## Front Matter of the Volume

### Title Page of the Series

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the three most recent centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which it is immediately clear to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture and in what places of their works. An extremely accurate edition, readily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially the fact that this collection—unified, systematic, and chronological—is the first in our library to gather together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; but the Eastern authors are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## In the Year of the Lord 1079

### John of Avranches, First Bishop and Subsequently Archbishop of Rouen

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. XI, p. 31.)

[Col. 0009A] After Maurilius died, the clergy of Rouen elected Lanfranc, Abbot of Caen, as their archbishop. According to Orderic Vitalis, he refused, and exerted all his strength both with that same clergy, with William, Duke of the Normans, and with Pope Alexander II, so that Bishop John might be placed over the widowed Church. He achieved this: sent by the duke to Rome to seek permission for the consecration, he returned from there carrying the pallium together with the authorization.

John, after receiving the apostolic legation, and after the election had been made by the common consent of all the bishops of the province and also of all the canons of that Church, obtained the metropolitan see, as is read in the acts [Col. 0009B] of the Archbishops of Rouen. John therefore passed from the see of Avranches—whence he also usually received the name “John of Avranches”—to the see of Rouen. He was the son of Ralph, Count of Bayeux and Ivry, and uterine brother of Richard, Duke of Normandy. The case of this archbishop concerning the cell of Saint Ouen at Gisors, between the monks of Saint Leutfred and of the Greater Monastery, was brought before the curia on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, 1070. In 1072 he held a council with his suffragans in his principal basilica for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline.

> “This man, according to the acts of the Archbishops of Rouen, was of noble birth and trained in the liberal disciplines. In other respects sufficiently energetic, he was most impatient in spirit. This disease grew harsh in him and, so to speak, was intensified both by the nobility of his flesh and by the [Col. 0009C] dignity of his prelate’s office. For these two things generally corrupt those placed at the summit, even to the point of bending them toward pride, when the very height of power flatters them: so that, forgetting the rule of justice, from which they seem to feed the fury of their spirit, they wish to assign it to zeal for justice. Sometimes, however, such men—who are not shepherds but cruel exactors—are, by the hidden judgment of God, rebuked before those whom they have unjustly harassed: [Col. 0010A] rebuked in exemplary fashion, so that they may be a terror to similar people in later generations and a source of hope to little ones.

> “All of this divine judgment displayed in this Archbishop John, of whom we are speaking, in the tumult which he unwisely raised against the monks of Saint Ouen. We have judged it right to write this, not in disparagement or insult, but for instruction. First, because it was extraordinary, unbelievable, and almost monstrous that so great a tumult and so great a disturbance should have occurred on that day without bloodshed. Second, so that this most noble place, free by the privilege of Charlemagne from every right or customary authority of the archbishops of this city, might possess a memorial by which they could prove that even in their great excesses they owed nothing to justice.

> “The circumstance was that William, Count of the Normans and glorious King of the English, was staying at Le Mans with his expedition [Col. 0010B]. Among the other nobles there was this John, archbishop of the see, a man of exceptional intelligence and no ordinary judgment; and also Nicholas, the revered abbot of the aforesaid monastery. The most celebrated feast day of Saint Ouen was approaching, a day to be received with every desire. Since it is customary for the archbishop to celebrate the solemn Mass there on that very day—not for any exchange of breakfast, but as if in recompense for his consecration, which no one of the said see may receive except in that church—he had sought leave from the king and was returning rapidly, while the aforesaid abbot remained occupied with more pressing matters.

> “What more is needed? The venerable day arrived. The clerics of the principal church gathered there as usual. Since John had sent word beforehand that he would come, the solemn Mass was meanwhile delayed. After some time, however, by common counsel, so that nothing might be taken away from so great a day while he was coming, it was begun. It was performed with such delay and such devotion that it is not surprising that the enemy of the human race burned with all his might to disturb this joy. He believed that it would be a great gain for him to infect with the poison of his wickedness the time which, meanwhile, he grieved to see slipping away [Col. 0011A].

> “Thus, when the Kyrie with its two sequences had been completed, and the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* had been finished—which had been begun by Abbot Richard of Sées and most solemnly carried through by the choir with its praises, all of this being spent in awaiting the archbishop—behold, he came rushing like a stormwind, confounding all the grace of the celebration. Conceiving in his mind the whole force of his indignation because he had not been awaited in every respect, he cursed everyone with grim eyes and furious mouth. Turning to the monks themselves, he excommunicated them; by the authority of God and of himself, he forbade the present service and caused it to cease, tore the abbot away from the altar, and prohibited the performance of the divine ministry.

> “It was full of grief and astonishment to see a feast of such joy, and so many and such great voices proclaiming it, fall suddenly silent [Col. 0011B]. He himself prepared to complete the service and ordered his clerics to finish it from the place where it had begun. We judge that nothing should be concealed here, lest, by appearing to favor one party through silence, we seem to attribute everything to the other in disparagement. The truth does not need the support of falsehood.

> “The brothers, although grieving that the adornment of so great a joy had been snatched from them, nevertheless yielded to pontifical authority. They stripped off their festive vestments and, amid considerable tumult, left the church. Some went here, some there, and others elsewhere, grieving and complaining to one another and to their own people about their disgrace. Suddenly a certain man, unable to endure the grief—whether one of the monks themselves or one of their servants is uncertain—gathering more fury and less counsel in his heart, hurried to the tower and struck the greater bell of the church [Col. 0011C].

> “At this, the idle populace rushed up. He shouted that the archbishop wished to carry the estate of Saint Ouen away to the principal church. Everyone sprang from his house: one seized a sword, another an axe, and others whatever first came to hand. They burst furiously into the church. Some, driven by curiosity, climbed onto the hidden upper structures of the monastery and removed certain things from the lofts, investigating what the enraged crowd intended to do. Very many were determined that, since the archbishop had interrupted the continuation of their great joy, he should not be allowed to complete the service himself.

> “The archbishop, terrified lest he be attacked by the surrounding bands of the furious, and fearing still more those threatening from above, fled from the altar to the monastery doors. He barely escaped within their enclosure before they were closed and took refuge there [Col. 0011D]. He had seats and benches piled up all around him. Some of his party, however, seized candlesticks, candles, and poles and, raging against the monks—who met them no less vigorously—brought about an outcome on that day so disgraceful an example that it is shameful to recount it.

> “It became sufficiently clear that the merit of the saint had been present for all on that day. By restraining the hands of the raging on the one side and rescuing the archbishop and his companions from such danger on the other, Saint Ouen was able, to the great wonder of all, to avert so great a sacrilege. For suddenly so dense a darkness of cloud occupied that part of the sanctuary in which the saints’ tombs were contained that it could scarcely be grasped even by the eyes of the curious. The miracle was appropriate to the event. Since Holy Scripture in various places represents by a cloud now the blindness of sinners, now the protection of the Lord, [Col. 0012A] it was rightly signified here in the very cloud.

> “From one side, the cloud of the senselessly raging, rising like smoke, disturbed the serenity of divine grace; from the other, Saint Ouen restrained by his merits the hand of the Lord, provoked by their guilt to strike. In saying this I have omitted nothing that contradicts the facts: the very logic, dependent upon the whole situation, supports it. Indeed, he might have considered—for the Most High is the rewarder of his patience—had he not, persisting in his obstinacy, withdrawn his mind from rational reflection. But the enormity of his impetuosity did not cease until, turning violently upon himself, it fell upon him.

> “Accordingly, as soon as the city’s viscount heard that the archbishop was thus surrounded, he feared that something rash might be done against him and that he himself might afterward be accused of the offense. He gathered a military force, displayed the king’s ban to all, and hurried to his assistance. He rescued him from the danger, by then offering no resistance and indeed completely despairing of himself. In such madness of tumults the day of so great a celebration was spent.

> “Let whoever is able consider what the court of heaven must have looked like then, and how unworthily it bore that the day of its most excellent citizen Ouen’s reward should have been so confused, so defiled, and so violently snatched away. Let him consider what misery it was for so great a patron to receive on that day nothing at all in his children which he might offer to appease the face of the Lord.

> “We, being ignorant of the secret of the divine counsel, pass over it and consider human matters in human terms. In so great a crowd, distinguished by sex, age, and rank, we do not believe that there were lacking those who, with a carnal mind, regretted that they had done too little harm, since they had considered no middle course by which they might have been deprived of so particular a joy; nor those of sounder counsel who attributed that disturbance to their sins, grieved that their vows had been snatched away, and, sighing for pardon from their patron, blushed over their actions.

> “The brothers chose some of their number for the following day, through whom the abbot might be informed of what had happened, and who might approach the king to lay the matter before him. But the archbishop’s messenger had preceded them and had turned all the odium back upon the monks. The matter thus tainted, they returned.

> “Although the king’s mind had been stirred against the monks by the prompting of the archbishop himself and of certain courtiers, nevertheless, weighing the matter impartially, he placed on just scales the one side, excessive arrogance, against the other, an ill-considered tumult. He therefore ordered the church to be reconciled immediately by the archbishop [Col. 0012D]. When he refused this with a sufficiently angry and resistant spirit, the king imposed upon Michael, Bishop of Avranches, the reconciliation of the place. He concealed his own shame while threatening future vengeance.

> “He therefore entrusted four monks of the place, whom he had heard were the authors of the faction, to an equal number of abbots of other monasteries, so that they might both satisfy the archbishop and pay for their less-considered wrongdoing in pilgrimage. Not long afterward, however, moved both by consideration of reason and by the request of their abbot, he recalled them into his presence and restored them reconciled to the Church.

> “In all these matters he was always careful to prevent the archbishop from arrogating anything insolently to himself in the affairs of that church, as though under cover of ecclesiastical authority. [Col. 0013A] Indeed, after he had been satisfied by the twofold exile of those brothers, he referred the matter to a council and convened an assembly. Because the archbishop had entered his abbey in anger and tumult; because he had been the cause and source of the whole disturbance; and because he had denied him the reconciliation of the place, he exacted three hundred pounds from him by the judgment of his leading men.

> “This punishment would have sufficiently expiated the offense if he had inwardly repented of the deed and had thought that the patience of the Lord should not be neglected. But he had not first then begun to harbor resentment against the monks of Saint Ouen, and in this way it could be intensified rather than softened. Three years had passed, and he continued to gnaw inwardly at the pain of his rejection, a fitting example of the fig tree in the Gospel. Hence someone wrote:

[Col. 0013B]

> “Awaited for three years, it bore no fruit.”

> “When, after that period, the same feast returned, he came to the solemnity, having been struck by paralysis a few months earlier but already recovering from the illness. Since he could not celebrate Mass himself, he entrusted his duties to Gilbert, Bishop of Évreux; he himself stood among the singers in the guise of precentor.

> “But when the Gospel began to be read—horrible to say!—he was suddenly so constricted by the flow of internal humors into a more secret passage that urine burst forth rapidly, staining the entire linen vestment up to the surplice and wetting the pavement on which he stood. After the offerings of the faithful, when he could no longer conceal the matter, he left the church [Col. 0013C], overcome with shame and grief to an extent that ought not to be described, and returned to his own quarters.

> “As soon as this became widely known among the people, who could estimate or express into what and how many cries it suddenly broke out? All together, however, they proclaimed the magnificence of the Lord and the merit of Saint Ouen. They applauded, rightly, that he had been driven away so disgracefully from the full enjoyment of the present joy which he had once so unworthily disturbed.

> “No one should be angry with us if we speak the truth, because we know that no one should reproach the judgment of the Judge of all, into whose hands it is dreadful to fall, and we greatly fear incurring punishment through another’s fault. Yet to marvel at the judgments of the Lord, which are like a deep abyss; to proclaim him in so holy a man, by whose piety he always protects and cherishes those who devoutly serve him; to do this is less sacrilegious than to cover it with ungrateful silence, as though its telling were irreverent.

> “Moreover, this greatly directs a pious intention: we must continually strive to serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him, but with trembling; we must soberly consider how bright a temple it is fitting that we ourselves should present to him, if he appears so zealous for this external worship in visible temples. For the Lord chose a place not because of those inhabiting it, but because of the inhabitants of the place.

> “But, to continue what we began, for another three years he suffered so greatly from the same infirmity that he could no longer perform the duties of his office. At last, urged by royal authority—or rather by the advice of everyone—he resigned the episcopate [Col. 0014A] and withdrew to one of his patrimonial estates called Saint-Philibert, where he survived for some time. In the twelfth year of his episcopate, he entered the way of all flesh and departed from this life. Nevertheless, he was then carried back to his own see.”

Thus far that writer. If he treated the prelate less cautiously and in harsher words than were proper, we are far from praising him for it. But when he seemed to see a miracle in a natural infirmity without revelation, we cannot refrain from censuring him. What, then, should be said of the editors of the history of Matthew Paris, who, both in the London editions of 1571 and 1640 and in the Paris edition of 1644, wrote this note in the margin [Col. 0014B]: “The monks of Saint Ouen kill John, Archbishop of Rouen!” Matthew himself had written, less imprudently, under the year 1073: “The monks of Saint Ouen attacked John, Archbishop of Rouen, while he was celebrating Mass on the feast of that same saint, with an armed band of men.”

But concerning the final years of the prelate, Orderic Vitalis reports, on page 550, that he was struck by a sudden seizure and thrown to the ground in the sight of the crowd, and that during the two years he survived he was without speech.

John had cultivated the beauty of the house of God with great devotion. An outstanding memorial of this survives even today in the little book of divine offices for the use of the metropolitan church, which he presented to his predecessor Maurilius. He also celebrated several councils: the first in 1072, of which we have already spoken; another in 1074, at which the priory of Saint-Victor at Cayeux was raised to the status of an abbey. Because he had prohibited his priests from keeping concubines, he was attacked with stones and forced to seek safety in flight; Orderic Vitalis relates this affair.

In 1074 he subscribed the charter of King William for the church of Bayeux. In 1075 he consecrated Cecilia, virgin and daughter of William the Conqueror, to God in the basilica of Fécamp. In 1077 he attended the dedication of the basilicas of Saint Stephen at Caen and of Blessed Mary at Bec. In the same year, ordered by King William, he refused to bury Hugh, Bishop of Lisieux.

Finally, concerning the end both of his episcopate and of his life: he was compelled to resign, both because of the king’s displeasure and because of paralysis or incontinence of urine. For this purpose Pope Gregory VII had sent Hubert as legate to the King of the English on the day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, which falls in the year 1078, to inquire whether he could bear the episcopal burden in view of his illness. If he were found unequal to so great a burden, another was to be canonically elected in his place.

He did not, however, have a successor until July of the following year, two months before his death. The histories of the Archbishops of Rouen, which assign his death to the twelfth year of his episcopate, must necessarily reckon the beginning of his episcopate from the death of his predecessor. Orderic Vitalis, on the other hand, who does not seem consistent with himself, assigns it at one point to 1069 and at another to 1072, when he says that John was buried in the baptistery of his basilica, toward the north, on the fifth day before the Ides of September.

Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, wrote three letters to him, and Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, wrote one. After Acherius and the *Library of the Fathers*, Pommeray published them in *The Councils of Rouen*, pp. 78ff., and Beslin published them in part II, pp. 15ff.

Orderic recites his epitaph:

> Here lies your metropolitan, city of Rouen,  
> Fallen from the highest summit, at whose death you collapse.  
> The wealth of the Church diminishes, the sacred order grows cold,  
> Whom your provident religion established.
>
> Here, restoring the decrees of the canons long neglected,  
> He instituted that priests should live chastely.  
> Under him no gifts of God were put up for sale;  
> He also bestowed abundant wealth upon the Church.
>
> Eloquent of speech, noble by birth, wise, and temperate in life  
> Was he whom this small stone covers.  
> It was the ninth day of September when John,  
> Stripped of the flesh, died. May true rest be his.

# The Book on Ecclesiastical Offices of the Reverend Father John, Bishop of Avranches and Subsequently Archbishop of Rouen, Addressed to Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen

First published from a manuscript codex of the Salicosan monastery, now enlarged and corrected from a manuscript codex of the Bigot Library; illustrated with the notes of Dom John Prevost, canon of the cathedral church of Rouen, and with more recent observations. In it various monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity, hitherto unpublished, are now brought to light for the first time from manuscript codices.

[Note: [Col. 0015] Rouen: at the expense and from the press of Bonaventure Lebrun, printer and bookseller, in the Palace Square, under the sign of Saint Bonaventure, with the approval of learned men and the privilege of the king. 1679.]

[Col. 0015]

## Preface

[Col. 0015B] It is customary for all who undertake to write about some subject to put certain things first, either so as to commend their labor to readers or to explain the purpose of the work they have undertaken. I have resolved neither wholly to break with this custom nor to observe it completely. For what need is there to praise a book whose author’s dignity and the usefulness of its teaching commend it in themselves?

It treats divine offices and the rites by which they are celebrated. In these, as Augustine testifies (*Letter* 119 to Januarius, chapter 7; *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 7; sermon 16, among the Paris sermons), there is a certain salutary eloquence adapted, by its admonition, to the disposition of those who are learning. Through it the spirit, cold toward the warmth of God’s Spirit, is aroused, while faith—which has its eye in the heart—rejoices in the invisible truth through the visible light of what it receives [Col. 0015C].

That same outstanding doctor of the Church, whom no praise can ever sufficiently honor, esteemed the exposition of these matters so highly that he judged it preferable even to the governments of the whole world, though they might be pacified by an unprecedented prosperity (*Letter* 119 to Januarius, chapter 16).

While considering these matters, I had long desired that the work of John of Avranches, first bishop and subsequently archbishop of Rouen, which had already become scattered and not readily available, might once again come to light, lest the homeland be deprived of its native ornament and many people be deprived of a highly useful work. But since the outcome did not proceed sufficiently according to my wishes, I silently awaited the more fortunate assistance of someone who might put the final hand to the unfinished work and heal its many mutilated parts.

Meanwhile, when I heard that a printer was preparing a new edition of it, the matter touched my heart and urged me all the more strongly because the printer did not wish to conceal his plan from me but encouraged me to join my efforts to his. It would have seemed mean-spirited to allow that opportunity, which God was providing for the accomplishment of the desired undertaking, to be spoiled, rather than to devote myself to it with all the strength at my command.

One thing delayed me and stood in the way of my undertaking: although I had diligently examined the libraries and searched the chests of my friends, I had not been able to find a codex complete in every respect, or even a better one than the Salicosan manuscript. Therefore [Col. 0017A], torn by conflicting thoughts, I wavered over what course to take. For, as King Theodoric wisely advises in Cassiodorus (*Variæ*, book IV, letter 31), one ought to bring to completion what the intention of prudent men seems to have undertaken. Deficiency of resources indicates either that judgment is faltering or that strength has failed; for just as things brought to completion produce perfect praise, so those abandoned in the middle of their efforts while still incomplete generate blame.

Although that labor did not have the desired outcome, I nevertheless did not lose heart. What had gone poorly by the first route, I decided to attempt by another. Thus, after searching everywhere for ancient manuscript codices intended for the use of the Church of Rouen, which generally agree so closely with the words of John of Avranches that an egg does not seem more like another egg, I thought that their assistance could illuminate various passages of his work and supply in the margins certain things missing from the printed book [Col. 0017B].

My judgment did not deceive me. We found the exposition of the sacred vestments, which appeared mutilated at the end of the printed book, complete in a manuscript codex of the exposition of the divine offices, five hundred years old, which the distinguished Emeric Bigot kindly lent, in accordance with his custom.

Nor did the kindness toward me of this man, no less distinguished for his gift of humanity than for his learning and noble birth, stop there. He gave me access to his extremely well-equipped library and had nothing hidden away relating to this matter which he was unwilling for me to use as though it were my own.

He also supplied a ritual book of the Church of Rouen, a manuscript approximately two hundred years old, from which I transcribed the rites of eight sacred processions [Col. 0017C]: namely, those held on Palm Sunday to Saint Gildard, in which the body of Christ, enclosed in a bier, is carried; the procession on the sacred day of Saint Mark; the three processions of the Rogations; that of Christ ascending into heaven “to lead captivity captive,” in which the recently absolved penitent takes part; the solemn feast of the Body of Christ; and the procession on the feast of Saint Ouen, when the clergy of the cathedral church proceeds to the basilica of that same saint.

If any differing and variant readings occur, the reader will find them noted in the margin from the manuscript ordinary of the cathedral church preserved in its sacristy.

From the same source I also extracted various rites already observed in the metropolitan church and in certain parish churches, though our author makes no mention of them [Col. 0017D]. Those who wish to follow the mother church as their guide in sacred rites may have recourse to these; if any difficulty arises, they may, as is proper, draw everything from its example, while first observing the ceremonies prescribed in the ritual.

From the same manuscript ordinary we present the blessings of the sacred chrism and the holy oil, taken from the Bigot codex.

Likewise from the same Bigot codex we present the order for the washing of the feet of both the poor and the clergy; the office of the so-called dry Mass, customarily celebrated on Good Friday; and the rite of the expulsion and reconciliation [Col. 0018A] of penitents, both of which, because they concern the same matter, we present together.

From an ancient manuscript pontifical of the cathedral library, at least seven hundred years old, we have added the archdeacon’s address to the Lord Archbishop for the absolution of penitents. It begins, “The time is at hand,” and is read in the cathedral church of Rouen. It is expressed in words that breathe an entirely fatherly kindness and compassion. It differs from the form found in the Roman Order and, so far as I know, has not previously been published.

This is followed by an Easter table which was attached to the Paschal candle in the year of the Lord 1678. Writing it, or having it written, belongs to the chancellor of the cathedral church. The wording is the same every year [Col. 0018B]; only the arithmetical or numerical signs are changed.

We have also drawn various rites from a manuscript ritual of the cathedral church, approximately two hundred years old. Since these rites are now obsolete and unused, we have separated them from the earlier rites of which we have spoken.

Among these the offices of the children, of the star, and of the sepulchre are especially notable. John mentions them, and we give their rites, words, and chant, all of which we have taken from two manuscript codices of the Bigot Library, approximately two hundred years old, intended for the use of the Church of Rouen. These offices had been received into use in several provinces, for John Beleth, William Durand, and other writers on sacred matters [Col. 0018C] write about them.

An old pontifical of the cathedral library, seven hundred years old, supplied us with the ordination of a bishop in the province of Neustria, together with the ceremonies and prayers to be recited over him at his consecration. It also mentions the Church of Rouen when it requires this profession from the person being consecrated: “Vis sanctae Ecclesiae Rothomagensi, etc.” (“Are you willing [the predicate is not quoted] for the holy Church of Rouen, etc.?”).

At the end of this Pontifical are contained the names of those who ought to have been summoned or even excommunicated. Among them are listed monks who held property as private owners. We did not think it irrelevant to report these names.

We have included an episcopal admonition for ordinands from a manuscript Pontifical of the cathedral library, three hundred years old, [Col. 0018D] in which many things worthy of observation are found. Above all, it requires eighteen years for the subdiaconate, twenty for the diaconate, and twenty-four and twenty-five for the priestly order.

From the same source we also give the blessing of an abbot, together with all the prayers to be poured forth over the abbot being ordained. It mentions the obedience to be shown to bishops, which abbots used to promise in the presence of the Church. Near its end is found the formula of this profession of obedience, which is perhaps the same one that Hugh of Amiens, archbishop of Rouen, used to require, as Pope Innocent II had ordered at the Council of Reims.

From the same source we have also taken the ordination of an abbot of canons and of an abbess of nuns.

[Col. 0019A] Three ancient pontifical blessings from a very old manuscript Pontifical of the cathedral library, at least seven hundred years old, likewise seemed worthy of inclusion. The first is for the dissolution of a synod; its first three verses are found in the Roman Order. The first of the other two is contained in the codex below the Mass celebrated at midnight on the Nativity of the Lord, and the second below the Mass of Holy Saturday. The bishop used to impart blessings of this kind during the solemn celebration of Mass, before uttering these words: “May the peace of the Lord be always with you” (see BONA, Book II, *On Liturgical Matters*, chapter 16). The aforesaid blessings are not found in Saint Gregory’s book of Sacraments.

We thought that the institution of the regular canonry of the priory of Saint Laud at Rouen should be appended to these. [Col. 0019B] It has been transcribed from the processional and collectary of that house. Each codex is about 160 years old. From this institution it is clear that an annual probation was not required, but that, after the candidate had been received, he put aside secular clothing and put on the regular habit. This consisted of a full-length tunic, a linen garment, and a hood; there is no mention of a biretta or of the almuce, which is now placed on the left arm. Then, after several prayers had been poured forth, he made his profession according to this prescribed formula of words:

“I, Brother N., offering myself, hand myself over to divine mercy, to serve in the church of Saint Laud according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, and I promise obedience to Lord N., prior of the aforesaid church, and to his successors [Col. 0019C] who canonically enter upon the office.”

Thereafter, having been admitted to the kiss of the prior and his companions, he confirmed by oath that he would observe the statutes of the order and keep the chapter’s secrets with him, revealing them to no outsider. Here one may observe that at that time they professed assiduity—or, as they call it, stability—in the same house.

This institution prepares the way for the Ordinary, or ancient ritual of the whole year for the use of the regular canons of the same church, which agrees in many respects with our author. For the regular canons, lest their name should seem ill-suited to them and they appear less obedient to the canons (Council of Vannes, 465, canon 15; Council of Epaon, 517, canon 27; Council of Girona, 517, canon 1; Second Council of Braga, 563, canon 1; Fourth Council of Toledo, 633, canon 2; Eleventh Council of Toledo, canon 3; [Col. 0019D] Council of Rouen, 1189, canon 1), by which it had been decreed that they should observe the order followed by their metropolitan fellow-provincials in celebrating the divine offices, conformed themselves to the diocesan rites: they recited the same office and sang the same psalms and hymns, adding at the end melodious repetitions of the antiphons, which are commonly called *pneumata*. In short, their fellowship and agreement with the canons of Rouen Cathedral were complete, as will become clear from various passages of this Ordinary.

The codex is four hundred years old, as is shown both by the script in which it was written and by the fact that, although it lists all the weekdays individually, it nevertheless omits the feasts of Saints Bruno, Dominic, Francis, and Louis, king of France, and even the feast of Corpus Christi. [Col. 0020A] In place of the latter it directs that on the Thursday after the Sunday dedicated to the Most Holy Trinity—for this church was dedicated to the Trinity—the weekday office should be performed. The codex is further given greater authority by the fact that its copyist states in the preface that he transcribed it from older books. Above all, this is worthy of observation: it was customary among the regular canons, on the days of Holy Week and on the vigils of other solemn feasts throughout the year, to kindle one another, through brief mutual exhortations, to celebrate with greater devotion the mysteries they were commemorating; and during Advent they abstained from meat and animal fat.

A manuscript codex from the Bigot Library, five hundred years old, supplied us with an exposition of the Canon of the Mass and of the divine offices by an uncertain author, never before published, and agreeing in many respects with our John. [Col. 0020B] Its author was both ancient and so well versed in Amalarius that he may rightly be called Amalarius’s abridger. We have added brief notes that may assist in understanding it. From this codex we took the portion of the exposition concerning the sacred vestments that, as we noted above, is missing from the printed book. We have nevertheless allowed it to remain here and have not torn it from its proper place in order to insert it into John’s text, so as not to disturb the sequence of the codex; rather, we preferred faithfully to represent that sequence as it stands.

After these materials we added excerpts from the charters of two very celebrated foundations: namely, the foundation of the college of chaplains of Albano, [Col. 0020C] from the archives of the archbishopric, and that of the college of Clementines, as they are called, from its archive. We added them because the divine office is always their song (Psalm 70), while the portion of the others is to confess the Lord seven times a day (Psalm 118) and to sing psalms to the name of the Most High (Psalm 9).

The first of these colleges recognized as its founder Peter of Colle-Medio of Rouen, first archbishop, renowned for his distinguished statutes, and later cardinal and bishop of Albano, in the year of the Lord 1245. The second, erected in 1350, rejoices in Peter Roger as its founder; he was eventually elected supreme pontiff after having been archbishop of Rouen and was called Clement VI.

The chaplains were established by both founders so that, in performing the divine offices, they might come as assistants to the canons, not so that [Col. 0020D] the canons—who perhaps think themselves freed from celebrating them—might be excused from doing so. For the statutes of God are “singable” to them in the house of his sanctification (Psalm 118; Isaiah 64), and they are all the more bound to attend to them because the Council of Trent, Session 24, *On Reform*, chapter 12, ordered them to perform the divine offices themselves, not through substitutes. Moreover, Christ rebuked those who “tie up heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matthew 23:4).

Among the matters worthy of observation in these documents, this is not the least important: even at that time the clerics lived a common life in food, drink, sleep, and clothing. This practice, after being interrupted for some time, had been happily restored on 1 April 1666, and things had been so wisely arranged [lacuna] that sacred reading should not be absent from the frugal table; [Col. 0021A] but we grieve that it was finally separated and abolished in December 1668.

We also include six sermons. The first concerns the respect with which the shepherds of the people ought to be honored and the duty of pastors and other clerics; the remaining five concern the office incumbent upon pastors: teaching the people and reproving the corrupt morals and crimes of human beings; the holiness in which priests ought to excel and which they ought to preserve whole and undefiled, even from the time they received baptism; the qualities and virtues with which they ought to be adorned; the vices that they themselves and clerics of lower rank must avoid; the faults that exclude men from the priesthood; the fact that priests must preach not only in word but also in deed and example; that they must possess the knowledge by which they can teach others; rebuke sins and sinners with grave words, without fear but with confidence; and finally be prepared to pour out their life for the salvation of the sheep entrusted to them, since it is wholly foreign to their condition to fear persecution or death.

Finally, after teaching them the bonds of duty by which they are bound, the author urges them to weigh the gravity of the burden imposed upon them in these words: “Consider, therefore, your burden.” Who the author may have been can be asked, since they do not identify him by name. If conjecture may be permitted in a doubtful matter, perhaps he was Ivo of Chartres. For among those we are discussing, three other works occur in our five-hundred-year-old manuscript in the Bigot Library, which have already appeared more than once under his name. Moreover, the manner of speaking and the diction are similar to those of the sermons on ecclesiastical matters published by Ivo, especially the sermons on pastors, which agree with the sermon he delivered on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter.

We have thought it superfluous to report the other points of agreement, both lest we weary the reader and because a diligent student will easily discover them. Certainly no one can deny that these sermons belong to some bishop: he speaks to priests as one possessing authority and as though he will have to render an account of their governance. Consequently, they seem to be synodal sermons. Nevertheless, let each person remain free to form his own judgment; for my part, it is enough to have explained the arguments that have led us to this opinion. I think no one will regret the labor spent in reading them, since they have not yet been published and abound in warnings that are by no means to be despised.

From the same manuscript codex we have appended an exposition of Baptism and the Eucharist.

To these sermons concerning discipline we thought that, as an appendix, there could be attached the synodal statute of Bayeux, issued in 1518 under the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Louis de Canossa, and then printed in Gothic type; likewise the synod of Évreux, promulgated in 1576 by Claude de Sainctes, who had attended the Council of Trent; and also the provincial synod of Rouen in 1581, whose canons he had arranged and rendered into the vernacular for the benefit of the less learned. [Col. 0022A]

The decrees demonstrate that this distinguished man was guided by the Spirit of God and that his house burned with zeal. Everywhere the eloquence of God shines forth, intensely aflame, together with an immense desire to correct the depraved morals of clergy and people and to bring wandering brethren back into the one fold of the supreme shepherd.

The aforesaid statutes were also made valuable by their rarity, which, always finding favor—as I may say in Tertullian’s words—“excites the desire to possess” (*On the Adornment of Women*, Book I, chapter 9). Indeed, they excited that desire in men of his diocese distinguished for piety and learning, and at their request we present them here.

The last place is occupied by those rites celebrated in the cathedral church in the presence of the Lord Archbishop, [Col. 0022B] because they are later in date and were published in the vernacular. They had been established in the year of the Lord 1632, on Tuesday, 6 April, with the chapter assembled by oath and in its houses. We present them here, excerpted from the records of that same chapter.

From all these materials, and from other old but published books of both the church of Rouen and the neighboring churches, we prepared notes which those men whose counsels it would have been irreverent to disregard judged necessary for a fuller elucidation of our author (whose books on the stole, the dedication of a church, and the maniple—mentioned by Lanfranc in the letter written to him—I wish we had been able to find and publish). We placed them beneath John’s book, interwoven with the notes that John Prevotius—whose name should never be mentioned without honor—had published on the same work, extracted from a manuscript of Salicosa (in the *Collection of the Councils of Rouen*, p. 78). [Col. 0022C] Yet, so that the learned man’s praise might remain undiminished, we distinguished Prevotius’s notes by the characters “Pr.” and appended his letter to Lord Francis II, archbishop of Rouen.

We say nothing of our own notes. “The ear tests words and approves them,” as is found in Job (Job 12 and 34). Our style is simple and has no affected brilliance, but it is perhaps for that reason no less suitable for explaining sacred matters: “For what does a golden key profit if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can? For we seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened” (Saint Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book IV, chapter 11).

Our diction has certainly pleased our friends—unless their judgment deceives them or their affection misleads them—and we wish that others may judge likewise. There may be some who complain that matters too minute and worn smooth by use have been recorded. But let them not suppose that all these things are addressed to themselves or to those like them; they are addressed to those who know nothing at all of our rites and are as strangers to our customs as they are free from our law. Let them consider that the stream of rivers would be poor if it were able to satisfy only the thirst of the great, and let them remember that the Apostle became weak to the weak and became all things to all.

Others may perhaps accuse us of clinging too closely to ancient customs, but:

> By ancient customs the Roman state and its men stand;

and antiquity itself, as the Ambrosiaster’s commentary says [Col. 0023A] on chapter 3 of the Second Epistle to Timothy, “is the strength of novelty.”

We venerate and report ancient rites in such a way that we now continue and observe wholeheartedly those customary rites prescribed by our bishops, remembering the divine oracle: “Do not despise your mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23). Yet, if it should happen that we slip somewhere—for we are human, and we consider nothing human foreign to us—we gladly declare with Jerome (Saint Jerome, Book I on Micah, chapter 2):

> I desire to learn from anyone what I do not know; I shall gladly profess myself his disciple, provided that he teaches and does not disparage. For nothing is easier than to discuss idly the labor of others.

Our one prayer will be what Saint Augustine’s once was:

> “May a brotherly spirit grieve in me over what you teach to be grieved over” (he says, addressing God; *Confessions*, Book X, chapter 4). Let that spirit be brotherly, not that of a stranger whose mouth speaks vanity; let it be brotherly, rejoicing in me when it approves me and grieving for me when it disapproves me, because whether it approves or disapproves me, it loves me.

It pleases us to conclude this already sufficiently lengthy preface with the words of Salvian (SALVIAN, in his letter to Salonius):

> Someone may perhaps ask who this author is. This may indeed be asked, and rightly, if the inquiry is capable of reaching some useful result. But if it is fruitless, why should curiosity labor when knowledge will gain no benefit from its curiosity? For in every book the benefit of reading is sought rather than the author’s name. Therefore, if there is benefit in the reading, and whoever he may be has something by which he can instruct those who read, what concern is it of his with a name that cannot help anyone except the curious?

He then gives reasons for the author’s silence:

> The first reason comes from God’s command, by which we are ordered in every way to avoid the vanity of earthly glory, lest, while we seek a little breath of human praise, we lose the heavenly reward.  
>   
> The second reason is that the smallness of the author’s person should not detract from salutary writings. For from now on everything said is valued according to the worth of the one who said it. The judgments of this age are so feeble, and almost so nonexistent, that readers consider not so much what they are reading as whose work they are reading; they think not so much about the force and power of the diction as about the dignity of the speaker.  
>   
> For this reason that writer wished to be hidden and concealed in every way, lest writings containing great healing power should perhaps be diminished by the author’s name.

Finally, we conclude with him in these words and ask the reader to pray to the Lord our God, and by praying to obtain that this little book, written for the Church of Christ, may benefit its author before God as greatly as he himself desires it to benefit everyone.

Farewell.

[Col. 0023]

## TESTIMONIES OF ANCIENT WRITERS CONCERNING JOHN

[Col. 0025A] Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in a letter to John II, archbishop of Rouen.

To the lord John, archbishop of the Normans, deservedly and conspicuously exalted for holiness, Lanfranc, unworthy to be called a bishop, wishes to join better things to what has been well begun.

Whatever Your Holiness has written about the stole has greatly pleased me and has never displeased me. But when you added that, because a bishop proceeding to dedicate a church ought, according to the institution of the episcopal order, to be clothed in sacred vestments, and in your exposition of those sacred vestments you included the chasuble, I was greatly astonished, because I cannot remember ever having seen anything of the kind.

Furthermore, since you stated that, in the conferral of orders, the maniple is given only to the subdeacon, I ask you to inform me by letter where you learned this. I hear that some do this, but I cannot remember whether it is prescribed by sacred authorities.

[Col. 0025B] Orderic Vitalis, monk of Utica, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V.

This man was the son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, and bishop of the Church of Avranches; thereafter he was raised to the archbishopric and flourished for ten years during the pontificates of Popes Alexander and Gregory VII.

William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Lisieux, in *The Deeds of William, Duke of the Normans and King of the English*.

For he appointed highly suitable pontiffs: Hugh of Lisieux, his own brother Odo of Bayeux, and John of Avranches. In their election, their worth prevailed in his judgment, not the high birth of those related to him. John, son of Count Ralph, though previously a layman by order, was learned in letters and had become renowned among the clergy, indeed among the leaders of the clergy, for his religious life. It was not the desire for the honor of the priestly rank that drove him, but the prayers of the bishops sought him as a colleague to be consecrated.

[Col. 0025C] William of Jumièges, monk, *History of the Normans*, Book VII, chapter 38.

John, bishop of the city of Avranches, was a man highly distinguished by nobility, happily imbued with spiritual wisdom, and exceedingly endowed with worldly prudence; for in accordance with the nobility of his lineage, he was the son of Count Ralph.

In the same work, concerning Ralph, John’s father:

He took as his wife a certain woman named Eramberg, very beautiful, born in a village in the territory of Caligny called Cavilla [Cacheville]. By her he fathered two sons, Hugh, later bishop of Bayeux, and John of Avranches, who eventually became archbishop of Rouen.

Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV.

After the death of his predecessor, Maurilius, the Church of Rouen elected Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, as its bishop; King William, with his nobles and all the people, most willingly consented. But the man devoted to God and intent upon humility refused the burden of so great a primacy and strove with all his strength to put forward John, bishop of Avranches, for this dignity. Then, so that this union might take place canonically, he went to Rome and obtained from Pope Alexander permission for the aforesaid appointment. He also brought back the sacred pallium, a source of glory to him and to all Normandy, together with the permission.

John, therefore, was transferred from the see of Avranches, which he had governed for seven years and three months, [Col. 0026A] and became metropolitan archbishop of Rouen. He burned with the ardor of virtue in words and deeds and, with excessive zeal, raged against vices like Phinehas. As for worldly dignity, he shone with the splendor of great nobility. For he was the son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, who had been the uterine brother of Richard, the elder duke of Normandy.

For ten years he conducted the metropolitan government vigorously and diligently, laboring greatly against unchaste priests to remove their concubines. When, at a synod, he forbade them under anathema to keep concubines, they attacked him with stones and he fled. As he fled from the church, he cried out forcefully: “O God, the nations have entered your inheritance” (Psalm 78:1).

*Deeds of the Archbishops of Rouen*, from manuscript codices of Saint Mary and Saint Ouen.

[Col. 0026B] After Maurilius’s death, William, king of the English, sent Lanfranc, abbot of Caen—whom he later placed over the metropolitan church of Canterbury—to Pope Alexander, asking his clemency and requesting that, by his authority, he consent to appoint John, bishop of Avranches, over the metropolitan church, and that he send apostolic letters so that no occasion might be given for resistance to this action. The pope, seeing that the king’s request was devout, consented and sent a letter concerning it to the bishop. The words contained in the letter are these:

> “Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends apostolic blessing to John, venerable bishop of Avranches.
>
> “Since the Church of Rouen has been deprived of a shepherd, we have learned from the report of the bishop of Séez and of Abbot Lanfranc that you are, by the election of your prince, our most beloved son William, king of the English, to be promoted to the greater see because of the integrity of your life and morals, provided that the authority of the Apostolic See, over which we preside by God’s authority, gives its consent.
>
> “Moved, therefore, by their prayers, for the salvation of that church and of all who are in your regions, we wish and by apostolic authority command your affection not to resist what divine providence has arranged concerning you, but to show yourself obedient to your election.
>
> “We therefore admonish the brotherhood of your sweetness [another reading: ‘the sweetness of your brotherhood’] that, if you have been faithful in a little, you should not cease to work well in a greater matter. Refresh the people with the nourishment of the divine word, so that you may deserve to hear that gracious voice of the Lord saying: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many’ (Matthew 25:23).
>
> “For the rest, you will hear more plainly the more secret intention of our mind through the truthful report of our legates.”

John, having received this apostolic legation, and the election having been made by the common consent of all the bishops of the province and of all the canons of the same church, obtained the metropolitan see. He was a man of noble descent, educated in the liberal disciplines.

[Col. 0026D] In the year 1061, John was bishop of Avranches in the month of September.

In the year 1069, John, son of Ralph, count and uterine brother of Richard, succeeded Maurilius. He had first governed the Church of Avranches for seven years and three months and thereafter, at the request of Pope Alexander and with the consent of William, prince of Normandy and king of the English, obtained the chair of the Church of Rouen.

In the year 1079, John, archbishop of Rouen, died.

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1079, John, archbishop, died in the eighth [eleventh] year of his governance and was buried in the baptistery of the basilica, to the north. [Col. 0027A] His monument [Note: [Col. 0027A] No trace of it seems to remain today.] was made of white stone, in which an epitaph of the following kind was skillfully inserted:

> Here lies your metropolitan, city of Rouen,
>
> from the highest summit of which you fall as he dies.
>
> The resources of the Church decline, the sacred order grows cold,
>
> though prudent religion had established it.
>
> [Col. 0028A] Here he reformed the decrees of the canons,
>
> long neglected,
>
> and instituted that priests should live chastely.
>
> Under him no gifts of God were put up for sale,
>
> and to this Church he brought abundant resources.
>
> Eloquence, lineage, wisdom, and sober life
>
> belonged to him, whom this small stone covers.
>
> It was the ninth day of September when JOHN,
>
> stripped of the flesh, died:
>
> may true rest be his. Amen.

[Col. 0027]

## JOHN, BISHOP OF AVRANCHES: BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES, TO MAURILIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Note: [Col. 0028] The notes of John Prevotius on this document were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 63–116. Numbers in parentheses in the text of *On Ecclesiastical Offices* refer to the notes in that separate document.]

[Col. 0027B] 1 (1) To the truly holy and worthy of honor for his merits, Maurilius, venerable (2) archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, John of Avranches, least in merit among all bishops, offers the service of complete obedience in body and spirit.

Because I have learned, from the very frequent questions we have discussed together, that Your Paternity’s holiness, always solicitous for the advancement of ecclesiastical dignity, is afflicted by its excessive decline with profound sorrow, and that this grief is increased for you by your ardent desire for its restoration, while the weakness of illness had withdrawn your strength for accomplishing it, my insignificance desired to support your most holy (2) intention—not inflamed by any arrogance, but moved by devout compassion—so that what is corrupted by the negligence of careless shepherds might be restored by the vigilance of your holy religion. [Col. 0027C]

Therefore, relying on your authority, I undertook the sayings of the holy Fathers; examining the practices and customs of various Churches, and considering those matters that pertain to the offices of divine worship and the mystical meaning they contain, I composed a kind of synthesis from this diversity. I now submit it, still hidden from everyone, to the examination of your sagacity, so that you may inspect this little work I have undertaken and, in inspecting it, I beg you to apply the diligence by which you may show us that you are the man whom you suitably present yourself to be in fatherhood and instruction.

It is your concern, then, if there are matters that you may wish to approve with fatherly affection, or, on the contrary, to correct with the judgment of an attentive teacher. If it is judged useful and acceptable by your authority, after [Col. 0027D] we see it flowing down from the metropolitan see, we shall endeavor, following the statutes of the canons, to offer it as a drink to our own people.

[Col. 0028B] Above all, the clergy ought canonically to observe the purpose of holy religion in morals, dress, and bearing (5), according to the Fourth Council of Carthage (canons 44 and 45): namely, that clerics should wear their crowns—not concealed but visible; (6) that they should not use garments of various colors or red garments, and that their capes in church should always be black. Let there always be one appointed time and one day for shaving. Whoever disobeys this precept should be subjected to strict correction.

(7) Since, according to apostolic teaching, we shave the upper part of our head, we are commanded to cut away from the mind—signified by the head—superfluous and temporal thoughts.

(8) By the crown of hair that we wear on the lower part of the head, we are admonished to govern temporal matters, without which the present life cannot be lived, with harmonious reason and to use them with ordered discretion. Holy religion observes this rule so that excessive hair may not cover the ears or eyes; it signifies that we must take the greatest care lest the concerns and riches of this age hinder the ears of the heart or the eyes from working toward the good.

But because (9) we shave the beard, by which bodily strength is signified, we are symbolically shown that we ought to lose the harshness of the mind and, according to the Apostle, become children in Christ (1 Corinthians 14:20).

Having disposed of this, let the hours of night and day be observed at fixed times according to canonical institution; and let the canons devoutly gather in the church, by whom, as it is written, the ecclesiastical offices shall be performed throughout the entire course of the year. [Col. 0028D] Since, however, subsisting through the four elements, we offend the Lord by night and by day, it is fitting that four times by night and by day we should strive to appease the omnipotence of God with hymns, psalms, and prayers, following the examples of the ancients; [Col. 0029A] for Ezra, returning from the Babylonian captivity, instituted the Israelite people (10) to sing psalms to the Lord four times by night and by day, so as to call forth his mercy (II Esdras 9:3). The prophet David, moreover, declares to us that he spoke praise to the Lord seven times a day and rose at midnight to confess to the Lord (Psalm 118).

For singing psalms to the Lord, the holy Fathers selected these hours above all others: Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, together with the Night Offices and the Matutinal Office.

Prime is so called because it is the end of night and the beginning of day. This hour, at all times except the three days of the Lord’s Passion and the seven days of Easter, is completed with the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, the Chapter, and the Collect. At this hour, because we have passed the night [Col. 0029B] in safety, we ought to give thanks to our shepherd and, asking his mercy through prayers and tears, wipe away whatever evil we have contracted through the five bodily senses. We ought also to entreat him to deign to defend his flock from every evil during the approaching day and to direct our five bodily senses according to his good pleasure.

Therefore (11) we sing five psalms, but join them together with a threefold glorification of the Holy Trinity, so that our senses may be fortified by faith in him. To these we add (12) the Catholic faith expounded by blessed Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, so that it may be an unconquerable shield for us against all visible and invisible adversities. (13)

Terce is observed because at that hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles; Sext, because at that hour the Jews crucified our Savior; and None, because at that hour the same Savior, hanging upon the cross, gave up his spirit. At these three hours (14) we sing twice three psalms with a threefold glorification of the Holy Trinity, for we ought to hold and venerate the faith of the Holy Trinity in mind and body. We complete these hours with a responsory, a verse, the Lord’s Prayer, prayers, and the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*), kneeling as we do so. On feast days, however, the Lord’s Prayer and the prayers, together with the psalm and kneeling, are omitted.

When these daytime offices have ended, (16) the nocturnal offices follow, among which Vespers is the first hour. [Col. 0029C] Since it is the end of day and the beginning of night, as at Prime we sing five psalms on account of the five bodily senses, so that whatever offense we have committed through them during the day may be forgiven us through the supplication of the psalms, and so that these same senses of ours, as night approaches, may be directed by the Lord according to his good pleasure.

Each psalm is to be sung with an antiphon, as blessed Ignatius, patriarch of Antioch, instituted. Through the psalm, which is sung by alternating choirs, the good works of the brethren are signified; through the antiphon, which one begins and the others sing together, charity is expressed, by which the minds of the faithful are joined into one.

Then the priest, who represents Christ, delivers a reading—that is, an exhortation to the people—not to grow faint but to persevere in good works. This is followed by the response—that is, the good work of the people who have been exhorted—and by the hymn, that is, the praise of God. After the verse has been said, (17) the hymn of holy Mary strengthens us by the examples of humility, obedience, and hope, and recalls the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation to arouse the devotion of our faith.

When the verse begins, according to what the Lord commanded Moses (Exodus 29:13), (18) incense is offered upon the altar by the priest. Thus, as at the other hours, (19) the office is completed with the Lord’s Prayer and the prayers, except on feast days; the prayer, however, is always said. [Col. 0029D]

(20) Since after Vespers we do not immediately rest, but engage in earthly tasks and attend to the needs of our bodies, which cannot entirely be avoided, we make amends at Compline for whatever we have done wrong in those activities. At this hour, therefore, according to the elements of our body through which we offend the Lord, we sing four psalms to appease the Lord. [Col. 0030A] After the Chapter and the hymn have been said, (21) we add again the hymn of the righteous Simeon, so that, guarded and enlightened by God, we may rest in peace.

Then, as at Prime, (22) we complete the hour with the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and the confession, arming ourselves against the snares of the night, together with the prayers and the prayer, which is preceded (23) by a reading drawn from the examples of the holy Fathers, to stir the souls of the brethren toward good.

(24) At midnight, according to the Prophet (Psalm 118), we ought to rise to confess to the Lord. Christ came to redeem the people sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, born of a virgin in the night season; he also illumined the night by his resurrection. Since at this hour we have remained silent until now, [Col. 0030B] overcome by sleep, we beseech the Lord to deign to open our lips so that we may proclaim his praise. Then, as at the beginning of the other hours, we invoke him as the helper of our work. (25)

After a hymn has been sung to appease him, (26) we sing twelve psalms, so that throughout the twelve hours of the night we may be protected by the Lord from every evil. Since this watch was necessary during the six ages of the world, we join the same psalms with six antiphons. Through the antiphons, as we have said, charity is expressed.

After a verse has been said to rouse the spirits, and the Lord’s Prayer has been completed for the cleansing of hearts, and after receiving the priest’s blessing, three readings are read, each followed by a responsory. Through the readings we preach; through the responses the good works that ought to follow are signified. [Col. 0030C]

For the six ages are concluded in three periods: the time of the natural law, the time of the written law, and the time of the law of grace. The same reality is represented on Sundays and feast days by the three nocturns.

When on Sundays in the first nocturn we sing twelve psalms with a threefold glorification of the Holy Trinity, joining four psalms by one glorification and one antiphon, we recall the twelve patriarchs from whom the Jewish people of God was propagated. They served the Lord devoutly, shining with the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—and binding those virtues together through faith in and charity toward the Trinity. We ought to be instructed by their examples.

The second nocturn signifies those who lived under the law, fortified by the same faith and charity. [Col. 0030D] The third signifies those who lived under grace, enlightened by the same virtues.

Through the nine readings, with which we sing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God”—we are shown that we ought to imitate the examples of these three periods in preaching and in action, so that we may deserve to be joined to the nine orders of angels and that the tenth may be restored from among us, one who will cleave incessantly to divine praises.

(27) Through the Matutinal Office we recall the baptism of the Israelite people, by which our own baptism is prefigured: it occurred at the morning watch of the Exodus, when, after the enemies had been slain by divine power, they crossed the Red Sea. In this office we also recall the Lord’s resurrection, which the angels announced to the women at first light. [Col. 0031A]

At this hour we sing five psalms to fortify the five bodily senses. After them, the priest’s reading, called the Chapter, exhorts us to persevere in good work; obedient to it, we raise a hymn to the Lord. Roused also by the verse, we sing together the hymn of Zechariah, in which we confess with praise that the Lord has visited us and fulfilled the redemption promised to us through Abraham.

When the verse has begun, according to what the Lord commanded Moses (Exodus 29), the priest burns incense upon the altar. Then, as at Vespers, after the antiphon has been sung, (28) the office is completed with the Lord’s Prayer, the prayers, and the prayer itself. On feast days, however, the Lord’s Prayer and the prayers are not said. When this has ended, as at the other hours, the Lord is blessed and all render thanks to him. [Col. 0031B]

This office also possesses another mystical meaning. The first psalm signifies the primitive Church from the Jews; the second, the Church from the nations; the third, to which one psalm is added under a single glory, signifies both peoples, Gentile and Jewish, who at the end of the world will be joined in one faith and one law. The fourth, which the youths sang in the fiery furnace, signifies the tribulation of Antichrist, which both peoples will suffer for Christ. The three psalms beginning *Laudate*, joined under one glory, signify the three orders represented by Job, Daniel, and Noah, who will reign with Christ in praise and glory.

(29) When the signal is sounded, before the office is released, the brethren are to assemble for Prime or for all the hours of night and day. (30) There they are to stand religiously, not moving this way or that, nor conversing with anyone; they are not to sit two together except at the appointed hours. At the *Gloria Patri* (31) they shall turn toward the altar and incline themselves. (32) They shall not leave the choir: the seniors without the dean’s permission, and the juniors without the cantor’s permission.

Whoever goes forward to read shall not pass through the middle of the choir without inclining first and afterward, (33) and shall proceed decorously, not noisily, so that religion may always be evident in their bearing and dress. Whoever goes from one side to the other under the pressure of the greatest necessity shall stop and incline reverently only once. Whoever violates this rule shall be subject to the proper correction.

After the hymn has been said, the psalms shall be recited with their appropriate antiphon. After them *Quicumque vult* shall be sung with the antiphon of the Holy Trinity, (34) except from the days of the Lord’s Nativity through the octave of Epiphany and on the days of Pentecost. [Col. 0031C]

The Chapter follows, with “Lord, have mercy” (*Domine, miserere*) on ferial days, and “King of the ages” (*Regi saeculorum*) on feast days. A responsory with its verse follows; after the prayers have been said and confession has been made with the prayers appropriate thereto, (36) the hour is completed with the prayer proper to it.

When Prime has ended, the brethren shall gather in the chapter house. The Martyrology is to be read, (37) lest any feast of a saint to be celebrated on the following day be negligently omitted. After the verse “Precious in the sight of the Lord” (*Pretiosa est in conspectu Domini*) has been said, the intercession of blessed Mary and of the saints is requested; God is then invoked through their assistance, and, after the Lord’s Prayer and the priest’s prayer, the gathering ends there. [Col. 0031D]

Next (39) a reading is recited from the canonical rule, (40) or from a pastoral work, (41) or from some other regular book. Then faults are examined; the examination is to be conducted canonically. Afterward they return to the church and sing the morning Mass. At it these prayers are said: first, “God of the faithful” (*Fidelium Deus*); second, “God, who among the apostolic…” (*Deus, qui inter apostolicos*); third, “God, giver of forgiveness” (*Deus veniae largitor*); and afterward the others that please the brethren. [Col. 0032A]

When the signal indicates it, Terce is sung. The Mass of the day is celebrated at the third hour, except during the time of fasting. For at the third hour Christ was crucified by the tongues—that is, by the words—of the Jews; during the time of fasting, it is celebrated at the ninth hour, at which Christ gave up his spirit.

The Mass of the day is celebrated in the following order. First, on ferial days two bells are rung, (42) and on feast days all of them. At the *Gloria Patri*, while the choir sings the Introit instituted by blessed Celestine, [Col. 0032B] the priest in the vesting room and the other ministers put on the sacred vestments according to order: the deacon, an alb, stole, and dalmatic; the subdeacon, an alb, tunic, and maniple; the remaining ministers only albs—namely, (43) two acolytes, one to sing the Gradual and carry the candlestick, the other to sing the Alleluia and carry the thurible. (44)

After the psalm has been said, when the choir begins the *Gloria Patri*, the priest and the other ministers proceed thus to the altar. The deacon goes before the presbyter; the subdeacon, preceding the deacon, carries the Gospel; (45) the candle-bearer, with his candle, precedes the subdeacon; and the bearer of the thurible precedes the candle-bearer.

When they have come before the altar, the subdeacon places the Gospel on the right-hand corner of the altar, where it remains until the Gospel. The altar signifies Jerusalem, in which the Gospel teaching resounded from the beginning of the Lord’s coming and from which it went forth publicly, as it is written: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). [Col. 0032C]

Afterward the subdeacon moves to the priest’s left and the deacon to his right. There, after they have confessed to one another, (46) the priest kisses the deacon and the subdeacon. For Christ first gave peace to the apostles and through them transmitted it to the world.

Then the priest and the other ministers pray briefly, standing in their proper order behind the altar. The first to rise from prayer inclines to the deacon who is inclining before him; the deacon inclines to the subdeacon who is inclining; and the subdeacon inclines to the choir that is inclining.

After his inclination, the deacon kisses both corners of the altar and offers the Gospel to the priest, who kisses the middle of the altar, to be kissed. Through the Gospel Christ, wiping out the bond of transgression, gave peace to the world; through its heralds he reconciled both peoples, Jewish and Gentile, to himself. The altar that the priest kisses signifies the Jewish people dwelling in Jerusalem, whom Christ reconciled to himself; the Gospel signifies the Gentile people.

Then the priest proceeds to the right-hand corner of the altar. For Christ always lived the right-hand life, and heavenly glory is acquired through the right hand. The deacon, imitating that life—or, perhaps, that way—stands behind him until the priest signals him to sit. [Col. 0032D]

The bishop’s seat, according to the decrees of Pope Urban (Letter on the Bishop’s Chair IV, chapter 35) and the Council of Carthage, ought to be higher than the others, and the episcopal chair is to be placed there honorably. For *episcopus* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “overseer” (*superintendens*); therefore a higher place is prepared for him, as for a vinedresser, to guard the vineyard of the Lord of hosts. When *Kyrie eleison* begins, the bishop ascends it with his ministers, some of whom stand and others sit.

Those who sit signify the members of Christ resting in peace; those who stand signify those placed in combat. When the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* begins, or when the pontiff says the prayer, the priest turns toward the east—not because the Lord is there alone, since he is present everywhere, not by spatial extension but by the power of his majesty, but because light rises from the east, by which the other regions are illumined, just as the supreme good comes from God, by whom the whole world is illuminated. [Col. 0033A]

Through the priest’s greeting and the people’s response their common and charitable affection is shown, alternately admonishing and wishing that Christ may always remain in them. The fact that the bishop alone says “The peace of the Lord” while greeting the people (49) shows that he is Christ’s vicar, who, rising from the dead, announced peace to the apostles.

Whatever the number of ministers, the greater part is to be on the right and the lesser on the left, since both blessings—temporal and eternal—are to be sought from God, although the eternal is to be sought more earnestly.

The candle-bearers are to hold the candlesticks from south to north until *Kyrie eleison*, (50) and, when it begins, to set them down there. The south, which is a warm wind, signifies the fervor of the Holy Spirit, which, from the rising of the true sun, spreads from east to west, illuminating the world. [Col. 0033B]

A third candlestick is placed in the middle, signifying that where two or three are gathered in the Lord’s name, the Lord is present (Matthew 18:20). The setting down of the candles when *Kyrie* begins (51) demonstrates that, while we beseech the Lord, we ought to humble ourselves with contrite heart.

When the presbyter greets the people, they hold them there. When the prayer has ended, they place them from east to west, for the four regions of the world are illumined by the two Testaments. (52) The seven candlesticks on feast days signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

When the subdeacon begins the Epistle, the priest sits beside the altar and signals the deacon to sit in his place. (54) The subdeacon, except during the time of his ministry, remains in the choir. [Col. 0033C]

The Epistle is followed at the appropriate times by the responsory, the Tract, or the Alleluia. Through the responsory, which is sung alternately, the active life is signified, in which the Church, by doing good, earns the eternal glory represented by the Alleluia. Through the Tract, which is sung without a response and whose melodies resemble a groan, the contemplative life is signified, in which perfect men, weeping over sins and devoting themselves to God alone, attain that same glory in a higher degree.
