The *pneuma* of the sequence, sung after the Alleluia, signifies the praise of eternal glory, where no verbal speech will be necessary, but only pure thought, always directed toward God. [Col. 0033D]

(56) The bone tablets held by the singers in their hands signify the strong perseverance in good works by which one ought to cleave to divine praises.

On feast days the readers of the Epistle and Gospel and the singers of the Gradual and Alleluia are to ascend the pulpit. For pastors and teachers ought, according to the prophet, to raise their preaching on high (Isaiah 40:9), and their works, for the instruction of God’s people, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled in them: “Let your works shine before men, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). [Col. 0034A]

When the deacon ascends the pulpit, he is to stand higher than the candle-bearers, for the Gospel of Christ surpasses the law and the prophets. The bearer of the thurible, who stands in the same place with the deacon, signifies the fragrance of Christ’s teaching and mighty works.

We make the sign of the cross upon our foreheads when the Gospel begins in order to drive away all evil suggestions, for the cross drives away every adversity of the mind.

At this same hour (57) bishops and abbots ought to lay down their staffs and, at the hearing of the word of the Lord, stand devoutly and humbly before the Lord.

When the ministers are vested in chasubles, after the prayer has ended, (58) the subdeacon removes his chasuble and reads the Epistle. After it has been read, he puts the chasuble on again and carries the corporal to the altar, handing it to the deacon, who arranges it on the altar.

When the Tract or Alleluia begins, the deacon removes his chasuble and places it beneath his right arm and over his left, leaving the right arm uncovered. For the Gospel has revealed to us the arm of the Lord that was hidden under the law.

The deacon’s putting on of the chasuble signifies the mystical time under the law; its removal represents the time under grace, (59) in which the mysteries are revealed. [Col. 0034B]

As the end of the Gospel approaches, the priest puts incense in the thurible. After the altar has been incensed, it is carried before the Gospel. The thurible, which emits a fragrant odor, signifies the good reputation that preceded the teaching. (60)

After receiving the priest’s blessing, the deacon takes the Gospel from the altar (61) and places it upon his left shoulder. The left shoulder signifies temporal life, in which the Gospel ought to be preached. The subdeacon carries a cushion before him.

The cushion that precedes signifies the law, which preceded the Gospel; the feathers concealed inside signify the mysteries contained in the law; and the lightness of the feathers signifies that the precepts of the old law are light in comparison with the new. In the former it is said, “You shall not kill” (Exodus 20:13); in the new, “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22). [Col. 0034C]

Thus, preceded by the candle-bearer and the bearer of the thurible, he proceeds in procession to the pulpit. After placing the Gospel there and incensing it, he turns toward the north and reads the Gospel. For the north signifies the unbelief of the nations, to whom the Gospel is preached by the apostles, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

When it has been read, the candlesticks are extinguished. For with the sacrifice of the true Lamb, the sacrifice of the figurative lamb ceased, as did the other mysteries contained in the law and the prophets, which were signified by the candlesticks.

Incense is offered to the priest in the thurible, and he first kisses the Gospel handed to him by the subdeacon; afterward the deacon kisses it. On feast days it is presented by the subdeacon to the entire clergy, with the incense preceding. [Col. 0034D]

When the Gospel has been read, the priest greets the people, and the Offertory begins; when it has ended, the verse follows. Meanwhile the subdeacon offers the bread and wine to the deacon, and the deacon offers them to the presbyter. (66)

On feast days the cantor brings water, covered with a cloth, to the deacon, who mixes it with the wine. Through the cantor’s sweet musical modulation the people are kindled to pious devotion and divine love; thus they run toward the Lord and become one body in Christ.

The wine signifies Christ; the water, the people; the cloth, the covering of the water, signifies the labor of the cantor’s modulation by which the people are freed from wicked thoughts, for labor is signified by linen. Water mixed with wine signifies the people united to Christ; wine without water is Christ; water without wine is the people without Christ. (67) On other days the acolyte supplies it. [Col. 0035A]

The priest arranges the offering so that he places the chalice on the right side of the host, for from the Lord’s right side flowed blood and water. Having covered it with the corporal, (69) he offers incense over it and then gives it to the deacon. The deacon carries it around the altar, then returns it to the priest, and afterward gives it back to the minister, who carries it to the clergy and people.

Moreover, the priest takes the paten from the altar and hands it to the subdeacon; if an acolyte is present, the subdeacon hands it to him. For no one is permitted to remove anything sacred from the altar except a deacon or a priest. [Col. 0035B]

Then, bowed before the altar, the priest alone prays, asking that he may be worthy to approach the altar and persist in divine worship, lest what happened to the men of Beth-shemesh happen to him, when they rashly looked upon the ark of the Lord (1 Kings 6:19). For before he suffered, Christ often spent the night alone in prayer, praying not for himself but for us.

The other ministers stand in prayer in their proper order. After this, the priest turns toward the people and instructs them to pray; then he turns toward the altar and says the Secret prayer. When it is completed, he speaks *Vere dignum*—“It is truly fitting”—with devout mind and sweet voice. At its conclusion the choir responds with the hymn *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus*, instituted by blessed Sixtus. [Col. 0035C]

The deacon and the ministers remain behind the priest through *Te igitur* until *Sed libera nos*, inclining themselves. For the apostles, grieving and fearing for the Lord who was suffering, shared in his sorrow. The inclination of the deacons signifies the sorrow of the apostles; that of the subdeacons signifies the sorrow of the holy women.

The subdeacons likewise incline themselves in the priest’s sight. Through them the holy women are represented: while the Lord was suffering and the disciples were fleeing, they remained attentive to what was happening to him, although struck by fear and sorrow. But after the Lord had been taken down from the cross and buried, they departed and prepared spices for the burial. Thus the subdeacons depart from that place and hasten to minister to the body and blood of Christ, bringing the paten by the hand of the deacon to the priest, so that he may break the Lord’s body upon it. [Col. 0035D]

After this, the priest completes the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood according to the institution of the holy Fathers, with pure and humble heart.

When he comes to *Nobis quoque peccatoribus*—“To us also, sinners”—he raises his voice and strikes his breast. The raising of the voice expresses, through the centurion, the confession of the Gentiles; the striking of the breast expresses the lamentation of the Jews who struck their breasts. [Col. 0036A]

When he comes to the words “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” the deacon approaches and takes the right side of the corporal with his right hand; together with the priest he uncovers it. As the priest says *Per ipsum*—“Through him”—he touches the four parts of the chalice. For through the immolation of Christ’s body the four regions of the world have been redeemed.

When the prayer has ended, the two of them raise the chalice, set it down together, and cover it. Then (74) the deacon kisses the altar and afterward the priest’s right shoulder. [Col. 0036B]

The priest’s shoulder signifies the stone on which the angel sat at the tomb. An angel must always be believed to be present at the immolation of Christ’s body. The deacon represents Joseph; the priest represents Nicodemus. The raising of the host from the altar represents Christ’s removal from the cross; its placing again upon the altar represents Christ’s burial.

After this the priest recites the Lord’s Prayer in a loud voice. The elevation of the Lord’s Prayer demonstrates the unity of our brotherhood (Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*). For God our Father, the teacher of peace and concord, taught us to pray for all as one, just as he bore all in one. [Col. 0036C]

When the clergy respond, “But deliver us from evil,” the priest completes the consecratory office. At the words “But deliver us,” the deacon and subdeacon rise and fix their eyes upon the consecration of the Lord’s body. For the Evangelist says that his acquaintances stood at a distance, striking their breasts (Luke 23:49).

When he comes to the place “Graciously grant peace,” the one who had held the paten, wearing the cloth, offers it to the subdeacon; the subdeacon offers it to the deacon, and the deacon to the priest. Upon it the priest divides the Lord’s body into three parts. He places one of these parts into the chalice and, saying aloud, “The peace of the Lord,” immediately adds secretly: “May the commingling of the body and blood of the Lord be for us who receive it unto eternal life.” [Col. 0036D]

He communicates himself, the deacon, and the subdeacon with another part. The third he reserves as a viaticum, if necessary, in the paten until the end of the Mass.

The particle of the offering placed into the chalice shows the body of Christ, which rose from the dead. The particle eaten by the priest or the people signifies Christ’s life-giving fellowship with his disciples after the resurrection. The third, which remains on the altar, the holy Church calls the viaticum of the dying, to show that those who die in Christ are not to be regarded as dead but as sleeping, since, under such a great guide, they are led to eternal life. (77) [Col. 0037A]

If it is not needed, the priest or one of the ministers receives the third part. The priest is not to communicate with bread dipped in the chalice, but, according to the decree of the Council of Toledo, with the body separately and the blood separately. The people, however, may be permitted to communicate with dipped bread—not by authority, but from the greatest necessity, because of fear of the shedding of Christ’s blood.

When the priest gives Communion to the ministers, (79) he first kisses each one, and afterward the person who is to communicate receives Communion from him after kissing the priest’s hand.

Finally the priest consumes the particle remaining in the chalice. Then he gives the chalice to the deacon to cleanse it and consume what remains. The deacon carries the chalice with the paten to the left-hand corner of the altar, where he takes one part for himself and gives another part to the subdeacon. After both vessels have been cleansed, both partake. The other acolyte brings the priest another chalice for washing his fingers. The subdeacon assists the deacon in cleansing the chalice and paten. [Col. 0037B]

After the paten and chalice have been cleansed, the acolyte holds both vessels, wrapped in the cloth, until the completion of the first prayer after Communion, together with the other ministers’ offices.

As we said above, after dividing the Lord’s body the priest says aloud, “The peace of the Lord.” (81) From him one of the canons receives the peace and distributes it among the seniors in both choirs. They in turn offer it to the others, so that no one moves from his place; each receives it from a superior and gives it to an inferior. One of the juniors in each choir receives it from the seniors and distributes it to the others in the prescribed order.

They must firmly observe the apostle’s command, “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:10): both those who give the peace and those who receive it are always to incline. Through the kiss of peace the benefit of our faith is signified. (82) [Col. 0037C]

The choir sings *Agnus Dei*, which Pope Sergius ordered to be sung during the breaking of the Lord’s body; the immolation of this Lamb redeemed the world. When it begins, the candlesticks are lit, for the world was illumined by the Passion of the Lamb. (83)

If the deacon is wearing the chasuble with which, as we said above, he had wrapped himself, he puts it on again when the choir repeats *Agnus* for the second time.

The priest greets the people and says the prayer. When he greets the people again, the deacon, at the appointed time, sings either “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite, missa*) or “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*). (84) The clergy respond, “Thanks be to God,” and the office ends. [Col. 0037D]

The Mass, as stated above, is to be celebrated at the third hour according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, for at that hour Christ was crucified by the tongues of the Jews; according to common custom, rather at the sixth hour, because at that hour he suffered at the hands of his persecutors; and during the time of fasting, at the ninth hour, because at that hour he gave up his spirit.

Those who, out of necessity, celebrate Mass before Terce or after None—not continually, but from the desire to offer the sacrifice—are not to be rebuked. For it is read that Leo, the supreme pontiff, celebrated Mass at dawn. [Col. 0038A]

A Mass for the dead is celebrated without the *Gloria*, the *Alleluia*, and the kiss of peace. There are certain churches in which, apart from burials, festive Masses for the dead are celebrated only on the Kalends of the months. We, however, offer sacrifice to the Lord for them daily, except on feast days and the days of Pentecost, and we commemorate their anniversaries festively.

At burials and on feast days with nine readings, we celebrate Vespers and Matins without *Deus in adjutorium*, *Domine labia*, and *Gloria Patri*.

## EXCEPTION

[Col. 0038B] During Advent and from Septuagesima until the day of the Supper, on the Saturdays of the four Ember seasons, and at festive observances for the dead, (86) the deacon and subdeacon are to wear chasubles. If a feast occurs during those periods, they are to wear dalmatics and tunics; likewise on the day of the Supper and on Holy Saturday.

At all feasts two candle-bearers are to be vested. The clerics shall sing the Gradual, Alleluia, or Tract in pairs. (87)

The *Gloria in excelsis* is always begun by the priest, facing east, after *Kyrie eleison* on feast days, except during Advent and Lent. Pope Telesphorus instituted it, adding the words that follow the angelic hymn; and Pope Symmachus ordered it to be sung every Sunday and on the birthdays of martyrs. (88) The priest completes it while censing the altar and saying it secretly with the ministers. Afterward he sits in his place beside the altar and grants the deacon permission to sit. The choir completes the aforesaid hymn by singing it solemnly. [Col. 0038C]

After the hymn has been said, the priest greets the people and says the prayer. The order of Mass written above is to be observed in its entirety.

On these days (89) the *Credo in unum Deum*—“I believe in one God”—is sung, begun by the priest: on all Sundays; on the eight days of Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord; on Epiphany and the Ascension; on all feasts of holy Mary except the Annunciation; on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; on the feasts of all the apostles, of the Holy Cross, of Saint Michael, of All Saints, and of the Dedication of the church.

It is not sung on Holy Saturday or on the Saturday of Pentecost, nor on any other feasts; instead, the priest’s greeting immediately follows the Gospel. [Col. 0038D]

On every day except during the time of fasting, Sext follows the Mass; (90) None is said at its own hour.

At Vespers and Matins several bells are rung separately; finally, as at Mass, two are rung, and Vespers begins. Each psalm is sung with an antiphon, (91) followed by the Chapter and then the hymn, which is never omitted. Ferial hymns are always sung, except on feast days and the days of Pentecost.

After the verse has been said, the *Magnificat* is sung with its antiphon, and (93) the office ends with *Kyrie eleison*, the Lord’s Prayer, and the prayers, with knees bent; and this applies not only to Vespers but to all the hours of night and day, except on Pentecost and feast days. [Col. 0039A]

The priest, recognizing himself as a sinner together with the others, kneels. Since he represents Christ, when he comes to the prayer he rises and says the prayer standing. Standing is the posture of one who fights; therefore the priest fights through Christ’s prayers against the ancient enemy on behalf of the people entrusted to him.

If the feast of a saint occurs, the prayer alone, without the prayers, is sufficient. If it is a feast of three readings, at Matins the invitatory and the hymn are sung from the saint; the entire nocturn is said, with the verses from the saint together with the responsories; and the Matutinal Lauds are celebrated with the hymn but without the prayers. (94) The readings, however, are taken from the saint’s history.

If the saint has an office designated in the official books, the Mass is celebrated for the saint; otherwise the Sunday Mass is sung. The prayer and the Alleluia, however, are said from the saint.

[Col. 0039B] From Advent until the Nativity, only the commemoration of Saint Mary the Virgin and of all the saints is to be celebrated in the community. From the Nativity until the octave of the Epiphany, only that of Saint Mary. From the octave of the Epiphany until the beginning of the fast, (95) the commemoration of Saint Mary, the angels, John the Baptist, Saint Peter, John the Evangelist, the holy apostles, blessed Stephen, all the martyrs, Saint Martin, all confessors, the holy virgins, and all the saints is always to be observed at Vespers and Matins. (96) At Mass, however, except on feast days, the second prayer is for all the saints; the third for the bishop; the fourth for all entrusted to him; (97) and the fifth for the ruler and all the people. At a Mass for the dead, the first prayer is for all the dead; [Col. 0039C] the second for bishops; the third for brothers and sisters; and the fourth for those entrusted to him.

From the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, this same commemoration is to be celebrated together with veneration of the holy Cross. Therefore, during these periods, (98) if on a Sunday the feast of a saint with nine lessons occurs, Vespers, Matins, and Mass are to be celebrated for the saint. Vespers also are to conclude with the office of that saint; and if on a Sunday the feast of a saint with three lessons occurs, for whom an office or passion is available, the invitatory and hymn are to be said for the saint; six lessons, with the same number of responsories, are to be read from the saint’s history; after the third nocturn, when the verse for the saint has been said, the Gospel concerning him is to be proclaimed, and the other lessons, together with the Matins lauds, are to be celebrated for the saint. But if a proper [Col. 0039D] office is lacking, the Sunday Mass is to be sung; the prayer, however, and the Alleluia are to be celebrated for the saint. If a feast with nine lessons occurs, the entire office is to be completed for the saint.

From Advent, therefore, until the Nativity, and from Septuagesima until Pentecost, if a feast with nine lessons occurs on a Sunday, the office of night and day is never to be changed; the feast is instead to be reserved for celebration on the following day. But if the feast of a saint for whom only three lessons are celebrated occurs on that very day, only a commemoration is to be made of him.

From Easter until the octave of Pentecost, only the commemoration of the holy Cross, Saint Mary, and All Saints is to be made at Vespers and Matins.

The office for the dead is to be celebrated throughout the whole year as follows, except from Easter until Pentecost, from the Nativity until the octave of the Epiphany, and on all feast days: from the Kalends of November until the beginning of the fast, only Vespers are to be said after the Vespers of the day; after the Matins lauds, the vigil of the dead is to be held together with their Matins lauds. (99) From the beginning of the fast until the Kalends of November, Vespers and the vigil of the dead are to be held after the Vespers of the day, and after Matins the lauds for the dead. This office is to end after the Matins lauds on the Wednesday of the Lord’s Passion. There, however, (100) it is to be celebrated festively with nine lessons, since it will not be said again until the octave of Pentecost.

The same is to be done at the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity: for it will not be celebrated again until the octave of the Epiphany.

### 32

On the First Sunday of Advent, on Saturday [Col. 0040B] at Vespers, the responsory *Behold, the days are coming* is to be said (101); on the preceding Saturday, at the announcement of the Lord’s Advent, it is first to be sung with great solemnity by two clerics clothed in copes. On this Saturday it is followed by the Advent hymn *Nourishing Creator*. The chapter, verse, and antiphon are to be said for Advent.

From this hour until the octave of Easter (102), no procession is to be made to the crucifix. Matins, with its proper invitatory, hymns, responsories, and antiphons, is to be celebrated festively. Matins is to be said with six prophetic antiphons and three final apostolic antiphons distributed among the several nocturns. In the first nocturn the Book of Isaiah is to be begun, and it is to be read throughout Advent until the Nativity; in the second nocturn, selections from the sermons of the Fathers; [Col. 0040C] in the third, expositions of the Gospels. The same arrangement is to be followed on Wednesdays and Fridays, on the Saturday of the seasonal fast, and at the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

If a feast occurs on one of these Sundays, as we have said above, it is to be reserved for celebration on the following day. On these Sundays, and on those from Septuagesima until Easter, *We praise you, O God* is not to be sung; instead, the ninth responsory is to be repeated. The order of the weekdays, as 33 we have noted above, is to be observed. On Sundays, after the first procession has ended, it is to proceed in such a way that it turns aside only from the crucifix; during it the processional Advent antiphons or certain responsories are to be sung.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

The solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity is to be celebrated as follows. (103) [Col. 0040D] The choir is to be directed by two cantors in copes; (104) after the chapter has been said, they are to sing with solemnity the responsory *O Judah*. After the hymn *Come, Redeemer* has been said, an antiphon is to be sung with threefold repetition over the *Magnificat*; the altar is to be incensed with two thuribles.

At Matins (105) all the bells are to be rung at the first vigil of the night; thereafter pairs are to follow in harmony. (106) The invitatory is to be sung by four clerics, followed by the hymn. As at Vespers, two are to direct the choir. All the responsories are to be sung by pairs, (107) with the third, sixth, and ninth singers clothed in copes; (108) at the second, fifth, and eighth responsories, and at *We praise you, O God*, as well as at the *Benedictus*, the altar is to be incensed.

(109) The lessons of the first nocturn are to be from the prophets, those of the second from the sermons of the Fathers, and those of the third from expositions of the Gospels. [Col. 0041A] (110) Three Gospels are to be proclaimed in copes, with incense and candelabra preceding them. 34 When the ninth responsory has ended, (111) the senior priest of the church, if there is one, is to come forward clothed in a dalmatic and chasuble and solemnly read the Gospel of Christ’s genealogy according to Matthew. When it has been read, he is to begin *We praise you, O God* in a loud voice; afterward, the clergy and people, after a brief interval, are to go out [the reading *lavātum* is uncertain].

Then (112) the clerics, clothed in sacred vestments, are to celebrate (113) Mass with Lauds and a sequence, which (114) the church secretary is to celebrate; the second [Mass] the cantor, and the third the bishop or dean. The reason Pope Telesphorus instituted the singing of Mass to the angels during the night is that the Savior of the world was born in it and was to offer himself as a holy sacrifice for the salvation of the whole [Col. 0041B] world; and in it the angels announced the Virgin’s childbirth to the shepherds, singing *Glory to God in the highest* in its praise.

When this has been completed, they are to finish the Matins lauds. When these have been completed, (115) the cantor is to begin the antiphon *Behold, these things have been fulfilled*; a suitable prayer of commemoration of Saint Mary is to follow it. (116) At the beginning of dawn, a second Mass is to be celebrated in the same manner as the first. Another is sung at the first light because, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, on that very day a new light arose for peoples sitting in darkness (Isaiah 9:2), and also because of the shepherds’ visitation to the Lord’s manger, where they found the bread of angels, 35 by which the souls of the saints are refreshed.

After Terce, a procession is always to be made on the Nativity of the Lord; when it has ended, the principal Mass is to be celebrated. (117) At Vespers [Col. 0041C] the hymn *From the rising of the sun* is to be sung, as at the Matins lauds; the responsory *The Word became flesh* is to precede it. When these Vespers have ended, (118) the deacons, clothed in diaconal vestments, are to come forward with candles, singing a responsory for Saint Stephen, whose birthday celebration is beginning. An antiphon with the *Gloria Patri* is to follow, and, after the prayer has been said, the evening synaxis is to be completed.

(119) At Matins the bells are to be rung as on the preceding night. The invitatory is to be sung by four deacons in copes, while the rest of the order of the preceding night is preserved in the lessons and responsories and in the number of singers. Three responsories, however, are not to be sung in copes. The Gospel is to be proclaimed by a deacon in a dalmatic, preceded by a thurible and candles. Two deacons in dalmatics are to direct the choir; [Col. 0041D] while incensing the altar, they are to begin *We praise you, O God*. Before the nocturn and at the lauds, hymns appropriate to the present feast are to be sung; at the *Benedictus* the antiphon is to be repeated three times. Mass is to be celebrated in copes. Those who direct the choir and sing the Gradual or Alleluia, and also read the Epistle or Gospel, are to wear dalmatics. 36 When the deacons’ Vespers have ended, the Nativity is to be commemorated (120) with an antiphon and the *Gloria Patri*.

(121) Then, with the priests proceeding in chasubles and carrying candles, the office is to be ended by singing the responsory *In the midst of the church*, together with an antiphon and a prayer. The Matins office is to be conducted in every respect as on the preceding two nights, but by presbyters. [Col. 0042A] The morning Mass is to be celebrated at dawn, as the authentic Missal demonstrates; and likewise on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. For both offered themselves to God as a sacrifice from the beginning of the light: the Evangelist through virginity, the Baptist through abstinence. The principal Mass is to be celebrated in copes; its officiants, who are (122) priests, are to wear chasubles. When Vespers have ended as above, the priestly office is concluded.

(123) When the office of the infants begins, everything is to be done as is to be done by the deacons in their office, although, as on the death of the Lord, *We praise you, O God*, *Glory to God in the highest*, and the Alleluia are customarily omitted in certain churches according to ancient practice. This is because, just as Christ was ordered to be killed, so many children were ordered to be killed; and, when they were killed, the death of Christ takes place according to Herod’s reckoning. Nevertheless, since this has pleased modern custom, it pleases us also that they be sung. Subdeacons and deacons are to use tunics and 37 dalmatics, although in certain churches the use of chasubles is observed on this day [f. adds: “the use”].

(124) On the feast of Saint Sylvester, the first six lessons are to be about the saint and the last three about the Nativity; the morning Mass is to be for the saint, the principal Mass for the Nativity. On the remaining days until the octave, the invitatory is to be sung by two clerics in copes. Nine psalms with the same number of antiphons; (125) three lessons with three responsories, sung by pairs. *We praise you, O God* is to be sung, and the office of the Mass (126) is to be performed with the lauds and the sequence.

The octave of Saint Stephen is to be observed like a Sunday feast; (127) that of Saint John like the feast of an apostle; that of the Innocents like a Sunday. [Col. 0042C] (128) The Day of the Circumcision, which is the eighth day of the Nativity, is to be celebrated like the feast of Saint John, except for the chasubles and the morning Mass.

The principal feasts are celebrated for eight days because the world declines through six ages; the seventh age lasts until the universal resurrection and is the rest of the holy souls; the eighth is the kingdom of God after the eternal resurrection. Therefore the eighth day is observed more solemnly, because in that kingdom Christ’s glory will be eternal and the exultation ineffable. And again, when we celebrate the feasts of the saints, we rejoice with the repose of their souls on the day of their solemnity, and on their eighth day with their resurrection in glory. 38

(129) The Day of the Epiphany is to be celebrated like the Day of the Nativity (130), without an invitatory. The lessons of the first nocturn [Col. 0042D] are to be from the prophets; those of the second from the sermons of the Fathers; and those of the third from expositions of the Gospels.

I think that our predecessors did not say the invitatory on the Day of the Epiphany because, by omitting the invitation, they seemed to distinguish themselves from Herodian deeds. On that day Herod invited the scribes and Pharisees for the purpose of having our Lord Jesus Christ sought out by them and treacherously killed. But (131) it is not entirely omitted, since it is recited within the order of the psalms. For Christ was often worshiped everywhere by his pious Virgin Mother, blessed Joseph, and all his other faithful, although not openly because of the fury of their persecutors, nevertheless secretly.

We say *God is our refuge* and the following psalms with alleluiatic antiphons [Col. 0043A] in the third nocturn with the responsories of the baptistery because Christ came in the third age, that is, the age of grace. When the ninth responsory has ended, (132) a priest in dalmatic and chasuble is to come forward and solemnly read the Gospel of Christ’s genealogy according to Luke.

At the Nativity of the Lord, his generation is read as woven by descending from Abraham, 39 the father of faith and obedience, to Joseph, the husband of Mary, who conceived and bore Christ through faith. For Christ, seeking the faithful, descended from the seat of majesty to the depths; by obeying the Father unto death, he redeemed those who had perished.

At his baptism, however, his generation is read as woven by ascending from Heli, his adoptive father, to Adam, who lost by sinning the glory first granted to him, through seventy-seven generations. [Col. 0043B] For seventy-seven is formed by saying the number seven eleven times. Through eleven, which is the transgression of the Decalogue, sins are expressed; and through the number seven, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through these, once original sin—which we contracted from Adam—and all the other sins have been erased in baptism, we become adopted children of God; and thus, by doing good works in faith and obedience, we attain the same glory that Adam received when he was formed.

Then (133) the office of the star is to begin. The procession is always to be made on the same day, as on the Day of the Nativity. On the remaining days until the octave, the daytime and nighttime office (134) is to be completed without *We praise you, O God* and *Glory to God in the highest*. The eighth day is to be celebrated in copes, like the feast of an apostle. [Col. 0043C] On the following day, the feast of Saint Remigius, Hilary, and Felix is to be celebrated. 40

After the feasts have passed, on Sundays until Septuagesima the procession is to proceed in such a way that it turns aside to the crucifix. The processional antiphons or responsories proper to that season are to be sung, and they are to end before the choir. (135) As they enter the choir, the cantor is to begin an antiphon or responsory for the saint to whom the church belongs.

On Sundays and weekdays at night, Paul’s Epistles are to be read; responsories are to be sung from the psalms. Except on Sundays and feast days, the prayers and the office for the dead are to be performed.

Since we omitted explaining the days between the Circumcision and the Epiphany, we think it useful to insert this here. On the day after the Circumcision of the Lord, we celebrate the octave of Saint Stephen in the Sunday manner; on the third day, that of Saint John, like the feast of an apostle; on the fourth, that of the holy Innocents, like that of Saint Stephen.

[Col. 0043D] (136) As for the vigil of the Epiphany, which the people observe in different ways—for some fast, while others dine—it seems fitting to us that we should fast. For we find no greater dignity of reverence for this day than for all the days of the Purification of Saint Mary, (137) on some of which we fast. And because so great a solemnity is approaching for us, in which the whole Trinity manifested itself to the world, we ought to purify ourselves. Simple fasting together with the fruit of good works is the true purification of the mind.

[Col. 0044A] The Day of the Purification of Saint Mary is to be celebrated festively, like the Assumption. Except at the vigil and octave, the procession is to proceed as follows: with candles and candelabra placed in another church, if there is one, the clergy and people are to go devoutly to it, (138) singing the antiphon *Hail, full of grace*, and there receive candles consecrated [that is, blessed] by the bishop or priest. When they have been lit, the cantor is to begin the antiphon *A light for revelation*. When it has ended, they are to return to the mother church through the cloister or around the church, singing *Adorn the bridal chamber*. Then, singing the responsory *He received*, they are to end before the choir. (139) A verse sung by two clerics is to follow; then, by repeating the antiphon, they are to enter the choir, and thus celebrate Mass festively with the lauds and the sequence.

[Col. 0044B] If the feast itself occurs within Septuagesima, a Tract is to be said in place of the Alleluia; the sequence is to follow without an Alleluia. At the Hypapanti, which is called the Presentation of the Lord, we present a light to the Lord, because on that same day Christ, the eternal light, was presented in the temple by blessed Simeon; by the light in our hands, good works are signified. 42

The Sunday of Septuagesima is to be celebrated as follows: on the preceding Saturday at Vespers, a sequence is to be sung in place of the hymn: *Let us all sing the melodious song*. At Matins (141) an alleluiatic invitatory is to be sung; the psalms with their antiphons and their responsories are to be sung. (142) In the first nocturn the Heptateuch is to be begun and read until the First Sunday of the Lord’s Passion, but in such a way that on Sundays its first three lessons are read from it; in the second nocturn, three lessons from the sermons of the Fathers; and in the third, from expositions of the Gospels.

[Col. 0044C] On Septuagesima, after *We praise you, O God* has been celebrated, (143) the Matins lauds are to end with alleluiatic antiphons and a hymn. From Septuagesima until Easter, (144) on Sunday nights at Matins two psalms are changed: *Have mercy on me, O God*, and *Give thanks to the Lord*. For we ought to lament our sins by saying *Have mercy on me, O God*. Once these have been erased by the lamentation of the heart, we ought, kindled by confidence in charity, to praise the Lord and exhort one another to confess to the Lord, for he is good. At First, however, *The Lord reigns* is used in place of *Give thanks*.

After Matins, only a commemoration of Saint Mary and all the saints is to be made, likewise with alleluiatic antiphons. 43 (145) [Col. 0044D] After *Let us bless* has been said with the Alleluia, it is not to be heard again until Holy Saturday; in its place, *Praise to you, Lord*, is to be said, and a Tract sung at Mass.

From that day, *We praise you, O God*, *Glory to God in the highest*, and the Alleluia are omitted until Easter. In place of the Alleluia, which is Hebrew and higher than the other languages, we say *Praise to you, Lord*, which is humbler. (For Greek and Latin, and the other languages, are called poor in comparison with Hebrew.) This signifies the affliction which during these seventy days we ought to undergo through contrition and humility of heart for our sins, so that, having attained true freedom, we may be worthy to return to the inheritance of our heavenly homeland. For the Israelite people are described as having spent that many years in captivity, doing penance for their offenses, and then having returned to their own land.

[Col. 0045A] (146) Seventy days are counted from the Sunday called Septuagesima until the Saturday after Easter. Although at Easter the yoke of our servitude was destroyed by Christ’s death, we shall not attain complete freedom until the true Sabbath, by which eternal rest is signified. For while we remain in this body, we are weighed down by many pleasures of the flesh and cares of the world. This is represented by the six days of Easter, on which we sing the Gradual and the Alleluia. Through the Gradual, as we have stated above, the life of actual good works is signified; through the Alleluia, the eternal glory of souls acquired through good works.

[Col. 0045B] When we reach the aforesaid Sabbath, which is signified by this day on which two Alleluias are sung without a responsory, we shall possess the kingdom of God, in which we shall possess the twofold glory of body and soul; having acquired perfect freedom, in the heavenly Jerusalem, with every servitude and burden of work laid aside, we shall reign perpetually with Christ our King, always at leisure in his praises.

(147) On that day, *Behold, most beloved*, or other antiphons suitable to this season [f. adds: “antiphons”], are to be sung in the procession, and likewise on the other Sundays until the day of Lent. These days, until the beginning of the fast, are to be celebrated like the preceding ones, except for the Alleluia. At Vespers, the responsory *My hope* is to be sung.

[Col. 0045C] Sexagesima ends on the Tuesday of Easter week. That Wednesday has a certain correspondence with the fourth age of the world, in which David and Solomon, the most renowned kings, reigned; through them Christ, the peaceful King, is signified. That age is signified by the glorious building of the most holy temple. In this age Christ, rising from the dead, built from the two peoples one most noble temple for God the Father.

Through Sexagesima, affliction and penitence are expressed. For sixty [f. adds: “days”] are referred to widows, whose life consists in tribulation. In the tribulation and affliction of our flesh, we ought to repent of our sins, so that, cleansed from every stain of sin and adorned with purity of mind and holy works, we may become one temple in Christ.

[Col. 0045D] Quinquagesima ends on Easter Day; it is itself the fiftieth, which mystically was once represented by the fiftieth, namely the jubilee year of remission and freedom. For on this day, after the enemy had been conquered through Christ’s death, the people of Christ were freed from his slavery and restored to true freedom. Therefore whoever, after baptism, by serving vices has again subjected himself to the devil’s power, should erase his offenses through contrition of heart and mortification of the flesh, and strive to keep the Decalogue with the five senses, so that on the day of the holy resurrection, freed from hostile servitude, he may deserve to attain perfect freedom.

[Col. 0046A] Lent, beginning on the Sunday after Quinquagesima, ends at the Lord’s Supper. This contains various meanings. First, because, following the instruction of Moses and Elijah—that is, of the Law and the Prophets (Exodus 24:34; 1 Kings 19)—and of Jesus Christ our Redeemer, we should correct through daily affliction whatever we, whose body subsists from the four elements, have contracted in thought and deed against the Decalogue. For according to the natural philosophers, the human body is fashioned within the mother’s womb in that many days until the day of birth. For that many cycles of days, by mortifying our flesh and doing good, we ought to be fashioned into one body with Christ.

That, according to Gregory (*Homily 16 de tempore*), the thirty-six days of fasting contain six weeks demonstrates that we ought to offer to God the tenths of the year through contrition of heart and mortification of the flesh. After the time of blessed Gregory, (148) four days were added by the holy Fathers in order to complete the number of the Lord’s fast.

[Col. 0046B] The fact that from the beginning of the fast until Easter, forty-six days of abstinence are counted between Sundays and weekdays signifies that we ought, by cultivating ourselves through good works, to restore within us the temple of Christ, destroyed by the assault of vices, for as many days as the temple of the Lord is said to have been rebuilt by the people of God after its destruction by the Babylonians: the temple was rebuilt in forty-six years. Through the Babylonians, vices are expressed.

At the beginning of the fast (149) the sermons of the Fathers are to be read; from the beginning of the fast until the day of the Supper, this is to be observed, except on Sundays. After the Matins lauds, (150) only the lauds of the dead are to be celebrated. When these have ended, (151) the seven psalms, with the litany and prayers, are to be sung while the brothers lie prostrate. After Terce, a Mass for the dead is to be celebrated; after None, the Mass of the day [Col. 0046C] is to be celebrated. (152) Prime is to be sung after sunrise. The chapter is to be reserved until after Terce, followed by the morning Mass; and immediately after Sext has been said, there is to be a short interval. None is to be said at its proper hour, followed by the Mass of the day. (154) When it has ended, Vespers for the dead are to be said; the evening office of the day is to follow them without interval.

Before Compline, when the bell gives the signal, the brothers are to gather in the church; (155) the vigil of the dead is to be held; then (156) the reading of the Collation is to be recited. When the signal is rung again, Compline is to be said.

Each hour of the day is to be followed, for the brothers, by one of these psalms: *When I was in distress I called upon the Lord*; *I have lifted up*; *I rejoiced*; *To you I have lifted up*; *Unless it was that the Lord*; *Those who trust*; *When turning*. For the dead, *Out of the depths* is always to be used.

[Col. 0046D] (157) In all the prayers of the hours, *Have mercy on me, O God* is always to be said; if it seems appropriate, one whole psalter of psalms may be added to it. In Vespers 48 and Matins no commemoration of the saints is to be made; instead, a prayer for sins is to be said: at Matins, *As I live, says the Lord*, followed by the prayer *Hear, O Lord, the supplications of your petitioners*; at Vespers, the antiphon *Who knows whether he may turn*, followed by the prayer *Our supplications*.

This is except only at Saturday Vespers and Matins, or at the Sunday Mass, at which the commemoration of the saints is to be made whose feasts occurred in the preceding week, in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Laodicea (canon 49), which, together with many other provisions, establishes that during Lent the feast of no saint is otherwise to be commemorated.

[Col. 0047A] Although the councils of Toledo (10, canon 1) forbid the Annunciation of the holy Mother of God to be celebrated during this period and decree that it should be anticipated to the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord, nevertheless we do not dare to introduce this observance without the judgment of your prudent discernment.

At the beginning of the fast, after None has been said, the clergy and people are to prostrate themselves before the altar, each person having made a private confession and received a penance, and are thus to be absolved by the bishop or the senior priest of the church. After this, (161) when the bishop has begun the antiphon *Let us change our garments*, (162) he is to distribute ashes with blessed water; then, with antiphons or responsories suitable to affliction, they are to proceed to a certain church or oratory. When they have arrived there, after the antiphons have ended, [Col. 0047B] they are all to prostrate themselves on the ground and say the Lord’s Prayer. But (163) before the procession, (164) the penitents are to be expelled. Thus they are to conclude with *Have mercy on me, O God*, with prayers and a prayer [f.: “are to conclude”].

At this point, rising, two boys are to begin the litany. This order is to be observed on Wednesdays and Fridays until Palm Sunday. On the following Saturday, or on Palm Sunday, when the offices are lacking, the office of the preceding Sunday, not that of the previous weekday, is to be celebrated.

During the first two weeks of Lent, (165) the hymns *Taught by mystical custom* at Vespers, *Most High Giver* at the nocturns, and *Hear us kindly* at the lauds are to be sung. During the next two, *Behold, the time*, *Bright glory*, and *Jesus of the forty-day fast*. During the following two, *The royal banners*, *Sing, my tongue*, and *Six days are completed*. During the final weeks, [Col. 0047C] all the hours of the day are to be sung with the responsories indicated there.

From the First Sunday of the Passion until Easter Day, the Book of the Prophet Jeremiah is to be read, on Sundays only in the first nocturn. During this period, neither at the Introit nor at the end of the third responsories is the *Gloria Patri* to be said; instead, the responsory is to be repeated.

The processional antiphons *When he sits*, *Christ*, *Father*, and *On the day when we shall come* are to be sung at processions on the Sundays of Lent.

On Wednesday of the fourth week, a variation is made (166) through the addition of one lesson and one responsory. On that day the scrutiny takes place, in which the catechumens are instructed in faith and conduct. For this reason (167) the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed are handed over to them, [Col. 0047D] which they must return on Holy Saturday of Easter.

(168) On the Saturday preceding Palm Sunday, ecclesiastical order commands the bishop or senior priest of the church to wash the feet of the poor, and each of the brothers, if he can, those of one poor person. On that very day Mary washed the Lord’s feet with her tears; and what she did on the head, we must do on the members. Therefore, since the office is vacant on that day, the office of the Sunday, not that of the previous day, is to be sung.

The Passion of the Lord is celebrated for two weeks, that is, through two periods: the first is represented by Noah and afterward completed through Christ. And through two periods, namely the natural law and the written law, the righteous, although they deserved good things, were tormented until the time of grace; for through Christ’s death the time of grace began.

[Col. 0048A] The Day of Palms is to be celebrated as follows. (169) After Terce, the clerics are to go in procession with palm branches; when it has ended, the office is to be celebrated festively. A Tract 51 is to be sung by four clerics in copes.

The Passion of the Lord is to be read on that day, and on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, in all churches. In all the Passions except that of Friday (170), *The Lord be with you* is to be said and *And with your spirit* is to be answered; but when the deacon says *The Passion of the Lord*, no one is to answer *Glory to you, O Lord*. The Passion is read on that day because on it he came to Jerusalem of his own will in order to suffer.

On the tenth day of the first month, the lamb that was to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded by the Old Law to be brought into the house—that is, on the fifth day before the day of the Passion.

[Col. 0048B] On Wednesday, a lesson is to be read, followed by a responsory; the second lesson is to be followed by a Tract. Through these two lessons, the twofold death of the first parent, which was erased by Christ’s single death, is signified. This is recalled on that day because on it Christ’s death was plotted by the counsel of the Jews.

Through the five verses of the Tract, the redemption of the transgression of the five senses is signified. In the Passion, as soon as it is said that the veil of the Temple was torn, (171) the curtain before the altar is to be taken down.

On that day the Vespers and vigil of the dead are not to be said. Instead, at Vespers on that day, as on feast days, (172) all the bells are to be rung out of reverence for the Lord’s Supper, and Vespers are to be celebrated festively. After Compline, 52 until Holy Saturday of Easter, the *Gloria Patri* is not to be said.

On Thursday at Matins, first the bells are to be struck individually, and afterward all together. [Col. 0048C] Beforehand, twenty-four candles are to be lit behind the altar; these are to be extinguished according to the psalms and readings. In the first nocturn, readings from Jeremiah’s Lamentations are to be read; in the second, from the exposition of the psalm “Hear my prayer, O God, when I plead”; in the third, an exposition of the Gospel. When the cantor begins the antiphon “But the traitor,” the one candle that still remains is also to be extinguished, and the *Benedictus* is to be sung in a loud voice.

When this is finished, two clerics standing behind the altar are to begin “Kyrie eleison,” which they are to pronounce three times in a loud voice; two others are to be in the middle, and two others at the entrance of the choir. After the first threefold repetition of “Kyrie eleison,” while those in the middle say nothing, the last two are to respond in a sweet voice, “Lord, have mercy.” The choir is to sing “Christ the Lord” in response through to the end. Likewise, the two together are to say “Christe eleison” once; those in the middle are to respond, “Who came to suffer.” Likewise, on another occasion the first are to say “Christe eleison,” while those in the middle respond, “Who, with arms outstretched upon the cross.” Likewise, the first and those in the middle are to say “Kyrie”: “Who prophetically proclaimed”; the last and the choir are to repeat what they sang at the beginning. Likewise, the first are to say “Kyrie eleison” three times together, while those in the middle make no response; the last and the choir are to repeat what they sang at the beginning.

In the same manner, Matins, with its readings and responsories, is to be celebrated on Good Friday and on Holy Saturday of Easter. From the moment the last candle is extinguished at the *Benedictus*, no light is to be kindled in the church until after the blessing of the fire.

On the day of the Lord’s Supper, the psalms at all the Hours except Compline are to be sung in a loud voice and with a tone. At Terce, Sext, and None, the responsory is to follow the psalms; and after the verse has been recited by a boy, everything that follows is to be done in silence. On that day, at the sixth hour, the people are to assemble at the church. If there is a bishop, the calling together and absolution of the penitents, and the consecration of chrism and oil, are to be arranged according to episcopal rite. But where no bishop is present, first both clergy and people, prostrate on the ground with tears and groaning, are to receive absolution of their offenses from the senior priest; then, proceeding in procession to the portico and saying “Have mercy on me, O God,” they are to go to the new fire struck from stone, which they are to bless with holy water and incense.

The fact that during these three days a new fire struck from stone is kindled in the church and from there carried to the other houses of Christians mystically signifies the light of the Godhead, which had been hidden in the Savior’s flesh until the Passion and which, through the Passion and Resurrection, shone forth in the church—that is, in the hearts of the faithful—and afterward resounded throughout the world as they proclaimed the new teaching to it. The fact that it is carried on a spear signifies Christ suspended upon the cross; the fact that it is carried in the form of a serpent signifies that same Christ, who was prefigured by the serpent in the wilderness.

The priest is immediately to take fire on a spear together with a candle and return to the altar, singing the psalm “The Lord is my light.” When all the bells are sounding, the service is to begin; with two cantors vested in copes, the deacon in a dalmatic, and the subdeacon in a tunic, it is to be celebrated festively. If there is a bishop, “Glory in the highest” is to be sung; otherwise, it is not. On this day the consecration of oil is celebrated and absolution is granted to penitents.

For Christ came to us in the fifth age, anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, seeking coheirs for himself, whom, anointed with that same anointing, he might make sharers in his kingdom. No one doubts that he could have done this without oil, since he created all things from nothing. But because, according to the Apostle (Heb. 11:3), invisible things are understood through visible things, he ordained that this mystery be enacted through the olive tree, which is called the emblem of peace and bears fruit whose richness restores the weary and infirm and provides the grace of light. Thus those wounded by the injuries of sins and weakened in the strength of virtues might be restored to eternal salvation and, when the darkness of sins had been driven away, carrying true peace in their hearts, might be enlightened by the light of faith.

For on that very day he brought the old law, which punished sins, to an end and instituted the first sacrifice of his body and blood, by which sins are loosed. The altars are also stripped, because when Christ, who is signified by the altar, was seized, the disciples abandoned him and fled (Matt. 26:56), and, struck with fear, hid for three days.

That no consecration of the sacraments is performed from that day until the Mass of the Lord’s night is observed in accordance with what the Lord said: “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in my kingdom” (Matt. 26:29). The kingdom of Christ was the glory of his resurrection; and on that very day he ate before his disciples. It also signifies that the sacrifice is not celebrated during these two days: the two-day affliction of grief and the fasting of the apostles.

“Agnus Dei” is not to be said; peace is not to be received. This is also to be observed on Friday, for he is betrayed by a false kiss of peace. In place of “Agnus Dei,” “The Lord Jesus” is to be sung as the Communion. When this is finished, the priest, holding the chalice in his hands, is to begin the antiphon “The cup of salvation.”

At this point all the bells are to sound; they are not to be struck again until “Glory in the highest” on Holy Saturday of Easter. In their place, wooden boards are to be struck. Six psalms are then to follow, namely: “I believed”; “To the Lord”; “Deliver me”; “Lord, I have cried”; “With my voice”; and “Blessed,” with their antiphons. When these are finished, the priest is to begin “As they were dining”; while the *Magnificat* is sung, the altar is to be incensed, and thus Vespers is to end with the prayer of Communion. [Col. 0050B]

On that day, several hosts are to be consecrated, so that clergy and people may communicate; half of the hosts, without wine, is to be reserved for the following day, so that they may communicate again. These hosts are to be carried honorably by the priest and the altar ministers, vested, in procession—that is, with candles and incense—to a certain altar, where they are to be carefully stored in the cleanest linen cloths. A light is always to burn there until the extinguishing of the last candle at Matins.

After the meal, everyone is again to assemble at the church. Stripping the altars and singing a responsory, they are to wash them with wine and blessed water; the walls and floors with water alone. The church washed with this blessed water signifies the minds of the faithful, which ought to be cleansed by holy confession and an overflowing of tears. For the Apostle says: “You are the temple of the holy God” (1 Cor. 3:17). The washing of the feet signifies the cleansing of human affections.

When this has been done, they are to assemble in a certain house and perform the *mandatum* according to the Lord’s example. The senior men, girded with linen cloths, are to begin “When the Lord Jesus,” wash the feet of the others, and dry them with linen cloths, singing the antiphons that belong there. Likewise, they are to provide water for the hands with towels. The same is to be done by one of the others for the seniors.

When this has been completed, the deacon, vested in a dalmatic and the other garments, is to approach in procession with candles and incense, and read aloud the Gospel “Before the feast day.” When it has been read, the deacon is to remain silent, and they are to proceed in the same procession to carry the charity [i.e. the charitable meal] to the refectory. The deacon is then to begin the Gospel again where he left off and read it through to the Passion.

Either the bishop or the dean is to provide each brother with a flask of wine. When this has been completed, he, the deacon, and the other ministers are to sit down and say Compline in silence. The *mandatum* for the poor is to precede the *mandatum* for the brothers; it must in no way be omitted, and charity is to be shown to them according to one’s ability.

During these three days every formula of the shepherd—that is, “O Lord, open my lips,” and “O God, come to my assistance”—is to be silent. Our shepherd Christ has departed; the rams of the flock, already predestined to be the shepherds of the Church, are scattered. Christ’s flock, struck with fear, venerates its Lord in the manner of the common people.

The extinguishing of the twenty-four candles according to the psalms, readings, and the hymn of Zechariah signifies the apostles’ sorrow by night and by day; and the extinguishing over the three days signifies the sorrow of the seventy-two disciples.

On Friday, all the Hours except Matins are to be said in silence as everyone assembles in the church. After Matins, the brothers are to say the psalter together in the cloister—or, if there is no cloister, in the church—with the litany. When this has been said, everyone is to remain inside the church, sitting in silence and making private prayers until the service.

At the ninth hour, the boards are struck as at Matins. Everyone, including the clerics, is to proceed in procession to bless the fire as on the previous day. After taking the fire, they are to return to the church and begin the service.

The service is to begin with a reading from the Book of Exodus, followed by a tract. Then, with genuflection, the priest is to say the prayer “O God, from whom Judas also [came]”; afterward the second reading, from Hosea, is to follow, and then the tract “Deliver me.” Next, the Passion of the Lord according to John is to be read. For this the deacon is not to say “The Lord be with you,” nor is the clergy to respond “Glory to you, O Lord.” On that day the greeting is to be omitted from the members, since a false greeting preceded from the betraying disciple at the head.

When the reading reaches the place where it says, “They divided my garments,” two deacons are to strip the altar of the linen cloths that had previously been placed beneath the Gospel. The altar signifies the Lord; the linen cloths signify the apostles, who abandoned the Lord when he was seized and fled.

The Passion is to be read in the manner of a reading, except that the voice of the Lord is to be rendered in the manner used elsewhere. When it has been completed, the senior priest is to say the solemn prayers [editorial reading: “to say”]. For Christ prayed in his Passion for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). During these prayers there is to be genuflection, except [editorial correction: “excepting”] during the prayer for the Jews, who mocked the Lord with a false genuflection.

When these things have been completed, two priests vested in chasubles are to bring a veiled cross while singing the antiphon “My people.” Two others, vested in copes and standing in the middle of the choir, are to respond with the Greek verses “Ἅγιος” (*Holy*), while all the others say “Holy”; this is repeated three times.

After it has been repeated three times, the priest is to come before the cross and begin the antiphon “Behold the wood,” and uncover the cross. As soon as they see it, all are to prostrate themselves on the ground and adore it with tearful hearts. Afterward the priest and subdeacon, prostrating themselves, are to adore the cross; after them, all the clergy; then the people.

The adoration of all is to be performed so that each person’s belly clings to the ground. For, according to Augustine in Psalm 43, when one kneels, something still remains to be humbled; but whoever is humbled so that his whole body clings to the earth has no further humility left in him.

When this has been done, the crucifix is to be washed with wine and water in memory of the blood and water flowing from the Redeemer’s side. After holy Communion, the choir [editorial correction: “clergy”] and the people are to drink from it.

After singing the responsory “Like a sheep to the slaughter,” they are to carry the crucifix to some place [editorial correction: “place”] arranged in the form of a tomb, where it is to be deposited until the Lord’s day. When it has been placed there, the antiphon “In peace, in the same place” and the responsory “The Lord having been buried” are to be sung.

Afterward, ministers of the cross, vested in chasubles, are to bring to the altar the Lord’s reserved body together with unconsecrated wine. There the priest is to incense it, and there alone the priest is to say “Let us pray: Instructed by saving precepts” through “But deliver us from evil.” “The peace of the Lord” is to be omitted, for Christ is betrayed by a kiss of peace.

Afterward, all are to communicate, from the senior to the junior. After the boards have been struck, Vespers is to be said individually; then they are to proceed to the meal of bread and water. They are to return for Compline, which they are to say individually.

On Holy Saturday, the entire church, together with its altars, is to be prepared. All the Hours of the day are to be celebrated in silence as on Good Friday. During these three days “Glory be to the Father” is not sung, because the Lord’s three-day burial is celebrated in them: humiliation is signified by death, and exaltation by glory.

But since Sunday, which is reckoned as the third day of the Lord’s burial because it extends through the night, cannot be devoted to the Lord’s burial on account of the glory of the Resurrection, the holy Fathers established a third celebration on the day of the Lord’s Supper. On that day he made known to the apostles that he would suffer for all his own, because he gave them his flesh to eat on the following day, when it would suffer, and likewise gave them the blood that would be poured out.

At the ninth hour of the day, after the boards have been struck, the people are to hasten to the church. The clergy are then to proceed in procession to bless the fire. After it has been blessed and incensed, one candle is to be lit. The bishop or priest, together with the deacon, is to carry it on a certain spear whose upper end bears the likeness of a serpent, while the clergy sing:

“The Lord . . . . . . , . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . his life”  
[Here considerable text is missing.]

That is, the joy of the soul and the incorruptible glory of the body; for the white garments signify the glory of the Resurrection. Those who have been baptized may wear white garments; chrismal garments may be worn only by priests [editorial reading: “in”] in divine worship.

Afterward light is placed in their hands, by which the Holy Spirit is received, so that they may be worthy to perform good works. The whiteness of the garment signifies purity of mind. The light received in the hands signifies good works.

That white and chrismal garments are worn for seven days expresses the course of this life, in which we ought always to be white—that is, radiant—in good works. Concerning this Solomon says: “Let your garments always be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9:8). Oil signifies charity.

The world is divided into six ages; the repose of souls is reckoned as the seventh age. By the eighth day, when the garments are removed, the kingdom of God is signified, in which charity and the other good works will cease, and we shall be clothed with blessed immortality.

After two others have begun the third litany with “Holy Mary, intercede for us,” the clergy are to return to the choir. At its conclusion “Agnus Dei” is to be sung, and then all the candles are to be lit, because through the Lamb of God the world has been enlightened.

After the verse “Receive our supplication,” “Glory be to the Father” is to be said, and “Agnus Dei” is again to be repeated. Then “Kyrie eleison” is to follow. After “Glory in the highest,” the altar is to be incensed, and the service is to conclude in a loud voice while all the bells are sounding.

After the prayer has been said and the reading read, two men in copes are to sing “Alleluia, Confess to the Lord” solemnly from the ambo. When this is finished, two elders in white garments are to sing the tract “Praise the Lord.” Through this Saturday and the *Alleluia* that follows the tract, the first life—which was not eternal but fell into misery—is signified.

By the *Alleluia*, glory is signified; by the tract, lamentation; by the gradual, which follows the *Alleluia*, the six ages of this world, through which one reaches eternal life by good works; and by the eighth Saturday, on which two *Alleluia*s are sung, the eighth blessedness is expressed—the double glory of body and soul, which will remain eternal without any sorrow following it.

After the Gospel has been read, neither the Creed nor the offertory is to be said. When the priest has said “The Lord be with you,” the choir responds, “And with your spirit.” After “Let us pray over the offerings” and “It is truly worthy,” the entire service of the Mass is to be celebrated in the customary manner.

When the priest has said “The peace of the Lord,” peace is not to be received. “Agnus Dei” and the Communion do not follow. Instead, after the clergy and people have communicated, Vespers is to be said with one psalm, “Praise the Lord, all,” and with an antiphon containing *Alleluia*. Then the priest is to begin the antiphon “But in the evening”; after the *Magnificat* has been sung and the altar incensed, he is to conclude the service with the prayer after Communion.

The fact that on Easter Saturday incense is not offered, but rather *thymiama* according to Roman order, signifies the spices prepared by the women. The fact that neither the offertory nor “Agnus Dei” is sung signifies the silence of the women, who, struck with fear, secretly announced the Lord’s Resurrection. “Sanctus,” namely the song of the angels, is said because they did not keep silent about the Lord’s Resurrection but foretold it to the women in an open voice.

The deacon is to say “Go, the dismissal is made”; the choir is to respond “Thanks be to God.” When this has been done, a responsory appropriate to it is to be sung with its verse, and afterward incense is to be blessed.

After the meal, they are to return for Compline, which is to begin with “O God, come to my assistance.” Three psalms are to be sung—“When I called,” “In you, O Lord,” and “Behold now”—without a chapter and verse as at Vespers. “Now you dismiss” is to be sung with an antiphon containing *Alleluia*, and the service is to conclude after the prayer has been said.

## THE ORDER OF EASTER

At the tenth hour of the night, a few vested clerics are to come, lift the crucifix with incense and *thymiama*, and honorably place it in its proper position while singing the antiphon “The Lord has risen from the tomb” [editorial addition: “singing”]. Afterward, when all the bells are sounding, they are to open the doors of the church and begin Matins.

Two cantors vested in copes are to direct the Matins service. The invitatory is to be sung by four clerics in copes, followed by three psalms with antiphons. The deacon, vested in a dalmatic, is to proclaim the Gospel reading. [Col. 0054A] Two others in copes are to read the other two lessons. Each responsory is to be sung by two vested clerics.

After the third responsory, the service of the tomb is to be celebrated. When this has been completed, “We praise you, O God” is to be sung, the altar being incensed; afterward, after each responsory, the altar is to be incensed.

After Matins, Lauds are to be celebrated with five psalms, their antiphons, the chapter, and the *Benedictus*, with the antiphon repeated three times. When the prayer has been completed, the cantors are to bless the Lord with thanksgiving.

Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline are to be said with psalms, the gradual, and the prayer. After the chapter, the antiphon “I saw water” is to be said while blessed water is sprinkled.

After Terce has been sung, a procession is to be made through the cloister and around the church, and the responsory “Mary Magdalene,” or some processional antiphon of the day, is to be sung. Then “The angel sat” is to be sung, so that it ends before the crucifix, where the verse is to be sung. When this is finished, they are to return to the choir singing “Christ rising,” and complete the service of the day with the greatest solemnity.

Vespers is to be celebrated as follows. First, the ministers of the Church are to vest; afterward they are to come in procession—with the cross, incense, candles, and the text—to the crucifix. There, without “O God, come to my assistance,” they are to begin Vespers with “Kyrie eleison.” After “Kyrie eleison” and “Christe eleison” have each been sung three times, when they begin “Kyrie eleison” again, they are to return to the choir and say there three psalms with an antiphon containing *Alleluia*.

Afterward two clerics are to sing the gradual. Those who have directed the choir are to sing the *Alleluia* of the day. After the verse has been said, the *Magnificat* is to be celebrated with the antiphon repeated three times. After the prayer has been said, “Let us bless the Lord” is to be said by those who sang the *Alleluia*.

After the cantor has begun the antiphon containing *Alleluia*, they are to proceed to the fonts while singing the psalm “Praise the Lord, children.” There, after the gradual has been said without its verse, the boys are to sing “Alleluia, Praise the Lord, children.”

For through the baptism that we receive in the font we attain the good work expressed by the responsory; through good work, the glory signified by the *Alleluia*. We omit the verse of the responsory not because of any symbolism, but merely to avoid tedium. Through “Praise the Lord, children,” which is said while going to the fonts, baptism is recalled. Through “When Israel went out,” the song of the people of Israel and the crossing of the Red Sea, by which it was freed from Pharaoh’s power, baptism is again signified. Pharaoh signifies the devil; the Red Sea, baptism. For through baptism we are freed from the devil’s power.

These six Easter days, on which we sing the responsory with *Alleluia*, signify the time of Christians, in which we perform good works by which we may attain glory. By Saturday and the period that follows until Pentecost, during which we sing two *Alleluia*s without a responsory, the kingdom of God is signified, in which, outside every temporal limitation, we shall be glorified with a double glory, namely of body and soul. Again, the six days on which the responsory is sung signify the six ages in which good works are performed; the seventh and eighth signify the repose of souls and the kingdom of God, in which we shall no longer work but enjoy praise and glory.

When this has been completed and the prayer has been said, they are to return to the crucifix while singing “When Israel went out” with an antiphon containing *Alleluia*. There, “The Lord has sent redemption,” or “Christ rising,” is again to be sung by two clerics, and the prayer is to be said.

Singing together the antiphon “Perpetual light,” they are to enter the choir and conclude the service with the prayer for the saints and “Let us bless the Lord.”

This order is to be observed throughout the entire week until White Saturday. At Matins “We praise you, O God” is to be sung; after the *Benedictus*, a procession is to be made to the crucifix, during which “Christ rising” is to be sung. Before the crucifix, “Let the Jews now say” is to be sung as the verse, and the prayer for the cross is to be said.

From there, as at Vespers, they are to enter the choir while singing the antiphon “Perpetual light,” and the service is to be completed with the prayer and “Let us bless the Lord.” All these seven days are to be celebrated festively in the same manner, in copes, with Lauds and the sequence, except for the procession of the Mass.

On White Saturday, however, a second *Alleluia* is to be sung in place of the gradual. At Vespers, “O God, come to my assistance,” five psalms, the chapter, the responsory “The Lord has risen from the tomb,” and the hymn “Choir of the new Jerusalem” are to be said. After Vespers, a procession is to be made to the crucifix, not to the font, during which a song about the Resurrection is to be sung.

Compline on that day is to be celebrated with its psalms, the hymn, “Now you dismiss,” the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and the prayer.

The eighth day is to be celebrated like the first. But all the Hours of the day are to be said there with their chapters and the verses belonging to them, as throughout the year; and at Vespers, “O God, come to my assistance” is to be said. The service of the day will lack the gradual but will have two *Alleluia*s.

On that day and on every Saturday, after five psalms have been sung at Vespers, two are to sing the responsory “The Lord has risen from the tomb”; the hymn “Choir of the new Jerusalem” is to follow; and after the *Magnificat* has been sung, the service is to be completed with “Let us bless the Lord.” On other Sundays, the hymn “To the supper” is to be said without a responsory.

In the same manner all the Hours of the day are to be celebrated from this time until Pentecost. Compline is to be sung with its psalms, the hymn “Jesus, redeemer of the world,” and an antiphon containing *Alleluia* at “Now you dismiss.”

On all Sundays until Pentecost, each nocturn is to be said with one antiphon containing *Alleluia*. Six readings are to be taken from the Apocalypse, and three from the Resurrection.

If anyone seems unwilling to resist these statutes of the holy Fathers because of the shortness of the nights, we permit, to avoid tedium, that only nine psalms be sung at the nocturns. Since there are eighteen, nine are to be said on one Sunday and nine on another. The ninth [the responsory appears to be missing] is to be sung by two clerics in honor of the Resurrection.

When it has been completed, the priest is to begin “We praise you, O God” while incensing the altar. After this has been said, Lauds is to conclude with the single antiphon “But the angel of the Lord,” the chapter, the hymn “Dawn of light,” the *Benedictus*, the antiphon “And very early,” and the prayer.

Afterward, as during Easter week, a procession is to be made to the crucifix. “Christ rising,” together with the aforementioned verse, is to be sung.

At Saturday Vespers and Sunday Matins, from that day until the Sunday before the Nativity, a procession is always to be made. Before Pentecost, a song about the Resurrection is to be sung; after Pentecost, one about the cross.

The service of the day is to be celebrated without tropes, Lauds, or a gradual, with two *Alleluia*s and the sequence. The morning Mass is to be one of the Resurrection; whoever wishes may celebrate the Sunday Mass, but the principal Mass is always to be one of the Resurrection. The processional chant is to be one of the Resurrection and of the cross.

After the octave of Easter, for as long as the responsory “Worthy are you” is sung, the Apocalypse is to be read. When this is finished, the canonical Epistles are to follow until Ascension Day.

On weekdays, at the nocturn, six psalms are to be sung—with “Glory be to the Father” three times and one antiphon—and three readings with the responsories of the same period are to be read. The Sunday Mass is to be sung throughout the week unless a feast of the saints occurs.

Only one *Alleluia* is to be sung on account of the joyful repose of souls, which they enjoy only before the universal Resurrection; on feasts, two are to be sung, in remembrance that after the judgment not only souls but also bodies will possess eternal glory.

If feasts occur, when celebrated at another time, minor feasts are to have three readings and major feasts nine. If a feast occurs on a Sunday during this period, it is to be reserved for celebration on the following day.

The general Office for the Dead is not to be celebrated, as we stated above, except at someone’s burial or anniversary.

If the Greater Litany occurs within the eight days of Easter, there is to be no fasting, no abstinence, and no mention of it, except for a festive procession. If it occurs at another time, everyone except children and the sick is to fast.
