After the sung Mass, following Sext, they are to proceed in procession to the church of Saint Peter of Saint-Ouen, where the priest is to be vested with the other ministers but without a chasuble.

Rogation antiphons are to be sung. When they have arrived, a responsory or antiphon for the saint is to be said. After the priest has finished the prayer, he is to begin “Kyrie eleison”; after all have said the Lord’s Prayer in silence, the prayers are to follow with “Have mercy on me, O God.” When this has been completed, they are to return to the church singing some litany; and, after None has been said, they are to proceed to the meal.

The Rogation days are to be celebrated in the same manner. If a feast of a saint whose Office is observed occurs on a Rogation day, the Mass for that saint is to be sung after Prime.

The Finding of the Holy Cross is to be celebrated as follows. The invitatory and the last three readings are to be about the cross, together with Lauds. The first six readings, with the same number of responsories, are to be about the saints whose feast is celebrated that day. Three responsories from these and three about the cross are to be sung by pairs of clerics. The service is to be celebrated festively with Lauds and the sequence. A procession to the cross is to be made at Vespers, Matins, and Mass.

The Ascension of the Lord is to be venerated as follows. At Vespers, the cantor is to direct the choir. Two clerics in copes are to sing the responsory; those who have sung it are to direct the choir. The hymn is to follow, and the *Magnificat* is to conclude with the antiphon repeated three times. After the prayer has been said, Vespers is to conclude with “Let us bless the Lord.”

A procession is to be made only for Mass. At Matins, all the bells are to be struck as at Easter; the invitatory is to be sung by four clerics in copes; the hymn is to follow; nine psalms with the same number of antiphons and nine readings with the same number of responsories are to be celebrated. Each responsory is to be sung by two clerics. The altar is to be incensed at the second, fifth, and eighth responsories, and at “We praise you, O God.”

Lauds is to conclude with the hymn, the antiphon repeated three times at the *Benedictus*, and “Let us bless the Lord.” After Terce, a procession is to be made. Then, with the church decorated as fully as possible, the service is to be celebrated with Lauds and the sequence. Vespers is to be conducted as at the vigil.

The eighth day of this solemnity is not celebrated with the greatest solemnity as at Easter, but only . . . [editorial note: “something is missing, perhaps ‘as the feast of an apostle’] will be celebrated. It is commemorated not merely for eight days but for ten, after the manner of the apostles, who after the Lord’s Ascension, always directing their minds toward heaven, awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, on all these eight days, “We praise you, O God,” “Glory to God in the highest,” and two *Alleluia*s are to be sung. From Ascension Day until the Sunday on which the historical reading “God of all” is sung, the Acts of the Apostles are to be read; afterward the Books of Kings are to follow.

On the vigil of Pentecost, the rite is to be celebrated as on Holy Saturday, except for the blessing of the candle, with Vespers celebrated within the Mass. At the eighth hour of the day the people are to assemble at the church. A senior is to read the first lesson, “God tested.” A chant follows it for this reason: through the faith for which Abraham is praised above all others, everlasting joy is acquired. The tract “Let us sing to the Lord” is to be sung by two clerics. Then the priest is to say the prayer “O God, who [in] Abraham thy servant,” and a senior is to read the second lesson, “Hear, O Israel.” The tract “Give ear, O heaven” is to be sung as the first was, followed by the prayer “O God, who through the mouths of the prophets.”

Likewise the third lesson, “Seven shall take hold,” is to be read; after the tract “The vineyard made” has been sung, “O God, who hast called us to celebrate the present [feast]” is to be said. When the prayer is finished, the fourth lesson, “Moses announced,” is to be read. The tract “As the hart” is then to follow, and afterward the prayer “Almighty everlasting God, who [hast instituted] this solemnity.” Let the entire remainder of the Office be performed as on Holy Saturday; but “Agnus Dei” and the Communion are also to be sung, and peace is to be exchanged.

At Vespers the vested cantor is to direct the choir. The responsory “They appeared” (*Apparuerunt*) is to be sung by two clerics in copes, who are afterward to serve as precentors. Five psalms are to be sung with one antiphon; after the chapter and hymn have been said, the *Magnificat* is to be sung with the antiphon repeated three times, and Vespers is to conclude with the priest’s prayer and “Let us bless [the Lord],” said by the precentors. After Vespers and Matins on that day, they are to make a commemoration of the Resurrection at the crucifix.

## How Pentecost Is to Be Celebrated

On the solemnity of Pentecost, the entire Office of the night and day is to be observed as on Easter Day, except without the service of the tomb, without the gradual, and without the procession to the font. Masses are to be said with hymns and responsories. The week is to be celebrated as Easter week.

The eighth day is to be celebrated with the greatest solemnity like the first, and the same Office of the night and day is to be completed in its entirety. Those who receive the imposition of hands from the bishop ought to observe the anointing with chrism for seven days, for the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of sevenfold grace, and his solemnity and mystery are rightly celebrated for seven days.

The only difference between Easter and Pentecost is that at Easter Matins no hymn is sung, whereas here two are sung. At the third hour, when all the bells are sounding, after “O God, come to my assistance,” the hymn is to be begun by three clerics in copes while they incense the altar. The entire church is to be illuminated, and all the clerics are to be vested as fully as the church permits. While the hymn is being sung, flowers of various colors, in the likeness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, are to be scattered from above, and the entire Hour is to be celebrated festively.

A procession is to be made on that day as on Easter Day. On the following day and throughout the entire week, if a feast of a saint occurs, the Office is to be sung for the saint. Otherwise, Matins is to be said with psalms [editorial addition: “readings and”] and responsories.

On Tuesday the Mass is to be of the angels; on the other days, the Masses established in the service book are to be used. On the following Sunday, the Office is to be celebrated in honor of the Holy Trinity with nine psalms and antiphons, and nine readings and responsories, with the same dignity as Ascension Day. The Epistle is to be read: “I saw a door”; and the Gospel: “There was a man of the Pharisees.”

On the following day the historical reading from Kings is to begin, with its responsories, and Chronicles is to be read until the Kalends of August; throughout the entire week the Sunday Mass is to be sung. From those Kalends, the book of Ecclesiastes is to be read until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. From that day, the book of Job is to be read until the Kalends. From the Kalends of September until the middle of the month, the book of Tobit and Ezra are to be read. From that day until the Kalends of October, Esther and Judith are to be read; from those Kalends, the Book of Maccabees is to be read until the Kalends of November. From then until Advent, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Twelve Prophets are to be read.

From the time when the celebration of the Holy Trinity begins until the Advent of the Lord, the ecclesiastical order is to be observed on Sundays and weekdays as previously prescribed between the octave of Epiphany and Septuagesima, except that after Vespers a vigil for the dead is to be sung, and after Matins only Lauds for the dead.

For the procession of the cross, a chant about the cross is to be sung at Saturday Vespers and Sunday Matins. When its prayer has been completed, a commemoration of the Resurrection is to be celebrated as seems fitting. The procession of the day is not to turn away from the crucifix; rather, when the processional antiphon has been completed, the cantor is to begin an antiphon or responsory and finish it before the cross.

From there, returning to the choir, an antiphon for the saint whose church it is is to be sung; then Terce is to be said, and the service of the day completed.

## The Four Ember Seasons

The Four Ember Seasons are to be celebrated as the season of Lent. On Saturday, however, when ordinations are conferred, the cantor shall direct the choir. At each prayer, except the last, the deacon shall say, “Let us kneel,” namely during the reading of the Three Children, who, worshiping God alone, refused to bend the knee before the statue of Nebuchadnezzar. (271) The last blessing is not followed by a blessing, (272) out of respect for the Lord’s night, on which the Mass office of that day is completed.

[Col. 0059B]

Since we subsist through the four elements—fire, air, earth, and water—it is fitting that, through the mortification of the fast of the Four Seasons, we cut away from ourselves all the vices of the body that sprout through the varying administration of the seasons. We observe each fast for three days, because with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength we are commanded, according to his teaching, to love the holy Trinity, the one God; and we, who subsist through these four elements, ought to govern ourselves according to his good pleasure.

The fact that the first is celebrated on the first Saturday of the first month, the second on the second Saturday of the fourth, and the third on the third Saturday of the seventh, while the fourth is not observed on the fourth Saturday of the tenth month, on which the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated, but, out of reverence for it, on the preceding Saturday—as is found in the writings of the holy Fathers—was omitted from our work, so as to avoid tediousness. (79) [Col. 0059C]

Accordingly, during these seasons, on Saturdays after None, (273) at the evening Mass—that hour being a part of the Lord’s Resurrection—the consecration of orders was established by Saint Leo the supreme pontiff and the other holy Fathers; it is to be conferred upon those who are fasting by those who are fasting. (274) Sacred authority prohibits its being performed before None.

Again, we fast each season for three days, since each season consists of three months. (275) On Sunday, however, the ordination of bishops shall be celebrated. For on that day the world was created and redeemed; on that day the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles.

Let one cleric sing each gradual before the altar. Let the responsory, the *Benedicite*, and the tract be sung by two clerics. At the end of Mass, “Bow your heads” is not to be said. [Col. 0059D]

On Wednesday of the Ember Seasons two readings are read, because those who are to be ordained ought to be instructed so that they may possess knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, and, according to the Apostle, shine through teaching and speech (1 Tim. 5:17).

## On the Feasts of the Saints

We ought to distinguish the feasts of the saints and how they are to be celebrated, lest they become burdensome to us if we act excessively, or lest, if we are too reticent, we be deprived of their assistance. Although they all have one glory in the kingdom of God, their feasts are nevertheless to be celebrated for us according to the precedence of their rank or the affinity of their bodies.

First of all, it is fitting to venerate with the greatest devotion the feasts of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, [Col. 0060A] but especially that feast on which our Lord Jesus Christ carried her with himself to his most glorious throne.

On the vigil, a festive Mass shall be celebrated at None, with one cope in the choir. Let all the people fast. At this feast, (276) two bells at a time shall be rung at Vespers. Five antiphons shall be sung with the evening psalms. After the chapter has been said, (277) two clerics wearing copes shall sing the responsory, and these same men, together with the cantor, shall direct the choir from both sides until they bless the Lord. Let the hymn be said, and let the altar be incensed with two thuribles. Let the *Magnificat* be said with the antiphon repeated three times.

At the beginning of Matins let all the bells be rung. Four clerics shall sing the invitatory, and two shall sing each responsory. (278) A deacon wearing a cope shall go in procession [Col. 0060B] to proclaim the Gospel. At the second, fifth, and eighth [responsory—addition], and at the *Te Deum laudamus*, the altar shall be incensed. At Nocturns and Matins let hymns be said. At the *Benedictus* let the antiphon be repeated three times.

After Terce, let them go in procession through the cloister, or, where there is no cloister, around the church. Let the Mass office be celebrated festively. (279) Let all the clerics be vested according to the ability of the church, and let Mass be celebrated festively with the *Laud* and the sequence. (280) Let the clergy, and whichever of the people desire it, receive Communion.

Let the Vespers of the day be performed like a vigil. Thus all the days up to the octave shall be celebrated according to the Sunday rite, except that (281) four readings shall be read at Nocturns. Let the *Te Deum laudamus* be sung. Let the eighth day be celebrated like an apostolic feast.

The Nativity of the same Virgin, her Purification, her Annunciation, [Col. 0060C] the feast of the saint to whom the church belongs, and (282) All Saints’ Day shall likewise be celebrated. So too shall her other feasts be celebrated, but without vigils and octaves; and the vigil of that saint, if he was a confessor, as well as All Saints’ Day, shall have octaves.

On the day after All Saints’ Day there shall be a festive celebration of all the dead. In it neither a hymn nor an invitatory shall be said. (283) Two clerics shall sing each responsory; two shall direct the choir; two clerics wearing copes shall sing the gradual; and four shall sing the tract. (284)

Matins and (285) the Hours of the day shall in no way be omitted, but, after these have been said according to the ferial rite, the festive Office of the Dead shall follow.

After Prime has been said, three psalms shall be sung in the tone, namely *Ad Dominum cum tribularer*, *Levavi*, and *Laetatus sum*; after the verse has been said, *Kyrie eleison* shall be sung. When the Lord’s Prayer has been completed, with only the first chapter, *Requiem aeternam*, the prayer shall follow. The same shall be done at the other Hours, except [perhaps “Vespers”] and Matins.

At Terce: *Ad te levavi* (“To you I have lifted up”), *Nisi quia Dominus* (“Unless the Lord”), *Qui confidunt* (“Those who trust”); the versicle shall be: “From the gate of hell.”

At Sext: *In convertendo* (“When restoring”), *Nisi Dominus aedificaverit* (“Unless the Lord builds”), *Beati omnes* (“Blessed are all”); the versicle: “Do not enter into judgment.”

At None: *Saepe expugnaverunt* (“They have often assailed”), *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”), *Domine, non est* (“Lord, there is not”); the versicle: “In everlasting remembrance.”

(286) At Compline: *Deus misereatur* (“May God have mercy”), *Deus in adjutorium* (“God, to my aid”), *Domine, exaudi orationem meam, auribus* (“Lord, hear my prayer; with your ears”); the versicle: “Eternal rest.”

(287) The feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the martyrdoms of the apostles Peter and Paul and of Andrew, the commemoration of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano, and the deposition of Saint Martin shall be celebrated in one manner. At these solemnities two bells at a time shall be rung. Five psalms shall be sung at Vespers with one antiphon only. Two clerics wearing copes shall sing the responsory; afterward they shall direct the choir until they bless the Lord. The altar shall be incensed with one thurible.

(288) At Matins three clerics shall sing the invitatory. Two by two they shall sing the responsories. At Nocturns and Lauds let the hymn be sung. Let there be no procession. On each day until the octave, unless a greater feast intervenes, something from those offices shall be sung, and the whole of Matins shall be said. (289) Let the eighth day be celebrated as Sunday.

The solemnities of the other apostles and evangelists; the Exaltation of the Holy Cross; the Beheading of Saint John; the dedication of Saint Michael in the Sea; Saint Peter in Chains; (290) the Conversion of Saint Paul; the feasts of the holy martyrs Laurence, Maurice, Dionysius, and Nicasius; the feasts of the holy confessors; the ordinations of Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, Nicholas, and Gildaldus; and the translation of Saint Benedict shall be celebrated according to an equal order.

At these feasts (291) the choir shall not be directed at Vespers or Matins. Two clerics wearing copes shall sing the responsory. At the *Te Deum laudamus* and at the *Benedictus*, the altar shall be incensed. Two clerics wearing copes shall sing the invitatory. Two by two they shall sing each third responsory. (292) The Office shall be celebrated with the Lauds and the sequence; and daily until the octave only their commemoration shall be recited.

On the eighth day, unless the feast of another saint occurs, something concerning them shall be sung and Matins shall be said.

These feasts of the saints are celebrated according to the Sunday rite, except that (293) Matins is not said: those of Sylvester, Sebastian, Vincent, Agnes, Cecilia, Agatha, the Chair of Saint Peter, and Gervasius; the translations of Saint Martin, Wandregisilus, and Germanus; the discoveries of Saint Stephen, Remigius, George, Leodegarius, (294) Romanus, Audoenus, Brictius, and Lucy the virgin; and others that may be desired, as well as those of all the holy bishops who have presided over this Church.

## On Sunday

Sunday shall be celebrated in this manner.

On Saturday, after the psalms of the day have been sung with their antiphons and the chapter has been said, (295) two clerics without copes shall sing the responsory, followed by the hymn. At the *Magnificat*, the altar shall be incensed.

At Matins two clerics without copes shall sing the invitatory, followed by the hymn. Nine readings and nine responsories shall be said. The *Te Deum laudamus* shall be said, except during Advent and Lent. Let the hymn be said at Nocturns and Lauds.

(296) At Matins, except during the aforementioned seasons, only one antiphon shall be sung. After Prime there shall be a procession, as stated above. The Office shall be celebrated by two cantors.

Let the ministers be vested as follows. The deacon shall wear a dalmatic, [Col. 0062A] the subdeacon a tunic, two shall wear albs and carry the candlesticks, and one shall carry the thurible. Two clerics in albs shall sing the gradual, and two wearing copes shall sing the Alleluia.

Since we have dealt with the divine mysteries, it is necessary to distinguish with what sacred vestments those who are to minister should be clothed.

The amice is therefore the first vestment. We wrap it around the neck so that the voice which comes forth through the throat may be protected from every evil utterance, and so that, according to the Prophet, we may guard our heart and not offend with our tongue.

The second is the linen shirt, which is called the white garment, or *poderis*, or *talaris* . . . . . . [lacuna] the knot of the body tightly [binding] the whole body without . . . . . . [lacuna], through which it is brought with great labor; it signifies the purity of mind and body, which is acquired through much fasting, [Col. 0062B] vigils, prayer, and the practice of good works.

Through the tightening . . . . . . [lacuna] the heart and all the limbs of the body . . . . . . [lacuna]; through the length of the *talaris* . . . . . . [lacuna] perfection; through the avoidance of wrinkles, by which . . . . . . [lacuna] the dispositions . . . . . . [lacuna]; the purity of the Catholic faith, through . . . . . . [lacuna].

Through the stole, which is called the *orarium*, [are signified] the Lord’s easy yoke and his light burden, by which . . . . . . [lacuna]. The purity of the stole . . . . . . [lacuna]. Through its length down to the feet, the virtue of humility. Through the belt by which the loins are tightened, chastity is signified . . . . . . [lacuna].

Next comes the tunic, concerning which the Lord said to Aaron: “You shall make for yourself a violet-colored tunic” (Exod. 28:31). This is worn beneath the dalmatic, and . . . . . . [lacuna] is called.

Hyacinth is rare; it is neither obscured by density nor does it shine uniformly. In a clear sky it becomes transparent, and it is pale, variegated, and of a color as though belonging to the heavens. Through the heavenly and variegated color it signifies the priestly life, which, intent continually upon heavenly desires alone, ought, according to the Apostle, always to have its way of life in heaven (Phil. 3:20).

Through the change of color it signifies brotherly compassion, as the Apostle says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice” (Rom. 12:15). The fact that this belongs specifically to the bishop signifies that understanding of sublime matters is not open except to the perfect. Because it is an inner garment and is not girded, it signifies that the virtues of the soul, known to God alone, must always be possessed without interruption.

The dalmatic, however, which is white . . . . . . [lacuna; the manuscript/editorial text supplies: “for it is white”] and is adorned before and behind with scarlet lines from top to bottom . . . . . . [lacuna], signifies purity together with the preaching of both Testaments and love of God and neighbor, with which priests and deacons ought to shine.

Through the twelve fringes contained in the two lines, [are signified] the twelve branches of the virtues which grow from the root of charity . . . . . . [lacuna]; these the Apostle also enumerates, saying: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4), and so forth.

The third line, which . . . . . . [lacuna].

The remainder is missing in the Salicosan codex (Gall. de Saulceuse), from which these excerpts were taken.

## Observations on the Book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*

### (1)

“To the truly holy and worthy of honor for his merits, Maurilius.”

The date of the work is immediately detected from the inscription. Since our John did not enter the episcopal office of Avranches before the year of Christ 1061, as we observed above, while Maurilius did not exceed the year 1067 in his pontificate, there is no doubt that the surviving book, dedicated to him, was written within that seven-year period.

Concerning Maurilius, a bishop of renowned sanctity—who completed and dedicated the principal church of the Mother of God—besides what is found in the commonly published authors, namely William of Poitiers in the *Deeds of Duke William*, William of Jumièges, *History of the Normans*, book VII, chapters 24 and 38; Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, books IV and V; William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of England*, book III; and others, the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Rouen* should be consulted from the manuscript codex of the metropolitan church.

Passing over other matters, since they are more extensive in that work, it will not be unwelcome to insert here two points worthy of notice.

1. In the ancient pontifical book of that same church there is said to be a profession of faith concerning the truth of Christ’s flesh and blood in the Eucharist, issued against Berengar and his successors in a provincial council presided over by Maurilius, “of venerable memory,” over this holy see—these are the words of the formula. We have thought it superfluous to transcribe it here in full, since, through the favor of the most religious lord archbishop, it has already been published together with his learned writings.

2. The place which was once made illustrious by the tomb, first of Maurilius and afterward of William, cardinal of Stoteville, but which is now empty because circumstances have changed, is seen in the nave of the basilica. It was always held in veneration by the clergy of Rouen, and for this reason it was accustomed to be incensed on appointed days.

The reason for this practice is not to be sought only in the holiness of the bishop, who left such a reputation among posterity that the place was popularly called “Saint Maurilius’s tomb.” It is also to be sought in the ancient tradition by which our ancestors were persuaded that the high altar had formerly been established there, as is plainly indicated by the letter of the canons of Rouen to the same cardinal, a copy of which is preserved in the church archives.

**John Prévost.**

### (2)

“Of the holy Church of Rouen.”

This is a familiar manner of speaking among those devoted to religious antiquity. So many examples of it occur everywhere in the monuments of sacred buildings, especially those of one’s own church, that anyone who disapproves of it or is unaware of it would seem blind at midday.

Without wandering farther afield, witnesses beyond all exception may be produced for this truth.

Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, wrote in a charter concerning the possessions of the same church:

> Riculfus, venerable archbishop of Rouen, brought to our serenity a precept of our grandfather, the emperor Charles of blessed memory. It contained the statement that, at the petition of the holy-memory archbishop Remigius, his predecessor, he had assigned certain estates to the men, the canons of the church of his holy metropolitan see of Rouen, who serve the Lord in the church of Saint Mary, and so forth.

Richard, duke of Normandy, wrote in a charter concerning the monastery of Fécamp:

> Having summoned all the bishops of our diocese, namely Robert, archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, and also Ralph, bishop of the holy Church of Bayeux, and so forth.

Robert, duke of Normandy, surnamed “the Magnificent,” and Robert, archbishop of Rouen, wrote in a charter concerning the possessions of the same church:

> We have resolved to confirm the possessions of the holy Church of Rouen, which is the chief and metropolitan church of our kingdom, and so forth.

Philip I, king of the Franks, wrote in a charter of the archiepiscopal archive dated in the year of Christ 1091:

> I grant the abbey of Saint-Mellon of Pontoise to Lord William, archbishop of Rouen, and to all his successors, and I give it in fee, so that they may hold it from me and my successors forever, for the honor and exaltation of the holy Church of Rouen.

Louis XII, king, in letters granting two *modii* of salt for the benefit of the canons of Rouen, issued at Blois in the year of Christ 1506, wrote:

> At this time, by the will of God the Creator, our dearest kinsman George of Amboise, cardinal of the holy apostolic see and of the Roman Church, our most approved legate *a latere*, and the most faithful patrician and counsellor of our empire, presides over this holy Church of Rouen.

**Prévost.**

### (3)

“John of Avranches.”

The forms *Bajocacensis* and *Parisiacensis* are likewise found among writers of that age for *Bajocensis* and *Parisiensis*. Perhaps *Abrincatensis* is more correct, as in Orderic, *Ecclesiastical History*, books III, IV, VIII, and XII.

Concerning John, besides the testimonies brought above at the beginning of the book, see the same Orderic, books IV and V, and Matthew of Westminster under the years of Christ 1073 and 1079. I would add the anonymous monk of Saint-Ouen, were he not somewhat unfair to John.

**Prévost.**

### (4)

“After we shall see [something] dripping from the metropolitan see.”

A Council of Rouen held under Walter of Coutances, archbishop, in the year of Christ 1189 according to the old reckoning of Gaul, on 11 February, canon 1, says:

> Following the footsteps of our ancient Fathers, we decree first of all that all our suffragan churches should imitate the usage of this most holy metropolitan church in reading and singing.

**Prévost.**

### (5)

“Likewise the eleventh Council of Oletanum, canon 3.”

“According to the Council of Carthage.”

That is, the fourth council, canons 44 and 45, one of which concerns the tonsure and the other the dress. So that no one might interpret the meaning of the former according to his own judgment, the Fourth Council of Toledo expressly prescribed the form of the tonsure in canon 41:

> Let all clerics and readers, like the Levites and priests, have the whole upper part of the head shorn, leaving below only a circular crown; not as readers in the regions of Galicia appear to do up to the present, who, with long hair like laymen, shave only a small circle at the crown of the head. For this practice has until now been that of heretics in Spain. Therefore, in order to remove the scandal from the Church, this mark of disgrace must be taken away, and there must be one tonsure, or one form of dress, as is the custom throughout Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.

The agreement of almost all places and periods supports this institution, so it is not surprising that ecclesiastical laws have acted so severely against those who despise it.

The ancient decrees of our province bear witness to this, especially the Council of Rouen under Walter, canon 5:

> Priests and clerics shall have broad crowns and a decent surrounding of hair. Violators of this constitution shall be suspended from ecclesiastical benefices. Those who have no benefices but nevertheless grow their hair long shall lose the clerical privilege.

The new statutes of Peter of Collemieu, archbishop, who began to hold office in the year of Christ 1237, say:

> Since priests ought to differ from laymen in their tonsure and especially in their dress, and since we find many offending in these matters in our times, we order that all shall have a large crown and a high, well-rounded tonsure. Whoever henceforth is found culpable in these matters shall be punished more severely.

The Council held at Pont-Audemer in the year of Christ 1267 [under Archbishop Odo Rigaud] ordered clerics, even married clerics, to be compelled by three admonitions to wear the tonsure and dress appropriate to a cleric, and added:

> Finally, if, after the admonitions stated above, any clerics persist in apostasy from the tonsure and dress, and it happens that they are seized by secular judges for their excesses, having been apprehended in their crimes, we shall not order them to be released through ecclesiastical censures.

Another council held in the same place in the year of Christ 1279 enacted almost the same provisions (*Collection of the Councils of Rouen*, p. 276).

When discipline had finally grown lax, the canons of Rouen established the following concerning tonsure and dress in a general chapter held in the year of Christ 1311:

> Inasmuch as our church surpasses the others in nobility, so should its ecclesiastical servants be distinguished from the rest by greater decency. We decree that all our canons, chaplains, and choir clerics henceforth wear an appropriate tonsure, almost equal in size to the tonsure of the altar boys, whose ancient custom preserves propriety in this matter. None of those mentioned above shall henceforth wear sewn footwear.

They also decreed:

> We further decree that whoever is entered on the roster for Mass, the Gospel, or the Epistle shall have his tonsure and beard shaved; otherwise he may not minister at the altar in his office until he has been shaved. We decree that this statute, and all the others enacted in this general chapter, shall be counted among those statutes which every canon swears to observe at his reception.

For further material on the tonsure, see Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 4; Albinus Flaccus Alcuin, *On Divine Offices*; Amalarius, likewise, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 5; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 3; Rupert, abbot of Tuitiensis, *On Divine Offices*, book III, chapter 25; the Council of Agde, canon 20; Pope Stephen II in his responses at the villa of Quierzy, in the year of Christ 754, canon 18; the Council of Aachen, A.D. 816, book I, which concerns the institution of canons, chapter 1; the Council of Coyaca in the year of Christ 1050; the Council of Westminster in 1175; York in 1195; Oxford in 1222; London in 1237; Ravenna I in 1286, rubric 3; Ravenna III in 1314, rubric 10; Ravenna IV in 1317, rubric 4; and finally, in the age of the Fathers, the Council of Rouen in 1581, title “On Bishops and Chapters,” section 7, and title “On Parish Priests and the Offices of Others,” section 9; and the Council of Reims in 1385, title “On Clerics in General,” section 18.

**Prévost.**

### (6)

“They shall use neither variegated nor red garments.”

The same thing was prohibited by many decrees of councils. It is not clear, however, from where the red *heteromallon* in the canons’ winter copes took its origin, for it is contrary to this institution.

### (7)

“Since, following apostolic teaching, we shave the upper part of our head.”

In the earliest times shaving the head seems to have been less customary than shearing it, for Saint Jerome says on Ezekiel 44:

> It is clearly shown that we ought not to be like the priests and worshipers of Isis and Serapis, with shaven heads.

Saint Gregory gives the moral meaning of this practice in *Pastoral Rule*, book II, chapter 7, and book I of the *Register*, letter 24.

It is said to derive from apostolic teaching either because we wear the tonsure in imitation of Saint Peter, as the Roman Order states—and he was tonsured in such a way as to commemorate the Lord’s Passion, as is read in Bede, *History*, book V, chapter 22—or because Peter instituted it, as Gregory of Tours relates, *On Miracles*, book I, chapter 28; as does the Council of Tribur, canon 20; and *The Jewel of the Soul*, book I, chapter 195.

### (8)

“Through the crown of hair which we wear on the lower part.”

It is therefore clear that clerics once customarily wore a circle of hair in the form of a crown, just as the Franciscans wear it today.

The same is prescribed in the Synod of Évreux of 1576, chapter 3, “On the Life and Decency of Parish Priests and Other Ecclesiastics,” article 3, and in the Rouen *Ritual or Manual*, published in 1651, part I, p. 383, in these words:

> Clerics, mindful of their profession, shall religiously wear on their heads the sign of the Lord’s crown and shall never abandon it. Those who act otherwise, as deserters from the ecclesiastical militia and despisers of the sacred canons, shall be subjected to strict correction and expelled disgracefully from ecclesiastical assemblies. The lower part of the hair shall likewise be cut in the form of a crown, so that the eyes and ears remain exposed.

The same work, p. 409.

### (9)

“We shave the beard.”

For the shaving of the beard, see the Roman Order and the Rouen *Ritual* in the same place.

### (10)

“Four times by night and by day.”

This clearly alludes to what we read in the Second Book of Esdras, chapter 9:

> They read in the book of the Law of the Lord their God four times in the day, and four times they confessed.

But the statement that they sang four times during the night is found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the edition of the Septuagint translators nor in the Latin Vulgate. Therefore our John seems to have borrowed this addition from Amalarius, book IV of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 3, and Amalarius took it from Bede on Esdras, whom he cites there.

### (11)

“We sing five psalms, but join them by a threefold glorification of the Holy Trinity.”

By the five psalms with a threefold glorification, understand the psalm *Deus in nomine* and the four groups, or divisions, of eight verses of the psalm *Beati immaculati*. These divisions we still sing under a double glorification, in agreement with *The Jewel of the Soul*, book II, chapters 60 and 61.

This also appears to be the practice in the Rouen Psalter of 1507; in another Psalter printed at Paris in 1540 by François Regnault; in the Lisieux Diurnal of 1542; in the Paris Breviary of 1557; and in the Avranches Breviary of 1592.

Perhaps at that time the ferial psalms were not recited at Prime in the Church of Rouen, as seems to be the case in the Paris and Avranches Breviaries mentioned above; otherwise six, not five, would have to be counted.

### (12)

“To these we add the Catholic faith expounded by Saint Athanasius.”

The Creed of Saint Athanasius was formerly sung in the Church of Rouen throughout the entire year, without a single day excepted, as seems to be shown in a manuscript ordinal for the use of the Church of Rouen from the library of the most distinguished and learned man, Lord Emeric Bigot. *The Jewel of the Soul*, book II, chapter 59, likewise agrees, in these words:

> The Church repeats the Faith, *Quicumque vult*, daily at Prime—the faith which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, composed at the request of the emperor Theodosius.

Likewise, in the Rouen Breviary printed in 1491, it is said throughout the entire year, even on ferial days. It is also found in the Rouen Psalters of 1507 and 1586, in the Lisieux Diurnal of 1542, in the Rouen Breviary published under Cardinal Charles of Bourbon, archbishop of Rouen, in 1578, and, as the Carthusian Diurnal states, it is read daily at Prime. It is also found in the aforementioned Paris and Avranches Breviaries; this Creed was assigned by Lord François de Harlay I in the Rouen Breviary to Sundays of the temporal cycle.

### (13)

“But the third.”

Isidore offers another explanation of the offices of Terce, Sext, and None in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 19:

> Daniel and the Three Children devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications, namely so that, from the rising of day until the time of prayer, three extended hours might declare to us reverence for the Trinity.

**Prévost.**

### (14)

“Two sets of three psalms.”

Here understand the same thing as above: that is, six divisions of this psalm, each division consisting of eight verses.

### (15)

“With the Lord’s Prayer, prayers, and the psalm *Miserere mei Deus*, kneeling.”

These provisions are found in the Rouen Breviary published in 1491; in the Rouen Psalters of 1507 and 1586; in the Rouen Breviary of 1578; in the Lisieux Diurnal of 1542; in the Paris, Avranches, and Fontevrault Breviaries of the year 1586; and in the Carthusian Diurnal.

Nevertheless, these practices are not observed in the Church of Rouen except on the ferial days of Advent, Lent, the Ember Seasons, and the fast. On those days the psalm *Miserere* is not said except at Vespers.

### (16)

“Night offices follow, in which Vespers occur.”

It is established, especially from Saint Jerome’s letter to Leta, that among the ancients Vespers belonged to the night and were customarily recited at its beginning. He says:

> Let her become accustomed, when the lamp has been lit, to offer the evening sacrifice.

Isidore, book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter “On Offices,” says:

> The evening office belongs to the beginning of the night.

The Council of Mérida, canon 2, says:

> In the evening, after the light has been offered, the evening office is said.

Many other Greek and Latin writers testify to the same, as Cardinal Bona discusses in *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 10, section 5.

Therefore the evening office was called *lucernarium* by the First Council of Toledo, canon 9; by Saint Basil, in chapter 29 of *On the Holy Spirit*, it was called the *lucernaria*, “thanksgiving”; and by Cassian, book III of *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 3, the “hour of the lamps.”

Although Saint Benedict wished Vespers to be celebrated before night in chapter 41 of his Rule, and Amalarius testifies that, already in his time, it was customary for the evening office to be celebrated before sunset in *On the Order of the Antiphons*, chapter 6, nevertheless Hugo of Saint-Victor, in book II of *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 5, assigned it to the beginning of night, when we go to sleep. He was later than our John.

### (17)

“The hymn of Saint Mary.”

By the hymn of Saint Mary understand the canticle *Magnificat*. Amalarius uses the expression in this sense for the same canticle in book IV, chapter 7, concerning the evening assembly.

### (18)

“Incense is offered upon the altar.”

Amalarius likewise says in the same place:

> Let the high priest, who represents Aaron in the Church, understand that he ought to offer incense to the Lord upon the altar; after this follows the hymn of Saint Mary.

William Durand also says this in *The Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book V, chapter 9, concerning Vespers.

The Rouen *Ritual* of 1651, part I, p. 392, likewise states:

> According to the custom of the cathedral church, the altar is incensed outside Mass by the celebrant wearing a cope, kneeling, with three swings and a kiss, in every office except the simple and ferial office, at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*. Thereafter the celebrant and choir are incensed by the acolyte. In a triple office it is also incensed at the hymn *Te Deum* by the same celebrant; and before the first reading of the homily by the deacon; and on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, before the eighth and also the ninth reading, by those who are to read, likewise wearing copes and kneeling.

This rite is observed in the cathedral church and in very many parish churches of the city of Rouen.

### (19)

“With the Lord’s Prayer and prayers, except on feasts.”

This was likewise the practice among the Carthusians and in the ancient Breviaries and Psalters of the Church of Rouen, as well as those of Lisieux, Paris, and Avranches.

Now, however, as we noted above, the prayers are said only on the ferial days of Advent and Lent and on fast days.

### (20)

“Since after Vespers.”

From this passage it appears that in John’s time Compline was customarily performed separately from the evening office. It would be desirable for this practice of genuine antiquity to be restored in collegiate churches and at least in the city churches.

**Prévost.**

### (21)

“The hymn of the righteous Simeon.”

That is, the canticle *Nunc dimittis*. Interpreters of the sacred rites sometimes use “hymn” for “canticle,” as we explained above. Understand the expression “the hymn of Zechariah” in the same way.

### (22)

“Fortifying ourselves with the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and confession.”

Except on triple and double feasts and during octaves.

### (23)

“Preceded by a reading concerning the examples of the holy Fathers.”

The same practice is found in the manuscript Rouen Ordinal throughout Lent. Saint Benedict likewise prescribes it in chapter 42 of his Rule, and the monks of Saint Benedict religiously observe it, for the reading is taken either from their deeds or from their works.

### (24)

“We ought to rise at midnight to confess to the Lord.”

Thus Saint Jerome writes in the epitaph of Saint Paula:

> In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours; in the evening and at midnight, they sang the Psalter in order.

Saint Athanasius likewise says in *On Virginity*:

> Rise at midnight and praise the Lord your God.

So too Saint Augustine, sermon 55 *On Time*:

> I ask you to rise earlier for the vigils.

See also Saint Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 22, concerning vigils; Radulfus, dean of Tongeren, *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 14; and other interpreters of the divine offices.

### (25)

“We invoke the Helper; and after the hymn has been said.”

This seems to indicate that immediately after the verse *Deus in adjutorium* the hymn is said, while the invitatory customarily used in the ferial office is omitted. If this is indeed the meaning, I do not understand the reason for the practice.

Durand writes in *The Rationale*, book V, chapter 3, and book VI, chapter 72, that the invitatory is not omitted except in the Office of Epiphany, during the three days before Easter, and in the Office of the Dead when the corpse is not present. In this he follows the ancient writers on the sacred offices: the Roman Order, Alcuin *On the Lord’s Supper*, Amalarius, book IV, chapter 21, and Honorius, book III of *The Jewel of the Soul*, chapter 88.

### (26)

“We sing twelve psalms.”

The Church of Rouen observes this on ferial days outside the Easter season. On Sundays, however, twelve psalms are sung at the first nocturn, and the verse *Gloria Patri* is appended to each, although in our John four psalms are joined under one glorification. William Durand agrees with this in *The Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book V, chapter 3.

### (27)

“Through the Matins office.”

Understand “Lauds,” for interpreters of the divine offices often call it by that name. Radulfus of Tongeren, proposition 14, says:

> They call the office which we call Lauds the Matins office.

In our author, however, the meaning of this word is ambiguous. In the order for Easter Day he understands the Matins office as Nocturns:

> Let two cantors wearing copes direct the Matins office. Let the invitatory be sung by four, and so forth.

After Matins he distinguishes Lauds from the Matins office. At the beginning of the work, however, he uses “Matins office” for Lauds, clearly separating it from Nocturns and from all the other Hours, which he lists individually there.

This meaning, which is the most proper in the judgment of the most eminent Cardinal Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 5, section 1, and which accords with the understanding of the ancients, is retained here.

### (28)

“With the Lord’s Prayer and prayers.”

This was also observed in the Church of Rouen sixty years ago, as is clear from the Breviaries of 1491 and 1578 and the Rouen Psalters of 1507 and 1586. It was formerly recited likewise in the Churches of Paris, Lisieux, and Avranches, as is evident from the Lisieux Diurnal of 1542 and the ancient Paris and Avranches Breviaries.

(29) **When the signal is sounded.** The Council of Aachen, canon 31: “For as soon as the signal has been heard, let everyone hasten to assemble in the church, which they shall enter not pompously, dishonestly, or disorderly, but with reverence and fear of God.” See the epilogue of the same council, canon 45. PR.

(30) **Where, standing reverently, they do not move about this way or that, nor does anyone engage in conversation.** Here clerics should observe with what modesty they ought to stand in the church of God. Thus the Council of Aachen, held in 816, canon 131, decrees: “Let all, therefore, discipline their hearing and tongue alike, refraining from idle conversations: standing in the church with fear and reverence, let them either pray, sing, or listen.” And Grodogangus, bishop of Metz, in the *Rule for Canons*, chapter 26: “As soon as the signal has been heard, let all the canons hasten to the church; and let them enter it not pompously, dishonestly, or disorderly, but with fear of God; nor, except for the infirm, should they carry staffs or cudgels in the choir, but they must stand and sing psalms there reverently.” He later complains that clerics, involving themselves in secular affairs, seemed unfit to perform the divine office [Col. 0070D]: “As soon as they have entered the church to perform the divine office, they appear so exhausted that they can neither devote themselves to prayer nor stand for singing psalms; instead, sitting down, they customarily persist not in divine but in frivolous conversation.”

The ancient statutes of the chapter of the cathedral church of Paris likewise state: “There let them stand simply and upright; let them beware of conversation, loud laughter, and laughter; let them sing psalms solemnly and modestly before God, remembering that their conduct will be an example to the other, junior ministers.” The Council of Basel, session 21, §§ 3, 4, and 6, lays down many further provisions concerning psalmody and the worship of God. Concerning conversation and wandering about in church, see the Council of Rouen held in 1522 under George II of Amboise, title 1; the Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, p. 387, agrees with it [Col. 0071A]:

“Within the choir there must be no conversations; no one should disturb the divine service by laughter or any other disorderly or insufficiently modest behavior; no one should sleep to the scandal of the others, or read letters or other writings; no one should privately recite the office or other prayers,” etc.

(31) **And at the *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”), turning toward the altar and bowing.** The Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, p. 388, likewise prescribes this. It is to be understood, however, that they rise at the verses *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”) and *Sicut erat* (“As it was”) at the beginning of the hours, at the end of the invitatory, psalms, and canticles, and at the same verse *Gloria Patri* at the end of the responsories. This is observed in part in the cathedral church: everyone stands, or rises, whenever *Gloria Patri* is sung [Col. 0071B]; only those in the lowest stall turn toward the altar, whereas in very many parish churches of the city and diocese everyone turns and bows.

(32) **They shall not leave the choir: the senior members without the dean’s permission, the junior members without the cantor’s.** The Rouen Ritual likewise states: “As long as the office is being celebrated, no one shall presume to leave the choir except for the sake of the office or because of pressing necessity.” Now, in the cathedral church, any canon may leave at will, without the order of the dean or cantor, after the recitation of the first psalm; but he thereby forfeits almost all the other distributions—apart from the bread which he receives in this way at Matins—unless he returns to the choir before the office is completed.

(33) **Let him bow before and behind.** The Rouen Ritual of 1651 likewise says: “They bow deeply toward the altar [Col. 0071C] and make reverence before and behind.” Similarly, in the old order for receiving a canon of the cathedral church of Paris: “Having made the required bows toward the east and then toward the west.” In the cathedral church of Rouen, however, reverence is made toward the altar and toward the choir on the opposite side. I think this should be understood as follows: “before and behind the altar,” namely, before the crucifix situated in the nave, or before the dean who used to stand near the door, as is customary on triple feasts. For this is how the monks of Grandmont observe this bow, which is also very frequently found in the more ancient customs of the monastery of Cluny. *Spicilegium*, vol. IV.

(34) **Except on the days of the Nativity of the Lord and Pentecost.** At those times the seasonal antiphon was taken from the Easter season, as appears in the Rouen breviaries of 1491 and 1578 and the psalters of 1507 and 1586, in which we read:

“Note that throughout the whole year, at *Quicunque* (‘Whoever’), some antiphon from those written above is said, except during the Easter season.”

And in the Lexovian Diurnal of 1542:

“During the Easter season, after the psalms and *Quicunque*, the antiphon is *Alleluia*.”

For this does not concern the *Quicunque* Creed, which according to the Rouen Ordinary manuscript and these breviaries and psalters is used throughout the year, even on weekdays.

(35) **With the chapter *Domine miserere* (“Lord, have mercy”) following, on weekdays.** At present, on weekdays throughout the year, the chapter *Pacem et veritatem* (“Peace and truth”) is said.

(36) **After confession has been made, with the prayers.** The prayers are not said, nor is confession made, on triple or double feasts, or during octaves.

(37) **When Prime has ended, let the brothers assemble in the chapter house.** The canonical rule of Saint Grodogangus, bishop of Metz, concerning Prime states:

“When this has been completed, they assemble daily in the chapter house; and, for their benefit, with God’s help, we have made this provision: each day they shall reread some chapter, except on Sunday, Wednesday, Friday, and the solemnities of the saints, when they shall read treatises, other homilies, or something that may edify those listening, etc. And the bishop, archdeacon, or whoever appears to preside in their place shall there command whatever must be commanded, correct whatever must be corrected, and diligently arrange whatever must be done. After the reading, the age of the month and of the moon [Col. 0072B], and the saints whose feasts the following day will celebrate, are recited, etc.”

The Council of Aachen, held in A.D. 816, book I, chapter 123, *On the Institution of Canons*: “Let them come daily to the conference, where they shall read through this institution and lessons from the other sacred Scriptures, ask pardon for their offenses, and receive a sentence proportionate to the offense committed; there they shall also deliberate concerning the common progress and usefulness of the Church.”

The customs of the Church of Rouen, written in the time of Richard de Coutances, dean, about four hundred years ago from an old codex of the same church, state:

“In the chapter house, when the reading has ended as appropriate, the table must be read; it must be arranged and written according to the requirements of the time and as suits the individual dignities and orders of the canons and choir servants, and afterward it must not be altered. Then the reckoning is usually made, and at that time and place canonical excuses are received or rejected; there also, if anything needs to be done, dispensations or favors are to be granted either by the dean or by the hebdomadary. After this, the complaints and offenses of the day and of the preceding hours are usually recited and punished there.

“Likewise, every Friday all the canons must assemble in the chapter house at the chapter hour, and when the foregoing matters have been completed, the affairs of the Church must be discussed there. The canons must not absent themselves or impede the discussion until the business has been concluded, unless they have received permission from the dean, or from the hebdomadary if the dean happens to be absent. Honor, propriety, and the Church’s advantage must be observed there, without deceit, partiality, injury to fidelity, or violation of conscience. Whoever does not come, or leaves without permission, shall forfeit one day’s bread.” PR.

The ancient statutes of the Church of Paris likewise state:

“From there they proceed to the chapter house, where, after the deeds of the saints and the diptychs of the dead have been read, prayers are made for their repose. Then, after God’s help has been requested three times, a verse with its collect is added, and the reader, having received the blessing, reads the canon or chapter of the rule, which all listen to with the greatest reverence while seated; and, after once again receiving the blessing from the hebdomadary, they depart . . . Every Friday the chapter shall hear the choir’s deficiencies during the week; the delinquents shall be examined and the errors corrected.”

Rouen Ordinary manuscript from the Bigot Library, p. 5:

“Then in the chapter house, and there let a reading from the Martyrology be heard. Verse: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* Prayer: *Sancta Maria* (“Holy Mary”), etc. *Per Dominum* (“Through the Lord”). Amen. *Deus in adjutorium* (“O God, [come] to [my] help”) is said three times: *Gloria Patri, Sicut erat* (“Glory to the Father; as it was”), *Kyrie eleison. Christe eleison. Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy”). *Pater noster* (“Our Father”). *Et ne nos* (“And lead us not”). *Et veniat super* (“And let [it] come upon [us]”). *Et respice in servos* (“And look upon [your] servants”). *Et sit splendor* (“And let the brightness be”). Let us pray: *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus dirige* (“Almighty everlasting God, direct [us]”). *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord [be] with you”). *Benedicamus* (“Let us bless [the Lord]”). Then let the death notice be read, if there is one, and let *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”) and the appropriate prayers be said there, as they are recorded in the Obituary. When this has been completed, let the boy say: *Jube, domne, benedicere* (“Command, lord, [me] to receive a blessing”). Blessing: *May almighty God direct us in the way of his commandments.* Amen. Let a reading from the sermons on the life of clerics follow.”

(38) **So that no feast of a saint to be celebrated on the following day may be omitted.** The Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, pp. 402 and 439, says the same. Grodogangus likewise states in the *Rule for Canons*, chapter 18, concerning Prime:

“We have established that every day all the clerics are to come to the chapter house, so that the soul may hear the word of God; and the bishop or archdeacon shall there command whatever must be commanded, correct whatever must be corrected, and diligently arrange whatever must be done. After the reading, the age of the month and of the moon, whose feasts the following day will celebrate, are recited.”

And Peter of Honestis, in the *Rule for Canons*:

“When the brothers assemble in the chapter house in the morning after Prime, the reader, having asked for the blessing, shall announce in the customary manner the end of the month, the age of the moon, the weekday of the following day, and the feasts.”

It may therefore seem strange that in certain churches where the Martyrology is read, the feast of that same day is announced, since, after First Vespers, Matins, Lauds, and Prime have been sung, the office has already been completed for the greater part.

(39) **A reading from the canonical rule.** Namely, that of Grodogangus, bishop of Metz, or of the Council of Aachen.

(40) **Or a pastoral work.** That is, Saint Gregory the Pope’s *Book of Pastoral Care* addressed to John, bishop of the city of Ravenna.

(41) **Or some regular book.** Here the subject is the *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, the *Life of Clerics*, published after the Rouen Martyrology, or their sermons. For in the cathedral Ordinary manuscript we read: “And let there be a reading from the sermons on the *Life of Clerics*”; sometimes: “Let the remainder of the exposition,” that is, the homily, “be read” [Col. 0073D].

(42) **On feasts, all of them.** On the more solemn feasts all the bells are rung; on double and semidouble feasts only three are rung.

(43) **Two acolytes: one to sing the Gradual and carry the candlestick, the other to sing the Alleluia and carry the thurible.** The Rouen Ritual of 1651, p. 399, says the same. I do not know why some disapprove of this rite, since it is found in our statutes. It is also clear from this that formerly, on weekdays, there was only one candle-bearer at the celebration of Mass in the Church of Rouen; now there are two throughout the entire year.

(44) **After the psalm has been said.** That is, a verse taken from the psalms [Col. 0074A]; for Honorius testifies as follows in book I of the *Gemma animae*, chapter 87:

“Pope Celestine instituted that psalms should be sung at the entrance of the Mass, from which Pope Gregory composed the introit antiphons by setting them to melody. Hence even now the first verse of that same psalm is sung, although formerly the whole psalm was sung at the entrance.”

(45) **The candle-bearer.** Among the Greeks he is called an acolyte, as Alcuin testifies in the chapter *On the Tonsure of Clerics*, as does Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 10; likewise Ivo of Chartres, sermon 2, *On the Life of Those to Be Ordained*. See also *Gemma animae*, book I, *On the Ancient Rite of Mass*, chapter 178.

(46) **The priest shall kiss the deacon and subdeacon.** At present he merely bows to them during the confession and does not kiss them. The ancient rite of kissing the ministers is nevertheless well attested by the Roman Order in the four orders of the Mass; Amalarius, book III, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5; Honorius, book I of the *Gemma animae*, chapter 7; and Hugh of Saint-Victor, *Ecclesiastical Mirror*, chapter 7. The reason, I think, is that, in the words of Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 10, they considered it impious to approach the sacrifice of peace without peace; therefore, so that they might approach it more prepared and fit, they preceded it with a sign of reconciliation. This is indicated by the Missal of the Church of Salisbury, published at Paris in 1555, which states:

“Then he kisses the deacon and subdeacon, saying: ‘Receive the kiss of peace and love, so that you may be fit to perform the divine offices at the holy altar.’”

(47) **The priest and the other ministers shall pray behind the altar, etc.** These practices are not part of the present usage of the Church of Rouen.

(48) **The deacon shall stand after him, following the same route, until he indicates that he should sit.** This was prescribed by the Council of Laodicea, canon 20, and by the Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, p. 398. While the presbyter is standing, neither the deacon nor the subdeacon should presume to sit contrary to the sacred canons; rather, the seated presbyter should indicate to them that they may sit.

(49) **He shows that he is Christ’s vicar.** Amalarius gives the same interpretation in book III, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5:

“The entrance of the bishop at Mass, since he is Christ’s vicar, recalls Christ’s coming to our memory.”

And in chapter 10, *On the Bishop’s Seat*:

“Since the bishop is Christ’s vicar in all the matters mentioned above, he ought also here, by enthroning himself, to recall to us Christ’s ascension and throne” [Col. 0074D].

Thus the priests are called Christ’s vicars by Pope Hormisdas, letter 60. PR.

(50) **They shall hold the candlesticks from south to north.** Alcuin says similarly in *On the Celebration of Mass*:

“When the cantor begins *Kyrie eleison* (‘Lord, have mercy’), the acolyte places the candles in order from the southern side toward the north, signifying by this action that the almighty Lord has had mercy on the world in the south and in the north.”

At present, however, they are placed toward the east in the Church of Rouen, except during the Gospel.

(51) **When the *Kyrie* has begun, the candles are set down.** The various orders and Amalarius, book III, chapter 7, say the same. PR.

The Rouen Ritual likewise, p. 444.

(52) **Seven candlesticks.** We are surprised that this number of seven candle-bearers, taken from the Apocalypse—for which see the Roman Order—has fallen out of use among us at pontifical Masses, where an equal number of deacons and subdeacons continues to be maintained. That it was formerly in use is clearly established by the old *Pontifical Book*, in these words:

“On the day of the bishop’s ordination, let Prime be sung and rung with great solemnity. After it, let them go to the chapter house, where the dean, archdeacon, cantor, and chancellor shall appoint the ministers who must proceed, as is customary on the greater feasts: namely, two acolytes with thuribles, two subdeacons with crosses, seven acolytes with candlesticks and candles, seven subdeacons with the Gospel books, seven deacons with the holy relics, twelve presbyters vested in chasubles, etc.” PR.

Concerning the number of seven acolytes at pontifical Masses, see the Rouen Ritual published in 1651, part I, p. 444. The *Gemma animae*, book I, chapter 4, likewise states:

“After the bells have sounded, the vested pontiff proceeds, preceded by seven acolytes with lights.”

The Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, p. 502, judges that this rite should be restored.

(53) **When the subdeacon begins the Epistle, the priest shall sit beside the altar.** This is also done today among the Carthusians; there the celebrant listens to the Epistle, Gradual, Alleluia, and Gospel. From this it is clear that the custom was introduced only recently whereby the celebrating priest is required to read what is read by the deacon or subdeacon, or what is sung by the choir.

(54) **The subdeacon shall remain in the choir except during the time of his ministry.** Among the Carthusian monks this is observed not only by the subdeacon but also by the deacon. As soon as he is not required for the ministry at the altar, he returns to his place in the choir and sings the office of the Mass with the others.

(55) **They follow the Epistle, responsory, tract, or Alleluia.** By “responsory” understand the Gradual, so called by John and other interpreters of the divine offices because it responds to the Epistle.

(56) **By means of ivory tablets.** Concerning these tablets, see Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book III, chapter 16. PR.

(57) **Bishops and abbots ought to lay down their staffs.** Amalarius teaches the same in book III, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18:

“Up to this office we were supported by staffs; now, since servants ought to stand before the Lord, we stand humbly, laying down our staffs from our hands.”

This is observed by the cantor of the cathedral church of Rouen.

(58) **The subdeacon, having removed his chasuble, shall read the Epistle.** Concerning this chasuble, which we call the folded chasuble (*planeta plicata*), the Rouen Ordinary manuscript, p. 3, states:

“On the Sundays of Advent and on the Sundays from Septuagesima to Easter, let the deacon and subdeacon be in chasubles at Mass; at the Epistle the subdeacon shall remove his chasuble, and after the Epistle has been read he shall put it on again. At the Gospel the deacon shall remove his chasuble and drape it over his left shoulder in the manner of a stole, and shall remain thus until the end of Mass.”

Amalarius likewise states in book III, chapter 15:

“The ministers remove their chasubles when they assume the office of reader or cantor” [Col. 0076A].

See also *Gemma animae*, book I, chapter 232. Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Special Observances of the Mass*, book III, chapter 9, says:

“On the days of Advent and Lent the ministers do not use such garments—namely, the dalmatic and tunic—but chasubles. Nevertheless, when they assume their proper office, they remove their chasubles, because in their proper office—that is, in reading the Epistle or Gospel—they represent those who were sent by the Lord to preach. The chasuble signifies works of such a kind as cannot be observed on a journey; for by its breadth it signifies the breadth of charity. This is required in speaking, because it is wrapped around the neck; in working, because it is folded over both arms; in thinking, because it covers the breast; and in bearing the burdens of others, because it encircles the shoulders.”

These practices are observed in the cathedral church of Rouen on the Sundays of Advent and Lent, except Palm Sunday, on which the ministers use the dalmatic and tunic, as prescribed in the Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, pp. 451 and 466, and in the Rouen Missal of 1668, *On the Rite of Celebrating Mass*.

(59) **The deacon puts on the chasuble.** The chasuble was not merely the distinctive garment of deacons and subdeacons in the ministry at the altar; formerly it was also the common vestment of all clerics, as Amalarius testifies in book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, *On the Chasuble*:

“The chasuble, which generally pertains to all clerics, ought to signify works that pertain to all.”

Likewise, the Roman Order for Maundy Thursday states:

“Immediately two acolytes, vested in black chasubles, shall begin to strip the altars until Vespers is finished; afterward they shall be removed.”

Ivo of Chartres agrees in his book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, sermon *On the Meanings of Priestly Vestments*.

(60) **After incensing the altar.** The altar is not incensed immediately before the reading of the Gospel, nor is a cushion carried by the subdeacon before the deacon for reading the Gospel, although the same practice is found in William Durand, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book IV, chapter 24, *On the Gospel*.

(61) **Let him place it upon the left shoulder.** That is, above the left side of the breast. The same is read in Amalarius, book III, chapter 18:

“The deacon carries the Gospel on his left arm,” etc.

(62) **With the candle-bearer and thurible-bearer preceding him, in procession.** That is, in the manner of a procession. Formerly, however—as we have read above—there was only one candle-bearer at weekday Mass in the Church of Rouen; a trace of this seems to remain in our Ritual, part I, p. 444.

(63) **When it has been read, let the candlesticks be extinguished.** Amalarius teaches the same in book III, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18:

“After the Gospel has been returned to its place following the reading, the candles are extinguished, because when the preaching of the Gospel has ended, the Law and the Prophets will cease.”

William Durand agrees with Amalarius, *Rationale*, book IV, chapter 24, as does the following exposition of the Mass, drawn from a Bigot manuscript [Col. 0077A]. At present, however, they remain lit throughout the entire office of the Mass; when it has ended, the celebrant and ministers withdraw to the sacristy, preceded by two candle-bearers with burning candles.

(64) **Let incense be offered to the priest in the thurible.** That is, let him be incensed; this is not to be understood of the incensing of the altar.

(65) **When it has ended, let the verse follow.** The Ordinary of the metropolitan church states:

“It has been decreed in the Church of Rouen that throughout the year the verses of the offertories are to be sung in their proper order, and it has been commanded under anathema that they are not to be omitted through the negligence of the clergy, unless the priest is ready for *Per omnia* (“Through all”).”

(66) **On feasts, let the cantor carry water covered with a cloth to the deacon.** Alcuin teaches the same in *On the Divine Offices*:

“Like Levites, who provided everything necessary for the tabernacle, the cantors fetch water at the fountain and keep it covered until the time of the sacrifice; thus they offer it clean.”

The *Gemma animae* likewise says concerning the ancient rite of Mass, book I, chapter 38, *On Cantors*:

“One cantor offers the oblation with the fan and the wine with the flask; another supplies the water to be mixed with the wine.”

This is not the present usage.

(67) **On other days, let the acolyte minister it.** In our diocese it is offered by an acolyte both on weekdays and Sundays and on feast days.

(68) **Let the priest arrange the oblation in this manner.** The *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 10, states:

“Once the oblation has been placed on the corporal, let the chalice be placed on the right side of the oblation, as though it were about to receive the Lord’s blood, which we believe flowed from the Lord’s side.”

(69) **Let him offer incense over it.** According to the decree of the Council of Rouen under John I, archbishop of Rouen, chapter 1:

“We have decreed that at the time when the Gospel is read, and after the Offertory has been completed, incense shall be placed over the oblation, signifying the death of our Redeemer.”

In the cathedral church, after the oblations and altar have been incensed, and the priest also incensed, the deacon carries the thurible around the altar. After incensing the tombs of the kings and the altar of Saint Mary, he returns the thurible to the acolyte, who incenses neither the clergy nor the people.

(70) **But the subdeacon, if there is one, shall give it to the acolyte.** The Roman Order says similarly, *On the Office of the Mass*:

“When the Canon begins, the acolyte comes with a linen cloth under his arm, tied around his neck, holding the paten before his breast on the right side until the middle of the Canon.”

And the *Gemma animae*, *On the Ancient Rite of Mass*, chapter 48:

“During the Canon the acolyte holds the covered paten, which here the subdeacon carries.”

The Church of Paris observes this rite; in the Church of Rouen, however, the subdeacon, not the acolyte, holds the paten.

(71) **The consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.** Among liturgical writers, the term “consecration” is understood in two ways: either as the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, or, to speak mystically, as the commingling itself of the body and blood.

Saint Ambrose is to be understood in the former sense in book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4, when he says:

“How can what is bread be the body of Christ? By consecration. By what words, then, and by whose utterances is the consecration accomplished? By those of the Lord Jesus.”

And shortly afterward:

“It was not Christ’s body before the consecration; but after the consecration I tell you that it is already Christ’s body.”

The words of Saint Laurence in book I of Ambrose’s *Offices*, chapter 41, refer to the latter sense, which is at issue here:

“To whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood, to whom the fellowship of completing the sacraments.”

Thus this passage, and the acts of Saint Laurence, should consistently be read from the ancient manuscripts as “the consecration of the blood,” not “the administration of the blood,” as the more recent editions incorrectly have it. For the consecration of the Lord’s blood—that is, the commingling of part of the oblation in the chalice—was entrusted to the deacon’s custody and ministry. The office is very appropriately called there “the fellowship of completing the sacraments.” PR.

The Council of Aachen, held in A.D. 816, p. 335 of Sirmond’s edition, chapter 7, likewise states:

“Without them the priest bears the name but not the office; for just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of the sacrament belongs to the minister,” etc.

Isidore says the same in book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 8.

(72) **Let the oblation touch the four parts of the chalice.** The same is found in Ivo of Chartres, letter 233, and in the Roman Order, in the ancient order of the Mass:

“The pontiff touches the chalice from the side, making two crosses.”

Three crosses are now formed; the commentators on the rubrics of the Missal warn, however, that care must be taken lest the host touch the lip of the chalice and fragments be made from it. Bartholomew Gavantus is among those who give this warning there.

(73) **When the prayer has ended, let both raise the chalice, and let them set it down and cover it together.** Today the deacon does not raise the chalice, but merely uncovers it and covers it again after the elevation. Formerly the chalice was raised and lowered by the priest and deacon together; in fact, it was not the chalice alone but also the host placed on the paten above the chalice, as is clear from Ivo of Chartres, letter 233.

Observe, however, that our author says nothing about the separate elevation of Christ’s body and blood, as is done today immediately after the bread and wine have been consecrated, so that they may be adored by the surrounding people. I do not think this rite is very ancient, since it is found neither in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory, nor in the printed sacramentaries, nor in Pamelius, nor in the ancient Roman Orders, nor in Alcuin, Amalarius, Walafrid, or Rabanus, nor in the exposition of the Mass published below, nor in the *Micrologus*, which mentions the elevation of the body made together with the chalice before the Lord’s Prayer is recited.

(74) **The deacon shall kiss the altar, then the priest’s right shoulder.** These practices are not observed in the Church of Rouen.

(75) **The subdeacon to the deacon.** The Church of Rouen retains this rite, but the *Gemma animae*, book I, chapter 48, states:

“During the Canon the acolyte holds the covered paten, which here the subdeacon carries; the subdeacon gives it to the archdeacon, who, after kissing it, hands it to one of the deacons to hold and to break the Lord’s body upon it.”

(76) **He shall communicate another with himself, the deacon and the subdeacon.** For the deacon, subdeacon, and people formerly received Communion from the same host, as is demonstrated below.

(77) **But if it is not necessary, let the priest or one of the ministers receive the third part.** Those who formerly ministered at the sacred altars were considered worthy to participate in this sacrament. As for the praise of the Council of Toledo, our John seems here to have suffered a lapse of memory: this prohibition is found not in the Council of Toledo but in the Third Council of Braga.

(78) **In the greatest necessity, for fear of the shedding of Christ’s blood.** A precaution worthy of the religious spirit of the age of Maurilius, but the practice of intinction was less approved. The *Micrologus*, chapter 19, warns that it should be avoided, and shortly afterward the Council of Clermont, A.D. 1095, abolished it by decreeing that the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood should be received separately. That abuse continued longer among the English, for at the Council of Westminster, A.D. 1175, it was forbidden to give anyone an intincted Eucharist as though it were a completion of Communion. PR.

(79) **Let him first kiss each one, etc.** The Roman Order, *On the Office of the Mass*, and the old manuscript Benedictional of the library of the cathedral church of Rouen agree with this passage:

“Therefore the presbyters and deacons, kissing the bishop, shall receive Christ’s body from him in their hands; but the subdeacons, kissing the bishop’s hand, shall receive Christ’s body from him in their mouths.”

(80) **Let him take one part for himself and give part to the subdeacon.** The Roman Order and the old manuscript Benedictional cited above likewise state:

“The deacon himself, holding the chalice and the tube, shall stand before the bishop until he has taken from the blood and body of Christ as much as he wishes; then he shall entrust the chalice and tube to the subdeacon. The same deacon must take the greatest care that nothing of the blood or body of Christ remains in the chalice or paten.”

These practices, and what follows, are not in use in the Church of Rouen.

(81) **From him one of the canons shall receive the peace, which he shall distribute among the senior members in both choirs, etc.** Formerly the kiss of peace was given at the end of the sacrifice, so that it might be evident that the people had given their assent to everything carried out in the sacred mysteries and celebrated in the Church. For the Roman Order, *On the Office of the Mass*, reads:

“When the blessing has been completed”—namely, the episcopal blessing after *Da propitius pacem* (“Graciously grant peace”)—“the priest comes and receives peace from the bishop, to offer the same to the others.”

Alcuin likewise states in *On the Divine Offices*, under the heading *On the Celebration of Mass*:

“Having therefore prayed for peace, the whole Church, beginning with the priest, gives one another the kiss of peace, so that, united in true peace, they may become a dwelling place for God.”
