And in his book *On the Meaning of Vestments*:

“In the church, kisses are exchanged by those persons who cannot compel anyone to awaken the least impulse of lustful suggestion.”

Amalarius teaches the same in book III of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 32, *On the Kiss of Peace*; Charlemagne, book I of the *Capitularies* in Ansegisus, chapter 53; and the *Decretals* of Pope Innocent:

“That peace be given by all after the mysteries of Christ have been completed.”

Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, states:

“Pope Innocent instituted by his decrees that peace should be given before Communion.”

See also the *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 18; Radulfus of Tongeren, *On the Observance of the Canons*, final proposition; *Gemma animae*, book I, *On the Ancient Rite of Mass*, chapter 90, *On the Canon*, and chapter 62, *On the Peace of the Lord*; John Beleth, in his exposition of the divine offices, chapter 48; William Durand, bishop of Mende, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book IV, chapter 53, *On the Kiss of Peace*; John Stephen Durandus, *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*, book II, chapter 54, *On the Kiss of Peace*; the exposition of the Mass from an ancient manuscript; and Odo, bishop of Cambrai, in his *Exposition of the Canon*:

“The end and completion of the sacrifice is made through peace, so that we may remain in peace; hence, at the completion of the sacrifice, we receive the kiss of peace, by which we both offer our assent to the sacrifice through participation and signify that we ought to remain in peace.”

The Rouen Ordinary manuscript agrees in several places, as does the Paris Missal manuscript, about three hundred years old, whose Canon, after the *Agnus Dei*, reads:

“Peace to you, brother, and to all the faithful of Christ.”

The Missals of the Church of Rouen from A.D. 1516, 1527, 1576, and 1604, and the Rouen Ritual under Charles of Bourbon, A.D. 1586, state in the Canon of the Mass:

“Here he shall receive peace, if it is to be received, saying: ‘Peace to you, brother, and to the holy Church of God.’”

The Missal of the Church of Salisbury in England, published in 1555, has the following in the Canon:

“Here the priest kisses the corporal on the right side and the rim of the chalice, and afterward says to the deacon: ‘Peace to you and to the Church of God.’ Response: ‘And with your spirit.’”

“The deacon receives peace from the priest on his right and gives it to the subdeacon. Then the deacon himself carries peace to the directors of the choir at the choir step, and they carry peace to the choir, each to his own side, beginning with the senior members.”

“On feasts and weekdays when the choir is not directed, the peace is carried to the choir by the deacon through the two outermost members of the second rank.”

The Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, p. 400, states:

“Moreover, by the same archiepiscopal authority it has been decreed that at all Masses, except those for the dead, peace shall be given after the prayer ‘Lord Jesus Christ, who said,’ etc. In giving it at solemn Masses, the order prescribed by the aforementioned John II in the Ritual Book must be observed. He, then bishop of Avranches, presented that book about 570 years ago to Maurilius, archbishop and his predecessor, as follows: ‘The priest,’ etc.”

See also the Rouen Missal of 1668, *On the Rite of Celebrating Mass*.

The ancient Fathers likewise mention this mystical kiss of peace: the author of the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter *On Communion*; Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2, near the end; Tertullian, *On Prayer*; Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 3, *On Peace*; Saint Chrysostom, book I, *On Compunction of Heart*, homily 3, *On Judas’s Betrayal*, near the end, and homily 51, *To the People of Antioch*; Saint Jerome, *To Theophilus of Alexandria*; Saint Augustine, sermon *On the Vigil of Easter*; Saint Paulinus of Nola, *Poem to Cytherius*; and Isidore of Seville, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 15.

From these testimonies it appears that the kiss or instrument of peace should be given in the sacrifice of the Mass, as is observed in many parish churches of the diocese of Rouen. Although this rite is unused in the cathedral church of Rouen, many members of the chapter have wished to restore it as an ancient and praiseworthy practice; it has not yet been restored.

(82) **The choir shall sing the *Agnus Dei*, which Pope Sergius commanded to be sung during the breaking of the Lord’s body.** Alcuin says the same in *On the Divine Offices*, as does Amalarius, book III, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 33:

“Pope Sergius established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung, as it is written in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*. He decreed that during the breaking of the Lord’s body the *Agnus Dei* should be sung by the clergy and people.”

See also Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 23; the *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 18; and *Gemma animae*, book I, chapter 90.

[Col. 0081B] **(83) If the deacon uses a chasuble, let him put it on again.** The same is stated in *The Soul’s Jewel*, book I, chapter 231, “On the Deacon’s Chasuble”: “When the ministry has been completed, the deacon is clothed in the chasuble.” The *Rouen Ritual*, published in 1651, likewise indicates this, part I, p. 466.

**(84) Let the service conclude with the clergy responding, “Thanks be to God.”** Hence it should be noted that at the end of Mass neither a blessing is given over the people nor was the Gospel of John formerly customarily read, just as it is not today among the Carthusians. The following also indicates this. *The Soul’s Jewel*, book I, chapter 3: “*Ite, missa est*” (“Go, the dismissal is made”) means permission to depart; “*Deo gratias*” (“Thanks be to God”) is an interjection of rejoicing. When these things have been completed, the people give thanks to God and return to their own affairs.

In the Missals of the Church of Rouen of 1516, 1527, and 1576, a blessing is included, but not the Gospel of John. In the Rouen Missal of 1604, under Charles of Bourbon, the following appears: “He turns toward the people and blesses them with his hand; meanwhile he removes the chasuble, saying, ‘The Lord be with you,’ and the Gospel according to John.”

In the Paris Missal, manuscript approximately 300 years old, in the old Roman Missal, approximately 200 years old, and in the Missal of the Church of Salisbury of 1555, neither blessing nor Gospel is included, but only *Placeat tibi, sancta Trinitas* (“May [it] be pleasing to you, O holy Trinity”).

The Salisbury Missal prescribes: “May [it] be pleasing to you, O holy Trinity.” When this has been completed, the priest is to rise, signing himself on his face and saying, “In the name of the Father,” etc. Then, having made an inclination, they are to return in the order in which they had previously approached the altar at the beginning of Mass, still wearing these vestments, with the candle-bearers and the other ministers. Immediately after “Thanks be to God,” None is to begin in the choir when it is said after Mass; as he returns, however, the priest is to say the Gospel, “*In principio*” (“In the beginning”).

**(85) On the days of Pentecost.** That is, during the paschal period of fifty days. So say Amalarius, book IV, chapters 29 and 46, and others. **PR.**

**(86) Let the deacon and subdeacon put on chasubles.** In John’s time the deacon’s and subdeacon’s chasubles seem to have been customary on the weekdays of Advent and Lent, but now only on the Sundays of those seasons. On weekdays on which the Office of the Dead is celebrated and on Ember Saturdays they use an alb, maniple, and stole, as is also read in the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 3: “On the weekdays of the aforesaid season they are to be in albs at Mass, and on the vigils of the saints and on the fasts of the Ember Days, September, Advent, and Lent.”

**(87) The *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) on feast days, except during Advent and Lent.** Formerly, on feast days during Advent and Lent, the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) was not sung, as is clear from this passage and from Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, under “The Purification of Saint Mary”: “On that day the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is not sung if it falls within Septuagesima.” The same is clear from the Missals for the use of the Church of Rouen of 1513, 1516, 1527, 1576, and 1604, in which the following is read for the feast of the Purification: “*Gloria in excelsis*, unless it is Septuagesima.”

**(88) And thus incensing the altar.** This incensing was still performed in our own age by the deacon kneeling. **PR.**

In our diocese the altar is incensed while the choir sings the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), as William Durandus notes, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book IV, chapter 10. After the kiss has been given, the bishop or priest, receiving the thurible from the deacon, solemnly incenses the altar. The Rouen *Ritual*, part I, p. 393, says the same. On all feast days—except simple feasts—in the Church of Rouen, while the *Gloria in excelsis* is sung, the choir is incensed by an acolyte.

**(89) “The *Credo in unum* (‘I believe in one [God]’) shall be sung,” namely, on all Sundays, etc.** The Rouen *Ordinary*, written approximately 200 years ago and preserved in the Bigot Library, says nearly the same.

**(90) Let None be said at its proper hour.** That is, at the ninth hour, three o’clock in the afternoon, which is observed by the metropolitan Church of Rouen, except on fast days, when this hour is anticipated until before midday, as in the monasteries.

**(91) Let the chapter be followed by the hymn.** Here no mention is made of the responsory *Tu exsurgens, Domine* (“You, arise, O Lord”), which is sung throughout Advent on Sundays and weekdays and is assigned in the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 5; in the Breviaries for the use of the Church of Rouen, published in 1491 and 1578; and in the more recent editions. Perhaps in John’s time it had not yet been sung in our province. Nor was it sung everywhere, as Amalarius testifies in *The Order of Antiphons*, chapter 80, but only in certain particular churches.

**(92) Let the weekday hymns always be sung.** At present, on the weekdays of Advent at Vespers, the hymn *Conditor* (“Creator”) is sung, as is noted in the old Diurnal of Lisieux and in the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578, as well as in the most recent editions.

**(93) Let them conclude with the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) and the Lord’s Prayer, kneeling, with prayers.** The same is found in the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578; in the Psalters of 1507 and 1586; in the Paris Breviary of 1557 and the Avranches Breviary of 1592, in which prayers are said at each Hour on weekdays; and also in the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 6, where we read:

“On Monday”—that is, of Advent—“at Prime: hymn *Jam lucis* (‘Now that the dawn’); antiphon *Veni* (‘Come’); Psalm *Deus in nomine* (‘O God, in your name’), etc.; antiphon *Gloria tibi, Trinitas* (‘Glory to you, Trinity’); *Quicumque* (‘Whoever’); chapter *Domine miserere* (‘Lord, have mercy’); responsory *Jesu Christe* (‘Jesus Christ’) is not to be said, but after the chapter the verse *Exsurge, Domine* (‘Arise, O Lord’) is to follow; at the *Kyrie eleison* they are to lie prostrate. *Pater noster* (‘Our Father’), and let the prayers be said, etc. At the chapter as noted above.”

**(94) Let the hymn of the saint be sung, etc.** At present only a commemoration of the saint is made at First Vespers, Lauds, and Mass.

**(95) A commemoration of Saint Mary, the angels, John the Baptist, etc.** These commemorations are not made in the Church of Rouen, but only those of the Cross, Saint Mary, the patron saint, Saint Romanus, and peace.

**(96) At Mass, however, etc.** At present, not five prayers as here, but generally three prayers are prescribed at a weekday Mass, 114 and the same number at a Mass for the dead, not four as is noted here.

**(97) The fifth for the prince.** Of all the Church’s practices, the Church of Rouen—nourished at the breasts of kings and mother of kings—has always most steadfastly observed the apostolic precept concerning supplications and prayers for kings. Hence the statement of Hugh III, archbishop, to Louis VII, king of France, letter 202, in *On French Affairs*, volume IV of the *Collection of French Historians*: “God knows that in all synods, consecrations of churches, assemblies, and Masses, we remember you in our prayers, because we love you exceedingly.”

Hence also Rotrodus, Hugh’s successor, in Peter of Blois, canon of Rouen, letter 28, concerning the same Louis, says: “Let the king of the Franks remember that the Church of Rouen is his own, for it continually makes special intercession for him as for its only king.”

The *Ordinary* of the same Church repeatedly prescribes that, if the archbishop celebrates, a commemoration is to be made of the pope and the king. Finally, in that same archiepiscopal Mass there is the solemn acclamation of the canons to the chant *Christus vincit* (“Christ conquers”): “Peace, health, and victory to N., king of the Franks.” **PR.**

**(98) If on a Sunday the feast of a saint with nine lessons occurs, etc.** This is not observed in our diocese unless it is a double or triple feast.

**(99) From the beginning of the fast until the Kalends of November, let Vespers and Vigils of the dead be held after the Vespers of the day, etc.** In the cathedral church during Lent, the Vigils of the dead are performed immediately before Compline, together with Lauds, at the ninth hour, three o’clock in the afternoon.

**(100) Let it be celebrated festively with nine lessons.** In the metropolitan church the Office of the Dead is celebrated with only one nocturn, except on the day of the deceased’s burial, as is noted in the Rouen *Ritual*.

**(101) The responsory *Ecce dies* (“Behold the day”), which is to be sung on the preceding Saturday.** On the Sunday preceding Advent, this responsory is sung at the station of the procession before the crucifix, but not on the preceding Saturday at Vespers, as it is described here; nor is it mentioned in the old Rouen *Ordinary*.

**(102) Let there be no procession to the crucifix.** That is, on Saturdays. At present, however, in the cathedral church a procession is held after Saturday Vespers throughout the year. The responsory *Sancta et immaculata virginitas* (“Holy and immaculate virginity”) is sung, followed by its prose *Inviolata* (“Unviolated”), and the psalm *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”) is sung to music, founded by Lord de Grigneuseville—although, strictly speaking, music is unsuitable to mourning. This foundation was established for the Saturdays of Advent and Lent, and at other times for the first Saturday of each month.

**(103) Let the choir be led by two cantors wearing copes.** The cope is the cantors’ proper vestment. Formerly it had a hood by which the head could be covered, as is read in Honorius, *The Soul’s Jewel*, book I, chapter 227, concerning the cope:

“The cope is the proper garment of cantors. Through this garment holy conduct is represented; therefore it is worn by each order. At the top it has a hood, which signifies heavenly joy.”

Today this hood falls onto the shoulders and is not worn on the head.

**(104) Let the responsory *O Juda* (“O Judah”) be sung by them.** Formerly this responsory was sung by two men; later their number increased to three, as is clear from the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 16:

“Three of the senior clergy in copes. Responsory: *O Juda et Jerusalem* (‘O Judah and Jerusalem’). Antiphon with threefold repetition: *Ecce jam venit* (‘Behold, he has now come’). Let the psalm *Magnificat* (‘My soul magnifies’) be sung in the sixth”—now only in the sixth—“and fifth tone. Meanwhile the altars are to be incensed by two priests in copes and afterward the choir by two boys.”

The number of those wearing copes who sing the responsory on triple feasts has today increased from three to four.

**(105) Let all the bells be rung at the first watch of the night.** Formerly there were three watches during the night, as Honorius of Autun testifies in *The Soul’s Jewel*, “On the Ancient Rite of Mass,” book II, chapters 1, 2, 7, and 11. The first watch was observed at approximately the tenth evening hour, the second at midnight, and the third approximately one hour before dawn.

Saint Jerome indicates these three watches in his letter to Eustochium, “On the Keeping of Virginity”: “One must rise twice or three times during the night.” William Durandus, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book V, chapter 3, “On the Nocturns,” explains them very clearly in these words:

“It should be known that in the primitive Church the ministers of the Church rose three times during the night, at intervals, to celebrate the divine office. They rose first around the first sleep, when the common people usually went to bed; second around midnight; third a little before daybreak. They arranged the office so that the nocturns would be finished and the lessons, with their responsories, read before it became light. When dawn appeared, after the bells had been rung, they sang *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”) and the morning Lauds.

“At the first nocturn the bishop and the ministers of the Church rose; it was sung without an invitatory, because no one was invited to it. It was called a vigil because it began from the shepherds keeping watch by night over their flocks. On the chief solemnities, however, the people remained throughout the night in the praises of God; but this practice was abolished, and a fast was appointed in place of that vigil.

“At the second nocturn the ministers and married people, women as well as men, rose together. It was said with an invitatory to signify the angels inviting the shepherds to see the newborn king. At the third nocturn everyone rose together. But afterward, as charity grew cold and all—both the ministers of the Church and the people—became reluctant to rise for the nocturnal office, it was decreed that everyone should rise at midnight and that the entire office of the night should be sung continuously; many still rise at that hour, as happens in the cathedral church of Paris and in many monasteries.

“Because certain people, devoting themselves more to nighttime pleasures than to the service of God, did not observe this institution, it was subsequently decreed that at least at the time of the final nocturn everyone should rise. Again, in memory of the devotion of the ancients who rose three times during the night, we say three nocturns, which received both their name and their origin from this practice.”

In the cathedral church of Rouen, on the more solemn feasts the nocturnal office with Lauds is performed at half past four in the morning; on other triple feasts at five; on double and semidouble feasts at half past five; and on simple feasts and weekdays at six.

**(106) Let the invitatory be sung by four clerics.** The invitatory is sung by four clerics wearing copes, as the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 17, states: “At Matins, four of the senior clergy in copes: *Christus natus est* (‘Christ is born’). Psalm: *Venite* (‘Come’).”

**(107) The third, sixth, and ninth wearing copes.** The responsories at the third and sixth lessons are sung by three men wearing copes; the ninth is sung by the four who sang the invitatory.

**(108) At the second, fifth, and eighth.** The *Ordinary of the Church*, in its rubric on Matins for triple feasts, says: “Let the altars and the choir be incensed at the second, fifth, and eighth lessons, and the altar at the Gospel.” **PR.**

In the cathedral church and in the other parish churches of the diocese of Rouen, the choir is never incensed at the responsories during the nocturns.

**(109) The lessons of the first nocturn shall be from the prophets.** That is, from the prophecy of Isaiah, as is found in the ancient Breviaries for the use of the Church of Rouen, which are still read on this night without a title.

It should also be noted that in the cathedral church of Rouen, throughout the entire year, even in summer, a burning lamp is carried by a boy preceding the acolyte who carries the lectionary. This indicates that the nocturnal vigils are to be said at night.

**(110) Let the three Gospels be proclaimed with men in copes, with incense and candlesticks preceding them.** All these practices are observed in the Church of Rouen. The altar is incensed before each person reads the Gospel, as the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 17, prescribes: “The seventh, eighth, and ninth lessons with candlesticks and thurible; and let the high altar be incensed.”

**(111) The chief priest of the church wearing a dalmatic and chasuble.** On that day, as at Epiphany, the priest wears not a dalmatic but only a chasuble, accompanied by the subdeacon, as the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 17, notes:

“When the prose has ended, a certain priest, vested in all the priestly vestments, together with the subdeacon vested in a tunic, is to sing the Gospel *Liber generationis* (“The book of the generation”) before the altar. When the Gospel has ended, the archbishop, or the dean, or another of the senior clergy from the right-hand choir, is to begin before the altar, with candlesticks and thurible: *Te Deum* (‘We praise you, God’).”

**(112) Let the clergy and people go out to wash.** I find nothing concerning this washing in the *Ordinary* or in the manuscript official books for the use of the Church of Rouen, nor among the interpreters of the divine offices. Perhaps a scribal error has entered here: the copyist may have written “let them go out to wash” (*lavatum exeat*) instead of “let them go to greet” (*salutatum eat*). For the greeting at the manger is mentioned in the official books and in the old Rouen *Ordinary* as follows:

“When the *Te Deum* has ended, let the office of the shepherds be performed according to the Rouen use in this manner. Let the manger be prepared behind the altar, and let an image of Saint Mary be placed in it. First, a certain boy is to be stationed above the choir, in the likeness of an angel announcing the Nativity of the Lord, to five canons of fifteen marks and pounds, or to their vicars from the second stall. The shepherds, entering through the great door of the choir and passing through the middle of the choir, are to approach the place where the manger has been prepared, singing this verse: *Pax in terris* (‘Peace on earth’), etc. Let the shepherds greet the Virgin . . . Then, when they have seen the child, let the shepherds adore him.

“When Mass has ended, the priest who has celebrated Mass is to turn toward the shepherds and say: ‘Whom did you see, shepherds? Tell us; announce to us who has appeared on earth.’ The shepherds are to reply: ‘We saw him who has been born,’ etc.”

**(113) Let them celebrate Mass: the church secretary the first, the cantor the second, and the bishop or dean the third.** The old Rouen *Ordinary* likewise assigns three Masses to three different priests, not to the same priest, as is commonly done in parish churches:

“If the lord archbishop is present, let him sing Mass, or the dean. Let the Mass of daybreak follow, sung by one of the left-hand choir . . . After the procession, let the archbishop, with seven deacons, an equal number of subdeacons, and the other ministers, sing Mass.”

Similarly, among the Carthusians three Masses are to be sung by three different priests, according to chapter 5 of the *Ancient Statutes*.

**(114) The church secretary.** Among the people of Rouen he is also called the custodian and sacristan; now, by the more customary name already adopted in sacred usage since Isidore’s time, he is called the treasurer. **PR.**

**(115) Let the cantor begin the antiphon *Ecce completa sunt* (“Behold, all things have been fulfilled”).** The old Rouen *Ordinary*: “Let the *Benedicamus*, *Verbum Patris hodie* (‘The Word of the Father today’), be sung by the shepherds. When this has ended, let the shepherds sing this antiphon in the pulpit: *Ecce completa* (‘Behold, they have been fulfilled’). Let the archbishop or priest say the verse: *Post partum* (‘After childbirth’). Prayer: *Deus qui salutis* (‘O God, who are the salvation’). *Benedicamus* (‘Let us bless’), by three boys.” These practices have been abolished in the Church of Rouen.

**(116) When dawn begins, let another Mass be celebrated in the same manner.** At present it is celebrated according to the double rite in the cathedral church, where it is sung immediately after Lauds; in the parish churches, however, it is celebrated at sunrise.

**(117) At Vespers, the hymn *A solis ortus* (“From the rising of the sun”).** Today, at First Vespers, the hymn *Veni, Redemptor* (“Come, Redeemer”) is sung, as is found in the old Rouen *Ordinary* and in the ancient Breviaries and Psalters.

**(118) The deacons wearing deaconal vestments.** The old *Ordinary of the Metropolitan Church* explains this rite of the deacons, as well as the following rites of the priests and boys, at greater length. Among other things, on the feast of Saint Stephen it prescribes that during the procession—if the feast falls on a Sunday—the deacons in silk copes are to be at the upper part of the procession toward the gate of Saint Romanus, while all the others in their black copes are to be toward the pulpit. The same is to be done by the priests and boys on the day of Saint John and of the Holy Innocents.

It also prescribes that at Mass all the deacons in copes are to lead the choir in the middle of the choir; that the deacon is to read the Epistle, *Stephanus plenus* (“Stephen, full [of grace]”); and that, at the place where it says, “He cried out with a loud voice, saying,” two deacons are to sing the prose *Stat ut agnus inter lupos* (“He stands like a lamb among wolves”). Three deacons are to sing *Sederunt principes* (“Princes sat”), verse: *Adjuva me* (“Help me”). All the deacons are to sing *Alleluia* (“Praise the Lord”), verse: *Ecce video coelos* (“Behold, I see the heavens”), in the middle of the choir in the form of a circle, etc. Finally, after the Gospel has been read, a deacon is to proclaim in chant: *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”). **PR.**

**Let the deacons proceed with candles.** That is, to the altar of Saint Stephen, as is found in the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 20:

“When Vespers have ended, let all the deacons of the church, in surplices and holding burning candles in their hands, come through the choir in procession, two by two, as far as the altar of Saint Stephen, singing the responsory *Sancte Dei pretiose* (‘Holy precious one of God’). Three deacons are to sing the verse *Ut tuo* (‘That by your’). When this has ended, let the antiphon *Beatus Stephanus, levita* (‘Blessed Stephen, Levite’) begin. Three deacons: verse *Gloria* (‘Glory’), etc. Prayer: *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus* (‘Almighty eternal God’). On the return, antiphon *Nesciens mater* (‘The mother, not knowing’), or a responsory of Saint Mary at will, and let it end in the choir. Two deacons are to sing the verse *Post partum* (‘After childbirth’), or *Speciosa* (‘Beautiful’). Let us pray. *Deus qui salutis* (‘O God, who are the salvation’). *Benedicamus* (‘Let us bless’) at will.”

This procession has been abolished in the Church of Rouen. The Bayeux Processional, published in 1624, nevertheless describes it as follows:

“When the last Vespers of this day”—that is, of the Nativity of the Lord—“have ended, the procession goes to the fonts through the upper exit of the choir. The subdeacon, festively vested, carries the arm of Saint Stephen in a silk shroud, and that shroud is red. The following responsory is sung: *Lapides torrentis* (‘The stones of the torrent’), etc. These things are observed only in the cathedral church. Prose: *Coelos vidit* (‘He saw the heavens’), etc.

“Then the chief cantor begins the following antiphon: *Infunde* (‘Pour out’), etc. Afterward the procession proceeds into the nave of the church, singing the responsory *Felix namque* (‘Happy indeed’), with its verse and *Gloria Patri* (‘Glory to the Father’), and the prose *Inviolata* (‘Unviolated’). On the return: responsory *Descendit* (‘He descended’), without a verse.”

The same Bayeux Processional contains processions on the following three days after Vespers and Terce. In the old *Ordinary*, or manuscript ceremonial, of the regular canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen, of the Order of Saint Augustine, they occur after Vespers and Lauds.

**(119) At Matins let the bells be rung as on the preceding night.** 120 The feast of Saint Stephen is now celebrated according to the double rite. The invitatory is sung by two men in copes, who lead the choir during the nocturns and Lauds. The following ceremonies, namely those for the feasts of Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, and the Holy Innocents, have completely fallen out of use. It nevertheless seems worthwhile to report what is found in the manuscript *Ordinary* for this feast:

“While the ninth lesson is being read, let all the deacons go to the vesting room. When it has ended, let them come out of the vesting room with burning candles, singing the responsory *O martyrum gemma* (‘O jewel of martyrs’). Before the altar, let it be completed in the form of a circle, with the verse and prose by three deacons. When this has ended, let *Te Deum* (‘We praise you, God’) begin, etc., as above.”

The old Rouen *Ordinary* describes the same processional rites for the feast of Saint John the Evangelist.

**(120) With the antiphon and *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”), a commemoration of the Nativity.** In the Church of Rouen a commemoration of the Nativity is made with an antiphon, verse, and prayer; the verse *Gloria Patri* has been abolished.

**(121) Then, with the priests proceeding.** Saint John was held in great veneration by the priests of our region from ancient times. Various reasons for this may be drawn from his various prerogatives, which are especially appropriate to the priestly order. This one, however, is particularly pleasing: among the apostles he alone prefixed the title “elder” to his letters.

On the morning Mass at the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, see Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book III, chapter 38. **PR.**

This Mass, however, was special and entirely different from the one celebrated after Terce, as is clear from the Paris Missal, a manuscript approximately 300 years old, and from the old manuscript *Ordinary* of the regular canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen.

**(122) Let the priests use chasubles.** How different these chasubles were from ours may be gathered from Rabanus, book I, *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 21, “On the Chasuble”:

“The seventh priestly vestment is what they call the chasuble. It is so called as a diminutive of *casa* (‘house’), because it covers the whole person. The Greeks call it a *planeta* (‘cloak’).”

This agrees with *The Soul’s Jewel*, “On the Ancient Rite of Mass,” book I, chapter 207, “On the Chasuble”:

“In ancient times chasubles were round, and their border, wandering over the arms, surrounded the entire body.”

Two such chasubles are preserved in the sacristy of the cathedral church of Rouen. They are made of foldable material, as the Rouen *Ritual* indicates. One, which is violet, is used by the celebrant on Holy Saturday of Easter and at the vigil of Pentecost while the prophecies are being read. The other, which is white, is worn by the priest who sings the genealogy on the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and Epiphany, so that the usage of this venerable antiquity may not entirely perish.

For this reason the Rouen *Ritual* prescribes that the form of the sacred vestments be maintained which the institution of the Fathers and the venerable antiquity of the cathedral church prescribe: namely, that the chasubles or *planetae* be extended on either side to such breadth that they at least cover the whole arms. They should therefore be made of convenient, foldable material so that they can easily be lifted by their borders and not impede the celebrant. Part I, p. 386.

It is enough to have reported these things so that those responsible for ecclesiastical ornaments may learn not to follow modern usage, but rather to obey ecclesiastical laws and restore them to their ancient form.

**(123) When the office of the infants begins.** That is, of the boys. Thus the infant readers of Carthage are called by Victor of Vita, book II, and in the Martyrology on the third day before the Ides of July. Concerning the office of the infants, which continued longer in the Church, the *Ordinary* provides more information for this day—**PR.**—which we transcribe after the observations from the same old Rouen *Ordinary*.

**(124) On the feast of Saint Sylvester, the first six lessons are about the saint and the last three about the Nativity.** The same is found in the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578. The old Rouen *Ordinary* agrees with them concerning both the lessons and the Masses, as does the manuscript *Ordinary* of the regular canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen.

At present the first three lessons are from the Epistle to the Romans; the three of the second nocturn are from the Life of Saint Sylvester; and the three of the third nocturn are from an exposition of the Gospel, *Sint lumbi* (“Let your loins be girded”). Conversely, the morning Mass is now of the Nativity, while the principal Mass is celebrated for Saint Sylvester.

**(125) Three lessons with three responsories.** Today nine lessons, with an equal number of responsories, are read in the Rouen Breviary.

**(126) With Lauds and the sequence.** The sequence and Lauds have been removed from this Mass.

**(127) The octave of Saint John as the feast of an apostle.** Now it is commemorated as a Sunday feast, as are the octaves of Saint Stephen and of the Holy Innocents.

**(128) Let the day of the Circumcision be celebrated as the feast of Saint John.** In the Church of Rouen it is celebrated according to the triple rite of the second class. At Vespers, two men wearing copes lead the choir; the responsory is sung by four in copes, and two of the senior clergy incense the altar.

Similarly, at Matins, four in copes sing the invitatory and the ninth responsory and lead the choir during the nocturns and Lauds. At Mass, the cantor in a cope intones the Introit; two men in copes from the second stall sing the Gradual; and four in copes from the senior stall sing the Alleluia with its verse.

At Second Vespers everything is as at First Vespers, but the altar is incensed by only one celebrant.

**(129) Let the day of Epiphany be celebrated as the day of the Nativity.** Except that the altar is incensed only at the seventh lesson.

**(130) Without an invitatory.** Alcuin teaches the same in *On the Divine Offices*, under “Epiphany”:

“On this day we omit one of the things that we celebrate at the Nativity of the Lord, namely the invitatory.”

Amalarius agrees with Alcuin in book IV of *Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 33, and in *The Order of Antiphons*, chapter 21. The Micrologus likewise says, chapter 40:

“On Epiphany, at the nocturns, according to the Roman Order, we refrain from the invitatory so that we may differ from Herod’s deceitful invitation.”

On that day the invitatory is not read in Honorius’s *The Soul’s Jewel*, nor in Beleth, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 37, nor in Durandus. In book VI, chapter 16, “On the Feast of Epiphany,” Durandus says:

“The invitatory is also not said for four reasons.”

And in the Dominican Breviary:

“On Epiphany at Matins, let neither the invitatory nor the hymn be said.”

Likewise in the manuscript *Ordinary* of the regular canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen:

“At Matins the invitatory and hymn are not said.”

At present, however, the invitatory is said. It is recorded as having been instituted in the Church of Rouen approximately 200 years ago, according to the Bigot manuscript *Ordinary*, p. 33.

[Col. 0090A] **(131) It is not entirely omitted, but is recited in the order of the psalms.** This agrees with what may be read in Durandus at the place cited above:

“Although the invitatory is not said on this day, the invitatory psalm, namely *Venite exsultemus* (“Come, let us exult”), is nevertheless said in the third nocturn at the seventh antiphon.”

In the Dominican Breviary:

“In the third nocturn, antiphon: *Venite adoremus* (‘Come, let us adore’), etc. The psalm itself.”

And in the manuscript *Ordinary* of the canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen:

“In the third nocturn, antiphon: *Venite* (‘Come’); the psalm itself is sung in its entirety while standing.”

**(132) Let the priest proceed wearing the dalmatic and chasuble.** Thus it is read in the old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 33:

“When the ninth responsory has ended, the priest, vested in the priestly vestments, is to sing this Gospel before the altar, with the subdeacon beside him, as is noted for the Nativity of the Lord: *Factum est cum baptizaretur* (‘It happened when he was baptized’). When the Gospel has ended, let the archbishop, or the priest of the week, begin before the altar, with candlesticks and thurible, the psalm *Te Deum* (‘We praise you, God’).”

**(133) Let the office of the star begin.** By “office” understand a spectacle, or, as they called it, a mystery, by which the story of the star’s appearance and the Magi’s adoration was presented to the people. The same sense is to be given to the “office of the sepulchre,” mentioned below in the order for Easter.

These and other inventions of later times, which the *Ordinary* shows to have persisted for a long time among our forebears, were rightly abolished by a more disciplined age, lest the sacred rites degenerate into theatrical entertainments and absurdities. **PR.**

In the old Rouen *Ordinary* it is called the “office of the three kings.” It was formerly performed after Terce; we append it to the office of the infants.

**(134) Without *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”) and the *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”).** Today they are said in the diocese of Rouen, as is customary during octaves.

**(135) As they enter the choir, let the cantor begin the antiphon or responsory for the saint to whom the church belongs.** On these unoccupied Sundays, at the entrance of the choir the responsory *Te laudant* (“They praise you”), *Confirmatum est* (“It has been confirmed”), or *Nesciens mater* (“The mother, not knowing”) is sung, as is noted in the manuscript *Ordinary*. Alternatively, a chant for the patron saint may be used, as is found in the Rouen Processional, or some antiphon of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

**(136) But the vigil of Epiphany.** That John formerly held this opinion among us concerning the fast of that vigil, but that in the course of time the pious custom died out through abuse or dispensation, is shown by the fact that nearly the same statement is found in the *Ordinary*, though with a certain qualification:

“On the following day is the vigil of Epiphany, which different peoples observe differently: some dine, others fast. For us, however, fasting seems appropriate. Since such a great solemnity is eminent among us, on which the entire Trinity first manifested itself to the world, we ought first to be purified.”

The Church of Rouen, however, does not fast on account of the solemnity of the Nativity of the Lord. **PR.**

**(137) During which we fast for several days.** From this it appears that in the Church of Rouen a fast for several days before the Purification was formerly in use. Although we have found no trace of it among the interpreters of the divine offices, nor in our manuscript Ordinaries and official books, it is nevertheless read in the Paris Missal, a manuscript 300 years old, and in the old Breviary of the Fontevrault order:

“Vigil of the Purification,”

which comes very close to prescribing a fast.

**(138) Let the clergy and people proceed to it.** Today the clergy do not go to another church; rather, during the movement of the procession this antiphon is sung: *Ave, gratia plena* (“Hail, full of grace”).

**(139) Let the verse follow, sung by two clerics.** It is now sung by four in the pulpit, as is observed on all triple feasts.

**(140) On the preceding Saturday at Vespers, let the sequence *Cantemus cuncti melodum* (“Let us all sing a melodious song”) be sung in place of the hymn.** In its place on Saturdays the hymn *O lux, beata Trinitas* (“O light, blessed Trinity”) is now said at Vespers, until the Saturday before the First Sunday of Lent. The old Rouen *Ordinary*, p. 46, also prescribes this.

**(141) An Alleluiatic invitatory.** The invitatory is sung without *Alleluia* (“Praise the Lord”), for it ceases at the Vespers of the preceding Saturday.

**(142) Let the Heptateuch begin in the first nocturn.** The manuscript *Ordinary of the Church of Rouen* states:

“In Septuagesima let the book of Genesis begin, and let it and the other legal books be read up to the Passion of the Lord: namely, the book of Exodus, the book of Leviticus, the book of Numbers, the book of Deuteronomy, the book of Joshua, the book of Judges, and the book of Ruth. On weekdays, three lessons are to be read; in the second nocturn, three lessons from a sermon; in the third nocturn, three lessons from expositions.”

The Rouen Breviary of 1491, part I, says:

“From the beginning of Septuagesima until the Passion of the Lord, readings are taken from the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth; on weekdays, three lessons.”

In the diocese of Rouen, readings are now taken from the book of Genesis until Ash Wednesday. Throughout Lent, expositions of the Fathers on the Gospels are read; on Sundays, however, the first nocturn contains readings from Genesis and Exodus.

**(143) Morning Lauds with Alleluiatic antiphons.** Today, after the final *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”) has been sung at the Vespers of the Saturday before Septuagesima, and *Deo gratias* (“Thanks be to God”) with a double *Alleluia*, *Alleluia* is omitted in every office until Easter. *Te Deum* (“We praise you, God”), *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”), and *Ite missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”) are not said except on feast days during Lent. The manuscript *Ordinary* prescribes the same.

125 **(144) At Matins.** That is, at Lauds. Lauds were called Matins, as is clear from the interpreters of the sacred rites; but because the nocturns and Lauds were joined together, we call both by the single name “Matins.”

**(145) Afterward, *Benedicamus* (“Let us bless”) with *Alleluia* (“Praise the Lord”).** This was corrected in John’s own time by Pope Alexander II, who ordered that *Alleluia* be omitted at Saturday Vespers before Septuagesima, as the Micrologus teaches in *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 47. **PR.**

**(146) For seventy days.** On the mystical significance of these days, see Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, and his letters to Charlemagne; Amalarius, book I, chapters 1–4; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Institution of the Clergy*, book II, chapter 34; and Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Special Observance of the Mass*, book III, chapter 16. **PR.**

**(147) On that day in the procession, *Ecce charissimi* (“Behold, dearest ones”).** This responsory is rejected in many churches because of its length, although it is noted in the Rouen Processional and in the manuscript *Ordinary*, p. 47, in the following manner:

“The procession follows: responsory *Ubi est Abel* (‘Where is Abel?’), with verse and return. At the station: *Ecce, charissimi, dies* (‘Behold, dearest ones, the day’). Verse in the pulpit: *Ecce mater nostra* (‘Behold our mother’). *Ut videatis* (‘So that you may see’). At the entrance of the choir: responsory *Igitur perfecti sunt* (‘Therefore they have been completed’), with verse and return.”

In the cathedral church it ends in the nave of the church, and the clergy do not enter the choir. When these things have ended, the archbishop is to preach to the people, and afterward Terce is to be sung.

**(148) Four days were added by the holy Fathers.** This is testified by Amalarius, book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7, “On Fasting,” and by William Durandus, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 28.

(149) Let the sermons of the Fathers be read—that is, the homilies or expositions of the Fathers on the Gospels read on the weekdays of Lent.

(150) Let only Vespers for the dead be celebrated. The same may be read in Radulfus of Tongeren, *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 20:

> It is a general practice, he says, among many that Vespers and vigils are said on the preceding day, and Lauds on the following day after Matins. But after the nocturn for the dead, Lauds for the same dead are said in the cathedral church before Compline.

[Col. 0092C] (151) Seven psalms with the litany. On this day the seven penitential psalms are not said after Lauds, but after None, without the litany. During Lent, however, every Wednesday fifteen gradual psalms are said after Lauds have been completed; on Friday the seven penitential psalms are said with the litany and prayers, provided that the office is for the weekday.

(152) Let Prime be sung after sunrise. The hymn indicates the hour: “Now that the star of light has risen” (*Jam lucis orto sidere*), etc.; but in the cathedral church it is sung at half past eight in the morning.

(153) After Sext has been said, let a short interval be made. On fast days and during Lent no interval is made, but None is said immediately, at its proper hour—as John of Avranches notes. What hour is proper for saying None scarcely any antiquarian fails to know: it is the third hour of the afternoon. None is said at that hour in the cathedral church, but on fast days it is anticipated by four hours, namely, to one o’clock in the afternoon.

During Lent, when None had been completed—the third hour after midday at which it was sung—Mass was celebrated afterward, and Vespers were sung. When these had been completed, clergy and people went to their meal, which was their only meal, as Saint Basil testifies in *Oration 1, On Fasting*; Saint John Chrysostom, *Homily 10 on Genesis*; Saint Augustine, *Sermon 56 on Time*; Saint Ambrose, *Sermon 33*; Saint Bernard, *Sermon 3 on Lent*; the *Micrologus, On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 49; and the Council of Rouen held in A.D. 1072 [Col. 0093A], under John II, canon 20, which likewise decrees:

> It has been established that no one in Lent shall eat lunch before the ninth hour has been completed and Vespers begun, for one who eats beforehand does not fast.

The monks of the Benedictine abbey of Saint Cyran observe this decree concerning fasting with the greatest devotion. From the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Lent they are content with one meal at the ninth hour, namely, three in the afternoon; during Lent, however, they eat after Vespers, namely, at six in the evening.

(154) When this has been completed, let Vespers for the dead be said, etc. The Rouen *Ordinarium* manuscript likewise states:

> In the rites for the dead, let this be done each day: before Vespers, let *Placebo* be said, except on Saturdays and triple feasts.

The cathedral church of Rouen had always retained this custom until the preceding year, when it placed the Vespers of the day before Vespers for the dead. This change was made only for the Lenten season, because of the excessive number of offices.

(155) Let the vigil for the dead be conducted. Here the manuscript *Ordinarium* agrees, reading as follows on page 53:

> After the meal, the vigil for the dead follows.

[p. 127] (156) Let the reading of the Collation be recited. This Collation was recited throughout Lent before Compline, as is stated in the manuscript *Ordinarium*, pages 53 and 56:

> On these four days—that is, from the beginning of the fast until the First Sunday of Lent—let a reading from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, etc., be read before Compline. Continue this practice until the Lord’s Supper. Likewise, on Monday of Lent, before Compline and until Palm Sunday, let expositions for the weekdays be read; and on the Sundays of Lent, let a reading be given from the remainder of that day’s exposition.

This spiritual Collation was afterward transformed among clergy and people into a bodily collation, or light meal. On this subject see Francolinus, *On the Time of the Canonical Hours*, chapter 38, no. 10.

(157) In all the prayers of the hours, always say “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*). The same appears in the Breviaries of 1491 and 1578 and in the Psalters of 1507 and 1586. Durandus likewise supports it in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 32, “On the First Sunday of Lent”:

> At this season that penitential psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” is regularly said eight times in the canonical hours.

In the Church of Rouen, however, that psalm is said only at Vespers on the weekdays of Advent, Lent, and the Ember Days. The psalms assigned there for the hours are not said; instead, after the chapter, the prayers prescribed in the Rouen Breviary are recited, followed by the prayer of the day and, at the end, the versicle “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*).

(158) Let one Psalter of psalms be added. Here understand a certain number of psalms, not an entire Psalter, as Radulfus of Tongeren indicates in *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 21:

> Since in holy Lent the holy Fathers wished the office of the Church to be increased in every way together with other good works, therefore, as an increase of divine worship during that season, on the weekdays of Lent, when the nine lessons are omitted, the Psalter is read after Prime in the following manner. Having received pardon while prostrate, the priest begins: “O God, come to my assistance”; “Glory”; “Praise to you.” Then, each day, ten psalms are read from the Psalter, two and two, with two under a single “Glory.” After the last: “Praise to you”; the versicle “Let it enter”; then the entire litany. When it has been said, while all are prostrate, the major prayers are said with the seven psalms and the prayers mentioned above; and at “Through the Lord” (*Per Dominum*) all rise.

(159) Let “As I live,” etc., be said for sins at Matins. These have been abolished in the Church of Rouen, both at morning Lauds and at Vespers.

(160) At Saturday Vespers, etc., let the memory of the saints be observed. Formerly no feast was celebrated during Lent; rather, at Vespers on Saturday and on Sunday [Col. 0094B], the memory was observed of those saints whose feasts occurred during the week, as the Council of Laodicea had decreed, chapter 49:

> It is not proper to celebrate the birthdays of martyrs during Lent, but their memory is to be observed only on Saturday and Sunday.

(161) When the bishop begins the antiphon “Let us change” (*Immutemur*). Today the cantor begins it, and the choir continues it.

(162) Let him distribute ashes with blessed water. The old manuscript *Ordinarium* of the regular canons of Saint Laud of Rouen prescribes the same for Ash Wednesday. Today blessed water is not sprinkled during the imposition of the ashes. The blessed ashes are imposed as a sign of penance, because formerly penance was performed in ashes and sackcloth—a matter on which the people should be instructed by their pastors. In testimony to this, on this day the Church sings the antiphon:

> Let us change our garment into ashes and sackcloth (*Immutemur habitu in cinere et cilicio*).

In the cathedral church of Rouen, at the public expulsion of penitents, a sackcloth garment is carried by a deacon, hung from a pole, in accordance with Durandus, *Rationale*, book VII, chapter 35:

> Ashes and sackcloth are the weapons of penitents.

On the expulsion of penitents, see the excellent sermon of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *On the Beginning of the Fast*, already published among his works.

(163) Before the procession. This procession, after the penitents have been expelled, proceeds to the altar of Saint Stephen in the same church while a responsory is sung. When the procession reaches the chapel of Saint Stephen, with everyone kneeling—formerly even prostrate, as is evident from the old manuscript Ceremonial—the prayers and collects are said as on the Monday of Rogation Days. When these have been completed, the short litanies are sung in full by two men from the second choir-stall, while the choir responds. This order is observed on Wednesday and Friday up to, but excluding, Good Friday: on Wednesday at the altar of Saint Stephen and on Friday at the altar of Saint John.

(164) Let the penitents be expelled. Durandus says this in *Rationale*, book VI, chapter 28:

> The penitents are then expelled from the Church with a procession and a cross, and on the day of the Lord’s Supper they are received back into it.

For the public expulsion of penitents and their convocation in the Church of Rouen, see what the manuscript *Ordinarium* prescribes after our observations.

[Col. 0095A] (165) Hymns at Vespers: “Taught by mystical tradition” (*Ex more docti mystico*), etc. The same hymns are found in the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578 and in the Psalters of 1507 and 1586. But every day at Vespers, until First Vespers of Passion Sunday, except on feasts, the hymn “Hear us, kind Creator” (*Audi, benigne conditor*) is sung; at Matins, the hymn “Taught by mystical tradition” (*Ex more docti*); and at Lauds, “Now, Christ, Sun of justice” (*Jam Christe sol justitiae*).

(166) By the addition of one lesson and one responsory. By “responsory” understand a gradual, as we have already said. Amalarius likewise reads in book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 8, “On the second variation of the fourth week of Lent”:

> On the Wednesday of the fourth week there is a variation through the addition of one lesson and one responsory. On the same day the third scrutiny is held, which is the greatest among the seven scrutinies [Col. 0095B] … On the same day they are instructed concerning the authors and beginnings of the four Gospels.

(167) The Lord’s Prayer and the Creed are handed over to them, so that, etc. Amalarius says in the same place:

> On the same day they receive the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, to recite them on Holy Saturday of Easter.

Guillermus Durandus teaches the same in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 46, “On the Wednesday of the fourth week.”

(168) On the Saturday preceding Palm Sunday, ecclesiastical Order prescribed that the feet of the poor be washed. Hence the old inscription of the day in the Sacramentary and Antiphonary:

> Saturday is free; the lord pope gives alms.

On this matter consult Amalarius, book I, chapter 9, and Rupert, abbot of Tuitien, *On the Divine Offices*, book V [Col. 0095C], chapter 6. PR.

Durandus agrees in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 66, “On the Saturday before Palm Sunday”:

> On this Saturday the lord pope was accustomed to attend to Christ’s poor by giving alms and celebrating the Mandatum.

See also *The Jewel of the Soul*, book III, chapter 71.

(169) After Terce, let the clergy go with palm branches to the procession. Here there is a significant silence concerning the procession to Saint Gildard, in which the body of Christ, placed in a bier, is carried by two priests. Although the precise time of the institution of this rite cannot be established, the same rite is at least found in the *Decrees of Blessed Lanfranc*, *Ordinary*, chapter 1, section 4, and in the old manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen. We describe the rite of this procession after the observations, from the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium*.

[p. 130] (170) Let “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*) be said. So state the manuscript *Ordinaries*, the manuscript official books, and certain Missals. But today “The Lord be with you” is said on no day during the Passion.

(171) Let the curtain before the altar be lowered. The *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen prescribes the same. Likewise the manuscript *Ordinarium*, page 74:

> At the Passion of the Lord, let the curtain hanging between the choir and the altar not be moved until “And the veil of the temple was torn,” and then let it be drawn from both sides and torn in the middle, and let it not be put up again.

This is observed in the cathedral church of Rouen.

[Col. 0096A] (172) Let all the bells be rung. In the cathedral church the rite is semi-double, as Vespers are celebrated on Saturdays; not all the bells sound, but only three, as on Sundays. Two men from the second choir-stall direct the choir, as on double feasts. The manuscript *Ordinarium*, page 74, agrees:

> At Vespers let “Placebo” not be said, but let the bells be rung festively as on Sunday, out of reverence for the Lord’s Supper; and let the antiphons over the psalms be sung festively and conclude with a neume. Antiphon: “Blessed is the man” (*Beatus vir*). Psalm: “Unless the Lord builds” (*Nisi Dominus aedificaverit*), etc., in order. Let two men from the second choir-stall, in black silk copes, direct the choir—now, however, in violet-colored copes—and two men from the principal choir-stall likewise wear copes. Responsory: “They surrounded me” (*Circumdederunt*). At the Magnificat, let the altar and choir be incensed. Let “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*) be sung by one person, as at semi-double feasts.

Likewise, in an old manuscript official book for the use of the Church of Rouen, we read:

> At Vespers let all the bells be rung as at the nine lessons, out of reverence for the Lord’s Supper.

The manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen prescribes the same.

(173) Let them all be rung together. The Rouen manuscript official book from the Bigot Library states:

> On Thursday, at the nocturn, first let the bells be rung one by one; afterward let them all be rung together.

The same is stated above.

(174) At the third, an exposition of the Gospel. It does not speak of an exposition of the Gospel, but of the First Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 11.

(175) Let the one remaining candle be extinguished. Thus the manuscript *Ordinarium*, page 75:

> Let the psalm *Benedictus* be sung festively, and let the candle that alone remained be extinguished.

The Rouen manuscript official book says the same and adds:

> Once the last candle has been extinguished at the *Benedictus*, no light in the church is to be kindled until after the blessing of the fire.

Nevertheless, on these days in the Church of Rouen it is kept in a box so that it may afterward be revealed, as Durandus records in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 72. The candle in the middle is not extinguished; rather, it is kept burning secretly in a window or box, so that it may afterward be revealed and illuminate the church. In the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1378, however, the wording is:

> And let the candle that remained be hidden.

(176) Let them sing in a loud voice. Now Vespers are usually recited in a moderate voice, according to the order of the divine office, like the canonical hours, except for the Nocturns and Lauds.

(177) After the versicle has been said by some boy. The choir adds the versicle, and it is not said by a boy except after Lauds, at the end of the tropes. The responsory after the psalms, mentioned by John, is found in the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the regular canons of Saint Laud of Rouen.

(178) The convocation of the penitents. The Church of Rouen has steadfastly maintained this ancient and salutary observance up to the present. It should also be noted from the *Ordinarium* that formerly on this day absolution was customarily given twice: once to the people after morning Lauds, and once to the penitents after None, followed by their reconciliation and a sermon. On the convocation and absolution of penitents see the Roman Order; Alcuin, *Book on the Divine Offices*, “On the Lord’s Supper”; Amalarius, book I, chapter 12; and Rupert, book V, chapter 19. PR.

(179) Let both clergy and people receive absolution while prostrate. According to the manuscript *Ordinarium*, there are two absolutions on this day: the first for clergy and people after Lauds, the second for public penitents after None. Thus it reads on page 76:

> Let one boy say in a loud voice: “Even the death of the cross.” Then let the choir say silently: “Our Father.” “But deliver us.” “Amen.” Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*). Prayer: “Look upon us, we ask, O Lord” (*Respice, quaesumus, Domine*); let each person say only “Amen.” Then let the lamp be uncovered. When this is finished, let the seven penitential psalms be said. Antiphon: “Do not remember” (*Ne reminiscaris*). Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury” (*Domine, ne in furore*), and the remaining psalms. “Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.” “Our Father.” “And lead us not into temptation.” Versicle: “Send them forth, O Lord.” Versicle: “Turn back, O Lord.” Versicle: “Let mercy be shown.” Versicle: “O Lord God of hosts.” Versicle: “O Lord, hear.” Versicle: “The Lord be with you.” Prayer: “Be present, O Lord, to our supplications.” Prayer: “O God, who made the human race.” Another prayer: “O Lord, holy Father.” Afterward let the lord archbishop, or his vicar, absolve the people: “We absolve you in the place of blessed Peter.” Afterward let him bless them.

The second absolution, which is for the penitents, we will present from the same manuscript *Ordinarium* after our observations, together with the archdeacon’s sermon to the archbishop of Rouen concerning the reconciliation of public penitents. This sermon has not yet been published and is preserved in an old manuscript codex of the cathedral church of Rouen, seven hundred years old.

(180) That a new fire is kindled on these three days. On the three-day rite of kindling the fire, the Roman Order and Rupert, book V, chapter 28, should be consulted. PR.

That blessed fire is distributed in the cathedral church and in certain parishes to the people on Holy Saturday, so that fire may be kindled from it in Christian homes. On this subject see the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen.

(181) If there is a bishop, let “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*) be sung; otherwise, not. Durandus teaches the same in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 75, “On the office of the Mass of Thursday.” Likewise the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium*:

> On this day in a parish church, “Glory to God in the highest” is not to be said.

Today, however, it is said in all the parish churches of the diocese of Rouen. In the cathedral church the consecration of chrism takes place during the Mass. We describe its rite and ceremonies from the manuscript *Ordinaries* of the cathedral church of Rouen and from the Bigot manuscript, after the solemn processions.

(182) Until the Mass of Sunday night. For this Mass, which is said on Holy Saturday, ought, according to the decrees of the sacred canons and Fathers, to be said at night, since it belongs to the night of the Lord’s Resurrection.

(183) With the priest holding the chalice in his hands, let him begin the antiphon “The chalice” (*Calicem*). Thus it is consistently read in the manuscript official book [Col. 0098A] and in the Missals for the use of the Church of Rouen dated 1513, 1516, 1527, 1538, 1576, and 1604:

> Then let Vespers be said in a subdued voice; the priest, holding the chalice in his hands, is to begin this antiphon: “The chalice,” etc.

Today it is begun by one of the senior members of the choir.

(184) In their place, let the wooden boards be struck. Thus Alcuin writes in *On the Divine Offices*, under “The Lord’s Supper”:

> The sound of signs and bells is suppressed; in its place, a lower sound of wood is taken up to gather the people.

Amalarius likewise writes, “On the Lord’s Supper”:

> The loud ringing of the bells, which was also produced by bronze vessels, is likewise laid aside; the use of wood, everywhere lower than the sound of bronze, is necessarily struck so that the people may gather at the church.

Rupert says in *On the Divine Offices*, book V, chapter 29:

> By striking with a wooden mallet a board suspended and sounding, and inviting the people to the church, we signify this.

John Beleth writes in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 100:

> For the Office of Tenebrae, one must not strike the bells, but wooden boards.

Guillermus Durandus writes in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 71:

> They no longer strike the bells, but a signal is made with a board … The use of wood, being lower than the sound of bronze, demonstrates this, and for that reason the Eastern Church still retains the use of wood, so that the people may be made humbler.

The Roman Missal of about two hundred years ago, and the Missal of 1658 for the day of the Lord’s Supper, agree:

> Once the signal has been made with the board, the brothers gather.

(185) Six psalms. Today only five are sung, and the *Benedictus* is omitted; but Vespers conclude with a second prayer, different from the prayer after Communion. In the cathedral church, the choir is directed by two cantors from the second choir-stall, wearing violet-colored copes. At the Magnificat, the altar is incensed three times by the celebrant, who wears a cope and also completes Vespers with the prayer.

(186) On that day let the clergy and people receive Communion. The manuscript *Ordinarium* and the Rouen Ritual of 1651, part I, page 400, likewise prescribe that on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper all the clergy, including the priests, receive Communion from the hand of the president or provost during the solemn Mass, mindful of the institution of the sacred table at which the Lord himself made the disciples participants in his body. The Roman Missal of two hundred years ago likewise says:

> Then the brothers immediately receive Communion, and afterward the Mass is completed.

(187) Let half the hosts, without wine, be reserved for the following day. The Roman Order says:

> When the Mass has been completed, let them receive Communion in the established order, and let them reserve some of the holy sacrament until the following day.

Alcuin says the same in *On the Lord’s Supper*. Concerning that same day, the Orders state that some of the Lord’s body is to be reserved for Communion on the following day. The prescriptions found in both sources for Good Friday agree: everyone is to receive Communion on that day in silence. Amalarius, however, in book I, chapter 13, on the basis of the response of the Roman archdeacon, observes that the practice of the Roman Church was contrary:

> At that station where the pope greets the cross, no one receives Communion there.

[Col. 0099A] (188) Let them receive Communion again. This practice had already prevailed before John; Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, says:

> On the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, at the vigil of Easter, and on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, all must receive Communion without exception.

*Capitula*, chapter 41. It continued afterward, for John Beleth says in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 99, that all religious persons who are obliged to do so receive Communion. The manuscript *Ordinarium* of the regular canons of Saint Laud of Rouen states:

> On these four days no one ought to withdraw from Communion except for a reasonable cause.

(189) While they strip the altars. On the stripping of the altars until Holy Saturday, consult the Roman Order, “On the Lord’s Supper”; Amalarius, book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, the chapter “On the Lord’s Supper”; *The Jewel of the Soul*, “On the Ancient Rite of the Mass,” book III, chapter 86, etc. Therefore priests who celebrate private Masses on these days should consider how little this agrees with the ancient institution and ecclesiastical discipline.

(190) With water alone, the walls and floors. Alcuin teaches that the walls and floor ought to be washed with water in *On the Divine Offices*, under “The Lord’s Supper”:

> On that same day the altars of the church and the walls or floors of the church are washed.

John Beleth, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 103, and G. Durandus, book VI, chapter 76, support Alcuin. In the Church of Rouen, however, only the altars are washed with wine and water.

(191) Let them gather in a certain house and perform the Mandatum after the Lord’s example. In the nave of the church the Mandatum is performed for the poor, not for the clergy today. Concerning the Mandatum for the poor, the autumn synod of 1641 prescribes in article 4:

> Let the Lord’s Mandatum be devoutly performed on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper in every church, if possible, especially in communities of clergy and monks: washing, drying, kissing, and serving the feet of the poor with all humility, as it is commendably observed in this holy metropolitan church, the mother and teacher of all the churches of our province. Let priests take note that this washing of the feet cannot be omitted, since it is the Lord’s command and was instituted by the Lord; therefore it must faithfully be performed by all, especially pastors, according to the Lord’s example.

[Col. 0099D] (192) Let them go to the refectory. The manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud likewise says so. Since today the cathedral church has no common refectory, however, they go to the chapter house, as the manuscript *Ordinarium* and the Rouen Processional prescribe. There the Gospel of John is read from the beginning of chapter 13 to the end of chapter 14.

(193) Let the bishop offer each of the brothers a small flask of wine. See below, after the observations, what the manuscript *Ordinaries* of the Church of Rouen and of the canons of Saint Laud prescribe concerning the Mandatum.

(194) Let the Mandatum for the poor precede the Mandatum for the brothers. Formerly there were two Mandata in the Church of Rouen, as is read in the manuscript *Ordinarium* and Rouen manuscript official book; see also Rupert, *On the Divine Offices*, book V, chapter 22, “On the Mandatum for the poor,” and the Roman Missal of two hundred years ago:

> After the stripping of the altars, at the proper hour, when the signal has been made with the board, the brothers gather to perform the Mandatum. The senior wash the feet of the junior, dry them, and kiss them.

The Rouen Processional of 1588 mentions the Mandatum for the poor and for the clergy as follows:

> After the meal, let the Mandatum for the poor be performed, and let the Mandatum for the clergy be celebrated in this manner. A priest vested in an alb, together with the deacon and subdeacon, performs the Mandatum after the Lord’s example; and let as many of the senior members as are willing, wearing albs, wash the feet of the rest.

The *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen discusses the two Mandata with complete clarity and at length, under Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.

[Col. 0100B] (195) All the hours except Matins. The *Ordinarium* of the metropolitan church states:

> Let the hours of this day be said in silence at the four corners of the choir, after the manner of the Jews who were taking counsel concerning the death of the Lord.

PR. The Rouen manuscript official book says the same.

(196) Let them commonly recite the Psalter with the litany. Here “Psalter” may mean the seven penitential psalms with the litany, which are customarily recited every Friday during Lent after Lauds, or perhaps the Psalter of psalms discussed above. It may be better to say “the entire Psalter,” for the *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen prescribes:

> On that day let each of them recite the entire Psalter together, in order, in the cloister.

[Col. 0100C] (197) Let it begin with the reading from the book of Exodus. It now begins with a reading from Hosea.

(198) Let two deacons strip the altar of its linen cloths. The Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium* and official book read:

> Let two clerics strip the altar of its linen cloths.

The manuscript *Ordinarium* of Saint Laud of Rouen and the Roman Order say:

> Two acolytes.

The Missals of the Church of Rouen from 1516, 1527, 1538, and 1576 state:

> Here two cloths placed above the altar are to be removed from its two sides.

Today they are not removed in the diocese of Rouen.

[p. 136] (199) Except for the voice of the Lord, which is to be said in the other manner. This passage should be restored from the *Ordinarium* and two manuscript official books for the use of the Church of Rouen, in which it reads:

> Let the deacon, in an alb before the altar, read the Passion in the manner of a lesson, except for the voice of the Lord, which is to be read in the manner of a Gospel.

(200) Two priests vested in chasubles, etc. This and what follows are contained in the Rouen *Ordinarium*, after our observations, in the same wording.

(201) Let everyone’s belly cling to the ground. Thus Alcuin writes in *On the Divine Offices*, under “Friday, also called Good Friday”:

> When we adore this cross, let our whole body cling to the ground … We prostrate ourselves bodily before the cross and mentally before the Lord.

Amalarius says the same in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 14, “On the Adoration of the Holy Cross,” and Guillermus Durandus in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 77, “On Good Friday.” The same is found in the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium* and official books in the office for Good Friday. See the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the regular canons of Saint Laud of Rouen for the same Friday.

[Col. 0101A] (202) Let it be washed with wine and water. This washing is mentioned in the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium* and official book from the Bigot Library, which read:

> Let the choir finish the antiphon. When it has been sung, let the small cross, in commemoration of the blood and water flowing from the side of the Redeemer, be washed with water and wine. From this, after Holy Communion, let the clergy and people drink, and let some be reserved for the use of the sick.

The Rouen Processional of 1588 says:

> After the cross has been adored by clergy and people, let it be washed with wine and water, and let it be lifted up; then let the following antiphon be sung: “Above all things” (*Super omnia*), etc.

(203) From this, after Holy Communion, let the clergy and people drink. This is otherwise among others, according to the testimony of the *Micrologus*, [Col. 0101B] which notes that, according to the prescription of the Roman Order, on Good Friday unconsecrated wine was consecrated—or, more correctly, sanctified—with the Lord’s Prayer and the placing in it of the Lord’s body, so that the people might fully receive Communion. PR.

(204) The ministers of the cross vested in chasubles, etc. This and what follows are found in precisely the same words in the Rouen manuscript official book. See the *Ordinarium* concerning the office of this day, after the observations.

(205) Let all receive Communion, from the senior to the junior. The manuscript *Ordinarium* and the Rouen Missals of 1513, 1516, 1527, 1538, 1576, and 1604 read:

> Let whoever wishes receive Communion, as on the preceding day.

The Roman Order says:

> Let all receive Communion in silence.

The Rouen manuscript official book says:

> Let him receive Communion, and all the brothers, without the kiss of peace.

The *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint Laud of Rouen says:

> Let him and the others receive Communion in silence.

(206) Let them go to the meal of bread and water. This severe observance of fasting, found in the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium* and official book, prevailed not only among our people but also in other regions, as is evident from the Roman Order and Alcuin. Thus Alcuin writes in *On the Divine Offices*, under “The Lord’s Supper”:

> From this night until Saturday, some servants of God, imitating the apostles, remain fasting; others are content with bread alone, herbs, and legumes, or fermented drink.

Durandus confirms the same in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 77, “On Good Friday,” where he says:

> On Good Friday we eat only one kind of food.

The manuscript *Ordinarium* of the regular canons of Saint Laud of Rouen states:

> At the table let nothing be served except bread and water and raw herbs.

After the meal, Compline is not sung separately but communally, in a moderate voice, as also on the day of the Lord’s Supper.

(207) At the ninth hour of the day. The Council of Rouen held under our John in A.D. 1072, according to Orderic’s calculation, states in canon 21:

> It has likewise been established that on Easter Saturday the office is not to begin before None. For it looks toward the night of the Lord’s Resurrection; out of reverence for it, “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia” are sung, as is also shown at the beginning of the office, namely, in the blessing of the candle.

PR. [Col. 0102A]

Durandus teaches the same in *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 78. Hugh of Saint Victor, however, disapproves of the current custom in *On Special Observances of the Mass*, book III, chapter 21:

> The ancients, he says, were accustomed to celebrate this office when the day of Saturday was nearly over; but the weakness of modern people, hurrying to their meals, anticipates the appointed time.

(208) After the boards have been struck. These are used in most parish churches, but in the cathedral church the doors of the church are struck with a wooden mallet.

(209) While the clergy sing: “The Lord.” The gap that follows can be supplied from the *Ordinarium* of the metropolitan church, which prescribes many noteworthy matters for this day. Among them is the instruction that the blessed fire not be extinguished until the blessed candle has been lit from it:

> Let there also be, according to the Roman Order, another candle which, having been lit from the blessed candle, is carried to the fonts for seven days and placed in the fonts at the appointed place.

The *Ordinarium* adds:

> By the candle of Christ is signified his humanity; by the light in the wax, his divinity overshadowed by virginal flesh; by the new fire burning in the candle, the new doctrine shining from Christ upon the apostles and from the apostles into the world.

It also prescribes that while the lessons and litany are being sung, the priests catechize the children. If there is no child to be baptized, chrism and oil are not to be poured into the fonts; if there is one, they are to be poured in. PR.

Exactly the same matters are found in the manuscript official book for the use of the Church of Rouen from the Bigot Library.

Here it should be noted that the year from the Incarnation of the Lord must be inscribed on the Paschal candle. This inscription is mentioned by Rupert of Tuitien, *On the Divine Offices*, book VI, chapter 29; Honorius, *The Jewel of the Soul, On the Ancient Titles of the Mass*, book III, chapter 102; Blessed Lanfranc in the *Decrees*, page 266; Guillermus Durandus, *Rationale*, book VI, chapter 80; and John Beleth in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 108, as follows:

> The year from the Incarnation of the Lord is indeed marked on the Paschal candle; the indiction, or era, and the epact are also inscribed on the Paschal candle.
