These things are observed only in the cathedral church, where the chancellor inscribes them on a Paschal tablet and attaches it to the Paschal candle. We shall provide the tablet in its proper place for the present year, 1678, taken from the same candle of the cathedral church.

[Col. 0102D] (210) Those baptized may use a white garment. Thus Alcuin says in his letter to the priest Oduin, and Rabanus Maurus in book I of *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 29. Likewise *The Jewel of the Soul*, book I, chapter 243:

> The baptized wear white garments because they signify that they have recovered the innocence they had lost.

(211) That white garments are worn for seven days. Alcuin says in *On Holy Saturday*:

> Every day until the octave they are to come to Mass and receive Communion.

Rabanus likewise says in book II of *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 39:

> We call them the seven white days because those baptized on the holy night wear white garments throughout the entire week; for seven days they customarily attend the sacred sacrifices in the angelic garment of purity and with the lights of heavenly brightness.

The Council of Rouen held under Malger in the year 1050 likewise prescribes, in canon 19:

> Let those baptized in the same church in which they received the grace of regeneration, and in which they are parishioners, be presented for eight days in white garments, with burning candles.

(212) On the octave when the garments are removed. Thus Alcuin says in *On the Saturday in White Garments*:

> Today those who were baptized on Holy Saturday are divested of their white garments.

Amalarius says in *On the Saturday in White Garments*, chapter 51:

> Those who have been baptized in Christ and are newly born lambs return today to the fonts to strip off their white garments.

(213) With two others beginning the third litany. Today this litany is sung in the choir by three men in copes from the principal choir-stall, and is brought to its conclusion there, as can be gathered from the Rouen manuscript *Ordinarium* and official books:

> The first is begun by seven boys; the second by five clerics from the second choir-stall, wearing surplices.

These three litanies are described in the Roman Order and by interpreters of the sacred rites.

(214) After “Glory to God in the highest,” let the altar be incensed. The *Ordinarium* states:

> Meanwhile let the archbishop, or the priest with the deacon and subdeacon, come with candlesticks and censers; and, having humbly recited the Confession, let him begin aloud: “Glory to God in the highest,” without tropes; and let the entire choir prostrate itself.

It adds:

> Meanwhile let all the bells be rung, and afterward throughout all the abbeys and parishes of the entire city.

This is different among us, for, as we said above, the altar is incensed while the choir sings “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*); and while “Glory to God in the highest” is said, the choir is incensed by an acolyte.

(215) Let two men in copes sing “Alleluia, Give thanks to the Lord” (*Confitemini*) solemnly from the pulpit. The Rouen manuscript official book for the use of the Church agrees with John. In the cathedral church, however, the *Alleluia* with its verse is sung from the pulpit by two canon cantors who sang the litany, wearing copes. Two other canons from the principal choir-stall, also vested in copes, sing the tract before the altar; after the Gospel has been read, they withdraw to the sacristy.

(216) After the clergy and people have received Communion. The *Ordinarium* says: “After the priests and any others who wish have received Communion, let Vespers begin as follows”; and the manuscript *Liber officialis* of Rouen: “After the clergy and people have received Communion,” etc. We are surprised that some recent writers should depart so far from the institutions of the Fathers as not to approve the giving of Holy Communion to the people at this Mass, on the grounds that it is celebrated at night. Surely, if this pious custom is to be observed at any time, it seems especially appropriate on this night, when the mystical Passover of Christians is celebrated. PR.

140 What Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book II, chapter 38, shows to have been not only permitted to all but even almost necessary:

> After baptism and the litanies comes the celebration of the holy Masses and the communion of the Lord’s body and blood. Whoever among the faithful abstains from sharing in this on this night, I do not know how I should call him a Christian—except for those who, having been excommunicated for capital crimes, are doing penance.

The same is found in the Missals of the Church of Rouen of 1516, 1527, 1538, and 1576: “After those who wish have received Communion, let Vespers begin as follows,” etc.

(217) After the *Magnificat* has been sung and the altar incensed. The same is found in the manuscript *Liber officialis* of Rouen, but today neither the altar nor the choir is incensed, as the Missal of the Church of Salisbury in England, 1555, also prescribes: “The altar and the choir shall not be incensed.”

(218) When this has been done, a certain responsory is to be sung. No responsory is sung, but after “Thanks be to God” has been said, everyone returns home, as the manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* records: “Let *Ite, missa est* be said solemnly, and, having received the blessing, let them depart.” The manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud at Rouen adds: “After the deacon has said *Ite, missa est*, let the Mass and Vespers end together.”

[Col. 0104B] (219) After the meal. “Meal” does not mean the midday meal, but the single meal. In the earliest periods of the Church, the entire night was devoted to this celebration. Later, as the number of those to be baptized declined, the service and the beginning of the night began to be shortened, and Vespers, the meal, and Compline followed one another. At Rome the introduction of Vespers occurred later than that of the meal. For the anonymous writer of the Roman Ordo—whoever he was—observes that in his time, on this night, nothing was done among the Romans concerning the evening assembly (*vespertinal synaxis*), either before or after Mass; and shortly afterward he adds that on the same day the lord pope and the other Romans ate eggs and *formaticum*, that is, cheese. PR.

(220) At the tenth hour of the night, etc. This has been abolished in the Church of Rouen.

(221) The deacon, wearing the dalmatic, shall proclaim the Gospel reading. Now, wearing a cope, and preceded by the candlesticks and thurible, he proclaims the Gospel after the altar has been incensed.

(222) Each responsory shall be sung by two vested clerics. 141 Today in the Church of Rouen the first and second responsories are sung by three men in copes, but the third by four, namely those who have sung the invitatory; this is observed on the triple feasts of the Easter season.

(223) After the third responsory, the Office of the Sepulchre shall be celebrated. John Belethus discusses the Office of the Sepulchre at length in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 113, and William Durandus in book VI, chapter 87; they agree with our Office of the Sepulchre, which may be seen at the end, after our observations.

(224) When the prayer has ended. Here the procession to the crucifix seems to belong. It is strange either that it was not then in use on this day, or at least that John omitted it, although he mentions similar processions on the following days. The *Ordinarium* describes it and teaches that it customarily ended with a solemn blessing. “When this has been completed,” it says, “let them be blessed by the archbishop, if he is present; and let him kiss all the brothers, saying to each one: ‘The Lord has risen.’” PR.

In Greece both clergy and people devoutly observe this rite, for on the holy day of Easter everyone greets others in this way: “Christ is risen” (*Χριστὸς ἀνέστη*).

[Col. 0105A] (225) After the chapter. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* likewise says: “Then, in the chapter house, let a lesson from the Martyrology be read by one boy, followed by the verse: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord.’ Prayer: ‘Holy Mary, this saint, and all the others,’ etc. ‘World without end. Amen.’ Then afterward let a canon-deacon read from an exposition of the Gospel.”

(226) After Terce has been sung, a procession through the cloister. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* arranges the procession as follows:

> A procession follows through the courtyard, in copes; the priest and deacon in albs, and the subdeacon wearing a tunic, with the cross, candlesticks, and banners. The cantor begins: “Mary Magdalene,” with its verse and repetition. When this is finished, three from the senior choir sing “Hail, festive day” up to the station. At the station the cantor begins the responsory: “The angel sat.” [Col. 0105B] Three from the senior choir—now four—in the pulpit sing the verse: “The Crucified One on the cross” [another reading: “in the flesh”]. “Do not be afraid.” At the entrance to the choir, the lord archbishop, if present, or otherwise the cantor, begins: “Christ, having risen,” with the verse: “Let the Jews now say.” When this is finished, the lord archbishop, if present, blesses the people, and Mass immediately begins. If present, the lord archbishop is to have with him seven vested deacons and an equal number of subdeacons, 142 twelve of whom are to be from the junior choir, etc. During the procession everyone in the choir wears a cope with the celebrant; the deacon wears a dalmatic and the subdeacon a tunic. In place of the latter, an acolyte wearing a tunic carries the cross.

(227) Let them complete the Office of the Day with the greatest solemnity. The often-cited *Ordinarium* says: “If he is present, the archbishop shall bless the people before the *Agnus Dei*. When the *Agnus Dei* has ended, all who wish may receive Communion.” PR.

We present three episcopal blessings formerly customary in the Mass, from a manuscript Pontifical in the library of Rouen Cathedral; the Rouen ritual, part I, p. 503, wishes them to be restored in pontifical Masses.

(228) With a procession, etc. In all these matters the manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* agrees. On Easter Day, p. 88, it reads as follows:

> At Vespers, three from the senior choir in copes are to sing “Hail, festive day” during the procession, with the vested deacon and subdeacon, the cross, candlesticks, thuribles, and banners. Let the procession descend along the right aisle of the church as far as the western door [Col. 0105D] of the church. Once the procession has been arranged in the nave, one of the cantors begins: “Lord, have mercy,” and the procession returns to the choir singing: “Christ, have mercy.” When “Lord, have mercy” has ended, one from the senior choir begins the antiphon: “Alleluia.” Those who sang “Hail, festive day” during the procession are to direct the choir, and one of them begins in the right choir the psalm: “The Lord said”; the psalm: “I will give thanks”; the psalm: “Blessed is the man.” Four antiphons: “Alleluia.”

The same is found in the manuscript Rouen *Liber officialis* and in Durandus, *Rationale*, book VI, chapter 89. Today nothing is done in the Church of Rouen concerning this procession before Vespers or concerning “Lord, have mercy,” although they are included in the Breviaries for the use of the Church of Rouen printed in 1491 and 1578, and in the Dominican Breviary:

> At Vespers, “O God, come to my assistance” is not said; instead, after the Lord’s Prayer has been said, let Vespers begin as follows: “Lord, have mercy,” etc.

(229) Let Vespers begin with “Lord, have mercy.” That pious rite, which ignorance of genuine antiquity finally abolished in our own age, had come down to us from Roman sources. The Roman Ordo says:

> On Holy Easter Day, the schola comes early with the bishops and deacons to Saint John in the greater church, to the place of the Crucified One. They begin, “Lord, have mercy,” and proceed to the altar. When the deacons have ascended the platform, the bishops and priests are stationed in their places, and the schola before the altar. When “Lord, have mercy” has ended, the archdeacon signals to the leader of the schola; he bows to the archdeacon and begins “Alleluia” with the psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord,” etc.

Alcuin, *On the Divine Office*: “On the same day the entire ecclesiastical order gathers early at Vespers at Saint John in the greater church, at the place called the Crucifixion; there the schola begins: ‘Lord, have mercy,’ and with that chant they proceed to the altar,” etc. PR.

(230) “Let ‘Let us bless the Lord’ be said by those who sang ‘Alleluia.’” Now it is said by three from the junior choir wearing surplices.

(231) Singing the psalm “Praise the Lord, children,” let them proceed to the fonts. This praiseworthy procession rite is still observed in the cathedral and in many parish churches of this city. It is described in the manuscript *Ordinarium*, p. 88, in these explicit words:

> One of the senior members begins: “Alleluia,” and one of those directing the choir begins: “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord. Alleluia. May the name of the Lord be blessed,” etc. “Alleluia.” Thus, singing the psalm, let the procession go to the fonts with the deacon and subdeacon, the vessels carried by two priests in albs, and the blessed candle carried by a dalmatic-wearing deacon from the junior choir. Let the choir finish the psalm and say four “Alleluia”s, and “This is the day” without “Alleluia,” with its verse. Then, before the altar of Saint John, let them sing “Alleluia,” with the verse “Praise the Lord, children,” and let “Alleluia” be repeated. When this has ended, let the priest say: “Let us pray. O God, who made your Church … Through Christ our Lord.” [Col. 0106C]

> Solemnly, one from the senior choir begins: “Alleluia,” and one of those directing the choir begins the psalm: “When Israel went out of Egypt. Alleluia,” with the verse: “Judah became his sanctuary,” etc. “Alleluia, alleluia”; [Col. 0106D] the verse: “The sea saw and fled,” etc., “alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.” Let it be carried through to the end, and at the end of the psalm let them say: “Glory to the Father. Alleluia. As it was, Alleluia, alleluia. The Lord has risen from the sepulchre. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.”

> Singing the psalm, let the procession descend through the other aisle of the church to the western door. Once the procession has been arranged in the nave of the church and the final verse of the psalm has ended, three—now two—from the senior choir sing “Alleluia” in the pulpit, with the verse “Redemption”; “Alleluia” is not repeated at the end. When this has ended, let the priest say the verse: “Declare it among the nations.” Let us pray: “O God, who for us gave your Son …”

> Then, in the same place, let there be a commemoration of blessed Mary, with the antiphon: “Gate of Paradise.” Verse: “After giving birth.” Let us pray: “We beg your grace, O Lord …” 144 At the entrance to the choir, a commemoration of all the saints, with the antiphon: “Perpetual light.” “If you loved me.” Verse: “A voice of gladness.” Let us pray: “Look, Lord, upon our infirmities …” Three boys: “Let us bless the Lord. Alleluia.”

The same is found in the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578 and in the Rouen Processional, p. 168 and following. This most ancient rite is mentioned in the Roman Ordo, in Alcuin, in William Durandus, in the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud at Rouen, and elsewhere; those who wish the memory of baptism to remain indelible in people’s minds cannot disapprove of it.

(232) Singing with it the antiphon “Perpetual light.” During the Easter season, in the procession to the crucifix, our John contains no commemoration of Saint Mary, nor does the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud. It is nevertheless found in the manuscript *Ordinarium* and official books, in the Processionals, and in the Breviaries for the use of the Church of Rouen.

(233) Seven days in copes, etc. In the cathedral church, not long ago, on Saturday in White Week, five boys dressed in albs or copes directed the choir at Mass. The same is read in the manuscript *Ordinarium*, p. 93:

> At Mass no one in the choir wears a cope, but five boys in albs are to direct the choir. Office: “He led out his people.” Psalm: “Give thanks to the Lord and call upon him.” The five boys mentioned are to sing “Lord, have mercy,” “King and Father,” and “Glory in the highest,” the sequence “Almighty Father”; the five boys sing the sequence, and the choir answers with the remainder. Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God …” No commemoration, except as indicated above. Epistle: “Putting off all …” Alleluia, with the verse “This is the day.” Five boys in the pulpit: “Alleluia,” with the verse “Praise the Lord, children”; another verse follows: “May the name of the Lord be blessed.” When this is finished, the five boys begin in the pulpit: “Rejoicing, resound,” and the choir answers with the neume.

Today in the cathedral church everything is done as on double feasts.

(234) After Vespers, let a procession be made to the crucifix. The same procession rite is described in the manuscript *Ordinarium* of Saint-Laud. Today a procession is held in the diocese of Rouen after Vespers. The cross is not carried in it, but candlesticks and a thurible are, according to the manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium*. While the responsory “You are worthy, Lord” is sung, the crucifix is incensed three times by the celebrant, who wears a cope and kneels. Two men in the pulpit sing the verse “O how …” The verse and prayer concerning the cross are said, and after the commemoration of blessed Mary, at the entrance to the choir an antiphon concerning the saints is said, with its verse and prayer.

(235) With the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. During Compline throughout the octave, neither the Lord’s Prayer nor the Creed is said. Instead, after the *Nunc dimittis* has been sung, the antiphon and prayer are said; after “Let us bless the Lord” has been said, Compline ends.

(236) Let the eighth day be celebrated like the first. It is not celebrated in the same manner, but according to the rite of a double feast.

(237) Let the responsory “He has risen” be sung by two. That is, by men in copes who direct the choir.

(238) Each nocturn with one antiphon. From this and what follows it is clear that among our forebears, during the Easter season, the Office of Sundays and feasts consisted of three nocturns. The later change was brought about by considerations of brevity, not by discipline—a practice strongly criticized by William Durandus, book VI of the *Rationale of the Divine Office*, chapter 89, and by Radulfus, dean of Tongeren, in *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 10. PR.

(239) Let six lessons from the Apocalypse and three concerning the Resurrection be read. It appears from this that formerly three nocturns were customarily said in the Church of Rouen; they are found in the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud at Rouen. The Roman Church still retains them, as do many cathedral churches. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* agrees concerning the lesson from the Apocalypse. We, however, read from the Acts of the Apostles—except on Sundays—until the third week, during which the book of the Apocalypse is read; afterward the canonical epistles are read until the vigil of the Ascension.

(240) Let the ninth responsory be sung by two clerics. That is, only by two from the senior choir wearing surplices. This is still observed in the Church of Rouen for the third responsory on Sundays during the Easter season.

(241) The Morning Lauds with one antiphon: “The Angel.” At Lauds on Sundays until the Ascension, the psalms are said under one antiphon: “Alleluia.”

(242) On Sundays, let a procession always be held at Matins. On Sundays only until the Ascension is a procession held at Lauds; on the other Sundays there is no procession at Lauds, but one takes place immediately before Terce after the sprinkling of water.

[Col. 0108C] (243) Without tropes and Lauds. Durandus explains what tropes are in book IV of the *Rationale*, chapter 5, and after him Pamelius at the end of volume II of *Liturgicon Ecclesiae Latinae*. To this type of chant belong the so-called prose litanies, such as “Lord, fountain of goodness.”

As for “Lauds,” liturgical writers use the term in various senses. It is usually taken to mean “Alleluia,” as in Isidore, book I, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 13. That meaning does not suit this passage, which concerns an office celebrated with “Alleluia” but without Lauds. Since tropes and Lauds are mentioned together here, we shall more correctly understand Lauds to mean some ecclesiastical chant related to tropes. Durandus, in the passage cited, also calls tropes “Lauds convertible at the Introit.”

An anonymous monk of Saint-Ouen gives support to this conjecture in his *History of our John*, appended to the deeds of the archbishops of Rouen, in these words:

> Thus, when “Lord, have mercy” with its two rhythms—by which, in our judgment, tropes are meant—had ended, and “Glory to God in the highest,” which had been begun by Abbot Richard of Sées, had been completed with the greatest solemnity by the choir together with the Lauds, the whole was spent in awaiting the archbishop.

From this passage it may be inferred that these Lauds were customarily inserted into, or at least appended to, the hymn “Glory to God in the highest” in solemn Masses. We observed shortly before, from the *Ordinarium*, that this hymn was sung without tropes at the Mass of Holy Saturday. Of this kind was the prose “You whom the heavenly citizens …,” which, according to the same *Ordinarium*, was sung on the night of the Nativity of the Lord by clerics acting as shepherds, after the hymn just mentioned; likewise “O glory of the saints,” there on the feast of Saint Stephen. Finally, the notable chant “Christ conquers,” discussed above, could perhaps be counted under the name of Lauds. PR.

(244) With two “Alleluia”s and a sequence. The sequence is not said, but four “Alleluia”s are sung.

(245) While the responsory “You are worthy” is being sung, let the Apocalypse be read. In the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578, the Apocalypse is read after the octave of Easter. The manuscript *Ordinarium*, p. 2, agrees:

> After the octave of Easter, let the book of the Apocalypse be begun, and let three lessons be read from it on weekdays until the Sunday on which “Sing joyfully to God” is sung. On the following day, let the canonical Epistles be begun, and let three lessons be read from them daily on weekdays until the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension.

The *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 54, likewise says: “In the octave of Easter we begin the history ‘You are worthy, Lord,’ and the Apocalypse according to its order.”

(246) On weekdays, six psalms at the nocturn. During the Easter season only three psalms are said on weekdays.

(247) Let only one “Alleluia” be sung. The *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 55, and William Durandus, *Rationale of the Divine Office*, book VI, chapter 89, say the same. But in the Church of Rouen, in the Office both of the season and of the saints, four “Alleluia”s are sung from Easter to Pentecost, except during the Rogation days and on the vigil of Pentecost.

(248) If it occurs at another time, let everyone except the little ones fast. This is indicated by the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the Bigot Library:

> Likewise, if it occurs on the eighth day, let the commemoration be reserved for both Vespers, Matins, and Mass, and for the following day with fasting. Likewise, if it occurs on the Saturdays or Sundays of the Resurrection, let the procession and fasting be reserved for the following day.

In the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the cathedral church, however: “A Mass of fasting shall be sung, and everyone shall fast.”

Two points follow from this. First, formerly the Church of Rouen observed a fast on the feast of Saint Mark when it did not coincide with the octave of Easter or with a Sunday during the Easter season. Second, everyone except children and the sick fasted. A similar command is found at the beginning of the Rouen Breviary of 1578 and the Avranches Breviary of 1592, under “On the observance of fasting”:

> Let the priests of the churches command all who have reached adulthood to observe the prescribed fasts, such as the fast of Lent, etc. Let them expressly forbid all the things mentioned above, under penalty of mortal sin.

That fast was later changed into abstinence from meat, likewise on the Rogation days.

(249) To the church of Saint Peter, of Saint-Ouen. The metropolitan church still observes this custom. For the antiquity and dignity of the church of Saint-Ouen, see Surius in the Life of that saint under 24 August; Dudo, *On the Customs and Deeds of the Normans*, book II; William of Jumièges, book II, chapter 18; and Orderic, at the beginning of book III and in book VIII, p. 710. PR.

[Col. 0110A] In a charter of Riculfus, archbishop of Rouen, one reads: “The monastery of the Lord Saint Peter and of the blessed Ouen.” In the course of time, however, it came to bear the single name of Saint-Ouen, whose body was buried in this church. See the rite of this procession below, after the notes.

(250) 148 After Nones has been said, let them go to eat. Except during Lent, on other fasting days the fast was broken at the ninth hour, as is clear from the *Micrologus*, chapter 49, “On the Beginning of the Fast,” and from several other sources.

(251) Let the Rogation days be celebrated in a similar manner. Concerning the fast of the Rogation days, Rabanus says in book II, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 4:

> Before the day of the Lord’s Ascension, it is therefore the custom of the churches of the West to observe a fast for the three preceding days and to perform litanies; and this is fitting.

See Amalarius, book I, chapter 37, *On the Greater Litany*.

(252) Let the first six lessons be about the saints. The manuscript *Liber officialis* of Rouen has exactly the same provisions. Now, however, one nocturn is said, in which the first lesson is from an exposition of the Gospel, and the second and third concern the cross. A commemoration of the martyrs is made at First Vespers, Lauds, and Mass.

(253) Let a procession to the cross be held at Vespers and Matins, and let Mass be celebrated. No procession is held unless it is Sunday—that is, the procession before Terce. Neither Lauds nor the sequence is sung in any office.

(254) At Vespers, let the cantor direct the choir. The Office of this day has been altered in almost every respect. Today two cantors wearing copes direct the choir; four others from the senior choir, likewise wearing copes, sing the responsory after the former have withdrawn to the vestry. Formerly there were three nocturnal vigils; today only one is said, namely three psalms with three antiphons. Three lessons from an exposition of the Gospel are read in copes, with an equal number of responsories: the first and second are sung by three men in copes, and the third by the four who direct the choir.

(255) After Terce, let a procession be held. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* places the procession immediately after Terce, p. 109:

> At Prime, “Now that the daylight …,” etc. Then let them go to the chapter house [manuscript: “in the chapter house”], where one deacon from the senior choir reads from the remainder of the exposition of the Gospel. Let the procession bell be rung solemnly. The hymn “Now, Holy Spirit” follows at Terce. Then the procession follows, etc.

On that day the cathedral church is so disordered by the influx of the people that Terce, Sext, Nones, and afterward the solemn Mass are delayed until the fourth or fifth hour of the afternoon, at approximately which hour the condemned man is led out of prison. One cantor in a Mass cope begins the Office of the Mass, which the musicians continue. Few canons and few chaplains are present, because men and women occupy their seats; thus everyone wanders about the church, and the church resounds with noise and tumult and shines with unsheathed swords and weapons like a military camp. When Mass has ended, Vespers is said immediately, as during Lent.

(256) “History: God of all.” Among writers on sacred matters, this term sometimes means a psalm, as in book III of *The Gem of the Soul*, chapter 19: “We sing the history ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger’ for penance.” Sometimes it means a lesson, as in *The Gem of the Soul*, book IV, chapter 118, concerning Advent: “The history ‘Cry out with strength’ belongs not to the Ember Days but to the week immediately before Christmas.”

Sometimes, however, it means responsories and antiphons. Radulfus of Rivo says in proposition 12:

> It should be noted that antiphons and responsories belonging to one day or observance are called a history.

But most often it means responsories, as in the *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 54: “In the octave of Easter we begin the history ‘You are worthy, Lord’”; and in Radulfus of Rivo, *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 16: “In a similar manner the history ‘You are worthy’ and the history ‘If I forget’ are observed.”

[Col. 0111B] In the Rouen *Ordinarium*, however, “history” is frequently used for responsories; there one also reads: “And the responsory from the history, ‘God of all.’” The same usage often appears in the *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud at Rouen.

(257) Let the Acts of the Apostles be read. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* likewise says, p. 2:

> On the day after the Lord’s Ascension, let the Acts of the Apostles be begun, and let three lessons be read from them throughout the week until the vigil of Pentecost.

Likewise, in the Breviaries of 1491 and 1578, three lessons from the Acts of the Apostles are to be read daily until the vigil of Pentecost, except on Sundays and the octave day. Now, during the octaves of the Ascension and Pentecost, the Fathers’ expositions of the Gospels are read.

[Col. 0111C] (258) At the eighth hour of the day, let the people gather at the church. That is, at two in the afternoon; today, however, at the fourth hour of the day, namely ten in the morning. The order of the lessons and tracts has been altered in some respects; everything else is as on Holy Saturday of Easter, except for the blessing of the fire and candle.

(259) Let the peace be received. The manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium*, p. 113: “The *Sanctus* and *Agnus* solemnly, and peace is given.” See what we have said about the kiss of peace in the observations on the Office of the Mass.

(260) 150 After Vespers and Matins on the same day, let them perform a commemoration of the Resurrection at the crucifix. Today no procession to the crucifix is held after Vespers and Matins in which a commemoration of the Resurrection is made; the manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* reads: “No commemoration.” Nevertheless, this procession is found at First Vespers in the Fécamp Breviary of 1627.

(261) Let the eighth day be celebrated with the greatest solemnity, like the first. Now, however, it is celebrated with the triple rite of the second class in honor of the Most Holy Trinity.

(262) Let the hymn be begun by three clerics in copes while incensing the altar. The *Ordinarium* and practice of the metropolitan church differ, for the number three has now increased to seven—not men in copes, but men in chasubles. PR.

Today in the Church of Rouen the hymn is begun by seven men in chasubles who incense the altar, and it is completed alternately by them and by the choir, as is recorded in the manuscript *Ordinarium*, p. 114:

> Seven priests from the senior choir, wearing chasubles and carrying seven thuribles, are to come before the altar with the vested deacon and subdeacon, wearing a dalmatic and tunic. The priest in the middle begins: “O God, come to my assistance,” and together they begin the hymn “Come, Creator Spirit,” while all the bells are rung. Let them say the entire verse kneeling and incensing the altar. Choir: Verse, “You who are called the Paraclete.” The seven priests: Verse, “You are sevenfold in your gifts.” Choir: “Kindle the light.” Priests: Verse, “Drive away the enemy.” Choir: Verse, “Through you may we know.” Priests: “Praise be to the Father.”

> When the hymn has ended, let the priests, turning their faces toward the choir and continuing to incense, begin the antiphon: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and finish it in full. Let the cantor then solemnly begin the psalm: “Teach me your law.” Meanwhile the priests privately say Terce among themselves; when it has ended, they withdraw.

[Col. 0112B] On Monday and throughout the week:

> At Terce, the priest who is to sing Mass, with the vested deacon and subdeacon—wearing amice, alb, and stole—begins in the choir before the choir stalls: “O God, come to my assistance,” with two thuribles and candlesticks. Together they begin “Come, Creator,” incensing while the verse is being sung by one side. The left choir finishes the verse that has been begun; the right choir sings another verse, and in this way the hymn is completed. Let this be done throughout the week by turns.

> Antiphon: “They were filled.” Let the cantor begin the psalm: “Teach me your law,” while the priest with the deacon and subdeacon sit on the choir stalls. When the antiphon has ended, let the priest say the chapter: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled.” Responsory: “The Spirit of the Lord,” etc. The priest says: “The Lord be with you. Let us pray. O God, who on this day …” 151 When Terce has ended, let them withdraw, and let the cantor begin the Office of the Mass.

These provisions are also read in almost the same words in the manuscript *Liber officialis* of Rouen in the Bigot Library.

(263) Let flowers of various colors be thrown. The aforementioned *Liber officialis* says:

> While the hymn is sung, let the altar be incensed, the lights lit, and the bells rung; and let flowers of different colors, like the gifts of the Holy Spirit, be scattered from above over the choir.

For about ten years now this custom has rightly fallen into disuse, both in the cathedral and in the parish churches. It is described in the manuscript *Ordinarium*, p. 114, as follows:

> Terce follows, and when “Come, Creator” is begun, the attendants of the treasurer stationed in the lower walkways of the towers before the crucifix—that is, below—shall throw, as far as they can into the choir, oak leaves, clouds, and burning tow in great quantity. At “Glory in the highest” of the Mass, they shall make small and medium-sized birds, but not large ones, fly toward the choir, with clouds tied to their legs in a suitable number. The foregoing shall continue until the Gospel, and all these things shall be at the expense of the treasurer and the chapter in equal shares.

(264) If the feast of any saint occurs, let the Office be sung for that saint. During the octave of Pentecost, if a feast of a saint occurs, it is transferred until after the octave.

(265) On Tuesday, Mass of the angels. Today a Mass of the angels is not said, but the proper Mass assigned in the Missals of the Rouen diocese is said.

(266) Let the Epistle “I saw a door” be read, and the Gospel “There was a man from among the Pharisees.” The same is found in the manuscript *Liber officialis* of Rouen in the Bigot Library and in the Missals of the Church of Rouen of 1516, 1527, 1538, and 1576. Today the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Romans, chapter 11, is read: “O the depth …,” etc.; and the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 28: “Jesus said to his disciples: ‘All power has been given to me.’”

(267) Let the history of Kings and Chronicles be begun. The books of Chronicles are not read in the Church of Rouen, but only the four books of Kings, until the Sunday nearest the Kalends of August.

(268) The Book of Tobit and Ezra. Ezra is not read, but only the Book of Tobit in the third week of September; in the fourth and fifth weeks, Judith and Esther are read.

[Col. 0113B] (269) After Matins, only Lauds for the dead. In the cathedral church, 152 they are said after the nocturn and before Compline.

(270) At Saturday Vespers and at Sunday Matins, let something concerning the cross be sung. In the manuscript *Ordinarium* of the canons of Saint-Laud:

> From the eighth day after Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, at every Vespers and Matins let a commemoration of the holy cross be made, except on double feasts.

At the procession after Vespers on Saturday, nothing concerning the cross is sung, but rather concerning blessed Mary, although the manuscript Rouen *Ordinarium* reads:

> Let the procession follow, with the antiphon: “O cross more radiant than the stars.” Verse: “All the earth.” Prayer: “O God, who …”

At Sunday Matins no procession is held outside the Easter season, unless one understands this to mean the procession held immediately before Terce after the sprinkling of water.

(271) The final blessing does not follow. That is, the prayer over the people, which Amalarius calls the “further final blessing,” book III, chapter 37. PR.

(272) On account of the honor of the Sunday night. From this it is clear that Mass on the Ember Saturdays was celebrated toward evening. Because of the length of the Office and the sacred ordination, Mass often extended into the night of Sunday; for this reason these days were occupied with the Office, and the Office of Sunday was taken up in the Mass, as the commentators on the divine offices note.

(273) At the vespertinal Mass, indeed, at the hour. That is, around the fifth or sixth hour after midday.

[Col. 0113D] (274) It is forbidden by sacred authority to take place before Nones. In the ordinations practiced today, the conferral of orders does not take place before Nones has been said, but the Office of Nones is anticipated by six or seven hours. After the notes, we present from a manuscript the admonition customarily given in the ordinations of clerics.

(275) On Sunday, however, the ordination of bishops shall be celebrated. We have extracted the rite of this ordination, after the observations, from a manuscript of the cathedral church dating back 700 years.

(276) At Vespers, let the bells be rung in pairs. On this day all the bells are rung at Vespers as at Matins.

(277) Let two men in copes sing the responsory. The responsory is sung by four men in copes, as are the invitatory and the ninth responsory at Matins. At Vespers the cantor does not direct the choir; instead, two cantors in copes direct it at the psalms. At Matins the third and sixth responsories are sung by three men in copes.

(278) The deacon, wearing a cope, shall go with the procession to proclaim the Gospel. With the procession—that is, with the thurifer and two candle-bearers—he proceeds in procession after the altar has been incensed. The first thurifer goes ahead, followed by the two candle-bearers; after them comes the deacon in a cope, who is to read the Gospel in the pulpit. This is observed on all triple feasts, both of the first and of the second class. At the second, fifth, and eighth responsories, however, neither the altar nor the choir is incensed.

[Col. 0114B] (279) Let all the clerics be vested as far as the resources of the church permit. Today at processions and on the more solemn feasts, everyone wears a cope as far as the resources of the church permit. Some wrongly disapprove of the variety of colors, since even a very wealthy church cannot provide as many vestments of one color as there are clerics. Let them consider that the bride of Christ is surrounded by variety and, as the royal prophet David testifies in Psalm 44, is clothed around with varieties in golden borders.

(280) Let the clergy and any of the people who wish receive Communion. It is an ancient rule and practice of the Church that, after the clergy have received Communion, the people should receive it. This has now been abolished in many parish churches. For what reason, I do not know.

[Col. 0114C] (281) At the nocturns, let four lessons be read. In the Church of Rouen only three lessons are read during the octaves. The manuscript *Ordinarium* likewise counts only three, as do the Breviaries of 1491 and 1578, etc. The first lesson is from an exposition of the Gospel; the second and third are from the Sermons of the Fathers.

(282) All Saints. This feast is celebrated in the same manner as the Assumption, except for what follows from the Rouen Ordinary manuscript, p. 254:

“On this feast proper blessings are said. The first, second, third, seventh, eighth, and ninth lessons are read in copes; the others in surplices. All the lessons are from the major seat. The first, second, third, sixth, and ninth responsories are sung in copes. The lord archbishop reads the first lesson. For the first responsory, three from the major seat, in copes. For the second responsory, the lord archbishop, together with the dean and cantor, in copes. For the third responsory, three from the major seat, in copes. At the second nocturn, three from the major seat, in red copes: ‘O steadfastness of the martyrs’ (*O constantia martyrum*).”

(283) “154 Let neither the hymn nor the invitatory be said.” The Rouen Ordinary manuscript begins Matins in this way: “Two from the major seat direct the choir as at Vespers. Antiphon: ‘Direct me’ (*Dirige*). Psalm: ‘Hear my words’ (*Verba mea*), etc.” In the Rouen Breviaries of 1491 and 1578, the following is read: “At Matins, antiphon: ‘Direct me’ (*Dirige*).”

The invitatory is not read in John Beleth, chapter 161, *On the Celebration of the Office for the Dead*, nor in G. Durandus, nor in Honorius of Autun; for in Book IV of *Gemma animae*, chapter 116, I read as follows: “In the office for the dead we imitate the offices of the Lord’s death or burial; therefore the invitatory is not sung, and blessings are not given at the lessons.” Likewise, there is no invitatory in the Lexovian ritual of 1661 for the day of the commemoration of all the faithful departed or for the deposition of the deceased, nor in the Paris Breviary of 1557, the Paris Manual of 1581, or the manuscript Ordinary of the regular canons of Saint-Laud of Rouen.

This invitatory was first instituted by the lord Francis de Joyeuse, archbishop of Rouen, in the Rouen Manual of 1612, and by his successor, the lord Francis de Harlay I, in the Rouen Breviary published in 1618.

(284) “Let two direct the choir.” The cantor directs the choir: the Gradual is sung by two in copes, and likewise the Tract by two vested in copes; but in the cathedral church it is sung by four, because Mass there is celebrated according to the threefold custom.

(285) “Let none of the hours of the day be omitted.” From this and what follows it appears that at that time in the Church of Rouen, in addition to the office for the dead, the office of the day was also recited, as is observed today in the Roman Breviary. This is also confirmed by the following words: “After these offices, said ferially, let the festive office for the dead follow.”

(286) “At Compline.” The manuscript Ordinaries make no mention of Second Vespers or Compline for the dead, nor does any Rouen Breviary assign either.

(287) “The feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, etc.” The feasts of Saint John the Baptist, of the Passion of Saints Peter and Paul, and of Saint Michael in September are celebrated throughout the diocese with the rite of a second-class triple feast, like the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.

(288) “Let the invitatory at Matins be sung by three clerics.” At triple feasts it is sung by four; at double and semidouble feasts by two in copes, in the middle of the choir; at simple feasts and on ferial days by one in his stall, wearing a surplice. It is never sung by three in the Church of Rouen. 155

(289) “Let the eighth day be celebrated as a Sunday.” It is now observed with the rite of a double feast.

(290) “The Dedication of Saint Michael in the Sea.” This feast is called the feast of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea in the ancient Martyrology of the metropolitan church, on 16 October. Its veneration also spread abroad. For in the Council of Oxford, held among the English in the year of Christ 1222, it is listed among the feasts to be celebrated by rectors of churches and chaplains in divine worship and praise, with the prohibition of lesser servile works. P. R.

[Col. 0116A] (291) “At Vespers and Matins let the choir not be directed.” At these Vespers and Matins the choir is directed by two men wearing copes, but at the *Te Deum* the altar is not incensed.

(292) “Let the office be celebrated with Lauds and a Sequence.” Nothing is done concerning these Lauds in the Church of Rouen; the cathedral church has retained Sequences only on triple feasts.

(293) “Let Matins not be said.” In the diocese of Rouen both a nocturnal and a diurnal office are nevertheless performed for these saints.

(294) “Romanus, Audoenus.” Since the author’s purpose was to transcribe this book for the use not of one metropolitan church but of the entire province, no one should wonder if he relegated the principal patrons of our Church to the lowest class of saints and moreover either omitted or passed over briefly many matters belonging to the particular ceremonies of that same church, knowledge of which may be sought in the Ordinary. Such matters include the solemn processions of Palm Sunday and the Ascension, and the feast of Saint Audoenus, which at the time of Saint John was, as his History establishes, exceedingly famous. We have wished to note this deliberately, lest anyone should seize upon it as an occasion for disparaging our rites. P. R.

The feast of Saint Romanus, patron and archbishop of the city of Rouen, is observed in the church with the rite of a triple feast, but not likewise by the populace, who on that day are wholly occupied with business and walking about, so that the church has good reason to mourn because there are none who come to the solemnity. The Council of Rouen of 1581, presided over by Charles of Bourbon, archbishop of Rouen and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, complains at length in its fourth article and following, concerning divine worship in general, about these fairs and public markets held on feast days, and punishes rebels with excommunication. The feast of Saint Audoenus of Rouen, likewise an archbishop, is celebrated throughout the diocese with the rite of a double feast; but solemnly and according to the triple rite, the canons of the cathedral celebrate it in the church proper to Saint Audoenus. On that day a procession goes there from the cathedral church, which, after the processions described in our account, is the last.

(295) “Let the responsory be sung by two clerics without copes.” On Saturdays throughout the year when there is a responsory at Vespers—that is, in Advent and from Septuagesima until Trinity—it is sung by two in copes. The same applies on all Sundays to the invitatory.

(296) “At Matins let only one antiphon be sung.” Now nine antiphons are sung over the psalms, except during Eastertide.

# Ancient Acts Mentioned in the Notes

To the most religious father and lord, the lord Francis II, archbishop of Rouen and primate of Normandy.

It happened most opportunely, most religious prelate, that while your providence was diligently attending to the restoration of the former splendor of sacred rites, the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* unexpectedly came into our hands. It was written with singular diligence approximately six hundred years ago by John, then bishop of Avranches, who afterward presided over your metropolitan church, and was offered for the use of the province to his venerable predecessor Maurilius.

This book, preserved for our age by divine providence in the solitude of the Salicosan monastery, where it had long lain hidden, and not without damage, we now at last bring back into public view under the auspices of your name. We do so with the greater confidence because, by the stronger right of origin and institution, a work properly belonging to your Church ought to be not so much dedicated to your Eminence as reclaimed for it.

The sacred law commands that a bishop’s pallium be buried with his body and forbids its use to his successors. The case of writings and works is very different: they pass on to posterity with their reputation and usefulness and revive after being buried, however deeply, in darkness and silence. Such is this book. We hope that knowledge of it will be all the more welcome because it contains many things that are either still religiously observed in part in your Church or, although carried away rather than abolished not long ago by a sudden surge of change, still remain fixed in the minds of many and can readily be recovered.

Thus it is entirely evident that this excellent witness and defender of sincere antiquity has been divinely awakened, as it were from a long sleep, to hold a torch before the public studies of the clergy and, above all, to assist your diligence with the well-earned authority of its teaching. Receive, therefore, most religious prelate, John restored to life in a small and mutilated codex, and raised up by the hands of the clergy; restore him, by right of return, to a share in the place and honor of his see.

Whatever our small labor has added to his distinguished studies, regard it with such calm favor that we may acknowledge that, through the protection of your patronage, as much has been added to our strength for study and discipline as has been added to our predecessor’s glory.

Most devoted to your Eminence,

George Ridel, James Malet, and John Le Prevost, canons of your Church.

[Col. 0117]

The solemn processions that are customarily held throughout the year in the cathedral church of Rouen now follow, taken from the manuscript Ordinary for the use of that same church.

(From the Bigot manuscript codex.)

# Procession to Saint Gildard on Palm Sunday

[Col. 0117A]

159 On Palm Sunday. When Matins has ended, let the Lord’s body be carried to the appointed [or: determined] place in a bier by two priests from the second seat, wearing albs. Let twelve servants be around the bier, carrying twelve torches which the lord archbishop is to provide; and let two from the aforesaid [or: first] seat carry two torches belonging to the choir, and let them accompany the Lord’s body as far as the atrium of Saint Gildard . . . .

Order on Palm Sunday. After Terce has been sung [Note: Now only in the cathedral church.], the clergy and people of the entire city shall assemble at the mother church and proceed in an ordered procession, with the cross uncovered and with candlesticks, to the altar of the cross, where the blessing of the palms is to take place. The cantor shall begin the antiphon “Six days before the solemnity” (*Ante sex dies solemnitatis*). Another antiphon follows: “Six days before Easter” (*Ante sex dies Paschae*).

When the antiphon has ended, the archbishop or priest shall say over the branches the prayer “Our deeds, we beseech you, Lord” (*Actiones nostras, quaesumus, Domine*). When the prayer has ended, the vested subdeacon, turned toward the people, shall read from the pulpit, as though it were a lesson, with the title “Tell the daughters of Zion” (*Dicite, filiae Sion*).

When this has ended, the cantor shall begin the responsory “They surrounded me” (*Circumdederunt*), verse “For” (*Quoniam*). When this has ended, the deacon wearing a dalmatic shall read from the pulpit the Gospel “When Jesus had drawn near” (*Cum appropinquasset Jesus*). [Or: add “when it has been read.”]

The blessing of the branches follows, and the prayers “God, who gathers what has been scattered” (*Deus, qui dispersa congregas*)—“through all ages of ages. Amen”—and “Eternal God” (*Aeterne Deus*), in the manner of a preface, “whose Son for the salvation…” are said.

Afterward the lord archbishop or priest shall sprinkle holy water over the branches, and this prayer follows: “God, who by the branches of the olive…” (*Deus, qui per olivae ramos*). When these things have been completed, let the branches be distributed, and let the cantor begin: “The children of the Hebrews, taking up” (*Pueri Hebraeorum tollentes*). Another antiphon: “The children of the Hebrews, their garments” (*Pueri Hebraeorum vestimenta*).

When this has ended, let the procession proceed to the appointed [or: determined] place, with the cantor beginning the responsory “When the crowd heard” (*Cum audisset turba*), verse “And when he had drawn near” (*Et cum appropinquasset*). The antiphon “Brothers, have this mind among yourselves” (*Fratres, hoc enim sentite*) follows. Let other antiphons follow at the cantor’s discretion, as many as may be necessary.

Antiphon: “When the people heard” (*Cum audisset populus*). Another antiphon: “But first” (*Prima autem*). Another antiphon: “When the Lord drew near” (*Cum appropinquaret Dominus*).

When they have reached the place where the station is to be held, let a sermon be given to the people. When it has ended, five from the second seat shall sing in albs, before the bier where the Lord’s body was carried [or: add, “to that place”], privately before the light of that day, the following verses: verse “Behold, the King comes” (*En rex venit*).

When this has ended, the lord archbishop or priest, the cantor, deacon, and subdeacon, together with the choir, shall kneel and, while incensing, answer “Hail, whom [we call] Jesus” (*Salve, quem Jesum*). Five clerics: verse “This is he who came from Edom” (*Hic est qui de Edom venit*). The lord archbishop, cantor, deacon, and subdeacon, and the choir, while incensing and kneeling: “Hail, light of the world” (*Salve, lux mundi*). The five clerics named above: verse “This is the one who, like a lamb” (*Hic est ille qui ut agnus*).

Meanwhile, as before, the lord archbishop, cantor, and the others: “Hail, our salvation” (*Salve, nostra salus*).

When this has ended, the lord archbishop, cantor, deacon, and subdeacon shall turn toward the bier and honorably incense the Lord’s body. The cantor shall begin, with the lord archbishop and the vested ministers, while incensing; it shall be repeated three times, and the choir shall carry it to the end: “You are worthy, O Lord” (*Dignus es, Domine*).

Another antiphon: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (*Hosanna filio David*). When this has ended, let the procession return, with the cantor beginning the antiphon “All the crowds began” (*Coeperunt omnes turbae*).

162 The following responsories are to be sung: “The Lord Jesus” (*Dominus Jesus*), verse “They gathered together” (*Convenerunt*); “When the crowd heard” (*Cum audisset turba*), verse “And while he was drawing near” (*Et dum appropinquaret*).

When the ordered [or: decorated] procession has reached the city gate, six boys shall climb the tower [Note: Now they climb into a room of a nearby house.] and sing festively the verses “Glory, praise, and honor” (*Gloria, laus et honor*).

The lord archbishop or priest and the cantor, with the vested ministers, shall begin “Glory, praise,” while incensing and kneeling, and the choir shall carry it to the end. Again the six boys: verse “You are the king of Israel” (*Israel es tu rex*). The choir, kneeling, and the lord archbishop, cantor, and the others: “Glory, praise,” as before.

Again the boys: verse “The assembly in the highest places” (*Coetus in excelsis*); the lord archbishop or priest and the others as before. Again the boys: verse “The Hebrew people” (*Plebs Hebraea*); “Glory, praise,” as above.

When this has ended, the lord archbishop or priest, with the vested ministers [or: add “the cantor”], shall begin the antiphon, and everyone shall kneel; the choir shall finish: “In the name of Jesus” (*In nomine Jesu*).

When this has ended, the cantor shall begin the responsory “As the Lord entered” (*Ingrediente Domino*), verse “When he heard” (*Cum audisset*). The procession shall enter the city.

The responsory “But they took counsel” (*Cogitaverunt autem*) follows, verse “Testimony” (*Testimonium*). At the entrance to the atrium, the cantor shall begin “The chief priests gathered together” (*Collegerunt pontifices*).

Four priests from the major seat, wearing red and green copes [Note: Today, black copes.], shall sing this verse before the church doors: “But one of them” (*Unus autem ex ipsis*); the choir: “Lest perhaps” (*Ne forte*).

When this has ended, let the procession enter the church. The bier containing the Lord’s body shall be held crosswise before the church doors by two priests, and the clergy and people shall enter after it.

When this has ended, let the crucifix immediately be uncovered. The lord archbishop or priest, cantor, deacon, and subdeacon shall begin, kneeling, “Hail, our King” (*Ave, rex noster*), and the choir likewise: “Hail, our King.” The lord archbishop and the others shall say “Hail, our King.” The choir shall say “Hail, our King,” and thereafter complete the entire antiphon “Son of David” (*Fili David*).

When this has ended, four deacons from the second seat, wearing black copes, shall sing in the pulpit behind the crucifix, facing one another, the responsory “They surrounded me” (*Circumdederunt*), with its verse and repetition.

When it has ended, at the entrance to the choir the cantor shall begin the antiphon “The chief priests” (*Principes sacerdotum*), and the procession shall enter the choir while singing. Another antiphon follows, if necessary: “A great crowd of Jews” (*Multa turba Judaeorum*).

When it has ended, the lord archbishop, if present, shall bless the people, and Mass shall begin.

# Procession to Saint Audoenus on the Feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist

At Sext: antiphon “In the shelter” (*In velamento*), etc. Meanwhile let the procession be prepared, and note that if this should occur within the octave of Easter, it is to be celebrated in the following manner.

As the procession moves, on the way to another church, three from the major seat shall sing, as many times as needed, these verses: “Hail, festive day” (*Salve, festa dies*). When they have reached the church, no Mass is to be sung there; instead, a responsory or antiphon for the saint of the church is to be sung, with its verse and prayer. When this has ended, let the procession return through the eastern gate, and let the litany “Lord, defend us” (*Domine, defende nos*) be sung by three from the second seat.

If it is another day, let the cantor begin the antiphon “Arise” (*Exsurge*), and let the priest say the verse “Show us, O Lord” (*Ostende nobis, Domine*); prayer: “May they ascend to you” (*Ascendant ad te*).

Finally, let the procession move, ordered from the choir, with the cross, candlesticks, and banners, and with the priest, deacon, and subdeacon vested. Let them proceed to the customary place, and there let Mass be sung for a fast: “And at the movement” (*Et in motione*).

As the procession moves, let the cantor begin the antiphon “Be favorable” (*Propitius esto*), and then another, if necessary: “In the name of the Lord” (*In nomine Domini*). After these have been sung, let a responsory or antiphon for the saints through whose parishes the procession passes be sung at the cantor’s discretion.

Afterward let the seven penitential psalms be said. When they have ended, let the antiphon “Do not remember” (*Ne reminiscaris*) be said. Then let the fasting office “He heard from the temple” (*Exaudivit de templo*), etc., be said, as it is found on the Monday of Rogation Days. After Mass, let a procession be made before the altar with the prayers and supplications belonging there.

Then let three from the second seat begin this litany: “Lord, defend us” (*Domine, defende nos*), and let the choir answer “Lord, defend us” (*Domine, defende*). Let the cantors sing “Holy Mary,” etc., throughout the litany until they come to the church.

# Procession to Saint Eligius on the Monday of Rogation Days

When Sext has ended, let the procession be prepared. The clergy and people of the entire city are required to assemble at the metropolitan and mother church with biers, crosses [Note: These are for the most part carried by laymen, to the disgrace of the clergy.], [Col. 0120B] ecclesiastical banners, and standards.

When they have gathered there, let the biers and portable reliquaries be solemnly brought out from the church treasury. Each bier is then to be carried successively and in order to the choir by two priests [or: chaplains] from the second seat, receiving the common allowance, whose names are written on the list at the discretion of the registrar, and wearing albs. The biers are to be placed upon the choir’s altars.

[Note: The cathedral manuscript adds: “Each of these chaplains shall receive six denarii from the lord archbishop’s purse for each day of these processions, except those who carry Saint Anne’s bier. Each shall also receive one pair of gloves from the brothers of the confraternities.”]

Whenever each bier leaves the treasury, the cantor shall begin aloud the proper antiphon for that relic, which the attending chaplains shall sing continuously while accompanying the bier with the brothers of the confraternities, who are required to attend, until the entrance to the choir.

A weekly or daily priest, vested in all the priestly garments [or: vestments] except the chasuble, shall offer incense to each bier from its departure from the treasury until its entrance to the choir, using a thurible handed to him by an altar boy. He shall be accompanied by a deacon and subdeacon similarly vested, with two boys carrying burning candles in candlesticks as far as the first step of the altar, beside the entrance to the choir on the right. There the boys shall remain with the candlesticks.

Another boy shall present the sacramentary to the priest, who shall say aloud there the verse and the collect appropriate to that relic, ending quietly with “Through Christ our Lord” (*Per Christum Dominum nostrum*).

When this has been completed for the first bier, the same shall be done for each of the others, in the following order: first the bier of the body and head of Saint Severus; second, the bier of All Saints; third, Saint Anne’s; fourth, the Blessed Virgin Mary’s; fifth, Saint Romanus’s.

When these things have been completed, the cantor shall begin aloud from his choir stall the antiphon “Arise, O Lord” (*Exsurge, Domine*), psalm “God, with our ears” (*Deus, auribus*), antiphon “Arise.” A priest vested in the choir before the eagle lectern, with the vested deacon and subdeacon, cross, and candlesticks, shall say the verse “Show us” (*Ostende nobis*). Prayer: “May they ascend to you, O Lord” (*Ascendant ad te, Domine*).

When this has ended, let the procession move and go to the appointed place through the Saint Stephen gate. Each bier is to be carried by the two aforesaid priests [or: chaplains] as far as the church gate; from the gate to the entrance of the church to which the procession is going, it is to be carried by the brothers of the confraternity [Note: Today by clerics in albs.]

At the entrance, the priests shall again receive the bier and carry it into the church, placing it in its customary place. Before each bier two clerics [Note: Now two laymen dressed in surplices.] from the aforesaid [or: first] seat shall proceed with lighted candles and the candlesticks of the confraternities that have come from their confraternity houses, together with the brothers, as far as the church. Two men shall remain in the church to receive the candles and candlesticks, and shall proceed before the bier of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

During the procession the cantor shall walk in its middle, between the chaplains.

[Note: The cathedral manuscript adds: “The parish priests of Saint Dionysius and Saint Vigor shall precede him, in the dress of the church, with flayed rods, to maintain order among the chaplains.”]

[Note: This is not in use.]

[The parish priests likewise return with the procession. During the procession described above the cantor shall begin in the choir the antiphon “Be favorable” (*Propitius esto*), and other antiphons shall be sung according to what the occasion requires and according to the order prescribed for this ferial day, together with responsories and antiphons of the saints through whose parishes the procession will pass.]

Before the procession comes, during these three days, to the customary places, on each of the three preceding days the monks shall first sing a responsory or antiphon for the saint of the church, with its verse and prayer. The choir shall immediately sing the same after them. When the prayer has been said, a sermon shall be given to the people; afterward prayers shall be said before the altar with prostration.

When these have ended, on the return journey three clerics from the second seat shall begin this litany: “Savior of the world, save us” (*Salvator mundi, salva nos*). Thus they shall come to the church singing, and the choir shall answer “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*).

When the procession reaches the church of the Holy Savior, it shall stop there. After the monks have sung, the cantor, with the canons and clerics gathered together in the atrium of that church, shall immediately begin this antiphon: “For these men are most great” (*Isti etenim maximo*).

When the antiphon has ended, the priest shall say the verse “Let the righteous rejoice” (*Exsultent justi*). Prayer: “Be favorable to us” (*Propitiare nobis*).

When the prayer has ended, let the procession separate, and let the cantors resume the litany where they left it. When the procession has reached the church, let the litany end in the choir.

[Note: The cathedral manuscript adds:]

“Note that on each of the three days of the procession the religious of Saint Audoenus are required to send, through their servants, to the house of the cantor of the Church of Rouen, or of his deputy, at lunchtime, one large loaf, one gallon of good wine, a respectable dish of fish, and one large flask of milk fat. Thus on the first two days the vessels are returned, while on the third day they are left and belong to the cantor.”

# Procession to Saint Gervasius on Tuesday of Rogation Days

On the second day of Rogation Days, let everyone assemble at the mother church as on Monday, and let the cantor begin the antiphon “Arise, O Lord” (*Exsurge, Domine*), etc., as above.

Meanwhile let the relics be incensed, and let the procession assemble as on the preceding day. Let it go to the customary place and leave through the Saint Romanus gate, with the cantor beginning the antiphon “From Jerusalem they go out” (*De Jerusalem exeunt*).

Another antiphon: “With gladness” (*Cum jucunditate*), and other antiphons as many as necessary. At the cantor’s discretion, let antiphons be sung for the saints through whose churches the procession passes.

The seven psalms follow. When the procession reaches the customary place, our singers, immediately after the monks, shall sing for the saint of the church the responsory “Grant” (*Concede*). The priest shall say the verse and prayer, as required, and afterward a sermon shall be given to the people.

When this has been done, let prayers be said with prostration. When they have ended, the cantor shall begin the responsory for the saints, “O steadfastness of the martyrs” (*O constantia martyrum*), and they shall depart when the responsory has ended.

Three from the major seat shall begin the litany “With humble prayer and sincere devotion” (*Humili prece et sincera devotione*), and the choir shall answer. Let it be sung as far as Saint Nicholas of Beauregard [Note: In French, Beauregard, in the cemetery now called Saint Maur’s.]

When the procession reaches the entrance to the atrium of Saint Nicholas, let the litany be suspended, and let the cantor begin this responsory: “One day” (*Quadam die*). It shall be sung while passing through the aforesaid church.

When the responsory has ended, the priest shall say the verse “Pray for us, blessed Nicholas” (*Ora pro nobis, beate Nicolae*). Prayer: “God, who blessed Nicholas” (*Deus, qui beatum Nicolaum*).

When the prayer has ended, let the procession depart, with the cantor beginning this responsory: “From his tomb” (*Ex ejus tumba*).

When the responsory has ended, three from the second seat shall take up the litany where the three from the major seat left it and shall sing it as far as the Great Bridge gate [Note: At the place now called in French *Lacrosse*]. There a station shall be made as at the Holy Savior.

After the monks have sung [Note: Here it is not monks, but musicians replacing them, from Saint Maclou, who sing the antiphon musically.], the cantor shall begin the antiphon “These are holy men” (*Isti sunt viri sancti*). There the priest shall say the verse and prayer, as above at the Holy Savior.

Then the procession shall separate as yesterday, and the cantors shall resume the litany “Audoenus of God” (*Audoene Dei*), etc., ending it in the choir.

# Procession to Saint Nicasius on Wednesday of Rogation Days

Formerly, to the Holy Trinity of the Mount.

[Col. 0122B] 171 On the third day of Rogation Days, let everyone assemble as above. Let the procession move and go to Saint Catherine’s Mount (now in French, *Mont Sainte-Catherine*), leaving through the Saint John gate, with the cantor beginning the antiphon “Arise, O Lord” (*Exsurge, Domine*), etc., as above.

When this has ended, let the cantor begin the antiphon “Rise, saints” (*Surgite, sancti*). Antiphon: “Have mercy” (*Miserere*). Antiphon: “Many are” (*Multa sunt*), and others as many as needed.

The seven psalms follow. As the procession enters the church of Saint Michael, let the cantor begin the responsory “You, holy Lord” (*Te sanctum Dominum*), and let the priest say the verse and prayer. When the prayer has ended, let him pause as he wishes.

Afterward let the cantor begin the responsory for Saint Michael, “Holy prince” (*Princeps sancte*), and let them depart. When the responsory has ended, let the fifteen psalms be said.

When these have ended, let the cantor, after the monks, begin the responsory “Honor, virtue” (*Honor, virtus*). There, when the prayer has ended, let a sermon be given to the people. When it has been completed, let prayers be said with prostration.

When these have ended, let the procession depart, with the cantor beginning the responsory “To the Most High Trinity” (*Summae Trinitati*). When it has ended, let the cantor begin the responsory “The kingdom of the world” (*Regnum mundi*).

When this has ended, let the following litany be begun by three from the major seat: “The lofty hope of the world” (*Ardua spes mundi*). Let them sing it until the procession reaches the fork of Saint Michael.

Then let the aforesaid litany be suspended, and let three priests from the second seat begin this litany: “King, Lord, have mercy” (*Rex, Kyrie*); the choir shall repeat it. The same three: “Holy Mary” (*Sancta Maria*). Then three deacons from the second seat: “King of virgins” (*Rex virginum*). Three subdeacons from the same seat: “To your servants” (*Servis tuis*).

Thus let them lead the procession as far as Saint Macutus (in French, Saint-Maclou), and let a station be made there. When the monks have sung and the prayer has been said, let the cantor begin in the atrium of Saint Macutus the antiphon “They rejoice in heaven” (*Gaudent in coelis*) [Note: Today “O how glorious” (*O quam gloriosum est*) is sung.]

When it has ended and the prayer has been said, let the procession separate and depart, with the cantor beginning the responsory “In your circuit” (*In circuitu tuo*), with its verse and repetition. When it has ended, let the cantors resume the litany and let it be sung as before as far as the gate toward Magdalen.

At the entrance to the church, let the cantor begin this antiphon: “Savior of the world” (*Salvator mundi*), and let it end in the choir.

# Procession on the Ascension of the Lord

[Col. 0122D]

The procession follows. Let it leave through the eastern gate and go to the old tower (in French, *la Vieille-Tour*).

First let the cantor begin the responsory “It is time for me to return” (*Tempus est ut revertar*), verse “I leave you peace” (*Pacem relinquo*), and other responsories with their verses, as many as desired.

When this has been completed, let three from the major seat sing these verses: “Hail, festive day” (*Salve, festa dies*) until they reach the place where it is customary to release the chained prisoner.

On the return journey, let the cantors sing this verse: “Release the chained” (*Solve catenatos*), and other verses until they come to the western doors of the church. There two priest-canons, dressed in albs, standing in the tower and facing the people, shall begin and complete the responsory “Men of Galilee” (*Viri Galilaei*).

When it has ended, the lord archbishop or priest and the cantor, with the vested ministers, shall begin “You, King of glory, Christ” (*Tu, rex gloriae, Christe*).

The right choir: “You are the eternal Son of the Father” (*Tu patris sempiternus es Filius*); the left choir: “You, for our deliverance” (*Tu ad liberandum*). Thus they shall sing alternately as far as “make eternal”; the lord archbishop and the others [continue], and the cantor shall begin “O King of glory, Lord of hosts” (*O rex gloriae, Domine virtutum*).

When the antiphon has ended, let the procession enter the church. The bier of Saint Romanus shall be held crosswise before the church doors by two priests in albs, and the people shall enter after it, with the cantor beginning the responsory “All beauty” (*Omnis pulchritudo*), with its verse and repetition. The procession shall ascend to the choir.

When the responsory has ended, Mass shall begin.

# Procession after Terce on the Feast of Corpus Christi

The procession follows in copes through the atrium. The bier containing Christ’s body shall be carried honorably by two priests dressed in white chasubles, and with them four boys in albs shall incense the bier.

[Col. 0123B] [Note: The cathedral manuscript adds: “And two other clerics who carry two wax torches around the bier.”]

As the procession moves, the cantor shall begin the responsory “A certain man made” (*Homo quidam fecit*), verse “Come” (*Venite*).

When the responsory has ended, three from the major seat shall sing “Hail, festive day” (*Salve, festa dies*), “By which God gave food” (*Qua Deus in cibum*).

At the station “The Word was made flesh” (*Verbum caro factum est*)—or “I am the bread” (*Ego sum panis*)—three from the major seat shall sing from the pulpit the verse “In the beginning was” (*In principio erat*), “full of grace” (*Plenum gratiae*).

When this has ended, the priest, with the deacon and cantor, shall sing before the bier, which is to be held crosswise in the middle of the nave, the following verses, while incensing and kneeling:

Verse: “Hail, true body, born” (*Ave, verum corpus natum*). The choir shall repeat the same [Note: It is not repeated; instead, the choir continues.]

Kneeling, verse: “Truly suffering” (*Vere passum*). The choir likewise.

Verse: “Whose side” (*Cujus latus*). The choir likewise.

When these have ended, at the entrance to the choir the antiphon “O how sweet it is!” (*O quam suavis est!*) shall be begun. When the antiphon has ended, the lord archbishop shall give the blessing, if he is present. Mass follows, etc.

# Procession to Saint Audoenus on the Feast of Saint Audoenus, Archbishop of Rouen

The procession follows to Saint Audoenus, and Vespers for Saint Audoenus shall be celebrated there festively.

Antiphon: “I shall make him like” (*Similabo*). Ferial psalms [Note: On this day the ancient custom of the Church of Rouen is retained.] Antiphon: “Confessor of the Lord” (*Confessor Domini*). Antiphon: “This is the one who before” (*Iste est qui ante*). Antiphon: “He loved him” (*Amavit eum*). Antiphon: “He led the just man” (*Justum deduxit*).

Chapter: “Behold the priest” (*Ecce sacerdos*). Responsory: “The soldier of Christ” (*Miles Christi*). Hymn: “This confessor” (*Iste confessor*). Verse: “Pray for us, blessed one” (*Ora pro nobis, beate*). Antiphon: “Receive our offering” (*Suscipe nostra*), with threefold repetition. Psalm: “My soul magnifies” (*Magnificat*). Prayer from the Common.

When Vespers has ended, let the procession return to the church.

On the following day, let the procession go to Saint Audoenus, as at Vespers, after Sext has ended and after the principal Mass [Note: This is said of Saint Bartholomew in the cathedral church]. Let everyone be in the procession with the monks, and let Mass be celebrated in copes.

[Note: The cathedral manuscript adds: “The abbot and Convent of Saint Audoenus shall pay the lords of the chapter, through their procurator, one hundred solidi. Each canon present is to receive two solidi, and each of the seven religious from Saint-Laud two solidi; the choirboys are to receive five solidi. The remainder is to be distributed among the chaplains receiving the common allowance. The altar boys are also to receive the vessel in which the holy water is carried, filled with good wine from the cellar of Saint Audoenus.”]

After Mass, let the procession return to the church. Let them depart in peace, and from there go to the meal.

[Col. 0123]

# Certain Fragments Taken from the Manuscript Ordinary of the Cathedral Church of Rouen

## First Sunday of Advent, at Matins

[Col. 0123C]

Three from the second seat: responsory “Looking from afar” (*Aspiciens a longe*), and each of them is to receive one gallon of wine [Note: Now solidi.] from the archbishop’s cellar.

On the ninth day before the Nativity of the Lord, let the antiphons beginning with *O* be begun. They are not to be followed by prayers, but commemorations are nevertheless not to be omitted.

The first is to be begun by the church chancellor, if he is present; if not, by one of the senior clergy who does not hold a dignity, from the left side. The same arrangement is to be followed on the right side.

The second antiphon is to be begun by the dean of the church. The third antiphon is to be begun by the cantor of the church. The fourth antiphon is to be begun by the sacristan of the church. The fifth antiphon is to be begun by the archdeacon of Vexin in France. The sixth antiphon is to be begun by the senior archdeacon. The seventh antiphon is to be begun at the cantor’s discretion, from the side of the weekly officer.

The lord archbishop shall begin “O virgin of virgins” (*O virgo virginum*). All the antiphons are to be repeated twice. After Compline [Col. 0123D], let them go to the customary places, or to the chapterhouse, and there let the following be begun: “O.” When it has ended, let them drink moderately and depart in peace. Amen.

And note that from the time these antiphons beginning with *O* are begun, the altars and choir are to be incensed while the *Magnificat* is sung.

## Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

Let the exposition of the Gospel be read by a deacon in a white cope [Col. 0124C] [Note: Now violet.] in the pulpit, with candlesticks and thurible: “When she had been betrothed” (*Cum esset desponsata*). Psalm: “Blessed” (*Benedictus*). Meanwhile let the altars and choir be incensed.

## On the Nativity of the Lord
