Then he shall continue the Mass. The Epistle to Timothy shall be read: “All Scripture is inspired by God,” etc. (II Timothy III, 16). The Gospel according to Luke: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful servant?” (Luke XII, 42).

“I believe in one God, the Father.”

Offertory. Then the new abbot shall offer two large loaves, two flagons of wine [another reading: two barrels filled with wine], and two torches with money fastened into them, according to the devotion of the new abbot, as an offering.

After the offering has been made, the new abbot and the assistants shall remain in their places before the altar. The bishop shall then proceed with the Mass and wash his hands, saying: “I will wash among the innocent,” etc. Then one host shall be administered for the new abbot.

The Secret follows.

“Receive graciously, we ask, O Lord, these gifts, and always and everywhere mercifully protect this elect servant of yours [another reading adds: and this]. Through the Lord.”

After the fraction, the blessing is given to the people, according to the manner in which the Mass is celebrated and the celebrant’s wishes.

After the “Lamb of God,” the bishop gives the new abbot the kiss of peace and gives him Communion.

Communion: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek,” etc.

### After Communion. Prayer

“May this Communion, O Lord, cleanse us from guilt and, in your gracious mercy, preserve your elect servant. Through the Lord.”

When the Mass has been properly completed, before the bishop withdraws from the altar, two assisting abbots—one on the right and the other on the left—shall lead the ordained abbot to the high altar, before the bishop’s presence. There the ordained abbot shall make his profession upon the altar in the following manner.

### The profession follows

“I, Brother N., humble abbot of N., such-and-such a place, promise verbally and confirm in my own hand the due subjection and obedience established by the holy Fathers, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to God and to holy Mother Church, to N., and to you, Father N., and to your successors.”

Then the abbot shall make a cross with pen and ink [French: *encre*, “ink”] in his own hand at the end of the document. Afterward he shall be led to his seat by the archdeacon, who says:

“Stand, and hold the place assigned to you by God; for God is able to increase his grace in you.”

Immediately the cantor shall begin: “We praise you, O God.”

When this is finished, all the brothers shall give him the kiss of peace, bending their knees before the father appointed for him by God.

[Col. 0149]

# BLESSING OF AN ABBOT OF CANONS

(From the same manuscript Pontifical.)

[Col. 0149C]

The election of an abbot of canons is arranged in the same order as the election of an abbot of monks described above. When everything has been completed according to the same rite—with psalms, litanies, and prayers—the following blessings are said over the elect.

Let us pray. Prayer.

“Be present to our supplications, almighty God, and let what must be performed through the ministry of our humility be brought to completion by the effect of your power. Through the Lord.”

### Blessing

“Bless, O Lord, this servant of yours, N., whom we elect to govern souls, so that he may exercise the most faithful care of his subjects: urging them to good, guarding himself irreproachably, always doing good, avoiding evil, and maintaining devotion in divine matters.

“Enlighten his heart, O Lord, with the grace of your Spirit. Filled with its fullness, may he despise worldly things, scorn prosperity, and remain strong and unconquerable in adversity. May he hate pride, love humanity, embrace charity, and always keep chastity before his eyes. May he always devote himself to the love of God and neighbor [manuscript reading: ‘may he always be called to it’]. May he rebuke vices, stand firm against the proud, lead the erring back to the way of truth, and make himself equal to the good.

“Unfold [manuscript reading: ‘unfold’] to him, O Lord, the treasure of your wisdom, so that he may know and understand, and teach others, the words of your sacred law. Instructed in the Old and New Testaments, may he do your will and bring it to perfection even to the end.

“Lord and Ruler, from whose gift everything good comes, give him the power to bind and loose his subjects, and to administer ecclesiastical affairs in such a way that he diverges in nothing from the truth. May he lead his subjects so that he makes them citizens of the heavenly homeland, and may he himself at the end deserve to hear from you: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew XXV, 21).

“May you deign to grant this, who live and reign, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Here the bishop shall hand him the rule of the canons and, reading it, say:

[Note: Something appears to be missing here.]

“Receive the pastoral staff of vigilant care, and thus keep watch over the Lord’s flock entrusted to you, so that, as a faithful and prudent servant, you may deserve to enter into the joy of your Lord.”

After this the Epistle shall be read, and the Mass completed up to the offertory. Then the new abbot must approach and offer two torches, with money depicted upon them according to his wish, together with two large loaves and two flagons of wine.

The collect, Secret, and post-Communion shall be said at Mass as stated above in the ordination of an abbot of monks. At that Mass the new abbot must receive Communion. Let the rest be done as stated above. Before the bishop withdraws from the altar, the new abbot shall make his profession in the same manner, and everything else shall be done as described above in the ordination of an abbot of monks.

[Col. 0151]

# BLESSING OF AN ABBESS

(From the same manuscript Pontifical.)

[Col. 0151A]

In the ordination of an abbess, the pontiff must celebrate Mass and bless her with two or three abbesses. Before the Mass or its Introit begins, some nuns from the abbey of which she has been elected abbess shall lead the elect before the pontiff, clothed in pontifical vestments and a chasuble. He must sit in the place of examination with his back turned toward the high altar. The aforesaid nuns shall then say:

“Reverend Father, our elect is present to receive her blessing.”

Question by the bishop: “Has she been elected according to the Rule of Saint Benedict by the sisters?”

The sisters shall respond: “The canonical election of the sisters has agreed upon her.”

The bishop shall also ask: “Do you have the written document concerning this?”

The sisters shall respond: “We do.”

The bishop: “Let it be read.”

When it has been read, the bishop shall say:

“Since, therefore, the votes of the sisters agree in her favor, we first judge her …”

And the rest as set out above in the ordination of an abbot of monks.

When everything has been completed according to the same rite—with psalms, litanies, and versicles—the pontiff shall say the following blessings.

[Col. 0151C]

### Prayer

“Hear, O Lord, our prayers, and pour out upon this servant of yours the Spirit of your blessing, so that, enriched with a heavenly gift, she may be able to obtain the gifts [another reading: grace] of your majesty and offer others an example of good living. Through Christ.”

Let us pray. Prayer.

“We humbly implore your almighty power, O Lord, that upon this servant of yours, whom you have deigned to admit to the sacred order (that is, sacred blessing or ordination), you may graciously pour out the gift of your blessing, and grant her the grace of consecration, so that what she receives she may, under your protection, preserve unharmed. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“Lift up your hearts.”

“We have them with the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

“It is right and just.”

[Col. 0151D]

“It is truly right and just, fitting and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God.

“Be present to our prayers, be present to our vows, be present to our acts of service, be present to our consecrations. You who wondrously arrange all things through your Word and provide what must be arranged; you who always adorn your Church with diverse flowers, illuminating her both with the examples of men and with the institutions of illustrious women; you who have also deigned to apply this servant of yours, from the inferior sex [another reading: weaker sex], to the service of your servitude: pour out upon this servant of yours, whom we faithfully dedicate to divine office, the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that her service may graciously please you at all times.

“May you deign to bless and sanctify her with the right hand of your power for the work of a ministry worthy of you, so that she may faithfully carry out the task of administration entrusted to her and be strengthened by the power of the sevenfold grace of that same Holy Spirit.

“May there rest upon her, therefore, we ask, O Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of wisdom and piety, and may the spirit of the fear of the Lord fill her.

“Grant her also gravity of conduct and disciplined living, so that she may meditate on your law day and night, keep your commandments, obey your words, devote herself to sacred reading, despise earthly and transitory things, and at all times serve good works.

“May she overcome every desire for wicked pleasure and hold to the love of honorable chastity, so that she may be able to meet you, her Bridegroom, when you come, with her unquenchable lamps, and be joined to the choir of prudent virgins. May she not be shut out with the foolish, but may she freely enter the royal door with the wise virgins.

“May every form of virtue abound in her: modest authority, constant modesty, attentive purity [another reading: purity of innocence], and spiritual observance of discipline.

“May the precepts shine forth in her conduct, so that by the example of her chastity she may offer all subject to her a pure model for imitation. Showing the good testimony of her conscience, may she persevere firm and steadfast in Christ Jesus, and, with your help, carry out the ministry she has received in such a way that, by your gift, she may deserve to attain eternal recompense. Through our Lord, etc.”

Then he shall give her the rule and, reading it, say:

“Receive the rule of holy conduct, together with the grace of sacred blessing. May he deign to help you, so that through this rule, together with the flock entrusted to you, you may be presented undefiled before the Lord on the solemn day of judgment—he who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Then the bishop shall give her the staff, reading and saying:

“Receive the staff of pastoral care, which you are to bear before the company entrusted to you, as an example of just severity and correction.”

The following prayer comes next, said by the pontiff in the manner of a prayer.

### Prayer

“Almighty Lord God, you caused Miriam, the sister of Moses, going before the other virgins [another reading: women] with timbrels and dances amid the waters, to come joyfully to the shore of the sea. We humbly beseech you [variant: we suppliants beseech you] on behalf of this faithful servant of yours, who today is established as abbess in the maternal chair over all the women subject to her [another reading: over all persons subject to her]: grant that she may so protect all your female servants [another reading adds: entrusted to her] according to the canonical [another reading: monastic] rule, so that, with your help, she may enter joyfully into eternal glory with them all. There, rejoicing [another reading: they rejoicing] with the angels, singing [another reading: they singing] new songs, may she follow [another reading: may they follow] the Lamb wherever he goes. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

### Prayer

“May your grace always bless this servant of yours, we ask, O Lord, and lead her blamelessly to eternal life. Through Christ.”

The collect of the Mass, the Secret, and the post-Communion shall be said, and everything else shall be done according to the same rite as previously stated for the consecration of an abbot.

[Col. 0153]

# BLESSING AT THE CONCLUSION OF THE SYNOD

(From the most ancient manuscript Pontifical of the library of the cathedral of Rouen.)

[Col. 0153A]

“May Christ, the Son of God, who is the beginning and the end, grant you the fulfillment of charity. Amen.

“And may he who brought you [manuscript reading: ‘us’] to the completion [another reading: absolution] of this council make you absolved from every stain of sin. Amen.

“Having been made freer from every guilt and also absolved [another reading: helped] through the gift of the Holy Spirit, may you return safely and happily to the dwellings of your own sees. Amen.

“May your care always advance, so that when the Judge comes your faith may keep watch and receive from the Lord the reward of vigilance. Amen.

“May he also give you the power to preach among the people, and may you always hold in your heart what you preach to others with your mouth. Amen.

“May the Lord hear you in the time of your prayer and give you counsel for uprightness, so that you may deserve to escape the punishment of Acheron. Amen.

“May he himself deign to grant this.”

[Col. 0153]

# EPISCOPAL BLESSING AT THE MASS IN THE NIGHT OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

(From the same manuscript Pontifical.)

[Col. 0153B]

“Favor your people, we ask, O Lord, with loving kindness, for whom you have deigned on this most sacred night to show your presence to the world. Amen.

“Guard with paternal mercy from every adversity your people, for whom you have deigned at this time to be born from a Virgin in the world. Amen.

“May it always recognize you as its Redeemer and truly comprehend your grace. Amen.

“May he himself deign to grant this. Amen.”

[Col. 0153]

# EPISCOPAL BLESSING AT THE MASS ON HOLY SATURDAY

(From the same manuscript Pontifical.)

[Col. 0153C]

“O God, who on this night, entering our death, conquered the Tartarus of hell by divine power, graciously receive the humble prayers of your household, offered with sincere devotion of mind. Amen.

“May those whom the consecrated water of baptism has cleansed from their ancient stains, purified through the bath by the aid of your protection, be presented before you in judgment such as they now emerged from baptism. Amen.

“And those who, by your mercy, have been recalled to paradise when sin had perished, do not allow to become exiles when the offense is renewed. Amen.

“And those who have once acknowledged you as Prince and Lord of the universe, may they never perceive an enemy tyrannizing over them through their invaded senses. [Manuscript: ‘who has once acknowledged …’] Amen.

“May he himself deign to grant this.

“The blessing of God the Father and the Son.”

[Col. 0153]

# ANCIENT ORDER FOR INSTITUTING A REGULAR CANON IN THE CHURCH OF SAINT LAUDUS OF ROUEN

(From a manuscript codex of the same church.)

[Col. 0153D]

The service for religious professed persons according to the use of Saint Laudus of Rouen follows.

The novice, coming after the offertory of the Mass with his master before the high altar, shall say while standing:

“Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live.”

[Col. 0154D]

Kneeling, he shall say:

“And do not put me to shame in my hope.”

He shall say this verse three times. When the verse is finished, the cantor shall begin the antiphon “We have received,” with “Glory be to the Father,” and afterward again “We have received.”

Likewise:

“The Lord is great.”

“Have mercy on me, O God.”

“Behold how good.”

Then the cantor: “We have received, O God.”

Afterward the litany is sung by two singers up to “Son of God.” Then the prelate shall bless the religious habit with the following prayers:

“We place the sign of our Lord Jesus Christ upon this garment, for guarding the divine purpose and so that the Holy Spirit may reign in the heart and body of the one receiving it.”

### Prayer

“O God, giver of good virtues and generous pourer-out of every blessing, hear our prayers, and deign to bless and sanctify this garment, which your servant asks to put on for preserving the purpose of holy conduct. Through the Lord.”

When this has been done, holy water shall be sprinkled.

Then the novice, still clothed in secular attire, shall approach the ordaining minister and, kneeling, stand before him. The minister, stripping him of his secular clothing, shall say:

“May the Lord strip you of the old man with his deeds. Amen.”

And, clothing him in a linen garment, he shall add:

“May the Lord clothe you with the new man, who has been created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth.”

The brothers shall respond: “Amen.”

Afterward he shall be clothed in the cappa or hood.

[Note: Here no mention is made of the square cap or the almuce.]

Then he shall return before the altar and kneel, and the prelate shall say the following prayers:

“Save your servant.”

“My God, who hopes in you.”

“Send him help, O Lord, from the holy place.”

“And from Zion protect him.”

“May the enemy accomplish nothing against him.”

“And may the son of iniquity do him no harm.”

“Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength.”

“Against the face of the enemy.”

[Col. 0155C]

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

Let us pray.

“O God, who do not desire the death of the sinner but always desire repentance and amendment, we humbly implore [addition: ‘help’] from your mercy: deign to pour out upon this servant of yours, who renounces secular actions, the grace of your abundant kindness, so that, enrolled in your army, he may be able, by serving you, to complete the course of this present life in such a way that, by your gift, he may receive the prize of eternal recompense. Through Christ.”

“Let us pray, most beloved brothers, to our Lord Jesus Christ for this servant, who, having received the religious habit, hastens to serve him: that he may give him the Holy Spirit, who will preserve in him forever the purpose of the religion he has undertaken, and defend his heart from the world’s hindrance and from secular desire.

“Just as his habit is changed, may the right hand of his power grant him increase; may it open his eyes from every human blindness and grant him the light of eternal grace. He who, with God the Father and the same Spirit…”

Let us pray.

“Holy Spirit, who have deigned to reveal yourself to mortals as God and Lord, coequal with God the Father and the Son, we ask for the immeasurable grace of your goodness. Just as you breathe where you will, grant this servant the disposition of devotion; and since he was created by your wisdom, may he also be governed by your providence. May your anointing, according to its customary grace, teach him about all things.

“Through the intercession of our most blessed father Augustine, whom you gave as the principal legislator of this holy institution, and of all the saints, turn him truly away from the vanity of the world. Since you are the remission of all sins, dissolve in him the burdensome bonds of wickedness.

“Make him burn eagerly for observing this holy purpose, so that amid tribulations and distress he may be able to breathe again through your unfailing consolation. May he, soberly, justly, and devoutly, grounded in true humility, obedience, and brotherly charity, complete with happy perseverance what, by your gift, he promises.

“May you yourself deign to grant this, who live and reign as God with God the Father and his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Then the novice shall rise and read aloud the profession written in his own hand:

“I, Brother N., offering myself, hand myself over to divine mercy, to serve in the church of blessed Laudus according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, and I promise obedience to Lord N., prior of the aforesaid church, and to his canonically entering successors.”

He shall place this profession upon the altar and, kneeling, pray. The prelate begins this antiphon three times:

“Confirm, O God.”

The choir responds:

“What you have wrought in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem.”

It is repeated three times.

The following prayer over him follows:

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

### Prayer. Let us pray

“O God, who kindle your servant N., turned from the vanity of the world, with love for the heavenly calling, enter into his purified breast and pour into him the grace by which he may persevere in you. Fortified by the protection of your guardianship, may he fulfill what he promised by your gift, and, having become the executor of his profession, may he attain what you have deigned to promise to those who persevere in you. Through the Lord.”

Afterward the prelate shall grant the novice, who is standing on his knees, the common fellowship of the congregation, saying this prayer of Saint Augustine.

### Prayer

“Although by the grace of baptism we are all brothers in Christ and have one Father in heaven, if we obey his commandments as we are able, without doubt we are united most fully when we are joined to one another through prayers and benefits.

“So it was with the primitive Church, in which there was one heart and one soul. Many, kindled by this love, sold their possessions and material resources, and, gathering together with the mother of Jesus, joyfully brought the proceeds into one common store. The apostles, having received them, distributed them to all according to their need.

“Thus this man also, inspired by God and strengthened by their example, desires to be joined to our fellowship. Therefore we grant him the common fellowship of life with us, insofar as we are able to merit it from God and it is ours to bestow, so that with the elect he may be able to receive the promised rewards from the rewarder of all good things.

“This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Then the novice shall kiss the prelate, afterward the superior, and all the brothers, beginning with the elders and proceeding in order. After the kiss of peace has been given, the prelate shall begin: “Come, Creator.”

When “Come, Creator” is finished, the prelate shall say:

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

Let us pray. Prayer.

“O God, who prepare a dwelling in heaven for those who renounce the world, enlarge the temporal dwelling of this holy congregation with heavenly goods, so that they may be held together by the bond of brotherly charity, preserve the precepts of continence with one accord, and, sober, simple, and peaceful, recognize that the grace given to them was given freely. May their life accord with their name, and may their profession be perceived in their conduct. Through the Lord.”

The prelate shall also make him swear, saying the following words:

“Do you swear to keep the rights of the Church, the statutes of the order, and the secrets of the chapter in this manner?”

He shall respond: “So I do.”

[Col. 0157]

# ORDINARY OF THE REGULAR CANONS OF SAINT LAUDUS OF ROUEN

(From a manuscript codex of the same church.)

[Col. 0157A]

## PREFACE

Since we have recognized that some of our predecessors or contemporaries in the church of Saint Laudus of Rouen, of which by the clemency of God’s call we are canons, have erred concerning the arrangement of the service—not in many matters, but nevertheless in certain ones—we have therefore resolved, with the cooperation of the grace of the same Lord and supported by the prayers of our brothers, to explain, in the brief compass of a small book, the service of our church, for its honor and their benefit.

This explanation concerns only the reading, chanting of psalms, and singing, without assigning the rationale for each individual matter, but observing as far as we could the use of the Church and the order of things. We do not undertake it while seeking titles of arrogance or temporal profits, but solely out of charity, serving—as we have said—the needs of the brothers.

Setting aside obscure wording and variation of sentences, we have aimed to make clear to the eyes not only of the prudent but also of the simple, in easy and lucid instruction, the manner and order of the nocturnal as well as the diurnal service. We have not at all abandoned the tenor of the ancient books, but have also inserted certain changes in the feasts made in our own times, adding carefully and faithfully whatever may have been lacking, insofar as the Lord may inspire us and bring it to our memory.

We begin from the start of Advent of the Lord, who may deign to come to our aid.

Let it therefore be known to all that Advent of the Lord is celebrated wherever Sunday falls between the fifth day before the Kalends of December and the third day before the Nones of the same month. Hence the verse:

“Nearer to Andrew’s feast, in whatever order,

The first weekday celebrates the Advent of the Lord.”

On Saturday before the first Sunday of Advent of the Lord, at Vespers:

Antiphon: “Blessed,” Psalm: the same.

Antiphon: “Forever,” Psalm: “I will exalt you.”

Antiphon: “I will praise,” Psalm: “Praise, O soul.”

Antiphon: “To our God,” Psalm: “Praise the Lord, for…”

Antiphon: “Praise, Jerusalem,” Psalm: the same.

Chapter: “It shall come to pass in the last days.”

Response: “Behold, the days are coming.”

Verse: “In the days…”

And this is it.

“Glory be to the Father.”

Hymn: “Nourishing Creator.”

The cantors of the week shall sing the responsory at the steps, in their habit.

Verse: “Drop down, O heavens.”

Antiphon: “Behold, the name of the Lord,” Psalm: “The Magnificat.”

While the Magnificat is being sung, the weekly priest shall put on a silk cope. With the candle-bearers preceding him, he shall incense the two altars and the prior, if he is in the choir; afterward the last stall shall be incensed, and then everyone, beginning with the elders.

Prayer: “Stir up, we ask, O Lord.”

“We bless the Lord,” said by the junior on the side where the weekly service is being performed.

If the feast of blessed Andrew occurs on that very day, the feast must be deferred until the following day. Nevertheless, a commemoration must be made of it at Vespers, after the first collect, under this antiphon:

“When he had arrived.”

Verse: “He loved Andrew.”

Prayer: “We ask, almighty God…”

Then follows the antiphon of Saint Laudus, “Worthy of praise,” etc. This commemoration is never omitted except on double or triple feasts; during the octaves of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost; during the three days before Easter; and during the octave of the Assumption.

During Advent, the prophet Isaiah is appointed for reading. The more elegantly and clearly he prophesied about Christ, the nearer to his Nativity his book is read.

It should also be known that on every Sunday throughout the year, when only the Sunday office is being celebrated, the first six lessons conclude with the book being read at that time, while the final three are taken from an exposition of the Gospel.

The following is also observed: at the end of lessons taken from the prophets, if they have been the Lord’s words, “Thus says the Lord” is said; otherwise, “But you, O Lord.”

On the first Sunday of Advent of the Lord, therefore, when Isaiah is begun, let the prologue together with the beginning of that book be read as the first lesson. This lesson is to be read by the cantor.

At Matins of that Sunday, the invitatory is *Ecce venit rex*, with Psalm *Venite*, sung by the two weekly cantors, etc. The first responsory is *Aspiciens*. The weekly cantors begin this responsory at the steps and sing the first verse, *Quique terrigenae*; repetition: *Ite obviam*; and the entire responsory is completed through all its repetitions. Then the cantor of the right choir entrusts the verse to the senior cantor of that choir, namely *Qui regis*, which he sings in his stall; the choir sings *Nuntia*, etc., in full. Meanwhile, the cantor of the left choir entrusts the third verse to the senior cantor of the left choir, namely *Excita, Qui regnaturus*. Thus the said cantors at the steps add *Gloria Patri*; after this, the precentor begins *Aspiciens* again, etc.

The ninth responsory, namely *Laetentur coeli*, is repeated, because *Te Deum laudamus* is omitted until Christmas; meanwhile the bell peal is sounded. This is always done on Sundays and on feasts when *Te Deum laudamus* is not sung. *Gloria in excelsis* is omitted until the Nativity of the Lord. For although good servants await the arrival of their lord with joy, they recall an even greater joy in his presence. Therefore *Gloria in excelsis* and certain other expressions of joy in the sacred office are postponed until the presence of the Lord’s Nativity, so that they may then be resumed with greater devotion and eagerness, and that angelic song, announced to the shepherds with great rejoicing, may then be repeated in their minds as though it were new.

At the chapter, the Gospel is *Cum appropinquasset*. Immediately after chapter, both on this day and on all Sundays—or on all days when a procession is held—the signal for the procession is sounded three times, followed by the summons to vest. The ministers then vest; meanwhile the signal is sounded for Terce. When Terce has been rung and *Pater noster* has been said, the weekly priest blesses the water. Then the weekly cantor of the choir in which the week’s service falls begins *Asperges me*. Meanwhile the priest sprinkles the water at the altars, as is customary, and likewise in the choir. Coming then to the steps, he says the verse *Ostende nobis*. *Dominus vobiscum. Oremus: Exaudi nos, Domine*. This prayer is to be said by singing on all Sundays except double feasts, on which another prayer is said, namely *Ascendant ad te*.

The procession then sets out, and this antiphon is sung: *Missus est*. The priest goes with the bearer of the blessed water, who sprinkles the water throughout the offices, first in the chapter, where he says this prayer: *Absolve, quaesumus, Domine*; then in the dormitory, etc., as contained in the collectary. At the cloister station, when the antiphon has ended, the priest says the verse *Fundamenta ejus*; prayer: *Via sanctorum*, read. Note that from Advent until Easter the procession’s station, customarily made in the middle of the church, is omitted. There, after the prior—or, if the prior is absent, the weekly cantor [“by the cantor”]—has begun an antiphon or responsory of Saint Laudo, the procession returns to the choir. At the steps the priest says the verse *Ora pro nobis, beate Laude*. Prayer: *Exsultet, quaesumus, Domine*, and it is said by singing; Terce also begins there.

Then the bell peal is sounded, and the Mass begins: *Ad te levavi*, etc., as contained in the books. At the end of Mass: *Benedicamus*. The reader for the table then comes to the steps seeking a blessing, saying three times: *Domine, labia mea aperies*, with the choir responding: *Et os meum*. At the altar the priest says: *V. Salvum fac servum*, etc., with the prayer *Averte, quaesumus, Domine*.

At this time, and from Septuagesima until Easter, at the principal Mass the deacon and subdeacon use chasubles unless the Mass is of a feast; on ordinary days during this period they are in albs, but during Lent they use chasubles. At a Mass of a lesser feast or of nine lessons, with solemn vesture—that is, tunicle and dalmatic—they serve the Mass. [Col. 0159B] When they use chasubles, the subdeacon removes his chasuble to read the Epistle and puts it on again after it has been read. While the Alleluia or Tract is sung, the deacon folds his chasuble over his left shoulder and wears it in this manner until after Communion; when he is to say *Benedicamus*, he puts it on properly again.

At Sext and None, as in the books. In the refectory, the homily *Cum appropinquasset*. Then another sermon, *Satis abunde*. When these have ended, Isaiah is begun if necessary.

At Vespers: antiphon *Sede a dextris*, Psalm *Dixit Dominus*, etc. Chapter: *Hora est*. Responsory: *Tu exsurgens*. Hymn: *Conditor*. Verse: *Rorate, coeli*. Antiphon: *Ne timeas*. Prayer: *Excita*.

Throughout Advent, the eating of meat and fat is discontinued; cheese and eggs are permitted.

## The Second Sunday

Note that on such Sundays with nine lessons, and on lesser feasts, at Vespers, Matins, and Lauds, the weekly cantors must begin the first antiphons and entrust the others in descending order, beginning with the seniors [manuscript: juniors].

On the Ember Saturday, at Mass on that same day, the office is *Veni et ostende*. It should be known that, since prayers are said before the Epistle on this day, *Dominus vobiscum* is said with none of them except the last, namely *Deus, qui tribus pueris*. On this day and on all Ember Saturdays, and at Easter and Pentecost, those who are to recite the lessons or Tracts at Mass must first recite them from a wax tablet on which they have been written. The tablet is to be made as follows:

“Today at Mass. The first lesson: such-and-such, namely one of the juniors. The second: another, ascending in order. The third: another. The fourth: another. *Angelus Domini*: one of the seniors, up to the verse *Benedictus es*. Tract *Benedictus es*: two.”

Four Graduals with their verses are likewise sung while seated. Tract *Benedictus es* [manuscript: *Tractus* for *Tractum*]: two at the steps, with the choir repeating *Et laudabilis* after each verse. At the end, *Benedictus es* is begun again. The Tract *Qui regis* is sung alternately by the two choirs, beginning the first verse on the side where the weekly cantor is serving. In the refectory, the reading is *Anno quinto decimo*.

The antiphons *O*, which are sung at the *Magnificat*, begin on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January and end at Vespers before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. Some, after beginning these antiphons, omit prostrations and prayers at Vespers; we, however, do not omit them but carry out the customary course. The first of these antiphons begins as follows: *O sapientia*, etc.

## The Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

On that day, after the morning Mass, the chapter signal must be rung more quickly and for a longer time than usual, so that all the brothers may be able to gather from wherever they are for the beginning of chapter. To ensure that no one is absent, this must be announced to everyone in chapter on the preceding day; for on the preceding day—or even earlier, if a Sunday intervenes—the brothers are shaved.

On this day, to demonstrate the joy and devotion of their hearts and to kindle them more fervently in love for the coming God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, the place where our redemption is to be announced—namely, the chapter house—should be prepared as honorably as possible. When the reader has announced it, saying, “In Bethlehem of Judah Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is born,” everyone shall immediately prostrate himself on the ground. While prostrate, they shall pray as devotion and reason dictate; when the superior gives the signal, they shall rise, and the reader shall continue with the remainder.

After this, when the Gospel has been announced, namely *Cum esset desponsata*, and the tablet has been read, the superior says *Benedicite*. Having therefore dealt with the matters to be dealt with in chapter, including the Masses to be said on the following day, the superior shall make arrangements for those who are to say them. [Note: [Col. 0159] Therefore the same priest did not celebrate several Masses.]

At the end of chapter, both on this day and on the eight following days, Psalm *Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes* is said. From this point no prostration is made at the Hours; from this point also the Hours of Blessed Mary and the familiar psalms are omitted; responsories with Alleluia are said over the Hours. So that everything may be completed unhurriedly and carefully, the lessons are heard immediately after chapter.

Accordingly, after everything that must be prepared inside and outside has been properly prepared before Mass, the entire bell peal is sounded. For this Mass the priest is honorably vested; the deacon wears a dalmatic and the subdeacon a tunicle. The entire office is performed festively, though it is sung more quietly than on the following day.

At Mass, the office is *Hodie scietis*. Prayer: *Deus, qui nos redemptionis*. The lesson is read in a surplice between the choir and the altar; it begins as follows: *Haec dicit Dominus Deus. Propter Sion*. When it has ended, the Epistle begins immediately: *Paulus servus Christi*. The Gradual *Hodie scietis* is sung and begun again by two in silk copes. Gospel: *Cum esset desponsata*, with candlesticks and incense. Offertory: *Tollite portas*. Communion: *Revelabitur*. At the end of Mass no signal is sounded; after a brief interval, two of the larger bells are rung for None.

In the refectory: *Cum esset desponsata*, followed by the sermon *Nativitatem Domini*, etc. Also from our Rule, namely *Ante omnia, fratres charissimi, diligatur Deus*, which is read once during the week by precept; the remainder is read through on the preceding day at supper or beforehand, as on the Wednesday before Easter. During octaves, however, it may be read at supper if necessary, especially on Saturday if convenient.

At Vespers, first two of the smaller bells are rung; at the second, third, and fourth signals, two and two are rung in their order, and then all are rung. During these signals all the church’s lights are lit: at the choir steps, a large candelabrum with seven candles; between the choir and altar, seven lamps; before the high altar, three candles in basins; around the crucifix, four candles; and before each altar, one candle.

Two men in silk copes direct the choir. The superior begins the first antiphon, which the right cantor assigns to the same prior, namely *Rex pacificus*, Psalm *Laudate, pueri*. The senior cantors begin the remaining antiphons in their order, assigned to them by those directing the choir. The chapter *Propter hoc sciet* is said by the superior in a silk cope, with the candle-bearers assisting him. Three men in red copes sing the responsory *O Juda*. The precentor begins the hymn *Veni, Redemptor*. Note that wherever the week’s service falls, when a double feast occurs, the right choir surpasses the left in such a way that at Vespers and Matins the items to be said or sung are begun in that choir.

The final verse of the hymn is *Laus, honor*. Verse: *Tanquam sponsus*. The antiphon *Dum ortus* is begun by the superior at both its first and final occurrences; the precentor assigns it to him, and it is sung three times. The superior, preceded by the candle-bearers and assisted by a cantor in a cope, incenses all the church’s altars. Returning to his stall, he is incensed by the cantor, while the candle-bearers remain there. Then those wearing silk copes are incensed in their order, first in the right choir and then in the left; afterward everyone is incensed, beginning with the seniors.

Prayer: *Deus, qui nos redemptionis*, which the superior says in his stall while the cantor assists him with the book. Three say *Benedicamus Domino*.

At Compline: antiphon *Miserere*, Psalm *Cum invocarem*, etc. Hymn *Salvator mundi*. Verse: *Custodi nos*. Antiphon: *Veni, Domine*.

## Matins

At Matins, the entire bell peal is sounded first. While the peal continues, two smaller bells sound until the brothers gather in the church. The invitatory is *Christus natus est*, sung by four men in silk copes. The choir is directed by two weekly cantors, who assign the antiphons as was said at Vespers, beginning with the seniors.

In the first nocturn, the antiphon is *Dominus dixit ad me*, assigned to the prior. The first responsory is sung by the weekly cantors in silk copes, namely *Hodie nobis*, verse *Gloria in excelsis*. All the remaining responsories, except the third, sixth, and ninth, are sung two by two. Three in copes sing the third responsory, and likewise the sixth, namely the prior and two of the seniors. Note that when the superior sings the sixth responsory with the others at the steps, the precentor must first begin the responsory before the superior and sing the verse with *Gloria Patri* for as long as the superior wishes.

The three Gospels are read in silk copes. The superior reads the final Gospel, *In principio erat Verbum*, preceded by two candle-bearers; whenever he reads in a cope, or says the chapter or a prayer, they assist him.

While the ninth lesson is being read, the deacon prepares in a dalmatic, the subdeacon in a tunicle, and the candle-bearers with the thurifer in surplices. They are to be ready for the repetition of the ninth responsory; then, proceeding in ordered fashion through the choir—preceded by the candle-bearers and followed by the thurifer, subdeacon, and deacon—they come before the superior. There the deacon offers incense to the superior. After it has been placed in the thurible, the deacon takes the Gospel book and asks for a blessing. Having returned the book to the subdeacon, he goes to the reading stand, honorably prepared between the choir and altar, with the ministers preceding him as they came, with great reverence. He announces the genealogy, not by singing but by reading it honorably.

When it has been read and the superior has begun *Te Deum laudamus*, the deacon places incense in the thurible and, with his procession, incenses the high altar and the morning altar [Note: [Col. 0161D] That is, the altar of the morning Mass.]. He then incenses the superior, to whom the subdeacon offers the Gospel book to kiss.

When these things have been completed and the candlesticks have been returned to their place, while *Te Deum laudamus* is sung in the choir, all the ministers who will serve the first Mass remain at the rear. The thurifer, having first incensed the deacon, carries the incense through the choir, followed by the subdeacon with the book. Meanwhile the priest vests honorably for the first Mass.

At *Te Deum laudamus*, two of the larger bells are rung; at the verse *Per singulos dies*, the bell peal—that is, all the bells—is sounded.

When *Te Deum laudamus* has ended, the superior says the verse *Ipse invocavit me*. Once *Deus in adjutorium* has begun, at the time when the first antiphon at Lauds is usually assigned, the precentor begins in the choir the Mass office *Dominus dixit ad me*, which is repeated three times. *Kyrie. Orbis Factor* is sung by two men in copes. The candle-bearers precede the priest; tunicle and dalmatic are worn.

The cantor presents *Gloria in excelsis* to the priest, and all sing it devoutly and solemnly. Prayer: *Deus, qui hanc sanctissimam*. The lesson is read in a surplice between the choir and altar; it begins: *Populus gentium*. When it has ended, the Epistle begins immediately: *Apparuit gratia Dei*. The Gradual is sung by two in silk copes and begun again, namely *Tecum principium*, verse *Dixit Dominus ad me*. Two sing the Alleluia, with a third in a cope joining them, namely *Dominus dixit ad me*. Sequence: *Nato canunt omnia*; the bells are not rung. Gospel with candlesticks and incense.

When Communion has been sung, the cantor immediately begins in the choir at Lauds the antiphon *Quem vidistis*, Psalm *Dominus regnavit*. While Lauds is being said, the priest and ministers remain silent. The second antiphon is *Genuit puerpera*, Psalm *Jubilate*. The weekly cantors assign this antiphon and the next three, and all end without a neume.

No chapter, hymn, or verse is said. When the antiphon has ended, *Parvulus filius*, without a neume, the priest immediately begins at the altar the antiphon *Gloria in excelsis*, presented by the cantor. Immediately after *Benedictus*, that same antiphon is begun and ended without a neume.

After this, following the prescribed order, the deacon adds *Ite, missa est*. When these things have been completed, all go to the dormitory with lanterns lit. On this occasion only, those who wish may lie down fully dressed. Note that at the Mass mentioned above the deacon brings the peace to the prior, and the cantor, receiving it from the prior, carries it to either side. If the prior is absent, the precentor receives and carries it, as stated.

When daylight has fully dawned, one of the larger bells is rung. On hearing it, all who are to serve at Mass hasten to wash and vest; the others rise promptly and sit in the choir until the bell peal is sounded.

For this Mass the priest and ministers vest as they usually do on Sundays, in white tunicles and dalmatics, as above. The sacristan must distribute candles in the choir to those singing, as at the first Mass. The office is *Lux fulgebit*, begun by the precentor. The lesson is *Spiritus Domini*, read as at the preceding Mass; when it has ended, the Epistle begins immediately, namely *Apparuit benignitas*. The Alleluia *Dominus regnavit* is sung by two, as the Gradual. Gospel with candlesticks and incense. The bell peal is not sounded.

When Mass has ended, they come into the cloister and wash their hands; after receiving books, they sit. Meanwhile the priests prepare for private Masses.

At Prime, two of the larger bells are rung. After Prime, chapter is held, in which only the love and sweetness of so great a solemnity should be discussed. Immediately after chapter, the procession signal is sounded. Whether it is Sunday or not, the procession takes place; the morning Mass is omitted. The procession is made without silk copes, except for the prior, who wears one. The subdeacon wears a tunicle and the deacon a dalmatic.

After Terce, when everything has been properly completed and the ministers are holding before the altar the items that must be carried, once the precentor has begun the responsory or antiphon, they proceed in this manner: first, the bearer of the blessed water; then the bearer of the cross; then the candle-bearers; then the thurifer; then the subdeacon with the book in a tunicle; and the deacon in a dalmatic. After them come the boys, and the others two by two, according to their order. The superior follows last in a silk cope.

As they proceed through the cloister, they make no station. Singing the responsory, they enter the church and, after making a station before the crucifix, stand until what is being sung has ended. At this procession the responsory *Descendit de coelis* is sung.

At the church station, the precentor begins the responsory *Verbum caro*; three at the lectern sing the verse *In principio*. At the entrance into the choir, the superior assigns the antiphon delivered to him by the cantor, *Hodie Christus natus est*. Then, after announcing the verse *Ipse invocavit me*, the superior says the prayer *Da, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus*. The bell peal is then sounded.

The office is *Puer natus est*. *Kyrie, Deus creator omnium*. *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is sung by three in silk copes. Prayer: *Concede*. The lesson *Propter hoc sciet populus* is read in a silk cope at the lectern; when it has ended, the Epistle begins immediately: *Multifarie*, etc. The Gradual *Viderunt* is sung at the lectern by two in copes and begun again. Alleluia: *Dies sanctificatus*, sung there by three in copes. Sequence: *Christi hodierna*. Meanwhile two of the larger bells are rung.

When this feast, or another double feast, occurs on a Sunday, the weekly priest first makes the holy water and immediately begins Terce. While it is being sung, he goes with the bearer of the water through the offices and completes the customary observances; afterward he returns to the choir to finish the Hour. At such feasts, all who do not sing Mass go to Communion, except those who deliberately abstain for some reasonable cause after consulting the superior. The same applies on all Sundays.

It should also be noted that whenever any double feast on which the superior is to celebrate Mass occurs on a Sunday, a blessing is given to the weekly reader for the morning Mass.

In the refectory, the reading is *In principio*, followed by the sermon *Vox spiritualis Aquilae* and other sermons; during the week they are taken up as needed after the daily Gospels.

At Vespers the bells are rung as at the vigil. The cantors direct the choir. The weekly cantor of the right choir begins the first antiphon, namely *Tecum principium*, Psalm *Dixit Dominus*. Another cantor of the left choir begins the second antiphon, *Redemptionem*, Psalm *Confitebor*. The other antiphons are distributed, and all end with a neume.

The superior says the chapter *Multifarie* in a cope with candles. Responsory *Verbum caro*: the cantors sing it in copes with a third cantor joining them. Hymn *A solis ortus cardine*. Verse: *Tanquam sponsus*. The superior begins the antiphon *Hodie Christus* at its first and final occurrences; it is sung in full, Psalm *Magnificat*. Meanwhile the superior incenses the high altar, and incense is also carried to the other altars. Prayer: *Concede, quaesumus*. The cantors say *Benedicamus Domino*.

Immediately three deacons in red copes begin at the steps the responsory *Sancte*. The procession then goes to the altar of Saint Stephen, which the superior incenses. The deacons sing the verse *Ut tuo propitiatus*. One of the deacons says the verse *Gloria et honore*. Prayer: *Da nobis*. The deacons add *Benedicamus Domino*. The procession then returns to the choir while singing *Inviolata*. Verse: *Post partum*. Prayer: *Deus, qui salutis aeternae*. The boys at the steps add *Benedicamus*.

At Compline: antiphon *Miserere*, etc.; hymn *Salvator mundi*. Verse: *Custodi nos*. Antiphon: *Alleluia, Verbum*.

## Saint Stephen

A simple double feast is celebrated for Saint Stephen. The invitatory is *Christum natum*, sung by three without silk copes. Hymn: *Deus, tuorum militum*.

In the first nocturn, the antiphon *Beatus Stephanus* is assigned by the deacon directing the singing to the senior cantor in the right choir after the prior; Psalm *Beatus vir*. The second antiphon, *Constitutus*, is assigned by another deacon in the left choir to the senior cantor there, etc.

The first responsory is *Stephanus autem*, sung by two at the steps. Likewise, all the responsories are sung two by two. The prior is assigned to the sixth responsory, as always on double feasts, and to the ninth lesson, etc. *Te Deum laudamus*. Verse: *Posuisti, Domine*, said by the superior.

At the *Benedictus*, the antiphon *Impii super* is begun by the superior after being assigned to him by the deacon directing the singing. The procession then goes to the altar. Meanwhile the superior incenses the high altar and the morning altar, and afterward the altar of blessed Stephen. When Psalm *Benedictus* and its antiphon have ended, the prayer *Da nobis, quaesumus, Domine* follows; the deacons say *Benedicamus Domino*.

On the return from the Nativity, the memorial is *Verbum caro factum est*. Verse: *Benedictus qui venit*. Of Blessed Mary the Virgin, the memorial is *Verbo*. Verse: *Post partum*. Prayer: *Deus, qui salutis*. The candle-bearers add *Benedicamus*.

At Mass, the office is *Etenim sederunt*. *Kyrie, Conditor* is sung by two in copes. The Epistle is read at the lectern: *Stephanus plenus gratia et fortitudine*. The Gradual, Alleluia, and Gospel are likewise sung or read at the lectern, etc.

At Vespers: antiphon *Tecum principium*, Psalm *Dixit Dominus*, etc., as above. Chapter: *Stephanus*. Responsory: *O martyrum*. Hymn: *Deus tuorum*. Verse: *Gloria et honore*. Antiphon: *Patefactae sunt*, Psalm *Magnificat*. Meanwhile the superior incenses the high altar and the morning altar. Prayer: *Da nobis, Domine, quaesumus*. Three cantors in copes say *Benedicamus Domino*.

Then three senior priests in copes begin at the steps the responsory *Apparuit*. The procession goes to the altar of Saint John, which the superior incenses. Verse: *Cumque complesset*. Verse: *Valde honorandus est*, said by one of the priests. Prayer: *Ecclesiam tuam*. The priests add *Benedicamus*.

On the return to the choir, the memorial from the Nativity is *Gaudeamus*. The memorial of Blessed Mary is *Alma Redemptoris*. Verse: *Post partum*. Prayer: *Deus, qui salutis*. The candle-bearers say *Benedicamus*.

## Saint John

A simple double feast is celebrated for Saint John, [Col. 0164B] which is called of the third dignity. In every respect the same observance noted for the feast of blessed Stephen is followed also for the Innocents and for Saint Thomas, without distinction.

After Lauds, a procession is made to the altar of Saint John. There, after the altar has been incensed and Psalm *Benedictus* has been said, the prayer *Ecclesiam tuam* is said. The priest-cantors add *Benedicamus*. There is a memorial of the Nativity, a memorial of Saint Stephen, and a memorial of Blessed Mary; the candle-bearers say *Benedicamus*.

At Vespers: antiphon *Tecum principium*, etc., as above. Chapter: *Qui timet Deum*. Responsory: *In medio*. Hymn: *Exsultet*. Verse: *Valde honorandus*. Antiphon: *In medio Ecclesiae*. Prayer: *Ecclesiam*. The cantors add *Benedicamus*.

Then three juniors, having taken silk copes, begin at the steps the responsory *Dignus a dignis*. A procession is made to the altar of the Innocents, which the superior incenses. Verse: *Accipiunt*. Verse: *Laetamini*. Prayer: *Deus, cujus hodierna*. The cantors say *Benedicamus*.

On the return there is a memorial of the Nativity, a memorial of Saint Stephen, and a memorial of Blessed Mary.

### Feast of the Innocents

At Lauds, a procession is made to the altar in the same manner as above.

At Vespers, the weekly cantors, with a third cantor joining them in silk copes, begin at the steps the responsory *Miles Christi*. A procession is made to the altar of blessed Thomas in the same manner as stated for the others.

### Feast of Saint Thomas

At Lauds, a procession is made to the altar as above.

## The Vigil of the Epiphany

At the vigil of the Epiphany, None is rung with two of the larger bells.

The solemnity of the Epiphany is celebrated with great reverence, because many mysteries are recalled in it. All the altars are prepared, and the bells are rung as stated above, except at Matins. Then, to awaken the brothers, the bell peal is not sounded, but two smaller bells are rung.

All the lights around the high altar are lit, except the three candles that are before the altar. One light is placed before each altar.

At Vespers the weekly cantors direct the choir in white copes. The first antiphon, *Tecum principium*, is assigned to the prior; the others are likewise assigned to the seniors, and they end without a neume. The prior, in a cope gilded with roosters, says the chapter *Surge, illuminare*. Responsory, in yellow and red copes: *Reges Tharsis*. Hymn: *Hostis Herodes*. Verse: *Omnes de Saba*. Antiphon *Magi* is assigned twice and sung three times. Prayer: *Corda nostra*.

At Matins the invitatory and hymn are not said. Instead, the antiphon delivered to the prior is begun by him as follows: *Afferte Domino*; the Psalm itself, etc. In the third nocturn, the antiphon *Venite* and the Psalm itself are sung entirely while standing.

Only on the day itself is the aforesaid antiphon sung with its Psalm. Throughout the octave: antiphon *Adorate Dominum*, Psalm *Cantate* I, etc. The homily is read in a cope with the candle-bearers. The ninth responsory, *In Columbae*, is sung by three in copes and is not repeated. To read the Gospel *Factum est*, the deacon comes with the procession, as stated for the Nativity of the Lord.

At Mass, the office is *Ecce advenit*. The cantors, with a third joining them, sing *Kyrie, Fons bonitatis* at the steps in copes. At the lectern: Gradual *Omnes de Saba*, Alleluia *Vidimus stellam*, etc.

In the refectory, the reading is *Cum natus esset*, with sermons relating to the same feast.

From the octave of the Epiphany until Septuagesima, the Epistles of blessed Paul are read. During the same period, food is taken twice daily, even on Friday, according to an approved custom.

Every possible care must be taken to finish the Epistles of blessed Paul before Septuagesima. Therefore, even if the time is short, they should be begun in the refectory on the day after the Circumcision. The history *Domine, in ira tua* is never begun before the Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany. When Septuagesima occurs on the first Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany, it is necessarily omitted.

On Monday, at Lauds: antiphon *Miserere*, the Psalm itself. The chapter at Lauds on all weekdays until Ash Wednesday is *Vigilate et orate*. Prostrations and prayers are resumed.

Note that if the period is long and the Epistles of blessed Paul do not suffice for the refectory reading until Septuagesima, readings from the saints are to be taken up.

On the Saturday before Septuagesima, Alleluia is said before None and is silent at Vespers. On this day, however, when the Purification of Blessed Mary occurs, since Vespers will be of the feast, Alleluia is said at Vespers and also at Compline; Septuagesima is then commemorated only at Vespers. From that day until Easter Vespers, at the beginning of the Hours *Laus tibi, Domine, rex aeternae gloriae* is said in place of Alleluia.

At Matins the invitatory is *Praeoccupemus faciem*, etc. At the first lesson the prologue with the beginning of Genesis is read. First responsory: *In principio fecit Deus*, etc. The ninth responsory is begun again. Verse: *Excelsus super omnes*.

From this point until Easter, holy Church suspends her instruments, namely the songs of joy: *Alleluia*, *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, and *Ite, missa est*.

Throughout Septuagesima, as was stated on the First Sunday of Advent, the deacon and subdeacon use chasubles at the principal Mass.

## Quinquagesima Sunday

In the refectory the reading is *Assumpsit Jesus*. Sermon: *Fides est religionis*. From this day onward, whatever feast occurs, the fast is not broken.

## The Beginning of the Fast

At the Beginning of the Fast the invitatory is *In manu tua*, etc. During these four days, only the proper chapters and prayers are said at Matins and Vespers, as on all the other days of Lent. At the Hours the Sunday collect is said, namely *Preces nostras*.

It should be known that from the Beginning of the Fast nothing is done concerning a feast of three lessons until Easter, except a commemoration and the morning Mass if it occurs on a Sunday, with the exception of Palm Sunday. It should also be known that if a feast of nine lessons occurs on the Beginning of the Fast, it must be transferred to the following day.

In chapter the reading is *Cum jejunatis*. On this day and on every Wednesday and Friday of Lent, silence is to be kept in the cloister. Moreover, in place of the procession customarily held on those days, immediately after leaving chapter each person must say Psalm *Miserere mei, Deus*.

After None, while the familiar psalms are being said, the sacristan rings one of the larger bells briefly three times. On hearing it, everyone in the choir removes his shoes, unless the superior grants them mercy because of the severity of the cold.

Then the superior comes before the high altar with the weekly priest and ministers, where a carpet must be spread. The superior begins the antiphon *Parce, Domine*, and those prostrate there say the seven psalms; the community likewise says them in the choir.

When the psalms have ended, with no litany but only *Kyrie, eleison*, the superior rises, takes the stole, and standing before the altar performs the absolution. Then, after the ministers have returned to their seats in the choir, the sacristan brings the ashes prepared from the palms of the preceding year. While the superior holds them, he blesses them and sprinkles them with blessed water, the subprior supplying the aspergillum. He gives the stole to the subprior, who first places ashes on him and sprinkles him with water. The superior then puts the stole on again and, as the subprior and the other brothers come with great contrition of heart and kneel before him, places ashes on each, saying to each: *Memento quia cinis es*, etc., while the subprior sprinkles each one.

Meanwhile the antiphon *Immutemur* is sung with the verses of Psalm *Deus misereatur nostri*; it is repeated as often as necessary.

After the ashes have been distributed and the procession has been prepared, the superior says from his seat in the choir the verse *Ostende nobis*. *Dominus vobiscum. Oratio: Concede nobis, Domine*. Then, after the antiphon *Exaudi nos, Domine* has begun, they go out through the cloister for the procession.

No one is to wear ecclesiastical vestments in this procession. After the antiphon has been fully sung before the refectory, with one verse of Psalm *Salvum me fac*, another antiphon, *Juxta vestibulum*, is added. When it has ended before the church entrance, two cantors begin the litany. As they announce *Sancte Joannes Baptista*, the procession enters the church. While the litany is being sung at the steps, the priest and ministers vest.

When the litany has ended, the office begins without a prayer: *Misereris omnium*. On this day and thereafter throughout Lent, every day until the Lord’s Supper, the deacon and subdeacon must serve at the principal Mass of the season in chasubles, including Sundays.

Prayer: *Praesta, quaesumus, Domine*, which the deacon must precede with *Flectamus genua*; the same is done on all weekdays of Lent. Epistle: *Convertimini ad me*. While it is read, the brothers put their shoes on again. Gradual: *Miserere mei*. Tract: *Domine non secundum*, to be sung alternately. Gospel: *Cum jejunatis*. Offertory: *Exaltabo te*.

At Vespers, the first signal begins to be rung when *Sanctus* is sung; at the second, *Per omnia*, it stops. After *Agnus Dei*, the second signal is rung. Communion: *Qui meditabitur*. When it has ended, the third signal is to be rung.

For the final prayer, which is said over the people, the deacon says *Humiliate capita vestra*. After this prayer the bell peal is sounded. The priest who celebrated Mass—unless it was a double feast, or a Saturday on which the weekly priest of the following week begins Vespers—begins Vespers there at the altar. After Vespers, following a brief interval, the bell is rung, and they go to supper.

### Friday

It should nevertheless be noted that from the Beginning of the Fast until the Lord’s Supper, on every day except Sundays, the seven psalms with the litany are said after Terce; on feast days, they are said immediately after Prime.

## The First Sunday of Lent

At Mass the office is *Invocavit me*, etc. Tract: *Qui habitat*, sung alternately by four, etc.

On this day after Compline, the sacristan extends the curtain between the choir and altar; at that time he also covers the crosses and images. From the second weekday of Lent until Easter, except on feasts, at the beginning of the principal Hour, when *Gloria Patri* is said, everyone together asks pardon over the choir stalls.

It should be known that in all Masses celebrated during Lent, the curtain must be gathered while the Gospel is being read; but once the Gospel has been read, it is to be spread out immediately. When, however, a feast is to be celebrated, the curtain is to be gathered immediately after the Mass of the preceding day has ended; nevertheless, on that day, while the Mass of Lent is being sung, it must be extended. During that Mass the brothers are not to bow over the forms at the Canon. On that day, after Compline, unless another feast occurs, the curtain is to be extended as usual.

It should be noted that on the Monday of Lent, at Collation, the Lenten homilies are to be begun. [Col. 0167A]

**Saturday of the Ember Days.** At Mass, the Introit is *Intret oratio*. The Collect is *Populum tuum*; at it *Flectamus genua* is said, and it is said without *Dominus vobiscum*, as are all the following collects, except the last one before the Epistle. The reading, *Angelus Domini*, is read up to the verse *Benedictus es in firmamento*; from that point the Tract begins. Half of its first verse is sung by four brothers together, and the remaining verses by pairs; but the choir takes up the first verse from the words *Et laudabilis*. Then, after the end of the other verses, it always repeats *Hymnum dicite* while seated. After the Tract has been completed by the four mentioned above, the first verse is begun again. They sing this Tract in their black woolen copes, sitting alternately, as was described above for the Sunday. *Dominus vobiscum*; the Collect *Deus, qui tribus pueris*, without *Flectamus genua*. The Epistle is *Rogamus vos*. The Tract *Laudate Dominum* is sung alternately in the choir. This Mass ends with only one Collect.

**The Third Sunday of Lent.** At Compline, the antiphon is *Media vita*, with the Psalm *Nunc dimittis*. When this antiphon is sung, upon reaching the place where *Sancte Deus* is said, everyone must prostrate themselves three times on weekdays, but on feast days merely bow.

**Passion Sunday.** At First Vespers: antiphon *Benedictus*, etc. Responsory *Circumdederunt*. Verse *Quoniam tribulatio*, without *Gloria Patri*; then *Circumdederunt* again. It should be noted that the responsories both at Matins and at the Hours, which are ordinarily said with *Gloria*, are begun again until Easter. If a feast happens to be celebrated, or a Mass is said that is not of the Passion, *Gloria Patri* is said in the usual manner.

**Palm Sunday.** At Lauds, the antiphon is *Occurrunt turbae*, with the Psalm *Benedictus*. It should be known that, while the procession of blessed Mary passes through the boundaries of our parish carrying the Lord’s Body to the appointed place, when the cymbal-signal of that procession is heard, two of the larger bells are to be rung in honor of the Lord’s Body. At Prime, the bell is rung in the morning, and the morning Mass is omitted. In the Chapter, the reading is *Cum appropinquasset*. Immediately after Chapter, the procession is announced by ringing. At Terce, the bell is rung; afterward the water is blessed, and the brothers are sprinkled in the usual manner. Then, after the prayer *Exaudi nos, Domine* has been said, the hebdomadarian begins Terce; while it is being sung, he himself sprinkles the workshops in the customary manner with the bearer of the water.

Immediately after Terce, the procession is arranged: blessed water, candelabra, and the uncovered cross. All must attend this procession, both the parish priests and the other brothers. Antiphon *Ante sex dies*, etc. At the entrance of the church of blessed Mary: Responsory *Christi Virgo*, etc. From there, after entering the choir of the church of blessed Mary, they are to conduct themselves as the others do.

The sacristan must take care to distribute blessed branches to each of our canons. While the branches are being distributed, the antiphon *Pueri Hebraeorum*, etc., is sung. On the return of the procession, antiphon *Coeperunt omnes*. Responsory *Dominus Jesus*. Also, Responsory *Cum audisset turba*. When the procession reaches the city gate, a station is made, while the boys sing *Gloria, laus* above the gate. At the entrance into the city, the responsory is *Ingrediente Domino*. Verse *Cumque audisset*. Then two of the larger bells are again rung. At the entrance of the church of Saint Laud, the responsory is *Circumdederunt me*. After the station has been made in the basilica, the verse is sung by two men.

When the responsory is finished, the prelate, kneeling, begins three times the antiphon *Ave, rex noster*, which has been brought to him by the cantor. He says only *Ave, rex noster*; each time, the community repeats the same words while likewise kneeling. Meanwhile the crucifix is gradually uncovered. Finally, the entire antiphon is sung.

At the entrance to the choir: Responsory *Collegerunt*. The verse *Unus autem* is sung at the steps by three of the senior brothers, while the community sits. After the antiphon *Ne forte* has been repeated, the aforesaid singer adds the verse *Benedictus qui venit*, and the choir responds, *Hosanna in excelsis*. The Collect is *Omnipotens sempiterne*. The ministers may then attend to what they require.

After the signal has been rung, the Office *Domine, ne longe* begins. The priest and ministers proceed to the altar carrying palms in their hands. The ministers are vested in chasubles. The Tract is sung by four, as on the First Sunday of Lent. At the Passion, *Dominus vobiscum* is said because it is Sunday, but *Gloria tibi, Domine* is omitted in its proper place. The Creed is said.

The Offertory is *Improperium*. While it is sung, the ministers first offer their palms; then the prelate and the others come in orderly pairs, and the sacristan receives them. Because of the labor of the Office, they sleep after dinner. When the time to rise has come, one of the smaller bells is rung. Upon hearing it, they come into the cloister, first washing their hands as usual, and then proceed after None has been rung.

This midday observance is to be maintained from Easter until the Kalends of October, except on fast days, when eating and sleeping take place after None. On this day and thereafter until the Kalends of October, the community is to maintain silence while seated in the cloister.

**Wednesday.** At Mass, the Passion of the Lord, without *Dominus vobiscum* and without *Gloria tibi, Domine*. *Appropinquabat dies festus*. At the hour when the deacon says, *Velum templi scissum est* (“The veil of the temple was torn”), the curtain is to be allowed to fall.

At Vespers and until the Mass on the following day, the bells are rung as on Sundays. The prelate must sing Vespers. At Vespers, the antiphon is *Beatus vir*, with the Psalm *Nisi Dominus aedificaverit*, etc. The Chapter is *Attende, Domine*. Responsory *Circumdederunt me*, which the cantors must sing at the steps in silk copes. Hymn *Vexilla regis*. The antiphon is *Tanto tempore*, which the prelate begins; he censes two altars. As soon as the antiphon has begun, *Magnificat* is begun.

The Collect is *Respice, quaesumus, Domine*, which is to be said at all the Hours during the following three days, except at Prime and Compline. The cantors in silk copes say *Benedicamus Domino*. Note that, if the Annunciation of the Lord occurs on this day, Vespers is celebrated for the feast. The Rule is read at dinner on this day. Compline is said in the usual manner, without prostration. On this day, if anything in the church, the cloister, or the other workshops needs cleaning, it is to be cleaned.

**Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.** The custodian of the church must carefully arrange that the brothers rise at the proper hour for Matins, so that the nocturnal Office may be completed at length in its appointed time before daylight. On this day, as on the following two days, prostration is made at the Hours.

At Matins on each of these days, twenty-four candles are prepared before the high altar each night; one of them is extinguished at the beginning of each antiphon or responsory. On this Thursday at Matins, after the signal has been rung, *Domine, labia mea aperies* is not said, nor *Deus, in adjutorium meum*. *Gloria Patri* is omitted entirely. The invitatory is not sung either; instead, the prelate begins the first antiphon in a moderate voice, as follows: *Zelus domus tuae*. The Psalm is *Salvum me fac*. When it is imposed, everyone asks pardon over the forms; they are to do this at Matins, Lauds, and each of the Hours throughout these three days.

The antiphons and versicles are to end without a neum. The prelate reads the ninth lesson. Responsory of the ninth lesson, *Revelabunt*, etc.; again, *Revelabunt*, while the signal is rung. When the ninth responsory has ended, the verse is not said; instead, the antiphon *Justificeris, Domine* is immediately imposed by the prelate, with the Psalm *Miserere mei, Deus*, etc.

While the Psalm *Laudate Dominum de caelis* is being sung, the sacristan puts away the light, and any lights in the church are extinguished. Then, when the antiphon has ended and the prelate has imposed the antiphon *Traditor autem*, the one candle that remained is suddenly extinguished. Thus *Benedictus* and the other things that follow are said in darkness.

After *Benedictus*, when the antiphon has ended, two brothers at the right-hand cross of the church first begin *Kyrie, eleison*, and two others at the left-hand cross respond in the same way, *Kyrie, eleison*. Then, when the first two again repeat *Kyrie, eleison*, two senior brothers at the steps, having been forewarned by the cantor, add *Domine, miserere*. The choir follows with *Christus Dominus factus est*.

Upon hearing this, those at the left-hand cross say *Christe, eleison*, and the two at the steps say the verse *Qui passurus advenisti*. Those at the right-hand cross say *Christe, eleison*, and the two at the steps say the verse *Qui discipulos*. Those at the left-hand cross say *Christe, eleison*, and the two at the steps say the verse *Agnus innocens*. After the verse has been said, the same men at the steps begin *Domine, miserere*. The choir responds: *Christus Dominus factus est*.

Again, those at the right-hand cross say *Kyrie, eleison*. Those at the left-hand cross say *Kyrie, eleison*. Again, those at the right-hand cross say *Kyrie, eleison*. At the steps: *Domine, miserere*. The choir: *Christus Dominus*.

When these things have been completed, as soon as the prelate has pronounced *Mortem autem crucis* (“death, even death on a cross”), they prostrate themselves over the forms. Each person says *Pater noster*, with the prayers and the Psalm *Miserere mei, Deus*, and the prayer *Respice, quaesumus*, ending with *Amen* on his own.

Afterward, when the prelate gives the signal, the light is brought out. With lanterns lit, they go to the dormitory. Rising in the morning, the brothers conduct themselves in the usual manner until Prime, except that they do not say the private Masses.

After Prime has been rung, they first say *Pater noster* while prostrate, and omit *Deus, in adjutorium* and the hymn. The hebdomadarian begins the antiphon *Justificeris*, with the Psalm *Deus, in nomine*. They sing *Beati immaculati* and *Retribue*, without *Quicunque vult*, more softly than usual.

When these have been said, the responsory *Unus ex discipulis* is immediately begun by the brother entrusted with singing the responsories over the Hours. He sings the verse, then begins the responsory again, adding the verse *Christus factus est*. After this, while prostrate, each person says silently on his own the customary prayers up to the confession. The confession is made aloud; then the following prayers and *Miserere mei, Deus*, with the customary prayer *Domine, sancte Pater*, are completed in silence.

At the signal they rise and enter Chapter. There, after the calendar has been announced, each person silently says *Isti sancti et omnes alii*. When this has been said, at the prelate’s signal the reading *Convenientibus vobis in unum* is read without *Jube, Domne* and without *Tu autem*. The table is then recited immediately. If there are deceased persons, they are announced, and after the absolution for them has been completed and *Benedicite* has been said, the order of business is first dealt with as usual; afterward the matters to be carried out up to the next day’s Chapter are arranged. At the end of Chapter they leave without saying anything, and throughout this time they observe complete silence in the cloister and in the other workshops, even more strictly than usual.

After Chapter, the prelate informs the provost and the almoner how many poor men are to be admitted for the Washing of the Feet. Before Terce, men sound in body are to be selected, so that they do not trouble the sick brothers: as many as there are healthy and sick brothers in the monastery, and as many as have died in that same year. Four are also to be brought for the prelate, together with as many others as he judges should be present for the household of the place at the Washing of the Feet.

The Hours of this day and of the following two days are sung in the same manner as was described above for Prime, with the prayers *Ego dixi, Domine* and *Respice, quaesumus*. On this day, however, they are said somewhat more loudly than on the following two days.

After Terce, Mass is said at the crucifix for the sick brothers, the household, and the poor who have been chosen for the Washing of the Feet [editorial addition: *sunt*, “are”]. When the Mass has ended, the almoner leads the poor to the place where their feet are to be washed with warm water. While Sext is being sung, he and the provost bring them into the cloister and have them sit in the part of the cloister next to the church, as follows: four poor men for the prelate are seated in the middle, and beside them others are placed on either side. Everything necessary for the Washing of the Feet—namely, warm water, basins, and towels for drying the hands and feet of the poor—is also prepared.

When Sext has ended, the brothers assemble in Chapter. There they remove their copes and, led by the prelate, follow in pairs. When he has taken his place before his poor men, the right choir passes to his right, while the left remains on his left.

When everyone has taken his place in order before his poor men and has turned toward them, the prelate, following the example of the Lord Jesus, girds himself with a towel and says the prayers: *Adjutorium nostrum in nomine Domini*; *Ostende nobis, Domine*; *Domine, exaudi orationem*; *Dominus vobiscum*. Prayer: *Actiones nostras*.

Then the cantor begins the antiphon *Dominus Jesus*. Meanwhile, the prelate humbly and devoutly first washes the feet of his own poor men, dries them with a towel, dries them even with his hair after the example of that woman, and kisses them. The senior who is at his right serves him with the basins.

No one except the prelate is to gird himself with a towel. Rather, the chamberlain distributes towels to everyone on one side and also assigns one of the brothers to do the same on the other side. While these things are being done, the antiphon *Dominus Jesus* is repeated after each verse of the Psalm *Beati immaculati*.

After everyone’s feet have been washed, the prelate again gives water for the hands of his own poor men. The almoner supplies four times four coins (sixteen), which the prelate offers to them, kissing their hands as he does so. Then, on each side, the brothers who have washed their feet give them water for their hands, observing the order already mentioned, so that those lower in rank receive the basins from those above them.

The chamberlain, with his colleague, supplies towels to the prelate and to all the brothers, just as he supplied the cloths. The almoner provides two coins for each poor person. The brothers offer these coins to all the poor to whom they have given water, likewise kissing their hands.

When this holy service, devoted to pious minds, has finally been completed, and the singing has ended, they bow and say three times *Kyrie, eleison*, followed by *Pater noster*.
