The prelate says *Et ne nos* and the prayers *Tu mandasti*; *Tu lavisti pedes discipulorum*; *Domine, exaudi orationem*; *Dominus vobiscum*. Prayer: *Adesto, Domine*.

They then wash their hands at the lavatory. After putting on their copes again and taking a short interval to attend to their needs, the poor are led to the almonry. There, after each has been given his allowance [Note: An allowance is the food necessary for sustenance.], they are left to decide whether to eat there or carry it away with them.

While None is being sung, the prelate and the ministers are ceremonially vested. Before the Hour ends, the secretary rings one of the larger bells three times, moderately.

The archbishop—or the bishop in his place—customarily gives absolution to the brothers on that day [Note: The canons of Saint Laud received absolution from the archbishop on the day of the Lord’s Supper.]. If it should happen that they are not present, then, after the seven Psalms have been said without *Gloria Patri*, as was done at the beginning of the fast, the prelate absolves them. After the absolution, all the bells are rung for a longer time than usual in a peal, and the ropes are then tied up until Holy Saturday.

Mass is celebrated solemnly and most devoutly. The Introit is *Nos autem gloriari*. The hebdomadarian cantors lead the choir in copes. The Collect is *Deus, a quo Judas*, without *Flectamus genua*. The Epistle is *Convenientibus vobis*. Gradual *Christus factus est*. Verse *Propter quod*, then again *Christus*. The Gospel, with candelabra and incense, is *Ante diem festum paschae*. The Creed is said; the proper Preface of the Cross is not said, but the common Preface is said.

The deacon places enough hosts for consecration to suffice for Communion today and tomorrow. During these four days no one should withdraw from Communion except for a reasonable cause. *Communicantes*. *Hanc*. *Qui pridie* are said as they are found in the Missal. *Agnus Dei* is sung, but the kiss of peace is not given.

After everyone has received Communion, and the Communion *Dominus Jesus* has been sung, the prelate imposes the antiphon *Calicem* at the altar. While the evening Psalms are being sung in the choir, he says those Psalms with his ministers and arranges in the corporals the hosts to be reserved for the following day. He places the folded corporals over the chalice and hands them to the deacon to carry. The deacon carries them with great care; the procession with which they came to the altar precedes, and the prelate follows. They go to a place suitably prepared for this purpose, where the prelate carefully and reverently receives the Lord’s Body from the deacon and places it there. The place is incensed before and after the reservation, and while the Lord’s Body remains there, a light is to burn continually.

When this has been completed, they return to the altar. The first Psalm is *Credidi propter*, etc. After the antiphon has been sung, the prelate immediately begins the antiphon *Coenantibus autem* at the altar, with the Psalm *Magnificat*. The antiphon is ended without a neum. The prelate immediately adds *Dominus vobiscum* and the prayer; the deacon says *Benedicamus Domino*.

After Mass, the community sits in the choir and waits until the prelate, having removed the vestments he was wearing, puts on a less valuable alb. Meanwhile the altars are stripped. As the prelate proceeds to wash the altars, with the subprior and secretary carrying water and wine before him, when they have come before the high altar the prelate says: *Adjutorium nostrum in nomine Domini*; *Domine, exaudi orationem*; *Dominus vobiscum*; prayer *Actiones nostras*.

Then the responsory *Circumdederunt me* must be begun in the choir, followed afterward by as many of the nocturnal responsories as are necessary, until all the altars have been washed. After the prelate has washed each altar with water, he pours wine over it in the form of a cross, saying the prayer of the saint to whom the altar belongs.

When all the altars have been washed in this manner, the prelate returns before the high altar and says the verse *Christus factus est*. Prayer *Respice, quaesumus, Domine*.

The prelate then removes his ecclesiastical vestments, and the community returns from attending to its needs. After a short interval, the subprior makes a sound at the refectory door with the instrument prepared for him by the cantor, announcing the meal; for neither today nor tomorrow is the cymbal or bell rung for the meal.

They then enter the refectory and stand in their places. At a signal from the prelate, *Benedicite* is said without a bell. Verse *Edent pauperes*, without *Gloria Patri* and without *Kyrie, eleison*. They say *Pater noster* silently. The hebdomadarian priest says in a subdued voice, *Oremus, Benedic, Domine*, etc. After *Amen* has been answered, the reading is begun without a blessing and ended without *Tu autem*.

When the meal has ended, at a signal from the prelate they say the verse *Memoriam fecit*, without *Gloria*, and the priest says *Agimus tibi gratias*. Then, singing the Psalm *Miserere mei, Deus*, they go to the church. When it has ended, they say silently, without *Gloria*, *Kyrie, eleison*, *Pater noster*, and the prayers, and then leave.

After this, while the servants are eating, everything is prepared for the Washing of the Feet of the brothers. In Chapter, the reading stand where the Gospel is to be read is decorated. Likewise, another reading stand is placed in the refectory before the last step, and a chair on which the prelate will sit is suitably arranged on the steps.

After the brothers’ feet have been washed in the infirmary, and everything has been prepared so that this holy service may be performed at length and devoutly, as is fitting, once the servants have eaten, the cantor strikes the table-sign for the Washing of the Feet at the proper time. When everyone has assembled in Chapter, the prelate—or, if he is absent, the one who is acting in his place—rises after the example of the Lord, removes his garments, takes a towel, girds himself, and pours water into a basin before the Chapter door. He then comes into Chapter with the hebdomadarian priest, who is to minister the water to him, and says before the steps the prayers and prayer as in the Washing of the Feet of the poor.

He first washes, dries, and kisses the feet of the subprior, who is seated in the prior’s place. Then, proceeding to the others as the order requires and beginning with the right choir, he performs the act of humility. Each brother, as soon as he has been washed in this manner, prostrates himself and humbly kisses the ground.

Meanwhile the antiphons are sung, the cantor beginning the antiphon *Mandatum novum*, etc. After everyone’s feet have been washed, the prelate returns to his seat. The subprior, girded with a towel, washes, dries, and kisses the prelate’s feet and those of the brother who ministered to him, while the hebdomadarian of the lesser Mass serves him.

After this, the prelate again takes the basins. With his assistant supplying the towel, he pours water over the hands of everyone in order, just as he had done for their feet, and kisses them. The subprior performs the same service with his assistant for the prelate and his companion.

The deacon who is to read the Lord’s sermon, and the others who are to serve him, leave at the appropriate hour to prepare themselves, after first washing their feet. The deacon puts on a dalmatic, the subdeacon a tunic, and the candle-bearers surplices. When the Washing of the Feet has ended, with *Kyrie, eleison*, the customary prayers, and the prayer *Adesto, Domine* having been completed, those from the vesting room proceed. As they enter, the community rises in Chapter.

Then the deacon, approaching the prelate with his procession, offers him incense according to custom and receives his blessing. Having received it, he goes to the reading stand and reads, in the manner of a lesson, the Lord’s sermon delivered at the Supper to the disciples. He begins as follows: *Ante diem festum Paschae*. The community stands until he has finished the first verse.

When everyone has sat down, the candle-bearers stand on either side with the thurifer. Then, when the deacon says, *Surgite, eamus hinc* (“Rise, let us go from here”), everyone goes in procession to the refectory. At a signal from the prelate they say *Benedicite*, and the prelate adds: *Potum charitatis benedicat dextera Dei Patris* (“May the right hand of God the Father bless the drink of charity”).

Then the deacon begins *Ego sum vitis vera*, etc. The subprior sits in the prior’s place, and the others sit in their own places. Beginning with the subprior, the prelate offers the drink of charity to each person, kissing each one’s hands. The refectorary, accompanied by another brother, goes before him, pouring the drink into cups. After everyone has been served, the prelate also offers the drink to those who served him. Then the subprior, while the prelate himself is seated in his place, serves him the drink in the same manner.

No one may presume to drink until he has received it from the prelate. After as much of the Sermon as the prelate wishes has been read, at his signal the deacon ends without *Tu autem*. At a signal they rise from the tables. After the prelate has said the verse *Benedictus Deus in donis suis*, they proceed to the church, preceded by the ministers, and say Compline.

Meanwhile the deacon and the other ministers, with their vestments folded, go together to the refectory to drink; having returned together to the church, they say Compline and rejoin the community.

At Compline, after the Psalms *Cum invocarem*, *In te, Domine, speravi*, *Qui habitat*, *Ecce nunc*, and *Nunc dimittis* have been said together, with the antiphon *Oblatus est*, and the responsory *Judas mercator pessimus* has been sung, with the verse *Christus factus est pro nobis* added, they say *Kyrie, eleison* in silence while prostrate, followed by *Pater noster* and *Credo*, with the customary prayers up to the confession. Only the confession is made aloud. *Miserere*. Prayer *Illumina, quaesumus, Domine*. After the triple prayer has been said, they rise, are sprinkled with holy water, and go to the dormitory.

**Friday.** This table is to be recited on wax in Chapter:

“Today, the first lesson: Brother So-and-so, namely one of the younger brothers. The second: Brother So-and-so, namely the hebdomadarian subdeacon. The first Tract, *Domine, audivi*: So-and-so and So-and-so, namely two of middle rank. The second Tract, *Eripe me, Domine*: D. So-and-so and D. So-and-so, namely two seniors. The Passion of the Lord: D. So-and-so, namely the precentor. *Popule meus*: D. So-and-so and D. So-and-so, namely the precentor and another of middle rank. *Agios* (“Holy”): D. So-and-so and Brother So-and-so, namely two younger levites. *Crux fidelis*: D. So-and-so and D. So-and-so, namely two of middle rank.”

Although the approved custom is thus established, the precentor may arrange the assignments according to the abilities of the persons.

### English meanings of the retained liturgical incipits

The retained Latin titles and quotations are translated here at their source-lemma occurrences: *Intret oratio*, “Let prayer enter”; *Populum tuum*, “Your people”; *Flectamus genua*, “Let us bend the knee”; *Dominus vobiscum*, “The Lord be with you”; *Angelus Domini*, “The angel of the Lord”; *Benedictus es in firmamento*, “Blessed are you in the firmament”; *Et laudabilis*, “and praiseworthy”; *Hymnum dicite*, “sing a hymn”; *Deus, qui tribus pueris*, “God, who [delivered] the three youths”; *Rogamus vos*, “We beseech you”; *Laudate Dominum*, “Praise the Lord”; *Media vita*, “In the midst of life”; *Nunc dimittis*, “Now you dismiss”; *Sancte Deus*, “Holy God”; *Circumdederunt [me]*, “They surrounded [me]”; *Quoniam tribulatio*, “For tribulation”; *Gloria Patri*, “Glory be to the Father”; *Occurrunt turbae*, “The crowds come out to meet [him]”; *Cum appropinquasset*, “When he had drawn near”; *Exaudi nos, Domine*, “Hear us, O Lord”; *Ante sex dies*, “Six days before”; *Christi Virgo*, “Virgin of Christ”; *Pueri Hebraeorum*, “The Hebrew children”; *Coeperunt omnes*, “They all began”; *Dominus Jesus*, “The Lord Jesus”; *Cum audisset turba*, “When the crowd had heard”; *Gloria, laus*, “Glory and praise”; *Ingrediente Domino*, “As the Lord entered”; *Cumque audisset*, “And when [he] had heard”; *Ave, rex noster*, “Hail, our King”; *Collegerunt*, “They gathered together”; *Unus autem*, “But one”; *Ne forte*, “Lest perhaps”; *Benedictus qui venit*, “Blessed is he who comes”; *Hosanna in excelsis*, “Hosanna in the highest”; *Omnipotens sempiterne*, “Almighty everlasting [God]”; *Domine, ne longe*, “O Lord, be not far [from me]”; *Gloria tibi, Domine*, “Glory to you, O Lord”; *Improperium*, “Reproach”; *Appropinquabat dies festus*, “The feast day was drawing near”; *Velum templi scissum est*, “The veil of the temple was torn”; *Beatus vir*, “Blessed is the man”; *Nisi Dominus aedificaverit*, “Unless the Lord builds”; *Attende, Domine*, “Give heed, O Lord”; *Vexilla regis*, “The royal banners”; *Tanto tempore*, “For so long a time”; *Magnificat*, “My soul magnifies [the Lord]”; *Respice, quaesumus, Domine*, “Look upon us, we beseech you, O Lord”; For the Thursday and Friday rites: *Domine, labia mea aperies*, “O Lord, open my lips”; *Deus, in adjutorium meum*, “O God, come to my aid”; *Zelus domus tuae*, “Zeal for your house”; *Salvum me fac*, “Save me”; *Revelabunt*, “They will reveal”; *Justificeris, Domine*, “That you may be justified, O Lord”; *Miserere mei, Deus*, “Have mercy on me, O God”; *Laudate Dominum de caelis*, “Praise the Lord from the heavens”; *Traditor autem*, “But the betrayer”; *Benedictus*, “Blessed”; *Kyrie, eleison*, “Lord, have mercy”; *Christe, eleison*, “Christ, have mercy”; *Domine, miserere*, “Lord, have mercy”; *Christus Dominus factus est*, “Christ the Lord became [obedient]”; *Qui passurus advenisti*, “You who came to suffer”; *Qui discipulos*, “You who [taught] the disciples”; *Agnus innocens*, “Innocent lamb”; *Mortem autem crucis*, “even death on a cross”; *Pater noster*, “Our Father”; *Amen*, “So be it”; *Deus, in nomine*, “O God, in your name”; *Beati immaculati*, “Blessed are the undefiled”; *Retribue*, “Reward”; *Quicunque vult*, “Whoever wishes”; *Unus ex discipulis*, “One of the disciples”; *Christus factus est*, “Christ became [obedient]”; *Domine, sancte Pater*, “Lord, holy Father”; *Isti sancti et omnes alii*, “These saints and all the others”; *Convenientibus vobis in unum*, “When you come together in one place”; *Jube, Domne*, “Command, Lord”; *Tu autem*, “But you [Lord]”; *Benedicite*, “Give a blessing”; *Ego dixi, Domine*, “I said, O Lord”; *Adjutorium nostrum in nomine Domini*, “Our help is in the name of the Lord”; *Ostende nobis, Domine*, “Show us, O Lord”; *Domine, exaudi orationem*, “O Lord, hear [my] prayer”; *Actiones nostras*, “Direct our actions”; *Et ne nos*, “And lead us not”; *Tu mandasti*, “You commanded”; *Tu lavisti pedes discipulorum*, “You washed the disciples’ feet”; *Adesto, Domine*, “Be present, O Lord.”

For the Mass, refectory, and closing rites: *Nos autem gloriari*, “But as for us, to glory”; *Deus, a quo Judas*, “God, from whom Judas [received his punishment]”; *Propter quod*, “For which reason”; *Ante diem festum Paschae*, “Before the feast of Passover”; *Communicantes*, “In communion with”; *Hanc*, “This [offering]”; *Qui pridie*, “Who, the day before”; *Agnus Dei*, “Lamb of God”; *Calicem*, “The chalice”; *Credidi propter*, “I believed, therefore”; *Coenantibus autem*, “But while they were dining”; *Edent pauperes*, “The poor shall eat”; *Oremus, Benedic, Domine*, “Let us pray: Bless, O Lord”; *Memoriam fecit*, “He has made a memorial”; *Agimus tibi gratias*, “We give you thanks”; *Mandatum novum*, “A new commandment”; *Surgite, eamus hinc*, “Rise, let us go from here”; *Potum charitatis benedicat dextera Dei Patris*, “May the right hand of God the Father bless the drink of charity”; *Ego sum vitis vera*, “I am the true vine”; *Benedictus Deus in donis suis*, “Blessed be God in his gifts”; *Cum invocarem*, “When I called”; *In te, Domine, speravi*, “In you, O Lord, I have hoped”; *Qui habitat*, “He who dwells”; *Ecce nunc*, “Behold now”; *Oblatus est*, “He was offered”; *Judas mercator pessimus*, “Judas, the most wicked merchant”; *Christus factus est pro nobis*, “Christ became obedient for us”; *Credo*, “I believe”; *Miserere*, “Have mercy”; *Illumina, quaesumus, Domine*, “Enlighten, we beseech you, O Lord”; *Domine, audivi*, “O Lord, I heard”; *Eripe me*, “Deliver me”; *Popule meus*, “My people”; *Agios*, Greek for “Holy”; and *Crux fidelis*, “Faithful cross.”

At Matins, the secretary shall make his customary sound at the dormitory door [Col. 0173A] to awaken the brothers at the proper hour. Matins shall be said in the same manner as was stated above for the Lord’s Supper. On this day, after the brothers have risen in the morning, they shall remain barefoot until the Office has been completed, unless ordered otherwise; the prelate may put on footwear because of excessive cold, but whenever this happens he shall be barefoot only during the Office. On this day each brother shall recite the entire Psalter in order, together, in the cloister.

The Chapter shall proceed up to the *Benedicite* (“Bless the Lord”), as on the preceding day. The reading shall be *Festinemus ingredi* (“Let us hasten to enter”; Hebrews 4). After the schedule has been recited and the *Benedicite* said, the customs pertaining to the Office shall immediately be read. Once these have been read, if there is no pressing need to speak, they shall leave at a sign from the prelate, saying nothing; but if some matter arises that cannot be deferred, it shall be handled as briefly as possible. For no hour of this day was free from the Lord’s Passion; therefore, at each of the Hours, we ought to have this material for meditating upon him, so that we may constantly remember how he endured spitting, insults, blows with the fist, slaps, the crown of thorns, scourging, the cross, nails, gall, vinegar, death, and the spear, and may meditate continually upon these things throughout the entire day.

The Hours—Terce, Sext, and None—shall not be said continuously, as some do, but separately, as on the preceding day, and shall be concluded in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0173] The practice of saying the canonical Hours consecutively and without interruption is rejected.].

Whenever, because of extreme cold, it has been necessary for the brothers to remain shod throughout this day, nevertheless, since they must attend the Office barefoot, immediately after None they shall go to the dormitory, remove their footwear, and return at once to the church.

After None has been sung, while the community waits in choir, the ministers of the altar shall hasten to vest. The ministers shall be vested as on ordinary days, except for the chasubles; the prelate shall vest in unornamented albs and in a purple chasuble, if he has one; otherwise he shall wear one of the middling ones. When the Hour has ended, he shall come to the altar barefoot, preceded only by the deacon and subdeacon, likewise barefoot and without candlesticks. He shall not make the confession, but, having said only the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”) and signed himself, shall immediately sit down when the lector begins the first reading [Col. 0173B–C].

The altar shall be covered with only one cloth, and no candles shall be lit around it. Both readings shall be read without titles. The first reading shall begin in the surplice between choir and altar: “Thus says the Lord: In their tribulation …” (*Haec dicit Dominus: In tribulatione sua*). When it has been completed, the tract *Domine, audivi* (“Lord, I have heard”) shall be sung at the steps by two men, the choir repeating after each verse: “I considered your works” (*Consideravi opera tua*). After the tract, the prayer *Deus, a quo et Judas* (“O God, from whom also Judas …”) shall be said, preceded by *Flectamus genua* (“Let us bend the knee”).

After the prayer, the subdeacon shall read the second reading, not as an Epistle but in the manner of a reading, beginning thus: “The Lord spoke to Moses” (*Dixit Dominus ad Moysen*). When it has been read, the tract *Eripe me* (“Deliver me”) shall be sung by two men and the choir antiphonally. All who read, sing, or serve at the altar with the candlesticks shall be vested only in surplices or albs; no one, however, is to wear an ornate alb today.

During the Passion, when the deacon says, “They divided my garments” (*Partiti sunt vestimenta mea*), let the two men who sang the final tract stand beside the altar, one on either side, and draw toward themselves the two cloths that had been placed there beforehand for this purpose [Col. 0173D].

After the Passion has ended, the prelate shall begin the solemn prayers. Whenever the deacon says *Flectamus genua* (“Let us bend the knee”) in all of them, he shall omit it only in the prayer made for the faithless Jews. Since, during the Passion, they bent the knee in mockery before our Redeemer, the Church, abhorring their crime, does not bend the knee in prayer for them alone:

“Let us pray, dearly beloved, to God …” (*Oremus, dilectissimi, Deum*, etc.).

Near the end of these prayers, the secretary shall spread a carpet before the greater altar, where the cross is to be adored, and place a cloth over it. When the prayers have ended, the prelate and ministers, having removed their chasubles, stoles, and maniples in the vesting room, shall come into choir in albs; the prelate himself shall stand last.

Then two priests in albs shall take the prepared cross from behind the altar and, standing to the right of that altar, present it covered to everyone while singing *Popule meus* (“My people”). Two levites standing between choir and altar in chasubles shall answer *Agios* (“Holy”), asking forgiveness three times. The choir, likewise bending the knee three times, shall add: “Holy, holy, holy” (*Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus*) [Col. 0174A].

Near the end of the choir’s response, the aforesaid priests shall advance a little; while the choir is silent, they shall say another verse: “For I led you out” (*Quia eduxi te*). The levites shall answer *Agios*, and the choir, “Holy.” Again the priests shall advance somewhat and sing a third verse: “What more ought I to have done?” (*Quid ultra debui*). The levites shall answer *Agios*, and the choir, “Holy.”

Then, when the priests have advanced far enough to stand at the place where the cross is to be adored, they shall suddenly uncover it and begin the antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis*—“Behold the wood of the cross.” All shall turn toward it, and as soon as they see the crucified Lord, with outstretched arms inviting us, after the example of his reconciliation, and the fountain of mercy flowing from the side of the hanging Lord, open for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman, appearing before the eyes of those who gaze, they shall show with what devotion they are inflamed toward so great a gift. Whenever the antiphon is begun, they shall prostrate themselves upon the ground and adore the Lord, kissing the very ground. At the end of the antiphon, when they say, “Come, let us adore” (*Venite, adoremus*), they shall bend the knee.

The antiphon itself shall be begun again three times by those holding the cross. After it has first been sung, the first verse of the psalm *Beati immaculati* (“Blessed are the undefiled”) shall be added; after the second repetition, the next verse shall be added; after the third, the antiphon *Crucem tuam* (“Your cross”) shall immediately be begun in choir. Whenever it is begun, they shall prostrate themselves on the ground. This antiphon shall also be sung three times, with three verses of the psalm *Deus misereatur nostri* (“May God have mercy on us”).

Afterward, two men in albs shall begin *Crux fidelis* (“Faithful cross”) at the steps of the choir, and the verses of the hymn *Pange lingua* (“Sing, my tongue”) shall be sung for as long as the cross is being adored, the choir repeating *Crux fidelis* after each verse [Col. 0174B–C].

When *Ecce lignum* is begun as the cross is first uncovered, the prelate shall immediately approach and prostrate himself bodily before the cross. Alone, as he wishes, either in a book or without a book, he shall say a prayer of his own, but a brief one. All the others, when they have likewise lain prostrate bodily before the crucified Lord, two by two, shall complete their prayers briefly, without a book but with the inmost intention of the heart, according to the inspiration of the one whom they adore. When the prelate is adoring, the subdeacon shall lie near him and adore with him. When the prelate has risen and kissed the cross, the subdeacon shall then approach.

Meanwhile, those who said *Agios*, having removed their chasubles, shall take the place of the priests who are still holding the cross. After adoring, the priests shall again hold the cross; then the deacons shall adore. After them, the members of both choirs shall come to adore, two by two, beginning with the senior members, in an orderly manner and with great reverence.

When they approach to kiss the feet of the crucified Lord, and the impressions of the nails and that little stream of blood by which the kisses are imprinted return to memory, one ought to consider rather than express what love and sweetness they should bring to the attentive mind [Col. 0174D].

The prelate, after adoring, shall not return to choir, but while the cross is being adored shall sit either at the altar in prayer or wherever seems best to him.

After everyone has adored, if people are present who ought to adore, the cross shall be carried to another place. If it is carried through the choir, all shall bend the knee, not simultaneously, but as it passes before each person. If the people delay in adoring, the secretary shall bring another cross. Those who sang *Popule meus* shall take it, raise it, and begin the antiphon *Super omnia ligna* (“Above all trees”). They shall then place it in an elevated position, while all, kneeling in adoration, complete the antiphon.

When this has been done, the prelate and ministers, having resumed their stoles and maniples—but with only the prelate shod and wearing a chasuble—shall go with the thurifer and candle-bearers to the place where they had deposited the Lord’s body on the preceding day. After censing it, the prelate shall hand it to the deacon to carry back. Meanwhile, the secretary shall spread another cloth over the altar. When they approach the altar, all shall adore on their knees the Lord’s body; the prelate, receiving it from the deacon, shall place it upon the altar in the customary manner.

Then, in its presence, the deacon shall pour wine and water into the chalice. After censing them, washing his hands, and making the confession with the ministers, he shall begin in a moderate voice: “Let us pray. Instructed by saving commands …” (*Oremus, Praeceptis salutaribus*), and conclude with the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), the choir responding, “But deliver us” (*Sed libera nos*). He shall then say in the customary manner, “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord” (*Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine*). When he has said, “For ever and ever” (*Per omnia saecula saeculorum*), and the response “Amen” has been given, he shall not say *Pax Domini* (“The peace of the Lord”) or offer the kiss of peace. He shall take a portion of the holy sacrament and place it in the chalice without saying anything. He shall then communicate himself and the others in silence; for the unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the Lord’s body placed into it.

This signifies that, in memory of his burial, the Lord’s body, reserved from Thursday, is received by the faithful on Friday, because on that day the Lord was buried by the faithful. The blood is not reserved, because it was poured out by unbelievers. Innocent therefore says that the sacraments are not celebrated on this day, as follows:

“For it is not fitting,” he says, “that on the day when the Truth deigned to be sacrificed for his own sake by unbelievers, the Truth should be sacrificed by the faithful in the sacrament.”

After everyone has communicated, the antiphon *Calicem salutaris* (“The cup of salvation”) shall be begun in choir. Together with the other antiphons and psalms that were said on the preceding day, Vespers shall be concluded gently, as the other Hours are, with the capitularies, prayers, and the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”). Each person shall complete the prayer *Respice, quaesumus* (“Look upon us, we beseech you”) individually.

The prelate, with the ministers, having arranged whatever must be arranged around the altar, shall return to the vesting room while singing Vespers.

After Vespers, everyone shall leave the church, wash their feet, and put on footwear. Then, after a short interval, when the board has been struck, they shall enter the refectory and complete everything before and after supper as on the preceding day.

At table, nothing but bread and water and raw herbs shall be served. The brothers’ food shall be cooked as on other days and carried from the kitchen for almsgiving; the customary food [read: drink] shall likewise be given to the poor. The superior shall take care of the weaker brothers who are in the community.

Since the Office is to be performed later than usual on the following day, because of the labor, after the collation in the refectory everyone shall receive the drink of charity. At the collation, a sermon of Saint John Chrysostom shall be read, namely: “On this day our Lord hung” (*Hodierna die Dominus noster pependit*) [Col. 0175A].

Compline shall be concluded as on the preceding day. On this night the subject for meditation shall be Christ: after all that he endured, his rest in the tomb, and, through his descent into hell, that ineffable and great joy long awaited by the wretched and presented so suddenly—the joy by which Christ, having taken death’s dominion captive, led them with himself out of hell. Thus, while the mind is led through these meditations, it may sleep and rest in peace together with him (*in pace in idipsum dormiat et requiescat*; Psalm 4) [Col. 0175B–D].

## Holy Saturday of Easter

Everything stated above concerning the Office of the night and day, up to the Office of the Mass, shall be completed in the same order. At Matins, the antiphon *In pace in idipsum* (“In peace in the same place”), etc. In Lauds, the antiphon *O mors* (“O death”), etc. *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) shall be said in the same manner as on the preceding day.

Early in the morning, the entire church shall be decorated, and the Chapter shall be held as on the Lord’s Supper. The reading shall be *Christus assistens pontifex* (“Christ standing as high priest”). Immediately after the Chapter, the brothers shall be shaved, so that all may be found shaved for the Office in joy at so great a solemnity; meanwhile, the chamberlain shall place clean and new undergarments on each person’s bed. After Sext, the readings shall be reviewed and the altars covered. Everything shall be decorated most splendidly, inside and out, in a festive manner to display the solemnity of such ineffable joy, so that above all the adornment of the mind may not be neglected amid the glory of the Resurrection [Col. 0176A].

After None, all the brothers shall go to the dormitory, remove their cloaks, and all put on clean surplices with hoods, if necessary. It is fitting that, at the solemnity of their restoration, they should appear pure both in mind and in clothing, like the angels who announced the joys of this festival in white garments. The ministers of the altar shall likewise put on more splendid vestments: the deacon a dalmatic, the subdeacon a tunic, and three men in surplices to carry the water, cross, and censer for the procession.

The prelate also shall be adorned in precious vestments. When everyone has been suitably prepared and the signal has been given, the community shall come into choir. Then, in an ordered procession, they shall proceed before the altar to the place where the new fire is to be blessed, in the following manner: first of all, the secretary shall walk with a staff into which a candle has been fixed, by which he will carry the fire; after him, the bearer of the water; then the one carrying the cross, followed by the thurifer; then the deacon and subdeacon; then the community, with the prelate last, wearing a silk cope [Col. 0176B].

When they reach the fire, all standing in order, the prelate shall approach and bless the fire, sprinkling it with holy water. Then the censer shall be filled with coals from the new fire, and the secretary shall light the candle on the staff. A candle shall also be lit in a lantern, from which the candle may be relit if it should happen to go out. In all the workshops and offices, after the old fire has been extinguished, the new fire shall be carried by certain persons.

Then the cantor shall begin the antiphon *Cum rex gloriae* (“When the King of glory”). The community shall return in procession to choir, singing the same antiphon throughout. After it has been sung, the incense shall be blessed by the prelate in this manner: “May almighty God come …” (*Veniat, omnipotens Deus*, etc.; blessing of the Paschal candle).

Meanwhile, the subdeacon shall stand last in choir, and the prelate shall sit in his seat. The deacon shall immediately approach for the consecration of the candle, as follows: “Let the angelic host now rejoice” (*Exsultet iam angelica*). While everyone stands attentive to the consecration of so great a light, when the deacon says, “Receive, holy Father” (*Suscipe, sancte Pater*), the thurifer shall be ready to offer him incense. The deacon, placing it in the censer, shall incense only the candle, into which the secretary must have fixed five grains of incense in the form of a cross before the Office.

After incensing the candle, the thurifer shall remain there with the smoking censer until the candle has been consecrated. Again, when the deacon says, “The shining fire for God’s honor” (*In honore Dei rutilans ignis*), the secretary shall light the candle from the new fire. When the deacon adds, “Although divided into parts” (*Qui licet sit divisus in partes*), he shall also light the two candles fixed in candlesticks on either side of the great candle [Col. 0176C].

The candle shall not be extinguished until after Compline on the following day; it shall also be lit throughout the entire week at the principal Mass and at Vespers.

When the consecration of the candle has been completed and the prelate and ministers have returned to the vesting room, the first reading shall immediately begin: “In the beginning God made …” (*In principio fecit Deus*). Then the two candles in the candlesticks shall be extinguished until Mass.

At this point the prelate, wearing one of the ordinary chasubles, shall proceed to the altar, accompanied only by the deacon and subdeacon, who have removed their dalmatic and tunic. He shall not make the confession, but, after first saying “Our Father” (*Pater noster*) and kissing the altar, shall sit with his ministers. The subprior shall read the first reading; the others shall read the remaining ones in their proper order, beginning with the first, and so forth [Col. 0176D].

When these things have been completed, the first litany shall be begun at the steps by boys, if any are present; if not, by three of the younger members of the community. This litany shall end in choir. Once the litany has begun, the prelate shall withdraw with the ministers to the vesting room; removing his chasuble, he shall put on a cope and return to his seat in choir.

When the first litany has ended, three other brothers shall begin the second litany. When they pronounce “Saint John the Baptist” (*Sancte Joannes Baptista*), they shall proceed in an ordered procession, with great reverence, to the fonts. The order shall be: first, the one carrying the cross; then the candle-bearers; after them, the one carrying the candle prepared for the consecration of the fonts; then the subdeacon with the book and the deacon with the chrismatory; then those saying the litany; and finally the community, with the prior last.

When they arrive, those carrying the sacred objects shall stand before the fonts. The three who are singing the litany shall finish it before the crucifix. When it has ended, the prelate, standing there before the fonts, with the deacon and chrismatory on his right and the subdeacon with the sacramentary on his left, shall begin the consecration of the fonts in this manner: “Let us pray. Almighty …” (*Oremus, Omnipotens*, etc.) [Col. 0177A].

While he performs this, the one holding the cross shall stand opposite him beside the fonts, facing the fonts; the candle-bearers shall stand beside him on either side in the same manner. The one holding the candle shall stand beside the deacon. The great candle is not to be carried to the fonts; rather, another candle, lit from the blessed candle, shall be carried to the fonts by one acolyte, if one is present.

After the fonts have been consecrated, the chrism shall not be poured in until anyone who may be present has drawn blessed water to carry home. The secretary shall also arrange to reserve some of this same water for the following day, so that, as is customary, the altars, brothers, and offices may be sprinkled with it; for on Easter Day the priest does not bless water in any way [Col. 0177B].

Then, as is customary, chrism shall be poured in together with oil, and the consecrated fonts shall be covered with a white cloth, incensed, and closed.

When this Office has been completed, the third litany shall be begun by three men in silk copes before the crucifix. When they pronounce “Saint John the Baptist” (*Sancte Joannes Baptista*), the procession shall return to choir. Meanwhile, the prelate shall withdraw with the ministers to the vesting room and solemnly prepare himself for Mass; the deacon shall put on his dalmatic and the subdeacon his tunic.

When the litany has ended, it must conclude after *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”) has been said three times, as is more fully contained in the books. When the cantor begins *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) for Mass, they shall proceed to the altar, preceded by the candle-bearers and thurifer. When they arrive, they shall make the confession in the customary manner.

Near the end of the litany, the secretary shall light all the church’s lights from the new fire, since every former fire ought to have been extinguished, so that we may be wholly illumined by the light of the eternal fire [Col. 0177C].

Afterward, while the chief cantor intones *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) slowly and at length, all the bells shall be rung in a peal. The Epistle shall be read between choir and altar. The precentor and those who lead the choir with him shall solemnly intone the *Alleluia*. After the verse *Confitemini* (“Give thanks”) has been sung, they shall repeat the *Alleluia*. Then the tract *Laudate Dominum* (“Praise the Lord”) shall be sung at the steps by two senior men in surplices, the choir singing half of each verse.

Before the Gospel, candlesticks shall not be carried, but only incense.

The Creed is not said, nor the *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”), nor is the kiss of peace given. While the *Sanctus* (“Holy”) is being sung, Vespers shall begin to be rung, as on double feasts, so that after everyone has communicated the bells may sound a peal. When it ceases, the cantor shall begin the solemn *Alleluia*. Then the psalm *Laudate Dominum* (“Praise the Lord”) shall be sung with great rejoicing. After that, the alleluiatic chant shall be concluded without a *pneuma*; from then until Vespers on the following Saturday, *pneumata* shall be entirely omitted both in antiphons and in versicles. Likewise, the antiphons said at the *Benedictus* (“Blessed”) and *Magnificat* (“My soul magnifies”) are not repeated.

After the aforesaid alleluiatic chant has been sung, the prelate shall immediately begin at the altar the antiphon brought to him by the cantor, as follows: “But in the evening …” (*Vespere autem*). When it has ended, he shall add the prayer after the *Magnificat* to complete the Office. After the deacon has said *Ite, missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”), Mass and Vespers shall end together [Col. 0177D].

Afterward, when they have left the church and an interval has passed, the cymbal shall be struck. Then, after they have entered the refectory and the small bell has been rung [Note: [Col. 0177D] *Scilla*, or *skilla*, that is, a small bell.], the customary verse shall be said: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (*V\ Edent pauperes et saturabuntur*), with the *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”) and *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). The weekly server shall say, “And lead us not …” (*Et ne nos*, etc.). The blessing shall be given before the reading.

In the refectory the reading shall be: “The evening of the Sabbath, which dawns …” (*Vespere sabbati quae lucescit*, etc.). The sermon shall be: “Mary Magdalene saw the risen Lord …” (*Maria Magdalene vidit Dominum resurgentem*, etc.).

After the meal, everything shall likewise be completed in the customary manner, except that the psalm of joy and exultation, *Confitemini Domino* (“Give thanks to the Lord”), properly concerning the Resurrection, shall replace the penitential psalm of mourning, *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”). It shall be used daily, both at dinner and supper, until supper on the following Saturday [Col. 0178A].

At Compline, after the four psalms—*Cum invocarem* (“When I called”); *In te, Domine, speravi* (“In you, Lord, I have hoped”); *Ecce nunc* (“Behold now”); *Nunc dimittis* (“Now you dismiss”)—have been said, with a brief alleluiatic chant and without a Chapter or hymn, only the versicle “Give thanks to the Lord” (*Confitemini Domino*) shall be pronounced. The confession shall be said, followed by *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and the prayer *Spiritum nobis, Domine* (“Give us your Spirit, Lord”). This Hour shall be said in the same manner throughout the entire week, with the responsory *Haec dies* (“This is the day”) added. After Compline, having made the threefold prayer, they shall go to the dormitory sprinkled with holy water.

## Easter Day

At Matins on the holy day of Easter, all the bells shall be rung in a peal, as stated above for the Nativity of the Lord. The homily shall be read in a silk cope.

Throughout the entire week, at Lauds and Vespers, no Chapter, hymn, or versicle shall be said. At Prime, without a hymn, the antiphon *Angelus Domini* (“The angel of the Lord”) shall be said, with the psalms *Deus in nomine* (“O God, in your name”); *Beati immaculati* (“Blessed are the undefiled”); *Retribue* (“Repay”). There shall be no Chapter throughout the entire week, just as the other Hours are said.

At all the Hours throughout the week, except Matins, the responsory shall be *Haec dies* (“This is the day”), with *Alleluia*, followed by the verse “Give thanks to the Lord” (*V\ Confitemini Domino*). The confession shall be said throughout the week, followed by *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”). The prayer shall be *Deus, qui hodierna die* (“O God, who on this day …”). Thus it shall be done at Prime throughout the entire week.

In the Chapter, the reading shall be “Mary Magdalene” (*Maria Magdalene*). At the end of the Chapter on this day and on the following six days—and indeed on all double feasts—the psalm *Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes* (“Praise the Lord, all nations”) shall be said [Col. 0178B].

From this point until the octave of Pentecost, whenever holy water is sprinkled, the antiphon *Vidi aquam* (“I saw water”) shall be sung. It must nevertheless be understood that immediately after the Chapter the signal for the procession is to be given, and afterward for Terce.

After Terce has been sung and the procession has been arranged, the cantor shall immediately begin the aforesaid antiphon *Vidi aquam*. While Terce is sung on this day and on all days when the procession is made in copes, the cantor shall distribute the copes throughout the choir.

In the procession on this day, which is to be led through the cloister, the antiphon *Sedit angelus* (“The angel sat”) shall be said. It shall be prolonged so that, after a station has been made in the church before the crucifix, the verses of that antiphon may be sung at the lectern by three brothers. Then, when the prelate has begun the antiphon *Christus resurgens* (“Christ, rising again”), they shall enter the choir and again sing the verse *Dicant nunc tres* (“Now let three say”) at the steps.

After the versicle “The Lord has truly risen” (*Surrexit Dominus vere*) has been pronounced and the prayer of the day has been said, the bells shall sound a peal and the Office of the Mass shall be solemnly intoned: “He has risen …” (*Resurrexit*, etc.).

In the refectory the reading shall be “Mary Magdalene” (*Maria Magdalene*), followed by the sermons that come afterward [Col. 0178C].

## Vespers

Vespers shall be conducted as follows. The antiphon *Angelus autem* (“But the angel”), psalm *Dixit Dominus* (“The Lord said”). Antiphon *Et ecce terrae* (“And behold, the earth”), psalm *Confitebor* (“I will confess”). Antiphon *Erat autem* (“Now it was”), psalm *Beatus vir* (“Blessed is the man”). Responsory *Haec dies* (“This is the day”).

Then the cantors, with a third added, shall say at the steps: *Alleluia, Angelus Domini* (“Alleluia, the angel of the Lord”), with both verses. Afterward the sequence *Victimae paschali* (“To the Paschal victim”) shall be added. When it has ended, without a versicle, the antiphon *Et respicientes* (“And looking back”) shall be intoned. *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), prayer *Concede, quaesumus* (“Grant, we beseech you”).

After *Benedicamus* (“Let us bless”) has been said, the procession shall immediately be arranged as follows: first shall proceed the one carrying the cross; the candle-bearers with the thurifer shall follow; after them shall walk the bearer of the candle with which the fonts were consecrated, and the deacon with the chrismatory.

Then, when the antiphon *Prae timore autem* (“But out of fear”) has been begun in the left choir, the community shall proceed in order, singing the psalm *Laudate, pueri* (“Praise, servants”), to the fonts. When they arrive, the fonts shall be incensed. After the antiphon has ended, without a verse and without *Dominus vobiscum*, the collect *Praesta, quaesumus* (“Grant, we beseech you”) shall be said.

When it has ended, with the antiphon *Sedit angelus* (“The angel sat”), they shall gradually turn toward the crucifix. After the altars there have been incensed and the antiphon has ended, the verse “Tell it among the nations” (*Dicite in nationibus*) shall be said, followed by the prayer *Deus, qui pro nobis Filium* (“O God, who for us your Son …”).

Then, after the antiphon *Respondens autem* (“But answering”) has been intoned in the right choir, they shall return to choir with the psalm *In exitu Israel de Aegypto* (“When Israel went out of Egypt”). After the collect—which is to be said without a verse and without *Dominus vobiscum*, namely *Praesta, quaesumus* (“Grant, we beseech you”)—the candle-bearers shall add *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”). In this manner Vespers shall be sung until Wednesday [Col. 0178D–0179A].

At Compline, the antiphon *Alleluia*, with the psalms *Cum invocarem* (“When I called”); *In te, Domine, speravi* (“In you, Lord, I have hoped”); *Ecce nunc* (“Behold now”); *Nunc dimittis* (“Now you dismiss”), shall be said without a Chapter or hymn. *Haec dies quam* (“This is the day which …”), the confession, and the rest shall be said as stated above.

## Monday

The psalm *Venite* (“Come”) shall be said in double chant for three days. If a feast of three readings occurs during this week, nothing shall be done concerning it during the first four days; on the remaining days there shall be only a commemoration. That commemoration is to be said after the final collect said in choir. The solemnity of nine readings shall be entirely reserved until after the octave of Easter.

It should also be known that the three days mentioned above are observed reverently as feasts of the third rank, while the remaining three are observed according to the custom of Sunday Office.

At Vespers, as on the preceding day, there shall be a procession to the fonts, as stated above [Col. 0179B].

## Low Sunday

At First Vespers, the antiphon *Alleluia*, psalm *Benedictus* (“Blessed”), etc.

On all Saturdays until the Ascension of the Lord, the Chapter at Vespers shall be: “If you have risen with Christ” (*Si consurrexistis cum Christo*).

R. “The Lord has risen” (*Surrexit Dominus*).  
V. “Who for us …” (*Qui pro nobis*, etc.).  
Hymn: *Chorus novae Jerusalem* (“The choir of the new Jerusalem”).  
V. “Remain with us” (*Mane nobiscum*).  
Antiphon *Surgens Jesus* (“Jesus rising”), psalm *Magnificat* (“My soul magnifies”).  
Prayer: *Praesta, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus* (“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”).

For the procession, the antiphon *Rex noster* (“Our King”). Then the community, with the thurifer, candle-bearers, and celebrant in a silk cope, without the cross, shall proceed to the crucifix while singing this antiphon. There, after the two altars have been incensed, the priest shall say, after the antiphon has ended, the verse “Tell it among the nations” (*Dicite in nationibus*), followed by the prayer *Deus, qui pro nobis* (“O God, who for us …”), unless some feast occurs of which a commemoration must be made; in that case the commemoration of the feast must come first.

Then, with the antiphon concerning the relics, *Lux perpetua* (“Perpetual light”), they shall return to choir. After the verse “The voice of joy” (*Vox laetitiae*) has been pronounced—not by the priest but by the last member—the prayer *Praesta, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus, ut sanctorum tuorum* (“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that of your saints …”) shall be said.

In this manner the procession to the crucifix shall take place on the other Saturdays until the Ascension of the Lord. It shall not be omitted for any feast, even a double feast. However, when the Finding of the Holy Cross falls on a Sunday, they shall go to the crucifix at Vespers, but with the chant for the feast, as written for that celebration.

After supper, the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”) shall be resumed [Col. 0179C].

On all Sundays until the Ascension of the Lord, unless a feast occurs, there shall be a morning Mass of the Resurrection. On Sunday, the Chapter reading shall be “When it was evening” (*Cum esset sero*). In the refectory the reading shall likewise be “When it was evening” (*Cum esset sero*).

When the homilies on the Easter Gospels have ended, the Acts of the Apostles shall immediately be begun. After they have been read, the Apocalypse shall be added, followed by the canonical Epistles.

From this Sunday after Low Sunday, the Office for the Dead, the familiar psalms, and the other things that had been omitted out of reverence for these days shall be restored. During this period, however, until the octave of Pentecost, the three psalms concerning peace, which are customarily said with prostration, shall be omitted. The genuflections that we call *veniae* shall be postponed during this period, except those imposed on people who make mistakes in singing or psalmody in choir [Col. 0179D].

## Monday of the Rogations

Immediately after *Pretiosa* (“Precious things”), the signal shall be given for Prime. After the Chapter, following a short interval, the signal shall be given for Terce. Immediately after Terce, the ministers of the altar shall vest again.

After Sext, the Office shall be *Exaudivit de templo* (“He heard from his temple”), etc. On this day, after Mass, while the brothers have gone to the dormitory to put on their cloaks for the procession, the secretary shall strike one of the larger bells three times, briefly. Then, when necessary, they shall return to choir. Meanwhile, all who must carry something in the procession shall put on albs [Col. 0180A].

Then, when the procession has been arranged, the cantor shall begin *Exsurge, Domine* (“Rise up, Lord”), with the verse *Deus, auribus nostris* (“O God, with our ears”), and the *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”). Meanwhile, the weekly server, remaining in his woolen cope, shall sprinkle the greater altar with holy water, then the community, and afterward say: “Show us your mercy” (*Ostende nobis misericordiam tuam*), *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), prayer *Praesta, quaesumus* (“Grant, we beseech you”).

Then the cantor shall begin *Surgite, sancti* (“Rise, holy ones”). As the procession moves, the banners shall proceed first; water, the cross, and candles shall follow in order; then the reliquary boxes containing the relics of the saints; afterward the community, with the prelate following last.

When the antiphon has ended, the responsory *Beatus Nicolaus* (“Blessed Nicholas”) shall follow; then, for Saint Hermeland, the responsory *Vir Israelita* (“An Israelite man”). At the entrance of the church of Blessed Mary, the antiphon *Alma Redemptoris* (“Nourishing Mother of the Redeemer”), verse *Post partum Virgo* (“After childbirth, Virgin”), prayer *Famulorum tuorum* (“Of your servants”). Then they shall enter through the left choir.

As the procession leaves from there, the cantor shall intone the responsory *O praeclare* (“O illustrious one”). When it has ended, with the verse, the antiphon for Mary Magdalene, *In diebus illis* (“In those days”), shall follow. Then, for Saint Martin, the antiphon *O Martine* (“O Martin”).

For Saint Clement, the responsory *Ora pro nobis, beate Clemens* (“Pray for us, blessed Clement”), with the verse. For Saint Vincent, the responsory *Agnosce* (“Recognize”), without a verse. Then the seven psalms *Domine, ne in furore* (“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury”), etc., shall be begun.

At the entrance of the church of Saint Eligius, the responsory *Miles Christi* (“Soldier of Christ”), verse *Ora pro nobis, beate Eligi* (“Pray for us, blessed Eligius”), prayer *Da, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus* (“Give, we beseech you, almighty God”). On the return, the responsory *Sancte Eligi* (“Saint Eligius”), with the verse *O sancte* (“O holy one”).

As the procession leaves Saint Saviour’s, two brothers shall begin the litany in this manner: *Salvator mundi* (“Saviour of the world”). This litany shall be lengthened or shortened according to the length of the route. When they have entered the choir, the bells shall sound a peal. After the litany, the priest shall say the verse “The voice of joy” (*Vox laetitiae*), followed by the prayer *Clamantes ad te, Domine* (“Crying out to you, Lord”).

After a short interval, the signal shall be given for None, and it shall be said [Col. 0180B].

## Tuesday

On this day, up to the movement of the procession, everything shall be done as arranged on the preceding day, both in the Masses and Hours and in the ordering of the procession.

When the procession moves, the cantor shall intone the antiphon *De Jerusalem exeunt* (“They go out from Jerusalem”), etc. The seven psalms shall follow: *Domine, ne in furore* (“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury”), etc.

At the entrance of Saint Gervasius: responsory *In circuitu tuo* (“Around you”), verse *Lux perpetua* (“Perpetual light”), verse *Vox laetitiae* (“The voice of joy”), prayer *Praesta, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus* (“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”). After the sermon, on the return, the responsory *Concede nobis* (“Grant us”), verse *Adjuvent nos* (“Let them help us”).

For Saint Nicholas, the responsory *Ex ejus tumba* (“From his tomb”), verse *Catervatim* (“In throngs”). On leaving Saint Nicholas, four brothers shall begin the litany in this manner: *Humili prece* (“With humble prayer”), etc. They shall proceed in this way to the church of Saint Laudo.

When the community has entered the choir, the bells shall sound a peal; the verse and prayer shall be as above. Then, after a short interval, the signal shall be given for None, and it shall be said [Col. 0180C].

## Wednesday

At Mass, the Office shall be *Omnes gentes* (“All nations”), etc. Immediately the signal shall be given for None, and it shall be said. Then the procession shall be arranged as before.

In the church of the Holy Trinity, the responsory *Honor virtus* (“Honor and strength”), verse *Benedicamus Patrem* (“Let us bless the Father”), prayer *Populum tuum, Domine* (“Your people, Lord”). On leaving that same church, the responsory *Summae Trinitati* (“To the highest Trinity”), verse *Praestet nobis* (“May he grant us”).

Afterward, four brothers shall sing the litany in this manner: *Rex, Kyrie* (“King, Lord, have mercy”). At the station before the church of Saint Audoenus: antiphon *Gaudent in coelis* (“They rejoice in heaven”), verse *Vox laetitiae* (“The voice of joy”), prayer *Propitiare, quaesumus, nobis, Domine* (“Be propitious to us, we beseech you, Lord”). On leaving, again *Rex, Kyrie* (“King, Lord, have mercy”). When the community has entered the choir, the bells shall sound a peal, and the prayer shall be said as above.

In the refectory the reading shall be: “Jesus, having lifted up his eyes” (*Sublevatis Jesus oculis*) [Col. 0180D].

## Eve of the Ascension of the Lord

At Vespers, Matins, and the other Hours, the bells shall be rung as prescribed for the Epiphany of the Lord.

At Vespers, the antiphon *Vado parare* (“I go to prepare”), psalm *Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum* (“Unless the Lord builds the house”), etc. [Col. 0181A].

At Matins, four men in silk copes shall sing the invitatory; the ninth responsory, *Viri Galilaei* (“Men of Galilee”), shall be sung by three men in silk copes. In the Chapter the reading shall be: “While the eleven were reclining” (*Recumbentibus undecim*).

After the Chapter the signal shall be given for the procession, and then for Terce. After Terce, the procession shall be arranged. In this procession there shall be no sprinkling with water, and *Exsurge* (“Rise up”) shall not be sung. Rather, as the procession moves, the cantor shall begin the responsory *Tempus est* (“It is time”), verse *Pacem meam* (“My peace”).

It should nevertheless be noted that in the procession on this day everyone wears only surplices.

Another responsory: *Non conturbetur* (“Let not [your heart] be troubled”), etc. At the entrance of the church of Blessed Mary, the antiphon *O rex gloriae* (“O King of glory”), etc.

On leaving the atrium of Blessed Mary, after making a station there, three brothers shall begin *Salve, festa dies* (“Hail, festive day”), the community repeating each verse, now *Salve* (“Hail”), now *Qua Deus* (“By whom God …”). After a brief station has been made before the church doors and the verses have ended, the prelate shall intone the antiphon *O rex gloriae* (“O King of glory”). Then, when the community has returned to choir, the prelate shall say the verse *Elevata est* (“She has been lifted up”), with the prayer *Deus, cujus Filius* (“O God, whose Son …”).

After a short interval, the ministers of the altar shall be honorably prepared for Mass. When the bells have sounded a peal, Mass shall begin with the Office *Viri Galilaei* (“Men of Galilee”), etc. The Epistle shall be read at the lectern.

In the refectory the reading shall be “While they were reclining” (*Recumbentibus*), followed by sermons on the same feast.

Saturday. On this day, when None has ended, the subprior immediately goes to read; the lessons are assigned to the seniors as on Holy Saturday. The prelate and ministers likewise vest as then, and proceed to the altar and return from it. At the beginning of the service the blessed candle is lit, and is not extinguished until after Compline on the following day. The first lesson is “God tested Abraham,” etc. Afterwards, whether in the procession to the font or in the litanies, everything is completed as on Holy Saturday. After the final litany, when the cantor begins “Kyrie, eleison,” all the church lights are lit; while “Gloria in excelsis Deo” is sung, the great bell is rung. “Alleluia, Confitemini Domino” is sung from the pulpit; “Alleluia” is repeated and ends with a jubilant neum. The Tract “Laudate Dominum” is sung at the choir steps; the Gospel is accompanied by candles and incense, etc. After Mass no bell is rung, but after a brief interval two of the larger bells are rung for None. In the refectory the reading is “If you love me.” The Office of this day and of the following week is to be performed with the same care and dignity as during Easter Week. [Col. 0181B]

At Vespers: antiphon “I will not leave you,” Psalm “Benedictus,” etc. At Compline, antiphon “The Paraclete Spirit, alleluia,” Psalm “Nunc dimittis.”

At Matins the entire great-bell sequence is rung first; all antiphons end with a neum; the homily is read in a silk cope. In the chapter the reading is “If anyone loves me.” Immediately after chapter the bell is rung for the procession; afterwards, when the bell has been rung for Terce, the cantor begins the antiphon “I saw water”; the altars are sprinkled, and then the choir. The procession is made in silk copes, during which three of the senior members sing the sequence “Alma chorus Domini,” with the choir repeating the same verse after each verse—namely, “Alma chorus Domini.” It should also be understood that while the singers recite their verse, the entire procession must stand.

When the sequence is finished, the prelate begins the antiphon “Today they have been filled”; meanwhile all the church lights are lit. After the antiphon, the prelate says the verse “They have been filled,” with the prayer “O God, who on this day….” Terce is immediately begun by the prelate. The hymn “Veni, creator Spiritus” is solemnly and devoutly begun by the prelate before the altar. Then, while all ask pardon—that is, while they kneel—the same hymn is sung slowly by both choirs together, with great exultation. Meanwhile all the bells are rung; the altars are incensed with two thuribles; then incense is carried through the choir. At this Hour the prelate imposes the antiphon and, after the psalmody, begins again “Accipite.” [Col. 0181C–D]

Monday: invitatory “They have been filled,” etc. For feasts of nine lessons, except on the first day, a commemoration is made at Vespers and Matins and at the morning Mass, and after Trinity the entire service is observed. For feasts of three lessons, a commemoration is made, and after the fourth day the morning Mass is observed. Every day at Terce the hymn “Veni, creator” is sung. The priest who says that Hour begins it, and it is sung simultaneously by everyone, as stated above. The altars, however, are incensed by the priest with one thurible, and then incense is carried through the choir. Only three lights are lit for this Hour after the first day. The priest begins the antiphon “Accipite,” etc. In the refectory the reading is “God so loved the world.” [Col. 0182A]

Saturday: at Mass all the prayers are said without “Dominus vobiscum,” except the one said before the Epistle. The lessons are read with their titles. “Blessed are you, Lord” is sung by two at the steps and repeated. The Epistle is “It is fitting,” etc. Alleluia 1: “Emit­te”; 2: “Laudate Dominum”; both Alleluias are sung at the steps, etc. Immediately after Mass, Sext is said. At None two of the larger bells are rung. After None the Paschal candle is removed. In the refectory the reading is “Jesus rose.” [332]

The feast of the Holy Trinity is celebrated in the manner of Christmas, with the same dignity and care. On the Holy Trinity, both at Vespers and at Matins, all the antiphons end with a neum. At Compline and thereafter: antiphon “Miserere.” [Col. 0182B]

After Compline, following a brief interval for the brothers’ needs, the great bell is rung for Matins. The first responsory, “May he bless us,” is sung by two in silk copes; the third responsory, “Who is God,” is sung in silk copes by three; the sixth responsory, “Honor,” in silk copes by the prior and two seniors. The homily is read in a silk cope. The ninth responsory is sung by four in copes and is repeated. The morning Mass is of Sunday. In the chapter the reading is “There was a man of the Pharisees.” Then the bell is rung for the procession, which must be made in silk copes.

Monday, at Matins, the invitatory is “Come, let us rejoice.” It should be noted that the hymns and ferial antiphons are said up to the Advent of the Lord in the same manner in which they are designated in the history of the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany, namely: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” The reading, both in church and in the refectory, is to be from the Book of Kings, as follows: “There was a certain man from Ramah”; responsory “God of all,” etc. The Sunday collect throughout the week is “O God, in whom those who hope….” From the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, on ferial days as well as Sundays, the chapters are said as from the octave of Epiphany until Lent. From the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, at every Vespers and Matins a commemoration of the Holy Cross is made, except on double feasts. During this period until the Advent of the Lord, on every Sunday the ninth responsory at Matins is to be taken from the history of the Trinity, except when that history is begun. On every Sunday during this period, the responsories from the Trinity are sung successively at the procession, except when a double feast or triple octaves are being celebrated. [Col. 0182C]

This history is sung in this manner, both on Sundays and on ferial days, until the Kalends of August.

Here begins the history from the Book of Wisdom, to be sung and read from the Kalends of August until the Kalends of September. [Col. 0182D]

Here begins the history of Job, to be sung from the Kalends of September until the middle of that same month.

Here begins the history of Tobit, to be sung together with the history of Judith, which follows, from the middle of September until the Kalends of October. [334]

The history of Judith follows, to be sung before the Kalends of October.

Here begins the history of the Maccabees, to be sung from the Kalends of October until the Kalends of November.

Here begins the history of the prophets, to be sung from the Kalends of November until the Advent of the Lord.

It should be noted that on whatever day the individual Gospels for the Sundays written above are recited in church—whether it is Sunday or another designated day—their homilies must be read in the refectory on that same day. The following order is to be maintained for beginning the books, both in reading and in singing: if the Kalends of a month fall on Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, the historical book, together with its responsories, is begun on that Sunday. But if the Kalends of a month fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the historical book and the responsories are deferred until the following Sunday. [Col. 0183A; Col. 0184A]

Here ends, with the help of God’s grace, the Temporal Office.

## On the Feasts of the Saints

### Preface

After discussing the order of the Temporal Office as seemed appropriate to us, it remains for us to undertake to insert into the present work how the feasts of the saints ought to be celebrated. To preserve the order we have begun, we arrange the beginning of our treatment with the feast of Saint Andrew, which is always commemorated around the beginning of the Advent of the Lord. [Col. 0183]

Throughout Advent we fast every day, and on all feasts occurring during it; on Sundays alone we eat twice.

When a feast of the saints is solemnized during Advent, before Terce the summons to vest is rung. When it has been sung, Mass follows, and immediately, without an interval, the bell is rung for Sext, which is said. After a brief interval the bell is rung for None, which is said before dinner. When the service is of the season, without a summons, Terce is said; when it has been sung, the summons to vest is rung, and Sext is said. When Sext has been sung, Mass follows; after a brief interval the bell is rung for None, etc., as above. [Col. 0183A]

### The Feast of Saint Andrew

At first Vespers one lamp is to burn, together with three basin-candles; the great bell is rung. The weekly cantor begins the antiphon “One of the two” in the choir where he is serving the week. The psalms are those of the day. The responsory “Man of God” is sung at the steps by two weekly cantors in silk copes. A lectern covered with linen is to be in the choir. The antiphon “When he had arrived” is to be imposed by the weekly cantor in the choir where he is serving the week, unless he is himself the senior; in that case he imposes it on the next-ranking cantor. The priest puts on a silk cope and, preceded by candle-bearers, incenses the high altar and the Matins altar. On returning to the choir he incenses the prior; afterwards he is incensed before the lectern. Then the right choir is incensed, beginning with the seniors, and afterwards the left. [336]

At Matins the bells are rung singly once and twice, and a third and fourth time, immediately followed by the great bell. [Col. 0183C] Two lamps are to burn between the choir and the altar, and one lamp at each altar; these are extinguished after Matins. The invitatory “Let us adore” is sung by two. In the first nocturn the antiphon “Andrew” is begun by the weekly cantor of the choir in which he is serving. The antiphon “I am of the cross” is begun by another cantor; the remaining antiphons are imposed beginning with the juniors. [337]

If it is before Advent, “Te Deum laudamus” is sung; meanwhile two medium bells are rung, and at the verse “Through every day” the great bell is rung. If it is during Advent, while the ninth responsory is sung the bell is rung as above, and when the responsory is begun again the great bell is sounded.

At Lauds, for the Benedictus, the weekly cantor begins the antiphon “Jesus walking” in his stall. The prayer is “Majesty.” At Prime two medium bells are rung. The antiphon “Living for two days” is begun by the junior of the choir in which the week is being served; likewise with the other antiphons at the Hours.

At Mass the great bell is rung, and three basin-candles are lit. The deacon and subdeacon are to wear the dalmatic and tunic. The Gradual “You will appoint them” is sung by two and is not repeated. The Alleluia is likewise sung by two in silk copes, but is repeated. The Gospel is accompanied by candle-bearers and incense. The Creed is said, and the text is carried through the choir with incense. This is the rule: it is not carried unless the Creed is said. In the refectory the reading is “Walking.” [Col. 0183D]

If it is necessary to transfer the feast of Saint Andrew to the following day, the feast of Blessed Eligius is likewise transferred to the next day. At Vespers three basin-candles are to burn; the priest in a cope incenses the two altars.

### Saint Nicholas

A simple double feast—that is, one of the third rank—is celebrated for Blessed Nicholas. The invitatory is sung by three, namely the weekly cantors and another. The prior is assigned the sixth responsory; he reads the ninth lesson in a silk cope, with candle-bearers. [338]

At Vespers five lamps and three candles are lit. The high altar is prepared, and the choir is conducted in silk copes. The psalms are those of the day. The prior says the chapter without a cope and without candle-bearers. The responsory “One day” is sung in copes by the cantor and the weekly cantors directing the choir. The antiphon “O shepherd” is imposed on the prior or his substitute. “Benedicamus” is said by three.

At Matins the bells are rung two by two as prescribed in the Order, with the great bell last; the lights are as above. The invitatory is sung by three. At Prime one large bell and one medium bell are rung.

At Mass the Office is “He appointed.” The Gradual “Lord, you went before” is sung by two in silk copes at the steps and is repeated. The Alleluia is sung by three. The sequence “Rejoicing together” is sung; meanwhile the bells used at Prime are rung. The Gospel is accompanied by candle-bearers. At Vespers the lights and ringing are as above. [Col. 0184A–B]

### The Conception of Blessed Mary

A simple double feast is celebrated, as above for Saint Nicholas. On whatever day it occurs, the entire service is of the feast, with a commemoration of Advent. [339]

At Vespers the antiphon is “Heavenly favor,” and the psalms are those of the day. Everything is done as at the Nativity of the same Virgin, except that wherever “Nativity” is named here “Conception” is to be named. It is additionally prescribed that proper prayers are said at Sext and None.

### The Vigil of Saint Thomas

At Vespers the psalms are those of the day. The responsory is sung in silk copes by two weekly cantors. The priest in a cope incenses the two altars, then the prior, and afterwards is incensed before the lectern in the choir. One lamp and three candles are to burn.

If at the vigil of Saint Thomas, or on his feast, the “O” is solemnized, after the feast antiphon, collect, and “Benedicamus,” the weekly cantor imposes the “O” on the celebrant. The entire antiphon is sung, followed by “Gloria Patri,” “As it was,” and then it is imposed and sung again. [Col. 0184B–C]

There are therefore certain feasts of three lessons that we call simple feasts. At them the ferial antiphons are said both at Vespers and at the nocturns, while the chapters and hymns, and Lauds with one antiphon belonging to the feast, are said, together with the antiphon for the Benedictus. At such feasts the prayers and prostrations are not omitted. If such feasts occur on a Sunday or during double octaves, only a commemoration is made of them, together with the morning Mass. [340]

### Saint Vincent

A simple double feast—that is, one of the third rank—is celebrated for Saint Vincent. At Vespers the choir is conducted in copes. The antiphon “Blessed is the man” is imposed on the senior after the prior. The psalms are those of the day.

At all double feasts the choir is conducted, and with a third cantor added the responsory is sung. The antiphon “This sacred…”; Psalm “Magnificat”: the antiphon is imposed twice on the prior and is sung the same number of times. [Col. 0184D]

### The Conversion of Saint Paul

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for the Conversion of Saint Paul. At first Vespers the responsory is sung in silk copes, as at all feasts of the middle rank: “Holy Paul.” “Benedicamus” is said by two in silk copes.

### The Purification of Blessed Mary

The solemnity of the Purification of Blessed Mary is celebrated in the manner of the Epiphany of the Lord.

After Terce, when the candles have been honorably arranged on a carpet before the high altar, the prelate comes there vested in an alb, stole, and silk cope. He first blesses them and then sprinkles them with holy water. When the prelate has returned to his seat in the choir, the sacristan distributes the candles, beginning with the prelate and the other seniors. As they begin to be lit, the precentor begins the antiphon “A light for revelation,” which is repeated three times with the verses of “Nunc dimittis.” The antiphon “Hail, full of grace” is likewise sung in its entirety in the choir.

Meanwhile the procession is prepared. As soon as the antiphon “Adorn the bridal chamber” is begun, they set out and proceed through the cloister, making a station before the refectory until the antiphon “Adorn the bridal chamber” is finished. The cantor then imposes the responsory “He received the answer.” With it they come before the crucifix, where three singers in the pulpit sing the verse “Today the blessed….” Then, when the prelate has begun the antiphon “When they brought him in,” they return to the choir. After the verse “He received the answer” and the collect “Hear, Lord” have been said, the great bell is rung and Mass begins. [Col. 0185A]

The entire convent holds the candles in its hands until the prelate comes to the altar. He and the ministers likewise proceed to the altar with candles. Once they have arrived, they hold the candles in their hands as long as they have use for them; in the choir, those who wish may place theirs before them.

The Office is “We have received, O God.” “Kyrie, King of virgins” is sung by three, not in silk copes because of dripping wax, but in woolen copes as earlier in the procession; only the prelate wears a silk cope. The deacon and subdeacon do not wear the dalmatic or tunic, although they have them for Mass. The Epistle is read from the pulpit.

If the Tract is to be said, it is sung by four, who begin and end together; they sing its individual verses two by two. “Nunc dimittis” is sung in the same manner. The Tract is sung in the same manner on the Annunciation of the Lord. [342]

While the Offertory is sung, the ministers of the altar first offer their candles. Then, beginning with the seniors, the members of the choir come and return in an orderly manner. The sacristan keeps a basin with water beside him; dipping the candles received into it, he extinguishes them so that no smoke may arise. The prelate’s candle—or that of the person celebrating Mass in his place—is placed on the altar and is not extinguished until the end of Mass.

In the refectory the reading is “When they had completed….” [Col. 0185B]

On this day and on every Sunday until Palm Sunday, there is to be an interval between the thanksgiving after dinner and None. During that interval, until the bell is rung for None, conversation is held outside the cloister in the church of Blessed Mary. The same applies on feasts of nine lessons until Quinquagesima, when “Esto mihi” is sung. On feasts observed in the manner of octaves, the same interval is observed, but immediately after chapter conversation is held in the cloister as usual, and there are two meals. On all other days, and on principal feasts if they occur, fasting is observed until Palm Sunday. From this point onward, the servers are required to attend None unless they have a canonical excuse.

This feast, namely the Purification, when it occurs on the first Sunday of Septuagesima, is transferred to the following day; when it occurs on either of the two following Sundays, it is not transferred. [343]

At Vespers the antiphon is “With you is the beginning,” begun by the weekly cantor of the right choir in a silk cope, etc. The responsory “Rejoice, Mary” is sung at cockcrow by the cantors together with the precentor, in a cope. All the altars are incensed. The antiphon “When they brought him in” is imposed twice on the prior by the precentor and is sung three times. Psalm “Magnificat.” [Col. 0185D]

### Saint Ansbert, Bishop

The section on Saint Ansbert, bishop, follows. At Vespers and at the nocturns the ferial antiphons appropriate to the day are said, together with the chapters of one bishop and confessor. At the Magnificat: antiphon “I shall liken.” At Lauds: antiphon “Behold the priest,” etc. At the Benedictus: antiphon “Priest and pontiff.”
