Likewise, at the succeeding Hours, the antiphons and chapters of one bishop and confessor appropriate to each Hour are said, with the prayer of the feast; nevertheless, the prayers and prostration are not omitted. What we say concerning this feast is likewise to be observed at all times when prostrations are made and prayers are said, for all simple feasts of three lessons that have their own days. [Col. 0186A]

### The Annunciation of the Lord

A double feast is celebrated for the Annunciation of the Lord. At Vespers: antiphon “Hail, Mary.” The psalms are those of the day.

### Saint Mark

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for Saint Mark. If this feast occurs on a Sunday after the octave of Easter, the entire service is of the feast, with a commemoration of the Sunday and the morning Mass; on the following day there are a procession and a fast. If it occurs during the octaves of Easter, the procession is entirely omitted that year, but the feast is celebrated after the octaves with first Vespers. [344]

At Mass the Office is “You have protected,” etc. After Sext, while the brothers have gone to the dormitory to put on their copes for the procession, the sacristan rings one of the larger bells three times briefly. Then, after a short interval, when everyone has returned to the choir, the cantor first imposes the antiphon “Rise up, Lord.” The weekly cantor, remaining in his cope, sprinkles the principal altar and then sprinkles the convent in the customary order. Afterwards he says the verse “Show us, Lord, your mercy,” “Dominus vobiscum,” and the prayer for the fast.

The procession is then arranged. The cantor begins the antiphon “In the name of the Lord,” and the other antiphons, as many as are needed, until the entrance of the church of Saint John. At the entrance of that church the responsory is “Among those born of women.” Meanwhile the priest and ministers quickly prepare themselves to celebrate Mass.

When the responsory is finished, the priest says the verse “There was a man sent” and the prayer “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that the household….” The Office is “He heard from the temple.” The prayer is “Grant, we beseech you.” A commemoration of Saint John is made with the aforementioned prayer; a commemoration of all the saints is made with the prayer “Grant, we beseech you,” etc.

For this Mass, everything necessary for the service must have been brought there in advance through the sacristan’s provision. When Mass is completed, two brothers standing in the middle immediately begin the litany “Lord, defend us.” Meanwhile the priest and ministers, having finished their duties, return to their proper order. When the cantors have pronounced, “Saint John the Baptist, pray for us,” the procession returns; the litany is lengthened or shortened according to the distance of the route. Those who lead it walk together in the midst of the convent. [345]

When the litany is finished, the priest says at the choir steps the verse “A voice of gladness” and the prayer “Crying out to you, Lord.” Then, after the copes have been removed, the bell is rung for None. In the refectory the reading is “Which of you, having a friend….” [Col. 0186B–C]

It should be noted that, when this feast occurs during Easter Week, its service is deferred until the Monday after Quasimodo. The procession, however, is celebrated on the actual day on which the feast occurs in the following manner. Once the procession has been arranged, two immediately begin at the steps “Hail, festive day”; the convent repeats each verse, now “Hail,” now “By which God….” Singing in this manner, they proceed to the church of Saint John.

At the entrance of the church the responsory is “Among those born,” with the verse “There was a man sent” and the prayer “Grant, we beseech you.” Mass is not celebrated there at that time. After whatever interval is appropriate, the procession is arranged; on the return, the cantors begin where they had previously stopped and continue the remaining verses as far as necessary. When they have returned to the choir, the priest says at the steps the verse “A voice of gladness.” The prayer is “Grant, we beseech you.” [346; Col. 0186D]

### Saints Philip and James

For the apostles Philip and James, at second Vespers the antiphon is “Lord,” etc. After Vespers, when the antiphon “Faithful Cross” has been begun, they go out in procession to the crucifix; from there they return to the choir with the antiphon for martyrs, “Daughters of Jerusalem.” At Lauds there is a procession to the crucifix; on the return, the commemoration for martyrs is “Perpetual light,” etc.

### Saint John the Baptist

A double feast of the first rank is celebrated for Saint John the Baptist. At Vespers the antiphon is “He descended.” The psalms are those of the day. The antiphon “When he entered” is imposed twice and sung three times. The Psalm “Magnificat” at both Vespers, at Matins, during the cloister procession, and with the neums of each antiphon is done in the same manner as at Trinity.

The altar of Saint John is curtained and decorated with rushes. At first Vespers there is no procession to the altar. After Vespers the procession goes with the cross and candle-bearers to the church of Saint John, carrying the reliquary of Blessed Laudus. As the procession moves, the cantor begins the responsory “O light,” with its verse and “Gloria.” At the entrance of the church of Saint John: responsory “Among those born.”

When the responsory is finished, the prior begins Vespers, which are said in the same manner as above. It should be understood that the body of Blessed Laudus is to remain there until after the next day’s Vespers, and that a candle prepared by the priest of that church must burn continually before the reliquary. After Vespers has been said, the convent returns without singing anything. [347; Col. 0187A]

After Compline, following a brief interval, the great bell is rung for Matins. The invitatory is sung by four, and everything else is as at Trinity. All the antiphons end with a neum. The homily is read in a silk cope, and likewise the ninth lesson in a silk cope, with candle-bearers present.

At Lauds, for the Benedictus, the antiphon “It was opened” is sung three times, the first time up to “And he prophesied, saying.” Psalm “Benedictus” is begun and imposed twice on the prior. There is a procession to the altar.

The morning Mass is celebrated at the altar of Saint John and is of the saint. The Office is “The just shall flourish like a palm tree.” The prayer is “Grant, we beseech you.” The Epistle is “The word of the Lord came to me, saying.” The Gradual is “The just shall flourish like a palm tree.” The Alleluia is “You, child.” The Gospel is “Zechariah said to the angel.” The Offertory is “In strength.” The Communion is “You have set, Lord.” [Col. 0187B]

At Terce the antiphon is “They beckoned,” etc. On whatever day it occurs, the procession is made in silk copes.

At Mass the Office is “From the womb.” “Kyrie, Almighty.” The prayer is “O God, who have made this present….” The Epistle, “Listen, islands,” is read from the pulpit. The Gradual is “Before I formed you.” The Alleluia is “Among those born.” The Gospel is “Elizabeth was filled.” The Offertory is “The just shall flourish like a palm tree.” The Communion is “You, child.” [348]

After Vespers the procession proceeds without singing anything to the church of Saint John. There, when two men have taken up the reliquary containing the sacred body, the cantor immediately begins the responsory “O truly spiritual,” with its verse and “Gloria.” At the entrance of the church: “O blessed bishop Laudus.” Verse: “Pray for us.” Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty….”

### Saint Eusebius the Confessor

At Matins there are three lessons. On this day the chapter (Latin *in capitulo*, read *capitulum*) is to be honorably prepared as on the vigil of Christmas. When the reader announces “The Dormition of Holy Mary,” everyone prostrates himself on the ground, remembering and considering within himself how many blessings we have received through this glorious Virgin. After a short interval, when the prelate gives the signal, they rise, and the reader continues what remains. Afterwards the Gospel lesson “A certain woman raised her voice” is read.

At the end of chapter, both on this day and on the eight following days, the psalm “Praise the Lord, all nations” is said. From then on the vigil is celebrated with great joy; prostrations and the customary psalms are suspended. The following Hours are said of the Virgin herself, even if it is Sunday, with the collect of the vigil. [349; Col. 0187C]

At Mass the Office is “Hail, holy Parent.” The Gradual “Blessed” is sung at the steps by two in silk copes. If it is Sunday, the Alleluia “After childbirth” is likewise sung in copes by three. The sequence, Creed, and proper preface are not said. The Gospel “It happened, while he was speaking” is accompanied by candles and incense. At the end of Mass no bell is rung, but after a brief interval two of the larger bells are rung for None. In the refectory the reading is “It happened, while he was speaking.” [Col. 0187D]

This solemnity is to be celebrated in the manner of Christmas. At Vespers the antiphon is “You are wholly beautiful.” Psalm “Praise, children, the Lord,” etc. All the antiphons at Vespers, Matins, and Lauds end with a neum. The antiphon “Christ ascended” is imposed twice by the precentor on the prelate and sung three times. All the altars are incensed.

At Matins all the bells are first rung in the great peal. The invitatory is sung by four in copes. The homily is read in a silk cope.

The procession is made in copes. At Mass the Office is “Let us rejoice.” “Kyrie, King of virgins.” The Epistle is read from the pulpit, etc. In the refectory the reading is “Jesus entered,” followed by sermons on the same feast. Throughout the octaves: “You compel me, O Paula,” etc. [350; Col. 0188A]

### Saint Bartholomew

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for Saint Bartholomew. At first Vespers the antiphon is “Be strong.” The psalms are those of the day.

It should be noted that on this day at Vespers, and on the following day at Mass, seven of our canons are customarily required to go to Saint Audoenus with the procession of Blessed Mary. Nevertheless, at our Vespers we make a commemoration of Saint Audoenus with this antiphon: “Receive our….”

### Saint Augustine

A double feast of the first rank is celebrated for Saint Augustine. At Vespers: “Rejoice, mother.” The psalms are those of the day. The antiphon “The day is present” is imposed twice and sung three times. All the altars are incensed. Psalm “Magnificat.” “Benedicamus” is said by three.

The procession is made in silk copes. At the pulpit the prose is sung by three, with the Fathers. At Mass the Office is “In the midst of the Church.” “Kyrie, Almighty.” The Epistle is read from the pulpit, etc. In the refectory the reading is “Blessed Augustine from the province,” etc. [Col. 0188B]

At Vespers the antiphon is “After death,” etc. The antiphon “Today the glorious one” is sung three times. Psalm “Magnificat.” “Benedicamus.” Afterwards three others in red copes begin at the steps the responsory “Among those born,” and there is a procession to the altar. The verse “There was a man” is sung; the verse “With glory and honor” is said by the last member of the right choir in a cope. “Benedicamus Domino.” [351]

### The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

A double feast of the second rank is celebrated for the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. At Vespers the antiphon is “Heavenly favor,” etc. The morning Mass is of Saint Adrian, unless it is Sunday. On this day the procession is not made in silk copes. At the principal Mass the Office is “Let us rejoice.” The Epistle “I am like a vine” is read from the pulpit. The Gospel is “The book of the generation,” etc.

### The Exaltation of the Holy Cross

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, except that the ninth responsory is double. At Vespers and Lauds there is a procession to the altar. On the return, the commemoration for the martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian is “These are the saints.” [Col. 0188C]

### The Solemnity of Saint Laudus

A triple feast is celebrated for the solemnity of Saint Laudus. At Vespers twelve candles are lit around the choir, in addition to the candelabrum and the other customary light. The antiphon is “In praise of Christ,” and the psalms are those of the day. The weekly cantors direct the choir in silk copes. All the antiphons, both daytime and nighttime, end with a neum. The chapter is said by the prelate in a silk cope. The responsory “O light of the world” is sung by three seniors in silk copes. The antiphon “By vow, by voice” is imposed twice and sung three times. Psalm “Magnificat.” The high altar is incensed with two thuribles. [352]

At Matins the great bell is rung first. The invitatory “One and true God” is sung by four in silk copes. The third responsory, “O light of the world,” is sung by three in silk copes. The sixth, “O truly,” is sung by three in silk copes—namely, the prior and two seniors. In the third nocturn the homily is read in a silk cope. The ninth responsory, “O rejoicing in gain,” is performed by four in silk copes and repeated.

At Lauds, for the Benedictus, the antiphon “Like the moon” is imposed twice and sung three times. All the altars are incensed. In the chapter the reading is “Watch, be vigilant.” At the end of chapter throughout the octaves the psalm “Praise the Lord, all nations” is said. After chapter the bell is rung for the procession. [Col. 0188D]

It should be noted that if the feast of Saint Laudus occurs on Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, the Ember fast is to be observed in the preceding week. [Note: On the patronal feast they did not fast.]

The procession is made in silk copes. In this procession the reliquary of Blessed Laudus must be carried honorably behind the convent by two bearers in silk copes, with two candle-bearers; two other men precede the cross, together with the thurifer. [353]

At the station in the church, four in silk copes say from the pulpit the responsory “O truly,” with the verse “With you as protector.” At the entrance of the choir: “O blessed bishop Laudus.” [Col. 0189A]

At Mass the Office is “He appointed.” A pneuma follows; then Kyrie, “God the Creator.” “Gloria in excelsis” is sung with the prose “O glory of the saints.” The prayer is “O God, who for adorning….” The Epistle is “Behold the priest.” The Gradual “Lord, you went before” is sung by three from the pulpit. The Alleluia is “Hail, gem.” The sequence is “Noble choir.”

In the refectory: the Life of Saint Laudus, followed by the sermon “The Lord and our Savior, dearly beloved brothers.” At Vespers the antiphon is “Blessed Laudus,” etc. Eight singers, or more or fewer at the precentor’s discretion, sing the responsory “O rejoicing in gain” around the choir. A commemoration is made of Saint Matthew.

### The Octave of Saint Laudus

A double feast of the third rank is celebrated for the octave of Saint Laudus. One candle must burn on the altar before the body of Saint Laudus at both Vespers and Matins.

### Saints Remigius, Germanus, and Vedastus

Three lessons are read for the holy confessors Remigius (1 October), Germanus, and Vedastus. From this day until Easter the midday sleep is suspended. From this day until the Kalends of November, unless it is a feast of nine lessons or a feast celebrated in the manner of an octave, None is sung immediately after thanksgiving. [Col. 0189B]

On feasts of nine lessons, however, the brothers must converse outside the cloister after dinner, until the bell is rung for None, up to the feast of All Saints. The table servers ought to attend None if they can conveniently do so. [354]

### The Translation of Saint Augustine

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for the Translation of Saint Augustine. At Vespers the antiphon is “Rejoice.” The psalms are those of the day. The procession is made to the altar common to Saint Augustine and Saint Nicholas. On the return, the commemoration for the martyrs is “They rejoice in heaven.”

At Matins, as at the other solemnity, while preserving the character of a feast of the middle rank, the middle lessons and middle responsories are nevertheless taken from the martyrs. At Lauds there is a procession to the altar; on the return, the commemoration for the martyrs is “When you hear.”

### The Dedication of the Church

A triple feast is celebrated for the dedication of the church. At Vespers the antiphon is “The architect,” etc. On the first day all the antiphons, both daytime and nighttime, end with a neum. The antiphon “The Lord sanctified” is sung three times. Psalm “Magnificat.” Only the high altar and the Matins altar are incensed. [Col. 0189C]

After “Benedicamus” a procession is made to the twelve crosses painted in the church. At each procession—namely, at Vespers and Matins—five candles are to be lit at each individual cross [editorial reading: *singuli*, “individual,” for the printed form]. For the procession the responsory is “Terrible is this place,” with its verse and “Gloria,” if needed. As he proceeds, the prelate must incense each cross together with its altar. In the choir: verse “Blessed are those who dwell.” The prayer is “Grant, we beseech you, Lord.” [355]

Before Matins the great bell is rung. The homily is read in a silk cope. At Lauds the procession is made as after Vespers. In the chapter the reading is “Jesus went out and passed through Jericho.” Afterwards the bell is solemnly rung for the procession, which is made in silk copes. The responsory is “Terrible.” At the station the responsory “Behold the tabernacle” is sung by three from the pulpit, with the verse “If anyone….” [Col. 0189D]

At Mass the Office is “Terrible is this place,” etc. In the refectory the reading is “Jesus went out.”

Throughout the octave, at the Hours and at Mass, the service is performed in the manner of a feast of the middle rank. The Alleluia is sung in silk copes; the ministers of the altar wear tunics and dalmatics. In the refectory there are sermons on the feast, as many as can adequately suffice.

### Saint Mellon

A double feast of the third rank is celebrated for Saint Mellon.

### Saint Romanus

A feast of the middle rank is celebrated for Saint Romanus. At Vespers the antiphon is “I shall liken.” The psalms are those of the day.

### Saint Fromond the Martyr

A double feast is celebrated for Saint Fromond the martyr. At both Vespers and Matins a candle burns before the bier. At Vespers the antiphon is “Blessed is the man.” The psalms are those of the day. [356]

If it is Sunday, the responsory “With glory and honor” is said at the procession. In that procession the reliquary of Blessed Fromond must be carried, with two candles beside the bier.

## On All Saints

The feast of All Saints is celebrated as a triple feast. Let all the antiphons end with a neum. Before Matins, let all the bells be rung in the manner of a signal. Let the first lesson [Col. 0190A] be read by the prelate in a silk cope, the second by the subprior without a silk cope, and the remaining lessons by the seniors according to their established order. On this feast the Gospel is not announced; rather, the seventh lesson begins as follows: “To the priests of Christ.” The eighth lesson is read by one of the younger members; for None, however, one of the priests is appointed to read the lesson, which must be read in a silk cope.

The first responsory is sung by four persons in silk copes: “To the Most High Trinity.” Verse: “May he grant us.” “Glory be to the Father” is added, and “To the Most High Trinity” is begun again. The second responsory is sung by the prelate together with two others, likewise in silk copes. The remaining responsories are sung by pairs, but not in silk copes; the ninth responsory, “Grant us,” is sung by three persons in silk copes. In the chapter-house the lesson is “To the priests of Christ indeed.” The procession on this day is not conducted in silk copes. For the procession, “Grant” is sung by three persons at the lectern: verse, “May they help.” The Mass proper is “Let us rejoice.” The Epistle is read at the lectern. In the refectory the lesson is “When Jesus saw the crowds.”

[Col. 0190B] From the Kalends of November until the Purification of Blessed Mary, immediately after grace has been said, with the Lord’s Prayer first, None is sung when there are two meals.

At Vespers, the antiphon “Savior of the world” is sung three times. Psalm: “My soul magnifies.” After Vespers, Vespers for the commemoration of the faithful departed is celebrated more festively than usual, as follows: let the precentor begin the first antiphon, and the weekly cantors the others; let the psalms be sung sitting, because, if a station were held and the antiphons were carried, there would thereby be two Vespers services in the community, which never occurs. Antiphon: “I am pleased”; psalm: “I have loved.” With this addition: at the end of each psalm, “Eternal rest,” etc., is said. Psalm: “My soul magnifies”; at the end, “Lord, have mercy” three times with singing, etc.; only one collect: “O God of the faithful,” etc. “May they rest in peace.” When this has been completed, let the signal be sounded for a while, while the community waits in the choir.

On the following day, the entire Office is celebrated for the dead in the manner of a double feast of the third rank. At Matins [Col. 0190C], let the bells be sounded two by two. After the signal has been sounded, with the Lord’s Prayer first, and the prelate having made the sound, let the weekly cantor of the right choir carry the first antiphon through the choir to the prelate, outside the stalls; let the remaining antiphons be carried to the senior members, at the end of each psalm. At all the Hours also, “Eternal rest” is said in place of “Glory be to the Father.” Antiphon: “Direct [my way].” Psalm: “Attend to my words,” etc. Verse: “From the gate of hell.”

The lessons are read at the lectern outside the choir and are taken from the First Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Corinthians, toward the end: “But if Christ is preached,” etc. The lessons are read without “Give [your blessing]” and without “But you, [Lord].” The ninth responsory, “Deliver me, Lord,” is sung by three persons. At the end, the prelate says, “May they rest in peace,” and, when “Amen” has been answered, all keep silence. Meanwhile, let the signal be sounded for a while, while the community waits in the choir. When the signal has ended, the prelate begins the antiphon brought to him by the weekly cantor: “They shall exult,” etc.

At Prime and at all the Hours, the weekly cantor of the principal Mass begins the antiphon in place of “O God, come to my assistance.” In the chapter-house, let everything be done as usual; the lesson “The time that intervenes between a person’s death” is read without “Give [your blessing]” and without “But you, [Lord].” At the end, the chapter is “Attend to my words.” As usual, after the chapter the bell is sounded for the procession, then for vesting, and afterward, when they have vested, for Terce.

When Terce has ended and the procession has been prepared with blessed water, a cross, candles, and a thurible, the prelate also vested and the ministers ready in white, with the cantor beginning the responsory “I believe that my Redeemer,” the procession goes out through the right-hand side of the church. The prelate sprinkles the tombs of the dead. Meanwhile, while the community waits in orderly fashion in the basilica and sings the responsories of the Office, namely, “I believe that my Redeemer,” etc., as much as is necessary, the prelate goes out with the ministers, the cross, the candles, and the blessed water to the common cemetery of the parishioners, and there sprinkles the blessed water around it.

Then, after the prelate has returned, the entire procession proceeds through the cloister, the prelate himself likewise sprinkling the blessed water. As he passes with [Col. 0191A] the ministers into the brothers’ cemetery, the community, standing in its proper order before the chapter-house, finishes the aforesaid responsories. When they have ended, “Lord, have mercy” is said three times with singing. The prelate says: “And lead us not,” etc.; “O God, giver of forgiveness”; “O God, by whose mercy.” At the end: “May they rest in peace.” “Amen.”

Afterward, the community returns to the choir with the seven psalms, without “Glory be to the Father”; the prelate goes with the ministers to the vesting room. At the end of the seven psalms, “Eternal rest” is said, followed by “Lord, have mercy” three times without singing. The prayer “Absolve” is then said again with the aforesaid petitions. After the signal has been sounded, Mass for the faithful is celebrated solemnly at the high altar.

The deacon wears a dalmatic, the subdeacon a tunic, and the weekly cantors direct the choir together with the precentor. The Mass proper is “Eternal rest.” Psalm: “To you praise is due”; “Eternal rest” is repeated, and, in place of “Glory be to the Father,” the verse “Hear my prayer,” etc., is said. “Eternal rest” is repeated. There is only one prayer, namely, “O God of the faithful.” The Epistle is “The hand of the Lord was upon me.”

The Gradual [Col. 0191B] “Though I walk” is sung by two persons at the steps in silk copes, and is begun again. The entire Tract “Out of the depths” is sung by three persons in silk copes. The Gospel is “As the Father raises up.” The Offertory is “Lord Jesus Christ.” Priest: “Sacrifices,” etc. Communion [Col. 0192A]: “Eternal light”; “Eternal rest.” At the end, no bell is sounded. At None, after the thanksgiving.

It should be noted that, if the feast of All Saints falls on a Saturday, the Office of the faithful departed is entirely postponed until the following Monday, to be celebrated in the manner described above. On Saturday at Vespers, that is, on the feast of All Saints, a commemoration is made only of Sunday.

The feast of Saint Rumpharius is a double feast of the second rank. At Vespers, the antiphon “I shall make him like” is sung, and the other antiphons with the psalms of the day; everything else—in hymns, antiphons, psalms, and responsories—is as on the feast of Saint Laudo, except that on this feast none of the antiphons ends with a neum. It should also be known that one candle must burn continuously before the reliquary of Blessed Rumpharius, from the beginning of First Vespers until the end of Second Vespers.

In the chapter-house the lesson is “A certain man went abroad.” Let the procession be held with the reliquary of Blessed Rumpharius, but not in silk [Col. 0192B] copes. For the procession, the responsory “Let your loins be girded” is sung; two candles are carried beside the reliquary if boys are present. The verse “Watch” is sung by three persons at the lectern. At Mass, the proper is “He established,” etc. The Epistle is read at the lectern.

[Col. 0191]

# Exposition on the Canon of the Mass by an Unknown Author

According to Amalarius [manuscript: Alarius].

(From an old Bigotian manuscript codex.)

[Col. 0191C] “The Lord be with you.” The priest greets the people and prays that the Lord may be with them.

“And with your spirit.” This is the people’s response and prayer: just as the priest prayed that the Lord might be with the people, so the people pray that the Lord may be with the spirit of the priest.

The priest says: “Pray, brothers.” He asks everyone to pray that his prayer may be heard.

And when he says, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” the priest prays to the Lord Father that the prayer may be completed through his Son, who is our Lord equally with the Father.

When he says, “Who with you lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God,” he wishes the people to believe and understand that the Son, with his Father, has reigned and lived from the beginning without end, and is God just as the Father is God; that the Holy Spirit has one power with the Father and the Son, one substance, and in all things the unity of the Godhead.

“Throughout all ages of ages,” that is, so that the Son, with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, may be believed to live equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit—as he lived and existed in the Godhead before all ages—in the present age also, and in the future age, where the righteous will remain with the angels and the unjust will be tormented with the devil; and he has no end.

“Amen” is the confirmation of the prayer by the people. In our language it can be understood as though everyone were saying: “May it happen just as the priest has prayed.” Its proper interpretation, however, is “truly” or “faithfully.”

“Lift up your hearts.” The priest admonishes the people to lift their hearts upward—that is, above themselves—to the almighty Lord, and to pray faithfully that help may come to them from above, from the heavenly God by whom they were created.

“We have them with the Lord.” This is the people’s response. Just as the priest commanded them to hold their hearts above, they profess that they do so.

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” The priest gives thanks to God in accordance with the profession of the people, who have confessed that their attention is directed toward the Lord.

“It is worthy and just.” The people give thanks to God together with the priest, because it is a worthy and just prayer to give thanks to God, since from him we receive all good things.

“It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary.” The priest commends the prayer, or profession, of the people and says that it is truly worthy and just to give thanks to God, that it is right—that is, proper or equitable—to give thanks to the Savior, or full of salvation that we should give thanks to him who gave us eternal salvation.

“To give you thanks always and everywhere.” After the people’s confession, he turns toward the Lord and speaks as though to one present, because we are always in the Lord’s presence and he sees our thoughts. The priest says this both of himself and of the people: “always,” that is, at every time; “and everywhere,” that is, in every place, to give thanks.

“Lord,” because you are the ruler of all and everything is under your dominion.

“Holy,” you who are holy, and through whom all things are holy, because you created all good things.

“Father.” In Greek it is called πατήρ (*patēr*), and in Latin *genitor*, “begetter,” because he himself begot the Son without any defilement or corruption.

[Col. 0192D] In Latin, “Father” (*pater*) is said to derive from *paternus*, that is, from *perpetrando*, “accomplishing,” which comes from “perfecting” or “helping,” because he perfects everything that has been made and helps everything that has been helped; and he wished us to become his adopted children through the sanctification by which he himself sanctified us.

“Almighty,” the one who can do all things. For this reason he is called Almighty, and no word is impossible with God.

“Eternal God,” that is, eternal, perpetual, and temporal. The eternal is that which had no beginning and will have no end, which always was, is, and will be. The perpetual is that which began to exist and will have no end. The temporal is that which had a beginning and will have an end. Therefore he is called here “eternal God,” because he alone is eternal: he did not begin to be and does not cease to be, but is always God.

“God” (*Deus*) is said to derive from *diligendo*, “loving,” because he loves and governs everything he created. Alternatively, “God” is said to derive from *divinando*, “divining,” because he is divine and knows all things, and divides all things as he wills.

“Through Christ our Lord.” “Christ” is Greek; in Latin it is called “anointed.” This Christ was venerably begotten before all beginnings, from eternity. At the time appointed by him, the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin Mary, anointed her womb with divine anointing, and he was conceived of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0193A] and born of the Virgin Mary.

For in the Old Testament priests and kings were anointed, and therefore were called *christs*, because they had been anointed with a temporal anointing. This Christ, through whom we give eternal thanks to the Father, is Christ, and with the Father he is eternal God. Through him we have been redeemed, and he is our Lord, who exercises lordship over us.

“Through whom your majesty is praised by the angels.” Through this Christ we give thanks to the Father. The angels praise the Father’s majesty because he is equal to the Father in divinity. “Majesty” is as if from “greater power,” because God’s power is greater than human power.

The angels praise God’s majesty through Christ, because Christ created the angels together with the Father. For “angel” in Greek is interpreted as “messenger.” “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature, because an angel announces; by nature, however, he is spirit.

The angels adore and rejoice in the herald of the human race, and they praise their Creator three times by a double and a single [act of praise]. For our death is double—that is, of soul and body—but the angels praise because our double death has been freed by Christ’s single death. Our resurrection likewise is double, of soul and body: of the soul, when it rises from unbelief to faithfulness; of the body, when it is restored from dust to incorruption.

The angels praise [Col. 0193B] because our double resurrection will be granted through Christ’s single resurrection. The angels praise a third time because we have been freed from death not only by Christ’s death, but through his resurrection we will rise on the last day.

“Dominions adore.” The dominions praise and adore the majesty of God the Father through the Son. The order of the dominions is the tenth order of angels; it fell [Note: [Col. 0193D] Some, with Saint John Damascene, think that the angels fell only from the lowest order, but do not acknowledge a tenth order among them. See Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, Part I, question 63.], and through pride was cast into hell, or became the devil.

[Col. 0193C] Nine, however, remained in their holiness. These are their names: angels, archangels, virtues, principalities, powers, thrones, dominions, cherubim, and seraphim.

The names of these two [orders] are Hebrew [reading: Hebrew]. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”; “seraphim,” “burning.” The remaining names of the aforesaid orders are Latin [addition: and Greek], such as angels and archangels. Angels are called “messengers”; archangels, “exalted messengers.”

Pope Gregory the Roman, however, in his homily on the Gospel reading—Homily 34 [add: where]—says: “Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him” (Luke 15:1). He expounded the aforesaid orders most fully. Let us now return to the order under discussion.

“Powers tremble.” He speaks of the aforesaid orders. He does not say this because the aforesaid orders are bodily, but speaks according to our custom, because we normally tremble and fear before our lords [manuscript: “we used to tremble and fear”]. He says that they tremble and fear so that we may understand that all things heavenly, earthly, and infernal tremble and fear before the sight of the divine majesty.

“The heavens and the powers of the heavens.” The heavens themselves obey the divine command, because they do not have the power to show themselves clear or cloudy. “The heavens and the powers of the heavens” are the aforesaid order of angels, as Gregory attests in his homily on the Gospel reading, “There will be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars” (Luke 21:25; Homily 1).

“And blessed seraphim.” The seraphim have already been mentioned above.

“They celebrate together with shared rejoicing.” All the aforesaid orders equally celebrate the Father’s majesty through Christ with complete rejoicing.

“With whom we ask that you command our voices also to be admitted.” Together with these is our petition: that the heavenly Father himself, through Christ his Son, through whom we give thanks, may deign to admit our voices and join them to the voices of the aforesaid orders of angels.

“Saying with humble confession,” that is, with a humble confession. What is more humble to confess than to commend ourselves to the eternal Father through the eternal Son and to presume nothing upon our own conscience or goodness? In accordance with the angelic voices, we are always to believe and proclaim him without ceasing, saying:

“Holy, holy, holy.” The Evangelist John wrote in the Apocalypse that he saw before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four elders and four living creatures standing there and saying without ceasing: “Holy, holy, holy,” etc. (chapter 4).

It is said three times “Holy” so that the Father is understood to be holy, the Son holy, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son holy. But although “Holy” is said threefold [manuscript: twofold], it is nevertheless not said in the plural number, “Holies.” Yet although there is one holiness and one eternity understood in these three persons—

“Lord God of hosts.” Many customarily interpret *Sabaoth* as “almighty”; many others as “Lord God of armies,” so that he himself might order all the armies of angels and human beings.

“Full are the heavens and the earth of your glory. Hosanna in the highest.” Why is *Hosanna* now said corruptly, when previously it was said *Hosyanna*? *Osy* is an interjection of one praising [manuscript: “of praise”] or magnifying; *anna*, “save.” But it is said corruptly as *Hosanna*, and it may be understood as “save” or “save, we pray.” “In the highest,” that is, in the heights.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9). When Christ came to Jerusalem, descending from the Mount of Olives, the children of Israel cried out, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13). But what did that coming of Christ to Jerusalem signify except the future resurrection, when he will come to judge the living and the dead and will appear to us in the same flesh in which he suffered for us?

Then, “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10), and the other things that the Apostle said.

# The Canon of the Mass

[Col. 0194C] “Therefore, most merciful Father.” “To you” is said distinctly, that is, “most merciful Father.” “Clement” is said as if from *clara mens*, “clear mind,” or “abundant”; he is most illustrious in mind and most merciful in heart, the Father.

We do not call him clement and merciful because he is composed of bodily members, or of a heart or mind, as a human being is. Rather, we cry out to him as clement and merciful so that we may call upon that clemency and mercy, may perceive it over us from him, and may understand from it why we owe thanks to the Savior.

“Through Jesus Christ your Son.” “Jesus” is Greek; in Latin it is called “Savior” or “salutary.” He is called Savior because he saves his people from their sins; he saves from sins because he has power on earth to forgive sins. He is called salutary because he gave us salvation, so that, if we keep his commandments, we may be able to obtain eternal life.

“Your Son, our Lord.” His only-begotten Son, because he alone is the only-begotten one from the substance [Col. 0194D] of the Father. We, however, are adopted sons through him, who is the only-begotten one, proceeding from the Father and co-eternal with the Father. Therefore, through him we ought to petition the Father, saying:

“We humbly beg and ask you.” “Humbly,” that is, as humble people, so that you may regard as acceptable and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and undefiled sacrifices.

“Gifts” are things given willingly. “Offerings” are things offered to God in some gift or payment so that sins may be forgiven. “Sacrifices” are things consecrated together with prayers. “Undefiled” means immaculate and removed from every stain of malice.

The gifts and sacrifices are undefiled to the extent that they are offered without the stains of scandals and have been acquired through just labor—not, as many say, because “undefiled” means “not dedicated.” Read the seven Conferences of the Fathers, and in the second conference of Theonas, in the ninth chapter, you will find what “undefiled” means (Cassian, [Col. 0195A] *Conference* 22).

“Especially those which we offer to you.” The words indicate for whom they are offered. They ought to offer first, that is, within one congregation, which you may deign to pacify, preserve, unite, and govern throughout the whole world.

“For those whom we offer first.” We offer first for this congregation of yours, so that you may deign to preserve it throughout the whole world in peace and unity, together with that servant—that is, with the one who occupies the seat of the Apostle Peter—because the Church in which Peter, prince of the apostles, sits is the head of all catholic Churches. For this reason Christ said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). Therefore we ought to pray for him, because he presides over that Church.

“And for our bishop,” that is, for our bishop, in whose parish—that is, diocese—we are. We ought to pray for him because he is our shepherd and preacher.

“Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, and all who stand around.” The priest has already prayed for the apostolic ruler and for his own bishop. If a bishop were celebrating Mass, he should not say “for our bishop,” because he himself is the bishop; if he is a presbyter, he should say it.

Prayer has already been made for the senior members; afterward prayer is made for the people. When the priest says, “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women,” he entreats God the Father to deign to remember all those present at the service of the Mass, whether men or women. Those called “the ones standing around” are the men and women who stand around.

The priest has now prayed for all who came to hear Mass. Then, finally, he prays for those who offer offerings, “who offer you this sacrifice of praise.” He says that they offer first for the praise of God [Col. 0195B] and afterward for themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and well-being. To you, the eternal, living, and true God, they render their vows.

They offer because the faith of all those standing around and offering is known to the living and true God, and all render their vows with acknowledged devotion. “Vows” are things promised willingly, because we ought gladly and willingly to make vows to God and fulfill them.

“Joining together and reverently commemorating, first of all, the glorious and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also your blessed apostles and martyrs.” To join together means to hold the memory honorably: Mary the Virgin became the mother of Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, who is God and human, through the coming of the Holy Spirit. Through him we entreat the Father, and we must share in the faith and believe that, when the Holy Spirit announced it, the Son of God was born from her and her virginity was not violated.

“And also your blessed apostles and martyrs.” In our language, “apostle” means “one sent”; “martyr” means “witness.” They are called apostles because they were sent by Christ; they are called martyrs because they are witnesses of Christ, who suffered for us, and they themselves suffered for Christ.

“Therefore, Lord, we humbly ask you graciously to accept this offering of our service [Col. 0195D], and also of your entire household.” The priest commends his offering and that of all who serve the Lord—that is, who are servants of the Lord—so that it may please the Lord and he may be favorable to us.

“Order our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal condemnation [alternative: ‘that we may be rescued from eternal condemnation’], and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect. Through Christ our Lord.”

For what the priest offers, the people ought to pray that the priest may be heard, that everyone’s days may be ordered in peace, and that they may be rescued from the eternal condemnation of which our Lord will say to the wicked at the end of the world: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” etc. (Matthew 25:41), and that we may deserve to be numbered by the holy angels among the flock of his elect, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (ibid., 34).

“Which offering, O God, we ask you to make in every respect blessed, entered [into the appointed place], that is, assigned so that it may please him; approved, that is, judged worthy to be offered in his sight [Col. 0196A]; rational, that is, full of right reason.” May he deign to make it so, because it is acceptable when we who believe rightly offer it with a just prayer. It is right to ask that the almighty Father sanctify the prayer or offering that we offer rationally.

“So that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Son is beloved by the Father, as he himself proclaimed from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son,” etc. (Matthew 3:17). We too ought to love him, because he first loved us (1 John 4:10) and suffered for us.

“Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and, with eyes lifted up to heaven, to you, God the almighty Father, giving you thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat from this, all of you. For this is my body” (Matthew 26).

“In like manner, after supper had taken place, taking also this noble chalice into his holy and venerable hands, likewise giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from it, all of you. This is the chalice of my blood, of the New and Eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins. Whenever you do these things, you will do them in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

“What we have omitted—‘Who, on the day before he suffered’—means: on the day before he himself suffered for us, he wished to hand over to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood, so that they might hand it over to us.”

Who would believe that bread could be changed into flesh or wine into blood, unless the Savior himself said so—the one who created bread and wine and made everything from nothing? It is easier to make something from something than to create everything from nothing.

The Savior himself wished to assume a human body and unite the human being to God, so that Christ Jesus, the human being, might become the one mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5). He wished us to offer bread and wine to him, and for these very things to be consecrated divinely; and he wished the faithful people to believe that there is one mystery, which he handed over to his disciples [Col. 0196C], saying: “Take and eat from this, all of you” (1 Corinthians 11:24).

When he lifted his eyes to heaven and gave thanks to the Father, he taught us that we must always entreat the Father to deign to accomplish this great sacrament through our hands. And when he said, “Whenever you do these things, you will do them in remembrance of me,” he commanded us to remember how much of that passion he endured for us.

Whenever we celebrate this sacrament, we must remember him at all times and place our confidence in his mercy, not in our own goodness.

“Therefore, Lord, we, your servants, and also your holy people, remember the blessed passion of Christ, your Son, our Lord.” We priests profess that we remember, and we testify that the people remember Christ, your Son, our Lord Jesus.

Therefore priests ought faithfully to remember, because they celebrate the Mass and offer the sacrifice instructed by Christ’s example. They ought to know what they are celebrating, because a request is foolish if the person asking does not know what he is asking.

“Your holy people” remembers because Christ suffered not only for priests but for the holy people. It is called holy because it has been sanctified by faith and baptism according to Christ’s command.

He now indicates what they should remember: the blessed passion, the resurrection from the lower regions, and the glorious ascension into heaven of Christ, the Son of God.

We ought to remember his passion because he deigned to suffer for us. We ought to remember his resurrection because righteous souls were freed from the dead through his resurrection. We ought to remember his glorious ascension because, without anyone’s assistance, he carried into heaven, by his own majesty, the human body he had assumed, joined to divinity.

For this reason he said, “without anyone’s assistance,” so that it might be understood that it was not human beings, angels, or any creature that ascended into heaven, but that he was raised by the majesty of the Father, of which he said in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

“We offer to your glorious majesty, from your gifts and bestowals, a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, holy bread of eternal life, and a chalice of everlasting salvation.”

Lord, remembering all the aforesaid goodnesses of yours, we offer to your majesty a pure victim [Col. 0197A], that is, with a pure heart, because the body that we believe is made from this bread is pure.

“A holy victim,” because you sanctified your body when you assumed the human being into God; and now sanctify this bread so that it may become your body.

“An immaculate victim,” because you suffered for us without the stain of sin.

“Holy bread of eternal life,” because you are the living bread who came down from heaven, and you wished us to receive your body in this bread sanctified by you; and through the chalice of your passion you wished us to receive you through your blood. Sanctify this victim so that it may become for us your body and your blood.

“Upon which may you deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance.” Here we entreat that the holy Father may deign to look upon the gifts offered by us with a kindly, gentle, and clear countenance [Col. 0197B], that is, to see them, and to accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and what your exalted Melchizedek offered to you: a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.

The Lord accepted Abel’s gifts because he offered to God whatever he found best; we too ought to offer just and pure gifts to God with a pure heart.

Abraham did not spare his son, but, obedient to the Lord’s command, wished to offer him. Melchizedek, the first priest, offered bread and wine to the Lord, and therefore it is written in the psalm: “You are a priest forever according to …” etc. (Psalm 109:5).

For just as he offered bread and wine, so Christ in his passion offered his body and blood to God the Father for us. In bread and wine he wished us to imitate the mystery of his passion, when, giving bread and wine, or the chalice, to his disciples, he said: “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26), and, “This is the chalice of my blood” (Luke [Col. 0197C] 22:20). We too ought to entreat that, just as the gifts of the aforesaid Fathers were acceptable to God, so ours may become acceptable.

“We humbly ask you, almighty God: command that these gifts be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar in the sight of your divine majesty.” We humbly ask that the heavenly Father command that our gifts, offered upon this altar that can be seen, be carried by the hands of his holy angel to that altar before his divine majesty, which we cannot see with our eyes because it is not bodily but spiritual.

And just as we cannot investigate the divine majesty of the Father but must instead believe:

“So that all of us who have received from this participation in the altar the most holy body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.” We ought to pray to the heavenly Father that all of us who have received the body and blood of the aforesaid Son from that altar upon which we offer to God the Father a commemoration of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, may deserve to receive every heavenly blessing.

“Remember also us sinners, your servants, who hope in the abundance of your mercies; deign to grant us some portion and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs, and with all the saints.” All these sacrifices are offered by both priest and people so that almighty God may not reckon our sins against us, but may grant us a share with his saints.

“Admit us into their fellowship, not as one who weighs merit, but as the giver of pardon, we ask.” We ask that he himself, who said, “At whatever hour the sinner turns back and does penance, all his sins will be washed away before me” (Ezekiel 33), may not assess the repayment due for sins, but may himself be the giver of pardon and place us within the fellowship of the saints.

“Through Christ our Lord.” Through him who created all these gifts, may he himself sanctify [Col. 0198A] and bless them, and grant it to us through Christ, through whom all things were made and with whom all things were made, because he is co-eternal with the Father. Let us always give thanks to the Father.

“Throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Warned by the saving commandments—by Christ’s commandments, which are full of salvation—because he himself is eternally supreme, we have been admonished and commanded. And formed by divine instruction—that is, we have received a pattern and example from Christ our Lord—we have dared to pray as he taught his disciples, and we believe that our Father is in heaven, who created us, and we say:

“Our Father, who art in heaven.”

Christ said after his resurrection: “I ascend to my Father and your Father.” He calls him his Father in one way, and our Father in another. He is his Father because he is the proper Son, begotten of the Father before all ages, coequal with the Father. He is our Father because he created us in time; we are his adopted children, and we ought to possess the heavenly inheritance of our heavenly Father if we fulfill by our deeds what we promised when we received the faith. [Col. 0198B]

“Heaven” (*coelum*) is so called from *celare*, “to conceal,” because it conceals divine secrets. Alternatively, heaven is named from its loftiness, because it is higher than earthly things. We say, however, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” to show that we believe in the heavenly Father; and just as children desire to fulfill the commands of their father, so may we desire to fulfill his commands and strive toward heaven.

“May thy name be sanctified” (Matt. 6:9): that is, may we be worthy to hold his holy name in our hearts. Just as the holy angels who are in heaven know and understand the holiness of his name, so may we who are on earth, with his help, deserve to know his holiness, so that “as in heaven, so also on earth” (ibid., 10) his name may be sanctified.

“May thy kingdom come” (ibid.): that is, may we deserve to know his kingdom and his power, and may the devil no longer reign over us because of our sins, but may his kingdom come, as it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). [Col. 0198C]

“May thy will be done as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10): that is, just as those who are in heaven do his will, so may we who are on earth do it. “Earth” (*terra*) is so called from *terere*, “to wear down.”

“Give us this day our daily bread” [alternative: “supersubstantial bread”] (Luke 11:3). *Pan* among the Greeks is interpreted in our language as “all”; and we pray that the almighty Father may deign to grant every kind of spiritual and bodily nourishment at all times.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). For one who demands a debt owed to him does nothing unjust. But if almighty God were to demand all our debts of us, no one would be found without debt. Therefore we ought to forgive the debts of our debtors, so that the Almighty may forgive ours, because he said: “If you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive your sins” (Matt. 6:15). And elsewhere: “All scandals will be taken away [alternative: gathered] from his kingdom” (Matt. 13:41). Again, a sacrifice is not accepted if it is offered with a scandal; rather, one is commanded to leave it before the altar until he has been reconciled with his brother, and then to offer it with a pure heart (Matt. 5:23). [Col. 0198D]

“And do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13): that is, may we not enter the temptation in which the devil tempts us and consent to him. Rather, may the Lord himself defend us, so that we are not led into diabolical temptation, because if God abandons us, we are immediately brought into the devil’s snare.

“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all past, present, and future evils.”

Here we ask that he himself deliver us from every evil, he who created us good and pure, from whom no evil comes. Past evils are those we committed previously while sinning, and for which we endure scourges. Present evils are those we commit daily. Future evils are those that may yet come through the devil’s persuasion. Therefore we pray that we may be delivered from all of them, because before the Lord’s presence there are neither past nor future things, but everything is present. [Col. 0199A]

“Through the intercession of blessed and glorious Mary, ever virgin and Mother of God, and of your blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, together with all the saints.”

We invoke the Mother of God to help us—she who was a virgin before childbirth and a virgin after childbirth—and the blessed apostles who handed down to us the celebration of these mysteries, so that they may intercede for us. For we ourselves are not worthy to merit forgiveness for past and present sins, nor protection from future ones, unless it is granted to us through their prayer.

We have now prayed to be delivered from evils; we pray next that, with the aforesaid saints intervening, he himself may grant us peace.

“Graciously grant peace in our days,” you who are powerful to deliver us from evil. Grant peace amid the devil’s temptation, so that we may not be led into it. Grant peace from every evil, so that we may not suffer its scourges. “So that, aided by the help of your mercy”—that is, aided by God’s help—we may always be free from sins and secure from every disturbance.

Through Christ our Lord. [Col. 0199B]

“May the peace of the Lord be always with you.”

Christ is the eternal peace who reconciled us to the Father through his passion, so that we would not be held in hell because of the sin of the first man. The priest prays that this peace may remain with the people and make them all concordant, so that, made peaceable with Christ, we may deserve to reign in heaven.

Therefore we make peace before receiving the Lord’s body and blood, to show that we have concord among ourselves and to receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ with concord in our own body. Without concord we are not worthy to receive holy communion, because our offerings are not accepted if we are at odds with our neighbors before we have been reconciled with everyone.

Then the clergy pray in song:

“Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

He is called the Lamb of God because of his innocence: he harms neither human beings nor beasts, and when he is led to the slaughter he does not injure those who are killing him, but by his death refreshes his slayers. So too Christ harms no one, as the Apostle says: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). After his passion, however, he turned and refreshed many of his persecutors through holy communion and the outpouring of his blood, and made them believers.

He took away the sins of the world when he gave us forgiveness of sins, because before his passion both the righteous and sinners descended into hell [Note: [Col. 0199B] Yet not into the same part of hell.] [Col. 0200B] For nowhere in the Old Testament do we read of the forgiveness of sins. Christ, however, promised us through repentance not only forgiveness of sins but also angelic joy, saying: “There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10).

We ask that this Christ himself, who is the innocent Lamb of God and suffered for the salvation of the world, have mercy on us, saying:

“Have mercy on us.”

# EXPOSITION OF THE DIVINE OFFICES

*(From the same Biaotian manuscript.)*

## What the Office of the Mass signifies

By the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, it must be explained what the Office of the Mass signifies, since it would have been sufficient for the body and blood of the Lord to be consecrated by the sole blessing of bishops or priests, without cantors [manuscript: “singers”], readers, and the other things performed there, as in the time of the apostles.

The use of signs was taken from the Old Testament, for the children of Israel had silver trumpets with which they summoned the people (Num. 10:2). We have bronze signs, louder and more durable, signifying the mouths of preachers. For then “God was known in Judah” (Ps. 75:2) alone; now he is known throughout the whole earth. Then temporal things were preached; now eternal things.

The clapper of the sign signifies the teacher’s tongue; the cord by which the sign is tied signifies the moderation of preaching; the wood from which the sign hangs signifies the mystery of the cross; the instrument by which it is tied signifies the prophetic oracles; the descent from the wood signifies the work of preaching; the upward movement of the rope signifies the teacher’s understanding, showing how far he advances in the height of virtues; the withdrawal of the rope to one side signifies consideration of how deeply he lies in one vice; the ring in the rope signifies the divine Scriptures’ indication of vices that must be kept silent.

## On the church

A church is called an assembly of the faithful. There are two reasons why we assemble in it: first, so that there we may hear our judgments, whether good or bad; second, so that there we may receive the Lord’s body.

Men ought to stand on the southern side of the church, women on the northern side, to show that they ought to stand more firmly against the heat of the temptations of the great ones of this age.

The arrangement of the church is said to be in the form of a cross and in the form of a human body. The chancel signifies the head; the cross, on either side, the arms and hands; the remaining part, toward the west, signifies whatever part of the body appears to remain. The sacrifice of the altar signifies the vow of the heart; the windows signify the senses of the human being or of the body.

## The Office of the Mass

Pope Celestine instituted the Office for the Mass. Previously Mass was celebrated after only the Epistle and Gospel had been read.

The censer with incense should go first; the acolytes with candles should follow, then the subdeacons, then the bishop between two presbyters.

The censer signifies Christ’s body; the coals, the Holy Spirit; the incense, the fragrance of Christ’s good work. For Christ, destined to come into the world, sent prophets, wise men, and scribes ahead of him.

In place of the scribes are the acolytes who carry the divine Scriptures and go before to illuminate the hearts of the faithful. In place of the wise men are the subdeacons, who wisely know how to arrange the vessels of the Lord. In place of the prophets are the deacons, who announce the future life in evangelizing. The bishop between two presbyters signifies Christ between the two Testaments.

The Office signifies Christ’s advent and the uniting of the people.

The bishop kisses the ministers first—afterward he goes to the altar—and then the Gospel. For Christ first reconciled the apostles, afterward the rest of the Jews, and then the Gentiles.

The Gospel remains on the altar from the beginning of the Office until it is read, because evangelical teaching remained from the Lord’s advent in Jerusalem, the place of the passion—signified by the altar—until it publicly went forth to the Gentiles.

Meanwhile the acolytes hold candles in their hands, because teachers ought to practice what they teach.

During the “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), the Church prays that the priest’s prayer may be pleasing to God. When “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) begins, the acolytes place the candles on the ground, one being placed in the middle between the others, so that teachers may recognize themselves as being on the earth in good work and preaching. The middle candle signifies him who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

The bishop’s passage from the middle of the altar to the right side signifies Christ’s passage from the passion, after the resurrection, to eternal life. On Sundays and feast days of the saints, “Glory to God in the highest” is sung there, because it recalls the saints to the glory of the angels through the Lord’s resurrection.

They minister behind in the same place, because although the faithful are still established in this life, they nevertheless always strive toward Christ’s eternity, as he says: “Whoever ministers to me must follow me” (John 12:26).

When the bishop greets the people by saying “The Lord be with you,” he presents his face to them, except at one point, where he shows the deepest devotion he has while offering the sacrifice. The inward feeling of both parties ought to correspond to this greeting and response of the bishop.

The bishop’s first greeting signifies Christ’s greeting to the disciples after the resurrection. The bishop’s prayer and blessing before Christ’s sitting [perhaps delete] signify the time when Christ blessed his disciples as he was about to ascend into heaven.

The bishop’s sitting signifies Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father after the Ascension. The sitting of the ministers signifies the sitting of those to whom it is said: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. 19:28).

Through the Epistle we understand the preaching of the Old Testament, which is more humble. The Responsory is so called because when one begins, the others respond; it signifies the preaching of the New Testament, which is more excellent. The readers and singers rise for the Office and have the Lord’s business, as it is said to them: “Trade until I come” (Luke 19:13).

## Why the Responsories are sung more loudly than the reading

The Responsory is heard more loudly than the reading so that, if someone with hardened ears of heart is not roused by the subdued admonition of the Old Testament, he may be roused by this.

In the verse sung by one person alone, he is admonished to reflect alone upon his frailty. Because of fear, he did not dare to begin the response loudly. When the verse is finished, however, he raises his voice more confidently. This represents those who, considering their own frailty, perform everything they do more humbly; the louder voice represents those who, confident—or presumptuous [that is, “presuming”]—in God’s mercy, attend more boldly to all their actions.

## What the Gradual signifies

The Gradual signifies good work, in which we sow the hope of the contemplative life in which we shall reap.

The Tracts of sadness precede it, but joy follows, because two days from the tomb precede and the third day of the glory of the resurrection follows.

The reader or singer rises above the step to perform his office, because by the perfection of his life a teacher ought to transcend the common people.

## On the significance of incense

When the Gospel is to be read, incense is placed in the censer over the coals so that it may emit the sweet fragrance of good works. This has been explained above.

Then the deacon, having received the blessing and having been fortified by the impress of the cross so that he may proceed securely, takes the Gospel from the altar and places it over his left arm, because in temporal life the Gospel must be preached.

The laying down of staffs signifies the humility of the faithful, or else that they should not appear like the Jews holding reeds in the presence of the crucified one.

The censer is carried above the tribunal before the Gospel because Christ’s works preceded his teaching, as it is written: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

The more exalted place of the Gospel signifies the eminence of preaching. The two candles that precede the deacon signify the Law and the Prophets, which preceded the Gospel. The placing of the candles on the ground signifies that the Law and the Prophets are lower than the Gospel.

After the Gospel has been read [Note: [Col. 0201D] So also John of Avranches, p. 19], the candles are extinguished because, when the preaching of the Gospel is finished, the Law and the Prophets will cease.

## 391 On the bishop’s admonition

After the Gospel, when the bishop says “The Lord be with you,” another Office begins [Note: [Col. 0201D] Namely, that of the faithful, after the catechumens have been dismissed]. By saying “Let us pray,” he admonishes each person to return to himself, examine his conscience, and offer himself as a holocaust to God.

## What the corporal signifies

When the linen cloth—that is, the corporal—is placed on the altar, the ministers or the people are admonished to be cleansed from every carnal desire, just as the cloth has been cleansed of its natural greenness and moisture. It shines with brightness; they with virtue.

Afterward, while the choir sings and the offerings have been received from the people, the bishop returns to the altar. Christ, having received the vows of the faithful, entered the temple amid the crowds of the faithful singing “Hosanna” (“Save, we pray”) in the highest, since he was soon to be sacrificed, as was necessary.

The offering of bread and wine signifies pious desires, whether through immolation or through a living victim.

Then the bishop raises his hands so that they may be clean from earthly bread, and he prays before the altar that he may be worthy to offer the sacrifice, lest what happened to the men of Beth-shemesh happen to him. Those who were not afraid to look upon the ark of the Lord were killed: seventy-five men of the people and fifty thousand of the common people (1 Sam. 6).

The censer placed above the prayer signifies Christ, through whom the Lord is propitiated for him.

## On the mixing of wine and water

The mixing of wine and water signifies the union of Christ and the Church.

The first Secret signifies the time when Christ came to the feast not openly but as if in secret; or it signifies what was hidden in Christ: the Paschal Lamb who was to be sacrificed, a mystery hidden from everyone until the day of the supper, when he disclosed it to the disciples.

In this Secret it is called an offering.

From “The Lord be with you” to “Holy” it is called a hymn, because it is full of the praises of the holy angels. It is called a preparation because it prepares the minds of the faithful for reverence toward the consecration that is to come.

It signifies the time when Christ sang a hymn in the upper room at supper and, after the hymn had been sung, went out to the Mount of Olives (Matt. 26:30).

Here too the altar signifies the Lord’s table, at which he feasted with his disciples; the corporal, the linen cloth with which he was girded; the napkin, the labor caused by his persecutors; and “Lift up your hearts,” the ascent into the upper room.

When the hymn “Holy, holy” is finished—the hymn inserted here by Pope Sixtus, whose first part contains the praise of the angels and whose last part contains that of human beings—the priests and deacons, standing behind and bowed, remain so until the end of the Lord’s Prayer.

They signify the apostles who, overcome by great tribulation during the Lord’s passion, did not dare to raise themselves up and confess that they were Christ’s disciples, yet nevertheless stood openly in the faith.

Just as there were two altars in the Tabernacle, one of incense and the other of holocaust, so there are two sacraments of the Church. One is that in which carnal impulses are put to sleep, extending from “Therefore, most merciful Father” to “Which offering”; the other extends from there to “And to us sinners,” in which it is necessary for carnal things to be slaughtered daily.

In this prayer, the linen cloth beneath signifies Christ’s humility in the passion; the napkin signifies labor.

As for the crosses that we usually make in different ways over the bread and wine, I have nothing to say in this place about them or about why more or fewer are made.

At the place where it is said, “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me,” the simple bread returns [Note: [Col. 0201D] “Returns,” that is, “has been changed.” The present is used for the past; the author speaks similarly in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3.] into the rational nature of Christ’s body and blood.

Hence, at “And remembering,” the passion begins.

At “A pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim,” the crucifixion begins.

At “We humbly beseech you,” this prayer, begun at the cross, extends from Psalm 21 [30] to “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” The bishop, bowed, signifies the giving up of Christ’s spirit with his head bowed. [Col. 0203A]

“And to us sinners.” This prayer extends to “For ever and ever.” Here the priest’s raised voice signifies the exclamation of the centurion saying: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54).

Again, “all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things” (Luke 23:49). The subdeacons signify these people.

At this voice the others rise and look into the bishop’s face. While the lesser disciples looked on in this way and the apostles remained hidden, Nicodemus and Joseph came, took down the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb (Matt. 27:59–60; John 19:42). The bishop and archdeacon signify them: while the subdeacons look on from afar and the deacons stand behind, they raise the chalice from the altar, wrap it in the napkin, and set it down.

The two crosses made beside the chalice teach that Christ was crucified for two peoples.

The offering in the chalice signifies the Lord’s body. The wine within the chalice: within the body and blood [the surviving text is elliptical].

The subdeacons’ withdrawal from the bishop’s presence when “Our Father” begins signifies the women’s departure from the tomb after the Lord had been buried.

The paten signifies the hearts of the women, made open by the breadth of charity in their service at Christ’s burial. At the reconciliation of the seventh day, when Christ rested in the tomb, the Lord’s Prayer—which contains seven petitions—is inserted.

The subdeacon gives the paten to the deacon because the women announced the resurrection to the apostles.

The part of the offering placed into the chalice shows Christ’s body risen from the dead.

The part eaten by the priest or by the people signifies Christ’s body still remaining on earth.

The part left on the altar, which the Church receives as viaticum, signifies the bodies of the faithful lying in the tombs. This part remains on the altar until the end of Mass because, until the end of the age, the bodies of the saints rest in tombs.

Corporal cleanliness signifies the purity of the faithful people.

The Lord, about to ascend into heaven, blessed his disciples; and the priest, when everything has been properly completed, blesses and greets the people [Note: [Col. 0203] By this blessing understand a prayer, as is clear from what follows below, or the greeting “The Lord be with you”]. Then, turning toward the east, he commends himself to Christ’s Ascension.

Nevertheless, the Mass extends from the offering to “Go, it is dismissed.”

The catechumens must not be expelled from the church before the Gospel, since they are instructed for preaching; rather, they must be dismissed before the sacrifice, which only those reborn may attend.

The devil attacks the human race more fiercely during Lent. Therefore, at the end of Mass, the priest confirms the human race with an added blessing, bowing his head humbly.

From the third hour to the ninth, Pope Telesphorus decreed that Mass should be celebrated, because at this time Christ offered himself as a victim to the Father for us. At the third hour he was crucified by the words of the Jews; at the sixth hour he ascended the cross; at the ninth he gave up his spirit.

For the Nativity of the Lord, the same pope decreed that Mass should be celebrated at midnight, because at that hour, when he was born, the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest.” It is likewise celebrated at the beginning of day, as though at the beginning of his birth, because he was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb. For the same reason it is celebrated very early on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

At a Mass for the dead, “Glory” is not sung, nor “Alleluia” (“Praise the Lord”), which signify sweetness [manuscript: “health”] and joy, because then we are more deeply affected by grief for our dear one and because the Mass is celebrated in imitation of Christ’s death. The kiss is not given there because there is the purification of the dead person through the priest’s sacrifice.

## On the Daytime Hours

Just as sheep kept watch over at night in their folds must, when they go out to pasture in the morning, have a shepherd to lead them, so we, rising at first light, must have a shepherd or teacher to lead us to spiritual pasture [Col. 0204A] and defend us from the devil’s snares. Therefore our same shepherd beseeches the supreme Shepherd, saying:

“God, attend to my help.”

The glory of the Holy Trinity follows, which we beseech to be present in our help.

Then follow the psalms, which defend and sustain us until the full third hour.

The Verse and “Kyrie eleison” prepare us for the Lord’s Prayer.

When we say “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), we recall the majesty of the Lord before he assumed humility [Amalarius reads: “humanity”]. Thus, by saying it once, we recall the one substance of the Godhead.

When we say “Christe eleison” (“Christ, have mercy”), we present our nature to Christ. We say it once because he alone lived among human beings without sin; we say it three times because he was not separated from the substance of the Trinity.

When we say “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) again, we recall the nature that Christ has after the resurrection with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The meaning of saying it once or three times has been explained above.

The Lord’s Prayer, the Creed—that is, the Apostles’ Creed—and the prayers that follow are said for lesser sins. The penitential psalms are for greater sins. In these psalms the priest takes the place of Christ remaining with us on earth and interceding with the Father for us.
