At each Hour, when the priest rises at the end, greets the people, and blesses them, he signifies Christ rising and blessing on the Mount of Olives at [manuscript: “after”] the Ascension.

The people, giving thanks to God, signify the disciples returning to their own homes; after the Ascension they returned to Jerusalem with thanksgiving.

At the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, and at that same hour we assemble for God’s service, so that the three psalms recited there may defend us until the sixth.

At the sixth hour Christ was crucified for us. Therefore we assemble at that hour to serve God, so that three psalms may likewise defend us until the ninth.

At the ninth hour, when Christ gave up the Spirit, we assemble again for the praise of God. From that hour three psalms guard us until the end of the day.

At these three hours we assemble during the day to confess God, following the example of the earlier people; and at four hours during the night: Vespers, Compline, Nocturns, and Matins.

At Vespers we sing five psalms antiphonally. The antiphon is a reciprocal voice [addition: “which”] that joins two choirs through the psalm, just as charity unites two brothers through good work.

Just as the five psalms daily wash away whatever the five bodily senses commit, so the Magnificat at the beginning of night chastises whatever thoughts boast in prosperity.

If pride carries someone outside himself during the day, let him return to himself at night when he hears: “He has scattered the proud.”

If desire for temporal things delights someone, let “He has sent the rich away empty” draw him back to himself.

If temporal affliction disturbs someone, let him reflect that “the Lord exalts the humble.”

If the power of this age steals upon someone, let “He has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble” suppress that power (Luke 1:52).

On ordinary days we kneel in prayer at the Lord’s Prayer and the intercessions, and at the penitential psalm because of more serious sins, recalling our pilgrimage.

On Sundays we do not kneel; neither the intercessions nor the psalm are said, because on those days the freedom of the future kingdom is recalled, in which Christ will reign with the saints, unhindered by any sin.

In the four psalms of Compline we commend the elements of our body to the Lord; in the hymn of Simeon we seek peace from all the tumult of this age.

On the Nativity of the Lord, on feasts, and on Sundays, the first three psalms suit those who believed in the Holy Trinity before the Law; the second three suit those who lived under the Law; and the third three suit those who live under grace.

Therefore “Alleluia” (“Praise the Lord”) is recalled more frequently on these days, because the joy of the angels—which those first two groups awaited—the latter, having been set free in this life, soon receive.

On the Nativity of the Lord, the resurrection, the Ascension, Pentecost, and Sundays, we pray standing, attending to the fact that Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father, who was born for us, rose, ascended, and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples.

Likewise, on the feast days of the saints we stand, recalling that they have been reborn into eternal blessedness.

On the birthdays of the saints, the nine readings signify the nine orders of angels with whom they have been joined.

On the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the resurrection, and the Ascension, we celebrate the first day, rejoicing in him who was born for us, appeared more fully, rose, and ascended into heaven.

The six days signify the six works of mercy by which we come to our birth, manifestation, resurrection, and ascension from this life into heaven—their commemoration we celebrate in these octaves.

Through the seven days of Pentecost we recall the work of the sevenfold Spirit; in the octave we recall the completion and fullness of that same work, which is always to come in eternal blessedness.

The octave of the Lord’s passion is taken away by the glory of the resurrection.

We celebrate the Lord’s passion in sadness because the apostles were uncertain about the resurrection.

We celebrate the passions of the saints in joy because we are certain of their glory, because of the passions of the innocent, and because of the martyrs’ grief.

On the birthdays of the saints we recall the rest of their souls; in the octaves, the resurrection of their bodies; and in the six days, the six works by which they came to the Lord.

The Verse in the nocturnal Office rouses hearts to the Lord’s Prayer. That prayer makes us attentive to the reading and raises us from the negligence produced by the security of sitting.

The same applies to the Magnificat and Benedictus, to which we ought to be attentive just as we are to the reading.

Prayer, blessing, and thanksgiving are always said at the end of the Hours, so that each person returning to his own home may be fortified by such protection against adversity.

What the readings and responsories signify in the Office of Darkness, we shall explain.

The Office of Matins signifies the period from the primitive Church until the judgment.

First, the primitive Church was established through Christ’s preaching, with Christ himself reigning in it. Hence the psalm in the Praises: “The Lord has reigned.”

Afterward, the Church itself announced Christ’s coming with the other prayers, saying: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” Offering his goodwill to the calling of the nations, it says: “God, my God.”

And because, before the persecution of Antichrist, it will come about that the people from the uncircumcision and the circumcision will be one in faith, two psalms are contained under one antiphon.

After these have been joined, the tribulation of Antichrist will come. Just as Nebuchadnezzar burned the three youths, so he will burn all who confess the Holy Trinity in the furnace of persecution. Like those youths, they will bless the Lord, having been delivered from every evil.

Therefore, while we sing “Alleluia” (“Praise the Lord”) in the other psalms, in this psalm we use Latin words in memory of so great a tribulation.

We do not say “Glory to the Father” at the end, because from the psalm itself we make use of the Holy Trinity.

After this there will be peace for the faithful for three years and forty-five days. During that peace, the praise of God contained in three psalms will be celebrated: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing to the Lord,” and “Praise the Lord in his holy places.”

And because there are three kinds of human beings—those who, according to the Gospel, are spoken of under the names of bed, mill, and field—from whom a portion will be gathered into the unity of faith, these three psalms are sung under one antiphon.

Septuagesima begins on Sunday and ends on the Saturday after Easter.

It signifies the captivity of God’s people in Babylon, who had departed from the Lord through sin, as though on Sunday, and return through God’s mercy to rest, as though on the Sabbath.

The period from Septuagesima to Easter signifies the time in which sinners are placed in affliction and sadness for their sins, before the days, and also the time in which they are nevertheless raised up through repentance and consolation, saying: “We became as those who are consoled” (Ps. 125).

The Sabbath signifies the time when, in the future life, we shall already receive complete rest.

Sexagesima begins on Sunday and ends on the Wednesday within Easter.

That Wednesday signifies the fourth age, when God’s people, glorious under David and Solomon, were triumphant.

Therefore on that day we conduct a procession with the banner of the holy cross raised. That triumph cannot be reached except through the Decalogue of the Law and the six works of mercy.

Quinquagesima begins on Sunday and ends on the day of the resurrection.

It signifies that if someone fulfills the Decalogue of the Law through the five bodily senses, he will reach the joy of the Lord’s resurrection—or of his own resurrection—securely.

Quadragesima begins on Sunday and ends on Thursday, extending over the two days until the baptism of the resurrection. Those who pass over to Christ through baptism reach him in the same number by which he deigned to come to us through his genealogy.

Following the Lord’s example, we extend the period of our fast over forty days.

The two weeks of the passion signify the two periods before the Law and under the Law; the time of Pascha signifies the period under grace.

On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, Mary anointed Jesus’ feet. In imitation of this, Pope Gregory gave alms; therefore the Office is omitted.

Five days before Easter, the lamb to be sacrificed is brought into the house; Christ is brought into the city.

On Wednesday the Jews took counsel to kill Jesus (Matt. 26:4). On Thursday and Friday the bells are silent; “O Lord, my lips,” the blessing, the chapters, and the prayer are not said, because our Shepherd, Christ, has departed. Therefore, because of fear of the Jews, all preaching and admonition by the apostles ceased; consequently, they perform their Office less fully in psalms, lessons, responsories, verses, and the examples of those who were known to be Christ’s disciples. The Invitatory is not sung because of the Jews’ evil assembly. The greeting and kiss are not given because of their treachery. [Col. 0206C]

In place of bells, wooden instruments are sounded; there are two of them, a hammer and a board. The hammer signifies the wood of transgression; the board, the fruitful wood, that is, Christ. Because of the threefold burial, our Office is made more humble for three days. In these three days, through the nine psalms, lessons, and responsories: through the nine psalms, which pertain to good works; through the nine lessons, which pertain to knowledge of God; and through the nine responsories, which pertain to the songs of the angels, it is shown that Christ descended to the underworld to free the three classes of the elect who existed before the law, under the law, and under the prophets, and united them with the nine orders of angels. Twenty-four lights are extinguished each day, signifying that the apostles hid for one day, that is, twenty-four hours. On Good Friday the Lord’s Body is not made, because Christ offered himself to God the Father as a sacrifice for us; but the sacrifice from Thursday is reserved, so that those who wish to communicate may have it. The Blood is not reserved, lest it be spilled; the wine is sanctified through the Body. The altar signifies the Lord; the vestments, the faithful; the washing with water, Mary’s tears; the branch, the hair; the wine, the ointment.

On Thursday absolution is performed, the new fire is blessed, the chrism and oil are consecrated, and the feet are washed, because Christ came into the world in the sixth age and retains in himself the sacraments mentioned above. The garments that are divided while the Passion is read are the apostles.

On Holy Saturday, whatever is done in the Office pertains in no way to the present day of the tomb, but to the coming night of the Resurrection; therefore, just as the sacrifice is not performed on Friday, so, note, neither is it performed on the seventh day. 406 The column of fire went before the children of Israel before the sea, and after the sea as far as Jerusalem; and the Paschal candle shines before baptism and afterward until the octave. Christ enlightens the soul until the Day of Judgment.

On Saturday incense is carried before the Gospel because of the women carrying spices. “Alleluia” signifies the Jews who were converted first; the Tract, the Gentiles who afterward came to believe. The glory that God gave Adam, had he not sinned, is given to those baptized on Holy Saturday; therefore “Alleluia” is sung. But because the way of life still remains, the Tract follows, signifying patience, by which they must await the eternal glory prefigured by the following Sabbath. Therefore on that Sabbath the Gradual is not sung, because good work is not necessary there; nor the Tract, because neither is patience necessary; but two Alleluias are sung, one for the glory of the soul and the other for that of the body. The Gradual is not said during the six days, signifying the good works of the active life. “Alleluia” signifies the hope of the contemplative life. The fifty days from the Resurrection until the octave of Pentecost signify the contemplative life, where there will be only “Alleluia.” The joy of this is signified by the number fifty, which is called a jubilee, that is, full of rejoicing.

Three psalms at the Lord’s Resurrection signify the three works of the Lord performed after his Resurrection in each believer: separation from unbelief, union with faith, and cleansing through baptism. The season of Lent signifies the present time of the Passion, since throughout every age we must labor and finally die. The Resurrection signifies the life that we shall receive on the Day of Judgment. Because Christ died at the ninth hour, those who are baptized into Christ’s death are baptized at that hour. They are baptized at the ninth hour on Saturday because of Christ’s burial. The frequent alteration of the chant invites the souls of the good to the Lord.

After fifty days we celebrate seven solemnities, because of the sevenfold Spirit, or because of the joy of those baptized. For seven days each person who has received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands celebrates his coming. The Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles like wind and fire.

Among the Romans, on the Saturdays of the Four Ember Seasons, six lessons were read— in Greek for the Greeks and in Latin for the Latins living there; therefore they are said to be twelve lessons. We fast four times, for three days in each season, because each season has three months. In each of these seasons we fast on Wednesday because on that day the Jews took counsel to kill Jesus (Matt. 26:4); on Friday because they killed him; and on Saturday because there was mourning among the peoples, by which God sanctified the Sabbath, and the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). On Wednesday two lessons are read, so that those about to be ordained may have knowledge of the law and the prophets; for in the fourth age the law and the prophecies flourished. On Friday one lesson is read, because in the sixth age the law and the prophecies are closed by the Gospel.

The clergy: the lot, that is, the portion of God. In clerics, because they are the Lord’s portion, or because the Lord is their portion, the head signifies our mind; the hair, our thoughts. The shaved upper part of the head signifies the mind contemplating the Lord; the unshaved lower part, the mind occupied with temporal matters through many thoughts. We shave the upper part when we cut away temporal thoughts from the soul; we level the lower part into a crown when, while considering temporal necessities, we arrange them through harmonious care. The hair must not grow over the eyes or ears, lest temporal thoughts impede the hearing or sight of the mind. It is not necessary to take great pains to investigate the authors of customs, if we can observe the customs themselves.

## On the Orders

In the Old Testament, doorkeepers guarded the doors of the temple, receiving the healthy and rejecting the sick; now in the Church they receive the faithful and repel the unfaithful.

In the Old Testament, readers taught the people openly and distinctly the words of the law; now, spiritually understood, readers are those who defend from demons those entering the Church.

[Col. 0208A] An exorcist, that is, one who adjures, in the Old Testament had power through the laying on of hands to drive a demon out of a person; now, through prayer, he ought to drive vices from the soul.

Acolytes, that is, candle-bearers, in the Old Testament prepared the Lord’s light; now in the Church they must always prepare the light of truth for the minds of the faithful.

### On Subdeacons

The Nathanaeans, who are hypodeacons, that is, subdeacons, just as in the Old Testament, so now receive offerings from the peoples; nevertheless, in the house of the Lord they themselves offer the vessels of the Body and Blood. The deacon arranges them upon the altar and does not receive them.

### On Deacons

In the Old Testament the Levites kept watch, guarding everything that pertained to the worship of God in the tabernacle and serving in his ministry. In the New Testament they are to provide everything necessary for the multitude that has one heart and one soul. Therefore it is their custom, keeping watch in the virtues and guarding the ministry entrusted to them, to arrange upon the Lord’s table whatever is necessary for the heavenly banquet. They receive the laying on of hands; through the hand and the distinction of the fingers they signify the works of the Holy Spirit, distinguished according to their kinds.

Presbyters took their beginning from the sons of Aaron in the Old Testament, and bishops from Aaron himself. Those who were then called priests are now called presbyters; those who were then called chief priests are now called bishops. Presbyters share many things with bishops, but differ from them in a few.

A bishop carries a staff so that he may rule his subjects and support the weak, and wears a ring so that he may not disclose the sacraments to everyone. The amice, wrapped around the neck, signifies the guarding of the voice; the alb, the chastisement of the body. Priests bind their hands and arms so that they may do nothing useless; the breast, so that they may think nothing useless; the belly, so that they may not desire delicacies; the genitals, so that they may not incline toward lust; the knees, so that they may not grow sluggish in prayer; the shins and feet, so that they may not run toward evil.

The belt signifies continence, as in: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). The stole, of which it is said, “The yoke of the Lord is easy,” signifies the Gospel of Christ. In that it is placed upon the neck, let him know that he is a minister of the Gospel, not its master; in that it descends as far as the knees, which customarily bend through humility, humility is signified.

The chasuble signifies works of righteousness, as in: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131:9). It is doubled behind, between the shoulders, and before the breast. By the shoulders, the burden of good work is signified. It is a double garment because works should be displayed outwardly to one’s neighbors while the heart within remains whole. It is double at the breast because both things ought to be present there: teaching and truth—teaching for everyone, truth inwardly. These two doubles are joined together because good ministry is performed when good work and true teaching agree.

By the white dalmatic is understood holy and undefiled religion: namely, to visit the sick and widows in their tribulations and to keep oneself undefiled by the world (James 1:27). It has two lines at the back and two at the front because the Old and New Testaments shine with love of God and neighbor: to be undefiled toward God, to visit the sick, and to love one’s neighbor. It has thirty fringes at the back and forty at the front; each line has fifteen on either side, because the line of charity in the Old and New Testaments, in prosperity and adversity, produces fifteen streams from itself, namely:

“Charity is patient, charity is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:4–6).

The left side has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things (Luke 10:41). The right has none because the contemplative life is at rest (ibid., 39). The width of the sleeves signifies the generosity of the teacher of the Gospel.

A deacon sometimes reads the Gospel wearing the chasuble wrapped around him, so that he may move freely toward the Gospel or prepare the Lord’s table [manuscript: “Mass”]. The chasuble is open on the left side, through which the arm is brought out, because the doer of the Gospel, whom the deacon ought to imitate, was pierced or transfixed by a lance in his right side.

The sudarium, with which the sweat and every flowing moisture of the body are wiped away, is carried in the left hand. It signifies the diligence of divine contemplation by which in this life we wipe away pleasures, weariness, and other excesses of the mind. It is clean; hence David says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:12), and Job: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done” (Job 1:21).

Sandals signify progress toward preaching. In them the foot is neither covered above nor bare against the ground: the Gospel must neither be concealed nor displayed to the earthly-minded. Since it is the preacher’s task to run here and there, the sandals are tied so that they do not fall from the feet; this is to be understood spiritually. The tongue that rises from them and is separate from the sandal leather signifies the tongue of those who give good preaching.

The sandals are black on the outside and white within, showing that the life of preaching is despised by worldly people, while its intention is inwardly pure before the Lord. The part of the sandals through which the foot enters is sewn with many threads so that the two leathers do not come apart, because at the beginning of preaching the teacher must apply himself to many virtues and sequences of Scripture, lest external works be separated from inward intention.

The tongue over the foot signifies the preacher’s tongue; the lines proceeding from both sides toward the middle line signify the law, the prophets, and the Gospel; the fastening signifies the incarnation of Christ. Sandals are also called soles. They are a kind of footwear worn by a minister of the Church: below, they have a sole protecting the feet from the earth, while above they have no covering and remain open. This makes clear what the apostles were commanded by the Lord to wear. It signifies that the minister of God’s word must not cling to earthly things but rather aspire to heavenly things, and must conceal his preaching from no one.

Next comes the shoulder garment, which is made of the purest linen [manuscript: “linen cloth”]. By linen, which is taken from the earth and brought to whiteness through much labor, the body is signified, since it consists of earth; worn down by many hardships, the body ought to be white and pure from every stain. Next comes the breast garment, which the common people call the alb.

The breast garment signifies perseverance in good action. Hence Joseph is described as having had a long tunic among his brothers. A tunic reaching to the ankle signifies good work continuing to its completion, for the ankle is the end of the body. He begins well who duly carries the uprightness of good work through to the end of his action: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Then comes the zone, which is called the belt, by which the breast garment is tightened so that it does not spread widely over the feet. It signifies the discernment of all virtues, for virtues without discernment are not virtues but vices; virtues are established in a certain middle point.

Next comes the orarium, that is, the stole, which is granted to orators, that is, preachers. It admonishes the one who wears it to remember that he has been placed under the yoke of Christ, which is easy and gentle (Matt. 11:30).

The dalmatic that follows is so called because it was discovered in Dalmatia. The use of dalmatics was instituted by blessed Pope Sylvester, for previously people used colobia. A colobium is a garment without sleeves; its being sleeveless signifies that every faithful person ought to be prepared for the performance of good works.

When the bareness of the arms was criticized by blessed Sylvester, as we have said, the use of dalmatics was devised. It is a garment in the form of a cross, reminding us that our Crucified One must be our help in the world, according to the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me” (Gal. 6:14). It also has fringes on its left side. The left signifies the present life, which abounds in various cares; the cares are signified by the fringes on the left side. The right, which lacks fringes, expresses the future life, in which no cares trouble the souls of the saints.

It is also seamless because in the Church, or in the heart of each believer, there ought to be no division, but an undivided integrity of faith. Alternatively, the left side has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things, whereas the right has none because the contemplative life has nothing on the left. The width of the sleeves signifies the generosity and cheerfulness of the teacher.

The mapula, worn on the left side, with which the discharge of the eyes and nostrils is wiped away, signifies the present life, in which we suffer superfluous humors. The chasuble, placed over all the vestments, signifies charity, which excels the other virtues; concerning it the Apostle says, after mentioning certain virtues: “But the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13).

The amice is therefore the first garment. We wrap it around the neck so that the voice issuing through the neck may be guarded from every evil word, according to the Prophet: “Let us guard our mouth, lest we sin with the tongue” (Ps. 38). The second is the linen shirt, which is called white, breast-length, or ankle-length; made according to the form of the body, it covers the entire body without a wrinkle.

By the whiteness to which it is brought through immense labor, the chastity and purity of mind and body are signified; these are acquired through much fasting, vigils, prayer, and the practice of good works. By the fabric of the garment, virtue is signified: the heart and all the limbs of the body are to be restrained from every evil deed. By its ankle-length, good work continuing to completion is signified. By the avoidance of wrinkles, which represent the convolutions of heretical perversity, the Catholic faith is signified. [Col. 0210C]

The belt signifies discernment, which is the mother of all virtues. The stole, called the orarium—“The yoke of the Lord is gentle and his burden is light” (Matt. 11:30)—signifies the Gospel. The whiteness of the stole signifies purity of doctrine [Note: [Col. 0209] From these materials the book of John of Avranches, pp. 85ff., should be corrected and supplemented]; its length down to the feet signifies the virtue of humility and perseverance.

By the girdle with which the loins are tightened, purity of mind is signified, in accordance with the Lord’s words: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

Then comes the tunic, concerning which the Lord said to Aaron: “You shall make a hyacinth-colored tunic” (Exod. 28:31). This is put on beneath the dalmatic and is called the undergarment. Hyacinth is neither thin nor obscured by density, nor does it shine uniformly; under a clear sky it becomes transparent, while under a cloudy sky it is pale, being of one, almost ethereal, color. By the ethereal and single color, the priestly life is signified: directed incessantly toward heavenly desires alone, it ought, according to the Apostle, always to have its conversation in heaven (Phil. 3:20). By the change of color, fraternal compassion is signified, as the Apostle says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). This belongs properly to a bishop. It signifies that the understanding of heavenly things is not open except to the perfect. By its being an inner garment and not being girded, the virtues of the soul, known to God alone, are signified as things that must always be possessed without interruption.

By the dalmatic, white and adorned before and behind from top to bottom with two scarlet lines, purity of mind is signified together with the preaching of both Testaments and love of God and neighbor, by which priest and deacon ought to shine. Through the twelve fringes contained in both lines, the twelve branches of virtue that hang from the root of charity are signified. The Apostle also enumerates them, saying: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4), and so forth.

The third line, placed between the two lines and joined before and behind by three fringes, demonstrates charity, which contains love of God and neighbor, marked by faith in the Trinity. Through the scarlet color, works of mercy toward orphans and widows are understood. Through the fringes of the left side, the solicitude of the active life is represented; through the right, which lacks fringes, the rest of the contemplative life; through the breadth of the sleeves, the generosity of almsgiving.

Through the chasuble, which is worn over all the ornaments, holiness and righteousness are signified, by which priestly glory ought to shine in every respect. Its being double between the shoulders signifies care and compassion for one’s neighbors, together with purity of inward intention; its other doubling at the breast signifies teaching among the people and the truth with which the mind ought to be adorned.

Through the linen footwear, which gleams with whiteness and is called linen, one is restrained from running toward evil and urged to hasten toward good. Through the sandals, which are open above but below prevent the feet from touching the earth by means of their soles, it is signified that preachers ought not to ascend toward earthly things but should aspire to heavenly things.

The pallium, which the archbishop wears over all the ornaments, signifies the chain that those legitimately steadfast customarily received. Through the circle by which it is fastened around the shoulders, fear and discipline of the Lord are signified; by these he ought to govern both himself and his fellow bishops, who are subject to him. Through the two lines running from top to bottom on either side, the preaching of both Testaments and uninterrupted love of God and neighbor are signified.

The corporal on which the Lord’s Body is placed ought to be nothing other than linen, since Joseph is read to have bought a clean linen cloth when he wrapped the Lord’s Body (Matt. 27). Linen is a pure growth of the earth, and the Lord possessed a true and pure body, not an apparent one. Just as linen reaches whiteness through much labor or sweat, so Jesus Christ, having endured many sufferings, departed from this world and was brought to the whiteness of resurrection and immortality.

Therefore, whoever desires to receive the Lord’s Body within himself must make himself clean and white through many labors of good works and through purity of mind and body. It should be [reading uncertain: *placari*, perhaps *plicari*, “folded”] in such a way that it has neither beginning nor end, for thus the sudarium was found in the Lord’s tomb.

The sudarium is a binding for the head. Through the head, divinity is signified, because the head of Christ is God. Its winding signifies that Christ, who in his humanity had a beginning by being born and an end by dying, has neither of these in his divinity, but always possesses being.

The body of Christ is threefold, namely, in the case of those who have tasted death and are destined to die. The first is the holy and undefiled body taken from the Virgin Mary; the second is the body that still walks upon the earth; the third is the body that lies in the tombs. Through the portion of the offered Mass placed in the chalice, the body of Christ who rose from the dead is shown; through the portion eaten by the priest or the people, Christ is shown still walking upon the earth; through the portion left on the altar until the end of Mass, Christ is shown lying in the tombs until the end of the world.

## On Those Who Ordered the Mass

The order for celebrating Mass was eventually composed in full by the apostles and apostolic ministers. The Church recited the Epistles and the Gospel according to the tradition of the ancients; they are unarranged in the book called the *Comes*, which Jerome is said to have written for Constantius.

Pope Alexander VII, who instituted the blessing of water [folio addition: “the use of blessing”] and the sprinkling, inserted the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion into the consecration of the Eucharist. Pope Xystus VIII was the first to introduce the hymn “Holy, holy, holy.” Pope Telesphorus IX, who instituted the Lenten fast six weeks before Easter, added the angelic hymn “Glory to God in the highest.” Pope Damasus XXXV instituted the singing of “I believe in one God” on solemn days, by decree of the holy universal synod celebrated at Constantinople by 150 bishops.

Pope Innocent XXXVIII decreed that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass. Pope Celestine XLI instituted the antiphonal composition of the Introit, Graduals, Offertories, and Communions from the psalms. Pope Leo XLIII added to the canon of the Mass “the holy sacrifice, the unspotted victim.” Pope Gelasius XLVI composed the Collects and Prefaces.

Pope Gregory LXI added “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy,” “Alleluia” outside the period of Quinquagesima, and in the canon: “And dispose our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect.” He also added the Lord’s Prayer after the canon of consecration, through which alone the apostles consecrated. To all this Pope Sergius LXXX added one final element: that, during Communion, “Lamb of God” should be sung by the clergy.

[Col. 0211]

# Foundation of a College of Ten Clerics of Albania

In the church of Rouen, in the year 1245.

*(From the archiepiscopal chartulary of Rouen.)*

[Col. 0211D] Peter, by divine mercy bishop of Albano [Note: [Col. 0211] Peter of Collemedio, who was archbishop of Rouen], to all who shall inspect the present letters, greetings in the Lord.

Not forgetful or ungrateful for the benefits that we have received in many ways from the noble Church of Rouen, we judge it right and highly necessary for our soul that, even if we cannot adequately repay either ourselves or that Church for all the benefits received, we should at least return something by which divine worship may be increased and, through this, its dignity and honor preserved in the future.

Accordingly, after careful consideration and for the honor of God, the glorious Virgin, and blessed Roman, in whose honor the said church was built, we have now decided to ordain that the archbishop who shall at the time be in the church of Rouen shall place or institute in it ten suitable and honest clerics [Col. 0212D]. They shall reside continually in that church, and at their reception they shall confirm this by their own oath. They shall also attend all the Hours in the same church, unless they are prevented by illness or by another sufficient, honest, and necessary cause.

Of these clerics there shall be four subdeacons, three deacons, and three priests. No one shall be appointed unless he has completed his twenty-first year and knows how to read and sing well. These clerics may be absent for one hour each day for any necessary reason, provided that they attend all the other Hours. If they do not attend all the other Hours, the stipend they ought to receive for that day shall be withheld from them.

No one may absent himself with impunity from Matins, Mass, None, or Vespers. If he misses one of these Hours, even if he has attended all the others, he shall be deprived that day of the stipend due to him, unless he can excuse himself on this matter because of a reduction [in duties] granted by the cantor or hebdomadary, or for another honest, sufficient, suitable, and necessary cause.

Each of these clerics shall receive twelve pounds Tournois annually. These shall be distributed faithfully day by day, according to the appropriate proportion, by someone from the church who is trustworthy and sworn to perform this task, appointed by the cantor with the advice of the major archdeacon and treasurer, if they are present, or of whichever one of them is present.

Whatever is withheld from the aforesaid clerics because of their failures shall be faithfully kept by the same archdeacon, who shall show favor to no one in this matter, and shall be spent for pious uses, as they deem expedient, through the hands of the cantor, major archdeacon, and treasurer, or of two of them.

For the purchase and assignment of these revenues, we allocate 1,500 pounds Tournois. We wish that, through the hands of the venerable Odo, archbishop of Rouen, our most learned friend, and also of Master Hugh the Pisan of Rouen, Peter of Pavia, and William of Rezeana, archdeacons of the church of Rouen; John of Campis, William Laudius, and Hugh of Alumnia, canons of Rouen—if they are present, or at least through the hands of two or three of those who are present—these revenues be purchased and assigned, together with the archbishop who shall at the time be in office, for the purposes stated above.

If our aforesaid friend the archbishop, or any of those named, should happen to die before these and the other matters contained below have been completed, the future archbishop shall take the place of the said archbishop, and his successor the place of the major archdeacon. In place of the two other archdeacons mentioned above, the dean and cantor named above shall succeed. If any of them should die before these and the other matters contained below have been completed, their successors shall take their places in carrying out the foregoing, so that the archbishop, together with all of them if they are present, or at least two or three of them, shall execute the matters stated above and those mentioned below.

But if, from the aforesaid 1,500 pounds Tournois, after the sum of 120 pounds of the same currency—which the ten clerics shall receive annually for their support—has been set aside, some revenues can be purchased, we wish the surplus remaining after the purchase of the revenues for the aforesaid 120 pounds to be converted into the purchase of revenues for buying choir capes each year for the clerics mentioned above.

For we intend that each of them, if possible, should have one choir cape annually, the price of which shall not exceed twenty solidi Tournois. These clerics shall all sleep together in one house; for beginning that house we presently allocate 200 pounds. In the same house they shall likewise eat together, if this can conveniently be done, and the archbishop who shall at the time be in office may compel them to do so if he considers it expedient.

Furthermore, if any of the aforesaid clerics behaves dishonestly, or proves negligent or remiss concerning the divine Office, or through his own fault becomes unfit to serve the church, then, upon the denunciation of the dean, major archdeacon, treasurer, and cantor who shall at the time be in office, or of two of them, the archbishop shall remove him without lengthy investigation and substitute another in his place.

For we do not intend that the aforesaid clerics be permanent, but rather temporary, so that they may receive the aforesaid benefits only for as long as they serve the church and conduct themselves honorably, as is fitting. Nevertheless, if through old age, an illness that comes upon them, or some other circumstance without their fault they become less useful for serving the church, we do not wish them to be removed on that account, lest affliction be added to the afflicted.

The archbishop who shall at the time be in office shall see to it that, when placing or instituting the said clerics in the same church, he keeps God alone before his eyes. He shall take care that, to the prejudice of divine worship—which we desire to increase in that church for the adornment of the house of the Lord—no favor be granted to anyone because of affection, prayers, or a desire to provide for a person rather than for the church. Our intention is that suitable, honest, and useful persons be assumed for service in the church without respect of persons.

We further wish and ordain that, if the archbishop who shall at the time be in office delays for more than one month after learning of a vacancy to place or institute the aforesaid clerics, or any one of them, in the said church, the dean and chapter shall take his place. If they delay doing this for more than another month, the power shall on that occasion devolve upon the dean, major archdeacon, cantor, and treasurer who shall at the time be in office.

Moreover, if any of the aforesaid clerics wishes to be absent from the church and to move elsewhere in order to remain there, he shall be required, one month before his departure, to announce this publicly to the chapter and to the archbishop, if he is present, or to the person acting in his place. Thus, when he departs, provision may be made for another to be substituted in his place, lest through his sudden departure the church happen for a time to be deprived of the service of one minister.

Furthermore, we ordain and wish that from the revenues of twenty-six pounds Tournois, which we purchased at Locum-Veris [in French, Louviers] and now give to the church of Rouen, our commemoration be made three times each year in the aforesaid church: namely, on the day of our death and at two other times to be assigned by the archbishop, dean, and chapter. At each occasion, seven pounds Tournois shall be distributed to the canons who attend the service, and thirty solidi to the clerics of the choir who attend, according to the custom of that church. The remaining ten solidi shall be distributed in bread to the poor on the day of our death, through the hands of the hebdomadary.

Furthermore, as long as the Lord in his mercy grants us life, we wish a Mass of the same glorious Virgin to be celebrated in the aforesaid church during the octave of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. To the canons who attend that Mass, seven pounds from the aforesaid twenty-six pounds shall be distributed, and thirty solidi to the clerics of the choir who attend, according to the custom of the same church.

On the day after All Saints, on which, while we live, we wish a commemoration to be made in the said church for the souls of our predecessors, the archbishops, and for the souls of our parents who have passed from this world, seven pounds from the aforesaid money shall be distributed to the canons who attend the service, and thirty solidi to the clerics of the choir who attend. On that same day, ten solidi from the aforesaid sum shall be distributed in bread to the poor through the hands of the hebdomadary.

The remaining eight and a half pounds Tournois shall be distributed to the canons and clerics of the choir of the aforesaid church who attend the Mass of the Holy Spirit, which we wish to be solemnly celebrated in that church on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, for as long as we live. The canons shall receive seven pounds and the clerics of the choir thirty solidi; neither the canons nor the clerics shall receive anything from it unless they attend the said Mass.

Finally, after, at the Lord’s calling, we have departed from this world, the aforesaid twenty-six pounds shall be disposed of as set out above.

Moreover, we wish that, from the revenues of sixty and ten Tournois solidi which we formerly purchased at Locum Veris and assigned in the said church for the use of lamps, if the said lamps do not burn in the church day and night, those revenues be distributed in bread, through the hands of the hebdomadary, on the day of our death and on the other two commemorations that will be held for us in the church of Rouen, so that one-third of the aforesaid amount may be spent at each term. [Col. 0215A] But the aforesaid sum of one thousand seven hundred Tournois pounds, which from now on we assign both for purchasing revenues, as stated above, and for beginning the house, we order to be deposited, registered, and carefully and faithfully preserved by the hands of the aforesaid persons in the treasury of Rouen, until the things that are to be done with the aforesaid money have been completed. Let each of them also promise in good faith that he will not permit the said money to be converted to other uses or ever be touched for another undertaking.

We further wish that, before they receive anything from the aforesaid twenty-six pounds, two terms of our commemoration be assigned by the archbishop together with the dean and chapter. Likewise, repeatedly bringing to mind the deficiency that occurred in the Masses sung at the major altar of the Blessed Virgin—a deficiency which, by our constitution, we wish at some point to remedy, but which, through the negligence of certain persons, has not yet, as is said, been remedied—we, considering that we were negligent because we did not compel the canons to serve, establish and arrange, in order to expiate our aforesaid negligence, that five hundred Tournois pounds be immediately assigned from the goods granted to us by God for the purchase of revenues. These revenues shall be assigned to the priest, deacon, and subdeacon who are canons and who will minister at the major altar at the High Mass. Thus they shall be divided equally among them each day according to their respective shares. This shall be done through the hands of the aforesaid persons, with the dean of Rouen nevertheless summoned, since he is bound diligently to conduct the chapter’s business.

We wish all the foregoing to be carried out during our lifetime. If it is not carried out during our lifetime, or at least within a year after our death, we establish, arrange, and, under threat of divine judgment, enjoin the archbishop who shall then be in office to make every effort, without delay, to distribute the aforesaid goods to the persons mentioned and their successors, and, without delay, to poor and pious places—namely, leper houses, poor monasteries of nuns and religious men, and also to any poor young women to be married, if any are found.

Nevertheless, we have deemed it right to retain the power to dispose of and arrange the said money otherwise, except for what we order to be done for the church of Rouen, as stated above, if during our lifetime the foregoing matters are not promptly fulfilled. Moreover, we wish that, for the execution of all the foregoing, our beloved associate M. Peter of Saint-Omer be consulted on account of his consent and presence. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Something appears to be missing here.]

432 Given at Lyon, in the year of the Lord 1245, on the feast of Saint Lawrence.

[Col. 0215]

# FOUNDATION OF THE COLLEGE OF SIXTEEN CLERICS OF CLEMENT

In the church of Rouen, in the year 1350.

(From the archives of the same college.) (G)*

[Col. 0215C] Clement [Note: [Col. 0216D] He was Peter Roger, archbishop of Rouen.], bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

Weighing the many talents entrusted to us by the Lord, and carefully considering that from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required, we are certainly frightened lest we, who are seen to have received more than others in this world, should for that reason be judged more severely by the Author of the world. For as gifts increase, so too do the accounts demanded for those gifts; and, weighed down by the burden of sins, we are not able to serve the Lord worthily.

Therefore, so that we may deserve to obtain, through the protection of others, the reward of divine grace, which our merits do not demand, for the praise and glory of almighty God, for the honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, his Mother, and of the other saints, and for the salvation of our own souls, of the souls of our predecessors and forebears, and of the souls of our faithful, we establish and also ordain, by apostolic authority, in the church of Rouen—which by divine disposition formerly had us as her bridegroom and now recognizes us as her father [Col. 0215D] and lord—sixteen perpetual clerics, or chaplains, as a number or college. We wish them to be called Clementine chaplains or clerics, namely of Clement VI, pope. We decree by the same authority that twelve of the said sixteen clerics or chaplains shall be constituted in the order of priests, two in the order of deacons, and the remaining two in the order of subdeacons.

Each of them shall receive fourteen denarii each day as their stipend; and, in addition to the aforesaid fourteen denarii, they shall perpetually receive two further denarii in the customary coin at every solemn procession. We further ordain that each of the twelve aforesaid clerics or chaplains constituted in the priesthood, as stated above, shall celebrate one Mass each for an entire week perpetually, six of them in the chapels of that church, secretly and by themselves, or, if prevented by a legitimate impediment, through other suitable priests; and that each of the remaining six shall likewise celebrate one Mass during another week in succession. Each of them shall receive, on the day when he celebrates as stated above, in addition to the aforesaid fourteen and two denarii, another four denarii in the same customary coin.

We also establish that all sixteen clerics or chaplains shall assemble together once each week in the chapel of Saint John, situated in the same church. As long as we remain among the living, they shall solemnly celebrate one Mass of the Trinity, or of the Holy Spirit, or of the Blessed Virgin, or of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, or of Saint Martial; after we have completed the course of this uncertain and fleeting life, they shall solemnly celebrate a Mass for the dead.

The priest who solemnly celebrates such a Mass, as stated above, shall receive a further twenty-four denarii; the deacon and subdeacon ministering to the priest shall each receive a further eighteen; and the remaining clerics or chaplains—namely, those who are present at such a celebration—shall each receive a further twelve denarii on each day on which such a Mass is solemnly celebrated in each week, in addition to the aforesaid fourteen, two, and four denarii, in the aforementioned coin.

In the distribution of the fourteen denarii established for the same clerics or chaplains as their stipends, we wish and establish that the following arrangement be perpetually observed: at Matins, at the High Mass, and at Masses for the dead, as well as at Vespers, each cleric or chaplain present at Matins, Masses, Vespers, and the aforesaid Hours shall receive two denarii for each of those Masses or Hours; and at the other Hours—namely Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline—and also at the offices for the dead, namely Placebo and Dirige, celebrated in the said church, each cleric or chaplain present shall receive one denarius for each such Hour or office.

We further establish that the said clerics or chaplains shall continually attend the Masses and other canonical Hours, both by day and by night, celebrated in the same church at the appropriate times, unless they have requested and obtained permission from the dean, cantor, or hebdomadary of the same church who shall then be in office, or from the aforesaid dean, according to the customary practice in similar cases concerning the other chaplains and clerics of that church who are then absent from it.

Furthermore, so that the aforesaid clerics or chaplains may be led to observe the foregoing both by hope of reward and by fear of punishment, we add the following provision: if any of the aforesaid clerics or chaplains is not personally present in the church mentioned at such Masses, Vespers, Hours, and offices, or at any one or more of them, he shall by that fact be deprived of the distributions—or of the distribution—of the Masses, Hours, or offices, or of the Mass, Hour, or office at which he was not present, and which, had he been present, he would have received.

We further ordain that, by the said dean and our beloved sons, the chapter of the church, one other cleric, outside the number of such clerics or chaplains, shall be appointed each week to observe the absences and other shortcomings of the sixteen aforesaid clerics or chaplains and faithfully record them in writing. At the end of each week he shall make a full and faithful report of them to the person whom the dean and chapter shall deem fit to appoint for this purpose. A fixed remuneration shall be assigned to the person appointed, as stated above, by the dean and chapter, so that he may perform the office entrusted to him more faithfully and diligently.

The stipends of fourteen denarii and the other denarii aforesaid shall be paid to these clerics or chaplains by the dean and chapter at the end of each week, according to our prescribed ordinance, after the dean and chapter have first retained and deducted whatever is to be deducted as penalties for the absence of those clerics and chaplains.

Finally, observing how good and how pleasant, according to the testimony of the Prophet, it is for brothers to dwell together as one (Ps. CXXXII, 1), we establish, wish, and also ordain by the aforesaid authority that the said chaplains or clerics live and reside together in one and the same house. We further ordain that the said dean and chapter, together with our beloved son Bertrand Chariti, archdeacon of Augi and apostolic nuncio in the same church, choose one house, manor, or lodging—or a single house, manor, or lodging—with its adjoining or contiguous gardens, orchards, houses, manors, or lodgings, which the said dean and chapter possess in the city of Rouen. A suitable and sufficient residence for these chaplains or clerics shall be selected.

After a faithful valuation has been made of the house, manor, or lodging, together with its adjoining or contiguous gardens or orchards, and the price for which it is found to be worth has been determined, we command by these presents that it be paid in full to the dean and chapter, or to another or others in their name, by the same nuncio from the funds of the Apostolic Chamber collected by him and to be collected thereafter.

The house, manor, or lodging thus to be selected, as stated above, we now give, grant, and donate to the said chaplains or clerics, and we also assign it to the same nuncio for their common residence. Nevertheless, by the same authority we command that both the valuation of the house, manor, or lodging, together with its adjoining or contiguous gardens or orchards, and any other necessary money for repairing that house, manor, or lodging and for arranging and establishing within it the necessary facilities for the common residence of the clerics or chaplains, be paid in full on this occasion from the funds of the said Chamber already collected and henceforth to be collected by the same nuncio.

We strictly forbid the said dean and chapter to presume to spend any of the money which they receive from the same nuncio, or from another person paying in our name, as the price of the said house, lodging, or manor, except on the purchase of perpetual revenues to be purchased for the same church; and, if they presume to attempt the contrary, we will that the aforesaid dean and chapter, and each individual person of the aforesaid chapter, be subject by that very fact to suspension and the sentence of excommunication.

The money that shall accrue from the penalties for the absences of the aforesaid clerics or chaplains shall be faithfully assigned and entirely converted by the said dean and chapter to the repair and preservation of the said house, manor, or lodging. From it, the salary established by the dean and chapter for the person appointed, as stated above, to inspect, record, and report the aforesaid deficiencies shall first be paid, just as payment is made to the keeper of the other sixteen clerics or chaplains, called those of Darnestallo, who were instituted in the same church long ago.

We further establish and ordain that no one be received or admitted as a cleric or chaplain to such clerical offices or chaplaincies unless he can recite the Psalter and Antiphonary by heart according to the histories; or, if such a person perhaps cannot be found, unless at least he is capable and fit to learn to recite the Psalter and Antiphonary in the prescribed manner within two years, calculated from the time of his reception.

Indeed, having full confidence before the Lord in the prudence and probity of our beloved son John of Novancuria, archdeacon of the Vexin of France, in the same church, we wish, and by the aforesaid authority also ordain, that, as long as we remain among the living, he—or, if it should happen that he is meanwhile taken from this life or promoted to another dignity, or if the archdeacon of the Vexin of France should cease to hold office in the said church, another person whom we shall choose for this purpose—confer and assign such clerical offices or chaplaincies, both on this first occasion and thereafter successively, whenever they happen to become vacant, upon suitable persons who know, or are capable and fit, to learn to recite the Psalter and Antiphonary, as stated above.

After we have been taken from this life, the free disposition of those offices or chaplaincies shall belong fully by right to the said dean and chapter. The dean and chapter shall also have full and free power to deprive of their clerical offices or chaplaincies those of the same clerics or chaplains who remain absent from the aforesaid church for more than two months without legitimate cause, or who are to be deprived for other just reasons, but only after our death; and to confer the clerical offices or chaplaincies made vacant by such deprivation upon other suitable persons who, as stated above, know how to recite the Psalter and Antiphonary, or are capable and fit to recite them.

We have also deemed it proper to provide decently for books, chalices, and other ornaments necessary in that church for the Masses and other divine offices to be celebrated by the clerics or chaplains. For the support of the aforesaid burdens, we assign annual revenues of three hundred and twenty small Tournois pounds, which we have caused to be purchased and amortized, and another two hundred and twenty pounds in revenues, which, apart from such house, manor, or lodging, we wish and command to be purchased. For the purchase of these, one thousand and seventy gold écus have already been assigned to the said chapter [addition: and dean] by the same nuncio, and we command and order by these presents that the remainder be paid by him.

From now on, by the same authority, we assign these revenues; and from now on we also give, grant, and donate to the said dean and chapter both the revenues already purchased, as stated above, and those yet to be purchased. We wish the dean and chapter to be permitted, wherever and in whatever things those revenues consist, to take possession of and acquire them by their own authority, and to convert them to the uses in question, according to the manner and form expressed above.

Nevertheless, the dean and chapter must swear for themselves and their successors, promise in good faith, and effectively bind themselves to incur and bear, for the repair and preservation of the said house, manor, or lodging, all necessary expenses beyond the money arising from such penalties and condemnation. They must faithfully collect these revenues and defend and preserve them, as well as the things, places, and goods in which they consist, to the best of their ability, just as they do their other common goods and rights. They must also pay in full, according to the prescribed order and perpetually from the revenues already purchased and those to be purchased, the stipends of the same clerics or chaplains.

They must likewise satisfy the other two perpetual chaplains instituted by us in the same church while we presided over it, according to our ordinance formerly made concerning their stipends. For these stipends also, we have deemed it right to assign certain revenues elsewhere, as appears from the public instruments drawn up concerning them. They must also perform the solemnity of Saint Martial and the anniversaries which we have until now annually ordered to be held in the said church, as well as the two Masses which the dean and chapter themselves established for us annually, at the time of our promotion to the height of apostolic dignity, for our salvation as long as we remain among the living, and perpetually after we have departed this life for the remedy of our soul [addition in the margin: “established”].

One of these Masses is to be celebrated on the Nones of May, the day on which we were taken up into the office of apostolic service; the other is to be celebrated on a day chosen by the aforesaid dean and chapter. The other two Masses instituted by us in the said church, as stated above, shall remain to be celebrated on their customary days and according to their customary order.

Furthermore, lest it perhaps happen through the absence of the dean that our will and intention concerning the foregoing ordinances, or any one or more of them, should be impeded or delayed, we add and declare that we wish all and each of the foregoing matters to be carried out by the said dean and chapter without summoning or awaiting the said dean if he should happen to be absent, while the rest of the prescribed form is nevertheless observed.

Moreover, we wish these present letters and all the individual instruments, both concerning the grant of the house, manor, or lodging itself and concerning the purchase of the revenues already purchased and also to be purchased, as stated above, as well as concerning the promise and obligation of the aforesaid chapter, together with an inventory of the books, vestments, and chalices assigned, and also to be assigned, for the celebration of the Masses and other divine offices, to be preserved in the public archive of that church, with copies thereof given in public form to the said chaplains or clerics by the said dean and chapter.

Therefore, let absolutely no one be permitted to violate this page of our ordinance, institution, statutes, wishes, commands, gifts, grants, ordinances, assignments, precepts, and orders, or rashly oppose it. Whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0220C] Given at Avignon, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

Thus signed on the fold:

“From the curia of Saint Stephen.”

[Col. 0219]

# SIX SERMONS TO THE PEOPLE BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

(From the manuscript of Bigot.) (G)*

## SERMON ONE. ON HONORING PRIESTS

[Col. 0219D]

The apostle Paul says: “There is no authority except from God. And those that exist have been ordained by God; therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Rom. 13:1–2).

Listen, dearest brothers, to what the Apostle of the Lord cries out to you. Authorities, whether of the world or of the Church, are not to be despised, because all have been ordained by God; and whoever contradicts and resists those ordained by God commits an insult against the one who ordained them.

It is therefore fitting that we visit and venerate our lord the pope, our counselor: visit him because he is our counselor; venerate him because he is our shepherd. For the bishops of the Church are to be venerated as teachers and as the vicars of the Lord.

The Lord wished his priests to be feared and venerated with such great reverence that in Deuteronomy he threatened, saying: “And whoever acts presumptuously and does not obey the priest or the judge shall die” (Deut. 17:12). Likewise, when Samuel was despised by the Jews, the Lord says to him: “They have not despised you, but they have despised me.” And the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me and the one who sent me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

After cleansing a leper, he said: “Go and show yourself to the priest” (Matt. 8:4). Later, at the time of his Passion, after he had received a slap from a servant of the priest, and when the servant said to him, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” (John 18:22), the Lord said nothing insulting against the high priest and took nothing away from the priest’s honor. Rather, asserting and demonstrating his innocence more fully, he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, give testimony concerning the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (ibid., 23).

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the blessed apostle Paul was told, “Do you curse God’s high priest?” (Acts 23:4)—although at that time, after Christ had been crucified, the Jewish priesthood was destroyed insofar as Christians were concerned—Paul nevertheless, venerating the office itself, although its name was empty, said: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people’” (ibid., 5; Exod. 22:28).

Since, then, the ancient priesthood of the old law was held in such great authority, and the Lord threatened death to those who resisted it, what do you think will be the fate of those who are enemies and rebels against the priesthood of the new law and against the Church of God? They neither heed the Lord’s warning—that is, they do not take precautions against it—nor are they terrified by the vengeance of the future judgment.

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who attempted to claim for themselves the right to sacrifice against the Lord, Moses, and Aaron the priest, immediately paid the penalty for their efforts. When the earth split open along its joints, it opened into a deep chasm, and the opening of the receding ground swallowed them while they stood alive. Nor did the wrath of the offended God strike only those who had been the leaders: fire from God, in a vengeance that proved his anger, also consumed the other two hundred and fifty leaders of the same rebellion (Num. 26). It thus warned and showed that whatever human beings attempt by human will to destroy God’s ordinance is done against God.

So also King Uzziah, carrying a censer and forcibly taking upon himself the sacrifice contrary to God’s law, refused to obey or withdraw when the priest Zechariah [Azariah] resisted him. He was confounded by divine indignation and marked on the forehead with a variety of leprous spots (2 Chron. 26:18), branded on that part where those who please the Lord are marked, but where he had offended the Lord.

It is therefore necessary to beware, dearest brothers, lest anyone dare rise up against God’s priests, lest the Lord choose to punish harshly those who perform his office in his place.

These men have been placed in the Church for our benefit: to provide for us, to render an account for our salvation, and to preserve the unity of the Church. Concerning this unity, the Lord wished us to be solicitous, lest, walking along byways and creating schisms, we should be separated from the unity of faith through various errors. For there is one Lord and one shepherd; thus he wished there to be one family and one flock. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “And there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16). And Israel says in the old law: “The Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4).

That there is one God, he shows in the Gospel when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And again it is written concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “And the three are one” (1 John 5:7).

The Lord therefore wished his own to be like him, so that, just as he was one, the Church might likewise be one. Hence the Lord says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my perfect one is one” (Song 6:8).

This mystery of unity was signified by the Lord’s seamless tunic. Concerning it the Gospel says that the soldiers who crucified him, because it was not sewn together from the upper part but woven throughout, said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to decide whose it shall be” (John 19:23–24).

Christ’s garment was whole from the upper part because the Church of God inseparably possesses the unity that comes from heaven—that is, from the Father and the Son—and the solid firmness of faith. The Lord did not wish his seamless garment to be torn because he does not permit the unity of the Church to be violated.

Paul therefore commanded concerning this unity: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you” (1 Cor. 1:10). And again: “Maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3).

> “For although the rays of the sun are many, the light is one; and although the branches of a tree are many, its strength is one, firmly grounded in a tenacious root. And although many streams flow from one spring, their number, though spread out and seemingly overflowing through the abundance of the outpouring, nevertheless preserves unity at its source. Tear a ray of the sun away from its body: the unity of the light does not permit division. Break a branch from the tree: once broken, it cannot put forth growth. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up. Thus the Church of the Lord, flooded with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; yet the light that is diffused everywhere remains one, and the unity of the body is not separated. She extends her branches throughout the whole earth with the abundance of her fruitfulness and spreads her flowing streams more widely through generous outpouring; yet there is one head and one source, and one mother, rich in the succession of her fruitfulness.”

(Saint Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*)

For the preservation of this unity, just as the lamb of the old law, slain as a figure of Christ, was to be eaten in one house—“You shall not carry any of the flesh outside the house” (Exod. 12:46)—so the flesh of Christ and the sacrament of the Lord cannot be carried outside. Nor is there any other house for believers besides the one Church. This house signifies the dwelling of unity, and the Holy Spirit announces it in the Psalms, saying: “God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7).

In the house of God, in the Church of God, those of one mind dwell who persevere in concord and simplicity.

Therefore, to preserve this observance, dearest brothers, the Lord wished to build his Church through one man, upon him to whom he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth …” (Matt. 16:18–19). And: “When you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

Peter is the foundation upon which the Church rests, for all the other members ought to adhere to his faith. He was made teacher and prince of the apostles, and shepherd of the faithful, because he prevailed in faith. When the Lord inquired into the faith of his own, saying, “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15), Peter, as the stronger in faith, answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16). When he heard the strength of Peter’s faith, the Lord granted him to be the foundation of the faith of the Church, saying: “And you are Peter,” and so forth (ibid., 18).

He has the keys of heaven because no one can aspire to heaven except through his teaching and instruction. It is therefore necessary that, when we are in danger, he should at some time turn toward us and strengthen us; for the Lord prayed for him that his faith should not fail (Luke 22:32).

Since Peter, then, is our teacher, our lord is his vicar. Therefore, we ought to visit the threshold of the apostles, visit our lord the pope, and seek counsel on how, amid so many and such great waves of this world, we can govern the Church of the Lord without danger. For storms arise daily in the Church of God [Note: [Col. 0221D] ‘Their’ is understood. ‘See manum qui,’ p. 454 (the printed reading is uncertain).], and there are those who wish to scatter its unity and extinguish the union of peace by sowing discord. They attack the pastors of the Church so that, by striking the head, the members may be shaken with terror. The Church suffers not only from outsiders but also from those within, from her own brothers; and internal wars, against which no precaution is taken, are worse than external wars, which can be foreseen.

At the beginning of the world, the just Abel was killed by his brother; Esau his brother persecuted Jacob as he fled; Joseph was sold by his brothers; and the Lord himself was betrayed by a disciple. But it is no disgrace for us to suffer at the hands of our brothers what Christ suffered, nor is it glory to do what Judas did.

We do not fear the insults by which they daily tear themselves and their own lives apart; we are not terrified by the clubs, stones, and swords that they brandish with murderous words. What are they? They are murderers before God. They cannot kill us unless the Lord permits them; and although we must die once, they nevertheless kill us daily by their hatred, words, and sins.

For this reason we will not be moved from our purpose of justice: ecclesiastical discipline must not be abandoned through fear, nor priestly authority dissolved.

They are like the devil, their father, who, immediately after he was created, rose up against his Creator and said: “I will place my throne above the stars of God; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds and be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

Those who trouble God’s priests ascend into heaven, wish to sit above the stars of God, establish their throne above the mountain of the covenant, and ascend above the clouds—as though they were saying: “They wish to reign over the bishops.” For bishops are heaven, the stars of God, the mountain of the covenant, the clouds of heaven, and the sides of the north.

They are heaven because they contain the secrets of God, as David says: “The heavens declare the glory …” (Ps. 18:1), and so forth.

They are stars because the Lord says concerning them: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).

They are clouds because they rain upon the minds of the faithful with the dew of preaching. Concerning them it is said: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8).

They are the sides of the north because they are neighbors to sinners, who, cold in their sins, persecute them; or because they offer their sides to endure the north—that is, the devil, who brings the cold of sin upon human beings. Concerning him the Song of Songs says: “Rise, north wind, and blow upon my garden” (Song 4:16)—that is, “Test my Church, so that, from the victory gained over you, she may receive glory.”

They are the mountain of the covenant because in them is the height of knowledge of both Testaments.

But you, who are children of the Church, defend the Church. “Let no one deceive you with empty words” (Eph. 5:6). The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated; she is incorrupt and chaste. Whoever abandons the bride of Christ has no share in Christ’s rewards; whoever does not have the Church as mother can no longer have God as Father.

Whoever wishes to divide the Church wishes to tear Christ’s garment. No good person abandons the Church of God or departs from the family of God. Truly, as the Lord says, “his sheep will recognize her” (John 10:14). He also cries out to all: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

The wind does not carry away wheat, nor does a storm overthrow a tree firmly planted by solid roots. Empty chaff is tossed about by the tempest, and weak trees are overturned by the attack of the whirlwind.

Let the children of God appear, so that the heavenly Father may reward them for standing firm in faith, and so that in heaven one God and one Church may become one throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON TWO. TO THE PASTORS OF THE CHURCH

On the pastoral office.

[Col. 0223C] Woe to the shepherds who scatter the flock of my pasture. Therefore the Lord God of Israel says this to the shepherds who feed his people: “You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your practices” (Jer. 23:1–2). Hear, dearest brothers, the sentence threatening you; yet he who threatens sinners wishes them to be converted. Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord commands you, because he had entrusted his flock to you to be fed, ruled, and guarded: you were to defend it from wolves lying in wait, and, when they were hungry, refresh them with the food of the heavenly word. Hence, when he had summoned his disciples, the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have compassion on the crowd, because [ms. *qui*] they have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. 15:32). Those for whom no table of preaching is set in this world are hungry on the way. The Lord has compassion when he sends preachers; you are the disciples of the Lord, sent to refresh the hungry.

[Col. 0223D] 454 What then, brothers? Behold, the Lord complains about you: shepherds have become wolves. Therefore the Lord threatens: “Woe to the shepherds who scatter and tear apart the flock of my people.” You tear apart those whom you ought to feed; behold, the sheep becomes the shepherd’s food. They tear them apart because, although they are evil, they incorporate them into themselves, tearing them apart by making them evil and like themselves, because they lead them to punishment. They scatter them because they divide them from the unity of the Church.

But hear what the Lord threatens you: “Behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your practices.” The Lord visits someone’s evils when he punishes them. Hence he says in the psalm: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not reckon sin” (Ps. 31:2). And why the Lord will punish the priests, he adds: “For the priests have been polluted, and in my house I have found their evil” (Jer. 23:11). They have been polluted by sins, although they ought to be clean, because they must make others clean. For the hand of the one who cleanses and washes the stains of a polluted vessel must be clean [Note: [Col. 0223] “His” is understood. See *Tempestates*, p. 450.], lest, when something filthy handles something filthy, it defile what is polluted still more. For it is written: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). They carry the Lord’s vessels who, by the example of their conduct, receive the souls of their neighbors in order to lead them into the inner sanctuaries.

The Apostle describes what a presbyter ought to be when he says: “The bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not irascible, not addicted to wine, not violent, not desirous of shameful gain” (Tit. 1:7). Here he calls not only a bishop but also a presbyter a bishop—that is, one who is irreprehensible, from the time, namely, when he was baptized. “How,” Ambrose says, “can he preside over the Church and remove evil from it who has fallen into a similar offense?”
