It follows: “As God’s steward.” A steward is one thing, a master another. A steward is a servant placed over his fellow servants; both the steward and his household are servants of the same master. Therefore it is not the steward’s task to strike his fellow servants, but to await the Lord, who will avenge what has been done wrongly. He ought, however, to give his fellow servants food at the proper time. Thus the presbyter has the people of God subject to him, but not as slaves. It is therefore not fitting for him to be a terror to God’s household, but to be humble, seeking, like a good steward, what benefits the many.

“Not irascible.” An irascible person is one who is always angry and is moved by the slightest breath of rebuke [the reading is uncertain] and sin, like a leaf by the wind. In truth, nothing is more disgraceful than a furious teacher. Although he ought to be gentle, and although it is written, “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be humble toward everyone, a teacher, patient, gently instructing those who oppose him” (2 Tim. 2:24)—or, according to another reading, “those who are opposed”—that man, by contrast, with a grim face, trembling lips, a wrinkled brow, and unrestrained insults, does not so much draw the erring back to what is good as drive them toward evil by his severity. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not repay evil for evil” [Col. 0224C] (1 Pet. 3:9); and again: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26); and the Lord says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12:19). Solomon says: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who conquers cities” (Prov. 16:52).

“Not addicted to wine.” For it is utterly disgraceful for a presbyter to be devoted to wine. Drunkenness blinds reason. Hence Solomon says: “Wine and women make the wise apostatize” [al. “the wise”] (Ecclus. 19:2). Moreover, it produces sexual excess; hence the Apostle says: “Do not get drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18). Drunk with wine, Lot lay with his daughters; Samson, drunk with wine, was handed over by a prostitute to his enemies. Isaiah also says: “Why do you rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that you burn with wine?” (Isa. 5:11).

In the old law, too, priests were commanded, when they entered the temple to minister to God, not to drink wine at all (Lev. 10:9; Num. 6:3). If priests who once entered the temple according to the old law were required to abstain, what must be said of you, who approach God’s altar every day? With how much sobriety ought you to live?

“Not violent.” After drunkenness he forbids violence, for quarrels commonly arise from wine. The servant of the one who commands, “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39), must not strike.

“Not desirous of shameful gain.” Desire for shameful gain must be alien to a presbyter. For there are many “teaching what they ought not, for the sake of shameful gain” (Tit. 1:11), and they think that piety is a means of gain (1 Tim. 6:5). Perhaps there are many among you who have presumed to accept the office of presbyter not for God’s sake but for earthly advantage. But those who seek earthly gains more than God “have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

Many shameful gains may be identified among priests who are unwilling to sing Mass, baptize, or bury the dead unless payment has been received, promised, or demanded. For “they seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s” (Phil. 2:21). They undertake the care of souls, but do not seek the salvation of souls. When one of their subjects dies, they desire not so much his salvation as his death. Parishioners’ deaths are desired because they believe that some advantage comes to them from the death. These, then, are shameful gains.

Moreover, some of them become moneylenders, although they customarily excommunicate moneylenders. If usury is judged a crime in a layman, should it not be considered more than a crime in a priest? Therefore the Psalmist says: “He who has not lent his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent” [ms. “does not accept”] (Ps. 15:6). If the one who does not accept such gifts is to be praised, then the one who accepts them must be condemned.

Shameful gain is also considered such in the canons if a priest or cleric buys grain or wine in order to sell it at a higher price. A priest then becomes a merchant. But the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business” (2 Tim. 2:4). He ought to be content only with sustenance. Again the Apostle says: “Those who serve at the altar should live from the altar” (1 Cor. 9:13), for “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7).

He said, “Let them live from the altar”; he did not say, “Let them become rich.” They should have food, but should not gather money from it. Hence, when the Lord sent his disciples to preach, he ordered them to carry neither purse, nor bag, nor belt (Luke 10:4), but to live from the possessions of those subject to them, saying: “Eating and drinking what they have” (ibid., 7). While despising earthly riches, they ought to announce those riches that must be sought elsewhere. If they preach and become shepherds solely for the sake of these riches, they deprive themselves of the heavenly ones.

Hence Gregory says: “If anyone preaches in order to receive here the reward either of praise or of payment, he undoubtedly deprives himself of the eternal reward.” Two rewards are owed for this office: one on the way, the other in the homeland. One sustains us in our labor, namely, food; the other rewards us at death, namely, glory. Yet he ought not to preach in order to receive a reward in this time, but to receive a reward so that he may be able to preach.

But what are we doing, shepherds, who obtain a reward and yet are in no way laborers? We receive the fruits, and yet do not labor at all in preaching. Behold, we live from the offerings of the faithful; but what do we do for the souls of the faithful? Rightly was it said of us through the prophet: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8). They eat the sins of the people who, by tolerating and encouraging the sins of wrongdoers, prevent themselves from losing temporal goods. They eat the sins of the people if they live from offerings and yet do nothing for those who make the offerings.

Therefore, dearest brothers, the Lord complains about you and threatens you; and on the other hand the Apostle instructs you. Consider, then, weigh carefully whether this complaint against you is deserved. Fear the threats that come beforehand from justice. Test whether you are such as the Apostle describes, so that you who have received the name of priest may strive to retain the reality signified by that name.

## SERMON III. TO THE PRIESTS

[Col. 0225D]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “A priest who has a blemish must not offer sacrifices to God; nor shall he approach his ministry if he is blind, or lame, or small or large, or has a crooked nose, or a broken foot, or a broken hand, or is hunchbacked, or bleary-eyed, or has a white spot in his eye, or a persistent skin disease. No priest who has a blemish shall approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord” (Lev. 21:17–21). “A man who is leprous shall not eat any of the things sanctified to the Lord” (Lev. 22:3).

Dearest brothers, all these commands concerning the priesthood in the old law appear to pertain spiritually to our priesthood. There the defect of the flesh in a priest is condemned; here the defect of the mind is indicated through the bodily defects. Let us therefore examine one by one whom the defect of the mind, at the Lord’s command, compels to be removed from the priesthood.

First he commands that a blind priest must not offer sacrifices to the Lord. A blind priest is one who does not understand the meaning of Scripture and, through ignorance, does not know where the steps of his teaching or conduct have become weak. Of such people it is written through Isaiah: “All the watchmen of Jerusalem are blind” (Isa. 56:10)—namely, those who ought to care for the Church of God and lead its people, but are blind, that is, ignorant of the Lord’s commands. How rightly such men are removed from the priesthood: they do not know how to rule God’s people, nor do they understand what they ought to teach. For the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, will not both fall into a pit?” (Matt. 15:14). The sins of both fall into the precipice, because both are ignorant of the way of truth.

[Col. 0226A] 461 To such shepherds the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are blind guides of the blind” (ibid., 15). The priests of God ought to be prudent in the Scriptures, so that from them they may feed the Lord’s flock and from them fortify themselves against the spiritual wolf. Hence Solomon, praising the eyes of the Church in the Song of Songs, says: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water” (Song 5:12).

The eyes of the Church are its pastors, who ought to keep watch over the Lord’s flock. They are said to be doves because they ought to be innocent and simple in their examination of the Scriptures, lest they corrupt a sound understanding with some heretical doctrine. They are described as being beside streams of water. By the streams, the meaning of the Scriptures is understood; different streams are different meanings. It is the nature of a dove to dwell beside flowing waters and, when a hawk approaches, to escape its ambush by plunging even into the water. In the same way pastors ought to have recourse to the protection of the Scriptures against the devil’s snares.

It follows: “If he is lame, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” A lame man has one foot straight and limps with the other. Hence pastors are compared to the lame when they proceed correctly in part by understanding rightly, but preach wrongly in another part. Jacob, lame in body, prefigured this mental lameness, because the people of Israel limped in mind when Christ came. They thought rightly about Christ when they regarded him as a man, but wrongly when they did not understand that he was God.

Those who limp in faith must be removed from the priesthood, lest they cause others, whom they ought to rule, to limp in the same defect.

It follows: “If he has a small nose, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” In the divine page, the nose signifies discernment, for by the nose good and bad odors are distinguished. Hence Solomon, describing the Church in the Song of Songs, says: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus” (Song 7:4).

The nose of the Church is its holy teachers, who know how to distinguish the fragrant teaching of the Catholic faith from the stench of heretical depravity. “Like the tower of Lebanon.” Lebanon is a mountain, and its name means “whitening.” The tower of Lebanon signifies the teachers because they are the defense and refuge of the faithful. “Which looks toward Damascus.” Damascus means “drinking of blood”; blood signifies bodily pleasures. Damascus therefore signifies the world, because it delights in blood, that is, in bodily pleasures. But that tower—that is, the holy teachers—is opposed to the world, and therefore it is said to look toward Damascus.

But let us return to the subject. If someone has a small nose, that is, little discernment—so that he cannot properly distinguish in his ministry what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, nor rightly discern by what spirit each thing is done, whether good or evil—he is not worthy of the priesthood. If he lacks true discernment, he will regard as good what is evil. Concerning this discernment the Apostle says: “To another is given the discernment of spirits” (1 Cor. 12:10).

It follows: “If he has a large and crooked nose, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” A man has a large nose when he strays into immoderate discernment, like those who investigate every matter beyond measure. To them the Apostle says: “Do not think beyond what it is necessary to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3). For when someone pursues the divine mysteries beyond measure, he falls into error, since he cannot attain by understanding what he was investigating. But, as the Lord says: “Whatever remains shall be burned with fire” [Col. 0227A] (Exod. 12:10); that is, what cannot be known must be entrusted to the Holy Spirit.

“If he has a broken foot or hand, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” A faithful person is said to walk the Lord’s way with two feet when he strives to complete in deed what he teaches with his mouth. But he has a broken foot who either preaches only and does not complete his preaching in action, or completes it in action but does not preach to others. Both must be removed from the priesthood: the one who remains silent about the truth to others, and the one whose life disagrees with his words.

The Lord notes those who preach well and live badly in the Gospel when he says: “They say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). To the priest who ceases to preach the Lord threatens through Ezekiel:

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear words from my mouth and announce them to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand”—that is, his soul. “But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul” (Ezek. 3:17–19).

The hand signifies the same thing as the foot: the hand signifies working, and the foot walking. In the divine page, walking and working mean the same thing.

It follows: “If he is hunchbacked, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” A hunchbacked priest is one whom the weight of earthly desire presses down and who therefore turns more slowly toward heavenly things. For while he longs for what is below, he remains bent over and bears the burden of anxiety like a weight.

The rich man who truly longs for earthly things is hunchbacked. The Lord indicated this in the Gospel when he compared a rich and avaricious man to a hunchbacked camel, saying: “As a camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle,” and so forth (Matt. 19:24; Mark 10:25; Luke 18:25). For all the priests strive after avarice, and “from prophet even to priest, all practice deceit” (Jer. 6:13).

It follows: “If he is bleary-eyed, he must not offer sacrifices to God.” A bleary-eyed man is one who sends out his intellect toward knowledge of the truth but obscures it by living carnally. There are some who can study the divine page well and would understand it well if they wished, but by devoting themselves to pleasures they obscure their intellect, and by living in filth they defile the light of their understanding.

He has a white spot in his eye who, although wise, places before the eye of his understanding a cloud of arrogance about his wisdom or justice. While he thinks he sees, he is blind and foolish, attributing to himself rather than to God what he knows. Or he has a blemish in his eye who, devoted to earthly rather than divine wisdom, thinks himself wise although he is foolish. Hence it is written: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

He has a persistent skin disease who does not repent of the other crimes by which he has been defiled.

All these, dearest brothers, the Lord commands to be removed from priestly office. But you who bear the name of priesthood, beware lest, because of all these defects, you be found unworthy of the dignity of your office.

## SERMON IV. TO THE PRIESTS

[Col. 0227D]

“The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

Listen, dearest brothers, to how great a treasure the Lord has entrusted to you and with how great a dignity of name he has honored you. He has handed over to you the treasure of knowledge and has called a human being an angel. Thus Malachi [ms. “Solomon”] says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge.” But because this is not commended to him for his own sake alone, but so that it may be spread to others—as he himself says, “What use are hidden wisdom and a hidden treasure?” (Ecclus. 20:32)—he therefore adds: “And people seek the law from his mouth.”

It is fitting that, because of his office, this should be imposed upon him: that others receive the words of the Lord from him, because he is “the angel of the Lord of hosts,” that is, the messenger and envoy of the Lord Sabaoth, that is, of the hosts—namely, of angels and the other orders.

You possess such great dignity that in the court of the heavenly King you are his intimates and know his counsels. Hence he says in the Gospel: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:14). He entrusts his commands to you so that you may tell them to others. You also possess such great intimacy with God that, through companionship and participation with him, you are called gods. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘You are gods’” (Ps. 82:6). And he says to Moses: “Regarding him who is to be brought to an oath, bring him to them,” that is, to the priests.

But what is the value of this honor and exaltation if you turn it into pride? Know this, all of you, my brothers: if you become proud, the very elevation will be your ruin, as it is written: “You cast them down while they were being exalted” (Ps. 73:18). He did not say, “You cast them down after they had been exalted,” but “while they were being exalted.” While they appear outwardly to rise, supported by temporal honor, inwardly they fall.

For this reason he says again: “Let them fade away as smoke fades away” (Ps. 68:2). Smoke, as it rises, diminishes and vanishes as it spreads. So it is with one who is exalted while he is proud: by the very thing through which he is shown to be high, he is brought to nonexistence.

And again: “My God, make them like a wheel” (Ps. 83:13). A wheel is lifted from its rear part and falls into higher places. Our rear parts are the goods of the present life, which we leave behind; the front parts are eternal and enduring things, toward which we are called. Paul testifies to this when he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13). The sinner, however, glories in the prosperity of present things; he is raised up by what is behind and falls forward into what is ahead—that is, into heavenly things.

There is another exaltation granted to you by God: he permits the Lord’s body to be handled and sanctified by you, and, through your blessing, his body to be made from bread. Great dignity! Great power! But see that this power does not become your condemnation. If you handle the Lord’s body unworthily, if you receive it unworthily, you will be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood, as the Apostle says: “Whoever eats”—and so forth (1 Cor. 11:27). “Let a person examine himself”—and so forth (ibid., 28). He commands that the examined person receive it: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11).

Therefore let there be no sexual excess and no impurity among you. We read that the priests of the old law, who were permitted to have wives, were commanded to remain in the temple during the year of their appointed service and to abstain from their wives, because it is written: “Be holy, for I am holy, I, the Lord your God” (Lev. 11:44). How much more, then, must those priests who have a priesthood without succession and serve continually preserve chastity from the day of their ordination? And since the Apostle says to laypeople, “Abstain for a time so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5), how much more must priests, whose continual duty is to pray and sacrifice, abstain continually from sexual excess?

One day David came, hungry, to the priest Ahimelech and said: “Give me something to eat.” He replied: “I do not have ordinary bread at hand, but only holy bread. Tell me: Are your young men clean from women?” He answered: “They have been so from yesterday and the day before yesterday, and the vessels of the young men have been holy.” Therefore the priest gave him the consecrated bread (1 Sam. 21:4–6).

If the priest asked whether they were clean from women on the day on which they were to receive the bread of the Presence, what ought priests to do continually because they are to receive the Lord’s body? But because you do not wish to receive it worthily, the Apostle says that these misfortunes occur: “That is why many among you are weak and sick” (1 Cor. 11:30), and so forth.

Therefore handle the Lord’s body with a clean vessel and a clean cloth, lest the Lord justly become angry at the unworthiness of his dwelling.

You must also, dearest brothers, provide for the relics, so that you may possess the remains of the saints with the greatest reverence. Hear what Gregory says concerning the presumption of handling and viewing relics:

“In the Roman regions and throughout the whole of the West, it is utterly intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone wishes to touch the bodies of the saints. If anyone should presume to do so, it is certain that this rashness will in no way go unpunished [al. ‘remain unpunished’]. For when someone wished to improve something concerning the most blessed body of Paul, because it was necessary to dig more deeply beside his tomb, the superior of that place found certain bones not actually joined to the same tomb. Since he presumed to lift them and place them elsewhere, he died a sudden death when certain signs appeared. Besides this, when Pelagius, the superior, similarly wished to improve something concerning the body of the blessed Laurence, while they were searching because it was not known where the saint’s body was, suddenly his tomb was opened without the knowledge—or, according to another reading, ignorantly—of those present. The monks who were present and laboring, and the keepers who saw the martyr’s body, all died within ten days.” (Gregory, Book III of the *Register*, Letter 30.)

Therefore, brothers, the relics of the saints must not be taken up or handled rashly.

You also act wrongly concerning penitents, because you do not investigate people’s sins, and, after investigating them, do not correct them or reveal them to us. But I tell you in the Spirit of God: I shall free my soul, but God will require it from your hand, because you consent. For Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0229D] Ambrosiaster, not Ambrose, in chapter 1 of the *Commentary on Romans*]: “To consent is not to rebuke when you are able.” The Apostle says: “Those who do such things deserve death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1:32).

Moreover, you do not dare to rebuke others because you yourselves do the same things repeatedly, as the Apostle says: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2:21–22).

But you say: “We suffer persecution; we endure wars; we see everything in disorder; we cannot guard the Lord’s flock.” Behold, you appear to be hirelings who flee when the wolf comes. Hear what the Lord admonishes: “Do not marvel if the world hates you” (1 John 3:13). “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. A servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:18–20).

What then, brothers, are you complaining about [f. “what are you seeking”]? Are you not members of Christ, who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life for his sheep? (Matt. 20:28; John 10:11.) “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5:10, 12).

Therefore do not be disturbed at all by such things, as Gregory says, because those who live after us will see worse times, so that, in comparison with their own time, they will consider us happy to have had such days [Note: [Col. 0230D] This is almost the same as Bernard, Letter 25 to Hugh, archbishop of Rouen.]. It is the greatest crown to be good among the wicked.

Hear what the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. 2:6). Job says: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). Paul says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15).

But some things must be endured with equanimity, while others must be corrected gently, as the Church says in the psalm: “Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 129:3), for burdens are carried on the back. “Sinners have built upon my back” when we patiently bear those whom we cannot correct.

I do not suppose that I am an Abel who has no Cain. If the good were without the wicked, they could not be perfect, because they would not be purified at all. The wicked are to the good what a furnace is to gold. Hence it is said: “And the elder shall serve the younger” (Rom. 9:12). Esau never served Jacob except by persecuting him; but while he persecuted him, he served him most, because he gave him a greater crown.

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not be terrified by persecutions, but labor and sweat to rescue the souls of the wretched from this tumult of the world, converting some to the contemplative life and others to the active life.

Imitate Jacob, who had two wives, Rachel and Leah—but first Leah, then Rachel. Leah was bleary-eyed, while Rachel was beautiful. He had many sons by Leah and few by Rachel. Jacob guarded Laban’s sheep, and Laban gave him animals of varied colors. Jacob took poplar rods and partly stripped them so that they were variegated, and placed them in the troughs where the water was poured out before the animals, so that, when they conceived, their offspring would resemble the rods. Thus there were more variegated animals than white or black ones, and Jacob’s flock became larger than Laban’s (Gen. 30).

This history looks toward you and shows what you ought to do. Laban is the devil; Jacob is any teacher of the Church [Col. 0230B], who feeds the sheep that the devil used to feed. The two daughters are the two lives. Rachel signifies the contemplative life, which is more beautiful; Leah signifies the active life, which gives birth to more children than the contemplative life.

Jacob stripped the rods, that is, the divine meanings, removing the allegorical sense from some [f. “the meaning”] but not from others. He is always laboring to make the devil’s children his own.

Therefore, dearest brothers, labor in the Lord’s flock, giving birth to some through the contemplative life and to others, who are married, through the active life, so that, after deceiving Laban—that is, the devil—you may return with a great multitude of sheep to the land of promise, where our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with the angels and saints, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. TO THE PRIESTS
Those who go down to the sea in ships, performing work upon many waters [Col. 0230C]; they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood, and its waves were lifted up. They rise up to the heavens and descend to the abysses; their soul melts away in troubles. They are troubled and stagger like a drunken man, and all their wisdom is swallowed up (Ps. 106:23–27).

The Lord, through David, complains, dearest brothers, about us priests, to whom he entrusted the governance of his Church and revealed his works and counsels, because we govern his ship badly and are not discerning either on the day of calm or on the day of storm. For he says:

The priests who descend from the height of their contemplation to the sea—that is, to endure the dangers of this world—placed in ships, that is, ordained to govern churches. For whoever assumes the care of governing condescends to God’s peoples and enters the sea, because the Church of God is surrounded by many waves of tribulations. And why they descend he adds: “performing work,” that is, for this purpose [Col. 0230D]—to perform work upon many waters, that is, among many peoples. Hence John says: “The many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15).

They ought to work because they are called workers, according to the saying: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few” (Matt. 9:37; Luke 10:2). They ought to work because, by the word of reproach, they must uproot vices from people’s minds and sow the seeds of virtues. They ought to work upon many waters because, by fishing people out of the depth of this age with the nets of the Lord’s commandments, they must rescue them; hence the Lord said to Peter and Andrew: “I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19).

And so that they might be able and know how to work wisely, the Lord revealed the Scriptures to them, for he says: “They have seen the works of the Lord.” They have seen in the Scriptures the works of the Lord: how he created all things, how by redeeming human beings he recreated them, and countless other works of his. They have also seen his wonders, that is, the hidden mysteries of God, such as the sacrament of the Lord’s body and of baptism, and all the other sacraments that have been revealed to the teachers of the Church but concealed from the rest of the people. These wonders are “in the deep,” because they are scarcely perceptible to the eyes of the heart.

You have heard, dearest brothers, how God entrusted the governance of his ship to priests, and with what purpose: namely, that they should work upon many waters. You have also heard how he instructs them, when he opens their understanding to comprehend the Scriptures. Understand, therefore, how they govern and how they conduct themselves in the office entrusted to them.

The Lord permits them to be tested by the storms of the adversary; and this is what he says, or implies: “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood, and its waves were lifted up.” The Lord spoke—that is, he willed it—and immediately the spirit of the storm, that is, the evil spirit who stirs up every storm in the Church of God, stood; that is, it raged against the rulers of the Church. And its waves, that is, diabolical temptations, were lifted up—that is, they were multiplied. For he tests the rulers of the Church both through prosperity and through adversity, both through their own circumstances and through those of their subjects.

But how will the rulers withstand this? “They rise up to the heavens and descend to the abysses, and their soul melts away in troubles.” Through great prosperity they rise to the heavens—that is, they are lifted up into excessive pride—and through great adversity they descend to the abysses—that is, they are cast down into despair. “And their soul melts away in troubles,” because, disturbed, it falls away from every good.

“For the hired man, and he who is not the shepherd, and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees” (John 10:12): not a shepherd, but a hired man, who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of inward love but for temporal wages. “He is a hired man who occupies the shepherd’s place but does not seek the profit of souls; he longs for earthly advantages and rejoices in the honor of pre-eminence” (St. Gregory, Homily 14 on the Gospels).

“The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep” (John 10:12) [Col. 0231C] when he drags one person into lust, inflames another with greed [ms. “ascends”], lifts another up in pride, and divides another through anger. He cannot stand in danger because he presides over the sheep not for the sake of the sheep but for profit, and therefore they tremble lest they lose what they love. The wolf seizes when someone oppresses the powerless [ms. “the powerful”], the poor, widows, and orphans.

The shepherd flees not by changing his place but by withdrawing his support. He flees because he sees injustice and remains silent. Therefore David says: “They are troubled and stagger like a drunken man, and all their wisdom is swallowed up.”

They are troubled because they do not know what ought to be done, like someone who is bewildered and shaken in a storm, concerning their poor subjects: they do not resist the rich but rebuke the poor. And because they conduct themselves rationally neither in prosperity nor in adversity, all their wisdom is swallowed up and destroyed, because it is empty and fruitless.

Thus the Lord describes us through the Psalmist. But what do we reply to these things? For Isaiah says: “As the people, so the priest; as the servant, so the master; as the maidservant, so her mistress” (Isa. 24:2). And Micah says: “The holy man has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings; all lie in wait for blood, each hunts his brother to death” (Mic. 7:2). We are more miserable than other people, because we both perish and cause others to perish.

For Moses says in Leviticus: “If the priest who has been anointed sins, he will cause the people to offend.” Who, indeed, is afraid to do what he sees his corrector doing? Therefore, when the Lord approached Jerusalem and, seeing the city, wept over it (Luke 19:41), he afterward entered the temple and drove out the buyers and sellers (ibid., 45), thereby showing that this was the greatest cause of the city’s destruction. And because we are the ruin of the people, the Lord says to us through Zechariah: “My fury is kindled against the shepherds” (Zech. 10:3).

A priest is the ruin of the people in two ways: by living badly and by governing without discretion. He governs without discretion when he produces either immoderate penance or things that ought to be neglected. Concerning immoderate penance, the Lord rebukes them, saying: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them even with a finger” (Matt. 23:4)—that is, they cannot observe even the least of those things that they command. Therefore the Apostle says: “If a person is overtaken in any offense” (Gal. 6:1), and so forth.

But concerning insufficient penance Augustine says:

“If someone has sinned against God, we are gentle and merciful in the matter of an injury to God; and we forgive God’s offense, as though it were within his power to will the injury or not to will it, with impunity and without the punishment of fitting penance. Yet, when something has been committed against us, we cannot allow even an insulting word to go unavenged, but exact vengeance according to the constitution of the holy Fathers and canonical authority.”

Do not therefore, brothers, be without discretion, lest it be said to you: “You are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, will they not both fall into a pit?” (Matt. 15:14.)

But so that you might have discretion, it was prefigured and indicated to you in Peter’s keys. For when the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to Peter, in Peter he gave them to all of you. There are two keys of the kingdom: power and discretion, so that we may bind and loose. But the person who is worthy is rightly bound and excommunicated if he is admonished repeatedly and is not corrected. Hence the Lord says: “If he will not listen to you or to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican” (Matt. 18:17). The person who is humbled by worthy satisfaction is rightly absolved.

Nor are you without discretion only with respect to your subjects, but also with respect to those belonging to others. For you accept another’s parishioners, over whom authority has not been given to you and concerning whom you are not to judge. Hence the Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls by his own master” (Rom. 14:4).

But if you see him in error, do what Moses commands: “If you see your brother’s ox or sheep wandering, you shall not pass by, but you shall lead it back to your brother” (Deut. 22:1). For you ought gently to admonish a parishioner belonging to another who is avoiding his own pastor and reconcile him to his pastor.

If you usurp authority, there is danger that you may incur the curse which Moses pronounced: “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary” (Deut. 27:17); and elsewhere: “You shall not take away or move your neighbor’s boundaries, which your predecessors fixed in your possession” (Deut. 19:14). For Pope Dionysius commands this (Dionysius, Letter 2 to Bishop Severus):

“We have assigned separate churches to separate priests and established a proper right for each, namely, that no one should invade the boundaries or right of another parish, but that each should be content with his own boundaries.”

Why, dearest brothers, must such great presumption be feared? Because many evils arise from it. Excommunicated people are often received through ignorance, and through this illicit conjugal unions come about. For when wicked men cannot marry in their own parish a woman who has been abducted, another man’s betrothed, or one who is forbidden to them, they flee to another parish and are illicitly blessed by the hand [Col. 0232D] of a foreign priest. But you gladly receive them for earthly profit and seek what is your own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21).

Many who have been suspended or degraded from office presume, at the devil’s instigation, to perform the divine office and, contrary to the Lord’s will, wish to minister after being forbidden by his vicars. Those who do this resist the Lord and are like Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who stood against Moses and Aaron and sought, by invasion, to rule the people of God. The earth swallowed them alive, together with their tents and possessions, and they descended alive into hell (Num. 16:32).

God severely avenges those who resist his vicar. Hence in the old law that sin was punished by death, for Moses says: “But the man who acts arrogantly and refuses to obey the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord shall die” (Deut. 17:12). In the Council of Toledo, however, they are ordered to be excommunicated, and if they refuse to be corrected, to be condemned to exile [Col. 0233A] (Toledo V, canon 5).

Concerning your carelessness and negligence in office, I have often admonished you to devote yourselves to reading and to learn what you ought to do and what you ought to preach. The Council of Orléans says of such men:

“Priests who do not know how to fulfill their ministry and do not strive, according to the commands of their bishops, to learn as far as they can, or who are contemptuous of the canons, are to be removed from their office until they have completely corrected these faults.”

For through ignorance of the Scriptures they err and cause God’s people to err, and they incur the curse pronounced by Moses: “Cursed is he who makes the blind man go astray on the road” (Deut. 27:18).

I have also often commanded you concerning the diminution of your titular churches, that no one should diminish them or permit them to be diminished. In the canons the following judgment is found concerning such a fault:

“Whoever, in any way, attempts to alienate in perpetuity from the right of his titular church gold, silver, gems, vestments, or any other movable goods given for divine adornment, whether as alienator or seller, shall be punished by the loss of his rank.”

What need is there to speak to you about each matter individually? You must be watchful in many things, because you are the eye of the Church: admonish the people of God to abstain from vices; rebuke public sinners; invite them to penance; treat the penitent in a spirit of gentleness; and admonish all who have not been confirmed to come for confirmation, because otherwise they are not yet complete. Baptism is given for the remission of sins, while the laying on of hands is given for the bestowal of virtues.

May God, whose vicars you are, who has given you judgment so that what you confirm in the world may be confirmed in heaven, himself govern and strengthen you in the office entrusted to you, so that you may present the flock entrusted or subjected to you to Christ when he comes. He lives and reigns forever, and so forth.

## SERMON VI. ON THE PRIEST

[Col. 0233C] “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars; and he placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. God also said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having a living soul, and the flying creature over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven” (Gen. 1:16–20).

Thus God willed, dearest brothers, to make the creatures of the world so that, at the beginning of creation, he might signify some mystery to us. Let us see what has been prefigured for us in the lights, in day and night, in the firmament, and in the earth, and let us imitate whatever in them is to be imitated. For this figure concerns us, brothers, because we are those lights of the firmament.

What is the firmament except Scripture, upon which the Church has been established? What are the lights of the firmament except the pastors of the Church, who illuminate it by explaining it to others? When you explain the Gospel, what else are you doing except clarifying the firmament of heaven—that is, Scripture?

There are two lights, the greater and the lesser, namely, the wiser and the less wise. Day likewise signifies the wise, and night the foolish. The greater light rules the day because wiser teachers instruct those who are more capable. What is Augustine except the sun in the Church? To whom does he speak except to the wise?

But you, priests who know less, are the lesser light. You rule the night because you rule the laypeople, who are ignorant of Scripture and move about in the darkness of ignorance. Yet whatever light you are, you are nevertheless light. “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14); “in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation shine as lights” (Phil. 2:15).

The other clerics who do not have authority over God’s people are called stars. Although they may not be able to shine through teaching, they nevertheless shine by their conduct over the earth, that is, over the Church.

The lights divide light and darkness because preachers discern the capacity of individuals, preaching humble things to the carnal and profound things to the spiritual.

It follows: “God also said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having a living soul [Col. 0234A] and the flying creature over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.”

After prefiguring the pastors of the Church, on the following day he demonstrated the duty of their offices [Hic. perhaps an addition: “the duty”]. For he created fish and birds from the waters. By the waters baptism is understood; by fish and birds, two kinds of faithful people regenerated through baptism are signified.

Some love worldly things and follow the broad roads of this world; these are called fish, concerning whom David says: “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass along the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:8). The sea is the world; the paths of the sea are the broad roads of this world. Others are birds, that is, flying toward heavenly things on the wings of virtues.

Both kinds of people are found regenerated in the sacrament of baptism; therefore fish and birds were created from the waters. To you, brothers, the ministry of regeneration has been entrusted: you beget children for God.

In this generation, the Holy Spirit is the Father and the water is the mother. Hence the Lord said to Nicodemus: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” [Col. 0234B] (John 3:5).

The first generation, from a carnal father, makes people carnal; the second, from the Spirit, makes them spiritual. Hence he says to Nicodemus: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit” (ibid., 6)—that is, from flesh come the carnal, and from spirit the spiritual.

Just as people are born carnally in order to enter the world, so they are born spiritually in order to enter heaven. Hence he says: “For otherwise he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

You are the ministers of this entrance; you make children of the devil into children of God. Behold, the gate of heaven has been handed over to you, since the water of baptism has been entrusted to you. But beware lest you be like the water of baptism: water washes away sins and afterward descends into foul places. Likewise, a wicked priest saves people through his office, but through his wickedness he deserves to fall into hell.

Furthermore, brothers, the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been handed over to you. For what is said to the apostles is said to you: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” [Col. 0234C] (Matt. 18:18).

There are two keys: one for closing and one for opening. The power of binding is one key, and the power of loosing is the other. One opens to penitents; the other removes access from the obstinate.

But it must be feared that you, who are doorkeepers of heaven, after admitting others may yourselves be unable to enter. Office does not arise from merit, nor merit from office. Many enter who do not possess the keys, and many possess the keys who do not enter. Alas! The sheep enter, and the shepherds are cast out.

When the Lord had driven the sellers and buyers out of the temple, the blind and the lame approached him, and he healed them (Matt. 21). Because he had driven unworthy priests out of his house, he receives and heals the blind in knowledge and the lame in action—that is, many sinners ignorant of God’s law—when they approach the temple through penance; while he often converts simple laypeople through inward inspiration and permits the wise, once liberated, to become blind.

And although they ought to be the eyes of doves, they become the eyes of ravens. Christ says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like doves” (Song 4:1).

Who are the eyes of the Church except its pastors? They are eyes because they ought to provide for those below them; they are compared to doves because they ought to be simple and innocent. These are the ones of whom it is said: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8.)

For you are clouds, who ought to rain upon others; you ought to fly toward heavenly things so that, by your example, you may show the way that you preach by your word. And although you are in a high place, you ought, like doves, to keep watch lest the hawk come. The windows are the Scriptures, through which you see God and through which you provide for the sheep.

You are light, eye, and salt. Light, so that you may shine; hence: “Let your light shine before human beings” (Matt. 5:16). Eye, so that you may provide care; hence it was said to Ezekiel: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). Salt, so that you may season your preaching [Col. 0235A] and destroy the worms of sins.

These three things are necessary for you: the light of good conduct, the eye of good discretion, and the salt of preaching and correction.

Concerning those who preach well and act badly, the Lord says: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works; for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). These are indeed light.

There are others who lack the eye of discretion. They do not discern sins and penances, or who ought to be bound and who ought to be absolved. Concerning them the Lord says through Ezekiel: “My priests have despised my law and polluted my sanctuaries; they have made no distinction between the holy and the profane, and they have not understood between the polluted and the clean” (Ezek. 22:26).

There are still others who do not know how to preach, concerning whom it is said: “Mute dogs, unable—or not knowing how—to bark” (Isa. 56:10).

If he does not have the eye of discretion, he looses and binds unworthily. If he is not salt, he is a dog around the Lord’s flock, but he does not drive away the wolf by the barking of preaching. If he is not light, he leads others in but does not enter himself.

All these things, therefore, are necessary for you together, brothers. If one of them is lacking, you guard the Lord’s flock dangerously [Col. 0236A]. For if you are not light, you handle the Lord’s body at your peril and are unworthy of your office. If you lack the eye of discretion, then the blind will lead the blind, and both will fall into a pit (Matt. 15:14). If you do not have the salt of preaching, then the Lord’s people will be hungry and will fail on the way. This is extremely dangerous for you, since the Lord says: “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they fail on the way” (ibid., v. 32).

Consider, therefore, your burden. The prophet Hosea cries out to you: “Hear this, priests, and pay attention, house of Israel, for judgment is against you” (Hos. 5:1). He then indicates why judgment awaits them: “Because you have become a snare for Zion and a net spread out” (ibid.), as though he were saying: You who ought to release others entangle them by your bad example.

Consider, therefore, what you are. You see to what ministry in the house of God you have been ordained. God has entrusted his money to you until he returns, saying: “Engage in trade until I come” (Luke 19:13).

May God, who said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), preserve his shepherds and his flocks, so that he may lead them into the heavenly Jerusalem, where there are peace, joy, and life. He lives and reigns, and so forth.

[Col. 0235]

## ON THE EXPOSITION OF BAPTISM AND THE EUCHARIST

[Col. 0235B] From the same Bigotian manuscript codex.) 488

Finally, it must be known that Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, Isidore, Hilary, Maximian, Innocent, and Gelasius firmly believe and define that baptism, the Eucharist, and chrism are neither increased by good priests nor diminished by bad ones.

But blessed Jerome, urging priests toward a holy and pure life, says with the same faith, although, as some think, in different words, in his *Exposition of the Twelve Prophets*, that it is life, and not words, that makes the Eucharist. This must be understood and piously interpreted in complete agreement with the other holy Fathers.

For almighty God, through the faith and solemn words of the priest, even if he is a sinner, changes the substance of bread and wine into the true substance of the flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But if the priest is pure, chaste, and devout, he causes the Eucharist to benefit, through his good life and prayers, both the priest who consecrates it and the person who receives it. The Eucharist itself is complete and perfect in itself, that is, from almighty God. That is, through the words and faith of the priest and the faith of those standing by, it is the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the Lord’s sacrament is holy and true in itself through the solemn words and faith, as has been said.

But if the priest carries out through good works what he believes and handles, he causes the Eucharist to benefit him and those who receive it for salvation. For the divine word is added and makes the sacrament (Augustine, *Tractate 80 on John*); it makes it, I say, in the sense that the good life of those who consecrate it obtains from God that it may benefit them when they receive it.

## APPENDIX TO THE OLD ACTS

[Col. 0235]

## SYNODAL CONSTITUTIONS

Issued and published by the reverend Father in Christ and lord, Lord Louis de Canossa, by the grace of God and of the Holy Apostolic See bishop of Bayeux, in his summer synod solemnly celebrated at Bayeux in the year of the Lord 1518, on 13 April, after Easter.

[Col. 0235C] The following statutes were promulgated in the summer synod in the year of the Lord 1515, on 17 April, by our immediate predecessor of good memory.

### I.

Following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we establish and ordain that the ecclesiastical men of our diocese of Bayeux, under penalty of a discretionary fine, are to wear decent clothing, neither marked by excessive length nor excessive shortness, but honest, suitable to their status, and respectable, both in churches and outside them. They are to be provided with the proper tonsure, under no circumstances grow their hair long, and go about with their ears uncovered.

### II.

Likewise, they are in no way to involve themselves in secular business contrary to the ecclesiastical state. Nor are they publicly to conduct commercial transactions for profit by buying or selling; nor are they to be lessees or lessors, renters, or *affirmatores* [probably leaseholders] of lands, especially lands belonging to laypeople; nor are they to act as agents in their secular estates and courts, or as receivers—especially those who hold benefices and those who have care of souls. We command such men to reside in the places of their benefices, as will be stated below. Nor are they to dare to involve themselves in royal taxes or subsidies by dictating or writing rolls, making collections, or interfering in them in any other way.

### III.

Likewise, they are not to keep in their residences women concerning whom some suspicion might arise, with scandal; nor are they to permit sons possibly begotten from illicit intercourse to serve them in churches or in divine offices.

### IV.

Moreover, under penalty at our discretion, they must beware of daring in any way to create insolence, disturbance, or scandal during the services for the dead. Nor are they to intrude upon or appear at such services in order to celebrate special Masses unless they have been specifically summoned and invited by the relatives, friends, or executors of the deceased [Col. 0237A].

### V.

Likewise, they are not at all to wear caps while officiating in churches, but are to have decent hoods. They are entirely to abandon disordered clothing in color and style, and are not to dare enter taverns to pursue feasting and drunkenness, except in a case of necessity as travelers. They may nevertheless send for drink to be sought for their needs in those same taverns.

### VI.

We further prohibit the rectors of the churches of this diocese and their vicars from keeping taverns in presbyteral houses, or having or permitting them to be kept there in any way. Nor are they to admit ecclesiastical men unknown to them to perform the sacred priestly office in their churches without a special license from us and our officials, even if those men are religious, unless they have letters from their superiors [Col. 0237B] of obedience and stating how they were sent by their superiors.

### VII.

Likewise, they are to strive to know the cases reserved to us, lest they deceive their parishioners by absolving them from those cases. They are also to ensure that, before the coming feast of Pentecost, they possess their own, not borrowed, copies of the *Manipulus curatorum* together with the present synodal statutes. At our Kalends, which are to be celebrated each year, they are to exhibit to our promoter the registers of excommunicated persons in their parishes and of wills passed before them, which they are required to make according to the synodal statutes issued both by us and by our predecessors. They are to appear personally at our synods and Kalends in decent clothing and surplices, unless prevented by a legitimate impediment.

### VIII.

Likewise, they are to minister divine services and ecclesiastical sacraments to their parishioners with due honor, seriousness, and reverence, and are not to attend clandestine betrothals. In the event that people are suddenly or accidentally killed or die, they are not to presume to bury them without our permission or that of our aforementioned officials.

### IX.

Likewise, ecclesiastical vessels and ornaments appointed and assigned for divine worship and service are to be kept clean and bright, polluted by no stains or dirt.

### X.

Moreover, because the vice of falsity has in these days multiplied in many ways—and, alas, has taken root—for certain people, using false names, obtain against others binding instruments, releases, memoranda, and mandates, and fraudulently have them passed so that they may keep others bound to them and evade those to whom they are obligated, and so that their own releases may, by carefully sought means, be falsely extorted and obtained. At times others use false and counterfeit seals, in fact excommunicating and almost absolving their neighbors and deceiving themselves. Still others devise various other forms of falsity and, as far as lies within them, bring them to their condemned result.

Therefore, desiring as far as we can to oppose this pestilential disease, we establish that from now on no ecclesiastical or secular person, of whatever condition or status, shall dare or presume fraudulently or deceitfully to commit such vices of falsity, or any others whatsoever, or knowingly to provide aid, counsel, or favor to those who commit them.

If anything contrary is thereafter attempted or presumed by anyone, we decree that the wrongdoers be punished with a grave penalty established for the aforesaid offenses. We charge the deans and priests subject to us to notify us, or our officials or promoters, as soon as possible, of whatever they know concerning the aforesaid matters. Otherwise we shall punish them with a similar and more severe penalty.

### XI.

Furthermore, we command all and each of the aforesaid curates of our diocese of Bayeux to reside personally in the places of their benefices [Col. 0238A], unless, where a legitimate cause exists, we or our vicars should decide to dispense them, and especially those residing in our diocese of Bayeux.

### XII.

We further enjoin, under penalty of a discretionary fine, all and each of the priests of our diocese of Bayeux not to presume to approach the altar to celebrate Mass unless they have first prepared for the Mass and possess everything necessary for its performance: namely, bread, wine, book, chalice, ecclesiastical ornaments, fire, and a cleric to answer the priest celebrating the Mass.

### XIII.

Finally and definitively, we command, establish, and enjoin upon all and each of our rural deans that, with every diligence, for the relief of our subjects, they make and report without delay or any excuse investigations concerning the crimes and offenses of anyone, and execute and cause our mandates to be executed without delay [Col. 0238B]. They are to report to our officials what has been executed and reported, under a monetary penalty and a discretionary fine for each defect—God forbid—that they commit in the foregoing matters. If they are found negligent and remiss in these matters, we wish them to be punished and corrected with a more severe penalty. The other synodal statutes and ordinances previously issued by our predecessors are to remain in force; through the tenor of these present provisions we renew them and wish them to retain their authority.

We have judged that these same statutes, renewing them, should be declared, and that several others should be added to them. First:

### XIV.

Concerning the excessive length or shortness of the clothing of ecclesiastical men, we declare that before the forthcoming feast of All Saints, their longer tunics are to extend as far as the ankles and no farther, while the shorter ones are to extend below mid-calf. Each day they are to wear a hood, a black-cloth *domino*, or a “cornet” [*corneta*]. With the cap and cornet removed, especially while officiating in church [Col. 0238C], they are thereafter to use, under penalty of a discretionary fine, the hood customarily called a *domino*, along with other clerical insignia.

### XV.

We further establish that no cleric of our diocese of Bayeux in future times is to be received or permitted to be promoted to the sacred order of subdeacon or to higher orders by virtue of a title assigned in any manner by parents or friends, unless first the person assigning the title and the cleric to whom it is assigned have appeared personally before our officials in court and, by their respective oaths, asserted the following.

The assignor of the title must assert that he intends to pay, and will in fact and without fraud pay annually to that cleric a sufficient sum, to which he will bind himself. The cleric in question must assert that he will effectively collect the sum assigned to him and in no way alienate or remit it, unless perhaps it should happen that the cleric is provided with a benefice of sufficient value. Even then he may not do so except with our license and permission; in our absence, he must proceed judicially before our officials, as stated above.

The person assigning the title and the person receiving it must also assert that they have not made, and will not make, any simoniacal or otherwise illicit agreement concerning the foregoing matters.

Nevertheless, we command that a proper investigation be made by our deans concerning the assignment of the said title and the other matters customarily investigated. For faithfully reporting this, they are to receive from those receiving titles the sum of only twenty-five Tournois sous, inclusive of everything. Otherwise, we decree that such a title, if assigned less than [or otherwise than] properly, shall lack force.

### XVI.

And because the law provides: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh” (Jerome, *Letter to the monk Rusticus, On the Form of the Spiritual Life*), therefore, desiring to provide as far as lies within us, we enjoin upon all clerics, especially curates and vicars serving in churches, that they frequently devote themselves to learning and purchase for themselves the treatise called *Fillon*, and the *Manipulus curatorum* [Col. 0239A], as well as the synodal precepts issued by our predecessors, within the next two months. They are to instruct themselves in these works under penalty of excommunication.

### XVII.

We further establish that clerics in sacred orders are not to play publicly or remove their clothing; nor are they to attend forbidden games. Rather, as far as they can, they are to draw laypeople away from every crime. They are not to attend to jesters and actors, and are to keep themselves entirely apart from dances. If anyone shows himself culpable in these matters, he shall be suspended from office and condemned to another penalty at our discretion.

### XVIII

We also prohibit our rural deans, under penalty of deprivation of their office, from daring to shelter or conceal—especially when he is a public and notorious offender in his sin—a criminal of whatever rank, status, or condition he may be, [f. conscii]. Rather, after first making a preliminary inquiry, they shall take care to disclose the matter promptly, so that, according to the circumstances of the case, the offenders may be restrained [Col. 0239B]. Otherwise, if they are found negligent and culpable in this matter, they shall be severely punished in addition to deprivation of their office. Let them take good note of this.

### XIX

From the decrees of our holy Fathers it is clear that we cannot please God without faith. And because it has come to our ears that very many of the people of our diocese of Bayeux are insufficiently instructed in the Catholic faith [8], wishing to provide a salutary remedy, we decree that henceforth each parish priest, or his vicar, shall have the Lord’s Prayer, *Our Father*, and both Creeds recited distinctly, in a loud and intelligible voice, on Sundays in the church porch before the parish Masses, so that the ignorant, the uneducated, and the weak may learn and retain them, and may not be ashamed at least explicitly to believe.

### XX

By the authority and decree of the reverend Father in Christ and lord, the lord bishop of Bayeux, all and each of the parish priests of the diocese of Bayeux are enjoined and strictly commanded to establish personal and continuous residence in their benefices within the next three months. For those temporarily dispensed from the obligation of residence, this period shall nevertheless be reckoned from the date on which their dispensation expires. Otherwise, once that period has elapsed, proceedings shall be taken according to law against non-residents, both by withholding their revenues and, if necessary, by depriving them of their benefices [Col. 0240A].

### XXI

Likewise, all and each of the parish priests of the said diocese and their vicars are prohibited from permitting any priests—even those promoted in another diocese, or in the Roman Curia itself—to celebrate the divine offices in their parishes unless they have obtained from the same lord bishop or his officials permission to celebrate in this regard, and have produced written evidence of it, under penalty of an arbitrary fine.

### XXII

Likewise, all and each of the rural deans of the said diocese are enjoined to warn all and each of the patrons of curial benefices in their deaneries, both ecclesiastical [Col. 0240B] and lay, that henceforth, whenever they present one or more persons to the same lord bishop for benefices subject to their presentation, they must send their nominee in person to request a letter of collation or institution, since henceforth no one shall obtain collation of a curial benefice through a procurator [9].

### XXIII

Likewise, the same parish priests are enjoined diligently to observe the synodal statutes previously issued and promulgated both by the same lord bishop and by his predecessors; and each of them shall keep with him a booklet called *Fillon*, or *The Mirror of Parish Priests*, as well as another book recently printed by the authority of the same lord, entitled *L’Instruction des curés*. They shall exhibit these booklets to the promoter of the same lord bishop on the Kalends, under penalty of an arbitrary fine.

[Col. 0239]

# STATUTES OF THE SUMMER SYNOD OF THE DIOCESE OF ÉVREUX

For the year of Our Lord 1576, by the Reverend Father Claudius de Saintes, its bishop.

To the most illustrious prince, Cardinal A. Bourbon, Archbishop of Rouen.

[Col. 0239C]

We are eagerly awaiting, most illustrious prince, your provincial synod, which may restore in our churches the piety and ecclesiastical discipline that have collapsed through the adversity of the times [10], and may at least fortify us against the unbridled freedom of the heretics through the fullest unity of faith and spirit. Meanwhile, as the day of the diocesan synod—which will be the first we shall hold—was approaching, and since we did not wish to appear to have accomplished nothing, we drew up certain statutes that we judged necessary, or at least beneficial, for our churches, provided that our people submit them to execution as willingly as they were written by us.

But since we clearly understood that this latter matter depended, after God, on your authority, not on ours, we took care, before proposing them to the clergy, to send them to Your Eminence, so that only those provisions which your archiepiscopal judgment and authority confirmed might come to light [Col. 0239D], leaving no room for anyone to accuse us. They are indeed somewhat lengthy, but subsequent ones will be shorter. Nor was it fitting for us at the outset to issue commands and statutes without instruction, lest we should seem to compel our people rather than teach and guide them. The provincial synod will refine the more serious and effective measures. For its convocation and successful completion, I pray our Savior Jesus Christ to grant your piety good health [Col. 0240C] and some release from the affairs of the commonwealth.

From our diocese, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, 1576.

The most humble ambassador of Your Eminence among your suffragans,  
Claudius, Bishop of Évreux.

# TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

[11] On the provision of benefices, especially curial benefices. On the residence of parish priests. On the life and propriety of parish priests and other ecclesiastics. On the office of parish priests and vicars. On the duty of the people. On the sentence of excommunication to be imposed. On schools and their teachers. On preachers. On the provision and reform of breviaries and other ecclesiastical books for the diocese of Évreux. [Col. 0240D] On rural deans. The privilege of Pope Urban, by which the bishop of Évreux may compel his subjects to receive orders and reside. The letter of Pope Gregory X on the same matter.

Claudius de Saintes, by the grace of God and of the Holy Apostolic See bishop of Évreux, sends greeting in the Lord to all and each of the rectors and curates of parish churches, and to the other ecclesiastical men subject to us [Col. 0241A].

Although human statutes vary according to the changing times, we nevertheless command you to observe and preserve, wholly and inviolably, all and each of the statutes and synodal constitutions made and issued by our predecessors, especially those not revoked by their superiors, under the penalties contained in them.

# On the Provision of Beneficed Persons, Especially Parish Priests

[12]

### I

The first and chief concern in religion ought to be for the rectors of churches, since without them, as the Apostle testifies, the people go astray and are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14), and are exposed to the attacks of wolves, like sheep without a suitable shepherd. Yet the cry to heaven is raised because almost no benefice is now provided to a capable man; rather, any man at random is provided with any benefice, and more often by illicit means [Col. 0241B].

In our diocese we have found that offences are committed in many ways, but especially through simony, or through the retention of revenues when the title has been entrusted to another for safekeeping. To begin remedying these and other evils, we warn all who have obtained an ecclesiastical benefice through simony, whether by explicit or tacit purchase and sale, or by exchange of land or any other temporal thing, that they live perpetually in mortal sin and under continuous excommunication; that no one except the supreme pontiff can absolve them, except at the point of death; and that they cannot obtain absolution unless they relinquish the benefice so obtained, or secure a new provision for the same benefice after absolution.

Meanwhile, whenever they celebrate or receive the most holy Eucharist, they eat and drink judgment upon themselves [Col. 0241C] (1 Corinthians 11:29), and store up wrath and punishments for themselves on the day of God’s just judgment (Romans 2:5). God himself frequently makes this manifest against them even in this world, either by uprooting the houses and families of sellers and buyers [13] through sudden calamities, or by removing from life through premature or sudden death those promoted in this manner, as experience permits us to observe.

Those who give a benefice into safekeeping, and those who accept it, we warn to be subject to the penalties contained in the bull of Pope Pius IV, and confirmed by his most holy successors, Pius V and Gregory XIII. These penalties are such that benefices entrusted, explicitly or secretly, in confidence or for safekeeping, become vacant by the law itself in the Roman Curia; those receiving the revenues do not make them their own but, in both courts, including their heirs, are bound to restitution; and those accepting the title of benefices under such an agreement incur, by that very fact, the penalty of major excommunication *latae sententiae* [Col. 0241D], from which they cannot be absolved except by the Roman pontiff, apart from the moment of death.

### II

Lest the gravity of either sin—simony and the safekeeping of a benefice—be unknown to our parish priests or go unconsidered, we decree that neither we nor our vicars general shall issue a grant of collation to anyone presented and nominated to a parish church unless he first appears in person before us or them, so that he may be questioned about the manner and circumstances by which he obtained the benefice, and this statute of ours may be read to him and, if necessary, explained.

Under threat of divine judgment, both in this age and in the future, an oath shall be required from him as to whether any stain of simony, or any agreement reserving the revenues under the title of having received the parish church for safekeeping, played a part in his provision.

### III

We further decree that, before he seeks collation [14], he must bring a proper testimonial, through the dean or parish priest—or the vicar of the parish in which he lives [Col. 0242A]—concerning his religion, life, morals, and learning, stating where and in what reputation he has lived during the past ten years. He shall also be examined by us or by our vicars on these matters. Finally, he shall make a confession of the Catholic, or Roman, faith according to the formula already customary in our diocese.

### IV

Furthermore, for the cleansing of these two sins, which offend and injure the whole Church, we wish all confessors, in the very sacrament of absolution, to question adults, both ecclesiastical and secular, especially whenever there appears to be suspicion that they themselves are conscious of either of these sins, or know others to be guilty of them. They shall declare the penalties imposed by the sacred canons and pontiffs.

We prohibit anyone from usurping an absolution not granted to him in dealing with those infected by such sins. As for those who merely know others to be infected with either sin, they shall administer absolution so as to require them, after they themselves have made fraternal correction, to disclose outside confession to us or to the local dean those who retain benefices thus unjustly acquired, so that we may apply a remedy [Col. 0242B].

# On the Residence of Parish Priests

### I

The rectors of churches ought always to discharge their office and care for their sheep, as though they were to render an account to God for each of their souls. They must, however, be far more circumspect and vigilant in every respect at this time, when Satan appears in France to have desired not only the churches but every individual person, in order to sift them like wheat [15] (Luke 22:31), and to have received full power to sow weeds everywhere.

Therefore, first we exhort and command in the Lord all rectors of parish churches in our diocese that, from the day of this synod and within two months, they reside with their flock more faithfully than before and be assiduous, lest, if they now flee or remain absent [Col. 0242C] when they see the wolf coming, they should show themselves mercenaries rather than shepherds who lay down their lives for their sheep.

### II

Lest anyone despise or neglect this statute as proceeding merely from our humility or from some other human invention, let him know that, after a long debate among the most distinguished bishops and teachers of the entire Christian world, it was agreed and declared in the Council of Trent that the residence of shepherds in bishoprics and smaller parishes is required by divine law. Those who transgress it commit mortal sin and do not make the revenues of their benefices their own; rather, they are bound to restore those revenues, which ecclesiastical superiors ought to distribute to the fabric of the churches or to the poor of the place. The obstinate may be compelled by ecclesiastical censures and other remedies of law, even to deprivation.

Confessors ought to warn non-resident parish priests of these matters, and absolution ought not to be granted to them in the court of conscience without an obligation to make satisfaction [Col. 0242D].

### III

We believe that formerly, especially in our diocese of Évreux, there was prolonged and extensive inquiry and litigation concerning which persons the bishop could judge to be dispensed from residence. It was therefore necessary more than once for our predecessors to consult the Apostolic See at Rome on the matter [16]. Through the popes Urban and Gregory X, of blessed memory, it replied that only those were exempt from residence who, by the very fact, served the universal Church in the Roman Curia, as is contained in their bulls sent to the bishops of Évreux. These are preserved in our archives, and we have had a copy of them transcribed at the end of these statutes.

In our own age, after the Council of Trent, not even the most holy Roman pontiffs Pius IV, Pius V, and Gregory XIII saw fit to exempt such persons. Instead, they either drove bishops—including cardinals—and parish priests from the Curia and the Roman Church into residence, or compelled them to surrender their benefices, and established the gravest penalties for non-residents [Col. 0243A], notwithstanding any privilege or custom.

We have judged that all these matters must be brought to the attention of each parish priest of our diocese at the present synod, to relieve our conscience, lest they seek excuses in their sins or suppose that it lies within our power or anyone else’s to release them, on any pretext, from the duty of residence—not only before God and in conscience, but even in whatever forum of the Church—especially at this unhappy and dangerous time, when the wolves do not spare the flock.

### IV

We know that what is chiefly required in the residence of parish priests is personal industry and diligence, rather than bodily presence and inactivity in one place. Among those who should be counted resident are rather those who, though bodily absent, watch over their flock in spirit and with constant attention than those who, though bodily present, feed themselves rather than the flock, to whose scandal they become a cause.

Nevertheless, in Moses, the faithful servant of God, and in other exceptionally vigilant shepherds, it has always been found that their prolonged bodily absence brought some great harm upon their sheep [17] [Col. 0243B]. Therefore we decree that, outside the period of absence granted to parish priests by the Council of Trent (Session 23, *On Reform*, chapter 1), if a parish priest does not perform the divine office in his parish on one of three consecutive Sundays, or at least does not attend it himself, he shall be reckoned as non-resident.

For if a layman is marked as a deserter of his church and subjected to excommunication when he fails to attend the more solemn Mass on any one of three Sundays, how much more justly should a parish priest be considered non-resident when he has deserted his church for so long a period?

### V
