If, because of illness, evident danger, or some new necessity, a parish priest cannot present himself at his church during that period, he shall be required to have the vicar publish the reason in the church porch at the principal Mass and warn the parishioners that, if they know it to be false or fabricated, they should announce this publicly before the Church, or report it privately to the dean [Col. 0243C], or to their churchwardens, so that it may be recorded in writing whenever the parish priest has wished to impose upon the Church how long, or how often on Sunday, he has been absent from it.

We also wish the rural deans to draw up a register of parish priests who are non-resident or absent at the proper time and to report it faithfully to us, under penalty of perjury against the oath they will swear to us.

### VI

Since there are persons who, through litigation and appeals to higher authority, defraud the sanctions concerning residence and the holding of multiple benefices, it seems equitable that anyone who receives the revenues of a parish church and enjoys possession of it should remain bound to the duty of residence while the litigation is pending.

### VII

We do not ignore that the penalties and fines established and customarily imposed against non-residents in our diocese [18] are applied to relieving the burdens of our episcopate, and that for this reason a large number of non-residents would be more advantageous to us. Nevertheless, we again ask and exhort in the Lord all parish priests [Col. 0243D] that they should rather deprive us of the fines due than place their flock’s presence and their own salvation below our interests.

Let them think instead of the more serious penalties that threaten transgressors of divine and natural law. Let them think, I say, that they live in perpetual mortal sin so long as they violate the divine command concerning the residence of shepherds. Let them think that, under both laws, a benefice is not owed to them except on account of its office, and therefore that they do not make its revenues their own if they have not performed their ministry, as the Council of Trent declared (Session 6, *On Reform*, chapter 1).

### VIII

For some, it is not enough unjustly to retain a benefice without performing any office. As though they wished to leave nothing undone that belongs to a thief and robber, they come to their parishes only at harvest or at the collection of revenues; after suddenly plundering and carrying these away, they flee and remain absent for the whole rest of the year, sometimes leaving no vicar at all.

Others hire wandering and disgraceful priests to perform ecclesiastical ministries during their absence, or even while they are present [Col. 0244A], or lease their priestly offices to such men on unworthy terms. From this arise innumerable and abominable scandals.

To remedy them, we decree, following our predecessors, that no one shall be received and recognized by the parishioners as vicar unless he has obtained from us at least once a year a letter of appointment certifying that he has done nothing unworthy during the entire year, for which he might be barred from the ministry.

We command the deans to inspect, from the day of this synod onward, the leases made to vicars or others of parish churches [19], lest they contain disgraceful or illicit conditions, and to arrange for a copy of each to be sent to us.

If in any place they find that no lease of the benefice has been made, but only that a priest has been hired to perform the function of vicar, we command them to establish a suitable vicar, in accordance with the Council of Trent (Session 6, *On Reform*, chapter 2), and faithfully entrust the revenues of the benefice to him, assigning him a portion of them, so that the care of souls may in no way be neglected and the benefices themselves may not be deprived of their due services, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal [Col. 0244B].

### IX

We hear—and have also observed during our visitation—that in our diocese several persons hold not merely two, but three or four benefices, both secular and regular, indiscriminately and without distinction.

As the Council of Trent enjoins us to remedy this abuse (Session 7, chapter 5), we command each beneficed person to present to us, before the next synod, his provisions and dispensations for examination and approval. Otherwise, we shall proceed according to the constitution of Gregory X, issued at the Council of Lyons against this abuse and renewed by the Council of Trent.

# On the Life and Propriety of Parish Priests and Other Ecclesiastics

### I

Although faith and truth ought not to be judged by morals, but morals rather by faith, nevertheless the religion and teaching of those whose life is despised are easily despised. On account of the corrupt life of ecclesiastics, our adversaries have alienated many from the Catholic Church and drawn them after themselves, rather than through any appearance of piety or truth.

Therefore, so that those who oppose us [20] may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us (Titus 2:2), we pray in the Lord not only for parish priests but for all ecclesiastics, that their integrity and purity may shine before men, who may see their good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16), and that those who have gone astray may not be ashamed to return to the way and to the bosom of the Church.

Above all, let all ecclesiastics beware of those vices by which God is especially provoked, his name is blasphemed among the nations (Romans 2:24), and the Church of God is afflicted. These are unchastity and violent greed, when piety or religion seems to be regarded as nothing but profit.

Because of these things the wrath of God came upon the sons of the high priest Eli and upon the ark of the Lord itself (1 Samuel 4). Therefore, especially let all parish priests live at home in such a way that they avoid not only the crime of unchastity but even suspicion of that crime. Let them keep no women in their homes concerning whom evil suspicion could be spread.

Let their conduct be free from greed; for every service, let them be content with what either the law itself or commendable custom has established for them. Let them not demand what is owed to them with excessive eagerness or inhumanity, and in all things let them take account of the poorer people.

We know that words and warnings have no effect upon those whom these vices have rendered senseless and blind. The priest Eli, chosen by God, did not save his soul by daily reproving his sons for these vices, but miserably perished with them, because he corrected them by word alone and not by deed.

Therefore, to free our soul from blame in this matter, we declare to all ecclesiastical men of our diocese that, unless from the day of this synod they remove from themselves any women whom they keep under suspicion, cease from unchastity, and stop trading in and selling sacred things [Col. 0245A], we shall proceed against those apprehended up to deprivation of their benefices and other penalties appropriate to their scandal, obstinacy, and defiance [21].

We command the deans to exercise every diligence in investigating these matters, to indulge no one, and to make no agreement with anyone through connivance concerning these crimes. Otherwise, we shall act against them as against ministers and abettors of other lusts and acts of plunder.

### II

Secular people could approve neither the austerity of John the Baptist nor Christ’s accessibility in food and drink. It is therefore better for ecclesiastics to avoid indiscriminate companionship with secular persons and instead to practice hospitality among themselves.

For this reason, we prohibit the deans and others from holding Kalends gatherings or other meetings of the clergy in public inns or secular houses. Rather, we command that everything be done by them in due order in the Church, as by the archdeacons and by us ourselves in the course of visitations, so that we may be neither a cause of scandal nor a burden to anyone [Col. 0245B].

We also desire, if it can be done, that ecclesiastical men in our diocese should not stay at public taverns, even while traveling, but should be received soberly and charitably by their fellow priests, though without imposing any burden. Everywhere they must avoid drunkenness, which is unworthy of every human being and much more so of a Christian priest. Anyone convicted of it shall, at our command, be confined in prison for a time, doing penance on bread and water.

### III

Finally, since according to Scripture speech, clothing, gait, and appearance reveal what a person is (Ecclesiasticus 19:27), just as every priest is separated from men and chosen for the things that belong to God, so he ought to be distinguished and separated from men who serve the age and the world [22], whether in speech or in any outward clothing and manner, so that it may be recognized that he serves God and not the world.

Therefore, in accordance with the prescription of the Council of Trent (Session 14, *On Reform*, chapter 6) and of our predecessors—and repeating their statutes here word for word—we decree, especially as was provided in the winter synod of the year 1573, that no ecclesiastical man shall wear clothing or garments inconsistent with the ecclesiastical state; nor shall he wear caps, especially while divine worship is being performed; nor breeches cut and gathered around the knees; nor frilled and open-necked undergarments, or shirts that we call *fronciatas*. Such garments are suitable only to secular and lay men, not to ecclesiastics. The gravest penalties shall be imposed upon those who wear them.

For this reason we enjoin our deans to pay attention to the matter and to report carefully and faithfully to us, under the obligation of their solemn oath, whatever they see or learn concerning violations of this statute, so that legal proceedings may be taken against the transgressors and the punishment of one may serve as a warning to many [Col. 0245C].

We further require all priests, deacons, and subdeacons, with the upper part of the head entirely shaved, to leave only the circular tonsure [Col. 0245D], and in no circumstances to wear a long beard.

### IV

Since the warnings of our predecessors appear to have accomplished nothing, and the evil has instead worsened day by day until it has become the defiance and conspiracy of many, we now increase the penalties against the obstinate according to the prescription of the Council of Trent (the same session). At the present synod we decree and declare that those who disobey and rebel against the statutes repeatedly issued by the holy Fathers and our predecessors, as well as against our own statute, incur excommunication by the very fact.

[23] Those who knowingly and obstinately sin publicly and against public statutes do not first require fraternal correction and admonition; rather, they deserve public coercion. Therefore we command that all ecclesiastics, especially parish priests, who dress in that secular fashion be avoided by everyone as excommunicated persons, and that their own parishioners and others prohibit them from entering the church. No one is to hear their Mass or any other sacred office [Col. 0246A].

If, notwithstanding this excommunication, they persist either in performing sacred functions or in wearing that secular habit while neglecting ecclesiastical dress, we shall proceed against them, as against those who despise ecclesiastical censures, to deprivation of the benefices they possess and to other canonical penalties. Their life and dress themselves announce that they prefer to serve the world rather than God; therefore we shall return them to the world, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, as the same sacred Council of Trent commands us to proceed (Session 22, *On Reform*, chapter 1).

We decree the same concerning ecclesiastics whose mouths offend pious ears with obscenity and daily oaths, bringing disgrace and scandal upon the Church. We warn others who dress more dirtily than befits the priestly order to make the purity and cleanliness of their minds shine forth also in their outward life and clothing, lest their ministry be blamed and despised and bring contempt upon the Church.

# On the Office of Parish Priests and Vicars

[Col. 0246B]

### I

[24] It amounts to the same thing for parish priests not to reside and for them to be idle while residing. Scripture requires all pastors to be capable of exhorting the people in sound doctrine and refuting those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). The need of our own time requires this much more, when the harvest is indeed plentiful but the laborers are few (Matthew 9:37; Luke 10:2), and when hostile men, the angels of Satan, openly sow weeds throughout the churches, not only while their rectors sleep but even while they keep watch.

It also generally happens that sheep listen more willingly to the voice of their own shepherd than to that of a mercenary, just as a pastor normally has, and ought to have, greater concern for feeding and teaching the sheep than a mercenary.

Let all parish priests therefore consider both the duty of their office and the need of the times, and often recall Paul’s saying: “Woe is me if I do not evangelize; necessity is laid upon me” (1 Corinthians 9:16).

If they despair because of their ignorance or inability to speak, let them hope in the Lord, who makes the tongues of the mute eloquent (Wisdom 10:21) and gives abundant power of speech to those who evangelize (Psalm 67:12). With that hope and with invocation of God, let them attend to reading. At least let them obtain homilies and sermons, both in Latin and in French, published by learned and Catholic men for the assistance of parish priests. Let them burn with zeal for the faith and salvation of their people. In this way it will come about that those who did not dare or were unable to speak will suddenly become teachers in Israel.

We do not, however, wish those who have obtained the gift of preaching to despise or entirely exclude from their churches other preachers sent by us, of whom we shall speak later. Rather, they should receive them as angels of God, offer them the right hand of fellowship, commend them to the people, and confer with them concerning doctrine and difficulties that arise.

If, through ignorance or inability to speak, someone lacks the capacity to teach the people, let him obtain a vicar to supply this duty, or occasionally invite a neighboring parish priest or priest who is not wholly ignorant of preaching. Alternatively, let him arrange for one of the religious preachers to visit his parish as often as possible [Col. 0246D], lest the people, through the ignorance or negligence of their parish priest, fail to know the true faith and instead imbibe heresy from elsewhere [25].

### II

Above all, parish priests must be concerned that no one, from the greatest to the least, be ignorant of at least what is necessary for salvation, such as the contents of the Apostles’ Creed and the Decalogue.

So that children, peasants, and others who are extremely uneducated may learn and retain these through hearing them repeatedly, we command that in every parish, on feast days at the first Mass designated for male and female servants—whether it is celebrated in a loud or a subdued voice—as well as at the principal and more solemn Mass, immediately after the *Agnus Dei* in both; and on Sundays after the pronaos (church porch), a child shall recite in French, in a loud, distinct, and intelligible voice to all, first both Creeds, then the Decalogue itself and the commandments of the elders, that is, the precepts of the Church, as they are given in French in the *Hours for the Use of the Diocese of Évreux* [Col. 0247A].

They may therefore be written on a tablet, which the child will hold in his hands while reciting them. We know that in certain dioceses these same texts are recited in the church porch by the celebrating priest. But, as is done in certain others, we have preferred to have them proclaimed by a child, because his voice affects everyone, and especially children, more strongly and makes them more attentive.

It is not enough to present and impress upon the people the articles of faith and the commandments of God unless provision is also made for their fulfillment in practice, and for repentance or punishment in the event of transgression.

### III

First, therefore, let parish priests be diligent in recognizing the faces of their flock and know how to call them by name. Especially in this unhappy time, let them go out to meet the wolves, pray, plead with, and rebuke [26] each of their parishioners, so that they may be sound in faith and guard against heresy and unbelief.

Let them exhort them to live more holily, to pray more earnestly, to produce fruits worthy of repentance through fasting, tears, and almsgiving, and to receive the sacraments more frequently—especially the sacrifice of the altar on the more solemn days—lest, as punishment for their previous sins, they be led into temptation and fall into heresy. Let them do this so that God may assist them and the soul may truly be strengthened by the presence of Christ’s body and the abundance of grace.

In all these matters, let the clergy lead and shine before the people: let them reform their lives for the better, increase public prayers and supplications, and offer the sacrifice of the altar each day with greater devotion for the law, the flock, the afflictions of princes and people, and the dangerous times into which we have fallen [Col. 0247B].

### IV

We therefore command that throughout this entire year extraordinary prayers and processions be held daily—or at least three times each week, including feast days—morning or evening, in all the churches of our diocese, within or outside those churches. In them, the litany shall especially be sung, together with collects and prayers imploring the mercy of God and the saints for the preservation of the faith and the Catholic Church, and for the tranquility of princes and people.

The collect said on Good Friday for heretics and schismatics shall be used, or another shall be said for them, so that at last we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and integrity (1 Timothy 2:2) [Col. 0247C].

We command resident parish priests and the vicars of absent priests to attend these private processions, as well as each priest established in a parish and other clerics, under penalty for the sin of rebellion and defiance [27], unless they have in conscience a just impediment that could not be postponed to another time.

We also command every priest of our diocese, whatever his condition or profession, to use such collects at every Mass, whether public or private, under the aforesaid penalty, unless the Mass being celebrated admits no commemoration.

Furthermore, each month, on some feast day, we command that a solemn procession be held in every parish and in every other collegiate or conventual church [Col. 0247D]. In cities and towns we wish it to be general, so that before or after it a Mass of the Holy Spirit, or of the Sacrament of the Altar, may be sung with the foregoing collects. Under the same penalty, those named above must attend it in decent dress together with the people.

### V

Since Christ has instituted many things for us against the temptations of the devil, the sacrament called Confirmation is especially commended. In it the flesh is anointed so that the soul may be strengthened for the struggle, and the flesh is signed so that the soul may be fortified by the Holy Spirit. The first Christians considered this sacrament so important that they regarded a Christian without it as imperfect for fighting and resisting the devil.

But Satan’s cunning has made this sacrament, like the other weapons of Christians by which he is defeated and repulsed, an object of contempt. Thus Confirmation is now sought by only a few, while very many do not consider it a sacrament, [Col. 0248A] or is thought to have no efficacy against vices and temptations.

Since the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (I John 5:19), and the devil has been released, possessing great wrath, let preachers and parish priests teach that this sacrament has perhaps never been more necessary to the people than it is now. Let them exhort them to present boys and girls to the bishop 28 as he travels through the parishes and visits them, as was formerly customary, so that they may receive Confirmation; and let adult laymen and women not be ashamed to receive what they ought to have received from childhood.

Let them, however, warn no one to be presented to the bishop for signing before that person knows and professes the articles of faith and has cleansed the soul through the sacrament of confession—a soul which is to be fortified and strengthened by the Holy Spirit for constancy in the faith.

### VI

In administering the sacraments, parish priests or vicars should display at least as much inward and outward holiness and reverence as they ought to require from laypeople in receiving them [Col. 0248B], lest they bring judgment and condemnation upon themselves through an unworthy administration, just as recipients do through unworthy participation.

Whether they are baptizing, absolving, or conferring another sacrament, it would indeed be right and pious for them, by some introductory explanation in the vernacular, to explain the power and efficacy of the sacrament—something which the Council of Trent commands them to do. If, however, until other provision is made, they are less capable of doing this, then at least by the propriety and dignity of the external signs they should show that divine and sacred things are contained there, and by the honor and gravity of their voice and gestures that these things are being handled and bestowed by them.

Therefore the vessels, linens, and all external signs of the sacraments must be clean and must display a certain divine character. Those administering the sacrament must pronounce the words and perform the ceremonies with great veneration, attentiveness, and distinctness.

Since, moreover, we have already experienced in these matters the extreme negligence—and even contempt—of many [Col. 0248C], we decree that offenders shall pay the due penalties for their negligence and contempt not only in money but in their own persons 29, through penances imposed upon them.

### VII

Since everything must be done in an orderly manner in the Church, just as parish priests and vicars are subject to the bishop, archdeacon, and dean, so it is right that all other priests holding benefices in a parish, whether arriving from elsewhere or otherwise, be subject to the parish priest or his vicar. Unless acting with their assent, they shall dare to do nothing in the church, under penalty of suspension from divine services incurred automatically, so that occasion for schism in that church may be avoided.

Let them nevertheless beware of abusing their authority over their assistants, under the same penalty. We also command them not to receive or admit priests of another diocese to perform any divine office unless they have brought letters concerning their priesthood, examined and approved by us, together with a profession of the Catholic faith.

### VIII

So that the same order of the Church may not be overturned, we do not wish anything new to be introduced into churches without consulting us [Col. 0248D], whether in ceremonies, singing, images, the divine office, confraternities, or in any other way.

Unless the greatest cause and necessity arise, we do not wish several high Masses to be celebrated simultaneously in the same church, several choral songs to be mixed together, or, on Sundays and other feast days, private Masses to be celebrated while the principal Mass is in progress—except after the *Agnus Dei*—lest, besides disturbing the order of the church, this provide an opportunity for certain impatient people to leave before the public service has been completed.

Anyone who acts contrary to this shall be regarded by all as rebellious, obstinate, and even schismatic.

### IX

Since, so that those who are approved may be made manifest, we are compelled to tolerate the weeds together with the wheat, and the harlot heresy 30 together with the legitimate bride of Christ, the Catholic Church, among the same people and in the same buildings, parish priests and vicars should first warn their parishioners that Scripture calls all heresies women who fornicate [Col. 0249A] and commit adultery against the truth.

They should not therefore think it lawful, or consider it in the least dangerous, to visit and hear heretical gatherings merely because they are permitted by the edicts of princes. For if, to avoid a greater evil, brothels are ordered to remain open in towns and cities, it would not on that account be honorable or lawful for a head of household to allow his wife or children to visit and frequent brothels.

### X

Furthermore, they should declare that those who have heard the sermons of heretics, attended their gatherings, read their books and kept them in their possession, or associated with them out of fraternity or friendship rather than necessity, are excommunicated automatically by the councils and by the Roman pontiffs of the Apostolic See. Consequently, it is not permitted to enter into marriage with them, conduct business with them, employ their craftsmanship or trade, converse with them, or live with them, except insofar as human necessity compels this, or a certain hope of winning them for Christ is evident, or duty requires it.

[Col. 0249B]

### XI

Nevertheless, so that Catholics may not be accused as disturbers of the commonwealth and human society or as disobedient to the laws of princes, parish priests should warn their parishioners neither to offend heretics by word nor by deed. They should allow them to enjoy the freedom of the laws which have pleased the princes, although the heretics cannot be approved; they should pray continually for them, demonstrate that they sincerely grieve over their destruction, and show themselves ready to do everything for their conversion, so that they may be recognized as children of their Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matthew 5:45).

31

### XII

If any parishioner has been overtaken by heresy, the parish priest or vicar should admonish him in a spirit of gentleness and employ every intercessor whom he thinks capable of recalling the fallen person. At the very least, he should teach that there is one Catholic Church, which we hold, outside which there is no salvation.

This Church is recognized as the true Church and the legitimate bride of Christ even by this sign alone [Col. 0249C]: it has always been oppressed and afflicted by all heretics, yet it has always ultimately prevailed and expelled all heresies, as handmaids, from the household of God and from the inheritance. It alone has remained there as the legitimate wife. It is to be hoped with equal certainty that the heretics of our time will meet the same fate as all those who came before them, however powerful they were in arms, influence, the multitude of those in error, the appearance of piety, learning, and authority from the Scriptures.

Nothing is said against the Church by recent heretics that was not said by those earlier ones, nor is anything done that was not previously done. Let the parish priest place before their eyes the disgraceful crimes by which the new religion was introduced and established; nor will Antichrist, when he comes openly to deny and attack Christ, display crimes more numerous or more execrable than these.

### XIII

If a parishioner does not heed the admonitions but leaves the church and goes backward after Satan, the parish priest or vicar shall order others to avoid him as a heretical person and one automatically excommunicated.

Nevertheless, he must not cease to seek the lost sheep by every means available [Col. 0249D]. If some affliction or illness gives the person 32 understanding, the parish priest should not wait until he is summoned by him, but should offer himself willingly and even invite him with tears to repentance and reconciliation with Christ and the Church. He should despair of no one so long as that person breathes.

If the person dies without the sacrament of repentance, or at least without having sought it when he could, he shall not be buried with Christian burial, nor shall prayers be offered for him.

### XIV

But if God should at some time grant him repentance (II Timothy 2:25), whenever he groans and returns to the Church, we wish him to be received with joy by the parish priest and the whole Church, and to be sent to our penitentiary so that his profession of faith may be examined, his conversion ascertained, and his penance received.

Although a contrite and humbled heart does not regard it as burdensome to make satisfaction publicly for sin and to undergo even the gravest things, nevertheless, if upon returning from heresy he alleges some just reason why he cannot approach our penitentiary [Col. 0250A], we decree that the reason be reported to us by the parish priest or vicar, so that we may entrust the matter to him or to another penitentiary.

We prohibit anyone from reproaching a person who returns from heresy. Let all remember their own condition, lest they too be tempted.

### XV

Just as parish priests or vicars must prepare a register of those reborn in baptism and of the dead, so we command them to record the names of those who have defected from the Church and no longer communicate in it, as though they were dead, together with the day on which they began to defect; and, in turn, the names of those returning to the same Church, as though they had come back to life.

As soon as either event occurs, the parish priests or vicars must report it to us by letters addressed to our secretary in the city of Évreux.

### XVI

If a man and woman returning to the Church have contracted and celebrated a marriage in a heretical gathering, we decree that, provided no other canonical impediment exists, they are to receive the priestly blessing in the face of the Church during a nuptial Mass from the parish priest or vicar [Col. 0250B], so that there may be no remaining doubt whether their marriage 33 lacks the character and grace of a sacrament.

We do not, however, wish any other nuptial solemnity to be repeated.

### XVII

Previously, learned and pious men had disputed whether baptism administered by Calvinists should be regarded as true baptism, since they supposedly did not intend to baptize for the remission of sins; or whether children baptized by them, when presented to the Church, should be poured over again with water, at least under the customary condition: “If you are not baptized, I baptize you.”

Before the decision of the Roman Apostolic See, perhaps each person was permitted to follow his own understanding. But after a debate and investigation concerning this difficulty had been held, Pius V, of happy memory, defined that the baptism used by the Calvinists was true baptism, since they employed the form and matter instituted by Christ with the general intention of doing what Christ instituted, even though they were mistaken in that particular interpretation [Col. 0250C] and singular intention, as nearly all other heretics have been mistaken either concerning the meaning of the baptismal form or concerning one of its effects.

For that reason, those baptized by Calvinists are not to be baptized again conditionally with the words, “If you are not baptized, I baptize you.” This clause was introduced for circumstances in which there is a legitimate doubt about the fact of baptism—when baptism was not performed publicly and there were no sufficient witnesses. This is the case when a midwife or another person baptizes secretly in an emergency and asserts that he or she has baptized, but that person alone cannot be believed before the Church.

Because the proof of the fact is then lacking, the precaution “If you are not baptized, I baptize you” is rightly prescribed. Since, however, the Calvinists baptize in a public assembly, the same pontiff decreed that there can be no doubt about the fact of their baptism, and that the clause is wrongly applied to a baptism known to have been publicly performed with the proper 34 matter and form and with the general intention. To do so would be nothing other than to repeat a true baptism or to call it into doubt.

The same Pope Pius [Col. 0250D], five or six years ago, graciously communicated this definition to us and to others who at that time were serving as preachers in Paris, by a brief transmitted through the apostolic nuncio, and forbade us to teach otherwise.

Therefore, lest a manifest error begin to take root in our diocese after the declaration of the Apostolic See, we prohibit all parish priests and priests, under penalty of automatic suspension from divine services and suspicion of schism and heresy, from daring to baptize again under that condition children brought to them who have already been baptized by Calvinists.

Instead, without any washing, they are to complete in them all the other rites of baptism omitted by the Calvinists. We order the same to be done with adults returning from heresy who received baptism not in the Catholic Church but in a Calvinist or other similar sect.

### XVIII

It has always been stated and established that heresies end in atheism and the kingdom of the devil, who works illicit arts and the evil practices of divination, sortilege, and magic in the children of dissension and unbelief [Col. 0251A]—practices by which our unhappy age, after innumerable heresies, is everywhere infected.

Parish priests should therefore look about to see whether any deceivers live among their flock, serving their belly and no religion, neither coming to church nor practicing heretical depravity. If there are any suspected and publicly noted for sortilege or witchcraft, we wish their names and condition to be reported to us, so that we may deliberate what must be done.

We command all confessors, after fraternal correction, to instruct each penitent to require each penitent, after fraternal correction, to reveal outside confession to the parish priest 35 or to us personally anyone whom he knows to be secretly obstinate and guilty of those crimes, as also of adultery, poisoning, usury, and other offenses by which God’s anger is provoked against the whole Church.

### XIX

Finally, parish priests and vicars should understand that it is their duty to see whether everyone—whether ecclesiastical or secular—properly performs his office, to admonish and rebuke those who err, and to report the obstinate to us.

They should inspect whether there are any illicit marriages [Col. 0251B]. Unless acting under our express mandate and license, they must not dare to give the nuptial blessing or join people in marriage outside the appointed times or without the required proclamations, under penalties to be imposed at our discretion.

Since apostolic dispensations in matrimonial cases and other matters are commonly entrusted to local ordinaries, and serious scandals arise from this because the petitions of those seeking them are often based on suppressed or insufficiently ascertained and proved truth, yet are nevertheless allowed to produce their effect, we decree that in future parish priests and vicars shall not execute such dispensations unless the case has first been examined by our promoter, approved by us personally together with our official, and the dispensation has been countersigned, so that nothing may be effected by surreptitious misrepresentation. Thus nothing may be committed through concealment or misrepresentation.

Parish priests should also strive to settle divorces and disputes among their parishioners, especially those arising from trivial causes. They should bar obstinate persons from communion in the sacraments and should not allow known excommunicates [Col. 0251C] to enter the church, just as they should not allow the sick to die without confession and viaticum, if this can be done.

To prevent this from occurring, whenever they hear that someone is ill, they should visit him as part of their priestly office and exhort him to provide for the salvation of his soul. They should not leave the parish unless they leave someone behind to take their place 36.

Just as disobedient parishioners do not deserve Christian burial, so parish priests and vicars, if they fail in their duty in this matter, will have to render an account on the day of the just judgment for the loss of their sheep and must be reduced to public penance together with those who negligently suffocate children.

We prohibit the consecration of the Eucharist in private and profane chambers, even for the use of the sick. The first Christians preferred, out of honor for so great a sacrament, to have it carried from the church to the sick even during times of persecution, or to keep it at home for sudden needs, rather than consecrate it in unsacred places.

Many simple priests, forgetful of their office and rank, dare [Col. 0251D] on feast days and other days to attend sacred services wearing a hat (*galerus*) and without a surplice, and disdain to assist the parish priest or vicar in the divine offices. They prefer to mingle with the laity and even, after completing their private Mass, to withdraw from the rest of the service.

Lest this scandal spread further, we declare that all priests are appointed for human beings in matters pertaining to God (Hebrews 5:1), so that they may perform all sacred functions for the people. Each priest is therefore bound to the parish in which he resides, so that he may serve it for the people in all matters pertaining to God and be distinguished within it from the people.

For this reason, whenever one of the priests comes into a church and refuses, in proper clerical dress, to perform the divine offices with the parish priest and the other members of the presbyterate, we order that he be regarded as no priest, suspended automatically from divine services, and reduced to lay communion with secular persons. He is also to be summoned by the dean before our Official to render an account for neglect of his office.

## The Duty of the People

[Col. 0252A]

37

### I

The people readily complain and lament over their calamities. But it is burdensome and hateful to them to think about the causes of those calamities, their own sins, and the remedies: the amendment of life, repentance, and the careful observance of divine worship and the heavenly commandments, by which God’s anger may be appeased and mercy implored.

Almost all, as though despairing of themselves, become worse through their miseries. They appear to themselves to be excellent people when they confess the Catholic faith in words but deny it by their deeds (Titus 1:16).

### II

Above all, let each person die in that religion and Church which has reached us through the consensus and succession of Christian peoples. To those who disapprove of it and advise a change, let them answer without contention with what David, Elijah, and the Apostle Paul taught should be answered in such controversies.

With David, let them say to God: “If I follow change [Col. 0252B], behold, I have rejected the generation of your children” (Psalm 72 [73]:15). With Elijah, in the utter desperation of his affairs, let them conclude for consolation: “It is enough for me, Lord; take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (III Kings [I Kings] 19:4).

With Paul, let them cry out: “If there is no truth in the Catholic Church, then have those who have fallen asleep in Christ perished?” (I Corinthians 15:18).

Let them consider how much more holy and happy life was, and how much more sincerely faith and charity—the perfection and end of the law—were practiced among human beings, for as long as the ancient religion prevailed among all.

Whenever they hear blasphemies, novelties, and disputes about religion, let them stop their ears and flee as far away as possible, just as Irenaeus speaks of the first Christians when they happened upon heretics.

38

### III

Nor should they imitate only the faith of their fathers, but also their piety and integrity, if they hope from God for an end to the public affliction—especially since his hand is still extended to strike and his fury is increasingly provoked by the freedom of heresies and [Col. 0252C] blasphemies.

### IV

Therefore, besides the things which we have commanded to be proposed and urged upon the people through the parish priests, let each person pour out his heart before the Lord in confession of the true faith, amendment of life, fruits of repentance, observance of the commandments, and daily and nightly supplication for forgiveness of public and private offenses.

### V

It would indeed be desirable for the people to pray without interruption and to devote every hour to worship and sacred duties. But since humanity was created to work the earth and, because of sin, is compelled to seek sustenance in the sweat of its face (Genesis 3) and to eat the labor of its hands (Psalm 127 [128]), it cannot and ought not devote itself constantly to prayer and heavenly actions.

Nevertheless, since neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (I Corinthians 3:7), every day, before a person goes out to his work, he should come, if possible, to the church to hear Mass. In it he should give thanks to God for what has passed, commend his own work and that of his whole [Col. 0252D] household to God’s blessing, and invoke him to avoid sins and dangers. He should not forget to pray for public peace, the Catholic faith, and the commonwealth.

If distance or another just impediment prevents a layman from coming to church, he should at least not omit to perform what is his duty toward God. He should teach and accustom his children, servants, and maidservants, and finally his whole household, to ask God for their daily bread, to profess the Apostles’ Creed, and to give thanks for all benefits, together with recognition and confession of sins. These prayers should include short petitions for the needs of the time and for the peace of the Church.

Moreover, since the annals of the Gauls recount that in difficult times our ancestors established the practice that, at the sound of the bell at sunrise, noon, and sunset, the people—wherever they might be working—were reminded to pray individually for God’s help, we wish that custom, interrupted in many places by heresy and [Col. 0253A] neglect of piety, to be renewed and maintained, especially since public calamity urges us to do so.

We would not insist on these things if we did not see most people carried with their families from sleep to food like brute animals, touched and affected by no sense of piety, but becoming more silent and stupefied the more heavily we are afflicted.

Parish priests, preachers, schoolmasters, and confessors are to warn and rebuke the people more severely concerning these matters.

39

### VI

According to Scripture, God instituted feast days as a memorial and remembrance of his benefits, so that people might acknowledge them and give thanks for them (Judith 16; Esther 16, and elsewhere), and so that, in imitation of God, who created heaven and earth and afterward rested, human beings might, after the days assigned to labor, know how to devote some time to rest, contemplation of divine goodness, and thanksgiving.

Thus the Sabbath had been imposed upon the Jews, so that on the seventh day they might rest in imitation of God, contemplate the works of creation, and devote themselves to giving thanks for them. God did not prescribe only that one feast, but many others as well, in remembrance and consideration of the many particular benefits he had bestowed upon them, for which they were to give thanks.

The Lord’s Day succeeded the Jewish Sabbath for Christians [Col. 0253B] as a sign and memorial of our redemption, as of a second creation and restoration which Christ accomplished on the cross, when he rested from the work of his Passion after completing it.

But just as the Jews were commanded not only to observe the one feast of the Sabbath, but whenever God bestowed some remarkable benefit upon them through Moses or other holy men, feasts were decreed for the perpetual celebration and contemplation of its memory, so the Christian people were not to be left with only the feast of the Lord’s Day. More were to be established for the individual gifts received through Christ, his Virgin Mother, the apostles, and other holy men and women, lest we be forgetful and ungrateful toward them.

A Christian, like a Jew, must especially cease from vices and sins on a feast day [Col. 0253C], since he must serve God, who is displeased by every sin and vice. But beyond this, it is fitting that he cease from every secular bodily work, from servile work, and from other work which is lawful and customary on other days. For from the creation of the world feast days were introduced so that the soul, together with the body, might cease from worldly affairs and be drawn away from the cares and labors of this world, while being occupied in the service of God, recognizing his benefits and returning thanks for them.

We believe that in no age has there been more serious or more frequent sin against the holy and legitimate observance of feast days than in our own. Many spend those days pursuing the pleasures of this world—in taverns, brothels, unlawful games, and other vain and even vicious activities—especially while the sacred offices are being celebrated. We are therefore not surprised that the evils which God threatens through the prophets against violators of feast days have overtaken us (Numbers 15; Ezekiel 20, and elsewhere).

Markets are held everywhere, along with every kind of dissipation [Col. 0253D] on those days. 40 Business dealings, commerce, driving, and transport are carried on, and activities that are permitted on other days are postponed until feast days, so that a double evil and sin may be committed.

Therefore parish priests or vicars, preachers, and confessors must be diligent in rebuking the people for their ingratitude toward God, for the mortal sin into which they fall by violating feast days against God’s ordinance, and for the punishment and vengeance that follow.

We decree that on feast days there shall be no buying, selling, leasing, auctions, dissipation, commercial dealing of any kind, or displaying of meat and other goods, especially in the courtyards and cemeteries of churches. Markets assigned to the feast days are to be moved to the preceding or following day, and this is first to be announced to the neighboring parishes.

We also prohibit driving, transport, and every work of human hands and animals, except when, during the harvest or grape harvest, the laws of the weather excuse it, or when at another time [Col. 0254A] the greatest and most evident necessity excuses it. 41

As for journeys which fall on feast days not through deliberate malice but because travelers from outside happen to be passing through our diocese, we nevertheless command that they be restrained at least from appearing in public until after the conclusion of the more solemn Mass. Taverns and other places of public corruption are likewise to be closed at least during the time of the divine Office.

All transgressors of feast days without evident necessity, and especially the obstinate and those caught in taverns, brothels, or illicit activities, are to be summoned before our Official. In addition to a fine, penance is to be imposed upon them for their sin and scandal; repeat offenders are either to be excommunicated or confined in prison.

We appeal to secular lords and judges to render obedience to God and to us 42 in this matter and to extend helping hands, lest, if so many sacrileges escape punishment, they bring God’s anger upon everyone.

### VII

We approve confraternities and fraternities, especially those devoted to charity in our diocese, and we praise nearly all the works of charity carried out through them [Col. 0254B], such as all divine Offices and church furnishings, burials and funerals even of those who have died of plague, as well as alms for the poor.

But since we have heard that feasting and drunkenness, and other associations and activities which, if not entirely evil, are nevertheless foolish, are being concealed under the name of charity, we warn and exhort the brothers not henceforth to commit anything in their assemblies unworthy of Christian men. Let them not feast so frequently or at such great expense, but take account of poorer brothers and of the public calamity, and instead devote themselves to multiplying works of true charity.

If anything in these or other fraternities of our diocese appears to require correction, we wish to be informed of it by the parish priests or vicars.

We prohibit one practice to all fraternities: they are not to have water or bread blessed in their private services on Sundays. Any priest, of whatever status or profession [Col. 0254C], who offers himself as minister for this in our diocese shall be suspended automatically from divine services, lest under the pretext of private services the people be drawn away from Mass and the parish Office, as nearly always happens. It is never permissible to omit or neglect what is commanded in favor of what is merely devotion and supererogation.

### VIII

Since a church ought to be the house of God and of prayer, and holiness ought to characterize it, we cannot fail to be moved by the irreverence of the people, who behave there no differently 43 than in a marketplace.

Since we know, however, that exhortations and warnings accomplish little with the people unless someone is present to rebuke them and break their hardness through constant attention, we decree that the parish priest or vicar, together with the priests, noblemen, judges, if any are present, and the church wardens, shall choose three men: one from among the priests, another from the fraternity of charity, if there is one, or from the people, and a third likewise from the people. They are to be men of good reputation and advanced in age, so that the others may respect their gray hair [Col. 0254D].

Those chosen must accept the election made of them by virtue of the holy obedience owed to God, the bishop, and their own parish priest. They shall be called church wardens, because we impose upon them the duty of observing and noting on feast days which priests and parishioners have been absent from the church Offices, and of inquiring for what reason they have been absent—whether in the meantime they have been spending their time in taverns, at games, or in other secular business.

Inside the church they must see what place and order each person ought to occupy. For, as is the practice of bad custom and ambition among some, certain people from the congregation occupy the first seats nearer the altar, before the priests, after whom it is fitting that everyone sit in due order according to his rank and condition.

In this matter the judgment and discretion of the church wardens shall prevail, so that the disputes and quarrels customarily arising in churches over this issue may cease.

Afterward they should observe what each person does in the church and how each behaves, from the least to the greatest: whether he uncovers his head, bends his knees when necessary, gives his mind and [Col. 0255A] ears to the divine Office, and applies himself to prayer.

They should rebuke those who act otherwise, with appropriate reverence and modesty, and compel them to attend the Office. They must not allow anyone to leave the church without a known reason until the sacred services have been completed and concluded. 44

So that they may perform all this more conveniently, we decree that the three shall take turns, with one standing in the choir, another outside the choir, and the third at the rear and far end of the church, so that they may see and observe all those attending.

If anyone requires fraternal correction because of disobedience, all three should approach him together, summoning the parish priest or vicar to accompany them. If he does not listen to them, we order the obstinate person to be summoned by the parish priest before us or our Official. Of whatever fine is imposed, one-third or one-half is to be assigned to the church wardens, and the remainder to the church fabric fund.

We also wish the church wardens not to be burdened, and therefore command that on feast days prayers be offered for them in the church porch as a service to God and the Church.

If they die while holding such an office, then, in recognition of their piety and gratitude toward them, we command that at their funeral the Office for the Dead with a public Mass be celebrated at the expense of the church fabric fund and the parish priest. We grant them [Col. 0255B] indulgences of forty days.

We trust that, because of their age and the election made of them, they will act against no one except maturely and in an orderly spirit of charity, seeking to please God more than human beings.

We wish them to remain in that office for as long as it is agreeable to those elected and to those who elected them.

### IX

Sheep ought to hear the voice of the shepherd and follow him. Yet, through some Satanic cunning, it happens that the people not only hear and follow outsiders more willingly than their own parish priests or vicars, but also set mercenaries against them—whether those whom they call parishioners’ vicars, chaplains, or any other outsiders—so that each person establishes a minister for himself.

We consider that the Apostle commands everyone to obey their superiors, who must render an account for the souls of each person [Col. 0255C] (Hebrews 13). 45 We also consider their daily solicitude, by which they satisfy the divine Offices and the uncertain needs of all; and finally, the struggles outside and fears within (II Corinthians 7:5), together with the continual troubles by which they are tormented on behalf of the people. Thus it is deservedly the case that many are wearied and repent not only of residing in their own parish but even of life itself.

We therefore appeal to secular lords, noblemen, and everyone else not to allow Scripture to reproach them for being like a people who do not obey the priest (Deuteronomy 17:12). Rather, through eagerness in respect, obedience, kindness, and gratitude, let them invite—and in a certain sense compel—their own pastor to remain with them and to carry out his ministry wholeheartedly.

If parish priests or vicars are thought blameworthy in some respect, although the Apostle warns us not to readily receive an accusation against a priest (I Timothy 5:19), we will nevertheless listen patiently [Col. 0255D] to the complaints of the people and will not allow the sins of parish priests to go unpunished.

But no one should report them on the basis of the opinion or report of wicked people, or because of some offense or indignation. The report must instead rest upon the established and proved truth of the crime.

Let the parish priests themselves strive to be loved and desired by their people rather than feared, and to preside not only by their office but also by their merits and good works.

### X. Hospitals, Administrations, and Leprosaria

By royal edict, hospitals, administrations, and leprosaria are entrusted to lay administration in our diocese, so that their revenues may be spent on works of piety. We have discovered, however, that in many places little or nothing from them reaches such works; rather, it is used to relieve the public burdens and even taxes of the inhabitants, or diverted to the advantage of certain individuals who take turns setting themselves over their administration, so that the faithful do not render accounts of the receipts, in which they customarily enter everything as spent on lawsuits, repairs, and other evasions, while they are meanwhile known to have diverted the funds to their own uses. Although it is the duty of bishops to oversee and safeguard all goods assigned to piety within the diocese, nevertheless, so that we may not be able to demand anything from those administrators, they assert that, by royal edict, nothing concerning them pertains to us.

We, however, at least to safeguard their consciences and lest we forget what belongs to piety and to our office, order the curates or vicars, in the church porch, to name and publicly declare excommunicated ipso facto by law all administrators of hospitals, administrations, leprosaria, and church-fabric funds as defrauders of the poor and sacrilegious plunderers—namely, all those by whom any of the goods of those institutions is alienated without public and ecclesiastical authority, or transferred or invested in their own advantage by any means, or placed at profane uses and at uses other than the works of piety to which they were assigned by their foundation. They are also to declare that all participants and accomplices in these acts are subject to the same excommunication, and that they and their heirs are bound to make restitution. We order their confessors to impose this obligation upon them, and not to grant absolution except with that obligation.

### On the Sentence of Excommunication

I. The people are accustomed to rush very quickly and very lightly to the sword-edge of excommunication against their neighbor; but, once it has been imposed in turn, they commonly regard it as nothing and neither feel nor consider the wound inflicted by it. Yet while all punishments inflicted by human beings kill only the body and do not pass beyond the boundaries of this world, ending in this age, excommunication ordinarily destroys in this world the body and everything a person possesses, but always strikes at the life of the soul—not only in this age but in the age to come, and not merely before human beings but also before God.

It is therefore by far the most serious of all punishments, to be exercised only for the gravest offenses and after every remedy has been attempted, and to be feared above any torment of this life. A grave offense, however, must be considered and assessed not so much from the seriousness and magnitude of the matter itself as from the perversity of the malice and obstinacy involved. For this reason, just as Adam, the first man, was expelled from paradise by excommunication because of the greatest disobedience and rebellion in eating a single fruit, a matter of the slightest importance, so in imposing a just excommunication one must attend not so much to the act itself as to the wickedness and obstinacy of the person acting.

Nevertheless, if the act was slight and did not bring with it public scandal, some other great evil, or manifest and hardened obstinacy on the part of the offender, we judge it unworthy of excommunication. Before excommunication is granted by any of our officials, however, if it is requested by name against someone, we wish it first to be established that admonitions and correction in charity have been employed. If it is requested on the basis of hidden matters that cannot be proved, we decree that the petitioners be questioned whether they have any suspects, and that their names be recorded; concerning these matters a letter is then to be sent to the curate or vicar, so that, before publishing the excommunication, he may summon them and privately admonish them with correction in charity.

Unless all the foregoing has been observed, we prohibit curates and vicars from proceeding to publication. We do not wish excommunications thereafter to be read and published perfunctorily by them, as though they were some ordinary popular mandate, and in haste; rather, they are always to be proclaimed with horror and a threat of divine judgment, as well as of public affliction upon the entire parish if the excommunicated person is tolerated within it. For this reason, we order that the pronouncement of excommunication be postponed as long as possible, awaiting the guilty parties and their accomplices so that they may come to penitence, confession, and reconciliation with those whom they have offended.

When the day of the pronouncement arrives, we order that, to strike terror into consciences and place the effect of excommunication before their eyes, a bier covered with a pall for the dead, with burning candles and holy water, be set up before the church porch. At the end of the pronouncement, the candles are to be extinguished and the holy water poured out. All are also to be warned that, whoever the excommunicated person may be, they must mourn him as truly dead rather than merely dead by bodily death, and must not associate with him any more than with a dead person whenever he is recognized.

It appears from Christian antiquities that the earliest Christians used almost this rite in proclaiming excommunication, and certain traces of it are still observed in some Churches. Moreover, whoever is convicted of having despised an excommunication which he knew he had incurred must be marked and avoided as a heretic, and brought to justice by everyone, lest, as the Apostle says when speaking of an excommunicated person, “a little leaven corrupt the whole lump” and the whole parish (I Cor. 5:6)—not merely by making everyone excommunicated, but by provoking God’s anger and public calamity upon all.

Therefore we order all confessors to examine not only whether those confessing are conscious of having incurred any excommunication, but also whether they have associated with known excommunicated persons, and to require them to disclose such persons outside confession. 49

### On Schools and Their Teachers

[Col. 0257B]

The hope and seedbed of religion, the Catholic Church, and the commonwealth lie in the schools, where the young are formed in true faith, piety, and learning, so that from them holy and capable priests, judges, and governors of the people may arise. Because what formerly used to be the first concern of parents, cities, and bishops has become the last—or rather no concern at all—everything has gone to ruin: the law has perished from the priest, jurisprudence from the judge, and counsel and foresight from the governor of the people. Piety, religion, and human concord have degenerated into factions and opposing interests.

For restoring and reestablishing all these things, therefore, one short path seems available: that from their earliest years people should become accustomed to living and being educated in the same schools, as though in the same sheepfold, imbibing the same milk of religion and learning, and holding and desiring precisely the same things.

We marvel at the diligence of our forebears in our diocese, since scarcely any populous parish is found to which there was not formerly attached a house and endowment assigned to a school. But, conversely, we detest the negligence—and not merely negligence but sacrilege—of our own age, in which noblemen and even ecclesiastics, or the parishioners themselves, have seized or alienated schoolhouses and endowments, so that now scarcely any school or teacher is found, not only in the villages but even in the towns and largest cities.

Where some remnant of a school and stipend still exists, a teacher is permitted, without residence or the duty of teaching, to enjoy—or rather abuse—those revenues and do whatever else he wishes, while the people look on and lament as their children are corrupted without discipline or instruction. Indeed, matters have reached such madness that many would rather hire a private tutor at great expense in their homes, or send their children, who have not yet learned their alphabet, to a famous university, than contribute a single penny toward restoring the public school—or even consent that some salary be established from the public treasury or from a hospital for a person capable of teaching the young.

We recount all these matters, known and witnessed by us, with sorrow, so that all may understand how just it is to remedy these abuses. Accordingly, we first order all schoolmasters, or those possessing offices, benefices, pensions, lands, and whatever revenues have been assigned to the heads and teachers of schools, that within two months of this synod they actually reside in the places and buildings assigned to their office and actually teach. They are not to involve themselves in other business or retain other benefices, since these are incompatible with residence at the schools and with the constant care and duty of directing and educating the young.

If they are incompetent for their function, or prefer to resign rather than be bound to such a burden, we prohibit them, when resigning their office, from attempting to reserve any revenues or pension, since those revenues are attached to the exercise of the office and not to the title. Those who, after the appointed time, persist in disobedience and rebellion we declare excommunicated and to be avoided by all as such; they are to be compelled, by withholding their future revenues, to restore the past revenues, which they could not make their own while they were neglecting the office. Another person is to be provided with the office, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, since this concerns the correction of a public corruption.

Next, we order all to whom this pertains to establish teachers in the cities, towns, and villages of our diocese. Within the same period they are to provide, together with the inhabitants, suitable persons and a just salary, unless the endowment is sufficient. If the endowment has in any way been alienated, they are to arrange for its full restoration at their own expense and that of the inhabitants. If they show themselves negligent in this matter, we wish proceedings to be taken against them either by withholding revenues, or by excommunication and other canonical remedies, or by depriving them of their rights over the schools.

So that occupied school property may be recovered, we order all curates and vicars, from the day of this synod, to warn everyone on each Sunday in the church porch, for a period of two months, who knowingly possesses anything belonging to the schools, under penalty of incurring excommunication after those two months, to return the property faithfully, or at least to reach an agreement concerning it under our authority.

They are also to warn all who know that anything belonging to the school is being withheld by anyone to disclose it to the curate or vicar within the prescribed period. They are likewise to warn those who, without ecclesiastical authority, have sold or otherwise alienated anything dedicated to God for the schools, so that they may have it returned or substitute compensation for it.

Lest schools be lacking where no such endowment exists, or where it is insufficient, we beseech in the Lord the patrons of parishes, priories, and chaplaincies, both ecclesiastical and secular, when presenting candidates, to prefer those capable of teaching, or those who have already labored in this work; or at least to reserve for them some pension, which the Council of Trent declared should justly be established from any benefice for the education of the young (session 23, *De reformatione*, chapter 18), as well as through the annexation of any benefices. 52

Moreover, since royal law has assigned the administration of hospitals and leprosaria to secular persons so that their revenues may be spent on works of piety, which fall under our direction, and since no works can be more important than those by which piety itself is impressed upon human hearts from early childhood and the Church and the entire commonwealth are built up, we inform the administrators of those places that they should entrust the titles of those benefices to schoolteachers together with some pension, or should not hesitate to devote some portion of such revenues to the use of the schools.

We further order fraternities and parish-fabric administrators always to remember the schoolmaster among those to whom they distribute stipends. Finally, we wish curates and vicars to warn the sick not to overlook the same teacher in their wills, as the father of the entire commonwealth.

For it is shameful that heretics wage wars and expend everything to obtain schools, so that impiety may be absorbed by their children, while Catholics neither assist schools of piety with public nor private support, but rather plunder and overthrow them.

II. Furthermore, lest the schools themselves serve to divide religion and the commonwealth rather than reconcile them, we first decree that there shall be one school for each parish, in order to eliminate dissensions and schisms. Under penalty of excommunication, we forbid any cleric or other person to dare privately to receive the children of individuals for instruction without the permission of the person who has charge of the school. Under the same penalty, we prohibit parents from keeping a private teacher at home unless with the approval and consent of the public schoolmaster.

If there are several parishes in the same city or town where public schools nevertheless exist, we wish the children of all the parishes to assemble there under the same penalty—at least those who are more advanced in letters, namely, those who know how to read and sing. It shall be permissible, however, to send the younger children either to the public school or to the parish school.

But lest heretics infiltrate Catholic schools, before anyone is appointed schoolmaster we decree that he must bring a testimony of his faith, religion, life, and integrity, at least from the curate or vicar and the churchwardens of the parish from which he comes, and must present himself to us or to our penitentiary for a profession of the Catholic faith and an examination of doctrine.

III. We order that the teacher be instructed above all to imbue the young, by example and word, with every form of piety and the Catholic faith, and to accustom them to fear and worship God, to keep and observe the commandments of the Decalogue, to hear Mass daily, to serve reverently at the offices of the Church, and willingly to pray. They should, if possible, know by heart the Hours together with the seven penitential psalms, as well as other exercises of piety.

He is not to allow vices to grow up in the children, but is to nurture them in the discipline and correction of the Lord. At every entrance to and departure from the school, both morning and evening, public prayer is to be offered by all, either by singing *Veni, Creator* or something else in which God, the Virgin Mother, and the saints are invoked for peace, religion, and the Catholic Church.

On the vigils of feasts they are to learn the Office and the chant of the Church, from the least to the greatest. On feast days, at some hour, either in the church or in the school, two or three are to be questioned in the presence of the others, in turn, about the Apostles’ Creed, the Decalogue, and the other contents of the catechism of Catholics, in Latin and French. The teacher is also to give there a simple and familiar exhortation and instruction in piety concerning the feast being celebrated. 54

On the more solemn feast days, and as often as possible, he is to accustom and teach the children to confess their sins, and those who have reached the age of discretion to receive the sacrament of the altar with a tested conscience.

He should attract and exhort the little ones to piety and study rather than compel them, lest they hate both before they know them. Nevertheless, since Scripture says, “He who spares the rod hates the soul of his child” (Prov. 13:24), he should resort to blows only when compelled. Just as we desire moderation in the severity of teachers, so we judge that the uncontrolled indulgence of parents must be punished: parents who wish their children to be allowed everything without discipline, and who, because of this, either withdraw their children from school or inflict some insult upon the schoolmasters. By this statute we give the teacher power to summon such parents before us or before our official, so that they may learn not to be angry with one to whom they ought to have given thanks.

Finally, we enjoin curates and deans to ensure that all these matters are put into effect, and to render us an account of any omission.

### On Preachers

The Apostle writes that true presbyters are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine (I Tim. 5:17). This is particularly necessary in our unhappy age, when false prophets are clamoring everywhere and very few are found who are able or willing to evangelize with great power. Yet, according to the same Apostle’s testimony, not everyone who is capable of evangelizing is to be heard unless he is lawfully sent (Rom. 10:15), lest the wicked mingle with the good, conceal wolves beneath sheep’s clothing, or deny by deed and life what they have affirmed in word or action—something that must especially be guarded against in our most corrupt age, in which even the elect, if possible, are led into error and depravity.

Accordingly, the holy Synod of Trent rightly decreed (session 5, *De reformatione*, chapter 2) that regular preachers of any order may not preach unless they have been examined and approved by their superiors with regard to life, conduct, and learning, and unless they have received their permission—even in the churches of their own orders. With that permission, they must personally present themselves before the bishops and ask their blessing before beginning to preach.

The same holy synod also forbids regulars to presume to preach in the churches of their own orders against the opposition of the bishop (session 2, chapter 24). In churches that do not belong to their orders, it commands them, in addition to the permission of their superiors, to obtain the permission of the bishop, without which they may in no way preach in those churches that are not of their orders; this permission, it orders, is to be granted freely by the bishops.

Since the general superiors of the regular orders, especially the mendicants, have sworn obedience to the decrees of this synod, we prohibit all preachers, including regulars, from henceforth presuming to preach throughout the parishes of our diocese without our express permission. Curates and vicars are neither to receive them nor permit them to address the people unless they have seen, or at least learned of, our permission. Nor are regulars to install a preacher in their houses located within our diocese unless he has been approved by us, under penalty of excommunication, contumacy, and perjury against the holy Council of Trent.

We further order them not to dare claim for themselves, without our permission, any places or territories as though they were owed to them by some right, as if it were not within the bishop’s power to send there others whom he knows to be more suitable. Nor may they leave or exchange an assigned station without this same permission; otherwise they are to be punished for desertion.

We beseech them in the Lord, and likewise the other preachers, to order their studies and their lives in such a way that they may be a help, an edification, and an ornament to our diocese, so that we may not be ashamed to send them out and prefer them as members of our household to any others.

In the cities and towns of our diocese where regular convents exist, the curates and vicars grievously complain that no sermons are preached on Sundays and feast days, and that the regulars produce impediments, dissensions, and scandals rather than the very modest assistance expected from religious observance. The rural people and curates likewise complain to us that they spend whole years without any sermon, except perhaps some hurried one during the harvest and gathering of fruits.

Therefore we again beseech the regulars in the Lord not to allow any feast day to pass without a special duty of preaching, especially in their own houses; to maintain peace with the curates, a peace confirmed by so many decrees of the pontiffs; and to understand that the Council of Trent does not even grant them the power to hear confessions in a convent without the bishop’s permission (session 33, *De reformatione*, chapter 15). They should also understand that all indults and privileges obtained from anyone whatsoever have most recently been confined by Gregory XIII, our lord pope, within the grants of the Council of Trent and the ancient canons, against which they cannot protest without sin.

We exhort them to devote themselves rather to reading, prayer, and exhortation than to sowing discord between clergy and people, and to emulate more the religious simplicity of their Fathers than to walk disorderly. Those to whom we have assigned a station are to preach there at least once each month throughout the year, or present to us another who will take their place in their absence, so that at least once each month all our parishes may be fed with the word of God.

If they fail in this, we order the curates to report it to us, so that we may provide others and prevent the collection of alms. Lest those who sow spiritual things be in need of temporal necessities, we order the curates and vicars to invite them to lodge with them and to receive them with joy and veneration, unless they prefer to lodge with noblemen or other wealthier parish priests. We prohibit them only from entering public taverns.

During Advent and Lent, the entire city, or the parish if there is only one, is to provide them with food and lodging, especially, if possible, in the house of some ecclesiastic. Such persons ought not to be exempt from providing for preachers, so that they may contribute with the others; rather, by their example they should encourage others.

We further decree that every convent be commended in its own territory in the church porch on all the Sundays of the year. We also declare that a just and deserved portion of the revenues of hospitals, leprosaria, and other administrations assigned to works of piety be distributed to the mendicant convents, and that the curates warn the dying not to forget them in their wills.

Just as they are called to share in our solicitude and in the assistance of all ecclesiastics, so it is right that all should make them participants in the benefits in which, because of their office, we rejoice.

Since the days are evil, however, we ask them to be prudent in their sermons and to strive rather to exhort our people in sound doctrine than to refute contradictions and heresies, especially where the people are not troubled by any large presence of heretics. Let them attack instead the vices and moral corruptions of the people, and draw more tears toward penitence and amendment than kindle fury or anger toward sedition.

Finally, let them address the people on all the matters that we have proposed concerning the duty of the curates and of the people themselves.

### On the Provision and Reform of Breviaries and Other Ecclesiastical Books for the Diocese of Évreux

[Col. 0261B]
