Moved by the prayers and complaints of many among the clergy, we have proposed, God being propitious, to inspect more carefully the Hours for the laity, the breviaries and missals for priests, and the manuals for the curates of our diocese; to reform them on the advice of devout men; and once more to commit them to a more accurate and elegant printing, especially since almost everywhere in our diocese there is now an extreme shortage of all these books.

But because printers do not now possess the abundance or resources that they formerly had, and because in a single printing a number of books must be produced sufficient for many years, so great an undertaking cannot be completed without the greatest expenses—expenses which the printers themselves neither wish nor are able to bear, and which we ourselves are not sufficiently powerful to meet.

Therefore, on the advice of prudent men, we have devised a plan by which this burden may in part be discharged: each abbot, prior, curate, and priest of whatever order, as well as the churchwardens, shall contribute with us, each according to the measure of his means and his need for those books, whether more or a single gold coin, or less than a gold coin. They are to deposit the contribution with those appointed by this synod to press this matter forward with us. Once the work has been completed, the price of the books that each person receives according to his need shall be reduced by the amount he previously contributed.

Accordingly, we order the deans to warn all the persons named above of this statute and to record in writing what each has offered, so that the deputies may determine whether the necessary sum of money can be assembled. Lest the money contributed perish, its custody is to be entrusted, with the consent of all the deputies, to one or more faithful persons who are solvent.

### On Rural Deans

Lest law and statute be issued in vain if no one observes them or ensures that they are observed in our absence, we order the deans, as though from a high watchtower, to look out over everyone and faithfully report delinquents and obstinate persons. For this purpose we give them power to summon anyone without any other special mandate, and we prohibit them from turning a blind eye or making any settlement with anyone in exchange for payment, under penalty before us of treachery and of perjury against God in violation of their oath.

At every synod we wish them to make and renew this oath in our hands, in the following form, taken from the holy canons:

“I, N., dean of N., swear by the living God and these holy Gospels that from now on, whatever I know or have heard, or may subsequently inquire into, which has been or shall be done against the will of God or sound Christianity in the deanery entrusted to me—if it occurs during my time and comes to my knowledge or is reported to me—I shall regard as a synodal matter and as belonging to the jurisdiction of my lord bishop. I shall conceal none of it from my aforesaid lord bishop, or from his envoy whom he orders to investigate it, or from his officials, whether because of love, fear, payment, or kinship. So may God and these holy Gospels of God help me.”

## PRIVILEGE OF POPE URBAN, BY WHICH THE BISHOP OF ÉVREUX MAY COMPEL HIS SUBJECTS TO RECEIVE ORDERS AND TO RESIDE

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Évreux, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You have informed us that certain rural deans and rectors of churches in your diocese refuse, when ordered by you, to receive sacred orders and to reside personally in their deaneries and churches, as the care of them requires. They claim that certain indulgences have been granted them by the Apostolic See, by which, it is said, they are not bound and cannot be compelled to do these things. They also refuse to perform the duties to which they are bound by reason of those deaneries and churches. Consequently, the said deaneries and churches are deprived of their due services.

We therefore, inclining to your supplications, grant your fraternity full and free authority, after prior admonition, to compel those deans and rectors, by withholding the revenues of the said deaneries and churches, to receive sacred orders at the appointed times; to reside personally in those deaneries and churches; and to perform the aforesaid duties as they are bound to do. No such indulgences, nor any apostolic letters prejudicial to truth and justice, shall stand in the way.

Finally, if their insolence requires it, while they remain in such contumacy for the prescribed period, you may deprive them of those deaneries and churches and confer them, insofar as pertains to you, upon suitable persons who are willing and able to serve in those deaneries and churches, in the orders required by their care. You may also restrain contradictors by ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal, except only those who are engaged in the service of ourselves or of our brothers.

Given at Orvieto, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the third year of our pontificate.

## LETTER OF POPE GREGORY X ON THE SAME MATTER

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Évreux, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You have informed us that certain deans, etc. (as above).

Given at Orvieto, on the second day before the Kalends of September, in the first year of our pontificate.

## Ceremonies Observed in the Cathedral Church of Rouen in the Presence of His Lordship the Archbishop

*(From the register of the chapter of Rouen.) Tuesday, 6 April 1632, the chapter being assembled by oath and in its houses.*

The articles drawn up in the chamber of accounts concerning the ceremonies to be observed in the presence of His Lordship the Archbishop, when officiating or present at the office, were placed before the chapter today, and it was ordered that they be observed and kept in every detail and entered in the register as follows.

[Col. 0263A] If it is Sunday and the said lord is present at the sprinkling of holy water, in the place where he sits when the office is not triple, after one of the gentlemen who is officiating has sprinkled the cross and, while passing, given holy water to the deacon and subdeacon according to custom, he shall descend. When he is before the said lord, after making a profound reverence and kissing the sprinkler, he shall present it to him so that he may himself take holy water and sprinkle the officiant; the officiant shall then continue the sprinkling according to custom.

But if the said lord is in his throne or near the altar, it seems that the officiant ought to present him with the holy water before distributing it to the deacon and subdeacon, because in that case there is no impropriety, as there would be if, from the lower part of the choir, he returned toward the altar to those deacon and subdeacon and then afterward began the sprinkling again for the gentlemen who were near the said lord.

As soon as the ministers and officiants, or other persons of the church, pass before the said lord, they shall salute him with the honor and propriety required by his rank and their order, always observing a distinction between this salutation and the adoration or reverence due to the Blessed Sacrament.

When the ministers and the officiant have entered the choir, the said lord shall go up to the altar for the confession. Afterward he shall bless the incense presented to him by the deacon in the boat, while the acolyte holds the open thurible before him; once this blessing has been given, he shall return to his place.

When the subdeacon goes up to the gallery or pulpit to read the Epistle, and returns from there to the altar, he shall be content to make a reverence to the said lord as he passes before him in both directions, according to the ancient usage of this church, without placing the book of the Epistles before him, kissing his hand, or kissing his ring.

When the ministers have arrived before the said lord on their way to the pulpit or gallery for the Gospel, the subdeacon shall take incense from the acolyte and present it to the said lord so that he may bless it as it is placed in the thurible. The thurible shall be presented to him by his almoner, who will previously have taken it from the acolyte. The deacon shall then ask him for his blessing with a profound inclination in order to announce the Gospel. After receiving it, he shall present for the said lord to kiss the crucifix in the Gospel book, saying: “We adore you, O Christ,” etc.

After the Gospel has been announced, the ministers shall return to the altar. There the deacon shall incense the priest, and the subdeacon shall present the Gospel text to him to kiss. Then, returning toward the said lord, the deacon shall incense him, and the subdeacon shall present him with the Gospel book or text to kiss. In all these actions the ministers must not kiss the hand or ring of the said lord, since this is not customary in this church and the said lord is not officiating.

The blessing of the water for the chalice and of the incense for the oblation shall be given by the priest who celebrates the sacrifice.

After *Ite, missa est*, the said lord shall give the pontifical blessing in the customary manner.

When the said lord officiates at Vespers, he shall leave the sacristy vested in his pontifical vestments, accompanied by one of the dignitaries as assistant priest. Two chaplains shall walk at his sides to lift the two sides of his cope. His cross and crozier shall be carried before him by two other chaplains, and another shall be assigned to hold his miter in his hands. All of them shall be vested in copes.

Having entered his throne, he shall say the customary prayers; then he shall begin Vespers by singing *Deus, in adjutorium*, and continue by saying the chapter. The antiphon of the *Magnificat* shall be announced to him by the coped minister, who shall use the word “Monsieur” when handing him the antiphon.

While the choir continues the antiphon, the assistant priest shall present him with the boat containing the incense and shall kiss his hand or ring. Once the blessing has been given, he shall leave his throne and go to the altar when the *Magnificat* begins, allowing time for the two officiating canons to carry the incense to the chapel of Notre-Dame.

When he has arrived at the altar, the assistant priest shall present him with the thurible, kissing his hand or ring; he shall do the same again when taking back the thurible.

When the incensing of the altar has been completed, he shall return to his throne. Meanwhile, the two aforementioned canons shall incense the tombs or burial places of the kings and the altar of the chapel of Notre-Dame. Having returned to the choir, they shall incense the said lord and, if required, Monsieur the Dean; the remainder shall continue according to the usage of this church.

After the *Magnificat* and the antiphon have been completed with the neume, he shall sing *Dominus vobiscum* and the prayer with its final clause, and at the end repeat *Dominus vobiscum*. If there are several prayers because of commemorations or the station of the *Inviolata*, he shall repeat *Dominus vobiscum* again at the end of the last prayer. When *Deo gratias* has been sung, he shall give the pontifical blessing to the people, either from his throne if there is no station, or in the nave if there is a station.

Done on the day and in the year stated above.

Signed, L. Patry.

## CHARTER OF JOHN BY WHICH THE PRIORY OF SAINT-VICTOR IN THE PAYS DE CAUX IS RAISED TO AN ABBEY

*(Year 1074.)*

*(Gallia Christiana, Instruments, vol. XI, p. 15, from Pommeraye, Council of Rouen, p. 97.)*
[Col. 0263D] John, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, to all the faithful of Christ, greeting, grace, and blessing.

Let it be known to all, present and future, that a petition from Roger of Mortemer and his wife Advita came before us, before Lord William, king of the English, and before me, as we sat and deliberated on ecclesiastical and secular affairs with the bishops assembled in a certain council in the city of Rouen. We sought to persuade Lord Nicholas, abbot of Saint-Ouen of Rouen and our kinsman, that, for the love of God and of us, he should permit an abbey to be established from a certain priory belonging to the church of Saint Victor in Caux, in which monks of Saint-Ouen lived. This church was called Saint Victor. A certain priest named Tormer, whose right it was, had given it as alms to the church of Saint-Ouen for the salvation of his soul, with the consent of William, then duke of the Normans; Malger, archbishop of Rouen; and Roger of Mortemer, in whose fief it lay. He had thereafter become a monk in the church of Saint-Ouen, together with a certain fosterling of his named Gilbert.

The aforesaid Roger granted that he would increase the revenues of the church of Saint Victor and of the church of Saint-Ouen sufficiently for the monks to serve God there honorably, and so that these revenues would adequately support them; and that the church of Saint-Ouen should eternally possess in the abbey the same dominion that it had previously held in the priory.

When the aforesaid abbot Nicholas, with the consent of his chapter, at our request and for the love of Roger and his wife, had granted these things, he sent a certain monk of his, Ralph, appointing him abbot and establishing him in the aforesaid place. With him he sent monks of Saint-Ouen: Fulbert, Gislebert Fauvetel, Hubert Treton, and William. The condition, however, was that the dominion of Saint-Ouen in the house of Saint Victor should in no way be diminished, but that, when one abbot died, Saint-Ouen should appoint another there, just as it had formerly appointed a prior, without prejudice to the dignity of Saint-Ouen.

This agreement was established between us as valid and firm forever, and we are witnesses of it on both sides. If, in appointing an abbot, monks or laymen should rebel against the church of Saint-Ouen, then we—King William, I, John, archbishop of Rouen, and Roger of Mortemer, in whose presence this was done—by the authority of Pope Gregory and by royal power, establish and firmly command all our heirs and successors that the abbot of Saint-Ouen shall receive the church of his priory of Saint Victor, with all its appurtenances then found there, including churches, tithes, and other possessions, and shall appoint a prior in that church as he formerly used to do. Thus the church of Saint-Ouen shall not suffer loss through fraud and deceit because of its generosity, for our predecessors founded it for the salvation of their souls.

We decree that this agreement, granted by Abbot Nicholas and Roger of Mortemer before the king by our authority, shall be valid; and we have confirmed it by the privilege of this present writing and by the authority of our seal. I, John, archbishop of Rouen, have forbidden under anathema [Col. 0266B] that any cleric or layman should thereafter dare to violate it, in the presence of these bishops, who join me in excommunication: Gislebert, bishop of Évreux; Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Hugh, bishop of Lisieux; and Robert, bishop of Sées. May all violators of this act be pierced by their anathema.

The aforesaid King William of the English likewise forbade its violation under penalty of twenty ounces of gold payable to the duke of Normandy and twenty pounds to the archbishop of Rouen, in the presence of the aforesaid bishops, Fulbert the archdeacon, and Roger of Mortemer, in whose presence this was done, in the year 1074 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Col. 0265]

CHARTER concerning the right of institution, removal, provision, correction, and other matters, which the bishop of Avranches fully retained over the monastery of Saint Michael, its abbot, and twelve canons. (Year 1061.)

(Petit, *Theodori Poenitentiale*, II, 664, from the *Pontifical Book of the Church of Avranches*.)

[Col. 0265C] In the year 1061 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Ranulf, abbot of Mont Saint-Michel, a prudent man in the governance alike of clergy and people and of the monastic order, approached John, the venerable bishop of Avranches, concerning certain burdens that were very frequently imposed upon the clergy and people of the Mount by episcopal threats. They were compelled to come to Avranches to answer any accusation against the Christian community. Neither the rising sea nor the ambushes of the Bretons could excuse them, since these obstacles could be anticipated; and thus they often incurred episcopal fines and compensations and were frequently wearied by oaths.

Because of these matters, the abbot offered the bishop, for the rights that he was to retain at the Mount, one garment each year from his own resources—one suitable for so noble and exalted a person to receive graciously and for the abbot of the Mount to give honorably—together with three pounds of incense, three pounds of pepper, six tablets of wax weighing nine pounds, and three candles at the Purification of Saint Mary: one of white wax, weighing one pound, for the bishop’s hands, and two of another wax, each weighing one pound, for the hands of the dean and treasurer.

The aforesaid bishop, noble in spirit and lineage, agreed to the abbot’s petition and made him his archdeacon at the Mount, but on the condition that, if he did anything improperly or was unable to do something, the bishop would correct it at Avranches and settle it by ecclesiastical judgment.

As for unlawful marriages, if legitimate witnesses came forward, they were to be heard before the bishop, and whatever had been presumed contrary to law was to be dissolved by their oath. For criminal offenses, penitents, confessors, or convicted persons were to come before the judgment and sentence of the bishop, after appearing before their own archdeacon. Those excommunicated by the bishop were to come to him for satisfaction and absolution. The trial by heated iron and boiling water was to be conducted at Avranches if clerics were found to have fallen into an offense deserving degradation, because ordination belonged to the bishop and degradation belonged to his judgment. Suspension from office for lesser offenses was to be entrusted to the abbot’s judgment as a corrective measure.

Such was the agreement made between the bishop and the abbot concerning the village of the Mount.

In the monastery of Saint Michael, however, the bishop retained the entire episcopal right over the abbot, the monks, and the twelve canons. In the monastery he has the duty of performing the dedication; whatever is offered at the altar during it belongs to the bishop, as does whatever is offered into the hands of his chaplains; and he and all who come with him must be provided for abundantly and honorably. Horses, fresh water, and all other necessities must be found in the monastery.

On that day the aforesaid garment for the bishop, wax, pepper, and incense must be ready, as well as three candles for the Purification of Saint Mary. Even if the bishop is absent, the abbot, with two of the canons, must attend the synod twice a year, unless he has remained away with the bishop’s permission, as must the priests of the Mount.

Whenever more serious cases arise, the bishop shall send word to the abbot and summon him; he must come unless he presents an unavoidable and legally valid excuse. The abbot shall not knowingly communicate with anyone excommunicated by the bishop, nor shall he excommunicate any named parishioner of the bishop residing outside the Mount without consulting the bishop.

On the Thursday of Pentecost the monks shall come to Avranches with the head of Saint Aubert, proceeding in a great procession of all the clergy and laity who hold houses to the church of Saint Andrew, in which the bishop himself once sat. They owe the cathedral church a penny’s worth of wax, as to the episcopal seat from which they receive care for their souls. The abbot, either personally or through his dean, is to provide oil and chrism for distribution and for the priests to perform Christian rites.

All the canons are under the bishop’s prior. When canonries—that is, prebends—become vacant, he must distribute them as he deems appropriate. Saint Aubert, to whom that Mount was granted as a divine gift, established them; and from his episcopal property he gave, for his own use and theirs, two estates to the church he had built, namely Ilium and Genecium.

[Col. 0267]

COUNCIL OF ROUEN, celebrated in the basilica of Saint Mary at Rouen by John, archbishop, with his suffragans, while William, king of the English, governed Normandy, in the year of Christ 1072, the eleventh year of Pope Alexander II, and the thirteenth year of Philip I, king of the French.

(Labbe, *Councils*, IX, 1225.)

TITLES OF THE CANONS

[Col. 0267C]

I. That the bishop consecrate chrism and oil at the proper hour and with twelve priests.

II. That all chrism and oil be renewed by the archdeacons.

III. With what care the deans are to distribute chrism and oil.

IV. That whoever celebrates Mass must receive Communion.

V. That a priest baptize fasting and wearing an alb and stole.

VI. That the viaticum and blessed water not be kept beyond eight days, and that consecrated hosts not be consecrated again.

VII. That Confirmation be administered to the fasting by the fasting and with fire.

VIII. That the sacred orders be conferred after Saturday, or on Sunday morning, upon those who are fasting by those who are fasting.

IX. That the observance of the Four Ember Seasons be exact.

X. That those who are secretly or improperly advanced to sacred orders deserve deposition.

[Col. 0267D] XI. Concerning those who abandon their tonsures; and that those to be ordained come to the bishop on Thursday.

XII. That wandering or expelled monks, and likewise nuns, be compelled to return to their monasteries.

XIII. That pastoral charges not be bought or sold.

XIV. Concerning the rite of marriage, that marriages not be contracted secretly or between blood relatives.

XV. Concerning married clerics: that they not minister in churches or receive revenues, and what archdeacons and deans ought to be.

XVI. That no one, after his wife’s death, take the woman with whom he had previously been accused of adultery.

XVII. That no one take another wife while a veiled wife survives.

[Col. 0268C] XVIII. That the wife of an absent husband not marry another before learning that her husband has died.

XIX. That clerics who have fallen into a public crime not be readily restored to sacred orders.

XX. That a bishop who cannot come to depose a fallen cleric send a representative.

XXI. That during Lent no one eat before the evening hour.

XXII. That the service of Holy Saturday not begin before the ninth hour.

XXIII. Concerning the transfer of saints’ feasts.

XXIV. That general baptism be performed only on Holy Saturday and Pentecost. Infants are to be baptized whenever they ask; no one is to be baptized on Epiphany except in case of illness.

PREFACE

In the year 1072 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a council was assembled in the metropolitan see of the city of Rouen, in the basilica of the blessed and glorious Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, over which John, archbishop of that city, presided. Following the footsteps of the Fathers, he provided in every way for the benefit of the Church, together with his suffragans: Odo of Bayeux, Hugh of Lisieux, Robert of Sées, Michael of Avranches, and Gislebert of Évreux.

First, they discussed the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity. In accordance with the decrees of the holy councils—namely, Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon—they confirmed and sanctioned it, professing that they believed it with all their hearts. After this profession of the catholic faith, the following chapters of catholic doctrine were appended.

CANONS

[Col. 0269A]

I. That the bishop consecrate chrism and oil at the proper hour and with twelve priests.

First, we decreed that, in accordance with the statutes of the Fathers, the consecration of chrism and oil for baptism and anointing should take place at the proper hour, that is, after None, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers. The bishop must also ensure that, during the consecration itself, he has with him twelve or more priests clothed in priestly vestments.

II. That all chrism and oil be renewed by the archdeacons.

Likewise, in certain provinces a detestable custom has arisen: some archdeacons, lacking a pastor, receive portions of oil and chrism from some bishop and mix them with their own oil. This too has been condemned. Rather, each archdeacon must present all his chrism and oil to the bishop by whom it is to be consecrated, as to his own bishop.

III. With what care the deans are to distribute chrism and oil.

Likewise, the distribution of chrism and oil must be carried out by the deans with the greatest diligence and propriety, so that while distributing it they are dressed in albs; and it must be distributed in vessels of such a kind that none of it is lost through any negligence.

IV. That whoever celebrates Mass must receive Communion.

Likewise, it has been decreed that no one should celebrate Mass unless he receives Communion.

V. That a priest baptize fasting and wearing an alb and stole.

[Col. 0269C] Likewise, no priest may baptize an infant unless he is fasting and clothed in an alb and stole, except in case of necessity.

VI. That the viaticum and blessed water not be kept beyond eight days, and that consecrated hosts not be consecrated again.

Likewise, there are some who keep the viaticum and blessed water beyond the eighth day; this too has been condemned. Others, lacking hosts, consecrate those that have already been consecrated; this is strictly forbidden.

VII. That Confirmation be administered to the fasting by the fasting and with fire.

Likewise, it has been decreed that the gift of the Holy Spirit be given only to those who are fasting and by those who are fasting, and that Confirmation itself not be performed without fire.

VIII. That the sacred orders be conferred after Saturday, or on Sunday morning, upon those who are fasting by those who are fasting.

[Col. 0269D]

It has also been decreed that, in conferring sacred orders, we must not be found violating apostolic authority. For it is read in the decrees of Pope Leo that sacred orders are not celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but after Saturday, at the beginning of that night which dawns into the first day of the week, the sacred blessing is to be conferred upon those who are to be consecrated, while they are fasting and by those who are fasting.

The same observance is maintained if the rite is celebrated on Sunday morning, with Saturday’s fast continued. The beginning of the preceding night is not separated from that time, and there is no doubt that it belongs to the day of the Resurrection, as is also made clear at the Lord’s Pasch.

IX. That the observance of the Four Ember Seasons be exact.

[Col. 0270A]

Likewise, the observance of the Four Ember Seasons is to be maintained by us at the proper times, according to divine institution and common observance: in the first week of March, the second of June, the third of September, and likewise in December, out of reverence for the Lord’s Nativity. For it is altogether unworthy that the institution of the saints should be neglected because of worldly occupations or concerns.

X. That those who are secretly or improperly advanced to sacred orders deserve deposition.

Likewise, clerics who, without being elected or called, or without the bishop’s knowledge, intrude themselves into sacred orders—some upon whom the bishop lays his hand as upon deacons, while others, without possessing the remaining orders, are consecrated deacons or priests—deserve deposition.

XI. Concerning those who abandon their tonsures; and that those to be ordained come to the bishop on Thursday.

Likewise, those who have received blessed tonsures and abandoned them are to be excommunicated until they have made adequate satisfaction. Clerics who are to be ordained must come to the bishop on Thursday.

XII. That wandering or expelled monks, and likewise nuns, be compelled to return to their monasteries.

Likewise, monks and nuns who, having abandoned their own churches, wander throughout the world, and those who have been expelled from monasteries because of their wickedness, are to be compelled by pastoral authority to return to their monasteries. If their abbots refuse to receive the expelled persons, they are to give them food as alms, which they may earn by the labor of their hands, until they are seen to have amended their lives.

XIII. That pastoral charges not be bought and sold.

Likewise, pastoral charges—namely, parish churches—are bought and sold by laymen, clerics, and even monks. It is forbidden that this continue.

XIV. Concerning the rite of marriage, that marriages not be contracted secretly or between blood relatives.

Likewise, marriages are not to be contracted secretly or after the midday meal. Rather, the bridegroom and bride, fasting, are to be blessed by a fasting priest in the monastery. Before they come together, the ancestry of both is to be carefully investigated. If any blood relationship is found within the seventh generation, they are not to be joined, even if one of them has been dismissed. The priest who acts contrary to this is to be deposed.

XV. Concerning married clerics: that they not minister in churches or receive revenues; and what archdeacons and deans ought to be.

Concerning priests, Levites, and subdeacons who have taken women for themselves, the Council of Lisieux is to be observed, so that they do not govern churches either personally or through their suffragans, nor possess any part of the benefices. The archdeacons who are to govern them must not be permitted to have either a concubine, an “introduced woman,” or a mistress; rather, they must live chastely and justly and provide their subjects with an example of chastity and holiness.

It is also necessary that such deans be chosen as know how to rebuke and correct their subjects, [Col. 0271A] whose lives are not infamous but who are deservedly placed above their subjects.

XVI. That no one, after his wife’s death, take the woman with whom he had previously been accused of adultery.

Likewise, it is forbidden that anyone who, while his wife was alive, had been accused of adultery with a woman should ever take that woman after his wife’s death. Many evils have arisen from this. Indeed, many men have killed their wives for this reason.

XVII. That no one take another wife while a veiled wife survives.

Likewise, no one whose wife has been veiled may ever take another while she is alive.

XVIII. That the wife of an absent husband not marry another before learning that her husband has died.

Likewise, if the wife of a man who has gone abroad or departed elsewhere marries another man before she has certainty of the first husband’s death, she is to be excommunicated until she has made adequate satisfaction.

XIX. That clerics who have fallen into a public crime not be readily restored to sacred orders.

Likewise, it has been decreed that those who are found publicly to have fallen into criminal sins not be restored to sacred orders too quickly. For, as blessed Gregory says, if permission is granted to those who have fallen to return to their order, the vigor of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since no one would fear to conceive desires for evil action through hope of returning.

Therefore this must remain established: one who has fallen into public crime is in no way to be restored to his former rank before completing his penance, except in the greatest necessity, and only after making adequate satisfaction through a long and worthy penance.

XX. That a bishop who cannot come to depose a fallen cleric send a representative.

[Col. 0271C]

Likewise, if someone who deserves deposition is found to have fallen, and as many fellow bishops as authority requires are needed for his deposition—namely, six for the deposition of a priest and three for that of a deacon—each one who cannot be present must send a representative with his authority.

XXI. That during Lent no one eat before the evening hour.

[Col. 0272A]

Likewise, it has been decreed that no one should dine during Lent before, after None has ended, the evening hour begins. For one who eats beforehand does not fast.

XXII. That the service of Holy Saturday not begin before the ninth hour.

Likewise, it has been decreed that on Holy Saturday the service not begin before None. It looks toward the night of the Lord’s Resurrection, out of reverence for which “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia” are sung. This is also shown at the beginning of the service, namely in the blessing of the candles. The *Book of the Offices* relates that no celebration of the sacrament takes place during these two days. It calls these two days Friday and Saturday, during which the mourning and grief of the apostles are commemorated.

XXIII. Concerning the transfer of saints’ feasts.

Likewise, if the feast of a saint falls on a day on which it cannot be celebrated, it is to be celebrated not beforehand but within the eighth day.

XXIV. That general baptism be performed only on Holy Saturday and Pentecost. Infants are to be baptized whenever they ask; no one is to be baptized on Epiphany except in case of illness.

Likewise, in accordance with the decrees of the holy Fathers, namely Popes Innocent and Leo, we decree that general baptism be performed only on Holy Saturday and Pentecost. This provision is to be observed, however, that infants are not to be denied the bath of regeneration at whatever time or on whatever day they ask for it. We altogether forbid anyone to be baptized on the vigil or day of Epiphany except in case of illness.

John, archbishop of Rouen; Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Michael, bishop of Avranches; Gislebert, bishop of Évreux; and many other venerable abbots consented to this council. At that time the monasteries of Normandy flourished nobly and maintained monastic discipline.

APPENDIX

[ACTS OF THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ROUEN]

[Col. 0271]

NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

(From Mabillon, *Analecta veterum*, old edition, p. 222.)

An anonymous monk of the monastery of Saint-Ouen in the same city committed to writing the acts of the bishops of Rouen. This edition has been prepared from his autograph. He lived under Pope Gregory VII, John, archbishop of Rouen, and Nicholas, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Ouen. Perhaps he was none other than Fulbert, a monk of that place, who dedicated to the same Abbot Nicholas his as yet unpublished book *On the Miracles of Saint Ouen*; or Theoderic, who likewise dedicated the metrical *Life of Saint Ouen* to Nicholas.

I refrain from adding more extensive notes to these acts, since the history of the bishops of Rouen has already been sufficiently illuminated by our fellow Francis Pomeraius, who composed it in the French language a few years ago with learning and accuracy, using the reading of the earlier Acts, which may serve as evidence for his history.

Here I observe only two things. First, among the bishops of Rouen these Acts assign no place to Hugh, son of Charlemagne, whose Life was written by Bishop Baldric, who incorrectly numbered him among the archbishops of Rouen, as I have shown more fully elsewhere in volume I of the third century of the Benedictine order.

Second, Archbishop Maurilius held a synod of the bishops of the province, at which a sentence was pronounced against Berengar and his heresy—namely, in the year 1063 from the Lord’s Incarnation. In that year he performed the dedication of the restored church of Rouen, with William, duke of the Normans, present together with all his suffragans. With them, says our Anonymous, he religiously and vigorously celebrated a council concerning the preservation of chastity and the restoration of the other institutions of the holy Fathers, which the negligence of pastors had carelessly set aside.

[Col. 0273]

ACTS OF THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ROUEN

[Col. 0273A] There are eighteen provinces of Gaul. One of them is Lyonnaise, called the Second, in which there is a noble and extensive city called Rodomus or Rotomagus, situated on the River Seine. The church of this city is consecrated in honor of the blessed and glorious Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary.

This is a metropolitan church. For beneath it are six episcopal cities: first, the city of the Baiocasses; second, the city of the Abrincati; third, the city of the Evatini, which is called Ébroicas; fourth, the city of the Salii, which is called Sées; fifth, the city of the Lexovii; and sixth, the city of the Constantii.

In the aforesaid city of Rouen, the distinguished Mallonus was first in succession. The placement of these words troubles some people who do not examine them carefully enough, since their desire to have the most blessed Niga­sius regarded as the first bishop of the aforesaid city is in no way contradicted by this statement, provided it is supported by a somewhat subtle explanation.

Let both clerics and monks therefore take care not to err. By examining the Scriptures more perceptively, let them judge that both claims can appropriately stand. Those who assert that Mallonus was first in the see of Rouen speak properly. No one preceded him with respect to the possession of the archiepiscopal office. Yet those who affirm that blessed Nigasius was the first archbishop of that same see do not speak falsely.

Indeed, I believe it has now been made clear to many that he was ordained at Rome by blessed Pope Clement as bishop of the city of Rouen, which was not yet subject to anyone’s pastoral yoke. Nor is this a trivial or uncertain matter, but firm and established, as his Passion testifies. With blessed Dionysius, by permission of Pope Clement, he came down to the Gallic regions; and before he could reach his own see, which, as we have said, he had received at Rome, he suffered martyrdom by decapitation, together with Quirinus and Scuviculus, though somewhat nearer the borders of the Northmen.

Thus each may truly be called “first,” but in a different manner: Nigasius according to ordination, Mallonus according to residence in the place. In this way it may be said: Nigasius was the first bishop of the city of Rouen to be ordained, whereas Mallonus was the first to be installed in the see.

[Col. 0273D] Thus the following verse can stand without contradiction:

The distinguished Mallonus was first in succession,

Adorned with character and born of a renowned lineage.

He shone in speech and excelled in noble deeds;

Generous in all things, merciful and liberal toward the needy.

He healed the weak in spirit through sacred doctrine,

And cleansed those tormented by demons through sacred power.

Ever watchful among the people, a devout shepherd and watchman,

He made himself a wall against the enemy on behalf of those entrusted to him.

Compassionate toward the sick, he strengthened the crushed.

[Col. 0274A] He continually sacrificed to the Lord by offering sacred rites,

Asking for perpetual peace and salvation.

He sweetly preserved enemies as dear brothers.

He was humble, temperate, and pure of heart.

Free from stains, he shone with the lamp of virtues. He died in Christ on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.

Avidiamus succeeded blessed Mallonus. Under blessed Pope Sylvester and the emperor Constantine, he governed the aforesaid Church. He was a prudent and vigorous shepherd among the people. He is found to have attended the first Council of Arles, which was assembled at the same time as the Council of Nicaea, together with Maternus, bishop of Cologne.

This blessed bishop was upright in intellect, distinguished in conduct, and provident for the salvation of those subject to him. Severus succeeded him; Eusebius succeeded Severus; Marcellinus succeeded Eusebius; Peter succeeded Marcellinus; and Victricius succeeded Peter.

Victricius had been raised at the royal court together with blessed Pope Innocent, as is found in the letter that the same pope sent to Victricius concerning the preservation of chastity and other institutions of the Christian religion. Among other things, he says:

“Moreover, certain of our brothers frequently strive to make clerics of court officials or persons occupied with various public functions. Later, when the emperor orders that they be recalled, greater sorrow than gratitude arises for them. Let the concern and sorrow of the brothers serve as an example—sorrow that we have often endured in the emperor’s presence, when we first pleaded for them, as you, who were present with us, know.

“He was insisting with great distress that not only lower-ranking clerics from among the court officials, but even those established in the priesthood, should be returned.”

For he was a most illustrious shepherd: stern in pursuing the crimes of the people, a most gentle father to widows and orphans, merciful to the poor, and compassionate toward all who were weak and afflicted.

Innocent succeeded him; Saint Evodus succeeded Innocent; Sylvester succeeded Evodus; Malsonus succeeded Sylvester; Germanus succeeded Malsonus; and blessed Gildardus succeeded Germanus. Gildardus was the brother of blessed Medardus, whose life blessed Fortunatus wrote in magnificent style. They were born on the same day, ordained on the same day, and likewise departed to Christ on the same day.

Blessed Flavius succeeded Gildardus. During his pontificate, a church was built in honor of blessed Peter the Apostle in the suburb of the city of Rouen, nobly constructed in the first year of Clothar, king of the Franks. The body of blessed Ouen, his successor, was buried there.

This blessed Flavius, in the five-hundredth year [lacuna] from the Lord’s Incarnation, endowed with many virtues and inflamed by the fervor of divine love, generous toward the poor, governed the church of Rouen.

Praetextatus succeeded him, a man of great holiness and hated by all the wicked. He lived in the time of King Chilperic, son of Clothar. Chilperic was a man of excessive cruelty and, together with his impious wife Fredegund, burned with intense hatred against the bishop.

The cause of this hatred was nothing other than Praetextatus’s great love for Chilperic’s brother, King Sigibert, who had been killed through Chilperic’s treachery, and the same love that he continued to show toward Sigibert’s son Childebert and his mother Brunhild.

For this reason Chilperic became angry and brought an accusation against him, alleging that Praetextatus had concealed a large part of his brother Sigibert’s treasure with himself, which he had returned to Childebert, his nephew, after Childebert had begun a lawsuit against him.

He persecuted him so severely that he removed him from the episcopate and expelled him into exile on an island in the sea belonging to the district of Coutances, and caused Melantius the archdeacon to be ordained bishop in his place.

The manner of his expulsion was as follows. The king summoned his bishops to a council, which Gregory, archbishop of Tours, a man of great authority and integrity, attended. Gregory gave no assent either to the crafty scheme by which the bishop was deceived or to his unjust deposition.

The king, however, through impious cunning, sent word to certain bishops [lacuna] that, if Praetextatus acknowledged the charges brought against him in the council and, prostrating himself before the king, declared himself guilty, the king would entirely forgive him. Deceived by the urging of the impious bishops, he yielded to the king’s fraudulent commands.

Then the king began to cry out: “You have heard him convicted of the crime; now determine a definite sentence concerning it.” And so they deposed him, and the king ordered him to be confined in the aforesaid exile.

After the king’s death, through the counsel and judgment of all the leading men and fellow bishops, and against the will of Queen Fredegund, he was recalled to his own church. Melantius was deposed, and Praetextatus was enthroned in his own see.

Melantius, however, remained in the intimacy of the most impious Queen Fredegund, who was always hostile toward and plotting against blessed Praetextatus. She eventually corrupted, through money, the minds of certain men together with the aforesaid Melantius, so that, as blessed Gregory of Tours relates in his writings, on the holy night of Easter they struck him with swords in the episcopal place where he was accustomed to stand and thus killed him.

As soon as he felt the wounds, he ran to the altar and embraced it. Fortifying himself with the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, he surrendered his soul to God.

All the leading men of the country, grieving with great wailing and lamentation over the desolation of the protection of so great a shepherd, committed his body to honorable burial.

Later Melantius, who had usurped the episcopate during Praetextatus’s exile, was restored to the same see through the counsel and influence of the aforesaid queen.

Bishop Hildulfus succeeded him, a prudent and honorable man. Blessed Romanus succeeded Hildulfus, noble by birth and illustrious in virtue. Saint Ouen, born of distinguished parents and exalted by the greatness of his virtues, succeeded blessed Romanus.

The renowned Ansbertus, a venerable bishop and glorious for his holy works, succeeded blessed Ouen. We have touched only briefly upon the memory of these three and of blessed Gildardus, because their deeds have been written out clearly among us by highly reliable authors.

The venerable Grippo succeeded Ansbertus. Ranilandus, a venerable and honorable man, succeeded Grippo. Saint Hugh, who was of venerable life and great integrity, succeeded Ranilandus, as his Life testifies.

Ratbertus, a prudent and vigorous man, succeeded Hugh. Grimo succeeded Ratbertus. This man was of great nobility and integrity and governed the people entrusted to him very well, both by the example of his good works and by his preaching. He increased the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, over whose see he presided, with his own estates and numerous benefactions. For he gave Fontanas, situated on the River Iton, with all its appurtenances.

Rainfredus succeeded Grimo, a man born of noble lineage and instructed in literary studies, who increased the church through his own benefactions. For he gave it, in the territory of Vexin, an estate called Cramisiacum, and acquired many benefactions from noblemen for the use of his church.

Rainfred was succeeded by Remigius, of blessed memory. He was the son of Charles, who was called mayor of the royal palace, and the brother of Carloman, who, having abandoned the portion of the kingdom that he possessed, became a monk on Mount Soracte, where he built a church in honor of Saint Sylvester; from there he transferred to the monastery of Saint Benedict on Monte Cassino. This Remigius was also the brother of Pippin, whom Pope Stephen consecrated king. This Pippin, at the prayers of his brother Carloman the monk, instructed the aforesaid Archbishop Remigius to go to the place called Floriacum and to return to Carloman’s envoys the body of Benedict, who rested there.

When Remigius came to the place and summoned the abbot who at that time governed the monastery—his name was Medo—he entered the church with the envoys, explaining the king’s commands. When they had approached the sepulchre of the blessed man, they were suddenly struck blind. Accordingly, shaken by great terror, they prostrated themselves flat on the ground before the aforesaid abbot and the brothers of that place, begging for mercy and asking them to pray to the Lord on their behalf, so that he might forgive them. Blessed Remigius promised that he would never again remove the saint’s body from that place. What more is there to say? They were immediately heard, and blessed Remigius and his companions recovered their former health.

He then asked the aforesaid abbot to provide them with relics of the blessed man’s body, lest the place where he had devoutly served God be deprived of so great a protection; the abbot willingly consented. Thus, when the envoys returned to their own country, blessed Remigius returned to his. He acquired many benefits for his Church and bestowed much from his own property. Over the flock entrusted to him he proved a most noble and vigilant man, distinguished also in character and conduct, and he rested in a blessed end.

Blessed Remigius was succeeded by Mainard, a venerable bishop; Mainard by Guillebert, who governed the bishopric decently and honorably in the time of the emperor Charlemagne. Guillebert was succeeded by Rainoward, worthy of episcopal rank. Rainoward was succeeded by Gunbald, noble by ancestry and distinguished by his zeal for good works. Gunbald was succeeded by Paul, a gentle and most prudent prelate. Paul was succeeded by Wanilo, a bishop devoted to God and most reverent in all things [Col. 0277A]. Wanilo was succeeded by Adalard, the nephew of Archbishop Gunbald, who was religious in all his works. Adalard was succeeded by Riculfus, a noble man, rich in many estates, with which he endowed the Church entrusted to him.

He lived in the time of King Charles, the father of King Louis, whose son was King Lothair; in Lothair the lineage of Charlemagne was utterly uprooted from the kingdom. For Duke Hugh, surnamed the Great, usurped the kingdom for himself and was consecrated king. He was succeeded in the government by his son Rotbert, a king devoted to God. The aforesaid Riculfus caused the charters of the Church to be confirmed by that king’s royal sanction. Riculfus was succeeded by John, a devout and religious bishop; John by Witto, an honorable and most reverent shepherd.

[Col. 0277B] Witto was succeeded by Franco, a prudent bishop and a good helper of the people. In his time Rollo, duke of the Danes, invaded the country called France, now marked by their name as Normandy. The ferocity of his mind he so softened—*dilinivit*—by divine words as well as by devout services that he governed the land he had acquired with peace and justice. Later, accepting the Christian law through the preaching of the aforesaid bishop, he was baptized by him, and, persevering in the Catholic faith, departed to Christ in a good end.

Franco was succeeded by Gunhard, a wise and provident man in all things. Gunhard was succeeded by Hugh. He was indeed distinguished by ancestry but ignoble in all his works. For he was a monk at Saint-Denis when William, the son of Rollo, duke of the Normans, bestowed the bishopric upon him [Col. 0277C]; but, setting aside the institutions of the holy Rule, he gave himself entirely to carnal wantonness. He fathered many sons, destroyed the Church and the Church’s possessions. For he gave Todiniacum, which belonged to the archbishop’s demesne, together with all its appurtenances, to his brother Radulf, a very powerful man, the son of Hugh of Calvacamp, and thus alienated it from the archbishopric’s demesne down to the present.

He was succeeded by Rotbert, a most noble and powerful man, the son of Richard I. This man was of great piety and honesty, and was so highly praised by secular men for his worldly wealth; but, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, he fathered many sons. He also did much good for the Church. For he began to build the present church with wondrous workmanship and great magnificence. Before his death, by God’s prevenient grace, he amended his life. He abandoned the woman [with whom he had lived] and did penance for this and his other wicked acts; and thus, with a good end, insofar as human frailty can attain it, he rested.

Rotbert was succeeded by his nephew Malgerius, for he was the son of his brother Richard. Since he had obtained the episcopal see in childhood not through the merit of election but through the carnal affection of his parents and the support of flatterers, deprived of all protection, he preferred to obey flesh and blood rather than the divine commands. Following pleasure in everything, he childishly distributed the Church’s ornaments and other benefices. Therefore, by the authority of Pope Leo, William, duke of the Normans and later king of the English, with the assistance of the aforesaid pope’s legate, namely Hermenfrid, bishop of Sées, and the other bishops of the province, deprived him of the episcopate in the church of Lisieux [Col. 0278A]. He later gave him a certain island situated in the sea in the county of Coutances, where he lived for many years, though not as was fitting; afterward, by what divine judgment is unknown, he was drowned in the sea.

After Malgerius had been deposed, Duke William chose a certain monk named Maurilius. Born of noble stock in the territory of Reims and educated in the church of that same city, he was then instructed in every liberal art in the Church of Liège and became head of the school of the Church of Halberstadt, a place regarded as exceedingly wealthy in Saxony, where he lived honorably for many years [Col. 0278B]. Later, inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland and scorning all that belongs to the world, he desired the monastic life. Thus, going to the monastery of Fécamp, he became a monk there, living holily for a long time and offering the others an example of sanctity.

Finally, burning with the fire of divine love and choosing a harsher life, he obtained permission from the abbot who governed the church and went to Italy. Living as a hermit and leading a solitary life, he supported himself by the work of his hands. When the abbot of the Florentine church—which had been built in honor of blessed Mary ever-virgin—died, the margrave Boniface, a noble and most powerful man, chose him. Thus, although unwilling, overcome by the admonitions of good men, he was ordained abbot of that place. There he governed his subjects holily and according to the Rule for a long time, to the best of his ability [Col. 0278C].

But since the life of the righteous is the ruin of the wicked, the monks who had lived without discipline in the time of his predecessor, unwilling to endure the strictness of the Rule of Father Benedict by which he had bound them to regular observance, and resisting him in every good work, plotted to destroy his life. Since he labored at this for many years and saw that he was making no progress with them, he took thought for his own safety, abandoned the abbey, and returned to his own place, namely Fécamp, where he lived holily until he was enthroned in the bishopric.

He completed the church begun by Archbishop Rotbert. With William, duke of the Normans and later king of the English, in attendance, together with all his suffragan bishops, he devoutly held a council in the church of Rouen concerning the preservation of chastity and the vigorous restoration of the other institutions of the holy Fathers, which through the negligence of pastors had been carelessly set aside [Col. 0278D]. After the church had been completed, he dedicated it in the presence of William, duke of the Normans, in the year 1063 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while Henry, the most noble king of the Franks, was reigning. The bishops of the province were also present: Odo of Bayeux, John of Avranches, Hugh of Lisieux, William of Évreux, Ivo of Sées, Geoffrey of Coutances, and the other venerable abbots; Pope Victor II was also presiding over the apostolic see. He did much good as well for the restoration of Christian law and ecclesiastical religion. Devoting himself to fasts, prayers, and almsgiving until his final day [Col. 0279A], he gave his soul to God on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

When the venerable bishop Maurilius had died, the aforesaid William, king of the English, sent Lanfranc, the most reverend abbot of the Church of Caen, instructed in all the liberal arts and adorned with holy character and works, to Alexander, the supreme pontiff and venerable pope. Lanfranc was later appointed bishop and primate of the English Church of Canterbury. The king asked the pope’s clemency to grant his consent, so that by his authority he might place John, bishop of the Church of Avranches, over the metropolitan Church, and command him by apostolic letters not to resist this on any pretext. Since Alexander saw that the request was devout, he granted it. He sent the bishop a letter. The words contained in the letter are these:

> “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, venerable bishop of Avranches, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> [Col. 0280A] “Since the Church of Rouen has been deprived of a pastor, etc.”

See, in the entry for the year 1073 under Pope Alexander II, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVI.

When Bishop John had received the apostolic legation, and his election had been made by the common consent of all the bishops of the province and all the canons of that Church, he obtained the metropolitan see. He was of noble birth and instructed in the liberal disciplines. He was otherwise sufficiently vigorous, etc. We have given this full account of John from *Gallia Christiana* in the preface to John, up to the words with which it closes: “And he is honorably buried in that very church on the fifth day before the Ides of September.” The *Acts* continue:

> “He was succeeded—or rather preceded—for he was enthroned two months before John’s death—by Lord William, abbot of the monastery of Caen, by apostolic authority, royal appointment, and finally common election, a man distinguished by nobility of birth [Col. 0280B] and pre-eminent in the excellence of his character.”

## In the Year of the Lord 1079. Arnulf, a Cleric of Milan

### Notice concerning Arnulf

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores, vol. VIII, p. 1, preface to Arnulf’s *Deeds of the Archbishops of Milan*, edited by W. Wattenbach.]

[Col. 0279C] Arnulf of Milan wrote a history of events that occurred at Milan in the eleventh century, down to the year 1077, himself an eyewitness, preceded by a brief narrative of events after the year 925. We have no certain knowledge of him apart from what can be inferred from this work. He indicated his name and lineage in Book I, chapter 8, where, having spoken of Archbishop Arnulf I (970–974), he adds this: “whose namesake I am, I, the writer of the present deeds, but the true great-grandson of his brother.”

Since the ranks of the Milanese were so distinguished among themselves that the standing of the capitanei was twice as great as that of the vassals, while the merchants followed the vassals at an equal interval, and then the rest of the multitude [Note: [Col. 0279D] See the peace of the year 1067, mentioned in III, 20], it is proper to count Arnulf among the first rank. For while the chief of the decumani was born from the people [Note: [Col. 0279D] Landulf II, 35], among the ordinary ranks were the sons of kings, princes, and capitanei [Note: [Col. 0279D] Arnulf I, 3; Landulf II, 35]. It is also both intrinsically probable and shown by the election of Wido that archbishops who were to be chosen from the number of the ordinary ranks [Note: [Col. 0279D] Arnulf I, 3] had never, during these centuries—from the time when they first held the leading place among the princes of Italy [Note: That is, of the kingdom of the Lombards, which writers of that age commonly called “Italy” and “the kingdom.” Provana has shown that Tuscany was included within its boundaries, *Stud. critici*, p. 258.]—been taken from a lineage inferior to that of the capitanei. Wido’s status as belonging to the order of the vassals caused him the greatest difficulties [Note: [Col. 0279D] Apparently; for I do not deny that the matter is uncertain. See Arnulf III, 2; Landulf III, 3].

It also matters that Arnulf himself openly reveals the nobility of his lineage in more than one place: he clearly favors the cause of the nobles [Note: [Col. 0280D] As Count Giulini already observed, *Memorie di Milano*, III, 363], and calls men humbly born those whom others praise as nobles [Note: [Col. 0280D] III, 2, 10], namely the lesser knights, while he speaks of the capitanei with restraint [Note: [Col. 0280D] As of Landulf and Herlembald, III, 10, 16]. Their sublimity is gazed upon with wonder from a lowly position by the monk Andreas, who wrote the *Life of Ariald*. If you observe this, many difficulties disappear: the assertions of contemporary writers may seem to conflict with one another, yet, although they use different words, they agree in substance.

Whether Arnulf was a cleric or a layman is not established by certain testimony [Col. 0280D] [Note: Unless perhaps you wish to interpret the words in I, 1, “yet a servant of the Catholic faith,” in such a way that he there professes himself a cleric. Arnulphus the subdeacon subscribed the pledge of Archbishop Wido preserved by Peter Damian (see below, III, 14), in Baronius under the year 1059, §55. Other editions omit this name, which may have been subscribed by our historian]. But his entire manner of writing, his knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs, and his mind, always occupied with the concerns of clerics [Col. 0281A], while turned away from laymen as from outsiders, forbid us to regard him as a layman.

He relates in V, 9 that he himself took part in the embassy sent by the people of Milan to the pope in 1077, so that they might be reconciled with the Roman Church. He himself had not been free from the guilt of the others, for he favored married clerics; but then, he says, “making satisfaction for the past, he promised to correct himself in the future.” He was evidently a genuinely modest man, distrustful even of his own judgment, but he had opposed innovations and the fury of Herlembald. Earlier he had agreed with many men of his own order, although he admitted that not all their actions met with his approval [Note: [Col. 0281D] III, 14]. Finally, however, he approved stricter discipline in the Church.

Since those disturbances seemed to him of great importance and especially worthy of remembrance—disturbances by which the entire condition of the Milanese Church was changed—after the election of Atto in 1072 he turned to recording them in writing, not from a desire for fame but lest the memory of events perish, events that would afterward be precious to his fellow citizens. For the present he wished the work to be hidden “under a bushel,” to be brought forth in its own time, but never to go beyond the boundaries of the city [Note: [Col. 0281D] I, 1].

Nevertheless, it seems to have been published immediately, since the first three books, which alone he had completed at that time, circulated separately, although Landulf appears to have had no knowledge of them. Arnulf later added a fourth and a fifth book, though they were not written at one time, as he gradually withdrew from his earlier position until, finally, as we have said, he was reconciled with the Roman Church.

At the beginning of the work he also prefixed a short preface—if indeed it came from him—with the names of the kings and archbishops, and altered some passages in the earlier books. These changes are not of great importance, but they are such as to reveal the author’s hand [Note: [Col. 0281D] I, 3, 6, 9, 11, 16, 20; II, 8, 12, 16; III, 2, 8, 14, 22]. He stopped in that very year, 1077, when the long schism was brought to an end; he himself was already advanced in age, since he says that he had learned by sight of events occurring after 1018.

The Palatine editors regarded Arnulf’s reliability as sufficiently poor, considering him a heretic and therefore a liar, while neglecting more careful investigation. But already in Muratori’s preface he is said to have written with sufficient accuracy; how true this was Giulini discovered by examining each matter individually. Nor does his judgment seem less worthy of praise because he first reported simply what he had heard and then what he had seen [Note: [Col. 0281D] In I, 1, he himself promises, in generally expressed words, “a simple narrative of the deeds performed by our kings and bishops, our fellow citizens in the city of Milan or outside it, and our compatriots in the Italian kingdom—deeds I myself saw, or heard from eyewitnesses, or heard at a slightly further remove”], rejecting the stories of the common people [Col. 0281D], which Landulf eagerly collected.

He began with the reign of Hugh, king of Italy, and briefly treated in Book I the events that occurred in the kingdom thereafter down to his own time, paying particular attention to Milanese affairs. He used no books to assist him, but, as he himself says, merely “blew away” whatever he had heard [Note: [Col. 0281D] II, 1. In I, 3, he once cites the privileges of the Church]. We shall therefore readily pardon him if he occasionally erred in these matters, since he alone preserved events worth knowing and can nowhere be accused of knowingly departing from the truth.

A man born of so noble a lineage could not lack a supply of suitable sources. Having thus prepared the way, after 1018 he endeavored to pour forth, “from abundance,” as he says, what he had learned by seeing it himself. In writing he used the acts of the Roman synod of 1027 [Note: [Col. 0281D] II, 5], the constitutions made by the Roman legates at Milan [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 14, 21], and the letters of the pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 12, 20, 22]. He does mention letters sent from Rome to the opposing party in III, 17 and IV, 2, but does not seem to have examined them.

Everything preserved from these sources confirms his reliability. Although he very often departs from Landulf, a writer of the same party, he almost everywhere agrees in his narrative of events with Abbot Andreas, later of Vallombrosa, the disciple and most ardent supporter of Ariald, and with Bonizo [Note: [Col. 0282D] In the *Book to a Friend*, edited by Oefele among the *Scriptores Rerum Boicarum*, vol. II], who was wholly devoted to the papal party. This is certainly the strongest evidence of his good faith, since he nowhere concealed that he strongly disliked the agitation of Ariald and the others. Yet he was so cautious and moderate that he either refused to pass judgment on Landulf [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 16] or admitted that the clerics were partly at fault [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 14].

He did not oppose better discipline of the clergy, nor did he wish to set himself against the Roman pontiff; but he abhorred actions carried out tumultuously, lay judgments concerning clerics, and the subjection of the Milanese Church [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 12, 13, 16, 17]. He praises the peace arranged through the Roman legates in 1067, in III, 21.

He therefore wrote these things while those disturbances still continued [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, 8], while Herlembald was alive [Note: [Col. 0282D] Chapters 16, 17] and Alexander II was alive [Note: [Col. 0282D] Chapter 17], and before Gotofred had been consecrated [Note: [Col. 0282D] III, end]—that is, before the spring of 1073. He had resolved thereafter to remain silent, but when the disturbances seemed to exceed all bounds, he nevertheless took up his pen again, lest the memory of events perish. He therefore added Book IV, carrying the narrative down to the death of Herlembald (1075), which he then thought marked the end of the schism.

At the completion of the work he openly declares that he wrote under the sole impulse of a love of truth, and that he did not dissent from the teaching of those who attacked the sale of ecclesiastical offices and the incontinence of priests, but disapproved of the manner in which everything had been done. Since this now conflicts with some statements he had made earlier, he expressly adds in the following chapter, chapter 13, that he now thinks differently from before and is ashamed when he compares what ought to be written with what he has written. He says that he had not committed barbarisms in his words, but had rashly judged the statements or actions of others, since hidden things are revealed to God alone. Observe, please, that he confesses himself guilty not of having perversely narrated facts, but only of having expressed an incautious judgment. In the first chapter of Book V he again rejects the charge of lying.

After this he adds a few remarks about the election of Thedald and the dispute between Henry IV and Gregory, now openly professing that the Roman Church had never erred [Note: [Col. 0283D] V, 7], until the work closes with the reconciliation of the Milanese with the pope.

He used a simple and sufficiently pure style, although he admits that he never climbed the “wheels of the quadrivium”—*curules quadrivii rotas*, an uncertain or figurative expression. He seems nevertheless to have read Sallust [Note: [Col. 0283D] V, 9]. In III, 2, he cites Orosius; in IV, 11, the *Etymologies*. We often find in him the repeated use at the ends of sentences of similar sounds of words, which seemed beautiful to the people of that time. He paid little attention to the description of dates. He pursued brevity so earnestly that he omitted many things we would like to know, while the more extended narratives of Landulf are both obscure and scarcely worthy of belief.

Thus it happened that those who later wrote about Milanese affairs, wishing to supply the poverty of the material handed down to us, allowed themselves to be led into errors by Landulf and Gualvaneus della Flamma, the most mendacious of all men. This happened even to Count Giulini on occasion, although he brilliantly elucidated many matters. After him the very learned Fumagalli treated certain subjects more accurately. Concerning matters relating to the political condition of the Milanese republic, much has most recently been discussed by the distinguished scholars H. Leo [Note: [Col. 0283D] *Development of the Constitution of the Lombard Cities* (*Entwicklung der Verfassung der Lombardischen Städte*). Hamburg, 1824, 8vo], who seems not rarely to have attributed too much both to Flamma’s fictions and to his own opinions, and A. de Bethmann-Hollweg [Note: [Col. 0283D] *Origin of Lombard Municipal Liberty* (*Ursprung der Lombardischen Städtefreiheit*). Bonn, 1846, 8vo], who, chiefly following Arnulf, proceeded more cautiously.

## On the Manuscripts

C. L. Bethmann, who used these manuscripts for a new edition during his Italian journey, transmitted the following information to us.

1. The Schönborn manuscript, preserved at Pommersfelden, no. 2802, parchment quarto, written in Italy in the thirteenth century, contains Arnulf copied in a continuous hand, followed by Otto Morena in another hand. Neither books nor chapters are distinguished, nor are chapter tables found; but wherever chapters begin in the other manuscripts, this codex generally begins a new line with a larger letter [Col. 0283D]. Its text is excellent, and we have followed it almost everywhere.

2. The Este manuscript, summoned for use by the distinguished Muratori, is from the thirteenth century, certainly not earlier; Muratori provided a specimen of it in *Mur. SS.* IV, p. 5. The chapter headings that Muratori adopted from this manuscript—since they are absent from the other manuscripts and seem to have been added by the copyist, like those occasionally written in the margin of codex 1—were noted at first among the variant readings, but later rejected entirely. It seemed unnecessary to collate again the codex that Muratori chiefly used in preparing his edition [Col. 0284A].

3. The Sitonian manuscript, of which Leibniz obtained a copy through the kindness of Giovanni de Sitonis. Muratori transcribed another copy from the same manuscript in 1699 at the house of Camillo Sitoni, Giovanni’s father, and later corrected it with the aid of the Este codex. The third and fourth books are there compressed into one; there are no chapter headings. We have marked with “3” what is found both in Leibniz and Muratori, and with “3a” what Leibniz alone has.

4. The Archintian manuscript, from which the two final books were copied by 5* and B2*. See the note at the end of III. When the Pavia manuscript was unavailable, J. P. Puricellus used this one [Note: [Col. 0283D] *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, p. 461]. It seems to have been divided into four books, so that Books III and IV formed one book and Book V was called the fourth. It comes closest to Muratori’s text, and therefore to 2 and 3. There is no division of chapters [Col. 0284B].

5. The manuscript of the Metropolitan Church of Milan, containing Landulf, Arnulf, and the catalogue of archbishops edited by Muratori, IV, 141 [Note: [Col. 0284D] Everything is written in the same character, and therefore it is later than 1176; see Muratori, *Anecdota* I, 237. He says on p. 238 that the script and form of the letters of this codex and codex B1 are almost one and the same. He repeats this in *SS.* IV, p. 51]. It had only the first three books, but because of the similarity of its wording to that of the earlier books it must be included among them; at the beginning it has a prologue and catalogues. The Palatine Associates used it, but Bethmann later sought it in vain.

5*. Codex of the most serene Duke Litta of Milan, written in 1703, paper folio, in a continuous hand. It contains Arnulf, the elder and younger Landulf, and some other works bound with it in another hand. The first three books of Arnulf were copied from 5, and IV and V from 4 [Col. 0284C].

These manuscripts, except 5, therefore comprise the entire work and at the beginning prefix a prologue with the names of the kings and archbishops. The manuscripts that we call B, which contain only the first three books, lack these materials and sometimes depart from the others in their wording so markedly that one can easily recognize an earlier edition of the work.

B1. Codex of Francesco Castelli, ordinary canon of the Milanese Church in 1574; afterward of the Milanese archpriest A. D. Ottaviano Forrerio; afterward of the Milanese chapter; finally, in 1822, returned among the Ambrosian manuscripts under no. 89, parchment quarto, written in a continuous hand in the fourteenth century [Note: [Col. 0284D] Compare Muratori, *SS.* IV], in two columns. It contains Landulf and then Arnulf. Four quires written by an entirely different hand have been sewn in, containing the younger Landulf and the Passion of Saint Ariald [Col. 0284D]. This is the manuscript that the Palatine Associates call M, but they collated it rather inaccurately.

The parchment is partly a palimpsest; everything erased from it displays the script of thirteenth-century documents, among which one should read: “Given as above.” It has three books, marked in red at the beginning. There is no division of chapters, but the scribe very frequently inserted their red signs into the continuous text wherever he pleased. The manuscript from which he copied had been corrected here and there, so that a better word had been written above an existing one, together with the word *vel* (“or”); the scribe, not understanding this, admitted both words into the text. Its text is much inferior to that of the others. A sixteenth-century hand frequently added notes in the margin, chiefly chronological ones [Col. 0285A].

B1*. Ambrosian manuscript no. 128, paper quarto, late seventeenth century. It contains Landulf and then Arnulf, which it copied from B1; it is therefore of no importance.

B2. The Pavia manuscript, from which J. P. Puricellus published some material in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae* [Note: [Col. 0285C] See p. 303], and more in his book on Saints Ariald and Herlembald. This manuscript was the source of the following copy.

B2*. Ambrosian manuscript 157, paper folio, previously copied in 1675 by the hand of Pietro Paolo Boscha from a manuscript “which I received from Master Matteo Valerio, prior of the Pavia Charterhouse. But that manuscript contained only the first three books . . . I obtained the fourth book in another copy, which . . . Count Ottavio Archinto supplied.” It agrees almost literally with B1, but in several places has readings lacking in that manuscript, so that it cannot have been copied from B1 itself. Boscha says that the chapters were not distinguished in the Pavia manuscript [Col. 0285B].

Arnulf’s work long lay hidden in libraries, known only to Milanese writers. Gualvaneus della Flamma, for example, transcribed some passages from Arnulf “at Saint Nazarius” in his *Manipulus Florum*—for his other works remain unpublished—but he used such license that his text is of no use for recovering Arnulf’s wording. At the end of the fifteenth century Tristanus Calchus mentioned him among his authors, but nevertheless preferred to follow Flamma along with the others.

He was also known to the author of the *Life of Mathilda*, who in chapter 5, section 4 [in Leibniz, *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium* I, 694] copied from a book “called the *Copia of Landulf of Saint Paul*,” with which Arnulf’s history seems often to have been copied. Later, in the seventeenth century, J. P. Puricellus made extensive use of Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0285C] Manuscripts 4, B1 (see *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 417; *De SS. martyribus*, p. 10), and B2]. But his complete history first appeared in 1711 among Leibniz’s *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. III, from the Sitonian copy [Note: [Col. 0285C] Reprinted in vol. IV of Burmann’s *Thesaurus*, 1772]. Muratori sent a corrected copy of that manuscript, based on the Este manuscript, to the Palatine Associates. With the addition of some readings from the Metropolitan manuscript 5 and B1, and a commentary not unworthy of consideration—although we have not now been able to repeat much of it—they published it in the fourth volume of the *Collection of Writers on Italian Affairs* in 1723 [Col. 0286A].

This is now our third edition, corrected according to manuscript 1 [Note: [Col. 0285C] We follow its spelling throughout, although it follows the Italian practice of the thirteenth century, for we do not know how Arnulf himself spelled his words. We have nevertheless restored the diphthong in place of the simple vowel *e*], by the distinguished W. D. Bethmann. He added all the variant readings of B1, omitting only differences of spelling, and included from 5* those that seemed to possess some importance.

We have retained the division of books indicated by the author himself, but marked with numbers the chapters distinguished by larger letters in manuscript 1. These numbers do not depart so far from the divisions of the earlier editors that different numbering needed to be added [Col. 0286B]. I have tried briefly to explain, by consulting the books of learned men, whatever required clarification. In particular, I have indicated passages in Bonizo and Andreas of Vallombrosa that are suitable for illustrating our narrative and confirming its reliability, and I have noted where they tell the story differently.

Since the *Life of Ariald* by Andreas deals so extensively with the affairs of the Milanese Church and with Ariald’s own deeds that it ought not to be included in this collection, I copied from it whatever seemed useful for knowledge of the events, using J. P. Puricellus’s book *On the Milanese Saints and Martyrs Ariald Alciatus and Herlembald Cotta*. Milan, 1657, folio. The *Life of Ariald* taken from that work was published again in the *Acts of the Saints*, June, vol. V, pp. 281–303 [Col. 0286C].
