The *Passion of Blessed Ariald the Martyr* that Puricellus added, written by an anonymous author [Note: Puricellus regarded him as Landulf of Saint Paul, relying on no adequate arguments, as Giulini already observed, IV, 18. Nevertheless, some more recent writers have followed him incautiously], is wholly derived from Andreas and Landulf, and seems to have been written considerably later.

Given at Berlin, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, 1846.

**W. Wattenbach**

# Arnulf’s Deeds of the Archbishops of Milan

Edited by L. C. Bethmann and W. Wattenbach.

## Here begins the book of recent deeds composed by Arnulf

[Note: [Col. 0285] “By Arnulf.” B1: “Here begins Arnulf’s book of histories concerning the deeds of the city of Milan, beginning in the year of Christ 923.” B1*: “Here begins the book called the *Copia of Arnulf’s histories*. It begins with the deeds of the cities of Milan and Pavia in the year of Christ 923.” B is missing the continuation down to “Multorum varios” and what follows.]

[Col. 0285D] This book contains the deeds of certain kings of Italy and bishops of Milan, from the time of King Hugh and Bishop Arderic down to the time of the writer, together with whatever other matters, besides these, have been inserted into those periods as they came to the writer’s memory [Col. 0286D–0287A]. Whoever desires to know these things should read them individually; without doubt he will find here something with which to nourish his mind—not with richer and more abundant foods, but with sound and digestible ones. The names of the kings and pontiffs have been written before the eyes below on the page [Note: [Col. 0287] “The names are these, namely,” 5*.].

Hugh, king of Burgundy. His son Lothair. Berengar the Lombard. Otto I the German. Otto II, son of the first. Otto III, son of the second. Ardoin the Lombard. Henry the German, likewise Huon [Note: [Col. 0287] Thus the manuscripts pronounce it: “Chuonon.”]. Henry, son, like his father. Henry, his son.

Arderic held the see for 22 years and 2 months. Manasses and Adelmann together held it for 5 years [Note: [Col. 0287] “For three years,” 3a, here and below. “Manasses and Adelmann held [it] for one year.” “Manasses and Adelmann together held [it] for five years in the bow, not in the cathedra,” 5*.]—not in the cathedra, but with bow and quiver. Walpert held it for 18 years. Arnulf held it for 3 years and 4 months. Gotofred held it for 5 years, 1 month, and 24 days. Landulf held it for 18 years and 3 months. Arnulf held it for 19 years, 9 months, and 6 days. Aeribert held it for 26 years, 8 months, and 19 days. Wido held it for 27 years [Note: [Col. 0287] 5* adds: “Gotofred from the king, Atto from the pope, Thebald from the king.”]

1. The varied inclinations of many people, and many different pursuits [Note: [Col. 0287] B: “many and varied”], please them; not everything pleases everyone [Note: [Col. 0287] B: “nor does everything please everyone”], nor does the same thing always satisfy each individual. Indeed, differing customs and the differing disposition of each person are often drawn toward different things [Note: [Col. 0287] B: “are drawn away”], by the manifold conditions of a single nature. To discuss these matters collectively, or to distinguish them individually [Note: [Col. 0287] B 1: “separately”], is neither the business of the present work nor within human power. He alone is good and capable who bestows diverse gifts of grace. Thus the Apostle says: “There are divisions of graces, but it is the same God who works all things in all people,” distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:6). And elsewhere: “Each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that” (ibid. 7:7).

For example, the gift of literary knowledge is given in many ways, as God distributes it among mortals [Note: [Col. 0287] Absent in B.]. Spiritual men interpret mysteries, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. And who is competent for this? Certainly not I, who do not presume to examine even one iota or one stroke of these matters except with reverent belief. But worldly men investigate secular affairs [Note: [Col. 0287] B 1: “forensic affairs”] in many ways, comparing carnal things with carnal.

Among them, I hide most shamefacedly, as though among trees thick with foliage in a dark forest; yet, as a servant of the Catholic faith, I blush to be seen—naked as I am of knowledge, and lightly clothed, as it were, in very few letters [Note: [Col. 0287] B 1 abbreviates “letters, very few” as “l. a.”], like the thinnest threads of a spider’s web. Moreover, since in the forest of the present age so many and such varied leaves of new events burst forth daily, I marvel that so many eloquent writers do not blow life into even one of them. For never in past times was there such a great opportunity for writing for writers [Note: [Col. 0287] “writers,” supplied by Muratori.]—learned and unlearned alike [Note: [Col. 0287] Muratori: “and”].

Reflecting on these things, I do not trust myself, for the poverty of my slender intellect constricts me so severely that the entrance into Aristotle’s labyrinth seems difficult to me, and access to Tully’s palace exceedingly laborious. I confess that I have never mounted the curule wheels of the quadrivium. Therefore, dearest reader, whoever you are, demand nothing from me beyond what I promise: namely, a simple narration, expressed in ordinary words, of the deeds performed by our kings and our pontiffs, by our fellow citizens in the city of Milan and outside it, and by our countrymen in the Italian kingdom—things which I myself saw, or heard from eyewitnesses or at only a slight remove, insofar as they also emerge from the treasuries of memory. You should expect nothing more from me.

If, through the narrator’s fault, the mind falters in recounting what it has heard, it will surely leap forward with greater confidence in recounting what it has seen, needing no one’s testimony. But if, for the present, those who know these things are bored by reading this work [Note: [Col. 0287] “of this kind” in B 1; “of this kind” in B 2*.], let them at least not begrudge it to posterity and to those who may perhaps wish to know, especially since I have prepared it for them alone [Note: [Col. 0287] Absent in B.]. For unless the style of writing preserved, however imperfectly, the deeds of the ancients [Col. 0288C], no memory of the past would remain for us at all [Note: [Col. 0287] Thus in 3 and 5*; “for you” in 1 and B 1.]. Let this work of ours, whatever its quality, remain meanwhile hidden under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0287] “subject matter” or “memory” above; B reads “they remember.”], to be brought forth at its proper time.

I ask that this private and singular volume not cross the threshold of its own city at all. If that seems too little, let it extend as far as the Roman Arch [Note: [Col. 0287] B 1 adds “thereafter”; in red it has: “Narrative: Now begin, reader, to learn the book.” Muratori also gives this from manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0287] On this arch, which Radevicus described carefully, see Fumagalli, *Antichità Longobardiche di Milano* I, pp. 200 ff.].

2. The proper order of narration descends from higher things to lower. But since the present depends upon the past, the account of events should run from the past to what is now at hand; yet, leaving antiquity aside, its beginning should be taken from recent memory.

3. [Note: [Col. 0287] Muratori places this first, from manuscript 2, where the heading is: “First, Hugo of the Burgundians reigns.”]

In the year 925 from the birth of Christ, Hugo, a Burgundian, reigned in Italy [Note: [Col. 0287] B: “Hugo, a Burgundian by nation, formerly reigned in Italy with his son Lothair; in order that he might act more securely in the kingdom …”]. In order to conduct himself more securely in the kingdom, he foresaw that he should claim for himself the distinguished city of Milan above all others. For he knew the ancient custom of the place: when a metropolitan died, one of the chief cardinals of the greater church, whom they call the ordinary clergy [Note: [Col. 0289] “cardinals” in B 1.], ought to succeed him. This, granted by the Roman bishops and by the emperors themselves under the authority of the canons, is testified by documents stored in the secretariat [Note: [Col. 0289D] These documents are presently missing. PAL. See also John VIII, Letter 221.]. [Note: [Col. 0289] B: “cujus.” Here Muratori’s and manuscript 2’s second chapter begins, under the heading: “Here he tonsured his son and attempted to kill the archbishop.”]

For this reason he decided that his younger son [Note: [Col. 0289D] Theobald; see Liutprand IV, 13.] should be tonsured in that church (936). But since he seemed entirely unfit for the episcopate at so childish an age, he temporarily substituted the aged old man Ardericus [Note: [Col. 0289] “Adderus” in 1 and 5*.] as bishop [Note: [Col. 0289] “bishop” or “prelate” in B 1 and B 2*.], hoping that he would soon fall. But since an expectation often deceives the one who forms it, the priest lived in this world for a very long time—twenty-two years [Note: [Col. 0289D] In fact twelve; but the same error was already made above.] and two months [Note: [Col. 0289] The words “twenty-two years and two months” are absent in B.]. When Hugo realized this, he immediately plotted his secret death.

When a general assembly of all the kingdom’s leaders had been arranged at Pavia, the emperor deliberately ordered the palace hirelings to quarrel with the Milanese, so that the old man might be killed when an opportunity arose. As they fought, a serious battle ensued, in which ninety prudent Milanese men are said to have been killed. But by the favor of God the bishop escaped unharmed.

When the treachery could no longer remain concealed [Note: [Col. 0289] B 1 reads “treacheries”; B 2* has “but not.”], the man responsible for so great a crime was deeply ashamed, fearing also blessed Ambrose, whose vicar that man had been.

4. [Note: [Col. 0289] Muratori’s third chapter, also in manuscript 2, has the heading: “His satisfaction and the deprivation of the kingdom, with Lothair elected.”]

It happened that, as a fitting satisfaction, he granted the Church the abbey of Nonantola [Note: [Col. 0289] Absent in B 1; B 2* reads “but not.”] for the ninety men who had been killed [Note: [Col. 0289D] If he received it, he did not hold it long, for it was soon given to the bishop of Modena; see Liutprand V, 17, and Tiraboschi, *Nonantola* I, p. 92.]. It is said to have been given this name because of its ninety estates under its own jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 0289D] See *Manipulus florum*, chapter 130, where Gualvagnus della Flamma treated what he himself reports as having been received by Arnulf.]. In addition, he gave a golden chapel with a cross, which had been placed above the altar in the winter church [Note: [Col. 0289D] Saint Mary’s, where the ordinary clergy performed the offices after the first Sunday of October, moving on Easter Sunday to the church of Saint Thecla; see Giulini, *Memorie di Milano* III, 423.] [Note: [Col. 0289] “placed” masculine in B 1; feminine in B 2*.], in a small structure [Note: [Col. 0290D] A vault erected over the altar; see Giulini II, 210.].

In the rest of his conduct he behaved too insolently, ignorant of the saying: “They have made you a prince; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sirach 32:1). He thus became intolerable to everyone. His son Lothair, who was much gentler, having been unanimously elected by all, Hugo was compelled by the common consent of the entire kingdom [Note: [Col. 0289] “so often” in B 1; “but not” in B 2*.] to return to Burgundy (946), never again to reign.

5. [Note: [Col. 0289] Muratori’s fourth chapter, manuscript 2, has the heading: “The conflict between Manasses and Adelmannus, and the episcopate of Walpertus.”]

At about that time (948), a destructive revolt broke out at Milan. When Archbishop Ardericus had been called to heaven, two rivals appeared, inflamed by ambition for the Ambrosian dignity: namely, Manasses, bishop of Arles, and Adelmannus [Note: [Col. 0289] “Aldemanus” in B.] the Milanese priest [Note: [Col. 0289] In the margin of manuscript 1, another hand appears to have supplied: “and he was a Milanese priest.”]. In truth, they had forgotten the apostolic pronouncement: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Gal. 5:26).

They contended for a long time: one through the king’s appointment, namely, that of Burgundy; the other through the faction of the people and of Milan [Note: [Col. 0289] “Milan” in 3a.]. For five years they quarreled stubbornly against one another, each forming his own party. Through their detestable dispute the Church suffered a very great loss, especially in all its treasures and sacred vessels, in which it abounded beyond comparison.

Amid these waves Walpertus swam cautiously, drawing to his side what was almost a current of counsel, until both men, willingly or unwillingly, yielded and he alone occupied the see [Note: [Col. 0290D] Rosmini, in *Historia di Milano* I, 87, cites a document that seems to prove that in March 959 Manasses was still acting as archbishop. But from the words he quotes it appears only that a priest named Erebert had at some time before 959 been sent by Manasses. See Liutprand, *History of Otto* I; Giulini II, 292.].

[Note: [Col. 0289] Muratori and manuscript 2 begin a new chapter here, headed: “Berengarius reigns, and Walpertus flees to King Otto.”]

Then Lothair died (950, November 22), and Berengarius the Lombard himself became king. Walpertus, then archbishop, regarded him with suspicion, since Berengarius was conscious of his own guilt. Anticipating his anger, and fearing that he might be overtaken by the king’s plots—for he had read, “The king’s indignation is a messenger of death” (Prov. 16:14)—Walpertus prepared for flight.

He went to Otto, king of the Germans (960), seeking assistance [Note: [Col. 0290D] That is, aid. This occurred before Otto’s second expedition; the first took place before Walpertus became archbishop.], and soon promised him the Italian kingdom if Otto would press his claim. Encouraged by this confidence, King Otto, taking with him Adelaide, once queen of Italy and the widow of Lothair, immediately began planning to seize the kingdom from Berengarius.

6. Having first sent envoys on Walpertus’s behalf, he pleaded for peace. When he could not obtain it, he dispatched Litulfus [Col. 0290C] with an army [Note: [Col. 0290D] Our author confuses several expeditions here and does not seem reliable in what follows.], his son by another wife [Note: [Col. 0289] “by another wife” in 3.]. The countrymen hated King Berengarius because of the excessive greed of his wife, whose name was Willa, and partly because of his own cruelty.

Therefore, abandoned by his own men, he was unable to confront the approaching enemy. Instead, he entered the town called the Island of Saint Julius and remained there in weakness [Note: [Col. 0289] B reads: “But he entered some impregnable place,” omitting “which is called the Island of Saint Julius.”]. When Litulfus had reconnoitered everything, certain soldiers among Berengarius’s household, pretending to be faithful and promising safety, led him outside and handed him over to the enemy. Truly, “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36).

When Litulfus saw him, he said: “Look to yourself, king, and humble yourself before the great Otto Augustus. If you do not, you injure yourself.” When Berengarius replied humbly, Litulfus continued: “Far be it from my faith that I should conquer by treachery, when I strive to overcome by strength. Beware henceforth, king, of soldiers of this kind.”

After saying this, he released him and thereafter served him loyally in every matter. O pious hostility and hostile piety! That pious man [Note: [Col. 0291] B and Muratori add “Litulfus.”] is later said to have been killed by Lombard treachery through poison (957, September 6).

7. Although Otto had lost his son, he relied on the counsel of his august wife Adelaide, as well as on that of Walpertus and the other leaders of the kingdom. With a strong hand and an outstretched arm [Col. 0291B], he came to Italy [Note: [Col. 0291] B reads: “He came to Italy with a strong hand and an outstretched arm.”] (961), the first of the Germans to be called Italian emperor.

When everything was subjected to him, he overcame Berengarius himself, who had fortified himself in a certain stronghold [Note: [Col. 0291D] Monte San Leo.], by blockading him under a prolonged siege (964), while his sons Wido, Adelbertus, and Cono were scattered all around. Otto captured Berengarius, along with his daughters and wife, and carried him with him to Swabia [Note: [Col. 0291D] More precisely, Babenberg.], where not long afterward he ended his days in bitterness of soul (966) [Note: [Col. 0291] B 1 reads “bitterness”; B 2* has “but not.”].

8. At the same time, when Walpertus died, Arnulfus assumed the see (970, November 6), truly turning away from evil and doing good. I, the writer of this present account, am his namesake; but I am the true great-grandson of his brother [Note: [Col. 0291] In the margin of B 1 the rubricator wrote: “Note that this author was called Arnulfus, the great-grandson of the brother of that Archbishop Arnulfus.”]. His life in the episcopate lasted three years, but now, having been transferred to a better dignity [Note: [Col. 0291] “Having been made” in 3; “made” in B.], it has become eternal (974, April 16).

Gotefredus succeeded him. At first he was rejected by the clergy and the people, because he had not yet advanced to the priestly or levitical rank and was only a subdeacon. But at the end he was received in peace through royal favor, and he fought against the sons of Berengarius. After Wido was killed [Note: [Col. 0291D] Already in 965, according to the Annals of Einsiedeln.], and Cono was quieted by an agreement [Note: [Col. 0291D] He seems to have retained the march of Ivrea and to have become ill there on September 30, 987. Together with his wife Ychila, daughter of the margrave Ardoinus, he granted certain estates to Saint Eusebius of Vercelli. See Provana, *Studi critici*, p. 331.], Adelbertus, bolder than the others, became a fugitive in every direction throughout all the days of his life [Note: [Col. 0291] B reads “throughout all days”; B 2* has “but not.”].

9. Then, when Otto died (973), his son of the same name reigned in his place [Note: [Col. 0291] B and Muratori read “his own.”]. He was fierce in arms and shrewd in intelligence. Having taken a Greek woman as his companion, he successfully consolidated the Roman Empire through the industry of his wise mother Adelaide.

After leaving Germany [Note: [Col. 0291] B omits “After leaving Germany.”], he held court at Rome, possessed Apulia and Calabria [Note: [Col. 0291] “Calabria” in 3.], and accomplished many notable deeds worthy of imperial majesty.

In his time, Saracens crossed the sea and attempted to invade the Calabrian territories. The emperor himself confronted them (982), though supported by only a small company of his men [Note: [Col. 0291] B reads: “although supported by a small force of his men.”]. Since an engagement of the few against the many is usually unequal, after fighting for a long time he ultimately weakened [Note: [Col. 0291] “Was defeated” in 3.]. What more need be said? Captured in battle [Note: [Col. 0291] B reads: “the engagement did not have a favorable outcome for him in war. What more? Defeated and captured.”], he was dragged all the way to the ships, for the enemy had occupied the nearby shores of the sea.

Realizing that, willingly or unwillingly, he would have to be carried away [Note: [Col. 0291] B 1 reads: “whether he wished it or not.”], he asked with feigned prayers that they at least permit him to exile himself with a single wife and a small retinue of female attendants, promising that he would take with him enormous quantities of gold and silver.

When permission had been granted [Note: [Col. 0291] B 1 reads: “When this had been granted.”], he ordered young men disguised in women’s clothing, but secretly girded with swords, to come very cautiously. When they had entered the ship, they immediately fell upon the enemy and, drawing their swords, slaughtered everyone indiscriminately.

Meanwhile, the emperor leapt swiftly into the open sea and, swimming, escaped to the shore, free and joyful. Terrified by this, the enemy withdrew to their own land [Note: [Col. 0291] B omits: “Terrified by this, the enemy withdrew to their own land.”].

Thereafter, planning to cross the sea with all Italy under his authority, he extended throughout the entire kingdom the order for military service [Note: [Col. 0291] B reads “to cross” instead of “to pass through.”]. But since God had otherwise ordained, he departed from human affairs (983, December 7), in accordance with the saying: “The heart of a man plans his way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps” (Prov. 16:9).

His son, a boy of the same name, survived him in the regions of Germany and had been made king while his father was still alive [Note: [Col. 0292D] “While he was alive, in June.”]

10. For Gotefredus had already been succeeded by Archbishop Landulfus, who suffered the bitter resentment of the people because of the excessive insolence of his father and brothers. They were making unusual efforts to abuse the authority of the city [Note: [Col. 0291] B omits this sentence and has instead: “in the customary manner.”]. Therefore the citizens, angered, bound themselves together in a single conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0291] “In a conspiracy” in B and Muratori.]. From this arose civil revolt and a division into factions.

As they quarreled continually, a great battle was fought in the city. Seeing that he was being pressed from every side and could not hold out, the bishop left the city with his brothers, abandoning his father [Note: [Col. 0292D] Landulfus II, 17, calls him Bonizo; the archbishop himself calls him Ambrosius in his testament. The former was his name, the latter his surname, as Giulini demonstrated with examples, *Memorie di Milano* II, 384. See also p. 443 and III, 76; Dominicus, also called Bonizo, p. 77; Nazaro, called Bonizone, p. 166; Andrea, or Bonizone.], who was already old and weak [Note: [Col. 0291] “Feeble.”].

For this reason the archbishop distributed the Church’s resources and many of the clergy’s benefices among soldiers. Then, having again gathered a force from various regions [Col. 0292D], he fought the same citizens in the field of Carbonaria [Note: [Col. 0293D] Carbonate, near Seprio, according to Puricellus; see Giulini II, 393.]. There was a very great slaughter on both sides, and he barely withdrew from the battle even on this occasion.

In the city, a certain household servant, hearing of his master’s death and rushing there, stabbed the bishop’s father, who was lying in bed, with a knife [Note: [Col. 0293] Muratori reads “a female servant.”].

After this and many other events, with God inspiring them and the wise counsel of both parties intervening, a new peace dissolved the old hatreds. The archbishop remembered his pastoral duty, while the people remembered the obedience of the flock [Note: [Col. 0293] B reads “civil obedience.”]. They forgave the past and were joined in perpetual peace.

Moreover, realizing that he had offended the Church by dispersing its resources, and wishing to reconcile the clergy and [Note: [Col. 0293] Thus in 3, 5*, and B; “the people” in 1.] the people, the bishop founded the monastery of the holy martyr Celsus and endowed it with many riches. When he had completed the allotted number of his days, he died and rested in his own tomb (998, March 23). Arnulfus succeeded him; more will be said about him later.

11. Meanwhile, while Otto III was reigning with his Greek mother, a certain Greek [Note: [Col. 0293D] John Philagathus.], the Greek lady’s chaplain, became bishop of Piacenza. It was said of him that he had cunningly attempted to transfer the glory of the Roman Empire to the Greeks.

Indeed, with the counsel and assistance of certain Roman citizens, especially a certain very wealthy Crescentius, he had already violently invaded the apostolic see, after removing the venerable pope who had occupied it at that time [Note: [Col. 0293] B adds: “Pope Benedict, who, after being captured by the aforementioned Crescentius, was strangled in the Castle of Saint Angelo on Christmas night.”] [Note: [Col. 0293D] The author confuses him with Gregory V, whom he also initially confounded with Benedict VI, who was killed by the elder Crescentius.].

When Otto heard this openly, he left Swabia and hastened to Italy (997).

12. Without delay, after taking counsel with the leading men of the kingdom, he set out for Rome with legions of Latins and Germans, terrifying all the surrounding places. At his entry (998), the whole of Rome was shaken [Col. 0293C].

The Greek himself cried out for mercy, while Crescentius prepared a rebellion, fortified in the fortress of the Tiberine Castle of Saint Angelo [Note: [Col. 0293] B reads: “having been fortified in the Tiberine fortress of Saint Angelo.”].

The emperor surrounded him with a siege on every side, attacking him daily with every engine of war, until, after some sort of agreement had been arranged, Crescentius surrendered himself to the emperor’s power. He was immediately ordered to be beheaded in the Neronian meadow.

His wife Stephania, however, was handed over to the Germans to be violated. The false pope, the Greek, after his eyes had been gouged out and his nose and ears cut off, was made to sit backward on a donkey, holding its tail in his hands, and was dragged throughout the entire city. Thus Rome, formerly changeable [Note: [Col. 0293] “noble” in B.], came to rest before the eyes of the king.

13. Some time earlier [Note: [Col. 0293] B reads: “But some time earlier.”], the emperor had decided to enter into marriage with a woman of his mother’s people. For this reason, the venerable Archbishop Arnulfus, having been warned by royal command, crossed the sea and proceeded to Constantinople.

Received with great honor by the remarkable monarch himself, he conducted himself sufficiently like a bishop in the imperial city. He was so beloved that whatever he asked for, he obtained easily [Note: [Col. 0293] B 2 reads “whatever he might ask”; Puricellus, *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 305, reads “whatever he asked.”]. At last, having settled the business for which he had come, he was courteously dismissed by the Basileus and hastened his return.

14. Meanwhile, Otto died in the first flower of his youth (1002, January 23), and in him the entire line of the Ottos [Note: [Col. 0293] B reads “the whole lineage”; manuscript 3 has “of Otto III.”] came to an end.

Then a certain nobleman, Ardoinus [Note: [Col. 0293] “Arduinus” in B; the text is apparently corrupt.] margrave of Ivrea, was elected by the Lombards at Pavia (February). Called emperor by everyone, he traveled throughout the entire kingdom, administering everything by royal right.

When he learned that the aforementioned bishop was returning, he met him on the road and tried, with whatever security he could provide, to attach him to his cause.

15. At the same time Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0293] “Henricus” in B; apparently correct.] was made king of Alamannia (June 29). Between them a great dispute arose over the Italian scepter.

The leaders of the kingdom, moving deceitfully between the two, openly supported Ardoinus but secretly favored Heinricus, pursuing the profits of greed, as the prophet said to Jerusalem: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves; they all love gifts and pursue rewards” (Isa. 1:23) [Note: [Col. 0293] “Thus” in 3.].

On their advice Heinricus sent his duke [Note: [Col. 0293D] Otto, duke of the Carinthians.] into Italy with an army. Ardoinus met him courageously and, when battle was joined in the field of Fabbrica [Note: [Col. 0293D] On the Euganean Hills, not far from the Brenta, there is a village currently called Fabbrica, owned by the family of the Counts Durini of Milan. Provana, *Studi critici*, p. 211; see also Thietmar V, 16; Adalbold, *Life of Henry* 15–17; and, on Mount Ungarico, Provana, p. 208.], laid many men low and drove the rest beyond the borders of the kingdom.

16. Not long afterward (1004), Heinricus advanced from Germany with a powerful German army and encamped at the threshold of Italy (April). Ardoinus, trusting in his strength and no less well equipped with arms, came to meet him at Verona, prepared not merely to defend himself but to rise against him offensively [Note: [Col. 0293] B omits “he came to meet him at Verona,” and continues: “But, with [p. p.] pressing, deprived of a large part of his men, and thus withdrawing, King Heinricus entered.” The abbreviated reading “p. p.” is unresolved in the supplied text.].

But, deceived by the treachery of the leaders, Ardoinus was abandoned by the greater part of his soldiers. When he withdrew unwillingly, Heinricus entered the kingdom and was immediately elected king (May 15); afterward, in due time [Note: [Col. 0294D] In 1014, February 14.], he became Roman emperor.

When he came to Pavia and found that it had not obeyed him as he wished, he burned the entire city in a single fire. All Italy shuddered at this, fearing something similar. From then on Ardoinus’s confidence was diminished, while Heinricus’s power prevailed everywhere.

Nevertheless, after temporarily recovering his strength [Note: [Col. 0293] “After regaining” in 3.], Ardoinus exercised vengeance against the treacherous as far as he was able [Note: [Col. 0293] “Meanwhile” in 1.]. He captured the city of Vercelli, besieged Novara, attacked Cumae, and destroyed many other places opposed to him.

At last (1015), worn out by labor and illness, deprived of the kingdom, he was content with only the monastery called Fruttuaria [Note: [Col. 0295D] San Benigno di Fruttuaria.]. There, after laying his royal insignia upon the altar and taking the clothing of a poor man [Note: [Col. 0295] “Poor” in B.], he fell asleep in his own time [Note: [Col. 0295D] December 14, according to the Necrology of Dijon; see Provana, p. 305.].

17. In those days the Normans first arrived in Apulia [Note: [Col. 0295] “Advent” in 5* and Muratori.], summoned at the counsel of the leaders of the land, since the Greeks were burdening it with countless oppressions.

After subduing the Greeks and driving them away across the sea, the Normans considered the inactivity of the Apulians and the region’s abundant wealth in every respect. Though few in number, they invaded part of the province.

Having sent envoys back to their homeland to encourage the others to this undertaking [Note: [Col. 0295] B omits “to this undertaking, encouraging the others.”], they gradually increased in number and filled all Apulia. They then possessed it as though by a right of their own, becoming more savage than the Greeks and fiercer than the Saracens; indeed, after casting out the former rulers, they themselves rose to power.

18. (1022.) It is unnecessary to recount what Heinricus did thereafter, how he besieged the noble Apulian city of Troy, or how he captured in a single act the four margraves of Italy—Hugo, Azo, Adelbertus, and Obizo [Note: [Col. 0295D] A did not preserve the chronological order here. They are thought to be the same men mentioned by Thietmar VII, 1 and VIII, 1, sons of Obertus II, margrave of Milan and ancestor of the lords of Asti; see Terraneo, *Contessa Adelaide* II, 62; Muratori, *Antichità Estensi* I, p. 137; Scheidius, *Origines Guelficae* I, p. 179.]—since the whole land trembled at his strength, so that if anyone was found to have favored Ardoinus’s party, he either fled or surrendered.

Among these, the bishop of Asti [Note: [Col. 0295D] Petrus; see Terraneo I, 1, chapter 5.] abandoned his own see and remained hidden at Milan until his death. For while the bishop of Asti himself was still alive and had been removed, the emperor had given the bishopric to a certain Oldericus [Note: [Col. 0296D] More correctly, Adelricus.], brother of the eminent margrave Mainfredus.

Archbishop Arnulfus vehemently detested this action and absolutely prohibited the consecration to which he himself had the right. But Oldericus [Note: [Col. 0295] “Odelricus” in 1 and B.] relied on his own power and that of his brother, went to Rome, and by a certain deception had himself consecrated by the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0296D] Giulini, *Memorie di Milano* III, 62, established that this occurred in 1008.] [an. 1008].

When this became known to Arnulfus, he was inflamed by entirely justified anger. He was indignant not only at the royal appointment but even more at the Roman consecration, which seemed worse.

19. When he therefore came before the assembly of the Milanese Church, he pierced the audacity of the consecrated man with the dart of anathema. Then, having gathered a large army from every side, he attacked the city of Asti together with the suffragan bishops. With the margrave and the bishop shut up inside the city, he surrounded it with a very dense siege.

He did not desist from ravaging and waging war until, after peace had been arranged, his will had been satisfied. The condition of peace was this: when they came to Milan, the bishop and the margrave were to walk barefoot from the third milestone outside the city. The bishop, carrying a book, and the margrave, carrying a dog, were to confess their respective guilt most devoutly before the doors of the church of Saint Ambrose.

Moreover, the bishop laid down upon the altar of the holy confessor the staff and ring of the pontificate he had received. Later, when the archbishop granted permission [Note: [Col. 0295] “When the bishop granted permission” in B.], he piously took them up again.

His brother Mainfredus the margrave gave the Church many talents of gold. From this was made that most beautiful cross which is carried to this day only on the principal feast days.

Then, barefoot as they had come, they proceeded through the middle of the city to the greater church of Holy Theotokos, where they were received in peace by the archbishop, the clergy, and the entire people.

20. Thereafter Arnulfus governed his Church priestly [Note: [Col. 0295] “Priestly” misspelled in B 1.], cherishing clergy and people and devoting himself fully to his duties. Many benefactions bestowed upon churches testify to his blessedness.

In his time [Note: [Col. 0295] B reads “in his time” with a different word order.] the relics of the holy confessor Mona were revealed in the church of Saint Vitalis near Saint Nabor [Note: [Col. 0295] B omits “in the church of Saint Vitalis near Saint Nabor.”].

He also founded the monastery of Saint Victor the martyr, with great honor and abundant grain, and was buried there, resting in peace.

Since the present day is not sufficient for rendering his praise, let this page now be closed, since another is to be opened afterward.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0295] Manuscript B 1 writes above this book: “The second book of Arnulfus’s histories begins. Another discourse comes, when the former one has now withdrawn.”]

1. In the preceding volume we attempted, however inadequately, to blow out only what we had heard. Now let us strive, from an abundance of material, to belch forth what we ourselves have come to know by seeing.

When Arnulfus, whose memory is blessed, was called from this world by heaven (1018, February 25), Heribertus was enthroned through the counsel of the city’s leading men [Col. 0296D] and by the gift of imperial power [Note: [Col. 0296D] “Aribertus, son of the late Gariardus, who was from the place called Antimianus and lived according to Lombard law”: thus begin the documents drawn up in his name. His mother’s name was Berlinda; see Puricellus, *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 371. On Antimianus, now Intimiano, see Giulini III, 385. He had been a subdeacon of the Milanese church since 1007; ibid., p. 56.].

From the time he was promoted, he devoted himself to his own affairs and those of others, occupied with many matters and experiencing great events. We have undertaken to narrate these, not to judge them.

In his days the empire of Heinricus came to an end (1024), with no surviving offspring. Then the people of Pavia, in revenge for the burning of their city, destroyed the royal palace that stood among them.

It happened that the leading men met together and deliberated collectively about establishing a king. Since different people were pulling in different directions, not everyone had the same mind.

2. While Italy was wavering amid such circumstances, Heribertus, avoiding the companionship of his peers [Note: [Col. 0297] “Companions” in 3, 5*, and B.], went alone to Germany, despite their opposition and resistance, intending to elect the German king himself.

When the Germans chose Chuonradus [Note: [Col. 0297] “Conradus” in 3a, 5*, and B.], Heribertus praised him [Col. 0297C]—he had met him at Constance at Pentecost, according to Wipo’s *Life of Conrad*—and crowned him before everyone’s eyes (1025).

In return, besides very many gifts, he received from Chuonradus the bishopric of Lodi, so that, just as he had consecrated the bishop, he might likewise invest him.

Returning secure in every respect [Col. 0297B], he overturned all Italy through his embassies, making some favorable by actual benefits and others by hope, until nearly everyone praised and accepted his chosen candidate.

Strengthened by such oars, Chuonradus came to Italy (1026) and was crowned king by Heribertus, as was customary. Then, led by the same man, he moved on to Rome.

At his arrival (1027), a great assembly of peoples from everywhere—bishops as well as secular leaders—was held at Rome, with Pope John presiding [Note: [Col. 0297] Absent in B.].

3. As the Easter solemnity approached (March 26), and King Chuonradus was about to be raised to the summit of imperial power by apostolic consecration in the basilica of the Apostles, Heribertus, archbishop of Ravenna, rashly seized and held the king’s right hand, doing what by right belonged to the bishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 0297] “Bishop” abbreviated and misspelled in 1.].

When this displeased everyone who saw it, the other bishops admonished him to desist from what was not his. Nevertheless, he obstinately held on.

Heribertus [Note: [Col. 0297] “Henricus” in B 1; B 2* has “Heribertus.”], the Milanese bishop, wisely took great care to avoid a popular disturbance, lest there be an uproar among the people on the feast day; he restrained all his supporters who wished to oppose the Ravenna bishop from any contradiction.

4. The king, stunned by the uproar of the rioters, finally learned the truth of the matter, planted his feet, and addressed the assembly as follows:

> “It is certainly clear, reverend fathers, that just as the consecration of the emperor is the privilege of the Apostolic See, so the election and consecration of the king is the privilege of the Ambrosian See. Therefore it seems right that the hand which blesses and first places the crown of the kingdom, if it is present, should represent the king before Saint Peter and his vicar when he is advanced to the empire. Thus, by the lawful testimony of Ambrose, he may rule who has learned to reign and has begun to reign through Ambrosian consecration.”

When this judgment of the king pleased everyone, he removed the right hand from the Ravennate and ordered the Ambrosian bishop to be summoned. The latter, in order to avoid the disturbance already mentioned, delayed coming.

5. Therefore, after the apostolic lord and all the bishops had consulted, he gave his right hand to Arderic, bishop of Vercelli and suffragan of that bishop, so that the father might be represented in the son and the master in the disciple. He [Note: [Col. 0297] Omitted in B.] fully performed the office of the archbishop of Milan in the imperial consecration [Note: [Col. 0297] B reads “he fully performed it.”]. A few days later, a synod was convened at Rome by apostolic authority (April 6). At it, it was decreed that in all pontifical affairs the Ravennate should in no way ever place himself before the bishop of Milan; and if he should presume to do so, he should be subject to canonical law [Note: [Col. 0297] The words “law should impose itself upon him” are missing in witnesses 1.]. Furthermore, everyone agreed that a document should be written concerning this matter [Note: [Col. 0297] Witnesses 3, 5*, and B2* read “in this matter.”] as an everlasting testimony [Col. 0298C]. From among many things we have selected the following few passages [Note: [Col. 0297C] This volume seems to have been preserved in the material reproduced below from the “New Beroldus” of the metropolitan chapter of Milan, written between 1265 and 1269. It reads as follows:

“Commemoration of the arrogance of the archbishop of Ravenna: how he presumptuously and arrogantly attempted to place himself before the archbishop of Milan at Rome, and how, defeated there, he was brought low and departed in confusion, to the glory and praise of God, who humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

In the year 1027 after the divinely assumed mortality [i.e. after Christ’s incarnation], in the third year of Lord John, universal pope, there was held at Rome a huge gathering of many bishops and secular princes, as well as clergy and laity, from Italy, Gaul, and Germany, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March [or April], on the holy day of Easter, in the tenth indiction. Since King Conrad, in the third year of his reign, was to be elevated to the summit of imperial power in the basilica of the Apostles through apostolic consecration, the enemy of the human race, the sower of weeds, envying the joys and delights of so great an assembly, deceitfully and with extreme danger—as is his custom—entered the mind of Heribert, archbishop of Ravenna, and spread over him the poison of his envy. The arrogance of pride compelled him to disregard the zeal for humility and justice and to presume to place himself before the archbishop of Milan [Col. 0298C].

“And because he insolently wished to appear superior, he disgracefully appeared inferior. It is known to all the faithful of Holy Church that the Ambrosian see has held, holds, and will hold primacy after the apostolic see, and that the vicar of Saint Ambrose is second to the apostolic see in all affairs [Col. 0298D]. For, just as Peter first taught at Rome, so Barnabas, his fellow apostle, first established the Catholic faith at Milan; he presided there for a long time and ordained as his successor and first among the Lord’s disciples Anatelon. By this apostolic right, just as the Roman see is considered first, so the Milanese see must be considered second.

“But, to return to the sowing of the ancient enemy, the aforesaid Ravennate, impelled by him, when King Conrad was to be led to imperial consecration, seized the king’s right hand with wicked and rash audacity, and inconsiderately—or rather violently—held it while the apostolic lord and the people were waiting in the middle of the church, as was customary. This had always belonged to the archbishop of Milan to do for kings being advanced to imperial power. When his rashness displeased all his fellow bishops beyond measure, and they rebuked and admonished him to desist, he despised everyone’s judgment, and his madness became rampant through headlong lack of restraint [Col. 0299C].

“But the lord Heribert, venerable archbishop of the holy Milanese Church—a vigorous and modest man, indeed also most patient [thus I conjecture; the manuscript reads ‘he came’]—lest a tumult arise among the people, opposed his savage insanity with holy restraint. He humbly avoided the whirlwind of so great a sedition and, by gentle persuasion, admonished his fellow bishops and all his own people, who condemned this rash act and wished to resist the rash man openly, to avoid scandal by humbling it. He urged them not to let an impetuous uprising grow among so great a crowd, nor to let the devil, author of every error, snatch the peace that the bishops had resolved upon—a peace whose presence is proper even among the laity.

“King Conrad, surrounded by the excessive pressure of the crowds, and not fully himself amid the tumult and uproar raised for various reasons, was unwillingly and as though unaware led into the apostolic temple [the manuscript reads ‘now in the temple’]. There he planted his foot and, recovering the strength of mind and body, spoke thus before everyone:

“‘It is indeed certain and manifest, reverend fathers, that just as imperial consecration is the privilege of the apostolic see, so election and royal consecration are the privilege of the Ambrosian see. Therefore it seems right that the hand of the one who blesses, anoints, and first places the crown of the kingdom upon the king, if he is present, should represent the king to Saint Peter and his vicar, so that he may be elevated to the summit of imperial power; and so that so great a consecration may not lack a true witness, he who first learned to rule and began to reign through Ambrosian consecration may lawfully rule with the testimony of Milan.’

“When everyone approved this judgment of the king, he took his right hand away from the Ravennate and, through his venerable messengers—namely, the archbishop and the bishops—summoned Lord Heribert, archbishop of Milan. He was prepared to meet him by returning to the church doors, so that what ought to be done might be fully accomplished there and Saint Ambrose might, through his vicar, retain the primacy of his honor. But because the immense pressure of the crowds prevented him, the lord archbishop of Milan could not go, and wisely, indeed patiently, [lacuna] [Col. 0300C]. Everyone unanimously praised his admirable patience and holy forbearance, and with equal vote and common agreement they advised and persuaded the king that, for the effective preservation of Saint Ambrose’s honor and the firm foundation of his empire, what Heribert, archbishop of Milan, ought by right to have done there should be done by Harderic, bishop of Vercelli and his suffragan. It seemed entirely just and appropriate that the vicar of Saint Eusebius should perform there the office of the vicar of Saint Ambrose, so that the master might be honored in the disciple and the father in the son.

“Their counsel pleased King Conrad, and he agreed. He gave his right hand to Arderic of Vercelli, who fully performed the office of the archbishop of Milan in the imperial consecration; and what the Ravennate had rashly attempted to seize, he disgracefully lost. Thus the Milanese is praised for the patience he displayed, while the Ravennate is judged infamous for his unrestrained insolence. After the imperial consecration, everyone gathered together; [Col. 0300D] and when they prolonged their discussion of this matter, a synod was convened by apostolic authority on the eighth day before the Ides of April. At it the apostolic lord first decreed and confirmed, and afterward all the venerable fathers gathered for the synod consented, that in all pontifical affairs the Ravennate should in no way ever place himself before the archbishop of Milan; and if he should presume to do so, he should be subject to canonical law, as is deserved by one who is not afraid to disrupt the peace of the Church. Everyone said, ‘Let it be done!’ And lest such a division should thereafter appear in Holy Church, everyone agreed that this writing should be made as a testimony. These things were enacted and promulgated at the city of Rome, while Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, presided there, and Lord Conrad ruled as emperor, happily in the first year of his empire. BETHM.”]

6. While these things were taking place, the Milanese and the Ravennates were arguing with one another [Col. 0299A]. As the quarrel grew, they joined battle against each other [Note: [Col. 0299] This is absent in B2*. B1 reads “they mutually came together.”]. But when the Milanese prevailed in force and courage, the Ravennates turned their backs, most of them wounded. Their opponents pursued them as far as their lodgings, plundering their baggage and all their belongings. Heribert himself, the Ravennate, scarcely escaped [Note: [Col. 0299] B reads “escaped,” where “having been rescued” is absent.] from the hands of his pursuers. Thereafter that entire dispute subsided. The emperor, returning from the Roman territories [Note: [Col. 0299] B adds “Conrad”], remained in Italy until he had subdued whatever opponents he had, with Heribert supporting him in everything; and the land was silent before him (1 Maccabees 1:3).

7. At that time it happened that the bishop of Lodi died. [Note: [Col. 0299] B reads “When.”] When the archbishop decided to appoint another in accordance with the investiture he had received from the emperor, the people of Lodi, indignant, boldly rejected the unfamiliar arrangement of their bishopric. Heribert disregarded their audacity and chose from among his own cardinals a sufficiently suitable priest named Ambrose. First giving him the staff and ring, he then consecrated him bishop, as was customary. Having done this, he violently attacked all the towns of the Lodigiani. After subduing them by force [Col. 0300A], he eventually reached the city, bringing his bishop with him. He surrounded it on every side with a siege and persistently attacked it. When the citizens saw that resistance was useless [Note: [Col. 0299] B1 reads “they saw that resistance was useless”], they proposed terms of peace [Note: [Col. 0299] absent in B] and finally agreed together to receive the bishop. Public oaths of promised fidelity were taken before the city gate; and thus the aforesaid bishop was received, afterward beloved by everyone, renowned both for his teaching and for his deeds.

From that time onward an implacable hatred prevailed between the Milanese and the Lodigiani. Consequently, for many years afterward they exchanged innumerable raids, burnings, and massacres. The Milanese, relying on their numbers, wealth, and strength of arm, frequently attacked them in war, surrounded them with a siege [Col. 0300B], and demolished their fields, vineyards, and all their suburban properties. The Lodigiani, few in number but fierce in spirit, poor in resources but burdened with strength, defended themselves now at the expense of their own people, now at that of others. If these matters were written out one by one, they would produce many volumes.

8. Finally, in those days, after the death of the king of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0300D] Rudolf III.] [Anno 1032, September 6], Conrad proposed to invade Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0300D] That is, for the second time. But Arnulf confused the two expeditions, as the Palatine associates have already observed.]. To invade it, he ordered the Lombard army to hasten there [Col. 0301A]. He himself, breaking through blocked passages from the neighboring side [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “breaking through passages from the contiguous side”], occupied the various fortified towns (Anno 1034).

From nearby Italy, elected leaders advanced with the other nobles [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “the leaders, as if the bishop himself were among them”], namely the bishop Heribert [Note: [Col. 0301D] After making his will at home, in March 1034; see Giulini III, 246.] and the distinguished margrave Boniface, the two lights of the kingdom. They reconnoitered those approaches which had been made passable by cutting through the rocks of the impregnable fortress of Bard [Note: [Col. 0301D] Bard is a castle on the Dora Baltea, defending the royal road from Aosta to Ivrea. BETHM.]. Leading the Lombard army through these routes, they crossed the steep ridges of Mount Jove [Note: [Col. 0301] B1 reads “Jovi”; B2* reads “Jovis”] [Note: [Col. 0301D] The Great St Bernard. PAL.]. Thus, entering the land by a violent incursion, they reached the emperor [Note: [Col. 0301] B adds “Conrad”]. Since the Burgundians were unable to resist, they hastened to surrender, submitting to Conrad under a permanent condition of subjection. And so it happened that all returned to their own lands in great glory [Col. 0301B].

9. At the same time, in June, on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul (Anno 1033, June 29), during the heat of midday, an eclipse of the sun appeared, bringing darkness upon the world for three hours. At another time afterward, the moon was seen at night [Note: [Col. 0301] B1 reads “by night”], darkened with a bloody color.

10. After many successful outcomes [Note: [Col. 0301] Witness 3 reads *prosperatus*, “having prospered”], Bishop Heribert ruled everyone somewhat too immoderately, considering his own will rather than that of others [Note: [Col. 0301D] He arranged the entire kingdom of Italy according to his own command. Henry III, in a charter of 1047, in Muratori, Antiquities VI, 218.]. Thus it happened that certain soldiers of the city, commonly called valvassors, secretly plotted against his actions, continually conspiring against him. When they learned of an opportunity arising from a powerful man’s being deprived of his benefice, they suddenly burst forth into open audacity of rebellion [Note: [Col. 0301] B1 reads “they burst forth into open rebellious audacity”; witnesses 1 and 2 read “the rebels” here], now being more numerous. When this became known to the bishop [Col. 0301C], he prepared through many counsels [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “first.”] to oppose their plots [Note: [Col. 0301] Muratori reads “their opposing plots.”]. But when he accomplished nothing, he attempted to overcome them by force. In the first battle they were defeated and severely worn down by fighting; leaving the city, they departed in mourning. Soon the people of Martesana and Seprio came to their aid [Note: [Col. 0301D] That is, soldiers from the counties neighboring Milan to the north, Seprio and Martesana], along with many other fellow soldiers of the kingdom, prepared both to die and to live together—especially the Lodigiani, mindful of the recent injury.

11. (Anno 1035) The archbishop, having gathered a force from everywhere he could, though not without his own faithful men [Col. 0302A], attempted to pursue and crush them all. When they dared to resist, they met in a field called Malus [Note: [Col. 0301D] Near Motta, a place between Milan and Lodi. SIGON.] from ancient times; and rightly “evil,” since it was destined to be watered with human blood [Note: [Col. 0301] Another reading has “and rightly evil.”]. There, when battle was joined in the open field, a great slaughter of the dead from both sides took place. While the aforementioned bishop of Asti, indeed the chief strength of the war, was passing through the middle of the battle, he was pierced and killed [Note: [Col. 0302D] 1035, according to Herimann of Augsburg.]. His death brought the battle to an end [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads: “Among them the aforesaid bishop Olderic of Asti fell, pierced by a spear; his death soon became the end of the war.”]. The bishop’s side, confounded by the loss of so great a brother, while the others, secure after the death of so great an enemy, withdrew from the battle and returned to their own homes [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “departed,” omitting “from the battle.”].

12. (Anno 1036) As so great a danger approached, the archbishop arranged to summon his emperor from Germany, hoping that he would become his helper [Col. 0302B]. The emperor came to Verona and from there to Milan (December 1037), where on the first day he was honorably received; on the following day, however, the people rioted and shouted against him, and he was gravely offended. For they had heard that the king had deprived Heribert of his right in respect of Lodi. The emperor [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “Conrad”], concealing his resentment, went to Pavia. There, having announced a general conference, he contrived a deceit, seized the archbishop, and held him, entrusting him to the patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0302D] Poppo] for custody.

Behold, the Milanese city shuddered in astonishment, grieving and lamenting that it had been deprived of its shepherd, from child to old man. O, what prayers to the Lord and how many tears were poured forth! When clergy, people, and soldiers cried out continually [Note: [Col. 0301] B reads “clergy and people”], an agreement concerning his release was made, hostages being given to the emperor. After receiving them, he nevertheless kept him, intending eventually to condemn him to exile [Col. 0302C]. Indeed, on the same day he also seized three other bishops [Note: [Col. 0302D] Somewhat later, when envoys joined with Heribert had sent a delegation to Odo, according to the Saxon Annals for 1037]: Arderic of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0302D] Arderic], Peter of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0302D] apparently Peter], and Hubald of Cremona [Note: [Col. 0302D] Hubald].

After two months the archbishop escaped [Note: [Col. 0302D] See what he himself recounts concerning this in a document of 1040, subscribed by Arderic, bishop of Vercelli. Campi, Piacenza I, p. 507; Ughelli IV, 103.]. When he came, the entire city ran out to meet him, so joyful that, like a servant before his master, no woman yielded to a man in running for joy [Note: [Col. 0301] Muratori reads *ita* (“thus”); witnesses 1, 3a, and 5* read *crederet* (“would believe”). In place of “After two months ... running,” B has: “Moreover, blessed Ambrose, entreated by the prayers of his Church, obtained from the Lord the liberation of his vicar, while everyone, including the emperor himself, remained unaware.”]. Behold, the city’s evening weeping was suddenly changed into morning joy (Psalm 29:6).

13. When Conrad saw that he had been deceived, he publicly declared Heribert an enemy of himself [Col. 0303A] and of the state. Therefore an edict was issued by the emperor Augustus that all the kingdoms under his authority should hasten to attack Milan [Note: [Col. 0303] absent in B1]. And so it happened that all Italy and all Germany assembled together, from one end to the other.

At the first assault he attacked a certain strong fortified town named Landriano [Note: [Col. 0303] B1 reads “its name”; B2* omits “toward it”] [Note: [Col. 0303D] It lies not far west of Lodi.]. Attacking it [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “assailing it”], he demolished it in a short time. From there [Note: [Col. 0303] B has “whence” or “from there”] he advanced to Milan (May), pitching his tents and encamping three miles from the city.

The Milanese, ready to resist, fortified every nearby position. From among them, selected young men, splendid in arms, trained in warfare, flying on horseback, practiced with their weapons, taunted the imperial soldiers, rode around the camp threatening them with their shields, and struck down their nearest opponents with spears [Col. 0303B]. After they had practiced these skirmishes for several days [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “preludes”], it happened on the holy day of the Lord’s Ascension (May 19) that all the imperial forces, with their emperor, burst from the camp: Germans fighting on the right, Italians on the left.

When the citizens met them from the opposite direction, the battle grew fierce everywhere, with different groups fighting in different places. On the front line, a certain tall and noble German and Wido, the Italian royal standard-bearer and margrave, were pierced amid the weapons. When they fell, and many others lay in their own blood, the ardor of battle gradually cooled. Finally, the imperial forces gathered their ranks and returned to the camp. The townsmen too abandoned the fields and sought their own homes.

14. The emperor therefore withdrew from the city and ordered all the places nearby and far around it to be laid waste [Col. 0303C]. While he was consuming everything with flames, he was caught by repeated strikes of lightning [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “strikes” in another form] and a storm of hail. Abandoning what he had begun, he withdrew in mourning. Moreover, Bertaldus, the royal secretary, on whose counsel everything was done, soon became deranged. (Chapter 14.) When the king ought to have been appeased by this, he became even more enraged, to such an extent that he judged Heribert deserving of deprivation of his own dignity.

After reaching this decision, he gave the archbishopric to Ambrose, a cardinal priest of the Milanese Church and his own chaplain, although the bishops witnessed it but did not wish it. When Heribert heard this, he likewise began to plot the king’s deprivation of his honor [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “plotted”]. Through a secret embassy he therefore urged Odo, the powerful count of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0303D] Count of Campania], to seize the kingdom of Italy with his support. Odo [Note: [Col. 0303] B1 reads “to whom”; B2* omits the adversative] delayed nothing; greedy for kingship [Col. 0303D], he violently invaded certain parts of Alamannia first [Col. 0304A]. Duke Gotefrid attacked him bravely and, after a fierce encounter, overthrew him in an instant (November 15). His severed head is said to have been sent to the emperor in Italy [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “whose head”]. Thereafter the emperor ordered all the leading men of the kingdom to swear to an annual devastation of Milan and, with an obdurate mind, returned to Swabia, sick in his feet and weak in all his limbs.

15. Meanwhile the Pseudo-Ambrose, openly carrying the staff and ring, was secretly lying in ambush like a wolf and plotting against Heribert in every possible way. Each day he made many promises, swearing many oaths to clergy and laity, in the city and outside it, while a faction was being formed. But when the dignity of the faithful perceived the plots of the traitors, they punished those caught in the crime both in their persons and in their own property. Thus, as Heribert’s power prevailed, all that fraudulent presumption vanished [Col. 0304B].

16. At the same time (Anno 1039) it happened that all the princes of the kingdom assembled from every direction to lay waste, as they had promised the king, the territory of the Milanese. Foreseeing the oppression that was to come [Note: [Col. 0303] B1 reads “providing”; B2* has another reading], the archbishop immediately ordered all the inhabitants of the Ambrosian diocese, armed from peasant to soldier and from poor man to rich, to assemble in the city, so that in so great a host they might defend their homeland against the enemy.

He established the following sign to go before his men as they went to battle. A tall beam, like a ship’s mast, fastened into a sturdy wagon, was raised high. At its top it carried a golden orb with two hanging strips of the whitest veil [Col. 0304C] [Note: [Col. 0303] B reads “with veils”]; at its middle a revered cross, painted with the image of the Savior and his arms extended wide, looked down upon the surrounding ranks, so that whatever the outcome of the battle, they might draw strength when they saw this sign [Note: [Col. 0303D] Heribert adapted this for war; it had already existed elsewhere for a long time, for example at the monastery of Novalesa. See the Chronicle of Novalesa II, 10. In any event, Ricottus proved in his excellent book, History of the Companies of Adventure, that the carroccio was always an emblem of infantry alone, not cavalry. BETHM.].

A grave conflict [Note: [Col. 0303] “Grave” is omitted in B.] would have taken place between the city and the kingdom unless a new rumor of the emperor’s death shook the minds of the enemy. So, when the camps were broken up, they rose in confusion and haste, colliding with one another [Note: [Col. 0303] One witness reads “they rose”; another “having been dispersed.” In place of all this, B has: “the minds of those who heard it. When the truth of the matter had been learned, both armies, intent upon battle, gladly came to rest, and everyone returned to his own place. After the emperor had died ...”]. Among them the standard-bearer from Parma fell and died disgracefully.

17. After Conrad’s death (Anno 1039, June 4), his youthful son Henry—created king while his father was alive—was called emperor by everyone. He was sufficiently well suited to govern the state. Not imitating his father’s disposition, he established a treaty of peace with the archbishop at the counsel of his faithful men (Anno 1040), and was afterward faithfully honored by him [Col. 0304D] [Note: [Col. 0304D] See the Saxon Annals for 1040.].

[Col. 0305A] 18. When all matters had therefore been pacified, internal quarrel and civil war followed—so detestable and lamentable that, apart from the innumerable disasters of war, the condition of the city and Church was altered. For it is entirely true that civil discords are nourished by idleness, and that iniquity often emerges as though from fatness (Psalm 72:7).

Since no external enemies opposed them, the citizens directed their hatred against one another. It happened that, in a private quarrel between them, a certain commoner was severely beaten by a soldier. The common people, indignant and stirred up by this, suddenly took up arms against the soldiers; the soldiers themselves, like unwary men, resisted as best they could. From this the tinder of hatred began to smolder, and very many oaths were sworn by the opposing factions.

A certain Lanzo [Note: [Col. 0305] B1 reads “a certain man”; B2* omits “a certain”], a freeborn soldier of the city [Note: [Col. 0305C] Waldo, also called Lanzo, notary and judge of the sacred palace, is mentioned in a charter of 1029, Giulini III, 516. In 1034 he wrote Aribert’s will; Giulini III, 267, gives reasons for considering him identical with the Lanzo mentioned by Arnulf. In 1035 he delivered a judgment as the emperor’s envoy, Giulini III, 517. In April 1042 he subscribed Aribert’s documents, but is absent in 1044. In November 1045 he took part in a judgment of Margrave Azo (Muratori, Antiquities IV, 9). In October 1046 he delivered a judgment with Arioald, Giulini III, 527. In February 1057 he drew up the agreement of Archbishop Wido with Odo, bishop of Novara, Monumenta Historiae Patriae, Charters, p. 586. Landulfus, born no less nobly, also served as a notary, as we shall soon see.], supported the common crowd particularly strongly, and through his encouragement it grew greatly in strength [Col. 0305B].

The rest of the nobility, angered by this, nevertheless joined the soldiers, partly out of affection for their own loyal men. At the same time many dreams and many prodigies were reported in the city. While the city hung in such uncertainty, a sudden cry arose there from a slight cause. Everyone rushed together; a savage battle began through the streets and corners, and for a long time they fought from rooftops and battlements on both sides. Finally, the small number of soldiers, surrounded by the multitude of commoners, was pressed from every side by flames and steel. Consequently they abandoned their homes in anger, together with their children and wives. A few days later, the archbishop too departed from the city, to provide for their situation [Note: [Col. 0305C] After issuing documents at Milan in April 1042, subscribed by Lanzo, Giulini III, 525.]. The people of Martesana and Seprio immediately came to their aid.

[Col. 0306A] 19. Strengthened by this support, they prudently arranged to fortify six strongholds near the city. Dwelling in them with all their families, they established a very firm siege all around, raging day and night with slaughter. For six groups, issuing from the towns, continually attacked the city from six directions.

The civil population was no less often bursting out through the gates [Note: [Col. 0305C] There were six principal gates, from which the divisions of the city and of the army took their names: the Roman, Ticinese, Vercelline, Comacine, New, and Eastern gates of Saint Renza. Giulini III, 372.], sometimes defending itself by fighting, sometimes attempting in its fury to attack them voluntarily. For scarcely a day passed without bloodshed.

When the factions had thus raged for three years, each had frequently tested, in alternating encounters, what it could do against the other. Then envoys came from the emperor, announcing an inviolable truce [Note: [Col. 0305C] In 1043, in April and June, Adalger, chancellor and royal envoy, held judicial sessions at Como and Asti, with Aribert present at Pavia. See Giulini III, 373–376; Monumenta Historiae Patriae, Charters, p. 552. Later, in the first months of 1045, the king held a Lombard assembly at Augsburg and arranged with them the administration of that kingdom. Annals of Altaich, 1045. There, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, he granted the monks of Saint-Denis a charter of confirmation. Puricellus, Sacred Monuments, p. 489.], which they confirmed by oath through the power and counsel of the entire kingdom.

[Col. 0306B] 20. At the same time the archbishop, residing at Monza, became gravely ill. When he was sick unto death, he ordered that, after arranging his household and all his possessions [Note: [Col. 0306C] He issued documents; Puricellus, Ambrosian Monuments, p. 414; Giulini IX, 36. Dated December 1044. Drawn up at the aforesaid place, Monza.], he be carried to the city.

After languishing there for several days, he was taken from the present life (Anno 1045, January 16). He was buried at Saint Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0306C] Giulini still saw his epitaph there and published it in III, 391, in these words:

“Here I lie, dust, though once the world shone brightly for me.

Then I was Heribert, and flourished in great splendor.

I served as archbishop, performing the office of a gracious bishop.

Now I am buried, Christ, servant of your servants.

For the merits of those who have deserved to please you,

I beg you, have mercy on me, redeemed by your blood.

Reader, coming here, say to the Redeemer: ‘Forgive him,’

And, living, may he always rest in that life.

He died in the year 1045 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the sixteenth day of January, in the thirteenth indiction.”]

where he himself had founded an elegant monastery. While still alive, he also provided for all the orders of the Church, bestowing many resources for the support of those living now and those to come.

21. In his days, the sacred relics of Archbishop John were revealed to a certain inhabitant of the city of Genoa. Since enough has been said about him, let our pen now cease, its edge already needing to be sharpened carefully for the third time.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK [Note: [Col. 0305] “Of the histories of Arnulf. What remains is now supplied by the third reading,” added by witnesses 2 and B1; omitted by B2*.]

[Col. 0305]

[Col. 0305C] 1. I remember having said recently that, because of the civil quarrel, the condition of the city and Church had changed [Note: [Col. 0305] B reads “I remember saying”]. Whether for the better or the worse [Col. 0306C] [Note: [Col. 0305] One witness reads “for the worse”], it was not appropriate to say, since a comparison of the past with the present will make the answer readily apparent [Col. 0307A]. Would that I did not know it! All these matters, however, will become clearer through writing.

2. After Heribert’s death (Anno 1045, July 18), many people discussed restoring the bishop. But the emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0307] “Henry, son of Conrad, who, because of the division, had neglected Milan,” according to B1 and B2*, which has “division”], keeping the Milanese discord before his eyes, disregarded the noble and wise clergy of the first rank and chose as bishop an ignorant man who came from the countryside [Note: [Col. 0307D] That is, neither learned in sacred letters nor enrolled in the urban clergy. Later authors call him Valvassorius of Velate, which may be true, for among Arnulf’s soldiers the lesser men are not nobles; see below, chapter 10, and the preface, p. 1. Wido’s kinsmen by marriage are mentioned in chapter 21, and his lineage in chapter 20.], whose name was Wido [Note: [Col. 0307] B has “Guido” in the constitution].

In truth, he took him from the sheepfolds and from behind the nursing ewes he brought him (Psalm 78:70). The Milanese offered little resistance to this act, whether through fear of the king, hatred among themselves, or partly through avarice—which, as a certain wise hagiographer says, first introduced every evil into Italy. From then on everything turned for the worse.

Afterward it happened that, turning against one another, each confronted the other [Col. 0307B] [Note: [Col. 0307] B reads “each confronted the other” in another form], laying his reproach before him, as well as the harm done to the city. Finally, after much deliberation, they joined together in treaties of peace in the presence of the holy Gospels, making an amnesty—that is, an abolition of evils—which, according to Orosius (II, 17), the Athenians are said to have instituted first and to have called by that name [Note: [Col. 0307] “as Orosius testifies” is absent in B.].

3. At that time the emperor Henry came to Italy and, after celebrating a synodal council at Pavia (Anno 1046, October 25), proceeded toward Rome. The pope [Note: [Col. 0307D] Gregory VI.] met him at Piacenza, having been enthroned while another was still alive and consenting [Note: [Col. 0307D] Benedict IX.]. After a general assembly of bishops had been held at Rome [Note: [Col. 0307D] More precisely, at Sutri; Suidger was elected at Rome.], it seemed to the king and to all the bishops that the pope himself was unjustly occupying the chair. He was immediately deposed, and a bishop from among the Germans was substituted in his place [Col. 0307C]. The king gave him the name Clement, changing his former name; from him he also received the imperial crown.

4. A third holy Leo then became distinguished (Anno 1048), through whose industry the condition of the Roman Church was restored. He most devoutly celebrated two synods in Italy, one at Pavia [Note: [Col. 0307D] 1049, in May] and the other at Mantua [Note: [Col. 0307D] 1053, in February], in the emperor’s absence.

Since he mercifully deplored the severe oppression with which the most impious Normans afflicted wretched Apulia, he attempted by preaching mixed with prayers to recall them from so many crimes (Anno 1053). When he achieved nothing, he attempted to restrain their savagery by arms (June 18), although the outcome of the war went against him. For the judgments of God are a great abyss (Psalm 36:7).

[Col. 0308A] 5. In those days, while Margrave Boniface [Note: [Col. 0307] “of Montferrat” is added by witnesses 3 and 5*, and by another hand in the margin of witness 1. I read it in B1, but that is an error of the Palatine associates; it is not found in B2*.] was crossing a shady grove, he was struck by a poisoned arrow from an ambush concealed obliquely. Alas, the old man, full of days, was overtaken by a timely death a little too soon.

6. At that time the emperor held a judicial assembly in the fields of Roncaglia [Note: [Col. 0308D] May 5, 1055, according to a charter in Muratori, Antiquities III, 645. It remains uncertain whether Arnulf refers to another judicial assembly held there. Nothing is known about that Adelbert.]. After examining many complaints, he investigated many matters legally. There he ordered Margrave Adelbert, against whom there had been an excessive outcry, to be seized with other criminals and bound in iron chains—quite deservedly.

Afterward, for many days, he fought according to circumstances, now with the Hungarians, now with the Leuticians. He triumphed nobly over all of them, constraining the defeated to pay tribute. One notable trophy of his is indicated by a gilded spear violently taken from the king of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0308D] Compare the Annals of Liège, 1043, and the Annals of Altaich, 1045.] and hung in the church of the Apostles at Rome [Col. 0308B] [Note: [Col. 0308D] Before the confession of blessed Peter, according to Bonizo, p. 801; later above the Guidonian gate, according to Ciampino, On Sacred Buildings, chapter 4, section 10.].

When he flourished in distinguished imperial power, he departed from the world beloved by everyone (Anno 1056, October 5), leaving behind a boy of his own name, to be cherished in the maternal lap of the empress Agnes.

7. During the reign of this child, the people of Pavia boldly rejected the bishop given to them by him, as was customary [Note: [Col. 0308D] Adalric, against whom the people of Pavia set up Henry, according to Robolini, History of Pavia II, 54.]. Showing deference neither to the royal appointment nor to the consecration carried out by apostolic authority, they continued to despise the rejected bishop until his death.

8. During these days (1059), a disagreement arose between them and the Milanese over civil matters [Note: [Col. 0308D] Berthold’s Annals, 1059.]. For each city was populous and renowned above the others of the kingdom. Nevertheless, in the estimation [Note: [Col. 0307] “innocence,” B.] of all, Milan held the advantage. Since they were neighboring cities, each was ashamed to yield to the other. Hence it came about that they repaid one another with killings, plunder, and fires, as well as robberies. It happened, then, that the Pavians, being the weaker party, hired troops from elsewhere at a price and advanced to devastate the Milanese territory; but the Milanese, having allied with the men of Lodi, rose against them, although a considerable part of the Milanese, under the leadership of the archbishop, was fighting elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0307] “that is, the parts are missing,” B.]. The two armies met in the fields in ordered ranks, raising their banners high (23 May 1061). There was a violent clash between the parties [Note: [Col. 0307] “against one another,” B., Mur.]; they raged in combat for a long time. At last the Pavians withdrew from the battle, while their adversaries pursued them from behind. A hired legion of foreigners soon came bravely to their aid, although shortly afterward it yielded and left the field to the Milanese [Note: [Col. 0309] “the words ‘shortly afterward it yielded and left the field’ are missing,” M.; “missing in B.”]. There was an immense slaughter of noble horsemen and a lamentable loss for the two cities. Finally, that day fulfilled the expression of an ancient word: for in former times the field on which they had fought was called “the Dead Man” [Note: [Col. 0309] “of the dead,” B.] [Note: [Col. 0309C] The name remained attached to a village situated between Milan and Pavia. The day is indicated by the Calendar in Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores, vol. I, p. 235; cf. Giulini IV, 48–58.].

9. At about the same time, the people of Asti likewise rejected the bishop given to them, as the Pavians had done; but through the prudence of the countess Adelaide, a very martial lady [Note: [Col. 0309] “duchess,” 1; “duke,” 3a, 5*.], after long struggles and after the city had finally been set on fire, they rejected the other whom they had chosen and accepted the former bishop.

10. At this same time an exceedingly great horror seized the Ambrosian clergy, as the people newly rose up against them and sins increased on both sides. “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
