Yet this horror, with the letter of the aspiration altered, produced error in many. Since the matter is still before our eyes, we shall relate its beginning and sequence as best we can. Let him himself provide the ending who, being Alpha and Omega, wonderfully orders all things.

A certain deacon from the decumanate, named Ariald [Note: [Col. 0309] “from the decumani,” B.], had been indulged by Bishop Wido with many pleasures and heaped with many honors. While devoting himself to the study of letters, he became a most severe interpreter of divine law [Note: [Col. 0309] “of divine law”; another reading: “of the honors” 1, B.; “yet not,” B. 2.], exercising harsh judgments against the clergy alone. Though he possessed little authority and had been born in humble circumstances [Note: [Col. 0309D] His biographer Andrew reports that his parents, Bezo and Beza, were quite noble (ch. 1, 6), though less noble than Landulf says (ch. 9). They were, namely, “of equestrian descent,” according to Bonizo, On the Persecution of the Church, p. 805. Later the Alciati family claimed them for itself. Cf. Landulf III, 5; Giulini IV, 10. In Peter Damian’s account he is called “Ariald the deacon of the chapel of the archbishop of Milan.” According to Andrew, ch. 33, he began to preach ten years before his death, first at Varese and then at Milan. Letter of Syrus to Andrew, ch. 36; Life of Ariald.], he foresaw that he should attach to himself Landulf, as though the latter were more noble and more suitable for this purpose, and made him his familiar associate and follower.

Landulf, however, being readier of tongue and voice and an excessive lover of popularity, suddenly became the leader of the preaching, usurping for himself, contrary to the custom of the Church, the office of preaching. Although he had not advanced through any ecclesiastical orders [Note: [Col. 0309D] According to Landulf III, 5, he was a notary and therefore not yet a subdeacon, which is the lowest of the ecclesiastical orders. Wido speaks similarly in a statute of 1067: “This pernicious commerce, which customarily prevailed in this holy Church, whereby whoever approached to be advanced to the clerical orders gave twelve coins for the subdiaconate, eighteen for the diaconate, and finally twenty-four for receiving the presbyterate, as though according to a fixed condition.” Cf. Alexander II [Col. 0310C] in Mansi, Collection of Councils XIX, 977. That he was a cleric is clear from the very words of Ariald, chs. 13, 16; but the office of preaching did not belong to a notary. Landulf, later called Cotta by subsequent writers, was “a cleric from the urban nobility, distinguished both in rank and birth,” Andrew of Vallombrosa, ch. 5; “of senatorial family,” Peter Damian, Opusculum III, 42; and brother of Herlembald, of whom see below, ch. 16. Anastasius, also called Amizo, the father of Herlembald, a soldier of Saint Ambrose, was sent and appointed by Emperor Henry around 1015, together with his son Herlembald. Giulini III, 75, 118, reasonably considers him to have been the grandfather of the two brothers.], he imposed a heavy yoke upon the necks of consecrated men, although Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light.

[Col. 0310A] 11. Among the other things that he daily pressed upon the ears of the people, one day he preached to them as follows:

“Most beloved elders, I can no longer keep within me the speech conceived in my heart. Do not, my lords, do not despise the words of a young and inexperienced man; for God often reveals to the lesser what he denies to the greater. Tell me: do you believe in the triune and one God?”

They all answered: “We believe.”

And he added: “Fortify your foreheads with the sign of the cross.”

And it was done.

After this he said:

“I rejoice with you in your devotion, yet I grieve over the great destruction that threatens. For many years now the Savior has not been recognized in this city. You have long been in error, since you possess no traces of the truth. Instead of light you grope in darkness, all of you having become blind, because your guides are blind. But can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into a pit?

“For manifold evils abound among priests and levites and the other ministers of sacred things, including that simoniacal heresy [Note: [Col. 0310D] According to Andrew, ch. 11, Ariald did not speak these words until after his journey to Rome; until then, “they had kept silent about it.” Afterward Guido, “and the greater part of the clergy and soldiers, as well as many of the lesser people, wicked men, seeing themselves, said to one another: ‘If this teaching succeeds, it will certainly not be possible for us or our sons to live. For what is our life except the benefices of the churches, which we continually sell and buy?’”]—and since they are Nicolaitans and simoniacs, they deservedly ought to be cast out. Therefore, if you hope for salvation from the Savior, beware of them entirely from now on, venerating none of their offices. Their sacrifices are no different from dog dung, and their basilicas are the mangers of beasts.

“Therefore, now that you have rejected them, let all their possessions be confiscated; let everyone have the power to seize everything, wherever such things are found in the city or outside it. For I too have committed many offenses deserving punishment; but, worst of all, by continuing until now to communicate with the unworthy, I have offended the King of heaven. Now, however, by the favor of the divinity, I am doing penance and intend to take precautions against such things in the future.

“Therefore, my beloved, be my imitators, and walk as you have us for a model.”

12. When these and many other things, which human memory cannot contain, had taken place, the people, always eager for novelties, were stirred to excessive zeal against the clergy. Some thought that by this they were devoting themselves to God; others were intent on the profits of greed. In addition, for many days Landulf himself, together with his accomplice Ariald, stirred the minds of many, proposing ever new and unheard-of things in his preaching in pursuit of the favoring breeze of popularity, as he knew the ways of the crowd [Note: [Col. 0311] “for these things,” B.].

To restrain his boldness, the leading men of the Church often assembled and set the sacred Scriptures and canonical decrees against him [Note: [Col. 0311] “and the canons,” B.]. He despised all these things and persisted nonetheless. Indeed, one day, coming to the church with crowds singing psalms from the marketplace, he violently drove them all from the choir [Note: [Col. 0311D] Cf. Bonizo, p. 805.], pursuing them through alleys and lodgings.

Then he cunningly arranged for a document—called a *phytacium* [Note: [Col. 0311] “*pytatium*,” B.]—to be written concerning the observance of chastity, extracted from secular laws while disregarding the canon [Note: [Col. 0311] “arising from the laws,” B. 1; “having arisen,” B. 2*.]. In it all the sacred orders of the Ambrosian diocese [Col. 0311B] were compelled to subscribe against their will, he himself coercing them with the aid of laymen [Note: [Col. 0311] “with lances,” B.].

Meanwhile, the city’s robbers, after demolishing certain houses in the city, ranged through the parish, searching the clergy’s houses and plundering their possessions [Note: [Col. 0311D] Cf. the words of the statute of 1067: “But all those clergy and laymen who swore that they would work through right faith so that these evils might not occur against simoniacal and incontinent clerics—and who consequently committed fires, plunderings, bloodshed, and many unjust acts of violence—we altogether prohibit from doing such things any longer.” Also Peter Damian’s account: “The greater part of the people, not only from the city but also from the suburbs, had already taken that very oath against simoniacs and Nicolaitans; their number, it is said, already exceeded a thousand.”].

The clergy, therefore, afflicted in many ways, first complained in humble embassy to the neighboring bishops and then to the Roman pontiff. At that time Stephen presided at Rome [Note: [Col. 0311D] 2 August 1057–29 March 1058.]. After weighing what he had heard, he ordered by apostolic letters that the people should be quiet and that the archbishop should convene a synod concerning this matter. Relying on that authority, Bishop Wido diligently endeavored to summon an assembly of bishops, instructing Landulf and Ariald to attend reasonably to the matters under discussion.

13. An episcopal synodal assembly was held at a place called Fontanetum [Note: [Col. 0311D] A town in the Novarese district, still existing under that name. PAL.]. When they had devoted three days to spiritual matters [Note: [Col. 0311] “was devoting himself,” 1, 5*; “had devoted themselves,” Puricelli, On the Saints, p. 183.], awaiting the arrival of those men, it seemed to everyone that such great boldness ought to be punished by a just anathema. And so it was done.

Landulf, however, treating all this as worthless, instead of being afraid became still more arrogant. From that point he insulted the bishops, especially the metropolitan; raging, he attacked the clergy alone, accusing them of the destruction of themselves and their fellows, while he fostered the laymen [Note: [Col. 0311] “favored,” B. 1; “but not,” B. 2*.], as brothers. Since he was thoroughly skilled in feigning and concealing and was loved by many, he twisted everything to his own will and himself became a wondrous spectacle to the world.

Having therefore acquired power, he imposed upon all the laymen a common oath, presenting as the object of attack the sexual sins of the sacred orders and their purchasable consecrations. Not long afterward he compelled the clergy also to swear it. From that time onward countless crowds of men and women accompanied him wherever he went and guarded him day and night. Having become united in purpose, they despised the churches and rejected the divine offices together with their ministers, declaring everything to be simoniacal. The rest of the populace mockingly called such people “Patarines” [Note: [Col. 0312B] “Paterines,” B.] [Note: [Col. 0311D] “The quarter of the transparent old rag-sellers, called by us Patarines.” Giulini IV, 98; *paterinos*, that is, “ragged men,” Bonizo, p. 805.].

Moreover, Ariald set out for Rome, carrying letters of defense [Note: [Col. 0312D] After reporting that the marriages of clerics had been destroyed by popular force, Andrew continues (ch. 8): “At that same time the faithful decided to send Landulf to Rome for the synod, because, as his rivals falsely accused them, they were going there.” Landulf was wounded at Piacenza, while Ariald reached Rome. The pope, “after showing him great honor, ordered him from which priests he should henceforth receive the divine mysteries, and under unavoidable command instructed him to return to the work begun and persist vigorously in it until he either completely eradicated the wicked practices or offered his blood. He says nothing about a synod. Landulf reports in III, 11, and Bonizo p. 805, that these events took place under Stephen XI.]. When he accused the Ambrosian clergy, asserting that all were Nicolaitans and simoniacs and utterly disobedient to the Roman Church, while he himself, together with Landulf, was devoted and fighting solely for the truth, he quickly won the favor of the Romans.

Since they desire to rule by apostolic right, they seem to wish to dominate everyone [Note: [Col. 0311] “everything,” 3a, B.] and subject all things to their authority, although the teacher of the Gospel teaches his apostles humility, saying:

“The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be like that; rather, let the greater among you become like the lesser, and the leader like the servant” [Col. 0312C] (Luke 22:25).

14. Because of the aforementioned upheaval, Roman legates frequently came to Milan: namely, Hildebrand, a cardinal archdeacon formerly a monk; Peter of Ostia; Anselm, bishop of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0311] “Alselmus,” 1. H.; “Bishop Anselm of Badagio, a citizen of Milan and formerly cardinal of the Ambrosian Church, but at that time bishop of Lucca, and the Roman pontiff were sent to Milan with the aforesaid,” B.]; and several others, each in his turn [Note: [Col. 0312D] Landulf III, 13, reports that Hildebrand and Anselm came to Milan with Ariald; Bonizo p. 805 reports that bishops were sent *a latere* with Hildebrand, who then proceeded to Gaul.].

If, when addressing the people, they had carefully attended to the apostle’s saying, “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10), they would certainly have provided appropriately for themselves and the clergy. Nevertheless, Peter of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0313C] He served as legate with Anselm under Nicholas II and later wrote a lengthy account of the mission to Hildebrand, published here by the Palatine Associates among his works, vol. III, opusculum 5, in Mansi, Collection of Councils XIX, p. 887. Cf. Bonizo p. 806. Andrew makes no mention of these events.], when the Ambrosian synod had then been assembled at Milan (1059), saw the noble order of the clergy, the rank of the persons, and the elegance of their dress; he also considered the excellence of their morals and the duties properly distributed among them, and testified truthfully that he had never seen such a clergy anywhere [Note: [Col. 0313] “never,” B., omitting “such.”].

Yet in the present assembly, because he was a Roman, he tried to preside over the archbishop. As a result, a sudden popular tumult arose in the city [Note: [Col. 0313C] See Peter, cited above. Landulf, then placed in the greatest danger, vowed that he would become a monk. Later, when he refused to fulfill the vow, Peter Damian rebuked him in a letter found among his opuscula, no. 42.]. Had his humility not yielded, the crowd would have made an assault [Note: [Col. 0313] “assault,” 3a, B.], not for Wido’s sake but for the honor of Ambrose.

Moreover, when Peter perceived the guilt of certain members of the clergy, he retained power over everything and judged their faults as he pleased. For, lest we tell a falsehood, not all of them were entirely free from the charges brought against them. Then, abolishing the old arrangement, he imposed a new one upon the Milanese Church through letters composed by him; the archbishop, together with the clergy, subscribed to it unwillingly, compelled and shouted at by the people.

15. O senseless Milanese, who has bewitched you? Yesterday you proclaimed the primacy of a single seat; today you are confounding the order of the whole Church, truly straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel (Matthew 23:24). Would it not have been better for your own bishop to arrange this [Note: [Col. 0313] “bishop, would he not have arranged this more holily?” 1; “has arranged this,” B.]?

Perhaps you will say: “Rome is venerable in the apostle.” It certainly is; but Milan in Ambrose is not to be despised either. Indeed, these things were not written without reason in the Roman annals. For it will be said in the future: “Milan has been subjected to Rome.” Behold, your metropolitan is summoned, contrary to custom, to a Roman synod [Note: [Col. 0313C] Not long afterward, however, Nicholas convened a synod at which Guido, bishop of Milan, is known to have sat, willingly or unwillingly, compelled by the Patarines; he brought with him the stiff-necked Lombard bishops, “bulls.” Bonizo p. 806.].

He went [Note: [Col. 0313] “Being summoned to Rome, he went to the synod,” B.], but, contrary to your desires, everything turned out favorably for him. He was treated with notable distinction [Col. 0314A] by the apostolic lord Nicholas, at whose right side he was seated in the present synod [Note: [Col. 0313] “placed,” 3, Puricelli p. 205.].

When that informer Ariald rose to accuse him, the bishops of Asti [Note: [Col. 0313C] Giselinus, according to Bonizo.], Novara [Note: [Col. 0313C] Otto.], and Turin [Note: [Col. 0313C] Cunibertus.], together with the other suffragan bishops, immediately stood opposite him and, before the whole assembly, refuted that false witness by the authority of the Scriptures. Thus confuted by all, he sat down on the ground in confusion.

Thereafter, when the archbishop promised the lord pope that he would henceforth be obedient, he received from him a ring of apostolic favor and of the whole ecclesiastical power, and returned glorious in every respect [Note: [Col. 0313] “he returned glorious in everything,” B.].

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place [Note: [Col. 0313C] That is, according to Andrew, before Ariald came to Rome for the first time; see above, ch. 13.], Landulf, intending to go to Rome [Note: [Col. 0313] “Landulf went to Rome,” B.], returned after being severely beaten and wounded by the people of Piacenza, unable to proceed farther. After this he did not cease to persecute the pontiff and the clergy with greater severity than before.

16. When it pleased the Most High, who searches the reins and hearts, the man who had long contemplated another’s weakness suddenly felt the unexpected pain of his own illness. Since he suffered for two years from a pulmonary disease, he was deprived of the use of his voice [Note: [Col. 0313C] Landulf III, 29. The time can scarcely be established with certainty; cf. Bonizo p. 807. A fragment of Alexander II’s letter to Landulf and Ariald is preserved in Ivo, *Decretum* XII, ch. 24, and Mansi, Collection of Councils XIX, p. 980.], so that in the very matter by which he had afflicted many he also became powerless, as Scripture says: “By the very things through which one sins, by those things one is punished” (Wisdom 11:17).

But lest we seem to accuse the dead, let us say nothing further about him, whose manner of life and death must be left entirely to divine judgment.

Ariald, therefore, deprived of such a companion, continually urged Herlembald [Note: [Col. 0313] “Herlembald,” B.; confirmed.] to undertake the cause of his dead brother [Note: [Col. 0314C] Andrew likewise testifies (ch. 16) that Herlembald was summoned into Ariald’s fellowship after his brother’s death. After consulting many hermits and monks, he finally went to Rome; there, under an unavoidable command from Pope Alexander and the cardinals—therefore after the middle of 1061—he was ordered to return and resist the adversaries of Christ bravely, together with blessed Ariald, in defense of justice, even to the shedding of his own blood. They also gave him, on behalf of Saint Peter, a wondrous banner, so that whenever the madness of the heretics raged beyond measure, he might hold it in his hand and restrain them. How steadfastly he fulfilled this charge for eighteen years—for he was killed in 1075—neither my tongue can fully tell nor my pen adequately express. For before the world Herlembald was a nobleman, like a duke in splendid clothing and among horsemen and weapons; but secretly before God he was dressed like a rustic hermit in woolen garments, and so forth.].

Although he was a layman, he presumed to undertake an act improper to him, supposedly out of fraternal devotion. He was so credulous toward Ariald’s words that those whom his brother had beaten with whips, he himself struck with scorpions (3 Kings 12:11), and what the locust had left, the bruchus consumed (Joel 1:4), judging, as he pleased, whatever sins of the clergy there might be [Note: [Col. 0313] “whatever,” B.]. While, therefore, he judged laymen, only the clergy suffered blows [Note: [Col. 0313] “but the clergy suffered,” B.].

[Col. 0315A] 17. Meanwhile, among the many other innovations that Ariald had introduced into the Church, he preached to his hearers that those litanies which the Ambrosians had celebrated with ancient and most devout observance after the Lord’s Ascension [Note: [Col. 0315] “had celebrated,” B., Mur.] were accursed [Note: [Col. 0315D] Fumagalli discusses these at length, *Antichità Longobardico-Milanesi* III, 229 ff. Andrew reports, ch. 21, and Bonizo p. 808, that Ariald disapproved only of the fasts and that he was expelled a few days later; cf. Landulf III, 30.].

Therefore, at his instigation, when the crowds were divided against one another for three days, a conflict arose in the city. In it, through God’s intervention, Ariald’s party was routed and defeated, with his men beaten and some killed [Note: [Col. 0315D] They plundered the canonical house established by Ariald. When the noble Herlembald and the other faithful heard of this, they took up arms and attacked the audacious and reckless populace; they immediately exterminated them all as though they were the vilest cattle. Then, coming with great courage and power to the greater church, they violently took from the impious whatever they had stolen from the house of the Lord. Andrew, cited above.].

Nevertheless, at his advice, Herlembald, in addition to the innumerable injuries he had inflicted upon the clergy [Note: [Col. 0315] “had expended,” B. 1.], when the archbishop was providing according to custom for the appointment of another abbot after the death of the abbot of Saint Celsus, entirely forbade it [Note: [Col. 0315] “the archbishop, according to the custom of his predecessors, appointed another, but Herlembald forbade it,” B.], scorning that man and utterly rejecting another already consecrated [Note: [Col. 0315D] Lanfranc; see Andrew, cited above, ch. 17.]. He armed a conspiracy of monks and their servants against him. In the same way he drove another man from the monastery of Saint Vincent [Col. 0315B] [Note: [Col. 0315D] Andrew does not mention this, but does mention Ariprand, who before 1064 usurped the monastery of Saint Ambrose.], accusing them of simoniacal ordination.

What more is there to say? He usurped all the ecclesiastical rights at once, having expelled from the city the pontiff whose soldier he himself had been by ancestral inheritance. A wondrous portent, unheard and unseen throughout the ages! Yet more wondrous is that the Roman [Note: [Col. 0315] “the assent of Anselm, who was already Alexander II—‘was favorable,’ adds B. 2* and Puricelli.] favors his ascent.

This is demonstrated by many indications: legations and letters marked with apostolic seals were repeatedly sent to him [Note: [Col. 0316D] Fragments of the letters sent to the Milanese clergy and people after the Roman synod of 1063 are found in Mansi, Collection of Councils XIX, pp. 978–979. Peter Damian sent letters to Ariald and Herlembald, V, 14–15.]. In them he confessed that in his actions he obeyed the Roman [Note: [Col. 0315] “papal,” B.; “obeyed,” Puricelli.] commands.

Supported, as it were, by this authority, the common populace execrated the divine offices on the pretext of simony, while entirely failing to understand the difference between the right hand and the left. Moreover, Herlembald himself boasted that he had received from Rome [Note: [Col. 0315] “from the apostolic lord Alexander,” B.] the military banner of Saint Peter [Col. 0315C] against all who opposed him.

Attached to a lance, it appears to be a sign of homicide; yet it is certainly impious to suspect such a thing of Peter, or [Note: [Col. 0315] “not,” B.] to suppose that he had any banner other than the one given in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” says the Lord (Matthew 16:24).

We speak faithfully, and therefore confidently: teachers must beware of Paul’s sentence when it is uttered absolutely: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9). In saying these things we are not opposing you, Roman elders, since our teacher Ambrose says: “I desire in all things to follow the Roman Church” [Note: [Col. 0315] “to follow the Roman Church,” 3, B. 2.]. With you we believe; with you we reject every heresy. But it seems right to us that ecclesiastical law should be presented by an ecclesiastical teacher, not by an ignorant layman.

18. During these days, when spring was already declining (April–May 1066), for the space of one month blazing comets spread a dreadful radiance across the sky [Note: [Col. 0315] “while the comet was blazing,” Mur.]. There were also frequent earthquakes throughout the world, so severe that on the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection it happened twice—namely, in the morning and in the evening [Note: [Col. 0316D] See the Augsburg Annals, 1067. Numerous annalists mention several comets. See the Annals of Benevento, the Lesser Annals of Saint Germain, and those of Lambert, Bernold, and Berthold, who uses the plural number.] (27 March 1065).

19. At that time Alexander presided at Rome as apostolicus [Col. 0316B]. He had first been made bishop of Lucca from the Milanese clergy; since he was sufficiently suitable, he later attained the apostolic dignity and was called Alexander of Anselm (1 October 1061).

Immediately an adversary arose against him: Cadalus, bishop of Parma, who was proclaimed pope through the initiative of the king and the empress mother (28 October). He went hostilely to Rome and pursued Alexander’s army to the walls of the City after a great slaughter of the slain (April 1062). At another time (1063), with the help and counsel of certain people from the City, he entered Rome, which they call New Rome, and climbed the fortress of Crescentius. Once factions had been formed in the City, battles followed battles every day. Finally, after long and varied conflicts, he withdrew sorrowful, confounded, and defeated, leaving victory to Alexander.

Herlembald went to Rome to consult him about the present affair [Note: [Col. 0316D] According to Andrew, ch. 23. When Ariald saw that Wido was ordaining novices in return for payment, he sent letters to the apostolic lord through Herlembald, asking him to decide what ought to be done with Guido, the adulterous, simoniacal, and perjured man. The continuation is related in the same way, but more fully, by Andrew and the Anonymous who copied him—for in Andrew the text breaks off here in a lacuna.], while Ariald raged against the bishop, stirring up both the urban and rural populace.

20. When his consultation had finally been concluded, Herlembald returned (1066), carrying letters of excommunication for the archbishop. This seemed to many a great disgrace to the city [Note: [Col. 0315] “which seemed to many,” B.]. Therefore it happened that on the holy day of Pentecost the bishop came forward and mounted the public pulpit of the church [Col. 0317A] to complain of the misfortune that had occurred (4 June).

Herlembald and Ariald stood opposite him, ready to answer what they heard. A violent tumult arose among the people, different persons shouting different things. Finally, when factions had been formed in the middle of the church [Note: [Col. 0317] “when a faction had been formed,” 3, 5*, B. 2*, and Puricelli p. 242.], they rose up against one another with a noisy assault. While they fought in different places, the bishop was left almost alone. The hostile party attacked him, cruelly beat him with clubs, and left him almost half dead; then, attacking the episcopal residence itself, they tore away everything valuable.

On the following day (5 June), when the citizens saw such cruelty, they were horrified and confused in mind. They therefore resolved together either to punish so great a crime or no longer to remain alive [Note: [Col. 0317C] Andrew asserts that, after money had been distributed, the party supporting Wido gained the upper hand [Col. 0317D]. Then, after an interdict had been proclaimed for as long as Ariald remained in the city, they forced him to flee. On his death, see Landulf III, 30.].

Thus Ariald fled from the city and remained hidden for several days. As he wandered through various hiding places, traveling only by night, he was betrayed by his companions and fell into the hands of those seeking his life [Note: [Col. 0317] “by the pursuers,” 1.]. They seized him and took him with them throughout that entire night. At dawn, after cutting off his ears, cutting out his tongue with his nose, and gouging out both his eyes, they killed him outright (27 June).

After his death, Herlembald concealed his anger for a little while, reserving it for the future. At that time almost the entire city favored the bishop. But, according to its custom, the people did not remain long in the same position. As soon as the bishop departed from the city, Herlembald impatiently approached to pursue him with renewed strength, declaring him an accomplice in the crime that had been committed.

He therefore again resorted to oaths, although the citizens were unwilling; and those whom he suspected he compelled to swear even more harshly. He continually forced rural crowds and urban bands to pursue Bishop Wido and destroy his entire family. He would certainly have done so had not the noble courage of Wido’s own faithful resisted [Note: [Col. 0317D] Wido must therefore be counted among the *capitanei*, unless we decide that these words refer to the household of Saint Ambrose.]. For they often gathered, prepared to undertake battle on behalf of their lord. Meanwhile, the robbers found no respite from plundering the possessions of the clergy.

21. To settle this dispute, it happened at that time (1067) that the Roman legates—Maginard, bishop of Silva Candida [Note: [Col. 0317] “Marnarelus,” B. 1; “Mainardus,” B. 2.], and Minutus, a cardinal priest [Note: [Col. 0317D] John, also called Minutus, cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere, subscribed to a bull in Tosti, *History of Monte Cassino* I, 426.]—came to Milan.

While they proclaimed peace to everyone in accordance with the apostolic command, they wisely arranged a treaty concerning Ariald’s death. Then, judging between the clergy and the people, they established in an elegant document what ought to be done in the future [Col. 0318A] [Note: [Col. 0318D] In that document, the judgments of laymen against clergy and the plunderings were condemned no less sharply than the vices of the clergy and were forbidden for the future. It was published here by the Palatine Associates and in the collections of councils among the letters of Alexander II, no. 6.] (1 August).

Yet Herlembald was not satisfied with this. He went to Rome and entered into a new consultation with the Romans. For it had long been an established custom of the Italian kingdom, persisting down to the present day, that when bishops of churches died, the king should provide successors, after being properly invited by the clergy and people of Italy [Note: [Col. 0317] “Italian,” B.].

The Romans deny that this is canonical. But that archdeacon Hildebrand, who was attempting to abolish the old arrangement and introduce a new constitution, declared openly that the Milanese division could not be settled except by having a canonical pastor, and that Roman consent would necessarily be required for his election.

Instructed by these arguments, Herlembald returned to Milan and hastily carried out what he had heard. First, therefore, he secretly summoned a few of his friends. From them he demanded a pledge that they would conceal what had been entrusted to them; then, cautiously, he introduced into the oath the matter of electing a future pastor after the departure of the present one. Thereafter, laboring day and night, he made every layman and cleric subject to that same oath.

Meanwhile, however, he did not cease pursuing Bishop Wido and all the relatives of his entire kinship.

22. But since the archbishop was unable to endure so many pressures threatening him, already advanced in years and with all his limbs weakened by prolonged illness, he judged it expedient to anticipate by destroying himself what he foresaw that another would do—namely, to grant his own dignity to another while he was still alive [Note: [Col. 0318D] Cf. Bonizo, p. 809.]. At about this time there was a certain subdeacon among the church’s ordinary clergy, named Gotefredus [Note: [Col. 0317] *cotefredus* 1; *gothofredus* B; *const.*] [Note: [Col. 0318D] Gotofredus, subdeacon of the order of the cathedral church of Milan, and envoy of the said archbishop Wido; he carried out this business in December 1061. Giul. IV, 530.], his one and only confidant above all others, who, as soon as he had penetrated his lord’s mind, strove by every means to transfer the honor to himself. Thus, after a secret agreement had been made with him, the bishop, once each had given an oath concerning the common pact, temporarily laid down his dignity, sending the staff and ring to the emperor through envoys. Gotefredus, however, having long before won the king’s favor through much effort, rejoiced to receive the episcopate from that same august ruler under the recently concluded pact. Nevertheless, in accordance with the truth of Scripture, laughter was mixed with sorrow, and grief seized the end of his joy (Prov. XIV, 13). For, rejected by the citizens, he was received nowhere in the bishopric, not even for lodging; he had become hateful even to the peasants. [Col. 0319A] The Romans, acting with the authority of the apostolic lord, immediately condemned him under canon law, sending the Milanese their letter of judgment concerning him [Note: [Col. 0319] *illos* B; *illo* Puric., p. 259.]. Encouraged by this confidence, Arlembald rose up more fiercely, not only against him but against all his supporters as well, destroying everything with fire and sword; against him he also intensified the oaths of many throughout the villages and castles. Consequently, whenever he tried to presume anything concerning the church’s property, he was utterly forbidden by everyone. But when he climbed the mountain of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0319D] Near Varese.], while an army from the city surrounded him, he barely escaped by fleeing during the night [Note: [Col. 0319] “When—escaped” is absent in B. In its place B has: “as happened in certain cases, of which it would be lengthy, indeed unnecessary, to judge by recounting them individually” (*indicare*, Puric.). “Meanwhile,” etc.]. Meanwhile Wido admitted that he had been deceived by Gotefredus’s plots, calling him a transgressor of their common pact. When he sought to recover what he had lost, or even his honor, he joined a peace treaty with Arlembald. [Col. 0319B] O the blind mind of mortals! For, coming to Milan under that man’s leadership, he was brought not into the city, as he wished, but to the monastery of Saint Celsus, made more private than a private man [Note: [Col. 0319] “and he was made” is found in B.]. There he was entrusted to guards and remained for many days without honor, deceived on this occasion as well [Note: [Col. 0319] “On this occasion also he was deceived” is transferred by 1 to the following chapter; B omits “also.”].

23. (Year 1071.) Gotofredus, now hemmed in by many obstacles, gathered with a portion of his followers in a town commonly called Castilio [Note: [Col. 0319] *colligit* B.] [Note: [Col. 0319D] Apparently Castiglione d’Olona, which lies five miles south of Varese.], truly an impregnable stronghold, fortified by its walls and by the nature of the site. Frequently sallying forth from it, and being excessively eager for plunder and slaughter, the Milanese, indignant, resolved to capture that towered fortress immediately [Note: [Col. 0319] *currit* B 1; absent in B 2* and Puricello.]. Without delay, having equipped an army and prepared what was necessary for military use, they all advanced and encamped [Col. 0319C] at the foot of the mountain; for it was a little more than twenty miles from the city. Soon they surrounded it on every side [Note: [Col. 0319] *circulantes*, B.] and attacked without interruption. They also urgently summoned all the peasants of that region to assemble, swearing to maintain a long siege. Thus they built stone-throwing engines and war machines of every kind, as well as slings and [Note: [Col. 0319] absent in B.] crossbows, and prepared a thousand snares of death. While the besieged resisted to the best of their ability, much blood was shed every day, so much so that during the very solemn observance of Lent there was no abstinence from human slaughter.

24. At this time, therefore, when the city’s sparse population enjoyed its security, sudden disaster attacked the unprepared city. I shudder to report it: on the first Saturday of Lent, the city was consumed by a great fire [Col. 0319D–0320A] [Note: [Col. 0319D] 3 Nones of March, 1070. The church of Saint Lawrence was burned. *Kalendarium Ambrosianum* in Muratori, *SS*, Ib, p. 235; [Col. 0320D] on the 5th Nones of March, in the year of the Lord 1071, Milan was burned by the fire from Castiglione. *Kalendarium Sitonianum*, ib., IIb, p. 1035. On the year, see below, IV, 8.] (March 19). Since a violent whirlwind was then blowing, it seized the balls of fire and carried them far and wide, burning many buildings, until the devouring flame consumed wood and stones; gold, silver, and all other metals likewise melted from the excessive heat. O what buildings of houses, and how splendid walls, were burned—of all of which scarcely anything remained except some ruined walls or the smallest fragment of charcoal! But what was worse than every loss, many basilicas of the saints were burned, both in the city and outside it. Saint Lawrence himself, once tortured by the fire of living flesh, again allowed himself to be consumed by flames. His church had been so magnificent above all others that it seems difficult to describe what were the carvings of wood and stone, the interlocking joints joined on either side [Note: [Col. 0319] *alteri secus*, 1; *intrinsecus*, B; *extrinsecus*, 3a.], its columns with their bases, the tribunals running around it, and above all the mosaic covering everything. O temple, to which nothing in the world was comparable! And O city, beside which the others had been villages! Alas! Those prophetic Lamentations seem almost to have been transferred to you. When such a dreadful report resounded through the camp, many immediately abandoned the siege and went to see the meager remains spared by the fire and the wretched people. Arlembald, however, retaining a portion of the troops with the others, persisted more stubbornly and did not cease fighting daily. Gotofredus, besieged now for three months, seeing that the force in the camp was small, secretly summoned his followers and carefully secured his friends [Note: [Col. 0319] B has “and his friends very cautiously”; Puric., p. 263, does not.]. When the Easter holidays were approaching [Note: [Col. 0320D] After Easter, according to Bonizo, p. 809.], they gathered together, immediately rose against the camp in battle formation with a considerable attack and outcry. The besieged, no less, broke open the barriers and sallied out from every side [Note: [Col. 0319] “from every side” is found in 3.]. Arlembald, placed in such danger, seized his weapons and dared, with his few men, to resist according to his strength, himself becoming standard-bearer. And if his own courage and that of his men had not fought, that day would have been his last. But when many saw the steadfastness of the few, they withdrew voluntarily, taking Gotefredus with them from the town. The Milanese pursued them far away, suddenly massing together—both those who had been in the camp and those who had remained in the city. They did not stop pursuing them for several days and nights, until they forced them, driven into the greatest necessity [Note: [Col. 0319] B reads “constructed in necessity, they forced”; not in B 2*; Puric. has “placed in necessity.”], to enter Castiglione again. [Col. 0320D]

[Col. 0321A] 25. After this, returning to the city, they determined by oath that Gotefredus should never be received, but rather that another should be chosen collectively from the catalogue of the major church. For that archbishop Wido had already departed from this world (August 23, 1071), and was buried in the place commonly called Berguli [Note: [Col. 0321] *Burguli*, 3; B.] [Note: [Col. 0321D] Alexandria was later built there; cf. Landulf III, 18, and the catalogue of the archbishops.], where, after the city’s burning, he ended his final day in bitterness of soul. From that day onward Arlembald devoted every effort—sometimes dealing with the clergy, sometimes with the people—to the election of a bishop, having received a new authorization from the Romans but rejecting the ancient provision of the kings [Note: [Col. 0321D] Cf. Bonizo, p. 810.]. Nevertheless, the greater part of the city, both clergy and prudent people, adhered to the ancient custom and the honor of the king. He himself, however, disregarding everything and the common oath, listened only to the advice of that Roman Hildeprandus [Col. 0321B] [Note: [Col. 0321] *ita*, 3; B; *consultiri*, 1.]. The day he himself had appointed for this action was now approaching, namely, the solemn feast of the Theophany (January 6, 1072). He therefore worked to summon those present and call the absent: clergy and laity, abbots and monks, not omitting the crowd of country people favorable to him. When the feast day arrived, a gathering of many took place in the winter church [Note: [Col. 0321] B omits “took place.”], although those with whom he had sworn to carry out this election were absent. After the solemn celebration of Mass, he preached as he pleased and recalled many things about a just [Note: [Col. 0321] “this,” B.] [Col. 0322A] shepherd. In the presence of a certain Bernard, a Roman envoy, he elected Atto [Note: [Col. 0321] B reads “elected”], who was still merely a cleric and a young man of tender age, against the will of the clergy and many of the people, so that they departed from the church in anger. Alas! [Note: [Col. 0321] B reads “from the church, in sorrow.”] It seemed then that the church’s most holy altar was shaken and moved from its place, when the excessive pressure of the people crowded it from every side. When Atto, with his followers, climbed into the episcopal hall to dine [Note: [Col. 0321] B reads “the episcopate”]—for abundant banquets had already been prepared on the tables—the enraged citizens suddenly attacked the house, searching its inner and outer rooms. The newly elected man, hiding in the corner of a room, was found, seized, and miserably torn [Note: [Col. 0321] B: “seized, torn apart, and”; Puric., p. 271: “seized, torn apart, and.”]; finally he was dragged by his shins and arms from top to bottom. While he stood in the church, prostrate before the altar in fear of death, the people shouted that he should mount the pulpit. There, after taking an oath in the hearing of everyone, he renounced the Ambrosian see for the present and forever. Meanwhile all his supporters fled through various hiding places; even the Roman envoy escaped only with difficulty, his clothing torn to shreds [Note: [Col. 0321] B 1: “and torn.”]. As for Gotefredus and Atto, both remained private men for many days afterward [Note: [Col. 0321] These words are absent in B.], content only with their own homes and possessions [Note: [Col. 0321] Here 5 and B 1 end; B 1 adds: “Thanks be to God, amen. The book of Arnulf’s copies ends.” B 1*, B 2. The following material is found in 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5* (which has in the margin: “Thus far from the revised codex of the chapter of Milan, where Arnulf’s history ends. What follows is taken from the manuscript codex of Archintus”). B 2* (from the same codex of Archintus).].

## THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0321] Thus in 2, where it is added: “The fourth describes what the third order left behind.” In 1 the books are not distinguished at all; in 3, 4, and 5* this still belongs to the third book. B 2* made this and what follows into the fourth book.]

[Col. 0321]

[Col. 0321C] 1. The resolve remained fixed in my heart that henceforth, in the account of present events, I should preserve silence, since things unheard of in former times gravely offend the minds of many, while matters delayed too long seem also to exceed proper measure, when the wisdom of God the Father, according to the truth of Scripture, disposes all things by number, weight, and measure (Wis. XI, 21). Nevertheless, turning back to myself, I judged it more useful to describe what I had begun in full once again, so that, once the quality of the deeds was known, judgment concerning them might thereby become more certain. For all praise and blame are assigned to the outcome of each undertaking, although it remains uncertain whether the Almighty will prolong our days until that conclusion. But may your will be done, Father most high, on earth as it is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0321] “according to the kingdom” in place of “on earth as it is in heaven,” 1.].

[Col. 0321D] 2. (Year 1072.) When he had heard what had happened to Atto, that same archdeacon Hildeprandus, now a cardinal, immediately judged that the oath imposed by violence was entirely invalid. The Roman bishop respected him so greatly that he presumed to do nothing without consulting him, although the holy Gospel plainly proclaims that the disciple is not above the teacher (Matt. X, 24; Luke VI, 40). It therefore happened that, after a council of bishops had been assembled at Rome [Note: [Col. 0321D] Gregory VII mentions it in Letter I, 15, written on the Kalends of July 1073; cf. II, 30. He says that Atto was lawfully elected in Letter III, 8.], and at Hildeprandus’s insistence, he publicly declared Atto lawfully elected and placed Gotefredus under anathema. Hildeprandus frequently reported all this in his letters to the aforementioned Arlembald. It is also said that from his own treasury, which was extremely rich, he sent him a large amount of gold and silver, so that, by distributing payment indiscriminately to anyone, he might gather as many supporters as possible. For the prophetic saying did not escape him: “From the greatest to the least, all are intent on greed” (Jer. VI, 13).

[Col. 0322D] 3. Meanwhile the suffragan bishops of the Ambrosian see, having received a mandate from the king [Note: [Col. 0322D] Through Rapoto V. Bonizo, p. 814.], gathered near the city of Novara and laid hands on Gotefredus in consecration, strengthening him as best they could, [Col. 0323A] although it is said that the royal command had been obtained through many gifts [Note: [Col. 0323D] Bonizo, p. 810.]. It is nevertheless certain that the king later repented and utterly hated the envoy who had intervened. Afterward Gotefredus attempted to seize certain castles belonging to the church, taking command of one of them, called Brebia [Note: [Col. 0323D] Brebbia, in the county of Angera.]. When shortly before he had attacked Leucum [Note: [Col. 0323D] Lecco, on Lake Como.], soldiers rushing from the city violently drove him out, after that most energetic soldier, the margrave, had been lost; the inhabitants of the place hurled him down from a high cliff and cruelly slaughtered him (April 21, 1073). While these things were happening, the apostolic bishop died.

4. After a short interval of days (April 22), Hildeprandus succeeded him, taking the name Gregory. In him Atto’s spirit immediately revived, so that Atto, going to Rome, placed himself under Gregory’s companionship. He himself, however, remaining firmly attached to his earlier purpose, summoned a general synod at Rome (March 1074) and denounced Gotefredus together with his consecrators [Note: [Col. 0323] Thus in 1, that is, “condemned,” as in chapter 7; 2 and 3 read “anathematized with his secretaries.” B 2*: “and when with his consecrators”; G: “and when.” Puric., p. 290, from which point onward used codex 4.] [Note: [Col. 0323D] For this reason Gregory VII wrote to King Henry on December 7, 1074, that the decree had been confirmed twice by synodal judgment; Letter II, 30.]. And since he had become accustomed to arrange many things according to his own pleasure, before the entire assembly he praised Atto as present, without the king’s assent and with the Ambrosian clergy and people absent. Hence it seems that a dispute arose between him and the emperor and continued—not over the condemnation of Gotefredus, but over this new election, conceived without the king’s authorization [Note: [Col. 0323] *litte*, 1.].

5. Moreover, while Gotefredus remained in the fortress of Brebbia alone, Atto, neglecting his own home and homeland, lived only at Rome [Note: [Col. 0323D] Bonizo, p. 810.], devoted to the pope’s constant service. Arlembald supported him at Milan with all his strength, laboring day and night and offering and promising gifts as well. Moreover, he sometimes persecuted Gotefredus’s entire faction with fire and sword, leaving nothing unattempted within his power, especially since Arlembald in no way yielded to the will either of the royal authority or of his peers and many others, relying solely on Roman support and confidence [Note: [Col. 0323D] Gregory VII’s letters to him, I, 25 and 26, dated September 7 and October 9, 1073, are extant. There he exhorts him as follows: “Trusting in the Lord and in your mother, the Roman Church, act manfully.” Cf. Letters 27 and 28.]; even going so far as to insult the bishops of the Ambrosian consecration, asserting that they had been excommunicated by the apostolic authority and rejecting all their ministry. Hence it happened that, on the Saturday of holy Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0323] Corrected from “Easter” by Leibniz.], he forbade baptism to be performed in the city.

6. Later, the sacred chrism which one of those bishops, as is customary in the absence of a bishop, had sent to the metropolitan church for the mystery of the Lord’s Supper, he poured out on the ground before all the people and trampled it underfoot, bringing forward his own chrism, although it was unknown by whom it had been prepared or from where it had come. Thus, setting aside the prerogative of that authentic Saturday handed down by the Fathers, he caused his own baptism to be celebrated on Friday in the octave (April 25), although Scripture forbids transgressing the boundaries established by the fathers (Prov. XXII, 28). As a result, his baptism did not know the joy of Easter, and for a long time afterward many catechumens were deprived of the grace of baptism. A great multitude of the people became involved in this error—some through simple-mindedness, some seduced by payment, and some by the impunity of crimes they had committed. From the very beginning, anyone wicked who joined his association was regarded by him as dear and innocent. Consequently, the number and power of the Patarines increased so greatly in the villages and towns, and in certain cities under his leadership, that he seemed to dominate all his fellow citizens [Note: [Col. 0324B] *convivium*, 1, instead of *concivium*.] [Note: [Col. 0324D] This is confirmed by the words of Gregory’s Letter I, 77, addressed to Beatrice and Matthew on April 15, 1074: “You should provide security for Guarnerius of Argentario up to the lord Erlembald, duke of Milan, knowing that he has been warned by our letter not to undertake anything adverse against you or your people in this matter.”].

7. Furthermore, when the emperor Henry, now a young man, saw the flower of his power gradually withering in this manner, he took counsel with his followers and sought to oppose the efforts of this man and of the Roman prelate [Note: [Col. 0323] Thus in 1 and 4; 3 has “prelate.”]. At that time the great Norman prince Robert ruled Apulia. While messengers traveled between him and the king concerning this matter, the aforementioned pope, having held a synod at Rome (February 1075), openly denied the king any right thereafter to confer bishoprics and excluded all lay persons from the investiture of churches. Moreover, having pronounced anathema, he condemned all the king’s counselors and threatened the king himself with the same unless he promptly obeyed this decree. [Col. 0324C] How mournfully the city of Milan suffered in those days, I say in grief and groan in lamentation, made a burden to myself, so that feeling withdraws from my mind.

8. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1075, in the thirteenth indiction (March 30), four years having passed since the fire mentioned above, as the most holy feast of Easter approached—namely, on the Monday of the authentic octave—the wretched city again felt divine anger, experiencing how terrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God. After the solemn celebration of Mass, when the sun was already declining, a dense smoke of darkness appeared in the middle of the city, driven and scattered through the air by a violent force of winds. A vapor vomiting flames followed it, consuming everything between heaven and earth. For many torches, as though lightning [Note: [Col. 0323] *fulmina*, 3a and 4; *fulmineae*, Muratori.], burst from that immense and inextinguishable fiery mass and suddenly flashed throughout the whole city, so that nearly everything the city had left after escaping that earlier fire was burned by the present flames and shaken down to the ground. Nor did this blaze entirely spare the buildings that had previously been burned and restored through much labor. What more can be said than that this fire was in every respect like the one described above? It was nevertheless more savage, because it burned many more and larger churches—namely, the summer church of the holy virgin Tecla, and also those of blessed Nazarius and the protomartyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 0325D] At the threshold of the new basilica these verses were inscribed, preserved by Puricello in *On the Holy Martyrs*, p. 308:

> The devouring flame consumed the ancient temple’s roof,  
> which in beauty and form yielded to none in the world.  
> For many years it had been the glory of this city.  
> Everything fashioned by human hands eventually suffers collapse.  
> It fell entirely; collapsed, it rises again from the foundations,  
> but the second cannot equal the beauty of the first.  
> People, seeing this, fear sin as the cause of ruin:  
> build yourself first, then restore what is material.  
> Be the temple of the Lord; the temple’s building pleases him.

[Col. 0326D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1075, indiction [lacuna] XIII, three days before the Kalends of April, Monday. Bonizo also mentions the fire, p. 813.], and many others, whose ruins, I believe, will remain visible for more than a thousand years. Among them, the mother of the others, the winter basilica of the holy Mother of God—O grief, and grief again [Note: [Col. 0325] absent in B 2* but not in Puricello.]—was allowed to burn, its walls having collapsed entirely. Its most holy altar cannot be seen, so great or of what kind it had been; the golden sheets melted from the excessive heat. But even the loss of a thousand talents of gold [Note: [Col. 0325] “a thousand pounds,” Muratori.] cannot be compared with it. Our sins deserved this calamity, because in our bitterness we offended the dove of the Holy Spirit; for, contrary to the divine command, what is holy has been given to dogs in our time, and the spiritual pearl lies indecently trampled beneath the feet of swine. The number of the remaining offenses cannot be reckoned.

9. Thus, amid so many hardships and such great sorrows, while the entire city mourned—people of every rank and age, of both sexes—only Arlembald’s spirit remained fearless and unbending. When the white days of Easter were at hand (April 4, 1075), he attempted, as he had done in the preceding year, to begin the baptismal rite with an unknown chrism [Col. 0325C]. When the cardinals of the church, whose duty it was to consecrate the fonts, refused to act contrary to custom, a certain priest named Liutprandus immediately appeared [Note: [Col. 0326D] Of the church of Saint Paul in Compito. Much about him may be found in the *History of Landulf of Saint Paul*, his nephew.], a household servant of the church descended from its founders, who by Arlembald’s command and authority usurped the office of the ordinary clergy and baptized those who came without proper consideration. This act of violence, added to the recent memory of the city’s burning, gravely offended many citizens [Note: [Col. 0325] *civos*, 1.], especially the soldiers, who had before their eyes the saying of a certain Roman [Note: [Col. 0326D] C. Memmius in Sallust, *Jugurtha* 31.] to recruits: “Hired slaves cannot endure the harsh commands of their masters, much less can you, Quirites.”

10. Consequently, after going out of the city together for several days, they swore, with a large part of the people, to uphold their justice and the honor of Saint Ambrose [Col. 0325D–0326A] [Note: [Col. 0326D] They said that they wished to swear to the integrity of Saint Ambrose. Bonizo, p. 813.], and to accept a shepherd from the king as a gift. When they entered the city together, Arlembald, as always unable to tolerate a partner, addressed the crowd standing beside him in his customary manner. But when he could no longer restrain his fury, he and his followers made an assault with shouting, hastily seized their weapons, and carried in his right hand the banner he called Saint Peter’s. He burst into the midst of the citizens, who rose against him from every side [Note: [Col. 0325] Thus in 1 and Puric., p. 326; “and against” in 3; “against” in B 2*.]. In the first instant and at the very outset of the battle, such a rush of opponents overwhelmed him that he could accomplish nothing memorable. When he was surrounded on every side, he was immediately pierced by repeated blows and, dying sooner than the word could be spoken, fell, while his small retinue scattered in every direction [Note: [Col. 0326D] Landulf of Saint Paul says that he was killed by Arnaldus of Raude. Cf. Berthold under the year 1077.]. His lifeless body, thrown naked upon the ground, was completely stripped of its clothing and beaten everywhere with clubs and stones, so that he who had terrified many while alive might, in death, lie subject to the mockery of many. When it was carried away for burial, no reverence of funeral rites followed him. Afterward, that aforementioned priest Liutprandus was found while fleeing; his ears and nose were cut off, so that he who had presumed to exercise another’s office might lose what he seemed to possess [Note: [Col. 0326D] See Landulf of Saint Paul, chapters 1, 6, 15, and 44.]. It therefore clearly appears that the assertion of the one who said this is true: “It is difficult for things to end well when they have been begun with an evil beginning.” At that same hour, after this notable triumph, all the citizens sang hymns of victory to God and to their patron Ambrose and, armed, went to his church. On the following day, laity and clergy together again proceeded to Saint Ambrose in litanies and praises, confessing their former guilt to one another. After the priests who were present had granted absolution, the whole people returned peacefully to their homes.

11. Here the end of this schism now appears, a schism that had continually sprouted from its very root and extended over nineteen years. From it the name “Patarine” first arose—not deliberately, but uttered by chance. While recently turning over several works in a volume of etymologies, I find the name written thus: “*Pathos* in Greek is called *perturbatio* in Latin,” that is, “disturbance.” Accordingly, following the small capacity of my own understanding, I immediately conjecture that the Patarines may properly be called “disturbers”; the outcome of events clearly proves this. Nevertheless, if someone at some time interprets it according to a more approved judgment, I willingly concede the point, provided that the name agrees with the work and the work corresponds to the name. For from the first sound of this word came the error of peoples and the force of wars; the whirlwind of winds also disturbed the world more violently than usual through the frequent occurrence of fires. This is proved in every way by experience of many calamities and by the increase of all evils.

12. Moreover, whatever the etymology of the word may be, no person of sound mind should suppose that anything we have recounted above concerning this matter was uttered in opposition to truth or in resistance to justice, since neither is permissible. For if there are good words or deeds of others, we do not reject them, nor do we in any way disagree with all those who condemn purchasable consecrations and the sexual misconduct of the sacred orders, provided that we do not depart from the authority of Paul. For he says: “Let all things be done decently and according to order” (I Cor. XIV, 40). The Mosaic law also agrees with this: “You shall pursue precisely what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20). This cannot be fulfilled in any other way than by preserving for each order and person the rights proper to each. The duties of clergy and laity, and of the members of each group among themselves, have been distributed separately. Just as in one body there are many members, but not all possess the same function (Rom. XII, 4), so, if they obstruct one another, the whole body is corrupted. Therefore, in the holy Church—that is, in the body of Christ—all things must be weighed with just moderation. Let clergy and people each perform their own office, content with the boundary assigned to them, as the Lord says: “I enclosed the sea with boundaries and said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and no farther shall you advance’” (Job XXXVIII, 10–11). The human heart is the sea. The bishops themselves should plainly attend to their own affairs, providing what is good not only before God but also before all people (Rom. XII, 17), lest it be said of them: “The wicked priests are the ruin of the people.” But if they prove negligent, the people will be scandalized. “Woe to that person through whom the scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII, 7). Truly, woe will be theirs—an exceedingly cruel woe—if, through their fault, the people, zealous against the clergy, rise up further.

13. As I pursue such matters, I now perceive them from afar, little by little, as though through narrow cracks, in a way different from anything I have seen until now. When I compare the present with the past and what must be written with what has been written, I blush faithfully and am ashamed; I am confused not because I have used barbarisms in my words, but because I have rashly judged the words or deeds of others, since hidden things are revealed to God alone. Yet blessed Paul comes to me in my trembling: first a blasphemer and persecutor of the faithful, afterward he labored more than the other apostles, blinded so that he might see. [Col. 0328B] Peter denied in order that he might believe; Thomas doubted in order that he might become more certain; Victorinus the Roman rhetorician, already advanced in age, was converted under the guidance of Simplicianus. The philosopher Augustine was saved through the teaching of Ambrose. And we know many others to have been changed from evil to good, and from good to better, some quickly and some slowly. For this is the change of the right hand of the Most High (Ps. LXXVI, 11). “The Spirit of the Lord blows where it wills” (John III, 8), and the Most High has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Rom. IX, 18). “So then it depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy” (ibid., 16). Therefore, Christ, I have made my sin known to you, and I have not concealed my iniquities. I said: “I will confess my iniquities to the Lord,” and you forgave the wickedness of my heart (Ps. XXXI, 5). From now on, Lord, we ask that you both go before our thoughts, words, and actions by inspiring them, and follow them by assisting them, so that all our activity may always begin from you and, begun through you, be brought to completion by you. To him be honor and glory, now and always and throughout all ages of ages.

## THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0327] Thus in 2, which adds: “But what has been promised by you, you shall observe and carry out.” Atto, 3, 4, and 5* call this the fourth book; B 2* joins it to what precedes.]

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327D] 1. Since at the very beginning of this little work I promised to narrate the deeds of my own time, I cannot remain silent without incurring the charge of falsehood, especially since I know that the Mosaic law has given this warning: “If you do not wish to make a promise, you will be without sin” (Deut. XXIII, 22). To proceed along the straight path of narration, it is therefore necessary to describe the deeds in an orderly manner, just as they occurred.

2. Since the matters mentioned above had not yet been fully settled, but remained in some confusion, the Milanese already mentioned sent an embassy across the mountains to King Henry to request a bishop, announcing the triumph of Arlembald’s killing. When the king learned this, he rejoiced exceedingly and promised to give them whichever bishop they wished [Note: [Col. 0327D] According to Bonizo, the king sent his counselor Everardus, who assembled a court at Roncaglia [Col. 0328D] and invited the Milanese to approach the king with their elected bishop.].

[Col. 0328D] 3. At that time there was a very bitter dispute between the king and the Saxons, the cause of which is not for our judgment to examine. Nevertheless, that extremely fierce people broke out into open rebellion under Duke Otto, so that, when the two sides engaged in battle, more than twenty thousand men are reported to have been killed. Yet victory smiled upon Henry.

4. A few days later, Duke Gotefredus, the son of Gotefredus, withdrew into seclusion and died after being pierced by a sword, leaving behind his wife Matilda, a daughter of Boniface and Beatrice and a woman of the highest distinction.

5. Meanwhile, when the Milanese envoys from the clergy and people approached the king concerning the matter mentioned above, a certain Tetaldus, a subdeacon of the Milanese church, was serving in the royal chapel [Col. 0329A] [Note: [Col. 0329D] Bonizo tells the matter differently, asserting that Tetaldus was sent to the king with the envoys. But Landulf IV, 1, indicates that he took part in the battle at Unstrut.]. The king, turning many counsels over in his mind and finally following his own judgment, granted him the Ambrosian episcopate, setting aside the investiture and anointing of the still-living Gotefredus, as well as the election of Atto, who was then residing at Rome [Note: [Col. 0329] B 3 omits this.]. What more need be said? That bishop was received by clergy and people, as they were habitually eager for innovations. The same suffragans who had consecrated Gotefredus also laid upon him the hand of blessing [Note: [Col. 0329D] This was done in disregard of Gregory’s letter of the sixth Ides of October [or, according to another reading, December] 1075, by which he forbade it; he himself had summoned Tedaldus to the synod at Rome. See Letter III, 8 and 9.]. It was a remarkable event, unheard of in all former times: in one city, with one bishop elected and another consecrated, a third should emerge at the same time.

### 6.

At that time there was in Rome a certain man named Cencius, who had always been hostile to Pope Gregory because of the ecclesiastical property he unjustly possessed. But, following wicked counsel, on the very night of the Nativity of the Lord (24 December 1075), while that holy father was celebrating the office of the nocturnal Mass in the basilica of Saint Theotokos after completing Matins according to custom, Cencius burst violently into the church with swords and clubs, and a great conspiracy of his followers, his sword drawn, in order to seize the pope—like Judas betraying the Lord at night.

After searching in various places, he found the priest beside the Lord’s altar, intent upon the saving mysteries. Rushing violently upon him, he dragged him away and wounded him severely; then, having set him upon a horse, he brought him all the way to his tower and kept him imprisoned there. At daybreak, however, when everyone was displeased by so detestable a crime, all the Romans rose in arms and surrounded the tower. Nor did they desist from the attack until they had snatched the lamb from the wolf’s jaws, breaking open the tower and plundering all its contents.

Nevertheless, divine vengeance followed human vengeance. For in that same year Cencius died, suffocated by an ulcer of the throat, just as the betrayer Judas was strangled by the tightening of the noose.

### 7.

At the same time, urged on by certain of his own people, the king rose up against Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0329] *se* in 3.], to such an extent that he offered him no obedience whatsoever. But the Roman prelate, very often prepared to forgive, dealt mercifully with everything, waiting a long while for the king and inviting him to conversion with many admonitions.

When he achieved absolutely nothing, he separated him and his supporters from communion with holy Mother Church (February 1076), imposing the sentence of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0329] *communicando*; Puricellus, p. 323, reads *excommunicando*.], while nevertheless maintaining the intention of a future and worthy conversion.

O unhappy times, in which, because our faults demand it, the holy Church seems to fight against herself, although Truth praises and commends her in these words: “My dove, my beloved, is one” (Song of Songs VI, 8). If she is one and beloved, I do not understand how she can be divided or become hostile to herself [Note: [Col. 0329] The reading is uncertain: “and become hostile to herself” (*q. scindica*) in 1; “and, being divided, become hostile to herself” (*q. scissa*) in 3a B 2* and Puricellus, *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 324, from 4.].

“Jesus Christ” are two names belonging to one person; from this it is clearly proved that kings and priests—namely, the anointed ones of Christ—ought to be united by one agreement.

What, then? Are both of them in error? Far be it. Certainly the Roman Church is never said to have erred, from the time when the divine voice said to Peter: “Simon, behold, Satan has sought you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 31).

Therefore, whoever dissents from the Roman Church is not truly a Catholic, as blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0330D] Cf. *On the Death of Satyrus* I, 47.]. Did those bishops themselves not read these things? And if they read them [Note: [Col. 0329] *legeret* in 1.], why, when they had gathered at Piacenza against the Roman prelate, did they conspire of their own accord? Why, when they afterward assembled at Pavia, did they proclaim for themselves an unjust—indeed, invalid—anathema, making, in accordance with the prophecy, not justice but cries [Note: [Col. 0330B] Isaiah V, 7: “He looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed”; the author has altered the expected wordplay from *justitiam* (“justice”) to *clamores* (“cries”).]?

For this reason they were most justly pierced by the apostolic sword. Let them answer, as they are accustomed to do, that they obeyed the royal command. But what does Scripture say? “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V, 29). Likewise: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew XXII, 21). And elsewhere: “Fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter II, 17) [Note: [Col. 0329] *timere* in 1.]. Honor, therefore, is not owed to the king unless the proper fear of God comes first.

### 8.

At the same time, that barbarous German people—especially the leaders Bertaldus, Rodulfus, and Welfo [Note: [Col. 0329] *Welfe* in 1.] together with the counts and bishops—having learned of the Roman excommunication, completely withdrew from the king’s fellowship and held no communion with him. Moreover, by accusing him of many crimes, they marked him with infamy.

Meanwhile, on the advice of the most holy abbot of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0329D] Hugh; cf. Lambert, under the year 1077.], as well as that of Agnes, the king’s mother, and of the most wise Matilda already mentioned, a general conference was arranged between the king and the apostolic pope, for the sake of peace and justice.

When the pope left the City to travel to Germany (January 1077), he came to Italy, relying on Matilda’s assistance. While he stayed there, she heaped many honors and attendants upon him. Henry hastened to meet him, avoiding the conference that had been arranged in his own country.

The countess possessed a town named Canossa, truly an impregnable stronghold, fortified on every side by many walls and by the nature of its location. There, while the apostolic pope was presiding (25 January 1077) [Note: [Col. 0329] *praevidente* in Muratori.], the king, walking barefoot and prostrate on the ground, after many tears obtained pardon, confirming the agreements of his faithful followers by oath [Note: [Col. 0329] *juramento*; Puricellus, p. 336, reads *juramenta*.], on condition that justice should be carried out.

Thus, through Matilda’s great prudence, the bonds of their peace were strengthened, despite the unwillingness of the bishops who remained engaged in the dispute.

### 9.

He withdrew [Note: [Col. 0331] The manuscripts offer several readings: *reprsit* in 1; *repressit* in 5*; *repressit se* in B 2*. The wording *manentibus* (“while they remained”) is followed by a difficult construction. Manuscript 3a has *Cum autem se* (“But when he…”), which is probably more correct; I regard the words following *recessit* as the apodosis of a sentence whose protasis has partly perished. Puricellus, *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 464, prints the passage from codex 4 as follows: “He restrained himself when the people of Milan, together with Bishop Tedaldus, recognized themselves as culpable, since the divine law forbade communion with an excommunicated person.”] from the arrangements, when the people of Milan realized that they were culpable through their association with Bishop Tedaldus, since divine law forbade communion with an excommunicated person.

They sent envoys to the lord pope to implore release [Note: [Col. 0331] *missis igitur* in Muratori.]. I myself took part in that embassy, making satisfaction for the past and promising to be corrected in the future.

The pope, following wise counsel, sent the venerable bishops of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm.] and Ostia [Note: [Col. 0331] Giraldus. Cf. Bernold and Berthold under the year 1077. See Anselm, chapter 3.] to Milan, to grant forgiveness to all who should request it.

When they entered the city, the whole community rejoiced. For three entire days, as citizens streamed to them, they preached the divine words, absolved everyone [Note: [Col. 0331] *absolventibus* in 1; *absolvunt* in Muratori.], and blessed them all.

Tedaldus bore this with great indignation and resentment, to such an extent that he attempted to stir up sedition among the people and bring about war; but he achieved nothing.

Meanwhile, the German leaders mentioned above, together with the counts and bishops in those regions, did not cease daily to deliberate among themselves concerning their agreement, the condition of the kingdom, and the election of a new king, asserting that Henry was unworthy of the crown for many reasons.

### 10.

Finally, when they assembled at Mainz in March, they unanimously entrusted the rights of the kingdom to Duke Rodulfus, confirming everything by oath.

When the king heard this, he was violently agitated within himself. For he was staying at Pavia; gathering all the Lombards he could command, he set out for Verona. There he took leave of everyone and returned to his homeland, intending to fight for the defense of the kingdom until death [Note: [Col. 0331] “the king”—namely, Henry—in 3.].

The pope, after remaining in Italy for several days, returned to Rome and was received with immense joy by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0331] In manuscripts 1 (written by the same hand and with continuous pen-strokes), 2 (according to Muratori, by another and later hand), 3, 4, 5*, and B 2*, the following words occur here; they will be given below, before the list of archbishops, since they have been placed here out of position and apparently were not written by Arnulf.].

## In the Year of the Lord 1079. Theodoric, Canon of Paderborn

### Notice concerning Theodoric

(R. P. Pez, *Introductory Dissertation on Part I of Volume II of the Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. IV.)

The age and status of this author, who until now was unknown to everyone, are revealed to us solely by the title of the very elegant and substantial little work he composed: “The Writing of Theodoric, canon of Paderborn, on the Lord’s Prayer, which he produced through the grace of the Holy Spirit, in memory of the venerable bishop Immabus, at the urging of the reverend priest Reinboldus.”

Immabus succeeded Rudolphus, or Ruthardus, in the bishopric of Paderborn around the year of the Lord 1052, and died after the monastery of Abdinghof had been restored following a fire in 1077—if the reckoning of Gabriel Bucellinus, *Germania Sacra*, part I, p. 20, is reliable. Bucellinus calls him not Immabus but Imadus.

Since Theodoric therefore composed this work in his memory, it is probable that it was written around the year 1079. We have been unable to learn anything more about Theodoric from elsewhere.

We found his work itself, written in an almost contemporary hand, in a large-format parchment codex in the library of Klosterneuburg. From that manuscript the most worthy prefect of the place, the Reverend Father Eugenius Pyrckbauer, extracted it and gave it for inclusion in our *Thesaurus*.

The booklet is indeed very brief, but in our judgment it surpasses many more recent volumes on this subject. The matters that Theodoric sets forth in chapters 5 and 6 concerning Christian faith and repentance seem especially worthy of notice. There he also answers not inelegantly those opponents whom a new interpretation of certain passages of Holy Scripture might provoke, and he warns them not to hasten to judgment concerning the grace of the Spirit.

“For I am confident,” he says, “that the same Spirit who distributed to others according to his will distributed also to me as he willed. The understanding is not the same in all of us, just as the activity is not the same in all the members,” and so forth.

These points ought to be impressed upon those to whom everything devised and discovered by more recent writers seems contemptible in comparison with the ancients—as though that divine Spirit who taught the Church in her youth had abandoned her in her old age. It is the mark of prudent men to inquire not how old a statement or written work is, but how true it is.

But more on these matters elsewhere.

## Theodoric’s Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer

Now published for the first time from a manuscript codex of the renowned canonry of Klosterneuburg in Austria, belonging to the order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, through the efforts of the Reverend Father Eugenius Pyrcklbauer, canon and librarian of that place.

(Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* II, II, 57.)

“The Writing of Theodoric, canon of Paderborn, on the Lord’s Prayer, which he produced through the grace of the Holy Spirit, in memory of the venerable bishop Immabus, at the urging of the reverend priest Reinboldus.”

### Chapter One. On the first petition: “Our Father, who art in heaven”
