That the Father of mercies is our Father is proved most clearly both by reasons and by authorities, each of which must be received in a holy and reverent manner.

For the Apostle, the chosen vessel, the contemplator of the hidden truth in heaven, says: “To God and our Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen.” And elsewhere: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father.”

Who could be so utterly devoid of shame, so shameless a mocker of truth, or so obstinate an advocate of falsehood that he would not agree that, if we are his children, he is our Father and we are his children? For it is written: “All are children of the Most High.” And again: “Come, children, hear me.”

Were these things not announced to us, who were covered and sealed under the same veil as carnal Israel until the revelation of our head, Jesus Christ? Therefore, he is the Father; he also possesses us through his love, made us from nothing through his power, and created us for good works through his grace.

Hence the Apostle says: “We are his workmanship”—that is, God’s—“created in Christ Jesus for good works.” Is he not therefore the Father who possesses us, made us, and created us?

Christ too, the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, and one who knows God, says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” Therefore Jesus Christ himself, when his disciples asked him how they should pray, said: “Pray in this way: Our Father,” and so forth.

Founded, then, upon Christ’s instruction and built up by the testimony of illustrious men, we consider it no robbery in our prayer to be encouraged to cry out in the Holy Spirit: “Our Father.” For Paul says: “In him”—that is, in the Holy Spirit—“we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’”

Who would dare to address the Almighty by such a familiar name as “Father” in his own spirit?

“Who art”—that is, who exists perfectly and uniquely. It was said to Moses: “He who is has sent me.” Who sent Moses? Was it not God? Therefore, “He who is” is God. And elsewhere: “I am who I am.” Who speaks these words except God, who is? Therefore, he is God.

That existence, however, is common in the form of the word both to the creature and to the Creator, yet is specially assigned to the Creator by a mode of speech in which many common terms are attributed, out of reverence for their greater excellence, to one participant alone.

For “god” is a name both of the true, rich, and omnipotent God and of a false, needy, and powerless image. But when “God” is said, the true God is understood.

“Lord” likewise is common to the Creator and to a certain creature; when it is uttered, our understanding is drawn toward the Creator out of reverence. When “just” or “holy” is said, he himself is understood. Hence the psalm says: “The Lord has magnified his holy one.” And elsewhere: “But the just man—what has he done?”

“Son” too is a common term, but when it is said by itself, the Son of God is understood. Hence he himself says: “If the Son sets you free…”

By the same mode of speech, when the Apostle is mentioned simply, Paul is understood.

Thus, since the being of the Divinity precedes all being, surpasses all being, creates all being, and governs all being, by assigning the term according to its prerogative we glorify the sublimity of God, understanding God when it is said, “who art.”

For the sake of brevity, this explanation may suffice here, although other explanations could also be added. His being is singular: it is not joined together by an assembly of parts. Rather, whatever is in him is God, and God is ineffably whatever is in him.

This is not so with creatures. The essence of a human being, being composed of soul and body, is again resolved into those same components. Nor is everything that is in this essence a human being, nor is a human being everything that is in this essence. A human being is not the soul, nor is the soul the human being; the same applies to the remaining elements.

Hence Boethius says: “No thing is that which it is”—that is, not everything that belongs to a thing’s essence is convertibly identical with the thing itself.

It is fitting, however, that at the beginning of the prayer we confess that he exists, as Jesus teaches us, so that we might not, like the foolish, say in our heart: “There is no God.”

Hence Paul says: “Whoever approaches God must believe that he exists.” Confession of his existence is the first foundation of faith. For we would believe nothing about him in vain unless we were certain of his existence—of him who created all things and whom all things glorify.

Accordingly, what follows is:

### Chapter Two. On the second petition: “Hallowed be thy name”

“In heaven hallowed be thy name”—that is, among those who are in heaven, may your power be glorified and worshiped.

We believe that the blessed angelic spirits, whom we call by various names, stand in God’s presence. Contemplating the glory of the Divinity and continually rejoicing in him, they praise and unceasingly sanctify him.

We also believe that the souls of blessed human beings, released from the bonds of the body, share the company of the angels and join in celebrating the praise and glory of the Creator, Redeemer, and Propitiator.

While they were bound in the prison of the body, they nevertheless sighed for him; although they saw only dimly through an enigma, they directed their gaze toward his brightness and glorified his power, virtue, and grace. How much more, now that they have been released, enjoy him, and behold him face to face, should they be believed to magnify his name?

Therefore, showing our devotion in glorifying God, we desire and ask that those who stand in his presence, who contemplate him as he is, and who enjoy him in blessedness, should praise and glorify him together.

It is as though we were saying openly:

“Because we, held fast in this frailty and corruption, cannot perfectly praise you, eternal Father, may your praise be completed by those spirits whom you have willed to cling to you inseparably, and by those souls whom you have taken pure from this filthy dwelling and set free to serve you.”

Therefore, with great desire to complete this praise through us also, we add:

### Chapter Three. On the third petition: “Thy kingdom come”

“Thy kingdom come.”

The holy Church is Christ’s kingdom, of which he himself will be ruler until he has placed his enemies beneath his feet, partly through the election of grace and partly through rejection.

Hence Paul says: “He”—that is, Christ—“must reign until he has put all his enemies beneath his feet.”

When this subjection has been completed and the kingdom has been most wisely ordered by its most wise king, he will hand it over to God the Father at the final time, as Paul says: “Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father.”

In that kingdom, received from God the Father, we shall comprehend as we are now comprehended; we shall know as we are now known—although we do not yet possess that perfection.

Hence Paul says: “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this to you also.” That is: if you do not perfectly understand God and his Christ, who gave you what you possess, he will reveal the remaining perfection in that kingdom.

There, too, we shall not fear human persecution; we shall not wither from hunger or thirst; we shall not grow numb with cold; nor shall we be subject to the slavery of the flesh, but free in the praise of God. Nor will the ancient enemy insult us, when Christ, as Paul says, has abolished every principality, authority, and power.

When, therefore, with the arrival of the kingdom of God the Father, we are freed from every necessity and every perfection of grace is bestowed upon us, so that his will may be done also in us—who, hindered by the corruption of the flesh, cannot in every respect serve his will—as it is done in those whom he has already established in heaven’s citadel, what could one ask for, or what more ought one desire, than the coming of this kingdom?

For this reason the following petition is added:

### Chapter Four. On the fourth petition: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

It is as though we were saying:

“Therefore, eternal Father, we desire your kingdom to come, so that we who are on earth may become such that we do not depart from your will, just as those who are in heaven do not depart from it—namely, Christ himself, your Son, our Lord, and all the saints who are with him.”

This may also be the continuation of the wording: “Thy kingdom come,” with the implied addition, “so that your will may be done,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, it is not inappropriate to understand this clause independently: “Thy will be done.”

First we desired that this age be brought to completion and that the Son hand over the kingdom of the Church to God the Father. When these things occur, there will be eternal exaltation in glory for the saints and unending abasement in punishment for those criminally defiled.

Therefore John, the faithful apostle and teacher, knowing that the coming of that kingdom would be harmful to us unless God’s will were done in us during the days of our flesh, immediately adds that this too must be requested.

God’s will is done in us when we are holy and blameless in his sight. Hence Paul says: “This is the will of God, your sanctification.” It will then be perfect when, through the armor of pure thought, we have driven hostile plagues from our spirit and, through self-control, scraped away the stains of proud flesh, finally trampling its defiance beneath the foot of perfect chastity.

Hence the same Apostle says: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness.”

This has already been perfected in those who, through the armor of faith, opposed themselves to the attacking enemy; having conquered him—or rather, having trampled him underfoot—they returned to the palaces of their supreme King and Leader and received with rejoicing the crowns of their rewards and the staff of perpetual freedom.

Yet, through the great wisdom of the Dispenser, the highest part of their rewards has still been withheld, without murmuring or impatience, from those who have earned it.

For those who have migrated from here to heaven have received part of blessedness, while awaiting us in the remainder, so that, when all things have been completed together and all rejoice together, a harmony of joy may arise in the house of the eternal King and Bridegroom such as befits his incomprehensible majesty: a household radiant with every adornment, a bridegroom advancing in complete chastity, and an immaculate virgin coming to meet him in his embrace.

Hence Paul says: “These did not receive the promise, since the Lord had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

It will indeed be better for all of us when, for the blessedness both of ourselves and of others, we rejoice together with one another in common.

Therefore, when we say, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth,” we implore that we who are still attacked in the camp of faithful service may be preserved holy and blameless, as are those spirits who stand before the brightness of his countenance—insofar as earthly things can be compared with heavenly things.

For no completion is comprehended here; rather, through the pledge of spiritual grace received here, we pursue perfection.

Hence Paul says: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have yet comprehended it; but I pursue it, if somehow I may comprehend it.”

For the completion of holiness, faith—which is the beginning of all good things—is supremely necessary. Through it, justice is conferred upon the fathers who came before, upon the brothers who are present, and upon the children who will follow.

Hence it is written: “The just person lives by faith”—that is, the just person is just by faith.

Therefore the Lord Jesus, the faithful teacher and the worker of everything for our salvation, taught us how to ask for it when he said:

### Chapter Five. On the fifth petition: “Give us this day our daily bread”

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

The bread that we ask for here—that is, sustenance—is understood as faith.

Through it, during the first age of the world, righteous Abel and Enoch, pleasing to God, were saved. Noah too, the head of the second age, and his household, were established as heirs of righteousness through faith.

The same faith also raised up the patriarchs, illustrious in the third age, into the grace of the promise. In the fourth age it crowned Moses, and in the fifth, David, as leaders.

In the sixth age, which the author of all things himself inaugurated and adorned with his presence, the apostles and their imitators were made partakers of Christ through faith.

Throughout every age of the world, as many as are just are just through faith; as many as are saved are saved through faith. For “without faith it is impossible to please God.”

These six divisions of the world, together with the seventh, which has no limit and is free from every laborious activity, resemble the division of the week into six days assigned to work and the seventh assigned to rest.

Since, therefore, this bread—that is, faith, which is sustenance and a firm foundation for salvation—has been necessary on every day, that is, in every preceding age of the world, we rightly call it “daily” and ask that it be supplied by God the Father today, that is, in this time of grace.

It is as though we were saying openly:

“O God the Father, give us who exist in this time of grace the faith with which you nourished all our fathers, whom you predestined for your glory in your eternal kingdom.”

If someone should happen to read these things and remember that the same passage has been explained differently by some interpreter of sacred speech, let him not therefore condemn this interpretation or hasten to judgment concerning the grace of the Spirit.

For I am confident that the same Spirit who distributed to others according to his will distributed also to me as he willed. The understanding is not the same in all of us, just as the activity is not the same in all the members.

Hence Paul says: “One person thinks this, another that.”

And what is surprising if the Wisdom of God has hidden many riches in the sacred words, when in a single grain he placed many natural properties and powers for reproducing itself, even though the different grains produced from one parent represent a single species of their kind?

What is surprising if different meanings of the Lord’s speech harmonize in one form, as it were, of truth? And since he makes every seed fertile by his blessing, why would he confine the seed of his word within the poverty of a single understanding?

Nor is it inappropriate for faith to be designated figuratively by the name of bread. For just as bread is the source of strength among bodily foods, so faith is the beginning and foundation among spiritual things.

Hence Paul says: “We have become partakers of Christ if we hold firmly to the beginning”—that is, faith—“of the substance.” And again: “Built upon the foundation”—that is, the faith—“of the apostles.”

But when we profess the faith of Christ, are crucified with respect to sins in baptism, and are buried there in the sign of the Lord’s burial, then, rising from there, and with our virtues raised together with us in the likeness of the resurrection of the dead with Christ, we become debtors to the whole of the Christian religion.

For just as circumcision in the flesh made the carnal Jew a debtor to the law given through Moses, how could sanctification in the spirit not bind the spiritual confessor to the debt of the grace proclaimed through Christ?

Hence Paul says: “I testify to every person who receives circumcision that he is a debtor to keep the whole law.”

But as we proceed to repay what we owe, the persecutor attacks, assails, and frequently conquers us; he violently snatches away what we carry, so that we may not bring what we owe to the storehouses of our Lord at the proper time.

What, then, shall we say to our Lord? Certainly what follows:

### Chapter Six. On the sixth petition: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”

“Forgive us our debts”—the debts we have not repaid, although we promised you.

“Forgive us, Lord, because in your name we forgive our debtors.”

But when the enemy ravages our fruit, he tries to burden us with the yoke of his iniquity and to impede our course, so that we do not hasten to our Lord to implore pardon.

His schemes are as varied as they are most destructive. First he delivers us over to the passions of desire; then he kindles us even to the accomplishment of crime; afterward he wraps our minds in darkness, so that, when we commit a mortal offense, we either judge it to be small and unworthy of repentance or do not even know that we have committed anything.

There are people who become entangled in the snare of greed, or who take pleasure in illicit love, and yet do not think that they have sinned or that, because of these deeds, they will be rejected from the kingdom of God.

But the Holy Spirit was in Paul. For he says: “I think that I have the Spirit of God.” And Christ spoke through him: “I do not dare to speak anything that Christ has not accomplished through me.” And elsewhere: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?”

Let us see, then, what those who preside testify through blessed Paul concerning the greedy person, the person defiled by illicit love, and others like them.

Writing to the Ephesians concerning those who deceive innocent hearts and commend themselves by praising the evil deeds of others, he says: “Let no one deceive you with empty words: no fornicator or greedy person will possess the kingdom of God.”

Fornication is everything of this kind that is committed without the lawful contracting of marriage.

When we fall into the devil’s snare—namely, into ignorance of the commission of our own crime—we are undoubtedly handed over to a wholly reprobate mind.

After listing the many sins into which the Gentiles had fallen and exaggerating iniquity upon iniquity, Paul added with grave lament: “Although they knew God, they did not acknowledge him.” Those who do such things are worthy of death.

He considered it the most pernicious evil that we should fall into ignorance of our own sins. For one who lies unknowingly swallowed up in the abyss of vices—how could he sigh for repentance? Who repents of a crime he does not know?

But if Satan cannot take away the sinner’s knowledge of his offense, he often persuades the sinner, after confessing the sin, to think that, while offering the sacrifices of repentance for his guilt, he may freely continue to wallow in the habit of the same offense.

There are people who sin through illicit love and similar conduct, yet flee to confession and amendment. But while they hasten through their offerings toward the cleansing of their guilt, they willingly defile themselves again in the same filth no less eagerly, falsely thinking that guilt is washed away through offerings while their mind, will, and action continue to roll about in the same impurity.

Hence Paul says: “For if we sin deliberately, no sacrifice for sins remains.”

Often, too, the persecutor induces the sinner to refuse to hear the words of God by which he is prohibited from doing evil, so that he may sin, as it were, more freely.

Paul shows how terrible this is when he writes to the Corinthians: “If anyone does not know, he will not be known.”

### Chapter Seven. On the seventh petition: “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen”

Since we are surrounded by so many ambushes of the ancient enemy, and if we are caught by them we shall surely die, it is necessary to invoke the assistance of our Leader and Savior, Christ Jesus.

Therefore we pray, saying: “And lead us not”—that is, do not permit us to be led—“into temptation,” namely, so that we might take pleasure in our minds in the very thing by which we are tempted by the devil.

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, from the delight of sin, whether our own or another’s.

“Amen.” It is as though we were saying:

“Through you, who are truth, may whatever we ask here become truth.”

## Around the Year of the Lord 1080. Berthold, Priest of Constance

### Historical and Literary Notice

(In D. Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Writers, volume V, p. 264.)

Berthold, a disciple and friend of Herman of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0339C] His name is disclosed by the Murensis codex under the years 741 and 1054; see note 3 below.], wrote, as the anonymous writer of Melk testifies [Note: [Col. 0339C] In the book *On Ecclesiastical Saints*, chapter 92.], a Life of his teacher and a Chronicle. Only fragments of it survive today in certain books, interwoven with the works of Herman and Bernold.

For the person who, in the middle of the twelfth century, copied a codex for the use of the monastery of Muri, in which he compiled a history [Note: [Col. 0339D] Under the year 741 he writes: “Up to this point Bede, the venerable priest, extended his chronicle in the greater book on the ages, containing, from the beginning of the world according to the Hebrew truth, 4,680 years; but many things have been intermingled from the chronicles of a certain abbot Regino of Bremen [read: Prüm], who, beginning from the Incarnation of the Lord, wrote down events extending to 906. From this point onward, what follows was taken from the writings of four authors, namely the aforementioned Abbot Regino, Lord Herman the Lame, his disciple Berthold, and Lord Bernold, priest of Saint Blaise. These writers continue in their works to the year 1006 of the Lord’s Incarnation.” But the year should apparently be understood as 1091.] from the creation of the world to the year 1091 of Christ, using the works of Bede, Regino, Paul’s account of the bishops of Metz, the genealogy of Saint Arnulf, and the *History of the Frankish Kings* [Note: [Col. 0340D] See *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Writers, volume II, pp. 324–325.], and then the books of Herman, Berthold, and Bernold, presented neither the complete text of Berthold nor anything more than the copyist of the once Gottwic codex [Note: [Col. 0340C] The Gottwic codex is now lost.] and of the Saint Gall codex did.

Rather, beginning with the year 1054, in which Herman’s Chronicle ends, he patched together material from Berthold and Bernold down to the year 1091. All doubt about this is removed by using Bernold’s autograph codex. The account of the year 1065 is complete and correct in Bernold alone, while in all the others it is corrupted in nearly the same manner. Whatever the Gottwic, Murensis, and Saint Gall codices have in common with Bernold must be attributed to Bernold, who proclaims himself their author [Note: [Col. 0340D] Bernold, under the year 1086.] and began writing in the year 1073 [Note: [Col. 0340D] Once these points have been set out, it will no longer seem necessary to repeat and refute the various opinions of earlier writers concerning Berthold. See Ussermann’s prefaces, volumes I and II; the *Prodromus of Sacred Germany*; Docen in *Archiv*, III, 1 ff.; Dumge and Mone, ibid., III, 209 ff.; Stenzel, *History of the Frankish Emperors*, II, 100–101.].

The remaining portion of the codices, which departs from Bernold’s brevity and clarity through its diffuse, involved, and somewhat obscure style, ought to be attributed to Berthold.

I shall therefore attempt, insofar as possible, to restore it. Using as my principal aid the text presented by Ussermann, especially on the basis of the Murensis codex, I have emended it with the help of all the supporting materials made available to me.

These are as follows:

1. The formerly Gottwic codex, cited by Ussermann but not examined completely, is now hidden from view—unless one should suppose it to be the same codex that

1*. is preserved in the Palatine Library at Vienna and is listed in Schwandtner’s catalogue, volume II, p. 451 [Note: [Col. 0341C] *Archiv*, II, p. 461.]. According to our Chmel, it was written on paper at the beginning of the eighteenth century.

It begins with the year 1053 in these words: “The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms with the lord pope,” and in the middle of a sentence under the year 1080 it breaks off with: “cast down by the judgment of God; but the treasure on account of which it ends…”

Like the Murensis codex, it presents excerpts from Bernold and Berthold intermingled. It is somewhat fuller in a few words under the years 1068 and 1076; under the year 1080 it alone of all the manuscripts preserved a fragment of Berthold; and it became known to Ussermann after being cited in 1727 by Hansiz [Note: [Col. 0341D] In *Germania Sacra*, volume I, pp. 264–266, he gave excerpts for the years 1076–1079.].

Although the book was written by an inexperienced or negligent person, it was nevertheless complete and had to be turned to our purpose. When I wrote to our Chmel about this matter, my wish was fulfilled, and in addition…

Source preparation: restored local supplied source, verified against canonical metadata.

1a.) I obtained the opportunity to collate with the edition of Muratori [Note: [Col. 0341D] *Antiquities of Italy*, vol. III, p. 933.] the codex of that same library, numbered among the secular historians as no. 672 (now no. 540), which contains the *Life of Herimannus*, and from which Muratori’s edition derives, though it is very corrupt. It occurs [Col. 0341C] there inserted in Otto of Freising’s *Chronicle*, between chapters 15 and 16 of Book VI, and, according to Chmel’s catalogue of the manuscripts of the Vienna Library [Note: [Col. 0341D] Vol. I, pp. 550–551.], is said to have been written in the thirteenth century.

2.) The codex of the monastery of Muri in Switzerland, which I examined on the spot in 1837, when it was still celebrated, is a parchment folio written in the middle of the twelfth century by a careful scribe, who nevertheless made only a few errors [Note: [Col. 0341D] Through mishearing, for example *coelo* instead of *zelo*.] and wrote several words in his own fashion [Note: [Col. 0341D] He sometimes uses the letters *c* and *p* in place of *t* and *b* in the words *justicia*, *vicium*, *precium*, *inimicicia*, *milicia*, *blandiciosus*, *nuncius*, *Wormaciensis*, and *pigricia*, and also in *optinere* and *optenebrare*. He writes both *Simoniacus* and *Symoniacus*.] [Note: [Col. 0341D] Ussermann did not correctly explain the abbreviations *quo* (= “because”) and *qncuque* (= “whenever”).] It consists of twenty gatherings, although the second has fallen out, with a bifolium added at the end. The first gathering contains inserted chronological tables, extending from the birth of Christ to the year 1175, followed by the years 1176–1218. The lost second gathering seems to have contained the beginning of the chronicle [Col. 0342A] from the creation of the world. The remaining gatherings present the text from the year 144 of Christ onward, drawn from the chronicles of Regino [Note: [Col. 0341D] Under the year 741 the heading described above appears; under 906: “Thus far the chronicle of Abbot Regino, and the chronicles of Herimannus follow”; under 1054: “Thus far the chronicle of Herimannus; from here Bertholdus.” [Col. 0342C] The continuation of Regino, copied down to 939, [Col. 0342D] leaves the scribe with the words *Caprimontem obsidione* (“Caprimontem under siege”); after leaving a space of nine lines, he gives the year 940 from Herimannus.], of Herimannus as it is contained in the manuscript of St Gall, and a composite text of Bertholdus and Bernoldus. In this portion it agrees with the Gottwic codex down to the end of 1079; then, omitting the fragment for 1080, it copies Bernoldus alone and stops in the words for 1091, “might perish amid the communion of the excommunicated.” The final two folios contain excerpts from Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*. A fourteenth-century hand has added numerous marginal notes here and there, and several poems have been inserted in the blank spaces. We append a specimen of the script.

The following was copied from the Muri manuscript, though one page has been omitted: [Col. 0342B]

2*.) The Engelberg codex, which I likewise examined in 1837 in the monastery situated among the high Alps, is a large-format parchment manuscript of the twelfth century; but its readings would not repay citation. It ends with the same words as the Muri manuscript.

3.) The formerly St Gall codex, printed by Johann Sichard in his Basel collection of chronicles in 1529, which, like the other manuscripts, I mentioned above on p. 74, already breaks off in 1066, in the middle of a sentence taken from Bernoldus: “two others, tearing their hands,” [Note: [Col. 0342D] Thus the first edition of 1529; in later editions the words from Bernoldus, “descended to the gates of hell,” are added.] certainly to the great disadvantage of our undertaking. For in it a text is preserved that is often somewhat fuller and that, as one can readily understand, comes closest to Bertholdus himself [Note: [Col. 0342D] For example, under 1056 it has *tenetur* (“is held”), where codices 1 and 2 read *tenebatur* (“was held”).], except for the *Life of Herimannus*, of which it gives only a brief mention.

With these aids, I proceeded in restoring the text as follows: for the years 1054–1066 and 1080 I printed chiefly the St Gall reading, arranging that material derived from Bernoldus should be printed in italic type; in the *Life of Herimannus* and in the remaining part of the work—namely, the years 1067–1079—I corrected the text with the aid of the Muri codex. Readers will readily perceive that this was not done without benefit.

Bertholdus is recognized from his own words as an Alemannian [Note: [Col. 0342D] Under 1075 he calls the Alemannians “our people.”] and an inhabitant of the diocese of Constance [Note: [Col. 0342D] Under 1069, “of our see,” namely, Constance.]. Nearly the same age as Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0342D] Bernoldus says that he died in 1088 “in a good old age, full of days.”], he appears to have been educated by him at Reichenau and, after his friend’s death, to have adorned his position [Note: [Col. 0342D] The statement under 1076 concerning the parties of Heinrich and Rudolf on this side of the Rhine, at Oppenheim, and on the far side of the Rhine does not serve this purpose; see below.] by teaching the students—an outstanding teacher [Col. 0343A] and especially well versed in sacred literature [Note: [Col. 0343C] He also indulged in etymology; under 1077 he derives the word *graviō* from the gravity of morals.] [Note: [Col. 0343C] Bernoldus, *Chronicle*, under 1088, and the *Necrology*, 15 March.]. He seems to have undertaken the writing of history under Pope Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 0343C] Under 1077 he writes: “The apostolic lord (Gregory), being, as he is, of no small compassion,” etc.] but only in 1076 [Note: [Col. 0343C] For under 1056 he writes: “Heinrich IV, son of Heinrich, reigns twenty years.”], a man not unknown to prominent persons [Note: [Col. 0343C] He may have seen Heinrich IV at Reichenau in 1074; he also knew the pope’s legates and the leaders of Rudolf’s party, including the bishops of Constance and Aquileia and others.], well acquainted with the events he recounts and supplied with abundant resources.

In the earlier part of the book [Note: [Col. 0343C] Whether one holds that he began the book with the year 1054, or that the chronicle which is copied from Herimannus and Bernoldus above, p. 265, and bears the title of the St Gall codex, also proceeded from Bertholdus cannot be asserted with certainty.] down to 1075, we find copied the *Chronicle of Bernoldus*, composed in 1073 and thereafter continued from time to time [Note: [Col. 0343C] See the passages printed in smaller type. He consulted Bernoldus’s text as we read it in the autograph—or even retained it literally; for example, under 1075, *Argentoracum*. Although he consistently wrote *Symoniacus* with Bernoldus, in one place he likewise adopted *Simoniacus* with Bernoldus.], and in 1076 Bernoldus is abandoned. Since Bertholdus stood on the side of Gregory VII and Rudolf against Heinrich IV [Note: [Col. 0343D] After Heinrich’s deposition he understands Rudolf by the designation “king”; in 1079 he calls Friedrich, whom Heinrich had made duke of Swabia, a count.], he carefully used for his own purposes the public acts issued by the supreme pontiff and his councils [Note: [Col. 0343D] For example, the Second Roman Council, in 1075 and 1077.], and placed such confidence in them that he very often incorporated in his narrative, in the same words, events reported by Gregory in letters to King Heinrich, to the Germans, and to the bishops of Germany or Italy [Note: [Col. 0343D] For example, the bishops of Mainz, Constance, Bamberg, and Aquileia.]. He also read Heinrich’s letters written to Gregory and used documents that no longer survive today [Col. 0344A]. In judging matters of public and canon law, he employed the writings of the papal party. In the years 1076–1080 he is entirely different from Bernoldus [Note: [Col. 0343D] For example, the matters that Bernoldus reports concerning Kadalaus are absent from our author.]; he relates the same events differently [Note: [Col. 0343D] For example, under 1076 he attributes the killing of Duke Godefrid, for which Bernoldus blames a cook, to a certain soldier; his wording is also cruder than Bernoldus’s. Under 1077 they report different outcomes for the battle at Strowi.], and generally proceeds in chronological order [Note: [Col. 0344C] At the end of 1078, guided by the connection of events, he reports the elevation of Eigilbertus to the see of Trier, although it occurred only in January of the following year.].

One cannot praise Bertholdus’s style very highly. He sometimes does not complete a sentence but breaks off in the middle [Note: [Col. 0344C] Under 1076, p. 33, line 3, of Ussermann’s edition.]; he uses accusatives absolute [Note: [Col. 0344C] Under 1077 and 1078.] instead of ablatives, deponent verbs with passive force [Note: [Col. 0344C] Under 1077, *praestolatos*.], *tacere* (“to be silent”) with a double accusative [Note: [Col. 0344C] Under 1079.], and the word *theutonizare* (“to speak German”) instead of *Theutonice sonare* (“to sound in German”), *returnare* (“to return”) for *reverti*, and *quamvix* (“hardly”) for *cito* (“quickly”) [Note: [Col. 0344C] Under 1079.].

The notes that Ussermann appended to the text I have retained wherever they seemed capable of offering some benefit to our readers; I have abridged quite a few [Col. 0344B] and removed many others as less necessary in a volume in which Lambertus, Bruno, and Bernoldus are presented together.

## THE ANNALS OF BERTHOLDUS

[Col. 0343B] Herimannus, who was also a great hero, etc. [Note: [Col. 0344C] In the margin of the parchment royal codex of the Berlin Library, numbered among the Latin manuscripts in folio as no. 307, which contains Herimannus Contractus’s book *On the Investigation of the Heart and the Hidden Matters of Astronomy*, written in a thirteenth-century hand, the following story is found: “Concerning this Hermannus it is read in the history that he was the son of a king [the codex reads ‘of the king’] and a queen, namely Tratia. While his mother was pregnant, it was divinely asked whether she would rather have a deformed and extremely ugly son, or one foolish but handsome beyond the sons of men. She is said to have replied that she preferred to have an ugly and wise son rather than one most beautiful and most foolish. This Hermannus was therefore born according to his mother’s wish—hunchbacked in front and behind, contracted, and lame. At the request of a certain person, he teaches him in this little work how to construct an astrolabe; but first he sets forth his preface.”] We have given this life, or eulogy, in the prefaces to Hermannus Contractus in volume CXLIII of *Patrologia*, col. 25.

A council [Note: [Col. 0344D] This appears to have come from Bernoldus, whose text at this point follows the year 1091.] was held by the emperor at Mainz. At it Gebehardus, bishop of Eichstätt [Note: [Col. 0343] “Of the people of Eichstätt,” in 3.], elected by the bishops and sent to Rome, was received there with honor and, in the following Lent, on Maundy Thursday, was ordained pope, the 154th, and took the name Victor II.

### 1055

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar, then prepared an expedition to Italy and celebrated Holy Easter at Mantua; Pentecost at Florence [Note: [Col. 0343] *Florenciis* in 1.]. There, in his presence, a general synod was held by the lord pope, and many matters were corrected [Note: [Col. 0344D] Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, p. 1079.]. The emperor released Adalbertus, who had been condemned to capital punishment, through the intervention of the bishops. At the same time, fifty or more armed soldiers secretly crossing the sea from Normandy, wishing to provide assistance to the Northmen against the emperor, were captured by citizens of Pisa [Note: [Col. 0343] Urstisius and Ussermann corrected this to *Picentibus*, but the subject could also be the Pisans.] and brought before the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0343] The words “At the same time ... were brought” are absent from 1* and 2.]

[Col. 0345A] The emperor sent Otto, bishop of Novara [Note: [Col. 0345] *Neovariensem* in 1*; *neofariensem* in 2.], to Constantinople. There he found, in place of the recently deceased Michael, a certain woman [Note: [Col. 0345] Ussermann notes here: “It was not Zoe, as the Gottwic codex has it, since she had died the previous year, but her sister Theodora, who died the following year and was succeeded by Michael Stratioticus, not preceded by him.” But no trace of such information appears in the Vienna copy of the Gottwic codex.] holding the monarchy of the entire empire. [XVII. [Note: [Col. 0345C] This year of Heinrich’s reign begins on 4 June. The emperor, returning from Italy through Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0345] The words “through Bavaria” are absent from 1* and 2.], celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the castle of Zurich, and there betrothed the daughter of Margrave Otto to his son, who bore the same name.

Herimannus, archbishop of the city of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0345] *Agrippinae urbis* (“of the city of Cologne”); 1* and 2 read *Coloniensis* (“of Cologne”).], died [Note: [Col. 0345] *obiit* (“died”)]; in his place [Note: [Col. 0345] *pro quo* (“in whose place”); 1* and 2 read *cui* (“to whom”)] Anno [Note: [Col. 0345] *Hanno* twice in 3.], previously provost of Goslar [Note: [Col. 0345] 1 and 2 read *Goslarensis praepositus successit* (“the Goslar provost succeeded”).], succeeded to the archiepiscopate. [Col. 0346A] In the same year [Note: [Col. 0345] The words “In the same year ... killed them” and “Heinrich” are absent from 1* and 2.] the Slavs called Liuticians, attacking the borders of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0345] Or “harassing”?], killed very many of their leaders together with Margrave Wilhelm. When the lord apostolic had been invited to him in the autumn, and Heinrich the emperor was staying in Saxony at Bothfeld [Note: [Col. 0345] 1* reads *apud bothfeldin*; 2, *(botfeldin)*.], weakened by an advancing illness and fortified by a good conversion through repentance and the purest confession, he forgave all his debtors from the heart; he returned everything he had acquired unjustly to those who were present, and for those who were absent he most carefully arranged by name, through the empress and his son, that it should be returned to them. Thus placing all his hope in God—oh, that he had done so happily!—he died on 5 October, in the thirty-ninth year of his age, the eighteenth of his reign, and the tenth of his empire [Note: [Col. 0345] 3 lacks “of his empire.”], in the tenth indiction. From there his body was carried away and transferred to Metz [Note: [Col. 0345] 1* and 2 read *Nemetim*], and he was buried in the church of Saint Mary, which he himself had built and which was still unfinished, beside his father and mother [Note: [Col. 0345] 3 reads “beside his father and mother.”], by the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0345] 3 adds “and his son.”]. His son Heinrich IV [Note: [Col. 0345] “Already made king by his father” (from Bernoldus), then seven years old; “he began to reign with his mother” (from Bernoldus), in 1* and 2.], being seven years old and undertaking the government of the kingdom in his place, was entrusted by the leading men of the realm to his mother, the empress, for upbringing [Note: [Col. 0345] “For upbringing” is absent from 1*.]. Famine afflicted many provinces [Note: [Col. 0345] The words “Famine ... provinces” are absent from 3.].

Heinrich IV, son of Heinrich, reigned twenty years, the ninety-sixth from Augustus [Note: [Col. 0345] The words “Heinrich IV ... from Augustus” are absent from 3; “from Augustus” is absent from 2.].

### 1057

King Heinrich celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Regensburg. On 25 April, the immense quantity of snow and frost destroyed a large part of the vineyards [Note: [Col. 0345] The words “On 25 April ... destroyed” are absent from 1* and 2.].

At Rome Victor II died; in his place Friedrich, brother of Duke Gotefridus, formerly archdeacon of blessed Pope Leo and at that time abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, was ordained the 155th pope and named Stephen IX [Note: [Col. 0345] 3 reads “VIII.”]. [Note: [Col. 0345] In place of this, 1* and 2 transcribe something from Bernoldus: “At Rome Victor II (1* adds ‘the 154th’) died. After him Friedrich, brother of Duke Gotefridus, formerly archchaplain of blessed memory Pope Leo, made a monk from a cleric and later promoted to abbot at Monte Cassino, ruled as Pope Stephen IX, the 155th, for nine months.”]

Duke Otho of the Alemannians died; Rudolfus [Note: [Col. 0345] *Rodolphus* in 1*.] received his duchy.

[Col. 0347A] This year stones of extraordinary size, mixed with hail, fell from the sky, and some people perished by lightning [Note: [Col. 0347] The words “and some people ... lightning” are absent from 1* and 2.].

### 1058 [Note: [Col. 0347] The number is absent from 3. What follows is omitted in 1* and 2, which instead contain certain material copied from Bernoldus: “At Rome, after Stephen, a certain Benedictus, elected contrary to the canons through the private favor of certain persons, presided over the Church without consecration for seven months. Expelled by Duke Gotefridus, Gerardus, bishop of Florence [“Burgundian by nation,” a fourteenth-century gloss], was appointed pope, called Nicholas II, the 156th, and presided for almost three years. He decreed that those who had then been promoted by simoniacs should be permitted to exercise their ministry; but thereafter, whoever was ordained by them should gain nothing from such promotion. This pope was also urged by Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, of blessed memory, to correct, in accordance with the canons, the incontinence of clerics.”]

[III.] Pope Stephen died at Rome. The Romans, having accepted money, elected a certain John [Note: [Col. 0347C] John, bishop of Velletri, under the name Benedict X; concerning him see Blessed Peter Damian, *Works*, vol. I, book III, letter 4, and Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 13. Ussermann.] contrary to the canons. After sitting for several days without consecration, he was expelled by Duke Gotefridus; the bishop of Florence was then made pope, the 156th, and called Nicholas II.

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0347] The words “At the same time ... displeased” are absent from 1* and 2.] Heinrich, bishop of Augsburg, held the highest position in the empress’s council. This greatly displeased some leading men of the kingdom, who could not tolerate his arrogance.

### 1059

[Col. 0347B] [IV.] This year there was a great mortality among human beings and [Note: [Col. 0347] The words “and ... animals” are absent from 1* and 2.] a plague among livestock. When war broke out between the Milanese and the people of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read: “A revolt arose between the Milanese and the people of Pavia, and more than one person fell in battle.”], many fell on both sides. Rudolfus, duke of the Alemannians [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 1* and 2.], took Mahthilda [Note: [Col. 0347] *Mahthildam* in the Engelberg Annals.], sister of King Heinrich [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 1* and 2.], as his wife.

At Fulda Abbot Eberhardus died, and Sigefridus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 add *et* (“and”).]

Andreas, king of Pannonia, after previously confirming peace and a treaty with King Heinrich through envoys, also obtained his younger sister Judith [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 3.] as bride for his son Solomon [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 3.], who was still a boy. Fridericus and his brothers of Glicheberga rebelled against King Heinrich, and afterwards surrendered to him.

### 1060

King Heinrich of Gaul died, and his son Philip [Note: [Col. 0347C] Absent from 3.]—still a boy [Note: [Col. 0347C] Philip I was then eight years old. Ussermann.]—undertook to govern the kingdom with his mother.

Liudpaldus [Note: [Col. 0347] *Luppoldus* in 1*; *Lupaldus* in 2.], archbishop of Mainz, died [Note: [Col. 0347] *decessit* (“died”); 1* and 2 read *obiit* (“died”).] [Note: [Col. 0347C] According to the Fulda Necrology, on 6 December.]; Sigefridus, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him.

[Col. 0348A] Chounradus, bishop of Metz, died [Note: [Col. 0347] *moritur* (“dies”); 1* and 2 read *obiit* (“died”).], and Einhardus, provost of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0347] The words “provost of Augsburg” are absent from 3.], was promoted in his place [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read “was substituted.”]. Mahthilt, the king’s sister [Note: [Col. 0348C] Wife of Duke Rudolfus. Ussermann.], died [V]. [Note: [Col. 0347] 3 reads *Mathildas*; 1* and 2: “Mahthilt, wife of Duke Rudolfus, died.”]

Count Heinrich of the Palatinate, having become insane, went to the monastery of Epternach [Note: [Col. 0347] *Ephtirnacha* in 3.] under the appearance of religion, as though abandoning the world; but after being taken away from there, he killed his wife.

And this year, as in the preceding one, mortality carried off many [Note: [Col. 0347] In 1* and 2 these words are read after the death of Mahthilt. The words “Winter ... damage” are absent from 1* and 2.]. A sufficiently severe and snowy winter, and one longer than usual, caused the greatest damage to grain and wine. [Note: [Col. 0348A] In Migne, the sections headed “Codices 1*, 2” and “Codex 3” are printed in parallel.]

**Codices 1*, 2**

In Hungary a certain Belo expelled his brother Andreas, already advanced in age, from the kingdom and brought about his death. Andreas, grievously wronged by his brother, was eventually struck by fever and sent all his treasures to the castle of Medelekka [Note: [Col. 0347] *Medeleka* in 1*; *medelekka* in 2.], as well as his son, to King Heinrich through Count Tietpaldus.

**Codex 3**

[Col. 0348]

Andreas, king of Pannonia, after suffering many injuries from his brother, who was devastating his kingdom on every side, was eventually struck by fever and sent all his treasures to the castle of Medilhecka [Note: [Col. 0348C] Melk in Austria.], as well as his son, to King Heinrich through Count Tiedbaldus.

### 1061 [Note: [Col. 0347] The number is absent from 1*.]

[VI.] A great famine consumed many [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read “killed.”]. Gebehardus, bishop of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0348C] This brother of Emperor Conrad II died in the preceding year. Ussermann.], died, and Otto succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read “and Otto succeeded him.”].

Chounradus, who ruled among the Carinthians [Note: [Col. 0347] *Carentanis* in 1* and 2.] in name only as duke [Col. 0348C] [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 1*.], died and gave way [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read “died.”]; Count Berhtoldus [Note: [Col. 0347] *Bertholdus* in 1* and 2.] of Swabian origin [Note: [Col. 0347] Absent from 3.] received his duchy [Note: [Col. 0347] 1* and 2 read “undertook.”].

At Rome, after Pope Nicholas died, the Romans sent a crown and other gifts to King Heinrich and appealed to him concerning the election of the supreme pontiff. He summoned all the bishops of Italy to himself and, after a general council had been held at Basel, was called patrician of the Romans after the same crown had been placed upon him. Then, with the common consent of all, he elected the bishop of Parma as supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, after many rewards had been given to certain persons, as they say, by simony. Meanwhile, while these events were taking place, Bishop Anselm of Lucca, with the support of certain Romans, usurped the apostolic see for himself [Note: [Col. 0349] Here 1* and 2 insert material concerning the bishop of Parma, given below: “The bishop of Parma ... remaining.” Then they add from Bernoldus: “This Alexander, a Catholic teacher, vigorously destroyed the simoniacal heresy and, under penalty of excommunication, forbade altar ministers to have intercourse with their wives according to the statutes of the canons; he also prohibited laymen, by public ban, from attending the offices of openly incontinent clerics, and thus wisely restrained their incontinence. The principal author of this decree was Hildebrandus, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, especially hostile to heretics.”]

Burchardus [Note: [Col. 0349] The sentence “Burchardus ... was dedicated” is absent from 1* and 2.] and Wezil of Zolorin were killed. The church of Metz was dedicated.

### 1062

At this time [Note: [Col. 0349] “And Agnes” in 3.] the Empress Agna, having laid aside her royal garments and been surrounded with the sacred veil [Note: [Col. 0349] Absent from 1* and 2.], dedicated herself to Christ and withdrew to the town of Fruttuaria [Note: [Col. 0349] *Fructerciam* in 1*? [Col. 0349C] In the Alps, within the diocese of Ivrea.]. On 8 February [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* reads “6 February 1062.”] earthquakes, lightning flashes, and thunder occurred. Pestilence and mortality followed and killed many [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 add, from Bernoldus, “and a great famine occurred.”]. King Heinrich celebrated Easter with his mother, the empress, at Utrecht, a city of Frisia [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 read “at Utrecht, and Easter together.”].

In those days Anno [Note: [Col. 0349] *Hanno* in 3.], archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 read “Anno of Cologne.”], with the support of certain leading men of the kingdom, forcibly seized King Heinrich from his mother, the empress, with the lance and other imperial insignia, and brought him with him to Cologne [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 add, from Bernoldus: “A great dissension arose between the empress and Guntharius, bishop of Bamberg.”]

The bishop of Parma, long since elected, went to Rome to be consecrated. When armed Romans met him and prevented his entry, a multitude of them were both killed by his soldiers and drowned in the Tiber; the rest were put to flight.

**Codices 1 and 2 [year 1061]:** The bishop of Parma, having gathered a large army from every side, determined by force to seize the see. When he reached the city of Rome in this manner, the Romans did not allow him to enter; hence a great slaughter took place there. Thus, after many Romans had been killed, he returned sadly to his Parma—not without a bloody victory—having usurped the apostolic title in name only, which he retained unhappily until the end of his life.

### 1063 [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2, from Bernoldus: “King Heinrich moved his army into Pannonia and restored Solomon, son of King Andreas, to his father’s kingdom. The winter was excessively severe and killed birds and ...”]

In the spring, in the middle of April, a fierce, windy, snowy winter lasted four days. It killed birds and livestock with the cold and destroyed a very large part of the trees [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 add “and caused a great scarcity of crops and wine.”] and vineyards.

Bishop Engilhardus of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 read “Engilhardus, archbishop of Magdeburg.”] died, and Werinharius, brother of the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0349] Absent from 3.], succeeded him. Heinrich, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Imbrico, a canon of Mainz, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 add, from Bernoldus: “A great slaughter occurred at Goslar in the presence of the king.”]

In the same year a certain woman near Constance gave birth to an infant with two heads and all the other limbs doubled down to the buttocks.

### 1064

King Heinrich celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne, but Easter at Liège [Note: [Col. 0349] Here 1* and 2 insert, from Bernoldus: “A great revolt arose between Adalbertus, archbishop of Hamburg, and the leading men of the kingdom.”] A synod was held at Mantua.

### 1065

King Heinrich celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 read: “He celebrated Easter at Goslar, but the Nativity at Worms.”], but Easter at Worms. The royal palace at Goslar was burned [Note: [Col. 0349] This likewise appears in 1* and 3, derived from Bernoldus through a mistaken reading.], and this also happened in [Note: [Col. 0349] *quod et factum est in* (“and this also happened in”) is absent from 1* and 2.] 27 March, in the third indiction. There he was girded with the sword, in the ninth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his age, and Duke Gotifridus was chosen as his shield-bearer [Note: [Col. 0349] 1* and 2 read: “In the same year from the incarnation of the Lord 1065, when Easter was celebrated on 27 March, on which day Christ rose, on the third day of Easter week, 29 March, in the third indiction, King Heinrich in the ninth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his age was girded with the sword in the name of the Lord, and Duke G. was chosen as his shield-bearer.”]

The bishop of Passau died, and Altmannus, the empress’s chaplain, succeeded him. At this time Sigifridus, archbishop of Mainz, Wilhelmus, bishop of Utrecht, and Guntharius, bishop of Bamberg, together with Otto, bishop of Regensburg, set out for Jerusalem with a large retinue and following. On that journey they suffered much at the hands of the pagans; indeed, they were forced to engage them in battle. On the same journey Guntharius died, and Ricimannus succeeded him by simony.

### 1066

Many nobles perished in civil war [Note: [Col. 0349] 3 wrongly adds “in the year 1065” to this notice.]. King Heinrich celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at [lacuna], but Easter at Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0349] Ussermann supplies “at Goslar.”]

[Col. 0351A] Eberhardus, archbishop of Trier, on 15 April, Holy Saturday [Note: [Col. 0351] 1* reads *sanctae* (“of the holy [day]”).] of Easter, after completing the offices of that day himself and while clothed in the very sacerdotal vestments, rested in peace. Chounradus, provost of Cologne, elected by the king, was supposed to succeed him; but he was rejected by the clergy and citizens of Trier. Therefore a certain count from the military force of Trier, named Theodericus, seized the same Chounradus while he was heading toward Trier and, after he had been long tormented in custody, handed him over to four soldiers to be killed.

When they had thrown him three times down a certain precipice and had been able to break nothing except his arm, one of them, moved by repentance, obtained his forgiveness. Another, wishing to behead him, cut off only his jaw. Thus he, a martyr worthy of God, departed to the Lord. He suffered on the Kalends of June in the year 1066 from the incarnation of the Lord and in the tenth year of King Heinrich’s reign [Note: [Col. 0351] The words “in the year ... of the king’s reign” are absent from 3.], and was buried at [Note: [Col. 0351] 3 reads *ad* (“at/to”) for *apud* (“at”).] an abbey called Doleja [Note: [Col. 0351] 3 reads *quandam* (“a certain”) for *nomine* (“called”).] A fitting vengeance later overtook the three soldiers who had caused his death. One of them was unable to swallow the food he had taken; the other two, tearing their hands [Note: [Col. 0351] Here 3 ends in the middle of the sentence.], thus expired and descended to the gates of hell. Besides this, many miracles occurred at his tomb, by which his venerable martyrdom is proved. Uto, a canon of Trier, was elected and appointed archbishop by the clergy after his death.

Comets were seen on the octave of Easter, that is, 23 April, and lasted for thirty days. The marriage of King Heinrich took place at Tribur. A comet was also seen. At this time the venerable Peter Damian, formerly a hermit [Col. 0351C], became a cardinal bishop and wrote many works; in his writings he refuted the incontinence of priests with sufficient reason, but treated those ordained by simoniacs, as they say, with excessive leniency.

Hugo, archbishop of Besançon, a religious, faithful, and prudent man, a servant of the Lord, happily entered into the joy of his master, to be set over many things. He was succeeded by a canon of that same church, canonically elected by his brothers.

### 1067

King Heinrich celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Speyer, but Easter at [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0351] Regensburg seems to be required. Ussermann.]

Saxony is suffering from civil discord; Burchardus, bishop of Halberstadt, devastated the people of the Liuticians with courage.

[Col. 0351D] Einhardus, bishop of Speyer, died on the Roman journey and was buried at Siena; a certain Heinrich succeeded him.

[Col. 0352A] In these times [Note: [Col. 0351D] Baronius and others generally assign this to the year 1063. Mabillon, however, takes a different view (Annales Benedictini, vol. V, p. 1 ff.), where, from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint Remigius at Reims, he proves that it occurred in the year 1067, in February, on the Wednesday of the first week of Lent, that is, on the twenty-eighth of that month. Mansi, however (Supplement to the Councils, vol. I, p. 1360), writes from another Florentine manuscript that it happened in the year 1068, on the Ides of February, the Wednesday of the first week of Lent, in the monastery of Septimo, that is, on 13 February. USS.] certain monks from the valley called Umbrosa, in the Florentine bishopric, refused to receive their bishop on account of the heresy of simony, and so turned the clergy and people away from him that they were unwilling in any way to receive his ministry. They also publicly declared in certain writings that the sacraments performed by him and by all simoniacal and married priests were entirely invalid and ought to be despised; and from this the greatest dissension and schisms arose, not only there but also in other neighboring places.

When Pope Alexander heard of this case and dispute, he summoned both the bishop and the monks to Rome, so that a Catholic judgment concerning these matters might be definitively established in a Roman synod. Accordingly, the judgment there [Col. 0352B] was defined, at the insistence of the bishops [Note: [Col. 0351] “the bishops themselves,” in 2.], so that, as though fire itself were the judge, the truth of the holy Church might be disclosed and made known. While this was being praised as something to be carried out by both sides, one of the monks declared that, with God as witness and discerner of his justice, he would himself submit to the same judgment. After this decision had been established and promulgated by the pope, they returned to Florence so that it might be carried out there in the presence of the clergy and people.

Finally, after a considerable council had been held there, a blazing fire, higher than a man’s stature and extending twelve feet in length, with an interval of two feet between its two parts, was carefully kindled in the church atrium from extremely dry wood. When Bishop Peter of Florence did not dare to enter its midst in order to establish himself and his associates as innocent of the alleged guilt and intention [Col. 0352C], the aforesaid monk [Note: [Col. 0352D] Peter, hence surnamed “Fiery,” and later made bishop of Albano and a cardinal. USS.], having received the Eucharist of Christ and prepared himself in the manner in which he had celebrated Mass there, entered barefoot, holding a cross in his hands. Under this sacramental test of God’s justice and truth [Note: [Col. 0351] “Roman,” in 1*.], he declared publicly before the whole Church in Christ that Peter, who was called the Florentine bishop, held the episcopate simoniacally [Note: [Col. 0352D] Bernold also reports the same thing, Opusc. IX, 5, p. 376. See also Opusc. XII, 3b, pp. 392, 395.], and that the sacraments performed by him and by the other simoniacal and married priests were in no way to be received by Catholics. Then, proceeding step by step into the midst of the flames, he successfully walked through them in the name of the Lord without any injury from the heat or fire [Note: [Col. 0351] “thus,” in 1*; “faithfully,” in 2.]. But when all the people saw this judgment, they unanimously gave thanks and praise to God, the righteous Judge on high.

Peter, however, was eventually summoned to Rome by the lord pope and, convicted on account of the guilt of the aforesaid heresy by the proof of this judgment, returned the episcopal staff and ring to the apostolic authority in confusion. Thus he departed, justly deprived of the dignity to which he had been unjustly elevated. For some time, nevertheless, with the aid of Duke Gotifrid, he seized the property of that church, hoping somehow to be restored to his see. When this hope finally failed him, he renounced everything he appeared to possess, turned to conversion, and became a monk at the monastery of Pomposa [Note: [Col. 0353D] Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. III, p. 73. USS.]. The Normans wished to invade Rome by force, but desisted when Duke Gotifrid threatened them.

## 1068

King Heinricus celebrated Christmas at Cologne, but Easter at . . . . Here, led astray by the error of his youth [Col. 0353B], he forgot his lawful wife to such an extent, and was reported to be entangled in such abominable crimes, that even his princes began plotting to deprive him of the kingdom. The whole year was rainy [Note: [Col. 0353] 1 1* adds: “Wernherus, second abbot of Saint Blasius, died.”].

## 1069

Peace and reconciliation among the people were confirmed at Christmas at Goslar by royal edict under oath.

King Heinricus devastated the people of the Liutizians.

Dedo, the Saxon margrave, rebelled against the king, but afterward was compelled to surrender.

Oudalricus, abbot of Reichenau, died. In his place a certain Meginwardus of Hiltinisheim was scarcely installed as abbot by the king, simoniacally and despite the rebellion of the brothers.

Rumaldus, bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 0353] 1* adds “thirty-six years.”], a most pious and humane man [Col. 0353C], who was also the most diligent restorer of the episcopal residence, which collapsed in his time, and the most attentive enlarger and provider of the ecclesiastical treasury, abandoned the shadowy vanities of this world and happily closed his final day on 2 November. He was honorably buried in the same house that he had already begun to build, on 4 November.

At that time the heresy of simony, no longer secret as formerly but openly and with irreverent arrogance, raged everywhere among our people, without respect of persons; and it had most miserably defiled the dove-like beauty of holy Mother Church with the contamination of its filth. Finally, it had compelled a certain Karlomannus [Note: [Col. 0353D] Commonly called Carolus. USS.], a canon of Parthenopolis and provost of Harcispurg, to enter the folds of the see of Constance—not through the door but by another way, namely through the wall—after he had given and promised to the king and his counselors a considerable amount of sacrilegious money, as well as ecclesiastical benefices [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 has “had compelled.”]. Thus that most wretched buyer, a man of hellish misery, strove with great determination, against all right, to be enthroned in our see, and schemed in every way to frustrate the canonical election of Sigifridus [Note: [Col. 0353D] Sigefridus is mentioned as the king’s chaplain among King Heinricus’s envoys to the rebellious Saxons in 1073, in Bruno. USS.], their brother and also the royal chaplain, whom the entire clergy and people had desired to have as their bishop [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 has “in every way.”].

Duke Gotifridus [Note: [Col. 0353D] Called “the Bearded” of Lower Lorraine, husband of Beatrice, marchioness of Tuscany. A short work by Saint Peter Damian, no. LVII (Works, vol. III), survives addressed to him; in it Damian criticizes his leniency in punishing crimes, and presses the same point in a subsequent treatise, setting before him the example of Hugh the Great, likewise margrave of Tuscany. USS.] was the most outstanding of secular men and the readiest to be moved to contrition and tears when remembering his sins. He was most generous in distributing alms, so lavishly dispensing all his possessions and treasures to the poor and to churches that he was almost left sitting naked, bearing only the naked cross. So completely was he transformed from one man into another by repentance so perfect and tearful that it is not permissible to doubt that he happily departed from here to the citizenship of the heavenly court [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 reads altera rather than alter.]—having commended his spirit into the hands of Him for whose grace he sighed with the utmost devotion, and, wholly intent upon heavenly things, joyfully breathing his last. At last, at Verdun, where he also died, he was buried with entirely fitting rites on 24 December. May he rest in peace [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 reads fit (“it happens”) rather than sit (“it is permitted”).].

## 1070

The king celebrated Christmas at Freising, and, after passing through those regions, arrived at Augsburg on the Purification of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0353] 1* adds: “Dietmarus, bishop of Chur, died, and Heinricus, a monk of Reichenau, succeeded him.”]. Accordingly, when the brothers of Constance came there to have their elected candidate accepted with the king’s support, they returned home sadly, whether they wished it or not, because that aforesaid simoniac was being imposed upon them by the king’s sufficiently threatening command [Note: [Col. 0353] 2 reads praedicta symoniana, “the aforesaid simoniacal [one].”]. Thus that excommunicated man, a stubborn invader, unhappily usurped the episcopal see. Without delay, he most diligently undertook the work for which he had come: namely, to sell worse what he had badly bought, to steal, to slaughter the sheep of others, and to destroy them. He secretly cut up and dismantled the sacred vessels, the liturgical vestments, and the altar panels covered with silver; and he presumptuously scattered the gold, gems, and the entire ecclesiastical treasury for his own and his associates’ uses, like a sacrilegious thief (Bernold, under 1071).

When the brothers had reported all this to Pope Alexander in a letter of complaint, the pope, by apostolic authority, forbade them to communicate with him at all. At the same time, he sent a letter to the archbishop of Mainz, commanding him not to consecrate this man as bishop unless he canonically cleared himself of the aforesaid heresy [Col. 0354D]. But, defending himself by whatever means he could through the promises and authority of the king and his associates, he prolonged his case into the following year.

France was suffering from civil discord. Otto, duke of Bavaria [Col. 0355A], was accused by certain people of treason against the king, and the king granted him the opportunity to clear himself by judicial combat. When he refused to do so, he took this as an occasion for rebellion, and Magnus, son of Otto, duke of northern Saxony, joined him. But when the aforesaid Otto, though lawfully summoned to make satisfaction, refused to come, the king deprived him of the duchy and his other benefices.

Dietmarus, bishop of Chur, died, and Heinricus, a monk of Reichenau, succeeded him.

Meginwardus, unwilling to endure the king’s exactions, commands, and services, voluntarily abandoned the abbey of Reichenau.

The winter was windy and rainy.

## 1071

The king celebrated Christmas . . . . [Note: [Col. 0355] Uss. inserts “at Goslar,” but it is absent both in 1* and in 2.].

Welf became duke of Bavaria.

King Heinricus, having suffered many ambushes [Col. 0355B] from the Saxons, passed through them all bravely.

Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, came with his associates to surrender to the king at Pentecost.

Karlomannus, that intruder at Constance, was synodically convicted at the council held at Mainz by order of Pope Alexander [Note: [Col. 0355D] On 15 August, according to Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. XX, p. 10.]. The canons of Constance had persistently charged him by accusatory letters with the aforesaid heresy and with the many sacrilegious acts he had committed. Since he could not deny that he had acted against the discipline of ecclesiastical rule—namely, that he had obtained a church by purchase—he was shamefully expelled from the see that he had invaded simoniacally, though not by the public deposition that ought to have occurred. For the king favored him as much as he could; and, with his heart still hardened and rebellious, he had returned the episcopal staff to him unwillingly—not in the synodal council, but in his own chamber.

If such a sentence awaits and condemns one not yet consecrated [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 has “condemns”], what will happen to the consecrated? And if this applies to bishops, what will be done about priests? Behold the argument for deposition from the greater to the lesser. Since, according to the precepts of the holy Fathers, no cleric may be permitted to be ignorant of the canonical statutes, let us not hesitate to commit to memory this one brief chapter from the decrees of Pope Saint Nicholas:

“Whoever has obtained a church by payment must be deposed in every respect, since he is known to have acted against the discipline of ecclesiastical rule. But whoever has expelled another priest lawfully ordained to a church by means of money, and has thus claimed it for himself, must have that vice, which has spread so widely, corrected with the utmost care.”

Otto, a canon of Goslar, was substituted by the king for Karlomannus.

A certain Roupertus, abbot of Bamberg, entered the abbey of Reichenau simoniacally after giving the king a large amount of gold. Later, having been anathematized, he was expelled [Note: [Col. 0355D] Gregory VII, Register I, 82, “to all the faithful”; Mansi, vol. XX, p. 122.].

## 1072

[Col. 0356A]

The king celebrated Christmas . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0355] Uss. conjecturally inserts “at Worms,” since it is absent in 1* and 2.] and overcame, almost without difficulty, those who rebelled against him.

Peter Damian, cardinal bishop of pious memory, long since crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on 7 Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0355D] Bernold has 8 Kalends of March; in the Necrology, the same date is given as 9 Kalends of March.]. The lord Geraldus, a monk of Cluny, distinguished in scriptural learning and not inferior in character to his predecessor, succeeded him in the bishopric.

Adalbertus, archbishop of Bremen, died. Liemarus succeeded him.

The king built many very strongly fortified castles for himself in Saxony and Thuringia, and unjustly seized more fortifications for himself; as a result he stirred up the minds of many against him.

In those days also the church of Milan remained vacant for some time after the death of its bishop. A certain man succeeded him after giving a very large sum of money to the king and his counselors. Although the pope had excommunicated him, the king ordered him to be consecrated. The clergy, however, had elected another suitable man for themselves, who is said to have been expelled by that intruder under compulsion to swear an oath [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 has “who” for “which.”] [Note: [Col. 0356D] Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. IV, p. 114, names the intruder as Gotifridus and the other as Otto. USS.].

## 1073

The king celebrated Christmas . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0355] Uss. adds “at Bamberg,” absent in 1* and 2.].

Roudolfus, duke of Alemannia, Bertholdus, duke of Carinthia, and Welf, duke of Bavaria, withdrew from the king because, after other counselors had entered in, they saw that their counsel had no influence with the king.

Count Theodericus, moved by repentance for the crime he had committed against the blessed Chounradus, appointed prelate of Trier [Col. 0356C], undertook to go to Jerusalem with many others in fervent faith, although many dangers stood in the way. When they had begun to enter the sea by ship at Laodicea, they were caught by a sudden storm. Immediately the day was darkened, so that they did not know where they were going; after four days [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 reads quadriduum rather than quatriduum, both meaning “four days”], while the storm continually battered the ship in the same direction, they were often cheered at night by a heavenly light descending toward them [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 has opt., an uncertain reading]. Then, no longer fearing death amid the dangers but contemplating eternal life, cleansed by the sea waves from the filth of their sins, they were shipwrecked and departed to the Lord on 13 Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0355] Bernold’s Necrology]. They were Count Theodericus, Wilderold, Marchward, and 113 in number with them.

Herimannus, margrave and son of Duke Bertholdus, still a young man and already striving toward evangelical perfection [Col. 0356D], became a true follower of Christ and a monk at Cluny, leaving behind everything he possessed, together with his wife and only son [Note: [Col. 0356D] Bernold’s text is entirely different; the Sanblasian scribe seems not to have understood him.]. After living there in complete observance of the Rule for only a little more than one year, he happily departed to the Lord on 7 Kalends of May. Through frequent revelations [Note: [Col. 0355] 2 has “miracles.”], he still remains a warning to the brothers concerning his hidden faults and negligences [Col. 0357A].

At Rome Pope Alexander died. In his place the venerable Hildebrandus, archdeacon of the Roman Church, a prudent, sober, and chaste man, was sought by the unanimous counsel of all to be made pope. On hearing this, he considered himself unequal to so great an honor—or rather burden—and could scarcely beg for a delay in replying [Note: [Col. 0357] Uss. reads impetravit, “obtained.”]. Thus, escaping by flight, he remained hidden for several days at Saint Peter’s in Chains. At last, scarcely discovered and forcibly brought to the apostolic see, he was ordained the 158th pope [Note: [Col. 0357] 159th according to the Annals of Engelberg and Bernold’s corrector] and called Gregory VII. By his prudence, the incontinence of priests was restrained not only in Italy but also in the German regions. What his predecessors had forbidden in Italy, he diligently attempted to forbid in the other parts of the Catholic Church as well.

All Thuringia and Saxony rebelled against King Heinricus on account of the aforesaid fortifications and many other things that the king had insolently and imprudently done in their region against the will of that people, things which they could no longer patiently and calmly endure. After forming a conspiracy with a great multitude, they deliberated on how they might unexpectedly constrain him, according to their intention.

When he learned of their plan, he hastily took his treasury and, as the circumstances of the moment allowed, scarcely escaped from them with a few men to Worms. There he was ill for some time. Afterwards the king prepared an expedition into Saxony. The Saxons, however, anticipating him, unanimously promised him satisfaction if he would grant them the laws and rights of their forefathers [Col. 0357C]. A conference was held at Würzburg for the sake of this agreement, but after many complaints about the intolerable injustices they had suffered, nothing else was accomplished there except that, contemptuously, they agreed—following the counsel of certain bishops and dukes already mentioned—to offer the king a false satisfaction again at Christmas.

After these events, one of the king’s counselors withdrew from him and publicly disclosed and accused him before the aforesaid dukes, claiming that the king, together with this counselor and his other intimates, had already formed a plan to kill everyone by whatever means possible. He openly declared that he himself had been designated for this very crime and compelled to it by the greatest rewards. Hence the greatest discord arose between the king and the princes [Col. 0357D], to such an extent that the king barely escaped their ambushes and entered Worms with the aid of its citizens. There, having gathered forces of auxiliaries from every direction, he awaited the day on which he would clear himself by judicial combat of the accusation of the aforesaid crime.

When the appointed day finally arrived, on which he was either to clear himself before the princes of the kingdom or be expelled from the kingdom, the king’s betrayer—the man who had turned rebellious against him—died a sudden death. Thus the matter of the aforesaid intention was postponed, since they rejected the king’s oath by which he wished to clear himself. He then gathered together from every direction whatever troops of soldiers and loyal men he could, and began day by day to pay little attention to the hostility of his opponents.

Ruotpertus, already anathematized by the pope and likewise expelled by the king, as was justly fitting for a sacrilegious disciple of Simon, was finally replaced by Eggehardus, one of the brothers of Reichenau, elected by them, who became abbot of Reichenau. In accordance with the provisions of his privileges, he was consecrated at Rome by the aforesaid pope after Easter [Note: [Col. 0357D] Gregory VII, Register I, 82.]. Ruotpertus, having become abbot at Gengenbach [Note: [Col. 0357D] Not until after the death of Acelinus, in the year 1074.], was killed by a certain minister of the church because he had attempted to take away a benefice from him [Note: [Col. 0358D] In the year 1075, on 12 December.].

## 1074

[Col. 0358B] King Heinricus celebrated Christmas at Worms, although amid the greatest dangers and anxieties. Then, having gathered from every direction whatever help he could, he suddenly attacked the Saxons on the Purification of Saint Mary. Fearing the force of war, they surrendered on the condition that the aforesaid fortifications, on account of which the rebellion had arisen, should be destroyed; and this was subsequently done. Thus, while the aforesaid dukes and the other leading men of the kingdom were absent, the king was reconciled to the Saxons in appearance only, and came with them as far as Goslar, though he placed little confidence in them.

Duke Roudolfus and the other rebels were reconciled to the king.

During this Lent, the empress [Note: [Col. 0357] A fourteenth-century gloss in 2 identifies her as the mother of this Emperor H.] and two bishops, legates of the apostolic see, came with her from Rome to Phorzheim in Alemannia, to correct the conduct of the king. The king celebrated Easter at Bamberg.
