From there, traveling to Nuremberg to his mother and to the other legates of the apostolic see, he placed himself, in the presence of the bishops of Mainz and Bremen and many others, into their hands as one accused, under a promise of correction. He also firmly promised the lord apostolic his assistance in deposing the simoniacs.

The king’s counselors likewise promised before the same legates, under oath, that they would restore all the property of the churches that they had unjustly acquired, since they had bought it from simoniacs and, by assisting those men in gaining ecclesiastical office through their counsel, had shown themselves unworthy of the same office. These arrangements having been made, the empress and the legates of the apostolic see returned.

That summer the king marched into Hungary to assist King Solomon, who, because of the insolence and disgracefulness of his crimes, had also been deprived of his dignity by his uncle and the other better men of the kingdom, while himself disregarding their counsel. But since the king was unable to accomplish anything there according to his wish—namely, to restore Solomon—he finally took back his sister, Queen Judith, Solomon’s wife, and returned home to Worms not under the good omen with which he had set out [Note: [Col. 0357] 2 reads homine rather than omine, “man” rather than “omen.”]. A son was born to the king [Note: [Col. 0358D] Conradus, born 12 February.] [Col. 0359A]. In the autumn, returning again to Bavaria and staying for some time in those regions, he proceeded from there through Augsburg and Reichenau to the city of Strasbourg.

## 1075

The king ceremoniously celebrated Christmas at Strasbourg with considerable forces of his nobles, in glory. There, under an openly proclaimed pretext, he and his loyal men were already craftily planning to march into Saxony unexpectedly with an army, as though the Pannonian expedition were to be renewed immediately after Easter. Thus, having prudently gathered from every direction a considerable military force, he hoped that he would be able to avenge his injuries all the more easily because he had now concentrated his entire purpose upon them, while his enemies were entirely unsuspecting [Col. 0359B].

During Lent, Pope Gregory gathered a synod at Rome with all his strength, in order somehow to suppress the innumerable and presumptuous outrages that were scandals to holy Mother Church, and to recall to observance, at least to some degree, the canonical constitutions of the holy Fathers—constitutions that our own age had almost entirely forgotten and abolished. For, trusting not a little, beyond hope, in the hope of the aid of the supremely mighty cultivator, he had found the Lord’s field, though for a long time already neglected through the careless sloth of his predecessors, overgrown with the harsh thickets of abuses arising from usurpations, and, through the hoary decay of ecclesiastical fruit, luxuriantly turning altogether into a lamentable wilderness [Note: [Col. 0359] Uss. inserts “he had found,” with 2 reading “becoming overgrown”]. Nevertheless, he himself undertook to cleanse it properly with the authentic axes of Catholic and apostolic correction. Its thorns, briars, and weeds had long been easy for his predecessors, in their own time, gradually to cut down through false discipline and to root out completely with the hoe of doctrine [Col. 0359C].

Therefore, with the entire holy council judging and agreeing, he firmly decreed by apostolic authority that the authentic rules of the holy Fathers, duly established in each of the councils up to the present, should retain their proper force; and that anyone who presumptuously resisted them in defiance should be wholly alienated from the members of the Church.

Furthermore, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, he issued the following judgment in the same synod [Note: [Col. 0359D] The passage beginning “According to the authority . . .” and ending “the people repent” is taken, with minor alterations, from a letter of Pope Gregory to Otto, bishop of Constance. Mansi, vol. XX, p. 404. The same letter appears in Bernold, Opusc. IV, 1, p. 272.]:

Those who have been promoted through the heresy of simony—that is, through the intervention of payment—to any rank or office of the sacred orders shall henceforth have no place for ministering in the holy Church. Those also who obtain or have obtained churches by the payment of money shall lose them entirely. Henceforth no one may presume either to sell or to buy them, or to make use of tithes, except according to the rule of canonical constitution [Col. 0360A]. Nor should those who lie in the crime of fornication celebrate Mass or minister at the altar according to the lower orders.

He also decreed that if the aforesaid contemptuous men should despise these constitutions—or rather, those of the holy Fathers—the people should in no way receive their ministry, since they had been alienated from the members of the Church; so that those who would not be corrected by fear of God and the dignity of their office might repent through worldly shame and the people’s rebuke.

But toward those who obeyed and truly repented of their error, he showed merciful indulgence, releasing them from their sin through apostolic gentleness and authority: thus he is to be believed without doubt, according to the Catholic faith, as the just judge and binder of the hardened, but the gracious forgiver and looser of the truly penitent [Col. 0360B].

There also he anathematized again the king’s counselors because of the Simoniacal heresy, since they had disregarded what they had promised the pope’s legates under oath [Note: [Col. 0360D] Roman Council II; Mansi, vol. XX, p. 443.]. The king, angered on this account, did not avoid them.

In the same synod, a sentence of both deposition and excommunication [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 has “excommunication.” USS.] was issued according to the just statutes of the canons against Heinricus, bishop of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0360D] Roman Council II, at the same place.]. He had long been canonically accused before the Roman see of simoniacal heresy and, summoned there so that his case might be examined, had disdainfully refused to come.

Now, in a remarkable manner, on the very day and at the very hour when he was judicially deposed at Rome from his rank and episcopate and excommunicated, he himself, luxuriously attended at Speyer in his customary fashion, rose from the table, and immediately his throat was fatally constricted by an extremely sharp dart of pain. Thereafter he could scarcely utter even a word, and that only until the following morning; in the afternoon he was removed from both episcopate and life by a most bitter death [Note: [Col. 0360D] Bernold reports the same event, Opusc. III, letter 5 to Alboin, no. 22.]. Thus the power and truth of God’s words were confirmed in this miracle: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

Behold, already unsheathed, Peter’s sword, a most discerning judge of frauds and most effective zealot against adversaries—the sword by which he had mortally struck Ananias and Sapphira when they defrauded the price of a field and lied to the Holy Spirit, by which he had also cast Simon, the arch-heresiarch, from his heavenly ascent down to earth to be torn apart in four pieces [Note: [Col. 0359] 2 has “in vain.”], and then down to the eternal condemnation of hell. Let it now and always be feared by all simoniacs, all the more anxiously because there is no shield of defense except perfect repentance by which so long, penetrating, and inevitable a vengeance may anywhere be warded off [Col. 0360D].

When the aforesaid and nearly all the statutes of the apostolic see had been promulgated among the various churches, either by letters or by commands, almost everyone resisted them. Hence the greatest hatred arose against the lord apostolic and against the very few who agreed with him, together with the greatest schisms everywhere, especially among the clergy. Since the causes were common, the lord pope ordered that a universal council be held at Mainz to define them canonically [Note: [Col. 0361D] Gregory VII, Register III, 4, addressed to Sigefridus, archbishop of Mainz.]. The archbishop had already announced to his suffragans on 16 Kalends of September that they were to observe it. But they, already contemplating disobedience, disregarded the apostolic command and left the matter undone [Note: [Col. 0361] 2 has “where,” and does not punctuate here.].

Outzmannus, a canon of the church of Speyer, succeeded Heinricus, who died miserably. King Heinricus celebrated Easter at Worms. After Pentecost, he suddenly advanced into Saxony with the considerable army that had previously been openly prepared for Pannonia [Col. 0361B].

The Saxons and Thuringians, having learned long before of this plan for so treacherous an invasion, themselves deliberated, after forming a conspiracy, on how they could meet the king with whatever strength the circumstances of the time allowed. Their agreement was this: if, with their bodily safety and integrity preserved by whatever means, and with the law of their ancestral rights retained, they could satisfy the king, they would humble themselves and surrender; but if not, they would prefer to die innocently in battle for their lives, their homeland, and all that was theirs under this disorderly coercion by the king, rather than imprudently deliver themselves and all their possessions to be intolerably tormented without guilt and, as before, plundered and enslaved by the king and his soldiers [Col. 0361C].

The king, however, had come with another intention: namely, that unless they surrendered themselves into his hands as guilty without any condition whatsoever, he would not accept their satisfaction at all, for the sake of preserving his honor; otherwise he would fight against them until he had subdued, at his pleasure, those whom he had conquered as guilty of rebellion against him.

They, judging the yoke of subjugation to be excessively heavy, or rather altogether most harsh, complained bitterly that it had become unequal and unbearable for their necks, and that they could no longer drag it farther upon their free shoulders.

Finally, after this plan had been shared, not very beneficially, with his counselors and the leading men of the kingdom, the king skillfully arranged his battle lines, fully equipped with weapons, so as to attack them first and unexpectedly [Col. 0361D]. Having cautiously sent before him the dukes of Alemannia [Note: [Col. 0361] Thus in 2.] and Bavaria with their warlike cohorts for the first engagement, as the Alemannic law also prescribes [Note: [Col. 0361] “Note: the Alemannic, that is, Swabian, law, according to which they must always fight in the first line.” Sixteenth-century gloss in 2.], he prudently stationed himself behind them with his chosen men, intending to provide support and assistance.

When the Saxons suddenly saw the attack of the warlike enemy, they were stunned and not unjustly terrified. although there was neither place nor time left for them to arm themselves by deliberation and arrange their lines for battle in the customary manner, they nevertheless took up arms in disorder and tumult in every way, as the fleeting moment allowed, and resolutely awaited the enemy [Col. 0362A].

The battle, boldly begun by our men, continued for some time with the two sides fiercely mingled against one another. At last the Saxons, unable to endure any longer the force and attack of the combatants, who were entirely equipped for battle, took flight. The pursuers cruelly followed them for nearly two miles, aided thereafter on both flanks by Duke Gotifridus and the Duke of the Bohemians [Col. 0362B] [Note: [Col. 0362D] Wratislaus.].

Nearly eight thousand of the Saxons fell. Many more were wounded and scarcely escaped by flight. Our men at last obtained a bloody victory; more than fifteen hundred of them were killed [Note: [Col. 0361] 2 has “a thousand.”]. After overrunning that homeland and devastating much of it with fires and plunder, they returned home, their cause unfinished and the king somewhat offended.

Otto, formerly duke [Note: [Col. 0362D] Of Bavaria; and Magnus of Saxony.], and Duke Magnus, together with the other leading Saxons, continued stubbornly in the same rebellion and resistance as before, even after the flight.

Then, therefore, in the autumn, the king, having once again gathered forces everywhere and hired military support from all quarters with rewards, equipped with no small army, undertook to subdue the remnants of the Saxons and make them subject to his will. By threatening speech at once and by promises, he approached them with considerable craft and importunity. He declared that henceforth and thereafter he would prove himself pious and truly gentle, reconciling, generous, and a most just judge and ruler toward all who obeyed him, respecting their ancestral laws and rights; and, as they say, he protested this very flatteringly under oath. But if, on the contrary, such rebels did not yield to these words, he persistently threatened, with sufficient menace and terror, that for as long as he lived they would find and endure him harsh, accusatory, wholly troublesome, an enemy even unto their destruction, and an exceedingly fierce plunderer.

After these and similar threats and promises had been most cunningly spread individually in both directions through smooth-tongued, enticing, and corrupting intermediaries, they eventually became excessively credulous and confident toward the king, who seemed to feign penitential grief on account of all the injuries he had inflicted upon them. This was especially so because, in addition to these matters, as they say, he had secretly sworn to them most solemnly on his side—above all, the security of their lives, which they most earnestly desired; an inviolable pact of peace and unfeigned fidelity; and complete freedom for their ancestral rights and laws—provided only that they did not hesitate to come to submission to him openly without any condition, honoring him in this matter.

Finally, after many such assertions and promises, so like truth and good faith, they expected nothing less than deceit or treachery. At the presumptuous urging especially of the bishops of Mainz and Augsburg, as well as of Duke Gotifrid and the others, who would have shrunk from engaging them in war unless compelled by the greatest necessity, they joined the king according to the terms of the promises and came together for surrender.

But soon, at the evil counsel of his whisperers, alas, he treacherously conspired against them. He ordered that they be dispersed among various garrisons and places of custody and that, with the pledge of his promises entirely set aside, they all alike be taken captive—since he was exceedingly eager to avenge more harshly the injuries of their rebellion. He himself thereafter, by a kind of royal right, invaded the possessions of some of them; and all the castles that he had previously seized for himself by plunder throughout Saxony he again, imperiously, occupied by placing his garrisons in them, without even a murmur from anyone.  
[Note: thus 2.]

Herimann, called bishop of Bamberg, was deposed from the clerical order and the episcopate by Pope Gregory on account of the heresy of simony, and was excommunicated. Having soon been reconciled by the apostolic authority through a feigned conversion, he sought the monastery of Suarza and professed there that he would become a monk. In his place the king soon installed a certain Roupertus, prelate of the provostship of Goslar and of many other establishments, an intimate associate of Herimann’s consecration, and almost universally disliked by clergy and people; and shortly afterward, on the feast of Saint Andrew, he was ordained by the bishop of Mainz at the king’s command.  
[Note: Compare Bernold, *Opusculum* I.2, p. 207; X.2, p. 379; XII.6, p. 395. See Gregory VII, *Register* III.1, to the people of Bamberg; III.2, to Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz; III.3, to King Henry.]

At the same time Anno, a faithful and prudent minister of Christ Jesus, archbishop of Cologne, who was exceedingly cheerful and a very generous distributor among Christ’s poor of the goods entrusted to him, and an industrious and lavish founder and provider for five new churches, after he had stored up in the heavenly treasury everything temporal that he seemed to possess, was himself brought thither through the efficacy of a blessed consummation, to be set over many things in the joy of his Lord and rewarded with never-failing prizes. Most blessed—would that it were so!—he entered there. Buried at the monastery of Siegburg, he had truly shone there as a most holy man through many miracles.

In his place a certain Hildulf, a canon of Goslar, himself a servant of the king, was installed only with difficulty by royal authority, despite the protests of clergy and people; he was ordained simoniacally, but at the next Roman synod was to be deposed on that account and for disobedience.  
[Col. 0363D Note: Compare Bernold, *Opusculum* I.2, p. 207; X.2, p. 379; XII.6, p. 395. See Gregory VII, *Register* III.1, to the people of Bamberg; III.2, to Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz; III.3, to King Henry.]

At the same time, in the summer, the lord pope, after so many of his promises and commands had been despised, still attempting the matter with apostolic gentleness, sent admonitory letters to the king, so that, by reflecting, he might remember what he had promised and to whom; that he might not obstinately set himself up as a falsifier or an offender, in contempt of and injury to God and apostolic dignity; and that he might not, as a contumacious and incorrigible man, nullify God, who had exalted him above others with such honor. Rather, he should always attend to this with the utmost prudence: “He resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”  
[Note: “Apostolic gentleness … gives grace,” Gregory VII’s letter to the Germans, Mansi, vol. XX, p. 375.]  
[Note: Books III, letters 7 and 10, and Book IV, letter 1; and, from the previous year, Book II, letters 30 and 31. USS.]

But for the victory which he had gained so magnificently, he did not, as he ought, offer the greatest thanks to God, who had enabled him to conquer and triumph. Rather, he continually attended wholly to how he himself, in his own judgment, might be pleased and delighted. The admonitions of apostolic mildness, by which the pope had repeatedly urged him toward a better life—rebuking, entreating, and reproving him—he pretended to accept as exceedingly welcome; but in practice, and by aggravating his error, he utterly trampled them underfoot.  
[Note: “But the admonitions … let it be his concern,” Gregory’s letter to the Germans, Mansi, vol. XX, p. 378.]

Several times he also sent the pope devout greetings and letters of apology, confessing and complaining sufficiently that he was hindered, first by his age, which was fleeting and fragile, and then because those in whose hands the court lay had often given him bad advice and counsel.  
[Note: See Henry’s letter among the Gregorian letters, after letter I.29. USS.] Several times he also sent him letters full of supplication and every form of humility, in which he professed himself greatly culpable and criminal before God and blessed Peter. He further offered prayers that whatever, through his fault, had been corrupted in ecclesiastical affairs against canonical justice and the decrees of the holy Fathers might be corrected by the pope’s apostolic foresight and authority, and that in this matter he would effectively find Henry’s obedience, counsel, and assistance not lacking.  
[Note: “Supplicants and full of every … assistance,” Gregory’s letter to the Germans, Book I.]

Now, however, he contumaciously regarded as worthless all these promises of correction—of himself and of so many churches—which he had so often made to the lord pope in so many ways through legates and letters. He presumptuously associated with his counselors and familiar companions, who had been excommunicated at the next Roman synod, and, as he had long been accustomed to do, did not cease to confuse and plunder the churches of God.  
[Note: Gregory’s letter to the Germans, Book I.]

When the lord pope learned these things and saw himself treated with such open contempt, he nevertheless resolved to attempt his hardened spirit once more. He sent back to him three religious men, his own faithful servants—two of whom he had already sent to him at Rome, as being more familiar with him—to address him still more familiarly and, according to evangelical teaching, to win him over. They were to recall him by the persuasive and secret promptings of friends, as well as by the flattering speech of friendly and sincere freedom, and urge him back toward worthy repentance for his crimes. They were also to set before him, by recounting them in part, matters that were horrible to say but nevertheless widely known, so that “every word might stand on the testimony of these three men.” Through them he also made it unmistakably known that if he would not listen to them speaking with him privately, his crimes would be disclosed to the Church in due order; but if he would not listen to the Church, the pope himself would separate him entirely from its members as a pagan and a publican.

They reached the king at Goslar around the Nativity of the Lord and, in accordance with what had been imposed upon them under obedience, carried out their mission with great caution, though not without the greatest danger to their lives. He received them without good temper. What they had spoken secretly into his ear he immediately had publicly recounted before his counselors, inflamed by no slight anger and indignation, complaining of it—so it is reported—with the intention that they should try all the more vigorously to defend not only his cause but their own. Soon afterward, contrary to what the apostolic lord had especially forbidden him, he deliberately and obstinately communicated with those who had then been excommunicated. He paid no attention to the tolerance of that fatherly charity and patience by which the pope had entrusted to him through these men, with the utmost fidelity, that he would embrace his salvation and honor within the bosom of holy Church if he repented. Nor did he fear the threatening sword of the pope’s severity, which he had likewise most unanswerably brandished against him if he persisted in his customary error and disobedience.

At the same time, in the autumn, the monastery of Hirsau, which had once been established with sufficient regularity, as is said, under King Pippin by a certain noble and religious senator named Erlefred, but had long since been destroyed and plundered through the invasion of his successors, had already for some time been restored by Count Adalbert, his wife Wieldruda, and their sons, who were of one mind in this matter. Now, under a testamentary grant and a full charter of royal liberty, it was transferred in every respect to the Lord God, Saint Peter, Saint Aurelius, and Saint Benedict.  
[Note: In fact, under Emperor Louis the Pious, in the year 830, when Count Erlafrid of Calw laid the monastery’s first foundations. See *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 267. USS.]  
[Note: *libertati*, “to liberty,” 2.]

Thus, wholly released from their proprietary dominion, they emancipated it entirely and freely, according to the customary renunciatory testimony of Alemannic law, before many witnesses at that same place and on the very feast day of Saint Aurelius. They confirmed it lawfully for the service of God, placing it under the free authority and care of Abbot Willihelmus and his successors, and assigning it for the necessary support of the brothers who would live there under the monastic rule.  
[Note: This donation was made at Hirsau in 1075, in the thirteenth indiction, on Tuesday, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October; the confirmation of Henry IV was on the seventh day before the Ides of October. Belsoldus presents the charter in *Documents of the Monasteries of Württemberg*, vol. I, p. 318, and the bull of Gregory VII on p. 333. USS.]

For the decrees of this most free foundation were to be strengthened by a privilege of apostolic authority. When Abbot Willihelmus of that place soon reached Rome and successfully accomplished before Pope Gregory what he had gone out to accomplish according to his wish, he was preparing to return home when he was immediately attacked by that most severe illness which the Greeks call *atrophia*, that is, “cessation of nourishment.” It results from a diminution and wasting of the flesh, arising from certain hidden natural causes and gradually recovering.

Moreover, weakened by wandering fevers, dysentery, hemorrhoids—that is, a flow of blood—and also greatly swollen by a certain tumor of the groin, he was afflicted by all these conditions together for approximately five months and was utterly despaired of even by the physicians; but he was not alone among his own people in suffering miserably. At last, when the time of mercy arrived through God Almighty, the physician’s compassion, he was anointed by the brothers with sacred oil and absolved from his sins, and the prayer of faith saved the sick man. Thus, soon recovering, he scarcely returned to his cell with the privileges and blessings acquired through apostolic generosity.  
[Note: Heymo’s *Life* contains nearly similar material, no. 4, in Mabillon, sixth century, part II, p. 727. USS.]

Dietwin, bishop of Liège, died, and Heinricus, provost of Verdun, succeeded him.

## 1076

King Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar, among Saxons who, though not a little hostile to him and not at all loyal, had been crushed by the savage and injurious animosity of his royal power.

Pope Gregory, as a good shepherd should, most diligently fortified Christ’s fold, watchful on every side against the wolf’s fury. He endured not only elsewhere but also in Rome itself certain antichristian adversaries and plotters on account of justice. Among them was a certain man named Quintius, a sacrilegious robber and criminal plunderer, a mad and sacrilegious despiser of all the sacred things of God.  
[Note: *Quintius*, thus in witness 2.] Rising against him on the most sacred night of the Nativity of the Lord, while he was celebrating Mass at Saint Mary Major, Quintius furiously burst into the church with a mad band of armed men. Before the pope had finished the Eucharistic service after the postcommunion prayer, Quintius dragged him wounded away from the altar, seized him, and, with the greatest disgrace, carried him like a sacrilegious robber into his own tower, where he imprisoned and cruelly confined him.  
[Note: *irrumpit*, “he burst in,” 1* USS.]

There, for a long time, with a sword furiously drawn over the pope’s neck, grim, threatening, and terrifying in every way, he did not cease trying to extort from him as benefices the treasury and the strongest castles of Saint Peter. But he could accomplish nothing at all. No sooner had this exceedingly lamentable sacrilege become known than the entire city was greatly stirred and wailed throughout the Church. With the greatest fervor of zeal for God they attacked the tower, rescued the lord pope from it—whom they had already thought dead—and destroyed it. In a short time they dispersed everything that belonged to Crescentius. Crescentius, having surrendered himself to the pope as guilty, was scarcely driven away alive from there only through the pope’s intervention; only one man, who had sacrilegiously wounded the pope in the head, was killed there.  
[Note: *Crescentius*, thus in witness 2.] Thus the apostolic lord returned joyfully to the altar and completed the Mass.

Quintius had deceived the pope through his customary folly. For while in his tower he saw the tumult of his fellow citizens and their most ardent zeal for God rising against him, fearing for his own life and that of his men, he confessed his sin to the pope and promised him obedience, worthy repentance, and satisfaction, though with a devotion that was only feigned. Treating all this as utterly worthless, he escaped by night in flight from the city. Thereafter the pope, having granted him a period of reprieve, recalled him to the penance he had imposed. But he not only became an apostate in this matter; he also occupied a certain very strong castle nearby, where he lived by robbery, plunder, and bloodshed. Therefore the pope had him condemned as excommunicated through the bishop of Palestrina. Yet, entirely compliant with the king, he continued to rage in this way for two years, hardened in contempt of God.

Finally, the king, moved by no slight fury after the departure of the aforementioned men and considering it unworthy that he should be reproved or corrected by anyone, did not repent. Rather, with still greater evasion, he rashly and dangerously went mad against what was right. For, after taking ill-fated counsel with his men, he summoned to Worms several bishops and princes of the kingdom, especially those whom he knew to be agreeable to his will.  
[Note: “Unworthy … to be corrected,” Gregory VII, letter to the Germans, Book I, p. 379.]

He compelled nearly all of them to deny the obedience owed to blessed Peter and to Gregory, the prelate of the apostolic see, and, having conspired together for this purpose, to renounce him publicly, each in his own name, written separately, but with the king’s own name placed first.  
[Note: “The obedience due … to renounce,” ibid., p. 380.] He then sent letters of renunciation through two bishops, the bishop of Speyer—Huzmannus—and the bishop of Basel—Burchardus—first into Italy, to the princes and bishops of that region, so that they might be associated with this conspiracy, and then to Rome.

Soon afterward, having held a considerable assembly near Piacenza, they all jointly resolved, not only by words and letters but also by an oath, that the proper obedience should not be shown to the lord pope. They feared greatly that they would be condemned by him for the heresy of simony. Finally, they hurriedly sent letters containing this disobedience through envoys—a certain canon of Parma and a certain servant of the king—to the Roman synod.

There, when the letters and commands had been publicly read before the entire assembly, the disobedience that had been resolved upon was proclaimed to the lord pope, and, on the king’s behalf, he was commanded with considerable menace to descend from the chair over which he presided unworthily. Let those who were present know what tumult, shouting, and disorderly attack upon those envoys arose there. Let it be enough for us to say only this: the apostolic lord, not without great danger to his own body, scarcely snatched them half-alive from the hands of the Romans.  
[Note: “But the Roman pontiff scarcely rescued the envoys from the hands of the Romans … and, silence having been made,” etc., Bernold, *Opusculum* I, p. 220.]  
[Note: *quamquam*, “although,” USS.]

At last, when silence had been made, the lord pope ordered the synodal decrees concerning these matters to be sought out and read aloud. These men, as though standing contumaciously in the midst of the whole Church, had rashly abjured the supreme pontiff and their ruler after God and had not blushed to profess their disobedience in writing under their own names. They did not understand or fear what applied to him and to the other teachers of the Church, namely what Paul says: “Always ready to avenge every disobedience.”

They ought rather to have paid closer attention to what Pope Saint Sylvester had already decreed irrefragably in a Roman synod: “No one shall judge the first see, because all sees desire to be regulated by the justice of the first see; nor shall he be judged by all the clergy or by all the people.”  
[Note: “Saint Sylvester … shall be judged,” Bernold, *Opusculum* I.3, p. 218.]  
[Note: Learned scholars have long agreed that this synod, and therefore the decree attributed to Pope Sylvester, is fictitious. See Bernold, *Opusculum* I, letter 3, no. 9, where the matter is treated more fully. USS.]

They ought also to have remembered the decree of blessed Pope Gregory: “We decree that kings fall from their dignities and be deprived of participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ if they presume to despise the commands of the apostolic see.” And many other statements of this kind.  
[Note: The same is read in Bernold, *Opusculum* VI.9, p. 361. This decree is drawn from Saint Gregory the Great’s letter 8 (book XIII of the new edition of his works, vol. II, p. 1223), to Abbot Senator; Gregory VII also appeals to it in writing on this matter to Hermann of Metz. USS.]

Therefore a synodal sentence was pronounced there, attested by the authority of divine and human laws: King Henry was not only to be excommunicated but also deprived of the honor of the kingdom without hope of restoration, so that he might remain in the company of the excommunicated, with whom he preferred to have a part rather than with Christ.

First, he had stubbornly refused to abstain from the communion of those who had been excommunicated for sacrilege and the crime of simony. Second, as a public despiser of God, he had refused not only to undertake penance for his criminal acts but even to promise it, never fulfilling what he had already promised to the apostolic legates. Moreover, in obstinate and public disobedience, he had not feared to resist the apostolic see contumaciously and thus to divide and scandalize the body of Christ, that is, the unity of holy Church.

For these crimes, therefore, by synodal judgment the apostolic lord excommunicated him, as well as all who knowingly and willingly persisted as guilty participants in that disobedience, and all great and small who deliberately consented to him in this matter. He permanently separated them from the members of the Church until worthy satisfaction, so that those whom gentleness could not recall, severity might, by God’s mercy, restore to the way of salvation.  
[Note: “First … should recall him,” ibid., p. 380.]

The empress Agnes, the king’s mother, was present at all these proceedings. The sword of his condemnation had wounded her soul not a little.

During these synodal days Duke Gotifrid, a major supporter and instigator of the Worms conspiracy, was returning from it when he was wounded from below by a certain soldier while sitting apart for the requirements of nature, and unhappily died, excommunicated.  
[Note: *Domum*, in witness 1.] His nephew, the son of his sister, and his namesake, acquired from the king his march, which he had scarcely purchased for forty pounds of gold; he was unjustly deprived of the duchy that his uncle had already obtained for himself from the king. The king appointed this nephew’s scarcely two-year-old son to preside over it.  
[Note: Antwerp. This Godfrey was the cousin of the slain man, who later became famous under the name of Bouillon. USS.]  
[Note: Conrad, from whom the king nevertheless took the duchy in 1089 because of his rebellion and granted it to Godfrey. USS.]

Afterward, when the king and his supporters learned of the apostolic anathema, almost all of them contradicted it, affirming that the action had been entirely unjust and not conducted according to canonical procedure, whatever had been done at that time in the Roman synod through such sacrilegious error. They regarded it all as wholly worthless. This was true only of the king’s associates and supporters; those whose minds were sounder did not think so.

Among the latter were certain bishops—the patriarch of Aquileia, the bishop of Salzburg, the bishop of Passau, the bishop of Worms, who was himself driven from his see by the king, and the bishop of Würzburg—as well as nearly all the Saxon bishops; and also Dukes Rudolf, Berhtold, and Welf, together with a considerable part of the other leading men of the kingdom. They unquestionably agreed with the apostolic lord and had refused to take part in the aforementioned conspiracy. Therefore, when later summoned by the king, they avoided him, both because of the anathema and especially because of the confidence they placed in the apostolic lord.  
[Note: *cum* corrected from *tum*, 2.]  
[Note: Namely, “in the apostolic lord”; Ussermann thought *maxime* should be inserted earlier; perhaps it should be omitted.]

The bishop of Paderborn died. Poppo, provost of Bamberg, succeeded him, though not entirely canonically, since he received the episcopate from the king, who had already been anathematized, while remaining in communion with him. Previously, however, the bishop of Utrecht had conditionally accepted the episcopate from the king as a gift for one of his relatives, on the understanding that he would not resist the ordination of the bishop of Cologne, who had entered not through the door but simoniacally, and that he himself would consecrate him. Thus deceived, he did not support the king with his whole heart, as he had earlier.

The king celebrated Easter at Utrecht, having gathered there from every quarter no small number of his supporters in rebellion and disobedience. At that time the church which the bishop had built over a long period with the greatest expense and effort, despised by God and Saint Peter, was wonderfully consumed by a punitive fire.

From there he returned through Lorraine to Worms, intending to hold a conference there with his peers at Pentecost.

Bishop Willihelmus of Utrecht, being somewhat angry with the king, withdrew from him. Returning home, he arranged with the greatest care to be served an extremely sumptuous meal. Thus, at a table where he was entertained for a third day, he was drawn away shamefully and excessively drunken, and, overtaken by sudden and unexpected death, died in great misery, himself unquestionably condemned by the dart of the anathema.  
[Note: *declamavit*, “he proclaimed,” 2.]  
[Note: Compare Gregory, *Register* IV.6, to Henry, bishop of Liège.]

Chounradus, chamberlain of Mainz, a diligent associate of the king and one who had pleased him by the granting of the bishopric, though not canonically, succeeded him.

The conference which the king had arranged to take place at Worms was convened, as they say, with the intention that the pope should there be prejudged, as it were canonically, by three bishops who seemed senior above the others, accused of the crimes charged against him, and condemned, so that he might somehow be deposed from the apostolic see and another, whom they would find compliant and obedient to the king’s heart, be immediately installed in his place.  
[Note: Omitted in witness 2. USS.]

These three had already been named in the conspiracy, but were delayed by divine predestination so that they would not reach the place. The bishop of Utrecht, as stated above, suddenly died; the bishop of Brescia was captured on the journey itself by Count Hartmann—an exceedingly hostile enemy of Henry—and, already excommunicated by the apostolic lord, was himself sent into custody; only the third, the bishop of Naples, arrived. But no one is condemned according to the command of the law when only one witness speaks against him.

Duke Gotifrid, who had boldly promised the king that he would bring the pope to Rome to be installed there, also, as everyone knows, died excommunicated.

When God had thus dissolved that conference, they assembled again at Mainz on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. There, in order to avenge themselves still more disorderly and to condemn more fully those who had been condemned by their own judges, they rashly excommunicated the apostolic lord through the sacrilegious audacity of their movement, treating him as though he had been judged on the basis of false testimony. They also confirmed, as if by a judicial sentence, that the anathema imposed by the apostolic lord through synodal judgment upon the king and the other participants in his alliance was rash, unjust, and of no weight, and therefore entirely to be trampled underfoot and despised.

They had not carefully considered that they had incurred guilt against apostolic majesty, in accordance with what the decrees of the holy Fathers irrefragably prescribe: whoever presumes to alter or retract the judgment of the apostolic see as though it were reprehensible, and whoever judges anything concerning it after having rejected that judgment, acts unlawfully; for such a thing has never been permitted to anyone.

Therefore Saint Sylvester, in the Roman synod to which 284 bishops, together with 40 presbyters and many deacons, subscribed in the presence of the emperor Constantine Augustus and his mother, Saint Helena, decreed as follows: “No one shall judge the first see,” and the rest, as set out above.  
[Note: *papa* is added in 1*.]  
[Note: *decretum* corrected to *decrevit*, 2.]

And blessed Pope Gelasius, in chapter 2 of his decrees, says: “The whole Church throughout the world knows that the holy Roman Church has the right to judge concerning every church, and that no one may judge concerning its judgment. For an appeal must be made to it from every part of the world, but no one is permitted to appeal from it. Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see has the power, without any preceding synod, to absolve those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and, without any synod existing, to condemn those who ought to be condemned. The most holy pontiffs Callistus, Fabianus, Xistus, Julius, and countless others all bear witness to this. They embraced the truth so completely that they resolved rather to die than to lie. In this, they acted for the sake of their primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter received through the word of the Lord and has always held and will always hold.”  
[Note: “Blessed Pope Gelasius … and will always hold” is found twice in Bernold, *Opusculum* I.4–5, p. 216, and *Opusculum* IV.23, p. 308. The words “Callistus … resolved” are found only in the second place.]

Blessed Pope Adrian follows him in chapter 18 of his decrees: “By a general decree we establish that whoever henceforth believes that the decrees of the Roman pontiffs are to be violated by any king, powerful man, or bishop, or permits them to be violated, shall be subject to an execrable anathema and shall always stand guilty before the Lord as a betrayer of the Catholic faith.”  
[Note: Chapter 80 in the capitularies of Adrian I to Charlemagne, Mansi, *Councils*, vol. VI, col. 1833; Bernold, *Opusculum* I.6, p. 361. USS.]  
[Note: XIII, 1*.]  
[Note: The edition reads: “henceforth the censure of the canons, in whatever matter,” etc. USS.]

No less should this be feared: Saint Leo decreed in his own decrees with exceedingly terrifying force: “Let everyone who strives through disobedience to nullify our definitions be struck by anathema; and let him who contumaciously contradicts our most salutary statutes be separated from the members of the Church for all time.”  
[Note: He seems to refer to chapter 5 of letter 1, to the bishops of Campania, Mansi, *Councils*, vol. III, col. 1294. USS.]

Therefore, whoever had come to doubt the judgment of the apostolic see ought to have debated it with the apostolic lord himself rather than with others; without him, what had been judged by him could in no way be retracted or changed. It is our duty to obey the apostolic ordinances without any hesitation and to avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, which generate quarrels and contribute greatly to the subversion of those who hear them. It is the duty of the apostolic lord to support his judgments by reason if anything in them should appear doubtful to anyone.

A different discussion was in fact being carried on among the members of the synod concerning this same excommunication of the king throughout the whole kingdom without interruption: whether it had been done justly or unjustly. Nevertheless, this was chiefly among contentious men, who had tried to serve not the truth but their contentions. For either they were ignorant, or deliberately pretended not to know, that two judicial procedures are gathered from the sacred Scriptures.[Note: [Col. 0372D] The same material, with a few changes, appears in Bernard, *Opusculum* I, 1, p. 187.]

The first applies to doubtful matters, where delays—of the sort over which they now argued most vehemently, claiming and asserting that they had not been granted—are necessary for obtaining witnesses and defenders. The second applies to public crimes, in which no delays are read as being granted, since, without accuser and witness, a judicial punishment is to be pronounced without delay against the contumacious and disobedient.

In doubtful cases, even when the matters are true but have not yet been made public, voluntarily confessed, or openly proved, delays must necessarily be granted for inquiry or proof,[Note: [Col. 0372D] “In doubtful cases … many things arise” is found in Bernold, *Opusculum* IV, 22, p. 306, except for the words “or voluntarily … to be proved.” Much the same material recurs in *Opusculum* I, 1, p. 187.] so that, in accordance with the decrees of the apostolic men, Pope Felix, Julius, and the others, the accused person may fully prepare himself against his accusers to clear himself of the charges brought against him. Hence also the blessed Eleutherius, the twelfth pope after blessed Peter, testifies in his decrees, chapter 1:[Note: [Col. 0373D] Labbé, *Concilia*, vol. I, col. 589. USS.] “Delays,” he says, “of no little length must be granted for inquiry, lest anything appear to be done precipitately by either party, because many things arise through surreptitious action.”

Therefore Saint Ambrose also testifies in his exposition of the Epistle to the Corinthians:[Note: [Col. 0373D] See the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose, vol. II, p. 127, to which this exposition is wrongly attributed. USS.] “It is not,” he says, “the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser; for the Lord likewise, although Judas was a thief, did not cast him out when he had not been accused”—and the same rule applies in all doubtful cases.

For this reason the Lord himself also gave us an example, so that we would not readily believe indiscriminately what we had heard but what had not been proved or examined. When he went toward Sodom in the likeness of angels, he said to Abraham: “I will go down and see whether they have actually done according to the outcry that has come before me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” But after he had proved true the outcry that he had, as it were, heard, immediately, without delay, the most present avenging rain of fire and sulfur rained down upon it from heaven from the Lord.

Those, however, who do not deny their own guilt—already long ago definitively condemned by the holy Fathers—but openly, as obstinate despisers, attempt by some means to defend themselves against the apostolic statutes, are most justly condemned without delays. Therefore witnesses need not be sought for a manifest case known to very many.

Hence the Apostle ordered that that fornicator among the Corinthians be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren, once everyone had learned what he had done:[Note: [Col. 0373D] “Therefore the Apostle … he had done,” with the order changed, is to be read in Bernold, *Opusculum* I, 2, p. 193. “Having learned … to be expelled,” [Col. 0374D] “everyone … could” are Ambrose’s words.] “You are puffed up,” he says, “and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be removed from your midst.” For they all knew his crime and did not rebuke him. He publicly kept his stepmother in the place of a wife; in this matter there was no need either of witnesses or of inquiry, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion. Therefore the Apostle did not postpone judgment against him: “Though absent in body,” he says, “but present in spirit”—whose authority, of course, is nowhere lacking—“I have already judged, as though present, the man who has done this deed.”

Thus the whole body of Scripture supports the judgments of the lord apostolic. Therefore their contradictors and perverters can very easily be convicted. [Col. 0373D] For he in no respect departed from the footsteps of the holy Fathers. In vain, then, certain contentious men muttered[Note: [Col. 0373] Thus in manuscript 2.] because delays had not been granted to the king and his accomplices, and because he immediately excommunicated them, after their crimes—so contumaciously publicized, so utterly despised, and so obstinately defended—had miserably defiled the holy Church, and after they had professed with excessive temerity, in no place other than the Roman synod, and there publicly in writing and by name, their disobedience, moreover, amid so many acts that were universally known.[Note: [Col. 0373] “Excessive” in manuscript 2.]

In the excommunication itself,[Note: [Col. 0374D] The author borrowed these words from the actual formula of excommunication; see Mansi XX, 469.] the lord apostolic, on behalf and in the name of the almighty Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority of Saint Peter, ordered all Christians that no one should thereafter obey or serve the excommunicated king as king in any way, or keep an oath that he had made or might make.

A considerable portion of the kingdom’s princes, taking this into account, repeatedly refused to come to him when summoned by the king,[Col. 0374B] laboring most diligently to possess the zeal of God according to knowledge. Although they knew that he had been excommunicated unjustly and uncanonically, nevertheless, according to the statute of the Council of Sardica,[Note: [Col. 0374D] Canon 17 of Dionysius, in Labbé, *Concilia*, vol. II, p. 649. USS.] they absolutely ought not to communicate with him unless they knew that he had been reconciled.

Therefore, fearing to communicate with the king while he remained hardened—for they could neither rebuke, punish, nor correct him—they strove, as was proper, to avoid him, since they abhorred consenting to him. For this reason, in the autumn, the leading men of the kingdom arranged to hold a conference with him at Parthenopolis concerning this matter, so that by common counsel they might determine what ought to be done concerning so great an affair, and where, once the king and their lord had been admonished, turned to repentance, and reconciled, they might lawfully serve him.[Note: [Col. 0373] The word is absent in manuscript 2; manuscript 1, 1* reads “Parthenopolim [is] Magdeburg.”]

After they had gathered there with no small military forces, the king, together with his flatterers, took up position on this side of the Rhine, at the village of Oppenheim, with a considerable group of his confederates,[Note: [Col. 0373] Thus in manuscript 2; “beyond” seems preferable; USS printed “near.”] threatening and emboldened by their exhortation and persuasion. The chief men of the kingdom who lived on this side of the Rhine discussed matters among themselves, and, with God as their giver, each one attentively conferred with the others concerning what ought to be determined by them about so monstrous a case.

Legates of the Apostolic See arrived there bearing letters appropriate to this case. In them the pope also imposed upon the bishop of Passau, to whom he had long before granted apostolic authority in his place, the task of canonically reconciling all who came—apart from the king alone—to a worthy satisfaction and repentance, namely, those who thereafter wished to stand on the side of Saint Peter.

Among these were the archbishop of Mainz with his troops; the bishops of Trier, Strasbourg, Verdun, Liège, Münster, the bishop-elect of Utrecht, Speyer, Basel, and the bishop of Constance, at Ulm;[Col. 0375A] these bishops,[Note: [Col. 0375] Hansiz, in the cited passage, reads “at Ulm”; nevertheless, it is clear from the manuscripts that “at Ulm” must be read, as in Bernold’s *Apology for Gebhard, Bishop of Constance* (*Opusculum* X, 4, p. 380), where Otto is said to have been restored to communion at Ulm. USS.] There were also many abbots, as well as a considerable crowd of high and lesser-ranking men,[Note: [Col. 0375] Manuscript 1* erased the words and the abbreviations “and abbots, etc., and no small number of greater and lesser men” a second time, and then continues as follows: “Trent or Trident, Cologne or Agrippina or Köln, likewise Metz or Mettis, Toul or Tull, Vence or Veins, Lausanne or Losanna, Freising or Frisingen, and many abbots, as well as a considerable crowd of high and lesser-ranking men, etc.”] who were reconciled and received into communion there, whether because of the guilt of communicating with the king, or because they themselves had been excommunicated for disobedience, or because they had accepted the masses and offices of priests condemned for sexual misconduct or simoniacal heresy.

Finally, after ten days had been spent in such deliberations, when the king saw and heard that so many and such important men had humbly yielded to apostolic authority, and that they had resolved to establish another king in his place, he too—although unwilling and reluctant, and scarcely possessing enough spirit to endure the pain—pretended that he had yielded, though only with great difficulty,[Note: [Col. 0375] “Although falsely,” USS.] not only to the pope but also to the princes of the kingdom in everything that they wished to impose upon him and require him to observe.

Then, among other things, they decided that first the bishop of Worms should have his see and city restored to him; that the queen should depart from there with all her followers; that the hostages of the Saxons should be returned to them; that the king should separate himself entirely from his excommunicated associates; and that he should immediately send a letter to Pope Gregory, firmly declaring that he would maintain due obedience, satisfaction, and worthy repentance. Meanwhile, he himself was to remain there according to their advice, awaiting the apostolic response and his reconciliation.

The king carried out these and all the other instructions immediately, although not with complete sincerity. Thereafter he sent to Rome, through the bishop of Trier, letters composed as they had agreed among themselves and sealed in their presence,[Col. 0375C] although he later secretly altered them and changed them at his own pleasure.

The leading men of the kingdom, fearing the king’s deceptions and the customary folly of his counselors, which they had so often experienced, also hastily sent to Rome their own envoys of good reputation, who had been present at everything done there, lest the pope be deceived by their tricks. They earnestly implored him, by the mercy of God, to deign to come to these regions to settle this dissension.

Moreover, so that they might bind the king more firmly to obedience to the Apostolic See, before they separated from one another they swore that, if he remained excommunicated through his own fault beyond a year, they would no longer have him as king. Then, fearing the future vengeance and injury of the king against them—for many of them had left him unseen, unsaluted, and greatly angered against them—they gave one another a pledge of mutual assistance if anything adverse should befall them on this account, and each returned proudly to his own territory.[Note: [Col. 0375] “They glory” in manuscript 2.]

When this conference ended around the Kalends of November, immediately, contrary to what was usual, an exceptionally heavy snow began to overwhelm the lands everywhere. This indeed, as a portent and sign of future evils, astonished not only the regions on this side of the Alps but also—what seemed even more remarkable—the whole of Lombardy with unprecedented excess.

For through the extreme freezing caused by the cold, the Rhine and the Po alike, to say nothing of the other rivers, became so solidly frozen that for a long time they presented themselves to all travelers as an icy road, as though across land. Thus a harsh, snowy winter, prolonged by the force of the frost, continued until the Ides of March—that is, from the conference just mentioned until the conference held at Forchheim by the leading men of the kingdom. On that very day the snow began gradually to diminish throughout all the regions of our lands,[Col. 0376B] melting in streams of varying character according to the nature of each place.

After the aforementioned conference at Oppenheim had passed, the king remained for some time at Speyer with the guardians and administrators assigned to him by the leading men of the kingdom, living for a while as penitents do. Thereafter, suspecting that, because of the aforesaid oath of the princes, their treachery and the crafty schemes by which they sought to undermine him were being directed against him, he gathered his counselors from everywhere, recklessly postponed the assembly of his leading men, and, so that he would not be deprived of the kingdom, guarded himself with every resource and the utmost vigilance, carefully combining all manner of investigations and counsels of his supporters.

The bishop of Toul, and likewise the bishop of Noyon,[Col. 0376C] soon arrived at Rome with many others, to whom this had been imposed by the bishop of Passau as an act of obedience. They presented themselves to the pope as guilty, with due satisfaction and obedience. He canonically reconciled them, but, testing their obedience for some time, had them alone confined in certain monastic prisons. They were scarcely brought out from there through the intervention of the empress and were permitted to return home, without any formal authorization,[Note: [Col. 0375] The edition lacks “not.”] solely by the pope’s permission to receive communion.

Immediately afterward the archbishop of Trier followed them with extreme haste, carrying letters from the royal embassy. He greeted the pope and presented him with the altered letters. The pope was unwilling to have them read except in the presence of the kingdom’s leading men, so that they might be present as witnesses to the reading,[Col. 0376D] since they had also been present and knowledgeable at their composition and dispatch.

When they had therefore been read, the envoys, recognizing that they contained material entirely different from what had been composed and sealed in the presence of the kingdom’s leading men, freely protested before the Lord God that they were not the same letters but altered ones, changed in various places.

Thus the archbishop of Trier, although at first he had begun to defend the letters, was finally convicted by them and reminded of the facts. He publicly confessed that the fraud was not his but that of someone else whose identity he did not know. In this way the lord apostolic, together with the empress, had diligently detected all the king’s fabrications—full of pretense and deception—concerning the obedience that the lying letter, rather than the truth of his heart, had represented.

Therefore, although the king had earnestly requested permission to come to Rome to be reconciled to the pope, the pope was entirely unwilling to agree. Instead, by apostolic authority he ordered the king to meet him at Augsburg, in the presence of the kingdom’s leading men, so that he might be heard and reconciled by him there. Through envoys of both parties he sent them the firmest assurance that, if the Lord willed, he would come to them around the feast of the *Ypapanti*,[Note: [Col. 0377D] That is, the Purification of Saint Mary.] and he repeated this promise with great certainty.[Col. 0377B]

After receiving letters of apostolic blessing—in which the pope had carefully and appropriately warned them concerning their duchy, their other necessities, and peace—they happily returned to their homeland, proclaiming the arrival of so great a guest.

Then all the leading men of the kingdom, joyfully receiving the contents of the letters as they had become known, prepared themselves with all the eagerness of their minds to observe these instructions in every respect, and were greatly encouraged by no small hope of restoring ecclesiastical religion and observance.

The king, however, whose mind was set upon an entirely different purpose, having learned the pope’s plan, devised with the greatest deliberative skill how he might meet him before he entered our regions.[Col. 0377C] He proposed either to frighten him into flight by collecting money, hiring troops by whatever means, and assembling the greatest possible military force of his followers; or, by corrupting the Romans and his other counselors with such great gifts and thereby making them his inseparable attendants, to force him to act according to his wishes.

If, however, those men, so treacherous and savage, resisted him so fiercely that they immediately drove him from the chair after inflicting injury upon him and substituted another in his place according to the king’s desire, then he would return gloriously to his homeland with his wife, having been elected and appointed emperor by that man. But if the king could make the pope, overcome by fear, threats, and the flattery of the Romans, entirely compliant with him, he foolishly anticipated that the pope would thereafter be gracious to him but most severe toward his adversaries.

Warned and encouraged by these and many other follies of his counselors, as rumor had it, he obstinately rose against the correction already determined by the leading men of the kingdom and against the recovery of Christian religion. He did not cease to oppress their authority by whatever means he could and to free himself entirely from them at his own pleasure.[Col. 0378A]

At that time a certain margrave named Opertus arrived from Lombardy and encouraged him above all others with the greatest zeal. Magnificently rewarded and honored by the king for this very reason, he was overtaken by sudden death while returning near Augsburg. He fell from his horse, and thus, although he had already regarded the apostolic anathema as worthless, he learned by experience how great its weight was. In this way that wretched man perished most damnably.

## 1077

The king celebrated Christmas at Besançon in Burgundy as best he could, staying there scarcely a single day. From there, taking his wife and son, along with his entire retinue and equipment, as had already been decided, he crossed the Rhône at Geneva and, scarcely climbing and crawling over the Alps by an exceedingly difficult route, entered Lombardy in haste through the diocese of Turin.[Note: [Col. 0377] “Turinese” in manuscript 2.]

After gathering from every direction as many men as he could, he reached Pavia and also drew to himself from everywhere a crowd of excommunicated bishops. As though he intended somehow to strengthen their case by the protection of his majesty, he announced to them, with considerable artifice, that he would address the pope not merely on his own behalf but rather on theirs, so as to inquire from him about the sentence of so injurious an anathema.

They, on the other hand, strongly dissuaded the king from even naming him “apostolic,” since they had utterly rejected him at the king’s command as one who had been so solemnly abjured, and since they had rightly condemned him together with the others and would perpetually cut him off from the body of the Church under the censure of anathema.

Nevertheless, lest he, the pseudo-king, rashly annul altogether the decision of the Teutonic princes and thereby justly incur their displeasure—for that unavoidable necessity constrained him—they considered it proper for him to yield and submit for a time. Thereafter, following this dispensation and this address to him, which was so necessary for his own purposes, he should work with all his strength and utmost diligence together with them to determine how he might completely free himself and the whole kingdom from such a sacrilegious man.

Otherwise, they thought, he could not fail to recognize that, because of the madness and majesty of that most crafty abuse of the sacred apostolic name and of that heretical usurpation, he himself would undoubtedly be deprived of the kingdom, his honor, and partly even his life; nor could he doubt that all who were always prepared to go with him, undefeated, into death and destruction would likewise perish and be condemned.[Col. 0378D]

After the king’s envoys and those of the kingdom’s leading men, dismissed by the pope, began to return home,[Note: [Col. 0378D] Compare Gregory VII’s letter to the Germans, *Register* IV, 12.] he himself, most ready to give his life for his sheep, hurried to the place and time that they had mutually agreed upon,[Col. 0379A] and there eagerly awaited the guides for his journey, as he desired.

But in vain. For when the Teutonic princes learned of the king’s unexpected and furtive flight across the Alps, fearing greatly his plots and attacks, they entirely ceased—even against their will and reluctance—from going to meet the pope or providing him with the agreed escort. Thus the pope waited for them for some time at the castle of Canossa.

But when they scarcely managed to send him word that, because of so many dangers standing in the way, they could not come to him at all, he was greatly distressed that he had come there in vain. Nevertheless, he did not despair that, out of necessity and for the sake of the holy Church, he might somehow reach the Teutonic regions later, and therefore decided to remain there for some time on this account.

At that time he also considered that the king’s journey and the activities of his counselors had not greatly benefited either himself or the holy Church. For the king had made the Lombards, whom he found rebellious against God and himself, even more rebellious, and had provocatively stirred up the peoples of the Germans, already divided among themselves by a considerable schism, concerning what they should do with so foolish a man. He had also disturbed the entire kingdom everywhere to no small degree.

Accordingly, as a truly apostolic man ought, he cast all his care upon the Lord. Day and night he persisted in tearful prayers, asking that God himself might inspire him from heaven and direct what ought rightly to be determined and arranged by synodal judgment concerning so great an affair.

At last the king, having accepted sound advice from his followers and entirely abandoned the earlier plan that, in his malicious and foolish zeal, he had devised against the pope, resolved—chiefly through the intervention and assistance of the lady Matilda the marchioness, of his mother-in-law Adelaide, likewise a marchioness, and of the abbot of Cluny,[Note: [Col. 0379D] Hugh, who had lifted the young Henry from the sacred font, as the king himself states in a letter addressed to him, D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 441 of the new edition. USS.] who had also recently come with the pope after being reconciled at Rome because of his communion with the king, as well as through the support of everyone whom he could draw to his side—to approach the pope and submit, yield, obey, and consent to him in every respect.

With this intention, although it was concealed as best he could among the Lombards, he sent messengers ahead to bring to him the interveners named above and then followed them himself little by little to the aforesaid castle.

They, hurrying to meet the king at the appointed place,[Col. 0379D] discussed at length among themselves, in varied conversation, the matter for which they had assembled, and weighed it carefully in every respect through diligent deliberation. But they had detected with very suspicious scrutiny certain deceitful and pretended twists in the promises—though I do not know precisely which ones—which they feared to bring to the pope as simple and entirely truthful statements, since he was truly most experienced in such matters through long practice and daily familiarity.

Nevertheless, immediately, since necessity demanded it, they returned and recounted to the pope in full truth, in sequence, whatever it was that they had judged to be disguised and treacherous.

The king immediately followed close behind them, rushing unexpectedly and precipitately with his excommunicated associates as far as the gate of the castle. Without an apostolic response or an invitation from the pope, he approached in grief and repeatedly knocked, earnestly begging to be allowed to enter.

There he remained outside the castle with his companions, clothed in wool and barefoot,[Note: [Col. 0380D] “Barefoot and clothed in wool.” Letter to the Germans, I, 1.] suffering from the cold, and lodged there until the third day. After being subjected to the strictest examination through many investigations and tests, and found obedient insofar as human judgment could determine, he tearfully awaited the grace of Christian communion and apostolic reconciliation, as is customary among penitents.[Col. 0380B]

The lord apostolic, who was unwilling either to be deceived or to deceive, and who, having so often been misled by the king’s many promises, did not readily believe his words, was brought only with difficulty, after many weighty conferences of deliberation, to agree that he would not refuse to receive him into Christian communion if the king came ready to confirm by oath the conditions of obedience and satisfaction that the pope was then about to impose for the welfare and standing of the holy Church—either by himself or through those whom he would name as witnesses—and if, in addition, he consented to entrust the keeping of this oath, firmly and permanently, to the hands of those interveners who were present, as well as to those of the empress, who had not yet arrived, and to bind this agreement in such a pact.

When the king received this response from the pope, he and all his followers judged the proposed terms extremely harsh. Nevertheless, since he could not be reconciled in any other way, he consented, deeply distressed, whether he wished to or not.

Finally, it was arranged with difficulty before the pope that the king himself should not swear. Two bishops, the bishop of Naples and the bishop of Vercelli, were chosen to swear the oath on his behalf, along with certain other members of his household,[Note: [Col. 0380D] Lambertus lists these men here. USS.] who were likewise to swear thereafter.

To recall the substance of the oath, they swore in this manner: that their lord Henry, whenever Pope Gregory should appoint within the year, would come into harmony and peace with the princes of the kingdom, according to the pope’s judgment or mercy; that neither he nor any of his men would inflict any injury upon the lord pope or his legates when they came into any part of the kingdom for the governance of the Church, whether by imprisonment or mutilation of their limbs; and that, if they were injured by anyone else, he would assist them in good faith as soon as he could.

If any obstacle prevented him from observing the period and delays that the lord pope might establish, he would thereafter hasten to observe them without delay, as soon as he could.

Under this agreement, as stated, the entrance and access to the pope were opened to the king, who was weeping with a great flow of tears, and to the other excommunicated men, who were also weeping greatly.

No one could easily describe how many tears were shed there by both sides: the lord pope, lamentably shaken by grief and weeping intensely for the sheep who had perished and needed to be sought out for God, gave them, as was appropriate after they had humbly prostrated themselves and confessed the obstinacy of their presumption, suitable exhortations toward canonical reconciliation and apostolic consolation. Having thus reconciled them by apostolic indulgence and blessing and restored them to Christian communion,[Col. 0381B] he led them into the church.

After the customary prayer had been made for them, and after he had graciously greeted the king and five bishops with the holy kiss—the bishops of Strasbourg, Bremen, Lausanne, Basel, and Naples—and the other leading men, the pope celebrated Mass. At the time of communion he called the king to himself and offered him the Eucharist,[Note: [Col. 0381D] This appears to have happened, though it was ill-advised: the king could have been bound by some other hidden sin. In this respect he is certainly to be praised, that he publicly declared himself unworthy, whatever the pontiff later decided. USS.] which he had previously forbidden him.

The king declared that he was unworthy to partake of it and departed without receiving communion. From this the apostolic, as though it were an indication of impurity and almost a testimony, revealed by the Spirit, of some hypocrisy hidden within him, prudently inferred something about him, and thereafter presumed not to place complete trust in the king’s words.

Finally, after food had been suitably prepared, they sat together at the same table and conducted themselves honorably with sober fare. Then they rose with thanksgiving and spoke with one another about the few matters beyond what was especially necessary: the obedience promised, the pledge given, the oath not to be violated, perfect repentance, and the need to beware of the anathema against the Lombards.

The king, having received apostolic permission and blessing, departed from there with his followers, except for the bishops whom the pope ordered to be imprisoned there, as he saw fit.

In addition, an oath-pact of a certain kind, which still remained to be discharged by members of the king’s household to the pope, was required of them. They attempted to pervert it through a contentious disagreement, in a manner far different from that in which it had been composed. Fearing that they would quickly be seized by the pope on the charge of perjury, they craftily evaded it by every means, so that they would not swear at all.

Among them, the bishop of Augsburg escaped secretly by night without permission and without having been reconciled. Thus, in the first pact that they had established among themselves, these liars departed after artfully deceiving and misleading the pope.[Note: [Col. 0381D] An absolute accusative is used in place of ablatives.]

Meanwhile, when the apostolic sent two bishops—the bishops of Ostia and Palestrina—to Milan, Pavia, and the other cities of those regions for the needs and governance of the holy Church, and when they were traveling to Piacenza with no little benefit, they were captured by the perjured and excommunicated anti-bishop of Piacenza,[Note: [Col. 0381D] Namely Dionysius, deposed by the pope in 1075 at the Roman synod. The legates were Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and Gerald, bishop of Ostia. See Arnulf, book IV, chapter 13. USS.]

The bishop of Palestrina was released shortly afterward, while the bishop of Ostia was sent imprisoned to a certain castle.[Note: [Col. 0382D] Compare Gregory’s letter to Udo, archbishop of Trier, *Register* V, 7; Mansi XX, p. 242.] While he was held there in chains for some time, and the king strove by every crafty means to pursue the profits of avarice with his followers, the king—although the pope had barely permitted him, on his Lombard journey, to accept from them the necessary service, while canonically requiring him wholly to avoid communion with them—showed the bishop no compassion, not even the slightest aid in a single word, having completely forgotten the oath he had made to assist the apostolic legates.[Col. 0382B]

But when the king wished to be crowned at Pavia according to the rite of the Lombard law,[Note: [Col. 0381] Manuscript 1* reads “royal law.”] and sent interveners to the pope to request permission for this, they received the response that, as long as Peter remained in chains, he would not have the permission of apostolic authority for this matter.

Even so, the king could not extract assistance from him. At last, with the empress and Lady Matilda helping, the bishop was released from prison after having been tested for some time.

At the same period, that Roman Quintius—who, to complete his own condemnation, had also kept the bishop of Como,[Note: [Col. 0381] Manuscript 2 reads “Cumadum.”][Note: [Col. 0382D] Reginald, bishop of Como. USS.] already captured near Saint Peter’s Church in Rome—endeavored to visit the king at Pavia with him and to make himself greatly favored by the king. For he had no doubt that he had earned from the king no small reward in gifts, not only for the bishop’s capture but also for the equally sacrilegious capture of the lord apostolic.

When he had arrived at court, the king, who had cautiously avoided him because of the anathema and did not dare to kiss or greet him as he usually greeted his friends, pretended that he was not yet able to receive him as he deserved and as his services merited, supposedly because of certain very important occupations. Thus he kept postponing the reception of his favored man from day to day.

Quintius, somewhat angered, complained that he was being treated with contempt and mockery, until at last, through his persistence, he extorted from the king a definite postponement of the due greeting and the rewards that were to be brought to him.[Note: [Col. 0381] USS inserts “of the postponement.”]

But on the very night of the appointed day, his throat suddenly being choked by a deadly swelling, he descended with extreme speed to the underworld, condemned to eternal death, without seeing or being greeted by the king.

Thus the king traveled throughout those regions, eagerly scraping together from every direction whatever abundant quantities of gold, silver, and garments he could obtain. During the whole of Lent he sought no further permission, as he ought to have done, from the apostolic, who had already placed the kingdom under interdict. He celebrated Palm Sunday at Verona in a very bold and agitated mood.

There, too, the intimate associate of his faction, the anti-bishop of Vercelli, departed from him. On the road along which he was traveling joyfully, he too was overtaken by sudden death: he immediately fell from the horse he was riding and expired most unhappily in an instant.

After the leading men of the kingdom had learned of the king’s treachery,[Note: [Col. 0383] Manuscript 2 reads “of the kingdom.”] the violation of the pact made at Oppenheim, his flight and simulated reconciliation, and all his crafty schemes throughout Lombardy, they gathered at Ulm after Christmas to deliberate about so great an affair.

Since only a few of them had gathered there, being hindered by the snowy winter and the extreme severity of the cold, they sent letters and envoys to their princes and bishops—the Lotharingians, Saxons, and also Bavarians. They earnestly admonished them, and repeatedly urged and entreated them, by the faith that they had pledged to one another and above all by the mercy of God, to assemble at least on the third day before the Ides of March at Forchheim, and there, after holding a conference and taking prudent counsel, to determine definitively whatever seemed best to them concerning the condition of the kingdom and the Church, with due regard for the necessities of their lives.
