Thereafter, since they were greatly anxious and sought to fortify themselves against every danger from every direction, they also sent to the lord apostolic, who was still staying at Canossa,[Col. 0383C] supplicatory letters full of urgent concerns. They informed him of the conference that had been arranged and of the plan they had resolved upon, and humbly begged him to send them, as was fitting in all their affairs, his counsel, authority, assistance, and letters of this kind,[Note: [Col. 0383] Manuscript 2 reads “daily.”] together with his envoys, as soon as possible.

The apostolic lord, being a man of no small compassion and kindness, had graciously carried this out with every diligent effort, just as they had so greatly desired; and for that same conference he had sent as legates the cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and the abbot of Marseille, Bernard by name in both cases [Note: [Col. 0383D] Both were named Bernard. Reg. IV, 23–24], with letters of admonition. He himself, although considerably saddened by so many and such great scandals and resistances of heretics and schismatics, remained in that same castle until the month of August [Note: [Col. 0383D] Gregory spent a considerable amount of that period at Carpineto [Col. 0384D]. Reg. IV, 23–28]; and from there, since the way to the German regions had not been open to him for settling so many disputes, he returned to his Rome in considerable glory, received with the greatest honor by the Roman citizens who came out to meet him and greeted him reverently.

[Col. 0384A] Duke Rudolf also, with the counsel of the other princes of the kingdom, after he had heard that the king had truly been reconciled, sent a messenger to him, earnestly and graciously beseeching him not to come at all into the German regions before he had sent either the pope or the empress there, so that they might diligently prepare for him a worthy reception and a peaceful welcome. The pope, indeed, when summoned and invited by that same envoy, had shown himself entirely ready to do this, but only after he had received from the king a security of peace and fidelity, confirmed to him by oath. King Henry, however, obstinately disdaining the embassy, did not deign either to provide security for the pope or to carry out the request for his timely advance dispatch.

Finally, on the aforesaid Ides, as had been determined, [Col. 0384B] a large part of the kingdom’s nobles assembled. There, after a conference had been held, they accused the king through very many most lamentable complaints and protests concerning the injustices and injuries inflicted upon themselves, the chief men of the whole kingdom, and the churches [Note: [Col. 0383] “many” in 2]; and because the pope had so strictly forbidden them to obey or serve the king, they deprived him of the dignity of the kingdom and judged him unworthy even of the name of king on account of his unheard-of thousandfold crimes [Note: [Col. 0383] “most lamentable” corrected from the feminine form to the masculine in 2]. Instead, they unanimously resolved to choose and establish another in his place.

When the legates of the apostolic see heard there of such a sacrilegious man, they were not a little astonished that they had endured him over themselves for so long. Nevertheless, they did not conceal what had been entrusted to them; rather, in the hearing of everyone they openly declared the admonition of their legation [Col. 0384C]: if it could in any way be achieved by some device of caution, they should not establish another king for themselves while this one was still being sustained in some fashion for a while longer. Otherwise, since they knew that they themselves had experienced the danger of their necessity much better, they might carry out whatever they judged best for themselves above all else, without opposition from the apostolic lord.

At this point apostolic letters were also read aloud [Note: [Col. 0384D] They are absent from Gregory’s Register]. In them, besides recalling the sequence and knowledge of the Christian communion granted to the king, it was stated that his subjects would have little cause to rejoice over the hope and progress of his repentance [Note: [Col. 0383] “progress” in 2; the editor reads “for progress”], since he had made the Lombards, whom he had found sufficiently disobedient, most disobedient and worse than evil. Therefore, all who had previously been under his hand and scepter were earnestly exhorted and advised by apostolic vigilance that, in order to overcome such necessities successfully, they should commend themselves solely to the Lord God, run daily with ever greater attentiveness and progress in the way and love of justice, and, persevering in it as they ran, deserve to be crowned by God.

Accordingly, placing very great confidence in and drawing strength from God’s grace, [Col. 0385A] the bishops separately and the senatorial order separately deliberated for a long time and at great length about appointing a king. At last, while the entire college of senators and people, eager for change, awaited with the greatest attention the bishops’ first, divine and spiritual vote—as spiritual men—to name and choose a king, Rudolf, duke of Alemannia, was first named and elected king by the bishop of Mainz, and then by the others. The entire senate and people followed them without delay, all legally submitting themselves to him for that same purpose with their customary fidelity to the oath.

This election was truly not heretical, since it was legally carried out with the common vote and acclamation of the entire people in the case of a man who neither desired nor wished it and was compelled. [Col. 0385B] Immediately afterward, having traveled through Bamberg and Würzburg, he reached Mainz in mid-Lent. There the same bishops and the assembly of the whole people acclaimed, anointed, and ordained him as their lawful king, ruler, and defender of the entire Frankish kingdom.

On that very day the citizens of Mainz deliberately began a battle against him. More than a hundred of them fell, while only two on the king’s side were killed; the others were scarcely saved from death by flight and the approach of night. Thus the king’s soldiers gained a remarkable victory and struck such terror into the citizens that at first light they immediately surrendered themselves as guilty to the bishop and their lord [Note: [Col. 0385] “lord” in 1], and, having obtained his favor, scarcely managed to secure the king’s favor as well, with the bishop intervening with everyone he could.

[Col. 0385C] The citizens of Worms also, having gathered not inconsiderable military forces from every direction, conspired in rebellion against the king and their own bishop. Therefore, after passing by that city, the king turned aside to Tribur; proceeding from there through Lorsch and Esslingen, and halting at Ulm on Palm Sunday, he continued as far as Augsburg in Vindelicia, intending to celebrate Easter there. During Easter week he had proposed to discuss and arrange there with his princes many matters necessary for the kingdom and the holy Church. But immediately they began to withdraw from him, each man separately, through the operation of some misfortune—I do not know what. Not only the new soldiers, but also the old, who had long before confirmed their loyalty to him by oath, apostatized, thinking little of perjury.

He had also decided to send leaders, after letters had already been sent from Würzburg to the pope inviting him to deign to come into our regions for the governance of the Church; but at that time he could not carry this out at all because of the shortage of soldiers. He scarcely gathered only three bishops with him: the bishop of Würzburg, the bishop of Worms, and the bishop of Passau.

The fourth, the bishop of Augsburg, most cunning in every ability at his disposal and hard-hearted with adamantine hardness, resisted for two full days with such obstinacy the legates of the apostolic see and their canonical judgments that he could in no way be compelled to obey the pope or the king. At last, although only hypocritically, he was scarcely convicted by everyone and confessed, in the communion of his lord King Henry, that he had sinned. For this reason he was deprived of his priesthood by the apostolic legates and subjected to fitting penance. Yet before they departed, when the king had humbly implored them in every possible way, they granted him his office only for a time.

There, on the holy day of Easter, while the king, all the clergy, and the people were solemnly standing in a considerable procession toward the church of Saint John, the apostolic legates issued and confirmed, not without reason and canonical authority, an order that this usurpation should no longer take place in the church—a practice rashly and presumptuously carried out by certain simpler brothers contrary to the decrees of Pope Clement.

For on Holy Saturday, before the chrism has been poured into the baptismal water, they customarily sprinkle all those standing around with it; and, having received some of it in their own vessels, they use it throughout the entire fifty-day period [Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, until Pentecost. USS.] in this merely usurpatory and disorderly sprinkling. They fail to heed the reasonable and unanswerable statute of Saint Pope Alexander [Note: [Col. 0385D] It is found in the canon *Aqua Sale*, *De consecratione*, distinction 3, from the first decretal letter of that pope, chapter 5, which everyone knows to be spurious. USS.], who commands that on every Sunday an exorcism of salt and water be performed by the priests, and that the people, their workshops, and their places be sprinkled from it.

At that time Lutold, a venerable brother of the same monastery, was appointed abbot over the cells of Saint Gall, having been regularly elected by the brothers [Note: [Col. 0386D] Compare Burchard, *Casus S. Galli*, chapter 7, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS II, p. 156].

After the king had celebrated Easter there with sufficient festivity, he returned through Ulm, entered the Reichenau, and from there reached Constance. The bishop of the city, carefully avoiding both an audience with the legates of the apostolic see and the presence of the royal majesty, withdrew to a certain castle of Count Otto [Note: [Col. 0386D] Of Bregenz and Buchhorn; see Stälin, *Württembergische Geschichte* I, 559], and remained there throughout that entire year. Although the apostolic lord had already completely forbidden him to exercise his office in the previous year, he nevertheless did not refrain from it on that account.

When he rose at Worms from the conspiracy of disobedience that had been written down [Note: [Col. 0385] “aforesaid” in the second witness], he then—as we note as a miracle of deserved divine vengeance—began to limp, and thereafter, weakened, continued to limp [Note: [Col. 0385] “he limps” in 1]. Nevertheless, he received communion, though not the office, from the bishop of Passau before the conference at Oppenheim [Note: [Col. 0385] “Oppenheim” in 2; see below, col. 390].

Although previously he could not in any way be compelled to this for two full years, from that time onward he did not cease to ordain clergy, consecrate churches, and repeatedly exercise the other episcopal rights, rebellious and contrary to law as he was. The apostolic legates, having summoned the college of brothers there, held a chapter with them concerning the flight and disobedience of their bishop, as well as his other rash acts, negligences, and presumptions [Note: [Col. 0387D] Compare Bernold, *Opusculum* X, 4, p. 379, where Otto, bishop of Constance, is treated in nearly the same order].

After granting him a period of delay, they summoned the bishop before them and firmly commanded, by apostolic authority, that no one should receive his office. They had entirely condemned, according to the sentence issued at the Roman synod, the Simoniac heresy and the Nicolaitan heresy [Note: [Col. 0387] “Nicolaitan” in 2] [Note: [Col. 0387D] Compare Bernold’s dispute with Alboin, apparently a canon of Constance, no. III; compare Gregory’s letters to Bishop Otto and to the people of Constance, Mansi XX, pp. 626–627], which reigned beyond measure in that bishopric, over which a very large population was subject.

They had also repeated there, as a special command above all others, that no Christian should receive the offices of clerics condemned for incontinence. When they learned that the judgments of certain priests and the testimony of seven of his fellow brothers concerning the reception of their churches were customarily accepted by that bishop, although they had been shown by the clearest testimony of many laymen to have acquired those churches through simony, they proved beyond contradiction, by canonical reasoning, that such judgments and testimonies could not at all be accepted. If, however, they were accused of any crime other than heresy, they did not reject judgments and testimonies of this kind.

But if any of the clergy was accused of heresy, they reasonably affirmed that the testimony of all Christians possessing the Catholic faith—clergy and laymen, men and women—ought to be accepted against him. Therefore, what they had declared must be done by the canonical authority of Scripture, they ordered to be observed in such cases through apostolic sanction and coercion.

Finally, King Henry reached Zürich and stayed there for a while. At that time the greater part of the incontinent and Simoniac clergy, despising the apostolic sentence, had stubbornly returned to their vomit, encouraged by the hope of assistance and protection from King Henry and his anti-bishops. Since they greatly feared correction by King Rudolf, they did not cease in every way to oppose and slander him, condemning, anathematizing, and detesting him.

Henry, whom almost the entire kingdom had previously trampled far from the Church in slanderous fashion as a man infamous for his widely known crimes and offenses, was now, by contrast, raised above the heavens with the most monstrous praises and proclaimed with abundant lamentation as though he had been unjustly condemned.

Yet this supremely flattering praise of the one, and hostile abuse of the other—may I say it without offense to them—was constantly being formulated, disseminated everywhere, and supported by unheard-of lies by the heretical and incorrigible persons of the antichristian bishops, together with the chorus of their subordinate clergy, canons, monks, village priests, and similar synagogues.

The crowd of common people, deceived by such persons, believed, did, and knew nothing except what they continually heard from their speeches and false testimonies. Hence very many divergent schisms plainly arose throughout the kingdom. No natural bond of kinship, no trust in friendship, no obedience owed by due subjection, no regard for the fear or love of God, no compact of faith, no obligation of justice, no honor or reverence for any person, nor nearly anything that divine law and right had always contained in its statutes, appeared to be observed among them even as a rule of merely customary practice or as an imagined order. Instead, from the least to the greatest, all had diligently and indiscriminately devoted themselves to avarice, attending neither to divine nor human concerns.

Discipline existed nowhere; modesty was indeed precious, truth exceedingly rare, and myriads of lies reigned everywhere. Thus the enormity of frauds, the harshness of scandals, and the whole number of evils of every kind never ceased to reveal themselves beyond measure.

King Henry, meanwhile, having spent Easter in the bishopric of Aquileia, after he had artfully drawn the Lombards to himself in every way, bound them by oath to their customary fidelity of subjection, and secured them as auxiliaries wholly in accord with his will, had entrusted his son to the care of the excommunicated Simoniac anti-bishops—the Milanese, the Piacentine, and the others throughout Italy [Note: [Col. 0387] “Simonians” in 2 and below, p. 302; the edition reads “Simoniacs”].

Then, taking his wife and the considerable amount of money he had somehow scraped together in those regions, he scarcely entered Bavaria secretly and unexpectedly through the rugged passes of Carantania with only a few companions. Soon at Regensburg, after conferring with the princes of the Bavarians, Bohemians, and Carantanians, as well as with the patriarch of Aquileia—an insufficiently reputable man whom he had brought with him from there—he tearfully laid before them, as he had recently done before the Lombards, very substantial complaints concerning his deposition. He urged them to help him avenge these matters according to his wishes, promising that he would gladly reward and honor them with their dignities and benefices, since he had raised them from certain poor men to such great lords.

At this they were immediately corrupted by magnificent gifts [Note: [Col. 0389] “to them” in 2], and by every device he could devise they were gathered from all directions with considerable eagerness to aid him [Note: [Col. 0389] “were gathered” omitted in the edition]. In a short time he assembled a considerable auxiliary army, nearly twelve thousand men, and, attempting to engage the new king, advanced with a military force to meet him.

Besides these, nearly the entire strength of the Burgundians, the anti-bishops of Basel and Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0389D] Burchard and Werner, reconciled with the pope at Canossa. USS.], who had recently been reconciled by the apostolic lord and professed that they would henceforth remain on the side of justice, a considerable part of the Franks, Count Hermann the Palatine [Note: [Col. 0389D] Of the Rhine], who was to become the son-in-law of King Rudolf, and most of the king’s soldiers—men whom he had long since sworn to himself and had no doubt would be wholly faithful—as well as almost all his relatives and close associates, to whom he himself had always been most faithful, had joined King Henry in everything. But each of them had withdrawn from Rudolf, disregarding their faith and oath [Note: [Col. 0389] “withdrew” in 2].

This occurred for three reasons, which we particularly noted above all others. First, they greatly feared being corrected by him according to the rule of justice, as has already been said. Second, it is almost natural for vicious citizens always to envy virtuous citizens. Third, such conduct is properly a form of serving idols. They all sought and demanded from him that the insatiable abyss of their greed should be stuffed through the monstrous abuse of unheard-of expenditure—that is, that the kingdom, which he had been compelled to undertake in a wretchedly scattered condition in order to gather it together [Note: [Col. 0389] The manuscripts and USS read “miraculously”; the editor indicates the emendation], should be dispersed among them even more wretchedly [Note: [Col. 0389] The manuscripts and USS read “more miraculously”].

Since he had not agreed with them in this, all but a very few persons of sound mind had flowed together astonishingly to their former disperser, as into a sewer to be defiled.

Therefore King Henry, strengthened by such a multitude of auxiliaries, invaded Alemannia to devastate it with plunder, robbery, and fire. There was no distinction between the sacred and the profane. For the Bohemians publicly violated women in the churches, carried away captives according to their custom, and counted the church and its stable as places of equal reverence. Thus, confusing right and wrong together, their heathen madness traversed a considerable part of that land with extreme hostility. From the lands of East Franconia and the River Main, through the River Neckar and the town of Esslingen, they somehow reached as far as Ulm and the Danube, though not without the greatest fear.

For they knew that King Rudolf was encamped with a considerable army in the siege of a certain castle beside the Danube, and was there awaiting the gathering of his soldiers whom he had been able to collect from every direction in so short a time.

At Ulm, after holding a conference with those whom he could, King Henry had King Rudolf, together with his dukes Berthold and Welf and the other leading men of Alemannia who agreed with him, condemned by sentence according to Alemannic law as men apparently deserving to be slaughtered, and deprived them alike of their dignities and benefices. He immediately enriched some of his own men with their benefices, and in his customary manner earnestly gathered these and all whom he could into his support, binding them by oath.

There the aforementioned patriarch, having letters forged as though they had been sent by the apostolic lord into these regions through him, read them aloud before the people. Defending his king in every way and commending him to everyone as though with this authentic majesty, he flatteringly declared him highly worthy to hold the royal power [Col. 0390B].

After such lying flattery, the patriarch at last hurriedly withdrew home, promising to spend himself zealously in military service of any sort in support of the king. Suddenly, however, he was seized by a mad frenzy. Afflicted for some time by this dreadful madness as an example to liars and apostates, in a demonic fashion, he died in the most insane state, with a damnable end [Note: [Col. 0389] “passion” in 2]. Thus, together with some of his men who likewise had been carried off by sudden death, he was taken back to his own see for burial [Note: [Col. 0389D] Compare Gregory VII’s letters to the people of Aquileia concerning the election of a successor, sent on 17 September, indiction 1, Register V, 5–6, Mansi XX, p. 239].

O how fearful is God, the Lord of vengeance, and how terrible in his counsels over the sons of men! This man, previously inflamed by zeal for God, had come the preceding year to the conference at Oppenheim with the most honorable men of God, the archbishop of Salzburg, the bishop of Passau, and the other soldiers of Christ. There, more diligently than almost all the other princes of the kingdom, he had applied himself to ecclesiastical correction, Christian discipline, and necessary improvement; and, like an angel of the Lord of hosts—and, according to his name [Note: [Col. 0390D] That is, “patriarch”], a prince of fathers—he had stood everywhere as a very threatening and terrifying man against King Henry and all who were disobedient and opposed to God and Saint Peter, with the two-edged sword of the Spirit.

Now, corrupted by no small allurements of mammon, he unhappily turned away from the zeal and justice of God as a very light-minded apostate and a prince of error [Note: [Col. 0389] “from heaven” in 2]. Therefore, by the judgment of God, who is most devoted to preserving equity, he too tasted beforehand, as an example for all who wished to observe it, a small portion of his cup; and, having tasted it, he will never cease, always thirsting, to drink it down forever and beyond, a draught that cannot be exhausted.

The bishop of Augsburg followed him no less unhappily. At the most recent Easter he had been very firmly allied with King Rudolf, although scarcely by homage and a pact of unfeigned fidelity. Yet as soon as King Henry returned, he promptly went out to meet him with congratulations, flattered him in every way [Note: [Col. 0391] “in every fashion” in 2; USS reads the adverbial form], and did not fail to serve and favor him diligently in the aforesaid company as far as Ulm.

There also, after celebrating the solemnities of Mass up to the place of communion, he turned to the king and the other hearers. After proclaiming in a somewhat flattering speech concerning the matters then at hand, he freely declared before everyone that he would receive the holy Eucharist as a test and judgment of this matter: that the cause of his lord King Henry was just, while Rudolf’s was wholly unjust.

Thus, as is customary in judgments, after first stating this sacramental condition—that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood should benefit him for the salvation of body and soul precisely to the extent that the cause of King Henry, his lord, in obtaining the kingdom was just and valid—the presumptuous examiner of justice, as though for the commendation of the people, communicated with these words.

Immediately afterward he was seized by a fatal illness and grew more grievously emaciated day by day, until, miserably tormented by the just judgment of God and confessing that the vengeance for his aforesaid presumption had fallen upon him, he too, overtaken by a most bitter death after only a few days, closed his final day.

Duke Welf promptly took care to report this judgment to the lord pope. The pope, himself no false prophet, immediately sent back the unequivocal reply that he had foreknowledge of this: that the bishop would never taste any of the new harvest’s produce that year. Shortly afterward, as the apostolic man had foretold, the outcome confirmed it.

Although these people had been sufficiently and more than sufficiently admonished by such signs and manifestations, scarcely anyone could persuade them that this very just and desirable support for King Rudolf had been undertaken for the sake of the Church’s necessity and its correction. Rather, they eagerly desired with all their strength to remain constantly attached to King Henry, the burner and devastator of all his own goods and the author and defender of so many heresies and schisms.

Then certain stubborn men preached openly a doctrine that was heresy and a seedbed of clerical error: that no judgment or sentence of the pope or of any magistrate ought to fall upon kings, even if they were heretics, worn out by every charge of crimes and offenses, bloodthirsty and utterly wicked, and profane and sacrilegious in every way.

They had not considered that the emperor Constantine, a follower of Paul [Note: [Col. 0391] “Paul” in 2; corrected in the fourteenth-century witness], bishop of Constantinople and a heretic, had been excommunicated at a Roman synod by Saint Pope Martin in the year 650 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0391D] Martin condemned not Constantine himself, or Constans, but only his type. See Pagi, *Breviarium Romanorum Pontificum*, I, p. 423. USS.].

They should also take note of Constantius, excommunicated by Pope Felix on account of the Arian heresy [Note: [Col. 0391D] See Bernold, in Hermann, under the year 358]. Let them not be unaware that King Haribert of the Franks was excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, on account of his sexual crime, and was condemned to descend to hell [Note: [Col. 0391D] Hermann of Augsburg under the year 563. The same is read in Bernold, *Opusculum* VI, 9, p. 360].

Let them also know that King Childeric of the Franks was deposed from the kingdom by the authority of Pope Stephen, tonsured, and sent to a monastery; and that Pepin was thus elected king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0391D] The same words appear in Bernold, *Opusculum* XII, 4, p. 393], and consecrated to the kingdom by Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz.

Pope Nicholas excommunicated Lothair, king of the Franks, because, having repudiated his lawful wife, he had presumed to keep Waldrada [Note: [Col. 0391] “Waldrada” in 2] as a concubine [Note: [Col. 0392D] Bernold presented the same example twice in similar words in the places cited above]. When he wished to excuse himself at Rome from the crimes brought against him, and judgment was imposed upon him that, if he were innocent, he should approach communion with confidence, he approached presumptuously and took judgment upon himself from the hand of the apostolic lord. For not long afterward he and all his supporters perished by sudden death [Note: [Col. 0392D] Hermann under the year 869].

The emperor Theodosius was driven away by Saint Ambrose from entering the church [Note: [Col. 0391] “entrance” in 2; corrected by the fourteenth-century witness to “from entering”] and, because of his crimes, was sent into confinement for eight months to perform penance [Note: [Col. 0392D] Theodosius’ penance is certain, but his confinement is legendary. USS. Nearly the same account is in Bernold, *Opusculum* VI, 9, p. 360]. The emperor Louis, laying down his arms, was confined by the judgment of the bishops in order to perform penance.

Why was it necessary to recall this and so many other examples of the same kind to those of sound understanding, except because of the most troublesome and false replies of certain foolish men’s chatter? They were producing in their synagogues of fables, with the ludicrousness of inept stories and trifles, very many privileges previously unheard of concerning kings, ignorant of public law and not even sufficiently knowledgeable about their own popular enactments (*scita*), though they are called from *scire*, “to know.”

According to the impulse of their desire [Note: [Col. 0391] “desires” in 2], they indiscriminately praised and blamed anything whatsoever on either side. Just as realities had long since lost their proper names, so among them even now it is not realities but names alone that receive praise and honor—names that, without their proper meaning [Note: [Col. 0391] “property” in 2] and functions, resound altogether emptily [Col. 0392D].

For just as *lex* (“law”) is derived from *legere* (“to read”), *sacerdos* (“priest”) from *sacer* (“sacred”), *dux* (“leader”) from *ducere* (“to lead”), *consul* (“consul”) from *consulere* (“to deliberate”), and *graviones* from the gravity of morals—or because a man is burdened by the weight of labor all the more heavily the more he is placed above others—so it is demonstrated that *rex* (“king”) is properly called or named from *regere*, “to rule.”

It is also known that *regula* (“rule”) is named either because he leads rightly and never draws in another direction, or because he governs, or because he provides a standard for right living, or because he corrects something distorted and wicked. The name “king” is therefore retained by doing what is right; otherwise it is lost. Hence the ancient saying:

> You will be king if you act rightly; if you do not, you will not be.

The two principal royal virtues are therefore justice and piety. Piety, however, is praised more in kings, for justice is true in itself [Note: [Col. 0393] Witness 2 has “so”; the edition reads “justice is true in itself”].

But if they neither judge justly [Note: [Col. 0393] “judge” in 2] nor show compassionate piety, and do not touch even the slightest part of the rule of their office—or even the image of its name—yet rather practice in every way the freedom of a criminal and luxurious life beyond the measure and even the extravagant madness of the heathen; if they suppress the people with the most savage majesty of domination, devour those whom they have most miserably oppressed, and consume them even to destruction [Note: [Col. 0393] The edition reads “to annihilation”], why should such men more properly be called tyrants, however powerful, than kings—who would be called so abusively and without truth to the reality?

For *tyrannus*, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as “powerful.” Among the ancients, powerful kings were called *tyrants*. Among the Greeks, because they support the people as though they were bases, they are called *basileis* (“kings”); hence they display bases and crowns twisted together upon themselves.

Christian kings must also take note of what is written about Octavian in Roman history. After he had been called Augustus because he enlarged the state, and had already been called Caesar and emperor, he was present at games and a spectacle of the Romans. When the people proclaimed that he should be called “god and lord,” he immediately resisted such disgraceful flatteries, turning away his hand and face, and as a man declined the title “lord.” On the following day he rebuked the entire people with the greatest severity and did not permit himself to be called “lord” thereafter, not even by his children.

If a king who was then an idolater valued this title so greatly, how much more valuable now is the noble pearl of Christian dignity? But it is enough to have said this against the triflers.

During these post-Easter days, letters of apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0393D] These letters are absent from Mansi] were sent to all who lived on this side of the Rhine, throughout Alsace, Lorraine, and German Francia, but specifically to the bishops [Col. 0394A]. Through them, all conspiracies, disturbances of the peace, and dissensions were forbidden them; and they were forbidden to obey or serve King Henry, as one customarily obeys a king.

The anti-bishops of Basel and Strasbourg, however, held these letters in complete contempt and thought nothing of them. The others, concealing themselves by whatever strategy or opportunity they could, as though the letters had never been sent to them, did not make them public, but as far as they were able carefully obeyed them.

At the same time the abbot of Marseille [Note: [Col. 0393D] See Gregory’s letter V, 7], together with Christian [Note: [Col. 0393D] Paul of Bernried reports that Bernard, abbot of Marseille, took with him an outstanding scholar named Christian, later bishop of Aversa, whose excellent work against Berengar of Tours survives. He is famous under another name, Guitmund. USS.], a most learned monk, while attempting to return to the apostolic lord—by whom they had been sent into the German regions to settle the dissensions among our people—were captured by a certain count, Ulrich [Col. 0394B], robbed, and imprisoned in the castle of Lenzburg [Note: [Col. 0393] “Lenzburg near the River Aar, in the district of Aargau,” a fourteenth-century gloss in 2] [Note: [Col. 0394D] He was its count].

When King Henry learned that they had been captured, he did not order them released, as he had already promised the apostolic lord by oath. Shortly afterward the abbot of Cluny sent him a letter of admonition, in which he rebuked him sufficiently and more than sufficiently for his perjury. The whole cause of the reconciliation and alliance between the pope and the king had been known to him, since he had been present as their principal mediator.

Moreover, with his face uncovered, he freely charged him that this was the clearest indication of his ruin: that, as an inhuman despiser of the apostolic see, he would not free such great and holy men of God who had been imprisoned for the sake of justice, but instead ordered them to be thrust into confinement.

By this admonition he was freely rebuked and scarcely broken down. Although not for God, at least because of the persistent urging of so great an admonisher, he agreed that God’s bound servants should depart released and free, while their possessions had been plundered. They waited for some time for the repayment of the goods stolen from them, according to the king’s order; but at last, having long been frustrated and deceived, they turned aside empty-handed and almost naked to the monastery of Saint Aurelius [Note: [Col. 0393] “Hirsau,” a fourteenth-century gloss in 2].

There, received with every form of human kindness by Abbot William and treated with great charity for almost the entire year, they awaited with no small sweetness the tranquility of peace and the possibility of their return.

King Rudolf, having gathered troops from everywhere, resolved, with God as judge, in high spirit to meet King Henry and attempt to engage him in battle. After receiving the unanimous counsel of his dukes and counts [Col. 0394D], as well as of his entire army, which scarcely reached a total of five thousand fighting men [Col. 0395A], they did not consider such an engagement a sound plan, but prudently decided that it should be postponed for a time, until he could thereafter industriously gather from every direction many myriads of fighting men, by whose numbers, at a favorable opportunity, he could subdue his adversaries without loss to his own men and, as a victorious king, compel them in every way to serve him. Although unwilling and reluctant, he yielded to their counsels. He graciously dismissed the multitude he had gathered, carefully warning his intimates to protect the kingdom and guard against the horrors of the wars that threatened; then, since the leading men of Saxony were earnestly inviting him, he hastened his journey into Saxony, taking with him three bishops—the bishops of Passau, Worms, and Würzburg—as well as a cardinal of the Apostolic See and some of his confidential attendants [Col. 0395B].

They received him with every mark of royal honor and glorification [Note: [Col. 0395] *totius* (“entire”) in the edition.], saluting and magnifying him most gloriously, as was fitting for their king and lord; with every expression and effort of submission and reverence, they joyfully honored him as one most welcome. There, as the most just arbiter of equity and of the ancestral laws of that people, he attempted judicially to settle before him all their complaints and accusations with the most careful scrutiny of justice, without respect of persons. Hence, not undeservedly, whereas the former ruler, always inflamed against them at the impulse of his own pleasure, had raged against them through seizures, plunder, and every form of oppression [Col. 0395C], this man, judging justly and correcting every wrong with the rigor of justice, was equally loved by all.

The king’s wife [Note: [Col. 0395D] Adelheid, sister of Bertha, Queen Henry IV’s wife, and Rudolf’s second wife. See under the year 1079. USS.], turning aside from Zürich toward Burgundy, remained for more than a year and a half in one of her castles, where she suffered many injuries from the Burgundians. For the anti-bishops of Basel, Lausanne, and Strasbourg, together with all whom they had drawn to themselves, soon devastated everything belonging to the king with seizures, burnings, and every kind of oppressive assault and persuasion, until they had subjected almost the entire region to themselves and to their king. But this did not happen without loss and harm to themselves. Twice the Burgundian bands that had invaded the Alemannic regions most arrogantly [Note: [Col. 0395] *superbisse* in witness 2.] with hostile force to plunder them were defeated, beaten, and put to flight by King Rudolf’s soldiers [Col. 0395D].

King Henry, meanwhile, hurried from Ulm into Bavaria. By distributing among his own men the benefices and church properties of Duke Welf and the other rebels against him—especially those of Passau—he gathered to himself, in his customary fashion, namely by oath, everyone whom he could obtain by any means and from anywhere [Col. 0396A]. Thus he most carefully prepared an expedition into Saxony against King Rudolf, and into Alemannia against the dukes Berthold and Welf and the other supporters of those men. Almost no Bavarian, except the archbishop of Salzburg and a certain Count Egbert [Note: [Col. 0396D] See below, cols. 401–402.], failed to support and obey him according to his will.

At the same time, certain counts among the Alemanni, formerly sworn soldiers and particularly devoted to King Rudolf, apostatized from him for the sake of shameful profit. Having seized the garrisons of certain castles, they ravaged throughout the province, with all their strength and every inhuman device, their own lord, Duke Welf, the property of the churches [Col. 0396B], and everyone who disagreed with them, through plunder, burnings, and every form of robbery and assault. Thus, throughout all the provinces, such disturbances were carried on for the whole of that year indiscriminately by the followers of both sides, as is usual in wars. Hence a very severe famine arose in our regions, both because the earth had not yielded its fruit and because the plunderers and robbers had consumed everything through the violence described above; it forced many to waste away and perish miserably. Neither divine laws nor secular legal ordinances were even mentioned in those days. Each person lived as he could, acting as his own judge and corrector. Hitherto unheard-of schisms born of discord, the disgrace of fraud and shameful gain, and countless sacrileges—even in the churches, into which everyone had brought his property in the hope of peace and protection—reigned everywhere openly and secretly, with lamentable arrogance, through the imperious power of despisers of God [Col. 0396C].

When the Apostolic Lord finally heard these things, he sent letters [Note: [Col. 0396D] From Gregory VII’s Register IV.23, addressed to the deacon Bernard and Abbot Bernard.] especially to his legates and also to all who were in the German regions, both great and small. He earnestly desired that, by whatever means he could, with our assistance, he might come into that country to establish peace. In these letters he instructed his legates to warn both kings most firmly that they should grant him a peaceful and secure route into those regions, together with guides in whom he could trust [Col. 0396D], so that, with God’s favor, he might settle such grave disorders. They were to separate from the members of the Church by public excommunication and condemnation anyone who refused to agree and obey him and the other wiser and better men of the kingdom in this matter; but to the one who obeyed they were, by apostolic authority, to confer the monarchy of the kingdom [Col. 0397A]. And they were to command all who were in the kingdom to obey, submit to, and serve that king as was proper, and in every way to honor him as one raised up for the stability and building up of the Church.

King Rudolf and all his men were ready to obey this instruction. But since King Henry held all the Alpine routes under his control, blocked on every side and filled with ambushes, Rudolf desired something that he could in no way bring about. King Henry, fearing the judgment of apostolic authority, gave strict orders to all his men that no one who carried an apostolic legation should be granted access to him—as though he could reasonably defend himself by this stratagem against the universally proclaimed charge. For he was now pursuing something else rather than obedience: namely, the expedition into Saxony [Col. 0397B] which all his men had already sworn to undertake. Accordingly, in July he withdrew from Bavaria into his own Franconia with as many men as he could, gathering there from every direction whatever forces he could assemble for a fairly large army.

When King Rudolf finally learned that Henry had assembled such a great body of military companies against him and his men, he did not delay long but industriously and repeatedly attempted to meet him and engage him in battle. Advancing as far as Würzburg, he delayed there for a while after besieging the city, for this reason: if he hastened toward the Rhine with so great a force of his army, the enemy, timid and terrified, might not dare to cross over to him. There he also awaited the auxiliary forces of the dukes Berthold and Welf and the other divisions of his Alemannic soldiers. With great skill he tried to destroy the city walls with certain engines and instruments of war [Note: [Col. 0397] *urbe* (“city”) in witness 2.]. The others, numbering about five thousand, were hastening joyfully to meet him [Col. 0397C].

When King Henry had reconnoitered their troop movements, he occupied for three days a certain point along their route, intending to bring war upon them with his not inconsiderable companies. They, eager for the encounter, advanced rapidly toward him. When they had come so near that they were no more than two miles apart, and all, armed for the same purpose, were boldly preparing to engage the king in battle, Henry withdrew from them by flight that same night with his men and, before sunrise, entered his own Worms ahead of the others, amid the mockery and insults even of their peasants [Col. 0397D]. When they learned of his flight, they hurried with terrifying speed and no small force to the place of his camp, intending to pursue him [Note: [Col. 0397] *persecutori* (“to the pursuer”) in witness 2.]. But when their scouts informed them that he had already gone so far from them and had been so thoroughly terrified, they abandoned the pursuit they had undertaken in the deepest grief; they proceeded proudly on their intended journey [Col. 0398A].

In those days the Roman cardinal [Note: [Col. 0397D] Bernard.] had graciously sent King Henry, as he had been ordered, a warning letter concerning the proposed apostolic journey to us, entrusting it to a certain monk of Würzburg. Before the monk could reach Henry, however, one of Henry’s confidential attendants, after carefully investigating the purpose of his journey, seized and mistreated him; they also grievously beat his servant and confiscated the letter. They profaned it in every way, treating it not as an apostolic letter but as though it were diabolical. Soon the same Roman cardinal again sent him a letter concerning the same matter, this time through a familiar knight of his. Henry received it when it was brought under another man’s identity and had it read aloud [Col. 0398B]; but, immediately hardening his ears, he became furious and treated the letter he had heard with utter contempt. He ordered its bearer likewise to be seized and imprisoned. Shortly afterward the man escaped from him and scarcely managed to flee custody with his life.

Meanwhile Henry had industriously gathered from everywhere, with all the effort he could make, a considerable army. Crossing the Rhine again with all whom he had collected, he pretended that he was going to meet King Rudolf. There, between the Rhine and the Neckar, they pitched camp after obstructing the river’s fords in every possible way, while awaiting the assistance of the Bavarians. When King Rudolf learned of their encampment, he abandoned the siege of the city [Note: [Col. 0398D] Würzburg.] and his destructive engines, and hastened toward them with great force, eager to bring battle upon them [Col. 0398C]. Reaching the very bank of the river with courageous intent to fight in defense of the kingdom entrusted to him and of the Christian religion, he found no way to cross, since the enemy, with their forces, occupied the opposite bank for almost three miles along its length. The bank on the other side rose so high that no one—not to mention a mounted man, but even a foot soldier—could find a way to climb there except at two extremely narrow fords.

Then King Rudolf repeatedly called out and appealed to King Henry and to the other commanders of the army: if Henry had resolved so stubbornly and with such a claim of right to possess the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0397] “to obtain” (*optinere*), witness 2: “to hold” (*r. optinere. s.*).], let him choose one of two alternatives. Either he should give Rudolf a place where he could cross over to him; or, if not, he should abandon the bank and position he had occupied, withdraw for two miles, and continue backward until Rudolf could likewise cross over to him with his entire army [Col. 0398D]. If Henry had no other confidence in that course, he should confirm the agreement inviolably by oath. Then both of them should devoutly entrust their cause to the judgment of the most just judge for decision; and, whether by single combat between the two of them, or—if that seemed preferable to the wiser and better men of the kingdom—by public war, they should immediately contend under the governance of the Lord God to prove their right [Col. 0399A].

King Henry, falling silent with deaf ears, gave him no answer. Rudolf, however, to show that he had made his demand in all simplicity and to provoke Henry by every possible means to such a judgment, moved away from his own position and camp with his men for about two miles, pretending to flee. The following day, when he perceived that even this had achieved nothing, he returned with a renewed charge of military force and boldly occupied the camp where he had been the day before, so that, if he could attempt it by skill or courage [Note: [Col. 0399] *se* (“if”) in witness 2.], he might endeavor to engage him in battle by whatever means [Note: [Col. 0399] *bellicos* (“warlike”) in witness 2.].

Then certain of King Henry’s leading men, entirely unwilling to fight, and eager to defend, under whatever pretext of honor—though falsely—the disgrace of their cowardice and their consciousness of manifest injustice [Col. 0399B], earnestly sought from Dukes Berthold and Welf a means of peace and an agreement of good faith, so that, in the immediate crisis of such great necessity, they might be permitted to confer with one another more familiarly. When the peaceful conference they had requested was granted [Note: [Col. 0399] *rogaverat* (“he had requested”) in witness 2.], those who seemed suitable from both sides promptly assembled for it.

After lengthy exchanges of differing speeches on both sides, the following agreement was finally defined as the substance of the conference: first, they were to make a firm peace with one another, entirely ending and calming the impending war on this condition—that shortly afterward all the greater men of the whole kingdom, except the two kings, should assemble for a conference near the Rhine [Col. 0399C]. There, together with the apostolic legates, they should deliberate and judge, by the most just examination of judicial reasoning [Note: [Col. 0399] *justissim’* (“most just”) in witness 2.], what was best and what was most just in so great a case. Whichever of the two kings did not agree with their decisions was to be despised, and they were to oppose him by common consent; finally, they were to agree with the other king and serve him with complete loyalty and submission, as is proper toward a king.

The bishops of Trier and Metz, together with certain of King Henry’s confidential attendants, at first utterly refused to hear the Roman cardinal at this conference. From the king they could obtain permission to hold the proposed discussion and make peace only after giving their word that they would not receive or hear the pope and his legate. At last, however, although extremely constrained, they both heard the same legate and the apostolic letters and decrees, and received them with all the reverence that was fitting [Col. 0399D].

Thus, to carry out the agreed conference, and so that neither king nor prince might impede it by any stratagem or faction, pledges were given and accepted by both sides, and a peace was likewise agreed to last until everyone had returned to his own territory. King Rudolf then returned gloriously with his men to Saxony [Note: [Col. 0399] *saxonia* (“Saxony”) in witness 2.].

King Henry, after waiting several days in the same place for his Bavarians [Col. 0400A] [Note: [Col. 0399] *pstolatos* in witness 2; *praestolatus* in the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0399D] That is, those for whom he had been waiting.], soon took them with him. They had almost encountered King Rudolf and were freed by the intervention of the peace just mentioned. After consulting with them, he again ravaged Alemannia most inhumanly with plunder and burnings, attacking the Alemannic princes, who had just returned from the aforesaid war, by a treacherous surprise. For at that time they thought there was peace and therefore were already confidently allowing their weary soldiers to return home. Nevertheless, he invaded that region only at the greatest cost to his own men.

On the same journey, in an open country, he observed the devastated region burning and smoking all around him from the fires, where, among many other places, one church had been burned and destroyed together with more than a hundred people [Col. 0400B]. There he imposed upon the church of Augsburg Sigifrid, his chaplain, in place of the man whom the brothers had already canonically elected, just as had been stated above concerning the unfortunate death of Bishop Imbricco. He did this not so that Sigifrid might govern the church, but so that he might stand by Henry with undivided assistance in the wars that were closing in. Subsequent events proved that this was indeed his intention.

On the same day and in the same place, he appointed over the abbey of the cell of Saint Gall a certain kinsman of his [Note: [Col. 0399D] Namely Udalric, son of Marquard, Duke of Carinthia. USS.], who was not a monk of that place, with the same intention [Note: [Col. 0399] *abb’* (“abbey”) in witness 2.], rejecting the man who had been regularly elected by the brothers and appointed abbot there by King Rudolf. Like the substitute imposed upon Augsburg, he thereafter skillfully organized, always wearing armor and not as a monk, unmonastic wars against King Rudolf.

At Aquileia also he installed as patriarch Henry [Note: [Col. 0399] *h.* in witness 2.], a canon of Augsburg and his chaplain, rejecting the man who had been canonically elected by clergy and people [Col. 0400C]. Then he set out on the route he had begun toward Bavaria. From there, after gathering auxiliary companies of his soldiers from every direction, he returned again to Franconia [Note: [Col. 0399] *ite* (“again”) in witness 2.]. Before doing so, however, he summoned the archbishop of Salzburg to himself under a pretended show of good faith and tested him with every device, trying earnestly and excessively—though in vain—to attach him to his side.

The archbishop, truly an immovable pillar of the holy Church, firmly set upon the foundation of truth by the weight of heavenly love, clearly perceived that he was being ensnared by so many schemes of folly and cunning. With all the effort he could make, he tore himself away from there, abandoning all his own men, and fled secretly by night, almost alone, into Alemannia to the men of his party and communion [Col. 0400D] [Note: [Col. 0400D] Compare the Life of Saint Gebhard.].

At last, when those greater and better men of the kingdom who had been summoned and named for this purpose had begun to assemble from every direction at the appointed time for the conference, King Henry once again gathered a considerable army. Treacherously breaking the pledge already made by the princes, and utterly disregarding the agreement of peace in his fury, he resisted them with every device he could employ, doing everything in his power to prevent their assembly [Col. 0401A]. When they had investigated this customary evasion of his folly, they realized that the purpose of their conference and the proposed future union of the whole kingdom against so many discords and schisms had been completely frustrated. Although deeply agitated and not without great murmuring, each returned to his own territory.

Henry, meanwhile, as he had already resolved, continued his customary burnings and plundering, stubbornly ravaging his rebels wherever he could with the force of royal authority. There the bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0401D] Werinher.], above all others in such affairs his chief instigator and helper at that time, one day returned to the camp, armed and wearing a coat of mail in military fashion. As the arm-leader and commander of so many evils and crimes, he was excessively cruel in serving his king. But when he lay down on his bed, he was suddenly struck by death in an instant [Col. 0401B].

His men were exceedingly terrified and greatly astonished, since they had so often been scandalized by the wickedness of his life. For, contrary to canonical command, he had shamelessly and publicly persisted in abusing a certain widowed concubine. She had been married to one of his soldiers, from whom he had taken her after purchasing her with a considerable sum of money and benefices. Later, when accused before the pope on this account [Note: [Col. 0401D] See Gregory VII, *Register* III.4, dated 3 September 1075.], he did not avoid her after swearing her away. In addition, although the infamous suspicion of a most abominable incest rested upon her, he never on that account separated himself from sexual intercourse with her.

Thus this energetic despiser of God, like that heretical bishop Paul of Samosata of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0401D] Bernold makes similar statements, *Opusculum* III.7, p. 252, and in the *Chronicle*, under the year of Claudius I.], who delighted in the company of women and granted the same liberty to his clergy so that they could not charge him with that crime, became a grave scandal to all his canons, to the clerics of his subordinate parishes, and to the whole Church. He earned the wrath of God and was destined to be struck by the severity of eternal condemnation: for woe to the man through whom such scandal comes. In the divine writings, “woe” is written for eternal mourning.

That heretic Paul, when condemned by the Church, refused to depart and was publicly driven out by force, to add to the measure of his disgrace. This man likewise, already canonically condemned by apostolic sanction for his heresies and crimes, was, by the sentence of the heavenly Judge, suddenly removed from life—and from the kingdom of God—as an unmistakable example to all. His men, having taken him up, carried him back by an ill-omened journey to his own seat, there to be buried [Col. 0401C].

King Henry, when he then intended, in his customary manner, to invade Alemannia for the third time in order to ravage it [Col. 0402A] [Note: [Col. 0401] *alemannam* in witness 2.], and had no doubt that Dukes Berthold and Welf, with the other Alemannic companies, would engage him in battle, prudently avoided meeting them. He went straight into Bavaria with his men, yielding the field. Then, taking with him the military forces of the duke of Bohemia, men of that province, he attacked Egbert, a count of considerable strength and courage who had rebelled against him. With plunder, burnings, and the sieges of his castles, he persistently and hostilely devastated him.

While carrying out this devastation, he and his men scarcely endured the excessive cold of the snowy season. After besieging three of Egbert’s castles for some time, and finally capturing and destroying them with military engines, the harsh invader wintered there. Since Egbert was entirely unable to resist him, Henry finally drove him into exile, fleeing to the king of Hungary with his wife [Note: [Col. 0401D] Compare the *Life of Blessed Adalbero, Bishop of Würzburg*, chapter 1, where Arnold, his father, is said to have had a daughter who—called Mechtild by others—“married Count Ekkebert, whose castle, called Neuburg, is situated on the bank of the Inn between Schärding and Passau. After the fortunate death of her brothers, the city of Putina, with everything belonging to it, fell to him as her dowry.” A little earlier Putina is called “the renowned and famous city, which, like a metropolis and mother of cities, was established in ancient times toward Pannonia, on the southern side, to repel the hostile incursions and devastations of the Pannonians,” and is now called Pitten. This explains both Egbert’s persecution and his flight: since he defended the cause of Bishop Adalbero of Würzburg, his father-in-law, who had been driven from his see by Henry, he too, after his castles had been overthrown—the principal one being Neuburg between Schärding and Passau—was forced to seek safer places, namely his city of Putina, situated on the borders of Hungary. USS.] and all his possessions.

At the same time, King Rudolf, after completing the aforesaid expedition, returned with his men to Saxony and recognized that the agreed conference had been prevented by King Henry’s faction and treachery. He had no better course, therefore, than to pacify the Saxon kingdom as the most equitable judge and, according to its laws, to examine and correct every wrong with the utmost justice. In addition, he restrained by royal authority certain Westphalians and Thuringians who had rebelled against him [Note: [Col. 0401] From “certain” through “Milan” (p. 305, line 26), the excised folio is missing in witness 1*.].

He also caused the Apostolic Lord to be informed of the entire sequence of events, sending a legate to Rome, and diligently sought his counsel and help regarding them. The pope sent him no other reply than that he knew Rudolf was awaiting with considerable eagerness the fulfillment of the contents of the letters which he had recently sent both to his legates and to all the princes of the German regions. Accordingly, that Roman cardinal, greatly encouraged, gathered at Goslar a council of the bishops and other princes of the Saxon province, as the letters prescribed. On 12 November [Note: [Col. 0402D] The words “from communion … the kingdom,” in a changed order, are taken from Gregory’s letter IV.23, cited above.] he solemnly excommunicated King Henry by apostolic authority, judicially condemning him from communion in the body and blood of the Lord and from the thresholds of the holy Catholic Church, and entirely forbidding him to govern the kingdom. The reason was that Henry, having become wholly disobedient to the supreme pontiff of the first Apostolic See [Col. 0402D] [Note: [Col. 0401] *pontifici* (“to the pontiff”) is absent in witness 2.], was rashly invading the kingdom—although the Roman synod had deprived him of it by a just sentence and had anathematized him after depriving him of it—without permission from the man who had condemned him. Moreover, as a despiser of God and the Apostolic See, he obstinately refused, even then, to allow the route and guidance needed to settle so many discords, schisms, and the criminal and disastrous conflicts of the whole kingdom.

By apostolic authority he confirmed Rudolf in the kingdom and firmly commanded all the nobles of the kingdom to support him as was proper toward a king. Throughout Alemannia, meanwhile, the warlike ranks of both sides, excessively hostile to one another, were thrown into turmoil by various movements everywhere, especially around the Danube. They raged as best they could, persisting in plunder, robbery, and burnings, and appropriating by public seizure the property of others, especially that of the churches [Col. 0403B].

At the same time, the Empress Agnes [Note: [Col. 0403D] Peter Damian also praises her virtues, both in letters addressed to her (*Works*, vol. I, pp. 112 ff.) and in *Opusculum* 56 (vol. III, p. 372). Compare Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, p. 617 ff., and vol. V, p. 115. USS.], who had long been striving with all her strength to calm such rebellions, happily closed the final day of her life on 14 December. For eighteen years [Note: [Col. 0404D] She became a nun at the end of 1061 or the beginning of 1062; see above.] after she had been consecrated in the sacred veil, she rejected for God’s kingdom both royal splendor and the voluptuous delights of worldly life, and eagerly undertook the course of religious life. She devoted herself tirelessly day and night to psalmody and prayer. Having truly followed Christ, she most genuinely denied herself and diligently crucified her flesh with its vices and desires [Col. 0403C].

For her, the tears divinely granted her amid the desirable contrition of her heart were continually her bread; thus, like Hezekiah, she always reflected upon all the years of her life in such bitterness of soul. As great as she had been in the magnificence of the world, so greatly did she humble herself in all things. Therefore the Holy Spirit looked upon her, humble and poor in spirit. Having laid aside her royal insignia and distributed them among Christ’s poor and the churches, she used cheap clothing, observing above all—not only in this but in everything—that nothing should be excessive.

In daily confession she was accustomed, at the beginning, to accuse and cleanse herself not only of her deeds but also of disordered thoughts and even dreams. She always kept with her, with the greatest care, as her inseparable companions, those teachers of obedience whom she knew to be more religious and prudent than others. Through their daily reading, instruction, discipline, and salutary supervision, she desired to be most discreetly fortified on every side. Whatever burden they imposed upon her through obedience, she bore willingly and without delay, submissive to God [Col. 0403D].

Her fasts were simple and not superstitious; her food was modest, sufficiently sober, and wonderfully temperate. At her little table there was always a reading from the divine books, which was also food and a delightful refreshment for her soul [Col. 0404A]. There Christ, as her guest, was diligently cared for in the poor. For she made friends for herself from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when it failed, they might receive her into the eternal dwellings.

Whatever she could possess from her estates, which were extensive and suitable to so great a person, she distributed every day for such purposes, apart from manifest necessities. She entirely avoided the comforts of baths and the softness of feathers. Her bed was most often the ground, or something else made hard—prepared with a small mat [*psiathium*: Note: [Col. 0404D] A small mat of the sort used by monks.], a carpet, or very sparse straw [Note: [Col. 0403] *praeparatum* (“prepared”) in the edition.]. When a brief sleep restored her fragile little body, she immediately became exceedingly energetic in returning to her customary vigils and prayers [Col. 0404B]. Christ was always in her heart, and psalm and word always sounded upon her lips. Only he with whom she had lived in such intimate communion knows what labor she then undertook [Note: [Col. 0403] *intimo* (“intimate”) in witness 2.].

She had compelled all her people, beyond measure, to labor day and night: with their own hands they sewed garments for the poor; they bathed, warmed, clothed, and visited the dirty poor, especially those who were scabrous, leprous, ulcerous, wasting away with running sores, or foul with any kind of disease. She served Christ most diligently through these works and showed herself wholly humble, most humane, and in every way generous toward all God’s servants. A chorus and multitude of people throughout the lands continue to proclaim these things with one voice [Col. 0404C].

For she attempted to share the gifts of her generosity with all persons of religious life anywhere in churches or monasteries, in whatever way she could; thus, privately and publicly, she most diligently shared in the memory of their brotherhood and prayers. Toward heretics and hypocrites, however, she was very severe. Without respect of persons, she possessed great freedom of speech and attack against all; she resisted them with the authority and correction of a teacher, and was especially hostile to Nicolaitans and Simonians.

At first, when certain leading men of the kingdom earnestly asked her to remain in the German regions as a more diligent and familiar motherly monitor and corrector, in order to restrain or moderate her son’s childish and later youthful errors, she consented for a while. But finally, after repeatedly warning, reproving, pleading with, and correcting her son and his confidential attendants by every art and device, both opportunely and importunately, and after not the slightest correction had resulted—in fact, while they were plotting worse things—her son became utterly abominable and even grievous to behold. Refusing to endure their many insolences, plunderings, envies, resistance, follies, and manifold insanities any longer, she withdrew entirely with all her people to Rome, to Saint Peter and the company of so many saints [Col. 0405A].

There she spent every day on the poor whatever she could possess of her goods. Thus, advancing daily in holy and religious life, always stretching forward to what lay ahead and forgetting what was behind, she pursued the prize of the heavenly calling, lawfully striving and completing her course, and there she triumphantly and gloriously attained it.

When the time approached for her to be rewarded for so many magnificent acts of piety in such a blessed life, she was joyfully seized, beyond her usual condition, by the weakness of fever. Although she was not unskilled in medical art and had often been accustomed to mitigate the violence of such fevers, for fourteen days her bodily strength continually diminished hour by hour, while her mind was more graciously enlarged and strengthened in Christ. At last she became extremely weak and wasted away [Col. 0405B].

Finally, when the end had come, after she had most carefully distributed her goods for the use of the poor and the churches, she first summoned to herself the Apostolic Lord and all the dearest persons among her faithful and friends. Bidding them her final farewell, she commended her soul to them [Note: [Col. 0405] *commendaverit* (“she commended”) in witness 2.], and arranged all her affairs according to her desire. Then, having received the Eucharist with the deepest devotion, while the others prayed and sang psalms, she too sang and gave thanks, and joyfully commended her spirit into the hands of God and of Saints Peter and Paul.

Finally, after the Apostolic Lord had solemnly celebrated funeral services, Masses, almsgiving, and vigils for several days on behalf of her soul, he reverently buried the sacred little body of the Empress Agnes—so often released from sins by his apostolic indulgence and absolution—in a sarcophagus in the church of Saint Petronilla, anciently called the Vatican of Apollo, beside the altar of the Lord, that is, at the side of Saint Petronilla. The entire holy Roman Church joined in harmony in hymns and praises at her burial [Col. 0405C].

In the summer of that same year, the prefect of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0405D] Saint Peter Damian calls him Cinthius and praises his virtues in Letters 1 and 2 of Book VIII, addressed to him; so too does Paul of Bernried, who calls him Cincius. It was this man who had thrown into prison the other Cincius, or Quintius, discussed in the preceding year [Col. 0406D], and thereby incurred Quintius’s hatred, which could be extinguished only by his blood. He writes that he was killed by agents of Heinrician persecution. Uss.] was treacherously killed by certain relatives of Quintius. He had long before made a complete confession of his sins to the apostolic lord and turned to God. He had wished, with the greatest eagerness, to abandon the world altogether, with all its alluring pleasures, and to strive toward the perfection of monastic life; but the apostolic lord entirely forbade him to do so under obedience and ordered him to remain in his prefecture, so that, armed with zeal for God and most observant as a judge of equity and justice, he might resist so many criminals and gratefully serve Christ in this obedience. This he also carried out in every way, with no little effort and to the best of his ability.

Hence he opposed Quintius, the chief of all criminals, with the most diligent and merited hatred, on account of all his robberies and banditry, and because that sacrilegious man, in contempt of God, had seized the lord pope while he was assisting at the altar during the solemn celebration of Mass, dragged him away, and imprisoned him in his own tower. In this contest of obedience, this man of God—a perfect zealot, hostile to heretics, a just judge, a generous distributor of alms, endowed in his assiduity of prayer with great grace of contrition and tears, and an outstanding lover of chastity and continence—had been lawfully married from boyhood and had shortly thereafter become a widower. From then on, in accordance with the apostle’s counsel, he manfully restrained the youthful ardor within him. He was charitable, humble, hospitable, gentle, approachable, steadfast, modest, patient and long-suffering, a follower of peace and truth, and a diligent soldier and administrator of remarkable religious devotion [Col. 0406B]. As a prudent recruit of blessed life and Christian service, he walked in the flesh but did not fight according to the flesh; triumphing in a fortunate martyrdom for justice and faith, he ended his temporal life and immediately gained in its place the ineffable immortality of eternal life, together with the desirable delight of the ever-green Paradise, to be preferred above all things.

He was mourned, as was fitting, by the Roman citizens, but especially by the leading men of the city, with great lamentation and wailing. After magnificent funeral rites had been duly and honorably celebrated according to Roman custom at Saint Peter’s, he was most devoutly placed in a marble tomb in the midst of that same Paradise, with the gracious offering of praises and hymns. Thus, in a burial most fitting for him, he was earnestly commended by all to God and to Saint Peter [Col. 0406C].

At last, however, it became clear to everyone how intensely he had served the civic community during his life and how truly he had used the world as though he did not use it, when his greatness before God became increasingly evident through so many miracles and virtues—not only to the Romans, but also to all who continually flocked there from every direction. Indeed, God performed so many great wonders there through his merits that some could scarcely be persuaded that they had truly occurred, namely, his rivals. Therefore, to refute publicly the envy-laden disbelief of such people, certain miracles performed there were publicly read out at the next Roman synod [Note: [Col. 0406D] In March 1078.], under the testimony of so many men of such great authority and reliability [Col. 0406D], and committed to writing. No one ought in any way to doubt the truthfulness of their account.

One event, which was regarded with no little wonder among the Romans, is reported to have occurred while he was still alive, in that same year as his killing. One day, when he had entered a certain oratory for the sake of prayer, before he had finished praying two hairs, a finger’s length, had grown from the thumb of his hand. When he saw this [Note: [Col. 0407] *uisa* (“seen”) in witness 2.], he was greatly astonished, together with all to whom he immediately showed it, and he used to wonder about it sufficiently both then and thereafter.

At the same synod, certain miracles were likewise read out that had occurred at Milan, at the tomb of the lord Erlebal[d]us [Note: [Col. 0407D] On Saint Erlebal[d]us, or Arlembard, see Arnulf of Milan, *History*, Book III, chapter 14 and following. The Bollandists discuss him more fully in volume V of the June *Acta Sanctorum*, under 27 June, p. 279 and following, where his killing is assigned to the year 1075; Pagi, however, in his *Critique of Baronius*, assigns it to 1076, although he also discusses him under the years 1057, 1061, 1066, 1067, 1071, 1072, 1074, and 1076. Arnulf likewise describes the death of Arlembard, as he calls him, in *History of Milan*, Book IV, chapter 10 (*Murat., Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. IV, p. 39, and *Leibnit., Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, vol. III, p. 727); there too his excessive zeal is not free from criticism. Compare Gregory VII, Book I, letters 25–28. Uss.], who himself had suffered for justice three years earlier. Credible persons testified there to the complete truth of these events, and the written records in which they had been preserved demonstrated their authenticity.

He too was a most eloquent preacher and, under secular dress, a most diligent champion of God; he restored canonical discipline and observance and resisted the heretical Nicolaitans and Simonians with such zeal for God that scarcely any of them remained uncorrected or unconverted throughout the entire diocese of Milan [Col. 0407B]. If anyone was found rebellious and disobedient to canonical rigor, he immediately took his military bands with him and compelled him to submit to canonical discipline, or drove him out, or captured and imprisoned him, and plundered and destroyed everything he possessed.

In revenge for this action, certain Milanese who had been respectful toward and flatterers of their simoniacal bishop [Note: [Col. 0408D] Gothefredus.], whom he himself had opposed with all the strength he could muster, and of King Heinricus, who had imposed that heretic upon them, treacherously and deceitfully killed this outstanding soldier of God for justice, faith, and the obedience that the lord pope Alexander had imposed upon them in such matters. They pierced him simultaneously with five lances. Then, after he had been killed, they brutally prevented his lifeless corpse from being given burial, leaving it in the city street for three days [Col. 0407C] under the force of gladiatorial violence.

On the third night, in the deepest darkness of that night, a light sent from heaven shone over his body for three hours. It was so brilliant that some people more than ten miles from the city did not doubt that the city itself was on fire. Among the many who gathered because of this sign were certain brothers who had been forewarned of it in visions during sleep. They boldly approached, carried away his body, and, after duly performing the offices of prayers and funeral rites and giving thanks to God as was fitting, buried him in the monastery of Saint Celsus the Martyr.

Finally, through many testimonies of virtues and miracles, it was clearly and indisputably demonstrated by divine power that this man of God, so diligent a zealot against heretical depravity, truly was and had been a friend of God [Col. 0407D]. May no soldier of the supreme King and defender of the holy faith hesitate to follow his diligence and intention strongly and joyfully in Christ, if he desires, once the lawful contest has been completed, to be crowned eternally with such a distinguished triumph of heavenly glory [Col. 0408A].

In the same year, a certain woman in Alemannia gave birth to a child who was not very lively and, together with it, to a solitary head resembling that of a human being, without any other human limbs. Yet it was alive and, in all its senses, entirely well formed in human fashion. While that infant was being baptized, as it was soon going to die, the midwives took it, but secretly, because of a certain shame, and gave it the name of a whole human being, baptizing it in the name of the Holy Trinity. But it died not long afterward.

## 1078

King Roudulfus celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously at Goslar in Saxony, with the greatest forces of the Saxon people. King Heinricus, however, staying at Regensburg for only two days in a makeshift and scarcely festive manner, hurried back again to besiege a certain castle from which he had come there [Note: [Col. 0407] *venerat* (“had come”) in that witness.]. He wandered uncertainly through the regions of the eastern part of the Noric Gulf until the middle of Lent, by whatever routes he could find, and devastated that country in a hostile fashion with repeated expeditions of no small extent. From there he also sent his legates, the bishops of Osnabrück and Verdun [Note: [Col. 0408D] Benno and Theoderic.], to Rome, to the apostolic lord and the Roman synod, to conduct his case there.

As for the apostolic legation and the letters of the Roman cardinal containing admonitions, he completely ignored them—with contempt, trampling, and disobedience, which he openly professed before everyone with all his strength—by means of an extremely crafty pretext, pretending as though he had never heard anything, or scarcely anything, about them.
