He also awaited the return of these men from the synod to Regensburg with no little anxiety; for, as his conscience itself deserved, he did not doubt that they would bring him something new from the apostolic see that he most earnestly wished not to hear.

King Roudulfus, likewise, together with all his supporters, had sent their legates to the same synod—not the men they would have preferred, but whatever men they could—and had sent them under every kind of contrived and evasive pretext. They charged them to offer the apostolic lord true obedience in every respect and, by unanimous request, diligently urged him to regard with paternal concern the tyrannical and most grievous desolation of the holy Church [Col. 0408D].

King Heinricus’s legates, because they could travel openly and accomplish everything they wished according to their peaceful convenience both in Lombardy and in the city of Rome, never ceased to draw everyone, from the least to the greatest, into favor of their king by gifts, lies, promises, flatteries, tearful complaints, and every art and device—for they were extremely experienced in such matters—corrupting, deceiving, and leading them astray. Conversely, they did everything to arouse the greatest hatred and calumny against King Roudulfus [Col. 0409A].

Then, at the appointed time [Note: [Col. 0409D] Lent began this year on 21 February.], that is, on the third day before the Nones of March, the synod was begun in canonical order. It consisted of nearly seventy bishops [Note: [Col. 0409D] In the acts of the council, *Mansi* XX, p. 503, the number 100 is read, and the date is given as the fifth day before the Nones of March.], among whom was Bishop Albanus [Note: [Col. 0409D] Peter; see above, col. 352.]. This was the same man who, among the brothers dwelling in the Florentine episcopate, in a place called Vallombrosa, passed unharmed through fire and a flame twelve feet long. By clear judgment he proved that Peter, who was called bishop of the Florentine Church, had truly been a simoniacal heretic and that, for this reason, he was not to be received, nor were his heretical offices to be accepted.

A bishop from the region of Gaul was also present there, the bishop of Die, who had become a bishop not by human but by divine election [Note: [Col. 0409D] This concerns Hugh, bishop of Die, formerly chamberlain of Lyon, who was installed in place of the simoniacal Lancelin on 19 October 1073, as Hugh of Flavigny writes in his *Chronicle of Verdun*. Uss.]. For, while he was traveling from his home toward Rome for the sake of prayer, he arrived at the city of Die, intending to spend the night there. The legate of the apostolic see, Gerald, bishop of Ostia, who at that very time had assembled a council there for the Church’s benefit and needs, saw him and was greatly pleased at his arrival, since he had known him and been his close friend.

He immediately kissed him and said: “You have come at the right time, because, with God as our guide, we shall have you as bishop and provider in place of the bishop of this Church, which has been deprived of and abandoned by its bishop.” [Col. 0409C] Smiling modestly, he thought that Gerald had said this jokingly. Then, when he realized that the words had truly been spoken seriously and not in jest, he scarcely managed to obtain from him a delay until the following day in which to answer.

Throughout that night he planned with all his strength how he might somehow evade the burden of pastoral care. Without his companions’ knowledge, he secretly slipped away from them alone and crept into a hiding place in a church there, intending to conceal himself. When morning came, and he could not be found despite a long and thorough search everywhere, the apostolic legate, taking with him the clergy and the entire people in sizable processions, went devoutly around those churches with litanies and supplications, seeking him from the Lord.

When they reached the church where the fugitive was hiding, a light sent from heaven shone over him and exposed God’s chosen man [Col. 0409D]. Thus exposed, he was compelled to undertake the summit of government, which he had humbly fled from the depths of his heart, submitting to the divine arrangement, although unwillingly.

He always kept with him men of such great authority and reverence. In their counsel, as a faithful and prudent dispenser of God’s mysteries, he most diligently placed the outcome of his concern and his faithful decisions [Col. 0410A].

At the same synod, King Heinricus’s legates, greatly encouraged and confident in the many supporters whom they had somehow attached to themselves, publicly promised on behalf of their lord, first of all, obedience to the apostolic lord in every respect and obedience that could be proved by any means. Finally, they complained at length about the injuries done to their cause—first before the apostolic lord himself, and then before the entire assembly—having been thoroughly equipped for this purpose with every method and device and being sufficiently fluent in rhetorical complaint.

All his supporters, as though it were an entirely just cause [Note: [Col. 0409] *justissima* (“most just”) in witness 2.], echoed their murmurs in agreement and strongly urged that it be decided by apostolic and synodal judgment [Col. 0410B].

The position of this case was as follows: Roudulfus, duke and soldier of King Heinricus, had been bound by the security of oaths to stand by Heinricus as a faithful man and indivisible supporter in everything relating to the protection of his kingdom. Yet, they claimed, Roudulfus had unjustly expelled Heinricus from his kingdom, as a perjurer and traitor together with his other supporters, and had thereafter rashly invaded the kingdom himself.

They declared that their lord had not brought this complaint because he was unable to suppress his adversaries—for he could do so very easily—but chiefly because it seemed just and proper to him first to appeal to the apostolic see for a decision in the matter. Certain judges who were favorably disposed toward their intention readily agreed that, for so manifest and sacrilegious a crime, King Roudulfus deserved to be condemned without delay by a sentence of apostolic anathema [Col. 0410C]. They pressed very strongly for this to be decreed judicially and carried out canonically.

The apostolic lord, however, fully understood the disturbance surrounding the case before him, and flattering argument could not easily lead him, as a man not readily seduced, into accepting persons’ claims. Before a careful examination of both sides, and while the truth concerning the excommunication already imposed by his cardinal still hung entirely in doubt, he openly declared that he could decide nothing about it.

He stated that he had heard many times of the obedience, legates, and proclamations of both kings. A considerable part of the kingdom’s leading men, bishops, wise men, and religious men followed each of them by different paths and in agreement with him [Col. 0410D]. He therefore announced that, for a matter of this kind, he would necessarily seek counsel at an appropriate time from the leading men and magistrates of the holy Roman see, as well as from everyone else whom he could consult and from all sound-minded men, lest the apostolic see decide anything unjustly against either of them [Col. 0411A].

He earnestly begged and admonished everyone to pray together to God with the utmost devotion for this purpose, so that God might deign to inspire him with the spirit of divine counsel, and, with God’s help, the holy mother Church, miserably scattered by so many heresies, schisms, and discord, might deserve to be united and pacified in Christ.

Thus the sentence was postponed until Saturday. Meanwhile, other matters beneficial and necessary for the Church were carefully considered and defined there with canonical diligence.

The apostolic lord and all those who counseled with him in Christ found and established the following prudent and sufficiently judicious plan concerning King Heinricus’s complaint: the apostolic lord himself, or suitable legates in his place [Col. 0411B], should come to the German regions; and, at a place most suitable for the purpose, the leading men, wise men, and all the nobles of the entire kingdom, excluding both kings, should meet them. There, after a conference had been held, the entire case of both kings would be most justly examined and debated, without regard to persons, and would be either justified or rejected by all. Thus, by the common, prudent, and most just judgment and counsel of everyone, it would be irrevocably decided how the kingdom—which had become so miserably schismatic and perjured against itself—might at least now not be completely destroyed, but rather might be rationally strengthened, united, and restored in the peace of Christ [Note: [Col. 0411D] On this and what follows, compare the acts of the fourth Roman council, *Mansi* XX, p. 503. The author also had before him Gregory’s letter to the Germans, *Register* V.15, p. 248, and 16.].

On Saturday, the apostolic lord, lawfully and properly prepared for this purpose, entered the synod with his suffragan bishops and publicly set forth the plan described above. When everyone had approved it, he immediately spoke with confidence and armed himself with apostolic authority. He universally condemned with the bond of everlasting and greatly feared anathema all persons—whether kings, dukes, bishops, clerics, or anyone at all, great or small—who by tricks, arts, schemes, factions, or any devices deliberately and willingly, in whatever manner, declined or obstructed the agreed conference so that it would not take place; likewise those who in any way opposed the legates of the apostolic see so that they could not reach that conference; and those who refused to uphold and observe irrevocably the decisions that, concerning this cause, this discord, and these enormous seditions, were to be established there by the apostolic legates and the other leading men, nobles, and wise men of the kingdom, named and chosen for this task, when all had agreed together on the same purpose [Col. 0411D].

Thus, while the apostolic lord and his suffragans canonically threw their burning candles onto the ground and extinguished them to complete the aforesaid anathema, this sentence of condemnation was defined. To test King Heinricus’s obedience in this matter first, the apostolic lord earnestly begged and entreated him by the Lord God, and for the sake of his own salvation, to keep peace with all his adversaries until the conference had been completed. Through Heinricus’s legates, he also admonished him with apostolic fatherly concern.

Then, in order to draw him diligently toward agreement by honoring him in every respect, he wisely sent his messengers together with Heinricus’s legates to him, so that, according to his own good pleasure, he himself might determine the time and place of the future conference. Once this had been unquestionably made known and announced to the leading men of the kingdom and to all who were to be summoned there, the apostolic messenger would return to Rome, so that the legates of the apostolic see appointed and chosen for this purpose might, at the proper time and by the right route, arrive at the gathering concerning the matter at hand as suitable advisers, mediators, and correctors [Col. 0412B].

The apostolic lord then dismissed the royal legates, but without the apostolic blessing that they were to bring back to the king. This was because rumor had spread everywhere that he had already been excommunicated by the apostolic legates [Note: [Col. 0412D] See the year 1077, cols. 401–402.], although this was only a doubtful supposition. He then turned effectively to the other matters that still remained to be completed synodally.

At the same synod, a sentence of anathema was pronounced against the bishops of Ravenna, Milan, Cremona [Note: [Col. 0411] The edition reads “of Crema.”], and Treviso, as well as against all simoniacal heretics and Nicolaitans who obstinately and disobediently persisted by their will and determination in the madness of their error [Col. 0412C]. It was directed especially against those who, within two years, in their rashness, obstinacy, and incontinence, had through apostate presumption resumed ecclesiastical orders that they had acquired for themselves by payment of money and then abandoned, as well as concubines forbidden to them.

There were indeed not a few of these in our regions, rising madly in public tyranny against the authentic sanctions of the sacred canons. By judicial sentence, all orders and consecrations—except baptism alone—were also irrevocably removed from those who had presumed to have themselves ordained, or rather de-ordained, anywhere by bishops deprived by apostolic sanction of office and priestly dignity, and not yet restored to their order either by themselves or through a properly appointed legate of the apostolic lord [Col. 0412D]. It was also judged and decreed there that any churches consecrated by them, since they had never been canonically initiated for God, ought to be reconsecrated from the beginning.

A sentence of anathema was also pronounced against laymen of every rank, against clerics, and against all persons who, contrary to the decrees of the sacred canons, presumed to give as a benefice to any cleric or any person, according to their former usurpation, bishoprics, abbacies, provostships, churches of any kind, tithes, or any ecclesiastical dignities. Likewise anathematized were those who presumed to hand over or grant, with a lay and unconsecrated hand, to be managed and arranged by consecrated ministers of God’s altar and ecclesiastical administration, what had first been legally assigned by canonical and legitimate transfer to the Lord God as property and service—as though it were some private and hereditary possession [Col. 0413A].

A sentence was also pronounced there that anyone who presumed to carry out plunder, robbery, or any contrived and reckless invasion in churches consecrated to God, or in their churchyards and cemeteries, or likewise in consecrated cloisters, or in any ecclesiastical goods, possessions, or appurtenances belonging to them, should be anathema [Col. 0413B]. These particular provisions are understood to apply especially to the daily prebends and every kind of provision of food and necessary expenses separately and, as it were, specifically designated and decreed for canons, clerics, priests, monks, holy virgins, and all who serve Christ under a rule.

The apostolic lord had chiefly aimed at this in such decrees: that, once peace had been established among the churches, even though wars and seditions might reign everywhere in secular affairs, the canonical praises and prayers of God among spiritual persons should nevertheless not cease for lack of external support [Note: [Col. 0413] *ab* (“from”) in witness 2.].

Since, however, the stumbling blocks caused by subordinates must sometimes prudently be disregarded, but at other times, once openly recognized, must be patiently endured until the proper time for their correction—and since remedies are appropriate only when the time is right—the apostolic lord, a prudent dissimulator and endurer, had deferred until a suitable time the heretical depravity, disobedience, and thousands of presumptuous scandals of many bishops and priests in the German and Italian regions. He did so in order that, after the great schisms of the kingdom’s princes and nobles, divided and warring among themselves in that highly seditious and more than civil controversy, had somehow been calmed by God’s agency and legitimately joined together in the peace of Christ, he might not delay applying his most diligent care to correcting, reproving, and punishing those matters as well [Col. 0413D].

After secretly and furtively dismissing King Roudulfus’s legates with a cautious and deliberately evasive permission, since he had no doubt that Roudulfus was entirely obedient and in agreement with him and with the apostolic see, he carefully instructed them to convey to him paternal love, compassion, and favor, together with apostolic indulgence and blessing. The same was to be conveyed to all, great and small, who continued unanimously in the peace of Christ to submit obediently to and support the commands and decrees of the apostolic see, both in their intention and in their will [Col. 0414A].

King Heinricus, finally, having awaited at Regensburg certain of his legates who had hurried ahead of the others and had gathered there with him, then departed from there somewhat sorrowfully and hastened to Mainz, where he intended to celebrate Palm Sunday. From there he proceeded to Cologne, gathering with him as many of his troops as he could. There too he celebrated Easter without much glory.

After his legates had returned to him with the messengers of the apostolic see and with the apostolic legation itself, he carefully learned from their truthful report everything that had been done and decreed at the Roman synod. He immediately devoted all his attention, with his usual crafty folly, to the familiar schemes, taking his secret advisers with him [Col. 0414B]. They all counseled and contrived with the greatest subtlety and exertion that they might appear to have freed themselves from that apostolic excommunication without observing or obeying the apostolic command and decree, and that they might impose upon King Roudulfus and all the associates of the opposing party, as though by the most reasonable justice, the burden of the Roman anathema that in reality threatened them because of their manifest guilt.

King Roudulfus, meanwhile, having gathered a considerable number of his Saxon princes and soldiers, celebrated Easter solemnly enough at Goslar. There, a certain canon of the Church of Augsburg, who had already been appointed provost of the Church of Saint Maurice and had been found to be a highly venerable and well-educated cleric named Wigoldus, was canonically elected by the clergy and people and by the better and greater part of the ecclesiastical army [Col. 0414C]. On Easter Day he was canonically consecrated and ordained bishop through the election and suffrage of the Roman cardinal, his metropolitan and archbishop of Mainz, and nine other bishops who had assembled there [Note: [Col. 0413] The words *ibi non* (“not there”) are absent from witness 1.].

After everything relating to his ordination had been lawfully completed, namely, after he had received the ring, pastoral staff, and episcopal chair from the archbishop of Mainz, the king carefully entrusted to him, on his own behalf, whatever belonged to royal jurisdiction in the administration of ecclesiastical goods. For, being obedient in all things, he took care to observe what had recently been canonically defined at the Roman synod and, after the judicial sentence had been pronounced, prohibited under anathema: that no layman should grant churches, ecclesiastical tithes, or dignities to anyone as his own property, or presume to usurp them against the canons [Col. 0414D].

Moreover, the archbishop of Mainz ordered Sigifridus, who had been noncanonically appointed bishop of Augsburg by King Heinricus, not rashly to invade his diocese any further after notice had been given. Otherwise he separated him and all who agreed with him entirely from the members of the Church by a just anathema. He threatened the same thing to the canons and people of Augsburg if they did not receive their elected bishop, as was worthy and just [Col. 0415A].

Thus the bishop of Augsburg, having received permission from the king, returned to his own country and prudently withdrew with his men to a certain castle near the Alpine passes [Note: [Col. 0415D] Füssen.], because it was extremely strong and well fortified, intending to await there the restoration of peace to the Church. Immediately, however, he was attacked and harassed by the people of Augsburg through the infliction of numerous injuries. He endured this for some time with whatever patience and long-suffering he could muster and devoutly commended himself and his men to God, the judge and defender.

After Easter, King Heinricus immediately returned to Mainz and gathered to his side everyone whom he could approach by whatever means. Therefore, by terrifying or flattering speeches and inducements designed to draw the Saxon nobles to him, he had it announced under the name and pretext of the apostolic legation and its sentence that, for the sake of arranging peace and calming the many schisms and discords of the entire kingdom, they should meet certain leading men and nobles of the kingdom at Fritzlar [Col. 0415B].

When the Saxon princes, gladly receiving this message and skillfully encouraged to the undertaking by King Roudulfus, tried to come at the appointed time and make the attempt, King Heinricus sent no one there from the leading men of the kingdom except certain of his secret advisers. Thus, when they realized that they had been deceived and decided to return from there in anger, they nevertheless agreed—because those court officials, masters of intrigue, earnestly begged them—to grant them an opportunity to confer with them and test their intentions [Col. 0415C].

There they heard nothing from them except lies and what amounted to threats supposedly made against them by the apostolic lord, on the grounds that they had unlawfully and unjustly deposed their lord and king as perjurers and faithless men. They made no truthful mention there of the proposed conference or of the apostolic anathema. In their false and stubborn determination, they imposed the entire sequence of that sentence upon King Roudulfus and his supporters.

Finally, after hearing these things and making it entirely clear why they had come there, the Saxons did not want the others to think that they regarded themselves as guilty of the charges brought against them or as afraid of the arrival and sentence of the lord pope. Rather, they wished to demonstrate that they were exceedingly eager and joyful. They all praised the conference that had been arranged and firmly declared, with steadfast courage and complete freedom of speech, that they would scarcely be able to wait for the arrival of the apostolic lord or his legates and that they would observe in every respect his decisions, as well as those of all the leading men of the kingdom concerning this matter [Col. 0415D].

They affirmed and entirely adjudged that all who were disobedient to the apostolic lord and who, by any device, trick, or folly, resisted his judicial sentence in this matter had been anathematized and truly separated from the members of the Church [Col. 0416A]. To settle such a controversy between the two parties publicly and reasonably, they had sent their own legate with them to their lord and to the other princes of the kingdom who agreed with him. Through him, the place and time of the conference would be announced to them, and he would declare that they were fully prepared and ready to come there, if the Lord willed, setting aside every necessity and doubt.

After this controversial exchange had continued for some time on both sides, but had finally been commendably concluded by the Saxons’ aforesaid unanswerable and just reasoning and obedience, peace was mutually commended until the future conference, and each party departed for home from the other.

King Heinricus’s advisers, taking the Saxon legate with them, set out toward their lord in the direction of the Rhine [Col. 0416B]. The just and truthful speech of the Saxon princes had not been agreeable to their hearts. They had gone out with an entirely different purpose and intention, namely, to make every possible attempt to bring the Saxons over to their side. When they could not accomplish this, they immediately returned and spread a false report everywhere: that the Saxons had certainly given hostages, entered into a peace agreement with their lord, and unquestionably secured the permanence of his favor.

They sent the Saxon legate back with this message: the king would not grant a place for a conference to anyone, but he was ready to do so for the sake of and out of love for the apostolic lord, so that anyone who rebelled against him might be received back into his favor, provided only that he showed himself submissive to the king with repentance and obedience [Col. 0416C].

The Saxons and King Roudulf, having learned this, openly judged and affirmed that he was excommunicated together with all his adherents, because he had so stubbornly and disobediently annulled the conference so irrevocably decreed by the apostolic lord. They also utterly disregarded the peace which the king’s secretaries and the Saxons had agreed upon among themselves, before the aforesaid legate returned to them: those who were on King Heinricus’s side had invaded and captured a certain castle, in violation of the pledged faith.

The bishop of Metz, together with many other Lotharingians who in those same days had come to King Heinricus, led by their loyalty, to see whether they could persuade him to incline toward the apostolic will, openly declared, after hearing of the contempt shown toward the apostolic legation, that they would remain and persevere on the side of the apostolic lord. They therefore returned home with his displeasure. He immediately pursued them, taking with him Duke Theoderic and other troops of his soldiers; by surprise and deceit he seized the city of Metz, drove out the bishop and the others, installed his own garrisons there, and proceeded to the city of Strasbourg, which he entered [Note: [Col. 0415] Uss. corrected *egressus* (“having gone out”) to *ingressus* (“having entered”), without evident reason.] [Col. 0417A].

There he remained during Rogation Days and, against the will of the canons and the ban of the apostolic lord, enthroned as bishop Thiepaldus [Note: [Col. 0417] The editor prints *thietpaldum*.], provost of Constance and also his own chaplain. The canons, because they had already been forbidden on the part of the lord pope to receive anyone from King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0417] The editor prints *est canonici* (“the canons have been”); the supplied text reads *est*.], had unanimously resolved canonically to elect for themselves, in Christ, whomever they should choose. But because those canons of Saint Thomas had given very great approval and praise to this man’s promotion, they soon experienced divine vengeance. For fire completely consumed the church, the cloister, all their buildings, and their fireplaces. Thereafter King Heinricus, intending to invade Alemannia but unable to gather enough men to carry this out without danger, turned aside into Bavaria. There he celebrated Pentecost at Regensburg, and Margrave Liutpaldus [Note: [Col. 0417D] Of Austria.] returned, somewhat offended with him.

The apostolic legate who had come to King Heinricus at Easter to arrange the conference decreed by the pope was initially kept in concealment for some time, because he had announced the apostolic legation with complete freedom, despite the king’s unwillingness and refusal and his utter disregard for the threats contained in the legate’s message. Thus, in the suspicion of many, he was thought secretly to have been killed or exiled. At last, however, he was treated and maintained by the king with public reverence and honor. Some suppose that he was detained for a time on this pretext: so that the king might, through him, defend himself in some fashion against the excommunication imposed upon him [Col. 0417C]. For since everyone saw the apostolic legate communicating with him, no one considered or avoided him as an excommunicated man; rather, they firmly regarded as a lie whatever was being said everywhere about the judgment of the Roman synod and the decree of the anathema. For just as King Roudulf could publicly display the Roman cardinal as a witness to his obedience, so Heinricus could display the apostolic legate before everyone as a witness to his own obedience and innocence [Note: [Col. 0417] The editor prints *ostendere* (“to show”) rather than *ostentare* (“to display”).]

King Roudulf magnificently celebrated Pentecost at Goslar, where a considerable multitude of Saxon and Thuringian princes had gathered. There, after taking counsel with them, he prepared and organized an expedition against King Heinricus. The envoys of King Philippus of France, of the Flemings, and of many Lotharingians, as well as of the king of the Hungarians, had also come to him there, promising most earnestly, for the sake of God and Saint Peter, to give him aid in defense of the holy Church and of the whole kingdom of the Germans—although they did not altogether fulfill their promise in the manner promised.

Thereafter, throughout the whole summer, numerous movements had arisen everywhere through Alemannia, Alsace, and Western Franconia [Col. 0418A]. In private wars, men on the side of King Heinricus were defeated, killed, and put to flight; these reckless violators had committed many plunderings, burnings, and sacrileges within the sacred churches themselves. The anti-bishops of Basel and Strasbourg barely escaped by flight, after their soldiers had been defeated and captured in a fierce battle by Margrave Berthold [Note: [Col. 0417D] Berthold II.], son of Duke Berthold [Note: [Col. 0417] The editor prints *B. 2.*], while the peasants whom they had compelled by sworn obligation from every district of their counties to come to their aid were partly castrated.

During that same period, Dukes Berthold and Welf had devastated much of Francia on this side of the Rhine with plunder and fires.

Meanwhile each king was preparing an expedition against the other with no little zeal and equipment, gathering military forces from everywhere and by every means [Col. 0418B]. Around the Kalends of August, the aforesaid dukes, with the Alemannic army, were planning to meet King Roudulf as he came forth from Saxony. But King Heinricus intervened with a very great army and prevented this from happening. Thus, while they daily expected a battle and eagerly sought opportunities to carry out their purpose, though not without considerable danger, they took up positions close to the king. Moreover, they had to endure nearby the country peasants, sworn together against them throughout all the hundreds of those regions and equipped with military arms, nearly twelve thousand in number, exceptionally warlike and hostile to them.

In this way King Heinricus, confident in his very great army, planned—first to triumph over the Saxons and then over the Alemannians—after separating the Saxons and Alemannians from one another and preventing them by every means from meeting or even deliberating among themselves through messengers about what they ought to do amid such pressing dangers [Col. 0418C]. He did not doubt that this could be accomplished very easily and without loss to his own men.

When he had communicated this plan to his followers, he deceitfully sent certain scouts, men of no low rank, to King Roudulf and to the leading Saxons, ostensibly to confirm peace between them. After this had been agreed between the parties and temporarily confirmed by the customary treaty on both sides, while the scouts were hastening back to their lord, Heinricus, having cunningly deceived them, suddenly and almost without warning attacked them with armed force and a warlike assault while they were unprepared [Col. 0418D].

King Roudulf, barely rushing out of the camp with his men as quickly as possible, prudently arranging and encouraging his battle lines against the threatening enemy as far as the circumstances permitted, engaged him with such exceptional courage that, with God granting the victory, he immediately gained a glorious triumph in the first encounter, overthrowing the first two legions within a short time. Without delay, the king himself, the first in rank, shamefully took flight with his closest companions [Note: [Col. 0417] *h.*—a fourteenth-century gloss in manuscript 2: “Heinricus.”] The rest of the army, seeing what was happening, unmilitary, fearful, and wonderfully terrified, also tried anxiously by every possible means to save themselves in flight in different directions [Col. 0419A].

The Saxons pursued them for more than three miles, pressing fiercely upon the fugitives from behind. On King Heinricus’s side, more than thirty of the nobility and, as they say, about five thousand of the lesser men lay slain; on the opposing side, they testify that only about eighty of the lesser men fell. Moreover, the bishops of that same side [Note: [Col. 0419] That is, Roudulf’s side; a fourteenth-century gloss in manuscript 2.], who were present there, having heard from certain fugitives who spread false reports that King Heinricus had won, fled in different directions with their men. Among them, the Roman cardinal was exposed to considerable danger. The bishop of Parthenopolis [Note: [Col. 0419] Manuscript 2 abbreviates this as *partenop.*] was struck by an arrow in the forests where they were seeking a hiding place from Slavic robbers. The bishop of Paderborn, captured and stripped, escaped from them almost naked; and the bishop of Worms, likewise captured, was handed over to King Heinricus together with a certain noble count, Herimannus.

After so many troops of the enemy had been routed [Note: [Col. 0419] Manuscript 2 reads *Profugatis* (“after being put to flight”) instead of *Profligatis* (“after being defeated”).] and killed, the Saxons returned joyfully to the site of the first battle and to their camps. Spending the night there, they took counsel with their king the next day and received from him, according to the law of their people, the assurance that they, victorious in battle, were not to advance farther. They therefore returned to their own Saxony with great rejoicing as triumphant victors.

King Heinricus, however, had proceeded without delay as far as Bavaria. For it is not surprising that he feared an attack by the Alemannians: on that very day, on the other side, they had fought against the allied hundreds of the Franks, utterly routed them in a very fierce battle, and castrated them [Note: [Col. 0419] I have corrected the supplied reading to *dimicabant* (“they were fighting”); manuscript 2 and the edition read *dimicabat* (“he was fighting”).] They too, having learned the truth about the flight of the enemy and the victory and return of their own king, rejoiced with their people in their success. After devastating everything in all directions with fires and plunder and storming many towns of their adversaries, they returned home triumphantly and exultantly.

At last, the falsifiers and fabricators of King Heinricus’s lies shamelessly asserted throughout the surrounding lands that their lord had returned victorious from the Saxon war. They had thus brought it about that he commended these inventions of theirs by letters to the lord pope, the Romans, and all the Lombards [Col. 0419D]. In those same days, the abbot of Marseille, a legate of the apostolic see who had been present with the Alemannian dukes during the aforesaid expedition and to whom the whole course of the wars had been completely known, perceived that he had neither achieved nor was likely to achieve any progress in the legation entrusted to him or in ecclesiastical usefulness among the adversaries of the apostolic see. He therefore hastened back to Rome to the one who had sent him, as an indefatigable destroyer of lies and a truly competent witness to sincere truth [Col. 0420A]. Thereafter he himself, and others as well, testified in orderly fashion to the lord pope and to the others about the indisputable course of events; the remarkable lies had caused many to waver greatly and had left them distressed [Note: [Col. 0419] Manuscript 2 lacks *nec* (“nor”).]

Then, as autumn followed, King Heinricus, having gathered military forces from every direction, once again pretended to organize an expedition into Saxony. When he learned that King Roudulf’s very large army had arrived to meet him in battle, he led into Alemannia to devastate it the perjured men whom he had gathered under oath against the Saxons.

There he hired the worst and most inhuman brigands from Bohemia, Bavaria, Burgundy, France, and wherever else he could, as well as from Alemannia itself. As a most savage despiser of God, he miserably persisted everywhere in plunder, fires, the destruction of castles and some towns, and unheard-of sacrileges against divine sanctuaries [Col. 0420B]. There was no distinction between sacred and profane, and amid so many miseries there was no compassion.

For the sacrilegious and presumptuous men had miserably burned and plundered the churches to which the inhabitants of the land had fled for the preservation of themselves and their possessions [Note: [Col. 0419] Manuscript 2 reads *mirabiliter* (“wonderfully”) instead of *miserabiliter* (“miserably”).] They trampled priests dressed in sacred vestments, leaving them half naked and cruelly beaten. They destroyed the altars of the saints after removing the relics from them. Upon the altars they defecated—something unheard of among pagans—and bloodied them by placing upon them the flesh of their plundered animals, torn into pieces. The women whom they had captured in the churches they shamelessly violated there as though in a brothel [Col. 0420C]. They set up stables for their horses and animals in the churches, as well as latrines. They also violated some women until death overcame them; many others, having been shorn like men and dressed in men’s clothing, they led away captive. At Altdorf and elsewhere they beheaded wooden images of Christ crucified, cutting off the head, hands, and feet.

Why say more? Violating every sacred and divine thing, they polluted it in every way with a madness worse than that of pagans.

All these things were done with the permission granted by the bishops who, together with them, had invaded the churches of God. This detestable trampling down and desolation of the holy Church occurred around the feast of All Saints. At that time, somewhat fewer than one hundred churches were violated during that expedition [Col. 0420D]. Yet these things were by no means done with impunity [Note: [Col. 0419] The editor inserts *omnia* (“all these things”).] For some of them, as they say, were seized by unclean spirits and tormented until death; others were killed, captured, or stripped by the Alemannian princes; and most of them were hacked to pieces and mutilated [Note: [Col. 0419] *euaricati* is a fourteenth-century correction in manuscript 2 for the supplied *enaricati*.]. Thus, after Alemannia had been miserably devastated, they returned home, burdened with no small loads of plunder and sacrilege, rejoicing though without a complete triumph.

In those days Duke Berthold, a devoted lover and zealous defender of the Christian religion, a man who, before God and the world, cultivated an honorable life with sobriety and order, most ardently devoted to justice and peace, moderation and discipline, mercy and zeal for God, and exceedingly skilled in carrying out the laws and dignities inherited from his fathers, a man of great counsel, exceptionally prudent, and sufficiently virtuous in every moral excellence, commended his whole soul, as was fitting, to God’s hands in hope and faith. Having prudently ordered his household, he closed the final day of his life in a happy consummation—oh, that it had been the happiest!

Hildulfus, that simoniacal bishop of Cologne who had been imposed upon it, condemned on earth by the judgment of apostolic authority as a heretic, thief, and robber, departed this world in the same autumn, eternally bound also in heaven.

A great synod was held at Rome, both because of the many necessities of the holy Church and especially to subdue, by whatever means possible, the tyranny of King Heinricus. At it, the envoys of both kings, speaking on behalf of their lords, protested and testified under oath that their lords were innocent, in that they would in no way, by any art or device, impede the conference which the lord pope had established under anathema at the next synod so that no one should obstruct it. The envoys of King Roudulf were believed by the best men with complete confidence; the others were accused of perjury.

At last they attempted to extort from the apostolic lord an anathema against King Roudulf for invading the kingdom. But, on the contrary, the whole synod scarcely supported them [Note: [Col. 0421D] That is, “abstained.”], lest it judicially turn that sentence against King Heinricus on account of his disobedience, the many sacrileges mentioned above, and his most crafty deceptions through lies [Note: [Col. 0421] Manuscript 2 reads *juridicialiter* (“judicially”) here.]. A truce for conversion and response until the next synod, or sooner, having been granted him [Note: [Col. 0421D] The subject of “might turn it” is evidently the synod.], they returned home in disgrace and confusion, without the apostolic blessing.

Among them was Eigilbertus, provost of Passau, who had already been judicially excommunicated by his own bishop. Returning to King Heinricus in this perjured state, he was placed by him, with his customary violence, over the church of Trier in a simoniacal manner, after the man canonically elected by the clergy and people had been rejected [Note: [Col. 0421] The editor adds *episcopus* (“bishop”).]—against the will and refusal of everyone [Col. 0421D]. [Note: [Col. 0422D] 8 January 1079.]

At the same synod the following decretal judgments were issued with universal agreement and subscription [Note: [Col. 0422D] Mansi, vol. XX, p. 507.]:

> “Whoever among soldiers of any order or profession has received or shall receive ecclesiastical estates from a king or secular prince, or from bishops, abbots, or any other rulers of churches, against their will; or has invaded or shall invade them; or has held them with their consent, unless he restores those estates to the churches, shall be subject to excommunication.

> “If any man of the Normans invades the estates of the monastery of blessed Benedict on Monte Cassino, or unjustly takes away any of the property of that monastery, and, after being admonished twice or three times, does not make correction, he shall be subject to excommunication until he comes to his senses and satisfies the Church.

> “Because we have learned that the investiture of churches by laymen, contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, is carried out in many parts of the world, and that from this many disturbances arise in the Church, indeed the ruin of holy religion, by which the dignity of Christian discipline itself is trampled underfoot, we have perceived and decree that no cleric shall receive from the hand of an emperor, king, or any lay person, man or woman, the investiture of a bishopric, abbey, church, provostry, or any clerical dignity. If anyone should presume to do so, let him recognize that the investiture is void by apostolic authority and that he is subject to excommunication until he has made worthy satisfaction.

> “If any bishop has sold prebends, archdeaconries, provostries, or any ecclesiastical offices, or has otherwise appointed them than the statutes of the holy Fathers prescribe, let him be suspended from office. For it is fitting that, just as he received the bishopric freely, so he should distribute the members of that bishopric or dignity freely.

> “Ordinations which are carried out with payment intervening, or through petitions, or through service rendered to some person for that purpose, or without the common consent of the clergy and people according to the canonical sanctions, and which are not approved by those to whom consecration belongs, we judge to be false and invalid. For those who are ordained in this way do not enter through the door—that is, through Christ—but, as the Truth itself testifies, they are thieves and robbers.

> “We call those penances false which are not imposed according to the authority of the holy Fathers and in proportion to the offenses. Therefore, whenever a soldier, merchant, or person devoted to an office that cannot be exercised without sin, entangled in more serious faults, comes to penance—that is, a person who unjustly retains another’s property or who harbors hatred in his heart—let him recognize that he cannot perform true penance by which he may attain eternal life unless the soldier lays down his arms and thereafter does not bear them except by the counsel of religious bishops and in defense of justice; and unless the merchant abandons his business, the official leaves his office, each restores whatever he has unjustly taken away, and he abandons hatred from his heart. Nevertheless, let him not despair in the meantime; rather, whatever good he is able to do, we exhort him to do, so that almighty God may enlighten his heart toward penance.

> “We prohibit by apostolic authority that tithes, which canonical authority has sanctioned as granted for the practice of piety, be possessed by laymen. For whether they have received them as property from bishops, kings, or any other persons [Note: [Col. 0423] *idem* (“the same”) is absent from the edition.], unless they restore them to the Church, let them know that they commit the crime of sacrilege and thereby incur the danger of eternal damnation.

> “Because the Sabbath day has been held in honor among our holy Fathers as a day of abstinence, following their authority we salutarily admonish that whoever desires to be a participant in the Christian religion abstain on that day from eating meat, unless a greater feast intervenes or illness prevents it [Col. 0423B].

> “We confirm by apostolic sanction that no abbot shall retain tithes, first fruits, or other things which, according to the statutes of the canons, belong to bishops, without the authority of the Roman pontiff or the consent of the bishop in whose diocese he dwells.

> “No bishop shall impose upon his abbots or clergy any burden or servile service arising from custom contrary to ecclesiastical norm, nor restore a priestly office under interdict when payment has intervened. If he does so, he shall incur the danger of his office [Note: [Col. 0423] The edition reads *id enim* (“for this”), instead of the supplied *idem*.].

> “If anyone has usurped for his own property the estates of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, wherever they may be located, or knowingly has concealed them and failed to reveal them, or has not rendered to Saint Peter the service owed from them, let him recognize that, as a sacrilegious person, he incurs the anger of God and of the holy apostles [Col. 0423C]. Whoever is discovered in this crime shall restore that inheritance to blessed Peter and pay a fourfold penalty from his own goods.

> “If any bishop, through prayers or payment, has consented to the fornication of priests, deacons, or subdeacons, or to the crime of incest in his parish, or has not opposed it by the authority entrusted to his office, let him be suspended from office.

> “Let every Christian take care to offer something to God at the solemn celebration of Mass and recall what God said through Moses: ‘You shall not appear before me empty-handed.’ For it is clearly evident in the Mass collections of the holy Fathers that all Christians, according to the practice of the holy Fathers, ought to offer something to God.”

At the same synod a sentence of anathema was pronounced against all Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, heretics who, hardened in the sect of their error, knowingly and deliberately resist the synodal definitions of the holy Fathers and their decretal statutes, stubbornly opposing them with the perseverance of apostates. Many other measures for the benefit of the Church were also promulgated there besides these, but it is not now the time to list them. It was enacted in the church of the Lord Savior at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of November [Note: [Col. 0423D] The acts give “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.”], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078, indiction 1.

Heinricus, bishop of Chur, died.

## 1079

King Heinricus celebrated Christmas at Mainz without much magnificence. There, contrary to the climate of our region, great flashes of lightning were seen and sufficiently terrifying thunder was heard; a whirlwind of storm tore away and threw to the ground a considerable part of the roof of the episcopal church. Since this happened at that time, it was regarded by everyone as a matter of no little wonder [Col. 0424B].

After this [Note: [Col. 0423D] Apparently at the end of December 1078.], contrary to the apostolic decree, the king appointed over the church of Cologne as bishop a certain Sigwinus, dean of that place, who did not enter canonically through the door. Presuming in turn to receive that investiture from the king’s hand contrary to law, the unfortunate man soon became subject to excommunication. Thereafter the king, remaining in some fashion beside the Rhine until the middle of Lent [Note: [Col. 0423] Manuscript 2 reads *circa* (“around”) instead of *juxta* (“until/beside”).], again gathered together all whom he could privately induce and provoke against apostolic authority, having sworn them to disobedience and rebellion. He not only plotted this privately and secretly, but rather had it proclaimed openly to everyone at Fritzlar, at a conference where the leading Saxons and his closest advisers had gathered in those days: he declared that, in no act or matter whatsoever that concerned him, would he have any care or regard for the apostolic lord [Col. 0424C]. He also proved this by the following action: he contemptuously refused to send the envoys whom the pope, at the previous synod, had decreed that he should send from him to Rome for the next synod, to give responses concerning his case.

After King Roudulf learned that, following the completed battle and the victory he had gained, his aforesaid enemy had again risen against him with a considerable army, he once more attempted in every way to meet him with the fiercest assault of his chosen fighting men. He drove him away from himself in every direction, terrified and stunned [Note: [Col. 0423] Manuscript 2 reads *omnifaria*; the edition reads *omni faria* or *omnino*.]. Having accomplished this, and supposing that on this occasion the other could do nothing except dismiss his army home, he returned gloriously with his men to his own Saxony.

But Heinricus, inflamed with savage fury, unexpectedly invaded Alemannia, as has been said, intending to devastate it. He compelled almost no notable man to surrender or submit to conditions of loyalty except Count Hugo [Note: [Col. 0423D] The Palatine count of Tübingen. We learn from the deeds of Trier that this castle had been besieged by Heinricus at the end of the previous year. Ussing.]. King Roudulf, after dismissing his Saxons home, devoted himself to peace and, according to their laws, to judgments and justice without respect of persons, as justly as he could, with their greatest possible assistance [Col. 0425A].

Soon afterward he was seized by fever and pleurisy with extraordinary violence. He suffered and wasted away for more than two months, so that many people altogether despaired of his life and of any recovery of his health. At last, recovering with great desire after God had healed him through so many dangers, he celebrated Christmas most gloriously and festively at . . . . . . with a considerable company of Saxon princes. Soon before Septuagesima he decided to hasten an expedition against King Heinricus, having gathered his troops from every direction.

When Heinricus first learned this and saw that he could not resist him within so short a period of time, he took counsel with his men and hastily sent envoys—not in his own name but in that of his leading men—to deceive the Saxon princes with the utmost cunning. They were to detest and denounce, in a pretended manner, the wars and seditions, the desolation of the churches, and the enormity of so many crimes; they were to declare most firmly that they and their lord, King Heinricus, agreed with the pope and with all the best men, and that they would obey in every respect in correcting such matters. If the Saxons did not otherwise believe their words, they were to prove them by oaths and the giving of hostages.

When the Saxons heard this, they quickly became too credulous toward men who flattered them so sweetly and, first of all, dissuaded their lord from the expedition he had begun [Col. 0425C]. Then they fixed a certain day in the coming Lent for a conference at Fritzlar. Thus, after secretly agreeing among themselves to a treaty of peace, they departed from one another for home with rejoicing.

When they finally met as they had agreed, the leading men of King Heinricus defended and concealed their inventions and madness as best they could, declaring that they had come for no other reason than to assist the Saxons before their lord, as far as they could, if only the Saxons were willing to submit. Although the Saxons perceived that they had come in vain and had been deceived by the usual frauds and tricks, they nevertheless patiently admonished them that they ought, for their part, to make themselves entirely ready for peace, concord, and obedience to the apostolic see [Col. 0425D].

The others, however, publicly proclaimed with loud cries that neither they nor their lord would have any concern for peace or for the pope. Thus, having renounced both their pledged faith and their peace with one another, they returned home, recklessly provoked.

In those days, before Lent, Duke Welf, taking his fellow soldiers with him, invaded the Raetia of Chur with a powerful force in order to devastate it and engaged in plunder and burning. He subdued the son of Count Otto [Note: [Col. 0425D] Count Otto is recorded as a royal provincial count in Raetia of Chur in a charter of Heinricus IV dated 12 July 1050. His son seems to have been Count Udalricus of Bregenz, as he is called in another diploma of the same king dated 1095 [Col. 0426D]; in both cases, certainly the same county is meant. Ussing. See also Stalin, *History of Württemberg*, p. 559.], together with certain other leading men who had been sworn to King Roudulf. Thereafter, having bravely captured a certain fortified enclosure or palisade, killing, capturing, and putting the enemy to flight, he returned victorious by God’s gift with the greatest force [Note: [Col. 0425] Manuscript 2 reads *egreditur* (“he goes out”) instead of *regreditur* (“he returns”).], intending afterward to subdue certain others.

That same Lent [Note: [Col. 0426D] In that year it began on 7 February.], a great synod was assembled at Rome in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1079, indiction 2, on the third day before the Ides of February. To it the Roman cardinal and the bishops of Passau and Metz came gladly, although traveling by secret routes and barely taking side roads, in order to bring before the apostolic see the many injuries done to themselves and to the churches. By God’s grace they safely passed through many dangerous ambushes and guards [Col. 0426B].

There, as they set forth their cases before the entire synod, the bishops were favorably heard and received. The envoy of King Roudulf [Note: [Col. 0426D] Mansi, vol. XX, p. 525.] carefully enumerated, in an extended complaint, the grievous miseries of the devastation of Alemannia. He also sufficiently exaggerated, in the manner of a formal accuser, the other insanities of King Heinricus’s tyrannical presumption throughout the whole kingdom wherever it appeared. He was graciously heard with his colleagues, amid the tearful sorrow of the lord pope and of very many who shared his compassion, as the circumstances required [Note: [Col. 0425] Manuscript 2 reads *eum* (“him”) instead of the supplied *cum*.].

The envoy of King Heinricus also set forth his lord’s case in some fashion, although it was truly not a very just one, with many people favoring him, as commonly happens [Col. 0426C]. But he and his men were convicted by the pope of falsehood; the others were believed sufficiently and with complete confidence by the best of the others.

Indeed, in public at the synod the lord pope declared that the legation of King Heinricus was deceitful. He also protested that he had judicially deposed him from the kingdom and had not afterward restored him in any way. Therefore he would have immediately anathematized him, except that all those present from both sides preferred that this should be postponed until the Ascension of the Lord, by continuing to wait, chiefly so that the Roman synod might not be accused of having acted precipitately or in disorder against him.

His envoy openly declared that his lord had not craftily but under compulsion of necessity failed to send, as the pope had decreed at the previous synod, envoys who could safely escort the apostolic envoys into the German homeland in order to settle so great a discord [Col. 0426D]. He swore, however, that his lord would send such men to Rome before the Ascension of the Lord and that, in the matter of the kingdom, he would obey the apostolic see in every respect. An oath was also sworn on behalf of King Roudulf that he too would obey the pope in the conference which the pope should establish [Col. 0427A].

Finally, the apostolic lord again excommunicated whoever had impeded, by any device or faction, the conference that was to have taken place in the previous year; likewise, he excommunicated whoever should impede the future conference which he had now established anew.

By these prescribed delays he so won over the minds of all the Romans that they asked that the anathema against King Heinricus not be postponed any longer if he should refuse to obey him. The pope now enacted nothing concerning the kings except what did not altogether displease the bishop of Passau, the bishop of Metz, and their other colleagues, insofar as the needs of the time required. All the better men, indeed, stood most firmly on the side of King Roudulf, whom they had proved entirely obedient to the lord pope [Col. 0427B].

Duke Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0427D] Of Lotharingia; compare Gregory VII, *Register* VI.22, dated 3 March 1079.] and Count Folmarus [Note: [Col. 0427D] Of Metz.] were excommunicated for invading the church of Metz. Likewise, all who had unjustly claimed for themselves the property of the bishops—namely, of the bishop of Mainz and of the others who had been expelled from their sees—were excommunicated.

The bishop of Milan and the bishop of Ravenna were also excommunicated, as were the soldiers of the bishop of Parma [Note: [Col. 0427D] Eberhardus, formerly a cleric of Cologne, who had succeeded Cadalus; compare Gregory VII, *Register* VI.18.] who had captured the abbot of Reichenau. The abbot himself had gone to the synod to bring forward his complaint. The bishop of Parma was suspended from office on account of the same capture.

At last, when the abbot [Note: [Col. 0427] “Of Reichenau,” a fourteenth-century gloss in manuscript 2.] realized that he could not otherwise obtain his freedom, he made an agreement with his captors by money and oaths. Released by them, he gladly reached Rome, as he had previously arranged. After his case had been settled before the pope according to his wish, he returned to his former monastery of Reichenau, not without danger. By Easter King Heinricus had installed there, in his customary manner, that anathematized tyrant whom he had also placed over the destruction of the cell of Saint Gall, as an anti-abbot.

The apostolic lord also sent letters throughout the German and Italian kingdoms to those who obeyed Saint Peter, in these words [Note: [Col. 0427D] These letters are not found among the Gregorian letters. Ussing.]:

> “If there are priests, deacons, or subdeacons who lie in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of Saint Peter, entry into the church until they repent and make correction. But if any prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you presume to listen to their office, because their blessing will be turned into a curse, and their prayer into sin. And so forth.”

Beringarius of Tours abjured his heresy there and professed the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0428D] Bernold discusses this case in *Opusculum* no. 17, as does Hugh of Flavigny. Compare the acts of the council, Mansi XX, p. 523.].

Heinricus, a cleric of Augsburg, who had already received investiture of the church of Aquileia from King Heinricus, testified there, with credible evidence, that his election was canonical. But because he had accepted investiture from a layperson, usurped against canonical and apostolic sanction, he was rejected by the pope. With the synod so judging, he publicly confirmed by oath that he had been unaware of, and had not heard, that decision.

Thereafter, while the entire assembly interceded for him with the pope in this matter, he first professed by oath, as is customary, a just and proper obedience, submission, and support for the Apostolic See and for Pope Gregory, the vicar of Saint Peter. From him he canonically received the ring, staff, and other insignia of the patriarchate of Aquileia; but afterward he did not deal faithfully with him in every respect.

Cardinal Bernard likewise did not altogether keep silent before the apostolic lord about the labor and dangers he had endured in our regions, how little he had been able to benefit the Church, and, among other things, how King Heinricus had first been justly excommunicated by judicial sentence, with Bernard’s consent, by the archbishop of Mainz and six other bishops; how Bernard himself, in accordance with the pope’s command, had excluded him and all who agreed with him from communion in the body and blood of the Lord; had expelled him from the church thresholds as a sacrilegious man; had forbidden him the governance of the kingdom as a tyrant and usurper; and had subjected him to King Roudolfus, as one wholly obedient to the Apostolic See. Nor did he fail to make all these matters known in detail to the leading Romans and to all the most distinguished men.

The apostolic lord, however, by some remarkable strategy, had endured all these matters, of which he was not unaware, for more than a year, as though pretending not to notice them. This caused great wonder to some, who asked why he had done so—unless perhaps he had not doubted that the conference which he had once again arranged, now under anathema, for settling so great a dispute would by itself suffice to accomplish what he desired. Or else, if they obstructed the conference and refused to obey him for the sake of peace and concord, he intended to impose this sentence, added as if unexpectedly to his earlier anathemas, as a most just and severe judge upon those all the more deserving of eternal condemnation [Note: [Col. 0427] *damnandis*; reading 2 has *damnand*], so that those who had despised him when he was gentle and withholding judgment might then experience him as the harshest avenger.

At the same Roman synod Pope Gregory, presiding, said [Note: [Col. 0428D] Gregory’s letters, *Reg.* VI.28–29, were issued at the sixteenth synod, on 17 February (*XIII Kal. Martii*), in the second indiction, therefore in the year 1079; not, as Ussermann holds, in 1078]:

**I.** We have decreed, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, that the ordinations of those who have been ordained by excommunicated persons are invalid [Note: [Col. 0427] “Chapter I,” in the margin, reading 2].

**II.** Likewise, holding to the statutes of our holy predecessors, we absolve by apostolic authority from their oaths those who are bound to excommunicated persons by loyalty or oath, and by every means forbid them to observe loyalty toward them [Note: [Col. 0427] “Chapter II,” in the margin, reading 2].

**III.** And since, because our sins demand it, we see many perishing daily on account of excommunication—some through ignorance, some through excessive simplicity, some through fear, and some through necessity—we, overcome by mercy, temper the sentence of anathema for a time, as far as we can and when appropriate. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we withdraw the following from the bond of anathema: the wives, children, male slaves, female slaves, or bondsmen of excommunicated persons; likewise peasants and servants; and all others who are not so influential at court that crimes are perpetrated on their advice [Note: [Col. 0429] *id est efficaces*, “that is, effective,” a fourteenth-century gloss in reading 2]; and those who unknowingly associate with excommunicated persons; and also those who associate with persons who associate with the excommunicated.

Whoever—whether a ploughman, a pilgrim, or a traveler—comes into the land of excommunicated persons, where he cannot buy or has no means with which to buy, we grant him permission to buy from and receive things from excommunicated persons. And if anyone wishes to give something to excommunicated persons, not for the support of their arrogance but out of human kindness, we do not forbid it.

Enacted in the church of the Lord Savior, on 3 March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1079.

The apostolic lord therefore resolved that another synod should be held during Pentecost week to decide the aforesaid case. He sent envoys to King Heinricus: the patriarch, Bishop Peter of Albano, a religious man, and Oudalricus, bishop of Padua, together with other faithful men of his. He instructed the king in due order concerning what the pope himself had decided about the matter at the synod and granted him permission to arrange, within a short time and at his own convenience and leisure with the aforesaid envoys, a definite time and place for the conference.

He demanded that the king now prove in reality the obedience which he had often ordered him by words to demonstrate at Rome. As evidence that this obedience was genuine, he also commanded him to establish a firm peace with all his opponents until the completion of the aforesaid conference; to grant the bishops whom he had already expelled from their sees unrestricted authority over their churches and possessions, together with safe and peaceful access and discretion to use and possess them, with every injury and treachery removed; and to send seven of his most powerful and religious men to Rome at the appointed time, so that they might give him security by oath that they would carefully bring his envoys, escorted peacefully to the aforesaid conference and fully protected in the mission entrusted to them there, safely back to Rome.

The patriarch, however, who had been one of King Heinricus’s closest associates, did not observe the mission entrusted to him with the best faith or diligence. He quickly sent a secret messenger to the king at Regensburg on his own behalf, to investigate the king’s will and obedience. He himself, meanwhile, delayed his fellow envoys on this occasion and returned to his own Aquileia, while the others turned aside to Padua [Note: [Col. 0429] *p. ad augiam*, “to the meadow,” reading 2; that is, Padua. See p. 318, line 41, for Oudalricus’s see].

The king, learning that this mission had been sent to him by the pope, did not particularly welcome it, in his customary insolence, since he had no intention of observing it. Nevertheless, pretending to be unaware of the apostolic mission, he sent the bishop of Osnabrück to the agreed-upon truce, equipped with no small store of deceptions and tricks, so that by every device and by his obedience—so often falsely feigned—he might once again deceive the pope and somehow frustrate him, especially with regard to the sentence of anathema and the synod, which had been arranged chiefly to restrain the king’s tyranny.

Finally, he spent Easter at Regensburg in some fashion, entrusting the duchy of Alemannia there to Count Fridericus as an encouragement to error. He also opposed the abbey of Reichenau—already twice sold by him through simony—to Eggihardus, who had been regularly elected by his brethren and was to be lawfully ordained by the pope according to the statute of that place [Note: [Col. 0429] *abbatiae*, “of the abbey,” reading 2]. Because Eggihardus had not dared unjustly to favor Heinricus’s party, he was now unjustly rejected and held in the aforesaid captivity [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Heinricus”]; and the king unlawfully installed there a certain tyrant, Oudalricus [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Oudalricus”], the invader and devastator of the cell of Saint Gall mentioned above.

In the eastern districts of Pagoria and Noricum, he ravaged the inhabitants and compelled Margrave Liupaldus, with certain others, to submit to him. The king remained there almost until Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0429] *vox supra lineam scripta*, “the word written above the line,” reading 2].

The wife of King Roudolfus, named Adelheit, daughter of Adelheida the margravine and sister of Bertha, the wife of King Heinricus, had lived somehow in the diocese of Constance, at the castle of Duello [Note: [Col. 0430D] Hohentwiel] and in other castles along the Rhine, ever since Heinricus entered Saxony. Worn down by poverty, grief, and various disasters of adversity, and finally afflicted for some time by the sufferings of fatal illnesses and fevers, she arranged her household and, as was fitting, made every provision in Christ for the salvation of her soul. Then, in a blessed—would that it had been joyful!—death, she most devoutly commended her spirit into his hands and was buried with due ceremony and every funeral observance at the monastery of Saint Blasius [Note: [Col. 0431D] This was the mausoleum of this family, as may be seen in C. Gerbert’s work on Roudolfus the anti-emperor].

King Roudolfus, now widowed, celebrated Easter magnificently at Goslar and prudently arranged his campaign against Heinricus, to be undertaken as soon as it seemed suitable to his nobles. Moreover, with all Saxony wonderfully united in the firmest peace, according to the lawful right and constitution of that people, he most diligently administered judgment and justice to all without respect of persons, with the utmost devotion to equity.

His son Bertholdus—the duchy of Alemannia had already been assigned to him by King Heinricus while he was still a child—was taken to Ulm by Duke Welfo together with certain elders belonging to him. There Welfo and the citizens submitted themselves to Bertholdus according to customary law, and by common vote and acclamation once again confirmed him as their lord and duke.

After those men had departed from there for home, Count Fridericus gathered troops from everywhere on behalf of his king—Austrasian Franks, Rhaetians, Vindelicians, Pagorians, and whatever military forces he could obtain—and invaded Ulm himself, not without danger, intending to spend Pentecost there. But when he heard that Duke Welfo was hastening against him with a hostile attack at that same place, he scarcely spent the night there before, with his three bishops driven out with him, he shamefully and fearfully abandoned the position like a coward.

The duke therefore entered the place. After a short time, when a very strong nearby castle had been besieged [Note: [Col. 0432D] Perhaps Kirchberg or Erbach], he waited there for more than two weeks, exceedingly bold and warlike, expecting Fridericus to meet him there in battle, to Fridericus’s injury. At last, with the ballistic engines that the Germans call *mangones*, he completely demolished, captured, and burned the castle, and forced all the castle’s defenders to surrender to him without any conditions.

Fridericus, after gathering everyone whom they could somehow assemble during so long a period [Note: [Col. 0431D] *potat*, reading 2], saw that he was still far too weak to engage the duke in battle. As his men scattered in different directions, he returned in great sadness and with no small disgrace.

After Easter, Bertholdus the margrave, son of Duke Bertholdus, a highly distinguished and generous young man who conducted himself energetically and virtuously with every kind of moral excellence, took Agnes, daughter of King Roudolfus, as his wife. She too was no less virtuous than her husband in all her qualities.

The aforesaid patriarch and the other legates of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0432D] Compare Hugh of Flavigny and Gregory’s letters to the legates and to the Germans. Ussermann; Gregory, *Reg.* VII.3; Mansi XX, 289], having learned through the messengers whom they had sent ahead and through the responses of the bishop of Osnabrück, King Heinricus’s envoy—responses that were obedient, though feigned—arrived at Regensburg to meet him around Pentecost. They were not received with sufficient magnificence, but nevertheless attempted with all their strength to carry out the business for which they had been sent.

At last, pressing and insinuating themselves upon the king with every kind of ingenuity and artifice, they scarcely extorted from him a merely verbal declaration, though under the pretense of peace: he swore by his envoy that he would hold a conference at Rome in the presence of the synod. They immediately sent envoys ahead to King Roudolfus in Saxony and to the other princes of the Saxons, as well as to Duke Welfo and the leading and principal men of Alemannia, instructing them to meet with them at Fritzlar on the appointed day in order to discuss the same matter. The Saxons, together with their king, were utterly obedient to the apostolic commands and, having received this mission, carried out what had been ordered.

Duke Welfo and the other Alemannians summoned there were fully prepared to come. But the guides whom King Heinricus had appointed for their safe conduct were withdrawn by him in his customary and treacherous folly, lest they lead them to the appointed place.

He also plotted the same treachery against the Saxons. While they had left the borders of their homeland and were going to meet the apostolic legates, he sent numerous bands of troops from Bohemia behind them. These broke into and ravaged their territory, plundered them with predatory violence, and harassed them in every hostile manner. But while they were invading the march to their own disadvantage, the forces of the march, gathered together, routed them in a military attack: some they killed, some they captured after defeating them, while only a very few escaped their plunder by flight.

The apostolic legates were received with the greatest honor at Fritzlar by the archbishop of Mainz and by everyone else, both great and small. They openly explained to all the cause and purpose of their arrival and proclaimed salvation and apostolic blessing to the lovers of peace, justice, and obedience.

After hearing this with joy, the princes of the Saxons with their king, together with all the united members of their party, declared that they would be wholly obedient to the apostolic lord in observing the proclaimed peace, in justly and judicially examining the cause of so great a dispute and rebellion, and in observing the decision of the conference. They stipulated only that the opposing party should agree to the same terms, giving hostages from both sides and confirming the agreement with mutual oaths. Otherwise, they declared that they would place little confidence in King Heinricus, having so often experienced his treachery and folly.

The patriarch and the king’s other household companions, whom the apostolic legates had brought with them in their retinue [Note: [Col. 0433] *secum*, “with them,” added in reading 2], long and repeatedly refused to approve such a pact, on the grounds that it was unnecessary [Note: [Col. 0433] *h.*, a fourteenth-century gloss in reading 2]. At last, when they perceived that the legates favored the Saxons’ position as the more credible, they ceased offering much resistance and professed, with a feigned and foolish promise, that they would force their lord—although he resisted—to accept this pact.

In this way the Saxons placed themselves, together with their king, wholly under the obedience of the mission of the Apostolic See, if it could be done with the security of peace. Then, when both sides had agreed upon the day and place of the conference at Würzburg, the Saxons returned to Saxony, while the others hastened back to their lord at Regensburg with the apostolic legates.

When they informed Heinricus of the pact of faith that had been agreed upon, he treated it with stubborn contempt in both heart and speech. Only when constrained by them did he profess that, out of honor for and love of the pope, he would show himself peaceful and favorable toward them—but only if they did not refuse to come immediately to him, surrender, and humble themselves.

Under that condition, he approved holding the conference with the Saxons—the conference which his envoy had sworn to hold at Rome in the synod and which, by authority of excommunication, had been decreed not merely not to be obstructed by anyone on either side, but rather to be observed in every respect. Otherwise, he said, he would not hold it at all.

When this became known to the leaders of the Saxons and Alemannians and to their other fellow soldiers, although they had already shown themselves ready to attend the appointed conference in obedience to the apostolic lord, they all together marveled at the stubborn folly of King Heinricus and detested his contumacious disobedience. They commended their anxieties and necessities wholly to God [Note: [Col. 0433] *alio altramento*, “with another ink,” written above the line; “to the lord pope,” editorial addition] and remained unanimously at home.

Heinricus, meanwhile, having gathered no small forces from bishops and other associates of his party from every direction, came rashly to the aforesaid city [Note: [Col. 0433D] Würzburg] around the Assumption of Saint Mary, together with the apostolic legates, as though by this means he could make himself excusable to the Apostolic See and free from the guilt of anathema and perjury [Note: [Col. 0433] *inmanem*, reading 2]. The legates themselves, as is said, had been partly corrupted with gifts, partly broken by fear and threats, and almost entirely seduced in his favor by flatteries, tricks, and every kind of artifice.

There he arranged this merely pretended synod according to his own pleasure, intending that through his own synod-members and advocates everything should be argued according to his heart’s desire. Then, with highly persuasive intent, he loudly brought complaints before the apostolic legates against the disturbers and usurpers of his kingdom, and demanded insistently that they strike Roudolfus and all his supporters with the anathema of apostolic authority.

He himself and all his followers noisily and aggressively contrived many inventions and clamorous accusations of this kind—though, as is said, not all of them were suitable in every respect. He asserted openly that he had obeyed the apostolic decision, that his adversaries had been convicted of disobedience, and that for this reason they were subject to excommunication, offering incontrovertible proofs of their guilt.
