At last, the legates of the Apostolic See—though they had not been strengthened by the spirit of freedom as they should have been [Note: [Col. 0433] *non* is absent in reading 1; *ut* is absent in reading 2]—declared that they had been sent to arrange peace and to establish the day and place of a conference, not such a conference as this, but the one decreed at Rome by the apostolic lord; to examine carefully the obedience of both parties; and to report their findings to the Apostolic See.

They also declared to those who so often accused them that they had not been appointed judges alone, but together with other suitable colleagues whom the lord pope would send thereafter, to settle justly the cause of the rebellions and wars for which they were then calling [Note: [Col. 0433] *dirimendat*, reading 2].

By this artful answer they scarcely freed themselves from those who were shouting accusations and causing tumult. They knew with certainty that King Heinricus and all who agreed with him had not merely failed to observe the conference established by apostolic authority, but had rashly obstructed it; that in this way he and his associates had openly subjected themselves to apostolic anathema; and that even the site of the present pretended synod, together with its inhabitants, had already been condemned by a just judgment of its own bishop. They also knew that they themselves had dangerously associated with all these persons and matters, contrary to law and canonical right.

Thus, this anathematized council, execrably begun through foolish evasion and ended still more execrably [Note: [Col. 0434D] accusatives absolute], King Heinricus—sufficiently turbulent and enraged—rashly moved off from there against the Saxons to ravage them hostilely, taking the apostolic legates with him and leading the considerable army he had gathered from every direction.

When King Roudolfus learned of the force of this hostile invasion against himself and his followers, trusting in God and strengthened by confidence in his mercy [Note: [Col. 0433] *miseratione*, reading 1; *miserationis*, reading 2], he too prudently advanced the considerable military force that he had diligently assembled and organized to meet Heinricus. He sent messengers to all the leaders of the hostile army and, earnestly appealing to them through the mercy of God, humbly begged them to observe with their lord the conference that the pope had already decreed for establishing peace, the unity of the Church, and concord throughout the kingdom. He asked them to grant him a place where he could observe it in good faith and without feigned peace.

There he strongly commended himself and all his followers as wholly agreeable and obedient to the apostolic lord and to the other leading men of the kingdom in the matter then impending. If, however, the rebels refused this, they should have no doubt that, with God’s favor, he would meet them in arms as their most relentless enemy and would punish them as hardened contemners of peace and justice ought to be punished.

When they heard this, and when their scouts had reported with complete certainty the presence of so many companies of his most savage and ferocious army, they were greatly frightened—not only by the imminence of battle but also by the consciousness of the injustice of their excommunication and disobedience. They therefore compelled their lord, although he resisted stubbornly for a long time with tearful lamentation, to dissolve the impending danger according to their advice and not refuse to free himself by whatever means from those whom he could not withstand or resist.

They unanimously asserted, after excluding all their bishops from this discussion, that the Saxons and their lord were demanding a just cause from them. Those bishops, brave only with their tongues, tirelessly and persistently urged them to test the matter of death by the sword. They were utterly depraved in thinking that the immense desolation, discord, and injustice of the holy Church and the entire kingdom—which had arisen and begun with them—should thus be pitiably defended and strengthened.

Without delay, they summoned the apostolic legates to them and exerted every effort with them to bind the lines of both parties indissolubly under threat of anathema, so that they would not rise against one another in war. Rather, united with one another in peace, they should establish a conference as soon as possible for the matter at hand, as ministers and fellow citizens of the kingdom, and through leading men whom they would choose for this purpose attempt to settle the cause of so great a dispute by the judgment of reason.

Some men on King Heinricus’s side, having received peace from the Saxons and having given it in return, acted as serious and peaceable mediators with them in the same matter, until both sides reached the agreement that they would all unanimously unite behind whichever party they determined to be in the right at the conference that had been proclaimed to them by apostolic command [Note: [Col. 0435] *condirent*, reading 2; the edition reads *condicerent*].

By this contrivance, artfully offered as a defense of their honor, they extricated themselves from the Saxons. The Saxons had previously rejected the peace pact outright; but the other side, now fortified by this most welcome assistance, departed thence with their king, deeply discomfited and scarcely managing a hasty retreat.

What had begun when a considerable part of the Bavarians, astonished at the Saxon advance, started to withdraw was then carried out tumultuously by the entire line of camps. Thus, somehow rushing home and treating the pact of conference with the deceived Saxons as worthless, the king once again exerted all his strength to force his men—who were highly susceptible to deception—into the same campaign, and bound them by oath to the same undertaking, as he had so often done before.

The apostolic legates, meanwhile, remained involved in these affairs, as they say, as though unwillingly. At last, richly rewarded, they returned to Rome, but not together and without having accomplished any of the tasks for which they had been sent.

One of them, namely the Paduan, corrupted by such great gifts, reached the apostolic lord before his fellow envoy, a very simple and holy man who had been left beyond the Alps. This Paduan arrived as a treacherous hypocrite, extraordinarily equipped with many ingenious fabrications and responses. He was determined not only to deceive the Lombards and the Romans in passing, but even the pope himself, and to please his own Heinricus by whatever means he could.

On behalf of Heinricus, this false envoy brought the pope a profession of the most humble obedience in every respect, together with every promise of service that he could devise for the future. He presented it as though Heinricus’s observance had been sufficiently proved in the conference and in the other matters for which he had sent him across the mountains.

When this shameless man, with such audacity and such falsehood, did not cease persistently deceiving everyone around him, together with his commendatory companions, a certain brother [Note: [Col. 0435D] perhaps Bertholdus himself?], sent there by King Roudolfus and his supporters and arriving before him, openly declared that he could not sufficiently marvel at the envoy’s impudence in lying openly and driving so many people mad with his falsehoods.

When the brother was brought before the apostolic lord and the other Romans, he resisted the envoy face-to-face as a most confident witness of the truth, until he publicly demonstrated that the envoy had been overcome by incontrovertible reasoning, had confessed, and had been disgraced together with all his fabrications.

For the brother had either himself often been present with that man in his transalpine activities and affairs, or had learned the whole matter from truthful informants who had carefully investigated and recounted it to him. He refuted him with such a weight of testimony because nothing concerning the entire affair was hidden from him.

Thus, justly disgraced and rejected by the apostolic lord, the envoy returned home in the deepest sorrow and with no small disgrace.

Afterward the pope sent letters and commanded Peter, that envoy’s colleague, to return to the Apostolic See as quickly as possible. Obeying the command, Peter revisited Rome honorably. Whereas the other envoy had testified through lies, Peter testified with the fullness of faith and truth, reporting to the apostolic lord all the disobedience, falsehoods, deceptions, unheard-of acts of folly, and everything opposed to God and justice that arose from Heinricus’s tyranny.

At last, having learned the deeds of his legates with complete truth, the pope asked nothing further about Heinricus. Nevertheless, he sent letters to King Roudolfus and the others who agreed with him [Note: [Col. 0436D] these letters are no longer extant], informing them that he was greatly troubled by the ineffectiveness of his mission. He declared before God, who was his witness, that although some judged him to have shown partiality toward Heinricus in this matter, there had been no such partiality at all, nor had he acted with any fickleness; rather, according to the understanding of his mind, he had until then favored and supported justice [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus Ussermann; reading 2 has *fuisse*].

As was his custom, he strongly encouraged them to persevere in the course of justice that they had begun, using paternal words of exhortation and persuasion.

King Roudolfus withdrew into his Saxony. When he perceived that the conference which the leading men and associates of Heinricus had very craftily arranged with the Saxons had been falsely approved and not observed, he was deeply saddened that their folly, which he had so often experienced, had deceived him so cunningly.

Nevertheless, he prepared himself prudently, magnanimously, and steadfastly to meet their conspiracy against him. He did not cease to consider with all his strength how, if an opportunity like the earlier one should again arise by God’s favor, Heinricus and his followers might not again roam about after deceiving him.

Heinricus, meanwhile, wandering throughout Bavaria and spending the autumn wherever he happened to be, did not cease by every means available to him to gather with his followers a very large body of soldiers, intending to invade Saxony soon after the Nativity of the Lord.

Through his most familiar intermediaries, he also persistently approached many of the Saxons with secret and lavish promises of gifts and possessions. Hastening by whatever means he could to join them to himself once they had been corrupted and bound by oaths, he acquired a firm hope of subjecting all Saxony shortly without a battle.

During these same days, the church of Chur, which had already been deprived of its bishop for more than a year, was violently assigned by Heinricus to Norbertus, provost of the church of Augsburg, an extremely avaricious simoniac. He could not easily find anyone equal to himself as a supporter of his error [Note: [Col. 0437] the word is superfluous]. He rejected the provost of that house, a highly religious man whom the clergy, knights, and people of the church had canonically elected, and appointed Norbertus over them against the will and refusal of everyone.

Norbertus immediately served his avarice with every means and art, as he had always been accustomed to do. Since he knew that he had entered the ecclesiastical sheepfold not through the door but by another way, he attempted to make himself a heretic by trying to submit to the heretical anti-bishop of Milan and to be ordained by him [Note: [Col. 0437] *pertemptatum*, reading 2; corrected by a fourteenth-century hand to *pertemptavit*].

He also attempted, by means of certain new and forged privileges, somehow to establish that the bishop of Mainz was not his metropolitan, although it is established that the church of Chur was his suffragan church. Nevertheless, he did not make much progress in this matter.

In fact, the church of Chur had originally been subject to the metropolitan church of Milan and was later subjected to Mainz around the time of Saint Boniface. Norbertus was finally ordained on 2 February 1085 by Wezilo, the schismatic archbishop of Mainz, and was deposed in the same year at the synod of Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 0437D–0438A]].

The summer of that year passed with excessive rain, but this bad weather nevertheless did not produce any great shortage of crops.

Eberhardus, bishop of Naples [Note: [Col. 0437D] that is, Nienburg, as the distinguished scholar Stenzel correctly observed], had already been condemned by the apostolic lord for the contumacy of his disobedience. King Heinricus, however, had rashly installed him in the church of Würzburg, contrary to law, in place of Adalbero, the legitimate bishop, who had been expelled from there.

Eberhardus himself was excommunicated and communicated with excommunicated persons with all his strength. He had closed his final day in deadly and ill-omened obstinacy, destined to share the portion of those whom he had willingly embraced and to be most justly excluded from the kingdom of God forever.

He was succeeded by … [Note: [Col. 0437D] Guntherus], a canon of the church of Naples, who was canonically elected in his place.

In the same year, Hecilinus, bishop of Hildesheim, departed from this valley of tears—would that he had departed joyfully!—to the Lord, and was to have Uto, a canon of his church, as his successor.

Naples also, during those same days, finally received Hartwigus, chamberlain of the church of Mainz, as its provisionally elected successor for its archbishop, who had already been happily martyred.

The abbot of Marseille, named Bernhardus, a man of no small holiness, wisdom, religious devotion, and charity, had steadfastly endured several injuries of persecution for the sake of justice. Because of the incomparable excellence of these virtues, the apostolic lord had chosen him uniquely as his intimate, familiar, and truly most beloved companion above all others. He therefore installed him at Rome as a suitably qualified primicerius of the church of Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 0438D] Gregory intended to unite this office with the church of Marseille, as is clear from his letter, book VII, letter 7; compare also VII.8].

As Bernhardus was planning to revisit his own Marseille, he was seized on the return journey by a fatal fever. With his whole heart joyfully suspended toward heavenly things, he entered the way of all the earth in a most blessed manner.

He was buried with the most devout funeral honors at the monastery situated on the royal road used by those traveling to Rome, where the river “Nar, white with water” is usually forded this side of Saint Dionysius. The note explains: “Nar is a river with turbid waters. Hence Lucan says: ‘The Nar, white with sulfurous water.’” [Note: [Col. 0438D] This is written in the margin by the same hand.] There he rests in the peace of Christ, on 19 July.

The monastery is thought by Ussermann to have been the Padoliron monastery, or Saint Benedict’s, in the Mantuan countryside between the rivers Po and Larion. But the river Nar is today the Nera, which flows into the right bank of the Arno below San Miniato; no trace of Saint Dionysius has been found [Note: [Col. 0438D]].

The Murensian and Engelberg codices, here and there, omit Berhtoldus and present Bernoldus’s text: “Doctor Adalbertus, eloquent in deed and word,” and so forth, continuing to the year 1091 [Note: [Col. 0437] From this point the Murensian and Engelberg codices, omitting Berhtoldus, give Bernoldus’s text].

**1080**
[Col. 0438D] King Rudolf celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with extremely magnificent royal pomp at . . . most solemnly. [Col. 0439A] There, after prudently and most carefully conferring with his men in the council that the situation required, he earnestly considered how he might resist Henry, who was already attempting to invade his Saxony, without suffering harm himself. Henry, meanwhile, staying at Mainz during those same days not with royal dignity but in some manner, and gathering no small military force from Burgundy, France, Alemannia, Bavaria, Bohemia, and from everywhere else,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “militia,” a small force, 1*.]

did not cease, immediately after the octave of the Epiphany, to advance into Saxony with the greatest violence and ferocity of a hostile expedition. King Rudolf, having likewise assembled a very large army of his own soldiers, resolved with great courage to meet him and to enter battle with the utmost steadfastness, greatly strengthened by confidence in the mercy and justice of God.

[Note: [Col. 0439] “minime,” “by no means,” 1*.]

With this intention he boldly advanced to meet him amid the terror of war,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “obvia,” “to meet,” 1*.]

[Col. 0439B] scarcely waiting for his arrival. For such a powerful ardor of zeal for God had inflamed him that, if by this means he could recover the condition of the holy Church and his own legitimate right, he would in no way have shrunk from exposing himself to every danger, even to death itself.

Henry, meanwhile, stupefying his soldiers with the customary madness of his cunning and falsehood, promised them—and, as they say, confirmed it by oath—that the kingdom of Saxony lay open to him without battle or any hostile resistance; that, through the leading Saxons, nearly all of whom he had bound to himself by oath and alliance, his enemy Rudolf with his men would easily be captured and delivered into his hands; that therefore no danger or difficulty stood in their way; and, rather, that they would soon be free to reign with him for as long as they wished, in return for all the labors they had undertaken.

Thus, having made them easily deceived and excessively trusting in him, he craftily hurried them toward death itself. For they had almost unexpectedly encountered King Rudolf with the great body of his army, who were exceedingly ready for battle. When Rudolf learned through his scouts that they had drawn so near to him, he pretended to flee from fear of them and, while moving backward with his men, artfully gave them an opportunity to invade the region. He had pretended this for the purpose that, if they came to battle with one another,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “bella,” “battles,” U.]

they would be less able to escape from him as he pursued them, since, within the borders of their own country, they could, with God’s favor,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “propitio,” “favorable,” U.]

be attacked and surrounded on every side by all their fellow countrymen.

The enemy, however, supposing that the Saxons’ flight was genuine and not deliberate, boldly pursued them,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “consequentes,” “pursuing,” *.]

and had presumed to press them everywhere with plunder and fires—above all, the Bohemian duke.

[Note: [Col. 0439] “praesumserunt,” “they presumed,” U.]

Therefore, after a council had been held for this very purpose with the archbishop of Salzburg and the other fellow bishops who supported him in this matter,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “suis,” “his own,” U.]

the archbishop of Mainz, whose ecclesiastical possessions in that region they had invaded while laying them waste,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “pervaserunt,” “they invaded,” U.]

had condemned Henry the sacrilegious leader of this devastation, together with all his accomplices, and had bound them with the fetter of anathema, a just sentence having been pronounced against them. Yet these men, as usual, utterly obstinate despisers of God’s justice and treating it as nothing, had approached the Saxon camp, breathing extreme rashness and bloodshed.

The winter, which had then become harsher than usual, had also presented both sides with no small impediment to the impending enterprise. Finally, when King Rudolf learned that the enemy was at hand, and advanced in a warlike and terrifying manner with his troops arranged and very thoroughly equipped for battle,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “ab,” “from,” U.]

trusting greatly in God and in His justice and strengthened by that trust, he awaited the enemies who were freely attacking him. For he considered it no small matter of name and glory that he was not the head and initiator of so great an encounter, but the defender and liberator of himself and his men, compelled to this by the greatest necessity, and that he both was and was called such.

[Note: [Col. 0439] “homo,” “man,” U.]

[Col. 0440B] Henry, however, having arranged his legions in a most terrifying manner according to the custom of combatants, engaged him with the fiercest attack, wholly intent on suppressing and in some way subduing him—partly by a frontal assault, partly by ambushes and reserve forces unexpectedly rebelling against him by every stratagem. But immediately in the first clash King Rudolf, fighting with such force, terror, and assault, pressed upon them violently, so that they were altogether unable to withstand his strength. Rather, some fell there slain, while others, weakened and unable to fight, freed themselves from him by a tumultuous flight.

[Note: [Col. 0439] “liberarent,” “would free,” 1*.]

The battle therefore began after the ninth hour and continued in various ways until night. And—what is believed to have been done by divine judgment—at the very beginning of the battle a violently wind-driven snowstorm so wonderfully darkened both sides that scarcely anyone could recognize his fellow soldiers, until the coming of night separated the fugitives and pursuers who were fighting in that situation.

[Note: [Col. 0439] “nimium,” “excessive,” U.]

[Note: [Col. 0439] “dirimisset,” “had separated,” 1*.]

The Bavarians and Franks, together with their king, were making off from so dreadful a slaughter with great speed and, terrified in no small degree,

[Note: [Col. 0439] “praefugare,” “to flee in advance,” 1*; “primum,” “first,” U.]

[Note: [Col. 0439] “minime,” “not in the least,” U.]

but feebly.

Of the Bohemians, however, who, confident in their great numbers, had entered that battle with the utmost eagerness—for they had especially desired this single reward for their servitude, that they might be worthy to engage the Saxons before all others—a particularly great slaughter and ruin occurred there. Their total is reckoned at 3,255. Besides these, the many Germans who fell there, and those captured from both sides, have not been fully or exactly counted.

Of King Rudolf’s soldiery, thirty-eight are reported to have fallen, all but two of them being commoners rather than sword-bearing soldiers. One of these was Meginfrid, a certain count of Parthenopolis, who had long since laid down his arms for God but had taken them up again as an apostate for the shameful profits of certain estates. Therefore he was pierced and perished there by the avenging sword of God, the just judge.

[Col. 0441A] After the enemies had been put to flight and driven in every direction by the force of war, some men from King Rudolf’s side, seeing a position where the guards, recruits, and shield-bearers of the hostile army were keeping watch, removed from the combat and awaiting the end of the battle, with their pack animals, vehicles, and bundles of food, provisions, clothing, and all their equipment,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “omnium,” “of all,” U.]

surrounded and attacked it from every side with considerable eagerness. They captured it and joyfully carried everything away with them into their camp, leaving the enemies, thus fatally despoiled, to their fate.

Thus Henry, so thoroughly defeated by the persecuting ferocity of his adversaries, by famine’s destruction, by the severity of the cold, and by the aggravation of such a dishonorable and unlucky flight, scarcely managed to return in some fashion to his Regensburg. The others, no less pitiable and disgraceful, wasting away under all these miseries no less than he, each returned to his homeland with little glory.

King Rudolf, having gathered his troops from every direction, victoriously occupied the battlefield until midnight. But because the great force of the cold, together with the exceptional labors of the recent battle, had exhausted and wearied them all, and had afflicted many of them with wounds of various kinds, they abandoned the place together with those who had been killed or still lay there half-dead. They turned aside for a time to a village nearby, where they could warm themselves and rest; then, returning there before dawn and triumphing most magnificently throughout the entire day, they joyfully spent the following day there.

The great duke and his uncle, Count Hermann, who had been captured in the preceding Saxon war and handed over to Henry, but had now been released and set free by him in accordance with the terms and promise of loyalty which he and the aforesaid duke had sworn to him, had attempted, by greatly violating the faith and assistance which they had earlier confirmed by oath to King Rudolf against all his adversaries,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “ipse,” “he himself,” U.]

to join themselves fraudulently to the aforesaid tyrant before the battle began, after gathering everyone they could. But, soon repelled and put to flight by certain leading Saxons who had discovered their treachery, they scarcely managed to escape from them alive and reach home.

By the same secret conspiracy of treachery, the margravine Adela and her son-in-law, the margrave Egbert,

[Col. 0441D]

[Note: [Col. 0441D] “Margrave of Saxony.”]

[Col. 0442A] allied themselves with all their men. After the battle, with their front now sufficiently exposed, they suddenly occupied certain very strong castles with the support of their soldiers and rebelled against their king in obstinate apostasy.

At last, with God’s favor, he compelled all of them within a short time to surrender to him, and not without losses—nor were these small ones. For he dispersed their soldiers, received into his own service those who had sworn allegiance to him,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “adjuratis,” “those who had sworn allegiance,” 1*.]

and distributed their estates, benefices, and margraviates to others who eagerly sought and accepted them. Driving and pursuing the rebels from place to place with royal majesty and subjecting them in every way, he constrained and humbled them with punishments of many kinds, until they learned by experience how foolish and destructive it is to resist their king and lord in any manner,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “quamlibet,” “in any way,” 1*.]

freely and treacherously.

Thus, after the aforesaid great war which he had waged with Henry, he returned victoriously to Goslar. Thereafter he had to labor anxiously, up to Lent, against the many rebellious and hostile movements of those who opposed him—movements that were scarcely less serious than the earlier ones—

[Note: [Col. 0441] “laboraret,” “would labor,” 1*.]

until he subdued them and, as was proper, brought them under his authority and surrender.

[Note: [Col. 0441] “adversariorum,” “of adversaries,” U.]

[Note: [Col. 0441] “subjectos,” “subject,” U.]

[Note: [Col. 0441] “dediditiosque,” “and surrendered,” U.]

Finally, when Henry was making no progress according to his wishes either through warfare or through the secret conspiracy that he was conducting with the leading Saxons—and, rather, knew that, as his own conscience testified, he was openly contumacious and disobedient to God’s justice, and that for this reason he and his men had already been excommunicated by apostolic censure—he at last pretended to fear the Apostolic See because of all the great sufferings and desolations of the holy Church which he and his men had inflicted upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0441] “quos,” masculine plural, 1*.]

He sent to Rome two of his anti-bishops, the bishop of Bremen and the bishop of Bamberg, though not without a great weight of gold and silver, with which, as they say, they attempted to corrupt the Romans according to his wishes.

[Note: [Col. 0441] “dixerat,” “he had said,” 1*.]

He also sent the bishop of Padua,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “Baduanum,” “of Padua,” 1.]

who had been dispatched as an apostolic legate to our regions in the preceding summer,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “quo,” “who,” 1*.]

laden and stuffed with an enormous amount of money, together with certain other members of his household, for the same purpose. This man, already considerably corrupted by gifts from Henry himself and intent on corrupting others as well,

[Note: [Col. 0441] “et” (“and”) is absent in 1*.] was deliberately pierced with a lance on the journey by one of his companions and, utterly corrupt, was suddenly cast down to hell by God’s judgment.

[Col. 0442D] The treasure, on account of which . . . [lacuna] The remainder is missing.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1079. JOHN, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP.

[Col. 0443]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. XI, p. 207.)

[Col. 0443A] John I was born in the region of Ravenna, the son of Robert. He was called Joannelinus because of his small stature and was surnamed d’Alye in Labbe’s Catalogue. Educated in letters and in the medical art at Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, which he had learned at the command of Abbot William, he became above all an assiduous imitator of that man, who appointed him as his successor in 1028, although he would have preferred to place him elsewhere.

Duke Robert, wishing to safeguard the liberty of the monastery of Fécamp under the new abbot, did not want the archbishop of Rouen to ordain him, but summoned Hugh, bishop of Avranches, through whom he had John blessed and consecrated abbot of Fécamp. During the tenure of this abbot, orders were more than once conferred by other bishops, without the archbishop making any objection.

In 1032 Roger, count of the Castle of Saint-Paul, entrusted to this same John the restoration of the monastery of Blagiac, over which John placed one of his own men as abbot. John reluctantly conceded—but nevertheless did concede—the monastery of Villarde, formerly donated to the monks of Fécamp by Richard II, to Duke Robert, who wished to restore the place to its former condition. In exchange, Robert gave the monastery of Saint-Taurin in 1035, and John subscribed his charter for the restoration of the convent of Villars. In the same year he subscribed the foundation charter of the monastery of Conques.

Around that time he reached an agreement with Rainald, chamberlain of King Henry, concerning the authority over Villars in the district of Senlis. In 1047 Duke William restored to John the land of Rainald the viscount, which his father Richard had granted to them and which John the abbot had later given as a benefice to Gozelin, son of Heddo; Gozelin had handed it over to his own men.

Some time later John had a dispute with Warin, abbot of Saint-Arnulf of Metz, on account of Benedict, formerly a monk of Fécamp but transferred to Saint-Arnulf, whom Abbot John demanded back in sharp language.

[Col. 0444A] During his time, Paschal II prohibited William, archbishop of Rouen, from using the pallium, because he had anathematized the monks of Fécamp on the grounds that they had not observed the interdict he had imposed upon the churches of Normandy. See the letters of Paschal, Saint Anselm, and Ivo of Chartres.

John served as a legate in Italy. On his return to France, around the year 1050, he suffered violence at the hands of Italians out of hatred for the Norman people, who had invaded Apulia. He complained about this in a letter to Leo IX.

When Halinard was raised to the metropolitan see of Lyon, John was summoned in 1052 to govern the monastery of Saint-Bénigne and resigned in 1056. He was present at the discovery of the body of Saint Denis in the abbey of that name on 9 June 1053.

At the end of 1054 he crossed over to England to attend to the affairs of his monastery [Col. 0444B] situated in that kingdom and to make King Edward well disposed toward him; Edward in fact increased his resources with several benefactions. Around 1058 he asked Letzelin, bishop of Paris, who had been sent by King Henry of France to Duke William of Normandy to establish peace between them, to celebrate Mass on the day of the Resurrection in the church of Fécamp. The bishop did so and, during the solemn celebration of Mass, ordained several of the monks as priests.

In 1066 John was present at the dedication of the convent of Caen. He went to Jerusalem and, after being detained there for a long time in prison, is said in Labbe’s Catalogue to have returned to the monastery. Two years later, full of days and merits, he died in 1078, on 22 February—that is, in 1079—and was buried in the chapel of Saint John the Baptist.

Some of his letters may be read in Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, pp. 381, 506, and 521; vol. V, p. 23; in the *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 160; and in Martène, vol. I of the *Anecdota*, col. 205 and following.

[Col. 0445]

A BOOKLET OF JOHN THE ABBOT, COLLECTED FROM SCRIPTURES AND THE WORDS OF THE FATHERS.

(In Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 120.)

[PREFACE]

[Col. 0445A] The following booklet survives in an ancient codex of the monastery of Saint-Arnulf at Metz. With the permission of the reverend father, the prior of that place, Dom Placidus Beuvillonius—whom I have already praised more than once—sent the codex to me.

I have thought it worthwhile to present this lengthy specimen because I believe it to be in the interest of the Christian commonwealth that the preceding little works be carefully examined. For this reason four or five matters must be investigated here: namely, the age or antiquity of the Metz codex; then the name of the empress to whom the first booklet is dedicated; next, the name and rank of the author; further, the little works themselves contained in the codex, which must finally be compared with the book of the *Meditations* published under Augustine’s name; and lastly, with Chifflet’s *Confession* of Alcuin.

[Col. 0445B] I. The Metz codex is oblong and of the finest quality. Without doubt it was written toward the end of the eleventh century, around the year 1080, as is demonstrated by the actual form of the writing and the style of script appropriate to that age. For example, the small elongated letters *r*, the large letters *A* without a transverse stroke, and several other features of this kind in the codex—which are easier to grasp with the eyes than to express in words—ceased to be used after the eleventh century.

Moreover, the manner of writing preserved in the same book corresponds especially well to those times. Examples include the syllable *in-* inserted in one continuous sequence into the composition of words: *intellego*, *neglego*, *inmensum*, *inperfectus*, where later writers use *intelligo*, *negligo*, *immensus*, *imperfectus*.

Finally, in that codex, written by the first hand, there is a prayer of Abbot William to be said before Mass on the feast of Saint Augustine. I shall reproduce it below, after the letters of William, abbot of Metz, to whom I think this prayer should be attributed. This William flourished during the pontificate of Gregory VII, at the time when John’s codex appears to have been written, apart from certain additions made by a later hand.

II. The empress to whom the first booklet is inscribed is identified by four indications: namely, that she was the widow of the revered and illustrious [Col. 0445D] and wise Emperor Henry; “that, after first receiving the palm of lost virginity, she dismissed the proposal of a second marriage; that she distributed her resources in works of mercy to widows, orphans, and other needy persons; that she traveled through almost the whole of Italy, visiting with the greatest devotion the relics of the saints and offering them precious gifts, and that, after returning to the regions of Gaul, she did the same.”

[Col. 0446A] Yet these facts fit neither Matilda, the wife of Henry I—both because this Henry was not solemnly crowned emperor and because, after her husband’s death, Matilda spent the rest of her life in Saxony—nor Cunegund, who was married to Henry II, since she is remembered to have preserved her virginity within the marriage and, after the anniversary of her husband’s death, withdrew until her own death into the monastery at Kaufungen.

Certainly all these details point together to Agnes Augusta, daughter of William, count of Poitiers, who married Emperor Henry III. After his death—which occurred in 1056—she traveled throughout Italy for the sake of devotion, especially visiting the monastery of Fruttuaria and also Monte Cassino, where she stayed for six months and offered precious gifts to Saint Benedict.

The same praises attributed to her in the preceding Preface are mentioned by Peter Damian in a letter addressed to Agnes Augusta, the empress, reported by Baronius under the year 1062. In it Peter gives salutary admonitions to Agnes, who was then living in Italy.

At Peter’s urging Agnes returned from Germany, where she had withdrawn for several years of pilgrimage, to Rome, where she completed the final day of her life in 1077, the year in which Baronius records her epitaph.

In the second century, chapter 77, of the Sebusian Library there is preserved an outstanding letter of this same empress, addressed to Albert—not Andrew—abbot of Fruttuaria. It will not be useless to cite a fragment of it here to illuminate this passage:

“A. [Agnes], empress and sinner, to A. [Albert], the good father and the brothers gathered at Fruttuaria, in the name of the Lord: the service of a handmaid whose eyes are in the hands of her mistress. My conscience terrifies me more than any specter or any apparition. Therefore I flee through the places of the saints, seeking a hiding place from the face of this fear. I have no small desire to come to you, since I have learned that your intercession is certain salvation; but our journeys are in God’s hand and not in our own will. Meanwhile, in spirit I adore at your feet,” and so forth.

[Col. 0446D] Baronius distinguishes Agnes’s various journeys to Italy as follows: the first, after she had indeed taken the veil, in 1062, a journey to which she devoted nearly three years; the second in 1066, lasting six years; the third in 1073; and finally the fourth, also in 1073. Therefore the *Booklet of Prayers*, which was dedicated to her after her pilgrimage in Italy and her return to the regions of Gaul, was composed during the interval extending from 1066 to 1075.

[Col. 0447A] III. From these facts we understand the period in which the author of this booklet lived; his name and rank must now be discussed in the third place. Both are stated at the end of the preface, which has no title, in these words:

“ I, John, the least of the servants of Christ, and the brothers who are with me, salute your blessedness.”

Therefore this John was an abbot. This is explained more clearly in the thanksgivings that he offers to God for benefits received, where he prays in this manner:

“I, the least of your servants, not unmindful of the benefits of your mercy which have been bestowed upon me, a sinner, give thanks to you, and so forth. You, Shepherd of shepherds and ruler of all, Christ God, who, not because of any merits of mine but solely by the graciousness of your mercy, called my littleness to this pastoral office, and so forth . . . . . . [Col. 0447B] For I am little, a man of no strength, possessing nothing in myself that ought to be desired or that is worthy of so great an office. Therefore, despairing of my littleness, I breathe only in your mercy.”

And below:

“Give me heavenly and earthly assistance sufficient for every need, so that I may have the means to feed and sustain your flock, both spiritually and bodily, and to receive those who come in your name without any hesitation; to order the places entrusted to me and prepare them for the rest and salvation of the brothers, as is fitting and necessary.”

Certainly this prayer appears to have the same author as the *Booklet of Prayers*.

From these facts it follows that John, the composer of the booklet, possessed the rank of abbot and that not one but several monasteries had been entrusted to him. But who, finally, was he, and of which monastery was he abbot? This must now be investigated.

I find two especially famous abbots named John at that time, both Italians: John Gualbert, founder of the Vallombrosan order, of whom I find no writings, and John, abbot of Fécamp. I consider the aforesaid booklet attributable to the latter rather than the former, for the following reasons.

First, the author repeatedly calls himself a *homuncionem*, *homunculum*, a little and insignificant man. John, abbot of Fécamp, was small in stature and was called Joannelinus because of his bodily smallness.

Furthermore, he was placed in charge not of one monastery but of several: Fécamp and other establishments subject to Fécamp, as well as the abbey situated in the place called Erbrestein.

In addition, he was esteemed by Henry III, as is demonstrated by the administration of Erbrestein, which he obtained in Swabia with Henry’s consent. From this arose the opportunity for familiarity with Agnes, who for that reason seems to have cultivated the monastery of Fruttuaria, since it had been founded by William, the abbot of Dijon, John’s teacher.

Moreover, John’s great learning and virtue are attested by John the chronicler of the monastery of Dijon, where John the abbot had been a monk. While John the abbot was still alive, the chronicler wrote of him in this manner:

“He was born in the region of Ravenna in Italy, educated in letters, and instructed in the medical art at the command of that Father. He proved himself, above all others, an assiduous imitator of his religious conduct, his learning, and all his virtues. Because of his small stature he was called Joannelius, a diminutive name; but such grace of humility, wisdom, discernment, and the other virtues shone forth in him that, as Saint Gregory wonderfully relates in the *Dialogues* concerning the priest Constantius, so in this man it was astonishing to those who looked upon him that such great gifts of God’s grace flourished in so small a body. But since he still dwells in an earthly house of clay, it is enough to have said this much.”

Thus far John the Chronicler concerning his contemporary and namesake John, who, as I have said, was first a monk in the monastery of Saint-Bénigne, then appointed prior of Fécamp by Abbot William; afterward, when William resigned, he became abbot in 1028; later, in 1052, he was appointed in place of the deceased Halinard to the abbey called Erbrestein; and finally he died in 1078, the year following the death of Agnes Augusta.

These facts are established by two chronicles, namely those of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon and of Fécamp, published in volume one of Labbe’s Library. There, too, in the catalogue of the abbots of Fécamp, John, surnamed d’Alie, is said to have gone to Jerusalem, to have been detained there for a long time in prison, and afterward to have returned to the monastery.

These are my conjectures concerning the author of the first booklet. It is now necessary to investigate his other little works.

IV. In his preface John mentions four or five of his little works. The first is *On the Instruction of a Widow*; the second, *On the Life and Conduct of Virgins*; the third, *On the Distribution of Alms*; the fourth, *On Divine Contemplation*; and the fifth, *On the Heavenly Jerusalem*.

The first three are absent from the Metz codex. Other works are found there, and it must be considered whether they should be attributed to John.

The works found in the Metz codex were copied partly by a first hand and partly by a second. The first hand wrote the first and later booklets of John, together with the subsequent prayers up to the eleventh; the twelfth prayer, like those following it, was written by the second hand.

All those belonging to the first category—apart from the prayer of Abbot William, which bears its author’s name in the codex—seem to me to have John as their author. I attribute the other prayers written by the second hand to Saint Anselm.

Among these prayers are three addressed to Saint Mary, which I believe to be those mentioned by Anselm himself in book I, letter 20, to Condulf. Abbot Durand mentions and attributes to Anselm the seventeenth prayer, beginning with the words, “My life terrifies me,” in letter 61 of the same book.

But whether the prayer to Saint John the Evangelist should likewise be attributed to Anselm is rendered doubtful for me by these words:

“If you recognize your name, I ask you, by that very love, to let me recognize your help in such great necessity. John, John,” and so forth.

From these and similar words it has been conjectured that the author’s name was John.

As I have said, not only the first booklet, which has John’s name written as its author, but also the second booklet and the prayers that follow up to the twelfth seem to belong to John, with the exception of the prayer of Abbot William.

The later booklet, *On Divine Contemplation*, certainly belongs to John the author. At its beginning the manuscript contains this title:

“Read also this other prayer, which has been composed in a similar manner concerning divine contemplation. For many things are found in this one that are not in the former.”

The same method of treatment and the same arrangement are preserved in this later booklet as in the first. For the later one, like the first, is divided into three parts: the first concerns the Divinity and the Trinity, the second the humanity of Christ the Lord, and the third the love of Christ.

In all these parts a particular psalm is prescribed in the title, as in the first booklet. All these features indicate the same author.

This is explicitly confirmed by the edition of the later book prepared in Paris in 1539 by Vascosanus. It is divided into three parts, as in the Metz codex, under the title: *A Theological Confession Completed in Three Parts*. Vascosanus, or someone else, discovered from certain fleeting marginal annotations in his old exemplar that the author of this confession was called John; but he wrongly interpreted the name as referring to John Cassian.

In the second prayer, *On Vices and Virtues*, which is appended to the later booklet, the author asks God for purity of mind, just as He had granted him bodily integrity from the time of puberty. Here he cites certain sentences from the sixth prayer, which is prescribed to be said before Mass, and in the prayers that follow he reveals himself to be a monk.

The third prayer begins with the words: “There are therefore many kinds of contemplation,” and so forth. Similar words are found near the end of the first part of Alcuin’s Chiffletian *Confession* and in Anselm; but after three or four lines there is no agreement with those authors.

The sixth prayer, to be said before Mass, begins, “Highest Priest,” and bears no author’s name in the Metz codex. Some attribute it to Ambrose, others to Anselm; but it seems to me to belong to John.

Certainly John repeatedly cites sentences from it in the later booklet, in the second and eleventh prayers and elsewhere. In Anselm the prayer is longer after the words, “in your commemoration for our salvation.” For what follows in Anselm and in other printed books up to the words, “I ask your mercy, that it may descend upon the bread and the cup,” is absent from John and appears to belong to another author who had pastoral care of the faithful as a bishop.

The preceding and following sections are expressed by the author in the singular, whereas the interpolator changes these intervening portions into the plural: “we pray,” “we ask,” and so forth. Moreover, the interpolator prays as a bishop for each category of people entrusted to him and for all their needs.

Therefore this prayer has John as its author—or certainly another author older than Anselm—while its enlarger may perhaps have been Saint Anselm, and for this reason later writers attributed it to Anselm.

Nor should it be considered an absurd idea that Anselm expanded John’s prayer. He did not claim it for himself on that account, and anyone may use such practical and everyday prayers as his own, whether by adding or subtracting whatever seemed appropriate.

Furthermore, many other things differ in that prayer from John’s codex, of which it is worthwhile to note only two. First, where the printed editions read, “May I be able to offer you with a pure heart,” John’s codex has: “May I be able each day to offer you with a pure heart.”

The second occurs near the end of the prayer, which concludes in the printed editions as follows:

“May I attain your kingdom, where we shall see you face to face, not in mysteries, as is done in the present time, but when you have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, and so forth.”

In John’s text it reads:

“May I attain your kingdom, where we shall see you face to face. Meanwhile, you have commended this to the Church: that this should be done, that this should certainly be practiced, until you come at the end of the age, when the saints will have their rest—not yet in the sacrament by which your members are joined together while what flowed from your side is being drunk, but already in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when you have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, and we no longer need any mysteries in that clear contemplation of your unchangeable truth. For then you will satisfy me with yourself,” and so forth.

For the rest, I would not easily persuade myself that John, who derived his writings from the ancient Fathers, especially Augustine, borrowed anything from Anselm, who was a young man when John was already old.

For Anselm became a monk of Bec at the age of twenty-seven in 1060; two years later he became prior, a position he held for fifteen years; and afterward, in 1077, he became abbot—an appointment that preceded the death of John, abbot of Fécamp.

From these facts it is more probable that Anselm, as a young man, borrowed certain things from John, an elderly man, than that John borrowed from the younger Anselm.

Indeed, the Prologue to the Ten *Meditations* in Anselm, with its order somewhat altered, was taken from John’s third part of the later booklet, just as the first chapter of those same *Meditations* was taken from the first part of the same booklet, although similar passages are also found in Alcuin’s Chiffletian *Confession*.

John, however, in the passages mentioned above, inserts lines here and there from this sixth prayer, as he usually does from his own writings. This is evidence that he was the composer of this sixth prayer.

Oration IX, which is more extensive, is filled with pious sentiments and repeats much from John’s earlier little book, especially these words, by which he proves himself an excerptor:

> “Therefore I greatly delight in speaking of you, hearing of you, reading of you, writing about you, and conferring about you, so that, having entered beneath the sweet shade of your sincerity, I may be hidden from the heats of this world in the temperate coolness of your refreshment. For this reason I climb the shady and densely wooded mountain, traverse pleasant meadows, pluck the greenest herbs of your teachings by reading, chew them by frequent repetition, and gather them by writing, so that I may store the sweetness of your tenderness and charity in the lofty seat of my memory.”

John writes similar things [Col. 0451A] in the second part of his earlier book:

> “I truly delight in speaking of you, hearing of you, writing about you, conferring about you, reading daily about your blessedness and glory, and turning over what I have read again and again beneath my heart, so that in this way I may pass from the heats, dangers, and labors of this mortal and perishing life into the sweet refreshment of your life-giving breeze, and, having passed over, may recline for a little while my weary head in your bosom, intending to sleep. For this reason I enter the pleasant meadows of the Holy Scriptures; I pluck the greenest herbs of their teachings by writing, eat them by reading, chew them by frequent repetition, and finally store them by gathering them in the lofty seat of my memory, so that, having tasted your sweetness in this way, I may feel less keenly the bitterness of this most wretched life.”

Here you can see the author of Oration IX using these words in imitation of the earlier book [Col. 0451B], in order to prove himself an excerptor and a flower-gatherer; yet he is not so bound to the wording of the earlier book that he deliberately reproduces it word for word. This is evidence that the same person is the author of both, and that neither is, in this respect, an excerptor of another’s work—for an excerptor’s task is to reproduce the syllables and words of others in exact measure. The same observation should be applied to the other orations as well: in them, in a similar manner, the same ideas found in the two books are repeated according to their sense, but not always deliberately repeated word for word.

Oration XI, in John’s codex, is a thanksgiving for divine benefits, beginning with the words “My hope, Christ God,” etc. It is indeed found in Anselm and is Oration 12. Yet it should certainly [Col. 0451C] be attributed to John rather than to Anselm. In it the author asks God for grace to govern the places entrusted to him—that is, monasteries—for whoever he was, he was clearly an abbot, as is evident from the sequence of the prayer. Anselm, however, governed only the monastery of Bec, whereas John governed two as abbot. But since John and Anselm were nearly contemporaries, what belonged to one could easily, through error, have been assigned to the other when the author’s name was not prefixed.

V. Now, if we compare both John’s earlier little book and the works that follow with the book of Meditations published under Augustine’s name, we shall find in both the same passages repeated word for word. I therefore thought I would be doing something worthwhile, and proposed this as the fruit of these observations [Col. 0451D]: to disclose which author borrowed these passages from the other. Yet in the Augustinian book of Meditations there are clear signs of plagiarism and patchwork compilation. This book is composed of several poorly connected and stitched-together parts. Each of these parts is excellent and pious in itself, but when joined together they produce a body badly woven and compacted. For disparate materials are heaped together awkwardly, although in John they are properly distributed among separate parts. Moreover, in the Meditations certain passages are inserted indiscriminately which do not fit well with what precedes or follows and which are absent from John. In addition, material that is read in continuous sequence in John is, with intervening portions cut out, forcibly joined together by the patchwork compiler. Finally, no copies of the Meditations are found from before John’s time; all are later. [Col. 0452A]

The book of Meditations consists of several parts torn apart from one another. The first part extends from chapter 1 to chapter 10. It is found in Anselm and is identical with Oration 10 in John, except that several verses have been cut out after the words, “sweetly into the fragrance of your ointments.” John’s codex adds other material there, which the compiler of the Meditations ineptly removed.

The second part of the Meditations extends from chapter 12—for chapter 11, consisting of only four verses, contains merely the glorification of the Trinity—to chapter 33. It presents the first two parts and the first section of the third part of John’s earlier book, which John dedicated to the empress Agnes, except for the hymn “On the Glory [Col. 0452B] of Paradise,” which the compiler inserted after chapter 25.

I define the third part of the Meditations as chapter 34, which is identical with Oration 4, appended in John’s codex to the later book.

The fourth part of the Meditations comprises chapter 35 and the two chapters following it. These correspond to the second, third, fourth, and fifth sections of the third part of John’s earlier book, except for the end of the fourth section, beginning with the words “May my memory sleep,” and the beginning of the following section, which the compiler of the Meditations cut out.

The fifth part of the Meditations consists of chapter 38 and is Oration 8 in John’s codex.

The sixth part contains chapters 34 and 40 of the Meditations, [Col. 0452C] which are absent from John, apart from a considerable number of verses from chapter 40, similar to passages found in John’s second oration.

Finally, the seventh part comprises chapter 41 of the Meditations and is identical with Oration 15 in the Metz codex, which is attributed to Anselm in the printed books.

From this comparison it is clearly established what I have undertaken to demonstrate: namely, that the compiler of the Meditations assembled a single body of Meditations from various short works of John, except for one or two chapters, and was therefore later than John. It therefore seems that matters proceeded as follows. By extracting sayings from the Fathers, especially Augustine and Alcuin, John composed two little books of prayers and other orations. In order to have these at hand [Col. 0452D], some compiler gathered them into one collection in a continuous but badly arranged sequence. Because this collection reflected Augustine’s style and sayings, later generations attributed it to Augustine. In this matter, by some fate, John suffered precisely what he had carefully taken precautions against in the Preface to his earlier book: he had adjured Agnes Augusta to take care that none of the scribes corrupt his writings, whether by adding, subtracting, or altering anything. Nevertheless, all these things were suffered at the hands of the compiler of the Meditations.

But who, finally, was that compiler? It is certainly not easy to determine. The judgment of the Louvain scholars is this: “The author is either blessed Augustine or someone who read his books with no little care.” Yet I have already demonstrated above [Col. 0453A] that this collection was almost entirely formed from the short works of John, the abbot, who repeatedly used Augustine’s sayings. Augustine, therefore, is not the author of these Meditations, but someone else later than John. Theophilus Raynaudus attributes them to Anselm, on the ground that some passages are taken from Anselm’s genuine books. But this argument proves nothing, nor is this collection constituted as much from Anselm’s writings as from those of John the abbot. Nor could I readily believe that Anselm, so great a man, would have patched together books from mere plagiarisms of authors contemporary with him, when he was capable of creating his own works from the sources of his own intellect; or that, if he had attempted such a thing, he would have carried it out so poorly.

Whoever that compiler was, he was certainly a monk. The evidence for this is [Col. 0453B] that in chapter 6 of the Meditations, where John has: “With your true and perfect servants,” [Col. 0454A] the compiler substituted: “with your true and perfect monks, whose footsteps I cannot imitate,” etc.

Moreover, if anyone wishes to possess these Meditations in a fuller, more corrected, and indeed better-arranged form, let him consult the Metz codex, which contains the short works of John the abbot—as I think, John of Fécamp—whose three letters I shall give below.

Now, since many passages found both in John’s short works and in the Augustinian Meditations likewise occur in the Confession of Faith published not long ago under Alcuin’s name, it is useful to explain here what I have been able to ascertain for the elucidation of that Confession. (What Mabillon says here that he will explain about the Alcuinian Confession was published separately, as being too extensive, at the end of volume [Col. 0454B] of the Analecta.)

## PROLOGUE OF JOHN THE ABBOT

To the widowed empress of Emperor Henry, concerning a work of various prayers composed by him from the Fathers.

[Col. 0453]

Some time ago, lady empress, you were pleased to ask me to gather from the Scriptures lucid and brief discourses in which, in accordance with the rule of your station, you could learn without great effort the norm of right conduct. For every rank, age, and sex has its own instruction for the ordering of life in the sacred writings, so that each person, walking most rightly in the calling to which he has been called, may be able to reach the kingdom in which there are many dwelling places.

Finally, after the death of your lord, the illustrious and wise Emperor Henry, formerly your husband, you embraced with all your strength the praiseworthy purpose of laborious widowhood. And although your nobility, wealth, and age invited you to enter marriage again, you nevertheless refused to incline your heart to the words of those who contend for falsehoods as though they were truths. Instead, lifting yourself upward, with your loins girded, you stood firmly upon your feet, so that, scorning the allurements of flesh and world, you might serve Christ the Lord in chastity and offer other noble matrons [Col. 0453D] a worthy example for imitation: namely, that, prompted by your continence toward better things, they might remain faithful to their deceased husbands and ask the Lord for the remission of their sins through heavenly sacrifice and constant almsgiving.

How seemly and honorable it is that a Christian woman, after the first palm of lost virginity, should thereafter strive to live chastely and soberly, so that, with the Lord’s help, she may both be and be called the wife of one man. This glorious virtue of a single union, unless I am mistaken, is declared worthy of observance by that one rib which was taken from the man’s body, from which the woman was formed.

Having learned, therefore, the pious desires of your heart, I immediately set to work and quickly excerpted several sayings from the short works of the Fathers, so that you might always have with you truthful instructions showing more fully the straight path along which a faithful widow ought to proceed justly and piously. In addition, I added another discourse on the life and conduct of virgins, to instruct the religious women [Col. 0454C] gathered in your monastery.

And because I discovered that you were devoted to works of mercy, I was not reluctant to write this also: that alms are unquestionably to be distributed not to ecclesiastical persons who possess many riches, but to widows, orphans, the sick, strangers, and especially those who are truly the poor of Christ. In doing all this, because of your great charity, I felt no labor in my labors.

Be silent, dogs of Scillae! Behold, with my ears stopped, I shall pass through the clamorous frenzy of your abuse. In your little gatherings, they say, this letter resounds from a canine snout. When you profess yourself a monk, and silence is proper to the monastic religion, what business have you with women? Whence do you have such authority [Col. 0454D] that you sit in the chair of teachers and, without shame, instruct women themselves with written pages?

Be silent, wretched men. You say this because you are blind, guides of the blind. Return, transgressors, to your senses, and carefully consider where you lie in disgrace. Would that your malicious mind might recover and strive in some measure to imitate the pious works of honorable women. Is not this woman worthy of all veneration, who preferred the love of Christ to riches and honors? Therefore, although she was mistress of kingdoms, she humbled herself and became the servant of the poor.

I shall say nothing of the fact that she traversed almost the whole of Italy, devoutly visiting the relics of the saints, offering them precious gifts, and giving very many alms in cities and villages and in all the places to which she hastened for the sake of prayer. [Col. 0455A] Since the narrowness of a letter does not allow me to linger longer on her praises, I shall also pass over the fact that, after returning to the regions of Gaul, she likewise consoled the poor and the churches of God with a generous hand, as it is written: “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever.”

But now, having driven far away those who blow upon the ground and raise dust into their own eyes so that they may not see themselves, I return to you, venerable handmaid of Christ, so that my discourse, which began to instruct you, may, as though I were present and conversing with you, reach the final completion of the work undertaken, with God as its author.

Although I think those little excerpts from my small resources, of which I spoke above, could suffice for your salvation, nevertheless, because I have learned from the report of friends that you desire and request that the little book I have published concerning divine contemplation, the love of Christ, and that heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of all the faithful, should also be copied out for you, my heart rejoices greatly, I confess, and glorifies in you God, the giver of all good things.

For unless, with Christ as your guide, you were ascending to higher things, walking from virtue to virtue, you would in no way be able to make such requests. Who would not marvel at so fervent a spirit, which, while drinking the little streams of sweet waters, never ceases to thirst? He is sufficiently foolish and excessively obstinate who spurns the pious prayers of such a woman and does not yield to her most just requests.

Behold, gladly and exultantly, according to the knowledge God has granted me, I am ready, venerable mother, to obey your will in all things. Would that there were in me a little spark capable of adding some increase [Col. 0455C] to your heated mind!

Receive, therefore, good soul, the illustrious example of holy widowhood; receive, I ask, with a wakeful mind what you desire—the little work of my excerpting, accomplished through Christ’s grace. In it you will find, for the most part, the sweet words of heavenly contemplation, which must be read reverently and meditated upon with due fear, lest the person who approaches tepidly and without devotion be judged presumptuous.

You should know, therefore, that the reading of this little book is especially appropriate for those who do not allow their minds to be darkened by carnal desires and earthly lusts. When these things are read with tears and exceptional devotion, the gentle reader then tastes with the palate of the heart what sweetness lies within.

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—let not a proud and disdainful mind presume to touch the secret and sublime words of the divine utterances, lest it slip into error; for blind eyes cannot behold the light. For this reason many have fallen through heresy into the abyss of eternal condemnation, dragging others with them to destruction, because the mysteries of Holy Scripture, whose roots are in heaven, are not here wholly disclosed even to any of the perfected.

Only those who are wise according to God, endowed with profound humility, grasp as much as the Holy Spirit deigns to reveal to them. Read these things frequently, therefore, and especially when you see your mind inspired by a heavenly longing. For it is just that you, who conduct yourself well in the active life, should assume the wings of contemplation [Col. 0456A] and, flying upward, draw from the fountain of heavenly sweetness, saying with the Prophet:

> “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.”

Likewise, those words read in the Song of Love, where the soul that loves God alone speaks to her beloved Christ, saying:

> “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women have loved you. Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments. My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows are removed.”

In this connection it must be understood that the supreme and immutable essence which is God cannot in any way be seen by mortal eyes in this land of the dying, nor has it ever been seen by any mortal since our first parent was expelled from the delights of paradise into these miseries. Hence the contemplative life begins here but is perfected there, where God is seen face to face.

For when a gentle and simple mind is raised into contemplation and, overcoming the constraints of the flesh, investigates heavenly things, the mass of the flesh pulls it downward and does not permit it to remain long above itself. Yet although it is quickly recalled to itself, struck back by the immensity of the heavenly light, it nevertheless makes great progress by the very fact that it can taste beforehand the divine sweetness. For immediately, kindled by an immense love, it hastens to go beyond itself; and, lifted up, it perceives that it cannot see what it ardently loves, although it would not ardently love it unless it perceived it to some degree.

There are some who make less progress and fashion God for themselves in images, because, dispersed in a distorted way among temporal things, they do not know how to contemplate intellectually that wondrous and boundless light. What else is the eye of contemplation for such people but a snare of destruction? They must be admonished that, content with the exercise of the active life alone, they should not presume to climb the mountain of contemplation, because, as it is written: “The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God,” and “to be minded according to the flesh is death.”

For unless the human spirit drives away from itself the desires of outward things, it does not penetrate inward realities. It sees invisible things with greater subtlety in proportion as it more perfectly despises visible things. Therefore, although God is invisible and incomprehensible in his nature, nevertheless, through a clean and holy mind [Col. 0456D] that longs for heavenly things alone, he is seen here without being looked upon, heard without sound, perceived without movement, touched without a body, and held without a place.

Having necessarily set these matters forth in advance, I ask your love that, if you find anyone who wishes to possess this little book, you admonish them to transcribe it carefully and reread what has been written frequently, so that they do not permit anything to be added, subtracted, or altered in it. We say this because of the carelessness of scribes, who not only corrupt the truth but also join falsehoods to falsehoods.

May God be with you, and may his hand strengthen you, so that, having become like a winged and many-eyed creature, you may make daily progress in both lives: now serving Christ with Martha in the active life, in his members; now sitting with Mary in the contemplative life at the feet of the Lord and listening attentively to the word from his mouth. Thus, by acting well and contemplating purely, may you reach that most blessed vision where the Son speaks openly about the Father.

May he himself, who descended to these lowly things so that we might ascend to those highest things; who bent down so that he might raise us up; who became weak so that he might make us strong; who assumed our life so that he might give us his own—may he, according to his piety and goodness, lead his servants and handmaids to that vision. [Col. 0458A] For he is the Only-Begotten, coeternal with the almighty Father, who with him lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

I, John, the least of Christ’s servants, and the brothers who are with me, greet your blessedness in Christ, pious mother of the poor and noble glory of widows. Farewell.

May the almighty Trinity always preserve you in its will.

## HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE BOOK

Collected from the Scriptures and the sayings of the Fathers, especially for the benefit of those who love the contemplative life.

[Col. 0457]

### Psalm: “May God have mercy on us.”

[Col. 0457B]

Most high Trinity, one power and undivided majesty, our God, almighty God, I, the least of your servants and a small member of your Church, confess to you. I confess and honor you with the sacrifice of praise that is due, for what you have deigned to grant to me, so small as I am, according to my knowledge and ability.

And because the offering of the heart is more precious in your sight, behold, I gladly and exultantly offer you the vows of praise that are within me, as a gift of your mercy, from an unfeigned faith and a pure conscience.

I believe you with my whole heart, King of heaven and earth, Lord; and with my mouth I confess you as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three in persons and one in substance, the true almighty God, of one, simple, incorporeal, invisible, and boundless nature.

You possess in yourself nothing greater or lesser, but are perfect in every way without deformity; great without quantity, good without quality, everlasting without time, life without death, strong without weakness, truth without falsehood, wholly everywhere without place, present everywhere without position, filling all things without extension, meeting all things everywhere without contradiction, transcending all things without movement, remaining within all things without being stationary, creating all things without need, governing all things without labor, giving all things their beginning without having a beginning yourself, making all mutable things without undergoing change yourself.

Infinite in greatness, almighty in power, supreme in goodness, immeasurable in wisdom, fearful in counsels, just in judgments, most hidden in thoughts, truthful in words, [Col. 0457D] holy in works, abundant in mercies, most patient toward those who sin, and gracious toward those who repent; always the same, eternal and everlasting, immortal and immutable.

Neither do spaces enlarge you, nor the smallness of places confine you; no receptacles constrain you; neither does will vary you nor necessity corrupt you; neither do sad things disturb you nor joyful things caress you. Neither does forgetfulness remove anything from you, nor does memory restore anything to you; neither do past things pass away, nor do future things succeed them. Neither will origin give you a beginning, nor times an increase, nor accidents an end. But before the ages, in the ages, and throughout the ages, you live eternally; and to you belong perpetual praise and eternal glory, supreme power and singular honor, everlasting kingship and dominion without end, through infinite, unwearied, and immortal ages of ages. Amen.

Thus far, almighty God, Trinity, inspector and searcher of my heart, I have confessed the omnipotence of your majesty and the majesty of your omnipotence. Now, however, just as I believe in my heart, for righteousness, so I confess with my mouth before you, for the salvation of the just, how you deigned to assist the human race at the end of the ages.

You, Father God, alone are nowhere read of as having been sent. Concerning your Son, however, the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.” When it says “he sent,” it sufficiently shows that he came sent into this world, when, born of Mary ever-virgin, he appeared in the flesh as true and perfect man.

But when the chief of the evangelists says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him,” he was sent there through humility where he always was and is through divinity. I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that this mission was the work of the whole Holy Trinity, etc.

It ends: “And the blessed vision and praise of you without end: where you, with him, and he, with you, in communion with the Holy Spirit, live and reign eternally and forever as God,” etc.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND PART

Concerning the love of Christ and that heavenly Jerusalem, our mother.

[Col. 0458D]

### Psalm: “My heart overflows.”

“My hope, Christ God,” etc. It ends: “And I shall manifest myself.”

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD PART

Where the soul devoted to God ascends to a higher degree of contemplation.

### Psalm: “We praise you, God.”

### Psalm: “Bless the Lord, all things.”

[Col. 0459A]

### Psalm: “Praise the Lord.”

I. Bless, my soul, the Lord, etc. It ends: “To our God be honor, power, and strength throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

II. PRAYERS BEGIN.

Of ardent desire, that the faithful soul may love Christ alone, because good and evil love cannot be contained together in one breast, as it is written: “No one can serve two masters.”

### Psalm: “Sing joyfully to God, all the earth.”

“Jesus, our redemption,” etc. It ends: “With the glorious Mother of yours, my Lady, and all the saints obtaining it. Amen.”

III. Here the sinful soul groans and grieves greatly, seeing the earth without water; therefore, out of longing, it pours forth devout prayers to the Lord.

[Col. 0459B]

### Psalm: “As the hart longs.”

“Christ the Lord, Word of the Father,” etc. It ends: “Through the prayers and merits of all the saints.”

IV. Here the devout mind desires with immense ardor and humbly asks God, the giver of all good things, that, supported by the protection of divine grace, it may steadfastly do what the Apostle commands, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.”

### Psalm: “How lovely.”

“Jesus Lord, merciful Jesus, who deigned to die for our sins,” etc. It ends in this manner:

> “In peace, in that same state, I shall sleep and rest. May my memory sleep, I beseech you, my God, from all things that are beneath heaven, while remaining awake in you, as it is written: ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake.’ May my soul, my God, be safe and always secure beneath the wings of your protection. May it remain in you and always be cherished by you. May it contemplate you in the ecstasy of the mind and sing your praises with jubilation, and may these sweet gifts of yours be my consolation amid these storms. Meanwhile, until I come to you, to true peace, where there is no bow, shield, sword, or war, but supreme and certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil security, joyful happiness, happy eternity, and eternal blessedness, and the blessed vision and praise of you throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

V. The man of desires and contemplator of heavenly things, weary of the present and longing for the future, groans from the depth of his heart and implores daily, grieving that he is not there where he may deserve to see his beloved with unveiled face, as it is written: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

### Psalm: “Sing joyfully to the Lord.”

“Christ the Lord, power and wisdom of the Father, who make the cloud your ascent, who walk upon the wings of the winds, who make your angels spirits and your ministers [Col. 0460B] a burning fire: I beseech and humbly ask you, give me enduring wings of faith; give me swift wings of the virtues, by which, raised upright, I may be able to contemplate eternal and heavenly things.
