Let my soul, I ask, cling after you, and may your right hand receive me; may it lift me above the height of the earth and feed me with that heavenly inheritance for which my pilgrimage sighs night and day. And because my dying limbs dull the vigor of the soul,

> Dispel the mists and burdens of earthly weight;
>
> Halt the wandering mind that rushes through many byways.

Grant that my mind may climb to the heavenly seat, so that, illumined by the light above, it may look down upon earth, look up to heaven, hate sins, and love righteousness. For what is more beautiful or sweeter than, amid the darkness and many bitterness of this life, to long for divine sweetness and [Col. 0460C] sigh for eternal blessedness, and there to hold the mind where it is most certain that true joys are possessed,” etc.

It ends:

> “Behold, I now see what I desired; I now hold what I hoped for; I now possess what I longed for. I am now joined in heaven to him whom, while placed on earth, I loved with all my strength, embraced with all my charity, and clung to with all my love. I praise, bless, and adore him, who lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

[Col. 0459]

# THE OTHER LITTLE BOOK

Concerning divine contemplation.

## FIRST PART

Concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0459D]

“Be present to me, true light . . . one almighty God. I invoke you into my soul: enter it, I ask, and fit it to yourself, so that you may possess it without stain and without wrinkle.”

It ends: “Neither will accident give you an end; but before the ages, in the ages, and throughout the ages, you live eternally; and to you belong perpetual praise and eternal glory,” etc.

## SECOND PART

Concerning the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us by the price of his blood.

### Psalm: “Sing to the Lord” 2.

“Thus far, almighty God, Trinity, inspector and searcher of my heart, I have confessed the omnipotence of your majesty,” etc.

It ends: “Where there is eternal day and one spirit of all, where you, with him, and he, with you, in communion with the Holy Spirit, live eternally,” etc.

## THIRD PART

In which the soul, burning with exceedingly great love, longing for Christ, sighing for Christ, desiring to see Christ, whom alone it loves, finds nothing sweet except to groan and weep, to flee, be silent, and rest, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I shall fly away and rest.”

“My hope, Christ God . . . . . I beseech, implore, and ask you that, with you as my ruler and guide, through you I may walk to you, reach you, and rest in you, who are the way, the truth, and the life. My God, my one hope and exceedingly great mercy, be for me a house of refuge and a fortified place,” etc.

It ends: “And I confess the eternal reasons of temporal things to eternal wisdom, and I give praise to your name. To you be blessing and splendor; to you thanksgiving; to you honor, power, and strength, Lord our God, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

# OTHER PRAYERS

I. These little verses have been collected from the Scriptures to awaken compunction of heart.

“Alas, man! Alas, man! Alas, wretched man! Why do you live like a horse, which has no understanding,” etc.

It ends: “The saints shall go to heaven with their King. Glory [Col. 0461B] to you, Christ,” etc.

II. PRAYER CONCERNING VICES AND VIRTUES

“Christ, God, power of our salvation, light from light, enlighten me, I ask, with the light of your grace. In your piety and goodness, grant that this may always dwell within me and rule me everywhere,” etc.

It ends: “May I reach eternal life through your mercy and gift, you who, with the Father,” etc.

III. A BRIEF AND TRUE RESPONSE TO AN APOLOGETIC DISCOURSE

“There are therefore many kinds of contemplation, by which the soul devoted to you, Christ, delights and makes progress; but my mind rejoices in none of them as it does in that contemplation which, when everything else has been removed, raises the simple gaze of a pure heart to you alone, God.”

It ends: “You have worked all our good works for us.” [Col. 0461C]

IV. HUMBLE CONFESSION OF A SINNER AND UNWORTHY PRAISER

“Forgive, Lord, forgive, merciful one, and do not reject me as presumptuous.”

It ends: “They shall praise you throughout the ages of ages.”

V. WHAT JUBILATION IS

“Jubilation is said to occur when the mind conceives ineffable joy.”

It ends: “The tongue of the speaker is sufficient.”

VI. PRAYER TO BE SAID BEFORE THE CELEBRATION OF MASS

“Most high priest and true pontiff, who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure sacrifice,” etc.

VII. PRAYER OF LORD WILLIAM, THE ABBOT

To be said in commemoration of Saint Augustine before the consecration of the Mass.

[Col. 0461D]

“Remember, Lord, the soul of your servant Patrick,” etc., published below.

VIII. HUMBLE CONFESSION OF A SINNER IN A TIME OF DISTRESS AND ILLNESS

“Have mercy, Lord, have mercy, merciful one, have mercy on me, the most wretched of sinners, doing what is unworthy and suffering what is deserved.”

It ends: “You know all things; you can do all things.”

IX. HERE BEGINS A BEAUTIFUL PRAYER, COMPILED THROUGH CONTEMPLATION, OR THEORETICAL MEDITATION

“My hope, Christ God . . . . . who are the way, the truth, and the life. But because in the great flood of this life, where we are driven about by storms raging all around us, no trustworthy anchorage and no higher place can be found where the dove’s foot [Col. 0462A] may rest, nowhere is there safe peace, nowhere secure repose,” etc.

It ends: “Glory to the Father, who made us; glory to the Son, who redeemed us; glory to the Holy Spirit, who sanctified us. Let there be praise; let there be blessing,” etc. The prayer is lengthy and devout.

X. ANOTHER PRAYER

“Lord, my God, grant that my heart may desire you; by desiring, seek you; by seeking, find you; by finding, love you,” etc.

It ends: “May it please you, according to the abundance of your mercies, through Jesus Christ,” etc.

XI. THANKSGIVINGS FOR THE BENEFITS OF DIVINE MERCY.

My hope, Christ God . . . . . I beseech, implore, and ask you [Col. 0462B] to complete in me the work of your mercy that you have begun. For I am the least of your servants, yet, not forgetful of the benefits of your compassion bestowed upon me, a sinner, I give you thanks: you, in your sole clemency, have freed me from the bonds of original sin through the water of holy baptism and the renewal of the Holy Spirit . . . . . You are the Shepherd and ruler of all, Christ God. Not through any merits of mine, but solely by the favor of your mercy, you have called my insignificance to this pastoral office for your sake and for the sake of your holy name. Make me fit for this ministry, so that I may govern your household wisely and be able in all things to feed your flock according to your will. Grant, for the honor of your name, that with abundant good fruit for the brotherhood I may be worthy to attain to your [Col. 0462C] glory . . . . . I know and am certain that you can produce good and great fruits from your flock through me, insignificant and weak as I am. For I am a little one and a manikin of no virtue, possessing nothing in myself that ought to be desired or that is worthy of so great an office. Therefore, despairing of my smallness, I breathe only in your mercy. Yet although you are great among the great, you work great things more gloriously in the least. Certainly your praise will be sweeter and more abundant, according to human custom, when you deign through one so very small as I am to accomplish great things from your flock . . . . . Give me heavenly and earthly assistance in full sufficiency, so that I may have the means to feed and sustain your flock, both spiritually and bodily, and to receive those who come in your name without any hesitation; and likewise to arrange and prepare the places entrusted to me [Col. 0462D] for the rest and salvation of the Franks, as is fitting and necessary . . . . . I ask two things of you; in your mercy, do not refuse me even one of them. I beg you, by all your mercies, grant me your heavenly consolation in my many tribulations! For I cannot bear this exceedingly heavy burden that has been laid upon my feeble shoulders, yet I am afraid to lay it down . . . . . I give you thanks, Lord, who have also separated me from the vain fellowship of this world and brought me to your holy service, etc.

## XII. PRAYER TO HOLY MARY

Virgin venerable to the world, beloved by the human race, etc.

## XIII. TO CHRIST

[Col. 0463A]

Lord Jesus Christ, my redemption, my mercy, etc.

## XIV. TO SAINT BENEDICT

Saint Benedict, whom heavenly grace has enriched with so abundant a blessing of virtues, etc.

## XV. FOR FRIENDS

Lord Jesus Christ, who displayed the charity greater than which no one has, etc.

## XVI. FOR ENEMIES

Almighty and merciful Lord Jesus Christ, whom I desire to be favorable toward my friends, etc.

## XVII. ANOTHER PRAYER

My life terrifies me. For, carefully examined, almost my whole life appears to me either sin or sterility [Col. 0463B], etc.

## XVIII. TO HOLY MARY

[Col. 0464A]

Holy Mary, and, among the saints after God, etc.

## XIX. TO HOLY MARY

Mary, you are that great Mary; you are that greatest of blessed Marys, etc.

## XX. TO SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Saint John, you are that John who baptized the Lord, etc.

## XXI. TO SAINT PETER

Saint Peter, most kindly and faithful shepherd of God’s sheep, etc.

## XXII. TO SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

Holy and blessed John, greatest of God’s evangelists, most beloved of God’s apostles, etc.

[Col. 0463]

# LETTERS OF ABBOT JOHN

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 450.)

## FIRST LETTER. OF WILLIAM [Note: [Col. 0463D] the Conqueror.] KING OF THE ENGLISH TO JOHN, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP

[Col. 0463C]

W., king of the English, sends greetings to John, abbot.

For a long time I considered with myself into whose hands and keeping I might commit and entrust the abbey of Saint Peter of Westminster, since I both hold it in the greatest veneration and ought to do so as a matter of duty. For there lies my lord, King Edward, of blessed memory; there also is buried the renowned Queen Edith, his wife; and there, through God’s merciful providence, I received the scepter and crown of the whole English kingdom. At last, on the advice of Archbishop Lanfranc and my nobles, I compelled Abbot Vitalis, though unwilling, to undertake it. Since he has raised the abbey of Bernay from very small beginnings to great eminence, as is evident, I understood him to be worthy of the abbey of Westminster, both for usefulness and prudence. Therefore, may I be permitted to do this which, by the common counsel of my nobles, I have arranged concerning him, with your permission and goodwill and that of the brothers’ community. I also wish you to know that I have chosen Osbern, the brother of Abbot Vitalis, to have the abbey of Bernay; and may I be permitted to do this with your permission. Farewell.

## SECOND LETTER TO WILLIAM, KING OF ENGLAND

John, by divine favor Father of the Fécamp monastery, to William, king of the English in great glory: victory over his enemies by the sword of the Lord and of Gideon.

Illustrious king of the English people, and duke of the Normans in warlike valor: behold, I, John, wholly yours in the Lord, humbly submit to you and inform you by letter [Col. 0464B] that I would have taken it badly if our brother, Lord Vitalis, had moved from one abbey [Col. 0464C] to another without our permission—were it not that I love you and wish to honor your counsels. Therefore I praise and confirm what your royal authority has decreed. But as for your having chosen Osbern, his own full brother, who is not a Fécamp monk, as abbot in a place under our jurisdiction, I gladly consent out of regard for your loyalty, provided that it is done according to the proper authority: namely, that, after obtaining permission from his own abbot, he become our monk and be obedient according to the Rule and order of Saint Benedict.

Having said this, I ask my lord, mindful of my old age, which is already bending me toward the end of life, to judge our causes and render us justice, so that I may die happy in the Lord. What are these causes? First, that he make full and willing compensation, as promised, for what we lost at Hastings. There are also many other urgent matters among our claims, which I ask the merciful king to judge and settle while he lives and has the opportunity, for the honor and glory of the most high Trinity, so that God himself, the Trinity, may raise him from among the English to the glory that is among the angels. Farewell.

## THIRD LETTER TO VITALIS, ABBOT OF BERNAY

John, abbot of Fécamp, sends greetings to his brother Vitalis.

I wish you to know, useful and honorable brother, that, for love of the king and because of the merit of your affection, I authorize your promotion and the appointment of Brother Osbern at our Bernay. But I and the whole community of the Holy Trinity ask and admonish you, mindful of your profession and mindful of our fellowship, to recognize and honor your place [Col. 0465A] better than have the many brothers who departed from us and through our house attained great honors. Farewell.

## NOTE ON THE THREE LETTERS ABOVE

The three letters above all aim at the same result: that Vitalis, abbot of Bernay, should be transferred to govern Westminster, in the London suburb; and then that Osbern, Vitalis’s full brother and a monk of Troarn, should be appointed in his place at Bernay.

Bernay is a town of Neustria on the River Carentonne, in the diocese of Lisieux. There Judith, married to Richard II, duke of the Normans, began the monastery; Richard, her husband, completed it and entrusted it to the venerable William, abbot of Fécamp, to finish and organize according to monastic discipline. Richard himself testifies in a charter issued at the Fécamp palace in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0465B] 1027, in the eighth indiction, that William had provided a small measure of counsel and assistance in laying its foundations.

Thus, since that monastery belonged by jurisdiction to the monks of Fécamp, William, king of the English and likewise duke of the Normans, commonly called the Conqueror, transferred Vitalis, abbot of Bernay, to Westminster only after obtaining the consent of the abbot of Fécamp and his monks, and appointed Osbern in his place. In this matter it should be observed that princes and kings, although they sometimes appointed abbots to abbeys founded by their ancestors and subject to themselves, nevertheless, in order to carry the matter out, sought the consent and confirmation of the monks to whom the election belonged.

Our William Filiaster extracted these letters and those that follow from a manuscript codex of Fécamp.

## FOURTH LETTER TO WARINUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ARNULF AT METZ  
### He demands the return of his monk Benedict

To Lord Father W., venerable abbot, Brother John, [Col. 0465C] a little servant of the cross of Christ, whatever is most fortunate in Christ.

More than once, both orally and in writing, I have petitioned your fatherhood on behalf of our monk named Benedict, asking you to return him to me; but you refused to listen, which was not a very charitable act. For you know what is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another”; and: “Charity bears all things.”

Therefore I again approach your fatherhood with humble supplication, asking that you not delay sending him back to me. If you are unwilling, I do not excommunicate you; but, by the authority of God, of our holy Father Benedict, and of all the saints, I separate and remove him from every Christian office as far as I am able, until I am shown by what right he is being taken from me [Col. 0465D]. I would say “farewell” if you were not defending our sheep [read: “detaining”]. Nevertheless, I shall say “farewell,” on this condition: that you return the sheep, setting aside every excuse.

## FIFTH LETTER. OF WARINUS, ABBOT, TO JOHN OF FÉCAMP  
### A response to the preceding letter

To Lord Abbot John, full in accordance with his name by the grace of God, Brother W., servant of him and of God’s servants, with faithful prayers, charity, and peace.

The Apostle’s words are: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all.” I say this in order to admonish and correct myself by the judgment of so great a teacher, lest, in answering your letter [Col. 0466A]—in which you recently addressed us too harshly, according to your pleasure and authority—I should, provoked as I am, blurt out something improper for you, that is, for so great a majesty (God forbid!), like a fool.

But since, as you say, charity bears all things, I pray, in accordance with the Apostle’s wish, that if I have spoken something foolish in my folly, you will bear a little with my foolishness and support me. For I propose nothing, command nothing, and threaten nothing; but, compelled to answer your letter, I reply in simple speech as follows.

Our brother, Lord Wimund, brought me your letter, saying that it had been sent by you for him to deliver to me. In the presence of that same brother who brought it, and of Lord Grimarius of Bézu, he presented it without any introductory greeting—which, as you say, was “not a very charitable act” [Col. 0466B]—and added that you commanded him to bring our brother, Lord Benedict, whom you wished to take away by force as though he were already yours, to you as quickly as possible, at your expense and with horses and servants. Certainly, if anyone other than yourself had done this, it would not have been a very religious act.

To say nothing for the moment of your person, to whom all honor is due, as to one who is my superior, earlier in rank, holier, wiser, and more religious, I shall speak of myself. If I had attempted such a thing against one of your brothers, and had warned him in a letter to come to me across so great a distance, especially to your loss, I should rightly be judged reprehensible by you and by everyone who heard of it, and contrary to the holy Rule, since we know that our holy Father Benedict forbids a monk to accept letters or gifts from anyone without the knowledge of his abbot. In such a transgression, the saying you opposed to me in your letter would more justly be applied to me: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

But let us set aside these matters, which might be borne lightly or counted as nothing at all if other, more serious matters did not spur us on, and let us, if you please, come to the very words with which you threaten us, so that, by answering them without contention, we may be found either guilty or innocent.

You complain that you have repeatedly sought from us, both orally and in writing, the return to you of your monk, as you call him, named Benedict, and that we refused to listen, and that this was not a very charitable act. To this I answer that, if I remember correctly, I received—God is my witness—from I know not what person [Col. 0466D] a certain letter, perhaps two years ago, in which I was urged to send back this same brother. I believe that he himself, and anyone else who read and understood it, laughed at it as worthless; I neither believed nor believe that it was yours. What it contained was so frivolous that I thought it had been mockingly fabricated by some buffoon rather than sent either by you or by any wise man, and therefore I considered it scarcely worth answering.

As for your saying that you sought this from me orally, with due regard for the truth of your statement—which I neither ought nor wish to call false—I affirm that I do not remember ever having had any conversation about this matter with you or with anyone of yours. If I had [Col. 0467A], I would have given then the answer I give now: namely, that I would most gladly have your counsel, assistance, and companionship, if I were worthy of so great a thing, and that, if you commanded it, I would repay it in the service of our house.

At present, however, since this is demanded with such force, I declare that we have no monk of yours; rather, that Lord Benedict was the convert, fosterling, and professed monk of the abbot of holy memory, Lord William. When William first received the governance of the place at Gorze, he ordered Benedict—no one can deny this—to come to that monastery with many others, some of whom, now dead, lie buried there, and to remain there as one of his own. This he did until, after several years, [Col. 0467B] with the agreement of Lord Sigifrid, abbot of Gorze, and of Lord Odo, then prior and later abbot, and by order of the aforesaid Lord Abbot William, Benedict was sent and assigned to the monastery of Saint Arnulf, which, by God’s direction, I, though a sinner, serve. There he has lived until now and continues to live; and, God willing, he will remain there—unless all the arrangements of our predecessors are to be annulled.

He awaited the death of our frequently mentioned father, Lord Abbot William, and took part in, approved, and supported the election and appointment of his successor, Lord Abbot Odo. After Odo’s death, without anyone warning or compelling him, he voluntarily and willingly, as I have said, promised obedience as a monk to me, though most unworthy, and confirmed it in writing, as can easily be seen.

By contrast [Col. 0467C]—if I may say so with your peace—he took no part, either in mind or body, in your election or appointment. Later, when you passed through and lodged in our regions, you made no mention at all, not even the faintest sound, of him. When we went to Saint Michael for the sake of prayer in past years and passed through your territory, where you received and refreshed us with sufficient kindness and the greatest generosity and charity, you made no mention whatever of him; nor, I think, would you have done so, unless Doeg—not that first Idumean but now another, half-Jewish—(whose name or face I do not know; but would that I knew from truth that his life was praiseworthy in good repute, as among us he is marked and condemned in bad repute) had lately appeared from overseas and come to you to corrupt peace between us; unless [the text has “not” for “unless”], I say, that man, infamous as he is said to be or praiseworthy as I would wish, had abandoned the monastic habit and life [Col. 0467D] and for a long time wallowed in the mire of the world. At last, drunk with the stench of carnal delight, which he drank down to the dregs from Babylon’s golden cup, he has now, driven more by entreaties than by threats, begun to threaten that he will not serve Christ in this way and will turn back from his perverse path and life unless, at the very beginning—not of his conversion but of his reversion—he acts against Christ’s commands.

For Christ says to those who come to him: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and brothers,” etc. But this man declares that he cannot serve without his fleshly brother.

[Col. 0468A]

Pay heed, I beg you, to the devil’s snares. A wolf lying in wait for sheep circles the sheepfold not with a free but with a cautious and watchful step; so the devil attacks those whom he seeks to deceive not with an open but with a feigned face. Paul, however, teaches that those who have made their first faith void must be avoided; therefore he says to his disciples: “I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ.”

I too fear that association with such men will produce this man’s ruin—God forbid!—more than the other’s salvation. But someone may say: “What if he cannot be otherwise held or retained?” Let the Apostle, not I, answer him: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.” For what gain is it to acquire one soul for God and lose another? If he takes away with him his gold—would that it had not been badly acquired—with which, as I hear, he abounds, let him take it. Would that it were not he, but, if it must hinder him, his money that should go to perdition!

Holy Church does not esteem such money or the perverse gifts of wicked men [perhaps: *impiorum*, “of wicked men”]; nor does Christ seek gold, but souls. He rejected the devil when the devil offered riches, so as to teach us to do the same, and at the apostolic calling he weighed the gold and silver of Matthew and Zacchaeus on the same scale as the boat and nets of Andrew and Peter.

But, O lamentable error of men! “Abbot William,” they say, “could not establish the monk in any place other than where he had been professed, except for the days of his life.” The Lord Christ did not wish the apostles to remain any longer in the upper room, but sent them throughout the whole world [Col. 0468C] to preach the kingdom of God [Col. 0468C]. The apostles themselves, divided throughout the whole world, sent their disciples, dispersed to preach in different regions of the earth: Peter sent Apollinaris to Ravenna, Clement to Metz, Eucharius to Trier, and many others, whose enumeration would be lengthy, to various places; and Paul sent Timothy, Silvanus, and the others.

The other apostles likewise filled the regions of the world assigned to them by God with disciples announcing Christ’s faith. And can the father of a monastery, whoever he may be, acting in Christ’s place, not establish a monk—dead to the world and living for God alone—in whatever place necessity requires, either for the winning of souls or for any other useful purpose, provided that it is done for God and according to God?

[Col. 0468D]

“No,” they say; “the monk must return to his own place.” I grant that a monk may return to his own place—but one who left improperly, not one who left obediently and remained obediently where he was ordered to stay. It is Bernard who fled and escaped against his abbot’s command, not Benedict, who, by order of his abbot, obediently left the monastery of his profession, came to us, and lives obediently among us.

How much better it would have been if your Bernard had remained with that same brother among us, rather than, while living elsewhere, nourishing for so long in an overseas workshop, among his other agreements, this fire of discord which he has now kindled between us—unless the God of peace should prevent it from consuming us.

If what we say is not conceded—namely, that a monk may, with the permission and command of his spiritual father, live according to God in whatever monastery—then, to break this contentious rope at last, let it be conceded [Col. 0469A] according to the heresy imputed to Origen—justly by Catholics if he is guilty, or unjustly by the envious if he is innocent: namely, that past ages should turn back again into the same things they once were.

Let the same or another Adam and Eve once more be deceived by the serpent; let the fires of Sodom arise again; let all living things perish once more in a flood; let Saul again search for asses and David feed sheep; finally—and it is horrifying to think and say this—let Christ again be born of the Virgin Mary, grow up, be betrayed, suffer, die, and rise again. Yet Paul says the contrary: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more.”

[Col. 0469B]

Let everything return to its first beginnings: Benedict to Fécamp, Warinus to Gorze, Lord Abbot John to Dijon, and all the other faithful of Christ who have been distributed and promoted through different places in the holy Church to feed, govern, organize, and teach the Lord’s flock. Let them return from where they came, be hidden away, and lie concealed under a bushel, although the Lord says the contrary: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden,” etc.

Let the souls of the dead also, according to the poets’ dreams, having drunk from the Lethean river and revolved through a thousand cycles of years, begin again to wish to return into bodies, so that your Bernard, achieving his desire, may happily mock us with the Mantuan [Col. 0469C] shepherd and sing:

> “The great order of the ages is born anew.”

If these things are absurd—and indeed they are absurd and contrary to the Catholic faith—let falsehood be rejected and truth upheld.

The most steadfast pillar of the holy Church, Pope Gregory, sent Augustine, Mellitus, and many monks of his monastery to preach the true faith to the English peoples; and they faithfully fulfilled this charge. After the happy death of so great a man, who among his successors, I ask, either urged or compelled any of these men to return as a monk to the monastery or as a cleric to the church? Did they not instead praise, foster, and assist the holy man’s praiseworthy deed?

[Col. 0469D]

This is what I expected you to do, first from your initial zeal and love of God, then from your devotion to and charity for the pious Father, and especially for your Lord Abbot William, who nurtured, loved, recognized, and honored you among the others with unique affection. I thought that what he had established should not be abandoned by you, but rather confirmed.

I would have more to write to your fatherhood in response to the dreadful words and deeds you ordered—for excommunication is no small matter—if reverence for you and the discipline of the Rule, which teaches us monks to maintain restraint in speaking, did not constrain me.

I have nevertheless said these few things to show and prove that I am neither taking a monk nor a sheep away from you, but am justly keeping and guarding in Christ’s sheepfold what has been entrusted to me. If he lives well there, as he is able [Col. 0470A], he will not be exposed to the wolf’s bites but will be preserved in Christ’s pastures.

For although we are sinners, we nevertheless confess Christ; we hold the Catholic faith; we have received Christ’s baptism and Eucharist; we read the Rule of Saint Benedict and observe it as far as we can; we stand in Christ’s battle line against the common enemy; we strike and are sometimes struck; by God’s sustaining power we stand, and at times, when weakness hinders us, we waver; if we fall through frailty, we rise again when God lifts us up, nor do we fail to the point of despair.

And I believe that in our place—which is small and poor both in wealth and, more dangerously, in religion—each faithful monk can, with God’s help, preserve and save his soul just as in any richer and more religious place, unless someone, being wiser than he ought, should transfer the heresy of the Donatists from Africa to Normandy. They said that true religion existed in Africa alone; such a person would assert that no monk can be saved except in the monastery of Fécamp.

Whoever says or believes this unduly confines him who is exalted above all nations, whose glory is above the heavens, and whose name is worthy of praise from the rising of the sun to its setting.

For the Apostle, understanding that every person must always fear the common enemy, admonishes both your people and ours, saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith.”

Unless, perhaps, the guardianship of angels—and the cherubim with their sword—has now so fortified your place [Col. 0470C] (which I do not think will happen in this life) that the prince of this world can no longer break into it. When he tested the one in whom he had nothing, he found him in the desert, on the pinnacle of the temple, and on a very high mountain, and tested him; but, being driven away, he departed.

These are the things we fear; these are the things we suffer. Yet we too trust that we can be delivered from him, just as others can, by the one who said: “Take courage; I have overcome the world.”

We have said this not by way of reproach, but by reasoning, and by patiently answering your letters, harshly as they strike, so that, if we cannot lead you to believe, we may at least lead you to judge that the sheep you call yours, even if it were yours without any opposition from us, would perish among us only through its own fault.

[Col. 0470D]

But the tablet now shows that it is full and can receive no more; nevertheless, the complaint justly, as I think, boiling up from our heart demands to be opened, at least in part if not wholly.

What, I ask, Father, what have we done against you that you should so suddenly, unexpectedly, precipitately, and fiercely wish to hurl against us the sharpest weapon of excommunication? We hoped that, as brothers, we would be aided by your prayers, so that we might deserve to be incorporated into Christ; and now you wish to separate us by an anathema from Christ’s body and from the holy Church, whose children by God’s grace through baptism we have deserved to become!

By his grace and mercy the Lord gave priests the power that what they bound on earth would be bound in heaven, and what they loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven. But that blessed Lamb who was sacrificed for sinners reserved this for himself alone: that he alone should take away the sins of the world. He did this lest some furious and frenzied person, through rashness of mind, destroy the innocent and preserve the guilty.

The Lord himself spared the hostile Israelites and the thief on the cross; and, opening the doors of mercy, he invites even us, unwilling as we may be, to himself, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”

And a person uncertain about himself, who does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, strives by a kind of violence to shut against another person and brother—whom he is commanded to love as himself—the gates of life, though he does not know whether those gates ought to be opened for him!

Mindful of my frailty, and fearing exclusion from God’s grace because of my sins more than because of anyone’s excommunication (God forbid!) [Col. 0471B], I give thanks to God and to you that, for the time being, you have refrained from excommunicating me, whether you ought to have done so or not.

As for that brother whom, as you write, you separate from every Christian office by the authority of God, Saint Benedict, and all the saints, I do not see by what reasoning or what just judgment you had or have grounds to do this.

For a monk living regularly under the Rule of Saint Benedict—in whose authority you have called upon us in this judgment—is entirely forbidden to follow the will of his own heart, and is forbidden to leave not only the bounds of the monastery but even the cloister. How, then, can your excommunication bind one who, having no power over himself either in body or in mind, cannot—even if he wishes [Col. 0471C]—fulfill that for which he is excommunicated, namely, the act he is ordered to perform?

Jesus blamed the Pharisees for binding heavy and unbearable burdens. But if those burdens were blameworthy because they were unbearable, these are more blameworthy because they are impossible.

But you say that you do this because it is permitted. Paul, however, says that everything is permitted to him, but not everything is beneficial. Would that, according to God’s good pleasure, nothing were permitted to anyone except what is beneficial!

But since good and evil, life and death, have been placed within our free choice, we must beware toward which side we turn, and fear what is said: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil!”

If this action had to be taken, the sentence ought more directly to have been directed against the man who, leaving his father’s house improperly and returning improperly, does not mitigate his father’s offense but [Col. 0471D] aggravates it. He ought now to be corrected with the sharp points of daggers, now encouraged with the soothing remedies of admonition, and finally deservedly struck with the dart of anathema, until, coming to his senses, he should say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants.”

Now the order has been reversed: the one who offended his father by departing receives good things in place of evil and feasts with his father; while the one who always remained with his father and never transgressed his command is anathematized in place of the kid he was awaiting.

I am compelled to cry out with the prophet: “Because the ungodly prevails against the just, therefore judgment proceeds perversely.”

But since this complaining speech of ours must now be brought to a close [Col. 0472A], we ask you, Lord Father, both to have and to display a gentler disposition toward us.

It is fitting for a servant of God and of Christ’s cross—which you confess yourself to be, and which we also acknowledge you to be—to do what he did who, by dying upon the cross, the sign of death, and redeeming us through it, changed it into a sign of life. He fulfilled what the Apostle both teaches and urges us also to do, when he says:

“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his bruises we have been healed.”

[Col. 0472B]

All the saints from the beginning of the world were more ready to bless than to curse; by this example they taught us to do the same.

Why should I mention Isaac blessing Jacob? Why mention Jacob himself blessing not only his sons but also Pharaoh? Moses blessing the twelve tribes, and Simeon also blessing the Lord, from whom all blessing comes? We even read that the foreigner Balaam was afraid to curse the Lord’s people. “How,” he said, “can I curse one whom the Lord has blessed?”

If I remember correctly, in the holy Gospel the Lord himself is said to have cursed only the unfruitful fig tree, although he is read to have blessed many in both the Old and the New Law. You know better than I why he pronounced that one curse upon the fig tree.

Behold this brother, whom with such severity you wish to separate by anathema [Col. 0472C] from every Christian office: you know better than I with what labor, skill, and ingenuity he was gathered to the faith and joined to Christ from the final remnants of the Jewish people—those remnants alone having once been foretold as destined for salvation. And now, for a most worthless, indeed nonexistent, cause, he is to be cut off from Christ’s body (God forbid)!

The blood of Christ must not be held so cheaply. He laid down his life for his sheep and deigned to die for his flock; to him be glory forever.

At the end of the letter, I ask with all humility and submission that you grant us your favor and charity, and that you receive and retain us as brothers and companions—or, as we prefer, as servants. Since we are weak and sinners, may you aid us more by your prayers [Col. 0472D], so that we may deserve Christ’s presence and the companionship of the saints, rather than excluding us from so great a grace by any curse or anathema (God forbid!).

If it pleases you to do this—not because of our merit, but out of regard for Christ and brotherly charity—we give thanks. If not, we shall attribute it to our sins, yet, without losing confidence in God’s mercy, with which the earth is full, we shall pray to him who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens, that by his grace alone he may receive us into the inner tabernacles.

At the end of your letter, when you came to the farewell, you hesitated for a long time over the word of leave-taking; finally, with a certain agreement, as you say, you poured out that farewell, as though you were speaking with a heretic, concerning whom the faithful are commanded: “Do not receive him into your house, nor bid him greeting.”

[Col. 0473A]

When I bid you farewell, I do not hesitate over the word of leave-taking. As a faithful and Catholic Christian, I sincerely say to you, Father and lord: Farewell. And often turn over in your heart, as you do, the Apostle’s words: “Bless those who persecute you.” I add: Bless those who do not persecute you, but love you; bless, and do not curse.

Again, farewell; and if I have sinned in speaking, forgive me, for I have spoken in the bitterness of my heart.

## NOTE

John’s entire dispute with Warinus concerns the reclaiming of Benedict, a monk of Fécamp, who, after being converted from Judaism and becoming a monk at Fécamp, was then transferred to the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz [Col. 0474A], where he had already resided for many years.

A certain Bernard was the architect of this conflict; for that reason Warinus called him Doeg. He had defected from the monastery of Saint Arnulf and taken refuge at Fécamp.

From Warinus’s letter it is clear that William himself, who was abbot of Fécamp, had also presided over the monastery of Saint Arnulf—plainly after Benedict, John’s second successor—and that Odo succeeded him. Warinus, the author of this letter, was appointed in Odo’s place. William was later substituted for Warinus; he wrote the letters that follow. From these letters the commonly transmitted list of the abbots of the monastery of Saint Arnulf must be corrected.

Moreover, Warinus’s letter teaches us that Warinus himself had been a monk of Gorze; and that John, abbot of Fécamp, whom I mentioned above as belonging to the monastery of Dijon, had been a monk before assuming its governance. Finally, before becoming a monk, Warinus had been a cleric of Liège, as Adelmann testifies in the rhythmic verses to be published below.

The following letters were published by D. Martène in volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, columns 206, 154, and 198.

[Col. 0473]

## LETTER VI. OF JOHN, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP, TO THE UNDISCIPLINED MONKS

*(D. Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum)*

Brother John, abbot of Fécamp, wishes “eyes in the head” to Brother M., formerly his son, and to his associates.

Setting aside the testimony of the many passages of Holy Scripture by which those who act according to their own judgment are reproved, let us return to the pure and simple authority of our most blessed Father Benedict. Read, among other passages, where it is said (chapter 49): “Whatever each person wishes to offer to God, let him inform his abbot, and let it be done with the abbot’s prayer and consent, because whatever is done without the blessing of the spiritual father will be counted as presumption and vainglory, not as a reward.”

In the chapter [Col. 0473C] of that same holy Rule where he depicts four kinds of monks, he commends the first, the cenobites—that is, the principal kind—which serves under a rule or an abbot; then he introduces the second kind, the anchorites:

“Those who, not through the fervor of a recent conversion, but through long testing in the monastery, have learned, already trained by the support of many others, to fight against the devil; and, well instructed, from the fraternal battle-line they go forth to the solitary combat of the desert, already secure, and without the consolation of another, with one hand or arm alone, by God’s help, able to fight against the vices of the flesh or of their thoughts.”

Listen, brother, and understand carefully whether prolonged testing, the purging of vices, and the command, will, or permission of the abbot advanced you to such an eminent life—or whether your own will rather enticed you. But if this seems either fictitious or authentic, you yourselves must judge; for it is fitting to walk by the straight path along the royal road.

Finally, if some provocation or transgression intervenes, we entrust its removal to the argument of your philosophy: charity does not seek corners. Clearly, the inner eye of your understanding has not rightly discerned whether I am shedding innocent blood or am cruel in the death of our sons. Consider which of us is the more cruel. For we know that it is God who puts to death and gives life, and that it belongs to him alone to forgive sins; and the one whom he raises up he commanded the disciples to absolve. Yet we also know this: as long as guilt remains, no one can in any way be absolved.

As long as the prodigal son fed swine in a distant land, no fattened calf was killed for him. But when, coming to himself, moved by repentance, he returned to his father, not only was the calf killed for him, but he was clothed in the first robe and ring, and received by his father with great honor.

Enough has been said about this to the wise or the foolish, since I am indebted to all of them. If you still wish to recall a more excellent way, listen for a little while: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1).

If you boast of speaking with an angelic tongue through the aim of contemplation, you have lost charity, which is the bond of perfection. God is charity: whoever thinks against charity loses God; whoever loses God has nothing. Whoever hates himself pretends to love another. He who voluntarily flees the yoke of obedience destroys himself; whoever diminishes obedience diminishes Christ, who became obedient to the Father unto death.

In this you have indeed lost the fruit of obedience, when you secretly shook your neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule. Therefore, he who balances weapons against obedience acts against Christ; he who acts against Christ is Antichrist.

Here it is clearer than daylight that I did not shed the blood of our sons, but that the sons themselves destroyed themselves. What more is there to say? The days will come upon us before the testimonies of Scripture fail us.

## LETTER VII. JOHN, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP, APPOINTS AN ABBOT IN THE MONASTERY OF BLANGY

[Col. 0474D]

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself clearly showed us that ecclesiastical ordination is not a matter of human judgment but of divine counsel. According to the truth of the Gospel, he showed the disciples whom he had chosen, his sheep, saying: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27).

To show them the way of salvation, he presented himself as their shepherd. Before the foundation of the world, divine providence had foreknown them, wishing to display in himself the form of the good shepherd, so that in their own time they might strive with more ardent devotion to imitate what they recognized as having preceded them in Christ, their head.

Therefore, those whom he himself first chose for this purpose, so that he might establish in them the foundations of his teaching, he made vicars of his Church, which he had acquired for himself with his own blood. Thus future shepherds in ecclesiastical government would cling all the more willingly to their teaching and example, believing without doubt that they had learned more familiarly from the mouth of the heavenly teacher whom they were to imitate.

For this reason, holy Church, established by the authority of the Fathers in its several orders, is strengthened by such rulers, lest through the negligence of its members what Christ the head instituted with such diligence should fail.

Therefore I, Brother John, unworthy Father of the monastery of Fécamp, to the brothers of this place called Blangy, yielding to the prayers of the venerable Count Roger [Col. 0475C], choose as abbot and appoint as their Father our most beloved son, lord …; specifically on the condition that the aforesaid count not neglect the same place, which, long destroyed and desolate, he has begun to restore for the salvation of himself and his people, but, insofar as he is able with God’s approval, ennoble and set it in order for the praise of God.

For as long as this place endures and the monastery of Fécamp does not deviate from the regular path, the man whom we have now chosen shall have no successor except one whom the brothers of Fécamp themselves choose, according to canonical and apostolic ordinance.

But if—God forbid, though we see and mourn that this has happened in many places—the aforesaid place of the monastery of Fécamp should at some time fall away from the institutions of the holy Fathers and from the spiritual life into secular ways, we grant the brothers of this place the freedom to choose a Father for themselves, provided only that it be done according to God and in no way offend canonical authority.

### Note: Diploma of Roger, Count of Saint-Pol, by which he grants the abbey of Saint Berthe at Blangy to the monastery of Fécamp

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Roger, count of the castle called Saint-Pol, together with my wife Hadwis and my sons, namely Manasses and Robert, wish it to be known to those now living and to those yet to come that I grant to the holy and undivided Trinity, the triune and one God, living and true, at the monastery called Fécamp, a certain gift for the redemption of my soul and those of my predecessors, as well as of my wife and sons—namely, the abbey of Saint Berthe in the place called Blangy.

Considering, therefore, the instability of the present life and the mortality of this changeable age, I have resolved to make God himself a partner and heir of the possession that almighty God has bestowed upon me. For I have chosen no one better to receive a portion of the whole than the one who, by his gratuitous goodness, gave me everything that I possess.

For, just as he himself proclaims in the Gospel, “The Lord praised the unjust steward because he had prudently provided for himself in the future” (Luke 16:8), and also: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41), moved by these and other divine admonitions I therefore make, as I have said, the monks of Fécamp my friends from my inheritance, so that, when I have died, they may receive me into the eternal dwellings.

The witnesses of this matter are: Richard the canon, Warin Trepellus, Guimer Grossus, Arnulf Glassellus, Acard the knight, Vitalis the marshal. On behalf of the holy Trinity: Adelelm Calvus the monk, Rainald the monk, Osmund the monk, Milo the cleric, Tetbald the layman, William of Ingliscavilla, Calvinus, Bernefredus, Rainald the marshal, and many others.

## LETTER VIII. TO SAINT LEO IX, POPE

See under **Saint Leo**, *Patrologia*, vol. 143, col. 797.

## LETTER IX. OF THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF FÉCAMP TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH

They complain of injuries inflicted upon them by the viscount of Arques and others.

[Col. 0476A]

To their lord, their sweetest lord, their most beloved lord W., by the grace of God king of the English—may God increase him by thousands and grant him health for many days—the people of Fécamp, extending the prize of justice among his subjects, with the Judge who judges justly going before them.

If it did not displease you, and especially if it were not burdensome, we would set forth at greater length in writing the misfortunes that surround us. We therefore complain first of all about your viscount of Arques, because he invades and disrupts everything that belongs to us, and we are unable to extract any justice from him. Every day he tears apart your poor people—I say “your,” not “ours,” because the abbey is yours and I am merely its guardian, nor will I permit it to be thrown into confusion in my hands. Either guard it as your own, therefore, or subject it to someone else’s authority.

Apart from these matters, we are compelled to suffer many accusations: concerning a certain guest of Pont-de-l’Arche named Boso, whom we have held in its entirety for more than sixty years without any dispute; and concerning land in the village of Amblie, which your wife gave to our monastery by your authority, after you received from us ten pounds of denarii and one horse worth one hundred shillings, with the approval also of Malger’s son.

Likewise concerning a certain guest from the village called Luc, whom Ralph son of Herluin offers to us; and also concerning land formerly held by Wesmannus, which Roger of Loventot now retains after invading it, as he says, by your authority and without any justice.

Because of these and many other matters, I and your prebendaries are afflicted and weep every day. Indeed, since we cannot peacefully perform the service of God, we finally wish to be released from this complaint by your clemency.

From this point onward, may you be well, flourish, and live happily through the ages.

# APPENDIX TO JOHN OF FÉCAMP

## PREFACE OF JOHN, THE MAN OF GOD, TO HIS COLLECTION FROM THE WORDS OF THE ELDERS, FOR THE INSTRUCTION OF THE YOUNGER

*(D. Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum I, 163.) (G)*

### IN THE NAME OF CHRIST BEGIN THE COLLECTIONS OF FATHER JOHN, SURNAMED THE MAN OF GOD, FROM THE WORDS OF THE ELDERS

Fraternal charity often urges the timid inexperience of my mind to speak briefly about instruction in life and conduct. But since the time has come for me, with the aid of him who inspired it, to undertake this work, I have considered it necessary to begin with that praiseworthy virtue called modesty. Although it is suitable to all ages, persons, times, and places, it nevertheless especially becomes adolescent and youthful minds.

There are three virtues, however, that are especially fitting for boys and adolescents: modesty, silence, and obedience. There is no doubt that, if they strive to possess these, they can, with Christ as their guide, ascend to the summit and perfection of the virtues.

For we undoubtedly see the insignia of character and the adornments of virtue in those elders who, trained in heavenly disciplines from the very apprenticeship of their earliest age until they became mature men, ran bravely along the Lord’s way. Their wisdom now flourishes and shines as much as old age itself becomes more learned through age, more seasoned through experience, and more prudent through the passage of time.

This wisdom produces the sweetest fruits of ancient study and restores others. For many old men, living long but making no progress because they gathered no riches for themselves at the proper time, infect the souls of the young who live with them with the disease of a corrupt life, leaving them destitute of every virtue.

Just as holy religion is destroyed by a vicious and foolish old man, so also it is destroyed by an immodest and reckless youth. After ignorant and wicked prelates, no plague is found more powerful for harming the weak within holy Church.

Finally, the generation of such people produces in countless numbers those times about which the Apostle foretold—alas!—when we see almost everything that is good ruined and thrown into confusion. Since it is extremely difficult for old men to change for the better from their ingrained habit of vice, we ought to extend a hand to adolescents. If they are willing to apply themselves, casting away all tepidity, they can certainly, through the grace of Christ, correct their lives, order their conduct, and improve their actions in every respect.

For this reason I have long desired, for the salvation of the young, especially those with whom I live, to gather by selecting a few passages from the little works of the Fathers that might be particularly suited to their tender age.

For, I confess, I have great sorrow and continual grief over their blindness of heart. Although they have learned in the school of Christ how they ought both to drive away vices and to labor at holy virtues, alas! armed with a spirit of rebellion, they rush with such headlong force down the cliffs of vice toward death that the charioteer presiding over them can restrain them with no bridle of discipline.

They ought certainly to shine in the house of God, like golden vessels, for the worship of divine honor, above every adornment. Why else were they educated from the earliest beginnings of infancy with such care and labor, unless so that, made strong in battle, they might manfully fight against the flesh and its desires, against the devil and his manifold temptations?

But what is astonishing and grievous is that the rule of discipline seems harsher and more severe to them than to others. Why is this, unless because they love secular life more? Certainly, scarcely one or perhaps no one among them is found who willingly follows the Father’s institution and loves the life of the elders—either because the laborious activity frightens him, or because continence is more difficult in slippery youth, or because life seems darker to vigorous adolescence, and therefore they turn to pursuits that they consider more applauded.

For many prefer present things to future ones. Therefore, the more excellent the cause, the more attentive the care ought to be. Unhappy is the person who holds the law of life in his hands but casts discipline aside and refuses to be governed by the teaching of his elders.

Such a person lives not according to God but according to himself: if he can, he stays with whomever he wishes; he goes wherever he wishes; he sleeps when and as long as he wishes; he speaks what he wishes and where he wishes; he eats and drinks when he wishes, what he wishes, and as much as he wishes; he laughs and jokes among whomever he wishes, and wherever and whenever he wishes. Finally, whatever is pleasant to his nostrils, whatever is soothing to his touch, whatever delights his eyes, whatever is agreeable to the other senses of his flesh, he practices and pursues.

But the person who lives according to God does not do what delights him carnally, but what builds him up spiritually; and whatever he desires or does, he wants to proceed not from his own will but from the will of God and the command of his elders.

Nevertheless, no one placed in the slippery condition either of adolescence or of intemperance should despair of his conversion. For an oleaster grafted onto an olive, having lost its bitterness, becomes fruitful. If agriculture can transform the nature of trees, could not devoted study of teaching and the constancy of discipline soften every disorder of the passions?

But lest the life of a child be lost through various falls, tender years ought carefully to be entrusted to the virtues mentioned above, so that good habit may grow together with age.

# CHRONICLE OF FÉCAMP

From the first year of Christ to 1220, with the Brennac appendix to 1246, from ancient parchment manuscripts in my possession.

*(R. P. Labbe, Nova Bibliotheca manuscriptorum, vol. I, p. 325.)*

The years from Adam, the first man, to King Ninus, when Abraham was born, are 3,084 years, as they are called by all historians. From Ninus—or from Abraham—to Caesar Augustus, that is, to the Nativity of Christ, which occurred in his time, when peace had been made with the Parthians and wars had ceased throughout the world, there were 2,015 years, during which writers devoted themselves to the leisure and business of the arts. In the 752nd year from the founding of the City, Our Most Blessed Lady, the Virgin, gave birth to Our Lord Jesus Christ, in the 42nd year of Caesar Octavian.

The rest of what follows is common material, and through the negligence of an inexperienced copyist has been attached most defectively to chronological epochs, so that it often strays from the straight path of truth by enormous parachronisms or metachronisms of ten, twenty, or even more years. I will select only a few items, especially those relating to the abbots of Fécamp and Norman history, which you may review more fully from the Chronicle of Rouen.

**415.** In these days the body of Saint Stephen was revealed by Saint Gamaliel to Lucian the priest, and his relics were carried to many churches of the West.

**486** *(read 496).* Clovis was baptized by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims.

**544.** Saint Benedict, Father of the monks, died.

**584.** Clotaire, son of Chilperic, became king of the Franks.

**636** *(read 646).* Saint Audoenus was ordained bishop.

**679.** Theodoric died; Clovis succeeded him.

**876.** Rollo, duke of Denmark, came into Neustria with his men, wishing to acquire it for himself.

**898.** Rollo besieged Chartres, but Bishop Wasquelin, calling Richard, duke of Burgundy, and Ebal, count of Poitiers, to his aid, drove Rollo away while carrying the shirt of Saint Mary in his hands.

**912.** Peace was made between Charles and Rollo, and Charles gave him his daughter, by whom he had no son.

**918.** William, duke of Aquitaine, who built the monastery of Cluny in honor of Peter and Paul, died.

**943.** William, duke of the Normans, was treacherously killed by Count Arnulf of Flanders; his son Richard succeeded him.

**963.** Abbot Girard died at Cluny.

**998.** Richard, duke of the Normans, died; his son Richard succeeded him.

**1001.** William the First, abbot of Fécamp.

**1014** *(write 1024).* Emperor Henry died; Conrad succeeded him.

**1026.** Richard, duke of the Normans, died; his brother succeeded him.

**1028.** John, second abbot of Fécamp.

**1031.** Robert, king of the Franks, died; his son Henry succeeded him.

**1035.** Robert, duke of the Normans, died; his illegitimate son William succeeded him. Because he was related to King Edward, he acquired England.

**1039.** Emperor Conrad died; his son Henry succeeded him.

**1056.** The establishment at Charity began.

**1058.** The donation of Saint Gabriel was made.

**1060.** Henry, king of the Franks, died; his son Philip succeeded him.

**1064.** Le Mans was subjugated by the Normans.

**1067.** William, duke of Normandy, became king of England after Harold was killed.

**1068.** Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, died; John succeeded him.

**1078.** John, abbot of Fécamp, died; William, the third abbot, succeeded him.

**1083.** Matilda, queen of the English, wife of King William and daughter of Count Baldwin of Flanders, died.

**1087.** William, the king who acquired England, died; his son William succeeded him.

**1090.** The monks of Charity came …

**1093.** Construction of Sainte-Foy at Longueville.

**1099.** Jerusalem was captured. William the Younger died; Henry succeeded him.

**1104.** Robert, the duke, came to England, wishing to acquire it for himself.

**1105.** The dedication of Charity by Pope Paschal, on the seventh day before the Ides of March.

**1106.** Henry, king of the English, captured his brother Robert, the duke.

**1108.** Philip, king of France, died; his son Louis succeeded him.

**1116.** William, count of Nevers, was captured.

**1120.** As King Henry was returning to England, his son William was drowned at sea with the chosen nobility of the knights.

**1127.** Geoffrey, count of Anjou, married the empress Matilda.

**1128.** William the Norman, count of Flanders, and Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, died; Hugh succeeded him.

**1130.** Henry became bishop of Winchester.

**1131.** The Cluniac church was dedicated by Pope Innocent II.

**1133.** Henry, firstborn son of Count Geoffrey and the Empress Matilda, was born in March.

**1134.** Robert Curthose, brother of King Henry, died at Gloucester.

**1135.** Henry, king of the English, died; his nephew Stephen succeeded him.

**1137.** Louis, king of the Franks, died; his son Louis succeeded him.

**1139.** The Empress Matilda came to Gaul with her brother Robert, count of Gloucester.

**1141.** King Stephen was captured on the fourth day before the Kalends of February and was freed on the Kalends of November by his brother Henry, bishop of Winchester.

**1144.** A certain boy was crucified by the Jews at Norwich.

**1147.** William, count of Nevers, died.

**1151.** Geoffrey, count of Anjou, died.

**1153.** Count Theobald died.

**1154.** Stephen, king of the English, died; Henry, son of the Empress Matilda, daughter of King Henry, succeeded him.

**1157.** King Henry led an army to Gravelines.

**1158.** The king of France gave his daughter to Henry, son of the king of England.

**1159.** King Henry led an army to Toulouse.

**1160.** Mary, abbess, daughter of King Stephen, married Matthew, count of Boulogne.

**1162.** Thomas the Chancellor was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury.

**1163.** On the first Sunday after Pentecost, a council was held at Tours by Pope Alexander.

**1164.** Saint Thomas went into exile.

**1165.** Philip, son of King Louis, was born.

**1167.** Matilda, the king’s daughter, married Henry, duke of Saxony.

**1169.** The abbey of Saint Mary of Valmont was founded by Nicholas of Stoteville.

**1170.** Henry, firstborn son of King Henry, was crowned by Roger, archbishop of York.

**1171.** Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, departed to Christ.

**1172.** Henry, bishop of Winchester, died, and the king crossed over to Ireland after the feast of Saint Michael, of Nicholas.

**1173.** The king returned from Ireland and crossed over into Normandy. The church of Valmont was dedicated.

**1174.** The king of Scotland was captured.

**1175.** King Louis and Henry the Young King besieged Rouen with the nobility of France.

**1176.** Peace was made between the king and his sons.

**1179.** King Louis came to Saint Thomas, and his son Philip was crowned. New coinage was made in England.

**1180.** Louis, king of the Franks, died; his son Philip succeeded him.

**1183.** Henry the Young King died.

**1185.** Robert of Stoteville died.

**1188.** Discord arose between Kings Philip and Henry. They took up crosses for peace.

**1189.** Henry died; his son Richard succeeded him.

**1190.** King Philip and King Richard went to Jerusalem with the chosen nobility of the knights.

**1192.** King Philip returned from Jerusalem and captured the castle of Gisors and other towns in Normandy.

**1193.** King Richard was captured in Germany.

**1195.** King Richard returned after being released from prison, liberated his castles in England from the hand of his brother John, who held them, and drove out King Philip, who had entered Normandy. The bishop of Beauvais was captured.

**1199.** King Richard was killed at Limoges. His brother John succeeded him.

**1200.** Discord arose between Kings Philip and John. The church of Rouen was burned together with the city.

**1201.** Louis, son of King Philip, took as his wife, for the sake of peace, the niece of King John, and peace was made.

**1202.** Baldwin, count of Flanders, remained at Venice, wishing to go to Jerusalem. War again arose between Kings Philip and John. Arthur was captured.

**1204.** King John went to England, and King Philip entered Normandy, which was surrendered to him.

**1207.** King John returned to Aquitaine and captured many towns.

**1209.** Louis was dubbed a knight. The Christians went against the Albigensians, and he commanded them.

**1214.** Philip, king of the Franks, defeated Ferdinand, count of Flanders, and Otto, who had been emperor.

**1215.** A universal synod was held at Rome under Pope Innocent.

**1220.** The translation of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, on the Nones of July.

*(These materials were first written at Fécamp or at the monastery of Valmont and brought to Brennac, where what follows was certainly copied in an entirely different hand from the preceding material.)*

**1204.** Agnes, countess of Brana, died.

**1218.** Robert, count of Dreux and Brana, son of Countess Agnes, died; his son Robert succeeded him.

**1223.** Philip, king of France, died; his son Louis succeeded him.

**1226.** Louis died; Louis, son of that same Louis, succeeded him.

**1227.** Henry, son of Robert, count of Brana, was elected archbishop of Reims.

**1229.** Discord arose between the queen and the clerics of Paris, and many were drowned in the Seine.

**1230.** Discord arose between the king of France and Peter, count of Brittany. The king, with all the nobility of France and Brittany, went to war, and peace was again made between the king and the count. In the same year discord arose between the count of Champagne, Philip count of Boulogne, Count Robert, and other nobles of France. They crossed the Marne, burned all the villages of Épernay, Vertus, and Sézanne, and drove away the count of Champagne. On their return they besieged the castles of … and Fismes, captured them, and burned the tower of Fismes.

**1233.** Philip, count of Boulogne, died, and on the fortieth day afterward Count Robert, lord of Brana, died; his son John succeeded him.

**1238.** The count of Champagne, the count of Brittany, the duke of Burgundy, and other nobles of France went overseas against the pagans. The count of Bar and the count of Montfort were captured.

**1239.** Henry of Brana, archbishop of Reims, died.

**1242.** Discord arose between the king of France and the count of La Marche. The king of France, with the greatest part of the French nobility, went into La Marche and captured many towns. Peace was again made between the king and the count. In the same year John, count of Brana, became betrothed to the daughter of Archambault of Bourbon.

**1245.** The holy synod of Lyon was celebrated by Lord Pope Innocent IV in the church of Saint John. Frederick was deposed, and the king of France took the cross.

**1246.** The body of Saint Evodius was translated to the monastery of Brana Castle by the venerable Fathers, the bishops of Soissons and Laon, under the direction of Lord Gerard, abbot of that place, into a shrine which Gerard himself had made to be constructed, in the presence of a great multitude of the people.

# CATALOGUE OF THE ABBOTS OF FÉCAMP

From approximately the year 1000 of the Christian era, copied and brought down to our own time from ancient documents.

*(Labbe, Bibliotheca manuscriptorum I, 328.)*

**I. William.** He ruled the monastery for twenty-nine years and was buried there, in the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene.

**II. John Dalye.** Born in Italy, he traveled to Jerusalem, where he was detained for a long time in prison. He returned to the monastery and died in the year 51; he was buried in the chapel of Blessed John the Baptist.

**III. William la Pucelle.** Of the diocese of Bayeux and archdeacon of Bayeux, afterward a monk at Caen, he then became abbot of Fécamp through the election of King William. He completed a very large part of the church, ruled for twenty-nine years, and was buried in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

**IV. Roger.** Born at Argentan in the diocese of Bayeux, he ruled the monastery for thirty-one years, when it had been left desolate by the absence of his predecessor. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Martin.

**V. Henry of Sully.** Descended through a sister of King Henry I of England, he was lord and heir of Sully. He died in the forty-ninth year of his ordination and was buried in the chapel of Saint Peter.

**VI. Ralph.** Born at Argentan in the diocese of Bayeux, he built half of the nave of the church and two towers of the stacks. He ruled for thirty years and was buried near the altar of Saint Taurinus, beneath a bronze tomb raised above the floor.

**VII. Aigard.** Nephew and pupil of Ralph, born in the same town, he ruled for only two and a half years and was buried in the chapel of Saint Nicholas. He increased the monks’ portion of wine by one third.

**VIII. Richard Morin.** Born at Paluel in the diocese of Rouen, a very simple man, after five years he was compelled to resign. A successor was elected by a legate named Romanus after certain dissensions. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Martin.

**IX. William Vaspail.** Elected from the priory of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, he was born near Caen in the village of Ros, in the diocese of Bayeux. A highly learned man, he ruled for thirty-one years. Summoned to a council against the Emperor Frederick, he was imprisoned by him with others and ransomed, after which he returned to the monastery. He sent good and famous scholars to Paris, for whom he provided well monetarily [the reading is uncertain]. He was buried in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin toward the chapel of Saint Andrew.

**X. Richard of Treigoz.** Born in the village of that name in the diocese of Coutances, he ruled for twenty-six years and was buried in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin on the left side.

**XI. William of Putot.** Born in the village of Putot in the diocese of Bayeux, he ruled for twelve years and was buried in the chapel of Saint Andrew toward the chapel of the Blessed Virgin.

**XII. Thomas.** Born at Saint Benedict in Umbris, in the bishopric of Coutances, he was the first personally confirmed at the Roman Curia, although the monastery of Fécamp in no way belongs to it. He ruled for ten and a half years and was buried in the chapel of Saint John on the right.

**XIII. Robert of Putot.** Born at Putot in the diocese of Bayeux. Under him the monastery flourished in religious discipline. He ruled for nineteen years and was buried between the chapel of Saint Andrew and the chapel of Saint John the Baptist.

**XIV. Peter Roger.** Of the diocese of Limoges, a solemn doctor of sacred Scripture and a very renowned preacher, a wise man. After many years he was transferred to the Church of Arras, and shortly afterward made bishop of Le Mans, then of Rouen; finally he became a cardinal. On the Nones of May 1342 he was made pope at Avignon and was called Clement VI. He died at Avignon.

**XV. Philip.** A Burgundian by nationality and prior of Longueville, he was summoned by apostolic authority. He sat for three months and died without having received the blessing.

**XVI. Robert of Brecy.** Of the diocese of Bayeux, from the suburb of Brecy, he ruled for two years and nine months. He was buried before the altar of Saint Taurinus on the left, near the wall.

**XVII. William Bourget.** From the town of Caen in the diocese of Bayeux, he ruled for two years. He was buried before the altar of Saint Taurinus on the left, near the wall.

**XVIII. William Chouquet.** Born in the city of Bayeux, he ruled for nine years. He was buried before the altar where the morning Mass is celebrated daily, on the left near the wall.

**XIX. Nicholas of Verneil, also called of Hauteil.** Formerly abbot of Saint-Médard at Soissons, he was transferred by Clement VI. Harsh toward his subordinate vassals and monks, by whom he was summoned before the Roman Curia, he resigned after fourteen years of rule. He died at Avignon.

**XX. John of Grangia.** Of the diocese of Lyon, from the village of Grangia, he had the abbey fortified. Having gained the king’s favor, he was transferred to the bishopric of Amiens after fifteen years of rule; he became a cardinal.

**XXI. Philip du Fossé.** He ruled for nine years and was buried where morning Mass is celebrated daily, on the right side.

**XXII. Peter Corvesye.** Born in the bishopric of Rouen, in the village of Riville, five miles from this monastery, he ruled for nine years. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Peter on the left, near the wall.

**XXIII. Estodus of Estouteville.** An outstanding doctor of canon law, he established a Mass for the clerics and choristers. He ruled for thirty-three years and was buried in the nave of the church, content with a humble burial.

**XXIV. Giles of Duremort.** He ruled for twenty-two years.

**XXV. John of Hanella.** He ruled for twenty-five years and was buried in the nave of the church.

**XXVI. John Ballue.** He ruled for twelve years.

**XXVII. Anthony of La Haye.** Of royal lineage and a professor of sacred Scripture, he ruled for ten years. Anthony Ruffi succeeded him, abbot of Saint George of Boscherville near Rouen, a highly learned professor of theology, elected by the entire community except one; but the king of France prevailed.

**XXVIII. Abbot Anthony Bouyer.** Although born in humble circumstances, he was abbot of Saint-Ouen and of this place, as well as archbishop of Bourges and a cardinal. He ruled for fifteen years.

**XXIX. Hadrian of Boisy.** He ruled for five years; he was a cardinal-priest and commendatory abbot after the elected abbots.

**XXX. John of Lorraine.** He ruled for twenty-six years and eight months.

**XXXI. Charles of Lorraine.** Cardinal.

**XXXII. Louis of Lorraine.** Cardinal of Guise.

**XXXIII. Francis of Joyeuse.** Cardinal.

**XXXIV. Henry of Lorraine.** Archbishop of Reims.

**XXXV. Henry of Bourbon.** Prince and bishop of Metz.

# AROUND THE SAME YEAR: BRUNO, CLERIC OF MAGDEBURG

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE CONCERNING BRUNO

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. V, p. 327.)*
[Col. 0485D] Bruno, a Saxon by birth and enrolled among the clergy of the Church of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0485D] C. 38, 39, 40.], was a member of the household [Note: [Col. 0486D] C. 38 and 52.] of Archbishop Werinher, who, when war broke out between King Henry IV and the princes of Saxony, was one of its principal instigators together with Duke Otto [Col. 0486D]. In 1075, he voluntarily surrendered himself to the king together with the other princes; and after he had returned to his homeland and, in 1077, raised Rudolf, Duke of the Swabians, to the kingship, he fled from the battle of Mellrichstadt [Col. 0487A] in 1078 and perished among the hands of peasants. When Archbishop Hardwig succeeded him in 1079, Bruno betook himself to Werinher, Bishop of Merseburg, his deceased patron’s friend and his partner in everything he had undertaken for the commonwealth; and, having been received into the bishop’s household [Note: [Col. 0487D] Preface.], wishing to show his most beloved lord a grateful spirit, he presented him in 1082 [Note: [Col. 0487D] He completed the work after 26 December 1081 (c. 131), while Werinher (+ 1101), Burchard, Bishop of Halberstadt (c. 83), (+ c. 1088), King Herman, and Duke Otto (c. 131) were still alive; the former died in 1087, the latter on 3 January 1083.] with the best book he could produce, concerning the war of the Saxons with Henry. It is readily believed that such a gift was agreeable and welcome to a man whom we know to have worn out Thietmar’s books by handling them [Note: [Col. 0487D] SS. III, p. 729.]. Bruno resolved to write “briefly and truthfully, as he was able to learn from those who had taken part in the events” [Note: [Col. 0487D] Preface.]. He himself, an assistant in counsel or action to the two bishops who played a large part in the war [Note: [Col. 0487D] C. 52; cf. c. 58.], committed to memory what he had learned in conversation with them [Note: [Col. 0487D] Cf. c. 96: “I heard more than once from his own mouth.”] and with other princes, not only of the Saxon but also of the Henrician party [Note: [Col. 0487B] C. 13.], and what he had himself seen in person [Note: [Col. 0487D] E.g. cc. 38, 40, 52; perhaps he had accompanied both Werinhers on their journeys, and perhaps he wrote letters in their name.] or had read in public documents of unquestionable reliability [Note: [Col. 0488D] Cc. 42, 48, 49, 51, 59, 65, 66, 67, 69, etc.]. Nor, in general, does it detract from his reliability that, led by love of his homeland and hatred of servitude, he attacks Henry with particular severity [Note: [Col. 0488D] He is accused of reporting nearly incredible things about him; but in our own time, too, we have seen with our eyes and heard with our ears things that seemed incredible to many.], since amid such a great upheaval of affairs it would scarcely, if at all, have been possible to find a man attached to no party, and our author himself declares that he learned from Henry’s intimates about the crimes perpetrated by the young Henry [Note: [Col. 0488D] It is clear that Bruno writes at the beginning of the work about the young Henry; hence some of the admonitions directed against him by the highly esteemed Stenzel, II, 55–66, lose their force.].
