He touched upon Henry’s affairs with Gregory VII only insofar as they related to the Saxon war, and he always placed the supreme pontiff after his homeland. Bruno therefore resolved to write about the civil war, which had not yet been settled, as it appeared to the princes of Saxony. The book stands out for the authentic documents inserted into it, its vivid manner of writing, at times humorous and playful [Note: [Col. 0488D] E.g. cc. 75, 77, 83, 96.], its simple style, and its sentences endowed with a certain rhythm and quite often ending in the same sounds. Although it could hardly have pleased writers of the opposing party, such as Ekkehard of Aura [Note: [Col. 0488D] Ekkehard seems to have known our work, but in his Chronicle he generally recounts different events for the years 1068–1080.] and others, it nevertheless appears to have enjoyed considerable authority among later generations, since most of it was copied at the end of the twelfth century by the Saxon annalist and at the beginning of the sixteenth century by the author of the Magdeburg Chronicle. Yet only one manuscript of the book exists: it was written at the end of the fifteenth century in the monastery of Altenzell, and from it the editions of Freher, Struve, and our own derive. It is preserved today:

1.) In the library of the Royal University of Leipzig [Col. 0487D], under the notable number 1323: a paper quarto of folios 2–55 containing Bruno, folios 55–66 containing certain passages transcribed from Platina, and folios 66–73 containing excerpts from Ekkehard of Aura [Col. 0488A], with this inscription: “The account of the Saxon war ends here; and with the end of Henry IV, 19 July 1500, by Brother M. S. T., then prior. Thanks be to God.” Folios 74–83 contain another manuscript presenting legends about Saint Anthony. The scribe, who used many abbreviations, generally followed faithfully and accurately the text as he had found it, though he seems not to have understood certain passages very well and, in the forms of proper names, to have expressed the usage of his own period rather than that of the text. The beginnings of chapters are indicated by a red letter.

Ib.) The Magdeburg Chronicle, whose manuscript, written on parchment in 1600, was sent by Marquard Freher to Meibomius [Note: [Col. 0488D] See the preface of the younger Meibomius.] and was later printed in volume II of Meibomius’s *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, took everything printed from page 288 through page 319, except for twenty-one lines on page 313 and three lines on page 314, from Bruno’s chapters 1–41, 44–47, 52–58, 60–65, 68, 74–102, 117, and 121–131—that is, omitting many documents. Its text follows the reading of manuscript 1 so closely even in the smallest details that it must be considered to have derived not from that manuscript itself but from a source common to it. For there are certain passages in which it is clear that the two writers understood and expressed the same word differently—for example, chapter 40, where the Leipzig reading *ymmo* had to be corrected from the Magdeburg reading *nimio*. Since, however, both manuscripts make other errors in the same way—for example, in chapter 56, where both, following an already corrupt source, give the name of Margrave Ekkibert as Erribert—it is fortunate that, in restoring the text [Col. 0488C], one may make use of—

2.) The Saxon annalist. In the years 1067–1082 he incorporated into his narrative a great deal from Bruno’s chapters 1, 5, 16, 2–15, 17–31, 32, 31, 33–47, 52, 47–51, 53–56, 64, 57, 58, 60–63, 65–68, 70–74, 82–88, 75, 74, 76–78, 80, 79, 81, 89–97, 99–101, 96, 101–103, 76, 77, 104–116, 98, 117–123, 122, and 123–131. He preserved the reading of the eleventh- or twelfth-century manuscript that he used, which is very often excellent, as well as certain sentences that, through a common fate, have dropped out of manuscripts 1 and 1b. Of these, however, I admitted into the text only those which the sense plainly required, or which were clearly derived not from other sources of the annalist—especially Ekkehard of Aura, from whom he occasionally inserts a few words. I used the authentic manuscript of the annalist [Col. 0488D], among the books brought from the monastery of Saint-Germain and now in the library of the Royal Library of Paris, marked with the number 440 [Col. 0489A]; its readings were recorded by our Waitz.

3.) In restoring the text of the letters of Pope Gregory VII and of the other letters, I consulted Gregory’s *Register* and Paul of Bernried’s *Life of Gregory VII*, and from the Trier manuscript I appended the end of the letter written to King Rudolf.

I used these aids in such a way that I placed manuscript 1 as the foundation—the copy of which was most willingly supplied to me by the highly learned men who have rendered great service in this matter, Dr. Ernst G. Gersdorf, prefect of the Leipzig University Library, and Gustav Haenel, its custodian—and corrected it, where necessary, with the help of the others, especially the Saxon annalist, both in the spelling of proper names [Note: [Col. 0489C] I consistently write *Heinricus, Adalbertus, Werinherus, Fridericus, Halberstadensis, —burg, Bawarii, Boemii, Merseburg, Magedaburg, Babenberg, Herimannus, Sigefridus, Wirtzeburg, exsurgo, exstirpo*.] and elsewhere; [Col. 0490A] the division into chapters follows the authority of the Leipzig manuscript.

Bruno was first published in 1600 by Marquard Freher, among the *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, volume I, pages 99–153. The text is that of the Leipzig manuscript, but it was often poorly disentangled and more often corrected either from the Magdeburg Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0489C] See, for example, chapter 65 at the end, “not by an oath,” [Col. 0490C] and chapter 40 below.] or by plausible conjecture. When this edition was reprinted in 1717, Burcardus Gotthelfius did so. Struve corrected some passages by consulting the Leipzig manuscript again, but corrupted others [Note: [Col. 0490C] Thus in chapter 40, in the Magdeburg manuscript, he wrote “deer fighting in the meadow,” following the Leipzig manuscript, although Freher had already correctly written “ravens” from the Magdeburg Chronicle, a reading also supported by the Saxon annalist.]. A comparison with our edition will show that quite a few corrections remained for us to make as well.

Bruno reckons the beginning of the year from the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0490C] Cf. the years 1076–1081, chapter 131.].

[Col. 0489]

# BRUNO’S BOOK ON THE SAXON WAR

## PROLOGUE TO THE SAXON WAR

[Col. 0489B] To his most beloved lord, never to be named without pious veneration, Werinher, the venerable prelate of the holy Church of Merseburg, Bruno—although a very small part of his household, yet whatever the devotion of a human being of either condition can offer.

Between the one who gives some gift and the one to whom it is given, this principle ought to be observed: when the former can find nothing more precious in his treasures to give, then the latter should receive nothing more pleasing than such a gift. Reflecting on this, when I wished to offer some gift to Your Paternity, whom I have always desired to serve according to my strength, indeed beyond my strength, by which I might also display outwardly, through the testimony of some work, the fervor of my mind, I searched through all the chests of my resources and found only one kind of gift [Col. 0489C] which I thought suited both your dignity and my devotion. For I consider this gift more precious than all the other things that human kindness can bestow upon one another, because its origin is nobler, its use more excellent, and its life demonstrably longer. Gold, and the other things that human beings regard as especially valuable, born from the bowels of the earth [Note: [Col. 0489] Thus the editions; *nato* in manuscript 1.], provide no improvement for the soul, but offer only brief support to bodily frailty or even a shameful service to luxury; and while they sustain human bodies, they cannot escape their own destruction. Even when they lie undisturbed, they are not safe, since, eaten away by the bites of moths or by rough rust, they cannot endure for long [Col. 0490B].

The study of letters, however, dug out with the mattock of reason from the more hidden dung-heaps of the soul [Note: [Col. 0489] The later editions read *secretioribus*.], ought to render no service to bodily weakness; rather, it forms and instructs the mind of the one whose industry has brought it forth. It is so ignorant of old age and destruction that even those things which are swept away to ruin by the violent torrent of time, the power of letters strives to rescue from time’s force and to display ever new, as though permanently stationed, to its readers. Therefore I wish to write briefly and truthfully about the war which King Henry waged with the Saxons, as I was able to learn it from those who took part in the events. It is memorable both because of its magnitude and because of the mercy of God, which we experienced in that very war, as anyone who deigns to read what follows will be able to recognize [Col. 0490C]. For in the scourge he mingled the oil of mercy with the wine of severity, so that we might joyfully acknowledge both that the prophet spoke truly: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2), and the Apostle: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

But before I begin to unfold the course of the war itself, I ought to preface it with a few remarks about the childhood and adolescence of that same Henry, so that when the reader has learned what sort of life he led as a boy or adolescent, he will be less surprised that, when he became a man, he began a civil war. Yet, lest anyone taking this work into his hands should immediately wish to spit upon it, I decided to fortify it by placing your name at its head, so that while your name appears on the first page [Col. 0492A], the work that follows may be protected from spittle. Therefore may your dignity deign to receive it with as much eagerness as the devotion with which it is offered by me.

# THE SAXON WAR BEGINS

[Col. 0491]

[Col. 0491A] 1. After the Emperor Henry departed from this world by a blessed death (in the year 1056), his son Henry IV, unhappily left alive in this world, received his father’s kingdom by common election. Since, as a five-year-old child, he was not yet able to govern it suitably, his mother, the venerable Empress Agnes, at the command of all the princes, took charge of caring for him together with the administration of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0491] The edition reads *causa*.]. But as time progressed, and although the boy advanced in age, he did not advance in wisdom [Col. 0491B], either before God or before human beings; and as, swollen with royal pride, he began to listen less to his mother’s admonitions, Anno, the venerable prelate of Cologne, forcibly took him away from his mother (May 1062). He took care to raise him with every diligence, as became an imperial offspring, looking not so much to the king as to the kingdom. For he was not unaware that “an unwise king will destroy his people, and cities will be inhabited through the prudence of the wise” [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *civitate*.] [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *per sensus*.]. Nor was he unaware that, just as virtues reveal some people born from humble stock, so those born from great parents, if instruction and good morals are lacking, are disgraced by guilt.

But after he had passed beyond childish simplicity and entered adolescence, which is the common field of all sins, he came to the fork in the road of the letter Y [Horace] [Col. 0491C]. Abandoning the narrowness of the higher right-hand path, he chose the broad descent of the left-hand road as his way, and, utterly renouncing the path of virtues, resolved with all his strength to follow his desires. To make this possible more freely—for under that teacher he was not permitted to do whatever he pleased—he first completely shook off that teacher’s authority; and he who had been chosen to govern the kingdom now disdained being governed by anyone. Thus, once the king had been released from the bishop’s authority (29 March 1065), and had begun to be his own master, he then revealed which way of life he had decided to follow [Note: [Col. 0491] I correct the text in this way; cf. chapter 11. The editions read *quam*, manuscript 1 *qa*. But “the way of life is the way of salvation.”]. For the briars of lust [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *lividinum*.], which at this age weary even those who dry them up in themselves by frequent fasts and uproot them by constant prayers, sprouted in him all the more fruitfully because he himself, burning with the fire of first youth and abounding in the luxuries of royal wealth, neither tore them from the field of his heart, nor did anyone dare to uproot them with the iron of correction, since he was a king who scorned admonishers [Col. 0491D].

2. At that time Adalbert, prelate of Bremen, was so swollen with the tumor of pride [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *typo*; manuscript 1b, *typho*.] that he thought no one equal to himself either in secular nobility or in holy conduct. When, on some great feast, he celebrated a public Mass in the king’s presence and, as usual, climbed to a higher place to speak the word of God to the people, he complained among other things that the good and noble had perished from the earth, and said that only he and the king remained of the nobility—placing himself before the king—although his two brothers, born of the same parents [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 2 reads *orti*.], stood there present. And although he did not bear the name of Peter, the prince of the apostles and his own brother, he nevertheless claimed to possess the same power that Peter could possess, or even greater, because he had never denied his Lord [Col. 0492B] as Peter had.

3. He ordered an abbess in his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *abatisse*.], who had committed some offense—who knows what—against him [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *quia*.], under penalty of obedience to leave this present life within fifteen days. Since she was ill at the time, that foolish man hoped that his command could be fulfilled in her case; and if she happened to die, he wanted it to be believed that she had died at his command.

On the fifteenth day, however, after she had recovered her health, she sent a messenger to the bishop, for some reason I do not know. When he saw the messenger approaching from a distance, he said joyfully to those sitting with him: “Can my power over this woman be less than that of my brother Peter over Sapphira? Look! This wretched woman is dead, my authority having commanded it!” But when the messenger came nearer and he learned that she was alive and had recovered from her illness [Col. 0492C], he was deeply confounded by his pride and fell silent.

4. Once, as usual, he was at the king’s court and loaded the king’s table every day with more sumptuous banquets than the king himself. One day, when everything pertaining to food had been consumed through excessive luxury, his steward had nothing which, according to his custom, was fine enough to place upon the king’s table for the king to eat [Note: [Col. 0491] This seems to require correction. Manuscript 1 reads *cum*; manuscript 1b has a lacuna.] [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 reads *imponerent*.]. Nor was there any money with which to buy an expensive dish, because he had spent all the silver for a similar purpose. Since the bishop knew this, he hid himself that day so that the steward could not find him, wishing the man to seek out by his own ingenuity, in whatever way he could, something suitable to place upon his table [Col. 0492D].

But after the steward had searched for a long time and finally learned that his master had taken refuge in a certain chapel, he knocked more confidently at the chapel door and asked to be admitted. When the bishop recognized his voice, he suddenly threw himself upon the ground as though in prayer. The steward entered; when he saw him lying there and could not rouse him either by coughing or by clearing his throat, he finally stretched himself out beside the bishop as though he too were going to pray, and said into his ear: “Pray,” he said, “that you may have something to eat today, for as yet you have nothing which can honorably be placed upon your table.”

The bishop, as though suddenly awakened from an ecstasy, said: “What have you done, you utter fool, who rashly snatched me away from conversation with God? If you had seen what Brother Transmandus [Note: [Col. 0493] Thus manuscripts 1 and 1b; manuscript 2 reads *Trosmandus*.] was privileged to see, you would never have approached me while I was engaged in prayers.”

The man was present at the time, and because he saw that such things pleased the bishop, he had already said that he had seen angels speaking with him while he prayed. He himself was a painter from Italy.

5. When this bishop therefore saw the king rushing like an unbridled horse over the precipices of vice, he sought to attach himself familiarly to his side—not in order to uproot from the roots with the hand of stern authority the thorns of vices that had sprung up, and to plant the seeds of virtues by episcopal preaching, but in order to water the shoots of vice with the water of flattery and, if any fruits of virtue emerged, to kill them with the bitterness of perverse doctrine.

For he did not, as of old, say with Tobit, so that Henry might guard against committing crimes: “Beware of all fornication, and bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your paths”; nor, so that he might wash away crimes already committed with tears of repentance, did he, like Nathan, wield beneath the veil of a parable the sword of reproof, so that, when the wound of the mind had been suddenly struck, the poison of conscience might flow out. Rather, he gave him what he represented as an apostolic command: “Do everything that pleases your soul; observe only this, that on the day of your death you may be found in the true faith” [Col. 0493C].

Yet Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires,” and again: “Do not sow evil in the furrows of injustice, and you will not reap it sevenfold.” He taught as though it lay within a person’s power to change his life in a single hour, although the proverb says: “A young man will not depart from his way even when he grows old,” and: “The odor that a fresh jar once absorbs it will retain for a long time” [Horace].

Thus, strengthened in wickedness by the bishop’s non-episcopal teaching, the king went down through the precipices of lust [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript 1 reads *lividinum*, as often.], like a horse and a mule that have no understanding; and he who was king of many peoples set up his throne in lust, the queen of all vices.

6. He kept two or three concubines at the same time. Not content with these, whenever he heard that someone had a young and beautiful daughter or wife [Col. 0493D], he ordered her to be brought to him by force if she could not be seduced. Sometimes he himself went by night, accompanied by one or two men, wherever he knew such women to be. Sometimes he achieved his evil desire; sometimes he scarcely escaped being killed by the parents of the woman he loved or by her husband.

He hated his wife, whom he had unwillingly married at the persuasion of the princes, although she was noble and beautiful, so greatly [Col. 0494A] that after the marriage had been celebrated he never voluntarily saw her [Note: [Col. 0493D] Only in 1071 did she bear him a son.], because he had not celebrated the marriage willingly [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript 1 reads *Quia*.]. Thus he sought in many ways to separate her from himself, so that he might then commit illicit acts with apparent license, since he would no longer have the lawful marriage that was permitted to him.

7. Finally, he ordered one of his intimates to seek intercourse with the queen and promised him a great reward if he obtained it. He hoped that she would not refuse him, because, having experienced a husband, she was now living as though abandoned. But the queen, possessing a manly heart beneath a woman’s body, immediately understood from what source this plan had come.

At first she refused as though indignant; but when the man persisted, as he had been instructed in advance, she promised orally to do what was requested. He reported the matter joyfully to the king and indicated the hour at which it was to be carried out [Col. 0494B].

The king, delighted, went together with the adulterer to the queen’s bedchamber, so that, when he himself saw them unite, he could lawfully cast her away from his marriage—or, what he preferred even more, kill her. But when the adulterer knocked at the queen’s door and she quickly opened it [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript 1 reads *volociter*.], the king, fearing that if the other entered first he himself would be shut out, rushed through the door. Recognizing him, the queen left the adulterer outside, closed the door as quickly as possible, summoned her maidens, and beat him so severely with benches and sticks, which she had gathered for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript 1 reads *colligerat*.], that she left him half dead.

“Son of a prostitute,” she said [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript 2 reads *it*; manuscript 1 lacks the word; manuscript 1b reads *inquiens*.], “where did you get the audacity to hope for adulterous relations with a queen who has the strongest of husbands?” [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscripts 1 and 1b omit *ut reginae, quae fortissimum habet maritum, sperares adulteria*; manuscript 2 adds *ea*.]

He cried out that he was Henry, that he was her husband, and that he had wished for lawful intercourse with her. She retorted that the man who had sought secret adultery was not her husband; if he were her husband, why did he not openly approach his own bed? Thus, after beating him almost to death, she threw him out of the bedchamber, closed the door, and went to her own bed.

He did not dare confess to anyone what had happened to him, but, pretending another illness, lay for almost an entire month in his bed. For she had spared neither his head nor his belly, but had bruised his whole body while leaving the skin intact. After he recovered, although severely chastened, he did not abandon his former crimes.

8. If any woman made a complaint before him about any injury and requested that justice be done to her by the king’s royal power [Col. 0494D], if her age and appearance pleased his madness [Note: [Col. 0493] Or *vel*, “or,” in manuscript 2.], then, instead of the justice she had sought, she received manifold injustice. For after the king himself had satisfied his lust upon her for as long as he wished, he gave her to one of his servants as though she were a wife.

Thus he dishonored noble women in this land still more disgracefully in servile marriages, after he himself had first shamefully abused them. That false and deceitful bishop saw all these things [Note: [Col. 0493] The initials *e. Adelbertus* occur in manuscripts 1b and 2.]; he saw them and did not prevent them [Col. 0495A]. Indeed, by his teaching he strengthened the king, as though by encouraging him, to do such things without fear or shame. For he said that it was foolish not to satisfy in every way the desires of his youth.

9. I deliberately pass over many other serious crimes of this kind, because I hasten to other crimes of another sort. Let this one, however, occupy the final place here: a just judge will not leave unpunished the disgrace he inflicted upon his sister [Note: [Col. 0495] The same thing seems to be hinted at by the envoys of the Saxons in Lambert, p. 198.]. He held her down with his own hands until another man, compelled at his command, had intercourse with her in the presence of her brother. It did not help her that she was the emperor’s daughter, that she was his only sister by both parents [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscripts 1 and 1b have a lacuna.], or that she had been betrothed to Christ by the sacred veil of her head.

10. But since abominable fornications usually generate still more abominable murders, just as that lustful man violated not one Bathsheba [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 and the editions read *Bersabe*.], so that cruel man killed not one Uriah. He committed so many monstrous crimes in the matter of murder that it is uncertain whether his greater disgrace lies in incestuous lust or in boundless cruelty.

He was horribly cruel to everyone, but to no one so much as to his closest intimates. Whoever shared all his secrets and was privy to or assisted in his crimes, while safely favoring him when he plotted the deaths of others, was compelled to suffer the death he had not feared. And for what fault? Because he had spoken one word against the king’s will, or, while remaining silent, had shown by some gesture that one of the king’s plans did not please him.

He had many counselors, but no one dared give him counsel except what pleased him [Col. 0495C]. If anyone, unaware of the danger, advised him to do something he did not want, he paid for the offense he had committed unknowingly by the shedding of his own blood. Nor did the king reveal his anger to anyone until he had the unsuspecting man’s life taken away.

11. One of his secretaries, named Conrad—a young man distinguished in nobility and character, if only God had granted him never to have been the king’s counselor—was one day at Goslar, certain that he enjoyed the king’s favor as fully as he had when he possessed it at its height.

The king, however, was in the castle of Hartsburg [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 reads *hertesburck*; manuscript 2, *hertesburh*.], to which, apart from those who were privy to and supporters of his crimes, no one ascended unless summoned by name [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 reads *propter*; manuscripts 1b and 2, *praeter*.]. The king therefore sent to Goslar, ordering Conrad to come to him immediately and to bring no one except his own armed attendant.

Thinking that he was being summoned to some council which no one but himself was permitted to attend, and wishing to show his greater loyalty, Conrad did more than he had been ordered: he became his own armed escort and rode out without a companion.

When he came into a forest, he saw an ambush but did not believe that it had been set for him. Nevertheless, because he was alone and feared so large a force, he quickly sought a nearby church [Col. 0496A]. Burchard, prefect of Meissen, the wicked leader of this brigandage [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 reads *latrocii*.], followed him to the church and promised on his word that, if Conrad wished to come out, he would suffer no harm.

Although Conrad had no confidence in him, he knew that if he did not come out voluntarily they would not spare the church. He therefore came out and entrusted himself to Burchard’s word. They led him into a deserted place and, exactly as they had been ordered, cruelly killed him; nor, even at the moment of death, did they tell him why he was dying.

No one ever truly learned why he had been killed, except that some muttered [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 reads *musitabant*.] that the king had charged him with having slept with one of his concubines. But the king, to remove suspicion of his death from himself, ordered all his friends to pursue the authors of the same death, whom he had commanded to hide for a time [Col. 0496B]. He had Conrad buried in an honorable place, attended his burial sadly, and, trained as he was in pretending everything, shed no small number of tears. Yet no one could believe that Conrad had not been killed by the king’s order, as indeed he had.

12. It was said that he had killed with his own hand one of his intimates, a most noble young man, while pretending to play; that he had secretly buried him; and that on the following day he had come, as though repentant, to his teacher, Bishop Adalbert, and received pardon from him without any satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 1 reads *pepercit*.]. But since I was unable to learn the truth of this matter, I decided to leave it among the uncertainties, although it was on nearly everyone’s lips.

13. I know of one of the king’s intimates [Col. 0496C] who once came from the court to his brother—the brother was a bishop [Note: [Col. 0495] Manuscript 2 adds: “The brother of that archbishop, Count Frederick the Palatine, once boastfully related the story to his brother, and so forth.”]—and boasted to him that no one at court enjoyed greater favor with the king than he did.

When his brother the bishop heard this gladly, and earnestly admonished him to seek by every means to preserve the king’s favor, since it would be honorable for him and useful to all his people, the man replied: “I would do so if, together with the favor of the earthly king, I could retain the favor of the heavenly one. But I have truly learned that, if anyone enjoys this king’s intimate favor, he cannot possess eternal life.”

Accordingly, like a prudent man, he gradually withdrew from the court. He approached the king’s secrets less and less, and was neither completely absent nor present as frequently as he had been accustomed to be [Col. 0496D].

When the king saw that he was less constant in his service, he did not inquire into the reason, nor did he show him any ill will. Rather, wishing now to spare his own sword, he sought to destroy him by another’s blade. Thus, for a reason—whether fabricated or genuine I do not know—he sent him to the king of Rus’ [Note: [Col. 0495] Thus manuscript 2; manuscript 1 reads *ruciae*.].

The man willingly accepted this embassy, first because by it he thought he had proved that he was not excluded from the king’s favor, since he did not hesitate, as before, to entrust him with secrets; then because he hoped that, by the labor of this embassy, he would earn a considerable reward from the king when he returned after successfully completing it. Nor was this the least of his reasons: he was glad to be away from court.

He therefore departed, still unaware of what had been decided concerning him. After several days, when evening had fallen and he had stopped at an inn, he ordered a good banquet to be prepared for him. When his companions had already drunk somewhat, a certain Slav, a person of low condition, sprang up and said: “I do not know what it is that I am carrying, which Bishop Eppo [Note: [Col. 0497] The edition reads *Eppo of Chichester*.] gave me and ordered me to deliver to the king to whom you are going.”

When the envoy asked that it be shown to him, the Slav produced a letter from the king sealed with the king’s image [Col. 0497B]. Without delay he broke the seal and ordered his clerk to explain what the letter meant. The clerk read and interpreted it. This was the sense of the letter:

“Know that you can show most clearly what sort of friend you are to me if you arrange that this messenger of mine never be able to return to my kingdom. Whether you accomplish this by perpetual imprisonment or, rather, by death, consider it to make no difference.” [Note: [Col. 0497] Thus the edition; manuscript 1 reads *q vre*.]

After committing the letter to the fire, the envoy cheerfully continued his journey, prudently completed his embassy, returned with a considerable gift, and brought royal presents to his lord the king.

14. I learned the following matter concerning one of the king’s closest counselors, whose name, like those of many others, I deliberately omit. I have decided to insert it here because it contains within it two of the king’s most serious vices, namely cruelty and lust [Col. 0497C].

This counselor was not born in Saxony, but he married a Saxon-born woman, a maiden as beautiful in body as she was noble in family. The king himself obtained her from her parents for him; the king himself attended the wedding, though it is uncertain whether more for the honor of the bridegroom or out of love for the bride [Note: [Col. 0497] Manuscript 1b reads *an*, “or.”].

She had not yet set aside the modesty of a betrothed maiden’s virginity [Note: [Col. 0497] Manuscript 1 reads *desposite*.] [Note: [Col. 0497] Manuscript 1 reads *pudicie*.] when the king, having set aside all modesty, asked the bridegroom to send her to his own bed.

“Although,” he said, “I would never wish to deny you anything—not even life itself—this is the one thing which it is neither fitting for you to ask of me nor possible for me to grant you.”

The king, a great dissembler, showed neither in face nor in words the grief that he held deep in his heart [Col. 0497D]. After not many days, when the counselor felt secure and feared nothing for himself, the king sent for him at about midnight, ordering him to come to him alone.

Although, knowing the king’s custom, he was certain that he was destined to die that very night, he went where he was ordered. But first he put on a triple coat of mail beneath his tunic.

When he reached the entrance to the royal bedchamber, behold, two swords fixed on either side of him would have met in the middle of his entrails [Col. 0498A] had not the strength of his breastplate repelled them. He nevertheless reached the king and told him how he had been received before his chamber. The king then ordered him, if he wished to live thereafter, never to let anyone know of this.

### 15

To all these evils he added this evil: he gave the former evils a foundation by which they might grow strong, and the new ones a beginning from which they might arise. For he appointed bishops not according to the merits of their character, as the decrees of the canons required, but if anyone paid a larger sum, or proved to be a greater flatterer of his crimes, that man was more worthy of any bishopric. And once he had given a bishopric to someone in this way, if another offered him more, or praised his crimes more extravagantly, he had the first man deposed as though he were a Simonian, and had the second consecrated in the same place as though he were a saint. Hence it happened that many cities in those times had two bishops at once, neither of whom was worthy of the name of bishop.

He gave the bishopric of Bamberg—rich in external possessions and venerable within for its learned men—to a certain money-dealer; indeed, he sold it for an incalculable sum. This man knew better how to assess coins of every mint than how to read the text of any book—not to speak of understanding or expounding it, or even pronouncing it correctly according to the rules. Once, during the sacred office of the Easter Vigil, he recited before learned clerics the first lesson in the customary manner: “Now the earth was formless and a cow!” He himself, plainly, although two-footed, was a brutish cow, empty of every virtue!

Yet although he spared neither his own gold nor that of the church which he had accepted as though to govern it, in order to win the king’s favor, he was deposed at the king’s own counsel, and the bishopric was given to another—not to one more worthy of the bishopric in life and wisdom, but to one who had been in every respect a greater flatterer of the king’s crimes.

### 16

Amid all these events, as his youth was already passing away, no sooner had he obtained Adalbert, bishop of Bremen, as his counselor than, persuaded by that man’s advice, he began to seek in deserted places high mountains fortified by nature, and to build on them castles of such a kind that, if they stood in suitable locations, they would at once be a mighty foundation and an ornament for the kingdom.

The first and largest of these he called Hartesburg. On the outside he fortified it with such a strong wall, towers, and gates; within, he adorned it with such royal buildings; in it he constructed such a monastery; in that monastery he placed such ornaments; and he gathered there from every direction so many clerics, that it might rival several episcopal sees in all their equipment, and even surpass some of them.

Whatever ecclesiastical ornament he saw any bishop possessing that made him especially splendid, whether obtained by command or by entreaty, he took pains to transfer to his own monastery. The other castles he worked to make not so beautiful as strong.

Blessed, indeed supremely blessed, would he have been if he had erected those same fortifications against the pagans. For by now they would either all have been Christians, or perpetual tributaries to Christian princes.

At first, however, the construction of these castles in various places seemed to our countrymen a childish game, because his evil intention was not yet known. Not only did they not prevent their construction, though they could have done so and still feared no danger, but they even helped him in the building, with money or labor, as though divining that this would make him warlike against foreign nations.

But after the garrisons stationed in those castles began to conduct raids in their vicinity, to carry away the people’s produce for their own use, to compel free men to servile labor, and to treat other men’s daughters or wives as objects of abuse, then for the first time they understood what those castles foretold. Even then, however, they did not dare to resist or defend themselves. Only those who were being harmed made secret complaints to those who lived farther from the castles and had not yet suffered any evil.

While the unharmed neglected to bring aid to the harmed, they granted strength to the tyranny against themselves. For it rose from the peasants to the knights, and from the fruits of the earth to the deprivation of liberty. The king asserted that Frideric of Monte, who was considered outstanding among free or noble men, was his servant. He also persecuted with such cruelty Wilhelm—who, because of his excessive devotion to the king, was called by the king “of Lotheslovo” [that is, “of Loth’s love,” because he had loved his daughters]—because Wilhelm had many estates but not much wisdom, that chiefly on account of these two a conspiracy was formed throughout all Saxony against the king, although the two themselves made the worst possible return.

For after all the Saxons had openly begun war against the king, those two, forgetting their sworn faith, were the first to abandon their homeland and, as contemptible deserters, defect to the enemy. This will become clear later.

### 17

When the people of Swabia heard of the Saxons’ calamity, they secretly sent envoys to them and made a pact with them: neither people would bring aid to the king for the oppression of the other.

For the king also wanted to oppress the Swabians by force and compel them to pay him tribute from their estates. If the Saxons had faithfully kept this pact, they would have been free both from the disgrace of treachery and from a large part of their calamity.

### 18

Sigifridus, archbishop of the see of Mainz, sent letters full of complaints to Werinherus, bishop of Magdeburg, and Burchardus, bishop of Halberstadt, because the king had chosen places in his bishopric suitable for carrying out raids and, having placed castles and garrisons there, was inflicting many evils upon the possessions of his church.

In the same letters he also asked them to join themselves to Archbishop Anno of Cologne in a most faithful alliance—not because they were divided by any hostility, but because their friendship did not unite them so faithfully that each dared entrust his secrets to the other as he wished.

This, he said, was necessary for the whole kingdom. If those two men, who were the greatest in the kingdom, came faithfully together as one, they could establish the entire kingdom in great security. Those two bishops could easily bring this about because one of them—namely, the bishop of Magdeburg—was the brother, and the other the cousin, of the aforementioned archbishop of Cologne.

Nearly all the princes of the German kingdom made the same complaint to one another. Yet no one dared acknowledge it openly, so great was the terror the king inspired in everyone. Thus, although the Saxons alone seemed to be openly beginning the war, it was not begun by their counsel alone.

When each of them was suffering so many and such great calamities and insults, they did not resist the common evil by common counsel: each grieved only over his own wound and did not sympathize with one who had been wounded while he himself remained untouched.

The king was planning universal ruin and drove away every obstacle to it, seeking everywhere the assistance by which his evil will might be fulfilled. They, however, thinking the evil peculiar to themselves, prepared no means of defense against the common destruction.

To oppress everyone more easily as he wished, he first tried to weaken them individually in whom their strength chiefly lay.

### 19. (A.D. 1070)

Finally, he sought by every stratagem to depose Otto, a prudent and brave man who, born in Saxony, was duke in Bavaria, because he had no doubt that Otto would aid the Saxons together with all the Bavarians.

Accordingly, he hired a certain man named Einnonus, who possessed no virtue except boldness, and enticed him with promises, so that he would say that he had discussed the king’s death with the duke and promise to prove this in single combat if Otto denied it.

When the day for that contest had been fixed, Otto was warned in advance by his friends, the bishops and other princes, that if he came to Goslar, where the duel was to take place, then even if he defeated his opponent, he would nevertheless not return from there alive.

He therefore chose to be unjustly deprived of his honor rather than undergo such a judgment, where he knew that violence was being done to justice itself. He withdrew to his own lands and, together with Magnus, duke of Saxony, waged a cruel war against the king for almost two years (A.D. 1071).

Then, compelled by the counsels of their friends, when they surrendered themselves to royal authority, the king kept Duke Magnus in his prison for a full two years, so that during that time no one knew whether he was alive or where he was.

### 20

Afterward he sent envoys across the sea to the king of Denmark (A.D. 1073) and asked him to meet him at Bardanwich. He himself went there with a few companions; no report attests that any king before him had ever reached those regions. He met the Danish king there, and held a private conference with him. Apart from Bishop Adalbert and one of the king’s counselors, no one attended that conference.

The conference did not, however, remain concealed for long. The man who alone was present with the bishop, since he could not prevent the plan they formed there, accomplished what he could: he ensured that the princes of Saxony whose interests were involved would not remain unaware of it.

For the Danish king swore to King Henry that he would bring him as much aid as he could, by land and sea, against all his enemies and especially against the Saxons. King Henry promised him in return that he would give him as his own all the regions adjoining his kingdom.

### 21

When that conference had ended and the Danish king had returned, King Henry considered the castle of Liuniburg, which was nearby. After examining its fortifications, he burned fiercely, in his customary manner, with desire for it, as though, if he held it under his authority, no one in those regions could resist him.

That castle had always belonged to the parents of Duke Magnus, and at that time had come by hereditary right to Magnus and his uncle Herimannus. From the few men he had with him, Henry therefore sent almost seventy of his most faithful followers into the castle, so that they might compel both it and the whole surrounding region to obey the royal command in servile fashion.

But when they had rashly entered, Herimannus waited until the king had departed from his territories, and then immediately surrounded the castle with a strong force.

What could they do? The castle was strong and impregnable to all except hunger; but, apart from a few loaves of bread left behind by the monks when they departed, it contained nothing that could be eaten. Hunger commanded them to abandon the castle, but the force of the weapons confronting them did not permit them to leave.

It was not safe for a small number to come into battle with an army. They therefore offered their surrender to Count Herimannus. He replied that none of them would depart unless Duke Magnus, his brother’s son, returned.

When he learned this, the king was in great distress and could not easily devise what would be useful to him. He could not free the besieged by force, because he did not believe he could gather an army from the Saxons, whom he had offended. From the other peoples subject to his rule he did not possess a force large enough to go there safely.

He did not wish to release the duke, because as long as he held him in chains he was secure from a Saxon war. Fear alone that Magnus might be killed had prevented the war from beginning despite all the injuries they had suffered.

But if he allowed so many of his most faithful men to perish—among them men who had noble and powerful relatives—he would find no one faithful to him thereafter, and he would have no safe time from their kinsmen.

He therefore released Duke Magnus and received back the multitude of his faithful followers. From this arose a proverb that spread throughout all Saxony: one Saxon could be bought for seventy Swabians, or seventy Swabians redeemed by one Saxon.

### 22

No Ciceronian eloquence could express how great the joy of all Saxony was at the return of Duke Magnus. They would not have rejoiced more over him if they had received him back alive from the dead.

To the extent that they had despaired of ever seeing him alive, so much greater was the joy with which they celebrated when they saw him alive. Nor did only his own people, relatives, or dependents rejoice over his safety: absolutely the whole population unanimously gave praise to almighty God, who had delivered him miraculously.

His uncle had been unable to redeem him at any price, however incalculable, in estates or money; divine mercy freed him in a manner that human prudence could never have devised.

Thus almost nothing was heard from the mouth of all Saxony except: “Thanks be to God for the duke Magnus’s marvelous liberation!” Those who had never seen him gave thanks to God for his rescue no less than if they had belonged to his family or household.

### 23

Then, as the feast of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, was approaching, the king ordered the entire multitude of the princes of Saxony to assemble at Goslar, so that if anything concerning the common affairs of the kingdom arose that deserved attention, he himself might discuss it with the common counsel of the princes.

They all hurried there eagerly, because they hoped that the calamities Saxony had endured for a long time would finally have some end.

When the feast had been solemnly celebrated and the appointed day for conducting business had arrived, the bishops, dukes, counts, and others gathered at the palace at dawn. They sat there waiting until the king came out to them or ordered them to enter, but they waited in vain.

For he, with the doors of his chamber closed, was inside amusing himself with his parasites at dice or with other childish diversions, and he cared nothing that so many great men were keeping watch at his door like the lowliest slaves.

The entire day passed, and neither he nor any messenger bringing a genuine message came out to them. When night had already fallen, one of his parasites came out and mockingly asked the princes how long they intended to wait there, since the king had gone out through another door and was hastening at speed toward his own city.

All those who had been treated with such contempt by the king’s arrogance were so shaken that, unless Margrave Dedi had restrained their fury by his prudence, they would all, at that very hour and having completely cast off fear, have openly renounced the king together.

That day and that incident first began the war; that day was the beginning of all the evils that followed.

For that same night, having eaten little, all the princes gathered by agreement in one church with those whom they trusted most, while everyone else was already asleep. After shedding no small number of tears, they said that it would be better for them to suffer any kind of death than to live such a life amid such calamities and insults.

They therefore fixed a day and place at which they would all meet with all the Saxons and deliberate together concerning the common liberty which they saw was about to be taken from them. Then each returned to his own place as though he would never again come to serve the king.

### 24

Not long afterward, great and small alike assembled as had been arranged at a village called Normeslovo [possibly Haldensleben]. Not everyone understood why so great an assembly had been held in so small a place.

Then Otto, who had once been duke but still bore the name of duke, ascended a hill from which he could be heard by everyone, and asked for silence. When this had been granted and all stood listening attentively, he began a speech of the following kind:

### 25

“Why your princes asked you, excellent soldiers, to assemble in such numbers at this place, almost all of you have individually learned. Nevertheless, so that none of you may be able to claim that he did not know, it seemed right to us that you should all recognize the reason together.

“The calamities and insults which our king has individually inflicted upon all of you for a long time are great and intolerable; but those which, if almighty God permits it, he is now planning to inflict are much greater and more serious.

“As you know, he has built many strong castles in places fortified by nature, and in them he has stationed a considerable number of his faithful followers, equipped with every kind of weapon.

“Since these castles were not built against the pagans, who have laid waste to the whole of our land bordering theirs, but in the midst of our own land, where no one had ever contemplated making war upon him, and since they have been fortified with such enormous effort, what they portend—and many of you have already experienced this in part—you will all soon experience, unless God’s mercy and your courage prevent it.

“Your goods, you who live nearby, are carried into those castles against your will. They abuse your daughters and wives for their own pleasure whenever they wish. They order your servants and animals to perform whatever labor they desire; indeed, they compel you yourselves to carry every burden, however shameful, on your free shoulders.

“But when I conceive in my mind what is still to come, I consider what you are suffering now tolerable. For after he has built his castles throughout our entire land according to his will, and filled them with armed soldiers and all the other things needed for this purpose, he will no longer seize your goods piecemeal. Instead, he will take away from you everything you possess at once, and, giving your goods to foreign newcomers, will order you yourselves—free and enfranchised men—to be slaves of unknown men.

“Will you endure all this being done to you, bravest men? Is it not better to die bravely than to lose shamefully a wretched and dishonorable life in which you have become the sport of their arrogance? Slaves purchased with money do not endure the unjust commands of their masters, and will you, born in freedom, tolerate slavery with equanimity?

“Perhaps, because you are Christians, you fear violating the oaths you have sworn to the king. Very well—but to a king. While he was my king and did what belonged to a king, I preserved intact and unstained the loyalty I had sworn to him. But after he ceased to be a king, there was no one to whom I was obliged to keep faith.

“Therefore I take up arms not against a king, but against the unjust thief of my liberty; not against my country, but for my country and for my liberty, which no good man loses except together with his life. I demand that you take up arms with me.

“Wake up, then, and leave to your children the inheritance handed down to you by your parents. Do not, through your sluggishness or negligence, permit yourselves and your children to become slaves of foreign men.

“But lest the cause for which we take up arms against the king seem insufficiently forceful to anyone—especially to us, who from childhood nourished him most generously in our land and were more faithful to him than the other peoples subject to his rule—let each man set forth before all of you the injuries he has suffered at his hands. Then let the common judgment decide whether a sufficiently great necessity compels us to repel those injuries.” (Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 31.)

### 26

Accordingly, Werinherus, archbishop of Magdeburg, said that his city had twice been attacked by the king with massacres and plundering. He further declared that he grieved over the common injuries no less than over his own, and promised that he would confront them as though he alone had suffered them all.

Burchardus, bishop of Halberstadt, complained that the king had unjustly taken for himself the estates of a certain nobleman named Bodo, although by right they ought to belong to his church.

Duke Otto complained that the king had unjustly seized the duchy of Bavaria from him—an office he had long possessed justly—by a contrived fraud, even though Otto had been convicted of no crime.

Margrave Dedi complained of estates belonging to him by right that had been taken from him unjustly.

Count Herimannus recounted what had recently happened: the king had cunningly occupied his city of Liuniburg, left to him by inheritance; and, if he could retain it, he intended to possess by unjust power, not by royal authority, the whole region which his parents had lawfully bequeathed to him.

Frederick, count palatine, complained that the king had taken from him by an unjust command the large benefice he had held from the abbey of Herolfesfelde, and that the king wanted him to redeem it with a hundred manses of farmland, although he was unable to do so.

Frideric of Monte and Wilhelm, called “the king” by surname—the former of whom the king wished to deprive of liberty, and the latter of inheritance—each made his own complaint. Their complaints moved everyone to pity more than the others, because they judged from those two men what he intended to do to everyone: namely, that if he could, he planned to take away from all alike both liberty and possessions.

Then each of the others in turn brought forward the injuries he had suffered; neither the page nor memory itself is sufficient to recount them.

All who had assembled there—and a very large army had assembled—therefore swore individually. The bishops swore that, insofar as they could without violating their order, they would defend with all their strength the liberty of their churches and of all Saxony against every man. The laymen swore that, as long as they lived, they would not lose their liberty and would henceforth permit no one to plunder their land by force.

### 27

Not long afterward (August 1073), they marched by the direct road with a large army toward Hartesburg, where the king was, and pitched their camp opposite the city, close enough that they could be seen from it.

When the king saw them, he was suddenly struck with astonishment and fear. But, being as dissembling as ever, he sent messengers as though he feared nothing. They were to say that he was greatly surprised by what such a large gathering of people wanted; he did not think he had deserved anything from them so serious that they should rightly begin a civil war.

They should withdraw from their arms. If they had some complaint, he was ready, with a peaceful mind, to hear it; and if anything needed correction, he would correct it with the counsel of his princes and friends.

The messengers were Bishop Frideric, Duke Bertholdus, and Sigefridus, the king’s chaplain. For Adalbert, bishop of Bremen, had recently died.

Duke Otto gave them this reply on behalf of all the Saxons: they had not assembled with hostile intent or wishing to begin a civil war. If the king wished to be king, they would serve him with complete loyalty. They asked him to destroy the castles he had built not for the fortification of the kingdom but for its destruction. If he refused, they would then understand why they had been built. They nevertheless wished, with the help of divine mercy, to defend their liberty and possessions against the violence of every man.

When the messengers returned and reported these things to the king, and although they tried very hard could not persuade him to do what had been requested, he no longer trusted even his close friends, since they had not given him the advice he wanted.

Having dismissed everyone, he deliberated alone with himself about what he should do. He did not consider it honorable to destroy suddenly the castles he had built over many years as though compelled by force; nor did he consider it safe to enter into any agreement with a great army prepared for everything, accompanied only by the few men whom he had already begun to trust less.

Known only to a few men to whom he entrusted the castle itself, he abandoned Saxony by night. Fleeing through the rugged forest paths that he had often traversed while searching for sites for castles, he reached eastern Francia with only a few companions.

When the princes who had been with him learned of his flight, each saying that he had been shamefully deserted, they hurried away to their own lands by a similar flight.

This flight took place in the year 1073 from the incarnation of the Lord.

### 28

When the Saxons learned of the king’s flight, which could not long be concealed, they delayed no longer. They left behind those who were to besiege this castle, which could not easily be destroyed; the others proceeded to destroy the remaining castles, which were not so strong.

Some of them crossed over to the Thuringians, made the whole sequence of events known to them, and joined them to their own alliance by oaths given and received.

Those who earlier, while the king was in the province, had not dared to swear with them, they now compelled—after the king had fled—either to follow the king by fleeing from their own land, or to swear with them in defense of their land against the king.

### 29

After all this had been properly carried out, since it had become extremely difficult within a short time to take Hartesburg castle—for, if it stood in a suitable location, it would be a site fit for a royal palace—and since abandoning it would have been dangerous for all Saxony, because, if only provisions were brought into it, it would remain impregnable to an army of any size, they built another castle equally strong.

By stationing garrisons there in rotation, they prevented assistance or provisions from reaching the enemy. Yet sometimes, when provisions were being carried to the new castle for the Saxons, the men in Hartesburg suddenly sallied forth and had the provisions carried inside their own walls.

By doing this they inflicted some damage or insult upon their enemies, but they thereby taught them to be more cautious and resourceful.

Thus almost every day the two sides fought bravely. The Saxons, however, were stronger because their own castle was situated on a higher mountain, so that no one in the lower castle was safe from stones unless he remained under cover. Fresh soldiers replaced the weary, and provisions came to them abundantly.

Everything was the opposite for the enemy. They could not easily throw stones upward; no others relieved the exhausted men; and hunger, their fiercest enemy, afflicted them severely.

It would have forced them, long before this, to surrender as conquered, had not certain Saxons secretly supplied them with food—men who had previously been their friends.

### 30

Meanwhile the king approached each of the princes of the German kingdom as a suppliant. He tearfully declared that he had been unjustly driven from the kingdom of Saxony, which he had received both by his paternal inheritance and by the election of all those princes.

In this matter, he said, the disgrace had been inflicted not so much upon him as upon all of them, who had been despised in his person. He humbly requested aid by which he might avenge both his own injury and theirs.

But his speeches moved few of them, because nearly all knew how many calamities he had inflicted upon the Saxons, especially since he had wanted to inflict the same evils upon the Swabians and the eastern Franks.

Nevertheless, they looked more to their own honor than to his, and promised to come to his aid on this condition: that, after summoning the Saxons to a hearing, they would carefully examine the claims of both sides. If the Saxons had violently expelled him without fault on his part, they would strive with all their strength to restore him to his kingdom. But if, credulous of foolish counsels, he had lost a land full of every kind of wealth through his own fault, they would advise him—if he wished to listen—to lay aside his fury and become just and merciful toward the nations subject to him, as was proper for a king, and not listen any longer to those by whose evil counsel he had been deceived.

They refused entirely to fight without cause against Christian men, innocent men, and men related to them by kinship.

The king therefore received these speeches as though they were pleasing, because he understood that what he intended could not be done: namely, that he should enter Saxony violently with an army without a hearing and make all those who were free unwillingly subject to his authority into slaves.

He therefore sent messengers to the princes of Saxony, promising every benefit if they allowed him to return peacefully to his kingdom. To Duke Otto, on whose decision he knew everyone’s counsels depended, he promised to restore the honor unjustly taken from him, with a great addition, if Otto wished to restore him to his former dignity.

### 31

He therefore gathered a large army, but one not prepared for battle unless great necessity compelled it, and planned to enter Saxony on the Kalends of February, when the year 1074 from the Lord’s incarnation had recently begun.

But when the Saxons learned of his approach, they advanced with a very large army to defend their land and met him at a town called Nachan [Vach, near the Werra]. They pitched their camp no farther from the king than the point at which each army could see the other.

Scouts were nevertheless sent between them, and carefully investigated the strength of both armies. Each side reported with complete certainty to its own men what it had seen.

The Saxon army was so large that it was believed to be twice the size of the king’s army. When those on the king’s side heard both of the Saxons’ numbers and of their military equipment—for the king had told his men that the Saxons possessed neither horses nor military experience, but were rustic men ignorant of warfare—they had previously been uncertain whether to fight, since they saw no sufficient cause for battle; now they became certain that they must not fight, because they lacked both a cause and forces with which they could safely confront so great a multitude.

At the command of his princes, the king therefore sent embassies to the Saxons and promised to do everything they themselves prescribed, provided that they did not deny him the paternal dignity which, as he admitted, he had lost through the fault of his youth and his evil counselors.

Then Duke Otto and the others, to whom great promises had been made, persuaded the rest to receive him on these conditions:

- He would destroy his castles and never restore them afterward.
- He would carry out no further raids in their land.
- In Saxony he would arrange everything according to the counsel of the Saxons and would admit no foreigner as counselor in the administration of their affairs.
- He would never avenge his expulsion upon any of them in any way.

When the king most faithfully promised that he would do all this and more, he dismissed his army, crossed over to the Saxons with a few companions, and was escorted all the way to Goslar amid praise and triumphal rejoicing.

The ill-considered formation of this pact became the source of the greatest evils for the Saxons. For the Swabians, who remembered the pact previously made with the Saxons and had refused to come with the king against them, were forgotten by the Saxons themselves when they made their pact with the king. Because of this, the Swabians became their most savage enemies instead of faithful friends.

If the Saxons had either not done this or had associated the Swabians with them in making the pact, they would both have escaped the charge of treachery and would not have had so many fierce enemies.

### 32

At the same time, however, we recognized God’s greatest mercy toward us, which we must never consign to oblivion.

The severity of the winter was so great that all the rivers and marshes provided a land route for those wishing to cross them. And while all the men had gathered together against the king, leaving only women and little children at home, the pagans—who had always been hostile to us—could have turned all Saxony to ashes after carrying away the women and children, unless God, by his wondrous mercy, had commanded them to remain at rest within their own borders, as though shut up there and forgetful of their innate cruelty.

33. Accordingly, when the king had come to Goslar accompanied by the Saxon army [Col. 0509A], he did not forget himself and began to seek excuses so that he would not have to destroy his castles at once, as he had promised. When certain of our princes saw him delaying, wishing to please him, they advised him to hand over that larger castle [Note: [Col. 0509] “that castle, Harcesburh” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0509D] namely, the Harzburg], which he wished to preserve, to one of the Saxon princes, as though in surrender, until the fury of the people, which was then burning fiercely, had cooled somewhat; then the castle, as he wished, could remain intact. For the people were insisting vehemently that it be demolished, and were loudly declaring that, unless this happened, they would immediately become rebels again.

But the king, placed in great difficulties, did not know what to do: he neither wished to destroy that castle nor trusted any of the princes who promised that, if it were handed over to them in some fashion, they would make it stand; and he greatly feared that the people might resume the renewed wars. For by what strength could he, almost alone and caught in the midst of the army, defend himself, or by what flight could he conceal himself, surrounded on every side by savage enemies?

Accordingly, returning to his usual ingenuity, he devised a deception, though it did not achieve the result he hoped. He secretly ordered certain of his old household companions to demolish only the castle’s principal fortification, and, when the people, seeing this, withdrew in the expectation that the whole structure would fall, to stop the demolition; thus, after a few ruins had been repaired, it would remain intact as he wished [Note: [Col. 0509] “so that it might remain” 1b.]. But, sparing themselves the labor, they brought in peasants from the neighborhood and ordered them, as they had been instructed, to demolish only the upper walls.

Once the peasants had received control of that place, where they had long before suffered many evils [Col. 0509C], they paid attention not to what they had been ordered to do but to what they had long desired to do. They did not cease demolishing until they saw that not one stone remained upon another. Thus they destroyed within a short time the royal buildings constructed over many years at royal expense, and in those vast walls left not even the foundations unexcavated. The king’s envoys did not dare say a word, because the peasants threatened to kill them as well if they contradicted anything.

Accordingly, they demolished to the foundations the monastery completed with laborious workmanship; they plundered the entire treasure amassed there, whether it belonged to the king or to the church; they smashed the sweet-sounding bells; they dug up the king’s son and brother, whom he had placed there, scattered their bones like any refuse [Col. 0509D], and permitted nothing whatsoever of that place to remain.

34. But when the king learned that his castle had thus been annihilated, he was inwardly disturbed by great anguish of heart, though he showed it by no outward sign, because he considered it pointless to display his grief to those whom he hated, since at that moment he could not satisfy his hatred against them according to his wishes by punishing them. The leading men of Saxony, knowing that the king’s mind was rightly, though he concealed it [Col. 0510A] [Note: [Col. 0509] “covered” 1b.], greatly disturbed, sought in every way to appease him. They cleared themselves, in whatever way he ordered, of any charge of having shared in the counsel or intention; and they tortured those who were implicated in the crime with whatever punishment he desired. But they accomplished nothing.

For the king was angry not so much with those who confessed that they had committed the crime [Note: [Col. 0509] “who had confessed” 1.] as with those who were clearing themselves of the crime they had themselves perpetrated. Disdaining to vent his anger on the peasants, he planned, when he found the opportunity, to kindle his fury against the greatest men of that region.

Meanwhile, however, he avenged his castle not as much as he wished, but as much as he was then able; and he ordered all the castles and every kind of fortification in that land to be demolished, except the ancient cities built for the honor of the kingdom. That this command proceeded not from the calm rigor of justice but from the troubled agitation of an angry heart could be recognized especially from the fact that he ordered certain castles, although accused of no wrongdoing, to be destroyed, while he commanded many others, convicted of plunder and brigandage, to remain untouched if money were paid.

After these things had been done, he left Saxony in the month of March, before it had ended (A.D. 1074), as though moved by no grief or contemplating any evil against Saxony, and crossed over to the inhabitants of the Rhine and the other parts of Francia with a mind far from cheerful [Note: [Col. 0509] “mind” 1.]. It is reported that, as he departed from our borders, he said under oath that he would never again wish to return to Saxony unless he had first acquired the power to do in Saxony whatever he pleased.

35. Accordingly, after assembling the princes of those regions [Col. 0510C], now individually and now all together, humbly prostrating himself before them [Note: [Col. 0509] “humble” 2.], he made his complaint, saying that the former wrongs of his expulsion now seemed light to him, whereas these seemed great and incurable; in the former he had been despised together with his princes, but in these the contempt of the heavenly host had truly been joined to the contempt shown to himself and his men—and, what was worse than all this, to contempt for the divine majesty.

For he told them with tears that, while yielding to their counsels against his own will and handing over his castle, built at royal expense, to the Saxons for demolition, they had not merely destroyed it in an inhuman manner beyond what had been permitted to them; in addition, more cruel than all the pagans, they had demolished from the foundations the monastery consecrated to God and the saints [Col. 0510D] [Note: [Col. 0509] “they demolished” 1.], smashed as profane objects, or seized by hostile plunder, the bells, chalices, and other things collected for the honor of God; and had pitifully dragged his brother and son—both royal offspring—from their tombs and scattered their limbs to the winds. What was more wicked than all these things, they had torn the relics of the saints from the sacred altars with accursed hands and scattered them through profane places like ordinary refuse.

Having concluded all this with abundant weeping, he kissed the feet of each of them and begged that, if they did not care to avenge his own wrong, at least they should not permit the insult inflicted upon God and God’s saints to remain unpunished [Col. 0511A]. He said that the Saxons should not be called Christians, since, by committing the crimes mentioned above in Christ’s house, they had shown that they neither loved nor feared Christ [Note: [Col. 0511] “nor Christ” 1.]. But they ought to demonstrate by this that they were faithful to Christ, if, burning with zeal for Christ, they did not hesitate, with his help, to avenge his wrongs.

While he repeated these complaints and supplications whenever an assembly of the princes took place, a whole year passed before his wish was fulfilled, so that he could lead an army into Saxony. For all who knew the pitiable miseries that he had inflicted upon Saxony, since every war is a harsh affair and the adequate justification for this war was not evident, sought every possible excuse for delaying it [Col. 0511B].

Had the Saxons not offended Duke Rudolf of Swabia when they were entering into the treaty with the king, as was said above, the king might perhaps still not have had forces against Saxony. Deceived by the Saxons, whose support he trusted, Rudolf was reconciled to the king as best he could, and first promised him that he would invade the Saxons hostilely with all his men. But this, as I have said, will be dealt with fully after a year.

36. Meanwhile, having sent envoys to all the neighboring peoples, and by giving gifts and promising greater rewards, he wished, if possible, to make everyone hostile to the Saxons, because he was seeking not so much to subject them to his authority—which could easily have been done without war—as to remove them altogether from the number of human beings [Col. 0511C].

He promised Wratizlaus, duke of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0511] “Wratislaus” 2.], the city of Meissen together with everything belonging to it [Note: [Col. 0511] absent in 1; present in 1b and 2.], and thus enlisted him to assist his party.

He loosened the restraints of the pagan Liutizi, whose cruelty toward the Saxons had always been great, and granted them as much territory as they could add to their borders. But they said that they had learned by experience, through many storms of war, what the Saxons were like, and that they had rarely or never rejoiced in their wars; their own land was enough for them, and they would be content if they could defend their boundaries.

He recalls the king of the Danes, whose promise had been confirmed by oath, and affirms that he would give him everything he had promised. He solicited Philip, ruler of Latin Francia, with many promises, asking that, mindful of their ancient friendship, he come to his aid whenever summoned. But Philip, likewise accused by his own people and almost deposed from his paternal throne, said that he could scarcely retain the honor to which he still clung, much less attempt to restore to this man the honor from which he had entirely fallen.

He summoned William, king of the English people, to his aid on the condition that he would repay him in equal measure if he should ever need him. But William replied that he had seized that land through the violence of war, and therefore feared that, if he left it, he might not afterward be received back into it [Col. 0512A].

He asked William, duke of the Poitevins and his mother’s brother, to take pity on his sister’s son and bring him aid, so that he might be restored to his father’s kingdom, from which he had been unjustly deprived. But William replied that such great forces of the French, Normans [Note: [Col. 0511] “Normans” 1.], and Aquitanians stood between them that he could not, by any strategy, pass through such strength with an army.

37. Thus deprived of all these men except the Bohemians, and lacking sufficiently great foreign forces against the Saxons, he devised the worst plan—one that he understood all too well: to divide Saxony and make Saxons fight against Saxons, so that whichever side was defeated might lie prostrate, while he, rejoicing as victor, triumphed.

Accordingly, he ordered the princes of Saxony [Col. 0512B] to come to him individually, inventing some major matter which, he said, he wished to resolve with their counsel. They came without hesitation to the place to which they had been summoned; indeed, they would not have failed to come even if they had simply been ordered to approach the king without any pretext.

When they arrived, he first received each one graciously; and when they had already remained with him for some time, he disclosed his intention to them and compelled them to swear that they would assist him to the best of their ability in crushing Saxony, and that they would reveal this to no one. Unless they did so immediately, they could not depart from him.

As a result, a father stood on our side and his son on the opposing side [Note: [Col. 0511] absent in 1]; one brother stood here and another there. Many of the leading men who possessed estates in both regions, in order to preserve both, voluntarily [Col. 0512C] left a son or brother here and went over to the king, or, remaining here themselves, sent their brothers or sons to the king.

He summoned many of the military class to him in the same way and, according as he perceived each man’s inclination, urged him toward civil war by threats or promises. He did not even disdain to summon servants and plead with them to earn the gift of freedom, or even to become masters of their masters, by killing or abandoning their lords. But all these things were still secret, because anyone who was compelled to swear his assistance to him was also compelled to swear faithful silence concerning it.

38. What shall I say of the bishops whom he could not draw over to his side? He sent them gifts of such a kind that they would deprive them simultaneously of their bishopric and their life [Col. 0512D], so that he might give the bishopric to persons who would assent to his will in everything.

Through a deceitful monk [Note: [Col. 0511] “false” 2.], he sent Werinher [Note: [Col. 0511] “Werenher” 1.] a splendid gift—a powder of spices—to the archbishop of Magdeburg, instructing him that it had been sent to him from Italy by his mother as a remedy beneficial against many illnesses. He ordered a portion of it, inserted into a crust of bread, to be given to a puppy; we saw the puppy die without delay, and we rejoiced that the bishop had not tasted such medicine [Col. 0513A].

39. But after the loquaciousness of rumor began to proclaim all these things throughout Saxony, and to foretell the future evils in the same order in which they later came, the common people, who do not know how to weigh causes, rejoiced and threatened, at the first assault, to overthrow all who had invaded their lands.
