The nobility, however, was afflicted by great anxieties as it carefully measured the king’s overwhelming strength against its own very small strength.

From that side they saw the Franks, holding both banks of the Rhine, the Swabians, Bavarians, Lotharingians, and Bohemians coming to battle; on this side, however, they found scarcely a third part of Saxony, because all the Westphalians and all who lived around Meissen, corrupted by the king’s gold, had defected from us [Note: [Col. 0513] “defected” 1.]. Even that third part scarcely remained loyal to itself, because royal promises continually solicited each of its members [Note: [Col. 0513] “who” 1.] [Col. 0513B].

All the bishops as well, except four—the bishops of Magdeburg, Halberstadt, Merseburg, and Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0513] “Paderborn” 1?]—either openly went over to the king or remained with us with wavering minds, so that, whichever side prospered, they could safely turn in that direction.

40. At the same time, we saw many signs occurring throughout Saxony, from which we could foresee the evils that later came upon us. I shall pass over what we saw in the field at Magdeburg: crows fighting so fiercely among themselves that some left others lying lifeless [Note: [Col. 0513] “it should be written thus; the event itself and the Saxon Annalist indicate it: deer” 1.], because I have more sacred signs to recount, no less prophetic of the future.

The pastoral staffs of our bishops, standing in chapels beneath a clear sky—indeed, in the burning heat of summer [Col. 0513C]—became so wet that, if anyone picked them up [Note: [Col. 0513] “perhaps grabbed them? touched them” 2.], they filled his hand with their own water.

At Steterburg there was a wooden image of Christ hanging on the cross. At that same time it poured forth such a river of sweat on summer days that, even when wiped with little cloths [Note: [Col. 0513] “cloths” 1.], it did not cease sweating, and it filled certain small vessels with the sweat it produced [Note: [Col. 0513] absent in 1.].

Werinher, bishop of Merseburg, while celebrating the solemn rites of Mass and, according to custom, placing a portion of Christ’s body into the Lord’s blood, saw that the piece sank to the bottom of the chalice, as though Christ’s flesh had been changed into lead.

A certain priest in the bishopric of Magdeburg, in the village of Wedding [Note: [Col. 0513] “in neither recension: ‘an eminent man in conduct in the village of Wedding’” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0513D] Today, Wedringen?], a man not distinguished either by the stain of vice or by the praise of virtue, had reached the communion during the preparation of the sacraments. When he raised the chalice, he saw the wine changed not only spiritually but also visibly into blood [Note: [Col. 0513] absent in 1; present in 1b.]. Terrified alike by its redness [Note: [Col. 0513] “perhaps its substance” 1.] and its density, he did not dare to consume any of it, but carried it with great fear to the city of Magdeburg, where it is still reverently preserved [Note: [Col. 0513] “in a silver shrine, v. 1b, Dresden manuscript”].

What else can we suppose that all these things signified except the suffering that we later experienced [Note: [Col. 0513] “experienced” 1.]?

41. Accordingly, when the king’s anger against us, inflamed excessively by the passage of time, could no longer remain concealed, and it became evident through definite signs what evils he was planning to inflict upon us, then our princes, individually and collectively, sent repeated embassies to the king, sometimes with letters and sometimes without. They asked him only this, with much supplication: that, after assembling his princes, he either show them guilty in their presence and punish them once they had been convicted by their judgment, or allow them themselves to demonstrate their innocence by whatever judgment he chose, and let them remain in his favor as they had hitherto done.

But when they received no answer expressing mercy from him and learned that he was bent in every way solely upon their destruction [Col. 0514B], they sent embassies to the princes who were with him and humbly asked them to try to appease the king’s mind. It seemed appropriate to insert one of these letters, which the archbishop of Magdeburg sent to the archbishop of Mainz, so that from it anyone may recognize all the others, since they were all of one kind.

42. “To Lord Siegfried [Note: [Col. 0513] “S.” 1.], most holy priest of Christ, Werinher [Note: [Col. 0513] “W.” 1.], though unworthy archbishop of the holy church of Magdeburg, and with him all the bishops, dukes, counts, and all the clergy and laity of Saxony together, great and small, offer equally a devoted prayer and submissive service.

The manifold and great tribulations which, because our sins demand it, afflict us without remedy unless divine mercy comes to our aid [Col. 0514C], compel us to seek humbly the mercy of all who either fear God or recognize that they are human beings. Therefore, since we know that Your Excellency both fears and loves God, we flee especially to the mercy of Your Holiness, humbly praying that, for the very fear of God, you weigh our case justly, and, if it is found to be just, grant us the aid of your mercy, for love of that justice which is Christ.

Our lord the king, after reaching adolescence, rejected the counsel of his princes and began to act as his own master; he submitted himself to the instruction of those who consider neither what is equitable nor what is good, and he continually sought to oppress us in an extraordinary manner, take our possessions from us, and hand them over to his intimates—his only reason being that they had little or nothing at home and saw that our land was fertile.

Accordingly, he occupied the more defensible places of our region with the strongest castles [Note: [Col. 0513] “occupied” 1.], in which he stationed not a few armed men who would either compel us to serve him like slaves or kill us if we wished to defend our freedom. How many dangers, how many insults, and how many losses we suffered there in our bodies, our wives, and our possessions, and how God’s mercy freed us from there for a time [Note: [Col. 0515] “has freed us” 2.], we believe is known to you, and we pass over it.

But after so great a storm had been calmed by God’s mercy and he had restored his peace and favor to us, we know of nothing that we did against him [Note: [Col. 0515] “that we offended” 2.] for which he ought rightly to renew the wars against us. We returned to his envoys the estates which he claimed had been taken from him, until the envoys themselves said that nothing remained which we ought to return.

We demolished all the castles and other fortifications in our territory which he ordered destroyed [Note: [Col. 0515] “we demolish” 1.], except those which he permitted to stand against our will [Note: [Col. 0515] “willingly” 2.]. When you hear how the destruction of his monastery, and the violation of the tombs of his son and brother and the scattering of their bones, took place, you will recognize that we are innocent.

He did not wish any of us to undertake the destruction of the castle itself where these things occurred, but imposed this task upon his servants and household companions [Note: [Col. 0515] “the f. and are absent” 2.]. They, being negligent and lazy, summoned all the peasants in that neighborhood so that they might complete more quickly what they had been ordered to do, and gave them power to demolish the castle.

The peasants, however, being ignorant peasants who had suffered many evils from that same castle, and with no one present to restrain them, wanted nothing left standing in it which could be rebuilt again [Note: [Col. 0515] “which” 2.].

Afterward, we repeatedly sent an embassy to our lord the king, like humble servants and with much supplication [Col. 0515C], asking that, if we appeared to have done anything against him in that matter or in any other, we might satisfy him before the judgment of his princes, either by denying the charge or by making amends. Since we were unable, even with anyone’s help, to obtain that he should yet be willing to receive this embassy, we all together, prostrate at your feet, beseech Your Holiness to wish to mitigate the anger of our lord the king toward us and to persuade him to do for the whole people what he would do for one man: namely, not to seek to devastate us first with the fury of war before showing us guilty before his princes and unwilling to make amends for our crime.

Let him accept from us the security which you and his other princes shall order, so that he may come to us without war and, according to your judgment, either punish us if we have deserved it or dismiss us in peace with his favor if we are found innocent.

If he is unwilling to do this [Note: [Col. 0515] “if he is willing” 1.], let him order his princes to assemble in any part of his kingdom, grant safe-conduct to whichever of us he wishes to be present, both for going and returning [Note: [Col. 0515] “for them to go and return” 2.], and carry out whatever you judge should be done concerning us.

Therefore, bring this suggestion to our lord and, for fear of God, persuade him to consider that we are human beings, lest, to the danger of his soul, he desire to destroy us, though we are innocent.

If Your Sublimity is sluggish or insufficiently merciful in carrying out these matters, the strict judgment of God will have to demand our souls from you [Col. 0516A]. But if the king should perhaps refuse to hear your pious counsel, we ask and beseech you at least not to allow him to have you and your men as instruments of his fury, lest, while ministering to his rage, you incur danger to your life [Note: [Col. 0515] “our” 1.] and soul.

Farewell.”

43. Our individual princes sent embassies, by letters or by spoken messages, containing the same message to all the princes on the other side. At last, they scarcely received from the king—overcome more by their persistence than softened by mercy—the answer that they could have his favor in only one way: if they were willing to surrender themselves, their freedom, and everything they possessed to the royal power without any condition [Col. 0516B]. They refused to do this, since they had often experienced that he possessed no mercy.

44. Thus, after a year and more had passed since the king departed from Saxony, while he was at Mainz, on the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection (A.D. 1075, April 5), a Saxon messenger came there with letters. He handed them to Udo, archbishop of Trier, who was celebrating Mass that day; while Udo was standing in the pulpit and addressing the people, the messenger asked him, on behalf of all the Saxons and for the love of God, to read and explain them to the entire people.

When the king prohibited this, the messenger himself confidently explained the substance of the letters to all the people in a brief speech. On behalf of all the Saxons, he asked everyone who feared God not to wish to invade Saxony with arms before it had been convicted of any crime [Col. 0516C].

But Duke Rudolf of Swabia, not forgetting the treaty suddenly made between the Saxons and the king, urged the king not to dismiss without vengeance the insult that had been inflicted both upon God and upon himself and all his princes, and promised him his support with all the strength he could muster. All the other princes did likewise: some were attracted by many promises, while more were driven by the necessity of an approaching death which they could not avoid.

45. When the Saxons heard this, they sent frequent embassies to the king and all the leading men, begging them not to invade innocent people with the sword [Col. 0516D], since, if they could be shown guilty of any offense against the royal majesty, they were prepared to submit to punishment at their discretion.

Then the king sent word of his favor to the archbishop of Magdeburg and certain others, and made known that his friends had advised him not to destroy the entire people without cause. He said that he wished to follow their advice if the Saxons would withdraw from their enemies and hand over to him Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, Duke Otto, Frederick, prefect of the palace [Col. 0517A] [Note: [Col. 0517D] that is, the count palatine], and the others whom he was still seeking [Note: [Col. 0517] “hand over” 1.].

The reply to this embassy, with the consent of those who were being demanded, was that they would present themselves to him on the condition that they stand under the judgment of both groups of princes, so that their sentence might either condemn them once convicted or reconcile them, if innocent, to the king’s favor together with the whole Saxon people.

But William, surnamed Rex, and Frederick of Monte, seeing that war had now openly begun, forgot the oath they had sworn with the other Saxons, the many calamities they themselves had suffered, and the fact that they themselves were the principal cause of the war’s beginning. They deserted their homeland as faithless men and, even more faithlessly, fled by night to the enemy of their homeland, the king. Thereafter neither citizens nor enemies trusted them, and among both sides they were base, faithless, despised, and miserable [Col. 0517B].

46. Accordingly, the king came with all the army he could muster to Beringa [Note: [Col. 0517] “Betinga” 1b; Dresden manuscript c.] [Note: [Col. 0517D] Beringen, near Langensalza], and there pitched his camp and settled in it.

On the other side, the Saxons placed their camp near Nechilstedi [Note: [Col. 0517] “the S. near” is absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0517] “Hechilstedi” 1; “Wichelstedt” 1b; Dresden manuscript c.; “Nechilstede” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0518D] Nagelstadt on the Unstrut], and waited while the king summoned them to a conference.

As they were preparing the words with which they intended to clear themselves of the charges brought against them, a royal messenger arrived, saying that the king wished to dispute with the Saxons not by words but by the sword [Note: [Col. 0517] absent in 1.], and fixing the following day for this dispute.

The messenger had scarcely finished speaking when another arrived, saying that the king was approaching with his entire army (A.D. 1075, June 13). At first they did not believe this; but when they realized that it was all too true—since there was neither time to hold a council nor to arrange the army for battle, as those caught unexpectedly ordinarily do—those few who had either courage [Note: [Col. 0517] “courage” 1.] or weapons ready went bravely into battle, while the greater number, whose courage or weapons were far away [Note: [Col. 0517] “was far away” 1.], turned to flight.

Those few who persisted in the battle nevertheless performed well, as far as they could, both their own part and that of those who had fled. For, unless God had determined there to humble our pride, our very few men would have put that entire army to flight.

The rearmost of the enemy, unaware that the greater part of our men had given themselves to flight, began themselves to seek the protection of flight; and, if they had not first recognized our flight, they would have left us victory by fleeing themselves. Whoever the fortune of war allowed to kill another could not recognize even the man he was killing, because such a great cloud of dust had been raised that scarcely anyone could distinguish between citizen and enemy.

This, however, we learned: our Margrave Udo [Note: [Col. 0517] “Udo, margrave of Stade” 2.] struck his cousin Duke Rudolf fiercely in the face with his sword, and, if the nose-piece hanging from the helmet had not faithfully protected him [Col. 0518A], he would have cut off the upper part of his head entirely.

Brothers were divided in that battle, fathers stood against sons, and others bound by affection were likewise set against one another [Note: [Col. 0517] “followers” 1.]. But if anyone committed a crime against his own kinsman, no one could know it.

It was an exceedingly savage battle, but it was completed in a very short time. For our men, few in number but great in courage—for the enemy themselves admitted that they had never heard such blows of swords—after they saw that they had been deserted by their own men, and after they themselves had become exhausted by killing many, gradually withdrew from the danger, fewer from an already small number, and left the king the glory of victory, but with great loss among his own men.

For on our side Count Gebhard, one of the greatest princes, fell; among the lesser nobles, Folcmar [Note: [Col. 0517] “Folomarus” 1.] and Suidgerus fell. On the other side there fell eight leading men, no less noble than the king himself.

This first battle took place in the year of the Lord 1075, on the Ides of June, Tuesday.

47. Accordingly, after winning a victory at the cost of much of his men’s blood, the king remained for several days within his camp, until he had gathered back those of his men whom fear had scattered [Note: [Col. 0517] “scattered” 1.], and had either had his dead buried or had them carried back to their homeland for burial.

Then he entered Saxony in great delight, judging that it had been so thoroughly overthrown that it would never rise again. He plundered and carried away whatever he encountered, or consumed it by fire. If pagans had defeated us in this way, they would not have exercised greater cruelty upon the vanquished.

It did not help the women to have fled into the churches or carried their possessions there. The men had scattered through the forests [Col. 0518C], or had hidden wherever they could find some hope of safety. The women were violated in the churches themselves, even if they had fled to the altar; after satisfying their lust in barbarous fashion, the attackers burned the women together with the churches.

Our princes, however, entered various fortifications and from there sent embassies to meet the king’s princes [Note: [Col. 0517] “princes” 1.], begging them either now to give thanks to God for their glory [Note: [Col. 0517] “victory” 2.] and to spare, for Christ’s name, their brothers in Christ even though defeated. It seemed appropriate to insert some of these embassies, so that from them the reader may recognize the others, since they all had the same meaning.

### 48

[Col. 0517] “To Sigefridus of Mainz and Adalbero of Würzburg, most holy prelates [variants: Adalbero, *alberoni* 1, *athelberoni* 2; Würzburg, *wertzeburg.* 1; prelates, *praesulis* 1]; Werinherus [*W.* 1], bishop of Magdeburg in name alone: whatever can be offered more humbly and devotedly.

[Col. 0518D] Because I do not doubt that you two burn more fervently than others with the flame of the two commandments of God, I flee especially as a suppliant to you two, asking and imploring that in this matter you prove the perfect love of God which I trust you possess, so that you may mercifully show compassion toward your wretched brothers.

[Col. 0519A] Consider that, as you know better than I, whatever divine grace grants to anyone is reckoned to him in place of a talent, for which he must render an account to the Judge who is to come. Therefore, since the mercy of the heavenly King has wished to grant you familiarity with our lord the king, make that familiarity beneficial to all who need your help, so that everyone who has been raised up by your assistance may rejoice in your good fortune, and God himself may grant you an eternal reward for the profit gained from your talent.

First, therefore, may your mercy mercifully handle my case with our lord: namely, that I have always wished and still wish, according to my strength and beyond my strength, to serve his honor. But if his majesty perhaps accuses me [variant: *incusat*] because [variant: *quod*] I recently came as though I intended to fight with him, answer—what Truth itself, who is Christ, knows to be true—that I came for no purpose of fighting, but solely for this reason: as had been settled before his legates, I wished to present to him, willingly or unwillingly, those whom he had called his enemies in our regions, so that, by your judgment and that of the other princes, they might either, if found guilty, undergo a just punishment, or, if found innocent, receive his favor through your intercession.

Since he did not deign to receive their case, what was fitting for me except to withdraw, as I did? If he lays any other faults upon me, to avoid prolonging matters, I shall submit to the judgment of you and of other men of the same order.

[Col. 0519B] Then may your benevolence suggest to our lord the king that he remember that he possesses both the office and the name of the heavenly King, who says that he desires mercy rather than sacrifice, and who came not to judge the world but so that the world might be saved through him. Thus, while reflecting on these things, may he strive to imitate in his actions the one whose member he is and whose name he bears [one witness omits this phrase], and may he deserve to be crowned with the glory of eternal blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0519C] For nearly an entire year we have approached almost all the princes of the kingdom through letters and other embassies, humbly asking them to obtain for us the opportunity to appear before them, so that by their judgment we might either be condemned if guilty or released if innocent. Since we were never able to obtain this, we again humbly ask you and all the faithful of God that, now at least—after he has satisfied his anger with our blood, after God has granted him the honor that was fitting—he lay aside his fury, return glory to God, and now do what he could have done before blood was shed, though so much blood has now been shed.

[Col. 0519D] Let him grant us a place where we may meet [variant: *possumus*] with you and with the dukes Rudolf, Berchtold, and Godefrid [variant: *bertoldo et g.*]; and in whatever matter we may seem blameworthy to you, we shall willingly submit to your judgment, having laid aside every preference of our own.

There was never such cruelty in any pagan that he would refuse to subdue, without danger or hardship to himself, those whom he could have subjected without danger, rather than subdue them at risk to himself and his people. But if he is laboring to shed our blood until none of it remains, let him consider that this cannot easily happen without some mingling of his own people’s blood [variant: *admixtione*, “admixture”]. Therefore, if he has resolved to show us no mercy, let him at least spare the hands and swords of his own men.

Suggest these things, then, and anything else you may find more suitable, to our lord; urge him to fear God and to preserve rather than destroy the people over whom he has been appointed ruler. Thus, if he listens to you, and if you give good counsel, both he and you may receive an eternal reward.”

### 49

[Col. 0519] “To the lords and holy priests N., and to the other men of the same virtue and order: Werinherus [W.], full of every misery, [wishes] a share in eternal mercy.

[Col. 0520B] Although all the supplications that I have made to your fatherhood in words or letters seem so far to have profited me nothing, nevertheless I do not cease again to implore your piety that, if neither the calamity of my innocence nor any compassion—which is accustomed to pity even the guilty—moves you, at least my importunity may conquer you through its very weariness.

By the clemency of almighty God, therefore, I ask and admonish you together, most holy prelates, to deign to consider yourselves in me, and not to permit me to be condemned when I have not only been convicted of no crime, but have not even been charged with any crime [variant: *illo*, “that crime”]. Let a fault first be laid upon me; let me be granted an opportunity of defense, where either, if guilty, I may be compelled by your judgment to undergo a punishment worthy of the offense, or, if innocent, I may deserve to enjoy your fellowship under the favor of our lord [variant: *d. n. regis* 2: “our lord the king”].

For who was ever justly condemned before having been accused of some crime? I have not yet learned that any fault has been charged against me, and already, as though convicted of many crimes, I have paid the most savage penalties.

If anyone accuses me of having been or being disloyal to my lord, he lies no less than the one who said to the Lord: “You have a demon.”

[Col. 0520C] Treat these matters, then, mercifully with our lord; persuade him to remember that he is a king [variant: *cogitet*, “let him think”], and teach him why he is called a king.

[Col. 0520D] May your wisdom also deign to weigh with him what sort and how great a crime it is to ravage the goods of churches and to pollute or burn the churches themselves. If this seems to be any grave crime at all, prove yourselves faithful to our lord in this matter [one witness: “in this matter you are nothing”], so that, while you turn him back from injustice, you may free his soul from the fire of Gehenna; lest, while he unjustly devastates the external goods of the saints, deprived of the saints’ grace, he justly lack their internal goods.

May your prudence also remember that the Apostle threatens death not only to those who do things worthy of death, but also to those who consent to them.”

### 50

[Col. 0521A] Fridericus, the venerable bishop of Münster, because he was born in our region and had once been a canon of the church of Magdeburg, sent a letter to the archbishop of Magdeburg. In it he admonished him, as one faithful to the land from which he was born, to strive by whatever means he could to make peace with the king. The archbishop of Magdeburg sent the following letter in reply:

### 51

[Col. 0521] “To the most holy priest of God Fridericus [F.]: Werinherus [W.], who is called unworthy, sends devoted expressions of fraternal service.

Although I am so filled with the grief produced by this new tribulation that no place for any joy can be found in the innermost recesses of my heart, nevertheless, as soon as I received your letter of consolation, I suppressed no small number of tears of sorrow, because I possess some relief from pain when I see even one brother grieving with fraternal grief [variant: *cordis*, “of the heart”].

I would then rejoice with solid joy if I saw that, just as you have considered the tribulation we have experienced, so also you considered our innocence [variant: “your innocence”], or if you were able to help make the peace about which you advise me into an actual reality.

[Col. 0521B] For what crime preceded the devastation of our land by fire and sword at the hands of our king and all the princes of the kingdom, especially our fellow bishops? Or, if there was some crime, in what council of priests, in what assembly of princes, was it declared and made public? When did we refuse to come when summoned for satisfaction [one witness omits this phrase]? By whom were we accused [variant: *vel*, “or”] and convicted?

Indeed, after we learned that the anger of our lord the king had blazed against us, although without cause, we humbly begged every prince, priest, and layman by letters and spoken appeals to obtain for us the opportunity to appear before him, so that we might either be condemned as criminals by their judgment [variant: *dampnaretur*, “might be condemned”] or, if free of crime, be dismissed with the peace and favor of our lord.

When we saw that this profited us nothing, we often sent an embassy to our lord himself like humble servants, begging him either to condemn us publicly by the judgment of the princes if we were found guilty [variant: *dampnare*, “to condemn”], or, if found free of crime, to grant us the serenity of his favor [variant: *sue g. sue*, “his own favor”].

[Col. 0521C] For this supposed fault, then, a savage devastator invaded our land and reduced it almost to a desert by fire and sword. If only laymen had been in that army, perhaps they would have spared the churches and ecclesiastical property. But now, because [variant: *quam*] many priests were present, they spared no sacred thing. They saw churches which either they themselves or their brothers [variant: “or their fellow-bishops”] had consecrated being burned with abominable fire, and they did not object.

What, then, were the laymen to do when they saw bishops consenting to, or even instigating, such acts?

[Col. 0521D] But although these things have happened [variant: *st*, “have happened”], and although we have been punished beyond measure before being found in any kind of guilt, and although we have been devastated by slaughter and fire without fault by those by whom we ought to have been defended even in an open charge, nevertheless we accept the counsel of your piety concerning the making of peace, if we see that it can be made without greater damage to us [variant: *majori*, “greater”].

[Col. 0522A] Let the princes of those regions come to some place where we can meet safely, and let them teach us by their wisdom what we ought now to do; for whatever pleases them, provided it does not harm us or our descendants, our agreement will carry it out unanimously.

If your fatherhood receives this pious task [variant: “this pious work”] and completes it in deed, then, together with a heavenly reward, you will always have all of us faithful as friends.”

### 52

[Col. 0522B] At that time almighty God showed great mercy to the city of Magdeburg through the merits of the saints, of whom many are held there, and defended that city and the entire bishopric so wonderfully from the king’s cruel invasion that no one who has learned of it may doubt that the city remained unharmed then through the merits of those saints.

For before the battle it had been revealed in a vision to a certain maidservant of God that, if the head of Saint Sebastian, which was kept in that same city with great veneration, were carried around the boundaries of the bishopric, no enemy would be able to enter those boundaries.

When she had reported this to Meginfridus, prefect of the same city [variant: *meinfrido* 1, 2; compare below, chapter 117], and the prefect had reported it to our archbishop in our hearing before they went out to battle [editorial note: “This shows that Bruno was among the familiar clerics of the archbishop”], after the battle had already been fought we had the head carried around all our boundaries before the king arrived [editorial note: “Ebra, near Sondershausen”].

[Col. 0522C] From the outcome itself we discovered that matters were exactly as the maidservant of God had foretold. For whenever the king came to those boundaries, terrified by divine command, he turned back and nowhere entered that bishopric.

### 53

But when the king came with his accompanying army to Goslar and was received there by certain of our bishops with triumphal honor, he asked his friends what he ought to do, and could scarcely find anything useful to himself.

For he did not accept the counsel given by almost all of them: that he should give thanks to God for his victory and, as a Christian king, receive the Saxons into his peace and favor [the transmitted text has *glam*, corrected by the editor to *gloriam*; witness 1 reads *daret*]. What he alone wanted—to subject them all immediately to his servitude—he could not accomplish at that time.

He was unable to capture all the princes, because they had been scattered in different directions; nor could he remain long with his army in that land, because famine had then been useful to us in that year, and the month of July had not yet yielded mature crops. Nor did he consider it safe to remain in Saxony then without an army.

[Col. 0523A] He therefore departed with his entire army and, as before, left Saxony uncertain. After he withdrew, the Saxons gathered together again, and humbly praised God because, while chastising them mercifully, he had not permitted them to be utterly crushed. They encouraged one another to fight with one mind and all their strength for their freedom, and from this they inferred [variant: *idem*, “the same”] that God’s mercy had not been entirely taken away from them [variant: *quod*, “because”]: for, having been scourged as by paternal kindness, they had received, through the king’s departure, a suitable opportunity to recover their strength.

### 54

[Col. 0523] Meanwhile the king again gathered his entire army so that, entering Saxony in October, he might consume—either by using or burning them—the crops he had seen in abundance in the fields in July, and might either give the whole population to be devoured by the sword as rebels or subject it, if humbled, to perpetual servitude [variant: *perpetuo*, “perpetual”].

[Col. 0523B] The Saxons, on the other hand, now made prudent by great danger, came with an army no smaller than his, no longer intending, as before, to flee and turn their backs, but to fight bravely for their freedom, so that either they might firmly retain it with God’s help or lose it together with their lives.

Both armies therefore met at a place called Everha [editorial note: “Ebra, near Sondershausen”], and were far apart from one another not in place but in spirit. Nevertheless, the king’s army was not as ready for battle as before, because it had discovered that the Saxons were not, as it had heard, unwarlike, and a large part of its former numbers was missing.

[Col. 0523C] For after the dukes Berchtold and Rudolf had returned from the earlier battle, moved by divine mercy, they publicly observed the forty-day fasts [editorial note: “for fear of God”], and faithfully vowed to God that they would no longer fight for the king against the innocence of the Saxons.

Then they sent to the Saxons. After pledges had been exchanged, the princes from both sides met in secret council. There they promised our men on their faith that, if they were willing to surrender voluntarily and thereby do honor to the king, so that all Saxony might remain quiet in peace, they themselves would not be held in either harsh or prolonged captivity.

We also learned by report that the king had sworn to his princes that, if they accomplished this to his honor, at the beginning of the coming November he would dismiss them all peacefully and with his favor.

[Col. 0523D] Therefore all our bishops, dukes, counts, and other leading men [variant: “the leading men of the Saxons and Thuringians”], having received from them a pledge of faith by hand, voluntarily surrendered themselves to the royal power (25 October), and ordered their very sorrowful people to return home.

### 55

[Col. 0524A] After our princes had been distributed among various guards, the king entered Saxony without his army with great glory, and was received with even greater glory by those who were at home. For they hoped that he would come peacefully and mercifully, as he had promised, and consign all his injuries to perpetual oblivion.

But he, forgetful of his promise, neither humbly returned worthy praises to God for the victory he had obtained so easily, nor believed that he would ever lose the glory he then possessed [text corrected: *disperditurum*; first reading *dispoturum*; printed edition *dispositurum*].

If the king had then humbly prostrated himself before the King of kings and shown God’s mercy toward the defeated, he would have made not only the Saxons whom he had conquered, but all the peoples over whom he ruled, both fear and love him, and he would have spread among even those nations that were not subject to him a reputation for glory worthy of universal praise.

[Col. 0524B] But because he was not mindful of his former cruelty and cared only to be feared, not loved, he held neither the Saxons faithful to him nor the other nations of his kingdom devoted, and he lost the great praise among foreign peoples that he could have possessed.

For he was no less cruel to his friends than to his enemies, except that he first exercised cruelty upon his friends, so that his enemies might learn from this what they could expect for themselves.

### 56

[Col. 0523] Finally, he first invaded the possessions of the margrave Ekkibert [variants: *Erriberti*; “Ekbert, margrave of Brunswick”], who had given the Saxons no assistance but, being closely related to the king, had supported him with all his heart; and he gave those possessions to Othelric [variant: *Otherico*], one of his counselors.

[Col. 0523D] This Othelric was born at Godesheim, and because he had entirely cast away the fear of God, he bore the nickname Godeshaz [variants: *godeshez*; *godeshetz*]. That is, “hatred of God.” For he truly came from hatred of God: he clung familiarly to the king and disposed the king’s mind according to his own will.

[Col. 0524C] Then he distributed among his parasites the goods of our captives—goods that ought to have remained intact for them if the king’s faith had remained intact—and he lied about everything he had promised his princes concerning goods for us.

At that point he entrusted the cities, castles, and whatever fortifications Saxony still possessed to his followers, and ordered them to exercise tyranny throughout the entire region.

### 57

[Col. 0523] He celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity at Goslar, when the year 1076 from the Lord’s incarnation began, after summoning [variant: *convacatis*] to himself the bishops of his party [variant: “with a large company of the princes of his party”]. His mind was not festive, because he intended to pollute the beginning of the feast of human salvation by the wicked killing of Otto [variant: *quam* for *quem*]; but Christ rescued Otto wonderfully by the same grace by which God at that time wished to become man in order to free the human race.

For he had entrusted the duke himself to Bishop Robert of Bamberg [variants: *Roperto*; *Roberto*], and the bishop had handed him over to his soldiers to be guarded in a certain castle while he himself went to the royal court.

[Col. 0524D] But the king sent there without the bishop’s knowledge and ordered that the duke be brought to him, so that, with the order of time reversed, they would travel by night and rest by day in place of night.

When he, unarmed, had been brought to Goslar in the middle of the night by four armed men, and they wished to proceed through the court toward the forest, he then first understood that they had been ordered to kill him secretly in the forest [variant: “to kill him secretly”].

[Col. 0525A] He therefore asked them to allow him to pray at a monastery. When this was denied him, he suddenly seized [variant: *appr.*] one of their swords by the hilt and, with the sword drawn, reached the chamber of his episcopal guardian despite their resistance [variant: “the bishop’s lodging”]. After the bishop had been awakened by the great commotion, he disclosed what was being done to him and begged him to save him from a secret death.

When this had been spread through the town, the king did not dare to destroy him as he had intended, but allowed him to go freely through the court wherever he wished.

[Col. 0525B] But he, being a prudent man in all things, frequently attended the king’s councils and, through his wisdom, soon earned the position that the king himself arranged especially according to his counsel whatever concerned the king’s honor.

Thus the man whom he had recently held as a most savage enemy he now began to have as his most faithful counselor (1076).

### 58

When we learned that those princes who were holding our men in custody were at Goslar, we sent them letters of supplication for the liberation of our princes, as did each city or province for the release of its own bishop or primate. Of these letters, we have decided to append only one:

### 59

[Col. 0525] “To Lord Udo, most holy shepherd of Christ’s holy sheep: the clergy and people of the church of Magdeburg [variant: *magdeb.*] send the most faithful devotion of both persons.

We severely accuse ourselves because we have not yet sought familiarity with and favor from so great a man by any service of our devotion; and we are all the more ashamed that no such service has made us known to you [variant: *nobis*, “to us”], because, though undeserving, we have received such great consolations of your kindness amid our many tribulations.

[Col. 0525C] Of all the tribulations that either long experience has already taught us wisely to endure or whose very novelty makes them, because unfamiliar, all the more grievous to us [variant: *insolitos*, “unfamiliar”], none has ever weighed upon us more heavily than being deprived of our lord archbishop [variant: *archi.*, abbreviated]—indeed, our most loving father—through the misery of so long a captivity, especially in these stormy times, when he would have been most necessary to us.

But because, as we have learned from his embassy, he enjoys much of your kindness, so that he confesses that he is not afflicted by the pain of captivity but is restored with great sweetness from the labor by which he had been greatly wearied, we willingly forget all the afflictions that we suffer. While we know that our head rejoices, we consider the pain of the members, however great it may be, as nothing [variant: *quos*, “which”].

[Col. 0525D] All of us, therefore, prostrate at the feet of your fatherhood with devoted hearts and one mind, offer you the greatest thanks for your kindness, because, by your mercy, you have mitigated the concern that afflicted us most of all [variant: *mitigasti*, “you mitigated”] and have enabled us to entrust all our other anxieties to the winds, to be carried to the Cretan Sea [the transmitted reading is corrupt: *mercium in Ercium*; the editor emends it to *Creticum* from Horace, *Odes* I.26].

[Col. 0526A] If, with divine clemency favoring you, your fatherhood should make this joy complete for us and assist our lord in returning more quickly to his own through the supplications of his people and his own, you will never regret having granted us your former benefits. You will always have our lord as your friend, fully prepared for every service, and all of us no less devoted and subject to you than your own clergy or people.

If your eminence wishes to strive for this with the zeal we hope for, we believe it can be accomplished without much labor, because we hold this certain: he is held captive as an innocent man, and the salvation of his church alone was the cause of his surrender.

[Col. 0526B] May almighty God therefore preserve you for a long time in this life as a consolation to his Church, and after this life grant you the eternal reward of blessed life.

Farewell [variant: abbreviated *Val.*].”

### 60

When the king had occupied the cities and all the fortifications in Saxony with garrisons of his faithful men, and thought that nothing stood in the way of his doing in Saxony whatever he wished, he passed away from us in the middle of Lent (1076), taking many hostages with him and leaving behind among us men to collect tribute from our regions.

[Col. 0526C] When he had entered his own territories, and his dukes and the others who had fought bravely in battle were expecting triumphal gifts, he prepared to give even then the gift that he was accustomed to lavish upon almost all his faithful [editorial note: “That is, death”] as the reward of their valor.

Grieving that none of the princes had fallen in battle according to his desire, he wished to take from them by cruelty the life which he believed they had preserved through cowardice [variant: *auferre*, “to take away”]. For, so that he alone might be lord of all, he did not wish any lord to live in his kingdom.

[Col. 0526D] Thus, in the middle of the night, he entered a certain deserted house with three very brave armed men and secretly brought in one of Duke Rudolf’s soldiers. When the man saw the swords, he was afraid, because he had nowhere to flee.

But when the king overwhelmed him with many promises if he would kill Duke Rudolf at the first opportunity offered him, he promised almost cheerfully that he would do so—not out of love for the promises, but from fear of the swords present—and confirmed his promise by oath.

[Col. 0527A] When morning came, and the duke, having been greatly praised by the king for his valor and faith, was departing after being dismissed with much graciousness, the man seized his weapons and quickly pursued him. Hurrying through the crowd with his lance extended, he loudly threatened to kill the duke.

But when the soldiers surrounded him and asked the reason for the terror, he disclosed the entire sequence of what had happened during the night. Throwing down his weapons, he made known to the duke what he had sworn and by what force he had been compelled.

### 61

[Col. 0527] At another time, when the same duke was leading the queen from a monastery under his protection, the king ordered a certain archer [variant: *sagitario*] to pierce him with an arrow beside the queen.

But after being warned by that same archer, the duke did not escort the queen; instead, finding some pretext, he hurried away from her.

### 62

A third time, when certain matters [variant: *quadam*, “a certain matter”] were being handled inside the king’s chamber and the duke was present with a few of his men, he was informed that two of the king’s servants were guarding the door with drawn swords, intending to stab the duke from both sides as he came out.

[Col. 0527B] He therefore secretly had some of his men arrive with concealed swords, made some of them enter the chamber, and stationed many more in front of the doors.

When everything had been arranged as he had ordered, he approached the door with his men and said: “Lord king, I would not have wished to see such doorkeepers in your chamber just now, nor do I ever again wish to see them.”

After saying this, he departed in great fury and declared—and carried out what he declared—that he would never again come to the king’s court.

### 63

[Col. 0527] By the same or a similar deceit he also sought to destroy Duke Berthold [variant: “Berthold, duke of Zähringen”], because these two seemed more than others to resist his malice.

And why do I mention his cruelty toward only two men, when I cannot declare any one of the princes safe from such danger?

[Col. 0527C] For one day, while he was staying in his chamber with his jesters and the bishops and other leading men were waiting in the vestibule, he is said to have spoken to those who were aware of and supported his wickedness:

“Behold these men who possess the wealth of my kingdom and have left me and all my people in poverty. If they were removed, I and all my familiar associates could quickly become rich. Therefore, if you are men and desire to possess wealth, attack these unarmed men boldly while armed, and take everything they possess.”

He always kept in his chamber many axes, gleaming with broad iron blades, against which neither shield nor helmet could resist by any strength.

Unless Archbishop Anno of Cologne had shortly beforehand been warned by one of those who was about to commit the crime with the others, that wretched deed would have been perpetrated on that day.

### 64

[Col. 0527D] But to return briefly to the earlier events: when our leading men had surrendered, the king ordered all the paths leading through the mountains into Italy to be closed, and permitted no person to pass along the road, lest the truth of the matter reach the apostolic lord before he himself, through his legates, had turned the apostolic lord to his own side.

Then he sent legates to the Roman pontiff to inform him that the bishops of Saxony, forgetting their order, had joined battle against him [variant: *congessi*, “I joined battle”], and to ask him to depose them from the priestly rank as faithless perjurers and instigators of civil war, so that he himself might put in their place men through whom the Church could be governed in peace [one witness omits “through whom”].

[Col. 0528A] But rumor had preceded the king’s legates to the apostolic lord and had truthfully reported to him the entire course of events.

He therefore sent letters to the king in which he accused him of many other crimes, and begged him to release the bishops from captivity and restore them fully to their churches and possessions. After this, he was to convene a council at a place to which the apostolic lord could come, where the bishops would either lose their episcopal dignity if they were deserving of such a penalty, or receive canonical satisfaction for the injuries they had suffered.

But if the king refused to obey the sacred canons in these matters [one witness omits the phrase “after this”] and to expel excommunicated persons from his fellowship, he threatened to cut him off, like a rotten member, from the unity of holy Mother Church by the sword of anathema.

[Col. 0528B] When this embassy had been received and confirmed by the arrival of those whom he had sent to the apostolic lord, the king was very sad, because he did not find in the apostolic dignity the assistance for his wickedness that he had hoped for [variant: “had hoped for previously”].

### 65

The king therefore came with his deceivers to Worms, and consulted individually or in pairs [variant: “with them”] about how he might make a worthy return for the insult that they had all heard the Roman pontiff had inflicted upon him: namely, that he had threatened to excommunicate him, although nothing of this kind had ever been heard of in all time.

After they had long revolved many plans in many ways, some of them finally thought it appropriate that, after a council of bishops had been held, they should condemn the pope by common agreement as though he were a Simoniac; and, after deposing him, that the king should appoint one of his friends in his place, who would carry out with complete willingness everything that pleased the king.

[Col. 0528C] When this plan had been devised and confirmed, he had all his bishops assemble and compelled them to prohibit submission and obedience to Hildebrand, who was called the Roman pontiff but was not one. To prevent any of them from later denying this, he made each one write with his own hand, under his own name, a renunciation of Hildebrand on separate sheets [variant: *cartis*, “sheets”], in the following form:

“I, N. [variant: *enim*], bishop of the city of N., from this hour and henceforth prohibit submission and obedience to Hildebrand, and henceforth I shall neither regard nor call him the apostolic lord.”

A few of them did this sincerely; they were themselves the authors of the plan. Most, however, wrote letters of renunciation through fear of death, but showed by this that they had acted unwillingly: as soon as the opportunity was given them, they sent the apostolic lord supplicatory letters of confession, acknowledged themselves guilty before him, and pleaded the necessity that had compelled them.

[Col. 0528D] Then he sent letters throughout Italy, inclining the princes of that land to his side with great gifts and still greater promises.

[Col. 0529A] Thus our bishops [variant: “the Germans”] renounced him only in writing, whereas those in Italy renounced him also by oath [variant: *non*, “not,” in 1b and the editions].

He also corrupted very many Romans with money and asked them, in such letters, to cast Hildebrand down from the honor of the apostolic see. He himself likewise sent the apostolic lord a letter full of insults, in which he threateningly ordered him quickly to abandon the apostolic name and see.

Here is an example of the letter:

### 66

[Col. 0529D] “Heinricus, by the grace of God king [V. *Legum*, vol. II, p. 46], to the clergy and people of the whole holy Roman Church: grace, salvation, and every good.

That faith is considered firm and unshaken [variant: *inconcussa*, “unshaken”] which is always and equally preserved toward the present and the absent, and which is not changed either by the prolonged absence of the person to whom it is owed or by the weariness of a long period of time.

[Col. 0529B] We know and give thanks that you preserve such faith toward us, and we ask that it continue in the same way—namely, that, as you do, you should always remain friends to our friends and enemies to our enemies.

Among these, marking out Hildebrand the monk, we stir you up against him, because we have discovered him to be an invader and oppressor of the Church and a plotter against the Roman commonwealth and our kingdom [variant: “we have comprehended him”], as is plainly evident from the following letter addressed to him by us.

[Editorial note: In manuscript 1 this begins a new chapter.]”

Source preparation: Supplied local archive source; all editorial apparatus and witness readings translated or glossed in context.

“Heinricus, by the grace of God king, to Hildebrand. Although until now I had expected from you the things that belong to a father, and had obeyed you in all matters despite the great indignation of our faithful, I received from you [Note: [Col. 0529] Missing in one witness.] the sort of reciprocal treatment that one ought to expect from him who was the most pernicious enemy of our life and kingdom. For when, at the outset, you had snatched away with arrogant audacity every hereditary dignity that was owed to me by that see, proceeding farther from there you attempted by the worst devices to alienate the kingdom of Italy. Nor were you content with this: you did not fear to lay hands upon the most reverend bishops, who are united to us like our sweetest limbs, and you harassed them, as they themselves say, with the most arrogant injuries and bitterest insults, contrary to divine and human laws [Note: [Col. 0529] “You aggravated” in two witnesses.].

“While I concealed all these things with a certain patience, you, judging this not patience but cowardice [Note: [Col. 0529] “Considering” in two witnesses.], dared to rise against my very head, issuing the commands that you know—namely, to use your own words, that either you would die or take away my soul and kingdom. Judging that this unheard-of contumacy had to be refuted not by words but by action, I held a general assembly of all the chief men of the kingdom, at their own supplication. When there the matters that until then had been kept silent through fear and reverence were brought into the open, it was made clear by their truthful statements, which you will hear from their own letters, that you could in no way remain in the apostolic see. Since their judgment appeared just and credible before God and men, I too, assenting to it, renounce every right of the papacy that you have seemed to possess, and I command you to descend from the see of the City, whose patriciate is owed to me by God’s gift and by the sworn assent of the Romans.”

“This is the text of our letter to the monk Hildebrand. We have therefore written it also to you, so that our will may be known to you, and so that your charity may satisfy us—or rather, God and us. Rise up [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 1 reads *Exurgite constanter*, “Rise up steadfastly.”], then, most faithful men, against him, and let him who is first in faith be first in his condemnation. We do not say that you should shed his blood, since after his deposition life will be a greater punishment for him than death; rather, if he is unwilling to descend, compel him, and receive into the apostolic see another whom we shall elect with the common counsel of all the bishops and of you—one who both wishes and is able to heal what this man has wounded in the Church.”

**67.** “Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0530D] V. Legum, vol. II, p. 47.], king not by usurpation but by the pious ordinance of God, to Hildebrand, no longer apostolic but a false monk. You have earned such a greeting, for your confusion [Note: [Col. 0529] “Confession” in two witnesses?], since you have passed over no order in the Church without making it a participant in confusion rather than honor, in cursing rather than blessing. To speak briefly and notably of many matters: the rulers of the holy Church—namely, archbishops, bishops, and priests—you not only did not fear to touch as the anointed of the Lord, but even trampled them beneath your feet like slaves who do not know what their master is doing. By trampling them you won popular favor; you judged that all of them knew nothing, while you alone knew everything. And you strove to use this knowledge not for edification but for destruction [Col. 0530C], so that we may rightly believe that blessed Gregory, whose name you have appropriated, prophesied about you when he said: ‘From the abundance of subjects, the mind of a prelate is often lifted up, and he thinks that he knows more than everyone, when he sees that he can do more than everyone.’ [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 2 reads *in hoc*, “in this,” before *beatum Gregorium*.]

“We indeed endured all these things while striving to preserve the honor of the apostolic see. But you understood our humility as fear, and therefore did not fear to rise against the royal power granted to us by God—power that you dared to threaten to take away from us [Note: [Col. 0529] ‘To be taken away’ in one witness.]—as though we had received the kingdom from you, as though kingdom or empire were in your hand and not in God’s; although our Lord Jesus Christ called us to kingship, but did not call you to the priesthood.

“You ascended by these steps: through cunning, which the monastic profession abhors; through money, influence through money, the sword through influence, and through the sword you reached the see of peace; and from the see of peace you disturbed peace, while you armed subjects against prelates, while you taught that our bishops, called by God, should be despised by you, who were not called, while you usurped their ministry for laymen over priests, so that they might depose [Note: [Col. 0529] ‘May depose’ in one witness.] or despise [Note: [Col. 0529] ‘May despise those whom they themselves’ in two witnesses.] those whom they had received to be instructed from the hand of the Lord through the laying on of bishops’ hands [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘Of episcopal men, to instruct’ in two witnesses.].

“You also touched me, who [Note: [Col. 0531] Missing in one witness.], although unworthy, have been anointed among the anointed for kingship; tradition of the holy Fathers teaches that I am to be judged by God alone and deposed for no crime unless, God forbid, we should deviate from the faith. For even the apostate Julian was entrusted by the prudence of the holy bishops to be judged and deposed not by them but by God alone. He himself [Note: [Col. 0531] “He himself also” in two witnesses.]—the true pope, blessed Peter—cries out: ‘Fear God; honor the king.’ But because you do not fear God, you dishonor me, his appointed servant. Therefore blessed Paul, who did not spare an angel from heaven if he preached otherwise, did not exempt you, who teach otherwise on earth. For he says: ‘If anyone, whether I or even an angel from heaven, preaches to you a gospel contrary to what we preached, let him be accursed.’

“Therefore, condemned by this anathema, by the judgment of all our bishops, and by ours, descend; leave the apostolic see that has been vindicated! Let another ascend the throne [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘The see’ in two witnesses.] of blessed Peter, one who does not cloak any violence with religion [Note: [Col. 0531] One witness reads *violencia*, “violence.”], but teaches the sound doctrine of blessed Peter. For I [Note: [Col. 0531] Missing in two witnesses.], Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0531] N. in one witness.], king by the grace of God, say to you together with all our bishops: Descend, descend [Note: [Col. 0531] Freher’s second edition adds from Lehmann’s Chronicle of Speyer, words that had already been read above in chapter 65: ‘The subscription of the individual bishops. I, N., bishop of the city of N., from this hour and henceforth forbid Hildebrand’s following and obedience, and hereafter I shall neither regard nor call him apostolic.’].”

**68.** When this letter had been brought to the lord pope, presiding over the holy synod in the Lateran basilica, and had been publicly read before the synod, such a commotion arose in the Church that the same envoy, unless he had found protection at the feet of the apostolic lord, would have perished miserably, torn limb from limb [Col. 0531C]. On the following day, however, the lord pope declared before that same synod [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 1 reads *ipso*, masculine, for *ipsa*.] how often and with how much gentleness he had reproved the king for his great crimes; with what great kindness he had asked—and by apostolic authority ordered—him to free the bishops from captivity [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads *utque*, “and that,” for *ut*.]; and how much bitterness of arrogance he had received in return for paternal tenderness. Then, when everyone cried out that such an insult must not remain unpunished, with the counsel and consent of all he condemned Heinricus by synodal judgment, deprived him of the king’s name and honor, and struck him with the sword of anathema. He sent letters into the kingdom of the Germans, of which it seemed appropriate to insert a copy here:

**69.** “Gregory [Note: [Col. 0531] N. in one witness.] bishop (Gregory VII, *Register* III.6), servant of the servants of God, to all who desire to be numbered among the sheep whom Christ entrusted to blessed Peter: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“You have heard, brothers, of a new and unheard-of presumption; you have heard the criminal babbling and audacity of schismatics who blaspheme the name of the Lord in blessed Peter; you have heard arrogance raised to the injury and insult of the holy and apostolic see, such as your fathers never saw or heard [Note: [Col. 0531] The *Register* agrees with witness 1.] and such as the sequence of Scripture never records as having arisen even among pagans or heretics. Even if any example [Note: [Col. 0531] The *Register* reads *aliquod*, “some” or “any.”] of this evil had ever arisen after the Church was founded [Note: [Col. 0531] Omitted in the *Register*.] and the faith of Christ propagated, all the faithful would nevertheless have cause to grieve and lament over such contempt and trampling of apostolic—or rather, divine—authority.

“Therefore, if you believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to blessed Peter by our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0531] The *Register* reads “by God our Lord” and “you believe them to have been entrusted.”], and if you desire through his hands to prepare for yourselves an entrance to the joys of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0531] The *Register* reads ‘to lie open’], you must consider how greatly you ought now to grieve over the insult inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘Injury’ in the *Register*.]. For unless here, where your faith and hearts are tested through the trials of temptations, you become companions in suffering, you are undoubtedly unworthy to receive a share in future consolation and, as sons of the kingdom, to obtain the heavenly crown and glory.

“We therefore ask your charity to strive earnestly to implore divine mercy, so that it may either turn the hearts of the wicked to repentance or, by restraining their wicked counsels, show how senseless and foolish are those who attempt to overthrow the rock founded [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘Founded by Christ’ in the *Register*.] upon Christ and to violate divine privileges [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘Privilege’ in one witness.] [Note: [Col. 0531] The *Register* adds: ‘But how and for what reasons blessed Peter bound the king with the bond of anathema, you can learn fully from the document enclosed with this one. The remainder is lacking. That deposition appears in III.5.’].”

**70.** “Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, bend, I ask [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘We ask’ in two witnesses.], your kindly ears toward us, and hear me, your servant, whom you nourished from infancy and have freed to this day from the hand of the wicked—those who hated and hate me for my fidelity to you. You are my witness, as are my lady, the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘Of the Lord’ in two witnesses.], and blessed Paul, your brother, among all the saints, that your holy Roman Church drew me, unwilling, to its helm, and I did not regard ascending to your see as a seizure; indeed, I preferred to end my life in exile rather than seize your office for the glory of the world or through secular cleverness. And therefore, by your grace [Note: [Col. 0531] ‘In God’ in two witnesses.], not by my own works—I believe that it was and is pleasing to you that the Christian people specially entrusted to you should obey me specially as your representative entrusted to me; and by your grace the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth has been given to me by God [Note: [Col. 0531] Omitted in one witness.].

“Relying, therefore, upon this confidence, for the honor and defense of your Church, on behalf of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by your power and authority I deny to King Heinricus, son of the Emperor Heinricus, who has risen against your Church with unheard-of arrogance, the governance of the entire kingdom of the Germans and of Italy; I absolve all Christians from the bond of the oath that they have sworn or shall swear to him; and I forbid anyone to serve him as king. For it is fitting that he who strives [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 agrees: *studet*, “strives.”] to diminish the honor of your Church [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *imminuere*, “to lessen.”] should himself lose the honor that he appears to possess.

“And because, as a Christian, he has scorned to obey, has not returned to God, whom he abandoned, has shared with the excommunicated, and has committed many iniquities, while, with you as witness, he despised my warnings, which I sent him for his salvation, and, by attempting to tear your Church apart, separated himself from it, I bind him with the bond of anathema in your stead. I bind him by confidence in you, so that the nations may know and acknowledge that you are Peter, and that upon this rock [Note: [Col. 0533] ‘This’ in two witnesses.] the Son of the living God built his Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

**71.** Then, after not much time had passed, the apostolic lord, lest it be thought that he had excommunicated the king more out of grief at his own injury than out of zeal for justice, sent these letters to the German regions, in which he testifies that he had justly excommunicated him [Note: [Col. 0533D] See Paul of Bernried, *Life of Gregory VII*, ch. 78.].

**72.** “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops, dukes, and counts [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in two witnesses.], and other faithful people in the kingdom of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0533] ‘German’ in one witness.] who defend the Christian faith: greetings and apostolic blessing [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in one witness.].

“We have heard that some among you doubt the excommunication that we imposed upon the king and ask whether he was justly excommunicated and whether our sentence proceeded with the deliberation required by the authority of lawful discipline. Therefore, as truthfully as we could, with our conscience as witness, we have taken care to make clear to the eyes and understanding of all how we were led to excommunicate him [Note: [Col. 0533] ‘How we are’ in two witnesses.]. We do this not so much to throw into public view, as it were through our outcry [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 reads *quasi in*, “as if in.”], the individual causes—which, alas, are too well known—as to satisfy the opinion of those who think that we seized the spiritual sword rashly and more from the impulse of our own mind than from fear of God and zeal for justice.

“When we were still occupying the office of deacon, an evil [Note: [Col. 0533] One witness reads ‘an evil report of the king’s actions.’] and highly dishonorable report about the king’s conduct reached us. Because of his imperial dignity and respect for his father and mother, and also because of our hope and desire for his correction [Note: [Col. 0533] One witness and Paul of Bernried omit: ‘imperial dignity and respect for his father and mother, and also because of.’], we often admonished him by letters and messengers to desist from his wickedness [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 2.] and [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *ac*, “and.”], remembering his illustrious lineage and dignity, to order his life [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *vitam suam*, “his life.”] according to the character that should become a king and, God granting it, a future emperor [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 reads *diceret*, “would say,” for *deceret*, “would befit.”].

“But after we had reached the summit of the pontificate [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *autem*, “however,” for *vero*.], although unworthy, while his age and his iniquity grew together, we understood that almighty God would demand his soul from our hand all the more strictly in proportion as greater freedom and authority had been given to us above others to rebuke him [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 1 and in Paul of Bernried.] [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *quantum*, “as much as,” for *quanto*.]. Therefore we exhorted him much more earnestly, by every means—arguing, entreating, and reproving him—to reform his life.

“When he [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *quod*, “because,” for *qui*.] often sent us devout greetings and letters, excusing himself both because, on account of his age, he was unstable and fragile [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *tum* for *cum*.], and because he had often been badly advised and counselled by those in whose hands the court lay [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 has *a. q.*; the abbreviated reading is uncertain.], he promised in words that he would most readily accept our warnings day by day; but in deed, and [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *atque*, “and also,” for *et*.] by increasing his offences, he utterly trampled them underfoot.

“Meanwhile we summoned to repentance certain of his familiars, through whose counsels and machinations he had, induced by payment [Note: [Col. 0533] Paul of Bernried reads ‘induced by them.’], polluted bishoprics and many monasteries with the simoniacal heresy, putting wolves in place of shepherds. We summoned them so that, while there was still opportunity for correction, they might restore to the venerable places to which they belonged the goods of the churches that they had sacrilegiously received through the intervention of so wicked a transaction, and so that they themselves might make satisfaction to God for the iniquity they had committed through the lamentation of repentance.

“When we learned that they scorned the time granted them to carry this out and obstinately persisted in their customary wickedness, we separated these sacrilegious men, ministers and members of the devil, from communion and from the body of the whole Church, as was fitting; and we admonished the king to expel them from his household, his counsels, and all his association as excommunicated persons.

“Meanwhile, when the case against the king of the Saxons was becoming more serious and he saw that the strength and support of the kingdom were for the most part inclined to withdraw from him, he again sent us a submissive letter full of every humility. In it, acknowledging himself deeply culpable before almighty God, blessed Peter, and us [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads *videns*, “seeing himself.”], he also offered prayers that whatever [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 reads *quae*, “which things,” for *quod*, “what.”] had been done through his fault in ecclesiastical matters contrary to canonical institution [Note: [Col. 0533] Thus emended; one witness reads ‘justice’; Paul of Bernried omits the words.] and the decrees of the holy Fathers might be corrected by our apostolic foresight and authority. In every respect he promised us his obedience, consent, and faithful assistance [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 reads *profidele*; the abbreviated form is uncertain.].

“Later, having undertaken penance, he confirmed the same promise in the hands of our fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 has *ita*; witness 1 reads *fratribus*, “brothers.”], Bishop Humbert of Praeneste and Bishop Gerald of Ostia, whom we sent to him, swearing by the sacred vestments that they held around their necks. Then, after some time [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in two witnesses.], when he had fought a battle with the Saxons, the king offered God such thanks and sacrifices for the victory he had won that he immediately broke the vows he had made concerning his amendment. Paying no attention to anything he had promised, he received excommunicated persons into his intimacy and fellowship and dragged the churches into the same disorder to which he had been accustomed.

“Struck by deep grief over this, although after his contempt for the benefits of the heavenly King nearly all hope of his correction had been taken from us [Note: [Col. 0535] ‘Although’ in two witnesses.], we nevertheless decided that his mind should still be tested, desiring more that he should hear apostolic gentleness than experience severity. Accordingly, we sent him letters of admonition, telling him to remember what he had promised and to whom; not to think that he could deceive God, whose anger, when he begins to judge, is all the more severe the longer his patience has lasted; and not to dishonor God, who honors him, nor [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 2 reads *neu*, “and not,” for *nec*.] to attempt to extend his power to the contempt of God and the insult of the apostolic see [Col. 0535B], knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

“Furthermore, we sent him three religious men, certainly his own faithful subjects, through whom we privately admonished him to repent of his crimes. These crimes are indeed said to be dreadful, but they are known to many and have been spread through many regions. On account of them, the authority of divine and human laws declares that he ought not merely to be excommunicated until he makes worthy satisfaction, but also to be deprived of every royal honor without hope of recovering it.

“Finally, unless he separated the excommunicated from his association, we could judge or determine [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 2 omits *discernere*, “determine.”] nothing else concerning him except that, separated from the Church, he should remain in the company of the excommunicated, with whom rather than with Christ he chose to have a share [Note: [Col. 0535] Two witnesses omit ‘with whom he himself.’].

“Certainly, if he were willing to accept our warnings and correct his life, we have called God as witness, and continue to call him, to how greatly we would rejoice in his salvation and honor, and with how much charity we would embrace him in the bosom of holy Church—as one who, appointed prince of the people and holding the reins of a most extensive kingdom, ought to be a defender of Catholic peace and justice.

“But how highly he valued either our letters or our words sent through legates, his deeds make clear. Unable to endure being rebuked or reproved by anyone, he not only could not be recalled from the crimes he had committed to amendment, but, seized by an even greater fury of conscience, did not cease until he had caused almost all the bishops in Italy, and as many as he could in the German regions, to suffer shipwreck concerning the faith of Christ. He compelled them to deny the obedience and honor owed to blessed Peter and to the apostolic see, which our Lord Jesus Christ had granted to it [Note: [Col. 0535] Thus in two witnesses; ‘and Ekkehard’ in one.].

“When, therefore, we saw that his iniquity had reached its height, we excommunicated him by synodal judgment for these reasons: first, because he refused to abstain from association with those who had been excommunicated for sacrilege and the guilt of simoniacal heresy; second, because, on account of the criminal acts of his life, he was unwilling not only to undertake repentance but even to promise it, having falsified the faith that he had pledged into the hands of our legates; and likewise because he did not shrink from dividing the body of Christ—that is, the unity of the holy Church.

“For these faults, I say, we excommunicated him, so that the one whom we could not recall to the way of salvation by gentleness, we might at least, with God’s help, recall by severity; or, if—God forbid—he should not even fear the rigor of discipline, so that our soul [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 1 reads *nostram ... animam*, “our soul,” in a different case construction.] might not succumb to the peril of negligence or fear [Note: [Col. 0535] One witness reads ‘our soul to the peril.’].

“If anyone should think that this sentence was issued unjustly or irrationally, if he is such a person that he refuses to offer his understanding to the sacred rules, let him deal with us about it, and, patiently hearing what divine authority teaches and decrees [Note: [Col. 0535] Omitted in one witness; another reads ‘discerns’ for ‘decrees.’], and what the harmonious voice of the holy Fathers judges, let him submit—not to what we say, but to what [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 1 omits *quid*, “what.”] divine authority teaches.

“We nevertheless do not think that any of the faithful who knows the Church’s statutes is held by this error, so that he would not acknowledge that this was rightly done, even if he does not dare to affirm it publicly, at least in his heart. And even if—God [Note: [Col. 0535] Omitted in witness 1.] avert it—we had bound him with such a bond without sufficiently serious cause or in a less orderly manner, as the holy Fathers assert, the sentence would not on that account be to be despised; rather, absolution would have to be sought with all humility.

“But you, beloved, who have refused to abandon God’s justice for the sake of royal anger or because of any danger, stand courageously and strengthen yourselves in the Lord against the folly of those who make light of execration and falsehood at the consummation [Note: [Col. 0535] The construction is lacunose; Mabillon supplies *consummationem ruunt*, “they rush toward consummation.”]. Know that you defend the cause of him who is judged the unconquerable King and glorious victor [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 2 reads *rex ac semper magnificus*, “king and ever-magnificent,” for the received description.], who will judge the living and the dead, rendering to each according to his work. You too may be certain of his manifold recompense if you remain faithful and unshaken in his truth to the end.

“For this reason we also pray continually to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0535] ‘To God’ in two witnesses.] for you, that he may grant you strength to be strengthened through the Holy Spirit in his name, and may turn the king’s heart to repentance, so that he too may at some time recognize that we and you love him far more truly than those who now obey and favor his iniquities. If, by God’s inspiration, he should wish to come to his senses, whatever he may plot against us, he will nevertheless always find us ready to receive him into holy communion, insofar as your charity may advise us.”

**73.** Afterwards, in order to confirm more fully the excommunication that he had imposed, the apostolic lord sent these letters into the German regions:
