“Gregory, bishop (Gregory VII, Register VIII.21; Codex Udalrici 156), servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, N., bishop [Note: Hermann of Metz, editor], greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that the fact that we understand you to be prepared to endure labors and dangers in defense of the truth is a divine gift. For this is its ineffable grace and wondrous clemency: it never permits its chosen ones to stray completely, nor allows them to be utterly shaken or cast down. Rather, after they have been tested by a useful trial during a time of persecution, it makes them, even after some fear, stronger than they were before.

Moreover, just as among cowards fear unmakes one man, so that he flees more shamefully than another [Note: “examines,” 1], so among the brave a manly heart is inflamed to act more vigorously than another and to burst forth more ardently [Note: corrupt, 1]. We have therefore taken care to commend this to your charity in the voice of exhortation, so that you may take greater pleasure in standing among the foremost in the battle-line of the Christian religion, the more surely you know that they are nearest and most worthy to the victorious God.

As for what you asked—namely, that you might be assisted and fortified by our writings against the madness of those who babble with impious mouth, claiming that the authority of the holy apostolic see could not excommunicate King Heinricus [Note: N., 1], a man who despised Christian law, that is, a destroyer of churches and the empire and an author and accomplice of heretics, nor absolve anyone from his oath of allegiance—we do not consider this especially necessary, since the pages of Sacred Scripture contain so many documents, and such certain ones, concerning this matter.

Nor do we believe that those who shamelessly detract from and contradict the truth, thereby adding to the heap of their damnation [Note: imprudently, 1], have fitted this to the audacity of their defense through both ignorance and the madness of wretched despair. Nor is this surprising: it is the habit of the reprobate, for the protection of their wickedness, to defend those like themselves [Note: “to strive,” added in the Register], because they regard it as nothing to incur perdition through falsehood.

For, to say little among many examples, who does not know the voice of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” (Matthew 16)

Were kings excluded here, or are they not among the sheep whom the Son of God entrusted to blessed Peter? Who, I ask, in this universal grant of binding and loosing, thinks himself excluded from Peter’s power, except perhaps that wretched man who, unwilling to bear the yoke of the Lord [Note: “at home,” 1], subjects himself to the burden of the devil and refuses to be numbered among Christ’s sheep?

Yet this does not help him toward a wretched liberty, because he casts from his proud neck the power of Peter divinely granted to him; for the more anyone refuses through arrogance to bear it, the more heavily he bears it at the judgment, to his own damnation.

The holy Fathers therefore received and preserved with great reverence this institution of the divine will, this foundation of the church’s administration, this privilege chiefly entrusted and confirmed by heavenly decree to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Note: “of the blessed,” omitted in 1]. In both general councils and their other writings and deeds, they called the holy Roman Church the universal mother. And just as they accepted its teachings for the confirmation of faith and instruction in sacred religion, so also they accepted its judgments. In this they agreed, as though united in one spirit and one voice: all greater matters and important affairs, as well as the judgments of all churches, ought to be referred to it as to a mother and head; no appeal should ever be made from it, and its judgments could and ought to be retracted or refuted by no one.

Thus blessed Pope Gelasius, writing to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10), instructed him in the following manner, supported by divine authority, concerning what he ought to think about the primacy of the holy apostolic see and how he ought to think it:

> “Although it is right that all the faithful should generally submit their necks to priests who rightly handle divine things, how much more ought consent to be given to the prelate of that see whom the supreme divinity willed to preside over all priests, and whom the continuing devotion of the universal Church afterward celebrated?”

Here your prudence clearly observes that no one can ever equal himself, by any merely human judgment, to the privilege or confession of him whom the voice of Christ preferred above all, whom the venerable Church has always acknowledged and holds devotedly as primate.

Likewise Pope Julius, writing to the Eastern bishops, says concerning the power of that same holy apostolic see (Letter 2):

> “It was fitting for you, brothers, to address the holy Roman and apostolic Church with care [Note: ‘to limit,’ 1], and not to speak ironically, since our Lord Jesus Christ himself addressed it appropriately, saying: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.’”

“For it possesses, by a singular privilege granted to it, the power to open and close the door of the heavenly kingdom for whomever it wishes.” To him, then, who has been given the power of opening and closing heaven, is it not permitted to judge on earth? Far from it. Do you not remember what blessed Paul the Apostle says?

> “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” [Col. 0538D]

Blessed Pope Gregory likewise decreed that kings fall from their dignity if they presume to violate the decrees of the apostolic see. Writing to a certain senator [Note: “abbot,” added in the Register], he said:

> “If any king, priest, judge [Note: judgment, 1], or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor [Note: omitted in 1], and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed. Unless he restores what he has wickedly taken away, or mourns through worthy repentance for his unlawful acts, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subject to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.”

If blessed Gregory, a teacher of exceptionally gentle character, decreed that kings who violated his statutes concerning a single hospice should not only be deposed but also excommunicated and condemned at the eternal judgment, who could reproach us for deposing and excommunicating Heinricus [Note: N., 1]—not merely a despiser of apostolic judgments, but also, insofar as it lies within him, a trampler upon the mother Church herself, and the most shameless plunderer and most savage destroyer of the entire kingdom and of the churches—unless he is like him?

As we have learned from blessed Peter’s teaching in the letter concerning the ordination of Clement, it says:

> “If anyone is a friend of those with whom he”—speaking of Clement himself—“does not speak, he too is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. Although he appears to be with us bodily, in mind and spirit he is against us, and this enemy is far worse than those who are outside and openly hostile.”

For under the appearance of friendship he does what is hostile, and he scatters and lays waste to the Church.

Take note, therefore, dearest brother: if Peter judges so severely one who associates, through friendship or conversation, with those toward whom the pope is hostile because of their deeds [Note: “adversely,” Register], with what severity does he condemn the man himself toward whom he is hostile because of his deeds [Note: “adversely,” Register]?

But to return to the matter: shall a dignity devised by secular people ignorant of God not be subject to that dignity which the providence of almighty God devised for his honor and mercifully granted to the world? His Son is undoubtedly believed to be God and man [Note: “is believed,” 1]; likewise he is held to be the supreme priest and head of all priests, seated at the right hand of the Father and always interceding for us. He despised the secular kingdom in which the sons of the age swell with pride, and of his own will came to the priesthood of the cross.

Who does not know that kings and rulers had their origin among those who, ignorant of God, driven by the prince of the world, namely the devil [Note: omitted in 2], sought, through pride, robbery, treachery, murder, and finally almost every crime, to dominate over their equals—over human beings [Notes: omitted in 2]—with blind desire and intolerable presumption?

When such men strive to make the Lord’s priests bow to their feet, to whom can they more rightly be compared than to him who is the head over all the sons of pride, who, tempting the supreme pontiff, the head of priests, the Son of the Most High [Notes: omitted in 2], and promising him all the kingdoms of the world, said:

> “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me!” (Matthew 4:9)

Who could doubt that the priests of Christ are considered the fathers and teachers of all kings, rulers, and faithful people? Is it not recognized as the height of wretched insanity if a son attempts to subjugate his father, or a disciple his teacher, and to subject him through wicked obligations to his own power—him from whom he believes that he can be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven?

As blessed Gregory recalls in his letter addressed to the Emperor Maurice (Letter IV.31), the Emperor Constantine the Great, lord of nearly the whole world’s kings and rulers, clearly understanding this, sat last of all in the holy Synod of Nicaea, after all the bishops. He did not presume to give any judgment over them; rather, calling them gods, he judged that they ought not to be subject to his judgment, but that he himself depended upon their decision.

The aforementioned Pope Gelasius, persuading the Emperor Anastasius not to regard the truth communicated to his mind as an insult, added:

> “There are indeed two powers, august emperor, by which this world is chiefly governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these, the burden of the priests is all the heavier, since they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.”

And after a few intervening words he says:

> “You know, therefore, that in these matters you depend upon their judgment, and that they do not wish to be reduced to your will [Note: ‘to be plucked,’ 1].”

Supported, then, by such institutions and such authorities, many pontiffs have excommunicated some kings and others emperors.

For, if a particular example concerning rulers is sought, blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom [Note: “Chrysostimus,” 1] from his see.

Another Roman pontiff, namely Zacharias [Note: added in the Register], deposed the king of the Franks—not so much because of his own wickedness as because he was not useful to so great a power [Note: omitted in 1]—and installed Pepin, the father of the Emperor Charlemagne, in his place. He also absolved all the Franks from the oath of allegiance that they had sworn to him.

The holy Church likewise often does this on the basis of frequent authority, when it absolves soldiers from the bond of an oath; and this was done in the case of those bishops who are deposed from episcopal rank by apostolic authority.

And blessed Ambrose, although a saint but not the bishop of the universal Church, excluded the Emperor Theodosius the Great from the Church by excommunicating him for a fault that seemed not so serious to other priests.

He also shows in his writings that priestly dignity is higher than royal power by a greater degree than gold is more precious than lead. At the beginning of his Pastoral he writes as follows:

> “The honor and sublimity of the episcopate, brothers, cannot be equaled by any comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of rulers, it will be far inferior, as the metal of lead is inferior to the brilliance of gold; for you see kings’ and rulers’ necks bent before the knees of priests, and, after kissing their right hands, they believe themselves strengthened by their prayers.”

And shortly afterward:

> “You ought to recognize, brothers, that we have prefaced all this for the following reason: to show that in this world nothing is more excellent than priests, and nothing more sublime than bishops.”

Your fraternity should also remember that greater power is granted to an exorcist when he is appointed as a spiritual commander to drive out demons than can be granted to any layman for the sake of secular domination.

Indeed, demons—alas, woe!—rule over all kings and rulers of the earth who do not live religiously and who, in their actions, do not fear God as they ought [Note: omitted in 1], and they confound them in wretched servitude. Such men, not led by divine love as religious priests are when they desire to preside for the honor of God and the benefit of souls, seek to dominate others in order to display intolerable pride and satisfy the desire of their spirit.

Of these blessed Augustine says in the first book of On Christian Doctrine:

> “But when anyone desires to dominate even those who are naturally his equals—that is, human beings—it is altogether intolerable pride.”

Exorcists, as we have said, have authority from God over demons; how much more, then, over those who are subject to demons and are members of demons? If exorcists have precedence over such beings, how much greater is the superiority of priests?

Furthermore, every Christian king, when approaching death, desiring to escape the prison of hell, to advance from darkness into light, and to appear absolved from the bonds of sins at God’s judgment, humbly and pitifully seeks the aid of a priest.

But who among priests—or even among laymen—when placed at the point of death, has implored the help of an earthly king for the salvation of his soul?

Which king or emperor can, by the sacred office entrusted to him, rescue any Christian through holy baptism from the devil’s power, number him among the children of God, and fortify him with holy chrism [Note: “and of the saints,” 1]? And, what is greatest in the Christian religion, which of them can produce the body and blood of the Lord with his own mouth? Or to which of them has power been given to bind and loose in heaven and on earth?

From these facts it is plainly gathered how greatly the dignity of priests surpasses all others.

Or which of them can ordain a cleric in the holy Church? How much less can he depose him for some fault? For in the ecclesiastical orders, deposing is an exercise of greater power than ordaining. Bishops can ordain other bishops, but they cannot in any way depose them without the authority of the apostolic see.

Who, then, even slightly knowledgeable, could doubt that priests are to be preferred to kings [Note: “taken away from kings,” 1]?

And if kings are to be judged by priests for their sins, by whom are they more rightly to be judged than by the Roman pontiff?

In short, good Christians of any kind ought much more appropriately to be understood as kings than wicked rulers. The former vigorously rule themselves while seeking the glory of God; the latter, seeking not what belongs to God but what belongs to themselves, become enemies to themselves and tyrannically oppress others. The former are the true body of Christ the King; the latter are the body of the devil.

The former rule themselves for this purpose: that they may reign eternally with the supreme ruler [Note: omitted in 1]. The power of the latter acts so that they may perish in eternal damnation with the prince of darkness, who is king over all the sons of pride.

Nor is it at all surprising that wicked pontiffs agree with an unjust king whom they love and fear because of the honors they have wrongly obtained through him [Note: “fear him,” 1, 2]; by ordaining people through simony, they sell God even for a paltry price.

For just as the elect are inseparably united to their one head, so the reprobate, especially against the good, stubbornly ally themselves with him who is the head of wickedness.

Against such men we should not so much argue as lament for them with tearful mourning, so that almighty God may rescue them from the snares of Satan in which they are held captive and at last, even after their dangers, lead them to knowledge of the truth.

This is what concerns kings and emperors, who, swollen with excessive pride in their singular glory, rule not for God but for themselves [Note: “who,” Register 55].

But because it is our duty to distribute exhortation to each person according to the rank or dignity in which he appears to flourish, we take care, with God as our author, to provide emperors, kings [Note: rulers, 1], and other princes with the arms of humility, so that they may be able to restrain the swelling of the sea and the waves of pride.

For we know that worldly glory and secular care commonly draw those who preside over others toward pride, so that, always neglecting humility and seeking their own glory, they desire to excel their brothers.

It therefore seems especially useful for emperors and kings that, when their minds rise toward high things and take pleasure in their singular glory, they should find ways to humble themselves and should recognize that what gave them joy is more greatly to be feared [Note: “may rejoice,” Register].

Let them therefore carefully consider how dangerous and how fearsome imperial or royal dignity is: very few are saved within it, and those who, by God’s mercy, attain salvation are not glorified in the holy Church as are the many poor [Note: “are enlightened,” Register].

For from the beginning of the world down to our own times, throughout all authoritative Scripture, we do not find even seven emperors or kings whose life was so distinguished, adorned with religion and the virtue of miracles, as was that of the innumerable multitude of those who despised the world [Note: “innumerable,” Register], although we believe that many of them found the salvation of mercy with almighty God.

To say nothing of the apostles and martyrs, which emperor or king shone with miracles as did blessed Martin, Antony, and Benedict? Which emperor or king raised the dead, cleansed lepers, or gave sight to the blind?

Behold Constantine, the emperor of blessed memory, Theodosius, Honorius, Charles, and Louis—lovers of justice, propagators of the Christian religion, defenders of the churches. The holy Church indeed praises [Note: “also,” 1] and venerates them, but it does not judge that they shone with such glory of miracles [Note: singular, “him,” 1].

Moreover, for how many kings’ or emperors’ names does the holy Church dedicate basilicas or altars, or establish that Masses be celebrated in their honor?

Let kings and other rulers fear lest, to the degree that they rejoice in being preferred to other human beings in this life, they be subjected all the more to eternal fires. Hence it is written:

> “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments.” (Wisdom 6:7)

For they will have to render an account to God for as many people as they have had subject to their rule.

If it is no small labor for a private religious person to guard his one soul, how great a labor awaits rulers concerning many thousands of souls?

Furthermore, if the judgment of the holy Church severely binds a sinner for the killing of one person, what will become of those who deliver many thousands to death for the honor of this world? Although they sometimes say with their lips, “My fault,” they nevertheless rejoice in their hearts over the killing of many, as an extension of what they regard as their honor. They do not wish that they had not done what they did, nor do they grieve that they drove their brothers into hell.

Since they do not repent of them with their whole heart, nor wish to abandon what was acquired or retained through human blood, their repentance remains before God without the worthy fruit of repentance.

It is therefore greatly to be feared and frequently recalled to their memory that, as we have said above, from the beginning of the world only very few holy kings are found throughout the various kingdoms of the earth, out of their innumerable multitude. Yet in one single see of pontiffs succeeding one another in order—that is, the Roman see—nearly one hundred are counted among the saints from the time of the blessed Apostle Peter [Note: “succeeding one another,” added in the Register].

Why is this, except that the kings and rulers of the earth, delighting in empty glory, prefer their own interests to spiritual things, as was mentioned above, while religious pontiffs, despising empty glory, place what belongs to God above carnal matters?

The former readily punish those who sin against themselves, but tolerate with equanimity those who sin against God; the latter quickly forgive those who sin against themselves [Note: “recognize,” 1, 2?], but do not lightly spare those who offend God.

The former, excessively devoted to earthly actions, regard spiritual things as of little value; the latter, diligently meditating on heavenly things, despise what is earthly.

All Christians who desire to reign with Christ should therefore be admonished not to seek to reign through ambition for secular power, but rather to keep before their eyes what the most holy blessed Pope Gregory admonishes in the Pastoral, saying:

> “Amid these things, what should be pursued and what feared except this: that a man rich in virtues should come to kingship under compulsion, while one empty of virtues should not approach it even under compulsion? But if those who fear God come under compulsion to the apostolic see, in which those rightly ordained are made better by the merits of the blessed Apostle Peter, with great fear, with how much fear should one approach the throne of a kingdom, in which even the good and humble, as is recognized in Saul and David, become worse?

“For concerning the apostolic see, as we have already mentioned, the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus [Note: omitted in 1], although we know it by experience, contain the following:

> ‘That one—that is, blessed Peter—sent to those who came after him an enduring endowment of merits together with the inheritance of innocence.’

And shortly afterward:

> ‘Who, after all, would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up? If the good acquired through merit should be lacking in him, what is bestowed by the predecessor of the place is sufficient; for either it raises distinguished men to these heights, or it enlightens those who are raised up.’”

Therefore, those whom the holy Church of her own accord, after deliberate consideration, summons to imperial power or rule should obey humbly, not for transient glory but for the salvation of many. They should always beware what blessed Gregory testifies in the same Pastoral:

> “For a man becomes like the apostate angel when he disdains to be like other human beings. Thus Saul, after the merit of humility, grew through the height of power into a swelling of pride. Through humility he was preferred; through pride he was rejected. The Lord bears witness, saying: ‘Were you not little in your own eyes when I made you head over the tribes of Israel?’” (1 Samuel 15:17)

And a little farther on:

> “In a wondrous manner, when he was little in his own eyes, he was great in the Lord’s sight; but when he appeared great in his own eyes, he was little in the Lord’s sight.”

It must also be carefully retained that the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “I do not seek my own glory.” (John 8:50)

And:

> “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the servant of all.” (Mark 10:44)

Let them always place God’s honor before their own. Let them embrace and preserve justice, maintaining each person’s rightful claim [Note: “vision,” 1]. Let them not walk in the counsel of the impious, but by always yielding to the religious let them cleave to them in heart.

Let them not seek to subject and enslave the holy Church to themselves as a handmaid; rather, by recognizing priests, teachers, and fathers as the eyes of him—that is, the Lord [Note: “those,” Register]—let them strive especially to honor them appropriately [Note: “decently,” 1].

For if we are commanded to honor carnal mothers and fathers, how much more spiritual ones? If the person who curses a carnal father or mother is to be punished with death, what does the one who curses a spiritual father or mother deserve?

Let them not, enticed by carnal affection, seek to place their own son over the flock for which Christ shed his blood, if they can find someone better and more useful than him; otherwise, by loving their son more than God, they will inflict the greatest harm upon the holy Church.

For plainly the person is shown not to love God and neighbor as a Christian ought who neglects, as far as he can, to provide for the great and necessary benefit of the holy mother Church.

When this virtue—that is, charity—is neglected, whatever good a person may do will lack all fruit of salvation.

By acting humbly in these matters and preserving love of God and neighbor as they ought, let them trust in the mercy of him who said:

> “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.” (Matthew 11:29)

If they imitate him humbly, they will pass from a servile and transitory kingdom to the kingdom of true freedom and eternity.”

Amen. [Note: “Given on the Ides of March,” added in the Register, where the remainder is lacking. Other additions occur in British Museum Codex Arundel no. 77, eleventh century, and in the Codex Udalrici.]

We admonish you, brothers and our fellow bishops [Note: bishops, 1], not to be so terrified by the countenances of rulers that you fear to tell them the truth, thereby incurring what Gregory says:

> “When anyone on earth fears a human being in opposition to the truth, he suffers the wrath of that same truth from heaven.”

## 74

When the king’s envoy returned (27 March 1076) and informed the king, who was then at Utrecht, that he had been excommunicated, the king, on the advice of Willehalm, bishop of that city, paid no attention to that excommunication [Note: thus, 1; 1b: “considered it worthless,” 2].

The same bishop, fearing that if the people heard this they would withdraw from the king as from an excommunicated man, delivered a sermon to the people during Mass and mockingly announced that the king had been excommunicated; but, being an eloquent man, he confirmed with whatever words he could that this excommunication was worthless.

How much it was worth, however, he was compelled to acknowledge in his own case—if only he had been permitted, by repenting, to recover from his pride. For in the very place where he was disparaging the Roman pontiff and laboring verbosely to annihilate his power, he was seized by a serious illness and held by it until the pitiable end of his wretched life.

As the illness grew increasingly worse, a certain royal official who was with him asked him to send him back to the king with his message. “This message,” he said, “I send him: he and I, and all who favor his wickedness, are condemned forever.”

When the clerics who were present admonished him not to speak such things, he said: “What else should I say except what I visibly perceive to be true? For behold, demons surround my bed so that as soon as I expire they may carry me away. Therefore, when I have been taken from the body, I ask you and all the faithful not to trouble yourselves by making supplications for me.”

Thus he died in this despair, reconciled to God by no prayers. He lay unburied for a long time, until word was sent to Rome and, after advice had been sought there, he was buried by apostolic command without the customary commendatory rites, lest the people be corrupted by the stench.

Not long after his death, he appeared to the abbot of Cluny [Note: Cluniac, 2], before the abbot knew that he had died, and said: “I am not alive, but truly dead and buried in hell.”

Thus that wise and in every respect honorable man, had he not been infected with the poisons of avarice [Note: thus, 1b; “poison,” 2], met a foolish and wretched end because he refused, while he could, to guard against it.

And why do I say that he alone died wretchedly, when it is evident that almost all of Heinricus’s associates and faithful men suffered equally wretched deaths—and that those who had been more faithful to him were more wretched, because that fidelity was truly treachery?

## 75

To pass over or anticipate certain matters, the patriarch, who had been the apostolic legate and the principal author of Heinricus’s renunciation and of the establishment of a new king, after becoming a renegade by attaching himself to the former king as though to a king, was overtaken by sudden death. Because he had shared communion with excommunicated persons, he was taken from this life without communion and without confession.

Yet because a man of such dignity ought not to go alone to hell, he had, as we heard, fifty of his own men as companions, seized by the same sudden death, lest he should have companions in retribution as well as partners in iniquity [Note: “in iniquity” omitted in 1].

## 76

Udo, archbishop of Trier, full of every kind of piety, was excessively mild and did not resist tyranny. He obeyed Heinricus more than was fitting, supplying the flame of his fury with the oil of his own consent, and granting permission for the churches to be plundered (see Chapter 103).

On the following morning [Note: thus, 1b, 2; omitted in 1], he was found dead, so that it was plainly evident to everyone that he had died such a death because, in the plundering of the churches [Note: “plunderings,” 2], he had not feared to give his consent.

## 77

Eppo, bishop of Cice, while seated firmly on a horse, was crossing a certain stream in the episcopal territory of Saint Kilian [Note: that is, Würzburg], a stream that anyone on foot could have crossed without danger. There was no cause for fear; nevertheless, when the horse fell, he died and perished in this manner (compare the Saxon Annals, year 1078).

Saint Kilian so disposed matters that he who, as a violent usurper, unjustly drank the wine belonging to that city, should also justly drink its water and seek no more wine.

And because he remained irreconcilable to us [Note: thus, 1, 2; “irreconcilable,” 1b], he departed this life unreconciled to God [Note: omitted in 1].

## 78

Godefridus, duke [Note: duke of the Lotharingians, Gozelo or Godefridus, 2], who had been the greatest enemy of Saxony, perished after being pierced by a savage blade in the most private part of his body. He was neither purified by a final confession nor fortified by holy communion.

## 79

When Godebaldus [Note: Godobaldus, 2] lifted the hind foot of his newly shod horse to see whether the shoe had been properly fitted [Note: replaced, 2], he was struck in the forehead by that very foot and was thus taken from this life.

## 80

Burchardus, prefect of Meissen [Note: made bishop of Meissen, 1], was attacked by the townspeople in a certain city of his over which he presided. After vainly wounding with his spurs the horse he was riding, he attempted to flee. The horse, which had previously often been praised for its speed, now, when the greatest possible speed was needed, stood still, as though saying:

> “I am not permitted to rescue him from you now, since, when it was permitted to him, he did not wish to correct himself.”

He therefore died in great peril to his soul, because he had often given his consent to the dangerous counsels of the most savage king.

## 81

Liupoldus [Note: Luidpoldus, 2], brother of Bertholdus, the king’s adviser, who was himself also the king’s adviser, was riding one day beside the king and conversing with him about various matters. The hawk he carried on his left hand began to flutter as though seeking prey.

As Liupoldus bent slightly after the bird, he fell heavily from his horse. The sword with which he was girded slipped from its sheath, its hilt fixed in the ground, and he received it in the middle of his chest.

He who had often been a partner in or author of wicked counsel departed this life without counsel for eternal salvation.

Having dealt with these matters in part and passed over many similar ones, I wish to return to the journey I had begun, which I abandoned not by wandering astray but by deliberately deviating from it.

## 82

(Year 1076, April–May.)

When the pontiff’s embassy and the excommunication or deposition of King Heinricus became known, all those who were holding our captives—since they could find no mercy with the king while he was king, and now, when he was no longer king, owed him neither loyalty nor submission—released them all freely into their homeland, without Heinricus’s knowledge.”

83. [Note: Bucco, or Burchard, in witness 2.] But I shall relate, to God’s praise and the consolation of all sufferers, how wonderfully Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt was delivered by divine mercy from a wretched condemnation. When Heinrich was beside the Danube and had with him Salomon, the husband of his sister, likewise driven from the kingdom of Hungary [Note: thus in witnesses 1 and 2], for in those times the deposition of kings was in force, and when his son-in-law was about to return to his homeland, where, possessing only a few cities on its frontier, he scarcely maintained his hold [Col. 0547C], Heinrich commended Bishop Burchard to him and earnestly begged him never to let the bishop be seen in German territory. The latter promised to do so.

When the bishop perceived this, he addressed the few friends he had there in a few words, as the urgency of the moment required, and begged them all, in God’s name, to consider how he might be rescued. Then a certain Othelricus [Note: Odelricus in witness 2] told him that an abandoned house stood not far from the shore, and advised him to try by some means to enter it.

The bishop was therefore placed in a boat with only one chaplain and was ordered to go ahead of the ex-king until Heinrich himself [Col. 0547D], after dining with his father-in-law, should pursue him swiftly down the running current [Note: “swift” in witness 1b]. The bishop, drifting gently downstream, did not fall asleep or occupy himself with idle conversation; rather, he lifted his heart to God with complete devotion and kept his eyes fixed on the shore until he saw the house that had been pointed out to him (June 24). When he saw it, he asked the sailors to put him ashore, so that, by relieving his belly, he might discharge nature’s obligations.

Suspecting nothing, they were merciful toward the unfortunate man and allowed him to go out with his chaplain. Why should I delay, when I see no delay in him? He was moved some distance from the shore, and while the sailors shouted that he must not go farther away, he approached the house. Knocking gently and calling devoutly upon God, he said, “Open.” [Col. 0548A]

Never had he said, nor would he ever say, “Open” with greater devotion of heart—unless he hoped that one day the door of the heavenly kingdom would be opened to him. Othelricus, with horses and companions prepared, received the bishop; resting by day and hurrying by night, with God’s mercy accompanying him, he brought him to Halberstadt [Note: “halberstatedi” in witness 1]. My dull pen cannot express with what rejoicing he was received by the whole people. Even those who had previously hated him ran joyfully and gladly to meet him [Note: “so that they might come together” in witness 2].

84. Almost all our princes, having returned home together from their various exiles, gave those who had remained at home great cause for rejoicing and opened the mouths of many in praise of God. For they found almost the entire populace assembled, taxes being demanded to be paid from their estates, and the hope of retaining their freedom already abandoned; the people were being ordered to do everything. [Col. 0548B]

But Herimannus, uncle of Duke Magnus, and Thiedricus of Katlenburg [Note: “Katelenburh” in witness 2]—for these had arrived somewhat earlier than the others—cried out, while everyone stood astonished:

“Do not,” they said, “excellent Saxons, do not accept the yoke of servitude; do not make your inheritance tributary; do not despair of God’s mercy! Behold, we, who gave ourselves into captivity for your sake, have returned by God’s clemency, against the will of him who held us, to fight for you and yours as long as we live. Therefore raise your necks free, having shaken off the yoke of servitude, never again to be oppressed by slavery, with God’s help.

“Keep your hands from paying tribute; retain your possessions free, just as you received them free from your parents. But you, abettors of iniquity, who sought the favor of a cruel tyrant through the oppression of the wretched populace, cease from oppression, desist from levying exactions, and from this hour either remain faithfully and under oath with us to fight for freedom, or at this very hour depart from us and from our homeland like treacherous and perjured enemies, never to return.” [Col. 0548C]

By such words the enemies, confounded, ceased their ferocity, while the citizens, encouraged and recovering their former courage, readily grew into unity. Finally united, they expelled Heinrich’s garrisons from all the castles and restored those castles freely to their former owners. Other possessions, which the tyrant had unjustly taken from their rightful owners and, still more unjustly, given to men who had no legal claim to them [Note: “donouerat” in witness 1], they seized and caused to be returned to their rightful possessors. [Col. 0548D]

When all this had been properly accomplished throughout our territories, they fixed a day and place where they would assemble to renew their agreement for the defense of the homeland. Those in whom suspicion of disloyalty remained they compelled either to leave their territories or to join them faithfully.

85. When Heinrich heard all this (June 29), he was greatly disturbed in mind and came to Mainz [Note: “Mogontina” in witness 1]. He ordered some of the remaining captives to be brought to him and negotiated with them the price at which they would ransom themselves and be released. [Col. 0549A]

Meanwhile, a quarrel arose between the people of Mainz and the soldiers of Babenberg. The city was set on fire by the Babenbergers, so that the whole city, or at least most of it, appeared likely to burn. While Heinrich himself and the entire populace hurried to extinguish it [Note: “the whole people hastened to extinguish it” in witness 1], our captives, left without a guard, found a boat and crossed the Rhine. Hurrying day and night, they reached their homeland.

Among them was also Gertrud [Note: “Gertrudis, the most noble woman, stepmother of Duke Magnus, whom Lodewig [captured]” in witness 2], widow of Herimannus, brother of the most noble Duke Otto. Lodewig had captured her nearly two years earlier and brought her to his lord Heinrich, so that he might extort money from her—which he did. [Col. 0549B]

86. Heinrich, the ex-king, seeing that everything opposed his will and understanding that he was accomplishing little by wolfish ferocity, thought of putting on a pellicia (“skin” or “fur garment”), not a corvina (“raven’s [skin]”) [Note: “Thus I correct”; “pellinam” in witness 1; “pellem” in witness 1b], so that by displaying piety and justice he might deceive those whom he could not overcome by violent cruelty.

He wished to send envoys to Saxony who would say that he desired their welfare more than they themselves did; that he would entirely cast away injustice, together with all vices, insofar as he could; and that he would submit to them in everything. But he found no one willing to undertake this embassy. None of his own people believed that he kept in his heart what he had uttered with his mouth, nor did anyone doubt that if someone brought this false message to the Saxons, who were already intensely exasperated, he would truly pay the penalty for false promises.

Two of our men still remained with him: Werinherus of Magdeburg and the bishop of Merseburg, who bore the same name. [Col. 0549C] Although they could have returned home against the king’s will, as the others had done, they did not wish to, because even in that impious man they feared offending God, from whom all authority comes.

He therefore sent them to Saxony with the embassy just described, but told them nothing about their return. They willingly urged the Saxons to do everything they had been ordered to recommend. But the Saxons, aware of so many of Heinrich’s lies, had no doubt that these promises too were infected with the poison of falsehood.

When the bishops wished to carry back their response, they were ordered to choose one of two alternatives: either to remain there from that moment onward or never to return there again. [Col. 0549D]

87. Our princes, therefore, assembled together and strengthened their union by exchanging oaths and hostages. In order to remain most firmly joined to one another, they deliberated on choosing a king to whom all would be subject.

But when they heard that the Swabians regretted having so cruelly broken their former treaty, they decided to send envoys to them to renew the alliance. Thus, meeting together again, they might overcome the bitterness of their hostilities with the great sweetness of mutual affection and, forgiving one another, stand united against the common enemy after choosing one of their number as king.

They also sent a letter to the lord apostolic, humbly asking him to come in person or through a messenger as a comforter to a people almost destroyed. [Col. 0550A]

88. After the Saxons had assembled an army of considerable size (October), they marched toward the Rhine against the settlement called Oppenheim. The patriarch had also come there with the Bishop of Passau, the Roman pontiff’s legate, as had a substantial number of Swabians. All of them were awaiting the arrival of the Saxon army.

When the Saxons approached (October 16), the patriarch and the other leading men went out to meet them. Although they had forgiven one another through mutual embassies, the swords of both sides were still wet with the blood of the recent battle. They feared that a quarrel, easily provoked among armed men by worthless individuals, might corrupt the treaty they had made [Note: “lest the treaty be shamefully corrupted” in witness 2]. They therefore went to meet the Saxons and urged them, now that they were present, to confirm the friendship they had renewed while absent. [Col. 0550B]

On one side stood Duke Otto, violently deprived of his honor; on the other, Duke Welph [Note: “walph” in witness 1; “Walterus” in witness 1b; “welpho” in witness 2], unjustly raised to the same honor. They exchanged the kiss of peace on this condition: once the new king, for whose election they had assembled from both sides, had been chosen, whichever of them lawfully retained that honor, the other would willingly concede it to him without resentment.

Likewise, the soldiers of the second and third ranks on both sides exchanged the kiss of peace, forgiving one another with many tears for whatever injuries they had inflicted.

Then, having all become faithful friends instead of enemies, they pitched their camps so close together that the people of each side could easily hear the conversations of the other. When they had begun discussing the choice of a king, the Saxons wished to choose one of the Swabians, and the Swabians one of the Saxons. [Col. 0550C] Heinrich, however, was held in the city of Mainz on the opposite bank of the Rhine, having abandoned all hope of retaining the kingdom.

Nevertheless, he sent messengers to try to bend them toward mercy, so that they might deign to accept his correction, since he had now been sufficiently chastised. But none of his embassies was accepted by any of our countrymen unless he was first released from the bond of anathema by the apostolic legate.

Thus, to make the narrative proceed swiftly, they promised that they would accept the penitent man’s humility on the condition that he wished to fulfill everything they proposed to him. When he had promised this, they first proposed that he restore the Bishop of Worms, who had long been expelled, to authority over his city.

Next, they required him immediately to have letters written in which he confessed that he had unjustly afflicted the Saxons. After our men had examined them, he was to have them marked with his image in the presence of our people and give them, sealed, to our messengers, who would send them throughout Italy and the German kingdom. He himself was to come to Rome and be freed from the bond of anathema through an appropriate satisfaction. [Col. 0550D]

The bishop was therefore at once led into the city with great honor. Letters sealed with the king’s bull in the presence of our countrymen [Note: “the letters likewise, in the manner stated, were sealed with a bull” in witness 2] were sent by our messengers through the cities of Italy and the German kingdom. [Col. 0551A] Heinrich himself prepared with all haste to cast off the bond of anathema through the Roman pontiff’s indulgence.

Our countrymen, each individually, confirmed by oath that unless Heinrich IV, son of the Emperor Heinrich, had been absolved from the ban by the apostolic authority at the beginning of February [Note: “released” in witness 2], he would never again, by any device of his own, be called or be their king.

The patriarch first took this oath, reduced it to writing, and placed it in his purse. Yet because he kept it better in writing than in action, as has been said shortly before, he later suffered a cruel punishment. The Bishop of Passau, the Roman See’s legate, then took the same oath, followed by all the bishops, dukes, counts, and other great and small men who were present. The bishops did more than the others in this matter, because they also kept the oath in writing. [Col. 0551B]

They then sent a legate and asked the apostolic lord to come to Augsburg at the beginning of February, so that, after the matter had been carefully examined before everyone, he might either absolve Heinrich or, binding him still more firmly, allow them with his consent to seek another man who knew how to reign.

After all this had been accomplished there, the two armies separated with great affection. Each returned to its own land, dancing for joy and singing praises to God [Note: “tripdudians” in witness 1].

89. The apostolic lord, proceeding toward Augsburg as he had been asked, intended to be there at the beginning of February, in the year of the Lord 1077, as the princes had arranged. Our countrymen were hastening there in the opposite direction, so that they might receive the lord pope reverently, as was fitting. [Col. 0551C]

But then the apostolic lord was informed that Heinrich had entered Italy with a large army and that, if he crossed the mountains as he intended, he wished to set up another pope in his place [Note: “for him” in witness 2]. The legate was therefore sent quickly to meet our men, while the apostolic lord, saddened and indeed fearing many things for himself [Note: “but” in witness 1; “sad and fearing many things” in witness 2], turned back in order to protect Italy from sword and fire.

90. Heinrich, wandering through Italy, was uncertain what to do—geographically, but even more in spirit—because whatever he did, he feared losing the kingdom. For he knew with certainty that unless he came as a suppliant to the apostolic lord and was released by him from the ban, he would not recover the kingdom.

But if he came as a suppliant to make satisfaction, he feared that the pontiff might take the kingdom from him because of the enormity of his crimes, or might double the bonds of apostolic authority against him if he proved disobedient. Thus he was divided among many anxieties in opposite directions. [Col. 0551D]

Although he did not doubt that in either course he was lost and would remain lost, he chose the one in which he thought there was some hope. Wearing woolen clothing and going barefoot, he came to the apostolic lord, saying that he loved the heavenly kingdom more than the earthly one and that he would humbly accept whatever penance the pontiff wished to impose upon him.

The apostolic lord, rejoicing at such great humility in so great a man, ordered him not to put on royal attire until he himself permitted it, so that the contrition of his heart might be more acceptable to Almighty God, since he displayed it outwardly through the testimony of his mean clothing. He also ordered him to avoid dining and conversing with those who were excommunicated, lest what God’s grace had cleansed in him through his own conversion should be made, through the contagion of others, more impure than before. [Col. 0552A]

When Heinrich promised to do both things, he was released under this condition and dismissed, being strongly warned not to lie to God. If he failed to fulfill his promises, not only would his former bonds remain, but stricter ones would also be added [Note: “and greatly warned” in witness 2].

When he returned to his followers and began to exclude them from his table, they began to create a great disturbance. They told him that if he now drove away those by whose wisdom and courage he had hitherto obtained the kingdom [Note: “by whose wisdom and help” in witness 1], the apostolic lord would be unable either to restore that kingdom to him or to acquire another for him. [Col. 0552B]

By these and similar words his mind was changed, and, following his customary course and the wicked counsel of wicked men, he returned to his former ways. He placed a golden diadem on his head and retained anathema in his heart, stronger than iron. He joined the company of the excommunicated, and the wretched man was excluded from the communion of the saints.

He thus made clear to everyone that what he had said—that he loved the heavenly kingdom more than the earthly—was not true. If only he had remained obedient for a little while, he would now possess the earthly kingdom in peace and would one day receive the heavenly kingdom to possess without end. But now, having become disobedient, he will not have even what he loves without great labor, and he will not receive the other except through a great transformation of his entire life. [Col. 0552C]

91. Meanwhile the Saxons and Swabians met at Forchheim. Envoys from other regions were also present, declaring that their own people would approve whatever these men might usefully decide concerning the commonwealth [Note: wording lacking in witness 1].

The apostolic lord’s legate was also present, prepared to confirm with the authority of the apostolic dignity whatever our countrymen usefully arranged concerning the kingdom. [Col. 0552D]

From among the many men whom they proposed as worthy by reason of their character, the Saxons and Swabians finally and unanimously elected Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, as their king [Note: “as king” in witness 2].

But when each man was expected to acclaim him as king, some wished to insert certain conditions, so that they would raise him as king over them only on the condition that he specifically promise them redress for their individual injuries.

Duke Otto, for example, did not wish to establish him as his king unless Rudolf promised to restore the honor unjustly taken from him. Many others likewise introduced their individual claims and wanted Rudolf to promise that he would correct them.

The apostolic legate, understanding this, forbade it. He explained that Rudolf would be king not of individuals but of everyone, and declared that it was sufficient for him to promise to be just toward all. He also said that if he were elected in the manner begun, with individual promises made beforehand one by one, the election itself would appear not sincere but polluted by the poison of the Simoniac heresy. [Col. 0553A]

Nevertheless, certain particular matters were excepted. Because abuses had unjustly prevailed in them, Rudolf was required to correct them: specifically, he was not to give bishoprics for money or friendship, but was to permit each church to make its own election, as the canons prescribe.

This too was approved there by common consent and confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff: royal power was not to pass to anyone by inheritance, as had previously been customary. Rather, the king’s son, even if very worthy, was to become king through a spontaneous election rather than by the line of succession [Note: a phrase is lacking in witnesses 1 and 1b]. If the king’s son were unworthy, or if the people did not want him, the people were to have the power to make king whomever they wished. [Col. 0553B]

After all these matters had been legally established, they escorted Rudolf, the elected king, to Mainz [Note: thus in witnesses 1 and 1b] with great honor. As he received the king’s consecration, they attended him reverently and resolutely, as soon became apparent.

He was consecrated by Sigifridus, archbishop of the city of Mainz, with many others present and assisting, in the year of the Lord 1077, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April [March 26].

92. On the very day of his consecration, a lamentable event almost occurred: one day might have become both the beginning and the end of his reign, and the proverb might truly have arisen that he was so watchful a king that he never saw sleep in his kingdom.

For on the day of his anointing, at the entrance of the Mass, the entire church of the faithful was invited under the name of Jerusalem to spiritual rejoicing [Col. 0553C], and nearly every church, even among religious communities, observes on that day a respectable custom of games. When the new king’s dinner had ended, his young men came to the customary game, for two reasons: both because of the royal consecration and, even more, because of the ancient custom [Note: “nevertheless” in witness 1].

When the townsmen saw this game, they were inflamed with savage zeal. Since they favored the ex-king more than the king, they planned to disrupt the game and introduce some seed from which a riot might arise, so that when the king came to suppress it, he might be killed by some means.

They therefore sent some of their young men to mingle with the courtiers’ game and, by one stratagem or another, create an occasion for violence.

One of them, as though secretly, cut off the collar (German Krause) of a certain nobleman from the court, ornamented with little mouse pelts [Note: precious mouse skins, which we read were sometimes dyed red]. He then withdrew as though wishing to conceal the theft, although he preferred to be caught, so that he might receive what he did receive [Col. 0553D].

The man whose respectable clothing had been dishonored pursued the man wearing the piece of his garment, merely struck him in the face, and recovered the fragment of his clothing.

Then the townsmen, who had assembled in reserve for this very purpose, attacked the unarmed courtiers with weapons. They wounded many of them severely and even killed some. [Col. 0554A]

For the courtiers’ weapons had been left in their lodgings while they themselves crowded around the king. The townsmen had seized the weapons and made sure that their owners could not find them.

When the king saw this, he wished to expose himself to danger, either to rescue his men or to fall with them. But those around him understood that the whole disturbance had been begun because of him and therefore did not allow him to descend from the palace [Note: “palace” in witness 1].

The courtiers and the entire army therefore withdrew into the great church of Saint Martin. There they gathered in a mass, strengthened by counsel and weapons, and suddenly burst out with great force. They either killed or captured the townsmen, except those who entrusted themselves to flight and, urged on by fear, escaped swiftly. [Col. 0554B]

On the following day all the leading men of the city came suppliantly before the king. For the evil they had committed, they submitted to the punishments the king wished to impose, and they swore that henceforth and forever they would remain faithful to him.

93. But the king did not trust them. He left the city and went to the Swabians; after staying there briefly, he crossed into Saxony. He celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection in the city of Augsburg [Note: “the feast” in witness 1], then came to Erfurt at Pentecost. From there he was escorted with royal honor by a considerable multitude of Saxons and celebrated with great devotion the principal feast of the chief apostles in the city of Merseburg [Note: “solemnity” in witness 2]. [Col. 0554C]

When leading and lesser men had gathered there from every part of Saxony and had unanimously confirmed the king in the kingdom, as he had been elected by the princes, the king said that it did not seem fitting or useful for the Saxons, as though they possessed complete peace, to sit quietly at home.

He urged them to assemble an army and invade the enemy’s territories voluntarily, so that by doing something bravely they might cast off the mark of idleness with which they had been branded [Note: “name” in witness 1b] and lessen the arrogance of the enemy, who was then swollen with pride at his victory. They gladly did so.

94. Therefore, in the month of August, King Rudolf besieged the city of Würzburg with a large army and ordered siege engines of various kinds to be prepared for its capture.

While these were being prepared, he himself, as a Christian king who feared God, reflected that if the city were captured, once the populace had been admitted to destroy or plunder churches and ecclesiastical property, even the king himself might not be able to recall them. [Col. 0554D]

He therefore sat there slowly and, by seeking various opportunities to prevent a battle from being fought at the city, remained there for nearly a whole month without accomplishing anything. He preferred the glorious disgrace of seeming unable to capture the city to gaining a dangerous glory in which, after the city had been destroyed, no sacred property would be spared [Note: “no sacred thing” in witness 1].

95. Meanwhile Heinrich, the ex-king, assembled an army neither large nor strong—for the greater part of it consisted of merchants—and prepared to go out against our men. Advancing slowly, he waited in vain for the Bavarians and Bohemians whom he hoped would come to his aid. [Col. 0555A]

When King Rudolf heard this, he gladly abandoned the siege and hastened to meet the savage enemy with still greater savagery. The two armies therefore met at the river called the Neckar and pitched their camps on opposite banks, with different intentions regarding battle.

Our men gave the enemy the choice either to withdraw farther from the bank and grant them the opportunity to cross, or to cross themselves after receiving a secure stretch of our bank and fight with our men.

Although the enemy was provoked by many insults to do either one or the other, they wished to do neither. After they had remained there for many days and our men had repeatedly and unsuccessfully offered them an opportunity to come over, they finally saw that they were neither equal to our men [Note: “to us” in witness 1] nor receiving the aid they expected. [Col. 0555B]

Unable to prevail by military strength, they tried by cunning to remove this war from themselves. They made a temporary peace with our men, so that, if possible, they might reach a permanent peace through mutual discussions.

After security had been granted for coming to one another, they asked what need our men had to settle the matter with them by the sword, since they themselves were ready to deal with it by words. If justice commended our cause, they said, they would abandon their lord and join our side, on the condition that, if their own cause proved the better, our countrymen would not disdain to join them under the same terms.

Our men approved this proposal, and our king himself promised that, so that a faithful peace might be established between them, he would willingly step down from the kingdom. A day was fixed on which they would come to settle the matter, with neither king present, and the two armies withdrew from one another. [Col. 0555C]

Then, behold, the enemy saw a large host of Bavarians and Bohemians arrive—the forces they had long been awaiting. When Heinrich learned this, he became exceedingly happy. Forgetting the peace that had been made, he would have attacked our men from the rear, when they were less cautious, if those princes who had been mediators or authors of the peace had not feared to violate their good faith.

Our countrymen therefore returned home in peace and remained for an entire year neither injuring anyone nor being injured by anyone.

96. In the following year, which was 1078 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the Saxon army was assembled again [Note: “assembled” in witness 1]. They sent an embassy and asked the Swabians to come to meet them, so that, with the strength of both peoples united, they might either compel all who opposed them to cross over to their side or wear down those unwilling to join them through the terrible hardships of war. [Col. 0555D]

When Heinrich learned this [Note: “recognized this” in witness 2], he intervened in the middle with a gathered force, and did not allow the two armies to unite.

The Saxon army therefore came to Methelrikestad [Note: “methelrikestadt” in witness 1; “methelrichestad” in witness 2; “macheltikestad” in witnesses 1b and 1c; near Dresden], where it found Heinrich with a considerable force. [Col. 0556A]

Why should I delay in telling the story, when they had made no delay in acting? Battle began bravely—or rather, cruelly (August 7). Fighting took place on both sides, and the battle had different outcomes here and there: these men fled, those men fled; our men were captured but rescued, while the enemy were killed.

The first among our men to flee were men who should never have come to battle: bishops of the same name but, so to speak, not of the same omen [Note: “less” in witness 1]. Both were called Werinherus.

The Magdeburg bishop was intercepted by inhabitants of that region and miserably killed. The Merseburg bishop, stripped of his possessions, returned naked to his homeland. Whoever reads this should understand that I say it not as an insult to him but as praise, for I heard from his own mouth more than once that he would not have refused to endure that nakedness in exchange for any weight of gold or silver [Note: the wording “not thus” is found in witness 1b; the passage is absent from witness 1]. [Col. 0556B]

In the same flight Bernhardus, archdeacon of the Roman See, Sigifridus, archbishop of Mainz, and Adalbertus, bishop of Worms, were captured [Note: “bishop” abbreviated incorrectly as “epos” in witness 1]. Divine mercy rescued the first two not long afterward; the third was brought into the presence of Heinrich, the cruel tyrant, but much later was liberated by divine mercy against the tyrant’s will.

Because all these men knew better how to sing psalms, having been raised in a religious life, than how to deploy armed legions for battle, the mere sight of the fighters turned them to flight. So great a multitude followed them that the king believed the entire army had utterly given itself to flight.

Since the king could not recall them either by promising a certain victory or by threatening perpetual servitude unless they returned, and since he thought himself left alone with a few men, he too began gradually to turn back and approach the borders of Saxony [Note: a phrase is absent from witness 1]. [Col. 0556C]

97. Meanwhile our men who had first joined battle bravely with the enemy, knowing nothing of what had been left behind them, resisted the strong among their opponents with strength. Against the weaker they pressed still more forcefully [Note: “the strong” in witness 1], compelling them to seek refuge in flight.

There one of our men, seeing an opponent before him, greeted him as though he were his comrade, saying, “Saint Peter!” This was the name that all the Saxons carried in their mouths as a battle cry.

But the other, exceedingly proud, began merely to mock the name. With his sword poised over the Saxon’s head, he said, “This is what your Peter sends you as a gift!”

He had not yet finished speaking when he had the sword of another Saxon in his brain. The Saxon said, “And take this gift as well, from your Heinrich, the raging tyrant.” [Col. 0556D]

98. On that same day, Hardwigus [Note: “Herderigus” in witness 1; “Hardewicus” in witness 1b], chief chaplain of the archbishop of Mainz, was surrounded by a multitude of enemies, so that there was no place for him to escape. He was destined, a year later, to enter the city of Magdeburg as archbishop (August 7, 1078). [Col. 0557A]

As the enemy mocked him like a captive, saying that they would rather see him then in the favor of his lord, as he had once been, he answered prudently. He framed his reply so that he spoke no lie and yet, by deceiving them, avoided the immediate danger.

In a few words, as the occasion required, he replied:

“As I see it,” he said, “none of you saw me last night in the chamber of the lord king. But let us hurry to our friends, lest our enemies suddenly catch us off guard!”

They were in fact not far from a small Saxon legion [Note: “thus I correct”; “one” in witnesses 1 and 1b]. When the enemy thought these men were their own and realized that they themselves were almost captured, Hardwigus said: “Go wherever you wish; I shall join my friends!”

99. Willehalmus [Note: “Count Willehelmus of Camburg, whose father was Gero and whose uncle was the margrave Dedo” in witness 2], son of Count Gero, was rashly traveling with a few companions when he was unexpectedly captured by Everhardus [Note: “Everhardus Barbatus, a most noble prince” in witness 2], who bore his nickname from the size of his beard. [Col. 0557B]

Everhardus’s soldiers led Willehalmus to their lord Heinrich, intending to present him as a large part of their triumph. Everhardus himself followed not far behind, keeping watch lest the captive be rescued by someone.

But behold, larger Saxon forces came upon them from the side and quickly killed Everhardus, who offered little resistance. When those who were leading Willehalmus saw this, they forgot their captive and hurried to their lord.

Willehalmus, however, did not forget himself and returned to his own men with all the speed he could muster.

100. Meanwhile Duke Otto and Fridericus, prefect of the palace [Note: thus in witness 2; “palace prefect” in witness 1], of Sommerschenburg [Note: “somerschenburg” in witness 1b], fought fiercely in different parts of the field. They did not stop until they had forced Heinrich and all his men to flee, and they pursued the fugitives until they saw them enclosed by the walls of Würzburg [Note: “he saw” in witness 1]. [Col. 0557C]

But Fridericus, unaware of what Duke Otto had done, returned dancing for joy to the place of battle. For the man who holds the field of slaughter after routing the enemy is considered the victor [Note: “had held” in witness 1].

Duke Otto, returning to the same place not long afterward, saw such a large multitude and thought they were enemies. Since he was very tired, he did not believe it useful to begin fighting them. Nevertheless, he sent a scout to discover the truth for him.

When the scout delayed there, Otto supposed that he had been captured or killed by the enemy, since the scout had found none among the companions whom he recognized. Thus Otto returned to his homeland victorious but not joyful, because he did not know what had happened.

101. Fridericus, meanwhile, gathered to himself those returning from the battle from various directions and spent that night in rejoicing, especially in divine praise. [Col. 0557D]

On the following day, after recovering everything that either allies or enemies had left there, they carried away with them the better things they could transport. They gave the rest to the flames, lest it benefit the enemy.

Then, returning with great joy and song, they devastated Schmalkalden [Note: “Smelekallan—Schmalkalden”] and the other neighboring settlements and villages with plundering and fires, because the inhabitants had stripped or killed our men as they fled the previous day. [Col. 0558A]

They also violently rescued Archbishop Sigifridus of Mainz, whom the enemy still held captive with many others, and brought him back with them to Saxony joyfully, singing hymns to God.

After all our men had gathered from their various regions and each had recounted to the others what brave deeds he had performed and what dangers he had escaped and how, they unanimously rendered many praises to God amid abundant tears [Note: “rendered” in witness 1]—both for the enemies who had been defeated and routed and for the liberation of so many priests.

102. From our side, therefore, apart from the Bishop of Magdeburg, who fell in the flight, no one worthy of the name perished in that battle. [Col. 0558B]

On the enemy’s side, however, the following most noble princes lay dead there: Everhardus Barbatus, who had been the fiercest instigator of this war; Poppo and Thiebaldus; and Heinrich of Lechsgemünd.

Thus this battle took place in the second year of the Lord 1078, on the seventh day before the Ides of August [August 7], on a Tuesday.

103. In the following October, Heinricus came to Regensburg and, after assembling the princes, told them that he had now brought his long labor to an end and had nothing left to do except make those who had shared his labor also partners in its worthy reward. For he said that the Saxons had been so utterly overthrown in the clash of the recent battle that, unless cultivators from foreign peoples came, the Saxon land—[Note: *soxonica* 1.]—would be left transformed into a wilderness, to be inhabited by wild beasts. Therefore he asked them to enter that land with him, since it was rich in every kind of crop, and faithfully promised them that they would find no one to oppose them as they entered.

To make this believable to them, he arranged for false messengers to come forward with carefully composed words. In the hearing of everyone, as they had been instructed, they said to the king in the name of Duke Otto and Count Herimann that they alone of the free men had been left in Saxony by the benefit of flight, since all the others had been killed in the recent battle; that they now bitterly regretted—[Note: *peniteret* 1.]—though too late, that they had ever dared to resist the royal power, trusting in the multitude of their people; that they were humbly awaiting the king’s arrival, so that he might provide cultivators for the land; and that they asked of him neither honor nor liberty, but only their lives, although they were unworthy even of that.

When those words had been delivered, just as the crafty man had dictated them, those who had received them with ears all too ready to believe already possessed the whole of Saxony in empty hope; and, as though they already possessed it, they swelled with pride, deceived by that empty hope. Therefore, with all haste, they hurried to follow wherever hope drew them. Nor did they wish the army to be very large—[Note: *ita* 2; *idigm* (*indignum*, “unworthy”) 1.]—lest each individual receive less of that region because more people would divide it among themselves; for nature dictates that the quantity of the parts becomes smaller in proportion as the number of those parts becomes greater.

When they came to the forest that separates the Thuringians—[Note: *turingos* (“Thuringians”), more than once 1.]—from Francia, they heard—and it was true—that on the other side of the forest the Saxons were stationed with so great a multitude as they had never before been heard to have assembled. For they had nearly sixty thousand armed soldiers, who were determined either to die bravely or to defend their land. At first they did not believe what they heard; but after sending scouts and learning that it was all too true, they hurried much more eagerly to return, driven by fear, than they had hurried to come, drawn by hope.

But Heinricus, the former king, so that he would not have assembled such a large army in vain, marched with the same force against the Suebi. There he spared neither the churches nor the church precincts, and made no distinction between sacred and profane things, in order to satisfy the insatiable greed of those whom he had deceived by promising them Saxony. There, as I have already narrated in advance (chap. 76), Udo, archbishop of Trier, miserably died a sudden death, because, having set aside the fear of God, he freely allowed profane hands to assault sacred things.

104. *(Year 1079.)* Meanwhile the apostolic lord, having forgotten apostolic vigor, for a reason unknown to us, changed greatly from his former judgment. Previously he had excommunicated Heinricus and all his supporters with apostolic severity, had forcefully forbidden him the power to reign, had absolved by apostolic authority all who had sworn allegiance to him from the bonds of their oath, and had confirmed by his consent the election of a new king. Now, however, he sent instructions by letter that, once a council had been held, both kings should be summoned and heard, and that the one whom justice permitted to reign should be securely confirmed in the kingdom after the deposition of the other.

So that what I say may be understood more clearly, I have taken care to place below a copy of these letters. They arrived in February of the year of the Lord 1079. [Note: The editions read *MLXXVIII* (1078). In fact, the two letters, chapters 105 and 106, appear to have been issued in the year 1078 and to have become known to the Saxons then. But Bruno attaches these letters to the later events.]

105. “Gregory, bishop—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—servant of the servants of God (Gregory VII, *Register* IV, 23), to his most beloved sons in Christ, Bernhardus—[Note: B. 1; reading 2, “to Bernhardus, deacon of the Roman Church.”]—deacon, and Bernhardus—[Note: B. 1; *Bernhardo, Massiliensi abbati* (“to Bernhardus, abbot of Marseilles”) 2.]—abbot, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“We do not doubt that it is known to your fraternity that we left the City, trusting in the mercy of God—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—and in the assistance of blessed Peter, for this reason: that we might cross into the regions of the Germans and establish among them, for the honor of God and the benefit of the holy Church, a peace. But because those who were to escort us according to the plan were absent, and because the king’s arrival in Italy prevented us, we remained in Lombardy—[Note: *longobardia* 1.]—among the enemies of the Christian religion, not without great danger; and even now we have been unable, as we desired, to proceed beyond the mountains.

“Therefore we warn you, and in the name of blessed Peter command you, that, supported by the authority of this command of ours—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—and girded in our place by that prince of the apostles, you admonish both kings, namely Heinricus and Rodulfus, to open for us a secure route by which we may pass through those regions and to provide assistance and an escort through persons whom you can trust, so that, with Christ protecting us, our journey may lie open.

“For we desire, with the counsel of the clergy and laity of that kingdom who fear and love God, to examine the case between them, with God’s favor, and to demonstrate which party justice more greatly supports for the governance of the kingdom. For you know that it belongs to the office of our apostolic see to examine the greater affairs of the churches and to determine them as justice dictates. The matter being conducted between them is, however, of such dignity and such danger that, if it were neglected by us for any reason, it would produce a great and lamentable detriment not only for them and for us, but also for the universal Church.

“Therefore, if either of the aforesaid kings should refuse to obey this will and deliberation of ours and to give heed to your admonitions—[Note: *aut vestra aut nostra* (“either your admonitions or ours”) 1.]—and, kindling the torches of his pride and greed against the honor of almighty God, should attempt to hasten the destruction of the entire Roman Empire, resist him by every means and with every resource, even unto death if necessary, in our place—or rather, by the authority of blessed Peter, oppose him by denying him the governance of the entire kingdom. Separate both him and all who consent to him from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the thresholds of the holy Church. Always keep in mind that whoever scorns obedience to the apostolic see incurs the crime of idolatry, and that blessed Gregory, that holy and most humble teacher, decreed that kings fall from their dignities if they rashly dared to act against the commands of the apostolic see.

“But to the other, who humbly obeys our command and offers obedience to the universal mother, as a Christian king ought, provide counsel and assistance in all things after convening a council—[Note: *consilio* (“counsel”) 1.]—of all the clergy and laity whom you can summon. In our place, confirm him in royal dignity by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and command, in the name of almighty God, all bishops, abbots, clerics, and laity living throughout the kingdom to obey him faithfully, as is proper toward a king.

“[Note: “Given at Carpineto, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction”; the *Register of Gregory VII* adds “in the year 1077.”]”

106. “Gregory, bishop (Gregory VII, *Register* IV, 21), servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ, archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and all the faithful of Christ, clergy and laity, both great and small, residing in the kingdom of the Germans, greetings and apostolic blessing. [Note: The words *dilectis in Christo fratribus* are absent from *Register* IV, 24.]

“We wish you to know, dearest brothers, that we have commanded our legates, namely Bernhardus—[Note: B. 1; *Bernardo* in the *Register*.]—a faithful son and deacon of the holy Roman Church, and likewise Bernhardus—[Note: B. 1; *Bernardo* in the *Register*.]—the religious abbot of the monastery of Marseilles—[Note: *abbati ...
