Massiliensis monasterii religioso* is omitted in the *Register*.]—to admonish both kings, namely Heinricus and Rodulfus, either personally or through suitable messengers, to provide me, so that I may examine the matter that has arisen among them through the agency of their sins, with a secure route by which, God willing, I may come to you.

“For our heart is tossed about in great sadness and grief if, through the pride of one man, so many thousands of Christian people are delivered to temporal and eternal death, the Christian religion is brought to shame, and the Roman Empire is led to destruction—[Note: *Romanumque* (“and the Roman [Empire]”) in the *Register*.]—. For each king seeks assistance from us, or rather from the apostolic see over which, although unworthy, we preside. Trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the help of blessed Peter, we are prepared, with your counsel—you who fear God and love the Christian faith—to decide the equity of the case on both sides and to offer assistance to the one whom justice is known to favor for the governance of the kingdom—[Note: *favore* (“by favor”) 1.]—.

“Therefore, if either of them, puffed up with pride, should by any device prevent us from coming to you, and, fearing the judgment of the Holy Spirit because of his injustice, should evade it—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—and, having become disobedient, resist the holy and universal mother Church, despise him as a member of Antichrist and a destroyer of the Christian religion, and preserve the sentence that our legates pronounce against him in our place, knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).

“But to the other, who conducts himself humbly—[Note: *h. se* (“he conducts himself”) in the *Register*.]—and does not despise the judgment—indeed, the decree issued by the Holy Spirit through us—[Note: *vos* (“you”) in 1 and in the *Register*.]—for we firmly believe that wherever two or three are gathered in the name of the Lord, his presence enlightens them—[Note: The *Register* reads *quod ubicumque* (“that wherever”); below, where *quod* is absent in the text, the *Register* supplies it.]—to him, I say, offer service and reverence according to what our aforesaid legates decree, striving and obeying him in every way so that he may honorably retain his royal dignity and come to the aid of the holy Church, which is now almost collapsing.

“For it must not escape your hearts—[Note: *nostro* (“our”) in the *Register*.]—that whoever scorns obedience to the apostolic see incurs the crime of idolatry, and that blessed Gregory, that holy and most humble teacher, decreed that kings fall from their dignities and be deprived of participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ if they dared to despise the decrees of the apostolic see. For if the see of blessed Peter releases and judges heavenly and spiritual matters, how much more earthly and secular ones?

“You know, dearest brothers, that from the time we left the City we have remained in great danger among the enemies of the Christian faith; yet we have been swayed neither by fear nor by love toward either of the aforesaid kings, and have promised neither of them any assistance contrary to justice. For we would rather undergo death, if necessary—[Note: *si hoc oportet* (“if this is necessary”) in the *Register*.]—than, overcome by our own will, consent to the Church of God’s being brought to shame. For we recognize that we have been ordained and established in the apostolic see for this purpose: that in this life we should seek not what is ours but what belongs to Jesus Christ, and that, following the footsteps of the fathers through many labors—[Note: *s. vest.* (“following the footsteps”) in the *Register*.]—we should, by God’s mercy, strive toward future and eternal rest.

“[Note: The *Register* adds: “Given at Carpineto, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction.”]”

107. After receiving these letters, Cardinal Bernhardus—[Note: B. 1.]—carried out what had been entrusted to him. But when our countrymen received the letters themselves, they fell from the great hope they had placed in the apostolic rock, because they had previously believed that heaven would stand or earth would move, rather than that the chair of Peter would lose Peter’s steadfastness. They therefore sent the letters back to him. By them they wished to rouse him, terrified by fear of the slave-woman—that is, of the present life—as though by the voice of a crowing cock, and, strengthened by regard for Christ, to call him back to the courage of his former steadfastness:

108. “To the apostolic lord and venerable Pope Gregory: the faithful of blessed Peter and his own, as much service as those oppressed are able to offer. We have already laid before this holy see many complaints concerning our various calamities. But because we have not yet obtained any justice or consolation, we attribute this not so much to your holiness as to our sins.

“If, therefore, we had undertaken the matter over which so many evils have overtaken us at our own counsel and by our own deliberation, it would have been less grievous if your gravity had been slow to rise to our assistance. But now, since we took up that burden solely at your command, your hand ought likewise to have been placed beneath it to lighten it.

“Your Excellency and your letters, which we possess as testimony, bear witness that you deprived our king of royal dignity not on the basis of our counsel or even for our cause, but because of the injuries inflicted upon the apostolic see; that with a terrible threat you forbade all of us to serve him as king; that you absolved all Christians from the bond of the oath which they had sworn or would swear to him; and that afterward you bound him with the chain of anathema.

“In all these matters we obeyed your fatherhood at great risk to ourselves—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—as is now evident. And because, together with the others, we refused to concur in your deposition of that same man—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—he exercised such cruelty against us that very many of our people, having lost all their property, laid down their lives in this struggle and left their children disinherited and, from wealthy, impoverished. [Note: *nos* (“us”) appears in reading 2.]

“Those who remain are daily anxious for their lives and have lost nearly all the means of sustaining life. But when he could not overcome us by any persecution, he himself was overcome, so that, although unwillingly, he presented himself before you and, to his own disgrace, rendered honor to the one whom he had dishonored. For this labor we received the following reward: the man who had been compelled, at the peril of our souls, to adore the footprints of your feet—[Note: *nostrorum* (“our”) 1.]—was absolved without our counsel and without correction, and regained the freedom to harm us.

“When that absolution from anathema became known to us through your letter, we understood that nothing had been changed in the judgment concerning the kingdom that had proceeded against him; nor do we now understand that it can be changed. For we are wholly unable to grasp how that absolution from the oaths can be annulled. Yet without observance of the oaths the office of royal dignity cannot in any way be administered.

“Therefore, since we had already been without a ruler for more than a year, another of our princes was installed by our election in the place from which that man had defected. And when great hope for restoring the Empire was growing in us from the one king elected for us—not from kings—behold, unexpectedly, your letters arrived, declaring two kings in one kingdom and decreeing a legation to both—[Note: *decerat* (“had decreed”) 1.]—.

“This plurality of the royal name and, in a sense, division of the kingdom was followed also by division among the people and by partisan factions—[Note: *divisio* (“division”) 1.]—, since they saw that in your letters the person of that transgressor was always placed first and that he was required, as a powerful man, to provide you with an escort into these regions so that you might examine the case.

“What the manner of this examination is, if we may speak without offending your favor, is astonishing in our eyes: namely, that the man who has already been deposed by synodal judgment, with no condition interposed, should now finally be summoned to account after another has been confirmed in the same dignity by apostolic authority; that what has been concluded should be begun again; and that a question should be raised concerning an indisputable matter—[Note: *indubitali* (“indisputable”) 1.]—.

“This too troubles our weakness: just as we are encouraged by words and deeds to persevere firmly in what we have begun, so hope is also suggested to the opposing party by words and deeds. For the associates of the aforesaid Heinricus, who are branded with infamy throughout the entire kingdom, who by serving him as king are manifestly disobedient to the synodal commands, and who, together with their head, have been separated from the holy Church by the apostolic legate, come to this see and are kindly received. They return not only unpunished but crowned with glory and honor; and, returning proudly to their former disobedience, they mock our misery.

“To us, however, it is reckoned as foolishness, almost as though we were ridiculous, that we abstain from the company of those whom our own head receives so charitably into communion.

“To the accumulation of our misfortune is added this: besides the offenses that we ourselves commit, the guilt of our adversaries is forged against us, since it is attributed to our negligence that we do not send suitable and frequent legates here. For it is clearer than daylight that those who promised you under oath that they would not prevent this are the ones who prevent it—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—. Now the violent closing of the sacred route and their manifest perjury are passed over in silence, while we are blamed for not sending messengers.

“We know, dearest lord, and from consideration of your piety we hope, that you are acting in all these matters with good intention and with some subtle deliberation. But we, inexperienced men, unable to penetrate that hidden dispensation, report to you what we have plainly seen and heard: that it has arisen, and daily continues to arise, from the strengthening of both parties and the postponement of certain matters in uncertainty—[Note: *ita* 2; *ceterarum* 1? (“of the remaining matters”)—the reading is uncertain.]—.

“These are internal wars, and more than civil wars; innumerable murders; devastations; fires, without distinction between houses and churches; incomparable oppressions of the poor; plunder of ecclesiastical property such as we have never heard or seen before; and the collapse of divine and secular laws without hope of restoration. Finally, in the struggle of the two kings, each of whom received from you hope of obtaining the kingdom—[Note: *accipit* (“receives”) 2.]—there has been such a destruction of royal resources that henceforth the kings of our regions will have to be supported by plunder rather than by royal revenues.

“These troubles would either no longer exist or would be much smaller if your judgment had turned neither to the right nor to the left on the journey you began—[Note: *intinere* (“on the journey”) 1.]—. You undertook a difficult journey out of zeal for the house of the Lord—[Note: *aggressi* (“you undertook”) 2.]—; advancing along it is laborious, but turning back is dishonorable.

“Do not, most holy Father, do not falter on the way. Do not, by further delay and by guarding against both sides, permit such evils to grow and multiply. If it is burdensome for you to speak on behalf of those who have placed their lives in great danger for you, nevertheless come to the aid of the Church, which in your time has been miserably destroyed and reduced to servitude by unheard-of oppression.

“If it does not seem prudent, because of the dangers now pressing, to resist its manifest destroyers openly and face to face, at least take care that what you have already done is not allowed to become void. For if what was defined in the Roman synod and afterward confirmed by the legate of the apostolic see—[Note: *postea* (“afterward”) 1.]—must be concealed in silence and treated as nothing, we have no idea what we should thereafter believe or regard as settled.

“We have spoken this to your holiness not arrogantly, but in the bitterness of our soul, because there is no sorrow like our sorrow. Since through obedience to the shepherd we have been exposed to the jaws of wolves, if we must also beware of the shepherd himself, we are more miserable than all other human beings.

“May almighty God rouse you in such zeal against the enemies of Christ that the hope we have placed in you may not put us to shame.”

109. When they had received no answer to these letters according to their wishes, they sent him the following letters once more. Since he had not been roused by the first crowing of the cock, just as Peter was not roused according to Mark, they ordered that, at the second crowing, as though the cock were calling, the people of the Church should raise their voice, so that, awakened with Peter from the torpor of hesitation to Peter’s steadfastness, he might rise:

110. “To the truly apostolic lord Gregory: the faithful of blessed Peter and his own, offering devoted service according to our strength. Your holiness knows, and it is known everywhere around us, with what difficulty and at what danger to our bearers we send legations to you—[Note: *difficiliter* 1.]—. For the road that at all times was open and passable to every people, tribe, and tongue is now closed and obstructed, especially to those who have labored not a little for the honor of the one whose body that same road leads to.

“It would accord with your honor and our necessity that what we accomplish with such difficulty should yield us some benefit and provide us with some consolation in our tribulation—[Note: *in* (“in”) 1.]—. But whatever question or complaint we direct to the see that has always been the teacher of judgment and justice, we receive no definite answer; everything is suspended in uncertainty for the future.

“For among the many other matters, we recently also reported to your holiness what sentence Lord Bernhardus pronounced against Heinricus, hateful to God—[Note: *B. m. n. deo* (“Bernhardus against the hateful-to-God [man]”) 1.]—and his associates, and what he decreed concerning King Rodulfus at your command. We were confident that, if this came to your knowledge, our whole case would advance and prosper through it.

“But after our long expectation, when the messenger finally returned, he brought us no consolation except that he said you had not believed what we had reported. And why, dearest lord, did it seem incredible to you that our brothers and fellow bishops—namely, the lords of Würzburg, Passau, and other religious men—reported the truth to you and testified that they had seen and heard it?

“Certainly, lord, we do not trust in words of falsehood to be delivered; rather, we believe that the truth will set us free. God, who is truth and who alone considers labor and sorrow, has not abandoned those who hope in him, but has visited us with mercy and compassion.

“For our king Rodulfus, strong in him who grants salvation to kings, has powerfully triumphed over the enemies of the Lord—[Note: A. 1078, 7 August; compare Berthold’s *Annals*.]—. Heinricus, however, as usual, was put to flight with his accomplices—[Note: *simplicibus* (“simple men”) 2.]—except for those who fell by the sword, together with that companion and associate whose wickedness you vainly attempted to overcome with goodness, namely Rupert of Babenberg, who is the author and instigator of all these things.

“Oh, if only you had by now been sufficiently instructed in the disgraceful deceit of him and his associates—[Note: *flagicia* (“disgraceful deeds”) 1.]—! Do not, dearest lord, do not continue to flatter such men, to the mockery of your holy name—[Note: *deest* (“is lacking”) 1.]—, and, after so many frequent refusals and shameful deceptions, ask them again and again for an escort.

“Your coming to us would be as desirable to us as it is necessary. But we know for certain that, of their own will, you will never come into our regions unless they are first certain that you favor their party, not on behalf of justice but according to their will. Therefore do not place your hope in the faith of those by whose treachery you have so often been deceived.

“Behold, you see how evils have multiplied throughout the land—evils whose number has no limit—and how the struggle begun by you and undertaken at your command is now being settled neither by you nor by your decrees, but is being abandoned to the judgment of swords.

“We therefore ask and beseech you in the Lord: once flatteries and delays have been removed, gird yourself with zeal for justice. If not for our sake, then at least for the honor of the holy see of the Church, confirm what the legate of that see has carried out, so that both by your living voice and by letters sent everywhere you may declare without ambiguity what must be held and followed in this division of the Church.

“If this had been done long ago, we are certain that the unjust party would by now have lost so much strength that it could no longer prevail against either you or us. May your holiness no longer add to certain matters decisions that are uncertain and wavering between both sides—[Note: *ugentia* 1.]—, decisions that until now seemed to favor us only insofar as they did not further provoke our enemies.

“But it is certain that you will in no way be able to free the Church entrusted to you from its misery unless you are willing to endure the hostility of its enemies—[Note: *tollerare* (“to endure”) 1.]—.

“We also ask that you not permit the canonical statutes to fail in this matter, so that you permit the bodies of the excommunicated who were killed while persecuting the Church to be buried in the church precincts—[Note: *corp.* 1; variant 2 reads “not permit.”]—; and do not permit their burial in church precincts—[Note: *corp.* 1; variant 2 reads “do not permit.”]—; wherever they have been buried, forbid the celebration of divine offices there. Many of them have been buried in the city of Augsburg—[Note: Compare the *Augsburg Annals* for the year 1078.]—. You can send your letters sufficiently to the communities of that place through traveling pilgrims—[Note: *perigrinos* (“pilgrims”) 1.]—.

“May almighty God direct you in these and all matters so that, just as you preside over the holy Church, you may also be able to benefit it.”

111. They also sent a third letter, which they ordered to be read in the Roman synod if the apostolic lord could be roused, through the intervention of the universal Church, to the rigor and steadfastness of apostolic dignity—[Note: *posset* (“could”) 2.]—:

112. “We complain to blessed Peter, and to his vicar, the apostolic lord Gregory, and to the entire council of the holy Roman Church, concerning the injuries and acts of violence which we have suffered and continually suffer from Lord Heinricus, for no other reason than that we are obedient to the apostolic see. It has come to our attention that at the holy Roman synod recently held [Note: [Col. 0567] omitted in one witness.] [Note: [Col. 0567D] February of this year.] it was asked and debated by some whether that aforementioned man should be excommunicated or not. Therefore, since this matter has become more clearly known to us through serious experience, we have thought it fitting to announce, according to our judgment, for how many reasons he not only should be excommunicated but already truly is excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0567] omitted in one witness.].

“This holy Roman Church is witness for how many crimes and with what unheard-of presumption he was bound at the synod of that same Church by the bond of anathema [Col. 0567B]—not, as we learned from the letters of the apostolic lord himself, until it had been demonstrated that, although he spurned many admonitions of the apostolic see, he always became worse after correction [Note: [Col. 0567] ‘had become’ in two witnesses.]. Let it therefore be considered concerning this man, who was found incorrigible three years ago: has he repented within those three years in such a way as to have been so corrected that there should now be doubt about pronouncing sentence against him? That he has been excommunicated, then [Note: [Col. 0567] One witness reads: ‘Excommunicated, therefore, as we have already said, how long a period of stubbornness…’; another: ‘how long a period…’], and that he has spurned apostolic punishment with how long-lasting a stubbornness, is known everywhere.

“At last, compelled by a necessity that is not unknown, he sought absolution, but could not obtain it until he promised by oath that he would make satisfaction for everything laid against him, insofar as the lord pope should set him a time. Absolved on this condition, he departed. When it pleased the apostolic lord, he sent legates and letters and demanded that Heinricus do what he had promised by oath. As the bearers of these letters approached him, some were captured by his supporters and thrown into custody until they could be ransomed with money, while others were flayed and had their hair torn out. When this had been reported to our people, they again sent an embassy and apostolic letters through another messenger. Heinricus heard the words of the embassy but made no reply, and refused to accept the letters that were presented to him.

“Many reliable witnesses testify to this, especially the legate of the apostolic see, Lord Bernhardus the cardinal, who had been sent to that region for this very matter. When he saw that his embassy was proving fruitless, although it was certain that the aforesaid man had been bound by the bond of the earlier anathema because of the perjury added to his disobedience—a bond from which he had already been conditionally absolved for a time—Bernhardus nevertheless imposed upon him what had been entrusted to him by the apostolic see. Therefore, by apostolic command, once again forbidding him the governance of the kingdom, he separated both him and all who consented to him from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the thresholds of the holy Church [Col. 0568A], and by apostolic authority confirmed another man in royal dignity.

“Disregarding these decrees of the holy Roman Church, as he has disregarded many others, and invading the kingdom that had now been forbidden to him for the second time, he has so demolished and scattered it that it can no longer be called a kingdom, since scarcely any royal possessions remain to it. When the resources of the kingdom did not suffice for him to win supporters, he stretched out his hand against the holy of holies and became a public invader of God’s churches—not in the manner, so it is known, in which some tyrants have already presumed to act. These acts of transgression are incomparable and without precedent. For he did not seize merely some estates or modest resources of the churches; rather, after driving away the bishops, he usurped a great many bishoprics [Col. 0568B], and devoted everything that belonged to the services or support of the bishops to his own uses and those of his followers.

“When the bishops protested over this, the lord pope, satisfying their complaints, excommunicated at the synod held on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December all who had invaded their property, out of his piety. When this became known to the aforesaid man, who is certainly established as the author and participant in that same invasion, he neither ceased the invasion on this account nor excluded from his communion, even for an hour, those who had been excommunicated together with him.

“We have heard that his defenders offer the following excuses concerning these complaints: that he himself had given nothing from the goods of the churches to anyone, nor received anything from his own hand, nor had anyone invaded anything at his command [Note: [Col. 0567] One witness has ‘offers’ instead of ‘offer.’]. We do not charge him with that. Rather, we accuse him—and we are very ready to prove it—of this: that his own men, with his permission, invaded ecclesiastical property, and that he granted this to them when they asked, dividing it among them as he wished; and that they were hired with this reward to lend their strength to his iniquity [Note: [Col. 0567] One witness reads ‘to his iniquity’ instead of ‘to his iniquities.’].

“Whatever remained of the bishops’ resources after that distribution, because it had not been granted to the soldiers, he uses as though it were his own; and they so plainly serve his uses as if they had come to him by hereditary right. If we, who are the accusers, are convicted of falsehood in this charge, we are prepared to suffer the punishment of the accused.

“Let the holy apostolic see judge; let the councils of the holy Fathers be consulted; let the decrees of the Roman pontiffs be examined: are those who do these things, or consent to those who do them, to be regarded as excommunicated and sacrilegious [Note: [Col. 0567] One witness reads ‘to be held’], and is communion to be extended either to them or to their supporters? Although they truly know that what we say about him is true, they knowingly share in his evil works. They regularly come here for this purpose: to provide hiding places for injustice through their defense and to become patrons of such great crimes.

“When they present themselves as envoys in the council of this holy Church, which has always taught abstention from the excommunicated, they are heard as patiently as our own people, with no distinction made between the injured and those who inflict injury. These men recently rose up, in the company of their lord, against those who obey the apostolic commands, in order to compel them to disobedience—namely, in the regions of Swabia, where innumerable sacrileges were committed through the burning of churches and the destruction of altars [Note: [Col. 0569] One witness reads ‘of altars’ in another form.].

“In this matter we neither accuse nor excuse them [Note: [Col. 0569] One witness reads ‘we do not accuse them in this way’; another has ‘nor do we excuse them.’]. But we firmly affirm that the plunder committed in the churches and their courtyards was perpetrated with the consent and permission both of the prince and of nearly all the leading men who were present, on the considered judgment that the sacrilegious army could not otherwise be maintained.

“The holy Roman Church also knows that the aforementioned Heinricus affirmed by oath to the apostolic lord that henceforth neither he nor anyone whom he could compel would prevent anyone traveling from any part of the world to the thresholds of the apostles. How he has kept that sworn promise, the evidence of the facts themselves makes clear, without our saying anything.

“Therefore, in addition to the sentence which both the ancient Fathers and your holiness have promulgated against transgressors of this kind [Note: [Col. 0569] The text is missing here in two witnesses; Eckhart supplied it.], the archbishop of Mainz, following the example of his predecessors and joined by seven bishops who had suffered the same kind of injury, for the defense of the Church entrusted to him [Col. 0569C] handed over to Satan, for the destruction of the flesh, the aforesaid man, who is his parishioner, together with all his accomplices.

“Likewise, the lord bishop of Würzburg, with the apostolic legate, Lord Bernhardus, present and cooperating, anathematized all those who had been guilty by act or counsel in the matter by which that man was prohibited from his see. The author of this prohibition is not unknown; he also resides most frequently in the city of that same see, in which scarcely anyone is not excommunicated.

“Behold, your holiness has heard in how many ways that man and his followers have been condemned and truly deserve condemnation. We therefore ask you, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by him whose place you occupy, that, if you do not think it necessary to add anything to the sentences already pronounced against these same men [Col. 0569D], you nevertheless prohibit with the greatest firmness that they be received into communion either at this holy see or anywhere else until they have made satisfaction to the churches whom they injured. Thus the flock entrusted to you will not be further contaminated by them, and that worst of leavens will not corrupt the whole mass.”

[Col. 0570A]

113. Then the synod itself sent the following letter to the German regions [Note: [Col. 0569] In Gregory’s Register these letters are said to have been issued at Capua on the Kalends of June, in the first indiction (1078).]:

“Gregory [Note: [Col. 0569] Gregory, bishop, servant; Register VI, 1.], servant of the servants of God (Gregory VII, Register VI, 1), to all clergy and laity established in the kingdom of Germany who are not held by the bond of excommunication: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We declared at the synod held at Rome during Lent of this year how great and how constant our concern has been and is that the plague, devastation [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘and devastation’], and desolation should be removed from your kingdom, and that peace [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘and peace’], honor, and its accustomed dignity should be restored to you.

“For by the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decreed and commanded that an assembly of all the bishops and laymen in your kingdom who fear God and desire peace among you should take place, and that, before our legates, it should be determined [Note: [Col. 0569] omitted in two witnesses.] which of the two men—namely Heinricus or Rodulfus, who are contending with each other over the governance of the kingdom—has justice more fully on his side. Then the less just party, defeated by reason and bound by the authority of blessed Peter, might more readily yield and, God being propitious, cease from the destruction of souls and bodies; while the more just party might trust God more fully, and, aided by the authority [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘power’] of blessed Peter and by the agreement of all who love justice, hope confidently for victory and fear neither death [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘and not fear either of the two deaths’].

“But because it has come to us that certain enemies of God and sons of the devil among you are attempting, contrary to the prohibition of the apostolic see, to render that assembly null, and are striving to fulfill their desires not through justice but through pride and the desolation of the whole kingdom, thereby destroying the Christian religion, we admonish you and command you on behalf of blessed Peter [Col. 0570C] to give such men no assistance and to have no communion with them.

“For at the aforesaid synod all these men have already been bound by the bond of excommunication and anathema [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads: ‘All are excommunicated and bound by the bond of anathema.’]. So that they may be unable to obtain any victory, they have been bound by the power of blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads: ‘They are bound by the power of blessed Peter’], in order that, at least when compelled, they may be confounded and recalled from the death of their souls and the desolation of their own homeland [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘of your homeland.’].

“But you, dearest brothers, should have no doubt about me [Note: [Col. 0569] omitted in one witness.], that I might knowingly favor the unjust party in any way. I would rather desire to undergo death for your salvation than seize the glory of the whole world for your destruction. If, however, some people, trusting in falsehood, tell you by letter or word something different, do not in any way listen to them [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness reads ‘to them.’].

“For we fear God and are daily afflicted for love of him [Note: [Col. 0569] omitted in one witness.], and therefore we regard the pride and pleasures of this age as insignificant, because we confidently believe that we shall soon be consoled in his presence. May almighty and merciful God, who in our tribulation has mercy on us and consoles us beyond hope and beyond merit, open your hearts to his law and strengthen you in his commandments [Note: [Col. 0569] Another witness adds ‘and confirm you in the peace of his service’], so that by the authority of blessed Peter he may lead you, absolved from all sins, to the heavenly kingdom, where you will reign.”

114. In reply to this, our people sent the following letter:

“We received some time ago a letter from your holiness stating that you had decreed at the Roman synod that an assembly of all the bishops and laymen who fear God should take place in our regions, in order to examine which of those contending over the governance of the kingdom has justice more strongly on his side.

“Here we are first astonished that your wisdom established something which plainly cannot happen. For we know that it has not escaped your memory—since it has been repeated to you in such persistent complaints—that nearly all the bishops who obey the apostolic see, expelled from their bishoprics [Col. 0571B], flee from the face of their persecutors and hide. How can these men meet and deliberate with their persecutors about the causes for which some of them have been killed, some led into captivity, and the rest stripped of all their possessions?

“Moreover, we consider it astonishing that we are ordered to discuss the cause of that man with those men whom the legate of the holy Roman Church, by your command, separated from the thresholds of the holy Church—both of them.

“But even if none of these things stood in the way, what concern is it of ours [Note: [Col. 0571] Two witnesses read ‘of yours’] that we should reopen the sentence of the Roman synod, long since concluded, and submit it again to examination? Why should we examine whether justice favors him in obtaining the kingdom, when three years ago, with the synod judging, you prohibited him from the governance of the kingdom [Col. 0571C]? Should not that judgment have been preceded by an examination, rather than followed by one only now?

“We know your discernment, because no synod has ever judged a matter that had not first been examined while you presided. What, then, is the need for a second examination? But if that man has not yet been examined, and, as you say, still must be examined, what reason was there for royal dignity to be forbidden to an unexamined man, by apostolic authority and without any qualification?

“If he has not yet been examined but still must be examined, why were we commanded by your authority to obey another king before it had been established that this man could not reign? Your letters in our possession bear witness to this: by your earlier command, the legate of the apostolic see, again forbidding that man the governance of the kingdom, separated him and all who consented to him from the thresholds of the holy Church; but the other man, who had been substituted in his place by our election, he confirmed in royal dignity by apostolic authority, and commanded all who lived in the kingdom of Germany, on behalf of almighty God, to obey him [Col. 0571D].

“Are all these things to be undone and counted as nothing? To say nothing of everything else, if only the release from oaths which you pronounced at the synod is to have effect, it is unquestionably clear that this man cannot be king. For how can he reign when no one henceforth owes him fidelity? How can he govern a people when, in legal proceedings, he cannot compel anyone by the obligation of an oath to render a just judgment?

“But if—God forbid—that apostolic indulgence is not to be regarded as valid, what will become of those bishops and others who, in hope of the aforesaid absolution [Note: [Col. 0571] One witness reads ‘because of the aforesaid absolution’], broke the oaths they had made to the aforesaid Heinricus? Are they not plainly convicted of perjury? For if he can reign justly, those men acted unjustly who threw off from themselves the yoke of the fidelity promised to him.

“Here is another matter: what will become of the oaths afterward sworn to King Rodulfus, to whose authority we have been subjected by your authority [Col. 0572B]? Behold the confusion of affairs! Let all who are sound in judgment consider and see whether anything of this kind has happened, whether such confusion has ever been heard of in the Church.

“See, dearest lord, for the earth has been shaken and troubled. If you wish to heal its wounds, persist firmly in what you have begun, and do not destroy what you have built. For if you wish to turn back on the road you began and, because of difficulty, seek side paths, you not only fail to heal the wounded but wound what is sound.

“If, by concealing the things established by your authority, you abandon us amid the storm which we have endured for your sake, heaven and earth bear witness against us that we have been unjustly ruined [Note: [Col. 0571] Two witnesses read ‘that we have been unjustly lost.’]”

115. Again, after some interval of time, our people sent the following letter to the apostolic lord:

“It is not hidden from your holiness how many persecutions we have suffered by obeying you, how we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter, how we have been made a byword and a reproach. If, then, by enduring such things for you we have deserved no favor from you, and are not worthy that effort should be devoted to our liberation, why at least is justice—which ought not to be denied even to enemies—denied to us?

“If it is just, as we have learned from many of your exhortations that it is just, namely that we should obey that sentence of yours which was issued against Heinricus, why are those who proudly resist that same sentence of yours not compelled according to justice? Why do they feel no censure from apostolic severity for this disobedience? Why is granted to them what has been forbidden both to them and to us? Or how is that permitted to them which has been made unlawful for us?

“Behold, without any opposition from you, they give assistance toward the acquisition of the kingdom to the man to whom you forbade the governance of the kingdom; they serve as a king the man whom you deposed from royal dignity so completely that you absolved everyone from the bond of the oath which they had made or would make to him; by sharing in his communion, they communicate with the man whom the legate of the holy Roman Church, again forbidding him the governance of the kingdom, separated from the thresholds of the holy Church [Col. 0573A]; and they devote all their strength to our oppression.

“For whatever evil we suffer, we suffer it from those whom you both ought and are able to prohibit. Since no authority of yours resists them, without a doubt the reins have been loosened for our destruction. Therefore, why does that famous vigor of yours—which, according to the Apostle, has always been ready to avenge every disobedience—not avenge this one? Why do you overlook it, especially such disobedience as produces unheard-of evils [Note: [Col. 0573] Two witnesses read ‘innumerable evils’], evils of which there is no number?

“When we, miserable sheep, have gone astray in some matter, the vengeance of apostolic severity has immediately and without delay proceeded against us. But now that we have reached the wolves, who with open jaws rage against the Lord’s flock, everything is deferred with patience and long-suffering; everything is endured in the spirit of gentleness.

“We therefore ask you, by the name of the Lord Jesus, whether fear of the sinful man, whose glory is dung and a worm, has made you stray, or whether the softened persuasion of familiar persons has ensnared you: return to your senses; remember honor and the fear of the Lord; and if you do not spare us for our own sake, at least take thought for your innocence in the shedding of so much blood. For if you allow those whom you ought and are able to prohibit to rage against us any further, we fear that before the just Judge you will have no defense for our destruction.”

116. Thus that entire year was consumed, so that almost nothing noteworthy occurred in our regions, except that apostolic legates frequently came to both sides and, promising apostolic favor now to us and now to our enemies, carried away from both parties as much money as they could collect in the Roman manner.

117. In the following year, which was 1080 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of January, Heinricus again assembled an army of considerable size and intended to invade Saxony, reckoning that the Saxons, as lovers of quiet while peace lasted, would not commonly go out during the winter.

“But the Saxons, already trained by many hardships and awakened from the sleep of repose by many disturbances, strove with all their strength to meet him and repel his attack from the invasion of their land [Col. 0573D]. Yet by his customary cunning he had separated the Saxons from one another by making many promises, so that shortly before the day of battle Widekin [Note: [Col. 0573] One witness reads ‘Widekint’; another ‘Widikin’], Wiprecht [Note: [Col. 0573] Another witness reads ‘Wipertus’], and Theodericus, son of Geron [Note: [Col. 0573] Another witness reads ‘son of Count Geron’], together with many others, crossed over from the Saxons to the enemy. Count Ekkibert, joining neither side with his legion, sat inactive not far from the combatants, uncertainly awaiting the outcome of the war so that he might congratulate whichever side won and join it as an ally.

“Thus both armies came together at a place called Flathecheim [Note: [Col. 0573] One witness reads ‘Flathechim’; another ‘Fladecheim.’] [Note: [Col. 0573D] Flarcheim, near Mühlhausen.], and took up positions so that a stream—not wide, but deep—lay between them. Our people, therefore, arranged to defend their bank and awaited the enemy as they came toward them on the slope of the mountain, intending, by descending with the advantage of the terrain, more easily to drive the enemy backward and throw them onto their backs. They ordered Duke Otto to be the first to join battle.

“While our people were thus arranged and watching for the enemy who were expected to come against them, the enemy, intending to fight by cunning as they had always done, surrounded our men unexpectedly. Although they were thought to be coming from the front, suddenly, when our men looked behind them, they appeared to be present at their rear [Col. 0574B].

“Then King Rodulfus sent a swift messenger to Duke Otto, adjuring him by God, and urging him, mindful of his ancient valor, not to shrink from beginning the battle first, as had been arranged. Duke Otto replied that if they had come against him first, as had been expected, he would in no way fear their violence; but now he could not turn the formation of his legion. He asked that those against whom the enemy had first come receive them with all their strength, promising that he would come to their aid as soon as he could.

“Finally, the battle began in a manner very different from what had been arranged. The last became first, and the first last. The fighting was fierce on both sides, but it ended in a brief moment. For the Saxons quickly wheeled around, showed terrifying faces to the enemy who had come against them from behind, and did not rest until they had forced those who had turned in flight to expose their backs to them.

“Thus the victorious Saxons returned, offering, as was fitting, many praises to the giver of all good things. Of our men, Meginfridus, prefect of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0573] So in another witness: ‘Meinfridus’], fell in that battle; of the other side, Folcmarus [Note: [Col. 0573] One witness reads ‘Falmarus’; another ‘Volcmarus’], prefect of Prague [Note: [Col. 0573] Also ‘Prague prefect’ in another witness], and with him a considerable number of Bohemians and others.

“Heinricus, who entrusted himself to flight as soon as the battle began, was led away by Lothowigus through hidden paths in the forest. His army, compelled soon afterward to seek refuge in that same flight, sat down exhausted near a certain fortress called Wartberg [Note: [Col. 0573] One witness reads ‘Wartberh.’] [Note: [Col. 0574D] Wartburg.], and there rested until their bodies were refreshed with food and repose. Our people, who held the fortress, suddenly attacked them [Col. 0574D], and after putting them to flight plundered almost everything they possessed: horses, weapons, golden and silver vessels, pepper and other spices, cloaks, and costly garments. For a patriarch and other princes of those regions were in that company, and they had carried great riches with them.

“This was the third battle, in the year of the Lord 1080, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, a Monday.”

118. [Note: [Col. 0575] The manuscript begins another chapter only with the word ‘Gregory.’] In that same year the apostolic lord sent the following letter from the synod to the regions of Germany [Note: [Col. 0575D] These letters seem to have been written in 1079; compare Berthold’s Annals above, p. 318. Paulus also assigns the earlier letter to 1079 in Bernold, chapter 105.] [Note: [Col. 0575D] The present text, like the following letter, has been collated with an eleventh-century copy in the Trier manuscript no. 102.]:

“Gregory, bishop [Note: [Col. 0575] Omitted in two witnesses], servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops and bishops residing in the German and Saxon kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0575] Another witness reads ‘dwelling there’], and to all princes, both great and small [Note: [Col. 0575] One witness reads ‘the lesser and greater’], who are not excommunicated and are willing to obey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since we know that from the quarrel and dissension which has existed among you for so long the greatest danger to the holy Church and the greatest harm among you everywhere are arising daily, it has therefore seemed good to us—and it has also seemed good to our brothers gathered in council—to burn with the greatest desire and labor with all our strength so that suitable messengers, distinguished both by religious devotion and by learning, might be sent from the side of the apostolic see to your regions. They would gather in your lands religious bishops and laymen who love peace and justice, and who are suitable for this work [Note: [Col. 0575] One witness reads ‘our lands’].

“Then, with the grace of the Lord going before them, on the day and at the place established by those men, they and those whom we must still join to them should either establish peace, or, after the truth has been ascertained, exercise canonical censure against those who are the cause of such great dissension [Note: [Col. 0575] Another witness reads ‘division.’].

“Yet because we know that some, fashioned by diabolical prompting [Note: [Col. 0575] One witness reads ‘consumed by diabolical instinct’], kindled by the torches of their iniquity and driven by desire, wish rather to create and witness discord than peace, we have decreed at this synod, according to the same form as at the previous one [Col. 0575C], that no person of any power or dignity [Note: [Col. 0575] ‘Or’ is omitted in one witness], whether great or small, prince or subject, should presume by any presumption to resist our legates [Note: [Col. 0575] One witness reads ‘dare to resist them’] or, after they have reached you, oppose the establishment of peace. Nor afterward should one person dare to rise up against another contrary to their prohibition [Note: [Col. 0575] One witness reads ‘rise up again’]; rather, until the day appointed by them, all should observe firm peace without any pretext or fraud [Col. 0576A].

“Whoever attempts to violate these statutes of ours by any presumption, we bind with the bond of anathema; and by apostolic authority we bind him not only in spirit but also [Note: [Col. 0575] Omitted in another witness] in body and in every prosperity of this life, and we take victory from him in arms, so that at least in this way they may be confounded and crushed by a double affliction.”

119. Likewise, the lord pope wrote to King Rodulfus:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to King Rodulfus and to all who defend the Christian religion together with him: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“That the kingdom of the Germans, hitherto the noblest among all the kingdoms of the world, is now being devastated, confounded, and destroyed by fires, slaughter, and plunder [Note: [Col. 0575] Another witness reads ‘devastated and confounded’], and how great a sorrow from this has settled in my heart, how constant a groaning afflicts my inward being, is known by him alone who searches and tests the hearts of all people.

“For embassies from Heinricus are now repeatedly brought to me, sometimes through his own messengers, sometimes through relatives, princes of other lands, and kinsmen, at one time promising every obedience, at another seeking to influence me by various devices, and striving with all their might to bring this about: that they may incline me to their wishes and to their side [Note: [Col. 0575] Another witness reads ‘to his party.’].

“But because the Roman gravity and the apostolic gentleness on both sides compel me to walk along the middle path of justice [Note: [Col. 0575] The reading is uncertain in one witness], I must devote myself in every way I can to discerning, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, true justice from false, perfect obedience from feigned obedience, and to carrying the matter through to the end in an orderly manner.

“These and other matters, if my legates reach you safely by God’s favor, they will testify to and explain better in person than this letter can [Col. 0576C].”

[Note: [Col. 0575D] The Trier manuscript adds: “I have indeed heard from my legate B. that the metropolitan church of Magdeburg has long been widowed and has continued to be troubled by the perverse contention of certain persons, so that it cannot be espoused. Resist, by the command of almighty God, of blessed Peter, and of me, all such attempts to prevail, and arrange, with the common agreement and election of all the religious—archbishops, bishops, clergy, and laity—to introduce through the door a worthy steward of the house of God.

“If you are willing to follow my counsel—for I hear that there are among you certain men of good reputation, namely A., dean of Goslar; G., son of Duke Bertaldus; and H., son of Count Sigifridus—then, with my command and consent, choose one of them and appoint him archbishop of the aforesaid church. But if no one worthy can be found among these three, turn to God in contrition of heart, praying and fasting, and ask that, by revealing his grace, he may show a person suited to this matter.

“Know this beyond doubt: just as I shall bind with the bond of excommunication anyone who enters irregularly through ambition for secular power, so I shall absolve from sins and bless with apostolic blessing anyone who has been canonically enthroned.”]

120. Likewise, the apostolic lord wrote to King Rodulfus:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to King Rodulfus and to all who dwell with him in the kingdom of the Saxons, bishops as well as dukes and counts, and also great and small: absolution from sins [Col. 0577A] and apostolic blessing.

“Since Truth itself says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to all who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, and the Apostle proclaims that no one can be crowned unless he has competed lawfully, do not, my sons, grow faint in this military struggle which has already harassed you for a long time. Do not, because of the lies of any deceitful person [Note: [Col. 0577] Possibly ‘of that deceitful person’], doubt our faithful assistance. Rather, labor ever more earnestly to defend ecclesiastical truth and the freedom of your nobility [Note: [Col. 0577] Another witness reads ‘your will’], and strive to bring the work to an end more quickly. Ascend against the enemy and endeavor to set yourselves and your bodies like a wall before the house of Israel.

“What was established in the two assemblies of our synod concerning King Rodulfus and Heinricus, and what was there defined concerning the peace and harmony of the kingdom, even with oaths [Col. 0577B], you can learn most clearly from our letters and from your legates, unless they have perhaps been captured [Note: [Col. 0577] Another witness reads ‘unless they are captured.’]. And if anything still remains [Note: [Col. 0577] Another witness reads ‘remained’], you may hear it as though it were ready at hand from the bishops of Metz and Passau and the abbot of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0577] An editorial reading gives ‘the abbot of Augsburg.’] [Note: [Col. 0577D] See Berthold’s Annals, 1079], who are staying with us while awaiting the conclusion of the matter and, when they themselves reach you, will make it known.

“Finally, we do not wish you to be unaware that, with all the persistence that is required—both through the continual assiduity of our prayers and through the seriousness of our office—we do not doubt that we are watching over your needs by giving counsel and giving counsel by watching over them.”

### 121

In that same year, namely in October, Henry, indefatigable in the labors of warfare [Note: [Col. 0577] thus in 2; *malicie* in 1], again gathered an army to invade the kingdom of Saxony. The Saxons, however, met him with a vast multitude at a place called Cancul [Note: [Col. 0577D] Perhaps Keula near Mühlhausen], and there, having set up their camp, they remained, intending with God’s help to defend their borders from hostile invasion.

When, after sending out scouts, he learned of our strength and did not dare engage it with his own forces, he turned to the art of malice; by crafty deceit he divided our army into two parts, so that what he had not dared to attack intact, distrusting his own strength, he would not fear to attack in separate portions if necessity compelled him. For, while avoiding battle and advancing with his entire army toward Erfurt [Note: [Col. 0577] *erpesfort* in 2], he sent the swiftest horsemen back toward Goslar, so that, after burning certain villages, they might hasten back to him.

But the Saxons, informed by their scouts of his route toward Erfurt [Note: [Col. 0577] *erpesfort* in 2], although they could easily have followed him or even overtaken him, saw the smoke behind them and all hurried there, so as to prevent him from reaching Goslar and those parts of Saxony. He, however, continued his journey toward Erfurt [Note: [Col. 0577] *erpesfort* in 2]; after the town had already been set on fire, he plundered it. When our army realized that it had been deceived, it left behind a great multitude of infantry together with cavalry and pursued him [Col. 0578A].

When our men were already approaching him and saw that he intended to burn the bishopric of Nienburg [Note: [Col. 0577] *nienburh* in 2] [Note: [Col. 0578D] Naumburg], they overtook him by a rapid march through the mountains and stoutly defended the city from the flames. When he learned this, he burned and ravaged everything in his path and reached the river called the Elster. Seeing its great depth, he did not wish to cross it and there pitched camp.

Here I came to know various opinions held by different people, but I was not permitted to learn which of them was closest to the truth. Some said that, since he had twice withdrawn from battle defeated, he no longer wished to test the fortune of war, but, after deceiving our men by his stratagem, intended to burn a large part of the region and then, without a battle, to turn back toward his own territory as though with the glory of victory; but, ignorant of the depth of this river, he had run into it and, compelled because it could not easily be crossed, had committed himself to battle.

Others thought that he had deliberately chosen this place for the battle, where those of his men in whom he did not fully trust would either have to fight bravely or, as the reward of a shameful flight, face the danger of the river. Others believed that he had sought those regions because he hoped for the assistance of the Meisseners or Bohemians, for whom he had sent envoys. If they had joined him as he expected, he could have crossed powerfully from there through Merseburg, Magdeburg, and all Saxony, laying waste to everything and subjecting it forever to his rule.

### 122

Accordingly, Henry established his camp on the bank of the Elster and, at first light the next morning, drew up his battle lines, since he himself wished there to be no delay in the fighting (15 October 1080). Then suddenly our men arrived, exhausted by great haste and the roughness of the journey, many having been left behind on the road from weariness [Note: [Col. 0577] omitted in 1]. When they heard that the enemy was present, they immediately prepared to defend their homeland [Note: [Col. 0577] omitted in 1; “their own country” in 2].

Since it was observed that there were very few infantry, with many unable to keep up, all the cavalrymen who did not have sufficiently strong horses were ordered to become infantry. Then, having been arranged in formation, they advanced little by little to meet the enemy. The bishops urged all the clergy who were present to sing Psalm 82 with great devotion.

Both armies came together at the marsh called Grona [Note: [Col. 0577] thus in 2; *grono* in 1]. Since the marsh had no ford, both armies halted there uncertainly, reproaching one another and urging the other to cross first. Each held its own bank without moving. At last our men learned that the head of the marsh was not far away and moved toward it [Col. 0579A]. When their opponents saw this, they proceeded along an equal route toward the same end of the marsh.

When they had safely come together there, they joined battle, and on both sides a pitiable deed was done. As soon as Henry saw them mingling with one another, however, he fled, as was his custom. His army pressed upon our men with such courage that, when some of ours gave ground, a deceptive report reached their camp announcing with lying words that the Saxons had been defeated [Note: [Col. 0579] *nuntiaret* in D; *p. q. II. a. c. s. c. T. D. l. g.*; accepted from 2; lacking in 1 and 1b].

While the prelates who were assisting Henry joyfully sang “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) with their clergy [Note: [Col. 0579] *cantaret* in 1; *canerent* in 2], Rappodo [Note: [Col. 0579] “Look, Rappodo” in 2], one of the chief princes [Note: [Col. 0579] “a prince of Henry’s party was being carried” in 2], was carried past dead. Those who bore him called from a distance to those in the camp: “Flee! Flee!”

Otto the duke then took a troop of infantry and repaid in equal measure those who had put our men to flight. He did not stop pursuing them as they showed him their backs until he saw them, hurrying through the middle of the camp, cross the river with considerable danger. For almost as many of the enemy perished in the river as in the battle.

Then the infantry, hoping that they had won a complete victory, wanted to attack the camp and seize its spoils. But Duke Otto, wise in warfare [Note: [Col. 0579] *prodens* in 1], fearing that some enemies might still remain behind them, warned them for the moment to keep their hands from the plunder, until, certain that no enemy was hiding behind them, they could safely ransack the hostile camp.

Returning, therefore, with the infantry, he found at the battlefield Henry of Laach with most of the army, already celebrating as though in triumph for victory and singing *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—with joyful shouts. When Duke Otto saw this multitude [Col. 0579C], he first wished to avoid it, because he saw that he did not have a force large enough to make it safe, in his judgment, to fight so great a host. But then, reflecting that it is not difficult for God to conquer many through a few [Note: [Col. 0579] “many among many and in few” in 2], he boldly attacked them; and, God granting them a spirit of fear, he quickly put them to flight.

When all had either been drowned in the river or driven in flight beyond it, Duke Otto said: “Now search the camp without fear; now, secure, take whatever you find; and whatever belonged to the enemy today, call your own, since your valor has granted it to you!”

Before these words had even ended, they invaded the hostile camp and hastily seized everything that was found. There they found many precious tents; many chests belonging to bishops, filled with sacred garments and vessels; many golden and silver vessels suitable for daily use; many plates of silver and gold; and a very large amount of coined money [Note: [Col. 0579] *multaque* in 1 and 1b]. There were also very many excellent horses, arms of every kind, changes of clothing, and other garments beyond estimation. In short, everything that the bishops of Cologne, Trier, and nearly fourteen others had brought with them; everything that Duke Frederick, Count Henry, and the other very wealthy men had carried with them; and everything they had seized at Erfurt—all of it our men plundered together and returned triumphantly to their camp.

### 123

Those who had escaped the sword endured such calamities in the river, the forests, and the marshes that no one can believe it unless he happened to see all those places with his own eyes. For the river has banks of such a kind on either side that on one side no one can enter it except by falling, while on the other no one can get out unless he crawls up by clinging to bushes or grasses.

Many of the fugitives, plunging headlong into the river on one side and leaping from their horses’ backs onto the bank on the other, cut at the bank with their swords in order to drag their horses out of the river behind them. At last, exhausted by cutting, they abandoned their horses and threw away their weapons, then anxiously took to flight.

Therefore, whatever Unstrut [Note: [Col. 0579] *unstrad* in 1], where we were defeated, inflicted upon us, the Elster [Note: [Col. 0579] *elstrad* in 1] avenged for us twofold. There we lost only our own possessions while fleeing; here, as the enemy fled and was killed, we took from them both the enemy property and our own, which the fleeing enemy had taken from us by plunder.

During the flight, very many strong men were killed by the axes and clubs of peasants; many noble and illustrious men were captured by people of low status; many, tortured by the most cruel hunger, did not hesitate to give horses or swords for a morsel of bread, nor did they spare any possession of theirs if they found bread for sale.

If any captives were brought to one of our honorable men, they were healed if wounded and sent back freely to their homeland, decently supplied with clothing and weapons. They were then told that Henry had sent after the Bohemians and that, when they arrived, he had intended to return to Saxony with the army that still remained. But they replied that, if possible, they would rather travel around the entire world than ever cross Saxon territory again [Note: [Col. 0579] *intrare* in 2].

### 124

Meanwhile the Saxons returned to their camp and found a great part of their joy diminished, because their king Rudolf, having received two wounds—one fatal, the other disfiguring—was grieving more for the people than for his own fate. But when he learned that his people had won the victory, he said: “Now, whether living or dying, I shall gladly endure whatever the Lord wishes!” Although his right hand had been amputated and he had a severe wound in his abdomen, extending down to the groin, he nevertheless confidently promised those whom he saw grieving over his death that he would not die at once [Col. 0580D], in order to console them.

Putting his own condition second, he showed his wounded men what medicine ought to be applied. Deeply moved by this courage and piety, our princes unanimously promised him that, if almighty God wished to preserve his life, Saxony would choose no other ruler while he lived, even if he were deprived of both hands.

Greatly rejoicing in this pledge, he was released by a blessed death [Note: [Col. 0581] “and from there was carried to Merseburg and honorably buried, as is evident today” in 1b]. This battle was fought in the fourth year from the Incarnation of the Lord, 1080, on the Ides of October, the fifth day of the week—that is, Thursday.

### 125

Then, in December, while our princes were gathered to discuss the condition of their kingdom, a messenger arrived and reported that Henry, having returned to his own men from the battle, had boasted that, after the king of the Saxons had been killed, he had subjected all Saxony to his authority and was now advancing with an assembled army so that he might celebrate Christmas at Goslar.

But our men, having gathered a large army over three days, went to meet him, intending by their valor to defend their homeland. When he learned this [Note: [Col. 0581] *agn.* in 2], he fell from his great hope, since he had thought that the Saxons, lacking a ruler, could easily be defeated.

Accordingly, he dismissed his army and changed his plan. He sent envoys to the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0581] “asking that” in 2], saying that, since they did not wish to be without a king, they should make his son their king, and promising to swear to them that he would never enter Saxon territory.

To this embassy Duke Otto replied, as he was accustomed to veil serious matters playfully with some rhetorical device [Note: [Col. 0581] *serie* in 1]: “Often,” he said, “I have seen a bad calf born from a bad ox [Note: [Col. 0581] *gnatum* in 1b]; therefore I desire neither son nor father.”

### 126

After the following Christmas had passed, with the year 1081 from the Incarnation of the Lord having begun [Note: [Col. 0581] “is beginning” in 1], the former king Henry was preparing to enter Italy in order to bring some end to the long labor of his affairs: either to win over Lord Pope Gregory by a feigned humiliation, or to remove the bonds of excommunication with which he was bound by compelling him through tyrannical force; or—which he desired more—to expel Gregory by force from the papal see and install in that see Wibert of Ravenna, who had already been justly excommunicated for three years, so that, with all support for his will coming from the Apostolic See, he might freely do whatever pleased his tyranny.

But his advisers did not think it safe to leave their borders exposed to invasion by the Saxons, who had been fiercely provoked by the recent battle. They had no doubt that the Saxons would attack if Henry went to Italy and left his homeland without military protection.

They therefore sent messengers to our princes, requesting a private conference and fixing a time and place at which chosen princes from both sides might meet to discuss the common good [Col. 0581D]. They met beyond the river called the Weser, in a forest called Capuana because it was understood to belong to the town called Capua [Note: [Col. 0581D] Kauffungen].

The bishops who met on that side (in February 1081) were those of Cologne, Trier, Bamberg, Speyer, and Utrecht; on our side were the archbishops of Mainz, Magdeburg, and Salzburg, and the bishops of Paderborn and Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0581] *hillinisheimensis* in 1; *hilhesheim* in 1b].

When those from the other side wished to hold a private discussion heard only by the princes, our men refused to enter into any conversation unless it was one that all who had assembled, great and small alike, were permitted to hear. For a long time both sides sat in silence: our men, who had been summoned to meet them, were waiting to learn what they wanted; while the others, wishing to appear not to have summoned our men but to have come at our men’s request, listened to discover what our men would ask.

At last our men broke the silence. To make the matter a public statement, they requested Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg. He rose. A man prudent and honorable in every respect, and one who added no small honor to the dignity he held, he expressed the thought of a wise and pious heart with modest countenance and measured voice:

### 127

“Venerable bishops and the other princes of Saxony whom you see present have deemed me worthy to undertake this task, so that through the service of my speech I should lay before you the sentiments of all our people.

Therefore, holy priests and distinguished prelates, I ask you all to listen to me patiently and to bring to the common cause, which I have been ordered to conduct, a calm mind with which you may recognize and examine the truth [Note: [Col. 0581] *a. et*; omitted in 1 and 1b]. For, if you are willing, it is no less in your interest than in ours to understand what I am about to say.

We confidently rely upon your own testimony [Note: [Col. 0581] *in nitimur* in 1; *inde nitimur* in 1b], because, although you have withdrawn from our fellowship, we trust that you have not withdrawn from the love of truth. By your testimony, I say, we wish to establish by how many injuries and insults we have been afflicted while, with our whole heart and will, as was proper, we were subject to the king’s service.

You yourselves know how often, individually or collectively, we sought your assistance, asking that, in return for our willing service, he might grant us through your intercession at least this favor: that he relieve us of the burden of the many calamities that weighed us down unbearably. You know very well that we often requested this, and you likewise know very well what we achieved by requesting it.

We do not therefore accuse you, because we know that you often labored on our behalf, although this benefited us little [Col. 0582D] [Note: [Col. 0581] *agn.* in 2]. But what final reward he gave our devotion—why need I speak of it, when it is clear to everyone’s eyes that at last he repaid us with the greatest evil in his power?

For he not only imprisoned priests who had been convicted of no crime and had not even been regularly accused, as though they were robbers, but also drove from their sees those whom he could not capture, stripped of all their possessions [Col. 0583A]. He handed over the goods of the churches—goods with which the bishops ought either to live themselves or to support God’s poor—to be dissipated by the accomplices of his crimes [Note: [Col. 0583] *dissipanda* in 1].

He has repeatedly ravaged our land with fire and sword. He has killed our kinsmen and soldiers, innocent within our own borders, although he had no cause for war except that he wished to have as slaves the sons of free men.

We often entreated him, and often entreated each and all of you, to lay aside the sword and bring his case before judgment together with us. We willingly promised that we would follow your judgment in every respect. What have we achieved by all this? We call you yourselves as witnesses.

Therefore we who are here now, together with all whom the land of Saxony holds, humbly beseech you, O most holy priests of Christ, and you, O most noble princes and bravest soldiers: remembering almighty God and your own office, consider that you have been called shepherds of souls, not destroyers, and that you received the sword for the defense, not the destruction, of the innocent. Do not wish to persecute us—your brothers in Christ and your kinsmen according to the flesh—with sword and flame any longer.

Whatever hardships we have suffered from you until now, we shall forgive you, assign them to our sins, and call them a correction of divine mercy, provided that henceforth we may be secure from injuries inflicted by you.

Lay down sword and fire, and, as befits Christian men dealing with Christians, conduct the case by arguments, not by slaughter. Grant now, at least, what we requested before bloodshed, even if you are satisfied with our blood.

Your lord Henry has indeed cruelly inflicted many hardships upon us and wearied us beyond measure with many calamities. Yet behold, we are ready to accept him as our king, as he once was. Behold, we are ready to swear allegiance and submission to him and faithfully and willingly to keep the oath once sworn.

Only establish this by true assertions, so that we may do it without violating our proper order, and so that the laymen may do it without detriment to the sacred faith. Nor will we leave this field until we have fulfilled everything I have said.

But if you are willing to hear our position, we shall show by true and evident arguments, firmly supported by the testimony of Scripture, that we cannot have Lord Henry as king with the salvation of our souls. Therefore, either show us convincingly that he can rightly reign, and accept us as faithful companions under his rule; or, allowing us to prove truthfully that he cannot rightly reign [Note: [Col. 0583] “that he cannot be king, permit us to prove it” in 1b], grant your friendly agreement to us—or rather, to the truth—and cease to persecute us as enemies against reason [Note: [Col. 0583] “and cease to persecute us against reason” in 1b].

If you object that you are bound by the oath you swore to him, we shall likewise establish that no oath can rightly compel you to persecute us [Col. 0584A].

This, then, is the sum of our petition: either convincingly show us that Lord Henry can rightly reign, or permit us truthfully to show you that he cannot. Once either matter has been demonstrated, cease to persecute us with fire and sword [Note: [Col. 0583] thus in 1b and 2; *desinatis* in 1].”

### 128

Then they replied that they had not assembled to discuss the case, nor were they so wise as to presume to undertake such a great matter without preparation [Note: [Col. 0583] *suscipere* in 2], especially since it seemed to concern not them alone but the king and all who were subject to his kingdom.

They requested that peace be granted by both sides from the beginning of the February that was then underway until the middle of June. During that period, after a meeting had been held, the same case that our men now wished to bring should be discussed by the common counsel of the whole kingdom, from both sides [Col. 0584B].

Our men, however, perceived their deceit: they wanted so long a period of peace in order that those remaining at home would be safe while those traveling to Italy insulted the Apostolic dignity. They replied that they wished neither to deceive nor to be deceived, but to give and seek a firm and complete peace up to the end of the period mentioned above.

When the others promised that they would grant peace to all the Germans who supported our side, Duke Otto said:

“Do you think us so foolish that we do not understand the plan of your cunning? You ask security of peace from us for your own side until you can dishonor the Apostolic dignity; and you promise us your peace until, if God permits, you mistreat according to your pleasure him who is our head.

Oh, what a fine peace is given to the body when, after the head has been cruelly severed, the body is mocked even more cruelly! Therefore grant peace to us and all our people, and accept peace for yourselves and all your people—either complete peace or none at all.

If you do not wish to grant full peace to us and all our friends, great and small, continue the journey you have begun. But understand this beforehand: you will soon have unwelcome guests in your own territories, and when you return from Italy you will not find your possessions protected as you would wish.

For we do not wish to conceal from you that, as soon as we can, we intend to have one ruler, who, with God’s help, will both defend us vigorously from injuries and repay those who have injured us with the due measure of justice.”

The common soldiers of the opposing side then cried out that our men were offering a just settlement, while their own princes neither accepted nor offered justice. They said that henceforth they would be less ready to fight than they had been previously, because they recognized that the cause of justice was with the Saxons, and that this conference had benefited us more than victory in three battles. For they themselves had heard, something they could never have believed, that our men were at once humbly requesting and offering justice [Col. 0585A].

Thus they departed from one another, peace having been granted on both sides for only seven days.

### 129

When March began, Henry entered Italy, intending to sow discord there as he had earlier done in the German land, so that he would leave no part of his kingdom at peace and would not corrupt the tranquility of peace with the poisons of civil war [Note: [Col. 0585] *ubi* in 1b].

### 130

The princes of Saxony sent envoys to all the peoples of the German tongue, enemies no less than friends [Note: [Col. 0585] *a. q. I.*], asking them to choose anyone else as ruler except Henry and his son. They promised to serve faithfully whoever he might be, so that all the members of the kingdom, as they had once done, might come together under a single king.

In June, having gathered an army, they advanced into eastern Francia. Ravaging it with plunder and fire, they avenged the many injuries they had suffered. Making a broad path with flames, they came near Bamberg. There they encountered the Swabians, their old friends [Note: [Col. 0585] omitted in 1], and by common counsel discussed the common business of establishing a king. After many deliberations, they all unanimously agreed to elect Herman king.

### 131

But when the Saxons returned home joyful and glorious, retaining no doubt about receiving their king, the princes of the opposing party, not forgetting their old art, sought by every means to disrupt his election before it could be completed, since they greatly feared the king who had been chosen.

They therefore asked Duke Otto to speak with them privately and tried, with many promises, to persuade him to waver in the election. Yet they could not induce him to promise them anything definite. Thus, while he hesitated and a large part of his people shared his hesitation, the whole summer passed, and his instability had stirred almost all Saxony.

In November he was again summoned by them to a private conference. By then he was entirely inclined toward the side of our enemies. But through God’s mercy, lest he lose at the end of his life all the labors he had endured for his homeland, the horse on which he was sitting [Note: [Col. 0585] *insidēbat* in 2] fell on level ground. It crushed one of the rider’s legs so badly that for almost an entire month he could not go anywhere except carried.

Thus, returning to himself through the movement of God’s grace, he understood that he had sinned and had been corrected by divine mercy. He therefore sent various embassies, renounced his enemies, and faithfully promised his fellow citizens that he would always remain loyal and united with them.
