The princes of Saxony were greatly delighted. A few days before Christmas, they received their king Herman at Goslar with great rejoicing. On the feast of Saint Stephen the protomartyr [Note: [Col. 0585] *steffani* in 1], he was solemnly anointed king by Siegfried, archbishop of the see of Mainz, when the year 1082 from the Lord’s Incarnation had already begun [Note: [Col. 0585] “begun. And thus much concerning the Saxon war and Henry IV, from this chronicle and history” in 1].

## Around the Year of the Lord 1080: Tomellus, Monk of Hasnon

[Col. 0585]

## History of the Monastery of Hasnon, by Its Author Tomellus, Secretary of Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, Surnamed Montanus

(D. Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 777, from a Hasnon manuscript.)

## Preliminary Notice

The history of the foundation of the monastery of Hasnon, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the district of Ostrevant on the Scarpe River in the diocese of Arras, has as its author Tomellus, a monk and secretary of Count Baldwin, surnamed Montanus—a serious writer who committed nothing to writing without a solid foundation.

Certainly, he drew the beginnings of the monastery, which from the outset was double, for men and women, whose first superiors were John and Eulalia, its founders, from the purest sources themselves, namely from the monastery’s archives, as he himself attests in more than one place.

For in chapter 1 he says:

“I shall not have as my authority in this writing any document deceitfully fabricated, because I am ready to substantiate from the archives of the same monastery whatever I say.”

And in chapter 3, when he is about to relate the succession of abbots and abbesses, he says:

“So that the reader may find the entire succession of the rulers of this place, let him read the following account, taken from the archives,”

which he then adds in chapter 4.

He also related the restoration of the monastery as he himself saw it, being an eyewitness. For he had been secretary to its founder Baldwin and dedicated his work to Rolando, the first abbot. After Rolando’s death, he added chapter 17 to the history, “On the Abbot Rolando of Blessed Memory and on the Excellence of His Character.”

Andreas Vallerius, however, was misled by the similarity of names in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, where he writes the following about our Tomellus:

“Thomellus, a monk of Elnon near Saint-Amand, flourished in the year 1070. At the command of his abbot, Blessed Roland, he wrote about the foundation, restoration, and dedication of the monastery of Elnon, and about the character of Count Baldwin, its restorer.”

For we have no abbot of Elnon at Saint-Amand named Roland, but there was one at Hasnon. Nor was Tomellus a monk of Elnon, but of Hasnon. Moreover, the matters that he committed to writing about the foundation, restoration, and dedication of his monastery and about the character of Count Baldwin do not belong to the monastery of Elnon but to that of Hasnon.

We copied this history from a Hasnon manuscript with the permission of the most reverend and illustrious abbot of that place. From him we also borrowed the cartulary of the lords of Avesnes, from which we excerpted many matters concerning Belgian history contained in the first volume of our works.

## On the Foundation of the Monastery of Hasnon

[Col. 0587]

## The Prologue of Tomellus Begins: On the Foundation of the Monastery of Hasnon, Addressed to Rolando, the First Abbot after the Restoration

[Col. 0587]

Although mortals regard the riches of this world as primary, yet the riches of salvation—wisdom, knowledge, and the fear of the Lord—are themselves its treasure. The Apostle glories in possessing this treasure in earthen vessels, because wisdom preserved in a humble heart is more powerful than all the rulers of this world.

This wisdom, Venerable Father Rolando, I embrace and venerate in you, leaving behind the wise men and seekers of this world. Your venerable and long life is not reckoned by the number of years but adorned with the graces of every virtue. To obey your authority is to gain authority; to be humbly subject to you is, not without glory, to preside [Col. 0587B].

Therefore I have resolved to obey whatever you command as though it were divinely commanded, and at your nod to proceed with every step of mind and body. For I know that you temper everything you do with the mother of virtues, so that it is something the strong desire and the weak do not recoil from.

You demand that I forge the ancient construction of the monastery of Hasnon in a new style and gather into one volume what has been scattered throughout the archives, and that I append how great a benefaction the margrave Baldwin of blessed memory bestowed upon that place in our own time.

To obey so great a man is, as I have said, glorious; but to lay an inadequate hand upon the work is by no means easy. Yet as I proceed beneath the burden, the staff of your holiness will support me. When I have put the finishing hand to the work, it will be your responsibility, if I please you, both to approve one part with your authority and to strengthen the other by your prayer [Col. 0587C].

The prayers of the Hasnon brothers under your care, who bear the weapons of righteousness in Christ’s camp, also come to the aid of my labor. In their mouths prayer never sleeps; in their hearts, love; in their strength, activity never grows weak. For them I desire and implore in prayer the tail of the sacrificial victim and, with Joseph, a long tunic—that is, good work lasting to the end.

## Chapter I: On John, an Illustrious Man, and His Sister Eulalia, the First Founders

[Col. 0588]

When I am about to speak of the foundation of the place of Hasnon, the subject requires attention to times and persons, to the place and its circumstances. For grammarians and orators alike share the practice of attending to place, time, and person in every undertaking.

The place, I say: where it was founded; the time: when it was founded; the persons: by whom it was founded. First I shall open my mouth in praise of the founder of the aforesaid place; then I shall relate as much as I can about how it was constructed by those same founders.

I shall not have as my authority in this writing any document deceitfully fabricated, because I am ready to substantiate from the archives of the same monastery whatever I say.

The Church possessed a precious stone of the Lord’s diadem, namely John, illustrious by birth and virtue, a most perfect layman and also an example for perfect laymen to imitate; most perfect, I say, because he obeyed the Lord’s word:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me.”

He put this into practice with such devotion that it will plainly appear in what follows. He certainly had as a companion in his goodness a sister no less good in flesh and spirit, named Eulalia. But from what parents they sprang, what persons were joined to them by the bond of kinship, and how through them the Hasnon monastery had its beginning, will easily be learned in what follows.

## Chapter II: On the Construction of the Monastery of Hasnon and Its Sacred Dedication

[Col. 0588C]

Just as the aforesaid John possessed the distinction of an excellent lineage, so he also possessed great wealth of patrimony. He resolved to appoint Christ heir on earth, so that he might make himself a co-heir with Christ in heaven; narrowing the cords of his earthly inheritance in temporal matters and splendidly widening them in heavenly matters, he could say with the Psalmist:

“The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me.”

At that time, a certain portion of his extensive patrimony was destined, not long afterward, through this illustrious man, to become a dwelling for the servants of God. It lay in the district of Ostrevant beside the Scarpe River. There, in order to build a monastery for God, he and his aforementioned sister Eulalia reached an agreement, and the effect followed their devotion; at last, with God cooperating, the work was completed.

This work was begun in the six hundred and seventieth year of the Word made flesh, in the fourth year of the reign of Theoderic, son of King Clovis and Queen Bathildis. When the architect had put the finishing hand to the work, Bishop Vindician of the venerable Church of Cambrai was summoned, and the place was dedicated to God and Saint Peter on the day before the Kalends of May.

Then holy Zion, joined to her Bridegroom, bore children of holy love, through whom she spread the fragrance of virtues far and wide, so that she could exultantly say:

“When the King was at his resting place, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

## Chapter III: On the Illustrious Founders and Rulers of This Monastery
Return to John, the venerable man, who had been the cause and beginning of this monastery and who was to bring the foregoing plans to completion. I shall record in writing from which parents he sprang and which brothers and sisters he had.

He was born of his father Autbaldus and his mother Grimoara. He had as brothers Aldo, Autgangus, Adalbodus, and Adalardus; and as sisters Eulalia, Bertrude, and Adalunara. They had an uncle named Deodatus, distinguished both by name and merit. These men and women, whose justice has not been forgotten, conceived the fervor of the Holy Spirit and brought forth the virtue by which they stripped themselves of their own possessions and enriched this place magnificently. The first of them, John, built this place with his sister Eulalia and governed it honorably; by the increase both of his possessions and of his virtues, he raised it to greatness.

His brother Aldo succeeded him. Leaving behind his possessions and his wife Oedila, and cutting off the hair of his head, he enrolled himself in the same place as a soldier of Christ. As he had resolved within his heart to ascend through the virtues, so he ascended through the ecclesiastical grades and obtained the dignity of the priesthood, which he rendered illustrious by holy deeds until the consummation of his life. And so that the reader may find the whole succession of rulers of this place, let him read the following account, taken from the archives. [Col. 0589C–D]

## CHAPTER IV. A remembrance of the rulers of this place

Abbot John and his sister Eulalia held the governance of the monastery of Hasnon for seventeen years.

Aldo the priest, brother of the aforesaid John, for forty years. Bertrude, his sister, with him for twenty years. Sigebolda, sister of the aforementioned Aldo, held the governance with him for eight years and, after his death, for four. Adalunara, likewise sister of the said Aldo, for ten years.

Savericus for thirty-one years. Gundrada, daughter of the aforesaid Savericus, for twelve years. Geroldus for six years. Rotfridus for twenty-six years. Martina for thirteen years. [Col. 0590A] Waltoarius for one and a half years; Alpaidis for one year. Amadeus for two and a half years. Adalulfus for seven and a half years. Algnitrudis for ten years. Ermentrude, empress and queen, together with her daughter, likewise named Ermentrude, for nine years.

The total is one hundred and ninety-four years. Under these rulers this place advanced over the course of time from day to day, and it remained a strict guardian of honorable discipline up to the final years of Charles the Bald. Nor should the reader be disturbed that persons of both sexes presided over the same place: it is clear that two communities existed there, one of monks and the other of holy women. The truth of this is readily established by the testimony of the ancient writers, as is shown by this comparison with similar cases. Indeed, divine grace had been greater in that place because the glory of God had resounded from the mouths of both sexes. [Col. 0590B]

## CHAPTER V. How the request of Queen Ermentrude obtained for this place the benefaction of Charles the Bald

The aforementioned Ermentrude was outstandingly distinguished by the title of nobility, which she rendered illustrious by exceptional merits and wisdom, so that, although she held the imperial insignia, you would marvel at her humility. She did not consider it of great value to reign without humility and charity; by these wings she learned to fly from earthly things to heavenly ones.

Accordingly, in both flesh and spirit, she had brought forth into the fellowship of her virtue a daughter who bore the same name but was equal to her in merit. By words and examples she instructed her and trained her to the standard of every goodness. Their virtue grew so greatly that, abandoning the pomp of the world, they crucified themselves to the world and the world to themselves; and, according to the rule prescribed in that place, they became female soldiers in the Lord’s camp. They enriched the place both by their counsel and by their possessions, and strengthened it by royal generosity as well as by privilege.

At that time France was ruled by its first prince, Charles Augustus, surnamed the Bald. The nobility on one side and Ermentrude’s own integrity on the other enabled the aforementioned Ermentrude to wield great influence with him. Hence, at her request, the royal majesty inclined itself toward this place and enriched it with generosity. Nor will it be burdensome to insert here, from the archives of the same monastery, the privilege of the king mentioned above, and thereby to provide readers with proof of what we are saying. [Col. 0590C–D]

## CHAPTER VI. A privilege of Charles the Bald, taken from the archives for the protection of the same monastery

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Charles, by the mercy of God emperor Augustus. If, by coming to the aid of the needs of God’s servants, we confer benefits, we have no doubt whatsoever that this will be profitable to us for eternal blessedness. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of God’s holy Church and of our own people, both present and future, know that, desiring to assist the needs of the brothers and sisters in the monastery called Hasnon, situated in the county of Arras, in the district of Ostrebant, upon the River Scarpe, under the protection of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, who serve there, and having had their necessities disclosed to us through our daughter Ermentrude, abbess, we decree, at the petition of the same Ermentrude, that the commands of our high authority be confirmed to them, so that, through our generosity, they may perpetually possess for their increase and benefit the things described below.
>
> “We therefore grant to the aforesaid monastery, within the monastery itself, two manses and two breweries, and one wood; moreover, from the abbot’s wood, enough to fatten sixty pigs. Also, in the aforesaid district, the estate of Azinium in its entirety, except for three manses; finally, in that same district, the estate of Azinium which is above the River Scarpe, in its entirety, except for five manses, together with two mills, one brewery, and two meadows. Likewise, in the aforesaid district of Ostrebant, we grant the estate of Ubanercinium in its entirety; and in that same district, at Scandinium, we have given them eight manses.
>
> “Of these, Guntramnus holds four by our command, at the request of the aforesaid abbess, for as long as she lives. Afterwards they are to be received for the use of the brothers. Furthermore, in the county of Tardenois, the estate of Aniciacum, situated upon the River Ubellula, with eleven manses; and from all the estates of the entire abbey we decree that the whole tithe be fully granted. And if this should not suffice for the uses of the brothers or sisters, all necessities are to be supplied from the demesne.
>
> “And so that this may remain inviolable for all time, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring. Sign of Charles, most glorious emperor Augustus. Odacrus, notary, acting in the place of Goselinus, examined and subscribed this. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the tenth indiction, in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of our lord King Charles in France and the second of his empire. Acted at the imperial palace of Quierzy, happily, in the name of God. Amen.” [Col. 0590D–0591C]

## CHAPTER VII. How the same place long flourished in divine religion but gradually grew lukewarm up to the time of Baldwin VI, marquis

Strengthened by the royal privileges and benefactions mentioned above, and receiving from God—something incomparably more precious than these—the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the place remained for a long time adorned by the delight of a devout way of life. But as iniquity increased and the charity of many grew cold, holy religion became the virtue of a few.

For, since—as it is written—dangerous times were approaching, and people were, indeed are, lovers of themselves, the more those who professed religion wandered toward external things, the more they grew weak in matters below. Thus, on this pretext, the place of Hasnon gradually departed from the great religious life in which it had flourished, while, by despising small matters, it carelessly exceeded the proper measure of strict discipline.

The canons of that place, enrolled—let me not say devoted—to canonical observances, to whom the Lord had given the land of the nations and the labors of peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law, were maintained freely, without the fruit of labor, by the stipends of the most holy place. One was carried away outside to an estate, another to business, one to curiosity, another to pleasure. [Col. 0591D–0592A] As the disease of this vice grew from day to day, it corrupted the house of God in that place, emptying it of all religion, until the destruction of souls, and it did not bring that corruption to an end even up to the time of Baldwin VI, the glorious marquis.

## CHAPTER VIII. The time of Baldwin VI, marquis, and his worthy conduct, deserving remembrance

Since the occasion of our discussion has brought Baldwin before us—Baldwin, I say, whom this sixth age of ours received as the sixth after Baldwin the Iron—it is not inappropriate to bring forward some ornaments of his virtues, sufficient as examples for good princes: a few from many, but great examples from great virtues, as astrologers are accustomed to depict the sphere of heaven on a small scale.

In the first years of his apprenticeship he was educated at the imperial court under Emperor Henry. Among the companions whom the court then possessed he was distinguished by precedence and equaled in affection. Then, as his years grew stronger and age advanced together with time, he entered the county of the Nervians—though not without some offense to the imperial majesty—and became renowned as a most powerful leader in war against enemies and in peace toward citizens.

The poor, orphans, and widows had him as a father; monks had him as an example of religious life; the afflicted had him as a shield of protection. You would marvel that the same man, in secular dress, was a powerful prince of the kingdom and yet concealed within himself a poor man of Christ.

During the sacred solemnities of the Mass, he devoted himself wholly, in soul and body, fixed upon God as though God were visible to his eyes; in prayer he offered God conversation and human beings silence. Accordingly, during the same solemnities of the Mass, he kept poor people with him as intercessors on his behalf before God. After presenting the offering to the priest, he distributed alms to them, offering them to Christ in the poor.

I have been a witness of this matter, O reader, whoever you may be—if indeed you do not doubt the fitness of so humble a witness—for when he had often graciously drawn me familiarly to his side, I heard that he secretly invited poor people to attend with him the sacred mysteries of the Mass. When, after some of the praises of the Mass had been completed, they asked for alms because they had neglected to attend, he quietly reproached them. Nor did he labor only at that time: whenever circumstances required, he worked through himself and through others at almsgiving, now secretly, now publicly. [Col. 0592B–D]

As hunger grew more severe, he distributed with a more generous hand to those in need and assigned this duty to the monasteries of his kingdom, so that from their own resources they might more wisely provide relief for the poor.

Evening will close Olympus before either pen or speech can equal his virtues. Nevertheless, we shall attempt to say how through him the monastery of Hasnon began to rise, changed from old to new and diligently improved from neglect to a better state.

## CHAPTER IX. How he was divinely admonished by a revelation concerning the restoration of this place

When, from the most pleasing disposition of his childhood, he was entering the years of adolescence, he fell into a grave illness—not merely to his bed but even to the point of despair. Just as, while he lived and was well, he had easily given his father hope and joy concerning him, so, when ill, he aroused fear in him not without sorrow. Thus you would have grieved to see the whole court grieving together, on one side because of the son’s illness and on the other because of the father’s sorrow.

But when heaven had inclined toward this great danger, divine mercy also inclined itself, and the visitation of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, together with the Holy of Holies, wiped away the affliction both of the son’s illness and of the father’s sorrow. For the aforementioned martyrs appeared to the half-awake sick man to stand beside him and burst forth into these words of consolation:

> “Know that you can be freed from this illness if you vow that you will become the restorer of the place of Hasnon.”

At that time a certain Winthericus remained in that place, abounding no less in vices than in riches, perverse in both, although in one of these two things he might have been at least somewhat good. For in one of them—that is, in wealth—everyone who possesses it is always liable to be bad, while in the other it often happens that someone is good.

The entire surrounding region was suffering under such a man as under a plague, and because of its affliction the voice of that whole land cried out to God. And behold, in this same revelation of his martyrs, the Lord remembered the footstool of his feet. For the holy martyrs whom we have named added the injunction that the sick and half-awake Baldwin should compel Winthericus, contrary in name and conduct to the kingdom, to migrate from that place.

Because we learned that this revelation had occurred at Bruchium through the report of faithful people, we faithfully believed it as a faithful account, and, believing it, committed it to writing. [Col. 0592D–0593C]

## CHAPTER X. How he obtained the same place through his father’s generosity, but forgot the divine admonition

At the time of the revelation, the glorious marquis Baldwin was sitting beside his son, who lay there already given up for dead. As though the boy were about to breathe his last at any moment, he held a burning candle before him. But the son, who had long kept his eyes closed in both ecstasy and illness, opened them. He scarcely moved his tongue into stammering words rather than forming a speech, and, when his father tenderly asked what he had seen and whether he was safe, he told him.

He added that he could become the possessor of his salvation if his father, inspired by the divine revelation, made him possessor of his vow. When the father, so exceedingly eager for his son’s recovery, anxiously asked what the son desired by his vow, the latter requested and obtained that the place of Hasnon be given to him as a gift.

For, with certain courtiers present—whom the marquis had admitted as spectators of his sorrow—he placed the burning candle in his son’s hands and, as though by a pledge supporting the act, made Hasnon a gift to him. It was possible to see, at one and the same moment, the son receiving a gift from his father and, through the saints, receiving the remedy of his illness and returning to life.

From then on he gradually grew somewhat stronger day by day, and, once he had recovered completely, he himself became a source of complete joy to many. But, as weakness of mind often creeps in together with health of body, the young marquis, in the day of good things, became forgetful of his troubles. When he entered the harbor of bodily health after the shipwreck of illness, he forgot the divine vision that he had seen.

## CHAPTER XI. How, wounded in battle and in danger of death, he was again reminded by a divine vision concerning this place

In the following period, when he had advanced to manly strength and had obtained, as we have said, the county of the Nervians, he stirred up a harsh war between the Easterners and the Flemings, the scourge of blazing discord.

Therefore the glorious marquis Baldwin, having summoned whatever forces he could, prepared to attack the territory of Antwerp, which bordered the frontier of his kingdom and was consequently all the more hostile. Dividing his army, with naval combat on one side and cavalry combat on the other, he placed himself over the ships and wished the younger marquis Baldwin to command the cavalry.

But while the younger marquis was leading the cavalry camp toward the place to which he had directed it, and, with a few men, was traveling somewhat farther ahead of the rear of the camp—as the outcome at that time showed—he unexpectedly fell upon an enemy who had been sent forward in ambush. With steadfast courage and as much prudence as he could, he armed himself and his men. The two sides engaged at close quarters; battle was joined; the fight was now with swords, not missiles. After a long struggle on both sides, the marquis attacked a stronger and more hostile enemy, a certain Hubert, wounded him, and, though wounded himself, cast him down. [Col. 0593D–0594C]

Hubert’s fall put the rest of the enemy to flight and removed the obstacle to victory. The younger marquis was carried by the hands of his men to Gaudavum and was afflicted for many days by the pain of a wound that was by no means slight.

When he was now almost in danger of death, he was admonished by Salako, once his guardian, concerning the divine revelation about Hasnon. He approached his father, who was then sorrowful, and spoke to him as best he could about this matter. Together they devised a plan to summon Winthericus, to whom Hasnon then belonged. Winthericus was summoned concerning an exchange of Hasnon; he was approached courteously, but, although they pleaded for a long time, he offered his ears but not his consent.

## CHAPTER XII. How the castle of Hasnon was burned by the younger Baldwin but rebuilt again by Winthericus

The often-mentioned Baldwin therefore recovered as the wound closed into a scar, and began to work toward carrying out the divine admonition. But what could he do? By no means could he bend the obstinate mind of the aforementioned Winthericus or incline his deaf ears toward consent—not to mention toward hearing.

Accordingly, by a circuitous path of reasoning, he resolved to attain what he desired. It secretly persuaded Winthericus’ younger brother, by flatteries and rewards, to hand over the castle of Hasnon; and, although with difficulty, it obtained an agreement for the surrender. Armed with this agreement rather than with weapons, and with not many of his men, he unexpectedly invaded the castle and, destroying it by fire, leveled it to the ground.

But once the deed was done, the marquis lost heart, because the matter had not succeeded according to his vow. For when Winthericus learned what had happened, and was not without suspicion of the surrender, he began, with the cunning he possessed and the effort of which he was capable, to repair the damage to his castle, as though he were restoring a fallen Troy. By rebuilding it, he achieved the object of his desire and temporarily frustrated the marquis’ plan. [Col. 0594D–0595A]

## CHAPTER XIII. How Winthericus was killed by his own soldier and removed from human affairs

When the most noble count had not only found no trace of fulfillment for his vow but had also been forced to despair of what was happening, he came to himself and believed that what he could not obtain by human means must be sought through divine assistance. Therefore, both personally and through others, he continued to offer unceasing prayers to the ears of God Sabaoth, asking that, just as through the divine revelation given by his martyrs he had conceived the desire for a good work, so he might also find its fulfillment.

But just as the promise of truth, which says, “Ask and you will receive; knock and it will be opened to you,” could not be made void, so a petition made in the name of Jesus could not fail to have efficacy for those who prayed. And behold, the sword of the Lord’s fury is unsheathed against the head of Winthericus and threatens a blow reaching even to his soul.

For while he was traveling one day with his men, he charged one of them with the crime of adultery involving his wife. When he received from the man an exculpatory denial of the deed, but was still not satisfied even by terrible oaths, matters proceeded to the point that he demanded a duel from the man before any preliminaries, without delay.

The soldier, however, fearing the Lord more than the alleged crime, sought the duel from another rather than from his lord. But when Winthericus not only refused to agree but also attacked the soldier with weapons, the soldier, under the pretext of self-defense, stabbed and brought down his lord, thus giving him simultaneously to the ground and to death.

So the hidden judgment of God, which had long delayed vengeance by enduring his conduct, took his life together with his castle through the soldier’s weapons. [Col. 0595A–C]

## CHAPTER XIV. How Baldwin VI, marquis, seized the castle of Hasnon, destroyed it by fire, and expelled its garrison

The fame of the deed flew abroad and became known to the younger marquis. He received the news with joy, attributing to God the fulfillment of his desire and giving thanks to him, from whom he had deserved to obtain what he could not obtain from a human being.

But, fearing that he might lose the gain of his desire if he delayed breaking into the castle of Hasnon, he summoned as quickly as possible whatever forces of his armed men he could, anticipated any delay on their part, and invaded the castle. The garrison had no easy means of resistance, being deprived of its leader and not sufficiently fortified either by the strength of the place or by weapons; moreover, necessity had overtaken them before they could take measures for their own safety. Thus, just as it was difficult for them to resist, so it was easy for the marquis to press his attack.

Breaking into the castle, he made a way for himself and his men with swords. He expelled the castellans without bloodshed, then committed the whole castle to fire, leaving nothing of it behind. Moreover, he leveled the embankment of the moat with the ground, making it as flat as a plain. Thus, secure concerning what remained, he resolved to transform that den of robbers into the house of God. [Col. 0595C–0596A]

## CHAPTER XV. How the canons of the same place were craftily won over by the aforesaid marquis’ kindness, and their stipends redeemed

At that time there were in that place, as we have said, canons who were soldiers in the divine camp in name only: they labored more than was right at external matters and less than was right at internal ones. Since the most illustrious man had determined to replace the canonical customs there with monastic ones, he devoted himself, after prolonged deliberation, to every aspect of the plan so that this might be done without violating the peace of either order.

He therefore summoned them, sometimes individually and sometimes all together, and urged them—usually toward a conversion of their conduct, sometimes toward the monastic way of life, and finally to hand over their stipends to him in exchange either for other possessions or for rewards.

Thus the persistent labor of the most serene man, pressing its case opportunely and importunately, overcame everything that the Holy Spirit had inspired him to desire. Although he achieved what he desired only through labor more tedious than he wished, he believed that it would nevertheless be accomplished soon, indeed that it would benefit many, if it were done well.

Why delay with many words? He succeeded in obtaining what he wanted. Having acquired the stipends from the canons, without violating their peace, he made both the place and the property belonging to the place his own, so that he might dedicate everything to God and to the uses of God’s servants. [Col. 0596A–B]

## CHAPTER XVI. How, when the canons had departed, the same place was assigned to monastic communities

When, as we have said, Baldwin possessed that place together with its dependencies in complete security, being, as it were, the sole master of what belonged to his own people, he devoted himself continually to making it worthy of monastic regulations.

First, having summoned a few monks from various places and having supplied the place with stipends sufficient for food and clothing, he caused it, like a tender infancy, to be taught the first steps for walking along the way of God’s commandments, so that in the course of time the monastic life there might flourish with the strength of maturity.

When the enemy of the human race saw this, he immediately became jealous. Since he understood that his own strength was being weakened, he prepared, through visible enemies, to plot invisibly. He stirred up certain kinsmen of the aforementioned Winthericus—members, so to speak, of his own body—against the servants of God. They could scarcely restrain their injury even with their hands, much less with words, and sought to compel them by any means to migrate from the place.

But in vain they raged against those who had God as their protector. Those who had plotted against stronger men through God were quickly torn apart like spiders’ webs by their weapons. [Col. 0596B–D]

## CHAPTER XVII. The construction of the place of Hasnon in greater splendor and its new solemn dedication

Because that monastery, together with its workshops, could scarcely accommodate the monks, the marquis decided to enlarge it. He summoned masons from everywhere and carried the desire of his mind into effect. As the buildings rose within a short time, he completed the final work on the construction.

At that time it happened that his father had left him the kingdom by right of succession. Not long afterward, once he had fully reached the heights of the kingdom with the favor of the entire court, he decided that the monastery of Hasnon, elaborately restored by skilled work, should be consecrated with chrism. To hasten this undertaking, he appointed the third day of June, the day after the feast of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, so that, by joining the day of the consecration to the solemnity of the aforementioned martyrs, the joy of the people of that land might be doubled by a double feast.

He carefully arranged this so that, on the feast of those same martyrs, what he had once received from them by revelation might be completed, especially since the place was protected by their present patronage. He also had a reliquary prepared for them with marvelous workmanship in gold and jewels and arranged for their relics to be placed in it on the approaching solemnity; and this was done.

For this translation and dedication he invited the bishops Lietbert of Cambrai, to whose diocese the place belonged, Ratbod of Noyon, and Rainer of Orléans. Together with them, and with very many abbots and the patronage of very many saints, he celebrated the aforementioned consecration of the monastery with considerable solemnity.

This dedication was performed in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul on the third day before the Nones of June, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1070, while Alexander presided as pope of the holy Roman Church and Henry, king of Lorraine, and Philip, king of France, were reigning. [Col. 0596D–0597B]

The dedication of this place after its restoration was carried out by three bishops: Saint Lietbert of Cambrai, Ratbod of Noyon, and Rainer of Orléans, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, in the eighth indiction, with epact VI, concurrent IV, and cycle IV, in the time of Pope Alexander, who had first been bishop at Lucca; of Philip, king of the Franks, son of Henry; and of Baldwin, count of Flanders. [Col. 0597B–C]

### The bodies of the saints that were present at the dedication

[Note: The author of the book *On the Translation of Saint Donatian, Archbishop of Reims, to the City of Bruges*, in Surius under 14 October, mentions this dedication in these words: “When the illustrious marquis of Flanders, Baldwin, a cultivator of justice and lover of peace, had, among his other zeal for good works, built the monastery founded in the castle of Hasnon, he made magnificent preparations for its dedication from his immense wealth and ordered all the nobles of Flanders, together with their people, to attend such a solemnity. He also wished the bodies of all the saints in his domain to be present, together with the bishops, provosts, abbots, and his subjects.” He then recounts the miracle that occurred at that time through the merits of Saint Donatian. In almost the same manner, at the solemn dedication of the collegiate church of Saint Peter of Lille, the bodies of the saints of the entire region were brought at the command of Baldwin, count of Lille, who had founded that church, as may be seen in Iperius.] [Col. 0597C–0598D]

Saint Marcellus, pope. Saint Piat, martyr. Saint Salvius, martyr of Valenciennes. Saint Innocent of Condé. Saint Amatus of Douai. Saint Donatian of Bruges. Saint Vedast of Arras. [Col. 0597D] Saint Amandus of Elnone. Saint Audomar of Saint-Omer. Saint Gislenus of Celle. Saint Vincent, count of Hainaut. Saint Bertinus of Saint-Bertin near Saint-Omer. Saint Vinocus of Flanders. [Col. 0597D–0598A] Saint Wandregisilus of Blandinium. Saint Bavo of Ghent. Saint Everardus of Ozoir. Saint Eubertus of Lille. Saint Landelinus of Crespin. Saint Hugh of Haspres. Saint Aicardus of Haspres. Saint Eusebia of Marchiennes. Saint Rictrudis, her mother, of Marchiennes. Saint Aldegund of Maubeuge. Saint Raginfledis of Donon. Saint Regina of Donon. Saint Waldetrudis of Mons.

[Note: Tomellus added this, together with the following chapter, to his work later, after the most devout Abbot Rotland had died.] Fifteen abbots were also present; their names are taken from the chronicle of Sigebert. [Col. 0598A–D]

[Col. 0598B] Rollandus, the first abbot of this place after the restoration. Lambertus, Adelardus, Guedericus, Ursio, Galterus, Guldericus, Remigius, Reynerus, Reinaldus, Fulcardus, Sygerus, Heribertus, Armengerus, Walterus.

[Col. 0598C] Two abbesses:

Fredesendis, Gerberga.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The abbot Rotland, of blessed memory, and his most pleasing uprightness of conduct

Since it belongs to monks humbly to be subject to one whom it is proper to appoint as superior, and since governing teaches one equally how to be useful, the often-mentioned count considered it appropriate to place one man over many in that place and to subject many to one, so that one might exercise authority over many with charity, and many might offer obedience with humility.

At that time there was in the monastery of Saint Amand a certain Rothland, radiant both in name and in monastic office, admirable in life and worthy of imitation by those who desired to live piously. The marquis had learned that he had long humbly obeyed; therefore, like a lamp long placed in concealment that ought to be set upon a lampstand so that it might become an example of goodness to those entering the house of the Lord, he selected him and appointed him to preside over them in the monastery of Hasnon.

Promoted to this honor and occupied by this office, he devoted himself to the burden rather than to the honor. To preside is an honor; to govern souls is a burden. Occupied fittingly with the latter, he strove more to be useful than to preside, so that in all the activities of the monastery he surpassed no one except by the merit of his life and by his pastoral staff.

Thus, by humility, he showed himself equal—or rather inferior—to the humble, while among the wicked, as their faults required, he showed himself superior through discipline. He kept in mind and fulfilled in practice the words: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock.” Likewise: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be as one of them.”

In the assembly of the brothers, he presented himself first at the beginning and last at the end of the divine praises. His bed was often a stone or the bare ground alone; when he wished to indulge his body somewhat more leniently, it was any cheap mat or the straw of a coarse blanket. His clothing was poor; he was sparing toward himself in food, but expensive and generous toward others. In all things he tempered matters with discernment and restrained them by discipline.

He shared table and bed with the brothers, unless perhaps, in the interest of special prayers, he occasionally spent the night in the oratory. Would that this were not said either to the shame or the condemnation of certain abbots who, more secretly than the common assembly of the brothers, have many chambers constructed for themselves, carve doors, paint cupboards, and feast at a more sumptuous table, living splendidly every day with that rich man who had no Lazarus. Finally, to speak in the words of that Flaccus, they demolish for themselves, build, and exchange square things for round.

Would that this charge were directed only against abbots and not also against monks who follow their prelates along precipitous paths. The Psalmist, observing them not with the spirit of one who wishes but of one who prophesies, says: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually.”

The eyes are those who, placed at the forefront of the highest honor, have undertaken the office of leading the way; those who follow them are, in turn, called backs. When the eyes are darkened, the back is bent, because when those who are perishing lose the light of virtue, all who follow are inevitably bent beneath the burden of sins. But we leave these matters to be examined more fully by wiser people in their proper place, while now we hasten to continue what we have undertaken to say.

Although much still remains that may be brought forward both to the praise of the abbot Rothland, of blessed memory, and to our own criticism.

## Around the same year. Renallus, master of the see of Barcelona

### Notice

*(Augustinus Theinerus, Critical Investigations, p. 357.)*

At the end of a codex of the Barberini Library in Rome, no. 2864, we discover certain verses written in addition, taken from Renallus’ work *On the Body of Christ*. Concerning this Renallus, who, as is clear from our heading, was master at Barcelona, we can provide no certain information. Nicolaus Antonius, the learned Spaniard, has nothing beyond his name except that he wrote a Life of Saint Eulalia, who suffered martyrdom under Diocletian. [Note: *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*. Madrid, 1788, vol. II, p. 376, folio.] But concerning this Life as well, Tamayo [Note: Under 12 February, vol. I, p. 100, of the *Spanish Martyrology*. Lyons, 1651, folio.] and the Bollandist hagiographers are completely silent. [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, on the date cited, vol. II, p. 576.]

The work of Renallus—or, as Antonius calls him, Raynaldus—appears to have been written in the time of Berengar of Tours, and indeed against his errors concerning the holy Eucharist. We have thought that the verses excerpted from it ought to be appended here.

### Excerpts from the verses of the book *On the Body of Christ* by Renallus, master of Barcelona and Girona

#### Four things are signified in the sacred sacrament concerning the body of Christ

The reason full of faith in God shows what is offered,  
by whom, for whom, or to whom it is given.  
Christ gives himself to himself: he gives himself in this,  
that he is human, but to himself because he is God;  
for Christ offers himself to the supreme Godhead,  
for the offspring of faith, namely the Church,  
which, taking part in the Godhead,  
he makes glorious by taking it into himself. [Col. 0599B–C]

#### How it is bread and only a sacrament, and not yet the Lord’s flesh

This bread of ours is at first common bread;  
when it is offered and received, it becomes flesh itself.  
It is a sacrament, a sign of sacred devotion,  
and the bread is not yet the true flesh of the Lord.  
Yet it is not common bread, removed from use,  
but a sacred sign because it signifies the thing. [Col. 0600C–0601A]

#### When it is both sacrament and the reality of the sacrament: sacrament because it retains the appearance of bread, reality because it is the true flesh of the Lord

After the priest consecrates it, with Christ consecrating,  
within the bond of peace and the embrace of faith,  
in the house of the Church, which is called union,  
through which the Church, the bride, is joined to her Bridegroom,  
with God inspiring, the former nature, once blessed,  
is the true flesh of the Lord, while the appearances remain.  
The reality is flesh, while it is a sacrament—  
the true flesh of the Creator.  
But it is called a sacrament for this reason:  
it retains the appearances, not because the force of bread remains.  
The former nature becomes the true flesh of the Lord. [Col. 0601A]

#### How bread is not received in the sacrament according to its forms, but according to its material and temporal force, which passes into an eternal force, namely eternal life

In the sacrament that bread is not received  
insofar as it possesses the force of bread, but according to that property  
by which it gives the one who eats it the life of this present time. [Col. 0601B]

This hidden force, sanctified by God,  
passes into an eternal power; the person who worthily receives it  
lives forever, filled with life by that power.  
It possesses those spiritual forms  
that cannot be seen by bodily eyes.  
It has the force belonging to the form that the bread possessed,  
but it does not receive or retain the nature of bread. [Col. 0601B–0602A]

#### How, when it is received, it ceases to be a sacrament and remains only the reality

The sacrament ceases to be a sacrament when it is received;  
the forms depart, and only the reality remains:  
that life-giving substance of the Lord  
by which our dead flesh returns to life.  
It refreshes us, redeems us, and unites us—  
by the supper, the cross, and the Father,  
by these three; these three the peace-making King accomplishes.  
While Christ’s flesh is consumed, devotion is renewed,  
and through renewed devotion our flesh becomes new. [Col. 0602A–B]

## Around the same year. Marianus Scotus

### Notice concerning Marianus and his chronicle

*(G. Waitz, Preface to the Chronicle of Marianus Scotus, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* V, 481.)*

The chronicle bearing the name of Marianus is read in several codices, and these differ greatly from one another. Among them, the first that must be named is: [Col. 0601C]

1) Codex Palatino-Vaticanus no. 830, parchment, eleventh century, quarto, consisting of 170 folios. Some have already called this manuscript an autograph [Note: [Col. 0601D] Pagius, *Criticism on Baronius*, year 853, no. 14, Lucca edition XIV, p. 425: “A copy of this manuscript is now preserved at Rome in the convent of Saint Isidore, but the autograph belonged to the Vatican Library or to some other library of the City.” Among authors of that period, however, this word signifies only the manuscript from which the copy was made. Perhaps Schannat followed Pagius; see *History of Fulda*, p. 60. Mabillon also mentions this manuscript, *Annals* IV, p. 583.]; and a more careful examination of the book seems to confirm this. For not only is the brief continuation added in different hands, but the *Chronicle* itself was written neither at one time nor by one hand. One scribe wrote folios 2–25 and 150 onward, another folios 26–149: the former in the letters commonly called minuscule, such as are found in most manuscripts of the eleventh century [Col. 0602C], the latter in an entirely different script, Irish or Hibernian, since it agrees completely with manuscripts written in that language. We call the latter hand the first; the former—the hand to which not only the final years of the *Chronicle* are owed but also very many additions made both in the text and in the margin—the second.

Which part is to be attributed to Marianus is disputed. In the upper margin, in the first hand, the following is written on folio 33:

> Soem [Irish; meaning uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0601D] We have not yet been able to obtain a certain interpretation of these passages. The subject is probably Mainz and perhaps also the monastery of Saint Alban, unless one wishes to refer *Aalbain* to Scotland. On the words *amélbrigte clusenair*, see below, note 19. *Diarmait* is an Irish name; what follows indicates the king of Leinster, whose death is known from the *Chronicle* to have occurred in 1072. As the distinguished Leo points out, *isin blia* (*bliadha?*) *irro marbat*, and so forth, should be translated: “in that year after Diarmait, king of Leinster, was killed”; *cetra blia* means “in the fourth year.” In the year 1076 (1098), that is, the fourth after 1072, Marianus wrote the book, as we shall see below.]

> dún indiv amélbrigte clúsenair in Magantia isin dardóen riafél Petair isin cetblia dendegàid [Note: [Col. 0601] Thus I read it; he seems subsequently to have corrected *dennegaid*.] i. isin blia irromqbat [Note: [Col. 0601] *irromarbat Diarmait* should be read.] Diqmait (rin [Note: [Col. 0601] I think that what I have enclosed in parentheses belongs here; see the specimen of the script and note 2.] Lagen. et isin fide) cetra [Note: [Col. 0601] *cetna*?] blia tanacsa Aalbain [Col. 0603A] [Irish, partly uncertain: “the enclosure of Maelbrigte the recluse at Mainz, on the Thursday before Peter’s feast, in the first year after Diarmait, king of Leinster, was killed; and in the fourth year I came [from or to] Alba (Scotland) on my pilgrimage”], and I wrote this book for love of you and of all the Scots—that is, the Irish—for I myself am Irish; folio 67:

> Sobenn dún indiv ámélbrigte clvsenaír diamairt [Note: [Col. 0603D] That is, on Tuesday, or the third weekday. Perhaps this concerns Marianus’s journey; see the *Chronicle*, year 1078 (1056).] 2 Kal. Aug. Manidern tais scoloca [Note: [Col. 0603D] The distinguished Leo translates this as: “a tenant of the monastery of Saint Maurice.” The rest is uncertain.] manestrech Mavritii Blaflacc dasa fleb erinn [Note: [Col. 0603] I doubt whether I have read this correctly.] nige (?) cotocenn, [Irish, partly uncertain: “[…] Maelbrigte the recluse, on Tuesday, two days before the Kalends of August (31 July). Manidern [was] a tenant of the monastery of Saint Maurice; Blaflacc … [the remaining Irish words are uncertain].”],

> “so that I fell with the tablets into the bottom of a dung-pit; but I give thanks, and I was not submerged in Frankish dung. Nevertheless, I ask the learners to pronounce a curse upon them.”

That some of these passages, written partly in Irish, were added by Marianus himself cannot be doubted; and consequently we cannot in any way regard the manuscript as a later copy. Yet when Marianus also speaks of himself in the *Chronicle*, most of the passages are written in the same hand; the note under the year 1050, however, was added later and by the second hand:

> “I, wretched Marianus, was in sin, born in this year,”

so that here too he seems to be found not merely the author but also the scribe. Moreover, on folios 147 and 148 this other hand wrote four lines in Irish in the margin.

There are therefore considerations favoring the attribution of both parts to Marianus. But there are also others opposed to this view, suggesting that either one part or both parts should be attributed to a scribe who either copied the autograph while Marianus was alive and was its author, or supplied his hand and pen while Marianus dictated. Although I do not doubt that the rough and highly distinctive writing found in the manuscript was the writing used by Marianus, I would by no means attribute to him the most atrocious errors and corruptions with which the manuscript abounds [Col. 0603C] and which appear to reveal a most unskilled and negligent scribe. Some may perhaps be explained by books that he followed having been badly written or badly read [Note: [Col. 0603D] For example: *facio* (“I make/do”) for *facto* (“made/done”), *flumina* (“rivers”) for *fulmina* (“thunderbolts”), *quia* (“because”) for *unice* (“only”) (year 242), *terrae* (“lands”) for *Terracon* (“Tarragona”) (year 278), *a consulis* (“of/from a consul”) for *agon solis* (“contest of the sun”; reading uncertain) (year 287), *Pausia* for *Fausta* (personal names; year 373), *judaicum* (“Jewish”) for *inductum* (“led in”) (year 396), *Paviam* (“Pavia”) for *Suaviam* (“Swabia”) (year 1100).]; others, however, are of such a kind as to show that the scribe poorly received and carelessly wrote down the author’s words [Note: [Col. 0603D] For example: *contentens* for *contendens* (variant forms of “contending”), *ordinator* (“one who orders”) for *ordinatur* (“is ordered/ordained”), *Hiberius* (“Irishman”) for *Hiber(i)os* (“the Irish”), *ex* (“from”) for *et* (“and”), and *et* for *ex*, *sextus* (“sixth”) for *sexus* (“sex”), *coeptus* (“begun”) for *coetus* (“assembly”), *statutis* (“statutes”/“having been established”) for *statuis* (“statues”), *cohortatus* (“having exhorted”) for *coartatus* (“compressed”), *indie* for *inde* (“thence”), *militibus* (“soldiers”) for *milibus* (“thousands”), *caessaris* (“Caesar’s”) for *caesis* (“the slain”), [Col. 0604D] *ab arbaris* for *a barbaris* (“by barbarians”), *sirium facit* (“he makes [something] Syrian”; reading uncertain) for *triumfavit* (“triumphed”) (year 21), *X* (“ten”) for *ducem* (“leader”) (year 313), *quadragesimo anno* (“in the fortieth year”) for *quadragesima. Anno* (“in the fortieth … year”; Archbishop of Cologne).]. These are found both in what was written by the first hand and in what was written by the second.

The latter hand—the one in which, as I said above, the passage concerning Marianus’s birth was written—also recorded his death after the *Chronicle* had been completed. No one will persuade himself that this was done by Marianus himself; rather, we detect a scribe who, while Marianus was alive, served him and entered into the manuscript whatever had to be written, and who, after his master’s death, thought it appropriate to add a brief notice of the venerable man’s death [Col. 0603D].

As for the other part, written by the first hand [Col. 0604A], nearly everyone considers it attributable to Marianus, and I would not altogether deny this, especially since it bears an Irish appearance and seems very well suited to a monk born in that land. Nevertheless, it should be noted that only a few marginal notes were written in this hand and, in addition, that this part above all is found disfigured by those atrocious errors and corruptions. I therefore come very close to concluding that this too was written by someone else, perhaps by a Scottish monk who migrated with Marianus to Germany and lent him his hand for writing the *Chronicle*. After his death or departure, it is probable that another succeeded him.

Nevertheless, who would deny that individual words or even longer notes were added by Marianus’s own hand, when, as those who have examined the manuscript testify, the script and ink frequently change, and it is extremely difficult to determine what was added, at what time, and by what hand? Accordingly, let us call the manuscript an autograph, but in this sense: it was not written entirely, or even for the greater part, by Marianus’s hand; rather, it presents the book as the author composed it and continued, corrected, and enlarged it over time, whether he himself committed these things to writing with his pen or employed the rough and unskilled hand of scribes.

The manuscript came from the monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz (on folio 1 one reads: “This book belongs to the library of Saint Martin at Mainz, 1479”). From there it was transferred first to the Palatine Library and then to the Vatican Library.

2) Codex Cottonianus Nero C. V., parchment, late eleventh century [Col. 0604C], a celebrated manuscript, from which Usserius and J. Vossius had already promised to publish a complete Marianus [Note: [Col. 0604D] See Stenzel, *Archive* IV, pp. 106–111.]. I shall briefly show that it by no means presents his genuine text. Wherever Marianus recounts events concerning himself, he speaks plainly: “I, Marianus, left the world, prayed, came” [Note: [Col. 0604D] Years 1074 (1052), 1078 (1056), 1080 (1058), 1081 (1059).], and so forth. This manuscript, however, either speaks as though of someone else: “Marianus the chronicler left the world,” “Marianus came”; or, where it retains his words, it thinks it necessary to add: “Thus says Marianus Scotus, the enclosed one” [Note: [Col. 0604D] Year 1080 (1058); compare 1065 (1043): “Thus says Marianus.”]. It even praises the author himself in these words:

> “Year 1028. In this year Marianus the Irishman, a likely Scot, was born; through his study and labor this excellent chronicle was assembled from various books” [Note: [Col. 0604D] Compare year 1065 (1043): “Marianus, the author of this chronicle—he prayed, who also related these things.”].

If these words are compared with Marianus’s genuine words [Note: [Col. 0604D] Marianus says: “I, wretched Marianus, was born in sins in this year.”], [Col. 0605A] one detects another hand at first sight. Whoever altered these passages corrected Marianus’s wording everywhere, so that generally the events themselves are the same, but the words here are very different [Note: [Col. 0605C] I thought it appropriate to give one or two passages from this recension; for example, year 1065 (1043):

> “Animchad, a Scottish monk and enclosed man at Fulda, died on the third day before the Kalends of February; lights were seen over his tomb and psalmody was heard. Over his tomb Marianus, the author of this chronicle, stood enclosed for ten years at his feet, singing Masses; he also related the following about the aforesaid Animchad. He himself says that, when he was in Ireland, on an island called Keltra, one day, when certain brothers arrived, he showed them charity with the permission of his elder, named Corcram. When some of them had gone out after the meal, those who remained sat warming themselves by the fire and asked him for a drink. Since he refused without permission, they compelled him. At last he consented; nevertheless, before drinking, he sent some of it to his elder as though a blessing. On the following day, when questioned by him about where he had sent the drink, he related everything that had happened; and immediately, solely because of this fault, his elder ordered him to leave Ireland. He humbly obeyed and, coming in this way to Fulda, lived as an enclosed man in holiness and died as he had foretold. My elder Tigernach related this to me when I had committed a small fault before him. While I was also listening, when he was enclosed at Fulda, a very devout monk of that same monastery, named Willehelmus, asked the already-buried Animchad to bless him; and, as he later confirmed to me, that same night he saw in a vision Animchad standing in his tomb, shining with snowy radiance and blessing him with outstretched hand. I too spent that whole night filled with a honey-sweet fragrance. Thus says Marianus.”

> “Year 1093 (1071): A certain cleric named Carolus obtained the bishopric of the city of Constance from King Henry. Consequently, when Sigifrid, bishop of Mainz, held a council in the presence of the aforesaid king, that same cleric lost both the bishopric and, not long afterward, his life.”]; moreover, it omitted many things that we cannot doubt were Marianus’s, especially those written either in the margin [Note: [Col. 0605D] Years 789, 790, 812.], or concerning the Scottish kings [Note: [Col. 0606C] Years 1026 (1014), 1056 (1034), 1062 (1040), 1079 (1057), 1087 (1065), 1088 (1066).], or concerning distant monasteries [Note: [Col. 0606C] Especially those of the island of Reichenau, years 880, 881, 886.]. But it also added other material, mostly concerning events at the monastery of Saint Alban at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0606C] Years 808 (786), 816 (794), 827 (805), 847 (825), 977 (955). Some of these, however, it drew from the same sources used by Marianus: years 832, 833, 834, 835. Compare years 1083 (1061), 1085 (1063), which would suit Marianus very well. Some may persuade themselves that he revised his work in this way on a second examination. But I cannot concede either that he could have altered those statements about himself in this way or that he ever attained the purity of language found here.], and seem to show that the author lived there. The manuscript also has a very brief continuation up to the year 1087, which I do not know whether I can attribute to the same person. For—

2*) The manuscript formerly at Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0606C] Miraeus also saw it, in addition to Schottus; see below, and his note on Sigebert, year 854, p. 107.], whose loss we mourn, presented the same recension as the Cottonianus [Col. 0605B], but those who saw it make no mention at all of a continuation. Nor—

2**) does the Liège manuscript 242, paper, fifteenth century, which I believe was copied from the Gembloux manuscript, contain it, although elsewhere it comes very close to the Cottonianus.

3) The manuscript formerly belonging to Saint Bartholomew, now no. 104 in the Frankfurt public library, parchment, fourteenth century, folio, contains a *Chronicle* continued to the year 1200, which all who followed the first editor attributed to Marianus Scotus and Abbot Dodechinus. But it cannot be proved that Dodechinus wrote the *Chronicle*, and at first sight it is clear that Marianus’s genuine work is not read here. It is a work compiled by a certain monk of Saint Dysibod—Disenberg near Mainz—from Marianus, Methodius, the Würzburg Annals, and other sources. With as much justification as this work, one might attribute Hermann’s *Chronicle* to Bede or even to Jerome.

For he not only enlarged the text with so many and such extensive interpolations that sometimes scarcely any trace of Marianus can be found, but also omitted much both at the beginning [Note: [Col. 0606C] Book I, chapters 1–8, and the whole of Book II.] and within the text itself. In particular, he compiled the history of the tenth and eleventh centuries in such a way that it agrees with Marianus [Note: [Col. 0606C] He had the genuine text at hand, not the text presented by manuscripts 2, 2*, and so forth. At individual points, however, he added certain things resembling this material concerning the monastery of Saint Alban [Col. 0606D]; compare years 816 (794), 990 (968). In the later part too he sometimes mentions this monastery: years 1085, 1095, 1096, 1116, 1119, 1130.], whose words about himself he nevertheless retained, only at a few points. The *Annals of Saint Dysibod* would be the more accurate designation.

With this preliminary matter established, let us briefly discuss both the life of Marianus and the character and method of his chronological work.

[Col. 0606B] Marianus was born in 1028 in Ireland, which writers of that period called Scotland [Note: [Col. 0606D] Everything I state is narrated by Marianus himself under these years.], and was apparently called Moelbrig in his native language [Note: [Col. 0606D] The verses with which the author first concluded his work (year 1098) seem to say that the first letter of each word contains his name. If these are collected, one obtains: “Moelbrigte clausenair romtin (l)ol.” *Moelbrigte* appears to be an Irish proper name; *clausenair* perhaps means “enclosed man.” The same words occur twice above, columns 601–603 (*amelbrigte clúsenair*); I myself understand nothing of the remainder.]. At the age of twenty-four he left the world and perhaps then took the name Marianus. Four years later, in 1056, following the example of many countrymen, he went from Ireland to Germany and was received at Cologne into the Scottish monastery dedicated to Saint Martin, which flourished in the eleventh century under Abbots Helias and Majolus.

Not long afterward, in 1058, he went to Fulda, accompanying Abbot Ecbert, with whom he first went to Paderborn to pray at the tomb of Paternus the Scot, who had allowed himself to be burned there. In the following year [Col. 0607A], he was ordained a priest at Würzburg by Sigefrid, abbot of Fulda, who had succeeded Ecbert, and was immediately enclosed at Fulda, following the example of Animchad the Scot. Standing at Animchad’s feet, as Marianus himself puts it, he sang Mass every day for ten years [Note: [Col. 0607C] Year 1065 (1043).].

Hardly before 1069, when he was released at the command of the archbishop of Mainz and the abbot, he went to Mainz, where he “was enclosed a second time for his sins.” He seems to have died there in 1082 or 1083, before being released [Note: [Col. 0607C] For under the year 1082, after the history has ended in the autograph manuscript, the same hand wrote: “Marianus the enclosed man died.” These words, later crossed out and supplemented by a brief continuation, are now read between the years 1086 and 1087, but can belong to neither year. The *Annals of Saint Dysibod* (manuscript 3), which assign his death to the earlier year, were copied from this manuscript; and Trithemius too, *Chronicle of Hirsau* I, p. 281, found that year there.], and he was buried at the monastery of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0607D] What Aventinus, who counts Marianus among the sources of Book V, relates about him (Ingolstadt edition, pp. 494, 553) concerns another Marianus Scotus of the same period, the abbot of Regensburg. See Raderus, *Bavaria Sancta* II, pp. 217–222; *Acts of the Saints*, February II, pp. 361 ff. (On p. 365 the life of this Marianus is published).].

One recognizes a man completely removed from secular affairs, who, enclosed in a very narrow cell and constantly engaged in contemplation of divine matters, sought to attain tranquility of mind and salvation of soul; [Col. 0607B] and one might therefore easily believe that he devoted himself solely to pious exercises and ascetic concerns. Yet he raised his mind higher: in the solitude where he lived, he devoted himself to study [Note: [Col. 0607D] In addition to the chronicle (see below, note 110), Trithemius also attributes letters to Marianus, *Chronicle of Hirsau* I, p. 207. I would think that he invented them in his customary manner, unless on p. 208 he expressly said: “To him—Arnold of Trier—Marianus Scotus, an enclosed monk, sent an elegant letter.” Vossius, *On Latin History* II.47, p. 385, attributes commentaries on the Psalter to Marianus together with Aventinus; these were written by another Scottish writer of the same name (compare no. 22). I believe the manuscript mentioned by Lambecius was written by the same person; see *Commentaries* II, p. 749. It contains Paul’s letters, copied by Marianus’s hand in 1079 and furnished with interlinear and marginal commentaries. What Vossius adds—“Indeed, the learned Cujacius also attributes to this Marianus Scotus the *Notice of the Roman Empire*, an outstanding work”—will no longer persuade anyone.], and by this gained no ordinary distinction both among his contemporaries and among posterity.

“Marianus Scotus,” says Sigebertus [Note: [Col. 0608C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 159; compare the *Chronicle*, years 1061 and 1082.], “journeying for Christ through Gaul and becoming a monk near Mainz, lived enclosed for many years and wrote a chronicle from the birth of Christ to the year 1082 after Christ’s birth. With remarkable subtlety he demonstrated the error of earlier chroniclers, who placed Christ’s birth in such a way that the year of his Passion, as regards chronological computation, does not agree with the evangelical truth. Therefore, adding twenty-two years [Note: [Col. 0608D] This should be read, not twenty-three as the edition has it; compare Sigebertus at the cited passage, chapter 171, which is published below.] to the year in which earlier writers say that Christ was born, he places in the margin of the page, alternately, on one side the years of evangelical truth and on the other the years of the false computation of the earlier writers, so that the truth and falsehood may be distinguished not only by understanding but also by sight.”

A similar testimony is offered by William of Malmesbury, the most celebrated writer of English history:

“Under this emperor,” he says [Note: [Col. 0608D] Book III, Hardy edition, § 292, vol. II, p. 470. I add Matthew of Westminster, who says as follows (Frankfurt edition, 1601, folio p. 229): “In the year of grace 1082 Marianus Scotus, lineally related to Saint Bede, examining all the books of that holy man together with many others, strove to resemble him in character and learning.” What follows he copied from Sigebertus (Robert of Torigni).], “Marinianus Scotus flourished. First a monk of Fulda and afterward enclosed at Mainz, he obtained the grace of the future life by despising the present. Having spent the long leisure of his life examining chroniclers, he detected the discrepancy between the cycles of Dionysius Exiguus and the evangelical truth. Accordingly, reckoning the years one by one from the beginning of the world, he added twenty-two years, which were missing from the aforesaid cycles; but he had few or no followers of his opinion” [Note: [Col. 0608D] For this reason William sharply castigates the sluggishness of his own age.].

In third place, let us hear also a Gaul, Orderic Vitalis, who says [Note: [Col. 0608D] Book III, Le Prevost edition, II, p. 159.]:

> “For Marianus was a monk in the monastery of Saint Alban the Martyr [Note: [Col. 0608D] This error arose because he had before his eyes the text interpolated at this monastery, as I said above, the text copied by Florence of Worcester.] near Mainz. There, following, according to his modest ability, Eusebius of Caesarea, Jerome, and other historians, he devoted himself diligently to study and generously offered to the sons of the Church, who were not themselves able to investigate matters of such importance, the sweet fruit of his long study and great labors, which he endured during a distant pilgrimage. Having carefully examined ancient and modern books, he accordingly published a chronicle in which, ranging from the beginning of the world, from the time when God fashioned Adam from the clay of the earth, through all the books of the Old and New Testaments and the histories of the Romans and Greeks, he gathered the best material and, counting the years through the periods of kings and consuls up to the day of his death, laudably divided the history into annual sections.”

From these testimonies it is clear that, already among contemporary and immediately subsequent writers, Marianus was praised not so much for the events he narrated as for establishing a firm chronological order [Col. 0608C] and defining the years elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord differently from the way the Church, together with Dionysius, had established them. Many before and after him treated the same questions, and although they could not alter common usage, they nevertheless seemed to themselves and their contemporaries to have accomplished something important [Col. 0609A] [Note: [Col. 0609D] Compare what Saint Hirsch, in his *Life of Sigebertus*, pp. 319–329, collected with his characteristic abundance of learning concerning this question, in solving which we see that Sigebertus was also engaged, while closely following Marianus’s traces.]. Marianus devoted himself entirely to these matters; let us now see how large a part of his book is occupied by them.

The following is read in the Roman manuscript [Note: [Col. 0609D] Most of this is also found in the Cottonianus (2), whose variants I thought should be added.]:

Folio 1. “Treatment of the following cycle.” On the following page, “varied according to the alphabet by a rule of letters concerning the two alphabets placed before the Kalends of the festivals, and long according to twenty-eight letters in accordance with the length of the solar cycle, but broad according to the length of the nineteen-year cycle, since it consists of nineteen letters; whatever letter you wish, look first”—[lacuna]—“and so it must always be observed.”

Folio 2. “There are nineteen solar cycles, which are contained in the great paschal cycle, and in each cycle there are twenty-eight years, which begin with the initial letters and the four concurrent letters.”

[Col. 0609B] Tables follow, displaying these cycles.

Folios 4–10. Marianus gives a catalogue of the Roman consuls, beginning as follows:

> “I. Lentulus and Marcellus. During their consulship, destructive dissensions concerning Pompey and Caesar were forged in the Senate-house at Rome. But Gaius Julius Caesar, coming to Rome from Gaul, [drove Pompey [Note: [Col. 0610D] I supplied the word in brackets from manuscript 2; it is read in manuscript 1, but has not yet been copied from it.] out of Italy, removed the gold and silver from the Roman treasury, and was the first of the Romans to hold sole power for four years and six months; he was killed on the Ides of March. Under him these consuls held office, as Cassiodorus testifies.”

> “II. Julius Caesar and Servilius,” and so forth.

554. [6. Justinian Augustus, consul for the third time.] Bede the priest and computist says the following, among other things, concerning this year, 532:

> “Dionysius, writing the paschal cycles from the year of the Lord’s [Col. 0609C] Incarnation 532, according to Dionysius himself—which is the 248th year of the tyrant Diocletian, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes—in that year the Code of Justinian was published throughout the world.”

Thus speaks Bede.

In the left margin, besides the years of the emperors, he also places the years from the birth of Christ, beginning them with year 42, under the consulship of Augustus, Lentulus, and Messala. In the right margin are placed the years of Dionysius, the first of which falls in the seventh year of Tiberius, under the consulship of Valerius and Aurelius.

Folio 10 follows:

“Another, second correction of the years of the Incarnation according to Jerome, who says that Paul spoke with Peter in Jerusalem seventeen years after his conversion; and according to Cassiodorus, who places four years between Nero and Vespasian; and according to Orosius, who says that Decius reigned for three years.”

34. “Christ suffered,” and so forth. [lacuna]

355. [3. Saint Julius the pope says the following in his decretal letter concerning this year: “In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, while Constantine and Constans Augustus were also reigning, in the fourth year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction,” and the rest.]

Year 3 is the third year of Constantius and Constans; the years of the emperors are always indicated in this way.

Folio 11 follows:

“Third correction of the years of the Incarnation, in a third line of evidence, according to the martyrology, the passions of the popes, and their decretal letters, which the aforesaid popes sent on particular Kalends and wrote under specified consuls. In these sources it is stated that Decius reigned for ten years, with ecclesiastical authority confirming this for each year, from Pope Fabian, who suffered under Decius, to Saint Laurence, who suffered under Decius.”

[Col. 0610B] Folio 12:

> “34. 18. 1. Tiberius Caesar, consul for the fifth time. Cassiodorus says as follows: ‘12. Tiberius reigned for twenty-three years. Under these consuls our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, 8.’”

Kalends of April, and so forth. [lacuna]

> “[267. 9. Valerian and Decius. 245.”

Another decretal letter of Pope Sixtus:

> “‘To our most beloved brothers established throughout the provinces of Spain, Sixtus the bishop sends greetings. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, under the consulship of Valerian and Decius.’

> “In the martyrology, concerning the conflict of Sixtus, Felicissimus, Agapitus, Hippolytus, Saint Laurence, and others against Decius, and since they suffered under him in the month of August, there is abundant and sufficient testimony throughout the whole Church. It will never be erased, and it must be believed much more than the chronicles.”

[Col. 0610C] “Gallus, Volusianus.

Cassiodorus, the expositor of the Psalter, says:

> “Under these consuls Decius built public baths and ordered them to be called by his own name.”

Decius was killed together with his son at Abritus, a place in Thrace, by the Goths. Gallus succeeded him, together with his son Volusianus; they reigned for two years and four months, but, as regards the consulship, for only two years, and the rest.

In the left margin are the years from the birth of Christ according to Marianus, as well as the years of the emperors. The third number, which is initially read as I–XIIII and I–XXV, is later omitted; I do not know what it signifies. In the right margin, as usual, he places the years from the birth of Christ according to the reckoning of Dionysius.

The following is added on the reverse of folio 14:

“Recapitulation [Note: [Col. 0610D] This is absent from manuscript 2.] of the empire. For a confirmation is a repetition commending each matter.”

The years of the preceding tables, corrected and expanded, are read again.

Folio 25 verso is blank, and at this point the second hand—which, as I said above, wrote the earlier folios of the book—comes to an end; then begins the hand that wrote the greater part of the book on paper. The Chronicle itself also begins here; the preceding material scarcely coheres with it, but seems to have been prefixed later in order to illustrate and explain the author’s opinion more fully. Since this is so, I believe that these folios 25 were written only after the Chronicle had been completed and were then placed at the beginning of the volume; I trust that the order of the quires will confirm this.

Thus, on folio 26, Marianus’s own work begins as follows:

## In the name of holy divinity

The inquiry into Christ’s resurrection begins, which Marianus the Irishman, the recluse, compiled.—We are instructed by a divine command that what we wish others to do for us, we should willingly bestow upon them. Therefore, since I would gladly receive from anyone an explanation of when the Lord’s resurrection day occurred, and [why?
