(absent in MS 1)] the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, according to the chronicle of Eusebius or of Bede the presbyter, or even the thirty-fifth year of the great cycle of Dionysius—this year, because the second year of that same cycle is said to be the year of the Lord’s birth [MS 1: *nativis*, “births”], is assigned to the Lord’s Passion—agrees with the evangelical truth and with the Church, which asserts that the Lord was handed over on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, that is, at the Jewish Passover, on the fifth day of the week, and was crucified on the sixth day, Good Friday, on the fifteenth day of the moon, and also with the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, which shows that he rose on 27 March, while those who hold the remaining [Note: [Col. 0613] MS 1, supplied by a second hand in the margin: *horum*, “of these”; MS 2: *nihil horum*, “none of these things.”] contradict—this I have finally obtained, though only with great labor, partly by magisterial authority [Note: [Col. 0613] MS 2: *magistra*.] and partly under the guidance of reason. If there is anyone who will accept what is offered in this spirit of charity, I present it devotedly, on the condition that, if it pleases him, he give thanks to God; but, if not, that he cease gnawing me with a dog’s tooth, especially since I recommend nothing that is not supported either by authority or by reason.

Three opinions, then, concerning Christ’s resurrection are handed down, and it is said that no one, or scarcely anyone, has been able to write down with certainty which of these is true, and so forth.

When this section is complete, the following is read on folio 27 verso:

## HERE BEGINS THE CLEAR CHRONICLE OF MARIANUS SCOTUS

The chapters of the three books follow, and finally the text itself.

In the first book, after prefacing chronological investigations, he brought the Chronicle down to the time of Christ; in the second, he treated chiefly the history of Christ and the apostles, illuminating the evangelists’ words, which he quoted beforehand, from the books of Augustine, Gregory, Bede, and others; in the third, he continued the account of events from that point to his own age. The index of chapters, edited below, will indicate more precisely what is treated in each book.

Marianus carried his history down to the year 1095 (1073), and added a chronological note and verses at the year 1098 (1076), with which he brought the work to an end. Afterwards he inserted events belonging to 1096 and 1097, and on folio [Col. 0614D] 166, in the same second hand, added a continuation down to the year 1104 (1082), apparently written at different times. After Marianus’s death, while the codex was being preserved in the monastery, others added a short continuation in new lines; most of it is taken from the Annals of Würzburg, or, more correctly, from the Annals of Saint Alban’s at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0613D] On the lower part of folio 166 verso, the following words were also added in a twelfth-century hand, as I mentioned above: “Marianus the recluse died.”]

[Note: [Col. 0613D] On the last folio, 170, this page was added in a twelfth-century hand: “With our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the times of the most devout and serene lords, the emperors Mauricius Tiberius and Theodosius, in the thirteenth year of that lord Mauricius, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifth day of the month of July, Pope Gregory, seated before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle, with all the bishops and presbyters of the Roman Church seated, and the deacons and clergy standing by, said: ‘In this holy Roman Church, over which divine providence has willed me to preside, a very reprehensible custom has long since arisen: certain men chosen as singers for the ministry of the sacred altar, and established in the order of deacons, serve with the modulation of their voices, though they ought properly to be free for the work of preaching and the practice of almsgiving. Consequently it often happens that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected, and the singer, the Lord’s minister, is encouraged in his morals while he delights the people with his voice. Therefore, by the present decree I establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar must not sing, but should perform only the office of reading the Gospel during the solemn celebrations of Mass; the psalms and the remaining readings, however, I decree should be delivered by subdeacons, or, if necessity requires, by those in the minor orders. If anyone attempts to act against this decree of mine, let him be anathema.’ And they all replied: ‘Let him be anathema,’ and so forth.”]

I have already said that, when composing his universal Chronicle, Marianus wished to treat chronology rather than history. He was therefore occupied chiefly with correctly determining the years from Christ’s birth and with other questions of this kind; he described the events themselves briefly from other books, and explained at somewhat greater length only those that seemed relevant to his purpose. Nevertheless, he collected and read a considerable number of volumes, using them as guides in narrating the history of ancient times. As far as I have been able to discover, the following materials were available to him [Note: [Col. 0615C] What Semler said about Marianus’s sources (Beiträge, p. 88, 142) concerns the interpolated text and is therefore of no importance. I have indicated the sources of the third book everywhere in the margin; I read Books I and II both in the Frankfurt and in the Cottonian codex, and although I sometimes cite Struve’s edition, I always took account of the manuscripts, so as not to foist upon Marianus material belonging to the continuator.]: Sacred Scripture; the works of Josephus [Note: [Col. 0615C] At year 53 and following. What is cited from his book Against Apion, p. 486 (Struve’s edition), seems to have been copied from Bede.] and Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History [Note: [Col. 0615D] II, 32; II, 49; III, year 67, etc.] in Rufinus’s translation [Note: [Col. 0615D] Rufinus is also cited at II, 23; some Ursinus or other at II, 62.]; Eusebius’s Chronicle, translated and continued by Jerome [Note: [Col. 0615D] Compare year 341. He cites the earlier part under Eusebius’s name.]; from Jerome’s genuine or spurious works: the letters to Damasus [Note: [Col. 0615D] p. 469 (I, 13).] and Vitalis [Note: [Col. 0615D] p. 499 (I, 17).], Against Helvidius [Note: [Col. 0615D] year 64.], the letter to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0615D] year 144.], the letter to Paula and Eustochium [Note: [Col. 0615D] year 35.], commentaries on Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0615D] p. 506 (I, 18), p. 524 (I, 21); II, 16.], Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0615D] p. 511 (I, 19).], Matthew [Note: [Col. 0615D] II, 49; compare II, 3, etc. Perhaps he also possessed the commentary on Luke inscribed with Jerome’s name, years 13 and 31.] and the Epistle to the Galatians [Note: [Col. 0615D] year 35.], the Book of Hebrew Questions [Note: [Col. 0616B] p. 457 (I, 11).], the Life of Saint Paula [Note: [Col. 0616B] year 425.] and the Martyrology that bore his name [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 24; III, year 33. These items, however, are not found in the martyrology published under Jerome’s name.]; the “Contests of the Apostles” [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 70, 71.]; Clement’s Book of Recognitions [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 70.]; Ambrose (on Luke?) [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 49, 67.]; Augustine, On the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 2, 24.] and especially the book On the Harmony of the Evangelists [Note: [Col. 0616B] Marianus follows this work throughout the second book; compare I, 13.]; homilies of Maximus [Note: [Col. 0616B] II, 23. Perhaps, however, he copied this passage and others in which he cites Tertullian (year 39), etc., from his own sources.]; the Passion of Saint Valentine [Note: [Col. 0616C] year 33.] and of other saints; Orosius’s History [Note: [Col. 0616C] p. 526 (I, 21); II, 6, 18, 19, etc. He used it very frequently in the third book.]; the chronicles of Prosper, Cassiodorus, Isidore (and Melitus [Note: [Col. 0616C] At A 551 he says: “as is found in the chronicle of Isidore the bishop or in the exposition of Melitus”; elsewhere he names Isidore, years 263 and 321.—We have identified the codex used by Marianus as the Parisian manuscript 4860, which formerly seems to have been Mainz property. It contains the chronicles of Jerome, Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes, Melitus—under this name he gives the title of Isidore’s book—Bede, and the paschal letters of Dionysius, Paschasinus, and others, finally the Annals of Augia together with that contemporary notice of William, archbishop of Mainz; we see that all of these were copied by Marianus. In Prosper’s Chronicle Marianus everywhere follows the text found here—the same text published by Canisius from the Augustan codex—except in the years 466 and 477, where he follows the common reading. It is easy to show that Hermann of Augia also used a similar codex, from which this one may perhaps have been copied.]); Bede’s Chronicles; the Tripartite History [Note: [Col. 0616D] Years 341 and following, which he attributes to Bishop Theodore.]; Isidore’s Etymologies [Note: [Col. 0616D] p. 511 (I, 19); II, 8.]; Jordanes’s book on the succession of kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0616D] He names it himself at year 496 and elsewhere]; Bede’s works, both chronological and theological: the books On the Reckoning of Time and On Times [Note: [Col. 0616D] Compare years 725 (703) and 747 (725). The Ecclesiastical History of the English People is occasionally cited by the second hand; see years 168, 201, 416, 431, 445 n.]; commentaries on Genesis [Note: [Col. 0616D] I, 10.], Daniel [Note: [Col. 0616D] p. 511 (I, 22).], the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0616D] Book II, passim.], and the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0616D] year 40 and following], as well as revisions [Col. 0616B] of this book [Note: [Col. 0616D] years 37 and 67.] and the martyrology [Note: [Col. 0616D] year 67 (80).]; Saint Lucian’s letter [Note: [Col. 0616D] year 437. It was published by Surius, Acta Sanctorum, August, day 3.]; the letters of Dionysius and Theophilus on the reckoning of Easter, which he copied in full [Note: [Col. 0616D] I, I, 3; compare years 459 and 548, V, n. 26.]; Paschasinus’s letter on the same subject [Note: [Col. 0616D] year 439, 466, V, n. 26.]; Victor’s letter [Col. 0617A] to Pope Hilary [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 554.]; the letters of Leo the Great [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 475; compare year 472.]; Gregory the Great’s Dialogues [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 521 and following] and Homilies on the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0617C] II, 6, 7, 15, etc.—II, 49. Gregory is cited on Mark.]; the Life of Gregory the Great [Note: [Col. 0617C] years 623 and 626.]; the Life of Saint Martin by Sulpicius Severus [Note: [Col. 0617C] years 337, 352, and following]; the Life of Saint Eliphius [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 381]; the Life of Saint Maurus [Note: [Col. 0617C] See note at year 625]; the Life of Saint Columbanus [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 611]; perhaps also the deeds of Saint Patrick [Note: [Col. 0617C] year 394 and following. I was unable to compare the older, three-part Life of Saint Patrick with Marianus.]; Ado’s Martyrology, from which he copied the Passions of the popes [Note: [Col. 0617D] I used the Roman edition of 1745, folio. Some material that is relegated here to the Appendix was copied by Marianus.]; he also possessed the Book of the Pontiffs, from which he inserted much, especially in his second revision [Note: [Col. 0617D] Later he added another series of popes on the basis of this work.], and perhaps another history of the Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0617D] Thus, at year 338, I would not suppose that the actual Book of the Pontiffs was in his hands. Perhaps he took everything written in the first hand about the Roman pontiffs from such a book.], certainly a shorter catalogue carried down to the tenth century [Note: [Col. 0617D] He copied this catalogue on folio 16. From it arose the error at year 987 (965) and following.]. He seems to have taken the decretal letters of the popes from the collection of canons falsely attributed to Isidore [Note: [Col. 0617D] I used the royal Paris collection of councils of 1715.]. Finally, in the first part of the Chronicle he used Paul the Deacon’s Roman History [Note: [Col. 0617D] II, 19, 26. In the third book he cites it on almost every page, from year 384, and appeals to Eutropius as still living. Perhaps he also used the Miscellaneous History.] and History of the Lombards [Col. 0617B]. It is therefore clear that he investigated the events of ancient times with great diligence; perhaps he even read Pliny the Elder himself [Note: [Col. 0617D] I, 10.]. When, however, he reached periods closer to his own time, he could not use so many sources; apart from Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne, Thegan’s Life of Louis the Pious, Regino’s Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0617D] He did not possess the continuation.], and finally the Annals of Augia [Note: [Col. 0617D] See V, n. 69.] and of Hersfeld [Note: [Col. 0618C] Compare what I said in Archiv, VI, p. 674. Perhaps he also used them at years 934 (912) and 937 (915). Later I found no trace of them, however.], he had no works to follow. Marianus likewise added nothing to the history of these years except a catalogue of the archbishops of Mainz and the abbots of Fulda, which he could easily have collected or compiled from local records. Deprived of these sources, he provides almost nothing beyond a brief account of the emperors, popes [Note: [Col. 0618C] He confused their order in a remarkable way; but he himself noticed the error, which arose because, after John XII, he inserted six popes in a second hand—of whom he apparently obtained the first three, John, Stephen, and Stephen, from an unknown source, while he placed the next three, Marinus, Agapitus, and Octavian, whom he had already listed once, a second time. “We are uncertain,” he says at year 987 (965), “about these popes.” Earlier, too, he forced Marinus into the sequence at year 907 (885), and Basil at year 912 (890).], archbishops of Mainz, and abbots of Fulda; in addition, from the eleventh century onward he reviews the periods of kings, abbots, and Irish monks, and finally briefly touches upon events in both Church and state during the last years. Some readers may value what he reports, both in Latin and in Irish, about the princes of that land; others will find it welcome that the travels of Irish abbots and monks and their various deeds are faithfully recorded. Everyone, however, will readily concede that German history itself will gain little from this book. It must nevertheless be kept in mind that Marianus in no way intended to write the history of his own time; he sought only to publish a very brief overview of events, arranged by years in what seemed to him the correct order. He was therefore especially useful to those who had a similar purpose, particularly to that famous writer of his age, Sigebert, who not only strongly approved Marianus’s method of computation but also transferred much from him into his own chronography [Note: [Col. 0618D] This was already perceived and explained with considerable acumen by the distinguished Hirsch, De vita et scriptis Sigeberti, pp. 113–122. In Bethmann’s edition, which had been printed before I could complete this work, some passages taken from Marianus are not indicated. Add year 1077: “Hildibrandus—they contradict,” “the emperor—devastates”; year 1079: “Heinricus—designates,” where Sigebert added only a few words of his own. The account given at year 1085 of Gregory’s death also seems to have been taken from Marianus’s Gembloux codex; see below, at year 1105.], undoubtedly using the Gembloux codex, which I mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0618D] Cols. 604, 606.].

In Germany I found Marianus copied only rarely by medieval writers, first in the so-called Annals of Würzburg, which were compiled at the monastery of Saint Alban’s in Mainz—where, as I have already mentioned, Marianus’s work was revised and expanded shortly after his death—from the Chronicle of Würzburg and Marianus [Note: [Col. 0618D] The following entries derive from Marianus: years 782, 792, 794 (“Fastrada—died”), 798, 801, 803, 805, 813, 824, 846, 855 (“Rabanus,” etc.), 863, 868 (“It was seen,” etc.), 879, 891 (“Sunderoldus,” etc.), (927, 936, 953, 968, 970?), 1001 (“at Mainz”), 1011 and 1020, namely the passages concerning the archbishops of Mainz.]; later in the Annals of Saint Dysibod, about which I have said enough above.

But when Marianus’s Chronicle was taken to England, it gained great authority among the writers of that land. For when Florence of Worcester undertook to write a new chronicle, he laid it down as his foundation, adding only material relating to English affairs [Note: [Col. 0618D] On these matters, compare Lappenberg, History of England, I, p. LVIII.]; he followed, if I am not mistaken, the Cottonian codex itself, or at least one very similar to it, since he faithfully copied both its continuation and its text [Col. 0619A]. Florence (d. 1118) carried the history down to the year 1117 (1139), and others continued it to 1131 (1153) and 1154 (1178) [Note: [Col. 0619C] Perhaps Orderic saw this book; he says, in the passage cited, that John of Worcester, at the command of Bishop Wulstan, composed the events of nearly one hundred years and inserted them into Marianus’s Chronicles, “in which he usefully and concisely disclosed many things about the Romans, Franks, Alamanni, and other peoples that he had come to know, worthy of narration.” He testifies that he saw this work at Worcester in England.]. Florence appeared to follow Marianus’s traces so closely that his Chronicle is usually entitled with Marianus’s name [Note: [Col. 0619C] Most manuscripts preserved in English libraries contain Florence; with the continuation to 1131 (1154): London, Lambeth Palace VII, 83; Oxford, Corpus Christi College manuscripts IV, 112 and VII, 94 (Petrie used both manuscripts in the new edition of Florence; see below); Bodleian 2468; manuscripts Arch. IV, 112 and VII, 90; and with the continuation to 1154 (1178): Bodleian 2182, Arch. VII, 90. I know nothing definite about the Cambridge manuscript of the eleventh century (Arch. III, 442; Arch. VII, 86) or the Middlehill manuscript (Arch. VII, 96); nor do I know the Oxford manuscript of Magdalen College, in which Roger of Hoveden—whose work is discussed by Lappenberg in the cited passage, p. LXI—is said to have continued Marianus (Arch. VII, 95). A London manuscript also shows that the History of Henry of Huntingdon is found under Marianus’s name: Arundel 46 (Arch. VIII, p. 754).]. Even before Florence, Robert of Hereford, who flourished at the end of the eleventh century [Note: [Col. 0619D] Compare William of Malmesbury, IV.], used Marianus’s work; he did not copy it in full, however, but abridged it, and the abridgment is sometimes embellished with Marianus’s name [Note: [Col. 0619D] In the Cottonian manuscript: “Here begins the book of Marianus Scotus by birth, excerpted from the books of the evangelists or from the teachers”; but in the Bodleian manuscript, more correctly: “Here begins Robert, bishop of Hereford’s excerpt from the Chronicle of Marinarius.” I took this from the Wrocław copy. Compare Stenzel, Arch. IV, p. 118.]. I have already said that William of Malmesbury and Matthew of Westminster praised Marianus’s work highly; nevertheless, I doubt whether they actually copied it [Note: [Col. 0619D] Lappenberg, in the cited passage, p. LXV, maintains that Matthew did so.]. I have often found other excerpts made from Marianus in English libraries [Note: [Col. 0619D] Compare the material collected by Stenzel, Arch. IV, p. 116.—The work of an Englishman, a member of Merton College at Oxford, written against Marianus’s errors and cited by Vossius in the cited passage and by Struve, p. 447, from Pithoeus’s De sanctis Anglis, appears to belong to a later period.], which show that this book, although not genuine, but nevertheless containing Marianus’s labors, circulated in the hands of many people.

At the end of the fifteenth century Trithemius saw Marianus’s Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0620C] He not only recorded the beginnings of the books (On the Saints of the Church, chapter 40), but also copied some passages from the Chronicle itself; see Chronicle of Hirschau, year 104, concerning Animchad the Irishman. What he reports there about the monk Clarus, citing Marianus—“Marianus Scotus, a monk of Fulda, records much about this most holy man in his compilations, and other miracles of saints who flourished in his time”—is not found there at all. See year 1062. He incorrectly distinguishes (On the Saints of the Church, cited passage) the books on the harmony of the evangelists and on computation from the Chronicle, since they constitute only parts of it. Nevertheless, the work sometimes seems to have been copied separately. Cave cites such a manuscript: Cotton E. 4, no. 26, now so badly burned that nothing apart from Bede’s On the Reckoning of Time can be made out (Catalogue of the Cottonian Manuscripts, p. 40).]; perhaps Aventinus as well [Note: [Col. 0620C] See above, n. 25.]. Apart from these, as far as I know, no one in Germany used it until Herold, having obtained the Frankfurt codex, published its first part under Marianus’s name: *Mariani Scoti chronica*—to which we added Martin of Poland’s History—“all now published for the first time,” Basel, J. Oporinus [at the end it reads: “by J. Parcus, 1559”], small folio. Pistorius followed this edition (I, p. 266; Struve’s edition I, p. 448) [Note: [Col. 0620C] Excerpts taken from it may be found in Bouquet V, 368–370; VI, 227; VII, 241; VIII, 269; XI, 73.]. Herold did not publish the book with the diligence and scrupulousness that were appropriate, but he was falsely accused of enlarging the text with arbitrary additions [Col. 0620A] [Note: [Col. 0620D] Stenzel also made this accusation, Frankish Emperor I, p. 136.]. For whatever we find attributed to Marianus is found in codex 3, whose scribe plainly intended not to copy Marianus at all, but to compose a new chronicle.

Therefore we may rightly say that Marianus’s Chronicle has until now remained unpublished. Many will join us in wishing that it be published in full [Note: [Col. 0620D] Miraeus, Schottus, Usserius, Vossius, Wadingus, and Hasius considered producing an edition of Marianus; compare the passages collected by Stenzel, Arch. IV, pp. 106–117. Everyone will regret with me that the distinguished Stenzel himself abandoned this plan.]. Nevertheless, this could not be done in this collection of German historical writings, in which we thought only the third book should be included, since, after the longer investigations have been completed in the second book, it contains a narrative of events beginning with Christ’s birth and is useful to us and to others for many reasons.

In preparing this edition I followed the Roman codex with the greatest possible accuracy [Col. 0620B]. Its final part, beginning with the year 741, had already been compared with printed editions several years ago by the distinguished Heyse; now the highly learned and most friendly Giesebrecht, while staying in Rome to collect new materials for the illumination of the history of Gregory VII, examined it with the greatest care, partly transcribing it and partly using it to correct the printed text. I do not wish readers to remain unaware that Giesebrecht was convinced that what was written by the first hand should be attributed to Marianus himself. Although I can scarcely, if at all, be brought to adopt the same position, I nevertheless took care to reproduce almost every word of the codex with the utmost accuracy and conscientiousness; and whatever was added by the second hand, whether in the text or in the margin, I enclosed in parentheses [Note: [Col. 0620D] Here and there the first hand also added material later; I indicated in the notes where and by whom such additions were written. But the second hand also wrote in the upper and lower margins material that has no connection whatsoever with the Chronicle and that was noted by the author for another purpose, especially excerpts from the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs. I omitted these. So that readers may not be surprised, I shall give one or two examples. On folio 101, where the third book begins, the following appears: “8 August, second feria: ‘Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven,’ and so forth. B. By the statement that on the sixth day they will gather twice as much, it is shown that manna was first given from heaven on the Lord’s Day; for the sixth day after the Lord’s Day is the Sabbath. Therefore the living bread descended on the Lord’s Day like rain upon the fleece (read: rain upon the earth).” On folio 106, in the upper margin: “Part five, canon 34; Pope Innocent, canon 52: If a catechumen has had a wife, and after her death has taken another after baptism, he cannot be a cleric. The marital union, because it is completed by God’s command, is not a sin, and therefore cannot be dissolved among sins at baptism. A bigamist, and likewise a man who is not the husband of one virgin wife, cannot, according to the apostle, be admitted to the presbyterate or the clergy. In the canons of the apostles, canon 17, in part five, canon 32: If anyone, after baptism, has entered into a second marriage or has had a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor in any way belong to those who serve in sacred ministry.” In the lower margin of the same place: “Gregory says in his Life: ‘If, having been established in the sacred order, you remember yourself to have been defiled by intercourse with a woman, after laying aside the honor of the priesthood you must in no way presume to approach ministry; know that you minister at the peril of your soul and will undoubtedly render an account to our God if, conscious of this crime, you wish to remain in the order in which you are, concealing the truth.’ Again Gregory: ‘The deacon Florentius of the church of Ravenna, who is remembered to have been chosen by all, if, after touching the most sacred Gospels, he gave an oath, as has been reported to us,’ and so forth.”]

I myself also believe that the codex’s distinctive orthography should be attributed to Marianus, and I did not wish to correct it. So that it may not offend the reader excessively, several points should be noted here. Sometimes a double letter is written where a single one should occur—*occuli*, *deffectio*, *martirologgium*, *civille*, *tulli*, *appollogeticum*—especially *ss* for *s*: *cassus*, *Caessar*, *Dionissius*, *divissio*, *misser*, *occissus*, *vissus*, *quassi*, *ressurrectio*, *ducentissimus*, *millessimus*, and many others; also *uu* for *u*: *manuus*, *Asiniuus*; *ii* for *i*: *imbrii*. At other times a single letter is written where a double one should occur: *efectus*, *Apia*, *suplicium*, *occurere*, *misio*, *pasio*, *possesio*, *posidet*, *grasari*, *scripsise*, *disperaset*. There is *b* for *v*: *Libius*, *labaretur*; *v* for *b*: *favae*, *-vit* for *-bit*; *st* for *z*: *Stacheus* for *Zacheus*, *Stenno* for *Zeno*; and *z* for *st*: *evangeliza*, *Zeppanus* for *Stephanus. There is *e* for *i*: *prespeter*, *demedius*, *marteribus*, *exteterunt*; and *i* for *e*: *disertum*, *disperare*, *comidebant*, *moriretur*, *inspiciret*, *terremotus*. There is also *te* or *ei* for *i* or *e*: *scribiens*, *preleio*. Sometimes an *e* or *i* is added: *thermeae*, *pupilice*, that is, *publice*.

The use of the letter *a* is distinctive: it is written for *e*, *i*, *o*, and sometimes without any apparent reason: *Alaxandria*, *Gallianus* and *Galleianus*, *adjactio*, *centias*, *mulliare*, *libare*; *aparatione* for *apparitione*, *margano* for *margine*; *Constantinapolis*, *videabaris*, *conhoartatur*, *Ticianum*, *Nicomedenasis* for *Nicomediensis*, *Laudacia* for *Laodicea*. As in the last word, *u* is also used for *o*—*consulatus*—unless this should rather be attributed to an error of the pen. Certainly I have either explained in this way or supposed to have been written for the sake of abbreviating words other forms that occur, especially where a syllable resembling the preceding one is omitted: *testa*, *vasta* for *testata*, *vastata*, *deputi* for *deputati*, *superstio* for *superstitio*. In other cases the practice is so consistent that it can scarcely be denied that these forms were written deliberately—for example, *sangis linga*; *eugelium* for *evangelium* occurs frequently and may perhaps have been the author’s pronunciation.

He follows a definite rule in using *i* for *ii* in the genitive, ablative, and so forth: *Juli*, *Antoni*, *Arri*, *Dionissi*, *euangeli*, *demedi* for *dimidii*; *operaris*. Yet forms are also found that violate the laws of Latin very seriously, and I remain uncertain whether to attribute them to the author or to the scribe. I therefore adopted the policy of correcting only the most offensive and obvious errors; elsewhere I preserved the codex’s reading and occasionally indicated what ought to be read. I could have done this more extensively by investigating and comparing all the sources, but I omitted it so as not to become too lengthy. For the same reason I indicated less often the corrections made by codices 2 and 3. I did not wish to report the additions of codex 3; but I edited what is found in 2, 2*, and 2**, as well as the short continuation from 2.

A copy of the Cottonian codex [Col. 0622B] (2) was partly made by the distinguished Faerber at the expense of our society and partly had already been transcribed by Usserius for the use of J. Vossius; it is now preserved in the university library at Wrocław, from which we received it through the kindness of the distinguished Elvenich, the library director. The same volume [Note: [Col. 0622C] From Vossius’s library it passed into Blondel’s, then into Burmann’s; from there to Frankfurt on the Oder, and finally to Wrocław. It was discussed by Hausen, *De antiquissimo codice chronici Mariani Scotti Gemblacensi exemploque ejus Schottiano ad edendum parato*, Dessau, 1782, quarto, and more accurately by Stenzel, Arch. II, pp. 105–111.] contains Herold’s edition from the Gembloux codex (2*), corrected by Schottus, apparently later from the Frankfurt codex (3), though rather carelessly. Bethmann, our colleague, transcribed the Liège codex (2**) more accurately and compared its most important readings with the printed editions. The distinguished Böhmer kindly sent the Frankfurt codex (3) to Hanover, so that I was able to use it [Note: [Col. 0622D] Apart from these I know no other manuscripts of Marianus. I have listed above the English manuscripts that contain Florence or other later chroniclers. The French manuscripts bearing this title contain Robert of Auxerre, a monk of Saint Marianus; compare Arch. VII, p. 195. The book of Count Forbin (Arch. I, p. 64) also seems to belong here.]; but I consulted it less often, since in another volume of this collection I shall publish the Annals of Saint Dysibod, which seemed not to belong here. Whatever in Florence’s Chronicle and its continuation contributes to the illumination of German history, however, I have thought it appropriate to add here.

Kiel, 1 May 1844.  
G. WAITZ

[Col. 0623]

## THE CHRONICLE OF MARIANUS SCOTUS, EDITED BY G. WAITZ, PROFESSOR PUBLICUS AT KIEL

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores V, 495.)

## HERE BEGINS THE CLEAR CHRONICLE OF MARIANUS SCOTUS

### HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK

(Folio 27)

[Col. 0623A] 1. On Dionysius Exiguus’s discussion concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection. 2. On the evangelical reckoning against him. 3. On investigating the beginning of the world and the beginning of the first week of the age. 4. On the paschal arrangement, and on the arguments and investigations concerning the Lord’s passion and resurrection from the beginning of the world. 5. On the contradiction of these matters according to Bede’s authority in the paschal arrangement. 6. On the beginning of the world, where it is according to Bede. 7. On the great year composed from the concurrent cycles by Bede, in order to show the discrepancy of the chronicles and historians concerning Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection, and on the treatment of this same great year. [Col. 0623B] 8. On the beginning of the world, the indictions, the great cycles, and the years from that point up to the Incarnation according to Dionysius and up to the present day. 9. On the first seven days according to the sun, moon, and weekday; and on the formation of created things during seven days, concerning the unformed matter [Note: Thus the manuscript, for *creatarum* (“created”).]. 10. On the fall of the first Adam, and on the threefold correction of that same fall through the second Adam, Christ, in the same order and on the same weekday and years, from the fall and from the beginning of the world up to the Incarnation and passion of the Lord, on the same weekday as the fall [Note: *Cassurae* (“of the fall”) was added by the same hand, apparently afterward, in paler ink; this is confirmed by the punctuation mark placed after *feria* (“weekday”).]. 11. On the first age of the world, beginning with its first day—that is, beginning on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, on the first [Col. 0623C] weekday—and passing in orderly succession [Col. 0624A] through each year from the birth of the fathers to their sons; and on the death of the patriarchs in that age, up to the Flood and Noah’s departure from the ark. 12. On the second age of the world, in the aforesaid order of fathers and sons, up to the birth of Abraham. 13. On Saint Augustine’s correction in the second age [Note: *Eatate* in the manuscript.], as witnessed by Bede. 14. On the loss discovered in that same second age, according to Luke the Evangelist [Note: *Eatis* in witness 1.]. 15. On the division of the earth among Noah’s sons; on languages, genealogies, and Nimrod’s tower. 16. On the third age according to the order of the patriarchs and leaders, from Abraham to David. 17. On the fourth age, arranged through fathers and sons, from David to the captivity and burning of Solomon’s [Col. 0624B] temple. 18. On Saint Jerome’s treatment, reckoning from Hezekiah’s sixth year to Ahasuerus. 19. On the feast days of the Law and the time of the burning [Note: Thus the manuscript, for *combustionis* (“of the burning”).] of Solomon’s temple by Nebuchadnezzar, according to Isidore and Jerome. 20. On the fifth age, arranged from the burning of the temple to the Incarnation of Christ, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixth weekday, when the archangel Gabriel announced it to Saint Mary. 21. On Saint Bede’s computation in the same age, counting seventy weeks—that is, 475 years—from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes to Christ. 22. On the individual years under their respective consuls, from Julius [Col. 0624C] Caesar to Christ.

## The Chapters of the Second Book Begin Here, Which Is from the Incarnation to the Lord’s Ascension (fol. 28)

[Col. 0623]

1. On investigating the birth of John the Baptist, guided by ecclesiastical authority. 2. On resolving that question. 3. On the announcement of Christ’s Incarnation to Saint Mary, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixth weekday, through the archangel Gabriel; and on Saint Mary’s departure to Elizabeth, remaining with her until the birth of John the Baptist. [Col. 0624C] 4. On the year of the reign, the nineteen-year cycle, the indiction, and the corresponding moon of the Lord’s conception according to the Law. 5. On the correspondence of the Incarnation and redemption through the second Adam, on the same sixth weekday and on the same day of the solar month on which the first Adam was created and transgressed. [Col. 0625A] 6. On the Lord’s birth in Bethlehem and the appropriate indiction of his birth. 7. How, according to Scripture, the Lord suffered after thirty-two and a half years [Note: That is, *dimidii* (“half”).], and also after thirty-four years; and how this can occur according to the Olympiads or the years of the kings, if he was baptized in his thirtieth and thirty-first years; how, according to the Gospel of John, he suffered after thirty-two and a half years [Note: That is, *dimidii* (“half”).], or, according to the Apocalypse [Note: The manuscript reads *apocolipsi*, but one letter has been erased by scraping in witness 1.], after thirty-four years. 8. On resolving the question, and on Bede’s reckoning according to the Hebrew truth [Note: Read: “truth,” not “unity.”], but the Olympiads according to the Seventy translators [Note: *Vero* (“but”) was added in witness 1.] [Note: *Computatur* (“is reckoned”) had been written, but *ur* was erased by scraping in witness 1.]. 9. On the deeds and the time of the Lord’s birth up to Herod’s death. [Col. 0625B] 10. On the Lord’s return from Egypt at the angel’s command. 11. On the Lord’s remaining in Jerusalem without his parents’ knowledge, and on the death of Caesar Octavian. 12. On Tiberius Caesar and his years, and on the Lord’s action [Note: *C.* was written below afterward in witness 1.]. 13. On the fifteenth year of Tiberius and his high priests, as treated by Bede. 14. On the harmony of the Evangelists [Note: Thus several times in place of *evangelistarum* (“of the Evangelists”) in witness 1.] according to Augustine, in the words of John the Baptist and the Lord. 15. On the Lord’s thirtieth year and baptism [Note: *De* (“on”) was added afterward in witness 1.], the dove and the assembly, according to Saint Gregory. 16. On Saint Jerome’s treatment of the prophet Ezekiel concerning the year and month of the Lord’s baptism. [Col. 0625C] 17. Likewise, Saint Augustine on the same year of Ezekiel and Christ, and on the Father’s words concerning the Son at the baptism. 18. On investigating the year of the Lord’s baptism—that is, the fifteenth year of Tiberius [Note: Thus the manuscript, witness 1?]—according to Eusebius’ or Bede’s chronicle, counting from that fifteenth year itself and the Lord’s baptism [Note: Added afterward in witness 1.] according to those chronicles up to Bede himself. 19. On demonstrating the error in the reckoning of the aforesaid chronicles, investigated even from the chronicles themselves. 20. On investigating the year of the Lord’s resurrection according to Bede, and Bede’s implicit testimony [Col. 0625D] that in that same year the Lord rose from the dead on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. 21. On the objection to the aforesaid reckoning [Note: “Of the world” was added by witness 2.]. 22. On Christ’s resurrection on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, with Bede as witness, according to the history of the Holy Gospel, and investigating it from the beginning of the world. 23. Why the resurrection is thought to have occurred on the eighth rather than the sixth day before the Kalends of April. [Col. 0626A] 24. On the passion on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and the resurrection on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, according to Saint Jerome. 25. On the same matter as Saint Augustine treats it in the fourth book of *The Holy Trinity*, and on how the Lord was in the tomb for three days and three nights. 26. On Saint Jerome’s testimony that Eusebius omitted many things in his chronicle, of which Jerome himself added several when he translated it. 27. On the Lord’s baptism on the eighth day before the Ides of January, on the Sunday of Epiphany; and on his departure into the wilderness on the following day, Monday, to fast for forty days and nights; and on the Lord’s victory over the devil on Friday, the fortieth day of his fast, concerning gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, in which the devil first cast down Adam on the same weekday; and on the Passover of that same year of the Lord’s baptism [Note: Added afterward in witness 1.]. 28. On the Lord’s first recognition by Saint Andrew and Simon, who was then first called by the name Peter; and on the calling of Saint Philip and Nathanael. 29. On Peter and Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee, being called for the first but separable time. 30. On the inseparable calling of the apostles, and on the Lord and his mother being called with his disciples to the wedding, and on the wedding’s taking place at Epiphany. 31. On the Passover and the expulsion of the merchants from the temple, while John had not yet been sent to prison. 32. On the Lord’s passage through Samaria, sitting and thirsty beside the well in the city of Samaria, Sychar; and on his passage through Galilee [Note: Added afterward in witness 1.], where he healed the son of the official who believed, together with his entire household [Note: *Domu sua* (“his household”) is written in witness 1, but signs show that the words are to be transposed; the same occurs elsewhere.]. 33. On the Lord’s second ascent to Jerusalem, as if at a second Passover, healing the paralytic. 34. On the healing of the man in the synagogue afflicted by an unclean spirit [Note: “Afflicted” (*vexati*) is to be supplied; this was added afterward in copy 2.], and of Peter’s mother-in-law from a fever. 35. On the election of the twelve apostles; the sermon of the Beatitudes while seated on the mountain; the similar sermon while standing in a level place; and the cleansing of the leper. [Col. 0626D] 36. On the centurion and his servant being healed, and on the scribe. 37. On the Lord’s passage across the changed sea [Note: *Freto motato* (“with the strait stirred”) was later corrected to *fretum mutatum* (“the sea changed”) in witness 1.], and on the words of faith, and on the blind men and the pigs. 38. On the Lord’s return across the sea, the healing of the paralytic, and the Lord’s city. [Col. 0627A] 39. On the calling of the apostle Matthew and the accusation concerning eating and drinking with tax collectors. 40. On Jairus’s daughter being raised and the woman [Note: That is, *muliere* (“woman”).] who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years being healed. 41. On the two blind men and Beelzebub [Note: *Belzpub*; afterward the letter E was written twice above it in witness 1.], and on Christ’s preaching, healing every disease and infirmity; on the harvest and the laborers; and on the sending [Note: *Demissione* in witness 1.] of the twelve apostles to preach, power over unclean spirits having been given to them. 42. On the names of the twelve apostles in order, and on the staff to be carried and not carried. 43. On Christ’s preaching after the sending of the twelve apostles; the son of the widow being raised; and the sending of two disciples by John, who was bound, to Jesus. [Col. 0627B] 44. On the Pharisee who invited the Lord to table, Mary Magdalene, and the alabaster jar. 45. On the Lord’s reproaching the cities, the confession, and the ears of grain on the Sabbath. 46. On the withered hand being healed, according to the harmony of the four Evangelists. 47. On the Pharisees and Herodians, and on the demon-possessed blind and mute man being healed. 48. On Herod and the passion of Saint John the Baptist; the miracle of the five loaves and two fish; the Passover; and the place of John’s beheading and burial. 49. On the Lord and Peter walking upon the waves while crossing the sea of Gennesaret [Note: The following words were added later in the margin by another hand in witness 1.]: during the fourth watch of the night, and on the Passover and the miracle of the loaves and fish. [Col. 0627C] 50. On the Canaanite woman and her daughter being healed; the deaf and mute man; the feeding of four thousand from seven loaves and a few fish; and the blind man being given sight, according to Mark. 51. On the Lord’s questioning his disciples, Peter’s contradiction, the Lord’s Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah, and the lunatic. 52. On the Lord’s coming from Galilee into Judea, and on the wife being dismissed. 53. On the little children and the laborers in the vineyard, the good man, and the Lord’s return to Galilee. 54. On the festival of Tabernacles. 55. On the solemn festival of the Dedication. [Col. 0627D] 56. On Lazarus being raised, the Lord coming from Galilee to Jerusalem, and one blind man being healed according to Luke when the Lord had drawn near to Jericho; and on two blind men being healed according to the other Evangelists when the Lord was leaving Jericho; and on Zacchaeus [Note: In place of “Zacchaeus,” the manuscript has *Stacheus*.] and the parables. [Col. 0628A] 57. On the Lord’s arrival at Bethany on the Sabbath six days before the Passover, and on the following day, Palm Sunday, on the tenth lunar day, in Jerusalem. 58. On the events of the first, second, and third weekdays [Note: *Que* (“and”) was added afterward in witness 1.], in order [Note: *Ordinem* (“order”) was added later in the margin in witness 1.], and many other matters. 59. On the two days before the Passover, that is, Wednesday. 60. On the first day of Unleavened Bread, that is, Thursday. 61. On the Lord’s Supper. 62. On the hymn [Note: That is, *hymno* (“hymn”).] that was sung and the Lord’s departure to Gethsemane, where he was arrested; on the events of that same night; and on Peter’s denial in order. 63. On the events of the day of Christ’s passion, his burial, and the linen cloths. 64. On the Lord’s tomb, the women, and the guards of the sepulcher. [Col. 0628B] 65. On Saturday evening, which dawns into the first day of the week, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on the seventeenth lunar day, on which Christ rose from the dead; and on the events of that day, in order, as Saint Augustine treats them according to the harmony of the four Evangelists. 66. On the testimony of the Evangelists and of Saint Paul the Apostle in the Letter to the Corinthians concerning the Lord’s appearances [Note: *Aparatione* in place of *apparitione* (“appearance”).], according to Augustine. 67. On the Lord’s bodily walking in Galilee, as Augustine treats it. 68. How many times the Lord was seen on earth and in heaven after his resurrection, as Augustine treats it according to the four Evangelists and Saint Paul. [Col. 0628C] 69. On the mystery of the Lord’s words when he said, “I will go before you into Galilee,” as treated by Saint Augustine. 70. On the passion of Saint Peter and the ordination of Saint Clement. 71. On the passion of Saint Paul [the Apostle; added afterward by another hand in witness 1.]. 72. On the passion of Saint Andrew [the Apostle; added afterward by another hand in witness 1.]. 73. On the passion of Saint James the Apostle, son of Zebedee. 74. On the falling asleep of Saint John the Evangelist. 75. On the passion of Saint Philip the Apostle [These words were added by the first hand at the very top of the margin, with a sign placed after chapter 74.]. 76. On the passion of Saint Bartholomew. 77. On the passion of Saint Thomas. 78. On the passion of the most holy Matthew. 79. On the passion of Saint James, the brother of the Lord. [Col. 0628D] 80. On the passion of Saint Thaddeus. 81. On the passion of Saint Simon the Cananaean. 82. On the death of Saint Matthias the Apostle. 83. On the seven deacons ordained by the apostles [These words were added by the first hand at the very bottom of the margin, with a sign indicating the place belonging to them in witness 1.].

## The Chapters of the Third Book Begin

[Note: The following also appears in copy 3, where many things are changed. Its heading reads: “The chapters of the following book begin.”]

[Col. 0627]

[Col. 0627D] 1. On the birth of the Lord; on his years, which are always written in red; and on the years of Caesar Octavian, written in black and arranged together in sequence under their proper consuls [Col. 0629A] [Note: Missing in witness 2.] according to Cassiodorus; and on the established events of each year up to Octavian’s death; and then [Note: The first hand continues with *tunc* after *Octaviani*; the letter *e* was added later in witness 1.], as will later be done for each king, on the total sum of the years of the Incarnation, titled from the Lord’s birth to the end of that king’s reign. 2. On Tiberius and his years, in black, but on the Lord’s years, in red, under the consuls and with the proper events, in the aforesaid order for each year, up to the nineteenth year of the Incarnation and the third year of Tiberius, where the Incarnation begins according to the chronicles of Eusebius and Bede the priest; and up to the twenty-third year of the Incarnation and the seventh year of Tiberius, [Col. 0629B] where the Incarnation begins according to Dionysius, which from that point is always written in black in the margin [Note: *Margano*, for *margine* (“in the margin”).], on the right-hand side. The kings also inscribed in the same Incarnation, as they reigned according to the chronicles of Eusebius and Bede, are arranged opposite the individual years of the Incarnation according to the history of the Holy Gospel, always in the margin on the left-hand side; and opposite those same kings, also inscribed in this Incarnation as they truly reigned, to show the error of the chronicles and of the years of the Incarnation according to Dionysius, up to the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius. 3. On the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John and the Lord baptized by him, according to the four [Col. 0629C] Evangelists, with Augustine as witness; on the Lord’s fasting [Note: *Junio* was corrected to *jejunio* in witness 1.] and his victory over the devil; on the preaching of Christ; and on the passion of John the Baptist. 4. On the Lord’s passion and the miracles during the passion; the appointment of James as the first bishop; the passion of Saint Stephen; Saint Paul’s conversion and arrival in Jerusalem, where he remained with Saint Peter for fifteen days [Note: Added afterward in witness 1.]; and the remaining events up to Claudius. 5. On Claudius; the famine and the passion of James, son of Zebedee; Saint Peter’s imprisonment; Saint Paul’s second ascent to Jerusalem in the fourteenth year after his conversion, speaking with Saint Peter; Saint Peter’s arrival at Rome; and the remaining events up to Nero. [Col. 0629D] 6. On Nero; Saint Paul, bound and sent to Rome; the passion of Saint James, the brother of the Lord; Christ’s resurrection on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as Bede thinks; Mark the Evangelist and his passion; the passion of Peter and Paul; Clement the pope and his decretal letter to Saint James, the brother of the Lord; the martyrs who suffered under Nero; and Nero’s death. 7. On Galba, his reign, and his death. [Col. 0630A] 8. On Otho, his reign, and his death. 9. On Vitellius, his reign and death, with Josephus as witness, who was then present. 10. On Vespasian [Note: *Vespasino*, with *a* written above it in witness 1.] and the destruction of Jerusalem. 11. On Titus, and on the consuls and events under him. 12. On the emperor Domitian; Pope Anacletus and his decretal letters; Saint John being cast into a cauldron of boiling oil and banished to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. 13. On the emperor Nerva; Saint John’s return to Ephesus, where he wrote the Gospel; and the martyrs. 14. On the emperor Trajan; the falling asleep of Saint John; and the martyrs. 15. On the emperor Hadrian; Pope Sixtus and his decree concerning the Mass; Pope Telesphorus and his decree; and the martyrs. [Col. 0630B] 16. On the emperor Antoninus; Pope Hyginus and his decree; Pope Pius; the angelic command concerning Easter; and Pope Anicetus and his decree. 17. On the emperor Marcus; Pope Soter and his decree; and the martyrs. 18. On the emperor Commodus; Pope Victor and his decree; and Easter. 19. On the emperor Helio, and on the consuls and events under him. 20. On the emperor Julian, with Orosius as witness. 21. On the emperor Severus; Pope Zephyrinus and his decree. [Col. 0630C] 22. On the emperor Caracalla [Note: *Caricalla* in copy 3.] and his name. 23. On the emperor Macrinus; Pope Callistus and his decree. 24. On Marcus Aurelius the emperor. 25. On Aurelius Alexander the emperor; Pope Urban and his decree; and the martyrs. 26. On the emperor Maximinus; Pope Anterus and his decree; and Pope Fabian and his decree. 27. On the emperor Gordian; and on the consuls and events under him. 28. On Philip, the first emperor to believe in Christ; on the completion under him of the thousandth year from the founding of the city of Rome, with every historian as witness; and on Pope Fabian’s decree. [Col. 0630D] 29. On the emperor Decius; Pope Cornelius, his decree and passion; and the martyrs. 30. On the emperors Gallus and Volusian; Pope Lucius, his decree, and his passion. 31. On the emperor Aemilian, who ruled for three months. 32. On the emperors Valerian and Gallienus; Pope Stephen, his decree and passion, and the passion of Saint Lawrence with others; Pope Dionysius and his decree; and the martyrs. 33. On the emperor Claudius; Pope Felix and his decree; and the martyrs [Note: Thus in witness 1, where chapter 33 was written in the margin by the first hand.]. [Col. 0631A] 34. On the emperor Quintillus, who ruled for seventeen days; and on Eutychian and his decree. 35. On the emperor Aurelian and Pope Caius and the martyrs. 36. On the emperor Tacitus, and on the consuls and events under him. 37. On the emperor Florian, who ruled for ninety days. 38. On the emperor Probus, and on the consuls and events under him. 39. On the emperors Carus and Carinus, and on the consuls and events under them. 40. On the emperor Diocletian; Pope Caius and his decree; Pope Marcellinus; and Pope Marcellus and his decree. 41. On the emperor Galerius; Pope Miltiades and his [Col. 0631B] decree; and the martyrs. 42. On the emperor Constantine; Pope Sylvester and his decree; the Council of Nicaea and the Catholic faith in their time; Bishop Theodorus, who wrote an ecclesiastical history; the cross; the death of the heretic Arius; the letter of Bishop Athanasius to Pope Mark and Mark’s reply to Athanasius; and Constantine’s death. 43. On the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans; the testimony of Saint Julius the pope; their fourth year, in the sixth indiction; the death of Antony the monk; and the sacred relics of Saint Timothy and Saint Andrew the Apostles, and of Saint Luke the Evangelist, brought to Constantinople; and Constantine’s death, according to the aforesaid Bishop Theodorus. [Col. 0631C] 44. On the emperor Julian; the temple constructed at Jerusalem at his command in hatred of Christ; the miracles that followed; and his most wretched death, with Bishop Theodorus as witness. 45. On the emperor Jovian and his death, with Bishop Theodorus as witness [Note: *Ivianus* was written above it with an *o* in witness 1; “with Bishop Theodorus as witness” was added in the margin by another hand.]. 46. On the emperor Valentinian; the monks; and Valentinian’s death, with Bishop Theodorus as witness. 47. On the emperor Valens, and on the consuls and events under him. 48. On the emperor Gratian, and on the consuls and events under him. 49. On the emperor Theodosius and his death, with Bishop Theodorus as witness. [Col. 0631D] 50. On the emperor Arcadius [This chapter was added in the margin by the first hand.]. 51. On the emperor Honorius; the testimony of Lucian, who was then alive; the seventh year of Honorius; the testimony of Bishop Paschasius to Pope Leo; the consuls, Easter, and the miracle at Easter in the ninth year of Honorius under Pope Zosimus; and Pope Celestine and his decree [Note: At the very bottom of the margin, after *ejus* (“his”), a sign was placed, and the first hand added these words: “In these times … Ireland”; after *Ireland*, a new sign was placed, to which nothing corresponds in the text, and the same hand added: “The most holy virgin … plays.”]. In these times Saint Patrick shines through his virtues in Ireland. The most holy virgin Brigid performs wondrous deeds in Ireland. 52. On the emperor Theodosius; his twenty-first year’s Easter; the letter of Bishop Paschasius to Pope Leo; Easter in that same year; and the consuls of Theodosius’s fourteenth year, up to Marcian [Note: *Marcianus* and what follows were written by the first hand at the very top of the margin, with a sign showing where they belong.]. The chronicles of Eusebius and Bede contradict the Incarnation according to the history of the Holy Gospel, and thereafter agree with it. 53. On the emperor Marcian; the consuls; Easter in Marcian’s fourth, fifth, and sixth years, with Saint Pope Leo as witness; and the plundering of the city of Rome. [Col. 0632B] 54. On the emperor Leo, and on the consuls and events under him. 55. On the younger emperor Leo, with Bishop Jordanes as witness, who composed a chronicle at that time. 56. On the emperor Zeno [The manuscript has *Stennone*], and on the consuls and events under him. 57. On the emperor Anastasius, the consuls, events, and popes. 58. On the emperor Justin; the consuls, events, and popes. 59. On the emperor Justinian; his five years under the consuls; and the events up to Dionysius’s cycle, that is, to the sixth year [Note: Missing in the text; added afterward in the margin by another hand.] of this Justinian, with Bede as witness. [Col. 0632C] 60. On Justinian’s sixth year, and Bede’s testimony according to the chronicle of Eusebius and his own, namely, that this is the same year as Diocletian’s 248th year; on the computation of these 248 years, from that same sixth year of Justinian—that is, the first year of Dionysius’s cycles—we have traced backward above to Diocletian according to the aforesaid chronicles of Eusebius and Bede, and again backward from Diocletian to the aforesaid sixth year of Justinian according to the testimony of Scripture, popes, and bishops who lived at that time; and there are found seven years missing from the aforesaid chronicles, across eight nineteen-year cycles—that is, from Constantine the Great [Col. 0632D] to Marcian, and afterward in orderly succession to Justin. 61. On the emperor Justin and the events under him. 62. On the emperor Tiberius. 63. On the emperor Maurice; his thirteenth year in the thirteenth indiction and his eighteenth year in the fourth indiction, with Bede as witness; and on Saint Gregory the pope and his decree concerning the Mass. Then the holy father Columbanus came from our most holy island of Ireland, which is called the island of the saints [Note: *Scor* in witness 1; it seems that *sanctorum* (“of the saints”) should be read. *Scotorum* was corrected to *sanctorum* in copy 2.], into Burgundy with Saint Gall and other proven disciples; and in these times there was Columba Baetinique [Note: Thus, or perhaps *Baetiinque* or *Baetririque* in witness 1; *Bethinique* in copy 2, whose Vratislav manuscript reads: “*cholon chillis*, thus superscribed in the Cottonian manuscript, in which alone this final clause occurs, and it appears to be an interpolation.”] in Scotland. 64. On the emperor Phocas and [Note: *Et* (“and”) was added afterward, but by the first hand, in witness 1.] his image. 65. On the emperor Heraclius, and on his sixteenth year in the fifteenth indiction, with Bede as witness [Note: Chapters 65, 66, and 67 were added afterward at the very top of the margin, with a sign placed after chapter 64. The letters are somewhat smaller but written by the same hand as the text.]. 66. On the emperor Heraclius and the heretics [same note]. 67. On the emperor Constantine [same note]. 68. On the emperor Constantine, and on his ninth year in the seventh indiction, with Bede as witness. 69. On the emperor Constantine and the six synods. 70. On the emperor Justinian. [Col. 0633B] 71. On the emperor Leo. 72. On the emperor Tiberius, and on Bede’s testimony concerning the year of the Incarnation according to Dionysius and the indiction of Tiberius’s fifth year. 73. On the emperor Justinian. 74. On the emperor Philippicus. 75. On the emperor Anastasius, and on Pope Gregory and his decree. 76. On the emperor Theodosius. [Col. 0634A] 77. On the emperor Leo, and on Pope Gregory and his decree. 78. On the emperor Pepin, also the first emperor from among the Franks. 79. On the emperor Charlemagne. 80. On the emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne. 81. On the emperor Lothar, son of Louis. 82. On Louis, also called Lothar, son of Lothar, and how he died by the vengeance of Christ’s body. 83. On the emperor Louis, his son. 84. On the elder emperor Charles, and on Louis the Stammerer, his son. 85. On the younger emperor Charles. 86. On the emperor Arnulf. 87. On the emperor Louis, his son. 88. On the emperor Conrad. [Col. 0634B] 89. On the emperor Henry. 90. On the emperor Otto. 91. On the emperor Otto, his son. 92. On the emperor Otto III, son of the second. 93. On the emperor Henry [Note: “Henry the Pious” in copy 2.] [Note: “Henry of Bamberg, who died without sons” in copy 3.]. 94. On the emperor Conrad [Note: “The Conrad of Speyer, how he is chosen for the kingship” in copy 3.]. 95. On the emperor Henry [Note: “Henry II” in copy 3.], his son. 96. On the emperor Henry, son of this man [Note: Copy 2 adds “on Pope Hildebrand and his decrees.” Copy 3 adds: “On Henry III and his son, how the son rebelled against him and how he died by poison in Italy, and on Pope Hildebrand and his decree”; and there it further adds: “97. On King Rudolf and King Hermann, how the Saxons set them over themselves and how they were killed. 98. On the emperor Henry and his son, how the son rebelled against him, how he was deprived of the kingdom by the counsel of the princes, and how they set his son up as king over themselves.”]. From Adam up to this point all the years have been written out in order.

We have omitted the first and second books.

## The Third Book Begins, in the Twelfth Indiction (Fol. 101)

[Col. 0633]

42. (JEROME.) Lentulus [Note: The letters printed in italics were written in red ink in copy 1.] and Messala, men of very distinguished rank and consuls. Quirinus, sent to Judaea by decree of the Senate, records the census of the people and their possessions. Christ is conceived on Friday, the eighth day before the Kalends of April; John [Col. 0633C] the Baptist is born on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. (CASS.) Our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, in these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies, is born in Bethlehem of Judaea on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on the Lord’s Day at night. (GOSPEL.) On the eighth day, also a Sunday, he is circumcised. On the thirteenth day he is adored by the Magi, guided by the star. On the fortieth day he is recognized by Simeon and Anna. Thereafter, at the Lord’s command, he is led into Egypt because of fear of Herod.

2. 43. (JEROME.) Caesar Augustus for the twelfth time and Paulus. Caesar makes peace with the Parthians. Sextus Pythagoras the philosopher became renowned.

3. 44. (JEROME.) Cossus Lentulus and Piso. Augustus adopted Tiberius and Agrippa as sons. Judas the Galilean urges the Jews to rebel.

[Col. 0634B] [In the manuscript, in the margin: The nineteen-year cycle begins in the fourteenth indiction, with one concurrent.]

4. 45. (JEROME.) Caesar Augustus for the thirteenth time and Paulus. When Herod had learned of Christ’s birth through the Magi’s report, he ordered all the infants in Bethlehem to be killed.

5. 46. (JEROME.) Vinicius and Alfenus. Asinius Pollio, orator and former consul, who celebrated a triumph over the Dalmatians, died in his seventieth year at his villa in Tusculum.

6. 47. (JEROME.) Servilius and Lamia. Herod died miserably and deservedly from a disease of retained fluid and worms swarming over his entire body.

7. 48. (JEROME.) Aelius and Sentius. Archelaus was installed in Herod’s place by Augustus for seven years, and his brothers Herod, Antipater, Lysias, and Philip became tetrarchs. (GOSPEL.) Jesus Christ our Lord is brought back from Egypt at the angel’s command [Note: Thus in witness 1?].

[Col. 0635A] 8. 49. (JEROME.) Cinna and Valerius. There was such a great famine at Rome that five modii were sold for twenty-seven and a half denarii. Philistion the writer of mimes, a Magnesian by nationality. Assianus [Note: Thus in witness 1; *Asiamus* in copy 2; *Magnesiamus* in Jerome.] is regarded as famous at Rome.

9. 50. (JEROME.) Lepidus and Aruntius. Caesar Tiberius brings the Dalmatians and Sarmatians under Roman authority.

10. 51. (JEROME.) Caecilius and Lenicius. Anthemodorus of Tarsus is regarded as a distinguished Stoic philosopher.

11. 52. (JEROME.) Furius and Nonius. Marcus Verrius Flaccus, a famous grammarian.

12. 53. (JEROME.) Sulpicius and Poppaucus. The Athenians, plotting a revolution against the Romans, are suppressed, after the leaders of the sedition are killed.

13. 54. (Luke 2:42, 46.) Dolabella and Silanus. [Col. 0635B] When Jesus was twelve years old [that is, as Jerome says, when he completed twelve years], he was found in the temple, sitting among the teachers of the Law, questioning them and listening to them. (JEROME.) The orator Messala Corvinus, two years before he died, lost his memory and understanding so completely that he could scarcely put a few words together; finally, after an ulcer developed around his spine, he wasted away through starvation, in the seventy-second year of his age.

14. 55. (JEROME.) Lepidus and Statilius. Augustus, conducting a census at Rome with his son Tiberius, found 9,370,000 people.

15. 56. (JEROME.) Caesar and Fonteius. Socio, an Alexandrian philosopher and teacher of Seneca, was famous.

16. 57. (BEDE.) Plancus and Silius. Archelaus, because the Jews could not endure him but accused his brutality before Augustus, was banished to the Gallic city of Vienne; and, to reduce the power of the Jewish kingdom and subdue its arrogance, four of his brothers were appointed tetrarchs in his place: Herod, also called Antipas; Antipater; Lysias; and Philip.

17. 1. (CASSIODORUS–JEROME.) Pompeius and Apuleius. In these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies, Octavian Augustus died in Campania, at the age of seventy-six, at Atella in Campania, in the fifty-sixth year of his reign, apparently in September; he was buried in the Campus Martius. Tiberius succeeded him.

3. Tiberius, third among the Roman rulers [Note: In the margin the second hand adds: “Tiberius reigned twenty-four years”; and likewise for all the emperors.], Augustus’s stepson—that is, the son of his wife Livia, born from an earlier husband—reigned twenty-three years and some days, according to Josephus; that is, up to the Kalends of October, in the fifth year after the Lord’s passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus. (JEROME.) Gaius Asinius Gallus, an orator, son of Asinius Pollio, whom Virgil also mentions, was famous and was put to death by Tiberius with dreadful punishments.

18. 2. Caesar Drusus and Norbanus. The historian Livy died at Padua.

19. 3. (JEROME.) Sisenna, Titilius, and Scribonius. The Incarnation begins according to the chronicles of Eusebius or Bede, while the years are counted backward for us up to the forty-second year of Caesar Octavian.

20. 4. (JEROME.) Pomponius and Caelius. The poet Ovid died in exile and was buried near the town of Tomis.

### 21. 5. (HIER.)

Caesar and Germanicus Caesar. Germanicus Caesar triumphed over the Parthians [Note: [Col. 0635] “he makes Syria” (?).]. Thirteen cities collapsed in an earthquake: Ephesus, Magnesia, Sardis, Mostuene, Aegae, Hiero, Caesarea, Philadelphia, Tmolus, Temus, Cimmerina, Apollonia, and Diahircania.

### 22. 6. (HIER.)

Silanus and Norbanus. Fenestella, a writer of histories and poems, died at the age of seventy and was buried at Cumae. The great Paschal Cycle begins here [Col. 0636B]; in its second year, according to Dionysius [in the third indiction [Note: [Col. 0635] added in a second hand in the margin: “1.”]], the Lord was born.

[The codex has this in the margin: “The solar cycle begins, as always, with four concurrent leap-year indicators.”]

### 23. 7. [I.] (HIER.)

Valerius and Aurelius. Tiberius never released the many kings whom he had summoned to him by flattery; among them he killed Archelaus of Cappadocia and, turning his kingdom into a province, ordered its most noble city Mazaca to be called Caesarea. The Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0635] “This was written twice in this year, after Aurelius, and here once.”] begins according to Dionysius in the fourth indiction [“written down” [Note: [Col. 0635] added here by a second hand: “1.”] in order, opposite the Incarnation, according to the Gospel].

### 24. 8. [II.] (HIER.)

Caesar and Drusus Caesar. Pompey’s theater burned down.

### 25. 9. [III.] (HIER.)

Harterius and Sulpicius. Tiberius makes Drusus his partner in the government.

### 26. 10. [IV.] (HIER.)

Asinius and Antistius. Drusus died by poison. Quintus Atherius, a ready and popular orator, grew old in the highest distinction almost until his ninetieth year.

### 27. 11. [V.] (HIER.)

Cornelius and Vicellius. Sevius Plautus, accused of having corrupted his son, killed himself in court.

### 28. 12. [VI.] (HIER.)

Asinius and Cossus Cornelius. Philip the tetrarch called Paneas, where he had built very many structures, Caesarea Philippi, and another city Julias.

### 29. 13. [VII.] (HIER.)

Calvissius and Getulicus. Pilate was sent by Tiberius as procurator of Judea.

### 30. 14. [VIII.] (HIER.)

Piso and Crassus. Votienus Montanus, an orator from Narbo, died in the Balearic Islands, to which he had been exiled by Tiberius in his fifteenth year (Beda). Herod the tetrarch, prince of the Jews, who reigned for twenty-four years, founded Tiberias and another city, Libias, in honor of Tiberius and his mother Livia.

### 31. 15. [IX.]

Silanus and Silius. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, the word of the Lord came to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness. And he came into the whole region of the Jordan (Luke 3:1–3). Matthew says: “Then Jesus came to be baptized by him in the Jordan” (Matt. 3:13), and what follows.

Augustine says the following [Note: [Col. 0637D] It is not clear whether the words that follow are Augustine’s or not; certainly I was unable to find them in the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*]:

What Matthew says—“Then Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized by John”—is according to the evangelist John: “On the following day,” and what follows. Mark says in the Gospel: “And he was baptized by John” (Mark 1:9). Eusebius says the following [Note: [Col. 0637] “The words of Eusebius are not read.” The words “Eusebius says the following” are missing in two or three places]: [lacuna] “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old” (Luke 3:23). This is what Luke says.

He was not yet fully thirty years old, that is, twelve months short; rather, according to Jerome and Luke, he was beginning his thirtieth year [when he was baptized, on the day] of the Lord’s Epiphany [on the thirteenth day of his thirtieth year]. According to solar years, however, he was then beginning his thirty-first year. [Col. 0637B] For the solar year at the end of which he was born is counted as the year of his birth. His year of age, consisting of twelve months, began at the end of the first year of his birth and was completed at the end of the second year of his birth, or solar year.

Mark says: “And immediately after the baptism the Spirit drove him into the wilderness” (Mark 1:12). This is according to Matthew: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days” (Luke 4:1), and what follows.

Therefore the Lord began his fast on Monday and, on the fortieth day, Friday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, overcame the devil in gluttony, vainglory, and greed—the very things by which on that same weekday the devil had first crushed Adam. From that point the Lord Jesus Christ preached to the peoples the way of salvation, as the blessed Peter testifies in the choice of the apostle Matthias:

“Therefore it is necessary that from these men who have accompanied us throughout the whole time in which the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day on which he was taken up from us into heaven” (Acts 1:21–22), and what follows.

(Gospel.) By signs and miracles he proves that the things he says are true. Of these, only a few are recorded in the Gospels. He calls the apostles and sends them to preach.

(BEDA.) [Note: [Col. 0637] Added here in the margin by the first hand.] Up to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, counting from Adam according to the Hebrews, as Eusebius marks in his chronicles, three thousand years must be noted; for in the fifteenth year of Tiberius was the beginning of the seventy-first jubilee according to the Hebrews. Three thousand years comprise sixty jubilees.

### 32. 16. [X.] (HIER.)

Rubellius and Fusius. [Eusebius says: “The beginning of the eighty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews,” that is, four thousand years from Adam to the present year. Among the Hebrews, a jubilee is called a fiftieth year.]

### 33. 17. [XI.]

Vinicius and Cassius. John the Baptist was beheaded.

[It is written in the *Passion of Saint Valentine* that the beheading of the Lord’s Forerunner took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as Saint Jerome also testifies in the *Martyrology* [Note: [Col. 0638D] These words are not found in the *Martyrology* published by D’Achery (*Spicilegium*, second edition, II, p. 6).]. The Gospel says that John suffered shortly before Easter, on the day before the Nones of April, on a Saturday, the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month. Our Easter, however, fell on the Nones of April, if it had occurred.]

### 34. 18. [XII.] (CASS.)

Tiberius Caesar, five times consul. Cassiodorus says:

“During these consulships our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and an eclipse of the sun occurred such as had never occurred before or afterward.”

(HIER.) Jesus Christ, the Son of God, according to the prophecies that had been spoken beforehand concerning him, suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the fifteenth day of the moon, according to the four Gospels, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, according to the Gospel of Saint John. On the third day, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on the seventeenth day of the moon, according to the account of the holy Gospel, he rose from the dead.

Phlegon [Note: [Col. 0637] “Flaccus,” according to a third-hand correction.] the historian says:

“In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad [that is, according to the Greeks], a great and extraordinary eclipse of the sun occurred, greater than all those that had taken place before it. At the sixth hour the day was turned into such darkness that stars were seen in the sky. An earthquake also overthrew many buildings in Bithynia and the city of Nicaea.”

This is what Phlegon says.

Josephus, likewise, a native Jewish historical writer, records the following concerning these events: on Pentecost, the priests first testified that they had felt a shaking of places and heard certain sounds; then from the sanctuary of the Temple a sudden voice burst forth, saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” Josephus also wrote that in the same year Pilate, the governor, secretly set up an image of Caesar in the Temple by night, and that this became the first cause of sedition and disturbances among the Jews.

(HIER.) James, the brother of the Lord, was appointed by the apostles as the first bishop of the church of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0638C] In the upper margin of folio 102, a second hand has written: “James, the brother of the Lord—that is, the son of Mary, the sister of the mother of the Lord, whom John also mentions—was appointed by the apostles immediately after the Lord’s Passion and governed the church at Jerusalem for thirty years. That is, until the seventh year of Nero. Beda says the following about the Acts of the Apostles (on chapter 21).” The same hand adds: “Lazarus is raised from the dead, destined to become bishop of Cyprus and to live for twenty-four years.” In the lower margin of folio 102: “Lazarus by name is raised, lest all the dead should be compelled to come out of hell; nevertheless he cries out at the tomb, the underworld is disturbed, all the dead await the permission, asking whether their names were being called: ‘Will the Lord raise us too?’ they say. Wherever Christ had stood, the underworld lay open.’ Suddenly one voice silenced the others. The most dreadful of the others, whose limbs were already flowing away, prevented approach; the eyes, wasting in their hollow sockets, had already settled there in a putrid condition; the softness of the nostrils was already failing; the gape of the mouth, with its teeth exposed, was already horrifying; the skin stripped away, loose at the temples, revealed the seat of the brain, [ [Col. 0639] “ses,” according to a first-hand reading], its covering thinned, paling, with the hair gradually becoming sparse. Even Mary and Martha, who had often seen Christ raise the dead, did not at all believe that their brother would be raised. Here Christ is proved to be God. Here he did as much as faith itself had not dared to hope.”]],

From this point one must consider how many calamities subsequently oppressed the Jewish people.

### 35. 19. [XIII.]

Unicius and Longinus.

[Note: [Col. 0639B] A mark placed here by a second hand indicates: “Seek on the second side of the following leaf.” The following leaf (fol. 103), after an addition, has on its first page a drawing of Christ’s crucifixion; the second page, written by a second hand, contains the numbers of the years 35–82 (19–22; 1–14; 1–25), 92, 94, and so forth. For the years 35–57 the following is written:

“Saint Stephen suffered, with Saul urging and present.” That Paul was converted in this year he confirms in the Epistle to the Galatians:

“When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. 1:15–16).

Jerome says (in the same passage):

“That is, without delay after the revelation of Christ he did not go out to the apostles and confer with the Lord among men, but went away to Arabia, and returned again from Arabia to Damascus; after three years he preached the Gospel, and only then came to Jerusalem” (*Commentary on Galatians*, IV, p. 234).

He himself testifies:

“Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away to Arabia, and again returned to Damascus” (Gal. 1:17).

To make these things credible to those who were absent, he confirms them under God’s testimony, saying:

“Now concerning the things I write to you, behold, before God I do not lie, for they are most true.”

These are the three years that Luke calls “many days” in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:23), during which Paul spoke the Gospel boldly in Damascus (Jerome, p. 235). For it is certain that immediately after he had been baptized and had received bread and been strengthened, he stayed for several days with the disciples who were in Damascus and, while all were astonished, preached in the synagogues of the Jews that Jesus was the Son of God. Then he went to Arabia and returned from Arabia to Damascus, and remained there for three years—the “many days” of which Scripture says:
