“When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him” (ibid.), and what follows.

Therefore his disciples took him and lowered him by night through the wall, letting him down in a basket, as he himself testifies:

“Then, after three years”—that is, of my conversion—“I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and remained with him fifteen days; but I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. In what I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:18–20).

Therefore, in the thirty-eighth year of the Incarnation, Paul stayed with Peter in Jerusalem. Then, that is, after the years and deeds mentioned above, he says:

“Afterward I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they had only heard that the one who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once sought to destroy, and they glorified God because of me. Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me” (Gal. 1:21–24; 2:1), and what follows.

Jerome says the following (same passage, p. 238):

“At the beginning” of his “conversion” and “faith, in passing, he saw the apostles” in Jerusalem—that is, three years after he was converted. “Then after years, as Paul himself testifies,” fourteen in addition to the three earlier years—that is, “after seventeen years” of his conversion—“he speaks fully with the apostles” in Jerusalem “and humbles himself,” and what follows.

This is what Jerome said.

Then Peter came to Rome. There he preached the Gospel for twenty-five years, five months, and thirteen days and presided as bishop of that city—that is, until the final year of Nero, in which he suffered with Saint Paul under the consulship of Silvanus and Otho, as the senator Cassiodorus testifies.]

Saint Stephen suffered, and Saint Paul was converted (Acts of the Apostles; Jerome). Cassius Verus, an outstanding orator, died in the utmost poverty in the year of his age [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0639] the word has been erased by a first hand], scarcely covered with a shameful scrap of cloth. Pilate, spending the sacred treasury, which is also called the *Corban*, on the aqueduct of Jerusalem [Col. 0639B], provided the seeds of a second sedition.

[Col. 0640B] Afterward, with the years 58–76 left blank, the following appears:

### 77. 25.

Cassiodorus said:

“Silvanus and Otho, distinguished men, were made consuls by Nero.”

During these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies, Peter and Paul suffered. Nero, living shamefully, was sought by the Senate for punishment. Fleeing from the Palatine, he killed himself at the fourth milestone of the City, on the suburban Nomentan Way [Note: [Col. 0639] so in the first hand], in the thirty-second year of his age. Galba succeeded him and reigned for seven months.

### 78.

After him Otho reigned for three months.

### 79.

After him, “Vitellius reigned for eight months and days. All of them reigned under the two consuls listed below.” This is what Cassiodorus said. Vitellius was killed on the third day of October, as the historian Josephus testifies (*The Jewish War* 5.13), since he was present at the time.

### 80.

Vespasian and Titus. Cassiodorus says:

### 81.

“Vespasian II and Titus II. During these consulships Vespasian assumed the imperial power for nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. Under him the following consuls were in office.”

The chronicles, however, state that Tiberius reigned for twenty-three years, that is, five years after the Passion; Gaius for four years; Claudius for fourteen; and Nero ruled for fourteen years. They omit the additional months during which kings reigned beyond their years, the intervals between rulers, and the ends of years in which rulers often died or lost the kingdom. Therefore, according to the chronicles, there are thirty-seven years between the year of the Passion and Vespasian, but forty-seven according to Saint Paul, as Saint Jerome testifies in his commentary on him addressed to Paula and Eustochium. Thus ten years are missing from the chronicles over such a span of time. Nevertheless, we follow the chronicles by another line of reasoning, as follows.

### 36. 20. [XIV.] (HIER.)

Sulpicius and Sitta. Sejanus, Tiberius’ prefect, who had very great influence with him, strongly urged him to destroy the Jewish people, as Philo says in the second book of his *Legation*.

### 37. 21. [XV.] (HIER.)

Priscus and Vitellius. Persius Flaccus, the satirical poet, was born at Volaterrae.

Paul says to the Galatians (chapter 1:15–20):

“But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away to Arabia, and again returned to Damascus. Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter and remained with him fifteen days; but I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. Now concerning what I write to you, behold, before God I do not lie,” and what follows.

Beda says the following (compare *Retractations on the Acts*, chapter 9):

“It is therefore established that Paul came to Jerusalem after three years of his conversion and was joined to the company of the apostles, because Luke says this in the Acts of the Apostles: Barnabas took hold of him and led him to the apostles.”

This is what Beda said.

### 38. 22. [XVI.] (BEDA.)

Gallus and Nonianus. Agrippa, also called Herod, son of Aristobulus, the son of Herod the Great, accused Herod the tetrarch and went to Rome. Tiberius threw him into chains, where he won many people to his friendship, especially Gaius, the son of Germanicus.

(HIER.) When Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the Christian doctrine, Tiberius referred the matter to the Senate, so that Christians might be received among the other religious observances [Note: [Col. 0641] “added afterward by a first hand.”]. But when the senators decided that Christians should be expelled from the city, following the counsel of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0641] “Vum” in the first hand].

### 39. 23. [XVII.] (HIER.)

Gallienus and Plautianus. By an edict Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death [Note: [Col. 0641] This belongs with the preceding year.]. Tertullian writes this (compare Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 2.2). Many senators and Roman knights were killed.

During these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies, Tiberius died in Campania, in the twenty-third year of his reign and the seventy-eighth year of his age [Note: [Col. 0641] “Tiberius” added afterward by a second hand], around the month of September.

[Gaius succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0641] added afterward by a second hand].]

### 4. The Romans

Gaius, also called Caligula, beginning in the same year in which Tiberius died, reigned for four years, ten months, and eight days, as Eusebius and Beda testify; that is, until the Kalends of August, in the tenth year after the Passion. During his reign the following consuls were in office [as Cassiodorus testifies].

### 40. 1. [18.]

Proculus and Nigrinus. In the sixth year after the Passion, the first year of Gaius, Saint Peter took possession of the chair of the church of Antioch on the eighth day before the Kalends of March and held it for seven years.

[Note: [Col. 0642C] A second hand writes in the margin: “Jerome: ‘When Peter came to Antioch, since Paul affirms it, we should believe that Paul resisted him to his face.’” (Compare the commentary on Galatians, IV, p. 242.)

“The same hand, but in different ink, adds: Beda on the Acts of the Apostles (on chapter 1): ‘The apostle Matthias was appointed before Pentecost, but the seven deacons were appointed after Pentecost through the apostles’ prayer and laying on of hands.’ Stephen is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *crown*. Hence Eusebius says (*Ecclesiastical History* 2.1): ‘Immediately after his appointment, Stephen was stoned by those who had also killed the Lord.’

“In another ink it continues: ‘They determined that Paul and Barnabas should go up to the apostles,’ and what follows (Acts 15:2). Beda on the Acts of the Apostles says the following (on chapter 15): ‘Paul himself writes to the Galatians about this ascent, saying: “Then after fourteen years I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me, and I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles,”’ and what follows.

“Here the number itself, which [ [Col. 0643] ‘q’ in the first hand; read: ‘which’] he set down, must be reckoned in years. ‘For we know that the apostles Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion, that is, in the final year of Nero, and that the blessed Peter occupied the episcopal chair at Rome for twenty-five years; and twenty-five years plus fourteen make not thirty-eight but thirty-nine. Therefore we must believe that the blessed Peter came to Rome in the same fourteenth year after the Lord’s Passion in which Paul addressed him in Jerusalem, in the fourth year of Claudius Caesar; and, unless I am mistaken, by this interpretation the apostle Paul is shown to have come to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered and rose again [lacuna] [ [Col. 0643] supply: ‘year.’]’”]

(BEDA.) Gaius made Herod Agrippa, his friend, who had been released from chains, king of Judea for seven years.

### 41. 2. [XIX.] (HIER.)

Julianus and Asprenas. Flaccus Acilius, prefect of Egypt, oppressed the Jews with calamities, with the people of Alexandria consenting and repeatedly raising clamors against them. He also polluted their synagogues with images, statues [Note: [Col. 0643] read: “statues”], altars, and sacrifices. Philo writes in the book also called *Flaccus* that all these things happened while he was present; for this reason he himself undertook an embassy to Gaius.

(BEDA.) Herod the tetrarch, himself seeking the friendship of Gaius, came to Rome at the urging of his wife Herodias; but, accused by Agrippa, he lost his tetrarchy. Fleeing to Spain with Herodias, he died of grief [in place of joy at the beheading of Saint John the Baptist].

[The codex has in the margin: “The second decade of the cycle begins in the seventh indiction.”]

### 42. 3. [XX.] (HIER.)

Publicula and Nerva. Gaius married the wife of Memmius Regulus, compelling him to register himself as his wife’s father.

(BEDA.) Pilate, falling into many misfortunes and being constrained by Gaius [Note: [Col. 0643] read: “constrained”], killed himself with the hand with which he had scourged Christ.

(HIER.) Gaius ordered Petronius, prefect of Syria, to place his statue in Jerusalem under the name of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. Throughout the Roman world, as Philo and Josephus write, statues, images, and altars consecrated to Gaius Caesar were set up in the synagogues of the Jews.

### 43. 4. [XXI.] (HIER.)

Caesar. Very many nobles were killed by Gaius. He condemned his sisters, with whom he had committed incest, to exile on islands. Gaius ordered all the exiles to be killed.

### 44. 5. [XXII.] (BEDA.)

Caesar [Note: [Col. 0643] The name “Caesar” has been erased by the first hand] and Julianus. While preaching in Judea, Matthew wrote the Gospel.

(CASS.) During these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies, Gaius was killed by his guards in the palace, in the twenty-fourth year of his age, around the month of July. Claudius succeeded him.

### 5. The Romans

Claudius reigned for fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days; that is, until the Kalends of April, in the twenty-fifth year after the Passion.

(CASS.) During his reign the following consuls were in office:

### 45. 1. [XXIII.] (HIER.)

Claudius Caesar II and Saturninus. This is the Claudius who was Drusus’ uncle and who has a monument at Mogontiacum.

### 46. 2. [XXIV.] (HIER.)

Saturninus II and Venustus. Eusebius says the following: The apostle Peter, after first founding the church at Antioch, was sent to Rome. There he continued as bishop of that city for twenty-five years, preaching the Gospel.

### 47. 3. [XXV.] (HIER.)

Tiberius and Gallus. Mark the evangelist, Peter’s interpreter, preached Christ in Egypt and Alexandria. Evodius was appointed the first bishop of Antioch.

### 48. 4. [XXVI.] (HIER.)

Crispinus and Taurus. Agrippa, king of the Jews, after ruling for seven years, died; after him his son Agrippa was appointed king by Claudius.

The prophecy of Agabus, by which he had said in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0643] It appears to have been written *actubus*, but corrected to *actis* by the first hand] that a famine would occur throughout the whole world, was fulfilled under Claudius. This is what Eusebius says.

[The codex has in the margin: “The fifteenth year of Tiberius according to the chronicle of Eusebius and the presbyter Beda.”]

Beda, however, says:

“In the fourth year of Claudius there was a very severe famine, of which Luke makes mention.”

This is what Beda says.

Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles:

“In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, named Agabus, stood up and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to occur throughout the whole world; this happened under Claudius. The disciples, according to each one’s means, determined to send relief to the brothers living in Judea; and they did so, sending it to the elders through the hands of Barnabas and Paul.

“At that same time King Herod laid hands on certain members of the church to afflict them. He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. It was during the days of Unleavened Bread. When he had seized him, he put him in prison” (Acts 11:27–30; 12:1–4), and what follows.

Luke continues:

“Set apart for me Barnabas [Note: [Col. 0643] A second hand adds in the margin of folio 104: “He was skilled in the art of making tents. The Greek word *skēnē*, ‘tent,’ derives its etymology from shading; among them a shadow is called *skēnē*. *Skēnai* or *skēnōmata* signify awnings, which were made from sewn linen, wool, or haircloth, or from the leaves and branches of trees. Beda. The Lord did not forbid making provision and taking care of the future in the human manner; rather, he forbade anyone to serve God because of these things, so that in his works he would look not toward the kingdom of God but toward acquiring these things. We should provide for them in such a way that, while serving in the army, we think of the kingdom of God, not of these things.”] and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

Beda says the following (on chapter 13):

“Paul, according to the order of the history, received the apostleship with Barnabas and took the name Paul in the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion; but in the fourteenth year after the Passion, in accordance with the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, he set out for the teaching of the Gentiles.”

This is what Beda said.

Concerning this ascent to Jerusalem, after saying—as we stated above (under year 35)—that three years after his conversion he had seen Peter in Jerusalem, he added:

“Then, after fourteen years, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me; and I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:1), and what follows.

This corresponds to Luke:

“Paul and Barnabas determined that they, and certain others from among them, should go up to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem” (Acts 15:2), and what follows.

Therefore we must believe that the blessed Peter did not come to Rome before that same fourteenth year after the Lord’s Passion, in which Paul addressed him in Jerusalem—that is, the fourth year of Claudius Caesar. Here the number of years that Saint Paul set down must be reckoned.

For we know that the apostles Peter and Paul suffered in the thirty-eighth year [that is, after the year of the Passion, in the final year] of Nero, and that the blessed Peter preached in Rome for twenty-five years, two months, and thirteen days, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, when he took possession of the chair, until the third day before the Kalends of July, when he suffered.

The twenty-five years of Peter and the fourteen years of Saint Paul, together with the year of the Lord’s Passion, make thirty-nine years. Therefore, in the forty-fifth year of the Incarnation, in the first year of Claudius, James, the brother of John, was beheaded with the sword by Herod, eight days before the Kalends of August.

Peter, however, in the second year of Claudius, during the days of Unleavened Bread, was put in prison—that is, when Herod, also called Agrippa, was struck by the angel.

Saint Peter, in the fourteenth year after the Passion—that is, the fourth year of Claudius—according to the chronicles, took possession of the chair at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.

(HIER.) Claudius triumphed over the Britons and added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire.

### 49. 5. [XXVII.] (HIER.)

Vinicius and Cornelius. Domitius, a distinguished orator, died at dinner under Nero from an excess of food. Clodius Quirinalis, a rhetorician from Arles, taught rhetoric at Rome with great distinction. An island of thirty stadia arose between Thera and Therasia.

[The codex has in the margin, beside numbers 50, 51, and 52: “The solar cycle begins; thus the concurrent days always occur in each solar cycle as in this one.”]

[The year of the Lord’s Passion according to the chronicle of Eusebius and Beda.]

[The fifteenth year of Tiberius according to Dionysius.]

### 50. 6. [XXVIII.] (HIER.)

Assiaticus and Cornelius. After a census of Rome had been taken, 6,944,000 Roman citizens were found. Thrace was reduced to the status of a province.

### 51. 7. [XXIX.] (HIER.)

Tiberius II and Vitellius. Under Cumanus, procurator of Judea, during the days of Unleavened Bread, such a great sedition arose at Jerusalem that, when the people fell at the exits of the gates, thirty thousand Jews perished [Note: [Col. 0645] supply: “thousand.”].

### 52. 8. [XXX.] (HIER.)

Vitellius II and Publicola. Palaemon of Vicetia, an eminent grammarian, was held in Rome. Once, when asked what difference there was between a *stilla* and a *gutta*, he replied: “A *gutta* stands; a *stilla* falls.”

### 53. 9. [XXXI.] (HIER.)

Veranus and Gallus. Antonius Liberalis, a Latin rhetorician, carried on the most serious enmities with Palaemon.

[Claudius ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, as Josephus says] [Note: [Col. 0645D] *Jewish Antiquities* 18.7; but Josephus says this of Tiberius.].

### 54. 10. [XXXII.] (HIER.)

Vetus and Nervilianus. When famine occurred in Greece, a *modius* was sold for six drachmas.

### 55. 11. [XXXIII.] (BEDA.)

Claudius and Orfitus. There was a great famine at Rome. At Peter’s direction, Mark preached in Egypt the Gospel that he had written at Rome.

### 56. 12. [XXXIV.]

Silvanus and Silvius. Claudius sent Felix as procurator of Judea. Before him the apostle Paul was accused and pleaded in his own defense. The Resurrection of Christ was on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, on the twenty-first day of the moon, according to Dionysius.

### 57. 13. [XXXV.]

Tiberius III and Antoninus.

[Lazarus, also bishop of Cyprus, died a second death, having lived twenty-four years between the two deaths, according to Ammularius [Note: [Col. 0646D] perhaps Amalarius?].]

(HIER.) Under Felix, procurator of Judea, many arose who deceived the people by their wicked persuasions. There was also a certain Egyptian false prophet who gathered many to himself; while attempting great things, he was crushed by the army of Felix, as Josephus writes, in agreement with the Acts of the Apostles, in which the tribune says to Paul:

“Are you not the Egyptian who, some days ago, stirred up and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men?”

### 58. 14. [XXXVI.] (Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities* 20.10.)

Silanus and Otho. Agrippina, his wife, after killing Claudius by poison so that she might make her son Nero king, suddenly sent Burrus, the commander of the army, with powerful tribunes to the camp. Nero was brought out and hailed in the manner of a prince during these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies.

Thus Claudius died in the palace, in the sixty-fourth year of his age, around the month of March. Nero assumed the imperial power.

### 6. The Romans

Nero reigned for fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days; that is, until the Kalends of December, in the thirty-ninth year after the Lord’s Passion.

### 59. 1. [XXXVII.] (HIER.)

Silanus II and Antoninus. Gaius Caligula was his uncle. While Felix was ruling in Judea, a sedition arose in Caesarea of Palestine and destroyed a great multitude of Jews.

[Linus, a chorepiscopus under the apostle Peter, cared for external affairs for eleven years and three months.]

### 60. 2. [XXXVIII.] (HIER.)

Marcellinus and Aviola. Festus succeeded Felix. In his presence, with King Agrippa present, the apostle Paul explained the principles of his religion and was sent to Rome in chains, during these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies.

In the second year of Nero, that is, the twenty-sixth year after the Passion, and after two years of free custody, he was released to preach freely in the fourth year of Nero.

[The Romans say that Peter was in Rome for fifteen years before Paul came to Rome.]

### 61. 3. [XXXIX.] (HIER.)

Nero and Vetus. Probus, the most learned grammarian at Rome.

### 62. 4. [XL.] (HIER.)

Nero II and Piso. Statius Ursulus of Toulouse taught rhetoric in Gaul with great distinction.

### 63. 5. [XLI.]

Nero III and Messalla. Nero killed his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister. There was an earthquake at Rome and an eclipse of the sun.

64. 6. [XLII.] (HIER.) Nero 4 and Cornelius. Nero was so luxurious that he anointed himself with cold and hot ointments. Albinus succeeded Festus as procurator of Judea. (BEDA.) James, son of Alphaeus and brother of the Lord, after having governed the church of Jerusalem for thirty years after the Passion, was stoned by the Jews on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the holy day of Easter, because they were taking revenge on him for their inability to kill Paul. [B. on the Acts of the Apostles: “It is established that blessed James completed his martyrdom in the thirtieth year after the Passion of the Lord.” Peter suffered in the thirty-eighth year, that is, the last year of Nero, and Peter wrote in his second epistle: “I am certain that the laying aside of my tabernacle is near, just as our Lord Jesus Christ also revealed to me by a revelation” [Note: [Col. 0647] read “revelationem” for “relevavionem.”]. Beda: “Hence it is clear that he wrote this epistle when his passion was imminent, since James had departed to the Lord long before” [Note: [Col. 0647] These words were written by a second hand in the lower margin of fol. 105, and there continue: “Blessed Peter, according to the deeds of the pontiffs, ordained two bishops,” etc.; these are written again below at year 71.].] Since, therefore, James suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April at Easter, and this happened in the thirtieth year after the Passion, it is sufficiently evident, according to the whole Church and all historians, that the Lord rose on the sixth day before the Kalends of April. Thus this is Nero’s fifth year [Col. 0647C] according to the reckoning of time, but according to the false computation of the Olympiads it is his seventh, in which we previously related, following Beda and Theophilus, that the Lord rose on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Saint Beda thinks that Christ’s resurrection occurred in this year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, because of the corrupt reckoning of Eusebius’s chronicle [Note: [Col. 0647] The “e” appears to have been added later.], and after it he composed his own chronicle from the Lord’s Incarnation, as he himself says.

After James had suffered, his brother Simeon, who is also called Simon, succeeded him on the throne. These men are called the Lord’s brothers because their mother, Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary, the Lord’s mother. John calls this Mary the wife of Clopas, either because Alphaeus was Clopas, or because, after Alphaeus died following the birth of James, Mary married Clopas and bore him a son, Symeon; Clopas was the brother of Joseph. [Jerome (*Against Helvidius*, Works IV.II, p. 138) [Note: [Col. 0647] Added in the margin by a second hand. From the words “brothers of the Lord,” the same hand, but in different ink.]: “This same Mary is also written as the mother of James the younger; she was the wife of Alphaeus and the sister of the Lord’s mother. John calls her Mary of Clopas, whether from her father, or from the nationality of her family, or for another reason; or she may have had two names.—The Lord’s brothers are called the sons of his maternal aunt Mary: they did not believe at first but afterward believed; or one of them believed immediately and another only after a long time. This is the mother of James and Joses, that is, Mary of Clopas, the wife of Alphaeus; this is the Mary called the mother of James the younger, who is the mother of James and Joseph according to Matthew.”]

65. 7. [XLIII.] (HIER.) Pius and Tupilianus. Nero competed in playing the lyre at Rome.

66. 8. [XLIV.] (OROS. VII.7.) Macrinus and Gallus. Nero fished with golden nets, which were hauled out with purple ropes. Lightning struck in front of Nero’s table.

67. 9. [XLV.] Crassus and Bassus. The evangelist Mark was stripped of the flesh on the holy day of Easter, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, as is read in the martyrology: “The birth of Mark the evangelist: the seventh day before the Kalends of May.”—(EUSEB. *Ecclesiastical History* II.15–16.) This man, the disciple and interpreter of the holy apostle Peter, wrote the Gospel when the brethren at Rome requested it [Col. 0648B]. Since he began it later than the others, he extended it over a longer period in writing. For he began with the origin of the Gospel preaching, which occurred through John, and continued up to the time when the apostles preached. When Peter heard it, he approved it and published it on his authority for reading in the churches.

After taking up this Gospel, Mark, sent by Peter, went to Egypt and, announcing Christ first in Alexandria, established a church. He possessed such great learning and continence of life that he compelled all Christ’s followers to conform to his example. Peter mentions him in his first epistle (V.13), naming Rome Babylon: “She who is gathered together in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark, my son.” After establishing and strengthening churches throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammonica, Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he was finally seized by the pagans [Bede’s martyrology] who remained in Alexandria.

When they saw him celebrating Mass on the holy day of Easter, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, they put a rope around his neck and dragged him to the places of Bucolia, which were beside the sea beneath the cliffs, where a church had been built. His flesh fell [into the ground], and the rocks were stained with blood. When evening came, they threw him into prison, where around midnight he was first strengthened by an angelic visitation. At dawn, while he was being dragged to the places of Bucolia, he died, giving thanks and saying, “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit,” and was buried with glory by holy men in a place of quarried stone [Col. 0648D], in the eighth year of Nero. This is in the martyrology.

That he celebrated our Easter, not the Easter of the Hebrews, is attested by Mark, and Beda likewise says in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles*: “It is already established that the apostle Peter celebrated Easter at Rome on the Sunday of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is also established that the evangelist Mark, sent by him, taught in Egypt.” This is Beda [Col. 0649A] (*Retractation*, chapter XXI).

Since, therefore, Nero’s first year began in the tenth indiction, in the twenty-second year after the Passion, and his eighth year ended in the third indiction, in the thirty-third year after the Passion, in which year Mark suffered on Easter Sunday, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, while the pagans scraped his flesh onto the ground, although he still retained his spirit until morning—is it not evident that Christ rose from the dead on the sixth day before the Kalends of April? For Easter on the seventh day before the Kalends of May is found neither earlier nor later than the aforesaid year by ninety-two years.—(HIER.) After Mark the evangelist, Anianus was the first bishop ordained for the church of Alexandria; he presided for twenty-two years.

68. 10. [XLVI.] (HIER.) Silanus and Paulinus. Perseus died in the twenty-ninth year of his age. Nero built baths, which he called Neronian [Note: [Col. 0649] Read “Thermae.”]. Nero competed at Rome in the contest of the lyre-players [Note: [Col. 0649] Read “contendens.”] and defeated them all. The poet Marcus Annaeus Lucan of Corduba, detected in the Pisonian conspiracy, offered his arm to a physician for the opening of his veins. In order to behold the likeness of burning Troy, Nero set fire to a very large part of the city of Rome. Three cities in Asia collapsed in an earthquake: Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae. Florus succeeded Albinus; under him the Jews rebelled against the Romans. Junius Gallio, Seneca’s brother, an outstanding declaimer, killed himself with his own hand. No action was brought before Nero by one appearing in his presence [Note: [Col. 0649] Read “presence.”].

69. 11. [XLVII.] Gensinus and Apuleius. Under Nero only two provinces were created: Pontus Polemoniacus [Col. 0649C] and the Cottian Alps, after King Cottius died. Many nobles were killed by Nero at Rome. Nero was crowned at the Olympic Games, surpassing cithara players, tragedians, and charioteers in various contests.

70. 12. [XLVIII.] Capito and Rufus. Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, Nero’s teacher and the uncle of the poet Lucan, died by opening his veins and drinking poison. Again, while celebrating the games at the Isthmus, Pythia, and Actia, Nero was crowned among cithara players, tragedians, and lyre-players. [Linus suffered martyrdom in these consuls’ year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Cletus the chorepiscopus succeeded him for twelve years, m. [lacuna]]

71. 13. [XLIX.] Italicus and Turpilianus. Nero, by decree of the Senate, provided an annual subsidy of ten million for expenses. Nero killed, among other distinguished men, his wife Octavia [Col. 0649D], and drove the philosopher Cornutus, Persius’s teacher, into exile [Note: [Col. 0649] One manuscript reads “fugati,” “were driven into exile.”]. Musonius and Plutarch were famous philosophers.

[Peter, as is found in the deeds of the pontiffs (in some manuscripts), consecrated Clement bishop and entrusted to him the chair and the administration of the whole church, saying: “Just as the power of binding and loosing, for governing, has been entrusted to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I also entrust it to you, so that, appointing administrators of various matters through whom ecclesiastical affairs may be carried out, you may not be found occupied with worldly concerns, but may devote yourself solely to prayer and to preaching to the people.””—Peter [Note: [Col. 0649] The same words are read above, book 1, under year 64.] ordained two bishops, Linus and Cletus, who would personally provide the whole priestly ministry in the city of Rome for the people and for those arriving. But blessed [Note: [Col. 0649] “Peter,” as above, year 64.] Peter devoted himself to instructing the people through prayer and preaching.]

—(*Book of the Pontiffs.*) Linus lived in the time of Nero, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio to that of Capito and Rufus. He was crowned with martyrdom and buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Cletus lived in the times of Vespasian and Titus, from the seventh consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Domitian [Note: [Col. 0649] One manuscript reads “Vespani.”; [Col. 0649] read “and of Domitian” for “in Domitian.”] to the consulship of Domitian and Rufus [Note: [Col. 0649] One manuscript reads “usque adoiano.”]. He suffered martyrdom and was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. Clement lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Tragalis and Italicus to the ninth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus.

[In the margin of the manuscript: The first persecution of the Church.]

72. 14. [L.] (HIER.) Silvanus and Otho. [According to Cassiodorus, in these consuls’ year Nero killed Peter and Paul and himself.] Lucius Annaeus Mela, brother of Seneca and Gallio, secured Nero’s favor for the property of his son, the poet Lucan.

(BEDA.) Nero, adding the first persecution of Christians even to all his other crimes, was the first to carry it out. In it, on a single day, blessed Peter was crucified and Paul was killed by the sword [in the thirty-eighth year after the Passion].

(HIER.) Against the Jews, who rebelled because they could not endure the avarice of Gessius Florus, Vespasian, military commander, was sent by Nero. Vespasian captured many cities in Judea. The historian Flavius Josephus, commander in the Jewish war, when he was about to be killed by the Romans, foretold to Vespasian Nero’s death and Vespasian’s own imperial rule.

Leo II, successor of Pope Agatho, says in his decretal letter: “Although Peter, prince of the apostles, knew Linus and Cletus as his assistants, he did not hand over to them the power of the pontificate, the rule of binding or loosing souls; rather, he handed it to Clement, his successor, who deserved to hold the apostolic see and pontifical power after him, when blessed Peter the apostle had entrusted these to him. For we do not read that Linus and Cletus ever performed anything by the authority of pontifical ministry, but only did as much as was commanded them by blessed Peter.” This is Pope Leo.

Thus Pope Clement was the first to hold the Roman church after the petition [reading uncertain] [Col. 0650D], or together with Linus and Cletus, just as it had been with Peter. After Peter—or rather, even with Peter—holy Clement was the first pope to govern the Roman church, as he himself testifies. The decretal letter of Clement, Roman pontiff: “Clement, bishop of the Roman church, to James, dearest bishop of Jerusalem” (Epistle 2, Labbé, *Councils* I, p. 50).

“Since, as we received from blessed Peter the apostle, prince and father of all the apostles, who received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, we must hold equally to the sacraments celebrated among holy things, it is fitting that we instruct you in due order. For the sacraments of divine mysteries have been entrusted to three grades: the presbyter, the deacon, and the subminister. These, with fear and trembling, must guard the remnants of the Lord’s body and its fragments, so that there may be no decay in the sacristy, that nothing may be handled negligently, and that no serious injury may be inflicted on any portion of the Lord’s body and blood.

“For if the communion of our Lord Jesus Christ is handled negligently, and the officers in charge fail to admonish concerning it, let the offender, struck by a grave anathema, be punished with a penalty worthy of judgment and humiliation. Certainly, as many sacrifices should be offered on the altar as ought to suffice for the people. If anything remains, it must not be kept until the next day but must be consumed with fear and trembling by the clergy.

“Those who consume the remnants of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy must not immediately come to receive ordinary food, nor must they think of mixing with food the holy portion which, digested through the intestines, is discharged into the privy. If, therefore, the Lord’s portion is administered in the morning, the ministers who consume it must fast until the sixth hour; and if they receive it at the third or fourth hour, they must fast until evening. Thus the sacraments are to be preserved through perpetual sanctification.

“Concerning the sacred vessels, this is how one must act: if the altar cloth, chair, candlestick, or veil has been worn out by age, it must be burned, since it is not permitted for things that have been in the sacristy to be handled improperly; they must be burned. Their ashes must also be buried in the baptistery, where there is no passage, or cast against a wall or into pavement pits, so that they are not defiled by the feet of those entering.

“No cleric should, through ignorance, think that a cloth from the altar may be used to wrap a dead person, nor should a deacon wish to cover the shoulders with things that have been on the altar. Whoever does this, even lightly—if he is a deacon—must be removed from the Lord’s altar for three years and six months, struck by a grave anathema. If a presbyter fails to admonish the clerics, let him be excommunicated for ten years and five months. He who has not taught them concerning these matters must afterward be reconciled to the mother Church with great humility.

“Let the altar cloths and veils of the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0651] So in one manuscript.] be washed inside the sacristy by deacons with humble ministers, lest by chance dust from the Lord’s body fall improperly outside the sacristy when the linen is carried out; whoever does this will incur sin. Therefore we command the ministers to guard them in the sacristy with every diligence. Let there be a new, clean basin, touching nothing else, for the service of the Lord’s altar, in which the altar cloths may be washed. The veils themselves, however, must not be washed in it but in another vessel.

“We also command that outside the church no layperson be given fragments of the offerings for his table. How do you know, you who indiscriminately hand the breads of the sacristy to the unworthy, whether those to whom you distribute them are clean from women? For this reason David, questioned by Abimelech the priest, when he declared himself clean from a woman for three days, ate the bread of the Presence.

“Presbyters or deacons serving at the altar must be chosen for the Lord’s duties from among those who have left their wives before ordination. If, after ordination, a minister should happen to enter the bed of his own wife, he must not enter the threshold of the sacristy, become a bearer of sacred things, touch the altar, receive an offering of sacrifice from those who offer it, or approach the portion of the Lord’s body [supplied]. Let him offer water to the priests’ hands, close the outer door of the church, and perform lesser duties; but he must not bring a jug to the altar or offer the chalice. If, by chance, a presbyter or deacon should sell something belonging to the sacristy or a veil, let him know that he will receive the punishment of Judas Iscariot.”

Clement later concludes: “Therefore obey these sentences well [Note: [Col. 0651] One manuscript reads “parate”; perhaps “parete.”], lest anyone believe that these commands are not to be fulfilled and suffer the torments of the eternal fire of God’s judgment, because he has neglected the sacred duties of ecclesiastical work. These things, therefore, dearest brother James, I heard from the mouth of holy Peter as he commanded them. If anyone does not keep these commands whole, let him be anathema until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. I received these commands from the holy apostle Peter, and I have taken care to make them known to you, dearest brother James, so that you may command that all be observed without blemish. If anyone listens to you, he will be a useful minister of Jesus Christ. But whoever does not listen to you—or rather, to the Lord speaking through you—brings condemnation upon himself. May almighty God, dearest brother, guard you by his protection and lead you, with abundant fruit of souls, to the heavenly homeland’s reward. May God guard you safe again and again, most reverend brother. Amen.”

Another decretal letter of Clement, bishop of Rome and Peter’s successor (Epistle 3, ibid., p. 53): “Clement, bishop of the city of Rome,” and so forth. Further on it says: “Concerning these matters, blessed Peter, our instructor and ordainer, also [spoke].” Shortly afterward: “The apostles received these things from the Lord and handed them down to us. We teach these things and command all of you, to whom it pertains, to hold and teach them without reproach.” And later: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, sending his disciples, commanded us: ‘In whatever city you enter, say, “Peace to this house,”’” and so forth.

Another letter: “Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, to his dearest brothers Julius and Julian,” and so forth. Another letter (Epistle 5, ibid., p. 61) [Col. 0652D]: “To our dearest brothers and fellow disciples residing at Jerusalem with our dearest brother James, bishop, Clement the bishop,” and so forth. Thus spoke Saint Clement.

Therefore Saint Clement was not only blessed Peter’s successor; while James was still alive, nine years before Peter’s passion, he also held the Roman chair, according to Scripture, and afterward, after Peter, for twenty-one years—that is, twelve with Cletus, or with Linus and Cletus—and nine years after them, until he was sent into exile. Thus Saint Clement was pope when he composed this decretal letter to Saint James. Yet no decretal letter is read as belonging to anyone except a pope. The nine years attributed to him are counted as though he alone held the chair after Cletus, while Pope Anacletus, who sat for ten years after Peter, is omitted, because four popes cannot be counted under the kings until the emperor Trajan. For James suffered in the thirtieth year after the Passion, and Peter in the thirty-ninth. Trajan also began to reign in the seventieth year after the Passion. Under him Saint Clement suffered. But Saint Clement would not have struck anyone with the sentence of a grave anathema, nor, with episcopal authority from the apostolic see, said: “Let him be anathema.”

Linus, at the command of blessed Peter, commanded that no woman enter the church with her head uncovered. Paul mentions him in his epistle to Timothy (ADON., *Martyrology*) [Col. 0653B]; Linus too is crowned with martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of December (2 Tim. 4:21).

At Rome, Processus, Martinianus, and forty-seven others who were baptized by blessed Peter and imprisoned in the Mamertine prison suffered martyrdom; also Torpes, Marcellus, and Apuleius. At Alexandria, the evangelist Mark in Nero’s eighth year. At Milan, Nazarius and Celsus. At Maceria near Aquileia, Hermagoras the bishop, Fortunatus the deacon, and Constantia.

The presbyter Orosius says as follows (VII.7): “But when Nero learned that Galba had been made emperor in Spain by the army, he collapsed completely in spirit and hope”; for after Peter had been killed in the city and Christians had been mangled by various punishments, Galba immediately arose from Spain.

(OROS., HIER.) Since Nero then contrived incredible evils for disturbing—or rather, for most shamefully overthrowing—the state, he was declared an enemy by the Senate. Fleeing in disgrace, at the fourth milestone from the city, that is, four miles away, in the suburban estate of his freedman between the Salarian and Nomentan roads, he killed himself in the thirty-second year of his age. In that year the entire family of Augustus was exhausted.

Roman ruler 7. Galba Servius came to Rome as soon as he learned of Nero’s death. (OROS. VII.8; H. Rom.) Although he was a senator of very ancient nobility and was sixty-three years old, he was chosen by the Spaniards and Gauls and soon willingly accepted by the entire army. His private life was distinguished among soldiers and in military and civil affairs: he was often consul, often proconsul [Col. 0653D], and frequently commander in very serious wars. His brief reign began with a good omen, except that he was inclined toward excessive severity.

Orosius says (VII.8): “Since he offended everyone by his greed, cruelty, and sluggishness, he adopted Piso, a noble and industrious young man, as his son and as heir to the kingdom. (H. Rom.) Together with him, he was beheaded by Otho’s treachery in the middle of the Roman city forum, in the seventh month and on the seventh day of his reign; he was buried in his gardens, which are on the Via Aurelia, not far from Rome.” This is Orosius.

Thus he reigned until the month of July, in the thirty-ninth year after the Passion, according to the reckoning of time.

73. 1. [LI.] (HIER.) Vespasian and Titus. Marcus Fabius Quintilianus was brought to Rome by Galba.

(OROS.) Roman ruler 8. Lucius, also called Otho, entered upon the imperial power amid disturbances and slaughter after Galba and Piso had been killed at Rome. (H. Rom.) He was nobler on his mother’s side than on his father’s, though neither parent was obscure. In private life he was soft and a friend of Nero, but in power he was unable to demonstrate his abilities. For when Otho killed Galba, Vitellius was made emperor by the Germans.

(OROS.) When Otho learned that Vitellius had immediately been proclaimed emperor in Gaul by the Germanic legions, he undertook a civil war. After first engaging in three minor battles—one in the Alps, another near Placentia, and a third near a place called Castor—against Valens and Caecina, the Vitellian commanders, and emerging victorious (Josephus, *Jewish War* V.8; H. Rom.), he fought a fourth battle at Bedriacum. When he saw that his men were being defeated, although he still had immense forces, and when the soldiers begged him not to despair so quickly of the outcome of the war, he said that he was not worth so much that a civil war should arise on his account. In the thirty-eighth year of his age, but on the ninetieth day of his reign, he killed himself—this was until the month of October, in the same year in which Galba was killed. Vitellius succeeded him.

Roman ruler 9. Vitellius reigned for eight months and eight days, until the month of October, in the fortieth year after the Passion.

74. 1. [LII.] (HIER.) Vespasian 2 and Titus 2. In these consuls’ year, according to Cassiodorus, Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the army in Judea.

(OROS.) After Otho was killed, Vitellius took possession of the imperial power and, victorious with immense glory, came to Rome with his own soldiers and Otho’s. (H. Rom.) He was born of an honored rather than noble family. His father was not of particularly illustrious birth, although he held three ordinary consulships. Marked by great disgrace and severe cruelty, Vitellius aggravated human life by his own vices, especially gluttony and greed; indeed, he is often said to have feasted for four or five days at a time. Most famously remembered is a banquet given him by his brother Vitellius, at which, besides other expenses, two thousand fish and seven thousand birds are said to have been served.

He wished to be like Nero and held this ambition so highly that he even honored Nero’s funeral rites, although Nero had been buried humbly.

(OROS.) When he learned of Vespasian, he first attempted to lay down the imperial power; afterward, encouraged by certain persons, he forced Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, who suspected no evil at the time, together with the other Flavians, into the Capitol. When the temple was set on fire, flame and ruin mingled together and brought them all into a single destruction and tumult.

Later, when support in Vespasian’s name had failed [reading uncertain], and he had been abandoned by his own army, with the enemy already approaching and himself terrified, he hid in a small chamber near the Palatine. He was dragged out from there in the most shameful manner and led through the streets and the city, publicly naked on the ground, with his hair standing upright and his head forced back so that his chin pointed upward; the executioners repeatedly threw filth into his mouth. He was led into the forum and subjected by everyone to every abuse. Finally, at the Gemonian stairs, by countless blows and repeated stabbings, he was dismembered with a sword wrapped in filth; then he was dragged by a hook and thrown into the Tiber, and was deprived even of a common burial.

(H. Rom. and OROS.) Vitellius was killed on the third day of October, as Josephus, the historian of the Jews, who was then alive, testifies (*Jewish War* V.13). Eusebius says: “Galba was beheaded in the middle of the Roman forum in the seventh month of his reign. (HIER.) Otho died by his own hand in the third month of his reign at Bedriacum. Vitellius was killed in the eighth month of his reign by Vespasian’s commanders and thrown into the Tiber.” This is Eusebius.

Neither Eusebius nor Beda counts this period between Nero and Vespasian. (OROS.) For many days afterward, in numerous and unspeakable ways (Josephus, same passage), Vespasian’s soldiers—namely, Antonius Primus and Martianus, the commanders of Vespasian who killed Vitellius—raged with indiscriminate slaughter against the Senate and the Roman people.

(OROS.) Vespasian (Josephus, same work VII.9), after he had shut up the Jews in the city of Jerusalem under siege, especially those gathered for the feast of Easter, learned of Nero’s death. At the urging of many kings [Note: [Col. 0655] Read “regum,” “of kings,” for “regnum,” “kingdom.”] and commanders, and especially on the advice of Josephus, commander of the Jews—who, when captured and thrown into chains, said with complete confidence, as Suetonius relates, that he would soon be released by that same Vespasian, but as emperor—he obtained the imperial power (HIER.). Entrusting the war to his son Titus, he set out for Rome by way of Alexandria. (OROS.) But after learning of Vitellius’s death, he stayed for a short time at Alexandria.

Titus was then proclaimed emperor by the army. He leveled all the city walls to the ground. Cornelius and Suetonius report that six hundred thousand Jews were killed in that war. Josephus, a Jew who himself commanded in the war and later obtained pardon and favor from Vespasian after the aforesaid imperial accession, writes that eleven hundred thousand perished by sword and famine. The survivors, dispersed throughout the entire world, are said to have numbered nine hundred thousand.—Vespasian and Titus were proclaimed emperors. (Cf. HIER.)

Roman ruler 10. According to all authorities, Vespasian reigned for nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days—that is, until the Kalends of October, in the fiftieth year after the Passion.

75. 1. [LIII.] (HIER.) Vespasian 3 and Nerva. The Capitol at Rome was burned.

76. 2. [LIV.] (HIER.) Vespasian 4 and Titus 3. In these consuls’ year, Judea was captured by Titus, Vespasian’s son. As Josephus says, eleven hundred thousand perished from famine and the sword, and one hundred thousand captives were sold.

The Gospel according to Matthew: “Amen I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matthew 24:2).

Jerome says: “According to the historical account, the meaning is clear: in the forty-second year after the Passion, under Vespasian and Titus, the city itself, together with its magnificent temple, was utterly overthrown, so that it was leveled to the ground.” This is Jerome.

Therefore, in the forty-second year after the Passion—that is, counting the year of the Passion, in which Vespasian began his second year—Jerusalem was captured during the days of Easter, Josephus testifying and being present there. [The Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0655] A sign having been placed, the words “first hand, as it seems, 1. Two are missing” are written at the top of the margin.] also spoke through the mouth of David: “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the sanctuary, and those who hate you have gloried in the midst of Easter,” and so forth.] When they refused to turn to repentance, although the Lord had awaited them for forty years, it was fitting that at the time when they killed the Lord they themselves should also be killed.

The Jewish Easter in the aforesaid year occurred on Wednesday, when all the chief priests and elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize and kill Jesus by deceit (Matthew 26:3–4). Our Easter, however, occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when they crucified the Lord; during those same days Titus captured the city, then burned the temple and leveled all the city walls to the ground. Josephus, the Jewish historian who was then present, writes that eleven hundred thousand perished by sword and famine, one hundred thousand captives were sold, and ninety thousand were dispersed. Jerusalem had such a great multitude at that time because people from all Judea streamed to the temple during the days of unleavened bread (cf. Orosius and Jerome).

77. 3. [LV.] Vespasian 5 and Titus 4.

78. 4. [LVI.] Vespasian 6 and Titus 5.

[In the manuscript margin: The fourth nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 15.]

79. 5. [LVII.] Vespasian 7 and Titus 6. Vespasian began to build the Capitol. A sedition occurred in Alexandria. Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes [Note: [Col. 0655] Read “Lycia, Rhodes” for “Aliciarchodus.”], Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, which had previously been free and under friendly kings, were reduced to provinces.

80. 6. [LVIII.] (HIER.) Commodus and Rufus. The Colossus was erected; it had a height of one hundred and seven feet [Note: [Col. 0655] “Feet” added later by a second hand.].

81. 7. [LIX.] (HIER.) Vespasian 8 and Titus [7]. Asconius Pedianus is regarded as a distinguished historical writer. In the seventy-third year of his age he lost his sight and afterward lived out twelve years in the highest honor.

82. 8. [LX.] (HIER.) Vespasian 9 and Titus 8. Gabianus, a rhetorician [Note: [Col. 0655] “By name” added by a later hand.], taught with great distinction in Gaul.

83. 9. [LXI.] Silvanus and Verus. Three cities in Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake. A great pestilence occurred at Rome, so that for many days nearly ten thousand dead were carried out each day.

84. 10. [LXII.] (HIER.) Domitian and Messalianus. Vespasian led out colonies. Apollinaris the bishop was sent to Ravenna and suffered martyrdom.

(REG.) Vespasian died from a flux of the bowels at his own villa near the Sabines, in the sixty-ninth year of his age [Col. 0657A]. (HIER.) [Titus succeeded him in these consuls’ year, according to Cassiodorus.]

Roman ruler 11. Titus, Vespasian’s son, according to Roman history, reigned for two years, eight months, and twenty days—that is, until the Kalends of June, in the fifty-third year after the Passion of the Lord.

85. 1. [LXIII.] (HIER.) Domitian and Rufus. Titus, Vespasian’s son, was highly eloquent in both languages and so good that, when one day at dinner he remembered that he had given nothing to anyone that day, he said: “Friends, I have lost a day today.” Mount Vesuvius erupted and cast such a quantity of fire from its summit that it burned the neighboring regions and cities together with their inhabitants.

86. 2. [LXIV.] (HIER.) Domitian 3 and Sabinus. Titus recalled the philosopher Musonius Rufus from exile [Col. 0657B]. Titus built the amphitheater at Rome, and at its dedication killed five thousand wild animals. Many houses at Rome were consumed by fire. Because of his outstanding gentleness, Titus was called “the delight of the human race.” Titus died at the villa where his father had died, in the forty-second year of his age, in the second year, eighth month, and twentieth day of his reign, according to Roman history. His younger brother Domitian succeeded him [in the aforesaid consuls’ year, according to Cassiodorus].

Roman ruler 12. Domitian reigned for fifteen years and five months, according to all authorities—that is, until the Kalends of November, in the sixty-eighth year after the Passion. Under him were the following consuls.

87. 1. [LXV.] (HIER.) Domitian 4 and Rufus. Domitian’s wife was called Augusta. [Cletus suffered martyrdom in these consuls’ year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, according to the deeds of the pontiffs.]

88. 2. [LXVI.] (HIER.) Domitian and Dolabella. By decree of the Senate, Titus was enrolled among the gods.

89. 3. [LXVII.] (HIER.) Domitian 6 and Rufus 4. Domitian prohibited eunuchs. Three Vestal Virgins were condemned for sexual misconduct. [Pope Linus: eleven years.]

90. 4. [LXVIII.] (HIER. [Note: [Col. 0657] In this year, the first hand noted in the right margin: “Vespasian: nine years, eleven months, twenty-one days”; and in the following years the names and years of the emperors are similarly recorded, corresponding to the years of the common era placed on the right.]) Flavius and Trajanus. Domitian sent very many senators into exile.

91. 5. [LXIX.] (HIER.) Domitian 7 and Nerva. Abilius was appointed the second bishop of the church of Alexandria; he presided for thirteen years.

92. 6. [LXX.] (HIER.) Trajan 2 and Gabrio. Domitian built a temple without the use of wood. Domitian was the first to order that he be called “Lord and God.” The Nasamones and Dacians, fighting against the Romans, were defeated. In his sixth year, Pope Clement was sent into exile, apparently after holding the chair for nine years, two months, and ten days after Cletus (the *Book of the Pontiffs*).

93. 7. [LXXI.] (HIER.) Domitian 8 and Saturninus. Two months were given different names: September Germanicus and October Domitianus.

Ancletus, the second pope after Peter, succeeded Clement and held office for ten years, as he himself bears witness: The decretal letter of Pope Ancletus (Letter 1, p. 63): “Ancletus, servant of Christ Jesus, in the apostolic see,” and so forth. And below: “No one, as blessed Clement, our predecessor, says,” and so forth. Another letter (Letter 2, p. 68): “Pope Ancletus to all the bishops established in Italy. Since your charity has shown me the due reverence owed to the apostolic see,” and so forth. And afterward: “And as we have been instructed by blessed Peter, the prince, by whom I too was ordained presbyter,” and so forth. “But the provinces had been divided for the most part long before the coming of Christ; and afterward that division was renewed by the apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor,” and so forth.

Another letter (Letter 3, p. 72): “Ancletus, servant of Jesus Christ, appointed by the Lord in the apostolic see and ordained presbyter by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. Since up to now we have known that these matters were established by blessed Peter the apostle and the other apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor and martyr, we cannot in any way deny them to you. But those who have been appointed in the metropolis by blessed Peter, at the Lord’s direction, and by our predecessor, the aforesaid Saint Clement, or by us, cannot all be primates,” and so forth.

And afterward: “But the other principal cities, which we send to you written down in a certain volume, received their primates and preachers from the holy apostles and from blessed Clement or from us. But this most holy Roman and apostolic Church obtained its primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord himself, our Savior, who said to blessed Peter the apostle: ‘You are Peter,’ and so forth, up to ‘They shall be loosed in heaven.’ The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel [Note: [Col. 0657] That is, *vassis*: ‘vessel.’], was also added in that same city of Rome; he was crowned by a glorious death together with Peter, suffering in the contest under the emperor Nero on one and the same day and at one and the same time.”

And afterward: “Therefore blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, speaking publicly and teaching the people about our holy predecessor Clement, instructed them how they ought to obey and observe him: ‘If Clement is hostile to anyone on account of his deeds, do not wait for him himself to say to you, “Do not be friends with that man”; rather, you must prudently observe this and comply with his will without communion [Note: [Col. 0657] Read: ‘admonition.’], and separate yourselves from him toward whom you perceive that he is hostile; nor should you speak with those with whom he does not speak. Thus, whoever is involved in this fault, while desiring to retain the friendship of all of you, should hasten to be reconciled with him who presides over all; and through this he may return to salvation once he has begun to obey the admonitions of his superior. But if anyone is friendly with those with whom he himself does not speak, he too is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God,’ and so forth.”

Thus speaks Pope Ancletus. But Eusebius entirely omitted Ancletus [Note: [Col. 0659] Not Anacletus but Cletus was omitted by Eusebius both in the *Chronicle* and in the *Ecclesiastical History*.], because Linus and Cletus, who were not popes, and Clement and Anacletus cannot all stand together under the rulers from Peter’s Passion in the last year of Nero up to Trajan. In place of the years of Clement, during which, after Peter, he held the see with Linus and Cletus—if Linus and Cletus were alive together after Peter—or with Cletus alone, Linus and Cletus have been placed; and in place of Pope Ancletus, who succeeded Clement for ten years, Clement has been placed.

### 94. 8. [LXXII] (JEROME)

Silvanus and Priscus. Quintilian, from Spain, a native of Calagurris, was the first to receive a public school and a salary from the treasury at Rome, and he became famous.

[Col. 0659B]

### 95. 9. [LXXIII] (JEROME)

Asprenas and Clement. Domitian sent very many nobles into exile and killed them; he drove mathematicians and philosophers out of the city of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0659] The first copy has *romamana*.]

### 96. 10. [LXXIV] (JEROME)

Domitian 9 and Clement 2. Many works were constructed at Rome, including the Capitol, the Transitory Forum, the Portico of the Divine Ones, the Iseum and Serapeum, the stadium, the pepper warehouses, the temple of Vespasian, Minerva Chalcidica, the Odeon, the Forum of Trajan [Note: [Col. 0659] *ni* was added afterward in the first copy.], the Baths of Trajan and of Ticiana, the senate-house, the morning school, and the Golden Mica.

In these consuls’ year Pope Ancletus died, according to the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.

### 97. 11. [LXXV] (JEROME)

Nerva 2 and Rufus. Domitian celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Germans. Domitian was so proud that he ordered golden and silver statues of himself to be set up in the Capitol.

[Col. 0659C]

### 98. 12. [LXXVI] (JEROME)

Fulvius and Vetus. Cornelia, the chief of the Vestal Virgins, convicted of adultery, was buried alive according to the law. Domitian forbade vines to be planted in cities.

### 99. 13. [LXXVII] (JEROME)

Sabinus and Antoninus. Flavius Josephus wrote the twentieth book of his *Antiquities* at this time. Domitian destroyed many nobles and sent some into exile.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The second persecution.”

### 100. 14. [LXXVIII] (JEROME)

Nerva 3 and Trajan 3. Domitian, the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, persecuted them; under him the apostle John was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil before the Latin Gate at Rome (Regino, Bede, Jerome), yet was not harmed, because he was free from the corruption of the flesh. Then, having been banished to the island of Patmos, he saw the Apocalypse, which Irenaeus interpreted.

[Col. 0659D]

In these consuls’ year Pope Clement suffered martyrdom, according to the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.

### 101. 15. [LXXIX]

[Note: [Col. 0659] From this year onward the popes belonging to these years are also placed in the right-hand margin, but by a second hand: 101. 79: Pope Cletus, according to Eusebius, 12 years.—113. (91.) Pope Clement, according to Eusebius, 9 years, etc.]

Senecio and Palma. Domitian once again expelled philosophers and mathematicians from Rome by an edict. Apollonius of Tyana and Euphrates were regarded as distinguished philosophers. At Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, was celebrated the nativity of Pope and martyr Ancletus, who suffered under Domitian (Bede, *Martyrology*) and who built and arranged the memorial of blessed Peter, where bishops were to be buried (*Book of the Pontiffs*).

[Col. 0660A]

Pope Evaristus, the third after Peter, held office for ten years and two months.

### 102. 16. [LXXX] (JEROME)

Trajan 4 and Fronto. Domitian ordered those who were of the lineage of David to be killed, so that no remnant of the Jewish kingdom would remain. Bruttius writes that very many Christians suffered martyrdom under Domitian, among them Flavia Domitilla, the niece through her sister of the consul Flavius Clemens, who was banished to the island of Pontia because she declared that she was a Christian. [Note: [Col. 0659] The first copy has *testa*.]

(H. R.) Many signs and portents occurred at Rome and throughout the world. Domitian was killed by a conspiracy of his own people in the palace, in the thirty-fifth year of his age; he was disgracefully carried away by undertakers of low birth—and Nerva succeeded him in these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies.

[Col. 0660B]

The thirteenth Roman ruler, Nerva, according to Eusebius and Bede, reigned for one year, four months, and eight days—that is, up to the Kalends of March, in the seventieth year after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 103. 1. [LXXXI] (JEROME)

Trajan 5 and Ofitus. At Alexandria Cerdo was appointed the third bishop and held office for eleven years. The senate decreed that everything Domitian had established should be annulled. Thus many whom he had unjustly cast out returned from exile and recovered some of their own property.

### 104. 2. [LXXXII] (JEROME)

Senecio 2 and Sura. They also say that the apostle John was released among those returning from exile and returned to Ephesus, where he had both a small dwelling and very devoted friends. (Bede.) He also wrote a Gospel against the heretics. Justus of Tiberias is recognized as a Jewish writer.

(Jerome.) At Rome, Eutychus, Victorinus, and Mauro suffered martyrdom; at the city of Amiternum, Victorinus, bishop and brother of Severinus.

(Regino.) Nerva died in the Sallustian Gardens at the age of seventy-two, after he had already adopted Trajan as his son, in these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies.

(Jerome.) Trajan, son of Agrippina, was made emperor in Gaul; he was born in Italica, in Spain.

[Col. 0660D]

The fourteenth Roman ruler, Trajan, reigned for nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days, according to every historian—that is, up to the Kalends of September, in the eighty-ninth year after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 105. 1. [LXXXIII] (JEROME)

Trajan 6 and Maximus. By decree of the senate, Nerva was enrolled among the gods.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The solar cycle begins.”

### 106. 2. [LXXXIV] (cf. Bede)

Senecio 3 and Sura. This year—that is, the year 84 from the Incarnation according to Dionysius—at the end of the following Sunday, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, John may have fallen asleep.

[Col. 0661A]

### 107. 3. [LXXXV] (JEROME)

Urbanus and Marcellus. For Irenaeus the bishop writes that the apostle John survived until the time of Trajan. After him his distinguished disciples were Papias, bishop of Hierapolis; Polycarp of Smyrna; and Ignatius, bishop of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0661] This should be joined with year 106.]

### 108. 4. [LXXXVI] (JEROME)

Condidus and Quadratus. Trajan celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians.

### 109. 5. [LXXXVII] (JEROME)

Commodus and Cerealis. After defeating King Decebalus, Trajan made Dacia a province.

### 110. 6. [LXXXVIII] (JEROME)

Senecio 4 and Sura 3. He received the Iberians [Note: [Col. 0661] Read *Hiberos*. This should be joined with what precedes.], the Sarmatians of Orozes, the Arabs, Bosporans, and Colchians into allegiance; he occupied and held Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon. He established a fleet in the Red Sea so that through it he might lay waste the borders of India.

[Col. 0661B]

### 111. 7. [LXXXIX] (JEROME)

Gallus and Bradua. The Golden House at Rome was burned. This year the Lord’s Day fell on the sixth day before the Kalends of January; it may have been the day on which Saint John died.

The decretal letter of Pope Evaristus (Letter 2, Council, p. 71) was addressed to Gallus and Bradua, most illustrious men, in whose consulship he suffered, according to the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.

### 112. 8. [XC] (JEROME)

Africanus and Crispinus. In an earthquake four cities of Asia were overthrown: Elaea, Myrina, Pitane, and Cyme; and two cities of Greece, Opuntian and Oritan.

[Col. 0661C]

### 113. 9. [XCI] (JEROME)

Crispinus 2 and Solenus. Primus was ordained the fourth bishop of the Alexandrian Church and held office for eleven years. Pope Evaristus died on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

### 114. 10. [XCII]

Piso and Rusticus.

Pope Alexander, the fourth after Peter, held office for ten years and five months.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The third persecution.”

(Bede, Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 132.) During Trajan’s persecution of Christians, Simon, also called Simon, son of Clopas, who held the episcopate at Jerusalem after James, was crucified, to everyone’s amazement, including that of the judge himself, because he endured the punishment of the cross as a man of 120 years.

[Col. 0661D]

### 115. 11. [XCIII] (JEROME)

Trajan and Africanus 2. Ignatius also, bishop of the church of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to the beasts; after him Oron was appointed the third bishop.

When Pliny the Younger, having governed a certain province and killed very many Christians during his magistracy, was terrified by their multitude, he asked Trajan what ought to be done [Note: [Col. 0661] The first copy has *facio*. It should have been written, with Jerome, “what ought to be done,” reporting this to him.], and reported that, apart from their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice and their meetings before dawn to sing to a certain Christ as God, he found nothing among them; furthermore, that they forbade murder, theft, adultery, robbery, and similar acts in order to bind their discipline together.

Trajan, angered by this, sent back a rescript that this class of people should not be sought out [Note: [Col. 0661] The first copy perhaps has *quidem* or *quidam*.], but that those who were brought before the authorities should be punished.

[Col. 0662A]

Tertullian reports this in the *Apology*.

Pope Alexander established that water mixed with blessed salt should be blessed and sprinkled in people’s dwellings (*Book of the Pontiffs*).

### 116. 12. [XCIV] (JEROME)

Celsus and Crispinus. Pliny the Younger of Novocomum, an outstanding orator and historian, was highly regarded; many works of his varied talent survive.

### 117. 13. [XCV] (JEROME)

Asta and Piso. Three cities of Galatia were torn apart by an earthquake. The Pantheon at Rome was burned by lightning.

### 118. 14. [XCVI] (JEROME)

Messala and Pedo. After Justus, Zacchaeus assumed the fourth episcopate of the Church of Jerusalem.

### 119. 15. [XCVII]

Aemilius and Vetus. After him Tobias was fifth; Benjamin succeeded him as sixth; then John as seventh, Matthias as eighth; and in Matthias’s place Philip was appointed as ninth.

[Note: [Col. 0661] This should be joined with year 118.]

[Col. 0662B]

### 120. 16. [XCVIII] (JEROME)

Niger and Apronianus. Trajan made Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia provinces.

### 121. 17. [XCIX] (JEROME)

Clarus and Alexander. The Jews who were in Libya fought against the foreign inhabitants living alongside them; likewise in Egypt and Alexandria. At Cyrene and also in the Thebaid they engaged in a great revolt; but in Alexandria the gentile party prevailed.

### 122. 18. [C] (JEROME)

Hadrian and Salinator. When the Jews of Mesopotamia rebelled, the emperor Trajan ordered Lusius Quietus to destroy the province; and Quietus, drawing up his battle line against them, killed countless thousands of them. For this reason he was appointed governor of Judaea by the emperor.

[Col. 0662C]

The Jews, after killing the gentiles in Salamis, a city of Cyprus, overturned it.

### 123. 19. [CI] (ADON, *Martyrology*)

Hadrian 2 and Rusticus. The martyrdom of Pope Alexander occurred on the fifth day before the Nones of May, at Rome on the Nomentan Way, seven miles from the city, together with the presbyters Eventius and Theodulus. He was beheaded under the emperor Trajan, with Aurelian as judge; yet Hadrian was not yet emperor, as it is read in the martyrology. [Note: [Col. 0661] The first copy has *sed I*.]

Pope Sixtus, the fifth after Peter, held office for ten years and eleven months. He established in the decrees that the sacred mysteries should be handled only by sacred ministers, and that during the celebration of the Mass “Holy, holy, holy” should be sung, and so forth up to “Hosanna in the highest.” (Cf. *Book of the Pontiffs*.)

(Regino.) At Rome Clement and Alexander, the popes, suffered martyrdom; Quirinus with his son; Balbina; Sulpicius and Servilianus; the virgins Domitilla and Seraphia; Nereus; Achilleus; and Ignatius, bishop of Antioch and disciple of John.

[Col. 0662D]

### 124. 20. [CII] (CASSIODORUS)

Servilius and Fulvius. In these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies, Trajan died at Seleucia in Isauria of a discharge of the bowels, in the sixty-third year of his age, in the ninth month and fourth day. The ninth month of the year, according to the Latins, is September.

(Jerome.) Trajan’s bones were placed in a golden urn and set up in the Forum beneath a column; he alone of all was buried within the city.

[Col. 0663A]

The fifteenth Roman ruler, Hadrian, reigned according to Roman history for twenty-one years, ten months, and twenty days—that is, up to the Kalends of August, in the 111th year after the Passion of the Lord. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 125. 1. [CIII] (JEROME)

Verus and Auger. Hadrian, born in Italica in Spain, was the son of Trajan’s cousin. Hadrian restored Alexandria, which had been destroyed by the Romans, at public expense. Envious of Trajan’s glory, Hadrian recalled the army from Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Armenia, which Trajan had made provinces.

### 126. 2. [CIV] (JEROME)

Aviola and Pansa. Hadrian captured the Jews when they rebelled against the Romans for the second time. The senate enrolled Trajan among the gods. Hadrian was extremely learned in both languages, but he was not sufficiently restrained with boys.

[Col. 0663B]

### 127. 3. [CV] (JEROME)

Paternus and Torquatus. Hadrian remitted the remaining taxes owed by the cities, after publicly burning the tax records; he also freed very many people from taxes. Plutarch of Chaeronea, Sextus, Agathobulus, and Oenomaus were regarded as distinguished philosophers.

### 128. 4. [CVI] (JEROME)

Gabrius and Apronianus. War was waged against the Sarmatians. After an earthquake, Nicomedia collapsed, and many neighboring cities were overthrown [Note: [Col. 0663] Read “neighboring cities.”], for whose restoration Hadrian contributed public funds.

### 129. 5. [CVII] (JEROME)

Asiaticus and Quintus. Euphrates the Stoic philosopher died. Hadrian led colonies into Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews. [Note: [Col. 0663] The first copy has *vasta*.]

### 130. 6. [CVIII] (JEROME)

Verus and Ambiguus. When the Athenians requested laws, Hadrian compiled legal regulations for them from the books of Draco, Solon, and the others.

[Col. 0663C]

### 131. 7. [CIX] (JEROME)

Gallicanus and Titianus. The river Cephissus flooded Eleusis. Hadrian, joining it to the sea by a bridge [Note: [Col. 0663] Read *ponte*, “by a bridge.”], spent the winter at Athens.

### 132. 8. [CX] (JEROME)

Torquatus and Libo. At Jerusalem, after Philip, Seneca was appointed as the tenth bishop. After him came Justus as the eleventh; Levi succeeded him as the twelfth; after Levi came Ephres as the thirteenth, Jesse as the fourteenth, and Judas as the fifteenth. All these bishops, who were from the circumcision, presided until the destruction that Jerusalem suffered under Hadrian.

### 133. 9. [CXI] (JEROME)

Celsus and Marcellinus. Hadrian, initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, gave many gifts to the Athenians. Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides of Athens, our philosopher, presented Hadrian with books composed in defense of the Christian religion.

[Col. 0663D]

[In the margin of the codex:] “The solar cycle begins.”

### 134. 10. [CXII] (JEROME)

Pontianus and Rufus. Serenus Granianus, a legate and a man of the highest nobility, sent a letter to the emperor, saying that it was unjust for the blood of innocent people to be surrendered to the shouting of the crowd and for people to be condemned merely on account of their name and sect.

[Col. 0664A]

### 135. 11. [CXIII] (JEROME)

Augurinus and Sergianus. Moved by this, Hadrian wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without charges of crimes being brought against them; a copy of this letter remains famous down to our own time. The emperor Hadrian was called “father of his country.”

[Note: [Col. 0663] This belongs to the preceding entry.]

### 136. 12. [CXIV] (ADON, *Martyrology*)

Tiberius and Silanus. Pope Sixtus suffered martyrdom on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

(Cf. *Book of the Pontiffs*, Adon, *Martyrology*, Jerome.) Telesphorus, the sixth pope after Peter, held office for eleven years. He established that all clergy should fast from meat for seven full weeks before Easter, that Masses should be celebrated on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, and that “Glory in the highest” should be sung at Mass.

Cornelius was appointed the fourth bishop of Antioch. Nicopolis and Caesarea collapsed in an earthquake.

### 137. 13. [CXV] (JEROME)

Sergius and Verus. Antinous, the king’s boy, of extraordinary beauty, died in Egypt. Hadrian, grieving for him intensely—for he had kept him among his pleasures—enrolled him among the gods; a city was also named after him.

Heuminus presided as the sixth bishop of the Alexandrian Church for thirteen years.

[Col. 0664B]

### 138. 14. [CXVI] (JEROME)

Pompeianus and Atilianus. A temple of Rome and Venus was built in the city under Hadrian. Salvius Julianus composed the perpetual edict.

### 139. 15. [CXVII] (JEROME)

Pompeianus 2 and Commodus. Hadrian, spending the winter at Athens, visited Eleusis. After constructing many distinguished buildings at Athens, Hadrian staged a contest and built a library.

### 140. 16. [CXVIII] (JEROME)

Laelius and Albinus. The Jews took up arms and ravaged Palestine, while Tinnius Rufus governed the province. Hadrian sent an army to suppress the rebels. Favorinus and Polemo were regarded as distinguished rhetors.

[Col. 0664C]

### 141. 17. [CXIX] (JEROME)

Camerinus and Niger. Basilides, the founder of a heresy, lived in Alexandria; from him came the Gnostics.
