Chochebas, leader of the Jewish faction, killed Christians with every kind of torture because they refused to provide assistance to his forces against the Roman army. [Note: [Col. 0663] The first copy has *necati*.]

### 142. 18. [CXX] (JEROME)

Antonius and Praesens. The Jewish war that was being waged in Palestine came to an end, with the affairs of the Jews completely crushed. From that time they were also deprived of permission to enter Jerusalem.

### 143. 19. [CXXI] (JEROME)

Antonius 2 and Praesens 2. First by the will of God, as the prophets foretold, and then by Roman prohibitions, Mark was appointed the first Gentile bishop at Jerusalem, when the bishops who had been Jews ceased to hold office. They numbered fifteen, from the Passion of the Lord through 107 years.

[Col. 0664D]

[The editorial note adds: “As Eusebius and Bede testify. Therefore add the Lord’s thirty-four years up to the Passion: 34 plus 107 makes 141 years, up to the year in which all the Jews were expelled from Jerusalem.”]

### 144. 20. [CXXII] (JEROME)

Severus and Sylvanus. Aelia was founded by Aelius Hadrianus. On the front of its gate by which we go out toward Bethlehem, a boar was carved in marble, signifying that the Jews were subject to Roman authority. Some think that it was constructed by Titus Aelianus, son of Vespasian.

[Col. 0665A]

Jerome (Letter 49, to Paulinus): “From the time of Hadrian until the reign of Constantine, for approximately 180 years, in the place of the Lord’s Resurrection an image of Jupiter was worshiped; on the rock of the Cross, a marble statue of Venus was set up and worshiped by the Gentiles, according to their custom. The authors of the persecution believed that they would remove our faith in the Resurrection and the Cross if they polluted the holy places with idols.” [Note: [Col. 0665] These words are written by a second hand in the margin of folio 113, without an indication of their place.]

### 145. 21. [CXXIII] (ISIDORE)

Rufinus and Torquatus. At this time Aquila of Pontus was the second interpreter after the Seventy translators; he translated Scripture from Hebrew.

Pope Telesphorus suffered martyrdom on the Nones of January (Adon, *Martyrology*).

[Col. 0665B]

Pope Hyginus, the seventh after Peter, held office for four years. He established the clergy and distributed the ecclesiastical orders (cf. *Book of the Pontiffs*).

(Adon, *Martyrology*; Regino.) At Rome Sixtus and Telesphorus, the popes, suffered martyrdom; Getulius, Sabina, and Seraphia, virgins; at Messana, a city of Apulia, Eleutherius the bishop with Anthia his mother; Dionysius the bishop, the Areopagite; at Tibur, a city of Italy, Symphorosa with her seven sons; at Athens Quadratus and Aristides flourished.

(Cassiodorus, *Roman History*.) In these consuls’ year, Hadrian died at Baiae in Campania from dropsy, in the sixty-first year of his age, in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the tenth month and twentieth day, as is recorded in Roman history. Antoninus Pius succeeded him. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

[Col. 0665C]

Orosius writes as follows:

“Titus Antoninus, surnamed Pius, the thirteenth emperor from Julius Caesar—after Galba, Otho, and Vitellius had been excluded from the number of the emperors—reigned with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty-three years, though not complete.”

This is what Orosius says (*VII, 14*). According to Eusebius and Bede, he also reigned for three additional months—that is, up to the Kalends of November, in the 134th year after the Passion of the Lord. Since it was customary among historians to assign to an emperor the year in which he died or ceased to rule, it can therefore be said that Antoninus Pius reigned for fewer than twenty-three full years, since he did not live to the end of the year.

### 146. 1. [CXXIV] (ISIDORE)

Torquatus 2 and Herodes.

[Col. 0665D]

[The note reads: “This Pius was called so because throughout the whole Roman realm he remitted the debts owed by people.”]

### 147. 2. [CXXV] (JEROME)

Aviola and Maximus. From this time Antoninus was called “father of his country.”

### 148. 3. [CXXVI] (JEROME)

Antoninus 3 and Aurelius. Under Hyginus, bishop of the city of Rome, Valentinus, founder of a heresy, and Cerdo, teacher of Marcion, came to Rome.

[Col. 0666A]

### 149. 4. [CXXVII] (JEROME)

Gratus and Seleucus. Justin the philosopher presented Antoninus with a book written in defense of our religion. Pope Hyginus died on the fourth day before the Ides of January (Adon, *Martyrology*).

Pius, the eighth pope after Peter, held office for fifteen years.

### 150. 5. [CXXVIII] (Book of the Pontiffs, Bede)

Antoninus 4 and Aurelius. Under Pope Pius, Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, in which the angel’s command is contained that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.

### 151. 6. [CXXIX] (JEROME)

Largus and Messalianus. At Antioch Eros was appointed as the fifth bishop.

### 152. 7. [CXXX] (JEROME)

Torquatus 3 and Julianus. At Alexandria Mark assumed the episcopate as the seventh bishop and held it for ten years.

### 153. 8. [CXXXI] (JEROME)

Orfiscus and Priscus. Valentinus the heretic was recognized and continued down to Pope Anicetus.

### 154. 9. [CXXXII] (JEROME)

Gabrius and Vetus. Mesomedes of Crete was recognized as a musician and poet of songs for the cithara.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The eighth decennial cycle begins; indiction 1.”

### 155. 10. [CXXXIII] (ISIDORE)

Gordianus and Maximus. Marcion, founder of a heresy, was recognized.

### 156. 11. [CXXXIV] (JEROME)

Gabrius 2 and Romulus. Taurus of Berytus was regarded as a distinguished philosopher of the Platonic school.

### 157. 12. [CXXXV] (JEROME)

Praesens and Rufus. Arrianus, a philosopher from Nicomedia, was recognized.

### 158. 13. [CXXXVI] (JEROME)

Commodus and Lateranus. Also Maximus Tyrius [Note: [Col. 0665] Read *Maximus*. This belongs to year 157.]. Apollonius the Stoic, by nationality a Chalcidian.

[Col. 0666C]

### 159. 14. [CXXXVII] (JEROME)

Verus and Sabinus. Also Basilides of Scythopolis [Note: [Col. 0665] The division is printed thus, but it belongs to year 158.], who were regarded as distinguished philosophers. [Note: [Col. 0665] The first copy has *philophi*.]

### 160. 15. [CXXXVIII] (JEROME)

Sylvanus and Augurinus. They too [Note: [Col. 0665] The division is printed thus, but it belongs to year 158.] were teachers of Verissimus Caesar.

### 161. 16. [CXXXIX] (JEROME)

Barbarus and Regulus. Celadion presided as the eighth bishop of the Alexandrian Church for fourteen years.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The solar cycle begins,” and below, “The fourth persecution.”

[Col. 0666D]

### 162. 17. [CXL] (JEROME)

Tertullus and Sacerdos. Crescens the Cynic was recognized. Because Justin, the philosopher of our doctrine, accused him of being a glutton [Note: [Col. 0665] After “philosopher” a lacuna was left; it is filled in the margin, with a sign, as follows: “of being a glutton himself.”] and of being a transgressor, he stirred up a persecution in which Justin shed his blood gloriously for Christ.

### 163. 18. [CXLI] (ISIDORE)

Quintillius and Priscus. Gallianus, a physician born at Pergamum.

### 164. 19. [CXLII] (JEROME)

Verus and Bradua. Pope Pius died on the fifth day before the Ides of July [Note: [Col. 0665] The words “5. Idus Julii” were added later in the margin, apparently by the first hand.] (cf. *Book of the Pontiffs*, Adon, *Martyrology*).

Pope Anicetus, the ninth after Peter, held office for eleven years and four months. He established that a cleric should not grow his hair long, in accordance with the apostle’s command.

[Col. 0667A]

### 165. 20. [CXLIII] (JEROME)

Antoninus 5 and Aurelius 3. Under Pope Anicetus, Polycarp came to Rome and corrected many who had recently been corrupted by the heretical stain of the teaching of Valentinus and Cerdo.

### 166. 21. [CXLIV] (BEDE)

Antoninus 6 and Aurelius 4. After Mark, Cassianus assumed the seventeenth episcopate of Jerusalem; after him came Publius as the eighteenth, whom Maximus succeeded as the nineteenth; then Julianus as the twentieth, Gaianus as the twenty-first, Symmachus as the twenty-second, Gaius as the twenty-third, Julianus as the twenty-fourth, and Capito as the twenty-fifth.

[Note: [Col. 0667] The remainder of year 167 is written here.]

### 167. 22. [CXLV] (JEROME)

Antoninus 7 and Aurelius 5.

### 168. 23. [CXLVI] (CASSIODORUS)

The proconsul. Antoninus and Aurelius.

[Note: [Col. 0667] In this year, in the margin by a second hand, one reads: “As Bede says in the *History of the English*”; I do not know what this refers to. Bede I, 4, calls Marcus Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus; but compare year 201.]

Antoninus Pius died at his own estate at Lorium, twelve miles from the city, in these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies. His sons succeeded him, namely Marcus Antoninus Verus, Lucius Annius, and Antoninus Severus. The following consuls served under them.

[Col. 0667B]

The seventeenth Roman ruler, Marcus Antoninus Verus, reigned with his brother Lucius Commodus after their father for nineteen years and one month—that is, up to the Kalends of December, in the 153rd year after the Passion.

### 169. 1. [CXLVII] (JEROME)

The two Augusti as consuls. These two first administered the empire with equal authority, since up to this time there had been only individual Augusti.

### 170. 2. [CXLVIII] (JEROME)

Rusticus and Aquilinus. While Lucius Caesar was sacrificing at Athens, fire was seen to be carried across the sky from west to east.

[Col. 0667C]

### 171. 3. [CLXIX] (JEROME)

Laelianus and Pastor. Vologeses, king of the Parthians, ravaged the Roman provinces neighboring his own territory.

### 172. 4. [CL] (JEROME)

Marcinus and Celsus. Fronto was regarded as a distinguished orator; he instructed Antoninus Verus in Latin letters. The Assyrian city of Seleucia was captured by the Romans together with three hundred thousand inhabitants.

### 173. 5. [CLI] (JEROME)

Orsitus and Pudens. At Pisae, the philosopher Peregrinus threw himself onto a pyre that he had constructed from burning wood [Note: [Col. 0667] Read “the pyre which he had built from wood,” etc.]. Lucius Caesar celebrated a triumph over the Parthians together with his brother.

### 174. 6. [CLII] (JEROME)

Pudens 2 and Pollio. Agrippinus presided as the ninth bishop of the Alexandrian Church for twelve years. When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom; written accounts of their passions are also circulated. Very many in Gaul were killed gloriously for the name of Christ; their struggles, recorded in books, have continued down to the present day.

[Col. 0667D]

### 175. 7. [CLIII] (JEROME)

Verus and Quadratus. A plague occupied many provinces, and Rome was partly affected. The Romans fought against the Germans, Marcomanni, Quadi, Sarmatians, and Dacians.

[Col. 0668A]

### 176. 8. [CLIV] (ADON, *Martyrology*)

Apronianus and Paulus. Pope Anicetus suffered martyrdom on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Pope Soter, the tenth after Peter, held office for nine years. He established that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium in the church or place incense there.

(Jerome.) Theophilus, whose many works of talent survive, was appointed the sixth bishop of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0667] Read “sixth”; the first copy has “seventh.”]

The emperor Lucius died of apoplexy in the ninth year of his reign—or, as some think, the eleventh—between Concordia and Altinum, while seated with his brother in a carriage.

### 177. 9. [CLV] (JEROME)

Priscus and Apollinaris. Asianus of Sardes presented the illustrious emperor Antoninus with an apology on behalf of the Christians. [Note: [Col. 0667] Read “the Sardian.”] Apollinaris the Asian, bishop of Hierapolis, was regarded as distinguished.

### 178. 10. [CLVI] (JEROME)

Cethegus and Clarus. The decretal letter of Pope Soter (Letter 2, Council, p. 101) was addressed to Cethegus and Clarus, most illustrious consuls.

[Col. 0668B]

Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, was regarded as distinguished, and Pinitus of Crete as a man of great eloquence.

### 179. 11. [CLVII] (JEROME)

Severus and Herennius. The pseudo-prophecy called Cataphrygian began, with Montanus and the insane prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla as its authors. Tatian the heretic was recognized; from him came the Encratites.

### 180. 12. [CLVIII] (JEROME)

Orfitus and Pluton. Bardesanes became known as the leader of another heresy. Oppian, a Cilician poet, was recognized; he composed the *Halieutica* with remarkable brilliance. Such a great pestilence raged throughout the whole world that the Roman army was almost destroyed to the point of annihilation.

[Col. 0668C]

### 181. 13. [CLIX] (JEROME)

Severus and Pompeianus. The emperor Antoninus, although many wars arose against him, was often present in person and often sent the most distinguished generals.

### 182. 14. [CLX] (JEROME)

Gallus and Flaccus. During these events, when Pertinax and the army that was fighting with him in the land of the Quadi were overcome by thirst, rain was sent from heaven by divine intervention; while, conversely, lightning pursued the Germans and Sarmatians and killed very many of them.

[Note: [Col. 0667] This belongs to year 181.]

### 183. 15. [CLXI] (JEROME)

Piso and Julianus. There survive letters of Marcus Aurelius, the most serious of emperors, in which he attests that the Germanic thirst was dispelled by a shower obtained, perhaps, through the prayers of Christian soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0667] That is, by rain.]

[Col. 0668D]

### 184. 16. [CLXII] (JEROME)

Pollio and Aper. Atticus, a philosopher of the Platonic school, was recognized. Pope Soter died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May (Adon, *Martyrology*).

(Bede.) Pope Eleutherius, the eleventh after Peter, held office for ten years and one month.

(Jerome.) Lucius, king of Britain, obtained through a letter from Pope Eleutherius that he should become a Christian. At Antioch Maximus was appointed the seventh bishop.

[Col. 0669A]

### 185. 17. [CLXIII] (JEROME)

Commodus and Quintillius. Antoninus made his son Commodus his partner in the kingdom. Antoninus triumphed over the enemies whom he had devastated while maintaining a stationary camp at Carnuntum for three years, together with his son.

### 186. 18. [CLXIV] (JEROME)

Orfitus and Rufus. The emperors gave many gifts to many people, granting to the provinces the money that was owed to the treasury; they ordered the debt registers to be burned in the middle of the Roman Forum; and, so that nothing might be lacking from their generosity, they tempered each of the older laws with new enactments.

(Regino.) At Rome Pope Anicetus suffered martyrdom, together with the presbyter Symmetrius; Felicitas with her seven sons; Julius; Antonius; Eusebius; Potentianus; Peregrinus; and Vincentius. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia many martyrs suffered under the judge Agricola; at Spoletium, Concordius; at Smyrna, Polycarp the bishop, disciple of John, and also Germanicus and Pionius; at Apamea, Alexander and Gaius; at Cortyna, a city of Crete, Philip the bishop; at Pergamum, a city of Asia, Carpus the bishop, Papyrus the deacon, and Justin the philosopher; at Lugdunum in Gaul, Irenaeus the bishop with many others, Photinus the bishop of the same city, Blandina with sixty-eight others, Epipodius, and Alexander; in Syria, Corona and Victor; at Milan, Faustus; at Cabillonum, Marcellus; likewise in the territory of Cabillonum, at the fortress of Trenorcium, Valerianus; in Alexandria, Ptolemy and Lucius. [Note: [Col. 0669] The first copy has *Educius*.]

### 187. 19. [CLXV] (JEROME)

Commodus 2 and Verus. After his victory, Antoninus was so magnificent in the staging of public spectacles that he exhibited one hundred lions at once. Commodus was called Augustus by the senate. The city of Smyrna in Asia collapsed in an earthquake; a ten-year exemption from tribute was granted for its restoration.

[Col. 0669C]

Julianus assumed the episcopate as the tenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church and held it for ten years.

(Cassiodorus.) In these consuls’ year, as Cassiodorus testifies, Antoninus died of illness in Pannonia, in the sixty-first year of his age; his son Commodus succeeded him. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

The eighteenth Roman ruler, Commodus, reigned according to all authorities for thirteen years and likewise eight months, according to Roman history—that is, up to the Kalends of August, in the 167th year after the Passion.

### 188. 1. [CLXVI] (JEROME)

Praesens and Gordianus. Commodus celebrated a triumph over the Germans.

[Col. 0669D]

### 189. 2. [CLXVII] (JEROME)

Commodus 3 and Rufus. The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned.

[In the margin of the codex:] “The solar cycle begins.”

### 190. 3. [CLXVIII] (JEROME)

Mammertinus and Rufus. Irenaeus, bishop of Lugdunum, was regarded as distinguished.

### 191. 4. [CLXIX] (JEROME)

Commodus 4 and Victorinus. The Baths of Commodus were built at Rome.

### 192. 5. [CLXX] (JEROME)

Marullus and Helianus. Commodus named the month of September after himself.

[Codex marginal note: The tenth nineteen-year solar cycle of the great cycle begins; the ninth indiction.]

### 193. 6. [CLXXI] (JEROME)

Maternus and Bradua. At Jerusalem Maximus was ordained the twenty-sixth bishop; after him came, as the twenty-seventh, Antoninus; the twenty-eighth, Valens; the twenty-ninth, Dulcianus; the thirtieth, Narcissus; the thirty-first, Dius; the thirty-second, Germanio; the thirty-third, Gordius; and, again as the thirty-fourth, Narcissus. With so many bishops at Jerusalem, we have been unable to distinguish their dates, because the years of their episcopates have not been preserved down to the present day. (Ep. 2, p. 101.) Lightning struck the Capitol, and, after a great conflagration, the library and all the neighboring buildings were burned.

[The decretal letter of Pope Eleutherius was addressed to Maternus and Bradua, VV., that is, venerable men, CC., that is, most distinguished consuls.]

### 194. 7. [CLXXII] (JEROME)

Commodus 5 and Gabrio. Commodus killed many members of the nobility.

### 195. 8. [CLXXIII] (JEROME)

Crispinus and Helianus. Commodus provided the Roman people with distinguished spectacles.

[Note: [Column 0669] “from 1.”]

### 196. 9. [CLXXIV] (ISIDORE)

Fuscianus and Silanus. Theodotion of Ephesus is regarded as the third translator.

### 197. 10. [CLXXV] (JEROME)

Duo and Sillanus. At Alexandria Demetrius was appointed bishop, the eleventh, and held the office for forty-three years. The emperor Commodus, after removing the head of the Colossus, ordered the head of his own image to be put in its place.

[Note: [Column 0669] The Cassiodoran codices likewise read this.]

### 198. 11. [CLXXVI] (JEROME)

Commodus 6 and Septimianus. Serapio was ordained the ninth bishop of Antioch.

### 199. 12. [CLXXVII] (JEROME)

Apronianus and Bradua. After a fire at Rome, the palace, the temple of Vesta, and a large part of the City were leveled to the ground. Pope Eleutherius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

*(According to the Martyrology.)*

Victor 12, pope for ten years and sixteen months.

### 200. 13. [CLXXVIII] (p. 103)

Commodus 7 and Gravius. [Note: [Column 0669] After “7,” witness I adds “post.”] The decretal letter of Pope Victor:

> “Victor, archbishop of the Roman and universal Church, to Theophilus the bishop and to all the brothers serving Christ at Alexandria, greeting in the Lord,”

and so forth. This letter was delivered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, when Commodus and Gravius, venerable and most distinguished men, were consuls.

*(REG.)* Many of those whom we mentioned above suffered during this period. But because the emperors’ names are similar, their sufferings cannot readily be distinguished. They nevertheless say that Irenaeus, bishop of Lugdunum, suffered under this emperor.

### 201. 14. [CLXXIX]

Commodus 8 and Pertinax. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, Commodus was strangled in the house of Vestilianus; Pertinax succeeded him. The following consuls served under Pertinax.

**19th Roman emperor.** Helvius Pertinax, according to all authorities, ruled for six months, that is, until the Kalends of February, in the year 168 after the Passion.

### 202. 1. [CLXXX] (JEROME)

Flaccus and Clarus. Pertinax, more than sixty years old, was ordered by a decree of the Senate to rule while he was serving as prefect of the City. When the Senate urged Pertinax to name his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, he refused, declaring that it was enough for him that he himself ruled unwillingly.

*(BEDE.)* Pope Victor, issuing widely circulated letters, established that Easter should be celebrated on a Sunday, as his predecessor Eleutherius had also decreed, from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day of the first month. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, supported his decrees. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, Pertinax was killed in the palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist.

*(Roman History.)* **20th Roman emperor.** Salvius Julianus, according to Roman history, seized control of the state after Pertinax. He was a nobleman and highly skilled in law, the grandson of Salvius Julianus, who under the deified Hadrian composed the perpetual edict. Orosius says as follows (VII, 16):

> “Julianus, after Pertinax had been killed, seized the empire; but soon, defeated by Severus in civil war at the Mulvian Bridge, he was killed in the seventh month after he had begun to rule. Thus one year was counted between Pertinax and Julianus.”

[Note: [Column 0671] Witness 1 perhaps reads “in.”]

This is what Orosius says. This period extends to the Kalends of September in the same year, 169 after the Passion.

*(CASSIODORUS.)* **21st Roman emperor.** Severus, a native of the province of Tripolitania, born in the town of Leptis, ruled for eighteen years, according to Cassiodorus, and also three months according to Roman history—that is, until the Kalends of December, in the year 186 after the Passion. [Note: [Column 0671] Witness 1 omits “after.”] The following consuls served under him.

### 203. 1. [CLXXXI] (JEROME)

Severus and Albinus. Severus, from the province of Tripolitania and the town of Leptis, was the only Roman emperor from Africa down to the present day. In honor of Pertinax, whom Julianus had killed, he ordered himself to be called Pertinax as an additional name, because he ruled six months beyond his eighteen years.

*[The word “eo” (“for that reason”) was added in the margin by the first hand.]*

Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, and Pantaenus the Stoic philosopher are regarded as most eloquent disputants in our doctrine.

### 204. 2. [CLXXXII] (ISIDORE)

Tertullus and Clemens. Symmachus is regarded as the fourth translator.

*(JORDANES, On the Summary of History.)* A certain Symmachus, a Samaritan—indeed, a Jewish proselyte—translated the divine Scriptures from the Hebrew language into Greek and produced his own edition. [Note: [Column 0671] “Samaritan” was written in the margin by the first hand, with a mark indicating its place.]

### 205. 3. [CLXXXIII] (JEROME)

Dexter and Priscus. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theophilus of Caesarea, as well as Polycarpus and Bacchylus, bishop of the province of Asia, are regarded as distinguished men.

### 206. 4. [CLXXXIV] (JEROME)

Lateranus and Rufinus. When a question arose among the bishops in Asia as to whether Easter ought to be observed on the fourteenth day of the month according to the law of Moses, Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, and Narcissus of Jerusalem, together with Polycrates, Irenaeus, Bacchylus, and many other pastors of the Churches, set down in writing what had seemed probable to them; the memory of these writings has survived down to us. The decretal letter of Pope Victor (Ep. 2, p. 105) was addressed to Lateranus and Rufinus, VV. CC.

### 207. 5. [CLXXXV] (JEROME)

Scoturninus and Gallus. A Jewish and Samaritan war broke out.

### 208. 6. [CLXXXVI] (JEROME)

Anulinus and Fronto. Severus defeated the Parthians and Adiabenian forces, and so thoroughly crushed the inner Arabs that he made their region a Roman province.

### 209. 7. [CLXXXVII]

Severus 2 and Victorinus. For these deeds he was called Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus.

[Note: [Column 0671] This belongs to the year 208.]

### 210. 8. [CLXXXVIII] (JEROME)

Fabianus and Mutianus. Pope Victor died on the Kalends of August. [Note: [Column 0671] “Kal. Aug.” was written below.]

Under Severus, the Severan Baths were built at Antioch, and the Septizonium was erected at Rome.

*(Book of the Pontiffs.)* Zephyrinus, the thirteenth pope, ruled for nine years. He established that ordinations of deacons or priests should take place in the presence of all the clergy and faithful laity, and that Masses should be celebrated by priests who were standing.

[Codex marginal note: The fifth persecution; the eleventh cycle; the fourteenth indiction.]

### 211. 9. [CLXXXIX]

Severus 3 and Antonius. In the fifth persecution Severus persecuted the Christians.

### 212. 10. [CXC] (JEROME)

Geta and Plautianus. Leonides, the father of Origen, was carried off by a glorious martyrdom.

### 213. 11. [CXCI] (JEROME)

Chito and Libo. Alexander is regarded as distinguished because of his confession of the Lord’s name.

### 214. 12. [CXCII] (JEROME)

Antonius 2 and Geta 2. Clement composed many and varied works.

### 215. 13. [CXCIII] (JEROME)

Albinus and Aelianus. Musanus is recognized as a writer of our philosophy.

### 216. 14. [CXCIV] (JEROME)

Aper and Maximus. After Clodius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lugdunum—

### 217. 15. [CXCV]

Antonius 3 and Geta. Severus transferred the war to the Britons. There, in order to make the recovered provinces safer from barbarian incursions, he constructed a wall for 132,000 paces from sea to sea.

[Note: [Column 0671] This belongs to the year 216.]

### 218. 16. [CXCVI] (JEROME)

Pompeianus and Avitus. Tertullian the African, son of a proconsular centurion, is celebrated in the language of all the Churches.

[Note: The solar cycle begins.]

### 219. 17. [CXCVII] (JEROME)

Faustinus and Rufus. Origen was educated through study at Alexandria.

### 220. 18. [CXCVIII] (JEROME)

Gentianus and Bassus. Severus died at Eburacum in Britain; his son Caracalla succeeded him.

**22nd Roman emperor.** Bassianus Antoninus, also called Caracalla, ruled, according to all authorities, for seven years and likewise two months, according to Roman history—that is, until the Kalends of February, in the year 194 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 221. 1. [CXCIX] (JEROME)

Duo and Asper. Asclepiades was appointed the ninth bishop of Antioch.

### 222. 2. [CC] (JEROME)

Antoninus and Balbinus. Alexander was ordained the thirty-fifth bishop of Jerusalem, while Narcissus was still alive, and governed the Church jointly with him.

### 223. 3. [CCI] (JEROME)

Messala and Sabinus. Antoninus was called Caracalla because of the type of garment he had distributed at Rome; conversely, garments of the same kind were called Antonianae from his name.

### 224. 4. [CCII] (ISIDORE—JORDANES)

Laetus and Cerealis. At Jericho the fifth edition of the divine Scriptures was discovered in a jar; its author is unknown. [Note: [Column 0673] “was discovered” was added in the margin by the first hand.]

### 225. 5. [CCIII] (JEROME)

Sabinus 2 and Venustus. Antonius built at Rome baths bearing his name.

*(BEDE.)* Perpetua and Felicitas were assigned to the beasts at Carthage in Africa, in the amphitheater, for Christ, on the Nones of March.

### 226. 6. [CCIV] (JEROME)

Presens and Extricatus. Antoninus was so lustful that he married his stepmother Julia.

### 227. 7. [CCV] (OROSIUS)

In the consulship of Antoninus, a man of the highest rank, Antoninus undertook an expedition against the Parthians.

### 228. 8. [CCVI] (CASSIODORUS)

In the consulship of Adventus, a man of the highest rank, Antoninus was killed in Osrhoene, between Edessa and Carrhae, according to Cassiodorus, at the age of forty-three; Macrinus succeeded him.

*(Roman History.)* **23rd Roman emperor.** Opilius Macer, who had been prefect of the praetorian guard, was made emperor together with his son Diadumenianus, but because of the brevity of his reign he accomplished nothing memorable. For, according to Roman history, he held the empire for one year and two months—that is, until the Kalends of April, in the year 195 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

*(JEROME.)* Philetus was appointed the tenth bishop of Antioch. During the Vulcanalia, the amphitheater at Rome was burned. Abgar, a holy man, ruled Edessa, according to Africanus. Pope Zephyrinus died.

*(Book of the Pontiffs.)* Pope Callistus, the fourteenth after Peter, ruled for five years. He established that a fast of the four seasons should be held annually, because of the abundance of wine, grain, and oil, in accordance with prophecy.

### 229. 1. [CCVII] (CASSIODORUS—OROSIUS)

Antoninus and Sacerdos. In their consulship, Macrinus was killed with his son at Archilaïs in a military mutiny, apparently in the month of February; Marcus succeeded him.

**24th Roman emperor.** Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the son of Caracalla, ruled for four years and also eight months, according to Roman history—that is, until the Kalends of December, in the year 199 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 230. 1. [CCVIII] (JEROME)

Antoninus 3 and Comazon. Marcus Aurelius, priest of the temple of Elagabalus, lived so immorally during his reign that he omitted no kind of obscenity.

### 231. 2. [CCIX] (ISIDORE)

Gratus and Seleucus, men of the highest rank. The sixth edition was discovered at Neapolis.

[Codex marginal note: The twelfth nineteen-year cycle begins; the second indiction.]

### 232. 3. [CCX] (Ep. 1, p. 109)

Alexander and Antoninus Augustus. “Pope Callistus to the archpriests,” and so forth. It was delivered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, when Antoninus and Alexander, men of the highest rank, were consuls; in this letter he established the fast mentioned above.

The temple of Elagabalus was built at Rome. (JEROME.) In Palestine the city of Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, was founded, with Julius Africanus, the writer of chronological works, undertaking an embassy on its behalf.

### 233. 4. [CCXI]

Maximus and Helianus. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, Antoninus was killed at Rome in a military mutiny, together with his mother, Symiasira.

**25th Roman emperor.** Alexander, son of Mammaea, ruled, according to all authorities, for thirteen years and several days—that is, until the Kalends of January, in the year 212. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 234. 1. [CCXII] (JEROME)

Julianus and Crispinus, men of the highest rank. Alexander defeated Xerxes, king of the Persians, with the greatest glory. Pope Callistus suffered martyrdom on the day before the Ides of October, under the emperor Alexander.

Urbanus, the fifteenth pope, ruled for nine years.

### 235. 2. [CCXIII] (JEROME)

Fuscus and Dexter, men of the highest rank. Alexander was such a severe corrector of military discipline that he discharged entire legions that had mutinied.

### 236. 3. [CCXIV]

Alexander 2 and Marcellus. “Pope Urbanus,” and so forth (Council I, p. 113), delivered on the Nones of September, when Alexander, a man of the highest rank, was consul.

### 237. 4. [CCXV] (JEROME)

Annianus and Maximus. Ulpian the jurist is regarded as Alexander’s most distinguished legal adviser.

### 238. 5. [CCXVI] (JEROME)

Albinus and Maximus, men of the highest rank. The Alexandrian Baths were built at Rome.

### 239. 6. [CCXVII] (JEROME)

Modestus and Probus, men of the highest rank. The presbyter Geminus of Antioch, Hippolytus, and Beryllus, bishop of Arabia, are regarded as distinguished writers.

### 240. 7. [CCXVIII] (JEROME)

Alexander 3 and Dion, men of the highest rank. Zebennius was appointed the eleventh bishop of Antioch.

### 241. 8. [CCXIX] (JEROME)

Gratus and Seleucus, men of the highest rank. Heraclas was ordained the twelfth bishop of the Church of Alexandria and held the office for sixteen years.

### 242. 9. [CCXX] (BEDE)

Pompeianus and Felicianus. Alexander loved his mother Mammaea because he was dutiful, and for that reason he was beloved by everyone. [Note: [Column 0673] Witness 1 reads “maia.”]

Pope Urbanus, after leading many members of the nobility to faith in Christ, suffered under Alexander on the eighth day before the Kalends of June and was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus.

Pontianus, the sixteenth pope, ruled for five years.

### 243. 10. [CCXXI] (JEROME)

Lupus and Maximus, men of the highest rank. Origen moved from Alexandria to Caesarea in Palestine.

### 244. 11. [CCXXII] (BEDE)

Maximus and Paternus. Origen was famous at Alexandria and throughout the whole world.

### 245. 12. [CCXXIII] (BEDE)

Maximus and Urbanus. When Mammaea, the mother of Alexander, wished to hear Origen, she summoned him to Antioch and treated him with the highest honor.

*(REG.)* At Rome the following suffered: Pope Callistus and Urbanus; the virgin Cecilia; Tiburtius; Valerianus; the presbyter Calepodius; the presbyter Austerius; and the consul Palmatius with his wife and children; and the senator Simplicius.

[Codex marginal note: The solar cycle begins.]

### 246. 13. [CCXXIV] (CASSIODORUS)

Severus and Quintianus. In their consulship Alexander was killed in Gaul, that is, at Mainz, in a military mutiny.

[The decretal letter of Pope Pontianus (Council I, pp. 115 ff.) was delivered on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, when Severus and Quintianus, VV. CC. SS., were consuls; and another was delivered on the Kalends of May, in the same consulship.]

*(Roman History.)* **26th Roman emperor.** Maximinus ruled for three years, one month, and a few days—that is, until the Kalends of February, in the year 216 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 247. 1. [CCXXV] (JEROME)

Maximus and Africanus. Maximinus, the first to rise from the military ranks, was elected emperor by the army without the authority of the Senate.

*(According to the Martyrology.)* Pope Pontianus was deported by Maximinus to the island of Sardinia together with the presbyter Hippolytus, and there, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, was killed with clubs. The blessed Pope Fabianus brought back his body and buried it in the cemetery of Callistus.

Antherus, the seventeenth pope, ruled for one month. The decretal letter of Pope Antherus:

> “Pope Antherus to his dearest and most beloved brothers,”

and so forth (ibid., p. 119), delivered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, when Maximinus and Africanus were consuls.

[And another letter, delivered on the Kalends of July in the same consulship. The council does not contain it; it seems to refer to Fabianus’ letter.]

*(Book of the Pontiffs.)* Pope Antherus suffered martyrdom on the third day before the Nones of January and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

Pope Fabianus, the eighteenth after Peter, ruled for sixteen years. The decretal letter of Pope Fabianus:

> “Pope Fabianus sends greetings in the Lord to all the fellow ministers of the Catholic Church everywhere,”

and so forth (ibid., p. 123). Later:

> “Finally, we likewise ordained seven deacons, who would supervise seven notaries and collect the acts of the martyrs truthfully and completely, and disclose them to us for examination. We also exhort all of you to do this, so that in the future no doubt or dispute may arise concerning any of these matters,”

and so forth. It was delivered on the Kalends of July, when Maximinus and Africanus were men of the highest rank.

[Codex marginal note: The sixth persecution.]

### 248. 2. [CCXXVI] (JEROME)

Perpetuus, a man of the highest rank, consul. Maximinus carried out the sixth persecution against the priests of the Churches.

### 249. 3. [CCXXVII] (BEDE)

Cornelius, a man of the highest rank. Maximinus persecuted the Church because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he succeeded, and of his mother Mammaea, and especially because of the presbyter Origen.

[Codex marginal note: The thirteenth ten-year cycle begins; the seventh indiction.]

### 250. 4. [CCXXVIII] (CASSIODORUS)

Pius and Proculus. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, Maximinus was killed at Aquileia by Pupienus; Gordianus succeeded him.

**27th Roman emperor.** Gordianus ruled for six years—that is, until the Kalends of February, in the year 222 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 251. 1. [CCXXIX] (JEROME)

Gordianus and Aviola, men of the highest rank. When Gordianus entered Rome, Pupienus and Albinus, who had seized the empire, were killed in the palace.

### 252. 2. [CCXXX] (BEDE)

Sabinus and Venustus, men of the highest rank. Origen wrote eight volumes in reply to a certain Celsus the Epicurean philosopher, who had composed books against us.

### 253. 3. [CCXXXI] (ISIDORE)

Gordianus 2 and Pompeianus.

[In Rome Flavianus was ordained bishop through the testimony of the Holy Spirit, appearing in the form of a dove descending upon his head, when he came to Rome; although some assert that this account more truly concerns Severinus.]

### 254. 4. [CCXXXII] (BEDE)

Atticus and Praetextatus. Origen was so diligent in writing that Jerome says in one place that he remembered having read five thousand of his books.

### 255. 5. [CCXXXIII] (JEROME)

Arrianus and Pappus. Gordianus, still quite young, after conquering the Parthian nation, was killed by the treachery of Philip, the prefect of the praetorian guard, not far from Roman territory, as he was returning victorious to his homeland.

### 256. 6. [CCXXXIV]

Peregrinus and Aemilianus. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, the soldiers built a tomb for Gordianus overlooking the Euphrates River, after his bones had been carried back to Rome.

**28th Roman emperor.** Philip, together with his son Philip, ruled, according to all authorities, for eight years—that is, until the Kalends of February, in the year 230 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 257. 1. [CCXXXV] (JEROME)

Philip and Titianus, men of the highest rank. Philip made his son Philip his partner in the kingdom, and was the first of all the Roman emperors to be a Christian.

### 258. 2. [CCXXXVI] (JEROME)

Presens and Albinus, men of the highest rank. During the reigns of the two Philips, the thousandth year of the city of Rome was completed.

### 259. 3. [CCXXXVII] (JEROME)

Philip 2 and Philip, his son. Athletes competed in celebration of the birthday of the city of Rome, and the contest of a thousand years was conducted.

### 260. 4. [CCXXXVIII] (JEROME)

Philip 3 and Philip 2. Philip founded in Thrace a city bearing his name.

### 261. 5. [CCXXXIX]

Aemilianus and Aquilinus. In their consulship, according to Cassiodorus, the thousandth year at Rome was completed. For this solemnity Philip killed countless beasts in the Great Circus and celebrated theatrical games in the Campus Martius for three days and nights, while the people kept vigil. Forty runners also competed in celebration of the birthday of Rome, and the contest of a thousand years was conducted. This is what Cassiodorus says.

But since, according to the Hebrews, the first Olympiad was placed in the first year of Joatham, and the city of Rome was founded in the first year of the sixth Olympiad, and since, as Jerome and Bede explain, from the first Olympiad to the Passion of the Lord there are 794 years, after subtracting twenty years—namely, the sixteen years of Joatham and the four years of Ahaz, which amount to five Olympiads—there are 774 years from the foundation of the City to the Passion of the Lord. From the Passion of the Lord to Philip’s final year there are 229 years; together, from the foundation of the City to Philip’s death, there are 1,003 years.

### 262. 6. [CCXL] (JEROME)

Decius and Gratus. Dionysius was appointed the fourth bishop of Alexandria and held the office for seventeen years.

[In their consulship Pope Fabianus suffered martyrdom on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs. Pope Cornelius succeeded him.]

### 263. 7. [CCXLI] (CASSIODORUS)

Decius 2 and Rusticus. In their consulship the elder Philip was killed at Verona, and the younger at Rome. Decius ruled for eight years.

The decretal letter of Pope Fabianus:

> “Fabianus the bishop sends greetings to his most beloved brother Hilary,”

and so forth (Ep. 3, p. 128), delivered on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, when Africanus and Decius, men of venerable rank, were consuls.

The Martyrology records it as follows:

> “At Rome, the commemoration of Pope Fabianus on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. After presiding over the Church for fourteen years, eleven months, and twelve days, he suffered martyrdom under Decius, at the beginning of his reign, and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.”

Bede records it as follows (Chronicle):

> “After Decius had killed Philip the father and his son, out of hatred for them he began a persecution against the Christians, during which Fabianus was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome. He left the seat of his episcopate to Cornelius, but Cornelius himself also suffered martyrdom.”

Pope Cornelius ruled for two years, eight months less five days.

The decretal letter of Cornelius:

> “Cornelius sends greetings to his dearest and beloved brothers,”

and so forth (Ep. 1, p. 131), delivered on the seventh day before the Ides of September, when Decius and Maximus, men of the highest rank, were consuls.

Another:

> “Cornelius the bishop sends greetings in the Lord,”

and so forth (Ep. 2, p. 132), delivered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, when Maximus and Decius, men of the highest rank, were consuls.

The Martyrology records it as follows:

> “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, the commemoration of Saint Cornelius, pope. During the persecution of Decius he had been assigned to exile at Centumcellae together with presbyters and deacons; [Note: [Column 0677] Witness 1 reads “deputi.”] many Christians came to encourage him. At that time the blessed Cyprian wrote to him concerning the lector Celerinus and how much he had endured for the faith and confession of Christ.

> “When the emperor Decius heard that many people were writing to him about the blessed Cyprian, he ordered him to be brought before him. Brought in and questioned by Decius about why he had received letters from Cyprian against the commonwealth, he replied: ‘I have received letters concerning the crown of Christ, not against the commonwealth.’

> “Angered, Decius ordered that his mouth be beaten with leaded scourges, and then that he be taken to the temple of Mars to sacrifice; if he refused, he was to be executed there. As he was being led away, one of the soldiers, named Cerealis, began to ask the blessed pope to visit his wife, who had lain paralyzed for five years.

> “When he entered the soldier’s house, he took the hand of Sallustia and raised her, saying: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and stand upon your feet.’ Immediately she stood up, crying out and saying: ‘Truly Christ is the Son of God.’ And she said to the blessed Cornelius: ‘Baptize me, for through Christ I adjure you.’ She ran, filled a vessel with water, and brought it to him.

> “Then all the soldiers threw themselves at his feet, asking to be baptized. After he had baptized them, he offered on their behalf a sacrifice of praise, and they all partook of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

> “When Decius heard this, he sent men to seize them all and ordered that they be taken with the blessed Cornelius to sacrifice; if they refused to obey, they were to be beheaded. [Note: [Column 0677] Witness 1 perhaps reads “plectentur.”] They were led outside the walls at the Appian Gate and, after spitting toward the temple, were beheaded together with the blessed Cornelius, twenty-one in number. Cerealis and his wife Sallustia were also martyred on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

> “That same night the blessed Lucina came with her clergy and household, took away the bodies of the martyrs, and buried them on her own property in a crypt in the cemetery of Callistus.”

The decretal letter of Pope Cornelius mentions this Lucina as follows:

> “To our dearest and most beloved brothers, the sons of the holy Church, Cornelius the bishop. I have decided to write to you what it is necessary to know at the present time,”

and so forth (Ep. 1, 11). Later:

> “Therefore I ask you to rejoice with us, because, at the request of a certain devoted woman and most noble matron, Lucina, the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul have been removed from the catacombs. First, the body of the blessed Paul was removed silently [Note: [Column 0677] Read *silentio*, “silently.”] and placed on the estate of the aforesaid matron, on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he was beheaded. Afterwards we received the body of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and were able to place it near the place where he was crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo, on the Golden Hill, in the Vatican, at Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July,”

and so forth. This letter was delivered on the seventh day before the Ides of September, when Decius and Maximus, men of the highest rank, were consuls.

After Cornelius had suffered martyrdom, Pope Lucius began in the third year of Decius and occupied the see for five months, until the fourth day before the Nones of March, at the beginning of Decius’ fourth year, under the prefect Valerianus.

From that point Pope Stephen held the see for three years and five months, until the fourth day before the Nones of August, when he suffered martyrdom under the prefect Valerianus, in the sixth year of Decius.

The decretal letter of Pope Zephanus:

> “Pope Zephanus sends greetings to his most beloved brother and intimate friend Hilary,”

and so forth (Ep. 1, p. 141), delivered on the fifth day before the Nones of May, when Valerianus and Gallienus, men of the highest rank, were consuls.

Another:

> “Zephanus, bishop of the holy apostolic and universal Roman Church,”

and so forth (Ep. 2, p. 145), delivered on the Nones of April, when Valerianus and Gallienus, men of the highest rank, were consuls.

The Martyrology records it as follows:

> “At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, the commemoration of Saint Zephanus, pope and martyr, under the emperors Valerianus and Gallienus. While a savage persecution was raging, he assembled all his clergy and encouraged them to receive the crown of martyrdom for Christ courageously.

> “He had ordained three presbyters, seven deacons, and ten clerics, with whom he continually taught concerning the kingdom of God. By the provision of divine grace, many among the Gentiles and honorable men came to him to be baptized. [Note: [Column 0679] Witness 1 reads “and.”] Among them were the tribune Nemereus with his entire household and his daughter Lucilla, who was blind and was given sight through the blessed Zephanus; and the other tribune Olimpius with his wife Exsuperia, his son Theodulus, and the others who believed in his household. These people later suffered martyrdom.

> “He celebrated Masses and councils in the crypts of the martyrs. It happened that Valerianus and Gallienus, persecutors of the name of Christ, sought the blessed Stephen with the utmost determination in order to afflict him or his clergy with various punishments. They therefore sent a multitude of soldiers, who seized him together with a multitude of clerics, presbyters, and deacons.

> “When he came before the tribunal of Valerianus, he entered alone. Valerianus said to him: ‘You are Stephen, who seek to overthrow the commonwealth and by evil persuasions and exhortations turn the people away from the worship of the gods.’

> “The blessed Zephanus replied: ‘I do not overthrow the commonwealth; rather, I exhort them, abandoning the demons worshiped in idols, to return to the living God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and to recognize that Jesus, the Son of the living God, is God. He alone, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is eternal, so that they may not perish with the devil in everlasting destruction.’

> “Then Valerianus ordered him to be taken to the temple of Mars and, if he did not worship the detestable image of Mars, to be beheaded there after the sentence had been pronounced. [Note: [Column 0679] Witness 1 perhaps reads “dicta” for “dictata.”]

> “The blessed Zephanus was led by the soldiers outside the walls at the Appian Gate to the temple. Raising his eyes to heaven, he said: ‘Lord my God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, you who destroyed the tower of the confusion of Babylon, destroy now also this place, where souls of peoples perish through devilish superstition in the worship of idols.’ [Note: [Column 0679] Witness 1 reads *superstione* for *superstitione*.]

> “Immediately there was a crash of thunder accompanied by terrifying flashes of lightning, and a very large part of the temple collapsed; the frightened soldiers fled.

> “But the blessed Zephanus went with all the Christians to the cemetery of Saint Lucia and, exhorting them with many sermons, offered a sacrifice to God on their behalf. [Editorial note: At this point several words are omitted from the martyrology narrative; it ends thus: “offering sacrifice to God.”] While he was fearless and steadfast and was completing the solemn rites before the altar, they beheaded him in that same place on the fourth day before the Nones of August.”

*(According to the Martyrology.)* His body was buried by the Christian people in the same crypt, together with the very seat where his blood was shed, [Note: [Column 0679] “where” was added afterwards in witness 1.] in the place that is now called the cemetery of Callistus.

*(Cf. Book of the Pontiffs.)* He established that priests and levites should not use sacred vestments in daily life, except in the Church.

After Stephen, Pope Sixtus succeeded for 2 years. A decretal letter of Pope Sixtus: “Sixtus, bishop, to his fellow bishop Grat[o], greetings,” and the rest (Ep. 1, p. 479); dated on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the venerable and illustrious Valerian and Decius. Likewise another: “To the most beloved brothers established throughout the provinces of Spain, Sixtus, bishop, greetings in the Lord,” and the rest (Ep. 2, p. 181); dated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Decius.

(AD Mart.) In the martyrology it reads as follows:

“Emperor Decius and the prefect Valerian seized the most blessed old man Sixtus, bishop of Rome, together with all his clergy, and shut them in the public prison; and they remained confined there for many days. It happened that Decius Caesar and the prefect Valerian ordered that blessed Bishop Sixtus, with his clergy, be brought before him at night within the city, at the Tellus. Decius Caesar said to him: ‘Do you know why you have been detained and brought before us in a public hearing?’ Blessed Sixtus replied: ‘I know, and I know well.’ Decius said: ‘Then, if you know, make everyone know as well, and you will live, and your clergy will increase.’ Blessed Sixtus replied: ‘Indeed, I have done and am doing this, so that my clergy may increase.’

“Then Decius said to him: ‘Sacrifice to the immortal gods and become chief of the priests.’ To this the holy man Sixtus replied: ‘I have always sacrificed, and I sacrifice, to the Lord God the almighty Father, and to our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, and to the Holy Spirit, a pure and spotless offering.’

“Then, at Decius’ command, the soldiers led him to the temple of the Mother, so that he might sacrifice. But because he refused to sacrifice, they shut him in a private prison with the two deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus.

“As he was being led away, blessed Lawrence, the archdeacon, began to address him with these words: ‘Where are you going without your son, father? Where are you hastening, holy priest, without your deacon? [Note: [Col. 0679] ‘without’ was added afterward in witness 1.] You were never accustomed to offer sacrifice without a minister. What, then, have I done to displease you, father? Have you judged me degenerate? Test, surely, whether you have chosen me as your minister. To whom did you entrust the consecration of the Lord’s blood? To whom the participation in the sacraments that must be completed? To this man you deny participation in your blood [Note: [Col. 0679] Witness 1 reads *hic*; read *huic*, ‘to this man’.]. See that your judgment does not fall into peril while courage is praised. The rejection of a disciple is the teacher’s loss. What is more, men who are more distinguished and excellent are surpassed by the contests of their disciples [Note: “rather than by their own,” according to the Martyrology.]. In the end, Abraham offered his son; Peter sent Stephen ahead; and you, father, show your strength in your son. Offer him whom you have instructed, so that, accompanied by the noble retinue of your judgment, you may reach the crown.’”

Then blessed Sixtus said:

“‘I do not abandon you, my son, nor do I desert you; but greater contests await you. We, as old men, undertake the course of a lighter battle; for you, as a young man, a more glorious triumph over the tyrant remains [Note: [Col. 0679] Witness 1 reads *trianno*.]. You will come soon; cease weeping; after three days you will follow me. This middle number is fitting between priest and Levite. It was not yours to conquer under your teacher, as though you were seeking an assistant. Why do you desire a share in my passion? I leave you my entire inheritance. Why do you seek my presence? Elijah left Elisha, yet did not take away his power.’”

And blessed Sixtus said to blessed Lawrence:

“‘Take the resources, or treasures, of the Church and distribute them to whomever you think appropriate.’”

Having received authority, Lawrence began carefully searching through the districts for wherever holy clerics or poor people were concealed; carrying the treasures, he distributed them according to each person’s need.

After this, blessed Sixtus was brought back to the Tellus to be heard, together with the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus. While Decius and Valerian were seated, blessed Sixtus was brought before them. Decius, full of anger, said to him:

“‘We are indeed concerned for your old age. Hear our commands and sacrifice.’

“Blessed Sixtus replied: ‘Wretched man, be concerned for yourself, and do not blaspheme; rather, repent of the blood of the saints that you have shed.’

“Then, at Valerian’s urging, Decius ordered that they be led to the temple of Mars; and if they refused to sacrifice, that they should be beheaded in that same place. When they had been led outside the walls at the Appian Gate, blessed Sixtus said to the temple of Mars: ‘Christ, the Son of the living God, will destroy you.’

“When all the Christians had replied, ‘Amen,’ part of the temple suddenly collapsed. Then blessed Lawrence began to cry out: ‘Do not abandon me, holy father, for I have already spent the treasures that you entrusted to me.’

“But when the soldiers heard about the treasures, they seized blessed Lawrence the archdeacon; while they led the holy Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus to the Clivus of Mars, before the temple. There they were beheaded on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

“At night the clerics and a very large part of the Christian community came, gathered the bodies of the saints, and buried Sixtus in a crypt in the cemetery of Callistus, on the same road. They buried the holy martyrs Felicissimus and Agapitus in the cemetery of Praetextatus. Four other men were beheaded with them, as is read in the Acts of the Pontiffs: Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen, subdeacons. Blessed Quartus also suffered with them, as blessed [Cyprian] writes.

“This blessed Sixtus was born at Athens and, having first been trained as a philosopher, afterward became a disciple of Christ. He held the see for one year, ten months, and twenty-three days. If, then, Saint Cyprian, who was present at that time, wrote these things, who can deny them?”

Blessed Lawrence was therefore seized by the soldiers and handed over to the tribune Parthenius.

(AD Mart.) He reported to Decius that Lawrence, the archdeacon of Christ who possessed concealed treasures, was being held in custody. Decius rejoiced and had him brought before him; after hearing him, he handed him over to the prefect Valerian, who in turn placed him in the custody of a certain Hippolytus, and Hippolytus shut him in with many others.

There was there a blind man named Lucillus. Saint Lawrence said to him: “Believe in the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and be baptized, and he will enlighten you” [Note: i.e., “he will enlighten you.”]. Lucillus replied: “I myself have desired to be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Then blessed Lawrence instructed him in the faith, took water, baptized him, and his eyes were enlightened.

When many blind people heard of this, they came to blessed Lawrence; he placed his hand upon their eyes, and they were enlightened. Seeing this, Hippolytus believed and was baptized.

By command, blessed Lawrence was brought before Valerian. Valerian said to him:

“‘Now put aside your stubbornness and give up the treasures that we know to be hidden with you.’

“Saint Lawrence replied: ‘Give me two or three days’ respite, and I will produce the treasures for you.’

“From that day he gathered the blind, lame, and helpless poor and hid them in Hippolytus’ house. Valerian then informed Decius that Lawrence, having been granted the respite he had requested, had promised to deliver the treasures.

“When the three days had been completed, Lawrence presented himself in the Palace of Sallust and Decius said to him: ‘Where are the treasures that you promised to present?’

“Blessed Lawrence gathered a multitude of poor people, brought them into the palace, and said in a loud voice: ‘Behold, these are the eternal treasures, which are never diminished or reduced, which are scattered among individuals and found in all.’

“The prefect Valerian said: ‘Why do you wander through so many places? Sacrifice to the gods and forget the magical arts in which you trust.’

“When blessed Lawrence had said to him, ‘Why does the devil constrain you to tell Christians to sacrifice to demons?’ Decius, enraged, ordered that he be stripped and beaten with scorpions.

“As he was being beaten, he said: ‘I indeed give thanks to my God, who has deemed me worthy to be joined among his servants. But you, wretched man, will be tortured by your madness and in your fury.’

“Then Decius said: ‘Take him away and administer every kind of torture.’ Iron plates, beds, weighted scourges, and hooks were brought before him [Note: ‘iron’ in one witness].

“Afterward blessed Lawrence was bound with chains and led to the Palace of Tiberius, so that he might be heard there according to the proceedings. He sat before the tribunal in the basilica of Jupiter.

(AD Mart.) When Lawrence had been brought before him and Decius had said, ‘Sacrifice to the gods and do not trust in the treasures that you have hidden,’ blessed Lawrence replied freely:

“‘Indeed I trust, and I am secure in my treasures.’

“Decius, full of anger, ordered that he be stripped naked and beaten with thorn branches. As he was being beaten, he cried out to the emperor:

“‘Behold, wretched man, recognize even now that I triumph over the treasures of Christ and do not feel your tortures.’

“Then Decius ordered that the clubs be increased and that burning iron plates be applied to his sides.

“Blessed Lawrence said:

“‘Lord Jesus Christ, God from God, have mercy on me, your servant, who, when accused, did not deny you, and when questioned confessed you as Lord Christ.’

“When he had been beaten for a very long time with weighted scourges, he said:

“‘Lord Jesus Christ, who for our salvation deigned to assume the form of a servant, in order to free us from the service of demons, receive my spirit.’

“And a voice was heard: ‘Many more contests are still owed to you.’

“Stretched out upon the rack and most grievously beaten with scorpions, he said with a smile and giving thanks:

“‘Blessed is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has granted us a mercy that we have not deserved. But you, Lord, because of your goodness, grant us grace, so that all who stand around may know that you comfort your servants.’

“Then one of the soldiers, named Romanus, believed in our Lord Jesus Christ and said to blessed Lawrence:

“‘I see before [Note: [Col. 0683] Witness 1 perhaps reads *in*.] you a most beautiful man standing with a linen cloth and wiping your limbs. I adjure you by Christ, who sent his angel to you, not to abandon me.’

“Then blessed Lawrence was lifted up and released from the rack and was returned to Hippolytus in the palace.

“Romanus came bringing water, threw himself at the feet of blessed Lawrence, and asked to be baptized. After blessing the water, Lawrence baptized him.

“When Decius heard what had happened, he ordered Romanus to be brought before him with clubs. Without being questioned, Romanus began to cry out: ‘I am a Christian!’ At Decius’ command he was led outside the walls at the Salarian Gate and beheaded on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

“His body was gathered during the night by the presbyter Justinus and buried in a crypt on the Veran Field.

“Decius Caesar then went at night to the baths beside the Palace of Sallust, and blessed Lawrence was brought before him again. Every kind of torture was brought out: weighted scourges, clubs, iron plates, claws, beds, and mallets.

“Decius said to blessed Lawrence: ‘Now put aside your faithlessness and magical art, and tell us your lineage.’

“Blessed Lawrence replied: ‘Since I am Spanish by birth, Roman by education and upbringing, and Christian from the cradle, I have been instructed in every holy and divine law.’

“And Decius said: ‘Sacrifice to the gods, for this night will be spent upon you amid tortures.’

“‘My night,’ he replied, ‘contains no darkness, but everything shines in the light.’

“When he was being beaten with stones, his mouth laughed, and he was strengthened and said: ‘I give you thanks, for you are the God of all.’

“Then a bed with three ribs was brought. Blessed Lawrence was stripped of his clothing and stretched upon an iron grid; mallets with burning coals were brought and placed beneath the iron grid. They pressed him from above with iron forks.

“Then he said to Decius: ‘Behold, I have offered myself as a sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma, for the sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.’

“But the executioners, pressing him, supplied coals, throwing them beneath the grid and pressing him from above with iron forks.

“Saint Lawrence said: ‘Learn, wretched man, how great is the power of my Lord God. Your coals provide me with refreshment; for you there is eternal punishment, because the Lord himself knows that, when accused, I did not deny him; when questioned, I confessed Christ; being roasted, I give thanks.’

“And with a most beautiful countenance he said: ‘I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because I have been found worthy to enter your gates.’

“And he gave up his spirit.

“At dawn, while it was still twilight, Hippolytus carried away his body and wrapped it in linen cloths and spices; he entrusted the matter to the presbyter Justinus.

“Then blessed Justinus and Hippolytus, weeping and deeply sorrowful, carried the body of the blessed martyr. They came by the Tiburtine Way to the estate of the widowed matron Cyriaca, on the Veran Field. The blessed martyr had himself visited her there at night and had given her the linen cloth with which she wiped the feet of the saints.

“There, already at the evening hour, they buried him on the fourth day before the Ides of August, and they fasted, keeping night vigils for three days with a multitude of Christians.

“Blessed Justinus the presbyter offered the sacrifice of praise, and all partook of it.

“On that same day, sixty-five soldiers suffered martyrdom at Rome: Claudius, Severus, Crescentius, and Romanus [Note: supply ‘with Lawrence’], on the very day on which blessed Lawrence suffered, three days after Saint Sixtus.”

—At Rome, on the Ides of August: the commemoration of Saint Hippolytus the martyr, under the emperor Decius and the prefect Valerian.

“When this blessed Hippolytus was serving as the vicar of Saint Lawrence, while he was in custody with him, Lawrence baptized him. Afterward, returning home from the burial of the saintly martyr, Hippolytus gave peace also to all his male and female servants, and shared with them in the sacrifice of the altar of the blessed martyr Lawrence.

“When the table had been set, before he took food, soldiers came, seized him, and led him before Decius. Seeing this, Decius smiled and said to him: ‘Have you too become a magician, since it is said that you carried away Lawrence’s body?’

“Saint Hippolytus replied: ‘I did this—not as a magician, but as a Christian.’

“Decius, seized by fury, ordered that his mouth be crushed with stones. He stripped him of the garment in which he was dressed in Christian fashion and said to him: ‘Sacrifice to the gods and you will live; otherwise you will perish amid tortures like Lawrence.’

“Saint Hippolytus said: ‘May I deserve to become like the example of the blessed martyr Lawrence, whom you, wretched man, dared to name with your polluted mouth.’

“He was therefore stretched out and beaten for a long time with clubs and hooks, until those beating him grew exhausted.

“Then he was lifted from the ground. Decius ordered him to be dressed in the military garment that he had worn as a pagan and said to him: ‘Remember your military service, become our friend, and before us make use of the former military service that you have always possessed [Note: [Col. 0683] Witness 1 reads *ute*.].’

“When the blessed martyr had said: ‘My military service is this: to serve as a steadfast Christian soldier. From this I desire to come swiftly to the palm of victory with its fruit,’ Decius, full of anger, said to Valerian:

“‘Take all his possessions and kill him by a cruel examination.’

“Valerian, having investigated all his possessions, found Hippolytus’ entire Christian household in his house and had them brought before him. He ordered blessed Hippolytus to be led outside the walls at the Tiburtine Gate together with the household.

“Blessed Hippolytus encouraged everyone, saying: ‘Brothers, do not be afraid, because I and you have one Lord.’

“They were beheaded, of both sexes indiscriminately, nineteen in number [Note: [Col. 0683] Witness 1 reads *sextus* (‘sixth’) for *sexus* (‘sex’)].

“But blessed Hippolytus, with his feet tied to the necks of untamed horses, was dragged through thistles and thorn bushes in this manner, and gave up his blessed spirit.

“During the night blessed Justinus the presbyter came, gathered the bodies, and buried them in the same field, beside the nymphaeum, near the estate of Veranus, on the Ides of August.”

From the emperor Decius up to this point, eight popes held the chair according to the chronicle of Eusebius; how long they sat according to the martyrology must now be stated.

Decius reigned for 16 years. Pope Fabian suffered martyrdom on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the first year of Decius. Then Pope Cornelius [reigned] for two years and eight months and suffered martyrdom on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the third year of Decius. Then Pope Lucius [reigned] for three years and five months and suffered under the prefect Valerian, in the seventh year of Decius, on the fourth day before the Nones of March. Pope Zephanus [reigned] for seven years and five months and suffered under the prefect Valerian, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the fourteenth year of Decius. Pope Sixtus [reigned] for two years and suffered on the Ides of August, in the sixteenth year of Decius.

(cf. REG.) Lawrence also, and Agapitus, Felicissimus, and Hippolytus suffered under Decius, if the Church is not mistaken.

Thus there is a discrepancy of 18 years in the chronicles of Eusebius and Bede, from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the tenth year of the Great Cycle. According to the history of the holy Gospel and the cycle of Dionysius, these years amount to the 16 years of Decius and the 2 years of Galerius, according to Bishop Isidore, who says that Galerius reigned for two years. But if anything conflicts with these calculations, let us investigate the Resurrection of the Lord in another way, according to the historical account [Note: At this point, in manuscript 3 and in the printed editions, the following is read: “Marianus Scotus placed 22 more years than the other chroniclers from the Incarnation of the Lord; he gathered them under the deficient kings, with complete months and days added to the years.”].

**Roman year 29.** Decius, according to Orosius, reigned for 3 years and 3 months, according to Eusebius, Bede, and Cassiodorus, beginning in the year 1004 from the founding of the City; that is, until the Kalends of May, in the year 232 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

[Codex marginal note: 7th persecution.]

### 264. 1. [CCXLII] (HIER.)

Gallus and Volusianus.

Decius was born at Budalia in Lower Pannonia. Decius [Note: [Col. 0685] added in the margin by the first hand.], out of hatred for the Philips, whom he killed, began a persecution of the Christians. Pope Fabian suffered martyrdom on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. (Mart.)

Cornelius, the nineteenth pope, [reigned] for 3 years and 5 months. [“Antony the monk is taught to have arisen from Egypt.”]

### 265. 2. [CCXLIII] (HIER.)

Africanus and Decius.

Antony the monk was born in Egypt. Paul of Thebes [CASS.] [Note: This is Paul the Theban, Antony’s teacher; cf. below, year 371. Grotefend.]

Under these consuls Decius built public baths, which he ordered to be called by his own name.

### 266. 3. [CCXLIV] (HIER.)

Maximus and Decius.

The amphitheater at Rome burned. After Alexander of Jerusalem had been killed at Caesarea in Palestine for his martyrdom, Babylas, Mazabanus, and Fabius were appointed bishops at Antioch.

(Mart.) Pope Cornelius suffered martyrdom on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

(REG.) At Rome, Fabian and Pope Cornelius suffered martyrdom, together with the virgin Victoria and the Miniates; at Antioch, Bishop Babylas; at the city of Apollonia, Leatus, Tirsus, and Gallinicus; at Jerusalem, Bishop Alexander; at Nazianzus, Trypho; in the Egyptian city called Thinis, Bishop Phileas and the tribune Philoromus, with many others; in Sicily, in the city of Catania, the virgin Agatha; in Persia, Polychronius, bishop of Babylonian Ctesiphon; at Perge in Pamphylia, Bishop Nestor; in the city of Córdoba, the presbyter Parmenius with his companions; at the Circensian colony, Marianus and Jacobus; at Tyre, Anatolia and Audax; in Africa, Nemesianus and Felix, the presbyter Rogatianus, Felicissimus, and Dioscorus with their companions.

(HIER.) Decius was killed with his son [Note: [Col. 0685] ‘in’ added afterward by the first hand.] at Abrutus, a place in Thrace, by the Goths in battle (CASS.).

**Roman year 30.** Gallus, with his son Volusianus, reigned for 2 years and 4 months, that is, until the Kalends of September, in the year 234 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 267. 1. [CCXLV] (HIER.)

Volusenus and Maximus.

A pestilential disease seized many provinces throughout the whole world, and especially Alexandria and Egypt, as Dionysius writes; and the book of Cyprian, *On Mortality*, bears witness to this. Novatus, Cyprian’s presbyter, came to Rome and joined Novatian and the other confessors to himself, because Cornelius had received repentant apostates. Demetrius was appointed fifteenth bishop of Antioch.

Lucius, the twentieth pope, [reigned] for 3 years and 5 months [Note: the number of years has been erased]. A decretal letter of Pope Lucius: “To all the most beloved brothers, Lucius, bishop, greetings in the Lord,” and the rest (Council, p. 137); and later: “In this holy apostolic see we decree that in every place two presbyters and three deacons are not to leave the bishop, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony,” and the rest; dated on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Gallus and Volusianus, most illustrious and venerable men. [Lucius suffered martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, according to the Acts.]

### 268. 2. [CCXLVI] (HIER.)

Valerian and Gallienus.

[Under these consuls, Stephen succeeded to the papacy according to the Acts of the Pontiffs.] According to Cassiodorus, under these consuls Gallus and Volusianus set out from the City against Aemilianus, who was stirring up rebellion in Moesia, and were killed at the Forum Flaminii—or, as some think, at Interamna. Aemilianus was killed in the third month after seizing the tyranny.

**Roman year 31.** Aemilianus, after killing Gallus and Volusianus, ruled for 3 months. (BEDA.) Origen died in the seventieth year of his age and was buried in the city of Tyre. (H. R.) Aemilianus was born in the greatest obscurity and ruled even more obscurely; for he was a Moor and was killed in the third month of his reign, that is, approximately in the month of November, in the same year in which he killed Gallus and Volusianus.

**Roman year 32.** Valerian, with his son Gallienus, reigned for 15 years, that is, until the Kalends of December, in the year 249 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

[Codex marginal note: Cycle 14; the decennalia begin; indiction 10.]

### 269. 1. [CCXLVII] (HIER.)

Valerian II and Gallienus II.

Valerian was proclaimed Augustus in Raetia; Gallienus was called Caesar at Rome by the Senate.

[Under these consuls Pope Stephen suffered martyrdom on the fourth day before the Nones of August, according to the Acts of the Roman Pontiff [Note: “g. p. R.” is absent in one witness].]

[Codex marginal note: 8th persecution.]

### 270. 2. [CCXLVIII] (AD Mart.)

Maximus II and Gabrio.

In the martyrology it reads:

“On the fourth day before the Nones of March, the birth [commemoration] of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr, who, during the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, was sent into exile for the faith of Christ and afterward, by divine will, was permitted to return to his own church; he completed his martyrdom by beheading and was placed on the Appian Way, at Saint Sixtus. He sat in the episcopate for 3 years and 5 months.”

Stephen, the twenty-first pope after Peter, [reigned] for 3 years and 5 months.

[Under these consuls Pope Sixtus succeeded.]

### 271. 3. [CCXLIX] (HIER.)

Valerian III and Gallienus.

Cyprian, first a rhetorician, then a presbyter, and finally bishop of Carthage, was crowned with martyrdom.

### 272. 4. [CCL] (HIER.)

Tuscus and Bassus, most illustrious men.

When Valerian had launched a persecution against the Christians, he was immediately captured and blinded by Sapor, king of the Persians, and there he grew old in miserable servitude.

[Under these consuls Pope Sixtus suffered martyrdom, according to the Acts of the Pontiff.]

### 273. 5. [CCLI] (HIER.)

Aemilianus and Bassus.

Sapor, king of the Persians, devastated Syria, Cilicia, and Cappadocia.

(Mart.) Pope Stephen suffered martyrdom on the fourth day before the Nones of August (Book of the Pontiffs).

Sixtus, the twenty-second pope, [reigned] for 2 years.

[Under these consuls Dionysius succeeded as pope on the eleventh day before the Ides of August, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus. Note: [Col. 0687] This notice is written again in the margin by a second hand: ‘Under these consuls Pope Dionysius succeeded, according to [the Acts].’] [A decretal letter of Pope Dionysius (p. 183), written on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, most illustrious men. Note: [Col. 0687] These words are written in the lower margin of folio 125 without an indication of the year.]

### 274. 6. [CCLII] (HIER.)

Secularis and Donatus.

When Valerian had been led away to the Persians, Gallienus restored peace to our people. (BEDA.)

Theodorus, also called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, moved a mountain by his prayers, among the other glories of his virtues, so that there might be sufficient space for building a church.

### 275. 7. [CCLIII] (HIER.)

Gallienus IV and Gentianus.

Paul of Samosata was appointed fifteenth bishop of Antioch. Pope Sixtus suffered martyrdom on the eighth day before the Ides of August. (Mart.)

Dionysius, the twenty-third pope, [reigned] for 6 years and 5 months. He assigned and established churches, presbyters, and parishes within the dioceses.

### 276. 8. [CCLIV] (HIER.)

Gallienus V and Victorinus.

When Gallienus had given himself over to every kind of dissipation [Note: one witness reads “having been abandoned”], the Germans came as far as Ravenna. The Alamanni, after devastating Gaul, crossed into Italy.

### 277. 9. [CCLV] (HIER.)

Albinus and Maximus.

Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were devastated by the Goths. The Quadi and the Sarmatians occupied the Pannonias [Note: one witness reads “and they”].

[Codex marginal note: Cycle.]

### 278. 10. [CCLVI] (HIER.)

Gallienus VI and Saturninus.

When the Germans held Spain [Note: read “the Spanish provinces,” specifically Tarraconensis], the land was conquered. The Parthians, holding Mesopotamia, invaded Syria.

### 279. 11. [CCLVII] (HIER.)

Valerius and Lucillus.

Maximus was ordained fourteenth bishop of the Alexandrian church and held the office for 9 years.

### 280. 12. [CCLVIII] (HIER.)

Gallienus VII and Sabinillus.

A Palmyrene decurion was appointed and, having gathered a force of peasants [Note: supply “he defeated the Persians”], pitched camp at Ctesiphon.

### 281. 13. [CCLIX] (HIER.)

Paternus and Archisilaus.

Hymenaeus held the episcopate of Jerusalem. Pope Dionysius died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. (Mart.)

(REG.) Felix, the twenty-fourth pope, [reigned] for 4 years.
