At Rome, Stephen and Sixtus, popes, suffered martyrdom, together with the deacons Felicissimus, Agapitus, and blessed Lawrence; Hippolytus; the virgin Eugenia; Jovinus and Basil; Bassilla, Rufina, and Secunda, virgins; Tertullianus, Protus, Hyacinthus, Valerianus, Nemesius, Symphronius, and Olympius in the Spanish city of Tarragona; at Verona, Zeno, bishop and confessor; Fructuosus, bishop, and the deacons Augurius and Eulogius; at Caesarea in Palestine, Marinus; in Africa, at the city of Turbuno; at Lucernaria, Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, virgin; in the territory of Cavilitanus, at the village of Mitanum, Privatus, bishop.

### 282. 14. [CCLX] (HIER.)

Paternus II and Marinus.

The cities of Gaul were recovered from Postumus, Victorinus, and Tetricus.

### 283. 15. [CCLXI] (H. R.)

Claudius and Paternus. (Orosius VII, 24.)

Under these consuls, according to Cassiodorus, Gallienus was killed, after 15 years of his reign, by the treachery [Note: supply “through the treachery”] of his commander Aureolus, abandoning the commonwealth and serving his lusts.

[A decretal letter of Pope Dionysius (p. 184), written on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus, most illustrious men [Note: written in the upper margin of folio 125 verso without an indication of the year; cf. year 273].]

[Under these consuls Pope Dionysius died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs. Felix succeeded him as pope.]

**Roman year 33.** Claudius reigned for one year and 9 months, that is, until the Kalends of September, in the year 251 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 284. 1. [CCLXII] (HIER.)

Antiochienus and Orbitus.

At Alexandria the *Brachium*, which had been besieged for many years, was finally destroyed. Claudius defeated the Goths, who were devastating Illyricum and Macedonia; for this reason a golden shield was set up for him in the senate-house and a golden statue on the Capitol.

### 285. 2. [CCLXIII] (cf. Mart.)

Valerian and Bassus.

Pope Felix suffered martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of June, according to Bede [Note: “January” is written above by a second hand]. He decreed that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs.

(cf. Book of the Pontiffs.) At Rome, Pope Felix suffered martyrdom, together with Marius, his wife Martha, and their sons; forty-seven soldiers baptized by Pope Dionysius; and the virgin Cyrilla. At Tarracina in Campania, the presbyter Felix and Eusebius.

(REG.) Valerian and Bassus. Under these consuls Claudius died at Sirmium, according to Cassiodorus (CASS.).

(H. R.) **Roman year 34.** Quintillus, the brother of Claudius, was made emperor with the agreement of the soldiers; with the agreement of the Senate he was also proclaimed Augustus. He was a man of exceptional moderation and civility, equal or superior to his brother.

Eutychianus, the twenty-fifth pope, [reigned] for 6 years. (cf. Book of the Pontiffs.) He decreed that only beans and grapes among the fruits should be blessed upon the altar, and that no one should bury a martyr without a dalmatic or a purple-colored colobium.

(CASS.) Quintillus was killed at Aquileia on the seventeenth day of his reign, according to Cassiodorus; that is, until the Kalends of October, in the same year in which Claudius died.

**Roman year 35.** Aurelian reigned for 5 years and 6 months, that is, until the Kalends of April, in the year 256 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 286. 1. [CCLXIV] (HIER.)

Quietus and Voldumianus.

Timaeus was ordained seventeenth bishop of the church of Antioch. When Tetricus betrayed his own army at Châlons, Aurelian recovered Gaul.

### 287. 2. [CCLXV] (HIER.)

Tacitus and Placidianus.

Zenobia was defeated at Hemesa, not far from Antioch. After killing her husband Odaenathus, she had held the empire of the East. In that battle the commander Pompeianus, surnamed Francus, fought against her with exceptional courage; his family still survives today near Antioch. From his line descended Evagrius, the presbyter who is especially dear to us.

[Codex marginal note: Cycle 15; the decennalia begin; indiction 14.]

### 288. 3. [CCLXVI] (HIER.)

Aurelian and Capitolinus.

Eusebius of Laodicea was held to be an eminent bishop. When Aurelian was celebrating a triumph at Rome, Tetricus and Zenobia preceded him on horseback. Tetricus afterward became governor of Lucania, and Zenobia grew old in the City in the highest honor; from her, even today, the families of the Zenobii at Rome take their name.

[Under these consuls Pope Felix suffered martyrdom, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs, on the third day before the Kalends of January.]

### 289. 4. [CCLXVII] (HIER.)

Aurelian II and Marcellus.

[Under these consuls Eutychianus succeeded as pope, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs.]

Aurelian built a temple to the Sun and surrounded Rome with stronger walls. The first contest of the Sun was instituted by Aurelian [Note: [Col. 0689] read *agon Solis*].

A decree of Pope Eutychianus:

“To the dearest brothers John and all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, Eutychianus, bishop, greetings in the Lord,” and the rest (p. 205); dated on the second day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Aurelian and Marcellus, most illustrious men.

[Codex marginal note: Ninth persecution.]

### 290. 5. [CCLXVIII] (HIER.)

Probus and Paulinus, most illustrious men.

When Aurelian had begun a persecution against us, lightning struck near him and his companions.

(AD Mart.) Pope Eutychianus suffered martyrdom on the sixth day before the Ides of December and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

(REG.) At Rome, Pope Eutychianus, Theodora, Basilides, Tryphon, and Mandalia suffered martyrdom; at Lingones, the holy Gemini; at Leontium, Conon; at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Mamas; near Praeneste, Agapitus; in the city of Salona, Anastasius; at Augustodunum, Symphronianus; in the territory of Vivarais, at a place called *Ad Gentibus*, the subdeacon Andeolus, the presbyter Andochius, the deacon Tyrsus, and Felix; in the fortress of Divona [Note: read “Divona”], the presbyter Benignus.

### 291. 6. [CCLXIX]

Probus II and Paternus II.

[Pope Eutychianus suffered martyrdom.]

[From Pope Eutychianus up to these consuls, the sixth year should be written.]

(CASS.) Under these consuls, according to Cassiodorus, Aurelian was killed midway along the road between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Cenophrurium on the Old Road.

(H. R.) **Roman year 36.** Tacitus obtained the empire after Aurelian and held it for six months. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

Probus III and Paternus III.

(BEDA.) Anatolius, an Alexandrian by birth and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, trained in the disciplines of philosophy, is celebrated in many writings. The greatness of his intellect can be recognized most clearly from the book that he composed on Easter and from his ten books on arithmetic. The madness of the Manichaeans arose.

Gaius, the twenty-sixth pope after Peter.

(H. R.) Under these consuls, according to Cassiodorus, Tacitus was killed in Pontus in the sixth month of his reign, that is, approximately in the month of September.

**Roman year 37.** Florianus, according to every historian, obtained the empire after Tacitus; he was killed in the third month of his reign at Tarsus, that is, up to the Kalends of January, in the same year in which Aurelian was killed. He accomplished nothing worthy of remembrance, owing solely to the brevity of his reign.

(H. R.) **Roman year 38.** Probus reigned for 6 years and 4 months, that is, until the Kalends of May, in the year 264 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

### 292. 1. [CCLXX] (HIER.)

Messala and Gratus, most illustrious men.

With great valor Probus restored Gaul, which had been occupied by the barbarians [Note: read “by barbarians”].

### 293. 2. [CCLXXI] (HIER.)

Probus IV and Tiberianus.

In the second year of Probus, according to the Antiochenes, the year was 325; according to the Tyrians, 400; according to the Laodiceans, 324; according to the Edessenes, 589; according to the Ascalonites, 380.

[The beginning of the eighty-sixth jubilee according to the Hebrews. A jubilee among the Hebrews is called a fiftieth year. Therefore, according to the reckoning of the Hebrews, as Eusebius says in his chronicles, from Adam up to the present time—that is, the second year of Probus—there are 4,200 years, namely, eighty-four jubilees and fifty years, that is, one jubilee. Forty jubilees extend from Adam to Abraham’s fiftieth year; and from Adam to the sixteenth year of Tiberius there are eighty jubilees.]

Gaius, the twenty-sixth pope, [reigned] for 15 years and 4 months.

### 294. 3. [CCLXXII] (HIER.)

Probus V and Victorinus.

Probus allowed the Gauls and Pannonians to possess vineyards, and gave the Alma and Ameus mountains, planted by military labor, to the provincials for cultivation.

### 295. 4. [CCLXXIII] (HIER.)

Carus and Carinus.

Quirillus was appointed eighteenth bishop of Antioch. Saturninus, commander of the army, began to found a new city at Antioch; afterward, when he attempted to seize the empire, he was killed at Apamea.

A decretal letter of Pope Eutychianus:

“To the most beloved brother bishops established throughout Sicily, Eutychianus, bishop, greetings,” and the rest (Ep. 2, p. 207). Dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the second consulship of Carus and the consulship of Carinus, most illustrious men, according to Cassiodorus.

[Under these consuls Pope Eutychianus suffered martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs. Under these consuls Pope Gaius succeeded him on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.]

### 296. 5. [CCLXXIV] (BEDA.)

Carus II and Numerianus.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in the Syriac language a book of his disputation against Mani, who had come out of Persia; translated by the Greeks, it is possessed by many.

297. 6. [CCLXXV] (HIER.) Diocletian, distinguished by the title *vir clarissimus*, being consul. Theonas, the fifteenth bishop, presided over Alexandria for 19 years.

[Col. 0691C] 298. 7. [CCLXXVI] (HIER.) Aristobulus, distinguished by the title *vir clarissimus*, being consul. In this consulship Probus was killed by a military uprising at Sirmium, in the tower called Ferrata.

Roman year 39. Carus reigned with his sons Carinus and Numerian for two years and likewise two months, according to Roman history—that is, until the Kalends of July in the year 266 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

299. 1. [CCLXXVII] (HIER.) Maximus and Aquilinus. Carus of Narbonne, after laying waste the whole region of the Parthians and beginning to capture Coche and Ctesiphon, the most renowned cities of the enemy, died from a stroke of lightning while pitching camp beside the Tigris.

300. 2. [CCLXXVIII] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the second time, and Maximian. Numerian, being carried in a litter because of pain in his eyes, was killed by the treachery of his father-in-law Aper; the crime was discovered only after several days, from the stench of the corpse. (REG.) At Rome, Chrysanthus and Daria suffered martyrdom; Claudius with his wife Hilaria and sons Jason and Maurus; seventy soldiers; and others.

(HIER.) In this consulship Carinus, defeated in battle, was killed at the Margus. [Decretal letter of Pope Gaius [Note: Written in the lower margin of folio 127 without an indication of year.]: [Col. 0691] “Gaius, bishop, sends greetings to his most beloved brother Felix, bishop,” and the rest (same work, p. 209). [Note: This is the same letter that is more correctly assigned to the year 309.]] It was issued on the Kalends of March, when Diocletian was consul for the second time and Maximian, distinguished men, for the second time.

[Col. 0692A] Roman year 40. Diocletian reigned for 20 years, that is, until the Kalends of July in the year 287 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

301. 1. [CCLXXIX] (HIER.) Maximian, for the second time, and Januarius. Diocletian, son of a Dalmatian scribe, was elected emperor and immediately struck down Aper before the assembly of the soldiers, swearing that Numerian had been killed without any crime on his own part.

[Codex marginal note: The solar cycle begins.]

302. 2. [CCLXXX] (HIER.) Bassus and Quintianus. Diocletian admitted Herculius Maximian into partnership in the rule; Maximian, after crushing the multitude of peasants who, through their faction, had assumed the name of Bagaudae, restored peace to Gaul.

[Col. 0692B] 303. 3. [CCLXXXI] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the third time, and Maximian, for the third time. Carausius [Note: The manuscript reads *Carus*; read *Carausius*.], having assumed the purple, occupied Britain.

304. 4. [CCLXXXII] (HIER.) Tiberianus and Dio. Narseus brought war against the East. The Quinquegentiani ravaged Africa.

305. 5. [CCLXXXIII] (HIER.) Hanniballianus and Asclepiodotus. Achilleus gained possession of Egypt; for this reason Constantius, Galerius, and Maximian were received into the imperial government as Caesars. Constantius was the grandson of Claudius through his daughter; [Maximian] Galerius was born in Dacia, not far from Serdica.

306. 6. [CCLXXXIV] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the fourth time, and Maximian, for the fourth time. Diocletian, in order also to join them to himself by kinship, gave Constantius his stepdaughter Theodora in marriage; by her he later had six children, Constantine’s brothers. [Note: This passage is to be joined with the entry for the year 305.]

[Codex marginal note: Solar cycle 17; indiction 3.]

307. 7. [CCLXXXV] (HIER.) Constantius [Note: The manuscript reads *constatius* for the first Constantius.] and Maximus. Galerius [Note: This passage is to be joined with the entry for the year 305.] took Valeria, the daughter of Diocletian, as his wife. Both men were compelled to repudiate the wives whom they had previously married.

308. 8. [CCLXXXVI] (HIER.) Tuscus and Anulinus. Busiris and Coptus, having rebelled against the Romans, were razed to the ground. [Note: The reading *bustris* is uncertain.]

309. 9. [CCLXXXVII] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the fifth time, and Constantius, for the second time. The peoples of the Carpi and the Bastarnae were transferred onto Roman soil. Decretal letter of Pope Gaius: “Gaius sends greetings to his most beloved brother Felix, bishop,” and the rest (same work, p. 209); issued on the Kalends of March, when Diocletian was consul for the fifth time and Constantius for the second time, distinguished men (compare the *Book of the Pontiffs*). In this letter Gaius established that anyone who was to become a bishop should ascend through all the ecclesiastical grades, namely acolyte, doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, subdeacon, deacon, and priest.

(AD. Mart.) Pope Gaius suffered martyrdom on the tenth day before the Kalends of May and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus [under the consuls already named, Diocletian for the fifth time and Constantius for the second time].

Marcellinus, twenty-seventh pope, held office for eight years.

[Col. 0693A] 310. 10. [CCLXXXVIII] (HIER.) Faustus and Gallus. Diocletian was the first to command that he be worshiped as a god and that gems be set into garments and footwear.

311. 11. [CCLXXXIX] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the sixth time, and Maximian, for the sixth time. Whereas all emperors before him were greeted in the manner of judges and possessed nothing more than a purple cloak beyond the dress of a private citizen, he [Note: “With the year 310” is to be joined here.] … [the text is grammatically incomplete]. [In this consulship Pope Marcellinus succeeded on the third day before the Kalends of July.]

312. 12. [CCXC] (compare BEDA.) Constantius, for the third time, and Maximus, for the third time. [Under these persecutors 7,000 suffered within thirty days.]

313. 13. [CCXCI] (HIER.) Titatianus and Nepotianus. Alexandria, having withdrawn from Roman authority together with all Egypt under the leadership of Achilleus [Note: The text reads “X”; a later hand has written *dux*, “leader,” above it.], was captured by Diocletian in the eighth month of the siege.

[Col. 0693B] 314. 14. [CCXCII] (HIER.) Constantius, for the fourth time, and Maximus, for the fourth time. Accordingly, very many throughout all Egypt were afflicted by severe proscriptions and exile, after those who had proved to be the authors of the rebellion had been killed.

315. 15. [CCXCIII] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the seventh time, and Maximian, for the seventh time. In the church of Jerusalem, the thirty-seventh bishop, Zabdas, was ordained. After ten years, the Britains were recovered by Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorium. Near Lingones, the Alamanni were cut down by Caesar Constantine.

[Codex marginal note: The tenth persecution.]

316. 16. [CCXCIV] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the eighth time, and Maximian, for the eighth time. Galerius Maximian, defeated by Narseus, ran before Diocletian’s carriage wearing the purple. (Compare the *Book of the Pontiffs.*) Veturius, master of the soldiers, persecuted Christian soldiers; gradually, from that time, persecution against us began. [In this consulship] Pope Marcellinus was led to sacrifice and did sacrifice; but afterward, moved to repentance, he was beheaded on the sixth day before the Kalends of May (AD. Mart.), together with Claudius, Quirinus, and Antoninus. He was buried thirty-five days later in a chamber on the Via Salaria by the presbyter Marcellus and the deacons, with hymns.

Pope Marcellus, twenty-eighth after Peter, held office for five years.

317. 17. [CCXCV] (HIER.) Constantius, for the fifth time, and Maximus, for the fifth time. Galerius Maximian, after overcoming Narseus and capturing his wives, children, and sisters, was received by Diocletian with great honor. The Baths of Diocletian were built at Rome, and the Baths of Maximian at Carthage.

318. 18. [CCXCVI] (HIER.) Constantius, for the sixth time, and Maximus, for the sixth time. In the church of Jerusalem, the thirty-eighth bishop, Thermon, was appointed. At Antioch, Tirannus presided as bishop for the nineteenth year. In the church of Alexandria, Peter was ordained the sixteenth bishop after Theonas; he later achieved a most glorious martyrdom in the ninth year of the persecution.

[Codex marginal note: Open persecution by edict. The first year of the persecution of the tyrant Diocletian.]

319. 19. [CCXCVII] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the ninth time, and Constantius. Diocletian and Maximian, the Augusti, celebrated a triumph at Rome with splendid ceremony; before their chariot were led the wife, sisters, and children of Narseus, together with all the booty by which they had despoiled the Parthians. In a terrifying earthquake at Tyre and Sidon many buildings collapsed and an innumerable population was crushed. In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, in the month of March, during the days of Easter, the churches were overthrown; but in the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign.

320. 20. [CCXCVIII] (HIER.) Diocletian, for the tenth time, and Maximus, for the seventh time. In this consulship, according to Cassiodorus, in the second year of the persecution, Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan.

Roman year 41. Galerius Maximinus [reigned] for one year, that is, until the Kalends of July in the year 288 after the Passion.

Decretal letter: “Pope Marcellus sends greetings to his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Antioch,” and the rest (letter 1, p. 221); issued on the Kalends of April, when Maxentius and Maximian, distinguished men, were consuls.

Another decretal: “Marcellus, bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of the city of Rome, to Maxentius,” and the rest (letter 2, p. 223); and afterward: “You, therefore, who urge the abandonment of divine worship, withdrawal from the true faith, and sacrifice to the gods,” and the rest. It was issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, when Maxentius and Maximinus, distinguished men, were consuls (AD. Mart.).

Marcellus, by order of the emperor Maximinus, was first beaten with clubs and expelled from his presence. Then, when Maximinus heard that Marcellus had made into a church the house of the holy Lucina, which he himself had condemned to confiscation, and was celebrating Mass there, he ordered that straw be spread in that church in the middle of the city for the animals of a stable, and assigned the bishop of that same stable to its service under public guard. There, after serving for a long time dressed in sackcloth, he died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. John the presbyter and the blessed Lucina embalmed him, and he was buried on the Via Salaria in the cemetery of Priscilla.

Eusebius, twenty-eighth pope after Peter, was ordained; he held office for eight months [he died on the sixth day before the Nones of October].

(REG.) In his time the Lord’s cross was discovered under Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, as it is recorded in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs (*Book of the Pontiffs*): “In these times the Lord’s cross was discovered on the fifth day before the Nones of May, and Judas, who is also called Cyriacus, was baptized.”

Pope Maelchiades, thirtieth after Peter, was ordained; he held office for four years. He decreed that no believer should fast on Sunday or on the second feria, because the pagans celebrate these days as if with a sacred fast.

321. 1. [CCXCIX] (BEDA.) Maximinus and Severus, distinguished men. In the third year of the persecution, in which Constantius also died at Eboracum, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by the emperor Galerius Maximian; among them, Maximinus added his sorceries and sexual crimes to the persecutions of the Christians. At that time Peter, bishop of Alexandria, suffered martyrdom with many Egyptian bishops; likewise Lucian, a noble man distinguished in continence, learning, and character, a presbyter of Antioch; and Timothy at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July. (OROS. VII.25.)

Meanwhile Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered that the churches be devastated and that Christians be afflicted and killed, in the tenth persecution after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all the preceding persecutions [Note: Orosius reads “preceding”]; for ten years it continued without interruption through the burning of churches, the confiscation of the property of the innocent, and the slaughter of martyrs.

In the second year of the persecution Diocletian compelled Maximian, against his will, to lay down the purple and the imperial power together with him, so that, after younger men had been substituted in the government, they themselves might grow old in private leisure. (BEDA.) Accordingly, on one and the same day Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down both imperial authority and its ceremonial insignia. In the second year of the persecution Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the purple. Bede.

Nevertheless, once begun, the persecution did not cease to rage until the seventh year of Constantine. Orosius [Note: Marginal annotation in witness 1] (same work): Galerius and Constantius, the Augusti, first divided the Roman empire between them: Galerius Maximian received Illyricum, Asia, and the East; Constantius received Italy, Africa, and Gaul. But Constantius, a man of the greatest tranquility, content with Gaul and Spain alone, ceded the remaining regions to Galerius. Galerius chose two Caesars, Maximus, whom he established in the East, and Severus, to whom he entrusted Italy; he himself was established in Illyricum.

Bede: In the third year of the persecution, in which Constantius also died at Eboracum in Britain in the sixteenth year of his reign, Maximus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximian.

Orosius: Constantius died in Britain and left Constantine, his son by the concubine Helena, as emperor of Gaul (VII.28). While Constantine was vigorously administering the government in Gaul, the praetorian soldiers at Rome named Maxentius, the son of Maximian Herculius, Augustus; Maxentius was living as a private citizen in Lucania.

The Augustus Galerius sent the Caesar Severus against Maxentius to Rome with an army. While Severus was besieging the city, he was abandoned and betrayed through the crime of his soldiers; fleeing from there, he was killed at Ravenna.

Maximian Herculius, the persecutor, now a tyrant in place of an Augustus, attempted to strip his son, whose imperial power was already secure, of the royal dress and authority. But, openly terrified by insults and the disturbances of the soldiers, he departed for Gaul, intending, by means of equal treachery joined with his son-in-law Constantine, to seize the empire. His plot, however, was exposed and betrayed by his daughter Fausta, because he was preparing a deception against her husband Constantine; fleeing, he was killed at Massilia. [Note: The phrase “her husband” is written twice in the manuscript.]

(HIER.) Then, after Severus had been killed, Galerius made Licinius emperor.

(OROS., same work.) After Galerius himself had increased the persecution begun by Diocletian and Maximian through savage edicts, and after for ten years he had exhausted the provinces with every kind of human suffering, his heart rotting within and his vital organs dissolving, he even vomited up worms beyond the horror of human misery. Since physicians could no longer endure the stench and were repeatedly killed at his command, a certain physician told him that his suffering was the punishment of God’s anger and that for this reason he could not be cured. Then he recalled the Christians from exile by extensive edicts; but he himself died.

Constantine granted peace to the churches after the ten years during which they had been harassed by the persecutors. Then, when civil war arose between Constantine and Maxentius, Maxentius was defeated and killed at the Milvian Bridge. This is what Orosius says.

According to the chronicle of Eusebius and Bede, the years of the persecution extend to the seventh year of Constantine: that is, the nineteenth and twentieth years of Diocletian, the year of Galerius and the sixth of Constantine. Bede counts the third year of the persecution—the year in which Constantius, Constantine’s father, died at Eboracum—between Diocletian and Constantine. He counts the fourth year of the persecution under Galerius, Severus, and Maxentius at Rome, while Constantine was ruling in Gaul. Isidore, however, counted the preceding third year of the persecution under Galerius.

(REG.) At Rome suffered Gaius and Pope Marcellus; the deacon Cyriacus; Largus; Smaragdus; Apronianus; Papias and Maurus; Claudius and Propedigna with their children; the presbyter Gabinius; Castulus; Pancratius; Arthemius with his wife and daughter; Sebastian; Marcus and Marcellianus; the presbyter Marcellinus; Peter the exorcist; Tranquillinus; Nicostratus with his wife Zoe; Primus and Felicianus; Claudius; Castorius; Victorinus; Simpronianus; Basiliscus; Faustinus and Beatrix; Tiburtius, son of Chromatius; Simplicius; the virgin Susanna; John; Crispus; Genesius; Felix and Adauctus [Note: The manuscript has *Adauctus*.]; Lucia; Geminianus; Sergius and Bacchus; Chrysogonus; Saturninus and Sisinius; the Four Crowned Ones; Theodorus; Pontianus; Pretextatus [Note: The manuscript has *pretexatus*.]; and Tharso.

(REG.) At Spoleto, the presbyter Gregory; Sabinus, bishop; and the deacons Exuperantius and Marcellus. In the Parmarian islands, Anastasia and Pamphilius, a presbyter and intimate of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, whose life Eusebius himself composed in three books. At Antioch, Julianus and Basilissa. In the cities of Spain: at Caesaraugusta, Vincent, deacon; at Barcino, Eulalia, virgin; Cucufas; at Gerunda, Felix. At Cumae, Juliana, virgin. At Tyre, Tyrannio, Silvanus, Plenus, and Linus, bishops, with an innumerable multitude. At Sirmium, Sirenus. At Nicomedia, Peter and Lucian [Note: Witness 1 perhaps reads *educianus*], an Antiochene presbyter; Anthimus, bishop [Note: A second hand adds: “the presbyter Hermolaus with others”]; Pantaleon; John; Adrian; Dorotheus [Note: The second hand has *Dorotheus*.]; Gorgonius; and Eleutherius. At Smyrna, the bishop Irenaeus. In Palestine, in the city of Gaza, Silvanus. At Milan, Victor [Note: The witnesses read *mediolis* and *mediolano*.] At Siscia, a city of Illyricum, the bishop Quirinus. At Tarsus, Boniface. At Aquileia, Felix and Fortunatus. In Cilicia [Note: The witnesses read *cilia* and *Sicilia*.], Vitus and Modestus with Crescentia, and the virgin Lucia. In Britain, Alban [Note: The witness has *abanus*.] At Massilia, Victor. At Augusta, Afra, in the province of Raetia. At Nicaea in Bithynia, Theodota with her children. In the Spanish city of Complutum, the brothers Justinus and Pastor. In the Sicilian city of Catana, Euplus, deacon [Note: The manuscript has *Epulus*; the second witness has *Euplus*.] At Pergamum, a city of Italy, Alexander. In the city of Chalcedon, Euphemia. At Naples in Campania, Januarius, bishop of Beneventum, and Sosius, deacon. In the city of Mesentia, Faustus and Desiderius. In Palestine, Peleus and Nilus, bishop. At Cyzicus, Fausta and Evilasius. At Agaunum, Mauritius with his companions. At Antioch, Cyprian, bishop, with Justina. At Aegeae, Cosmas and Damian. In Gaul, at the fortress of Solodorum, which is above the river Arola, Victor and Ursus. At Cologne, Gereon with his companions. At Tarsus, Taracus [Note: Either *Trachus* according to one witness, or *Taracus* according to another.], Probus, and Andronicus. In Venusia, a city of Apulia, Felix, bishop, and Audax and Januarius, presbyters. At Soissons, Crispinus and Crispinianus. At Sidon, Zenobius, presbyter. In the territory of Agaunum, Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentia. In Scythia, at the metropolis of Phrygia, Salaria and Mennas. At Antioch, Romanus. At Alexandria, Peter, bishop. In Africa, in the city of Colonia, Crispina, virgin. In Tuscany, Barbara, virgin. In Spain, Leocadia; and in the city of Merida, Eulalia and Julia, virgins.

(BEDA.) Then, within one month, 17,000 martyrs suffered for Christ.

Roman year 42. Constantine the Great, son of Constantius by the concubine Helena, beginning with the fourth year of the persecution and the second indiction, reigned for 30 years and 10 months—that is, until the year 318 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

322. 1. [CCC] (HIER.) Proconsuls: Diocletian, for the eleventh time, and Maximus, for the ninth time. Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximian, was proclaimed Augustus by the praetorian soldiers at Rome. Severus, Caesar sent by Galerius Maximian against Maxentius, was killed at Ravenna. [In this consulship Pope Melchiades succeeded on the Nones of July.]

323. 2. [CCCI] Proconsuls: Diocletian, for the twelfth time, and Maximus, for the tenth time. Licinius was made emperor by Galerius at Carnuntum. Herculius Maximian, exposed by his daughter Fausta because he was preparing a plot against her husband, was killed while fleeing at Massilia. Quirinus, bishop of Siscia, was gloriously killed for Christ. For after a millstone had been tied around his neck and he had been thrown from a bridge into the river, he floated on the surface for a very long time; and, speaking to the onlookers, lest his own people be frightened by his example, he scarcely obtained by prayer that he might be submerged. [Note: One witness reads *terrentur*, “are frightened.”]

324. 3. [CCCII] (HIER.) Maximus, for the eighth time, and Licinius. (OROS.) Galerius Maximian, the persecutor of the Church, died of worms.

325. 4. [CCCIII] (HIER.) Constantine, for the second time [Note: The witness reads *Constantius*.], and Licinius, for the second time. Maximian, after persecuting the Christians, died at Tarsus, when he was already about to be punished by Licinius. Pope Melchiades died on the fourth day before the Ides of January (compare the Martyrology).

Silvester, thirty-first pope, held office for 20 years.

[Codex marginal note: The decennial cycle begins; indiction 7.]

326. 5. [CCCIV] (BEDA.) Constantine, for the third time, and Licinius, for the third time. (HIER.) [Peter, bishop of the church of Alexandria, suffered martyrdom.] In the church of Alexandria, Achillas was ordained the seventeenth bishop.

327. 6. [CCCV] (HIER.) Volusianus and Annianus. Maxentius was defeated and killed by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge.

328. 7. [CCCVI] (HIER.) Constantine, for the fourth time [Note: The witness reads *Constantius*.], and Licinius, for the fourth time. The Cibalense War was fought against Licinius. Our peace was restored by Constantine after ten years of persecution.

[After Constantine had been baptized by Pope Silvester, his mother Helena wrote to him from Britain, urging him to follow the Jews by denying Christ. Then, in the consulship of Constantine for the fourth time and Licinius for the fourth time, on the Ides of August, 120 of the wisest Jews assembled with Helena at Rome, together with the emperor Constantine and 24 bishops under Pope Silvester; and the Jews were defeated in every point of divine Scripture.]

329. 8. [CCCVII] (HIER.) Sabinus and Rufinus. In Jerusalem, the thirty-ninth bishop, Macarius, was appointed.

[Codex marginal note: The solar cycle begins.]

330. 9. [CCCVIII] (HIER.) Gallicanus and Bassus. Diocletian died not far from Salona, in the palace of his country estate; and, alone among all men, he is recorded as a private citizen among the gods.

[Col. 0698C] 331. 10. [CCCIX] (HIER.) Licinius, for the fifth time, and Crispus. Crispus and Constantine, sons of Constantine.

332. 11. [CCCX] Constantine, for the fifth time, and Licinius. Licinius the younger, son of the Augustus Licinius and grandson of Constantine through his sister, were called Caesars. [Note: This entry is to be joined with the year 331.]

333. 12. [CCCXI] Constantine, for the sixth time, and Constantius. Lactantius educated their son Crispus in Latin letters; he was the most eloquent man of his age. [Note: This entry is to be joined with the year 331.]

334. 13. [CCCXII] Crispus, for the second time, and Constantius, for the second time. Yet he was so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities. [Note: This entry is to be joined with the year 331.]

335. 14. [CCCXIII] (HIER.) Probinus and Julianus. Licinius drove the Christians from his palace. Basil, bishop of Amasia in Pontus, was crowned with martyrdom under Licinius.

[Col. 0698D] 336. 15. [CCCXIV] (HIER.) Severus and Rufinus. In the church of Alexandria, Alexander was ordained the eighteenth bishop. Arius, a presbyter expelled from the church by him, joined many to his impiety. To refute their perfidy, a synod of 318 bishops was assembled at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, and by its opposition in favor of the *homoousion* (“of the same substance”) it destroyed all the devices of the heretics.

337. 16. [CCCXV] (OROS. VII.22.) Crispus, for the third time, and Constantius, for the third time. Constantine prohibited the killing of Christians and ordered the temples of the pagans to be closed. (Compare the *Life of Saint Martin.*) [Saint Martin was born.]

[Saint Martin [Note: These words are written in the margin elsewhere.] was born at Sabaria, a town of Pannonia, but was raised at Ticinum within Italy.]

338. 17. [CCCXVI] (BEDA.) Paulinus and Julianus. The catholic faith was discussed at the synod of 318 bishops assembled against the Arians in Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, on the nineteenth day of the month Desius according to the Greeks—that is, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July—in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, according to Bede.

Decretal letter of Saint Pope Silvester. (Compare the *Book of the Pontiffs.*) In the time of Pope Silvester and Constantine, the most devout Augustus, a great council was held in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. By the regular summons of that same Pope Silvester, 318 catholic bishops gathered there, set forth the complete, catholic, undefiled faith, and condemned Arius, Photinus, Sabellius, and their followers.

(Compare AD. Mart.) At the same time, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, when the great council mentioned above had assembled at Nicaea (compare the *Book of the Pontiffs*), Silvester himself, after a canonical summons, assembled 277 bishops in the city of Rome with the counsel of Constantine and condemned the aforesaid heretics. They established that an Arian presbyter who repented should not be received unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and confirmed him with holy chrism through the laying on of episcopal hands, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be given by heretics.

With the agreement and subscription of all, they also established that no layman should bring a charge against a cleric, nor a cleric of a lower rank against one of a higher rank—that is, a presbyter against a bishop; that the body of Christ should be offered in pure linen; that chrism should be prepared by a bishop; that a presbyter should anoint the baptized; that dalmatics should be used in the church; that the left shoulder of the subdeacons should be covered with a linen pallium; and many other matters.

339. 18. [CCCXVII] (HIER.) Constantine, for the seventh time, and Constantius, for the fourth time. Constantine, son of Constantine, was made Caesar. Licinius was killed at Thessalonica as a private citizen, contrary to the terms of his oath.

340. 19. [CCCXVIII] (HIER.) Constantius, for the fifth time, and Maximus. Nazarius is regarded as a distinguished rhetorician. Crispus, son of Constantine, and Licinius the younger, son of Constantia, the sister of Constantine, and of Licinius, were brutally killed.

341. 20. [CCCXIX] (HIER.) Januarius and Justus. Constantine’s twentieth-anniversary celebrations were held at Nicomedia and published at Rome in the following year.

Up to this point Eusebius, the companion of the martyr Pamphilus, writes the history; we have added what follows [that is, Jerome]. [Note: Five lines have been erased after this point.]

In the history called the *Tripartite History*, the following is found (II.18): Helena discovered the cross and sent two parts of it to her son. Constantine placed one of them on a statue in the Forum of Constantine, upon a porphyry column; he enclosed the other in a silver reliquary and kept it in the city.

(III.6.) Arius, writing a fabricated confession of faith, was recalled from exile by Constantine. When he returned, Arius swore to Constantine: “If we do not believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as the catholic Church has believed, may God be our judge, both here and in the future.” Although Constantine rejoiced at this, he nevertheless did not permit him or the other heretics [Note: One witness reads *hereti*, “heretics.”] to communicate in the church until the bishops had judged them.

(III.10.) Constantine, meanwhile, preferring to approve Arius, brought him to the palace and questioned him under oath about the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. But Arius, secretly keeping his sect under his cloak, swore in this manner. Since that day was a Saturday, Constantine ordered that Arius be admitted to communion on the following Sunday.

Then Arius was honored by the soldiers of the bishop Eusebius, who was also an Arian, and was escorted with honor and display through the middle of the city. But when he came to the Forum of Constantine, where that part of the cross was, Arius trembled and became confused. When he needed to relieve himself, he discharged his bowels together with his entrails and died quickly.

342. 21. [CCCXX] (HIER.) Constantine, for the eighth time, and Constantius, for the sixth time. Arbonius is regarded as a renowned rhetorician in Africa. When he taught young men declamation at Sicca and, still a pagan, was being compelled toward belief by dreams [Note: One witness reads *sontis*.], and could not obtain from the bishop the faith that he had always opposed, he composed brilliant books against his former religion and finally obtained the agreement of his piety as if by certain pledges. Constantine founded and restored the Bithynian city of Drepanum in honor of the martyr Lucian and named it Helenopolis after his mother. At Antioch the church called the Golden Church began to be built.

343. 22. [CCCXXI] (HIER.) Constantius, for the seventh time, and Symmachus. Constantine killed his wife Pausia [Note: Read *Fausta*.]. Donatus became known; from him came the Donatists throughout Africa. At Antioch, after Tirannus, Vitalis was ordained the twentieth bishop; after him Philogonius the twenty-first; Paulinus succeeded him as the twenty-second; after Paulinus, Eustathius became the twenty-third. After Eustathius was driven into exile for the faith, the Arians held the church down to the present day.

344. 23. [CCCXXII] Bassus and Ablabius. The Arians [Note: This entry is to be joined with the year 343.] gained control of the church—namely, Eulalius, Eusebius, Euphronius, Placillus, Stephen, Lentius, Eudoxius, Meletius, Euzotus, Dorotheus, and again Meletius. I have not separated their periods because I judge them enemies of Christ rather than bishops.

[Col. 0700D] [Codex marginal note: The decennial cycle begins; indiction 11.]

345. 24. [CCCXXIII] (HIER.) Pacatianus and Hilarianus. Juvencus, a presbyter by rank and a Spaniard by birth, explains the Gospels in heroic verse. (CASS.) Porphyry, having sent Constantine a distinguished volume, was released from exile. [In this consulship the city previously called Byzantium, its name having been changed, was named Constantinople by Constantine.]

346. 25. [CCCXXIV] (HIER.) Dalmatius and Zenophilus. Athanasius was ordained the nineteenth bishop of Alexandria. Constantinople was dedicated, almost to the point of stripping all other cities bare. The philosopher Metrorus became known.

347. 26. [CCCXXV] (HIER.) Optatus and Paulinus. By Constantine’s edict the temples of the pagans were [overthrown]. (Vita S. Mart.) [When Saint Martin was ten years old, he fled to the church against the will of his parents, since they were pagans, and asked to be made a catechumen. [Note: The manuscript may read *catechuminus*.]]

348. 27. [CCCXXVI] (HIER.) Constantius and Albinus. Constans, son of Constantine, was advanced to the throne. An innumerable multitude perished from pestilence and famine in Syria and Cilicia. [Note: One witness reads *Ciliaque*.]

349. 28. [CCCXXVII] (AD. Mart.) Nepotianus and Fecundus. In the martyrology: On the day before the Kalends of January, the birthday of Pope Silvester, who held office for 23 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He held office from the Kalends of February until the second day before the Kalends of January; he was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, on the Via Salaria, at the third milestone from the city of Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of January, [when Constantius and Volusianus were consuls], and the episcopate was vacant for 15 days.

Note the two months during which the episcopate was vacant: from the fourth day before the Ides of December, when Pope Milichades died, until the Kalends of February, when Silvester began his episcopate, and then the additional 15 days. This period is not counted against the pontiffs. If, therefore, something in the time of the pontiffs is lacking, whose birthdays are celebrated annually, how much more may there be a discrepancy in the period of the emperors?

Marcus, thirty-second pope after Peter, was ordained; he held office for eight months. [Under the consuls already mentioned, Nepotianus and Fecundus, he succeeded on the Kalends of February.]

In a decretal: “To the holy lord Marcus, venerable for the dignity of the apostolic summit, pope of the holy Roman and apostolic see and of the universal Church, Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt. We do not doubt that it has reached you how much and what sort of suffering we endure daily from the heretics, and especially from the Arians, so that we are now weary even of living. They have devastated our possessions to such an extent that they left us not even the smallest utensils; they burned our books down to the last one.

Therefore we beseech you, most blessed father—for we do not doubt that you possess complete copies of the Council of Nicaea—that you send us, under secure guarantee, those copies that belonged to your predecessor, Silvester, of holy memory. For when we took part in the aforesaid synod with Alexander, our bishop, a pontiff worthy of God and bishop of the city of Alexandria, in the office of deacon, the seventy chapters were sent to the aforesaid Pope Silvester, under a supporting guarantee, in the presence of Victor and Vincent, blessed presbyters and apostolic representatives.

Indeed, while we were present, eighty chapters were discussed in the aforesaid synod: forty issued by the Greeks in the Greek language, and forty by the Latins, issued in Latin. But it seemed good to the 318 fathers assembled in the aforesaid council, filled with the Holy Spirit, and especially to the aforementioned Alexander and the apostolic representatives, that ten chapters should be joined to the others and inserted in appropriate places, so that the chapters of so great and excellent a council would correspond to the seventy disciples and the seventy languages, and would instruct the entire Christian world; and that all who live under the priestly and Christian name should be governed by one faith and one priestly and clerical rule, with nothing discordant from its head.

Now, as was said, the enemies of the holy Church of God, especially the Arians, by whom we are daily consumed, attacked, and oppressed, burned with fire the aforementioned seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea. These are the chapters that I brought from the aforesaid synod, at the command of my already-mentioned lord Alexander, by decree of all the bishops, and that I read aloud and transcribed before everyone. We desire that, through the authority of the Church of your holy see, we may be worthy to receive them through the bearers of this letter,” and the rest (Council I, p. 553).

“Marcus, bishop of the holy Roman apostolic see and of the universal Church, sends greetings to all the venerable brothers Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt. I grieve, brothers, and am exceedingly distressed over your affliction,” and the rest (Council I, p. 555).

“Regarding the truth [Note: Read *veritate* for *capitulorum*, ‘chapters’.] of your chapters of the Council of Nicaea, concerning which your brotherly letter indicated that you were present, we made more careful inquiries from our people who were present together with you. They explained the entire order to us just as your letters testified and confirmed that your letter was true in every respect—not because we suspected anything sinister on your part, but because we desired that we, you, and they should all agree without any future hesitation, and that the holy Roman Church, which has always remained undefiled and, with the Lord’s command and the help of blessed Peter, will remain so in the future, should stand firm and immovable at all times without any attack by heretics.

After these matters had been carefully investigated, we found in the holy archive of our apostolic see the same seventy chapters that had been sent to my predecessor Silvester of holy memory, unharmed, just as you reported. Because of the authority and writing [Note: Perhaps *subscriptionem*, “subscription,” rather than *scriptionem*.] of so many fathers and of that great council, we did not send those very documents to you. Instead, in the presence of your representatives, we arranged for other documents containing the same number, the same matters, and the same subscription to be written and sent to you under a firm guarantee,” and the rest.

It was issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, when Nepotianus and Fecundus, venerable and distinguished men, were consuls.

Marcus died on the Nones of October and was buried in the cemetery of Balbina, on the Via Adriatica, which he himself had caused to be built through his efforts. (ADON. Mart.)

Pope Julius, thirty-third after Peter, was ordained; he held office for 16 years and 9 months [in the consulship of Felicianus].

### 350. 29. [CCCXXVIII] (HIER.)

Felicianus and Titianus. Callocerus, who was plotting a revolution in Cyprus, was suppressed. Constantine, together with his sons, sent letters of honor to Antonius.

### 351. 30. [CCCXXIX] (HIER.)

Ursus and Polemius. At Constantine’s thirtieth anniversary, Dalmatius was named Caesar. The rhetorician Pater taught most gloriously at Rome. The daughter of the rhetorician Nazarius equaled her father in eloquence. Tiberianus, an eloquent man and prefect of the praetorium, governed Gaul. Eustathius of Constantinople was recognized; through his industry a martyr-shrine was constructed at Jerusalem.

### 352. 31. [CCCXXX] (SULP. SEV.)

Constantius II and Constans. (*Life of Saint Martin*) [When Saint Martin was fifteen years old, he was seized and chained and bound by the military oath, with only one servant as companion. (ch. 2.) For when the emperors had issued an edict that the sons of veterans should be enrolled for military service, his father betrayed Martin, because he begrudged his son’s virtuous conduct. He spent almost three years under arms before baptism, but remained innocent of vices. (ch. 3.) Within those three years, he clothed Christ with half his cloak. (ch. 2.) From adolescence he served in the armed forces among the cavalry units of the imperial guard (*scholares alae*) under Emperor Constantius, and afterward under Caesar Julian.]

(HIER.) [A later hand—the same one that wrote the continuation for 1126–1128—adds: “Jerome says thus.”] Constantine, at the end of his life, was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and turned toward Arian doctrine. From that time down to the present, the plundering of the churches and discord throughout the whole world followed. When Constantine was preparing war against the Persians, he died at Achiron, a public estate near Nicomedia.

Theodorus says the following in his *Tripartite History*: “Constantine died at Nicomedia, at the estate of Achiron, after he had been baptized by Eusebius, the Arian bishop of Nicomedia.” (cf. III, 13.)

He died in the sixty-sixth year of his age and the thirty-first of his reign, on 25 May, during these consulships. [The entire passage from *Obit*, “He died,” to *consulibus*, “consulships,” had been written after *moritur*, “he dies,” and was afterward transferred here.]

[OROSIUS, as follows.] The forty-third Roman ruler, Constantius, gained the imperial power in the year 1091 from the founding of the City, together with his brothers Constantine and Constans. He held it for twenty-seven years, that is, until November in the year 345 after the Passion, during these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 353. 1. [CCCXXXI] (HIER.)

Acyndinus and Proculus. Ablabius, prefect of the praetorium, and many nobles were killed. Sapor, king of the Persians, after laying waste Mesopotamia, besieged Nisibis for nearly two months. Dalmatius Caesar, whom his uncle Constantine had left as partner in the kingdom for his sons, was killed through the faction of his cousin Constantius and a military uprising. Jacobus of Nisibis was recognized as bishop; at his prayers the city was often delivered from danger.

### 354. 2. [CCCXXXII] (HIER.)

Marcellinus and Probinus. From this point Arian impiety, supported by the protection of King Constantius, first persecuted Athanasius and then all bishops who did not belong to its party, through exiles, prisons, and various kinds of affliction. [Pope Julius was in exile for ten months; but after the death of Constantius he returned with glory to his see.] (*Book of the Pontiffs.*)

### 355. 3. [CCCXXXIII] (HIER.)

Constantius III and Constans II. Constantine, waging war against his brother, was killed near Aquileia. Constans fought against the Franks with varying success. [At this point the names of the consuls of the following year, and apparently also the note “Audeus–Audiena,” had been written, but were erased and supplied in the margin by a second hand. Thus what follows formerly belonged to the year 356, but now belongs to 355.] (SULP. SEV.)

Many cities of the East collapsed in a terrible earthquake. [Saint Martin, when he was eighteen years old, was baptized; and when his tribune’s term of office had ended, he promised that he would renounce the world. For almost two years after his baptism he served in name only.] (ch. 3.)

In a decretal letter of the blessed Pope Julius it is written:

> “In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, while the Augusti Constantine and Constans were reigning, in the fourth year, on 24 September, in the sixth indiction, with the holy and most blessed Julius presiding as pope of the apostolic see of the city of Rome, with the holy and venerable Gospels set forth, in the church of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, which is called Constantina, and with the venerable men also seated and hearing together with him—Benedictus, bishop of Aquileia; Rufus, most holy bishop of Fartanum; Agapitus, bishop of the church of Ravenna; Julius, bishop of the church of Milan; Lucianus, bishop of Mauriana; and the others with them, one hundred and sixteen bishops in all—the aforesaid Julius, most holy bishop of the city of Rome, said…”

and so forth. (*Council* I, p. 567.)

Thus the fourth year of the Emperor Constantine was the sixth indiction; according to the chronicle of Eusebius or Bede, it was the twenty-eighth year of the Great Constantine, but according to Dionysius, the year 333 from the Incarnation.

### 356. 4. [CCCXXXIV] (HIER.)

Placidus [The note for this year was already written by a second hand; see variant reading 260 above.] and Romulus. Audeus was held in high esteem in Coele Syria; from him came the heresy of the Audiani.

### 357. 5. [CCCXXXV] (HIER.)

Leontius and Sallustius. The Franks were subdued by Constans, and peace was made with them. Hermogenes, master of the soldiers, was dragged from Constantinople by the populace because of Bishop Paul, whom he was expelling by the king’s command and through the faction of the Arians. The Golden Church at Antioch was dedicated.

[Codex marginal note: The solar cycle begins.]

### 358. 6. [CCCXXXVI] (HIER.)

Constantius IV and Constans III. Macedonius, a man of great skill, was installed by the Arian bishops in Paul’s place; from him came the Macedonian heresy. Paul was strangled through the cruelty of the prefect Philip—for Philip was a supporter of the Macedonian party—and through the plots of the Arians.

### 359. 7. [CCCXXXVII] (HIER.)

Amantius and Albinus. Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was held in high esteem [and Martin, bishop of Mainz; during their time Eufratus of Cologne, a heretic, was condemned—added by another hand, the same hand that wrote the first continuation]. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, when Constantius was seeking him for punishment, was received honorably by Maximinus. Sapor, king of the Persians, persecuted the Christians. Neocaesarea in Pontus was overthrown, except for the church, the bishop, and the others who were found there.

### 360. 8. [CCCXXXVIII] (HIER.)

After the consulship of Amantius and Albinus. Titianus, an eloquent man, administered the prefecture of the praetorium in Gaul. Athanasius was restored to Alexandria in response to letters from Constans.

### 361. 9. [CCCXXXIX] (HIER.)

Rufinus and Eusebius. Dyrrachium collapsed in an earthquake, and Rome trembled for three days and nights [MS. 1 reads *natavit*, “swam,” for *nutavit*, “trembled”]. Many cities of Campania were also afflicted.

### 362. 10. [CCCLX] (HIER.)

Philippus and Sallia. At great expense to the state, the harbor of Seleucia in Syria was completed. Sapor again besieged Nisibis for three months. Eusebius of Emesa, a standard-bearer of the Arian faction, wrote many works.

### 363. 11. [CCCXLI] (HIER.)

Limenius and Catulinus. There was a solar eclipse. A night battle against the Persians took place near Singara; in it we lost an indisputable victory through the stupidity of the soldiers. Nor indeed was any of Constantius’s nine serious battles against the Persians more severe. For, to omit other matters, Nisibis was besieged, while Bezabde and Amida were captured.

Maximinus, the fortieth bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, died. After him the Arians invaded the church—namely, Cyril, Eutychius, then Cyril again, Hirenus, Cyril a third time, Hilarius, and Cyril a fourth time. This last Cyril, although he had been ordained priest by Maximus, and although after Maximus’s death the episcopate was promised to him by Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, and the other Arian bishops if he repudiated Maximus’s ordination, served as a deacon in the church. For this impiety he was rewarded with the recompense of the priesthood: by various frauds he enticed Heraclius, whom Maximus on his deathbed had appointed as his successor, and degraded him from bishop to priest.

[Codex marginal note: The nineteenth decennial cycle begins; the fifteenth indiction.]

### 364. 12. [CCCXLII] (HIER.)

Sergius and Nigridianus. When Magnentius seized the imperial power at Augustodunum, Constans was killed not far from Spain, in a fortress called Helena, in the thirtieth year of his age. Consequently, when the state was thrown into confusion, Vetranio was made emperor at Mursa and Nepotianus at Rome. The Roman people, rebelling against the supporters of Magnentius, were betrayed by the senator Heracliada. The head of Nepotianus was carried on a spear through the city, and many proscriptions of nobles and killings took place.

### 365. 13. [CCCXLIII] (HIER.)

After the consulship of Sergius and Nigridianus. At Naissus, Constantius granted Vetranio the insignia of kingship. Magnentius was defeated at Mursa; in that battle the Roman forces collapsed. Gallus, Constantius’s cousin, was made Caesar.

### 366. 14. [CCCXLIV] (AD. Mart.)

Constantius V and Constans, Caesar. Pope Julius died on the day before the Ides of April and was buried on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone from the City, in the cemetery of Calepodius. He had been cast out for ten months under the Arian Constantine, son of Constantine, but after Constantine’s death he returned to his own see.

Liberius, the thirty-fourth pope after Peter, was ordained; he sat for eighteen years.

### 367. 15. [CCCXLV] (HIER.)

Constantius VI and Constans II. Gallus suppressed the Jews who, after killing soldiers during the night, had taken up arms to wage war; he killed many thousands of people, including those of innocent age, and delivered their cities—Diocaesarea, Tiberias, and Diospolis—and many towns to the flames. Several nobles were killed by Gallus at Antioch.

### 368. 16. [CCCXLVI] (HIER.)

Constantius VII and Constans III. Magnentius killed himself with his own hand in the palace at Lyons, and Decentius, his brother, whom he had sent as Caesar to defend Gaul, ended his life by hanging at Sens. Gennadius, a distinguished forensic orator, was held in high esteem. Minervius, a rhetorician of Bordeaux, taught with great distinction.

### 369. 17. [CCCXLVII] (HIER.)

Arbitrio and Lollianus. Gallus Caesar, summoned by his cousin Constantine [the name as supplied], who had become suspicious of him because of his exceptional character, was killed in Istria. Silvanus, who had attempted a revolution in Gaul, was killed after twenty-eight days. The rhetorician Victorinus and the grammarian Donatus, my teacher [that is, Jerome’s], were distinguished at Rome; Victorinus also practiced in the Forum of Trajan. Paulinus and Rodanus, bishops of Gaul, were driven into exile for their faith.

### 370. 18. [CCCXLVIII] (HIER.)

Constantius VIII and Julian. The rhetoricians Alchimius and Delphidius taught with great distinction in Aquitania. Donatus, from whom we mentioned above that the Donatists in Africa took their name, was expelled from Carthage. Some of his followers are called Montenses, because they began to have their first church at Rome on a hill. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli; Lucifer and Dionysius, bishops of the churches of Cagliari and Milan; and also Pancratius, a Roman priest, and Hilary, a deacon, were condemned to exile in places separated from one another by the Arians and Constantius.

Julian, the brother of Gallus, was proclaimed Caesar at Milan.

### 371. 19. [CCCXLIX] (HIER.)

Constantius IX and Julian II. Antony the monk died in the desert in the 105th year of his age. He was accustomed to tell many who came to him about a certain Paul of Thebes, a man of marvelous holiness; we have described Paul’s death in a short work. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who three years earlier had been driven into Phrygia by the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, and the other Arians who were with him, composed books on our religion. The relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople. Sarmata, Armatus, and Macarius, disciples of Antony, were held in high esteem.

Pope Liberius of the Roman Church was sent into exile. [After he had been driven into exile for the faith, all the clergy swore that they would accept no other man. But when Felix had been installed in the priesthood by the Arians, many broke their oath, and after a year they were expelled together with Felix, because Liberius, overcome by the weariness of exile and subscribing to heretical depravity, had entered Rome as though victorious. (*AD. Mart.*) Felix, after being deposed from his episcopate, lived on his small estate on the Via Portuensis, where he died on 29 July.]

(HIER.) Great forces of the Alamanni were defeated by Caesar Julian near the town of Argentoratum in Gaul.

### 372. 20. [CCCL] (HIER.)

Titianus and Cerealis. When the Saracens attacked the monastery of blessed Antony, they killed Sarmata [MS. 1 spells the name *sarmatatam*, for *Sarmatam*, “Sarmata”]. Upon Constantius’s entry into Rome, the Constantinopolitans received the bones of the apostle Andrew and of Luke the Evangelist with marvelous enthusiasm.

Felix, the thirty-fifth pope after Peter, was ordained; he sat for one year.

### 373. 21. [CCCLI] (HIER.)

Eusebius and Hipatius. Nicomedia was utterly destroyed by an earthquake, while the neighboring cities were partly damaged. Paulinus, bishop of Trier, died in exile in Phrygia. [“Paulinus … died” was written again in the margin by another hand.] (See above.) Evanthius, the most learned of grammarians, died at Constantinople; Chrestus was brought from Africa to take his place.

Pope Liberius returned from exile.

### 374. 22. [CCCLII] (HIER.)

Constantius X, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. A council was held at Ariminum and at Seleucia in Isauria, in which the ancient faith of the Fathers was first condemned through the betrayal of the ten legates, and afterward through the betrayal of all the others. Honoratus, formerly prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, was made the first prefect of the city at Constantinople. Gratian, now emperor, was born. Hilary [bishop of Poitiers], after presenting a book in his defense to Constantius at Constantinople, returned to Gaul. Macedonius was expelled from Constantinople. Nearly all the churches throughout the world were polluted under the name of peace by association with the Arians and the king.

### 375. 23. [CCCLIII] (HIER.)

Julian, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. The largest of the churches at Constantinople was dedicated. Meletius, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, was transferred to Antioch by the Arian bishops Acacius and George. After a short interval, when he had received the priests who had been deposed by his predecessor Eudoxius, he frustrated the just cause of his exile by a sudden change of faith.

### 376. 24. [CCCLIV] (HIER.)

Faurus, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. [Through Hilary, Gaul condemned the treacherous devices of the Ariminian perfidy.]

### 377. 25. [CCCLV] (ISID.)

Florentius, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. [The heresy of the Anthropomorphites arose in Syria, Macedonia, and Constantinople.]

### 378. 26. [CCCLVI]

Mamertinus, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*).

### 379. 27. [CCCLVII]

Nevitta, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*). [Bishop Theodorus says the following in his *Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts* (IV, 50): “Constantine died at Mopsucrenae, between Cilicia and Cappadocia,” in the forty-fifth year of his age.] Coming to Constantinople, he died on the third day of November.

The forty-fourth Roman emperor, Julian, according to everyone, reigned for two years and eight months, that is, until 1 July, in the year 348 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 380. 1. [CCCLVIII] (HIER.)

Julian IV, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. After Julian had turned to the worship of idols, there was a gentle persecution, enticing rather than compelling people to sacrifice; in it many of our people fell of their own accord. After George, who had been installed by the Arians in Athanasius’s place, was burned by a popular uprising, Athanasius returned to Alexandria. Eusebius and Lucifer returned from exile. Lucifer, together with two other confessors, made Paulinus, a priest of Bishop Eustathius who had never defiled himself with communion with heretics, bishop of the Catholic party at Antioch.

### 381. 2. [CCCLIX] (HIER.)

Sallustius, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. The Athenian sophist Prohaeresius, when a law had been enacted forbidding Christians to teach the liberal arts, voluntarily abandoned his school, although Julian had granted him a special exemption to teach as a Christian. Aemilianus was burned by the vicar at Dorostorum because of the destruction of altars [the editor reads *ararum*, “of altars,” for the supplied *ararium*]. The churches at Antioch were closed, and the gravest storm of impending persecution was lulled by God’s will.

### 382. 3. [CCCLX] (ISID.)

Julian V, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. Out of hatred for Christ, Julian permitted the Jews to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem, and Jews gathered from all the provinces laid new foundations for the temple. But suddenly, when an earthquake arose during the night, the stones were shaken from the depths of the foundations and scattered far and wide; a fiery globe from within the temple building struck many of them down with its flames. Terrified by this, the survivors unwillingly confessed Christ. And lest they should think that this had happened by chance, the sign of a cross appeared on everyone’s clothing the following night.

(REG.) At Rome suffered: Piscus the priest, Priscillianus, Benedicta the woman, Pimenius the priest, Gordianus, Demetria the virgin, Johannes the priest, also Johannes and Paulus, Faustus and Dafrosa; at Ostia, Hilarianus, bishop of Jerusalem, Quiriacus, and Judas; at Alexandria, Gallicanus; at Vercelli, Bishop Eusebius; at Arezzo, Bishop Donatus; at Antioch, the priest Theodericus.

(HIER.) Julian set out against the Persians, having vowed our blood to the gods after victory. There, led into the wilderness by a pretended deserter, he lost his apostate army through hunger and thirst and, wandering too incautiously from his own ranks, was killed by an enemy horseman whom he happened to encounter: the rider pierced his flank with a spear. He died in the thirty-second year of his age. (cf. *Tripartite History*.) When he put his hand into the wound and sprinkled [the blood] into the air, he said: “You have conquered, Galilean”—that is, “Christ.” (VI, 47.) For he always called Christians “Galileans.” He died on 26 June.

(HIER.) On the following day Jovian, formerly chief of the household troops, was made emperor, as Bishop Theodorus testifies (VII, 1), together with Eutropius, who was then still alive.

(*Life of Saint Elifius*) [Saint Elifius, after being beheaded in the presence of Caesar Julian because he refused to worship the gods, rose and carried his own head with both hands for one mile to a high mountain. There a white rock opened its breast and gave him a hollow, suitable place on which to sit. The mountain is called Saint Elifius’s Mountain; there, beside the aforesaid stone, an oratory was built over his tomb. It lies midway between Frumentosa and Grandim, six miles from each; to the north it has the city of Toul, and to the south it faces Grandim. He suffered in a pleasant meadow on the bank of a river called the Vera, on 16 October.]

The forty-fifth Roman emperor, Jovian, according to everyone, reigned for eight months, that is, until 1 March, in the year 349 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

[Codex marginal note: The twentieth decennial cycle begins; the fourth indiction.]

### 383. 1. [CCCLXI] (HIER.)

Jovian and Varronianus. Compelled by necessity, Jovian handed over Nisibis and a large part of Mesopotamia to Sapor, king of the Persians. A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his supporters, in which, rejecting *homoousion*, “of the same substance,” and *anomoion*, “unlike,” they upheld the Macedonian doctrine of *homoiousion*, “of similar substance,” as a middle position between them. [Christ is called *homoousios*, “of the same substance,” with the Father because of the unity of substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit.] (H. R.)

Jovian died at Dadastana in the thirty-fourth year of his age, through indigestion—or through the smell of the excessive charcoal he had ordered to be burned—and through the glare of the freshly plastered walls, which was oppressive to those resting there. He died on 16 February, as the aforementioned ecclesiastical history records (VII, 6).

After him, when the army had arrived at Nicaea in Bithynia on 25 February, it proclaimed Valentinian, a tribune of the shield-bearing guard (*scutarii*) from Pannonia and a native of Cibalae, as Augustus. He made his brother Valens govern with him at Constantinople. (HIER.)

The forty-sixth Roman emperor, Valentinian, reigned with his brother Valens for eleven years and five months, that is, until 1 October, in the year 360 after the Passion of the Lord. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 384. 1. [CCCLXII] (HIER.)

Valentinian and Valens. Valentinian was an outstanding emperor, otherwise resembling Aurelian in character, except that people interpret his severity as excessive. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, composed writings on our religion of many kinds.

### 385. 2. [CCCLXIII] (HIER.)

Gratian and Dagalaifus. An earthquake occurred throughout the whole world, and the sea overran the shore. It overwhelmed the cities of Sicily and of many islands in numberless places. Procopius, who had seized the tyranny at Constantinople, was killed in Phrygia Salutaris, and many of Procopius’s party were killed and proscribed. Pope Liberius died on 24 April.

Damasus, the thirty-sixth pope after Peter, for nineteen years. (HIER.) Not long afterward, Ursinus was made bishop by certain men and seized the Sicinian basilica with his followers; when the people of the Damasians’ party streamed together, exceedingly cruel killings of persons of different sexes were committed. Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted our people. (*Book of the Pontiffs.*)

[In the *Deeds of the Pontiffs* it is written as follows: “Felix, a Roman by nation, son of Anastasius, sat for one year and three months, and so forth. He declared Constantine, son of Constantine, a heretic, and said that he had been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, near Nicomedia at the estate of Aquilon [*Aquilone*, as supplied here]. Because he had made this declaration, he was beheaded by that same Constantine Augustus, son of Constantine Augustus, on 11 November in the city of Corana. The clergy then snatched him away and buried him in his own basilica, which he had built while he was a priest, on 20 November on the Via Aurelia, at the second milestone; and the episcopate remained vacant for thirty-eight days. He purchased land around the same basilica and gave it to that church, which he had built on the Via Aurelia. He conducted ordinations in the city of Rome during December: twenty-one priests, five deacons, and nineteen bishops in various places.”]

[Codex marginal note: The solar cycle begins.]

### 386. 3. [CCCLXIV] (HIER.)

Lubicinus and Jovinus. Gratian, son of Valentinian, was made emperor at Amiens during these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies. So great a storm arose at Constantinople that hailstones of extraordinary size fell and killed some people. At Arras, wool mixed with rain fell from the sky.

### 387. 4. [CCCLXV] (HIER.)

Valentinian II and Valens II. Bishop Hilary of Poitiers died. Nicaea, which had often collapsed previously, was utterly destroyed by an earthquake. Libanius of Antioch, a distinguished rhetorician, was held in high esteem.

### 388. 5. [CCCLXVI] (HIER.)

Valentinian, “most noble boy” (*nobilissimus puer*), and Victor. Valens returned from Constantinople. Athanaric, king of the Goths, after launching a persecution, killed very many Christians and drove them from their own settlements into Roman territory. Bishop Eusebius of Vercelli died.

### 389. 6. [CCCLXVII] (HIER.)

Valentinian III and Valens III. At Constantinople the shrine of the apostles was dedicated. There was a great famine in Phrygia. Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, died; together with Bishop Gregory of Spain and Philo of Libya, he had never joined in the Arian depravity.

### 390. 7. [CCCLXVIII] (HIER.)

Gratian II and Probus. Maximinus, prefect of the grain supply, was ordered by the emperor to investigate sorcerers and killed many nobles at Rome. Valentinus was suppressed in Britain before he could seize the tyranny. A priest was most unjustly beheaded because he was unwilling to destroy Octavianus, a former proconsul who was hiding with him.

### 391. 8. [CCCLXIX] (HIER.)

Modestus and Arintheus. Didymus of Alexandria composed much about our doctrine through secretaries; after his fifth year he was deprived of his eyesight and was also ignorant of the elements. The Illyrian count Equitius stripped the provinces he governed through most unjust exactions of tribute before they were devastated by the barbarians.

### 392. 9. [CCCLXX] (HIER.)

Valentinian IV and Valens IV. Eunomius, a disciple of Aetius, was recognized at Constantinople; from him came the Eunomian heresy. The Saxons were defeated at Deusone, in the territory of the Franks. About eighty thousand Burgundians, something that had never happened before, descended to the Rhine. Clearchus was recognized as prefect of the city at Constantinople; through him, necessary and long-awaited water was brought into the city in accordance with the people’s prayers.

Peter was ordained twentieth bishop of Alexandria. After the death of Valens he was so accommodating in receiving heretics that he gave some people grounds to suspect that he had accepted money.

[Saint Martin, in the fifty-sixth year of his age, was consecrated archbishop of Tours, a city of Gaul, on Sunday, 4 July; he lived most holily in that office for twenty-six years. (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II, ch. 5.) At the time when Saint Martin was first appointed bishop, Valentinian was then in possession of the greater power. He refused to rise before Martin until the fire had burned the royal chair and the king’s buttocks; thus the proud king was driven from his throne and rose unwillingly for Martin.]

### 393. 10. [CCCLXXI] (HIER.)

Gratian III and Equitius. Melantia, the noblest of Roman women and daughter of the former consul Marcellinus, left behind her only son, who was then praetor, and sailed to Jerusalem. There she displayed such a miracle of virtues, especially humility, that she received the name of Thecla.

### 394. 11. [CCCLXXII] (HIER.)

After the fourth consulship of Gratian and the consulship of Equitius. After Auxentius’s late death, Ambrose was made bishop at Milan, and all Italy was converted to the true faith. The clergy of Aquileia were regarded as a choir of the blessed. Because the Sarmatians had devastated Pannonia in the preceding year, the same consuls remained in office.

Theodorus says the following (VIII, 1): The monk Pior ate while walking, lest he please his flesh. Pambus refused to learn more than one verse, namely, “I said, I will guard my ways,” until he had fulfilled it. When someone asked him about that verse, he replied: “I can scarcely fulfill it in forty-nine years.” When Bishop Athanasius asked him to leave the desert and come with him to Alexandria, he wept [at the sight of a woman’s adornment].

Macarius the Egyptian; Macarius of Alexandria. Aemonius, when he came to Rome with Athanasius, saw nothing there except the basilica of Peter and Paul. When he was dragged toward the episcopate, so that he would not become a bishop, he cut off his own ear. John, father of three thousand monks. Serapion, father of ten thousand monks. Dioscorus, father of one hundred monks, who before communion examined the consciences of each of the brothers. Theona remained silent for thirty-five years. Hellin carried fire in his bosom. Elias, a priest and monk, lived alone in the desert for seventy years, at the age of 110. Apelles the smith, pulling raw iron from the furnace with his hand, struck at night the face of a demon that had taken the form of a beautiful woman. Isidorus closed his monastery, keeping necessities inside. Apollo lived for forty years in the outer desert. Dorotheus’s food was six ounces of bread, one bundle of greens, and water. The priest Piamon, when he was once offering the sacred Body, saw an angel near the altar erasing the names of absent brothers and writing down those who were present. Mark was given Christ’s Body by an angel at the hour of communion. Moses filled the brothers’ vessels with water at night, drawing it over ten, twenty, or thirty *stadia*. When four robbers attacked his lodging, he bound them and intended to carry them the next day on his back to the common dwelling of the brothers. Paul, father of fifty monks. Stephen, tested for forty years and well known to the great Antony, was afterward so afflicted that his limbs were cut off. Julian Accepsemas remained shut up in a cell for seventy years, neither seen nor speaking for that length of time.

[Saint Patrick was born on the island of Britain, to a father named Calpurnius; Calpurnius himself was a priest, the son of a deacon named Fotid. Patrick’s mother was Conchess, sister of Saint Martin of Gaul. His baptismal name was Sucat. His name was Cothraege. *Diambae icfogna docet hartreb* [the supplied Irish is uncertain; see the editor’s parallel and English meaning below]. Germanus called him Magonius; Pope Celestine called him Patrick, that is, “father of citizens.”]
