[Note: [Col. 0711D–0712D] “Cothraighe was Patrick’s name; see the Irish poem in O’Connor, *Writers on Irish Affairs* (*Rerum Hibernicarum Scriptores*), I, 1, p. XC. I do not understand the rest. But in that poem it reads: *Ceathar trebhc dia fognad*, that is, ‘because he served four tribes.’” The parallel’s meaning is preserved here without pretending that the editor deciphered every word of the supplied Irish.]

### 395. 12. [CCCLXXIII] (H. Trip. VIII, 11.)

Valens V and Valentinian. (HIER.) During these consulships Valentinian, violently enraged against the Sarmatian envoys, died at Brigetio on 17 September in the fifty-fourth year of his age, the eleventh of his reign and the fifth month, from a rupture of the veins—what the Greeks call *apoplexy*—through a flow of blood.

The forty-seventh Roman emperor, Valens, reigned with Gratian and Valentinian, his brother’s son, for four years, that is, until 1 October, in the year 364 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 396. 1. [CCCLXXIV] (BEDA.)

Gratian IV and Merobaudes. Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army and ordered those who refused to be killed with clubs. Theodosius, father of the later Emperor Theodosius, and many nobles were killed.

(HIER.) Photinus died in Galatia; by him the doctrine of the Photinians was introduced [following the editor’s correction; see the textual note]. Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Cappadocia, was held in high esteem; he lost many good qualities of self-control and intellect through a single fault, pride.

### 397. 2. [CCCLXXV] (HIER.)

Valens VI, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*), consul. About thirty thousand Alamanni were slain by Gratian’s army near the town of Argentaria in Gaul. Florentinus, Bonosus, and Rufinus were held in high esteem as monks. Florentinus was so merciful toward the needy that he was commonly called “father of the poor.”

The nation of the Huns devastated the Goths. The Goths, received by the Romans without surrendering their weapons, were compelled by the greed of the commander Maximus, through hunger, to revolt. After defeating the Romans in battle, the Goths poured into Thrace.

### 398. 3. [CCCLXXVI] (HIER.)

Valentinian XI, “most distinguished man” (*vir clarissimus*). Valens, compelled to leave Antioch, recalled our people from exile in a late repentance [the codex has a lacuna here, as Giesebrecht noted].

(HIER.) A mournful war took place in Thrace. When the cavalry support deserted, the Roman legions were surrounded by the Goths and slaughtered to the last man. The Emperor Valens himself, wounded by an arrow as he fled and often slipping from his horse because of the pain, was carried to the hut of a certain small estate. When the barbarians pursued him there and burned the house, he was deprived even of burial. Thus far Jerome.

(CASS.) Cassiodorus says the following: [Theodosius, son of Theodosius, succeeded him in the East; Gratian admitted him as his partner in the kingdom. Thus, when Gratian had reigned for fourteen years, he reigned with Theodosius for six years. The following consuls served under him. Therefore, according to Cassiodorus, the fourteen years extend from the third year of Valentinian, in which Gratian was made emperor, when Lubicinus and Jovinus were consuls, until the death of Valens and the second imperial rule of Gratian.]

(PROSP.) The forty-eighth Roman emperor, Gratian, reigned with his brother Valentinian for six years in all, that is, until 1 October, in the year 370 after the Passion. The following consuls served under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

### 399. 1. [CCCLXXVII] (PROSP.)

Ausonius and Olybrius. After his uncle’s death, Gratian enrolled Theodosius, son of Theodosius, as a partner in the empire and entrusted to him the rule of the East. At that time Priscillianus, a bishop from Gaul, founded the heresy named after himself from the doctrines of the Manichaeans and Gnostics.

### 400. 2. [CCCLXXVIII] (PROSP.)

Gratian V and Theodosius. Bishop Ambrose wrote many lofty responses in defense of the Catholic faith. [Ambrose was renowned during these consulships.]

### 401. 3. [CCCLXXIX] (PROSP.)

Siagrius and Eucherius. Martin, bishop of Turin [Some material is missing. What follows must be referred to King Athanaric.], was killed at Constantinople on the fifteenth day after he had been received.

(CASS.) [During these consulships, as Cassiodorus testifies, Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours in Gaul, was held in high esteem.]


## Textual and editorial notes, keyed to the annal years

- **354, “various kinds” [Col. 0703]:** *modiis* is to be understood as *modis*, “kinds/modes.”
- **355, Saint Martin’s baptism [Col. 0703]:** The notice was written by a second hand in the lower margin without a year indication; compare year 352.
- **358, “prefect Philip” [Col. 0703]:** MS. 1 reads *prefecit*, “he appointed,” for *prefecti*, “of the prefect.”
- **359, Neocaesarea [Col. 0703]:** Printed *Necessaria* is to be understood as Neocaesarea; it is not the ordinary adjective “necessary.”
- **360, “prefecture” [Col. 0705]:** The apparatus queries *prefectus an. 1?*, apparently asking whether MS. 1 reads *prefectus*, “prefect,” for *prefecturam*, “prefecture”; its uncertainty is retained.
- **363, the Persian war [Col. 0705]:** The editor directs that the corrupt *illum … gravis … fuit* be read *ullum … gravius fuit*, “any … was more severe,” producing “Nor indeed was any … more severe.” MS. 2 is reported in abbreviated form as *ullum … gravibus plus prosperum c. P. f. —* “any … among the serious [battles] was more successful against the Persians.” This is a different evaluation of the battle. At the promise of the episcopate, MS. 1 may read *et*, “and,” for *ei*, “to him.”
- **364, Vetranio [Col. 0705]:** MS. 1 has *vetranto* here and below; the scribe very frequently writes *t* for *i*. At “were made emperors,” MS. 1 has *facit*, “he makes,” for *facti*, “made.” *Philo* is to be read as *pilo*, “on a spear.”
- **366, Julius’s burial [Col. 0705]:** MS. 1 reads *militario*, an altered form of *miliario*, “milestone.”
- **367, the suppression of the Jews [Col. 0705]:** MS. 1 has *cessaris*, a corrupt-looking form at *caesis*, “having been killed,” and *militibus*, “soldiers,” for *milibus*, “thousands.” The latter changes the numeral noun, not the word *hominum*, “people.”
- **368, the defense of Gaul [Col. 0705]:** MS. 1 spells *tutendas* for *tuendas*, “to be defended.”
- **370, the places of exile [Col. 0706C]:** The supplied correction *in[ter] se* inserts *ter* to form *inter se*, “from one another,” in place of *in se*, “in themselves.”
- **371, Timothy’s relics [Col. 0705]:** MS. 1 spells *Reliquae* for *Reliquiae*, “relics.”
- **372, Constantius’s entry [Col. 0707]:** The editor reads *ingresso*, “having entered,” for *ingressio*; “upon Constantius’s entry” follows that correction.
- **374, the council [Col. 0707B]:** The source brackets the completion “and afterward through the betrayal of all the others [the ancient faith] was condemned,” and identifies Hilary as “[bishop of Poitiers].”
- **375, Meletius [Col. 0707]:** MS. 1 reads *armentorum*, “of herds,” for *Armeniorum*, “of the Armenians.” The editor directs *Armeniorum episcopus*, “bishop of the Armenians,” supplying *episcopus*, “bishop,” after the place-name Sebaste.
- **379, Theodorus’s notice [Col. 0707]:** This was written by a second hand in an erased space.
- **380, persecution [Col. 0707]:** The editor corrects *implens*, “filling,” to *impellens*, “compelling,” yielding “enticing rather than compelling.”
- **382, Julian’s death [Col. 0707]:** *Ovio* is to be understood as *obvio*, “encountered.” The source supplies “[blood]” as the object of “sprinkled” and “[Galileans]” as the name Julian used for Christians.
- **382, Saint Elifius [Col. 0709]:** This passage was written in the margin by a second hand without a year indication. Compare the *Life* written by Rupert of Deutz in Surius, V, p. 246; Rupert followed an earlier author.
- **383, the Antiochene synod [Col. 0709]:** MS. 1 possibly reads *omocoque*. The editor directs *omousio anomoeoque* in place of the corrupted sequence: the positions of “same substance” and “unlike” are rejected for the intermediate position of “similar substance.” At Jovian’s death, the editor corrects *crudelitate*, “cruelty,” to *cruditate*, “indigestion”; the translation follows the correction without making cruelty an alternative cause of death.
- **385, Liberius’s death [Col. 0710A]:** Compare the *Book of the Pontiffs*. The source places the account from Ursinus’s occupation of the basilica through Valens’s persecution in brackets.
- **388, Valens’s return [Col. 0709]:** MS. 1 has *constantinopi* for *Constantinopoli*, “Constantinople.” Jerome’s parallel is cited as *Agon Constantinopoli*, “A contest at Constantinople.” How that very compressed citation relates to the supplied return notice is unclear; it has not been silently substituted for the notice.
- **390, Valentinus [Col. 0711A]:** “[Tyranny]” is supplied in the source.
- **391, Didymus and Equitius [Col. 0711]:** MS. 1 gives the sequence *ignarus. Fuit illiriricus*, “unlearned. There was an Illyrian …,” rather than *ignarus fuit. Illiricus*, “he was unlearned. The Illyrian …”; *illiriricus* is its spelling. The editor corrects *iniquissimus*, “most unjust” qualifying the count, to *iniquissimis*, “most unjust” qualifying the exactions; MS. 2 reads *iniquissimus comes*, “a most unjust count,” in that order. At *erasit*, “stripped/erased,” MS. 1 possibly reads *evasit*, “escaped.”
- **392, the Saxons [Col. 0711]:** The editor corrects printed *Dehusone* to *Deusone*, the place-name. MS. 2 instead reads *de hassia*, “from Hesse.” At Peter’s reception of heretics, MS. 1 has *jam*, “already,” for *tam*, “so.” The Saint Martin passage beginning “At the time” was added later in the margin of MS. 1.
- **393, the son left behind [Col. 0711]:** The editor corrects *unito*, “united,” to *unico*, “only.”
- **394, Patrick’s parentage [Col. 0711D]:** “Although what is read in Marianus about Saint Patrick agrees fairly well with other sources, I cannot refer it to a definite author.” MS. 1 abbreviates Calpuirn’s name as *Cal.* [Col. 0711]. The Irish note and its supplied English meaning are given immediately after the Patrick notice above.
- **396, Photinus [Col. 0713]:** MS. 1 gives *judaic* at printed *judaicum*, “Jewish/Judaizing”; the editor directs *inductum*, “introduced.” The main translation follows the latter while preserving both other forms here.
- **398, Cassiodorus’s chronology [Col. 0713]:** MS. 1 abbreviates the consuls’ names and endings as *Lubicini’ et Jovin’*, “Lubicinus and Jovinus.” Giesebrecht’s notice of a gap after Valens’s recall from exile is retained at its exact point above.
- **400, Ambrose [Col. 0713]:** “Ambrose was renowned during these consulships” is written in the margin of MS. 1.

[Codex marginal note: The twenty-first decennial cycle begins; the eighth indiction.]

402. 4. [CCCLXXX] Antoricus and Siagrius. Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, dedicated to Theodosius, [son] of Gratian, a computation covering a cycle of one hundred years, [at the beginning of the consulship of Antonius and Siagrius]. (BEDA.) A synod of one hundred and fifty fathers was held in the imperial city against the Macedonians, under Pope Damasus and Gratian. (cf. *AD Mart.*) At Rome: the feast of Saint Damasus, pope, on 11 December, on the Via Ardeatina, in his own basilica [Col. 0714B]; he sat for eighteen years. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) He established that the psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches.

403. 5. [CCCLXXXI] (PROSP.) Merobaudes II and Saturninus. (CASS.) Arcadius, son of the emperor Theodosius, is proclaimed Augustus. Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours in Gaul, is renowned.

404. 6. [CCCLXXXII] (PROSP.) Ricomer and Glearchus. Honorius, son of Theodosius, is born.

(PROSP.) Ursinus, also called Siricius, was pope for fifteen years, the thirty-seventh. [Note: [Col. 0713] Pope Damasus died on 10 December; what follows has been erased here.]

During these consulships, in Britain, in a military uprising, Maximus was made emperor. When he soon crossed over to Gaul, Gratian was defeated at Paris through the treachery of Merobaudes, master of the soldiers; while fleeing, he was captured and killed at Lyons [Col. 0714C]. (BEDA.) Maximus made his son Victor his colleague in the kingdom.

**Romans 49.** Theodosius, son of Gratian, reigned with his uncle Valentinian for eleven years and four months, that is, until 1 February, in the year 382 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, according to Cassiodorus.

405. 1. [CCCLXXXIII] (PROSP.) Arcadius and Bauto, *vir clarissimus*. At this time the presbyter Jerome, already renowned throughout the whole world, lived at Bethlehem, serving the universal Church with exceptional talent and devotion.

406. 2. [CCCLXXXIV] (HIER.) Honorius and Euodius. Priscillian, realizing that he was about to be condemned at the synod of Bordeaux, hastened to the emperor Maximus. After being heard at Trier by Evodius, prefect of the praetorium, he was condemned to the sword, together with Eutrotia, wife of the governor Delfi [Note: [Col. 0713] “Eutroti Adelfi,” first hand], and Latronianus and other associates in his error.

407. 3. [CCCLXXXV] (HIER.) Valentinian III and Eutropius. At Bordeaux, a certain female disciple of Priscillian, named Urbica, was killed by stoning during a popular riot because of her persistent impiety.

408. 4. [CCCLXXXVI] (HIER.) Theodosius II and Cynegius. The tyrant Maximus was stripped of his royal garments by the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius at the third milestone from Aquileia, brought before them, and condemned to death; his son Victor [Col. 0715A] was killed by Arbogast in Gaul in the same year.*

*Another hand has added in the margin:* During these times Saint Alban was martyred.

409. 5. [CCCLXXXVII] (HIER.) Timasius and Promotus. The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius, who had been the accusers of Priscillian, were deprived of communion with the Church because of his execution.

410. 6. [CCCLXXXVIII] (BEDA.) Valentinian IV and Neoterius. Jerome composed his book *On Illustrious Men of the Church* in the eighth year of Theodosius. [Saint Patrick, together with his two sisters, namely Lupuit and Tigress, was sold into Ireland. Saint Patrick himself was sold to a king named Miluc [Note: [Col. 0715] According to O’Connor, II, p. 81, Milcuon was a dynast of Dalaradia in Ulster], son of the grandson of Buain, in northern Ireland. Patrick was the keeper of his pigs, and the angel Victor often spoke with him. His two sisters, however, were sold in Conaille Muirthemne [Note: [Col. 0715B] On fol. 141, in the lower margin, a second hand has again written: “Saint Patrick, a Briton by birth, when he was sixteen years old, was sold in Ireland to Milcon, king of Dalaradia. He served him for six years and was always comforted by the angel Victor, speaking with him from a certain stone, which remains there.” It is added: “This ought to have been written six folios earlier, that is, here.—Also on fol. 144v are written passages that had originally been assigned to the year 475, but now, with the signs erased, are assigned to no definite year: ‘Saint Patrick personally returned a mass of gold to his master. For when his master refused to release him except for a mass of gold, Patrick, at the command of the angel Victor, kept certain pigs of which he was the herdsman; one of them dug up the mass.’ Cf. year 416.]]

411. 7. [CCCLXXXIX] (cf. ISID.) Titanus and Symmachus. John the anchorite monk is held in renown.

412. 8. [CCCXC] (PROSP.) Arcadius and Rufus. Valentinian, driven to despair of life by the excessive severity of Arbogast, master of the soldiers, perished by a noose at Vienne. Arbogast, commander of the army, after Valentinian’s death—an outcome that weighed upon him—made Eugenius emperor in Gaul.

413. 9. [CCCXCI] (BEDA.) Theodosius III and Abundantius II. [From the west and from the north, the Scots and Picts ravaged the island of Britain.]

[Col. 0715D] [In the margin of the codex: the solar cycle begins.]

414. 10. [CCCXCII] (PROSP.) Arcadius III and Honorius II. (CASS.) John the monk, endowed with the gift of prophecy, foretold to Theodosius, who consulted him about the outcome of the war he was conducting against Eugenius, that he would be victorious.

415. 11. [CCCXCIII] (PROSP.) Olibrius and Probinus. Theodosius defeated and killed the tyrant Eugenius. Augustine, the disciple of blessed Ambrose, outstanding in eloquence and learning, was ordained bishop of Hippo in the region of Africa [Col. 0716A]. The distinguished poet Claudian was held in renown.

416. 12. [CCCXCIV] The emperor Theodosius died at Milan on 17 January, in the sixtieth year of his age, as is read in the *Ecclesiastical Tripartite History* [Note: [Col. 0715] Added in the margin: “as Bede says in the *History of the English*.”] (X, 50). [When his master refused to release Saint Patrick except for a mass of gold, Saint Patrick, at the command of the angel Victor, kept certain pigs, of which Patrick was keeper and herdsman; one of them dug up the mass of gold, which Saint Patrick gave to his master for himself.]

**Romans 50.** Arcadius, son of Theodosius, reigned with his brother Honorius for fourteen years and three months according to all accounts, that is, until 1 May, in the year 396 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him.

[Col. 0716B] 417. 1. [CCCXCV] (ISIDOR.) Arcadius IV and Honorius III. Donatus, bishop of Epirus [Note: [Col. 0715] “Epi...,” first hand], killed an enormous dragon by spitting into its mouth. Eight yokes of oxen could scarcely drag it to the place where it was burned. It was therefore burned, lest its putrefaction corrupt the air.

418. 2. [CCCXCVI] (PROSP.) Caesarius and Atticus. The Council of Carthage, where the decrees of the Council of Hippo were confirmed and incorporated. [Saint Martin died on Sunday night, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.] (GREC. Tur.) [Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0715] These words are written in the margin], bishop of Tours, died in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate, at midnight on Sunday, in the consulship of the illustrious Caesarius and Atticus.]

419. 3. [CCCXCVII] (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Honorius IV and [Col. 0716C] Eutychianus. Pope Siricius died on 21 February. Anastasius, the thirty-eighth pope after Peter, held the see for five years. He established that whenever the sacred Gospels are read, the priests should not sit but should stand bowed down.

420. 4. [CCCXCVIII] (PROSP.) Manlius and Theodorus. When this consulship began, the eunuch Eutropius was in office; shortly afterward he was deprived both of his honor and of his life. [In the fourth year, Eugenius was killed.]

[In the margin of the codex: the twenty-second cycle begins; indiction 12.]

421. 5. [CCCXCIX] (PROSP.) Stilicho and Aurelian. The Goths entered Italy, under Alaric and Radagaisus as leaders.

422. 6. [CCCC] (PROSP.) Vincentius and Fravitus. John of Constantinople and Theophilus of Alexandria were regarded as distinguished bishops; discord obscured both of them, and it advanced so far that John, oppressed by Theophilus, was driven into exile in Pontus, although the greater part of the bishops, following the example of the Roman pontiff, preserved communion with him.

423. 7. [CCCCI] (PROSP.) Arcadius V and Honorius V. A fierce battle was fought at Pollentia against the Goths, with heavy losses on both sides.

424. 8. [CCCCII] (AD Mart.) Theodosius Augustus and Rumoridus. Pope Anastasius died on 27 April.

[Col. 0717A] Pope Innocent, the thirty-ninth, held the chair for thirteen years. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) [Pope Innocent established that a fast should be observed on Saturday, because on that day the Lord was in the tomb and the disciples fasted.] [When Saint Patrick was thirty years old, he came to Tours and was tonsured with a monastic tonsure by Saint Martin, because until then he had worn a servile tonsure. Then he crossed the Alps and went to the southern western part of Italy, to Germanus, bishop of a city named Alsiodorus, and studied divine Scripture with him for thirty years on an island called Alanensis.]

425. 9. [CCCCIII] (PROSP.) Honorius VI and Aristaenetus. A Council of Carthage was held concerning the Donatists. [HIER. (*Life of Paula*) Saint and blessed Paula [Note: [Col. 0717] These words are written in the lower margin of fol. 139a] died on 25 January, on the third day of the week after sunset, and was buried on 28 January, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus VI and Aristaenetus.]

426. 10. [CCCCIV] (PROSP.) Stilicho and Anthemius. Radagaisus, after many thousands of Goths had been killed in Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0717] A lacuna in the codex], was defeated and captured by Stilicho, who was leading the army.

427. 11. [CCCCV] (PROSP.) Arcadius VI and Probus. The Vandals and Alans entered Gaul, having crossed the Rhine, on 30 December.

428. 12. [CCCCVI] (PROSP.) Honorius VII and Theodosius II. The tyrant Constantine arose in Britain and crossed over to Gaul.

429. 13. [CCCCVII] (BEDA.) Bassus, *vir clarissimus*, consul. God revealed the bodies of the holy prophets Habakkuk and Micah.

[Col. 0717C] 430. 14. [CCCCVIII] (CASS.) Philippus, *vir clarissimus*, consul. The emperor Arcadius died at Constantinople on 1 May, as is read in the aforementioned *Ecclesiastical History* (X, 35).

**Romans 51.** Honorius reigned with Theodosius, the son of his brother, for fifteen years according to all accounts, that is, until 1 May, in the year 411 after the Passion.

431. 1. [CCCCIX] (PROSP.) Honorius VIII and Theodosius III. The Vandals occupied Spain. Attalus was made emperor at Rome; shortly afterward, deprived of his kingdom, he joined the Goths [Note: [Col. 0717] In the margin, in a second hand: “as Bede says in the *History of the English*.”]

432. 2. [CCCCX] (PROSP.) Varane and Tertullus. Rome was captured by the Goths under their leader Alaric. For this reason there was only one consul from the eastern regions, and this arrangement was observed in the following year as well.

433. 3. [CCCCXI] (PROSP.) Theodosius IV, consul. Constantine was defeated and captured near the town of Arles. His son Constans, who had begun to reign in Spain, was killed by the count Gerontius, who transferred the tyranny to a certain Maximus.

434. 4. [CCCCXII] (PROSP.) Honorius IX and Theodosius V. Maximus was deprived of his kingdom in Spain and was granted his life, because, through modesty and humility, he did not deserve the odium incurred by the threats of his attempted imperial power [Note: [Col. 0717] Read: “humility”] [Col. 0718A] [Note: [Col. 0717] First hand: “the attempted rule perished.”]. The Goths entered Gaul under King Athaulf [Note: [Col. 0717] Read: “under King Athaulf.”]. At the same time, Heros, a holy man and disciple of blessed Martin, while presiding as bishop in the town of Arles, was driven out by the people of that city, although he was innocent and subject to no accusation. Patroclus was appointed in his place, a friend and associate of Constantius, master of the soldiers; through whose favor Patroclus was seeking the office. This became a source of great discord among the bishops of that region.

435. 5. [CCCCXIII] (PROSP.) Lucius, *vir clarissimus*, consul. Lucius, a most illustrious man, was consul. His colleague in the consulship was Herodianus, who, accused of revolutionary activity in Africa, lost both his office and his life. The Burgundians occupied the part of Gaul near the Rhine. The brothers Jovinus and Sebastianus, having seized a kingdom in Gaul, were killed. At this time Pelagius the Briton [Note: [Col. 0717] Read: “Briton,” not “Brutus”] brought forth the doctrine bearing his name against the grace of Christ, with Caelestius and Julian as his helpers, and drew many into his error. He taught that each person is governed toward righteousness by his own will and receives as much grace as he deserves, because sin harmed Adam alone. Consequently, he held that it was possible for those who wished to be entirely free from sin; the transmitted wording concerning Adam’s descendants is corrupt and uncertain. and that all infants are born as innocent as the first man was before the transgression. They therefore should not be baptized in order to be freed from sin, but to be honored by the sacrament of adoption.

436. 6. [CCCCXIV] (PROSP.) Constantius and Constans. Attalus, with the support and protection of the Goths, presumed to exercise tyranny in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0717] The ending “-dio” had already been written in the line and was later erased by a second hand in the margin].

437. 7. [CCCCXV] Honorius X and Theodosius VI. [In the seventh year of the emperor Honorius], when Honorius had already been consul ten times and Theodosius six times, and in the year 415 of the Incarnation according to Dionysius, indiction 13, Saint Lucian, presbyter of Jerusalem, in the letter he wrote concerning the discovery of the most blessed body of the protomartyr Stephen and of the saints Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibos [Note: [Col. 0717D] See Surius, *Acta Sanctorum*, 3 August], as it had been revealed to him by the Lord, clearly demonstrated among other things the following concerning that same year:

> “On Good Friday, that is, on the sixth day, which is 3 December, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus X and Theodosius VI” (cf. BEDA),

and so forth. After the regular seven days of December had therefore been set aside, the four concurrent days of the aforesaid year remain: namely, 1 December, Wednesday; 2 December, Thursday; and 3 December, Friday, in the seventh year of Honorius, in the aforesaid consulship, in which the sacred bodies were revealed by the Lord. He wrote this revelation in Greek for the use of all the churches; the presbyter Avitus, a Spaniard by birth, translated it into Latin [Col. 0718D] and, adding his own letter, sent it through Orosius to the eastern churches (BEDA). Orosius, arriving at the holy places in Jerusalem—for Augustine had sent him to Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul—received the relics of Saint Stephen and, returning to his homeland, was the first to bring them to the West.

(PROSP.) Attalus, neglected by the Goths as they migrated to Spain and left without protection, was captured. Athaulf, wounded by a certain relative by marriage, died; his kingdom was seized by Wallia, after those who were understood to desire the same thing had been killed. The Pelagians, already condemned in advance by Pope Innocent, were resisted through the firmness of the Africans and especially through the efforts of Bishop Augustine [Note: [Col. 0719] First hand: “was resisted.”]

438. 8. [CCCCXVI] (PROSP.) Theodosius VII and Palladius. Wallia, seeking peace from Honorius, returned Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius, whom the Goths had captured at Rome and whom Athaulf had taken as his wife; Constantius secured her marriage. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Innocent died on 29 July.

Pope Zosimus, the fortieth after Peter, held the chair for four years.

439. 9. [CCCCXVII] (PROSP.) Honorius XI and Constantius II. Honorius entered Rome in triumph, with Attalus preceding his chariot; he ordered Attalus to live freely [Note: [Col. 0719] That is, “as a free man”] in exile. [Note: [Col. 0719D] See below, year 466.]

—(PASCHASIUS, letter.) The latter half of the letter of Bishop Paschasius to Pope Leo:

> “Therefore let a difference of one day not frighten us, lest, while avoiding this, we fall into error. Thus, in the time of the blessed memory of my lord, your predecessor Zosimus, in the eleventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius, when care was taken that Easter should not be kept on 10 Kalends of May, it was celebrated on 8 Kalends of April—that is, a common year was reckoned instead of an embolismic year—and a very serious error arose. To such an extent was this so that the truth was demonstrated by a certain miracle, since it is administered through the gift of the Holy Spirit. I have therefore believed that this should be explained, because that very place is also well known to my holy and venerable brother, the deacon Libanus. The miracle of this mystery is as follows.
>
> “There is a certain very poor estate called Meltinas, situated among steep mountains and extremely dense forests. There is a very small and cheaply constructed church there. In its baptistery, on the most sacred Paschal night, at the hour appointed for baptism, although there was no channel, no pipe, and no water anywhere nearby, a spring filled itself. After the few who were there had been consecrated, since it had no conduit, the water descended as it had come. At that time, therefore, as I said above, under my former lord of holy memory, the most blessed Pope Zosimus, when an error had arisen among the westerners, after the customary readings had been reviewed on the sacred night, the presbyter sought the hour for baptism according to custom. Since the water did not come until daylight, the unbaptized who were to be baptized departed [Col. 0720A].
>
> “To tell the matter briefly: on that night which dawned into Sunday, 10 Kalends of May, the sacred spring filled at the proper hour. Thus, by an evident miracle, it became clear that the error had belonged to the western regions. I have written this, as far as I could and as the brevity proper to a letter permitted, at the command of your apostolic office.”

[In the margin of the codex: the twenty-third cycle begins; the decade begins; indiction 1.]

440. 10. [CCCCXVIII] (PROSP.) Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII. At this time Constantius, a servant of Christ who lived at Rome as a former vicarius and who devotedly resisted the Pelagians for the sake of God’s grace, suffered many things through the faction of those same men, and these sufferings joined him to the holy confessors. A council of 214 or more bishops was held at Carthage, and the decrees of the synod were carried to Pope Zosimus. After they were approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world. Valentinian, son of Constantius and Placidia, was born on 3 July. A council was held at Carthage against the Pelagians. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Zosimus died on 26 December.

441. 11. [CCCCXIX] (PROSP.) Monaxius and Plinta. Constantius made peace with Wallia, giving him Second Aquitaine and certain cities of the neighboring provinces for settlement.

Boniface, the forty-first pope after Peter, was ordained; he sat for four years.

[In the margin of the codex: the solar cycle begins.]

442. 12. [CCCCXX] (PROSP.) Theodosius IX and Constantius III. Constantius was admitted by Honorius as a colleague in the kingdom [Col. 0720C]. The presbyter Jerome died in the ninety-first year of his life, on 21 September.

443. 13. [CCCCXXI] (PROSP.) Agricola and Eustachius. The emperor Constantine died. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Boniface decreed that a slave could not become a cleric, nor be liable to the curia or to any other obligation.

444. 14. [CCCCXXII] (PROSP.) Honorius XIII and Theodosius X. At this time an army was sent against the Vandals in Spain; its commander was Castinus, who, through inept and insulting command, turned Boniface, a man distinguished in the arts of war, away from participation in the expedition. For Boniface considered it dangerous and beneath his dignity to follow a man whom he had found to be contentious and arrogant, and he quickly withdrew to the port of Rome and from there to Africa. This became the beginning of many hardships for the commonwealth. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Boniface died on 25 October.

445. 15. [CCCCXXIII] (PROSP.) Marinianus and Asclepiodotus. The empress Placidia, driven out by her brother Honorius, set out for the East with Honorius and Valentinian. (PROSP.)

Celestine, the forty-second pope after Peter, held office for nine years.

Honorius died at Rome, and John succeeded to his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0719] At this point a second hand has added in the margin: “as Bede says.”]

[Col. 0721A] **Romans 52.** Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigned for twenty-seven years, that is, until 1 May, in the year 438 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him.

446. 1. [CCCCXXIV] (PROSP.) Castinus and Victor. Theodosius made Valentinian, the son of his aunt, Caesar, and sent him with his August mother to receive the western empire. At that time John, while attempting to recover Africa, which Boniface controlled, by war, was weakened in his efforts at self-defense.

447. 2. [CCCCXXV] (PROSP.) Theodosius XI and Valentinian. The empress Placidia and Caesar Valentinian, with remarkable success, crushed the tyrant John and, as victors, recovered the kingdom, granting pardon to Aetius, because the Huns whom John had received through him returned to their own country through Aetius’s efforts. Castinus, however, was driven into exile, because it seemed that John could not have presumed to seize the kingdom without his connivance. By decree of Theodosius, Valentinian was proclaimed Augustus. Archilar, a noble town of Gaul, was attacked with great force by the Goths until, when Aetius approached, they withdrew without having gone unpunished [Note: [Col. 0721] Read: “withdrew.”]

448. 3. [CCCCXXVI] (PROSP.) Theodosius XII and Valentinian II. Patroclus, bishop of Arles, was killed by a certain barbarian tribune, after being mangled by many wounds. (PROSP.) This crime was attributed to a secret order from Felix, master of the soldiers; at his instigation, it is believed, Titus the deacon, a holy man who distributed money to the poor at Rome, was also killed.

[Col. 0721C] 449. 4. [CCCCXXVII] (PROSP.) Hierius and Ardabures. Boniface, whose power and glory within Africa were increasing, had war declared in the public name at the command of Felix, who refused to come to Italy. The commanders were Mabornius [Note: [Col. 0721] Read: “Mabortius and Galvio”; “Mabortius and Galvio”], Calvio, and Saoneces. Through the treachery of Saoneces, Mabornius [Note: [Col. 0721] Read: “Mabortius and Galvio”; “Mabortius and Galvio”] and Galvio were killed while besieging Boniface; soon afterward Boniface himself detained and killed Saoneces by treachery. From that time, when peoples who did not know how to use ships were called upon by the combatants for assistance, the sea was made passable, and the direction of the war begun against Boniface was transferred to the care of Signisvultus [Note: [Col. 0721] First hand: “insignis vultus”]. The nation of the Vandals crossed from Spain to Africa.

450. 5. [CCCCXXVIII] (PROSP.) Felix and Taurus. Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempted to introduce a new error, teaching that Christ was born from Mary as man alone, not also [as God], and that divinity had been conferred upon him according to merit. The efforts especially of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and the authority of Pope Celestine opposed this impiety. The part of Gaul near the Rhine, which the Franks had occupied for possession, was recovered by the count Aetius.

451. 6. [CCCCXXIX] (PROSP.) Florentius and Dionysius. After Felix had been elevated to the rank of patrician, Aetius was made master of the soldiers. Agricola the Pelagian, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, corrupted the churches of Britain by introducing his doctrine [Col. 0722A]. But through the agency of the deacon Palladius, Pope Celestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, as his representative; after expelling the heretics, he restored the Britons to the Catholic faith. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Celestine established that David’s one hundred and fiftieth psalm should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice; previously, the epistle and the holy Gospel were read.

452. 7. [CCCCXXX] (PROSP.) Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III. Aetius, together with Felix, his wife Padussia, and the deacon Grannitus . . . [Note: [Col. 0721] Half a line is blank.]

(BEDA.) Saint Augustine died in the seventy-sixth year of his life, on 28 August, having completed forty years in the clerical or episcopal state.

453. 8. [CCCCXXXI] (PROSP.) Bassus and Antiochus. A synod of two hundred priests was held at Ephesus [Col. 0722B]. Nestorius was condemned, together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who were helping [Note: [Col. 0721] Read: “helping”] the doctrine akin to their error. Palladius, ordained by Pope Celestine, was sent as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ. [After him] Saint Patrick, a Briton by birth, was consecrated by Pope Celestine [and] sent to the archbishopric of Ireland [where, for sixty years,] preaching with signs and miracles, he converted the whole island of Ireland to the faith.

454. 9. [CCCCXXXII] (PROSP.) Aetius and Valerius. Boniface came from Africa to Italy by way of Rome and received the rank of master of the soldiers. After defeating Aetius, who resisted him, in battle, he was killed by illness a few days later. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Pope Celestine died on 8 April.

Sixtus, the forty-third pope after Peter, held office for eight years.

(PROSP.) Aetius, after laying down his authority and living on his estate, was attacked there suddenly by an enemy. He fled to Rome, and from there reached Dalmatia, then traveled through Pannonia to the Huns. Having obtained their friendship and assistance, he secured peace among the rulers and a restoration of his interrupted power.

455. 10. [CCCCXXXIII] (BEDA.) Theodosius XIV and Maximus. Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, returned from Jerusalem, bringing with her the relics of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, which are venerated after being placed in the basilica of Saint Laurence.

456. 11. [CCCCXXXIV] (BEDA.) Aspar and Ariovindus. [Col. 0722D] Pope Sixtus built the basilica of the Mother of the Lord, which the ancients called Liberiana.

457. 12. [CCCCXXXV] (PROSP.) Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV. Peace was made with the Vandals, and a portion of Africa was given to them for settlement. At the same time Aetius defeated Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians living within Gaul, in war, and granted him peace when he begged for it [Note: [Col. 0721] The margin reads: “gave it to him”; Pr.]. He did not enjoy it for long, however, since the Huns destroyed him and his people root and branch.

458. 13. [CCCCXXXVI] (PROSP.) Isidorus and Senator. The Goths disturbed the terms of the peace and occupied several townships [Col. 0723A] near their settlements, showing especial hostility toward the town of Narbonne. When it had long suffered from siege and famine, Count Lattorius freed it from both dangers: by bringing two measures of grain for each horseman, he vigorously put the enemy to flight and supplied the city with provisions.

459. 14. [CCCCXXXVII] (PROSP.) Aetius and Sigisvultus. War was waged against the Goths with the assistance of the Huns. In Africa, Geiseric, king of the Vandals, wishing to overturn the Catholic faith into Arian impiety within the boundaries of his realm, persecuted some of our bishops so severely that he expelled them from their cities after depriving them of the legal possession of their basilicas, although their steadfastness yielded to none of the terrors of the most arrogant king [Col. 0723B]. The emperor Valentinian set out for Constantinople to the emperor Theodosius and took his daughter in marriage. In the same year the barbarians engaged in piracy.

At the same time four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychianus—had long been held in high regard by Geiseric because of their wisdom and faithful service. To make them more closely attached to himself, the king ordered them to convert to the Arian sect. But they most steadfastly rejected this deed. The barbarian was roused to furious anger; they were first proscribed, then driven into exile, and finally killed by various deaths. Thus they met their end in a glorious and wondrous martyrdom.

A boy named Paulillus, brother of Paschasius and Eutychianus, was highly favored by the king because of his handsome appearance and intelligence. Since no threats could disturb him in his profession and love of the Catholic faith, he was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to the lowest slavery. Apparently he was not killed so that even that age might not boast of the defeat of the skill of the impious man (cf. the letter of Dionysius in Petavius, p. 874).

Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, composed a ninety-five-year cycle, beginning from the year 153 of Diocletian [Note: [Col. 0723] See also the preface and letter of Cyril himself in Petavius, p. 881].

460. 15. [CCCCXXXVIII] (ISIDOR.) Theodosius XVI and Faustus. The Devil appeared to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses and promised to lead them across the sea on foot to the promised land. But when many had been submerged and killed, the survivors were saved and converted to the grace of Christ.

[Col. 0723D] 461. 16. [CCCCXXXIX] (PROSP.) Theodosius XVII and Festus. Julian of Eclanum, the most boastful advocate of the Pelagian error, whose immoderate desire for the episcopate he had lost had long driven him on, attempted by many deceptive methods to insinuate himself into communion with the Church while holding out hope of correction. Pope Sixtus, acting watchfully against these ambushes at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no opening for his deadly efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the exposure of the deceitful beast, as though at that moment the apostolic sword had first severed the head of the most arrogant heresy [Note: [Col. 0723] Pr. reads: “to rejoice.”].

Peace was made with the Goths, since after the grievous experience of a doubtful battle they had sought it more humbly than ever before. While Aetius was occupied with the affairs being settled in Gaul, Geiseric, whose friendship had seemed to offer no cause for fear, invaded Carthage by a deceitful pretense of peace and, after subjecting its citizens to various forms of torture, converted all its wealth to his own possession [Col. 0724A]. Nor did he refrain from stripping the churches, which he emptied of their sacred vessels and deprived of the ministry of their priests; he ordered them no longer to be places of divine worship but dwellings for his own people.

(PROSP.) He was savage toward the entire population of captives, but especially hostile to the nobility and religion, so that it could not be determined whether he had waged war more against human beings [than] against God.

462. 17. [CCCCXL] (PROSP.) Valentinian V and Anatolius. After the death of Bishop Sixtus, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience the deacon Leo, who at that time was detained in Gaul arranging the renewal of friendship between Aetius and Albinus. Leo was therefore summoned by a public embassy and presented to his rejoicing homeland; he was consecrated as the forty-fourth pope of the Roman Church and sat for twenty-one years. (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) While Geiseric was severely afflicting Sicily, he received news of Sebastian’s crossing from Spain to Africa and quickly returned to Carthage, judging that it would be dangerous for himself and his people if a man experienced in warfare were to take charge of recovering Carthage. (PROSP.)

463. 18. [CCCCXLI] (PROSP.) Cyrus, a most illustrious man, consul. The emperor Theodosius undertook war against the Vandals, sending a large fleet under the commanders Ariobindus, Ansila, and Germanus. By delaying the undertaking for a long time, they proved more a burden to Sicily than a defense for Africa.

464. 19. [CCCCXLII] (PROSP.) Dioscorus and Eudoxius. While the Huns were devastating Thrace and Illyricum with savage destruction, the army that had been staying in Sicily returned to defend the eastern provinces. Peace was confirmed with Geiseric and Valentinian Augustus, and Africa was divided between them by fixed boundaries.

465. 20. [CCCCXLIII] (PROSP.) Maximus II and Paternus. At this time Pope Leo’s diligence made it known that very many Manichaeans were hiding within Rome. He brought them out of their secret places and exposed them before the eyes of the entire Church, making them condemn and reveal all the disgraceful features of their doctrine, while their books were burned.

466. 21. [CCCCXLIV] (PROSP.) Theodosius XVIII and Albinus. This year Easter [the Lord’s Easter] was celebrated on 23 April, and there was no error, because the day of the Passion had fallen on 21 April. Out of reverence for it, the anniversary of the city of Rome passed without the Circensian games.

—The letter of Bishop Paschasius to Pope Leo begins, instructing him to write back concerning the question [Col. 0725A] that had arisen [about the same year]:

> “To the holy and most blessed lord . . .”

[Note: [Col. 0725D] It exists in the Paris codex, formerly, it seems, Mainz; it was printed among the letters of Saint Leo I, no. 64. We have judged that it should be omitted here.]

> “Let a difference of one day not frighten us,”

and the rest, concerning which we spoke above in connection with the eleventh year [Note: [Col. 0725] Read: “ninth”] of Honorius. Therefore, the year 417 of the Incarnation according to Dionysius is the ninth year [Note: [Col. 0725] “XI” corrected to “IX,” first hand] of Honorius, and the year 444 of the Incarnation according to Dionysius is the [twenty-first year of Theodosius].

467. 22. [CCCCXLV] (cf. *Liber pontificalis*) Valentinian VI and Nonius. Leo established that at Mass one should say, “the holy sacrifice, the spotless offering”; and that a nun should not receive a head-covering blessed by the bishop unless her virginity had first been tested.

468. 23. [CCCCXLVI] (BEDA.) Aetius III and Symmachus. The Britons were defeated by the Scots and Picts. When they promised submission to the Romans in return for assistance, a legion was sent which freed them, drove the Scots from Britain, and, on its return home, ordered the Britons to build a wall across the island between the two seas. Built more with turf than with stone, as the Romans departed, the Scots arrived in ships and, finding the Britons before them like a ripe harvest, cut them down, trampled them, and devoured them. When the Britons again requested assistance, the Romans returned, drove away the Scots, and together with the Britons established a stone wall between the cities, solid from sea to sea. On the shore of the southern sea, from which the enemy was feared, they also erected towers at intervals to watch the sea.

When the Roman army withdrew from Britain, however, the Scots and Picts returned and seized the whole of Britain from the north as far as the wall, which itself had been breached. The Britons then sent a tearful letter to Aetius, a man of Roman authority and three times consul, in the twenty-third year of the reign of Theodosius, but they obtained no assistance. The Scots returned home, and shortly afterward the Picts returned and occupied the farthest part of Britain, where they were to dwell then and thereafter [Note: [Col. 0725] First hand: “were to inhabit.”].

The Britons, however, by unanimous decision with their king Vortigern, chose to invite the Angles to them as defenders of their homeland. But when they had received them, they found them to be attackers, after the Angles fabricated the pretext that the Britons were paying insufficient wages to those who were fighting on their behalf.

469. 24. [CCCCXLVII] (PROSP.) Alibius and Ardabures. Eutyches, the heresiarch and presbyter of Constantinople, relying on the friendship of the emperor Theodosius, attempted to assert that Christ was not a perfect man [Note: [Col. 0725] “assert” in witness 1]. [Col. 0725D] Against him Flavian, bishop of that same city, took action; but, together with his priests, he was condemned, at the instigation of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. Against Dioscorus Pope Leo sent a bishop, a presbyter, and a deacon, who, having suffered injury, reported that Flavian had perished amid the gravest outrages in defense of the Catholic faith. [Col. 0726A]

[Cod. in margin: The solar cycle begins.]

470. 25. [CCCCXLVIII] (PROSP.) Postumianus and Zeno. The emperor Theodosius summoned Pope Leo of Rome to himself in defense of Eutyches. When Leo wished to go, but was prevented by the people, he sent presbyters and deacons.

471. 26. [CCCCXLIX] (PROSP.) Asturius and Protogenes. The Catholics were summoned again to be heard.

472. 27. [CCCCL] Valentinian VI and Abienus. A council was held at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0725D] More probably at Chalcedon. I have been unable to find the certain source of this passage [Col. 0726D]; cf. Leo, letters 24, 29, 31] against the presbyter Eutychian, who presided over the famous monastery at Constantinople and said that the Lord was Christ alone, not a man. In this council the deacon Hilary and Julius, bishop of Puteoli, were sent as representatives of Pope Leo. Because that deacon cried out there on behalf of the violated faith, he secretly fled [to Rome] for the sake of his life [Col. 0726B] [Note: [Col. 0725] At this point a new year began, but the numbers and consuls have been erased].

(PROSP.) The emperor Theodosius was escorted with great pomp by Placidia and Leo, together with the entire senate, and was laid to rest in the mausoleum at the Apostle Peter’s.

[Note: [Col. 0726B] Witness 2 adds at this point: “In the time of this Theodosius, when a council had been held at Carthage by the most impious king of the Vandals, Honoric, and when other bishops too were being driven from their sees, Saint Theonestus, driven from Philippi, the city of his see, came to Rome with four of his disciples during the time of Pope Leo, whether for the sake of pilgrimage or to receive consolation. He was received favorably by him and stayed there for some time; then he proceeded to blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan. He too received him charitably and presented him through his own agency to the emperor Theodosius, who was then staying there. Finally, after being dismissed peacefully by both men, he came to Augusta Vindelicum, the first city of Raetia, where one of his disciples, Ursus, also suffered. Departing from there, he came to King Sigismund of the Allobroges, and from him to Paulinus of Trier; then, traveling by ship, he reached the city of Mainz. There, while he fought most vigorously against the heretics with sound doctrine, he left behind another disciple, Alban, who was truly whitened like snow by martyrdom.”]

[Col. 0726C] Roman emperor 53. According to some, Marcian reigned seven years; according to the historian who wrote at that time [Note: [Col. 0726D] Prosper’s Chronicle indicates the version that we read in the Augsburg and Mainz manuscripts], eight years; according to Roman history, seven years and two months—that is, approximately until the Kalends of July in the year 445 after the Passion. The following consuls held office under him, as Cassiodorus testifies.

473. 1. [CCCCLI] (PROSP.) Marcian and Adelfius, men of clarissima rank. A battle was fought in Gaul between Aetius and Attila, king of the Huns. After a slaughter on both sides, Attila was driven back into upper Gaul.

[Col. 0727A] 474. 2. [CCCCLII] (BEDA.) Herculanus and Asporacius. John the Baptist revealed his head to two monks near the dwelling of Herod; it was carried with great honor to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia. The people of the Angles, or Saxons, arrived in Britain in three longships and subdued nearly the whole island from east to west.

475. 3. [CCCCLIII] (ISID.) Opilio and Vincomalus. The Synod of Chalcedon was held, at which Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned. Saint Pope Leo writes thus (letter 61): “Concerning the observance of Easter, Theophilus of holy memory, writing to the elder emperor Theodosius, calculated the sequence of the feast-day over one hundred years from the first consulship of that emperor; the seventy-fourth year of that reckoning is now passing, in which the sacred solemnity was celebrated on 12 April, with Opilio as consul.” [Col. 0727B]

476. 4. [CCCCLIV] Aetius and Studius. Hence [Note: [Col. 0727] These words must be joined to the preceding year] “in the following year [Note: [Col. 0727] The same words are read twice in witness 1], consequently, on 5 April,” and so forth. But the year that would be the seventy-sixth seems to disagree, since Easter is placed on 24 April, whereas, as it seems, it ought to occur on 17 April (PROSP.). Deogratias was ordained bishop in the basilica of Faustus on Sunday, 25 October. On 21 September the emperor Valentinian killed the patrician Aetius and Boethius at Carthage [Note: [Col. 0727] An error arising from an imperfect understanding of Prosper’s manuscript].

477. 5. [CCCCLV] (PROSP.) Valentinian VIII and Anthemius. Valentinian was killed by Aetius’ friends on 20 March [in the Campus Martius] (PROSP.). Maximus, a man of two consulships and patrician rank, assumed the imperial power at Rome on the following day, 21 March. [Col. 0727C] Two months later, when the arrival of King Geiseric from Africa was announced to him and many noble citizens were fleeing the city, Maximus, frightened and wishing to depart after granting everyone permission to leave, was seized by Valentinian’s servants on the seventy-seventh day of his reign, torn to pieces, and thrown limb by limb into the Tiber; he was denied burial as well.

After this followed the Roman captivity, deserving of many tears. For when Geiseric seized the City, empty of every defense, on 12 July, a Tuesday, Pope Leo the holy bishop met him outside the gates. His supplication, by God’s agency, so softened Geiseric that, although everything had been handed over to his power, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and punishment against the city. Rome, however, was emptied of all its wealth by fourteen days of secure and unrestricted plunder [Col. 0727D] [Note: [Col. 0727] “emptied” in witness 1]; many thousands of captives, together with the queen and her daughters, were carried off to Carthage, each according to his age or skill.

In this year—that is, 455 from the Incarnation according to Dionysius—Easter was rightly celebrated on 24 April, in accordance with the reckoning of Saint Theophilus [Note: [Col. 0727] The manuscript continued: “which Saint Pope Leo declared ought rather to be celebrated on 17 April according to the reckoning of Saint Theophilus,” but the words have now been erased]; Pope Saint Leo subsequently declared that it ought rather to be observed on 17 April.

[Col. 0728A] 478. 6. [CCCCLVI] (CASS.) Varan and John. After Maximus, Avitus assumed the imperial power in Gaul.

[Cod. in margin: The 25-year decennial cycle begins in indiction 9.]

479. 7. [CCCCLVII] (CASS.) Constantine and Rufus. Avitus was deposed at Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0727] At this point a new year began, but the numbers and consuls have been erased]. After Marcian died at Constantinople, Leo assumed the imperial power in the East and Majorian in Italy [Note: [Col. 0728A] Witness 2 adds here: “Up to this point is the chronicle of the emperors, at whose end the following is written:

‘After the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus, Geiseric, king of the Vandals, entered Carthage on 19 October; he reigned there for twenty-seven years, three months, and seven days. After him his son Huneric reigned seven years, ten months, and twenty-eight days. At the end of the seventh year of his reign he began a persecution of the Catholic Church, closed all the churches, and bound all the Catholic priests of the Lord, together with Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, in exile. He himself, by the judgment of the Lord, died swarming with worms.

After him Guntamundus, son of Gentunis, the brother of that same Honoric, reigned eleven years, nine months, and eleven days. In the third year of his reign he ordered that the cemetery of Saint Agileus at Carthage be given to the Catholics, after Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, had already been recalled from exile by him. In the tenth year of his reign he opened the Catholic churches and, at the request of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, recalled all God’s priests from exile. These churches had been closed for ten years, six months, and five days—that is, from the eighth year of Honoric, from 7 February, until the eleventh year of King Guntamundus, 5 August, when the aforesaid ten years, six months, and five days were completed. The aforesaid King Guntamundus afterward lived two years and one month.

After him Trasamundus, son of Gentunis, reigned twenty-six years, eight months, and four days. From the beginning of Avitus’ imperial power until the twenty-sixth year of Trasamundus, and from the fourteenth year of the reign and death of Valens until the twenty-second year of Trasamundus, there are … years. After him Hildiric, son of Honoric, reigned eight years and eight days. At the beginning of his reign he ordered Boniface, bishop of Carthage, to be ordained in the church of Saint Agileus and restored liberty to all Catholics.

While he was reigning, the tyrant Geilimer seized his kingdom. He reigned three years and an equal number of months, committing such wicked murders that he spared not even his relatives. Thus from the beginning of Geiseric’s reign until the end of the Vandals there are … years; from the death of Valens, which occurred in the fourteenth year of his reign, until the aforesaid time, there are … years. The sum of all the years from Adam to the destruction of the Vandals is therefore 5733.’—All this was taken from Prosper’s Mainz manuscript]. Under these emperors the following consuls held office, as Cassiodorus testifies.

[Col. 0728D] Roman emperor 54. According to everyone, Leo reigned seventeen years, that is, until the Kalends of July in the year 461 after the Passion, under the following consuls, as Cassiodorus testifies.

[Col. 0729A] 480. 1. [CCCCLVIII] (CASS.) Leo Augustus and Majorian Augustus. Majorian prepared an expedition to Africa.

481. 2. [CCCCLIX] (ISID.) Ricimer and Patricius. Alexandria and Egypt languished under the error of the heretic Dioscorus.

482. 3. [CCCCLX] (ISID.) Magnus and Apollonius. The heresy of the Acephali appeared; they opposed the Council of Chalcedon. They are called Acephali, that is, “headless,” because its author did not appear.

483. 4. [CCCCLXI] (JORD.) Severinus and Dagalaifus. (CASS.) Majorian was killed near the city of Dertona on 6 August through Ricimer’s machinations; Ricimer caused Severus, a Lucanian by birth, to succeed him at Ravenna. [Pope Leo died on 28 June (AD. Mart.) [Note: [Col. 0729] Written by a second hand in an erased place].]

[Col. 0729B] 484. 5. [CCCCLXII] Leo II and Severus. Hilary was consecrated as the forty-fifth pope on 12 November; he held the office for seven years and six months.

485. 6. [CCCCLXIII] Basiliscus and Vivianus. (BEDA.) Theodore, bishop of the city called Cyrus, because it was founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians, wrote concerning the true incarnation of the Lord against Eutyches and Dioscorus, who denied the human flesh in Christ. Victor [Note: [Col. 0729] The same words were written again in the margin of folio 145 by a second hand], at Pope Hilary’s command, composed a paschal cycle of 532 years.

486. 7. [CCCCLXIV] (CASS.) Rusticus and Olybrius. Beorgor, king of the Alans, was killed at Pergamum by the patrician Ricimer.

487. 8. [CCCCLXV] (CASS.) Arminericus and Basiliscus. Severus was treacherously killed by Ricimer with poison in the palace at Rome. [Col. 0729C]

488. 9. [CCCCLXVI] (BEDA.) Leo the Younger, in his third consulship. The aforementioned Theodore, bishop of Cyrus, wrote an ecclesiastical history called the Tripartite History (BEDA.), beginning at the end of Eusebius’ books—that is, from the twentieth year of Constantine the Great—up to the time of this emperor Leo, in whose reign Theodore himself also died.

489. 10. [CCCCLXVII] (CASS.) Puseus and John. Anthemius was sent to Italy by the emperor Leo; at the third mile from the City, at a place called Brontotas, he assumed the imperial power.

490. 11. [CCCCLXVIII] (CASS.) Anthemius Augustus, in his second consulship. Marcellinus was killed in Sicily.

491. 12. [CCCCLXIX] (CASS.) Marcianus and Zeno, men of clarissima rank. Arabundus, attempting to seize the imperial power, was deported into exile by order of Anthemius. [Col. 0729D]

492. 13. [CCCCLXX] (CASS.) Severus and Jordanes. The Roman patrician, aspiring to the imperial power, was beheaded. Pope Hilary died on 21 February.

Simplicius, the forty-sixth pope after Peter, sat for fifteen years.

493. 14. [CCCCLXXI] (CASS.) Leo Augustus IV and Probianus. Aspar, aspiring to tyranny at Constantinople, was killed by the emperor Leo.

[Col. 0730A] 494. 15. [CCCCLXXII] (CASS.) Festus and Marcianus. The patrician Ricimer, having made Olybrius emperor at Rome, killed Anthemius, contrary to the reverence owed to the prince and to the law of kinship, with grave destruction to the city; Ricimer died on the fortieth day of his ascendancy. Olybrius, however, ended his life in the seventh month of his imperial rule.

495. 16. [CCCCLXXIII] (CASS.) Leo Augustus V, in his fifth consulship. At the urging of Gundobad, Glycerius assumed the imperial power at Ravenna. In the same year the emperor Leo made his nephew Leo his associate in the imperial power.

496. 17. [CCCCLXXIV] (CASS.) Leo the Younger Augustus VI, in his sixth consulship. Nepos succeeded Glycerius in the kingdom at Rome. The emperor Leo died in this year. Cassiodorus, bishop Jordanes, writes the following in the chronicle he composed at that time (JORD.):

“Leo, appointing Leo the Younger, his nephew through his daughter Ariadne, as emperor in the East, died in the sixteenth year of his reign.”

(JORD.) Roman emperor 55. Leo the Younger, although he had ruled as a child for only a few months, with his father nevertheless appointing him, departed this life after crowning his son-in-law Zeno with his own hand and establishing him as emperor. Zeno, an Isaurian by birth and son-in-law of the emperor Leo, reigned seventeen years. This is written by Bishop Jordanes; and according to Roman history this means that Leo the Elder nevertheless reigned sixteen years and six months [Note: [Col. 0729] The Historia miscella says that he reigned seventeen years], that is, until the Kalends of January.

(cf. BEDA.) In the same sixteenth year, in which Leo died, King Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0729D] Bede is speaking of Odovacer] seized Rome, during the time of Leo the Younger.

Roman emperor 56. According to everyone, Zeno reigned seventeen years [Col. 0730C], that is, until the Kalends of January in the year 479 after the Passion. Under him the following consuls held office, as Cassiodorus testifies.

497. 1. [CCCCLXXV] (CASS.) Proconsul of the younger Emperor Leo. Orestes, after driving Nepos into Dalmatia, gave the imperial power to his son Augustulus.

498. 2. [CCCCLXXVI] (CASS.) Basiliscus II and Armatus. Odovacer killed Orestes and his brother Paulus and assumed the title of king.

499. 3. [CCCCLXXVII] (ISID.) Proconsuls of Basiliscus and Armatus. This Zeno sought to kill Leo, the emperor’s son.

500. 4. [CCCCLXXVIII] Ellus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. But [Note: [Col. 0729] This must be joined to the year 499] his mother presented another man of similar appearance in his place.

[Col. 0730D] 501. 5. [CCCCLXXIX] Zeno Augustus II, in his second consulship. He secretly made Leo [Note: [Col. 0729] This must be joined to the year 499] a cleric.

502. 6. [CCCCLXXX] Basilius the Younger, consul. He lived in the clerical state until the time of Justin [Note: [Col. 0729] This must be joined to the year 499].

503. 7. [CCCCLXXXI] (CASS.) Placidus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Odovacer defeated and killed Odiva in Dalmatia.

504. 8. [CCCCLXXXII] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Severinus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Pope Simplicius condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, as Eutychians. [Col. 0731A]

505. 9. [CCCCLXXXIII] (ISID.) Faustus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. The body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of Matthew, written in his own hand, were discovered, he himself revealing them.

506. 10. [CCCCLXXXIV] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Theoderic and Venantius. The apostolic Pope Simplicius died on 2 March.

Felix, the forty-seventh pope after Peter, was ordained; he sat for eight years.

507. 11. [CCCCLXXXV] (BEDA.) Symmachus, a man of clarissima rank. The Arian king of the Vandals, Honoric, after driving more than 334 Catholic bishops into exile, closed the churches and afflicted the people with various punishments; cutting off the hands of countless people and severing their tongues, he nevertheless could not take away the speech of the Catholic confession. [Col. 0731B]

508. 12. [CCCCLXXXVI] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Decius and Longinus. Pope Felix also condemned Acacius and Peter, the Eutychian bishops.

509. 13. [CCCCLXXXVII] (CASS.) Boethius, a man of clarissima rank, consul. After defeating and capturing Feva, king of the Rugians, Odovacer gained possession of the kingdom.

510. 14. [CCCCLXXXVIII] (CASS.) Dynamius and Sifidius. King Theodoric entered Italy [under these consuls, as Cassiodorus testifies].

511. 15. [CCCCLXXXIX] (CASS.) Probinus and Eusebius. Odovacer prepared for battle against him at the Isonzo, but was defeated and put to flight with his entire people. Again, in the same year, Odovacer was defeated in battle at Verona.

[Col. 0731C] 512. 16. [CCCCXC] (CASS.) Faustus the Younger, consul. Theodoric defeated Odovacer at the river Adda [in a third engagement], and Odovacer, fleeing to Ravenna, was besieged.

513. 17. [CCCCXCI] (CASS.) Olybrius the Younger, consul. Odovacer, having gone out from Ravenna by night with the Heruli [Note: [Col. 0731] Read: “Herulians”], was overcome by Theodoric in a memorable battle at the Candidian Bridge. Then the Vandals, after humbly requesting peace, ceased their customary plundering of Sicily.

[In the same year the emperor Zeno died.]

[Saint Patrick, archbishop of Ireland, died in the most blessed manner at the age of 132 (122) years [Note: [Col. 0731] 132 corrected to 122 in witness 1?; 122 in witness 2]. He is said to have been sold at the age of 16, spent six years in slavery, forty [Note: [Col. 0731] The number appears to have been erased in witness 1; absent in witness 2] in the Roman territories, and preached in Ireland for seventy (sixty) years [Note: [Col. 0731] 70 corrected to 60 in witness 1?; 60 in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0731] On the numbers, cf. O’Connor, II, p. 124, n. 96; I would like you to supplement the text from that passage].]

Roman emperor 57. According to everyone, Anastasius reigned twenty-seven years, that is, until the Kalends of May in the year 506 after the Passion. [Col. 0731D] The following consuls held office under him.

514. 1. [CCCCXCII] (H. R.) Anastasius Augustus and Rufus. He denied, following Eutyches, the two natures—that is, of humanity and deity [Note: [Col. 0731] Thus in witness 1] [in Christ].

[Cod. in margin: The 27th decennial cycle begins in indiction 2.]

515. 2. [CCCCXCIII] Albinus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Gelasius, the forty-eighth pope after Peter, sat for four years and ten months.

[Col. 0732A] 516. 3. [CCCCXCIV] (CASS.) Asterius and Presidius. King Theodoric entered Ravenna and killed Odovacer, who was plotting an ambush against him.

517. 4. [CCCCXCV] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Victor, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Pope Gelasius restored to his church Misenus, the bishop condemned by Pope Felix.

518. 5. [CCCCXCXVI] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Paulus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Pope Gelasius composed books against Eutyches and Nestorius and died on 19 November.

519. 6. [CCCCXCXVII] (JORD.) Anastasius Augustus II, consul. The emperor Anastasius deserved to hear no vengeance from his enemies, just as he himself did not preserve the rights of the Church.

Pope Anastasius, the forty-ninth after Peter, sat for one year and six months.

[Col. 0732B] 520. 7. [CCCCXCXVIII] (BEDA.) Paulinus and John. Trasamundus, king of the Vandals, sent 225 bishops of the Catholic churches into exile in Sardinia. (Liber pontificalis.) Pope Anastasius died on 28 May. [Pope Anastasius wished secretly to recall Acacius, the condemned bishop of Constantinople, but was unable to do so; he too was struck down by divine will.]

521. 8. [CCCCXCXIX] (Liber pontificalis.) John, a man of clarissima rank. Pope Symmachus, the fiftieth after Peter, sat for fifteen years. [Because of the election of Pope Symmachus and Laurentius, Festus, a most noble former consul, and Probinus, a former consul, acting on Laurentius’ side against the former consul Faustus and the others on Symmachus’ side, caused slaughter and murders in the middle of the City, and killed many clerics. Hence the holy deacon Paschasius was also placed after his death in punishment, because he remained opposed to the people in the election of Laurentius until the end of his life, as is read in the Dialogues (GREG. Dial. IV, 40). This too was a very minor sin, namely, a fault of ignorance, because he thought before God that what he had done was more correct than the alternative.]

[Simplicius was pope from the consulship of Paulinus until the second consulship of Senator [Note: [Col. 0731] Thus written elsewhere in the margin by a second hand; supply: “the deeds of the popes”].]

522. 9. [D] (CASS.) Patricius and Hipatius, men of clarissima rank. King Theodoric came to Rome and treated the senate graciously.

523. 10. [DI] (CASS.) Avienus and Pompeius. King Theodoric gave grain rations to the Roman populace.

524. 11. [DII] (CASS.) Avienus the Younger and Probus. [Col. 0732D] King Theodoric brought water to Ravenna and restored its aqueduct at his own expense, since it had long before been reduced to the ground.

525. 12. [DIII] Caetheus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Through the power of King Theodoric, after the Bulgarians had been defeated, Sirmium was recovered for Italy.

526. 13. [DIV] (BEDA.) Theodorus and Sabinianus. [Col. 0733A] Pope Symmachus built many church works from their foundations or restored ancient ones.

[Cod. in margin: The solar cycle begins.]

527. 14. [DV] Messala and Ariobinna. He built dwellings for the poor beside Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Laurence [Note: [Col. 0733] This must be joined to the year 526].

528. 15. [DVI] Anastasius Augustus III and Venantius. Every year he supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the bishops who were in exile.

529. 16. [DVII] (CASS.) Venantius the Younger and Celer. Theodoric sent an army against the Franks.

530. 17. [DVIII] Importunus, a man of clarissima rank. He acquired for his own empire the Gauls, thrown into confusion by Frankish plundering, after defeating and routing the enemy [Note: [Col. 0733] This must be joined to the year 529].

531. 18. [DIX] (ISID.) Boethius, a man of clarissima rank, consul. At Carthage, a certain Olympius, an Arian, blasphemed the Holy Trinity in the baths. [Col. 0733B]

532. 19. [DX] Felix and Secundinus. But immediately, when fiery darts threatened, he was visibly consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 0733] This must be joined to the year 531].

533. 20. [DXI] (ISID.) Paulus and Muschianus. A certain Arian bishop, Barnabas, while baptizing someone contrary to the rule of faith, said: “I baptize you, Barrabas, in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately the water that had been brought for the baptism disappeared completely. Seeing this, the person who was to be baptized at once went to the Catholic church and received the baptism of Christ.

This is the second year of the Lord’s birth according to the course of the sun and moon [Note: [Col. 0733] Written in the margin by the first hand].

[Col. 0733C] 534. 21. [DXII] Probus and Clementinus.

[Cod. in margin: The 28th decennial cycle begins in indiction 6.]

535. 22. [DXIII] (ISID.) Senator, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Bishop Fulgentius flourished in confession of the faith and in knowledge.

536. 23. [DXIV] (CASS.) Cassiodorus, consul, writes: “While I too am consul, to the praise of your times, with the Roman clergy [or people] assembled, the desired harmony returned to the Church.”

537. 24. [DXV] (CASS.) Florentinus and Anthemius. King Theodoric joined his daughter Amalasuntha to the illustrious Eutharic, with God’s favor [Deo auspice]. [Pope Symmachus died on 19 July.]

Pope Hormisdas, the fifty-first after Peter, sat for eight years. [Hormisdas [Note: [Col. 0733] These words were written in the margin by a second hand, which also indicated by a sign that the words “Hormisdas … eight” belong with the year 535] held office from the consulship of Senator until the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius.]

538. 25. [DXVI] (CASS.) Peter, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Eutharic Cillica was accepted by the senate and people for the consulship.

539. 26. [DXVII] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Eutharic Cillica and Justinus. Pope Hormisdas organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms.

540. 27. [DXVIII] (H. R.) Anastasius IV, a man of clarissima rank. Pope Hormisdas sent Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, [Col. 0734A] and others to instruct the emperor Anastasius. (JORD.) But Anastasius, scorning them and favoring the heresy of Eutyches, persecuted the Catholics in various regions and, surrounded by troops of enemies, often groaning, perished by a thunderbolt from heaven. Bishop Jordanes wrote the following history at that time: “The emperor Anastasius, grieving and raging, more than eighty years old and in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, departed this life.” [Note: [Col. 0734A] The hand that wrote the continuation for the years 1126–1128 added: “Saint Remigius, converting the Franks to the faith of Christ, baptized three thousand of them with their king Clovis in one day. King Clovis of the Franks sent a golden crown to Saint Peter at Rome under Pope Hormisdas and the emperor Anastasius.”]

[Col. 0734B] Roman emperor 58. According to Roman history and Bishop Jordanes, who composed a chronicle at that time and lived during it, Justin the Elder ruled for nine years; according to Bede, only eight years—that is, until the Kalends of January in the year [514 after the Passion].

541. 1. [DXIX] (H. R.) Rusticus and Vitalis, men of clarissima rank. Justin began to extinguish the name of the heretics and had their churches everywhere consecrated to Catholic use.

542. 2. [DXX] (JORD.) Valerius and Justinianus. Justin killed Amantius, the palace superintendent, and Andreas, the chamberlain; he sent Misael and Ardabur, chamberlains, into exile at Sardica.

543. 3. [DXXI] (Liber pontificalis.) Symmachus and Boethius. Pope Hormisdas died on 6 August [under these consuls, according to the deeds of the popes—that is, under Maximus [Note: [Col. 0734C] Thus the second hand assigned this note to the year 544]]. [Saint Brigit the Scottish virgin died in Ireland [Note: [Col. 0733] These words were first written under the year 544 and later transferred here].]

544. 4. [DXXII] Maximus, a man of clarissima rank, consul. John, the fifty-second pope, sat for two years and ten months [under these consuls, according to the deeds of the popes].

545. 5. [DXXIII] (H. R.) Opilo and Justin Augustus. Theodoric, the Arian emperor of Italy, sent Pope John, together with Theodore and Agapitus, men of consular rank, and Agapitus the patrician, to the emperor Justin at Constantinople, threatening that, unless the heretics were released to live in peace, he would himself put all Italy to the sword. (BEDA.) When Pope John came to Constantinople, at the gate called the Golden Gate, crowds of people running to meet him, he restored sight before everyone to a blind man who asked him. [Col. 0734D] (H. R.) The emperor Justin, moved by tearful entreaties and by the certain prospect of a slaughter of the Catholic people, yielded to releasing the heretics. [Columcilli was born in Ireland.]

546. 6. [DXXIV] (BEDA.) Probus the Younger and Philoxenus, consuls. When Pope John, returning, had reached Ravenna, Theodoric, driven by jealousy because Justin, the defender of Catholic piety, had received him honorably, killed him and his companions by the affliction of imprisonment. (cf. Liber pontificalis.) In that year, the consulship of Probus the Younger, he also killed the patrician Symmachus at Ravenna. Pope John died on 20 May; his body was transferred and buried in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter. Saint Pope Gregory mentions this John in the third and fourth books of the Dialogues (III, 2; IV, 30).

547. 7. [DXXV] (BEDA.) Olybrius, a man of clarissima rank, consul. (H. R.) Theodoric died suddenly at Ravenna in the following year. The Goths set Athalaric, born of King Theodoric’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0735] Supply: “daughter”], over themselves together with his mother. (BEDA.) Hilderic, [king] of the Vandals, ordered the bishops to return from exile and the churches to be restored, after seventy-four years of heretical profanation. (ISID.) After Trasamundus, Hilderic, born from a captive daughter of the emperor Valentinian, assumed the kingdom of the Vandals. Bound by an oath imposed by Trasamundus not to aid the Catholics in his kingdom, he nevertheless, before assuming the kingdom, ordered the bishops to return from exile and commanded that their churches be restored.

Felix, the fifty-third pope, sat for four years and two months.

The heresy of the Acephali was rejected [they said that the apostle Paul had commanded in his letters that women ought to become deacons, because he mentions them after deacons]. (Liber pontificalis.) [Under the consulship of Olybrius, Pope John was buried on 27 May.]

548. 8. [DXXVI] Maburtius, consul. [Maburtius, consul. Felix succeeded him.] In this year Dionysius began his reckoning, saying among other things (Letter 2, in Petavius, p. 877):

“Let us show an example from the present year. For it is the fourth indiction, and the lunar cycle is 11, the nineteen-year cycle 14. And because it is the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle, it must be an embolismic year. Let us therefore inquire carefully how many days there are from the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the fourteenth of the present one, and without doubt we shall discover when we ought to celebrate Easter. When the preceding year had passed, in indiction 3, the fourteenth moon of Easter was on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 24 March—which person can doubt it?”—and so forth.

A little earlier he says (Letter 1, ibid., p. 874):

“We point out that this cycle of ninety-five years, which we have constructed, does not return entirely into itself; and therefore, after the completion of the ninety-five years, the reader should not proceed to the fifth cycle of Saint [Cyril], who began his cycles from the year 153 of Diocletian [Col. 0735D], which fifth cycle we necessarily placed before us, but to our first cycle, which we began from the year 248 of that same Diocletian,” and so forth.

(BEDA.) Benedict the abbot shone with the glory of miracles, which Saint Gregory recorded in the Dialogues. (ISID.) Justin, making Justinian, his sister’s son, emperor at Constantinople four months before his own death, died.
