Roman emperor 59. Justinian, according to every historian, reigned thirty-eight years, that is, until the Kalends of January in the year 552 after the Passion. Under him the following consuls held office, as Cassiodorus testifies.

549. 1. [DXXVII] (ISID.) Justinian Augustus II, consul. The patrician Belisarius triumphed wonderfully over the Persians.

550. 2. [DXXVIII] (ISID.) Decius, a man of clarissima rank, consul. Belisarius, sent by Justinian to Africa, destroyed the nation of the Vandals.

551. 3. [DXXIX] (cf. Liber pontificalis.) Lampadius and Orestes, men of clarissima rank, consuls. [Under these consuls Pope Felix died on 12 October.]

Pope Boniface, the fifty-fourth after Peter, sat for two years. [Pope Boniface died on 18 October in the consulship of Lampadius, according to the deeds of the popes [Note: [Col. 0735] Supply: “the deeds of the popes”].]

552. 4. [DXXX] (BEDA.) Proconsuls Lampadius and Orestes again. The body of Saint Antony the monk, revealed by God, was carried to Alexandria and buried in the church of blessed John the Baptist.

[Col. 0736B] 553. 5. [DXXXI] Again, Lampadius and Orestes, men of clarissima rank, consuls.

(cf. Liber pontificalis.) Pope Mercurius, the fifty-fifth, sat for two years. [Under these consuls Boniface died on 17 October. Mercurius, who was also called John, died as pope on 27 May, in the consulship following that of Lampadius.]

Up to this point the great paschal cycle of 532 years extends. In its thirteenth year our Lord Jesus Christ suffered on 25 March, the fifteenth day of the moon, and rose from the dead on 27 March, the seventeenth day of the moon, in the eighteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, according to the history of the Gospel.

The great solar and nineteen-year paschal cycles begin together.

### 554. 6. [DXXXII] (P. D. II, 25.)

Justinian Augustus [Col. 0736C] 3. Justinian compressed the laws of the Romans, which had been set out at excessive length and with useless inconsistency in many books, into twelve books, forming a single work which he ordered to be called the Justinian Code.

Saint Bede says this:

> “Dionysius writes the Paschal cycles, beginning from the year of the Lord’s incarnation 552, which is the 248th year of Diocletian, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes; in that year the Justinian Code was promulgated to the world.”

Thus far Bede. Therefore, when Bede says, reckoning from Diocletian up to the cycle of Dionysius, that the first year of Dionysius’ cycle was itself the 248th year of Diocletian, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, he sufficiently demonstrates what is true: that the first year of Dionysius’ cycle was Justinian’s sixth year.

Beginning, therefore, from that first year of Dionysius’ cycle—that is, from Justinian’s sixth year—and counting upward to Diocletian [Note: [Col. 0735] “idem,” witness 1?] according to the chronicle of Eusebius or Bede, and from there again up to the cycle of Dionysius according to Sacred Scripture and the apostolic men who, at that very time, also discussed those years accurately—not merely, as we have shown, to expose the falsehood of the chronicles, but to defend the most sacred evangelical truth and the Catholic men of the Church who, after the Gospel, testify that our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on the seventeenth day of the moon, namely Jerome and Augustine.

Victorius likewise writes to Pope Hilary as follows (in Petavius):

> “On the first day of Unleavened Bread our Lord Jesus Christ, dining with his disciples, after revealing the sacraments of his body and blood, proceeded to the Mount of Olives, as the holy Gospels testify, and there he was arrested by the Jews, when a disciple betrayed him. Then, on the following sixth day, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, he was crucified and buried; on the third day, that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on the Lord’s day, he rose from the dead,”

and so forth.

Cassiodorus also, senator and expositor of the sacred Psalter, writes in his chronicle:

> “In these men’s consulship our Lord Jesus Christ suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and an eclipse of the sun took place such as had never occurred before or afterward,”

and so forth.

From that first year, therefore, of Dionysius’ cycle, Justinian reigned for five years, up to the year 527 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 13.

Then Justin the Elder reigned for eight years, up to the year 519 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 40.

Then Anastasius reigned for twenty-seven years, up to the year 492 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 57.

Then Zeno reigned for seventeen years, up to the year 475 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 74.

Then Leo reigned for seventeen years, up to the year 458 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 81.

Then Marcian reigned for seven years, up to the year 451 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 108.

Then Theodosius reigned for twenty-seven years, up to the year 424 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 123.

Then Honorius reigned for fifteen years, up to the year 409 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 136.

Then Arcadius reigned for thirteen years, up to the year 396 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 147.

Then Theodosius reigned for eleven years, up to the year 385 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 153.

Gratian [reigned] for six years, up to the year 379 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 157.

Then Valens reigned for four years, up to the year 375 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 168.

Then Valentinian reigned for eleven years, up to the year 364 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 169.

Then Jovian reigned for eight months, up to the year 363 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 171.

Then Julian reigned for eleven years and eight months, up to the year 361 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 195.

Then Constantine reigned for twenty-four years, up to the year 337 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 226.

Then Constantine the Great reigned for thirty-one years, up to the year 306 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. From the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign, according to the chronicle of Eusebius or Bede. 227.

They assign the third year of the persecution—which began in Diocletian’s nineteenth year—to no one. Bishop Isidore, together with many others, also recorded this year along with the second year of Galerius Maximianus [247].

Then Diocletian reigned for twenty years, up to the year 285 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. According to the chronicle of Eusebius or Bede, however, this continued up to the year 289 of the incarnation, that is, four years longer. Thus the chronicles of Eusebius or Bede contradict the holy Gospel concerning the years of the incarnation.

Between Diocletian and the cycle of Dionysius, thirteen nineteen-year cycles lack seven years. We can investigate these years accurately according to Sacred Scripture as follows.

For Diocletian, beginning in the year 278 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, reigned for twenty years. In his nineteenth year, that is, in the year 287 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, in which Easter fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, this agrees with what Eusebius says in his chronicle:

> “In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, in the month of March, during the days of Easter, the churches [were overthrown].”

(Hieronymus.)

In the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign. In the second year of the persecution Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia, and Maximian at Milan. It therefore appears that there was one year between Diocletian and Constantine; according to many, however, there were two years, during which Galerius, Diocletian’s son-in-law, reigned.

Galerius therefore governed the third year of the persecution, beginning in Diocletian’s nineteenth year and ending in Constantine’s first year, that is, in the year 299 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Constantine, therefore, beginning in the fourth year of the persecution, reigned for thirty years and ten months, up to the year 330 of the incarnation according to Dionysius; in that year, in the third indiction, he died on the twenty-fifth day of May.

Then, according to Orosius, Constantine reigned for twenty-seven years, up to the year 357 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

In the decretal letter of Saint Pope Julius of the Apostolic See the truth is then declared as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, while the Augusti Constantine and Constans were ruling, in their fourth year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction,”

and so forth, as above (see col. 702).

Constantine died on the third day of November, as is read in the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

But if Constantius reigned for twenty-seven years according to Orosius, or if Valentinian and Valens reigned for seventeen years and Gratian for seven, or Arcadius for thirteen, as is found in the chronicle of Bishop Isidore or in Mellitus’ exposition, this cannot be established with certainty from Sacred Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] “Because,” witness 2.] That the fourth year of Constantine and Constans, which is the year 333 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, was the sixth indiction, and that the ninth year of Honorius, his eleventh consulship with Constantius’ second, which ended in the year 417 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, was the fifteenth indiction, is beyond doubt according to Scripture.

Between these two years, over four nineteen-year cycles, four years are missing.

Julian, therefore, beginning in Diocletian’s eightieth year, reigned for two years and eight months; he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of July in the year 360 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 83.

Jovian, beginning in Diocletian’s eighty-third year, reigned for eight months; he died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March in the year 361 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. [84 [Note: [Col. 0737D] Thus in the margin, 1.]]

Valentinian, beginning in Diocletian’s eighty-fourth year, reigned for eleven years and five months; he died on the seventeenth day of September in the year 372 of the incarnation according to Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0739] At this point LXXXIIII was written but later erased, 1.].

Valens, beginning in Diocletian’s ninety-fifth year, reigned for four years, up to the year 376 of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 95. [99b].

Gratian, beginning in Diocletian’s ninety-ninth year, reigned for six years, up to the year 382 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Theodosius, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and fifth year, reigned for eleven years; he died on the seventeenth day of January in the year 393 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Arcadius, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and sixteenth year, reigned for fourteen years; he died on the Kalends of May in the year 408 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Honorius, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and thirty-first year, reigned for fifteen years, up to the year 423 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

In his ninth year, which ended in the year 417 of the incarnation according to Dionysius (see year 439), although Easter ought to have fallen on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, it was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. But when the hour for baptism came, [Note: [Col. 0739] “for baptizing” is written in witness 2 and should be read here.] water did not come into the baptistery, and therefore baptism did not take place that night.

On that night, however, which dawned into the Lord’s day, the tenth day before the Kalends of May, the sacred font filled itself at the hour for baptism. This happened at the end of Honorius’ ninth year.

Theodosius, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and forty-sixth year, reigned for seventeen years, up to the year 450 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

This is how it is read in the books, as Saint Prosper testifies; at that very time he added a section to the chronicle of Eusebius:

> “In this year, that is, in Theodosius’ twenty-first year, Easter was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, as stated above” (col. 725, year 466).

Concerning this same year Paschasinus, bishop, also writes to Pope Leo, as above.

This is the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, which is the 444th year of the incarnation according to Dionysius, in which Theodosius’ twenty-first year ended.

Marcian, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and seventy-fourth year, reigned for seven years and two months, according to Roman history—that is, up to the Kalends of July in the year 457 of the incarnation according to Dionysius (see year 477).

Prosper says again:

> “In Marcian’s fifth year Rome was captured on the fourth day of the Ides of July. In that same year Easter was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, as Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, had ordained,”

and so forth.

> “Saint Pope Leo, however, declared that Easter ought rather to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May,”

and so forth.

Saint Theophilus correctly established Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of May in the year 465 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, since Easter was celebrated neither in the thirty preceding years nor in the ten following years on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

The last year, therefore, of the nineteen-year cycle is Honorius’ ninth year . . . [Note: [Col. 0739] “if likewise?”; two words are missing.] and Marcian’s fifth year.

Leo, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and eightieth year, reigned for seventeen years, up to the Kalends of July in the year 474 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Leo the Younger reigned for six months, that is, up to the Kalends of January in the same year in which Leo the Elder died. 180.

Zeno, beginning in Diocletian’s one hundred and ninety-eighth year, reigned for seventeen years, up to the year [492] of the incarnation according to Dionysius. 198.

Anastasius, beginning in Diocletian’s two hundred and fifteenth year, reigned for twenty-seven years, up to the year 518 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Justin the Elder, beginning in Diocletian’s two hundred and forty-second year, reigned for eight years, up to the year 526 of the incarnation according to Dionysius.

Justinian, beginning in Diocletian’s two hundred and fiftieth year, reigned for five years, up to the first year of Dionysius’ cycles, which is Diocletian’s two hundred and fifty-fifth year, according to the foregoing calculation of the holy men—not the year 248 according to the [unjust chronicles], but 250.

For it is certain that Constantine and Constans’ fourth year, which is the year 333 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, was the sixth indiction, as Saint Pope Julius testifies [Note: [Col. 0739] “pope” is written in witness 1; the first “pope” is a scribal error.] when he also wrote about this matter at that time.

[Note: [Col. 0739] The codex now continues in a second hand.] It is likewise certain that Honorius’ ninth year, which is the year 417 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, was the fifteenth indiction, in the eleventh consulship of Honorius and the second of Constantius, as Paschasinus, bishop, testifies together with Saint Pope Leo.

Likewise, Theodosius’ twenty-first year, which is the year 444 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, was the twelfth indiction, as the same bishop Paschasinus testifies together with Saint Pope Leo.

Also, Marcian’s fifth year was the eighth indiction, and was the year 455 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, as Saint Pope Leo likewise testifies, as above.

Therefore, Constantine and Constans’ fourth year was the sixth indiction, as the most holy Pope Julius wrote.

In Honorius’ ninth year Easter was on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, as Bishop Paschasinus testifies together with Saint Pope Leo.

In Theodosius’ twenty-first year Easter was on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, as Bishop Paschasinus testifies together with Saint Pope Leo.

In Marcian’s fifth year Easter was on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

No pope or bishop sends a letter, or writes a decretal letter, unless he himself knows [Note: [Col. 0739] “knows,” witness 1.] what he writes or sends in it.

### 555. 7. [DXXXIII]

Pope Agapitus, fifty-sixth after Peter.

(H. R.) Meanwhile Athalaric, king of the Goths, who had ruled for eight years, died. His mother Amalasuntha associated Theodahad with herself in the kingship, but after a few days Theodahad ordered her to be strangled in a bathhouse.

Because, while still alive, she had commended herself and her son to the emperor Justinian, the emperor Justinian was angry with Theodahad. To induce the emperor to forgive him this offense, Theodahad sent Pope Agapitus to him at Constantinople.

Agapitus converted the emperor, who had fallen into the heresy of Eutyches, to the faith. He also forced Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople and defender of that heresy, who denied the two natures in Christ, into exile, and consecrated Mennas bishop in his place (see the Book of the Pontiffs).

### 556. 8. [DXXXIV]

Pope Agapetus died there at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [he was buried at Rome on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0739] The words enclosed in parentheses were written later in the margin by the same, second hand.]].

Pope Silverius, fifty-seventh after Peter, [held office] for one year and two months.

[Col. 0741A] (H. R.) Meanwhile, to Africa, which the Vandals had possessed for many years, Justinian sent the patrician Belisarius with an army, and he destroyed the nation of the Vandals.

(BEDA.) Carthage also was recovered in the ninety-sixth year of its seizure, after the Vandals had been expelled and defeated and their king Gelimer [Note: [Col. 0741] Or Gelesmer?] had been defeated in battle, captured, and sent to Constantinople.

Carthage, however, had withdrawn in the year 439 of the incarnation according to Dionysius, the sixteenth year of the younger Theodosius.

(H. R.) After Agapitus died, the emperor Justinian sent the patrician Belisarius against Theodahad. When Belisarius had delayed in Sicily, Theodahad died. Wittigis succeeded him.

Belisarius, seeing that the time was unfavorable for fighting, fortified himself within the city of Rome. Wittigis, however, together with the Goths, besieged Rome for a year and plundered everything belonging to the Romans with fire and sword, including even the remains from the tombs of the saints, so that in that year mothers ate the limbs of their children from hunger.

### 557. 9. [DXXXV]

(H. R.) Then, immediately, at the command of the empress Theodora, with the consent of the emperor Justinian, Belisarius, although unwilling, expelled Pope Silverius to the island of Pontia, because he refused to restore Anthimus, the heretical bishop of Constantinople whom Pope Agapitus had expelled; Silverius died there on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July (see the Book of the Pontiffs).

### 558. 10. [DXXXVI]

Pope Vigilius, fifty-eighth after Saint Peter, held office for eighteen years and six months.

### 559. 11. [DXXXVII]

(H. R.) Belisarius, having captured Wittigis in war, brought him with him to Constantinople before the emperor Justinian.

[Col. 0741C] ### 561. 13. [DXXXIX]

(H. R.) Belisarius came to Africa again with an army.

### 562. 14. [DXL]

(H. R.) Belisarius killed Guntharic, king of the Vandals.

### 563. 15. [DXLI]

(H. R.) Belisarius brought the Vandals under the Roman state.

### 564. 16. [DXLII]

(H. R.) Belisarius, coming to Rome, presented to blessed Peter through the hands of Pope Vigilius a golden cross weighing one hundred pounds and adorned with the most precious gems, inscribed with his victories [543]. [Note: [Col. 0741] This was written in the year 569.]

### 566. 18. [DXLIV]

[Note: [Col. 0741] This passage, and those for years 567–569, were written in this year.] In the thirteenth year of the great Paschal cycle, that is, Justinian’s eighteenth year, the second year of the Lord’s Passion is contained—not earlier, that is, in the first year of the Passion and now the second.

From Christ’s Passion, therefore, up to the aforesaid year, there is a great Paschal cycle of 532 years.

### 568. 20. [DXLVI]

[At these times in Africa an Arian king of the Vandals imposed silence on bishops who would not agree with him in Arian depravity either by words or by gifts.

Nevertheless, since they did not remain silent in defense of the Church, lest they appear to have consented, the king cut out their tongues by the roots.

Yet the bishops, speaking, formed words afterward just as well as before with their tongues, saying:

> “Behold, without tongues we now speak just as well as before.”

But one of them, after falling into sexual excess, subsequently became mute.

[Note: [Col. 0741] This passage appears to have been written in the upper margin on folio 150r and associated with this year by a sign that has now been cut away.]]

### 570. 22. [DXLVIII]

[Note: [Col. 0741] This passage, for years 570–572, was written here.] (H. R.) After King Wittigis was captured, the Goths beyond the Po established Hildebad as their king; in that same year he was killed. Eraric succeeded him, and was killed before a year had passed.

### 573. 25. [DLI]

[Codex, in the margin: The second nineteen-year cycle begins, indiction 14.]

### 574. 26. [DLII]

(H. R.) Baduila, also called Totila, succeeded Eraric.

### 575. 27. [DLIII]

(H. R.) Pope Vigilius, for the same reason as his predecessor Silverius, was brought to Constantinople through the indignation of the empress by Anthimus the notary, and from there driven into exile.

(Book of the Pontiffs.) [He was later recalled to Rome, came to Sicily, died in the city of Syracuse, and was buried at Rome on the Salarian Way near Marcellus.]

### 576. 28. [DLIV]

Pope Pelagius, fifty-ninth, [held office] for eleven years and eleven months.

### 577. 29. [DLV]

[Note: [Col. 0741] This passage was written in the years 577 and 678.] (H. R.) Totila invaded all Italy with the Goths. Then, traveling through Campania and past the monastery of the holy man Benedict, he surrounded Rome with sieges [Note: [Col. 0741] “circumludit” in witness 1.]. At that time a famine almost like the preceding one occurred.

### 579. 31. [DLVII]

(H. R.) When the Romans were exhausted and unable to defend the walls, Totila entered the city through the Ostian Gate [in the thirteenth indiction, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs].

Having captured the city by night, he ordered trumpets to be sounded so that the Romans might at least briefly escape the fury of the enemy. For a short time he lived with them as a father with his children.

As may be conjectured, he acquired this kindness of spirit—though previously he had been excessively cruel—from the admonitions of the blessed Father Benedict, whom he had heard when he was about to come to Rome; Benedict rebuked Totila and foretold his death to him after nine years (see Gregory, *Dialogues* II.15).

### 580. 32. [DLVIII]

(See the Book of the Pontiffs.) Pope Pelagius began to build the church of the blessed Philip and James.

### 581. 33. [DLIX]

[P. D. II, 25.] At Rome Cassiodorus, formerly consul, then senator, and afterward a distinguished monk, was held in esteem.

[Codex, in the margin: The solar cycle begins.]

[Col. 0742D] ### 582. 34. [DLX]

(IBID.) Arator, a subdeacon, wrote out the Acts of the Apostles in Rome in hexameter verse.

### 583. 35. [DLXI]

(BED.) Victor, bishop of Capua, writing a book on Easter, refuted the errors of Victorius.

### 584. 36. [DLXII]

The most holy man Herculanus, my foster-father and bishop of the city of Perugia, was beheaded upon the wall of his city at the command of Totila, king of the Goths, and so forth. Saint Gregory said this (*Dialogues* IV.13).

At these same times the blessed Father Benedict first shone forth in the place called Sublacum, which lies forty miles from the city of Rome, and afterward in the fortress of Casinum, which is called Aurum, through the merits of his great life and apostolic virtues (P. D. II, 26). [Note: [Col. 0743] The remainder was written in the year 585.]

[The following is what Saint Gregory relates in the second book of the *Dialogue*, chapters 14 and 15.]

[Columcille fought the battle of Cúl Dreimhne [Note: [Col. 0743D] “Battle of Cúl Dreimhne”; see the annals of Tigernach in O’Connor, II, p. 142.]]

### 586. 38. [DLXIV]

(P. D. II, 23.) Priscian the grammarian was renowned at Constantinople (Book of the Pontiffs).

[Pope Pelagius died on the sixth day before the Nones of March.]

[That Saint Gregory lived in these times, he himself relates in this way in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 11:

> “The venerable man Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, also gave great proof of his holiness in our days. For, since he was very devoted to the practice of hospitality, he hid soldiers in his lodging so that they would not be killed by the Goths. The treacherous king Totila of the Goths, at a place called Merulis, where he was sitting with his army, handed him over publicly to an enormous bear that cruelly devoured human beings. But the bear licked the bishop’s feet with the gentleness of a sheep,”

and so forth.]

Roman emperor 50. Justin the Younger reigned for eleven years, that is, approximately up to the Kalends of January in the year 563 after the Lord’s Passion.

### 587. 1. [DLXV]

Pope John, sixtieth after Peter, [held office] for thirteen years.

[When Columcille of Ireland, at forty-two years of age, was about to preach in Britain [Note: [Col. 0743D] See the annals of Tigernach, cited above, p. 143, and the note on p. [Col. 0744D] 144], he afterward preached for thirty-three years.]

### 588. 2. [DLXVI]

(H. R.) The patrician Narses came to Italy, killed Totila, and restored all Italy to the Roman state.

### 589. 3. [DLXVII]

(BEDA.) Then, out of resentment from the Romans, for whom he had labored much against the Goths, he was accused before Justin and his wife Sophia of oppressing Italy. He withdrew to Naples in Campania and introduced the Lombards into Italy.

(ISID.) Leovigild, king of the Goths, brought certain rebellious regions of Spain under the power of his kingdom by conquering them.

(BEDA.) Pope John completed and dedicated the church of Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun.

### 592. 6. [DLXX]

### 593. 7. [DLXXI]

Germanus, bishop of Paris, died.

### 594. 8. [DLXXII]

(P. D. II, 13.) Fortunatus the poet was renowned in Gaul.

(ISID.) The Armenians accepted the faith of Christ.

### 596. 10. [DLXXIV]

Redemptus, distinguished bishop of the city of Ferentinum, as is read in the *Dialogue* (III.38).

### 597. 11. [DLXXV]

(P. D. III, 11.) The emperor Justin died in madness.

Roman emperor 61. Tiberius Constantine reigned for seven years, up to the year 561 after the Lord’s Passion.

### 598. 1. [DLXXVI]

(BED.) Gregory, then apocrisarius at Constantinople and afterward pope, composed an exposition of Job.

[Pope John died on the third day before the Ides of July, at the same time as Narses died (Book of the Pontiffs).]

### 599. 2. [DLXXVII]

Pope Benedict, sixty-first, [held office] for four years and two months.

[Col. 0744B] ### 600. 3. [DLXXVIII]

(BEDA.) Gregory convicted Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, in the presence of Tiberius, so that Tiberius, destroying Eutychius’ book on the resurrection through his Catholic arguments, determined that it ought to be burned in the flames.

Eutychius had written that our body in the resurrection would be intangible and more subtle than winds and air, contrary to the Lord’s statement:

> “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

(Gregory, *Dialogues* III.28.)

[In the fifteenth year, before the *Dialogues*, the Lombards killed forty captive country people because they would not eat sacrificial food with them; other captives were beheaded because they would not worship a goat’s head with them.]

### 601. 4. [DLXXIX]

(BEDA.) The nation of the Lombards, accompanied by famine and pestilence, invaded all Italy under their king Alboin and laid siege, as a devastator, even to the city of Rome.

### 602. 5. [DLXXX]

(See the Book of the Pontiffs.) Finally, when the Lombards were laying waste to everything around it and famine was abundant, Pope Benedict sent many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt and relieved Rome through an act of mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0744D] In the *Book of the Pontiffs* these things are related about the emperor Justin.]

### 603. 6. [DLXXXI]

(ISID.) The Goths, divided into two factions through Hermenegild, the son of King Leovigild, were devastated by mutual slaughter.

[Pope Benedict died on the second day before the Kalends of August (Book of the Pontiffs).]

### 604. 7. [DLXXXII]

Pope Pelagius, sixty-second, [held office] for ten years and two months.

[Saint Pope Gregory says in the *Dialogue* as follows (IV.26):

> “Ten years ago, in my monastery, the monk Gerontius, weighed down by a serious illness, dreamed that abbots and most distinguished men had descended from the heights into my monastery. One of them said to him: ‘We have come for this purpose: to send some brothers from Gregory’s monastery into military service.’ Another said to him: ‘Write down Marcellus, Valentinian, Agnellus, and others, and this Gerontius.’ They died in this way.”]

[Col. 0745A] Roman emperor 62. Maurice reigned for twenty-one years and four months, that is, up to the Kalends of May in the year 592 after the Lord’s Passion.

### 605. 1. [DLXXXIII]

(P. D. III, 20.) Pope Pelagius was ordained without the command of Maurice, because the Lombards were besieging Rome on every side, so that no one could go outside.

### 606. 2. [DLXXXIV]

(BEDA.) The Suevi [Note: [Col. 0745] Read “Suevi.”] were subjected to King Leovigild after the Goths had been conquered [Note: [Col. 0745] Read “having been conquered.”].

### 607. 3. [DLXXXV]

(BEDA.) Hermenegild [Note: [Col. 0745] Written in the years 607–609.], son of Leovigild, king of the Goths, was deprived by his Arian father of his kingdom because of his unshakable confession of the Catholic faith, and was thrown into chains and prison.

At last, on the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, struck on the head with an axe, he deserved to possess the heavenly kingdom as king and martyr in place of an earthly one.

His brother Reccared, as soon as he received the kingdom after his father, converted all the Gothic people over whom he ruled to the Catholic faith, at the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, who had also instructed Hermenegild.

[Codex, in the margin: The solar cycle begins.]

### 610. 6. [DLXXXVIII]

(P. D. III, 20.) Pope Pelagius sent a very useful letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; Saint Gregory, while still a deacon, composed it.

[Codex, in the margin: The fourth nineteen-year cycle begins, indiction 7.]

### 611. 7. [DLXXXIX]

[Note: [Col. 0745] Written in the years 611–613.] (See P. D. IV, 49.) (*Life of Saint Columba.*) The holy Father Columbanus came from the island of Ireland of the Scots into Burgundy with Saint Gall and several other approved disciples. There, with the permission of King Theuderic, he built the monastery called Luxeuil.

Afterward, driven out by Brunhilda, he entered Alemannia, where he left Saint Gall. He himself, crossing into Italy, built the monastery called Bobbio, where he became the father of many monks.

### 614. 10. [DXCII]

(P. D. III, 23.) At this time, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, a new flood occurred, so that the river Tiber flowed over the walls of the city of Rome. Along the channel of that same river, together with a great multitude of snakes, a dragon of extraordinary size descended through the city as far as the sea [Col. 0745D].

The pestilence called the bubonic plague immediately followed this flood, so that few survived from the multitude. Pope Pelagius was the first to die in it [on the eighth day before the Ides of February].

### 615. 11. [DXCIII]

(P. D. III, 24.) Pope Gregory, sixty-third, held office for thirteen years and six months.

He was chosen by everyone during this tribulation. When he ordered a sevenfold litany, eighty people suddenly died in a single hour while they were praying to God.

It is called a sevenfold litany because the people were arranged in seven orders: first, the clergy; second, abbots with monks; third, abbesses with their communities; fourth, children; fifth, all laymen; sixth, widows; seventh, married women.

### 616. 12. [DXCIV]

(ISID.) The Avars, fighting against the Romans, were driven away more by gold than by weapons.

Gregory says in the *Dialogue* (IV.55):

> “Three years ago, in my monastery, a monk named Justus, a physician, shortly before his death informed his brother, whose name was Copiosus and who also served him, that he secretly possessed three gold pieces. We had him buried with them in the dung heap,”

and so forth.

> “In that same year, when the monk had been buried by us, he called the monk John, who remained at the tomb after we had left, and, pale and trembling, reported to us; ten days later he died.”

### 617. 13. [DXCXV]

(BEDA.) In the thirteenth year of Maurice’s reign, in the thirteenth indiction, Pope Gregory gathered twenty-four bishops in synod at the body of the blessed Apostle Peter and issued decrees concerning the needs of the Church [Note: [Col. 0745] “Is missing?” Witness 2 adds here: “Among other things, also this: ‘In the holy Roman Church, over which divine providence has willed me to preside,’ etc.” These words were added later in codex 1, fol. 170; see above, p. 490, n. 42.]

(GREG. D. III.30.)

[Two years before the *Dialogues*, when a church of the Arians near Rome, in a place called Subura, was being consecrated as a Catholic church, the relics of Saint Sebastian and Saint Agatha were brought into it. The devil passed through the people outside in the form of a pig. A few days later a cloud descended from heaven and filled the whole church with a marvelous fragrance.]

### 618. 14. [DXCXVI]

(P. D. IV, 18.) The monastery of Saint Benedict the abbot was invaded by the Lombards at night. The monks fled to Rome, carrying with them the book of the holy Rule, a measure of bread, and a measure of wine.

### 619. 15. [DXCXVII]

(See the Book of the Pontiffs.) Gregory added to the Mass the words “And our days” through “to be numbered among the flock.”

[Five years after the river Tiber left its channel and flowed over the walls of the city of Rome, Saint Gregory composed the *Dialogue*, as he himself testifies in Book III, chapter 19 (Dial. III.19).]

[Gregory says in the *Dialogue* (III.16):

> “Recently also, in a part of Campania, a highly venerable man named Martin led a solitary life on Mount Narsicus. He fastened an iron chain [Note: [Col. 0745] Written twice in witness 1.] to his foot and attached it at the other end to a rock, so that he would not go farther away. When the venerable man Benedict, whose memory I mentioned above, heard this, he arranged through his disciple to send him this message: ‘If you are a servant of God, let not a chain of iron hold you, but the chain of Christ.’”

At these words Martin loosened the chain and afterward never went farther than the length of the chain.

Redemptus, bishop of the city of Ferentinum, who died about seven years ago, told me, while I was still living in my monastery, that in the time of my predecessor, Pope John, the martyr Yuticius, while he was sleeping, said to him beside his tomb:

> “Redemptus, are you awake?”

He replied:

> “I am awake.”

And he said three times:

> “The end has come for all flesh.”

Soon afterward the Lombards entered that land and brought about its end.]

### 620. 16. [DXCXVIII]

(BEDA.) Gregory converted the Angles to Christ by sending Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with several other God-fearing monks, to Britain.

[Columbanus died.]

### 621. 17. [DXCXIX]

(BEDA.) Indeed, after Æthelberht had believed, together with his people of Kent over whom he ruled and the neighboring provinces, he also endowed Augustine, his bishop and teacher, and the other prelates with episcopal sees.

But the peoples of the Angles situated north of the River Humber under the kings Ælle and Æthelfrith had not yet heard the word of life.

### 622. 18. [DC]

[Note: [Col. 0747] Written in the years 622–624.] (BEDA.) In the eighteenth year of Maurice, in the fourth indiction, Gregory decreed, writing to Augustine—and likewise to the bishops of London and York—that, after receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See, they should be metropolitans.

In Gregory’s *Life* (VII.63):

> “We read that the Apostles sang nothing else at Mass except the Lord’s Prayer.”

### 625. 21. [DCIII]

(P. D. IV, 27.) The emperor Maurice was killed, together with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus.

If the holy Father Benedict the abbot died, as his biographers write [Note: [Col. 0747] This seems to refer to the *Life of Saint Maurus*; see Mabillon, *Acta* I, p. CXII.], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Holy Saturday of Easter, he appears to have died in this year.

For unless he died ninety-six years before this year, his death cannot be placed here; at that time, if he had been born, he would have been very young, whereas in this year he could have died at approximately ninety years of age.

[Col. 0747C] Roman emperor 63. Phocas reigned for eight years, up to the Kalends of May in the year 600 after the Lord’s Passion.

### 626. 1. [DCIV]

The image of Phocas was brought to Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, as is read in the *Life of Saint Gregory* (IV.20). After the clergy and senate had acclaimed it in the Basilica of Julius, it was placed, at the command of Saint Gregory, in the Basilica of Saint Caesarius, established in the Lateran Palace.

### 627. 2. [DCV]

(See the Book of the Pontiffs.) Saint Pope Gregory died on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the eighth indiction.

### 628. 3. [DCVI]

Pope Sabinian, sixty-fourth, [held office] for one year and ten months.

[Codex, in the margin: The fourth nineteen-year cycle ends in indiction 11.]

### 629. 4. [DCVII]

(Book of the Pontiffs.) [Pope Sabinian died on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.]

(ISID.) [Civil wars arose between Prasini and Veneti throughout the East and Egypt, and they struck one another down in mutual slaughter.]

### 630. 5. [DCVIII]

(See the Book of the Pontiffs.) Pope Boniface, sixty-fifth [Note: [Col. 0747] “LXIV. 1?”], [held office] for ten months.

He obtained from the emperor Phocas that the Roman Apostolic See should be the head of the Church, whereas previously Constantinople had declared itself first of all.

(Book of the Pontiffs.) [He established in the church of blessed Peter, with seventy-two bishops, thirty-three priests, deacons, and all the clergy, under anathema, that no one should presume to speak or form a faction for himself while a pontiff or bishop was alive, but only on the third day after his deposition. Then, with the clergy and servants of the Church assembled, an election should take place.]

Pope Boniface died on the third day before the Ides of December.

### 631. 6. [DCIX]

Pope Boniface, sixty-sixth [Note: [Col. 0747] “LXV. 1?”], [held office] for six years and nine months.

### 632. 7. [DCX]

(P. D. IV, 37.) This man obtained from Phocas that, in the ancient temple called the Pantheon, built by the emperor Domitian, a church of All Saints should be consecrated, where the worship of all the gods had been conducted.

633. 8. [DCXI] (Ibid.) The Persians, waging extremely serious wars against the Roman state, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself; destroying churches and profaning holy things, they also carried away, among the ornaments of sacred or public places, the banner of the Lord’s cross. Heraclius, who ruled Africa, deprived Phocas of his life.

Among the Romans, Heraclius 64 reigned for 27 years, that is, until 1 May in the year 627 after the Passion of the Lord.

634. 1. [DCXII] (Bede) Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0747] These entries were written for the years 634–636], a Persian monk, later nobly suffering martyrdom for Christ. Born in Persia, as a boy he learned magical arts from his father. But when he had learned the name of Christ the Savior from Christian captives, he immediately turned to him with his whole heart. [Pope Boniface died on 25 May.] (Book of the Pontiffs)

637. 4. [DCXV] Deusdedit, also called Theodatus, 67, pope for four years.

638. 5. [DCXVI] (Bede) Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0747] These entries were written for the years 638–648], having left Persia, sought Chalcedon and Hierapolis in search of Christ, and then proceeded to Jerusalem. There, having been baptized four miles from the city, he entered the monastery of Abbot Anastasius, in which he lived according to the rule for seven years. When he had come to Caesarea in Palestine for the sake of prayer, he was captured by the Persians and suffered many beatings for a long time amid imprisonment and chains at the hands of the commander Marzaban. At last he was sent to Persia, to their king Chosroes, by whom he was beaten three times at intervals. Finally he was suspended by one hand for three hours of the day and then beheaded; thus, together with seventy others, he completed his martyrdom. Soon afterward, a demoniac wearing his tunic was cured. Meanwhile, Prince Heraclius arrived with an army, defeated the Persians, and joyfully brought back the Christians who had been taken captive. The relics of blessed martyr Anastasius were first brought to his own monastery and then to Rome; they are venerated in the monastery of blessed Paul the apostle, which is called “at the Salvian Waters.”

640. 7. [DCXVIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Pope Deusdedit established a second Mass among the clergy. At the same time, a very great earthquake occurred in August, in indiction 6. After this there followed a plague among the people, namely an outbreak of scabies, so severe that no one could recognize his own dead; and Pope Deusdedit died on 8 November.]

641. 8. [DCXIX] Boniface 68 was pope for five years.

645. 12. [DCXXIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Boniface died on 25 October. He established that no one should be dragged from the church.]

646. 13. [DCXXIV] Honorius 69 was pope for twelve years.

[In the margin of the codex: The sixth decennial cycle begins, indiction 15.]

649. 16. [DCXXVII] (Bede) In the sixteenth year of Heraclius, indiction 15 [Note: [Col. 0749] These entries were written for the years 649–653], Edwin, king of the English in Britain, of the Northumbrian people, received, together with his people, the word of salvation, while Paulinus the bishop preached; Paulinus had been sent from Kent by Archbishop Justus. In the eleventh year of his reign—about 230 years, more or less, after the arrival of the English in Britain—he accomplished this. He himself gave Paulinus the episcopal see of York. As an omen of the faith to come and of the kingdom of heaven, earthly power also increased for that king; for he was the first of all the English to subject the whole of Britain to himself.

654. 21. [DCXXXII] (Bede) At that time [Note: [Col. 0749] These entries were written for the years 654–659] an error of fourteen years arose among the Scots in their observance of Easter. Pope Honorius rebuked them by letter; John also, who succeeded his successor Severinus, argued the same point. While he had still been elected to the pontificate, he wrote to them concerning that same Easter. John also wrote against the Pelagian heresy, which was reviving among them.

657. 24. [DCXXXV] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Pope Honorius died on 12 October; the episcopate was vacant for one year, seven months, and seventeen days.]

Severinus 70 was pope for one year. [Pope Severinus died on 2 August.] (Book of the Pontiffs)

658. 25. [DCXXXVI] John 71 was pope for one year and ten months.

659. 26. [DCXXXVII] (Isidore) The Jews in Spain were made Christians. For Sisibut, the most glorious king of the Goths, subjected by warfare many Roman provinces in Spain and cities of the Roman military, and converted the Jews who were subjects of his kingdom to the faith of Christ.

[Col. 0749D] 660. 27. [DCXXXVIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Pope John died on 12 October.] (P. D. IV, 51) Heraclius died at Constantinople.

Among the Romans, Heraclonas 65, son of Heraclius, reigned with Martina for two years, until the year 629 after the Passion.

661. 1. [DCXXXIX] (Bede) Theodore 72 was pope for six years and six months. Cyrus of Alexandria, and Sergius and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, reviving the heresy of the acephali, asserted as doctrine that there was one operation of divinity and humanity in Christ and one will.

[Col. 0750A] Of these, Pyrrhus came to Rome during these times under Pope Theodore from Africa. With a repentance that later proved feigned, he presented to that pope, in the presence of all the clergy and people, a document bearing his signature, in which everything that he or his predecessors had written or done against the Catholic faith was condemned. Therefore he was kindly received by him as though he were the pontiff of the imperial city. But because, after returning home, he resumed his domestic error, the aforementioned Pope Theodore summoned all the priests and clergy to the church of blessed Peter the apostle and condemned him under the bond of anathema.

662. 2. [DCXL] In these times Isidore, the bishop of Hispania, was held in high regard.

Among the Romans, Constantine 66, son of Heraclius, reigned for six months, almost until 1 November in the year 629 after the Passion.

(Bede) Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, afflicted Catholics not only with the insane doctrine of his predecessors but also through open persecution. He harmed the representatives of the holy Roman Church, who had been sent to correct him, some by imprisonment, some by exile, and some by beatings. He also overturned and plundered their altar, consecrated in the house of Placidia, in the venerable oratory, forbidding them to celebrate Mass there. Therefore he too, like his predecessors, was condemned by the apostolic see with the just punishment of deposition.

Among the Romans, Constantine 67, son of Constantine, reigned for 28 years, until the year 657 after the Passion.

[Col. 0750C] 663. 1. [DCXLI] (Bede) He was deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been by the aforementioned bishop Sergius. For this man published a Type against the Catholic faith, defining that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ should be believed, as though Christ should be believed to have neither will nor operation.

666. 4. [DCXLIV] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Theodore died on 14 May.

[In the margin of the codex: The solar cycle begins.]

667. 5. [DCXLV] Martin 73 was pope for six years and two months.

668. 6. [DCXLVI] [In the margin of the codex: The seventh decennial cycle begins, indiction 4.]

669. 7. [DCXLVII] (Bede) Pope Martin [Note: [Col. 0749] Written for the years 669–672], on account of the aforementioned heresy, assembled a synod of 105 bishops at Rome. In that synod he condemned under anathema Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, the aforementioned heretical bishops. The synod was held in the ninth year of the reign of Constantine, in October, indiction 7. (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) After this, the emperor sent the exarch Theodore, who removed Pope Martin from the Constantinian church and brought him to Constantinople. From there he was sent into exile at Cherson in the province of Lycia, where he died on 10 November; he shines there with many signs of virtue.

[Col. 0751A] 673. 11. [DCLI] Eugenius 74 was pope for two years and ten months.

674. 12. [DCLII] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Eugenius died on 2 January.

675. 13. [DCLIII] Vitalian 75 was pope for fourteen years and six months.

676. 14. [DCLIV] (Bede) When Pope Vitalian had recently been ordained, the emperor Constantine sent blessed Peter the apostle golden Gospels, wonderfully ornamented around the edges with immense white gems.

682. 20. [DCLX] (Bede) He himself [Note: [Col. 0751] It is clear that these entries, written in different years (676–686), are to be joined together] came to Rome after several years [Note: [Col. 0751] “several”: 1], [on 5 July, on the fourth day of the week, indiction 6].

683. 21. [DCLXI] Then [Note: [Col. 0751] It is clear that these entries, written in different years (676–686), are to be joined together] he offered [on Sunday] upon the altar of Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold.

[Col. 0751B] 684. 22. [DCLXII] And [Note: [Col. 0751] It is clear that these entries, written in different years (676–686), are to be joined together] he entered the church with his entire army carrying candles.

685. 23. [DCLXIII] But this [Note: [Col. 0751] It is clear that these entries, written in different years (676–686), are to be joined together] took place in indiction 6, in the twenty-third year of the reign of Emperor Constantine.

686. 24. [DCLXIV] In the following year [Note: [Col. 0751] It is clear that these entries, written in different years (676–686), are to be joined together] there was a solar eclipse, remembered by our age, at about the tenth hour of the day, on 3 May. [Bede]

687. 25. [DCLXV]

[In the margin of the codex: The eighth decennial cycle begins, indiction 8.]

688. 26. [DCLXVI] (Bede) Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, a man equally learned, sent by Vitalian, enriched many churches of the English with the fruits of ecclesiastical learning.

[Col. 0751C] 689. 27. [DCLXVII] (Book of the Pontiffs) When Constantine had offered the pallium, he remained in Rome for twelve days. Then, in indiction 7, he entered Sicily, where he remained until indiction 12.

690. 28. [DCLXVIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) In that indiction he was killed by his own men in Sicily [on 15 July] in a bath. Not long afterward Pope Vitalian died [on 27 January].

Among the Romans, Constantine 68, son of the preceding Constantine, reigned for seventeen years, until the year 674 after the Passion.

691. 1. [DCLXIX] (Book of the Pontiffs) Adeodatus 76 was pope after Peter for four years and two months [he died on 26 June].

[Col. 0751D] 692. 2. [DCLXX] (Bede) The Saracens invaded Sicily; after carrying off enormous booty with them, they soon returned to Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0751] Written for the year 693].

694. 4. [DCLXXII] This Emperor Constantine instituted the sixth synod.

[In the margin of the codex: The solar cycle begins.]

695. 5. [DCLXXIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Conon 77 was pope after Peter for one year and six months [he died on 11 April].

696. 6. [DCLXXIV] The island of Ireland is considered sublimely filled with countless holy marvels of the saints.

[Col. 0752A] 697. 7. [DCLXXV] Pope Agatho 78 was pope after Peter for two years and seven months.

698. 8. [DCLXXVI] (Bede) At the request of the most devout emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, Pope Agatho sent his representatives to the imperial city. Among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward a bishop, to bring about the union of the holy churches of God. They [Note: [Col. 0752D] In the margin these words are written (Book of the Pontiffs): “When they entered the imperial city, that is, Constantinople, on 10 November, indiction 9; on 18 November, a Sunday, they were honorably summoned to the emperor Constantine’s procession. On 17 February, a Sunday, Patriarch Gregory was questioned concerning the Catholic faith”], having been received most graciously by Constantine, the most reverent defender of the Catholic faith, were ordered to investigate the true faith in peaceful discussion, with philosophical disputes set aside; they were given from the Constantinopolitan library all the books of the ancient Fathers that they requested.

One hundred and fifty bishops were also present, with George, patriarch of the imperial city, presiding, and Macarius of Antioch. Those who asserted that there was one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified many statements of the Catholic Fathers. When the dispute had ended, George was corrected, while Macarius, together with his followers and his predecessors—Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—was anathematized. In his place Theophanius, an abbot from Sicily, was made bishop of Antioch.

Such grace accompanied the representatives of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, celebrated the public Mass in Latin on the Sunday of Easter week in the church of Holy Wisdom, in the presence of the emperor and patriarch.

This is the sixth universal synod, celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, in the time of Pope Agatho, under the direction and presidency of the most devout Emperor Constantine within his palace, with the representatives of the apostolic see and 150 bishops likewise in session.

The first universal synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, with 318 Fathers, in the time of Pope Sylvester, under Constantine the Great. The second was held at Constantinople, with 150 Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city. The third was held at Ephesus, with 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the emperor Theodosius the Great and Pope Celestine. The fourth was held at Chalcedon, with 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo, in the time of Emperor Marcian. The fifth likewise took place at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius, under Emperor Justinian, against Theodore [Col. 0752D] and all heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] On folio 154, in the upper margin, these words are written: [Col. 0753A] “Arius said that the Father was greater, the Son lesser, and that the Holy Spirit was a creature. Macedonius denied the Holy Spirit. Nestorius said that Holy Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being. Eutyches, the Constantinopolitan abbot, said that Christ, through the assumption of humanity, did not exist from two natures, but that only the divine nature remained in him. Theodore said that the Word was one God and Christ another, and that Mary was not the mother of God. Macarius, the bishop of Constantinople, said that there was one will and one operation in Christ.”] This is the sixth.

[Pope Agatho died on 10 January.] (Book of the Pontiffs) [In the time of Pope Agatho, indiction 8, the moon underwent an eclipse on 18 June.]

[Col. 0753A] 699. 9. [DCLXXVII] (Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Leo 79 was pope for eleven months [Note: [Col. 0753] “Before ‘months’ was written, but it has been erased: one year]. 700. 10. [DCLXXVIII] The holy priest Bede, an English computist, was held in high regard in these times.

701. 11. [DCLXXIX] Pope Benedict 80 was pope for four years and ten months.

702. 12. [DCLXXX] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) From an early age he served in the Church, and he always proved himself a lover of poverty for Christ.

703. 13. [DCLXXXI] (Bede) The holy virgin Æthelthryth [Note: [Col. 0753] Written for the years 703–705], daughter of King Anna of the English, was joined to three distinguished men. After sixteen years of burial, her body and the garment in which she had been wrapped were found incorrupt.

706. 16. [DCLXXXIV] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Benedict died [after Easter] on 8 May and was buried at blessed Peter.

707. 17. [DCLXXXV] (Book of the Pontiffs) John 81 was pope for one year and one month. [In his time Justinian reigned, after his father, the Augustus, had died, at the beginning of September, indiction 14. Pope John died on 2 August.]

[Col. 0753D] Among the Romans, Justinian the Younger 69, son of Constantine, reigned for ten years, until the year 684 after the Passion.

708. 1. [DCLXXXVI] (Bede) Pope Conon 82 was pope for one year and eleven months.

709. 2. [DCLXXXVII] The holy Scot Kilian, born on the island of Ireland and bishop of Würzburg, was held in high regard. [Pope Conon died on 21 September.]

710. 3. [DCLXXXVIII] (Book of the Pontiffs) Sergius 83 was pope for thirteen years and nine months. Pepin, son of Ansegisus and Arnulf, ruled the Franks for 27 years.

[Col. 0754A] 711. 4. [DCLXXXIX] (Bede) Justinian [Note: [Col. 0753] Written for the years 711–713] established peace with the Saracens for ten years, by land and sea. The province of Africa was also subjected to the Roman Empire; it had been held by the Saracens, and Carthage itself was captured and destroyed by them.

712. 5. [DCXC] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Pope Sergius established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, the Agnus Dei should be sung by the clergy.]

714. 7. [DCXCII] (Bede) Because Pope Sergius had refused to favor or subscribe to the heretical synod that Justinian had held at Constantinople, Justinian sent his protospatharius Zacharias and ordered Sergius to be transported to Constantinople. But the army of the city of Ravenna and the neighboring regions forestalled the emperor’s wicked commands [Note: [Col. 0753] Written for the year 715], and drove that same Zacharias from the city of Rome with insults and injuries.

716. 9. [DCXCIV] (Bede) Pope Sergius ordained the venerable man Willibrord, surnamed Clement, bishop for the Frisian people; he was born in Britain and of English descent.

717. 10. [DCXCV] (Bede) Justinian, deprived of the glory of the kingdom because of his faithlessness, withdrew into exile in Pontus.

Among the Romans, Leo reigned for three years, until the year 686 after the Passion of the Lord.

718. 1. [DCXCVI] (Bede) Pope Sergius found, through a revelation from the Lord, in a very dark corner of the shrine of blessed Peter the apostle, a silver chest that had lain there for a very long time. In it was a cross adorned with various and very precious stones. When four panels containing gems of immense size were removed, he saw inside a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross. From that time onward, every year on the day of its Exaltation, all the people kiss and venerate it in the Basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana.

719. 2. [DCXCVII] (Bede) The most reverend Cuthbert, bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne in Britain, formerly an anchorite, led a life distinguished by signs of miracles from childhood into old age. Although his body remained buried for eleven years, it was afterward found incorrupt, almost as though at the very hour of his death, together with the garment in which it had been covered.

720. 3. [DCXCVIII] (P. D. VI, 13) Tiberius rose up against Leo and invaded his kingdom; he kept him under guard in the same city for as long as he himself reigned.

Among the Romans, Tiberius 71 reigned for seven years, until the year 694 after the Passion of the Lord.

721. 1. [DCXCIX] (Bede) The synod of Aquileia, because of ignorance concerning the faith, hesitated to accept the fifth universal council until, instructed by the saving admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed and consented to this council together with the other churches of Christ [Note: [Col. 0753] Written for the year 722].

722. 2. [DCC]

[Col. 0755A] [In the margin of the codex: The solar cycle begins.]

723. 3. [DCCI] (Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Sergius died on 9 September [indiction 14].

724. 4. [DCCII] John 84 was pope for three years and three months.

[In the margin of the codex: The tenth decennial cycle begins, indiction 1.]

725. 5. [DCCIII] In the book On Times, in the year in which he composed it, the priest Bede says as follows (chapter 14):

“If you wish to know how many years there are from the incarnation of the Lord according to Dionysius, find out how many cycles of indictions there have been; for example, in the present year, the fifth of Tiberius, 46. Multiply these by 15: they make 690. Always add the regular number 12, because according to Dionysius the Lord was born in indiction 4, and add the indiction of whatever year you wish—for example, in the present year, one—and they make 703. These are the years from the birth of the Lord according to Dionysius.”

Thus Bede.

726. 6. [DCCIV] (Bede) Gisulf, duke of the Lombard people at Benevento, devastated Campania with fire, sword, and captivity. Since there was no one able to resist his attack, the apostolic Pope John, who had succeeded Sergius, sent priests to him with very many gifts; he redeemed all the captives and made the enemy return home. Pope John died in indiction 3, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs. (Book of the Pontiffs)

727. 7. [DCCV] (Bede) Pope John 85 was pope for two years and eight months. Among many distinguished works, Pope John built, with exceptionally beautiful workmanship, an oratory to the holy Mother of God within the church of blessed Peter [Col. 0755C] the apostle. King Herebert of the Lombards restored to the jurisdiction of that see many estates and patrimonies of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the rights of the apostolic see but had long been taken away by the Lombards; he sent this donation, written in golden letters, to Rome.

Among the Romans, Justinian II reigned together with his son Tiberius for six years, until the year 700 after the Passion.

728. 1. [DCCVI] (Bede) Having recovered his kingdom with the aid of Interpellus, king of the Bulgars, he killed the patricians who had expelled him, as well as Leo, who had usurped his place, and his successor Tiberius, in the time of Pope John, according to the Acts of the Pontiffs. He sent Gallinicus, the patriarch, to Rome with his eyes torn out, and gave the episcopate to Cyrus, who had been an abbot in Pontus and had supported him in exile. [Pope John died on 18 October, indiction 6.]

729. 2. [DCCVII] (Book of the Pontiffs) Sisinnius 86 was pope after Peter for one month. [Pope Sisinnius died on 6 November.]

730. 3. [DCCVIII] Constantine 87 was pope for seven years and one month.

731. 4. [DCCIX] Justinian ordered Pope Constantine to come to him; he received him honorably and sent him back. He ordered him to celebrate Mass for him on Sunday and received Communion from his hand. Prostrate on the ground, he asked him to intercede for his sins, and he renewed all the privileges of the Church.

732. 5. (Bede) When he sent an army into Pontus [Note: [Col. 0755] “When,” to be joined with the year 731], to capture Philippicus, whom he had left there, the entire army, despite the apostolic pope’s strong opposition, went over to Philippicus’s side and made him emperor there.

733. 6. [DCCX] Returning with him to Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0755] To be joined with the year 731], he fought against Justinian at the twelfth milestone from the city. After Justinian had been defeated and killed, Philippicus assumed the kingdom.

(Book of the Pontiffs) [At the command of Emperor Justinian, Pope Constantine left Rome on 5 October, indiction 9, and came to Hydruntum, where he delayed because it was winter. Emperor Justinian then ordered the pope from Nicaea in Bithynia to come to Nicomedia to meet the king arriving from Nicaea. There the pope and the king met together. The pope departed from Nicomedia and entered Rome on 24 October, indiction 10; then, after three months, he learned that Philippicus had killed Justinian.]

Among the Romans, Philippicus reigned for one year and six months, until the year 702 after the Passion of the Lord.

734. 1. [DCCXII] (Bede) He expelled Cyrus from the pontificate and ordered him to return to Pontus to govern his monastery in the capacity of an abbot. He sent letters of erroneous doctrine to Pope Constantine, who rejected them together with the council of the apostolic see. For this reason he caused paintings to be made in the portico of Saint Peter, containing the acts of the six holy universal synods. For when Philippicus ordered similar paintings to be removed from the imperial city, the Roman people decreed that they would accept neither the name of the heretical emperor nor his documents or the image of his coin. Accordingly, neither was his likeness brought into the church nor was his name pronounced at Mass.

735. 2. [DCCXIII] (P. D. VI, 34) Anastasius rose up against him and deprived him of both his kingdom and his eyes.

Among the Romans, Anastasius reigned for three years, until the year 7 after the Passion of the Lord.

736. 1. [DCCXIV] (Bede) He sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, the patrician and exarch of Italy, in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a preacher of the holy sixth council. [Pope Constantine died on 8 January.] (Book of the Pontiffs)

737. 2. [DCCXV] Gregory 88 was pope for eighteen years and ten months. He was a chaste and wise man who ordained Boniface, whose father and mother were Scots, bishop for the see of Mainz. Through him he preached the word of salvation in Germany and illumined that people, sitting in darkness, with the evangelical light. (Book of the Pontiffs)

[This Boniface was sent from Ireland together with Willibrord, an English bishop, as is read in his Life by Willibrord [Col. 0757A] [Note: [Col. 0757] These words were written in the lower margin of folio 155, where the following also appear: “Pope Constantine, at the command …,” etc., which we placed above under the year 733; then: “Of Gregory,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0757D] See the Life of Boniface by its author Willibrord, chapter 6.] [In the time of Pope Gregory, indiction 14, the moon was seen reddened until midnight.] (Book of the Pontiffs) This Gregory lived in the times of the emperors Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo.]

Pepin, son of Ausgisius, called Anchises the Trojan by name, reigned among the Franks in Gaul and died. His son Charles, also called “the Mayor of the Palace,” succeeded him in the kingdom for 27 years, until his sons Carloman and Pepin, the first emperors of the Franks. (Bede) Liutprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed, at the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps that King Herebert had made and Liutprand had reclaimed. Ecgberht, a holy man and priest of the English people, adorned by monastic and pilgrim life, converted by devout preaching many provinces of the Scottish people to the canonical observance of the time of Easter, from which they had long strayed, in the year 716 from the incarnation of the Lord according to Dionysius.

738. 3. [DCCXVI] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0757] The same material, written later for the year 737, had formerly been recorded here but has now been erased] established that during Lent there should be fasting and the celebration of Mass, which had not existed before him.

Among the Romans, Theodosius reigned for one year, until the year 705 after the Passion of the Lord.

739. 1. [DCCXVII] (P. D. VI, 36) When the emperor Anastasius Augustus sent an army with a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens, he turned back halfway through the journey and made Theodosius emperor, compelling him and confirming him on the imperial throne. Theodosius later defeated Anastasius in a severe battle near Nicaea, in which seven thousand of the army fell. After Anastasius had been captured and had given him an oath, he had him made a cleric and ordained a priest. But when Theodosius began to reign, since he was a Catholic, he immediately restored in the imperial city to its former place that venerable image depicting the six holy synods, which Philippicus had removed.

(Bede) The river Tiber, overflowing its channel [indiction 15], caused much destruction at Rome, rising in the Via Lata to a height of one and a half statures, so that the waters descending from the gate of Saint Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge joined together. It remained for seven days, until, when the citizens had performed frequent litanies, it finally receded on [lacuna]. Bede says as follows:

“Many English came from Britain to Rome, among them also my most reverend abbot Ceolfrith, aged 74, who had been a priest for 47 years and an abbot for 35 years. When he reached Langres, he died and was buried in the church of the Twin Martyrs. Among other gifts, he sent to the church of Saint Peter a Pandect translated by blessed Jerome into Latin from a Hebrew or Greek source.”

[Col. 0758A] Among the Romans, Leo reigned for nine years, and thereafter for fifteen years, until Pepin, the first emperor of the Franks—that is, until the year 729 after the Passion of the Lord.

740. 1. [DCCXVIII]

741. 2. [DCCXIX] (Bede) The Saracens [Note: [Col. 0757] These entries were written for the years 741–747] besieged Constantinople [the city] with an immense army for three years, until the citizens, with great persistence in prayer, cried out to God. Then very many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, and pestilence. The Saracens, weary of the siege, withdrew. Afterward, on their return, they attacked in war the people of the Bulgars, who live beyond the Danube. Defeated by them also, they fled and returned to their ships [Note: [Col. 0757] This was written for the year 747. “They proceed” belongs to the year 755.]

[Col. 0758B] [In the margin of the codex: The eleventh nineteen-year cycle begins, indiction 5.]

744. 5. [DCCXXII]

745. 6. [DCCXXIII] The oath of the holy Scottish archbishop Boniface (Council III, p. 1857), in the church of Saint Peter the apostle before Pope Gregory II, in the sixth year of Emperor Leo and also of Constantine, his son, as emperor.

747. 8. [DCCXXV] In this year Bede the computist composed a shorter book of computation, as he himself testifies:

“If you wish to know how many epacts there are for each individual year, take the years of the Lord according to Dionysius, however many they are—for example, in the present eighth indiction, 725. Divide by nineteen: nineteen times thirty is 570; nineteen times eight is 150 plus two; three remain. Multiply these three again by ten: they make thirty-three. Remove thirty: three remain. These three are the epacts of the present year.”

Thus says Bede (On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 50).

749. 10. [DCCXXVII] Another letter of the same Pope Gregory II [Note: [Col. 0758D] That is, of the pope mentioned under the year 745] to Boniface (Council III, p. 1858), dated 22 November, in the tenth year of Leo’s reign and also the eighth year of Constantine’s reign, indiction 10, and so forth.

753. 14. [DCCXXXI] (Book of the Pontiffs) [Pope Gregory died on 11 February, indiction 14, while Leo and Constantine were emperors.]

754. 15. [DCCXXXII] Gregory 89 was pope for eleven years.

755. 16. [DCCXXXIII] (Bede) The aforementioned Saracens [Col. 0759A] [Note: [Col. 0759D] See the year 741], when they were making for the open sea, were overtaken by a sudden storm; many of them were drowned and killed. For many of their ships were wrecked and broken apart along the shores [Note: [Col. 0759] Written for the year 756].

757. 18. [DCCXXXV] (Bede) Liutprand [Note: [Col. 0759] Written for the years 757–759], king of the Lombards, heard that the Saracens were corrupting the holy places. He heard that, after Sardinia had been devastated, they had also defiled the places where the bones of Saint Augustine, bishop, had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the devastation of the barbarians. Therefore he sent agents, and, after paying a great price, obtained them and transferred them to Pavia; there he buried them with the honor due to so great a father.

759. 20. [DCCXXXVII] Bede the computist died on 31 December.

[Col. 0759B] 760. 21. [DCCXXXVIII] (cf. Book of the Pontiffs) The aforementioned Pope Gregory established in the Mass: “whose solemnity is today [Note: [Col. 0759] Written for the year 761],” and so forth, up to “receive us, giver, through Christ our Lord.” (A. of Hersfeld) [Beginning of Herolvesfeld.]

762. 23. [DCCXL] (Book of the Pontiffs) He himself died on 28 November and was buried in the church of blessed Peter.

[Letter of Gregory III to Boniface the Scot, archbishop of Mainz (Council, Mansi edition XII, p. 285), dated 29 October, in the twenty-third year of Leo’s reign and the twentieth year of Constantine, his son, indiction 8.]

(Book of the Pontiffs) [Gregory [Note: [Col. 0759] Written in the margin for the year 1] the Third lived in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine, while the persecution was raging that they had initiated for the deposition and destruction of the sacred images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God, and of all the holy apostles, saints, martyrs, and confessors. For the pope, so that they might come to their senses and abandon this error, sent the decrees of the apostolic see through the priest George. Because, out of fear of the emperors, George did not return with them to Constantinople, the pope sent him again from Rome to the imperial city, and he delivered the same decrees a second time. He retained in part the writings in the island of Sicily, did not allow them to be taken farther to Constantinople, and banished the bearer into exile for one year.

Therefore, in a council of 23 bishops, together with priests, deacons, the entire clergy, nobles, consuls, and the remaining Christian people, before the body of blessed Peter the apostle, the pope decreed (Book of the Pontiffs) that if anyone thereafter, despising the faithful practice handed down by the ancient custom of the apostolic Church, should become a deposer, destroyer, profaner, or blasphemer of those same images, he should be excluded from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the unity and structure of the whole Church. He solemnly confirmed this by his subscription together with the entire council.

He sent these synodal decrees in defense of the sacred images through Constantine the Defender to the emperors. They likewise held on to them, imprisoned the bearer for one year, and then sent him back with insults and injuries. The entire Roman province also unanimously sent to those same emperors, through Sergius, the patrician and military governor of the island of Sicily, [Note: [Col. 0759] From this year onward V. Cl. Heyse collated the codex with the printed edition; he seems to have indicated the marginal notes on cycles and the like less accurately, and did not always correct the orthography.] a written petition in defense of the restoration of the images. The emperors seized the documents, kept the bearers for eight months, and then sent them back with reproaches and injuries.

Again the pope, through Peter the Defender, to the imperial city—both to Anastasius, usurper of the see of Constantinople, and to the emperors Leo and Constantine.]

[In the margin of the codex: The nineteenth cycle, number 12, begins, indiction 9.]

765. 2. [DCCXLIII] Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was held in high regard. 766. 3. [DCCXLIV] (cf. Annals of Hersfeld, Fulda) Saint Boniface began the monastery of Fulda in the Bochonia wilderness.

767. 4. [DCCXLV] (cf. Royal Annals) King Carloman, the emperor’s brother, discussed with his brother his intention to renounce the world.

[Col. 0760D] 768. 5. [DCCXLVI] (Annals of Augsburg) Carloman, relinquishing the empire, entered Alamannia.

769. 6. [DCCXLVII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Carloman, going to Rome, was tonsured by Pope Zacharias. (Einhard, ch. 2.) But because of the insolence of the Franks visiting Rome, who did not wish to pass him by as though he were not their former lord, he withdrew to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated at the fortress of Monte Cassino, where afterward he lived according to the rule.]

771. 8. [DCCXLIX] (Annals of Hersfeld) Grifo returned again from Saxony.

772. 9. [DCCL] (Annals of Hersfeld) By decree of Pope Zacharias, Pepin was anointed emperor by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz; for this reason the bishop of Mainz was afterward regarded as second after the pope [Note: [Col. 0761] “down to the present day” is added in witness 3.] (ibid., year 746).

773. 10. [DCCLI] (Annals of Hersfeld) [Burchard, the first bishop of Würzburg, was consecrated, and held the see for 40 years [Note: [Col. 0761] superscribed in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0761] IX. 3.] (Annals of Hersfeld).]

[Col. 0761B] 774. 11. [DCCLII] (Pontifical Book) Grifo died. Pope Zacharias died on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction.

775. 12. [DCCLIII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Stephen, the 91st pope after Peter, for 5 years and 1 month. (cf. Royal Annals) Pope Stephen and the aforesaid Carloman, the monk from Monte Cassino, came to Pepin in Francia, seeking protection against Haistulf, king of the Lombards.

776. 13. [DCCLIV] (Annals of Hersfeld) Stephen anointed Pepin’s two sons, Carloman and Charles the Great, as emperors on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. (Pontifical Book) Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 0761] this is in the upper margin in witness 1.] came from Rome on the fourteenth day of October, in the seventh indiction; and on the fifteenth day of November, with the permission of Haistulf, king of the Lombards, he came from the city of Pavia, in the seventh indiction, to Francia. Pepin and Pope Stephen, having killed the Lombards in battle and put their king Haistulf to flight, besieged the city of Pavia on the eighth day before the Ides. Haistulf then gave hostages.
