The Romans 78. Charles the Great, son of Pepin, reigned for 46 years and 4 months.

791. 1. [DCCLXIX] Stephen, 93rd pope, for 4 years.

792. 2. [DCCLXX] (Einhard) When King Pepin died, the Franks, in a general assembly, divided the whole kingdom equally between his sons Charles and Carloman. Charles received their father Pepin’s portion [Note: [Col. 0763] “his” in witness 1? Witness 3.], while Carloman received the portion of their paternal uncle Carloman [Note: [Col. 0763] “paternal uncle” in witness 1.]. (Royal Annals) After governing the kingdom for two years, Carloman died at the villa of Samoussy on the second day before the Nones of October, and Charles was established as king over the whole kingdom.

Adrian, 94th pope, for 23 years.

795. 5. [DCCLXXIII] (Einhard, chs. 5–6) After Hunold, who had attempted to wage war against Charles following Waifarius’s death, had been put to flight and Aquitaine subjected, Charles went to Italy at Pope Adrian’s request.

796. 6. [DCCLXXIV] (ibid.) Charles, after wearing down Desiderius, king of the Lombards, by a long siege, took him under his authority. He drove his son Adelgis, in whom everyone was placing their hopes, out of Italy, subdued all Italy, and restored to the Romans and to Pope Adrian everything that had been taken from them by the Lombard kings. He then reached Rome for the first time on Holy Saturday. (cf. Pontifical Book)

797. 7. [DCCLXXV] (Einhard, chs. 7–8) Once Italy had been subjected, the Saxon war, begun two years before the Italian war, was renewed and lasted for 33 years. Of those Saxons Charles dispersed 10,000 captives, together with their wives and little children.

799. 9. [DCCLXXVII] (Einhard, ch. 9) Charles subjected Spain and returned with his army unharmed.

800. 10. [DCCLXXVIII] (Einhard, ch. 10) He also subdued the Britons who lived in the west of Gaul along the coast.

[Manuscript marginal note: The fourteenth nineteen-year cycle begins in the second indiction.]

801. 11. [DCCLXXIX] (Annals of Augsburg) Charles again entered Saxony; and there was a great famine and mortality in Francia. [Col. 0763D] (cf. Annals of Hersfeld) Saint Sturm, first abbot of Fulda, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

802. 12. [DCCLXXX] Baugolf succeeded him as abbot.

803. 13. [DCCLXXXI] (Annals of Augsburg) Charles captured Saxony.

804. 14. [DCCLXXXII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles went to Rome for the second time, and there his son Carloman was baptized; Pope Adrian changed his name to Pepin.

805. 15. [DCCLXXXIII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Queen Hildegard died, leaving Charles three sons—Charles, Pepin, and Louis. (cf. Thegan, ch. 2)

806. 16. [DCCLXXXIV] (ibid.) After this Charles took Fastrada as his wife.

807. 17. [DCCLXXXV] (Annals of Hersfeld [Q.]) The conspiracy of Hardrad and the easterners.

808. 18. [DCCLXXXVI] (Annals of Hersfeld [Q.]) Charles proceeded to Italy and buried his mother Bertrada with great honor in the basilica at Saint Denis beside her husband Pepin. (Einhard, ch. 18.) Charles went to Rome for the third time, and the sign of the cross appeared on people’s clothing. (Annals of Hersfeld, Augsburg) Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, at the second hour of the day. Richolf succeeded him for 27 years. [Note: [Col. 0764B] “He began the basilica of the most holy martyr Alban from its foundations, completed it with marvelous workmanship, and enriched it inside and out” [“outside” is absent from witness 2?]; added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**.] Richolf [Note: [Col. 0763] in the margin in witness 1. In witness 2, the year 320 is read.] was ordained bishop of Mainz on the fourth day before the Nones of March, a Sunday, in the monastery of blessed Peter at Fritzlar (Annals of Hersfeld). Blood flowed from heaven and from the earth.

809. 19. [DCCLXXXVII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles went from Rome to Benevento, to Saint Benedict, and through Alamannia came to Bavaria.

810. 20. [DCCLXXXVIII] (Annals of Augsburg) Bavaria was captured, and its duke Tassilo was deposed.

811. 21. [DCCLXXXIX] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles subdued the Slavs called Wiltzi [Note: [Col. 0763] “wilzi” in witness 3.].

812. 22. [DCCXC] (Annals of Hersfeld [L.]) The basilica of Saint Boniface at the monastery of Fulda was founded.

813. 23. [DCCXCI] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles proceeded to Pannonia [Note: [Col. 0763] “per annoniam” in witness 3.].

814. 24. [DCCXCII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles subdued the Avars and ravaged the kingdom of the Huns. (Annals of Augsburg) [In the twentieth year of Pope Adrian, in December, in the fifteenth indiction, the river Tiber, swelling across the plains, tore out the gate called Flaminia from its foundations up to the arch, which [Note: [Col. 0763] “which is called” in the *Liber pontificalis*.] brought it down by three *fulcidas* [reading uncertain]; it surpassed the walls in several places as far as the gate of Saint Peter, and the waters descended as far as the Milvian Bridge for three days (Pontifical Book).]

815. 25. [DCCXCIII] (Annals of Hersfeld) The conspiracy of his son Pepin against his father Charles. When the plot was discovered, Pepin was tonsured, while some of his associates were beheaded [Col. 0764D] and others hanged.

816. 26. [DCCXCIV] (Annals of Hersfeld) The heresy of Felician [Note: [Col. 0763] read: Felician.] was condemned at a synod held at Frankfurt. (Einhard, ch. 18.) Queen Fastrada, of German stock, died [Note: [Col. 0764D] “She was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban on the north side before the altar of the holy Mother of God,” added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**; “and she was buried at Saint Alban” is also added by witness 3.]; afterward Charles married Liutgard of Alamannia.

817. 27. [DCCXCV] (ibid. and ch. 19) Pope Adrian [Col. 0765A] died on Christmas Day; Charles mourned him as a brother or dearest son. [Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0765] in the margin in witness 1.] died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction (Pontifical Book).]

818. 28. [DCCXCVI] Leo, 95th pope, for 20 years and 6 months.

819. 29. [DCCXCVII] (Royal Annals) The Romans seized Pope Leo during the Greater Litany, blinded him, and cut out his tongue by the roots. Placed in custody, he escaped at night over the wall and came to Charles’s legates, Abbot Wirundus and Winegesius, duke of Spoleto; he was taken to Spoleto. He then reached King Charles in Saxony at Paderborn, in the presence of Richolf, bishop of Mainz, and was received by them with the highest honor. Charles was anointed emperor by Pope Leo.

[Col. 0765B] 820. 30. [DCCXCVIII] (Manuscript marginal note) The fifteenth nineteen-year cycle begins in the sixth indiction.

821. 31. [DCCXCIX] (Einhard, ch. 26) Charles most diligently improved the discipline of reading and singing psalms.

822. 32. [DCCC] (Einhard, ch. 28) Charles went to Rome for the fourth time with Pope Leo to restore the condition of the Church, which had been greatly disturbed; there he spent the entire winter.

823. 33. [DCCCI] (Annals of Hersfeld) At that time Charles was also called Augustus by the Romans.

824. 34. [DCCCII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Amarmurmulus, king of the Persians, sent an elephant and other gifts to King Charles.

[Col. 0765C] 825. 35. [DCCCIII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles built a bridge 500 paces long across the Rhine at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0765] “of Mainz” in witness 3.], for the river is of such breadth there. (Einhard, ch. 17)

826. 36. [DCCCIV] (Annals of Hersfeld) Pope Leo came to Francia.

827. 37. [DCCCV] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles, son of Emperor Charles, ravaged Bohemia, killing Lecho, its king. [The church [Note: [Col. 0765] in the margin in witness 1.] of Saint Alban was dedicated this year [Note: [Col. 0765C] “was dedicated this year on the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction, which is Richolf’s twentieth year after receiving the bishopric but the eighth year after he was consecrated bishop [“a. o.” in witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**], that is, 805, in the thirteenth indiction.], that is, in 805, in the thirteenth indiction.]

828. 38. [DCCCVI] The first year of the indiction. A very great mortality arose [Note: [Col. 0765] “morta” in witness 1.] in the monastery of Fulda, so that very many of the monks themselves died.

829. 39. [DCCCVII] (Einhard, ch. 26) Charles cultivated with the greatest holiness and devotion the Christian religion with which he had been imbued from childhood; he was especially devoted to supporting the poor [Note: [Col. 0765] “toward the year 831” in witness 1.] and giving alms. (Einhard, ch. 27)

832. 42. [Note: [Col. 0766A] Pepin, son of Emperor Charles, died (from Thegan, ch. 5). A very great mortality of cattle devastated almost the whole of Europe (cf. Annals of Weissenburg). Added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**.] [DCCCX] (Einhard, ch. 22) Before he died [Note: [Col. 0765] corrected from “before he departed” in witness 1.], Charles was repeatedly seized by fevers for four years.

[Col. 0766A] 833. 43. [Note: [Col. 0766B] Charles, the emperor’s firstborn, died (from Thegan, ch. 5). “The emperor Charles himself” is added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**.] [DCCCXI] (Einhard, ch. 33) In the forty-third year of his reign in Francia, the thirty-sixth in Italy, the eleventh year of his empire, in the fourth indiction, Charles divided his treasures, clothing, and everything else into three portions. Of these, he distributed two portions among the twenty-one metropolitan cities known to be in his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0765] “which are known to exist” in witness 3.], allotting one part to each; their names are as follows: Rome, 1; Ravenna, 2; Milan, 3; Forum Julii, 4; Grado, 5; Cologne, 6; Mainz, 7; Juvavum, also called Salzburg, 8; Trier, 9; Sens, 10; Besançon, 11; Lyon, 12; Rouen, 13; Reims, 14; Arles, 15; Vienne, 16; Darantasia, 17; Embrun, 18; Bordeaux, 19; Tours, 20; Bourges, 21. Each metropolitan bishop was to give one part to his own church and two to his suffragans.

The third portion was to remain in daily use either until his death or until he wished to be rid of it [Note: [Col. 0766C] “until the daily use remained” and so forth. The portion itself was eventually cut into four divisions. The first was added to the twenty-one portions mentioned above; the second went to his sons, daughters, and grandchildren; the third was distributed to the poor; the fourth to the male and female servants serving in the palace. To the third portion were added vessels and utensils of bronze, iron, and other metals, together with weapons and clothing and every kind of household equipment for various uses, such as curtains, blankets, carpets, felt coverings, leather, pack saddles, so that the distribution of alms might reach more people. He decreed that the chapel—that is, the ecclesiastical treasury that had come to him by inheritance—should be preserved intact, except for anything he himself might have added to that chapel in vessels or books; whoever wished could purchase these. The price of these objects and books, of which he had a large collection in his library, was to be distributed to the poor (from Einhard). Added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**.]; its first portion was then to be added to the portions of the aforementioned metropolitan bishops; the second was to be distributed among his sons, daughters, and grandchildren; the third among the poor; and the fourth among male and female servants. He ordered that the price of his books, of which he had gathered a great supply in his library, be distributed to the poor.

[Col. 0766D] 835. 45. [DCCCXIII] (cf. Einhard, ch. 17) The bridge at Mainz, which Charles had built of wood over ten years with immense labor and marvelous workmanship [Note: [Col. 0767A] “so that it seemed capable of lasting forever,” added by witnesses 2 (or 2*?) and 2**.], burned down in three hours during the year before his death, and not even a single splinter remained of it. The aforesaid bridge [Note: [Col. 0767B] It is said that Bishop Richolf ordered the bridge itself to be burned because of the robberies carried out there at night, when robbed men were thrown into the river [“thrown into the river itself” in witness 2*.] and killed; but Einhard, who wrote this Charles’s life, reports that it happened accidentally. Added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**.] stood across the Rhine at Mainz. Because robbers used it at night to plunder people thrown into the Rhine, Richolf, bishop of Mainz, ordered it burned.

(Annals of Hersfeld) Richolf, bishop of Mainz, died; Haistulf succeeded him for 11 years. (Einhard, ch. 30) Around the Kalends of November, after holding a general assembly, Charles summoned his son Louis to him from Aquitaine. While admonishing him, on a Sunday he ordered him with his own hands to place the imperial crown upon his own head at the great altar at Aachen; after being given great gifts, Louis returned to Aquitaine.

When Charles [Note: [Col. 0767B] “The emperor, however, was seized by a fever in January after bathing. After suffering for seven days, on the seventh day he received the body and blood of the Lord, to confirm his departure, and struggled through that day and the following night. When daylight came on the next day, knowing what he was about to do, he marked his whole body with the sign of the holy cross with his right hand as best he could. Then, drawing up his feet and extending his arms over his body, with his eyes closed, he sang this verse: ‘Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.’ In a good old age he died, and so forth.” Added by witnesses 2 (or 2*?) and 2**; from Thegan, ch. 7.] was wintering at Aachen, he was seized by a fever in January. He died there on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, at the third hour of the day, in the seventh indiction, in the seventy-second year of his life, in the year 814 [Note: [Col. 0767] erased in witness 1; absent from witness 3.] (Einhard, ch. 31); and on that same day he was buried there at Aachen in the basilica of the Savior and of the holy Mother of God, which he himself had built from the foundations with marvelous workmanship.

[Col. 0767C] The Romans 79. Louis reigned for 26 years and 11 months, up to . . . .

836. 1. [DCCCXIV] (Thegan, ch. 13) Louis investigated and restored all the injustices of his kingdom.

837. 2. [DCCCXV] (Annals of Hersfeld) Baugolf, abbot of Fulda, died on the eighth day before the Ides of July. It was ordered that all the monks should sing the course of Saint Benedict. Ratger became abbot for 5 years.

838. 3. [DCCCXVI] (Thegan, chs. 15–16) Louis’s armies defeated the Slavs, and Pope Leo died.

[Manuscript marginal note: The sixteenth nineteen-year cycle begins in the tenth indiction.]

[Col. 0767D] 839. 4. [DCCCXVII] (Thegan, chs. 16–17) Stephen, 96th pope, for 2 years [Note: [Col. 0767] “X. 2” in witnesses 2 and 2*; corrected to “II” in witness 1; the number is erased in witness 3.], 7 months. When Pope Stephen met Louis in the great field of Reims, he anointed him emperor on the following Sunday before the whole people and, placing upon his head a golden crown of wondrous beauty, magnificently adorned with precious gems and brought with him from Rome, he placed another golden crown upon Queen Irmingard’s head, naming her Augusta.

840. 5. [DCCCXVIII] (ibid.) Pope Stephen, after being given great gifts and honorable assistance on his journey, was dismissed by the king to Rome and died not long afterward.

841. 6. [DCCCXIX] (Annals of Hersfeld) The monastery of Saint Boniface at Fulda was dedicated on the Kalends of November.

842. 7. [DCCCXX] Ratger, abbot of Fulda, died on the eighth day before the Ides of December. Abbot Egil succeeded him for 5 years.

Paschal, 97th pope, for . . . years [Note: [Col. 0767] “VII” in witness 1, corrected from an earlier figure in witness 3; the rest is absent from witnesses 2 and 2**; these entries are assigned to the years 841–840.]. (Annals of Hersfeld) Emperor Louis subdued Britain, killing its duke Murcomann. On his return he found Queen Irmingard suffering from a fever; she died shortly afterward. (Thegan, ch. 25)

843. 8. [DCCCXXI] (Annals of Hersfeld) Emperor Louis took Judith, daughter of Welf, duke of Bavaria, as his queen and held his general assembly at the royal villa of Ingelheim. (Thegan, ch. 26)

[Col. 0768B] 844. 9. [DCCCXXII] (Thegan, ch. 27) Emperor Louis ravaged the eastern Slavs with his army and put their duke, named Liduit, to flight.

845. 10. [DCCCXXIII] (Thegan, ch. 28) At a general assembly Emperor Louis joined his firstborn son Lothar in marriage to the daughter of Count Hugh [Note: [Col. 0767] “conjuxit” in witness 1.].

846. 11. [DCCCXXIV] (Thegan, ch. 29) From the general assembly at the palace of Attigny [Note: [Col. 0767] “Attinco” in witness 1.] Emperor Louis sent his son Lothar with his wife Irmingard into Italy. From there he came to Frankfurt and celebrated Christmas.

Pope Paschal died.

(Annals of Hersfeld) Eugene, 98th pope, for 3 years. Haistulf, bishop of Mainz, died.

847. 12. [DCCCXXV] (Annals of Hersfeld) Bishop Otgar . . . years [Note: [Col. 0768C] When he had been sent to Italy with others because of the emperor’s disagreement with his son and had reached Pavia, a certain cleric came to Otgar with the relics [absent from witnesses 2 and 2**] of Saint Severus [absent from witness 2?], bishop of Ravenna, as well as those of his wife Vincentia and his daughter Innocentia, which he had stolen; he disclosed to Otgar what he had done. Otgar rejoiced, received the relics, and brought them with him to Mainz. He placed Saint Vincentia on the southern side of the monastery of Saint Alban, Saint Innocentia on the northern side, and Saint Severus beside the altar of Saint Alban. He afterward transferred the relics of Saint Severus to Erfurt. Added by witnesses 2, 2*, and 2** (cf. Lambert, year 836).] (Thegan, ch. 31) Emperor Louis [Col. 0768C] ravaged Britain.

[Col. 0768D] 848. 13. [DCCCXXVI] Egil, abbot of Fulda, died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. Rabanus succeeded him for 20 years. At Aachen envoys of the Bulgarians brought gifts to Emperor Louis. (Thegan, ch. 32)

849. 14. [DCCCXXVII] (Thegan, ch. 33) At Ingelheim Louis raised Heriolt of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0767] “of the Danes” in witness 1.] from the baptismal font, and Queen Judith raised his wife. He gave him a large part of Frisia and dismissed him with his envoys and honorable gifts.

Valentinus, 99th pope.

850. 15. [DCCCXXVIII] (Thegan, ch. 34) Emperor Louis, sending an army against the Saracens, met them [Note: [Col. 0769] that is, “to meet them.”] and put them to flight.

851. 16. [DCCCXXIX] (ibid.) From Ingelheim Louis came to Compiègne after the general assembly.

852. 17. [DCCCXXX] (Thegan, ch. 35) At Worms Louis gave Charles, Judith’s son and his own [Note: [Col. 0769] “his son” in witness 1; “his son by Queen Judith” in witnesses 2 and 3.], Alamannia, Rhaetia, and part of Burgundy, in the presence of his sons Lothar, Louis, and Pepin. These three brothers were angered by this. The bodies of Saints Valentinus and Senesius came to the island of Reichenau on the fifth day before the Ides of April [Note: [Col. 0769] “sixth” in witness 2.].

853. 18. [DCCCXXXI] (Thegan, ch. 36) Pope Gregory, the 100th.

Judith [Note: [Col. 0769B] Emperor Louis came from the palace at Aachen to Compiègne. There his son Pepin, accompanied by many treacherous men, came to meet him, wishing to drive him from the kingdom; but the emperor’s namesake son opposed him [“his” in witness 2?]. Those traitors told him that Queen Judith had been violated by a certain Duke Bernard, who was of royal descent, although they were lying about everything. Thus they forcibly veiled her and sent her to a monastery. The same was done to her brothers, and so forth. (from Thegan, ch. 36).] the queen, supposedly violated by Duke Bernard, who was of royal descent and the emperor’s godson through the sacred font of baptism [Note: [Col. 0769] omitted in witness 3; “Bernard, who was of royal descent” in witnesses 2 and 2*.], was veiled by the kingdom’s leading men and sent to a monastery. They also tonsured the queen’s brothers Conrad and Rudolf and sent them to a monastery. King Louis defeated them at Neufchâteau on the River Vaal; he received the queen, who came to meet him at Aachen, at the command of Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0769] “at the command of Pope Gregory and the other bishops, he received her after a just judgment” in witnesses 2 (or 2*) and 2**.] (Thegan, ch. 37).

[Col. 0769C] 854. 19. [DCCCXXXII] (Thegan, ch. 38) Duke Bernard cleared himself at the palace of Thionville before the king and his sons, since no one had made him guilty in relation to the queen, not even by arms.

855. 20. [DCCCXXXIII] The king’s sons attempted to seize the kingdom, dishonoring their father.

856. 21. [DCCCXXXIV] Emperor Louis was deprived of the empire by his sons [Note: [Col. 0769] “by his sons” absent from witness 1.], Pepin, Louis, and Lothar, who came to meet him with Pope Gregory in the great field between Strasbourg and Basel. (Thegan, ch. 42) They then separated the queen from him and sent her to Italy, to the city of Tortona. Pepin went to Aquitaine, and Louis to Bavaria. Lothar led his father to the palace at Compiègne and from there to Aachen, shut him in custody, and celebrated Christmas there while his father was still confined.

857. 22. [DCCCXXXV] (Thegan, ch. 48) After Epiphany, Lothar, because Louis was with his father against him, compelled his father to go with him to Compiègne. Louis followed them with a multitude [Note: [Col. 0769] This is absent from witness 1.]; when Louis was near, Lothar fled. Louis then led his father to the royal seat at Aachen, and there they celebrated Easter together.

858. 23. [DCCCXXXVI]

[Col. 0770A] [Manuscript marginal note: The seventeenth nineteen-year cycle begins in the fourteenth indiction.]

860. 25. [DCCLXXXVIII] (Annals of Augsburg) Paul [Note: [Col. 0769] “Paudus” in witness 3.], a palace deacon, fell into Judaism.

861. 26. [DCCCXXXIX] (Annals of Augsburg) An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third day before the Nones of May, between the eighth and ninth hours, on the eve of the Ascension of the Lord.

862. 27. [DCCCXL] (Royal Annals) While Emperor Louis was pursuing his son Louis across the Rhine, he was weakened by illness. He was taken by boat through the Main into the Rhine and, scarcely reaching the island of Ingelheim, died there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. From there, in the month of March, he was carried and buried in the basilica of Saint Arnulf. Immediately afterward Lothar left Italy and seized the empire.

The Romans 80. Lothar reigned for 15 years.

[Col. 0770B] 863. 1. [DCCCXLI] (Royal Annals) Louis and Charles, deprived of their paternal kingdom, defeated their brother Lothar in battle at Fontenoy.

864. 2. [DCCCXLII] (Royal Annals) The three aforementioned brothers divided the kingdom of the Franks among themselves. Charles held the west, from the British Ocean to the River Meuse. Louis held the east—that is, all Germany as far as the Rhine and certain cities [across the Rhine, with the adjacent districts because of the abundance of wine; absent from witness 1?]. Lothar, the firstborn and emperor, held the middle kingdom between the two, together with all Provence and all the kingdoms of Italy, including Rome. From this Lothar the kingdom has until now been called the kingdom of Lothar (*regnum Luthorium*) [Note: [Col. 0769] “lotringun” in witness 3.].

866. 4. [DCCCXLIV] Sergius, 101st pope.

[Col. 0770C] 868. 6. [DCCCXLVI] (Annals of Hersfeld) Otgar [Note: [Col. 0769] “Otgar” in witness 1.], bishop of Mainz, died. Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him for 9 years.

869. 7. [DCCCXLVII] Hatto succeeded Rabanus [Note: [Col. 0769] “Rabanus” in witness 1.] as abbot at Fulda and held office for 15 years.

873. 11. [DCCCLI] (Royal Annals) Queen Irmingard, wife of Lothar, died. [This entry was written under the year 874 in the margin.] The queen left three sons, Louis, Lothar, and Charles.

875. 13. [DCCCLIII] Leo, 102nd pope after Peter.

876. 14. [DCCCLIV]

[Manuscript marginal note: The nineteen-year cycle ends in the second indiction [Note: [Col. 0769] “third” in witness 2.].]

877. 15. [DCCCLV] (cf. Annals of Hersfeld) Rabanus, bishop of Mainz, died on Monday, the Nones of February. Charles succeeded him as bishop for 8 years. The basilica of Saint Kilian [Col. 0770D] was burned. Emperor Lothar, having summoned the leading men of the kingdom, divided the empire among his sons. (Royal Annals) He gave Italy to Louis and had him called emperor after himself; to Lothar he granted the kingdom that was named after him; and to Charles, the younger among them [Note: [Col. 0769] *hessorum* in witnesses 2 and 2**.], he entrusted Provence. Having arranged matters in this way, he renounced the world. He went to the monastery of Prüm, received the habit of the monks’ holy way of life, and died that same year on the third day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0771A] The Romans 81. Louis, also called Lothar [Note: [Col. 0771D] Marianus does not correctly distinguish Louis the emperor from Lothar the king, and therefore says that the former succeeded the latter.], reigned for 15 years.

878. 1. [DCCCLVI]

[Manuscript marginal note: The second year of the eighteenth nineteen-year cycle, in the fourth indiction.]

879. 2. [DCCCLVII] Benedict, 103rd pope after Peter.

880. 3. [DCCCLVIII] (Annals of Augsburg) Folcwin [Note: [Col. 0771] Absent from witnesses 2 and 2**.] died as abbot.

881. 4. [DCCCLIX] (Annals of Augsburg) Waldarius [Note: [Col. 0771] Absent from witnesses 2 and 2*.] succeeded him as abbot.

882. 5. [DCCCLX] (Annals of Augsburg) Meginrad, the hermit, suffered martyrdom.

883. 6. [DCCCLXI] Hatto, abbot of Fulda, died on the day before the Ides of April.

[Col. 0771B] 884. 7. [DCCCLXII] Thiodo succeeded him as abbot for 13 years.

885. 8. [DCCCLXIII] (Annals of Hersfeld) Charles, bishop of Mainz, died. Bishop Liutbert succeeded him for 26 years.

Saint Nicholas, 104th pope.

886. 9. [DCCCLXIV] (A. Aug.) Walter, abbot, died. [Note: [Col. 0771] Missing in witnesses 2 and 2*.] Hecco succeeded him.

(REG.) Emperor Lothar, wishing to repudiate Queen Teutberga, his lawful wife, whom he detested because of his concubine Waldrada—whom, when he was a young man, he had loved excessively in his father’s household—became involved in no small difficulty as a result. [Note: [Col. 0771] Read *indie* in witness 1.] Accordingly, the queen’s brothers brought the matter before Pope Nicholas at Rome. Pope Nicholas therefore sent his bishop Arsenius, his representative and counsellor, to Francia in his place that year. When Arsenius arrived and had summoned an assembly of bishops, Lothar, compelled by necessity, whether he wished it or not, received the queen in marriage before he could immediately be struck by the sword of anathema. He confirmed this with an oath: that he would not separate her from himself, nor, while she lived, take another woman over her.

But afterward, when the queen had been cast aside and Waldrada brought in in her place, Saint Nicholas excommunicated Waldrada from all fellowship with the holy Church by a sentence of anathema, on 4 February, at the Purification of Saint Mary. [Note: [Col. 0771] “The queen’s brothers … excommunicated” was written in the years 887–890.]

890. 13. [DCCCLXVIII] (A. Aug.) A comet was seen with the greatest clarity this year.

891. 14. [DCCCLXIX] (A. Aug.) Pope Saint Nicholas died on 6 December. A lightning strike occurred on 1 July at the tenth hour. [Col. 0771D]

892. 15. [DCCCLXX] (REG. year 868.) Adrian, the 105th pope, reigned for three years. When Lothar heard of the death of Pope Nicholas, he sent to Pope Adrian, asking that he receive him into favor. The pope replied that, if Lothar knew himself to be free from the charges mentioned above, he should come to the blessing he desired from Saint Peter; but if he were guilty, he should accept the appropriate remedies of penance, and in any event should come without delay. [Col. 0772A]

(REG. year 869.) When Lothar had reached Rome, Pope Adrian received him honorably. When the pope asked him whether he would observe the commands of Saint Nicholas—indeed, of blessed Peter—and his oath concerning the Lord’s body, he replied that he had observed everything as though it had been divinely commanded him. His nobles and leading men also bore witness to this with him.

The pope said to him: “Then, dearest son, you ought to partake of Christ’s body with us, so that through this participation you may deserve to be joined to the members of Christ in the body from which you seemed to have been cut off.”

After the Mass had been sung, at the time of Communion the pope took the body of Christ in his hands and said to Lothar: “If you are innocent of the charges mentioned above, may this Communion be forgiveness for you; but if not, do not presume to receive it, lest it perhaps come to you for judgment and condemnation.” But the king, mentally overpowered, hardened and blinded at once, received Communion without hesitation.

Afterward the pope said individually to the king’s followers and supporters: “If you have not shared with your king in the adultery mentioned above, may this communion of Christ’s body be for you unto eternal life.” Yet no one who consented to the king in this crime received Communion [Note: [Col. 0771] “who” is absent in witness 1.], and no one of them lived another year.

Emperor Lothar, however, after leaving Rome, was seized by illness and, reaching the city of Piacenza, died on 8 August. From this event also the greatest mortality spread among the people.

(REG. year 870.) After his death, his kingdom was divided into equal portions by Ludowic and Charles the Elder, his two brothers, at Marsana near the Meuse, together with their nobles and leading men. Charles went to Heristal, whose palace had fallen to his share. [Col. 0772C]

Romanorum 82. Ludowic [Note: [Col. 0771D] Marianus does not properly distinguish the emperor Ludowic from King Lothar, and therefore says that Ludowic succeeded him.] son of Lothar or Ludowic, reigned four years.

893. 1. [DCCCLXXI] (REG. A. Aug.) Ludowic returned to the palace at Aachen. Abbot Hecco died; Ruadho succeeded him.

894. 2. [DCCCLXXII] Pope Adrian died. John, the 106th pope, succeeded him and reigned twelve years.

895. 3. [DCCCLXXIII] (A. Aug.) Worms was burned by a lightning strike.

(REG. years 871, 872.) When Emperor Ludowic came to Rome and held an assembly there before Pope John, Adalgisus, duke of Benevento, corrupted by Greek persuasion and raising his hand against Emperor Ludowic, was proclaimed by the senate a tyrant and an enemy of the state, and war was decreed against him. Abbot Thiodo of Fulda died on 7 August. Sigehart succeeded him for twenty-two years.

[Cod. in margin: The nineteenth-year cycle begins in indiction 7.]

[Col. 0773A] 896. 4. [DCCCLXXIV] (REG.) Emperor Ludowic Caesar of Italy died, and Charles the Elder, king of Gaul, went to Rome.

Romanorum 83. Charles reigned two years.

897. 1. [DCCCLXXV] (REG.) Charles therefore reached Rome, gave great gifts to Pope John and the Romans, and was made emperor.

(REG.) King Ludowic, Charles’s brother, died at the palace of Frankfurt on 28 August and was buried in the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch. By Queen Hemma he had three sons: Carloman, the father of Arnolf; Ludowic; and Charles the Younger, later emperor.

When Charles the Elder and emperor heard of his brother’s death, he went to the palace at Aachen; after staying there a few days, he departed for Cologne. Carloman, Ludowic’s firstborn, entered the regions of Italy because Charles the Elder had withdrawn from there. Charles, his brother, remained in Germany. Ludowic, who had been present at his father’s death, resided at Frankfurt, the principal seat of the eastern kingdom.

He defeated Charles the Elder in battle on 8 October in the district called Meginense, in Ripuaria, not far from the castle of Andernach beside the Rhine, with more than fifty thousand men fighting against him. [Note: [Col. 0773] Witnesses 2 and 2** read *moinense*.]

Then the three brothers divided their father’s kingdom among themselves at a place called Sualifelt. Carloman held Bavaria, Pannonia, Carinthia, and the kingdoms of the Slavic Bohemians; Ludowic held eastern Francia, Thuringia, Saxony, Frisia, and part of Lothar’s kingdom; Charles held Germany and certain cities from Lothar’s kingdom.

898. 2. [DCCCLXXVI] (REG.) Emperor Charles went to Rome for a second time. Returning from Rome to Bracham, he married his brother Boso to Irmingard, daughter of Emperor Ludowic and of Queen Richildis [Note: [Col. 0773] “son” is absent in witness 1.], with great magnificence. He gave him Provence, placed a crown upon his head, and ordered him to be called king.

A few days later he entered Pavia. While he was organizing public affairs there, it was suddenly announced to him that Carloman had entered the Lombard kingdoms with a huge armed force. Immediately seized with terror, Charles crossed the Ticino [Note: [Col. 0773] Read “Ticinum.”] and the Po and hastened with all effort to return to Gaul. But before he reached the high ridges and narrow passes of the Alps, he was struck down by illness, from which he died at once on 6 October.

His men carried his body in a bier out of Italy, but, compelled by its intolerable stench, they were forced to commit it to the earth. Some years later his bones were transferred and honorably buried at Paris in the monastery of Saint Denis.

899. 1. [DCCCLXXVII] (REG.) After Charles, his son Ludowic reigned, also called the Stammerer, because his speech was impeded, for two years. [Note: [Col. 0773] “After” is written as *post* in witness 2.]

900. 2. [DCCCLXXVIII] (REG.) Ludowic the Stammerer died, leaving three sons. Two of them, Ludowic and Carloman, were born by a girl named Ansgard, whom he had married against the prohibition of his father Charles and without his counsel. His father therefore joined him to a wife named Adalheid; after her husband’s death she bore a son named Avi, that is, Charles. A solar eclipse occurred on 29 October. (A. Aug.)

[John [Note: [Col. 0773] In the margin; witnesses 2 and 2** omit the following.] pope, because of certain oppressions of churches, while in the regions of Gaul in the year of the Incarnation 878, indiction 12, on 11 August, held a synod of thirty-one bishops in the church of Saint Peter at Troyes. [Note: [Col. 0773] Witness 1 perhaps reads *tritasina*.]]

Romanorum 84. Charles the Younger reigned for ten years after his first entry into Italy. [Note: [Col. 0773] “With crooked legs” is added in witness 3.]

901. 1. [DCCCLXXIX] (A. Aug.) Charles the Younger, son of Ludowic and brother of Carloman and Ludowic, first entered Italy.

902. 2. [DCCCLXXX] (REG.) Boso, kinsman of Charles the Elder, striving to seize the kingdom, was pursued and driven out by the sons of the Stammerer during his lifetime.

903. 3. [DCCCLXXXI] (REG.) Carloman, senior king of Bavaria and father of Arnolf, died of paralysis on 7 April and was buried at Ötting in Bavaria. Ludowic, his brother, possessing his own kingdom, granted Arnolf Carinthia, which his father had previously given him.

904. 4. [DCCCLXXXII] (REG.) Charles the Younger departed from Germany, took possession of the Lombards’ territories, and within a few days received all Italy. When he reached Rome, Pope John and the senate received him favorably; he was anointed with consecrated oil with great ceremony and made emperor.

905. 5. [DCCCLXXXIII] (REG.) King Ludowic, the emperor’s brother, died at Frankfurt on 20 August and was buried at Lorsch in the monastery where his father also lay.

906. 6. [DCCCLXXXIV] (REG.) Ludowic, son of the Stammerer, died at Saint Denis and was buried there. His brother Carloman held his kingdom.

Bertulf, bishop of Trier, died on 10 February. Rabbodus succeeded him on 6 April and also consecrated Ruodbert bishop of the church of Metz on 22 April.

[Col. 0774D] 907. 7. [DCCCLXXXV] Marinus, the 107th pope.

908. 8. [DCCCLXXXVI] (REG.) Carloman, son of the Stammerer, died and was buried at Saint Denis with his brother and grandfather.

909. 9. [DCCCLXXXVII] (REG.) Agapitus, the 108th pope. Emperor Charles began to suffer illness in body and mind. In November, coming to Tribur around the feast of Saint Martin, he summoned an assembly.

Then, seeing that the leading men of the kingdom had perceived the emperor to be failing not only in bodily strength but also in spirit [Col. 0775A], they drew Arnolf, son of Carloman, into the kingdom of their own accord. [Note: [Col. 0775] In Migne, the letter in square brackets is printed above the letter after which it appears here: *attra[c]hunt* in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0775] Witness 1 reads *solummodo* (“only”) instead of *solum*.] Within three days they abandoned the emperor so completely that scarcely anyone remained with him to perform even the offices of ordinary humanity. Only food and drink were supplied at the expense of Liutbert, bishop of Mainz. At his request Arnolf granted him several royal estates in Germany.

Romanorum 85. Arnolf reigned twelve years.

910. 1. [DCCCLXXXVIII] (REG.) Arnolf, having successfully settled affairs in Francia, returned to Bavaria.

(REG.) Adrian, the 109th pope. Emperor Charles died on 2 June and was buried on the island of Reichenau.

[Col. 0775B] 911. 2. [DCCCLXXXIX] (cf. A. Hersf.) Liutbert, bishop of Mainz, died on 17 February. Sunderold succeeded him for two years.

(REG.) After Charles’s death, one part of the Italian people made Berengar, son of Eberhard, who held the duchy of Friuli, their king; others decided that Wido, son of Lambert and duke of Spoleto, should be raised to royal dignity. But after many slaughterings had taken place between them, Wido emerged victorious and expelled Berengar from the kingdom.

912. 3. [DCCCXC] Basil, the 110th pope. [Note: [Col. 0775B] The following note is written here in the edition:]

“Saint Adalric, bishop of Augsburg, was born.” Added in witnesses 2, 2?, and 2**.

913. 4. [DCCCXCI] (A. Aug.) Sunderold, bishop of Mainz, was killed by the Northmen at Worms on Saturday, 26 June. (REG.)

914. 5. [DCCCXCII] (cf. A. Hersf.) Hatto succeeded him as bishop and held office for twenty-one years and eight months.

915. 6. [DCCCXCIII] Stephen, the 111th pope.

[Cod. in margin: The twentieth nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 11.]

(REG.) King Arnolf entered Lombard territory with a strong force and powerful army and reached as far as Piacenza. Turning back from there, he entered Gaul across the Pennine Alps and reached Saint Maurice. [Note: [Col. 0775] The remainder was written under the year 916.] [Note: [Col. 0775] Witness 1 reads *maurum*, witness 2 *mauritium*.] Abbot Sigehart of Fulda died on 5 September. Huogi succeeded him for twenty-four years.

917. 8. [DCCCXCV] (REG.) Wido, who governed Italy in the emperor’s name, died. His son Lambert, taking possession of the kingdom, had the imperial diadem placed upon him by the pope at Rome. [Col. 0775D]

918. 9. [DCCCXCVI] (REG.) A synod of ninety-six bishops, together with abbots and many distinguished clerics, met at Tribur in the monastery. Against several laymen who had attempted to diminish episcopal authority, they confirmed numerous decrees written concerning the state of the holy Church.

(REG.) Formosus, the 112th pope. [Note: [Col. 0776B] Another hand writes in the upper margin: “Formosus, pope, to Hatto, archbishop of Mainz: ‘We have kindly received the letter of Your Holiness and, considering your petition in matters relevant to the case, we grant your request. For we grant the use of the pallium, warning and declaring that you should not suppose it was bestowed upon you for the pomp of the world,’ and so forth.]

King Arnolf came to Worms. There, when all the leading men of his kingdom had met him, he held a public assembly. With everyone applauding, he placed his son Zwentibold over Lothar’s kingdom.

Then Arnolf entered Italy for a second time and reached Rome. With the consent of Pope Formosus, he captured the city by force; this had once previously been done before the Nativity of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0775] Witness 3 reads *fecerat* (“had done”).]

Lambert’s mother, who had been left behind to defend her son [Note: [Col. 0775] Witness 3 reads *fecerat* (“had done”).], secretly fled with her followers. Arnolf entered the city and was received with great honor by Pope Formosus. He was anointed and crowned before the confession of Saint Peter and made emperor.

That same year Lambert, who bore the title of emperor [Note: [Col. 0775] The edition reads *imperatoris* (“of the emperor”); no note records the reading of the manuscripts.], died. Ludowic, son of Boso, brother of Charles the Elder, invited by the Lombards, left Provence and entered Italy.

[Col. 0776B] 919. 10. [DCCCXCVII] (REG.) At the urging of his father Arnolf, Zwentibold took Oda, daughter of Count Odo, as his wife after Easter.

Pope Boniface [Note: [Col. 0775] Written in the margin under the year 919 or 920.] [Note: [Col. 0775] “Pope 113” in witnesses 2 and 2*, and likewise below.] for fifteen days. Pope Stephen in his first year, three months.

920. 11. [DCCCXCVIII] (REG.) Many battles were fought in Italy between Ludowic, son of Boso, and Berengar. At last Ludowic drove out Berengar and entered Rome, where he was crowned by the pope and proclaimed emperor.

921. 12. [DCCCXCIX] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians ravaged Italy extensively. Emperor Arnolf died on 29 November and was buried at Ötting, where his father also lies. (REG.)

Pope Romanus, the 117th, held office for four months. [Note: [Col. 0775] Witness 2 reads CXV, and so forth.]

Romanorum 86. Ludowic reigned twelve years.

922. 1. [CM] (REG.) Theodorus, the 118th pope, for twenty days.

Ludowic, son of Arnolf, whom Arnolf had begotten in lawful marriage, was in the seventh year of his age. On 4 February the nobles and leading men of the kingdom set him up as their king, and, assembled together at Forchheim, raised him to the height of the kingdom after he had been crowned and clothed in royal ornaments. [Col. 0776D]

923. 2. [CMI] (A. Aug.) King Zwentibold, son of Arnolf, was killed.

Pope John, the 119th, held office for two years.

924. 3. [CMII] (REG.) Count Stephen, brother of Walo, was sitting in seclusion and relieving his bowels during the night when he was struck by an arrow through a window. He died that same night. [Note: [Col. 0775] This was written under the year 925.]

925. 4. [CMIII] Benedict, the 120th pope, for three years and five months.

[Col. 0777A] 926. 5. [CMIV] (REG.) Focho, bishop of Reims, was killed by a certain soldier of Count Baldwin named Winimar. Heriveus succeeded him; together with many other bishops, he excommunicated that same Winimar with perpetual anathema for so great a crime.

927. 6. [CMV] (REG.) Ludowic, son of Boso, who had assumed the title of emperor, expelled Berengar from Italy and possessed the whole kingdom. Presuming on his security, he dismissed his army and entered Verona with a few men, at the urging of Adalard, bishop of that city.

When the citizens, with the greatest haste, made promises to Berengar—who was then an exile in Bavaria—and announced that the city gates would be opened to him, Berengar deprived Ludowic of his kingdom and his sight and obtained the kingdom of Italy.

Leo, the 121st pope, held office for fifty-seven days.

928. 7. [CMVI] (REG.) Count Conrad, father of the younger Conrad, was killed in battle in Hesse, at a place called Fritzlar, by Count Adalbert, on 27 February.

In July of the same year King Ludowic held a general assembly at Tribur, a royal estate. He besieged Adalbert in the fortress called Terasso and beheaded him on 9 September.

Christophorus, the 122nd pope, held office for four months.

929. 8. [CMVII] (A. Aug.) The Bavarians were killed by the Hungarians. Sergius, the 123rd pope, held office for seven years, three months, and sixteen days.

930. 9. [CMVIII] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia.

931. 10. [CMIX] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians ravaged Alamannia.

932. 11. [CMX] (A. Aug.) The Franks were either killed or driven away by the Hungarians.

933. 12. [CMXI] (A. Aug.) King Ludowic died, and Conrad was raised to the kingship.

Romanorum 87. Conrad reigned seven years.

[Cod. in margin: The twenty-first nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 15.]

934. 1. [CMXII] (A. Hersf.) Hatto, bishop of Mainz, died. Heriger succeeded him for fourteen years and six months.

935. 2. [CMXIII] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians ravaged Alamannia and were killed near the river Ina by Bavarians and Alamanni.

[Col. 0777D] 936. 3. [CMXIV] (A. Aug.) The winter was exceedingly great and harsh.

(A. Aug.) Anastasius, the 122nd pope [Note: [Col. 0777] “Pope 122,” and likewise below, in witnesses 2 and 2*.], held office for two years and two months.

937. 4. [CMXV] (cf. A. Hersf.) The Hungarians ravaged all Alamannia and Thuringia with fire and sword, reaching as far as Fulda.

938. 5. [CMXVI] (A. Aug.) Erchanger and Bertolt were beheaded. Lando, pope, held office for five months.

939. 6. [CMXVII] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians came through Alamannia into Alsace and as far as the borders of Lothar’s kingdom. Pope John held office for fourteen years, two months, and three days.

[Col. 0778A] 940. 7. [CMXVIII] Huogi, abbot of Fulda, died on 8 June. Helmfrid succeeded him for one year.

(A. Aug.) King Conrad died on 23 December and was buried in the monastery at Fulda beside the altar [of the Holy Cross]. [Note: [Col. 0777] “of the Holy Cross” is absent in witness 1?]

Romanorum 88. Henry reigned seventeen years.

941. 1. [CMXIX] Abbot Helmfrid died on 6 December.

942. 2. [CMXX] Haicho succeeded him and held office for six years.

945. 5. [CMXXIII] (A. Aug.) The most precious treasure of the Lord’s blood came to Reichenau on 8 November. Perhaps it was the blood that flowed from an image of Christ when he was suffering at the hands of the Jews the same things that the Lord suffered from them.

947. 7. [CMXXV] Haicho, abbot of Fulda, died on 28 May. [Col. 0778B]

948. 8. [CMXXVI] (A. Aug.) Hiltibert succeeded as abbot at Fulda and held office for four years. The Hungarians ravaged all Francia, Alsace, Gaul, and Alamannia with fire and sword. [Note: [Col. 0777] This was first written under the year 958 (935), but was transferred here in witness 1.]

949. 9. [CMXXVII] Heriger, bishop of Mainz, died on 1 December.

950. 10. [CMXXVIII] Hiltibert succeeded as abbot of Fulda and held office for nine years and five months. Hadamar, the thirteenth abbot at Fulda, succeeded him and held office for twenty-eight years. [Note: [Col. 0777] Witness 1 has *tert.* (“thirty-third”).]

[Cod. in margin: The twenty-second nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 4.]

953. 13. [CMXXXI] King Henry made the king of the Obodrites and the Northmen Christian.

Pope Leo held office for seven months. [Note: [Col. 0777] In witness 1 these popes are written in the margin under the years 951–958; in witness 2 under 951, 956, 957, and 958.]

[Col. 0778C] 954. 14. [CMXXXII] (A. Aug.) Stephen held office for two years and two months.

956. 16. [CMXXXIV] (A. Aug.) The Hungarians were killed by King Henry’s army, and many of them were also captured.

957. 17. [CMXXXV] John, the 126th pope [Note: [Col. 0777] Witness 2 has CXXVII, and witnesses 2 and 2* continue according to their own sequence.], held office for four months. (A. Aug.) King Henry died on 1 July. [Note: [Col. 0777] Read “6 July.”] His son Otto was established as king.

Pope Leo, the 127th [Note: [Col. 0777] Witness 1 has CXX; witness 2 has CXXVIII.], held office for three years, six months, and ten days.

959. 1. [CMXXXVII] (A. Aug.) The monasteries of the holy Scots, Saint Gall, and Saint Boniface were consumed by fire. 963. 5. [CMXLI] Otto then returned, came to Brisach, and besieged it; Ludowic withdrew.

Pope Marinus, the 130th, held office for three years, six months, and fourteen days. [Note: [Col. 0779] In the margin of witness 1, perhaps under the year 964.]

972. 14. [CML].

1012. [CMXC] 6. [Pope Marinus, the 116th.]

1020. [CMXCVIII] 14. [Pope Agapitus, the 117th.]

1024. [MII] 18. Emperor Otto III died on 23 January and was buried at Aachen.

Romanorum 92. Henry reigned twenty-two years.

[Col. 0782A] On Sunday, 9 June, Henry II was acclaimed king at Mainz by the election of the people. On that same day he was consecrated and crowned king at Mainz by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, before the altar of Saint Martin the Confessor.

1025. [MIII] 1. Kilian, abbot of the Scots of Saint Martin at Cologne, died on 14 December. [Pope Octavian, the 118th.]

1026. [MIV] 2. Helias the Scot succeeded him for twenty years.

1029. [MVII] 5.

[Cod. in margin: The twenty-sixth nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 5.]

1031. [MIX] 7. Bruno, bishop, [was martyred]. [Note: [Col. 0781] “Was martyred” is absent in witness 1.] [Pope Leo, the 119th.]

[Col. 0782B] 1033. [MXI] 9. Willigis, bishop of Mainz, died on Friday, 23 February. Ercanbald, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him for ten years and six months.

1036. [MXIV] 12. Brian [Note: [Col. 0781] This is absent in witnesses 2, 2?, and 2**.], king of Ireland, was killed on Good Friday, Friday, 23 April, while intent upon God with hands and mind. [Note: [Col. 0781C–D] See the *Annals of Inisfallen*, in O’Connor, *Scriptores rerum Hibernicarum*, II, pp. 60 ff.; and the *Annals of the Four Masters*, ibid., III, p. 552.]

At this point I have judged it appropriate to display the catalogue of the kings of Ireland, which is written on folio 15 of the manuscript:

“These are the *flathi* [that is, emperors or kings] of Ireland who ruled from half of it, that is, from *do leth Chuinn* [that is, ‘Conn’s half’; see the *Annals of Inisfallen* for the year 201, in O’Connor I, p. 7], from Conn the Hundred-Battled [*o Chunn cetchatach*] to Flann son of Maelsechnaill:

Conn, Art, and Cormac reigned sixty years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] These are three kings: Conn, Art, and Cormac.]

Corpri son of Cormac reigned thirty years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] See the *Annals of Tigernach*, loc. cit., p. 48.]

Fiache Multach the Broad reigned twenty-five years.

Muredach Tirech reigned four years.

Euchu Mugmedoin reigned twenty-five years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] *Euchu* is corrected to *Echu* in the manuscript; read *Eocha*.]

Conlae Uoiss reigned four years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] The manuscript has *Roiss*?; *uais* or *uois* means ‘illustrious’.]

Niall reigned twenty-seven years.

Nathi reigned sixty years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] Commonly *Dathi*, but *Nathi* is also found in other chronicles; see O’Connor II, p. 84.]

Loegaere son of Niall reigned sixty-six years. [Note: [Col. 0781D] Compare the oldest catalogue of the kings of Ireland, which O’Connor compiled from all the annals and the ancient metrical writers, ‘collated’ together, *L. Ep. nunc.*, p. LXXV ff. It begins with Laoghaire son of Niall.]

Aillill Molt, son of Nathi, reigned twenty years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] The manuscript often has *m*.]

Lugaed son of Laegaere reigned twenty-three years.

Murchertach son of Erca reigned twenty years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] *Cercca* corrected to *ercca*. “Called by his mother M. son of Erca,” O’Connor, loc. cit.]

Tuathal Mailgarb reigned eighteen years.

Diarmaet son of Fergus reigned twenty years.

Fergus and Donnall, two sons of Muircertach son of Erca. [Note: [Col. 0782D] That is, “Fergus and Donald, two sons of Murcertach son of Erca,” O’Connor, p. LXXVII.]

Muiredach Munderg reigned twelve years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] This is absent in O’Connor, loc. cit.]

Anmire son of Setna reigned four years.

Baitan son of Muirchertach and Echoid son of Donnall son of Murchertach reigned four years.

Baetan son of Murchada reigned sixteen years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] O’Connor’s catalogue differs.]

Anmire reigned seven years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] This is absent in O’Connor, loc. cit.]

Colman Bec son of Diarmata and Aed son of Aumerech reigned thirteen years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] O’Connor has *Ainmerech*.]

Suibni son of Colman Mor reigned three years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] This is absent in O’Connor, loc. cit.]

Aed Slane son of Diarmata reigned four years.

Aed Alaenn son of Donnall reigned seven years.

Oengus son of Colman reigned nine years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] This is absent in O’Connor, loc. cit.]

Suibni the Illustrious, son of Fachtna, reigned seven years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] ‘Suibhne Meann,’ that is, ‘Suibne the illustrious,’ O’Connor.]

Donnall son of Aed reigned thirty-five years.

Conall and Cellach, two sons of Mailecoba, reigned fifteen years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] That is, two sons.]

Bladmecc and Diarmait, two sons of Aed Slane, reigned nine years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] That is, two sons.]

Sechnasach son of Bladmecc reigned five years.

Cendfaelad son of Bladmecc reigned four years.

Finnachta son of Dunchad reigned eighteen years.

Longsech son of Oengus reigned nine years.

Congal son of Fergus reigned seven years.

Fergal son of Maeleduim reigned twelve years.

Fogartach son of Cernach reigned two years.

Cinaid son of Isigalaig reigned four years. [Note: [Col. 0782D] O’Connor has *Iorgalaigh*.]

Flaitbertach son of Longsig reigned six years.

Aed son of Fergael reigned ten years.

Donnall son of Murchada reigned twenty years.

Niall son of Fergael reigned fifteen years.

Donnchad son of Donnall reigned eighteen years.

Aed son of Niall reigned twenty-two years.

Conchobor son of Donnchad reigned nineteen years.

Niall son of Aed reigned thirteen years.

Maelsechnaill reigned thirteen years.

Aed son of Niall reigned fourteen years.

Flann son of Maelsechnaill [Note: [Col. 0783D] He is said to have died in 916; O’Connor, p. LXXXIII.] was succeeded by his son Donnchad, who reigned fifty-one years, but did not rule even a quarter of Ireland.”

1039. [MXVII] 15. [Pope Benedict, the 120th.]

[Col. 0783A] 1042. [MXX] 18. In the presence and hearing of Emperor Henry, and also of the highly reverend man Richard, abbot of the see of Saint Boniface, Pope Benedict celebrated publicly at Fulda, on 1 May, the Mass of the Apostles Philip and James upon the altar of Saint Boniface. . . [Note: [Col. 0783] One word was erased in witness 1.]

1043. [MXXI] 19. Erkanbald, bishop of Mainz, died on 17 August.

1044. [MXXII] 20. Aribo succeeded him as bishop for nine years and six months.

1045. [MXXIII] 21. [A solar eclipse occurred at the ninth hour in springtime.] [Note: [Col. 0783] Added by another hand.]

1046. [MXXIV] 22. Pope Benedict died on 7 April. Emperor Henry died on 14 July and was buried at Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0783] in the mountain of Babo, that is, Babenberch, 2]. Pope John. [John, [Col. 0783B] 121st pope.]

93rd of the Romans: Conrad, a Frank by birth, reigned for 15 years.

1047. [MXXV] 1.

1048. [MXXVI] 2.

[Codex marginal note: Cycle 27; the nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 9.]

1050. [MXXVIII] 4. [I, wretched Marianus, was born in this year in sins. [Note: [Col. 0783] Added by another hand, 1.]]

1053. [MXXXI] 7. Aribo, bishop of Mainz, died on Tuesday, 8 April.

1054. [MXXXII] 8. Saint Bardo succeeded him for 20 years, receiving the staff on 3 June, the day of Pentecost.

1055. [MXXXIII] 9. [Bardo [Note: [Col. 0783] These words are written in the margin near the year 1047; numbers 2 and 3 are absent.] bishop received the pallium from Pope John in indiction 15, in the month of January.]

1056. [MXXXIV] 10. Moelcoluim [Note: [Col. 0783] These words are absent in witness 2 (2*? 2**).] [Note: [Col. 0784D] That is, Malcolm, in Irish Maelcolaim. Concerning him, see the Annals of Tigernach, under this year, book I, II, p. 284.] king of Scotland died on 26 November. Donchad, his daughter’s son [Note: [Col. 0784D] She was called Beatrix; see the same work, p. 288, n. 48.], succeeded him for 5 years and 9 months.

1058. [MXXXVI] 12. Because of his strict religious observance and excessive discipline, and because of certain Scots whom he had with him, Helias the Scottish abbot—who governed together the monasteries of Saint Pantaleon and Saint Martin in Cologne—was told by Piligrinus, bishop of Cologne, incited by envious men [Note: [Col. 0783] “By envious men” in witness 3; “by certain envious monks from the monastery of Saint Pantaleon” in witness 2.], that, until Piligrinus himself had returned from the royal court, neither Helias nor any other Scot was to remain in the monastery of Pantaleon. Then Helias and the other Scots to whom the bishop had spoken agreed: “If Christ is in these pilgrims, may Bishop Piligrinus never come alive at all to Cologne from the royal court.” And so the Lord fulfilled it; and Helias governed the two monasteries.

1059. [MXXXVII] 13. Piligrinus [Note: [Col. 0783] “Pilgrinus” in witness 1?] bishop of Cologne died on 25 August. Herimannus, bishop, succeeded him for 19 years. [Brun [Note: [Col. 0783] In the margin of witness 1, near the year 1057; absent in witness 2.] bishop of Würzburg died.]

Saint Archbishop Bardo, in the presence of Emperor Conrad, in indiction 5, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, which was also a Thursday—the day on which chrism is consecrated [Note: [Col. 0783] Read: “crisma,” chrism.] and on which many other holy and good works are performed, and on which, indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ sanctified bread into his body and wine into his blood for us, and which is the most honorable day of the whole week after Sunday—consecrated the monastery of Saint Martin, the seat of the archbishopric of Mainz—indeed, of all the Franks—in honor of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, with many bishops and venerable men.

1061. [MXXXIX] 15. Emperor Conrad died on 12 June and was buried at Speyer. Richard, abbot of Fulda, of blessed memory, died on 20 July. He also kept many holy men of the Scottish race in the common life of the brethren, and provided them with a separate chamber and dormitory, while also supplying them together with the brethren, like a father. Sigiwart the abbot succeeded him.

94th of the Romans: Henry, son of Emperor Conrad, reigned for 17 years.

1062. [MXL] 1. Donnchad [Note: [Col. 0783] These words are absent in witness 2.] king of Scotland was killed in the autumn [Col. 0784C] on 19 August [Note: [Col. 0783] In the margin of witness 1.] by his own commander, Macbethad mac Finnloech, who succeeded him in the kingship for 17 years [Note: [Col. 0784D] See the note to the Annals of Tigernach, in O’Connor II, p. 288.].

1064. [MXLII] 3. Helias the Scottish abbot died on 11 April, a prudent and religious man; and for that reason the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, together with his own—that is, Saint Martin’s—had been entrusted to him. He burned with fire, for the community of monks at the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, an excellent mass book written by a Frankish monk without permission, so that no one else might write without permission or do anything of that kind. Majobus [Note: [Col. 0783] Thus in witness 1, here and under the year 1083; “Majolus” in the other witnesses.] the Scot succeeded him, a patient and wise virgin, for 18 years.

1065. [MXLIII] 4. Animchad, a Scottish monk and recluse, died on 30 January in the monastery of Fulda. Lights were seen above his tomb and psalmody was heard [Note: [Col. 0785C] “This is that Leo who composed the new chant concerning Saint Gregory the Great,” witness 2 adds.]. I, Marianus the Scot, spent ten years enclosed above him, standing daily at his feet and celebrating masses. Willihelmus, a converted monk, priest, cleric, and learned man, the strictest and most religious of all the monks of Fulda, as we ourselves saw, asked Animchad to bless him. That very night, as Animchad confirmed to me, who was enclosed beside him, he dreamed that Animchad was standing in his tomb, shining with immense radiance, and that, extending his hand, he was being blessed by him. Since the grave for my burial beside his had remained open and unfinished during the night, I spent that whole night, as it were, amid a honey-sweet fragrance.

Because he had, with the permission of his superior named Corcram, shown charity to the brothers on the island of Kelta, but, when only a few remained after the others had departed and were asking for drink, had provided it without permission—and had then also sent the superior a drink, as at first—his superior expelled him the following day not only from the island of Kelta but from all Ireland. He accepted this humbly. Thus Tigernacb [Note: [Col. 0785] So in witness 1.] Borchecb pronounced me guilty of some slight fault.

1066. [MXLIV] 5. Pope Benedict succeeded John. After Benedict had sold his papacy [Note: [Col. 0785] “Had bought it” in witness 2.], Emperor Henry went to Rome and appointed Clement pope in his place, since, according to the words of Saint Peter, both the buyer and the seller of spiritual grace in Simon Magus were condemned.

[Marginal note in the codex: Cycle 28; the nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 13.]

[Col. 0785C] 1067. [MXLV] 6.

1068. [MXLVI] 7. Clement, first [Note: [Col. 0785] “The 143rd, proceeding in his order,” witness 2.] after blessed Peter, pope.

1069. [MXLVII] 8. Pope Clement died on 9 October. Pope Bopo, also called Damasus, succeeded him. There was so much snow in the west that it broke the forests.

1070. [MXLVIII] 9. Pope Bobbo died. Pope Leo, first . . . after Peter, succeeded him for 6 years.

1072. [ML] 11. Macbethad, king of Scotland, distributed silver at Rome by scattering it among the poor.

1073. [MLI] 12. Saint Bardo, bishop of Mainz, died on 10 June.

1074. [MLII] 13. Liuboldus succeeded him [Col. 0785D] for 8 years and 4 months. I, Marianus, abandoned the world.

1075. [MLIII] 14. Aed the cleric [Note: [Col. 0785] “Aedericus” in witness 3.], bearded, a very famous man in Ireland and of wondrous religious observance—for he cut the hair of women and boys by tonsuring them in the manner of clerics, and preached that converted women ought to have their crowns and their uncovered heads [Col. 0786A], and he had a large school of them, as well as of girls, boys, and laymen—was expelled from Ireland on that account.

1076. [MLIV] 15. Pope Leo died on 16 April.

1077. [MLV] 16. Pope Victor, first . . . after Peter, succeeded him for 3 years.

1078. [MLVI] 17. Herimannus, bishop of Cologne, died during Lent [Note: [Col. 0785] “In the fortieth year,” witness 1.]. Anno succeeded him as bishop. I, Marianus, became a pilgrim for the sake of the heavenly kingdom, borrowed a homeland [Note: [Col. 0785] That is, “mutuavi,” I borrowed.] for myself, and at Cologne, on Thursday, 1 August, became a monk. Emperor Henry died on 3 October and was buried at Speyer, where his father also lies.

95th of the Romans: Henry, son of Emperor Henry, reigned for 10 years.

1079. [MLVII] 1. Pope Victor died on 28 July. [Macfinlaeg [Note: [Col. 0785] These words are in the margin of witness 1 and absent in witnesses 2, 2*, and 2**. [Note: [Col. 0786D] See the year 1062.]] was killed in August. Lulach succeeded him and was killed in March; Moelcol [Note: [Col. 0786D] That is, Malcolm.] succeeded him.]

Moelcoluim [Note: [Col. 0786D] That is, Malcolm.], son of Donchaed, rules Scotland. [Donchad [Note: [Col. 0785] The following words are in the lower margin. [Note: [Col. 0786D] See the years 1056 and 1062, and the poem on the kings of Scotland in O’Connor I, Prolegomena 1, p. CXXX.] reigned for 5 years, that is, from the mass of Saint Andrew to the same mass and in addition to the Nativity of Saint Mary. From then Macfinlaeg reigned for 17 years until the same mass of Saint Mary. Lulach reigned from the Nativity of Saint Mary until the mass of Saint Patrick in the month of March. From then Moelcoluim reigned for 20 years until the mass of Saint Patrick.]

1080. [MLVIII] 2. Pope Stephen, first . . . , succeeded. The city of Badaebrunna, with two monasteries—that is, the episcopal monastery and the monks’ monastery—was consumed by fire on the Friday before Palm Sunday [Col. 0786C]. In the monks’ monastery there was a Scottish monk named Paternus, who had been enclosed for many years and had also foretold the fire. Seeking martyrdom, he did not leave his enclosure for anything outside, but, burned in his cell, passed through the fire into refreshment. Some good things are also related about his tomb.

On those very days, on the Monday after the octave of Easter, while I was leaving Cologne for Fulda with the abbot of Fulda in order to be enclosed, I prayed upon the mat in his cell, where he had been burned and suffered above that same mat.

Pope Stephen died on 29 March. Pope Nicholas.

Ecbert, abbot of Fulda, died on Tuesday, at the seventh hour, on 17 November. Sigfridus succeeded him on the Nativity of the Lord, in the first year.

[Col. 0786D] 1081. [MLIX] 3. I, unworthy Marianus, was ordained to the priesthood with Sigfridus, abbot of Fulda, beside the body of Saint Kilian the martyr at Würzburg, on the Saturday in mid-Lent, 13 March; and on the Friday after the Ascension of the Lord, 14 May, I was enclosed at Fulda for ten years. Liuboldus, bishop [Col. 0787A] of Mainz, died on Tuesday, 7 December; Sigfridus succeeded him.

1082. [MLX] 4. On Sunday, the day of the Nativity of the Lord, Sigfridus, abbot of Fulda, went from Fulda to the royal court; on Friday, on Epiphany, he received the staff of the archbishopric of Mainz, with Pope Nicholas’s legate Alexander—who not long afterward became pope—also consenting to this at the royal court. Witratus, dean of Fulda, succeeded him as abbot at Fulda for 10 years. Pope Nicholas died. Pope Alexander, first . . . , succeeded him for 10 years.

1083. [MLXI] 5. Majobus, abbot of the Scots at Cologne, died. [Note: [Col. 0787A] “Foillanus succeeded him,” witnesses 2, 2*, and 2** add.]

[Col. 0787B] 1085. [MLXIII] 7. [Note: [Col. 0787] The solar cycle and the nineteen-year cycle begin together. Added by witnesses 2, 2*, and perhaps 2**.]

1086. [MLXIV] 8. The great Paschal cycle [third [Note: [Col. 0787] Absent in witness 1?]] begins in the second indiction. Many rich and poor people, with the archbishop of Mainz, the bishop of Utrecht, the bishop of Bamberg, and the bishop of Regensburg, after the passing of Saint Martin, went to Jerusalem, more than 7,000 in number. Where the bishops sat, hanging back-cloths were displayed, and they had golden and silver bowls and vessels; from these they ate and drank together in splendor.

1087. [MLXV] 9. The Arabs, attracted by the report of the money, killed many of the aforesaid on Good Friday (25 March). When the others could not hold out, our men fled into a certain empty castle called Carvasalim [Col. 0787C] [Note: [Col. 0787] “Quotam” in witness 1.]. After closing it, they defended themselves with stones and clubs against the Arabs’ arrows, as the Arabs sought all their money—or their lives together with their money.

Then one good soldier, in no way prevented from leaving the Lord’s Sepulchre, came out naked. The Arabs immediately stretched him out in the form of a cross, lying on his back, with his hands and feet pierced into the ground by nails; and, cutting open his entrails and throwing them over his face from the bottom of his belly to his throat, they examined how human viscera are arranged. Then, dividing him limb by limb, their leader first threw a stone upon him, and each man after him did likewise.

Then, while all our men in the castle watched, they said: “You will be treated in this way if you do not hand over all your money to us.”

When our men promised to give all their money except their provisions, they allowed the Arab leader to enter among the Christians with sixteen men and the same number of swords. When he saw the glorious bishops with many soldiers, the hanging back-cloths, and the other things, as is the custom of pagans to hold captives, he placed a thong around the neck of the bishop of Bamberg, as though impressed by the stature and beauty of our lord and by his bodily appearance, and said: “You and all these things of yours will be mine.”

The bishop, through an interpreter, said: “What will you do to me?”

He replied: “I will suck the beautiful blood from your throat, and I will hang you like a dog before the castle.”

Then the bishop seized his head and struck the leader to the ground with a single blow [Note: [Col. 0787] “Colopho” in witness 1.]; all the others were bound. Those who were outside, hearing this, rushed upon the castle. But the bound men, placed upon the wall beneath their swords against the arrows of their own people, begged their sons and friends to restrain the others, and they did so. Thus a battle arose among the robbers: many chose money, while many chose their fathers and friends.

On Monday after Easter (28 March), when the others who had escaped begged him, the commander from Ramla came with a large force and, driving away the Arabs, took five hundred golden bezants [that is, large denarii; [Note: [Col. 0787] Written above the line in witness 1.]], as well as capturing the Arab leader, who had long been an enemy of the king of the Saracens. He led the Christians to Jerusalem and from there to the ship. The Lord carried them by a favorable wind as far as the Christians; fewer than 2,000 of the 7,000 returned.

Nial [Note: [Col. 0787] These words are absent in witness 2, as are the remaining passages concerning the Irish kings.] mac Eochoda [Note: [Col. 0787D] That is, Nial, son of Eochod, king of Ulster; compare the Annals of the Four Masters, under 1062, and the Annals of Ulster, under 1063.] king of Ulad [Col. 0788C] died on the Ides of November.

Grifri, king of the Britons, died in the autumn.

Donnchad [Note: [Col. 0787D] Concerning him, see the year 1036 (1014). Tigernach’s and other Irish annals mention this pilgrimage under the year 1064.], son of Brian, king of Ireland, and Echmarcach [Note: [Col. 0787D] Eachmarcach is called “king of the foreigners” in the Annals of Tigernach under 1052. He is said to have died this year; see the Annals of Ulster IV, p. 342.] king of Innarenn [Note: [Col. 0787] “Inarenn” in witness 1; I do not know whether I have explained it correctly.], men not undistinguished among their own people, died while coming to Rome.

1088. [MLXVI] 10. Donnchad, descendant of Mathgamna, king of Ulad (Ulster) [Note: [Col. 0788D] That is, king of Ulster; see the Annals of the Four Masters III, p. 624.], was killed in the church of Bennchuir [Note: [Col. 0788D] “Bennchair” in witness 1; it is called “Benucoir” in the Annals of Ulster under this year.] in the spring. Domnnall, descendant of Loigsig, king of Arad (Dalaradia) [Note: [Col. 0788D] That is, Donald O’Loigsig, king of Dalaradia . . .; see the Annals of Tigernach and the Annals of the Four Masters and of Ulster under this year.], of the Cenél Eógain, was killed; the intervening Irish words, “ifeltigernaeg cluana,” are materially uncertain. Hetbartus, king of the English, after reigning for more than 30 years, died on the Nativity of the Lord.

1089. [MLXVII] 11. Araldus succeeded him. Araldus, who was also called Arbach [Note: [Col. 0787] That is, “of battles.”], king of the Northmen, came with fewer than a thousand ships in September, intending to rule England. At York in the autumn [Col. 0788D] he killed in battle more than a thousand laymen and a hundred priests from among the English. But Araldus, king of the English, arrived immediately with seven battle-lines [Note: [Col. 0789] In the margin of witness 1.] and, finding Araldus unprepared, without armor and without the other equipment of war, killed him in battle in October. Meanwhile Willihelmus, also called the Bastard, entered among the English with the Franks; after immediately killing Araldus, king of the English, in battle, he ruled the English. [In this year a comet-star was seen.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] Gloss in witness 1: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” Simon Magus, however, in Samaria, where he believed and was baptized, wanted this comparison from the apostles.]

1090. [MLXVIII] 12. Two popes were in Rome: the bishop of Parma, who had been expelled, and the bishop of Lucca, who became pope.

Murchad Sciath guerr [Note: [Col. 0789D] This is an epithet, translated “of the short shield”; see the Annals of the Four Masters III, p. 628.] oa Briaen was killed in September.

1091. [MLXIX] 13. Murchad oa Moelnambo oa Briaen died in the spring [Note: [Col. 0789D] See the cited annals under 1070, where he is called the son of Diarmait, son of Malnambi.].

I, wretched Marianus, by order of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda, on the Friday before Palm Sunday, 3 April, after ten years of my enclosure, was released and led from my cell at Fulda to Mainz [Col. 0789B]. The chapel of the enclosure of the monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz was dedicated in honor of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle on 10 July, Friday, on the feast of the seven brothers. On that same day I, Marianus, was enclosed a second time in that cell for my sins.

The new monastery of Saint Mary at Mainz was consecrated on 23 November, Monday, the day of Saint Clement.

1092. [MLXX] 14. While the Scots and Franks were laying waste to the English, the English were scattered and died of hunger; they were compelled to eat human flesh, to kill people for this purpose, to season the flesh, and to hang the victims.

[Col. 0789C] 1093. [MLXXI] 15. One of the clerics, named Carolus, like Simon Magus [Note: [Col. 0789] Gloss in witness 1: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” Simon Magus, however, in Samaria, where he believed and was baptized, wanted this comparison from the apostles.], who had asked the apostles for a spiritual gift in exchange for a price, bought from King Henry the bishopric of the city of Constance. At the gathering of bishops and abbots held in the monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz on the Assumption of Saint Mary (15 August), he was accused by Sigfridus, archbishop of Mainz, before King Henry because he had not entered through the Lord’s door [Note: [Col. 0789] “While” in witness 1.]. He left the gathering without the staff; thereafter he did not live for a year.

1094. [MLXXII] 16. Diarmait [Note: [Col. 0789D] See the Annals of Tigernach, p. 308, and the Annals of the Four Masters, [Col. 0790D] p. 633.] king of Leinster was killed on 6 February, Monday. Cuulad [Note: [Col. 0790D] See the same work, p. 635.] oa Flathrae was killed on Friday, 10 February.

Sigfridus, bishop of Mainz, set out on Sunday, 9 September, ostensibly for the sake of prayer, to Galicia, to Saint James. When he was at the monastery of monks called Cluaneca on the Sunday before the mass of Saint Michael (23 September), he entered the cloister and rejected the world. But when mercenaries wished to purchase the bishopric of Mainz for a price, Sigfridus was violently compelled, in violation of the obedience he owed to the abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0789] “Obidendentia” in witness 1.], to return to Mainz on 6 December.

1095. [MLXXIII] 17. In this year everything occurs according to the course of the sun and moon as in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, in which the Lord was baptized: namely, the day of his baptism was 6 January, the day of Epiphany, on a Sunday; and on the following day, Monday, the beginning of the Lord’s fast; on 15 February, the fortieth day of his fast, Friday, his victory over the devil when he overcame gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, in which same Friday the devil had first cast down Adam. Thus from the baptism of the Lord in the fifteenth year of Tiberius until now there are two great cycles, that is, 1,064 years.

Conchobor [Note: [Col. 0790D] See the cited annals under this year.] oa Maelsechnaell, king of Meath, was killed on 24 March, the Sunday of Palm Sunday.

Pope Alexander died on Sunday, 21 April. Illdibrandus, Roman archdeacon, succeeded him.

1096. [MLXXIV] 18. The aforesaid pope decreed, by the commandment of the Apostle Peter and Saint Clement, as above, and by the canons of the Fathers, under the ban of God, Peter, Paul, and himself, by synodal judgment of many bishops—and, contradicting them, he prohibited—that priests, deacons, and all clerics should have wives or live altogether with women, except with those whom the Rule or the Nicene Council permitted them to have.

He also decreed that, under the sentence of Saint Peter, not only the buyer and seller of any consecration or ecclesiastical office—namely, a bishopric, priesthood, diaconate, provostship, deanery, church, or tithing—but also the associate of the transgressor should be condemned with Simon. For the Lord said: “You received freely; give freely.”

Therefore legates of the pope were sent from the aforesaid synod to Henry, king of the Romans—namely, two bishops together with the queen, the mother of that king—in order that, both at a universal synod before the king and by the common prohibition of all the bishops, they might separate women from the clerics, and especially from priests. They refused to be with the king at Easter in the city of Bamberg (20 April), and would neither accept food from nor associate with Hermann, the bishop of that city, who had formerly bought the bishopric and served the king at that Easter.

[Dunatus [Note: [Col. 0789] In the margin of witness 1.], bishop of Dulim [Note: [Col. 0789] Perhaps “Tulini” in witness 1. [Note: [Col. 0790D] That is, Dunanus, archbishop of Dublin.] died on the Ides of May.]

1097. [MLXXV] 19. Since certain clerics preferred to remain under the sentence of the apostolic prohibition rather than be without women and wives, so that they might at least be punished through others, the pope decreed by a synodal legation also in this year that, as in the preceding year, no Christian should hear the mass of a married priest.

On 16 July Widradus, abbot of Fulda, died. [Note: [Col. 0790D] Ruozelinus succeeded him; witnesses 2 and 2** add this.]

[Col. 0791A] 1098. [MLXXVI] 20. In this year the Lord’s Passion occurs for the third time according to the course of the sun and moon, that is, two great cycles after Christ’s Passion, namely 1,064 years.

Eighty [Note: [Col. 0791] “From Adam until this year there are five thousand years and additionally two hundred and eighty,” witnesses 2 and 2**. The remainder is absent.] two hundred and five thousand

All the years’ time from Adam until this point stands complete.

Much [Note: [Col. 0791C] Concerning this passage, see the preface, p. 484, n. 19.] we read from extracted barbarian accounts,

Kings to be justified and turbulent deeds for the needy.

Gather the preceding letter [small, turn over the sum;

Let the numbered author arise; search within;

The straight [line?] has carried me all into a new [that is, book] in the order of praise.

1099. [MLXXVII] 21. At a council of 24 bishops, many abbots, and many clerics, held at Worms [Note: [Col. 0791] “Urmatia” in witness 1 and below.] in March [Note: [Col. 0791C] January, in the year 1076; see Leges, II, p. 18.], in the presence of King Henry, it was decreed that no one should heed the ban of Pope Ilibrandus [Note: [Col. 0791] “Illibrani” in witness 1.], and that he should not be pope.

But the pope excommunicated the king and his followers during Lent for three reasons: because of the infamy of their sins, because of their unity with the simoniacs, and because of this schism of the Church between the pope and the others. Thereafter, on an apparently just pretext, the chief men of the kingdom opposed the king as though he were excommunicated, attempting to cast him out of the kingdom.
