[Bilis [Note: [Col. 0791] In the margin of witness 1; absent in the other witnesses.], brother of Bopo and Gotobaldus, a soldier and canon of Saint Kilian at Würzburg, praiseworthy in character, age, and singing, and very useful in the choir, lay dying in December, crying out and groaning because of the terrors, threats, and calumnies of the present devil. He suffered miserably because of his singing; for God was not appeased by empty shouting and the false addition of many letters [Col. 0791C] to one letter [Note: [Col. 0791] That is, addition.], or by beauty of sound, but by a contrite heart through attentive words. Therefore, what he had always sung beautifully in the choir like an angel . . . [Note: [Col. 0791] Illegible in witness 1.]—as he was dying, he heard himself harshly tormented by the devil [Note: [Col. 0791] The reading is not entirely certain; “carpit acrit” seems to be intended.]

1100. [MLXXVIII] 22. Thus King Henry and Pope Ilibrandus met in March [Note: [Col. 0791C] January, in the year 1077.] in Lombardy: the king received absolution from the pope, while the pope received the apostolic see from the king.

When the Swabians and Saxons, and Walp, duke of Bavaria, met, together with seven bishops from Saxony and six others—the bishops of Passau, Salzburg, Würzburg, Worms, and Mainz—near Bamberg [in the margin: Forchheim], on the third Sunday of Lent [Note: [Col. 0791C] That is, 12 March, more correctly 13 March.], they set up Rudolf, duke of the Swabians, over themselves; and on the middle Sunday of Lent (26 March), at Mainz, they anointed him king and fortified the roads across the Alps against Henry.

When Henry learned this, he went by way of Aquileia to Regensburg after Easter and hastened to Swabia against Rudolf, who was attempting to fight him. When Rudolf fled, Henry plundered Swabia. They also met near the Rhine, between Mainz and Worms, in August, but were prevented from fighting. After an agreement had also been made in the same place on 1 November, Rudolf did not come to meet Henry [Note: [Col. 0791] Witness 2 of the codex, the Vrat. copy, adds: “In this year Anno, bishop of Cologne, died.”]. Henry plundered Swabia and destroyed the castles throughout the winter.

1101. [MLXXIX] 23. Gregory [Note: [Col. 0791] “Gregory—your” in two codices; the words occur after “priests” under the year 1097 (1075), and certainly belong either here or to the year 1074; compare n. 54.] pope, also called Ilibrandus, bishop, servant [Note: [Col. 0791] Absent in witness 1.] of the servants of God, sends apostolic blessing to all throughout the Italian kingdom and the Teutonic [Note: [Col. 0791] “Teutonicorum” in witness 1.] regions who offer due obedience to Saint Peter.

“If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons who lie in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, in the name of almighty God and by the authority of Saint Peter, entrance to the church until they repent and amend their ways. But if any prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you dare listen to their office, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: ‘I will curse your blessings,’ he says.”

King Henry deposed Pope Ilibrandus at Pentecost at Mainz (31 May 1080), and made Vugbertus, bishop of Ravenna, pope in his place at the Nativity of John the Baptist (24 June), at Pressea [Note: [Col. 0791] “Preslea” in witness 2. [Note: [Col. 0792C] That is, Brescia.].

He also killed Rudolf, king of the Saxons, in battle at Merseburg, where Rudolf was buried on the Ides of October. Mainz, with its walls, was so shaken by an earthquake on 1 December that, at the monastery of Saint Victor, about half a mile from Mainz, the earth threw up a dead man with his coffin.

1103. [MLXXXI] 25. From Pentecost, for forty days, King Henry attacked Rome against Pope Ilibrandus (23 May–June [end date uncertain]) but could not enter [Note: [Col. 0791] Read: “was not able to.”]. During the octave of Pentecost, the city of Mainz, for the greater part, and the episcopal monastery and three other monasteries were consumed by fire (August).

In the autumn the Swabians made Conrad’s brother, Hermann, son of Henry of Laach [Note: [Col. 0791] “Lacha” in witness 1.], king in place of Rudolf; and on the Nativity of the Lord he was anointed king in Saxony.

[Col. 0793A] 1104. [MLXXXI] 26. The first Paschal moon appeared for the whole world on 2 April, although it ought to have been on 4 April. There were many murders and acts of plunder between King Henry and Pope Ilibrandus, so that on the night of Palm Sunday many were killed (17 April) [Note: [Col. 0793] The same hand immediately added below, on folio 166: “Marianus the recluse died”; afterward lines were drawn, the years were written, and a brief continuation was added.].

## First Continuation

From the Roman codex.

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A] 1105. [MLXXXIII] (A. Wirzb.) Rome was captured by King Henry, and a great pestilence occurred.

1106. [MLXXXIV] 28. Henry the emperor returned from Italy, and Augsburg was besieged and captured by him. Archbishop Sigefridus died.

[Col. 0793B] 1107. [MLXXXV] Emperor Henry laid waste to Saxony. A synod was held at Mainz, at Saint Alban’s. Meginhardus was appointed bishop of Würzburg. Pope Gregory, also called Hiltibrant, Dietmarus, bishop of Worms, and Hermannus, count palatine, died.

1108. [MLXXXVI] Battle was joined near Bleihefelt on 11 August. Hermannus laid down the name of king and soon afterward perished. Würzburg was captured by the Saxons and shortly afterward recovered by the emperor.

[1109. [MLXXXVII] Empress Bertha died.]

[1110. [MLXXXVIII] Wezel, archbishop of Mainz, and Meginhard, bishop of Würzburg, died. Buggo, bishop of Halberstadt, was killed at Goslar. [Col. 0793C] A battle was fought near the castle of Glicho, situated in Thuringia near Erfurt, between Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0793] “Heinric’” in the codex.] and Margrave Eggibert, on the Sunday vigil of the Lord’s Nativity; in it Burchard, bishop of Lausanne, was killed.

Bishops Sigewinus of Cologne and Otto of Regensburg died. Ruothardus was appointed bishop of Mainz, Hermanus bishop of Cologne, and Emehardus bishop of Würzburg.]

1112. [Note: [Col. 0793] The codex corrects 1111 to 1112.] [MXC] The emperor set out for Italy. Huozmannus, bishop of Speyer, Hermannus [Col. 0794A] of Metz, Duke Liudolfus, and Duke Berhtolfus, son of Rudolf, died. Margrave Eggibert was killed. Adelbero, bishop of Würzburg, died.

1113. [Note: [Col. 0793] The codex corrects 1112 to 1113.] [MXCI] Mahthildis of Lombardy rebelled against the emperor.

[Col. 0794B] 1115. [MXCIII] Fratizlaus, duke of Bohemia, suddenly fell from his horse while hunting and died a sudden death.

1117. [MXCV] Ladizlaus, king of Pannonia, a man of pious memory, and likewise Margrave Liupoldus and Hermannus, count palatine, died.

1123. [MCI] Conrad, the emperor’s son, perished by poison in Lombardy. The archbishops Engelbert of Trier and Liemar of Bremen died.

1124. [MCII].

[Marginal note in the codex: The nineteen-year cycle begins in indiction 10.]

1126. [MCIV] Henry, withdrawing from his father because of the excommunication, accepted the protection of the Catholics. [Note: [Col. 0793] The remainder was written by another contemporary hand.]

[Col. 0794C] 1127. [MCV] King Henry and the archbishop of Mainz, R. [Note: [Col. 0793D] Ruothardus.], came with an army as far as the castle while the emperor held Mainz, and, having been frustrated, departed. Nuremberg was captured. The father was wonderfully defeated by the son at Regensburg.

1128. [MCVI] The cross, lance, crown, and the other insignia of the kingdom were handed over to the son before the princes of the kingdom.

1155. [MCXXXIII] In this year, on 2 August, at about the ninth hour of the day, a solar eclipse occurred so great that the stars could be seen in the sky. [Note: [Col. 0793] These words were added by another hand. The numbers through the year 1335 (1313) are found written on the final folios of the codex.]

## Second Continuation

From the London codex.

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793D] 1105. [MLXXXIII] 27. Henry broke into and captured the city of Rome and installed Wicbertus [Note: [Col. 0793] “Wibbertus” in the codex.] in the apostolic see. Iltebrandus, however, went to Benevento, where he remained until his death. Henry returned to the German homeland.

1106. [MLXXXIV] 28. Hildebrandus [Note: [Col. 0793] “Pope II” in the Vrat. copy.] died [Note: [Col. 0794D] In the year 1085.].

[Note: [Col. 0795A] [This note appears at the top of column 795, but the callout symbol (*) has not been printed in the text.] Florentius has it thus:]

“Pope Hildebrand, the Apostolic, when he was near death, summoned to himself one of the twelve cardinals, whom he loved greatly. He confessed to almighty God, Saint Peter, and the whole Church that he had sinned greatly in the pastoral office entrusted to him for governance, and that, at the devil’s prompting, he had stirred up hatred and anger against the human race. Afterwards, however, he said that he had adopted the sentence which had been spread throughout the world for the advancement of Christianity. Then at last he sent the aforesaid confessor of his to the emperor and to the whole Church, asking them to grant him pardon, because he was contemplating the end of his life. In silence he put on the angelic garment, released and dissolved for the emperor and for the entire Christian people—living and dead, clergy and laity—the bonds of all the bans he had imposed, and ordered them to leave Theodoric’s house and Henry’s friends to ascend, with the archbishop of Mainz as witness. Not long afterwards he died.”

In the first folio of Codex 2 these words are read:

“We wish you to know, who are concerned with ecclesiastical care, that the Apostolic Hildebrand, now near death, summoned to himself one of the twelve cardinals, whom he loved greatly above the others, and confessed to almighty God, Saint Peter, and the whole Church that he had sinned greatly in the pastoral office entrusted to him for governance. At the devil’s prompting he had stirred up hatred and anger against the human race. Afterwards, he said that he had adopted the sentence spread throughout the world for the advancement of Christianity. Then at last he sent his aforesaid confessor to the emperor and to the whole Church, asking them to grant him pardon, because he was contemplating the end of his life. And [printed: *tam cito*, ‘so quickly’; apparently for *tacito*, ‘in silence’] he put on the angelic garment, released and dissolved for the emperor and the entire Christian people, and for dead clergy and laity, the bonds of all his bans, and ordered his men to leave Theodoric’s house and Henry’s friends to ascend. With the archbishop of Mainz as witness.”

These words also seem to have existed in the Gembloux manuscript, from which Sigebertus received them.

[Note: [Col. 0795D] See Hirsch, *De Vita Sigiberti*, pp. 139–143; Bethmann, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, VI, p. 365. Here I will add a brief narrative, first transcribed by Mabillon (*Annales Benedictini*, V, p. 214), and later by me from the Laon manuscript (*Archiv*, VII, p. 220):

“Agano, bishop of Autun, returning after two years from Jerusalem, attended the deposition of the lord pope Gregory. He asserts that Gregory had foretold the day and hour of his death eight days beforehand, and had not lain down in bed at all; on the very day of his passing he went to the church and publicly addressed, together with the clergy, the people of the whole city of Salerno—first concerning belief in the body and blood of our Lord, and then concerning the purpose of all his work. Having put on his stole, he absolved all whom he had in any way anathematized. Afterwards, proceeding on knees and hands, he approached the altar and received from it the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood. Returning home in this manner, he died at the hour he had foretold, charging the aforesaid prelate with the entire duty of his burial, including the distribution of the small amount of property he possessed.”

Finally, the following passage from Codex Udalricianus, no. CLXVI, must also be added:

“When the lord Gregory VII, pope of blessed memory, had begun to fall ill at Salerno with the illness from which he soon died, Roman cardinals and bishops of other cities, religious men, stood by him and asked him to indicate whom he wished to be appointed in his place as bishop. After thinking briefly to himself, he finally gave them this reply: ‘Whichever one of these three you are able to have—namely, the bishop of Lucca, or the bishop of Ostia, or the bishop of Lyons—choose him as bishop.’

“Again, when questioned about the excommunicated, he replied: ‘Except for the aforesaid King Henry and Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, and the other principal persons who by counsel or aid support their impiety or wickedness, I absolve and bless everyone in the place of the apostles Peter and Paul; and whoever will unhesitatingly believe that I possess this power.’

“These, moreover, were his final words: ‘I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.’”]

[Col. 0796A] **1107. [MLXXXV] 29.** Henry [Note: [Col. 0795] H., King, Florentius] defeated the Saxons in battle, gained possession of the country, and compelled them to swear allegiance and obey him. But after he dismissed his army, the Saxons secretly began to gather against Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0795] “the emperor. Henry,” manuscript 2.], intending by treachery to kill him. When he discovered their plot, he avoided their ambush by departing from that province.

**1108. [MLXXXVI] 30.** Henry [Note: [Col. 0795] H., King, Florentius], having engaged the Swabians and Saxons in battle near Würzburg, was abandoned in the very conflict by the support of some of his own traitors, who turned to the enemy [Note: [Col. 0795] *hostes* (“enemies”), Florentius; Vratislav apograph, corrected], and was also struck on the head with a sword by one of his companions. He fled with a few men. The enemy pursued him as far as the aforesaid city, captured it, and there restored Bishop Albero, whom Henry had expelled for treachery [Note: [Col. 0795] *a* (“by”); *ab* (“by”), Florentius], after Bishop Mainard [Note: [Col. 0795] *Menander*, Florentius]—whom Henry had installed there [Note: [Col. 0795] *a* (“by”); *ab* (“by”), Florentius]—was expelled.

Shortly afterwards Henry gathered an army, besieged and captured the same city, and granted Bishop Albero permission to remain, because he was Henry’s godfather, provided that he remained faithful to him and bishop of the city. But when Albero refused to submit to Henry, Henry, being excessively merciful, allowed him to depart freely.

William, king of the English [Note: [Col. 0795] Florentius lacks this passage, expressing the matter differently and omitting what follows], ordered all the possessions of the whole of England to be recorded: its fields, people, all animals, all dwellings from the largest to the smallest [Note: [Col. 0795] lacking in the exemplar of Vratislav], and every tax that could be rendered from all the lands. As a result, the land was afflicted by many calamities.

**1109. [MLXXXVII] 31.** William, king of the English, died on 9 September. William, his son, was anointed and made king on 4 October [Note: [Col. 0795] The years are written through 1122 (1099).]

## From the History of Florentius of Worcester

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795C] **1113. [MLXXXXI] 35.** … There were two men who, as was reported in England, were called Roman pontiffs. They were at odds with one another and dragged the divided Church of God after them: Urban, namely, who had previously been called Odo, bishop of Ostia; and Clement, who had been called Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna. This matter, to say nothing of the other parts of the world, occupied the Church of England for many years to such an extent that, from the time Gregory—who was also Hildebrand—died, it had refused to submit or obey any pope anywhere up to this time. It had already accepted Urban as the vicar of blessed Peter in Italy and Gaul …”

**1118. [MXCVI] 40.** … Pope Urban came to Gaul, and, when a synod was held at Clermont during Lent, urged the Christians to set out for Jerusalem to fight the Turks, Saracens, Turcopoles, and other pagans. At his urging, during the synod itself Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, and with him many others marked with Christ’s cross, promised that they would undertake the pilgrimage for God and carry out what he had advised.

When the others heard this, the Christians from Italy, Germany, Gaul, England, and elsewhere vied with one another in preparing for the same expedition. Their leaders and principal men were: Aimeric, bishop of Le Puy; the bishop of Ostia, with very many other bishops; Peter the monk; Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the French; Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; Stephen, count of Chartres; Robert, count of the Normans; Robert, count of Flanders; the two brothers of Duke Godfrey, Eustace, count of Boulogne, and Baldwin; the aforesaid Count Raymond; and Bohemond, son of Robert Guiscard …

[Col. 0797C] **1120. [MXCVIII] 42.** … The city of Antioch was captured by the Christians on 3 June, a Wednesday. A few days later, the spear with which the Savior of the world was wounded while hanging upon the cross, revealed by the most gentle of the saints, the apostle Andrew, was found in the church of the apostle Saint Peter. Encouraged by this discovery, the Christians went out of the city on 28 June, a Monday, carrying it with them. Having engaged the pagans in battle, they put to flight Curbaran, commander of the Persian sultan’s army, and the Turks, Arabs, Saracens, Publicans, Azimites, Persians, Agulans, and many other peoples, killing many thousands of them with the sword; by God’s power they gained a complete victory. An unusual brightness shone for almost the entire night of 27 September …

Roger, duke of Apulia, having assembled a great army, besieged Capua, which had revolted from his authority. Pope Urban, accompanied by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, as he had ordered him, set out for the council which he had arranged to celebrate at Bari on 1 October. At that council many matters concerning the Catholic faith were expounded by the Apostolic in eloquent and fluent speech. When a question was also raised by the Greeks, who sought to prove by evangelical authority that the Holy Spirit has procession only from the Father, the aforesaid Anselm treated, explained, and resolved the matter so effectively that no one at the gathering remained who did not acknowledge himself satisfied by it.

**1121. [MXCIX] 43.** In the third week after Easter, Pope Urban held a great council at Rome. There, after cutting away what had to be cut away and establishing what had to be established, the pope, with the whole council, imposed a sentence of excommunication upon all laymen who gave investitures of churches, upon all who received those investitures from their hands, and also upon all who consecrated persons to such offices after they had been so appointed.

He also bound with the chain of anathema those who became the men of lay persons for ecclesiastical honors. He said that it appeared exceedingly detestable that hands which had grown to such eminence that they created God, the creator of all things, with their own sign—the privilege granted to none of the angels—and offered that same God, for the redemption and salvation of the whole world, before the sight of God the supreme Father, should be thrust down into such disgrace as to become the servants of hands polluted day and night by obscene contacts or stained by devotion to robbery and the unjust shedding of blood. “Let it be done, let it be done!” everyone shouted, and the council was concluded. Afterwards the archbishop proceeded to Lyons …

On 15 July, a Thursday, Jerusalem was captured by the Christians. Afterwards, on 22 July, the same weekday, Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, was elected king by the whole army. Pope Urban died on 29 July, a Thursday. On 12 August, a Thursday, the Christians fought a great battle before Ascalon with Amiraviso, commander and second in authority throughout the kingdom of the king of Babylon; by Christ’s favor they gained the victory. Paschal, a venerable man who had been ordained priest by Pope Hildebrand, was elected by the Roman people on 13 August and consecrated pope on the following day, that is, 14 August, a Sunday …

**1122. [MC] 44.** Pope Clement, also called Wibert, died …

Meanwhile, Counts Robert of Flanders and Eustace of Boulogne first returned home from Jerusalem; afterwards Count Robert of the Normans returned to his homeland with the wife whom he had betrothed in Sicily …

**1123. [MCI] 43.** Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, son of Eustace the elder, count of Boulogne, who had been the powerful duke of the Lotharingians, ended his life and lies buried in the church of Golgotha. After his death, the Christians unanimously elected his brother Baldwin as their king.

**1128. [MCVI] 48.** … In that year a most detestable conflict arose between the emperor of Alemannia and his son …

**Romans 96.** Henry IV died; his son Henry succeeded him and reigned for nineteen years …

**1132. [MCX] 4.** King Henry of the English gave his daughter in marriage to Henry, king of the Germans …

**1133. [MCXI] 5.** Henry, king of the Germans, came to Rome, captured Pope Paschal, and placed him in custody. Afterwards, at the Salarian Bridge, where they celebrated the Paschal feast in the open field, he made peace with him. The reconciliation between the king and the lord pope was made in the following manner, and this was the king’s oath [Note: [Col. 0799D] See *Monumenta Legum*, II, p. 72.]:

“I, Henry the king, shall set free and cause the lord pope, the bishops, and the cardinals, and all the captives and hostages who were captured for him or with him, to be brought safely within the gates of the Trastevere district on the next Wednesday or Thursday. I shall not thereafter capture, or permit to be captured, those who remain faithful to the lord pope Paschal. I shall preserve peace and security for the Roman people and for the cities of Trastevere and the Island, both in persons and in property, through myself and my men, for those who preserve peace toward me.

“I shall faithfully assist the lord pope Paschal so that he may hold the papacy peacefully and securely. I shall restore the estates and possessions of the Roman Church which I took away, and shall assist him in good faith to recover and retain everything that he ought to possess according to the custom of my predecessors. I shall render obedience to the lord pope Paschal, saving the honor of the kingdom and empire, just as Catholic emperors do to Catholic Roman pontiffs. I shall observe all these provisions in good faith, without fraud or malicious design.”

These are the king’s sworn guarantors: Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Gebhard, bishop of Trent [Note: [Col. 0799] so the edition]; Burchard, bishop of Münster [Note: [Col. 0799] so the edition]; Bruno, bishop of Speyer; Albert, chancellor; Count Hermann; Frederick, count palatine; Count Berengar; Boniface Martius [Note: [Col. 0799] so the edition]; Albert, count of Blandracco; Count Frederick; Count Godfrey; and Warnerius Martius [Note: [Col. 0799] so the edition].

The lord pope Paschal [156] [Note: [Col. 0799D] See the same work, p. 71.] shall grant to the lord King Henry and to his kingdom, and shall confirm and strengthen by his privilege under threat of anathema, that a bishop or abbot freely elected without simony, with the king’s consent, may be invested by the lord king with ring and staff. A bishop or abbot invested by the king shall freely receive consecration from the bishop to whom he belongs. If anyone is elected by clergy and people but is not invested by the king, he shall be consecrated by no one; and archbishops and bishops shall have the freedom to consecrate those invested by the king.

Furthermore, the lord pope Paschal shall not trouble the lord King Henry or his kingdom and empire on these matters. The lord pope Paschal shall not trouble the lord King Henry or his empire or kingdom concerning the investiture of bishoprics or abbeys, nor concerning the injury inflicted upon him and his men; nor shall he inflict any harm upon him or anyone else on this account. He shall never impose anathema upon the person of King Henry, and nothing shall prevent the lord pope from crowning him as prescribed by the order. With the assistance of his office, he shall help him to hold the kingdom and empire to the best of his ability. The lord pope shall fulfill these provisions without fraud or malicious design.

These are the names of the bishops and cardinals who, at the command of the lord pope Paschal, confirmed by oath the privilege and friendship with the lord emperor Henry: Peter, bishop of Porto; Cencius, bishop of Sabina; Robert, cardinal of Saint Eusebius; Boniface, cardinal of Saint Mark; Anastasius, cardinal of Saint Clement; Gregory, cardinal of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul; another Gregory, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus; John, cardinal of Saint Potentiana; Rhisus, cardinal of Saint Lawrence; Rainerus, cardinal of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Vitalis, cardinal of Saint Balbina; Dunzo, cardinal of Saint Martin; Theobald, cardinal of Saints John and Paul; and John, deacon of Saint Mary in the Greek School.

Paschal [Note: [Col. 0800D] See the same work, p. 72.], bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his dearest son in Christ, Henry, king of the Germans and, by the grace of God’s work, august emperor of the Romans.

“Divine providence has ordained that your kingdom should be specially joined to the holy Roman Church. Your predecessors obtained valor, together with the greater grace of prudence, as well as the crown and empire of the Roman city. To the dignity of that crown and empire divine majesty has also raised your person, dearest son Henry, through the ministry of our priesthood.

“Therefore, we too grant to your devotion that prerogative of dignity which our predecessors granted to your predecessors, the Catholic emperors, and confirmed in the pages of their privileges; and we confirm it by the page of this present privilege: you may confer the investiture with staff and ring upon the bishops or abbots of your kingdom who have been freely elected without violence or simony. After investiture, let the person receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom he belongs. But if anyone is elected by clergy and people without your consent, let him be consecrated by no one unless he is first invested by you. Bishops and archbishops shall certainly have the freedom canonically to consecrate bishops or abbots invested by you.

“For your predecessors enlarged the churches of their kingdom with such great royal benefactions that the kingdom itself ought to be fortified chiefly by the estates of bishops and abbots, and, after the many dissensions that frequently arise from elections, these matters ought to be restrained by royal majesty. For this reason you must diligently attend to the care of prudence and authority, so that, with the Lord’s favor, the dignity of the Roman Church and the welfare of the other churches may be preserved through benefactions and services.

“If any ecclesiastical or secular person should attempt, with rash presumption, to violate this page of our concession, let him, unless he repents, be bound by the chain of anathema and suffer the loss of his honor and dignity. May divine mercy protect those who observe it, and grant that your person and power may happily rule to its honor and glory.”

By these agreements and oaths, peace was made between the lord pope and the king at the Paschal feast. Afterwards the king came to Rome on 13 April. While celebrating Mass in the church of Saint Peter, the pope consecrated him emperor, absolved him and all his men, and forgave every injury inflicted upon him.

**1134. [MCXII] 6.** In the thirteenth year of the pontificate of the lord pope Paschal II, in the fifth indiction, in March, on 18 March, a council was held at Rome in the Lateran, in the Constantinian basilica [Note: [Col. 0801D] See Ekkehard, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, VI, p. 246, and what I noted there.].

When the lord pope had taken his seat [Note: [Col. 0801] The edition reads *redisset*, “had returned”] with the archbishops, bishops, cardinals, and a diverse multitude of clergy and laity, on the final day of the council, after making a profession of the Catholic faith before everyone so that no one might doubt his faith, he said:

“I embrace all divine Scripture, namely, that of the Old and New Testaments; the Law written by Moses and the holy prophets. I embrace the four Gospels, the seven canonical epistles, the epistles of the glorious teacher, blessed Paul the apostle, the holy canons of the apostles, and the four universal councils, like the four Gospels: Nicaea, Ephesus, Constantinople, and Chalcedon; the Council of Antioch; and the decrees of the holy fathers, the Roman pontiffs, especially the decrees of my lord Pope Gregory VII and of Pope Urban, of blessed memory. What they praised, I praise. What they held, I hold. What they confirmed, I confirm. What they condemned, I condemn. What they rejected, I reject. What they forbade, I forbid. What they prohibited, I prohibit. In all these matters and through all things, I shall always persevere.”

When this had been completed, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, legate in Aquitaine, rose on behalf of everyone and, with the common consent of the lord pope Paschal and the whole council, read this document before all:

“That privilege which is not a privilege, but truly ought to be called a *pravilege* [Note: [Col. 0801] The edition reads *privilegium*, “privilege”], extorted by King Henry’s violence from the lord pope Paschal for the liberation of captives and of the Church, we all, gathered in this council with the lord pope, condemn by canonical censure and ecclesiastical authority, by judgment of the Holy Spirit; we judge it null, utterly annul it, and, so that it may possess no authority or effectiveness, excommunicate it completely. It has been condemned for this reason: the privilege contains the provision that one canonically elected by clergy and people is to be consecrated by no one unless he has first been invested by the king [Col. 0802A], which is contrary to the Holy Spirit and canonical institution.”

When this document had been read aloud, the entire council acclaimed: “Amen! Let it be done, let it be done!”

The archbishops who were present with their suffragans were these: John, patriarch of Venice; Sennes [Note: [Col. 0801] The edition reads *Semies*], of Capua; Landulf, of Benevento; the archbishops of Amalfi, Reggio, Otranto, Brindisi, Capaccio, and Girgenti; and the Greek archbishops of Rossano and Santa Severina.

The bishops were: Cencius of Sabina; Peter of Porto; Leo of Ostia; Cono of Palestrina; Gerard of Angoulême; Calo of León, legate for the archbishops of Bourges and Vienne; Roger of Volturno; Geoffrey of Siena; Roland of Populonia; Gregory of Terracina; William of Troia; Gibinus of Syracuse, legate for all the Sicilians; and nearly one hundred other bishops.

The bishops Siguinus and John of Tusculum were in Rome on that day but did not attend the council. Afterwards, when the condemnation of the privilege had been read, they consented and approved it …

**1136. [MCXIV] 8.** Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of the English, was betrothed at Mainz to Henry, emperor of the Romans, on 6 January, and was consecrated empress …

**1137. [MCXV] 9.** That year the winter was extremely severe, so that almost all the bridges throughout England were broken by the ice. After Emperor Henry had long besieged Cologne [Note: [Col. 0801D] See Ekkehard, under the year 1114 and following] and had lost many of his men in a pitched battle, he made peace by oath at the city of Neuss [Note: [Col. 0801] The edition reads *missam*, “Mass”] …

**1139. [MCXVII] 11.** … In Lombardy a great earthquake occurred and, as those who experienced it testified, continued for forty days; many buildings and houses collapsed. And, something astonishing to see and recount, a certain very large village was suddenly moved from its original position and was seen standing at a place far removed from everyone.

At Milan, while men of the city’s leading families were sitting together beneath a certain tower and discussing public affairs, a voice sounded outside in everyone’s hearing, calling one of them by name and asking him to come out quickly. When he delayed, a certain person appeared before them and, by entreaty, prevailed upon the man who had been called to go outside. As he went out, the tower suddenly fell and crushed all who were there in a miraculous disaster.

[Note: [Col. 0801D]

In the continuation of the anonymous author, only a few matters concerning the emperor Lothair—whom he calls “Leodegarius” under the year 1125—and the popes Anacletus and Innocent under the year 1137, the Saxons victorious over the Thuringians, perhaps from Widukind, under the year 1138, and a miracle performed in the monastery of Prüm under the year 1138, are worth noting. It is useful to transcribe them here:

**1159.** The Roman see had still been wavering for seven years, since 1137, because of the papacy of two men: Gregory, also called Innocent, and Peter, also called Leo. On their account war arose between Lothair, emperor of the Romans, and Roger, duke of Apulia. Both were rich. One was superior or more distinguished in religion and dignity; the other, to his own disgrace, was superior in gold. Nevertheless, imperial majesty, as is worthy and just, surpasses every royal dignity in all things.

Both appointed the aforesaid men as bishops of bishops at Rome: Lothair granted the papacy to Gregory, canonically elected; Roger granted it to Peter Leo. But since this division between them displeased the authority of the cardinals and the dignity of the prefecture, the cardinals, out of love of money, now admitted Gregory to the Apostolic See by expelling Peter, and now Peter by excluding Gregory.

Finally, Gregory, appointed by Lothair, governed the Apostolic See. Peter Leo, elected by Roger as though he were another pope, sat in the Lateran—the descendant of the earlier Peter Leo. Ambition for dignity spurs both of them on; neither pleases God. While such things take place in the world, they are preserved for God’s judgment, whose judgments are a great abyss.

Because of this great dissension, which had existed for many years at Rome, the head of all the churches throughout the world, the common council of the leaders appointed a day on which a duel should take place between the Romans and the Apulians, and almighty God, the judge of all, should grant victory to whomever he determined.

When an almost innumerable army had been assembled, Emperor Lothair, although weakened by illness, encamped in Apulia. Roger came against him, surrounded by a multitude of many thousands of infantry and cavalry. They fought on both sides. But, God so disposing, the emperor and his men prevailed and triumphed, while Roger and his men were defeated and fled. Roger’s royal crown, which he had made for himself so that he might be crowned king, splendid with gold but nevertheless discovered through an ambush, was presented as an acceptable gift to the imperial majesty. After returning home, Roger lost both his kingdom and his life not long afterwards …

**1160. 1. Romans 99.** Conrad, duke of the Bavarians, nephew of the earlier Henry, who had taken as empress the daughter of Henry, king of the English, reigned for twelve years.

Long ago, a certain people came from the northern region and entered the land of Thuringia to settle it. The inhabitants of that land, since the people from the foreign country requested it, granted them a considerable portion of their settlement. The population grew and multiplied greatly. After a long time had passed, the newcomers denied the Thuringians the tribute that was due.

For this reason the two sides assembled with arms, as was customary among that people, so that the debt might be demanded and paid. This happened once and again, without bloodshed; a third time it was decided that both sides should meet without arms under a peace agreement. The great multitude of foreigners, perceiving the weakness of the Thuringians and that their land was governed well neither by counsel nor by courage, gathered. On the appointed day they entered the agreed meeting, secretly carrying long knives in sheaths for their own precaution and protection.

They did not negotiate in a spirit of peace but amid great discord. What more need be said? The Thuringians were defeated, and the foreign and savage people triumphed. For the use of the long knives, now drawn from their sheaths, caused no small shedding of blood among the Thuringians. The Thuringians were driven in disgrace from their land and ancestral stock; almost their entire country passed to those whom fortune, turning in their favor, had smiled upon in victory.

Finally, the land that had until then been called Thuringia was renamed after the long knives and their victorious outcome—not Saxonia, but, in the English language, Sexonia …

When Peter Leo, the invader of the Apostolic See, died in the ninth year of his invasion, the venerable Pope Gregory, also called Innocent, who governed the holy Church, received in reconciliation all who had supported Peter against him. After peace had been made with everyone, on Easter Day at Rome he consecrated Alberic, abbot of the church of Vercelli, bishop of the church of Ostia. The report of this miracle flew throughout the surrounding region.

In the archbishopric of Trier there is a distinguished monastery called Prüm, dedicated in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. It was founded in ancient times by Pippin, king of the Franks and father of Charlemagne. It is reported by everyone living there that the following unusual event occurred. One morning, and so forth. They caught a demon in the wine cellar and made him a monk; but afterwards, when they stripped him of his monastic habit, he vanished like smoke from between their hands.”]

.

# 1045–1100. LANDULF THE ELDER, CLERIC OF MILAN

[Col. 0803]

## THE HISTORY OF MILAN BY LANDULF

Edited by L. C. Bethmann and W. Wattenbach.

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 32.)

## NOTICE CONCERNING LANDULF: HIS AGE, BIRTH, HOMELAND, DEEDS, AND WRITINGS
[Col. 0803A] The schism in the Milanese Church after the second Arnulf prompted Landulf to write. He supported the same side as Arnulf, but wrote much more bitterly, and, so far as we know, never afterward changed his position—guided more by loyalty to a party than to truth, and sometimes carried away by blind fury.

The subscriptions of the manuscripts indicate his name, as does the letter L., placed at the beginning of the preface in lieu of the name. His social origin is unknown, but Count Giulini has already rightly observed that he favored the common people more than the nobility [Note: [Col. 0804C] *Memorie di Milano* III, 363.]. For when recounting the battles that broke out between the two sides around 1045, he shows himself a partisan of the populace; and while praising Archbishop Guido, he fiercely attacks the clerics who disliked him because of his humble birth.

He himself indicates that he was a cleric, III, 1 [Note: [Col. 0804C] With the words *mei animi vel ordinis* (“of my spirit or order”).], and this is confirmed by his style and his knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs. The letter prefixed to the work, addressed to the archpresbyter of the Milanese Church, seems to assign him a place among the ordinary clergy.

Nothing certain has been handed down to us about the time when he wrote. If the manuscripts are to be trusted, the archpresbyter’s name began with the letter L.; but during those years I have found no one to whom this fits [Col. 0805A]. There is, however, a period between Anselm, who is found in 1100 [Note: [Col. 0805D] From 1096 onward, after Gotefred, who subscribed in 1095; see Giulini IV, pp. 301, 328, 427, 539, 544, 545. Ulric became archbishop in 1120. On 18 October 1128, Tetald of Landriano is mentioned; in 1148 Obert, or Obizius, succeeded him. But perhaps the archpresbyter L. should not be sought among the ordinary clergy, although the wording seems to oppose this.], and Ulric, who was elected in 1110.

Nor can we descend beyond the latter year, since after the death of Heribert (1045) he promises to write about events that occurred in his own time (II, 34), having been shaken by many tribulations, as though he himself and his order had suffered them [Note: [Col. 0805D] III, 1.]. Yet, unlike Arnulf, he did not write in the midst of the events themselves. It is remarkable that he nowhere mentions events of particular importance that occurred after 1085, and the poem prefixed to Book II seems to have been written amid those disturbances. The two greater counts of the Ambrosian see, wandering abroad, whom he mentions there may, I suspect, be Gotefred and Atto, and thus he may have written while they were still alive. [Col. 0805B] But we do not know when either of them died, and from the *History of Landulf of Saint Paul* we learn that the same partisan divisions continued to trouble the Milanese for a long time.

The wretched condition of the Ambrosian clergy that he laments fits well the period of Grosolanus, who disturbed that see from 1102 to 1112, as the author of the catalogue soon to be published says. Nothing in our Landulf’s work proves that all of it was written at a single time. He carried it down to the year 1085, and in III, 30 mentions an event that occurred in the second year of Anselm IV, that is, in 1099 or 1100. He may have added this later. Another consideration, however, shows that he was writing about events already sufficiently remote: for since he entirely neglected chronological order everywhere, even in matters treated at the end of the work, [Col. 0805C] he confused everything most shamefully.

He says that Tedald, who became archbishop in 1075, had been present at the battle in which King Henry defeated the Saxons before his election; in the same battle, he reports, King Rudolf was killed. Nor did he arrange what follows much better. Hence it seems to me quite probable that Landulf, already an old man, wished to console his mental distress—when the opposing faction had long been dominant—by explaining the causes that had brought the clergy down from its position. He says that these matters were firmly fixed in his memory [Note: [Col. 0805D] If *tabulas carnales* in III, 1 may be interpreted in this way.], and that he would now commit them to writing for the protection of posterity.

One thing is surprising: that he was permitted to address such material to an archpresbyter elected by the victorious papal party. He complains that no one had yet undertaken to write down such great events, from which it appears that Arnulf’s work was unknown to him. He himself, remembering—as he says [Note: [Col. 0805D] II, 34.]—from what greatness and how many honors the clergy had fallen, carefully gathered everything that could illuminate its former magnificence, [Col. 0806A] and then began the continuous narrative with Walpert.

He was himself a witness of the latest events; others he learned from those who had seen them [Note: [Col. 0806D] III, 19.]. But the events that occurred before 1045, he asserts, he discovered with much toil and labor, by questioning all the old men and searching through the pages of books from all the cities of Italy [Note: [Col. 0806D] III, 2. Compare the prologue.].

From these statements he himself indicates, besides Sacred Scripture and the theological works of Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory the Great, from which he quotes very extensively, Paulinus’s *Life of Ambrose* [Note: [Col. 0806D] I, 1; II, 15; III, 12, 30.], Gregory’s *Register* [Note: [Col. 0806D] III, 6, 9.] and *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0806D] III, 7.], the book *On the Situation of the City of Milan*, together with the lives of its first bishops [Note: [Col. 0806D] II, 2, 15. It was published in *SS. Rer. It.*, vol. Ib.], and the *Pontifical of the Romans* and the *Deeds of the Lombards* [Note: [Col. 0806D] II, 2, and the heading of chapter 15. Paul’s *History* contains none of what chapter 2 relates; but perhaps he had a manuscript enlarged at the end.]. Yet he sends readers to these works rather than actually drawing material from them himself. He also used verses inscribed on the Nazarene basilica and on the cenotaph of Fronto [Note: [Col. 0806D] I, 6; II, 3.].

Besides these, in II, 8 he mentions a book found at Genoa, which, unless I am mistaken, is the same work that he indicates in the obscure words at the end of the prologue. From this book, it seems, he drew the narratives full of legends about the early fortunes of the Milanese Church with which the first part of the work is filled.

We nevertheless learn the names of the individual authors from the chapter headings: Ambrose himself, Datius, Constantius, Benedict, and Thomas, bishops of Milan. But the reliability of these headings is highly uncertain. None of the manuscripts known to us is earlier than the fourteenth century, and they differ greatly in their chapter titles. The manuscript that we call B. supplies a title for chapter III, 30 that certainly was not written by Landulf; but A., [Col. 0806C] at II, 30, likewise supplies a heading that I am convinced originated with some later person.

Moreover, it seems scarcely likely that those authors whom we find named only in the chapter titles were never mentioned by Landulf in the actual text—as Gregory was—if he had either possessed such sources or invented them. I therefore incline entirely to the view that Landulf himself occasionally supplied lists of names for the chapters, while the rest were added by later hands.

First, the statement at I, 11 that the material is by Blessed Ambrose is manifestly absurd. What is entitled “The Sermon of Constantius” at I, 4 appears to have arisen from a misunderstanding of words at the beginning of chapter 8. As for Benedict, Landulf himself may have named him at II, 15, since his name appears in the speech itself, although that speech was composed much later than Benedict.

Chapters I, 10–14, which are entitled “The Sermon of Blessed Thomas,” are also found in a thirteenth-century manuscript called the *New Berold*, but [Col. 0807A] without the author’s name. No one who has read them will doubt that Archbishop Thomas could not have written them.

Only Datius therefore remains, to whom chapters 1, 2, 4, 12, and 13 are attributed. But this is false, as the distinguished scholars Muratori [Note: [Col. 0807D] In the appendix to *Anecdota*, vol. I, and in the preface to Landulf.] and Fumagalli [Note: [Col. 0807D] *Antichità Longobardico-Milanesi* III, 333.] proved long ago.

Landulf mentions Datius, but says not a word about his writings [Note: [Col. 0807D] Indeed, at I, 12, he says that after explaining the orders of the Church he will now narrate the catechumens “according to the order which I have seen with my heart, learned by experience, and learned from the faithful.” If these words are compared with the prologue, there can be no doubt that Landulf, not Datius, is speaking.].

I therefore believe that it was through no fault of his that not only those chapters but the entire work was, through some extraordinary error, attributed to that Datius. In 1574 Franciscus Castellus inscribed the manuscript: “The *Chronicle of Datius, Archbishop of Milan,” [Note: [Col. 0807D] See Muratori, *Anecdota* I, 236.] and rightly so, since it is established that it was already being called by this name at the beginning of the fourteenth century.

For Galvaneus of La Flamma names Datius and Arnulf among his sources [Note: [Col. 0807D] At Saint Nazarius, *Manipulus florum*, chapter 1.], and invokes Datius as a witness when he reports events drawn from Landulf’s history. Our manuscripts were written around the same time, and attribute the work to Datius, Archbishop of Milan. In the following century the author of the *Life of Mathilda* quotes Landulf’s words from “the book called Darius” [Note: [Col. 0807D] *Leibniz, SS. Rer. Br.* I, 694. We owe this information to a note by Horatius Blancus.]. Bernardinus Corius also calls him Datius.

The origin of this designation is entirely obscure. Moreover, no mention is made of the writings of this Datius, except that a few words are attributed to him in the *Deeds of the Bishops* [Note: [Col. 0807D] See Sylverius.] and in the *Miscellaneous History* [Note: [Col. 0808D] Book XVI, p. 107, Muratori.], apparently taken from a certain letter.

I therefore think that Landulf composed the narrative down to II, 35 partly from writings that he found, composed by authors unknown to him and therefore bearing no authors’ names, and partly from stories that were commonly circulated. I believe that he inserted the poem about King Albert, either because it had been written down or because it was still customarily sung by his fellow citizens. In the continuous narrative after Walpert, he seems to have lacked the assistance of books and to have reported what he had learned by hearsay until he reached events that he himself had known by seeing them.

But in both the earlier and later material he handled his sources with considerable freedom, and seems to have enlarged and embellished many things [Note: [Col. 0808D] The passages at II, 2 and 15, taken from the book *On the Situation of Milan*, provide examples; Landulf added much to them himself.]. Among these, the speeches inserted throughout the work deserve particular notice. I do not know whether he invented them himself or incorporated them after receiving them from others—for who could believe that they were actually delivered?

He nowhere cared about chronological order, and, blinded by partisan zeal, departed from the truth very often. Thus we can scarcely use him in constructing a history of events; at the very least, every individual statement must be examined with the greatest care [Col. 0807D].

He uses a careless style, scarcely disciplined by the rules of grammar [Col. 0808A], which has been corrupted still further in our manuscripts. These manuscripts are late, and all descend from a single copy, already mutilated, since the lacunae at the ends of the chapters are common to all the manuscripts known to us.

Nor can we correct him from the words of Galvaneus of La Flamma, since Galvaneus has rarely preserved Landulf’s wording. The *Life of Ariald*, whose author abridged certain chapters of Landulf, is no more useful.

The passages of Ambrose and other writers that Landulf quotes, when compared with other copies, show that the wording in our manuscripts is very defective [Note: [Col. 0808D] For example, Ambrose at II, 3; III, 24, 26.]. Yet I have not dared to correct it, since the author’s own carelessness is plainly evident in the same passages. For example, he quoted the same passage of Gregory three times [Note: [Col. 0808D] II, 3, 35; III, 23; see also III, 30 for how he misused Ambrose’s testimony.], but always in such a corrupt form [Col. 0808B] that it makes no sense.

He sometimes altered even the passages of Sacred Scripture that he quoted from memory so greatly that one can scarcely recognize them; several I searched for entirely in vain. It is nevertheless apparent that the books he used differed somewhat from other copies, and that some were pseudepigraphical works—for example, the words of Augustine about frogs at III, 8.

Until now there has been only one edition, prepared by Horatius Blancus in Muratori’s *Scriptori di cose italiane*, vol. IV, from two metropolitan manuscripts, one of which has since perished [Note: [Col. 0808D] Puricellus also knew both of them, *De sanctis martyribus*, p. 14. But he used manuscript B, from which he published much.]. Muratori had earlier copied for his own use a more recent transcript in the Ambrosian Library, which he thought had descended from one or the other of those two manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0808D] *SS.* IV, p. 51.].

Our Bethmann followed him and, because he trusted the transcript A* more, regarded Blancus’s text as less valuable. But [Col. 0808C] when I noticed that some readings from manuscript A reported by Blancus [Note: [Col. 0808D] II, 19, 20, 35.] differed completely from the others, this no longer seemed so certain to me. I therefore decided that Blancus’s variant readings should be reported, although I have rarely dared to admit them into the text—at first all of them, and afterward only those of greater importance.

Let us now present the description of the manuscripts themselves, as Bethmann transmitted it to us:

**[A.]** A manuscript formerly belonging to the metropolitan church of Milan, the same one that we designated 5 in Arnulf’s history, now lost. It can be known only through two copies of it; these are:

**A.** Ambrosian manuscript no. 128, seventeenth century, which in Arnulf we called B 1. It copied Arnulf from Ambrosian manuscript no. 89 and Landulf from A. In the chapter titles [Col. 0808D] it differs so greatly from A** and B that it seems to have composed them independently [Note: In my view, if any of these titles are genuine, they appear to have been preserved in this manuscript—for example, II, 15, 34; III, 1, 4, 7, 19, 31.]. Muratori used it.

From it was copied manuscript A of the Brera Library, F, X, 6, on paper, in folio, beginning of the seventeenth century; it contains nothing but Landulf.

**A\*\*.** A manuscript of the most serene Duke Litta of Milan, dated 1703, which we called 5* in Arnulf. In Landulf it follows A* very closely, except in the titles, where it generally agrees with B.

**B.** A manuscript formerly belonging to the metropolitan church, now Ambrosian, no. 89, fourteenth century. It differs greatly from A, especially in the first part, because it omits sometimes individual words, sometimes several words, and even condenses entire sentences and, indeed, chapters. It occasionally altered the chapter titles, which it wrote in red, on its own initiative; it also sometimes added notes in red to the margins.

This is Bethmann’s account. He transmitted to us a text corrected chiefly according to the authority of manuscript A*, while retaining the orthography of manuscript B [Col. 0810A] [Note: In particular, *e* and *i*, *s* and *ss*, and *sc* are often interchanged. That these and other features had already become common at an early date in manuscripts written in Italy is shown, for example, by the ninth-century manuscript now in Vienna; see our *Annals* VII, 275.].

I have retained this orthography, since we do not know Landulf’s own practice; and in some passages that remain doubtful, it will be useful to keep the scribes’ orthography before one’s eyes. In passages taken from Ambrose and other writings, I added the variant readings of more recent editions, which clearly reveal how badly the scribes handled the text.

Where they are unnecessary, I relegated the chapter titles to the variant readings, since it is evident that many were added later and we cannot distinguish the genuine titles by any certain method. As for the historical matters, I added only a few notes, since Arnulf’s *History* is available for comparison, while the reliability of most of these matters is so uncertain that determining what truth lies beneath the legends would require a longer investigation.

**W. Wattenbach**

## Prolegomena to Landulf’s *History*, by Ludovico Antonio Muratori

(*Scriptori italiani*, vol. IV, p. 49.)

[Col. 0809]

[Col. 0809B] Landulf the Elder, the Milanese historian, now brought forth into the light, will have difficulty winning favor with fastidious readers once they uncover his faults and blemishes. Yet the fact that he himself hints at these blemishes, and thus early warns the reader against the writer’s slanders, ignorance, and spitefulness, will, I think, so disarm his otherwise foolish venom that I do not expect anyone in the future to fear him.

This historian, whose chronicle extends approximately to 1085, lived in the time of Gregory VII, and certainly flourished before the year 1100 after Christ. In his homeland, that is, at Milan, the morals of the clergy were then greatly corrupted: some were infected with the crime of simony, while others refused to observe sacred continence. Consequently, especially the marriages of priests and of other clerics were customary there, and no account was taken of ecclesiastical discipline—a discipline that had prevailed, at least in the Western Churches, from the apostolic age down to that time.

Nor was the Milanese clergy alone infected with this stain. To pass over other cities, the disease afflicted Rome itself so successfully that Pope Stephen IX, in 1057, was compelled to convene the clergy and people of the city in frequent synods and to insist especially on abolishing the marriages of clerics and priests [Col. 0809D], as is attested by Leo of Ostia, Peter Damian, Baronius, and others.

Indeed, the supreme pontiffs—namely the renowned Stephen IX, Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII—expended very great effort to restore, especially in the Milanese Church, the discipline that had collapsed in this respect, as the learned Giovanni Pietro Puricellus once demonstrated at length in his book *On the Holy Martyrs Ariald and Herlembald*.

It was in those times that our Landulf lived at Milan and composed this *History*. He himself may perhaps have been a married priest, and certainly he was a most ardent patron of married or concubinary clerics. Hence it is no wonder that his books are filled with both extravagant abuse of the Roman pontiffs and astonishing insolence toward all good men who opposed incontinence, while he returns, opportunely or inopportunely, in various places to the defense of the depraved custom and to accusations against those who thought otherwise.

What else could one expect from a man so extraordinarily disturbed by such passions? It will therefore be the task of the prudent and learned reader to despise and laugh at everything he freely pours forth against the holiest men and against the Roman Church itself, to which honor must always be paid and from which it is a most grievous sacrilege, in the sight of God, to depart.

[Col. 0810C] Moreover, Landulf is disfigured by considerable ignorance and no ordinary shamelessness. Read the chapter *On Priests with One Wife*, where he either invents or foolishly believes that Saint Ambrose supported the marriages of priests, and makes him write statements that either are nowhere found in the books of that holy bishop or occur there with another meaning. For it is otherwise certain that Ambrose recognized, in more than one passage, that it was unlawful for priests to beget children.

His words are perfectly clear in Book I, chapter 1, *On Duties*:

“You recognize that the ministry must be presented unharmed and undefiled, and must not be violated by any marital intercourse—you who, sound in body and incorrupt in modesty, and even removed from marital companionship itself, have received the grace of the sacred ministry.”

Read the remainder there, together with Mabillon’s notes. Then, in Letter 63 to the Church of Vercelli, class I, no. 62, he says:

“These are the things I have set down which I have learned must be avoided. The Apostle is the teacher of virtues: he teaches that those who contradict must be reproved with patience; and when he commands that a bishop be the husband of one wife, this is not so that he may exclude one who has no share in marriage—for that would go beyond the requirement of the law—but so that he may preserve the grace of his purification in marital chastity. Nor is he thereby invited, on apostolic authority, to beget children while in the priesthood; for he says ‘having children,’ not ‘begetting them.’”

In many other passages as well, one may see Landulf’s reliability wavering. The complaint of Blessed Benedict, Archbishop of Milan, concerning the consecration of the bishop of Pavia, which appears here and which I had already published in volume I of the *Anecdota*, Appendix, chapter 5, is a speech falsely attributed to that archbishop, as I showed there in chapter 7.

This writer similarly assigns speeches to other men according to his own fancy, so that he may sell his opinions—sometimes quite futile—under another person’s name, to say nothing of the miracles and visions that he recalls, or, more accurately, invents, with excessive readiness for the benefit of his own side.

What is still more surprising is that Landulf is inept not only in ecclesiastical learning but also in the narration of events themselves [Col. 0811A], even events that occurred no more than a few centuries or years before his time. Most worthy of notice is what he reports about the reign and age of the Emperor Lambert.

If we believe what he writes in Book II, chapter 3, Lambert ruled in Italy in the sixth century of the Christian era. For after Landulf has narrated his death, he immediately continues: “At that time, when the fiercest Lombards came into Italy…” Yet everyone knows that Lambert, king and emperor of Italy, lived until the end of the ninth century and was killed in the year of Christ 898—that is, not even two centuries before our Landulf. One can scarcely understand how a writer living so near those times could have been so blind in so notable a matter.

I pass over other errors of this sort, which at least show this historian guilty of considerable negligence, and I leave aside his style, in which solecisms, not to mention barbarisms, abound to satiety—faults that one could hardly attribute entirely to the copyists.

[Col. 0811B] But I seem already to hear someone asking: Why, then, do I wish to publish an ignorant, unreliable writer who is hostile to the Roman pontiffs—someone whom it would be more equitable to leave buried in his own oblivion?

Those who move in the inner sanctuaries of ancient learning will answer on my behalf. They know very well how much it matters for the humanities that even these historical trifles, whatever their quality, be brought into public view.

It is already well established that the Middle Ages suffered from a lamentable scarcity of writers, during which ignorance and barbarism deprived us, above all, of nearly every use of the sciences and arts. Hence the complaints of our own age: that we lack monuments from those times and that an immense darkness now confronts us in Italian history. If anyone devotes himself to dispelling it by diligently examining ancient manuscripts and archives, the learned owe him great thanks.

For although historians of those centuries are often inept when they report events somewhat distant from their own age—a fault that Godefridus Guilielmus Leibniz justly charges against them in the *Introduction to the Collection of Historical Material on Brunswick*—they nevertheless generally have this merit: they faithfully describe events close to their own time, whether contemporary or nearly so. When compared with other sources, they can also help to confirm or explain more fully events of greater antiquity.

Mixed, to be sure, with legends and certain errors, they contain much historical truth, which an acute and prudent critic must afterward separate out. The very events that Landulf reports about Lambert, although they depart extraordinarily far from chronological calculation, easily indicate the period of Theudebert, king of the Franks. From this we learn only what tradition in Milan related about Lambert’s deeds and death approximately one hundred and eighty years after his death.

But who would deny that the matters nearer to Landulf’s own time can contribute something to the clarification of history? I particularly ask the reader to notice what he says in Book II, chapter 16: that Otto III Augustus, having lost his wife, by whom he had not fathered a male child, was averse to marriage but eventually arranged a marriage with the daughter of the emperor of Constantinople.

Godefridus of Viterbo relates that Maria, the wife of Otto III, solicited a certain count of Modena to engage in an illicit embrace. Because he recoiled from so great a crime and was consequently accused by the impious queen of having used force against her, he was beheaded. When the dead count’s wife defended his innocence before Otto by undergoing the ordeal of fire, Otto executed his queen by public punishment.

Some accuse this great event, reported by no contemporary writer, of being false. Among them the most distinguished Pagi, in his *Criticism of Baronius* under the year 998, no. 17, adopts the view and writes: “Otto III never took a wife.”

Yet our Landulf, who lived not long after the time of Otto III, testifies that this Augustus truly had a wife. Why should we not believe him on this point? Certainly, after hearing this testimony, one would not dare immediately to consign Godefridus’s account to the realm of fable.

Although Landulf’s spirit was embittered and unjust toward the supreme pontiffs themselves, he should not be condemned with such severity that, in the deplorable scarcity of writers from his age, the republic of letters should be deprived of this literary offspring. What, I ask, has the Chair of Peter or the Catholic Church to fear from such an inept writer, when Landulf’s abuse may rather redound to the praise of those pastors whose zeal restored the Milanese Church to its former dignity?

There ought to be such confidence in the truth and in the good cause that, however badly someone may have served the Roman Church—as I believe Landulf did—anyone who wished, with nothing but a harsh frown, to proscribe its enemies and to permit nothing, or even the slightest thing, differing from our opinions to be published from antiquity would be acting wrongly.

Let the guilty person fear for himself and avoid the light. For this reason the leaders of the ecclesiastical republic did not take offense when certain pamphlets of the ancient heretics themselves came to light, provided that remedies were joined with the poison.

We have other historians, and indeed not a few, resembling Landulf, and they have free circulation through the hands of the learned. Even in our own time, with Rome not dissenting, the *History of the Bishops of Ravenna*, formerly composed by Andreas Agnellus and illuminated by the distinguished Benedict Bacchinius, was restored to the light from the Este Library and reprinted here in volume II, although it presents material not unlike that of our Landulf.

All such works must be tolerated under the one justification that they contribute to weaving history together more accurately and truthfully.

It remains now to say something further about the *History* itself and its author—matters perhaps more agreeable to the learned.

The manuscript exemplar from which I once made my copy is preserved in the Ambrosian Library and was written in a more recent hand. It was made from one of the two manuscript codices held in the library of the metropolitan chapter of Milan [Col. 0812C].

There are, I say, two manuscript codices there, both written many centuries ago. One contains, besides the *History of Landulf* that we are now publishing, the *Chronicle of Arnulf*, which we have likewise published, and a catalogue of the bishops of Milan extending to Galdinus, who died in the year of Christ 1176.

Everything in it was written in the same script, so that one can easily determine the age of the codex. The other manuscript contains the same histories of Landulf and Arnulf, in a script not unlike that of the first codex, and also contains the *History of Landulf of Saint Paul*, which will likewise be published in our collection.

At the beginning of this second codex, however, appears the following title, written in a more recent hand: “The *Chronicle of Datius, Archbishop of Milan.”

It should now be noted that a famous controversy exists among scholars as to whether the authors of the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* were the holy bishops Ambrose and Augustine. Those who defend this view rely chiefly on the testimony of Saint Datius, Archbishop of Milan, who flourished under the Emperor Justinian, and who, they say, confirms the matter.

They report that Saint Datius was the author of a certain chronicle. Gualvaneus Flamma, Corius, Alciatus, and other ancient and modern writers on Milanese affairs say this, and even testify that they drew much material from that same chronicle. On these documents above all Father Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo formerly based his defense of his opinion concerning the authors of the hymn, in a published investigation of the matter.

Nor is it necessary to enumerate all the others who have mentioned Datius and his chronicle. But the distinguished Jean Mabillon must not be passed over. When he learned that a manuscript copy of this chronicle was preserved in the metropolitan library, he inquired about it by letter of Antonio Maria Pusterla. Mabillon later published Pusterla’s replies in the *Analecta veteris aevi*, vol. I, p. 3.

[Col. 0813A] I myself undertook to examine this same question in volume I of the *Anecdota*, p. 221. There, in a work entitled *Propempticon* and addressed to the aforementioned Father Eustachius of Saint Ubaldo, concerning the ancient right of the metropolitan of Milan to the episcopate of Pavia, chapter 6, I argued that the *Chronicle of Datius, Archbishop of Milan*, frequently cited by historians, was nothing other than this very chronicle of Landulf, which I am now making public.

I also argued that there was no sufficiently firm proof that any chronicle had been written by that most ancient Archbishop Datius. Therefore the argument for the authors of the hymn *Te Deum*, drawn from the authority and antiquity of Saint Datius, collapsed or at least became doubtful.

Moreover, it is clear that the history mentioned under Datius’s name by Flamma, Corius, Alciatus, and others cannot be attributed to Saint Datius, since it contains very many things—indeed, most things—that happened long after Datius’s time and extends down to the age in which our Landulf flourished.

Father Eustachius was displeased by this opinion of mine. In a preface addressed to me, attached to his *Dissertation on the Metropolitan Church of Milan*, published at Milan in 1699, he therefore tried to persuade me and others that I had denied without adequate grounds that any chronicle had been written by Saint Datius.

It could not be inferred, he argued, simply because Landulf’s *History* contains material that some people admit they copied from Datius’s chronicle, that Landulf’s book was identical with Datius’s work. He did indeed concede that no history written by Saint Datius was extant; but he maintained that such a work had once existed, or could have existed, and that Landulf had incorporated it into his own work.

He held that Puricellus considered Datius to have been different from Landulf, and that this Datius wrote after the middle of the eleventh century after Christ, while Landulf, his contemporary, committed similar matters to writing at the same time.

Furthermore, he argued that Landulf’s *History* differed from the chronicle of this later Datius, since Gualvaneus Flamma, Corius, and Alciatus say that they drew certain material from Datius’s chronicle which is absent from Landulf’s books or is reported there in a different [Col. 0813C] form.

This was his position. But although Father Eustachius’s arguments were offered in anger, I was unable to respond to them at the time, being hindered by other occupations and studies. Perhaps I might have settled the dispute more clearly, or freed it from some points that I consider false or doubtful, when I formerly lived at Milan after being summoned to the Ambrosian Library.

Now that I am removed from that beloved and splendid city, it is not equally easy for me to debate these matters. Nevertheless, let readers receive from me some observations on the question which, if I may anticipate their judgment, will not prove entirely useless.

First, then, I maintain that it cannot be proved that Saint Datius, Archbishop of Milan, was the author of any chronicle. Paul the Deacon and Anastasius the Librarian write only that Datius, bishop of Milan, reported—perhaps by letter—that the bodies of children had been devoured by their own mothers to relieve the famine that at that time was cruelly ravaging the people of Insubria [Col. 0813D].

But none of the more recent writers who have praised the *Chronicle of Datius* praise a history composed by Saint Datius the archbishop. Rather, they refer to a work either compiled by another Datius after the middle of the eleventh century after Christ or circulated under his name.

This is certainly established by the fact that most of the material taken from Datius’s chronicle belongs to periods immediately following the death of Archbishop Datius. The material that Landulf reports from Bishop Datius, however, comes from an author who is unreliable in other matters, so that we cannot safely rely on him.

Moreover, Puricellus thinks that the bishop’s name was rashly added to those chapters by a copyist, contrary to Landulf’s intention. Certainly Landulf himself, when he mentions Archbishop Datius, does not attribute any history to him.

Puricellus’s opinion follows, holding that Datius and Landulf, two different men, lived in the same eleventh century and composed histories; that the former’s *Chronicle*, later cited by others, can no longer be found, whereas the latter’s still survives. The learned man observed, namely, that certain things are written by Gualvaneus as though excerpted from Datius’s *Chronicle*, although they appear otherwise in Landulf’s *History*. But I still hold the opinion that under the name of Datius Gualvaneus and the others meant one and the same *History of Landulf*; nor have the arguments of Puricellus and Father Eustachius yet drawn me away from that opinion.

First, because at least most of what Gualvaneus and others report from Datius’s *Chronicle* occurs in the same words in Landulf’s *History*. Yet one can scarcely understand Landulf to have been so witless that, when he undertook to write a history for himself, he should so openly and so frequently plunder one Datius and compose nearly his entire history from Datius’s books, without even changing the wording—especially since that invented Datius, as Puricellus is compelled to maintain, carried his histories at least as far as the year 1074 [Col. 0814B] after Christ, indeed, as Puricellus himself asserts in chapter 39 of the *Dissertatio Nazaren[a]*, up to the liberation of Gregory VII by Robert Guiscard, that is, to the year 1084, at which very time Landulf was both living and writing.

Second, it may seem strange that Gualvaneus and the others, who diligently sought out the earlier histories of their city and even mention many of those which we now regret to have perished, should so often mention Datius alone, but never Landulf, although Landulf’s *Chronicle* certainly still existed in their age, since it was preserved in that same city down to our own times in at least two copies, and those ancient ones. On the other hand, since Gualvaneus asserts that in his own day there was not merely one copy of Datius’s *Chronicle* at Milan, and since copies of the same work still survived in the time of Corius and Alciatus, Puricellus’s view necessarily requires that all those copies should have disappeared within a brief period, while Landulf’s survived—although, as Puricellus himself is compelled to admit, the ancients had taken no account of Landulf. Certainly everyone will admit with me that it is more plausible that no copies of a Datian *Chronicle* perished, because none ever existed, whereas copies of Landulf’s *History* were preserved because they had always existed and had formerly been cited only under Datius’s name.

Third, on the first page of the older manuscript of the Metropolitan Library, where the histories of Landulf and Arnulf are found, this title is written:

> *Chronicles of Datius, Archbishop of Milan. By me, Francesco Castelli, ordinary of the Church of Milan, 1575.*

Do you see how Francesco Castelli, otherwise a learned man, erred in appending that title? For that *Chronicle* could indeed have been attributed to some Datius, but certainly never to Datius, Bishop of Milan, who could not have committed events to writing many centuries after his death—unless he had been a prophet. From this we can learn that Castelli—living in the same century as Corius and Alciatus, although younger than they—thought Datius’s *Chronicle* to be nothing other than [Col. 0814D] Landulf’s *History*. For although, and this must especially be noted, the following words are written at the end of the Metropolitan manuscript in very ancient characters:

> *Here ends the book of the Histories of Landulf the historiographer*,

nevertheless this did not prevent Castelli from entitling that *History* as belonging to Datius, since he knew perfectly well that when the ancients mentioned Datius’s *Chronicle*, they were referring to no other work than Landulf’s *History*. Moreover, in the very Preface the author of the *Chronicle* reveals himself when he writes: “L., least of all.” That is, he expressly identifies himself as Landulf, the author of this *Chronicle*, which was later called among the Milanese Datius’s *Chronicle*.

Fourth, what has strengthened and continues to strengthen me all the more in my opinion is this: when Gualvaneus Flamma enumerates the books from which he composed his *History*, he mentions, among others, Datius’s *Chronicle* in these words: “The Chronicles of Datius and Arnulf.” Yet in two ancient manuscripts of the Metropolitan Library we saw the histories of Landulf and Arnulf joined together, for among the ancients Arnulf customarily followed Landulf. How then could we fail to understand that Gualvaneus’s *Chronicle of Datius* was the same work as our *Chronicle of Landulf*? Why, however, Landulf’s *History* was cited under Datius’s name, we cannot determine from certain evidence. Nor is it necessary to labor over the matter, since everything else converges upon this conclusion: this *History of Landulf* was known to the ancients and cited under Datius’s name, and there is no need to invent another Datius contemporary with Landulf—an expedient to which Father Eustachius was finally compelled to retreat after abandoning the earlier opinion.

“But,” say Puricellus and Father Eustachius himself, “Gualvaneus, Corius, and Alciatus produce certain passages from Datius’s *Chronicle* which now are either sought in vain in Landulf’s *History* or are presented there differently. Therefore,” they infer, “the Datian *History* was different from Landulf’s.”

At first sight, not without reason. But one must first observe [Col. 0815B] that the few passages which Father Eustachius adduces to demonstrate this difference are not all correctly represented.

Next, this difference must be attributed to Gualvaneus, who either expands matters from other histories or explains Landulf’s ideas according to his own ingenuity and learning.
