Finally, there formerly were—and still are—copies of Landulf’s work that disagree among themselves; perhaps the same scribe, or someone else, added to, reduced, or altered what had previously been written. All this could be confirmed at greater length at Milan. Nevertheless, I have these matters noted from long ago.

Gualvaneus Flamma writes as follows in the *Politia*, chapter 124:

> “Datius’s *Chronicle* says that the Roman princes, etc., built six very lofty dwellings over the city’s six gates, etc.”

Here Father Eustachius says: “Flamma reports from Datius that there were six gates at Milan, and six dwellings over them.” Landulf does not speak of the number of gates or dwellings. In fact, the word “six” is absent from one of the Landulf manuscripts, namely the copy in the Ambrosian Library; but in the other, that of the Metropolitan Library, six gates are enumerated. Read book II, chapter 1.

Father Eustachius adds that Gualvaneus derives the following additional matter from Datius:

> “They built a triumphal arch outside the Roman Gate, two miles long.”

Father Eustachius adds that Landulf contains a little about this arch but says nothing about its length. I read Gualvaneus’s manuscript preserved in the Ambrosian Library at that passage, and I did not see Datius cited there as a witness, but rather the *Campanian Chronicle*. Gualvaneus’s words are:

> “And the Campanian *Chronicle* says that this arch was two miles long.”

Again, in chapter 690 of Gualvaneus’s *Greater Chronicle*, Gualvaneus reports from Datius, if we are to believe Father Eustachius, that Archbishop Walpert of Milan and Guald, Bishop of Como, were sent to Otto I, King of Germany, so that he might enter Italy against Berengar, the enemy of the Church. In Landulf’s *Chronicle*, however, as Father Eustachius observes, there is no mention of Guald, Bishop of Como, and the matter is narrated differently.

Yet Father Eustachius should also have observed [Col. 0815D] that Gualvaneus drew this account not from Datius’s *Chronicle* alone but also from the *Pantheon*, since he concludes his narrative with these words:

> “Thus the *Pantheon* and Datius’s *Chronicle*.”

It is certain, however, that Gotfrid of Viterbo reported the matter in part XVII of the *Pantheon*, just as Gualvaneus relates it; and Datius is therefore cited there by Gualvaneus as a second witness because he too narrates the matter, although in different words and from different historical records. There Albert is the same as Adelbert, who was reigning in Italy together with Berengar, his father.

I pass over the other examples produced by Father Eustachius, in which it could plainly be shown that Gualvaneus sometimes gathered his statements from different histories, and that when, after a long narrative, he calls Datius his witness, not everything must always be attributed to that same Datius. In any case, nothing taken by Gualvaneus from Datius’s *Chronicle* fails also to occur in Landulf’s *Chronicle*, sometimes with a few additions but generally in precisely the same words. All this finally leads us to believe without hesitation that Datius’s *History* and Landulf’s *History* were one and the same. This will become even clearer to readers of Gualvaneus’s own *Greater Chronicle*, where the Datian *History* is so often cited and entire chapters are reproduced from it which one later finds in the manuscripts of Landulf.

If Corius, in book I of his *Milanese History*, has three verses from Datius which are not read in Landulf, this may be attributed, among other causes which I omit, to the differences among the manuscripts of Landulf’s *History*.

Puricellus, in *On Saints Ariald and Herlembald*, chapter 92, using I do not know what manuscript, gives the following words of Landulf from book I, chapter 11, under the title “On priests who have one wife, according to the teaching of Saint Ambrose”:

> “While Saint Ambrose was seated, a very serious disagreement arose before the apostolic representative at a synod, between priests who had one wife and others living in virginity or chastity. Since this had occurred, and the apostolic representative commanded it while the other bishops agreed, the matter was submitted to the judgment of Saint Ambrose, so that whatever he said should be held sacred and firm. But Saint Ambrose, recognizing that human inclinations are prone to sin, especially because of incontinence, and knowing that someone might not even preserve virginity, etc., said this and restrained all dissension. Thus Greek priests, etc. And if it should happen that one’s wife dies, they either live chastely while retaining the priesthood, or they lose the priesthood if they thereafter have carnal relations with another woman, etc.”

Compare these few passages, omitting others, with the manuscript from which we transcribed Landulf’s *History*, book I, chapter 11. You will understand that the manuscript copies of Landulf’s *History* do not all agree in these matters and that much was either added or removed.

Moreover, as Father Eustachius observes, Andreas Alciatus, in *On the Affairs of the Fathers*, p. 150, states that Saint Mona, Bishop of Milan, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. He then adds: “Datius prefers the Kalends themselves of April.” Likewise, after recounting the death of Saint Protasius, Bishop of Milan, after he had completed twenty-two years in the episcopate, Alciatus adds: “Datius adds three years to them.” But Father Eustachius tells us that these statements are not found in Landulf’s *History*.

Furthermore, let readers know that in that parchment manuscript of the Metropolitan Library, where our Landulf’s and Arnulf’s histories are joined together, there is also a catalogue of the bishops of Milan, which, as we indicated above, extends as far as Galdinus. Alciatus drew these statements of his from that catalogue, and therefore summoned Datius as a witness because Milanese historians customarily cited the same manuscript under Datius’s name. Hence here too you may understand that the Datian *History* is wrongly distinguished from Landulf’s, and that there was no need to invent a Datius later than Landulf.

In addition, Possevinus, Gavantus, Peter Maturus in the notes to Saint Antoninus’s *Chronicle*, Jacobus Perez de Valentia, Bellarmine, and others, whenever they write on the authority of Datius that Saints Ambrose and Augustine were the authors [Col. 0816D] of the hymn *Te Deum*, cite as their witness Datius’s *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 10. These statements correspond to the *History of our Landulf* if one counts the prologue of book I together with the following chapters.

These are the points I have at present on which I would discuss this question. I would give fuller treatment if, standing now in the arena, I could consult and compare—as I once could without difficulty—all the manuscripts of Landulf and the manuscript works of Gualvaneus and others preserved in the Ambrosian Library. But no more is needed in a matter which, as I may say, appears to me clearer than the noonday sun from what has so far been presented.

Finally, I judged that the reader should be informed that I had once intended not to publish everything Landulf committed to writing, but only the first two books, from which historical learning, although interspersed with and disfigured by not a few fables, might hope to obtain some light and support. For what follows in Landulf’s *History*, comprising the third and fourth books [Col. 0817A], pursues only particular disputes that arose in the Milanese Church on account of the clergy’s hatred of continence. They abound in foolish speeches, almost all fabricated, which seem either to possess no charm at all or even something of an unpleasant color, having been devised in defense of error and as a safeguard for vices.

But the final decision prevailed that nothing belonging to Landulf’s chaff should be concealed: first, lest anyone hostile to the Catholic Church should imagine that we had omitted these passages through fear or because of a bad conscience, thinking that what was hidden was better than what came to light; and also because these passages are so badly stitched together that to set them forth once is to refute them. Puricellus has moreover already published most of this material [Col. 0818A] and shown its emptiness and absurdity in his *Life of Saints Ariald and Herlembald*.

Finally, nothing more effectively commends the present condition of the Church of Milan—and indeed of the entire Catholic Church—and shows the clergy steadfastly devoted, by the gift of God Almighty, to holier counsels than to contemplate the corrupt customs of the eleventh century and the way in which they were purged through the zeal of the Roman pontiffs. Nor should one grow angry when the ravings and crimes of the ancient heretics are exposed; rather, one should congratulate our own times, which think rightly and, with Christ as their guide, follow a better manner of life in the Catholic Church.

But now let us hear Landulf himself speaking.

# LANDULF’S MILANESE HISTORY

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae VIII, 36.)*

## LETTER OF THE HISTORIOGRAPHER SENT TO THE ARCHPRIEST

[Note: Thus B: “The first book of the historiographer, concerning the archbishop, clergy, and laity of Milan, especially a letter directed to L.” A*]

To L., endowed with the evidence of every virtue, supported by knowledge of many sciences, and religiously instructed by divine teaching, appointed to govern the holy Milanese Church as archpriest, and dear both to God and to human beings; and to L. [Note: Thus, apparently, in codex B: “and L.” W.]—the least of all, servant of your servants [Note: Thus in B in the specimen published by Muratori, p. 55; it appears to be absent from the remaining copies. W.]—may you enjoy the happiness of this life and the fellowship of the angels in the eternal kingdom.

Diligently recalling the love of your charity and devotion which, as a son, you have had and, with God’s consent, will always have for the Ambrosian Church and its clergy, and carefully contemplating the reverence due to your watchful fatherhood, I—my spirit shaken by many tribulations, through which almost all Italy has been stained by false prophets running about in detestable hypocrisy—have been kindled by the heat of God’s fire and, as if awakened from a heavy sleep, have risen.

Therefore, considering whether I should devote myself diligently to secular works or divine worship; whether I should narrate the brave and magnificent deeds accomplished in our times [Note: Or: “whether I should narrate,” according to B; “magnificent deeds,” according to Blancus.], or whether, among other things, I should recount the tribulations which the Ambrosian clergy suffered from treacherous citizens and from wicked priests who encouraged them—I resolved to narrate them [Note: “to narrate,” B.]. Thus, reflecting on where I might exercise the ability of my mind, unwilling to pass through this wretched life in silence, and moved by the numerous and great histories flying about everywhere, by love of my homeland and my city, and also by devotion to that same clergy [Note: Thus the manuscripts: *diligentia* (“devotion”), according to Blancus.], I resolved to write in humble style, beyond all histories, the deeds of the archbishops accomplished before God and human beings against emperors detestable to both, together with the tribulations and dissensions carried out by false prophets not born in this city.

Accordingly, very many who seemed, by their false preaching, to belong to the ecclesiastical order, but who in their deeds miserably and diligently practiced hypocrisy, hiding themselves like ravenous wolves beneath a sheep’s skin, abandoned their flocks and broke the canons. Many others, instructed in the Roman rite and envious of the honor of the holy Ambrosian Church, like tyrants showing no reverence to the Ambrosian order, descended upon the city of the Milanese, whose laity had been bewitched and among whom tares had been oversown by the tricks of Antichrist [Note: Thus the manuscripts: *imbuerunt* (“they imbued”), Blancus.]. Through their fault [Note: *unio* in the manuscripts, apparently a corruption.] the Ambrosian Church, once exalted and adorned by the eloquence of many priests and Levites, and of very many wise men of both orders [Col. 0818C], was utterly worn down and trampled into nothingness both in its ministry and in its persons.

For what the Roman pontiffs and cardinals, rivals of this holy mystery, had once been unable to accomplish despite much toil, these false “Cathari,” disturbing the order itself, so utterly crushed that thereafter there was no hope of restoring either the mystery or the order. It appeared far worse [Note: *potius* (“rather”), B.] than in the speech of Saint Eusebius, who once said:

> “This city has perished; the Church has collapsed. Therefore, with the prophet, I shall lament: ‘Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep for the sins of my people? My own womb-born ones have become my enemies; they have unjustly stripped me and, to swords of my enemies seeking my life, have pitilessly handed me over.’”

Since my tears were overflowing, I shall say, lamenting with a certain wise man:

> “The songs I once composed when study flourished  
> I am compelled, alas, in grief to take up mournful measures.  
> Behold, the Muses, wounded, dictate to me what must be written,  
> And water my face with true tears of elegy.”

*(From Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, at the beginning.)*

Therefore, venerable father, although for a long time I have been shaken by many and various sorrows, seeing the loss of the virtues of our Church [Note: Thus A** and Blancus, according to A. *injustum* (“wrong”) in A*. B.], and remembering what it once suffered and endured from wicked kings and detestable priests—men who had been nourished from the very cradle by the sweetness of the order of the holy Ambrosian Church [Note: *dulcedinis* (“of the sweetness”), Blancus.] [Col. 0819B], for whom it would have been glorious to endure death for the welfare of their Church—I shall faithfully endeavor to disclose and narrate for the benefit of posterity the few things I found in various books and papers trampled in the streets, learned from very worthy and Catholic men, and discovered by investigating the cities of Italy.

Furthermore, whatever honor, reverence, and greatness the Ambrosian clergy possessed in the many preceding ages, and how it was honored by many great men, as well as what it later suffered when the city was full of the dregs of the world, I have decided diligently to write for the protection of posterity and the salvation of souls—what I saw with my eyes [Note: Absent in B.], heard with my ears [Note: *et* (“and”), Blancus.], and understood with my heart.

But before I recount what I have decided to say, I shall proclaim, moved by the reverence due to God, a spark of fire which, aided by God’s mercy, I committed to memory and found in a certain chest filled with the finest pearls, poor on the outside but overflowing with riches within, to the honor of God and the praise of blessed Ambrose. Would that all these things might remain to the end [Note: *fine* (“end”), Blancus.] so dear to the Ambrosian Church as they are acceptable, so sweet as they are health-giving, so lovable as they flow from a brotherly heart.

Farewell, father! May you happily enjoy everlasting joys with all the lovers of the saints of the Ambrosian Church.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

## 1

Since wise and outstanding men, endowed with great knowledge, have left behind accounts of the ages, changes in circumstances, deeds of leaders, battles of kings, seditions of cities, and disturbances of peoples, treating them elegantly for the protection of the young [Col. 0819C] and the guardianship of the old, and [Note: Absent in B.] leaving posterity a safeguard and consolation amid many things, it is now much more fitting that religious men, filled with the divine Spirit, should kindly communicate and most clearly explain to their followers—indeed, to their brothers—for the caution of their souls and bodies alike, whatever increase or decline they have observed [Note: *perspexerint* (“have perceived”), B.].

Thus their followers, foreseeing the pit of serpents, the lair of asps, the den of dragons, and the forests of lions, may, kindly instructed and carefully armed, both rescue themselves from those dangers and, by warning others, free them from death, remembering what Solomon says in his Wisdom:

> “Therefore I shall possess this immortality and eternal remembrance among those who will come after me.”  
> *(Wisdom 8:13.)*

For this reason I shall strive, insofar as my little knowledge can express it, and according to what I have discovered and learned in truth, to elucidate how clearly and brilliantly the Church of the holy and most glorious confessor Ambrose shone throughout the whole world through hymns, organs, symphonies, melodies, and the like.

Ambrose, the teacher, resplendent in episcopal vestments like an excellent shepherd, magnificently adorned the Church of God and, like a noble athlete, decorated it with the armor of spiritual virtues; he joined it to himself as his bride [Col. 0820B]. Sent here by divine command through the most merciful emperor Valentinian of the whole world, he deserved to hear:

> “Go; act not as a judge but as a bishop.”

For the Lord adorned him with such grace and such great mercy that he converted his enemies with the greatest patience and, as a true teacher and doctor of the Church, lovingly administered to his sheep—indeed, to his children—the first principles of the Catholic faith.

As the first—that is, the greatest—to govern the metropolitan see, he most clearly established the ordinations of priests, deacons, subdeacons, clerics, laypeople, old men, young men, soldiers, peoples, sacred virgins and women remaining unmarried, married women [Note: *maritorum* (“of married men”), Blancus.], widows, orphans, pilgrims, and guests. In establishing them, he carefully attended to what the religious character of each order required; and in carrying it out, he gently instructed others, remembering the Gospel saying:

> “Jesus began first to do, and then to teach.”

For he was exceedingly wise in preaching, eloquent in judgment, most gentle toward all the faithful, and mild, peaceful, humble, and serene toward all unbelievers. He was a provident steward, giving pasture to the strong, food to the young, nourishment to the old, and sustenance to adolescents, remembering the Apostle’s saying:

> “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all.”  
> *(1 Corinthians 9:19.)*

The Lord had provided for himself, from Ambrose’s very cradle [Note: Thus Blancus: *cunalibus* in A* (?) and B.], the blessed Ambrose as shepherd of himself and of his Church, through the honeycomb dripping around his lips [Col. 0821A]. Through the Holy Spirit, he knew that this saying had been spoken of him:

> “Honey and milk proceed from the mouth of the prudent; a dripping honeycomb is his lips; his tongue is the sweetness of honey.”  
> *(Proverbs 16:24; Song of Songs 4:11.)*

Under the guidance of the divine Spirit, he endeavored to teach each person according to that person’s capacity, knowledge, and age, knowing what the Apostle says:

> “Feed the flock of God, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock from the heart, so that when the chief Shepherd appears you may receive an unfading crown.”  
> *(1 Peter 5:2.)*

And again, in the words of the Apostle Peter:

> “In your faith supply virtue, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge self-control, in self-control endurance, in endurance piety, in piety brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love.”  
> *(2 Peter 1:5.)*

Firm in the way of God, firmer still in the Catholic faith, and indefatigable in his good purpose, he fulfilled what the most wise Solomon says:

> “Be firm, my son, in the way of God and in the strength of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice pursue you.”  
> *(Ecclesiasticus 5:12.)*

By establishing bishops throughout all the cities of Italy, he extended the branches of the most honorable religion and of the honor of God’s Church so widely that Solomon’s wisdom spoke of him under an alternative figure, saying:

> “I spread out my branches like a terebinth, and my branches are branches of honor and glory.”  
> *(Ecclesiasticus 24:22.)*

And again, to strengthen and praise the faithful, the same wisdom sounded forth in the person of the Lord and of the Church, exhorting them and saying [Note: “And he exhorted and said,” B. The words “I spread out … honor” are absent from A**.]:

> “I blossomed like a vine with fragrant sweetness, and my flowers are the fruit of honor and uprightness. I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.”  
> *(Ibid., 23.)*

But when our Lord, the Redeemer of the whole human race, our King and Savior Christ, through the Apostles and teachers and by the administration of the Holy Spirit, had most gently unveiled the Gospel of salvation to every human creature, it pleased him to exalt the most distinguished and learned man Ambrose, supported by divine knowledge, among those teachers who were present at that time, in the ordering of his Church and its mysteries, symphonies, melodies, hymns, and spiritual songs [Note: Paulinus, chapter 13, and Augustine, *Confessions* IX, 7, report that these things were instituted by Ambrose, but on another occasion and without revealing anything about the constitution of ecclesiastical orders. See Fumagalli, *Antiquities of Milan* III, 101 ff.].

Thus, by divine providence, just as the Apostle John—preeminent among the evangelists and holding a privilege among the other disciples, admonished by the divine breath—was worthy to say:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; he was in the beginning with God.”  
> *(John 1:1.)*

so blessed Ambrose, the teacher and doctor, outstanding among the other teachers [Col. 0822A], exalted and magnificently adorned the Church of God in every way and with every effort, meditating, writing, reading, and preaching day and night, according as God, through his mercy and the Holy Spirit, granted and permitted the Church to him.

After the perfidy of the Arians had been subdued and the wickedness of the schismatics conquered, one day before the Lord’s Nativity, while he was dictating alone—but he was not alone, for God was with him—he began to consider how or in what manner he should establish priests, deacons, and the other orders, together with chants, Masses, Vespers, psalms, and everything else suitable and appropriate to divine worship; whether he should designate the first chant or establish the orders and clerics beforehand for the degrees of the office [Col. 0822B].

It seemed good and pleasing to him to appoint ecclesiastical men instructed in the Catholic faith, to keep them continually with him, and, with the grace of the Lord administering through their counsel, to arrange everything. As he surveyed all the sacred and holy Scriptures and the accounts of the patriarchs and prophets, in which they had prophesied Christ, God and our Savior, for the salvation of all posterity and the benefit of others who believe in Christ [Note: Thus the editor corrects the manuscripts: *prophetaru*; *prophetarum*.], it seemed to him that, above all the others, the patriarch David had prophesied most clearly and brilliantly concerning the incarnation of the Lord through the Virgin’s childbirth, the Passion through Judas the betrayer, the resurrection, the appearances after the resurrection, and how he would ascend into heaven while clouds received him in the sight of his disciples.

Foreseeing through the Holy Spirit granted to him that the Church of God would be adorned with faithful people and devoted to God, humbly and with the greatest devotion believing in Christ, he confirmed this by prophesying in many arguments and, by confirming it through many examples, offered the Church to God as a bride adorned with every virtue, through wise men, singers, musicians, and teachers.

Therefore blessed and holy Ambrose, the doctor and teacher [Note: “Blessed and holy doctor and teacher” is absent from B.], like a vigorous soldier looking toward the standards of the commanders who had gone before and toward the battles that were approaching, all breathing as one, strove to imitate the distinguished prophet David. Following his model and imitation, and with God’s aid and the administration of the Holy Spirit, he strove to compose and establish psalms, chants, symphonies, melodies, clerics, and all the offices of the Church [Col. 0822D].

For when the almighty Lord and our Savior was preparing a wall for his Catholic Church against its enemies and raising David as a tower for the house of his Church and as a wall for Israel, in order to defend his bride from unbelievers and free the flock entrusted to him from ravenous wolves, Ambrose, for as long as he lived, insofar as God in his mercy granted it, cared for the Church of God, his people, and many cities. Whenever anything was reported to him through a messenger, as we find written about him in his sacred history, he watched diligently as a good shepherd, carefully going about among diverse peoples and cities, converting tyrants, kings, and leaders—all of them—to Christ. For every city, and for all the faithful who asked and devoutly sought it, he appointed a bishop, and consecrated the one appointed with the greatest joy.

The Church of God flourished so greatly in his hands that all the unbelievers gathered together and, silently placing a finger upon their lips, said:

> “Truly, the finger of God does this and works in him.”

For as long as life accompanied him, laboring on behalf of many faithful people, he was never accused by anyone who unsheathed a sword. Therefore, grieving that he could not be what he wished to be, he said in a hymn [Note: “Grieving in a hymn,” B.]:

> “We cannot be martyrs, but we have found martyrs.”

And as we read in the Book of Chronicles through the prophet David:

> “God did not permit anyone to slander them, but rebuked kings for their sake, saying: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.’”  
> *(1 Chronicles 16:22.)*

And again, mutually and silently marveling in their hearts, they glorified God, so that what was written by the most wise Solomon might be fulfilled:

> “Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples, for the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and terrible above all gods.”  
> *(Ibid., 24.)*

Then what is said through the same author was fulfilled:

> “Let the sea and its fullness resound [Note: Absent in Blancus.]; let the fields rejoice and all that is in them. Then the trees of the forest will rejoice before the Lord, because he has come to judge the earth.”  
> *(Ibid., 32.)*

And since the Lord and our Savior, through his clemency and mercy, so greatly magnified, exalted, and adorned the deeds and wonders of the most learned and religious teacher and confessor Ambrose—more than many distinguished books could contain, and more than many vigorous and most wise men and teachers of schools could recount and explain to posterity with immense toil and labor [Note: Thus Blancus: *quievit* (“rested”) in the manuscripts.]—it is not fitting for me, a man filled with little knowledge, to linger over each of his deeds. For it seems better to me to remain entirely silent about such great miracles of our patron and such outstanding deeds than to say too little.

But in order to come to the matters toward which my intention and greatest zeal aspire, I do not cease to invoke the Holy Trinity itself and all the saints with heart and mouth, so that through his Holy Spirit he may grant me to write what must be written and to keep silent about what must be kept silent [Note: Thus A** and Blancus: *suum* (“his own”); *tuum* (“your”), A*. B.].

## 2

[Note: [Col. 0823] The manuscripts preface the title: “Exposition of the orders of Saint Ambrose, issued by Datius, bishop of Milan, of holy memory.” Since this author attributes every one of the diverse rites and various kinds of clergy of the Milanese Church to Saint Ambrose, let the reader pardon a man insufficiently learned. But let him recognize that their antiquity is altogether earlier than Ambrose’s age. Puricellus adds this in the margin in B and A**.]

Therefore Saint Ambrose, imbued with divine knowledge and filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed a fast for all the clergy and for all Catholic lay faithful, so that the Lord might deign to open the hearts of his people for the honor of his Church and the praise of divine worship. On the fourth day, as though in accordance with the four Gospels, through God’s clemency and by revelation of the Holy Spirit, he ordained seventy-two priests—who in the primitive Church were called bishops, as the doctor Blessed Jerome asserts in one of his books [Note: [Col. 0823D] Letter 82, to Oceanus. BL.]—imitating the true teacher and Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ.

For just as our Lord and Redeemer, after his incarnation and baptism—which, in the Jordan, he received from John the forerunner and baptizer, who is said to be more than a prophet, after turning three times through the Holy Spirit—chose seventy-two disciples to proclaim the divine Gospel, as is read in the Gospel of the evangelist Luke and is held without doubt as authoritative, so the good disciple, following the wise teacher, chose his priests—indeed, his sons, and, as I have said, his bishops—for the work [Note: [Col. 0823] Bl. reads “of the mystery.”] of priestly ministry. Confirming and praising them, he exhorted them, saying:

“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his possession.”

Indeed, he admonished them so thoroughly in conduct, morals, humility, knowledge, patience, and obedience [Note: [Col. 0823] A** reads thus. A. has “in conduct and morals”; A* “in conduct and humility, knowledge, patience, and obedience.”], as well as in the care of their clothing and in every respect, that if anyone happened to see them in the clergy, he would not say that they were the sons of men but would affirm that they were companions of angels.

There is another reason why he ordained so many priests, and it presses upon me and urges me, as though impatient, to explain it. Since the human race, once united by a single language, is later read to have been spread and scattered through pride, as though into seventy-two varieties of languages, just as is found in the Book of Genesis (XI, 1), Moses says—the one with whom God spoke as a friend speaks with a friend:

“For the whole earth had one language and the same words. And when they had come into the land of Shinar, one said to another: ‘Come, let us make for ourselves a name, a city, and a lofty tower whose summit may reach to heaven, and let us make our name famous before we die.’ But the Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building, and said: ‘Behold, they are one people, and all have one language. Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor!’ And so the Lord divided them from that place throughout all lands, and they ceased building the city and the tower because of the excessive confusion of their languages. Therefore its name was called Babel, that is, ‘confusion,’ because there the language of the whole earth was confused.”

Thus it was made manifest that, to the same degree as their purpose was wicked and perverse before God and his angels, it should become known to every nation and every people, leaving an example for posterity—as though he were saying:

“You to whom knowledge of the mind, together with strength of body and practical intelligence, has been abundantly showered by the most high God in his goodness, like rain gently falling upon grain, take careful and diligent heed for yourselves, lest anything that deservedly befell us through pride and folly happen to you as a warning, so that what is ill-sweetened to us you do not believe [Note: [Col. 0825] Bl. reads “to you”], you may someday believe for yourselves, wearied by many sighs. [Note: [Col. 0825] A. reads “lest something happen to you”; F. has “to them.” Hor. Blancus.]”

For when Adam had been formed by God in paradise and fashioned in the image of God, as we know, the Lord saying through Moses, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us,” and when all that was in God’s paradise had been granted to him except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, concerning which the Lord had commanded him not to eat, saying, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die,” then, if he had carefully and diligently kept God’s admonition and commandment, he himself would have been immortal, and we would have been like God.

Therefore I earnestly beg you: because Adam grievously sinned through disobedience, and because we have been confused through excessive pride and scattered throughout all the regions of the earth, so that we do not understand one another, and rightly so, on account of the diversity of languages—God, out of the fullness of his love, became human, died, and was raised again, graciously granting you the means of restoring what the angels lost in heaven through pride—if you remain steadfast in faith, diligently and carefully, with the Lord’s help, guard what has been entrusted to you, and, while guarding the holy faith, perform good works, so that, when you reach the perfect end, you may at the final examination of judgment be placed at God’s right hand and joyfully deserve to hear what the Lord mercifully said:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

For this reason Saint Ambrose wished to ordain seventy-two priest-disciples: so that, as many as were the varieties of peoples produced by the dispersion of languages, so many priests might exist for the salvation of our souls.

But when the human race, once spread and scattered throughout the world, wandered like cattle and, trusting and tearing one another apart without law or treaty, was governed—and was also to be protected from the incursion of enemies—God permitted and ordained that it be ruled by seventy-two kings. When Saint Ambrose saw that these kings governed the world through the effectiveness of the supreme Roman empire, it pleased him, for their salvation and that of all peoples, to ordain, with God’s confirmation, seventy-two priests [Note: [Col. 0825D] That these men, called *decumani*, were instituted only toward the end of the ninth century was demonstrated by Giulini, *Memoirs of Milan* 70 I, 295, and Fumagalli, *Antiquities of Milan* III, 340.], so that he might deeply affect each royal king through each individual priest, confirm him in God by teaching the faith of Christ, and strengthen him in every good virtue through that confirmation, so that, attaining the prize, they might one day, with God’s permission, reign with Christ in heaven [Note: [Col. 0825] Absent in B.].

## 3

[Note: [Col. 0825] The manuscripts have the title “Concerning the *primicerius*.”]

When these matters had been properly arranged and beneficially ordered, he appointed a certain religious priest, a man who was to be called the *primicerius*. As a kind of co-bishop, he received from Saint Ambrose, his teacher, authority over all who were struggling with sin, so that whatever the bishop could not accomplish personally, the co-bishop called the *primicerius* might diligently strive to accomplish among them.

He also designated a place where they could all meet, which is still called the presbytery by everyone. There all the city’s priests, assembling on Friday or on the Kalends, carefully examined one another concerning the divine ministries [Note: [Col. 0825] B reads “examined”; the remaining witnesses “was examining.”] and thus religiously and unceasingly exercised themselves in those ministries. When all were seated in that place, he taught whatever God inspired the bishop to teach. Then [Note: [Col. 0825] Bl. reads “finally.”] the sub-bishop, who is still called the co-bishop [Note: [Col. 0825] These words are absent in Bl.] and the *primicerius* [Note: [Col. 0825] Absent in B.], admonished them according to what God directed, saying:

“Against folly, provide wisdom; against wantonness, chastity; against dullness, understanding; against rashness, counsel; against fear, courage; against ignorance, knowledge; against hardness, piety; against pride, humility.”

Concerning this, a certain wise man [Note: [Col. 0826D] Gregory I, *Exposition of the Third Penitential Psalm*, verse 3.] says:

“Whoever gathers virtues without humility is like one carrying wind into dust” [Note: [Col. 0825] The Paris edition reads “carrying dust into wind.”]

And there is also this saying:

“Humility conquers all things, and it is itself conquered by no one.”

In addition to these matters, he instructed them to possess love of God and neighbor. When these things had been completed, he beneficially dealt with whatever was appropriate to each person’s particular case.

Everything among them was done so peacefully and was handled so honorably, without deceit or envy, that what is read in the Acts of the Apostles was fulfilled in them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). Although their faces were different, they had one heart and one soul.

As they lived excellently and conducted themselves religiously, everything worked together for good, as the Apostle testifies [Note: [Col. 0827] B reads “testified”], saying:

“Brothers, we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Romans VIII, 28).

They also heeded the words of the *chirograph*:

“Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Psalm CXVIII, 2).

But how attentive they were to their ministry and order, no one [Note: [Col. 0827] B reads “indeed”; the remaining witnesses “except.”] except one who lived at that time could relate, since they feared what is said [Note: [Col. 0827] Bl. reads “says”]:

“Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah XLVIII, 10).

It happened, therefore, that when a certain Gothic commander of foreign stock, named Ruilus, unexpectedly saw them on the feast of the saints Nazarius and Celsus—elegantly dressed and walking with the bishop in silence—he believed and declared that they were not merely priests but bishops, saying:

“Certainly, although at the command of the emperor Valentinian I have traversed almost the whole world [Note: [Col. 0827] The words “almost the whole” are absent in B.] and observed, investigating their customs and practices, especially those of religious bishops, I have never before been so struck dumb with amazement or overwhelmed by such ineffable wonder.”

After seeing and admiring these things, he remained for a short while; at last he departed, wondering to himself at what he had seen.

As these men acted in this way, the fragrance of mercy, piety and charity, chastity, humility, brotherhood, knowledge, and every virtue spread around all peoples, especially the neighboring cities, like the sweetest aroma. Concerning this the Lord said to Moses:

“Take for yourself spices: stacte, onycha, galbanum of good fragrance, and the clearest frankincense; you shall make incense compounded by the art of the perfumer, carefully mixed and pure” (Exodus XXX, 34) [Note: [Col. 0827] B reads “by the work of the perfumer.”]

Their blessed teacher and doctor Ambrose admonished them daily by singing, saying:

“Let us love one another, because love is God; and whoever loves his brother is born of God and sees God. In this the love of God is perfected; and whoever does the will of God remains forever.”

## 4

[Note: [Col. 0827] The manuscripts add the title “According to Datius, concerning the twenty-four cardinals of the Milanese Church”; the words “twenty-four according to Datius” are absent in A** and Bl.]

When blessed Ambrose, by God’s arrangement, had ordained the priests mentioned above, it seemed right to him and to the other brothers that twenty-four priests, who would be like cardinals, should be established.

Our Lord and Savior confirms these men through the revelation of the Holy Spirit in the Apocalypse, where John says:

“I saw, and behold, twenty-four elders, who fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever, and they cast their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created’” (Apocalypse IV, 10) [Note: [Col. 0827] Bl. reads “they were worshiping.”]

And:

“They fell before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints, and they sing a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy to receive glory and honor and to open the book and its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us, Lord, by your blood, from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and they shall reign upon the earth’” (Apocalypse V, 8).

There is another reason why he ordained twenty-four cardinal priests: just as the natural day is completed by twenty-four hours, so the mystery of the Ambrosian Church would be revealed and governed through twenty-four cardinals. Concerning the day, Saint Ambrose says in the *Hexaemeron* (I, 10):

“He established the law that we should define the hours of day and night only by the name ‘day,’ as if he were saying: ‘The measure of twenty-four hours is the period of one day.’”

After ordaining these men, he placed an archpriest over them, so that whenever they deviated in any office, they might be calmly corrected and gently reproved and live with a good disposition and good will [Note: [Col. 0827] Bl. reads “he proposed.”]. His name in Latin means “chief of the priests,” for *archos* in Greek means “chief” in Latin.

## 5

[Note: [Col. 0827] The title in the manuscripts is “Concerning the seven deacons.”]

At the same time blessed Ambrose ordained seven deacons, blessing and ordaining them by laying hands upon them through the Holy Spirit, as though through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0827] B omits “and.”]. He imitated the Lord’s apostles [Note: [Col. 0827] B omits this clause and abridges what follows as: “who ordained seven deacons in the unity of the Catholic Church through the grace of the Paraclete. Therefore, after …”], who, after graciously receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem—which is called “Vision of Peace”—assembled together and ordained seven deacons through the Holy Spirit.

He consecrated seven because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are bestowed by God upon the faithful Catholics [Note: [Col. 0827] Omitted in B.]; or so that, like seven lamps, they might shine most brightly each day before God’s throne, kindling others through a good life, excellent conduct, and teaching [Note: [Col. 0827] B omits “or.”]

Therefore Saint John says in the Apocalypse:

“Seven burning lamps proceed before the throne; they are the spirits of God” (Apocalypse IV, 5) [Note: [Col. 0827] B adds “seven” and presents what follows as: “The seven spirits of God. Then he added twenty-four beneath them for the honor of God, and after he had ordained all these, the teacher …”].

Foreseeing these things, the holy doctor Ambrose blessed twenty-four subdeacons by ordaining them for the honor of God and his Church [Note: [Col. 0827] This number is likewise found in chapter 13 and in Galvagnus Flamma, *Manipulus Florum* 40. But later there were seven, as Landulf himself testifies, II, 35.]. After ordaining these men in the Catholic manner, he appointed masters over them all, one of whom was to be called archdeacon and another archsubdeacon.

## 6

[Note: [Col. 0827] The title in the manuscripts is “Concerning Saint Simplicianus.”]

At the same time, a holy man named Simplicianus was archdeacon. He was a man of complete goodness, complete religion, complete holiness, complete charity, complete piety, and complete chastity, filled with divine grace. Traveling to Rome on a mission from blessed Ambrose and instructed by him in knowledge [Note: [Col. 0829] B reads: “At that same time Saint Simplicianus, a man of every goodness and of all virtues and of divine grace, went to Rome …”], he restored the Church of God and of blessed Peter the apostle, which had been torn apart, scattered, and divided by many heresies, to the unity of the Catholic faith. Concerning this the Lord had said to Peter:

“I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 32) [Note: [Col. 0829] B omits the words from “concerning this” through “your brothers.”].

Disseminating the Gospel of God throughout all the districts of the city of Rome, like a good and vigorous farmer gathering a hundredfold, a thirtyfold, and a sixtyfold harvest, he converted many to Christ [Note: [Col. 0829] B omits “and vigorous”]. Among them was a certain philosopher, a very wise man named Victorinus, who believed, despite his great riches [Note: [Col. 0829C] See Augustine, *Confessions* VIII, 2.]. The Roman Quirites loved and revered him as a father and lord, as he deserved.

Moreover, through the revelation of God’s grace, he splendidly and with the utmost devotion deposited and adorned the relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with religious men who were called cardinals and with all the Romans whom the Catholic faith had made devout [Note: [Col. 0829] B abbreviates the following passage. Its surviving text is: “R. [the Romans] as father and lord loved. Q. e. r. Deo r. a. P. e. P. c. cardinalibus et c. o. R. m. e. o. Then b. S. from Rome to blessed Ambrose the relics of Peter and Paul the apostles gratefully offered; when these had been received, b. A. the relics of the other apostles acquired and a most beautiful basilica in m. c. i. R. p. i. p. which is called Roman, and a. q. R. t. d. h. c. i. q. o. a. r. with devotion and a great gathering of bishops and neighboring cities, and such verses exist in memory of this foundation.” The abbreviations and lacunae in B do not support a fuller reconstruction.].

When blessed Simplicianus returned from the city of Rome to blessed Ambrose, the revered teacher, he carefully and with the utmost devotion presented him with a portion of the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0829] A* reads thus; A** and Bl. have “a portion of the relics.”]. After this, blessed Ambrose, with the greatest joy and gladness, diligently acquired the relics of all the other apostles [Note: [Col. 0829] Omitted in A** and Bl.].

Having acquired them, he honorably built a most dignified basilica in the form of a cross in the Roman district, between the gate called the Roman Gate and the arch called the Roman Triumph. In it he placed the relics of all the apostles with the greatest care and zeal, amid the great gathering of bishops, clergy, laypeople, women, young people, and [Note: [Col. 0829] Omitted in Bl.] old people from the neighboring cities. Hence, even to this day, it is called the Basilica of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0829C] The *Kalendarium S. Mariae* in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* IIb, 1035, assigns its translation to 10 May. It was also called the Church of Saint Nazarius.].

But what the same holy Ambrose composed concerning this church, and how he versified the honor of Saint Nazarius, I learn by hearing it from his own mouth:

> Ambrose built this temple and consecrated it to the Lord,  
> With the apostolic name, gift, and relics.  
>
> The temple is shaped as a cross, the temple of Christ’s victory;  
> The sacred triumphal image marks the place.  
>
> At the head of the temple is Nazarius, life-giving and noble,  
> And the lofty floor is marked by the martyr’s remains.  
>
> Where the cross raised its sacred head in a curved circuit,  
> This head is the temple, and a dwelling for Nazarius.  
>
> The victorious one who cherishes eternal rest through devotion—  
> The cross was his palm, and the cross is also his bosom.  
>
> But the third, in the middle, death obstructs the things raised aloft [Note: [Col. 0829C] Puricellus noted that this verse is absent from all the other witnesses that transmit this epigram. It appears to be highly corrupt.].

## 7

[Note: [Col. 0829] The title in the manuscripts is “Concerning notaries, lectors, and the ten *ferulae*.”]

At that time he ordained notaries, who are still called acolytes, and placed a master over them [Note: [Col. 0829] Bl. reads “appointed.”]. He also confirmed the lectors as he found them, praising and magnifying them greatly [Note: [Col. 0829] Bl. reads “and praised them.”]. Since he knew that they had been ordained for many years by many bishops together with their *primicerius*, he hesitated to say anything; but, encouraging them in all things, he gave thanks and blessed them [Note: [Col. 0829] B omits everything from “since” through “blessed them.”].

To make everything perfect, he placed ten religious men [Note: [Col. 0829] Bl. reads “religious men.”] over ten orders, as though according to the ten commandments of the Law [Note: [Col. 0829] A** and Bl. read “men”]:

first, the *primicerius* of the priests; second, the archpriest; third, the archdeacon; fourth, the archsubdeacon; fifth, the master of the notaries [Note: [Col. 0829] Omitted in A*.]; sixth, the *primicerius* of the lectors [Note: [Col. 0829] Bl. reads: “in the sixth he praised and confirmed the *primicerius* of the lectors.”]; seventh, the master of the boys, who is called the master of the school [Note: [Col. 0829] Thus A**; B agrees, while A* omits it. Here A* and A** insert: “8. Concerning the priests … were called,” which has clearly been displaced from its proper place. B greatly abridges what follows: “All these duly observed their orders, and kept obedience to their superiors and charity toward their brothers according to the Apostle’s teaching: ‘Obey your superiors in the Lord, and be subject to them.’ Thus love among them was without pretense, abhorring evil … and the rest according to the Apostle’s teaching in the same epistle. — Concerning the *decumani*. Later blessed Simplicianus, seeing that the labors of the aforesaid seven orders increased with the growth of God’s Church under his charge, added three … they received [the tithes]; hence the *decumani*, as it were *decimani*, are called from tithes; or because they assisted the *ordinarii* in the offices of the whole metropolitan church, they were called *decumani*, as it were the ‘glory of the greater men,’ that is, of the *ordinarii* or cardinals. — Concerning the staff with leather. When all had thus been ordered, elegantly … to show office or dignity in …, so that each corrected his subordinates with rod and staff, according to the Prophet: ‘Your rod … are.’ Therefore the *primicerius* admonished his subordinates through … me. The archpriest [admonished] his, saying: ‘Do not make a graven image or any likeness of idols.’ The archdeacon [admonished] his: ‘You shall not take my name in vain.’ He arranged the remaining matters as suited each order: that, as many were the plagues against Pharaoh in Egypt unto death, so many remedies of salvation unto life should be in the Old and New Testament; hence, if anyone sinned once, he made amends ten times. When these had been most religiously ordered … he strove to sing psalms with men trained in musical art, according to that Davidic saying: ‘God, a song …’; God’s [Church] through him flourished like a lily among thorns …; but how brilliantly he ordered all things is not for me to explain, but for God, who has known all things more clearly than the eternal sun.”]; eighth, the master of the doorkeepers, who are called custodians; ninth, the master of the men and women devoted to God [Note: [Col. 0830C] Fumagalli, *Antiquities of Milan* III, 308, believes this was the school of Saint Ambrose, founded in the ninth century.], who offer bread and wine each day, signifying the New and Old Testament. For these people offer bread and wine to God daily, so that the people may not appear empty. Tenth, the master of the secular men [Note: [Col. 0830C] That is, the *vicecomes*. See II, 35.].

When all these matters had been completed, constituted, and ordered, they devoutly observed their order, and all obeyed one another. Concerning them the Apostle says:

“Obey your superiors in the Lord, and be subject to them” (Hebrews XIII, 17).

And again [Note: [Col. 0831] Omitted in Bl.]:

“Through charity serve one another” (Galatians V, 13).

In their example the Lord admonishes his disciples, saying:

“By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if …” (John XIII, 35), etc.

Thus, as the Apostle says:

“Love was among them without hypocrisy: hating evil, clinging to what is good, loving one another with brotherly charity, anticipating one another in honor, not sluggish in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer, sharing in the needs of the saints, pursuing hospitality” (Romans XII, 9);

“having gifts that differ according to the grace given to them [Note: [Col. 0831] Bl. reads “or giving”]: if prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; if ministry, in ministering; whoever teaches, in teaching; whoever exhorts, in exhortation; whoever gives, with simplicity; whoever presides, with diligence; whoever shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (ibid., 6).

## 8

[Note: [Col. 0831] See above, the preceding note.]

Seeing this labor, blessed Simplicianus later observed that the Lord was causing his Church to flourish, grow, and abound greatly in his hands [Note: [Col. 0831] A** reads thus; A* omits the phrase.]. He added three men skilled in singing, as well as twenty-eight priests, who, joined with the other seventy-two, make one hundred; for this reason they are called *Deciesdeni*.

This is why they are called *decumani*: either because, after fulfilling the offices of this city together with the twenty-four cardinals, they later received the tithes of all things from everyone; or because they diligently carried out the governance of the entire metropolitan church in all its offices, and for this reason were called the “ornament of the greater men.”

When all these men had been arranged and ordered according to the dignity that he had received from blessed Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0831] Perhaps “they had received.”], they wore elegant clothing and carried daily in their hands rods ornamented above and below with leather, to show what office or dignity each possessed, so that each might correct and amend his subordinates with the rod and staff.

Concerning this the Prophet says:

“Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me, O Lord” (Psalm XXII, 4).

Therefore the *primicerius* of the priests admonished those entrusted to him by the rod of God, saying to Moses:

“You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus XX, 3).

The archpriest, in the second place, taught those under him, saying:

“You shall not make for yourselves a graven image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven or on earth” (ibid., 4).

In the third place, the archdeacon taught those under him:

“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (ibid., 7).

And these commandments, because they are greater, appear to have been entrusted to the greater officials. He arranged and ordered the remaining commandments according to what suited each order: namely, that as many plagues as afflicted Pharaoh in Egypt unto death, so many remedies of salvation should exist in life, in the Old and New Testament.

Thus it happened that if anyone sinned by straying in some matter, one offense was corrected tenfold.

When these men had been completed and most religiously ordered, they strove, together with the men mentioned above, who were wonderfully trained in musical art, to compose, teach, and sing antiphons, responsories, psalms, and the other things suitable for divine worship, so that they might sing according to the Davidic saying:

“I shall sing a new song to you; on the ten-stringed psaltery I shall sing praise to you” (Psalm XLII, 9).

And so the Church of God began to germinate, flourish, and spread; and, like a lily among thorns, it gave the sweetness of its fragrance throughout all peoples.

For how brilliantly and how wisely he established and ordered everything through God’s dispensation is not for me to explain, but for God, who nourishes and arranges all things, to whom it must be attributed and assigned as his gift.

## 9

[Note: [Col. 0831] Title: “Concerning Saint Augustine.” B greatly abridges this chapter and the following two chapters.]

At that time it happened that a certain wise man named Augustine, although led astray by the error of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0831] Bl. reads “the error of the Manichaeans.”], armed with dialectical arguments and later living as a faithful and Catholic bishop of God, came into the winter church—not out of a desire for prayer, nor for the useful purpose of seeing and hearing the Lord’s mystery, but in order to criticize blessed Ambrose as he was explaining and preaching to the people about the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0831] Bl. reads “having found.”].

Forgetting himself and all his thoughts, he grew pale and trembled and became rigid, as all who were present could see [Note: [Col. 0831] Bl. reads “were present.”].

When the admonition that blessed Ambrose had delivered to the people was finished, Augustine came privately to him. But blessed Ambrose, recognizing his learning and perceiving the extent of his training and what he was capable of in the arts, and knowing through the Holy Spirit how he differed from the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0831] Bl. reads “perceiving his disagreement”] and how he would become faithful and Catholic, received him with the greatest gentleness and charity.

Thus blessed Ambrose rejoiced over him, just as in the Gospel we read of a certain father who, falling upon the neck of his son whom he had lost and placing his ring upon his finger, wept and kissed him, and, reproaching another brother who had been driven by excessive jealousy, said:

“This brother of yours was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 32).

And likewise, as we read in another Gospel about the good shepherd who, leaving the ninety-nine in the desert, searched for and found the sheep he had lost, placed it upon his shoulders, rejoiced, and, coming home, called together his friends and neighbors, saying:

“Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which I had lost” (Luke XV, 6).

Therefore the Lord says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: there is greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance” (ibid., 7).

And elsewhere we read of that woman who rejoiced over the drachma she had lost and called together her friends and neighbors, saying:

“Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost” (ibid., 9).

At last, by divine will, after not many days, just as he had publicly gone astray, as many people witnessed and agreed, so, with God’s help, he was baptized and confirmed by blessed Ambrose in the fonts attributed to Saint John [Note: [Col. 0833] Augustine was therefore baptized in the Church of Saint John at the Fonts, which stood between the greater church and Saint Thecla, which had been completely destroyed. A. adds this in the margin.], while all the faithful of this city stood by and watched, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

At these fonts, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance, they sang the *Te Deum laudamus*, with all who were present hearing, seeing, and marveling together. In later generations they produced what is held by the entire Catholic Church and is devoutly sung to this day.

And, as though enriched with many riches and priceless pearls, they rejoiced together in God; they ate their food with thanksgiving, rejoiced with great joy, and were strengthened in God.

## 10

[Note: [Col. 0833] B greatly abridges this chapter. The manuscripts prefix the title “Concerning the four councils to be observed.”]

Meanwhile, in addition to those matters with which he instructed his clergy daily [Note: [Col. 0833] Bl. reads “in which, or how many, he instructed them daily.”], he earnestly entrusted the priests with certain things to be preserved, held inviolably, and guarded above all else—namely, that they should hold the four principal councils in which Greeks, Latins, and Catholics faithfully agree [Note: [Col. 0833D] Yet two of these councils are much later than Ambrose.], and in which the Catholic faith remains whole and inviolate.

He also said that these four councils, confirmed by the apostles and by other holy bishops, were so holy and firmly established that if anyone added or removed anything from them, he would remain anathematized and excommunicated.

Therefore, just as the four Gospels are to be observed, held, and believed, so too are these four councils in every respect.

How greatly these councils were objects of fear, love, and reverence to blessed Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0833] A** reads thus; the other witnesses have *beato Ambrosio*; A* omits the words.], he himself shows in his letter addressed to the most merciful emperor Valentinian concerning the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0833D] I, 21 in the Paris edition.], saying:

“And rightly I abhor that council [Note: [Col. 0833D] Ambrose specifies the Council of Ariminum.], following the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, from which neither death nor the sword will be able to separate me. This faith your merciful father, the most blessed emperor Theodosius, both follows and approved; this faith Gaul holds, and Spain guards it with a devout confession of the divine Spirit.”

In those councils there is a provision—though the passage is corrupt—that no one, seeing himself or his brother to be incontinent, should under any pretext incur a shameful vice, unless he deceives in a transaction [Note: [Col. 0834D] “In the councils”? I confess that I do not understand this passage and consider it corrupt.].

For this reason it was established in the universal Church that priests would either be virgins or live chastely with their wives, so that, if God had ordained that someone should come to the episcopate with God’s approval, he might be found either a virgin or a man of one wife.

Therefore the Apostle says:

“It is necessary that a bishop be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, respectable, hospitable” (1 Timothy III, 2).

### 11. [Col. 0833]

[Note: Title: “On monogamous priests, by blessed Ambrose.” The words “by blessed Ambrose” are absent in A** and Bl.]

After many years had passed, while blessed Ambrose was still living, a very serious disagreement arose before the apostolic authority in a synod between the monogamous priests and others living under virginity or chastity. As a result, the disagreement between the monogamous priests and others who merely pretended to live chastely came almost to death and the ruin of their own people and of others. This matter was brought, at the command of the apostolic authority and at the urging of many Catholic bishops, before the judgment of our blessed patron Ambrose by both parties, who affirmed that whatever he said they would observe and regard as firm and holy. [Col. 0834B]

But blessed Ambrose, seeing and understanding human dispositions, holy counsels, and everyone’s inclination to sin—especially because of incontinence—and knowing that no one can possess either virginity or chastity except from God, opened his mouth and said what he had already dictated in the book *On Duties* (I, 50):

> “What shall I say about the monogamy of priests? Only one union is permitted, and it is not to be repeated; and this is the law: marriage is not to be repeated.”

[Note: On chastity, see the passage beginning “When ...”; also: “And therefore even in marriage ...”; Ambrose. Cf. below III, 24.]

And saying this, he immediately restrained those who seemed to have perfected their chastity but possessed no compassion or charity toward their brothers. Concerning this the Apostle says:

> “If I have such faith as to move mountains, and if I give my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

Yet they did not see themselves and did not understand what the Apostle says:

> “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he shall stand” (Rom. 14:4).

But recalling the apostolic word to brotherly love, he introduced it by saying:

> “God does not desire forced service; therefore do not grieve your brother, nor betray him, for whom Christ died” (cf. V, 16).

Thus the Greek priests, holding Ambrose’s opinion, have to this day established and regard as sacred law that when they are ordained to the priesthood, they either promise thereafter to remain virgins or are joined to wives in the presence of good men as witnesses. If it happens that one’s wife dies, they either live chastely while retaining the priesthood, or they lose the priesthood if they join themselves to another woman.

Blessed Ambrose imitated their Church with reverence in very many practices. Indeed, at the most celebrated festivals, especially at the Lord’s resurrection, he blessed, confirmed, and consecrated their sacrifice—namely, the leavened bread—with ours—namely, the unleavened bread—in order to praise, confirm, and strengthen it, with angels ministering and sanctifying. [Col. 0835B]

Therefore the same holy Ambrose says:

> “The angels stand beside the altar, and the priests sacrifice the body and blood of Christ, singing and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest.’”

But God and our Lord, wishing to honor and glorify so great and magnificent a bishop, like a veteran soldier triumphing and laboring long in the service of his Lord, with many rewards, many honors, and ineffable recompense, commanded him to depart from the prison-house of the flesh into eternal glory, accompanied by angelic choirs. [Col. 0835C]

Therefore the Apostle says:

> “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

As he was dying, he earnestly commended to God—the one in whom all the treasures of knowledge are hidden—the clergy entrusted to him and the sheep committed to him by God, with prayers, words, and lamentations.

Moreover, understanding through the Holy Spirit that many false Christs and false prophets would come in sheep’s clothing and overthrow God’s Church and his peoples by false teaching—of whom the Lord says through the Gospel:

> “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15)—

holy and most reverend Ambrose, foreseeing this, armed the clergy and people each day by praying to God and saying:

> “Deliver us from heretics, from Arians, from schismatics, and from barbarians, because you alone are Lord, you alone are Most High, O Christ.”

When he departed from the body, the extent of the sorrow of the nobles, the groaning of the clerics, the lamentation of the orphans, and the frequent sighs of the monks that followed I cannot recount with my tongue or write with my pen; nor do I have time to relate how greatly his funeral observance shone with miracles. But after the most blessed Simplician was appointed to the episcopate, with God’s help he completed what seemed lacking, and what he found established he preserved and strengthened inviolate, so that no bishop thereafter added or diminished anything. [Col. 0836A]

### 12. [Col. 0835]

[Note: Title: “On the *chrismon* of Saint Ambrose according to Datius, bishop of Milan.” A** and B: “On the ...”; A: “by Datius, bishop of Milan”; A*.]

After the ordinances of the holy Ambrosian Church had been determined and defined, and rational figures had been supplied in which God, through his clemency and by the intercession of Saint Ambrose, graciously allowed himself to be revealed to posterity, I shall now faithfully explain how, with his assistance, the catechumens enter the winter church, according to the order that I saw and understood in my heart and learned from the faithful. I shall also explain charitably why they do not enter through the western doors of that church, and why they are brought before the holy *chrismon* by the subdeacon and the doorkeepers to be instructed. [Col. 0836B]

[Note: The words “with his assistance” are absent in B.]

Thus the catechumens, to whom God in his supreme mercy has already granted permission—after they have tasted the salt of wisdom, after the priest has anointed their nostrils and ears with spittle, after they have renounced the world and its pomp, and after the priest’s hand has in a certain way granted them permission to enter the church—enter the church from the eastern side, led in by the subdeacon and the doorkeepers.

Why from the east? Because the supreme Wisdom of God, the dawn from on high, illumined those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, as the prophet testifies:

> “Upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, light has risen” (Isa. 9:2).

And again the outstanding prophet David says:

> “Light has dawned in the darkness for the upright in heart” (Ps. 111:4).

[Note: B reads “and the prophet.”]

When all these have entered, the priest and deacon, with the Gospel closed, meet them so that they may recognize that the unworthy are not permitted to see the secrets of the holy Gospel, lest those who ought not see should see, and those who cannot preserve what they hear should hear. The subdeacon comes with a censer of incense, so that through the work of good fragrance they may one day appear in the sight of God, and so that the devil, who had assailed them for many ages, may flee from them irrevocably, abandoning them through their devotion to the holy faith. With a burning candle also, signifying the presence of the Holy Spirit, they go to meet them. [Col. 0836C]

When this has been done and they have been led to the holy *chrismon*, they are carefully and reverently taught what it signifies.

[Note: Concerning this sign, see Allegranza, *Sacri Monumenti*, p. 18, where its image, taken from an ancient stone, is given.]

> “You whom God, foreseeing all things from the beginning, graciously created in his image and likeness: understand and receive with your heart and the ears of your soul what this sign containing alpha and omega signifies. Therefore, believe that the Α and Ω which you see signify the first and last Creator of heaven and earth and the author of all creatures. Hear and understand what the prophet Isaiah, filled with the Holy Spirit, says concerning him:
>
> “‘Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none. I am, I am the Lord, and there is no savior besides me. I have wiped away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. I am, I am he who wipes away your iniquities for my own sake, and I shall not remember your sins’” (Isa. 43:10; 44:22; 43:25). [Col. 0837A]

Having thus set forth the knowledge of almighty God—how he was and is and will be before the ages, in the ages, and after the ages—learn with what mercy he permitted the Word, with whom from the beginning and before the ages he made all things and prepared the heavens, to become incarnate when the Holy Spirit conceived him; and learn how, born as a human being from a virgin, he redeemed the human race with his precious blood, and, wounded and led like a sheep to slaughter, he suffered.

The ash whose powder you see entirely marking the *chrismon* is the Lord Christ, who, taking flesh from the virgin, became ash as a mortal human being, God from God and light from light, conceived through the Holy Spirit.

[Note: B omits “the Lord”; B also omits “light from light”; Bl. reads “became the Son.”]

The cross that you see in the cross is Christ, God, the Lord, and our Redeemer, who redeemed us, though unworthy, by the precious blood he shed on the gibbet of the cross, led like a sheep to be sacrificed.

Therefore the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth in humility” (Isa. 53:7).

Again:

> “He was wounded because of our iniquities; he was afflicted because of our crimes” (ibid., 5).

Having suffered death and many injuries for us, he admonishes us each day, saying:

> “Return to me, for I have redeemed you. Praise, O heavens, for the Lord has shown mercy” (Isa. 44:22).

[Note: Bl. reads “for I redeemed you.”]

Moreover, the hair-cloth that you see beneath these figures shows you that you are sinners and that you lost the glory of the eternal kingdom through the transgression of the first parent. Therefore, weeping over your sins before God, turn to him in body and soul. Concerning these things the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2:13), “for I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us imitate the prophet in ash and hair-cloth; let us fast and weep before God, because he is greatly merciful in forgiving our sins. [Col. 0837D]

When, with God’s consent, you soon come to the sacrament of holy baptism, instructed in the teachings of the Catholic faith, believe that through perseverance in good works you have acquired the blessedness of eternal glory, which the first-formed parents once foolishly lost by transgressing God’s command.

Moreover, because you see all these signs made from ash, recognize that you are mortal and hope in him who deigned to redeem you with his precious blood. [Col. 0838A]

But the eight rods that you see extending toward the sphere signify the eight beatitudes promised by God to the faithful, to remain eternally with Christ. Or, because there are eight ages of this present and future world, running day and night as though in a sphere, concerning which a certain wise man says:

> “There are six ages of this world, distinguished by the most familiar divisions of time, in which it is necessary to labor for God and to work for a time in order to obtain everlasting rest. The seventh age is the rest of those who are not in this life but in another, lasting until the time of the resurrection of souls. The eighth age is the very day of resurrection, blessed without any end of time.”

[Note: A** and B read “Thus a certain wise man”; A* reads “concerning which the venerable man says.” B has “clearly distinguished” instead of “distinguished.” Bl. reads “another.”]

But where are these beatitudes except in the sphere—that is, in God, who is not enclosed by an end nor increased by beginnings?

[Note: B reads: “who is not confined by beginnings nor enclosed by an end.”]

Indeed, that round sphere, without end or beginning, which you see containing all these things, is the very one who speaks in the Apocalypse, saying:

> “I am alpha and omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8).

[Note: Bl. reads “omega”; B omits the clause.]

### 13. [Col. 0837]

[Note: Title: “The antiphon of the cross by Datius”; B: “according to Datius, archbishop of Milan.”]

The antiphon of the cross, by which the mystery of God and the prerogative of the holy Ambrosian Church are adorned each day, is rightly understood to contain and express a most reverent allegory.

For when the song that Zachariah, the father of the prophet John, prophesied in honor of God is sung, and after the readings have been completed, the readers, together with their master, and the doorkeepers, after the higher orders have been dismissed from the choir, take three silver crosses from the sacristy. Carrying them outside the church with the greatest reverence, with three candles burning above each of them and signifying the presence of the Holy Spirit, they enter the royal doors of the church in proper order. [Col. 0838C]

[Note: The base text has the singular *significans* (“signifying”); Bl. reads the plural *significantibus* (“signifying”).]

The crosses are rightly taken from the sacristy, because Christ appeared to us from the secrets of God; protected by his cross, and with him defending us, we are freed from every aerial power.

The crosses are taken from the hidden place because, coming forth from the secrets amid the terror of the nations, the peoples carrying the cross of Christ devoutly enter the thresholds of God’s Church in order to follow Christ.

Therefore the Lord thunders through the Gospel, saying:

> “Whoever carries Christ’s cross shall be saved.”

There are three crosses so that all three parts of the world—namely Asia, Europe, and Africa—may actually confess the Unity in Trinity and the Trinity in Unity, recognizing the Creator of heaven and earth and believing in the holy Word born from the Virgin and conceived through the Holy Spirit.

Our most faithful Catholic Fathers, instructed by God in the Catholic faith, confessed all these things in the Council of Nicaea and said:

> “The Catholic faith is this: that one God in Trinity and Trinity in Unity is to be worshiped.”

[Note: B omits the words “instructed by God in the Catholic faith.”]

As the readers and doorkeepers enter with the signs, they find the archbishop outside the choir, with the archdeacon guiding his right side and the archpresbyter his left, and themselves supporting him like the true Moses. Thus, through the grace of the holy Gospel, he is confirmed by the teachings and figures of the New and Old Testaments, or the holy Church is supported and nourished by human beings as though by columns through love of God and neighbor, so that, with God’s consent, it may deserve to ascend and fly to the joys of heaven. [Col. 0839A]

[Note: Bl. reads “the true Moses.” B reads “and of neighbor.” B has “so that they may be supported and nourished.”]

Therefore Saint Prosper says:

> “Whoever lacks these twin wings of virtues has no means by which to fly to the kingdoms of heaven.”

When these have entered and been arranged according to order, they sing, with the Prophet praising God, “In the highest,” in accordance with what is said:

> “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the highest” (Ps. 148:1).  
> “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and all things were created” (ibid., 5).

From there they see twenty-four cardinals and many notaries on the eastern side, and on the other, western side, seven deacons and twenty-four subdeacons, their faces turned toward the east, according to what is said:

> “They will come from the west and the east, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matt. 8:11). [Col. 0839B]

Meanwhile, with the signs raised as the discipline of the order requires, the antiphon is sung six times outside the choir, throughout the body of the church, in a loud voice. Therefore the prophet Isaiah says:
