> “All you inhabitants of the city, you who dwell upon the earth: when the sign has been raised on the mountains, you will see it, and you will hear the sound of the trumpet” (Isa. 18:3).

After the antiphon has been sung six times, they come to the choir, where all the orders together sing it once in loud and resonant voices. [Col. 0839C]

Thus, when it has been sung seven times, with everyone standing in his own place, they show that the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit have mercifully been given to the faithful for the honor and glory of God.

But so that what I have said and am saying may appear true, I have taken pains to confirm and approve it by the judgments of the saints and of our most glorious confessor Ambrose.

[Note: B reads: “by the judgments of the saints and especially of blessed Ambrose.”]

Hear not me but him himself, who explains in what ways and for what reasons he sang hymns and songs, in his treatise *On the Blessed Immaculate One* (VII, 25):

> “For what we hold well, we are accustomed to sing; hymns are ours, song is ours, psalms are for us matters of justification. I shall sing with the spirit; I shall sing also with the mind.”

[Note: The apparatus gives *justificationes Domini sunt* (“the Lord’s justifications”) and then “Let us sing, let us sing and ...” in Ambrose; Bl. reads *psallamus* (“let us sing”) in both places.]

To expel and drive forgetfulness from his holy house, the true Solomon made singers for himself who would devote their whole spirit to seeking knowledge of divinity, so that singers would not be lacking in his Church, and so that the evil spirit might be driven away by their singing. [Col. 0840A]

The prophets too, when they prophesied, saw those skilled in singing sing, so that spiritual grace might be poured forth after being invited by the sweetness of the sound.

[Note: B apparently reads: “The prophets too, when they prophesied, judged those skilled in singing to be singing, so that spiritual grace might be poured forth after being invited by sweet spiritual delight.”]

And in the Gospel we read that in the house of the father who recovered his son a harmony resounded, by which the faithful who were feasting were delighted, while the unbelieving man heard it impatiently.

Sweet, therefore, is the song that does not weaken the body but strengthens the mind and spirit.

For that reason it is called a song while the testament is proclaimed, because in the evangelical Scriptures they sing together the remission of sins and, finally, the Lord’s righteousness with the joyful exultation of the mind. [Col. 0840B]

The Lord himself did not disdain to say:

> “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Luke 7:32).

And the Prophet says:

> “Your ordinances were songs for me” (Ps. 118:54);

and again:

> “I shall sing to you, O God, upon the lyre, O Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Ps. 70:22).

[Note: B omits “O Holy One of Israel.” Bl. reads “redeemed” rather than “have redeemed.”]

He sang these things joyfully, as though he were being nourished by these better feasts.

Finally, Moses sang, the one who received the Law. Mary also, Aaron’s sister, sang with tambourines and dances.

And so that he might soothe the minds of the people, who were divided among themselves like a sea by stormy tempests, he says in *Exameron* (III, 5):

> “The Church is often compared with the sea. At first, with the advancing ranks of the people entering, it spews out waves throughout all its vestibules; then, in the prayer of the whole people, it roars like waves flowing back, when the harmonious crash of the waves resounds through the responses of psalms and the song of men, women, virgins, and children.” [Col. 0840C]

[Note: The edition of Ambrose reads “song” instead of “songs.”]

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0839]

[Col. 0839C]

[Note: Heading: “The excellent prayer of the historian to God and his Trinity, in which anyone who reads it will discover the purpose of this book and the schism of the entire Ambrosian clergy, through which many were miserably treated.” A* and A**; also Bl., in which “the second book” is absent. B has: “The historian’s prayer to the Lord.” In B these verses close Book I, as also in Blancus.]

### Jesus Christ, splendor of the Father

Jesus Christ, splendor of the Father, way, life, truth,

Kind Redeemer of all, the equity of all,

Your charity fills all who seek you.

God the Father, Word of the Father, Spirit the Comforter,

Three persons, one God, forever undivided,

Ruling and restraining all things, seated as the Most High.

You graciously fill those whom you will with the spirit of knowledge,

And make the speechless possess great eloquence,

Please extend to me a drop of your living spring. [Col. 0840C]

Blessed and worthy of praise in the glory of the saints,

Whose mutilated bodies exude fragrance like lilies,

To whom the hosts of angels owe supreme praise.

Since you, Savior, are the sole defense of us,

You who granted jubilation to the Jewish people,

May your power, my nourisher—

[Note: Possibly “protector”; W.]

—be present to me forever.

From you I ask forgiveness for so many sins,

For whatever I did by sinning in my youth in this world,

So that when you come as judge in your judgment. [Col. 0841A]

Woe is me, who have lived so many years in this world!

I have never knowingly accomplished good things in my heart,

Burning inwardly, blazing outwardly, without any end.

To all young men and to the clergy I speak, especially,

To whom age and appearance shine at this time:

Please greatly refrain from vain words and jokes.

The once golden age has come into a silver one,

And now the unhappy bronze age has sent an iron one upon us,

And now, to our misfortune, it has found us made of clay.

The Antichrist-worshipping people, already greatly seduced by a long plague,

Bear witness to this and recognize it:

he who, through diabolical art, permits true things to be mingled with false.

For now we see the Ambrosian see and its clergy,

The two chief Counts and their peoples,

Wandering through certain schismatics. [Col. 0841B]

Foreseeing them, the noble and kindly teacher Ambrose

Asks and implores God through the voices of the clergy

That the schismatics may depart with their devices.

They swarm and proliferate beyond counting;

feigning chastity along with every virtue,

these priests gnaw at the clergy beyond what is fitting.

And, frenzied like dogs, they long for precipices,

Treating all just and unjust things indiscriminately,

Filled with anger and hatred, which is an evil beast.

I ask God, who sent Barnabas the Apostle here,

And afterward sent the renowned Ambrose,

To grant me a gentle manner of speaking about our dissension. [Col. 0841C]

[Note: “The first book ends. The second begins. It begins the second prologue of the second book.” A**, B, Bl. “The second book of the most faithful historian, who, investigating all the matters stated above and those that follow, found them in books from various places.” A*.]

### 1

Amid many troubled and storm-filled times, disturbed by wicked men, during which all the senses of my body are confused and dragged in different directions because of the variety of many sects, after great inward struggle I have deliberated much in my mind how to narrate and explain, as far as my small talent can manage, the schism that the Ambrosian Church suffered from false brothers and false prophets, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

I remember that Ambrose, the teacher of the churches and most reverend shepherd, said:

> “Do everything with counsel, so that you will not regret your work.”

[Note: Bl. reads *consiliis* (“with counsels”). B reads, in place of the introductory attribution, “mindful that blessed Ambrose said.” The citation is *Exposition on Psalm 118* VIII, 32.]

I shall diligently narrate what dissensions and disturbances it endured from its own sons through counterfeit rudiments, and what losses it suffered—not in the lofty words of philosophers, but in plain style and composed speech, as God may grant through my glorious confessor and patron Ambrose.

[Note: B reads “through blessed Ambrose.”]

I have not aimed to describe the wars of kings, disclose the uprisings of peoples or the seditions of cities, labor over the refinements of words, or waste time in idle speech, knowing that the Lord thunders through the Gospel:

> “Do you not know that you will have to give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment?” (Matt. 12:36).

Therefore, anticipated by fear of the Lord and relying on the prayers of blessed Bishop Ambrose, I shall keep silent about what must be kept silent, and what I have decided to write in my heart I shall, with God’s help, faithfully explain for the protection of souls and the defense of bodies in generations to come. [Col. 0842B]

I do not seek human glory from men, nor earthly riches, nor displays or adornments of clothing, nor houses, servants, or maidservants—all things that emperors, magistrates, and Roman consuls once customarily bestowed above all others.

[Note: B reads “above poets.”]

I seek only the salvation of posterity, of their bodies and souls. Having seen such great signs and such great virtues, and having heard of such great disasters and disturbances, let them take precautions and guard themselves, and remember me in their divine supplications.

[Note: Additional apparatus and editorial matter, keyed to the translated lemmata above. Abbreviated bibliographical references are retained as printed.]

- 11, title ([Col. 0833]): *De monogamis sacerdotibus a b. Ambrosio* (“On monogamous priests by blessed Ambrose”); *a. b. A.* is absent in A** and Bl. At *De monogamia*, the note refers to *de castimonia autem q. l. Quando u. t. nec repetita p. c. Et in ipso ergo conjugio l. e. n. i. c. Ambros.*; cf. below III, 24. A* reads *et est* (“and is”) for *et*, and *parata* (“prepared”) for *peracta* (“perfected”). At Ambrose’s departure, Bl. reads *stipatum* (“accompanied”) for *stipatus*.

- 12, title ([Col. 0835]): A**, B, and Bl. have the title *de crismon sancti Ambrosii*; A has *a Datio ep. M.* (“by Datius, bishop of Milan”); A* is also cited. At “with his assistance,” B omits *ipso adjuvante*; at “according to,” B omits *secundum*. B also omits *summam* (“supreme”) both in the opening account of mercy and in the explanation of the eastern entrance. At the Isaiah citation B has *propheta sic dicente* (“the prophet saying thus”); at David’s citation it has *Et prophetam David* (“And the prophet David”).

- 12, entrance and *chrismon*: B reads *cognoscat* (“may recognize,” singular) for *cognoscant* and adds *cum* (“with”) before the burning candle. Bl. reads *significante* (“signifying”) for *significans*. At alpha and omega, Bl. supplies *omega* after *alpha et ho*; the reading *A. ω videtis* (“the A and omega which you see”) is found only in B and is absent from the remaining witnesses. B reads *de celo* (“from heaven”) for *deleo* (“I wipe away”). Bl. adds *et* in *ab initio et ante saecula* (“from the beginning and before the ages”); B instead reads: *homo natus ex virgine, suo sanguine nos redemit, et sicut ovis ad occisionem ductus sit* (“born as a human being from a virgin, he redeemed us by his blood, and was led like a sheep to slaughter”).

- 12, ash, cross, and penitence: Bl. reads *cinis* (“ash,” nominative) for *cinerem* (“ash,” accusative), *filius* (“Son”) for *factus* (“made/became”), and *redemi* (“I redeemed”) for *redimi* (“I have redeemed”). B omits *lumen de lumine* (“light from light”), *Deus dominus ac* (“God, Lord, and”), *de* in *de quibus* (“concerning which”), and the phrase “with his precious blood” at the later exhortation to hope; it reads *propterea* (“therefore”) for *praeterea* (“moreover”). Bl. has *propheta dicit* (“the prophet says”), *habitu* (“in garb/attire”) for the printed *ambitu*, *dimittens* (“forgiving”) for *dimittere* (“to forgive”), and *cognoscentes* (“recognizing”) for *cognoscite* (“recognize”).

- 12, eight rods and sphere: B has *promissas cognoscite sive* (“recognize [them as] promised, or”) at the introduction to the alternatives. A** and B read *de quibus* (“concerning which”); A* reads *de quibus reverendus sex* (“concerning which the venerable [man says] six”). B reads *condistincte* (“distinctly distinguished”) for *distinctae* (“distinguished”); Bl. has *altera* (“another”) for *alia*. B reads *qui initiis non coartatur nec fine concluditur* (“who is not confined by beginnings nor enclosed by an end”). Bl. supplies *omega* in the Apocalypse citation; B omits *loquitur* (“speaks”).

- 13, title and procession: The title is *De crucis antiphona a Datio* (“On the antiphon of the cross, by Datius”); B reads *secundum Datium archiepiscopum Mediolanensem* (“according to Datius, archbishop of Milan”). B reads *ab inferna potestate* (“from infernal power”) for *ab omni potestate aerea* (“from every aerial power”), orders the continents as *Asia scilicet Africa et Europa* (“Asia, namely Africa and Europe”), and omits *sanctum* (“holy”) before “Word.”

- 13, Nicene fathers, archbishop, and song: B omits *fidelissimi catholici, catholica fide a Deo imbuti* (“most faithful Catholics, instructed by God in the Catholic faith”), has *vero* for *verum* in the comparison with Moses, reads *ac* for *et* before “neighbor,” and pluralizes *sustentarentur et alerentur* (“might be supported and nourished”). B has *alas* (“wings,” accusative) for *alis* (“by wings”). It also omits “from his Church” after “so that singers would not be lacking.” Bl. omits *Et* (“And”) at the opening of the Gospel example. In the final quotation, the Ambrosian edition reads *cantus* (“song”) for *canticis* (“songs”).

- Prayer before Book II: Bl. orders the opening words *via, veritas et vita* (“way, truth, and life”); all manuscripts support *cunctorem aequitas* (“the equity of all”) as printed in the apparatus; Bl. reads *noster* (“our”) for *nostris* (“of us/our”). W. queries whether *nutrix* (“nourisher”) should be *tutrix* (“protectress”). B has *cleri* (“of the clergy”), while the other witnesses have *clerici* (“clerics”); Bl. reads *multa* (“many things/greatly”) for *multum* (“much”), and *argentea* (“silver,” nominative) for *argenteam* (“silver,” accusative).

- Book II, chapter 1: Bl. omits *a falsis fratribus* (“from false brothers”). Bl. has *dissensiones* (“dissensions”) for *dissessiones*. B reads *per beati Ambrosii* (“through blessed Ambrose”) and omits *antistitis* (“bishop”) in the appeal to Ambrose’s prayers. At the list of worldly goods, B reads *poetis* (“poets”) for *ceteris* (“others”).

## 2. Saints

[Note: [Col. 0841] Title: “On King Lambert’s siege of Milan.” A**, Bl. A*: “Begins: On …” B: “How the city of Milan was destroyed by King Lambert.”]

During the time of Saint Honoratus, archbishop of Milan, when the most unfortunate King Lambert was ruling Italy after usurping its sovereignty [Note: [Col. 0841C] Honoratus was archbishop in 568; Lambert, about 896, captured the city, which had been destroyed by the Goths in 539. Our author confuses all these matters. See Count Giulini, *Memorie di Milano* II, pp. 45 ff., who discusses them admirably.], an immense hidden plague attacked the city of Milan with the utmost violence.

For this city, honored fittingly and exalted appropriately by magnificent emperors who claimed the whole world for themselves through their empire and laws, flourished again. Because of the pleasantness of its situation and the healthfulness of its air, they loved it even more than Rome, and at that time raised it above all the cities of Italy, augmenting it with many imperial adornments.

But, so that you may believe truly and without doubt what I say, hear what I found in the most truthful annals and in a description of the site of Milan: how the Augustan emperors of old adorned it with royal authority, placing there, according to ancestral custom, an imperial palace worthy of the dignity of the Augusti, a most splendid theater, an *aumatium*, and baths—that is, hot bathing establishments—where the queens, the emperors’ wives who were residing in the city for a time [Note: [Col. 0843] Bl. reads “who were residing”], were cleansed elegantly and separately from the men; and where the whole population of the city, whenever time and need required, eagerly gathered to bathe, men separated from women.

Then they built a garden, like the Paradise of God, made pleasant by trees of various kinds. They also constructed an arena adorned with stones and various workmanship, in which the soldiers of all Italy could sit and hear and properly understand a single orator.

Moreover, enlarging the city beyond the size to which the Gallic Senones had built it—the same people who captured Rome apart from the Capitol [Note: [Col. 0843] This is omitted in Bl.]—they built and completed, for as many days as there are in a year, that many closely packed towers of massive construction.

Furthermore, above the city’s six gates they built very lofty, round dwellings, together with a very lofty triangular outer gateway, in most elegant workmanship, so that these structures might strive to prevent the barbarian enemy from entering, as though fortified by nature.

For these reasons the emperors afterward began very frequently to visit, inhabit, and honor the city, especially because it possessed the most suitable tempering of the healthiest air and a location altogether prepared for domestic uses.

The most impious and wicked King Lambert hated this city intensely, chiefly because Duke Ilduynus, who governed it [Note: [Col. 0843D] He has confused Count Maginfred with this man; moreover, I have found no trace of Ilduynus.], was by no means favorable to him.

With three kings and many dukes of France, Saxony, Normandy, and Germany, and with an innumerable multitude of barbarians, he besieged it for ten years. Many of his own dukes, cavalrymen, and infantrymen died from arrows and various engines, and he accomplished nothing.

But when he had already labored for a long time in vain with his men [Note: [Col. 0843] A** omits “for a long time”; B reads *per multum tempus*, “for a long time”; Bl. reads *per multum temporis*.], had been deprived of every hope, and saw that the resources of his kingdom had been spent uselessly, he was filled with immense grief and miserably took the road by which he might depart.

Meanwhile, a most wicked peasant, after the king had gone three days on his way with his army, arrived before him in sorrow, proclaiming that the kingdom had been conquered and trampled underfoot. With his clothes torn, like a truly mad man, he came to the king.

When he had reached the king, he advised him that the king, together with all his men, should renew the abandoned siege with the strongest assurances; and meanwhile that a few very trusted men should make an agreement with the citizens and Duke Ilduynus: the king should enter and leave the city with his men only, while all the citizens remained unharmed; thirty of his own dukes should affirm this upon the holy Gospels.

Then, once he had entered the city, he should appear as lord of the city and its inhabitants and, as they deserved, should endeavor to exercise his men after breaking the agreements [Note: [Col. 0843] So the manuscripts.]; and he bound himself by oath never to enter the city gates.

Thus, after this detestable plan had been adopted, Lambert carried out in due order everything that the devil had spoken through the mouth of the most wicked peasant.

At that time, when the citizens saw the harsh siege renewed and were filled with various anxieties, they heard and fearfully accepted the king’s proposal: forty very powerful dukes swore under oath to preserve the integrity of the city and the safety of all its citizens. Their hearts, interpreting the truth of the matter favorably, did not perceive the wickedness of Lambert’s heart. Desiring peace and quiet, they received the king—worse than a Saracen—with his men, so that he might quickly enter and depart, just as he had sworn upon the holy Gospels.

Finally, on the third night after his departure, he entered the city of Milan, after certain traitors had broken through the city walls beside the church now called Saint Andrew’s, at the breach in the wall. Thus, as the king had sworn, he entered not through the city gate but through the breach, so that he might appear to observe his oath.

After this had been done, the most savage Lambert, forgetful of faith and of God, drew his swords and, filled with demonic fury, inhumanly slaughtered an immense number of citizens—children and old men, young men and infants alike.

He also destroyed with hammers and mangonels [Note: [Col. 0843D] That is, engines of war.] the city’s palaces, towers, and municipal buildings, together with all the defenses of the citizens, which the Gallic commander Brennus, Nerva, Trajan, the cruel Maximian, and other emperors had built for the city’s protection.

At the same time, Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0843] The words “and Saint” are omitted in B.], seeing the citizens and the city being devastated and consumed by the enemy, appeared to Lambert on the night of Saint Severus [Note: [Col. 0843D] Saint Severus is commemorated on the Kalends of February.] and said to him, the wicked man:

> “O enemy of God and of men, denier of God and deserving of a condemnatory death, unjustly destroying the city and its defenses, which I blessed and consecrated to the honor of God and for the benefit of the Christian inhabitants! You have slaughtered like a pagan the people whom God, hanging upon the cross, redeemed with his precious blood. Know, therefore, that neither you nor your heir will long hold the empire, and that you will die a most shameful death, like a dog.”

When he heard this, Lambert abandoned the city and, taking with him into something like exile the son of Ilduynus, whose name was Azo [Note: [Col. 0844D] Liudprand calls him Hugh, I, 12. I do not know whether Adalbert’s rebellion, which occurred at that time, gave rise to the name Azo.], set out for Parma.

By divine providence he loved the boy, who was still young, so greatly that King Lambert did nothing without him.

After he had stayed in those regions for three years, he one day wished to go out for a walk. He was led hunting near the woods; the dogs were scattered and sent into the forest, and the hunters, with clever skill, were trying to discover the woodland animal [Note: [Col. 0843] Bl. reads *ut*, “as.”]. Lambert, overcome by very deep sleep, rested in the lap of Ilduynus’s son, while Ilduynus’s servant stood nearby [Note: [Col. 0844D] Compare the *Chronicon Novaliciense*, p. 127.].

When Azo, the son of Ilduynus, saw this, encouraged by the servant and remembering all the evils Lambert had inflicted upon him and his father, he resolved, after much deliberation, to kill the king.

When he could find no sword with which to cut his throat, he saw beside him a large and extremely sharp thorn. Seizing it, he treated him like a dog, as blessed Ambrose had foretold, and immediately killed him by striking him in the breast.

Terrible vultures and ill-omened ravens buried his flesh as they greedily devoured it with their beaks. [Note: [Col. 0845D] This little tale seems to have arisen from the name of the estate *Spina Lamberti*, now Spilamberto; see Giulini, cited above, p. 66; Leibniz, *Annals of the Empire*, II, p. 175.] And the boy Azo [Note: [Col. 0845] B omits *et*, “and,” before “the boy Azo.”] mounted the royal horse and hurried to Milan, where he restored the ruined city as best he could, while the king was torn apart by wild animals.

After three days, Lambert’s soldiers, wandering all around, found him with his flesh gnawed away and only his bones visible. His clothing was completely filthy with decay, worms, and stench. Sad and miserable, they did not give him burial as a king.

At that time the savage Lombards came into Italy, sparing neither young nor old. They too, behaving like pagans in a pagan manner, came to Milan.

The blessed archbishop Honoratus, foreseeing their arrival and knowing that the city had been devastated, that it had also been afflicted by a most cruel plague of worms, that innumerable people had died, and that the city’s warrior citizens had been torn apart by the sword of the most cruel Lambert, seized the entire treasure of the church and, heading for Genoa, faithfully carried it away in order to rescue it from the hands of the Lombards.

A few days later the city was captured by the Lombards. Since it had been devastated, its walls and towers could not long be maintained. Yet, by God’s mercy and through his forbearance, it obtained the greatest friendship of the king and the Lombards, so that, through many privileges and many ceremonies, whatever belonged to the archbishopric remained untouched and unharmed by every people and by the king.

Later, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, became a Christian through God’s mercy and built there, for the remedy of his soul, a church of Saint Vincent and a monastery for monks, adorning them with many estates and castles [Note: [Col. 0846D] Giulini I, p. 80, called this into doubt.].

Adrian, afterward Roman pontiff, having learned of Desiderius’s very grave deeds, was the first to give Charlemagne, son of Pepin, episcopal staffs for investing bishops and rings, contrary to right and law, so that he might rescue his cities from the hands of Desiderius—thus, as it were, drive out one nail with another.

But whoever does not believe me should read the *Roman Pontifical* or the *Deeds of the Lombards*, for there he will find faithfully treated what I have said [Note: [Col. 0846D] Namely, that Adrian summoned Charlemagne; for the rest you will search there in vain.].

But before I speak of the hidden plague that attacked the clergy of the entire Ambrosian church with the utmost savagery, like a grim lion, I shall not cease to explain who first contaminated and violated the seat of blessed Ambrose through the heresy of simony.

[Note: Chapter 2, [Col. 0841]: B and its copy A* read *haec etenim*, “for this”; A** and Bl. omit it. B omits *vere*, “truly.” The description of Milan was published by L. A. Muratori, *Scriptores*, I.b; p. 204 reads: “which, as is found in the most truthful annals from ancient times, possessed rank and dominion as the second great empire after illustrious Rome,” etc.]

[Note: Chapter 2, [Col. 0842C]: The cited description reads, in the editor’s abbreviated quotation, “They enlarged [it], placing in it, in the ancestral manner, a palace outstanding in its fitness for the dignity of the emperors, a theatre, an aumatium [the name of this facility is unclear], baths, and a garden.” The same is repeated below in chapter 15. On these buildings see Fumagalli, *Antichità milanesi*, I, p. 137 ff.]

### 3. Fronto, Ordained Bishop of Milan by Simony

[Note: [Col. 0845] Title: *On Fronto, appointed bishop of Milan by Constantine.* A*: “On Fronto, an archbishop ordained by simony.” A**, B, and Bl.]

After all the bishops who had piously and catholically held the episcopate before the admirable confessor Ambrose, and after Ambrose himself and those bishops who followed him as disciples of the Lord had gone rejoicing with Christ into the kingdom of heaven, Fronto invaded the Ambrosian chair, unworthy and undeserving, like a thief and robber.

In him were all the treasures of malice, the quivers of wickedness, and the perverse designs of every kind [Note: [Col. 0845] Bl. reads *malitiae*, “of malice”; the other manuscripts read *militiae*, “of military service.”].

Born of noble parents, he devoted himself neither to knowledge of God nor to divine worship. Rather, he was wealthy in gold and silver, rich in necklaces, and exceedingly well supplied with male and female servants.

But how naked and poor he was in every good virtue, the following account will show.

He was full of avarice, which is increased neither by abundance nor extinguished by poverty. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “The greedy and avaricious will not enter the kingdom of God.” In addition, he was ambitious beyond what can be believed.

This came about after Bishop Honoratus died—honorable both in name and in office, and the eighteenth who had occupied the see after blessed Ambrose. The nobles and a vast Catholic people, together with the entire clergy, were piously and catholically seeking and desiring a bishop according to God. Suddenly, when many on both sides—the people and the nobles—had been bewitched [Note: [Col. 0845] So B.; omitted in the other witnesses.], an immense disturbance arose.

Thus, when the election had been thrown into confusion, Fronto, stripped of every good quality and clothed in many vices, filled with an evil spirit, knowing that he could not obtain the episcopate through the catholic election of the clergy and people, hastened with a vast weight of gold and silver, and with a few nobles, by rapid journey to the emperor’s detestable court.

After taking counsel, in addition to what he had paid in hand to obtain the episcopate, he promised immeasurable quantities of gold and silver to dukes, counts, and all who daily served the imperial commands.

The emperor, however, having learned of his wickedness and foreseeing Fronto’s entire purpose, was greedy for gold and did not care how or in what manner Fronto behaved toward catholic ecclesiastical offices. Having received an immense weight of gold and silver, he gave him, with only slight hesitation, a certain execrable investiture of the bishopric of Milan.

After receiving Fronto’s oath of loyalty, he also gave him a county [Note: [Col. 0845] Omitted in Bl.], under whose protection Fronto might defend himself in the heresy of simony, while the emperor is represented as innocent in this matter [Note: [Col. 0845] Bl. reads “might be held responsible.”].

After this, Fronto exulted with great rejoicing. Accompanied by many Lombards who at that time served in the imperial court [Note: [Col. 0845] Bl. reads “in the imperial service.”], he came to Milan like a thief and robber.

He was the first who, seeing that he could not obtain the episcopate through the arms of justice and a catholic election—through a good life and reputation, preaching, good morals, chastity, and fasts—drove the nobles and a large part of the populace, by distributing great gifts and making many promises, into allegiance without entering through the gate.

Concerning this the Lord thunders terribly, with true and living voice, through the Gospel:

> “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate is not the shepherd of the sheep, but is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1).

Blessed Ambrose, teacher and master of truth [Note: [Col. 0847] “Teacher and master of truth” is omitted in B.], follows this by saying:

> “O wretched man: what you gave was gold; what you received is leprosy” [Note: [Col. 0847] So Bl.; the manuscripts read *lepta*, “a small coin.” “What he received was money, and what he gave was leprosy” is said of a bishop selling ordinations in chapter 5 of the *Pastoral Book* falsely attributed to Ambrose. W.].

Accordingly, Saint Ambrose says concerning Luke (4:52):

> “For the guilt of a mystery that has been sold is inexplicable, and grace passes from vengeance before the eyes to posterity” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ambrose reads “inexpiable”; B: “and grace, vindicated by the law, passes from the eyes to posterity”; A**: “and grace from the law of the flock”; A*: “and grace is vindicated by the law”; Bl.: “and grace vindicated by the law.” The Ambrosian text also reads *caelestis oculis*, “before heavenly eyes.”].

Again, concerning Luke (9:19):

> “Those who do not deem themselves worthy of the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot have fellowship in the Church of God” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ambrose reads: “who traffic in grace.”]. “For you received freely; give freely. Finally, Peter answered Simon, who thought that the gift of sanctification could be conferred upon him for a price: ‘May your money be with you for destruction, because you think you can obtain the grace of God with money. You have neither part nor share in this faith’” (Acts 8:20).

Again, concerning churches in the same work (9:17):

> “For our God [Note: [Col. 0847] Bl. reads *Deus enim noster*, “for our God.”] does not want his temple to be a merchant’s lodging place, but a dwelling of holiness; nor does he fashion the use of priestly ministry through a saleable religious office, but through free devotion.”

Finally, Fronto lived for eleven years, treating all good and evil, justice and injustice, indiscriminately, and consumed almost all the treasures of this holy Ambrosian church, both inside and outside, by wasting and misusing them.

One day, accompanied by a crowd of his soldiers, with dogs and huntsmen arranged, he went to the wood that is still called Caminadella [Note: [Col. 0847C] The place-name still survives beyond the Porta Tonsa; it is called the Wood of Caminadella. Puricelli.]. When he was leading the animal he had found toward death, suddenly, overtaken by God’s wrath and a very swift scourge, he came upon a place called the Well of Averanus, and the marsh swallowed him. Just as Dathan and Abiram provoked God’s anger, so an inundation of earth swallowed him.

Thus, after Fronto had died badly and been buried even worse, let us hear what his epitaph says—an epitaph that I later found, after many years had passed, on a polished stone, with the dust of his body absent. Let us also carefully hear how cruelly and savagely he behaved toward the golden chalice of blessed Ambrose, which Ambrose himself had consecrated with his own hands, and toward the gold that the emperor Theodosius had given to Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0847] Bl. reads “how he had behaved.”].

[Note: [Col. 0847] Rubric: “Verses of Fronto, bishop, who first invaded the see of Saint Ambrose through a wicked election and simony.” A*, A**, Bl. B: “Verses found where Fronto’s tomb was supposed to be.”]

> After Ausonia’s rule had received [Note: [Col. 0847] Bl. reads *excipit*, “receives,” for *excepit*, “received.”]  
> The flourishing reins of the Lombards’ Church,  
> Ancient report throughout many walls proclaims  
> That Fronto first mounted the supports of the see.  
> His promised payment pressed him repeatedly, and when  
> He had no remaining means even for food,  
> He is said to have handed over to the fire for melting  
> The holy chalice that Ambrose and the catholic Caesar  
> Theodosius had once made together.  
> Alas, the ill-fated man died shamefully.

### 4. How Saint Gregory Dealt with the Universal Office

[Note: [Col. 0847] Title in B: “Sermon of Constantius, archbishop of Milan, on how blessed Gregory dealt with the ordering of the universal office.” A** and Bl. read *tentavit*, “attempted,” for *tractavit*, “dealt with.” A*: “The ordering and arrangement of all Latin ministers, composed and arranged by Saint Gregory, Roman pontiff. Constantine wrote these things to bishops and archbishops, that they might be seen in the world.” Bl. reads *propter*, “because of,” for *praeter*, “except for.”]

After a considerable time, Pope Gregory, the most reverend shepherd and pontiff, came after blessed Agapitus [Note: [Col. 0847C] After Pelagius II, in the year 590.] had been pontiff of the city of Rome. Instructed by the divine Spirit, he saw that all the churches of the Latin language differed greatly in their various offices.

With God’s assent, he restrained and recalled all of them to the unity of the Roman Church, except for the Ambrosian mystery, saying:

> “O brothers and venerable fathers, a fitting and appropriate principle is attributed to us. Since the Apostle Paul says through the Holy Spirit, ‘One God, one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5), so there ought to be one mystery for the whole Latin language.”

When all the religious men who presided over those churches heard this, they were terrified. Gregory knew that many holy men of different lands had ordered various offices according to what God had granted to each, faithfully and wonderfully singing praises to the Holy Trinity and Unity.

In the end, the arrangement was praised and confirmed. But when he saw that the Ambrosian mystery had been established by divine instruction, he stopped in fear.

### 5. How Constantius Protected the Ambrosian Office

[Note: [Col. 0847–0849] Title: “On Constantius, through whose probity the Ambrosian ministry was kept safe and defended from the envious.” A**, Bl. A*: “Begins: On …” B: “How, through the labors of Archbishop Constantius, the Ambrosian office was protected from the envious.”]

At that time, in the year 593, Constantius, a catholic bishop who had been catholically ordained, third after Fronto, was a deacon of the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0848C] Rather, of the church of Milan; see Gregory I, *Epistles* III, 29.], whom blessed Gregory the author of the *Dialogues* had consecrated while he was a deacon.

Constantius had gone to the council that blessed Gregory was holding, accompanied by reverent men, by his own and blessed Ambrose’s many suffragan bishops, and by a large force of very capable soldiers [Note: [Col. 0848C] But at that time Constantius was living in exile at Genoa; see Fumagalli, *Antichità di Milano* III, 135.].

When this had happened, through the administration of the Holy Spirit, and while Constantius the archbishop, together with all the faithful clergy and laity and the religious bishops, was petitioning—partly out of fear of God and of blessed Ambrose, knowing that Ambrose had once labored with many great exertions in the divine service, and partly because of love and affection for Bishop Constantius—Gregory said:

> “Let the Ambrosian Church remain in its own state.”

### 6. How Saint Gregory, Instructed by the Ambrosian Book, Ordered His Own Office

[Note: [Col. 0849] Title: “On the order of the Ambrosian book, and how Saint Gregory, instructed by it, arranged his own mystery.” A*, A**, Bl. B: “How blessed Gregory, instructed by the Ambrosian office, ordered his own office.”]

Not long afterward, Gregory ordered his faithful to present to him the Ambrosian order, which Constantius had greatly commended to the apostolic pontiff. This was done when, by divine will, the messengers sent to him returned. Gregory had instructed them to ensure that the order of the Ambrosian mystery should be presented to him at the appointed time, with every obstacle removed.

But while he was in the palace discussing important matters with all the cardinals who had spoken in the synod about the mystery of Saint Ambrose, the messengers arrived. Suddenly, a considerable light shone forth. All except the apostolic were thrown to the ground by excessive fear, and, since they did not know what this was, the pope alone was greatly astonished.

Meanwhile, the messengers returned from blessed Constantius, bishop of the city of Milan. After greeting the apostolic, they gave him the book. Filled with great joy, he opened it and carefully examined throughout how blessed Ambrose had arranged the books of the Old and New Testaments for reading in his church, and how he had ordered in writing the Gospels, the Epistles of Paul, the prophecies, the solemn celebrations of the Mass, and everything else suitable for divine worship.

Having learned this, Gregory drew many shining flowers from the splendid sequence of that book, as though from a most pleasant meadow, and grafted them into Roman worship like a good and fruitful olive branch into a wild olive tree. With these things the Roman Church, adorned like a bride with various ornaments, has remained to this day, with hymns, prayers, and glorious songs.

Blessed Gregory, seeing and recognizing how excellent and dignified all that had been ordered by blessed Ambrose, the pillar of the Church, was, and how it had been established by the Holy Spirit like stone upon stone, called them by distinctive names: an Ambrosian hymn, an Ambrosian responsory, an Ambrosian antiphon, an Ambrosian invitatory, an Ambrosian prayer [Note: [Col. 0849] The reading may be *insignivit*, “he distinguished it.” W. reads “as a sign of the divine hymn”; A. reads “the Ambrosian hymn”; Bl. reads “the Ambrosian response and the Ambrosian antiphon.”].

For whenever blessed Gregory inserted and arranged anything from his own orders, he always used the name Ambrosian like a kind of seal, saying “Ambrosian.” A* reads *unicuique*, “to each,” for *ubicumque*, “wherever.”

How great the love and reverence of the Ambrosian Church were toward the apostolic majesty is apparent from the distinguished and friendly matters that the most reverend Pope Gregory described concerning blessed Datius in the *Dialogue*. It is also apparent from the brilliant letter he issued to the Ambrosian clergy, whom false brothers and wicked, utterly evil laymen [Note: [Col. 0849] Bl. reads “from false brothers and from evil and very wicked laymen.”] were unjustly persecuting because of the election they had conducted catholically and canonically. That letter still remains in his register.

Thus Datius, because he was a bishop and is described as possessing greater dignity, should precede as a father precedes his children. Concerning him blessed Gregory described, among the other miracles he narrated with Peter, something magnificent and wondrous, saying (*Dialogues* III, 4):

### 7. The Account of Archbishop Datius by Blessed Gregory in the *Dialogue*

[Note: [Col. 0849] Title: “What blessed Gregory relates in the *Dialogue* about Datius, archbishop of Milan.” A**, B, Bl. A*: “On Datius, archbishop of Milan, ordained by blessed Gregory.” We have added the various readings of the Paris edition, omitting those that differ only in word order.]

> “In the time of the emperor Justinian, when Datius, bishop of the city of Milan, was traveling to Constantinople after being harassed and driven out on account of the faith [Note: [Col. 0849] The Paris edition reads *exactus*, “expelled.”], he came to Corinth [Note: [Col. 0849] The edition reads *Corinthus*].
>
> “While he was looking for a large house in which to lodge, one that could accommodate his entire retinue, and was scarcely finding one, he saw at a distance a house of suitable size and ordered it to be prepared for his lodging.
>
> “When the inhabitants of that place said that he could not stay there because the devil had inhabited it for many years, and that for this reason it had remained empty, the venerable Datius replied:
>
> “‘Indeed, for that very reason we ought to lodge in the same house, if an evil spirit has invaded it and driven human habitation away from it’ [Note: [Col. 0849] The Paris edition reads *inhabitationem*, “human habitation,” for *habitudinem*.].
>
> “He therefore ordered the house to be prepared for him [Note: [Col. 0849] B has this reading; the other witnesses omit it.] and entered without fear, prepared to endure the struggles of the ancient enemy [Note: [Col. 0849] The edition reads “that house.”].
>
> “Thus, in the stillness of the night, while the man of God was resting, the ancient enemy began, with immense voices and great clamors, to imitate the roars of lions, the bleating of sheep, the braying of donkeys [Note: [Col. 0849] The edition reads “the braying of donkeys.”], the hissing of serpents, the squealing of pigs, and the cries of mice [Note: [Col. 0849] The edition reads “of mice. Then.”].
>
> “Suddenly awakened by the voices of so many animals, Datius rose in great anger and began to shout loudly against the ancient enemy, saying:
>
> “‘It has gone well for you, wretch. You are the one who said, “I will set my throne in the north and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). Behold, through your pride you have become like pigs and mice; and you who presumptuously wished to imitate God, behold, as you deserve, you imitate beasts.’
>
> “At these words, the evil spirit was ashamed of his humiliation, so to speak. But did he not also become ashamed and thereafter cease to enter that same house to display the monsters he was accustomed to display? Thus the house afterward became a dwelling of the faithful, because, when one truly faithful man entered it, the lying and faithless spirit immediately departed from it.”

[Note: Chapter 7, [Col. 0849]: The Paris edition reads *exactus*, “expelled,” for *exagitatus*, “harassed/driven out”; *Corinthum*, “Corinth,” for *Corinthii*; *hospitandum*, “for lodging,” for *ad hospitium*, “to a lodging”; adds *hunc*, “this [man],” after *in ea*, “in it”; reads *inhabitationem*, “habitation,” for *habitudinem*, “association”; changes *sibi igitur*, “therefore for himself,” to *igitur sibi*, with the same meaning; reads *illam*, “that [house],” for *illa*; *ruditus*, “braying,” for *rugitus*, “roaring”; and *soricum. Tunc*, “of mice. Then,” for *suricum. Cum*, “of mice. When.” B retains the printed *igitur*, “therefore”; the other manuscript witnesses omit it. B also gives the abbreviated rearrangement *i. c. a. h. et m.*, apparently *incipit clamare adversus hostem et magnis*, “[he] begins to cry out against the enemy and with loud [voices],” with *vocibus*, “voices,” supplied by the continuing text. The abbreviation does not indicate a manuscript gap.]

### 8. How Blessed Gregory Confirmed Deusdedit as Archbishop

[Note: [Col. 0849] Title: “How blessed Gregory confirmed Deusdedit as archbishop.” A**, B. Bl.: “Consecrated.” A*: “On Deusdedit, archbishop, by blessed Gregory.”]

After some time, while blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome and of the whole world, was diligently expounding the divine utterances by dictating them, he heard that, after Constantius, bishop of the city of Milan, had died in the year 600, a catholic election had been made by the clergy of the Ambrosian Church in favor of Deusdedit.

I found this, as mentioned above, in a book discovered in the city of Genoa, and I have recalled it briefly [Note: [Col. 0851] Omitted in B. The source explicitly states that B omits *ut*, “as,” in this parenthetical assertion.].

Events soon proved the truth of this report. Messengers came from the Ambrosian clergy, dear to Gregory, and carefully explained how Constantius had departed this life. They also fully recounted how catholically and canonically they had carefully elected to the episcopal dignity the deacon called Deusdedit [Note: [Col. 0851] Bl. reads “had elected.”].

Moreover, they explained how many hardships the clergy and priests were unjustly suffering from the Lombards, from faithless soldiers, and from part of the populace, because they did not consent to the will of those people, on account of the election that they themselves had irregularly and disorderly made in favor of Agilulfus [Note: [Col. 0851C] He seems to attribute the name of the king to the person elected.].

When the apostolic heard this, he grieved very deeply over the death of Constantius, formerly his deacon and most faithful foster-son. Finally, he rejoiced partly over the catholic election and partly displayed his evident sympathy with their suffering.

Meanwhile, he received the messengers kindly, since they represented so great a city, so great a clergy, and so many orders—people whom the blessed apostolic loved above all cities in affection, devotion, love, and reverence for blessed Ambrose.

Blessed Gregory loved this church and these orders because he saw that they had been arranged and composed in every respect by blessed Ambrose, as a father loves his son and a mother her only child. He did not love them superficially or with any worldly intention, but with good affection and a sincere heart and pure mind.

What more is there to say? The letter that he sent through the messengers to the Ambrosian clergy, firmly exhorting them concerning the canonical election they had made in favor of Deusdedit, demonstrates this to the present day. But so that anyone who reads these things may be able to believe them fully and with greater certainty, let him listen with attentive ears and a watchful mind to that very letter, recorded in Gregory’s register (XI, 4).

### 9. Letter of Blessed Gregory to the Milanese Clergy

[Note: [Col. 0851] Rubric: “Letter of blessed Gregory to the clergy of Milan.”]

> “We cannot fill a written statement with the measure of grief with which the death of our brother and fellow bishop Constantius affects us. If only those neighboring regions might perceive how many good things they have lost in that man through this sudden calamity [Note: [Col. 0851] The Paris edition reads *partes illae in uno homine*, “those regions in one man”; Bl.: “if only they might perceive the sudden calamity”; Gregory: “may they perceive the calamity that has suddenly occurred.”].
>
> “For we are not unaware how careful he was in the discipline of ecclesiastical rule, or how vigilant he was in defending your city.
>
> “But since, when a shepherd dies, it is not fitting for you to remain without your own bishop, we have received with complete firmness and gratitude your declaration, made with God as its author, that you unanimously elected your deacon Deusdedit to the office of bishop [Note: [Col. 0851] Gregory’s text reads: “with the bishop having died, you ought altogether not to be without [a bishop].”].
>
> “Therefore, since no delay ought to impede the desires of good men [Note: [Col. 0851] The edition reads “the desires of good efforts”], we hasten, with God’s grace, to fulfill your wishes in him.
>
> “And because the aforesaid man is known to us not by his character but only in outward appearance, you must be the more careful, if you recognize that in this election not only your own advantage but also God’s cause is at stake [Note: [Col. 0851] B omits the words beginning “if …”; the Paris edition reads “inasmuch as …”].
>
> “You must therefore investigate carefully, so that there may be nothing in his former life that could oppose him through the sacred canons on account of a crime; and, if he is found suitable for maintaining discipline or exercising governance, and the agreement of all has been reached in his election, as you write, then, with the support of divine grace and by the authority of the present document, we have solemnly decreed [Note: [Col. 0851] The edition reads *decernimus*, “we decree,” rather than *decrevimus*, “we have decreed.”] that he be ordained.
>
> “But let not what you have reported to us in writing concerning Agilulfus disturb your affection. For we in no way give our consent to a man who is elected not by Catholics, and especially not by Lombards; nor, if he has been made through the usurpation of some presumption, do we receive that priest into the place or order of a priest [Note: [Col. 0851] The edition reads *hominem*, “a man,” in the accusative, for *homine*, “in a man”; it reads *factum* for *factus*, and “the place or order of a priest” for “that priest into his place or order.”], because he is plainly shown to be an unworthy vicar of Saint Ambrose if he is ordained after being elected by such men.
>
> “Nor should this matter frighten you or impose any necessity upon you, since the [resources] from which sustenance can be provided to the clergy serving Saint Ambrose are not in enemy territory but, under God’s protection, in Sicily and in other regions of the republic [Note: [Col. 0851] This rendering follows the cited edition’s *sed*, “but,” for the supplied main text’s *et*, “and,” in the corrupted coordination *nichil in hostium locis et in Sicilia*. The edition also reads *unde possunt*, “from where [provisions] can [be supplied],” and Bl. *unde etiam*, “from where also,” for the opening *inde possit*].
>
> “Therefore, so that no delay may occur in ordaining the man whom you have elected, we have sent our notary Pantaleon. With the support of the authority of our consent, he is to arrange for him to be consecrated according to custom.
>
> “We have also instructed him in the present matter concerning the little estates [Note: [Col. 0851] The transmitted *possiundiis* is corrupt. The manuscripts read approximately this way; the Paris edition supplies: “and concerning the small properties which a certain presbyter Magnus had formerly held in trust, or concerning other utilities.” The sense is that Pantaleon was instructed what care or other action he should undertake concerning the church’s possessions.] that a certain Magnus had held in trust, and concerning the care of the other interests of our church, or whatever else he ought to do [Note: [Col. 0851] A** and Bl. read “what work he ought to do”; the Paris edition: “what else he ought to do.”].
>
> “May your affection show itself devoted to him in all things, as it ought, and strive to demonstrate this devotion [Note: [Col. 0851] The edition reads “devoted”; Bl. and the Paris edition: “as is fitting.”].”

### 10. Karuli

[Note: Chapters 10–14 are also found in the “new Beroldus” of the venerable metropolitan chapter of Milan, written between 1265 and 1269 by Johannes Boffa; we have noted all its variant readings. No title is written there. In A**, B, and Bl this title appears here: “The sermon of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Milan, concerning how the Ambrosian Office was defended through blessed Eugenius by Pope Adrian and the Emperor Charles with the clearest miracles.” A* has: “Here begins [the work] of blessed T., archbishop, concerning how the mystery of Saint Ambrose, through the merits of blessed Eugenius the Confessor, with God helping, while Adrian was seated and Charles was reigning, was protected and strengthened, and endured through the greatest and most evident miracles.”]

[Note: Concerning this fabulous account, see Fumagalli, *Antichità di Milano*, III, pp. 131 ff. On Eugenius, also see Giulini, *Memorie di Milano*, I, 161; cf. IX, 7; Frisi, *Memorie di Monza*, III, 152.]

In the time of Charles I [Note: Beroldus reads “II”], when he was magnificently enjoying the imperial power at Rome, surrounded by an indescribable army of soldiers, and when Pope Adrian was seated [on the apostolic throne], a vast synod was held, with many bishops assembled from different lands. After they had dealt with many diverse matters, they indiscreetly intruded upon the mystery of God and of the blessed teacher and confessor Ambrose, remembering little or nothing of how much reverence and love blessed Gregory had once shown toward the Ambrosian Church [Note: the words “teacher and confessor” are absent in B]. Therefore, as though blinded and crazed, and without any judgment, they began somehow to discolor [Note: Beroldus reads “disfigure”] and obscure what had been renowned, firm, and sanctioned for many ages—and, I will say more, to destroy it completely.

The Emperor Charles was therefore instructed by a great many bishops to proceed throughout the Latin-speaking world and to erase everything that he found differing from the Roman [rite] in song and divine ministry [Note: Bl has *mysterio*, “mystery,” instead of *ministerio*, “ministry”], and to unite everything with the unity of the Roman mystery. Accordingly, when the emperor came to Milan, after devastating Pavia—which he hated with an unquenchable anger because of his rival, the Emperor Desiderius, whom the soldiers of Pavia had vigorously defended with arms and strategy against Charles’s imperial power—he burned all the books sealed with the Ambrosian title that he had been able to obtain by purchase, gift, or force; others he carried with him across the mountains, as though into exile. But religious men, seeing such great and important books, preserved them reverently.

God, however, who sees all things and knows everything, who foreknows how to investigate and disclose the secrets of hearts, foresaw the minds and intention of all. He knew that the Ambrosian rite had been ordained for the praise and honor of his name by the Holy Spirit dictating it to Saint Ambrose the bishop [Note: A. reads “ordering it for the praise and honor of his name”; Beroldus]. Therefore, he did not permit it to be violated or torn apart by wicked men.

### 11. The journey of blessed Eugenius to Rome

[Note: B has *proficit* for *proficiscens*. A**, B, and Bl add the heading: “How blessed Eugenius went to Rome.”]

Bishop Eugenius, of glorious memory, a transalpine, a lover and almost a father of the Ambrosian mystery, as well as its protector and the spiritual father of Charles, went to Rome on account of the council. He found that the apostolic lord Adrian—who had first given Charles rings and staffs for the investiture of bishoprics—had already held the council for three days.

Eugenius carefully investigated everything in the order in which it had occurred. He was a discerning man, provident in counsel and wisdom, calm in spirit, serene in countenance, gracious in teaching and speech, and, as his dignity required, more benevolent than all others. Whatever seemed worthy of praise to him he appropriately affirmed. At last, as though by force, he extracted from them how and in what manner the synod had conducted itself regarding the Ambrosian mystery.

When Eugenius heard this, he was exceedingly frightened and grieved. Calling himself wretched in a voice full of tears, with tears flowing from his eyes like water, he said:

### 12. The lament of blessed Eugenius over the Ambrosian mystery

[Note: The title “The lament of Saint Eugenius over the Ambrosian mystery” is added. A* has “The lament of blessed Eugenius concerning the proceedings of the synod”; the others, except Beroldus, have the following title.]

“Wretched man, what shall I do? The world and its judge have perished; the teaching of the world, obscuring all the things of this life—which are vanities—is slipping away. The glory of the whole Church, both Latin and Greek, is being clouded; what is good, just, and holy is being driven out. The pillar of the Church, the foundation of faith, the defender of justice, the lover of God’s word, is being cast down. The outstanding teacher, trained in knowledge of every art, is being torn asunder. The mystery of mysteries is perishing—the mystery concerning which our lord and most reverend Pope Gregory feared to utter anything sinister, and concerning which blessed Master and Doctor Gregory, carefully gathering so many and such great things like the brightest flowers and inserting them into the Roman mystery, joined them to it down to the present day.” [Note: In B and Bl, “the blessed master and doctor” are omitted.]

At last recovering his spirit and courage, and at the pope’s command, with the praise of a large part of the Roman nobility and the approval of the people as well, he recalled to the court of the supreme pontiff all the bishops, archbishops, abbots, and all the religious, laymen, and clerics whom he knew had been present at the council, although they had departed from Rome three days earlier.

When they had assembled, blessed Bishop Eugenius bitterly complained to them, in a kindly voice, about the Ambrosian mystery, concerning which they had dealt so disorderly [Note: Beroldus has the singular, “concerning which he had dealt disorderly”]. When they heard this, the foreign clerics, recognizing that he was a very upright man and a lover of justice, began partly to wonder greatly and partly to feel ashamed.

Why say more? The apostolic lord, all the bishops, the entire clergy, and the whole Roman people unanimously declared and acclaimed that the Ambrosian book and the book of blessed Gregory should be placed upon the altar of blessed Peter, both carefully sealed—indeed, marked most clearly with the apostolic seal [Note: Bl has “with the seal of the apostolic lord”]—by religious men. Moreover, all the doors of the church were to be sealed most openly, and, after a fast had been proclaimed, everyone, from the least to the greatest, was to fast devoutly for three days. Thus, with God favorable, whichever book they found opened and unsealed, they were to retain with the greatest devotion and without doubt; and whichever they found unmoved and sealed, they were to burn by an unmistakable dispensation.

This was done [Note: Beroldus omits this phrase]. After all the bishops [Note: Beroldus has “all the people”] and the entire Roman clergy and people had observed the fast, on the third day, a Tuesday, of that week in which the Ambrosians still devoutly sing “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” everyone gathered together for a miracle unseen and unheard of. With the apostolic lord standing by [Note: Bl has “with the apostolic lord present”], the doors of the church were opened and opened of their own accord.

When they entered, they found both books sealed and wholly untouched, just as they had left them. When everyone saw this, marveling, utterly astonished, and groaning deeply, the books broke their bindings by themselves and produced a great and terrible sound, heard by all [Note: Beroldus has “a terrible sound”; the manuscripts have “terrible”]. Opening themselves by the finger of God, both books were opened in such a way that no one could find one of their leaves more on one side than on the other [Note: Beroldus omits “by themselves”]. Immediately an immense joy seized everyone, their tears having abruptly ceased.

Meanwhile, after both books had been seen and the manner of their opening had become apparent, everyone proclaimed as though with one voice:

“Let the Gregorian and Ambrosian mysteries be praised and confirmed by the universal Church, and let both be fully observed.”

They also said:

“It is evidently the will of almighty God and of the blessed apostle Peter that these mysteries be praised and firmly observed by all the bishops of the whole world.”

Some, however, thought this declaration good, while others considered it difficult and exceedingly harsh. At last, by the pope and the other wise and discerning men, it was approved that the Ambrosian see—within which the mystery had been ordered and exalted by blessed Ambrose—should remain content with that mystery alone; and that the rest of the world, which appears to resound with the sounds of the Latin tongue, should, with all other rites omitted, diligently and carefully observe the Gregorian rite [Note: Beroldus has “which appears to harmonize with the words”].

When all these matters had been done, concluded, and settled, Eugenius, rejoicing and dancing with great joy, came to Milan as though hastening to his own children.

Only a few days earlier, the emperor, at the command of the council in which he had taken part at Rome, had desired utterly to erase the entire Ambrosian mystery from the face of the earth. After slaughtering many clerics of both the lower and higher orders, he scraped away all the Ambrosian books, whether written in the texts of the New or Old Testament or composed according to Ambrose in the musical art. Nothing remained except the missal, which a certain good and faithful priest, hidden in mountain caves, faithfully preserved for six weeks.

Later, with Bishop Eugenius present, a most faithful bishop gathered together learned men among both the priests and the clerics, who retained much by heart; with God’s help, they found the Manual [Note: Beroldus and Bl have *manuale*] as whole as it had formerly been and handed it down to posterity.

### 13. The exhortation of blessed Eugenius

[Note: A* has the title “The exhortation of Saint Eugenius.” The others, except Beroldus, have: “How blessed Eugenius gathered the dispersed clerics of Milan and restored the Office.”]

At that same time, blessed Eugenius withdrew from the city of Rome, after Charles—hostile to the Ambrosian Church—had devastated and burned many of its most revered books. He summoned the dispersed and wounded clerics. Seeing them excessively sad and miserable, and feeling profound compassion for them, he encouraged them as much as he could.

He faithfully disclosed to them everything that had occurred concerning the Ambrosian mystery at Rome before the supreme pontiff, with many bishops present, and how greatly he himself had labored, with God favoring the prayers of blessed Ambrose.

When they had heard all this, they rejoiced like a father over an only son who had died and was afterward restored to life by God’s mercy [Note: Beroldus omits this phrase], and they were glad in proportion to the sorrow with which they had been filled.

At last Eugenius, after lovingly exhorting them at length to the honor of God in the ministry of blessed Ambrose, wished to leave the city. He had remained there for nearly fifteen days. The clergy and the elders who at that time were nourished in Milan by his teaching with Ambrosian milk, although they were very few, began most faithfully to entreat and implore Eugenius to remain with them, if it pleased his dignity and goodness.

When he heard this, he who loved blessed Ambrose and his offices and songs beyond expression, answered them kindly, with a peaceful and serene countenance:

“Let your charity know, dearest brothers, that, for love and reverence of blessed Ambrose, in whose honor I have already labored to some extent, and because of your brotherhood, I desire not merely to remain with you in this church, to be with you, and to live with you, but also, if necessity or the disturbance of the times should demand it amid evils that are continually increasing, to hasten with willing spirit with you even into prison [Note: Beroldus adds “and into death”].” [Note: B omits “your charity”; A* has *crescentibus* where other manuscripts read *crebrescentibus*; Beroldus omits the words.]

Afterward, while blessed Bishop Eugenius lived for a few days, he patiently instructed everyone in life, conduct, and good examples. Finally, full of knowledge and piety, charity and chastity, and every virtue, he died and paid the debt owed to nature.

### 14. Concerning the revelation of blessed Eugenius

[Note: A* has the title “Concerning the revelation of blessed Eugenius, bishop, ‘paternus’ of King Charles” [the final word/relationship is uncertain as printed]. The others, except Beroldus, have: “How the body of blessed Eugenius was revealed by the saint himself to a woman.” Beroldus omits the title.]

After many years had passed, when the memory of Bishop blessed Eugenius—both his name and the place of his burial—had slipped from the hearts of all the inhabitants of this city, it pleased God, who reveals all hidden things to his faithful and continues to disclose his faithful servants and soldiers for the honor of his name—those who once triumphed through fasts, prayers, vigils, and the other weapons of virtue—to reveal the bishop’s name and the place of his burial through a certain matron who had been afflicted for many days by numerous illnesses and by paralysis.

Indeed, it happened by divine will that, while she was resting in her bed as usual, weak, sick, and helpless in all her limbs, her wealth greatly diminished because she had spent it on various physicians in the hope of being freed from the illness that afflicted her, she was consumed by anxious thoughts. Reflecting on how she had imprudently squandered almost all her property, she immediately fixed all her hope of recovery upon God, beyond her own will.

When, with great eagerness of mind, she had again and again begun to think about many ecclesiastical matters, concerning various and very numerous services to the honor of God, behold, suddenly, by God’s will, a man worthy of reverence appeared to her: venerable in face, clothing, and bearing, with the hair of his head already turning gray, holding a pastoral staff in his hand, clothed in episcopal garments [Note: A** reads “clothed in garments”; A* and Bl, “dressed in clothing”; B and Beroldus, “dressed in vestments”], and suffused with an immense and infused light [Note: Beroldus has “immeasurable light”].

“Greetings,” he said, “mother! Your prayers, your alms, your tears, and your patience have been presented before God and heard by him. Rise early, you and your husband, with two diggers of the earth [Note: A**, Beroldus, and Bl read “diggers”; A* and B have “diggings”], and go to Saint Eustorgius, where his body lies, not far from the fountain in which the martyrs Protasius, Gervasius, and Secundus, athletes of God [Note: A* has *adhelete*; Beroldus, *athleta*], were baptized. There, when you find a place somewhat damper, dig it up, and you will find my body. Then, once it has been raised, have it placed in the church of Saint Eustorgius.”

When the woman heard this, eager for health and anxious for the restoration of her body, and born of a noble lineage, she desired to kiss the feet of that holy man. With abundant tears flowing, she earnestly began to beg him at least to make his name known to her.

Eugenius replied to her:

“You will undoubtedly find my name and my body in a sarcophagus, if you carefully carry out everything I have said.”

Having said this and instructed her in all these matters, he departed.

The woman awakened her husband, who knew nothing at all of what she had seen and heard, and took care to recount everything to him in order, asserting that she herself had been restored to health, that she knew the place where the saint’s body lay, and that she was going to carry out everything.

At last her husband, almost incredulous but nevertheless glad because of what his wife affirmed, took some diggers at the first light of day and hastened to the place, instructed in every detail by his wife.

Meanwhile, the woman, whom her husband had left at home as weak and ill as she had formerly been—he knowing that she was wholly unable even to move herself—arrived among them at a swift run, healthy and unharmed, while the diggers themselves were hesitating about the place [Note: Beroldus omits this phrase].

They were greatly astonished. Since God had restored her former health, she herself split the earth with a digging tool, as though reproaching them, while religious men whom she had summoned stood by and diligently sang psalms. With God’s consent they reached the body.

Looking inside, they found beside the head, just as the saint had reported, a leaden plate on which his name and the time of his death had been written. They rejoiced to find not only this, but also his body and clothing exactly as they had been on the day when they were placed in the tomb.

Finally, good and religious men reverently placed him on a litter. Beside the chest of blessed Eustorgius, on the right side [Note: B has “beside the altar of Eustorgius”], he was honored with many spices, many prayers, vigils, hymns, psalms, solemn Masses, and abundant alms, and was magnificently buried in a precious marble sarcophagus.

When this had been done, the woman, who by God’s favor and through the merits and prayers of blessed Eugenius had been restored to her former health, still burning with zeal for the exaltation of so great a man, resolved to make a most fitting image in his honor.

Therefore, after consulting her husband, who objected somewhat because he knew that she had little wine or grain for such a work, she nevertheless fixed all her hope upon God, summoned the master builders and their servants, and diligently undertook the work [Note: The readings are: B, *eorum* (“their”); A* and Bl, *eorumque* (“and their”); Beroldus, *eorum quorumve* (“their, or whosever [they were]”).]

By divine goodness the work was at last completed with the greatest care. All its vessels, both those for grain and those for wine, were found just as full as they had been at the beginning of the undertaking, after the masters had been generously refreshed, together with her entire household and family, and many poor people had been provided for.

When this had been completed, the noble matron, thinking little of what she had done, began to consider deeply how the feast of blessed Eugenius might be honored forever with hymns, frequent prayers, and repeated visits by clergy and people.

Meanwhile, when her husband learned of this intention, which she had already disclosed to him, and knowing that she was deeply devoted to the service of God, he faithfully and devoutly granted her authority and permission in everything that he knew she desired.

She, having received her husband’s governing authority, summoned secular priests—namely, judges of human law—and many men of the highest nobility. She assigned and firmly established estates from which the feast of blessed Eugenius could be celebrated honorably every year with all the orders.

From these estates, down to the present day and forever, with God’s favor and with blessed Eugenius interceding for her and for all devoted to Christ, the feast is celebrated with the greatest devotion [Note: Beroldus omits “down to the present day and forever”].

### 15. (Ann. 711.) The Complaint of Blessed Benedict, Archbishop of Milan

[Note: “At Milan, in a synod, because Pope Constantine had deprived that archbishop of the consecration of the bishop of Pavia, contrary to ancient custom.” A**, B, and Bl. “The complaint of Benedict, archbishop of Milan, concerning the consecration of the bishop of Pavia, which his predecessors had performed peacefully and charitably down to his own time, while Constantine was pontiff of the Roman see. But although he ought to have treated and decided all ecclesiastical affairs with the highest dispensation, thinking that the rule of the whole world through the Lord meant nothing if the Church of Pavia lacked its consecration, he unlawfully and without cause, through the arrogance of injustice, usurped this honor for himself. And if you read, kind reader, the Roman pontifical book, you will find how the church was unlawfully deprived of what he acquired without rational cause.” A* has this note.]

[Note: Muratorius, *Anecdota*, I, p. 240, proved this speech to be fictitious. On the historical matter itself, see Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, VI, 29, and the *Life of Pope Constantine*.]

“To the supreme creator of the heavens, the maker of all the lands, the author of all nations, the creator of all creatures, the support of heaven and earth, the one memorial of angels, human beings, the catholic faith, and the apostolic see, the firm support of orphans, widows, and all churches, I return immense thanks to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit because, in his ineffable piety, he mercifully chose and compassionately ordained such a man as pontiff for the holy apostolic see.

“Therefore, let the entire choir of bishops and the college of priests diligently remember that he benevolently and mercifully provides for the human race, since in his supreme piety he has chosen to place over this holy see, and to appoint beforehand, such a discerning, illustrious, orthodox man, who does not cease to strengthen the world entrusted to him by good works and holy admonitions, and to teach those who err.”

Concerning him Truth says:

“‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers’” (Luke 22:32).

“Therefore, supported by the presence of God, of you, venerable father, and of this holy council, and strengthened by its compassion, I, Benedict, archbishop of Milan, have resolved, led by the reverence and due love owed to it, to present before you and this holy assembly the case of our church, which has flourished through God’s ordinances and through the teachings and miracles of the blessed apostle Barnabas, and now shines, adorned with the disciplines of the most glorious confessor Ambrose and resplendent in virtues. Though worn out by great age, I shall strive to disclose and lay it open with such voice as I possess.

“Therefore, since the Church of Milan, exalted by the deeds [Note: A** reads “deeds”; A*, B, and the corrected text have a form meaning “trifles”] and virtues of God and blessed Ambrose, and elevated for many preceding ages by many bishops, now complains to you humbly and devoutly because it has been unjustly stripped of the consecration of the Church of Pavia:

“Among the other suffragan churches of our church, Pavia has until now held, with the greatest strength, the privilege belonging to the first-ranking church, by the merits of blessed Syrus. But now, ambitious for the dignities of the Roman see and the honors of its ancestors, unlawfully abandoning and unjustly deserting its own proper metropolitan, it approached the Roman pontiff in order to receive the consecration secretly.

“Our church has possessed Pavia for many ages, through the long course of years, from the time of the blessed apostle Barnabas until my own presence—I who have resided in the Milanese see for forty years [Note: Bl reads “I reside.” The editor notes that Benedict was not elected until 681 and that the entire passage seems corrupt; Gregory is not found among the bishops of Pavia]—and has humbly consecrated there the bishop Gregory, and, with God’s help, has retained it charitably.

“Now, therefore, with your compassion coming to our aid and with the holy canons approving, we faithfully and devoutly beg that our church may recover what it unjustly lost.

“May your wisdom, which must be preferred to all disciplines, benefit us. For he who presides over all ought, with due fatherly care, to benefit all, to harm no one, and to envy no one; he ought not to usurp the honor or prerogative of dignity belonging to any church. As a discerning man and judge, he weighs everything in the scales of supreme justice, condemning those who inflict injuries unjustly, while mercifully and graciously defending and supporting those who suffer unlawful oppression at the hands of wicked men, by his right hand and by the ceremonies of the law.

“But the judge of iniquity, overturning all affairs for a price, obscures what belongs to the law and criminally exalts what gives temporal pleasure. From such things the lover of justice guards himself daily, with God’s right hand protecting him.

“Let us therefore learn justice, concerning which the prophet Isaiah, filled with the Holy Spirit, says:

“‘Learn justice, you who dwell upon the earth’ (Isaiah 26:9).

“Venerable father, may divine reason prevail over the authority of the Roman eminence. Hence blessed Ambrose says:

“‘It is fitting that reason should prevail over authority.’

“Judge the case of our complaint with a just judgment. Hence the Lord speaks through Zechariah, saying:

“‘Judge a just and peaceful judgment, and do not retain the malice of your brother in your hearts’ (Zechariah 8:18).

“And David says:

“‘From your presence let my judgment proceed; let my eyes see equity’ (Psalm 16:2).

“But so that I may disclose more clearly and most truthfully the truth of our church and of our complaint, kindly take note of the privileges of ten Roman pontiffs. I speak of those privileges which assert the consecration of the Church of Ticinum [Pavia] and strictly prohibit, under the sword of anathema, all bishops from violating it.

“Moreover, carefully consider how our city, from its very beginnings, was cultivated and exalted and remained under the diligent care of our ancestors through Roman emperors, consuls, and patricians who were inhabitants of that same city, when the world was governed by a single empire.
