“Yet, as I discovered in the description of its site [Note: Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, I, p. 204], the Roman kings and princes later increased and exalted it far more magnificently after expelling the peoples of the Senones, placing in it, according to ancestral custom, an outstanding imperial palace worthy of the dignity of the emperors [Note: The *Anonymous Description of Milan* omits this phrase], a theater, an *aumatium* [a possibly corrupt or uncertain term], baths, and a pleasant garden, delightful with varied flowers and diverse fragrances [Note: The words from “pleasant” through “appropriately” are absent in the Anonymous description]. They also built an arena, wondrous for its stones and workmanship, in which all the citizens of Italy could sit and from which one speaker could appropriately address the assembly.

“For this reason, and because it possessed an especially healthy climate and a place indisputably well equipped for domestic needs, it began to be visited, inhabited, and honored by those same emperors above all the cities of Italy [Note: The cited source omits the words ‘for what reason’ and has a different construction].

“From that time, venerable father, when holy Christianity appeared to the whole world, Milan immediately believed in God upon hearing the faith, with the holy apostle Barnabas sent there by the Holy Spirit and faithfully preaching the orthodox faith. From the very beginnings of our church, by God’s merciful dispensation, it held the primacy of Italy through the metropolitan see, and, by God’s gift, it will hold it forever.

“Therefore the chair of Milan, exalted and suitably elevated by that apostle, flourished appropriately through God’s right hand and through the oar of blessed Peter.

“For what we find most truthfully in our annals, in the account of his arrival and in the life of Saint Anatalon, one of the Lord’s disciples, says most faithfully and certainly:

“‘The aforesaid city, Milan, which was already then regarded as second only to the most famous Roman citadel, was indeed lofty in equal dominion and, as I have said, stretched forth the imperial insignia of the western emperors’ [Note: The *Anonymous Description* has “held” for “stretched forth”; it also has “the most famous city” rather than “the most famous citadel,” and a different reading for the final phrase].

“Thus, by God’s merciful dispensation, the holy apostle Barnabas decreed that the Milanese Church—which he knew the emperors had exalted above all the cities of Italy—should perpetually be regarded as the principal seat of ecclesiastical eminence and the metropolitan church of the other churches in that province, just as he himself had first founded it through holy preaching [Note: The cited source adds: ‘so that Milan, which he himself had founded, might be held as…’].

“Indeed, as I found in the life of Saint Anatalon, whom he had consecrated there before proceeding to Jerusalem, Saint Anatalon knew that his master had granted that city such a gift of privilege that, just as among the other cities of the Italian provinces—specifically those extending from the bosom of Italy as far as its western boundary [Note: Bethmann corrected the reading, and the same form is found in the Anonymous description; the manuscripts have a different word]—it appeared, after the Roman citadel, as the foremost in eminence beneath the imperial throne [Note: The Anonymous description has a reading referring to the structure’s lofty elevation], and as the chief in the most crowded assembly of courtiers [Note: Bl has “peoples”; A** has “little ears”; the Anonymous description has “courtiers”], so in ecclesiastical jurisdiction its prerogative excelled all others after the Roman see [Note: The Anonymous description has “appeared to hold primacy”].

“In this manner that aforesaid bishop himself, differing in nothing from his founder [Note: B has a form meaning “dissipating”], established the same metropolitan see for future ages as belonging to the faithful in Christ, so that the bishops of neighboring peoples—that is, of Venetia, Liguria, Emilia, Raetia, and Alpiscotia—whoever in future might exist within holy Mother Church throughout these aforesaid provinces, should have, after the Roman pontiff, the metropolitan bishop of the Milanese see as a certain head and distinguished honor [Note: The Anonymous source has “should have,” rather than “were obliged to have”].

“Thus the Church of Milan, supported and adorned by these and many other oars [that is, aids or supports], reached almost down to my own time, through the mercy of God and the merits of blessed Ambrose, with devotion, bearing all these honors.

“But so that you may hear the testimony of certain holy bishops of Pavia, by which the cause of our complaint is fittingly fortified and competently defended among its many grounds, listen to the testimony of Crispinus and Epiphanius.

“When Saint Crispinus saw that he was hastening toward death, as is recorded in the life of Saint Epiphanius (chapter 4) [Note: The author of the life is Ennodius; see *Acta Sanctorum*, January II, p. 364], he brought Saint Epiphanius to Milan and said to Bishop Protaxius and the clergy whom he found there:

“‘Behold, sons, my age has now completed the course of my life. [Note: Ennodius reads: “My age compels me to depart; now the earth calls back to its own right the original particle.”] I commend the city; I commend the church; I commend this man, to whose labor and grace I owe the fact that I have lived to this time, aged and weak; his bodily strength [Note: Another reading has “solidity”] and the virtue of his soul have carried my weakness without annoyance.’

“Likewise, in the same life (chapter 5):

“‘Blessed Epiphanius was led to Milan while still resisting and promising great gifts if he were released; but, so that this might happen, he refused to promise even the smallest thing. He was then consecrated by blessed Protaxius, the predecessor of Saint Ambrose and the most steadfast defender of the catholic Church, with the greatest devotion and universal solemnity’ [Note: The cited source adds “with the full solemnity of all”; the manuscripts omit this phrase].

“Moreover, venerable father, accept the most certain testimony, which the holy fathers have decreed it dangerous and criminal to doubt or resist. For in the life of Saint Ambrose (chapter 46), our patron and protector of all churches [Note: B has “protector of all”], we read:

“‘After the priest of the Church of Ticinum had been ordained, he fell ill.’

“It is therefore your concern, venerable father, as Pope Saint Fabian asserts in his decree [Note: In the letter to the eastern bishops, in the collection of Pseudo-Isidore]:

“‘You must take care that those things which have been ordained by the apostles and their successors and established by the grace of the Holy Spirit may neither be neglected through indifference nor disturbed by any presumption’ [Note: The cited vulgar collection has a different expanded reading, meaning “and established under the prompting of the Holy Spirit”].

“But just as what reason’s usefulness required ought to have been decided, so what has been decided must not be violated [Note: B has “so also what has been decided must not be violated”; A* and Bl have a different wording].

“Venerable father, I earnestly and charitably implore the reverence of your fatherhood and the charity of this holy council, entreating you on behalf of God and Saint Ambrose, that no bishop, especially the bishop of Pavia, concerning whom I complain to the mercy of this holy council, should presume, as a disturber of your brotherhood, to retain or ordain a suffragan of our church.

“If this should occur, let the ordination of the one who receives him and of the one who ordains him be forever invalid and void.

“Therefore, Saint Pope Sixtus, divinely admonished in his decree [Note: The letter of Sixtus II to the Spaniards, in the collection of Pseudo-Isidore], says with authoritative instruction:

“‘Let no bishop presume to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner without that bishop’s consent. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so too will his judgment be’ [Note: The vulgar collection has “and likewise his judgment”]. ‘For he who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him’ [Note: The vulgar collection has “in no way” rather than “not at all”].

“Venerable father, every metropolitan church and apostolic see, which surpasses all in dignity, still maintains the boundaries established and duly ordered by the holy fathers. Concerning these, Pope Callistus says in his decree [Note: Letter to the Gauls, in the same collection; the present passage is abbreviated there]:

“‘Let no one unlawfully usurp another’s boundaries, concerning which the Lord speaks, saying: “Do not cross the ancient boundaries that your fathers established”’ (Proverbs 22:28).

“Therefore, every church that desires to preserve the faith handed down by its holy ancestors and strives to honor the decrees of the saints should faithfully and charitably take precautions on behalf of our complaint, so that it may not suffer similar treatment.”

[Additional apparatus omitted above: In chapter 10, Beroldus reads *imperium*, while A** and Bl have *imperio magnifico*; Beroldus and Bl support *per affectum*, whereas the other manuscripts read *vel affectum*. B omits *doctoris et confessoris* and reads *emendati* (“corrected”) for *ementati* (“deranged”); Beroldus omits *quod* and *omnino*, reads *ut* for *et*, and has *decolorare*, while the manuscripts have *decolare*. Beroldus reads *mysterio* for *ministerio*. A has *ordinante* (“ordering”) in place of “with the Holy Spirit dictating”; Beroldus has the expanded *Ambrosio episcopo ordinante*.

In chapter 11, B omits *nec non et* (“and also”), and Beroldus reads *perplurimum* (“very exceedingly”). In chapter 12, Beroldus has *justum et sanctum* in place of the separated “just, holy,” and *infit* (“he begins”) for *inquit*; B and Bl omit *magister et doctor*, and B and Bl read *sapientum* for *sapientium*.

In chapter 13, B reads *ac* for *atque*; B omits *vestra* in “your charity”; A* reads *crescentibus* for *crebrescentibus*; Beroldus omits *crebrescentibus malis*; and the manuscripts read *exposcere animo cupienti praeparare* rather than *animo cupienti properare* (“to hasten with a willing spirit”).

In chapter 14, Beroldus and Bl read *accidit* (“it happened”) for *accedit*; B omits the conjunction in “your prayers and your alms”; B and Beroldus read *nobilisque* for *nobilique*.]

[Further chapter-15 apparatus: The Anonymous *Description of Milan* omits *annosam* (“ancient”) and reads, in the following clause, *frequentari coepit et incoli eo quod* (“it began to be frequented and inhabited because”). It reads *quoniam* for *qui* in the quotation concerning Milan, and preserves an expanded formulation after Barnabas’s decree: “besides this, that Milan, which he himself had founded, should be held …” The note on Anatalon also records *a suo magistro* (“from his master”) and the fuller phrase *tantum privilegii munus … concessum*.

Ennodius’s reading in the Crispinus passage includes *et grandaevus* (“and aged”), and has *soliditas* (“solidity”) for *felicitas* (“well-being”). In the Epiphanius passage he reads *cum omni celebritate cunctorum* (“with the entire solemnity of all”). Bl reads *contendo* for *contendendo* (“entreating/contending”).]

## 16

[Cols. 0863–0866. Title: “Here begins the account of Archbishop Walpert and King Albert” (A*); “How Archbishop Walpert deprived King Albert of his kingdom” (the remaining witnesses).]

Textual notes: “securely” (*ita*, A**; A* reads *secutus*, “following”; B omits); “Milan,” Bl.; “had flourished,” Bl.; B adds “for it” after Ambrose’s intercession; B reads “all things” for “all”; the phrase concerning devastation reads *regnum quodam negotio* (“the kingdom by some undertaking”) in Bl.; “honorably received” is the reading of A** and Bl., while A* and B have “received”; B lacks “in every matter.”
Among all the great and remarkable deeds in which the Ambrosian Church, torn apart by treacherous kings and most savagely afflicted by cruel enemies, suffered the utmost violence, I shall strive to record one especially great and worthy of praise. I have learned that it must be investigated when and how this occurred, by which king and by which archbishop, and for what reason.

Thus, in the time of King Albert, when he magnificently enjoyed the highest summit of Roman imperial power, as befitted so great a man—being born a Frank and deriving the origin of his lineage from that people—he had defeated and overcome the Gothic peoples who had gathered in the regions of Italy to ravage its boundaries, cities, and inhabitants, and had also driven far away and kept at a great distance the Hungarians, whom the Italian people, long grievously worn down by them, had come to know.

As King Albert traveled securely through the regions of Italy, surrounded by a great company of very capable soldiers, he eventually directed his journey to Milan. He knew that, for many years after the death of Breno—who had magnificently adorned Milan after constructing all the cities of Italy and had exalted it, once adorned, with many honors—the city had flourished above all the cities of Italy like a most delightful rose. It had later been exalted by all the Roman emperors, since it was beneficial to all human affairs, and especially by Hadrian, by his son Nerva, by the most honorable and distinguished King Trajan, and also by the most cruel King Maximian, who, by imperial commands, had magnificently raised palaces above its seven gates.

When he came to Milan, Albert ordered the palace of Maximian, situated within the city walls, or Trajan’s palace, located beside the baths of Saint George, to be prepared at once. He was unaware—or, as he later pretended, unaware—that since the time of blessed Ambrose no king had entered this city, because under Ambrose’s protection the city of Milan had acquired freedom, above all the cities of Italy, from the entry of an emperor.

When the citizens heard this, they became somewhat suspicious. Quietly trying to determine whether Albert had conceived this plan because of an enemy attack, civil unrest, or some other wicked intention, they were disturbed. What more need be said? With God’s consent and blessed Ambrose’s intercession, entry into the city was entirely forbidden to him.

At last, seeing the people’s resolve, and pretending to be somewhat pleased, as though he had thought little of the matter, while holding beneath his breast a wound deeper than anyone supposed, he took up residence at the Ambrosian palace, not far from the church of the same name.

At that time Walpert was archbishop and governed the Ambrosian see. He was a man of good character, though still young, and, as the times required, a military man. He served the king with great devotion, applying himself carefully to counsel and to the arms of his soldiers. The bishop was dear to the king, worthy of reverence for his counsel, and in all imperial affairs an exceptionally faithful judge. Thus, whenever he sought to pronounce judgment on any matter in the presence of many judges, all immediately obeyed him with one accord.

After several years had passed, while Walpert, proven by the king to be entirely faithful, administered all the affairs of the kingdom carefully and diligently, the palace dogs—swollen with excessive envy like frogs—secretly brought malicious accusations against Walpert before the emperor.

Accordingly, the king, having seized upon a false pretext, began to rage and roar like a lion against Walpert and the whole city, with burning eyes and threatening death through various tortures. Walpert therefore recognized that the king was deranged and insane, and that he had been stirred to irrational anger. Relying more on knowledge of the mind than on the strength of arms, and [apparently intending] to lay waste to the kingdom with immense slaughter, he pretended that he was going on some business beyond the mountains. He then set about establishing Otto the German, duke of almost the whole of Germany, in opposition to Albert. Relying on Roman support and on the votes of his bishops and the Milanese soldiers, he undertook to have Otto take control of the kingdom.

After counsel had been arranged, Otto, trusting above all peoples and treasures in Walpert and his advisers, came to Italy within a few days, accompanied by Walpert and surrounded by an indescribable multitude of soldiers.

When these events had taken place, Walpert summoned all the bishops, dukes, margraves, and every leading man of Italy. He complained of the arrogance of Albert, who had been honorably received at Milan.

Thus, scorning the arrogance of Albert and of his entire people, who ruled Italy as though it were a maidservant, Otto was elected and raised to the kingship by everyone, amid triumphs, at Milan.

Meanwhile, while Walpert was celebrating the divine mysteries and many bishops stood around him, the king placed upon the altar of blessed Ambrose all the royal insignia: the lance in which the Lord’s nail was kept, the royal sword, the battle-axe, the belt, the imperial cloak, and all the royal garments.

While all the clergy and all the Ambrosian orders completed and celebrated the mysteries of the divine solemnities, the great-hearted archbishop Walpert clothed and anointed Otto. He was dressed in all the royal garments, with the subdeacon’s maniple, and with the crown placed upon him; all the suffragans of blessed Ambrose, together with many dukes and margraves, stood present. Otto the king was praised and confirmed in every respect with the utmost propriety and splendor.

After this, the king remained at Milan for a few days. Instructed by Walpert’s counsel—for he regarded Walpert’s integrity and energy as surpassing those of all other wise men—he hastened to anticipate Albert in every matter. Accompanied by all the bishops from the cities of Italy, as well as by dukes, margraves, captains, and vassals who followed Otto out of love for Walpert, and by an innumerable and indescribable multitude of brave foot soldiers, he set out toward Rome.

Walpert went ahead of the king for three days so that he might crown him before the multitude of all the nations. With God’s help, Otto arrived.

When Albert learned of King Otto’s reputation and magnificence, and saw that he could not resist him by force of arms, and when he recognized Walpert’s virtues, he repented too late of what had brought him shame. Hated by almost everyone, by heaven and earth alike, and abandoned by all peoples—as his deserts demanded—he fled secretly and swiftly, sad, wretched, powerless, inert, and miserable, to the island called Corsica. He would never return to the kingdom, and fled like a thief and robber.

At that same time, after Otto the king had defeated and driven out Albert, while everyone rejoiced and the peoples of all nations in Rome acclaimed and praised him through the apostolic authority, he was crowned, with Walpert alone standing beside him (2 February 962).

Meanwhile, after he had acquired the rule of all the kingdoms without the slaughter of peoples and without any dangers of war, King Otto exalted Walpert. In the regions of Italy he gave him many royal towns, suitably and honorably bestowed upon him; he exalted, magnified, and honored him, and raised him above all and in all things by honoring him.

### Song on the condition of King Albert

Come, come now, Albert, beyond Decius in your arrogance;

Learn, wretched and pitiable man, what you were and what you are.

Otto the king is present, governing the scepter of our peoples,

To whom the kings of the kings of the ages owe supreme praise.

Surpassing kings in knowledge, ruling powers above the strong,

He now rightly surpasses all whom this world possesses.

Strong of hand and joyful, warlike and discerning,

With the countenance of angels, and father of orphans.

Albert, the grove befits you, while glory awaits Otto.

For the disgrace done to Walpert, the seaweed of a kingdom befits you [A* reads *algat*, an uncertain form];

Instead of a queen, now use a sea-latrine [Bl. reads *latina*, “Latin [woman/thing]”];

For our royal scepter, enjoy the ship’s beak;

Use the sea-sails, and now enjoy Salonica [one witness reads *Salonichina*],

So that you may defend this life while seeking clothes and flour.

## 17

[Cols. 0866–0868. Title: “The account of Walpert ends; that of Bishop Landulf and his father Bonizo begins” (A*); “On Landulf of Carcano, archbishop of Milan, and his father Bonizo” (the remaining witnesses).]

Textual notes: Compare Arnulf I.10; compare Andrew, chapter 16 (Herlembald was noble and, in secular affairs, as though a duke). A*—and B before correction—reads “men,” where B after correction has “all”; B reads “hiding” for “lying hidden”; its reading is “threatened” for “raged/threatened violently.” The difficult phrase concerning the enemy’s spoils is transmitted in A* and B as “in whose [spoils] those rejoicing might [fall]”; manuscript g and Bl. read “of the slain,” and the editor queries whether “of the wicked” was intended. The possessive after “Tazo’s household servant” is feminine in B.
Meanwhile, as I recalled the dignity and magnificence of the archbishops mentioned above, and, observing them, described some portion of the great things they magnificently accomplished for God and for the world, I suddenly leapt over Landulf. He, wicked like a scorpion, striking at the end with his menacing tail, dishonored beyond all measure, irrationally, and unjustly the chief men of the ecclesiastical order: namely, the archdeacon, the archpriest, and the other leading officers, as well as the chief priest of the presbyters, who is called the co-bishop, and the other archpriests of this city’s churches. These men had been raised with the greatest distinction, above all the clergy of this world, for many years. Landulf, driven by a kind of madness, dishonored them without compensation, without judgment, and without justice.

For in order to retain the archbishopric, which he himself had acquired through his father’s harsh and wicked dealings, he handed over to savage and most cruel laymen all the ecclesiastical honors and dignities that the aforementioned orders had governed and possessed for many years for the honor of the churches and of blessed Ambrose.

But before I proceed by narrating the events of this affair, I shall explain in whose king’s time it occurred, of what lineage and power Landulf was, and from which father he was descended.

Thus, in the time of the first Otto, Roman emperor, Bonizo—from whom Landulf derived the origin of his birth—held this entire city as though he were its duke, having received authority from the emperor and administering it as a fortress.

There was an immense scarcity of good soldiers and very capable citizens, for a pestilence of loathsome and unheard-of worms had almost entirely consumed the people. These worms, hiding beneath the dust, were extremely small and, like a dreadful serpent, biting them, had nearly consumed them.

For this reason, at that time a sextary of wine was sold throughout the city for one denarius, a modius of grain for four denarii, and a single cartload of wood for one denarius. Sheep, pigs, and other larger animals were sold for prices beyond what anyone now could readily believe. [A note adds: “Pigs, rams, and great oxen found no buyer; indeed, they were given away for nothing.” See Flamma, chapter 132; cf. Giulini II, 378.]

At that same time, after the death of Archbishop Gottofred (19 September 979), whose memory scarcely resounds among us, Bonizo, originally from the town of Carcano and exceedingly desirous of dignities, acquired the archbishopric of Milan for his son Landulf, at a great weight of gold and silver and against the will of all the orders of the clergy.

After Landulf had remained a few years, his father having died an evil death in his bed at the hands of a certain household servant of Tazo, he fled at speed and made his way to Emperor Otto.

When he had come into the king’s presence, he recounted all the wars that his father had waged for the honor of the royal imperial power, and how faithful a soldier of the king his father had been. He also implored Otto, with many tears and many promises, to surround Milan with arms and troops from various nations, both for his own honor and the dignity of the empire, and out of affection for Bonizo—whom Otto had loved above all others after finding him excellent in good deeds and outstanding service—and in order to restrain and humble the pride of so great a city.

King Otto II, moved like a lion, therefore came to Milan with Landulf, accompanied by an indescribable host of barbarian peoples and very capable soldiers. He surrounded the whole city with engines and various instruments of war, yet settled there without any battle.

That very night a reverent vision came to Landulf, exhausted by long labor and a hard journey. It showed him, in the sweetest words, all the torments of hell that he deserved, as well as how pleasant were the places and how eternal the rewards prepared for those who fear God and faithfully persevere in good works to the end. The vision terrified him.

Accordingly, Landulf, inwardly exasperated by divine words, was touched by fear of God and reverence for blessed Ambrose. He saw that the people, whom he had heard would soon perish, were being exposed solely for his honor; he saw that the citizens had through a kind of obstinacy become enemies to one another; and he saw that sons who had shortly before been dear to him were now wickedly gathered with swords and savagely prepared for death. He recognized and saw that the king’s anger might fall upon them, amid the rejoicing of the nations as they seized the spoils of their enemies—or perhaps of the slain [the final word is uncertain; one witness reads “of the wicked”]. He was utterly overcome with horror.

He therefore summoned some of the nobles of the city, at first without the king’s knowledge, and afterward only with the king’s most reluctant consent. Promising them all the parishes, all the dignities, and all the hospitals—which the chief ordinary officers, the chief of the decemani, the archpriests, and the treasurers of this city’s churches held—he made, under oath, a pact that was utterly detestable.

The king was by no means unaware of what had been done. Although he had threatened the citizens cruelly for many reasons, he nevertheless rejoiced exceedingly when the friendship of the city was restored.

After this deed, Landulf entered the city, while King Otto, having taken leave of everyone, withdrew into the regions of Liguria.

At that time Landulf, after stripping the churches’ clergy unjustly, raised up all the leading soldiers whose valor enabled him to hold the archbishopric, by granting them those parishes through a detestable investiture.

Moreover, from the property of the archbishopric of blessed Ambrose—which Landulf himself, unworthily, enjoyed—he granted forty thousand modii of land and its produce in fief to his relatives whom he had in the town of Carcano, so that he might enrich them beyond all their neighbors.

## 18. (998)

[Cols. 0868–0870. Title: “The account of Archbishop Landulf ends; that of Archbishop Arnulf begins” (A*); “On Archbishop Arnulf and his deeds” (the remaining witnesses).]

Textual notes: The preceding Bonizo notice is compared with Arnulf I.10. All manuscripts transmit the obscure wording *a filio conjugali*; Muratori proposed *consilio* (“by counsel”). B has “king’s” for “king”; B reads *sociaret in conjugio* (“might join [her] to him in marriage”); B omits “archbishop”; A* and B read *cicotgitronum* for *cicotergitronum*. Bl. has “very many who” for “very many, who.” The bronze-serpent episode is cited to Giulini III, 9.
Arnulf, the fifth after the great Walpert, came to govern the bishopric vigorously. After the death of Otto, whom Walpert had anointed king, he suitably served at the royal court of King Otto III, son of Otto II, according to the circumstances of the time. For the text calls Otto the son of Otto II and then gives the corrupt phrase *a filio conjugali* (“from/by a conjugal son”), adding that his wife had died without bearing him a male child; all manuscripts transmit this reading, while Muratori conjectured *consilio* (“by counsel”).

Seeing that through human frailty he could not remain chaste, and judging it a most grave crime either for a king to be befouled by adulteries or to be polluted by fornications, he at last ordered Arnulf to be summoned, so that he might consult him suitably about a wife. When Arnulf came before the emperor, the king rose from his throne and honorably received him. Having taken counsel, he formally dispatched Arnulf, laden with an immense weight of treasure and silver, to the emperor of Constantinople, that he might give him his daughter—more splendid than all virgins—in marriage.

Arnulf, abounding in every wealth, was honorably received at the court of Constantinople. Attended by a remarkable host of soldiers and clergy, he stayed some days and, after refreshing himself and all his party exhausted by the long journey and toil, had the imperial horse—which Otto, emperor of the Romans, had given him as solace for this labor—carefully equipped with a splendid cloth beneath it, golden shoes, and silver nails, its hoofs pared.

News of this promptly spread through the royal palace; the palace soldiers, hearing of this unheard-of thing, were greatly astonished as they stood before the emperor according to custom. Arnulf had done it for the honor of the Roman Empire, the eminence and magnificence of King Otto, and all Italy.

At length Arnulf the archbishop, attended by a great company of soldiers whom he had adorned with marten- or sable-skins, with various reindeer skins and ermine—garments with which the emperor had splendidly furnished him—having obtained assurance from the emperor concerning his daughter, sat alone before him on the *cicotergitronum* [reading uncertain], while many bishops and others of the highest dignity stood by, though they were not permitted to sit in the emperor’s presence. After much discussion through an interpreter, what Arnulf was within appeared outwardly.

Meanwhile the emperor asked Arnulf to go hunting with him, as though to dispel bodily heaviness. Arnulf, in a kindly voice, first reflected silently for a little upon the ecclesiastical order and upon the pursuits in which he ought to exercise himself, and finally said:

“If it please you, at the hour when I am accustomed to pursue my hunt, I shall come to you tomorrow at midday, prepared with my arms and my soldiers.”

The emperor did not understand, despite the interpreter’s stammering, what arms and soldiers Arnulf meant.

On the appointed day Arnulf came to the emperor, honored and wearing episcopal vestments and a stole, without which he was never accustomed to be abroad or in the city when affairs or disturbances arose; he brought chrism, the most honorable orders of clergy whom he had with him, and three dukes.

The emperor, seeing him, marvelled greatly to himself. Seeing so great a man religious in God’s work, wise, discerning, and kindly, he was somewhat ashamed of what he had said about hunting; praising and magnifying Arnulf in every way, and extolling him in Greek speech, he stood still.

The Greek bishops, archbishops, and priests then attending the court marvelled greatly at this deed. Not believing that such religion existed among the Latins, they repeatedly blessed blessed Ambrose, saying:

“It was fitting and proper that, just as blessed Ambrose to this day nourishes us with divine food and instructs his own children with the milk and honey of the divine word and with most holy admonitions, so Lord Arnulf, successor of so great a man and patron, should now instruct us by his examples, fashioning us [*colifizando*, an uncertain word] in this way.”

Meanwhile the emperor and Arnulf met with a few bishops and deliberated in secret. Arnulf stayed with the emperor for nearly three months and, having obtained the king’s favor, requested and was granted the bronze serpent which Moses, instructed by divine command, had raised before the children of Israel in the desert. On returning he set it up in the church of Saint Ambrose.

Of it Saint Ambrose says in the *Hexameron*: “And he himself, raised up like a serpent, devours the serpents of the Egyptians.”

At last, endowed with many great gifts of gold and gems, Arnulf, happy and joyful, had come almost to the port of Bari with the emperor’s daughter, whom he was to give in marriage to the Roman emperor. Suddenly there resounded a royal human voice announcing that Otto, emperor of the Romans, was dead (23 January 1002).

Hearing this report, Arnulf was somewhat alarmed; but, courageously exhorting everyone and looking upon them all with an episcopal voice, he said:

“O brothers, this is a phantom voice, come to frighten us: it is the voice of him who deceived the first-created humans, who long ago tempted our Redeemer twice and thrice, and of whom Truth itself said (John 8:44): ‘He is a liar from the beginning and his father’ [as transmitted; the quotation is grammatically defective in the source]. No one imbued with the Catholic faith ought to give it credence. Therefore, putting aside all evasions, let us hasten with sails lowered toward the harbor of salvation.”

After they had remained three days in the harbor, the report was found true. Thus, amid everyone’s bitter groans, great laments, and great sighs, Arnulf and the king’s daughter, with all their party, returned separately to their native homes.

## 19

[Cols. 0870–0871. Title: “On the death of Emperor Otto” (A*), with A* adding “and of Stephania.”]

Textual note: In the description of Arduin, Bl. reads *ignarus*, “ignorant,” for *gnarus*, “skilled/knowledgeable.”
King Otto III had for many years besieged in Rome the castle of Crescentius, which Crescentius had built with remarkable workmanship against his imperial authority; at last he took both the castle and Crescentius himself by stratagem, not by arms or bodily strength (29 April 998). He further ordered Crescentius, of noble birth, first to have his eyes disgracefully torn out, then all his limbs cut off, and finally to be beheaded.

Not long afterwards (1002), King Otto was tormented by a severe illness. Although every physician diligently serving his court and commands had been tried, and neither their medicines nor antidotes had benefited the king at all, he was almost deprived of all hope of recovery.

At last a chamberlain reported to him that Stephania, Crescentius’s wife, understood this disease better than anyone. When the king ordered her summoned, desiring by good deeds and promises to soothe her grief over her husband, he ordered great gifts of gold and silver to be presented to her.

Stephania cautiously inquired somewhat into his illness. Holding a hard wound within her breast, she pretended that she would employ the medicines of the most wise Galen or Hippocrates to free the king from his hateful illness.

After tending the king for twelve days with many ointments and experiments, and having power to enter and leave either alone or with a maidservant, she saw that she had now seized the time prepared for avenging her husband. Pretending to take counsel, she summoned the palace soldiers and said:

“Soldiers, if you seek the emperor’s health and see that his life is necessary to you, bring me at the greatest speed a fresh, bloody deer-hide. It is very necessary for the king’s recovery. It is worth the effort that the king be very carefully wrapped in this deer-hide after it has been anointed with many ointments.”

The soldiers, compelled by the emperor’s order and suspecting no evil, promptly carried out the command and brought the hide. Stephania then cautiously and most secretly anointed it at once with ointments infused with poison.

When all was prepared, she came to the king, pretending zealously to perform these things, and, with many soldiers standing by, stripped him completely naked and tightly wrapped him for a long time in that hide. Having done so, she enjoined silence on the king and, arranging a diet by which he was to be fed, pretended that she was going to treat a certain dearly loved duke.

And the medicine thought to preserve the king’s life was found to cause his death.

Arnulf, a man most inquisitive in every respect, carefully investigated all this in sequence and discovered that everything had happened at Rome exactly as related. Laden with movable goods of many kinds, in gold, silver, and diverse fabrics, he visited the relics of the apostles and many martyrs, with whom Rome, adorned and honored by them to this day, is frequented by many peoples. He also greeted the pope and, leaving that city, set out on the road back to Milan.

Meanwhile Arduin, a noble and lofty margrave, rich in gold but scant in learning, wise in arms and skilled in contrivance [one witness reads *ignarus*, “ignorant”], had, with the consent of few Italian magnates, risen almost furtively as king after Otto’s death.

Hearing this, Lord Arnulf delayed a few days, honored the churches of Holy Mary and Saint Ambrose with gold, silver, fabrics, and diverse gems, and appointed a meeting at Roncaglia with all the magnates of Italy. After they had variously deliberated there on the affairs of the kingdom, he rejected Arduin’s rule, which he had usurped by wicked arts, and chose Henry I the German [another manuscript reads “Conrad”], distinguished in learning, very strong in arms, abounding in troops and rich in wealth.

Henry I was summoned [the manuscript tradition also gives “Conrad, who by another name was Cyno”]. Coming to Italy and supported by Lord Arnulf’s aid, he courageously ruled and held the Roman Empire after driving out its enemies (1004).

## 20

[Cols. 0871–0872. Title: “The account of Archbishop Arnulf ends; that of Archbishop Heribert begins” (A*); “On the deeds of Lord Heribert, Archbishop of Milan, 1017” (the remaining witnesses).]

Textual notes: Bl. reads “not merely” for “not, however”; another manuscript reads “Cono” for “Henry I.” Giulini III, 160 judged both the conference and the following narrative fictitious; Rainaldus was then bishop of Pavia, and no other evidence for Eusebius exists.
Heribert, the second successor after Arnulf, came to the episcopate: strong in resources and active in a still stronger age, powerful in divine knowledge and shrewd in worldly intelligence. Concerned to restore everything ecclesiastical which the archbishopric had foolishly lost through the fault of certain persons, he sat vigorously in the seat of the Ambrosian see, radiant in episcopal vestments.

In his time (1018), a famine, not indeed terrible [another reading: “not only terrible”], held Italy for twenty years and grievously afflicted all peoples.

Blessed Heribert, however, moved inwardly by divine mercy, saw the many poor and needy, and the immeasurable multitude of orphans and widows. He ordered five masters of the baking craft to be summoned.

When they came, he expounded a few divine sayings to animate them in God’s service; having agreed their wages, he commanded them under divine obligation that, day and night, for as long as famine remained in Italy, they should put aside every other labor and diligently attend to this work, so that every morning they should deliver to his servants eight thousand loaves of mixed flour and grain (*mixturae panes et cereris*; the exact construction is uncertain).

He also summoned his household cooks and commanded them, after receiving legumes from his servants, carefully and diligently to provide each morning eight *modii* of beans for almsgiving.

Moreover, around the Kalends of every month he gave many coins and new garments with his own hands. Throughout his life this was continually fulfilled, with the utmost devotion and God’s favor, except during those years in which he was occupied by diverse affairs with the king, margraves, dukes, foreign peoples, or the populace.

Meanwhile Lord Heribert courageously recovered and restored the archbishopric, wickedly and variously torn apart by many. With all things prospering for him, he watched zealously before God in every episcopal matter, like a good shepherd restoring the sheep and bearing his flock heavily on his shoulders.

Moreover, led by his close friendship with Emperor Henry I [another manuscript: Cono], whom the king himself had exalted above all mortals in the kingdom and in counsels serving the king with royal trust, he suitably convened at Roncaglia a conference with many dukes and bishops for the stability of the kingdom.

[The conference and the following narrative appeared fictitious to Giulini III, 160. Rainaldus was then bishop of Pavia, and no other evidence mentions Eusebius.]

## 21

[Cols. 0872–0873. Title: “On the bishop of Pavia and Archbishop Heribert” (A*); “How the bishop of Pavia, rebuked by Heribert, rejected the cross which he had sent before himself” (the remaining witnesses).]

Textual notes: B reads “Roman” for “in a Roman synod”; B has “made [the daughter] a handmaid” for “bound [the church] to himself as a handmaid from a daughter.”
At that time Eusebius, bishop of Pavia, had a cross carried before him as though he were a metropolitan. He was wealthy and descended from the town of Copiosa, and, lifted up by the supreme arrogance of pride, desired to make himself equal to the dignity of the Milanese prelate. He arrived late at the assembly.

When Lord Heribert saw him approaching from a distance, he was inwardly touched with grief of heart. For a long time he sighed silently to himself; then, to the astonishment of everyone, he began to speak aloud in their midst:

“Most high and eternal God, who order all things by your wisdom; who established a law for kings and princes, so that they might be content with what belonged to their jurisdiction; and who, like the most careful physician, graciously prescribed for metropolitan archbishops and subordinate bishops that they should remain diligently content with the spiritual laws issued by the holy fathers and with their parishes: where have these men come from, who, driven by an excessive zeal for iniquity, try to obscure the beauty and honor of the holy Ambrosian metropolitan church, having forgotten the paternal law and the reverence due to their ancestors?

“For the one who once, when our holy and most reverend predecessor Benedict complained in a Roman synod about the consecration of the bishopric of Pavia, unjustly brought the matter forward—assuming the mind of a duke rather than retaining the affection of a father—illicitly and usurpatively drew him to his own residence for consecration, without the law of a shepherd: he neither loved the city of Pavia, which had one charitable obedience toward our predecessors, and whose church he gathered to himself as a daughter made into a maidservant, nor did he love the see of Saint Ambrose with the paternal affection with which the holy apostolic predecessors loved it.

“Therefore great and doubled sorrows cling to my heart, as I carefully recall the holy devotion of blessed Juventius and Crispinus, and also of the most reverend Epiphanius, which they devotedly offered in our church while supporting it as a mother. When our church, once deprived of a pastor through the savagery of emperors and tyrants, had eventually flourished, sustained by God’s help, they cherished it with kindly exhortations and consecrations. They held the primacy of this holy church and the prerogative of oversight over all our bishops.

“Above all, how great was the love and diligence shown toward our holy confessor Ambrose, who, although burdened by bodily illness, took care to ordain there, with his own hand, a priest as bishop.”

When these words were heard, the hearts of all who stood around burned more and more fiercely. They had endured many savage and bitter battles out of love for blessed Ambrose, with immense slaughter and victory granted by God.

The cross that Eusebius had presumptuously sent ahead of himself was then rejected by Eusebius himself, with the utmost humility and due devotion, before the whole multitude. It is still preserved to this day, containing a great deal of crystal, in the sacristy of Saint Mary, as a testimony for posterity.

## 22.

**[Note: [Col. 0873] Title: Concerning the exceedingly harsh Emperor Conrad and the lord Archbishop Heribert. A*: How Archbishop Heribert was captured by the emperor at Pavia. Other witnesses.]**

At that same time (1037), when Emperor Conrad had taken his seat at Pavia, surrounded by his army and resplendent with the imperial dignities, he resolved—as the rigor of his empire required—to proceed and judge according to human law all who had invaded ecclesiastical benefices, or had unjustly committed homicides, or had devastated and destroyed the estates of orphans or widows, and all who were being unjustly tormented by treacherous men for any reason.

Accordingly, observing that many people were scattered throughout the regions of Italy, offending one another inhumanly, without law or treaty and having cast off all fear, he decreed that, in order to recall them all from evil to good, those who had illicitly engaged in every kind of promiscuous activity while possessing everything without law should be strictly judged according to law. He therefore issued an edict throughout the various provinces of Italy and appointed a day for this purpose.

When this was heard, many orphans and many widows, very many dukes and many bishops, like water in a cistern, streamed to Pavia before the emperor’s presence, each complaining of his own injury. There, according to the nature of the offense, some were required, in amends for their deed, to restore a pound of the finest gold or a mark of silver; others, according to the circumstances of the case, were judged according to law **[Note: [Col. 0873] They were judged, B.]** **[Note: [Col. 0873] The words *l. q. e. a. s.* are absent in Bl.]**. Indeed, in accordance with the commands of the law, some had their hands cut off, others had their eyes completely torn out, and finally another had his life—which is more precious than gold—taken away by the royal sword, his head being severed.

Meanwhile, a certain man from beyond the mountains, in the presence of the emperor and with a great crowd standing around, lodged a complaint against Archbishop Heribert concerning the estate of Leuci. When Heribert heard this, he was disturbed by the accusation and did not prepare either to answer or to defend himself. At last, rising from his seat, he asked, in words of the following kind, that the king grant him a period of time under a truce.

At this, while many people barked against him and provoked the king to anger, they showed excessive hostility toward Heribert. Therefore, when the emperor learned of it, moved by anger and by the words of evil men, he forgot that he had made a treaty with Heribert. Filled with savage rage, he commanded the archbishop to render judgment according to law to the complainant.

When Heribert refused, the king himself rose from his royal seat and ordered that Heribert be seized. But the soldiers, knowing how great was Heribert’s dignity and magnificence, feared to lay hands on him and held back for a while. At length Heribert tried in vain, with lofty words, to recall the king to their former friendship, reminding him how he himself had aided the king in his kingdom and had served him valiantly with all his strength.

Then the court dogs and the fiercest Germans arrived—men who do not know what lies between the right hand and the left **[Note: [Col. 0873] A proverbial expression, also used by the author in III.12 and by Arnulf in III.17.]**—together with many beasts, and detained Heribert.

When this had been done, all the force of the king and of the law **[Note: [Col. 0873] Thus A*.; “yoke,” B; “yoke” or “burden,” Bl.]** was dissolved, while all the judges and dukes, as well as the bishops and marquises, were stirred by a certain anger and were shouting in protest **[Note: [Col. 0873] “Stirred,” p. B.]**.

Once he had been detained, news very quickly reached his fellow citizens, his sons, and his adopted children in God. Therefore the nobles of this city, running without delay throughout all the regions of Italy and urging many bishops, dukes, and cities to action, devised a remarkable plan.

Meanwhile all the citizens of Milan, old and young, priests, clerics, noble matrons, and religious women, casting aside all their ornaments and clothed in ashes and sackcloth, visited the bodies of the saints, entreating God with fasts and prayers, litanies, and frequent vigils. And when they prolonged their fasts almost until nightfall **[Note: [Col. 0873] Absent in B.]**, they gave to the poor, with the greatest reverence, the cooked food that they were supposed to eat. They stood there with sorrowful faces and grieving hearts, as though their children were dead and all the possessions of the inhabitants had been stripped away by the power of wicked men.

The priests and monks, however, celebrating litanies diligently every day with inward sighs and great lamentations, and supplicating the Lord, blessed Ambrose, and all the saints barefoot amid many great sacred rites, wore themselves out without ceasing **[Col. 0874D]**.

But God, who searches out all hidden things and knows all things openly before they happen, seeing all Heribert’s faithful fellow citizens, as well as the neighboring and distant peoples, obstinate even unto death in liberating and avenging Heribert, and prepared in spirit and arms for an immense slaughter of Conrad and his satellites, freed Heribert from the hands of the wicked before the appointed time for battle, without war and without the slaughter of the peoples on either side, through the counsel of the abbess of Saint Sixtus, whom Heribert himself had consecrated.

For when Heribert had been detained by Conrad, an envious and hateful man **[Note: [Col. 0875] “By the emperor,” B and Bl.]**, yet was not bound as other condemned men usually are, but was courteously guarded by the Germans, he came, by God’s dispensation and guidance, to the river called the Trebbia, not far from Piacenza. There, while the tents and the other furnishings had been set up, he remained and rested for several days.

Meanwhile, seeing and recognizing the Germans’ gluttony and their spirits given over to wine **[Note: [Col. 0873] “Wine and …” are absent in B.]**, Heribert took one of his most faithful household servants, whom he had with him, and sent him carefully instructed in everything he wished to the abbess of Saint Sixtus, whose monastery was situated within the city of Piacenza.

When the servant had recounted to the abbess in due order everything that had unjustly happened to Heribert and had disclosed to her the plan with which he had been instructed, she, being a prudent counselor, began to investigate most carefully and secretly among herself by what ingenuity or plan she might snatch Heribert away from the hands of the Germans and set him free.

Therefore, seeing that the Germans were accustomed to become excessively drunk, even after dinner, while playing with small nuts and larger walnuts in the finest wine, as was the custom of that wild people **[Note: [Col. 0875] Thus V. D. Grotefend conjectured; the manuscripts have something like *utro fere gs*; Bl. reads *mos f. g.*]**, and that they delighted in this indiscriminately and thoughtlessly, the abbess, wishing to deceive them in this way, magnificently sent Heribert twenty loads of various meats and ten wagons of different wines, together with many grains and other provisions.

Taking aside the faithful servant whom Heribert had sent to her, she instructed him quietly and wisely, with careful admonition, that on the first evening, when the provisions had been presented to Archbishop Heribert, they should do everything in their power to make the Germans, bloated from their excessive meal, completely drunk by diligently breaking for them the walnuts and small nuts in which they took pleasure, as they were accustomed to drink more abundantly; moreover, all Heribert’s household should pretend to drink and eat very much while remaining sober and free from wine. By acting in this way, they were finally to lead the Germans, carefully and cautiously, into drunkenness until the third or fourth crowing of the cocks.

“But when the drunken Germans, already stupefied by their excessive intoxication from wine, pouring wine over themselves here and there, utterly unaware of what they are doing, and at last exhausted by wine and the labor of military service, have thrown themselves down and fallen asleep in their accustomed places, then, together with all your clerics, leaving behind the packhorses and mules, quietly rouse Lord Heribert, who is resting in bed. Whether he wishes it or not, take him up, mount the horses that I have prepared outside the camp, surrounding him as you ride, and with the boat made ready conduct him with the utmost care, casting off all fear, to the landing-place of the Eridanus.”

## 23.

**[Note: [Col. 0875] Title: Concerning the liberation of Lord Heribert, Archbishop of Milan. A*: How Archbishop Heribert was freed from captivity. Other witnesses.]**

When Heribert’s household servant heard this, he pondered the matter silently in his heart and entrusted its outcome to God’s hand. As he had been instructed, he privately encouraged and carefully instructed all the other most faithful members of the household in every detail.

By God’s dispensation and with his mercy assisting, everything happened in due order, without bloodshed, just as the abbess, consecrated to God, had foretold.

Accordingly, when Heribert’s household had won the friendship of the Germans with many gifts and many promises, and on the first evening had prepared for them many and varied dishes and wines of different kinds, fragrant with the scent and powers of herbs, they delighted the Germans by their willing participation in these pleasures and offered them abundant servings of various wines among the others. The Germans became drunk beyond measure.

When, already overcome by excessive drunkenness, they continued drinking almost until midnight, each man urging his companion to drink more and more, as they jested and competed with golden and silver cups **[Note: [Col. 0875D] That is, goblets.]**, they now threatened one another with wild eyes and terrifying voices, and now, swollen with food and drunk with wine, with tearful faces and tears streaming abundantly, they did not know at all what they were doing and could no longer make their individual limbs perform their functions. They threw themselves down here and there **[Note: [Col. 0875] “From wine” is absent in B.]**.

When Heribert’s household saw all this, they rejoiced with immense joy and carried the Germans one by one, as though they were dead, placing them on richly furnished beds.

Meanwhile, when the Germans in whose custody Heribert was had fallen asleep and been thoroughly bewitched **[Note: [Col. 0875] Thus in the text; that is, “fascinated” in A and B; “stuffed” or “gorged,” Bl.]**, his most faithful servants, seeing that the time appointed for the undertaking was approaching with favorable success, and that the Germans, drenched in excessive quantities of various wine, their limbs almost dead and their minds completely dulled, were sleeping disgracefully and snoring terribly, secretly roused Heribert, anxious for the safety of their sincere and true lord. Although he resisted, they removed him from among them without shoes, with no one noticing, mounted their horses, and reached the landing-place very quickly.

They had already boarded the boat when, behold, the Germans, raging with the terrible heat of the wine, ran about with dreadful cries and discordant voices, gnashing their teeth in their own language. Like savage animals running here and there with the fiercest barking, they rushed about in immense distress, as when they suffer from their own wounds, from an arrow shot by a hunter’s skill, or from the loss of their young, whom they had already loved with paternal and maternal affection. Carrying many large torches and running about amid many kinds of fires and heaps of straw, they raised a dreadful howling as they searched for Heribert.

At last, with God’s assistance and without bloodshed, while the Germans were frustrated and laboring in vain, and while Heribert was aided by the prayers of his clerics and citizens, he returned to Milan that same day with the greatest joy, marvelous honor, and immense reverence, where the clergy and the entire people received him **[Note: [Col. 0877] “And,” B.]**.

After greeting everyone and being refreshed by the food of souls **[Note: [Col. 0877] “Refreshed,” B.]**, he gave immense thanks to God and blessed Ambrose. With all the citizens rejoicing, and assisted and liberated, as we saw, by his own almsgiving, he took his seat courageously and prospered happily.

## 24.

**[Note: [Col. 0877] Title: Concerning the siege of Milan undertaken by King Conrad together with four other kings. A*: How the city of Milan was enclosed in a siege by Emperor Conrad because of Heribert’s flight. Other witnesses.]**

When the outcome of this affair had been reported in detail to Emperor Conrad—how and in what manner it had happened—he recognized Heribert as a worthy man, endowed with the counsel of most valiant soldiers and strong infantrymen and exceedingly rich in gold and silver. Recalling inwardly all the evils he had inflicted upon him, he was touched in his human heart; his face grew pale and he stiffened.

At last, wishing to exercise cruelly the tyranny that he was nurturing in his heart, and desiring to have Heribert and the entire city placed in chains, he resolved to establish and firmly carry out a siege, granting all their sons and possessions as plunder to his soldiers.

Accordingly, summoning four kings **[Note: [Col. 0877D] Above, Lambert also attributes three kings to the counts.]**, and gathering together all the dukes, marquises, counts, and bishops whom at that time he could command either by flatteries or by threats, together with an immeasurable multitude of infantry, he came to besiege Heribert and the whole of his city, threatening to surround it with famine, iron, and unquenchable fire.

When he had reached Milan for this purpose, with the army spread and scattered around him—no one being able to draw him back from the undertaking—and had set up his camp beside the river called the Vitabilis **[Note: [Col. 0877D] La Vecchiabia; concerning it, see Giulini III, 305–311. [Col. 0878D] Fumagalli, *Vicende di Milano*, p. 297.]**, which formerly, together with the river Lambro, joined all the riches from overseas to the Po and daily presented them to us like a mother **[Note: [Col. 0877] “Which,” B.]**, he sat down, exhausted, after fixing his camp and tents not far from the city.

After refreshing his army there for several days and arranging the standards and commanders of the legions, on the third day he sent all the soldiers and the companies of infantry to fight at each gate of the city, like wild beasts, in order to demolish the city completely.

Once they had been sent out, one fought for love of the emperor, another from fear of him, another because of gifts, presents, and promises, another in hope of plunder, another attracted by the city’s wealth, from which he himself had inspired his troops, and another filled with anger and hatred toward the city, according to the demands of his people’s nature. Fighting with a dreadful sound and unheard-of shouting, they initially terrified the citizens somewhat and, rushing at close quarters, hurled spears, arrows, and other weapons appropriate to battle, wounding many of our men who were caught off guard.

But our men, as they had been instructed, with the gates, bars **[Note: [Col. 0877] Thus Bl.; the manuscripts read *sedis*.]**, outer gates, and towers strongly fortified, and with the triangular outer gate—called the *anteportale*, set before the gates and barring the enemy’s entrance—and with three hundred and ten walled towers **[Note: [Col. 0878D] Rather scarcely one hundred; see Giulini III, 301.]** densely distributed around the circuit of the city, so that all those who guarded them could converse with one another as neighbors sitting nearby **[Note: [Col. 0877] “Sitting together,” B.]**, met the enemy army courageously, first beside the triumphal arch, which Heribert had marvelously fortified with arms, defenses, and engines of war, placing a tent above it and stationing strong men upon it **[Note: [Col. 0877] “Which,” B.]**.

When they saw such a multitude of people and heard the unprecedented clamor of weapons, they overestimated them, thinking them more numerous than the grass. At the first clash of battle, while the enemy rushed hand to hand, they held out for a while, sending weapons with the greatest force.

Meanwhile, once our men had gradually recognized which of the enemy were effective in arms, in the blows of weapons, or by the skill of war, they slaughtered them everywhere like wretched animals scattered in all directions, with spears and swords, javelins and arrows, and other instruments of war.

When the enemy approached from a distance, each man, uttering discordant cries according to the provinces of the various lands from which they came, rushed at our men with the greatest force, hurling weapons. For this reason our men paused somewhat and received all kinds of missiles capable of being thrown, turning them aside from the enemy.

Thus, having skillfully intercepted the enemy’s missiles, the soldiers and infantry, firmly wielding their own weapons as they had been instructed by the masters of war, fought competitively, carefully guarding their assigned positions in the order in which they had been arranged.

No one rushed against the enemy to strike him without counsel; no one abandoned his position without a serious clash with the enemy or without wounding him; no one, even if he saw an enemy conveniently exposed, dared to spring out alone from among his comrades to strike him.

But whenever the battle grew heavier in one direction and its burden became overwhelming, not everyone, but the legion to which the man stationed on the tower gave the signal, immediately came to its aid with its standards arranged.

Therefore, when they had gathered together and were tightly massed, and the enemy had already begun to break in confidently, one wielding a sword and another holding a spear in his hand, they struck the Germans and the other enemies with savage force. Another terrified them by striking and diminishing their ranks with arrows and other engines of war; another slaughtered with iron hooks those enemies whom he could drag toward himself.

After doing these things, and slaughtering many of the enemy with the sword, the cavalry fought against cavalry and infantry against infantry for several days.

But the soldiers, by whose valor, knowledge of warfare, and bodily skill the battles were conducted, secretly sent out hundreds of the boldest and strongest soldiers to attack the enemy wherever they could: now on the left flank, now on the right, now in front, now from behind. Especially when the enemy were weary from battle, they killed very many of them in the fighting, abandoned the spoils entirely, turned their horses’ reins, and rapidly threw the king’s army into confusion on every side.

## 25.

**[Note: [Col. 0879] Title: Concerning Eriprand the Viscount and King Baiguerius. A*: How Eriprand the Viscount beheaded Baiguerius, Conrad’s nephew. Other witnesses.]**

It happened that Eriprand the Viscount **[Note: [Col. 0879D] A dignity already hereditary at that time, which passed into the name of the family, as Giulini thinks, III, 314. Eriprand’s son was Otto the Viscount; see Giulini IV, 203.]**, a knight commanding a thousand men, descended from royal stock **[Note: [Col. 0879] “From,” B.]**, a man whose intelligence and bodily strength made him superior even to the king, protected our army on every side like a giant, surrounded by many most valiant soldiers.

By chance, as often happens to soldiers in war, he encountered a certain exceedingly proud German, the emperor’s nephew, named Baiguerius and born among that people, who had approached with a few men to reconnoiter the enemy companies.

Trusting in his strength and in his great multitude, Baiguerius had sworn and declared with terrible words that he would not first taste bread or drink wine until, with that very lance of his and with his own hand, he had struck the city’s gates and their iron bars.

When Eriprand and his men saw and learned this, their spirits were stirred like lions. With burning eyes and snorting horses, which the most valiant soldiers had properly trained for battle, they charged with extended lances and produced a monstrous crash.

But when the soldiers struck one another with the utmost violence, their lances broke, and the horses and shields, resounding like thunder, produced a terrifying noise. Forgetting to strike with their swords, almost every man seized the other by the nose-guard of his helmet. Thus, as the horsemen charged together in one direction, they carried their masters along with them.

Meanwhile Eriprand, fighting for his homeland, for which he desired to die, and triumphing for himself and his people, placed his sword beneath the man’s chin and, cutting through his armor, beheaded the proud man, like another David who once courageously beheaded Uliah.

When he was dead, the city’s infantry seized his severed body and, to the emperor’s disgrace, after drawing out his entrails, sent it up onto the triumphal arch, spreading the entrails out in the open.

From it, one of our men, when the king’s innumerable army was surrounding the place, covering the earth like locusts **[Note: [Col. 0879] “Covering the earth” is absent in B.]**, flung himself down unharmed, as though flying, with shields arranged on both sides.

But King Conrad, frustrated in all his hopes, having already lost, contrary to his desire, many very valiant soldiers and innumerable infantrymen, and seeing that he had labored in vain for fifteen days, with heavy sorrow added to sorrow, was struck down by God’s anger with many hailstones from above and below. He fled toward Pavia, threatening the city bitterly **[Note: [Col. 0879] Thus B; “holding,” A*; “proceeding toward Pavia,” Bl.]**.

Struck by the terror and anger of God from above, and overcome by the swords of the Milanese **[Note: [Col. 0879] “Sought,” Bl.]**, they were shattered by the scourges of both blows and fled in such distress, although no one pursued them, that many soldiers and infantrymen were crushed beneath the feet of the horses and met death without human assistance.

Among them was Hugh, Marquis of Transpadana **[Note: [Col. 0879D] Muletti conjectures that he was the son of Anselm of Montferrat, *Saluzzo* I, p. 341.]**, who had rushed to destroy the city in Conrad’s aid with many soldiers. Falling from his horse, when no one could help him because of the excessive density of the crowd, he too was trampled beneath the horses’ hooves and given over to death.

When the king had remained at Pavia for several days, still filled with excessive anger, he came by some unknown plan to Corbetta **[Note: [Col. 0879D] Corbetta, where Wipo says this happened during the siege, lies twelve miles from Milan and five from Buffalora. [Col. 0880D] The *Annals of Hildesheim* place Conrad in the field near Milan and say that on 29 May he issued laws during the siege of Milan.]** (in the year 1037, 29 May), where he treated everything as indiscriminately his own, divine and human alike, to such an extent that he allowed his horses to fill the churches.

There, struck by divine anger, his daughter-in-law also died by lightning, while many others perished **[Note: [Col. 0880D] She died on 18 July 1038.]**.

Then, grieving and hating all the elements, he carried his daughter-in-law, embalmed with balsam **[Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in B.]**, with him to Germany. After remaining there a few days, he died, overcome by a serious illness (in the year 1039, 4 June).

## 26.

**[Note: [Col. 0879] Title: Here ends the account of Cono’s siege. The account begins of the siege undertaken by the capitanei against the people asserting the liberty of their ancient ancestors. A*: Concerning the civil discord that existed on one side between the capitanei and valvassores, and on the other between them and the people of Milan. Other witnesses.]**

Not long afterward, the citizens, having obtained victory over their enemies, became, as is the way of the human race, enemies to their enemies and most faithful friends to their friends, returning evil for evil and good for good, and became active in these matters.

Indeed, although they had peace with other men and their enemies had now everywhere disappeared, they turned their swords against one another and became enemies to themselves.

The cause of this war was that the leaders who had formerly governed and protected this city through strength of mind and bodily valor had, through a certain negligence, lost their authority. In accordance with the demands of their dignity and nobility, they had formerly lived for periods in the palaces beside the church of Saint Protasius **[Note: [Col. 0880D] It was given to monks; see Fumagalli, *Vicende di Milano*, p. 270; Giulini I, 308, concerning the duke’s estate.]**, carefully providing everything honorable for the city, diligently and wisely repairing whatever had been broken through carelessness, and immediately arranging by some means to correct whatever had been unjustly done and to make the offender give satisfaction.

They were a defense for orphans, a help to the afflicted, a support for widows, nourishment for little children; they were law for the unjust, justice for the treacherous, and a terror to robbers.

All the merchants and peasants, plowmen and ox-drivers, lived securely while attending to their own affairs and taking care of their possessions. Concerned for the honors of the churches and clergy, and with everything prospering, they lived in peace.

There was no dignity or protection from one’s ancestors that would undertake to correct anyone acting unjustly against another, or defend and free anyone resisting the commands of the leaders **[Note: [Col. 0881] The manuscripts read *quem*; Bl. has *qui*.]**.

Indeed, except during the periods when they were engaged with the utmost valor and propriety in the wars of kings or against the companies of enemies scattered far and wide, they humbly and devoutly enjoyed peace and joy.

But after the leaders, I know not for what evil reasons, gradually began to give the honor and magnificence of their dignities to newly established capitanei **[Note: [Col. 0881] Thus A*; “recently,” B.]**, they were stripped of their greatest honors, forgot the reverence owed to their ancient ancestors and their own forebears, and were deprived of all their honors.

Thus the entire people exacted from a few capitanei, who had exalted the leaders, the reverence and due service that they had been accustomed to render to the leaders. Yet, while the leaders still governed the greater affairs of the city by their authority and counsels, the capitanei selected valvassores in order to hold their new grants more securely.

Meanwhile, seeing that their evils had increased under various and different lords, and finding the rule of their fellow citizens harder than that of their former leaders, the people resolved, by testing the varying outcomes of war, to defend and free themselves from the rule of those men.

Accordingly, while Heribert still occupied the Ambrosian chair—Heribert, whom we have learned to have courageously overcome, through the strength of his mind and the valor of his soldiers, the powerful and grand actions of proud princes and of the aforementioned king—very serious wars began in the city. The people fought against the nobles to obtain the liberty that their ancestors had once lost because of the excessive scarcity of men.

Therefore, whenever in any district of the city the capitanei and valvassores overcame the people, they slaughtered them inhumanely **[Note: [Col. 0881] “Savage,” B.]**.

But the people, as is customary, angry without mercy, preferring to die rather than to live dishonorably, and judging it sweeter to behold death than to lead a long life in the deepest disgrace, wherever they defeated those men with arms and various javelins, put them to death everywhere like the most savage serpents or dragons.

At last, when the capitanei and valvassores saw that they were entirely unable to resist the people within the city, they judged that they could overcome and defeat the people through excessive siege, by famine, iron, and many necessities, and reduce them to their ancient servitude. They therefore left the city secretly and unanimously.

When this had happened, the people, seeing that their life was about to lie in their own hands, hoped for safety more through weapons **[Col. 0882A]** than through any benefits. Burning zealously day and night for the work of war and the exercise of their minds, strong in poverty, exceedingly strong in their pursuit of liberty, anxious about wealth but more devoted to freedom, they worked with care and propriety, using javelins, various engines, different fortifications, and every ingenuity by which they might free themselves from their fellow citizens, who had now become mortal enemies.

Their leader and protector was the noble and eminent capitaneus Lanzo, by whose counsel and by whose exercises of mind and body all affairs were directed.

The capitanei, however, arranging outposts around the city and surrounding it carefully day and night at a distance of one mile, treated the citizens not as citizens but as enemies.

With the assistance of the Marciani and the people of Seprio, they constructed six strongholds around the city **[Col. 0882B]**, and for three years, worn down by many battles every day, countless men fell.

During this period, whenever they could capture someone, as happens in war, they either killed him as an enemy or thrust him into a dark prison and wore him down with various punishments, extracting from him with the greatest harshness everything he possessed either personally or through his friends.

Likewise, if the people, through some outcome of battle or by some ingenuity of mind aided by bodily valor, could capture any of the nobles, they honored them with precisely the punishment, and even a somewhat more severe punishment, with which the capitanei slaughtered members of the people.

Thus encouraged by these and other actions, there was no day on which, as I have said, the capitanei or valvassores did not invade the city.

But they did not dare to approach the wall before the city gates, which defended themselves almost by nature, because they feared the ballistae and engines of various kinds and feared the citizens themselves, who were harder than the serpents of Ethiopia **[Note: [Col. 0881] “As though,” Bl.]**.

At that time, if some recruits from the people, now made exceedingly brave, hot in spirit and most inflamed by anger, who did not at all refuse either to die or to kill, happened by chance to pursue them, they either struck them very heavily as enemies or, defending themselves, withdrew into places of the greatest safety.

By now the city had almost been consumed by famine, which is harder than iron, after several periods had passed, to such an extent that it lacked bread and wine altogether, except insofar as the plowmen could reap within the city’s boundaries and the vine-growers could labor with careful cultivation. Meat and fish, however, were obtained by theft; the people were gaunt, light in battle, strong in spirit, and most ardent in war.

If you had seen it from within, with its towers and palaces abandoned and already threatening ruin, you would have called it a deserted Babylon rather than Milan, once the seat of noble kings.

Therefore, after many citizens had secretly fled, the towers and city wall, the gates and outer gate, and the other fortifications of the city, magnificently furnished with a human army, were carefully guarded day and night.

The same Lanzo, prudent in judgment, commendable for bodily strength, and most attentive to military affairs, [Col. 0883A] found himself in desperate straits, anxious about victory over the enemy. When at last he realized that no one among the citizens could come to his aid and that he could no longer resist the capitaneis and valvassors, he was prepared to die rather than criminally surrender to the enemy the city and the people—small in number, indeed, but entrusted to his faith. Relying on the aid of God and blessed Ambrose, yet instructed by the counsel of a few, he went courteously, laden with gold and silver, to the emperor Henry, who had recently risen to power, though contrary to Heribert’s will. He was accompanied by Alberius, one of the valvassors, who had always remained his companion in sufferings. [Note: [Col. 0883] Absent in B.]

When he came to the royal court with some soldiers, as a nobleman descended from a great city, and had carefully distributed many rich gifts among the palace officials, he was received with honor. Meanwhile the king asked Lanzo very little about Heribert’s successes, but inquired at length about the affairs of the city; expressing sympathy in these matters, they sat together for a while. For Heribert, because Henry traced his origin to the line of Conrad—whom I recalled above in my own accounts—and because he wholly opposed the kingdom which Henry had seized for himself against Heribert’s will, was diligently working so that Rome and Italy might have another king. Therefore, since Henry discovered that Heribert was hostile to him above all others in his claims to imperial dignity, he regarded him and all his men with suspicion. [Note: [Col. 0883] Bl. reads *assertione* (“claim/assertion”) for *assertionibus*.]

Returning to the affairs of the city, which had suffered for some time, and passing over many disturbances, I shall briefly relate Heribert’s will—how he neither stood with the people nor supported the will of the nobles. When Heribert first saw that the spirits of the capitaneis had become immoderately and irreversibly unbridled through luxury, avarice, and other evil practices, he repeatedly admonished them, as was fitting for so great a man, to remain in the laws of their fathers. Yet he could move them neither by threats nor by flatteries to take up arms against the people. Bound by the love of God and nourished with the people on the milk of blessed Ambrose, though raised by illustrious parents, he neither aided the soldiers who disturbed the city daily nor sought to harm the besieged citizens; thus he harmed neither party, nor did he take care to assist the other.

But King Henry, having learned from many reports that Italy was hostile to him because of his father’s treachery, and that all those in Italy who opposed him could not be restored to obedience through Lanzo and the citizens of Milan, said through an interpreter:
