“If Lanzo shall confirm by oath, faithfully and under the sanction of the Gospels, that he will receive within the city of Milan and admit four thousand of my knights, subject to my authority, without evil or wicked intent, and that he will aid them, as far as he can, against all the enemies of my empire until my arrival; and if he promises, with the same assurances, to secure the fidelity of all his fellow citizens toward me, I shall not fail, at the appointed time, to fulfill everything he has requested concerning these affairs, under penalty of my imperial authority. I shall faithfully hand over to his will and that of his people all the enemies of the citizens, without any excuse being admitted; whatever vengeance they wish to exercise against them shall not be refused by me. Toward those with whom they make peace I shall be wholly peaceful, and against those upon whom they wage war my sword shall crush them.”

When Lanzo heard this and understood that it exceeded what he had hoped for, being a man of great intelligence and great cunning, he eagerly and wholeheartedly hoped easily to achieve great and numerous results from these arrangements. He agreed after giving and receiving the oath and fixing the appointed times. [Note: [Col. 0883] B has “many and great” instead.] After exchanging greetings and taking leave of the king, he returned to Milan as quickly as he could.

When he approached, and the report of this affair had already reached the ears of the people, immense joy and immeasurable delight began. When Lanzo arrived in Milan, his fellow citizens received him gladly with fitting honor and boundless praise. On that same day, after he had conveyed the king’s greetings to all the people assembled and had briefly recounted much of the matter, he was received by his friends and servants in his house as though it were a royal palace.

Lanzo remained there for a few days. As a man discerning in counsel, prudent in spirit, cunning in deliberation, and most exact in his daily exercises, he turned over and weighed in his agitated mind all that he had done and how great a danger it would be for his party to oppose its adversaries. Thus, regretting somewhat what he had previously done, he secretly summoned a number of nobles and diligently laid bare, in sequence, everything he had arranged with the emperor for the protection of the people and the establishment of peace. He also showed what increase or loss they, their wives and children, and their possessions would suffer at the hands of the Germans—a people without judgment and without mercy—so that they might come as quickly as possible to unity of peace with the people, abandoning all their former disputes, on account of which they had until then been exacting their demands from the people by hostile fighting. Having interspersed his speech with harsh and bitter words, he sat down as though exhausted.

When that group of nobles had carefully investigated all these matters from Lanzo and learned how they had occurred, after their minds had long been divided among many conflicting opinions, [Col. 0884D] they finally asked Lanzo to give them the more salutary counsel. Lanzo, having foreseen every plan and determined the dangers of war, advised them to enter peacefully the city which they had attacked and to consider what belonged to peace, and to deliberate more securely about the reconstruction of their own fortunes and of all Italy. As for the murders and lost possessions that commonly arise from such negligence, he weighed everything between the two sides as though on a balance and judged that silence should be maintained.

What more need be said? After many counsels had finally been approved, they entered the city with their wives, children, and all their property, though the city gates had been opened. Their faces were cast down to the ground in deep shame, and the murders and reproaches that had shortly before passed between them and the people had been mutually forgiven.

### 27.

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading: “Concerning the heretics of Monteforte, who seduce others with heated arguments.” A*: “Concerning the heretic Girard with his companions, the heretics of Monteforte.”]

At that time, when Lord Heribert [Note: [Col. 0885] Absent in B.] had already visited nearly all the suffragan bishops of the city of blessed Ambrose—on whose account he had traveled through Italy—he arrived at Turin, surrounded by a great company of good clerics and a large number of vigorous soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0885] Heading: “Concerning the heretics of Monteforte, who seduce others with heated arguments.” A*: “Concerning the heretic Girard with his companions, the heretics of Monteforte.” The remaining witnesses: same general heading.]

After staying there for several days, he exhorted the bishop and clergy of the city, and the people of the whole city, with prophetic and apostolic admonitions, as was fitting for so great a man. He then heard of an unheard-of heresy which had recently gathered in a castle above the place called Monteforte. [Note: [Col. 0885C] Landulfus occupied the see from 1011 to 1039; Wido succeeded him.] [Note: [Col. 0885C] Compare Rodulfus Glaber, IV.2; Anselm of Liège, 62–64; Terraneo, II, chapter 18, who believes that these events occurred in 1034.]

When Heribert heard this, he immediately ordered that a man of that heresy be brought to him from the castle, so that he might learn the truth of the matter. When the man came before him, he stood ready and eager to suffer, glad if he should end his life under the most grievous torments, and prepared to answer everything with a cheerful face.

When Heribert saw him ready with such steadfastness, he began carefully and in sequence to inquire about his life, his conduct, and their faith. After permission had been given and silence ordered, Girard began:

“I give immense thanks to God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because you take such care to inquire about me. May he who knew you from the beginning in the loins of Adam grant that you may live for him and die for him, and that, reigning with him throughout the ages, you may be glorified.

“I shall tell you about my life and the faith of my brothers, however you may inquire about it. [Note: [Col. 0885] B reads *scisitatis* for *sciscitetis*, ‘you inquire.’] Above all we praise virginity. Among those who have wives, the one who is a virgin preserves virginity; but for one who has been corrupted, if our superior grants permission, it is permissible to preserve perpetual chastity. None of us uses his wife carnally; rather, he keeps her with affection as though she were a mother or sister. We never eat meat. We continually fast and pour forth prayers without ceasing. Our superiors always pray by turns, day and night, so that no hour may pass without prayer. We hold all our property in common with all people. None of us ends his life without torments, so that we may escape eternal torments. We believe and confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We believe that we are bound and loosed by those who possess the power of binding and loosing. We read daily and retain the Old and New Testaments and the holy canons.”

When Girard had said these and many other things with the sharpest intelligence, some regarded them as great and terrifying. Meanwhile, Lord Heribert, recognizing the wicked cunning and ingenuity of the man, ordered him clearly to explain what he and his companions meant by each of the words he had spoken, and especially what they believed concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; furthermore, he ordered him to explain each individual point. [Note: [Col. 0885] The word *et* (“and”) is absent in B; B reads *postea* (“afterwards”) for *praeterea* (“furthermore”).]

Upon hearing this, Girard began joyfully:

“When I said ‘Father,’ I meant the eternal God, who [the text is uncertain: ‘all things … from the beginning’] and in whom all things subsist. When I said ‘Son,’ I meant the human mind loved by God. When I said ‘Holy Spirit,’ I meant the understanding of divine knowledge, by which all things are governed in due order.”

Heribert replied:

“Friend, what do you say about Christ Jesus our Lord, who was born of the Virgin Mary, the Word of the Father?”

He answered:

“Jesus Christ whom you mention is the mind born sensibly from the Virgin Mary; that is, he was born from Holy Scripture. The Holy Spirit is the understanding of the holy Scriptures received with devotion.”

Heribert asked:

“Why do you take wives, except to beget offspring from whom the human race might be born?”

He replied:

“If the entire human race joined together without experiencing corruption, the human race would be generated without intercourse, just as bees produce their kind without sexual union.”

Heribert asked:

“Where is the absolution of our sins found—in the apostolic see, in a bishop, or in some priest?”

He answered:

“We have a pontiff—not the Roman one, but another—who daily visits our brothers scattered throughout the world. When God provides him for us, forgiveness of our sins is granted with the greatest devotion.”

Heribert asked:

“How does your life end in torments?”

He replied:

“If we perish through torments inflicted upon us by evil men, we rejoice. But if nature at some time brings us to death, our neighbor kills us by whatever means he can before we give up the soul.”

When Heribert had heard all this with attentive ears, he silently marveled, while the others nodded their heads. He then asked whether Girard believed the Catholic faith held by the Roman Church, baptism, and the true Son of God who was born from the Virgin Mary according to the flesh, and whether he believed that the body and blood which the Catholic priest, however sinful, sanctifies by the word of God were truly present.

He replied:

“There is no pontiff other than our pontiff, though he has no tonsure of the head; nor is there any sacrament.”

Upon hearing this, the truth of the matter became evident, as their reputation had indicated.

Heribert then sent a great number of soldiers to Monteforte and captured all whom he could find. Among them he captured the countess of that castle, who held these heretical opinions. [Note: [Col. 0887] Thus in B. A* and Bl., after *duxisset*, instead offer the following: “and, above all, the countess of the castle, holding these heretical opinions.”]

When he had brought them to Milan and labored for many days, through his own priests, to restore them to the Catholic faith, he was deeply distressed, fearing that the people of Italy might be contaminated by this heresy. Yet those most wicked men, ignorant of what part of the world had brought them into Italy, behaved as though they were good priests and daily, in private, sowed false rudiments drawn from the divine Scriptures among the peasants who had gathered in the city to see them.

When the leading laymen of the city discovered this, they kindled a remarkable pyre and erected the Lord’s cross on one side. Although Heribert did not wish it, when all the heretics had been brought out, this law was imposed upon them: if they wished, they could cast away all perfidy, adore the cross, and confess the faith held by the whole world, and they would be saved; otherwise they would enter alive into the blazing flames and be burned.

And so it happened that some came to the Lord’s cross, confessed it, and professed the Catholic faith, and were saved; while many, placing their hands before their faces, leapt into the flames and, dying miserably, were reduced to miserable ashes.

### 28.

[Note: [Col. 0887] Heading: “Concerning the danger of famine, which grievously invaded Italy for twenty-five years, and the alms of Lord Archbishop Heribert.” A*: “Concerning the miracle of fertility in the time of Lord Archbishop Heribert, during the famine which lasted twenty-five years.”]

At the time when these events were taking place, I shall set down in suitable writing a miracle most worthy of remembrance, which appeared in our land while Heribert was still alive and, above all, occurred by God’s power and was brought about through his mercy in the region around this city.

After twenty-five years had passed, during which the pestilence of famine, thinning nearly the whole earth, had invaded known and unknown peoples, the venerable archbishop Heribert—having learned the truth, as I said above, [Note: [Col. 0887] The words “as I said above” are absent in B.] and having been taught by divine mercy from the beginning of his office—carefully ensured that immense alms were distributed daily, so that God’s mercy might approve the completion of his course, and that this might be clearly demonstrated to all the faithful and unfaithful.

The ploughmen and ox-drivers came and, with their customary care, had worked the furrows of the earth; the little furrows opened their bosom to receive what was due from the cultivators through the seed. So that the farmers might sow the seed more abundantly and generously, as though the pleasantness of the season itself were encouraging them, they devoted great exertions and great labors to the work.

When the seeds had been sown and the clouds driven from the sky, the cultivators went around from day to day, touching the cultivated fields with their hands. Meanwhile the earth, dried so completely by the winds, neither moistened by rain from heaven nor held fast by frost poured down from above during the winter, lay dusty and barren like the land of Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0887] B has “and the earth.”]

Winter had already passed, and the cultivators of the fields, uncovering the seed with their fingers and by scattering the dust, found it sound and whole, as though they had always kept it in the safest vessels. When they saw the seeds, they were wholly stupefied and marveled beyond words.

Therefore the entire clergy and people, matrons and poor women, trusting in the mercy of God and humbly entreating God and his saints daily and without ceasing through prayers, vigils, fasts, and almsgiving, continued for many days in their weariness. Then God, who does not permit his own to be tested beyond what they can bear, graciously chose, like a most merciful father, to open and reveal the affection of his compassionate kindness. When the Lenten fast had hastened to its appointed end, and palms and olives had been distributed to the faithful, and the fonts of holy baptism had been sanctified according to the ordinance of blessed Ambrose, which he had established with the Holy Spirit administering it, God’s mercy was openly disclosed: clouds, at first sending down very fine drops gently, poured out the most abundant rain.

When this was seen and had occurred, all rejoiced with the greatest exultation, celebrating the most sacred day with supreme devotion and giving immense thanks to God. They rejoiced and exulted in their joy, and through God’s mercy they finally obtained a harvest such as had never been gathered even in a time of the greatest fertility. [Note: [Col. 0887] Bl. has “he gave.”]

### 29.

[Note: [Col. 0887] Heading in the manuscripts: “Concerning the reverence which all Italy diligently (and, A*, devoutly) paid to Lord Heribert.”]

When the Lord our King, Christ Jesus, creator of heaven and earth, who exalts all the humble and casts down all the proud, had for a long time and through many ages raised the city of Milan, city of blessed Ambrose, above all the cities of Italy by its clerics, most vigorous soldiers, many wise men, and imperial buildings, he determined, after the death of the illustrious priest and archbishop Heribert—with whom all the honors of the Ambrosian Church and its clergy departed—to restrain and suppress it, as the merits of the wicked citizens demanded.

After he had raised and exalted the Ambrosian Church above the other churches through continual and most fitting successes, and especially through the worship of God, while the abundance of religious priests and most learned ordinary clergy flourished in divine writings, at Heribert’s death he brought down almost to nothing those orders which blessed Ambrose had established and instructed for the honor of God, because of the merits of the people who then existed and those who were to come.

The Lord had exalted that city so greatly through the merits of such a man that, if a duke or marquis of all Italy acted unjustly against another, whether inferior or superior, and overcame him by excessive force, and if Heribert’s pastoral staff were sent and fixed in the place or estate from which the disagreement had arisen, the proud man did not immediately consent to the reconciliation requested by the injured party through humble prayers, nor did he dare to inflict any violence upon the other until the matter itself had been legally investigated.

### 30.

[Note: [Col. 0889] Heading: “Here begins an extract concerning the Truce of God, which appeared at Jerusalem.” A*: “Concerning a certain thing which appeared at Jerusalem.” A** and Bl.: “Concerning a certain thing.”]

In his time a holy law and a new and good commandment was given from heaven to all Christians, both faithful and unfaithful, as holy men asserted. It stated that all people might remain secure while conducting their affairs from the first hour of Thursday until the first hour of Monday, whatever their guilt might be. Whoever violated this law—namely, the Truce of God, which had recently appeared upon earth through the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ—would without doubt be condemned to exile and suffer bodily punishment for a period of time. But whoever observed it would, through God’s mercy, be released from the bonds of all sins.

### 31.

[Note: [Col. 0889] Heading in the manuscripts: “Concerning the miracle (A*, ‘wonderful miracle’) of the staffs of Saint Ambrose.”]

Although the Lord and our redeemer and savior of all, Christ Jesus, had already, through many preceding ages, adorned with estates [Note: [Col. 0889] Bl. reads *prodigiis*, “miracles,” for *praediis*, “estates.”] all the ecclesiastical institutions of blessed Ambrose—institutions which Ambrose himself had splendidly furnished for divine worship and the honor of God, in the most suitable manner for each—and had exalted them by miracles through the right hand of his majesty, as though all these things had already been consigned to oblivion, he nevertheless chose, through a supreme miracle in the glorious staffs of the chief bishop Ambrose and in the time of the blessed archbishop Heribert, to make them manifest. He also humbly chose, by an unheard-of and unseen miracle, to reveal how great the reverence and diligence owed by all the faithful, both those now living and those yet to come, were toward all the Ambrosian practices.

It happened, then, that the staffs of Saint Ambrose—which, together with the pastoral staff, he himself had been accustomed to drag penitentially in the Church of God for as long as he lived in this life—were secretly stolen by thieves. After the sacrilegious men had broken them and stripped away the gold and silver with which the staffs were encased and adorned in honor and reverence of blessed Ambrose, they secretly placed the bare wood in a most shameful privy, so that it might never again be found. But they gave the sheets of gold and silver to a master of the goldsmith’s art, valuing them for the goldsmith’s payment while pretending that they had bought them from certain Allobroges, so that they might commit their crime separately.

When the furnace had been lit [Note: [Col. 0889] The words “when the furnace had been lit” are absent in B.] and the sacrilegious men were standing by, the goldsmith took the sheets of gold in his hand and placed them upon the glowing coals. When they had been placed there and the coals had been heaped improperly upon them, immediately, as God’s command pressed upon the furnace, they leapt out of the fire.

The master and the sacrilegious men gathered them and placed them again upon the coals in the furnace. Finally, through the operation of the divine will, the fire cast out the sheets even more violently. At last the master, angered and initially entirely ignorant of why this unprecedented thing was happening—something he had never before seen—seized a hammer. In extreme anger he bound all the sheets together and cast them into the fire.

But when God wished to disclose the theft committed by the sacrilegious men through the merits of blessed Ambrose, and could no longer tolerate their perfidy, the sheets, making a great noise and leaping forth terribly, burned the master and the sacrilegious men miserably in their faces, making God’s anger utterly manifest.

All who had previously gathered to witness these events—the goldsmith’s household and his neighbors—testified that the sheets were venerable, and with loud voices denounced the sacrilegious men, gnashing their teeth. A number of the city’s nobles were then summoned, and the thieves were taken to the dark prison where the condemned were customarily confined; worn down by various punishments and bound with harsh chains, they were reduced to captivity.

Moreover, their lives were spared until morning on the condition that they either plainly confess how they had discovered and carried out the deed, or else be hanged from the highest beams and punished most severely. For it had been established that this sacrilege had been committed neither by the custodians of the treasury nor by any citizens, and it had been disclosed to no one.

What more need be said? The sacrilegious men, undoubtedly realizing that they would suddenly face death if they completely denied what God was gradually revealing to the faithful through the merits of blessed Ambrose, summoned a few priests. After receiving from them an assurance of safety, they disclosed in sequence everything they had done; they also described in the clearest words the place where they themselves had hidden the wood of the staffs. [Note: [Col. 0889] B has “the wood” instead of “the woods.”]

When the priests heard this, they were deeply shaken and almost overcome with distress. Meanwhile a certain cleric, whose spirit yearned to see the wood—not to remove it—ran at the swiftest pace to the most horrible place identified by the sacrilegious men. Looking inside, he saw the pieces of wood broken and hanging, so that they were neither soiled by the mud nor touched from any side.

When the priests had themselves found the truth of what the cleric had discovered, they summoned the entire people and immediately announced all these matters in sequence. Thus the people and all the clergy, giving immense thanks to God and blessed Ambrose and recognizing the order in which these things had occurred, rejoiced. When the staffs had been restored to their former use and encased in gold and silver, with no sign of the break made by the wicked men, they rejoiced in God.

### 32. (A.D. 1045)

After many years had passed, during which Lord Heribert had flourished most worthily in the Ambrosian see and, according to the circumstances of the time, had been vigorous as an administrator in all ecclesiastical offices, he ordered the greater part of the leading nobles and soldiers, who until then had been the protectors of the Church and clergy, to be summoned. [Note: [Col. 0889] Heading: “Concerning the death of Lord Heribert, archbishop of Milan” (B omits “of Milan”), A.D. 1045.]

Commending the benefits of the churches and the episcopate of blessed Ambrose, for which they had often fought manfully, he exhorted them magnificently and said that, if they were overcome by death while liberating the churches’ benefices from the faithless, this would be as valuable to them as the death of the saints had been.

When he saw that the course of his bodily life was hastening toward its temporal end, he distributed many estates and many castles to the primicerius, to all his priests, to the decumani, and to the other greater and lesser ordinary clergy. He also made arrangements for many monasteries, for the souls of all Christians, especially for the defenders and lovers of the Ambrosian Church, and for his own soul. He then rested for some time in illness.

Meanwhile, after summoning the priests and deacons, he received with the utmost devotion penance for all his sins, made confession before everyone, and received absolution from the priests through the laying on of hands, with the Holy Spirit cooperating. He then humbly and devoutly received the holy Eucharist.

After this, while the priests, deacons, and others present awaited the departure of his blessed soul with venerable psalms, commending it to God and the angels, he awaited temporal, not eternal, death, trusting in the aid of God and blessed Ambrose.

While these things were happening, Ubertus, who was also his chancellor, was deeply sorrowful, recalling with tearful eyes and frequent sighs all the good things that Lord Heribert had done for him. When Heribert asked him, in the voice he could manage, why he was weeping, he replied:

“O venerable father, honor of Italy, father of orphans, protection of clerics, ornament of priests, protector of widows, the poor, and merchants, until now the manly defender of the entire Ambrosian Church, both far and near, in divine and human affairs—where are you going? Father, to whom can you leave us, who will be able to equal you?”

Heribert answered these words with all the effort he could summon:

“Dearest brother, if you have ever loved me, do not grieve. For I am going securely to the feet of my father and yours, blessed Ambrose.”

The blessed Lord Heribert departed to the Lord on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, A.D. 1045, and was buried at Saint Dionysius. He had exalted and magnificently adorned that monastery and church for the honor of God and blessed Dionysius, enriching and honoring it with many estates and many distinctions. [Note: [Col. 0891] B has “for he”; another hand of the fifteenth century added in the margin: “Before Heribert’s tomb, on the face of the wall, these verses are inscribed on stone: ‘Here—indeed.’ See Arnulf II.20.”]

### 33.

After his death, when the solar year had almost administered ten months to the human race in the customary manner (September), and Lord Heribert had been carefully buried, and the golden axis of the sun had withdrawn from its customary course as summer turned and lost its heat, the law of the season had been preserved—the season in which, by the frailty of the human race, the bodies of all people, once deprived of their souls, usually decay excessively.

The monks whom he himself had ordained and consecrated there, moved by a certain anger—especially because the possessions that Lord Heribert had given to the Church of Saint Dionysius and to them were being unlawfully and unjustly seized by the faithless—uncovered Archbishop Heribert. As though they wished to complain to him, they dug away the great stone that sealed the tomb and exposed him to the gaze of the citizens. [Note: [Col. 0891] Heading: “How Heribert’s monks opened his tomb after ten months and found him so splendid that he appeared as he had been when he died, so that they thought him alive” in B; A** and Bl.: “Concerning how the monks of the saint opened the body of blessed Heribert after many days”; A*: same.]

Blessed Heribert, after so many days had passed since his death, had a bright face and eyes slightly open—the eyes that, before all the other limbs, usually decay in the bodies of the dead. His hand held the pastoral staff which he himself had raised while alive, as though his soul were still in his body. His stole and all his episcopal vestments, with which he had been clothed as befitted so great a man, shone so sound and bright as though they had remained in the safest chest.

When word of this flew through the city, all the citizens, stirred to extreme anger as though they saw themselves being struck by many lightning bolts and devastated by many hailstorms, rushed at the swiftest pace to the monastery of Saint Dionysius. Without any questioning, as a people commonly moved without mercy, they beat and tore apart with their hands all the monks whom they could find, nearly killing them.

On the following day, with extraordinary honor from clergy and people, after all that had been lost had been restored and the usurpers had renounced everything before the people, he was buried in the same place around the Kalends of October, as though he had only just departed to the Lord. His sarcophagus was bound with iron and lead on all four sides, and, with God’s aid, he will rest there in peace until the Day of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0891] In B the same fifteenth-century hand added in the margin: “This tomb of Heribert was overturned by a stroke of lightning on 23 August 1403 and opened. When the monks saw this, they transferred his relics to the high altar. Thus he lay in that tomb for 358 years. Afterwards, on the first Sunday of September 1403, Lord Matthew, primicerius and ordinary of Canchana, by order of Lord Peter, archbishop of that place, transferred his bones once more into that tomb.”]

### 34.

[Note: [Col. 0891] Heading: “Here begins concerning the orders of the holy Milanese Church, both in God and in the world, both in divine and human studies, both in the nurturing of clerics and in the support of little children and orphans, both concerning priests’ rods and rings and concerning the admonitions of all laymen.” A*: “Concerning the orders of the Milanese Church in divine and human studies, in nurturing clerics, supporting little children and orphans, and instructing priests.”]

Since all things proceed toward their destruction, and what has fallen apart does not return to its course, while the end of the world turns everything toward its setting, and since even the highest things have been denied permanence for long, with divine and supreme foreknowledge governing all heavenly and human affairs, the Ambrosian clergy, together with the Church itself—which for many ages had stood magnificently through the efforts of its clerics, whose hymns and symphonies harmonized carefully before God each day, and which had flourished far and wide among the other virtues through the courage of its soldiers and people—appears, after the departure of blessed Heribert, to have been left almost without a shepherd.

Through the merits of wicked citizens, with the most savage disagreements arising among both clergy and laity, it has been reduced almost to nothing. Indeed, it was so utterly destroyed in so short a time that, if Saint Ambrose himself were now to appear bodily, he would not acknowledge either the clergy or the city as the one in which, while he still lived, he had governed the episcopate.

[Additional apparatus: [Col. 0887] In the famine account, Bl. reads *sata* (“sown fields/crops”) for *serta*; Bl. also reads *et ut* (“and so that”). A* and Bl. read *misericordiae et pietatis affectu* (“with an affection of mercy and compassion”); A* omits *finis*, while Bl. reads *fini*. [Col. 0887–0889] In chapter 29, B omits *atque* (“and”); B reads *dum* (“while”) for *cum* (“when”), and Bl. has the corrupt reading *Qui d.*; at *vi* (“force”), A** omits *vi*, A* and B read *s. vi vir virtute*, and Bl. reads *vi aut virt.* In chapter 30, B reads *lex quidem sancta* and Bl. *quaedam lex sancta* for *lex sancta*. In chapter 31, B omits *igitur fornace jam accensa* (“therefore, once the furnace had been lit”), consistently reads *lamas* for *laminas* (“sheets/plates”), and omits *induciis usque mane* (“with their lives spared until morning”). [Col. 0891] In chapter 33, the manuscripts read *x[i]* at “the golden axis of Christ’s sun,” and B reads *recesisset* for *recessisset*. In chapter 34, B reads *iterant* (“repeat”), while A* and Bl. read *intrant* (“enter”).]

When I remember how greatly that clergy fell through its own negligence, from the greatness and honors through which the Church of blessed Ambrose had shone most brilliantly and flourished for so long, I now weep with tears, like a son mourning his mother as dead—the mother by whose aid, support, and other nourishment he had been raised. With many sobs shaking my breast, I shall tell posterity, insofar as I can, though not in every detail but in certain portions, what happened in my own time, so that they may guard themselves against such things.

### 35. [Note: [Col. 0893] Heading: “On the ordinances.”]

But [Note: [Col. 0893] B reads “And afterward.”] before I speak of the matters on which my mind is intent, I shall set forth a few ordinances that were wonderfully established and remained in good order until the death of the lord Heribert. Yet will I be able to show them to faithful posterity by recounting and writing how pre-eminent they were above all others? Certainly not. For, so that I may omit nothing, I shall strive to unfold and make clearer how the rectors and teachers of the churches—who governed both themselves and the people in love of God and neighbor—diligently devoted themselves to the divine office, and admonished and exhorted their subjects to apply themselves courteously to divine worship by day and by night. [Col. 0893C]

Thus, in the church of blessed Mary—which was, and by the Lord’s favor always will be, the second head of this archbishopric under the Lord, and which to this day is called the Winter Church—Wibertus, venerable in life and name, presided over the archdeaconry, as blessed Ambrose had ordained. [Note: [Col. 0893] The manuscripts read *archiepiscopatu* (“archbishopric”); a later hand in A, as reported by Blanco, correctly emended it to *archidiaconatui* (“archdeaconry”); see below, III, 21.] Thoroughly trained in Ambrosian chant and learning, and also endowed with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, he daily held in his own hand a staff ornamented above and below with leather, and guarded everyone with the most vigilant care. The clergy of every order, both major and minor, revered him as a father whom they owed obedience and loved him as a brother.

For every day he governed and corrected the ecclesiastical offices; and, whenever necessary, he corrected the order of the boys either himself or through learned masters. He was especially attentive to those whom he was to admit to sacred orders, whether from the city or from the parishes. Together with the primicerius, he carefully questioned each one as to whether they were adorned with chant, reading, and other good morals; whether they were free from crime; whether they were husbands of one wife, or virgins; and whether they could remain virgins or were capable of living with a wife. If someone who had no wife confessed that he could not remain a virgin, he, knowing that human and fragile nature cannot be restrained without the help of God’s mercy, immediately, in the presence of good men and according to human law, after receiving permission from the bishop, betrothed to him a wife who was nevertheless a virgin. Hence the Apostle says: “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Cor. 7:9).

Everyone, except on account of fornication, had his own wife; and once he had taken her, he was no less revered and loved than if he lived without a wife. For those who appeared to live a life in the priesthood without a wife were always suspect to married men of both orders, lest they be dishonorably ensnared by them.

The custom of the entire Church, both Latin and Greek, had for many ages been as follows: when a priest was found to be the husband of one wife, and the faithful had learned that he had governed his household and family well, he was promoted to the episcopate with the greatest devotion, many of the faithful praising him. Whoever in the clergy was found to be a concubinarius, whatever his order, was promoted no further; for they judged it a most serious sin, of which the Apostle says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her” (1 Cor. 6:16).

Those who possessed neither age nor learning nor good morals, so that they could diligently learn from their masters what was necessary, were kindly exhorted to come in due time, God willing, to receive this office, and to appear better instructed.

In the choir, the archdeacon and the archpriest—one on one side of the choir, the other on the other—religiously governed the choir itself, diligently applying themselves by day and by night so that the other orders might chant the psalms, hymns, chants, and the remaining offices of divine worship. If one of them behaved improperly by singing, reading, or standing, or by muttering and chattering with another in the choir, he either immediately corrected himself of the fault in which he had sinned, or, whether he wished it or not, was corrected by the archdeacon after his undertunic had been removed, in the sacristy, with rods. [Note: A* reads “they sinned, they were corrected”; in the passage beginning “where he corrected…” through “by the archdeacon with rods,” A* lacks the intervening words.]

For there was no man who would dare rescue him from the archdeacon’s hands, even if the person being beaten had been born of marquises, counts, or captains. Thus the ecclesiastical offices were celebrated religiously and courteously, by day and by night, in all things with fear and reverence for these men.

No one dared enter the choir without a white toga. No one dared enter the choir without his head covered by the hood of a birrus. None of them dared enter while walking improperly. No one, stammering with his tongue, intruded upon any office. No cleric wore various or mismatched garments. No one dared assume lay dress, whether in his birrus, his clothing, or his footwear.

What more need be said? They all lived in their own houses as though in another’s, attentive to the divine offices and most careful concerning the customs of the Church and their own households. They had been so nurtured in clerical dress, over the long antiquity and habitual practice of the world and through many passing generations, in face, clothing, and gait, that if you encountered anywhere in Burgundy [Note: B reads “Gorburgia”], Germany, or France someone from the entire Ambrosian choir devoted to literary studies, even if you had never seen him before, you would immediately affirm, merely from his slight familiarity with the customs of this church, that he belonged to it.

Finally, in that same church there were ten staffs, each carefully governed by its masters and each guarding its own proper order among its subjects by day and by night. Two of them remained outside the choir: one was held by the master of blessed Ambrose’s school, and the other by the viscount, a layman himself governing laymen.

There were twenty-four priests of the major order, seven deacons, and just as many subdeacons; many notaries; and eighteen readers of the church, bearing its burden and learned in chant, reading, and the psalter. [Note: According to Blanco’s testimony, A and Beroldus read “eighteen”; Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae* IV, p. 861, and the remaining witnesses read “twenty-eight.”]

Besides these orders there were twelve decani-priests, namely, men of good testimony and good reputation belonging to the decani order. They performed their office in the Winter Church; and, during the summer, did what was necessary for the people at morning-time (*manicanti*, a materially uncertain reading). [Note: B omits “which were necessary.”] [Note: The ordinary clergy, during the summer, performed their office in the church of Saint Thecla.] There were sixteen custodians, good men and courteously trained in every ecclesiastical office.

In the school of Saint Ambrose there were ten clerical men; with them were an equal number of women, already growing old, who had changed their clothing and the adornment of their heads, and who daily offered bread and wine for the whole people. All these, persevering daily in the service of God, blessed Mary, and the entire city, performed their office each day for God and for the people who desired it.

There were also two schools where the masters of chant gathered daily to teach the boys, in the atrium before the doors of that church. When necessary, the archbishop paid money, and the boys were corrected by their masters. [Note: B reads, “for money was given.”] As the prophet Ezekiel confirms when he says: “Outside the inner gate were chambers for the singers” (Ezek. 40:44).

In the inner atrium, which was beside the gate facing north, there were also two schools of philosophers skilled in various arts. There city clerics and outsiders were diligently imbued with the teachings of philosophy. So that the clerics who were devoted to their exercises might be carefully taught, the archbishops of earlier times had long established the arrangement whereby the chamberlains of the archbishop then in office annually honorably paid the masters’ stipends. The prelate himself often came there, driving from himself the worldly cares by which he was burdened, exhorting the masters and students in their studies, and finally withdrawing into the Ambrosian palaces.

There were also hospitals: some received foreign clerics; others only poor and foreign women; others little children who, weakened by extreme poverty, were sent by parents unable to nourish or care for them. They were fed like children through wages and stipends assigned to midwives.

Over all the priests dwelling in this city presided the master who was called the primicerius and co-bishop. The priests of the entire city and of all the parishes obeyed him humbly and devoutly. Although he had been born among the people, he was dear to God and to men; at the proper times, he gathered them in the place called the presbyterium and carefully expounded the commands of divine law and the Catholic faith. When the merits of his subjects required it, he also often opened up to them, as God enabled him, the love of God and charity toward one’s neighbor—without which no one will please God—and the other weapons of justice, armed with which they could stand firm and resist their adversaries.

Besides the other priestly offices to which the ten prelates mentioned above courteously devoted themselves, all the city priests, except during Lent, daily carried a staff devoutly in their hands. It was round and smooth, bore uprightness and a most becoming dignity without reproach, and was polished free of every stain. At the bottom it was surrounded by a metal band that held a sharp spike, displaying to the priests the power of governance. Thus the roundness of that staff imparted to the Ambrosian priests a rounded and joined-together charity, perfect and mutual.

For whatever is sound and round, having no fissure, is perfect. Of this divine Scripture cries out: “God does not dwell in the clefts of the mountains”; and charity, which covers a multitude of sins, is one and perfect. Of it the Apostle says: “Charity is patient, is kind; it does not seek its own; it is not jealous; it does not act wrongly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not think evil; it is not provoked; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:4–8).

Of this Gregory says: “He who gathers virtues without charity carries wind into dust, as it were.” [Note: See above, I, 3.]

The charity that God bore toward humankind, immersed in the sin of its first parent [Note: That is, *immersum*, “immersed”], lifted up on the cross God himself made man. And the charity that had lifted God upon the cross itself sowed forgiveness for the murderous Jews, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The same charity had loved Saint Stephen [Note: Or perhaps “had animated”]. Through this charity they served one another, of which the Apostle says: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Hence Truth itself says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

They carried a sharp spike on the staff so that they might diligently and devoutly prick sinners and criminals with the discipline of God’s word. Hence wise Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccles. 12:11).

The staff was straight because under the bishop they governed God’s people. It was straight because they were bound to hold to the uprightness of the Scriptures. It was straight because they held to the rule of the Catholic faith through the uprightness of good works and perseverance. It was straight because the old were supported by the support of good preaching, and the young were refreshed by correction through discipline.

The staff was straight because, cutting the earth beneath with sharp iron, it pricked and recalled to repentance hard hearts weighed down by the burden of sins. Of these goads Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply.”

That staff was straight which our priests carried in their hands in imitation of that staff of which the Lord said to his disciples: “Do not carry gold, silver, or bronze in your belt, but only a staff” (Matt. 10:9). [Note: The Vulgate reads “nor a staff.”]

The staff was straight because it bore the *timpum* [perhaps “head” or “knob”; the printed word is uncertain] of that staff which once devoured the staffs of the Egyptian magicians while Pharaoh, that most hardened king, stood by. For just as the staff of Moses, through the operation of God’s finger, annihilated the magical staffs of those magicians, so the staff of our priests abolished the idols of the pagans and immediately made them most faithful Christians by converting them to God when their ears heard. Of these David, the strong-handed one, speaking in the person of the Lord, said: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45).

Blessed and straight was the staff of our priests, the like of which is scarcely found in the world—in chant, adornment, or any other divine worship. It bore the *timpum* of that staff which once, striking the rock of Horeb for the people of Israel, supplied them with flowing waters from abundant veins.

Straight was the staff that followed the image of that one which once opened the sea three times for the Hebrew people, when, with Pharaoh and his pursuing army behind them, they had almost despaired of their salvation, Moses striking the sea three times through the working of God’s Spirit. When Pharaoh and his army had been submerged in the sea, the waters closed on both sides [Note: B reads “now” (*jam*); Blanco reads “on both sides” (*utrimque*)], and the pillar of fire went before them, opening the way of salvation. Hence the eminent prophet David rightly said: “Your rod is a straight rod, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44:7); and again: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me, O Lord” (Ps. 22:4).

If you had come upon them, especially on the feasts of the saints, at the psalmody that among the Romans is called a procession, you would have said that they were bishops rather than city priests: so splendid in their clothing, praiseworthy in propriety and devotion. The ordinary clergy who preceded the archbishop—the deacons, subdeacons, priests, and very many notaries—shone in such varied ornaments, according to the rank of each, that they appeared like choirs of angels possessing human form together with many divine powers.

All the laymen, however, having one lord, though himself a layman, revered as manifest gods the man associated with the staff and rod, and the one who governed ten priests [the printed syntax, *qui baculum ferulae uni*, is corrupt]. Of these the prophet says: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). All orders, both clerical and lay, were corrected by them when necessary.

When some business or serious trouble required it, or when the faults of the young or the old had to be cut away, all the orders, corrected devoutly through love of God with rods or sacred admonitions, consoled one another. Of these rods and staffs the prophet cries out: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me, O Lord” (Ps. 22:4).

### 36. [Note: On the ring.]

Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0897] B reads “so that” (*ut*) and lacks the remainder of the material.] all the city priests daily wore rings on their right hands, so that they might show themselves to be spouses of the Church, and, possessing knowledge of the divine Scriptures, might appear religiously before all the faithful as the seal and expression of sincere faith.

Hence blessed Ambrose, master and teacher, said in the treatise that he himself wrote on Luke (VII, 231, §232):

> “What else is a ring except the seal of sincere faith and the expression of truth? He who has the ring also has the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, which signifies God [Note: The Paris edition reads, “because God has sealed us”], whose image is Christ; and he gave the pledge of the Spirit [Note: The edition reads “the Spirit”] in our hearts, so that we may know the seal of this ring [Note: The edition reads, “of the ring”], which is given on the hand [Note: The edition reads, “which is placed on the hand”], by which the inner things of the heart and the mysteries of our works are sealed [Note: The edition reads, “the ministries of our works”]. Therefore we have been sealed, as we also read: ‘Believing in that in which you have been sealed by the Holy Spirit’” [Note: The edition reads, “He says: believing, you have been sealed…”].

The other clerical ornaments, and likewise the footwear, were clearly distinguished from all lay ornaments by unmistakable signs. Maintaining a golden mean, beloved by their neighbors and most dear to all the citizens, they prospered in every business and were obeyed in every discipline.

For the love of God and the remedies provided by their ancient parents meant that there was no one in this city who, every year, according to his means, did not receive in his house, with the greatest devotion, two priests, or four, or twelve, or more, to refresh them, mindful of the evangelical saying: “He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me” (Matt. 10:40).

And so that they might receive the prophets’ reward, they welcomed them with great humility and charity. [Note: A certain Nazarius confirms this in Andrew’s *Life of Ariald*, chapter 6, speaking of priests: “I call them into my house to bless it; according to my means I refresh them, and afterward, kissing their hands, I offer a gift.” For the rest, I wish to set beside this a very different account by Andrew of Vallombrosa concerning the morals of the priests, chapter 3: “For at that time the ecclesiastical order had been led astray into so many errors that scarcely anyone could be found who was truly in his proper place. Some, wandering here and there with dogs and hawks, devoted themselves to slippery hunting; others were tavern keepers and worthless stewards; others were impious usurers. Almost all, living shamefully with public wives or prostitutes, sought what was their own and not what belonged to Christ. For what cannot and ought not to be said or heard without groaning: all were so entangled in the simoniacal heresy that, from the least to the greatest, no order or rank could be obtained unless it was bought in the way livestock is bought. And what was worse, no one then appeared who would resist such great perversity; but although they were ravenous wolves, they were thought to be true shepherds.” —Chapter 4. “To expose and correct their perversity, Ariald was undoubtedly sent by God to Milan, where this iniquity was more abundant in proportion as the city was more populous than the others.” He then introduces him speaking as follows: “Your priests who can become richer in earthly possessions, more exalted in building towers and houses, prouder in honors, more beautiful in soft and luxurious garments—these are thought to be happier. Behold them, as you see, openly taking wives like laymen, pursuing fornication like wicked laymen; and for committing this abominable deed they are all the more powerful because they are less burdened by earthly labor.” Alexander II likewise testifies in Letter 35 that all benefices in the Church of Lucca had gone the same way. Paschal I had already reproached the Milanese with this; see Mansi XIV, p. 378.]

Thus, through these and many other alms of mercy, whatever offense clung to the laity was dissolved, while the priests filled them with good morals. Charity, which covers a multitude of sins, guarded everyone, rich in every good thing, like a mother.

Moreover, the age was peaceful, without invasions by neighboring peoples or disturbances by foreign enemies, and among men and women it was complete, sound, and joyful. Although during the few preceding periods they had devoted themselves to leisure, they did not in the least pursue lust or various desires. Such steadfastness existed in the hearts of men and women that no one knew any woman except his own wife.

And, what seems incredible, men and women were thirty years old before they gave themselves to marital affairs. Thus, if they encountered a man two or three feet tall, they judged him not a man but a monster: men and women were whole, strong, and complete.

Our age was whole and healthy, abounding in every resource; a suitable, peaceful, joyful, pleasant, charitable, and salubrious time among all the peoples whose speech resounded within our borders.

[Col. 0899] **HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK** [Note: A* adds “in prosperous circumstances.”]

**HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK.** [Note: A* adds: “In it Queen Discord, the source of every evil and the occasion of diverse iniquities, having dismissed all love and despised all fear, openly brought about discord among clerics and ecclesiastics, among laymen and laymen, among levites and levites, among old men and old men, among priests and priests, among bishops and bishops, while two pontiffs held the Roman see.” A** and B add: “In it the discord of the clerics is discussed, which arose from the preaching of Ariald and Landulf at the urging of Anselm, who later became Pope Alexander II.”]

[Col. 0899]

### 1.

Since many things try to draw the desire of my mind in different directions, and since I have been shaken by many tribulations of my mind and order—tribulations which, if it is permissible to say so, I unjustly suffered from wicked Christians—I shall continually return to those matters which I remember having marked down in my cardinal tablets for the protection of posterity, leaving aside the other causes that present themselves.

But because I know that many of the ecclesiastical order, wearied by a certain disgust with most wicked sloth, did not take pains to hand down to posterity many rudiments of the sacred Scriptures, by which they could have defended and freed themselves from pseudo-priests, these men, while through feigned chastity and fictitious fasts offering false preachings, wholly pretending to possess charity, and preaching for gifts and private riches in widows’ houses or at street corners, furnish the sharpest swords. Of them the most eminent of the prophets says:

> “That they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:2);  
> “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongues sharp swords” (Ps. 56:5).

And the Lord says:

> “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing” (Matt. 7:15).

They bind heavy and unbearable burdens, but with their finger they do not wish to move them; they bind those who should be released and release those who should be bound; and by subtle preaching they plunder widows of very great possessions. Of such blessed Ambrose says in his sermons:

> “It makes no difference to God whether someone seizes another’s property by force or by deception, so long as he possesses what belongs to another by whatever means.”

And again the prophet says:

> “Woe to you who tithe mint and cumin and dill” (Matt. 23:23), “and strike with the fist wickedly.”

These are they who, as Truth testifies, provoke the anger of God. Of them Saint Gregory says:

> “Those who provoke God’s anger are worse than those who deserve it.”

The Ambrosian city, which for many ages had been free of them, is now, through the merits of wicked citizens, besieged by them and polluted and stained, as though pearls of divine letters and of many sciences had been thrown before swine. [Col. 0900C]

For, by the Lord’s favor, the Ambrosian Church abounded in wise priests, levites, and subdeacons above the other churches of Asia. Hence the proverb arose:

> “Milan in clerics, Pavia in pleasures, Rome in buildings, Ravenna in churches.”

But it often happens that the wiser people are than many others, the less they provide for posterity by their own efforts; and thus, like unlearned and feeble men, they pass this wretched life miserably in silence. Those who could have benefited others by keeping watch, laboring, and writing, so that they might one day prepare living water for their thirsty souls, made no effort to do so. Of this water of charity and mercy the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying:

> “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

But I, although such a very little man, wearied by hardships and tribulations, trusting, as I believe, in the merits of my posterity—who, seeing these things, will recognize that I labored for the honor of their dignities—shall hasten to undertake and pursue what I began. [Note: The reading has been corrected by Blanco in this form; A* reads “to which I was hastening”; A** reads “to which he was hastening”; B likewise.]

### 2. [Note: Heading: “Recapitulation.” This heading is absent in A**; Blanco says that the following chapter is called the second, and so thereafter.]

Having defined and determined the affairs of our archbishops—which I discovered with much sweat and labor by carefully questioning all the ancients who nevertheless loved the truth, and by examining and almost scrutinizing the pages of the books of all the cities of Italy, and which, gathering much together in brief as best I could, I entered beneath my own hand—I shall now return to the sequence of the histories, which some person skilled in reading may relate as it was and as I discovered it in truth.

### 3. (2.) [Note: Heading: “On the election of Guido as archbishop.”]

A few days after the death of the illustrious Heribert had passed, the whole body of the citizens was gathered together. It is worthwhile for me to tell why the city was assembled.

For when the citizens—both clerics and laymen—had come together and offered lengthy prayers among the people, in order to take counsel concerning the obtaining and election of an archbishop, they chose four wise men of the major order, of excellent life and good reputation. Once these men had been chosen, all the orders of the city sent them with the greatest care to the emperor Henry, who had newly arisen and had newly freed that people from the hands of their great men. When they had been presented to the emperor, he was to provide prudently, after examining the counsels, so that, praising one of these four as archbishop, he might confirm him with ring and pastoral staff, and so that, once confirmed, the citizens, great and small, might hold him without doubt.

But Guido, relying on the emperor’s support—for he himself had criminally disclosed to the emperor the secret counsel of the lord Heribert—followed them with a few companions. When the elected deacons saw Guido at the royal court, they silently reflected inwardly on the agreement he had made with the emperor, each despairing of himself, and examined the implications of this event.

What more need be said? The appointed day came (18 July 1045), on which the emperor was to confirm the archbishop, praising him together with all his leading men. Thus the ordinary clergy, the captains, and the others who had gone with them at the city’s command stood before the emperor. Having set forth their business in very eloquent words, as nature gave them speech, while many bishops and leading men stood by, they relied on the dignity and counsels of their ancestors and finally sat down.

The emperor answered them, hesitating somewhat over other matters. Seeing men who were wise, discreet, gracious, and rich in learning, he appeared for a long time to examine silently among themselves the matter of Guido and of these men. At last, in his own voice, he called forward Guido, who had been standing behind all the others there. When he had been summoned, he began to question them all as to whether they wanted him as archbishop. Three times they replied:

> “We ask, we want, we desire.”

Then the emperor said:

> “If with all your heart you ask, want, and desire him, accept Guido.”

When they heard this, all the clerics and laymen, who had not at all expected to hear such a thing at first, refused with pale faces and subdued voices.

Hearing this, the emperor began to question them, saying:

> “What feast are you celebrating today?”

They answered:

> “That of Saint Maternus.”

> “Who was this Maternus?”

They answered:

> “The primicerius of our readers.”

> “Of what lineage was he?”

They answered:

> “Whatever his lineage may have been [Note: B omits this phrase], we accepted him.”

> “Then, if you accepted him whatever his lineage was, and Maternus was your archbishop, accept this Guido as a good man.”

Thus, after completing and arranging the counsels which the emperor had carefully conducted with Guido, partly in private and partly publicly, he sent him to Milan greatly honored and exalted in every respect.

When Guido came to Milan, whose fame concerning the matter had shortly before flown ahead of him through the city, he was received honorably and devoutly, in accordance with ancient custom and the urgent commands of the emperor. He governed the Ambrosian archbishopric peacefully for twenty years and, as circumstances required, strove to guard and magnify all clerical and secular offices courteously and devoutly, like his predecessor.

He was shrewd in secular conversations and secret counsels, eloquent in expressing words, but very little learned in divine matters.

Meanwhile all the ordinary clergy, whom he had been unable to calm and appease through the many benefices and honors by which he tried to relieve the pain of mind and indignation of body with which they had previously been notoriously imbued at the royal court, daily slandered him with dishonorable words, although secretly because of fear of the people, so that idleness might be vigorously exercised against him.

Their minds were so filled with anger, hatred, and detestable ambition, and they served while wasting away, that one day, when they had come with Guido in orderly procession before the altar of blessed Mary to celebrate the divine mysteries, magnificently adorned as the rank of each required, they provoked the anger of God. They ought, with the gravest tears, to have sought from God the forgiveness of their sins, for their own and their posterity’s great misfortune.

For all of them, leaving the archbishop alone, fled like demons scattering sacred incense, while the entire people watched and wondered, and they vanished amid harsh mockery and hissing. [Col. 0903A] After this, Guido, bathed in many tears, celebrated the solemn mysteries as best he could.

O most wicked zeal! O most cruel envy! O most criminal anger! Did you not know that Lucifer himself, whom God had exalted above all the angels in knowledge, splendor, and every other dignity, fell irrecoverably through excessive envy of God’s honor? At least you should have feared to reveal the intention of your minds, out of reverence for blessed Ambrose—whose chair, although unworthy, he himself governed—and out of reverence for the bishops, your orders, and the Church of the entire world.

For, because your sins demanded it, while you thought to insult him, you will be rebuked when, after no long time, you fall without mercy together with him. You struck him with words and many mockeries, and you will be struck with innumerable popular scourges. While envy consumed you, you wished to confess your sins before God; but God himself, who will not spare you, will disclose your crimes.

You left your archbishop alone at God’s altar so that you might oppress him more openly by evil arts; and God will leave you before a theater, with a cruel people standing by, badly prepared and most wretchedly treated, vainly invoking the name of the Lord.

### 4. (3.) [Note: Heading: “On the dispute between the Ambrosian and Ravennate sees.” A* reads: “On the dispute of the Ambrosian church and Ravenna in the Roman court.” B and Blanco read: “On the Ambrosian and Ravennate Church in the Roman hearing.”]

At that time (April 1050), the lord Guido was accused at Rome before the Roman pontiff Leo, while Leo himself presided over a council with many bishops, who had previously held a synod at Pavia with clemency.

Guido, magnificently honored by many wise clerics and very brave soldiers, fought against the accusations in the council with many varied arguments, as though with lead itself, and overcame all the crafty snares of his enemies by canons and other arguments. [Note: A** omits “magnificently honored by many wise clerics and very brave soldiers”; A* reads “had helped” instead of “had opposed.”]

Suddenly, however, while his own household and the archbishop of Ravenna were disputing, asserting that the Ravennate archbishop ought always to sit at the right hand of the apostolic bishop above the Milanese archbishop, a most serious conflict arose.

When it was over, by God’s favor the Ambrosian Church, through Guido, courageously defeated Ravenna in that very matter of precedence, and it will religiously retain it today and forever.

A certain soldier named Anselm, who had been severely wounded in the right hand during that struggle in defense of the honor of God and blessed Ambrose, appeared the following day completely unharmed through the merits of blessed Ambrose.

5. (4.) [Note: [Col. 0903] They add the title: “The beginning of the schism of the Milanese Church, by which the ecclesiastical order of the whole Latin world was torn apart by hypocrites and trampled by laymen, unlawfully oppressed without hope amid the most precious pearls of sacred writings.” A*. “How Anselm of Badagio, made bishop of Lucca from an ordinary cleric of the Church of Milan, urged Landulf and Ariald to preach that wives should be separated from priests.” A**. B. Bl.]

At that time (1057), Anselm [Note: [Col. 0903] B reads “Anselm of Badaglio.”] of Badagio [Note: [Col. 0903D] Baggio, near Milan to the west.], whom Guido himself had shortly before ordained to the priesthood, was seeking to usurp all the orders, both major and minor, of the priests, under a certain obedience of all the orders, although it was common to his parents and to himself; and he was dishonorably agitating the matter through many conflicts. [Note: [Col. 0903D] Arderic, abbot of Saint Victor, makes similar complaints about the violence of Anselm and his brothers in a letter [Col. 0904D] in Giulini III, 538.] Therefore, so that Guido might put an end to these two evils, he took Anselm across the mountains to the king, intending that the king himself should judge the matter prudently. At length, after many aspects of the affair had been examined, and after Guido had received sound advice that the whole city might have lasting peace, Anselm having withdrawn the dispute under oath, the emperor assigned him the bishopric of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0904D] In 1057.].

For Anselm was powerful in speech and rich in possessions; he too used to preach the holy Gospel of God elegantly to the people at the appropriate times. But when Anselm was enjoying the episcopate of Lucca, Guido chose and ordained seven deacons for the work of God’s ministry and of his preaching, all of them wise and of good reputation. When each one preached with great clarity on successive Sundays of Advent, the report of this matter flew to Anselm of Lucca. [Note: [Col. 0903] B reads “of this kind.”] Hearing it, he was extraordinarily indignant; he bristled like a lion and seethed inwardly, driven by anger and hatred, and, like a bear chewing its words in a cage, he poured forth unintelligible speech.

Accordingly, stirred by excessive passion, he came secretly with a few clerics of his city on the day [Note: [Col. 0904D] December 25.] when the saying of Saint John, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,” was being expounded to all the people and clergy. He entered the winter church and appeared face to face before the preacher himself, as though under cover.

On that day Ambrose Biffus—“Biffus” as though bifarius, “bifarius” because he delivered the Gospel’s sayings in both Greek and Latin—treated those sayings wonderfully according to the holy doctors, especially according to the teaching of blessed Ambrose. He explained the Greek in Latin, handling the matter not as a man but as though he were announcing it as an angel.

Anselm, pale in face, livid with anger, trembling at the lips, turning the matter over and over in his mind but nevertheless annihilating everything he had heard, withdrew with his clerics and returned to his ancestral home, while all the clerics of the city were entirely unaware of the matter. But the clerics who had come with him, ignorant of his intention, praising God and blessed Ambrose for what they had heard, were filled with wondrous amazement. They testified repeatedly that no human being had ever spoken so fully about the deity and humanity.

At these words Anselm, carrying a great beam beneath his breast, like a lion stirred by excessive anger, stammering, as nature allowed him [Note: [Col. 0905] B reads “and”], said:

“Certainly, unless all the priests and Levites of this city had wives, they would be quite capable in preaching and in other good conduct.” [Note: [Col. 0905D] After becoming pope and bishop, Anselm wrote to the Milanese in Letter 1: “We hope ... that during the time of our ministry the holy chastity of the clergy will be exalted and the luxury of the incontinent, together with the other heresies, will be confounded.”]

When his clerics resisted him with many arguments and many examples—especially by announcing to him what he himself had been or might become, so that he might recognize it by observation—he, exhausted by anger and other evil practices, lay on his bed fasting until evening and not sleeping at all, and then rested.

At that time a certain cleric named Landulf, descended from a noble family, attended the choir of the glorious virgin Mary courteously day and night [Note: [Col. 0905] A** reads “thus”; A* and B, “of these”] [Col. 0905B] and served as one of the notaries. Pierced by the sword of ambition, especially with regard to the archbishopric, toward which he openly panted every day like a dog, he continually agitated all the orders. Since all the greater and lesser clerics gave him no support, although his soul desired it with panting longing, he daily persecuted them as suspects and enemies [Note: [Col. 0905] A* adds “and pierced”], with the most shameful words and actions. Thus, pouring forth now sweet and now bitter water through his most disgraceful speech, secretly and openly slandering everyone, he had hardened their hearts like a diamond.

Moreover, he associated with himself another foreign cleric, a mere deacon, named Ariald, whom Guido himself had ordained, born at Cuzago near Cantù [Note: [Col. 0906D] Now Cantu.], a master of the liberal arts [Note: [Col. 0906D] Andreas I, 6, discusses his studies.], so that he might exercise more and more the desire of his own mind, which was indiscreetly inflamed against all the orders. This Ariald, burdened by the zeal of a certain pride, had shortly before been accused and convicted before Guido, in the presence of many priests, of a certain most abominable crime. Moreover, partly because the city priests did not at all allow foreign clerics wearing the toga to enter the city, nor permitted them to possess civic churches except through the tonsure [Note: [Col. 0906D] Giulini IV, 15, translates this as “not of simple clerical status.”], he was everywhere seeking an opportunity to remove all priests from their wives by agitating the people toward virtue. Returning evil for good [Note: [Col. 0905] A** and A* read “returning”; the latter also has “which were being done.”], he was driven not by the divine Spirit but by the human spirit.

Therefore, when Anselm had sufficiently observed and recognized by certain experiments the minds and intentions of these men, he ordered them to be summoned secretly to him in the silence of a stormy night. When they had been called, he welcomed them somewhat, and first exposed the pride and evil deeds of certain clerics—things he could remember about himself—in order to inflame them, so that, once inflamed, they might burn. Then, inserting many speeches, he encouraged them to separate all priests from their wives, with the greatest disgrace, by his commands and counsels [Note: [Col. 0905] B reads “might be separated.”].

When Ariald and Landulf heard this, they rejoiced and examined the counsel. It had not been wholly given by God, but had flowed from the fountain of malignant iniquities; it was laden not with the love of God but with envy and hatred; it was supported not by mercy but by anger, ambition, and detestable madness—as later became apparent and was openly seen. Bound by oath, they mutually confirmed that from that day forward they would not permit any priests or Levites to have wives, and that they would diligently and openly, fearing neither life nor death, disclose to the people and to all the citizens how dangerous and wicked were all the acts of the priests that they had carried out up to that time.

After the counsel had been formed, Anselm promised them under oath every support by which he could help and sustain them. When morning came, without greeting the archbishop whom Guido himself had ordained to the priesthood, he secretly withdrew from the city like a serpent.

Once these counsels had thus been joined and confirmed, Landulf, remaining in the city, bound all the scholars he could find by the oath he himself had sworn, misleading them now privately and now publicly. Ariald, for his part, binding the scholars whom he governed by the same oath, remained at Varese [Note: [Col. 0906D] Varese, west of Como.].

None of these things escaped Archbishop Guido. With a calm expression, he smiled daily at their most insane intrigues and regarded them as insignificant. O God, who sees all hidden things of the heart, who examines everything with a just balance, who holds and measures heaven and earth with closed hand, and by your word orders the sea and the abyss, whom all creatures obediently obey: what beginning did these men have in such good matters, and what intention? [Note: [Col. 0905] Thus B; A* and A** read “these men [had] life.”] For if they had begun this purpose of God with a good intention and good will, he who is the helper of the work would also be the protector of the labor, since God does not desire forced service, as the Apostle testifies. [Note: [Col. 0905] Thus corrected; the manuscripts read “by the people.”]

Why, then, having forgotten the Gospel of God, did they practice a detestable conspiracy with terrifying oaths among the people under the pretext of God’s purpose—a conspiracy later called the *pataria*? Had God, because of their merits, erased from their hearts the evangelical command that cries out to this day:

“He who does not swear does not perjure himself; do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by the hair of your head, because you cannot make one thing white or black” (Matthew 5:34). [Note: [Col. 0905] A** reads “do not swear.”]

Or had you forgotten the teaching of the doctor who says:

“He who does not speak does not lie; but you will have to give an account for every idle word” (Matthew 12:36)? [Note: [Col. 0907] The continuation, “If this is so ...,” through “you will have to give an account,” is absent from B and from A* and A**.]

If this is so, for how many evil oaths and evil words will you have to give an account!

If you acted from some hatred, you labor in vain. Of this the Lord says through the Gospel:

“You have a beam in your eye, and you wish to cast the speck from your brother’s eye? Hypocrite, cast the beam from your own eye first, and then you will see to cast the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:4).

If anger made you active, see what our lord, pastor, and teacher, Saint Ambrose, says in his book *On Joseph* (chapter 13):

“Anger often brings even the innocent into accusation, because when we become excessively angry with the just and wish to restrain another’s sin, we commit more serious sins.”

Therefore the Apostle says:

“Do not judge yourselves, beloved, but give place to anger” (Romans 12:19),

and the Lord through the Gospel:

“He who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22).

Hence the Apostle says:

“For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:20).

6. (5.) Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0907] Title: “Here begins the account of Ariald and Landulf.” A*: “How Ariald began to disclose his purpose through preaching.” A** and B.] while Ariald was staying at Varese, one day, wishing to sow grain from what was incorruptible and almost frantic, grain which he had cleaned by winnowing it badly, he climbed the church steps and earnestly set about defaming the priests in every respect, so that they might be wrongly separated from their wives, stirring up the common people with the most disgraceful rustic language. [Note: [Col. 0907D] Syrus the priest, in Puricellus, p. 120, testifies that this was where he began preaching. They replied to him: “You speak these things to us because you know us to be unlearned; but if you wish to be considered a credible teacher, go and say these things in the city, without fear.”]

When the rustics and priests heard these things with astonished ears, not believing them at first, they were stunned and amazed beyond measure at what Ariald was saying. They particularly affirmed that no one can possess chastity unless it has been given to him by God, as the Apostle says:

“For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father” (James 1:17).

Thus the whole assembly gathered and clerics and laypeople unanimously hastened to Archbishop Guido to report in order everything that Ariald had recently disseminated.

Therefore Guido summoned Ariald and Landulf, lest they should criminally disturb the ancient practice and good customs of both the Ambrosian Church and the whole Latin-speaking world, and of the whole Latin and Greek world, by agitating the indiscriminate crowd. As far as he could, he privately and carefully corrected and admonished them. He also made clear and explained in detail that many other evils, many dissensions, and various crimes could arise from these things. Among other words, he kindly set forth certain words of evangelical teaching:

7. (6.) “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matthew 7:6).
