[Note: [Col. 0907] Title: “Exhortation of Archbishop Guido against Ariald and Landulf, that they should cease from vain disputes and dissensions by which they were agitating the people against all priests and all orders, and that they should be calmed and removed by many examples of the holy Fathers.” A*: “How Archbishop Guido summoned Ariald and Landulf and vainly exhorted them to desist from the preaching they had begun.” B: “He exhorted them.” A**.]

“Beloved, see what the Apostle cries out, saying: ‘If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another’ (Galatians 5:15). And hear what the teacher Gregory says concerning you: ‘It is advantageous for us to endure many things that seem dishonorable and inappropriate, and it is much better that we should do so, lest dissension or scandal should thoughtlessly arise in the Church of God.’

“Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Woe to him through whom scandal comes’ (Matthew 18:7). And the Apostle says: ‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand’ (Romans 14:4). Again: ‘Do not scandalize your brother, for whom Christ died’ (ibid., 15).

“Hence Truth says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea’ (Matthew 18:6).

“Let Augustine also touch you, speaking in human terms through himself (*Sermon on the Mount* 2.61):

‘Let us not rebuke what is manifest in such a way that we despair of healing; and we shall avoid the judgment of which it is now said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure by which you measure, it will be measured out to you”’ (Luke 6:38).

“Moreover, listen carefully and devoutly to what blessed Ambrose says concerning Luke:

‘Unless you first empty your inner self of every stain of sin, lest dissensions and quarrels proceed from your disposition, you cannot bring medicine to others. Begin peace from yourself, therefore, so that when you yourself have become peaceful, you may bring peace to others. For how can you cleanse the hearts of others unless you have first cleansed your own? You have a beam in your eye, and you wish to cast the speck from your brother’s eye? Hypocrite, cast the beam from your own eye first, and then you will see to cast the speck from your brother’s eye’ (Luke 6:42).” [Note: [Col. 0907] Thus Ambrose; the manuscripts perhaps read “in you”; Bl reads “before.”]

Augustine likewise says (Book 1, chapter 63):

“Those who love to blame and condemn more than to amend and correct are quick to criticize.” [Note: [Col. 0908] The citation continues in the next chapter.]

“(Chapter 64.) This is a fault of pride or envy. Therefore one must watch piously and cautiously, so that when necessity compels us to rebuke or reprimand someone, we may first consider whether it is a fault that we have never had, or from which we have already been free. If we have never had it, let us consider that we too are human beings and could have had it; but if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, may precede that rebuke or reprimand. If, however, when we examine ourselves, we find that we are in the fault in which the person whom we were preparing to rebuke is found, let us neither rebuke nor reprimand him, but merely groan together with him, and invite him not to obey us but to strive together with us.”

Hence:

“I became as a Jew to the Jews, so that I might win the Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20).

And again:

“I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak; I became all things to all people, so that I might win all” (ibid., 22).

“You say that it is impossible for priests not to commit adultery and to sacrifice, and you speak truly. But our priests, thanks be to God, are not adulterers to this day, nor have they been called such; rather, they carefully observe the apostolic command that they be husbands of one wife.

“Hence blessed Ambrose says concerning Abraham (I.7):

‘No one may know a woman except his wife; therefore the right of marriage has been given to you, lest you fall into the snare of iniquity and sin with another man’s wife. You are bound to your wife (IX.84); do not seek release.’ Hence Solomon says: ‘A wife will be prepared for a man by God.’” [Note: [Col. 0909] B, corrected, reads *conjugii* (“of marriage”); A* reads *conjugi* (“for a spouse”). These words do not follow in Ambrose’s works, but Landulfus adds them in the same form in chapter 23.]

“If they sin in something, as human frailty is prone to do, apart from capital offenses, they are justified by God through true confession when they confess their sins. Hence our teacher Ambrose mercifully said in his letter concerning the Emperor Theodosius:

‘He who accuses himself when he has sinned is just; not he who praises himself.’

“Again, blessed Ambrose says in his treatise on the Blessed Immaculate (IV.11): [Note: [Col. 0909] The words “blessed Ambrose” are absent from B.]

‘He who accuses himself, even if he is a sinner, begins to be just, because he does not spare himself and confesses the justice of God, whom he believes unable to have anything hidden from him. Therefore Scripture says: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.”’

“Moreover, dearest brothers, understand how many evils, how many most abominable dissensions, how many murders, and how many adulteries can arise from these words.”

8. (7.) For their minds, sweetened by these and other words, were being softened as they weighed in their hearts everything prosperous and adverse that might happen to them. And behold, a certain most wicked man, whose spirit was in his nostrils, uttering the most shameful words against them with a mad mouth, stirred with excessive anger the minds that Guido had mitigated as best he could.

Thus, stirred by extreme indignation, they unanimously rose before Guido himself, who was deeply grieved by these things, and affirmed in terrifying words that they would never be silent about them [Note: [Col. 0909] B reads “that they would never be silent about themselves”], as long as there was breath in them and a tongue remained in their throats.

While uttering these prophecies, unaware of what they were saying about themselves, they left the Ambrosian palace without greeting the archbishop, running swiftly like a savage beast struck by a deadly arrow.

At that time, while the translation of the blessed martyr Nazarius was being devoutly celebrated by all the citizens of both sexes with great and numerous burning candles [Note: [Col. 0909] B reads “great and many”; May 10.], and people of every sex had humbly and devoutly gathered to celebrate the service, Landulf and Ariald, remembering the oath they had sworn, having somewhat defamed the priests throughout the streets and districts of the city because of marriage, gathered together at Saint Celsus, swollen like marsh frogs, and quarreled with the clerics in the most empty words, like pigs with dogs.

Since Saint Ambrose was alive at the time of this translation, understand, reader, what, we say [Note: [Col. 0909] Bl reads “what we learned”], he did when he was commanding the noisy frogs. Saint Augustine, a holy witness, affirms:

“When the abundant croaking of frogs disturbed the ears of the devout people, the priest ordered them to be silent and to show reverence for the sacred prayer. Then suddenly the surrounding noise ceased, and to this day the marshes are silent, so that you would scarcely, or perhaps never, find a frog croaking, especially at that time.”

9. (8.) Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0909] Title: “Concerning the indignation of a priest against Ariald.” A*: “Concerning the indignation of the priest, with a slap.” A**: “Concerning the indignation of a certain priest rebuking Ariald, with a slap.” B and Bl.], behold, a certain priest, flying like an arrow from a bow, gnashing his teeth and rolling his eyes like an animal, saw Ariald and Landulf spreading their newly sweetened but evil teachings, with which they had by then imbued almost the whole city. He rushed toward Ariald himself and threatened to lay hands on him.

After questioning Ariald with words trembling from excessive anger, asking whether what he had recently heard as it spread through the city was true, and whether Ariald had spoken so indiscreetly and thoughtlessly throughout the city and streets, defaming the priests, the latter, like a madman facing a madman, immediately shook his head and replied:

“What I said, I say; what I say, I affirm; what I affirm, I shall undertake to prove by competent reasoning.”

Hearing this, the priest, stirred by extreme indignation, raised his right hand and struck him hard across the face [Note: [Col. 0909] The manuscripts read *alpizando* for *alapizando*]. He addressed him:

“You alone, through detestable hypocrisy, dare to defame the life of priests throughout the whole world. Are you alone, through execrable *pataria* and countless evil and detestable oaths, kindling against us the flame of the people, which surges like the sea in its violence? Are you better than Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; than Solomon; than the prophets and the outstanding David? Are you better than the Apostle Paul, who was called by God the vessel of election?

“Or are you alone more just than the many holy and venerable Fathers through whose good life and conduct the primitive Church blossomed and, with God’s favor, will always flourish? Are you alone going to disregard and annihilate the many counsels of the saints? Are you alone going to criminally sow dissension in the Ambrosian Church through your false chastity, which was formerly tested in the Ambrosian palace in the presence of Guido?

“If God had supplied you from heaven with perfection in good works, you should correct us now privately—and, if necessary, at some time publicly—by good words and good examples, humbly and devoutly, publicly as in our presbytery. Hence the Apostle says:

‘If your brother sins, rebuke him between yourself and him alone’ (Matthew 18:15).

“Christ the Lord could have subjected the world to himself by one word and by his commands. But so that through patience and humility we might attain in heaven the kingdom that the proud one lost, he instructed us on earth with charity, saying:

‘What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.’

“He could even have drowned alive those who crucified him, as he did Dathan and Abiram. Tell me: whose path of the saints are you following?

“For, to speak the truth, I have never found a just man who converted the wicked to God against their will through dangerous oaths and the worst defamation. The wicked generally become harder rather than gentler, and through punishments they usually become more cruel rather than being softened.

“Hence the Apostle says: ‘God does not desire forced service.’ And Paul likewise says:

‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand’ (Romans 14:4).”

With these and other sayings, the priest Anselm, seeking to recall him from such a way of thinking, agitated him beyond recall, as fire agitates a furnace and anger a lion.

When news of this matter flew to Landulf, and what they had said in secret was being spread more and more upon the housetops, he abandoned the veneration of the martyr, for which everyone had devoutly gathered, and neglected the veneration of the ancestors. Seizing Ariald by the hands, he proceeded furiously and wickedly with a few men to the theater [Note: [Col. 0911D] Fumagalli demonstrated that this word indicates nothing other than the forum adjoining the metropolitan church, adapted for the people’s assemblies, *Ant. Mil.* I, 164 ff. Concerning the signals by which the people were summoned, Peter Damian says in *Opusc.* 5: “The bells resound; the enormous bronze trumpets there, and the clamors of the whole city, thunder forth.”].

Accordingly, they sent written notices through the city’s alleys and streets by messengers [Note: [Col. 0911] A* reads “to all [men]”; Bl, “to men.”]. With many great bells clanging and women chattering, they worked to bring everyone together in unity—young and old, wise and foolish, upright and reckless—so that they might hear attentively whatever might contribute to edification and the salvation of their souls.

When all the citizens had been summoned, Ariald, wholly aflame, climbed the common platform. With eyes blazing like a lion’s, stirred by excessive anger, he poured forth many detestable things concerning the priests, rolling out stones, woods, men, and cattle like a river swollen by a massive flood, as though offering a gift [Note: [Col. 0911] Bl reads “one”] and a hard parasite. Under the pretext of religion, he spewed before the laughing people every disgrace that can indecently be uttered by a human mouth.

At that time God did not permit divine words to come out of his mouth, except for two verses which, in my view, were quite discordant with him:

“He who serves me, let him follow me; follow me, if you do not wish to offend.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ disclosed and explained these words while indicating to all his disciples and all the faithful that they should preserve humility and have charity toward everyone:

“He who serves me follows me, and where I am, there also my servant will be” (John 12:26). [Note: [Col. 0911] B reads “there.”]

Later, when he was betrayed, he showed this saying to the man whose ear was being cut off, saying:

“Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?”

By this word and command he armed his apostles, protected them once armed from the arrows of all demons, and crowned them eternally once protected.

By this word Saint Lawrence was strengthened and overcame the savage torments of the most wicked tyrant and the blazing masses of fire; he conquered the cruel tyrant himself, half-burned and deserving the wrath of God.

By this word Saints Nazarius and Celsus, relying on the aid of God’s angels, were worthy to tread fearlessly upon the stormy surface of the sea as upon dry land.

By following this word devoutly, virgins, martyrs, and all the saints followed the highest and true religion and were found worthy to receive an eternal reward with Christ.

10. (9.) When Ariald had ended his most shameful speech, having gravely and criminally defamed the priests before the people, and when Landulf, as eloquent as he was, had repeated it in a still more serious style, they stirred up the people against the priests like lions and the fiercest tigers, anxious for prey and warm blood, disclosing and spreading among the people what even the most disgraceful men would have been ashamed to reveal [Note: [Col. 0911] B reads “she-asses”].

After these words had been pestilently disseminated, many people from whom another’s money was being exacted with extreme harshness, and whom severe poverty was slaughtering both within and without, seeking any opportunity by which they might revive and support their wretched children and wives, who were often beaten, praised them with immense applause. Others, simple and ignorant, beating their breasts, regarded their words as though they were the words of Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0912D] Such was that moneyer Nazarius, who eventually lent his support to Ariald. Andreas, chapter 6.].

What more is there to say? All their fellow citizens, bewitched like the fierce storm of the sea and the summer lightning that often overwhelms and kills many who are unprepared, ran through the city like a she-bear deprived of her cubs and barked most disgracefully like hungry dogs. First they rushed about plundering the homes of the priests; afterward, with the greatest disgrace to the women, they carried out divorces without law, without right, without the bishop, loving not God but their money, using swords and clubs.

Meanwhile the unarmed priests, knowing none of these things [Note: [Col. 0913] A** reads “into the sea”; Bl conjectures “to turn aside”], raised their minds and eyes to heaven and lay exposed like cattle before wolves. But the nobles of the city, by whose valor the priests had shortly before been protected, stirred by excessive anger and indignation, some left the city, while others waited for an opportunity to put an end to the stormy calamity.

Meanwhile many among the people, having received permission from the men already mentioned, abandoned all the occupations by which the wretched life of this world nourishes the body, clothes it, and cares for children and wives. Loving robbery more than God, they plundered the homes of the priests without mercy and, seeking increasingly to deserve God’s anger by these and other deeds, persecuted the priests and their families with the most shameful words and blows.

Then, when the city priests had been thoroughly worn down by the midday wolves and the wealth they had wrongly acquired had been exhausted, the people, desiring to extend their rage, left the city. Ariald diligently encouraged them and, under the pretext of religion, enticed them like dogs to hunt boars. They went around the villages, castles, and townships, treating all the priests they could find in the same way, and somewhat more harshly, seeking not God but money.

11. (10.) [Note: [Col. 0913] Title: “What happened to Landulf at Rome, when there (B: ‘there’) he had defamed the priests.”]

Therefore, when part of the nobles and many among the people saw the priests being indiscriminately torn apart, they were moved by compassion and protected them through many conflicts. While these things were taking place, after some time had passed, Ariald, taking Landulf and Oldeprand with him [Note: [Col. 0913D] He means Cardinal Hildebrand; see below, chapter 15.], whom he had associated with himself at the beginning of this affair, so that he and his followers might exercise themselves more and more in these acts as though by apostolic permission, secretly set out for Rome to the apostolic lord Stephen, who had recently arisen and taken office at that time [Note: [Col. 0914D] The editions give August 3, 1057–March 29, 1058.].

When he had been brought before the apostolic lord, he took care to make known, in the presence of many clerics, laypeople, and cardinals, everything he had done at Milan and how he had separated the priests from their wives with the greatest disgrace. But he was not received then as he had wished.

Hearing this, all who were present, seeing that the whole body of priests, both Latin and Greek, was being bound by the same law, and that no one could possess chastity unless it had been given from above, were astonished, as were the Romans generally.

One of them, a cardinal named Dionysius [Col. 0913D], who had been raised in the Ambrosian Church during his childhood, knew all the Ambrosian orders and how they had lived devoutly and without disturbances for many years. Running through many examples of the holy Fathers, he rebuked Ariald and all who had come with him before the apostolic lord, saying:

12. (11.) “When you conceived the plan of stirring up this unheard-of Pataria [Note: [Col. 0913] Heading: “Cardinal Dionysius’s speech against Arialdus before Pope Stephen.”], whatever your intention may have been [Col. 0914A], you ought first to have consulted the apostolic ruler or some religious man, with many fasts, before beginning so great and dangerous an undertaking with unlearned men; and what you ought to have taught with humility, patience, and good admonitions, this you carried out with lances and clubs, as you claim, while laymen ran against priests. Did you not know the Gospel of God, which says: ‘Whoever touches you touches me’? And David, the foremost of the prophets, recognizing through the Holy Spirit that Saul himself had been condemned by God, said, to instruct us: ‘It is not lawful to lay a hand upon Christ the Lord’ (1 Sam. XXVI, 11).

“Unless you are aided by God’s mercy, you deserve to be tied to a stone and plunged into the depths of the sea, because [Note: [Col. 0913] *qm.* in B; *quantum* in A* and A**.] you have rashly scandalized the most glorious and most illustrious Church of God [Col. 0914B], in which blessed Ambrose labored and toiled greatly! This schism, cruelly disseminated and, as I see, newly born, will very swiftly invade the whole world, with laymen eagerly thirsting to attack priests. The true Church of God, so that schism or scandal might not arise, long nourished with holy provisions, has been accustomed to endure and suffer very many things.

“This schism is the one through which an infinite number of children, crushed by various deaths without baptism, will be cruelly killed; this is the occasion by which many young men, unable to exercise their nature, fall into sin by acting against nature, and, unable to render to a wife the debt they would owe her [Note: [Col. 0913] *haberet* in B.], lust after another man’s wife. At least let blessed Ambrose touch your heart: when a certain woman attempted to touch him, he said with episcopal lips (ch. 11): ‘Even though I am unworthy of so great a priesthood, it is not lawful for you to lay a hand upon Christ the Lord.’

“Whether they wish it or not, you make them chaste by clubs and various blows; indeed, you openly make them incestuous in mind and body, although the Apostle says: ‘God does not desire forced service.’ And if you, together with your followers, were just, chaste, modest, holy, and good by God’s mercy, consider what the Teacher of truth says to his disciples: ‘When you have accomplished everything, say that you are useless servants’ [Note: [Col. 0913] *quia* in B.] (Luke XVII, 10). But you have handed over the priests of God—whom the whole world until now has regarded as good and dear, just and faithful, and whom it devoutly obeyed in all things, although they are unworthy of so great a priesthood—to all the criminals and seditionists who do not know what lies between the right hand and the left.

“With these words you have given the lives of all priests, the customs of all the churches, and their long-established practices to the most savage Christians, like rabid dogs, to be gnawed under the pretext of chaste religion. What divine piety required to be handled and corrected justly, devoutly, and with the greatest humility, through excellent morals and good examples, you entrusted to the clubs, lances, and swords of an unthinking populace to be dealt with—or rather trampled underfoot [Col. 0915A].

“For our Lord Jesus, Redeemer of the human race, could by a single command of his majesty have made all the unbelieving Christians of the world perfect, and in one moment plunged into hell all those crucifying him. But so that we might overcome and overthrow with supreme patience the ancient enemy, the most savage serpent, the enemy of the human race, Truth kindly admonished us, saying: ‘By your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke XXI, 19).

“I know, and truly I know: your words appear good and reasonable and worthy of praise; but because you did not begin from zeal for God, may you be deprived by God of every reward. It is fitting that all ecclesiastical dignities and all honors should be such that no one can find fault with them [Col. 0915B], and that priests should be good in every respect. But God says to one who questioned him: ‘Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone’ (Luke XVIII, 19).”

13. (12.) When Dionysius had said these and many other things to Arialdus and his associates, and was mocked with dishonorable words by many clerics, the apostolic ruler commanded silence with his hand. Meanwhile, the same apostolic ruler, speaking very little, conducted himself in such a way that he neither praised the cardinal nor condemned Arialdus. When Arialdus heard this, utterly disappointed of the glory he had hoped to obtain at Rome, and realizing that all those present sympathized with the Church of Milan, he trembled and grew pale, stiffening like a corpse.

At last, after examining many and various counsels [Col. 0915C], and after several days had passed, he joined to them Anselm, bishop of Lucca, whom I mentioned above, so that he might put an end to so great a disaster, free the priests from all the treacherous men, and strengthen what Arialdus himself had begun, so that, in a certain sense, the Church of Milan might obey his commands [Note: [Col. 0915] B has *et ut*]. He sent Arialdus, Anselm bishop of Lucca, and Hildebrand, now made archdeacon of the Roman Church, to Milan, all agreeing in one mind. One of them, livid with the anger described above, and the other, moved by excessive indignation against the dignity of the Milanese Church, were burning with the most wicked zeal.

When they reached Milan, they handled everything differently from what the apostolic ruler had indicated to them. At that time various crowds of citizens—some out of compassion for the priests, who were being badly treated by Arialdus and his party—were fighting daily, killing one another like enemies [Col. 0915D]. Therefore Anselm and Hildebrand, fearing the fury of the people, secretly summoned whatever citizens they could and, in words as harsh as their tongues could express, proclaimed without mercy or charity, cunningly and angrily: “Do you not heed the Gospel of God, which says: ‘Do not cast pearls before swine, lest they turn and trample them under their feet’ (Matt. VII, 6)?”

Finally, they blackened the archbishop himself, Guido, who at first had treated all these matters as insignificant and had consecrated Anselm to the priesthood, calling him a Simoniac and condemning everything about him. What more need be said? They sowed so great a collapse, schism, and evil discord as Nabuzardan, commander of the army, once introduced among the people of Israel; as much as Haman, who was condemned and hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai; and as much as Absalom unjustly stirred up against his father David.

14. (13.) [Note: [Col. 0915] Heading: “Here begins the account of Herlembaldus.” A*: “How Arialdus and Landulfus associated with themselves the knight Herlembaldus.” A**, B, Bl.] After almost seven years had now passed, during which the parties on both sides had encountered alternately prosperity and adversity in harsh military struggles [Col. 0916B], Arialdus and Landulfus secretly began, with heated minds, to investigate whom among the *capitanei* or *valvassores* they could place over such affairs for military action against the priests, so that, secure through his counsel and sword, they might preach freely and strive to teach and accomplish their aims courteously [Note: [Col. 0915] B has *et curialiterque*].

While these things were taking place, behold Herlembaldus, Landulfus’s brother, born from a great lineage of *capitanei*, a knight as naturally vigorous as could be, wearing a beard almost purple, as ancient custom required, with a slender face, eagle eyes, a lion’s chest, and an admirable spirit; cautious in delivering speeches to the people; as stern in war as Caesar, yet mild and very conspicuous in adversity; lofty in heart, with a delicate and well-proportioned body, and most becoming limbs and legs [Col. 0916C]; with exceptionally slender shins and feet; skilled in spending the night awake because of enemies; and very prudent in counsel, so that nothing natural to military life was lacking in him—had recently returned from Jerusalem, having become disgusted with his elders [Note: [Col. 0915] “Recently returned from Jerusalem, he then wished to leave the world and devote himself to monastic life. Andrew, ch. 16.”].

There, while he was flourishing in the bloom of youth, had betrothed a wife according to customary practice, and had discovered with certain indications that she had in fact been jesting with a certain cleric, he silently fled, abandoning the marriage altogether. Herlembaldus, Landulfus, and the other brothers were, as I have learned with certainty, born from an illicit union; their father and mother were people whom Archbishop Heribert, despite great efforts, could not separate by the sword of God’s word.

When Arialdus and his brother Landulfus had surrounded him at night under the pretext of visiting him, and had exchanged kisses with him, they addressed him in these words [Col. 0916D]: “O Herlembaldus, venerable in every respect, we give immense thanks to God, praising him for your return. Just as God in his kindness has resolved to preserve and restore you to us after you had been shaken by many storms on land and sea, just as you have hitherto been a soldier of the world and its vices, so it is fitting and appropriate that from now on you should become a most vigorous soldier of God and the Catholic Church [Col. 0917A], and that, aided by your right hand, we may be able to fulfill and accomplish what we have so far been unable to complete.

“Be like Mattathias or his sons, who died for the temple of God and the liberty of his people and, possessing eternal life, were happily crowned in Christ. Let us free the Church of God, besieged for many years and held by married priests: you by the law of the sword, and we by that of God. Preserve the reward you deserved to have when you visited God’s sepulchre. You freed [Note: [Col. 0917] Andrew in the *Vita Arialdi*, ch. 16, has “visited”] God’s sepulchre; therefore free his Church.”

While they were saying these and many other things, Herlembaldus drew deep sighs, seeing in his mind with great speed the good and, even more quickly, the adverse consequences that might befall him; and, as though exhausted, he sat down. Remaining silent for a long time, and doubting whether to mingle in all the things they had done in the city against the priests [Col. 0917B], and how people of high and low rank were daily harassed by fierce battles, he refused to answer, being wholly reluctant to involve himself in such actions.

At last, by many stratagems, they obtained his agreement to go to Rome and accept the counsel of the apostolic ruler [Note: [Col. 0917] Andrew’s testimony confirms this; but both Andrew and Arnulf attest that Landulfus was already dead at that time.]. At that time, Stephen, whom I mentioned above, had died by a divine scourge—he had held the apostolic see for scarcely nine months—and Anselm, bishop of Lucca, now made pope and called Alexander, governed the apostolic see through all its successions [Note: [Col. 0918D] 1061, Sept. 30–1073, Apr. 21.]. I shall omit how he acquired the Romans’ confidence, while eyes scrutinizing the abyss examined the matter.

Accordingly, leaving Landulfus at home, Arialdus went to Rome at a suitable time, taking Herlembaldus with him [Note: [Col. 0918D] Andrew reports that Herlembaldus went to Rome alone.], and presented himself with him to Anselm, who was called Alexander by another name [Col. 0917C]. When Alexander learned of them, he rushed upon their necks and rejoiced greatly; then, summoning them into an inner chamber, he privately questioned them about the condition of the city and ecclesiastical affairs. But Arialdus, seeing that the apostolic ruler was prepared to do everything he might demand—especially since he was carrying out matters previously undertaken on his advice—said among other things:

15. (14.) “Reverend father [Note: [Col. 0917] Heading added by B and Bl.: “Arialdus’s speech to Pope Alexander, a Milanese by birth, asking him to make Herlembaldus standard-bearer of the Church.” B and Bl.: “Arialdus’s words to the apostolic ruler Alexander, urging him to give Herlembaldus the military standard.” A* and A** have *adhortantis*.], I give immense thanks to the Creator of all, who in his mercy has resolved to exalt and raise you to such a summit of honor. Now, therefore, my spirit, weakened by many difficulties, recognizes what your love once promised me in friendship.

“To omit everything else, I humbly and earnestly beseech the clemency of your fatherhood to assign this soldier Herlembaldus to me as a defender—a man proven in war, most vigorous in counsel, confirmed and encouraged in all things, fortified on God’s behalf and by blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0917] B lacks *and by blessed Peter*] and by you—and to let him receive the standard of victory, so that, fighting more securely, he may defend us and humble those of yours who were formerly rebellious.”

After urging him with many exhortatory speeches [Col. 0918A], he brought the matter to an end. When the apostolic ruler heard this, he was greatly astonished inwardly; recognizing how grave a danger it was to encourage civil wars, he granted three days for deliberation on the matter.

Meanwhile Arialdus hurried to Oldeprandus, the chancellor and archdeacon who had been made one from a monk, and who, seated in the palace, governed the Roman soldiery almost like an emperor. Arialdus approached him and disclosed all the lofty and magnificent deeds of the Milanese people, archbishops, and priests, as well as the long-standing insolence they had shown toward the Roman pontiff, so that he might animate him more and more. When he heard this, immediately setting aside all the other affairs in which he was involved, Oldeprandus said that he would urge the apostolic ruler to grant everything Arialdus requested.

What more need be said? Alexander and Oldeprandus agreeing in one purpose, Herlembaldus and Arialdus were summoned, with many people standing by. Holding a certain standard in his hand, and blessing it as best he could, Alexander assigned it to Herlembaldus under a certain obedience and unprecedented authority. O father, where were you? You struck your sons with scorpions!

After this, Arialdus, confident like a lion and rejoicing in everything, was received as a guest; and when he came to Milan, he laid before his assembled followers everything he had done at Rome. When Herlembaldus and Arialdus arrived in the city, they began to denounce the priests somewhat more than usual in all their actions and words, on the pretext of their having wives, with very many laymen joining them. When everything prospered in their hands, they became increasingly inflamed.

If by chance they found a priest celebrating the divine service who had not obeyed their instructions, they immediately, as though driven mad, dragged him away from the sacred altars amid much abuse. Meanwhile, as Herlembaldus had made the beginning of the undertaking [Note: [Col. 0917] B has *et*], he secretly caused the strongest young men of the city, from both classes of the populace and from the nobility, to be brought to him by day and night. Embracing them and throwing himself upon each man’s neck, he carefully enticed and pressed them by many gifts and promises to swear the oath that Arialdus and Landulfus had previously sworn, so that they might maintain the *patalia*.

Those whom he could not attach to himself by gifts, promises, or any flatteries, he associated with himself either by threats or by blandishments, drawing their sons from the sacred baptismal fonts. While these things were taking place, Herlembaldus, Landulfus, and Arialdus suddenly sprang into the theater and disgracefully harangued the priests before the entire people [Col. 0918D]. Thus, having tested the disposition of everyone, they relied on the oaths of the young men and on the multitude of the mob, whose voices and actions could be moved for a paltry price, and permitted the priests whom they could find married to be disgracefully mistreated.

16. (15.) At that time Guido, the archbishop whom I mentioned above, governed the chair of the Milanese Church with the greatest disgrace [Note: [Col. 0919] Heading: “Here begins the account of the council’s proceedings which Guido held at Novara with many suffragans.” A*: “How Guido the archbishop held a provincial council at Novara …”; the remaining manuscripts differ]. At first, relying on the eminence of his office and treating the priests’ secret storm as insignificant, he delayed assisting them. Later, when the time had come near, he abandoned the support of his fellow priests and was able neither to aid them nor to strive to help himself.

For when Herlembaldus, Landulfus, and Arialdus had arranged all the priests’ affairs according to their own wishes, stretching out the arrows of their words to the utmost, they condemned Guido as a Simoniac, as though he were a bishop in a synod. Therefore Guido, summoning the suffragans whom he could obtain, held an immense synod at Novara with the permission of Alexander the apostolic ruler, whom Guido himself had consecrated to the priesthood [Col. 0919B] [Note: [Col. 0919D] “Concerning the council at which Arialdus and Landulfus were excommunicated, held in the Novara region in 1057 or 1058, see Arnulf III, 13. It seems very unlikely that another council of this kind was held, and we have already seen that the chronology is greatly confused by our author.”].

There, in the presence of all his clergy, he humbly lamented the great evils and the great schisms that had unexpectedly and irreparably come upon him and his clergy, and begged that they consider how these evils might be brought to an end [Note: [Col. 0919] B has *pertractatum*]. Meanwhile all the bishops begged the Milanese priests to live honorably with them, insofar as they could assist them, disregarding all the citizens of the city of Milan [Note: [Col. 0919] The reading *coadjuvarent* has been conjectured by the distinguished scholar Grotefend; the manuscripts have *quoad juvaret*]. They refused, preferring punishment at home to rejoicing abroad.

After they had remained there for nearly fifteen days, and had taken counsel together, they honorably sent envoys to Arialdus, Herlembaldus, and Landulfus, asking that, if they wished, they should come to the synod with a few men, without violence, fury, military attack, or evil quarrels, and humbly and devoutly declare the justice which they seemed to be claiming through fierce battles and savage disputes, and prescribe with justice what ought to be condemned [Note: [Col. 0919] B has *perscriberent*].

When they heard this, Herlembaldus, Arialdus, and Landulfus smiled and refused, replying that they would absolutely not attend the bishops. But all the suffragans, recognizing the will of Herlembaldus, Arialdus, and Landulfus, on the final day, after the council had been held, saw that the enormous evils afflicting the metropolitan Guido and his priests were growing worse day by day. They condemned them and their supporters to the divine scourge until they should humbly and devoutly come to worthy amendment, and they declared:

“May the sickles of the canons and the swords of the apostolic see, bent against rebellious subjects who do not obey their prelates, be upon them and their supporters, on behalf of God, blessed Peter the Apostle, and also blessed Ambrose, until they have come to worthy amendment.”

At that time Leo, bishop of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Leo had died long before. Gregory was then seated at Vercelli.”] [Col. 0920A], a discerning man and supremely wise in all divine matters, holding a pastoral staff in his hands, raising himself and the bishops’ crown, and gazing into Guido’s face, said, with tears flowing frequently from his eyes:

17. (16.) “Beloved father, O reverend Guido, O rector of the Ambrosian Church, venerable above very many, and O Milanese choir, instructed in divine things above all the choirs of the Latin tongue! Although you are now overwhelmed by the false justice of evil clerics and your citizens, you who have flourished for so many years among all men, remember what Truth cries daily through the Gospel: ‘Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil on account of the Son of Man; rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven’ [Note: [Col. 0919] B has *multa*] (Luke VI, 22).

“And again: ‘All the hairs of your head are numbered. Do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows’ (Matt. X, 30). Just as our order is not permitted to glory in prosperity, so it is not fitting to be troubled in adversity. Hence the wise teacher says: ‘Let prosperity not lift you up, nor adversity trouble you.’

“O dearest brothers and fathers, it is fitting for us to recall, with much sweat and labor, all the souls of the faithful, however they may have gone astray through whatever causes of schism, to the bosom of the holy Church, and, once recalled, to rejoice with them in God. But if we cannot recall them in any way, and they seek by subtle pretexts to drown us and unjustly strive to suffocate us entirely, we have the Gospel of Truth daily admonishing us: ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee into another’ (ibid., 23).

“In truth, dearest fathers, we find Truth itself saying in the Gospel: ‘A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and among his own kin’ (Matt. XIII, 57). For many of your citizens, seduced by the detestable vice of hypocrites, of whom the Lord says, ‘Woe to you, hypocrites, who lead innocent souls astray,’ seek, like the Jews once did against Christ, to bite you and tear you apart like dogs.

“But when the Lord soon vindicates you by the fire of his Holy Spirit, and you see them lying dead like dogs in the streets, while their survivors remember the evils that they unjustly inflicted upon you [Col. 0920D], say to them, groaning, as Christ once said to the daughters of Jerusalem: ‘Daughters of Zion, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children’ (Luke XXIII, 28).

“When I recall from heart and from the books of ancient volumes the many kings and dukes who, down to that time, sought unjustly to disturb and trouble the Milanese Church, nourished by Ambrose’s milk, and how afterward they were disgraced and reduced to nothing by God’s right hand, I hope, with God’s mercy aiding you, that you will very soon be freed.

“And if God, on account of our sins and our deserts, has permitted them to fulfill and accomplish all their detestable purposes against us, believe without doubt that this has been granted by God for the destruction of their bodies and souls. For if they wished peacefully to discuss and investigate the Catholic faith, the Simoniac heresy, or ecclesiastical affairs, they would attend this holy council; and either we would quietly agree to their matters once they had been canonically determined by arguments, or we would refute them by open judgments through the rectitude of the canons, which cannot lie.

“But because they seek to invade you and your property under a worthless pretext and with ruinous intent, they now savagely tear you and your orders apart with the worst words, like rabid dogs, and have refused, with the most shameful words, to attend our council humbly and devoutly, as is fitting.

“Behold, fathers, the time has come of which blessed Ambrose lamented in his *Pastoral Book* [Note: [Col. 0921D] “I have searched for this passage there in vain,”] when he said: ‘We grieve that, contrary to the warnings of the fathers of old, the most destructive desires of later generations have grown strong. For the more frequently those earlier fathers forbade harmful things, the more zealously these later ones do not cease to commit what was forbidden’ [Note: [Col. 0921] B has *volemus*].

“For behold, Jeremiah says: ‘Wicked men have been found among my people, lying in wait like bird-catchers, setting snares and traps [Col. 0921C] to catch men, like a decoy filled with deceit. Behold, I will bring ruin upon this people, and fathers and sons will fall together in it; neighbor and kinsman will perish’ (Jer. V, 26; VI, 21).

“Likewise the prophet Ezekiel says: ‘Destruction has gone forth; the rod has blossomed; pride has budded; iniquities have risen up on the rod of impiety’ [Note: [Col. 0921] The Vulgate has *surrexit*] (Ezek. VII, 10).

“Therefore, just as Isaiah spoke against Jerusalem, so I speak through the same Isaiah against Milan: ‘How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a prostitute? Justice once dwelt in her, but now there are murderers; your silver has become dross, your wine mixed with water’ (Isa. V, 21).

“Thus, grieving over the Church’s honors and dignities, so greatly diminished, I shall weep like Jeremiah, saying: ‘Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night? Let each person guard himself from his neighbor, and let no one trust his brother, because every brother utterly supplants, and every friend proceeds deceitfully’ (Jer. IX, 1).

“David foresaw their end when he said: ‘He lies in wait to seize the poor, to seize the needy while he draws him into his snare; he will humble himself and bow down, and with his weapons he will fall into death’ (Ps. IX, 9). ‘The snare they do not know will come upon them; the trap they concealed will seize them, and they will fall into that very snare’ (Ps. XXXIV, 8).”

After saying these things, he turned back to the priests and, as though beginning these words for the first time, said:

“Fathers and dearest brothers, although you have been afflicted and troubled by many evils and for a long time, it is nevertheless fitting for you, as circumstances require, to remember what Truth cries: ‘By your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke XXI, 19). And again: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’ (Matt. X, 28).

“Among other things, hear and receive in your hearts the counsel of blessed Ambrose, confessor of every tongue, which he expresses in his letter from Vercelli (I, 43, 63): ‘Let there be no sloth among you; let there be no perverse mouth, no bitterer tongue [Col. 0922B]. Do not sit in the council of vanity; for it is written: “I did not sit in the council of vanity” (Ps. XXV, 4). Do not listen to those who slander their neighbors (Ps. C, 5), lest it be said to each of you: “Sitting, you slandered your brother” (Ps. XLIX, 20).’

“Again, in *The Blessed Blameless One* (VIII, 35): ‘Let each person consider how he directs his foot and restrains his hand, lest, driven by a rush of indignation, while he thinks he is repelling an injury, he himself inflict upon another a blow notable for its slaughter’ [Note: [Col. 0921] The manuscripts have *inlibat*].

“And: ‘Although salvation is far from sinners, let no one despair, because the Lord is rich in mercy. “I will have mercy,” he says, “on whom I have mercy.”’

“Dearest brothers, in what blessed Ambrose says, we believe what he said and what he spoke through the Holy Spirit. Again, in *The Blessed Blameless One*: ‘He who thinks himself gold here possesses lead; and he who thinks himself a grain of wheat possesses straw that can be burned.’ Yet many here seem to themselves to possess gold. I do not envy them.

“But to bring this speech to an end, I shall say with blessed Ambrose what he said about you: ‘May the Lord grant you to be ignorant of shipwrecks of faith, to possess deep peace, and, if there is anything that stirs up the heavy waves of this age against us, to have the Lord Jesus as a vigilant helmsman for us—he who commands the storms by his word and calms them, restoring tranquility to the sea’—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.”

18. (17.) When these events had taken place, and Guido, having greeted all the bishops, had returned to the city [Note: [Col. 0921] Heading in the manuscripts: “How Guido’s garments were torn by the citizens as by dogs.”], behold Herlembaldus, Arialdus, and Landulfus, together with all their followers, were stirred by excessive indignation against the aforesaid council, especially because they had heard that they themselves had been included under its canons. They were irrationally inflamed like wild beasts.

Thus, one Sunday, relying on a very large crowd of people, a great hired multitude, and a portion of the nobility already dulled by daily warfare, while the bells throughout the whole city rang loudly, they entered the theater furiously, accompanied by a few clerics, priests, and the priest Leoprando [Col. 0923A], who was the chief stimulus of the affair, having recently joined them, possessing the spirit of a lion rather than of a man, and whom Guido had consecrated to the priesthood.

They spent a long time delivering many extended speeches, courteously applying themselves to inflaming the mob more and more against Guido. What more need be said? Guido, driven by the excessive violence of the people—and with Herlembaldus himself shouting disgracefully at him, threatening to bring ruin upon him, while the minds of the mob were moved like leaves by the wind—pulled himself into the theater despite the danger.

When silence had been made, so that Guido, at the command and urging of Herlembaldus, who threatened him harshly with eyes, hands, and beard like a tyrant, should either retract the excommunication he had pronounced or irrevocably abandon the archbishopric, many among the people, irrationally inflamed like wild beasts, immediately rose against him [Col. 0923B]. In various places they tore his garments like rabid dogs and left him almost entirely naked.

After this, all of them, as they were—like madmen and lunatics—left the theater. With different people holding different opinions, they made a din through the city streets with unclean hands and mouths, grunting like pigs [Note: [Col. 0923] B has *civitatibus*].

When the report of this affair had swiftly flown through the city, and the leading nobles had learned the whole truth, the nobles of the Ambrosian curia gathered unanimously around Guido, prepared, as though for death, to avenge him for so great a disgrace. Among them was Guido of Landriano, a man of great counsel and supreme dignity, who deeply sympathized with Guido’s disgrace and that of the nobility. With brilliant words, tears streaming from his eyes, and many others weeping, he urged them all to the harshest war, so that either they should immediately defend Guido, to whom they had sworn fidelity, and courageously restrain the arrogance of Herlembaldus and his companions by the sword [Col. 0923C], or else promptly leave the city with him, together with their sons and wives [Note: [Col. 0923] A** has *autem*].

For by then the leading men could scarcely resist Herlembaldus. Certain priests—if it is permissible to say so—were living under a kind of assumed chastity, as it seemed to some, and were daily inciting the people; while Herlembaldus, Landulfus, and Leoprando [Note: [Col. 0923] This Leoprando was priest of St. Paul in Compito; B has this written in the margin in red ink.] remained united every day, as though prepared to confront enemies.

Meanwhile they had inflamed the mob by their vain actions: slippery in will, frenzied in conduct [Col. 0924A], and most stubborn in obstinacy, so that they cared no more about the opportunity to oppose their fellow citizens than if those citizens had been proven Saracens or pagans [Note: [Col. 0923D] *vulgum* in A* and A**, and originally in B, but corrected here; *accenderat* in A*, A**, and Bl.].

But, to omit the many and various speeches, the numerous wars of civil strife—wars sufficient for the times of Sulla, Marius, or Catiline—and the very many killings, all of which I have considered too lengthy to write out, I shall now set down much in a few words.

Accordingly, when Guido saw all the citizens running together daily, partly to protect him and partly to expel hostile poverty through the expulsion of the leading men and the seizure of the priests’ property [Note: [Col. 0923D] That is, “partly so that…”], and saw conspiracies being made not only privately but publicly, by day and by night, he quietly said to a few:

“For the salvation of my soul is better served if, content with a small place, I die in peace with God’s consent, than if, supported by riches and honors, while so many citizens lie in wait for me, I should one day die and be plunged into hell with the impious. Therefore I shall tirelessly strive to be content with Vergilio [Note: [Col. 0923D] Arnulf III, 25.], so that another archbishop may enjoy the honors and riches.”

At that time there was a certain Gottofredus of the order of the leading men, a wise and upright priest, born from a noble and distinguished lineage. He too, at appointed times, had recently been nourishing the people with the provisions of the divine Scriptures.

Guido ordered him to be summoned to him in the presence of many nobles and, while everyone was unaware, entrusted the archbishopric to him with ring and staff, declaring that he would in no way concern himself with it any further [Col. 0924C] [Note: [Col. 0924D] After 1067; see Arnulf III, 22].

This action did not escape Herlembaldus and Arialdus. Therefore Herlembaldus, moved by excessive indignation—for he himself had labored greatly over this matter so that the bishopric might be refused to him alone—undertook, under the pretext of guarding it, to take control of all the villages, castles, fortifications, and revenues of the archbishopric. Like a commander who had driven out the enemy, he secured all these possessions against Gottofredus with terrible oaths, so that he would have none of them, whether he wished it or not [Note: [Col. 0923] A* has *ullum*, A** has *et nec ullum*].

He even strove to resist and oppose him in the mountains and valleys with a remarkable force of men. While these things were taking place, in the year 1073, Gottofredus was consecrated at Novara with the greatest honor and glory, in the presence of many suffragans [Note: [Col. 0924D] See Arnulf IV, 3.].

## 19. (18.)

At that time, when Alexander unjustly resolved, through a certain wicked zeal, to defame and oppress the Ambrosian priests, those whom he himself had sent against those same priests under a kind of obedience, encouraging them with many accusations as though they were pigs, soon set ambushes for him, while an utterly disgraceful report spread abroad.

The wise Solomon, in the wisdom granted him by God, therefore says: “He who prepares a pit for another falls into it himself” (Prov. 26:27).

For certain suburbanites, ensnared in diverse and varied doctrines, together with Ariald himself and the very man whom he loved above all others in his heart, and with some laymen who almost entirely agreed with the opinions of Girard of Monteforte—men whom he had recently embraced and kissed as sons—nearly twenty in number, when they saw that by their plots and barking they had accomplished something at Milan, came to Rome, thinking it of no account, to test the apostolic lord and utterly bring him down.

When they had assembled in the Lateran palace, they began to defame Alexander in the plainest terms, saying that he had invaded the apostolic see and, like a thief and robber, had entered not through the door but by way of the roof; “and what he ought to have possessed by God’s gift, he acquired through detestable simony. Therefore he can celebrate no divine mystery. Accordingly, if the Roman people wish it, we are entirely prepared to undergo whatever judgment they wish or demand, so that what we assert about him may appear without delay, openly and manifestly.”

Thus many upright, wise, and discerning Romans, who, while they were in Italy, had gathered at Milan on the king’s business and had discovered that the clandestine plague which Alexander had introduced there through such men had been carried on amid much bloodshed, were saying:

“It is a just and fitting thing that the man who entrusted his sons to pigs and serpents should in turn be defamed and condemned by them; and that, when he intended to oppress them through such men, he should be torn apart and dragged down by those who were born and raised with him in the same homeland, and should be called and convicted as a simoniac. What they had been imbued with through his accusations and exhortations, they fittingly turn against his own head; and, like pigs, they tear apart all the priests and bishops of the churches, sparing no bishop, so that what the Truth says may be shown.”

Meanwhile, when this report had flown over the districts of the city of Rome, behold, Oldeprand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, who was himself also lying in wait as Alexander’s rival and who dominated every affair except the control of the apostolic see, ordered all these men to be secretly summoned to him. After questioning them at length about every aspect of their case, and being somewhat aware of Alexander’s conduct, he incited them further against him in this matter.

What more need be said? When the day arrived on which, although the apostolic lord was absent, judgment was to be carried out by means of red-hot iron, with God and the blessed apostle Peter consenting, they gathered such an oath against him from the testimony of the cathedra that it revealed what was true and silenced what was false. Thus, when their false religion had been stopped, they left the City under cover of darkness, lest they be worn down by various tortures.

The man who related these things to me was one of them. At that time he himself, surrounded by excessive superstition and the most vain religion like the sons of Sceva, had taken part in this great and ill-considered deed with the others, and with other *cathedrae* [possibly “judgments” or “tribunals”]—[Col. 0925D] himself also being present, as he recounted in terrifying words.

### Editorial note

The title in A* reads: “Here begins the account of the dissension that occurred at Rome concerning Pope Alexander, who, when he resolved to oppress the Ambrosian priests through certain schismatics whom, as an author dispensing affairs, he once cherished as sons, was defamed and criminally attacked by those same men after they had learned the accusations with which he had instructed them, yet remained in his see.”

The other witnesses read: “How Pope Alexander, exalting certain clerics in order to depress others, was unjustly defamed by his own men at Rome, and thus remained in his see” (B, in the margin in red ink).

Another marginal note reads: “Here Gotofredus was deprived by Pope Alexander because he was an intruder; hence he is not written in the catalogue of archbishops.”

## 20. (19.)

Meanwhile, when Ariald had come to Milan, and saw all the offices of ecclesiastical men trampled with a kind of utterly mad and senseless cruelty by evil Christians or filthy pigs, the holy Scriptures perverted by the arguments of Arians and savagely torn apart like dogs, and when he himself regretted his conduct, he began sorrowfully to examine what he should do with himself, as though with another person.

When he learned that, according to the customary practice of all the priests and of the whole city, the assembly of a single body of men, together with their primicerius, was to meet on the appointed day in the presbytery—a venerable place—for their own and common affairs, he came privately into their midst, accompanied by only one cleric and carrying the Lord’s cross.

After remaining silent for a long time, thinking inwardly, with tears flowing most abundantly, he finally began with these words:

“O assembly and O fathers, spare me, for the sake of that supreme and customary reverence due to your priesthood, in the abundance of your mercy, although I am undeserving and entangled in all the crimes with which miserable human frailty offends.” [Col. 0926C] “Now forgive me, wretched man, the punishments I deserve for my crimes.

“I am the man who, acting against the holy Gospel, indiscreetly surrendered the holy things to dogs thirsting most greedily for the blood of men, attending neither to myself nor to my order. Indeed, I am the man who, by defaming you and yours, wickedly and without reflection handed you over to hateful men and beasts of the earth.

“Therefore I see, as demanded by my sins and those of the people, the order of Saint Ambrose and the dignity of that church trampled underfoot and destroyed before my eyes. Moreover, I recognize and discover in truth that many little children have suffered death without baptism—a most cruel and exceedingly grievous sin—and that, under the pretext of false religion, innumerable adulteries and many different Sodomitic fornications have been committed.

“Among other things, I see very many men, corrupted in their understanding and seduced by Arian doctrine, perverting the holy Scripture. They now confess neither a priest, nor a bishop, nor the Roman supreme pontiff, nor, finally, any church at all.

“Therefore grant me pardon and humbly pray for me for the peace of the Church. With God’s consent I will henceforth devote every effort to ensuring that the schismatics depart with their arguments and that you live happily in lasting peace and your customary charity.”

When Ariald had ended these words and had inflamed them all by recalling past evils, everyone remained silent and answered nothing. Then, as though he had been beaten with the heaviest blows, he withdrew, threatening, burning with anger, and without being greeted.

At that time, when Count Anselm had devoutly hurried to Rome with his soldiers for the sake of prayer, he too was questioned by the apostolic lord Alexander about the state of the city and of the ecclesiastical order. He replied:

“From the time when our Patalia resounded in the city, everything divine and human has been trampled down by civil wars, with citizens fighting one another most fiercely and priests being criminally reviled under false pretexts, so that now nothing at all remains common to the order of our church.”

Then Lord Alexander, moved by reverence for his mother, drawing long and profound sighs, said:

“God has turned their heart, so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. Let him be condemned with the anathema *Maranatha*, whoever caused that agreement with me to be initiated.”

When he had said this, a voice without a person answered: “Let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.”

## 21. (20.)

When these things had taken place, while Herlembald knew nothing of them, and after the captains had been expelled from the city as though they were enemies, with the greater part of the people fighting excessively on his side, he furiously turned all his anger and rage against the priests—more violently than had ever before been heard.

Indeed, so as to deserve the anger of God, whose anger is slow and whose reconciliation is swift, he inflicted many unspeakable sufferings upon priests on account of women and upon women on account of priests.

When he had no coins or gold with which he daily retained his loyal men, he immediately, like an emperor, sent a law concerning priests through thirty men, saying:

“If a priest or levite can swear with twelve witnesses, using the words of the Gospel, that from the days on which he received consecration he has not had intercourse with a woman, let him remain free. Otherwise, let him be deprived of all the property he possesses.”

Other palace dogs, inside and outside the city, abandoning their brooches, needles, and other occupations by which they earned their living, together with donkey-drivers, whose lives were daily supported by the most disgraceful work with asses—men to whom Patalia supplied a livelihood through evil arts—secretly brought women’s ornaments by night through the windows into the houses of priests, without the priests’ knowledge.

After this had been done, they burst through the doors with loud creaking and great destruction, rushed in amid loud barking, and, taking away what they themselves had placed there, declared in the most terrifying terms that the woman had slept with the priest. With no one defending him, they dragged the priest away and stripped him of all his possessions.

O God! The gentile emperors, wholly ignorant of the true God, did not issue such a law for their priests. But this new ordinance issued new commands, which Julius Caesar, Nero, or Maximinus would never have praised, even if they were still alive in mind and body.

That same Herlembald, since he did not have a house large enough to receive his men, criminally seized a large palace with a courtyard and a wonderful, delightful garden, situated before the church of Saint Victor of the Forty Martyrs, so that it might receive his supporters and also shelter his horses and mules.

## 22. (21.)

After several days had passed, but at Herlembald’s command, members of both parties—only those of the ecclesiastical order who were eminent by birth and learning—assembled in the secretarium, so that they might examine this matter against one another by means of authorities and arguments, and so that whichever party was defeated by reason might submit and obey the other.

On one side were Guibert the archdeacon, a master of both languages; Ambrose Biffus, who was also a deacon; Arderic, also a deacon, whose voice was like the sound of many waters; and, from among the decumani, the priest Andrew, a man distinguished in divine and human matters and in Greek and Latin speech.

On the other side were Ariald, Landulf, and Aginulf, who had assembled on a new footing from different parts of the city.

When they had taken their seats so that they might debate their arguments and interests calmly, the leading speakers were given permission to speak.

After they had long disputed on the basis of the apostle Paul and the canons, Ariald and Landulf began to shout, saying:

“The old things have passed away, and everything has become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). What was once permitted by the holy fathers in the primitive Church is now unquestionably forbidden. Let the blessed teacher and doctor Ambrose alone, whose order we maintain, condemn or affirm you.”

Then Guibert the archdeacon, after silence had been made, began:

### Here begins the speech of Guibert against Ariald and Landulf.

## 23. (22.)

“Let us now invoke and beseech the holy Trinity and the unity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, with heart and soul, so that, with his assistance and with all indignation and anger removed—for anger makes even the just into criminals—we may be able, in peace and charity, to set forth matters conducive to the edification of both souls and bodies. Concerning charity the wise doctor Gregory said: ‘He who gathers virtues without charity carries wind into dust.’

“Hence the Apostle says: ‘If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal’ (1 Cor. 13:3). ‘For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God’ (Jas. 1:20).

“Concerning this, blessed Ambrose says mercifully in his treatise on Joseph (13): ‘Anger often brings the innocent into accusation, because, when we become excessively angry with the just and wish to punish another’s sin, we commit more serious sins.’

“Therefore the Apostle says: ‘Do not judge yourselves, dearest brothers, but give place to anger’ (Rom. 12:19).

“That you have now removed all opinions from this matter except those of Ambrose pleases and greatly delights us, brothers, because all disciples accept and praise the opinions of the teacher whom they have recognized as wiser and stronger than all others in disputing and examining.

“Therefore let Ambrose, that excellent doctor and teacher of the churches, now and always, come and sit again among you and converse with you. Let us understand what he says in the *Hexameron* (5.7). He says:

“‘Let each of the faithful behold the beautiful ornaments of souls, and let them delight in the maturity of prudence, the splendor of faith, the beauty of confession, the loveliness of justice, and the abundance of mercy, so that it may be said to you: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house.” Do not seek another’s bed; do not lie in wait for another’s union. Adultery is a grave matter; it is an injury to nature. In the beginning God made two, Adam and Eve—that is, man and woman, woman from man, that is, from Adam’s rib—and he commanded both to be one body and one spirit. Why do you separate one body and divide one spirit?’

“Likewise, in his work on Abraham (1.7): ‘No one may know a woman except his wife. The right of marriage has been given to you, lest you fall into a snare and sin with another woman. You are bound to your wife; do not seek release. Hence Solomon says: “A wife will be prepared for a man by God”’ (9.84).

“Perhaps you think that he speaks only of laymen, about whom there is no doubt that they may have a spouse. Yet all laymen and clerics, whoever they are, are sons of the Church and are priests.

“Hear how holy Ambrose speaks against priests in his work on Luke, when he discusses David (5.33):

“‘How, then, did that observer and defender of the Law himself eat the loaves and give them to those who were with him, although no one was permitted to eat them except priests? It was so that through that figure he might show the priestly food passing over to the use of the peoples; or because we must all imitate the priestly life; or because all the sons of the Church are priests. For we are anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.’

“Moreover, understand what he says in his sermons: ‘No one can change nature except the one who is Lord of nature. For adultery against religion is more serious than adultery of the body.’

“Hence, in his work on Luke: ‘Learn that the fault belongs to the person, not to the sex. The sex itself is holy.’

“Besides these things, hear the apostle, the chosen vessel:

“‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife’ (1 Cor. 7:1).

“Dearest brothers, we know that God has granted bishops, priests, and levites the task of prophesying and humbly and devoutly announcing the mysteries of the Gospels to the faithful and the unfaithful. But I do not know by what prophet or by what Gospel you have been instructed, since with spears and clubs you criminally judge those at whose feet you have always stood, after wickedly defaming them as though you were emperors.

“Concerning them blessed Ambrose says in the book *Paradise*:

“‘For God knew that you were frail; he knew that you could not judge. Therefore he said to the more fragile, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.” Since he knew that you were weak for judging and wished you to be obedient to the command when he said, “Do not judge,” the apostle Paul says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; but he will stand”’ (Rom. 14:4).

“Likewise, hear what he says about those who judge another unjustly, in his treatise *On the Blessed Immaculate* (20.26):

“‘Forgiveness is more readily granted to one who errs than to one who unjustly judges another. For it is necessary that the same form of judgment which you yourself thought should be imposed on another return upon you.’

“Each person, therefore, should strive to possess the fire of charity toward God and toward his neighbor with the utmost humility and devotion, so that his brother may be built up.

“Let us hear and understand in our hearts what Ambrose says concerning this fire of charity in his treatise *On the Blessed Immaculate*: ‘He who has the fire of charity here will not be able there to fear the fire of the sword.’

“And again:

“‘If no silver is found in me, alas, may you cast me down into the deepest hell, or may I burn entirely like straw. But if gold or silver is found in me—not through my own deeds, but through the mercy and grace of Christ, through the mystery of the priesthood—perhaps I shall say: “Indeed, those who hope in you will not be put to shame.” No one should claim anything for himself; no one should boast of merits or power. Let all turn to the Lord Jesus. We shall all stand before his tribunal; from him I shall ask pardon, from him forgiveness. For what other hope is there for sinners? He who thinks he has gold has lead; he who thinks he is a grain of wheat has straw that can be burned. Yet many here seem to themselves to possess gold; I do not envy them.’

“Again, in the same work: ‘Even if you are chaste and sober, beware lest you be negligent. He does greater injury to Christ who rejects him when he comes.’

“Therefore, brothers, receive deeply with your inner ears the judgment of our most glorious confessor Ambrose. It is unquestionably dangerous for a Catholic and criminal for an unjust person to oppose it.

“For he says in the book *On the Conflict of the Virtues*:

“‘What you profess—that at the beginning of the human race the Lord created male and female so that they should be joined in mutual embraces—you say entirely and most truly. But permission to marry is granted to some, namely those who have not professed virginity, chastity, or widowhood; while it is not granted to others, namely those who have decided to remain virgins or continent.’

“Furthermore, dearest brothers, listen carefully to what Saint Ambrose says. In the book *On Flight from the World* (3) he says:

“‘The law of men was able to close the mouth; it was not able to change the mind.’

“And in the seventh book of his work on Luke (8.7):

“‘From the beginning there is the law of God. What is the law of God? “A man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Therefore he who dismisses his wife cuts his own flesh and divides his body’ (4). ‘Do not dismiss your wife, lest you deny that God is the author of your union. Hear what God said: “He who dismisses his wife makes her commit adultery,” for she to whom it is not permitted to change her marriage while her husband lives may be overtaken by the desire to sin. Therefore he who is the author of error is also guilty of the fault. How dangerous it is if you offer the fragile age of a young girl to error! How impious it is if you abandon the old age of one whose youth you have despoiled! You who obey men, fear God. Hear the law of the Lord (5), which even those who make laws obey: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (6). But not only this heavenly commandment is dissolved; a work of God also is dissolved.’

“But hear what Saint Chrysanthus says in his passion, where he could not lie. He says:

“‘They are in error who think that they can attain perfect chastity by their own efforts. Unless bodily flames have been extinguished by your rain, O Lord, the soul cannot reach the place toward which it strives. Desire is an evil beast, which in the forest of this world is incited by flesh and the devil to devour souls. Whoever escapes its death gives thanks to you, O God, because what he has escaped is yours.’”

### Editorial notes

A further apparatus note at [Col. 0925] gives *iique* (Bl.); another gives *dñm* (= *dominum*, “control/lordship”) in B. The word *cathedris* is perhaps the same as *Chateri* in chapter 29; compare chapter 31. A* reads *terribilissimis* (“most terrifying”) for *terribilibus*.
- Chapter 21 bears the heading: “Concerning Herlembald’s fury against the priests.” B reads “and others” for “other.”
- Chapter 22 bears the heading: “Here begins the conflict of the two parties, while the king ruled through Herlembald”; the other witnesses have: “Concerning the disputation of the two parties from the testimony of the Holy Scriptures.” B reads *sive* for *seu*; it lacks “teacher and doctor”; and it lacks the heading “Here begins.”
- The closing heading of chapter 23 has this note: “The speech of Ambrose Biffus, learned in Latin letters and Greek; for this reason he was called Biffarius” (A**, B, Bl.).
- The title reads: “Concerning Ariald’s confession, when anger appeared with the spirit in his nostrils beneath the words, spoken with great speed” (A*).
- Another version reads: “How Ariald tearfully confessed in the presbytery that he had erred.”
- The note at [Col. 0927] reads: “The teacher and doctor are absent” (B).
- “Thus” is found in A**, Bl.; “I” in A*, B.
- “Gregory; see above, I.3.”
- The printed text at [Col. 0933] has *muniti*; the editor corrected it to *muniri*. A*, A**, B read *muniti*; Bl. has *munitis me*.
- The reading *doceat* is found in a later witness; the common text has *docet*.
- In the Vercelli-letter quotation, the common text reads *servet … gratiam* (“may preserve … grace”) where the present text reads *fruet ablutionis suae gratia* (“may enjoy the grace of his washing”); A** and Bl. read *absolutionis* (“absolution”) for *ablutionis* (“washing”). The present author has omitted several statements here, and again after “There is no fault in marriage, but there is a law.”
- The common text has *suscipiendi* (“to be undertaken/received”) for *supradicti*; in the following phrase it has *iteraverit* (“has repeated”) for *intraverit* (“has entered into”).
- The reading *stabilitatem* is found in the common text; the present text has *subtilitatem*.
- The common text has *expetat*; the present text has *expectat*.
- One witness has *hoc* instead of *hic*.
- The phrase “Therefore, he who joins his virgin in marriage does well” is omitted either by the copyist or by Landulf.
- A marginal note gives the common reading “Of chastity, however.”
- A marginal note gives the common reading “of repeated marriage, for the choice.”
- The common text has “the fault can be remitted in baptism.”
- The common text omits “not” in “not in the marriage.”
- The common text has “This whole passage is greatly abbreviated here.”
- At the opening of chapter 24, A* and A** read *unico de* for *de unico*; the editor notes, “I searched for it there in vain.”
- The source’s further apparatus is as follows: the common text reads *doceat* for *docet*; *stabilitatem* (“steadfastness”) for *subtilitatem* (“refinement”); *expetat* (“should seek”) for *expectat* (“awaits”); and *hoc* for *hic*. The clause “Therefore he who joins his virgin in marriage does well” was omitted by either the copyist or Landulf. The common text’s heading is “Concerning chastity, however,” rather than “Concerning the monogamy of the priesthood.” It reads, in the next passage, *Quod plerisque mirum videtur, cur* (“Why this seems remarkable to many”); *iterati conjugii ad electionem muneris* (“of repeated marriage, for election to office”); *baptismo culpa dimitti* (“that guilt is remitted in baptism”); and omits *non* before *solvitur*.
- B reads *queri* (“to be complained of”) for *conquaeri*. The common text gives the title as *Against Eutropius and Paulinus*, rather than *Against Paulinus and Eutropius*, and omits “which covers a multitude of sins,” “freed from these things,” and the words after “like the sun,” beginning “Then fully and perfectly.”

### Colophon

Here ends the speech of Wibert the archdeacon; here begins that of Ambrose, learned in Greek and Latin expression, who was also a deacon.

## 24. (23.)

“May God, who is the fountain of goodness, the perfection of chastity, the teacher of charity, the lover of true virginity, and the author of every virtue, be for us in this matter the guardian of truth, the helper of humility, the defender of our adversaries, the increase of true virtue, the minister of righteous speech, and the ever-growing source of sincere charity.
