“The apostle Paul magnified this charity above all virtues by praising it, as you already know. Concerning it, Saint Augustine, supported by knowledge of every kind of judgment, wrote in the book *On One Baptism* [the source is uncertain here], saying:

“‘Let them see how many and how great things are of no benefit if the one thing that is lacking is absent; and let them see what that one thing is. Let them not hear me as a man, but the Apostle: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but do not have charity, I am nothing.”’

“Therefore, even if during some persecution they hand over their bodies with us to the flames for the faith which they confess together, yet because they do these things while separated, neither bearing with one another nor striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, since they do not possess charity, they cannot attain eternal salvation with all those things which are of no benefit to them.

“The sword slew idolaters among the people of God, but a cleft in the earth swallowed schismatics.

“Yet because a great matter now lies before us, one which it is fitting to discuss with the greatest humility, let us now withdraw from such subjects and rest.

“Let us therefore now recall what the teacher of the nations and master of truth, the apostle Paul, the trumpet of salvation, thunders forth:

“‘He who cannot contain himself should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn’ (1 Cor. 7:9).

“And again:

“‘I wish that all men were as I myself am, but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that. I say to the unmarried and to widows: It is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn’ (ibid., 7).

“Likewise, in the Letter to the Romans:

“‘We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do what I wish, but I do the very thing I hate. But if I do what I do not wish, I agree with the law that it is good’ (Rom. 7:14).

“For, dearest brothers, fearing greatly in heart and soul, I tremble when I observe so many priests, outstanding in knowledge and action, cruelly slaughtered by faithless Christians under some unheard-of pretext. In sorrow I now perceive that the time has hastened upon us which the soul of the apostle, radiant with the Spirit and knowledge of God, foretold in many prophecies, saying:

“‘In the last times some shall depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared, forbidding to marry, and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth’ (1 Tim. 4:1).

“Would that, dearest brothers, this ordinance had begun in God with charity, humility, and discretion! For if that had happened, God would certainly, by clear indications and without such wounds and hardships as now oppress our order and especially the whole Ambrosian Church, mercifully have approved its good middle and its end, which are the beginning and end of piety and charity.

“Concerning these matters blessed Ambrose complains in his sermons, saying:

“‘This miserable life is so filled with evils that, in comparison with it, death is thought a remedy rather than a punishment.’

“But because malice and ill will, anger and hatred, and avarice—which cannot be increased by abundance or diminished by poverty—have been filled with these vices, exercising them without compensation, the matter will lack good beginnings as well as better endings.

“Let us hear what the teacher and blessed Ambrose says concerning this wickedness of malignity in his Vercelli letter (45):

“‘Malignity does more harm than malice, because malignity possesses neither pure simplicity nor open malice, but hidden ill will.’

“But, to come to the matters to which my mind is directed: with what breastplates, with what weapons, or with what shield can I, however fruitlessly, arm and defend myself against such men? Let Ariald and Landulf, together with everyone else, attentively hear and understand—not me, but our holy apostle Ambrose—what he says in the Vercelli letter (62):

“‘The apostle is the teacher of virtues. He teaches that those who must be reproved and those who contradict should be instructed with patience. He commands a man to be the husband of one wife, not because he excludes one who is without marriage—for that is above the commandment of the law—but so that, through conjugal chastity, he may enjoy the grace of his washing.’

“‘There is no fault in marriage, but there is a law.’

“Therefore the Apostle established the law, saying: ‘If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife.’ Therefore, whoever is without blame as the husband of one wife is to be held to the law of the priesthood mentioned above. But whoever enters into marriage does not indeed have the guilt of defilement, but is deprived of the privilege of the priesthood.”

Likewise, in the same letter (39):

“‘A good physician, wishing both to preserve the subtlety [the common text has “stability”] of virtue in the strong and to give health to the weak, gives counsel to some and shows a remedy to others, saying: “Let the weak person eat vegetables and take a wife; the strong person awaits the stronger food of virtue.” And rightly he added: “He who has resolved firmly in his heart, having no necessity but possessing power over his own will, and has judged in his heart to preserve his virginity, does well”; and he who does not join [her] in marriage does better.’

“And through the prophet the Lord says: ‘Let my priests marry once.’

“Again through the prophet: ‘Let the priest take a virgin as wife, and likewise the levite’ (Lev. 21:13).

“But now, to bring these words to an end, hear what blessed Ambrose writes in the book *On Duties* (1.50):

“‘What shall I say about the monogamy of the priesthood, when only one union is permitted and it may not be repeated? In marriage itself, therefore, there is a law: not to repeat marriage and not to enter upon a second marital union—a matter that seems astonishing to many.

“‘Even repeated marriages before baptism create impediments through delay in the privilege of appointment and ordination, although offenses ordinarily do not hinder one if they have been remitted through the sacrament of the bath. But we must understand that baptism can remit guilt, while it cannot abolish the law. In marriage there is not guilt but law. Whatever therefore belongs to guilt is loosened in baptism; whatever belongs to the law is dissolved in marriage.’”

Likewise Jerome says:

“‘The Church seeks a priest who is either holy through virginity or adorned through monogamy.’

“I praise, dearest brothers, what brothers Ariald and Landulf have now sown among the peoples and what they have made all the faithful desire—especially priests and levites: chastity. But, as Augustine says in the book *Against Paulinus and Eutropius* (11), ‘Who can be continent unless God grants it?’

“‘The charity of God,’ he says in the same work, ‘which covers a multitude of sins, is poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’

“And again in the same work (34):

“‘When the just king has sat upon the throne of his majesty, who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin? Then, freed through his mercy from these things and fully and perfectly cleansed, the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun; and the Church will be fully and perfectly without spot or wrinkle.’”

I remember saying many things while passing through the holy Scriptures. But we grant you this option, although unjustly, since it is fitting only for bishops to do what you are doing: to have permission to investigate openly the whole city and all the peoples.

Accordingly, weighing crimes, murders of little children who innocently and cruelly suffer death without baptism, perjuries committed for the love of women and for self-defense, and also adulteries and various fornications of young men and consecrated virgins, as well as the practices through which all Christendom, happily spread throughout the whole world, has until now enjoyed loving God and man, we entrust these matters, as we are able, to the judgment of your souls.

As for priests whom you find to be digamists, trigamists, or concubinarians, let them either be deposed or separated. Those whom you find to be husbands of one wife according to the customs of the whole Church, let them remain, lest they fall into worse things.

Only take vigorous care that you do not intolerably impose upon our order the yoke which our ancestors once could not bear, knowing how the heat of human nature is inclined toward sin. Remember the Lord’s Gospels, where, when he saw that his disciples were being lawfully reproved by the Pharisees, who said:

“‘Your disciples do what they are not permitted to do on the sabbaths’ (Matt. 12:2), plucking ears of grain and eating them.”

But Jesus, defending them like a good shepherd, said to them:

“‘Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him? Or have you not read in the Law that on the sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the sabbath and are without blame?’”

Any human being can humble the natures of lions; only God, not man, can change human nature.

Hence Holy Scripture says:

“No one can change nature except the one who made it.”

### Colophon

Here ends the speech of Ambrose Biffus, also called Biffarius, against Ariald and Landulf.

### Editorial note

The title reads: “The speech of Ariald and Landulf against Guibert and Ambrose, proving from the testimony of Holy Scripture that priests ought not to marry” (A**, B, Bl.).

Here begins the speech of Ariald and Landulf against Wibert and Ambrose.

25. (24.) “O fathers and O brothers, pre-eminent among all the leaders of the whole of Italy in rank, dignity, and lineage, and worthy to be preferred—if only you had taken care to preserve the vigor of our order insofar as our reason requires—we rejoice exceedingly, wearied as we are by what we have already heard from such men, that you have spoken with us until now so wisely and judiciously.

“Good is charity, which is the fullness of the Law and the Prophets; good is charity, which, after the first-formed human beings had been condemned for many ages by the demands of their sins, mercifully drew them from the jaws of hell; blessed is charity, which, through the supreme mercy of the Godhead made human, mercifully strives to free us from the punishment of the first man and, in freeing us, grants us to rejoice with it forever in the guilt of our age. With this charity he armed his disciples, saying: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall possess the earth (Matthew 5:7)’; and again: ‘By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John 13:35).’ Of this the Apostle said: ‘Love without hypocrisy: hating evil, cleaving to what is good (Romans 12:9).’

“‘I say’ [Note: [Col. 0935] “I say,” that is, “I assert”: A*. A**. B. “I, a man, say”: *a. k. homo q.* Bl.], also, dearest brothers, that whoever sees a brother going astray through some negligence or weakness of nature and does not correct him under a pretext furnished by a certain marital union [Note: [Col. 0935] *corripuerint* (“do not correct”): A*. A**.; *corripuerit* (“does not correct”): B.] no longer walks according to charity but according to the most unjust kind of pity; and, as the Apostle says, he will rightly be judged on account of perdition [Note: [Col. 0935] *pernice?*, reading uncertain], or condemned for negligence.

“But whoever gives counsel in matters of doubt, as we see being done today, ought to be free from anger, hatred, and mercy. For anger, as the wise teacher says, often hinders the mind from being able to discern the truth. What more shall I say about hatred than what the Gospel cries out when it says: ‘He who has a beam in his own eye cannot remove the speck from his brother’s eye’? But whoever practices mercy in such a way that he completely forgets justice no longer walks according to charity. Hence Augustine: ‘If your brother has a wound on his body which he wishes to conceal because he fears being cut, would he not be cruelly left unspoken of by you if, moved by mercy, you remained silent, and mercifully judged?’ And the Apostle says: ‘If you see your brother going astray and do not correct him, you will be judged for negligence or condemned for it.’

“You say, brothers: ‘Few are chaste in mind and body, and very few priests are virgins.’ But I would rather be crowned in Christ with the few than placed in darkness with the many.

“We cannot all do everything, for we are not all equally capable. Concerning this the Apostle says: ‘To one is given the word of knowledge, to another the word of wisdom, to another discernment of spirits, to another different kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of words (1 Corinthians 12:8), to each one as God has apportioned the measure of faith (Romans 12:3).’ Yet, thanks be to God, each of us excels so greatly in knowledge of divine and human matters that, although trained by long practice in the sacred Scriptures, he is unable from the beginning to recognize and free himself from the path of truth, whether straight, deviant, or winding. Hence the prophet says: ‘Prepare the way for the Lord; make his paths straight (Isaiah 40:3).’

“Turn aside, brothers, from your own ways; perceive what Scripture cries out, saying: ‘Woe to the man who walks on two paths.’ Let what the foremost of the prophets cries out enter your understanding, brothers: ‘I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments, O Lord (Psalm 118:30).’ And again: ‘I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart (ibid., 32).’

“Let us give honor to God and bear him in our body, putting ourselves to death in all the acts of this world, through whom, as the Apostle says, the world has been crucified to the world, and I to the world (Galatians 6:14) [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *mihi* (“to me”) for the first *mundo* (“to the world”)]. Let us love him in mind and body, for he eternally crowns all who legitimately triumph in glory and honor with an indescribable crown; and let us first love him with the devotion of brotherhood and sincere charity.

“Thus Saint Augustine, treating devotion with careful attention in the book which he composed for the presbyter Jerome [Note: [Col. 0935D] Epistle 167, Paris edition], says (chapter 11): ‘What is devotion except the worship of God? And from what source is he worshiped except from charity [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate omits *ex* (“from”)]? Charity, therefore, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, is a great and true virtue [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *est* (“is”)], because it is itself the end of the commandment.

“‘As death tears the soul away from the senses of the flesh, so charity tears it away from carnal desires [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *avellit*, “tears away”]. When, therefore, charity is full and perfect, nothing of vice will remain.’

“Guibert, dearest brothers, testified that the Apostle had said: ‘You are bound to a wife; do not seek release (1 Corinthians 7:27),’ and so it is. But why did he not say what follows, namely: ‘You are released from a wife; do not seek a wife’? You brought forward the Apostle’s judgment: ‘Let each man have his own wife’; but I say: ‘Those for whom it is permitted.’

“Moreover, hear the apostolic counsel concerning souls and bodies: ‘Brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh; for if you live according to the flesh, you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live (Romans 8:12) [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *autem* (“but”) for the second *enim* (“for”)].’

“You quoted what pleased you from the letter of Vercelli, but why did you not bring forward what follows, where it says in the same letter (chapter 62): ‘Nor meanwhile is the apostolic authority to be changed [Note: [Col. 0935] *mutetur* (“be changed”); the Vulgate reads *invitetur* (“be invited”)] so as to create sons in the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *iterum*, “again”]; for one who has sons [Note: [Col. 0935] The Vulgate reads *dixit* (“he said”) for *enim* (“for”)], not one who makes them, nor is he to repeat marriage.’

“The same Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may serve the one who has approved him (2 Timothy 2:4).’ Again, to Timothy: ‘Keep yourself chaste (1 Timothy 5:22).’

“It is astonishing and exceedingly terrible that a priest or Levite engaged in the work of marriage should be able to offer sacrifices to God, when God’s angel is called a priest: ‘The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts (Malachi 2:7).’ Thus you know what the holy canons say, especially where it says: ‘Priests who have taken wives are to be deposed.’ [Note: [Col. 0937] Readings: *ita* A**. Bl.; *qui* A*. B.; *qui habet qui s. c. d. s.* Madicant; *scitis maxime c. d.*]

“Moreover, Holy Scripture cries out: ‘God will judge fornicators and adulterers (Hebrews 13:4).’ For a priest ought always to be clean and spotless; but if he has been defiled by any corruption of a woman or of himself, he cannot offer holocausts to God.

“In former times, many things seem to have been granted to many people on certain unjust occasions, though dangerously. Now, however, it is expedient for all of you to act so that we may walk along the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left. I see you standing as though armed with much knowledge of the Scriptures; but your shields will be turned into pumpkin leaves, and your swords into cold lead.”

The address of Ariald and Landulf ends [Note: [Col. 0937] A**. B. Bl. read: “The address of Andrew, priest and dean, against Ariald and Landulf.”]. The address of Andrea, priest and dean, against Ariald and Landulf begins.

26. (25.) “Brothers—and would that you were truly dearest brothers—you have now and often inserted charity and mercy into your teachings, as you have indicated with your mouth; would that you had confirmed them in the same way by the example of good works.

“You had much to say about charity at the beginning of your speech, but its conclusion openly stripped bare the source from which your words had flowed. For if you had begun from charity, you would have ended in charity, which is God. Where, then, are you heading, when you walk in the wind of pride?

“You said: ‘Whoever exercises mercy in anger forgets justice completely [Note: “Mercy,” that is, “injustice,” completely: B.], and no longer walks according to charity.’ It is true; but whoever does this, and behaves in this way toward sinners, is not faithful and is not worthy to be called a Christian.

“Nevertheless, consider what the Lord says: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice (Matthew 9:13)’; and again: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will be gracious to whom I please (Exodus 33:19).’

“You ought to have taught, admonished, and persuaded us over a long period with charity, humility, patience, kindness, and discernment, which is the mother of virtues. Now, however, as though we were condemned and criminal, you chastise us with the most savage blows, together with your chairs, though your tongue remains uncovered. By whose example are you doing all this to us and to the people?

“For many years we governed our order while living peacefully and chastely. By reviling us you have now stirred up a grave civil war. Moreover, hear the Apostle saying: ‘God does not desire forced service.’ And again: ‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he shall stand (Romans 14:4).’

“For I see that no one will be able to recall you, or those whom you have enticed over us by your customary speeches, from such actions. But civil wars, homicides, unspeakable oaths and perjuries, and the multitude of little children incurring death without baptism ought to terrify you. Keep before your eyes the limbs of these children—what sort and how many [Note: [Col. 0937] Bethmann corrects to *membra qualia* (“what sort of limbs”); A*. A**. B. read *membra equalia*; Bl. reads *membra aequalia*]—which were found this year in the theater cistern when it was cleaned by the sewer-workers [Note: [Col. 0937] *clocariis*, that is, *cloacariis*, “sewer-workers”], though few people felt compassion.

“And if you do not believe me concerning human nature, do not at least disbelieve me concerning our order, which, the more tightly it is constrained, is inflamed all the more toward unlawful acts. Believe yourself, who once were—or may be tomorrow—what we are.

“By forbidding one’s one and proper wife, you permit a hundred acts of fornication and many adulteries. Moreover, let the detestable vice that ensnared some of your own followers deter you by touching you as a friend. Pretending to live chastely, they dismissed their wives under a false religious pretext; infected with this detestable vice, they were shamefully dragged through the theater and branded on the forehead [Note: One witness reads “on the fountain”: A*. A**.].

“You also said to Lord Guibert: ‘You are released from a wife; do not seek a wife.’ But why did you not say what follows? Rather, the Apostle says: ‘If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.’

“You said: ‘As the Apostle says, we are debtors not to the flesh.’ It is so; but do we not therefore serve the flesh so that, in spirit and body, at the proper time, we may serve God?

“For this reason hear blessed Ambrose [Note: Rather, Augustine.], who says in the book *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 25): ‘Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the mind; but the virtue of the mind is sometimes manifested in action and sometimes lies hidden in disposition.’ (Chapter 26.) ‘And wisdom is justified by her children, who see that the virtue of continence must always exist in the disposition of the mind but must be manifested in action according to the opportunity presented by circumstances and times.’

“You defamed us and our order at Rome and among our fellow citizens, whose goodwill you maliciously sweetened, in order to display your knowledge or loquacity. But where you believe you will have good fruit, there you cannot have a seedbed of good fruits. Blessed Ambrose attests this in his treatment of the Psalm ‘Blessed are the Immaculate’ (II, 25), where he says:

“‘It is dangerous not only to say false things but also to say true things, if someone discloses them to those to whom he ought not. This vice has four forms: flattery, avarice, boasting, and reckless loquacity. For when someone wishes to flatter the person to whom he is speaking, he pours out a mystery. Some, driven by zeal for profit, pursue the reward of perdition, selling by their speech what ought to be concealed in silence. Others, so that they may seem to know more and may boast of their knowledge, reveal what they ought to conceal; and, by speaking without judgment, they utter a word which they cannot recall [Note: The Vulgate reads “many”].’

“Concerning such people the Lord says: ‘You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts (Luke 16:15).’ For whoever has lost the divine things cannot possess either a posterity of the soul or a seedbed of merits.

“O friend, if God had entrusted you with the task of accomplishing everything, you ought, with the Truth as your witness, to say: ‘I am an unprofitable servant.’ But if you imitate the Apostle, you ought to think with him, saying (Romans 15:1): ‘We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, for edification.’

“Moreover, understand what Saint Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels* VII, 4): ‘You who are superior, consider one another, especially your neighbors who are not entrusted to you [Note: [Col. 0939] The Vulgate reads “who have been entrusted to you”], because, although you see some of them committing wrongs, you do not know what good things may lie hidden within them. Therefore let everyone strive to be great, but in some way let him not know himself to be great [Note: [Col. 0939] B omits *se* (“himself”)], lest, while arrogantly attributing greatness to himself, he lose it. Thus it is said through the prophet concerning Saul in his pride: “When you saw yourself small, I made you great above the others”; but because you see yourself as great, you are judged small by me.’ [Note: [Col. 0939] One witness abbreviates the passage beginning “When you saw yourself small.”]

“If, as you think, we sin through the weakness of the flesh, we have the consolation of blessed Ambrose. For he says in the book *On Flight from the World* (chapter 11):

“‘If, through the weakness of the flesh and the allurements of the world, we cannot shape our mind in this way, let us lessen sin by reverence for paternal offspring [Note: The Vulgate reads “by reverence for paternal generation and diligence toward offspring”]. For charity covers a multitude of sins. Whoever could not be in the image of God, let him be so in the fullness of charity [Note: The reading “therefore … could” is found elsewhere].’

“He says in the book *On Repentance*: ‘The law of this flesh, contrary to the law of our mind, reigns in us and leads us captive into sin, so that we do what we do not wish.’

“Again, in his commentary on Luke (1:30): ‘It is not without purpose that, at the very beginning [Note: [Col. 0939] Ambrose reads *statim* (“immediately”); B *statuty*; A*. A**. Bl. *stat ut*] of Genesis, marriage is joined by God’s command [Note: [Col. 0939] Vulgate *jussu* (“by command”)], unless it is so that heresy may be destroyed. For God approved marriage in such a way that he joined the couple.’

“Our nature, after all, is feverish every day in many ways. Hence Saint Ambrose, commenting on Luke: ‘Our fever is avarice; our fever is lust, because desires are inflamed.’ Thus the Apostle says: ‘If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9).’

“Many seem chaste and pure before human beings, but before God they appear entangled in the most shameful vices. Hence the same author, commenting on Luke (1:18): ‘Not everyone who is righteous before men is always righteous before God [Note: [Col. 0939] “Not always” is absent from A** and Ambrose]. Human beings see one way, but God sees another: man sees the face, but God sees the heart.’

“Indeed, so that we might be freed from the snares of death by which this life is beset, we encounter lesser dangers in order to avoid greater ones. For, as the psalmist says, the proud have hidden many snares along this road (Psalm 139:6). And what are these snares? Hear Saint Ambrose commenting on Luke: ‘The eye of a prostitute is the sinner’s snare; there is a snare in money, a snare in religion, and a snare in the pursuit of chastity.’

“You have separated us from our wives—you who are more righteous than the Apostle, holier than the prophets, and purer than the patriarchs—not through justice or charity, but through lances, swords, and the harshest insults. These were handed down lawfully from the beginning of Christianity by our predecessors, who did violence to themselves and to us because of the defect of nature.

“Therefore, if it pleases you and your followers, hear what Saint Ambrose says concerning Luke (8:4): ‘How dangerous it is to expose the fragile age of a young girl or young man to the error and guilt of sin [Note: [Col. 0939] “Of a young girl or young man” is absent from the Vulgate]. Hear the Lord’s law, which even those who enact laws obey (chapter 5): “What God has joined, let no man separate.” From the beginning this is God’s law. What is God’s law [Note: [Col. 0939] Ambrose reads *quae est lex Dei*; the manuscripts read *lex eque est Dei*] (chapter 7)? “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh (Genesis 1:24).” Therefore whoever divides a wife [Note: [Col. 0939] The Vulgate reads “dismisses”] cuts his own flesh, divides the law, separates the body [Note: [Col. 0939] The Vulgate reads “cuts, divides”], and makes them commit adultery. “Virginity,” as blessed Ambrose says, “may be recommended; it cannot be commanded.”’

“What, then, will you answer concerning those who have already been joined to the marital bed for fifteen or twenty years?

“You said: ‘God will judge fornicators and adulterers!’ This is plainly true. But concerning your brothers, whom you see believing with you in one Father, holding one Catholic faith, and, as you say, permissibly using one wife of their own, you have sinned. For Saint Ambrose states in the letter of Vercelli (chapter 11): ‘We say that whoever has been baptized in Christ should no longer be regarded as a fornicator.’

“Perhaps you are still entangled in that opinion with which those men from Monteforte once imbued you: they asserted through false teachings that the whole of Christianity must not touch a woman and that the human race is born without male seed, like bees.

“I too wish and desire that the whole ecclesiastical order be clean, spotless, pure, and holy. But the Apostle says: ‘No one can be free from sin and holy.’ Job, seeing the frailty of the human race, says: ‘Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? (Job 6:12).’

“Moreover, since you have defamed us in many ways, crying out that a priest touched by any defilement cannot offer sacrifice to God, you ought to have recognized what the Lord says in the Apocalypse: ‘I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last. Blessed are those who wash their robes [Note: The Vulgate adds “in the blood of the Lamb”], so that they may have authority over the tree of life and enter the gates of the city (Revelation 22:13).’

“There are stains that are washed away by confession alone; this washing is signified by the aforesaid statement of John. Indeed, hear from the testimony of the Lord what things defile a person. He says: ‘It is not what enters into a person that defiles him, but what comes out of a person (Matthew 15:11).’ Adulteries, homicides, and perjuries are what defile a person. You know well enough how prone the clerical order is to sin because of incontinence.

“Hence Saint Gregory, in the *Moralia*, affirms the Apostle’s statement, saying (XXXII, 39): ‘When Paul saw some people in the Church who were incontinent, he permitted lesser things so that they might avoid greater ones [Note: The Vulgate reads “they might turn aside”], saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife (1 Corinthians 7:2).”’

“Again, in the second book of the *Register*, writing to Bishop Sabinus among many tangled expressions, he wrote something to the entire clergy who were guilty of sacrilege [Note: Bl. reads “what”]. I searched for this passage in vain [Note: The passage could not be found]: ‘Besides what I said above, let it be your care to urge these same brothers of ours, the bishops, so that those placed under them in the sacred orders may be admonished to preserve in every respect, in imitation, what they themselves observe. This one qualification, however, must be added: that they, as canonical authority has decreed, should govern the wives they have blamelessly.’

“You say: ‘You cannot serve God with wives.’ It is true, if we loved them more than God. Hence the Truth itself says: ‘Whoever loves father or mother or brothers or wives is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37).’ What the holy Fathers say about bishops you apply indiscriminately.

“For we are not what we ought to be. Yet God loves us as we shall be, not as we are, as Augustine himself says in the book *On the Trinity*: ‘For those whom God loves, he preserves forever.’ Again, Augustine himself says: ‘Even if I have no outward gifts to offer, within myself I nevertheless find something which I may place upon the altar of your praise. For although you are not nourished by our giving, you are better pleased by the offering of the heart.’ Nothing is richer toward God than good will.

“Augustine also says against Julian, in the third book: ‘What cannot be raised to something better must be cared for according to its own kind.’

“You said: ‘A priest who takes a wife is to be deposed.’ You speak well, and I say the same: if he takes a wife after receiving the priesthood, let him incur the danger appropriate to his order. But if you find in the priesthood a man who is the husband of one wife, why do you separate what you are not permitted to separate? Why do you divide the body? Show me Saint Ambrose, our holy teacher, separating the wife of one of our order from her husband against the will of either party; then let us believe and always hold to this.

“Moreover, hear what Saint Pope Gregory says to the patrician Theoctista [Note: Not to the patriarch Teostites, but to the patrician Theoctista] at Canobium (Letter XI, 45):

“‘There are some who say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion. But it must be understood that, although divine law prohibited this, human law permitted it [Note: Gregory’s wording is: “Human law permitted this, although divine law nevertheless prohibited it”]. For the Truth itself says: “What God has joined, let no man separate.” He also says: “A man may not dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication.” Who, then, could contradict this heavenly lawgiver? For we know that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh.” If, therefore, husband and wife are one flesh, and for the sake of religion a husband dismisses his wife—or a wife her husband, who remains in this world or perhaps turns to unlawful things—what kind of way of life is this, in which one and the same flesh partly passes into continence while partly remains in pollution?’”

27. (26.) [Note: The heading reads: “How Herlembald, through Landulf’s address, attempted to incite an attack upon the priests.”]

When an end was being imposed upon the speaking of both parties, behold, as though rising in the anger of God, Landulf the elder rose furiously from the assembly of the leaders. His face was pale and his tongue hissed; stirred by the abuse of a certain cleric with whom he had quarreled tooth and nail like a dog, he wished to deliver an address, but everyone was trying to restrain him because of his excessive agitation, and he sprang forward.

Thus, in extreme indignation and great anger, stirred like a she-bear whose cubs have been seized, he cried out that he wished to be killed by a clerical knife [Note: Andreas reports in chapter 2 that Landulf had once been wounded by a cleric]. Furiously springing from the sacristy into the theater, he summoned everyone and delivered a highly inflammatory address against all the orders, with Herlembald present; he spoke bitterly and tearfully.

When Herlembald had urged them on and, like a king, commanded them, the people immediately rushed upon the priests. If they had found them in the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0941] B reads *aut* (“or”)] or in the church, where they showed no reverence at all, they would certainly have killed them all that very day with swords and clubs [Note: [Col. 0941] “All” is absent from A*.].

28. (27.) [Note: The heading reads: “Here begin the miracles performed by the finger of God.” A*. A**.; B. Bl.: “Certain miracles that appeared during the persecution of the priests.”]

While the mercy of Almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit reigned, and his right hand diligently and mercifully flashed forth in powers and miracles over irrational human beings and over the priests of God, who had been deprived of all human aid but relied upon God’s help, unseen and unheard-of miracles appeared.

One day, when the priest Liprand—suspected by men of the ill-named party of those “pleasing God”—appeared before certain people and was going to the church of Saint Nazarius for prayer, he was abused with the most obscene words. Clubs were hurled after him amid loud barking, and in great anguish of spirit he fled into the hollow beneath the altar of Saint Nazarius, over the body of the saint.

When a certain utterly wicked man, more shameless than the others, dragged him out, striking him with slaps and using the vilest words and gravest threats in order to gratify the minds of himself and his like-minded companions, mad as pagan Gentiles, the power of God intervened: shortly afterward all his limbs contracted and he miserably dried up.

Another man, in the same church, received the holy Eucharist from a certain priest at the Nativity of the Lord, out of fear of that priest and not from love of God. Outside, subverted by a heretical sect, he put it into/on a wall [the precise construction is uncertain]; nevertheless, a certain faithful person saw this and reported it to the priest.

Hearing this, the priest of God gathered the holy body of the Lord with the greatest reverence and put it away. But that wretched man, who had been unworthy of the holy body, remained insatiable for all food until the end of his life, tormented by every kind of anguish; when he died, he did not deserve to possess the body of Christ.

Five others, after they had shamefully dishonored a certain priest by dragging him about on account of a woman, died like dogs in that same year.

Moreover, another man entangled in a detestable sect rejected the holy incense which the priest carries from house to house on the Lord’s Nativity, shutting his door and forbidding entry. That same night the devil, most faithful to those engaged in schism, came upon them and snatched the man’s son from his mother’s hands, beat him while he wailed in the air, and finally, disappearing as he fell, left the boy dead.

29. (28.) [Note: The heading reads: “Concerning Gotofred, intruded into the archbishopric.”]

At that time (March 1071), when Herlembald heard that Gottofred, whom I mentioned above, was intruding into every episcopal affair, among both clergy and people, against his right and will, he prepared an immense army and, with a contingent of nobles, encamped near Castiglione like an emperor.

After he had labored there unsuccessfully for many days with siege engines, crossbows, and various forms of combat, many among the people having been miserably lost, and after the wrath of God had burned through the city of Milan from end to end—through houses and churches alike, through marble and beams alike—a fire not hidden from the camp, he withdrew in sadness, deprived of all hope.

After these things had happened, and a short time had passed, Herlembald, instructed by the counsel of Oldeprand, who is also called Gregory VII and who was the head and seedbed of this movement, resolved to have an archbishop, together with his associates, who had long disturbed every royal affair as well, without staff or ring and without the king’s consent, against whom Gregory was plotting with every effort.

Herlembald brought forward a certain Anton and, with Anton’s agreement, elected him by his own mouth and unlawfully before the entire multitude (January 6, 1072). When the multitude of great and small—both his supporters and his opponents—saw this, having recently sworn loyalty to the emperor, they took up arms and, in a great battle, forced Anton, newly elected, to reject the archbishopric irrevocably, amid many wounds and oaths.

On the following day, when Herlembald realized that he had been unexpectedly and rashly deceived [Note: Thus Bl.; “deceived,” superscribed in B.; A*. has “made”; A**. has “about to make.”], he gained control of the whole city while armed, scattering silver coins [Note: Bonizo confirms that he prevailed on the following day].

Meanwhile, when Herlembald, like a pope for judging priests and like a king for crushing peoples, had already overcome the city with the sword [Note: [Col. 0943] B omits *ferro* (“with the sword”); A*. adds it by correction, but in the same scribe’s hand], gold, and many different oaths—so that none of the nobles could resist him—the wrath of God, which he had already merited with his followers, turned against him like a double-edged sword and became obstinate [Note: [Col. 0943] Reading uncertain: perhaps *obinanita*] . . . [Note: [Col. 0943] After *merebant*, A*. A**. and B. leave space for approximately two words. In the margin, the rubricator of B. wrote: “Landulf dies.” A**. adds: “Martyr Landulf,” in red letters.]

For when Landulf discovered that he had been frustrated of the hope of the archbishopric which he had previously cherished, and, excessively ambitious for gold and honor, he fell into a grave illness in sorrow.

As he died, he thrust out his tongue, almost like that of an ox, horrible—the tongue with which he had greatly offended, which had no covering, and for which torments were plainly being prepared. Finally, when he was carried to the tomb, he could not be enclosed until his legs had been broken like those of robbers of old (around 1061).

### 30. (29)

[Note: Title: “On the death of Ariald.” A, A*, A**. “How Ariald was crowned with martyrdom by the treacherous.” B.]

Ariald, while during the Easter solemnities (29 May–1 June 1066) he was devoutly celebrating the litanies in the church of the Milanese, both preaching and disputing with the clergy, firmly maintained that Ambrose had asserted that no fast ought to be observed on those days, and that during those three days it was lawful to eat both meat and drink wine. When these words were heard throughout the city and the said litanies had been interrupted, a great battle was begun by both sides. As they fought, and many were wounded by swords and stones, six men fell dead in the battle.

From this, reader, you will be able most certainly to learn and investigate what kind of judgment, knowledge, and continence Ariald possessed. For we know, indeed we truly know, Ariald, that during these fifty days the Church knows no command of fasting, as Saint Ambrose, together with many saints, bears witness.

[Note: Not at all; for Saint Luke says, VIII, 25: “Therefore, during these fifty days, the Church knows no fast.”]

Or do you not know what Truth cries out in truth: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when the bridegroom has been taken away from them, then they will fast in those days” (Luke 5:34)? For we believe that the apostles, after the Lord’s departure, when he ascended into heaven, fasted while praying in Jerusalem until the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Would that you understood the prayer which is read at the gates of our city before all the people—

[Note: “God, refuge of the afflicted,” etc.; see Fumagalli, *Antiquitates Longobardicae Mediolanenses* III, 232, who thinks that it was instituted by Saint Lazarus in the fifth century.]

—ordered and written by Saint Ambrose, as the support of the whole Church, and believed what is read in his *Life*:

[Note: Chapter 38; but Landulf altered the wording.]

“He fasted throughout the whole time of his life, except on Saturday and Sunday and on the feasts of the more celebrated martyrs.”

When these things had happened, Ariald, seeing the city stirred up most violently against him by the immense grief over the dead and by the daily division caused by discord, remembering inwardly everything that had previously been done and stirred up by his own activities, prepared a route by which he could secretly flee.

As he fled by night, he was seized and captured near Legnano by the retainers of the lady Oliva, niece of Lord Guido (27 June 1066).

[Note: The castle belonged to the faithful Herlembald; Andreas, chapter 27, reports that he was handed over by a certain priest.]

When his likeness had been shown at the fortress of Arona, he was immediately taken, by her command, to a certain island near Lake Maggiore, in the greatest secrecy, since she remembered the suffering of her uncle.

[Note: Apparently Isola Madre. Giulini IV, 114.]

There he was questioned whether he would acknowledge Guido as archbishop,

[Note: Andreas, chapter 29, likewise has this.]

the man whom the Roman Church had confirmed with the pallium and the cardinals. He answered and said: “As long as I carry a tongue in my mouth, and my spirit remains sound and my mind tranquil, I shall neither recognize him as archbishop nor regard him as such.”

At these words, Oliva’s servants furiously attacked him, pulled his tongue out from beneath his chin, and left him half-dead on the island. Indeed, on the following day (28 June), by the command of that same Oliva, lest he should be found dead or alive by his own people and lest she be harshly besieged by Herlembald, they very carefully concealed and buried him, already dead, in a fortress at Trevali, in the storehouse of Saint Ambrose.

[Note: The name remains in Valtravaglia, the valley on the left bank of the lake, near the Swiss frontier. While searching for him there, Andreas was thrown into prison, as Syrus the priest relates in Puricellus, at the cited place, p. 119. *Acta Sanctorum*, June, V, p. 301.]

After several days had passed, the stench of his corpse filled the entire castle, so that everyone fled in nausea. Therefore those who knew of this crime, terrified by great fear lest they be discovered because of the corpse, filled the storehouse itself with water up to the navel, thereby suppressing the stench, though only with the greatest labor.

[Note: Andreas, chapter 30, says that he was submerged in the lake.]

Thus, as you have heard, when both had been deprived of their tongues, God—who sees everything and disposes everything by his own judgment—clearly demonstrated, through the open examination of [lacuna] intention, what their furious words were.

[Note: A*, A**, and B leave space for one word after *aperto*.] When this wicked deed had been carried out, and when the outcome of the affair had reached Herlembald’s ears (1067) in a shadowy form, not as the truth had occurred, he immediately gathered an immense force to besiege Oliva, who was supported by knowledge of almost every kind of wicked art, especially enchantments, so that she might without delay surrender Ariald’s body to him.

[Note: The body had been found on 3 May on the lakeshore and was then carried to Arona.]

Accordingly, envoys were sent to her, while the army was encamped in the field of Rocho.

[Note: In the margin of the other manuscript, namely A: “Rho, today Raude.” Bl.]

As night came on, a certain voice, thinly sounding above them like the wind from a phantom apparition, rang out in the hearing of everyone, saying:

“Run, run to the bank of the Ticino! Run, run, for our saint Ariald has arrived and is about to be shown to us there on the bank of the Ticino.”

[Note: “And behold, when the next day dawned, a joyful voice rang through the camp, saying: ‘Indeed, on the bank of the Ticino the body of blessed Ariald has been placed in a boat.’” NDR, chapter 32.]

Believing that all had heard an angelic voice, they abandoned the camp with a great shout and ran to the place mentioned. When they had gone there at a swift pace,

[Note: A** has “the clerics.”]

a body long since mutilated, almost completely withered (the syntax of *mulieris* is uncertain), and not at all foul because of the water in which it had lain, whose every limb—of whatever sex—had decayed, exceedingly horrible and most dreadful to see, was handed over to them.

[Note: Thus A*, A**, and B; in B another correcting hand inserted *ca* before *mulieris*. Bl has *m. causa* (“by a woman’s agency”).]

Thus, while many doubted, many rejoiced, and very many believed, it was finally placed in a litter with a pallium laid over it (17 May). After it had been taken up and adorned as though he were a levite with a stole, it was buried in the monastery of Saint Celsus amid the greatest litanies, loud exaltations, and the attendance of very many people (27 May).

[Note: In B the same rubricator wrote in the margin:

“Verses over the tomb of blessed Ariald:

‘Ariald the martyr and levite lies in this urn;  
Mutilated, he dies, yet merits the gifts of life.  
In this mausoleum—read *mausoleo*, with Flamma in Giulini IV, 408—  
he was reverently laid in a worthy resting place.  
For these twin causes Ariald, having suffered at their hands,  
Is buried here in the Church as martyr and levite.  
Anselm the shepherd transferred the venerable body.’

“These three verses concern Ariald and Herlembald:

‘Honor everywhere these beloved holy treasures,  
These champions of Christ, O noble people of Milan,  
From whose holy blood these men were born.’”

A** presents exactly the same material, but awkwardly placed it in the text itself as follows: “it was buried.” The initials of the words that follow—“H. i. p. H. s. c. o. m.”—were written as though in red letters in the margin: “Verses over …” through “born,” as if they constituted a new section.]

After these things had been completed, Herlembald and all his followers honored Ariald as a new martyr with great ceremonies. They had been deceived by a phantom apparition, as later became clear during the time of the fourth Archbishop Anselm, yet they continued to venerate him assiduously and devoutly.

For when, two years after his consecration—

[Note: Thus B’s rubricator in the margin: namely 1096.]

—that is, in 1099 or 1100—

[Note: Therefore, in 1099 or 1100.]

Lord Anselm discovered how badly Ariald’s bones and body had once truly been buried, he proceeded ceremonially with a few clerics to the place, gathered the bones that he could find, and buried them in the church of Saint Dionysius (1075).

At that time the capitanei, whom Herlembald had expelled from the city together with their factions, preferring to die rather than live dishonorably, having restored their strength and gradually entering the city, swore that the citizens whom they could secure would stand with them and retain their feudal holdings by right.

After a short time, when the ordinary clergy had devoutly brought the holy chrism in order to consecrate the fonts for Holy Easter, they were constrained and compelled by Herlembald with clubs and threats to carry it into the theater on Holy Saturday.

When it had been brought there, and Herlembald had long harangued them, bitterly slandering them over this affair and imposing new dishonorable names upon them,

[Note: B omits the phrase, leaving a space.]

he was seized by the fiercest furies. He snatched the holy chrism from their hands with the greatest disgrace, poured it onto the ground with his own hands, and caused it to be trampled underfoot and beaten with clubs by many men—as though it were mud—who had no reverence for the divine sacraments.

[Note: He seems to have confused events that occurred in 1074 and 1075.]

O people without God! O judgment without truth! What offense has this sacrament, consecrated by the word of God, committed? “For,” as blessed Ambrose said,

[Note: Rather Augustine, *On the Gospel of John* X, 80.]

“the word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.” And understand what Saint Augustine says: “Although those who perform the rite are impure and unclean, its own holiness cannot be polluted, and that which is holy through the evangelical words remains holy even when performed by adulterers and upon adulterers.”

What shall I say about this mad people, forgotten by God? Since God’s wrath was openly being poured out upon the city through many judgments, and the holy baptism of Holy Easter had been criminally interrupted, they came to the day of Holy Week on which the capitanei, no longer privately but publicly, were carefully striving to retain their own feudal property and possessions.

While these things were happening, Herlembald, believing that all this had been prepared through his own efforts and judging that his life was already in his hands, alone, like a commander in the theater, organized the necessities of battle while encouraging and exhorting his followers to war. First of all, he arranged for himself a standard, soldiers, and infantrymen who would carry ladders for capturing houses and storehouses, as well as various engines. He also secretly arranged crossbows and slingers, and triangular iron ladders, standing by themselves at the lower end, twenty cubits long.

When these preparations had been made, and after he had delivered an eloquent speech in which he promised his followers great heavenly riches and the highest earthly honors, he ordered the soldiers and the rest of the multitude to assemble fully armed in the theater at the signal.

On the other side, the capitanei, together with part of the people who had learned of Herlembald’s intention, recognized his skill and expertise in battle and understood that civil war was being carefully prepared against them. Fearing that a shameful death would be inflicted upon themselves, their children, and their wives, they armed themselves and prepared manfully for war somewhat earlier than Herlembald.

When Herlembald heard this, he put on a remarkable cuirass, mounted a horse prepared for combat, and himself carried the standard. Armed with only a few men and accompanied by the priest Leoprandus, who likewise carried a cross in his own hand—not to calm the war, but rather to incite his own fighters against the combatants—he himself sprang forward as an enemy. He even drew his beard out from his cuirass, so as to inspire greater terror, and gave himself to the fight.

Since he was the first to begin the battle, without waiting for his armed followers or for the signal, trusting greatly in his own strength—especially because he had previously driven them from the city—he was pierced by spears and swords and fell first among the first.

[Note: In B the rubricator wrote in the margin: “Herlembald is killed by Arnald of Raude, as is found elsewhere,” namely in Landulf, June, chapter 44. A little farther below: “Verses over Herlembald’s tomb in Saint Dionysius, whom Urban II entered in the catalogue of holy martyrs and whose body he buried with Archbishop Arnulf of Milan in 1091”—rather, 1095—“because Herlembald, standard-bearer of the Church and defender, was killed by the adversaries of the Roman Church:

‘This Herlembald, a soldier reverend in Christ,  
Slain, is covered here, and now possesses the heavenly seat.  
He reproved incest and simony, and because he condemned them,  
The servants of Venus and the wicked followers of Simon killed him.  
Urban, supreme pontiff, also called the Second,  
And our shepherd Arnulf, pious and kindly,  
Buried the transferred limbs of this blessed man.’

A** likewise noted these things in the manuscript that he copied, writing in the margin in red letters.”]

When the battle had been completed, however, and by God’s mercy few had died, all those whom an evil cause—not the love of God—had armed were defeated and put to flight, without the slaughter of many, despite what some of them had confidently asserted. The entire city was filled with immense joy and peace. The only priest among the clergy who had been the foment of the whole dispute, Leoprandus, had his nose and ears mutilated several days later.

For if victory had been granted to the enemies because the merits of the whole city demanded it, and if the armed men had assembled somewhat earlier—as we have most certainly learned—and if the engines of various kinds that had been prepared for this crime had been deployed, then, as those citizens who were hard-pressed maintained, the entire body of nobles, together with the people supporting them, would have perished on that very day by swords and various weapons, as in the time of Sulla or Marius.

### 31. (IV, 1)

[Note: “Here begins the fourth book, concerning the Emperor Henry and Rudolf, and concerning the deeds of Countess Matilda and Cardinal Hildebrand, who after Alexander became Pope Gregory VII.” A** and B. “Here begins the account of the Emperor Henry, Rudolf, and the Saxon war, in which, after Countess Matilda and Hildebrand had undertaken it, an unheard-of slaughter of nobles and common people was carried out.” Chapter 31. A*. Also attested by Horatius Blandus, manuscript A.]

When these matters had been concluded, through which these three men ended their human lives, I shall faithfully explain the rest for future generations who are faithful and love this Church, so that they may take warning for themselves, from what source all these events flowed through the exchange of many letters.

Accordingly, when Countess Matilda, seeing herself the sole survivor after the death of her two brothers, whom she believed to have been killed through the cunning of Emperor Henry IV, sought to deprive the emperor himself of his kingdom by the sharpest deceits rather than by arms, she joined Gregory in his seventh year.

[Note: So A**, while B has “in the fifth year”; the rubricator corrected it to “the seventh year.” A* has “the fifth, sixth, or seventh.”]

Previously, while still a virgin, she had taken as her husband Gigon, a most prudent man and duke of Normandy. After living with him for a few years,

[Note: V. Math. has *secum manens*, “remaining with him,” and above it *in persona alicujus habere dominium*, “to have dominion over another person.”]

she came to regret having a master over her. After consulting with a most faithful servant, she had him most carefully killed with a sword through the buttocks while he sat on a privy over the lake.

For, since she alone exercised power over almost the whole of Tuscany and as far as Rome, she made a most secret agreement with Oldeprand (Hildebrand), who at that time held the rank of deacon in the Roman Church, and, after scattering among many Romans the “bones” of Albinus and Rufinus—

[Note: That is, gold and silver. Compare the verses widely circulated in the eleventh and twelfth centuries: “Whoever possesses at Rome the bones of the martyr Albinus and the bishop Rufinus can obtain everything”; and the proverb: “At Rome God is not threefold but fourfold.” Also compare the *Gospel concerning the Coin*, where the same saints are cited as especially powerful at Rome.]

—to ensure that he should be elected and consecrated to the Roman pontificate without the emperor’s consent (February 1076).

Thus, after Oldeprand had been elected and consecrated as Gregory, he remained only a short time before, at the first synod and on the counsel of Lady Matilda, excommunicating the Emperor Henry without any advocate, granting only the briefest delay unless Henry himself renounced the investiture of all bishoprics and abbeys.

Afterward, when he saw that everything favored him, and especially because Herlembald, together with all his *cathedrae*—

[Note: That is, *cathedras*; compare chapter 19.]

—served him in every respect with the greatest joy as though he were the Apostolic Lord, he was warned by many letters and inflamed by the numerous flatteries of Countess Matilda. Persisting zealously in this matter, he was the first to strive for canons and a register by which clerics who accepted investiture from the emperor’s hand would be removed from office.

Finally, having rejected the peace and concord of all the churches and of the entire secular world, and encouraged by the pleasant arts and diligence of Matilda, with whom he himself also laughed, he sent Rudolf, Duke of Saxony, a magnificent crown set with precious stones, so that Rudolf might enter into the Roman Empire against King Henry IV.

[Note: The text appears to require correction here; the reading is uncertain in the vicinity of this part of the book.]

He declared that he would excommunicate Henry with many excommunications and would fight manfully with Rudolf’s splendid arms and with the swords of the Saxons.

Rudolf had humbly and devoutly held from Emperor Henry the duchy of Saxony itself, together with almost the entire tetrarchate of that land—

[Note: Thus A** and Bl; A* and B have *thetarcarum*, an uncertain form.]

—having received it through his fidelity to the imperial authority and to all his own honor, until this time.

When all these matters reached the emperor’s ears in order, he was stirred by monstrous anger and grief. Seeing this clandestine evil unexpectedly rising up against him, and Rudolf already almost threatening him and his kingdom through perjury—for Rudolf had also armed all Saxony against him—he took up arms against Rudolf with all the men he could gather.

Therefore, when an indescribable multitude from both sides had assembled, a battle was fought and completed such as I have neither learned from written accounts, nor seen with my eyes, nor heard with my ears, and which no one could believe unless he had been present.

In this battle, while the emperor had been sitting in his camp with all his men for two days before, and while everyone was encamped at the entrance to Saxony, he gave this order: on the first day of battle, whatever good or bad fortune might occur, three fires were to be lit when night came, “so that all who had been scattered and divided by various events, as usually happens in war, might assemble, and finally gather together around the largest fire before me, whether to pursue the enemy or to renew the battle.”

When, in the first clash of the battles, he had lost twenty thousand chosen soldiers while arranging and sending them forward upon a rock, and when they had been swallowed up by the enemy as Jonah once was swallowed by the sea-monster, he hastened to the aid of his men with all his soldiers except those who were protecting the lance in which the nail of God had been enclosed, the support of the Roman Empire, against its fiercest enemies. By coming to their aid, he rescued many through his valor.

When the two kings had met at a distance, fighting fiercely like the most savage lions, and neither side had gained victory throughout the day, as they raged against one another with ferocious swords and an innumerable slaughter had been made on both sides, the day came to its end in night.

Then, after the three fires had been lit and all the soldiers who had been scattered had been gathered together, the emperor began to exhort the whole multitude whom he had been able to collect in groups to battle, with many tears and with eyes blazing from excessive anger. He had eaten a most wretched meal. From then on, he showed how he himself had fought with his right hand, displaying the nerves of that hand, exposed after he had cut down Saxons with the greatest strength from the sword’s hilt. In royal fashion he encouraged the entire multitude, promising royal gifts to the living and to the sons and daughters of the dead, preferring to die rather than be defeated by his perjurer, and preferring that his own body and those of his soldiers be bravely cut to pieces in the battle or mingled with the field.

When the second day arrived, Emperor Henry, at the earliest dawn, having gathered and encouraged the strength of all his soldiers, and with Lord Tealdus, notary of the holy Milanese Church, himself guarding the lance, attacked the enemy with twenty thousand soldiers who were eagerly thirsting for this battle. By the valor of his armed men and the sharpness of their courage, he immediately and unanimously drove the enemy into flight, striking them vigorously with spears, swords, and arrows.

[Note: But Tealdus was elected archbishop in 1075 or 1076. Our author confuses the battle at the Elster with the battle fought at the Unstrut.]

Finally, after innumerable men from both sides had been slaughtered over two days, and after the perjured king Rudolf had been killed by one of the emperor’s soldiers, who himself lay among the dead on the field but, grievously wounded, raised himself with great difficulty, the soldier cut off … of him … entirely with a German sword.

[Note: A*, B, and A** leave spaces after *vulneratus* and after *et*.]

In addition, sixty chosen noble soldiers whom the emperor’s orders had allowed to be gathered and identified amid so great a slaughter were burned in a heap. The emperor then entered Saxony in fury for four days, mutilating and cutting down everyone he could seize, both men and women.

### 32. (IV, 2)

[Note: Thus A*. The manuscripts add: “On the election of Thealdus as archbishop and the siege of the Roman city by Henry IV.”]

Meanwhile, after a few days, the clerics and laymen of Milan, acting by common agreement, expelled the dregs of those same citizens—wicked, crafty, and deceitful men who provoked God’s anger—purified the error of the most wicked sects, and drove away the many clerical tares. They unanimously sent three deacons and a notary to the emperor, so that they might accept as archbishop whichever man he approved with ring and staff.

This had formerly been granted to the Roman emperor by the Apostolic Lord and by many bishops, because, when each city ought canonically to conduct the election of one priest or levite—

[Note: A* and Bl have “ought,” rather than “ought to.”]

—as we know happened at Rome and in many other cities, the Milanese were striving to conduct two elections with much bloodshed.

When they had been presented at the royal court, the emperor silently reflected on what these men, or Thealdus, whom he had long known to excel in knowledge of mind and body, might accomplish. Finally he produced Lord Thealdus, a most capable man, honorably dressed from the royal chamber, elevated with ring and staff, and praised by the voices of all who were present. In the presence of the citizens, and of all those who were absent, he gave him the office and commanded that he be honorably received and amicably treated in Milan.

After a few years, when the emperor perceived that Rome was the source and foment of all his evils, and that he should besiege that city and Gregory, who opposed him and plotted against him in every way, he came into Italy surrounded by an indescribable multitude of soldiers and by a company of many bishops.

When he arrived, and the leading men were consulting at Rome about choosing a pontiff, and when all had decided to elect Lord Thealdus, who refused that office, they elected Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna and cardinal. After his election, they consecrated him with the greatest diligence and with the praise of all, with the utmost devotion, this Clement, who was overflowing with Greek pleasantries.

[Note: He was elected in June 1080 and consecrated on 24 March 1084.]

[The events are dated to 1081.]

After this, while the emperor, together with the whole multitude, was borne by the Po, rigid with intense frost, as though it were serving him, and while Lord Thealdus and all his suffragans were present—except those whom Gregory himself had illicitly removed from the church of Saint Ambrose amid savage mockery during the conflict which he himself had provoked,

[Note: Namely, the bishops of Como, Chur, and Augsburg; see Giulini IV, 253.]

because of the Ambrosian mystery, which he hated beyond all bounds of right and wrong—and while he was supporting a thousand soldiers and chosen men, whom he himself maintained at his own great expense, he established his entire camp before Rome in December 1082.

After the emperor had labored in vain for seven months with weapons and engines, one day he approached unexpectedly, while all the Germans and the various peoples, released from battle, were resting in their camps. Two very bold men, Amizo, a baker from the household of Lord Thealdus and Saint Ambrose, and Hugo, a chamberlain who had long guarded the enemy’s chamber, both accustomed to battle and daring exploits, armed and girded with swords, wished secretly to investigate the city’s defenses and the arrangements of the guards of the towers and walls. Encouraging one another, they gradually and cautiously climbed the wall, which had been partly undermined by engines (June 1083).

When they saw the city’s guards sleeping and universal silence prevailing, they immediately drew their swords and boldly cut down some of the sleeping men and threw others, unarmed, from the towers. After this, they showed themselves at once from the towers and secretly made a signal with their shields so that the emperor might come to them as quickly as possible.

Meanwhile, when Lord Thealdus saw this, frightened for his men, he urged the emperor to come quickly to him and his followers. Therefore, after the Germans—an envious people toward the Lombards—had been angered, the emperor immediately armed all his soldiers, captured the city, and cut down a few men. They even pursued Gregory himself and besieged him while he was taking refuge in the safest fortified places of old Rome.

After these events, on the third day before the Kalends of July, the emperor splendidly rewarded Lord Thealdus with gold and silver, as well as the new and honored soldiers whose boldness and exertions had caused Rome, once captured, to submit to the emperor. He also gave various gifts to the other leading men, elevating them with different honors. He alone retained the Germans with him and sat in the imperial palace.

### 33. (IV, 3)

[Note: The title in the manuscripts: “On the death of Oldeprand, who was called Gregory VII” (A* has: “who was called Gregory”).]

Meanwhile, Gregory, seeing himself abandoned by the citizens and by very many cardinals, and having lost every hope of gold and silver—which he had stripped bare by scraping the royal doors, grilles, and altars of Saint Peter—by which he had kept the Romans fighting with him, since they loved gold more than the Apostle Paul, and seeing that he could not leave the place where he had fled because of the exceedingly severe and prolonged night-and-day siege, very cautiously and secretly sent envoys to Robert, Duke of Apulia, asking him to gather an immense force as quickly as he could and come to his aid, after surrendering to him the royal treasures of Saint Peter.

For Robert, formerly a poor soldier from Normandy with his companions, had recently and unjustly invaded Apulia, Calabria, and many maritime cities, together with the many crimes of his followers.

Accordingly, Robert gathered an immense force and all the Saracens whom he could obtain. Within a few days he entered old Rome by force of arms, while the Romans failed entirely to defend themselves, their sons, and their wives, and while the relics of Rufinus and Albinus were no longer protecting them (May 1084).

[Note: B has “Rubertus” here and below.]

When he had entered, he found that after a few days the emperor had left the City. Thus this foreign people, ignorant of God, trained in crimes and murders, accustomed to adulteries and various fornications, had plunged furiously into every crime normally carried out by such enterprises with sword and fire. They even violated consecrated virgins, committed incest with the wives of the wretched Romans, and cut the rings from their little fingers.

What more need be said? After burning three parts of the city and many palaces of the Roman kings, Gregory, whose sons had been badly anointed and whose daughters had been consecrated still worse, and for whom there was now no hope of living in the city, finally fled from Rome with Robert and went to Salerno. After living there for a short time, he died, as one who had earned the punishment for his evils (25 May 1085).

### 34. (IV, 4)

[Note: Title in A** and B: “On the passing of the priest Anselm and how he appeared unharmed on the following day.” A*: “On Saint Anselm’s passing, and how his spirit passed unharmed before the altar of Saint Mary through an angel of God.”]

While all these things were happening, and the schism of the clergy and the furious battles of the laity held power, there was a certain priest named Anselm, whom Lord Thealdus had ordained to the priesthood. One day, during the vigil of Saint Maurice, while he was reciting the collect of all the saints before the altar of Saint Mary at Funticulum, after the vesper service of Saint Mary had ended, he suddenly fell and died, in the sight of the clerics. Yet his face retained its color and his veins continued to pulse.

[Note: On this place, see Giulini V, 373.]

When this was heard, many people of both sexes came out from the city and saw a sight wondrous and terrifying to everyone. When crowds had gathered in groups to witness this unheard-of event, some believed it to be a deception, while others fearlessly pricked his feet with an awl or needle, as though he were dead.

On the following day, around midday, in the sight of many astonished people, he seemed to have been released from his confinement. Crying out for repentance, with his spirit restored, he quickly raised himself. He revealed with many tears, as best he could, the many torments that he had seen—unbelievable to unbelievers and usurers—and the honors and glory that he had seen above the holy men, while an angel showed him all these things and carried his spirit through various places.

[Col. 0953] Here ends the *Book of the Histories* of the historiographer Landulf.

[Note: Thus A* and B. A**: “The end of the history of the elder Landulf.”]

## APPENDIX TO LANDULF

[Col. 0953]

### I. CATALOGUE OF THE ARCHBISHOPS OF MILAN

Edited by L. C. Bethmann and W. Wattenbach.

(*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, edited by Pertz, *Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 101.)

### Editorial Notice

We append to the histories of Arnulf and Landulf a catalogue brought down to the same endpoint as theirs, namely to Archbishop Thealdus. We present it from three manuscripts:

1. The Ambrosian manuscript C. 133 of the lower section, formerly marked P. 246 and B. 245, is a parchment folio. Before the *Lives of the Saints* and the sermons of blessed Ambrose, it contains a catalogue written continuously up to Laurentius II. At that point the pen changes, but the same hand remains, and the text continues without interruption until after Guido, in 1075.

All this therefore derives from an older exemplar completed by at least two hands, as Papebrochius already observed. One person appears to have composed the first part, up to Laurentius in 573, because the style is uniform throughout. The second part, from 573 to 1075, sufficiently reveals another author—or, if one prefers, several authors—through the expressions “the bishop,” “he died,” and “he was buried.”

The remaining portion, from 1075 to 1206, was added to the manuscript by different people at different times, as the archbishops died; it is therefore autograph and generally equal in date to the events it narrates. Mabillon first published it in *Museo Italico* I, 2, 109. Papebrochius then illustrated it splendidly in *Acta Sanctorum*, 7 May, p. 54. We now present it again from the manuscript itself. At our request, the very reverend Bartholomew Catena, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, examined it most carefully and arranged for a collation to be made for our use. We owe it to his distinguished kindness that we have now been able to present the catalogue more accurately here and to provide reliable information about its varied handwriting.

2. The catalogue itself, after it had finally been brought down to the year 1126, was copied into another metropolitan manuscript, concerning which see above, p. 4, note 5; that manuscript has now been lost. From it Muratori published the text in *SS.* IV, 141.

The copyist altered many words, and we have judged it useless to record all of these changes. He added some material of his own, which we have reported accurately. After Ulricus, beginning in 1126, he continued on his own initiative until 1176.

### 3)

This same catalogue appears to have been copied from manuscript 1, around the beginning of the thirteenth century, into the book of the chapter of Milan known as the *Beroldus*. There it was continued by various hands, both in prose and verse, and enlarged by a preface concerning Barnabas, the first bishop. This *Beroldus* has perished; but in 1296 or shortly afterward John Boffa copied the entire catalogue, with its continuations, in a single continuous hand and inserted it into the *New Beroldus*, which he had already completed between 1265 and 1269. Someone else later added a few items at the end after 1371. From this *New Beroldus*, Muratori had already published the catalogue up to the year 1262 (*SS* I b, 228); we give it in full, just as our Bethmann copied it in 1845, when the most reverend Francesco Rossinelli, a canon of Milan, graciously made both the book and the place available to him. It is a pleasing duty on this occasion to praise the singular courtesy of that distinguished man.

We have supplied in the margin the years of the Lord, which are not found in the manuscripts, calculated from the reckonings of Papebrochius and Saxi, although many uncertainties remain; later we followed the calculations of Count Giulini.

## HERE BEGIN THE NAMES OF THE BISHOPS OF THE CITY OF MILAN

[Note: Thus manuscript 1. The heading in manuscript 1 reads: “Here begins the commemoration of the bishops of this holy Milanese church, insofar as they lived in this age or where they were buried. The first pontiff of the Milanese church was the blessed Barnabas, apostle of Jesus Christ, as the blessed Jerome attests, among other things that he wrote to Chromatius and Heliodorus [I could find no trace of this anywhere in Jerome’s works; but nearly the same words are found in the book of Dorotheus], saying: ‘Barnabas, who ministered the word with Paul, first preached Christ in Rome, and afterward became bishop of Milan.’ That the blessed Barnabas was also the first pontiff of the Milanese church is plainly asserted by the blessed Dorotheus, disciple of the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, in the book that he composed concerning the acts of the apostles. For the Milanese church was founded by that very apostle. Indeed, it is read in the most ancient histories now preserved in the city of Milan [in the book *On the Situation of the City of Milan*, Muratori, *SS* I b], that the blessed Barnabas himself moved from the city of Rome to the city of Milan, and, preaching in it the word of life, converted the citizens of Milan to the worship of Christ and instructed them in faith and conduct. He likewise converted the citizens of Brescia to Christ through his companion Anathelon, whom the apostle sent to them. This blessed Barnabas, having organized the metropolitan church of Milan, decreed that it should perpetually be regarded as the principal seat of authority and the metropolis of the other churches in its province. First, after himself, he appointed and consecrated the aforesaid Anathelon archbishop of the Milanese church and first bishop of the church of Brescia, entrusting him with the care of both churches. Hence the verses:

> Barnabas, illustrious bishop of Milan’s city,  
> Consecrates Anathelon pontiff for himself;  
> He raised him to metropolitan dignity  
> And led him to the light of faith and likewise to the light of virtue.  
> Brescia, which through him had been joined to Christ in faith,  
> At once receives Anathelon as its first shepherd.  
> This noble region, founded under so great a patron,  
> Should rightly praise him and reverently honor him.
