Manuscript 3 adds a picture: on the left Milan is shown, on the right Brescia, each represented by several houses with citizens emerging from them; in the middle Saint Barnabas places a mitre on Saint Anathelon. The scribe then continues: “Saint Anathelon,” and so forth. All this, except the verses, is also found after the history of Arnulf in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5*, and B 2*. But it does not appear to have come from Arnulf, as was already observed by Muratori, who first published it, *SS* IV, 45.]

### Manuscript 1

(1126) From the election of Lord Anselmus of Pusterla until the election of Lord Ribaldus (1135, August 3, manuscript 3), who was then bishop of Alba, there were 9 years and 29 days.

### Manuscripts 2 and 3, and a later hand in manuscript 1

(1136) **Anselmus, called of Pusterla**, held office for 10 years, 1 month, and 14 days; he died on 19 Kalends of September [Note: Manuscript 1 has “October”; manuscript 2 adds, “and he was buried at Rome at Saint John Ycolanus Lateran.” At Milan there was a church of Saint John Ycolanus, later commonly called Saint John Lateran. *Vicende di Milano*, p. 259] and was buried at Rome at Saint John Lateran.

[Note: In Migne, the sections headed “Manuscripts 1 and 3” and “Manuscript 2” are printed in parallel.]

### Manuscripts 1 and 3

(1135) **Robaldus** held office [Col. 0961C] for 10 years, 4 months, and 26 days; he died on the third day before the Kalends of January and was buried in the church of the Blessed Mary called the Winter Church, beside the pulpit. From his death until the election of Lord Obertus there were 26 days [Note: Manuscript 3 has 23 days.].

(1146) **Obertus** held office for 20 years, 2 months [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “2 months”], and 6 days; he died on 6 Kalends of April and was buried in Benevento, an exile for the faith, [Col. 0961D] in the church of Saint Sophia. From his death until the election of Lord Galdinus there were 20 days.

(1166) **Galdinus** held office for 10 years, being consecrated and dying on the same day. He died on 14 Kalends of May above the pulpit of the Blessed Thecla, preaching to the people the word of faith and truth, especially against the Cathars. He was buried in the same church beside the pulpit. From his death until the election of Lord Algisius [Col. 0962B] there were 10 weeks and 4 days [Note: Manuscript 3 adds: “The fourth year of the Incarnation, 1176, on the eighteenth day of April.” From this point in manuscript 1 the hand of the fourteenth century continues.].

[Col. 0961B]

### Manuscript 2

**Roboaldus** held office for 10 years [Col. 0961C] and was buried in the winter church beneath the pulpit. **Ubertus** held office for 20 years and 9 weeks—that is, 64 days—and was buried in the city of Benevento at the monastery of Saint [Col. 0961D] Sophia. He died on 7 Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1167.

[Col. 0962A]

**Galdinus** held office for 10 years and was buried in the church of Saint Thecla. He died on 13 Kalends of May, on Sunday the fifteenth day after Easter; at that time Easter fell on the fourteenth [Note: Read “fourth.”] day of April. He became sick and died on the same day, and that year of the Lord 1176 was a leap year [Note: Here manuscript 2 ends.].

[Col. 0962B]

(1176) **Algisius** [Note: Manuscript 3 adds “of Pirovano”] held office for 8 years and 9 months, less 5 days. The see was vacant for 1 month and 11 days. He was buried [Note: Manuscript 3 omits this] in the winter church beside the pulpit.

(1185) **Lord Ubertus** [Note: Manuscript 3 adds “Crivellus”], who was also Pope Urban, held office for 2 years, 4 months, and 10 days [Note: Manuscript 3 has 6 days]. The see was vacant for 1 month and 16 days. He was buried in the church at Ferrara.

(1187) **Milo** [Note: Manuscript 3 adds “of Cardano”] held office for 7 years [Note: Manuscript 3 has 8 years], 8 months, and 8 days. The see was vacant for 26 days [Note: Manuscript 3 adds: “He was buried in the winter church.”].

(1195) **Ubertus of Terciago** held office for 9 months and 5 days. The see was vacant for 29 days.

(1196) **Philippus** [Note: Manuscript 3 adds “of Lampugnano”] held office for 10 years, 4 months, and 7 days. The see was vacant for 24 days. He was buried [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “He was buried … in Milan”; manuscript 1 ends here] in the church [Col. 0962C] of Saint Mary Major in Milan.

### Manuscript 3

1207 [1206]. On Saturday, 11 Kalends of January, Lord **Ubertus of Pirovano**, who was a cardinal of the Roman Curia, was elected. He held office for 4 years, 3 months, and 2 days. He died on 9 Kalends of October, on Holy Saturday [Note: According to this calculation, which Giulini challenged with many arguments], and was buried on Easter Day in the winter church beside the pulpit. The see was vacant until the fourth day of May.

(1211) **Lord Girardus of Sessa**, who had been elected bishop of Novara and was legate of the Apostolic See, held the office only as an elected bishop, neither consecrated nor even confirmed, from the fourth day of May until the sixteenth day of December. He died at Cremona and was buried there. The see was vacant amid great litigation and discord for 10 months and [Col. 0962D] 20 days. The cause of this dissension was a threefold division during the examination of the election. One party gave its support to the lord archpriest, another to the lord archdeacon, [Col. 0963A] and the third to the bishop of Vercelli [Note: Ariprando of the Visconti], who was the ordinary of this church and, after the death of the aforesaid legate and elect, had become legate of the Apostolic See before this examination.

Yet none of the elections was formally proclaimed by the electors according to the customary procedure, since each party asserted that its own election ought to be put into effect. One party claimed that it was larger in number and therefore that its candidate ought to be declared elected; each of the other two parties, while admitting that it was smaller in number, argued that it was nevertheless more worthy and therefore that its election was the more effective.

This dispute lasted a long time, though it was to some extent quieted. The question was neither properly discussed nor fully argued before the judges, and therefore it still remains unresolved.

Because of this dispute, Lord Pope, having summoned the messengers of the chapter to him, elected as pastor Lord **Henry of Setara**, treasurer of this church and apostolic subdeacon, who was studying at Bologna, in the year of the Lord 1213, on the fourth day of November.

And note that a short time earlier, after the death of the blessed Galdinus, there had been an almost similar, though less prolonged, dispute between the archpriest and the archdeacon. Because of their dispute, the electors and bishops of this church, rejecting both of them, elected Lord **Algisius of Pirovano**, who was likewise treasurer and a priest, than whom no one afterward, up to the present, was more useful to this church.

> Once these things had been done, let the man eager for honor be warned  
> That by strength, applause, pride, threats, or cunning  
> He strives in vain to make anyone illustrious  
> And to avoid the supposed fasces of Christ’s companions.  
>   
> For, trusting in these things, unless they climb by them,  
> They remain brothers though they had wished to be fathers.  
>   
> Do not form factions, man, if you wish or desire strongholds,  
> Nor applaud your brothers’ faults in order to increase your own strength.  
>   
> Do not crush the humble through pride, threats, or cunning.  
> Whoever does these things drives away the honor he seeks.  
>   
> Do not desire gifts; how unjust is the one who seeks them  
> Is indicated clearly in the twenty-fifth Psalm [Note: That is, it is intimated in Psalm 25].  
>   
> Therefore let no one ensnare you with gifts; be like a fish  
> Wounded by a curved hook beneath whatever gift is offered.  
>   
> Do not plant thistles while throwing violets and lilies,  
> Magnifying the guilty while trampling the gentle as worthless.  
>   
> Do not anoint the fat while letting the lean waste away,  
> Giving to the rich and showing no pity to the needy.  
>   
> Do not strive to feed bears, horses, and swift birds  
> While a poor man cries in vain before your door: “Have mercy!”  
>   
> Do not attend to the flesh, soon to become food for worms;  
> Instead, be mindful of the soul that will be without a tomb.  
>   
> If you disdain these things that I have now warned you of, with an evil heart,  
> You will not climb where you wish, but will remain deservedly below.  
>   
> Even the one who climbs, if he does not observe these things,  
> The higher he rises, the more he will incline downward.  
>   
> But if, on the other hand, you disdain them and this man here fulfills them kindly—  
> O may he come! You both shall reign forever.

The aforesaid Lord **Henry of Setara** died at Brescia in the year of the Lord 1230, on 16 Kalends of October, and was buried in the church of Saint Victor at the Elm. His body has now been transferred to the church of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix, and there it lies.

He remained in the episcopal see for 16 years and 10 months less 12 days. The record says that he “remained,” and not that he “held office,” as is said of most of those written above, because standing is the posture of one who fights or labors, whereas sitting is the posture of one who rests. For almost the whole period of his government he was engaged in labor and no small struggle: for defending the liberty of the whole church, for preserving the honor of this major [Col. 0964B] church, for expelling heretics, and for recovering bishops who seemed to have been released from subjection to the Milanese church.

Thus Lord **Henry**, after many labors and expenses, a prolonged dispute, and an extended case conducted with Lord **Omnebonus**, bishop of Cremona, in the Roman Curia, finally overcame him and had him condemned by sentence. Omnebonus, who for many years had refused to show this church the reverence due to it and entirely denied that he was bound to obey, was made to render the required fidelity by the customary oath to Henry and to the Milanese church, publicly in the middle of the church of the blessed Thecla before all the clergy of this city and an innumerable multitude of people of both sexes and of all ages—children, adolescents, young men, and old men—in the year of the Lord 1229, on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Mary, at the third hour. The clergy came in procession from Saint Mary at Beltrade according to the established custom.

The episcopal see was vacant for 28 days, namely until the day before the Ides of October, when **Lord Guilielmus of Ruzolio**, the venerable archdeacon of this church, was elected with complete peace and concord and with the consent and support of the entire chapter.

> May Christ double the gifts bestowed upon him,  
> So that he may hear this happier song of praise with due honor!

Since divine law commands, and the provisions of the law itself teach, that in a work in which some deficiency appears, the person who comes closest to supplying what is lacking ought rightly to be regarded as having completed it in practice, and since we found some things written about Lord Guilielmus, the venerable archbishop, but not everything suitably completed, I proposed to insert this account, so that I might set down in writing what I had learned and understood about him as worthy of remembrance. I do not hope thereby to receive a reward; rather, I wish these writings of mine, composed about so great and noble a man, to shine in the light of day and not grow dim in darkness—that is, that they may illuminate you who are present and afterward shine forth among posterity.

Hence my verses continue in this order:

> The years of the Lord were then running to twelve hundred,  
> To which the number forty-one had now been joined,  
> When on the fourth day, which came before the Kalends  
> Of that month which is called April [1241, March 29],  
>   
> Guilielmus of Ruzolio, the beloved shepherd,  
> Departed from this world to the everlasting citadel.  
>   
> For two lustra he triumphed in the cathedral see,  
> And beyond these, faithfully, for five months  
> And fifteen additional days he remained.  
>   
> Piety redeems him, divine law reforms him,  
> His conduct praises him, and blessed life crowns him.  
>   
> Trained in the arts and filled from the divine fountain,  
> By his own example he taught us all.  
>   
> In eloquence this man is Marcus Tullius Cicero;  
> In war he is Turnus, when the fierce enemy acted;  
> In peace he was another Cato, whom tranquil peace assisted.  
>   
> For he granted peace to the one who desired it whenever it was sought from him.  
>   
> What more shall I say? My lyre can no longer sound.  
> For if God himself had given me a hundred tongues,  
> I could not write all his praises.  
>   
> Therefore let us pray to God the Father with devoted mind,  
> Who himself gave the shepherds their talents and requires them back,  
> So that he may grant him rest and also bestow eternal life.  
>   
> Whoever reads these verses, I admonish and earnestly beseech him  
> To say that Christ now spare him. Amen.

The aforesaid Lord **Guilielmus** held the episcopal see for 10 years, 5 months, and 15 days; he died in 1241, on the fourth day at the end of March. The see was vacant for 2 months and 19 days. [Col. 0965C] He was buried in the monastery of Clairvaux [Note: Chiaravalle, near Milan.].

**Leo**, archbishop, descended from the noble family of the *valvassores* of Perego, held office for 16 years, 3 months, and 30 days. He was elected in 1241, on the feast of Saint Vitus, June 15; he died in 1257, on the fourteenth day of October, and was buried in the church of the Savior at a place called Legnano, having been banished by the populace of the city of Milan.

He and the ordinaries of the Milanese church were banished by those same townspeople because he and the aforesaid ordinaries refused to enroll certain members of the populace as titular clerics of that church. They were not only banished for this reason but also stripped of their property by them.

The said Archbishop Leo, as a pilgrim and expelled by them from the city of Milan, died at the place mentioned above in the year 1257. A vigorous and steadfast man, he defended the liberty of the Milanese church until his death. Because of his death, the see was vacant for 4 years, 9 months, and 7 days.

In the year of our Lord 1262, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [July 22], at the time when the Torriani ruled the city of Milan, Lord Pope Urban IV, dispensing rewards proportionate to merits and endeavoring to provide the Milanese Church with a shepherd, after a careful examination of Lord Otto, then archdeacon of the aforesaid Milanese Church, who derived his origin from the ancient and most noble lineage of the Visconti, provided for him at Monte [Col. 0966A] Flascone, recognizing that his character and life shone with integrity. Since the circumstances have offered an occasion to speak of his life and character, although reason counsels that something should be related, nevertheless there is not much need to do so, because his integrity, diligence, and expertise are most clearly revealed in the articles of necessity by his endurance, and in the repayment of favors by his mercy. For, when fortune turned against him, he patiently endured the stings of many adversities; and, amid abundant prosperity, clothed in the mantle of humility, he showed himself approachable to the poor and— as will be related—merciful and protective toward his own enemies.

When it had been made known to the aforesaid Torriani that the said Lord Otto had been provided for as archbishop of the aforesaid Church, they, fearing his industry and power as things frightening to themselves, were distressed. Therefore, preventing the said archbishop from his see so that he could not govern his people, and moved by a pretext rather than a cause, they shamefully expelled from the city as many as they thought would be favorable to him. But the aforesaid lord archbishop, often considering with himself the hardships of his friends and the desolation of his people without government, and intending to remedy these two deficiencies, entered Arona with his exiled friends assembled around him (in 1263, April 1). When this came to the knowledge of the Torriani, relying on the support of the marquis Pallavicini [Note: [Col. 0965D] Uberti.], who at that time had dared to make himself hostile to Mother Church, they expelled the aforesaid lord archbishop, with his adherents, from Arona with a prepared army, and compelled him to undergo an outrageous exile from his own see for about fifteen years [Col. 0966C].

Finally, divine providence, seeing the people of blessed Ambrose, its father, perishing in desolation through lack of his guidance, and bringing a fitting end to the misery of shepherd and people, while unwilling that they should appear to have been driven from the borders of their own commonwealth, in the year 1277 strengthened the said lord archbishop with such power and favor that, on the feast of blessed Agnes (January 21), he defeated and overcame the aforesaid Torriani and their accomplices, who were at the village of Desio [Note: [Col. 0966D] Desio, ten miles distant from Milan.], in a great battle. In that engagement a great number of the Torriani and their accomplices were slain, and many were captured and brought into the presence of the said lord archbishop. Among them was Lord Napoleone, together with certain other leading members of his household.

Then the mercy of the compassionate father was stirred, sympathizing with the adversity of his enemies [Col. 0966D]. He forgave them the offenses they had inflicted upon him over the preceding years, and with the sign of the holy cross absolved them from the bond of excommunication to which they had been held bound on account of their offenses. In this one deed the preeminence of the mercy of so great a father shone forth: although, after suffering grave injuries at the hands of Lord Napoleone and the other captives, they were attempting to attack him and others with swords, the lord archbishop, in no way forgetting divine compassion, threw himself before the violent intention of many, extinguished their fury, [Col. 0967A] and preserved the lives of those captives from their savage anger.

When these matters had thus been accomplished, the aforesaid lord archbishop, arranging the duties of his dignity according to three aims—namely, the exaltation of God’s glory, the increase of his archbishopric, and assistance to Christ’s poor, whom he recognized as messengers of Christ—entered the city of Milan with his friends, without the elation of triumph, and entered his own see.

Therefore, recognizing that the victory described above had proceeded from divine dispensation through the prayers of blessed Agnes the virgin, on whose feast the power of the aforesaid Torriani had been overthrown in the manner described, he built, for the honor of God and of that blessed virgin, a chapel in the winter church of Saint Mary, and endowed it sufficiently, as is set out below [Col. 0967B]. For the disciplining of the Milanese clergy in sacred Scripture, he established in the same Church an ordinary teacher in that sacred science, one who should be from the house of the Visconti if a suitable man were found in that house.

He granted the church of Saint Bartholomew at the Wood, the hospital of Saint James on the road at the Cuman Gate, and the church of Saint George of Legnano, with their appurtenances, to the common table of the chapter of the Milanese Church, which was insufficient, for daily distributions. To increase the table of his archbishopric, he also adorned its possessions and lands with most beautiful buildings: namely, the splendid fortress of Angera; the also handsome fortress of Travaglia [Note: [Col. 0967D] Travallia, at Lake Verbano.]; the beautiful castle of Cassiano [Note: [Col. 0967D] Now Cassano Magnago, near Gallarate.]; the village of Legnano with precious palaces; and the village of Abbiate with houses [Col. 0967C] more suitable and attractive [Note: [Col. 0967D] Abbiate Grasso, or Biagrasso.]. He acquired for the archbishopric possessions and wealth at Casorezzo [Note: [Col. 0967D] Casorezzo, in the parish of Legnano.], together with many other buildings and possessions.

At last, that most spiritual father, whose whole intention was directed toward God, and who did not strive to enrich those joined to him by carnal union, arranged his affairs in the following manner. He endowed the new hospital, of which he had been the founder, with a large estate situated at Trivulzio. From its revenues he ordered that sixty pounds be given annually to the chapter of Saint Agnes the Virgin, one hundred pounds to the doctor of theology as his salary, and twenty pounds for his annual commemoration, in the currency then in circulation.

Finally, in his last will he bequeathed all his immovable patrimonial goods to the hospital of the Jerusalemites for the aid of the Holy Land, and all his movable goods for the construction of a hospital for the use of the poor. The trustees of this bequest built a suitable hospital at Saint Donatus on the road.

While diligently attending to these works, that most devout father, after sitting in the archiepiscopal see for thirty-three years and twenty-three days, in the year 1295, on August 8, was summoned from the darkness [Col. 0968A] of this life and departed to the heavenly homeland. His body lies in the aforesaid chapel of blessed Agnes, in a finely carved marble sarcophagus raised there behind her altar; may his soul, through God’s mercy, rest in peace. Amen.

All the foregoing is briefly declared in the following verses, written in golden letters on the sarcophagus of the said lord archbishop:

That illustrious father, light of his fatherland, glory of fathers,

Radiance of justice, foundation of faith, ark of wisdom,

Giver of forgiveness, harbor of mercy for the needy,

Fearless shepherd, whom no harsh difficulty of labors overcame,

Who was destined to bring peace to his people;

That pious prince and gracious bishop, in whom

All the lofty splendor of virtues had come together;

By whom Milan shone with so great a lamp,

And the whole region gleamed, but now grows pale at his removal:

Bright offspring of the Visconti, venerable Otto—

O grief! O wound! He has become ashes in this marble.

Christ, Father of life, may his spirit rest in you!

For eleven years, three times six years, and three times days,

He presided over the Ambrosian Church as a good shepherd [Note: [Col. 0967] Here the scribe ends in the middle of the page. Another hand added what follows on the next page in the mid-fourteenth century.].

Lord William, son of the late Lord Thomas of Pusterla of Tradate, was table chaplain to Lord Pope John XXII, as well as provost of Pozsony [Note: [Col. 0967D] Now Pressburg.] in Hungary, archpriest of the Church of Saint John of Modetia, ordinary and cimeliarch (keeper of the church treasury) of the Milanese Church, and canon of the Church of Saint John at Castel Seprio [Col. 0968C]. Thereafter, Lord Pope Clement VI declared the said Lord William patriarch of the Church of Constantinople, granting him all the aforesaid benefices in commendam. Finally, Lord Urban V [Note: [Col. 0968D] Rather Innocent VI, if the year has been correctly given; see Giulini, continuation II, 105.] transferred the same Lord William to the archbishopric of the Milanese Church, commending to him the patriarchate and the other aforesaid benefices. This transfer took place in 1361.

The aforesaid Lord William held the patriarchate for sixteen years and seven months, and the archbishopric for nine years and four months, together with the patriarchate and the other benefices mentioned. He was buried at Avignon in the house of the Friars Preachers (in the year 1371).

[Col. 0968D] In Book I the following is added at the end:

1344 [1342] [Note: [Col. 0968D] More probably July 17, 1342; see Giulini, continuation I, 430. He died in 1354; ibid., p. 538.]

Lord John Visconti became archbishop of Milan and lived in the archbishopric for eleven years. He died on Sunday, October 5, 1355. He was also lord general of the cities of Milan, Bologna, Genoa, Parma, Piacenza, Bobbio, Lodi, Brescia, Bergamo, Cremona, Como, Vercelli, Novara, [Col. 0969A] Asti, Tortona, and Alessandria. He had prepared, and was preparing, many good things for his Church; but if his heirs had left them to that Church, he himself could not reach them—namely, books for the liturgy and theology, chalices, crosses, images of saints, golden mitres, croziers, and so forth.

[Col. 0969]

## II. JOHN PETER PURICELLI’S DISSERTATION

Whether Saint Ambrose permitted his Milanese clergy to marry a virgin once.

(Printed in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* IV, 120.)

### NOTICE

The errors that Landulf scattered everywhere throughout his History originated from the claim that Saint Ambrose had permitted his clergy to marry a virgin once, according to the custom of the Greeks. Hence also his complaints against and hatred of the Roman pontiffs, who, together with Saints Ariald and Herlembald, had undertaken to restore the ancient discipline in the Milanese Church.

John Peter Puricelli dealt with the matter against the testimony of our Landulf in his special dissertation, chapter 92 of the *Life of Saint Herlembald*, by means of several utterly conclusive arguments, so that he removed all room for doubt. Therefore I, who had adorned Landulf’s edition, having been scandalized by this most biting-tongued man’s writing, feared that the pious ears of readers might be offended by it. For that reason I have deliberately appended the learned man’s praised dissertation here, so that it might serve as a present correction both to Landulf and to all who share his opinion, and so that for all the devout it might provide a most splendid triumph over the malice and falsehood of the schismatic.

## DISSERTATION

### I

Among all the adversaries of Ariald who, while he was alive, resisted him openly, and likewise resisted his supporters, I have certainly not yet found anyone who expressly asserted that the marriages of the Milanese clergy had been permitted or even approved by our Ambrose, formerly a bishop and now a saint. Accordingly, no such statement by any adversary can even be gathered from the whole of our work thus far, although in it so many other arguments are brought forward here and there by which both our own clergy and clergy from elsewhere stubbornly tried to defend marriages of this kind.

### II

Nevertheless, other writers of histories later appeared who expressly and no less confidently attributed patronage of such clerical marriages to that exceedingly wise and holy teacher. The first of these, in my view, is Datius, that chronologer whom many of us have believed to have been a holy archbishop and to have been commended by Saint Gregory Pope the Great. I refuted him in chapter 39, number 10, of my *Nazarene Dissertation* [Col. 0969C]; shortly afterward the second to subscribe to the same fiction was that Landulf the Elder, whom I identified in that same chapter 39, number 13, and also in the preface to Book I of this work and in chapter 2 of that first book.

His contemporaries extended their Histories: Datius at least to the year 74 of Christ, Landulf to the year 1085, as I concluded concerning Datius in that chapter 39, number 14, and concerning Landulf in Book I of this work, chapter 2, number 3.

### III

Let us hear Datius himself. Although his Chronicle is nowhere to be found at the present time, we nevertheless possess his very words on this matter through Gualvaneus Flamma, who in his own day had two copies of it at hand for his use. Thus, in his *Major Chronicle*, according to the copy preserved in the Ambrosian Library, chapter 397, Gualvaneus left the following, transcribed from it for posterity [Col. 0970B], which I likewise quoted in chapter 39, number 11, of my *Nazarene Dissertation*:

“From the Chronicle of Datius:

‘At the synod of Damasus I, of one hundred and fifty bishops, held at Constantinople, where blessed Ambrose was present, a very serious disagreement arose between priests who had wives on one side and priests living without wives on the other. The priests without wives said that married priests could not be saved. The supreme pontiff entrusted this question to blessed Ambrose. He said:

“Perfection of life consists not in chastity but in charity,” according to the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians 13: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” and so forth. Therefore the law permits priests once to take a virgin as wife, but not to repeat the marriage. If, however, after the death of his first wife, a priest takes another, he loses the priesthood.’”

These, then, were Datius’s very words on this subject, according to the testimony of Gualvaneus Flamma, who also rashly agreed with them, as we shall see shortly.

### IV

As I was saying, that Landulf the Elder later followed Datius in agreement. In Book I, chapter 11, under the title “On Monogamous Priests according to the Teaching of Blessed Ambrose,” he expressed this opinion in a somewhat different form:

“While blessed Ambrose was seated, a very serious disagreement arose before the apostolic authority at a synod between monogamous priests and others living in virginity or chastity. At the command of the apostolic authority, and with the other bishops consenting, the matter was submitted to the judgment of blessed Ambrose, so that whatever he said would be held sacred and firm.

“But blessed Ambrose, recognizing that human inclinations are especially prone to sin on account of lack of self-control, and knowing that no one can possess virginity or chastity except from God, said what he had already set down in the book *On Duties*:

“‘What shall I say about the monogamy of priests, when only one union is permitted and it may not be repeated? This is the law: not to repeat the marriage.’

“By saying this, he silenced all disagreement. Accordingly, Greek priests, holding to the opinion of Ambrose, to this day regard it as sanctioned and as a sacred law that, when they are ordained to the priesthood, they must either promise virginity from that time onward or join themselves to wives in the testimony of good men. If it happens that their wife dies, they either live chastely while retaining the priesthood, or lose the priesthood if they thereafter have carnal relations with another woman.

“Their Church he also imitated reverently in many observances. Indeed, on the most celebrated festivals, especially the Resurrection of the Lord, he blessed their sacrifice—that is, the leavened bread—together with our unleavened bread.”

Such was that Landulf the Elder, himself, as has often already been said, exceedingly devoted to priests with wives in those times.

### V

But what of Gualvaneus Flamma and certain others after him, who undoubtedly otherwise condemned such clerical marriages and rightly professed that they had eventually been forbidden? See how he incorrectly traced their first origin all the way back to apostolic times. For he entitled chapter 226 of his Chronicle, mentioned shortly before, “Priests and bishops had wives,” and immediately developed and supported the claim with arguments:

“Blessed Barnabas was able to appoint a successor and organize Churches, and those who were ordained were able to have wives. Hence the Apostle says, in 1 Timothy 3: ‘A bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife.’ And the same Apostle, speaking of deacons in the same Epistle: ‘Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own households well.’ And the same Apostle says to Titus, in chapter 1: ‘Appoint presbyters in each city, as I also appointed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children.’ And in Luke, chapter 1, it is stated that Zechariah the priest fathered John the Baptist by Elizabeth.

“From this it plainly appears that bishops, priests, and deacons have the legal right to have wives, both in the New Testament and in the Old. [Col. 0971C] The same is found concerning Heribert of Arzago, archbishop of Milan, who took in marriage a noble woman named Useria, who donated Useria to the monastery of Saint Dionysius. But after Pope Alexander of Badagio, from Milan, decreed that no cleric should take a wife, with the approval of a sacred council, thereafter no cleric was permitted to marry, especially because in the order of the subdiaconate every cleric solemnly professes perpetual chastity.”

This is what Gualvaneus says there. Later, in chapter 397 (otherwise 396), entitled “Divine Worship Is Enlarged through Blessed Ambrose,” after he had listed from Datius’s Chronicle various orders of sacred ministers instituted by Ambrose in the Milanese Church, he added:

“He blessed them all and granted that each of them might take a virgin as wife. After she died, they were to remain widowers.”

The matter is treated above, in chapter 227, or in that same chapter 226 that I cited above, according to the numbering given there by Gualvaneus himself [Col. 0971D]. Nor was he content with this; he continued the present chapter in the following way:

“Gloss. Chronicle of Datius:

‘At the synod of Damasus I, of one hundred and fifty bishops, held at Constantinople, where blessed Ambrose was present,’”

and the rest, as I quoted it in the third section.

Again, in chapter 737, writing about our archbishop Heribert, he relates:

“His wife, called Useria, an exceedingly wealthy woman, donated to the monastery of Saint Dionysius an estate called Useria.”

Such is Gualvaneus in that Chronicle. In another Chronicle of his, which he called the *Handful of Flowers*, he likewise listed the same orders of ministers from Datius, and at the end of chapter 40 added the following:

“Blessing all these, most blessed Ambrose permitted them to have one wife; after her death, they were to remain widowers forever. This custom lasted seven hundred years, until the time of Pope Alexander, whom the city of Milan had produced.”

For this reason, later, in chapter 152, he began to relate how this very controversy had been disputed by that same pontiff when he was still a cardinal or ordinary canon of the Milanese Church.

### VI

That manuscript Chronicle, *Flower of Flowers*, whose testimony I used in Book I above, chapter 6, had already been read by me before the year 1645, and before I printed the monuments of the Milanese Ambrosian Basilica and monastery, in which frequent mention is made of the same Chronicle.

But after I had returned it to its owner, Aloysius ab Ecclesia, whom I shall always remember with grateful affection; and when afterward, in 1653, I was writing the *Life of Our Archbishop Saint Lawrence of Litta*, and immediately delivering the work, prepared hastily in sections, to the printer during the autumn holidays; since at that time I could not have that codex at hand—just as I could not have the autograph of Tristanus Chalcus [Col. 0972B], which I shall likewise discuss later—I supposed that the author of that Chronicle, who was accustomed to agree with Gualvaneus Flamma in almost everything, had also agreed with him in what he attributed to Saint Ambrose concerning priests’ marriages.

Accordingly, in chapter 20, number 16, I affirmed the same thing. But in this my memory deceived me, as I have recently noticed. For the author of that Chronicle, following Gualvaneus Flamma, continues at length and in detail in describing Ambrose the bishop and all the orders of ministers instituted by him; yet concerning permission granted to them to marry, he says not a word—plainly following a sounder judgment than Gualvaneus.

Only afterward, in the case of Heribert the archbishop, among many other things, he says the following on folio 128, page 2:

“This archbishop had Useria, a noble woman, as his wife; she donated her dowry to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, which to this day is called Useria.”

What I think of this addition, however, I shall explain in its proper place in this very chapter [Col. 0972C].

### VII

Certainly Peter Azarius also agreed with Gualvaneus Flamma in this respect. I likewise used his testimony above, in Book I, chapter 7. For, after mentioning the clergy instituted by Saint Ambrose in the metropolitan Church, he immediately spoke in the following way, together with Gualvaneus Flamma:

“Blessed Ambrose, blessing all these, permitted them to have one wife; after her death, they were to remain widowers forever. This custom lasted seven hundred years, until the time of Pope Alexander, whom the city of Milan had produced.”

### VIII

I also thought that Tristanus Chalcus had fallen into the same error—not, indeed, according to the printed edition of his Milanese History, prepared in this city in the year of our Lord 1627, in which that error really ought to have been omitted, just as, on the contrary, it had already been decreed against Bernardinus Corius, as we shall see shortly—but according to his manuscript copy, indeed his autograph, preserved in the Ambrosian Library.

Thus, in the *Life of our archbishop Lawrence of Litta*, chapter 20, number 16, I included Tristanus Chalcus, on the basis of that autograph, among several other followers of his error. Nevertheless, when I was recently composing the present chapter and again examining those places in which I had seemed to myself to have once read this, I found nothing of the sort. I therefore now pass over him in silence, and for the time being also acquit him of this charge.

Yet on this very occasion I again denounce him as guilty of the error that I attributed to him in this same work, Book IV, chapter 10, number 42. For just as that error undoubtedly exists in the printed edition, so too it exists in the author’s autograph and in another manuscript copy, likewise preserved in the Ambrosian Library.

Therefore I see no reason at all to consider a third copy that was recently lent to me by a friend most obliging toward me and also exceedingly learned, abundantly supplied with selected books and other historical materials—namely, John Baptist Blanchinus, this year, 1656, the most deserving consul of justice in this city. In that copy there is absolutely no mention of that provostship or of the metropolitan provost.

For another person, different from the author, deliberately omitted it—as I interpret the matter—because he knew well and accurately the original establishment of that provostship and wished to free Tristanus from the stain of that error.

### IX

I now come at last to Bernardinus Corius, made famous in the mouth of rumor by this very error against clerical celibacy and by the censure rightly pronounced against him.

For in the first part of his Milanese Chronicle, according to the Venetian edition of 1565, page 12 [Col. 0973B], after treating individually the sacred orders of ministers instituted by Saint Ambrose in the Milanese Church, or metropolitan basilica, he ends with these words:

“‘I also appointed many priests, readers, and doorkeepers; and I blessed them all; and I granted them that they might have a virgin wife, and that, when she died, they should thereafter remain widowers, as is clearly read in the First Epistle to Timothy.

“And that this is true is plainly seen from the fact that Heribert of Antimiano, archbishop of Milan, of whom we shall treat at length in the course of the History, had as his wife a noble woman named Useria, who donated to the monastery of Saint Dionysius [the reading should nevertheless be here: “who donated to the monastery of Saint Dionysius”; as Gualvaneus Flamma likewise stated above, in section V] a fruitful vineyard, which to the present day is adjacent there and is called Useria’s Vineyard after her name.

“But afterward, in the course of time, Pope Alexander III [in truth, this pontiff was not the third of that name [Col. 0973C] but the second] ordered that no priest or cleric should take a wife. This was also approved by the sacred council, which added that they should observe chastity perpetually. For this reason, in the year 1062, when Herlembald Cotta wished to persecute married clerics, he was cruelly killed by them. Therefore, as Leo writes in his Annals, since he was regarded as a martyr, the republic had him buried with the greatest reverence in the church dedicated to Saint Dionysius, in a coffin surrounded by iron plates.’”

I have already quoted the testimony that Corius added here concerning Cotta’s sanctity, in Book I, chapter 9.

### X

Thus far we have considered the authors who, by their assertion, claimed that our holy bishop Ambrose granted marriages to priests. We must now show how false and detestable such an assertion is, and how unworthy of a Catholic writer.

To begin here: the Sacred Congregation of the Index long ago condemned this claim in Bernardinus Corius himself, who had first published it in print, and decreed that it should be removed from his Chronicle. This is clear from the following letter, written not long afterward to our cardinal archbishop Federicus Borromeus and preserved among the books of the Ambrosian Library, in these words:

“Most illustrious and most reverend Sir, my most respected lord,

“Since the Sacred Congregation of the Index has considered how desirable and useful is Bernardinus Corius’s book on the History of Milan, which the edict of March 16, 1621, orders not to be permitted unless corrected; and since no other errors have been noted in it except that on folio 12, according to the Venetian printing, it asserts that Saint Ambrose permitted priests to take wives, and on folio 629 it says that the supreme pontiff granted the Milanese Church a plenary indulgence even to the unrepentant [Col. 0974A]—errors that are also found in the old Milanese edition of 1503—the most illustrious gentlemen, my colleagues, have been pleased that I should inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship, as I do by this letter, that, once those two passages alone have been corrected or removed, you may give everyone in your diocese free authority and permission to read and possess that History, and that it may circulate everywhere in that corrected form and even be printed again.

“With this, humbly kissing Your Most Illustrious Lordship’s hands, I offer myself to you wholeheartedly. Rome, October 6, 1621.

“Your Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lordship’s most humble and devoted servant,

“Cardinal Bevilacqua.

“To Cardinal Borromeo, Milan.”

Mention of the foregoing decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Index is also found in the *Index of Prohibited Books*, compiled by Franciscus Magdalenus Capiferreus, secretary of that congregation [Col. 0974B]. Under the letter B it reads:

“Bernardinus Corius’s *Milanese History* is not permitted unless corrected. In the decree of March 16, 1621.”

### XI

How false and spurious this assertion is, Saint Ambrose himself demonstrates through his golden writings, approved throughout the universal Church. He demonstrates it especially in the passage to which Landulf himself appealed above, in section IV.

That passage is without doubt the fiftieth and final chapter of Book I *On Duties*. Accordingly, in another of Landulf’s copies, preserved in the library of the metropolitan chapter, I saw that same chapter marked in a fairly recent hand in the marginal space beside Landulf’s text, together with the following censure, which in my judgment is entirely truthful:

“See the passage wrongly reported and wrongly understood. Hence the greatest corruption of the Ambrosian Church, and the destructive disturbances and complaints expressed throughout this entire book.”

### XII

In that passage, then, Saint Ambrose, after saying much about the virtues necessary in a Levite and minister of the altar, continued in this way:

“But what shall I say about chastity, when only one union is permitted, and it may not be repeated? Therefore, even in marriage itself, the law is not to repeat the marriage, nor to enter into union with a second spouse.”

It is now clear to us how that passage was wrongly reported by Landulf. Let us now examine how it was likewise wrongly understood by him.

The true meaning of Ambrose in this passage is that it is not permissible for an evangelical Levite to be ordained, or promoted to such a sacred order, if he has already repeated a marriage—that is, if after the death of his first wife he has taken another and has therefore become a digamist. He was required to be monogamous only, and thereafter, once promoted, to abstain completely from marital relations; for this is what the law has established.

There is no doubt that Ambrose’s words just quoted refer to this, as do the words that follow and are about to be quoted.

### XIII

For Ambrose proceeds in this sense as follows:

“What seems remarkable to many is why even a repeated marriage before baptism should create impediments to election to office and to the privilege of ordination, when even sins are not usually an obstacle if they have been forgiven through the sacrament of the washing. But we must understand that in baptism guilt can be forgiven, whereas the law cannot be abolished. In marriage there is not guilt but law. Therefore what belongs to guilt is released in baptism; what belongs to law is not dissolved in marriage.”

As Cardinal Robert Bellarmine wisely taught in Book I of *On the Members of the Church Militant*, which is *On Clerics*, chapter 24, section “But as for Jerome”:

“It should be observed that there was a controversy among the ancient Fathers: whether a man who had had one wife before baptism, and after her death took another after baptism, should be considered a digamist or not. For Saint Jerome, in his letter to Oceanus, maintained that such a man was not a digamist, on the grounds that through baptism he had become a new man from the old, and that none of the things he had done before baptism could harm him.

“And indeed the seventeenth Apostolic Canon strongly favors this opinion, since it expressly forbids anyone who has celebrated two marriages after baptism from becoming a bishop. Ambrose, however, together with Innocent and Augustine, in the passages cited, maintained that anyone who had had two wives should be considered a digamist, whether before baptism or after baptism. For baptism washes away sins but does not dissolve marriages; it renews a person with respect to the oldness of vices, but not with respect to things that are rightly ordered.

“This latter opinion ultimately prevailed and was received by the whole Church. Nor does the Apostolic Canon stand in its way. Perhaps at that time, because of the scarcity of men, the apostles dispensed with those who had had one or more wives before baptism, provided that they had not had more than one after baptism. For this command of the Apostle—namely, Paul, in 1 Timothy, chapter 3—is not altogether incapable of dispensation.”

Thus far Bellarmine.

For confirmation of the same opinion, let us also hear Saint Augustine in the passage indicated by Bellarmine himself. In Book 20 of *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, he held the following view:

“They understood this more perceptively who judged that even one who had had another wife as a catechumen or pagan should not be ordained. For the issue concerns a sacrament, not sin, since all sins are forgiven in baptism. Because of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman, even if she was violated while still a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it was not unreasonably judged that a man who had exceeded the single number of wives had not committed some sin, but had forfeited a certain norm of the sacrament—not one necessary for the merit of a good life, but one necessary for the sign of ecclesiastical ordination.”

But let us return from this to Ambrose.

[Col. 0975C] **XIV.** He immediately goes on to ask: “How, then, can one who has himself frequently married be an exhorter to widowhood?” Although this type of argument is directed by Ambrose specifically against those who passed from a first marriage to a second, and who for that reason were denied advancement to the sacred order, Catholic doctors reasonably apply it, by analogy, also to ministers who, after sacred ordination, engage in marital intercourse. Bellarmine, specifically, in Book One of *De clericis*, chapter 19, while listing various impediments that marital intercourse would impose upon priests and other consecrated persons, also lists this one: “Third, it impedes the effectiveness of preaching, as Ambrose teaches in Book One of *De officiis*, at the final chapter. For how will one effectively exhort widows and virgins, who is perpetually occupied with children?” Likewise Gregory of Valencia, in *De caelibatu*, chapter 5: [Col. 0975D] “The use of marriage likewise obstructs the duty of teaching and exhorting. For one who is entangled in marital custom certainly cannot, with sufficiently great effectiveness and authority, exhort virgins and widows, and others among the people who are not yet joined in marriage, to continence, as Saint Ambrose noted in Book One of *De officiis*, at the final chapter.”

**XV.** The words of Ambrose that immediately follow in the same place plainly show how consistent with reason—and indeed how necessary—he judged it to be that sacred ministers, after sacred ordination, should thereafter abstain permanently from marital intercourse, if they had previously married and still had their own wife surviving. “You recognize,” he says, “that the ministry must be presented unoffending and immaculate, and must not be violated by any marital intercourse—you who received the grace of the sacred ministry with body intact, uncorrupted modesty, and estrangement even from marital companionship. I have not passed over this because in many more remote [Col. 0976A] places, while carrying out the ministry or even the priesthood, they fathered children; and they defend this as an ancient custom, on the grounds that when the sacrifice was offered at intervals of days, the people nevertheless were purified for two or three days so that they might approach the sacrifice pure, as we read in the Old Testament: ‘And he washed his garments.’” Ambrose immediately refutes this pretext with the following argument: “If there was such observance in the figure, how much greater must there be in the reality? Learn, priest and Levite, what it means to wash your garments, so that you may present a clean body for the celebration of the sacraments. If the people were forbidden to approach their sacrifice without washing their garments (Exod. 19), do you, unwashed alike in mind and body, dare to intercede for others, dare to minister for others?”

**XVI.** Thus far, then, we have sufficiently examined that earlier passage of Saint Ambrose which Landulphus misappropriated as testimony in support of his error. Let us now see how this same holy doctor explicitly expressed the same opinion in other places as well. [Col. 0976B]

**XVII.** Certainly, in *De dignitate sacerdotali*, chapter 4, explaining the words of the Apostle Paul in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3—“The bishop must be the husband of one wife”—he writes as follows:

“If we look only to the surface of the letter (that is, to the literal sense), it forbids a bigamous man to be ordained bishop. But if we ascend to the higher (that is, the mystical) sense, it forbids a bishop to usurp two Churches. And if you search still further inward into deeper matters, it warns that, after the Catholic doctrine, the bishop must not be found to possess a heretical belief, but must associate with himself only a Christian, orthodox, and Catholic faith, so that the bishop may be called the husband of only one wife—that is, of the Catholic Church.”

A little later, explaining the further statement found there from the same Apostle—“To rule his own household well, having his children submissive with all chastity”—he likewise says:

“He can rule his household well who has preserved the chastity of his body. ‘His household,’ he says—that is, he should rule his own [Col. 0976C] body by such a right that it is not subjected to its own will, lest, given over to the desire of lust, he plunge headlong into destruction; rather, by his example of chastity, he should teach his children the rule of purity. For if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? This is what we said above: He who cannot cultivate the house of his own heart—how will he care for the many?”

**XVIII.** Again, in the letter to the Church of Vercelli—which, according to the Roman edition corrected by Pope Sixtus V while he was still a cardinal and later commended by a papal diploma, is the twenty-fifth letter of Book Three of the *Epistles*—he writes:

“I have set down what I have learned must be avoided. The Apostle, however, is the teacher of virtues. While he teaches that contradictors are to be reproved with patience, and commands that a man be the husband of one wife, he does not thereby exclude one who is without [Col. 0976D] marriage—for that would be a command above the law—but so that he may preserve the grace of his cleansing through marital chastity, and so that he may not again be invited by apostolic authority to beget children in the priesthood. For he said ‘having children,’ not ‘begetting them,’ and not repeating marriage.

“I have not passed over this because many argue as follows: that ‘the husband of one wife’ refers to one taken after baptism, since baptism washed away the fault that had constituted an impediment. Indeed, all vices and sins are washed away, so that if someone had defiled his body with many women to whom he was joined by no law of marriage, all this is forgiven him; but marriages are not dissolved if someone has repeated marriage. For the guilt is removed by the washing, not the law. There is no guilt in marriage, but there is a law. Therefore what belongs to the law is not forgiven as guilt, but retained as law.

“Thus the Apostle also established the law, saying: ‘If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife.’ Therefore he who is without blame, the husband of one wife, is bound by the law concerning the reception of the priesthood; but he who has repeated [Col. 0977A] marriage has no guilt of defilement, yet is stripped of the prerogative of the priest.

“We have stated what belongs to the law; let us also state what belongs to reason. But first let us recognize that the Apostle established this not only concerning a bishop and presbyter, but that the Fathers, in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, also added that no cleric should be one who had contracted a second marriage. For how can he console a widow, honor her, and exhort her to preserve widowhood and remain faithful to her husband, when he himself did not preserve fidelity to his first marriage? Or what difference would there be between the people and the priest if they were bound by the same laws? The priest’s life ought to outweigh that of others, just as his grace does. For he who binds others by his precepts ought himself to observe the lawful precepts.”

Thus far Saint Ambrose in that letter.

**XIX.** I now proceed to the prayer which Ambrose himself first composed in order to prepare himself and his fellow priests for the celebration of the most sacred sacrifice of the Mass. This prayer is also read near the end of the fifth [Col. 0977B] volume of his works—that is, before his hymns. There, not far from the beginning, he poured out the following prayers to God:

“King of virtues, God who loves chastity and integrity, extinguish in my body, by the heavenly dew of your blessing, the whole burning fuel of lust, so that the condition of complete chastity of soul and body may remain in me. Put to death in me the goads of the flesh and every stirring of lust, and grant me true and perpetual chastity, together with your other gifts that please you in truth, so that with chaste body and pure heart I may be able to offer you the sacrifice of praise.

“For with what contrition of heart and fountain of tears, Lord Jesus Christ, with what reverence and trembling, with what bodily chastity and purity of spirit, must this divine and heavenly sacrifice be celebrated—where your flesh is truly received, where your blood is truly drunk, where the highest things are joined to the lowest, where the presence [Col. 0977C] of the holy angels is present, where you are wonderfully and ineffably constituted both Priest and Sacrifice! Who could worthily celebrate this unless you, almighty God, made the one offering it worthy?”

**XX.** Finally, in testimony to the same truth that we are defending, we must also bring forward the commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul, which are more commonly attributed to Saint Ambrose and which, in the Roman and more carefully corrected edition mentioned above, are also numbered among his genuine works.

In the commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, at the words of chapter 3, “The bishop must be the husband of one wife,” he interprets them in precisely this way:

“Although it has not been forbidden to have a second wife numerically, nevertheless, if someone is to be worthy of the episcopate, he must reject even what is lawful, because of the sublimity of that order; for the one who desires that office must be better than the rest.”

A little later, at the words, “Let deacons be the husbands of one [Col. 0977D] wife,” he continues:

“What he had said more briefly concerning the ordination of deacons he now adds. He also shows that they must be husbands of one wife, so that those may be chosen for the ministry of God who have not departed from God’s ordinance. For God decreed one wife for man, with whom he might be blessed; no one is blessed with a second wife.

“If he has governed his children and his households well—that is, his servants or domestic dependents—they may become worthy of the priesthood and have confidence before God, knowing that they can obtain what they ask, while henceforth restraining themselves from intercourse with women.

“For this reason the practice of having wives was formerly permitted to Levites or priests: they had much time free from ministry or priestly service. There was a multitude of priests and a great abundance of Levites, and each served the divine ceremonies at a fixed time according to David’s institution. He established twenty-four classes of priests, so that they might serve by turns. Thus Abijah belonged to the eighth class, in whose turn Zechariah [Col. 0978A] served as priest (Luke 1), as is contained in Chronicles; and so, during the time when it was not their turn to serve at the altar, they attended to their households.

“But when the time of ministry approached, they purified themselves for several days and came to the temple to offer sacrifice to God. Now, however, there ought to be seven deacons and several presbyters, so that there may be two in each church, and one bishop in the city; and consequently all must abstain from association with women, because it is necessary for them to be present in the church every day, without having time afterward to purify themselves lawfully, as the ancients did.

“For an offering must be made every week, and, if not daily for strangers, at least twice a week for residents; nor are there lacking sick people who are baptized almost every day. The former were permitted this because they were not seen in the temple for a long period, but were private persons.

“For if Saint Paul commands laymen to abstain for a time for the sake of prayer, so that they may devote themselves to prayer (1 Cor. [Col. 0978B] 7), how much more should Levites and priests, who must pray day and night for the people entrusted to them, do so? They must therefore be purer than the rest, because they are God’s ministers.”

**XXI.** Thus speaks our most holy bishop Ambrose in these commentaries—provided, that is, that he truly is their author. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine certainly assumed this as established and beyond doubt in Book One of *De clericis*, chapter 19, under the section “Ambrose,” when he alluded to the preceding text, and again in chapter 20, under “But as for this.” Yet in *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis* he evidently held a different opinion. For, when discussing Saint Ambrose of Milan under the year 374, or composing an observation concerning his works, he concluded as follows:

“In the fifth volume are the Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul. Many do not believe them to be by Ambrose, and not without reason.”

On this subject I may consult Alfonso Salmeron, volume 13 of his *Commentaries*, which is the first on all of the blessed [Col. 0978C] Paul’s Epistles and the Catholic Epistles, specifically Book One, disputation 19; and Cornelius à Lapide, in his commentaries on all the Epistles of Saint Paul, in the section at the beginning of the work where he discusses the interpreters of Saint Paul’s Epistles, page 24, and on chapter 7 and verse 11 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

I also remember having read many years ago a substantial short work on the same subject, published separately, composed by Nicolaus Rusca, and approved by Cardinal Baronius. When I lent it—as has often happened to me—to a certain religious man of the Order of Preachers, who was also related to the Rusca family, I lost it.

That Nicolaus Rusca was a doctor of sacred theology, archpriest of Sondrio in the Valtellina, especially dear to our cardinal archbishop Federico Borromeo, and a very close friend of mine, as well as a most zealous defender of the Catholic faith. For this reason he was eventually put to death most unjustly by the heretics in the year of our Lord 1618. His [Col. 0978D] life and death, written in Latin by Giovanni Battista Bojacha, a lawyer of Como, and published at Como by its printers in 1621, are in circulation, as is also a book by Nicolaus himself, published in 1598, containing the proceedings of the Tirano disputation against Calvin and the ministers who defended Calvin.

But let us return to the proper subject of the present chapter. In support of his own opinion and that of others, Bellarmine collects many causes and arguments. Among them he expressly lists this one in third place: that, among the many matters which the author of these Commentaries explained contrary to Saint Ambrose’s opinion, he interprets in the Commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy the words “King of the ages, immortal, etc.” in a manner plainly contrary to the way Ambrose himself truly interpreted them in Book Two of *De fide*, chapters 1 and 3, and in Book Three, chapter 2.

But what if those Commentaries really were composed by Saint Ambrose, [Col. 0979A] though later corrupted in some places by another person? Perhaps this occurred specifically in those passages which Bellarmine and others of the same opinion criticize, but not in the passage that I cited above, since it plainly agrees with the other works attributed to our Ambrose without dispute and corrupted by no one.

Accordingly, if anyone should insist on arguing the point stubbornly and contend doggedly that those Commentaries can in no way be attributed to our Ambrose, I shall not now strongly resist him. For the purposes of the present question and chapter, the other passages drawn from the places cited above are sufficient for me, as I shall shortly undertake to show in summary.

**XXII.** They contain these three parts: namely, a literal exposition of those words of Saint Paul by which it was prescribed that the bishop should be the husband of one wife; abstention from marital intercourse after the sacred order has been received; and the difference [Col. 0979B] between the ministers of the Old and New Testaments. These parts are more than sufficient for my present purpose.

**XXIII.** According to Ambrose’s exposition, therefore, Saint Paul prescribed in that Epistle that a man who, after the death of his first wife, had taken another should not be admitted to the episcopate or the diaconate.

Bellarmine, in Book One of *De clericis*, chapter 23, while examining the true understanding of these words of Saint Paul, did not hesitate to affirm:

“The judgment of the Catholic Church has always taught that those words of blessed Paul must be understood in such a way that it is forbidden to initiate into sacred orders those who in any manner have been bigamous. We can prove this opinion by three arguments.”

He then proves it most effectively: first from Sacred Scripture; second from the time at which Saint Paul wrote these things; and third from the authority of the Fathers, who always understood this passage concerning monogamy in such a way that a man who has had two wives, even at different times, may not be made bishop or [Col. 0979C] deacon.

Among these Fathers, after Tertullian and Saint Epiphanius, he also makes use of Ambrose’s testimony. His words are as follows:

“Tertullian, in Book One *To His Wife*: How greatly second marriages detract from faith and hinder holiness, the discipline of the Church and the Apostle’s prescription declare, when they do not permit bigamists to preside and do not allow a widow to be chosen for ordination unless she is a woman of one husband.”

Bellarmine immediately adds to these words of Tertullian:

“There is no doubt that by ‘bigamists’ he means those who have had two wives, not simultaneously but one after another. For he speaks of this digamy throughout the entire book; indeed, he exhorts his wife not to enter a second marriage after his death. He says similar things in *De monogamia* and in *De exhortatione castitatis*.”

A little later he writes:

“Epiphanius, *Against the Cathars*, heresy 50: Those requirements handed down concerning the priesthood, because of the excellence of the celebration of the sacred [Col. 0979D] rites, the Cathars thought applied equally to everyone, when they heard that the bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, and continent; and likewise the deacon and presbyter. For holy preaching of God truly does not admit, after the coming of Christ, those who, after their wife has died, have joined themselves to a second marriage, because of the eminent honor and dignity of the priesthood. And this the holy Church of God certainly observes with sincerity.”

He speaks here most clearly of the successive digamy of several wives, calling those men digamists who, after the death of one wife, take another, and criticizing the Cathars, who from this passage of Paul also forbade second marriages to laypeople.

From this Bellarmine proceeds to the testimony of Saint Ambrose:

“Ambrose, in Book X, Letter 82, to the Church of Vercelli, treating this passage of Paul, ‘the husband of one wife’: ‘He who has repeated marriage,’ he says, ‘has no guilt of defilement, but is stripped of the prerogative of the priest.’”

And a little later:

“Ambrose says similar things in Book One of *De officiis*, at the final chapter, and in *De dignitate sacerdotali*, chapter 4.” [Col. 0980A]

**XXIV.** The second part, briefly drawn by me from those indisputable testimonies of Ambrose, was this: even monogamous men who had been promoted to sacred orders while their wives were still alive ought nevertheless thereafter to abstain permanently from marital intercourse.

This in particular plainly refutes the use of marriage that prevailed in Ariald’s time among the Milanese clergy as well as among the Greeks. What the practice was then among the Milanese we have already seen in chapter 3, number 1, of the present fourth book. What it was likewise among the Greeks at that time, I do not regret having learned long ago from the learned Bellarmine’s Book One of *De clericis*, nor am I now ashamed to quote his words on the subject.

When, in chapter 19, he was arguing that celibacy was most rightly attached to sacred orders by apostolic law, so that after ordination it is not permitted either to marry or to use wives previously married, [Col. 0980B] by positive law—though a most ancient and equitable one, and one that ought by no means to be relaxed in our time—he then set out two errors for refutation, one of the Greeks and the other of the Lutherans.

Concerning the error of the Greeks he says:

“The first error is that clerics ought to marry wives before receiving sacred orders, because after receiving sacred orders they may not do so, and one who lives without a wife exposes himself to too great a danger of fornication. Some make Nicolaus, one of the first seven deacons, the author of this error. But whatever the truth of that may be, it is certain that Vigilantius explicitly taught this error. Concerning him blessed Jerome says at the beginning of his book against Vigilantius: ‘Woe to the crime! He is said to have bishops as partners in his wickedness—if indeed those are to be called bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives, trusting no celibate person’s chastity.’”

Bellarmine then continues: [Col. 0980C]

“The Fathers of the Council of Trullo adopted this error around the year of our Lord 700, as is clear from canon 13, where that profane synod expressly condemns the canons of the Roman Church and establishes the contrary—namely, that clerics should marry wives before the subdiaconate and afterward live with them while established in sacred orders.

“At the time of this synod the practice of the Greeks that now exists began. It was increased and confirmed in the time of Leo IX, when the division of the Greeks from the Latins grew most sharply in many other articles as well. Hence there exists a book written at that time by Cardinal Humbert on this matter against Nicetas the abbot, who then defended the Greek custom with great vehemence.”

Later he adds: [Col. 0980D]

“The Trullan Synod, in canon 6, prohibits bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons from marrying a wife after their ordination, and in canon 48 commands that a bishop not cohabit with his wife.”

In the same chapter Bellarmine later concludes:

“The custom of the Greeks that they now have did not exist during the first six hundred years, as is clear from the same authors—of whom I have already produced many—and also from Chrysostom, Jerome, and Leo in the places cited.”

Again, in chapter 21:

“To the third objection I reply that those canons belong to no approved council. For the true Sixth Synod issued no canons, as is clear from the Seventh Synod, sessions 4 and 5. But after the Sixth Synod certain bishops assembled at Constantinople, in the palace of the emperor Justinian II, which was called the Trullus, and issued these canons in the name of the Sixth Synod.

“Moreover, not only did no Roman pontiff approve these canons, but Pope Sergius, who was then seated, openly disapproved them, as Bede writes in *De sex aetatibus*, under Justinian, and Paul the Deacon in Book VIII, chapter 9, of *De rebus Romanis*. Bede calls the assembly of those Fathers who issued these canons an errant synod.”

A little later, concerning this Trullan Synod, he adds:

“It does not permit any [Col. 0981A] cleric to marry after receiving sacred orders, but only permits the use of a wife taken before ordination. And even this it does not permit to bishops, but only to lower clerics, as is clear from canons 6, 12, and 48.”

Thus far Bellarmine for our present purpose, so that it might be clearly understood what the use of marriage among the Greeks was in the time of our Ariald, and how consistent it then was with the practice of the Milanese clergy.

Now consider how Bellarmine argued against such a use of marriage, whether among the Latin or Greek clergy, using the testimony of our own Ambrose, in that same chapter 19, after he had brought forward many other Greek and Latin Fathers against that practice:

“Ambrose, in Book One of *De officiis*, at the final chapter: ‘You recognize,’ he says, ‘that the ministry must be presented unoffending and immaculate, and must not be violated by any marital intercourse—you who received the grace of the sacred ministry with body intact, uncorrupted modesty, and estrangement even [Col. 0981B] from marital companionship. I have not passed over this because in many more remote places, while carrying out the ministry or even the priesthood, they fathered children.’

“The same in Letter 82 to the Church of Vercelli: ‘Having children,’ he says, ‘the Apostle said, not begetting them,’ and so forth.

“And in the first chapter—more accurately, the third—of the First Epistle to Timothy: ‘Henceforth,’ he says, ‘they are to abstain from intercourse with women,’ and so forth.”

For Bellarmine counted such a Commentary on this Epistle of Saint Paul among the genuine offspring of our Ambrose, as I also observed above.

**XXV.** It is worthwhile, together with Bellarmine, to examine also that third part in Ambrose’s testimonies which I indicated, and to reason from it together with him.

In that chapter 19, when he had collected many statements from the New Testament in support of the celibacy of clerics, which he had undertaken to prove, he also confirmed his proof as follows:

“Moreover, in the Old Testament we see that continence [Col. 0981C] from wives was especially required of those who were about to draw near to God or handle some sacred matter. For in Exodus 12 it is prescribed that those who are to eat the paschal lamb should gird up their loins; by this, as Gregory explains in Homily 22 on the Gospels, it was signified that those who eat the paschal lamb ought to subdue the pleasure of the flesh.

“In Exodus 19, when the people were about to receive the law from God, Moses said to them: ‘Be ready for the third day, and do not approach your wives.’ Ambrose uses this testimony in Book One of *De officiis*, at the final chapter, to prove the continence of clerics.”

This is precisely what we are concerned with here; nevertheless, together with Bellarmine, let us proceed to a fuller proof. He adds:

“Likewise, in Exodus 28 God commanded that Aaron and his sons, when they entered the tabernacle, should be covered with linen undergarments from the loins to the thighs. Bede explains in Book Three of *De tabernaculo*, [Col. 0981D] chapter 9, that this signified that the priests of the New Testament ought either to be virgins or to have dissolved the covenants made with their wives.

“Likewise, in First Kings, chapter 21, the priest Ahimelech was unwilling to give David the bread of the Presence to eat until he had first learned that David had abstained from his wife for some time. From this blessed Jerome deduces, in his commentary on the first chapter of Titus, that perpetual continence from wives is required of priests who consecrate, eat, and distribute to others the body of Christ, which was signified by that bread of the Presence.

“Finally, from First Chronicles, chapter 24, and Luke 1, it is gathered that the priests of the Old Testament were accustomed to minister in their appointed turns and, throughout the entire time during which they ministered in the tabernacle, to remain away from home and wife. From this Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himericus, and Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius, as well as Bede in his commentary on the first chapter of Luke, conclude that if those priests abstained from their wives during the time when they ministered, then it is altogether fitting that our priests, who minister not by turns but continually, should continually abstain from their [Col. 0982A] wives.”

Thus Bellarmine in that place.

**XXVI.** Since those indisputable testimonies of Saint Ambrose contain this teaching, and since it is simultaneously assumed as certain that he never judged otherwise concerning the celibacy of sacred ministers—whether Greek or our own—than he clearly and expressly judged in his books, it necessarily follows that anyone who nevertheless contends that he favored the marriages ever practiced by Greek or even by our own priests cannot escape the charge of inexcusable rashness and impudence.

For that divine doctor denies—and denies precisely—that such marriages were approved by the holy Apostle Paul if they had been contracted by those who were soon to be promoted to Sacred Order. He denies that their use is lawful for those promoted to Sacred Order, and likewise denies that their use is compatible with the ministry proper to the New Testament, which is far greater in dignity and holiness than the ministry of the Old [Col. 0982B] Testament.

These points are already entirely clear from Ambrose’s own words quoted above. But they will become somewhat clearer still if we examine more minutely and accurately the assertions of the historians whom we previously set against him.

**XXVII.** Datius first asserted that Ambrose had been appointed arbiter of that dispute by the Fathers of the council assembled in the city of Constantinople, which he himself also attended at that time.

By the name of that council he could certainly have meant nothing other than the ecumenical Council of Constantinople, which, as Baronius correctly calculates, was celebrated in the year of our Lord 381, and which was attended in that city, beyond all controversy, by 150 bishops.

Yet it is equally certain on the contrary that neither Pope Damasus nor our Ambrose attended it; only Eastern bishops were present, and consequently no one other than those Eastern bishops ultimately [Col. 0982C] subscribed to it. For that council was indeed convened by the authority of Pope Damasus—whether through his letters, transmitted by the emperor Theodosius the Elder to the Eastern bishops—but Damasus himself did not go there, nor did anyone else from the Western bishops.

This is attested with the greatest certainty by the unanimous agreement of all the ecclesiastical historians of that period. Accordingly, Bellarmine, in Book One of *De conciliis et Ecclesia*, chapter 5, after counting this Council of Constantinople as the second among the general councils approved by the Roman pontiff, adds:

“It must be observed that no one from the Western provinces was present at this council. For Pope Damasus had convened a synod of Westerners at Rome and had invited to that place the bishops who had assembled at Constantinople, so that in this way a most complete council might be celebrated at Rome. But because the Eastern Fathers could not come to Rome for legitimate reasons, Damasus accepted their excuse, and the two synods were united in mind and judgment as though they had been one and the same. Because of this union, the Council of Constantinople was regarded as one of the ecumenical and legitimate synods. See Theodoret, Book One of the *History*, chapters 9 and 10.”

Thus Bellarmine. Baronius, however, in the year of Christ 382, held a somewhat different view concerning the excuse of the Easterners.

Ambrose therefore was not actually present there, and consequently the Fathers of that council did not reserve the judgment of that dispute to him alone.

**XXVIII.** Moreover, no ancient writer is ever read to have asserted that such a dispute was raised at that council.
