Even if it had been raised there, and Ambrose himself had likewise been present, it does not seem credible that the Fathers would have wished to reserve this judgment to him alone, since otherwise it concerned a very serious matter. [Col. 0983A] Just as they unanimously enacted decrees concerning certain other matters of lesser importance, so they would likewise all have judged that question together.

But let us proceed from this to the argument by which Ambrose was said by Datius to have been moved to pronounce a judgment in favor of married priests.

**XXIX.** “The perfection of life,” he says, “consists not in chastity but in charity.”

A plainly irrational statement, and one utterly unworthy of Ambrose—and, as something he would have regarded as completely worthless, also something he in fact treated as completely worthless!

Why, then, did Ambrose not similarly, for the same reason, grant permission to virgins who wished to be admitted to the sacred veil to contract marriage once? For, according to that statement of the Apostle, just as the perfection of life does not consist in chastity, neither does it consist in virginity, but in charity.

Why, moreover, did he not grant even to sacred ministers permission not merely to marry once, but also a second and third time, indeed as often as it was lawful for laypeople? For the perfection of life, according to that statement of the Apostle, consists in charity at all times—not only during the period of a man’s first [Col. 0983B] marriage—but never in chastity.
, which otherwise would concern a matter of truly grave importance [Col. 0983A]. For just as they had unanimously issued decrees concerning certain other matters of lesser importance, so also they would all together have decided that question. But let us proceed from this point to the reasoning by which Ambrose, as Datius was said to have been moved, pronounced a judgment in favor of married priests.

### XXIX

“Perfection of life,” he says, “consists not in chastity but in charity.” A plainly irrational statement, and utterly unworthy of Ambrose; and, just as it was something he evidently regarded as completely worthless, so too it was something he actually made completely worthless! Why, otherwise, did Ambrose, for the same reason, not likewise grant permission to virgins who wished to be admitted to the sacred veil to marry once? For, according to the Apostle, just as perfection of life does not consist in chastity, so neither does it consist in virginity, but in charity. Why, moreover, did he not grant even to sacred ministers that they might marry not merely once, but also a second and a third time, indeed as often as it was lawful for laymen to do so? For perfection of life, according to the Apostle, consists in charity not only during the time of their first marriage, but at every time, and not in chastity [Col. 0983B].

### XXX

Before, however, we press Datius more sharply with consequences of this kind, it will certainly be most convenient and useful to explain clearly how, according to the truth of the matter and according to the judgment of the Apostle Paul, the perfection of spiritual life consists in charity.

Bellarmin, in the second book of *On the Members of the Church Militant*, which is *On Monks*, chapter 2, taught this very aptly:

“Certain points must be noted here. First, true perfection consists in charity. For the perfection of each thing lies in its being joined as closely as possible to its ultimate end. The end of man is God; but charity unites man with God most of all, according to 1 John 4: ‘He who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him’; and according to Colossians 3: ‘Charity is the bond of perfection,’ that is, the bond which, by binding man to God, makes man perfect; or, as Chrysostom explains it, the bond which, by binding and holding together all the virtues in man, makes man perfect.

“For just as the human spirit binds and holds together all the humors and parts which would otherwise disperse, so the Holy Spirit, dwelling in our hearts through charity, holds together all the virtues, which would otherwise easily disperse. The same Apostle also shows this when he says, in 1 Corinthians 13: ‘Charity is patient, is kind,’ and what follows.

“Thus Irenaeus, in the fifth book, shortly before the middle, explaining the Apostle’s statement in 1 Thessalonians 5, ‘that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved whole,’ says that the perfect man consists of three things: body, soul, and the Holy Spirit dwelling in him through charity. For just as, if body or soul is lacking, he is imperfect in the order of nature, so, if charity is lacking, he is imperfect in the order of morality.

“Nearly all the Greeks understand Paul’s passage in this way as well: Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Theophylact; and with them Jerome, in his letter to Hedibia, at the last question.

“Finally, it is clear that charity is Christian perfection from the fact that everything is referred to it. Matthew 22: ‘On these two commandments depend the whole Law,’ and 1 Timothy 1: ‘The end of the commandment is charity.’” [Col. 0983C–D]

### XXXI

He then continues as follows:

“Note secondly, from blessed Thomas in his short work *On Perfection*, that there are four degrees of charity and therefore also four degrees of perfection. For that is called perfect which lacks nothing in relation to some end. Hence it is not contradictory for something to be perfect and imperfect if it is compared with different degrees or even different ends.”

### XXXII

He assigns these degrees or ends as follows. But since the first does not pertain to any creature, and the second does not pertain to man’s present life, I therefore pass them over and turn to the third and fourth.

“‘The third degree,’ Bellarmin therefore adds, ‘is to love God not as much as he is lovable, nor as much as any creature can love him absolutely, but as much as a mortal creature can love him after removing from itself all impediments to divine love and consecrating itself wholly to God’s service. Those who are at this degree are imperfect in comparison with the blessed, but perfect in comparison with other human beings, including the just and devout.’”

### XXXIII

And again:

“‘The fourth degree,’ he concludes, ‘is to love God not as much as he is lovable, nor as much as a creature can love him either absolutely or in this life, but nevertheless in such a way that one loves nothing equally with or more than God—that is, one admits nothing contrary to this love. This degree is commanded to everyone and possesses a certain perfection, although in comparison with the higher degrees it is imperfect.

“‘Hence 1 John 2 says: “He who keeps his word, truly in him the charity of God is perfect.” Yet in Matthew 19 the Lord says to the one who declared that he had kept all the commandments: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything,” and so forth. John is speaking of this fourth degree; the Lord, however, of the third.’” [Col. 0984A–B]

### XXXIV

With these points thus prefaced by us, if we now ask in what sense Ambrose, in Datius’s opinion, asserted that perfection of life consists not in chastity but in charity, according to that testimony of the Apostle Paul—a testimony so clear and authoritative in support of the virtue of charity, indeed of charity as queen of the virtues—Datius could certainly give no other answer than that Ambrose was speaking of the perfection of life necessary for each person’s eternal salvation, and that he was therefore speaking of charity according only to that degree of perfection which Bellarmin had just placed in the fourth degree.

Certainly, approved interpreters unanimously explain that passage of the Apostle in precisely this way; and Ambrose himself explained it no differently, both in the *Commentary*—if it is really his, as I qualified it in section 21—and in book 4, letter 33, near the end, where he writes to the sacred virgin Demetrias.

If, therefore, Ambrose had argued from that passage of the Apostle in the manner Datius claimed, he would plainly have supposed no other kind of perfection to be necessary in the sacred ministers of the New Testament than that which was necessary in every layperson in order to attain eternal salvation.

Unless he supposed this, his argument would plainly have been most deserving of laughter and derision. For it could have been answered immediately and irresistibly that the perfection of such ministers belonged to a higher order than that of laymen, and that it consisted not in chastity alone but in charity together with chastity, just as it unquestionably consists in charity together with virginity; and that, by Datius’s own admission—for this cannot be denied by him, if only he is willing to be consistent with himself and to suppose Ambrose consistent with himself—after the death of the first wife of those ministers, it consists in charity together with chastity, or with abstinence thereafter from the use of the marital office [Col. 0984C–D].

Therefore, with regard to that first marriage of the ministers of the New Testament, the reasoning drawn from that testimony of the Apostle has no force whatsoever, unless it is meanwhile supposed that their perfection was of no higher order than the perfection necessary even for all laymen to attain eternal salvation.

But Ambrose does not suppose anything of the kind—not even provisionally. On the contrary, he certainly supposes the opposite, as we have already seen from section 12 and many subsequent passages. It is therefore reasonable not to believe that he argued in the way Datius attributed to him; and in this respect he would have been foolish, inept, and insufficiently consistent with himself.

### XXXV

Would anyone of sound mind further believe that Ambrose was so disposed as to dare to issue such a law in favor of married priests, one that would contradict the decrees of the holy apostles and of the sacred First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea? That the celibacy of sacred ministers was prescribed by the apostles themselves may be shown by the canons of the apostles, cited by Clement I, pope. Their twenty-seventh canon reads:

“We command that those who have been advanced to the clergy while unmarried may, if they wish, take wives; but only readers and singers.”

After citing this canon, Bellarmin, in book 1 of *On Clerics*, chapter 19, added:

“What is said concerning readers and singers is to be understood also of the other minor orders, since the same reasoning applies to all.”

Consequently, conversely, according to the sound understanding of this canon, all unmarried men who had been promoted to sacred orders were forbidden to take wives.

This understanding also agrees perfectly with the sixth canon of those same apostles, which prescribed:

“Let a bishop, presbyter, or deacon not cast out his wife under the pretext of religion. But if he casts her out, let him be separated; and if he persists, let him be deposed.” [Col. 0985A–B]

This canon concerned bishops, presbyters, and deacons who had taken wives before ordination and who therefore ought carefully and religiously to guard against using them thereafter. Thus, lest under the pretext of religion—or of that precaution which was otherwise necessary because of the law of celibacy—they should abandon responsibility for their wives, fail meanwhile to support them, or fail to provide the other necessities of life, this canon was established, as learned men have wisely affirmed. Severinus Binius also lists many of them in the first volume of the *Councils* published by him, in his notes on this same canon.

Pope Calixtus I, who governed the Roman Church from the year of the Lord 221 to 226, likewise supports the same position. For in Gratian, distinction 27, chapter *Presbyters*, he says:

“We entirely forbid presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and monks to have concubines or to contract marriages; and we judge that marriages contracted by persons of this kind are to be dissolved, in accordance with the definitions of the sacred canons.”

Gregory of Valencia, in his book *On Celibacy*, chapter 3, aptly observes concerning this passage, among other theologians:

“In this passage, since Calixtus, himself an ancient pontiff, cites even older sacred canons in support of this matter, there is an argument that this law of celibacy is apostolic.”

The same conclusion is also sufficiently clear from the testimonies of sacred councils, Roman pontiffs, and the ancient Fathers, which Catholic teachers collected in defense of the same celibacy against heretics, especially Bellarmin in book 1 of *On Clerics*, chapter 19.

Of these testimonies I now wish to present just one: that of the Council of Carthage, more commonly numbered the Second. Baronius discusses it under the year of Christ 397, and Binius, in the first volume of the *Councils*, page 541, states that it was celebrated during the time of Pope Celestine I—who held office from the year of Christ 423 to 432—and approved by Pope Leo IV, in chapter *On Booklets*, distinction 20. The words of that council, canon 2, were:

“It pleases all that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and those who handle the sacraments, guardians of chastity, should also abstain from their wives, so that we too may observe what the apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved.”

Thus we see that the law of celibacy for sacred ministers was enacted by the holy apostles and likewise observed from ancient times [Col. 0985C–D].

### XXXVI

As time went on, however, there were some who deviated to a certain extent from that ancient and apostolic discipline, particularly in the Eastern Church. For this reason, several councils of that same Church successively attempted, through various decrees, to restore the discipline to practice.

### XXXVII

The Council of Ancyra presents itself first. It was assembled at Ancyra, in the province of Galatia, in the year of the Lord 314; eighteen bishops, eminent men, were present—as Baronius rightly observed under that year, sections 77 and 78—as were many of them later at the Council of Neocaesarea, and most of them at Nicaea. We shall speak of those councils shortly.

After the Council of Ancyra had enacted various canons for receiving into Catholic communion those who had fallen away from the Catholic faith during the persecution of the tyrant Maximinus, it decreed in canon 9, or 10 in another numbering, as Baronius expresses it under that year, section 88:

“After such remedies had been supplied to the lapsed, the Fathers added other rules for preserving ecclesiastical discipline without corruption, especially that rule which seemed to concern the sacred ministers of the Church above all: that they should lead a celibate life without a wife. By this law, as has been said elsewhere, not only priests but also deacons had been bound from the very beginning of the nascent Church.

“They wished to exempt from this rule only those deacons who, when they were ordained unwillingly, had likewise declared that they could not live continently and therefore wished to take a wife. Whoever had protested in this way and nevertheless had been ordained—the Fathers agreed that such a person could take a wife after receiving the sacred order of the diaconate—establishing the following rule, in canon 9, or 10:

“‘If any deacons who are ordained declared at the time of ordination and stated that they wished to be joined in marriage because they could not remain as they were, let them remain in the ministry if they subsequently take wives, since the bishop had given them permission. But all who remained silent and accepted the laying on of hands, professing continence, and were afterward bound by marriage, must cease from the ministry.’” [Col. 0986A–C]

Thus far Baronius, following the edition of Dionysius Exiguus. He then adds:

“‘The second edition adds’”—the edition which Baronius himself had said in the preceding section 81 was by an uncertain author—“‘that they receive communion only as laymen.’”

From these words Baronius observes:

“Namely, no longer with the sacred ministers, but with the people outside the rails.”

Finally he concludes:

“From this you may see how firm, stable, and universally affirmed the celibacy of sacred ministers was both throughout the universal Catholic Church and in the East. These matters were treated at greater length in the first volume of the *Annals*.”

The Fathers of the Council of Ancyra, then, as I too may finally conclude here according to my own judgment, supposed that there was an established law forbidding the use of marriage to sacred ministers generally, although the bishop could relax it in the manner prescribed by them, so that such men were permitted to make use of marriage only under those conditions [Col. 0986D].

### XXXVIII

“After Ancyra,” Baronius continues under the same year 314, section 90, “the Council of Neocaesarea was celebrated. In what year, however, we do not know. But, as far as conjecture can determine, since nearly all the bishops who attended the Council of Ancyra are likewise recorded as having subscribed to the council celebrated at Neocaesarea, including, among others, Basil, bishop of Amasea, whom we said, in the persecution of Licinius that followed shortly afterward, to have suffered martyrdom, it is plainly necessary to affirm that not long after Ancyra nearly the same bishops again assembled at Neocaesarea, before Licinius began to afflict the Eastern Church with persecution.”

A little later he says:

“At Neocaesarea in Pontus, whose bishop at that time was the renowned Longinus, as was recently mentioned, when those most holy Fathers were holding their assembly, they considered nothing more important than to safeguard the integrity of the priests’ lives. Therefore, concerning their leading a celibate life, they established the following, in accordance with the ancient custom of the Church, in canon 1:

“‘If a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order. But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled altogether and subjected to penance.’

“These words are from the version of Dionysius.”

As for the reason for this decree, at least in its first part, I interpret it as follows: some of the deacons who had been granted permission to marry at the Council of Ancyra were reserving the exercise of that permission for the time when they had also received the priesthood. The Fathers therefore judged such marriages unseemly for an order already assumed and consequently forbade marriages of that kind [Col. 0987A].

### XXXIX

The 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia in the year 325 for the sacred and holy Ecumenical Council were not satisfied with these decrees of provincial councils, by which something had been relaxed from that ancient and apostolic discipline of sacred ministers. For, while not permitting such ministers to live with their wives, they also unanimously denied all of them the celebration and use of marriage.

The third canon of that council reads verbatim:

“The great synod altogether forbade that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy should have a woman introduced into the household, unless perhaps she were his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escaped suspicion.”

Why should we not, together with Bellarmin in book 1 of *On Clerics*, chapter 19, argue from these words in the following way?

“No mention is made of a wife, who nevertheless should have been placed first if it were lawful to live with her. Again, why is cohabitation with women forbidden to clerics if they may be married? Can they not have wives as servants in the same house?”

Why should we not also argue, together with the same author, later in chapter 20, near the end?

“How does the account of Paphnutius agree with the third canon of the Council of Nicaea, where bishops, presbyters, and deacons are forbidden to have any woman in the house except a mother, sister, or aunt?”

Bellarmin opposed this very point in that chapter to an argument of the following kind:

“Calvin’s fifth and final argument is drawn from Socrates’ *History*, book 1, chapter 8, and Sozomen’s book 1, chapter 22, where they say that, when the Council of Nicaea wished to enact a law forbidding clerics to sleep with their wives, Paphnutius the Confessor rose, the whole synod adopted his view, and continence from one’s wife was left to each person’s discretion.”

To refute this argument, Bellarmin first of all points out what those two Greek writers nevertheless freely conceded:

“For both authors,” Bellarmin says, “testify in the same passage that Paphnutius added that it seemed good to him that, according to the ancient canons, clerics should be forbidden to take wives in any way after ordination, but should be permitted to make use only of those whom they had taken before ordination.”

He then demonstrates through many arguments of great weight that those authors are not reliable in this account, which, as we have seen, he nevertheless contends is refuted by that same third canon of Nicaea.

Gregory of Valencia, in *On Celibacy*, chapter 6, in his response to the thirteenth argument, and Baronius, in the third volume of the *Annals*, under the year 325, sections 148 and following, also refuted their account with nearly the same arguments. Baronius was additionally singular in this respect: in section 151 he confirmed his interpretation of that third Nicene canon with the testimony of Saint Basil the Great, excerpted from his seventeenth letter to Paregorius. The testimony is so relevant and appropriate to the present subject—including parts omitted by Baronius—that I have decided to reproduce it here in full.

According to the Paris edition of 1603, page 1040, it reads verbatim:

“Basil to Paregorius the presbyter.

“I read your letter with great composure of mind, and I wondered how you attempt to remedy incurable matters with lengthy speeches, when you have resolved to remain in matters about which you are accused, although you are able to satisfy us briefly and easily by the facts themselves.

“Neither were we the first, Paregorius, nor are we the only ones who enacted that women must not cohabit with men. Read the canon established by our holy Fathers in the Council of Nicaea, which clearly forbade anyone to have a woman introduced into his household. The honor of celibacy consists in this: that a man withdraws from the bond of a woman.

“Therefore, if someone professes celibacy in name only but in reality does what married people do, it is clear that he displays the honor of virginity in name, while meanwhile he does not cease from inappropriate pleasure.

“You could have yielded to our admonition all the more easily because you assert that you are free from bodily passions. For I do not believe that a man seventy years old could cohabit with a woman and be subject to such passions. Nor did I make this determination because you had indicated anything absurd, but because we have learned from the Apostle that no stumbling block or scandal should be placed before a brother.

“We know, however, that what some people do rightly becomes for others an occasion of sin. For this reason, following the constitution of the holy Fathers, we have ordered you to separate from the woman.

“Why, then, do you accuse the chorepiscopus and mention an old enmity? Indeed, why do you accuse us as though we were ears inclined to admit accusations? Why do you not rather reproach yourself for delaying to abstain from the woman’s companionship?

“Cast her out of your house, therefore, and hand her over to a monastery. Let her be among virgins, and serve among men, so that the name of God may not be blasphemed because of you.

“Until you have done this, even if you make countless complaints in your letters, you will accomplish nothing; but you will die as an idle man—that is, without the exercise of the presbyterate, as is noted there in the margin—and you will give an account to the Lord for your idleness.

“But if, without correcting yourself, you dare to retain the exercise of the priesthood, you will be anathema to all the people; and if anyone receives you, they will be excommunicated throughout the whole Church.” [Col. 0987B–0988C]

Thus far Basil, truly Great alike in doctrine and holiness, a very close associate of our bishop Ambrose, and, as Baronius correctly calculates, taken from this mortal life to immortal and blessed life on the first of January in the year of Christ 378.

Therefore, no one should now doubt that the Council of Nicaea truly forbade sacred ministers, through that third canon, to use marriage for all time thereafter, and that the same law was subsequently received as a general practice—appropriately, indeed, in obedience and faith, which are most justly owed to so holy and so authoritative a council.

### XL

How holy and authoritative that council was may also be inferred from the account given by Theodoret in book 1, chapter 7 of his *History*, where, describing the bishops who attended the council, he says:

“The number of bishops assembled was 318. The Roman bishop, worn out by old age, was not present in person; nevertheless, he sent two presbyters to take part in the settlement. Many at that time excelled in apostolic gifts; many bore in their bodies, according to Saint Paul, the branded marks of the Lord Jesus.

“Among them was James, bishop of Antioch in Mygdonia, which the Syrians and Assyrians call Nisibis. He was said to have raised the dead and restored them to life, and to have performed countless other miracles. Since these have been set out separately in the *History* entitled *Philotheos*, I did not think they belonged in this account.

“But Paul, bishop of Neocaesarea—a fortress on the Euphrates—had experienced the fury of Licinius. He carried both hands crippled, contracted by white-hot iron, with the movable nerves of the joints seized and destroyed. Some had had their right eyes torn out; others had had their right arms crippled. Among the latter was Paphnutius the Egyptian.

“To conclude briefly, in that assembly one could see a people of witnesses to Christ.” [Col. 0988D–0989A]

Thus far Theodoret’s words.

That Paphnutius, leaving the others aside, was the same man mentioned shortly before by Socrates and Sozomen, and likewise mentioned in the *Life of the Holy Abbot Antony*, written by Saint Athanasius, as well as in the Roman Martyrology and in Baronius’s notes added under September 11, is clear.

Concerning him, Ruffinus of Aquileia left the following account in book 1, chapter 4:

“Constantine”—that is, the emperor—“held him in such great veneration and affection that he frequently summoned him into the palace, embraced him, and kissed with eager kisses the eye that had been torn out during his confession of the faith.”

It is reasonable to understand that this Paphnutius—whom, together with Baronius and others, we suppose to have been bishop of Upper Thebaid—was entirely different from that Jerusalem bishop whose eye, likewise torn out by persecutors for the Catholic faith, Constantine often kissed, as Saint Pope Gregory VII affirmed for us in the preceding chapter 59, section 2.

If this bishop too happened to attend the Council of Nicaea, his name was certainly Macarius. For among the bishops of the province of Palestine who attended that council, Macarius of Jerusalem subscribed first.

The following considerations also lend substantial support to this conjecture in favor of Macarius: he governed the Jerusalem Church from the year 312 to 331 and was a man worthy of the blessedness of his name and adorned with many good qualities, an encomium by which Theodoret commends him in book 1, chapter 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; meanwhile, “at his urging, the holy places were cleansed by Constantine”—to whom the sign of the Cross had first appeared from heaven in that same year 312—“and by Helena, and were adorned with sacred basilicas,” as the Roman Martyrology records on March 10; moreover, “from the beginning of Arius’s heresy he always resisted Arius most vigorously,” as Baronius rightly proves in his notes under the same day; and finally, it may rightly be believed that he resisted no less vigorously those persecutors by whom the faithful had just previously been tested through various tortures and enticed into apostasy.

But let us return from this point to the authority of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0989B–C].

### XLI

We take as certain and indisputable that this was the first of the general councils and that it was approved by the Roman pontiff, as Bellarmin carefully taught in book 1 of *On Councils*, chapter 5.

Accordingly, we also take it as certain, as a matter of the Catholic faith, that it could not have erred either in faith or in morals, just as Bellarmin excellently argued in general concerning all councils of this kind in book 2 of *On the Authority of Councils*, chapter 2, and many subsequent chapters.

We also have particular testimonies concerning this same council, especially the following. Saint Athanasius, in his letter to Epictetus—which Saint Epiphanius also cites under heresy 77—expresses wonder that anyone should dare to raise a question concerning matters defined at that council, since decrees of councils of this kind cannot be changed without falling into error.

“With what audacity, then,” he says, “do they institute disputes or questions after the authority of so great a council? If they belong to the number of the Arians, it is not surprising that they attack with slanders what was promulgated and written against them, and so forth.

“But if they are among those who, while appearing to be Orthodox and seeming to embrace what was issued by the Fathers, nevertheless attempt to overturn it through disputation, they do nothing other than carry out a manifest subversion, fighting with verbal quarrels—not for anyone’s benefit, but for the ruin of simpler people.”

In his letter to the bishops of Africa, Athanasius likewise testifies that the same council pronounced an anathema against all who held opinions contrary to its own confession:

“To this council,” he adds, “the whole world gave its assent. Although many synods have been held, everyone nevertheless remembers this one: in Dalmatia, Dardania, and the other islands; in Sicily and Cyprus; in Isauria, Pamphylia, Lycia, and all Egypt and Libya; and most people in Arabia acknowledged and admired it and approved it by their subscriptions. Thus, if anyone remains who has sprung from the Arian root producing bitterness”—I speak of Ursacius, Valens, and the others who share their opinion—“they are found to have been cut off and rejected by these very writings.

“Therefore what was confessed at Nicaea is sufficient and possesses power in itself, as we said above, both for the overthrow of impious doctrine and for the protection and benefit of ecclesiastical teaching.”

A little later he adds:

“The word of the Lord through the Ecumenical Council of Nicaea remains forever.” [Col. 0990A–B]

Did not the emperor Constantine himself, in Eusebius, book 3 of *On His Life*, when writing a letter to the Churches, expressly call the decrees of that council “heavenly commands”?

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus likewise did not hesitate to affirm, in his oration on Athanasius, that the bishops had been gathered by the Holy Spirit for the General Council of Nicaea.

Saint Cyril, in book 1 of *On the Trinity*, called the decree of that council “a divine and most holy oracle.”

Accordingly, Saint Basil, in letter 78, taught that the decrees of the Council of Nicaea should be presented to those whose faith was suspect, since it would thereby become clear whether they were heretics or Catholics.

If we wish to add others who were later than Ambrose, the holy pontiff Leo I, in letter 78 to Leo Augustus, expressly asserted that those who resisted the Council of Nicaea could not be counted among the Catholics; and in letters 53 to Anatolius and 54 to the emperor Marcian, he stated that the canons of the Council of Nicaea had been established through the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, Saint Gregory the Great, in book 1, letter 24, went so far as to write:

“Because belief with the heart leads to righteousness, while confession with the mouth leads to salvation, I confess that I revere and venerate four councils just as I do the four books of the Holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected.

“With complete devotion I embrace them and preserve them with wholly sound approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises and the rule of every life and action is established. Whoever does not hold to their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.” [Col. 0990C]

For this reason, when Bellarmin was about to present the testimony of that council in book 1 of *On Clerics*, chapter 1, he prefaced it as follows:

“Let the First Council of Nicaea, Ecumenical, most ancient, most numerous, and most renowned, come forward—not from individual men but from assemblies of men. Its authority was always so great among all the ancients that Eusebius, in book 1, chapter 18 of *On Baptism*, calls it the council of the whole world; Athanasius, in his letter to the bishops of Africa, and Leo, in letter 53 to Anatolius, compares it with the oracles of the Holy Spirit; and Gregory, in book 1, letter 24, compares it with the Gospel itself.” [Col. 0990D]

Since, therefore, this council possessed such great authority, and since it forbade sacred ministers the use of marriage, it is plainly unbelievable that Ambrose wished to permit them that same use and actually did so.

### XLII

Nevertheless, I do not therefore deny that there were meanwhile some who nonetheless appropriated to themselves this same use of marriage; [Col. 0991A] but just as they appropriated it to themselves contrary to what that sacred ecumenical synod had decreed, so I deny, and deny again, that Ambrose permitted it to them or to others of the same kind. Such ministers Ambrose unquestionably condemned, as shown above in section 15; and he would have condemned no less those whom Saint Epiphanius described—or rather condemned—in Heresy 59, that of the Cathari.

For, according to the Parisian and Greek-Latin edition of 1622, corrected through the study and work of Dionysius Petavius, Epiphanius says there, among other things:

> “If anyone after baptism has married a second wife, he is no longer admitted by them. This, indeed, is plainly foolish.”

A little later he says:

> “For they judge that what has been specially assigned to the priesthood because of the singular dignity of that office belongs equally to everyone. They have heard that a bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife; and likewise a deacon and a presbyter. [Col. 0991B] The matter certainly stands thus: after Christ’s coming into the world, God’s most holy discipline rejects all those who, after their first wife has died, have bound themselves by a second marriage, because the honor and dignity of the priesthood are beyond belief. And this is precisely what the most holy Church of God preserves with every precaution and diligence.
>
> “Moreover, even a man who is still living in marriage and raising children, although he is the husband of one wife, is by no means admitted to the order of deacon, presbyter, bishop, or subdeacon; only the man who has abstained from marital relations with one wife, or who has been deprived of her, is admitted. This is especially the practice in those places where the ecclesiastical canons are carefully observed.
>
> “Yet in some places presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons still have children. I reply that this does not happen by authority of the canon, but because of human negligence, which at certain times customarily acts carelessly and connives on account of the excessive multitude of the people—namely, when those who apply themselves to these offices cannot easily be found. [Col. 0991C]
>
> “As for the Church itself, since it has been well ordered and constituted by the Holy Spirit, and since it considers what is more fitting in all matters, it has made it its chief concern that the ministries rendered to the divine Majesty should, insofar as possible, be distracted by nothing, and that all spiritual offices should be performed with the best and most joyful conscience.
>
> “This, then, is what I say: because of sudden duties and offices, it is fitting that a presbyter, a deacon, and a bishop should be wholly free for God. For if the Apostle commands even those who belong to the people to devote themselves for a time to prayer, how much more does he prescribe this for a priest? He must plainly not be called away by any impediment from what, in spiritual matters according to God, is performed in the very exercise and administration of the priesthood.”

Thus far Saint Epiphanius. He was a contemporary of Saint Ambrose, as can be understood from Baronius’s *Annals*. Ambrose governed the Church of Milan from the year 374 until 397. Epiphanius, meanwhile, governed the Church of Constantia, or Salamis, the principal city of Cyprus, from approximately the year 370 until about 402. [Col. 0991D]

Indeed, Epiphanius must be remembered by us especially under this further title: in the year 382—or, more precisely, after the Council of Constantinople had been celebrated, at which Datius was said to have claimed that Ambrose had judged in favor of married priests—he unquestionably took part in the Roman council celebrated under Pope Damasus. Ambrose likewise unquestionably took part in it, and Bellarmine mentioned it above, in section 27.

At that Roman council, as Baronius rightly observes under that year, it was also prohibited, according to the prescription of the Nicene canon, that Masses should be sung before the third hour on feast days; on other days, however, it was permitted to celebrate them from the middle of the fourth hour until the ninth. From this we may also understand how entirely foreign it was to Ambrose to enact any law for married clerics contrary to the Nicene canon. [Col. 0992A]

### XLIII

If anyone still remains doubtful about this matter, let him listen to Ambrose himself, and at last be ashamed to doubt.

In the preface to Book I of *On the Faith*, he wrote to Gratian Augustus:

> “You ask me, holy emperor, for a little book on the faith as you set out for battle. For you know that victory is usually sought more through the faith of an emperor than through the courage of soldiers. Abraham, too, led 318 men to war (Genesis 14) and carried away trophies from countless enemies. Under the sign of the Lord’s cross and name, after the strength of five kings and their victorious bands had been subdued, the enemy was conquered, and he recovered both his brother’s son and a triumph.”

A little later, indicating the Council of Nicaea, he says:

> “With regard to councils, I shall follow above all that council in which 318 priests, chosen as Abraham’s judgment had chosen them, victorious through the harmonious strength of their faith, raised a trophy over the impious conquered throughout the whole world. Thus it seems to me divine that, in councils concerning the faith, the oracle is found in the same number in which the history contains an example of piety.” [Col. 0992B]

Later in the same book, chapter 9:

> “You have rightly received as condemned those who assert such things”—namely, the Arian propositions he had just reviewed—“not through human skill or through some arrangement, but 318 bishops, as I said above, assembled for the council. Yet, so that the Lord Jesus might prove that he was present at the council through the sign of his passion and name, there is the cross in the 300 priests and the name of Jesus in the 18.”

Furthermore, in Book *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, chapter 7:

> “For it is not that one who is of the same substance is one person, but one thing. For when, in the account of the Council of Nicaea, they confessed the Son to be of the same substance as the Father, they believed not in one person, but in one divinity in the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0992C]

Likewise, in his exposition *On the Manner of Celebrating Easter*, he begins:

> “That it is no small evidence of wisdom to determine the day of the Easter celebration is taught us both by divine Scripture and by the tradition of our ancestors. When they assembled at the Nicene synod, among those decrees of the faith that were as true as they were admirable, they also addressed the celebration just mentioned. Gathering the most skilled calculators, they worked out a cycle of nineteen years and, as it were, established a certain circle from which an example might be generated for the years that followed. They called this circle the *Enneacaedecaeteris*”—that is, the nineteen-year cycle—“etc.”

A little later:

> “Nor do I think it absurd that we should derive an example for observing the month from the place where Easter was first celebrated. Therefore, if anyone pays careful attention, our ancestors in the account of the Council of Nicaea also judged that this same *Enneacaedecaeteris* should be established, and they rightly observed the month of the New [Moon], because in Egypt new grain is cut in that first month.” [Col. 0992D]

Also, in Book II, Letter 13, to Valentinian Augustus:

> “The Arian who says that Christ is a creature agrees very well with them—something which even pagans and Jews most readily confess. This was written at the synod of Rimini, and I rightly abhor that council, following the account of the Council of Nicaea, from which neither death nor the sword will be able to separate me. The most blessed emperor Theodosius, the father of Your Clemency, both follows and has approved this faith. Gaul holds this faith; Spain holds it and preserves it together with the devout confession of the divine Spirit.”

To these statements of Ambrose concerning the Council of Nicaea add what we already quoted above in section 18. It will then become perfectly clear how great was the reverence with which he regarded it and how faithfully and religiously he always wished to preserve the account of the Nicene council—or all its decrees—both those concerning the Catholic faith and those concerning ecclesiastical discipline. The canon forbidding those sacred ministers the use of marriage certainly belonged to that discipline, as we have already amply proved. [Col. 0993A]

### XLIV

Now observe with what words, suitable and convenient for understanding, Datius expressed the law that he imagined had been proclaimed by Saint Ambrose for married priests. His words were these:

> “Therefore the law permits priests to marry a virgin once, but not to marry again. If, however, after his first wife has died, a priest marries another, he loses the priesthood.”

To understand these words in their pure and genuine sense, I would explain them as follows. Just as it is one thing to beget children while in the priesthood and another to have children, as Ambrose rightly observed for us in section 18 in his commentary on the Apostle Paul’s Epistle, so without doubt it is one thing to marry a wife while in the priesthood and another to have a wife.

A priest may have a wife whom he married before entering the priesthood; moreover, he may have her in such a way that [Col. 0993B] he either makes use of her meanwhile or does not make use of her ever again. Accordingly, the Greeks too—as was already explained in section 24—were permitted under the Trullan Synod to have a wife even for marital relations, provided that they had married her not after, but before, entering the order of subdeacon. The same practice was likewise eventually observed by the Milanese clergy in the time of Ariald, as we have already seen in this fourth book, chapter 3.

I now ask, therefore, what the genuine and lawful meaning of that law was. On the one hand, it seems to have granted priests permission to marry even after they had already undertaken the priesthood. For just as by that same law priests who were already exercising the priesthood were forbidden to contract a second marriage and to marry another woman after the death of the first—and therefore those who did so were required to lose the priesthood, not one that they were subsequently to acquire, but one already acquired—so, conversely, priests already promoted to the priesthood seemed to have been permitted to marry a virgin once. [Col. 0993C]

But if this was granted to priests, why would it not have been granted even more to deacons and subdeacons? There you have Ambrose granting those sacred ministers a faculty altogether different from, and much broader than, the one they later practiced. Yet who could believe this?

If, on the other hand, one prefers Datius’s view—that by this law Ambrose granted priests permission to marry only before the subdiaconate, and in precisely the order that we eventually know to have been observed by the Greeks after the Trullan Synod and by our Milanese clergy in the time of Ariald—it cannot be denied that a law expressed in such words is exceedingly ill-suited to that meaning and, for this reason also, must appear unworthy of the learned Ambrose.

### XLV

This is enough for now. We have examined individually that principal testimony of Datius. As for the testimony of Landulf the Elder, which followed in second place—or rather its more important portion—we have already replied in section 11. [Col. 0993D]

Now we would gladly ask Landulf himself what synod he had in mind. If he were to answer that it was the Council of Constantinople, the one explicitly named by Datius, then, like Datius, he too would be held convicted of error in this matter. If he were to say that it was a different council, would he not thereby admit that Datius had erred, and be the first to show us how little weight should be given to his authority and historical reliability? Would not the pretext of a different synod likewise be refuted by almost all the same arguments by which the pretext of that Council of Constantinople was refuted?

### XLVI

Far be it from me to deny that Ambrose knew and understood very well that human affections are inclined to sin, especially because of lack of self-control, and likewise that virginity and chastity can be obtained from no other source than God.

Yet even this great doctor of the Catholic Church could not have been ignorant of what the Fathers and sacred theologians of that same Church [Col. 0994A] teach everywhere and by common agreement: namely, that continence is indeed a special gift of God, but that it nevertheless lies within human choice and power, provided that a person is willing to use the remedies necessary for attaining it, instituted by God and made available for our use.

On this matter, more than any other theologian of our age, I would recommend consulting Cardinal Bellarmine: in Book I of *On Clerics*, chapter 21, in his response to the fourth argument of the adversaries; and at somewhat greater length in Book II of *On Monks*, chapter 31. There, among many other testimonies of the Fathers proving that celibacy lies within our power with the help of divine grace, one may also see the testimony of our bishop Ambrose, expressed in these words:

> “Ambrose, Book III of *On Virgins*: ‘The Lord,’ he says, ‘who knew that integrity ought to be preached to all but imitated by few, says: Not all receive this word.’ And in *On Widows*: ‘There are eunuchs [Col. 0994B] who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; but this is not commanded to all, though it is demanded of all.’”

And further:

> “The Creator of all knows that the dispositions of individuals are various, and therefore he summoned virtue through rewards rather than binding weakness with chains.”

These are the words of Ambrose. Bellarmine immediately adds:

> “So much for him. Here you see continence preached to all and demanded of all—plainly, if they themselves wish to obtain its rewards.”

### XLVII

Moreover, Landulf the Elder was also mistaken in the way he described the Greeks’ custom of marrying. He described it in these words:

> “Therefore the Greek priests, holding the Ambrosian opinion, have sanctioned and regard as law to this day that, when they are ordained to the priesthood, they either promise virginity thereafter or join wives to themselves in the presence of good men.”

In this, I say, he was unquestionably mistaken, and he is very clearly refuted by the canons of the Trullan Synod themselves, faithfully set forth by Bellarmine, as we have already quoted in section 24. For the Greeks did not perform this act when they were ordained to the priesthood—as they do not perform it today—but before they were initiated into the subdiaconate. [Col. 0994C]

### XLVIII

Nor does Landulf appear free from error in supposing that all priests without exception lived as monogamists not under chastity, but thereafter kept their wives with them and even had marital relations with them. This, however, is false. For according to the sacred canons and according to the Catholic teaching of Saint Ambrose explained above, this was forbidden to them.

### XLIX

We now return to the testimony of Gualvaneus Flamma, quoted in section 5, and likewise point out his particular errors.

He first erred in wrongly interpreting those admonitions of Saint Paul to Timothy and Titus, against that perpetual and common judgment of the Catholic Church which we indicated, together with Bellarmine, in section 23. [Col. 0994D] There is also that exceedingly certain rule of Tertullian, recorded in Book *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 17:

> “An adulterating interpretation obstructs the truth as much as a corrupting style.”

Accordingly, Gualvaneus judged corruptly and perversely—and even contrary to those apostolic canons that we cited in section 35—that from the very beginnings of the Christian Church deacons, priests, and bishops had been permitted to have wives and meanwhile to have marital relations with them. This was unquestionably Gualvaneus’s meaning.

### L

Likewise, in the argument he drew from Zachariah, the father of Saint John the Baptist and a priest of the Old Testament, to the priests of the New Testament, he was unquestionably mistaken. In this he is refuted even by Saint Ambrose himself, as we have already seen in sections 15, 20, and 23.

### LI

Whether that Archbishop Eribert—whom I customarily call Aribert—really had the wife whom Gualvaneus mentioned does not seem to me true or even plausible.

Aribert was raised [Col. 0995A] to govern the Milanese Church in the year of the Lord 1019 and remained in that office until 1046, as I have recorded in the monuments of the Ambrosian basilica and monastery, sections 213 and 246. At that same time, the historians of Milanese affairs, Arnulf and Landulf the Elder, whom we have so often brought forward as witnesses, were also living.

Both of them therefore recorded the deeds of that archbishop clearly and at length in their histories; yet neither made any mention whatsoever of a wife whom that prelate supposedly had at the time. They certainly ought to have done so if it were to appear how greatly the married priests of that period—whom they exclusively favored, as we have often said—followed even the example of their archbishop.

Concerning the monastery of Saint Dionysius, Arnulf says only this in Book [Col. 0995B] II, chapter 11:

> “Aribert was buried at Saint Dionysius, where he himself had founded an elegant monastery.”

Landulf, after writing for many chapters in Book II of his *Histories* about the deeds of that archbishop, likewise states in chapter 32:

> “For the blessed Heribert”—such was the author’s esteem for him—“departed to the Lord on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in 1045, and was buried at Saint Dionysius. He himself enlarged and adorned its monastery and church for the honor of God and the exaltation of blessed Dionysius, raising it to distinction by enriching and honoring it with many estates and many privileges.”

I myself have also read—and even copied out—many public and authentic documents of that monastery. From its first foundation—which, in the monuments of the Ambrosian basilica and monastery, section 228, I dated to the year 1023 of Christ—up to the year 1164, they enumerate individually, in their own terms, [Col. 0995C] all its immovable properties and possessions. Yet I have never seen that singular vineyard, called by its proper name Useria, included among them. It is supposed to have been adjacent to that monastery and, for that very reason, would have seemed all the more deserving of inclusion if it had already been in the monastery’s possession.

This vineyard, therefore, had not yet been donated to the monastery; consequently, it was not donated to it by a woman who was the wife of that Archbishop Aribert.

In 1642, Bernard Bellonus, a canon of the Ambrosian basilica and procurator of Cardinal Antonio Barberini, then commendatory abbot, lent me such documents from the abbey archive, being fully assured by long experience of my good faith. I had already mentioned him in the monuments of the Ambrosian basilica, section 280, and again in my dissertation *On the Nazarene*, chapter 107, section 12.

I shall quote the first three documents of this kind verbatim in the following chapter. The remaining documents are of the following sort.

The fourth [Col. 0995D] is a privilege of our Archbishop Obertus, granted to the same monastery “in October of the year 1146 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth indiction.”

The fifth is a privilege granted likewise to the same monastery by Pope Eugene:

> “Given at Vercelli through the hand of Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1146 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugene III.”

The sixth is a privilege of Pope Adrian:

> “Given at the Lateran through the hand of Albert, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, acting in the place of Lord Roland, cardinal presbyter and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.”

The seventh is the privilege of the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, [Col. 0996A] finally subscribed as follows:

> “I, Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of the Italian kingdom, have confirmed this in the year 1158 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh indiction, while the most glorious Lord Frederick was reigning as emperor of the Romans, in the seventh year of his reign and the fourth of his empire. Amen. Given at Roncaglia on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.”

The eighth and final document is a privilege of Pope Alexander:

> “Given at Sens through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of November, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.”

At that time—horrible as it is to recall—this most noble city of ours had already lain for the second year in a pitiable condition, destroyed by the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa himself and stripped of its citizens, who had been forced to depart. [Col. 0996B]

In each and every one of these privileges granted to the same monastery, all its estates and immovable possessions are individually enumerated. Indeed, in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and eighth, “the tithe of the lands that are beside the monastery itself” is expressly named; yet that vineyard distinguished by the name Useria is never named or indicated in any other way.

For this reason, it does not appear to have been in the monastery’s possession even at that time, and therefore it was not donated by Useria, who was supposedly the wife of Archbishop Aribert.

Furthermore, neither Saint Ariald nor any other of his supporters is ever reported, amid their innumerable complaints about the marriages of priests, to have hinted at any marriage by which one of our archbishops had at some time been bound.

Consider also the abuses that the apostolic legates sent here endeavored to remove from the Milanese Church, especially Cardinal Peter Damian [Col. 0996C] and Anselm, Bishop of Lucca, about whom we spoke particularly in chapter 10 of this fourth book. These abuses will certainly be found to have been nothing other than simony—for which both the archbishop and the clergy were guilty—and the incontinence of ministers inferior to the archbishop.

For this reason Archbishop Guido himself also promised in that same chapter 10, section 24:

> “We likewise condemn the heresy of the Nicolaitans, and we promise, insofar as it shall be possible for us, under the same testimony as above, to exclude not only presbyters but also deacons and subdeacons from the shameful association of wives or concubines through our efforts.”

Finally, concerning the sacred ministers of the Milanese Church who had wives in those times, it seems that the matter must be understood according to those laws of this kind that were likewise commonly in use among the Greeks during the same period. Among them, however, it was decreed and [Col. 0996D] inviolably observed that bishops should not have wives with whom they cohabited, as we have already seen testified most clearly in section 24; the matters that we shall see below in section 64 agree with this as well.

For these reasons especially, I cannot be persuaded to believe Gualvaneus—who flourished more than 250 years after Aribert’s death—when, without any authority, he asserted that our archbishop had that wife, with whom he could meanwhile have relations in the manner practiced at that time by the inferior ministers of this Church.

### LII

Let us nevertheless deal generously with Gualvaneus and grant him even this point. Should Aribert therefore be believed actually to have had a wife because Saint Ambrose granted him permission to marry and, specifically for this purpose, blessed even his successors?

Aribert certainly practiced simony during the same period [Col. 0997A], as can also be inferred from what we quoted in the preceding chapter, chapter 10, section 30; yet he had not received permission to practice it from Saint Ambrose. Why, then, should we not similarly believe that he did not receive permission from Ambrose to marry, just as the rest of the clergy did not receive from him the permission that we have maintained throughout?

In this abuse, Aribert seems rather to have imitated the Greek clergy applauding that errant Council of Constantinople. Perhaps he even made further and bolder advances, relying on the law contained in Book VII of the *Capitularies of the Emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious*, chapter 353, entitled “On the Rules of Clerics,” page 1116, expressed in these words:

> “Let clerics also strive to preserve chastity of body inviolate forever, or at least let them be bound by the bond of a single marriage.”

The seven books are entitled as follows:

> “Seven Books of the Capitularies, or Ecclesiastical and Civil Laws, of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, most Christian kings and emperors, collected by Ansegisus the abbot and Benedict the Levite.”

They are likewise contained in the same codex [Col. 0997B] of *Ancient Laws*, printed at Frankfurt by Johann and Andreas Marinus and associates in 1613.

Certainly, however, even in the time of the Emperor Louis—which lasted from the year 814 of Christ until 840, just as Charlemagne’s had lasted from 800 until 814—simoniacal corruption disgraced the Milanese Church, as we have already seen in this fourth book, chapter 3, section 5.

To the same point also surely belongs what is read on page 431 of the second volume of the *Ancient Councils of Gaul*, edited by Jacques Sirmond at Paris in 1629. There, after the Synod of Aachen, celebrated in the year 816 of Christ, the third year of the Emperor Louis the Pious, in the tenth indiction, capitularies subsequently enacted in the palace of that emperor are recited. Among these is the sixteenth, entitled “On the Bishops of Italy,” and [Col. 0997C] expressed in these words:

> “With regard to the bishops established in Lombardy, who were accustomed to receive or demand from those whom they ordained oaths and gifts contrary to divine and canonical authority, it is prohibited in every way that this should happen any longer, because according to the sacred canons both parties who do such things must fall from their proper rank.”

### LIII

To conclude our examination of the testimonies of such writers, only this remains to be observed concerning Bernardino Corio: he seems to have made no distinction whatsoever between *having* and *marrying* a wife.

Accordingly, when he first explained what Ambrose had granted, he expressed it in these words:

> “He granted them that they might have a virgin wife.”

Then, explaining how this same practice was later forbidden to them, he put it this way:

> “It was ordained that no priest or cleric should take a wife.”

Hence even the censor of Corio—at whose suggestion the Sacred [Col. 0997D] Congregation of the Index decreed that this very passage of Corio ought to be corrected—used these words, which we quoted in the letter of that congregation in section 10:

> “He asserts that Saint Ambrose permitted priests to marry.”

### LIV

This opportunity having arisen, we must not pass over in silence the manner in which the Roman Catholic Church forbade sacred ministers not so much to marry as to have a wife for marital relations, as Dominicus Soto wisely observed in Book VII of *On Justice*, question 6, article 2; Bellarmine in Book I of *On Clerics*, chapter 18; Gregory of Valencia in *On Celibacy*, chapter 2; and others.

Gregory’s words are these:

> “As Soto most aptly observed”—in the place recently cited—“it must be forbidden for anyone to marry after ordination because of the very act of contracting and marrying, since it is forbidden for anyone to engage in marriage after ordination. For those in sacred orders are not forbidden to have a wife”—since that act is holy and religious, most honorable, and constitutes a sacrament—“but because of the use of marriage itself, which seems less befitting the dignity and office of sacred men, as we shall show later.”

Bellarmine likewise writes in the same sense:

> “Marriage does not conflict with holy orders in its essence, but because of the office or exercise of marital relations. For if God had forbidden marriage to priests, he would certainly have forbidden it because of the marital act, which makes a person wholly carnal and unfit for divine things, and because of the care of household and children, which produces very many distractions; not because of the sacrament of marriage alone, or because of the marriage contract, which is completed by the sole consent of the minds and is a very brief and most honorable matter.” [Col. 0998A]

### LV

It is now time to turn from this sort of accusation [Col. 0998B] collected against those historiographers to a more agreeable consideration of several other supporters of our cause, especially Saints Jerome and Augustine, contemporaries of Saint Ambrose and exceedingly well versed in his writings. They were also knowledgeable about the ecclesiastical affairs of Milan. No prudent person, therefore, could believe that any of them might have been unaware whether Saint Ambrose had enacted that law concerning the marriages of Greek or of our own priests, or whether it was subsequently practiced by them either at Milan or in Greece.

### LVI

Consider how much Jerome supplies us in Letter 50 to Pammachius, or in his *Apology for His Books against Jovinian*. Not far from the beginning he says above all:

> “If worldly people are indignant that they are of a lower rank than virgins, I am astonished that clerics, monks, and continent persons do not praise what they themselves do. They castrate themselves from their wives in order to imitate the chastity of virgins; [Col. 0998C] and do they want married women to be the same as virgins? Let them therefore be joined to their wives, whom they had renounced; or, if they abstain from them, even while silent they will confess that what they preferred to the work of marriage is better.”

A little later:

> “Behold, we have plainly said that marriage is permitted in the Gospel; yet nevertheless that those who remain in its office cannot receive the rewards of chastity. If husbands take this amiss, let them not be angry with me but with the sacred Scriptures—indeed, with bishops, presbyters, and deacons, and with the entire priestly and Levitical choir, who know that they cannot offer sacrifices if they serve the work of marriage.”

Finally, near the end of the letter:

> “Apostles are chosen either as virgins or as continent after marriage; bishops, presbyters, and deacons are chosen either as virgins, as widowers, or at least as men who, after priestly ordination, remain chaste forever.”

These are Jerome’s words in that letter.

### LVII

Here is what he says again near the beginning [Col. 0998D] of his book against Vigilantius:

> “Shameful indeed!”—he exclaims, speaking of Vigilantius—“It is said that bishops have accomplices in his crime, if those are to be called bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first married, believing no celibate person to be chaste. Indeed, they show how holy their own lives are by suspecting everyone, and they do not confer Christ’s sacraments unless they have seen the wives of clerics pregnant and infants crying as they emerge from their mothers’ wombs.
>
> “What will the Churches of the East do? What will Egypt do, and the Apostolic See? These Churches either accept virgins or continent men as clerics; or, if they have had wives, they cease to be husbands.”

Later, explaining this passage in his scholia, Marianus Victorius wrote:

> “From this passage it is clear that in Saint Jerome’s time there were also celibate sacred ministers of the Church in the East, and not married men, as is said; and that afterward the Greeks, having disregarded the canons, mixed marriage with the sacred ministries. This is also asserted by Saint Basil, as may be seen in his letter to Gregory—or rather to Paregorius. [Col. 0999A] The same is asserted by Eusebius in Book I of *The Evangelical Demonstration*, by Maximus in his answers to the *Questions of Thalassius*, by Ephrem the Syrian in a certain letter to a monk who said that it was better to marry than to burn, likewise by Epiphanius against the Cathari, and by others.”

Thus far Marianus Victorius.

### LVIII

But what prevents us from interpreting the Milanese Church also as included among those Churches of the Apostolic See—either because, according to Jerome’s judgment, it truly was one of them, or at least because, together with its bishop Ambrose, in so serious a matter and one confirmed by such solemn decrees, it in no way dissented from the judgment and commands of the Apostolic See?

How highly Ambrose esteemed that see can be recognized most clearly from the passage which Peter Damian, in this same fourth book, chapter 10, no. 13, and Arnulfus, chapter 17, no. 4, indicated, and which is contained in Ambrose’s third book *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1. There he was discussing the custom—commonly observed at Milan at that time—of washing the feet of the baptized, when he says:

> “We are not unaware that the Roman Church does not have this custom, whose type and form we follow in all things. Yet it does not have this custom, namely, that of washing the feet. See, therefore, whether perhaps it has declined from it because of the multitude. There are nevertheless those who say and attempt to excuse the matter, because this is not to be done as a mystery, nor in baptism, nor in regeneration, but as though the feet of a guest were to be washed. One thing belongs to humility, another to sanctification. Finally, hear that it is a mystery and sanctification: ‘Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me.’ I say this not because I reproach others, but because I myself commend my own duties. In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church; nevertheless, we too are human beings and possess judgment. Therefore, what is more rightly observed elsewhere, we also rightly preserve.”

Thus far Ambrose.

Examining this passage in the *Life of that same holy Ambrose*, under the year of Christ 384, Baronius discussed it in these words:

> “Furthermore, to say something incidentally concerning what relates to the Saturday fast and certain other ecclesiastical rites: although Ambrose observed them in a manner different from the practice of the Roman Church, he certainly did not do so in such a spirit as though, approving only his own customs, he despised those others. Hear what he himself professes when, treating of this matter in book 3 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1, he says: ‘We are not unaware that the Roman Church does not have this custom’—namely, washing the feet of the newly baptized—‘whose type and form we follow in all things.’ And shortly afterward: ‘In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church,’ and so forth. For such variations of rites, provided that the unity of the Catholic faith and charity is maintained, and that the Holy Roman Church, the Apostolic See, is recognized as the mother and teacher of all Churches, do not prevent us from all being one in Christ.”

### LIX

Certainly, however, when the situation is considered in the opposite direction, the sacred ministry of the New Testament was not of such a kind that Ambrose could have thought it more rightly preserved elsewhere than in the Roman Church, or that it could therefore rightly be observed by him differently from the way it was observed there.

Elsewhere—for, as we have already seen, only among a few—it was preserved together with the practice of marriage, but contrary to the sacred canons of the apostles and of the Council of Nicaea; contrary to the singular excellence and holiness of so great a ministry; contrary to the common agreement of the holy Fathers; and finally contrary to the command of the Roman Church itself and of the Apostolic See.

Anyone who dissents from that Church and See “is not truly a Catholic, as blessed Ambrose says,” as Arnulfus also declared to us above, chapter 17, no. 6, and chapter 57, no. 12. By these words Arnulfus was referring to Ambrose’s *Oration on the Death of His Brother Satyrus*, in which—if not in those exact words, certainly in substance—that maxim is expressed.

There, concerning Satyrus, after he had miraculously escaped unharmed from a shipwreck at sea and reached the shore, we find the following, commended in the words of that same Ambrose:

> “He summoned a bishop to himself and considered no grace genuine except that of the true faith. He asked him whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops—that is, with the Roman Church. Perhaps at that time the Church of that region was in schism. For Lucifer had then separated himself from our communion; and although he had gone into exile for the faith and had left heirs to his faith, Satyrus—and with him Ambrose—nevertheless did not consider faith to exist in schism. For although they retained faith toward God, they did not retain it toward the Church of God, whose limbs they allowed to be divided, as it were, and whose members to be torn apart. Since Christ suffered for the sake of the Church, and the Church is the body of Christ, it does not appear that those display faith toward Christ by whom his passion is rendered void and his body torn asunder.”

For the present, these testimonies of the saints Jerome and Ambrose concerning the matter proposed are sufficient.

### LX

The testimony that follows next is that of Saint Augustine, who was baptized in this city by Ambrose himself. It is taken from his second book *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 20:

> “We are accustomed to propose even the continence of the clergy to those who do not consider manly excellence to consist in anything except license to sin, when we warn them not to perish eternally by clinging to adulterous marriages. Clerics are often compelled unwillingly to undertake that same burden, and, once they have accepted it, they carry it through to its appointed end, with the Lord’s help. We therefore say to them: ‘What if you too were compelled by the pressure of the people to undertake this? Would you not preserve the office, once accepted, chastely, turning suddenly to ask from the Lord for the strength about which you had never previously thought?’ But they reply: ‘Honor greatly consoles them.’ We answer: ‘Let a greater fear restrain you. For if many ministers of God suddenly and unexpectedly accepted what was imposed upon them, hoping to shine more illustriously in the inheritance of Christ, how much more ought you to live continently by avoiding adultery, fearing not that you will shine less brightly in the kingdom of God, but that you will burn in the fires of hell?’ We say these and similar things, as best we can, to those who, whenever they depart from their wives in whatever manner, or dismiss them because of adultery, wish to marry other women and, when forbidden to do so, plead the weakness of the flesh against us.”

Here, then, we see how, in Augustine’s time, clerics in the Latin Church commonly professed continence, “hoping to shine more illustriously in the inheritance of Christ.” For just as by living chastely on earth they professed a higher degree of perfection than married persons, so also they could rightly and deservedly expect a more excellent degree of blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

### LXI

Augustine departed to heaven in the thirtieth year after the four-hundredth year of Christ, whereas Jerome had died in the twentieth year of that same century. Ambrose, however, had preceded them in the ninety-seventh year of the preceding century.

### LXII

To establish with greater certainty that the same point is also true of the Eastern Church, behold other suitable witnesses from the same period, especially Saint Gregory, who, by the merit of his faith, conduct, integrity, and wisdom, was most worthy to be called the brother of Saint Basil—as Vincent of Lérins celebrates him in his *Book against Heresies*—and who, though married, was bishop of Nyssa and had attended that Constantinopolitan synod which, as we said, was held in the year 381 and which he was still living to see in 394.

In his book *On Virginity*, at the final chapter, he says:

> “How can you perform the priesthood of God, you who were anointed precisely for the purpose of offering the gift? How will you offer these things themselves to God, when you do not obey the law that forbids the impure person to perform sacred rites? And if you desire God to appear to you, why do you not listen to Moses, who commands the people to be pure from marriage if they are to behold the appearance of God?”

### LXIII

Saint John Chrysostom was also elevated to the archiepiscopal chair of Constantinople in that very year in which Saint Ambrose was taken to his blessed dwelling in heaven, and he lived until the year 407.

In his second homily *On the Patience of Job*, he left us the following written testimony:

> “The Apostle Paul said, ‘the husband of one wife,’ not with the intention that this should now be observed in the Church. For the priest ought to be adorned with complete chastity.”

### LXIV

The same opinion concerning the celibacy of Eastern clerics is also supported by that council which Chrysostom himself celebrated in the city of Constantinople in the year 400, as Baronius correctly calculates. Palladius the deacon wrote extensively about it in his *Dialogue on the Life of that same Saint John Chrysostom*, chapters 13 and 14.

Among many other things, he writes:

> “In the thirteenth distribution—or indiction, as Baronius also correctly observed—the bishops of Asia came to Constantinople on account of ecclesiastical necessities and remained with us, since Palladius himself was also present there at that time. Other bishops were present as well: Theotimus from Scythia, Ammon the Egyptian from Thrace, and Arabiano from Galatia, all metropolitans, together with elders who brought the number to twenty-two bishops.
>
> “When all had assembled and communicated, a certain Eusebius, bishop of Valentinopolis, appeared before the assembled council on a Saturday and handed petitions to the synod, addressed, as was proper, in John’s name, against Antoninus, bishop of Ephesus. They contained seven Chapters.”

Palladius then recites these Chapters one by one in order. The sixth was expressed in these words:

> “That, after he had renounced his own wife, he again had intercourse with her and fathered children by her.”

After relating further matters, he added the following:

> “They therefore order the petition to be read, and the aforementioned Chapters were read. Afterward the elder bishops say to John: ‘Although each individual Chapter is impious in itself and everywhere forbidden by the sacred laws, nevertheless, so that we may not appear to devote all our attention to the matters laid before us, let the investigation begin with what is more horrifying to state. For if that matter is found to be true, there will be no dispute concerning the remaining Chapters, since the root of that Chapter displays every form of iniquity.’”

Thus far Palladius.

From these words Baronius appropriately and opportunely warned, under the same year:

> “Thus you may become more certain of what has been repeatedly stated above: that even in the Eastern Church married men chosen as bishops were accustomed to be ordained only after dismissing their wives, and thereafter no longer to make use of them.”

I myself also discussed this matter separately in numbers 51 and 52.

### LXV

Finally, we must confirm the opinion established in the present chapter by a pontifical decree which we mentioned from Saint Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, in chapter 20, in the *Life of Our Archbishop Saint Laurence of Litta*, which we published in print in the year of the Lord 1653.

Such a decree was enacted by the authority of Saint Pope Symmachus in the year 502 and was immediately promulgated by that archbishop to his provincial bishops. By it, both the archbishop himself and the priests and deacons were commanded to have female companions as witnesses to their chastity. The clergy of Milan was likewise professing that chastity at that time, which had been perpetually preserved from the ancient days, and specifically from the time of Saint Ambrose.

If you please, therefore, read that chapter attentively, as well as Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals* under the year of Christ 502, article 32, and several of the following articles.

For the present, we quote only the following from that decree:
