> “Therefore we wish no priest who obeys the ancient and modern laws, and no Levite, to remain anywhere without a person whose worth has been well tested; or, if poverty of means has not allowed someone to have a companion, let him himself become the fellow-resident of another. Let everything that is done among religious persons be public; let secret obscurity be rejected. He who owes innocence to God should have many aware of his actions. Let rivals take note: whoever brings forward witnesses wishes to be proved. Let conduct that does not wish to be known be judged evil.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, in accordance with the ordinance of God and our Redeemer, which is to remain in force, we decree, relying upon the authority of blessed Peter, the Apostolic See, and its pontiff, whose desire is that vices be eradicated from the roots, that no religious person of the aforesaid orders dare conduct himself otherwise than we have stated. Whoever presumes to do so shall suffer loss of his honors with disgrace. How great an evil it is when a person dedicated to God does not obey salutary admonitions, let him say. No one shall keep strange women with him, except the persons designated by the canons, lest, by acting in this way, even if his life is innocent, he incur damage to his reputation.”

Thus far the decree.

Its final clause plainly shows how well it agrees with the canon of the Council of Nicaea which we quoted in number 39. The following statement of Pope Gregory the Great also aptly belongs here, from book 7, letter 39, addressed to the Roman Defender:

> “It has come to our attention that certain bishops, under the pretext of companionship, live in one house with women. Therefore, lest this provide either a just occasion for reproach to mockers or an easy opportunity for the ancient enemy of the human race to deceive, we command you by the tenor of this instruction to show yourself energetic and vigilant.
>
> “If any of the bishops within the bounds of the patrimony entrusted to you live with women, restrain this altogether, and henceforth do not allow them to dwell there in any way, except those whom the judgment of the sacred canons permits: namely, a mother, aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no evil suspicion can arise. Yet they do better if they also abstain from living with such persons. For it is written that blessed Augustine did not consent to live even with his sister, saying: ‘Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.’ The caution of so learned a man ought therefore to be a great instruction to us. For it is the mark of foolish presumption that what the strong fear, the weaker do not fear. He wisely overcomes what is unlawful who has learned not even to use what is permitted.”

Thus spoke that holy Pope Gregory, truly great and an outstanding teacher of the Church; and with these words we too now gladly bring the present chapter to its conclusion.

## Between 1080 and 1095

### Saint Gerald, First Abbot and Founder of Silva-Major

[Col. 1003]

## Life of Saint Gerald, by an Anonymous Monk, His Contemporary

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictine Saints, IX, 886, from manuscript codices and the Bollandist April volume.)*

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Later writers spell the name of this blessed abbot in various ways. Some call him Gerald or Girald, some Girard, and most commonly Gerard; but in the older copies of his *Life* he is consistently called Geraldus.

This is confirmed by Baldric, then abbot of Bourgueil, in various epitaphs that he composed immediately after the death of blessed Gerald, and by Stephen, bishop of Tournai, who in the immediately following century published a sermon, hymns, and other works to be sung on Gerald’s feast.

Indeed, in the old documents of the monastery of Silva-Major—of which very many survive, including several written by the blessed abbot’s own hand or recorded at his dictation—Geraldus is found written everywhere, except in one or two documents where he is called Geraudus. He himself consistently calls himself Geraldus or Giraudus.

### 2

We possess two Lives of him, both written in the monastery of Silva-Major shortly after his death. The name of the author who produced the first is unknown; the other writer is called Christian in the Corbie manuscript, from which Henschenius says that he obtained it.

Both were monks, and specifically monks of Silva-Major, as is evident from the content of their works. It is therefore surprising that the editor of the second Life nowhere praised the first, although it contains almost nothing—apart from a few miracles performed at the blessed man’s tomb—that is not narrated in the first Life, and indeed at greater length.

The author of the later Life reports, in no. 27, a miracle which, he says, had been “committed to writing” by Peter, the seventh abbot of that place. Since the same miracle appears in the first Life, no. 30, someone might suspect that Peter, whom the later author praises, was the author of the first Life—namely, that same Peter who was received as a monk by blessed Gerald, afterward became his chaplain, and finally, in advanced old age, became the seventh abbot of Silva-Major.

Two principal considerations, however, prevent us from accepting this. First, the author of the earlier Life repeatedly praises Peter himself. “Peter,” he says in no. 28, “relating many of his [Saint Gerald’s] miracles, testified that the following miracle had been performed”; and in the following number: “The aforementioned abbot Peter also related another kind of miracle.”

Then the same author states in no. 32 that he received the miracles he narrated from others “who had most certainly seen and heard them.” This does not fit Peter, if he himself had witnessed them and heard them with his own ears.

Whether the later author, by those words in which he praises a miracle written down by Abbot Peter, intended to designate the first Life—which he may have thought had been written by Abbot Peter—we cannot determine.

Certainly, the author of that earlier Life, whoever he may finally have been, nowhere mentioned any writing of Peter concerning the miracles of blessed Gerald; nor, if such a writing ever existed, has it survived to the memory of posterity.

Besides these two authors, John of Guisia, abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon at the end of the fourteenth century, also wrote a Life of blessed Gerald. But this Life is nothing other than an abridgment of the earlier Life.

Of these works, we present the first Life, collated against three manuscripts; the second may be found among the Bollandists. We shall say something below about Baldric and the other authors who celebrated blessed Gerald on various occasions.

It is nevertheless surprising that both writers of his Life, who lived at Silva-Major, said almost nothing about the distinguished deeds of the blessed abbot in that monastery. We have therefore thought it appropriate to discuss them somewhat more fully, especially the spread of his institution into various provinces, which occurred while he was still alive, as is clear from several documents.

But first, a brief account must be given of his election to the abbacy of Saint Medard, since some do not hesitate to call it into question.

### 3

Lisiardus—or rather Hariulfus—in the *Life of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons*, which we published above under the year 1087, testifies that blessed Gerald was elected abbot of Saint Medard of Soissons after Arnulf’s resignation.

Some recent writers deny this, because no mention of his election occurs in the two Lives of blessed Gerald, nor even in any of the monuments of Silva-Major. Yet many such documents survive in which Gerald himself testifies that, after relinquishing the administration of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon and after various pilgrimages, which are individually recounted in both Lives, he arrived in Aquitaine.

Hugo Menardus, who cites this passage of the *Life of Saint Arnulf* in his observations on the Benedictine Martyrology for 5 April, suggests that the passage concerning Saint Gerald’s election to the abbacy of Soissons was added by copyists, since, as he says, nothing similar is found in the *Life of Saint Gerald*.

The authority of the old manuscripts contradicts this conjecture. We collated the *Life of blessed Arnulf* against them, and in all of them the election of blessed Gerald—who afterward became the founder of the monastery of Silva-Major in Aquitaine—to the administration of Saint Medard is described in the same words and in the same manner.

Moreover, Lisiardus, who revised this Life, and Hariulfus, its original author, were contemporaries of the blessed Arnulf and Gerald, and, as may be inferred, were not strangers to either of them.

Lisiardus, a disciple of blessed Arnulf and ordained subdeacon by him, was at Soissons at precisely the time when Gerald is said to have been elected abbot of Saint Medard. Hariulfus, however, was living at Centula, where he had embraced the monastic life, while Gerald was at that time managing the affairs of the monastery at Corbie.

We therefore may not doubt this election. I readily believe, however, that Gerald never actually took possession of this abbey, since Pontius, the usurper of the monastery, relying upon the power of Queen Berta, expelled the blessed man.

Nor does the author of the *Life of Saint Arnulf* seem to imply more than this. It is therefore not surprising that the writers of the *Life of blessed Gerald*, and even Gerald himself, nowhere mentioned this election, since there was no reason to commemorate it.

Gerald, never admitted to the administration of the monastery, could accomplish nothing there worthy of being related by the writers of his Life. And since Gerald himself recorded in the documents of Silva-Major only what happened to him after he had resigned the abbacy of Laon, he ought not to have mentioned that election to the monastery of Saint Medard, which more probably occurred before that resignation, when, weary of the faithlessness of his monks, he was considering a change of place.

For the authors of both Lives state that he departed immediately after relinquishing the administration of the monastery of Laon; the author of the second Life adds that Gerald did this in order to withdraw to the desert.

But now we must discuss his deeds at Silva-Major.

### 4

Besides what the author of the *Life* says about blessed Gerald’s arrival in Aquitaine and the beginnings of the monastery of Silva-Major, we learn much from the old documents of that place, which were written through the care of the holy man himself.

One of them explains how the pious abbot acquired the estate through the generosity of Ogerius and other noblemen, who voluntarily offered the place to be consecrated to God in favor of so great a man.

Only Drogo, abbot of Malliacum, caused some difficulty. He wished to claim the place where the monastery was being built because one of his monks had inhabited it for some time, with the permission of the matron Ermentrude. But his case failed.

The manner in which Gerald finally obtained full possession of the place must be learned from his own account, preserved in the Silva-Major Chartulary:

> “When I, Gerald, although unworthy, had been called abbot and had first come to Silva-Major with my fellow soldiers, and when we had decided to remain in the place anciently called Altus-Villaris, we sought out the owners of that place so that, with their permission, we might live there.
>
> “There was a certain man named Autgerius of Rions, to whom one half of the allod belonged, while many persons shared the other half. Yet the jurisdiction and tithe of the entire allod belonged to Autgerius.
>
> “This Autgerius, therefore, anticipated by divine inspiration, gave us whatever he possessed in that allod. Likewise Olivarius of Turre and his brothers Guillelmus Guilfrandi and Arnaldus, as well as Ostendus and Bonaefusus of Saint Severinus, and many others who claimed a share in that allod, freely gave us whatever they possessed there.
>
> “Among them was a certain matron named Ermengardis of Gistris, who also gave us her share. But this matron had granted a dwelling on her portion to a certain monk of the monastery of Malliacum who wished to lead a solitary life, under the condition, as was reported, that he might inhabit it for as long as he wished.
>
> “When he had begun to live there and had made an oratory of earth, the place displeased him as a dwelling. He moved his residence to another territory and allowed the chapel he had built to fall into abandonment.
>
> “When he heard that the entire allod had been given to us, with no exception made for his portion, he went to his abbot, named Drogo, and informed him of the whole sequence of events.
>
> “The abbot came to the council that was held at that time in the city of Bordeaux and there complained that we had invaded the possession of his church.
>
> “But since we preferred to abandon everything rather than retain anything through litigation—we who had left our own possessions—we asked Lord Amatus, the Roman legate, and Lord Guillelmus, of revered memory, Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitiers, whose counsel and assistance had enabled us to remain in the aforesaid place, to obtain from the abbot that he peacefully surrender this portion to us, since he would derive no profit from it and would not prefer there the dwelling of wild animals to that of human beings and servants of God.
>
> “But when he was petitioned by them and by many other bishops and good men, he replied that he could not do this without the consent of the brothers of his monastery.
>
> “Then Lord Amatus went with him to the monastery of Malliacum and took with him one of our monks, named Litherius.
>
> “When the brothers of that place had assembled in the chapter-house before their abbot Drogo, Lord Amatus stated our petition before them all. At first they strongly opposed it. But finally, convinced by the reasoning that it was not compatible with charity to oppose a request for the service of God, from which they would receive no assistance, they gave their consent.
>
> “Accordingly, Abbot Drogo, with the consent of the monks, surrendered whatever claim he had in the allod given to us and granted it to us freely, in the presence of Lord Amatus, the Roman cardinal, with his chaplains Litgerius and Artaldus, and of our monk Litherius with his servant Erluinus.”

### 5

Having thus obtained full and free possession of the territory of Silva-Major, Gerald approached the archbishop of Bordeaux, in whose diocese it lay, so that he might obtain from him the liberty of his monastery.

The pious bishop readily consented to the holy man’s requests and granted him a most ample privilege. To prevent it from being violated in the future, he arranged for it to be confirmed at the Council of Bordeaux by the other bishops and abbots.

The blessed abbot himself relates this in the record made concerning the matter, which he arranged to have copied into the monastery’s Chartulary for the memory of posterity, in the following form:

> “All things that arise perish, and things that grow old decline; human life is not extended very far, and its memory is shown to be extremely brief. But lest oblivion entirely swallow up the past, it is necessary that writing preserve a record of things done, so that what is changeable may not remain unknown to those who come after.
>
> “Therefore let the present Church not be ignorant of this, nor let posterity remain uncertain about what was done in our presence.
>
> “I, Gerald, by God’s generosity abbot, though unworthy, had long desired to be snatched from the worldly waves by which I was battered more severely than a fragile spirit could bear. Moreover, those subject to me obeyed me less and less, and their iron hearts could not be softened, since worldly affairs had hardened them excessively.
>
> “Finally, when divine mercy showed me the harbor of salvation, I resolved to seek the caves of solitude, where there would be no secular dwelling of human beings.
>
> “Having therefore commended the care of the flock entrusted to me to the bishop, I departed from the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon with a few companions, entirely unaware where the journey would lead.
>
> “But at length, with the Lord guiding us—for he is never absent from those who hope in him—we reached Lord Willelmus, Count of Poitiers, a man of outstanding nobility and also Duke of all Aquitaine. He assigned to us a suitable woodland called Silva-Major.
>
> “He granted us that allod so completely that no one could claim any right there, as another charter also testifies.
>
> “When I wished to begin a monastery there, I went to Lord Goscelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, in whose bishopric the aforesaid allod lay, to ask his favor. With the intervention of the aforesaid duke, he granted the monastery, already begun, such complete liberty that neither he nor anyone after him—neither archbishop, archdeacon, archpriest, nor any person of any order—could have any right or authority in it, so that the monks living there might serve God freely and without any disturbance.
>
> “He also established, at the request of Willelmus, that if the town should ever grow, by Christ’s will, the archbishop or any of his ministers should nevertheless have no jurisdiction there, either over clerics or over laymen; rather, everything should be referred to the disposition of the abbot or the congregation.
>
> “He also provided for himself and for us that, nevertheless, when necessary, we should receive the consecration of churches, sacred orders, and chrism from the archbishop.
>
> “This constitution was again confirmed by him at the next council, in the presence of the Roman legates Hugh and Amatus and a large college of other bishops.
>
> “It was also decreed that if anyone attempted to violate this decree, he should know himself to be excommunicated until he had made satisfaction, both by the archbishop and by all who had been present at the council.
>
> “Moreover, on the advice of Lord Amatus, we established that this monastery should be subject solely to the Roman Church and, for its protection, should pay the Apostolic Lord each year a gift of five solidi.
>
> “But I, already declining into the weakness of extreme old age, was now wishing to relinquish the care of the monks and yield my place, as one less useful, to a better man.
>
> “When our brothers nevertheless asked Lord Amatus to intervene, although I resisted with all my strength, he declared to me, on behalf of the Apostolic Lord, that obedience was required of me and entrusted their care to me.
>
> “This confirmation was enacted in the city of Bordeaux at a council in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1080, indiction 3, epact 26, on 7 October, in the eighth year—year 7—of Pope Gregory, while Philip was reigning in France.

> “The signature of Willelmus, Duke of Aquitaine. Confirm this, O God.  
> “I, Amatus, legate of the Apostolic See, confirm. +  
> “I, Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See, confirm. +  
> “I, Gocelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, grant and confirm in the presence of the council. +  
> “The signature of Rodulfus, archbishop of Tours.  
> “The signature of Willelmus, archbishop of Auxerre.  
> “The signature of Boso, bishop of Saintes.  
> “The signature of Ademar, bishop of Angoulême.  
> “The signature of Willelmus, bishop of Périgueux.  
> “The signature of Raymundus, bishop of Bazas.  
> “The signature of Hugh, bishop of Bigorre.  
> “The signature of Donaldus, bishop of Agen.  
> “The signature of Peter, bishop of Aire.  
> “The signature of Odo, abbot of Saint John of Angély.  
> “The signature of Drogo, abbot of Malliacum.  
> “The signature of Raynaldus, abbot of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers.  
> “The signature of Bertrand, abbot of Saint Julian [or Saint Junianus of Nobiliacum].  
> “The signature of Hildebert, abbot of Nantilly.  
> “The signature of Fulchradus, abbot of Saint Saviour of Blaye.  
> “The signature of Acelinus Gocelinus, archdeacon of the Church of Bordeaux.”

### 6

In that same year, 1080, many noblemen of the neighboring region, emulating the zeal of the bishops toward Silva-Major and inspired by the example of Guillelmus, Duke of Aquitaine, unanimously granted complete liberty to the Church of Silva-Major, which Gerald was establishing, “so that,” as they said, “freed from earthly powers, it may serve God alone in security.”

This is likewise attested in an old document transcribed from the Silva-Major Chartulary by our Stephanotius.

There, after citing the example of Willelmus, or Guido, Count of Poitiers and Duke of all Aquitaine, who had done the same “with all the nobles of his military following consenting and willing,” and after praising the decree of the Council of Bordeaux, by which the legates of the Apostolic See and the other bishops had decreed, under threat of anathema, that no one should violate the liberty of the monastery of Silva-Major, they declare that they accept and approve this grant of liberty.

Indeed, so that no difficulty might later arise concerning the use of this immunity, they explain under what principal conditions it was to be established. The document sets out the matter as follows:

> “It is necessary to state briefly what that liberty is, and what protection was granted to that Church by the aforesaid men: namely, that no one except the abbot and monks should have any right, authority, or advocacy whatsoever in any matter throughout the entire allod belonging to that same church,” and so forth.

Among these noblemen the more illustrious are listed: Peter, viscount of Gavarret, who confirmed this liberty “with the entire fellowship of his army”; and Guillelmus Amaneus of Amanjeu, who did the same, saying that “all the nobles of our region approved it.”

With him subscribed Bernard, his brother; Bernard of Rions and Vidianus, his brother; Arnaldus; Raymundus of Bordis; Boso of Montremblant; and Bernard of Scutianus of Escoussans.

Besides all these, Bernard of Boiville, viscount; Arnaldus of Blancafort; and many other noble knights who were present there promised that they would be future defenders of the Church of Silva-Major, and so forth, against anyone whatsoever.

The same liberty of the Silva-Major monastery was solemnly confirmed with an oath sworn upon the holy Gospels on the holy day of Easter by these same men—or certainly by their descendants—together with other noblemen of the entire region, under Gaufridus, the sixth abbot.

In subsequent times the dukes of Aquitaine and other nobles confirmed all these possessions and immunities.

The authority of the Apostolic See was also added, as is clear from the bulls of Alexander, Lucius, Celestine, and other Roman pontiffs. But it is not relevant to pursue these matters more fully here, since we have undertaken to illuminate the deeds of blessed Gerald, not to present a history of Silva-Major.

### 7

The fame of Gerald and his disciples’ holiness therefore soon spread throughout Aquitaine and flew also into distant and foreign provinces. Many flocked to the new monastery [Col. 1009D] so that there, under the discipline of so great a Father, they might renounce the world’s pomp and serve as soldiers of Christ. Others, who could not do this, at least consecrated their possessions to God by donating estates and property to the monastery.

But since the narrowness of a single monastery could not contain so great a multitude of disciples—and indeed other provinces were not to be deprived of so great an example of virtue—monasteries were first established in neighboring regions for monks from Silva-Major, and then also in distant places. Saint Gerald sent colonies of his disciples there and caused them to flourish in the careful observance of the Benedictine Rule. These were the first beginnings of the congregation of Silva-Major, which later became celebrated not only in [Col. 1010A] Aquitaine or Gascony, but also throughout Gaul, Belgium, England, Navarre, and other provinces of Spain. While Gerald was still alive, it was propagated through almost all these regions.

Pope Celestine lists individually the places that were subject to Silva-Major in the following century, in a bull issued to Peter, the abbot, in 1197. Here, however, it has seemed appropriate to discuss only those whose beginnings Gerald himself took care to have recorded in his monastery’s cartulary.

### 8

Not long after the construction of the monastery of Silva-Major, Gerald himself laid the foundations of the small monastery of Trajectum, situated on the bank of the Garonne. Raymond-William supplied the site, as is clear from the foundation charter, in which this same Raymond gave “to Lord Gerald, first abbot of Silva-Major, part of the allod [Col. 1010B] of Trajectum on the bank of the Garonne, where a monastery may be built with its workshops, gardens, and orchards, and with access from the river to the nearby millpond.”

This nobleman placed the charter, “with all his sons, upon the altar of God’s Mother and of the holy apostles Simon and Jude”—that is, upon the altar of the church of Silva-Major—for greater security. William, duke of Aquitaine, gave this new colony the same “protection” that he and the other nobles had granted to Silva-Major.

### 9

Not long afterward Peter, viscount of Gavarret, built on his estate, called “Gavaret,” a monastery in honor of the Holy Sepulchre. He endowed it with numerous lands and revenues and wished it to be subject “to Lord Gerald” and to his successors, the abbots of Silva-Major [Col. 1010C]. Thus, he says in the foundation charter:

> “Let the abbot of Silva-Major always be the abbot of the Holy Sepulchre, and let him cause the same kind of religious observance and way of life maintained there to be maintained here also. Let him have in this monastery the same authority over its monks, property, and possessions as he has in that church, so that the place of Silva-Major and the Holy Sepulchre may always be one in God’s service and in good religious observance; and let them likewise share poverty and abundance, without prejudice to the authority of the archbishop of Auch and the bishop of Aire.”

The charter was subscribed by William, archbishop of Auch; Peter, bishop of Aire; Arnold Roger, the donor’s brother; Stephen of Caumont; Raymond; William of Mezerolles; Peter of Vico; Amanevus of Tilliacum; Odo of Pardailhan; [Col. 1010D] and others.

Peter, the founder’s son, solemnly confirmed the same donation. A record of this is preserved in the Silva-Major Cartulary, and we hope that no one will find it unwelcome if we reproduce it here:

> “Peter, viscount of Gavarret, son of Peter the viscount, came with the greatest devotion to the monastery called Silva-Major and humbly requested the benefits and prayers of the place from Abbot G. and the other brothers. The abbot and the community of brothers gladly consenting to this most praiseworthy request, they brought him into the chapter and there, with the book, as is customary, granted him investiture in the benefice. He, however, without hesitation, at that same place and hour gave and conceded to them whatever his father had previously given: namely, the monastery of Gavarret with all its appurtenances, both those already acquired and those yet to be acquired.” [Col. 1011A]

Other charters likewise show that the viscounts of Gavarret were extremely generous toward the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre. Indeed, not long afterward, following the death of blessed Gerald and under the rule of Abbot Geoffrey, the viscountess Agnes founded a nunnery beside the monastery of the men, where she herself became a nun.

Although no year is given in most charters of this kind, it is nevertheless clear that the first foundation of this place took place before 1092. Peter, bishop of Aire, who subscribed it and is said in another charter to have made certain gifts to the same monastery, is said to have died in that year, 1092, according to the old Necrology of the monastery of Saint-Sever at the head of Gascony, where we read: [Col. 1011B]

> “On the Ides of June, the deposition of Lord Peter, bishop of Aire, of blessed memory, in the year 1092.”

The nunnery of Gavarret is believed to have been united in the fourteenth century with the monastery of the men, which stood nearby. The latter, however, was plundered by the Calvinists and thereafter supported no monks. There nevertheless remains today a fairly spacious and well-kept church, together with the prior, who supports several priests there to perform the divine offices as best they can. Gavaret is a town in modern Gascony, formerly in the diocese of Aire and later, despite the protests of the people of Aire, assigned to the diocese of Auch.

### 10

The beginnings of the monastery of Saint Nicholas on the island of Rugiana—Royan—in the territory of the Santones should likewise be assigned to the year 1092. Elias of Didonne, together with his wife Avicia and their sons Walter, Gifard, and Elias, supplied the monks of Silva-Major with a suitable site for its construction and many possessions for its endowment [Col. 1011C].

The charter of donation gives the year 1092, at the castle of Royan itself, in the fifteenth indiction. Among others, the following were present: “Stephen, abbot and hermit of the island of Cordouan,” and Herlegius, prior of Silva-Major, with many others whose names it is not necessary to list individually.

### 11

At the same time, Dimo, a nobleman, together with his wife and children, granted the monastery of Silva-Major the church of Saint Peter of Neronis-Villa, situated in the diocese of Sens, where several monks were established.

We infer that this foundation was made during the lifetime of blessed Gerald from the consent of Richer, archbishop of Sens, who died in 1096 [Col. 1011D]. An extraordinary miracle provided the occasion for increasing the resources of this place. It is reported in the old record of the Silva-Major Cartulary, without any indication of date, in these words:

> “There was a certain knight named Fulco Faicus, who had a clerical son named Garmund. In his youth, this son had devoted himself excessively to the activities of secular life, had subjected himself to the yoke of every carnal pleasure, and—what is worse—having fallen into the Simoniac heresy, had perpetrated many unlawful acts against God’s will. At length, struck by a severe illness of the limbs and believing death to be near, he gave himself to the church of Saint Mary of Silva-Major and to the church of Saint Peter of Neronis-Villa; and, receiving the religious habit from a certain monk of that place [Col. 1012A], he was immediately restored to his former health.”

Various donations are subsequently listed, which Fulco, Garmund’s father; Hauvinus, his brother; and other noblemen made to the church of Neronis-Villa after witnessing this miracle. That church is said there to have been “consecrated by the hand of God.”

### 12

The fame of Gerald and his disciples was no less celebrated among the people of Orléans. It is said to have occasioned the conversion of many and the establishment of the monastery of Sedes-Meri, or Semoy, situated not far from that city.

It was founded at this time by a nobleman named Tecelin, who gave the monks of Silva-Major the church of Saint Bartholomew, together with many possessions for the support of the monks brought from Silva-Major. They continued there until almost our own time [Col. 1012B]. The place has now been reduced to what is called a simple priory and still remains subject to Silva-Major, although scarcely anything survives except the small ruins of the ancient monastery.

The Silva-Major Cartulary presents various donations subsequently made to this place by Albert, Tecelin’s son, and by other noblemen. “Houses, a garden, a courtyard,” and so forth, were possessed by the monks of Silva-Major among the people of Orléans while Saint Gerald was still alive, as we learn from an old record made by Gerald himself. In it he testifies that he sent Theoderic there to recover some possessions of his monastery from calumniators. It reads as follows:

> “In the name of Christ, I, Giraudus, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Silva-Major, wish it to be known to the faithful of God’s holy Church, both present [Col. 1012C] and future, that a certain brother named Theoderic, son of Anselm, despising the worldly service which he had practiced and seeking the salvation of his soul, fled to us and was devoutly received. Together with his own person, which he offered through our hands to God, Saint Mary, and Saint Benedict, he also contributed from his own property and that of his parents, apart from what he brought with him, houses in the city of Orléans with a garden and courtyard, and the adjoining land which he held. In the very view of the city he also possessed seven arpents of vineyards . . . After not much time had passed, however, his mother and brother brought an unjust claim against a certain part of these possessions. Therefore I, the abbot, and my brothers sent our fellow brother Theoderic so that he might fully [Col. 1012D] settle whatever he had contributed to the monastery of blessed Mary. By God’s grace, this was done,” and so forth.

Gelduin, a member of King Philip’s household, gave the same monastery a furnace situated in that city and other possessions located in neighboring villages, as we learn from another record, which explains the matter as follows:

> “A certain member of the household of Lord Philip, king of the Franks, named Gelduin, with the king’s consent and counsel, abandoned all the glory of the world, surrendered himself and his possessions to the church of Silva-Major, and received the habit of holy religious life from Lord Gerald, the first abbot of that place. This man, therefore,” and so forth.

The possessions contributed by Gelduin are then listed.

### 13

In the year 1083, in the twenty-third year of his reign, Philip, king of the Franks, gave “to the church of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, which is called Silva-Major,” the chapel of Saint Leodegar in the forest of Lesgia—l’Esgue—with its appurtenances.

The chief officers of the kingdom subscribed the royal charter. It was reread by Gislebert, the king’s cleric, in the place of Gosfrid, chancellor and bishop of Paris. In another charter Philip testifies that he did this after hearing much about the holy way of life of the monks of Silva-Dei from two monks whom Lord Gerald, the first abbot of the place, had sent. The chronological notices found in our copy of this later charter, however, are corrupt.

It is certain that monks of Silva-Major had already been established there, or at least were established shortly afterward. Indeed, in a bull issued by Celestine III in the following century, among other places are listed “the priories of Saint Leodegar and Saint [Col. 1013B] Paul of the Forest, and Bellaevallis, in the diocese of Soissons.”

### 14

More celebrated than all these, however, was the foundation of Saint-Denis near Mons in Hainaut. Richildis, countess of Flanders and founder of the place, wished this abbey to be subject to Saint Gerald and his successors. It is useful to reproduce here the foundation documents from the Silva-Major Cartulary.

> “I, Richildis, countess, mother of Count Baldwin, son of the great Baldwin, who held the principality of both the Flemish and Hainaut districts, seeing the whole world rushing toward destruction and all mortals more subject to the darkness of sins than to the light of truth, began to consider the salvation of my soul and that of my son, and how we might please the heavenly Judge by raising up the fallen condition of holy Mother Church.
>
> “As I often pondered and lamented these things, the thought occurred to me of restoring a certain small place dedicated to Saint Denis and establishing there brothers who would serve as soldiers according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. At the time when these matters occupied my mind, a monastery had been begun in a place called Silva-Major, where God was wonderfully increasing his servants, since they served him with complete devotion.
>
> “It therefore pleased me to subject the aforesaid place to that church, so that it might always receive an abbot from so noble a congregation to govern the church of Saint Denis properly. From our surrounding property I contributed enough to the place for the abbot to be maintained honorably. Accordingly, Lord Gerald, the first abbot of Silva-Major, sent monks of his own there and appointed the first abbot.
>
> “A rent of twelve gold denarii was established there, to be paid each year at the beginning of Lent to Saint Mary, in whose honor the monastery of Silva-Major is dedicated. We have entirely freed this place and everything belonging to it from every authority, so that no one may have any right, lordship, or advocacy there except the abbot and brothers of the church.
>
> “Lord Gerald, bishop of Cambrai, also gave to God, for the cultivation of the Christian religion, whatever episcopal right he possessed in the church or at the altar, so that the monks residing there might be wholly free from every disturbance. If at any time—which God forbid—the abbot of Saint Denis should act against the Rule, let him come to the abbot of Silva-Major, who shall correct his wrongdoing; and likewise any monk who rebels against the abbot.
>
> “So that these provisions might have greater authority, they are strengthened by the testimony of noblemen whose names are written below: the subscription of Saint Gerald, bishop of Cambrai; the subscription of Anselm of Ribemont; the subscription of Baldwin of Tournai; the subscription of Gislebert, provost of Nivelles; and those of many others who were present at this declaration.”

> “These things were therefore done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1082, in the fifth indiction, with an epact of eighteen and a concurrent of five, while Henry, king of the Romans, was reigning. The subscription of Count Baldwin. The subscription of Richildis, his mother.”

The monastery of Saint-Denis in Broqueroy, near the city of Mons in Hainaut, is still famous today.

[Col. 1014B]

### 15

Not long after the death of blessed Gerald, Hugh, count of Rethel, founded the monastery of Novy. Monks from Silva-Major were established there, and it continues to exist to this day under the title of a priory—one preferable to many abbeys—subject to Silva-Major.

It is situated not far from the town of Rethel in the diocese of Rheims and is now inhabited by the Reverend Fathers of the congregation of Saint-Vanne. The congregation of Silva-Major was also propagated into the neighboring dioceses—that is, throughout the whole of Belgica II, or the province of Rheims—where the name of Gerald, its own alumnus, was no less famous than in Aquitaine. Indeed, across the sea, among the English, the careful observance of regular discipline by the monks of Silva-Major was also celebrated. As the eleventh century drew to a close, they were already flourishing in that region, but they made much greater progress in Spain.

### 16

At that time Sancho, son of Ramiro, was reigning among the Aragonese. After adding Navarre to his kingdom, he founded and endowed a considerable number of churches in those regions, thereby giving many clerics and monks an opportunity to approach him.

Among these were several of Gerald’s disciples. The pious king kindly received them and established them in a church near the village of Rosta, so that they might devote themselves there to the exercises of monastic life. Since they were subsequently oppressed by extreme poverty, he later endowed them with various possessions.

We learn all this from an old record preserved in the frequently mentioned Silva-Major Cartulary, where Sancho himself relates the matter as follows:

> “Until now,” he says, “Christian religion has rarely been preserved in Spain. But after the Roman law established by the holy Fathers was introduced in our times, and murky error was driven away by the coming of the light, the Church of Christ was enlarged by clerics and monks arriving from various regions.
>
> “Accordingly, certain monks came to me who said that they had been sent by Lord Gerald, abbot of Silva-Major. This abbot and his disciples had been widely proclaimed throughout Spain; having departed from their homeland, they practiced at Silva-Major a service worthy of God.
>
> “To these monks I first gave a church in a village named Rosta, which I freed for them from every form of lordship. But they received too little from it for their needs, although, content with this, they led a sufficiently austere life.
>
> “Afterward, when I had come to visit them and had learned of their extreme poverty, I gave them another church not far away, dedicated to Saint James. Through their assistance and prayers, I hoped that my soul might be helped before God.”

He then lists various donations made to these monks by himself and by a certain hermit named Hugh. The king himself, together with his son Peter, is said to have granted and confirmed all these possessions.

In the era 1122, the same prince gave the Silva-Major monks the mosques of Essoya—*Meschitas* (V., “mosques”)—without doubt seized from the Moors, together with tithes and other revenues. Besides his son Peter, his wife Felicia, queen and Peter’s mother, also subscribed this donation.

He made considerably more donations in the era 1131, in October—that is, shortly before his death. He was killed in the siege of the city of Huesca the following year, namely in 1094, [Col. 1015B] on 4 June. At the same king’s urging, Peter, bishop of Pamplona—who, according to Tamayo’s notice in the catalogue of the bishops of Pamplona under 7 April, had been transferred to this see from the monastery of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières in Gaul—gave Argilense Church, with its appurtenances and other revenues, to Saint Gerald in the era 1125.

### 17

Gerald, mindful of so many benefits received from the pious king, decreed that one poor man should always be maintained in the Silva-Major monastery in place of that king or of his successors. It is useful to reproduce here the decree made concerning this matter:

> “Testament of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Silva-Major to King Sancho of Aragon. By the authority of God the almighty Father, at the request of King Sancho, I confirm, and I command our successors to observe, that for King Sancho and for each one of his successors, one poor man shall be received into this community, so that he may become a monk entirely without money, be clothed in the king’s place, eat, drink, and pray; and likewise for his successors. If one of the poor men who have become monks for the kings dies, another shall be substituted in his place. The whole chapter answered: Amen; let it be done, let it be done.”

After receiving these letters, the king thanked Gerald, as we learn from his reply, which we likewise reproduce here from the Silva-Major Cartulary.

> “Reply of King Sancho to blessed Gerald. Because you have confirmed such provisions in your chapter for me and my successors, may God repay you, and, if life permits, we shall not be ungrateful. For the present, by the authority of God and our own, we confirm—and propose that our descendants confirm—that all the gifts which I have given you, or which I or our successors shall give, be everywhere as free as our own palaces, so that neither an ecclesiastical nor a secular person may dare to disturb them. Whoever disturbs them, or consents to those who disturb them, shall incur God’s anger with bodily punishment. For those who guard them, life and peace.
>
> “This I grant; this I confirm; this I leave as a memorial with blessing to my descendants. This is the sign of divine acknowledgment, and these are the witnesses in whom the testimony remains.”

### 18

The pious abbot was no less concerned for William, duke of Aquitaine. It is useful to reproduce here the statute which he arranged to be observed for William both while he was alive and after his death, as a perpetual memorial of gratitude for the many benefits received from him.

To prevent this institution from falling into disuse after a long passage of time, Gerald summoned the brothers to chapter. Since they willingly consented, he wished it to be entered in a public document, which is preserved in the Silva-Major Archives in the following form:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy Church, both future and present, that Lord William, the venerable duke of Aquitaine, gave to Saint Mary whatever he possessed in the territory called Silva-Major and endowed it with complete freedom.
>
> “Therefore I, Gerald, by God’s providence its first abbot, [Col. 1016B] together with the entire community of brothers, decreed—and established the decree in the congregation—that, for this and the many other benefits which he has bestowed upon us, he should always be remembered especially in our prayers, so that he might deserve a reward from Christ.
>
> “We also established that a special Mass should be sung for him each week, and that each day an allowance equal to that assigned to each brother should be set aside for him and distributed to the poor on his behalf. This was determined so that, just as it is done during his life, it should be done after his death with no less devotion, for as long as the church endures.
>
> “We therefore considered it necessary to commit this to memory and writing, lest it be lost through the negligence of future generations. Two similar little charters have therefore been written, so that the aforesaid duke may have one and the other may remain with the church.
>
> “If anyone should presume to oppose this decree, he shall be liable to the danger of anathema until he has obeyed by making satisfaction. To confirm the testimony of this matter, we have subscribed the names of those who were present at the decree: the subscription of Robert of Burgundy; the subscription of William Elias of Bordeaux; the subscription of Peter, viscount of Châtillon; the subscription of Amanevus of Marcha; the subscription of Rodulf of Saint-Eloi.”

### 19

The pious abbot prescribed in detail what was to be done for each deceased person, whether one of the monks of his monastery or someone else joined to it by a spiritual bond. He took care to have all these provisions written in a book designated for that purpose.

In the necrology he also wished the names of other benefactors to be inserted, so that at least some remembrance of them might be observed each year in the brothers’ assembly on the day of their death [Col. 1016D].

What he instituted should be said or done for the monks of his own congregation we learn from a record which blessed Abbot Gerald himself issued on this subject:

> “Let all present and future generations know that I, Gerald, abbot, though unworthy, of Saint Mary of Silva-Major, concerned for the welfare of the living and the dead, have established the following with the common counsel of the entire congregation, and have ordered it to be committed to writing so that it may endure forever.
>
> “If anyone from our congregation departs from this world and is buried with us, bread and wine shall be given to the poor on his behalf for a year, and for thirty days Masses and the vigils of the dead shall be celebrated communally by all [Col. 1017A]. The first seven Masses and vigils, however, shall be performed solemnly, with all the bells rung. Each priest shall recite seven Masses for him; whoever is not a priest shall recite three psalters; whoever has not yet reached the psalter shall sing seven psalms every day for thirty days; whoever does not know these shall say the *Miserere* seven times each day; and whoever does not even know the *Miserere* shall say the *Pater noster* seven times each day,” and so forth.

The spiritual associations of the monks of Silva-Major with the communities of other churches and monasteries are subsequently listed, but there is no time to pursue them here in greater detail.

Papebrochius reports the association which Gerald himself entered into with Odo, abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, in the chapter of Silva-Major, in his preliminary observations to the Life of blessed Gerald, no. 18. Anyone may consult it there [Col. 1017B], together with the names of most of the churches that maintained a fellowship of prayers with Silva-Major.

Several scribal errors have nevertheless entered these lists. Thus “Saint Mauritius of Uzerche, of Geneva” is written in place of Saint Maurinus, an abbey in the diocese of Agen; “of Uzerche,” that is, Uzerche among the Limousins; and “of Generes,” commonly Saint-Pé-de-Generez in the diocese of Tarbes.

### 20

No one, it seems, can deny that Gerald’s death must be assigned to the year 1095. This is stated in explicit terms by the author of the second Life, by Hugh of Flavigny, an exceptionally accurate contemporary writer in the Chronicle of Verdun, and by the author of the Chronicle of Maillezais, or Saint-Maixent.

The day of his death also seems no less certain, since both Lives state that the holy man departed to heaven on the Nones of April. Hugh of Flavigny does not disagree: he records that in the year 1095, on Wednesday, the eleventh day before the Nones of April, stars were seen falling from the sky from midnight until dawn; he then adds:

> “On that same night Gerald, abbot of Silva-Major, migrated to the Lord.”

The author of the Chronicle of Maillezais, however, writes that this occurred on the following day; he records the death of Saint Gerald and the falling of the stars from heaven on the eighth day before the Ides of April. His authority must be preferred neither to that of Hugh nor to that of the authors of both Lives of Saint Gerald.

Indeed, Gerald is commemorated on this very day in the ancient Necrology of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres. In the Necrology of Corbie, written not long after Gerald’s death, [Col. 1017D] we read:

> “On the Nones of April, Gerald, abbot of Stephen of Silva-Major [reading uncertain], and a monk of our congregation, died.”

His feast is prescribed for the same day in the ancient calendar of Silva-Major.

For this reason Hugo Menard rightly entered Gerald’s name in the Benedictine Martyrology under 5 April, where he is called “a man of great patience and humility.” Those who assigned his commemoration to other days seem to have confused this blessed man with other saints of the same name.

This undoubtedly happened especially on 13 October, the day on which the memory of Saint Gerald of Aurillac, the most celebrated count among the Auvergnats and therefore in Aquitaine, is recorded in ancient documents. On this day, therefore, Molanus, in the *Natales of the Saints of Belgium*, citing the Martyrology of Rubeaevallis, where the memory of Saint Gerald the confessor is found, recounts praises of our Gerald from an ancient poet and from Lisiardus.

Ferrarius, in his general catalogue of the saints, praises on the same day our Gerald together with Gerald of Aurillac and another abbot of that name from the Limousin. Bucelinus, although he had already entered our Gerald under 5 April, nevertheless repeats his commemoration on 13 October. It is not useful to pursue these matters at greater length.

It must nevertheless be acknowledged that the principal feast of blessed Gerald was celebrated in ancient times on 21 June, because on that day his sacred body was raised from the earth. This is clear from the letter of Otho, duke of Aquitaine, which we shall reproduce below.

The Silva-Major Calendar commemorates a double feast of Gerald: his death, as we have just said, on 5 April, and his Translation, on 21 June.

### 21

The holiness of blessed Gerald had been so widely celebrated, even while he was still alive, that immediately after his death no one hesitated to call him a saint and to venerate his relics and tomb, even before he had been formally enrolled among the saints by the supreme pontiff.

This is clear not only from both authors of his Life but also from Balderic, then abbot of Bourgueil and later archbishop of Dol. After receiving news of the death of the blessed abbot, who had been his friend, Balderic immediately composed, according to the custom of that period, verses to be sent to various churches. In them he calls Gerald “most holy” and says that he had no need of prayers, as other dead people did; indeed, he begs Gerald not to disdain helping him and the other living.

We think that no one will find it unwelcome if we reproduce some of these verses here. Anyone wishing to read the rest may consult Chesne, volume IV of the *Writers of French History*, if he wishes.

> When the faithful are accustomed to pray for the dead,  
> And to prolong their tears for those dear to them,  
> Nothing of either is needed for Father Gerald,  
> Who lived on earth as a citizen and inhabitant of heaven.  
>
> Here lies the most holy abbot of Silva-Major,  
> The splendor of abbots and the glory of monks.  
>
> Rejoice, Gaul, in Gerald, whom you brought forth,  
> And here venerate his sacred ashes.  
>
> Pray for us, Gerald, reverend Father:  
> We need ask nothing further for you.

### 22

As miracles frequently occurred over time at blessed Gerald’s tomb, it was considered worthwhile to transfer his sacred body elsewhere, “where it might be kept more secretly and securely,” as the author of the second Life seems to suggest, lest someone steal it.

Both authors of the Life relate that this was done under Peter, the seventh abbot, who had formerly been the holy man’s disciple and chaplain. Bishops, abbots, and other noblemen were summoned for this solemnity.

Gerald was not, however, publicly enrolled among the saints by decree until the end of the twelfth century. At that time two monks of Silva-Major went to Rome and presented to the pope—then Celestine III—letters written by the archbishop of Bordeaux and the other bishops, abbots, and noblemen of the province. These letters asserted Gerald’s holiness, which was firmly confirmed by his blameless conduct while he lived and by the almost innumerable miracles performed through him both during his life and after his death.

After these documents had been examined and weighed, and their testimony had been confirmed by several Gallican bishops and others who happened to be in Rome at the time, the pope decreed that Gerald’s name should be entered in the catalogue of the saints and wished his feast thereafter to be celebrated in the province of Bordeaux. He issued a document, which we reproduce here because it explains the proceedings of this canonization more clearly.

> **“Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ established throughout the province of Bordeaux [Col. 1019B], greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> “Just as golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (*Revelation* 5:8), emit before the Most High a sweet fragrance to cleanse the corruption of our sins, so we believe that it greatly benefits our salvation if we keep a celebrated memory on earth of those whose merits we recall with solemn praises and whose continual intercession in heaven we hope will assist us.
>
> “When our beloved sons G. and P., monks of Silva-Major, had come to the apostolic see and had fully informed us concerning the holy conduct, life, and merits of blessed Gerald, founder of that monastery, both through letters from our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Bordeaux and his suffragans, and through letters from others, namely abbots [Col. 1019C] and noblemen; when they had presented to us and our brothers very many proofs of these matters; and when, through our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Rouen, the bishop of Châlons, and certain others who had more fully learned of the miracles which the Lord worked through the merits of that holy man, we had been made even more certain—after hearing also of the signs of his virtue and miracles, and that among worldly people he had maintained a spiritual way of life and among human beings an angelic one—we canonized him, with the counsel of our brothers, since he had been dissolved bodily and deserved to be with Christ, lest we should in some way seem to detract from his due honor and glory if we allowed one sanctified by the Lord to remain deprived of the veneration of human devotion. We decreed that he be numbered in the catalogue of the saints.
>
> “Since his lamp burned so brightly in this world that by God’s grace it deserved to be placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand (*Luke* 11:33), so that, burning within himself through works of charity, he might shine upon others by his example, we ask, admonish, and command all of you, by the authority we exercise, that, being devoutly and beneficially moved to venerate him, you honor him each year with a solemn feast on the appointed day, so that, appealed to by votive prayers, he may intercede for us before the Lord.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate,” namely in the common era 1197. Celestine had been appointed in April of 1191, in place of the deceased Clement III. [Col. 1020A]

The same pontiff shortly afterward—that is, on the sixth day before the Ides of May of the same year, in the fifteenth indiction—granted Peter, the abbot, who had chiefly managed the entire affair of Saint Gerald’s canonization, and his brothers a very extensive diploma. In it all the privileges and possessions listed there are asserted and confirmed for the monastery of Silva-Major.

### 23

The same pontiff wrote to Otho, duke of Aquitaine, to inform him of blessed Gerald’s canonization and invite him to celebrate the feast of so great a man.

We have not been able to see Celestine’s letter, but we have before us two letters of Otho concerning this matter. In the first, he admonishes the archbishops and other prelates of Aquitaine to proclaim the feast of Saint Gerald in their synods [Col. 1020B]. In the second, he commands his own officials to provide complete security for all who gather for the feast of Saint Gerald and for the fairs which, on that occasion, he had granted as entirely free from restrictions.

These letters are preserved to this day in the Silva-Major Archives, where they read as follows:

“Otho, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, to the venerable archbishops and bishops, and to the other prelates of the churches established in the duchy of Aquitaine, greetings.

You should know that the lord pope has informed me by his letters that Saint Gerald, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Silva Major, having been crowned long ago in heaven with glory and honor, as many great and manifold signs and miracles attest, has recently, [Col. 1020C] by the counsel and decree of the Roman Church, on account of the distinction of his merits and virtues, which the Lord performed through him, been canonized by that same Roman Church and enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, in the presence of very many archbishops and bishops and other prelates of the churches; and that his feast was solemnly celebrated at Rome with the devout service of praise. The pope has commanded me to celebrate his feast devoutly, so that I may deserve to be aided by his merits and intercessions, and to honor and venerate this saint of God with sincere devotion, and to induce others to do the same by my example and exhortation.

Therefore, devoutly receiving and reverently embracing the apostolic command in this matter, I ask you to announce to the faithful entrusted to you, in your synods, churches, and assemblies, that this is to be done and carefully observed out of reverence for the same saint, so that he may intercede with the Lord for us all. Moreover, to all who come to visit his holy body and to attend his feast-days, or to the fair and market which I grant entirely free to the same monastery and establish there to be held every year on the day of his Elevation [form: Relevationis], the fourth day before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, I provide full security in coming and going. I command all my seneschals, provosts, and bailiffs to have the fair announced and proclaimed when requested by the brothers of the same monastery, and to observe inviolably the liberties and safeguards established, [Col. 1021A] and to ensure that others likewise observe them.”

24. Otto wrote similar letters on this matter to his officials.

“Otho, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, to all his seneschals, provosts, and bailiffs established in the duchy of Aquitaine, greetings. You should know,” and so forth, as in the preceding letters.

“I ask you to venerate this same saint, for your own salvation, with the honor due to him, following my example, so that he may intercede with the Lord for us all. I also firmly command you and all my seneschals, provosts, and bailiffs that, when requested by the brothers of the same monastery, you cause the feast of this saint and the fair on the day of his Elevation, the fourth day before the feast of Saint [Col. 1021B] John the Baptist, to be announced and proclaimed in the places entrusted to you by me. Moreover, to all who, etc. We command you to observe inviolably the liberties and safeguards established, and to ensure that they are firmly observed by others. Witnessed by me in person, at Vasatum, on the ninth day of March.”

25. In these letters Otto seems to imply that at least two celebrations were already customarily held in honor of blessed Gerald—for he calls them “feasts”—but he did not state by whom they had been instituted. Certainly P. Papebrochius was mistaken when he supposed that Pope Celestine, in the bull mentioned above, had commanded the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Châlons to establish the feast of blessed Gerald. Celestine says nothing about this [Col. 1021C] in the bull in question; nor is there any trace, in the ancient or recent breviaries, martyrologies, or necrologies of Silva Major, of the feast supposedly instituted by them on 13 October.

It is much more likely that these feasts of the blessed abbot were proclaimed by the archbishop of Bordeaux, or indeed by all the prelates of Aquitaine, in some provincial synod. Nevertheless, to state frankly what I think about the matter, I rather believe that both feasts of blessed Gerald—namely, that of his deposition and that of his elevation (relevatio) or translation—were celebrated before Saint Gerald’s canonization, at least with the greatest concourse of the people. Since it is certain from both of his Lives that people frequently came to his tomb even from distant regions, there can be no doubt that this occurred rather on the anniversary of his deposition, or certainly of his translation—which indeed had been a very celebrated translation—than on other days.

Although the feasts of the blessed man were not yet celebrated with a public office composed in his honor, nevertheless, as may be conjectured, on those honored days his solemn memory was observed, as it is still customary today in most monasteries of our order according to the ancient institution of our Fathers, where the anniversaries of the first abbots and founders are celebrated each year with the greatest solemnity on fixed days. These solemnities, therefore, which at first, as it seems to us, were observed merely in memory of blessed Gerald, were transformed, once he had been canonized, into true feasts; and it was then, for the first time, [Col. 1022A] that a public office began to be celebrated in his honor.

26. As for the lessons, antiphons, and other prayers of the divine office, this much is certain from the letters of Stephen, bishop of Tournai, a man then renowned for piety and learning. The abbot and monks of Silva Major asked him to compose these things in honor of Saint Gerald, and he granted their request. Stephen himself testifies to this in Letter 277, written “to the abbot and chapter of Silva Major.”

The following letter, however, is incorrectly addressed “to the archdeacon of Bordeaux.” In fact, it was written by the archdeacon himself to Stephen, asking him, on behalf of the abbot and monks of Silva Major, indeed of the whole “diocese of Bordeaux,” “according to the grace” that had been “given” to him, “to provide the office in the antiphons over the psalms, in the responsories over the lessons, and in the prose and collect.”

When Stephen had carried this out, the same abbot and the entire convent of the monastery sent him a cypress staff as a gift and returned him their greatest thanks. They also granted him “the brotherhood of the monastery in the general chapter,” that is, they made him a participant in all the good works performed by the monks of Silva Major, “both in life and in death,” so that after his death the same prayers would be offered for him as were customarily offered for the brothers of that monastery. This is described more fully in their letter, among Stephen’s other letters, no. 279.

The office composed by Stephen himself—that is, the lessons, hymns, collect, and one responsory, published as a specimen of the others—was printed at Paris in 1679, at the end of the same Stephen’s letters, which R. P. Claudius du Molinet, a canon regular of the Gallican Congregation, illustrated with notes and observations.

27. Moreover, the archdeacon of Bordeaux, in the letter just mentioned, not only praises Gerald’s holiness at length but also praises the monks of Silva, because they surpassed the other religious men of their age in observance of regular discipline and in the vigor of their order. It is worthwhile to quote his words in honor of the blessed abbot and his sons.

“Blessed Gerald,” he says, “who drew his origin from the regions of Gaul, whose praiseworthy life flourished before men, and whose beautiful and precious death shines in the sight [Col. 1022D] of the Lord, attested by signs and radiant with miracles, came to the region of Bordeaux and founded the monastery of Silva Major from its first stone, and reformed it according to regular disciplines. This year, having been authenticated at Rome by the lord pope with the due solemnity of Masses, he deserved to be inscribed in the catalogue of the saints. But how the order in the aforesaid monastery flourishes and burns with spiritual vigor beyond the common rules of monks, your greatness will learn more faithfully and effectively from the proclamation of its reputation than from the work of a pen.”

Elias, who at that time was archbishop of Bordeaux, likewise praises them because they were always devoted to spiritual matters. “We know,” he says in the charter of the donation of the church of Campanias, “and from the frequent association which we are known to have had with you we recognize without any doubt that, as spiritual men, you always embrace and seek the things that are Jesus Christ’s, and that you are continually engaged in those matters that pertain to works of charity,” and so forth.

Much the same appears in various charters, which there is no time to cite individually. Yet it is impossible to pass over a notable passage in the record of the visitation made by Simon, archbishop of Bourges, in 1284 through the provinces of Bourges and Bordeaux. It reports that when the archbishop had come to Silva Major, he was compelled to eat above the monastery gate, because it was not permitted to eat meat within the precincts of the place; indeed, it adds that when the monks learned that the abbot of Saint-Sulpice had sat at table with the archbishop and eaten meat with him, they took this violation of the rule very badly.

“[The lord] came,” as the record itself states, “to Saint [Col. 1024A] Gerald, the abbey of Silva Major, and was received there with great honor and solemnity. There are black monks there, and the place is very distinguished. Since meat is not eaten within the body of the abbey, the lord and his companions ate above the gate, and there they ate meat. Certain monks then came to the lord and forbade the abbot of Saint-Sulpice to eat meat there, because by doing so he would act against the constitution of his order.”

Such was the fervor of the monks of Silva even in those latest times. Furthermore, the monastery of Silva Major still remains famous, united to our Congregation of Saint Maur, where, among other sacred relics, the body of blessed Gerald is preserved, enclosed in an old reliquary decorated with bronze plates and silvered statues. His sacred head, separated from the rest of the body and placed in a silver vessel representing his likeness, was transferred there several years ago.

# LIFE OF SAINT GERALD, ABBOT

[Col. 1023]

## 1. The author’s period

“Wearing the habit of the Christian religion and desiring the salvation of all God’s faithful, [I wish] salvation in the Lord for the whole Church. Since I see that many things done in former times have been entrusted to little written records lest they be erased by forgetfulness, it has also seemed fitting that the things done in our own days should be transmitted to posterity through the work of our little talent. If those Fathers of ours took such pains to make known to us things done merely for the sake of vainglory, how much more ought we to labor that the things of God not be suppressed by silence.

Let us therefore turn their examples to our good, and let us do for divine glory what they did for human approval. Let us undertake, then, to narrate what we have begun, and let it no longer be pleasing for us to wander away from the work once undertaken. First, we beseech the Maker and Redeemer of all things to deign to extend his hand to us as we enter upon so great a sea, so that, explaining—if not as it deserves, then at least in whatever manner we can—how the most blessed Gerald, first abbot of Silva Major, lived in the exile of this life, what temptations the ancient enemy inflicted upon him, how bravely, strengthened by divine aid, he fought against those temptations, and how great a mercy almighty God bestowed upon him, we may, carried in the vessel of charity, with faith filling our sails and the grace of the Holy Spirit swelling our canvas, be able to reach the harbor of salvation by the path of righteousness.

Therefore, let the reader imitate in God’s servant his steadfastness, in the infirm his patience, in the patient his long-suffering, and in long-suffering his unremitting perseverance. Let him not prejudge the excess of what is said, because neither the finger by writing nor the tongue by words can equal it as it was; especially since Gerald himself would scarcely have wished these things to be reported, lest he appear to speak for his own praise.

Let no suspicion of false praise, therefore, be attached to him, because this account was written not for his glory but for God’s. Let no one consider it burdensome or unworthy that so great a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit should be called holy; for if he knew and practiced righteousness, saw great wonders, and entreated the Most High, he was without doubt found among the number of the saints.

Whoever reads or hears these things should forgive the writer’s ignorance and attend not to the style in which the work was made but to what it concerns; let him not seek the craftsman of the book. No person of sound judgment ought to attend to embellished fabrications of words [another reading: harmonious composition], but should carefully discern, by the insight of his mind, whether what he considers is Catholic.

Having called upon God as witness to this truth, let us come to the narrative.”

## 2. Gerald was born at Corbie and educated there. Like Saint Nicholas

Gerald, therefore, born at Corbie of parents who were not unknown, was handed over by them in the very monastery of Corbie to serve God. There he practiced the years of his childhood in such holy conduct that he appeared entirely estranged from the pleasures of this sort which boys commonly embrace, and he was loved by all who were in that same monastery more than his peers.

The boys loved him because he invited boys to every good thing; the young men loved him because in him they found examples of every virtue and patience; the old men admired him because they saw him striving beyond the strength of his age. What more need be said? He was so loved by all who were in the monastery, both monks and laymen, that almighty and wondrous God was praised in him.

Nor is this surprising, for he whom God had drenched with grace necessarily had to be loved by all. Persevering in humility—which is rightly considered the guardian and mother of the virtues—and armed with the weapons of obedience, he strove to follow the one who, obedient to the Father even unto the death of the cross (Philippians 2), had descended into the exile of this life. Truly made a boy of the Most High, he showed Jesus wondrous in himself insofar as he could.

Who could ever sufficiently admire the wonders of God? Nothing is difficult for God, whether he chooses to work through little things or greater ones; for whether a person is a child or of whatever age, all must serve him completely if he wills and assists them.

We have heard that Saint Nicholas, while still hanging at his mother’s breasts, drank milk once a day on Wednesday and Friday, and remained content with this throughout the whole day. Considering the works of God, we cannot keep silent. Hearing that this boy of our own times, so blessed, showed himself to everyone in such a way that he was loved by all, we have not dared fail to proclaim the wonders of God.

Let us praise the Lord in most holy Nicholas, and let us also magnify him in this boy, so wondrously filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Yet we do not dare to equate him with Saint Nicholas; rather, in both we wish to proclaim the wonders of God. For God is wondrous in his saints (Psalm 67), now and always, and throughout endless ages of ages.

## 3. Dear to Abbot Fulco. He is placed in charge of external affairs

At that time, when the laws of death begrudged us [Abbot] Richard, Fulco inherited the same see and honor. [Note: Gerald himself calls Richard “of blessed,” or “of happy,” memory in Book I of the Miracles of Saint Adalhard, where more is said about him, cited above, fourth century, part I, pp. 361 ff. Fulco succeeded him in 1048 and was very famous for his distinguished deeds; the following year he attended the Council of Reims under Leo IX. Many thought that he lived until 1097. But Evrard, his successor, attended the Council of Compiègne in 1085.]

When the aforesaid boy entered the years of adolescence, he did not forget what he had done in childhood but reached toward higher things; and, climbing from virtue to virtue with God’s help, he presented himself as a model and mirror to all good people. Not forgetting the Lord’s ordinances, the adolescent asked him for understanding so that he might live by them—for God gives abundantly to those who seek him with their whole heart, and does not reproach them.

He was truly one of the husbandmen to whom the care of the Lord’s vineyard had been entrusted, who returned fruit to his lord at the proper time, continually meditating day and night on the profit of the talent entrusted to him, and greatly fearing the condemnation of that slothful servant who hid his master’s money. Happily, he did not cease to conduct his business, so that when his master came he might return the talent multiplied (Matthew 21, 25).

When the abbot under whom he lived saw him admired by everyone in the manner described, he wisely began to consider that, if he lived, he would accomplish something good through him; and he devoutly prayed to God, whose gift he saw this to be, that Gerald might be preserved and progress toward better things.

Finally, taking him to himself and assigning him to his service as a monk, the abbot began, as was his custom, to travel wherever the affairs of his church required, taking Gerald with him as an assistant and, wherever possible, as a prudent counselor. The youth of good character, having physically left the cloister and been brought into public view, destined to become an example of virtue to many, appointed the Holy Spirit as his guardian; and the Spirit kept him free and exempt from every worldly desire.

For wherever he went, as he had been accustomed to do in the monastery, he devoted himself to fasts and prayers as time and circumstance allowed, and tried to discharge the entire task of psalmody, lest he ever fail in what he had promised God. When he returned to his mother’s bosom after diligently completing the assigned duty, he paid little attention to what he had seen outside, and strongly afflicted his flesh with vigils, prayers, and fasts.

## 4. Wonders follow upon wonders

He was so engaged in worldly affairs that he did not lose custody of his mind; and he kept such vigil in fasts and prayers that he nevertheless traveled everywhere for the needs of the church. If we attend to the Gospel sayings, this is not surprising. God promised that he would be present to all who believed in him. For he says in the Gospel: “Do not fear, for I am with you all the days of your life, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). And elsewhere: “Have confidence; I have overcome the world” (John 10). And again: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

Understanding these words of the Lord, the aforementioned youth devotedly obeyed and joyfully hastened to him so that he might fulfill those promises. Completely abandoning the pride and pomp of the world, he humbled himself entirely under the Lord’s command and, gentle as a sheep, submitted without hesitation to the Lord’s instructions. His submission to the abbot was so great that the abbot’s affection for him surpassed that shown to all others. Thus, although unequal in rank, honor was equal to the burden [Bollandus: equal to the burden], since he was present everywhere, as the nature of that ministry required.

## 5. Excessively fatigued. He suffers a headache

Since the place was somewhat destitute through the poverty of the times and the turmoil of wars [Note: Gerald himself speaks of these matters in Book I, chapter 3, of The Miracles of Saint Adalhard; that book was published in the fourth century, part I, p. 358], the abbot began at every hour and with every resource to labor for its relief. Neither night, nor the heat of day, nor the time for eating or drinking kept them from laboring for the good of the place. Their entire former routine was changed: sometimes they anticipated the hour, sometimes prolonged the fast, sometimes took more than usual, sometimes less, and moreover transgressed the natural pattern of sleep by observing it irregularly. This could not happen without grave danger.

By this change, therefore, both incurred a serious illness, but the young man the greater, because he was less mature in character and age. He suffered such a severe illness as no human being could explain—not by tongue, writing, or any form of description [Bollandus: treatment]. There was no measure to the illness that any mortal could endure unless sustained by God’s clemency.
