It was located in his head; and how grave a place this is appears from the fact that this part of the body normally directs the other members. There is no comparison for this illness: if it had been possible, decapitation alone would have seemed a remission of the pain. From the chin to the crown he was bound, not by iron but by the still heavier fetters of illness, and could move his head nowhere except by turning the whole mechanism of his body.

All the adamantine veins of his head tortured the youth without interruption. There was no relief from pain; all the hours of the day were unequal, every time inconvenient, every place a source of suffering. If he went out into the sun, he seemed to see the whole world turning; if he looked up at the sky, it seemed to him to fall down upon his head; if he rode, he feared that he was about to fall headlong; if he sat on a roof or in the monastery [another reading: dwelling], it seemed to him that he was supporting the entire mass of the building with his head.

He thought that he had incurred this illness through the unaccustomed alteration of food, drink, and sleep. Yet, as will be shown below, in reality it occurred by the prejudicial will of the Supreme Judge, although he diligently sought to attribute all these things to his own sins. Whatever the cause, no one knew how great the anguish under which he labored except one servant of his, his namesake, whom he had drawn into such intimacy that the servant could assist him in this affliction.

A certain regard for modesty still remained in the youth, while everything else was hidden except what the redness of his eyes and the sorrow of his weakened face revealed. He avoided exposing his condition to everyone, lest the devotion occasioned by the illness make him softer [another reading: better, or more contemptible].

What, then, was he to do? Where could he turn? It was a misery and a sorrow to see the flower of his first youth withering, not without grave harm. Anyone who saw his eyes flooded with tears [manuscript 1: pierced], and his suffering face changing through various colors, could not doubt how great the anguish and sadness were that disturbed him inwardly.

## 6. He has recourse to physicians in vain. He awaits healing from God

At last, unable to endure any longer, he began to seek the opinion of physicians. Since among human beings there are so many opinions, one asserted that he should be cured by incision of the frontal vein; another, by administering potions and every kind of medicine. He endured all this with a patient spirit.

If he were burned alive, he would regard it almost as a remedy, since every skill and diligence of the physicians was having the opposite effect. For what benefit could human medicine provide for one whom God had reserved to be cured by the magnificence of Saint Adalhard? (below, no. 14.)

After spending much on physicians without benefit, he began to reflect that God is not as man, and that, whoever the physician may be, salvation belongs to the Lord. Therefore, as his illness grew worse, he withdrew all his hope from man and sought God as the physician of his illness.

Finally, with only the aforementioned servant aware of it, wherever he was able and from whatever he could, he took away from his own mouth and ministered to Christ in the poor. Through the physicians’ pretext he received from his friends whatever he could obtain; from it he selected three poor men, in imitation of the Lord’s Supper, and established them for himself. Every day he washed their feet, watered them with tears, wiped them with his hair and shirt, and set food and a table before them.

Then, throwing himself down in the same place before their feet for prayer, as though he were seeing the Holy Trinity visibly present there, he cried out in tears: “Holy Trinity,” he said, “take from me this illness which I cannot bear. Where is your promise, O God? ‘At whatever hour you call upon me, I shall say: Behold, I am here’ (Psalm 115). Where are your many mercies, your many compassions, your many acts of clemency? But you endure, because in your loving intention you delay.”

## 7. He accompanies the abbot on his journey to Rome

While the wounds were still recent from the incision, and the arteries were burning with the most severe inflammation, Abbot Fulco, planning to go to Rome for the benefit of the church and for the sake of prayer, urged the aforementioned youth to go with him as a faithful friend. The youth willingly obeyed and declared himself ready, failing in body but not in good will.

When people who saw the youth from outside informed the abbot that such a journey would be dangerous for him, the abbot again affectionately urged him to remain at rest. But Gerald humbly resisted with all his strength, with the sole intention that, if he should depart this life, God might have mercy on his soul; and that, if by God’s clemency he reached Rome, he might implore from Saint Peter, whose servant he was, the mercy of health.

What more need be said? Humility conquered in the one, friendship in the other. Gerald plundered his friends, carefully taking money from them with which he might relieve the destitute along the way. Thus he undertook the journey, and what a perfectly healthy person could scarcely accomplish, the sick man attempted, laboring under the pain of his wounds and the excess of his illnesses.

He always rode alone at the rear, because even what should have been a relief—the speech of his companions—was burdensome to him; indeed, unless God’s clemency sustained him, he sometimes almost lost consciousness. Yet whenever he encountered poor people, with the strength he possessed he descended from his horse and secretly closed coins and half-coins in their hands. He kissed them sweetly and, as though crying out to God visibly present—as was truly the case—with groans and tears, he said: “Lord God, help me with all your mercies.”

Then he mounted his horse again and went on, dazed, his mind—the only part of him that remained sound—always clinging to God.

## 8. He climbs the Alps

They reached the place called the lodgings of Saint Dionysius, still known by his name. There the servant assigned to Gerald, observing the incisions as he was accustomed to do, said: “Alas, lord, your condition grows worse every day. You will not be able to complete the journey. It is necessary for you to take counsel with our senior.”

He then made this report to the abbot. The abbot, saddened, summoned his brother and urged, entreated, and advised him in every way either to remain there or to return with whichever men he preferred.

He said this because, still unaware of the interior illness and seeing only the external condition, he had concealed his situation from his abbot, as he had from the others, precisely so that the abbot would not impede the journey he had begun.

Humbly resisting the abbot’s advice with every kind of entreaty, Gerald said: “No, lord, I undertook this journey not for turning back but for proceeding, if God and you permit it. I came in obedience to your command; beyond that, another necessity remains to be fulfilled. Therefore, for the love of God, I beg your fatherhood not to impose upon me, by ordering me to return, a command that I would be unable to resist.”

When the abbot saw the youth’s perseverance, he yielded to his will and to the desire of his good intention.

When they reached the Mountain of Jupiter (Montjoux), Gerald climbed not only the Mountain of Jupiter but also that of Bardon, not on horseback but on foot—not so much for the sake of his soul as to bend God’s mercy toward the recovery of his health. Such was the force of the pain, such the love of attaining health, that in comparison with it all the things created by the Maker of the world had become worthless.

When he climbed the Mountain of Joy, walking barefoot and with his hooded head covered, he secretly nourished his pain with tears and sobs.

## 9. He reaches Rome

He reached Rome. He had sought it with as many anguishes as steps, burning with desire for it. Lodging was sought, and they went to pray. Who could recount how many tears he shed there before his Lord? There is no need to recount them if someone wishes to compare his love and pain, his desire and illness.

They remained there for eight days, during which the youth thought that he had satisfied his vow with his tears. But how could he be satisfied as long as such anguish pressed upon him?

Every day he came to the church and, as though he were about to converse face to face with Saint Peter, entered the sanctuary enclosure up to his waist [Note: Through the window that was there. See Gregory of Tours, Book I, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 20]. Striking there with the devotion of faith—not only in the affection of his heart but also in the movement of his body—and opening the little doors of his memory, he washed and watered everything there with tears and weeping, with God and Saint Peter alone as witnesses.

While the others slept, he kept vigil; and, rising secretly, he revisited Saint Peter after securing the guards by payment [Note: That is, winning them over by payment; as Papebrochius thought, no change of this word [Col. 1030D] to lucratis (“having won them over”) is necessary].

The whole substance of his petition was this: if he did not deserve to obtain health because his sins stood in the way, then Peter might at least obtain for him this pardon from the clemency of the supreme Judge, so that he would not lose the little spark of soundness of mind that still remained.

O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are your judgments, Lord! You did not wish to grant Peter at Rome what you had reserved for Saint Adalhard at Corbie.

## 10. On the journey through Apulia he is attacked by robbers. He visits Cassino

When the eight days had been completed, the abbot, for the benefit of the church, proceeded farther, following Saint Pope Leo, who was then heading toward Mount Gargano. Although his body was failing, the youth’s spirit grew stronger in following him—not because his illness was diminishing, but because it was worsening; and thus, after enduring serious hardships, he afterward endured even more serious anguish.

For a storm of war had broken out between the Romans and the Apulians, more violently than usual and with the greatest danger. Each day the riders awaited the outcome of fortune. Fortune did not fail to play its trick: falling in with robbers, they lost everything they possessed.

Thrown from his horse, the abbot would have wished at that moment to be nowhere on earth less than there. Gerald likewise, as he always did, rode alone and hanging back, and was carrying the abbot’s gold and silver with him. What could he do? How could he escape? He was attacked, thrown from his horse, dragged, shoved, and stripped; and, to increase his illness, he was also severely beaten.

His companions fled as best each could, thinking that they had lost nothing so long as they were still alive. After a certain soldier recovered their horses, they reached Mount Cassino. There the youth again sought Saint Benedict on foot and with tears. After they had remained there for two days, he revealed his illness to the abbot of the place, following counsel.

The abbot sympathized with him in tears and sighs and said: “Alas, brother, under how great a danger you labor! One of our brothers incurred the same illness that afflicts you. He endured it, miserable man, with such great affliction and suffering for a long time, until finally all sense and every human faculty ebbed away from him, not without the greatest harm.”

The youth, astonished at this, departed more despairing than before from the man whose counsel he had hoped would free him from the illness.

## 11. He climbs Mount Gargano, becomes a priest, and returns to Corbie

They reached Mount Gargano. As devoutly as he could, Gerald prayed to the archangel Michael and repeatedly sprinkled his head with drops of dripping water.

But what more need be said? The judgments of God are hidden. It was not Saint Michael on his Gargano, nor Saint Benedict on his Cassino, nor Saint Peter in his Rome, but Saint Adalhard in his Corbie who obtained what Gerald sought in this matter.

After finding Pope Leo, Gerald did everything he could to unload the burden of his sins before him. But since there was no opportunity to approach him and no special time for remaining with him, Gerald began to grieve and struggle, wondering how he might bring the matter to an end.

Meanwhile, he saw a certain bishop named Hubert [Note: Thus in Corbie and Silva Major; others read Robert, Ubertus, or Menardus reads Gubertus. Papebrochius suspects that he was the archbishop of Siponto]. Gerald disclosed his entire conscience to him, revealed the illness from which he suffered, and explained how, having abandoned medicine, he had entrusted all his hope to spiritual guardianship.

The bishop adjusted the measure of his penance to the measure of his illness, praised the youth’s purpose, urged him to persist in what he had begun, and ordered him to do nothing further without the abbot’s permission.

When the matter had thus been completed, and both Gerald and his abbot had also been made priests by the pope, Gerald returned with his abbot to Corbie, not without great danger to his life.

Having now despaired of bodily health, he sought the salvation of his soul more attentively: he devoted himself to almsgiving, served the poor, clung to the churches, and frequently celebrated Masses, since he had recently been ordained. While he stood at these Eucharistic celebrations, he became so stunned by the anguish of his illness that, unless God’s clemency held—or protected—the one whom he held in his hands, he would have been completely beside himself.

## 12. He becomes sacristan and adorns the church

After he had completed a year in this manner following his return from Rome, the custodian of the church, who held that office at the time, departed this life; Gerald succeeded him in obedience. He succeeded obediently, although he was hindered by his illness—not from any other motive, since he did not belong to himself, nor was he enticed by ambition, but so that through such obedience he might merit from God the grace of recovering his health [Col. 1031B].

Nor was there any lack of opportunity for so great a desire, despite the opposition presented by the intentions of his predecessors. For the newly founded temple had been entirely abandoned [Note: [Col. 1031D] The principal church of Corbie had been set on fire in the time of Abbot Richard, as Gerald himself relates in Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Adalhard*, cited above in the notes to no. 5.]. It was open to sheep, pigs, and cattle; it was so full of rainwater, like a public square, that geese and ducks swam through it; its pavement consisted of a dung heap a cubit deep. It was offensive to everyone, and all who passed by shook their heads at it.

The young man began to devote himself to this work, seeking by whatever means he could to incline divine regard toward compassion for him. Although he was hindered by the poverty of the times, God nevertheless providing for him, he cleansed the temple, arranged seats, adorned the choir above with small columns and bases, cleansed the crypt and the ambulatory passages, and suitably set the altars in their places. Why delay? The monastery, which had long been abandoned by everyone, he fitted out within a fairly short time so thoroughly that it appeared suitable for the service of God and entirely necessary for so great a community. One day, then, the brothers who held the greater authority in the monastery, seeing that it had been, as we have said, excellently arranged, went to the abbot and brought him to see what they had seen. They advised that the bodies of the saints who were in the old monastery should be removed and placed with the highest veneration in the place that Gerald had so appropriately cleansed. Their advice was given and approved; whatever was lacking for this purpose was sought out, and everything was carried out, as we have said, with joy, with the confirmation of the neighboring bishops, and with the firm testimony of the people [Col. 1031D]. Thus the young man, laboring more and more earnestly at the work he had undertaken, adorned it with everything necessary, while the one whose desire and love had prompted these actions supplied what was needed.

## 13. He implores the aid of Saint Adalhard

He was indeed making progress toward his goal, but as yet no remedy brought him relief from his illness. Nevertheless, he did not desist; knocking at the sanctuary of supreme piety, he was doing violence to the kingdom of God. The opportunity afforded by the church and by prayer kept him constantly present and attentive [Col. 1032A]. There was no limit to his prostrations, to such an extent that knots rose at the joints of his fingers and the callus became harder than stone. For what limit could there be to crying out to God, whose power to afflict had no limit [*cui* in the edition]?

At last, seeing that his prayers still achieved nothing and that all his labors, humanly speaking, were coming to nothing, moved by divine inspiration he approached Saint Adalhard with every kind of petition, above all others and beyond all others. Standing before his altar, already overwhelmed almost to despair, he poured himself out in every prayer with the pitiable humility of contrition. But he was pitied from above by the one who draws near to the brokenhearted, and he reached the point at which, if he had done so earlier, he would already have been freed by God’s mercy.

For he made a praiseworthy vow to Saint Adalhard: namely, that, to the best of his ability, he would always and everywhere magnify his glorious name, if the saint would grant him the assistance of his favor. When he had bound himself by this vow, he began little by little to feel the loosening of his illness. Thus, daily more and more encouraged by divine mercy to make his petition, after Compline [Note: [Col. 1031D] That is, after Compline, unless I am mistaken. The author of the other *Life*, however, who makes no mention of Saint Adalhard, writes that this happened after Gerald had celebrated Mass [Col. 1032D].], he once poured himself out before the altar in the fulfillment of all his prayers. His words were interrupted by sobs, and he nearly melted into flowing waves of tears. At last his loosened voice found a passage, and his released groans burst forth in these words:

“Saint Adalhard, friend of Christ, receive me, wretched above all and the last of all, as I flee to you.”

## 14. He heals him; Gerald celebrates his praises

When, therefore, he seemed to himself to have sufficiently equipped Saint Adalhard as an advocate before Christ the Judge, he rose, wiped his face, and returned groaning to his bed. As he sat there, still sobbing and bewildered, a globe of radiance flew from the side of the altar in the form of a flash of lightning; it struck his eyes with reflected brilliance and illuminated his entire body. He remained stupefied and motionless, when suddenly, the knots of his illness bursting apart, his very head gave a great crack between the skin and, as it were, certain little cords. Unable to endure the pain, he cried out in a pitiable voice, “Saint Adalhard, help me!” Then he immediately restrained himself in silence, because together with the pain he felt that a power had been wrought within him.

Thus freed from the very illness whose removal he had desired and for so long endured with weariness, he praised his liberator in an unconstrained voice. Nor did he fail to fulfill the vow he had shortly before made to the saint; wherever he could, he exalted his glory and, by exalting it, magnified it in this manner as well [Col. 1032D]. He had the saint’s life, which offended the minds of its readers through elegiac apostrophes and excessive elaboration, extracted from those thickets of excess; and, having plainly restored it to the flower of history, he adorned it mystically with hexameter verse [Note: [Col. 1032D] The *Life of Saint Adalhard* was first written by Saint Paschasius-Radbertus, the celebrated abbot of Corbie. We published it, together with the one written by Gerald and with the same saint’s two books of miracles—the first of which was also written by Gerald—in the fourth century, part I, under the year 826 [Col. 1033D].].

Very little had previously been done in memory of the saint’s feast, but Gerald composed antiphons and responsories and caused it to be venerated with a solemnity both lofty and worthy [Col. 1033A], not without arousing the envy of many, whom nevertheless, through God and the saint acting together, a marvelous victory refuted. Saint Adalhard had illumined the eyes of those still living with many signs, but their negligence had consigned them all to oblivion. The young man, Gerald, carefully sought these signs from those who had seen them and in whom they had occurred, and afterward committed what he had learned to writing.

## 15. His progress in the way of the Lord after his healing

When the man of God, as the brightness receded, recognized that he had been freed from his illness and had been visited so miraculously by divine grace, as we have said, he remembered the evangelical saying, “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24). He therefore showed himself tireless in God’s service and began to mortify himself before the altar of Saint Adalhard and the other altars of the church more than he had done before [Col. 1033B].

O man worthy of praise, whom neither illness delayed even for a little from the service of God, nor the health so miraculously recovered lifted outside himself! O mercy of our Lord and Savior, worthy of proclamation everywhere, which sustained its servant in illness so that he would not fail, and mercifully preserved him after restoring him to health so that he would not become proud!

The aforesaid man, not exalting himself because of the benefit bestowed upon him by God, but always recognizing his own frailty and persevering in humility, did not deviate from the straight path. Advancing toward what lay ahead, established in mind and conduct upon the mountain of the Lord, he wholly encouraged himself to attain the palaces of heaven. For he had read the Lord’s words in the Gospel: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened [Col. 1033C] to you” (Luke 11). Trusting in this word of the Lord, the servant of God did not cease asking so that he might receive; he strove to seek so that he might find; and he endeavored to knock so that the Lord might graciously open to him.

And so it happened. He had been afflicted, as we said, with a most grievous illness, and in response to his petition divine mercy had miraculously freed him. He sought that the grace of the Holy Spirit might graciously visit him, and he found it before the eyes of the Most High. He did not cease knocking at God’s ears with prayers and tears, and God himself graciously opened the depths of his mercy.

## 16. He is refreshed by a divine vision

At one time it seemed to him in a dream that he was standing before the oratory of Saint Michael, which is within that monastery, and that the Lord Jesus Christ, inside it [Col. 1033D], was preparing to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass with an innumerable multitude of angels and archangels and all the saints. Angels stood by, archangels ministered, and they prepared what was necessary for so great a mystery. When they had ministered everything, and the saints who were with him had been placed on either side in the choir, like singers standing in their ranks, the Lord Jesus himself began to inquire whether all who ought to be present had arrived.

When they answered the Lord, saying, “We are here,” he said: “No, because that brother has not yet entered, who is standing beside the outer door.” At his command, therefore, that brother was brought in [Col. 1034A] and placed in the midst. Then, as the Lord proceeded to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass, the office began: “Let us all rejoice in the Lord.” Thus the office was brought to its conclusion, and the vision vanished; the brother awoke and began to ponder within himself what he had seen.

He understood clearly that he was pleasing God in his actions. If previously he had kept himself devoted to God’s service, afterward he began to restrain the movements of body and soul with greater severity.

## 17. Another vision; he resolves to go to Jerusalem and carries out his plan

At another time, as it seemed to him, he was in the monastery of Saint Peter at Corbie and was standing before the cross that is in the middle of the church. Such a multitude of men and women had gathered that, as it appeared to him, they filled the entire church [Col. 1034B]. As he stood before the cross and all the people looked toward it, the image of the Lord that was upon the cross descended from the cross and approached him, who was in the midst of the people. Gently and softly calling him by name, it began to stroke his head with its hand, saying:

“Take courage, son, in the Lord and in the power of his might.”

Then, departing from him, it ascended the cross in the sight of everyone, just as it had been there at first. When this had happened, the brother awoke, and, deeply troubled by what he had seen, began earnestly to pray that God would make the vision favorable to him.

It then came into his mind that he wished to visit the holy places beyond the sea and adore the Lord at his tomb in Jerusalem. While he was turning over in his mind how this might be accomplished, he heard [Col. 1034C] that certain faithful men in the same village where he was living were preparing their journey so that they might adore at the Lord’s tomb.

When he learned this, he became exceedingly joyful and gave thanks to almighty God, who had provided the means necessary for what he desired. But since he lived in the monastery under an abbot and a rule, it seemed very improper to him to do what he was attempting without the abbot’s counsel and permission. He therefore approached the abbot, disclosed his intention, and asked and earnestly entreated him to grant permission.

The abbot, however, seeing the brother’s purpose and fearing that he might remain somewhere on the road, either enclosed as a recluse or as a hermit, refused and tried, if he could, to turn him back from such an intention. But because a planting planted by God cannot be uprooted, the often-mentioned man did not withdraw from his purpose [Col. 1034D]. What he could not obtain by himself, he afterward secured through the prayers of many holy men.

At last the abbot gave his consent, but on the condition that, if God granted him the ability, he would unquestionably return to him. The venerable man, having received permission, accepted this obedience and prepared his journey. By God’s grace he visited many holy places and adored at the Lord’s tomb, which he desired above all things. He returned to his own monastery, as he had promised his abbot.

How many torments and sufferings he endured on the journey is not ours to relate, since, concerning the things God deigned to accomplish through him among us, the tongue can scarcely stammer sufficiently. After entering the monastery’s cloister, he began to exercise himself in God’s service and to recall to mind the things he had heard and seen concerning the saint’s wonders.

## 18. On his return he becomes abbot

Meanwhile, when one of his own brothers by blood [Note: [Col. 1035D] This was Reginerus. The abbey of Saint Vincent, situated on the other branch of Mount Laon, still exists today and is affiliated with the Congregation of Saint Maur.] had departed this life—the man who had assumed responsibility for the brothers in the monastery of Saint Vincent near Mount Laon—Gerald was advanced to the abbacy. He accepted this reluctantly and only after holding back for a long time; although he knew that presiding over the brothers was no small burden, whether he wished it or not, he obeyed.

With so heavy a burden placed upon his shoulders, he did not abandon himself to forgetfulness; rather, insofar as he could, he presented himself to his disciples as a model and mirror. The brothers under him, however, being more concerned with earthly advantages than heavenly ones [Col. 1035B], did not agree with his way of life; instead, as is read concerning Saint Benedict (Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 3), they held opinions contrary to his holy admonitions.

When he saw that they were unwilling to consent to living without personal possessions, as he wished, he thought, following the example of our most holy Father Benedict, of dismissing them and living by himself. In his monastery there was a most holy recluse [Note: [Col. 1035D] Bollandus suspects that this was Saint Arnulf, afterward bishop of Soissons; but he is mistaken. For the recluse mentioned here lived in the monastery of Saint Vincent, as is clear to the reader, and this cannot be said of Saint Arnulf. I would rather believe that he was Ebroinus, mentioned below in no. 22.]. Gerald sought his advice about how he might dismiss those whom he had undertaken to govern, and the recluse gave him advice that was entirely suitable and very necessary for him.

Meanwhile, soldiers of no little distinction in worldly terms had come to this same recluse, complaining to him about their sins. They had confessed that they no longer wished to serve the world and had asked him for advice about how they might do so. The holy man, recognizing both the intention of the aforesaid abbot and the desire and understanding of the soldiers, gathered them all together, disclosed to them the plans of both parties, and entrusted the laymen, as though they were receiving the beginnings of faith, to the providence of the most holy abbot.

O inexpressible piety of Christ! O incomparable mercy of the Savior! To his servants who sought him with their whole heart, he supplied a teacher to lead them in overcoming the allurements of the world; and to his servant, so that he might serve him more devotedly, he added companions and disciples.

After such men had been joined together in the Lord, the abbot, not forgetting the brothers whom he had undertaken to govern, approached the bishop Helinard, from whom he held the burden of the abbacy. He disclosed to him the advice he had sought and entrusted to his care the burden of governance that he bore [Col. 1035D].

## 19. He gives up the abbacy and visits various places of the saints

Thus these soldiers of Christ were subjected to the most holy abbot, and, following the example of our holy patriarch Abraham, they went out from their land and their kindred (Genesis 12:1) [Col. 1036A]. A joyful union was formed, a pleasant exultation arose: the disciples rejoiced in their teacher, the teacher rejoiced over his disciples; the abbot exulted in the company so wonderfully provided for him by God; and the soldiers of Christ rejoiced because they saw and understood that everything they desired had come to them according to their will, not from man but from God.

Having therefore laid aside worldly honor, they entered upon the way by which they might follow Christ, and gathered from every direction as far as the house of Saint Denis, the place they had chosen for themselves. Having adored the Savior’s mercy at the tomb of the holy martyrs and invoked the patronage of those martyrs and of the other saints for their assistance, they directed their steps, under the guidance of Christ’s providence, toward Orléans, in order to adore there at the church of the Holy Cross [Col. 1036B] [Note: [Col. 1035D] This is the cathedral church, still famous under that name today. It was destroyed by the Calvinists but restored to its former splendor a few years ago [Col. 1036D].].

When they had departed from there and were approaching Tours, where the body of the most holy confessor Martin rests, they met pilgrims returning from Saint Peter’s in Rome. These questioned them closely about where they came from, where they were going, and what they had in mind. When the pilgrims had learned of their desire, they approached the abbot and asked him to direct his journey toward their lands, so that he might build a church from their estates and allodial lands, which they intended to give to God for his service.

This would have been done, had God not arranged their dwelling elsewhere. Since God so willed it, the pilgrims went on their way, while the abbot and his companions, with God as their guide, reached Poitiers.

## 20. He arrives at Poitiers; Count Guido receives him and commends him to Ralph; he goes to Silva-Major

When they entered the city, behold, the venerable count of Poitiers, Wido [Note: Guido, surnamed Gofridus, son of William V, duke of Aquitaine, succeeded his brothers William VI the Fat and William VII the Bold in the duchy of Aquitaine under the name William VIII. He died in 1086 and was buried in the new monastery at Poitiers, which he had restored from its foundations.], arrived from the opposite direction by God’s providence.

When the abbot learned this, hoping that it would not be inappropriate to speak with him, he went to him and told his companions to follow. When the count saw them, he returned their greeting and carefully asked where they had come from and where they wished to go. The abbot disclosed everything that he had in mind and added that, having left their lands and kindreds, they were following the Lord.

When the count learned of their desire and recognized God’s providence in it, he began to ask the abbot and his companions, for the sake of Christ, whose love had inspired them to do these things, to remain wherever they wished in his land; he himself would take care to provide them with his counsel and assistance in everything [Col. 1036D].

While they were speaking with one another about these matters, behold, a certain provost from Bordeaux, named Ralph [Note: Papebrochius thought this man was an ecclesiastic; but from the other *Life*, where he is called a *ministerialis*, it is certain that he had been appointed by the duke as provost at Bordeaux to administer justice.], came, sent by God [Col. 1037A], and invited the count, if he wished, to let him lead them to a suitable place. The count therefore became exceedingly joyful and entrusted the abbot and his companions to the custody of this provost, so that the provost might guard them as though they were himself. He promised without hesitation that whatever place they chose throughout his entire land, he would grant them by his authority without any dispute.

Why say more? The provost Ralph gladly received them and led them to the place called Silva-Major, between the two seas. There he showed them a small church constructed not of stone but of earth. The surrounding forest had grown so densely with brambles and thorns that no one could approach the church without first cutting a path with a sword or some other tool.

When the abbot and his companions came to this church, such a love for remaining there arose in the abbot that he promised God that, if God were favorable to him, he would go nowhere else.

## 21. He obtains it from the lords and is encouraged by a vision

At that time the lord of that land and owner of the forest was a certain knight named Augerius of Riontium [Note: John Guisius writes *Ogerius*. Riontium was a village in the time of Saint Gregory of Tours, who mentions it in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 48. It later grew into a town that is still famous today, commonly called Rioms, on the Garonne, about four leagues above Bordeaux and seven from Silva-Major.] together with many others, whose names are known to the one who created them.

The abbot dealt with all of them in such a way that they donated the place to God and to his holy mother Mary and made it forever free from every service. Thus the holy Father Gerald, greatly rejoicing, returned to the little church and thereafter had a dwelling built for himself and his companions.

One night he began to pray fervently to God that, if their settlement there pleased him, he would show this to them and direct all their actions toward the good according to the riches of his goodness [Col. 1037C]. When he fell asleep, tired from praying, it seemed to him that from the eastern side there came a chariot drawn by two oxen. After some time, the two oxen were changed into a single horse, and the horse followed the same path on which the oxen had traveled. Finally, the horse was changed into the Son of God, hanging in the same manner as he had earlier hung for us upon the cross. The lower part of the cross touched the earth, while the upper part rose up to heaven [Note: [Col. 1037D] The author of the other *Life* says: “Nevertheless, that cross was not seen materially; rather, there was a certain brightness formed in the shape of a cross, which illuminated the entire place with the greatness of its marvelous splendor.”].

When the most holy man saw these things, he rose from the place where he was and adored Christ as he hung upon the cross. Strengthened by so great and marvelous a vision, the servant of God awoke. After awakening and pondering for a long time what he had seen, he recognized that it was a vision from God, and understood that he ought to found a church in the place where the sign of the holy cross had been fixed. He recognized that his journey and his undertaking pleased God, since it was by God’s gift and grace that he had been enabled to adore him in this manner [Col. 1038A].

When these things had been accomplished, the soldiers who had come with the abbot, still wearing lay clothing because they had vowed to make a journey to Saint James, entered upon that journey, with the abbot’s permission and blessing. They had promised that they would do nothing without his command.

## 22. The names of his companions

At last, when their pilgrimage had been completed, they returned to him and devoutly received the habit of Saint Benedict, entrusting themselves wholly to God. If anyone wishes to know the names of those who first came with the abbot, he will undoubtedly be able to learn them by reading with understanding the following page:

Gerald the abbot, and three monks who came with him out of love for him from the monastery he had formerly governed: one was Martinus [Note: He is mentioned in the necrology of Silva-Major on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.], who afterward governed the church of Saint Denis of the Mount; another was Ebroinus, who, leaving military clothing behind, fought bravely as a recluse [Note: Apparently the same man who was a recluse in the monastery of Saint Vincent under our Gerald, mentioned above in no. 18. He is mentioned in the necrology of Silva-Major on the eighth day before the Ides of July with this eulogy: “Ebroinus of blessed memory, companion of Blessed Gerald, died.”]; and the third was Alerannus [Note: He was the third abbot of Silva-Major and is praised in the necrology in these words: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, Lord Alerannus died, a man venerable in life, nephew of blessed Gerald and third abbot of this church; he lies in the chapter house where the abbots receive their vestments.”], the abbot’s nephew.

These three had already become monks when they came, and in that same place they made their profession, as the Rule of Saint Benedict prescribes. Five others also came, still wearing lay clothing, who followed him for the love of God as their teacher and father.

One of them was named Berlegius [Note: Menardus has *Herlegius*. Some material is lacking here in Bollandus through the copyist’s fault.], a man of excellent conduct, prudent in counsel, distinguished in speech, vigorous in martial prowess, joined in friendship with all good men, ardent in charity, and fully endowed with worldly riches and rank. He was a Frenchman, one of the king’s soldiers, and not of the lowest rank; he came from the city of Noyon in France and was the brother of the castellan of that city [Col. 1038C].

As long as he was involved in worldly affairs, he was always more beloved than all the others by everyone who was with him, wherever he might be. He abounded in wealth and handled it generously, not as its slave but as its master. His parents had devoted him to the study of letters in childhood, but after he entered the years of adolescence, he abandoned literary study and devoted himself to military service. Since he was noble and born of noble stock, he could not restrain his mind from such pursuits, especially when he saw his peers inclined toward similar occupations.

Why say more? Having embraced military service and taken up military arms, he exercised himself in warfare for a fairly long time, until, touched by the right hand of God, he recognized that he was not acting rightly. He abandoned his arms and, baptized again in waves of tears and pure confession, followed Abbot Gerald to Silva-Major. As the evangelical word urges and commands, he renounced everything that he possessed (Luke 14:33) [Col. 1039A].

## 23. The other companions are named; the beginnings of the monastery’s foundation

Another was Wido, born in the city of Mount Laon in France [Note: This is the city of Laon itself, situated on the summit of the mountain. There is, however, a small town in the territory of Laon called Mons in the district of Laon, commonly Mons-en-Laonnois. But the author of this *Life*, above in no. 18, clearly designates by the name Mount Laon the city of Laon itself, beside which the monastery of Saint Vincent is situated.], a soldier of the bishop, rich in wealth and sufficiently distinguished by worldly nobility. This man was a counsellor of virtue, a vigorous ruler of his own spirit, and most refined in every form of goodness.

The third was Teszo, a young man indeed, but strong in spirit. As long as he lived in the world, he never surrendered his arms to another, nor did he ever change his course through fear of a single soldier. Wherever he was, he always strove to win victory and the palm above all his companions. This Teszo came from a certain castle in Gaul called Coucy [Note: The material that follows, up to “The fourth,” is lacking in the edition. The castle mentioned here lies between the cities of Laon and Soissons, closer to the latter but within the diocese of Laon, on the very summit of the mountain at whose foot the abbey of Nogent stands. It is called *Codiciacum* or *Coceium*, commonly Coucy, and had the powerful lords of the Enguerrand family, famous in history.], and was a young man of good character and noble birth [Col. 1039B].

The fourth was Valterus, likewise from the city of Mount Laon: a military and upright man, discerning in deed and speech, strong in counsel, not excessive in anything, and temperate in all his actions.

The fifth was Litherius [Note: Menardus has *Lucherius*. John Guisius has *Eutherius*.], from Laon, likewise an honorable and generous man, quite capable with weapons, serving everyone and loving everyone. He disdained being inferior in virtue to the other soldiers, always raising himself toward greater military exercises, and striving in every way, by deed and intention, to undertake whatever he recognized as fitting for a good man.

All these men, pierced by the finger of divine mercy, renounced everything they possessed and, leaving their lands and kindreds, followed Christ. Those who had formerly shone in costly garments afterward appeared shabby, clothed in the cheapest garments [Col. 1039C]. They became mighty uprooters of thickets and forests, though previously they had been vigorous warriors.

In them, therefore, the prophetic word was fulfilled: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isaiah 2:3). They had never read the Scriptures, yet they fulfilled what Scripture commands. And because they had often previously committed unlawful acts, afterward they abstained from lawful ones beyond what could be believed. Many times they even fasted from bread itself during the day and sometimes refused to drink water, so that they might restrain bodily pleasures within themselves more and more.

## 24. The monastery of Silva-Major is built

After blessed Gerald had founded the monastery in that same place, as was said above, where he had seen and adored the Lord Jesus on the cross in a vision [Col. 1039D], the work began to grow and improve from day to day. Nor is this surprising, for “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28), and every planting that the heavenly Father plants is not uprooted (Matthew 15:13), but always prospers.

O how greatly that day ought to be revered by the inhabitants of this region, on which the blessed man, sent by God, came here from distant parts of the earth! In the year 1079 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1040D] In the chronicle of Maillezais Gerald is said to have arrived two years earlier, where it reads: “In the year 1077, Giraud began to build the monastery of Saint Mary of Silva-Major.” See the following note.], Lord Gerald came with his companions to Silva-Major on the feast, as is said, of the apostles Simon and Jude.

In the second year [Note: [Col. 1040D] That is, the second year after his arrival, namely 1080. For this is how it is read in the old martyrology of Silva-Major: “The fifth day before the Ides of May: the beginning of the monastery of Saint Mary and of the holy apostles Simon and Jude at Silva-Major, in the year 1080 from the Incarnation.”] the monastery was begun, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in honor of the Lord, the blessed Virgin Mary, and the holy apostles Simon and Jude [Note: [Col. 1040D] Among the sacred relics preserved at Silva-Major, the principal ones are almost half of Saint Simon’s skull, part of Saint Jude’s head, and the point of the lance believed to have pierced Christ’s side.].

The fame of so great a man spread rapidly through various regions [Col. 1040B], and people gathered together and began to flock to him in crowds, so that they might enjoy his presence and that, through the ploughshare of his preaching, their hard hearts might be made fit for the seeds of divine grace. For he had an angelic appearance, a chaste body, a devoted mind, eloquent speech, and was adorned with various flowers of virtue; he was constant in prayer and distinguished in his life by many signs.

Before his arrival, the inhabitants of this region were rude and almost uncivilized, and had little understanding of the goodness of holiness and religion. But the chosen servant of God repeatedly softened their fierce hearts both by his example and by his preaching, and incited many of them to repentance and confession. For when a very great multitude often came to him to confess their sins [Col. 1040C], he imposed upon all of them alike this penance for the remission of their sins: that they should fast on Friday and abstain from meat on Saturday.

## 25. He shines through miracles

When the reputation of the holy man had spread through various regions, a certain man from the bishopric of Limoges repeatedly entreated him with tears on behalf of his little son. The child had had twisted and extremely deformed feet from birth. The father said:

“O holy Gerald, if what is said about you is true, remove the reproach from my house.”

While the father continued in this manner, the boy, through the merits of God’s servant, obtained perfect health. The father, astonished and exceedingly joyful at so great a miracle, brought the boy into the man’s presence and, with great devotion, gave thanks for the benefit he had received [Col. 1040D].

Nor should this be left unmentioned: many who were ill or feverish, if they happened to eat bread blessed by him, and likewise those who drank of a stone ground up by the brothers and prepared for his burial, returned home unharmed, giving thanks to God and to Saint Gerald [Col. 1041A].

## 26. He saves a monk from shipwreck

When the fame of the aforesaid man of God had spread through the various peoples of Gaul, a certain monk of Saint Peter of Chartres, hearing of his renowned deeds, frequently and earnestly prayed that he might not see death before enjoying the sight and conversation of the man of God.

But when he happened to plan to cross the English Sea, he boarded a ship. As stormy waves rose, he suffered shipwreck. Amid the waves, after his companions had been drowned and the ship battered and lost, the monk was swept about and spent that day and the following night in such peril [Col. 1041B].

As he was carried here and there by the swelling waves and expected nothing but the imminent arrival of death, he remembered the one whom he had heard led an angelic life on earth and whom he had so greatly desired to see. Drawing sighs from the depths of his breast, he said:

“O holy Gerald, servant of the Most High God, whom I have so greatly desired to see: if you have any power in the presence of God, help me and have mercy on me.”

While he repeatedly cried out these words, a ship immediately arrived at swift speed and, through the merits of the man of God, snatched him from the brink of death. Those who later saw the monk relating these events to Saint Gerald, not without great weeping, also reported them.

[Col. 1041C] **27. He dies.**—Thus, flourishing happily in life through these and similar virtues, after he had snatched many souls from the mouth of the bloodstained lion seeking whom he might devour, and, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, had led very many submerged in the darkness of ignorance back to the light of faith and religion, mature in years and blessed in merits, he departed to the Lord on the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 1041D] The author of the other Life describes his death more fully; see Bollandus]. He was buried in the church that he himself had founded, on the right-hand side of the altar of blessed Mary.

At his passing, a considerable multitude of noblemen, clerics, laymen, farmers, and women gathered. Having heard of his departure, they had flocked from towns and villages, and even from the city of Bordeaux. They raised a cry to heaven, tore their cheeks, and with tremendous weeping lamented that they had lost their most devout Father and teacher of the right way; they bitterly mourned from the depths of their hearts that the light of their entire homeland had been extinguished.

It would therefore be lengthy—indeed impossible—to explain how many good works the Lord deigned to perform through him, how many wonders he displayed during his life, and how many people were drawn from darkness to the true light, namely Christ. Of the many signs and virtues that he performed after his death, let us briefly discuss a few, so that we may not appear to have kept entirely silent [Bollandus reads *signis et* (“signs and”) for *signorum eius* (“of his signs”)]. For the signs that he performed during his life have, through negligence, been for the most part consigned to oblivion [Note: [Col. 1041D] The author of the other Life bears witness to the same thing]. Therefore, with the Lord’s approval and through the intervention of his holy merits, may our discourse—which we undertake to write in his honor—receive a good beginning and an end.

**28. His miracles after death. His elevation. A tooth that was taken away is restored.**—At the time when blessed Gerald was still drawing the breath of life, a certain man named Peter was received by him as a monk [Note: [Col. 1041D] In catalogues of the abbots he is called Peter of Amboise. He was the seventh abbot of Silva Major, and his letter to Louis, king of the Franks, written on behalf of the prior of Seruvium—which place is in the suburb of Orléans—is cited by Chesnius, vol. IV of the *Histories of France*, no. 344. The necrology of Silva Major records the following concerning him: “14 Kalends of May. The lord Peter, seventh abbot of this church, and disciple and chaplain of Saint Gerald, died.”]. He had been his chaplain for many days; he himself closed Gerald’s eyes and, together with the other brothers, honorably committed him to burial.

When Peter had become advanced in age, he was chosen by the brothers as Gerald’s seventh successor in the dignity of abbot. Recounting many of Gerald’s miracles in those days, he declared that the following miracle had taken place:

“Once the brothers decided that the man of God should be transferred from the tomb in which he had first been buried. Accordingly, after a sizeable gathering of bishops, abbots, clerics, and noble laymen had assembled, reverent men raised the holy man’s bones as was fitting.

“A large crowd of nobles was present at that time, and among the others a faithful man from the people was standing there, eagerly trying to obtain something from the relics, if he could somehow manage it. At last, when the saint’s head was being shown to the people, the man mentioned above stretched out a garment underneath it, and one of the teeth happened by chance to fall into the garment. When the man saw this, he drew the garment toward himself, hid the tooth, and went away believing that he had been well rewarded.

“But after he had left the village and proceeded a short distance, he was struck senseless by divine will and wandered here and there, unable to walk along the straight road. At last he understood that his journey had been obstructed through the merits of the saint whose relic he was carrying. He returned, though unwillingly, to the monastery, reported the matter to the abbot and the brothers, and produced the relic. Thus he departed joyfully.”

**29. Soldiers wonderfully preserved.**—The aforementioned abbot Peter also related yet another kind of miracle [the edition reads *aliud*, “another”]:”

“A certain noblewoman, who had two sons serving as soldiers, venerated blessed Gerald with the greatest devotion. She often came to his church and earnestly commended both herself and her sons to him.

“One day her sons wished to set out with other soldiers in an army. Since their mother had been unable to keep them from joining the army, and they were already prepared to depart, she is said to have spoken to them with a groan while kneeling on the ground:

“‘O my sons, I commend you to God and to holy Mary, and I commend you entirely to the protection of Saint Gerald of Silva Major, whose handmaid I am.’

“While they were thus positioned for battle, one of the enemy attacked one of them with a lance and struck him forcefully on his body, which was unprotected by armor. But through God’s power and the merits of the holy man to whom their mother had commended them, the blow could do him no harm.

“For although the attacker drove the lance’s iron into his body with great force, the iron bent back as though it were soft wax, so that the point of the iron, which had previously been straight, was turned backward toward the shaft.

“When the mother heard of this astonishing event and that her son had been snatched from death through the intervention of the blessed man, she came with her sons to his tomb to offer thanks. She brought the lance’s iron with her, and for many days that iron hung above the saint’s tomb as testimony to the miracle.”

**30. A dropsical man is healed.**—In the monastery of Silva Major one of the brothers was afflicted with a bodily disorder [Note: [Col. 1043D] The author of the other Life testifies that this miracle too was transmitted to posterity by Abbot Peter; indeed, as he himself says, Peter also committed this and other miracles to writing and confirmed them with his attested testimony]. He suffered from a severe illness: his entire body had swollen violently, his skin inflated like a wineskin, and he expected nothing except death.

One night, when he had anxiously surrendered himself to sleep, he saw himself in a vision standing at the tomb of the blessed man. The tomb, as it seemed to him, had been opened, and he was repeatedly making the sign of his illness with one of the saint’s teeth.

When he awoke and reflected upon what he had seen, he went in the morning to the man of God’s tomb, although he was weighed down and exhausted by the severity of his illness. He earnestly begged that through his merits Gerald might obtain from the Lord the grace of healing for him. He was healed in this manner, and faithfully related the event to us.

**31. A dying man recovers.**—At another time, a certain brother of the same monastery [Note: [Col. 1043D] In the other Life he is called the monastery’s custodian] was sick almost to death. For he remained nearly three days without a voice, and caused all of us who looked upon him [Note: [Col. 1043D] So the Corbie manuscript. Other manuscripts read *nos, qui intuebantur* (“us, whom they were looking upon”); hence the Bollandists’ reading *eos, qui*, etc.] to despair of his recovery.

When matters had reached the point that the attendants were preparing to remove him from his bed and hasten to lay him on the ground in a hair shirt, as is customary with the dying, he became exceedingly sorrowful and turned toward the wall. He began to pray that the Lord would have mercy on him and, as best he could, to invoke Saint Gerald for help.

As he himself testified, when he had closed his eyes as though falling asleep, suddenly an old man stood before him, venerable with white hair and dignified in appearance. It seemed to him that this could be none other than the holy man whom he had shortly before invoked.

When the old man touched the sick man and turned him to the other side, the illness immediately departed, and a great quantity of blood flowed from his nostrils. Thus he declared that he had been freed from the danger of death through the intervention of the blessed man.

**32. A poor woman finds money.**—The same saint also performed another miracle, certainly extraordinary but marked by compassion. A woman from a distant region, having exhausted everything she possessed, came to his monastery and repeatedly called upon his name. As though he himself were alive and physically present, she diligently asked him for food. When she was already approaching the monastery gate in order to leave, she found twelve coins lying on the ground. She took them, departed joyfully, and gave thanks.

**33. Another man finds a lost key.**—A similar event occurred when one of the monastery’s custodians lost a small key. He searched around for a long time but could not find it. At last he went to the blessed man’s tomb and prayed that Gerald might help him in this necessity. As soon as he rose from the tomb, he found the key before the altar. He was greatly astonished and gave thanks.

**34. A captive is wonderfully freed; the author’s testimony.**—A certain soldier named Oliver, son of that Augerius of Riontio who had earlier given the site of Silva Major to Saint Gerald [above, no. 21], was captured by enemies. He was taken to a fortress called Montrevel [Note: [Col. 1044D] Papebrochius thought this place was the well-known town of that name in the province of Bresse, commonly called Montravel. Here, however, the reference is to a small town in Périgord, commonly called Montravel, situated on the Dordogne not far from the district of Bazas. It lies seven leagues from Silva Major and two from the town of Castillon].

There he was loaded with a great weight of iron, stripped naked, smeared with milk, and exposed to the sun so that the flies would attack him more avidly.

But blessed Gerald, not forgetful of the benefit he had received, appeared visibly to the man in such distress—not at night but by day—and said: “How are you, brother?”

He replied: “Badly.”

“Rise,” said the saint. “Rise.”

“And how, lord,” said the soldier, “can I rise, weighed down as I am by such a burden of chains?”

“Rise,” said the saint. “Rise as quickly as possible; do not be afraid.”

When he tried to stand up, all the chains immediately fell to the ground. Astonished, he said: “Who are you, lord?”

“Do not trouble yourself to learn who I am,” the man replied. “Take your fetters and hasten to the monastery of Saint Mary of Silva Major. Give thanks to God there.”

The man saw that the guards were not absent and that very many people were walking about in the street, and he was afraid to leave. The saint again said to him: “Do not be afraid, for no mortal will be able to hinder you until you reach the place I have mentioned.”

“I beg you, lord,” he said, “to reveal your name to me.”

The other replied: “Know that I am Gerald, abbot of Silva Major.”

After saying this, he immediately vanished from the eyes of the man who was looking at him.

At last encouraged by the promise of so great a man, Oliver left the town without anyone preventing him. Taking the fetters with him, as he had been ordered, he departed and came joyfully and cheerfully to the monastery of Saint Mary of Silva Major. There he gave thanks to God and to Saint Gerald and related the miracle in order to the brothers serving there.

They immediately rang the bells with the greatest joy and solemnly sang the *Te Deum laudamus*. These signs, and the others that we relate, we have received from no one except those who saw and heard them with complete certainty, or those upon whom they were bestowed.

[Col. 1045A] **35. Miracles at his tomb.**—Nor should we remain silent about the manifest signs that were frequently performed at his tomb [Note: [Col. 1045B] The author of the other Life adds several, which are found in Bollandus. Menard adds here: “For those who drank water mixed with powder from a piece of his tombstone were healed.”]. Many men and women who had lost their senses were brought to his tomb by parents or friends. After vigils had been held for three or four nights, they were restored to their former health and brought an annual payment back to the monastery.

The Lord deigned to grant him such great grace that he unhesitatingly ordered countless captives, who had been fiercely bound by their enemies with iron, chains, and fetters—not only from neighboring places but also from the distant ends of the world—to depart free. Thus, some captives even came from the regions of the Northmen to his monastery with chains, fetters, and other instruments of torture to offer thanks. They faithfully declared that they had seen him face to face and that through his command and merits they had been released from their bonds. They hung their fetters above his tomb, imposed an annual payment upon themselves, and returned joyfully to their homeland.

Many inhabitants of the region, afflicted by pain in the head, eyes, hands, feet, or other limbs, invoked his name and often fashioned wax likenesses. Suspending these above his tomb, they faithfully confessed that through his merits they had recovered their former health.

We also repeatedly saw a ship made of wax and hung at his tomb by a certain shipwreck survivor, who declared that, when he had been placed in great peril at sea, he had been miraculously saved from death by the sole invocation of Saint Gerald’s name.

**36. The author writes at Silva Major.**—Why, then, should we speak of his miracles, when this alone is sufficient to demonstrate his merits: that through him so great an example of religion shone forth in this homeland; that countless sinners, abandoning the world, escaped death; and that in the monastery he built, young men and maidens [Note: [Col. 1045C] Papebrochius interprets this as referring also to nuns living at Silva Major, where he observes that the ruins of a women’s monastery can still be seen today. Certainly, in many monasteries of our order, some nuns lived in neighboring houses not far from the church. Oregundis is said in an ancient document to have received from Saint Gerald the habit of holy religious life. Other women are mentioned in various places. Among the other locations of the monastery of Silva Major mentioned in a bull of Celestine III, there appears a women’s monastery at Pomeret in the diocese of Cahors, together with its priories, etc. There was another at Gavaret in Occitania, subject to Silva Major], the old together with the young, praise the name of the Lord?

For the place that had once been a den of robbers, a hiding place of wolves and wild beasts, became, upon the arrival of the man of God, a house of prayer [Col. 1046B], a place of sanctification and religious peace.

Who he was, and how great was his holiness or what kind of life he led, is made much clearer by his deeds than by words; his end proves his actions. Therefore, lest excessive length of speech weary the readers, let us bring our writing to an end, glorifying above all and in all things God, who wondrously sent so outstanding a teacher, the most blessed Gerald, from distant regions for the illumination of this land. To him belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1045]

# LIFE OF SAINT ADALARD, ABBOT OF CORBIE, BY SAINT GERALD, ABBOT OF SILVA MAJOR

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines, vol. V, p. 345.)*

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1045D] **1.** Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, glorious and magnificent in his saints. He himself is the crown of the saints, their hope, exultation, and joy. Their singular vision of him is their universal delight. Through their exultation the whole earth is established: Mount Zion, the northern slopes, the city of the great King, the universal Church.

This Church, adorned with the numerous offspring of marriage and made fruitful through them in a varied order of children, embellishes Jerusalem with chosen citizens—that is, that city of heaven, whose image this earthly Church prefigures [Col. 1046D]. In this Church the hope of that city is possessed; in the other, the desired reality is held. This makes people blessed; that restores the elect.

Nor is this Church without those citizens, for God is known in their houses, where emperors bow before the tombs of fishermen, fishermen are honored through the succession of pontiffs, and pontiffs through the religious life of abbots. Therefore let it delight us to submit to the supreme Good, and let it be our pleasure to be subject to the Lord, who is not only the supporter of the growth of those who advance, but also mercifully provides remedies for those who fall. He ensures that angelic assistance is not lacking to us and grants us the patronage of the saints, whom we do not hesitate to implore as intercessors for our offenses.

Although it is fitting that we honor all of them everywhere with common services, he mercifully assigns particular saints to particular places, whom he has wished us especially to embrace and to pray to with greater devotion.

**2.** Among these, blessed Adalard, the light of his homeland, was a worthy abbot of Corbie. He shone forth not only as the jewel of the Franks but also as the rising star of the Saxons. He fathered children for the Church and nurtured Fathers at Corbie.

Saint Anscar, who was chosen at Corbie by Waldo, the brother of Saint Adalard, to be sent by King Louis with Heriold, king of the Danes [Col. 1047B], to preach to the Danes—and who afterward suffered many punishments from them for the faith of Christ and at last rested in his archbishopric at Bremen, adorned with many merits—was a disciple and foster-son of this same Saint Adalard.

Ratbert, also called Paschasius, likewise abbot of that place, who composed a splendid book on the Body and Blood of the Lord, deserved through worthy sonship to receive Adalard’s fatherhood. Corbie is also made illustrious by his body, together with the relics of the others.

These men, each in different ways, attained merits of diverse holiness in Christ. What kind of man Adalard was, and how great, is attested in a certain letter by Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, who at that time was considered the wisest among the learned. It would be lengthy to insert it here.

**3.** Let us turn our pen to Saint Adalard, from whom we have digressed for a little while [Col. 1048A]. In the expansion of his charity, his son’s love for him burned so greatly that one of them composed his Life with such prolixity, such a breadth filled with lamentation, and such an amorous languor of the *Song of Songs*, that it may be called an epithalamium rather than the text of any history.

The custodian of the church at Corbie at that time [Note: [Col. 1048D] Namely Gerald himself, who was first sacristan and afterward cellarer at Corbie] was considerably offended by this disorder and often urged the abbot to have all superfluous matter cut away. But while the latter was occupied with worldly concerns, this man, moved by reverence for the saint to whom he was bound by a special privilege of love, ordered that the flowers of his Life be gathered from so great a meadow of luxuriance.

By obeying his command in abbreviated form, he does not detract from the judgment of the earlier writers, except for the judgment of the one who did not treat this history authentically in his account of the translation of Saint Vitus, since he entered this way of writing only at the end.

For how else could he have inserted the New Corbie, which Saint Adalard built, although he described the translation itself, carried out by Adalard’s successors, down to the last detail? Nevertheless, he erred disorderly concerning the chronicles of the rulers and the saint’s successors.

To remove the falsehood of this error, the testimony of that same writer should suffice for all readers: even what he asserts in ignorance, he advises us to seek in this history. Therefore let us now pardon him for this disorder, on the understanding that in those matters where he thinks otherwise than the facts warrant, no one should believe him in every detail. Let us thus turn our pen toward the truth of the matter.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1047]

[Col. 1047C] **4. Adalard’s lineage.**—At the time when Charles held the scepter—that Charles, namely, whose fame ended with the age, crowned by the palm of virtue—Adalard, a boy of good character, was training at the palace.

Antiquity does not conceal his parents; therefore posterity cannot conceal how noble he was. According to the genealogy of his entire nobility, tracing his line of birth from the freeborn kings of the Franks, he had Bernard, brother of the great King Pippin, as his father.

He also had as a kinsman his namesake Pippin, Pippin the Younger, and as his cousin and fellow student beneath the scholastic wings, that same Emperor Charles. He was a Frank by nation—the people called Franks because of their ferocity—and of Trojan stock: under the leadership of a certain Antenor, the Trojans were led through the Illyrian bays and settled in the Maeotian marshes.

Thus he shared a civil kinship with the Romans who followed the Aeneid standards, and the common affinity of one empire once existed and ought still to exist between them. This was at the time when Charles was called, and truly was, Roman emperor. He alone was the man whom the world, according to fame, regarded as the greatest.

**5. Educated with Charles.**—After the blessed boy had passed through the fountain of the liberal arts—not with unwashed feet—he began to flourish among the foremost of the palace in age and wisdom and to be regarded as first beneath the scepter-bearing ruler.

Nevertheless, he feared God and guarded his heart with every vigilance. He had two brothers and an equal number of sisters, whom he surpassed in age as well as in merit.

Although, as a young man, he was naturally pliable and inclined toward vice, he was free from the vices by which that age is usually stained. The testimony of justice was always in his mouth; hatred of injustice was always in his heart; and the younger he was, the more perceptive he was.

[Col. 1048D] **6. Angered with Charles for repudiating his wife, he abandons the world.**—But at that time, the truth that their service to him had earned from certain men made them his enemies. The emperor had married, in a legitimate marriage, the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Italians. Later, however, because he hated the injury inflicted by her father, he repudiated her and, through perjured Frankish nobles, brought another woman into the kingdom in a public adultery.

How detestable this action was, even now the East can announce to the West. And if it did not entirely displease those who were just, I believe that it could not please the good and perfect.

Therefore the young man, utterly detesting the illicit marriage of his kinsman and publicly declaring that the Frankish nobles were perjurers, chose—though still a boy—to set aside the palace and the world together rather than appear to share in and consent to such conduct. Since he could not prevent his kinsman from acting contrary to it, he would at least show his dissent by fleeing.

**7. He withdraws to Corbie.**—Having laid aside the insignia and training of the palace, and being in his twentieth year—when the youthful mind is considered especially prone to sin—he resolved to take up Christ’s yoke, ennobling his freedom through service to Christ.

Because he intended to serve him sincerely, he sought a monastery in which he might receive an example of such service. A suitable workshop of that religious life was found in the place called Corbie. His hope did not deceive him, for what he devoutly sought came to him even more devoutly.

How noble that place then was is still sufficiently clear to those who see the traces of so great an ancient ruin. To speak of its praise more modestly than is fitting, it was truly the palace of God and, without the desire for forbidden fruit, another paradise.

And what was it then, when now it scarcely preserves the signs of Corbie? It was certainly such a place as befitted a soldier of the supreme Emperor.

[Col. 1049C] **8. Where he is rightly trained.**—At this place, then, he knocked and, by knocking, was admitted. He was to be formed according to the rule of Saint Benedict. First laying down his burden and secular clothing as he entered, he began to run along the way of God’s commandments.

He immediately became a disciple of divine law—he who had previously been an accomplished teacher of worldly knowledge—and through attaining the highest humility he quickly grasped the perfection of both laws. For this he had come; therefore learning was not a great labor for him. The grace of the Holy Spirit also made everything teachable and entirely possible for him.

Whatever was commanded, he obeyed as though it had been commanded by God. In humility he was second to no one, and although a novice, he was nevertheless first among all in religious observance. Toward his superiors he was inclined with worthy reverence; toward his juniors he was moved by fatherly affection.

Thus he became all things to everyone, and shortly afterward surpassed in every virtue those whose attendant he had been shortly before. After professing his conversion in conduct and habit, he made himself a victorious solitary combatant in the monastery—the monk he had sought to become. Strengthened by the right hand of God, he fought against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

**9. He cultivates the garden.**—When he had already blossomed to such a degree that within monastic discipline he was believed—and truly found—to have his mind more occupied with heavenly than earthly things, he was assigned an obedience so that this new monk might be tested in every respect.

He was entrusted with the care of cultivating the garden, in order that he might thereby reap the fruit of obedience and, as some say, by royal command, as though this obedience were intended to wound his spirit and bend him back toward the palace.

He accepted this obedience as a monk, willingly and devoutly, and fulfilled it as best he could with all his ability. He cultivated the garden, and with Mary sought Jesus risen in the garden.

It was a new sight to see the recent courtier, who had lately held his place among the foremost of the palace, now tearing the nettles from the earth with a rake and a hoe. It was a new sight to see the young gardener laboring in a cowl that was not his own, though shortly before he had been dressed in silk among the courtiers.

But this change was the work of the right hand of the Most High, who chooses for himself whom he wills and as he wills. This was entirely the road by which he was to travel to the stars.

**10. Fleeing his relatives.**—Nor did this road seem sufficient once he had become accustomed to advancing along it and thought that it could be maintained. He sought a narrower one, so that he might ascend from virtue to virtue.

This beginning of conversion seemed worthless to him unless it led to a greater advancement in virtue. He considered it no small obstacle that his relatives and parents were in the way. His family loved him exceedingly, and therefore visited him beyond his own wishes. Their visits were not a consolation to him but a desolation of mind.

Having chosen not to be Christ’s disciple only intermittently—for he had wholly abandoned even himself—he did not want his purpose to be obstructed by his parents. He hated the soil of his birth, because he had heard that those who abandoned such things received a hundredfold in return.

He therefore advanced in spirit to the point of deciding that he must avoid such visits by fleeing, since he could not avoid them otherwise. For if he had asked permission, he knew that it would certainly be denied him.

What, then, was he to do? It seemed irreligious to depart in this way, but it was more irreligious to remain among friends who were struggling against his purpose.

**11. He withdraws to Monte Cassino.**—While he turned such matters over and over in his mind, a good intention destroyed every hesitation. Like another Elijah, he immediately slipped away in flight, fleeing the pleasure of the flesh so that he might be found by himself.

The place to which he withdrew bears witness to the reason for his departure from his own place. He did not seek some retreat of a more relaxed life; rather, in will and in journey, he directed his steps toward Mount Cassino, where he was received with considerable honor. There he devised nothing concerning the matter that pressed upon him or the purpose he had sought, but instead planned one thing in place of another.

**12. He is recalled through the prophecy of a hermit.**—Yet he could not remain hidden for long whom God did not wish to remain hidden—indeed, whom God wished to glorify more magnificently through this flight.

A certain hermit lived there who, while speaking with the servant of God in the kindness of hospitality, foretold everything that would happen to him: who he was, where he came from, and for what purpose he had arrived.

He added matters that greatly displeased him—namely, that the emperor’s envoys, who had followed him in order to bring him back, would arrive without delay.

When the man of God heard this, he concealed his feelings, but became sad. After they had exchanged a brief conversation, they asked each other to pray for the other and consoled one another. Then Adalard withdrew to the monastery’s father and at last confessed the reason for his coming.

He asked for advice and help; he begged for permission, opportunity, time, and a place to depart, so that he might be allowed to move farther away, to somewhere where even his name would not be heard.
