The abbot praised his intention but did not reject his request; instead, he delayed his answer. Because of this delay in answering, they were immediately intercepted by the emperor’s petitioning embassy.

A year passed while they were devising their plans, and suddenly their plans were dissolved. The imperial command was heard, and, once it had been heard, they returned to the monastery.

**13. Confined at Corbie.**—Because the undertaking he had begun did not provide what he desired, he decided that, in his own place, he would be whatever he had resolved to be in a foreign place.

He remained among his relatives and yet fled his relatives, for he treated the cloister as a desert and devoted himself to prayer. He had nothing except himself, and sought to acquire the kingdom of God for himself through himself. He devoted himself to vigils and tormented himself with fasting.

**14. He is elected abbot. He directs King Pippin in Italy.**—He became such a man that he deserved to be elevated not only in rank but also in honor. Nor was there any delay in his elevation, for God was disposing the hearts of all toward it.

The monastery’s father, feeling himself deprived of bodily strength, appointed Adalard as his successor with everyone’s approval. Invested with the honor of this dignity and lawfully enthroned by the ruler of the kingdom, he did not become *philopompus* [Note: [Col. 1051] Perhaps *philocompus*, φιλόκομπος, “pompous” or “ostentatious”; for the author later uses *pompolentus*, which means the same as *philopompus*], nor, as many customarily do, ostentatious.

He wanted his people to be as he himself was, and drew them toward this by his example and urged them toward it in his words. Nor did his preaching lack varied learning; rather, he founded learning in the hearts of his listeners through exceedingly sweet eloquence.

How nobly he excelled in this was proved by all Gaul, which relied upon his counsel and was thereby pacified. Italy especially, which had been entrusted to him by Charles so that he might instruct Pippin the Younger in governing and shape the Italian kingdom according to the balance of justice [Col. 1051C], confirmed it.

There he performed justice so completely that he won from the people praise worthy of an angel. In judgment he accepted no one’s person, nor did he seek a knot in a reed—that is, he did not look for needless difficulties or pretexts.

At his arrival he laid aside every tyrannical power, especially that of those who, like robbers, exercised a tyrant’s power of plundering among the people. He restored to each person what belonged to him, thereby removing the cause of quarrels among them and establishing united peace.

**15. Praised by Pope Leo. How generous he was.**—After arranging the kingdom in this way, he reached the territory of the Romans, where Pope Leo received him with a familiarity such as no Frank is known to have previously enjoyed.

This did not happen by chance, for Leo found him to be such a man. Therefore he gave him this testimony:

“Know, excellent Frank, that if I find you to be anything other than what I have formed in my mind, I shall henceforth trust none of your people.”

He was a man of great authority, whose slight deviation from the truth would have brought about the ruin of an entire kingdom. But how could Adalard deviate from it, when he devoted himself to restoring it in those who deviated and even communicated it in writing to emperors?

In this respect he was indeed rich, but he willingly brought upon himself the poverty [*aporia*, “lack”] of worldly possessions, because he wished to be poor in Christ. He borrowed from many so that he might always give and always possess, yet he was always in need because he had to repay.

He always held generosity in his hands, and it flowed toward him through distribution. He distributed and abounded; he was enriched when he gave, because divine recompense always preceded him.

This was once revealed through divine goodness to his own people, who did not believe it but regarded his conduct with indignation.

**16. An outstanding example.**—Once he practiced such generosity toward those who asked that absolutely nothing remained for the brothers’ meal: neither fish, nor cheese, nor any food other than the monks’ bread.

A brother who had been assigned responsibility for such matters became more indignant than was just and said:

“I marvel, Father, at what such great expenditure is meant to accomplish, and why no repayment comes from anyone. You do not recall the brothers’ poverty as you ought; you assist those in need, and you yourself are in need.”

But he smiled and, concealing his intentions, replied:

“Do not be troubled, brother. Those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.”

“You always make that promise,” the brother replied, “but what you continually pour out will not immediately be supplied in this way. The brothers will feel the one who spends before they see the one who repays.”

The son of charity regarded the Father, provoked by the brother’s indignation, and endured the brother’s indignation for the sake of charity. Then he extended the hand of generosity.

Immediately two carts appeared at the gates, brought there by divine agency, not through the service of oxen but through the service of God: one loaded with cheeses, the other with fish.

The blessed Father was relieved by this visitation. He rejoiced even more over the brother’s rebuke than over the relief itself. He gave an order, and the one whom he summoned immediately appeared.

When the brother arrived, Adalard said:

“Nothing is ever lacking to those who fear God. Blessed is the man who hopes in him. See: what you feared is refuted by God, and your unbelief is plainly disproved. Now that you have been convicted, blush, accept what you were demanding, and do not despair again.”

The brother departed in confusion. He was simple—dove-like, though not without bile—and said:

“Father, I beg you to forgive me. From now on I shall believe that everything will turn out according to your desire. What you gave has been returned, because you have what you received: the grace that you deserved.”

It was a true confession, and not inconsistent with his merit. For he was not half-generous but wholly and completely so. I would be lying if I lacked testimonies to support this.

**17. With compassionate discernment.**—Whenever fortune brought two needy people before him and he did not have at hand a meal sufficient for both, he judged it better to give everything to one than for both to seem to depart almost without alms.

To one he gave the benefit of compassion; to the other, only the affection of goodwill.

### 18. Endowed with the gift of tears

[Source cols. 1053A–1064A; individual column breaks omitted.]

Nor was he empty of the inward parts of compassion; how much of it dwelt within him he could scarcely conceal from his heart, and even less from his eyes. For tears always streamed from them as though from some watercourse; as could be seen, they were witnesses to sweetness, not to the conscience of one doing penance. When those closest to him asked him the reason for his lamentation, he would say:

> “I weep for myself, my sons—not to display my humility, but to bring my conscience to account. I know myself inwardly and in my mind; therefore I weep for what I have done.”

He said this not because he was such a man, but because he was one who invited men of that kind to lamentation. Whenever some worldly matter occupied him—as temporal administration in such circumstances required and still requires—shortly after being released from it he would be wholly absorbed in divine things. At once a flood of tears would pour forth, and amid his tears the murmuring of psalms would sweetly whisper.

### 19. Especially during the divine office

Whenever he entered for the divine office, he set all secular thoughts aside beside the entrance door, and advanced wholly with himself, as it were before God. While others sang psalms, he wept; for he was dissolved in tears by a sweeter music, through which he was wholly sustained. He was of such sweetness and of such a sweet attentiveness to God that, even if he were attending royal councils, he could in no way restrain himself from weeping when he heard some melody. Nor is this surprising, since the sweetness of his homeland—the homeland in which he found sweetness, and for which he always sighed with a new song—dissolved him through that sweetness.

### 20. He walks apart on the road

Even when he traveled on the business of the Church—a service from which one is sometimes, though rarely, able to withdraw—he walked apart from all the others. Nor did he abandon the observances of the Rule: he devoted himself to tears in place of reading, and to prayers throughout the rest of the community’s routine. His companions, who were accustomed to such things, went before and behind him, attending to their own amusements; he lightened for himself the roughness of the journey by singing psalms.

### 21. He restores peace among those at variance

Wherever he walked, peace accompanied him: he waged war against war and entered into alliance with peace. Once, when he arrived at Benevento, he found that Benevento had taken up arms against Spoleto. They were raging against one another with such fierce combat that everything they possessed was being annihilated by weapons, plunder, and flames. Bellona was raging toward the destruction of all, and it seemed beautiful to everyone to recover what had been lost through the midst of the enemy. This was the measure of the war: to perish before being defeated.

At last the man of God walked between them as a herald of peace and brought forth from his heart counsel for peace to both sides. Nor did he cease before he restored their treaty even to the point of kisses, reestablished peace between the parties, and restored their ancient customs and boundaries within fixed limits. By such acts and others like them he indefatigably united the kingdom.

### 22. He is banished because of his zeal for justice

But at that time justice seemed to be departing from the earth. Mortals suffer an eclipse while the sun shines, because among them the color and beauty of things are perishing. At last Charles, the light of the world, the emperor, entered upon the way of all flesh and died, making his son Louis emperor by his death—but not making him as good a son as the empire required. For he did not follow his father’s way, but took his stand with Rehoboam, the son of Solomon. Whatever his father had loved, he hated; whatever had pleased his father displeased him. His father’s counselors were removed, and new men, haters of the former counselors, were brought in.

Their long-standing perversity immediately lamented that public affairs were prosperous, precisely because, in Plato’s manner, it saw their rulers embracing wisdom. They were the men who, in Charles’s time, had envied the man of God, who had been advanced in wisdom and honor; they preferred right and wrong to be confused rather than that he should rule. When the time for their envy arrived, inflamed by vengeance, they strengthened their conspiracy so as to separate him from the king’s side. Thus, with justice having no defender, the kingdom would lose justice, and iniquity would eventually recover a place of domination through the frauds by which it would itself be caught.

Nor was the undertaking particularly difficult, since place, time, and person were all available. As they say, good men are more suspect to kings than bad men. Another’s virtue is always terrifying to such men. Nothing proved more clearly that this was so in the case of the man of God, who, stripped of his honorable dignity without a judicial hearing, endured exile for the benefit of the commonwealth, and thus received evils in return for good deeds. O morals! O times, changed from golden to earthen! Yet “blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” For that righteousness, as though exile from the world were not enough, he received without trial the sentence of a second exile—not, however, without judgment, since he was thereby destined to be gloriously rewarded by God.

### 23. And even his own kin

Thus that happy brotherhood was dissolved which, like some constellation, appeared to be the splendor of the entire palace. There were five brothers and sisters, differing in sex and age but united in the same goodness. Saint Adalhard held the first rank in age and holiness. After him came Walo, a man of the highest distinction, heir to their rank, justice, and equity.

The holy virgin Gundrada, attached to them at their side, differed in sex but not in holiness. Alone among the palace’s amorous flowers, she deserved to escape the fire of youth. The remaining two were Bernharius and Theodrada. The latter, having laid the fruit of marriage at the feet of Jesus, chose to hear the word of God with Mary. She governed the life of the nuns at Soissons; he assumed the form of a disciple of Christ at Corbie.

### 24. These innocent flowers of the palace are sent to different places

These flowers of the palace were therefore sent, though innocent, to different places. Saint Adalhard, by God’s providence, obtained at Heri the place in Aquitaine that he had previously sought through flight. Walo, through God’s providence, was received at Corbie, so that Corbie, which had been desolate, weeping and grieving over the departure of so great a father, might be consoled by the succession of that same brother in holiness and rule.

Bernharius was sent to Lérins. Theodrada, as though more innocent than the others—although all were innocent—was left at Soissons. Gundrada was sent to Poitiers, where one worthy woman was assigned to another worthy woman, namely to serve Saint Radegund.

O hearts so united, why were you separated by the world’s intervening distance? Those whom God joined, why did man separate? This proscription was not a lawful judgment, but a furtive report. Yet in place of the goodwill that had been received, it excluded every injury arising from ill will.

### 25. While all mourn, he alone is joyful

When they departed from the palace together, Adalhard went forth, giving thanks that he had been found worthy to suffer insult; he softened his weeping brothers and sisters with kisses, persuaded his friends to show strength of mind, offered the palace nobles examples of virtue, and displayed to everyone the remarkable steadfastness of his mind.

Many followed him, since they could not do otherwise, showing by their tears and contrition of heart that the matter displeased them. When he bade them farewell as they departed, and departed from them after they had bidden him farewell, they withdrew in tears. Two archbishops, who promptly and warmly stood beside the king, said:

> “Do you suppose, Emperor, that you have taken vengeance because you dishonor this man by such a proscription? Either you have been badly advised or you have not thought the matter through. In fact, you do not dishonor him; as he sees it, you honor him completely. You have taken vengeance not upon him, but upon yourself for him, because he has never had as much exultation and joy as he has today. Today he rejoices that he has recovered his former liberty in Christ, and openly confesses that you could not have given him any joy like this. Therefore you may know beyond doubt that we have never seen him happier.”

At this the emperor was covered with shame. He regretted having done what now seemed to him capable of rendering his shame useless; yet, had it been undone, it certainly ought not thereafter to have been done. While everyone charged him with the matter as a crime—for otherwise it could not have been, since one committing a sin could not be without sin—the man of God resisted the accusation in every way:

> “It should not be charged against him—against him, I say—that which is not in human power. He has made use of God’s permission, and it is clear that we have sinned in every respect. If this is stirred up against us by the Lord, it is fitting that the sacrifice of humility should give off its fragrance.”

### 26. He benefits the monks at Heri

After preaching these and other things, he departed for the place destined for his use and desired by him with every longing. How great were his humility and grace there, the brothers can properly testify, among whom he led an angelic life for seven years. The more free he was from worldly cares, the more attentively he sighed after divine and heavenly things.

He was constant in prayer, after prayer in reading, and after reading in relieving the brothers. He refreshed them with honeyed reasoning, offering himself as a mirror for them to follow in their conduct. He was small among the lesser, lesser among the greater; he honored the greater as lords and cherished the lesser as sons. They rejoiced in his fatherhood and, as though under their own abbot, displayed worthy filial conduct. They sought him when he admonished them and in everything listened to him as a counselor.

His speech was seasoned with salt, and he supported everyone against adverse circumstances. The father of the monastery revered him in the place of a father and judged that nothing should be done without his counsel. For him, however, giving such counsel was a very small matter, since he was accustomed to arrange the manifold [reading uncertain] care of the empire, unless the diligence or charity of the brothers overcame his reluctance. But because, according to Paul, his citizenship was in heaven, divine contemplation always held him; he scarcely ever withdrew from it except when the charity of the brothers or the refreshment of food drew him away.

To conclude this brief account—for a complete definition of his virtues cannot be given—he displayed himself there as one whom no speech can adequately comprehend.

### 27. After seven years he is recalled, with everyone rejoicing

After he had completed seven years in such veneration, still as new in God’s service as though he had not yet completed two years, God—in whose hand the king’s heart is held—by his customary favor released him from exile. For the Lord looked upon the earth, and justice looked forth from heaven. Equity returned to the kingdom, the iniquity of many cooled, the color of things revived, and the churches’ flowers regained their color.

The time of pity had now come, the time had come for them, because God’s mercy inspired Emperor Louis to recall Saint Adalhard from exile. At his recall there was such exultation throughout the empire as though the divine visitation itself had visibly descended from heaven. Nor was the reality otherwise, because through him God was visiting mortals.

The monastic communities rejoiced; the dignity of the churches resounded with gladness; the arrogance of the proud was humbled; the patience of the humble was exalted. The people flocked together, their former dignity restored to them, because he who had been taken away from those sitting in the darkness of error now shone forth as the Sun of righteousness. When their father was received again, the orphans became mothers, and widows and orphans received a governor.

### 28. Except for the men of Heri

But as great as the joy of these men was, so great was the sorrow of those from whom he was departing. They rejoiced and grieved, because they always wanted to have him, yet preferred that he return to his own seat. This was discordant concord among them, and likewise concordant discord.

They wept around him with the tender sweetness of loving affection—for during the seven years they had not yet been satisfied with him, although seven years commonly become tedious to many because of their length—and only with the force of their love were they compelled to let him go.

### 29. Especially Raginard

Among them there was one especially bound to him by affection, Raginard, who was to become abbot of that place after the man who then held it. Burning with a unique love for him, he rejoiced and grieved by turns.

He rejoiced because the defender of truth was returning to his homeland; but he grieved beyond measure because he was being deprived of the presence of so great a man. When Adalhard was already leaving the monastery and the brothers followed him, bidding him farewell and escorting him with tears, Raginard concealed himself in the valley of weeping and satisfied his grief with groans and tears, because he could not bear to witness the presence of the departing man.

Adalhard repeatedly sought him, and repeatedly stopped to wait for him. He resolved not to depart at all so long as there remained a brother to whom he had not said farewell. When at last Raginard was found, and people asked him not to impede the departure of one who wished to leave, he said:

> “Please do not reveal me to those who are looking for me, because, while absent, I can bear the departing man more gently.”

The saint was informed and shown the place where he was hiding. Immediately he returned to his brother on the feet of charity, lest he remain without a farewell. When he suddenly arrived, Raginard sprang up, stricken in spirit, and cried through his tears:

> “Alas for me, Father! I have added sin to sin. I did not wish to come out to you, and so, wretched man, I have compelled you to come back here. But forgive me, because I hoped to remain hidden. Indeed, I do not know what to do now that I have delayed you; yet, now that you are present, I can scarcely bear my longing for you. But let no delay on my account entangle you in any way. May the Lord’s grace accompany you, because, whether I wish it or not, your presence will always remain with me.”

After these words, they exchanged farewells and remained for a long time in the affection of their embrace. Thus the saint departed with the others, Raginard accompanying him as well.

### 30. He boards a ship and departs

Ropes were prepared, the ships were pushed out, and, with their sails opened to the breeze, the anchors were released. With their arms bared to the shoulders, the rowers and yards were made ready. The brothers uttered groans, and the ships gave forth their sound. They stood for a long time on the bank, fixing their gaze upon the departing man, until, with their eyes growing dim, they seemed to see many men in place of one.

### 31. He is honorably received at the palace

After some days he finally reached the palace, having departed from their bodily sight but not from their hearts, his body worn down by prolonged emaciation. There he was favorably received by the king and the nobles, who tearfully asked him for forgiveness. They confessed their error and found him forgetful of the injury.

When he saw them covered with shame—though formerly they had felt no shame in envying him even to the point of carrying out their designs—he forestalled their attempts at satisfaction. With lowered eyes, he soothed them as they now sought to make amends, saying sweetly:

> “Nothing, Caesar, happens on earth without a cause; nothing, nobles, happens in the world without God’s judgment. If God rebukes us for our sins, what is that to you? We shall see to ourselves. You could do nothing without God’s permission; now let us make use of God’s command. ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven’ (Luke 6:37). I shall be the first to do so; follow me.”

All was done by everyone without delay; everything was set right.

### 32. He resumes care of his monastery

When these matters had been settled, his sons begged him to resume his former seat. To them, wearied by longing, those seven years seemed longer than a hundred years multiplied a hundredfold. He accepted and did not refuse—for according to the canons he could not refuse; indeed, the charity of his sons commanded him—and thus, amid a great escort of his own people, he returned to Corbie.

O what a joyful day then shone upon the men of Corbie! That day was a day of joy, a day of exultation and glory. Who could adequately describe the splendor of his reception? A procession of monks advanced in their cloaks, preceded by a white-clad procession of clerics. Every sex and every age rushed to meet him. Nothing could be heard except the united harmony of a single praise: namely, those praising Christ’s clemency because of the Father’s return.

Their voices agreed and disagreed, because it was sex, not praise, that changed the voices. The desolation of his departure had not shed more tears than the consolation of his return now poured forth again.

### 33. Afflicted by fever

But there was no lack of an impediment that for a time diminished their joy. The man for whom these joys smiled was attacked by the destructive flame of fever, which further weakened the limbs already emaciated by exile through the disease of illness. This diminished their gladness, but it increased the tears flowing from both sides, tears arising both from joy and from sorrow.

They were comforted only by the fact that they preferred to have him ill rather than not to have him at all, even if he were well. Therefore, as they gathered around him with every form of kindness, they performed the service of charity with gracious filial affection.

### 34. He returns honorably to the palace and secures the return of the exiles

When he had rested somewhat more easily and, whether he wished it or not, had improved a little through rest, he was summoned again by the Augustus. He who had previously been received gloriously was now received in the palace still more gloriously.

As he entered, such grace accompanied him; as he spoke, such wisdom; and as he displayed wisdom, such eloquence, that everyone’s folly immediately became apparent. They marveled and were astonished, and stood perplexed before his reasoning, because those who had previously seemed to themselves perfect rhetors now stood almost speechless, with a finger placed upon their mouths. Whatever they had discussed was rendered void; whatever he uttered was confirmed.

Thus the captivity of many was dissolved, especially that of those connected with the royal family by marriage. In this way his fortunate brotherhood was first restored, and complete liberty was returned to all together. Everyone was recalled from the various regions, except those whom death, more fortunately preceding them, had sent back to their homeland. The tonsure that some had received without legal right passed through him into a crown, and what had been inflicted as a disgrace was freely offered to God.

### 35. He reforms the conduct of the courtiers

The glorious emperor, undertaking public penance, made himself humbler than all others in respect of his offenses. He had been carried away by royal arrogance and had become another Tarquin. Whatever he had made others do wrong by his example and permission, once instructed by salutary counsel he finally healed through royal satisfaction, leading back to the path of repentance all those for whom he had become the way of deviation.

He listened to Saint Adalhard in everything and asked him to restore the empire to its former integrity. Nor did Adalhard fail to do so: he restored justice and equity to their proper seat. He restrained innovations in speech and rash presumptions among the people. And because, when he departed, he had changed his dwelling but not his mind, he restrained the changed empire through fear and love and made it ten times greater than when he had departed.

Moreover, he was ordered to direct all the churches. For them he appeared a master in counsel and prudence, but a disciple in humility. Nor did he cease until he had made the kingdom of the Franks grow young again in all its glory.

### 36. He reluctantly retains the office of abbot; he is severe toward himself

When affairs had thus been settled in peace, he considered once more divesting himself of secular cares so that he might spend the remainder of his life in divine things. But he was not permitted to do so by his sons, whose greatest hope after God he was, and their father in a mother’s place.

The more mature he was in age, the more useful he seemed to those striving toward virtue, and the more perfect for every task that had to be done. No one could undertake that work above him, especially since the vigor of the Holy Spirit and the freshness of his still-unexhausted flesh gave him such strength that no young man could follow him in the labors and business of affairs, much less overtake him.

He was so perfect in action that he handled everything sweetly while treating himself without sweetness. Who was ever so much the master of a servant as this man was of himself? Who was ever so cruel toward another as he was toward himself, acting as his own judge? When his sons sometimes begged him, with filial reverence, not to be so severe toward himself—he who treated others with such great discretion—he would immediately promise before them to correct himself, but shortly afterward would resume his vigils and hunger.

### 37. Yet he had a gracious countenance

Nevertheless, he was handsome with the grace of dignity, and his moderate emaciation left him sufficiently full of color. No disfigurement overshadowed his face; rather, constant cheerfulness gave him a becoming appearance both when he ate and when he fasted.

His gray hair adorned him with snowy whiteness, and, like a lily upon rose-colored garments, the hair of his head shone above his ruddy complexion. Had he been chosen from among thousands, no one whiter or more ruddy could have been chosen.

### 38. Generous toward everyone

There is no adequate measure by which his other qualities can be praised. In person, nobility, wisdom, and uprightness he did not fall short of the very art of his ministry. Corbie will testify, for as long as it endures, how well he arranged the affairs of the Church.

There he was a harbor for the poor, a regard for the rich, a mother’s house for orphans; and by his example it still remains a refuge for all who ask. No undowered rich person and no unprovided poor person returned from him. He assigned unmarried men and widows to receive stipends in the individual villages; wherever they received from him a hospice in suitable places, they held the Church’s possessions jointly as their patrimony.

For a treasure in heaven was being prepared for himself and his people, and the house of God was being wisely administered by a wise man.

### 39. He wore humble clothing

His clothing was scarcely sufficient against the cold, and yet it protected his limbs rather than contributing any honor or luxury. In truth, he needed no bodily adornment, for he lacked nothing of human beauty and nothing of the beauty within his soul.

His appearance was incomparable, his stature tall, his walk virginal. His voice, with the sweetness of a swan, soothed the hearing of those who listened, and his speech made everyone who heard it mindful of him.

### 40. How solicitous he was for his own

He had such a remembrance of his sons in his paternal heart that he not only watched their conduct but always had their number and names written in his hands, so that he would not forget for whom he would have to render an account to God, or for how many.

Therefore, because he exercised the greatest care over them, he did not leave any one of them without a conversation during the week, lest the enemy, finding them unoccupied, sow tares over their hearts.

### 41. He orders the monastery properly

Anyone who wishes to know how effective he was in arranging and organizing his institution may read, not without great admiration, the book written about these matters.

> **Note:** They call this book the *Statutes of Adalhard*, concerning which see the preliminary Observations.

There he will also perceive how wisely the house of the church of Corbie was arranged by a wise man.

### 42. Skilled in languages and learned

What, indeed, should be praised in him first, since in arranging affairs he was neither inferior to Moses nor below Solomon, and since he fulfilled everything that the Holy Spirit wished to suggest to him?

If he spoke in the vernacular—that is, in the Roman language—he would have been thought ignorant of all other languages; and this is not surprising, for he had been liberally educated in every respect. If he spoke German, he excelled even more perfectly; if Latin, he was more accomplished in no other field. His many letters, addressed to very many people and regarded as exceptionally polished, bear witness to this.

For he could not fail to know letters with sufficient breadth, having been brought up and educated among scholars together with his cousin, the Emperor Charles. After he renounced the world, he devoted himself with sufficient zeal to monastic learning.

### 43. Strong in counsel

Thus, perfected in both disciplines, secular and divine, and made all things to all people, he was a mediator between kings and princes, great and small, most equitable in everything, pleasing to God and to human beings.

The counsel of the whole homeland was vigorous in him. Although his sole desire was to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he was nevertheless overcome by the prayers of his people and arranged the peace and integrity of the empire everywhere.

### 44. The beginnings and progress of Saxon Corbie

Pursuing these responsibilities, he came to Saxony on another definite mission as well. The purpose of that mission was that he had once resolved to establish there a contemplative religious community. To establish it, through a certain boy named Theodradus, who had been brought from Saxony to Francia by the king and made a monk at Corbie, he had obtained from the boy’s parents a place for building.

> **Note:** [Cols. 1059D, 1060D.] Paschasius does not mention this Theodradus, nor the foundation of Corbie undertaken by Adalhard before his exile. Gerard took both details from an anonymous author who described the translation of Saint Vitus, below. But what Paschasius wrote about this matter in Book I of *The Life of Abbot Wala* is to be preferred.

At that place he sometimes planned to build a church suitable for the use of monks. But because he realized that the site was not sufficiently suitable, he continually postponed the undertaking through repeated delays. He prolonged this delay until Charles’s death, and after Charles until his own banishment into exile. During the time of his exile, whoever had previously received property belonging to him brought everything under his own control.

### 45. But he had there a certain son in Christ

But he had there a certain son in Christ who, above all his monks, was especially close to him—one who bore the same name. This man, so that no one else might enter, took possession of the aforesaid site in his place.

Because he already knew that Adalhard had wished this earlier, and out of affection for him, he began to build a cell there from Corbie’s resources. He began it but did not complete it until the saint returned from exile. When Adalhard returned, he set in order whatever had been disordered among his possessions.

### 46. He reaches Saxony again and seeks a suitable place

When he came to Saxony on this occasion, he inspected the place on every side and understood that it was entirely useless. His mind was suspended between alternatives: he did not wish to abandon the religious work he had begun, yet, having no more suitable place, he saw that this one was unfit.

At last he went to the king and asked him to give him a buildable site. The king did not hesitate for a moment. Rejoicing in his religious purpose, he resolved to allow Adalhard to choose wherever he found a suitable place. Adalhard went, searched, found one, and reported back. Having gladly received the authority to build, and having in addition been presented with many gifts through royal generosity, he abandoned the cell and began to build a monastery.

### 47. The site of the new monastery

The site lies on the River Weser and is of such great beauty and such a favorable tempering of the elements that it plainly seems to have been created from the beginning for the use of monks.

It spreads across the level ground of a valley, shaped like the letter Δ. Toward the east it has a riverbed, beside which a mountain extends directly outward. To the south, another mountain rises from the riverbed and stretches westward with an expanded curve. To the north, a third mountain lies opposite in a similar arrangement, until they seem to join one another by leaving a road through the middle.

Thus, with the very level valley remaining in the center, the place appears like another paradise, blooming with the pleasantness of its entire temperate climate, and, in this way, insofar as the arrangement permits, expressing the figure of a triangle.

### 48. The generosity of the Saxons toward the new Corbie

At this place he built a church with its associated buildings and adorned it with the best monks he could find. He instructed the monks in morals, endowed the place with resources, and did everything for everyone that Saint Benedict had commanded.

He called the place Corbie, so that it might be a sign to posterity of the source from which it had taken the matter of its existence, and he established it as the daughter of the Corbie of the Franks. And rightly so, since whatever it was began from that mother, from the egg, as it were.

It was not long before, in resources, though not in dignity, it was able to rival its mother. The good odor of its monks spread far and wide, for the most holy Father brought from the mother’s bosom to the daughter all the chosen monks. Such generosity from the emperor and all the nobles flowed toward the church that the will to receive failed before the will to give.

Such reverence burned toward the holy Father and his sons that they preferred to register the church rather than their own children as heirs to their possessions.

### 49. Adalhard sets a limit to possessions

When he saw that the church had been sufficiently endowed—with as much land, gold, and other property as was available—he set a limit to what it would receive. By daily preaching he rooted out from the hearts of his subjects the vice of covetousness.

> “We ought,” he said, “to be dead to the world, and our life ought to reign with Christ. But behold, many who appear to have renounced the world are found, because they possess an excess of things, to serve the world again. Consider with us how absurd this is. Otherwise it does us no good to have stripped ourselves of our possessions, since the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (2 Timothy 2:4).
>
> “It is not ours to become rich so that others may become poor, nor is it ours to rejoice in what causes others to grieve. Let us be content with sufficiency; for even the poverty of Christ, who, though rich, wished to become poor for us, ought to be sufficient for us.”

### 50. He often travels between the two Corbies

Preaching these and other things, he often traveled from one Corbie to the other, rejoicing as he heard that they were a good odor in Christ. He rejoiced in such worthy plantings and delighted in their unity, now firmly rooted.

They were common to one another; and because the younger was already sistered with the elder under the same father, they were dearly beloved sisters. Happy the Father in such daughters! Happier the daughters under such fatherhood! Happiest the sons, if they should remain in this unity!

For behold, the Father is departing: he abandons those whom he had nourished in the world, but he does not abandon them in Christ. The time has come to be dissolved and to be with Christ, the time to die on earth and to be reborn in heaven.

### 51. He is seized by fever

The solemnity of solemnities was therefore approaching, namely that solemnity on which, through the mystery of his incarnation, the Lord placed his tabernacle in the sun. Adalhard had returned from Saxony to Gaul so that, having founded his daughter in Christ, he might celebrate the Lord’s coming at the mother, Corbie.

The aged Simeon had already prepared to meet the coming Lord and joyfully to receive in his arms the King of kings proceeding from his bridal chamber. But behold, three days before the Nativity of the Lord, a very powerful fever struck him as he prayed and wept according to his custom in the basilica in the middle of the night.

He persevered through the entire vigil together with the brothers, singing psalms with them and weeping as he sang, until daylight, consecrating to the Lord in his heart an offering of jubilation.

### 52. He declares that his death is near

As daylight continued, he ordered the brothers to assemble before him. With them standing in his presence, he admonished each one about his particular concerns, announced that the time of his dissolution was at hand, and addressed them all concerning the peace and unity that should govern the future election according to God.

After reciting the Creed with a prayer, he commended himself to the others as they wept, but retained those with whom he had to deal concerning the ordering of affairs.

### 53. What he does meanwhile

As his weakness grew daily more and more severe, he arranged everything with such foresight as though he were suffering no evil. Above all, he labored lest the holy solemnity receive less honor or service because of the tedium caused by his illness.

He was equally diligent in arranging the remaining matters, lest anything imperfect appear to remain unfinished after him. Once the day had been completed with all the veneration he could offer to the supreme divinity, who had deigned to assume our humanity, the remaining days were ordinary days for him, because the deadly fever began to grow more fiercely diseased within him.

Nevertheless, every day he went to the oratory of blessed Marnus, whose memory he recalled with the others but, by the privilege of love, above the others. There, hearing Mass, he received holy Communion.

### 54. He rejoices at Hildemannus’s arrival

Meanwhile, Bishop Hildemannus of Beauvais heard that he was ill. Adalhard had raised him as a monk and had advanced him to that honor with the king’s permission. Hildemannus was not detained by the celebration of the approaching feast; rather, he exchanged its joys for a visit to his father in compassion for his illness.

The holy Father rejoiced at his arrival with such animation that, unless his illness had been at its final stage, he would almost have forgotten his sickness amid so great a consolation. He gave thanks to God and to Hildemannus that he had not been deprived of his desire. For he had wished to see him and to die in his hands.

### 55. He is anointed by him

When he was asked whether he wished to be anointed by Hildemannus with the oil of blessing, he raised his eyes toward heaven and prayed in every way that it might be done. The bishop was summoned and came, and immediately what Adalhard had requested was carried out.

From the moment he arrived, Hildemannus scarcely ceased attending to him. Placing a small seat before the bed, he always sat in his presence. One day, however, when he had gone out of the room for a short time and Adalhard had remained inside alone, suffering from fever, Adalhard began to cry out after being visited by the presence of God. When the bishop returned, he said:

> “Run quickly, Bishop—I command you—and kiss the feet of my Lord Jesus Christ, for behold, he is present with me.”

At this the bishop trembled violently. Not knowing what to rely upon, he stood there perplexed; and the saint withdrew silently.

### 56. He speaks to his own people

On the eighth day after Christmas—that is, on the day of the Circumcision—he began more eagerly to persist in prayers to God, asking that, once the festive days had been celebrated, he might at last be permitted to depart from here. His prayers were not without fulfillment.

When the middle portion of the night had passed, foreknowing what was to come, he summoned the brothers and addressed them in this manner:

> “O sons, the fruit of my old age in the Lord, I have completed the appointed number. Know that today I shall depart from here. It has been granted me to enter upon the way of all flesh and to appear before the presence of my Redeemer. The course of my struggle is finished. I do not know what reward I shall receive; but come to my aid, I beg you, so that I may rejoice in the Lord because of you, and you because of me.”

### 57. He conferred with the elders concerning himself; having received the Viaticum, he dies

After saying these things, he gave permission for the brothers to leave, retaining some whom he urged to get ahead of the morning office as quickly as possible. When these matters were finished, he received the Viaticum; and after receiving it, his tongue fell silent in the praise of Christ.

But the tongues of his sons did not fail him—the tongues he had instructed in the praise of God. Commended to the Lord by their psalms, prayers, and tears from the first hour, he released his spirit around the ninth hour and struck his people with a sorrowful swoon.

58. The voice of those commending his soul to Christ followed, and sobs interrupted their speech. For who would not weep, even if he had been born of stone? Very many things were present to draw forth tears. His orphaned sons stood there, and Corbie, their widowed mother [Col. 1064B]; their grief and mourning penetrated even the courts of heaven. The sheep stood without a shepherd; silent grief grew without a voice.

For he himself was, good Jesus, he whom I found, among all, the one and only abbot [Note: [Col. 1063B] Gerard here appropriates words uttered by Paschasius. From this you may understand that great discrimination is needed in judging these passages [Col. 1064B], lest you rashly take an interpolator for the primary author.]; he himself was the one whom I found seeking another’s good more than his own. Just as a mother loves her only son, so he loved each of them most tenderly and invited them to receive more substantial nourishment.

[Col. 1063]

# The Miracles of Saint Adalhard

## Book One of the Miracles

Written by Saint Gerard himself, abbot

## Author’s Preface

[Col. 1063C]

### 1. The praises of Corbie. Its three churches

Whoever might remain silent about the renown that Corbie formerly possessed, its stones proclaim it—not only to the ears but also to the eyes of posterity. For three principal churches are found there [Note: These three churches still stand: the first belongs to the monks; the second is the parish church and belongs to the Canons, whom they call the Charitables; the third is likewise a parish church. All are situated around the monastery walls.], in which the confession of the Holy Trinity can rightly unite the hearts of the faithful.

The first presents Peter the fisherman; the second, the fisherman and Evangelist John; the third, Stephen the protomartyr, the evangelizer. It is a beautiful order, certainly arranged by God. I would not call Queen Balthild its founder, but rather the grace of the Holy Spirit, who inspired her—as he inspires all good things.

### 2. The situation and pleasantness of Corbie

Accordingly, its situation is healthy and very suitable, flourishing with every kind of usefulness and pleasantness [Col. 1063D], and altogether well adapted to the needs of the monks, for which purpose it was sought out and found. On one side the river Somme flows past; on the other, the stream called the Corbie, flowing together with it, gives its name to the place—but immediately falling into the Somme, it loses there what it gives here.

Thus, with meadows, waters, and fields stretching far and wide, it is both like and unlike the Corbie of Saxony, that place whose ruler and founder was likewise Saint Adalhard.

### 3. The precious death of Saint Adalhard

When his deeds and manner of life, related above, have been completed, the noble account of his precious death follows [Col. 1064C]. He was buried beside the principal church of Saint Peter, lying midway before the lower step of the chancel rail. The language of the epitaph is one thing, but the burial itself has no corresponding likeness. There the ashes long return to ashes, awaiting with the elect the resurrection of the flesh, until that generation had almost entirely produced another generation, and all except the learned were unaware where so blessed a treasure rested.

The burial remained hidden for a long time, so that the rest of the earth might be trampled by everyone; no passerby and no person praying was obstructed. At last, the Discerner of merits, wishing by making the burial known to magnify it, made the merit of the buried man the beginning of this glorification of his servant.

## Chapter I. The remarkable revealing of his burial through a man whose feet clung to the pavement

[Col. 1064D]

### 4. A man’s feet cling to the pavement before Saint Adalhard’s tomb

A certain man came to pray for the intercession of the saints, through whom so great a church flourishes. Since custom required it, he first sought the Prince of the Apostles. He sought Peter and found Saint Adalhard: he found him hidden, but reigning in his hiddenness.

For, unknowingly, he prostrated himself upon the confessor’s tomb, and by prayers and vows gained the favor of those above. He prayed and was heard; he rose—I do not know whether he had been answered. But when he wished to depart with his face marked with the sign of the cross [Col. 1065A], his feet clung to the pavement as though they had been nailed down.

The wretched man was astonished, and in his astonishment began to cry out piteously. Since he could not move his feet, he turned his face about tearfully. The novelty of the event drew many to the tomb, especially the monks, who were astonished and amazed, yet rejoiced at the novelty of the signs: the man could not move, and yet he remained healthy.

He asked them whether someone was buried there, and they asked him whether any awareness of guilt tormented him.

“I know, lords,” he said, “that I am a sinful man; but I beg you, help me from here, by your prayers on the one hand and by your counsel on the other.”

Both were done at once. They prayed for him, and, instructed by the event, he made a vow to the saint—namely, to Adalhard—to construct a tomb. Thus, bound by himself to the one who held him, he was released without delay [Col. 1065B].

Joy arose for both parties: for him, permission to depart; for the monks, the magnificence of their patron. Nor did the saint fail to receive a reward for binding and releasing. For when the man returned, he built a fitting tomb and further established, for every day of his life, an anniversary day on which he would pay the census.

## Chapter II. A woman crippled and healed by God through the merit of the saint

### 5. Ulfiardis is healed

This binding afterward became the release of many. From this celebrated event the place began to be frequented with great veneration. The healthy and the afflicted gathered there: the former seeking the health of their souls, the latter that of their bodies.

Among them was a certain crippled woman who seemed, by remaining continually beside the burial, somehow to exert force upon the man of God. No night excluded her, except the first watch; no day, unless she was restoring her body with food. Her name was Ulfiardis, and she was always at hand because she was a resident of Corbie. She was so crippled that she seemed to walk more by the feet of those carrying her than by her own. If bearers were absent, one would have thought her not a two-footed creature walking, but a quadruped crawling on little stools.

Apart from the mercy of Saint Adalhard after God, no hope of recovering her health remained. One night, as usual, she came to the tomb; with her head she sought the earth, but with her prayers she sought heaven. After praying, she sat because she could not stand. Holding a candle, she drew the eyes of the monks who were singing toward herself, by her tears and the misery of her condition. She multiplied her prayers because she was seeking not someone else’s but her own healing.

At last divine mercy was present, because the intercession of the one she had lost was present. The cracking of sinews was heard, as sinew sprang back to sinew and joint to joint. Feeling that she had been healed through the intercession of Saint Adalhard, the woman called to her attendant, who was sitting behind her. The attendant approached the caller and, sooner than could be said, found her healthy and standing upright.

Those who were present were amazed; they asked for the same favor and were now made increasingly certain of their own healing. Such exultation also came upon the monks that, in praising the servant, they seemed to interrupt the praises of the Lord.

Abbot Ingelramnus was present at Matins [Col. 1066A] [Note: Ingelramnus governed the monastery of Centula after Ingelard, who had been taken from the Corbie monastery and restored monastic discipline at Centula around the year [Col. 1066D] 980. Ingelramnus succeeded him at the beginning of the eleventh century and died in 1045.]. At that time he surpassed the others in learning; and the fact that he was a witness of this sign was not due to chance, but because Saint Richarius was the shepherd of his flock.

Heribert, the abbot of Corbie, approached him and made a sign with his hand. Saint Benedict had imposed silence upon him, since, if the Matins hymns were interrupted, he would have sung the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. Ingelramnus refused and indicated that Matins ought to be brought to an end; thus everyone celebrated the event with praises.

The woman took part in the praises, and herself became, by the testimony of her recovery, known to those who knew and those who did not know. The crippled woman, well known to all the people of Corbie, gave complete credibility to the miracle by being healed.

## Chapter III. The healing of a woman’s hands through the merits and intercession of the holy confessor

### 6. A woman’s hands are restored

There was also a woman in the monastery at Corbie who suffered from various bodily ailments. Her fingers had adhered to the roots of her palms so completely [Col. 1066B] that she had entirely lost the use of both hands.

Placing all hope of her recovery in the holy man of God, whose mercy she often saw recall many sick people from the very danger of death, she came daily to the tomb and, among the other sick, implored the help of God and Saint Adalhard. Although she often saw many depart healed, even though she herself had approached more eagerly and attentively than they, she did not fall into despair; rather, she was encouraged to ask. She attributed the lesser efficacy of her petition to her own sins.

Therefore she asked and received; she sought and found; she knocked and entered. Because she did not desist, she was saved in her faith, like the Canaanite woman [Col. 1066C].

After she had long implored the saint’s mercy and daily awaited the result of her petition beside his tomb, at last, on the first Sunday of the Lord’s Passion, she happily obtained what she had long sought. Standing before the tomb with an attentive mind, where the holy body had been buried, she began, amid prayers and tears, to extend the knots of her fingers.

The palm of each hand was restored to freedom; now each palm could grasp and release. The hands returned to their proper function; the body that had suffered from infirmity was restored to health.

Thus, by singing *Te Deum laudamus*, the glorification of the saint was referred to the praise of God. And so that everything might be established by testimony, a suitable witness was present: at that time a boy, but later Abbot Fulco, who received the burden and honor of Corbie after Abbot Richard had been taken from human life [Col. 1066D].

## Chapter IV. The elevation of the saint, the burning of the church, and the danger to the kingdom

### 7. Fire at Corbie and famine in France

But enough of these matters. It must now be told how his elevation was celebrated.

At that time many misfortunes had fallen upon Corbie, and still more upon the kingdom of the Franks. The principal church of Saint Peter at Corbie was set ablaze through the envy of the devil; almost all Gaul was given over to the danger of famine. King Rotbert was exercising his office in the Frankish kingdom [Col. 1067A], while Richard was abbot at Corbie in the place of Christ: both were acting successfully, except that fire reigned cruelly with the one and famine with the other for seven years.

Hunger handed so many peoples over to death that the sisters seemed to break their threads not with their fingers but with a sword. This plague of the dying afflicted all the other regions severely, but the territory of Amiens most of all.

### 8. Peace is made between Amiens and Corbie

Compelled by this necessity, they decided to provide themselves with a remedy as quickly as possible: namely, to appease God, whom they had offended by evils of many kinds, with certain good deeds. Indeed, it seemed that this punishment had been imposed upon them from heaven because they had never preserved the peace that the Lord alone loves and commands to be loved.

Such a habit is naturally ingrained in the kingdom of the Gauls: more than other nations, they always wish to practice the fury of wars [Col. 1067B]. But what now? It is no longer necessary to wish to die in war, since they are dying in crowds by the sword of famine and pestilence.

The world cannot endure the anger of the Judge. A council is held with the Ninevites. Peace and justice come together; the reign of Saturn is now pleasing to restore. For those in despair, one course alone remained among all others: to seek the intercession of the saints in order to appease the anger of the heavenly Judge.

The relics were sought. The relics were sought; the neighboring places gathered at the relics, and there the inviolable pact of peace was confirmed. Thus the people of Amiens and Corbie came together with their patrons, established a complete peace—that is, peace for the entire week—and unanimously promised God that each year they would return to Amiens on the feast day of Saint Firmin to confirm it.

They bound themselves by the vow of this promise, and bound the vow again by an oath. The promise was this: if any people quarreled among themselves in some dispute, they would not avenge themselves by plunder or arson until, on the appointed day, a declaration of peace had been made before the bishop and the count outside the church [Col. 1067C].

### 9. Miracles at the gathering of the relics

How pleasing this plan was to the Lord of lords was demonstrated more clearly than daylight by the gathering of saints that took place there. On that day Corbie proved how great before God was the merit of the intercession of its patrons.

When their relics had been set apart in the place chosen by the abbot and monks, all the afflicted who came there to pray were immediately made healthy and unharmed. Thus, after peace had been arranged, each returned to his own home.

From then on, the fame of such events began to spread so far and wide that Corbie was rightly considered worthy to be called another Rome. In the end, those present and absent, the bound and the imprisoned [Col. 1068A], when they invoked the name of the saints of Corbie, immediately experienced the sovereignty of Saint Peter.

### 10. The decision to elevate Saint Adalhard’s body

As the fame of so great a good became brighter from day to day, it pleased the Author of these things to magnify the place more nobly by demonstrating the merits of blessed Adalhard, whose body was still covered by a burial tomb.

It was covered in the church that had been burned by fire. The brothers, however, had moved with the relics of the saints to the nearby church of Saint John the Evangelist. How and by what signs he revealed himself there, and how gloriously God magnified him at the tomb after his elevation, must also be told—but the former first, the latter afterward.

## Chapter V. By what signs Abbot Richard was encouraged to elevate the holy body

[Col. 1068B]

### 11. Himoldus’s vision of Saint Adalhard and the devil

A certain priest named Himoldus, who enjoyed a sufficiently good reputation according to his way of life, was staying in the aforesaid monastery of Saint John the Evangelist, because he was regarded as the custodian of that church.

One night, in a dream [that is, in a vision], the same confessor appeared to him and led him through the chambers of the burned church. He revealed many wondrous and astonishing things to him, which Himoldus, made sleepless, considered worth recounting to many.

Among other things, he saw what seemed to be a certain man, cloudy, misshapen in stature, black, filthy, covered with rags and years. He leaned his jaw upon his hand and was entirely, so to speak, not the sign of one who suffered but of suffering itself.

The priest, questioning his holy guide about him in his dream, said: “Who is this, lord, who displays such great grief?”

“This,” said Saint Adalhard, “is that demon whose sole desire is to drag everything to destruction, and who handed this sanctuary over to the devouring power of fire. But because he now sees, contrary to hope, that the best monks are striving to restore the house of God more elegantly than it had been before, this is why he afflicts himself with as much grief as you see, and grieves over the fact that you are made joyful by it” [Col. 1068C].

At this the priest was astonished, and, astonished, awoke. He did not become a deaf hearer, but a truthful preacher of his vision.

### 12. Abbot Richard receives permission to elevate the body

Thus, by these things, by those mentioned earlier, and by many signs that were often plainly visible, it seemed to Richard, abbot of blessed memory [Col. 1068D], that God both wished him and showed him by his will not to delay through negligence.

Accordingly, he sent messengers to receive the blessing of Pope John, who at that time was regarded in Rome, within the pontifical hierarchy, as the vicar of Saint Peter [Note: Bollandus corrects this expression, as though Gerald had erred in calling the supreme pontiff the vicar of Saint Peter, since he ought to have been called the vicar of Christ and successor of Saint Peter. But not only Gerald, but also other authors used the same expression down to the thirteenth century, when the pope began to be called the vicar of Christ as a distinctive title; previously that name was common to other bishops. It would take too long to cite the various authors here; I note only a few. Alcuin calls the pope the Vicar of blessed Peter in Letters 6 and 72; Einhard, under the year 799; the *Life of Louis the Pious*, under the year 816; Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, in Letter 84; Anastasius, in the commonly circulated account of Pope Stephen II and elsewhere; the Council of Pavia concerning the imperial dignity of Charles the Bald; Aimoïn in *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 1; Leo of Marsica in *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book I, chapters 12 and 15; Anselm of Bec in his letter on leavened and unleavened bread; and others. Indeed, the Roman pontiffs themselves generally assumed no other title for themselves, as Pope Nicholas I does in Letter 30 to Charles the Bald, before the middle, and at the end of his letter to Roland, archbishop of Arles; and Hadrian II in his letter to the Fathers of the Council of Douzy and in his letters to King Charles and his wife. Hadrian I explains this expression in Letter 89 of the *Codex Carolinus*, when he says that he had taken the place of blessed Peter [Col. 1069D]. At that time, indeed, it was a distinctive title of the Roman pontiffs. Bishops, however, were commonly called vicars of Christ, and even kings and abbots were so called. Hincmar, in the letter prefixed to his book *On Predestination*, calls bishops “vicars of Christ, our God”; and in the *Admonitions to Louis, King of Germany*, chapter 7, they are so named. Gunthar, bishop of Cologne, says in a letter to Hincmar: “I have fled to you, who are God’s vicar.” In the twelfth century, Guibert, abbot of Gembloux, repeatedly gives the same title to Philip, bishop of Cologne, in manuscript letters, one of which bears this heading: “To Philip, the revered Father, vicar of Christ and officer of the heavenly court’s key-bearer,” etc. Saint Bernard, in Sermon 1 on the Ascension, also calls all prelates vicars of Christ. From this it follows how unjustly Gervase of Tilbury expresses indignation against the Roman pontiff because he is called the vicar of Christ and successor of the apostles. Since the title was once common to other bishops, it could be reserved for him without arrogance, just as the title “pope” came to be adapted. From that time supreme pontiffs were called vicars of Christ; bishops were sometimes called vicars of Saint Peter, as is clear from Peter of Blois, Letter 148, and Peter of Celle, Book VIII, Letter 7. In this case, however, the title was given to bishops not so much as a common designation as for the sake of honor.], and was not merely permitted but even commanded by apostolic order to do what he would gladly have done without being ordered.

Because Fulco, bishop of Amiens, was absent—whom the abbot, following the counsel of the brothers, had arranged to have present for this solemn rite—Drogo of Thérouanne was summoned, a man praised by the testimony of every good reputation.

After the ministers had been prepared with the twofold disposition required, of heart and body, the holy body was lifted from the tomb on the sixth day before the Ides of October and offered for veneration to the waiting people by the hands of the bishop and the abbot. The crippled, deaf, mute, maimed, and blind were immediately healed.

The crowd of those approaching grew dense. There was no counting the offerings of the faithful, for there was a lack of space and time before there was any lack of willingness among the offerers. From that time, therefore, the title of confessor was inscribed among the other patrons of Corbie [Col. 1069B], with whom he protects Corbie to the present day and will always protect it.

This elevation of the holy body was celebrated in the year 1040 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: Rather, in the year 1025, to which all the chronological indications agree, not the year stated in the text, in which Pope John XX, Conrad, and Rotbert had already died. The feast of this elevation is solemnly celebrated every year at Corbie on 10 October.], in the eighth indiction, with Conrad ruling among the Romans and Rotbert among the Franks.

## Chapter VI. A mute and deaf man healed before the tomb of the holy confessor

### 13. Roger, mute and deaf, is healed

Nor must we allow to pass into oblivion how God afterward deigned to glorify him, as I learned from the very man who rejoiced in that glorification.

It was the vigil of the celebration on which the heavenly key-bearer ascended through the passion of the cross into heaven. Every road in the surrounding region seemed to lead to Corbie—so highly did Peter value the glory of his Corbie. Some came to pray, some to earn merit, and some to be relieved, since the church that Christ had founded upon such a rock had been burned [Col. 1069C].

Among them a certain boy named Roger was brought. Nature had reserved for the mercy of Saint Adalhard the use of speech and hearing that he lacked. After the parents had visited the other prayers of the saints, at the first hour of the feast day they came to the tomb, which Saint Adalhard had made glorious with his ashes.

The tomb was in the church abandoned after the fire, while the body, together with the other relics, had been honorably placed in the church of Saint John the Evangelist. The parents prayed for themselves and for their son, invoking Saint Peter often and Saint Adalhard more often. Both were present—or rather, God was present because of both.

For the boy, having recovered his health, began to address and hear those who were present [Col. 1069D]. O heavenly condescension! And lest anyone attribute to the others what God had granted uniquely through Saint Adalhard, this mercy occurred not before the body but before the tomb.

The event was announced to the abbot and monks. The joy of the feast increased; a swift procession began. Saint Adalhard was carried about with the people following. They came to the tomb, where they sang and prayed the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. A brief account of what had happened was delivered, and then they departed [Col. 1070A].

## Chapter VII. A deaf and mute man, crippled in hands, feet, and his entire body, is healed over the tomb

### 14. Gislebert is healed

There was another man in Normandy named Gislebert, who was almost deprived not only of the natural form of his body but even of human appearance. His whole body was contracted; he was bent, his face twisted backward, deaf and mute, with only his eyes preserved, so that he could see his misery [Col. 1070B].

His people brought him to Corbie, where for a long time he remained among the others, receiving the brothers’ alms. At last Saint Adalhard appeared to him in a dream and instructed him that, as soon as he arose, he should go to his tomb to pray.

When he awoke, he wished to go; but although he had already been visited by the saint, he was entirely unable to move. Since he had often been instructed by watching the monks’ signs, he indicated that his companions should help him.

Moved by compassion for his misery, they carried him to the place where the saint lay with the others, toward the church of Saint John the Evangelist. But Gislebert gestured to turn them away and directed himself toward the tomb, so that no one could doubt by whom he had been visited.

They immediately carried him and placed him before the tomb. He lay there for a short while, prayed, and obtained his request [Col. 1070C]. He felt the power, rose, gave thanks, and departed healed.

## Chapter VIII. The indignation of the people of Amiens, and the healing of a mute and deaf man

### 15. The annual gathering of Amiens and Corbie

A new kind of religious observance had also grown up between the people of Amiens and Corbie, and from that observance a custom had sprung up that was repeated every year.

On the octave of Rogationtide, both sides came together in one place, and the bodies of the saints were brought together there. Lawsuits were settled, those at odds were recalled to peace, and the turns of prayer were exchanged by the people. The decrees of both places were renewed, the people were addressed, and then everyone returned home.

But as time went on, the practice itself sometimes began to lose its value through use, and irreverence arose from excessive veneration [Col. 1070D]. Both men and women devoted themselves to laughter and games, began dances, and acted irreverently; thus almost everyone neglected the bodies of the saints. This displeased good people, and especially the monks.

### 16. Saint Adalhard is carried alone

Richard, abbot of Corbie, was in charge—a truly blessed man of memory. When he had seen such things occurring for several years, one day, as the procession was about to set out, he summoned the brothers and said:

“I fear that the saints who are accustomed to being carried are being offended. For you see how much irreverence is shown to them each year. But if it seems good to you, let them remain resting in their resting places.”

“It is not appropriate,” the brothers replied, “because the Amiens people, who will come with their saints, will judge us proud if we meet them in any other way.”

“Let it be,” said the abbot, “as you think best. But if you wish, carry Saint Adalhard, since none of the others will be carried.”

What he had ordered was approved. No one could oppose it; indeed, God had arranged it in this way. Thus Saint Adalhard, as though less worthy than the others, suffered the insult that he had been ordered to accept on their behalf.

They set out for the procession and came to the appointed meeting place [Note: This place is still called *Indictum*, or *Lendict*, midway between the city of Amiens and Corbie.]. The people of Amiens came with Saint Firmin, and the people of Corbie with Saint Adalhard. When they arrived together, they began the antiphons according to custom.

Both sides stopped and prayed with due reverence. Yet from a brief ignorance a great grace was eventually obtained. Some people took offense, as though the monks had disdainfully refused to bring there the other relics of the saints—namely, those of Saint Peter and Saint Gentian. In truth, however, the omission had been made only for the reason explained above: because of the irreverence shown to them by the people [Col. 1071C].

But many people say many things while the actual state of affairs is unknown to many. The monks therefore placed Saint Adalhard suitably close by and attended to their patron with the diligence they owed him.

The people of Corbie followed their custom: they honored Saint Firmin with gifts and sought his help in prayer. Saint Adalhard was placed opposite, but he was not visited with the veneration he deserved. No one prayed before him; no one asked anything of him. Yet, although no one had yet asked, he was already preparing to give.

### 17. Retbert, mute and deaf, is healed

The Lord therefore did not tolerate the abasement of his servant. Through the restoration of one man, he immediately showed those present how great the saint’s merit was in his sight. He exalted his chosen one and magnified him above all those who had been carried before him [Col. 1071D].

A certain Retbert [or Rotbert], as he had been instructed in a dream, came with the people of Amiens. He was the servant of a certain Roculf from the castle of Ailly. In full view of everyone, he began to pray beside the bier, all the more intently because he was entirely deprived of hearing and speech.

He was drenched in a shower of tears and expressed by groans and nods of his head what he could not express by voice. He sought the saint with a talkative heart, as though he saw the saint speaking with him. Everyone fixed their attention upon him, while he fixed his upon no one [Col. 1072A]. He stood beating his breast and kissing the bier.

At last divine mercy looked upon him, in order through him to display the merits of the holy confessor. When he had felt the power of God within himself for a short time, he began, after yawning repeatedly and at length, to strive toward speech.

He moved many people to pity, and even more to tears. Straining with all his strength toward speech, he again expelled through his nose, mouth, and ears a stream of blood, which sprinkled the entire bier drop by drop.

With his voice now released, he burst forth with what he had previously wished but could not utter: “God, help me,” he said, “and you also, Saint Adalhard!”

This was the first voice he recovered with his health. Immediately everyone began to run toward him, while he himself, scarcely able to stand, began to stagger like a drunk man. He was received and gently seated [Col. 1072B]. When questioned, he confessed by explaining the power that had been worked in him.

Both peoples rejoiced, and both orders and both sexes offered their praises. There could be no doubt, since the healing had been plainly manifested. There was, moreover, abundant material for belief: the man’s identity was known to the very people of Amiens with whom he had come, and he had recovered the use of speech and hearing.

Roculf himself, whose servant he was, faithfully bore witness. God too, who had performed the miracle, had left an evident sign to inspire belief: the blood that had sprinkled the bier wiped the poison of unbelief from everyone’s hearts.

### 18. The people honor Saint Adalhard

How certain this event was to the clergy of Amiens may also be judged from the fact that one of them immediately climbed to a more elevated place and addressed the people for some time about this event and the others.

Voices worthy of praise resounded, and the tumult of such great rejoicing increased. Access to the body became impossible because of the crowd; prayers were poured out, gifts were offered, and the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* was begun. Both orders and both sexes resounded with it.

Thus Saint Adalhard vindicated the saints from the insult that he had been sent to endure on their behalf.

When everything had been settled, the gathering dispersed and the monastic procession began. The body was carried back to its proper place, with the people of Amiens following. The fields answered with his praises, and the neighboring people came to meet him with due veneration.

Some of the monks went ahead to the church, dressed in white garments and capes, and carrying the other relics of the saints [Col. 1072D]. When they had returned together to the church with hymns and had placed Saint Adalhard’s body upon the altar, the man who had been healed again prostrated himself before the body on the pavement and gave thanks, once more emitting blood through his ears, mouth, and nose.

The entire church resounded with joyful voices; no one ceased praising and singing hymns within it. Nor was this undeserved, for he is worthy of such honor who has been deemed worthy by God to be honored.

# Book Two of the Miracles

Written by an anonymous author of the twelfth century

[Col. 1073]

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 1073A]

### 1. The virtues and miracles of Saint Adalhard

Whenever the power of divine action deigns to illumine its saints in the present by virtues and miracles, it is fitting to transmit them to posterity in written form, so that their hearts may be stirred to praise the power of God and may burn more ardently to show honor to the relics of the saints.

Accordingly, we briefly record certain miracles that, in our own times, our patron—namely Saint Adalhard—has performed; or rather, that divine power has performed through him.

We did not witness these events with our own eyes, but learned of them from the reports of faithful men who saw them and were present. Full faith must be given to their testimony, since they are commended both by the holiness of their conduct and by the respect due to their age.

For neither would their own welfare be increased, nor would glory be added to the saint, if one now established him by lies when it is clear that he had already been glorified by many miracles. As we received these accounts from them [Col. 1073B], so we also relate them in what follows.

## Chapter I. Why Saint Adalhard was carried to Flanders

### 2. Corbie is granted to Baldwin the Elder

Henry, king of the Franks, who had succeeded his father Rotbert in the kingdom, had a sister named Adela. He joined her in marriage to the margrave of Flanders, namely Baldwin the Elder, and granted him Corbie, which bordered his kingdom, as a dowry along with many other possessions.

On account of this union, the king and the count entered into an alliance, and great friendship flourished between them as long as they lived. But since, as a certain philosopher says, “Friendship is often disinherited,” after both had yielded to mortal nature—that is, after the king and the count had died—the alliance of friendship was broken between their sons, namely King Philip and Count Rotbert.
