King Philip, considering it a loss to himself that his kingdom had been diminished, as it were, by the deprivation of Corbie—which his father, as we said above, had given in marriage to his sister—entered Corbie with royal pomp and compelled its townsmen to swear allegiance and security to him as king [Col. 1073C].

### 3. The dispute over Corbie

When Count Rotbert learned of this, he was distressed that an injury had been done to him. Since, as anger demanded, he could not immediately avenge it upon the king, he turned it against the church of Corbie, which had deserved no such treatment.

He immediately invaded its villages and estates, which were widely scattered throughout his territory, and denied the brothers serving Christ there the revenues assigned to the needs of their clothing.

Therefore Abbot Fulco, who at that time presided over the church of Corbie, and the brothers, greatly troubled, poured forth a tearful complaint in the king’s presence and implored his counsel and assistance in the matter.

But since, whether through the king’s inability or negligence, they recovered none of what they had lost, and since they had suffered great damage by being deprived of their revenues for almost two years, they began, while considering what ought to be done, to waver in mind over these matters [Col. 1073D].

At last, casting their thought upon the Lord as upon a harbor, they fixed the anchor of their salvation in him. For they jointly resolved to flee to divine aid and to present Saint Adalhard to the count, so that the count, moved by his presence, might restore his allodial property to him and to Saint Peter.

## Chapter II. The carrying of the saint to Flanders, and how the church doors were opened at his arrival
4. Therefore, having chosen brothers of sounder counsel to accompany the saint, and having prepared everything necessary for the journey, they set out with great honor, as was fitting, and reached Flanders, not despairing of God’s mercy and the saint’s merits.

[Col. 1074A]

The count had heard beforehand from rumor that the saint was to be presented to him by the brothers, and had forbidden the entrance of any church to them, supposing that in this way they could gain no access to him. But matters turned out otherwise than he had thought. For as they were traveling toward the village called Curba, where a church was held by hereditary right of Saint Peter, the priest, following the count’s command, had locked the church doors and withdrawn secretly with the keys, so that he could not be found.

At last they reached the church; the keys were demanded; the priest was sought everywhere, but the power to find him was denied to those searching. A wondrous thing to tell! As the saint sought a faithful hearer, while some delay occurred in the search for the priest of the church, suddenly, of their own accord, the church doors opened: the locks were shattered, the bars flew apart, and they stood open to the saint and to all who accompanied him. No magic, no mechanical art, worked there; rather, to reveal the merit of Saint Adalard, heavenly power appeared [Col. 1074B] in the opening of the doors.

Behold another Peter in this deed, comparable to the holy Peter, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted, in such a miracle. For when Saint Peter had been freed from prison by an angel, the iron gate opened of its own accord; so likewise, when this man had already been led out by the angel of counsel from prison—that is, from the prison-house of the flesh—the hard strength of the doors yielded of its own accord. O wondrous condescension! He received from the Lord the grace that had been granted to the heavenly key-bearer.

It was also just that Saint Peter’s church should open to him in a foreign land: at Corbie he had been given lodging in Saint Peter’s church, and, as though bound by a pact of companionship, he was acting as an envoy to seek the goods belonging to that church. Thus the saint was carried into a church previously inaccessible, while the people of both sexes who had gathered followed him. The monks and clerics offered praises to the divine Majesty with rejoicing of voice and heart, while the people applauded and gave thanks to the Lord.

### CHAPTER III. How the Count Returned to Him Everything He Had Taken

[Col. 1074C]

5. On the following day he was carried away from there, and the journey was hastened to seek the count. Wherever the saint’s arrival was heard of, an immense multitude of people came out from afar to meet him, because the miracle had already become widely known. They not only strove to open the doors of churches to him, contrary to the count’s command, but ecclesiastical and secular persons alike requested that the saint be brought into their churches, fearing that they might incur divine displeasure more than the count’s.

When the brothers heard that the count was staying in the district of Tournai near the town of Schelmas (Schlin), which he had surrounded with troops in a siege, they turned their journey there and at last reached the place toward which they had set out. When the count heard that the saint was being brought to him, he hastened to withdraw from his presence.

Then the princes who were accustomed to stand at his side, and upon whose counsel all his decisions depended, began to reproach him on this matter. They said that nothing would go well for him [Col. 1074D] so long as he despoiled the churches of the saints of their possessions. They advised him to meet the saint humbly and to make amends for whatever offense he had committed against him.

The count accepted their prudent counsel and went humbly to meet the saint. You might have seen another king of the Ninevites descending from his throne, walking barefoot in humility and laying aside his dignity. With such devotion, while a troop of soldiers attended him, the count approached the saint’s bier. Taking the carrying-pole in his own hands, he carried it into a nearby church, while the soldiers eagerly relieved one another in lightening his burden.

There, in the presence of the saint and before his leading men, he returned everything he had taken from the church of Corbie. Whatever offense he had committed against [Col. 1075A] Saint Peter and Saint Adalard, he repaired, asking that through them the Lord’s forgiveness be obtained for him. The brothers, acting in the place of the Lord, who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, and of Saint Peter, to whom the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing, absolved him. Then, rejoicing and commending him to their prayers, they sent him back to the siege of the town.

From there, grateful for the divine mercy by which, through Saint Adalard, they had obtained the count’s favor, they offered immense praises to the most high God, whose ear—upon which they had knocked with their prayers—had heard the preparation of their hearts.

### CHAPTER IV. How the Countess Wished to Keep Him

6. Thus, rejoicing that the labor of their journey had not been in vain, they set out with the saint to return home. But some distressing trouble intervened, so that greater joy might follow. For it happened that they reached the town called Insula (l’Isle) and carried the holy man of God [Col. 1075B] into the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, which was situated there.

In those days Countess Adela, whom we mentioned above, was staying in the same fortress, while the count—her son—was occupied in besieging the aforementioned town of Schelmas. When she heard that the holy confessor of God had arrived, she rejoiced greatly that an opportunity to retain him had been offered to her.

Accordingly, she summoned the monks and said among other things:

> “Know, my lords, that Saint Adalard is related to me by common kinship and is close to me; therefore, so that he may prepare for me the grace of honor in heaven, I wish to exalt his honor on earth. It is therefore my intention to retain him in this land, since here I shall be better able to carry out what I desire.

> “Either I shall have a new church built for him and endow it with immense resources, appointing monks or clerics to serve the saint; or I shall have him carried to the monastery of Blandinium, situated in the fortress of Ghent in honor of the holy apostle Peter, [Col. 1075C] where I shall see that honor is shown to him above all the saints who are there.

> “I therefore forbid you to move him from the church of Saint Stephen. Return to your own place; or, if you prefer, remain here with him.”

Finally, she ordered the doors to be locked and the roads and exits to be watched by guards, lest the saint be carried away secretly in the silence of night.

### CHAPTER V. How the Holy Relics Were Carried Away Through the Midst of the Watchmen

7. What were the monks to do? Being in a foreign land and deprived of the help of their own people, they could not oppose the countess’s power by using any violence against her in carrying away the saint. They immediately returned to Saint Adalard and, finding themselves beyond hope, deliberated what they ought rather to do.

As they sought counsel concerning the matter, they spoke to one another in lamentation:

> “What shall we do? Where shall we turn? Returning to our own people without Saint Adalard [Col. 1075D] is of no use to us, for perhaps they will drive us away or—even worse—bury us under stones. Indeed, disgrace and dishonor prevent us from returning, because if we do not return, they will attribute so great a loss to our consent and our schemes.

> “Yet although we might obtain their favor without presenting the saint, the removal of our father will bring desolation upon our mother church. For our mother, who has cherished us like sons in her bosom, will be left like a shelter in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber field.”

Thus their little boat was first tossed upon the sea; and because Christ was asleep within them, they began to sink in their doubt. But when they cried out, “Lord, save us; we are perishing,” the Lord immediately arose and commanded the winds and the waves.

8. While they were taking counsel, a plan inspired from heaven came to them: in the silence of the dead of night, they should remove the relics of the holy confessor from the bier where they had been exposed, [Col. 1076A] and, using them as the means of escape, provide for themselves and their companions.

The Savior himself is read to have done this and to have warned his followers to do likewise: “When they persecute you in one city,” he said, “flee into another,” though we may understand this figuratively.

Therefore, while everyone throughout the village was overcome by sleep, the monks denied rest to their eyes, seeking an opportunity to bring to completion what was in their minds. At midnight they approached the silver shrine in which the precious treasure was enclosed and exposed it with bold—or, rather, faithful—hands.

They then wrapped it, more precious than gold and topaz and surpassing by its fragrance the scent of every spice, first in a clean cloth and afterward in a deerskin. They entrusted its transport to one of them, namely Lord Everard, who appeared more skillful for this task.

While the others remained with the shrine of the saint, he was deeply anxious in mind over the treasure entrusted to him, wondering how he might [Col. 1076B] leave the city because of the watchmen’s guards. While he was wholly occupied with this concern, the morning hour dawned, when, with evening expelled, grief yields to joy through Christ’s resurrection.

Then Christ, who is the true Sun of justice, driving away the darkness of error and sadness, showed him the path of salvation and joy. For at that very hour a certain monk presented himself to him, as though sent by the Lord. The archbishop of the city of Reims had sent this monk to the count on his own business.

Joined by this man who was carrying the holy relics, Everard passed through the midst of the watchmen’s ranks and went out through the open gates. By God’s providence—through the merit, namely, of Saint Adalard—he left behind the guards whose watch had been rendered futile.

9. A miracle was surely renewed in this deed, like the one that occurred at the tomb of the risen Christ, if we dare to compare the power of the soldier with the glory of the king. Yet we do not diminish the king’s glory when we proclaim the soldier’s power, because the soldier’s power is the king’s glory.

A guard of soldiers had been placed at Christ’s [Col. 1076C] tomb so that he would not be stolen by his disciples; likewise, the diligence of watchmen had been assigned to the gates and exits of the roads so that the body of Saint Adalard might not be carried away secretly by his monks.

At dawn Christ rose and rendered useless the soldiers guarding the sealed tomb; likewise, at daybreak Saint Adalard, going out, eluded the watchmen observing the gates and exits of the roads. When Christ rose, the soldiers became as if dead from fear; after Saint Adalard had been carried away, the guards were rendered senseless by overwhelming astonishment.

Thus the body of the holy confessor was brought back to Corbie and received by the monks amid great rejoicing of clergy and people. It was honorably restored to the church treasury, as its dignity required, and by his presence it adorned the church that his absence had first rendered dark.

The brothers then offered immense praises with devotion of heart for this divine goodness. They considered it insignificant if the shrine should be lost [Col. 1076D], since the restoration of the precious treasure had made them blessed and rich. The former loss could be repaired; if they had lost him, the loss would have been irreparable.

But the one who willed to restore the treasure of the body also deigned to send back its vessel, so that just as the saint’s merit had been revealed in the carrying away of his body, it might also be revealed in the restoration of the vessel.

### CHAPTER VI. The Return of the Shrine, and How a Lame Man Was Healed at Its Presentation

10. Meanwhile, when rumor had flown and the countess had been informed that Saint Adalard had been carried away by the monks in this manner, she was displeased that she had been so deceived. Yet, understanding that this was the will of God and that she could no longer stretch out her arms against the current, she granted them leave to return home with the shrine of the holy confessor.

Thus, as though they had come out of Egypt, where they had been detained almost as captives, and as though a cloud of heavenly protection sheltered them from being burned by the sun of tribulation, they arrived, [Col. 1077A] led by our new Moses, in the land of peace and security.

11. When they had already drawn near to Corbie, they sent messengers ahead to inform their brothers that they should come quickly to meet the shrine of Saint Adalard with the arm of the same confessor.

Immediately new joy was added to their still-fresh joy. Trumpets were sounded; the church was adorned with carpets and hangings; it was also illuminated with many lights. Finally, when the people had gathered, a festive procession began, and they went out to meet the shrine with the arm of Saint Adalard preceded by candles and crosses.

Then, like the children of Israel receiving the ark of the Lord brought back from the Philistines and returning it to the tabernacle of God, they went before it singing with David “with the voice of rejoicing and confession,” while various kinds of musical instruments sounded all around to increase the joy.

12. Now a certain lame man was lying at the gate of the temple. Both his feet were so contracted that the soles [Col. 1077B] of his feet—an astonishing sight—were bent backward against his buttocks.

He had come there, crawling as far as he could on his hands and knees, not only to ask alms from those entering but also to beg Saint Adalard to attend to his pains. When he saw the saint’s bier being carried in at the head of the long procession, he began, as far as his illness permitted, to cry out for the saint to have mercy on him.

But Saint Adalard, in the manner of blessed Peter, did not give him gold or silver; rather, by the grace of God, he granted him something better. For, wondrously, you might immediately see the previously contracted sinews extended, the skin torn open, blood flowing, and his feet and legs returning to their natural position. The man, however, was exhausted by his extreme anguish, so that he almost seemed to be failing.

At last, standing upright on his own feet, and no longer needing anyone’s assistance, he approached the saint’s bier.

O gift of God worthy of praise! O merit of the saint worthy of proclamation! The bodily presence of the saint was absent, yet [Col. 1077C] the Lord displayed such great things in the vessel of his body. But he could display this in the vessel of his body who had been able to heal the sick through the shadow of Saint Peter’s body.

Then the man who had been healed, following and carrying the bier, gave thanks to the Lord, imitating [Col. 1078A] that Gospel leper who returned and gave praise to God.

With such joy that the sons had been received into the bosom of their mother church, they brought forth from the treasury of their conscience a sacrifice of hope and faith, while the fervor of charity had kindled an altar in their hearts; and before the altar of the divine Majesty they sang the hymn, “We praise you, God” (*Te Deum laudamus*).

### CHAPTER VII. The Restoration of the Holy Relics to the Shrine

13. Finally, having ascended the steps of the pulpit—having climbed from the valley of weeping by the steps of the virtues to the mountain of rejoicing—they descended to the lowly people lying below, who were unable to climb to higher things, by offering them a life-giving sermon suited to the event and the present time.

They did not omit, for the confirmation of their sermon, what had happened to them on the journey: how great the Lord’s grace had been with them in everything, and by how many miracles he had declared to them the beloved confessor [Col. 1078B].

And so that none of them might remain uncertain that Saint Adalard had been brought back, they had his relics brought from the sacristy, where they had previously been placed. They lifted them up in the sight of the assembled people and displayed them for all present to see, as was right to believe, brighter than ancient ivory and pleasing to behold because of their rarity.

After every cloud of doubt had been removed from them by the presence of the saint, they honorably restored him to the same shrine, which had shortly before been brought back with rejoicing.

14. When this had properly been completed, they placed Saint Adalard beside Saint Gentianus, blooming in the house of God like the rose of martyrdom, while he himself flowered before God like the lily of chastity.

Happy the hall supported by such columns! Happy the church illuminated by such lamps! To say nothing of the others whose presence makes the Church itself flourish, it is protected by these guardians against blasts of wind and lightning storms. Because these illuminate it, [Col. 1078C] the dark shadows of darkness and the clouds of sorrow are driven away from it.

Let us therefore honor them; let us venerate them on earth, so that they may deign to remember us in heaven.

---

## CHARTER OF SAINT GERALD, ABBOT

### Concerning Prayers to Be Made for the Brothers of His Congregation and for Others United with Him

*(Around the year 1091.)*

*(Dom Martène,* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, *vol. I, col. 255, from the cartulary or Necrology of Sylva Major.)*

[Col. 1077D] Let all know, both those present and those who will come after, that I, Gerald, abbot—although unworthy—of Saint Mary of Sylva Major, caring for the welfare of the living and the dead, have established by the common counsel of the entire congregation, and have ordered to be committed to writing so that it may remain forever, that if anyone of our congregation departs from this world and is buried with us, bread and wine shall be given to the poor on his behalf for a year, and for thirty days Masses and vigils for the dead shall be celebrated communally by all.

[Col. 1078D] The first seven Masses and vigils, however, shall be performed solemnly, with all the bells rung. Each priest shall recite seven Masses; he who is not a priest shall recite three psalters; he who has not yet reached the psalter shall sing seven psalms daily for thirty days; he who does not know them shall say “Have mercy” (*Miserere*) seven times daily; and he who knows neither this shall likewise say “Our Father” (*Pater noster*) seven times.

If another person should die within two days, or four, or even more, when both are placed together, whatever is diminished for the one at the beginning [Col. 1079A] shall be restored when the office for the other has been completed.

The entire congregation shall sing psalms prostrate before the altar after chapter for the first seven days. If someone dies in a cell far from the monastery, everything shall be performed for him that is performed for one present, except that bread and wine shall be assigned as alms for a year in the cell where he died, as has already been said.

As for the congregations that have entered into fellowship with us or will enter into it, if anyone dies and a messenger reaches us, we shall perform seven Masses and as many vigils communally. The first three vigils shall be with nine lessons, all the bells being rung; the remaining four with three lessons.

On the very day the messenger arrives, however, after [Col. 1079B] chapter, with the bells sounding, the psalm “My words” (*Verba mea*) shall be sung for him; the priest shall say a Mass; the others shall recite one psalter; whoever does not know the psalter shall recite seven psalms; whoever does not know seven psalms shall say “Have mercy” seven times; and whoever knows neither shall say “Our Father” seven times.

The congregations in our fellowship are these: the congregation of Saint Sicarius of Branstosma, of Saint Florentius of Saumur, and of Saint Faith of Conques.

This is the indissoluble covenant of the monasteries of Major Monastery and Sylva Major: namely, that for the brothers of both monasteries, both chapters and every spiritual and bodily benefaction shall be common to all on both sides, and that fellowship shall exist in every respect.

For the deceased brothers, once each year [Col. 1079C] we celebrate a full vigil and a festive Mass; and upon receiving the notice, immediately after chapter, we shall perform “My words,” with its appendices, for the absolution of the brothers whose names have been read, with the bells rung.

Let it be known to all, present and future, that Lord Odo, abbot of Saint John of Angers, came to the chapter of Saint Mary of Saint-Maur. By the counsel of Lord Gerald the abbot and of all the brothers, they mutually established the following for deceased brothers: on the very day when his notice should arrive, a most complete vigil should be celebrated with all the bells rung; on the following day, likewise, a most complete Mass; and likewise for seven days—but without ringing the bells, the psalm “My words” [Col. 1080A] after chapter. On that day a provision of bread and wine shall be given for him.

For the abbots of both congregations they established this same practice forever, as is done for a brother of the same place. The same is done for the congregation of Saint Benedict of Nantilly.

The same is observed for the congregation of Luçon; and for its abbots a thirty-day office is performed. Likewise for the canons of Saint Mary of Pamplona, Saint Michael of Eremo, Saint Maurinus of Agen, and the canons of Saint Romanus of Blaye.

Similarly, we act for the monks of Saint Mary of Dol, Saint Vincent of Laon, and Saint Peter’s church of Ferrières. For the abbots, a thirty-day office shall be completed, both in Masses and in vigils, and their names shall be written in the martyrology, so that an anniversary commemoration may always be made for them.

Likewise for Holy Cross [Col. 1080B] of Quimperlé and Saint Savior of Carrof; but more is done for those of Carrof: for thirty days, at every hour, the psalm “With my voice” (*Voce mea*) shall be said with the familiar psalms, and after matins, “My words.”

Similarly, we act for the congregation of Saint Peter of Maillezais. For the abbots of Maillezais, a provision shall be given for thirty days, and all the brothers of that place shall be written in our martyrology.

For the monks of Saint Paul of Cormery, upon receiving the notice, after chapter, with the bells sounding, we perform the absolution; for seven days, seven complete offices with as many Masses; and for thirty days, “My words” and “With my voice.”

Similarly, we act for the congregation of Userche, for the brothers of the monastery of Generensis, and for the monks of Saint Laumer of Blois. On the day when the notice has been read, [Col. 1080C] a provision of bread and wine shall be given.

Likewise for Saint Peter of Chartres, Saint Mary of Guistre, and Saint Stephen of Beania; for the clerics of Saint Martin of Ruricourt, three vigils and three Masses; and on the first day, with the bells rung, we do the same for the sisters of Saint Mary of Soissons.

Similarly, we act for the monks of Saint Peter of Solignac and for the monks of Saint Martin in the Fields: after chapter, absolution, one complete vigil, and one Mass.

For the congregation of the monastery of Exmes, seven Masses with vigils, and a provision on the very day when the notice is read in chapter. The same is done for the canons of Saint Stephen of Agen.

## Around the Year of Our Lord 1080  
### Folcard, Monk of the Monastery of Sithiu near Arras

[Col. 1083]

### Historical Notice

*(Cave,* Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers, *p. 531.)*

Folcard, a monk of the monastery of Sithiu near Arras, flourished in the year 1060 and lived for a long time thereafter. For a man of the age in which he lived, he was not unlearned. He was very familiar with William, king of the English, whom we call the Conqueror. After conquering England, William appointed him provost of Torneia, where for nearly sixteen years he served in the place of an abbot.

He remained for a long time in England, until disputes arose between him and the bishop of Lincoln, whereupon he withdrew to his monastery of Sithiu. He first wrote in abbreviated form, and afterward revised and expanded, two books *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Bertin, Abbot of Sithiu*, which he dedicated to his abbot Bovinus.

Mabillon published these from manuscripts of Bertin and Vedast in *The Benedictine Centuries*, III, part I, p. 104. He also appended Book II of the *Miracles*, written by an anonymous author around the beginning of the tenth century.

Bale, indeed, lists a certain Folcard of Canterbury, a monk of the monastery of Canterbury and a most learned man, illustrious in the year 1060. We think that he was the same as our Folcard. Bale reports that, at the command of Aldred, archbishop of York and his great Maecenas, this Folcard wrote two books *On the Life and Miracles of John, Archbishop of York*, dedicated to Aldred, as well as certain other works.

Certainly, Orderic Vitalis, a writer of nearly the same period, testifies that our Folcard composed gracefully the histories of Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and of other English saints. He mentions him in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, under the year 1118, where he provides further information about Folcard.

The life of John, archbishop of York, written by Folcard, is also mentioned by the anonymous author of *The Life of Saint John* in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I. Like Bale, this author calls Folcard a Canterbury monk—[the printed text reads uncertainly here, “*montu chum*,” apparently for *monachum*]—not, as Mabillon incorrectly has it, the archbishop of Canterbury.

Mabillon published the life itself in *The Benedictine Centuries*, III, part I, p. 433. He was unable, however, to find the *Book of Miracles*, which Bale also mentions.

Mabillon will teach you more about the other writers of Bertin’s life—an earlier anonymous author; Folquin, abbot of Lobbes; the anonymous compiler of the *Acts of Saints Audomar, Folquin the Bishop, Winnoc, and Salvin*; and finally Simon, abbot of Sithiu, who was distinguished at the end of the twelfth century—in the preliminary observations cited above, p. 104.

---

## Life of Saint Bertin, Abbot of Sithiu in the Morini  
### By Folcard

*(In Mabillon,* Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, *third century, part II, p. 104.)*

### Preliminary Observations

[Col. 1083A] 1. Many people have committed to writing the deeds of Saint Bertin, abbot. I find six works altogether on this subject.

The first is by a certain anonymous author, whom the others afterward followed. The second is by Folquin, abbot of Lobbes, who dedicated the *Acts of Saints Audomar, Bertin, Folquin the Bishop, Winnoc, and Silvin* to Walter, the Bertinian abbot who died in the year 996.

The third and fourth have Folcard, a monk of the monastery of Sithiu, as their author. The fifth and sixth were composed in verse: one by an anonymous author, the other by Simon, as they think, abbot of Sithiu toward the end of the twelfth century, although John Iperius, when discussing Abbot Simon, does not, if I am not mistaken, mention this matter.

We received the last four works from the monastery of Sithiu through the kindness both of the most religious lord Dom John Le Pecqueur, subprior, and of the most courteous lord Gerard du Val, a monk of the monastery. Here we present only Folcard, intending to say a little about the other authors.

2. The very ancient anonymous author of Bertin’s life is praised by the author of the book *On the Deeds of Saint Winnoc, Abbot*, by Folcard, and by others.

Folquin is frequently cited by Jacques Malbrancus, especially in the scholia to chapter 1 of Book III of *On the Morini*. There he says that Folquin, in the *Acts of Saints Audomar, Bertin*, and others, passed over many things that can be found in other authors because he wished to insert only those matters that could be adapted to the readings of the Breviary.

They think this Folquin was the deacon and Bertinian monk who gathered into one collection the diplomas of princes and kings and other documents, and adapted the years of the kings to the years of the Lord’s Incarnation. In this matter he often deviated from the true calculation.

The anonymous work was read and compared with the work of Folcard presented below by Dom de With, a Bertinian monk who died thirty years ago. We shall place his observations, communicated by Dom Gerard du Val, in the marginal space.

### 3. Folcard, a monk of Bertin, first wrote a Life of Saint Bertin in abbreviated form, which he later promised to expand. Thus he writes in the dedicatory letter to his earlier work:

> “To his lord Bovo, his most desired Father, Folcard—one who ought to be inserted into no page, which is the highest distinction before the supreme Pontiff—sends greetings.
>
> Perhaps, my Father, you rightly grow more frequently angry with your native son, nourished once by your milk and brought up on your provisions, because I occupy only the ground, like that useless fig tree, and produce none of the instruction that you once planted in me when I was a boy. I admit that it would be right for what you planted to put forth some kind of shoot, even if not worthy; but, excellent Father, my strength fails amid my desire, and I am compelled to hide ignobly among private persons. Hence I shall rightly concede that you have often been angry at my inactivity, and I shall gladly acknowledge this as the greatest favor you have bestowed upon me.
>
> Therefore I have endeavored, at your fatherly command, to improve what I have hitherto done with insufficient judgment. While reflecting on this, there came to mind the Life of our most blessed Father Bertin, which I have begun to rewrite, impelled by several considerations. If this work proves appropriate, your scales of judgment will test it.
>
> For when I intended to say or do something good, I preferred to take my beginning from no one but you, who daily devote yourself to so many advantages for us all. In addition, I ought to satisfy the devout petition of certain brothers, who, although they seem to ask for something small, are recognized by their very request to be commanding it.
>
> Yet, I admit, they do not ask—as I believe, or as I understand them—to have this work brought into public view while the old one is set aside or neglected. It would be exceedingly absurd for me to undertake anything of that sort among so many and such men—as I may say, cloud-dwellers. But if you so command, let this account of my smallness be preserved together with the old one, in accordance with what is said about wooden and earthen vessels being kept with golden ones in the temple of the Lord.”

Another Prologue follows, beginning: “The mercy of the divine Trinity…,” which Prologue differs in the Cistercian copy. The Life itself begins as follows:

> “The blessed boy Bertin is said to have been born of a noble line of ancestors in the territory of Constance,” etc.

He finally concludes the book in this way:

> “Let these few statements from among many suffice. We have brought them to an end in a concise account, but we intend to clarify them by arranging them in a fuller sequence of text.”

You see that a longer work is promised here. Later he also promises to write a book on the miracles of Saint Bertin, in these words:

> “Therefore, accommodating ourselves to the satisfaction of the reader, as though we had already refreshed ourselves with the Life of our most renowned Father, we shall next unfold in writing the account of the signs that the Lord God of hosts performed through him.”

He fulfilled both promises by publishing books On the Life and On the Miracles of Saint Bertin, which we now print for the first time. Although the handwritten books do not bear the author’s name, we nevertheless infer it from the author’s age, which he indicates in Book I of the Miracles, chapter 11. The second book On the Miracles, however, seems from its beginning to have an older author; Folcard appears to have added the rest.

Orderic Vitalis, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, under the year 1108, praises “Fulcard, a monk of Saint Bertin of Sithiu, strong in extensive learning. After William, king of the English, had conquered England, he appointed him provost of Thorney, where Fulcard acted as abbot’s deputy for nearly sixteen years without receiving the abbot’s blessing. He was,” Orderic says, “affable, cheerful, and charitable, and highly skilled in grammar and music. Accordingly, he left in England precious monuments of his learning for future generations. For he composed many memorable poems, and he skillfully fashioned delightful stories for singing about Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and other saints whose lineage came from Britain. Later, when certain disputes arose between him and the bishop of Lincoln, he withdrew”—namely, to the monastery of Sithiu, where he undertook to embellish the Life of Saint Bertin.

### 4. Bovo, abbot of Bertin, to whom Folcard dedicated his first work, was responsible for the elevation of the body of Saint Bertin, which Folquin, bishop of the Morini, had secretly concealed because of the attacks of the Northmen. Bovo committed an account of this event to writing; we publish it, extracted from manuscript copies, after Folcard, who abridged the same history in Book II of the *Miracles*.

Bovo governed the monastery of Sithiu from 1043 to 1065, as we learn from John Iperius’s *Bertinian Chronicle*, chapter 37. Iperius also included the deeds of Saint Bertin in his *Chronicle*, chapter 1.

### 5. Of the two poets, the Anonymous author and Simon, there is nothing for us to record. It did not seem worthwhile to commit their works to print. Simon governed the monastery of Bertin from 1176 to 1187, when he resigned the dignity of abbot, afflicted by quartan fever and other ailments; he survived for four years thereafter. See John Iperius’s *Chronicle*, chapter 103.

Simon’s poem on Saint Bertin begins as follows:

> I, your son and brother by right, O pious mother,  
> let us, people of Sithiu, celebrate you with boundless praise.  
> Since I deem one greeting insufficient for you,  
> you may think that I bring you a thousand greetings together with the Father.  
> Therefore, gracious Father, I pray, favour Simon [and] Leo (*Leoni*; the sense is uncertain),  
> for I have now begun to write  
> what I conceived long ago: the illustrious festal deeds of our Father,  
> in praise of God.

### 6. The authentic Martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and the addition of Florus to Bede celebrate the memory of Saint Bertin.

“On the Nones of September,” says Usuard, “in the territory of Thérouanne, Saint Bertin, abbot.”

Ado writes on the same day:

> “The feast of Saint Bertin, abbot, a man of great holiness and innocence.”

Florus writes:

> “The burial of Saint Bertin, confessor and monk, who, wise in divine matters and simple in the face of evils, shone with divine virtues.”

Moreover, the concealment of Saint Bertin’s body by Folquin in the ninth century is entered in ancient Calendars under the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. Its elevation, celebrated in the eleventh century by Guido, archbishop of Reims, is recorded under the seventh day before the Nones of May. Finally, its translation into a more precious shrine, carried out in the thirteenth century by Peter, bishop of the Morini, is recorded under the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. We shall discuss these events below in their proper places.

### 7. Whether Bertin was the first abbot of the monastery of Sithiu may reasonably be doubted. The author of the *Life of Saint Audomarus, bishop of Thérouanne*, published in the second Benedictine century, assigns the first place to Mummolinus and the second to Bertin.

John Iperius completely removes Mummolinus from the catalogue of the abbots of Sithiu. The Sammarthani, in *Gallia Christiana*, place him after Bertin, but certainly without justification. For Mummolinus succeeded Saint Eligius in the see of Noyon in the year 669 and presided over it for twenty-six years, as the author of the *Life of Saint Audomarus* testifies; consequently, he ceased to live long before Saint Bertin.

It is likely that Mummolinus had been abbot for fourteen years before entering the episcopal office, at the Old Monastery, which has retained his name to the present day, and that he supervised the construction of the new monastery of Sithiu. He did not, however, govern the monks there, unless perhaps for a short time, since he was taken to the episcopate when the monastery had scarcely been completed. Bertin, on the other hand, soon put the finishing hand to the building and was placed over the monastic community.

### 8. The monastery of Sithiu, or Sithien, began to be built around the year 660 in the territory of Thérouanne. From its earliest foundation it was very extensive, and to this day it is celebrated under the name of Saint Bertin. It is enclosed within the walls of Saint-Omer, a city that arose from the monastery’s renown and was endowed with an episcopal see a hundred years ago, after Thérouanne was destroyed.

Almost from the beginnings of the monastery, there were two communities of monks there. One was in the basilica of Saint Peter and consisted of one hundred and fifty monks. The other was in the church of Saint Mary, built on the site of the cemetery, and had forty religious men. Fridogisus, a secular abbot, turned these into secular canons. Eventually an episcopal see was established in this church of Saint Mary, while the community of monks continued in the other.

As time passed, women religious were also admitted there, as in many other places; they were called “conversae” and were expelled by Cardinal Romanus, deacon of Saint Angelo, during the pontificate of Gregory IX. “At that time,” says Iperius, chapter 46, part XX,

> “there were in this monastery nuns who were called conversae. They lived under a religious habit, though not under a regular profession, between the two gates of the monastery, near the church of Saint Martin. They lived on the monastery’s alms, served the poor in the hospital, and, when necessary, sewed and washed the sacred vestments and church ornaments. Since women were not permitted to enter the monks’ monastery, they received our mothers, sisters, and female relatives when they came to visit us.”

### 9. To understand what is said about the various basilicas of the principal monastery, it is useful to append here Iperius’s words from chapter 3:

> “It should be noted that this church was successively called by different names at different times. At first it was called Sithiu, after the name of the village or place called Sithiu. Blessed Bertin founded this church in honor of the blessed apostle Peter, who still remains its Father and patron.
>
> “Then, when Blessed Bertin had been added to the number of the saints, because he had been our first founder, the place was named after him: the monastery of Saint Bertin of Sithiu. To compensate the name, a church was built for Blessed Peter on the western side of the temple, toward the north; from it the gate there is still called Saint Peter’s Gate.
>
> “A church was built for Saint Martin beside what is now the parish church of Saint Martin on the island. Between these two churches of Saints Peter and Martin, a hospital for the poor, or house of alms, was built. There was also an open way by which access was available from one church to the other and from the hospital to both.
>
> “Finally, after the churches of the blessed apostle Peter and of Bertin had been consumed by an accidental fire, in the time of Lord Roderic, abbot—who began to preside in the year 1021—it was arranged, and remains so to this day, that the high altar of our church, indeed the entire church itself, should always be consecrated in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of the blessed confessor of Christ, Bertin. The second altar, at which the morning Mass is customarily celebrated, is always assigned and consecrated in honor of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours.”

Thus far Iperius.

### 10. This monastery flourished in such devotion and observance of the holy Rule through the many changing vicissitudes of the human condition “that the Church now solemnizes twenty-two holy monks of that church,” says Iperius in his Prologue.

Locrius numbers twenty-five in his *Belgian Chronicle*: Bertin, abbot and founder of the monastery; Ebertramnus, abbot of Vermand; Count Walbert and his son, the younger Bertin; Mummolenus, bishop of Noyon; Winnoc, abbot of Wormhout, together with his companions Quadanocus, Ingenocus, and Madocus; Erkenbodus, the fourth abbot of Sithiu in the eighth century; Humfrid, formerly a monk of Prüm and abbot of Bertin; Fulco, archbishop of Reims and likewise abbot; Wocard, Winebald, Ragenard, and Gerwald, monk-martyrs of the ninth century; Grimbald, abbot of Winchester, together with his companions John and Asser, and Gerard, abbot of the tenth century; Lambert, Simon, and Leo, abbots of Sithiu, together with the monks Joscione and Bernard, in the twelfth century.

### 11. Many others also emerged from this same monastery and were raised to episcopal rank. Men of distinguished nobility likewise renounced the splendor and dignities of the world there.

“Guntbert,” says Iperius, chapter 11, part III, “born of a noble family, with Gorbert as his father and Ebertruda as his mother”; “Count Honrocus, father of Abbot Adalard,” chapter 13, part III; “Zoppo, deputy of King Charles the Bald,” chapter 15, part I; “Megenfridus, a noble boy, offered by his father Ruodwaldus,” chapter 16; and others.

To these should be added Childeric, the last king of the Merovingian line, “tonsured in the monastery of Sithiu,” and William, count of Flanders, who, when death was near, put on the religious habit and was buried in the monastery of Sithiu, as Orderic Vitalis testifies in *History*, Book XII, where he reports William’s epitaph under the year 1127.

### 12. Moreover, fourteen worthy monasteries took their origin from this abbey—or, to use the words of Iperius’s Prologue, “were derived from it”—so that the Church of Sithiu “held the first place in the region after the cathedral church of the Morini.”

Concerning the monasteries of Wormhout, Bergues, Alciacum, Hunulfricurt, and the others that proceeded from the seedbed of Sithiu, see the often-mentioned Iperius.

### 13. This place was not only a seedbed of saints but also a refuge and sanctuary for saints. Saints Anselm and Thomas, archbishops of Canterbury, withdrew there.

Monks from Canterbury, driven out by kings, were also admitted there more than once: first, out of hatred for Saint Thomas, by Henry IV; and later, in the year 1207, by King John. Iperius discusses the former in chapter 44, part II, and the latter in chapter 46, part XII, where he writes:

> “When they arrived, the lord abbot and the convent went out to meet them in procession with a cross, candles, and thuribles, proceeding as far as the church of Saint Dionysius. They brought them from there into the monastery. There were seventy monks and as many as one hundred attendants. They all remained together with us here for twelve days, until pairs or groups of three had been sent by their prior to the surrounding abbeys. The prior himself remained with us, together with sixteen monks, for more than a year,” etc.

A truly outstanding example of Christian charity and religious hospitality!

## PROLOGUE OF THE AUTHOR

*(From an older anonymous author.)*

### 1.

Abundant thanks and praises must diligently be rendered to the almighty Lord, giver of good gifts, who, existing as the creator and governor of all visible and invisible creatures, sent his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, into the world to teach and redeem every nation; and the rest, as in the *Life of Saint Audomarus* below.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

### Chapter I. In what region Blessed Bertin was born, and how he became a monk in childhood

### 2.

The blessed boy Bertin is said to have been born from a noble line of ancestors in the territory of Constance, beneath whose walls the Rhine flows and becomes almost stagnant for three miles in the lake called Apotamus. From there the city looks nearby toward Bavaria, on the other side toward Burgundy, and to the south toward the Alpine peaks.

This child, therefore, a very dearly loved pledge to his parents, was carefully raised in infancy, destined to become so great in the Lord. Although God supported him with the dignity of earthly nobility for worldly distinction, from his very infancy the love of a greater service to Christ grew together with him.

As soon as he reached the appropriate age, he dedicated the beginnings of his childhood to God through evangelical perfection. He renounced his parents and homeland in order to follow the Lord; and, so that nothing might be lacking to the perfection of a servant of the Lord, he professed himself a monk in the monastery of Luxeuil under Father Eustace.

How rich that man’s life and instruction were in spiritual grace can be understood from the excellence of the flock over which he presided, especially now, when the more evident signs of holiness are apparent in those whom we know to intercede before the Lord for many lands through their merits.

The boy Bertin, young in age but mature in understanding, strove, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to imitate the tender life and conduct of these men. After the Holy Spirit had claimed him through the gifts of his grace, he placed him among such great Fathers so that he might be instructed by their examples. At last, strengthened in childhood by every aid of a more perfect life and endowed in adolescence with the inexhaustible vigor of heavenly desire, he advanced.

### Chapter II. How, while still a very young man, he came to Saint Audomarus

### 3.

When the Lord had decided to reveal his soldier more openly to the world, lest so great a lamp shining with such brilliance in concealment delay the spiritual benefit of so many mortals, Bertin set out with only two companions, Mummolinus and Ebertramnus, men of very great holiness. Joined to them as the third, he reached Gaul as a perfect worshiper of the Holy Trinity.

**[Note: The Cistercian copy reads as follows: “He reached the territory of the Morini, where at that time his countryman and, as is said, kinsman, the distinguished bishop of Christ Audomarus, was dispensing abundant streams of divine teachings.” John Iperius proves this kinship in chapter 1, parts I and V, where he asserts that Audomarus and Bertin descended from the family of Saint Arnulf. On this matter, if it is worth the effort, see Malbrancus, Book III, *On the Morini*, chapter 1.]**

When these holy men—Bertin, that is, and his companions—saw there a great harvest but few laborers, they began earnestly to spread the word of life far and wide throughout all Gaul. Many religious men joined them, and they were refreshed by these men from morning until evening with the nourishment of eternal life. Likewise, not a few nobles of the palace, temporarily setting aside their royal service, flocked to them and proposed their modest way of life as an example for their own upright conduct.

### 4.

At that time Lothair, son of King Louis, governed the unified kingdom of the Franks. When repeated reports of the outstanding conduct of Bertin and his companions had reached his ears through the accounts of his nobles, he immediately ordered them to appear before him.

When they had been brought before the king, the man of God Bertin and his companions were honorably received and, for a long time, retained with the greatest care within the royal palace. After a lengthy period, the aforesaid men approached Saint Audomarus, then bishop of Thérouanne, whose countryman and kinsman Saint Bertin was, so that they might accompany him in preaching and thereby deserve from God to become participants in equal glory in the eternal reward.

Saint Audomarus graciously received these servants of God and gave thanks to almighty God, who had sent him such assistants for preaching the Gospel. They were perfect in the Catholic faith and learned in ecclesiastical disciplines and divine Scripture. They therefore undertook the duty of their legation through continuous labor in preaching.

### Chapter III. The Donation of Adroald

### 5.

**[Note: From the text of the older Anonymous author.]**

Meanwhile a certain very noble man, exceedingly wealthy in possessions, named Adroaldus, who had no son, began to discuss with Blessed Audomarus and the aforesaid servants of God how he might make the Church heir to his possessions.

Blessed Audomarus, inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, urged him to bestow on Saint Bertin and his aforementioned companions whatever he could possess, so that, by building a monastery there in honor of Blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, they might gather together a considerable company of monks.

In the presence of Blessed Audomarus and all the nobles of the city of Thérouanne, Adroaldus fulfilled this with great joy of heart, giving the village belonging to his property called Sithiu, in the year 626 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

**[Note: Folquinus writes in the *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 2, that this occurred in the eleventh year of Louis, in the year of Christ 645; more correctly, in the year 648 or the following year, to which the eleventh year of Chlodoveus is assigned. A charter of this event, drawn up by Adroaldus, exists in Miraeus, chapter 3, *Donations*, and in John Iperius’s *Chronicle*, as we observed in the *Life of Saint Audomarus* under the year 657.]**

It occurred, moreover, in the eleventh year of the reign of Chlodoveus, son of Dagobert, on the eighth day before the Ides of September.

They therefore began to build a monastery in a certain territory of this village; that place is called the Old Monastery to this day.

### Chapter IV. Why the holy man of God sought a more suitable place

### 6.

**[Note: From the older Anonymous author.]**

Meanwhile, when Acharius, bishop of the city of Noyon, had died, the venerable Mummolinus was raised to the bishopric of that same city, and Ebertramnus was placed by Mummolinus over the monastery of Saint Quentin. Saint Bertin, however, remained for fourteen years in the place granted to him by the Lord.

**[Note: Mummolinus succeeded not Acharius but Saint Eligius in the see of Noyon, as has been noted in the *Life of Saint Audomarus*.]**

**[Note: The first author does not state the number of years. He adds the following: “To speak to those who do not know the situation of that place, it is situated on a low hill, with the river Agniona and marshy waters on one side, and on the other a forest extending above it for a long distance.” Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, compelled to leave his native land, is said to have come to the Old Monastery, once the hermitage of the glorious confessor Bertin, where he remained hidden for three days; on the fourth day he withdrew to the abbey of Sithiu. See Iperius, chapter 44, part II. It is now the village of Saint-Mummolin, commonly called Saint-Momelin, one league from Saint-Omer.]**

Because that place was very small and not spacious enough to accommodate the construction of a large establishment, the holy man of God Bertin began, together with those gathered around him, to seek a more suitable place for building a monastery.

But as he turned over in his mind the saying of the Lord, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and committed himself wholeheartedly to the providence of God, who arranges all things, he immediately boarded a ship without pilot or oarsman on the broad lake beside which the aforementioned little monastery stood.

The ship was moved solely by God’s will. You could also see, through the ministry of angels, the vessel driven against the current of the rushing river until it came to rest at a suitable harbor. Then the venerable Bertin brought forth this verse from the Psalter, chanting it in order:

> “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it” (Psalm 131:14).

Recognizing that the Lord had chosen that place for him, he left the ship without delay and began to build a monastery called Sithiu in that same place, in the name of God and in honor of Saint Peter.

As religious men flocked there from every direction, within a short time he gathered a multitude of monks, namely one hundred and fifty.

**[Note: The Cistercian copy has two hundred brothers.]**

He lived many years with them in the service of God. As a shepherd, he kept watch with attentive care over the flock entrusted to him by the Lord, under the strict yoke of the sacred Rule, knowing what is written: “To whom more is entrusted, from him more is required” (Luke 12:48; Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 2).

By preaching the Lord’s and the apostles’ commandments to the blessed servants of God who lived under his care, and by his own strict conduct and religious actions each day, he offered a great example of right living, fulfilling what is written:

> “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father” (Matthew 5:16),

lest, in accordance with the apostolic command, he should preach to others and himself be found reprobate.

Nor, by the Lord’s providence, were the necessities of their life lacking. For relatives and every noble person devoted to Christ, instructed and admonished by him, bestowed on him many gifts of lands and estates, as will become clear below.

### Chapter V. The Donation of the Estate of Worinhoud

### 7.

**[Note: This chapter is absent from the ancient Anonymous author.]**

After the aforesaid donation of Adroaldus, by which he first offered himself in the beginnings of the construction of that place, a certain wealthy man named Heremarus gave to God and Saint Bertin an estate belonging to his property, called Worinhoud.

**[Note: It is called Worimholt in the *Life of Saint Winnoc* below, under the year 717.]**

That blessed man, not ungrateful for such gifts of divine generosity, consecrated whatever was bestowed on him by the faithful of God to heavenly purposes, truly concerned for their salvation. For on the aforesaid estate he sent Saint Winnoc, whom he had instructed from childhood in his discipline, together with his other fellow soldiers, and ordered them to build a cell and a church in honor of Saint Martin for the reception of the poor. The aforesaid men, united in the Lord, completed this through strenuous labor in a short time.

After establishing a small community of brothers, he placed over it his disciple Saint Winnoc, his rival in every exercise of holiness, because he had no doubt about Winnoc’s life and conduct. Bertin had raised him with himself from infancy under the school of the Lord’s monastery.

Thus Blessed Bertin became the founder and father of all the monasteries in the territory of Thérouanne, and he bore fruit for the advancement of the Church of Christ through so great a growth. Omitting for now all the details of the great care with which he provided everything necessary for the place of his own habitation, we shall relate them in the subsequent narrative.

### Chapter VI. How he acquired a cemetery

### 8.

After obtaining every convenience for the brothers of his place, he could not acquire a cemetery, since the site lay in a marsh. Concerning this matter he did not delay seeking the counsel and assistance of his beloved helper in all things, the bishop of God, Audomarus.

That illustrious bishop offered his customary service of charity. After sharing in the counsel and labor, he enclosed the cemetery with a ditch and consecrated it to the same monastery on the summit of the aforesaid hill. A basilica was built in its center in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God.

When it had been completed through their common work, he granted it entirely to Saint Bertin and his monks in the year 660 from the Lord’s Incarnation. He confirmed his donation by recording it in a charter of grant, in which he commended himself to the prayers of that blessed Father and of all the brothers serving God under his protection. He also requested that, after he had entered the way of all flesh, they bury his lifeless body in that same cemetery.

We have taken care to transcribe a copy of this charter here, just as we received it as having been made at that time by the aforesaid bishop of Christ, Audomarus.

### Copy of the Charter of Saint Audomarus Concerning the Cemetery

*(From the Chartulary of Folquinus, monk of Saint Bertin.—See Migne, *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVI, col. 1189.)*

### 9.

Therefore, when Lord Audomarus, bishop, had died, in the thirty-fifth year after the donation of the aforesaid cemetery and chapel in the village called Waurantis, situated nearly four miles from the monastery of Sithiu, his body was brought from there by Lord Bertin, in accordance with the request of that blessed man expressed in this charter. He was buried in the basilica mentioned above, before the altar of the holy Mother of God. From that time onward, the basilica itself was subject to Lord Bertin.

### 10.

The generous rewarder of good works, therefore, seeing his soldier Bertin’s tireless struggle against the devil’s persuasions—for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers” (Psalm 33:16)—and observing his great care for the sheep entrusted to him, glorified him with life-giving signs and miracles. With the Lord’s favor, we shall relate a few of these in the following account.

### Chapter VII. The Donation of Walbert

**[Note: Taken verbatim from the ancient Anonymous author.]**

### 11.

There was a certain noble and distinguished man, a count according to the vain dignity of this age, named Walbert. His wife was called Regentrudis.

Blessed Bertin was this Walbert’s confessor, and also his spiritual co-parent, according to the praiseworthy custom preserved among Christians for joining the bonds of fraternal charity.

**[Note: He is termed a *confessarius* (confessor); concerning this ministry or office, see the preface prefixed to this century.]**

Blessed Bertin often preached the divine word to both of them. Consequently, the pious Walbert frequently used to visit Blessed Bertin, both to hear divine commandments from the blessed man and, after receiving the body and blood of Christ, to be blessed in the customary manner by his sacred mouth.

One day, therefore, when the aforesaid Walbert came to the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, where Blessed Bertin had also buried Saint Audomarus, and had completed his prayer there, some necessity suddenly drawing him back, he neglected to visit Blessed Bertin and imprudently returned to his own home.

Then his disciple, named Dodo, informed Blessed Bertin, saying:

> “Most venerable Father, I am greatly surprised that your faithful friend in Christ, Walbert, traveling near us today, has insolently gone home without asking for your blessing.”

Then Saint Bertin, confessor of Christ, filled with the prophetic spirit, said to the disciple:

> “Before Walbert, my son, reaches his home, to which he now hastens, believing that he will soon arrive, he will deeply regret having left this place today without the gift of our blessing.”

The outcome of events confirmed the word of the blessed man, who had foreseen it. On that same day, after sunset, a messenger from Walbert quickly came riding to Blessed Bertin, according to his lord’s command. As soon as he reached the holy man’s presence, he fell at his feet and said to him in a trembling voice:

> “Lord, your kindly friend in Christ, Walbert, now placed on the boundary between life and death, begs you in God’s name to pray for him, according to the customary compassion of your charity, that through your glorious prayers before the eternal King he may receive relief from the deadly danger that has recently befallen him.
>
> “For after he had set out today, wishing to hurry home without your blessing, he was suddenly thrown from the horse on which he was riding swiftly in the middle of the road and fell carelessly upon stony ground. Many parts of his body were bruised, and his thigh, most blessed Father, was completely broken. He thinks that death is upon him unless, as he believes, divine mercy saves him through your holy prayers.
>
> “For he knows that this danger came upon him through his own negligence, because, without the protection of your blessing, some necessity drawing him back, he left this place today through the cunning of the crafty enemy.
>
> “Therefore, in God’s name, he begs you, asking pardon for this negligence, to send him, before he dies, a drink blessed by your holy mouth and signed by your sacred hands.”

Then the venerable old man, moved by the accident of his faithful friend, immediately ordered his disciple to draw wine from the wine vessel that had been placed in the sacristy, so that it might be sent as quickly as possible to the sick man.

**[Note: That is, from a vessel containing wine.]**

The young man replied gently to the holy abbot:

> “Most blessed Father, as I believe, it has been a full month or more since there was even one cup of wine in the vessel of which you speak.”

The holy confessor of Christ, full of perfect faith and charity, said to his disciple:

> “Go, my son, in God’s name, to the vessel of which you speak. Our Lord, to whom all things are possible and who is present in times of need—for ‘the Lord is near to all who call upon him’ (Psalm 145:18)—will, I believe, provide a healing drink for our sick friend.”

Then the young man obeyed the holy man’s command. Entering the aforesaid sacristy, he found the vessel of which he had just told the holy abbot—that there had not been even one cup of wine in it—now, by the grace of God’s generosity, full of excellent wine. Its marvelous fragrance had filled the aforesaid room.

Then Saint Bertin, confessor of Christ, gave immense thanks to almighty God and said to Walbert’s servant:

> “Take some of this wine with you and return quickly to your master.”

That same night the man, filled with immense joy, returned to his master. He told him the entire miracle that had occurred and gave him a healing drink from the aforesaid wine.

After he had drunk from that blessed beverage, he was made well at that very hour by the healing hand of God. He gave immense thanks to almighty God, the author of his salvation, and, filled with contrition of heart, gave to Blessed Bertin a large part of his inheritance—namely, the estate of Arkas and many other properties, as antiquity records—and permanently assigned them to the use of the brothers serving Christ at Sithiu.

Thus, little by little renouncing worldly possessions and yearning with every effort for heavenly things, and now desiring to become a monk, he relied on the encouragement and counsel of Saint Bertin and promised, with irrevocable devotion, to receive the religious habit at Luxeuil.

**[Note: For this reason some infer that this Walbert is none other than Saint Walbert, abbot of Luxeuil; we rejected this identification in his Eulogy, in the second century, under the year 664.]**

### Chapter VIII. The Donation of Hunulfricurt

**[Note: Absent from the ancient Anonymous author.]**
12. A certain illustrious man named Amalfridus handed over to Lord Bertin the monastery that he himself had built on his own estate, called Hunulfricurt, in the district of Cambrai, on the River Scheldt. There, too, his daughter, a noblewoman named Auriana, appears to have been abbess and ruler of the nuns, on the following condition: that during his lifetime he himself should hold it by precarious tenure; but after his death and that of his daughter Auriana, the aforementioned Abbot Bertin or his successors should have, hold, and possess it, and should have permission to appoint there whichever provost they wished. Thus also testifies the copy of that grant preserved among us to this day: it was executed in the year 677 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the sixth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] More correctly, Iperius: “Executed at Vermand, when February had eight days, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord, the most glorious King Theuderic,” that is, in the year of Christ 684. Iperius adds in chapter 1, part XIV: “Amalfridus caused it to be confirmed by a royal privilege, which begins as follows: ‘Whenever a rightful petition…,’ dated on the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth year of our reign, at the palace of Barisiacum.” Then, after Amalfridus and Auriana had died, the successors of Saint Bertin forbade the nuns there to succeed and established monks there instead. How it was alienated, and withdrew from this obedience of ours, our writings do not relate. See the Life of Saint Austreberta under the year 704.]

## CHAPTER IX. How the Lord performed many signs through him, although they are hidden from us

[Note: [Col. 1096D] The wording is taken from the ancient Anonymous.]

13. Moreover, the divine power performed wonders through the holy man, although he concealed some of them from a desire for secrecy, while at that time the negligence of those present concealed others. Yet beyond all miracles, his tireless labor in God’s service must be preferred, together with his ever-watchful care for the souls entrusted to him.

Throughout his life, therefore, he labored in preparing the place entrusted to him by God. Divine grace so assisted his work that, in his time, the monastery became equal to the ancient monasteries built with royal resources, both in the number of holy relics and in abundance of possessions.

Thus Saint Bertin, Christ’s confessor, after Adroald had granted the site at Sithiu, in the fifty-seventh year of his rule appointed as his successor a venerable monk of his own named Rigobert. He himself, living thereafter in seclusion for the remainder of his life, withdrew into divine contemplation.

He had also built an oratory while his beloved Audomar, bishop of God, was still living. Constructed on the eastern side of the church of Saint Peter, he had it dedicated by that same bishop in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God. There, spending most of the night in prayer, the tireless soldier of Christ completed his days with fasts.

The venerable Abbot Rigobert, diligently carrying out his turn of watch over the Lord’s flock, built, at the command of that Father, the monastery in honor of Blessed Martin within a short time and with great effort.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] That is, the church of Saint Martin, which is now a parish church. Likewise, below, “the monastery of Saint Peter” means the basilica; that basilica no longer exists.]

For he was profoundly devoted to this confessor of the Lord and served his memory and devotion to him with the greatest dedication.

## CHAPTER X. How the man of God was tempted by the devil in the form of a woman and visited by Saint Martin

14. Our elders relate that this same man of God, having been bled one Saturday, was tempted by an evil spirit in the guise of a girl of royal status, and at first did not perceive the tricks of so great an ambush.

But when he was about to leave, while the brothers were waiting for him to perform the service commanded by the Lord—which is customarily celebrated among monks every Saturday—and when she tried to detain him, speaking as though about some necessary matter concerning the monastery but in reality longing, if she could, to take the servant of God captive through shameful intercourse, the aforementioned bishop of God, Saint Martin, appeared to him. Addressing him sweetly as a brother and friend, he exposed the mockeries and deceits of the enemy lying in ambush in a woman’s guise. The young soldier of the Lord immediately drove her away from him by the sign of the cross. Then he rose, sought the brothers who were calling him to the service commanded by the Lord, and went to praise God for such great mercy.

Indeed, such joy over his holiness filled the heavenly beings that they not only deemed him worthy to have them as intercessors with God in heaven, but also stood ready to serve his salvation in person on earth, lest they lose in heaven a fellow heir of so great a reward and glory.

Therefore the pious Father, considering that it was altogether unsuitable for monks to associate in any way with the female sex, entirely excluded women, under anathema, from entering the approaches of that monastery.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] The use of this prohibition continued until the end of the thirteenth century, as is clear from Iperius, chapter 52, part IV. Compare Book II of the Miracles, chapter 12.]

In our own time this was observed by a certain religious woman: she had learned that women were not to go farther than the place established by the man of God, and she would not proceed beyond it. After her death, her body also observed the same boundary. For when they carried her, placed in a coffin, and reached the limit of the ancient boundary established by him, she was immediately fixed there by such a divinely imposed weight that she could not be carried farther, even though the assembled crowd exerted itself to bear her onward. Thus the old woman, who had honored the saint’s command throughout her life, could not allow her dead body to cross the boundary that her living soul had desired to observe.

## CHAPTER XI. How he entrusted his monastery to Erlefrid after Rigobert

[Note: [Col. 1098D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

15. After laboring for a few years, Rigobert obtained the indulgence of his pious master and withdrew himself into spiritual rest. By this change he showed himself to be a perfect disciple of so great a Father, instructed by his teaching and example.

That excellent Father appointed as his successor the abbot Erlefrid, whom he had nourished from childhood. Inferior to no other, Erlefrid did not degenerate from his father’s instruction.

## CHAPTER XII. The passing of Blessed Bertin

16. Desiring to repay the holy man with rewards worthy of his labors, Christ caused him, when he was full of days and perfect in merits, to pass over to him. The aforementioned Abbot Erlefrid and the whole company of monks buried him with the greatest honor, as was fitting for so great a Father, in their own monastery, which had been built in honor of Saint Martin, Christ’s bishop.

This athlete of God passed away on 9 September, in the year 698 from the Incarnation of the Word; he was 112 years old, in the fifteenth year of Childebert, king of the Franks, and in the fifty-ninth year since he had begun to build this place.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] The fifteenth year of King Childebert corresponds to the year of Christ 709, when fifty-nine years had already elapsed since the foundation of the monastery at Sithiu. Folquinus, however, assigns Bertin only fifty-four years of rule in the *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 21—perhaps through a scribal error.]

At that same time the venerable King Childebert, after reigning sixteen years, departed to the Lord, and his young son Dagobert reigned after him for five years. During his reign the aforementioned Abbot Erlefrid began to rebuild on a larger scale the basilica of Saint Martin over the tomb of Saint Bertin, constructing an altar of veneration at the head of the tomb. There the Lord performed many miracles through the merits of the blessed man, of which, with the Lord’s favor, we shall relate a very few from among their great number.

[Col. 1097]

# THE MIRACLES OF SAINT BERTIN

## BOOK ONE OF THE MIRACLES

Composed by the same author.

## CHAPTER I. The fisherman who was healed

[Note: [Col. 1098D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

[Col. 1097D]

Three men skilled in fishing, servants of that place, went aboard a boat on the Lord’s Day at night on the River Rhône, near the monastery of the blessed martyr Maurice. They cast out nets to catch fish.

[Col. 1098D] Then, during that same night, an extraordinary multitude entered their nets, so that during all the long years in which they had been accustomed to cast nets in that river, they had never seen fish of such size, nor had they ever caught such a multitude of fish in a single night.

Thereupon they joyfully sailed toward the harbor where they usually put in after fishing, but they were unable to move the aforementioned boat. Two of them were so crushed throughout their bodies that they lost the use of their feet and hands. The third, deprived of the use of his feet, also became deaf. Divine retribution had come upon them because they had violated the night of the Lord’s Resurrection.

The man who had lost both hearing and the ability to walk resolved to visit holy places for the sake of prayer, supporting himself on two staffs and relying on the assistance of companions, so that through the glorious merits of the saints he might deserve to recover the health of his body.

After some time, therefore, having traveled through many places, he came to the venerable tomb of the aforementioned confessor of Christ, Bertin, located in the monastery at Sithiu.

While the brothers living there were singing the nocturnal vigils on the night of the Lord’s Resurrection in the same church where the body of the blessed Bertin rests, the aforementioned man, seized by immense illness, was brought into the church by his companions.

After praying for a long time with tears and asking the Lord to restore his health through the merits of the holy Father Bertin, when the Gospel reading had been recited according to custom, he saw many lights shining around him. Gradually he felt his illness depart from him; his hearing returned, and the use of his feet was restored. Suddenly, by the gift of divine grace, he was made well in the presence of the brothers.

After the synaxis, he gave thanks to almighty God and Blessed Bertin, and joyfully and in good health walked back to his own home on his restored feet.

## CHAPTER II. A certain sacrilegious man

[Note: [Col. 1099D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

A certain man, unknown to us in origin but, as the outcome later proved, filled with an evil spirit, pretended to be a religious person. For three consecutive days he entered the church of our aforementioned Father Bertin as though to pray, repeatedly prostrating himself on the ground as if he were pouring out prayers with a contrite heart. But whenever he went out, he carefully examined the locks of the doors, while pretending to be doing something else in the presence of the guards.

Sometimes he bent down as though to retie loosened straps; at other times, pretending that his sleeves had fallen, he bent over at the same exit and picked them up. Having thus investigated everything he wished to know, he noted the hour at which, after Sext, the brothers went to the refectory to receive bread for their meal.

He then attacked the wood with a knife, pressing it between the joints of the doors where the two were fastened across one another. Since they were not secured elsewhere by an iron bolt, raising the end of the bar upward gave him an opening through which to enter.

Then that wretched but undeserving man revealed the result of his wickedness. After entering, he stole the silver vessels that hung beneath the crowns and lamps before and behind the altar.

But when he began looking for a way out through the door, he saw, astonishingly—as he later related—that a great number of terrifying enemies were standing before him. Tempted by the devil, he had indeed been permitted to seize the plunder in his greed, but he was not permitted to carry it away completely.

Thus, since the open doors offered him no means of returning, he turned back, took a path through the middle of the monastery, and made for an island situated within the marsh belonging to the monastery, intending to deposit there, with an acquaintance, what he had stolen from the sacred place.

Meanwhile, the guards of the church came out of the refectory with the brothers. When they saw that the sacred vessels were missing, the monks immediately assembled in a crowd. They were so overwhelmed that they could find neither what to say nor what to do nor where to turn; but they unanimously cried out that this had happened because of their sins.

The merciful Lord, through the merits of his confessor Saint Bertin, did not allow the spirits of those who continually served him to remain in danger for long.

The unfortunate thief, seeing on one side bands of enemies and on the other the obstacles of water and marsh—for, to explain the place to those who do not know it, the site is such that for a thousand paces and much farther there is no access except by boat, apart from a single western gate through which pedestrians, horsemen, and those driving carts ordinarily have free entry—began to make leaps as though over precipitous walls and roofs.

When those living there saw this, all doubt was removed. They cried out that this man was guilty, that he was the thief of the sacred treasure, and that this was why he was being driven about by a demon.
