After they had detained him, they questioned him by whatever means they could, asking what had happened to him and why he had become deranged. He immediately disclosed the truth of the whole affair.

What more need be said? Judgment prevailed against him, and he was sent to Nervium,

[Note: [Col. 1099D] Turnacum, Tournay, on the River Scheldt, on the boundary of Hainaut and Aptesia; it is the city of the Menapii, as Abbot Philip of Bonne-Espérance calls it in the *Life of Saint Amand, Bishop*. Julius Caesar also, in *The Gallic War*, Book II, chapter 4, Book III, and Book IV, chapter 38, associates the Menapii with the Morini. Ferrari’s opinion concerning the Menapii must therefore be corrected.]

to a notorious place, namely the fortress of the Menapii.

The unanimity of the aforesaid community felt compassion for him. They sent to the count of that place, and he was released. But since he was later found to have been entangled in many other crimes, he perhaps had only a very brief period for repentance: he survived for only a week.

[Col. 1100D] Oh, how brief is the time of the present life in comparison with eternity! Therefore we exhort all who have heard these things to abandon evil and pursue good.

## CHAPTER III. A certain fugitive named Benjamin

[Note: [Col. 1100D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

As many crowds of secular people were flocking to the often-mentioned monastery out of love for God and burning with desire for the monastic life, among them was one named Benjamin. Noble by worldly birth, he contributed a great deal from his own inheritance to the monastery and sought entry into the religious life. With a commendable simplicity, at least as he appeared outwardly, he devoted himself entirely to the monastery.

He was received and placed among the other brothers. But after not much time had passed, struck by the devil’s arrow, he began to defend his evil deeds, to be deceived by the enemy’s excessive prompting, and to give his consent to deadly suggestions.

Although he was frequently rebuked by the spiritual brothers, he was not only not corrected but came to hate those whom he saw to be greatly saddened by his perversity. After he had been tolerated in this perversity for a long time, he finally left the monastery.

Leaving the monastery, he began to visit the houses of his relatives and to seek someone willing to let him live with him—someone, of course, who would consent to his wicked deeds. But when he found no one, and all hated him because he had abandoned his resolve, he finally began to practice theft frequently, to defile himself with excessive sexual immorality, and to commit other unspeakable crimes.

As he pursued such things day after day, the clemency of almighty God—which calls the ungrateful to the kingdom through scourges—caused him to lose his bodily sight through an intense pain in his head.

Only after suffering such a terrible affliction of the flesh did he scarcely obtain from his relatives that they should offer him some assistance of kinship, in whatever manner seemed right to them. He was received by them, but was continually beaten with insults.

For his salvation, the merciful Lord had taken away the light of his eyes and had not allowed him the comfort of his relatives. One day, therefore, when he was deeply saddened by the constant insults, compelled by divine prompting he asked to be guided to the monastery of Blessed Bertin.

When this had been done, he prostrated himself daily before the church doors and strove to appease the Lord for his past negligence, persisting in fasts, prayers, and continual tears. Singing psalms, he said:

“But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 22:7); “but you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory; you will lift up my head” (Psalm 3:4).

When the Father of the monastery saw his humility, he understood that his heart had been visited by the Lord, and he placed him at the gate, providing him with daily food.

The man, persevering in penance as has been said, kept his mind stretched like a bow, so that, watering the ground with his tears again and again, he might deserve to hear: “Your sin has been forgiven.”

One day, while the brothers were singing the synaxis of the third hour, the aforementioned brother stood beside the altar situated in the middle of the church, where the relics of the Lord’s Nativity are venerated. Suddenly he fell to the ground.

The brothers quickly ran to him and lifted him from the ground. Seeing him stretching out the pupils of his eyes with perfect clarity, they immediately asked him how the Lord had granted him the restoration of his sight.

He told them that, while he was entreating the Lord with pure intention of mind, he saw two torches thrown from the tomb of Saint Bertin, pouring an exceedingly bright light into his eyes; thus the light of his eyes had been restored.

Then it became clear to everyone that through the merits of Blessed Bertin he had been restored to his former health. Immediately and without delay they recalled him to his former place, showing him even greater honor and veneration than at the beginning of his monastic life.

He, however, neither fell through his former humiliation nor was exalted within himself by the abundance of his present honor. From then on he followed Christ along the paths of good works, walking with the straight foot of faith, and frequently sang to him:

“I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me and have not allowed my enemies to rejoice over me. O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. Lord, you brought my soul up from the underworld” (Psalm XXXIX, 2).

Thus, gradually growing, he attained charity, which casts out fear when it is perfect (1 John 4:18). After this he lived for many years in holy conduct, sustained by the gratuitous mercy of the Lord Christ, who is blessed forever.

## CHAPTER IV. A certain penitent freed from iron bonds

[Note: [Col. 1101D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

A certain citizen of Orléans named Adam, from the village of Pruniac (Prunay), had been bound by order of the bishop of the city of Orléans with iron bonds around his belly and arms because of fratricide.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Thus the people of that time commonly paid for homicides; others did so by paying a price called *wergild*; others by flogging and mutilation of limbs. Those who fled to a church, or sent intercessors, were punished more lightly, either with iron bonds or with a monetary fine. Einhard, in Letter 18 to Marchradus, *vicedominus*, asks that Willirannus and Otbertus, who had fled to the threshold of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, be allowed to pay the *wergeld* for their brother, who had killed one of his companions, and that his limbs be spared. In Letter 25 he makes a similar request for another man who had taken refuge there after committing homicide: that, with the integrity of his limbs and the penalty of flogging remitted, he might make satisfaction and repair what he had committed through ill will by a payment of money. From this it is clear that not only accidental but also intentional homicides were then customarily expiated, not by capital punishment but by lighter penalties, and that penalties were reduced for flight to holy places. See the *Miracles of Saint Berta* below under the year 725.]

For several years he endured the burden of this great affliction while visiting the shrines of the saints. At last, at the threshold of the Apostle Blessed Peter, which he frequently visited in Rome, he obtained the release of two of the bonds.

Then, as he himself testified, he was warned in a vision to seek out over long stretches of land the monastery of the soldiers of Christ, Audomar and Bertin, and to entrust himself devoutly to their patronage.

Obeying this warning, he reached the designated place by long and winding routes. On the night of the octave of the Apostles, the second day before the Nones of July, while the brothers were celebrating the nocturnal praises in the basilica of Saint Peter and the lector was reciting the first lesson, he was suddenly surrounded by considerable terror and immediately fell. At once the iron bond was broken and driven far away from his arm.

The brothers lifted him from the ground as he gave thanks to God and Saint Bertin in tearful cries, while they themselves also offered due thanks and praise to God the author and to their patron Bertin.

## CHAPTER V. A certain crippled girl

[Note: [Col. 1103D] From the ancient Anonymous.]

[Col. 1103A]

A certain girl from the household of the saint himself, from a district called Mellingasele, had been entirely deprived of the use of her legs from her earliest years, so that she could scarcely crawl on her hands across the ground she needed to cover.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when our countrymen, according to local custom, were gathering for the feast of John the Baptist, she too attended, supported by the necessary assistance.

When the signal for the evening synaxis sounded for the third time, she placed herself on the ground some distance from the church, as far as women were permitted to approach, and begged almighty God to be reconciled to her through the patronage of the blessed man.

Immediately, shaken by a tremor, all her limbs began to stretch out. At once she recovered the use of her feet, giving thanks to her Creator,

[Col. 1103B] who, through the merits of her holy patron Bertin, restored her to the health for which she had long prayed.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Here the ancient Anonymous ends.]

## CHAPTER VI. How Fridogisus expelled the monks and established canons

Jesus performed many other signs through the merits of his confessor Bertin, which have not been written in this book. Why they were omitted or neglected, we do not know, unless perhaps because of the negligence of the writers, or because of the great persecutions and disorders that the holy mother Church, and especially this place, suffered at that time.

Of all these matters, we have decided to insert here one misfortune alone for the memory of posterity.

During the reign of the glorious Emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne and himself emperor, this ancient and then royal monastery had until that time been greatly ennobled, from the days of the most blessed Bertin, its principal founder, by the sacred observance of the monastic order; and, according to the statutes of the canons, its governance had been entrusted to the election of the brethren.

It happened that a certain Fridogisus,

[Note: [Col. 1103D] This is the Fridogisus mentioned in the catalogue of the enrolled brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall preserved by Goldastus, together with other monks from the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours. Were monks therefore still present there at that time, along with the canons? He was the first secular abbot of the people of Sithiu, a secular canon, says John Iperius in chapter 11.]

an Englishman by birth and abbot of Saint Martin at Tours, in the year 820 from the Incarnation of the Word and the seventh year of the aforementioned King Louis, received the abbacy of the monastery of Sithiu by royal grant and undertook its governance.

At the beginning of his tyranny, when he saw that the entire abbacy had been assigned to the use of so many monks—namely, 130 monks living in the two monasteries, those of Saint Bertin and Saint Audomar—and that nothing had been set aside for his own pleasures, he was blinded by the dart of avarice. He shamelessly attempted to destroy the monks’ way of life, so that he could more easily enslave to his own wantonness the goods that the faithful had entrusted for their use.

What he conceived in his mind through diabolical suggestion he carried out by a wicked deed. In the place of the chief of the apostles, namely Saint Bertin, where eighty-three monks served the Lord, he retained sixty, more for human praise than for the love of God. The rest, men of stricter life whom he judged unwilling to consent to his perversity, he expelled from the monastery and allowed to depart.

In the monastery of Saint Audomar,

[Note: [Col. 1104D] Originally Saint Mary; see the monastery or church in the *Life*, chapter 6.]

where forty monks living according to the rule had been present, he appointed thirty canons to serve there in the ministry of Christ.

Afterward, as he traveled around the villages belonging to the entire abbacy, he granted the monks a double portion of the villages because they were twice as numerous. To the canons, because they were fewer in number, he assigned a single portion in contrast with the monks. He reserved for his own perverse use whatever pleased him most.

And because he was a canon, he lived a secular life with the canons in the monastery of Saint Audomar.

Why should I say more about this abbot’s cunning, when I could truthfully say that he was the first downfall of this place? Here, too, in accordance with the truthful word of Truth, “when others had labored, he entered into their labors”; not only did he enter, but through reckless presumption he destroyed what they had labored to establish.

He was also the destroyer of fraternal charity between the two monasteries. The monks claimed for themselves the just honor of reverence handed down from the ancient Fathers and rightly defended the canons’ subjection to them; while the canons, through the deceitful assertion of their canonical abbot, claimed that primacy over the monasteries belonged to them.

For all these things and the other acts of his tyranny, he has been reviled by everyone up to the present day, and there is no doubt that he will also be reviled by those who come after.

## CHAPTER VII. The subjection of the canons of Saint Audomar to this church

When the aforementioned Fridogisus died in the fourteenth year of his rule—or rather of his tyranny—Hugh succeeded him in governing the monastery. Hugh was the venerable son of the great King Charles and brother of the Emperor Louis.

In the year 844 from the Incarnation of the Word, Hugh, grieving over the most unhappy and wretched division and separation of the venerable monastery of Sithiu caused by the infamous Fridogisus, obtained from Lord Folquinus, then venerable bishop of the Morini, that the monasteries should be restored to their former unity according to ancient custom. He also caused this to be confirmed by a privilege.

The privilege is as follows:

### Copy of the charter of Saint Folquinus concerning the same matter

“I, Folquinus, by the grace of God bishop of the Morini, to all the faithful, present and future…”

For the remainder, see the *Chartulary of Folquinus*, *Patrologia Latina*, volume CXXXVI, column 1223.

## CHAPTER VIII. The translation or removal of Saint Audomar

At this time we find the following recorded in the nineteen-year tables of the years of the Lord’s Nativity: it was the year 843, in the sixth indiction.

After the aforementioned Abbot Hugh—otherwise a man praiseworthy in all things except the matter I am about to relate—had commendably established this place by his constitution, and had justly subjected the canons of Saint Audomar to the monks of Saint Bertin by a capitular decree, he also appointed a monk from the lower monastery to guard Saint Audomar, as stated above.

But, struck by the devil’s arrow [sic], he began to devise how he might quickly carry the body of Saint Audomar to the monastery of Saint Quentin at Vermand, since that monastery too was under his governance. Through the help and assistance of Saint Audomar, together with his companion Bertin, the people of Thérouanne were governed.

Nevertheless, fearing the people’s resistance, he assembled a crowd of Vermandais and attempted to carry it away by force, in case the populace should obstruct him.

Meanwhile he arrived, and, with a certain monk named Moro serving as guardian, took up the sacred body of our holy bishop and patron and carried it with his assembled multitude as far as a village called Liesgensburtz—Lisbourg, according to Iperius.

By God’s providence, they remained for three days in the aforementioned village with the sacred body. When this was reported to the holy bishop Folquinus, he pursued the aforementioned abbot and his men with the greatest haste, accompanied by a very large crowd of people who had gathered throughout those three days, until they reached the village named above.

But when the others eagerly tried to lift the holy body and flee, they were entirely unable to raise it from the ground, despite all their numbers. Then, without delay, they hastened their flight, leaving the saint’s body behind.

The blessed Folquinus allowed them room to flee, took up that treasure more precious than all gold,

[Note: [Col. 1105D] The neuter noun *thesaurum* is not infrequently used by medieval authors in this way. Alcuin uses *thesaura* in Letter 49 and Epigram 115.]

and, retracing the road, carried it back with the entire multitude of the people. Taking precautions for the future, lest the holy body be carried away in a similar manner or by any other device, he buried it underground on the island of Sithiu beside the body of Blessed Bertin.

## CHAPTER IX. How the body of our Father Bertin was first translated by Saint Folquinus

It is recorded in the public archives of this place that Saint Folquinus, bishop of our see—whose body, famous for great miracles, also rests in this church—

[Note: [Col. 1105D] Folquinus died in the year of the Lord 855, the fifteenth year of King Charles and the fourteenth year of Abbot Adelard, in the fortieth year of his episcopate. He was buried to the right of Blessed Bertin’s tomb. We preserve one processional cope of his, together with a mitre, gloves, sandals, and three stoles. Iperius records this in chapter 13 and states, on the basis of his contact with these objects, that women are daily freed from the danger of childbirth. His body is said to have been elevated in the year 928, on the Ides of November; see chapter 22, part II.]

when the barbarity of the Danes was raging through the coastal regions with fire and sword, had shortly before the day of this devastation buried the body of Saint Bertin underground on a certain day.

When, for what reasons, and for how long those sacred members lay hidden beneath the earth, let us disclose briefly, to the praise of God and the honor of this saint.

During the reign of the glorious Emperor Louis, son of the great Emperor Charles and himself likewise emperor, this ancient and then royal monastery had until that time been greatly ennobled, from the days of the most blessed Bertin, its principal founder, by the sacred observance of the monastic order; and, according to the statutes of the canons, its governance had been entrusted to the election of the brethren.

But when it had unfortunately been given as a benefice to a certain Englishman by birth, a canon named Fridogisus, as has already been stated, it began to wither away from the brightness of the entire holy religious life, to fall into foreign hands, and to decline from its former integrity.

Finally, he reduced the number of monks serving there, who had numbered eighty-three. He seized for himself the villages and the more fertile estates assigned for the monks’ food. He completely overturned the monastery of Saint Audomar, which had been one with the monastery of Saint Bertin, for after expelling forty monks he substituted thirty canons in their place and assigned to their use a third of all the property belonging to the monastery of Saint Bertin.

What else, then, was this man but the scourge of this monastery? He was also rightly the eleventh among the abbots counted by Blessed Bertin, because by overturning what his ten predecessors had well ordered, he exceeded the limits of the Decalogue.

Let this brief account of these matters suffice for our present purpose, so that it may become clearer through what sins such evils arose from God’s sanctuary, and under what pressing circumstances the saint’s body, like a pearl, was buried.

## CHAPTER X. The division of the Frankish kingdom

After the aforementioned emperor had departed from this world, his sons Lothair, Louis, and Charles, each seeking to rival his father’s empire, soon began to disagree among themselves.

At length, peace was made, and they divided the Frankish kingdom among themselves. At that time the eastern regions belonging to us fell to King Charles.

Yet peace did not put an end to evils. While each brother desired to rule over his own kingdom and to extend himself according to his father’s magnificence, they brought ruin upon themselves and their possessions by throwing everything into confusion.

## CHAPTER XI. How Saint Folquinus buried the body of Saint Bertin underground
During the reign of that same Charles, in the third year of Abbot Adalard’s administration [Note: [Col. 1106D] This Adalard was the son of Count Henry, a soldier of Charles the Great. As a young man he was offered by his father to God, Saint Peter, and Saint Bertin in the monastery of Sithiu; but afterward, under Fridogisus, he was made a canon at the church of Saint Audomar. Later, when he was older, after the death of Hugh, he assumed this abbacy in the year of the Lord 844, according to Iperius, chapter 13. By order of King Charles he was deposed in 859, and Hugh the younger, son of Conrad and Charles’s maternal uncle, was appointed in his place. Restored after two years, he died in 864; he was succeeded by Saint Hunfrid, bishop of the Morini, formerly a monk of Prüm.], the aforesaid prelate placed the venerable remains of Saint Bertin, wonderfully arranged in a more secluded place than before, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 846. He also decreed that this holy translation should be celebrated more magnificently by the entire people of his diocese on appointed days, so that whatever they celebrated less worthily at the saint’s deposition, because September coincided with the urgent demands of the harvest, they might discharge more freely through this solemnity of the translation.

After so great a treasure had been assigned to hidden places, not long afterward all the peoples of this land, shaken on the one side by the distress of a most severe famine that had arisen, and on the other fearing the sudden fury of a Northmen invasion, began to depart. Almost all the nobility of the land, except for the few whom abundance of wealth and estates, or confidence in castles and fortifications, had detained, withdrew after their lords or wherever seemed safer to them. Moreover, the remnant, though somehow delivered from danger while still in the grip of famine, was at last assailed by the furious persecution of the Danes, which cruelly tore it to pieces. When they burst in here as enemies to vent the violence of their tyranny, they found none of the brothers here except four, who were awaiting the palm of martyrdom (concerning them, Book II, chapter 1).

What then, do you think, would have happened if the body of the aforesaid saint had at that time been duly venerated after being placed in a more prominent or secure location? Would it not have been carried away, unless the strong hand of the Lord rescued it? Was it not then all the more necessary that what the aforementioned priest of God had done shortly beforehand, prompted by the forewarnings of so many evils, should be done for the preservation of the holy relics? As yet no fortification of a castle or rampart defended this place; and so, especially because the weight of sins pressed upon it, the incursion of the enemies broke in with great ease. Nor did they cease ravaging the boundaries of Sithiu once only, but twice and three times, until, worn down in many ways by the merits of the aforesaid saint, they were forced to return to their own sheath.

While the disasters of this divine vengeance afflicted this land for nearly a hundred years, it was again, as though by a kind of flood, washed away, exhausted by these tribulations. Therefore, forewarned by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, the priest of God Folquinus concealed the venerable body of Saint Bertin, while he lived, in an unknown place where it would least be suspected, allowing no one except a few to know of it. And lest it be exposed publicly in any way, he bound those same few by solemn threats and oaths. He established this day as a solemn feast for us—the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August—on which our nourisher and shepherd lay hidden until these latest times of ours, namely for two hundred and fifty years [Note: [Col. 1107C] The same total of years is read in the account of Bovo, from whom the author borrowed this material. Nevertheless, one should read “two hundred and ten years”: for the body of Saint [Col. 1108C] Bertin was covered in 846 and, according to what follows, uncovered in 1056.].

## CHAPTER XII. The miracle that occurred at the translation of Saint Bertin

The feast day of the translation of the body of blessed Father Bertin, celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, was approaching, and the priest announced what was to be celebrated, according to the proper manner and the reverence customary for the occasion. A certain woman, however, postponed and neglected that same feast day and worked at a servile task until midday. Afterward she hurried to wash some clothes that she needed to have cleaned; but at that same hour something other than what she had expected happened to her. Suddenly the clothes first became red, and then, soaked with blood, they began to drip blood.

She persisted in washing the clothes, striving to overcome the increasing blood; but the more she washed them, the more abundantly the blood increased. At first it dripped drop by drop; afterward it flowed as water usually drips through a gutter. What was she to do? She stood astonished and stunned by so great a miracle. Immediately [Col. 1108B] news of the sign flew abroad. The neighbors gathered; those present marveled; and one of them spoke the truth, saying: “You have violated this feast day; you worked when you were least permitted to work.” She hastened to the church, sought pardon, and was assigned penance. The flow of blood ceased.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning a certain woman who did not observe the feast of the translation

Another woman, on the same day, cleaned grain in a winnowing basket, intending to grind it after it had been cleaned. But before she began that task, some people reproved her because she was not observing the feast day. Irritated by their words, she is said to have replied: “As many years as there are, and as many suns as are counted, so many feast days are inscribed in our priest’s book.” She said this and insisted on grinding.

At the first turn of the mill, a piece of wood adhered to her fingers and palm; then her entire arm also became rigid. Immediately the mill stood motionless, and the wood attached to her hand dragged it toward itself. She tried to pull it away but could not. At last, confessing her shame with a blush, she displayed her right hand attached to the wood, confessed the guilt of her error, and went to the church. At the priest’s instruction, those present offered a prayer, and the wood fell away. She returned home rejoicing; from that time onward, every feast day was a source of fear to her.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning blood flowing from ears of grain

At another time, also on this day of his solemn celebration, he drenched ears of grain that had been plucked with an abundant flow of blood, thereby rendering them useless for human purposes.

# BOOK TWO OF THE MIRACLES

Written by another anonymous author, around the beginning of the tenth century, chapter 10.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 1107C] Our most reverend Fathers, who were not only exceedingly eager for every good study of their time but also, in the affairs of their place, as truly and faithfully as possible previewed the virtues of our most blessed patron—being both its most solid pillars [Col. 1108C] and its brightest lights—have thus recounted these matters. Yet afterward many events worthy of narration have remained unmentioned, not, God forbid, because of a poverty of writers or a deficiency of authors, but because of the many adversities that arose with the passage of time.

From their great number we undertake humbly to add a few, lest we be marked by the fault of frivolity or falsehood: only those things that we ourselves saw, or that we learned had been seen by reliable persons. We do not rely on the audacity of our own presumption, but rather on the confidence of him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, although our account may be less elegant.

And although we are slow in understanding and unskilled in speech, we undertake to make these things known as best we can—not out of the vanity of boastful display, but from the devotion of a simple heart and a presumptuous humility. We would rather, if any wish to become our rivals, expose ourselves to the bites of their yelping than sluggishly conceal the miracles performed, in our presence, through the merits of God’s chosen one for the praise and glory of his name, allowing them to be erased from the memory of those who come after us. Therefore, although we are idle, our heart is now set on beginning what has been proposed and publishing what has been begun with the utmost devotion, according to our ability.

## THE MIRACLES BEGIN

[Col. 1109]

## CHAPTER I. The coming of the pagans

[Col. 1109B]

In the time of the divinely remembered Charles [Note: [Col. 1109D] That is, Charles the Bald, who succeeded to a portion of his father’s kingdom in 740 and was acclaimed emperor in 875. In the Northmannic Chronicle, published by Chesnius in volume II of the *History of France*, the Northmen are said to have plundered the monastery of Sithiu twice, namely in 845 and 881.], son of Louis, formerly king and afterward emperor, when the savage tyranny of the pagans arose, rushing along the famous rivers Seine and Loire and raging throughout all Neustria, it consumed with sword and fire not only the surrounding territories but also a large part of Armorica. At length, after not many years had revolved, they withdrew, partly driven away by stratagem and especially repelled through consideration of divine mercy, and returned to their homeland, declaring that they would in no way ever again return to ravage the borders of that kingdom.

Yet not long afterward they falsified this pledge through a fraud friendly to themselves, like dogs, which the more they are enticed, the more fiercely they pursue: greedy for money, practiced in robbery, ravenous for plunder, and falsely professing a thirst for blood. For in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord Christ 860, having again gathered an immense force and retracing their familiar route with a great fleet, sailing with all their strength across the open sea, they vied with one another in cleaving the foaming waters. With persistent course they reached the territory of the Menapii, at the inlet called the Port of the Yser [Note: [Col. 1110D] Iperius, chapter 14: now Nieuwpoort, commonly Nieuport, a town at the mouth of the Yser.].

There they leapt ashore and, turning aside from no public road, refraining even from the fires and slaughter proper to their purpose, hurried secretly toward the celebrated resting-place of Christ’s confessors Audomar and Bertin, eager covertly to seize the treasures of the churches and hoping to capture the servants of God there by surprise. Traveling through the brief passages of the night, namely on the Saturday of Pentecost week at the second hour, they reached [Col. 1109D] the place toward which they were making their way.

But by the constant providence of God, who protects those trusting in him, they found none of the brothers there. Instead, obeying the command of the Lord who ordered them—as he says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23)—they had withdrawn for a time, preserving themselves for better and more favorable circumstances. Four alone remained behind, having vowed that, if it pleased God, they would rather end their lives there in martyrdom than survive the desolation of their place.

That God arranged matters otherwise in part became clear from what followed. The names of those who made this vow were these: Worardus [also Woradus] and Winebaldus, priests; Gerwaldus and Raynardus, deacons.

Worardus, who had been raised from almost the cradle under the discipline of monastic religion and, although already decrepit with age, was a veteran soldier in Christ’s service, was struck with terrible blows of the fist and beaten nearly to death by three days of nakedness and cold. Winebaldus, although he had been weakened by the extreme affliction of his body and emaciation for the sake of God’s name, was tormented with sharp beatings and, by liquid poured through his nostrils, had his entrails distended; he was left half-alive.

Gerwaldus likewise, although older, because he seemed more vigorous and stronger than the others, was subjected to various and much heavier forms of mockery and abuse. Yet the Lord preserved him and granted him life, even if not his former health; thus he was not deprived of the martyrdom that he eagerly desired with all his heart.

The fourth of them, Raynardus by name, younger and more robust—as we have said—was broken by various tortures. When the Northmen departed and tried to take him with them, he resisted with what strength he had so as not to go with them. He preferred, if in any way he could be forced by the enemies, to commend his soul to God there in martyrdom in confession of Christ’s name, to have his body buried in the cemetery of his fathers, and to have his name inscribed in the brothers’ diptychs, rather than be polluted by the most execrable filth of their mockeries.

Nevertheless, bound as he was with dreadful chains, he was dragged miserably to a village of his own native region—“from the mother’s abundance” (the reading is uncertain)—named Miramo, three miles north of the monastery. Surrounded by a multitude of wicked men, and because of the great number of those surrounding him and the density of the night—for they passed through it at twilight—he did not know where he was. His fellow captives, who knew the place, said to him: “Look, we are going straight toward the gate of the place where you were born.”

When he realized this, he suddenly collapsed to the ground. The enemies who were leading him, turning their weapons aside and beating him, compelled him to rise, but he declared that he would in no way do so and that he preferred to die there for Christ. Pierced by repeated thrusts of spears [Col. 1111A], he breathed out his soul amid the shedding of his blood and offered it to Christ.

## CHAPTER II. How the Danes hanged Danes

Nor do I think that an event accomplished by divine judgment through the merits of Saint Bertin at the very hour of their departure should be left unmentioned. They threw an enormous quantity of silver offerings upon the altar of the church where he rested and entrusted them to one of the brothers mentioned above for safekeeping, lest anyone seize them.

While the invaders were hastening out in a wedge and throng, some of them secretly remained behind and rashly stole away the money. When this became known to their leaders after the others had departed, they halted, sounded their trumpets in the space between the two monasteries, and gathered themselves together until the culprits were sought, found, and brought before them. After they had been convicted and condemned by the judgment of the sacrilegious, they were hanged on the southern side beside the entrance to the monastery gate. The Lord most clearly proclaimed, even through the judgment of unbelievers, by what brief punishment and torment sacrilegious persons will be punished perpetually under the pretext of Christianity, unless the sacrilegious repent.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must observe with the utmost diligence how mercifully the Lord, who allows our sins to continue as though drawing out a long rope, deigned to correct and chastise us through the sudden—indeed, unseen—incursion of the enemies. In the same way, we must consider with the most exact vigilance how mercifully he preserved the place at that time and spared its inhabitants through the gratuitous compassion of his kindness. It should also rightly be counted among the merits of the patrons of the place that, at the same time, all those who had been taken captive soon returned, rejoicing and glad [Col. 1111C].

## CHAPTER III. How a certain craftsman, falling from the summit of the church to the ground, suffered no harm

After the aforesaid danger had been averted, the brothers of that monastery assembled. Their faces stained with tears of joy no less than of grief, they afterward became more composed and began to deliberate wholeheartedly how they might make the Lord, whom they had offended, propitious to them and render themselves pleasing to him.

As an indication of this intention, like obedient sons receiving the admonition of a kindly father, they agreed unanimously that they wished to become more grateful—or rather, more reformed—through this chastisement. The superiors also, with prudent care [Col. 1111D], consulted with the elders about what occupations in particular could make recompense for their former negligence.

Thus it was commonly resolved that they should not merely repair the roofs of the churches, which age had consumed, and the leaking roofs of the other buildings, but renew them completely, without interruption or the intrusion of another task. As this work was begun with the greatest devotion, so, with God supplying the means through our labor, it was completed beautifully and energetically sooner than expected.

The church containing the resting-place of Saint Bertin was also very quickly covered with lead through marvelous workmanship. They likewise took down its tower, although it had recently been superimposed, because it had been constructed in the ancient manner, and undertook to build another of marvelous size and workmanship. Its length, while it lay upon the ground, equaled the height of the roof of the church upon which it was to be placed.

Nor is this surprising, for it had been made, to use the common expression, with three tiers—three rows of tripods—apart from the highest *claxendix* [Note: [Col. 1111D] That is, the uppermost bell tower, commonly called *le clocher*.].

When the structure had been placed upon and raised over the church and joined at each of its joints, a fruit-shaped dome was being lifted aloft together with the victorious sign of the cross. Around the same upright shaft, the uppermost wheel—against which the rods and planks of the aforementioned *claxendix* were to lean and be fastened—was being fitted by being lifted into place.

One of the craftsmen, named Bertus, standing upon that circle, seized a hammer. As though rejoicing that the completion of so marvelous a work was almost at hand, he drew back for a longer blow, somewhat boastfully, and struck carelessly. But alas! When the wheel sprang back and shook, he lost his balance, his feet slipped, and he fell headlong from so great a height to the ground.

But—marvelous to say and still more marvelous to behold!—he suffered no injury whatsoever, except that he was shaken by his fall from such a height. Thus there can be no permissible doubt that he had been supported by the wings of the assistance of the most blessed Father Bertin, whom he served.

As confirmation of so great a miracle, we add the amusing and cheerful answer that he gave without any distress of pain to those who ran up and offered him water as though for refreshment. Since he had always been cheerful in his work and labor, he said that they should know for certain that he habitually rejoiced more in quenching his thirst with wine [Col. 1112C] than with water, and that he had no need of the liquid then being offered.

Immediately, on hearing of what was thought to be so great a misfortune, the brothers and the rest of the household ran together in groups as though to his funeral; discovering that he was unharmed, they rejoiced and led him into the church, changing their mournful weeping into tears of joy. Together they rang the great bells with their customary prolonged peal and solemnly offered hymns to the Lord, the author of the miracle, and to blessed Bertin, its helper. The craftsmen too, not merely inspired by this power but made stronger and bolder by it, brought the work they had begun to completion, steadfast and joyful.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning a certain citizen of Verdun, naturally deaf and mute, healed at the tomb of Saint Bertin

In the course of time it happened that an unknown man, unknown both by origin and by name—and this was not surprising, since he had been miserably bound by a twofold disease—came as a pilgrim to the monastery of the aforesaid Father. From the earliest hour of his birth he had been without hearing and deprived of speech.

He spent a long time there. Since, as we have said, he could not speak, he begged alms by striking clattering tablets. He never turned aside anywhere, and the Christians of the place, reflecting on his unbroken perseverance and continual attendance at the churches, and recognizing that such a sign had not occurred without God’s direction, began to receive him more humanely. They assigned him a dwelling in the hospice appointed for the daily reception of the poor [Col. 1113A].

After he had lived there for nearly a year, on the tenth day after the completion of the week of the Lord’s Resurrection—that is, on Wednesday—the monks were performing the evening office due in the church. The cantor began the antiphon for greeting the cross, beginning: “Go, announce to my brothers.” A boy then recited the verse: “Declare among the nations,” while the others, as usual, followed in a drawn-out and subdued manner.

At that very hour, which was almost one of silence, the deaf and mute man mentioned above began, babbling, to imitate the voices he had heard from those singing psalms. The brothers, terrified by so strange and alarming a sound, stopped and signaled to the steward of the poor to investigate the cause.

When the steward signaled to him as usual but accomplished nothing, he began angrily to rebuke him with words [Col. 1113B]. The man attempted to answer by babbling those very same words, since he did not know how to speak anything else.

Then the brothers immediately understood that the Lord, through the merits of blessed Bertin, had granted him hearing and speech. With hymns of praise, together with the ringing of bells, they gave thanks with all their strength to God and to his healer.

Rejoicing in the celebration of this power, and because he was at the first beginnings of a flourishing youth, they sent him to the school of the canons to be instructed in letters as much as he could manage. As soon as he had learned the daily chapters and the evening psalms, he asked to have the hair of his head cut.

Before long, however, he began to grow weary. He declared that he wished to go to Rome. After receiving permission, he joined some overseas Saxons who were traveling to Rome. When he had reached the region beyond the city of Langres with them, merchants from Verdun, who were traveling the same road, joined them until the road divided toward Spain.

There it became known what had previously been unknown: that the man himself was a citizen of Verdun. For there he recognized his own people, although they could scarcely recognize him because of the unexpected cure of his inborn diseases. He nevertheless completed the journey he had begun with vigor and, returning from there, revisited directly the place of his healing, without any desire to turn aside on the way home, and gave thanks to God and to his restorer.

He also then disclosed the name given to him at baptism, which he had previously not known until he learned it from acquaintances: he was called Ermenfridus. Thus, bidding farewell to his benefactors, he returned home happily, filled with an abundance of blessings [Col. 1113D].

## CHAPTER V. Concerning a certain man blinded for two years and restored to his former sight

Just as some people are endangered for a time because of their negligence, so many are saved through the most healthful chastisement of divine providence, as is clearly evident in the present event.

A certain man of the same church’s territory, from the town attached to it called Gimiacum, named Letfridus, proved less zealous than the rest of his fellow citizens in Christian devotion, as the appropriateness of the event later made clear. It therefore happened that, on a certain Sunday, while the citizens of that place were hastening to church according to their custom, with no less devotion of mind than speed of foot, and while the leading men called upon him with the gentle persuasion of familiar speech [Col. 1114A] to go with them, he not only refused to go but also ignored their salutary admonitions. Instead, he went to tend the few animals that appeared to belong to him.

Before he reached the pasture, anguish of mind came upon him, together with intolerable fear and excessive shuddering. As we later learned from him himself, it seemed to him as though he had been completely drenched in the heat of boiling water.

To speak in terms familiar to strangers: the location of that estate where this happened is such that the churches of Christ’s confessors Audomar and Bertin are visible there to travelers. Although the wretched man was not pitiable because of his hardness of heart—or because of the miracle that followed—he tried, though late, to turn toward them in the hope that he might be helped by their prayers [Col. 1114B]. He could not do so, however, and fell almost lifeless to the ground—not struck by an attack of *scotoma* (vertigo), but deprived, for the salvation of his soul, as later became clear, and rather for the praise of God’s name and by his disposition, of the delightful sight of his eyes. He remained in the bitterness of this blindness for two years or more.

While he was still languishing in the sluggishness of his torpor, almost entirely despairing of the restoration of his health, he finally went at the urging of his family to visit the threshold of the most blessed Father Bertin. He brought whatever he could obtain, especially wax offerings, by which—if it should please God and the most merciful Father just mentioned—he might deserve through his merits to receive the lost light of his afflicted eyes. He promised and affirmed [Col. 1114C] that, whatever divine mercy might decide concerning this, he wished to spend the remainder of his life there.

God, the knower of hidden things, seeing his inward devotion of heart and his most steadfast confession, restored him to sight and sight to him through the merits and prayers of the most merciful Father. He did so with such clarity of vision that, since the man had been raised and educated from childhood to adulthood in the household of a certain most noble man of that region, and had been taught in his women’s quarters to spin, sew (*cusandi*, that is, stitching), weave, and perform every craft of women’s work, he undertook with attentive care whatever in the aforementioned church needed to be adorned or repaired, and whatever ecclesiastical garments needed to be washed.

He eagerly aspired and humbly prayed that, just as he himself labored in making and repairing whatever was necessary and cleansing what was soiled [Col. 1114D], so the merciful kindness of divine compassion might deign to wash away the impurities of all his offenses, so that he might happily attain the summons of the Author of his restoration.

## CHAPTER VI. How the Danes returned a second time

At that time, when the boundaries not only of France but also all the principal places of the kingdom and the province of Armorica were being cruelly—though justly—invaded through the long-continued sacrilegious oppression of the Danish people (whose details it would take too long now to enumerate), because of the many and overwhelming offenses of the common people and indeed of every rank and order, that fleet, which was called a great army by everyone because of its size—as we may speak *epithetically* (*epitheticῶς*)—assembled in the twelfth year after its arrival in the kingdom.

It ascended the river called the Yser from the whole region where it had been dispersed, gathering at a place called Confluence because of the meeting there of notable waters. By both cavalry and ship it reached as far as the city of Noyon, constructing a fortification around a village on the southern side, naturally defended by water and forest, called Chyrisiacus [also Kyrisiacus]. They intended, if they could not capture the city quickly through a close and prolonged siege, to take it because it seemed small.

But when they had spent half a year accomplishing nothing there—not merely failing to make progress but being so constricted by hunger, thirst, and every kind of deprivation that they almost perished—they formed a plan, as the outcome afterward revealed: they would go into the former kingdom of Lothair. They planned to cross by the coastal routes, seize the castles recently built there, and kill all the inhabitants unless they surrendered.

When this was discovered, five hundred and fifty young men who seemed more agile and bolder than the rest selected themselves without the knowledge of the others. Secretly carrying themselves away at night, as though proceeding as usual to another place, they took an unbroken route and headed directly toward a small fortification in the district of Tervana, at a place called Sithiu, near the monastery of the excellent bishop Audomar.

It had been constructed at scant cost by a small, though valiant, band of inhabitants, with sticks, clods, and turf—both with great skill and with great strength. On the way they boastfully sported in advance, declaring that they wished to break it at the first assault and that, because of the weakness and small number of its inhabitants, it could easily be captured.

Yet with the help of God and the protection of the saints who had chosen that place for their repose, and who intervened according to their custom, Christ’s anger turned their presumptuous boasting directly into a deserved punishment. To proclaim that punishment, we now turn our pen.

## CHAPTER VII. At what time they came, and how they accomplished nothing

For fourteen days after the holy day of the Resurrection of Easter had passed, on a Sunday at the hour when the principal public assembly for Mass was being held, the invaders mentioned above suddenly appeared, descending the slope of the mountain that rises above the village called Locus-ecclesiae [Col. 1115D] [Note: [Col. 1115D] Iperius, part III, chapter 20: the Holy Field, commonly called *Helechvelt*, is now called *Hellefaut* under a corrupted name. He assigns this event to the year [Col. 1116D] 891. This village lies two miles from Audomaropolis.], because the most blessed martyrs Fuscianus and Victoricus are said to have built there, at the forefront of the Christian inhabitants of the land, the first church. It faces the monastery on the western side.

When the sentries saw this and supposed that a much larger force would follow—as rumor had earlier spread that this was the case—they immediately reported it to the people assembled in the church. The people were not greatly terrified by the news. Rather, becoming more composed, they entrusted their cause to God and to the protection of the saints. With contrition, they baptized one another anew through mutual confession [variant, probably: *compuncti se*, “being contrite themselves”], and fortified themselves through humble reception of the mystery of the body and blood.

They gave one another their right hands, promising that, for the sake of liberty and the defense of the place, they would either die swiftly or defend it bravely. Then, armed with the best weapons—as is customary among the inhabitants of the region—they climbed the wall and, together with the weapons of war prepared beforehand, very securely equipped the fortress.

When the previously arrogant enemies learned of this steadfastness, and saw some of those enclosed boldly coming out to meet them beyond the fortification, God struck them with the greatest terror. Their proud boldness was softened, their boasting suppressed, their courage slackened and dissolved, and they did not dare to attack. Instead, they turned to seize the cattle grazing through the fields, wishing to return quickly even with so small a booty [Col. 1116B].

The rest of our men, stirred by this invasion and especially trusting in God’s help and in the intervention of the witnesses, suddenly burst out of the fortification and attacked them from behind. The horsemen, taking shortcuts and moving ahead of them on the level ground of the mountain from which they had previously descended—for the invaders were slowly driving the cattle—held such audacity in contempt. The foot soldiers followed behind, placing the enemies between them.

When the invaders realized that they were being surrounded on every side and that all were preparing to flee, they broke desperately toward the east through the left wing of those surrounding them, making for a certain grove of oaks. They thought that there they might somehow defend themselves or escape.

Our men pursued them, killing them. It was the ninth hour of the day when they left the castle; before evening came, they had destroyed in God’s battle the entire large force of chosen warriors which the invaders themselves had boasted of, though not without loss on our side—yet their loss was greater.

The slaughter took place at a place called Windigamo [also Windingahamo]. All of them were killed there, except that as many of our men as had died were matched by that many of the enemy who escaped in flight. Only nine out of that great number escaped; of these, five were found dead on the road by those pursuing them. Only four, as we learned afterward from those who had taken part in the army at that time, reached their companions, condemning the audacity of their rashness and carefully examining the outcome of their presumptuous undertaking [Col. 1116D].

They also divided the spoils into three portions: one they granted to the churches, another they gave to oratories and the poor, and the third they shared equally between the nobles and the lower-ranking men. And rightly so. Let us consider, for example, in human terms to whom such a victory ought more properly to be assigned—to those who pray or to those who fight, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Saint Audomar appeared to a certain monk
Moreover, beloved brothers and fellow soldiers of Christ, with what petitions of the heart or hymns of praise could we be sufficiently capable of giving thanks to God for the unexpected [Col. 1117A] rescue from so great a danger? And with what boldness may we say that an undertaking of this kind would have been begun, unless it had been inspired by great zeal for the merciful God? For it was dreadful to relate, and still more dreadful to undertake. Almost all the nobility of that land had long since departed from their native country, out of love for, or in submission to, their beloved lords, except for a few who were so endowed with hereditary estates that they had no need to submit except to public ordinances.

Some of these, together with the most noble and religious monks of that place, and with the most devoted to God and most vigorous canons—whom no tribulation of persecution had ever been able to terrify—sustained and encouraged the place in their resolve not to abandon it; and together they strengthened the [Col. 1117B] nearly dispirited hearts and feeble hand of the remaining populace. In particular, they confidently assumed the anchor of the safest hope and the boldness of trust in the Lord, since the matter concerned their lives. In earlier times, namely under Folco, the most noble man and then abbot of that place, and afterward most reverend archbishop of the holy mother Roman [Note: [Col. 1117D] Perhaps *Remanae*, that is, of the Church of Reims, over which Fulco presided after Hincmar from 882 to 900. This passage deserves notice, since from it we learn that Fulco had been abbot of the Sithiu monastery; Frodoard makes no mention of this. Hear Iperius, chapter 18: [Col. 1118D] “Saint Fulco, the eighteenth abbot of this place, a canon of the church of Saint Audomar, was appointed abbot here after Hilduin, namely in the year 877, when Rodulfus died after eight years of governance; he was elected abbot again in 893.”] Church, while the inhabitants of the land were still rich in every abundance and flourishing in complete prosperity without diminution, the circuit of the castle had been agreed upon, measured out, and distributed for completion through the authorities and officials. A considerable part had already been undertaken, but, alas, it remained unfinished because of sins that obstructed it, and was hindered and abandoned under the pretext of the circuit’s great extent—an impious and disastrous pretext. [Col. 1117C]

As time passed—namely, in the year of grace 891—when the whole land had already been burned and laid waste, and almost all its people had been consumed by hunger and driven into dispersion by flight, God, at last regarding and pitying the very few remnants, showed that salvation does not depend upon the multitude of the people, but rather upon his mercies and compassions. He also revealed that he deigns, through the prayers of his elect, to grant effect to the fitting petitions of the needy, in response to their supplications according to his will. He therefore willed that the blessed Audomar, most readily moved to mercy, should appear in a vision to a certain monk of the monastery of Saint Bertin—namely, the sacristan of the church of that prelate—a man of memorable character named [Col. 1117D] Herricus.

As he himself afterward used to recount pleasantly before many listeners, the saint was tall in stature and venerably gray-haired. On his forehead were marks that spread apart the radiance of an exceedingly beautiful baldness. His face was handsome and slender; his nose moderately long and slightly aquiline; his hands, with very long fingers, were beautifully slender and almost translucent in their leanness. He was dressed in episcopal vestments and, in a sweet voice, addressed him as follows:

“Are you burdened, brother, with sleep, [Col. 1118A] or are you awake?”

Trembling at this unusual visitation, the monk replied that he was not entirely asleep, nor could he keep himself from sleep because of the anxiety naturally present in him—for fear commonly induces drowsiness—and that his limbs, wearied by excessive labor and relaxed by anxiety, could not otherwise be refreshed. The apparition extended his arm and seemed to reach out his hand toward him, adding:

“It is more necessary for you to be watchful in mind and body, and to labor with the utmost diligence according to my instructions for your salvation, than to idle in sluggish laziness. Therefore rise, and earnestly urge the remaining people, wholly devoted to their salvation, to persevere without ceasing, as far as they seem able, in strengthening the fortress day and night.”

Partly filled with joy and partly terrified by the vision, the monk nevertheless first summoned a gathering of suitable persons and consulted them. Then he earnestly announced the vision of the Father, who had admonished, encouraged, and diligently commanded them. Rejoicing with contrite hearts and weeping joyful tears, they all unanimously cried aloud to heaven with their vows raised on both sides, saying:

“We give thanks to almighty God, who has deigned, by providing for us, admonishing us, and consoling us through the salutary visitation of our Father, to refresh and strengthen us. We promise that we desire most diligently to fulfill these wholesome instructions with whatever strength we may possess.”

They immediately began to carry out this promise with the greatest urgency and strove to complete it with the utmost perseverance. Thus, aided by the merciful providence of God and encouraged by the exhortation of the pious Father, they were worthily aided not only in the danger already mentioned but also in the later danger, which was far greater and more perilous. Indeed, they had been saved by the experienced, customary, and provident protection of the Fathers. From then on, with still greater outpourings of devotion, they continually and joyfully praised the Lord and their own protectors there.

## Chapter IX. How the remaining pagan army came on the following Sunday in greater numbers, but achieved nothing through the merits of Saint Bertin

Nor was there a long delay after the aforesaid slaughter of the enemy. That ancient Leviathan, insatiably hungry and thirsty, does not allow his members to delay in plotting against the human race or in persecuting and injuring the godly. Inflamed by the bile of envy, he grieved that our men were fervent with their recent benefit and supreme devotion. Nor is this surprising, since at that time he became all the more hostile insofar as he perceived them growing stronger in their resolve to do God’s will.

Therefore he compelled the relatives, companions, and fellow tribesmen of those who had fallen, along with many others, to blaze with all the force of his cruelty in savage anger and most cruel vengeance for their own people—if God had permitted it. He suggested that the forces of the entire kingdom should quickly be gathered and concentrated in the narrowest confines of a single estate. For after the slaughter mentioned above had taken place, on the following Sunday, I believe at the second hour, while a mist, naturally [Col. 1119A] formed in the morning because of the character of the place, still stained the air, foot soldiers of immeasurable number appeared descending by the same slope as the earlier ones. [Note: The author uses this same expression more than once below, in Chapters X and XI, and likewise more than once above.] Making swiftly for the castle, they did not enter it, but waited before the outer entrance gate for those who were to follow.

The horsemen, innumerable as sand, turned aside toward a certain place of battle, moved by nothing other than this: as at the sight of a new spectacle the grief of their murdered companions was renewed, so elephants are roused to anger and battle by the sight of blood. In the same way these men were sharpened to avenge the blood of their own people more harshly and cruelly. After grieving and deliberating there for some time, and accomplishing nothing else except seeing the emaciated and rotting corpses, they set out at a swift run and, as though they would capture the little fortification at the first assault, reached their companions. Bursting in with a furious roar, they decided that the infantry should set the defenders of the castle ablaze with a dreadful attack.

The horsemen, by God’s gift, hurried toward the naturally fortified place: the monastic monastery of Saint Bertin, the most pious protector of his people and their most ready liberator in the greatest necessities. We believe that such things did not occur without God’s dispensation, just as we immediately and clearly experienced them by his will: wherever the common victory was to be greater and completed through an abundance of divine assistance from heaven, there the greater multitude of the enemy was assembled.

When they arrived at once, at that very moment, they sent their horses through fodder-seekers to pasture near the villages, and with such zeal hastened to build dwellings as though, after breaking through the little fortification, they intended to remain there for a long time because of the strength of the place and the suitability of the *gromnae* [Note: [Col. 1119D] *Gromnae* or *gronnae*: marshy and [Col. 1120D] grassy places; another manuscript reads *grumarum*.].

Meanwhile, from the moment of their arrival, the foot soldiers did not cease fighting all day with the more agile horsemen against the castle’s defenses. By turns and successive attacks, in dense groups and wedges, they harassed their opponents with various and unfamiliar kinds of contrivances, allowing them no respite, or scarcely any. They hurled flaming implements and pieces of glowing iron at them like molten hail, and did not cease pouring upon them showers of arrows. They devised many other obstacles, which it is both tedious and difficult to enumerate. Finally, after constructing trenches around the fortification of remarkable depth and breadth, they filled them, like walls of wicker, with straw and every kind of dry material, attempting to destroy the defenders by fire where they could not prevail by other devices and engines.

When they withdrew from the attack for a little while, our men, by God’s gift and with a favorable whirlwind of wind blowing toward them, cautiously applied fire to the same heaps of straw and piles of wood. Without the enemy’s knowledge or expectation, they likewise brought fire against them to produce the same result. As the straw burst into flame, many of them were burned, barely escaping the danger of death. By God’s favor, none of our men were seriously endangered during the prolonged period of conflict, except for one brother [Note: [Col. 1120D] At this time clerics and canons were also called “brothers”; hence here “brother” means a member of the monastic order, to distinguish him.], a member of the monastic order, who was struck by an arrow beneath the groin between two wooden levels of the bulwark where he was standing. He too recovered.

Nevertheless, God permitted another brother of the same order to repay the enemy with a fitting recompense, since, being less stirred to vengeance by arms and therefore less cautious, his servant had been wounded.

## Chapter X. Concerning the monk who killed a tyrant by shooting him with an arrow

There was a certain tyrant among the opposing forces who, as it seemed, was harsher and stronger than all the others and more cunning in the art of warfare through ingenious stratagems. He never ceased fighting vigorously, even for a moment, and urged the others on as though they were about to capture the walls without delay.

On our side, although the repeated attacks of the enemy made them persist more tenaciously in defense than in assault, they nevertheless resisted bravely and actively with whatever skill and strength they possessed. All of them fought with the utmost intensity in every way, seeking somehow to hinder that most hostile enemy. But none of them was granted this, because God wished to make them understand—and to signify to those standing on the border of life and death—from which side he had mercifully decided to send them relief from their impending danger.

Therefore, as we have said, he decreed that a young man in monastic dress should take up a bow, although handling weapons is unlawful or unsuitable for this order. Carefully taking aim at the man who was rushing forward to attack, though doubtful of his own strength but by no means uncertain of God’s help, he fitted an arrow to the bow, invoked God’s assistance, drew the taut string with force, and, through the impulse granted by divine direction, drove it manfully into the forehead of the aforesaid tyrant.

When he had died, the others ceased the tumult of the attack and immediately sent messengers to report the event to their elders. They remained in the courtyard of the aforesaid monastery, while the officers sat in council in the church of the blessed Peter. When the report of what had happened was brought to them, and although it troubled them somewhat, yet did not greatly distress them, they deliberated more slowly and securely about what should be done that evening.

During this interval, one of them ran up and took down the cross standing behind the altar of Saint Bertin. Returning to his companions, he irreverently began to dismantle it before them with an iron implement called a *sol*, with which fire is customarily struck from flint. The aforesaid messengers, inflamed with anger by so great a delay, attacked them with insolent insults and began to rebuke them harshly, saying:

“What you are doing is deeply disgraceful and unworthy. You are not angry over the vengeance for our murdered men; you do not burn with anger over us who are fighting and in part falling for your sake; nor, if only you wished it, do you hasten to attack them over the capture of the castle, which would cause no delay. Moreover, you pay no attention to the untouched booty, for if these men are granted merely the space of this night, they will either bury all their possessions or conceal them in wells or in any hidden places, since they are certain to fear that they must surrender or die.”

Then those men turned to anger and burst into furious rage. Immediately leaping up from their seats, they made vows to their gods: if they could capture the fortification that evening, they would spare no male person until morning.

No one ought to doubt that these proud words of boastfulness and threats of dreadful recklessness were, through the intervention of the blessed apostle Peter and the prayers of Christ’s readily heard confessor Bertin—in whose churches, as though in insult to them, these things had been done and said—humbly conveyed to the ears of God’s compassion, which indignantly bore them.

For at once, as we believe to prevent so cruel a decree, the aforesaid violator of the saving sign was struck with an incurable affliction. His mouth suddenly contracted together with his ear all the way to the back of his head; his eyes were twisted by a reversal of their position; and he rolled on the ground, foaming and trembling.

When those who had shortly before raged arrogantly saw this, they began to be distressed, grow pale, and tremble. They cursed their beloved comrades, who had been struck down, as though they were now detestable, and considered an escape route their only refuge, if they were permitted to retrace the way by which they had come.

Thus, some struck by God’s vengeance and others terrified, they hastily seized their own banners, which had been leaning against the walls of the churches. Receiving them there, shining white with linen, they were astonished to find them black as pitch. In this way they burst at a rapid pace, staggering precipitately through the midst of the churches—not drunk with wine, but overwhelmed by God’s indignation and the offense against the saints. It seemed too slow for them to reach the monastery gates, so that at that moment they rejoiced more over their departure than earlier over the entrance they had long desired.

After they had gone out and recovered their breath, which had almost failed them, they remembered the remaining weak men. Yet none of them dared to return for them. Instead, they summoned a vigorous young man, formerly captured from the estate of Saint Wulmar, who had been involved in this affair from the beginning. They ordered him to try to return as quickly as possible and bring the men back if they were alive.

When he returned to carry out the order, he found them wandering and groping about here and there, as before, and the contracted man lying almost lifeless as before. Since he could not leave, he remained there and lived miserably for many days on the alms of good people. With the barking noises he was able to make, he bore witness to the miracles of God accomplished there.

The aforesaid young man took one of the blind men by the hand. Thus, clinging one after another to one another, they were dragged to the others. Meanwhile, trembling with fear of death, they repeatedly urged one another on with loud cries, and the shrill trumpets signaled—or rather compelled—flight more than they encouraged battle.

When the entire great host [i.e., troop] heard this, wherever they were—whether stationed around the castle, in the tents, or in the pastures—they were terrified by the familiar lament of flight and still more by divine power. They did not return for their lords, companions, or acquaintances, but fled headlong wherever they saw a way by which they could more quickly escape or hide.

The aforesaid leaders, joining themselves to those whom they could keep with them and hastening to leave the region of the fortification through the entrance gate, did not merely approach it, nor did they dare turn their faces in that direction. Although evening was coming on, they did not dare remain that night within six miles of it. Instead, they went straight to the once-renowned stronghold of the Menapii. The Lord Christ mercifully freed them as his own people, while striking the others, alienated from him, with the fitting torments of calamities, terrifying them divinely, and driving them far away—even to the point of destruction.

From the report of faithful men who took part in the battle, we learned that when they reached the place toward which they were heading, twelve noble warriors among them were defeated in a single battle encounter, God graciously repaying them with a fitting return for the number of their killings and sacrileges.

## Chapter XI. How the pagan standard, when set up, was exceedingly bright, but was found most dreadful

A further event worthy of mention was sent from heaven and seen at the same time.

Behind the outer courtyard of the gate of the monastic monastery, not long before these events, a certain religious monk of that place had planted a very beautiful and fruitful grove. In its middle there was something like a burial mound, on the summit of which stood a pear tree whose pears were of extraordinary size and exceedingly sweet flavor. The elders related that it had been planted by the most blessed Father Bertin.

For this reason, the diligence of the Fathers decreed that every year, on Easter Monday, the brothers—solemnly dressed, with relics and psalmody, as was customary throughout that entire week at the various offices—should visit the same orchard and, after completing a prayer on the little hill, return to the public solemnities.

Because this grove lay between the two monasteries, the Christians decided to uproot it, lest it become a hiding place for the enemy. The pagans therefore came, as we have related, and planted their principal standard on the summit of the aforesaid hill, fixed to a tall pole. This standard is said to be called a *labarum*, and they set it there to inspire terror in those who saw it from a distance.

But in the same place the merciful Lord also wished to reveal most clearly that he looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God (Psalm 13:2). For the aforesaid *labarum*, which had been placed there in the brightest condition, was snatched away and torn out in a most dreadful state. At the time when the aforesaid wonders began, a cloudy darkness covered the entire grove, so that those on the hill could not see those below, nor those below those on the hill.

A column of cloud, suspended from heaven in the midst of the darkness, was also seen above the hill itself. In the color of its appearance it imitated the varied hues of a rain-bearing rainbow, and in its breadth matched the width of the hill beneath it. It did not withdraw from the sight of the faithful who watched it intently until the entire great host [i.e., troop] of the enemy had completely departed.

By this visible manifestation, the almighty God clearly showed—or rather mercifully urged us—to fix continually, in every necessity, both our outward and inward eyes with the whole attention of our minds and the entire devotion of our hearts upon the place to which he deigned to invite us through the redemption by the blood of his most precious Son. He lives, is glorified, and reigns with God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1123D] What follows appears to be by a different author.]

## Chapter XII. Concerning the entrance of women

[Col. 1123B]

After our venerable Father Bertin had been tempted by the devil in the form of a woman, and had been visited and freed by Saint Martin, he judged that it was altogether unsuitable for monks to have contact with the female sex in any way. Under anathema, therefore, he entirely excluded the entrance of women from the approaches of the same monastery.

This was carefully observed by everyone from the time of the blessed Bertin until the time when Adala, the most noble wife of Count Arnulf, abbot [Note: [Col. 1123D] In the year 944 he arranged for the collapsed discipline of the Sithiu monastery to be reformed through Saint Gerard, according to Iperius, chapters 23 and 24.] of this place, had been very frequently afflicted by grave illnesses. She began to desire that the monks grant her permission to enter this monastery, so that she might be allowed to prostrate herself before the altar of Saint Bertin and pray for her health.

For this reason, the venerable bishops Wicfrid [Note: [Col. 1123D] Frodoard, in his *Chronicle* under the year 935, says: “Archbishop Artald ordained a certain monk named Wicfred”—namely, a monk of Sithiu, according to Iperius, chapter 22, part II—as bishop of the Church of Terwaan. From this author we learn that Wicfred, bishop of Thérouanne, took part in the Council of Trier in the year 948. See Iperius, chapter 23, part II.] of the Church of Thérouanne and Folbert of Cambrai were summoned, and she disclosed her desire to them. After permission had also been obtained from the monks, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 938, the fifth year of King Louis, on Easter Monday, the aforesaid bishops introduced her into the same monastery, not without great trembling. She was the first to presume to do this, since before her no queen had either desired or dared to undertake it.

After she had been brought in and had prostrated herself before the altar of the blessed Bertin, she received complete bodily health after pouring out a devout prayer. By entering, she also bestowed very many ornaments upon this place [Note: [Col. 1123D] Among them, says Iperius in chapter 28, was a curtain of extraordinary size and workmanship, which still survives.], and for as long as she lived she never ceased giving gifts.

## Chapter XIII. Concerning the man who offered his son, near death, to Saint Bertin

[Col. 1123D]

At the same time, Rodulfus, the civic governor of that castle, seeing that his son named Walter was near death from the illness that physicians call smallpox [Note: [Col. 1124D] Commonly called *la petite vérole*. Physicians call it *boam*.], carried him in his own arms to the altar of Saint Bertin. He promised that he would make him a monk if he were helped by the saint’s pious intercession.

When the boy was soon restored to health, he offered him to the Almighty as a servant and to Saint Bertin as a monk, promising that he would remain one perpetually [Note: [Col. 1124D] Here what Iperius says in his *Chronicle*, chapter 27, part II, should be supplied: “Abbot Ragenoldus, at the command of Count Arnulf, surnamed the Old, carried the relics of Saints Audomar and Bertin across the Rhine beyond Nijmegen, where the emperor was then residing, so that they might claim his lands for him.
