During this journey a miracle occurred at the port of Tiel: the custodian of that church blasphemed the saints and prevented them from entering the church; there he was struck down and killed by God. Read also in the same author, chapter 39, part II, about another transfer made in the year 1087 to the village of Ostresela.”]

## Chapter XIV. How this place was rescued from the danger of fire through the merits of Saints Vincent, Audomar, and Bertin

The diligent report of truthful men who were present established how, in the time of the venerable man Lord Odbert, abbot, the site of the Sithiu monastery had formerly been divinely rescued from the danger of fire through the merits of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, and the holy confessors Audomar and Bertin [Col. 1124B]. Since this account appears so beneficial to its hearers, although it had long remained hidden through the negligence and carelessness of writers, it is nevertheless considered worthy of being committed to memory by the work of the pen.

In ancient times no solemn observance was held there for the aforesaid martyr of Christ except with three readings and an equal number of responsories. But when the responsories proper to him were brought here by certain brothers, the brothers immediately perceived the harmony of their sweet and pleasing melody. Since they were exceedingly delightful, the community’s youth took great pleasure in them and was fully instructed from that time onward for the celebration that was to be observed in the future.

Thereafter, the deposition of the aforesaid saint began each year to be honored more appropriately than before with twelve readings, and the brothers’ devotion toward the saint of God grew daily ever greater. After several years had passed in this way, with the brothers continuing in such holy devotion, it happened one year, shortly after his solemn deposition had been duly celebrated—namely, on the very feast of Saint Gregory, which falls in Lent—that a large building adjoining the cloister and monastery caught fire from a spent candle-wick and began to burn.

The fire was powerful, spewing forth dreadful flames and concealing with smoke and fire that part of the cloister where it stood. It threatened destruction to all the monastery’s offices, and the brothers, already despairing of the rescue of so great a place, occupied themselves only with removing the church’s treasures and its various furnishings [Col. 1124D].

Then, through God’s favorable providence, three doves, white as snow, descended from heaven—as I believe, and as subsequent events demonstrated—and were seen openly by many people to fly three times around the bell tower. Now here, now there, they alternated their perches upon the pinnacles. Some who saw this believed that such things were being brought about by the Lord, and prayed and desired that by such signs this place might be preserved from so great a danger of fire.

Although the fire was so immense that it threatened the principal cloister [perhaps “the cloister of the chief church”; or “the cloister of Saint Peter”], scarcely any interval separating them, and although the blaze spread so violently that it reached and consumed buildings far away, with a large part of the castle also destroyed, thanks be to God not only was the whole place rescued from the loss caused by so great a danger, but not long afterward it was also glorified by a clearer revelation of that rescue.

At that time the ancient monastery of Saint Peter, said to have been built by Saint Bertin, our patron, still stood. A very small crypt provided access to it from the oratory of Saint Martin. A certain brother named Rambertus, a monk of this place, remembering it with love because of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Bertin, its builder, used to visit it every night after completing the offices of Matins and spend the night there in psalmody and holy meditation.

During the same Lenten season, a short time after the threat of the fire mentioned above, he was engaged in these practices one night after Matins had ended. Since Matins had been sung earlier than usual that night, and he was tired from the vigils, he sought a seat and, as human weakness allows, began to sleep lightly, overcome by drowsiness.

It seemed to him that a magnificent man, clothed in a white dalmatic and deacon’s vestments, stood beside him and asked whether he was asleep. When, out of fear, he could not respond, as it seemed to him, the apparition said:

“Do not be afraid.”

Then he added:

“But do you know who I am?”

The monk replied:

“I do not know, lord.”

Then the apparition said:

“I am Brother Vincent, and I give you thanks for observing my feast and for the proven devotion that you show toward me. Are you also unaware of what those three doves, white as snow, signified when they appeared here amid the immense fury of the fire?”

The monk replied:

“It is hidden from us, holy man of God. We thought that such things had been revealed by the Lord as an auspicious sign of our protection.”

“You were right to think so,” he said. “For I was there with Saints Audomar and Bertin, and we came here to protect you. Because the sins of certain people demanded it, the Lord had handed this entire place over to the flames. But because the memory of me is celebrated here by you in such distant lands, and because the feast of my deposition is observed with such devotion, I, together with the saints whose deserving bodies are venerated here, stood before the majesty of the Lord as a timely intercessor for you. Having obtained from the most merciful Jesus the rescue of this monastery, we came here without delay for your preservation.

“Reveal all these things to Abbot Odbert and to the entire congregation of brothers. Warn them to become more corrected through these rebukes of the merciful Lord, lest they at some time be struck more severely by his correction. Do not neglect to render great thanks on my behalf to all of them: for the affection of devotion that they show toward me, and because they have instituted the observance of my feast and arranged to honor it so becomingly and humbly.”

After these words, the dreamer awoke, and the apparition vanished. His spirit, made sweet as by honey from the nectar of this revelation, was drenched in a shower of tears.

When morning came, he was uncertain whether to keep silent or make the matter public. He summoned one of the senior brothers, named Grimwaldus, and consulted him about what should be done. Grimwaldus urged and advised him that the saint’s commands must be obeyed and ought not to be concealed. Together they went to announce the matter to the Father, and afterward, at that Father’s command, to the entire small phalanx of the congregation.

The brother’s tears testified that everything being reported was true, for as he recounted it, his tears flowed in an abundant flood. When the brothers heard, amid weeping and the telling of these things, that thanks had been conveyed to them on behalf of so great a martyr, they all immediately burst into tears, fell upon the ground, and kissed it. Greatly rejoicing together over these events, they praised and blessed the most merciful Lord in songs of their lips and on harps (Sirach 39:20), for he is appeased and is said to be carried toward us in our iniquities by the intercessions and merits of his saints.

On account of this, the aforesaid abbot, together with those subject to him, carefully considered how they might more worthily exalt and venerate Christ’s foremost soldier, so that they might continually deserve so great an intercessor before the divine majesty. After completing what now remains of the oratory of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 1126C], he ordered the martyr’s altar to be established there. From that time onward, every year his feast was most devoutly and fittingly observed in white vestments.

But we, dearest brothers, having experienced the more severe correction foretold by the earlier threat—for in our own time we saw with our own eyes our entire place handed over to desolation and consumed by fire, our sins having deserved this—we must finally recognize that the time of our visitation has come. Whatever we perceive in ourselves to be displeasing to our Lord, let us hasten to remove from his sanctuary, that is, from our hearts. Let us strive to drive far from us the nations of vices that have entered into his inheritance, lest they make Jerusalem a watchman’s hut in an orchard (Psalm 78:1). [Col. 1126D]

Let us also remember the Lord’s threat against Jerusalem: that not one stone would be left upon another that would not be destroyed (Matthew 24:2), because they did not recognize the time of their visitation (Luke 29:44 [sic]). After so great a desolation by fire, now that by God’s grace our monastery and everything in it have been rebuilt and restored for the better, let us make every effort to become more chastened and corrected by this mirror. Let us cleanse ourselves day and night and drive away the armies of innumerable vices that never cease attacking the holy Jerusalem of the Lord—that is, ourselves—with Christ as our leader. Let us adorn the sanctuaries of our Lord with the beauty of holy virtues, so that we may at some time deserve his coming to us. [Col. 1127A]

Let us also continually invoke the saints and elect of God for our aid, whom through this revelation we have learned to be so ready to come to our assistance. Following their examples, let us crucify ourselves through the mortification of vices and desires, so that our Lord may possess us as children of those who have mortified themselves. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1127D] What follows also appears to have been written by another author.]

## Chapter XV. A miracle in the village of Gaumont
Part of the inheritance of our holy Father Bertin lies adjacent to the city of Noyon. For there is situated the village of Caumont, which belongs wholly by right to that same Father: for it is certified that it was handed over to him in ancient times by authoritative title. But a certain tenant of this village, [Col. 1127B] abusing his tyrannical power, oppressed their property excessively, taking it away sometimes by force, and at other times by whatever means he could. His madness therefore turned toward this crime and grew worse, so that he invaded part of the estate of that village and claimed what he had seized as subject to his own right and authority.

When the steward whom the abbot had appointed in his place to administer all the affairs of the village saw the violence of this invasion, he resisted with all his strength the man plotting such wickedness, opposed the enraged aggressor, and proclaimed that an injustice was being done to God and to the holy Father. At last, after he had protested so loudly and so often—and since several others likewise knew the truth of the matter and opposed the mad undertaking—the case came to court, for the other man placed great confidence in his own strength. The former demonstrated the cause of the injury, [Col. 1127C] while the latter denied that any injustice had been committed by him. Thus the dispute was conducted, and arguments were advanced on both sides. The case was first presented and publicly established; afterward it was confirmed by deliberation. Finally, the concluding stage of the judicial proceeding followed.

“If you deny,” said our champion, “that this estate of the village, which you unjustly claim for yourself, belongs to God’s dominion and to the right of the holy Bertin, you will nevertheless be defeated and confess it; once defeated, you will restore it to the saint and will in no way acknowledge it as yours.”

“I will stake my head,” he replied—and he pointed to his head with his right hand—“upon the danger, relying solely upon God’s justice and his own assistance.”

“And conversely,” said the other, “you will find me myself ready to fight; you will never say that I have been defeated.”

[Note: In judicial combats undertaken to settle disputed matters, pledges (*vades*) were given on both sides, so that the victorious party would have a sure security for the case. Abbot Guilbert of Nogent, in Book III of his *Life*, chapter 14: “After pledges had been given,” he says, “he attacked him, intending to fight him with his fists.” See Acheri’s notes on this passage.]

Thus pledges were given, the duel was confirmed, [Col. 1127D] and the day was fixed.

After the matter had been secured by such a legal arrangement, the steward did not forget it, but went to Abbot Odbert—for at that time he governed the monastery of Sithiu—and laid out the entire sequence of events in order. He begged him to assist him, so that on the appointed day he might either be present himself or send in his place men of good reputation; above all, he asked that the abbot himself be present.

The abbot promised that he would indeed do this and that he would assist him personally by his authority. Then, prostrate before the holy altar, he earnestly and for a long time [Col. 1128A] committed himself wholly to God’s providence and prayed that God would have mercy on him. At last, after receiving the abbot’s blessing, he returned more swiftly than usual, as if endowed with a certain agility. First, however, he repeatedly and earnestly begged the abbot not to forget him.

When the appointed day arrived, he prepared himself for the duel, yet awaited, in accordance with the promise, the arrival of some men to assist him—or of the abbot himself. After the priest had celebrated Mass, and he had devoutly completed his prayer and worthily received the Eucharist, he happened to sit outside the church upon a large stone. Turning his eyes toward the place of Sithiu mentioned above, he held out his palms and kept his face raised; moving only his lips, he cried aloud with a great and pure heart.

But, perhaps by God’s providence, so that the worthy merit of his soldier might be revealed, the abbot, [Col. 1128B] being occupied elsewhere, neglected the promise he had made. Meanwhile the adversary hurled threats at him, provoked him with words, and reproached him for delaying; several who favored the other side repeated insults and abuse, accusing him of cowardice. He nevertheless remained, waited, and prayed, paying little attention to those who tried to provoke him.

At last he burst out: “I will wait a little longer for my lord.”

Then, behold, he saw from afar two doves, whiter than snow, cleaving the air with their wings. He kept his eyes fixed upon them for a long time, wishing to know where they were directing their flight and what sign their flight might portend. For he had once heard that the merciful Father Bertin deigned to reveal himself and, in a vision, to retain the likeness of this bird.

Thus, flying swiftly, they circled the entire battle line [Col. 1128C] three times and afterward vanished from the eyes of those who were watching. At once he rose and, thundering terribly and flashing like lightning with his shield, went against the enemy with his staff. It is reported, moreover, that when he rose and struck the stone with his staff, the stone sent forth a little stream of blood.

O event worthy of being strengthened and confirmed by a second sign—marvelous to relate, marvelous to behold, blood flowing from a stone! Yet it is truly God’s nature to be able to do all things.

At last the treacherous invader, overcome by repeated blows, was defeated and thrown to the ground. Then, so badly beaten that he repeatedly declared himself vanquished, he proclaimed that he had unjustly invaded that village’s estate. Scarcely rescued from the victor’s hands, he was carried home, and three days later he died. The entire neighborhood declared that this had happened deservedly, celebrated the signs of the miracle, and devoutly honored the holy Father [Col. 1128D] Bertin by exalting him.

### Chapter XVI. A second miracle concerning the same village

Yet what sometimes causes the good to fear, and by which those striving after virtue are especially corrected and inwardly made radiant by divine grace, gives the wicked outwardly an occasion for boldness. They add sin to sin, setting truth aside; blinded by the cloud of mortal wrongdoing, they follow what is worse. In them that prophetic saying is fulfilled: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2)—that is, the wicked person persistently adds evil to evil, whether crooked or utterly depraved.

Thus another tyrant, nourished on crimes, arose in the aforesaid city of Noyon. Fierce in spirit and still more monstrous in wickedness, he thirsted for blood day and night above all others. Since his reputation for wickedness was such, he spread plots and deceptions in every direction. He caused the slaughter of the wretched people, sparing neither man nor woman nor even a little child.

But when he had already devastated most of the surrounding estates, the village of Caumont was by no means safe from his madness. It greatly feared him, and what it feared afterward came to pass. When he heard—and truly knew—that the former aggressor had been slain by the outcome of the duel, and that the holy Father Bertin avenges those who act unjustly against the village and inflict injury, his deranged mind did not in any way rest or cease from its customary rage and fury. Rather, he considered a suitable place and an appropriate time at which to invade the village.

But when he lacked any place upon which to turn the boldness of his rage—for he had already consumed nearly everything else by fire and plunder—he armed two hundred horsemen and set out toward the village of Caumont. At first, however, he advanced by indirect routes, pretending that he was hurrying elsewhere. Then, suddenly, he rushed upon the village from the opposite direction, surrounded it with armed men, and plundered all the property that was within it.

By chance, all the village’s animals—beasts of burden, sheep, and cattle—had gone out that day to pasture. When they were returning, he found them scattered about, grazing in the fields. Alas, alas! A double misfortune suddenly befell them. Whatever was better within the village was plundered; outside it, whatever cattle were grazing were driven away.

Then, behold, a monk named Winradus, a man of good memory [Col. 1129C] and worthy of praise, sent by Abbot Roderic—[Note: Roderic, formerly a monk of Saint-Vaast, was made abbot after Hemfrid in the year 1021 and died in 1043. Bovo, a son and heir worthy of such a father, succeeded him.]—and in those times useful and necessary to the Church of God and to our community, arrived at the devastated village.

When they saw him, their cries and lamentations redoubled. “Help, help, excellent man, good lord!” they repeated. “Hurry! Go after the enemy; pour out pleading words to him. We are certain that when he sees you, he will immediately return to you everything he has carried away, for he has plundered all that was within the village.”

The gentle man was inwardly moved by the magnitude of all their complaints. He quickly pursued the man at a gallop, caught up with him, and greeted him. But the other, in the arrogance of his pride and the fierceness of his spirit, did not look back at all, nor did he show reverence to the monk, God’s servant, who greeted him—not even returning a word.

The monk nevertheless pressed his horse with the spurs, controlled it with the reins, and approached more closely. He spoke more boldly: “You are unjustly carrying away this plunder from the village of the holy Father Bertin. Return it, then, lest through the rashness of your injustice, or because of the severity of your wrong, you deservedly incur God’s anger.”

The man refused to look back and disdained to give an answer to the one who pleaded with him. He did not know what to do; for through ignorance he doubted, and by doubting he remained ignorant of what course of reason or counsel he might take. He saw that he was being despised and perceived that his prayers were being scorned. Nevertheless, he considered that he might soften the man’s fierceness by offering him something.

He decided to offer him two things, a heavenly good and an earthly one. He offered the first, but did not offer the second, for there was neither the occasion, the reason, nor the time for it. In a subdued voice and humble speech, while preserving in his expression the reverence that he bore both in habit and in mind, he began to say the following:

“I promise you—indeed, I surely pledge you—two hundred Masses.”

When he wished to complete the sentence, the other, indignant, cut off the unfinished words from his mouth. To use a common and ordinary expression: the monk devoutly said “two hundred Masses,” while the other wickedly and contemptuously said “two hundred exhausted ones.” Three times, finally, he repeated the same words and urged his horse fiercely with the spurs.

The contemptuous word was still on his lips [Col. 1130B] when suddenly he fell from his horse, plunged headfirst, and drove his helmet into the ground. His neck suffered the impact of the fall, and the human and secret contents of his belly burst forth through their natural passage.

He was therefore deservedly punished and chastised with a fitting penalty from the part of his body by which insults against the holy Father had issued. Rightly and deservedly he emitted stench below, since above he had rolled a similar source of foulness upon his lips and tongue in his mouth.

Meanwhile his men continued to drive away the plunder, unaware that their lord had suffered such a fall. But when the news compelled them, they abandoned the booty and hurried to their lord. They found him dead, punished by the vengeance of heavenly anger. At last the plunder was restored to its owners; the Lord’s name was praised by all, and the protection of the holy Father Bertin was honored.

These people celebrated joyfully the happiness of a splendid triumph [Col. 1130C]; those others conducted a mournful funeral. O Lord omnipotent, glorious in his saints! O God, wondrous in the height of his majesty and in the power of his greatness! Who would doubt that this palm of noble triumph may be ascribed to the merits of the holy Father Bertin?

As a testimony to the faith, therefore, the monk arrived, approached humbly, and poured out pleading words before God, who never despises those who hope in him, always humbles the proud, and gives grace to the humble, repaying each according to his works; he lives and reigns forever and ever.

### Chapter XVII. The third miracle of Saint Bertin, concerning the village of Caumont in the time of Abbot Bovo

A certain man named Bodera was acting as deputy in the affairs of a certain powerful lord who claimed for himself the advocacy of the village belonging by its own right to Saint Bertin, called Caumont. Since he desired both to be feared and to please, he oppressed the villagers excessively—indeed, beyond measure—with labor imposed upon them.

Because of this undertaking and the injustice of so great a dispute, a certain monk named Heribert, who succeeded Abbot Bovo in governing this monastery, took charge of the village by order of the aforementioned Bovo, of venerable memory, and repeatedly tried to admonish this man to desist from his wicked conduct and from oppressing everyone.

[Note: That is, in the year 1065, according to Iperius, chapters 37 and 38.]

But, as if fearing the monk who openly accused him of crime, he fled from him, while secretly slandering him and craftily preparing schemes against him. The monk, distressed by these matters, went to the man’s lord and disclosed both the wrong done to his people and the wrong done to himself.

“I myself,” he said, “will first deal with this man by threatening him; and if he continues to commit such acts, he will suffer financial loss.”

When the monk was returning, the other man mentioned above happened to arrive. His lord said to him: “The monk Heribert is angry with you, saying that you subject the peasants to my service.”

The man returned armed with his lord’s command and spewed forth the evil of hidden poison. For he seized the monk’s oxen, which were grazing in a field, subjected them to his lord’s service, and kept them for three full days. When it pleased him, he returned them, as usually happens, extremely thin and much afflicted by so many labors.

The monk was deeply angered and attacked the wicked man with words:

“Until this time our estate has been free from every service and has remained under its own authority; none of those who came before you ever dared to claim any right or exercise any force of seizure over it. Why, then, did you drive away our oxen and claim them for the service of another?”

Little wonder, indeed, that a wicked man utters perverse things with his mouth; this was a still greater outrage, as though he had said: “If your Saint Bertin were an ox, he would be yoked to my yoke and groan under labor, since you complain that your oxen have sweated at my work.”

But the monk said: “What did you say, wicked man? Even if you had considered what is unlawful to say, you would never have uttered it openly. Suffer, wretched man, the penalty you deserve; you will be punished by the rod of heavenly anger.”

As the monk, greatly angered by these words, turned away, the wicked man was struck with a deserved and fitting blow. For his face was immediately twisted backward, so that the back of his head appeared to be his forehead, and his forehead his occiput, while his face was distorted from its proper form. His neck was crooked and swollen; his lips were likewise swollen and turned in a direction different from that which they should have taken; and the pupils of his eyes were turned backward, so that he looked in the opposite direction.

And what more should I relate? Marvelous to say, and even more marvelous to see, those who looked upon him could discern nothing human in him. Thus he was carried home. Emitting the bellowing of bulls, he stirred the entire neighborhood by the torment of his punishment. It was misery itself to look upon the man.

At last, at his own request and that of others, and because he wished to see the man punished, our monk Heribert came there with others. When the afflicted man perceived his presence—for he could not recognize him by sight, only by his voice—he earnestly begged him to pray for him, asking again and again.

Moved by compassion for the wretched man—for who among mortals could see him in such a condition and not pity him?—Heribert asked whether he wished from then on to repent and thoroughly correct his former life.

“Let this same affliction strike and punish me incurably,” he replied, “if, once soundly healed, I fail to reform in every respect.”

The good man therefore believed his promise, returned immediately, and prayed. The man was restored to health. On the following day he appeared dressed in fine clothing, stronger and healthier than before.

Everyone who had known him when he was afflicted marveled that he had recovered so suddenly. But he himself invented another explanation, composing a story and twisting his words away from the truth.

When a man grows accustomed to standing against the truth by lying, constant practice nourishes boldness; boldness doubles the crime, and the crime brings a deserved death. Before three days had passed, he seized the oxen of a poor man, subjected them to the authority of a false claim of right, and kept them laboring, according to his pleasure and for as long as the time allowed, under excessive toil.

He had not yet returned the oxen and was perhaps already considering undertaking still greater actions when he was suddenly struck by the same affliction as before. He fell to the ground and again seemed not to be a man or to utter human sounds. Instead of human speech he produced bellowing; instead of lamentation he imitated the fury of wild beasts. He begged his friends to pray for him, but it did not help. He pleaded with messengers to have the monk come to visit him, but he did not deserve even that.

Thus, on the very day when he was struck again by the same illness, he lost the life he had previously cast aside and saw, encountered, and suffered the death he had pursued.

### Chapter XVIII. The discovery of Saint Bertin’s body

In our own times, because of the iniquities we had committed, divine vengeance, as had been shown by a heavenly oracle and as we find recorded in our memory of Saint Vincent the martyr, hung over us as a consequence of divine indignation. It would have struck us even to the soul, unless that same holy martyr, together with our holy patrons Audomar and Bertin, had risen as intercessors for us before the Lord.

But the merciful Lord, moved to compassion by the intercession of his saints, postponed the correction of his indignation for a time, awaiting the fullness of confession and improvement in holy conduct. Terrified unanimously by this rebuke and led for a time to repentance, we ought to have striven with holy zeal to attain completely the sincerity of the new man; yet some returned once more to the mire.

At last the heavenly Judge, provoked by the enormity of our iniquities, determined miserably to give his outer house over to fire for destruction, as he had long before threatened divinely. And, as it is written, “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9:6): the houses of God were suddenly attacked by fire. In its rapacity the fire swept around the boundaries of the entire cloister and destroyed everything without interruption.

After these things had been consumed, on the following night one of our elders dreamed that he saw a magnificent man standing in a certain place of the cloister, clothed in a whiteness like snow and with a face flashing like lightning. After carefully looking around at everything, he extended his right hand and blessed the entire site of the monastery.

From this it is also inferred that the place had already been cleansed of certain offenses and would eventually, by God’s mercy, be restored to its former or even greater beauty.

Meanwhile, with our buildings laid bare, necessity again compelling us, the roofs were repaired and placed upon the walls, which still stood on both sides. When everything had been repaired, or rather whitewashed, as circumstances and our ability allowed, it became necessary to move the altar of Saint Martin, the principal altar [Note: The cardinal altar, called below the chief altar in chapter 31, is the first altar in the apse or at the front of the basilica, placed behind the greater altar. The morning Mass customarily celebrated there was called the cardinal Mass; see Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 7. Certainly the altar of Saint Martin still exists in that same place, and the first Mass is celebrated there every day. The cardinal altar is called the principal altar below.] in order to build a crypt there. This could not properly be done without the presence of a bishop.

For this reason the bishop was summoned and came readily enough. He arrived with many people to demolish the altar, overturned it, and returned home. While the ground was being dug more deeply at that place to lay the foundations, and a great quantity of earth was being removed, behold, directly beneath the consecrated site of the altar a certain subterranean chamber was encountered, carefully constructed of hard stones, tiles, and ancient cement.

[Note: *Apogaeum*: a subterranean vault, a crypt.]

It was not permitted either to cover it again or to uncover it further, lest, if it were opened and dismantled without the testimony of good men, or if the brothers of that place tried to conceal it for some time after it had been covered, they should be accused through the slanders of any rivals.

At last, after the matter had been discussed with prudent men, while several suitable witnesses stood around, they approached with processions, prepared crosses, and candles. Meanwhile the brothers sang litanies as was fitting. To the wonder of all, the subterranean chamber was uncovered, and with the great labor and sweat of many people it was scarcely broken open with iron tools from the first hour of the day until evening.

When at last it was opened, a leaden chest appeared to the eyes of everyone present to be enclosed within it. When the chest was opened, the venerable remains of a certain saint were revealed to all standing around. Beneath the saint’s right shoulder a silver cross was found and brought out and presented to the brothers. It bore only this inscription of three words:

**Saint Bertin, abbot.**

### Chapter XIX. The miracle that occurred at the very moment when the holy man’s body was discovered; Pope Leo’s authorization for its elevation

When the body of the most blessed Father had been found and identified by such signs—more precious than gold and topaz—and when until then the whole earth had been parched and ruined by a long and grievous drought, behold, at that very moment, after many thunderclaps and flashing lightning, a great rainfall followed. When the earth had been sufficiently drenched, it began, revived by fresh hope, to expand once more toward new crops for its cultivators.

The discovery of this most sacred body took place in the year 1050 of the assumed humanity of Christ, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

After the sacred body had been revealed and uncovered, as has been said, it was ordered that the same urn be covered again and that the burial chamber be rebuilt as it had previously been, until the elders could deliberate what should be done with it.

At that time Lord Pope Leo, called Bruno, presided over the holy Roman Church. The reputation of his wisdom and probity breathed throughout the world the fragrance of a sweet perfume. Because of the urgent necessity that the brothers of this place might be strengthened by the authority of their superiors, a trustworthy envoy was sought and found and sent to him, so that whatever the apostolic lord, together with men of weightier counsel, judged outstanding concerning these matters, he would not delay to communicate to them in the name of the Lord through that envoy.

When the envoy had approached him and had been admitted into his presence, having received permission to speak, he briefly explained the event to the lord pope, who was at that time occupied with many affairs. He displayed before his eyes the testimonies of Scripture and the cross found with the sacred body, which he had brought with him as evidence.

When these things had been seen, and when they had been shown to those who happened to be present with the pope—those who had then assembled for the Roman council, namely the patriarch of Aquileia, archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, and other prominent men—the pope said that in the face of such signs of truth they ought by no means to doubt, but rather to believe more securely and firmly. This was especially so because many historical records make it possible to find that nearly the whole territory of Gaul, and particularly our region and the other coastal areas, had been devastated by frequent Danish incursions, plundering, and fires. For this reason, some bodies of saints had been transferred from less secure places, while others had been secretly buried, as is clearly known to have happened with Saint Bertin, either within walls or beneath the earth.

When these responses from the apostolic lord had been reported by their messenger to Abbot Bovo and to the brothers of this place, Lord Wido, archbishop of Reims, and Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne, were invited, together with many distinguished persons. Various abbots from different places also arrived with them, and countless multitudes of people hurried here.

### Chapter XX. The elevation of our same protector, Bertin

In the year 1052 of the incarnate Word, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, after bishops, abbots, monks, and canons had assembled, and certain prominent laymen had also been admitted as witnesses, they approached the holy place in procession. The singing of the litanies was begun, and workers were ordered to excavate the chest containing the sacred body.

### Chapter XXI. The miracle that occurred while the most holy body was being raised from the earth

When the limbs of the most holy Father Bertin were being brought out by the hands of bishops and abbots, and were being venerated as was fitting and purified by sprinkling with water and wine, a certain cleric named Berwoldus stood apart. He was deprived of the sight of one eye.

Previously he had possessed equal clarity of vision in both eyes, but some time before, because of an illness whose nature I do not know, he had had a vein near one eye cut in order to be treated. As a result, he had lost all sight in that eye. Because of shame, however, he had concealed this from nearly everyone except a few members of his household.

He earnestly begged for the protection of Saint Bertin, so that through the Lord he might recover the sight he had lost. He greatly desired to have his eye touched by any of the sacred limbs that were being handled there, but he feared that he would not be permitted to approach.

While the brothers were devoutly occupied in singing psalms for so great an event, the cleric, who lacked the sight of one eye and hesitated to approach the sacred limbs, begged a certain brother to touch one of them lightly with his fingers and to make the sign of it upon his blinded eye.

When this had been done, he was immediately endowed with the sight for which he had long waited.

What the Lord had permitted to happen for the praise of his name and for the revelation of the saint’s merit, Berwold himself wished to keep silent out of foolish shame. But afterward, perhaps at that very time, he murmured to a certain Arnold who was closely attached to him that it was a favorable omen that he had been admitted there, because through the touch of the saint then present he had received back the sight he had long ago lost. He earnestly charged Arnold to keep this secret and never reveal it to anyone.

But the other did not agree to conceal such insensibility on his part. He immediately disclosed the matter to those standing around. When one of the brothers learned that it had truly happened, he extended his hand and signaled silence to everyone. Then he proclaimed that the man who had long been condemned to the sight of only one eye had now been restored, through the saint’s merits, by the gift of the sight for which he had waited.

### Chapter XXII. A second miracle performed on the same day

A certain woman stood outside the church, in the atrium, with her son, whose arms and legs were contracted, intending to pray to Saint Bertin for his healing. Previously, when she had considered carrying the twelve-year-old boy to Cologne, to seek the intercession of Saint Heribert and the other saints resting there, so that he might perhaps deserve to obtain the use of his limbs through their merits, the boy—although still a child—had said that he had already been warned three times in a vision not to be carried anywhere before first coming to Saint Bertin’s side to test his merits.

When he had also come there in a vision and prayed, he said that he had seen four very white doves flying away; the monastery itself and the altar had trembled like a leaf, and he had prostrated himself before it. Without delay he had risen from there sound through the merits of the saint.

When the boy had reported this to his mother, and the fame of the saint’s elevation was already spreading, she hurried there with the boy and many companions. Awaiting the Lord’s intervention through Saint Bertin before the doors of the monastery, she remained there humbly with her son.

When she pressed through the crowd trying to kiss the saint’s bier, and, after being pushed back, returned again, making every effort to bring the boy up to the saint’s bier, God granting her request, the boy’s arms and legs were straightened and he was restored to health.

When many people saw this, some of those standing nearby went to the aid of the oppressed mother, while others lifted up the boy. Then the cry of the countless, excited multitude rose up, and throughout the crowd God, wondrous in his saints (Ps. 67:36), was proclaimed. They had known the boy only a little earlier as scarcely able to crawl; now they saw him walking before their eyes, with his mother leading the way.

Meanwhile the brothers were singing the Mass in the choir, and the sweet report of this event reached them. While they were still asking one another whether it was true, the boy, healed through the merits of Saint Bertin, entered. Standing upright in their midst, led by his mother, he prostrated himself before the altar according to his ability in order to give thanks to God.

After the Gospel had been read, and with the lord archbishop present before the altar beginning the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, while the choir followed repeatedly, one could see many rejoicing with Christ over what had occurred and many others weeping for joy.

### Chapter XXIII. The third miracle on the same day, concerning a blind woman

The hymn had not yet been completed, and many were still weeping for joy, when it was announced that a certain blind woman, a resident of this city and therefore well known to all the brothers, had also recovered her sight. She herself came before everyone bearing this report and joined the boy, prostrating herself for the praise of God and the proclamation of Saint Bertin’s merit.

No account would suffice fully to convey with what exultation and with what solemnity people rejoiced and delighted in the Lord on that day. When these things had been accomplished, that most celebrated day was brought to an end with indescribable glory.

On the following day they again assembled, and a written record serving as testimony to the event—containing its order, time, persons, and witnesses—was read aloud before an innumerable crowd. After it had been read, it was placed together with the cross that had been found [Col. 1136C] and with the sacred body. The document, thus arranged, was sealed with the seal of the supreme prelate; the chest was closed, tightened with iron bands and nails, sewn and bound, and made inseparably secure. Amid the rejoicing of the innumerable multitude, it was carried with the other relics into the Holy of Holies, where it was to be honored.

[Note: That is, into the sanctuary or the place of the principal altar. Iperius, chapter 28, says that Mathilda gave a curtain of marvelous size and workmanship, which still survives today and is the one we use during Holy Lent, separating the Holy of Holies.]

There it is still venerated and, with the Lord’s favor, will be venerated forever and ever. Thereafter the supreme prelate and our lord bishop ordered that the day of the sacred elevation be commemorated and venerated by all the people of this diocese and celebrated every year with great devotion.

When these matters had been completed, and the lords, bishops, and abbots had obtained some of the holy relics, each receiving a gift, they returned home in great joy.

### Chapter XXIV. A certain blind man enlightened by a tooth of Saint Bertin

One of them, namely the abbot of Saint Valery—[Note: This was Wazo, abbot of the monastery of Leucone or Valery at the mouth of the Somme into the Ocean, mentioned below in chapter 31]—having obtained a portion of the holy relics, returned home after the solemn celebration of the sacred elevation.

A certain peasant, blind because the pupils of both eyes were covered with thick spots, approached him, being led by a boy who directed his steps, intending to ask for some kind of treatment.

The abbot said to him: “I know of no remedy that can bring healing to such an illness, except the intervention of our all-powerful and saving Lord Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, very recently I joined several people in the most holy service of the elevation of a famous saint, and although unworthy I took part in such a sacred undertaking. There the Lord revealed to all of us how great that saint’s merit was by numerous and marvelous miracles.

“Returning here, I was also enriched by the gift of one of his sacred teeth. I brought it back rejoicing in such a gift. If you believe that you can be healed through the merits of that saint, I will order it to be brought before you.”

“I believe,” the man replied.

The abbot immediately ordered it to be brought in the sight of those present. When it had been brought and applied to both his eyes, his eyes were instantly opened and he began to see clearly. After blessing the Lord’s name for this, he returned home safe and joyful.

### Chapter XXV. A certain woman bound with iron chains and released at the tomb of the holy man

A certain woman from Lorraine had both arms bound with iron chains as a penance. In this monastery, in the year 1125 of the incarnate Word, while many people stood by, she was released from those chains through the prayers of our most holy Father Bertin.

### Chapter XXVI. A certain girl whose sinews were contracted

A certain girl named Goduina had sound limbs but suffered from contracted sinews. At the tomb of the blessed man, in the year of grace 1126, her legs were straightened.

### Chapter XXVII. The abbot of Lobbes

[Col. 1137C]

A certain abbot of Lobbes named Leonius, later summoned and appointed to govern this monastery of Sithiu, built a church in the parish of Saint Bertin, in the territory of Furnes, in the year of grace 1135, without the consent of the chapter of that saint. A violent wind shook it through the merits of the aforementioned saint and made it fly up from the ground, so that not even a joint of its timbers remained attached to another.

### Chapter XXVIII. A certain abbot of Clairmarais

In the year 1171 of the assumed humanity of Christ, during the time of Lord Godescal, of good memory, abbot of this place, an event occurred worthy of renowned and illustrious remembrance, and terrifying and dreadful to all who invaded the possessions of the people of Sithiu.

For not long after David had been consecrated abbot of the church of Clairmarais, he raised his heel against the church of Blessed Bertin and undertook to construct watercourses and ditches through the middle of the land of the aforesaid church, in the village of Arques. That village is known to have belonged properly and freely to the same church from ancient times, without disturbance by any claim.

Not content with this presumption, he entered the church of Saint Bertin and arrogantly and proudly threatened that he would carry out, according to his will, what he had presumptuously begun, even though the monks opposed him. But divine vengeance, intolerant of such arrogance and presumption, followed not long afterward, so that this was fulfilled:

“Stop speaking grandly: God breaks every proud man.” For on the following day, when he had undertaken the aforesaid work and was about to instruct his laborers according to his own pleasure in making the watercourse, his horse began to kick beneath him at that very place, and he was thrown to the ground. There he broke his leg; though he had arrived sound on horseback, he was carried home in a litter on the hands of his servants. From then on he desisted from invading our land, leaving, as has been said, a terrifying and dreadful example for invaders of the lands of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Of a certain man who did not observe the saint’s feast.

In the town of Saint-Omer, in the year of the incarnate Word 1214, a certain man named Michael, by profession a barber, was rebuked by some of his neighbors because he did not observe the feast of the saint and nevertheless continued to work. He reviled the saint in words and burst into insults. Seized by a demon, he lay for a long time bound with ropes in a wooden vessel of the sort in which dough is kneaded. After he had recovered some measure of health through the mercy of God and the patronage of the saint, we saw him improved in our church, before the holy altar in the choir, with Lord Abbot John III and many monks standing by; he was humbly and devoutly entreating God’s mercy and imploring the intercession of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXX. Of a certain priest who cursed Saint Bertin and everything belonging to him.

[Col. 1138C]

Since the priest of Remynghem was not permitted to eat in the refectory on the deposition-feast of Blessed Bertin, he ate angrily in the town. As he was returning home, he began, in a boat with the canons of Watten, to curse God’s saint Bertin, to excommunicate him, and to curse everything belonging to him. The sword of God, taking vengeance upon him, cut him almost in half when he was submerged in the river, having been thrown into it—he did not know by whom—unless the canons had dragged him out. Because he repeated this with a blasphemous mouth and a wicked heart, the same thing happened again.

[Col. 1138D]

Likewise, concerning another priest who blasphemed God’s saint.

In the same year, John, a priest from Rubrouck, was playing with someone at dice—or, I do not know, at chess. When he lost, he began to curse God’s saint Bertin and everything belonging to him. After uttering many words of blasphemous insult, he heard a sound as though a powerful wind were coming; receiving a great slap on the cheek, he fell back upon the chessboard or gaming table, and remained for three days without food, hearing nothing and seeing nothing.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A copy of the translation of Saint Bertin.

“Peter, by the grace of God bishop of the Morini, and Asso, by the grace of God bishop of Arras, to all the faithful of Christ to whom knowledge of the present document comes, eternal salvation in Christ.

“Since, for the honor of God, who is believed to be honored in his saints, a translation was made of the body of Blessed Bertin, abbot, from the shrine in which it had lain for one hundred and eighty-five years, as could clearly be established from a written document found there, that most holy body was found carefully wrapped and bound in the aforesaid shrine with silk cloths, although greatly worn by age, and marked with authentic seals. When it had been unbound and opened, a silver cross was found among the sacred bones, on which the following words had plainly been inscribed in capital letters: SAINT BERTIN, ABBOT. Then, when the searchers examined the aforesaid cloths more carefully, they found hidden within them the document mentioned above, whose text was as follows:

> ‘In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, in the fifth indiction, while Henry was reigning as king of the Franks in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and in the eighteenth year of the episcopate of Lord Wido, archbishop of the Church of Reims, and the twenty-ninth year of Drogo, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne, while the illustrious marquis Baldwin—namely, Baldwin of Lille—held the principality of the region of Flanders in the seventieth year, and in the fifteenth year of the rule of Lord Abbot Bovo, the body of the most blessed Father Bertin, which had been found not quite two years earlier beneath the altar of Saint Martin, was raised on the sixth day before the Nones of May by those same lords, the bishops, from the leaden shrine and from the place where it had formerly been translated and deposited by Saint Folquin.

> ‘The cause of this discovery—or rather, of this raising—was the following. The monastery, devastated by fire, threatened ruin. While a crypt was being constructed for its restoration and its foundations were being laid, the mass of that most holy body unexpectedly appeared. It had lain for almost one hundred and forty-nine years in the sarcophagus in which it had been buried by Helfrid, whom he himself, while still alive, had appointed abbot; but in the leaden shrine in which, as we have said, Saint Folquin had placed it beneath the altar, it had remained for two hundred and six years, until our own time.

> ‘It was raised in the presence of men of good reputation and exemplary life: namely, Wido, the archbishop, and Drogo, the bishop; in the presence of Lady Athleta, countess and wife of the aforesaid marquis, who most devoutly served God and Saint Bertin in this undertaking; and also in the presence of these abbots: Bovo, abbot of this place; Heremar, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius; Renuld, abbot of Saint Winnoc; Gervin, abbot of Saint Richarius; Folbert, abbot of Saint Bavo; Heribert, abbot of Saint Josse; Wazo, abbot of Saint Valery; and Alfrid, abbot of Saint Wulmar. Also present were the canons of the Church of Reims: Ulric, Constantius, and Hugh; the clerics of the Church of Thérouanne: John the archdeacon, Theodoric, Gozelin, Baldwin, and many others; and from Saint-Omer: Regard, Norbert, Aubert, Odbert, Marger, and Rembold. In the presence of all these, together with an innumerable multitude, he was raised and placed in this shrine, blessed in every respect. Amen.’

[Note: [Col. 1139C] Read Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, and wife of Baldwin of Lille. After her husband’s death in 1057, she founded a convent of nuns at Messines. Visiting the thresholds of the apostles devoutly, she received the widowed habit from Pope Alexander II. Thus she returned to her monastery at Messines, where she lived most humbly and died full of works of piety; she was buried there. So Iperius, part II, chapter 38.]

“On that same day the Lord also worked three miracles through his merits. Accordingly, the aforesaid body was transferred by us from the aforementioned shrine into another new one, suitably, and was placed in a new reliquary of gold and silver and precious stones, honorably prepared for this purpose, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, namely on the fourth [Note: [Col. 1140C] Read fifth: for in that year Sunday had the letter D.] weekday before the feast of Mary Magdalene, in the year of grace 1237, while the most excellent king of the Franks, Louis, son of Louis, was reigning, and his illustrious brother Robert held the county of Artois at the beginning of his county. All this was done under the guidance and with the cooperation of the grace of God our Savior, who will restore the bodies of the saints, conformed to the glory of his own body.

“This translation was solemnly carried out by us and through us in the church of the aforesaid saint, in the presence of many abbots and provosts, together with other prelates of the churches and other good men, while James, then the venerable abbot of the Church of Blessed Bertin, presided. As testimony to this matter, we caused the present document to be confirmed with our seals, in the year of the Lord 1237, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.”

(Here an index of the chapters is added in manuscript codices.)

[Col. 1141]

## Account of the discovery and raising of Saint Bertin the abbot, which took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, composed by Bovo, abbot of Sithiu.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, third century, part III, p. 153, from manuscript codices of Sithiu and Clairmarais.)

### Letter of Bovo to Wido, archbishop of Reims

[Col. 1141A]

To the most distinguished lord Wido, archbishop, Brother Bovo, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, sends a blessing among the blessed.

Since, lord Father, you have been established as the more eminent member in the body of the holy Church of God under Christ, its supreme head, and since, so to speak, you ought to be joined and attached to the head as its neck, I desire your Reverence to flourish in every respect in the health of both parts, namely of soul and body, so that we, the most remote and feeble members, may through your salutary mediation be incorporated with our Lord, the sound Head. Otherwise—God forbid!—if we act differently, we may be cut apart by his penetrating sword, according to the saying of the Gospel: “I have not come,” he says, “to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34).

That I have addressed your sublimity in such words does not arise so much from presumption as from the prompting of charity, which, according to the Apostle, hopes all things, believes all things, and endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). For the safety of the shepherd is the secure hope of the flock. After I had deserved to be commended to the kindness of your paternal charity, although I may have been of very little use, I have nevertheless always been concerned for your welfare. Whenever those coming to us from those regions arrived, I used to inquire about your circumstances; when I learned that your nobility was safe and well, I rejoiced, and when I learned that it was ill, I grieved, since you are regarded as our spiritual father and supreme shepherd.

Moreover, your paternal devotion, which formerly served so readily and devoutly in the causes surrounding the raising of the body of Saint Bertin, has made us liable to your fidelity by a weightier debt, so that we ought continually to sigh for your welfare and to pour the same constant prayers into the ears of God. This matter also, as your charity remembers, compelled me to make my insignificance known to your magnificence. For this reason, when I had visited your fatherhood to seek your counsel on the matter, I returned home happy—not only instructed by sufficiently useful advice for my investigation, but also encouraged by the promise, which I had hoped for, of your coming.

There, lord Father, when on the appointed day you were present together with the holy assembly of your clergy, and when you yourself served with sufficient devotion at the raising of the sacred limbs, no one with your experience can know better how honorably and wonderfully that celebrated raising of the saint was accomplished. For it was exalted by the power of your high office and supported by your authority.

Since this is so, the loving insistence of our brothers urges my ignorant hand to describe the event itself and make it known to posterity—not because I possess any knowledge superior to theirs, since they all surpass me in uprightness and some also in intellectual insight, but so that the sequence of the holy raising may be considered more worthy if it is marked by a title of greater distinction, namely the name of an abbot.

Yet I neither wholly resist nor wholly yield to their efforts; rather, I leave the matter to the more judicial judgment of your decision and declare that I will follow whatever your fatherly highness judges most appropriate. If, however, you deem the matter worthy of being reported and compel my insignificance by the commanding power of your authority to record it, I shall promptly obey your holy commands to the best of my ability. Whatever I have gathered comes, in some fashion, into the hands of your paternal excellence: let whatever is superfluous be pierced by the obelisks of apostolic authority, and let what has been said too briefly be clarified by asterisks. Thus, just as the magnificent and awaited presence of your holy authority made that sacred raising glorious, so may its record be strengthened by the same supporter and presiding authority.

### Wido’s reply

[Col. 1142C]

Wido, archbishop of Reims, to the venerable abbot Bovo.

Since it is honorable to recount the works of the Lord, we consider it fitting to respond to your inquiry, which you have poured out before us concerning the description both of the discovery and of the raising of the body of Saint Bertin. We rejoice and judge that the event should be committed to written record, since it has pleased God to distinguish your church so sublimely.

And as you indicated in your letter, when these matters have been written out in your style, we command that they be referred to us. We enjoin your fatherhood to describe them exactly as they happened, so that when your account reaches our hands nothing will need to be added or removed. Such things must plainly be described faithfully and truthfully, so that they may please the one who makes himself known as the Truth. Farewell.

### Bovo’s dedicatory letter to Wido

To the glorious lord Wido, archbishop by the grace of God, and to all the clergy of the holy Church of Reims entrusted to his care, Brother Bovo, a sinner whom they call abbot of Sithiu, wishes a blessed portion with the sheep of the right hand.

Having received your reverent command, most magnificent prelate, by which you order the raising of our most holy Father Bertin to be begun with the record of our poor style, I undertake to narrate it as best I can: prompted by the pious devotion owed to that saint, by the injunction of your apostolic authority, and by the daily persistence of our brothers’ entreaties. I do not wish to appear opposed to the command of your highness.

Although I am less than capable, I shall attempt the task according to the measure of my small intelligence. As I prepare to run along the path of truth and have already spread the sails before the winds with the hands of my weakness, if perhaps the whirlwinds of a hostile storm threaten shipwreck and danger, may I be received and refreshed in the shelter of your harbor, and defended by the protection of your faithful hand. It is fitting that I, confident in the protection of your nobility, should be guarded by the wall of your defense, since at your command I have undertaken, fragile though I am, to carry so great a burden.

Next, I humbly beseech you, sons of the holy Church of Reims, our lords: remembering the bond of brotherhood, be my support now. Whenever this heap of our foolishness, extended by an apostolic right hand, reaches your hands, do not turn your reverent gaze away from it. Rather, at the command of the lord archbishop, do not refuse to season whatever is tasteless in it with the salt of your expertise. Thus may you help brothers bear one another’s burdens at the Apostle’s command (Galatians 6:2).

This work has not been gathered so that the skill of the learned may honor it, but so that our simpler brethren may be occupied in meditating upon it, or at least so that the material for dictation already prepared may somehow be available to some learned person. In this way, according to the Apostle, who did not labor for himself alone but for all (1 Corinthians 15:10), the sequence of our discourse may be arranged for all who earnestly desire to labor in Christ. Let it imitate, as far as we can, both the example of the Just One and the mirror of a good man.

Let it therefore be such that the delicate may find what they desire, and travelers burdened by hunger and thirst may find something by which they may reconcile the Lord to themselves. Who they are, and with what provisions they should be supplied, is suitably explained by the Egyptian boy who, wearied on the road, was abandoned by his Amalekite master. Found by David while David was pursuing him and sufficiently refreshed with food, he was not only joined to him in pursuing the Amalekite, but, under his guidance, that impious man was found and killed.

When some were invited to these provisions and offered various excuses for their circumstances, the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame, found at the crossroads, were admitted. Let our simpler brethren sit down with these; let them alone rejoice to share in taking our milk. And lest your magnificence, apostolic men, should grow weary of the sufficiency of those rich foods, be willing for a little while to attend with your companions to these vegetables of our lowliness, until the judgment of your examination determines whether they are considered worthy or unworthy even for the use of little children.

Therefore, with the affection of a child who wants to repeat whatever he has heard but is not yet able fully to form words, I recall that certain congruities of events have previously come to me through written accounts. I have seen many of them myself, and have learned some from the reports of serious and respectable men. I would rather stammer out a preliminary account of them here than remain silent, so that, when these things are joined to others, it may shine more clearly to everyone how the Lord has gloriously displayed his mercies toward us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Thus the whole community of our religious house may more worthily rejoice in the praises of God and of his saint Bertin.

Next, let the diligent reader not be angry with me if I first set forth the purpose of this little work for the benefit of our simpler brethren, lest, when they encounter passages harsher than usual, they become frightened, but rather understand more fully how and to what they refer. The labor of bees is sweeter to us if a bad taste has first touched our mouths. The stars shine more gratefully when the south wind has driven away the thickest clouds.

In the same way, as I am about to hand down to the memory of posterity the Lord’s threats and chastisements, together with the events and the subsequent advance of divine mercy, I shall piously and justly say many times that our Lord, the righteous judge, terrified us, who were guilty in many ways, sometimes with his threats, and often corrected us worthily with the harsh blows of his rebukes. Thus, after being embittered for a time by a taste of that same evil, we might later be gladdened by the more welcome gifts bestowed upon the flock of God. Always remembering the visitation so often made upon us, may we be more corrected throughout the remaining years of our lives.

Nevertheless, let no one’s ears be offended by these scourges of the Lord’s denunciation. Rather, let all who have corrected themselves through them rejoice that they are to be received as sons, remembering what holy Scripture teaches: “The Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6), and so forth.

## The author’s narrative

### 1

It is very well known to all the sons of the holy Church of God that Jerusalem once, as the Gospel’s testimony confirms, moved our Savior to compassionate lamentation; that he foretold all the disasters of that city by threatening its future ruin; and that afterward everything happened according to the Lord’s prediction.

Likewise, in our own times, because of the demands of our iniquities, as was shown by a heavenly oracle and as we find recorded in the memory of Saint Vincent the martyr, divine vengeance was hanging over us in indignation and would have struck us to the very soul, unless that same holy martyr, together with our holy patrons Audomar and Bertin, had risen before the Lord as intercessors for us.

But the merciful Lord, moved to pity by the devout intervention of his saints, postponed for a time the correction arising from his indignation, awaiting the repentance of our confession and improvement in holy conduct, for as the prophet recalls: “He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18:23).

Thus, terrified exceedingly by this rebuke and led for a time to repentance, although we ought to strive with holy zeal to the very end for the sincerity of the new man, some returned again, in the manner of swine, to the mud of their former ways. At last the heavenly Judge, provoked by the enormity of our iniquities, had determined miserably to deliver our outer house to the fire for consumption, since, under the pressure of our evil deeds, it had been made into a den of thieves, just as he had long before threatened.

Let no one doubt whether the disasters of this conflagration came upon us by chance or because of the matter just mentioned. For when the fire arose and grew far from the monastery, the wind rose with it and strengthened it. Crossing several buildings, it drove toward the church with a more violent blast—or rather, with sin pressing it onward. And as it is said, “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6), the seats of God were suddenly attacked by fire and lamentably melted in the voracity of the devouring flame. What had been accomplished through long and great labor was then, alas, consumed in a single hour of a single day.

Afterward, in its rapacity, the fire circled the boundaries of the entire cloister and destroyed everything, leaving nothing untouched. Yet, as it is said, “Nothing happens on earth without cause” (Job 5:6), and we must not believe that the Lord allowed his house to perish for no reason. Rather, it was so that it might be thoroughly purified from its long-standing evils, and so that those dwelling within his inner house might be deterred from their wicked actions, lest, if they refused to renounce their sins, they should afterward be punished more severely by the condemnation of eternal fire.

Here also comes to mind the fact that this disaster befell us during the observance of Lent, when all who practice the sound faith take particular care to punish the faults of other times and to cleanse themselves from them by worthy repentance. Thus, yes thus, may the patient, most merciful, and truthful Lord have examined this monastery and its monks at that time, striking us with so great a punishment of fire for all the impurities of sin; and may he, if only he wills it, make us more corrected for the remainder of our lives, so that, made more disciplined by this extinguishable fire, we may escape the torments of the eternal and inextinguishable fire!

For God’s wisdom often moderates the sending of his rod when he corrects, so that it may piously punish what must be corrected in those who have sinned, and afterward, within the very chastisement, foster by his mercy something good, which he reveals at the proper time, as the diligent reader will find in its place.

### 2

After these things had been consumed, on the following night one of our elders—whom, because he is still alive, I do not wish to name—seemed in a dream to see a magnificent man, snow-white in the brightness of his clothing and lightning-like in the splendor of his face. He stood in a certain place of the cloister, and, after carefully surveying everything, blessed the whole monastery with his right hand extended.

From this it may also be inferred that the place, having already been purified from certain offenses, would eventually, through God’s mercy, be restored to its former or even greater beauty.

Meanwhile, after we had been exposed to the open sky and the walls had been stripped of the dignity of their roofs, necessity soon compelled us to repair the roofs and to place them upon the walls, which still stood in some fashion. What more need be said? After everything had been repaired, or rather whitewashed, according to the circumstances and our ability, some of our number soon forgot the visitation and returned irreverently to the practices they had renounced. The dregs of their evil deeds had not yet been emptied, and at last they were caught in the snare of diabolical wickedness.

Then, behold, the divine majesty, intending to terrify us, after the passage of some years brandished its sword against us (Psalm 7:13) and struck a large part of our community with sudden pestilence, even to death. There was then no rest for the dying; day after day they fell like diseased sheep. While the burial of one or more of the dead was still being attended to, behold, the sudden deaths of others were announced.

Meanwhile, many, afflicted by the terror of the same pestilence and each fearing sudden death for himself, began again to feel deep repentance for their sins and to appease the face of our Lord, embittered by their evil deeds, with the innermost sighs of their tears. Then one could see the apostolic saying fulfilled: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

Nor was anything of anyone’s private property kept back. Every little possession was brought forward and laid before Lord Abbot Roderic; everything was baptized anew in worthy repentance and streams of tears—or, to conclude more briefly, they renounced all these and every other evil and clung to every good.

Yet even then this deadly plague did not cease throughout the whole Lent, until eleven of our number had died and the days of the entire year, which we had abused for so long, had been reduced by a tenth in such mourning and anxiety. Then the celebration of the paschal solemnity drew near, and God’s mercy wiped every tear of that disaster from our eyes.

That the number eleven pertains to sin is sufficiently demonstrated by the authority of holy Scripture. Just as the Decalogue is completed by the sum of ten, so it is exceeded by the addition of eleven. Therefore, just as the observance of the Decalogue is represented by ten, so transgression of sin is represented by eleven.

Why these things also corresponded to the season of Lent, and what has been noted above about that same season, let the diligent reader consider; with lively understanding, let him grasp how events follow events and seasons follow seasons here. But, having briefly digressed from the text of the narrative I began, I now turn my pen back to the same subject.

### 3

Meanwhile, after the Lord’s rod had scourged us in this way and driven us toward a better path, several years passed. Then the walls of the sanctuary, partly through age and partly through the fire, began to disintegrate and threaten ruin over the heads of those who looked upon them.

Therefore, after consultation with our leaders, we laid hands upon it in order to destroy it, with the intention of improving it, so that once it had been renewed we might extend our efforts to the remaining structures that needed renewal.

In the meantime, some of our simpler brethren came to us and urged us to persist firmly in the work we had begun. They promised that the Lord would cooperate with us, that after not much time the monastery of Sithiu would be magnificently visited by the Lord, and that he would reveal something great concerning it.

At the time I paid little attention to this, turning immediately to other matters and devoting myself especially to the practical administration of the work we had begun. Thus, while we were laboring, four years passed. In the fifth year, when the exterior wall had already risen somewhat in height, the principal altar of Saint Martin had to be moved in order to build a crypt there; and it was scarcely proper for this to be done without the presence of the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1147D] Note the religious practice of that period, when it was not permitted to move an altar from its place without the assent of the bishop who was present.]

While preparations were being made after the octave of Easter, and while, in the bishop’s absence, the great masses of earth surrounding the altar were being removed by our order, the affliction of a very severe illness suddenly attacked me and immediately laid me powerless in bed. Thus the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it was beaten with many blows.

Nor do I believe that I, so great a sinner and subject to every guilt, could in any way have deserved to take part in such a holy undertaking, since I had first to be purified by so great a blow from the Lord. For this reason the destruction of the altar was postponed for some time. Meanwhile, the earth dug out around the altar was carried away.

When, after the Wednesday fast, I had recovered somewhat from the affliction of my illness, some of our elders came to me and said that the altar, now deprived of the mass of earth that had surrounded it, was wavering and that, unless help were quickly provided, it would fall. For this reason, they said, the bishop—who was then at Thérouanne—ought to be summoned more quickly.

On this account he was called and came with considerable kindness. On the Friday of that same fast he arrived with many men to destroy the altar. After it had been overturned, he returned home that same day, against our wishes.

At that place, on the following day—that is, on the Saturday of the fast [Note: [Col. 1148D] Namely, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year from the Incarnation 1050, as it is read in Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 19]—while the ground was being dug more deeply in order to lay foundations and a great quantity of earth was being removed, behold, directly beneath the holy site of the altar we encountered a subterranean chamber carefully constructed of hard stones, tiles, and ancient cement.

When this was discovered, we hurried there to see it ourselves, and, seeing it, we were greatly astonished. We were not permitted either to cover it again or to uncover it further. If it were opened and disturbed without the testimony of good men, or if we tried to conceal it for some time after covering it, we might, through our own imprudence, expose ourselves to the accusations of any hostile critics.

Nor could the bishop be approached that day, since, as has been said, he had returned home immediately after the altar had been removed on the preceding day. Our minds turned now here, now there, in great anxiety over what course should be chosen. At last, after our community had discussed the matter, it seemed better to turn to this course: relying upon the witnesses whom that day had brought, we should proceed to investigate whatever might be hidden there.

We sent a messenger to the vicedominus, the castellans, and all the principal clergy, inviting them all to come to us quickly. Since it was Saturday, and some were assembling to attend to the legal procedures of the marketplace, before long a considerable crowd of notable persons arrived.

Moreover, because the report of such a matter stirred up the common people, it could not remain hidden from the multitude. They came running separately, making a foolish uproar. When we yielded the approach to the leading men and permission was given to view the little chamber, Lambert, the urban magistrate, immediately declared, while other men of rank likewise shouted, that he would not move his foot from that place until he knew the truth about the matter hidden there.

By then we were certain that the body of some saint was contained there, but of no one did we have less expectation than of the one who, beyond all expectation, was to be found.

Meanwhile, while everyone stood around for the investigation of so great a matter, processions were made with crosses and candles. Then, while we sang the litanies as was fitting and everyone looked on in wonder, the chamber was uncovered. With the great labor of many men, it was scarcely broken apart with iron tools from the first hour of the day until evening.

At last, after the covering had been removed through a sufficiently elaborate operation, a leaden shrine appeared before the eyes of all present. When it was opened and its contents were revealed to all who stood around, the remains of a certain venerable saint appeared.

His name, however, was not yet visible, and everyone’s eyes were intent upon discovering it. After the entire tomb had been searched once, twice, and three times, a silver cross was finally found beneath the right shoulder of the same saint. It was taken out and brought before us, marked only with these three words:

**SAINT BERTIN, ABBOT.**

Nor is it unrelated to the praise of this saint that, although we were still unaware of it and had formed no prior plan concerning the matter before it happened, the discovery of the holy remains of so beloved a Father took place so suitably during the fast of the fourth month.
