It was fitting and highly appropriate that, as we approached so sacred an encounter, we should first be made somewhat more purified by the restraint of the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday of that fast, and should thus hasten somewhat more worthily to investigate the saint’s most venerable limbs.

Whatever can be known before it happens can, according to its measure, be governed by providence. But since none of us had any knowledge of this beforehand, who could have arranged it in such a way except the foreknowledge of God? And so forth.

### 4

When, by such signs, the body of the most blessed Father had been found and discovered—more precious than gold and topaz—until then the whole land had been scorched and ruined by a long and most severe drought, so that the farmers complained that all hope of crops had now been entirely taken from them.

But at that very moment, after many preceding thunderclaps and flashing lightning, a great inundation of rain followed. The earth, thoroughly drenched, immediately began to grow green again by producing fruit, and began to unfold itself to its cultivators in revived hope of new crops.

From that time onward, all the fields, refreshed by the life-giving dew, rose beneath the blowing breezes. Though the harvest was immense, the number of laborers could scarcely suffice for the work, so that, by God’s grace, the cycle of the coming year might provide the inhabitants of the earth with every sufficiency of crops.

### 5

When these things had been said, the sacred body, now uncovered and exposed, was ordered to be covered again in the same urn, and the little tomb was restored as it had previously been, until, after consultation with the elders, it could be deliberated what ought to be done about the matter. How many vexations and blasphemies we suffered in the meantime, may the Lord know for our purification and forgive them. At that time the lord pope Leo, surnamed Bruno, presided over the holy Roman Church; the fame of his sagacity and probity breathed throughout the whole world the fragrance of a sweet perfume.

When necessity required us to be strengthened by the authority of our superiors, a faithful envoy was sought and found and sent to him, so that, whatever the apostolic pontiff himself, together with men of weightier counsel, judged excellent concerning these matters, he might not delay to communicate to us through that envoy in the name of the Lord. When the envoy had approached him and, having been admitted into his presence, had received permission to speak, he briefly explained the matter as it had occurred to the lord pope, insofar as he was then occupied with many affairs. He presented before him the scriptural testimonies, as well as the cross found with the sacred body, which he had brought with him as evidence.

After seeing these things, and displaying them to those who happened at that time to be with him—men who had then gathered for the Roman council, namely, the patriarch of Aquileia, archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, and leading men—he said that such indications of the truth ought by no means to be distrusted, but rather believed with greater security and firmness. This was especially so since it could be found sufficiently in many historical records that almost the whole territory of Gaul, and above all your regions and the other coastal areas, had been ravaged by frequent Danish incursions, plunderings, and burnings. For this reason, many bodies of saints had been transferred from less secure places; others had been secretly hidden—as is known to have happened in the case of Saint Bertin—either within walls or beneath the earth.

When these apostolic replies had been brought back to us by our messenger, I came to myself and began to remember something in the *Life of Saint Folquinus* that spoke about this very matter. When that work had been brought, the passage I was seeking was read aloud: it explained how that same holy pontiff had transferred and reburied the venerable body of the saint, and how he had instituted that the festive day of this translation should be celebrated every year throughout his entire diocese.

It seemed appropriate to record this here also as an example: he transferred and reburied the body of Saint Bertin, and decreed that this solemn day should be observed by us; it is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [16 July]. Popular opinion long added this detail to the matter: the aforementioned bishop had done this secretly, with no one recognizing it except a few, and had bound them by severe threats and oaths lest it in any way become public.

Having seen this, but with it not yet sufficiently clear for what reason or in what year of the Lord’s Incarnation it had been done, I immediately went through various annals and histories of ancient events, comparing the scattered passages that seemed useful to our investigation. Within the limits of my small ability, I composed the conclusion that this had occurred through a great foreshadowing of divine providence: namely, that the venerable body had been transferred by the work of the aforementioned bishop from its known place into a more secret location.

To make this clearer, let the comparison of these excerpts be set forth. But lest the order of the argument already begun seem to be interrupted, let these matters be reserved for fuller treatment elsewhere.

### 6

When the glorious emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne and of the emperor, was reigning, this ancient and then royal monastery had by that time been greatly ennobled, from the time of the most blessed Bertin, its principal founder, by the sacred observance of monastic discipline; and, according to the regulations of the canons, its governance had been entrusted to the adoption of brothers. At that time, however, it was given as a benefice—alas!—to a certain man of canonical rank, an Englishman named Fredegisus. From then on it began to wither in the purity of its entire holy religion, to pass into foreign hands, and to decline from its former integrity.

Finally, he reduced the number of monks serving the Lord there from eighty-three to sixty, and appropriated for his own possession the estates and more fertile lands assigned for the sustenance of the monks. He completely overturned the monastery of Saint Audomar, which was the same institution as the monastery of Saint Bertin: after expelling forty monks, he substituted thirty canons in their place and assigned for their use a third part of all the goods belonging to the monastery of Saint Bertin.

What, then, was this man other than the scourge of this monastery? He also rightly became the eleventh in the number of abbots after Saint Bertin, because, by overthrowing what his ten predecessors had well ordered, he exceeded the bounds of the Decalogue. Every sin is called “undecimal” because whenever something unlawful is committed, the sum of the Decalogue is violated, insofar as it lies within the sinner’s power.

This usurper, then, Fredegisus, was rightly called as though *Frigidus*—“Cold”—because, unless that north wind, the possessor of his heart, had existed within him, he would never have aspired to such presumptions. Since, therefore, the presumption of this “Cold One” became the beginning and cause of so great a ruin for this monastery, his action was both a sin and the punishment of sin and the cause of another sin.

It was a sin, indeed, and even sacrilege, when what had been assigned to the monks’ table passed into the legal possession of another. It was also the punishment of sin, because, unless some very grave sin had previously occurred in Fredegisus—through which, being already filthy, he was bound to become still filthier—the Lord would never have permitted him to be so blinded that he could conceive such a sacrilege. That same sin also supplied the cause of another sin to Fredegisus’s successors, because what he claimed as his own possession remained an inextricable matter among all his successors down to the present time.

Let it suffice that I have touched upon this very briefly for our young men, so that it may become clear from what sins arising in God’s sanctuary such great evils sprang, and for what urgent reasons the pearl of the holy body was hidden.

When the aforesaid emperor had departed from this world, his sons Lothair, Louis, and Charles, each vying for their father’s empire, soon began to disagree with one another. After a most savage struggle had arisen among them, they engaged in a bloody war in the district of Auxerre. There, while the nobles of the Franks and all the nations subject to them were laying one another low in mutual slaughter, Louis and Charles finally gained the victory after putting Lothair to flight.

As the discord arising from this conflict continued for five years, nearly all the regions of the Franks, together with their inhabitants, were reduced to nothing. At last, peace was made, and they divided the kingdom of the Franks among themselves; at that time our western regions fell to King Charles.

Yet the evils did not cease because of this peace. While the paternal empire was divided into three parts, each brother wished to act as father in his own kingdom and to extend himself according to his father’s magnificence; thus they brought ruin upon themselves and their possessions by confusing everything. For the word of the Lord had not fallen to the ground: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house” (Luke 11:17).

While that same King Charles was reigning, in the third year of Abbot Adalard’s administration, the aforementioned bishop placed the venerable remains of Saint Bertin in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 843, wonderfully arranged in a more secluded place than before [read: *compositos*, “the remains … arranged”]. In a similar manner, he secretly restored to its own place the venerable body of Saint Audomar, which had earlier been furtively removed but divinely entrusted to his diligence, lest this land should ever be deprived of so great a patron; he also committed it to a more hidden place.

He decreed that their holy translations should be celebrated with greater magnificence by all the people of his diocese on distinct days of the year, so that whatever they celebrated less worthily at the saints’ depositions in September, because of the pressing need of the harvest, they might perform more freely at the solemnities of these holy translations.

After so great a treasure had been assigned to hidden places, not long afterward all the peoples of this land were thrown into confusion: on one side by the severe distress of a famine then arising, and on the other by fear of the sudden fury of a Norse invasion. Almost all the nobility of this land, except a few whom the abundance of their works and estates or the security of castles and fortifications detained, departed after their lords, or wherever seemed safer to them.

Moreover, after the remaining people had somehow been stripped of the danger of the terrible famine, the raging Danish persecution attacked and cruelly tore them apart. When the Danes had burst in here hostilely to complete the fury of their tyranny, they found no brother here except four, awaiting the palm of martyrdom. The text of the *Life of Saint Bertin* explains clearly what punishments they inflicted on three of them, by what kind of death they were punished in the case of the fourth, and how, after plundering everything they could find, they burned the monasteries and all the workshops and destroyed everything.

> [Note: Read here Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 1. From this passage it is clear that this book, like the first, was written not by Folcard but by another, earlier author.]

What, then? If the bodies of the saints mentioned above had at that time been duly honored in more prominent or secure places, do you think they would have been carried away and seized by the strong hand of the Lord? Or was it not then greatly necessary that what the aforementioned priest of God, foreseeing so many evils, had done shortly before for the preservation of the saints’ relics should take place?

No fortification of a castle or rampart yet protected this place; and therefore—indeed, even more because the burden of sins pressed upon it—the incursion of the wicked broke in with great ease. Nor did they devastate the borders of Sithiu only once, but repeatedly, returning two and three times with renewed invasions, until, worn down in many ways by divine vengeance through the merits of the aforesaid saints, they were forced to return to their scabbard.

Then, so that a third scourge of the world might also be examined, the bestial fury finally pursued the survivors of famine and barbarian devastation wherever they were. It slaughtered those whom it had miserably suffocated, and, tearing them limb from limb, destroyed them without burial. As these calamities of divine vengeance occupied this land for nearly a hundred years, it was again washed away, as though by a flood, after having been parched by such tribulations.

### 7

The priest of God Folquinus, therefore, forewarned by the illumination of the Holy Spirit of such great evils, while he was still alive concealed the venerable body of Saint Bertin in an unknown place, where it would least be expected. There our nourisher and shepherd remained hidden until these very last times of ours—namely, for two hundred and fifty years—until the principal altar was overturned for the purpose of founding the crypt, as has already been noted, and revealed it.

> [Note: Rather, for two hundred and nine years. For that is the number of years between the translation said above to have been made in 843, when the body of Saint Bertin is said to have been hidden in the earth, and the translation made in 1052.]

Having now been made more certain by these indications, I received a letter from our bishop and proceeded to Reims to seek the archbishop’s advice concerning them. When we arrived, we went forward to speak with the lord archbishop. After we had been admitted into his presence and he had fully set himself to hear the sequence of our account, we first reported to him in order the novelty of what had occurred. Then I placed in his hands the letter of the lord bishop, together with the testimony of Scripture that spoke about this very matter and the title of the cross.

He immediately summoned abbots, archdeacons, and all the monks and canons of sounder judgment. In the presence of two hundred people, on the third day before the Ides of January, at the feast of the deposition of Saint Remigius, the same letter was read aloud in these words:

#### The Bishop Drogo, of those called Morini, to the lord Wido, archbishop of Reims by the grace of God

Since, by divine gift, you possess the summit of the highest dignity, and, as a distinguished shepherd, you care for the pastors placed under you with both authority and vigilance, our actions depend upon you and our counsels look to you. If these are arranged wisely and laudably, the benefit is yours as well as ours.

Therefore, whenever something unusual occurs in our churches, where, because of the importance or novelty of the matter, we are not fully sufficient to give counsel, it is fitting that we turn to you as members to the head, so that your authority may make us more certain in our doubts. Our humility presumes to define nothing on its own that requires higher consideration and deliberation.

Let your fatherhood know, then, that something new and wondrous has occurred these days in our diocese. It seemed to me advisable to write to you about it and to request your judgment concerning it. The place called Sithiu is a monastery of men of God and a parish of our see; it is not the least among those foundations which ancient memory records as having once been established and endowed by kings.

It is truly most renowned for the relics of many saints resting there. Among them, as though by the privilege of a special merit, the blessed Bertin stands out, being himself the principal rector of that place.

The matter required that the central altar be moved in order to construct a crypt, and the abbot undertook to do this, with higher counsel, in our presence. When, after the destruction of the altar, the earth was dug out more deeply, a certain repository, constructed of brickwork and mortar and almost impossible to break apart, appeared before the eyes of those standing by.

At last, after it had been destroyed with much labor, it revealed a lead chest containing bones of a body reduced to ashes, together with a sufficiently clear mark of a seal. The seal was a silver cross; the inscription was: “Saint Bertin, Abbot.”

When this event, so extraordinary and unexpected, filled some with joy but disturbed others with distrust and immense astonishment, the testimony concerning it returned to the memory of the abbot and brothers and was brought to the attention of others who were less inclined to believe. We have also briefly indicated its meaning to you.

It is read in the public archives of that place that Saint Folquinus, bishop of our see—whose body, celebrated for great miracles, also rests in that same church—when the barbarism of the Danes was raging through the coastal regions with fire and sword, had shortly before that devastation buried the body of this saint in the earth on a certain day. But when or by whom it was afterward found, there is no mention at all, except in the rumor of the people, which, just as it often introduces the certain in place of the uncertain, so it also often introduces the false in place of the true.

This testimony satisfies us concerning the credibility of the event. But there is another matter that troubles us in part, while it greatly troubles the less discerning crowd. For what ought to be done with the relics venerated in the same church under the name of that saint, if the recently discovered body of the saint is transferred to its proper honor? No decision that accords with our wish supports us.

We therefore beseech you, by Him who appointed you as bishop over us, and by the mutual bond of holy charity, that, after calling upon men whom knowledge of divine law enlightens and whose testimonies approve a praiseworthy life, you take counsel concerning both matters and, by a rescript of your authority, provide us with advice concerning both. Thus, when every cloud of ambiguity has been removed, all scandal of disagreement may also be driven away, the harmony of peace may increase among us, and the name of the Lord may be praised in all our works. Amen.

When this had been read, after consultation with everyone and in accordance with everyone’s wishes, he ordered another letter to be written containing replies of the following kind:

#### Wido, archbishop of Reims, wishes his brother and fellow bishop Drogo to live happily in both worlds

Because wisdom always acts wisely, and Solomon says, “My son, do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24), we praise, dearest brother, your prudence in properly seeking counsel from us concerning the relics of the recently discovered saint.

After taking counsel about this matter with our own people, as you requested, we decree that the body found is indeed that of Saint Bertin, since we altogether place uncertain things after certain ones. The testimonies of Scripture that you sent us confirm this, as do the dignity of the place in which it was found and the evident indication, namely the sign of the cross.

Therefore, lift up the very body of the saint with due honor and place it in a reverent location, as is fitting. But place the relics of the other uncertain saint, as you say, beside the body of Saint Bertin, trusting in the mercy of God, because in the time when He wills and in the manner in which He wills, it will also be revealed whose they are.

> [Note: Later writers say that these relics, which until now had been enclosed in one chest together with the relics of Saint Bertin the abbot, belong to Saint Bertin the Younger, son of Count Walbert, mentioned in the *Life of Saint Bertin the Abbot*. Bertin the Elder received Bertin the Younger from the baptismal font. I have read of no earlier mention of Bertin the Younger than Lambert, priest of Ardres.]

For the revelation both of the uncertain saint and of the certain one, we have decreed that a three-day fast be proclaimed for the people, so that, appeased by the prayers and fasting of His people, the Lord may reveal to us when He wishes and in whatever manner He wishes. Amen.

### 8

When these things had been completed, we privately summoned certain members of his household and, through them, humbly entreated the same supreme prelate that, with God’s help, he should honor the day appointed for the elevation by the presence of his arrival and strengthen it by the authority of his dignity.

He immediately asked when we intended to undertake this with the Lord’s assistance. When he learned from our reply that it would be on the first or second day of May, he kindly promised that he would be present, provided that life and health accompanied him.

Thus, having become somewhat more easy in mind, we received the written account and permission and hastened home. When we reached Thérouanne, we found the lord bishop there. After being admitted into his presence, I placed in his right hand the letter rewritten in the form of his words. After it had been read, he promised that he would have everything proclaimed throughout his diocese according to the counsel of the supreme prelate.

Then, after we had returned home, we devoted ourselves with all our limited ability to seeking from the depths of our hearts the mercy of God and the protection of the saints through prayers, fasts, and vigils, and to attending in every way to the preparations for the approaching celebration. Meanwhile, certain people were making great disturbances of opposition, troubles, persecutions, and insults against us and were striving greatly to obstruct the sacred rites that were to be performed.

To say nothing of ourselves—for we did not receive a punishment sufficiently worthy of our offenses—how great a crime it is to attempt anything against the saints of God is clearly shown by the ark of the covenant, which was tilted by the kicking oxen. When the Levite rashly tried to steady it by handling it, he was immediately condemned by divine vengeance and deprived of mortal life.

In the same way, whoever attempts to reproach anything done in the administration of God’s servants should beware lest, unless they repent, they may at some time be struck by a more severe condemnation of their souls.

After we had been harassed by many tribulations, at last, through Christ’s favor, we were freed from these people.

What more is there to say? On the first day of May, the lord Wido, supreme pontiff,

> [Note: Here an archbishop is called “supreme pontiff”; this usage belongs to the middle of the eleventh century. Above he is called “supreme prelate.”]

arrived with many distinguished persons; Drogo, our bishop, also arrived with his honorable clergy; and various abbots came with their entourages. The lady Adhela was not absent either, accompanied by her brother Odo and a large body of noble soldiers.

In addition, countless crowds of people came rushing here from different places, and the churches were filled to their walls. Nevertheless, since the lord archbishop, together with his companions and the other guests, was tired from the journey and rested that day, we meanwhile took care to prepare whatever was necessary and postponed all the rites concerning the saint until the following day.

For when I had earlier deliberated that this should be done on the first day of May and had sent a messenger to seek the agreement of our lord bishop, he immediately, with wiser counsel, ordered it to be postponed until the second day of the same month. He did this lest the most celebrated solemnity of the holy apostles Philip and James, which fell on that same day, should appear to be diminished in its own celebration, and so that, after it had come first and the feast of the Invention of the Life-giving Cross followed afterward, all who came here or returned from here might enjoy the festive rejoicing of leisure.

Although we did not yet know this, we believe that the matter was arranged by divine providence, so that the coming day might be adorned with an appropriate observance: just as the deposition of Saint Walbert had been magnificently celebrated, so the elevation of Saint Bertin might finally be magnificently celebrated, since the readings of one life commended both saints and the same responsories celebrated them together.

Leaving these matters aside, early on the following day, when the bishops, abbots, monks, and canons were ready, and certain leading laymen had also been admitted as witnesses, they proceeded in procession to the most sacred place. The singing of the litanies began, and the workers were ordered to excavate the chest of the sacred body.

The orders were not delayed. After the earth had been removed, the sacred place was prepared until access was easy for everyone to draw out the saint’s chest. Then our bishop, together with four abbots of proven life, was stationed around the limbs of the sacred body. When the chest had been opened, the supreme prelate began to sing the responsory, “Let my prayer be directed,” and the choir took it up: “As incense in your sight, O Lord.” The same prelate then censed the interior and exterior.

After this prayer had been sung, while the same precentor continued with the verse of the responsory, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice,” something that previously had been attempted by several people for whatever reason but had been prevented by a certain difficulty, the chest was then drawn out with agility and ease by the hands of a few men. It was raised onto a higher arrangement of benches, while we all, seeking the earth, venerated it; it was again censed, and the sacred limbs were revealed to our then-stained eyes. They were purified by being sprinkled with water and wine.

> [Note: It was the custom among the ancients to wash the relics of saints with water whenever they brought them out of a tomb, as Bede shows in the account of the elevation of Saint Æthelthryth, Book IV, chapter 19.]

### 9

Meanwhile, a certain cleric named Berwold stood apart, deprived of the sight of one eye. Previously he had possessed equal clarity of vision in both eyes, but, because of some illness, he had earlier had a nearby vein cut in order to treat the eye, and as a result he had lost all sight in that eye. Out of shame, he had concealed this almost from everyone except a few members of his household.

He was earnestly imploring the patronage of Saint Bertin, asking that the sight he had lost might be restored to him by the Lord. He greatly longed to have his eye touched by any of the saint’s limbs that were being handled there, but feared that he would not be allowed to approach.

While we were carefully attending to so great a matter, and meanwhile certain appropriate chants had been sung, the responsory of the holy Trinity was appointed and sung: “Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who does wonders.” Then the responsory of the same saint was taken up by the choir to be sung slowly:

> “Therefore glorious Bertin, athlete of God and distinguished priest, serving the heavenly King with fasts and prayers throughout a long life, receives today the rewards of his merits in the choir of angels.”

While this was being sung, the aforementioned cleric—sound in every respect but lacking the sight of one eye—feared to approach the sacred limbs, as has been said. He begged one of our brothers to touch one of the sacred members lightly with his fingers and to make the sign upon his blinded eye with those same fingers.

This was done without our knowledge. But, because of the devotion inspired by the saint present, when the end of the responsory still further delighted the minds of those singing, the man immediately received the sight he had been expecting.

Indeed, what the Lord had granted to occur in him for the praise of His name and the proclamation of the saint’s merit, he himself wished to conceal through foolish embarrassment. But perhaps at that time he muttered to a certain Arnold, who was closely attached to him, that he had been admitted there under a good omen, since through contact with the saint who was present he had recovered the sight lost for so long; and he emphatically instructed him to keep this silent and never reveal it to anyone.

The other, however, did not yield to such great insensitivity on his part, but immediately disclosed it to those standing nearby. When a certain Walter learned that this had truly occurred, he extended his hand and commanded silence from everyone. Then he proclaimed that the man, who for a long time had been condemned to the sight of only one eye, had now been restored through the saint’s merits by the expected gift of vision.

When they heard this, they were greatly exhilarated and poured out tears of joy. By this event we were already consoled with a certain hope: that, through whatever indications of divine grace, doubt might be driven from the hearts of all who were distrustful.

### 10

Then one of our own household, who until that time had disagreed with us excessively in this matter and had been quite unaccustomed to it, was for the first time overcome by much repentance and drenched in a great flood of tears. Yet he still did not sufficiently believe the matter. With whatever vows he was able to make, he humbly prayed to the Lord, the fountain of mercy, that, if the body then being handled there was truly that of Saint Bertin, He would deign to declare it to everyone by a threefold sign of miracles.

### 11

Meanwhile, after the sacred limbs had been arranged as they had formerly been joined together in the body, they were wrapped in a white linen cloth and a precious mantle, which the countess had willingly prepared for this purpose. The lord archbishop reverently placed them in the immense chest.

Then the aforementioned venerable matron, revealing the desires of her great devotion toward the saint, legally transferred to that same saint, in the presence of everyone who was there, a certain salt-producing estate as a gift.

### 12

When these things had been done, the body was lifted in the arms amid the immense rejoicing of those singing psalms and carried out of the crypt into the venerable sanctuary. At that moment, the other bodies of the saints resting there were extended before the doors of the crypt to meet it.

The archbishop was then about to celebrate Mass, but because the crowds were pressing and rushing forward, no easy exit was available. Therefore everything was ordered to be carried outside the monastery precincts, so that, with the greater multitude of the people accompanying it, the supreme pontiff could enter the Holy of Holies without impediment to celebrate Mass.

When this had been suitably accomplished, and the great majority—that is, the crowds—had followed the relics of the saints, the cardinal Masses were celebrated after the supreme pontiff had entered the sanctuary.

### 13

Meanwhile, a certain woman stood outside the church in the courtyard with her son, whose arms and legs were contracted. She had come to ask Saint Bertin for his healing.

Earlier, when she had been considering taking him, a twelve-year-old boy, to Cologne to seek the aid of Saint Heribert and the other saints resting there, so that perhaps through their merits he might obtain the use of his limbs, the boy had said that he had already been warned three times in a vision not to be carried anywhere until he had first been taken to Saint Bertin’s side and tested the saint’s merits.

When he had also come there in a vision and prayed, he said that he had seen four exceedingly white doves flying out of the monastery, and that the altar itself had been shaken and trembled like a leaf. He had prostrated himself before it and, without delay, had risen from there restored through the saint’s merits.

When the boy reported this to his mother, and the report of the saint’s impending elevation was already spreading, she hastened there with the boy and a large retinue. Awaiting the Lord’s intervention through Saint Bertin before the monastery doors, she remained there with her son in supplication.

When she forced her way through the pressing crowd to kiss the saint’s bier, and, after being driven back, returned again with importunity, attempting with great effort to place the boy against the saint’s bier, the boy, by God’s assent, was given upright limbs and restored to health.

When many people saw this, some came to the aid of the mother, who had been crushed by the crowd, while others lifted the boy up and carried him away. After this, the uproar of the countless tumultuous multitude rose high. The words “God is wonderful in his saints” (Psalm 67:36) were proclaimed everywhere, because they saw before their own eyes the boy whom they had known shortly before as scarcely able to crawl now walking with his mother going before him.

Meanwhile, as we were singing the Mass in the choir, the sweet report of this event reached us. While we were still asking whether it was true, the same boy, healed through the merits of Saint Bertin, entered. Standing upright in our midst, he was led by his mother and prostrated himself before the altar, according to his ability, to give thanks to God.

After the Gospel had been read, and the lord archbishop had begun the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* before the altar, while the choir followed repeatedly, you could see many rejoicing with Christ over what had occurred and many shedding tears for joy.

### 14

The hymn had not yet been completed, and some of us were still weeping for joy, when it was announced that a certain blind woman, a resident of this city and therefore well known to all our people, had also received her sight. She herself, illuminated in this manner, accompanied the messenger in the sight of everyone and joined the boy, prostrating herself to the praise of God and to the proclamation of Saint Bertin’s merit.

No account could fully convey how greatly and with what dignity people rejoiced and delighted in the Lord on that day. For after we had been so greatly embittered by the disturbances, troubles, and insults of certain people, the grace of our God then flashed over us with greater favor:

> “We became like those who are comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with rejoicing” (Psalm 125:1).

### 15

Now the cause of the singular grace mentioned above shines forth; now that good thing which, as I remember, I had foretold would be nurtured by God’s mercy and brought to completion in its own time flashes forth. May this grace leave none of our people ungrateful; may it henceforth make all of us more devoted to Christ; may it urge all of us to be more watchful for the praise of God.

As I reflect on these things, I am also reminded of the three words engraved on the little cross that was found. For the elevation became clear then through three more evident signs. Just as, at the discovery, no one would have known what it was if the three words had not spoken, so also at the elevation it would not have been sufficiently believed by everyone unless the truth had been clarified by these indications of three miracles.

What, then? Would we remain unmoved by such great correspondence among these events? Three words proclaim the discovery; three miracles proclaim the elevation. O how great is the consistency of God’s works, how great the harmony that shines forth!

By this light of words and signs (the text supplies “light”), all shadows are driven away from everyone by God’s grace; through it the merits of so great a patron now flash forth.

### 16

After the sacred offices of the Mass had been completed with such magnificent glory, and the other bodies of the saints had been returned to their places, the chest of Saint Bertin, still unsecured, was exposed upon the altar of the holy cross for the people to visit. The sun was already inclining toward its setting. Guards were appointed, and the chest was kept safe until the following day, when it was to be sealed.

After these things had been properly done, the bodies were cared for according to the circumstances, and that most celebrated day was brought to completion with indescribable glory.

On the following day they approached again, and, in the presence of an innumerable multitude of people, the written testimony of the event was read aloud. It contained the sequence, time, person, and witnesses of what had occurred. After it had been read, it was attached, together with the found cross, to the sacred body. Thus arranged, it was sealed with the seal of the supreme prelate. The chest was closed, fastened with iron bands and nails, sewn and bound, and joined together indissolubly. Amid the rejoicing of the innumerable multitude, it was carried into the Holy of Holies with the relics, there to be honored.

There it is venerated to this day and, with the Lord’s assent, will be venerated forever and ever.

### 17

Afterward, the supreme prelate and our lord bishop ordered the day of the sacred elevation to be commemorated and venerated by all the people of this diocese thereafter, and to be celebrated each year with great devotion.

When these matters had been completed, and the lord bishops and abbots had obtained certain portions of the holy relics, each returning to his own place, they went back more joyfully, each presented with his own gift.

18. One of these, namely Wazo, abbot of Saint-Valery, having obtained some of the holy relics, returned home rejoicing after the solemnity of the sacred Elevation had been completed. A certain peasant, blinded because the pupils of both eyes were covered with severe dark spots, approached him, being guided by a boy, to ask for some kind of remedy. He said to him:

“I know of no antidote capable of saving one from such an illness, except the intervention of our all-powerful and saving Lord Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, I recently attended, though unworthy, the most holy Elevation of a certain renowned saint, when a number of people had gathered for it, and I took part in such a holy undertaking. There, too, the Lord revealed to all of us how great that saint was by various mighty miracles. Returning here, I also brought with me, rejoicing in the gift, one of his holy teeth, which was given to me. If you will believe that you can be healed through the merits of that saint, I shall immediately order it to be brought to you.”

He replied: “I trust.”

The abbot at once ordered it to be brought into the presence of those standing by. When it had been brought and applied to both his eyes, his eyes were immediately opened and he began to see clearly. After blessing the name of the Lord for this, he returned home safe and joyful.

[Note: [Col. 1159] The body of Saint Bertin is preserved by our Bertinian brethren in a silver reliquary above the high altar; his head, enclosed in a gilded shrine, is kept in the sacred treasury.]

[Col. 1159]

SERMON ON THE FEAST OF THE SAME SAINT. (Fragment.)

[Col. 1159C]

Rejoice, dearest brothers, in the Lord, you who have gathered for the solemnity of our most holy Father and protector, namely Saint Bertin. Be glad with spiritual joy, and from the innermost affection of your hearts praise together the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in his goodness has led us from the errors of idolatry to the knowledge of his holy name through the preaching of this holy priest.

Let us unanimously follow the footsteps of so holy a teacher. Let us not be degenerate sons of so great a Father, but imitate the holiness of his life by the nobility of our conduct. Let us cast away from ourselves the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day (Romans 13:12), because the night of ignorance has withdrawn and the light of true knowledge has shone upon us, so that as children of light we may walk in all chastity and godliness.

[Col. 1159D]

Let there be no hidden seeds of any wickedness or malice within us, because “man looks upon the face, but God considers the heart” (1 Kings 16:7), and nothing can be hidden from the eyes of his omnipotence. Let us also prepare ourselves in every good work, so that our illustrious shepherd and devout preacher, Saint Bertin the abbot, may bring us joyfully before the tribunal of the supreme Judge on the last day. Thus his glory may be increased by the multitude of his children, and with him may we deserve to hear the blessed sentence:

“Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

From the heavenly homeland he does not cease daily to assist our struggle with devout prayers, desiring that his dearest children, whom he fathered in Christ with paternal devotion, may reach the glory of everlasting blessedness. Therefore, dearest ones, let each person in his own order, according to the measure of his strength, resist the devil’s suggestions bravely, so that he may be made worthy to receive with our devout father the eternal crown of triumph.

“For the sufferings of this present time,” as the Apostle says, “are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

Thus divine goodness has willed that the time of our labor should be brief, that the reward of our struggle should be everlasting, and that for temporal affliction we should rejoice in the recompense of enduring glory. We heard, therefore, when the Life of the priest beloved by God was read, how greatly he was devoted to every good work; how he chastised his body through the rigor of abstinence; and how, through acts of charity, he strove to benefit everyone.

Let us follow with complete eagerness of mind and the full strength of our abilities the footsteps of that life, so that we may deserve to become sharers in the blessedness in which he reigns with Christ. Therefore let no carnal desire and no worldly ambition impede our path. The citizens of the eternal city await us; and the King himself, who wills all human beings to be saved, ardently desires our salvation together with that of his saints, and so forth.

[Col. 1161]

THE LIFE OF SAINT JOHN OF BEVERLEY, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, BY FOLCARD, MONK OF SITHIU.

(In Bollandist, May, vol. II, 7 May, p. 166, from an English manuscript.)

PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

[Col. 1161B]

1. Beverley, a large and populous town, according to Camden, lies in the eastern part of the county of York, commonly called the East Riding, not far from the River Hull, which flows from there after several miles into the estuary of the River Humber. Bede calls that district Deirawood, that is, “the forest of the Deirans.” There Saint John, whom we are discussing here, found a parish church dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist. After acquiring the site and lordship of this place, he converted the aforementioned holy church into a monastery and assigned it to monks. There he built the presbytery—that is, the choir of the church—while the prior of Saint John’s Church occupied a place in the nave. On the southern side of that church he built an oratory of Saint Martin, where he later placed nuns. He associated with these monasteries seven priests and an equal number of clerics in the nave of Saint John’s Church. He acquired for his monasteries the manor of Riding. He then built the Church of Saint Nicholas on the estate belonging to his lordship. All this is indicated from Leland’s Collectanea in the first volume of the Monasticon Anglicanum, page 170, where a representation is given of the carved structure of Beverley monastery [Col. 1161C] and of the western façade of the conventual church.

Saint John withdrew here when, weighed down by old age, he had resigned the archbishopric of York. Finally, on 7 May in the year of Christ 1221, he surrendered his holy soul to Christ, renowned for miracles during his life and after his death.

2. The venerable Bede discusses the virtues and deeds of Saint John in several places, especially in book V, chapter 2 and the following chapters of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People. Later, Folcard, a monk of the Church of the Holy Trinity at Canterbury, collected his deeds into a single volume at the request and insistence of Aldred, archbishop of York, as the title prefixed to these acts indicates.

He seems to have written this when Saint Edward the Confessor was ruling England. Edward died in 1056; in the preface to this Life, which we present from an English manuscript sent to us from Saint-Malo by the reverend Father Leander Prichard, a Benedictine monk, Folcard recalls that he was assisted in the desolation of his monastery by Queen Edith, Edward’s wife, through the recommendation of Archbishop Aldred.

In the Monasticon Anglicanum cited above, page 169, it is stated that Folchard of Canterbury wrote the Life of the blessed John, archbishop of York. It is not, however, said that Folchard was archbishop of Canterbury, as John Mabillon interprets those words; rather, Mabillon corrects the statement and asserts that he was a Bertinian monk who lived in England at the beginning of the eleventh century.

This Folcald, however, seems to have been somewhat younger than the other Folchard of Canterbury. He was summoned to England by King William and placed in charge of the monastery of Tournai. Orderic Vitalis testifies that he governed it for nearly sixteen years—without benediction, performing the duties of an abbot— in book XI of his Ecclesiastical History, under the year 1108. This places him at the beginning of the twelfth, not the eleventh, century.

Mabillon appends a certain Life of Saint John, taken from a manuscript legend of the monastery of Saint Gildas in the Forest, believing it to have been written by Folcard the Bertinian monk. In fact, it is merely an abridged extract from the longer Life that we present here. We also possess another, more condensed account on an ancient parchment, written by Henry of Huntingdon in the twelfth century. Another Life of him, printed in 1516, appears in the English legendarium of John Capgrave.

Passing over all these, we append notable miracles written by four different authors, almost all eyewitnesses, and sent to us by the aforementioned Leander Prichard. The first is called William Kecellus. He reaches the times of William the Conqueror, so that he appears to have written at the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the following century. The names of the subsequent authors are not given.

The author who wrote the nearest in time of these miracles mentions King Stephen, who obtained the royal crown in 1136, and the final years of Archbishop Thurstan, who is said to have died in 1140. The third author indicates that the miracles occurred within a period of five years. The fourth mentions the general interdict under King John to which England was subjected, and appears to have appended the final miracles under Henry III.

3. Among the ten writers of English history printed in London in 1652 there is the Chronicle of Thomas Stubbs, or Stubeus, a Dominican, written in the fourteenth century, On the Deeds of the Archbishops of York. In it, columns 1691 and following contain the deeds of Saint John the archbishop. Near the end we read:

“He withdrew to his monastery, which he had founded at Beverley, and there, distinguished by the glory of miracles, he happily completed his life on the Nones of May. He was buried there in the church, where from that time until now his glorious powers have never ceased to be publicly proclaimed.”

Then, concerning Archbishop Alfric, who presided over that Church from the year 1023 until 1051, he writes:

“He caused a shrine to be made at Beverley of gold, silver, and precious stones, with incomparable workmanship. Then, having raised from the tomb the precious body of the glorious Father Saint John, archbishop, from a wooden coffin carved with marvelous artistry, he placed it most honorably in the shrine, amid the great rejoicing of clergy and people and with many relics added.

“He also acquired for the Church of Saint John, with his own money, land at Milletune and at Holm from a certain wealthy man named Forceo, together with five bovates at Fredichthorp, including the money and the men attached to it.”

Thus far his account. A bovate is as much land as a single ox can plow.

This translation of the relics took place on 25 October 1044. It is clear from the account of the miracles that this day was celebrated with solemn observance, just as his natal feast was. In the thirteenth miracle of the second author, a woman who had been crippled for seven years is said to have been healed at one of his solemnities, called the Translation of the saint’s body, while the writer was singing psalms with the others.

Another translation is reported to have taken place in 1307 in the Monasticon Anglicanum.

4. Edward Maihew discusses the earlier translation on 25 October and inserts the following memorandum:

“In the year of Christ 1415, the most invincible King Henry, fifth of that name, on that very day sacred to his translation—namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of November, that is, 25 October—won the famous victory against the French at the place called Agincourt. Attributing it to this most holy bishop, he returned to England and arranged that both his deposition, or natal feast, and his translation should be solemnly celebrated throughout the province of Canterbury—for in the province of York, it seems, they had already been celebrated.”

Indeed, among the provincial constitutions of England, under the title “On Holidays,” there is a decree of Henry Chichele, archbishop of Canterbury, issued at the provincial synod held in the year of Christ 1416. Its opening words are: “The English Church.” A little farther below it contains these words:

“By the will and consent of our brothers and of the clergy present at this council, and no less at the special insistence of our most Christian prince and king, Henry V, we have judged that the memory of the most holy confessor and bishop John of Beverley should everywhere throughout our province be exalted with votive and devout affection. Therefore we decree, and so forth.”

As stated, he decreed that both of John’s feasts should be celebrated. Concerning the later portion of this decree, which relates to the feast of the translation, the most learned William Lyndwood writes:

“On this day, 25 December”—which at that time fell on a Friday—“the battle of Agincourt in Picardy took place in the year 1415. Because of its victorious outcome, the said King Henry V caused the English Church to establish the arrangement set out here. Thus this feast may be counted not only among the solemn holidays, but also among the sudden ones,” and so forth.

Thus he writes. Let the reader observe that not only in earlier centuries, but even in these latest times, the most blessed bishop John of Beverley has been present with the kings of England in their wars.

Thus far Edward Maihew.

5. In a very ancient missal preserved in the monastery of Jumièges and written around the year 1000, the feast of Saint John, bishop of Beverley, is prescribed for 7 May. We possess an ancient martyrology written in England in which, on these Nones of May, the deposition of Saint Leotard, bishop of Canterbury, who had died, is placed first, followed immediately by these words:

“And the natal feast of Saint John, archbishop of York.”

The martyrology printed at Cologne and Lübeck in 1490 has:

“At Beverley, the natal feast of Saint John, bishop and confessor of York.”

The authors of the Florarium manuscript follow these: Grevenus, Molanus, Canisius, Galesinius, the modern Roman Martyrology, the English martyrology, and various monastic calendars, several of which assign his translation to 25 October.

In the Breviary according to the Use of Salisbury, printed in 1499, the feast of Saint John of Beverley is prescribed for this 7 May in the calendar, in red letters, as principal feasts customarily are, with the direction of the choir. The appointed lessons contain an abridgment of his Life, and the following prayer is added:

“O God, who hast consecrated the present day by the departure of blessed John, your confessor and bishop: grant that your Church may worthily rejoice in his solemnity, so that through your mercy we may be helped by his example and merits.”

In the Sarum Breviary printed in 1557, a sacred commemoration of his solemnity is also prescribed for 25 October. In certain manuscript calendars, some notice of him is found on 17 January and 28 April, as we observed at that time among the entries passed over.

6. Having established these points, we take up the History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford, printed at Oxford in 1674, whose author, as we gather from the preface, was Anthony Wood. From page 2, where the claims of the Oxford schools—flourishing in the time of the Britons and Saxons, that is, before King Alfred—are discussed, we quote the following:

“First, then, I shall begin with Saint John of Beverley, who died around the year 720. Several ancient writings report that he devoted himself to the liberal arts at Oxford; painted indications in the windows also shed abundant light on this matter.

“For the writer who flourished in the year 1373, in the Life of the same Beverley” (which begins, “The more ancient land of the Britons …”), “states that he was born at Harpham among the peoples of Deira, but spent his youthful years in study at the monastery of Saint Hilda. He is said to have been the first among the English to be honored with the degree of doctor or master.”

His teacher, that writer says, was Theodore, a foreigner, “who rose to the highest position at Oxford,” and so forth.

Leland also reported this from an anonymous author concerning Beverley and the saint of that place, in a work divided into three parts. I believe the author was a certain William Asketell, who, during the reign of Edward II, took up the same subject and published books likewise divided into three parts. He had, in my opinion, learned much from the libraries of Deira and other regions beyond the Humber, whose monks, when the Danes were ravaging England everywhere, rescued their histories and antiquities from repeated disasters with the utmost diligence.

To this may be added the words of the sacristan of Beverley, also mentioned by the aforesaid Asketell, who records that Saint John of Beverley was the first master of arts at Oxford.

These claims are also admirably confirmed by an image of Beverley himself, formerly adorning the sixth window on the left side of the Salisbury library—indeed, I do not know whether it may still be seen there—with this inscription:

“Saint John of Beverley, holy doctor, was the first master of the liberal arts at Oxford …”

I could produce other testimonies highly suitable for supporting what has been brought forward concerning Beverley, but the concise brevity of the work assigned to me draws me elsewhere.

Thus far the passage. At the end of page 12, the author concludes that during those years Oxford possessed the general studies so called, or an academy equipped with professors of arts and sciences and with distinctions of certain degrees, since Saint John of Beverley received the degree of master there.

7. The same author, in book II of the History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford, page 61, when discussing writers before Alfred restored the academy, places Saint John of Beverley first. Concerning him he adds the following:

“When, on 14 September 1664, a sexton was digging a grave in the central part of the collegiate church at Beverley for the burial of a poor woman, he uncovered a brick vault. In it he found two small boxes: one contained ashes, while the other enclosed human bones. On one of them these words were inscribed:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1188 this church was burned in the month of September, on the night following the feast of the apostle Saint Matthew; and in the year 1197, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, an examination of the relics of Blessed John was made in this place. These bones were found in the eastern part of the tomb and were reburied here; and dust mixed with cement was found and reburied in the same place.”

THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1165]

PROLOGUE

[Col. 1165A]

1. To Aldred, the shining and burning lamp in a dark place, archbishop of the English: his least devoted brother, Folcard, sends greetings with faithful service.

In undertaking the command of your service, my most reverend Father and Lord, my lowliness must remember not only our old friendship and your frequent kindness, but also—and this is more important than those things—your authority, which among human beings is the Christ of God. Supported by so great a privilege of heavenly gifts, you bear the weight of command, and consequently a heavier judgment threatens anyone who resists it.

Although these considerations persuade my timidity to submit to your order, the memory of the mercy you showed us by this act of commendation gives me the greatest support.

[Col. 1165B]

2. When the sea of my storm-tossed monastery was in turmoil, and nearly all the beloved members of the monastery were groaning because the one who had assumed the place of shepherd and physician pursued in the suffering little sheep not the burden of guilt but the old loss of a familiar hatred; and when, gathering all the strength of his mind, he did not attempt to protect his companion sheep from an attacking—and, alas, overly familiar—wolf, but by an improperly acquired secular power drove us from the monastery’s ship and cast us into the waves of the sea;

when the waves in turn rushed upon us and overwhelmed us, and only destruction threatened, with no hope of escape, then this woman at last shone upon us like the star of the sea with a pious radiance. She received her shipwrecked man into the harbor of her compassion and, pitying the pains of wounds still gaping and fresh, with motherly care sent him to you, like a skilled physician, to be treated and consoled for the time being.

She faithfully imitated the example of that chosen Samaritan who, when a man had been wounded by robbers and neglected by the priest and Levite, took pity on him and came near; washed the wounded man with wine, soothed him with oil, bound him with compassion, and entrusted him to the innkeeper for care, promising payment.

So that all later generations may know that such great compassion was shown by a queen, I say that the woman who did this was one whose virtues no eloquent rhetoric, however gifted, could ever unfold in sufficient speech. We therefore believe that she was joined by divine providence to the royal side so that the benefit of the present kingdom might be wisely secured through the great diligence of her vigilant industry.

[Col. 1165C]

3. To return to what I left above: through your consolation and healing, my most loving Father, the wounds are indeed closed, but I tremble at the nearby arrows secretly lying in wait from certain envious people. Yet I breathe again at length, placed under the authority of my patroness and, indeed, under the protection of your recommendation. By God’s grace, there is nothing to fear: while you are our protector and guide, no storm, however threatening and treacherous, can overwhelm us.

For, with the Lord’s grace always going before us, I shall hope beneath the shadow of your wings until the wickedness of every ambush has passed. But enough of this. Let my discourse now turn to the weight of your authority. In accordance with its proper consequence, it must briefly preview how the holy Church of York, during the time of your episcopate, cast off its former rusticity through the growth of divine service, and, in its raw newness instructed by your teachings in the praises of God, grew fittingly to maturity.

I would say that this has been divinely added to your crown: the clergy, formerly indistinguishable from secular people by their customary clothing, now celebrate God’s praises in the wedding garment and conduct the synodal assembly in long tunics. They also undertake the work of mercy, formerly neglected to an excessive degree, in almsgiving and offerings to the poor; and you have continually impressed upon them the memory of the faithful departed.

I say this not to cast upon you the snare of flattery, but rather—if I may say so—to kindle you toward those deeds which you rightly recognize that you necessarily owe to God, arising from the office of leadership undertaken with the dignity of the honor imposed upon you.

[Col. 1166C]

4. In this respect also you show yourself a worthy successor to the holy bishops who preceded you in your see, since you diligently strive both to celebrate their deeds and to commend their lives in writing. Hence it happened that, when you had ordered responsories for the most holy John to be composed according to the limited measure of my lowliness, you instructed me to turn my pen to beginning his Life.

This work is recognized as all the more difficult and arduous because it is all the more well known. Therefore, in the name of the Lord, take up the oars, spread the sails, and entrust our course to God. If he applies his grace to your prayers, we shall happily reach the shore and tread the sand of the beach, secure and unconcerned about the barking dogs of the turbulent sea. For the more sharply they raise their crests in barking, the more nature reveals their weakness.

[Note: [Col. 1166D] After this prologue had apparently ended, the manuscript adds the following in the manner of a rubric. Here Brother Folcard returns to his subject, Saint John. From this one may infer that the other rubrics inserted subsequently in the manner of capital headings do not belong to the author but to the copyist. Nevertheless, out of reverence for antiquity, we would have wished to append them here in continuous sequence, had we not found them to have been copied rather recklessly, as will become apparent immediately after no. 8.]

CHAPTER ONE. His studies, sermons, the bishopric of Hexham, the archbishopric of York, and miracles.

[Col. 1167A]

5. The eternal mercy of the compassionate God, coming to the aid of the lost world, through his incarnate Son dissolved the ancient judgment of human condemnation, so that just as through the transgressing Adam we had become children of death and hell, so through Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God and the Virgin, we might be restored as children of life to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

Through him, who reigns with God in heaven and dwells among human beings on earth, God disclosed the mystery of his providential plan—namely, with how great a mercy God had determined to save the children of men, since he handed over his only Son to death in order to give them life.

Having received the insult of the outrage inflicted upon him, he used this law of mercy against his despisers: where guilt abounded, there the examples of his mercies might overflow all the more abundantly.

After confirming his disciples, our teachers, through the doctrines of the divine commandments, he had already marked almost the whole world with the Christian name derived from himself. Their words penetrated the boundaries and corners of the earth, and thus the faith reached the knowledge of every language.

For, as the faithful account of our fathers has handed down, although the boundaries of all Gaul had long since been illuminated by faith, the word of God was brought later to this island of Britain. Britain followed the example of that younger son in the Gospel who at first resisted his father’s command but afterward, moved by repentance, persisted more earnestly in cultivating the fruits of his father’s vineyard.

Thus, the later it saw itself come to the faith of Christ, the more devoutly it began to advance in the religion it had received.

[Col. 1167C]

6. From that time the favorable goodness of Christ began to produce sweet figs among thorns, to multiply beautiful grapes in the bramble, and to make the stock of its newly established people fruitful with a brood of holy children.

Among the other lights divinely bestowed upon the still-uncultivated Britons, then kindled more brightly by God to drive away the darkness of ancient errors, this blessed boy John shone like the morning star. From the very beginning of his name he was initiated into the grace of Christ, and as a glorious soldier of God he remained in Christ’s service to the very end.

First he placed his hand under the rod of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, under whose teaching and care he had been educated; from this supreme teacher he climbed to the highest summit of philosophy.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Saint Theodore is commemorated on 19 September. Consecrated at Rome, he came to Canterbury in 699 and died in 690. Thomas Stubbs asserts that John, named “the grace of God,” received from him an exceptionally lively intelligence in the Scriptures. More about him is related below, in no. 15.]

Because of the excellence of his gifts, he was detained for some days in the monastery of Streaneshalch by Abbess Elfleda.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] We have discussed the Life of Saint Elfleda on 8 February; there, in no. 60, this residence of Saint John is cited from Thomas Stubbs. Bede, book IV, chapter 23, states that five bishops came forth from this monastery of Streaneshalch, all men of exceptional merit and holiness, among whom John is numbered.]

But merciful God, unwilling to allow so great a light to remain enclosed for long in a small vessel, brought it out from its bushel’s hiding place and set it upon a lampstand, so that it might shine for all who entered his house.

7. Departing from there, and admonished by fraternal charity, he began to evangelize the word of God among the still-uncultivated peoples of the English.

Abundantly endowed with divine generosity, he was an eloquent rhetorician in the worthy outpouring of his words. His holy life also lent appropriate support to his continual preaching, since the example of his conduct never departed from the path of the instruction he had heard.

Moreover, the power of God accompanied the power of his word, and all who were sick were healed through him, so that Christ’s promise might be confirmed in this faithful servant of his:

“The signs that I do, you also shall do, and greater than these shall you do” (John 14:12).

Enriched by so great a gift of divine grace, he multiplied the talent received from his Lord by various forms of profitable exchange, so that he might enter joyfully, at his calling, into the gladness of his Lord.

8. Imbued with an abundant supply of learning, he devoted himself with diligent vigilance to teaching his disciples. Among them he embraced Bede, renowned among the teachers of the Church, with affectionate regard according to the strength of his capacity.

As an industrious young beginner, Bede followed him, abundantly instructed by so great a teacher. He excelled both in explaining the Gospels and in arranging historical matters. By setting out the most subtle calculations of chronology and computation, he purged the inborn dullness of the British people and ennobled the dignity of his writings through the authority acquired from the Roman See. Greater still, preserving the innocence of his life, he faithfully strove to please God to the very end, so that with the holy he might be holy and, with his most holy chosen teacher John, remain in the election of Christ’s discipleship.

In due course, John, who had consecrated Bede to God from the first orders of the sacred degrees, advanced him, together with certain other men trained by him, to the dignity of the priesthood as worthy helpers of God. Thus they might cling more tenaciously to Christ’s vine, the more closely they had embraced its branches.

But because the memory of some of these men had necessarily to be introduced into the rest of the Life in accordance with the circumstances of the narrative, let us now return to unfolding the events of the account we have undertaken.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] The following title had been inserted here: “How Saint John was elected archbishop of the Church of York.” But what is related at the beginning concerns his bishopric of Hexham, while his archbishopric of York had been improperly inserted below, in no. 14, and has therefore been brought back here at the end.]

9. While the illustrious king of the English, Aldfrith, was reigning, and the bishop Eata had passed from this human life,

[Note: [Col. 1168D] This is Alfrith the illegitimate or younger, not distinguished from the elder Alfrith by William of Malmesbury and others. He succeeded his brother Ecgfrith, who was killed around Pentecost in the year 684. Consult Richard, prior of Hexham, chapter 10.]

[Note: [Col. 1168D] Saint Eata, according to the same Richard, died in the year 685 and is entered in the English calendars on 26 October.]

the votes of all calling for it—and especially through the agency of God’s will—this beloved man of God succeeded him in the episcopate. Anointed as the Lord’s Christ, he increased his works of piety and faith, appropriate to so great an office and divine dignity.

Although we cannot recount all these works because of their number, let us at least gird ourselves to explain some of them, for the honor and glory of the Lord. We have learned these things as handed down by truthful witnesses, and especially from the blessed Brithun, who was first his deacon and later, through John’s gift and consecration, became the most worthy abbot of the monastery that John had built from the foundations and that is called Beverley.

[Note: [Col. 1170D] In Bede she is called “the abbess’s natural daughter.”]

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Bede, book V, chapter 2, has the following: “The most reverend and truthful man Berhthun, formerly his deacon and now abbot of the monastery called Inderawuda, that is, ‘the island of the Deirans,’ is accustomed to relate these things.” In the Life published by Mabillon, the reading is: “Now abbot of the monastery called Beverley.” In volume I of the Monasticon Anglicanum, page 170, Brithun is said to have died, as the first abbot of Beverley, on the Ides of May in the year of the Lord 733 and to have been buried beside Saint John. We discuss his Life on 15 May.]

10. The same beloved bishop of God had dedicated a church in honor of the blessed archangel Michael in a little village called Carnesboc, [Col. 1169B] not far from the flowing stream of the River Tyne [Note: [Col. 1169D] Bede adds: “not far from the church at Hagustald, that is, at a distance of about a mile and a half.” Thomas Stubbs seems to call it Arneshange, that is, “Eagle’s Mount.”]. Here Saint John frequently remained, especially during Lent, since the place was more remote from the crowds of ordinary people, devoting himself to fasting, prayer, and generous almsgiving. On one occasion, when he had ordered a crowd of poor people to be admitted for consolation, as was his custom, a man of pitiable appearance came among them. He was mute from birth and so hideous from the jaundiced foulness of his head that, since his entire scalp had been overrun by a skin disease, sparse and bristling hairs stood up in place of hair, like the bristles of pigs [Note: Bede says: “He had so much scurf and dandruff on his head that no hair could ever grow on the upper part of his head; only horrible hairs seemed to stand around its circumference.”].

The holy bishop knew him well, for he had often seen him among the other poor receiving his alms. At last, then, the sight of such misery pierced more deeply the soul beloved of God and moved him to greater compassion. He laid his hand upon the poor man’s chin, for he was exceedingly kind, blessed him [Note: Bede: “He impressed the sign of the holy cross upon his tongue,” and gives the rest more fully.], and commanded him in God’s name to speak. The bishop first pronounced certain letters and words; the man who had been mute followed, speaking the same words from the bishop’s mouth. Then, after the words, he gradually entered into the sentences of the prayer, insofar as the holiness of the bishop required. All that horrible infection of the head also fled from him, and he was clothed with a mass of curly black hair. Thus, after the other poor had been consoled with simple food, he returned, through the merits of Saint John, enriched by the abundant manifold mercies of God [Note: This passage had been wrongly transferred to no. 25 through the fault of copyists; we have restored it here, as it also stands in the Life published by Mabillon. Richard asserts that he presided over the church of Hagustald for only one year, and perhaps not even a complete year. He would therefore have become archbishop of York in 686, namely, as Bede says in book V, chapter 5: “When Wilfrid had been restored to the episcopate of the church of Hagustald, John was appointed at York in his place after the death of Bishop Bosa.” We gave the Life of Blessed Bosa on 9 March, when we stated that he died in that year, 686. We illustrated the Life of Saint Wilfrid on 24 April.].

11. After this, therefore, Blessed Bishop Wilfrid, who had long been expelled from his episcopate, returned to his homeland after receiving a letter from the Roman council and from the lord Pope Agatho. He recovered the episcopate of the church of Hagustald with the approval of a synodal council, while Saint John received the episcopate in the city of York and held it nobly for thirty-three years.

12. On another occasion, while the Saint of God was traveling, he came to a village called Yatadini, where there was then a monastery of handmaids of Christ. It was governed by an abbess named Hereburgis, a woman full of faith, who, with her daughters in Christ, rejoiced greatly at the arrival of the man of God [Note: Yatadim, Bede’s Vetadum or Wetadum; in the Life published by Mabillon, Humedatum.].

The devout mother immediately reported with grief that one of her sisters was being overwhelmed by a serious bodily illness and that no hope for her life remained. She earnestly begged the holy bishop to deign to visit her, saying [Col. 1170B] that she placed great confidence in God’s mercy and in his merits, and that the sick woman would be better if he laid his hands upon her.

The blessed bishop asked the cause of the illness. From the abbess he learned that the woman had been bled on the fourth day of the moon and that, after the condition of her body had been disturbed, her arm had swollen miserably. Once he learned this, he declared that it had been done imprudently. He recalled that, when he was a boy and his disciple, he had heard from Blessed Theodore, archbishop and his teacher, that bloodletting during the fourth lunar phase was extremely dangerous, and that such treatments ought not to be undertaken when the waxing moon was still young or when the flow of the sea had only recently broken out.

At last, overcome by the tears and prayers of the grieving abbess and the sisters, he entered the sick woman’s room [Col. 1170C]. Seeing the excessive swelling of her arm, he imposed the sign of the cross, offered God more fervently the incense of pure prayer, consoled the woman lying there, and went out of the house. Yet, while the woman remained ill, the blessing remained effective, and as the bishop departed, all the swelling departed with him.

The saint had scarcely sat down to eat when Capuburgis—for that was her name—sent a messenger to his deacon Brithtun, asking that he grant her an interview. When the man went, after receiving the bishop’s blessing, he met her coming toward him already healed, and learned that the cure had come to her through the bishop’s prayer. Afterward she lived a long time in good health, often recounting with joy the healing bestowed upon her by the blessed bishop.

13. This bishop, chosen by God, was also invited to dedicate the church of a village called South Burton [Note: Bede, chapter 4, says that the village was separated from the monastery of Beverley by a distance of nearly two miles. Its owner was called Puch; his daughter Yolfrida became a nun at Beverley and died on 13 March in the year of the Lord 742. Her bones were buried at Beverley. Puch gave the manor of Valkingione together with his daughter. Thus the Life of Saint John in the English Monasticum.]. A diligent executor of his office, he went there and dedicated it. When everything had been completed, as customary, he wished to return to his own place.

But the owner of the village, who had invited him, together with his household, pressed him with the humblest entreaties to enter his house and accept a meal as an act of service. Saint John of God replied that it was more fitting for a bishop to return to the monastery and serve God in the persons of his poor than to feast in the houses of the rich. Nevertheless, he was persuaded by promises of numerous alms to be given on this occasion, especially when Blessed Brithtun made the same promise, and at last he yielded to their requests.

14. The lady of the house, the wife of the man who had invited him, was suffering from a serious bodily illness [Col. 1171B], so that she had lain in bed for more than three weeks and was in danger of death. When the man of God, the true physician of souls and bodies, learned this, he ordered her to drink some of the water consecrated for the dedication of the church and to be sprinkled with the same water wherever the pain of the illness pressed most severely.

When this had been done, the whole illness suddenly fled, and she was restored to a new vigor of health. The woman immediately rose, prepared herself in her finest clothing, entered, and asked for a blessing. She then gladly waited upon the guests at table. The extent of the health granted to her became known to everyone, so that, serving the pious bishop and those seated with him drink as a faithful cupbearer, she did not withdraw even once to rest.

Consider, I ask, how in blessed John was fulfilled what Christ promised his own: “The works that I do, you also shall do.” Our Lord entered a house, found Peter’s mother-in-law suffering from fever, drove away the fever, and ordered her to minister to him. In both cases one and the same work was performed; but there the Lord acted without a servant, whereas here the faithful and prudent servant acted through the Lord and with the Lord.

15. The Lord likewise glorifies his servant John through a similar work. A certain rich man named Adam invited him to consecrate a new church [Note: Bede, chapter 5. It may be added that the same events are related there.]. The rich man had a servant who was very dear and useful to him. Because of an illness that had seized him, the servant had reached the point at which a bier suitable for his body was being prepared beside his bed, shrouds were being made ready, and everything appropriate for a funeral had been placed at hand in the sick man’s presence.

The man of God, our physician, was invited again, so that he might meet severe afflictions with stronger remedies.
