When he saw the funeral preparations, the great intercessor was wholly lifted up toward heavenly things and obtained what he asked. Then, turning immediately to his command, he ordered the man to be healed and rise quickly, and at once withdrew.

When the illness had been driven away and he had been restored to life, the man remained for a while in astonishment, scarcely knowing whether he was himself. His flesh, restored to life, began to demand the necessities of life. He sent a message to his master, who was dining, and asked him to send him something [Col. 1172A] to drink. Everyone rejoiced that the man who shortly before had caused concern about his funeral was now asking for drink.

The illustrious bishop immediately offered him a cup of wine and ordered him to refresh his thirsty thirst from it. After drinking it, he put on his clothing, entered among those dining, and, since he had not eaten for a long time, confessed that he was hungry and asked for food. You would have seen all the guests solemnly rejoicing over their companion restored to life, venerating the holy man of God, glorified by such holiness in the world, and undoubtedly praising the Lord, who in his favor worked such things through his John.

## CHAPTER II. Other Miracles before and after His Death. The Duration of His Episcopate and His Death

16. The Lord magnified him in the sight of kings [Col. 1172B] and displayed his glory and merit in the assembly of princes. By royal decree the leading men of the kingdom gathered; this man of God also came with the others. King Osred himself was present, a man of religion and faith, and by common deliberation the faithful established regulations there concerning many useful matters.

In that assembly injuries were corrected, the laws of God were confirmed, the equity of peace was strengthened, and the property of churches and monasteries was secured by the king’s protection. When these matters had been happily settled, the lord archbishop—John, by the grace, name, and office of God—invited the king and his companions to his table. The king courteously obeyed, as was fitting, and, reclining with his nobles, took his place at the bishop’s command. He partook of bodily food together with heavenly admonitions.

When all had been abundantly refreshed, listen, I ask, with attentive hearts; listen also here to the Lord’s work, and see here the Gospel’s assertion: “The works that I do, you also shall do.” “Fill,” Saint John said to his cupbearers, “fill three jars: one with wine, another with mead, and the third with ale.”

17. When they had been filled to the brim, John, who was also filled with the grace of God, extended his hand, blessed them, and ordered the drink to be served. The cupbearers drew the increasing liquid from the jars into abundant cups and repeatedly returned to serve the happy guests. They drew without exhausting the supply, and nothing appeared to have been taken from the jars so often; they continually overflowed to the very top.

The drinkers themselves marveled at the renewed nectar. They were astonished that what they drank increased, overflowing with gentle sweetness and wondrous heavenly abundance. As you reflect on the increasing power of this drink, remember the wedding at Cana of Galilee, where the master of the feast declared that the wine was good.

But in the overflowing of the three jars, remember the Lord’s banquet, at which he satisfied five thousand men and more, and consider in your hearts what the Lord performs through his John. There we read that, when they saw the sign of the wine, his disciples believed in Jesus. Here also King Osred [Note: Osred reigned from the year 705 until 716, when he was killed in the misfortune of war.] and his princes, having experienced this sign, learned that the grace of God was in his John.

The king venerated the man of God and summoned his cupbearer, named Brithdred. Rejoicing with royal delight, he said: “You have served very well in your service. We have been abundantly refreshed by the best and most wondrous drink from your lord, and we have been gladdened by the holiness of the saint whom we have seen. Now we must depart with his grace.”

18. Listen, I ask, still further to the Lord glorifying his John in the likeness of his own works and displaying a new sign of his holiness. Whenever John happened to remain in the metropolis of York, the seat of his archbishopric, he had a great affection for the basilica of the archangel Michael and kept vigil there according to his customary practice. It was adjacent to his residence.

On one occasion, while he was secretly carrying out his prayers there, the majesty of the Holy Spirit visibly appeared to him in the form of a shining white dove, flashing with fiery brightness, and deigned to place the glory of its dwelling above the head of the praying bishop. O eternal and most merciful God, from how pure a heart those prayers proceeded which obtained the presence of the Holy Spirit—the same Spirit, I say, who appeared in the Jordan when Jesus, the Son of God, was baptized!

How pleasingly did those prayers rise into the sight of the Godhead, carried even to the faithful by messengers who reported the effect of such power! The immense brightness of the majesty enclosed there shone through every opening and window of the basilica, as though the sun, having left the heavens, had moved into that place and enclosed its radiance within the narrow confines [Col. 1173C] of the building.

To pursue the truth of the matter with a fitting novelty of praise: truly the Sun of Justice, God, was enclosed there, enclosed in his John, illuminating him with the grace of the Holy Spirit and allowing no error to darken him.

19. Everyone who saw this was astonished, as at an extraordinary event, and wondered what those lights could be, and from where so many rays of light shone with such brilliance and flashed with such radiance. At last his deacon Sigga [Note: Saint Sigga is called Saint John’s deacon in the English Monasticum.] approached, unfastened the bolt, opened the door, and shared in the glory of the vision.

He saw the holy bishop, his eyes raised and fixed upon heaven and his hands lifted up, pouring out his soul before God like water, and a dove, white as snow, upon his head [Col. 1173D]. At the sight of its brilliant brightness, the deacon, as though scorched, suffered the punishment of his rash intrusion: his face contracted into wrinkles and his entire skin was affected.

The holy man of God perceived that the deacon had shared in the vision. Although annoyed, he nevertheless did not abandon the demeanor of his gentle devotion. He summoned the deacon to him, cleansed him with the touch of his right hand, restored his face to its former beauty, and entreated, protested, and adjured him not to reveal that vision to any mortal as long as he himself lived.

You have heard how the Lord Jesus, after displaying the glory of his divinity on the mountain to Peter, James, and John, enjoined them to keep silent until the Son of Man had trampled death by his resurrection and restored life to the dead. Here also you see John, imitator of his Lord, a witness of his divine glorification, as though hiring a witness at a price: he binds him by prayers to keep silent about what he had seen until he had put off mortality and clothed himself with the glory of blessed immortality.

There is therefore no doubt that this holy man of God possessed great purity in the sight of God in heaven, since he was endowed with such radiance before human beings on earth.

20. He also had another witness of the signs which the merciful God performed through him: namely, Herebald [Note: Bede reports this in chapter 6, saying: “Herebald, who was then living in his clergy, now presides as abbot over the monastery beside the mouth of the River Tyne,” as is also said here toward the end.], of the monastery of Tynemouth. He had been John’s disciple from childhood, had been formed by his teaching, and lived continually with him as his companion.

Herebald often testified that he had learned by personal experience that Saint John was truly a man of the holiest life. Among the many benefits he bestowed upon the sick, John had brought Herebald himself back from death and restored him to sudden health.

He said that on one occasion this beloved man of God was traveling with his companions and came to a pleasant stretch of level road. Delighted by the smoothness of the plain, the young men, following military custom, begged their lord to allow them to test their horses across the unobstructed level of the field.

At first the man of God refused, regarding the request as frivolous. But when they persisted in asking, he said: “Go ahead as you wish; but let Herebald remain with me.” When Herebald heard this, he began to grieve with youthful impatience, for he wished to test the horse he was riding, which the bishop had recently given him.

21. At last, when the whole field resounded with the horses racing about on loosened reins, Herebald, as though unwilling and unable to restrain the horse that had been urged on, disobeyed and flew away, driving the swift-footed animal into its course with still looser reins.

Herebald used to testify that he then heard the bishop shouting behind him: “You are doing wrong by leaving me, and you will learn this in such a way.” Scarcely had the holy man finished his threat when Herebald’s horse slipped. Herebald was thrown upon a huge stone; he fell headlong, fractured his skull, suffered internal injuries, and was left disabled in hand and thumb.

All were disturbed and ran to him. Leaving their horses, they leapt to the ground. But the injured man seemed more senseless than conscious and was thought more likely to die than to live. A canopy was stretched over the dying man, and because of him its shade was extended across a broad space. Everyone grieved that he had taken part in the race, but they did not know what God himself had foreseen through that race.

22. The holy man of God especially mourned the fall of his beloved disciple. With the sacks drawn tight, he passed a sleepless night in the tent and prayed with supplications and tears that the merciful Lord might show mercy to his disobedient servant.

Very early in the morning he entered to the weakened man. First he prayed, and then, with tender affection, addressed Herebald by name. It is remarkable that, although Herebald had lain almost lifeless from the seventh hour of the preceding day until that morning, when called by the saint of God he opened his eyes as though awakened from deep sleep and fixed them upon the man of God.

The merciful teacher asked whether he recognized the one speaking to him. The sick man immediately replied in a tearful voice: “You are John, my bishop and my most beloved lord.”

The bishop then asked: “Do you think you can escape alive from the danger that threatens you?”

“I know and believe that I can,” he replied, “if God grants this to me through your prayers.”

What more need be said? The bishop laid his hands upon the fractured head, sprinkled the weakened body with consecrated water, invoked God and, bending down, breathed upon him; then he marked him with the cross, and God granted sudden healing.

Herebald himself often recounted this afterward, living for many years. When he had reached a more mature age, he became a most vigilant abbot in the place where the sea flows into the River Tyne; hence it is also called Tynemouth.

23. That venerable abbot of whom we spoke above also related that on one occasion Saint John of God went to the monastery at Beverley for two reasons: namely, to remind the flock of God dwelling there of their salvation in the service of God, and to ensure that nothing was lacking in the administration of their temporal resources that might prevent them from devoting themselves to divine things.

There he made clear to everyone, through God’s ready generosity, how great a reputation for integrity this great servant of his possessed before God. The venerable abbot had prepared a bath for the bishop, already wearied by advancing old age. After the old man had bathed following his customary, extended celebration of psalms and prayers, the abbot asked him to enter the storeroom and deign to bless the provisions that God had supplied there for the use of his servants.

When these things had been done according to the abbot’s desire, the weary old man sat down. The abbot humbly asked whether, after his bath, he would like to taste a little wine.

With calm expression the bishop replied that he would be pleased if some could be brought to him. The previous day a merchant had brought the abbot a flask of wine from the city. The abbot had gladly received it and ordered it to be placed in the storeroom for the use of this most holy man.

24. Brithred the cupbearer was summoned and ordered to serve the bishop wine in a glass cup. While he hurried to obey, acting too quickly out of his eagerness to serve, he carelessly left the aforementioned flask of wine hanging on the wall. Falling from above, it broke through the middle, so that it was divided into two parts.

But since the one for whom that drink had been reserved was a vessel of chosen integrity before God, it is no wonder that God himself preserved the drink within the divided parts of the vessel. For the two pieces stood separated from one another, and each contained the wine within itself like frozen liquid or solid crystal.

Disturbed by the sound of the falling flask, the cupbearer Brithred ran inside and found what had been divinely done there. Since he knew that an account of this event would be unwelcome to the one whose merits were responsible for it, he summoned a certain brother named Plechelm and brought him in to see the unusual and wondrous sight, so that he might have a witness when the event was reported.

They then received the wine into another vessel and gave thanks to God, who performs such things in Saint John, the vessel pleasing to him as the dwelling of his presence.

25. The Lord performed many other signs through the same man. For all who touched his clothing in faith rejoiced that they had quickly received healing from all their illnesses [Note: Here there had been inserted the praise of the disciples, which we have transferred to the end of the following number, together with the election to the archbishopric of York, which we have restored to its proper place, no. 11.].

One day, when a great crowd had come to Bishop Saint John to receive the anointing of sacred chrism, he anointed among the others a certain young man who was dead and thus brought him back from death to life. Similarly, he expelled a demon from a certain man. He also always healed the insane and the sick wherever he found them. He even possessed power over storms through the strength of the Holy Spirit.

26. It is no wonder that this chosen John of God was gracious before God and human beings, since he had been sufficiently instructed by a most illustrious teacher and one of the most eloquent among theologians, namely Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. Saint Bede reports the following about him in his Ecclesiastical History of the English:

“In the time of Bishop Cedd there was in Rome a certain monk named Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia. He was a man sufficiently instructed in both secular and divine learning, in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew; upright in morals and venerable in age. Ordained by Pope Vitalian, he was sent to Britain and came to his own church at Canterbury in the second year after his consecration.

“This Theodore also received many people from the British region into his instruction. Among them he had a disciple of great holiness named John, whom we later saw ordained, in the time of King Alfrid, as archbishop of the metropolitan church of Blessed Peter at York. The Lord Jesus Christ loved him so greatly that, while he was celebrating the divine mysteries, he sent the Holy Spirit to him in the form of a dove.

“Theodore remained in the archbishopric of Canterbury for twenty-one years, three months, and twenty-six days, and thus departed to Christ. John, for his part, sanctified many in the order of the diaconate and honored many with the dignity of the priesthood. Among their company was the saint Bede, who wrote many useful works concerning the apostolic faith.”

John himself also had a deacon of great holiness named Brithian, whom he appointed abbot of his monastery called Beverley, a man of holy conduct. The same Bishop John converted all who came to him to the way of truth, and continually and without ceasing prayed for the flock entrusted to him and for the whole Christian people.

27. This athlete of Christ, John, remained in the episcopate [Note: In both episcopates, that is, from his ordination as bishop.] for thirty-three years, eight months, and thirteen days. Then, when advanced age made it impossible for him to travel around the episcopate, he entrusted the episcopate of York to his priest Wilfrid, with the election of the entire people [Note: This is Saint Wilfrid the Younger, whose Life we gave on 27 April.].

He himself, with the counsel of Saint Brithun, his abbot, went to Beverley. Remaining there for a long time in the service of God, he happily ended his life on 7 May [Note: Bede says, “and there he completed a manner of life worthy of God,” omitting the word “long,” in place of which Thomas Stubbs and the author of the Life of Saint Brithun substitute “four years.” Richard asserts three years, but we find scarcely two complete years. For since Easa died in the year 685, perhaps on 26 October, and even if John was ordained bishop only a few days afterward and remained in that administration for thirty-three years, eight months, and thirteen days before leaving the see for Beverley, he would have arrived at the year 719 and beyond the eighth day of July. Thus, by 7 May of the year 721, scarcely ten months beyond a year could remain; this is sufficient for it to be said that he remained there “for a long time.”].

Thus ascending to the heavenly kingdoms, he was buried in the portico of Saint John the Evangelist, in his own monastery, in the year 721 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In the same place where he was buried, through his merits the sick are healed, demons are driven away, the blind are enlightened, the ears of the deaf are opened, speech is restored to the mute, and the lame are granted the use of their feet. Every kind of suffering is driven away, and through his intercession our sins are wiped out and heavenly joys are granted, by the power of him whom all things serve.

28. [Note: The miracles that follow, as a new beginning makes clear, have been added from another source.] Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ performed many miracles through his beloved John. The first of them is this:

On one occasion a certain man, overcome by the heat of fevers, reached the holy man’s tomb. Having lost his senses, he remained there for a long time, rolling about; at last the evil spirit was driven from him. Restored to complete health through the merits of Saint John, he took up his staff and returned to his own house. Afterward he was never again attacked by the same illnesses.

29. At a later time the abbot Brithun invited the abbot of Swina to Beverley on Saint John’s anniversary [Note: The monastery of Swina in the territory of York is prominently mentioned in the English Monasticum, p. 1026. Its antiquity is established from this passage, since these events occurred before the year 733, when Abbot Brithun died.]. The latter brought with him a certain priest named Druchwald, who was afflicted by such serious illness that he could scarcely make the journey there.

When the abbot of Swina afterward planned to return home, Abbot Brithun, at his request, received the sick priest into his care until he became well, especially because of the invocation of Saint John’s name and his love. The abbot of Swina also left with him one of his deacons, named Adde, so that the priest might be attended more carefully. Abbot Brithun had assigned to him a priest named Welverd, who was to serve the sick priest and provide everything necessary for him.

The sick priest then asked Abbot Brithun to permit his body to be buried in that cemetery if he should die there. “For,” he said, “that holy bishop formerly raised me to the priestly rank.” After he had obtained this request, the priest himself gave Brithun thanks with humble and devout prayer.

30. During the following night his illness became so severe that he was thought quite unable to survive it. When morning came, the abbot himself went to him and said: “I believe that you will soon be better if you are carried to the monastery where there are many relics of holy martyrs.”

The priest replied that he believed the same, and immediately declared that, after the third hour, he should be carried to the monastery itself. He gave thanks to God that he had been granted to enter it alive [Col. 1178B].

After praying fervently before the altar of Saint John the Evangelist, he went from there to the tomb. With humble prayer he begged Saint John to deign to aid him in his illness as his physician. Recalling more than once the grace he had obtained through John’s favor with God, he went onward and entered the monastery of Saint Martin, which also contained many relics of holy martyrs.

When the sign of the holy cross had been impressed upon his forehead through the power of those relics, he returned to the tomb of the holy confessor and was immediately cured of the illness that afflicted him. He afterward returned home healthy and unharmed, and often and joyfully recounted the miracle that had been performed in him.

31. On another occasion it happened that a certain nun from Esech, whose hands were contracted and whose entire body was held by illness, came to the tomb of the holy confessor and there received without delay healing from all her infirmity through the intercession of that holy Confessor.

After receiving her health, on the very day on which she was healed she served many people by pouring out drink for them, and afterward lived for many years in that health. These things were done through the intercession of this holy confessor, to the praise and honor of our Creator Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God forever and ever.

[Col. 1179]

## THE POEM OF FOLCARD ON SAINT VIGOR

(Achery, *Spicilegium veterum*, fourth edition, p. 576.)

[Col. 1179A]

The festive day of Father Vigor shines forth, worthy to be celebrated,

Vigor, whom Bayeux calls its father and Arras rejoices to call its brother.

His mother, a noble woman pleasing to God,

Receives as a pledge from so great a heavenly protector

The son whom she carries; divine power blessed him,

Consecrated him to itself, and consecrated him also to the whole world.

Thus the boy is born, beautiful in appearance, and becomes another

Samuel, worthy of the Lord from his tenderest years.

Soon he bends his gentle neck beneath the Lord’s yoke,

And the boy-monk is brought into the flock of Arras.

Making progress among all the fathers, he advanced through their instruction,

That illustrious boy, gladly subject to them all.

Now the blessed novice meditates on a greater undertaking:

That he may become, like the patriarch, a stranger far from his homeland.

[Col. 1179B]

Thus this exile, a sower of the word, goes into distant exile,

Making his way toward the people divinely appointed for him.

There is the city of Bayeux, which ancient Neustria displays.

He approaches it to teach those whom impious error held.

The grace of Christ’s virtues accompanies his disciple.

Whatever he teaches and admonishes, he proves by signs and fulfills by deeds.

He restored those exhausted in strength and drove away serpents;

By poured-out prayer he drew one whose life had ended to the world above.

When the people saw these things, they devoted themselves to the sacred waters;

And through the honor of the sacred font

You beget this people for God, Saint Vigor,

To whom we offer sacred hymns.

Master of flames, who suppresses the fires of the world,

[Col. 1180B]

Restrain the flames of Gehenna, lest they consume us.

## DOUBTFUL LITTLE WORKS OF FOLCARD

[Col. 1179]

## LIFE OF SAINT AUDOMAR, BISHOP OF TERUANNE

Written by an anonymous author who seems to have lived before the Norman devastation; abridged in Surius and perhaps interpolated by Folcard, a monk of Sithiu, in the eleventh century; restored from the Corbie copy.

(In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, second century, p. 559.)

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1179C]

1. We ought to offer manifold thanks and diligent praises to the almighty Lord, giver of spiritual gifts and great virtues, who, being the Creator and governor of all visible and invisible creatures, sent his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, into the world to teach and redeem every nation, and so forth.

He who chose twelve apostles from the multitude of the whole human race also commanded sixty-two others of another order to be his disciples in the white regions, so that laborers might not be lacking for the abundant harvest. Filled with the holy breath in the upper room of Zion and enriched with the wondrous gift of all languages, he commanded these disciples to go and teach and baptize every nation, and so forth.

After these men, and after their successors, he granted that other men, holy and endowed with the grace of God, filled with the same Spirit, should be vicars of the apostles in every part of the world, and so forth.

Therefore, for the western regions of the world, he gave Audomar, adorned with divine gifts, an apostolic teacher known through signs and virtues in many parts of the earth. For this reason, almighty God, through the glorious patronage of that bishop, we beg you to grant that the abundant streams of your wisdom from above may sprinkle our minds, stained though they are, so that we who desire to learn about the merits and virtues of so great a man, and about what your grace accomplished through him, may at least be able to draw out small things from great matters and a few things from many.

For who can know and recount his daily conduct, his steadfastness in the service of God, and all the labors that he performed in secret, with God alone as witness?

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 1181]

[Col. 1181A] **2.** This holy bishop Audomarus was born to parents who were noble and illustrious according to the dignity of the world and instructed in the Catholic faith, in the region of Constance, not far from the city of Constance (Constance on the Rhine), and specifically in the place called Aurea-Vallis (in the vernacular Imperio, Guldindal).  

[Note: [Col. 1181D] Saint Bertinus, who was his countryman, is said to have been a blood relative of Saint Audomarus; concerning this matter, see the Acts of Saint Bertinus in the following century. Johannes of Ypres, or Iperius, abbot of Sithiu, adds in his manuscript Chronicle, which he brought down to the year 1295, that in a certain instrument of Charlemagne Audomarus is called by the emperor himself his kinsman.]

His father, distinguished among his people, was called Friulfus; his mother was named Domitta. These devout parents, with the support of divine grace, raised the aforementioned boy from his cradle according to the rites of the Christian religion in ecclesiastical disciplines; for they had Audomarus as their only son. After the death of his aforementioned wife, while the boy was increasing in age and grace, Friulfus likewise strove, with divine mercy assisting him, to submit himself to Christ’s sweet and easy yoke, encouraged and persuaded by his son Audomarus.

**3.** Thus both of them—namely, his father Friulfus together with his blessed son Audomarus—fulfilled what is written: “Go, sell everything that you have, give to the poor, and come; follow me, and you will have eternal life” (Matthew 19:21). Dead to the world and alive to God, poor in things that pass away and rich in things eternal, subject to God and rebellious against the devil, alike in mind but different in age, they proceeded to the monastery of Christ’s soldiers called by the famous name of Luxeuil. It had been founded in the region of Burgundy in God’s name by the abbot, the blessed Columbanus, a man of Irish origin and holy memory.

At that time Saint Austasius governed the holy and blessed multitude of monks in the aforesaid monastery. Audomarus and his father, united in purpose, disclosed to him their religious desires, following what is written: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you, and your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32:7). When Saint Austasius saw them burning with the love of God and recognized divine grace in the face and words of blessed Audomarus, he gave these servants of God sound and perfect counsel, in accordance with the authority of sacred Scripture. He urged both of them—sometimes together, sometimes separately—to persevere with him in God’s service under regular discipline.

Both of them, therefore, burning with divine love and following the counsel of their spiritual father Austasius, devotedly subjected themselves to the yoke of the sacred rule. Blessed Austasius, filled with immense joy, joined them to the holy fellowship of the monks.

Thereafter Saint Audomarus, filled with spiritual grace, young in age but strong in faith, subject to the strict rigor of the rule, was instructed among the holy multitude of monks and, by the prompting of divine grace, became beloved by all Christ’s soldiers dwelling in the aforementioned monastery. For he was chaste in mind and body, filled with obedience and humility, instructed in divine knowledge, full of charity and gentleness, disciplined by strict fasts of abstinence, and continually watchful through prolonged nocturnal vigils, knowing what is written: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:37).

**4.** Thereafter the fame of blessed Audomarus spread through many places and reached the notice of Dagobert, king of the Franks—for “a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14). After many years had passed, he was summoned by the most reverend prince Dagobert and by the entire Frankish people, with the assistance of Saint Acharius, bishop of Noyon, to teach and govern the people of the city of Thérouanne. With great humility of mind he accepted the episcopal dignity. In that office, sowing the divine word in the hearts of believers, curing the sicknesses of souls and bodies, ransoming captives and prisoners, and caring above all for widows and the poor, he rightly governed the people entrusted to him by the Lord.

Before the arrival of blessed Audomarus, the people of Thérouanne had indeed heard the divine word from the companions of the martyr Dionysius—namely, Fuscianus and Victoricus—at the same time that Saint Quintinus was preaching in the city of Amiens. Nevertheless, many of the Thérouannais still clung to the worship of idols. After the two blessed men mentioned above, Fuscianus and Victoricus, had departed from the city of Thérouanne and had been crowned with martyrdom in the city of Amiens, the Thérouannais returned again to the worship of idols. Not only those who had earlier refused to accept the name of the Lord, but also those who had been baptized by the aforementioned Fathers, led astray by the same error, worshiped idols.

The supreme bishop Audomarus therefore entered that city and delivered the saving commandments of the divine word to the foolish hearts of the pagans. He illuminated their savage minds, blinded by the foul darkness of ignorance, with the abundant light of the Gospel; he handed over their empty images to be destroyed by fire; and he utterly overturned the sacrilegious worship of idols in that city. With divine grace assisting him, he converted the entire population dwelling there to the Catholic faith, for “God works together with everyone who does good” (Romans 2:10). For, as the Apostle testifies, “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Romans 8:31).

**5.** After the aforementioned bishop had converted that people to the worship of the true God, he preached the divine word as crowds gathered to him from every direction, and freed many people from various illnesses in the name of God. Divine generosity granted him signs of great powers, of which the following account now hastens, with Christ’s favor, to extract a few from his glorious deeds.

One day the distinguished confessor of Christ, Audomarus, was staying in the city of Boulogne. At dawn, after the nocturnal vigils, he rose as usual and entered the church to pray. There he preached the word of God for a long portion of the summer day to the crowds standing around him. He sang Mass for the Christian people and laid hands on the sick suffering from various kinds of disease. At midday the venerable old man, weary, lay down on his bed.

Then, wishing to allow his little body, fatigued by many labors, a short time for rest, one of his attendants, a young man given to youthful frivolity, approached him and said: “Lord, grant me leave now; I wish to go to the places near the sea.” The old man said to the young man, who was making this request before the crowd: “You do not have permission, my son, to go outside yet. For I think it better that you wait here a little while, until you see me rise safely from sleep.”

The prudent guardian, filled with the prophetic spirit, foresaw that it would be harmful for the erring young man to leave. Then the old man, overcome by sleep and weariness, fell silent. But the young man, despising the commands of his excellent patron—as is customary among the young, to despise the orders of the old—then hurried rapidly toward the sea.

Seeing a small boat standing on the shore, which people commonly used to cross the little river that the inhabitants of those parts call the Elna (Elne), the young man, forgetful and blinded by his love of amusement, foolishly climbed into it alone, wishing to play on the banks of that stream. But a powerful force of wind swept him out into the open sea.

Suddenly a fierce storm arose upon the water. The little boat, shaken by swelling waves, having neither rudder nor helmsman, drifted here and there upon the sea that separates Britain from the Franks by its vast waters and often brings destruction here upon the strongest ships when they founder. The wretched young man could see neither his own land nor any other. He then regretted that he had despised his patron’s words. Amid the battling winds and waves he believed that he was about to die; neither boat nor young man could resist the sea.

Then, when he prayed, God, through the merits of Audomarus, immediately brought the trembling youth to Saxon [English] land. Seeing unfamiliar fields, he was again bewildered and trembled with fear that robbers would strip him if he attempted to remain there alone any longer.

[Note: [Col. 1183D] Boulogne, also called Bolonia or Boulogne, not far from the Ocean at the river Elna, was the episcopal seat of the Morini, as Thérouanne was once a city at the little river Lys, destroyed by Emperor Charles V in 1553. According to the circumstances of the times, the bishop resided in either city. The see of the Morini is now divided among Boulogne, Saint-Omer, and Ypres.]

**6.** Acknowledging his known fault of disobedience and pouring out abundant tears as he begged for help, he called upon Audomarus his patron in a trembling voice and, trusting in the Lord, quickly returned to the boat. At once the Almighty granted him a favorable wind and commanded the sea, which had previously been swelling, to grow calm. Floating again across the tranquil sea, he soon returned safely to the harbor from which the strong east wind had earlier carried him away, namely to the aforementioned stream Elna, where it enters the sea.

The sailor immediately rose, recognized the familiar fields, left his boat unharmed on the shore, and, treading the seaweed of the shore with rapid steps, gave manifold thanks to the Almighty. Repentant, he returned again to his patron. The bishop was still staying in the same place where he had previously left him asleep, and, by the wondrous mercy of almighty God, the swift traveler returned within those same hours.

When he approached the doors of the hall where the old man was praying, the wretched youth quickly threw himself to the ground, confessed his fault with a tearful face, and, sighing with sobs, sought pardon with abundant tears. The old man gently rebuked him, saying: “Son, I told you beforehand what would happen and that it was not fitting for you to go out today. Why did you afterward dare to despise our word?”

The trembling young man replied to his patron: “It is my fault, lord—truly my fault. Forgive me, wretched man that I am, brought back from death through you.” Then, as we have said, he related his dangers: alone in the swelling waves of the Ocean, amid the devouring surges of the currents around the reefs, in a small boat, he had suffered much upon the sea and had not believed that he could escape alive, unless God, through Audomarus’s merits, had freed the wretched man, who had despaired of human help, from death.

The sober old man then ordered the young man to be silent and humbly restrained the careless disciple: “Do not bring this statement forth from your mouth again,” he said, “nor may you tell such things about me to anyone while you see me enjoying this brief life, lest the devil overcome us through the fault of boastfulness. Do not seek praise from the mouths of men, lest empty glory lift our heart on high.”

After the old man’s death, that disciple who had suffered upon the waves related all these events in order.

[Note: [Col. 1184D] Thereafter, in the Paris copy of the manuscripts from Fécamp, an account is given of a temptation of the flesh which Saint Audomarus is said to have overcome, after the example of Saint Benedict, by the stings of nettles and thorns.]

**7.** Not long afterward, three men from the aforementioned region of Constance came together in spirit to blessed Audomarus: Mummolinus, Ebertramnus, and Saint Bertinus. In accordance with the Lord’s command, they likewise left their parents, homeland, and all their relatives (Matthew 19:29).

Saint Audomarus graciously received these servants of God, giving immense thanks to the almighty Lord who had brought him such helpers for preaching the Gospel. For the men mentioned above were perfect in the Catholic faith and instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines and divine Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 1184D] Ebertramnus later became abbot of the monastery of Saint Quintinus near Vermand, or Saint-Quentin; concerning the others, see below.]

**8.** After a short period of time had passed, Saint Audomarus, prompted by divine grace, conceived the plan of founding a monastery in God’s name together with the blessed men mentioned above. By the gift of divine mercy, he had a suitable place for monks to inhabit.

There was a certain powerful man named Adrowaldus, exceedingly rich in the vain riches of this world. Blessed Audomarus converted him from the error of paganism to the Catholic faith and baptized him together with his entire household. Adrowaldus, however, wisely despising the deceptive riches of the present world and having no son, offered to God and blessed Audomarus a large part of his inheritance together with all his numerous possessions—namely, a villa commonly called Sithiu.

Blessed Audomarus had built a church in that villa before the arrival of the aforementioned men, in the very place where his little body now rests in peace. After the servants of God mentioned above had come to him, he granted them permission to build a dwelling for monks wherever they wished in the aforesaid villa.

Thus the holy men Mummolinus and Bertinus, together with their other companions in Christ, began to build a monastery in a certain place, which to this day is called the Old Monastery.

[Note: [Col. 1185C] Adroaldus, Iperius writes, wished to have his donation confirmed by written testimony so that it might remain more secure for future times. It therefore begins as follows: “To the holy lords and fathers Bertinus, Mummel[inus], etc.” The donation was made on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord King Chlodoveus. It was executed at the royal villa of Sithiu. Yet Miraeus, Donations of the Pious, chapter 3, reads: “Executed at the royal villa of Ascio.” Chlodoveus’s eleventh year corresponds to the year of Christ 648.]

But after remaining there for only a few years, they wished, at the prompting of divine grace, to choose another place.

[Note: [Col. 1185D] Surius reads “the old temple.” Iperius writes: “At the command of blessed Audomarus, the three holy men mentioned above built a little church and a cell in the territory of the same villa, in a place which is still, for this reason, called the Old Monastery, above the river Agniona, in the year 626”—read, “about the year 649.” “In that place the holy men mentioned above lived almost as in a hermitage, confined with a small community, for fourteen years,” and so forth.]

**9.** These blessed men, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, found a perfect plan. Immediately they boarded a boat without a helmsman or oarsman and without making any provision for food or drink. Sailing here and there upon the broad pond adjoining their aforementioned dwelling, they begged the almighty Lord to lead them unharmed to the place that his mercy had prepared for them. They said to one another that they would not disembark from the pond until, when their boat had found a suitable landing-place, it should happen that they could sing, in the proper order of the Psalter, the following verse: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it” (Psalm 131:14).

The merciful Lord, who is everywhere present to his servants—for “the Lord is near to those who call upon him”—immediately brought the boat in which the blessed men were traveling to land after a certain interval that had been foreseen for them. Then, singing the verse mentioned above, they joyfully left the boat without delay and went ashore, recognizing that the Lord had granted them that place.

Thereafter, with the favor of Audomarus, their pious father, they began to build in God’s name the monastery called Sithiu, named after the aforementioned villa, above the river Agniona.

As religious men flocked from every direction to the servants of God mentioned above, blessed Audomarus placed Mummolinus over the multitude of monks. Not long afterward, however, the venerable abbot Mummolinus was elevated, by the gift of divine grace, to the episcopate of the city of Noyon, and for twenty-six years rightly governed the people of that city entrusted to him by the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1185D] The monastery of Sithiu, also called Ulterense, was named from the river Ultro—which is also called Agnio, Agniona, and Enneno, and is now called the Aa. It is now called Saint Bertinus, either by that very name or because of its exceptional renown. We shall discuss it more fully in the Acts of Saint Bertinus.]

[Note: [Col. 1185D] That is, after Eligius, who, having been ordained bishop in the third year of Chlodoveus II, the year of Christ 640, governed the Church of Noyon and Tournai for nineteen years and in 649 made way for Mummolinus. In the Life of Saint Eligius, book II, chapter 44, Mummolinus is said to have been rebuked by the abbot of the basilica of Saint Eligius for having stolen the holy man’s horse; there Saint Audoenus calls Mummolinus an apostolic man. Mummolinus therefore died in 684, on 16 October, the day on which he is commemorated in the Benedictine and Gallican Martyrologies. His body is preserved in the principal church of Noyon, and part of his head in the monastery of Sithiu. Nothing else occurs in his manuscript Acts except that he is said to have been promoted to the episcopate by Chlotharius, son of Chlodoveus.]

**10.** After Mummolinus, the glorious bishop Audomarus placed the blessed Bertinus over the holy choir of monks in the aforesaid monastery.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Nevertheless, Iperius assigns Bertinus the first place in the catalogue of the abbots of Sithiu, entirely omitting Mummolinus.]

Bertinus was beloved and dear to the holy brothers who served God in that place under the rigor of strict discipline. For he was a venerable man, wise in divine matters and a provident shepherd of his flock, but simple and innocent in evil, according to the Lord’s command: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

**11.** After many years had passed, blessed Audomarus lost his bodily eyes and was deprived of temporal light, so that, illuminated by perpetual light, he might always behold the Lord, as blessed David says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 24:15); and again: “To you I lift up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens” (Psalm 123:1).

By the loss of his bodily eyes he was filled with spiritual light and continued to govern the people entrusted to him by the Lord according to the same order.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] In the Life of Saint Vedast, Alcuin writes that Audomarus took part in the translation of Saint Vedast: “During that translation, blessed Audomarus is said to have received the light of his eyes, but immediately, by his prayers, to have obtained again the blindness which he had voluntarily borne.” Fulbert likewise testifies to this in the Acts of Saint Autbert.]

**12.** After a few years had passed, when the venerable old man Audomarus had been wearied by the excessive heat of a fever and had recognized that the day of his death had arrived, he rose that same day from the little bed on which he lay. Entering the church, he prostrated himself before the altar and prayed with tears to the Lord for himself and for the people standing around him.

After receiving the body and blood of Christ and preaching to the crowds surrounding him, he lifted his eyes toward heaven. With trembling hands, which fever and old age caused to shake, he blessed his disciples with devoted mind, saying: “I beseech the immense mercy of the almighty Lord that I may deserve to see you, my little sons, happy in the kingdom of God.”

When all these things had been duly accomplished that day, he returned again to his little bed. Lying there with his whole body extended in the usual manner and with a serene face, the soul of his holy confessor, surrounded by angelic hosts, departed to the almighty Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Iperius says that this occurred in the villa of Waurantis (Wauvrant), about three miles from Sithiu, where Saint Austreberta is said to have received the veil from Audomarus.]

Those who were present in that house at the same hour testified that such a fragrance entered their nostrils and mouths as though the entire house had been filled with every kind of spice, as has often happened at the passing of other saints: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15).

**13.** The aforementioned venerable abbot Bertinus, when divine grace revealed this to him, immediately went with his monks to the place where the venerable old man had died. With psalms, hymns, and songs he brought the sacred body of blessed Audomarus to the place of burial, and with the immense mourning of the surrounding people they buried him in the aforementioned church, which that blessed bishop had built at Sithiu.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The interpolator writes: “His body was translated by the most reverend abbot Bertinus and the choir of monks and buried with honor in the monastery of Sithiu, in the basilica which that illustrious bishop himself had built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, for the burial of the bodies of the monks.” Read the Life of Saint Bertinus. Iperius writes in his Chronicle, chapter 11, section 1, that Fridogisus, the secular abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, expelled forty monks from the chapel of holy Mary, Mother of God, which blessed Audomarus had dedicated for the burial of the monks, and established thirty secular canons there. It is now the cathedral church of Saint-Omer.]

Saint Audomarus had previously instructed blessed Bertinus and all the brothers serving the Lord at that time in Sithiu that, whenever death should overtake him at his final hour, they should bury his little body in the place mentioned above.

After a short interval had passed following the burial of the venerable man’s body in that place, a lamp suspended above his tomb, filled with divine light, dripped luminous oil for many long years. To those who carefully contemplate the divine mercy in this, it becomes evident how great a glory blessed Audomarus, God’s confessor, possesses in the sight of the eternal King, since glorious signs have so often been displayed beside his venerable tomb even to this day.

Many people afflicted with various illnesses, when they come to the tomb of blessed Audomarus, suddenly receive health by the gift of divine grace. For the almighty Lord not only performs glorious deeds through his servants while they live this life, but after their blessed death he does not cease to glorify them with signs and wonders in different parts of the world. Thus through his blessed confessor Audomarus he performed many miracles after his death, which, with the Lord’s favor, we shall relate in the following account.

**14.** Shortly after blessed Audomarus’s death, a certain man inflamed by the fires of avarice and, as is said, full of depraved morals, went to his godfather and asked him to lend him one silver solidus until an appointed time. He also pledged in a deceitful oath that he would return it to him at the appointed time.

The other, trusting his godfather with a simple heart, lent the silver to his cunningly pleading friend. When a few days had passed, the appointed time came, and he went to him saying: “Return to me the silver that I lent you; the time fixed by your promise has arrived.”

Then the deceitful friend looked at him with hostile eyes, spoke harsh words to him, and boldly swore, denying that he had ever received even a small coin from him. The man who had lent the solidus replied with sound reasoning: “Let us go together to the venerable tomb of blessed Audomarus, the confessor of Christ, so that there you may confirm by oath, through the glorious merits of that bishop, what you are attempting to deny here.”

Then the wretched mortal, blinded by love of gain and further encouraged by the prince of lies, the devil—who was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth—set out in a mad frame of mind toward the basilica of blessed Audomarus, prepared to complete his perjury by persevering in his wickedness.

Speaking harsh words to one another, the two traveled along the same road toward the venerable basilica of blessed Audomarus and approached it as they saw it. Then the man demanding the solidus said to his godfather: “Why do we need to come closer to the basilica of blessed Audomarus? God is present everywhere. Swear to me here, where we are standing, by the merits of blessed Audomarus, that you did not receive the solidus lent to you by me.”

Then the wicked man stretched out his hands, moved his tongue to utter the perjury, and lifted his eyes toward the basilica of Audomarus. At once, struck by divine vengeance, he fell face down upon the ground, and his eyes burst at that very moment. His life was nevertheless prolonged for two days, evidently to terrify others who saw him in such distress; on the third day he died a most wretched death.

[Col. 1188D] **15.** There is therefore another miracle which is undoubtedly believed to have been performed through the merits of blessed Audomarus and which, through the working of divine power, is still demonstrated by reliable signs to the present day.

One day, as he was traveling from the city of Thérouanne to nearby places, he wished to allow his little body a short rest at midday and lay down beneath a certain tree not far from a villa called Orneacus. When the venerable man awoke, he immediately fashioned a wooden cross and fixed it beneath the tree under which he had lain.

On the following night, immense light appeared in the same place where the holy confessor of Christ had lain. All who lived in the surrounding area saw this miracle and said: “This place too now shines with such a light because, when blessed Audomarus rested here for a short time on the preceding day, it was consecrated and blessed by him.”

[Note: [Col. 1189A] The interpolator relates other miracles of Saint Audomarus: a criminal near the basilica where Saint Audomarus lay, released through the saint’s merits; a certain plunderer of the vineyard of Sithiu, punished and healed; and a boy rescued unharmed after falling into a well. Omitting the others, he concludes the Life as follows: “He governed the Church for a period of thirty years, and when these had been completed, at the final hour of his deposition, surrounded by a multitude of weeping disciples, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, full of the Holy Spirit, he departed to Christ. His body was translated—that is, carried away—by Saint Bertinus and buried in the monastery of Sithiu, while … reigned,” and so forth. We therefore place Saint Audomarus’s ordination around the year 647, which was the penultimate year of Dagobert, and his death around the year 647. From this you may understand that Audomarus did not subscribe to the Council of Rouen under Ansbert in the name of an abbot, as some after Baronius assert. In the proper Acts of those saints, Audomarus is said to have consecrated Waldetrudis to the priesthood and Austreberta and Waldetrudis to the veil. In Usuard’s genuine Martyrology he is commemorated on the fifth day before the Ides of September in these words: “In the territory of Thérouanne, Saint Autmarus, bishop and confessor.” Ado likewise writes: “The feast of Saint Audomarus, bishop of Thérouanne, whose glorious way of life is praised by the proclamation of miracles.” His body is kept in the church of the monastery of Sithiu, except for his head and certain bones, which are preserved in the church of Saint Mary at Saint-Omer. We shall discuss his various translations in the Life of Saint Bertinus in the following century.]

And to the present day many sick people receive healing in that same place, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout eternal ages. Amen.

[Col. 1189]

# Life of Saint Oswald, Bishop of Worcester and Archbishop of York, by an Anonymous Author of Uncertain Date

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fifth century, part 1, p. 727, from Capgrave and Bollandus.)

## Preliminary Observations

[Col. 1189C] **1.** Of those three outstanding bishops of England whom we have often praised—Dunstan, Æthelwold, and Oswald—Oswald outlived the other two, namely “Dunstan by five years and Æthelwold by ten,” says William of Malmesbury in book III, where he discusses the bishops of York. He inspired such admiration for himself in England that he seemed alone to display the authority of the one, the effectiveness of the other, and the holiness of both.

Senatus Bravonius is said to have written Oswald’s Life; he is reported to have flourished around the year 1170 as superior of the monks of Worcester. Yet it is clear that another author had accomplished this earlier. Among these was Fulcardus, a monk of Saint Bertinus at Sithiu, whom King William, according to Orderic Vitalis in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, appointed provost of Tournai around the year 1108.

Orderic adds that Fulcardus was affable and pleasant, charitable, and highly skilled in grammar and music; hence he left in England precious monuments of his learning for future generations. For he published several treatises worthy of remembrance and composed delightful histories for singing, skillfully and pleasantly, of Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and of other saints whose stock came forth from Britain.

I do not know whether this is his work, which Capgrave first published in print, Surius polished, and Henschenius restored to its native style.

[Col. 1189D] **2.** Much is read about the monastery of Ramsey, whose founder was Oswald and whose founding duke was Æthelwine, in the Acts of Saint Abbo, abbot of Fleury, and in William’s book IV *On the Bishops of the English*, where he discusses the bishops of Dorchester, as well as in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 231 onward, where the genealogy of Duke Æthelwine is given.

His father, Æthelstan, called “Semirex,” became a monk at Glastonbury. A colony of twelve monks was brought to Ramsey in the year 971 from the monastery of Westbury, which likewise traces its origin to Oswald.

But more illustrious than these was the monastery of Saint Mary, founded by Oswald at Worcester near the cathedral church; by this means the cathedral church easily passed to the monks. Hence William of Malmesbury writes in book II *On the Kings*, chapter 8: “He filled the episcopal see of Worcester with regular monks, not by forcibly expelling the clerics, but by surrounding them through holy stratagem.” Earlier, Bishop Æthelwold had expelled the clerics from Winchester by royal command, and so forth.

Together with Dunstan, Oswald crowned three kings of England: Edgar in 973, Edward two years later, and Æthelred in 978.

[Col. 1190C] **3.** Concerning the death of Saint Oswald, Florence of Worcester records the following: “Saint Oswald, archbishop, on the fifth indiction, on the day before the Kalends of March, a Monday, passing from this life, ascended to the joys of the heavenly kingdom, and rests at Worcester in the church of Saint Mary, which he himself had built from the foundations.”

These chronological indications coincide in the year 992, which was a leap year; consequently February in that year contained twenty-nine days, the last of which was Oswald’s final day. English writers report this year as marked by his death; the *Martyrology*, however, must be corrected, since it assigns the event to the following year.

Saint Oswald is mentioned in the more recent Martyrologies on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Molanus praises him on 15 October, and Thomas Maihew, who had promised to discuss Saint Oswald on that day, assigns that date to his translation. In fact, his first translation took place on the day before the Ides of May, as we shall soon relate. Henschenius writes that another saint was inserted under the name of Oswald on 15 October.

[Col. 1190D] **4.** Oswald was succeeded in the see of York by the venerable abbot of Medeshamsted, that is, Burch, Adulfus. Like his predecessor Saint Oswald, and with the permission of King Æthelred, Adulfus also held the bishopric of Worcester in his hands, as Thomas Stubbs testifies.

In the twelfth year of his episcopate, after gathering his fellow bishops, abbots, and many religious men, he raised the bones of Saint Oswald, archbishop, from the tomb in the twenty-fifth year of King Æthelred, in the fifteenth indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [the text reads “seventh”; read “seventeenth”], a Wednesday, and honorably placed them in a shrine that he had prepared. Not long afterward—that is, on the day before the Nones of May—he himself died and was buried in the church of Saint Mary at Worcester.

Florence of Worcester records the same events under the year 1002, when this elevation took place. Both writers copied Simeon of Durham in his book *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*. William of Malmesbury also mentions this same elevation in his account of the bishops of York. “Then,” he says, “having been buried in the church of blessed Mary, after twelve years he was raised from the earth when divine signs appeared.”

“What marvel this may be—that, although his whole body has been reduced to dust, the priestly stole with which he was clothed has suffered no damage from decay to this day—is reserved for the Lord’s judgment.”

Then, concerning Adulfus: “Adulfus, formerly abbot of Burch, succeeded him in both sees, a holy and, as they say, venerable man. His holiness excuses him for holding two sees contrary to the canonical rules, since he did so not from ambition but from necessity. This was not so in the case of Wulstan, who differed from him in holiness and in habit.”

Godwin of Malmesbury indignantly attacks William for approving Adulfus as bishop of two churches while charging Wulstan with this as a crime. Yet he gives the legitimate reason for the distinction: in Adulfus there was holiness free from ambition and the necessity of the Church, neither of which was present in Wulstan.

“Adulfus lies at Worcester,” William adds, “and ought also to be praised at the monastery of Fleury for the abundance of gifts with which he strove to rival Oswald’s generosity.” Read the Acts of Saint Abbo.

Thomas Stubbs records that in his own time Oswald’s priestly stole—purple, adorned with gold and gems, and shining with its ancient beauty—was preserved in the church of Beverley.

[Col. 1191B] 1. Saint Oswald, archbishop, born of the noblest lineage, shone in graceful appearance. While still a boy, he began to avoid childish follies and to train himself in works of holiness. His father’s brother was Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, eminent in discernment, grave in conduct, devoted to justice, and circumspect in all his actions. His nephew Oswald was entrusted to him by his parents to be imbued with learning and instructed by good examples and conduct. At length, fully trained in secular knowledge and Sacred Scripture, he was made a canon by Saint Odo at Winchester. While the others, despising the discipline of their order, followed the desires of their hearts, he tirelessly carried out the canonical way of life. Thus, made dean within a short time, while still a young man he undertook to correct the sullied life of the elders and to empty their childish minds through the diligence of heavenly discipline. But they, wishing rather to keep to the ancient paths of corrupt custom, declared that they would in no way listen to him in such matters.

2. When he understood this, he rejected secular pomp and riches and resolved to go to Fleury, where the body of Saint Benedict rests. Having sent letters of recommendation and many gifts from Saint Odo, he commended the young man both by word and deed. Saint Odo himself, when he was a young man, had crossed the sea and received the monastic habit at Fleury. [Col. 1191D] Having therefore received the sacred habit,

[Note: [Col. 1191D] William says: “At Fleury,” he says, “he was changed into a monk, according to a custom familiar to the English at that time: if any good men were inspired by the desire, they would receive the communal habit in the monastery of the most blessed Benedict, from whom this kind of religious life had originated. In this place, therefore, he broke the slipperiness of youth, serving religion and letters for many years.” Oswald received the monastic habit at Fleury [Col. 1192D] not from Abbot Wifald, who began his rule in 962, but from his predecessor Archembald. On him, read Aimoinus, Book I, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapters 13 and 14, and the notes on Aimoinus in the preceding volume.]

he who had come to be taught by others showed himself such that in him they found enough to teach and to imitate. He was sparing of sleep, moderate in food, prudent in speech, and constant in prayer. How patient, humble, kind, gentle, and benevolent he was can be judged from the sincere charity in which he shone beyond human estimation. [Col. 1192B] The abbot assigned him a secluded place in the church, where he might cleave to God more familiarly. There, removed from the disturbance of others, he was accustomed to devote himself to prayer, meditation, and contemplation of eternal life, and thus he supplied the human race’s enemy with abundant fuel for envy and hatred.

3. One night, while he was giving himself to contemplation and prayer, an evil spirit appeared. Producing terrifying sounds, it tried to frighten the man of God into abandoning what he had begun and attempting such things more sluggishly or not at all. But he, protected by the shield of faith, was no more frightened by the roar of a lion or the hiss of a serpent than by the bleating of a sheep. That wicked spirit assailed him with the voices of these and other beasts, but, undaunted, he mocked them all together with their Author. When the demon perceived this, it disappeared; but immediately transformed into an angel of light, it appeared to the same holy man. The man of God, however, fortified himself with the sign of the cross, knowing that the angel of light should not be provoked, but that the angel of darkness should be driven away from a distance. And so it happened. For when the wicked tempter saw the sign of the cross, it vanished from his eyes like smoke.

4. At last, when Saint Odo heard of the holy conduct of his nephew Oswald, he gave immense thanks to almighty God. He sent various gifts to the abbot and monks and expressed his gratitude for his nephew. He also informed them that he greatly desired to enjoy Oswald’s presence: first, because he knew that, exhausted by old age, death was near him; and second, because he intended through Oswald to train men of his people in a regular way of life. On hearing this, they were cast down by deep sorrow, yet, not daring to oppose the bishop’s will, they entrusted Oswald to his direction with due honor.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] William: “Although he was invited by the archbishop, he resisted through frequent letters, alleging the novelty of his clothing and his tender inexperience in religion; and he came only late, shaken by the messenger of his uncle, who was already ill and reclining.” [Col. 1193D] Read *lying ill* instead of “reclining.” *Discumbere* is a dining-room term, used of several people seeking different couches for the purpose of dining. *Decumbere* is used of the sick: “Struck by the fatigue of the journey, I lie ill for some days” (Apuleius, *Apology*); “With fever approaching, I had lain ill” (Gellius). Editor of the *Patrology*.]

Now, when Oswald had arrived at Dover and heard that his uncle had died, he was scarcely prevented from returning immediately to Fleury. But, warned by his companions that the needs of his parents must not be neglected, after paying the final rites to the holy archbishop he went to Oskytel, archbishop of York, whom he reached by the nearest degree of kinship. Captivated by Oskytel’s kindness, he enjoyed his religion and companionship for many years.

Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, died in 961. Oswald’s return to England therefore occurred in that year, while Archembald was abbot of Fleury, as I have just noted.

Before he could reach Canterbury, however, Saint Odo paid the debt of human flesh. At that time a certain Oskytel presided over the church of Dorchester. [Col. 1193A]

[Note: [Col. 1193D] The Ramsey chronicler below likewise calls him bishop of Dorchester; William calls him bishop of York. That he successively presided over both sees is proved by the same [Col. 1194C] chronicler.]

When he heard of the arrival of his nephew Oswald, Oskytel received him kindly, loved him sincerely, and made him a confidant of his secrets. When Oskytel was eventually raised to the archbishopric of York, Saint Dunstan made Oswald a member of King Edgar’s household after commending him to the king, and, by the king’s command, placed him over the church of Worcester.

[Note: [Col. 1194C] Simeon of Durham and Roger Hoveden refer this below to the year 960; they assign Odo’s death to 958, although it occurred three years later, as was proved in the *Life of Saint Odo*. Oswald was therefore not promoted to the see of Worcester before 961.]

5. Oswald gathered twelve monks at a place called Westbury. [Col. 1194D]

[Note: [Col. 1194D] On the monastery of Westbury in the territory of Worcester, read the *Monasticon*, volume I, p. 125.]

He used frequently to visit them, offer instructions concerning eternal salvation and consolation, and devote himself to fasts, vigils, and prayers.

6. It also happened that Earl Ailwin had suffered for many years from the daily and painful torment of gout in his feet. One of his fishermen, named Walgit, had entered the water called Ramsey Mere in his little boat to fish for his lord the earl. After laboring fruitlessly for a long time and becoming exhausted by extreme weariness, he finally began to fall asleep. Saint Benedict appeared to him and said:

“When dawn rises, cast out your dragnet, and you will meet a great multitude of fish and obtain what you desire. Offer the largest of the fish caught, called a *haket*, that is, a pike, to your lord Ailwin on my behalf, and tell him that, kindly accepting my gift, he should without delay strive to build on this island a monastery for the pious mother of mercy, Mary, for me, and for all the holy virgins. Let him observe how his animals lie down on the island at night, and when he sees a bull rising with its right foot, let him hasten to strike the ground there and erect an altar. So that he may believe my commands more surely, raise this outer finger of yours, which is bent; once he himself has been freed from the bonds of gout, he will have it restored and straightened for you.”

When he awoke, he enclosed a great multitude of fish and offered the largest to his lord on behalf of the saint, repeating what he had seen and heard. He earnestly begged Ailwin to straighten his bent finger. Then Ailwin raised the man’s finger, which was attached to his hand, and hastened to the island as best he could. When he entered the island, he was completely cured of his illness. A bull rose from among the animals and, striking the ground with its foot, divinely indicated the place where the altar was to be built.

The earl therefore praised God and immediately constructed a chapel there after cutting timber. Not long afterward, when Earl Ailwin had granted extensive possessions, Saint Oswald built a notable monastery there within five years and solemnly dedicated it in the year of the Lord 974. He appointed the monk Ednoth abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] On Earl Ailwin, see the other *Life*. The *Monasticon*, p. 231, says that Oswald sent twelve monks from Westbury to Ramsey.]

7. At the same time, by the authority of Pope John, Archbishop Dunstan convened a general council and established and confirmed by decree that all canons, priests, deacons, and subdeacons should either live chastely or relinquish the churches they held.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] On this council, see the *Acts of Saint Dunstan* above.]

King Edgar was a faithful helper and firm defender in this matter. The execution of this decree was entrusted to Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester. Blessed Oswald therefore built seven monasteries in his diocese, expelled the clerics who were living insolently, introduced monks, and appointed abbots over them.

8. Meanwhile, the abbot of Pershore whom Oswald had appointed, named Fudbertus, was well mannered and a fervent defender of monastic religion; yet, toward his subjects—which was strongly criticized in him—he was excessively and indiscriminately severe.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] On him, see Pits at the year 980, where he calls him Fuldebert. On him and the monastery of Pershore, read what was said above, p. 641 of the fifth century.]

When he had been brought to the point of death, had been taken from this life, and had been placed in a coffin, he recovered his spirit. While everyone trembled, he raised himself and said that Saint Benedict had led him in a vision into the presence of God, that God had forgiven his sins through the merits of his beloved Oswald, and that he had revived in order to make Oswald’s holiness known. Having said this, he fell silent. After receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body, he lived for half a day and then ended his life by dying a second time.

9. In other parts of England also, for the reason stated above, he emptied distinguished churches of clerics and elevated them through men of monastic religion. Their names are these: the church of Saint Alban, that of Saint Etheldreda the virgin at Ely, and the church established at Beamfleet, which was considered honorable.

He appointed Elfric abbot of the church of Saint Alban,

[Note: [Col. 1194D] There was also another Alfric or Elfric, abbot of Abingdon after Saint Ethelwold; Alfric himself wrote his *Life*, as we saw above. Godmann was abbot of Thorney, according to the second *Life* and the acts of Saint Ethelwold.]

who was later raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In the church at Ely he appointed Brithnoth abbot, and in the church at Beamfleet he appointed Godmann abbot. He took care to visit the monasteries he had built and, in word and deed alike, to provide with a fatherly affection whatever contributed to salvation.

10. He also placed at the monastery of Ramsey Abbo of Fleury, a monk distinguished by holiness of conduct and exceptionally well trained in knowledge of letters. Abbo was to teach the monks, direct the schools, and be useful in regular discipline and literary learning. At Dunstan’s urging, the same Abbo also laudably wrote the passion of Saint Edmund, king and martyr. Later, having returned to Fleury and become abbot, he was killed by his monks.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Not by the monks, but by the monastery’s servants, who were rioting against the rule, as is stated below in his acts.]

11. When he had begun to build a monastery at Worcester, within the episcopal seat itself, where he could live with monks, a square stone lay not far from the work, entirely necessary for the construction. When the craftsmen tried to lift it, it clung to the earth as though rooted there and could not be moved by any effort.

Great astonishment seized everyone, and the matter was reported to Father Oswald. He came and saw a great crowd sweating around the stone in fruitless labor. Standing in wonder and amazement, and silently praying to God, he looked upon the stone and saw an Ethiopian sitting on it, mocking the laborers with obscene gestures. He immediately made the sign of the cross against the demon and forced the terrified creature to seek safety in flight. The stone, which eighty men had been unable to move, was then easily lifted by a few and set into the building.

When the church had been completed in honor of Blessed Mary and some monks had been gathered there, several of the clerics at the episcopal seat rejected the world and received the monastic habit. The episcopal seat was transferred from the clerics at the church of Saint Peter to the monks at the church of Saint Mary.

12. When the archbishop of York died,

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Namely Oskytel, praised above. Ingulf, Simeon of Durham, Roger Hoveden, Florence of Worcester, and others assign his death to 972.]

Oswald was appointed archbishop, urged on by King Edgar and Saint Dunstan and with the consent of all the clergy. And lest the monks whom he had established should be shaken by any temptation beyond what they could bear, if deprived of pastoral care they had no support on which to rely, by the authority of Saint Dunstan he carefully governed the bishopric of Worcester together with the archbishopric.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Radulfus de Diceto suggests the reason for this action: the Danes had ravaged Northumbria.]

13. When the monks of Ramsey, with Bishop Oswald standing on the bank, wished to cross the water by boat, the vessel, being too heavily loaded, began to sink. The disturbed monks, fearing death, implored the aid of the holy bishop. When the saint saw this, he made the sign of the cross, and the boat, rising from the depths of the water, was carried smoothly to the bank as though it bore no burden at all.

14. When it was reported to him that a certain monk of Ely had fallen from the church building and died suddenly, he was distressed by intense sorrow. He knew that the monk had not lived an entirely happy life. He summoned the monks at Ramsey, recounted what had happened, and urged them to pray more earnestly to the Lord for the dead man’s soul.

They devoted themselves to vigils, psalms, and tears, and knocked at the door of the Redeemer’s mercy. One night, while the bishop was persisting in prayer, the same dead man visibly appeared to him. When asked who he was, he replied that he was the one for whom the bishop had prayed.

The bishop, drawing breath, said: “Brother, how was it with you, and how is it now?”

“Until now,” he replied, “it was very bad; but now it is very good. For yesterday the Lord, through his angel, rescued me from the punishments by which I was tormented, through your merits and prayers. I have come to make this known and to give you thanks, and also to tell you that, because of this and other things, you ought rightly and deservedly to be in God's favor.”

After saying this, he disappeared.

15. At suitable times he traveled throughout his diocese, striving by fatherly correction to rebuke and amend whatever he could discern in the conduct of his people that offended the eyes of the supreme God.

Once, while engaged in this work, he came to Ripon, where the blessed Wilfrid had once earned burial in a noble monastery that he had built.

[Note: [Col. 1196D] We related the acts of the elder Wilfrid both in the first part of the third century and in the appendix to the fourth century, where the monastery at Ripon was discussed.]

That place, however, had formerly been largely destroyed by barbarians, although it remained suitable as a lair for wild beasts. There, while keeping constant watch in prayer by night, Oswald learned through divine revelation that the bodies of saints had been buried in that very place, and that, if he investigated, he would undoubtedly find them together with the names of each.

When morning came and they dug the ground, the bodies of the saints were found together with a tablet bearing this inscription:

“Here rests Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York, and the venerable abbots Tilbert, Botwin, Albert, Sigred, and Wilden.”

For the time being he placed the relics in a suitable location. Later, he reverently laid the body of Saint Wilfrid in a suitably prepared coffin,

[Note: [Col. 1196D] On the younger Wilfrid, read the poem on the bishops of York in the appendix to the third century; on this translation, read the monk Gervase and the chronicle of John Bromton.]

since he knew that Wilfrid was related by blood to the great Wilfrid, founder of that place. The body of the elder Wilfrid had long before been translated by Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 1196D] Having placed the relics in a coffin, he conveyed them to Worcester with great honor.

16. A powerful man was seized by a severe fever and sent word to the man of God that he was ill. Oswald blessed a loaf of bread, sent it to him, and ordered him to eat it with faith in obtaining health. When he had done so, he felt himself restored to perfect health.

As the bishop was sitting at table, blessing bread and distributing it among those seated with him, a shrew, happening to come upon crumbs that had fallen, began eagerly to gather them. It was immediately suffocated and died, and could not vomit up what it had swallowed.
