So that no one might ascribe this to his own praise, the holy man ordered the lifeless creature to be thrown away from the sight of those watching.

17. After bathing, a certain monk began to sleep in the place where the bishop frequently used to sit. Suddenly, several exceedingly terrible spirits appeared there. After a strict examination, they asked him why he was not afraid to rest in the place of so great a bishop. They attacked him, tortured him, tore him, and dragged him here and there, snatching him upward from below and throwing him down again from above. At last, crying out in a dreadful voice, he openly recounted to everyone what had happened to him.

18. Every day, in addition to the countless others whom he fed daily, he was accustomed to wash the feet of twelve poor men, kiss them, dry them with his hair and a linen cloth, pour water over their hands, give them money, and serve them food and drink at a set table. At Easter he dressed them in new clothing and kept them with him in his household for several days.

No bodily illness held him back from these things. Rather, the weaker he felt in body, the greater strength he imposed upon himself to serve them.

19. One day, after leaving the oratory with his attendants, he stood beneath the open sky and fixed his eyes intently on heaven. With devout heart and fervent prayer he addressed Christ, for whom he longed. He did not quickly lower his raised eyes, as is usual; instead, as though contemplating something new and delightful, he kept them fixed for a very long time upon the place where he had set them.

When asked what he had seen, he said:

“I behold the destination toward which I am tending, and tomorrow, while both you and I remain silent, the event itself will make it known. For the eternal salvation for which I have labored on earth until now is near; and tomorrow will not pass before my Lord, as he promised, brings me into it.”

Returning to the oratory, he summoned the brothers and urged them to administer to him the ministry of holy anointing together with the viaticum of the Lord’s body.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] At that time the anointing of the sick was everywhere administered before the viaticum, as we have said elsewhere.]

20. On the following night, forgetting his illness, he entered the church, completed the office, and spent the remainder of the night in divine praises. In the morning, according to his custom, girded with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of the poor, kissing and drying them. When he had sung the fifteen psalms that he was accustomed to chant during this ministry, he added: “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.”

When the poor men rose and offered their customary thanks, he himself, saying “and to the Holy Spirit,” surrendered his spirit into the hands of Christ before their feet.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The Ramsey chronicler below says that his death occurred on the third Sunday of Lent; others, and more correctly, say Monday, as was stated in the preliminary observations.]

When his body was being carried to the church that he had built, a white dove was seen descending from heaven and, with wings spread, protecting the bishop’s body in slow flight. They also saw a fiery sphere, like a shield, fall from heaven upon the coffin.

When the holy body had been placed before the altar, the vision that had appeared, as though indicating the place of burial, turned toward the southern part of the church near the altar and vanished from the eyes of those watching.

Earl Ailwin, overwhelmed after the holy man’s death by excessive anguish and grief of heart, entered the way of all flesh and was buried in the monastery at Ramsey.

[Note: [Col. 1198D] The Ramsey chronicler below says that his death occurred on the third Sunday of Lent; others, and more correctly, say Monday, as was stated in the preliminary observations.]

21. When Saint Oswald, in his youth, was living a wholly holy monastic life in the monastery at Fleury, there was near the place where he used to pray a certain crypt. Before its doors twelve poor men lived, receiving their daily sustenance from the monastery’s service. One of them used to serve the man of God when he offered the sacred hosts.

One day, after the Gospel, while the saint was preparing himself for prayer with his eyes raised toward heaven, his servant saw a person of most venerable appearance, holding a very white loaf—small in quantity—with due honor between his hands, which he had raised as far as his head. Although overcome with great terror and amazement, the servant endured and did not immediately flee.

But when he saw the same bread gradually increase during the priest’s progress through the Mass, growing until it became of extraordinary size, he dared remain no longer and fled outside through the doorway. The priest therefore remained alone, together with the angel who seemed to be standing at his right hand.

The servant repeatedly thrust his head through the doorway and anxiously observed what was happening around the altar. When the servant of God said, “World without end,” and other words, and the servant did not dare to respond in any way, he heard the angel responding to each phrase and rendering service to the priest.

When the Mass had been completed, the servant looked in and, not seeing the angel, approached the man of God in fear. He explained the reason for his flight and asked whether Oswald too had seen the angel.

“Yes,” he replied, “I saw him clearly and heard what you say. But blessed be the name of almighty God, because although I was abandoned by you, I was not abandoned by him in the sacred mystery of God.”

He forbade the servant as strongly as he could to make the matter known to anyone while Oswald lived.

Saint Oswald died in the year of grace 992, in the thirtieth year of his episcopate,

[Note: [Col. 1198D] He was therefore ordained bishop of Worcester in 962 or the following year, as we established above.]

on the day before the Kalends of March.

22. In the twelfth year after his death, Aldulf, archbishop of York, warned by a divine revelation, hastened to Worcester, where Saint Oswald had chosen to be buried. He raised the bones of the holy bishop from the earth and placed them in a shrine with the greatest honor.

[Note: This translation, or elevation, is mentioned above in the preliminary observations.]

The water with which the bones were washed restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and health to all who were infirm. All the garments were found intact and undefiled in the tomb, fragrant with an exceedingly sweet odor.

23. A certain monk at Ramsey was so afflicted by a cancerous ulcer in his jaw that, after the skin and flesh had been consumed, the bare jaw and exposed teeth appeared with the gums.

On the feast of Saint Oswald, he drank with great devotion and faith from the cup from which that same saint used to drink. After taking the drink, he immediately placed the empty vessel against his diseased jaw and pressed it tightly to it. After a short time he removed the little vessel from his jaw, and all the corruption and putrefaction of the disease clung to the vessel. The jaw, restored from its illness, showed no sign whatever of the former disease.

As evidence of so great a miracle and of God’s power, that jaw remained forever somewhat redder than the other.

24. A man who had been mute from infancy, on a certain feast of Saint Oswald, saw an unknown man of venerable appearance, shining with beautiful gray hair, dressed in priestly clothing, and carrying a staff in his hand. He seemed to be hastening toward him from the place where the holy bishop’s tomb was located.

As the man passed before him, the mute humbly inclined his head. The stranger raised his staff, struck him on the neck, and disappeared. Terrified by the blow, the mute immediately began to cry out when a great mass of clotted blood fell from his mouth onto the ground:

“Help, I beg you, help! And lest the Lord’s church be stained with my blood, quickly remove me from here!”

After he had been led outside the church, he shed abundant blood and explained to those standing around the manner of his cure.

25. Once, when a devouring fire was consuming the city of Worcester, as soon as the flames reached the saint’s coffin, the fire weakened and, unable to consume anything further, died out.

The house of a certain poor man, roofed with reeds, stood there. One half of it remained whole and sound from its middle, while the other half had been burned as though by a plumb line from the top all the way to the ground.

26. On another occasion, when the city mentioned above was burning and the monks were carrying the saint’s coffin to a village, a man who had recently built a beautiful house came toward them and cried out:

“O holy Father and shepherd Oswald, behold, I give you my house, exposed to devouring flames, and place it under your dominion to possess by perpetual right. If it pleases you, deign to free it from its present danger.”

When the coffin had been brought into the house, while the neighboring house was entirely consumed by fire, the hall commended to Father Oswald could neither be touched by the fire nor retain any trace of it.

27. Once, a savage plague ravaged the province of Worcester, striking men and women, young people and children with sudden death. People walking or standing would suddenly fall and die unrepentant and without confession.

The monks, however, carrying the coffin of the holy bishop around the city, devoutly pleaded for the people’s salvation while singing litanies. Immediately the plague not only completely left Worcester, but also abandoned the surrounding villages, from which the inhabitants had come to implore the saint’s aid.

## In the Year of the Lord 1081: Eusebius Bruno, Bishop of Angers

[Col. 1199]

## Historical Notice on Bruno

(*Gallia christiana*, old edition, volume II, column 126)

[Col. 1199C] Eusebius Bruno succeeded to the episcopate of the church of Angers in the year 1047, on 8 December, according to the Chronicle of Vendôme. In that year he consecrated the church of Saint Martin at Bellopratum, as the records of Saint-Laud relate.

He took part in the Council of Reims in 1049 and then subscribed the donation of the church of All Saints made by Geoffrey Martel to the monks of Vendôme. Around the year 1053 he made an agreement with Frederick, abbot of Saumur, concerning the churches in the territory of old Saint-Florent. Shortly afterward, in 1058, he attended the inauguration of the basilica of Saint John of Angers in Saintonge, and in 1059 he is named in a charter of Count Geoffrey by which he ceded Mount Hidulf to the Major Monastery.

On 4 April 1062 he dedicated a new monastery at Angers. In a notice of the abbey of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, concerning the church of Vieux-Champ and issued at the castle of Craon in 1067, he designated the nineteenth year of his episcopate. [Col. 1200C] He later confirmed by his signature, in August 1074, a document of the abbey of Vendôme, and in 1077 a charter of Count Geoffrey written at Calmont for the collegiate church of Faye. In that same year he entered into an agreement with the monks of Saint-Aubin concerning the pensions owed to them by the churches dependent upon them.

The same Eusebius redeemed the church of Saint Maurice, which Lord Castrigunther had held in lay possession. In 1081 he gave judgment between Geoffrey, cantor, and Marbod, master of the schools of the church of Angers, later bishop of Rennes. He died on 27 August of that year, as the Chronicle of Vendôme records. A charter of Saint Martin of Tours calls him a faithful man of God and a friend of the clerical order.

This Eusebius was accused of holding an erroneous opinion concerning the sacrament of the altar. At this same time Berengar, the archdeacon and archchancellor of Angers, was also branded a heresiarch. As a young man, Berengar had been a student of the exceedingly learned bishop Fulbert at the school of Chartres. Falling into error, he denied the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist and dared to assert that the Lord’s body was merely a shadow and figure. It is said that, in order to promulgate this view more freely, he brought Bruno, bishop of Angers, over to his error.

Condemned, therefore, at the Roman, Vercellian, and Tours synods, where he swore to the heresy, he later arrogantly attempted to defend it again. After relapsing so many times, he finally repented and abjured it.

In the year 1060 the Chronicle of Tours says of him:

“Berengar, the grammarian, archdeacon and treasurer of Angers, as well as master of the schools and chamberlain of Saint Martin, was distinguished in grammar and philosophy and highly skilled in necromancy. Departing from Rome, he came to Tours, and there, on the island called Saint Cosmas, renouncing the pomp of the world, he served the Lord faithfully for twenty-eight years. Many other canons of Blessed Martin, having changed their clothing through the Holy Spirit and his salutary admonition, withdrew to that island.”

At length he died on the feast of the Epiphany in 1088, at the age of ninety, and was buried at Tours in the cloister of Saint Martin on the left side. Hildebert, later bishop of Le Mans, wrote his epitaph. Hildebert was a man of great learning and holiness among the Gallic bishops, and was also praised in this encomium by Baldwin, abbot of Bourgueil, in his historical poems:

> All the eloquence of the Latins, withered, flourishes,
>
> While it lived under Berengar’s instruction at Tours.
>
> Yet the eloquence of the Latins, once flower-filled, now withers,
>
> When envious fortune at Tours has taken away so great a light.
>
> For you, teacher, the door of life is closed in January,
>
> Or rather, in January the door of life opened for you.
>
> Behold, great old man, beneath this vault lies your mound,
>
> Sighing for the return to its own condition.
>
> And although the hope of your merits may promise you pardon,
>
> May the reader hasten it by offering pious prayers.

Eusebius, therefore, accused of having been excessively intimate with Berengar, was believed either not to have adhered to his heresy at all, or at least to have negligently fallen asleep in it. At last, however, he attempted to abolish the most destructive heresy—which he could have extinguished at its birth—and to clear his reputation by writing a letter to the heresiarch. The distinguished Dom Menard of Angers was the first to recover that letter from manuscript leaves and publish it.

Read the learned and comprehensive notes of John Picard on Saint Anselm of Canterbury’s book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*. From them you will easily conclude that those who attribute the letter against Bruno, bishop of Angers, and Berengar to Durand, bishop of Liège, were deceived. It must be restored to its rightful author, likewise Deoduin, bishop of Liège. The error arose from the single letter D, the initial of both names. Valerius Andreas did not notice this in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, and the most illustrious father of ecclesiastical history overlooked it when referring that letter under Durand’s name to the year of Christ 1035. The letter is also found in volume III of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, which includes the published authors in volume VI who wrote against Berengar: Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; Adelmann, bishop of Brescia; Alger of Corbie; and Guitmund of Aversa.

On this matter, Sigebert’s Chronicle should also be consulted at the year 1051. Vincent should likewise be read, Book XXV, chapter 30, and Saint Antoninus from him, title 16, chapter 1; Bellarmine, volume II, Book I *On the Eucharist*, chapter 1, and Book III, chapter 8; and Baronius at the year 1088, where he discusses Berengar’s death and the epitaph or funeral poem that Hildebert placed upon his friend Berengar.

[Col. 1201]

## Letter of Eusebius Bruno to the Master Berengar: On the Sacrament of the Eucharist

(Edited by Franciscus de Roye, former official of Angers, in his book entitled *The Life, Heresy, and Penance of Berengar*. Angers, 1656.)

[Col. 1201D]

To his brother and fellow priest B. E., worthy of embrace with the devotion of sincere affection, greetings.

You wrote that, according to the credible report of witnesses, Gaufridus Martini had arrived to support, with the utmost exertion and public proclamation, the absurdity and madness of Lanfranc; and, inserting certain other matters, you earnestly implored me to allow you and him to be heard before a judge, in the book of blessed Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*. Attend patiently and calmly to what answer or advice I have for you—if you deign to accept it.

Whether this controversy arose and was stirred up for the sake of asserting the truth or of seeking reputation, God knows; but after it had traversed almost the greater part of the Roman world, it finally assailed us with the sharpest reproaches from both distant and neighboring regions. Against this, although relying on my own humble and dull understanding, I chose—with the counsel of learned men and of those better than myself—a form of response that would deviate from the path of truth by no byway of error and would rightly give no cause for offense or scandal to the more exalted persons of the universal Church, whether in dignity or in learning. It had also to be accessible to the simpler faithful, while not appearing to overreach the learned through any arrogance.

Accordingly, abandoning the turbulent streams of disputation, we judge it necessary for ourselves, and propose to all who may wish to join us, to drink from the very source of truth, flowing forth in the purest abundance, with a salutary singularity of its own. This source is as follows:

The Lord Jesus, on the day before he suffered, taking bread into his holy and venerable hands, lifted his eyes to heaven, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat, all of you, from this; for this is my body.” In like manner, taking the glorious chalice, giving thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you; for this is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal covenant, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do these things, you will do them in memory of me.”

By the power and efficacy of this word, through which all things were made, we believe and confess that, after the priest who consecrates has consecrated the bread with these words, it is the true body of Christ, and that the wine, in the same manner, is truly his blood.

If anyone asks how this can happen, we answer him not according to the order of nature but according to God’s omnipotence: “God made this and everything whatsoever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths.” For no abundance of words can explain how, according to the order of nature, the Word—God, in the beginning with God—could be conceived from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, or how, after the resurrection, the true body of the Lord Jesus could enter to his disciples through closed doors and be touched. Nevertheless, it is absolutely necessary to believe, firmly and faithfully, that these things truly took place according to God’s omnipotence.

If, however, anyone should ask us what our Fathers and teachers thought about this matter, or what they left written, we refer him to their books, provided that he is competent to consult them, so that he may read carefully what he finds there, understand it purely, and choose for himself, with gratitude and a desire for fraternal concord, whatever he judges most suitably accordant with the truth of the Gospel.

As for us, we do not despise the writings of the Fathers; yet, in this dispute over so great a matter, we refrain from relying on their opinions—while preserving the reverence due to them—as we read the Gospel. For they themselves, while living and writing, did not intend that this should be done, nor did they wish it to be done in their little works. We refrain lest, if we were to put forward the Fathers’ views inappropriately—whether they had been corrupted in some way, or had not been properly understood by us, or had not been fully investigated—we should fall into the very scandal that we so earnestly avoid.

When one of Christ’s little ones is scandalized, he is judged worthy to have an ass’s millstone hung around his neck and to be cast into the depths of the sea. Therefore we rightly and deservedly shudder at scandalizing the whole Church. Nor do we conceal from ourselves that, on this account, we may be exposing ourselves to danger without necessity, since we can live safely and peacefully, content with the simple abridgment and sufficient firmness of holy faith contained in the most sacred words of Christ set out above, insofar as we understand them and know that many men far superior to us understand them likewise.

By this counsel the complaint that arose in the presence of Lord Geraldus, then papal legate at Tours, was brought to an end. By this same counsel the tumult that had boiled over in the hearing of Lord Eldebrarinus in that city was quieted. By this truthful confession the demand of our present prince, in the little chapel mentioned in your letter, was satisfied; and the revived pestilence, which had raised its head after being stirred up by the wickedness of certain men, was crushed by the authority of the archbishop of Besançon and of the learned men who were present.

You should know that I neither seek nor intend ever to pursue, assemble, or convene any other dispute or controversy on this matter—neither accusers nor defenders, witnesses nor judges, advocates nor hearers. To all who, with my consent—or, if that is too little, despite my opposition, though it be disregarded—wish to assemble a public gathering for this cause, I will give no agreement. From those who come together I will withdraw my humble person; from those who quarrel I will withdraw a hearing; from those who persist I will withdraw communion. For the case has been settled three times by the judgment of our province and, a fourth time, extinguished by the decision of a synod of the Apostolic See.

Farewell, E.

[Note: This letter shows altogether how great Eusebius’s faith was, and how devout his simplicity: he stubbornly asserts, from Christ’s words alone, that the true body and blood of Christ are present in the most holy Eucharist. He so subjects his understanding in obedience to that most holy faith that he is unwilling either to dispute about it, to raise controversy over it, or to seek it elsewhere than in Christ’s words. So far was he from adhering to Berengarius that he rather avoided him and did not wish to hear him or admit him to a meeting or conversation.

Whence, then, did such a suspicion arise concerning this Bruno of ours? Was it because, when Berengarius had been summoned to Tours, he immediately chose him as archdeacon? But at that time he was of sound mind. Was it because he offended his rivals through his virtues? For he was both most devout and most learned, as the author of *Gallia Christiana* immediately makes clear. Was it because, returning from the Council of Rheims—at which he had been present among the leading men—he surpassed envy by his glory? Perhaps certain abusive detractors, ill-disposed toward him, shamelessly spread among the people that Bruno adhered to Berengarius.

They did not heed the anathema: “Whoever acts arrogantly against the priest shall die” (Deuteronomy 17). Nor did they heed this other saying: when Samuel was rejected by the Jews, the Lord said: “They have not rejected you, but me” (1 Samuel 8:7). For this reason, too, the sacred canons do not permit a bishop to be reproached or accused by the common people or by ordinary men, lest a stain be rashly placed upon one who has been chosen—canon *Non est*, II, q. 7. From all these considerations, Bruno appears to deserve vindication from that suspicion.]

ANNO DOMINI MLXXXII. GEBUINUS, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS.

[Col. 1205]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV.)

[Col. 1205A] Gebuinus, who was also called Gibuinus, indeed Geboinus, and, in the course of time, when the first letter of his name was changed to J, a letter of the same sound, Jebuinus—as may be seen in the ancient list of the bishops of Lyons reported in the antiquities of the island of Barbara—was finally called Jubinus by the apocope of one letter, as may be seen in Missals and Breviaries for the use of the Church of Lyons. From this latter name came the French *saint Jubin*, by which he is designated by the common people. He was the son of Hugh III, count of Dijon, and was afterwards archdeacon of Langres.

The Chronicle of Verdun thus relates his election to the bishopric: “At the Synod of Autun, held in 1077 by Hugh, bishop of Die and apostolic legate, on the fifth day, since the see of Lyons was vacant of a bishop because Humbert of Simiane had been expelled and had become a monk in the Jura region, the archdeacon Gebuinus, a man distinguished by uprightness of character, was elected by the assent of the whole council. The bishop of Langres bore this with difficulty, complaining that the Fathers had torn out his right eye by taking away his archdeacon, a man most necessary in ecclesiastical and secular affairs, in whom resided his own counsel and the consolation of the whole diocese. But the unanimous judgment of the council prevailed, because thus it had been predetermined and had pleased the Lord. Without delay, on one day, namely Sunday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, he was consecrated at Autun by the legate amid the utmost rejoicing and celebration of all. Nor was this all: Hugh immediately requested the pallium for him in these words:

[Col. 1205C] ‘We most earnestly ask that through Lord Valentinus, bishop, you send us the pallium to confirm the ordination of the most devout archbishop of the Church of Lyons against the barking heretics and those who carnally boast of the king’s indignation against God’s ordination. For he himself, setting aside every inconvenience and danger of hardship and travel, would most devoutly present himself before your Holiness, if the Church entrusted to him, so long languishing and deprived of a shepherd’s consolation, could in any way endure his absence without great loss. Command Bishop Valentinus [lacuna], so that about the feast of Saint John the Baptist, as we have agreed with him, his church may receive him to celebrate the office, because he seems very suitable for assailing the arrogance of the provincials.’” The pope refused nothing, moved by so many outstanding endowments of the new bishop.

In 1078 he is mentioned in a charter of Widelin, count of Forez, granting certain things to the monastery of Savigny; for its date is written thus: “While Lord Henry IV Augustus was waging war against King Rudolf, while holy Pope Hildebrand was seated on the apostolic throne, and while the archbishopric of Lyons rested under the rule of Lord Gebuin; while also Lord Dalmatius held the staff of Savigny [lacuna], in the month of May, on Monday, and on the fifteenth day, in the year of the Lord 1078, indiction I, concurrent VI, epact IV.” In the same year—or rather the following year according to the modern manner of beginning the year—Peter, bishop of Albano, cardinal of the Roman Church and papal legate in Burgundy, informed Landric, bishop of Mâcon, and Gebuin, archbishop of Lyons, that on the pope’s behalf he would excommunicate them unless they refrained from the molestations which they inflicted on the monks of Cluny. “Done at Anse, near Saint Bernard, 8 February, indiction II.”

[Col. 1206B] About this same time Gebuin seems to have gone to Rome with some of his canons. This is indicated by Gregory, Book VI, Letter 36, from which it is clear that the canons of the cathedral church then lived a regular, common life without private property. For, having been struck with anathema by Landric, bishop of Mâcon, who had been made the pope’s examiner in this case, because they had divided the common goods of the Church among themselves in order to live privately, and since some had gone to Rome to obtain both absolution and blessing, the pope not only did not grant these, but by apostolic authority commanded that those who had acquired property in this manner should entirely give it up. He wished the Church of Lyons, which had shone among all the Gallican Churches in the example of religious life, to guard that distinction vigilantly even now, so that it might begin to increase in religious observance the glory which it had hitherto possessed above the others in dignity.

In 1080, asked by Hugh, abbot of Cluny, he favoured the election of Walter, bishop of Chalon. He gave the Church of Savigny the basilica of Saint Mary of Jo[lacuna] at Lyons, in the court of Saint Nicetius, while the bishop himself lay there ill. He certainly suffered from stone and bore the sharp paroxysms of that illness with such patience that he is said, as the reward of his virtue, to have great power in curing it; for that reason he is invoked by the people of Lyons and their neighbours. In the old Martyrology of the Church of Lyons, the end of his life is entered as 18 April. In the Necrology of Saint Benignus of Dijon one reads: “15 Kalends of May: the deposition of Lord Gibuinus, archbishop of Lyons.” He lies in the church of Saint Irenaeus. Over his tomb an altar has been placed, consecrated to God in his name, and he is venerated as a saint in his Church.

As for the year of his death, it is not stated in ancient records. M. de Lamure extends his life to the end of 1087, and proves that it should be so extended from an old manuscript of the monastery of Savigny containing its old cartulary and recording three charters in which Gebuin is still mentioned as living in 1086 and 1087. The first is on folio 123 of the codex under this title: “Concerning the church of Saint Mary of Diniciacum [lacuna], and the church of Comiacum [lacuna], and also the chapel of Montelard [lacuna]. This gift was approved by Archbishop Gebuin in the choir of the Church of Lyons, Landric, bishop of Mâcon, Bladinus, dean, and others witnessing [lacuna]. Done in the chapter at Savigny, on the sixth day before the Nones of February, sixteenth and fifteenth, indiction nine, epact three, lunar cycle nineteen, while Henry reigned in Burgundy. Written by the hand of Stephen, vice-chancellor, in the year of the Lord 1086.”

[Col. 1207C] The second appears on folio 122 of the cited codex, by which Agna with her sons gives to Saint Martin of Savigny, for her son Lenchon, whom she delivers to the monastic order in that place, a half share in the church of Saint John of Dnerna with its tithes and appurtenances. “Done in the district of Lyons, at the monastery of Savigny, with the approval of Archbishop Gebuin, in June, Wednesday, the fifth moon, while Philip reigned in France and Henry in Burgundy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087, indiction ten.” The third lies in the same place and on the same folio. By it, to the Church of Savigny [lacuna], where Lord Iterius the second seems to preside as abbot, Ermengard gives for her burial the church of Saint Veranus at Graziacum. “Done in the district of Lyons, at the monastery of Savigny, with the approval of Archbishop Gebuin, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087, indiction seven, in June, Wednesday, the fifth moon, while King Philip reigned in France and Henry in Burgundy.”

These things indeed appear very strong, even indubitable, if M. de Lamure copied correctly; that is, if the instruments which he presents are originals and not later copies. Yet I hesitate; indeed, compelled by the force of truth, I must adopt the contrary opinion: the instruments which he reports are not originals. This is highly probable from the fact that they are contained with innumerable others in one and the same codex, which could not possibly have been written except by one and the same copyist. Thus an error may have crept in through the scribe’s carelessness or ignorance; or the Hebrew-style numerical signs may have been corrupted because the copyist’s eye was deceived. That they were in fact corrupted is clear from the fact that, in charters of 1087, one joins indiction ten and the other indiction seven to that year. Again, in the first charter the day is assigned as the sixth before the Nones of February, a date which never existed in that month. Finally, what the first charter has—“Done 6 February, sixteenth and fifteenth”—is neither genuine nor intelligible.

On the other hand, if anything can be established in historical matters of this sort, it is shown that Hugh occupied Gebuin’s place before 1087, indeed before 1086. It is necessary to give the arguments—not all of them, but the principal ones.

First, Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, in a letter written to Pontius, abbot of Fraxinet, formerly a monk of La Chaise-Dieu, which Mabillon reports, mentions the venerable Father Hugh, archbishop of Lyons; and at its end orders that the lord archbishop of Lyons be greeted in his name. Since, therefore, in the Life of that same Anselm, written by one of the canons of his church, it is said: “In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1086, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, indiction IX, he fell asleep in the Lord on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April,” it is certain that Hugh was bishop at Lyons before that year.

The second argument is supplied by Pope Gregory VII. Thus in Book IX, Letter 19, he writes: “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ H[lacuna], archbishop of Lyons [lacuna].” He can be no one other than Hugh, Gebuin’s successor: first, because H is the initial letter of his name; secondly, because the man to whom he writes was legate of the Roman See, as is clear from the context, a dignity Gebuin never held. Moreover, Letter 32 of the same book is addressed to the venerable archbishop of Lyons and likewise legate of the Apostolic See, as is evident to anyone reading it. Gregory the pope, moreover, is known to have died in 1085, on 25 May. Therefore Hugh already occupied the see of Lyons before then.

[Col. 1208C] Our third and unanswerable proof comes from the Life of Gregory VII himself, written by a contemporary author, namely Paul of Bernried, where the following is read: “When Pope Gregory, lying at the point of death, was asked to designate a successor for himself amid so great a disturbance of the faithful [lacuna], he proposed three choices: Desiderius, cardinal and abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, and the most reverend bishops Otto of Ostia and Hugh of Lyons.” And it is added: “But because [lacuna], surveying his rulership from afar, he was absent, he advised the election of the nearby Desiderius.” This is confirmed by the Life of Desiderius, or Victor III, where the following is read: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, indiction VIII, Gregory VII, three days before his death, having been asked by the bishops and cardinals then present with Desiderius what he ordered concerning the ordering of the Roman See after his death, answered that, if by any means they could, they should advance that same Desiderius to this office; but if they could by no means bend him to this, after his death they should hasten as quickly as possible to elect as pope either Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, or Otto of Ostia, or the bishop of Lucca—whichever of these they could obtain first.” These statements are so clear and explicit that it seems scarcely possible to depart from them. Hence the Bollandists, in the appendix for 25 May, vol. V of the same month, part I, p. 1951, say that he died in 1082, on 16 April, or, as others wish, 17 May.

[Col. 1209]

LETTER OF GEBUIN, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, TO RODULPHUS OF TOURS.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis*, vol. XVI, p. 768.)

[Col. 1209B] G., unworthy priest of the Church of Lyons, to the distinguished and especially revered Father R., archbishop of the see of Tours, and to the flock committed to him: the glory of eternal blessedness.

O how good and how sublime is humility, which casts down proud and lofty persons from the seat of pride and raises humble poor persons from the dunghill (Psalm 112:7)! For its power is so great that through it we must pass from toil to rest, from death to life, and from punishments to glory. Through it the strong are humbled and the humble exalted. Indeed, God, remaining above all things by humility, nobly triumphed over the strong man armed; and the humility of God drove out from the world which he held captive—wherefore “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

We have thus found your graciousness to be full of this virtue, since, following the custom of your predecessors, you do not disdain to render to my holy Church of Lyons the service of such most humble devotion, such charitable entreaty, humility, and total obedience. Therefore let the greatness of your discernment consider with how much sweetness and with what fervour of charity we love your humility, being certain that we know ourselves to be loved by you; for Scripture says: “The soul loves one who loves it.” Further, let your love know that we love you with such sweetness that, if your need required it, with the love by which the Apostle professes that he would give his eyes for the Galatians, we likewise would not hesitate to tear out our own eyes for you and give them for you.

[Col. 1209D] For when you show humility to your mother, what else is accomplished by doing this than that you become ours by obligation, and we yours by charity? Therefore your reward with the merciful Redeemer will be all the more abundant the more diligently you retain the humility through which the concord of all brothers and the unity of the whole holy Church are preserved. Accordingly, trusting in your charity as truly in a dearest friend, we do not hesitate confidently to knock at the ears of your mercy, firmly believing that you will not suffer us to be saddened, especially in a matter by which your soul can be greatly helped.

There is a certain abbey belonging to you, called Savigny, a place most noble from ancient times, still, thanks be to God, preserving its ancient nobility, which has long been bereft of its shepherd. For it I ask; the Church of Lyons asks. I would have come here to implore you for it, had I not been oppressed by so many and such grave infirmities that I can scarcely breathe, let alone go to you. Now therefore, because I cannot be with you bodily, but remain always with you in spirit, I beg that, gathered in one spirit, you earnestly urge, entreat, and persuade on our behalf and yours Lord B., abbot of Marmoutier, that he not delay to provide for me, his beloved, and the desolate brothers who ask his mercy. Let him send a father, let him send a shepherd, who may guard his flock with such caution that no entrance may be opened in any respect to the ancient enemy through which he might ever break into that flock. Farewell. May almighty God prolong your life through the course of many years and, after a long time, receive you at the table of the heavenly homeland. Farewell again; persist in your commands.

ANNO DOMINI MLXXXII. GALTERIUS, SURNAMED SAVEYR, BISHOP OF MEAUX.

[Col. 1211]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VIII, p. 1608.)

[Col. 1211A] Galterius, called Saveyr, that is, “the Wise,” gave the brothers of the monastery of La Celle two altars in the villages of La Celle and Vaire on 29 March 1045, in the sixteenth year of King Henry, completing what his predecessor Bernerus had planned but had been prevented by death from fulfilling. By the king’s command, he subscribed in 1047 for the monks of Saint-Médard against Robert of Coucy; he also subscribed the king’s diplomas of 1048, concerning the cell of Saint Aigulf to be joined to the monastery of Saint Peter of Troyes and concerning the canons of Chartres. In the same year he attended the council at Senlis, where the Castle of Vico was restored and confirmed to Saint-Médard.

In 1050 King Henry sent him with Wascelin of Châlons into Russia to seek Anna, daughter of King Gerisclon, in marriage for Henry after the death of his former wife; the king of Russia received this gladly. He was present at the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Dionysius and his companions in the church of Saint-Denis in 1053. He attended the consecration of King Philip I in 1059, and in the same year the Roman synod, where the complaint of the monks of Saint-Albin against those of Vendôme was decided, Galterius being one of the arbitrators. He subscribed King Henry I’s diploma for the restoration of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in 1060. He is mentioned in King Philip’s writs of 1064 for the monks of Saint Peter of Sens, and of 1066 for the monastery of Saint-Nicaise. He attended the dedication of the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and subscribed King Philip’s diploma for that church in 1067; in the same year he subscribed the letters of Villanus of La Chapelaude confirming a gift made to Saint-Denis.

[Col. 1211C] At the Council of Bordeaux in 1068, his letters were read, testifying that the case concerning the cell of Crécy had been decided in the Roman synod by Pope Nicholas in favour of the men of Vendôme against the monks of Saint-Albin. He attended the dedication of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais in 1069. He subscribed an instrument of Geoffrey, bishop of Paris, for the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 1070; King Philip’s diploma, issued in 1071 at the Council of Sens, confirming the gift of the church of Saint Andrew by Hugh of Troyes to the ascetics of La Celle; and, in the same year, the writ of Burchard, count of Corbeil, for the church of Saint Exuperius.

Counted among the Fathers of the Council of Paris held in 1071, he subscribed King Philip’s diploma confirming all the goods of the Church of Compiègne. He attended the Council of Sens in 1080, and likewise that of Meaux, at which Saint Arnulf was made bishop of Soissons after Ursio’s removal, and Lambert of Morin was excommunicated. About that time he approved the land of Morissart for Abbot Gautier and the monks of Pontoise. He subscribed the judgment delivered by King Philip at Poissy on 6 January 1082 in favour of the monks of Saint-Germain against the knight Hugh, surnamed Stavellus. He also affixed his seal to the charter of Richer, archbishop of Sens, granting the church of Saint-Baldus to the monastery of Saint-Remigius in that city, in the twenty-third year of King Philip.

Galterius’s death is recorded on 19 October 1082 in the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif. In the Necrology of Meaux he is commemorated thus: “On 24 October died Galterius Saveyr, bishop of Meaux, who gave the church of Saint Martin to the church of Blessed Stephen.” Fulcoius gives 20 October in this epitaph, in which he says that Galterius was buried in the Major Church, which he had rebuilt:

Here lies the devout bishop Galterus, for whom
This worthy house was safely mother and bride.

Lest, in accordance with your vows, you should repent [uncertain],
The glorious man obtained both the thing and its reward.

Though it was lifeless, uncultivated, and naked at once of beauty,
He raised it as much as he could, in body and in mind.

He renewed it, adorned it, and reformed it in worship and art;
He made it a church, though it had previously been ruined.

Twice ten days of October marked his departure:
A mournful day, such as his people had not known before.

[Col. 1213]

LETTER OF GALTERIUS TO BARTHOLOMEW, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, CONCERNING THE CELL OF CRÉCY, AWARDED TO THE MEN OF VENDÔME IN THE ROMAN COUNCIL UNDER POPE NICHOLAS.

(Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 901.)

[Col. 1213A] Hugh, bishop of Nevers, to B., archbishop of Tours, E., bishop of Angers, and Count Geoffrey: the gift of perpetual happiness to each one.

Last year, while we were at Rome in the holy synod, a disputed complaint concerning a certain church of Saint Clement at Crécy came to the ears of Pope N. The brothers of the Church of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme and the monks of Saint-Albin had laid their respective claims to it before us. But the pope, occupied with many matters, ordered that the question be investigated separately by the bishops of Metz and Troyes, and by me, bishop of Nevers, and by the bishops of Le Mans, Arezzo, and Limoges: to which party the aforesaid church should be awarded according to right. What we heard from both groups of monks we reported to the pope. In the plenary synod he awarded the aforesaid church to the monastery of the Holy Trinity, because we judged that no one can grant to a church a fief which he holds from someone else, nor grant it to anyone except by permission of the person from whom it derives. Farewell.

ANNO DOMINI MLXXXV. ALPHANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF SALERNO.

[Col. 1213]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, p. 380.)

[Col. 1213B] Alphanus, an outstanding ornament of the Church and city of Salerno, was born of most noble parents, piously brought up from his earliest infancy, and remarkably learned in the Holy Scriptures. He became a learned cleric, skilled in ecclesiastical affairs, distinguished in verse and prose; and, at Desiderius’s urging—Desiderius who later became Pope Victor III—he voluntarily embraced the monastic life about the year of the Lord 1056 in the monastery of Monte Cassino, having laid aside the belt of clerical soldiery. Not long afterwards, at Prince Gisulf’s request, he was first made abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Salerno, then created archbishop of Salerno, and received consecration from Pope Stephen IX in 1058. The Chronicle of Monte Cassino, Book III, chapter 7, makes known the beginnings of his career, his progress in monastic discipline, and the time of his ordination, in these words:

“Desiderius, falling into a considerable illness through excessive abstinence and many vigils, went to Salerno for treatment. While he stayed there for some time, Alphanus, who later obtained the archbishopric of that same city, a most prudent and noble cleric, became closely acquainted with him. By frequent admonitions he exhorted Alphanus’s mind to contempt for the world, and finally obtained from him the promise that he would become a monk, if first he were allowed to go to Jerusalem, as he had long conceived in his mind. This agreement having been made between them, Desiderius returned to Benevento and, after not many days, summoned Alphanus to come to him.

[Col. 1214B] When all the noblemen and clerics began to frequent Alphanus and to honour him fittingly because of his great wisdom, his purpose of taking the road to Jerusalem gradually began to grow lukewarm in his mind; he declared that he wished in no way, at no time, ever to be separated from Desiderius’s side. They spent some time at the monastery of Saint Sophia. Then news spread that Pope Victor had come from beyond the Alps to Rome and would soon come to these parts. Alarmed by this news, Alphanus, knowing without doubt that his brothers would be accused over the murder of Prince Guaimar, resolved to forestall the apostolic pope and humbly begged Desiderius to go with him. Because he had marvellous skill in singing and no small knowledge of medicine, he had brought from home with him several books of that art and fully trusted that he would be held in high esteem at the supreme pontiff’s court. Having therefore prepared and made ready all the remedies he could, he set out with that city’s archbishop for the Roman pontiff in Tuscany, and they found him staying at Florence. In a short time they acquired great familiarity with him and were treated quite honourably.

[Col. 1215A] But when Desiderius, after staying there for some time, had learned for certain that the pope would not come to these parts and was, moreover, soon going beyond the Alps, and when he considered that life at that pontiff’s court was quite useless for his purpose, he began urgently in every way to press Alphanus to seek from him, without delay, permission to return. A few days before, the brothers had elected Peter abbot of this monastery; to announce his ordination he had then sent two brothers of that place to the pope. Desiderius therefore, having found the opportunity he had long desired, went with Alphanus to the Roman pontiff; falling together at his feet, they requested leave to depart. They added a request that, in order to live more religiously, he would send them there through the monks who had come to him from the monastery of Monte Cassino, and deign to commend those monks to the abbot and brothers by his letters. The apostolic pope agreed, and so they were sent with those brothers to the monastery as they had proposed. They were received fittingly by the abbot and honourably joined to the brothers; for some time they lived among them with the greatest honour and humility, were held in great affection by all, and received monastic consecration from that abbot, Frederick rejoicing more than enough at their arrival.”

And chapter 8: “In those days Desiderius had seen a vision not to be despised, whose fulfilment soon commended the matter. He saw himself with Alphanus standing in a certain church and in a very beautiful tower situated beside the brothers’ chapter house; in it Father Benedict appeared to be sitting upon a most fitting seat. While they were struck with amazement and fear at the sight and did not dare at all to approach more closely, Blessed Benedict cheerfully beckoned to Desiderius and, stretching out his hand, commanded him to sit beside him. But Alphanus, because he had not been summoned by him, took offence as though slighted and went out of that house. This vision seemed very plainly to signify both that Alphanus would not remain long in this place and that Desiderius would take on the role of Father Benedict in this monastery. Not long afterwards, therefore, Prince Gisulf requested Alphanus; he was first made abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Salerno, and afterwards obtained the archbishopric of that same city.”

After his consecration by Pope Stephen himself, Alphanus obtained a privilege specifying on which days he was to use the pallium in celebrating solemn Masses. By the same letters he was granted the authority to nominate, elect, and consecrate eleven of his suffragan bishops—namely, those of Paestum, Conza, Acerenza, Nola, Cosenza, Bisignano, Melfi, Policastro, Marsica, and Cassano. We have not seen these letters, but Musca cites them. As for the statement contained in them that the Churches of Cosenza, Conza, and Acerenza were at that time suffragans of the archbishop of Salerno, [Col. 1215D] I think that they were subject by virtue of primatial right, since those churches had then been distinguished by archiepiscopal rank, as we shall say in their proper places.

In the year 1059 Alphanus took part in that celebrated Roman council convened by Nicholas II, at which Berengar, having abjured his heresy for the third time, professed the Catholic faith before 113 bishops. At the same council the constitution concerning the election of the Roman pontiff was issued: the election was restricted to the cardinals and bishops of the Roman Church, authority over it was assigned to them, and the election was decreed.

In the same year Alphanus attended another synod held by the same Nicholas at Benevento, and subscribed himself first after Humbert, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida.

In 1066 Alphanus ordained Riso, the first bishop of Sarno, and furnished him with a privilege, a copy of which is recorded among the bishops of Sarno.

In 1067 Pope Alexander II confirmed to Alphanus, the archbishop, and to the Church of Salerno its ancient privileges in the following diploma, [Col. 1216A] a copy of which we present from the archive of the archiepiscopal table, written in these words:

“Alexander, etc.

“‘In consideration of pastoral care,’ etc.” See under ALEXANDER II, privilege no. 55, volume CXLVI of the *Patrologia*.

In the following year, 1068, he went to Salerno, as was customary, to inspect the affairs of Campania, and held an assembly of bishops and abbots. Gisulf, prince of Salerno, Robert, the duke, and his brother Roger, the count, were present. There William, son of Tancred, restored to the Church the property he possessed, and Alexander adjudicated it to Archbishop Alphanus in the following manner:

“Alexander, etc.

“‘Let it be known to all the sons of Holy Church,’ etc.” See under ALEXANDER II.

A few years afterward, namely in 1071, Alphanus wrote a diploma for Leo, abbot of Cava, concerning the exemption of the Church of Saint Nicholas of Palma, [Col. 1216B] with all its rights and possessions. With the consent of the chapter and clergy, he exempted it from all jurisdiction belonging to himself and his successors. It was executed in the twenty-ninth year of Gisulf’s principate, indiction IX. We give its copy below.

According to the accounts, while Alphanus was archbishop, Duke Robert of Apulia, elated by the success of his undertakings in Sicily, brought an army to Salerno and began to attack it fiercely, calling upon his brother Richard, prince of Capua, for assistance. When Gregory VII learned of this, he sent Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, to settle the dispute between Gisulf, prince of Salerno, and Robert. Gisulf’s untimely obstinacy made an agreement impossible. Robert, however, approached the walls with a very large force, and after part of them had been demolished by siege engines, opened a passage for himself into the city. On the Ides of December, while the prince was perhaps still resisting, he brought it under his authority. He afterward adorned the city magnificently with various buildings, and at his own expense caused a temple of extraordinary beauty [Col. 1216C] and size to be built for the blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew in the year 1075, the first year after he captured Salerno.

After Michael, son of the emperor Constantine, arrived in the city of Salerno in 1080 to visit Robert Guiscard, Pope Gregory absolved Robert himself and congratulated Alphanus on having discovered the bones of the apostle Matthew, which had been unknown, and having placed them in the new temple. He urged him to exhort Duke Robert and his wife to embrace them with the highest reverence. The history of the translation was written from an ancient monument by Archbishop M. Antonius Marsilius Columna in *The Life and Deeds of Matthew*, chapter 8.

Duke Robert, founder of the temple, died after many triumphs and victories on the island of Corfu in Greece, at the age of seventy-two, in the year of Christ 1079 and the twenty-third year of Alphanus’s episcopate. His body was brought to Venosa and buried in the principal church in a most honorable tomb, [Col. 1216D] and his son Roger succeeded him in the principate.

In the following year, 1080, Duke Robert restored to Archbishop Alphanus numerous possessions that had been seized from the Church of Salerno, as appears in the following document:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, by the favor of divine mercy duke.

“We do justice, and at the same time enlarge the commonwealth, when, preserving the rights of the churches inviolate, we confirm them to those churches out of regard for divine mercy. Therefore we wish it to be known forever to all that, knowing and acknowledging through the legitimate documents shown to us, the castle of Olibano, the estate of Liciniano, the Church of Saint Angelo of Monte Auro, the estate of the Cosenza people, the Church of Saint George situated near that same estate, the estate of Salsanico, the estate of Saint Victor, the estate of Scalcinato with all its people, and especially their holdings at Doleave and Pressano, Portus and Lintus with its crossing, and the small canals [Col. 1217A] in the river Sele, the holdings at Pecta and Fasanara, the larger lake, the sea caves of the Tusciano, Castelluccio of Battipaglia, as well as the woods of Laurito, Maleuritunde, Calezano, and Lama, and other cultivated and uncultivated lands situated in the Tusciano and in Foria of our city of Salerno, belong by rightful title and true ownership to the Church of Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist in the aforesaid city of Salerno, over which the lord Alphanus, venerable archbishop, presides, and that all these and many other immovable possessions are justly held and peacefully possessed by that Church and the aforesaid lord archbishop, by divine regard and at the command of the lady Sicalgaita, our wife.

“All the aforesaid possessions, individually and collectively, and all others which that Church rightfully holds and peacefully possesses, together with the tithes of all the revenues of our city of Salerno and of the land of Eboli, we grant and forever confirm to the Church of Saint Matthew, to the aforesaid lord archbishop, and to his successors. If anyone should, with rash daring, violate any part of this grant and confirmation, let him know that he shall pay fifty pounds of the purest gold, half to our treasury and half to the party of the Church of Saint Matthew.

“We ordered the text of this grant and confirmation to be written by the hand of John, our notary, and strengthened with our leaden seal in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1080, in October, indiction IV, and in the twentieth year of our dukedom.

“When this privilege had been shown and read, because it was in the interest of the same lord archbishop and of his aforesaid Church that it should be published or formally entered, the same lord archbishop, imploring my office, asked me to admit this privilege for publication or formal entry. I, assenting to his requests because I saw that they accorded with reason, admitted the privilege for publication or formal entry, transcribing the whole of it, in due order, word for word, with nothing added or changed, through the hand of the aforesaid Philip, public notary of Salerno, into this public instrument. I, the aforesaid Philip, public notary of Salerno, having been requested, was present while it was reduced to this public instrument, wrote it, and marked it with my customary sign. What above has been distorted reads ‘of his beloved wife.’ Place of the sign.

“I, the judge Matthew mentioned above.

“I, the aforesaid Matthew of Silices, am a witness.

“I, the aforesaid notary James, am a witness.

“I, the aforesaid notary John Scant[ianus], am a witness.”

During the episcopate of Alphanus, a notable miracle occurred at the monastery of Saint Benedict near Salerno in the year 1078, as the *Chronicle of Cassino*, book III, relates:

“At that time,” it says, “a very notable miracle occurred in the monastery of our blessed Father Benedict, which was built within the walls of the city of Salerno and from the very beginning of its construction was subject to this monastery of Cassino. From the household of that monastery, a ravenous wolf secretly attacked and carried away a little boy. The mother, pierced with grief, cried out after it:

“‘I adjure you, beast, by blessed Benedict, whose servant he is: do not carry my son any farther, but release him with all speed.’

“When the wolf heard this, it immediately dropped the boy it was carrying from its open mouth. But then it suddenly sprang upon another boy, tore him to pieces, threw away his mutilated corpse, and swiftly carried off the severed head, fixed between its teeth, to its lair.”

At approximately the same time Peter Damian records another miracle in book IV of his letter to the bishops, which perhaps occurred at Salerno:

[Col. 1218A]

“This,” he says, “is what the venerable Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, recently reported to have happened to one of his priests. That priest, in order to increase his monetary gains, had been collecting no small amount of interest from widows and living thereafter in carnal conduct. Once, while he was celebrating Mass, during the very breaking of the Lord’s body, three sparks of fire were seen to burst forth from the heavenly sacrament itself and to strike terribly against the breast of the celebrant. What this could have been, the judgment of a prudent person who investigates carefully will decide.”

At this time the Church of Saint Michael the Archangel at Salerno was famous, and it is mentioned in a certain instrument of the nuns of Saint George:

“In the year,” it says, “1079, in the time of the lord Robert, glorious duke, I, Lando, formerly of John . . . through the accidents of human frailty fell ill and lie in bed, etc.; and for the salvation of my soul I dispose of my possessions in the Church of Saint Michael the Archangel, which was built in the jurisdiction of the place called Padulecta, and the property itself, etc., to be made over to the aforesaid Church and its rectors, to do with it whatever they wish, without any opposition,” etc.

Moreover, Alphanus adorned three parts of the apse of the temple of Saint Matthew with the most elegant workmanship, called mosaic. There, in the year 1085, he interred with solemn ceremony in a most elegant tomb—an outstanding work of Duke Robert—Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff, whom he had received into hospitality as an exile and who had died.

The Salernitan writers report that, while living at Salerno, this most holy pontiff selected for the service of the altar twenty-four canons, whom he also called cardinal priests, and four deacons, whom he likewise called cardinal deacons. By later pontiffs they were subsequently granted the privilege of wearing silk mitres, which they call *de damasco*—“of damask.” They continue to use such titles and mitres to this day.

Alphanus, remarkable in countless services to God, in the salvation of souls, the advancement of religion, and the adornment of his Church, departed to the Lord in the twenty-ninth year of his priesthood, in the year of salvation 1085, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, full of days and virtues. He was buried near the tomb of Gregory VII, the most holy pontiff, who had been summoned to heaven shortly before, and is said to have been numbered among the saints.

That Alphanus produced many monuments of his genius is attested by Peter the Deacon of Cassino in his book *On the Illustrious Men of That Monastery*, recently published by our learned friend John Baptist Mari, canon of Saint Angelo in the Fish Market, who also furnished it with notes:

“Alphanus,” says Peter, “archbishop of Salerno and monk of the monastery of Cassino, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures and fully instructed in knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines, composed in a plain and very lucid style the passion of Saint Christina; two hymns, moreover, concerning the same virgin; verses on Saint Benedict for Pandulf, bishop of Marsica; the songs of Saint Sabina; verses on Saint Christina; on Saint Peter the apostle; in praise of the monks of Cassino; on the situation, construction, and restoration of the same monastery; a Sapphic hendecasyllabic meter on Saint Maurus; also hymns concerning him; three hymns on Saint Matthew; two on Saint Fortunatus; on Saint Nicholas for Acto, bishop of Chieti; for Gisulf, prince of Salerno; for William, grammarian of that same place; for Guido, brother of the prince of Salerno; for Goffridus, bishop of Aversa; for Hildebrand, Roman archdeacon; for Romuald, advocate of Salerno; for Rofridus, monk of Cassino; a heroic meter in honor of the twelve Holy Brothers; his metrical Confession; verses on the Church of Saint John the Baptist at Cassino; very many epitaphs of distinguished men; and other works that have not come to our knowledge. He lived in the time of the emperors mentioned above. He was buried at Salerno.”

Thus far Peter.

The works noted by Peter, apart from the verses he composed in praise of Romuald the advocate and of Sigismund of Cassino, have been published at the end of our *Italia sacra*. In addition to these, the same Mari reports in his notes on Peter that Alphanus wrote other little works:

“On the union of the Word of God and man, one book; on the union of body and soul, one book; on the four humors of body and soul, one book. The aforesaid little works existed in the Cassinese library, manuscript shelf 8, on the left. The Passion of the twelve holy martyrs, the brothers of Benevento, addressed to Rofridus, monk of Cassino, is found in Lippomanus, volume IV, and Surius, volume VII, under the first day of September.”

The same John Baptist Mari will publish, corrected and complete in every respect, many other little works and verses of Alphanus, according to the evidence of a manuscript codex.

What I have wished to note at the end concerning this highly praised archbishop Alphanus as an author of poems is intended to prevent anyone from being misled by the note of Antonius Caracciolus in the index under Alphanus II, who immediately succeeded the first. Caracciolus falsely attributes to Alphanus II the poems preserved in the Cassinese library and mentioned by Baronius, volume XII; for from what Peter, Alphanus’s contemporary, and the *Chronicle of Cassino* wrote, it can easily be established that Alphanus I composed the poems.

I also wish to copy here the donation of a certain John, a Salernitan blacksmith, which he made to the Church of Saint Sophia before Sico, count and judge, in the same year and month in which Alphanus died. Alphanus, his successor, then priest and custodian of Saint Maximus, was present with several other Salernitan priests and custodians of churches. Thus it appears in the copy:

“In the name of the eternal God and of our Savior Jesus Christ. In the year from his Incarnation 1085, in the time of our lord Roger, most glorious duke, in the month of October, indiction IX.

“Before me, Sico, count and judge, came John, priest and custodian of the Church of Saint Sophia, which was founded within this city of Salerno, and witnesses came with him. They are: Alphanus, priest and custodian of the Church of Saint Maximus; Peter, priest and custodian of the Church of Saint Mark, built near the Rotense Gate; Manso, cleric and primicerius (chief cleric) of that same Church of Saint Mark; Peter, priest and custodian of the Church of Saint Gramatius; and Maurus, priest of that same Church of Saint Sophia.

“These witnesses testified that, before them and six or more others, John the blacksmith, son of Radecis, and Isa, his wife and daughter of Maraldus, of their own good will and for the salvation of their souls, had offered to the same Church of Saint Sophia, over which the lord Muscanus, venerable abbot, presides, all their possessions that belonged to them in any manner and that belong to them outside this city, in the places of Saraniano and Pelliciano, with the boundaries and names and appurtenances of those places, together with everything within them and all their appurtenances, with the right of way along their roads and with the documents [Col. 1220A] relating to them.

“The arrangement was that these things should always remain in the power of the custodians of the Church of Saint Sophia, and that the party and rectors of the same Church should have the license to do with them whatever they wished; and that they should forever defend the aforesaid possessions, whole and entire, belonging to him, his wife, and their heirs, as stated above, for the party of that Church against all men. Whenever the party of that Church wished, it would have the power to defend them itself, in whatever manner it wished, with all documents and legal claims it could produce concerning them.

“Nevertheless, as long as the man and his wife lived, they were to retain the aforesaid property in usufruct by their own authority and were to do with its usufruct whatever they wished. If John should die while his wife was alive, half of the usufruct would immediately pass into the power of the party and custodians of the aforesaid Church of Saint Sophia, to do with it whatever they wished; the other half of the usufruct would remain in the power of the said Isa as long as she lived. If she should die before her husband, then one quarter of the usufruct would pass into the power of the party and rectors of the Church of Saint Sophia, to do with it whatever they wished, while the remaining three quarters of the usufruct would remain in the power of the said John. After the death of both of them, John and Isa, the whole usufruct would return to its ownership.

“By agreement, the man and his wife gave a *guadia* to John, the custodian, on behalf of the Church of Saint Sophia, and they could provide sureties to him on behalf of the same Church. By that *guadia*, the man and his wife offered themselves and their heirs to pay to the party and custodian of the Church of Saint Sophia fifty solidi of Constantinopolitan gold if they did not fulfill the agreement as stated.

“They also undertook to fulfill the agreement as stated; and Isa said that she had done these things with the consent of her aforesaid husband. When I had heard the witnesses certifying these matters as stated, I asked them whether they could legally affirm their testimony. Having heard this, they said and promised that, whenever necessary, they would confirm under law what they had testified and would bear witness to it.

“What is written above between the lines is to be read ‘the man and his wife.’ Therefore I ordered you, John the notary who were present, to write this, since you promised to be a witness to what the said man and wife had done.”

“+ I, the judge mentioned above.”

At approximately the same time Gauferius of Salerno, a monk of Cassino, a most learned and eloquent man, lived with the greatest devotion and left many monuments of his genius. They are recorded by Peter the Deacon in his book *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, and also in book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*.

[Col. 1219]

# Poems of Alphanus I, Archbishop of Salerno, Contemporary of Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiff, and Several Other Works Containing Many Matters Relevant to Sacred History

A copy from an ancient manuscript written in Lombard letters, obtained from the Cassinese library through the labor of more than one person, is now for the first time given to the public for its benefit.

*(Ughelli, Italia sacra, volume X, column 47.)*

## I. Verses of Alphanus, Archbishop of Salerno, to Pandulf, Bishop of Marsica

These verses were composed at Pandulf’s request in praise of the blessed Sabina, a most illustrious martyr, in whose honor his episcopal church was consecrated.

[Col. 1220C]

Beloved bishop, loved far more than you believe,  
See the work composed by a reverent mind.  
I have fulfilled, as best I could, what you commanded;  
Songs, they say, render meter more sweetly than prose.  
Your voice instructed me, and in instructing, asked me  
To sing the praises of Sabina the martyr.  
Perhaps I wished to avoid the labor of composing a poem,  
But I feared that I might displease you.  
I know your desire, and I have already learned  
That it could not be discharged by a small offense against affection.  
I am not so fortified in mind that I could willingly  
Endure being deprived of your commission.  
This is a most praiseworthy thing in friendship:  
Whatever is fitting may be done in harmony.  
He is miserably barbarous who lives without this custom,  
Content to remain alone amid the Getic wilderness.  
Rejoicing in the hope of pardon, I ask only this:  
Grant that I was previously too slow to obey your commands.

[Col. 1221B]

It was a great undertaking, beyond my strength,  
To set difficult deeds in dactylic meters.  
Yet I did it rightly, because I reverently clung to you;  
Your voice, surely, lifted away my disgrace.  
According to varying order and numerous rules,  
Consider these two hymns composed not without labor.  
The members of the antiphon are almost marked  
By two verses, since eight lines rightly contain two equal parts.  
There are three times seven, as the ancient custom requires,  
And each part corresponds to those born from it.  
There remain for you three times three responsories,  
As in these I have written three times nine feet without fault.  
At last I wrote the martyr’s acts in free meter;  
This task was unfamiliar to me as a service.

[Col. 1221C]

The study of Cyprian, often reread, had helped me,  
The man said to write so excellently for martyrs.  
In the ancient books he burns like a backward-moving star,  
Giving the Church’s faith a particular light.  
There it was permitted to use his rhetorical flowers  
And often to play with ornamented jokes.  
Now it is permitted—and will be permitted to those who write lawfully—  
And custom here is accustomed to possess the force of law.  
This matter cannot be discharged by any arguments  
Unless the remaining obligations are discharged at the same time.  
You, wise judge, alone must discern these things,  
If they can bring you a place of joy.  
Be whatever you wish to be; it will not harm me for my own sake.  
Here too there remains a pledge of faithful friendship.  
Nor do I fear being properly refuted by the words of others,  
So long as I shall enjoy you as my judge.

[Col. 1221D]

The bees of my heart flee from you, whose caves are Cyclopean,  
And your weapons are not equally able to sting.  
I have not seen a breast so filled  
With the gift of virtues as yours plainly is.  
You alone taste the bitter sweetness of nobility  
And bring sufficient help to your servants.  
Again, these writings of your kinsman will make that certain,  
With whom, as I hope, under your leadership I shall be safe.  
I now use them as a wall, weary as I am from enemies;  
In them life has granted no defect.  
They do not cease to remember you by night and day;  
For you they often gather before God.  
Oderisius presses with tears, Theodinus with prayers,  
[Col. 1222A]  
But Transmundus does what each of them does.  
I know the others, but I know them as skilled in these arts:  
With their mouths they sing only through voices and signs.  
May this goodness also benefit them, as it benefited those men,  
So that they may strive together to look ahead attentively.  
Nevertheless, as I can, I proclaim without reserve  
Those whom I have named, as long as I live—those whom I love and fear.  
Accept the rewards I have been able to bring you at your request;  
They are slight, but nevertheless suited to peaceful places.  
So that the payment for so great a labor may not be empty for me,  
See to it that you implore the resources of this martyr.  
And beyond this, I ask you to remember Pandulf’s wishes  
And, like a devout father, to deem them worthy of assistance.  
May the complete goodness of the boy Leo be pleasing to you,  
And may it not displease you to love him, so that you may be loved.

[Col. 1222B]

So that he may always love you  
And often be able willingly to render you service.  
He lives devotedly in an order with a sufficiently gentle spirit,  
In which the work of the Almighty is perfected.  
Now let these things be sufficient for you; may you prosper.  
May the sought title (*onoma*) of the poem bear both your name and mine.

## II. Hymn of the Same Author in Praise of Saint Sabina

Grant, Christ, to those who sing  
The gift of joy in your martyr,  
So that the sacred rewards of your Sabina  
May be proclaimed alike by voices and lyre.

Born of illustrious parents,  
Powerful through marriage to an exceptional husband,  
Outstanding in beauty,  
She was sufficiently full of virtues and rich in possessions.

The virgin Seraphim had carefully taught her  
By her admonitions  
To abandon idols with her whole heart  
And hasten to trust her Maker.

She despised the laws of the powerful  
And did not fear the harsh form of punishment;  
But, offering her head to the sword,  
She rightly reaches the rank of a hundredfold harvest.

Thus, once in death, hiding her eyes,  
She sees her own people forever in triumph.  
The radiance of the perpetual sun,  
Never failing, will be her day.

Happy is she, more powerful than the world,  
Who receives heaven in exchange for her blood;  
Her reward is paradise,  
Overflowing with the delights of life.

There the purple flower of the rose  
And nard are present; the amaranth blooms;  
Saffron flowers with violets;  
Incense, thyme, lilies, and balsam give forth their fragrance.

The angelic choirs sing hymns;  
The apostles resound with a worthy song;  
The martyrs sing psalms beautifully,  
And the virgins strike the drums with their plectra.

Holy one, save forever  
Those whom you praise in the midst of this company.  
From that company we now ask you especially  
To regard the gifts of the Marsicans.

Praise, salvation, honor, power, dominion,  
And light without end be to the eternal One.  
To you, Christ, King of kings, be these things,  
With God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## III. Another Hymn in Her Praise

To the honor of the best Father,  
With the innermost voices of your hearts,  
Sing, renowned choirs,  
The praises of the martyr Sabina.

She climbs to the heights of heaven  
In place of the holy martyrs  
And joins to herself the Son of the King  
By the covenant of virgins.

In whose diadem,  
Like hyacinthine gems,  
She shines for her highest merits,  
Which she deserved through faith in Christ.

Her heavenly dignity,  
Implanted in her sacred blood,  
Knows how to discharge its rewards,  
Unaware of any limit of time.

Her glory always surpasses  
The annual cycles;  
It becomes more beloved  
The more precious it becomes.

Let the pleasures of the world possess  
The foul place of death,  
Whose form of punishment  
May be made the reward of life.

Pray for your servants,  
Noble martyr by birth,  
But much nobler still  
Through the interest of sacred blood.

Disperse the mass of sin;  
Ask an end to dangers;  
And to those languishing with the fever of death,  
Grant the gift of health.

Implant in our minds  
The duty owed to Christ,  
Lest the strong laws of powerful judges  
Destroy us.

Grant this, best Creator,  
Who remain God with the Father,  
And also with the Holy Spirit,  
Who reign without end. Amen.

## IV. Sapphic Hendecasyllabic Meter on Saint Maurus, Abbot

What should please us more on your day  
Than to strive more strongly for you  
With prayers or hymns,  
Best Maurus?

You once learned this, as a boy,  
Under sacred instruction:  
The greatest devotion of enduring life,  
From which you shine with glorious triumphs.

You remember how great your faith was  
When the gentle wave bore your steps,  
And, rushing forth, you lifted Placidus  
From the deep spring.

Among your miracles, this is very sweet to us:  
That here in this stronghold you restored  
Both his languid step  
And his speech.

From far away you saw a road  
Spread with cloaks and flashing with torches,  
Which our Father Benedict  
Once ascended to heaven.

What you once asked might be done for you—  
That, living austerely under the rule that now governs us,  
By your unceasing prayer  
We might live forever—

We ask that the founder of peaceful rest  
Make this happen for you with himself.  
For what we desire, if you are willing,  
You are able to bring about.

May the Author of mercy grant you  
What you wish to be,  
God the King, with whom the equal Son  
Reigns without end, and the gracious Spirit  
Of them both. Amen.

## V. Another Meter by the Same Author
