Brothers, today it is fitting for us to rejoice  
And to cast away every sorrow of the heart  
In the highest joy of the blessed man  
Whose odes we sing with these instruments.

This is the day when the spirit of Maurus,  
Freed from the body, entered heaven;  
Thus, having completed the service of his King,  
He carried away the rewards of such great rest.

Made steward of the heavenly palace,  
He kindly grants what is fitting to those who ask.  
May he soon illuminate our hearts  
With the gracious light he has received as his own gift.

Once he completely healed the wretched limbs  
Of Arderadus, crushed in an accident,  
When both his mind and body  
Were shining throughout the world.

He healed Sergius’ broken foot,  
And gave sight to Linus, the blind;  
He lifted from death the one deprived of sensation,  
And at his prayer the dead man lived.

O blessed Maurus, we ask you: use fully  
The power you once possessed.  
May the sweet soil of Cassino now learn  
What such glory, in which you shine, can accomplish for you.

Do now what your charity is asked to do;  
For equity, by the laws of justice, grants  
That everyone ought to die for his homeland.  
You live—but make us live for you.

*(The final four verses and the conclusion of the hymn are missing.)*

## VI. On Saint Matthew the Apostle

The noble victory of the apostles,  
And the glory repaid for their labor,  
Make heaven and earth rejoice together,  
As the highest proclamations of praise  
Bring them their honors, whose mother is the Church.

This is the senate which, together with the glorious King,  
Will preside as judge on the final day  
To judge the whole seed of Israel.  
His power knows how to close the lofty bolts  
And once more to open them with the key of the tongue.

In this blessed college of princes  
Matthew rejoices in a gracious reward.  
Having immediately abandoned his profitable business,  
He followed Christ and, first of all,  
Wrote his humanity for everyone.

He is the first and wondrous charioteer of the chariot;  
He preserves the figure of the river Pishon,  
And among the evangelists he is granted above the others  
To bear the form of supreme beauty;  
For among them he alone is conspicuously human.

He shines with a threefold dignity of gifts,  
So that the whole age may proclaim in song:  
Evangelist, martyr, and apostle.  
Such a reward appears never to have befallen  
Any of his companions.

He made the nations scorched by the neighboring sun’s climate,  
And inwardly stained with the soot of sins,  
Shine in mind, so that they would not turn  
Toward the black darkness of death,  
While he faithfully freed them through signs and gracious nourishment.

Matthew, apostle, receive now  
The due thanks of your citizens, worthily.  
Make them safe from every crime,  
So that at the future judgment  
They may know that, with such a patron, they served faithfully.

To the Trinity be supreme praise and glory,  
Perpetual salvation and honor, and power,  
Simple and one, and eternal . . .  
Which all created things confess,  
Through all the ages of ages. Amen.

## VII. Another by the Same Author

Rejoice, mother, as you bring forth children;  
Ever fertile, wash them clean,  
Whom water and the Spirit bring forth to you  
Through all the movements of time.

In the first and most sacred mystery of salvation  
You shine from the college of the apostles;  
You shine in his illustrious struggle,  
To whom the world gives triumphs of praise today.

This is the noble feast of Matthew.  
Let the Church make sweet-sounding melodies  
With lyres, flutes, and drums,  
So that the song composed by you may surpass them all.

Use the same one, apostle, for your own people  
In the place of the Teacher; and if anything sounds discordant  
When the people sing, correct it  
With clear doctrine, suitably, as you please.

You more clearly exposed the perverse deceits  
Of certain demons once carried out,  
By which they had secretly made so many guilty  
And inflicted the worst penalties of death.

By prayer you raised the only son  
Of the king, fallen into both kinds of death.  
After this, when you rebuked the tyrant Irtacus,  
From here you ascend the stars as a martyr,  
From here as an apostle.

Glorious evangelist, endowed with acceptance,  
Obtain now, we ask, the heavenly kingdom  
For the faithful, among whom you are seen  
To be a diligent guest.

May the heavenly Son grant this,  
With the Father and the equally holy Spirit,  
To whom all praise and due honor belong,  
And perpetual power without end of time. Amen.

## VIII. Another by the Same Author

Be present, Holy Spirit,  
As we sing your praises  
On this noble feast  
Of the apostle.

You immediately made him an apostle,  
Though he had diligently devoted himself  
To profit while the marketplace was open,  
Transforming him from a publican.

Here he provided healing through words  
To hearts weakened  
By the burning of sins,  
Which had already been entrusted to him by you.

By sacred baptism he washed  
The king together with his wife;  
Their son, who had died,  
He powerfully raised again.

By righteous speech he confounded  
The tyrant’s unlawful marriage;  
For this, adorned with the martyr’s crown,  
He crossed beyond the heavens.

Grant now, Paraclete,  
That at this time we may all  
Live freely  
Through his triumph.

It is attributed to your grace  
That he is called a citizen  
And father of our own homeland—  
A claim plainly believed as well.

Glory to the highest Father,  
Victory to the Son,  
And due praise to you,  
Throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## IX. On the Holy Martyrs Fortunatus, Gnius, and Anthes

Praise, honor, and glory to the holy martyrs,  
Who, consecrated to the Lord of heaven  
By their own blood, retain  
The place of the heavenly army  
With unconquered faith.

They strove manfully to endure strong conflicts,  
To break hostile ranks bravely,  
Using their bodies as a barrier,  
So that after death they might live.

Now placed in the King’s diadem,  
They shine more brightly than the light of the stars.  
Christ, the Son of God, has given  
These gifts to his soldiers.

Among their number are those for whom  
The people today gladly bring forth songs—  
Our pious people, as is fitting,  
The great light of this homeland.

Fortunatus, enjoy your prosperous circumstances,  
Whose name agrees equally with your merits.  
By your prayer grant that we too  
May rejoice forever.

And you, Gnius, consent by your good character  
To blunt our hearts continually,  
And help us happily receive later  
What we now ask.

Anthes, splendid in perpetual light,  
Equal to these in merit and rightly not the least,  
Ask the common Lord so often for us  
As often as you can.

May the Godhead, our King, grant this to us,  
Binding together our discordant composition,  
So that with you, in stable peace through all things,  
We may live for you through the ages. Amen.

## X. Another on the Same Martyrs

Hail, day dedicated  
To our protectors,  
Distinguished by praises  
And adorned with the highest virtues  
Of the martyrs.

While they rightly preferred  
Eternal things to temporal,  
They were swiftly proved  
Soldiers of Christ by the sword’s blow.

Wonderful are the things believed  
To have happened to them after their passing.  
Birds guarded  
Their shining bodies.

Their homeland, besieged  
And almost delivered to death,  
Suddenly remained free  
Through the victory of these men.

Now secure among your fellow citizens,  
Holy Salerno, give your victors  
The sweeter proclamation  
Of a new praise.

These are the men for whom  
It is fitting that you rejoice most often,  
By whose gift you are thought  
To live with fear suppressed.

May they drive away from you  
Visible and invisible enemies;  
May they provide increases of peace  
And the rewards of the highest life.

Glory to the highest Father,  
Victory to the Son,  
And due praise to the Spirit,  
Throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## XI. On Saint Nicholas

King of kings, God of all,  
the honor and glory of the saints, who always make the leaders  
of the sacred warfare distinguished by new gifts:

You adorn them also with the everlasting diadem  
of the kingdom, which they may likewise enjoy with you,  
since they lived with you before the day  
that marked the beginning.

Therefore the annual festivals of these men are present,  
celebrated with devout praises,  
while the world proclaims its rewards  
through the measured regions of its climates.

Grant what those who ask you seek,  
so that Nicholas, resplendent, may approach the stars  
with sweet-sounding songs.

[Long lacuna.]

On the fourth occasion this boy once nursed,  
and on Friday he suckled at the breast—  
a wondrous meal,  
which is believed to have been accomplished by you, not by chance.

When his boyhood years had passed,  
he frequently attended the thresholds of the Church;  
you wished him to become  
heir to his patrimony.

With no small amount of gold  
he relieved the poverty suffered by a wretched man,  
who, through shameful desire, was intending  
to give his three noble daughters, born from him,  
to prostitution.

This the metropolis of Myra  
rightly obtained as a worthy bishop for itself—  
the one whom the divine voice, heard by your faithful,  
identifies as bishop.

Compelled by prayers, he quickly restrained  
the great danger of the sea,  
and restored those almost overwhelmed  
by the deep to a state of complete tranquility.

He diminished nothing for the sailors  
of the grain granted in their narrow hour of need;  
rather, for a full two years  
it had been an abundant supply for all the citizens.

[Col. 1228D] Opposing the frauds of the enemy,  
he orders at once that the vessel carrying oil  
be emptied into the sea;  
the oil burned up the substance of the waters,  
which had long been burning.

Afterward, he swiftly snatches three men  
condemned to capital punishment from death;  
for, by his power,  
even barred double doors open of their own accord.

Now in dreams he fiercely terrifies the Caesar,  
now the Exarch;  
and, placed at a great distance,  
he drives away the funerals already prepared  
for three princes.

Nicholas, bringer of salvation,  
be forever the protector of your servants,  
all who celebrate you  
at this festival with peaceful praises.

Noble Greece worships you wondrously,  
praises and magnifies you;  
indeed, all the world rejoices  
to pay you these gifts.

Rome, the head of the world,  
always celebrates you as equal to the apostles;  
it seeks and obtains your frequent help  
with no great number of prayers.

Who would not regard this day  
as a festival above the others,  
when a father restores to their parents  
sons snatched away to the yoke  
of various servitudes?

Watching over the many gulfs of the sea,  
whenever you are asked with an easy prayer,

[Col. 1229B] you rescue the wretched,  
whose ships have been submerged in dreadful storms.

## XII. In Praise of Saint Christina

Christina, virgin dedicated to God for us, show favor;  
may this day be honor and rest for all.

The people, very well instructed, press upon you  
with friendly praises,  
so that they may remain safe through your help.

You declare that the customs of your homeland’s law  
are nothing,  
to teach your companions what faith must be.

You shatter idols and defeat the prefect  
by your doctrine, believing that he is God  
who sits above the stars.

First you drive away sharp whips, the wheel, and swords;  
then, after the wave had submerged you,  
it brought you forth again.

[Col. 1229C] But the treacherous father, wretched and unjust,  
killed his enemy;  
he himself sought your death,  
but God rescued you.

A jar quite full of dark liquids is broken;  
the golden image of the deceived sun falls.

The crowd, bearing this ill, thunders against  
the judge’s doors;  
and the censor himself becomes the defendant  
in your case.

He had delivered your limbs to the flames  
of a terrible furnace,  
which nevertheless could not destroy them  
as he wished.

Marsus, skilled in the bites of serpents, perished;  
but, in the name of the Lord,  
he remained unharmed.

Then you are deprived of your tongue,  
both breasts are cut away,  
you are pierced by arrows—  
thus swiftly you seek the stars.

Therefore teach, virgin instructed by a heavenly teacher,  
what your people should do,  
that they may come to the place  
where you shine.

## XIII. On the Same

With undefiled faith, come to the aid of our ruin;  
he himself gave you strength,  
by whose love you live.

Despising your father, joined to the heavenly King,  
you mock quarrels and fear no blows.

Because Christ the Savior possesses you within,  
anger, fury, and the sword have no power outside.

You scorn the commands of rulers  
and despise your parent’s orders;  
thus the King preserves his bride  
in the struggle.

Urbanus burns with rage; Idion and Julianus rage.  
Who can overcome the weapons of chastity?

But because in your mind you worship Christ,  
whom you proclaim by name,  
a strong spirit dwells in a fragile sex.

By heaven’s power the fire of the burning furnace grows cold.  
The sea does not retain the virgin body.

[Col. 1230A] Neither the wheel, nor iron, nor a thousand raging darts  
changes your mind, blessed virgin.

At the virgin’s prayers, a young man, rising from death,  
is subjected to the commands of the heavenly King.

What are you doing, Julianus? Why do you, unjust censor, delay?  
You are defeated, as I see, by a woman’s breast.

Complete what remains; attempt what is harder still.  
Let savagery not cease; let impiety not rest.

Take away the tongue still, wretched man;  
take away both breasts.  
But, though she does not speak,  
she enjoys God in her mind.

Most holy virgin Christina,  
we ask you to protect us, committed to you,  
with perpetual assistance.

May the gift of eternal love abound in us,  
so that your flock may come to the homeland  
which you worship.

## XIV. On the Same

Virgin, exalted in the starry dwellings,  
insert yourself among your peoples, Christina,  
so that they may now discharge to you  
the duties of praise with peaceful hearts.

You are resplendent in your father’s radiant offspring,  
but far more splendid in character and faith;  
while you flee the world with a chaste body,  
you acquire God as your companion.

Carrying out his commands by virtuous deeds,  
you do not fear betraying him to savage rulers;  
with a steadfast heart you despise  
the dreadful kinds of punishment.

What battles, and how great, you fought:  
fire with swords, clubs, and wheels,  
chains, scourges, and the fierce  
blows of weapons testify.

Now that you are entering the highest regions of heaven,  
make them open to us by this prayer.

And if you remember us who always remember you,  
may you wish that we be happy in remembrance.

So may your Deity, O King, grant this to us,  
binding together the discordant collection of these meters,  
that with you, in steadfast peace throughout all things,  
we may live for you through the ages.

## XV. On the Same

Bestow, O merciful Jesus, the fountain of everlasting grace—which you are—  
on the servants prepared for you  
in praise of so great a virgin.

For she first marked you by name,  
then by doctrine;  
thus, as the bride of the Bridegroom,  
she had determined rightly to enjoy his glory.

Hating the pageants of the world,  
she sought you as the form of goodness;  
fixed upon dreadful instruments,  
she never ceased to praise you.

Now, picking pleasant grasses  
among rosebuds,  
she bears a crown of light  
sparkling with brilliant gems.

[Col. 1231A] Truly, with greatly increased fruits,  
she brought back a hundredfold seed;  
when such blood had been duly shed,  
such light was won for you.

Through the ages of ages  
glory to the supreme Father;  
may power be yours, O Son,  
with the Spirit, the Paraclete.

## XVI. On Saint Peter the Apostle

The nourishing day shines, most celebrated throughout the whole world,  
which Peter adorned forever with his own blood.

The lofty temples are dyed with purple triumphs.  
Equal praise remains, balanced in a twofold number.

Behold, the boat is driven forward with full sail;  
the credulous beast is already caught on the sickle-shaped hook.

Help your servants, Father and chief apostle;  
bring us also safely to God in winding nets.

When you leave the net and the boat at Christ’s command,  
you are regarded as a key-bearer in heaven  
and a fisherman on earth.

You believe him to be God,  
whom the crowd associates with the prophets.  
Therefore you remain renowned, Peter,  
prince of the churches.

The ignorant Malchus is deceived  
by such a great soldier as you,  
when, sluggishly, he lifted the blow  
delivered by the striker.

You also answer when the whole people accuse you:  
“This impulse is not of strong wine,  
nor is it the utterance of Joel.”

The lame man asks for wealth,  
but he does not have it, because gold was lacking;  
in the name of Christ, however,  
you restored his power to walk.

As Simon departs, a dead man begins to live.  
His own power becomes nothing;  
Simon stands defeated by Simon.

[Col. 1231C] That wretched man flies through the air  
and says that he is going to the heavens,  
from which he falls still farther  
when his wings fail him.

After wicked Nero sees his pestilential friend extinguished,  
you are added to the heavenly shores,  
having been given to die on the cross.

Now receive Rome, consul,  
and Caesar’s senate.  
Behold, the entire world under the stars serves you.

We ask you, Peter, to be humane to all servants,  
powerful on our behalf,  
and a bringer of salvation to the whole world.

O most glorious God,  
Father of the eternal Word,  
grant that we may ascend  
the walls of Peter’s heavenly mind.

## XVII. On Saint Benedict

With the golden ray of the sun, the whole world  
is adorned on this everlasting day,  
so that, happy in Benedict’s festivals,  
it may appear more resplendent.

Rich wars, wondrous deeds,  
and signs of virtues—  
the special gift of the Rule—  
offer him everlasting praises.

He shines from his tenderest years  
in the character by which you ordered his life,  
when you gave yourself to no pleasure  
deep within your heart.

A broken vessel, a woman’s loss—  
you restored it whole by tearful prayer.

You quickly displayed a holy discipline,  
having abandoned the highest studies;  
you fled your father’s possessions  
and were blessed with a saving garment.

You had cherished your limbs in a small cave  
through nine times four months;  
there, remaining known to no human being  
but to one alone, you were held.

Festivals pleasing by divine command  
provided food for you;  
you seemed to be hiding.  
The fame of it arose, and every wound of the mind  
was healed by the wound of the flesh.

Thus the glass cup of poison is broken by his sign;  
the wandering mind is driven away  
by the touch of a little branch,  
and water flows from hollowed marble.

[Col. 1232B] Iron leaps back from its handle.  
A gentle wave governs human footsteps,  
by which the seized Placidus  
is said to have seen his cloak.

A dear bird carried the terrible food.  
You weep greatly, moved by the death  
of the guilty enemy;  
leaving your accustomed place,  
you sought the pleasant Liris.

The slippery serpent rages on the paved altar;  
it increases the burden and crackles with false fire,  
but it has no power to inflict anything  
against the work begun.

Limbs crushed by a collapsed wall  
are restored healthy;  
the evil deed is proved to the brothers,  
and the ruler’s action is disclosed.

He who tasted poison dies,  
and the ruin of the chosen dwelling is revealed.  
Spirits are seized;  
the hydra is seen hiding in stolen wine.

You accuse the brother of having done  
what was useless;  
you inspect the rebellious mind completely,  
expose his abundance,  
and, full of sleep, serve as a judge.

The earth drove the treacherous limbs far away.  
The dragon stops the wanderer;  
the royal ulcer yielded;  
coins took their place,  
and the dreadful plague fled.

What falls as glass proves to be sound.  
Vessels produce oil;  
the chelydrus is driven away by the hand,  
and the vision releases the places of the hands.

When the boy is restored to life,  
you see the soul of your sister  
entering the heavenly dwellings;  
and, as if beneath a single ray of the sun,  
you see all things.

You ascend, holy bishop, through the fiery sphere.  
On the road to heaven, you blaze with torches,  
when the third of the third day before the Kalends  
of April approaches.

The joyful choir of angels sings you,  
as well as patriarchs and apostles,  
and prophets—blessed by the merits  
of every rank.

[Col. 1233A] So that this people may remember such praise,  
love to be called their father here;  
teach them suitably, nourish them generously,  
and grant them the ascent to heaven.

Christ, reward of devoted labor,  
grant that we may be helped by this man’s prayer;  
by his example we have abandoned  
the foul, perishing world.

This hymn of ours, Prince Benedict,  
may it always be pleasing to you,  
for you are the salvation, light, honor,  
and everlasting praise of your monks.

The precious goal of the heavenly King  
makes you famous with true trophies.  
Therefore we always ask you often,  
night and day.

Let glory remain with the exalted Father,  
and the sacred diadem with his Son;  
and to you, holy Spirit,  
let there be the equal power of both.

## XVIII

The following hymn, by the same author and composed in senarii, appears to treat the virtue of humility and the vice of pride. It is quite elegant, but in composing it he uses, in the manner of comic poets, much metrical license. I regret, however, that I found in it certain expressions corrupted through the fault of the copyist, which I have been unable to correct.

Rejoice, just, gentle, and peaceable people,  
and all upright in heart, glory;  
you possessors of the prize that always remains,  
sons of God, beholders of the Lord.

Thus the order of sacred speech bears witness.

In us, indeed, that holy Spirit continually resides—  
the Spirit of piety, wisdom,  
understanding, fear, knowledge,  
counsel, and fortitude—  
filling each person sufficiently and generously.

Inexpressible is the Lord’s kindness,  
who loves humble hearts so greatly  
that, filling them with sevenfold grace,  
he makes them dwellings of his Spirit,  
whose fruit is joy, peace, and love.

He casts down the exalted; arrogance pours forth;  
with his arm he crushes the illustrious.

Thus once, for the sake of pride alone,  
he expelled from perpetual happiness  
an angel crowned with supreme glory.

He was so beautiful and comely  
that nothing within the paradise of the Lord  
could be compared with his beauty.

The crown of the plane tree, cedar, and fir  
was not equal to his foliage.

He was a beautiful seal of God’s likeness,  
exceedingly splendid in appearance.

On his garment shone  
carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, sardius, chrysolite,  
emerald, onyx, beryl, and topaz.

Unhappy human being, when you have grown proud,  
what will you suffer for the crime of exaltation,  
if the just Judge grants no pardon  
to him who received such a great light of brilliance,  
so that he might rightly be set before all the angels?

But happy is the one who possesses these things:  
a good mind, a pure heart, an innocent life,  
whose reward in heaven is greater than the world,  
and whose name the great book contains—  
the book the Almighty had written before time.

There, by the gift of divine mercy,  
[the supplied text is corrupt: “Vos oderis. . . tudine. . . tras mudule.”]  
you shine, inscribed with the character of life.

The choir of apostles, martyrs,  
confessors, and virgins rejoices there.

After the station of the world has ended,  
when that ancient one summons you who are written there,  
the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven  
will soon open it.

The Virgin Mother of the eternal King receives you,  
and immediately joins you to the angelic choirs.

The whole army of the saints sings together.  
Jubal is first among those who sing in the choir;  
Mary, Aaron’s sister, beats the tambourine;  
King David sounds the psaltery;  
and Benedict, the reward of the Rule.

He sees distinguished men, through the doctrine of his law,  
shining equally with wondrous brilliance  
among fiery and condensed stones;  
he marvels at the work and praises the craftsman.

Then he examines the origin of the school.  
Maurus, Honoratus, Placidus,  
Constantine, Faustus, and Simplicius approach.

[Col. 1234C] They all report these things to blessed Peter,  
who marvels that they have emerged from Cassino.

Our Desiderius polished us,  
to whom the gracious Father gives countless thanks  
and declares worthy rewards.

He asks the Author of all things  
that he may be permitted to rejoice with him  
in the heavenly glory of the angels.

Meanwhile, shining seraphim,  
proclaiming “Holy, holy, holy,”  
offer you immeasurable joys  
and command you to sing the song of songs.

So that those thirty-six thousand, four times counted,  
playing zithers with a virginal song,  
may fittingly sing psalms to the purple Lamb.

You praise him in choir and with tambourine;  
you sing to him on strings and with the organ;  
you rejoice to the Lord of heaven and earth.

Having been made participants in his glory,  
I now ask you always to remember me.

Make him favorable to me,  
so that he may deem me worthy to join you among the blessed,  
from where I may look upon you, even from afar.

## XIX. On Mount Cassino

Good mountain, may you be greeted, giver of peace and rest,  
which is believed to be the easy way to the heavenly kingdom.

You preserve in your breast those stones fixed there,  
by which the palace of heaven is marked as constructed.

[Col. 1235A] How much a human being, made in your image,  
owes you, good Christ—  
the power of the mind cannot penetrate it,  
nor can the tongue unfold it  
by any masterly art.

The rhetorician’s office perishes;  
the end and art of learned study fail.  
Nor do the philosophers’ doctrines,  
however ingenious, help them sufficiently—  
those who think they know everything.

You, the creditor, can count these things;  
no rewards given escape you.

You alone exact the profits,  
you who make everything possessed in the world  
yield to your command.

And by your mercy you had conferred upon him  
things far better than these.

For, so that you might make him a participant  
in the citadel of heaven,  
you allowed yourself to die willingly on the cross.

Moreover, it is to his honor  
that you possess the form of flesh,  
in which you shine on the Father’s throne,  
born of a Virgin by a new right—  
both almighty God and human being.

Until now this human appearance  
had been despised by the heavenly citizens;  
but now, because they have a human lord,  
they venerate it  
and offer dutiful obedience.

You bind them gravely together  
so that they may also remain in perpetual peace.  
Therefore heaven and earth, yours alone,  
seem to be—and are—one homeland,  
where so great a commonwealth shines.

When this law has been set down,  
the lowest part enjoys it,  
so that it may pass into another’s joys—  
indeed, may now receive its own reward,  
which Adam’s sin had caused it to lose.

After the former sin had been corrupted,  
no flesh remains without stain;  
it slips continually through guilt,  
and humanity itself again flees.

So it possesses what it has deserved by faith.  
Punishment is now given for crime;  
grace is returned for good work.  
Indeed, no one can otherwise move  
the splendid standards of your warfare  
except through good military service.

By giving themselves to these studies,  
they give themselves to living in many ways.

And since one rule of duty  
is not sufficient for everyone,  
they will be capable according to their merits.

For virgins, widows, men,  
married people, and sacred orders,  
the hall of heaven stands open.

It is usually more familiar  
to the pious who labor and to monks.

Behold, Cassino abounds in such people:  
the venerable mountain, the palace of God;  
another Mount Zion, leader of faith;  
the mountain where God gave the laws to the people,  
written by his own finger.

You are the supreme wisdom of the Father,  
who know everything without doubt.

Grant that the pleasantness of this place,  
as it truly is, may be represented there  
by the work that pleases you.

To those who wish to know this,  
the mind now tells me to speak;  
the rest remains in your goodness,  
for you prepare manifold rewards  
for those who serve here.

In Italy’s bosom lies a plain  
covered with mountains;  
green vine leaves adorn it.

It is somewhat wooded, but famous for its waters,  
its varying waves,  
and rich in every respect  
for its native inhabitants;  
it is richer still for visitors.

For from here there is a road  
to the apostolic City,  
still mistress of the entire world.

[Col. 1236C] Its hills contain the graceful olive,  
the cedar, and the tall cypress.

The remaining wooded trees  
rush pleasantly through their parts like a lyre,  
and water and nourish the land as they water it.

There the mountain bearing the name of Cassino  
rises above everything.

It carried on its breast ancient walls,  
within which there was an altar  
where Apollo is said to have been worshiped.

Here, before the monastery,  
Father Benedict established himself,  
possessing tokens of heavenly light,  
by which the ignorant people  
might be rescued from demonic disgrace.

But, by the judgment of the almighty Father,  
that same structure fell,  
after it had shone splendidly  
and then collapsed.

From that time the house, renewed over a long period,  
remained even in these times;  
because it had not been well founded,  
it gave signs recognized through its disasters.

[Note: The final part of this hymn is missing in Ughelli. D. Ozanam published the remainder from the Casinensis manuscript no. 47, folio 22 verso, in the book entitled *Unpublished Documents for the Literary History of Italy, from the Eighth Century to the Thirteenth*.]

The material and the workmanship were slipping;  
not even one cell of the monastery  
was suitable for its duties.

But by the Father’s counsel—which I cannot convey in this song—  
they were duly razed to the ground,  
and now, at whose command,  
they are endowed with continual light.

For this reason the name of the workman  
cannot be entirely passed over.  
And since the use of the name as a proper name requires it,  
the preceding syllable may become long instead of short.

Therefore it is permitted and appropriate here  
that the name Desiderius, who, O Benedict,  
gave you such precious rewards of a dwelling,  
led by love for you,  
should be present.

Outside, the structure is of marble stone;  
inside, the wall of the church  
is splendid.

Yet it was not easy, through rough labor or crude art,  
for every column brought from the city  
to be completed.

All the other broad features of the place,  
purchased at excessive cost,  
were obtained from every direction;  
and the craftsmen of Hesperia  
are not sufficient for the work.

For these works, Thrace is hired at a price.

Their outstanding labor is applied  
rather to glass material;  
for, varied with colors,  
it adorns the human form  
so that one person does not appear unlike another  
in the image.

Nine times ten lustrums pass,  
showing that the labor of this work  
was beyond the cities of Italy;  
a foreign undertaking, after long delay,  
now becomes our own.

Here alabaster makes the stone shine;  
porphyry and green stone do so as well.

With these, proconnesian marble—[the text reads *pavita*, perhaps corrupt]—  
is joined together,  
so that the work here seems to be  
a glassy sea.

So great is the glory of beauty  
that I judge Rome itself  
not to make more of its own;  
and thus Desiderius’ vows  
have grown strong through the Father’s kindness.

Golden vessels, or rather vessels  
of another noble weight,  
in which a very precious gem  
shines, sparkles, or glows—  
he supplied them from here  
with innumerable resources.

In chasubles, cloaks, and stoles  
there is a very great quantity of value.

The gray altar shines more precious  
through its own workmanship,  
and the double doors surpass  
Carian bronze in costliness.

Almost everything by which this place  
is adorned and made famous  
the Father himself generously provided.

They are new, good, and solid,  
and sufficiently suited to their proper duties.

[Col. 1238A] Through the power of his goodness  
he raised patricians, counts, and dukes to this place;  
and the house, famous enough in every direction,  
shines throughout the world  
like the sun’s clear mirror in heaven.

Who, Cassino, established walls  
better than yours with their porticoes?

The golden house of Cyrus itself,  
nor Solomon’s work,  
could shine more splendidly  
in these dwellings.

The halls of Justiniana  
would have preferred this site for themselves.

Your merit is exceedingly great;  
it is said everywhere beneath the sky  
that your dwelling is holier.

You are the beautiful window of God,  
nearest to the heavenly lights,  
toward which souls are seen  
to tend;  
and here the world of humanity  
is seen by the eyes of One.

Like the pleasant paradise of Eden,  
you are fragrant with every heavenly beauty  
through its aromas.

You have no other delights,  
unless they are perhaps equal to its own.

You compose songs harmonious  
with angelic voices and melodies;  
you seem, in heart and mouth,  
to seek God with continual prayers,  
rather for the sin of the people.

[Col. 1238C] Now, Father Benedict,  
you can enjoy the angelic promises.

This house is sufficiently richer  
than it has been before;  
but, by your merits,  
make it as blessed as it once was.

You good, you merciful, you Lord,  
holy God, almighty Father,  
for whom nothing is difficult to give:  
grant, I ask, that it may be clear  
to those dwelling here  
that the way to heavenly light is open.

Thus may our assembly now please you,  
as the ancient one pleased you,  
which wholly deserved  
to enter the luminous realms of heaven  
from the parts of this guesthouse.

## XX. Song in Praise of Blessed Margaret, Virgin and Martyr

If the world, swollen with boastful poetry,  
recounts its deeds, will our hand be able to lie idle,  
not striking the lyre with its voice  
when it tells of heavenly things?

Therefore let every voice that sings words in choruses  
of vanity fall silent;  
let it banish all empty games;  
but let our lyre carry divine things.

Once Antioch, from its citizens, brought forth  
into the great world a radiance  
of the female sex.

After being cleansed by God in baptism,  
she deserved not to be dear to her earthly parent;  
rather, for this reason she pleased the heavenly Father more,  
and drew the heavenly beings greatly to herself.

Margaret caught the eyes of mortals;  
the governor, with dishonorable gaze,  
looked upon the girl brought before him,  
seeking to soothe her.

But while she refused him,  
she confessed her faith with confident lips.

Believing that he could strike  
a tender mind with threats,  
he found a manly heart hiding  
in the tender girl.

He could not overcome her  
in the dark prison cavern;  
not with rods striking her flesh,  
from which streams of blood ran,  
nor did she draw sighs from her breast  
in the manner of girls.

An iron claw was joined to these instruments,  
tearing her and exposing her bones;  
her entrails could endure more suffering  
than the hand, moved by pity,  
could inflict upon her steadfast mind.

She is shut up in darkness,  
which a ray from above drives away.

The enemy appears in the form  
and terror of a vast dragon;  
softened, defeated, and fleeing,  
he then turns to other,  
long-established inventions of deceit  
and is defeated there also,

when the virgin’s foot tramples  
his empty neck.

Nor was he permitted to recover  
the shades from which he had been led away  
without the virgin’s command.

Then, steadfast, she scorns  
the sacred rites of the gods;  
a burning lamp is joined to her side  
as a wound.

But while the flesh suffers,  
the mind is raised entirely to higher things.

And when, bound, she is given to a barrel  
so that her wounds may be torn open,  
she felt the people’s voices  
being raised to the stars.

Those who confessed God  
receive the gifts of heaven.

Finally, so that the whole people  
would not believe in Christ,  
she was ordered to go  
to the place of bloody combat.

After her prayer had been offered,  
she was struck;  
and while her flesh lay there,  
her mind was carried into heaven.

## XXI. Ode in Praise of Saint Ursula

The splendor of her appearance pleased men,  
but the beauty of her mind pleased the heavenly troops—  
Ursula, deservedly powerful,  
of noble birth.

She brought consolation to her father’s grief,  
not fearing the fury of the perishable king,  
relying upon the virtue  
of the mighty Lord,  
the chaste virgin.

A bridegroom is sought for her;  
she draws the bridegroom,  
and, while she presents herself,  
she seeks companions.

Joyful at what was to come,  
she swiftly gathers  
the ministers of the feast.

She is joined to the sacred company of her companions,  
the holy and celebrated band of the clergy;  
a shining order of fathers,  
eager for the crown, arrives.

The chief shepherd offers the honor  
entrusted to him and returns it,  
not fearing a lesser loss;  
he dedicates the companions  
of the blessed virgin to Christ  
through baptism.

The savage killer rushes in with his sword,  
dripping with the blood of the sacred band;  
their spirits ascend into open heaven,  
their bones remaining for the inhabitants.

Therefore pray to the Lord who is being entreated,  
so that our small virtue may be aided by merits  
while we are surrounded on every side  
by great snares of evils.

## XXII. Song in Praise of Saint Catherine, Virgin

Exceedingly beautiful, wishing to admit no bridegroom  
whose form did not possess the perfection of complete beauty,  
she sought one powerful in virtue,  
who knew all things,  
and who was especially kind through piety.

The chaste virgin Catherine, martyr of God,  
obtains what she desires  
while abhorring the wicked enticements of the flesh.

While she rejects wealth  
and scorns empty honors,  
she is subjected to blows  
and shines victorious through each trial.

Strengthened by God’s help,  
she boldly resisted mortal snares,  
not troubling herself over the harsh promises.

The learned woman, herself a teacher,  
was not afraid to confound learned hearts,  
nor did she fear enduring scourges  
in tender youth.

Higher than imperial authority,  
she is shut in a dark prison.

No hunger could strike the holy mind,  
because God, giving what is suitable for life  
to his servant, visits the maidservant—  
and the Queen visits the imprisoned woman.

She does not suffer the darkness,  
while light spreads within.

A crowd of servants, aware of the matter,  
approaches; receiving faith,  
it sought the palm at the proper time.

The wheels could not wheel away  
her steadfast prayers.

Nor did she fear death,  
bearing a crown from death.

When the wound ought to have poured out  
streams of blood, it gave milk;  
and the heavenly host gave her body  
an honorable burial  
and poured out healing drops.

## XXIII. Ode in Praise of the Same Virgin

The girl’s great goodness compels us  
to stir praises in our song.

Although she despised the few things  
her parents had left her,  
she was sustained by abundant riches.

While she left behind the scepter  
of the fragile king,  
a lofty crown adorned the young woman.

Catherine shone with very great beauty,  
but abundant virtue made her more beautiful  
and made her worthy to be joined  
to the only Son of the supreme Father.

Desiring to be cherished in his embrace,  
she did not desire anything  
that the earth could give.

She neither sought anything prosperous  
nor fled anything evil.

Therefore not even the prefect  
could remove her courage  
with his threatening face.

She also refused to favor  
what pleased him.

She displays the deeds of reason  
with skillful speech,  
things that would illuminate faith  
even for elders in the toga.

She conquered, and the conquered were pleased to submit,  
as at the end they entered  
a life free from death.

The executioner tears the tender girl  
with iron,  
but by chance he could not pierce her heart.

She hid in the foul cavern of the prison,  
but the splendid beauty of the Most High  
was revealed.

And she prepares profit for Christ  
among the multitude.

Now a new weight of wheels has fallen;  
she carried before her  
the sacred sheaf.

But at last, ordered to have her head cut off,  
she asks Christ to show favor  
to those who pray.

The wound inflicted gives white fluid.  
The heavenly host buried her bones;  
purity pours forth healing oil.

## XXIV. Another Ode in Her Praise

Let us not be reluctant to bring forth in song  
the praises the virgin deserved.

The distinguished virgin whiteness,  
the exceptional brilliance,  
the wisdom that shone,  
and steadfast courage  
rightly seek to be raised  
by new titles.

The number of virtues in which she flourished  
during the brief span  
of her fragile life  
raises Catherine’s snowy glory.

The many advantages that do not tear her apart,  
the appearance that does not exalt itself,  
the free portion of the female sex  
that does not collapse through riches—  
great understanding is seen beneath tender youth.

She brings forth the mystical doctrines of faith  
to those who know many things  
through secret knowledge.

The conscious assembly does not introduce anything,  
holding the lights of the radiant victor;  
and, losing souls,  
they find them again.

She tested strength in an excellent but fragile tree,  
the governance that held her hands.

While she strikes with prayers,  
while the threatening fury  
places her flesh in darkness, tearing it,  
so that, once food is taken away,  
it may hasten her to death,

splendor gathers the servant’s joys;  
it prepares food  
so that they may nourish her flesh.

The word bears fruit;  
she gathers its shoots.

The strong woman did not fear  
the terrifying wheels,  
and she endured death  
so as not to undergo destruction.

And she obtains white milk  
after the wounds.

They place the funeral on a mountain summit;  
the right hand of the heavenly beings,  
from which liquid flows back,  
returns strength to weakened limbs.

## XXV. The Virgin Mary Speaks to the Newborn Jesus

You have come well, our infant,  
to look upon these darknesses of the world,  
you who spread lights through the broad heaven.

My Son, and Son of God,  
new inhabitant, hail.

But who are you, and where are you hastening,  
equal to the Father?  
From above, where are you springing forth, my Son,  
where are you coming?

You who fill the decreed regions of heaven—  
does this bosom of earth please your limbs more?

Do you perhaps come to be enclosed,  
you who had no end?

You who, standing, move all things,  
have come to be moved in flesh?

You who carry in your right hand  
the weight of the world’s mass—  
will you be carried in the palm  
of a maidservant and a trembling old man?

The heavenly beings are fed by your gift;  
yet have you been pleased to suck  
the small breasts which you yourself filled?

The choirs above sang of you;  
for whom blessed minds once rejoiced,  
have you come to utter lamentation?

Come now, my Son,  
enter our arms.

A small mother will carry the great one;  
the fragile woman will carry the powerful one;  
she will carry the Maker,  
the work, and the beauty of the clouds.

The poor maidservant stands before you,  
to cover your tender little limbs  
with a soft cloth.

This renowned house does not provide luxury;  
the maidservant lacks resources,  
and the attendants are idle.

When Boreas rages,  
I will warm you neither with fire nor with a pelt.

Behold, I am ready to place  
your tender body in a little box.

[Col. 1242A] Behold, a manger is spread out for you  
as a bed, broad enough.

Whatever you choose, my Son,  
I shall prepare for you in such a manner.

## XXVI. In Praise of Saint Lucia, Virgin and Martyr

You who once established the lights of heaven  
to scatter light over the earth,  
through the gift of light that drives away darkness—

Although pale clouds may cover us at night,  
pressed down by darkness,  
we nevertheless rejoice  
whenever we can behold the light here.

A virgin, famous in faith,  
carries clear lights beneath her standard;  
she taught us, radiant through steadfast battle,  
to stand firm,  
while she seemed to overcome the thundering Lord  
with prayers and to offer aid to her mother in sickness.

The demon, the power of the flesh,  
and the world prepare many battles.

Instructed, she strikes the enemy  
hidden in the clouds with a dart;  
shining with the light of faith,  
she conquers the assaults of the flesh.

She does not join herself to the torches  
of an earthly lover.

What, indeed, is more excellent  
than the covenant of the heavenly Bridegroom?

He cherishes her,  
spreading gifts through her smallest limbs.

The world rises more powerfully against her,  
as a second Mars.

Then the sinister one is present, swelling  
with word and blow.

No force beneath fragile flesh  
can break the manly mind enclosed within her;  
from whose strength mortal mass  
has drawn its strength,  
for she seemed capable of standing firm.

Driven by human efforts of many kinds,  
she was led to places of destruction  
so that she might be dragged  
into shameful dishonor.

She overcomes burning flames  
and did not fear the wounds of death.

Nourished by sacred grace,  
she left her limbs to the earth,  
but her spirit ascends to heaven.

Here your dwelling shines  
at the summit of the light-bearing one.

Here the sacred Bridegroom, entwined with you,  
offers you kisses.

May your radiant prayers also draw us here,  
O shining virgin.

## XXVII. Ode in Honor of the Innocents

Let us admire the shining heap  
of the new harvest, the choir,  
who lead tender throats  
before the Prince with songs.

The newly appointed commander  
rejoices to send forth  
his advance troops.

The boy rejoices,  
gathering the first fruits  
of equal flowers.

Here he rejoices to speak of titles  
which his age, entirely unaware  
and without guilt,  
was giving him.

Thus the first one is sung  
as worthy.

You press upon the innocent one;  
if they lack the service of their tongues,  
the bloody redness cries out.

The slain resound with the honor  
which the living cannot speak.

What do you want, harder than a tiger?  
Why rage, worse than a savage dog?  
Why do you leave your companions empty?

Do you suppose that the pledge of the heavenly ones  
is being crushed by your hands?

But let fury swell in vain;  
let the boy, magnificent to you,  
drinking beneath his mother’s breasts,  
conquer you and tame you by fleeing you.

## XXVIII. On Saint Agnes, Virgin and Martyr

If it perhaps seems difficult for you  
to possess what strong men were able to possess,  
what virgin would disdain to embrace  
what is called by the name Agnes?

Nature did not make her strong at birth,  
nor did the experience of a long period  
make her practiced in wisdom.

Her appearance was pleasing outwardly,  
but more pleasing was her form within.

Thus she pleased human eyes,  
but abundantly, through each deed  
of her excellent nature,  
she exhaled fragrance for the heavenly beings.

She cherished the things which sacred faith  
had given her to hope for.

She joined such a purpose  
to herself with such strength  
that nothing pleasing or harsh  
could make her mind afraid,  
as one who considered all mortal things nothing.

What woman—or perhaps a more robust heroine—  
could overcome such a kind of battle,  
if there were beautiful appearance,  
the passing softness of youth,  
someone offering abundant gifts,  
and a noble suitor present?

Yet, overcoming these things,  
would she fear the scourges inflicted?

When these advantages surrounded  
this sacred young woman,  
they were not instruments of vice,  
but those she possessed of virtue.

Thus the hidden virtue of the tender girl  
might grow still more  
and kindle fearful minds  
for lofty deeds.

The son of the unjust prefect  
prepares snares.

A lover of the flesh,  
he urges her not to reject his marriage  
and gently offers her his gifts.

“I have,” the virgin replies,  
“a better bridegroom than you,  
one who loves me.

“Go far away, food of death,  
servant of crime.”

Every power yields to his virtue,  
and the starry splendor of beauty  
adores its summit.

Her face is indeed fitting,  
touched with cheerful radiance;  
her voice is sweet with holy devotion,  
her speech knows no anger,  
and, not harsh toward the wretched,  
her mind sits free from grief.

Hence no outward appearance of hers was seen to be troubled.

There is whiteness in her, and shining beauty, and a bloom of color;  
the Father makes him excellent—how beneficial is the likeness!—  
and royal birth, together with abundant virtue of spirit.

Thirsting, she touches perpetual riches, powerful to warm  
hearts from which want is wholly removed.  
With him, my beloved, I was well pleased; with him I entered into marriage,  
which no power whatever can change.

**[Col. 1243D]**

A golden ring encircles my finger, so that I may be  
his faithful bride; he graciously gave me many gifts,  
adorned with which I am. My face is decorated with blood;  
I have received a garland woven of the radiance of gems,  
and an excellent kind of garment, lest I should appear  
so unlike my bridegroom, or unworthy to be admitted  
to the bridal chamber, among all those whom I have chosen.

Thus he joined himself to me, and I too am joined to him.

Let not caresses draw me away, nor the hailstorm of threats break me.  
Behold, if the enemy prepares war, I shall shine forth victorious in combat.  
If he shamefully exposes my tender limbs,  
my thick hair will cover me in place of a fitting garment.

If I am also placed untouched in the darkness of a brothel,  
the protecting hand of an angel will guard my limbs.  
If the place is infamous, my vows will be dedicated to the Lord.  
If the appearance of the place is dark, bathed in fresh light  
it will shine more brightly, and a garment will be provided.

If his freedwoman maliciously sends young men to me,  
then, if they know how to govern their hearts wisely, they may return  
unharmed; but the one who does not fear the divine will perish.

Yet I hope that he will grant this with poured-out prayers—  
Christ, who joined me to himself by a special gift,  
whose titles she will sing, rising from death.

Then the fury that arose will compel evil ministers to rage;  
another will be appointed to pursue what has been begun.  
And she will prepare to turn his limbs to ashes.  
When these things have been cast upon the pyre and the flame divided, it will rest;  
and, so that at last I may be joined to my bridegroom in heaven,  
I shall be pierced in the throat, but my mind will fly to the heights.

### XXIX. On the same woman

**[Col. 1244B]**

Radiant with the fire of divine love,  
Agnes overcame the sex of the body,  
and the chaste barriers of the flesh  
prevailed over flesh.

She is compelled to be stained by the crowd’s lusts,  
to enter naked into the notorious brothel;  
but an angel guards the modest  
limbs of the chaste girl.

White garments come from heaven;  
the Lord shines brightly over the obscene place,  
and splendor, with its pleasant fragrance, surpasses  
the arches of the brothel.

**[Col. 1244C]**

The young man lost the beauty of life,  
having dared to violate an untouched body;  
but the virgin recalls the bitter corpse  
to true salvation.

The flame, under divine command,  
grows cold, imitating summer dews,  
when it is ordered to burn the body  
of the virgin dedicated to the Lord.

Dying, she poured forth streams of snowy milk  
mingled with sacred blood;  
the savage executioner buried a deep sword  
in her side.

The white spirit is received by the heavenly hosts,  
and they raise it above the stars of heaven;  
the chaste bride is joined to the chambers  
of her blessed bridegroom.

**[Col. 1244D]**

Now, divine woman, have mercy on our condition;  
and whoever celebrates your triumph  
may obtain for himself forgiveness of guilt  
and salvation.

Restore to the praying people a peaceful  
ruler of heaven and Lord of earth;  
may he, in his goodness, grant peace  
and times of tranquil life.

Let us celebrate with praises the gentle Lamb,  
whom Agnes chose as her chaste bridegroom,  
who governs the stars of heaven  
and directs all things.

### XXX. On the same woman

**[Col. 1245A]**

The prefect’s son burns for the face of the untouched girl,  
but she, steadfast, returned such an answer  
to the young man with chaste lips:

“Why do you seek my bridal chamber in vain,  
food of death and snare of life?  
Depart far from here, foul author  
of obscene crime.

The precious gifts which you, rich man, boast of  
may move the heart of a poor girl;  
but a worthier bridegroom offers  
far better gifts.

Brighter than the moon and the rays of the sun,  
to whom all the elements of the world are subject,  
he gave himself to me as bridegroom, and the stars  
as an everlasting dowry.

Already we enjoy a chaste embrace;  
already flesh rejoices joined to flesh;  
already sacred blood has dyed  
her shining face with purple.

Why do you seek mortal forms, doomed to perish?  
Our features have pleased the heavenly one;  
this love will live on earth,  
it will live among the stars on high.

And let no one wonder that the blessed virgin  
despised all the memorials of death,  
for she always loved the Lord of life  
with enduring devotion.

At your altars, Agnes, we ask  
that this love may burn in our inward parts,  
restraining with holy breath  
the goads of tender youth.

Burn the wanton marrow of human beings,  
so that the spirit, safe, may flee sweet storms,  
and, having subdued the flesh, may triumph  
as victor.

Let the devout vows of virgins praise the King,  
whom every kind of sacred praise befits,  
whose one Godhead we venerate  
in a threefold divine being.”

### XXXI. Sermon to the clergy in praise of the martyr Vincent

**[Col. 1245D]**

Until now, recounting the deeds of blessed men,  
we have clothed them in the covering of prose; but now, fathers  
and brothers, new things have pleased us more. It is not pleasing  
to preserve what has grown old; the very table demands that its food be renewed.

Therefore the reason of the food has drawn you here;  
offer not what the body loves, but a fresh taste,  
and whatever the Lord gives, we shall carry in a joyful mouth.

And so that your willingness may be more fully renewed,  
let us hasten, as usual, with honor to the Mother of the Lord.  
What we should bring to her, an angel taught us long ago.  
After we received help from heaven, from that source  
hearts are strengthened and the speaker’s tongue grows vigorous,  
as you know, reverend company, brothers and fathers.

All life passing through this decline is engaged in warfare.  
Therefore it is worthwhile to overcome enemies, since the ardor  
of the mind acts more fittingly when a crown is promised—  
how great is it to ascend the realms of the lofty heavens!

For here life is freed from deadly fear,  
and no adversities stand in the way to break salvation.  
Here the divine abyss feeds the thirsty soul;  
here abundance overflows with lavish gifts.

Here the one who has stood firm is raised to supreme honor;  
here glory, which never ceases, surrounds the worthy.  
No murmuring, no rumor breaks the bonds there.

If the mind can weigh anything, or if the speaker’s tongue  
can say anything, or if the eyes can see anything,  
would you now compare it with these things? Would you dare  
to speak of such matters? Would you attempt to touch  
the joys of merit?

Whoever desires these things, let him become victorious  
in vigorous combat. A garland and the sweetness of manna  
will be given to the victor.

**[Col. 1246B]**

Do you seek friendship? First conquer raging enemies.  
For we know that three enemies have been set against us.  
These three attack our breasts with death-dealing weapons,  
and do not cease to weary a man unless he casts down his neck beneath them  
and, with his strength broken, gives his defeated hands.

Oh, how many the wicked assailant of the flesh, lurking unseen,  
has thrown down; how many the world has dragged to the depths;  
how many the voracious robber of darkness has thrust below!

These dragged our first fathers to their first deaths.  
Their offspring was first struck down by an abominable wound,  
by which the defeated Sodomite perished, cast into the ruin  
of sulphur. By their blow the blessed psalmist fell,  
and the radiant offspring; already a great multitude falls—  
for who leaves the world without a wound?

O exceedingly happy is the one who has driven back so many blows!  
Let praises and titles mark him; let a golden crown  
mark such a man, if one like him is present among us.

Yet let him forgive the excellent man if he is not equal in honor;  
nevertheless, let this song be sweet in his ear,  
if it is modest, and if he wishes heavy things to be raised  
to the heights.

You have heard, reverend phalanx, whom the holy Mother adorns with praise,  
singing hymns, psalms, and responses.  
It is also lawful for us to describe him in our verses.

He is the victor born in the western region;  
he came forth, and the name Vincentius belongs to him.  
Hence radiant beauty encircled the young man; within him was a higher  
splendor, by which he was powerful to behold the highest and the lowest;  
the ranks of virtues made him more illustrious.

He subjected his limbs to the service of God, not of the world.  
When he saw so many hearts defeated on the field,  
and leaders fleeing in fear, and voluntarily yielding to enemies,  
their arms immediately thrown down by themselves,  
he groaned and bore deep grief in his heart.

He wished to avenge himself and was ashamed to endure  
the enemies’ triumph. Yet, when he rashly attempted  
to oppose them unarmed, he hastened to ask for weapons  
and prepared for war with threatening gesture.

The sisters standing on either side rejoiced.  
They did not permit an external soldier to encircle his limbs,  
but wished to gird him with their own hands.

“Behold,” said the first sister, “the shield,”  
her serene face darkened by a veil.  
She is called by the name of Faith.  
This will help you, so that hostile things may not harm you.

The second, who would provide a helmet for his head, brings it—  
she who hopes in the hidden things of God  
and in lofty salvation.

The third gives a breastplate able to encircle the whole body,  
which many fasten with a succession of rings:  
this is the love of the mind, which joins innumerable things.

The fourth gave a firm cuirass, clothed in the beauty of righteousness,  
and brought a sword suitable for the thigh.

The chaste virgin, carrying what was akin to her own modesty,  
gave woven coverings: the weapon was threefold prudence.  
Sacred law fortified the fighter with a strong bow,  
from which he could pierce enemies with powerful arrows.

The double greave which the humble virgin brought  
was fitted to his legs, and she gave spurs  
to both feet.

**[Col. 1247B]**

On one side love, on the other fear, keeps the horse subdued by reins;  
sobriety trained the horse. Patience brought the saddle.

At last, gleaming in a golden covering which the king had bestowed,  
he sought his hostile enemies; and, conquering, he went forth  
to conquer. There the proud battle lines stood,  
and he himself stood shining in heavenly armor.

First, beside the battle line, came the flesh.  
It threatens no wounds and displays no grim faces in the ranks,  
but deceptively imitates the appearance of gentle love.

Giving kisses entangled with deadly poison,  
smiling, it prepares weeping; singing, it prepares sorrow.  
It brings beautiful things before the eyes, and to ears that prey upon the soul;  
it attempts to strike the sluggish soul with sweet-sounding melodies.

Then, returning the soul, it caresses the nostrils  
with manifold fragrance and draws the taste  
with varied art of flavors. In food it renews  
the ferment, enticing the touch with softness;  
and then, by sin, it confounds the wretched mind.

O you who have conquered such great enemies, how happy you are!

When the young man perceived this one secretly setting up war,  
he could not bear to mix his noble arms with it;  
and, disdaining the fighter’s allurements, he rejected them as wicked.

Thus, fleeing, he conquered—for thus it is honorable to flee.  
He drives the horse with his heels and puts on rigid reins.

The world appears against him and draws up a threefold army.  
The burden of errors leads the way: dreadful tyranny,  
having imagined that God was a god who sculpted fictile images,  
had scattered deadly darts from its deceitful mouth.  
He opposed blows with a shield and conquered the proud one.

Behold, another army is set before the fighter to be conquered:  
vain love—love by which a beautiful house is loved,  
or a wife, by which sweet offspring is loved,  
by which beautiful gold is sought.  
The soldier overcame these through heavenly love.

Meanwhile the fear of the age, arriving to strike  
his robust mind, attempted to attack the strong man in his helmet.  
He repelled the assault, while no hostile force of evils  
could overthrow the mind of the blessed soldier.

“Give the command,” he said, “illustrious Father;  
I shall oppose words to the tyrant.”

He gladly commands. “What words, unhappy tyrant,  
what words do you utter? Why do you order our sacred things  
to be denied? Do you think that I—I—fear your face?  
Do you think that threatening terrors strike my mind?

I shall torture you more if you torture me;  
and punishment itself, taking vengeance, will punish you.  
You will be struck by the blow which the bow draws.”

Thus the soldier had overcome the hostile enemy.

**[Col. 1248A]**

Then, from afar, he orders the dishonorable armed troops,  
arrayed for war, to stand—those once hurled down  
from the summit of heaven. Their former intrigues  
sought to prepare deceptions.

The Christ-bearing athlete, mocking the drawn weapon,  
guarded against its wounds. The scattered ranks could not  
endure the fury of Mars; everything fled into the shadows,  
and the troop feared the fighter’s appearance and weapon.

Then a savage troop of bloodstained executioners  
is set against him; this race follows the tyrant’s standards.  
With varied skill in tortures, they are assigned  
to rage against the holy young man.

One man wishes to oppose them all; leaning upon his saddle,  
he drives his swift four-footed beast forward,  
pressing it with twin spurs, and unmoved  
urges his enemies toward the wounds.

The crowd strikes the fighter, and by striking  
is itself struck more severely.

**[Col. 1248B]**

For he was able to endure more powerful evils  
than the hand could inflict, set on fire by love of Christ;  
and the one whom they think they conquer, raised to heaven, conquers them.

The Prince, surrounded on every side by lofty companies,  
meets him—the Prince who once had supported the fighter with arms,  
who gave him splendor in battle and brought help with his hands,  
concluding the palm of victory with an eternal gift.

Let this mirror draw us onward; let this manly nobility  
of spirit instruct us. He was seen to endure immense labor;  
a still greater rest follows him, while they think  
that life is being taken from him—a life which no end  
can ever close.

While the fighter casts off his small dwelling,  
the lofty palace of the heavenly home is given to him,  
because he endured wounds from the combs, whips,  
and fire, or from the prison’s cavern;  
as victor, he receives surpassing gifts from on high.

Reproach has passed away, punishment is completed,  
and labor is finished; but the palm, destined never to fall,  
now rejoices in heaven.

Beloved phalanx of this man, if we lean upon powerful arms,  
if we delight in pursuing his deeds, if we are pleased  
to overcome hostile hands in battle with equal stride,  
he who gave the fighter the palm will also help our hearts,  
granting beauty from the enemy when he has been overthrown.

May the victor from on high obtain this for us  
by his poured-out prayer.

### XXXII. Here begins an exhortatory ode to the soldiers of Christ

Why do you stand? Why, fighter, cling to idleness?  
Let the fervor of war move you.

But if frivolous courage should draw you back,  
behold, the right hand of Christ gives help,  
carrying the weak upon its shoulders.

Pay attention to the form of the commander which you take.  
The life of the righteous will be your model.  
A golden crown will be given to the brave.

Let prudence protect you in front,  
and let righteousness cleanse what follows.  
And so that you may not grow proud, despise prosperity.

Hold the left firmly with strength.  
Receive the commands of the highest Master.  
They preserve the fragile, if you preserve them well.

By sacred speech the enemy is struck down.  
Take this sword for yourself, a safe one,  
and the cross will not permit you to be subdued by the enemy.  
Whoever stands by this does not fear him.

**[Col. 1249A]**

The soldier is covered, and, pouring forth his vows,  
Moses protects the people by praying.

Receive the shield of faith fervently;  
as victor, you will be able to ward off blows.

Let hope provide the helmet which covers the head.  
Take the cuirass covering the limbs,  
which the right hand of righteousness holds out.

It also helps greatly to gird the loins,  
and to place the ankles beneath the boots of peace.  
The lurking enemy will fall by these weapons.

### XXXIII. Also, a metrical prayer, or confession

Christ, who washes away the ancient sins of the world  
with your own blood, make my words worthy prayers to you.

Only you yourself, who are powerful, can teach me  
by what means I may obtain this. For I deny  
that anything good is given unless you give it.

In the beginning, no good can arise from evil,  
because in the beginning good things were generated by you, the Good.

Therefore whatever my tongue can say of good,  
I shall certainly believe that you have bestowed upon me.

I shall keep my mouth open in David’s manner of speech;  
may you fill it, remembering your promise.

You are the living fountain, a fountain clearer than the sun;  
whoever drinks from it thirsts from nowhere else.

Your morning is not interrupted by any darkness of night.  
Whoever walks in this will not fall.

Give me this fountain; give me light. After this,  
I may not doubt that I shall possess what I ask.

Why should I, wretched as I am, trust so greatly in you,  
when I am held by such great crimes?

I ought to, pious King; I ought to, for you became flesh,  
a victim, and a ransom, so that mankind might be freed from destruction.

Your death was the life of all, and life was life—  
though different things prove that they are the same.

This was not the merit of mankind, but your grace accomplished it;  
that grace will always be my right of confidence.

As long as I am able to trust in you, I shall not doubt,  
because whoever is preserved by your love does what is right.

The fisherman burned with this love, and the publican with this love:  
the former suddenly rejected his nets, the latter his boat.

Hence the greatest redemption is given for the least things:  
the one is the key-bearer of heaven, the other the lawgiver of God.

He burned with your love who gladly received you as guest;  
as host and prince, he burned with your love.

**[Col. 1249D]**

She burned with your love whose equal faith  
could not be found even in Israel; she burned with your love.

She burned with your love who, often rejected,  
obtained salvation for her child; she burned with your love.

She burned with your love whose disease  
your fringe halted with blood; she burned with your love.

She burned with your love who wiped your feet  
with her hair, washing them with tears; she burned with your love.

But none of them burned except when you willed it.  
If you will this, I too shall be worthy of the gift,  
whether it be faith, or hope, or love itself.

Whatever helped them, I say, was grace.  
I say that grace gave good things to suffering mortals;  
the things truly given were given by grace.

There was no sick man after credulous Eve  
had broken the man with the apple, and the serpent had overcome him.

Man lived wretchedly after he had carried himself  
from the threshold of life into this miserable lodging of death.

That was without stain, but filthy corruption broke it.  
I think that “world” received its name from its opposite.

The world was clean when you created a clean world;  
it began to be unclean through the filth of man.

That man, that guilty one, driven by a sacred desire,  
was the first in the new world to break the laws.

He was the beginning of strife and the example of fury,  
the first to sprinkle the earth with human blood.

Yet although this blood pronounced punishment upon the world,  
it proclaimed beforehand the great work of the sacrament.

For blood dripped from the wound in his side;  
it drove away punishments and washed away every wickedness.

**[Col. 1250B]**

O pious voice of the thief, worthy of this blood,  
to whom the stream of blood opened a way to life!

For, sprinkled with this powerful liquid,  
he first set foot upon the heavenly sphere.

To the rulers he said: “Lift up your gates,  
and let the heavenly realms open to their Lord.”

Whence comes this new kind of thing, and such glory of triumph—  
that the cross should serve both for punishment  
and for salvation?

Why does unexpected love for the just leader, on account of a crime,  
dare to utter such a thing in God’s presence: “Remember me”?

Is this not, O God, a change wrought by your right hand?  
By this word the former thief becomes your standard-bearer.

Thus, too, sins resembling the red worm  
will become white, like the color of snowy wool.

For if these were counted with the grains of sand,  
I think that, when you show mercy, they would suddenly be erased.

Thus the one who carries the lost sheep on his shoulders  
to the rest of the hundred taught us to believe.

Thus the harlot taught us to believe; she departed cleansed,  
though Mary had been full of every vice.

Thus he taught us to believe who washed away sins with tears,  
especially when Peter denied him.

I would ask that your mercy consider me worthy of so much,  
but the sand of the sea yields to my sins.

Nevertheless, in this manner I shall ask as David himself did;  
I know that you, a just Judge, will give equal justice to equals.

O my good Jesus, how great a madness it seems  
to grant that I should be equal to David!

But what shall I do, when throughout the whole world  
nothing exists that could be equal to my crime?

Every day I sin; at every moment I go astray,  
and, like a dog, I often lick up my own vomit.

I pass over every created thing in deadly vices.  
There is no hope in my plans of anyone who might provide for me.

What shall I do, what shall I do, to whom shall I turn,  
O best Father?

Behold, that final, dreadful day is approaching.  
What shall I do, what shall I do, when there is no one to set me free,  
while no guilty person can deny his deeds?

What shall I do, what shall I do, when the wrath of so great a Judge  
condemns all the guilty to everlasting fire?

You tell me what I should do; you, the only Counselor,  
advise me, for you are wholly the way of forgiveness.

You tell me what I should do; you who created all things  
tell me, for you could have made none of them exist.

You tell me what I should do; you who possess the waters of the river,  
the stars, the earth, and the sea in which they may be washed.

Idle boy, how much wicked pleasure has stolen time from you,  
since from your earliest age, all the way to old age,  
you indulged with impunity in such delights,  
when salvation was near and weakness itself  
was the only medicine prepared for your ruins,  
which could be used without labor.

Now strength itself is needed. These are no longer merely ulcers  
to be entrusted to soft ointments, nor suitable for a swelling.  
A sponge will provide help for a powerful disease.

It is useful for you to indulge in such bitter things  
and to restrain pleasure. The flesh has led you  
to guilt with the greatest delight until now;  
let suffering not lead you back to it.

**[Col. 1251B]**

Act steadfastly according to your strength; watch continually,  
labor by night and by day; destroy every crime with your hand.

Give drink to the thirsty, coverings to the naked,  
and food also to the hungry.

Wash yourself with tears, cleanse yourself with weeping;  
empty your mind of every vice and fill it with virtues.

Let your fasts be moderate, your reading continual,  
your psalmody frequent, your prayer diligent.  
Let no burden move or release you; measure your labor  
by your promises, your work by its reward,  
and your brief struggle by eternal triumphs.

Whatever you labor at is small if you look toward the rewards—  
not as if the ascent to the shining heights were easy:  
consider how much sweat is endured by the one  
who strives to reach the highest ridges.

What do you seek, that you may go to heaven?  
Blessed life awaits you as the greatest reward.  
Only make sure that you follow the laws marked out for you.

Always remember: let no burden move or release you.  
A man who fears hardship is not considered a soldier;  
when courage is idle, it withers.

O my good Lord, my hope, my light, Christ,  
who are power in your words and healing in your commands!

Until now, guilt demanded that I, fallen, suffer punishments;  
now, together with the punishments, my guilt has been forgiven.

Yesterday illness broke my limbs with powerful pain;  
but today they are healed by the help of mercy.

Late I was dashed against the rocks and all the waves;  
in the morning a safer harbor is present for me on the shore.

I affirm with truth that all those are deceived  
who deny that forgiveness is granted to the fallen repeatedly.

Whoever denies that you grant forgiveness to the fallen  
after a thousand falls cannot receive forgiveness even once.

Whoever believes that you grant forgiveness for crimes  
after thousands of crimes will not be denied it after thousands more.

You are wholly mercy, wholly indulgence,  
wholly peace, wholly grace, wholly love.

How light a burden you give, a mild and faithful command,  
a fruitful counsel, a sweet yoke!

These things are light for the gentle,  
but always hard for the proud,  
and this labor is heavy for the ignorant.

How great is the burden of labor which you impose above me!  
May no burden of sin weigh upon me now.

I expose myself to your commands; I shall cut through the depths of the sea.  
Favor me, so that my sails do not turn backward.

Guard me so that nothing at all from the world hinders me—

**[Col. 1252A]**

the world into which man, made by your hands, rushes.

For, after more than six thousand years have passed,  
this inhuman race fights without end.

It is skilled in ambushes, deceptions, and arts of harming;  
its craft is to know how to inflict harm.

It has learned through experience all the things of antiquity,  
and carries them wherever virtue does not remain unfallen.

Did it not attack Job with curses, slaughter, and ruin,  
so that he was entirely flowing with wounds into corruption?

And unless you had then commanded that only his soul be preserved,  
it would have destroyed him inwardly, as it did everything outwardly.

Hence your lineage is natal, and hence the second great one,  
David, is shown to have fallen beneath it.

Yet when he wept, he destroyed every crime with his weeping;  
having fallen defeated, he returned victorious.

**[Col. 1252B]**

That enemy did not spare Solomon, either through his wisdom  
or through the royal honor increased by his immense wealth;  
he overthrew him completely with his customary deceptions.  
The cause of his fall was wicked passion.

O how often, under your shepherd,  
it urged captured sheep toward ruin through evil pursuits!

O how often it hurled souls, whom the lofty court awaited,  
down into Tartarus’ waters!

O, if earth, air, and sea could now become what Olympus was then,  
may hell alone possess him!

Forbid the impious Leviathan  
to hurl sulphurous stones and fiery weapons.

His most wicked limbs also attack this head;  
but crush the head, and the limbs suddenly fall.

Now abandon childish words, boy,  
and set a limit to your trifles. Your vows demand long silence;  
make yourself silent. An abundance of speech will yield no profit,  
while the loss of your affairs remains.

You possess a king’s spirit, so that enemies may not violate you.  
You suffer for a moment whatever is permitted to you;  
the right which we have over you is produced by love—  
this is desired, that excess of love for you.

For what is surprising in this? Do you think that evil men  
produce evil things, or that the wicked bring harm?

Is anything wrong with a ship if a crafty man lies in wait,  
an enemy pursues, or an adversary harms?  
Does not a son offend, a servant do wrong, a friend stumble?

Human nature bears wicked and faithless people.  
You may fear, but you must endure what you fear;  
you must fight what you fear.

**[Col. 1252D]**

This struggle summons the happy and burns the wretched.  
It attacks kings and provokes the empty crowd.

It spares no one; victory will settle this dispute  
and, at the end, calm this fury.

Do not fear, do not be afraid, do not, God forbid, despair!  
You will be able to restore salvation, often by resisting.

To repel every missile, you have the strength of faith.  
The son of light fears the harms of darkness,  
or the dangers of night, whose father is day itself,  
or threatening signs, whose leader is unconquered.

Trust me: I shall help you. Do not doubt that you are my creature,  
the work of my hands, whom I redeemed at such a price,  
with so great a payment.

Would I allow you to perish? What would descent and rising,  
hunger and thirst, provocation, weeping, and fear,  
what would blows, spittle, thorns, reed, and scourges,  
what would cross, nails, vinegar, sponge, and gall,  
spear, death, tomb, descent to the depths,  
or even the final thing, have accomplished for redemption?

While you look upon these things, do not fear:  
we have provided such weapons for you from far away. [The source has a long printed lacuna here.]

When you trust in these things, the enemy fears these signs;  
he fears them and flees them. At last he has felt  
his strength broken; here he is nerveless and weak.

But through countless falls, his callus has grown durable  
in his sinewed knee. And whenever he falls, he is nourished,  
yet cannot rise and struggles from his blood;  
he fights from his knee, but, weakened, has no strength  
with which to strike.
