This is a light but persistent quarrel;  
though the quarrel of the limbs has arisen from this quarrel,  
and though each dispute tends toward an unjust end,  
it presses on in order to scatter human minds.

Yet the reason of the divine mind is one,  
though there are two things to be conquered:  
patience breaks one, strength the other;  
after the battles, it will give a palm worthy of that victory.

This is the kingdom of heaven. The heavenly powers rejoice  
in these wars; the prophets rejoice; the patriarchs rejoice.  
The apostolic senate is glad in them.

These things are sweet to martyrs;  
virginity, too, beholds such joyful triumphs;  
blessed souls exult in these events.

These are a pleasing crown to me,  
which I myself repay to the victors according to their merits,  
so that they may strengthen their spirit continually  
for enduring everything.

Let the human race know that I have a fatherly  
and stern spirit, pleased to send its children frequently  
to their studies, granting them no leisure  
even on holidays, often shaking sweat from them,  
and sometimes tears.

He does not preserve them in the shade or cherish them in his lap;  
he makes them grieve, weep, and suffer.  
They endure great things; through rich weariness they grow weak.

Whatever movement these things have been stirred by labor,  
they fail beneath their own burden. No unharmed prosperity  
will withstand a blow.

And who among the vigorous does not judge leisure a punishment?  
Every industrious man undertakes great things,  
unless he refuses to be reconciled with greater peace.  
For one prepared to conquer, being conquered is neither praise nor glory.

The brave man asks from the one with whom he wrestles  
to exert himself against him with all his strength;  
he gladly allows himself to be struck, beaten, and harassed,  
unless an equal opponent is found.

When he is exposed to many, what patience can do  
and how powerful it is become clear.  
Consider that this must be done by good men.

Or do you perhaps fear those whom the image alone  
of good things makes conspicuous, whose minds are like those  
deceived by long dreams, whom the world has adorned  
with ivory, gold, and silver?

You look upon them as happy; but if you examine  
what lies hidden, not what meets the eye,  
you will see them wretched, foul, and base,  
dressed outwardly according to the manner of their construction.

That prosperity is not stable, but glass-like,  
a crust, and thin. While they are permitted to stand  
and appear to possess what they desire, they shine;  
when something arises to disturb them and expose them,  
the filth that had been hidden beneath their splendor  
soon appears in alien form.

Give certain gifts to the good, so that the more you turn them over  
the more they may appear outwardly in better forms;  
they do not shine outwardly, for their good things  
are always turned inward.

They do not need prosperity as a good;  
prosperity is merely the opportunity to mock the powerful  
and to prove miserable those whose heavy anger  
aims at the weak, in the mind’s treacherous pursuits,  
the deadly arrows of its quiver.

The hands of wickedness, the bow of death,  
the weapons of impiety, and the face of evil  
are the material of torment.

Those whom they harm, they delight to hate;  
they make guilty those whom they have harmed,  
and think it the highest thing to be feared by those  
whom they themselves fear.

How happy they are whenever they have lain  
at the feet of those whom, in proud arrogance,  
they often drove away from their own feet;  
how happy whenever the punishment prepared  
for those whom they envied has rebounded upon them;  
how happy whenever the one who often refused forgiveness  
himself seeks it!

The envious person whom a happier man torments  
must rightly be considered happy—so be it.

Let them be happy; tell me where those are whom you know  
to be triumphing in a lofty seat, giving laws  
to conquered peoples.

They were glass vessels; they have been shattered.  
The hail has melted. River bubbles have burst.  
The shadow has withdrawn. The smoke has passed away.  
The cloud has disappeared.

These are the things you fear; these are they.  
You do not wish to fight—withdraw.

But in a foreign region you fear living as a poor man.  
And who lives as poor a life as the one in which he is born?

Free yourself from these delights, from these possessions,  
and free yourself from the world.  
The more you flee them, the more you cling to me.

Christ God, maker of true and nourishing life;  
Christ God, creator of beauty and goodness;  
Christ God, through whom what is not returns to being,  
and what is made is believed to have come from nothing.

Christ, who do no evil at all, and cause things to be,  
so that the worst things may not come to be  
and good things may attain their end.

Christ, who are no evil,  
who prove yourself truly good to those who flee to you  
by reason.

Christ God, through whom all things exist,  
even with their left-hand portion,  
perfectly created, beautiful, and good.

Christ God, whoever can love you loves you,  
whether he knows or does not know what he loves.

**[Col. 1254D]**

Christ, merciful Father, who delight in nothing  
but the pure knowing what is true and perfect  
and finding it.

Christ, sower of truth, through whom all things are true,  
and through whom all things that have understanding understand.

Christ, merciful Father, perfect and supreme life,  
by whom everything that possesses life lives in the highest life.

Christ God, whose kingdom is the whole structure of the world,  
whom no mind can comprehend.

Christ God, from whose kingdom comes into these things  
the law which rules, and the power of righteousness.

Christ, merciful Father, from whom to turn away is to fall,  
and toward whom to turn is to rise. I proclaim you,  
Christ, merciful God: from you to depart is death,  
and to return to you is life, to remain is salvation.

Christ God, whom, unless deceived, no one abandons,  
and whom no one can seek unless first forewarned.

Christ, merciful Father, whom no one finds  
unless purified, unless cleansed, I call upon you.

Christ, merciful Father, to whom to hasten, to love,  
and to behold you is to possess what truly is.

Christ, whom true faith awakens and raises us toward,  
whom hope joins to us, and through whom we conquer every evil.

Christ, merciful Father, who in pity lead us back to yourself,  
who are the true gate, life, and way.

Christ God, who deign to honor us with your own honor,  
and who make us your co-heirs.

My peace, my praise, my hope, my possession, my light, Christ,  
I glorify, venerate, bless, and worship you.

In you alone I rejoice; in you alone I am glad;  
you alone I embrace, desire, love, seek, and follow.

Even if all the stars became tongues,  
and this were true of the sand of the sea,  
of every seed of the earth,  
of the drops of rain, the waves of the shore,  
and all that no number can count,  
they could not repay you praises according to your merits,  
for what you do for me, Christ, though I do not deserve it.

Your mercy has given me words full of mercy;  
those words are the way by which I may come to you.

While I cannot behold you, I can behold your words;  
the words of God, once seen, will give me sight of the Word.

Your words are seasoned with the new flavor of honey;  
whoever has once tasted them knows nothing but sweetness.

Your speech is infused with the new fragrance of life,  
by whose odor life returns to corpses.

**[Col. 1255C]**

No one without you could sense this flavor by experience,  
and without you no one possessed this fragrance.

You are the newness of the heart, the liquid you pour into mouths;  
and what you pour into minds is a new aroma.

In me this taste expelled what had been bitter,  
and this fragrance drove far away what had stunk.

Therefore, after your virtue has driven vices far away,  
remain here, God, in this temple, lest they return.

Remain here, God; defend it outwardly,  
guard it within, so that this whole house may be empty for you.

While I dwell on earth, make me fit for you  
as a future inhabitant of the kingdom  
and a participant in you.

And since you are first, since through the love of mercy  
you protect the human race by sharing its suffering,  
protect Gregory, the archapostolic one  
who shines at the summit of honor; you know that he loves Peter.

As seventh in number, may he always possess  
the seven gifts of your watchful Spirit.

Favor faithful kings with the people in peace,  
so that the Church may be able to remain in secure tranquility.

I beseech you: make yourself mindful of Queen Agnes,  
who gave herself and her own to the King of kings.

I speak to you of her desire, O best Father of the father;  
always attend to her desires.

With eyes upon eyes, by which you behold the whole world,  
see how great Casinum is in its devotion.

See Benedict’s dwelling: he himself brought all this splendor  
to the praise of your name.

See the dwelling which is governed under your protection;  
see the companies professing your holy law.

**[Col. 1256A]**

Bless these things, and pour over them that sacred liquid  
which the Father and your gracious Spirit possess.

See the priests, see the deacons, see the other ministers  
of the Church, and all its people.

They all gather together and, by nights and by days,  
at hours and moments, sing you without end.

They have Christ in place of hands, Christ in place of light,  
Christ in place of lips, Christ in place of the hearth of the heart.

Return exchange for exchange; repay merit with merits.  
Mutual gifts ought to be given to you in a greater measure.

The vineyard planted and adorned by your beloved hands  
produces clusters; you, Christ, gather the grapes.

Let there be no bitter or harmful foreign vine in it,  
lest an alien hand seize its fruits.

**[Col. 1256B]**

May the Father, may the Lord, preserve this vineyard  
with continual protection; may hope, love, and faith  
be its hedge.

And as the cherubim are the defenses of paradise,
On every side a flaming sword encloses it.

### XXXIV. To Gisulf, prince of Salerno

There is nothing more certain than urban nobility alone,  
which proves that deeds are fortified  
and refutes everything that frivolity reveals,  
especially, prince.

Whatever the world possesses that is good,  
all of it the goodness of the City had made;  
this the Senate resolved to preserve  
at home and in warfare  
under an enduring law.

In strength of mind and body, and in force,  
you follow the Augusti; no gravity of Cato  
surpasses you. You alone are rightly held  
to survive among the rulers of the world.

What soldier anywhere is more worthy  
to bind a leafy laurel around your temples?  
If the victor of Carthage were here,  
the consul himself would willingly yield to you.

The Tarpeian rocks, accustomed to seeing  
victorious eagles, immediately,  
when every sorrow has been driven away,  
rejoice that Caesar’s deeds  
can be renewed under your leadership.

For it is pleasing that Gallic commanders,  
their necks bound with heavy chains  
in the ancient manner, should be seen—  
provided they now see themselves  
restrained by you in renewed warfare.

[Col. 1256D] Rome recalls, when it sees you,  
the Pauluses, Fabii, Cornelii,  
Gracchi, Fabricii, and Luculli,  
and shows that in virtue and arms  
you are their worthy equal.

Your sword already hastens  
to shatter the resources of Pyrrhus,  
the ancient fortunes and madness  
of Hannibal,  
so that it may bring the world  
under its accustomed laws.

### XXXV. To Guido, brother of the prince of Salerno

Once you have recognized the reason for my strength,  
most courageous Guido, you may accept  
this modest work of song.

I do not bring you riches: it is love,  
to which you will give no gifts worthy  
of a generous hand unless you grant them.

[Col. 1257A] Fame constantly proclaims your triumphs everywhere,  
which my lyre cannot conceal.

You are shown to have drawn your lineage  
from a royal stock,  
to be the son of the great Duke Guaimarius.

Under his rule, Salerno,  
which is now impoverished,  
was richer than any other principal city of Latium.

The Lucanian, Beneventan, Calabrian, Capuan,  
and Apulian peoples had each been subdued  
by his warfare.

Its beginning was the city and palace;  
its end, too, was the city and palace  
[“lyris” as printed, sic].  
Yet this was not enough for him.

Babylon raised it up with foreign goods  
and with gold,  
as broad as the celestial sphere  
in the regions where the sun descends.

Carthage, excessively rivaling Roman prosperity,  
gave many gifts  
under a treaty of peace.

The kings of the Germans were often presented  
[Col. 1257B] with splendid gifts,  
measured by their weight and value.

At that time it flourished so greatly  
in the medical art  
that no illness could find a place there.

But after the father of the homeland—and your own father—  
was pierced by swords before the eyes  
of his relatives,

whatever glory this life had possessed before  
perished in a moment;  
it became smoke and shadow.

For just as a single plague among cattle  
is accustomed to weaken an entire herd  
in every way through corrupted air,

so the numerous race of the Gauls,  
by a great slaughter at Salerno,  
when its prince had died,  
struck the whole land.

Perhaps this did not happen without divine providence:  
so that it might itself become stronger  
through your own strength.

Finally, when your noble youth  
had twice nine times seen the sun  
turn through its cycles and return,

[Col. 1257C] you rushed wholly into arms,  
and nothing delighted you  
except rewards appropriate to war  
and the places of military service:

impetus, anger, fury, toil, impatience, virtue—  
and whatever else remains near  
to these passions.

The spear, flashing helmet, shield, cuirass,  
quiver, horse, bow, and sword  
are your wealth.

Who now, as Philyrides once instructed Achilles,  
bestows upon you instruments of luxury?

So great a man struck an empty lyre,  
which Hector himself would one day  
experience by his hand.

No contrary desire was powerful enough  
to keep you from the path  
once you had begun it.

To preserve the public laws  
through continual labor  
is preferable to living  
or enjoying reason.

[Col. 1257D] This conviction remains in your mind;  
and although it may sometimes be useful,  
you prefer not to devote yourself  
to private pursuits.

Having sought every means of arms  
for their proper use,  
you move your battle line  
against the enemy’s standards.

There are harbors in the Lucanian region  
of Velia, where the pleasant valley  
of the Britians lies.

Because it had long been extremely rich  
in possessions,  
the hostile people had thoroughly  
subjected it to themselves.

Here your right hand especially showed  
what it could do;  
this was a great ruin for the harsh enemies,

whose multitude was far larger  
than your own army,  
and not every one of your men  
was a vigorous soldier.

The allies have little praise  
in so great a conflict;  
all the enduring glory belongs to you.

You alone rush like a lion  
among so many thousands,

[Col. 1258A] and suddenly destroy the guilty men  
in slaughter.

One falls here by a javelin;  
a spear’s blast deprives another of life;  
another, overwhelmed by many weapons, perishes.

Neither the protection of a shield  
nor that of a cuirass  
can guard the body  
once you have struck it with your sword.

You give no thought to laying ambushes;  
you dare everything by force,  
and no deceit pleases you.

Many perish by force;  
the surviving crowd takes flight,  
and all the goods they leave  
belong to you as victor.

What praise did he deserve  
against whom such a host,  
until then unconquered,  
had yielded and now appeared defeated?

The burden and presumption  
of the battle you began were greater;  
but virtue, by its victory,  
drives away the burden of failure.

Now, as victor, seated in the lofty hall  
of the castle’s [“pale” as printed, sic] enclosure,  
you have the means  
by which the weariness of your homeland  
may at last be driven away.

[Col. 1258B] You have now created the hope  
that the remaining things can be conquered  
and subjected—  
although I do not believe  
that they were ever truly their own.

The land of Sicily marvels  
at the heap of Arabs  
whom your sword and spear  
themselves gave to death.

You are a terror to powerful nations,  
and a new cause of terror,  
as that greatest Macedonian boy  
once was.

Therefore see that you conquer  
whatever resists and threatens  
your citizens,  
and destroy whatever you judge harmful.

The noble practice of arms, Guido,  
will make you the equal of Caesar  
in the praise and honor of knights.

Your court had already given you  
the name “Augustus”;  
we too owe you this name,  
O knight.

How I wish you could—  
and I think you will—  
make Caesar’s world,  
the kingdoms of Constantinople,  
subject to you.

[Col. 1258C] How much gold the Caesarian age would require  
for the sceptres in your hand,  
purple for your shoulders,  
and jewels for your feet.

Swift in arms, you would take from the Parthians  
as many Greek pledges  
as they possess of shame.

Neither the pestilential weapons  
of their quivers  
nor the sharp impact  
of a swift horse’s charge  
would preserve them.

And now farewell,  
but do not abandon these undertakings.  
Let your zeal awaken  
the Greek trophies.

### XXXVI. To Gosfrit, bishop of Aversa

Gosfrit, treasure of the bishops’ joy,  
may you remain well for a very long time;  
may no evils be able to harm you.

Never has devouring envy, anger,  
or pride defiled your breast,  
which is filled with loves  
and virtue.

For charity reveals itself  
in no one more than in you,  
whose merits have freed you  
from the onset of vices.

No one has called you  
a greedy bishop,  
nor will anyone ever say:  
“You are an avaricious prelate,”  
while life remains.

Thus, tranquil in the ways of your life,  
you look upon everything around you  
as Sardian gold is bound  
by a gleaming jewel  
[“Sardina gemma,” literally “Sardian gem”].

You shine purer than Parian marble;  
you gleam more brilliantly  
than the flashing rose-colored sun.  
See how beautiful you are.

So radiant outwardly,  
you are more beautiful within;  
yet it is not lawful to say  
that in either appearance  
you are inferior to anyone.

You are the light of the Church  
over which you now preside;  
you are the clergy’s glory and protection,  
and the hope and strength  
of your people.

In devotion to studies,  
you surpass the remaining philosophers  
so greatly  
that you would not be unequal  
even to the best men of Athens.

Under your guidance,  
the instruments of music  
have been established—  
instruments able to restrain  
the swiftly moving rivers  
more than Thracian songs can do.

Send thanks, Parthenope,  
to Gaul,  
because, rejoicing in its gifts,  
you possess so great  
and so excellent a light.

May Paul, steward  
of the heavenly homeland,  
save you by his prayers,  
glory of bishops,  
and preserve you forever.

### XXXVII. To Atto, bishop of Teano

You promise many things  
that will rightly have to harm you;  
neither unrestrained laughter  
will protect you,  
nor the honor of a prelate  
will help you, Atto.

The sacred statutes of the canons  
condemn a lying prelate,  
and forbid the common people  
to approve anything  
by the law in contracts.

You willingly gave me  
six heifers selected from your herd—  
perhaps a remarkable gift,  
and at that time an unheard-of one—  
with Casino as witness.

For the first of these six,  
as though she had been set apart  
when Ninus first built  
the lofty walls of Babylon,  
experienced the Flood in the ark.

The second plainly taught you  
to speak in every language,  
and in that of birds;  
blessed would you be  
if you knew how thus to render  
your Latin words to the world.

The third had been skilled  
in the studies of the seven liberal arts  
and in almost every branch of learning;  
she represented you as Timaeus,  
Plato’s companion.

The fourth, by which you are happily refreshed,  
continually blows suitable gold  
to you from its tail;  
unless it has lifted the sky  
with its horns, you will not go.

The fifth gave birth to Pontius,  
half-clad in a hood,  
as companion in your lawsuits;  
with him you are regarded  
as wholly and endlessly deceitful.

The sixth protects you  
from black fevers.  
With joyful flowers,  
with their colors and herbs,  
this potion becomes healthful  
to your savage stomach.

If you can, prelate Atto,  
do not lie to me voluntarily.  
Honor an ally as a faithful friend should;  
soon no cause  
will harm you.

### XXXVIII. To Transmundus, a scholarly boy

[Col. 1260A] Sisters skilled in composing  
sweet song in metrical praise,  
make Transmundus worthy of it;  
as you wish to do with a high voice,  
sing of him with Phoebus’ sweet lyre.

In scarcely one month,  
by studying one art,  
he refutes the subtle heresies  
of the philosopher Aristotle  
and the arrogance  
of Plato’s eloquence.

This is not an Attic school  
that grants him victory,  
but the Zetina marsh,  
always harmful  
to those suffering from digestive,  
uterine, and splenic disorders.

He often mocks  
a ten-year course of study;  
but whenever he wishes,  
leaving this mountain behind,  
he happily hastens there  
at the season of spring,  
because he may learn so many things  
more quickly.

He is said to know homilies  
by heart, reading forty of them;  
but after so many returns  
he is entirely without  
the benefit of this work,  
as he was long ago.

He knows Virgilian verses  
so well, having learned them  
from childhood,  
as he knows the books  
that the angry Sibyl burned  
because the purchaser refused  
to buy them.

Such grammarians  
the Aternus sends forth.

Here forgetfulness, close beside  
hated love, makes philosophers inert.

Happy are those  
to whom this is unknown.

[Col. 1260C] If you believe me, Transmundus, my friend,  
finally cease to use such studies.  
Take care to learn  
what a monk professes,  
so that you may be considered  
truly wise.

### XXXIX. To Guillelmus, a monk and grammarian

Often, Guillelmus,  
I remember you as a boy,  
overflowing with laughter  
at night after dinner,  
when you now praise too highly  
the very thing  
you used to condemn in monks.

Let no one’s desire  
be fulfilled in these matters,  
at least not for the defense  
of the law of nature,  
without the prior’s appointed word.

[Col. 1260D] Let them show, by their dark clothing,  
a bird that is denied  
the enjoyment of water  
so many times  
as a fig remains  
unripe on its tree.

You used to say  
that only the rich deserved  
to be called blessed,  
because the world, made for human use,  
provides them with everything  
without burden.

You yourself belonged  
to their number;  
the wealthy city of Aversa  
gave you, through your studies,  
a sharp mind,  
an abundant income,  
and the summit of sweet honor.

By the supreme power of your head,  
and by the company  
of so many companions,  
tell me for what reason  
you entered the profession  
that you had condemned.

No amount of consideration,  
and no dignity of honor,  
would finally have freed me  
from wretched crowds,  
unless I had been safe  
under this rule.

This world overcomes its friends  
with snares—  
the friends with whom it played  
under a better promise—  
and in one moment strips them  
of their excellent possessions.

I think this is told  
in ancient fables;  
if you listen patiently,  
you will surely approve  
that it was done  
with fitting reason.

The vicious fox,  
worse than savage wolves,  
advises the lion to go by ship  
across the sea,  
so that the lion might become king  
even of the marine beasts.

Then the wandering multitude  
of beasts, each according  
to its assigned duty,  
enters the vessel  
and fulfills every command  
of the sailor and the captain.

When the wind blows,  
the ship goes through the deep  
with its sails raised;  
but once it has been taken  
out into the open sea,  
the growling beast  
begins to hunger greatly.

The bear falls first;  
after him it slaughters the others,  
as the constant appetite  
and gluttony  
of its belly demanded each day.

[Col. 1261C] Now the fox alone,  
together with the lion,  
scorns the thought of fighting  
and accuses himself greatly  
of having delayed  
the undertaking and counsel  
of his agreement.

Then, near the shore,  
where a thousand deer  
whose lot it was to steer  
the vessel had almost been killed,  
he swears,  
with wavering deceit,  
that he sees them.

The savage lion orders her  
to descend and to drive them  
at the fastest pace  
of which she is capable.  
The fox, facing death,  
obeys willingly.

But when he reached  
an overhanging rock,  
he said: “I do not wish  
to be the companion  
of a sailor  
whose meals are savage beasts.”

[Col. 1261D] Thus the world destroys  
its own followers,  
whose gifts must altogether  
be feared.

They dedicate to poverty,  
in the place of a king,  
those whom it clothes in purple.

Now, if I wish,  
empty-handed before the robber,  
I can sing safely  
through the inhospitable woods;  
no dark wheel of this world  
will roll me back.

I do not lack purses  
filled with coins,  
nor honor,  
nor the banquets of kings,  
provided that Ceres  
and a full wine-jar  
are given to me together.

### XL. To Hildebrand, archdeacon

[Col. 1262A] We have thought—and still think—  
that your knowledge lies hidden here:  
how great a glory has often been bestowed  
on those who protect the public interest.

The same path is reported  
by sacred and Latin tradition;  
and the exceptional summit  
of the Capitol teaches  
that it is a throne  
powerful with imperial authority.

But why are you troubled or ashamed  
by that arduous labor  
or by envious deceit?

For it harms good men  
more than sudden pestilence.

The hidden poison of envy  
places its illness  
in miserable circumstances  
and brings death and danger  
to these and no others.

But it is fitting for you  
to be envied, not to envy,  
through the expertise  
that makes a good and virtuous man  
uniquely master of his own merit.

Every right favors  
your judgment;  
without it, no one can give me  
either the nourishment of approval  
for my purpose  
or a reward.

The exceptional strength of your heart,  
and the best works  
that have followed your noble life,  
certainly prove  
the genius of your law—  
the law whose arts  
you now employ.

By these arts Rome, head of cities,  
is made more just, and nearly  
the whole world fears them.  
Break the strength and assaults  
of savage barbarism—[the phrase concerning  
“illustrious lineages” is textually uncertain]—  
with these arts and with the fiery sword  
of Peter, chief apostle,  
so that it may feel its ancient yoke  
to the very end.

[Col. 1262D] What power an anathema has!  
Whatever Marius once did,  
and whatever Julius did,  
with the greatest slaughter  
of soldiers,  
you accomplish  
with a moderate word.

What more did Rome owe  
to the Scipios  
and to the other Quirites  
than to you,  
through whose efforts  
she has found the path  
to her own power?

Since they had properly  
conferred so many benefits  
upon their homeland,  
they are prevented  
from enjoying perpetual peace,  
from the light,  
and from regions superior  
to those you possess.

A glorious life,  
enduring forever,  
awaits you, endowed with merits,  
so that you may be compared  
with your fellow citizens,  
the apostles.

### XLI. Epitaph for Stephen, cardinal

Stephen, what sort of priest  
and how great a one you were  
in Peter’s church,  
Gaul and Latium know.

This land produced you, nourished you, and feared you;  
that same land loved you, cherished you,  
and advanced you.

By the judgment of the canons  
you knew how to terrify the guilty,  
and without law  
to raise the accused  
by means of the laws.

Nobility, gravity, probity,  
sharpness of mind,  
and great strength of spirit  
were yours.

For five [lacuna] were to remain  
when the sun ought to—  
you are enclosed  
in this urn.  
May Christ grant you rest. Amen.

### XLII. Epitaph for Atto, bishop of Teano

Casino, you entombed  
the limbs of Bishop Atto;  
Marsia had previously rendered him due rites  
[the final relation to “yours” is syntactically uncertain].

The house from which  
his ancestry sprang  
shows that his line  
was derived from the Gallic kings.

Born of Marsian princes  
from the stock of the Quirites,  
he received from Thetis the honour of a seat  
in the morning [text uncertain].

For the Virgin, Mother of works,  
appointed this man to you,  
so that he might display  
the rights and labour  
of her Church.

He was the one kind of friend  
who knew how to have  
more useful companions  
than either Marsia or Thetis.

Seven days before the sun  
was in Pisces,  
he was thirty-eight years old.

### XLIII. Epitaph for Leo, a most noble Roman, written by Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno

Here lies Leo,  
a man faithful in all things,  
at the time when  
the Apostolic See flourished.

Born in Rome, rich in possessions,  
upright, and ennobled  
by a mother’s blood  
of very high lineage, he was.

Prudent and wise,  
known and celebrated  
under almost every sky,  
he always remained in the City.

The Virgin had been with the sun  
for three times six days  
when he ended the span of his life.

[Col. 1263D] The poems that follow  
were published most recently  
by D. Ozanam in the work cited above.

### XLIV. To Romualdus, advocate

Sweet orator, vehement and grave,  
among all advocates  
your practice has granted you, Romualdus,  
an everlasting glory in the law.

Through the strength of your own wealth  
or your father’s money,  
and through studies  
that labor at golden morals,  
you emerged distinguished  
and near to the world.

No stain of crime  
could ever mark you;  
now you firmly follow everywhere  
the path of a prudent man,  
now that of a wise man.

Among all citizens  
during this span of time,  
no one, in the serenity of fortune,  
has prevailed  
to smile so happily  
as you recently have.

How exceedingly rich you were  
in money and houses,  
in land;  
how renowned for uprightness;  
what an excellent wife  
and children you had—  
Salerno knows well.

And when you shone happily,  
like a star in the world,  
you despised the world  
lying in its rose-colored bloom,  
and at the same time  
the advantages of its possessions.

Although this may seem bitter  
to the people,  
you nevertheless did rightly,  
with my judgment approving,  
because you were going to enjoy  
a better life.

What one is pleased to call life here  
is more truly death:  
great bodily pains  
and cares of the soul  
destroy us here.

I do not wish to move you  
from your undertaking  
or from the movement of a penitent heart;  
it is sufficiently clear to you  
that despising the world  
will be beneficial.

### XLV. Epitaph for John of Salerno, a most noble man

How pitiable was the crime  
of the forbidden wood  
is sufficiently clear  
from the single fact  
that every human being perishes.

Simplicity protects the child;  
no force protects the young man;  
nor can a doctrine of intelligence  
help the old man.

He had fulfilled these stages;  
as a young man,  
he was perhaps buried here,  
but none of this availed  
when savage death seized him.

Immense is the grief  
of those for whom Salerno  
is now known:  
they mourn from afar  
the lifeless man;  
he had been the flower  
of his homeland.

When the third light  
gave itself to the lands  
of the bow-bearing one,  
he went free of guilt  
to his homeland of peace.

I commend John’s soul  
to all these saints;  
I beg that they receive him  
with themselves  
before God.

### XLVI. Verses on Saint Sabina the martyr: antiphons and responsories

#### Invitation

Sing for joy to the heavenly King,  
you peoples redeemed;  
the devout festivals  
of the outstanding martyr Sabina  
are approaching.

#### At night

Grace has been poured upon your lips;  
therefore the same God  
has always blessed you.

a

The Lord sanctified her,  
the one who created her;  
the true river’s current  
makes her glad.

a

The King chose you,  
the only offspring  
of the highest Father;  
in the likeness of Jacob  
God became your heir.

a

Rejoice, Mount Zion;  
rejoice together, daughter of Judah;  
by Christ’s judgment  
you, a martyr,  
went above the heavens.

a

Let your people rejoice in you,  
greatest King of kings;  
to you they have turned,  
and you return  
the gifts of peace.

a

Gate of Zion, beloved by God  
above Jacob’s courts,  
the Creator’s voice  
confers upon you  
the praise of love.

a

The confession of his martyr  
remains before God,  
and a bright beauty  
that no stain marks.

a

Today light has shone  
for the just and upright in heart;  
in it, Sabina,  
rejoice over  
your highest triumphs.

a

Sing wisely with voices  
and psalms, you saints,  
whom the Lord makes  
companions in life  
with Sabina.

a

The King, girded with strength,  
had clothed you in beauty;  
clothe us in the wings  
of righteousness,  
greatest martyr.

a

Sabina now rightly rejoices  
to God with a joyful heart;  
she has deserved  
to enter into his presence  
in this way.

a

Blessed Sabina keeps vigil  
before God, happy in the light;  
in him her holy mind  
had thirsted  
so exceedingly.

a

As much as the furnaces  
gave fire to the three boys,  
so many torments  
did the wretched tyrants  
give you.

a

Glory, life, and honor  
belong to all his saints,  
with whom you have always  
received an everlasting life.

**R\ br.**

Behold, added to garlands  
of roses, lilies adorn  
your illustrious head;  
you have no fear.

Ravished away  
by a hostile hand,  
look upon us, we pray,  
and make us always safe  
from our enemies.

**R\**

Precious before God’s face  
is the death of Sabina,  
who, dying to the world,  
lives above the heavens  
for Christ.

**V\**

Today is the martyr’s feast;  
rejoice, faithful ones.

**R\**

With a steadfast mind  
she had endured  
the tyrant’s torments,  
so that she might reach  
the homeland  
of heavenly life.

**V\**

When exceedingly rich  
in worldly possessions,  
she left everything behind.

**R\**

You receive the fullness of joy  
through a wave of blood;  
this reward has always  
been owed to martyrs.

**V\**

Joys worthy of God  
are heaped up  
by so great a trophy.

**R\**

How devout, how happy,  
how holy you appear, Sabina;  
it has been granted to you  
to dissolve  
the bond of sins.

**V\**

In every way, behold,  
we ask you:  
grant our request.

**R\**

Beautiful is your appearance:  
your hair is like the purple  
of a king;  
your eyes gleam  
like the waters  
of the fountain of Hesebon.

**V\**

Your neck shines above your arms  
like an inaccessible tower.

**R\**

Sweet friend of God,  
associated with the light of day,  
ascend, by the gift  
of the pious King,  
to the chamber of rest.

**V\**

When the hostile crowd  
comes to meet her  
in the middle of the night,

**R\**

Dissolve, by your prayers,  
the bonds of our guilt,  
lest any law of the Judge  
destroy us for our offense.

**V\**

If you can obtain pardon,  
you can rightly ask  
for protection.

**R\**

We fear true judgment  
with trembling heart,  
when God judges  
all the guilty  
and the just.

**V\**

We ask you to make us yours  
and remember us  
at the end of our days.

**R\**

Give hope to our hearts,  
Creator of the world,  
and always increase faith  
through Sabina’s merits  
and prayers.

**V\**

May true love be present,  
the love commanded  
by the ancient law.

#### At vespers

a

Christ, who shines  
with splendors among the saints,  
have mercy on us, we ask,  
through Sabina’s prayers.

a

You fulfilled all  
the faithful commands of Christ;  
grant also that,  
after your struggle,  
we may be of pure heart.

a

Glory and everlasting riches  
are yours, Sabina.  
Employ with us too  
whatever power your virtue possesses.

a

He whom the boys praise  
led you, the humble one,  
to the stars;  
by the strength  
of good virtues,  
raise us, poor in morals.

a

Praise the Lord fittingly  
with the peoples and nations,  
you who desire  
to seek the gift  
of this martyr.

a

Sabina’s holy spirit  
magnifies the Lord;  
it rejoices and exults  
and will never again  
be saddened.

When Christ looked upon her,  
humble outwardly and inwardly,  
he increased and adorned her  
and placed her above  
the stars of heaven.

### SERMON OF ALPHANUS on the Gospel: “As Jesus was passing through his own city, he saw a man sitting at the customs booth, named Matthew, and said to him: ‘Follow me,’” etc.

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. X, col. 79.)

[Col. 1267A] The Gospel reading that has now sounded  
in your ears, beloved,  
like an outstanding oracle  
among the other teachings of the Lord,  
revives the sorrowing conscience of sinners;  
raises up minds that are wasting away;  
drives out the cold of cowardice  
and distrust;  
and lifts the person cast down  
to conceive the hope of pardon  
into the heights.

For who could despair  
because of the enormity  
of crimes, however monstrous,  
when he hears that blessed Matthew,  
who was intent upon the profits  
of financial gain,  
was not only suddenly called,  
but also appointed  
to obtain two distinguished offices  
of the heavenly court?

Namely, that he should ascend  
to the summit of the apostolic senate  
and, among his fellow evangelists,  
receive the dignity of privilege  
in being the first.

Neither office was bestowed  
on anyone else at all  
except Matthew alone  
[Col. 1267B] and John.

And because John is said  
to mean “grace of God,”  
Matthew is also interpreted  
as “given,”  
while each earned gifts  
of a twofold dignity.

Thus, as I have said,  
the grace of the heavenly gift  
was certainly poured out,  
so that the saying might be fulfilled:  
“Where sin abounded,  
grace abounded still more”  
(Rom. 5:20).

Because Matthew began  
the writing of evangelical truth,  
he possesses the distinction  
of leader and teacher  
among the other evangelists.

The saying applies to him  
with particular fitness:  
“He is faithful  
and worthy of all acceptance,”  
because “Christ Jesus came  
into this world to save sinners,  
of whom I am the first,  
so that in me first  
he might show all patience,  
as an example to those  
who would believe in him  
for eternal life”  
(1 Tim. 1:15).

[Col. 1267C] Hence it happened,  
as the Gospel history  
has now recounted,  
that “while he was reclining  
at table in Matthew’s house,  
many tax collectors and sinners  
came and reclined at table  
with Jesus and his disciples”  
(Matt. 9:10).

Those whom the biting conscience  
of their crimes  
could keep away  
from approaching the Redeemer  
were encouraged to approach  
by Matthew’s familiar companionship  
with the Lord.

And when they saw  
a tax collector near  
the fountain of mercy,  
already presuming  
with fortunate boldness,  
they did not hesitate  
to approach the fountain itself  
with the other sinful tax collectors.

Of this public sharing  
in the eternal fountain  
the prophet says:

“On that day there shall be  
an open fountain  
for the house of David  
and for the inhabitants  
of Jerusalem,  
for the washing  
of the sinner  
and of the menstruating woman”  
(Zech. 13:1).

The covered and hidden fountain  
is God, the only-begotten one  
of the invisible Father.

The open fountain  
is the same God incarnate,  
who is rightly called  
the open fountain  
of the house of David,  
because there is no doubt  
that our Redeemer came to us  
from David’s line.

This fountain of mercy,  
Pharisaic pride,  
you prepare to obstruct,  
while with an arrogant brow  
you strive to keep  
the thirsty and the parched  
from approaching it.

Here, through Isaiah’s mouth,  
a drink was promised to you,  
when he said:

“For I will pour water  
upon the thirsty land  
and streams upon the dry ground;  
I will pour out my spirit  
upon your seed  
and my blessing  
upon your offspring,  
and they shall spring up  
among the grass  
like willows beside  
flowing waters”  
(Isa. 44:3).

Here again it was promised  
when he said elsewhere:

“And you shall be like  
a watered garden  
and like a spring of water  
whose waters do not fail”  
(Isa. 58:11).

But you, shamelessly raised  
into the pomp  
of swollen self-exaltation,  
and coquettishly inflated  
by the singularity  
of a false righteousness,  
insolently despise  
the fountain of eternal salvation  
freely set before you,  
and disdain the life-giving streams  
of the heavenly fountain.

For you approach  
the Lord’s disciples,  
swollen and arrogant,  
pouring out the poison  
of the pestilential Pharisaic pride  
that was in your breast,  
and blowing out  
the wind of exaltation  
that you had conceived  
with a swollen mind  
through the breath  
of a mouth too swift  
and foully foaming.

“Why,” you say,  
“does your teacher eat  
with tax collectors  
and sinners?”

He plainly eats with such people  
in order to make  
the just from tax collectors,  
the holy from sinners,  
and apostles from criminals.

For he calls sinners  
so that, justifying them  
by his own power,  
he may make them innocent.

Thus, indeed, elsewhere,  
while you, Pharisee,  
arrogantly enumerate  
your good deeds  
as you stand in the temple,  
and condemn the other tax collector  
by preferring yourself to him:

he ascended  
from the abyss of his guilt,  
justified so as to obtain pardon,  
while you unhappily fell  
from the summit  
of your false righteousness  
before the eyes  
of almighty God.

Thus, in this way,  
while you presume  
on the painted brilliance  
of your empty righteousness  
and maliciously nibble  
at others,  
judging them for their offenses,

your righteousness  
is turned into sin  
through exaltation,  
while their wicked deeds  
are restored to the attainment  
of pardon  
through the grace of humility.

Hence the prophet also says:

“And the wilderness  
shall become a fruitful field,  
and the fruitful field  
shall be counted as a forest”  
(Isa. 32:15).

### LIFE AND PASSION OF SAINT CHRISTINA, VIRGIN AND MARTYR, WRITTEN BY ALPHANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF SALERNO

(Published by Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. X, col. 80.)

### Prologue

[Col. 1269A] We have decided to say something  
about the celebrated and splendid triumph  
of Christina, a most noble virgin,  
to hand down to the memory  
of posterity some account  
of her admirable deeds,  
and especially to pursue  
what she endured,  
while still in the tender flower  
of adolescence,  
as she contended for the love  
of the eternal King  
against the most stubborn persecutors  
of the Christian profession.

When these things are recounted,  
the honor of God is recognized;  
praise is offered to martyrs,  
and the souls of warriors  
are urged more diligently  
toward festive battles.

For it is entirely certain  
that in human conflicts  
the fierce spirits of soldiers,  
terrified and weakened  
by sudden fear of war  
or by some accidental crash,  
become soft,  
so that they are forced  
to flee rather than seize their arms.

But when they remember  
the ancient victories,  
glory, honor, and freedom  
of the bravest men,  
as well as their own  
most illustrious deeds,

[Col. 1269B] those who had been cowardly  
suddenly become vigorous  
and fiercer,  
and leap into the ranks  
of the most closely assembled enemies.

So, in the arena  
of divine combat,  
when those about to fight  
against the tyranny of lust  
with savage torments  
and the seductive assaults  
of demons have wavered,

they set before themselves  
the most glorious sufferings  
of the martyrs  
and everlasting crowns  
after victory,  
and strive to contend  
with the greatest hope of triumph.

Thus, after their happy struggles,  
they too attain  
the eternal joys they sought.

And when, by the merits  
of their labors,  
they are enthroned  
before the tribunal  
of the eternal chamber,  
they become companions  
of the angels  
and friends of almighty God.

Through dining halls  
radiant as dawn,  
and through most pleasant fields  
flowering with roses,  
white with lilies,  
and purple with violets,  
they walk forever  
according to the distinction  
of their allotted rank.

Everything there is suitable  
for a peaceful dwelling;  
everything is fresh  
with delightful greenery,  
and in peace  
they enjoy all that they desired.

These, then, are the rewards  
that spur the timid  
to become brave;  
these compel  
the well-equipped soldiers  
and warriors of the divine battle  
to carry victories  
in their right hands  
[“reportare” printed as an alternative to “portare”].

### Here begins the life and passion

[Col. 1269] Therefore Christina,  
a most glorious virgin,  
sprung from the patrician family  
of the Anicii,  
had already been taught,  
in the earliest years of childhood,  
the arguments of the ancient philosophers.

She had been trained  
in the art of speaking,  
had used the poems  
of poets,  
and seemed, beyond all  
her companions,  
able to dispute subtly,  
to act with civility,  
and to play in meter.

But when she had been  
more fully instructed  
in such disciplines,  
at the beginning of adolescence—  
the age in which there is  
the greatest uncertainty  
about the pursuits of life  
with which each person wishes  
to become involved—

after deliberation,  
when she saw two paths,  
one of pleasure  
and the other of virtue,  
she entered at last  
upon the one concerned  
with honor, dignity,  
and chastity,  
with ardent care.

For the girl was fortunate  
not only in the nobility  
of her family and intellect,  
but was also adorned  
with the appearance  
of the most precious beauty.

Because of this,  
many young men sought her  
in marriage.

But she shrank from them  
as though she were always  
opposed to the torches  
of marital love  
and the enticements  
of wedlock.

Her father, however,  
named Urbanus,  
unwilling to fail  
in such a laudable wish  
of his daughter,  
supposed that she desired,  
through the inspiration  
of a Vestal,  
to enjoy perpetual virginity.

He therefore urged her  
to pay, without any delay,  
the sacrifices owed  
to the immortal gods,  
together with twelve maidservants  
joined to her  
by long familiarity,  
according to the custom  
of her ancestors,  
whose benefits  
to the Roman republic  
had been very great.

Although the sight of this  
shook her  
because of her father’s command  
concerning the ceremonies  
to be performed,  
nevertheless, since he possessed  
the power to compel her  
if she resisted,  
she made a promise  
with a feigned intention,  
just as he had ordered.

There was a tower  
of astonishing height  
and astonishing construction.

Dedicated to these services,  
Christina was shut up there  
with her foster-sisters,  
who were dressed  
in the most careful garments  
and adorned  
with distinguished ornaments.

Urbanus ordered them  
to teach her magnificently  
the ritual of sacrifices  
and at the same time  
to exalt the majesty  
of the sacred divinities  
with the most carefully chosen words.

He also threatened them  
with capital punishment  
unless they obeyed  
his commands.

[Col. 1271A] In that pyramid,  
on the western side,  
stood statues  
of Jupiter and Apollo,  
both cast from the purest gold.

When the maidservants,  
remembering the Lord’s command,  
arranged to sacrifice  
at the appointed time,  
they prostrated themselves  
before the sacred couches  
and offered incense.

They urged their mistress  
to do the same;  
she refused.

They pleaded,  
and she denied them.

She declared openly  
that she was the bride of Christ  
and therefore ought never  
to submit to handmade images.

At this declaration  
her companions began to shout  
against her.

They suddenly tore apart  
the garments they were wearing  
and, rending themselves  
with their hands,  
assailed the girl  
with these cries:

“Speak, sacrilegious girl!  
In reliance on what  
are you sinking into this madness?  
From where have you spewed  
this unspeakable crime,  
which must be kept silent,  
from your polluted mouth  
to your own destruction?

What has driven you  
to such obscenity?

You lacked neither beauty,  
nor lineage,  
nor wealth.

Is this what the life’s work  
of your father Urbanus  
has come to?

Has it really been brought  
to such misery  
that the daughter whom he first  
wanted to be instructed  
in the honor of the immortal gods,  
and then in the liberal arts  
of the Senate,  
the plebs,  
and the Roman people,

should, through you above all,  
receive the disgrace  
and ruin  
of his most illustrious family?

Even if he may seem  
to have committed  
no savage crime  
in his homeland  
on any other account,  
he will nevertheless  
most deservedly be judged  
among the greatest criminals  
because he raised  
a daughter like you.

Is it for this,  
with stubborn heart,  
that you curse  
the sweetest marriages?

Do you recoil  
from the embraces  
of the most illustrious young men,  
than which nothing sweeter  
can even be imagined,  
so that you may destroy  
the marks of your virginity  
for a ruined man?

And do you shrink  
from the divinities,  
to whose greatest advantage  
you could be useful  
if you wished,  
for the punishment  
of your own destruction?

Or is it hidden from you  
that ever since  
this portent of such disaster  
crept into the city,  
the condition  
of the Roman Empire,  
assailed by the battles  
of foreign peoples,  
has declined  
and been delivered  
into various calamities?

Therefore, while you can,  
show the gods  
an obedience pleasing to them,  
lest, if you provoke them  
to anger still further,  
you experience  
an untimely death  
through the movement  
of the Augustal sentence.”

When they added other insults, Christina said: “Please, to what end does this rashness of corruption lead? You rave excessively against the mistress; come to your senses in this matter, since, as you know, Minerva teaches nothing. Following the customary practice of disputants, let us proceed, taking turns and submitting to the testimony of learned authorities, so as to establish the truth of the matter.”

And they said: “If you can, you begin by proposing what you think should be done.”

But the girl, being aflame with devotion to the studies of orators, first attempted to win them over to herself by appealing to their goodwill:

“Do you remember, companions, how much destruction, in prosperity and adversity alike, is shared between both of you toward me, from whom I have never been absent either in mind or in body? I had often resolved within myself that, after the final days of my father and mother, I would regard the entire sum of the patrimony as my own, while its use and administration would remain in your hands; I would treat you as grandparents in place of my parents, and as relatives in place of my family. Moreover, I decreed that these things now before us—the necklaces, bracelets, rings wonderfully adorned with gleaming gems, purple garments embroidered with the purest gold, and everything with which royal offspring are magnificently adorned—should belong equally to me and to you. I entrusted my hope, fortune, authority, and the whole substance of my policy to your judgment, because I had long since found your loyalty to be exceedingly advantageous to me. If you deny any of this, I shall convict you by the facts, which are plainly before us.”

But her companions, as she wished to say more, attacked her with arguments of this sort:

“You will more easily wrench a key from Hercules’ hand than detach us—who, from our cradles, have devoutly offered sacred rites to the gods—from our religion and attach us to the Christian sect through your fervent studies in rhetoric, without a promised debate. If you have any hesitation about the divinity of the gods, let Jupiter be the starting point. If you prove, by the testimony of poets or philosophers, that he is not omnipotent—since then we must remain silent about the others—you will see us assent to your assertions without hesitation. But if you cannot establish this, fairness requires that you submit yourself, together with us, to the authority of our gods in the same way.”

The most wise virgin replied:

“Let it be according to your judgment. I think you hold in your hearts the matter I am about to discuss, but for the present you disdain to follow the author’s judgment step by step. For in that little book of Apuleius entitled *On the Sacred God*—which, because of its incredible abundance and sweetness of expression, we often and at length used to study—he speaks openly not only of Jupiter’s powerlessness but also of the crimes committed by him against those within his power.

“For when this Jupiter of yours, omnipotent through the glory of supreme power, ruled the kingdom of the Cretans—for so we have found it recorded there—he was violently and laboriously attacked by his son Ascribas and, unable to resist, was driven from his throne. Since he was held up to mockery by his own accomplices, he remained uncertain for a long time in his search; nevertheless, having taken auspices, he threw himself into the heavens, offered sacrifices to the gods, and asked those gods to aid him. With their support, the enemy was conquered, and thus Jupiter emerged crowned with laurel.

“Clearly, as I think, you and I can mark him more sharply as incapable of accomplishing what was impossible for him: he abandoned to the enemy, in openly demonstrated wars, the kingdom he had claimed as his own right; and the man with whom he alone was ashamed—or certainly afraid—to engage in combat, he killed with the assistance of others, whom he won over by tears.”

A little later the same Apuleius begins speaking as follows about his incestuous crimes:

“Awake, most beautiful matrons. The festivals of Father Liber are indeed entering the following month—certainly, in turn, his image passes through the countryside, the crossroads, indeed through the city . . . [lacuna] . . . Marcus Varro also makes clear to readers what he attached to this Vesta whom you worship in his *Digests*. ‘Vesta,’ he says, ‘who until recently boasted of the privilege of virginity, was defiled by Jupiter’s adultery. When an inquiry was being held into her corruption, at the prompting of her corruption she filled a sieve with water from the Tiber; and because the water did not run through, she removed the dispute about her deed.’

“O delirious mind! O man polluted by the filth of every crime! O accursed monster filled with every deformity! He yielded to violence of this sort, though not willingly; he violated the modesty of his daughter; he deceived the offspring of Agenor in the form of a bull; he committed every crime that pleased him; and he was not ashamed, through impious opinion, to usurp for himself the majesty of divinity.

“Behold what sort and what kind of god the Romans rejoiced to entrust with the protection even of the Capitoline citadel. But when the whole city, in the dead of night, was surrendered to the power of hostile peoples, that celebrated stronghold of the empire would certainly have been captured along with the same guardian, had not the vigilant geese awakened the guards of the citadel while Jupiter slept more carelessly than he should have done. It is therefore astonishing that men so shrewd could have been deceived into such worship afterward.

“But since, through the testimony of illustrious men, the argument I have set forth concerning Jupiter’s powerlessness and disgrace seems to me to have been brought to completion in every detail, if you think anything ought to be opposed to this, bring it forward as an objection to what I have said, so that you may confirm it.”

And they said:

“By the clearest judgment of reason, our little tiger is excluded from divinity, which he rashly claimed for himself. We offer no objection. We ask only that you now explain to us most lucidly what you believe concerning Christ’s divinity.”

Christina said:

“You are investigating the divinity of the omnipotent God quite properly, having shaken off the error of superstition, so that you who are blinded in mind by the dark filth of errors may shine eternally in the true light, who is Christ. Therefore prepare your minds for what you ask, and listen carefully while I speak simply.

“Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whose divinity you knowingly question me, his servant, is true God before the origin of the world, begotten from true God, through whom all things were made—not adopted, nor imaginary, but the only-begotten Son, consubstantial and coessential with the omnipotent Father.

“After many cycles of years had passed since the world was created, not under compulsion but by his own will and that of the Father, in order to free the human race entangled in the bond of original sin—which, contracted through the fault of the first parent at the devil’s instigation, had fallen from that everlasting happiness of the angels into the abyss of eternal death—he came from heaven into the womb of the Virgin. He whom the circuit of heaven and the capacity of the whole world cannot contain, the Virgin carried within a narrow womb.

“Clothed in our mortal flesh, he presented himself to the endangered world as perfect God and man. He was seen by human beings and lived among them, becoming the friend of sinners and tax collectors and the companion of poor fishermen. From these he made apostles, whom he appointed patriarchs, heralds of truth, and judges of the world.

“And so that what I proclaim to you may become better known, he adorned this man—once a fisherman content with a small hook and a little net, but now one to whose footsteps people hurry from the whole world to pray—as prince of the world and key-bearer of heaven. Through such ministers he revealed the secrets of his majesty, and by their preaching taught them to recall humanity, led astray by the allurements of demons, to the grace of its Creator.

“And so that faith might be given to their words and the power of his divinity might shine forth, he cleansed lepers, healed paralytics, gave sight to the blind, and raised the dead.

“Finally, so that this alone would not be considered too little an aid to our freedom, he willingly took upon himself the scaffold of the cross. The Lord of life dies; the glory of the world is buried; the earth is shaken; the sun is darkened; the elements do not obey the law of nature, whose Lord has been crucified.

“His flesh was enclosed in the tomb, while the power of his divinity shattered the barriers of hell. The peoples condemned to continuous death through so many ages hasten to him. The first parent of earth-born humanity appears and recognizes the sign of his beginning. With one accord they beseech their Creator and point out the origin of their transgression, to excuse themselves before him.

“Meanwhile the Lord, moved by compassion, binds the enemy of the human race with eternal chains. Taking with him those whom he wished, he returned to the body and, on the third day, as he had foretold to his disciples, rose again.

“After forty days he returned most manifestly to the heavens, from which he had come, with his body. This is most certainly confirmed by the unimpeachable authority of the holy apostles, who were condemned to a blessed death for their love of the truth. The most glorious martyrs also bear witness to it; amid racks and flames they, as victors, do not fear to proclaim the Creator of all things.

“While establishing these truths, they compel the minds of their hearers toward the heavenly kingdoms. Completely despising this life, which is only so called, they gain another life that knows no death and knows no end. To that life, without doubt, you too can go, dearest companions, if you wish.”

And they said:

“We wish it now. We all greatly admire the power of the divinity, but we are especially astonished at such and so great a form of piety. This piety appears to us indescribable and, in our judgment, incomparable with the whole structure of the world. Come, then, and without delay safely carry out for us whatever the Christian profession requires of you in order to obtain such great joy.”

Then Christina, the most prudent virgin, filled with the joy of so great a triumph, hurried with the greatest speed to the images of the idols. Striking Jupiter first with the little rod she was carrying in her hand, she said:

“Test your strength against me, if you possess any, and, if you can, avenge the injury inflicted upon you according to your accustomed custom.”

As she continued to heap such insults upon each of them in turn, she seized them all together, gathered them into one pile, and on the following night lowered herself through a window with the aid of small cords. She handed everything over to the hidden Christians, and through their hands distributed it among the poor.

When these things had been accomplished, she retraced her steps to the place from which she had come and reported in order to her companions what she had done.

Meanwhile, while these events were taking place, Urbanus arrived with a large crowd of soldiers, since he was governing the prefecture of the city. A festival was then being celebrated among them. As he approached the trunk of Apollo in order to burn incense to the one for whom he had come, he saw no image. For a long time he stood stunned in deep astonishment; then he first asked his daughter politely where they were.

Christina replied:

“For the eminence of your honor, I have always worshiped the only-begotten Son of God, and for the welfare of the whole state I have adored Christ, who is in heaven. By his prompting and through confidence in him, I judged it most harmful to attribute divine majesty to the most criminal and wretched little men and, by praying to their images, to offend the Creator of all things. I therefore resolved to smash them with my own hands and distribute whatever silver or gold they contained among the poor. This was accomplished last night.”

Urbanus could in no way accept this, since the entrance was secured and the height of the lofty tower prevented human beings from entering it. As he turned many things over in his mind and, driven by excessive grief, walked obstinately through the house, he happened by chance to lean against a window. Suddenly he saw the small cords, which provided evidence of what had happened there.

Then, inflamed with boundless anger and raging against his child more fiercely than was proper for a parent, he attacked his most gentle daughter with slaps and kicks. The soldiers standing around him suggested that he should treat her as a father and inquire through persuasive words into what had happened. They added, pretending to advise him, that it was not plausible that a woman so clever and so learned in Roman law would have wished to inflict such an injury upon her father; accordingly, under civil law, she would rightly be declared disinherited by her father’s will, and thus seemed rashly or deliberately to be harming herself by depriving herself of her hereditary property.

Blessed Christina replied:

“If the laws establish this, if this is their will and purpose, that all who heap insults upon their fathers should be deprived of their possessions, then by your own judgment you will rightly be punished, you who, separated from your Creator—who created you in his own likeness—voluntarily offer yourselves to demons.

“But I lawfully possess his inheritance, in which Christ is my co-heir, the angels my fellow citizens, the apostles my partners, the martyrs my companions, confessors my friends, and virgins my relations. There no heir will be substituted for me; no praetor will be able to deprive me of possession of my goods; no collector will dare harass me with fiscal exactions.”

Urbanus said:

“Come to your senses, reckless girl, and turn your mind away from your wicked purpose. Bring out the gods whom you hid and offer sacrifice to them; otherwise you will experience in your limbs as many kinds of punishment as you fear you have seen inflicted upon others.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“Stop searching any further for your gods, Urbanus. When you have considered whether anything praiseworthy has been done by them, how can you be so ill-disposed and forgetful of yourself as to tolerate images of demons carved in the precious brilliance of metal, rather than remove such abominable monsters with all possible speed?”

Urbanus said:

“So you destroyed the golden image of mighty Jupiter?”

Blessed Christina replied:

“I distributed the whole mass, disgraced by such pollution, into pieces, so that I might erase the senseless effigy of Jupiter, along with whatever else . . . [lacuna].”

At once Urbanus, seized by an incredible fury, said to the soldiers:

“Stretch her out upon the ground and let her be cruelly punished with clubs, so that it may be recognized how great a death she deserves who has violated the immortal gods with atrocious injury.”

By divine judgment, the twelve men chosen to carry out his commands in turn immediately found their steps driven backward. They clung to the nearby wall as though with the steps of old men, so that the tyrant might plainly recognize that the soldiers, expelled from the slaughter of the girl, had yielded through forces not their own.

Then blessed Christina, secure amid this great wonder, said:

“You recognize that your punishments are ineffective, Urbanus. You see what power your soldiers possess against me, if they believe in it. Let the gods come forward, and, since they cannot supply help to those fighting on their behalf, let them aid themselves. Let them test upon me whether they possess any divine power, because I have brought no small disgrace upon them: by refuting them in words I despised them; by despising them I mocked them; by mocking them I shattered them. I tore out their eyes, stopped their wicked mouths, cut off their fleeing feet, broke their arms, and crushed their limbs, rendering them incapable of action.”

Hearing this, Urbanus was overwhelmed by excessive grief. He bound her delicate neck with iron chains and shut her in a subterranean place in the lower part of the prison. Then he hurried home and, raging and turning many things over in his mind, revealed to his wife, who asked the cause of his sadness, the unfortunate outcome that had befallen him in this unexpected affair. In the presence of many people he disclosed that his daughter Christina had become a Christian.

Suddenly a meeting of friends took place, and matrons came running from every direction. The house resounded with various kinds of grief and was filled with the lamentations of men and women, friends, and servants.

While these things were taking place among them, most blessed Christina devoted herself for a while to prayer, asking that the Lord grant her an impenetrable shield of faith against the armies of the devil.

After she had prayed, she suddenly sprang up. Before her eyes appeared a most splendid young man surrounded by fiery radiance. He said to her:

“The Lord Jesus Christ has sent me—whose servant you have confessed yourself with all your heart to be—so that I may be for you the helmet of eternal salvation and a breastplate more impenetrable than any assault.”

As he said this, he offered her the bread he had brought with him and ordered her to eat.

After a short interval, behold, her mother—softened by womanly weakness, her hair disheveled, her clothing torn, and covered in mud and filth—came to the place of her daughter’s calamity and saw her daughter bound in iron chains. From this arose irremediable torment, incomparable mourning, unheard-of grief. The whole city gathered to witness so deadly a spectacle. The wretched old woman did not know what to do or where to turn.

She began to call for her daughter, but breath cut off her voice. She did not know what she wanted, and whatever she seemed about to do displeased her. She saw the matrons seated in a circle; she addressed each one by name, asking, begging, and imploring them, moved by maternal compassion, to return her only daughter to her.

They therefore approached blessed Christina and addressed her with persuasive words:

“Christina, the chains in which you are bound contradict the courage and intelligence we had believed you possessed. As we see, you have stained your most distinguished learning with a disgrace unworthy of your nobility. The common proverb seems appropriately to be applied to you: ‘The higher the glory after triumph, the lower the disgrace after a fall.’

“Where did you acquire such an iron heart? Did tigresses give birth to you? Did Gorgon-like parents raise you? You are found to possess outwardly only the appearance of a human being, while inwardly you bear a monstrous savagery, since you make the mother who bore you a spectacle and the cause of such great grief.

“Does it please you that she, driven to such madness, should be held up to the mockery of watching eyes? If other considerations—which are numerous—or the endearments with which she cherished you when you were little, ought to move you, then by this beautiful head and by this body adorned with every grace, we beg you to abandon this impiety and bring the mother, already in danger, the remedy of consolation.”

Blessed Christina answered them briefly:

“You have spoken at length and skillfully about the duties owed to parents, and you have accused me of impiety toward my mother, arranging what had to be said with verbal and rhetorical distinctions whose art is not unknown to me. But the divine laws decree that whoever loves father, mother, brothers, sisters, or children more than God is not worthy of God.

“Consequently, the piety toward my mother that you urge upon me makes the servant impious toward the Lord; and thus, in the judgment of those who see the truth, this kind of piety is considered impiety.”

When they could not in any way change her mind, they returned home with her mother, their sorrows multiplied.

Then, when Urbanus learned from those who had been present that his daughter would not yield, he remembered a certain Fulvius, son of a senator, whom his father ordered killed after he had been brought back from the journey on which he had conspired with Catiline. Thinking that he would make a great example in his prefecture if he acted similarly, he ordered Christina to be brought before him.

Christina was led forward, bound in iron chains, before the eyes of the spectators, who wondered what outcome such a deed would have. A great outcry rose everywhere that an innocent woman appeared to be condemned without legal examination, to the detriment of the state.

But as soon as she came into the tyrant’s presence, he addressed her as follows:

“You would act much better, Christina, if you were to consider your own safety, since nothing ought to seem more useful to you. It does not seem right to me to seek death with a reckless mind and in every way resist what is good and beneficial.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“Not everything that seems so to you must necessarily be so. Otherwise your Jupiter, whom you worship, would be a god; but I deny that he is, and I consider it honorable to die in this conviction.”

Urbanus said:

“There are two things I want you to show me: first, that Jupiter is not a god; second, that it is honorable for you to die. I ask you to teach me both most clearly.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“Anyone judged to be of sound mind understands that there is no other God except the one who made all things.”

Urbanus said:

“No living person is unaware of this.”

Blessed Christina said:

“Then Jupiter made all things, if he is a god.”

Urbanus said:

“That is perfectly clear.”

Blessed Christina said:

“If he made all things, nothing could in any way have been made without him. Yet Saturn, who begot him, could have come into being without him. Therefore Jupiter did not make all things. It is consequently established by the clearest reasoning that Jupiter is not a god.

“There is what you asked for. You must confess that it has been necessarily concluded without any contradiction on your part. As for the other matter, which you likewise asked me to demonstrate, I shall show it by the clearest reasoning, if before those present you acknowledge the things truthfully put forward which you are unable to refute.”

Urbanus said:

“One must not digress to a question raised later when the opposing party may still criticize the arguments of the first question. Therefore, adhering to the earlier arguments, I shall refute your reasoning by changing a few words and turning against you what you directed against me.

“Tell me, then: is your Crucified One, whom you proclaim to be the only-begotten Son of God, God? Did he make all things? If he made all things, nothing could have been made without him. Yet his begetter, whom he himself did not make, could have come into being without him; and thus you too are convicted by the same demonstration of not having made all things and of not being God.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“Do you understand God to be the creator or a creature?”

Urbanus replied:

“The creator.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“The creator of all creatures, or of some?”

Urbanus replied:

“Of all.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“If God is not a creature but the creator of all creatures, and if both the Father and the Son are God, then neither is the Father the creator of the Son nor the Son the creator of the Father.

“Thus, when you appear to argue that the only-begotten Son of God did not make all things because he did not make his Father, and therefore is not God, you have plainly lied, all ambiguity removed. It is therefore clear that the only-begotten Son of God the omnipotent Father is both God and creator of all things, although he did not make his Father.”

Urbanus said:

“All this is more appropriately understood of Saturn and Jupiter, whom all things that have been made obey, and by whose disposition everything has been governed from the beginning.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“You are mistaken, prefect; you err, skilled judge. You say that everything has been governed from the beginning by their disposition, although it is known that many thousands of human beings and many ages existed before them, as the poets relate and the philosophers prove.

“Learn that they were human beings, not gods—incestuous and murderous. For that reason they were thrust into Tartarus, where they await you and their other worshipers, to burn with them in everlasting fires.”

Then Urbanus, driven by the furies of impiety, ordered a wheel to be brought, the sharpest swords to be fitted upon it, and a great fire to be kindled beneath it.

When, by order of the tyrant, blessed Christina was bent beneath such cruelty, her most precious body was torn apart and burned as the wheel revolved.

Then the tyrant, insulting her together with his supporters, said:

“Be steadfast, Christina. Do not fear while suffering this for the sake of that Crucified One, who, although he could, did not wish to come down from the cross.”

Blessed Christina replied:

“Now, wretched and unhappy man, listen: the more humble are the things he suffered for me, the more I owe him. When you have completed every kind of torture against me, I shall praise the Crucified One. But as for me, far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ! (Galatians 6:14) On that cross I triumph over my enemies, and I set it against all who oppose me.”

As she continued speaking, the wheel overturned and crushed a large part of the unbelievers standing around it.

The prefect, immediately struck with immense terror, dismissed the assembly and ordered her to be consigned to prison custody.

When blessed Christina entered the darkest part of the prison, an angel of the Lord appeared to her like the midday sun and said:

“The Lord Jesus Christ has sent me—on whose account you have suffered grievously—so that I may restore health to your limbs.”

As he said this, all her wounds were so completely healed that no mark of the cuts remained upon them.

On the following night, Urbanus, believing it best to attempt once more to recall her mind to the worship of the gods through gentle conversation and flattery, had her brought before him. When he could extort no answer from her at all, he had her bound to immense weights and consigned to the waves of the sea.

But when the sailors threw her into the middle of the sea, aided by angelic assistance she was carried safely and joyfully to the shore.

Meanwhile Urbanus was seized by a demon and died.

After not much time had passed, when the most wicked Idion was chosen prefect in Urbanus’ place, blessed Christina was seized by persecutors and compelled to sacrifice to the image of the Sun.

When she refused to consent, she was brought before the most depraved judge. The prefect, raging against her, said:

“Are you Christina, who repeatedly deceives our omnipotent gods by philosophical argument?”

Blessed Christina replied:

“It is just, and in no way contrary to reason, that things deserving contempt should be mocked and that things which are vain should be considered utterly worthless. You worship not gods but demons—not inhabitants of heaven but impure human beings condemned to hell for the enormity of their crimes—in metallic images.”

Moved by these words, the prefect immediately ordered her to be beaten with clubs. Then he ordered a bronze vessel, shaped like a cradle, to be brought with great speed. At the prefect’s command, the soldiers filled it with oil, pitch, resin, and sulfur and placed it over a fire so that, once heated, these substances would melt. When, under the excessive heat, the mixture began to boil, the prefect said:

“Choose one of two things, girl: either burn incense in worship of the god, or drench your body in this most delightful dew.”

Blessed Christina made upon herself the sign of the most glorious cross and threw herself with great speed into the boiling cauldron.

Immediately the cradle split apart, and whatever had been in it flowed out through the fissures; blessed Christina, however, remained unharmed and rose up.

The prefect, instantly enraged, had her tortured naked and, after shaving her head, led her to the temple of the Sun.

In the middle of the temple stood a tribunal raised high, with silver walls; its upper sections were covered with gleaming ivory. Upon it shone a golden image of the sun, flashing rays from its radiant hair, and it seemed to move with great speed along the zodiac, retracing the course of the stars. Six signs on the right and an equal number on the left seemed alternately to set and rise, each pair standing opposite the other. There the hours, there the days, there the months, there the year revolved within their appointed intervals.

> There was a golden axis, a silver order of rays;  
> Chrysolites, strung in an unbroken order, gleamed.”

Blessed Christina was brought to this spectacle, the prefect having decreed that, if she refused to sacrifice to the sun-god, she should immediately die by the sword.
