Blessed Christina therefore at once asked for silence and, raising her hands toward the stars, prayed to the Lord in these words:

“Most unconquered King, omnipotent Father, immense God, who, shaping crude and unformed matter into the four elements, wonderfully fashioned the perfect constitution of the world in its perfect parts; and who, at the very birth of the world, cast down from the highest summit of heaven the angel of immoderate pride, who had usurped the north as his seat against your will, moved solely by the impulse of his mind: grant to me, your servant, that from this image of the Sun, in which that most wicked deceiver dwells . . . [lacuna] . . . this mechanical work, fashioned by the craftsman himself, may be shattered, so that this entire senate and people may recognize that every creature is bound by its duty to obey you, the Creator of all.”

When she had said this, behold, a fiery demon appeared. It shattered the whole mechanical and magical work and hurled the greater part of the metal upon the prefect; striking his neck, it immediately killed him.

After these things had been accomplished, the judge Julianus ordered blessed Christina to be seized and burned in a furnace of blazing fire.

The soldiers immediately carried out the wicked orders of the most wicked and cruel prince.

When the most holy virgin had been in the furnace for three hours, the tyrant, believing that she had been consumed, ordered the fire to be removed.

Then a sweet voice of singers suddenly rang out from the furnace, and amid choirs of angels the sacred face of the virgin Christina shone forth.

The matrons who had come there to watch, astonished at what they had seen, believed. But Julianus, hearing this, was moved by fierce indignation and ordered her to be brought before him. He said to her:

“We are weary, girl, of the insults you have inflicted upon us and upon our gods—many enough, and with no one resisting or avenging them. Therefore you shall suffer punishments against which magical arts will be of no avail.”

Immediately, as ordered, one of the company of magicians—at that time regarded as the most celebrated in Rome in the detestable art—brought forward two dragons and sent them against Christ’s servant so that they might devour her.

At once blessed Christina opposed to them the sign of salvation. But, by divine judgment, they turned back, seized the magician, and killed him in an instant before the face of the entire assembly.

With the censor and his whole retinue standing stupefied, blessed Christina approached the place where the dead man lay and said so that all could hear:

“In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified, rise, wretched man, so that this whole crowd may understand that he alone is the true, living God who reigns for ever and ever.”

At this command the corpse, having received back its spirit, rose before everyone’s eyes, declaring and proclaiming that there is no other God except the one whom Christina proclaims, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meanwhile the dragons returned without harming anyone to the place from which they had come.

Julianus, therefore, fearing that an uproar might arise among the people and seeking to avoid the terrors of revolt rather than satisfy reason, ordered her breasts and tongue to be cut off. Then he had her led into the hippodrome and pierced with volleys of arrows until she breathed out her spirit.

The passion of the unconquered martyr Christina was completed on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, under Julianus.

Why do you rage so senselessly, Urbanus? Why do you seethe, most depraved Idion? Why do you strive so savagely, Julianus? Devise new punishments more grievous than the former ones; multiply the blows; heap up the penalties.

But what does it profit you to rage against flesh that she willingly offered to be torn apart, and against a soul that she wished to preserve rather than destroy?

Learn at last, wretched men; learn her joy, and thus behold your own destruction.

Behold, the most beautiful virgin, after clubs and chains, after fire and the wheel, after tortures and blows, after the cradle and the shaving, after mutilations and arrows, is carried by angelic hands to the bridal chamber of the eternal King.

You, on the contrary, while making for the Elysian fields, offer a ram to Acheron; yet the Stygian marsh absorbed your boat, weighed down by the burden of your evils, and mighty Cerberus devoured it.

You will be punished with a penalty greater than can be expressed, because you disdained to believe in the Crucified One.

But you, most devoted bride of the Son of God, friend of the omnipotent Father, now possess what you desired; now you obtain what you asked; now you enjoy the indescribable joy of light. You dwell within the lofty secrets of divine majesty, where, rejoicing in closer intimacy with God, you have found the Bridegroom reclining at midday, joined to his young bride.

Now through the pleasant valleys of purple turf you pluck blooming violets, gather unfading roses, and reap stalks of spikenard. Now you sit beside the flowing waters and at the edge of the glass-clear spring, singing wedding songs in a gentle murmur.

You shine among virgin choirs, illumined by a royal diadem. You sit beside the throne of Christ, made a participant in the eternal kingdom.

Hail forever, maidenly beauty, virginal modesty, example of virtue. Hail forever, you who devoted your beautiful limbs to perpetual chastity. Hail forever, you who, knowing nothing of every form of lust, gave yourself as a temple to the Holy Spirit. Hail forever, you who fled spacious porticoes and vast stretches of estates and, receiving the inheritance of God, became Christ’s co-heir. Hail forever, you who, subjected to punishments so great, rejected the laws of your homeland and flew with all desire to the banner of the cross. Hail forever, you who, despising the commands of rulers, were condemned to a cruel death as a witness to the truth. Hail forever, you who, now exalted to the heights of heaven, are worthy of the Son of God as bridegroom and Lord.

And because you see us faithful to you in our vow of obedience, hear what we ask; consider what we desire to obtain through you. Obtain for us also the blessedness of the promised heavenly life, to which we dare not ascend without your aid, since our sins deserve this.

Therefore ask the Creator of all for forgiveness of our offenses, so that, as a merciful judge, he may forgive what has been committed against him and not inflict upon us servants many punishments worthy of our merits. While we dwell for the brief time of this fragile life, protect us, preserve us, bless us, defend us, and govern us as subjects of your authority; make our minds fit to praise you.

Behold, blessed virgin, we have narrated the deeds of your glorious triumph and briefly indicated the abundant reward of your great labor. If anything has been said less suitably than it should have been, or otherwise than was proper, kindly spare us, virgin; mercifully forgive us.

Therefore, most blessed brothers, since we celebrate with solemn festivity the triumphal day of blessed Christina, let us claim for ourselves, as far as we can, something from her virtues, so that she may show herself toward us all the more favorably as our courage strives all the more fervently to attain her.

For this reason the Lord has placed before us examples from the female sex: so that the strength of manly spirit, which we have lost through wicked living, may at least be stirred by the virtue of women, and we may recover it by walking along the straight path. Thus, joined to the labors of the blessed, may we be able to climb by Jacob’s ladder to the place where the Lord Jesus Christ dwells, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

The passion of Saint Christina ends here.

In the year of the Lord 1084. Guaiferius, Casinensis monk.

[Col. 1281]

## Historical Notice on Guaiferius

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Low Latin Authors*, III, 25.)

Benedictus, also called Gauferius, Guaiferius, or Gaviferius, a Salernitan and Cassinese monk, wrote around the year 1060, according to Peter the Deacon, *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, chapter 29, for Stephen, bishop of Troia:

- *The Life of Saint Secundinus of Aecae, or the Trojan Bishop*, and his song *Verses in Praise of the Psalter*.
- *On the Miracle of the Man Who Killed Himself and Was Restored to Life through Saint James*.
- *On the Conversion of Certain Salernitans*.
- *In Praise of Saint Martin* [Note: [Col. 1281] Not “Marbinus,” as it was erroneously printed in the distinguished Leyser’s *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 348].
- *In Praise of Saint Secundinus*.
- Hymns concerning the same.
- A homily on Advent.
- [Col. 1283] Sermons on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, Septuagesima, and Palm Sunday.
- *The Passion of Saint Lucius, Pope*.

Of these works, *The Life of Saint Secundinus* was published by Ughelli in volume I of *Italia sacra*, p. 1336. Also published there, on p. 1341, is an elegiac poem in his praise beginning:

“May the whole festive day be present at your feasts,”

and a hymn in Sapphic meter, whose opening is “Christ, King of kings, price of the devout,” on pp. 1342 and following. Henschenius published from a Cassinese manuscript *The Life of Saint Lucius I, Pope*, who died in A.D. 255, although the final portion is mutilated, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume I, March 4, pp. 304–307. John Baptist Marus had promised in 1655, in his notes to Peter the Deacon, to bring the remaining works to light, but death overtook him, and he left their publication to others.

[Note: [Col. 1283] Ughelli was the first of all to publish the account of the discovery of Saint Secundinus, not, however, his Life. Bollandus reproduced the same work on February 11, though somewhat differently, from a manuscript codex. Gattola observes that both versions differ somewhat from the Cassinese autograph, *Cassinese History*, sixth century, p. 187. He especially notes the difference in the preface. Where Bollandus’s edition gives “Holy fellow-bishop,” by which the episcopal dignity of Gauferius would be asserted, the genuine authorial codex—preserved, I believe, in the Cassinese library—reads “Holy bishop.” This, then, is how it should be read, although Gattola’s printed edition also contains the typographical error “Holy fellow-bishop”; Gattola himself makes this observation. MANSI.]

[Col. 1283]

# Poems of Gauferius, Cassinese Monk

(Partly first edited, and partly reviewed against the manuscripts, by Dom Ozanam in the book cited above, *Documents inédits*, etc., pp. 272–287.)

## I. Verses in Praise of the Psalter

[Col. 1283A]

Hold fast the words of life, which the Word, Life itself, recorded;

The royal tongue uttered them, from whose seed the King of kings

Willed to be born into the world without human seed.

Therefore, let it please you to use those things by which you lived:

He himself, who brought forth life through these words, himself received it,

And, becoming an example, taught those who were falling into the death of sins

That they could return to the life of virtues,

And, as veterans who had earned their service, be summoned to worthy rewards.

But you ought to imitate in weeping, groaning, and tears

The one with whom you wish to be equal in pardon, virtue, and triumph:

How he lamented his transgression who ate

His bread as ashes and mingled his drink with weeping!

How he groaned and clung fast, the man who had forgotten to take bread

[Col. 1283B]

Because of his groaning; and how the one who roared with groaning

From the excess of his heart poured forth streams

Of tears—he who watered his bed with another kind of spring

Through the nights, matching his sins by the accumulation of his tears!

With what longing, with what love of weeping, did he weep,

For whom tears were bread, dwelling, and delight,

For whom tears were drink both night and day!

He calls the flood “tears,” and tears “the abyss,”

Because neither flood nor abyss dissolves more than these,

Nor is any abyss deeper than the tears that penetrate

The foul abyss of the mind.

In this flood you cling more closely to the Lord:

Here God dwells, and this abyss calls to the abyss.

Clearly, it embraces every depth of compassion.

By these tears the Psalmist escaped the tears of Hell;

By these he earned pardon and deserved restoration through virtue;

[Col. 1283C]

By these he became whiter than snow, and, with purified

Inmost parts, his upright spirit was renewed.

By these God is seen; by these the gracious Spirit is possessed;

By these the saving joys of the Father are restored.

By these also the Spirit who is Father confirms him:

These are the seeds that produce the harvest of supreme joy;

[Col. 1284A]

These are the living shoots that send forth fruitful growth,

And such a planting bears health-giving clusters.

Behold instruction for one who ought to mourn his guilt;

Behold the first lesson in hope, the rule of vigilance.

You have sinned; you are guilty: with the king, mourn your guilt.

You are grievously wounded: with the Psalmist, hope for salvation.

You are righteous; therefore beware. For who was ever more righteous than this man,

Or more beloved by the Almighty because of his righteousness,

Of whose fruitful loins he swore that he would set one upon his own throne,

And did so; whom he repeatedly bears witness to have been his servant,

And to have been anointed with his own oil?

Yet so great a man fell in so great a ruin.

Nevertheless, soon afterward, by the lifting of his grief, he sat up from the place where he had fallen.

[Col. 1284B]

You, however, having heard of pardon, refuse to sin again,

Either because you would not be able to endure such great labors,

Or because the short span of fragile life would resist this,

And because before your transgression you do not possess such virtue

That you can be free from vices, stand firm in virtue,

And enjoy the blessed lot of the saints.

In his own little book he teaches these things in various places:

The plague of avarice is the source and head of vices,

Which desires partly possessions and partly honors,

And from this arise treachery, filth, sleeplessness, anxieties,

Schemes, frauds, murders, thefts, and robberies,

Along with the rest of its innumerable offspring-generating progeny:

From it come envy, contempt, wars, furies,

And things of that kind, with the rest that it creates in abundant fertility.

From one side it strips others of the spoils by which it is itself burdened;

[Col. 1284C]

From the other, it strips its own people in order to enrich others,

Whose purchased tongue loudly proclaims those laden with vices to be filled with virtue.

From one side it rages with hidden arrows, from the other with open ones;

It bears the limbs of a wolf, while on one side it assumes the appearance of a sheep.

This disgraceful and foul thing has no concern for appearing ugly;

So many vipers grow upon each of its two heads!

[Col. 1285A]

Thus it spreads its deadly poison on both sides,

So that every evil may flow from an ignoble source.

Destroy the two-headed monster, and its monstrous offspring will perish;

And in place of the double vice, a double and supreme virtue—

Abundant love toward the rapacious one—

Will succeed.

Love is the head of virtues, and this is the head of vices:

Just as every vice is enclosed in this vice,

So every virtue is held together in this virtue.

Certainly, if you speak with human and angelic tongues

But do not possess this love, you have become like sounding brass.

If you are a prophet and know all mysteries

And everything that can be known, and possess faith so complete

That you could move mountains, still without this you are nothing.

If all your possessions are distributed to the poor,

Or if your body is handed over to be burned in fire,

[Col. 1285B]

But you do not possess this virtue, it profits you nothing.

It is not impatient, not ambitious; it is kind.

It does not act wrongly; it does not seek what belongs to it.

It is not irritated, not puffed up; it meditates

Only on what is good. It rejoices with truth;

It does not rejoice in wickedness; it is not envious; it believes all things,

Endures all things, bears all things, hopes for all things.

It will never fall away; it will never be brought to nothing,

Whether prophecy should cease, or knowledge, or

Tongues should cease. It remains while hope and faith remain;

And when these have passed away, it will remain greater, without end.

Imitate it and love it; embrace this love.

Honor, possess, and hold fast this love with your whole strength,

[Col. 1285C]

Whose flame, if it surpasses every measure, number, and extent,

Burns up the mass of sins like straw;

Whose sweetness, with a certain sweetness of heavenly

Nectar, sweetens minds, and this love gives a taste

Of a certain future joy even in this world,

So that you may see those placed on earth as though they were dwelling in heaven.

In martyrs it possesses unconquerable strength;

In virgins it preserves an inviolate vow.

The claw, torture, sword, wheel, blows, and flames—

Every kind of punishment is overcome by this love.

This love fights; this love conquers; this love itself triumphs.

From it comes the laurel for martyrs and the crown for virgins;

From it every righteous person receives the ample reward of labor.

And you, whoever reads these things, filled with this love,

[Col. 1285D]

Repay with a fitting prayer the one whose work has been written for you

As though for himself; for if you remember another,

God himself will remember you. The law of this love

Grants that, by helping others through this work, you yourself may be helped.

## II. On the Miracle of the Man Who Killed Himself

Guilt plunged you into the monstrous ruin of death;

The death of Christ raised you up, human being.

Death alone redeemed you; it alone gave life, hope, and salvation.

But, forgetting such great hope of life and such great blessings of salvation,

You return to the things that dragged you down and still drag you

Under the cruel authority of the tyrant who holds you captive.

But Christ, rising from death, no longer dies,

And the most holy body whose punishment was the cause of your salvation—

[Col. 1286A]

The nails, scourges, cross, and spear will no longer afflict it.

That saving blood will not flow freely again;

Nor will Christ, your life, be enclosed a second time in the tomb;

Nor will the soul, recalled from darkness to the dwelling of light,

Descend into the depths of the abyss.

What new means, then, could there be by which you might be rescued

From so pitiable a yoke? The renewed bonds clasp more tightly;

The prison seals you in more closely, once bound;

Strength is less and greater [thus], and the second fall is more grievous.

No patience could any longer wear down the enemy,

Nor will death, once perishing through death, perish through death again.

Nevertheless, hope—hope in him. The life of the one whose life triumphs

Will triumph, and he will conquer in heaven

Who conquered in the tomb.

For once the wave of that blessed blood, poured out,

Restrained the savage dragon,

[Col. 1286B]

So that the one who had swallowed the world with his dreadful jaws

Should himself groan beneath the world and no longer possess the right

To claim anyone as his own, as before, when the ruin was rising

By which human beings rise.

He rules only over those who do not repent of their crimes

Or refuse to believe.

Therefore, once the precious robe of salvation has covered you,

Whiter than snow and brighter than Phoebus himself,

Confident in hope, when your crimes darken you,

Direct to Christ your mingled tears, accompanied by groaning.

For even now tears and groans will be sufficient

To wipe away the immense stains of sins.

Lamentation will not merely obtain pardon for the one who confesses;

It will restore the lost rewards forfeited through guilt.

Nor need faith be sought through a long and ancient history:

[Col. 1286C]

It is enough that there is an example from our own age,

A miracle manifold and wondrous in its manner, though one in number,

Adding great hope for the fallen and caution for those who stand.

A company of Gauls was traveling through the lands where Iberia shines,

Seeking, according to the custom of their nation, the apostolic body,

So that devoted love, while visiting the holy places,

Might lighten the burden of sins through the very hardship of the journey.

Among them was one extremely simple and childlike by nature,

Easy to bend in whatever direction one wished.

When the late hour compelled them to seek lodging,

The simple man alone turned aside from the group,

Moving a short distance from the road. There he found the author

Of fraud and deceit, in the likeness of a youthful body.

The crafty man begins a dreadful battle with the simple one,

At first moving no scourges or swords, but words bearing

[Col. 1286D]

The appearance of peace: “Brother,” he said, “where are you being led?”

But what did this simple man know of such things? A human face,

A calm expression, and speech friendly in its use of the name “brother”—

Things that might ensnare even well-disposed and highly proven men—

Drew his foolish mind into a wretched conversation.

He revealed where he was going. The other followed up:

“Why are you willing to endure so much labor?”

Here is the route and the advice concerning the route:

“Without danger and without delay, you can obtain what you desire.”

And, in order to ensnare the wretched man more fully, he made his face still more serene;

Caressing him with his voice, he said: “Do you recognize the person speaking?”

The simple man honestly confessed that he did not know who the young man was.

Then the other said: “I am that apostle

[Col. 1287A]

Whom you are seeking.” The wretched man believed him and at once,

Prostrate on the ground, begged for help and relief from his sins.

Soon the author of death burst forth with his deadly plan,

But first he secured the man’s belief in what he was about to advise him to do.

Then he said: “Unless you yourself release your limbs from the structure of your soul,

You cannot hope for the salvation you desire.

Do you wish to live a life that will last forever?

Take away from yourself this fleeting life.”

He shuddered at so great a crime in his brutish heart,

And dared to say that this was contrary to faith . . .

But, persuaded by the wicked counsels, he yielded.

He therefore asked for the manner in which the crime could be carried out.

They should return to the lodging; after dinner, when conversation

Had closed the anxious heart and all his companions were immersed in sleep,

He was to pierce the deepest part of his throat with a sword,

[Col. 1287B]

And, after the wound, to transfix the middle of his belly

With the same sword. The wicked man advised what he desired.

The simple man went and dined; and as soon as his companions,

Weighed down by sleep, had fallen asleep together, he plunged the weapon into his throat,

Cut through his veins, and severed the tendons along with his throat.

Without delay he pierced his chest; but the pain itself

Compelled the wretched man to cry out against both crime and death:

“Woe is me! I am lost; my own right hand has committed this crime.”

And he fell lifeless. Soon a crowd of savage spirits seized his soul,

And, driving, snatching, and dragging it through the highest valleys

And through the lowest, they carried it along.

Suddenly the enemy who had persuaded him to commit the crime appeared

And declared that the soul was his property and that he was the cause of the crime.

He is beaten; he pursues; alone he presses harder than all the others.

Thus they journey toward places near the Roman walls.

Here a voice sounds: “Leave him.” The foolish spirits withdrew for a little while.

But when the voice fell silent, they seized the soul again and hemmed it in.

The same voice thundered nearer, now more terrifying:

All the enemies fled in sudden terror,

And they no longer shook the soul, released by the holy voice.

Behold, in true form, a most beautiful young man stood there.

The spirit, as though foreknowing it, recognized the form

Of the apostolic countenance. He followed him,

And they came over the lofty roofs of the reigning Prince of the Church.

In heaven the Mother appeared to stand, surrounded by choirs of virgins.

James approached as an intercessor for so great a stain.

He heard from the pious mouth that, unless the soul should return

To its fleshly prison and, with the flesh, pay the guilt committed with the flesh,

[Col. 1287D]

The soul, condemned for so great a crime, could not be released.

Therefore, returning suddenly, now free, on its swift course,

It entered the bedchamber to which it was led by the apostle.

The corpse yawned, rose, spoke, and walked.

The event itself gave proof to his companions, for they saw alive

The man whom they had seen die. But the sole witness was a scar,

Visible in each of the two wounds, so clearly

That no one could doubt that such a man had returned to life

Through restoration.

Nearby, it is said, were the sacred places of the monastery of Cluny,

Over which Father Hugh, a man of no small merit, presided.

The man sought this monastery and begged Hugh to give him the habit,

Confessing everything that had happened to him.

But the discerning father, investigating the man’s actions and character

And his skill and practice, found that he was content

With the cobbler’s craft by which he had supported himself and his mother,

Whom Hugh ordered him not to abandon.

Thus he returned to his mother, now himself a reason for caution

And an example of hope to those who have fallen into any crime.

## III. On the Conversion of Certain Salernitans

A sufficiently great and unprecedented event is reported to have occurred at Salerno,

Full of holy tears and celebrated with praises.

An affluent, eminent, learned, and powerful household

All at once put on the arms of the sacred robe.

There were the husband and wife, and their seven beloved children:

Five males, the others female.

What man, good sir, has fulfilled the Lord’s commands better than you?

Or who in these times has fulfilled them in this way?

The Almighty commands that one leave wife, offspring, mother, and father,

[Col. 1288B]

And whatever one possesses for oneself.

You, leaving all these things at once, carry everything with you to Christ.

Therefore you do more than the Gospel commands.

What woman now offers so sweet a gift to God—

A great-hearted wife, now herself the husband’s sister?

Few are found who give what is theirs; scarcely anyone gives himself.

But you give what is yours, your own people, and yourself to the Lord.

What made you submit so completely to your parents’ command,

Eminent offspring, hope and honor of your homeland?

You were not yet of that age which, wearied by the labor of the world,

Would compel you to do this, hope and honor of your homeland.

You do not know that law by which offspring is said to be subject

To the father’s will, hope and honor of your homeland.

If you had wished to resist this command,

By their laws your father and your homeland would have claimed you for themselves.

[Col. 1288C]

Yet your father and mother would certainly have had less glory,

Nor would complete joy have been yours apart from them.

Law and custom grant that the son is his father’s heir:

You, glorious offspring, have your father as your heir.

The parents have received their return willingly and swiftly;

Indeed, they receive much more than they have given.

The portion of possessions that is given is received with complete certainty;

For unless it had been received, it would now have been less alienated.

Behold the lords of possessions, the seven sweetest children:

Both parents give them, together with their possessions, as though they were possessions.

Therefore he who goes to be sacrificed when his father himself calls him

Did not once offer more to his parent than you have offered.

The Father’s love, Christ, has sacrificed you also at the altar,

While, killing you to the world, he himself gave you to God.

O holy company—father, mother, and blessed offspring—

These things are holy, good, and fittingly done.

But you may rejoice, because rewards will be repaid,

Rewards which no sense and no mind can comprehend.

Estates, farm, field, and household goods have all been abandoned,

And the sweet affection of friendship has been rejected.

But heaven will be given, and paradise itself will be given,

And Christ; and the heavenly company will be your friend.

How happy and joyful you will then be, parents,

When your offspring shines above the stars with you!

And how happy the holy company will appear,

When both parents feed you among the sheep!

How great a band of rulers will envy your triumphs,

Grieving that it did not strive for your triumph alone,

When, after the delights of the world and its love, there follow

[Col. 1289A]

Perpetual and abundant hunger and the Stygian abyss!

And while black little blankets, a frugal diet,

And measured food carry you to heaven through holy vows,

These others will be fed by everlasting worms and fires.

For you there will be angelic bread to eat,

Which always satisfies and never brings disgust;

Its touch gives life, and its fragrance restores.

That I too may share in this food, holy assembly,

Pour out unceasing prayers to the Lord, I beg you.

And I ask you to remember your brother John,

So that he may love what you love and do what you do.

For, without his own stock, to wish to enjoy almost the whole world alone

Is disgrace, not honor.

## IV. In Praise of Saint Secundinus, Bishop of Troia

[Note: [Col. 1289] Ughelli had already published the poem on Saint Secundinus in *Italia sacra*, volume I, column 1341.]

[Col. 1289B]

Be wholly present, festive Troia, at your festive days,

To which another Troy has yielded.

That other land produced many men powerful by land and sea,

Yet it could not always keep them.

It experienced the wealth and honors of those who lived;

When they died, whatever honor they possessed perished.

But you, new Troy, possess leaders powerful in heaven and on earth,

Who are more present to you when they die.

One of these is present here, one who, by his own custom, seconds

Everything; rightly he bears the name Secundinus.

Prepare yourself for his distinguished festival;

Let mind, clothing, and face express joy.

Take up the lyre; let it please you to strike the middle strings;

Let tongue and hands resound with a song of joy.

It is fitting that the city should honor him and love him,

Since he loves the city, which loves him greatly;

That is sufficient proof of the love she bears him.

He lay unknown when you lay destroyed;

When you rose with your walls, he too rose for you.

The many beautiful stones discovered by the excavator

Tell that you became beautiful and spacious.

But the sacred treasure of the discovered body,

More splendid than every stone, makes you still more beautiful.

Sing how, while the bishop displayed the bishop’s hymns [reading uncertain],

He laughed and nearly proceeded to his final punishment.

Behold, the man who had just destroyed him begs, entreats, and prays,

And, when the cause of pain is gone, he is free from pain.

Thus the holy man, mocked, punishes and helps when entreated;

Thus virtue shines; thus the work of compassion shines.

Therefore the same bishop, once resistant in belief, manifests his faith,

[Col. 1289D]

While testing the sacred relics by fire.

The fire surrounds the relics, but has no power to burn them.

Thus the bones fly out, burned yet unharmed.

The man whose mouth the fire could neither burn

Nor hold for long rests in the highest places of refreshment.

Therefore let the bishop place the sacred, holy limbs upon the altar,

And let him give to his own Secundinus what is not alien to him.

He praises, honors, loves, venerates, entreats, and prays:

These things are yours indeed; city, do the same.

You can count, O Troy, many more of his triumphs,

But this praise will be sufficient to add to the heap.

It was not enough for all Latium to see the rewards of virtue

And the glorious deeds of your leader.

Gaul itself came as a spectator of such great blessings,

And came as the very material and witness of them.

A people of Gauls had come, according to their custom, to pray

At the celebrated church of Saint Michael.

One of them was afflicted throughout all his limbs

By an unheard-of, severe, and sudden sickness.

The disease contracted his entire body so tightly

That the mass appeared as a sphere rather than a man.

His legs and feet were joined to his buttocks in an immovable structure;

His tongue and hands scarcely performed their functions.

The remaining limbs were afflicted, nor did these escape their pains.

He who died so many times was scarcely permitted to live.

The fame of Secundinus, already known in many lands,

Flew to the Gauls, who were then close at hand.

[Col. 1290B]

At once a great hope of unexpected healing arose,

And the possibility that the disease could be expelled became a present salvation.

Therefore he was carried to the venerable church of Secundinus,

Although his feet could nowhere carry him.

Psalms are sung, prayers offered, tears shed, vows made,

And gifts promised. What is requested happens quickly.

He who had lost at once the use of his arms, hands, thighs, and feet

Recovers all their functions at once.

Now he walks, speaks, and is invigorated throughout his whole body—

He whose entire body had nearly been dissolved.

The immediate withdrawal of the disease makes him mindful of his vow

While the event is new, but forgetful when it is old.

After several days he prepares to return to his homeland,

Not knowing whether he would anywhere be safe and sound.

Yet not without penalty: as soon as he enters the city,

The former punishment, much harsher, returns.

If he sought his homeland, his health denied him a step;

If he wished for Troy, his foot was free.

Therefore, having recovered his health, he gladly returns to Troy

And gives himself into the service of Secundinus.

Obedience makes his restored health firm and stable,

And restored health strengthens his obedience.

Let it suffice for the praise of so great a Father to have reported these things,

In which you may see what his merits were.

Certainly neither compassion, uprightness, that will

Which gives each person his due, nor that twofold love,

Certainly neither gravity nor any other virtue

Could have departed from the dwelling of the mind of this man,

Whom the King and giver of virtues and blessings

Hears and answers, glorifies, and honors.

[Col. 1290D]

Now look upon your citizens, best Father; look upon your disciples;

Look upon your heralds, heavenly Herald, your own.

If a land not your own receives your intercessions,

Justice grants that this land should receive more of what is yours.

Since you newly procure acquaintances through illness,

Care for your devoted followers, who have long been yours by choice.

When he is healed, the sick person becomes a debtor to the healer;

The herald whom he proclaimed may be able to act as creditor.

Therefore let us, your disciples, attain in some measure the merit

Which these inexperienced people have now attained while wholly undeserving.

Destroy the evils of body and heart; establish health,

So that neither part may ever be empty of your praise.

## V. Hymn on Saint Secundinus

[Note: [Col. 1291D] It appears in Ughelli, at the place cited, column 1342.]

[Col. 1291A]

Christ, King of kings, price of the devout,

We worthily sing to you the fitting deeds

Of Secundinus, who serves you;

Grant fitting vows.

His distinguished and celebrated life,

His noble character, ancient triumphs,

And the newly revealed wonders

Of his virtues make them known.

He strikes the one uttering falsehood with the dart of grief;

Here he sees his guilt,

Repents of his word;

His punishment leaves him repentant.

The warmths of eternal spring delight his soul,

And the heavenly breeze of rest cherishes it;

Fire cannot harm his limbs.

When a man was almost deprived of all his limbs,

The right that alone could protect him,

While he poured out prayers,

Quickly restored health through his tongue.

Illness binds the sound steps of one attempting

To render the bishop’s great deeds and vows void;

The same illness releases them when he prepares

To discharge those vows.

A candle brought into contact with the fringes of the cloth

Adorning the altar is completely burned;

But the fringes suffer

No burning at all.

[Col. 1291C]

May eternal splendor, honor, and triumph be yours

With the Coeternal Father,

And, likewise, with the sacred heavenly

Breath, O Son.

**R.**

Behold Secundinus, having gained the heavenly seat,

Passes from this life, truly a good Israelite.

Now let the choir exult and follow him with psalms as he departs.

He passes, etc.

**R.**

Well done, good worshiper of the King of God, faithful servant,

Happy in much because you were faithful in little!

**V.**

Present double the five talents entrusted to you.

[Long lacuna] because, etc.

## VI. In Praise of Saint Martin, Bishop

[Col. 1291D]

Gem of priests, attend to the prayers of your people,

That worthy songs may resound for your merits.

The deeds of your triumphs are celebrated everywhere,

When you shine first under the title of faith.

The one whom you clothe on earth is your witness above the heavens:

A part of your cloak lends to the heavenly Lord at interest.

A thief becomes the herald of your virtues,

Professing heavenly faith at your words.

[Col. 1292A]

Your exceedingly powerful speech drives the strong enemy far away;

Every harm of hellebore is absent through the force of prayer.

What the thief was is revealed by his most dreadful appearance,

To whom the martyr’s obedience and honor are granted.

Three times the greatest virtue conquered the dark abyss;

It raises up those pressed down by crimes and the guilty.

When you move the weapons of the cross, the people stand like a mass of stone,

And can go wherever they wish only when you wish it.

When you approach, the pine tree overturns and falls;

It falls on the side where it had seemed unable to fall.

The fiery force flees when you go out to meet the flames;

It burns only in those places where it has been commanded.

While the people resist, you, covered with heavenly arms,

Destroy the entire work of the demonic building.

When one or another wicked man attacks you with a sword,

[Col. 1292B]

One falls, and the other loses the sword from his hands.

How many do you save by prayer who are seized by illnesses and demons!

You cure the leper by your kisses alone.

The fringe of your garment drives away countless illnesses;

A written page dispels fevers wherever your words are written.

When your limbs were broken in exceedingly dreadful ruins,

You were healed after being smeared with angelic ointment.

You use angelic words, sparing human beings,

And heavenly faces visible to you.

What the unwilling enemy does for you, the wicked one reveals;

Your deeds are not hidden from you; often future things are disclosed.

When the appearance of a fleeting tunic is displayed for you [reading uncertain],

It soon vanishes; the feigned art perishes.

The enemy falsely represents Christ in a purple cloak;

Recognized by you like a shadow, he slips from your eyes.

[Col. 1292C]

While you handle the great gifts of the heavenly sacrament,

Your head shines with its own divine fire.

While you, the holy man, lift your outspread hands to heaven,

Your bare arms are seen covered with jewels.

This abundance of virtues is brought to you by the wealth of your character,

Which plainly surpassed the limits of human nature.

Therefore, dying, you can almost say alone against the enemy:

“You cannot find anything deadly in me.”

When you depart from your body, the number of the saints

And the angelic choir sing of you in heaven.

The entire heavenly court of the King comes to meet you,

And God himself is given as the glorious palm and honor.

Noble glory comes to your members on earth,

Which surpass the sun itself in radiant brilliance.

Thus holy, adorned, and blessed in every respect,

[Col. 1292D]

You reap worthy rewards here and in the heights.

Therefore we ask, Father, for those whose hope you are: be their help;

And look with care upon those who fear you yourself.

We are not wearied by age, nor tired of labor in the world,

If, under your guidance, we may live while they remain strong.

May it be your will, Martin, to protect us in heaven,

Where whatever you wish will at once be possible without labor.

[Col. 1293]

# Life of Saint Secundinus, Bishop of Troia, by Gauferius, Cassinese Monk

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 1336, from a Cassinese manuscript.)

## Notice

Saint Secundinus belonged to Aecae in Apulia, today called Troia. His body was discovered, with an inscription and amid great rejoicing by the people, when the foundations of a new basilica were being excavated. The history of this discovery is preserved in the Vallicellana Library at Rome. His feast day is celebrated on February 11.

Pliny, book III, chapter 11, mentions the people of Aecae. Aescae, or Escae, appears in Antoninus Augustus’s *Itinerary*. Aecana—more properly an adjective—was later called Troia [and therefore “Trojan”; E. P.], an episcopal city of Daunian Apulia, built on higher ground, near Luceria and Bovino, eight miles away, thirty miles from the metropolitan city of Benevento, and twice as far from Naples. The period in which Secundinus flourished is still unknown to me.

# The Prologue to Stephen, Bishop of Troia, Begins

[Col. 1293]

[Col. 1293A]

On the goodness of love and obedience, brother and fellow-bishop S., both from that dark and densely packed description of the stone Tablets and from the Gospel’s clear and open discourse, a rule, standard, and discipline are presented to us.

For the supreme Maker himself, the incomprehensible God who rules the whole world, was pleased first to mark instruments of this kind, under the veiled face of Moses, with a certain sacramental sign. Through them he would afterward provide the nations destined to believe in him, after the mystery of the Word made flesh, with the strongest support of manifest compassion.

Nothing on earth is more acceptable to him than a company of human beings who, joined together mystically by the wave of sacred baptism and by the Spirit, devote their activity, labor, and finally their diligence to these things.

[Col. 1293B]

The pillar of cloud and fire had also signified this to that Israelite people.

We are commanded to love God with our whole heart; we are commanded to admonish our neighbors and obey our parents. These are divine teachings, and certain commands designated by the finger of God on both Tablets.

These are also the foundations for building hope, the supports for strengthening faith, the nourishment for fostering the heart, the guides for directing one’s journey, and the defenses for obtaining salvation.

From this source, flowing from the origin of the prophets and proceeding from the law, comes that very brief discourse which waters everything: the stream of faith that works through love.

But you may know why I have prefaced these remarks. You asked me, through the Cassinese abbot whom, out of respect, I call Desiderius—a man praised among good prelates for his work and religion and approved for his character—whether, if his friendship could grant me any leisure, I would devote it especially to writing the History of the confessor Secundinus.

[Col. 1293C]

I shall undertake a task difficult for me, but I shall pursue an easy cause. I shall neither fail him when he urges me nor you when you ask me, since I owe him obedience and you charity.

I shall therefore undertake the work long desired by your soul, and charity, which bears all things, will not fear what is harsh and difficult.

The very secluded setting of Cassino will certainly provide the greatest advantage for so great a work: there, the duration of peace has strengthened sacred leisure in honor of the venerable founder of rest.

Antiquity also reports that the famous Varro, celebrated through so many ages, was the founder of this church; and, according to Marcus Tullius’s judgment, he surpassed some Romans in religious devotion, others in the memory of their deeds, but all in knowledge of literature.

This too will be of interest to me.

I shall also come to Troia, whose name is your boast. At the bank of the cold Simois I shall gaze upon famous Tenedos; I shall climb to Athens, the inventor of every branch of learning,

[Col. 1294B]

where the highest power of speech was both discovered and perfected.

Door by door I shall seek the plane tree whose branches spread widely to provide shade, beneath whose shadow Socrates sat.

From him I shall borrow the method of speaking, the arrangement of words, wit, sweetness, and grace, so that I too may not fall short of urbanity, and so that the history may flower through knowledge of its subject and the discourse may overflow.

For history is “the witness of times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, and the messenger of antiquity” (Cicero, *Orator* II, 9), commended by the orator’s voice in enduring inscriptions.

On the other hand, many come naked and unarmed, despite the lofty praises set before them for eloquence and the attainment of glory, adorned by no knowledge of things and no learning, like the man who, after touching this very History that we have in our hands,

[Col. 1294C]

utterly damaged and confused it.

But while writing and reflecting on these matters, I am more reminded of blame than praise.

For it is clear that, where the glory of elegant eloquence is due, the disgrace of incompetence is due instead.

[Col. 1295A]

Therefore, brother dearest to me in Christ, help with your prayers the man devoting his labor to the fruitful vine; and obtain through your intercessions that holy Secundinus may second this work according to his own wish and mine.

Once these matters about him—which are fewer among us—have been dispatched, along with the miracles (for you possess other accounts that are not found in these copies), we must recall our mind and attention to the studies from which, through your love, we descended to these matters.

In these matters we ask and pray that by the hand of his mercy he may grant us protection for living well and the possession of eternal happiness; the remaining transmitted clause is corrupt: “[f, quae] is received from a worthy heir by grant and in undivided possession, [and] may acquire it, as the price of reward, for those meriting it by their deserving merits.”

# The Life Begins

[Col. 1295]

[Col. 1295A]

Once upon a time, Troia, distinguished by leaders, wealth, and military renown, whose long-standing misfortunes and various destructions are known throughout the same regions as the course of the sun, lay in the region of the Peloponnese, in a most serene setting, on fertile soil, in a countryside made pleasant by water and every kind of greenery, near Pontus and the island of Tenedos.

From there, in the first crisis and in a terrible storm, when the entire exchange of such a great city was being lost in ruin, several very brave leaders eventually escaped.

Among them was the son of Anchises, a vigorous and energetic man, from whom the Quirites—the rulers of the world, who would later avenge the enemies of the Trojans by retaliation—received the noble beginning of their lineage and glory.

Troia lay there for a long interval of time, deprived of every consolation:

No wealth, no splendor, and finally no religion.

Only walls half-ruined and eaten away by fires remained standing;

the Xanthus, the Simois, and the island of Tenedos indicated that Troia had once been there.

At last, however, she rouses herself and gathers herself together, mindful of her former virtue and glory.

She brings back a long line of descendants from the generation of great-grandchildren, repairs her hearths, and applies herself to that remarkable and singular military oath of hers—only to be devastated, as a supporter of the dictator Sulla, by Fimbria’s siege on behalf of the Marian faction; to be shaken by engines of war; and to fall again, a mother beneath the swords of her sons.

From that disaster until nearly the present time, only the name lived on without a body, hated equally by all nations outside Latium because of the Roman monarchy, although Troia herself had been its cause and the beginning of its distinction.

[Col. 1295C] There was also, on the soil of Apulia, a certain city inferior to no other land in abundance of grain; there, too, many things pleasant to the taste, which nature desires, are produced from the earth and trees, both with easy abundance and with outstanding sweetness. The vines and trees there are low-growing and cannot raise themselves very high above the ground; yet among them some remain evergreen, while others, stripped bare in winter, put forth leaves when warmed by spring, and pour forth fragrant flowers and produce exceedingly rich crops.

Now this city, if we attend to the meaning of its name—for it was also called Ecana—was most ancient, as the marble facing of its monuments, the columns of its theaters, and the height of its roofs indicate. In Troy’s refoundation this name is fittingly bestowed upon it, so that the title of an illustrious name may lend authority [Col. 1295D] to the novelty. We think that this may satisfy those seeking confirmation whom the city’s designation under the name of Troy has moved to inquire about Ecana. Now let us return to the subject of the History.

Since, therefore, the people were greatly occupied, through the diligence of their leaders, in building churches and establishing walls—so that, once these were safe, they themselves too might be safe—while some were engaged in laying marble slabs, others in polishing stones, others in digging out bricks, and still others in various tasks to which each had been assigned, those whose desire was to complete a temple in honor of the life-giving cross discovered, in the cemetery of the blessed evangelist Mark—for a basilica had been built there—a tomb laid with precious marble. While it was being examined with curious eyes, they noticed, because of the great number of tombs surrounding it, an engraved epitaph, although its lower portions had already been worn away; what could be read was as follows:

[Col. 1296B] “Here rests the holy and venerable Bishop Secundinus, who renewed the structures of the saints, snatched away into rest, on the third day before the Ides of February.”

Many men were therefore sent in with mattocks; they cleared and opened the place. When the mound had been exposed, a most precious pearl was found in a magnificent lower basin, which protected the monument externally from damage. At once the whole city gathered around the treasure of the body that had been found. They thought it right—as was pious—to kiss the relics, invite them by vows, proclaim them with praises, and ask through their intercession: pardon for the guilty, protection for the innocent, assistance for those in need. They prayed collectively for the condition of the city, for the common safety, and for the hope of all blessings. [Col. 1296C]

Do not suppose that such joy affected only the skin; it moved the very breast and entrails. Everyone’s desires had been satisfied for the remedy of all; every source of delight had overflowed. The venerable body was carried in the hands of priests to the place where the foundations of the new city were being laid, where a new name, after the former had been extinguished or transformed into an addition to a stronger one, was arising. In the sanctuary of the life-giving cross they deposited it with great dignity and adornment.

As the blessed relics, through signs and miracles, daily kindled the hearts of the citizens to love them, and as the shoots of religion, bursting forth into ripe clusters of blessedness, spread abroad, the bishop of the city nevertheless attached no faith to such events. He charged the citizens with a crime against the salvation of their country, accused the people of folly, denounced the leaders for rashness, and indicted the Church for stubbornness. There was no insult of reproach, madness, or mockery that he did not heap upon it.

The city could indeed have degenerated from its best institutions into manifold evil, had not blessed Secundinus, [Col. 1297A] with the hand of mercy, held it back as it was almost falling and already rushing toward ruin, insofar as he was able. What are you doing, bishop? Do you think that one who has placed himself upon the heavenly summit, from which no one is cast down, is vulnerable to any injury? What does it matter to you, even though you have hurled many darts of abuse against him? He has a breastplate impenetrable to every assault. Do you not know the hardness of the stones from which the city of the supreme King is built, unconquerable by the iron of insult? You strike heavenly adamant and wear down, with insolent words, what blunts everything that attacks it. Look to the hardness of refined gold, whose substance no surrounding flame can defile; there are many things of this kind that ordinary fire cannot harm. Look to the cliffs thrust up into the heights: they break the sea, but, beaten for thousands upon thousands of years, show no trace of any violence.

Secundinus is safe from every injury; he has been removed beyond the range of weapons. Whatever you try insolently, wantonly, or arrogantly against him, you will attempt in vain. Heavenly things escape human hands; no missile shot at the sun reaches it at all. There will be—there certainly will be—one who avenges him; there will be one who directs against you darts of suffering, not shaken by that bowstring so as to fall uselessly and short of their mark, but driven into your side, your entrails, and your very heart by the force of torments.

Meanwhile the bishop was unexpectedly struck by a weapon in his side. Whichever way his pitiable body turned, it sank beneath its pains; his eyes were suspended in a long vigil; reliefs became tortures, remedy became pestilence, medicine became poison, and life became destruction. The household mourned, the city was thrown into confusion, and the physicians, laboring to apply remedies, accomplished nothing. For whatever protection of the body they found was turned to the opposite purpose; the stronger tortures rejected the remedy, and incurable diseases fled from medicine.

There were many who, when he was almost at death’s door, reminded him of the abuse he had uttered [Note: “Improprie,” improperly, for “commonefacerent,” they should remind him; that is, they recalled to his mind his own insult. ]: “While there is still room for repentance, change your purpose, return to the way, reject your error, and do not despair of Secundinus’s virtues.” The bishop turned to his admonishers and promised, in a subdued voice—for he could not do otherwise—that he would do what they had urged, hoping that, if only time for repentance intervened, he might obtain health [Col. 1297D] and pardon through Secundinus’s merits, whom he addressed by name as follows:

“Blessed Secundinus, whom God, the Father of all things, appointed father of the Trojan fatherland, and for whose benefit you devote yourself wholly to conferring blessing, establishing salvation, and preserving liberty: assist me, unworthy as I am, through your good will, and do not allow a part to be separated from the whole, since it is within your power to show mercy to all and restore them completely!

“Woe to me! Am I accused of a crime, or of sin? Certainly of both. For I did not solemnly honor in you what I ought to have honored; rather, I stirred up the people to forget what I ought not to have caused them to forget about you. Yet release me from the yoke of sin; set free the slave of irremediable pain; impose upon me any other torment of repentance. For it is unjust that one should be punished as a criminal who, not through hatred but through the madness of folly, raged against a most powerful prince.”

Then he turned to those standing around him:

“Remember, my sons,” he said, “remember the Father; remember love; remember mercy; remember dignity. You know what my love, my virtue, my gravity, and, finally, my diligence have brought you. Help me with your prayers; preserve me for my country, preserve me for yourselves, preserve me for your children. May you be willing to ask for salvation from him from whom you have plainly received many benefits.”

At these words of the bishop the whole household dissolved into tears. Prayers mingled with groans, and they asked the Mother of God and her confessor Secundinus to grant their intercession. You would have seen [Col. 1298B] the citizens, for the bishop’s recovery, pouring out much of their own possessions, making numerous vows, and imploring the omnipotence of God in every manner.

While they persisted in such actions, the bishop felt the assistance of their prayers. He declared that the pain had completely departed and pronounced himself free from his manifold affliction. How great was the Trojan people’s thanksgiving and how great the joy that arose when they thought that what they had done for the shepherd’s recovery, by common prayer, with one mind and one strength, had prospered!

Accordingly, no time, force, or opportunity held the bishop back from the benefits obtained through Secundinus’s generosity. Immediately, using his hands in place of his feet, he went to where Secundinus’s relics were. The priests followed with perfumes, and the people with candles [Col. 1298C] and offerings. When they reached the temple of the life-giving Cross, the bishop prostrated his whole body on the ground, asking him who had already brought healing to his pain-stricken body to forgive his sins. He also gave and expressed the greatest thanks to the holy bishop Secundinus, because he had obtained what he had vowed, because he had entered into the favor of the one whom he had offended, and because through him he hoped to be able to set foot in the possession of eternal life.

Some deliberately urged the bishop—for they thought he was uncertain—that he, whose duty it was to provide for his subjects, labor to establish belief, and show each whom they ought to obey and whom they ought to follow, should cast a portion of the relics into fire to test it, so that every wound of doubt might be cut away from the hearts of the many. Yet the proven power of the relics dissuaded the bishop from what they proposed; nevertheless, because he perceived that it could lawfully be done for the benefit of the people, he lent his support to those who urged it.

The relics were thrown onto the embers; from every side the flames were urged by blowing, and the pieces became red. At last they leapt out of the fire. No mark of burning was found upon them, as those who were present reported. The people rejoiced at the astonishing event and took courage from its favorable outcome.

The bishop then came before the assembly amid great anticipation. He declared that they possessed exceedingly useful protection for their country, if they chose to use it under the guidance of honesty. He gave thanks that they rejoiced over his safety as over the common safety of all. He urged them to devote themselves to establishing the church and finally to complete it, so that it might be worthy of the venerable Secundinus; from it he could always behold, always have Troy before his face, Troy in his eyes, Troy on his lips. But enough of this; now let us come to what follows.

A certain man named Teuzo, an Aquitanian by birth, came to Rome, to the chief of the apostles, out of devotion to prayer—for this is especially customary among that people—with the encouragement of his mother, who, out of affection, offered herself as his companion on the journey. After solemnly making the appropriate offerings during his circuit of the holy places—for the journey was taking him through other venerable sites—he went to the house of the blessed archangel Michael, [Col. 1299B] situated above the highest summit of Mount Garganus. Because it was remote and because he had decided to devote himself to prayer, he prolonged his stay there for a long time. His mother, who had followed him, died.

Having been almost deprived of every consolation of life, and having devoted himself to prayers, tears, and lamentations—for it often happens that greater sorrows produce more grievous illness—he was struck by what appeared to be an incurable disease. Some of his limbs moved against his will; others were so dry that he had no sensation whatever in them. His eyes and hands could scarcely perform their functions; his legs and feet, clinging to his buttocks, had deprived him of the ability to walk. [Col. 1299C] Only his tongue, and not even that properly, retained the benefit of nature.

What could he do, far from his parents, far from home, and—to speak more truly—far from himself? Passersby pitied his helplessness, though they could not assist his health. He was told of Secundinus’s miracles; but if he wished to go, he could not, and if he were to be carried by others, he had nothing with which to hire them. Nevertheless, those who were daily distressed by his misery began to discuss the journey. Men sent from home traveled with him toward Troy at the greatest possible speed. They hurried because the solemn day for depositing the confessor Secundinus’s relics was approaching.

When they reached the city and laid the man, weakened in all his limbs, before Secundinus’s shrine, they said: “As far as we were concerned, we seem to have fulfilled your vow. For the rest, act as you wish. Yet we advise you, on this great day of present celebration, to devote yourself to prayer; for we believe—and are convinced—that this will greatly benefit you, and we ourselves will strive with all our strength for your recovery.”

And so it happened. The time had already come for the bishop to enter upon the service. The people, having carefully arranged everything for the honor of God, stood inside and before the doors of the church. Many were also brought to these solemnities from villages, neighboring fields, and lodgings; many, finally, who lived far away were brought from their homes.

The bishop entered, accompanied by all the choirs of the church, and began to perform the pontifical rites. While this was taking place, the sick man turned with all his heart to God, drew deep sighs from the bottom of his breast, filled everything with tears and mourning, and uttered words [Col. 1300A] capable of inclining God’s mercy. He raised himself wholly in spirit, as though praying and pleading before Secundinus’s visible eyes, and vowed that he would never leave him if he restored his former health.

As he moved his tongue and other limbs without knowing how he was doing so, the thought came to him: he tried in truth to move his hands, and moved them; to extend his feet, and extended them; to rise, and rose; to walk, and walked. He cried out as loudly as he could that his feet were sound and that all his limbs were performing their functions.

This voice, heard with immense longing, raised the spirits of the priestly order to some degree for their edification. For such was the splendor of the true praise, such the people’s jubilation, and finally such the joy among the clergy that the entire assembly exulted beyond measure. You would have seen [Col. 1300B] the restored man most affectionately promise to devote his service to the physician, to remain steadfast, and to surrender himself to him as had been agreed. He proclaimed him the author of his bodily health, the guardian of his soul, and the giver of his benefit.

He remained in this resolve for only a very few days. Thinking that it was in his interest to return to his homeland and visit his friends, he broke the pact he had established in God’s presence, changed his decision in haste, and denied the promise he had made without necessity. Because he was afraid to undertake so long a journey alone and without companions, he went to Rome to find fellow travelers.

When he had found companions and set out, his former illness took away his ability to walk. He prepared to turn back, and his steps resumed their function; he prepared to depart, and once again his feet, hands, and entire body were disabled. Terrified by the worsening affliction, because he saw the evils already erased from him returning, he did not wish to remain subject any longer to so great a calamity. He brought back his steps to the place from which he had taken them, and there he remained, for as long as he lived, most devoted in the service of the confessor Secundinus. [Col. 1300C]

Moreover, when the Trojan people saw that such authority and such power of Christ’s confessor shone forth increasingly each day, they unanimously and harmoniously applied themselves to adorning with every kind of ornament the church in which he had been buried. Their hope depended upon him, their confidence upon him, and especially their concern upon him; concerning him—as the bishop of the city, as its guardian, and finally as its ruler—they deliberated among themselves every day.

You would have seen every person providing for his house as for his own household and children, content in private affairs to live with the slightest and humblest adornment, but preparing everything for dignity, glory, and splendor in its public furnishing. There were continual transfers to him not only of inheritances but also of deeds of purchase and even of codicils concerning all possessions. Perfumes smoked, candelabra shone, and the entire dwelling glittered with wax candles and lamps by night and by day.

One night, when the altar was being encircled by those carrying a great row of candles for the people’s devotion, as is still customary today, it was requested that the custodians allow them to remain lit for a long time during prayer. The lights were therefore left burning, and when the custodians turned their attention to other matters, the postponement of extinguishing them slipped from memory.

Between the candles [Col. 1301A] and the altar, in the front part, there was a space formed by the width of the step to which the candles, with their burning heads, were attached; on the other sides, only the altar-cloth formed the intervening space. The fire therefore continued to burn, and there was no end to its burning except when its material was exhausted.

Meanwhile, concern for the morning hymns deprived the custodians of sleep. Each rose to his own duties: one to open the doors and strike the cymbal; another to bring out the books and kindle the incense. When they came to the altar with the censer, no one seemed to remain from that multitude of candles. The custodian turned around the altar, looked, and saw ashes lying in straight lines, just as the arrangement of the candles had been ordered.

Great amazement seized the custodian: the fringe of the altar-cloth was wrapped in ashes, yet remained intact. When he brought his hands near it, he found, as he had seen, that it was untouched by the fire. Finally, thinking that it would be appropriate to make the event especially credible to those who saw it, he decided to preserve it just as he had found it.

After the morning psalms had been completed, the clergy invited the people to so great a spectacle. At this sight everyone raised their hands to the stars and offered manifold thanks to the Creator, who does not despise his workmanship, who makes himself known to human beings through miracles, and who very frequently causes Secundinus to shine from virtue to virtue.

Immediately afterward orders were given to summon the entire city, to distribute suitable gifts, and to make known such great glory to the neighboring districts as well. This true virtue of the blessed man procured the greatest dignity for the citizens, the greatest joy for the neighbors, and the greatest benefit even for distant cities.

[Col. 1301]

## Life of Saint Lucius, Pope and Martyr, by the author Guaiferius

(From the *Acta Sanctorum* of Bollandus, March, volume I, day 4, p. 304, from a manuscript of Monte Cassino.)

### Chapter One. Praise of Martyrdom. The Birth and Holy Youth of Saint Lucius

[Col. 1301B]

#### 1

The most courageous and distinguished pursuits of virtue, formed as an instruction in the sacred faith for the common benefit of believers, we see most deeply carved and impressed above all in the armor of the martyrs. For they brought themselves there, through labor and steadfastness, and by the greatness of their spirit to that summit from which their deeds, renowned everywhere among nations and throughout the world, are presented as an eternal memory before the eyes of all.

This is brought about by the steadfast endurance of discipline, which not only kept delicate and soft things far from them, but also granted strength to exhaust the hands of their beaters and to overcome every force of the entire hostility. Christ, the virtue and wisdom of God, enrolled these men in that most frequent and singular service of his. He consecrated this chosen class of warriors, through a new oath of service, among the soldiers of his imperial court: armed with courage of spirit, they were to come beneath the blows with naked bodies; they were to fear nothing harsh, dread nothing difficult, and consider nothing intolerable; they were to despise all human things and perform everything gravely, steadfastly, and splendidly; finally, they were to overcome the world itself not merely in battle but in war.

Moreover, this consecration of the eternal Emperor was established for his glory—not because he has need of anyone—and was also prepared for the protection of the human commonwealth. Otherwise, just as a solid ship, fashioned from durable material, strengthened by a tenacious framework, decorated with various colors and gold, equipped with a movable rudder, strong ropes, a lofty mast, a distinguished yardarm, gleaming sails, and finally all the equipment both useful for service and pleasing to behold, would easily be sunk by the sea or driven by a storm onto the rocks if no helmsmen guided it and no rowers propelled it, so through the beautiful and exceptional creature of this kind—the beloved creature of the Creator, the image of God, the likeness of the Redeemer, the mirror of the world, the dignity of heaven—the principalities and powers of this world and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places would be destroyed by frequent, violent, and customary assault if many martyrs had not fought for it under divine instruction.

#### 2

But against such battle-lines and their forces—powerful tyrants spread throughout all the cities of the whole world—resistance was made not by a multitude of soldiers, a great number of legions, shining weapons, or limitless money, but by only twelve leaders, who together performed the offices both of Emperor and of soldier. They exposed themselves to danger, did not know how to give the signal for retreat, and in no way avoided battle. They were distinguished by no material armor, not even light armor; they had been forbidden even a staff.

Among these leaders was Simon, by far the most excellent of all, prince of all and standard-bearer of all. From the firmness of his faith and his love toward the Lord Savior, the name Peter was given to him. In the City, where the throne and dignity of earthly empire shone, he pitched the camp of his virtues. So great was this man, filled with God, in overcoming, that no one after him would dare either to hope for a similar triumph or to wish for one. For he would not have fought a task worthy of him if he had compared himself with others who could have been defeated without the highest praise and glory.

He ascended to the arduous and difficult heights of the Capitoline fortress, so that, once Jupiter had been shaken from his throne, the other demons elsewhere in the cities might more easily be overtaken by the same downfall. Devoted, therefore, to this most diligent work, he instructed disputants and judges according to his own rule, so that they too might subdue monstrous apparitions through the power of the Crucified, cleanse the world of its filth, and overcome wickedness; so that they might restrain anger, envy, greed, lust, and every plague from human minds. They themselves were naked, possessing no support in their household affairs and no advantage of riches beneath the sky.

They were to change the consulship into the pontificate, empire into the episcopate, magistracy into the priesthood, praetorship and prefecture, and finally senatorial dignity and the remaining offices of that kind into ecclesiastical dignity. Through their flashing standards they would so subdue the world that today you may see all nations, all kingdoms, and even the empire itself serving the decrees and commands of the Roman priesthood.

#### 3

Against them, however, that Roman power moved its victorious standards, though not with solid success. It directed its strength against them with spirits more savage than against any other enemies, attacking them as sorcerers, as traitors to their country, as men born for the destruction of the public welfare, with every kind of torture.

Against Peter it tried the cross; against Clement, exile; against Marcellus, servitude; against Alexander, chains; against Lucius, the sword. Although throughout the world it afflicted some members of Christ’s household like rabid beasts, killed others as fierce and untamed creatures, sent iron against others as against something diseased, extinguished others as monstrous offspring, and slew others as misshapen and weak, it could not turn its savage cruelty away from its own associates, its own household, or even from itself.

Behold this Porphyrian Lucius, a Roman citizen and supreme pontiff, whose title of triumph this day celebrates. He belonged to a family distinguished by the dignity of its name, a family that, so that Rome might survive, imposed a limit and an end upon the Carthaginian and Numantine fury—indeed, upon the whole world. Because of his valuable service to the Roman people, he was put to death under the emperor Valerian by a capital sentence.

#### 4

It seems worthwhile, for the benefit of posterity, to unfold in order how a man of complete integrity and advanced age, a patrician, endowed with prudent intelligence, polished in speech, most eloquent among legal experts and most learned in law among the eloquent—one whose majesty, greatness, and priestly dignity had destined him for heaven—having forbidden himself pleasures and vices, devoted himself wholly from early youth to sacred morals and duties.

He led those who had been abandoned by piety, mercy, and humanity, and even those grown old in the reins of treachery, lust, and hatred, not by austere severity, diffuse laxity, or grim solemnity, but by the strategy of varied and vigorous speech, full of spirit, sweetness, and truth, into the citadel of peace, quiet, and religion.

Nor would it be irrelevant to explain how, in the matter of the title of Christianity, when he was matched against a raging Caesar, and when Roman and foreign laws seemed to be serving him, he proceeded prudently and splendidly through the stages of litigation: from the formulation of the charge to its rebuttal, and from rebuttal to the final position. Through the contest of words he spoke of matters grounded in civil society, common sense, nature, and morality, and was always superior.

For the greatness of his spirit had raised him into an open field, where Christ, the principalities, and the powers were spectators, and where prizes had been set before him. Fighting from behind a rampart against the enemy’s position, he was never brought down, bent, or even moved, so that he might carry away, by the greatest favor, the triumph born of virtue to the heavenly empire.

#### 5

Considering that the thing which he had recognized as the source and beginning of every disturbance must be utterly rejected if he wished to seek this glory and nobility, he first closed the doors of his spirit against the monster of intemperance—which is, of course, a departure from right judgment and from every rational principle, so that once the mind has been infected by it, it can neither be ruled nor restrained—by admitting temperance, the moderator and mistress of virtues, into the dwelling of his mind.

He made his desires obedient to right reason, so that, as a frugal man, he might preserve sound judgments, do everything rightly, and possess a moderate, steadfast, and tranquil spirit; so that he might not waste away through troubles, be broken by fear, exult in empty brilliance, or burn for anything except heavenly desire.

When virtue had withdrawn into the highest and most elevated place, from which it could survey the entire scene it had illumined, and had used its powers well, it dedicated the breast of the blessed man as a free and wondrous treasury to its companions alone. From that treasury good, useful, and honorable things could easily be sought: justice, self-restraint, prudence, greatness of spirit, generosity, piety, friendship, hope, faith, charity, and the other virtues opposed to vices.

Thus divine providence ordained that such ornaments should befit the man who was to preserve laws, the City, and true sacred things; who was to proceed into the forum, onto the rostra, and into the senate-house to speak about Christ.

Intent upon the human race as the work of the supreme divinity—or rather, as the likeness of God—he looked around and saw everywhere a broad and continual supply of evil: some laboring under poverty, others troubled by ambition, others numb with idleness, others befouled by luxury; some shaken by impatience, others swollen with savagery; some driven mad by anger and fury, others by cruelty.

Against these pitiable afflictions the good man tested the labor and strength of his heart. In accordance with the Apostle (1 Corinthians 9:20), he became all things to all people; he bore for each person whatever concerned everyone, and offered each one moderation, indulgence as to a brother, reverence as to a parent, and respect as to a superior. He pitied one, restrained another; he came to the aid of one and instructed another. To all who, amid so many errors, labored day and night under the burden of an evil mind, he showed the safest and most renowned path to living happily and eternally.

### Chapter Two. Saint Lucius’s Exhortation on Despising Earthly Things, Imitating Christ, and Acquiring Virtues

#### 6

All things are slippery and uncertain, and those things cannot be called good which, attractive but through deceptive pleasure, entice wretched mortals: money, rank, power, and other things of that kind. Drawn toward them, so many people grow numb with blind desire. They are acquired with labor, viewed with envy, make everyone anxious, no one truly happy, and no one truly secure.
