No one stands in a stable place. Everyone is tossed about, hangs suspended, and fluctuates; they collide with one another. Some drag down those who are falling; others are the ruin of others. This is slaughter, not life, and a heap of people falling one upon another.

Let each person answer himself according to his desire and believe that pleasure is the highest good, placing the glory, displays, and ultimate vices of the age among supreme happiness. Nevertheless, all human things are brief and perishable, and do not extend into any longer portion of time. They pass quickly and are enclosed by an untimely end before they can grow, so that they are not granted a long existence.

Let us even extend, if we wish, the boundary of our age to those things that boast of antiquity; few reckon its middle point as reaching the hundredth year. Let the mind then proceed to the longest and infinite stretches of time. Compared with eternity, what proportion would these periods possess, even if our life were granted a thousand years?

Since such things are so, we surrender this small and brief interval in which we are compelled to live according to the custom of others wholly to negligence and idleness, so that the very thing we live is plainly death. Human life flows away from childhood through luxury and intemperance: inert through sluggishness, exhausted by wantonness, suspended by ambition, eager for buying and selling, wandering, unstable, and displeased with itself. Vices press upon it and surround it on every side. They do not allow it to be properly established, devoted to any good thing, to raise its face, or to lift its eyes toward the vision of truth.

At last it compels itself, wretched as it is, to worship gods fashioned by its own fingers. It rejoices to bow its captive body before foolish images, foolish creations, and utterly impious monsters. It prefers to lower its exalted posture toward heaven and its face raised toward its God, bending it down with the other animals toward the earth.

#### 7

For this life, sailing amid so great a storm, upon such a changeable sea and such a tempestuous ocean, there is no salvation except loss, no rest except shipwreck, and no harbor except death.

We must therefore abandon all the enticements of the world and the idols invented by human error. We must go to God and direct ourselves toward heavenly things. Look there; raise your eyes there; lift your heart, hanging in suspense, there. Do not prostrate yourself before the shrines of dead men; do not fall before a creature created for your service. Preserve your dignity, preserve your sublimity, preserve the likeness of God. Persevere as great as you are; be such as God made you. Look at yourself; make yourself present to yourself; return to your mind. If you wish to know God, first recognize yourself.

For those who believe in him, he makes heaven their homeland and builds their dwelling above the sun and stars, where honors are eternal, joys infinite, peace everlasting, and rest perpetual. With immeasurable love he adopts human beings as children for these things and makes them share in the name and dignity of divinity, which belong to him alone. Therefore, from this brief and perishable passage of time, let us give ourselves with our whole heart to those things that are immeasurable, eternal, and better than all better things.

To these we are led by Christ’s love alone. There no duration of the world excludes us; all are admitted; we are neither bound nor reduced to servitude, but, safe, free, and eternal, we enjoy the open and unrestricted heaven. There no terror will invade us, no anger torment us, no disease afflict us, no suspicion attack us, no envy pursue us, no fear trouble us, and no fickleness disturb us.

Or, if you judge rightly, would we not, in a certain sense, choose these places of eternal blessing for ourselves alone, once they had been seized and taken away from us?

Come now: suppose that from this very day a magistrate, whether for an investigation or merely to test your spirit, ordered you to be led away, so that first you would be beaten with rods, then bound to a stake, and expose your neck to the executioner to be struck with an axe; and thus, while your relatives and close friends, your wife and children, stood by, you would become an abominable spectacle to the people. Suppose that petitions were made on every side for your deliverance, but achieved little. If, amid the terror of so great a danger, you understood the weight of that empty and airy happiness, and recalled it throughout the whole of your life, then certainly, if it were possible for you freely to assess the greatness and those glittering goods, you would perceive—by sorting through and reviewing all the days of your life—that no day worthy of memory, but that all had been equally lost and equally destructive, had remained with you.

You would find yourself more wretched and unfortunate than that Syracusan, who, amid all that highly coveted splendor, saw a sword hanging by a horsehair from the ceiling over his neck.

8. Do you think those live who are grim, savage, and utterly frantic in the violence of grief, weapons, blood, and punishments—whose expression is threatening, brow gloomy, face fierce, stride hurried, hands restless, complexion altered, sighs frequent; whose eyes flash, hair bristles, breath is stunned, lips tremble, and teeth are clenched; who stamp the ground with their feet, repeatedly clap their hands, and agitate their whole body—hideous to behold, horrifying in appearance, deformed by every manifestation of anger? Or do you, by your own right, grant life to those who are stirred by some dishonorable act or word of another, if someone proud has rejected their conversation or laughed openly; who, if they have not been admitted to dinner with others, or, if admitted, have perhaps been placed not in the middle but at the very end, or if someone whom they greeted has failed, not deliberately, to return their greeting, believe that these things were seriously done as an insult to them?

What do you think of the envious, who are saddened by another’s prosperity and delighted by another’s misfortunes; who, in order to obtain some advantage, violate others, overturn the laws of nature, depart from humanity, and remove the human being from the human? Is this not eternal misery and an inhuman pleasure? Do you not think those dead whose long-prepared wealth, abundance of possessions, and magnificence of royal dwellings are always a source of fear, lest some magistrate’s cruelty or some intervening fault plunder such great displays?

When they are tormented by diseases and pains to which iron and fire are applied, whose bones we see broken and injured, whose veins are drawn out and limbs amputated—do they live? What of those fickle people who cannot bring their instability to rest, who shun tranquility, who are thrown into turmoil by every movement of the mind, whom regret for what they have begun holds back and fear prevents from beginning; who are weak in enduring everything, patient neither of toil nor of pleasure; who frequently change their plans and keep circling back to the same things; who in a sense flee from themselves, leave no room for novelty, and find life and the world itself wearisome? All these, upon whom such pestilent emotions descend, I should rightly call dead in misery rather than alive, especially since, while held back by the guardianship of the body, they are allowed little of what they desire, to abuse their pleasures; and since an unanswerable judgment will bring torment upon those cast out beyond everything that can be called miserable—wretched and beyond remedy.

9. The mind must therefore be restrained when it tends downhill and driven toward the heights; there is no doubt that, as it ascends, it will strive upward. Patience, courage, and perseverance must resist, so that endurance may subdue the vices that make a human being utterly wretched, and so that a creature born so bright and shining, beautiful in no single form alone, may not be brought down by an infernal plunge from the heights of heaven.

Let us therefore abandon the pleasures of the world, which is the better and more equitable course; and let us renounce riches, which ought more truly to be called occupations. Once these are admitted, all good things are overturned. The things necessary for human protection are, moreover, small and capable of satisfying the body’s desires: cold is removed by a simple covering, hunger and thirst are quieted by moderate nourishment. You have no reason to accuse nature; everywhere and in every place lie the things by which you can nourish yourself.

Finally, what difference will it make to you whether the stomach is served and the appetite excited by elaborate arts, and the belly filled? These things will not last long. Here we are guests—indeed, we are visitors; we remain in another’s house. Do you wish to prove it? Wait a little, and you will utterly forget both luxury and the beloved lodging.

Let us correct the errors to which we have indulged too much; let us return to our boundary, Christ, who will not allow us to go astray. Whoever walks boldly in him does not stumble; whoever advances more swiftly does not slip; in him speed encounters no interruption. Behold, he summons us, enrolled in the heavenly army, to receive our donative. The gifts he promises for so great a campaign are, as we have said, immense and equally divine. We shall attempt nothing in vain; nothing will be forbidden us. Everything will yield, everything will obey. Thus indeed we shall change service into command, slavery into freedom, and what is no longer subject to change into change itself.

## CHAPTER III. The Deeds of Saint Lucius in His Pontificate. The Persecution Begun against Him

10. When Lucius had said these things, the numerous people began to extol the Christian religion to heaven, to give their names, and to seek the faith, some striving to do so before the others. The faithful, meanwhile, were daily inflamed by no small longing to entrust the pontificate to him as soon as Cornelius should attain heaven, acclaiming him as the most suitable for the succession, capable of administering the Roman priesthood by both doctrine and virtues.

While Cornelius was being displayed to heaven, radiant with the laurel of martyrdom, Lucius, with the assent of the whole Church, took possession of the supreme pontificate. It had long been his practice to pay the debts of one unable to pay; to intervene even with the praetorian faction so as to free those oppressed by lawsuits; to pity orphans, console the afflicted, and provide for the needs of the poor; to defend the stranger and the widow.

For he cherished Job, that very courageous man, as both the memory and the model of our fathers. Scripture had taught him Job’s following and other most generous words concerning such duties:

“I saved the poor from the hand of the powerful, and I assisted the orphan who had no helper. The mouth of the widow blessed me; I was clothed with judgment and surrounded by equity. I was the eye of the blind and the foot of the lame. I was the father of the helpless; I examined causes without partiality, and, breaking the jaws of the unjust, I snatched the plunder from the midst of their teeth.”

11. Although he devoted himself so completely to these duties that he was scarcely thought to have enough leisure for other institutions of piety and religion, he nevertheless used to weigh the whole order of affairs on an equally balanced golden scale, turning minds and eyes with equal and great admiration in either direction.

He consecrated seven bishops, as though they were craftsmen and guardians of human life—for it was fitting that the Paraclete, powerful in the reality and number of his gifts, should display his inhabitant in this way—according to the law that governed the office. They were to receive the breast and the right shoulder, the portion set apart, so that they might be priests, ascend to the Lord’s altar, and offer the saving sacrifice; men full of knowledge, full of diligence, full of greatness, full of faith, full of every divine understanding—in short, full of all the virtues of God.

Finally, with this most suitable office, he established them in possession of judgment and defense, to hear cases, so that in the Church, by the word of doctrine, great solicitude, and the labor of vigils, they might win the goodwill of sinners, leading them rather to follow the path by which they could arrive at knowledge of the true God, from whom they had departed.

Such bishops the Prelate of prelates, Pontiff of pontiffs, Priest of priests, Prince of princes, King of kings, and Lord of lords approves for carrying the Lord’s vessels. They must have nothing negligent or dissolute, fearing no lapse of soul or body, so that they may be holy in body and spirit and be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

Lucius therefore wished none of these to be common—for they would otherwise belong to many—but to God alone, as the separated portion of the sacrifice showed. Nor did he wish them to go to war or fight against an enemy, but, with Moses, to pray with hands raised, so that, while they devoted themselves to prayer, the people might triumph over the invisible enemy and drive the worst Amalekites—that is, demons—far from their very position; lest, if they ceased and lowered their hands, they should discover that they, the victors, had been defeated by the vanquished when the legions were restored.

12. Among them the ancient custom of ecclesiastical order was also preserved in the performance of the sacred ministries with exceptional ceremonial. A great and fortunate multitude of ministers thronged the service, since access to the divine mysteries was solemn; and they wore the legal vestments, so that the Roman pontiff, with his face veiled and invested with lituus or crown, might seem in outward adornment no inferior to the chief pontiff of the idols, although he was distinguished by the more splendid adornment of his mind.

[Note: That is, to make the Roman pope, dressed in this way, appear no less richly adorned than the chief pontiff of the idols. Coins, statues, and other monuments of Roman antiquity display those profane pontiffs with their heads covered by the rear part of the toga, drawn upward. They often represent the same augur’s staff, or augural rod, as a pontifical emblem, as well as a crown—although in the manuscript one might rather seem to read *cornu* (“horn”) in place of this, whose use in sacred rites I do not know.]

This most zealous man also devised for all of them a better garment, so that it might increase the delight of the eyes and the care bestowed upon their appearance; it was called the *dalmatica*.

[Note: This is a tunic with sleeves, whose name and use are thought to have come from Dalmatia. Dominicus Magrus, in his *Notice of Ecclesiastical Terms*, writes that the emperor Pertinax was accustomed to use it. “At first,” says Walafrid Strabo, cited by Octavius Ferrarius, book I, *On Clothing*, chapter 39, “priests were dressed in dalmatics before the use of chasubles. Later, when they had begun to use chasubles, they granted dalmatics to deacons; for Sylvester ordained that deacons should use dalmatics in the church,” as the same author says. “But Lucius had merely granted permission for them to use it; for he is said to have devised this garment for priests.” We infer from the Acts of Saint Caesarius of Arles that this concession was made only to the Roman clergy. Moved by the outstanding dignity of his merits, Pope Symmachus wished the deacons of Caesarius to use dalmatics just as the deacons of the Roman Church did.]

The *dalmatica*, both in itself and by reason of the dignity of the priesthood, appeared more precious than the embroidered toga, the palm-patterned tunic, and the purple cloak marked with broad stripes and fastened with golden brooches.

[Note: Ferrarius, cited above, book II, chapter 8, discusses these garments; they are triumphal vestments. The embroidered toga, he says, which is now so called, was formerly called purple and had no embroidery. Pliny says that the Phrygians taught the art of working it with a needle, and therefore were called *Phrygiones*. That this embroidery was golden can be shown from many other passages, and most clearly from Ausonius to Gratian: “This is the embroidered garment, as it is called, not so much by its own gold as by your words.”]

[Note: Festus says that the palm-patterned tunic was so called from the size of its *clavi* (stripes), because it was distinguished by broad stripes resembling the palm of the hand; and then from the kind of embroidery, because it had palms woven into it. Servius, commenting on the eleventh book of the *Aeneid*, says that it was deserved by those who had won the palm from their enemies.]

He also granted the Levites permission to use such garments.

Thus this extraordinary man, endowed not only with virtue, steadfastness, and gravity but also with distinguished ornaments, proceeded with his attendant senate before the divine rites and ceremonial sacrifices, bringing to peoples thirsting for the sacred laws, the tablets of the Testament, and the privilege of the Gospel the streams of life. The pontifical vestments gave him authority, and the abundance of the sacred word gave him credibility, as he strove to raise a city broken by misfortunes, cast down by fear, and weakened by luxury toward hope of heavenly dignity and freedom.

Thus, remarkably, religion prevailed through long labor amid the very crimes, so that throughout the city of Rome the name and faith of Christ were celebrated from street to street in lawful words and free speeches.

13. At this the pontiffs of the Capitol—flockmates of demons, storm of the fatherland, whirlwind of peace, tempest of leisure, every crime and abomination—recklessly hurled against the bishop Lucius every assault of discord, every torch of envy, and every weapon of poisonous hatred, through violence and fury.

They suddenly drove throughout the city the fanatics under their control, the refuse of every shrine, to conspire against the professors of the Christian name. Then through the forum and the public platforms they assembled all the common people whom they could, with as much zeal as possible, as accomplices in that crime; they prepared them for this kind of proceeding, either goading them with the sharpest hatred or winning them over with gifts.

With these witnesses equipped and accusers appointed, they burst into the senate-house, the crowd loudly declaring that they had come to appeal to Caesar and the Senate. They said that the issue was virtually one of diminishing majesty and overthrowing the state, unless provision were made at once. Therefore all other matters had to be set aside; concern must be shown for wives and children, altars and hearths, and especially the immortal gods; and care must be taken lest, when sudden ruin had overwhelmed them, the gods should be invoked in vain—gods who are as hostile to those who violate their sacred rites as they are unwilling to avenge those who refuse to do so.

This speech not only struck the Senate and the other dignitaries with fear but also deprived the city and Caesar himself of courage. They immediately granted the speakers permission to say freely whatever they wished in the atrium of Jupiter.

When the Senate had granted them leave, the most prominent among them, both in rank and age, said:

“I shall use my right to speak, Caesar—by your leave and that of the magistrates—in accordance with the authority which Jupiter Optimus Maximus, in this temple, first entrusted to the pontiffs and kings, then to the consuls, and finally to you in private confidence. For you may not rightly take offense at my opinion, which has been spoken not against you but for you—men whom, after your recent admission into our college by a fresh favor, our ancient authority to instruct and correct has compelled us to address.

“Let me be angry and bear things bitterly, provided that I do not allow the state to be shaken by silence through so lamentable a loss; provided that I accuse of indolence those who, if they may rightly be called its guardians, are so; provided that, not merely in speech but with every power of mind and body, I defend the trust of the immortal gods, oppressed, abandoned, and destroyed by wicked and frenzied men. For those who neglect such matters will have no lasting impunity against the fiery darts of heaven, as though they were bringing light to heaven…”

The remainder is not found in the manuscript.

### Canons

I. That the bishop consecrate the chrism and oil at the proper hour, together with twelve priests, 269.

II. That all the chrism and oil be renewed by the archdeacons, 269.

III. With what care the deans ought to distribute the chrism and oil, 269.

IV. That whoever celebrates Mass must communicate fully, 269.

V. That the priest baptize fasting and wearing an alb and stole, 269.

VI. That the viaticum and holy water not be kept for more than eight days, and that consecrated hosts not be consecrated again, 269.

VII. That Confirmation be conferred upon those who are fasting, by those who are fasting, and with fire, 269.

VIII. That Holy Orders be conferred after Saturday, or on Sunday morning, upon those who are fasting and by ministers who are fasting, 269.

IX. That the observance of the Ember Days be exact, 270.

X. That those who are furtively or improperly advanced to Holy Orders deserve deposition, 270.

XI. Concerning those who abandon the tonsure; and that those to be ordained come to the bishop on Thursday, 270.

XII. That wandering or expelled monks, and likewise nuns, be compelled to return to their monasteries, 270.

XIII. That pastoral offices not be sold or bought, 270.

XIV. Concerning the rite of marriage: that marriages not take place secretly or between blood relatives, 270.

XV. Concerning married clerics: that they neither serve in churches nor receive their revenues; and what sort of men archdeacons and deans ought to be, 270.

XVI. That no one, after his wife’s death, take the woman with whom he had previously been accused of misconduct, 270.

XVII. No one with a veiled wife still living may marry another, 271.

XVIII. That the wife of an absent husband not marry another before learning with certainty of her husband’s death, 271.

XIX. That clerics who have fallen into public crime not easily be restored to the sacred orders, 271.

XX. That if the bishop cannot come for the deposition of one who has fallen, he send a vicar, 271.

XXI. That during Lent no food be taken before the evening hour, 272.

XXII. That the office of Easter Saturday not begin before the ninth hour, 272.

XXIII. Concerning the transfer of saints’ feasts, 272.

XXIV. That a general baptism not be held except on Easter Saturday and Pentecost. Infants are to be baptized whenever baptism is requested for them; no one is to be baptized on Epiphany except from necessity caused by illness, 272.
